# External Binding

->**[The Front Cover]**<-

The manuscript is encased in a fine example of a <term>blind-tooled</term> <note>“Blind-tooling” refers to the technique of impressing designs into leather using heated metal tools without adding gold leaf or color, resulting in a subtle, textured relief.</note> leather binding.

The design features a central rectangular panel decorated with a series of repeating circular motifs. This central field is framed by a complex border containing star-shaped elements and floral geometric accents.

<note>This style of decoration is characteristic of European craftsmanship from the late medieval or early modern periods. Such an elaborate cover indicates that the text contained within was considered highly significant and valuable by its creators and owners.</note>

# PIETRO d’Abano.
### 7470. The Conciliator of Differences; Treatise on Poisons.
Thomas of Hermannstadt, with Johann Burster. Mantua. 1472.

<term>Folio</term> <note>A large book format made by folding sheets of paper once.</note> ; <term>signatures</term> <note>Letters or marks at the bottom of pages used by binders to assemble the book in the correct order.</note> [a-g<sup>10</sup> h<sup>8</sup> i<sup>10</sup> k<sup>8+1</sup> l-p<sup>10</sup> q<sup>12</sup> r<sup>10</sup> ; s-bb<sup>10</sup>, cc-dd<sup>12</sup> ee-ll<sup>10</sup> mm<sup>12</sup>; nn<sup>8</sup>] ; 363 leaves (the first and last blank) ; 2 columns ; 56 lines ; <term>roman characters</term> <note>A style of typeface based on Italian humanist handwriting, easier to read than the "Gothic" blackletter types.</note> ; {Mantua, press iii, type 1} ; <term>capital-spaces</term> <note>Blank spaces left for an artist to hand-paint large initial letters after the text was printed.</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from the modern bibliographic description and provenance notes of the previous pages to the original 14th-century text. It begins the Prologue of Peter of Abano's masterpiece, where he outlines his philosophical motivations and the structure of the work.</meta>

# THE CONCILIATOR OF THE DIFFERENCES OF PHILOSOPHERS AND ESPECIALLY OF PHYSICIANS: BY THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, PETER OF ABANO OF PADUA, HAPPILY BEGINS. PROLOGUE.

**N**ow, concerning the triad: and all those things which they might put forward from it. Once again, you have compiled the opinions of illustrious physicians and philosophers. Indeed, in the seventh book of the *Politics*, Aristotle says: "All men desire to live well and seek happiness. But the power to obtain these things belongs to some, while not to others, on account of a certain fortune or nature." Whereby the natural desire of anyone for life and happiness is primarily indicated. However, some are subsequently hindered by fortune or nature so that they are least able to obtain it. First, it is evident since all things desire the good. Hence they are praised for testifying to this at the beginning of the *Ethics*. Moreover, to live and to be blessed stands as the highest good, because to live is the form of a living being; hence, from the second book of *On the Soul*: "To live is the being of the living." Indeed, this life is desired most as something more perfect and divine than other things; its opposite confirms this. For every animal avoids death and destruction, as stated in the third book of *The Consolation of Philosophy* <note>original: "de consolatione i trio"</note>. Finally, happiness is a certain operation of the soul and a practice according to perfect virtue, from the tenth book of the *Ethics*. Also from the second book of *The Consolation*: "Happiness is a state perfected by the gathering together of all goods." Clearly, there is implanted in all men by nature a desire for knowing, which they conclude with happiness as if by a touch. Therefore, every single thing desires to live and be happy, but especially that which is perfect. 

Furthermore, they are deprived of life whose beginnings at birth were depraved and disproportionate, caused by intrinsic and extrinsic factors, and whose acts of virtue are deficient in every way. One may find not a few of this kind. Yet, in proportion to them, their malice and difference will be opened in the sixth [book]. The moral philosopher, detesting the brutal acts of these people, incites those marked with the principal virtues to possess them through no short habit. For some are slaves by nature, not only in body but also in soul. Finally, the fortune of such people is similarly hindered by lack of nobility, wealth, power, and their opposites—altogether good fortune and misfortune—as the second book of the *Rhetoric* testifies. In this, I think the sidereal force of one’s origin <note>Latin: *vimus geneseos*; Peter of Abano was a famous astrologer and believed the stars influenced birth and character.</note> should not undeservedly be included by You. For some are deprived of life and happiness, having mistakenly estimated good fortune as if it were bad. For even if fortune provides the protection for happiness, it must be modified by how much, what kind, where, and when it is expedient. You, therefore, choose to live by virtuous acts and to possess eternal life and happiness more and more in the future; not only by example, but also by helping others who aspire to this. For the knowledge that gives life is by no means bound by the chains of death.

Indeed, I have decreed to weave together a book from problems, together with the understanding of my dearest companions, having now investigated these things publicly for two lustra <note>A "lustrum" is a five-year period; Peter is saying he has been researching this for ten years.</note>. In this book, certainly, the apparent disagreements of philosophers and physicians in medicine might be put to rest, preferring the truth continuously for anyone speaking. For this reason, I preferred to call it *The Conciliator*. I thought this work should remain hidden for a long time, had I not been obliged to hear the frequent and worthy prayers of those seeking it, and had I not feared the risks of acting inconsiderately. I have raised this work up to be sufficiently instructed in the primary sciences, philosophy, and medicine above all others. 

<margin>
The division of the entire book into three parts:
1st
2nd
3rd
</margin>
I will separate this into three parts, following the reverence for the Trinity and also for the gods. For all things, according to the philosophers, end in the first and supreme Trinity. In the first part, common and external matters will be established, concerning the modes and matters of both parts of medicine: namely the theoretical and the practical. Once these are known and explained, the mind of anyone will be able to more easily consider the very reason and way of the art, as stated in the preface of the *Old Rhetoric*. The second part will contain the doubts of theory. In the third part, the final matters which are subject to practice will be placed, along with five appendices that occur. I will separate the parts by "differences" <note>Peter uses the term *differentia* (difference) to denote a specific point of contention or a "problem" to be solved.</note>, since each one is not a little distant from the rest. Indeed, I will number these in the order of natural numbers until the end of the entire volume, for the sake of brevity in citation. Finally, I will depict these with the figures of the Algorism <term>Algorism</term> <note>This refers to the use of Hindu-Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3...) which was becoming more common in scholarly texts of this period compared to Roman numerals.</note> for ease of finding. In the same way, I will indicate the discourses brought from the wise men, which I will also try to transcribe as they lie, and rightly derive them here from the source in smaller letters.

<margin>
Method of proceeding in each of the differences.
</margin>
In each of the differences, four steps will always enter, besides the arguments of both sides. Some of these will receive a subdivision. These are:
1. First, the exposition of the terms to be doubted.
2. Second, what has been previously felt about it by others.
3. Third, the showing of the truth with its motivations.
4. And finally, the fourth: the solution to the arguments.

<summary>In this prologue, Peter of Abano introduces his "Conciliator," a monumental effort to harmonize the conflicting views of ancient philosophers and medical authorities. He explains his philosophical framework, rooted in Aristotelian ethics and astrology, and outlines the book's three-part structure.</summary>
<keywords>Peter of Abano, Conciliator, prologue, Aristotle, medicine and philosophy, happiness, Trinity, Arabic numerals, Scholastic method</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page continues the prologue of Peter of Abano’s "Conciliator," a massive medieval effort to resolve contradictions between ancient medical authorities like Galen and philosophical ones like Aristotle. Having established the human desire for life and knowledge, Peter now outlines the systematic structure of his work, justifying his selection of specific debates (or "differences") that he will address in the following chapters.</meta>

Out of a love for brevity—than which nothing was more beloved by the ancients, as noted in the fourth book of the *Method of Healing* <note>original: "terapentice methodi quarto"—referring to Galen's work</note>—I will explain some matters in two or four differences <note>A "difference" is Peter's term for a disputed question or scholarly contradiction</note>. For the rest, I will subscribe to the established views, following the first, second, third, and fourth things that must be known.

### The Sufficiency of the Ten Universal Questions

Since medicine is the <term>science</term> <note>theorica: the study of principles</note> of the human body insofar as it is capable of being healed and cared for—the subject to which this present writing is devoted—it can be considered in two ways, just as with other sciences. For it may be viewed either according to those things that are external to it, or those that are internal. If the former, it is viewed either according to its <term>formal cause</term> <note>the essence or definition of the thing</note>, its <term>material cause</term> <note>the substance it is made of</note>, its <term>efficient cause</term> <note>the agent that brings it about</note>, or its <term>final cause</term> <note>its ultimate purpose</note>.

If it is referred to the formal cause, it is either universal or particular. The first occurs in two ways: either by reason of its perfection, from which arises the first of all the "differences," or by reason of its method, which is the second. If, however, they are considered more specifically, it is either regarding its whole being (the third difference), or its parts; and this is either in respect to the intellect (the fourth) or the emotions (the fifth). If viewed regarding the material cause, it is also twofold: either as it is ordered toward knowledge (the sixth) or toward permanence (the ninth). If it is intended according to the efficient cause, it is either by reason of the practitioner (the seventh) or the art itself (the eighth). If it is referred to its final purpose, the tenth difference arises from there.

If, however, it is viewed according to its internal aspects, it is twofold: either according to the <term>theoretical</term> or the <term>practical</term>, and so on. Indeed, this method of "sufficiency" <note>a Scholastic term for proving that a list is complete and logically exhaustive</note> could be adapted to other questions, as is the study of some. But because it brings about more curiosity and lengthiness than utility, it shall be omitted in the questions hereafter.

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page begins the formal text of Peter of Abano's "Conciliator Differentiarum Philosophorum et Praecipue Medicorum" (The Reconciler of the Differences of Philosophers and Especially Physicians). Having completed the index on the previous page, Peter now opens "Difference One," where he begins his signature method: posing a controversial question, presenting arguments for and against, and then "reconciling" them with a definitive middle ground.</meta>

# FIRST DIFFERENCE.

<margin>first reason</margin>
**I**T IS SHOWN that it is not necessary for a physician to know all the schools of speculation. This is first seen through Hippocrates of Cos, the most distinguished of physicians and, according to Galen, the first of all, whom God clearly brought forth for the merciful provision of the human race as one who never erred. In his transmission of perfect medicine—and in certain <term>problems</term> <note>original: "ppleumaticus," likely referring to the *Problemata*</note> attributed to Aristotle which were translated by me—he did not hold to other schools, since they had not yet been invented. For, according to the prologue of the *Metaphysics*, the arts and sciences that are most necessary were discovered first, and medicine is numbered among these.

<margin>2nd</margin>
Furthermore, science and sense-perception follow their subjects, as is the reasoning in the book *On the Soul*. Since, therefore, the things with which medicine is concerned are separate and distinct from the things with which other sciences are concerned—for sciences gain their diversity and unity from the diversity of their subject matter, just as powers are defined by their objects—medicine will therefore be deep and distinct from the others. Consequently, the physician is defined by medicine alone. Since the sciences are distinct, there will be different necessities arising from them, so that one is not necessary for that which belongs to another. Otherwise, anything would be necessary for everything, and thus all would be confused according to <note>Anaxagoras was an ancient Greek philosopher who taught that "everything is in everything."</note> Anaxagoras, and nothing would be distinct.

<margin>3rd</margin>
Moreover, every art and discipline intends to supply that which nature lacks, as stated in the *Politics*, Book 7. But what nature lacked was the preservation of health and the removal of sickness; the science of medicine removes this defect, as its own introductory descriptions suggest. For it promises to guard health and remove sickness. Also, according to the <term>physicists</term> <note>Referring to natural philosophers or followers of Aristotle's *Physics*</note>, that thing is in vain which nature does not include for a higher cause if it were naturally suited for it. Medicine, however, is ordained toward the possession of health. Whence it is said at the beginning: the intention of the medical art is health, but its end is the possession of it. If, therefore, another science were necessary for the possession of health, then medicine would be in vain. But nothing is in vain in nature, according to the first book of *On the Heavens and the World* and the third book of *On the Soul*. And for this reason, it is not in vain in art, since art is the image and follower of nature. Again, it seems the same for this science and others: for who can obtain one of the others without the rest, such as grammar, logic, or rhetoric? From which it is concluded that it will not be necessary to know other schools for medicine.

On the opposite side is Hippocrates in the book *On Airs, Waters, and Places*; Galen at the beginning of the *Therapeutic Method*; and <term>Haly Abbas</term> <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician</note> at the beginning of the *Theorica*. Furthermore, that thing whose knowledge and perfection depends on the knowledge and perfection of others necessarily requires those others for its own perfect knowledge. Such is the condition of this science and many others. For subsequent sciences are not perfected at all unless they are clarified by prior ones, until they are finally raised to that science which is called <term>Metaphysics</term>, as appears in the beginning of the *Metaphysics* and the first book of the *Physics*. Because of this, it is necessary for a physician to know all the schools of speculation.

---

In order that the truth of this inquiry may be held, its terms must first be explained. For the principle of every demonstration is "that which a thing is," as the prologue of *On the Soul* declares. Second, let us express what some have felt. Third, let the truth be demonstrated. Fourth, let the opposing arguments be removed.

Regarding the first, it should be known that a physician is a diligent minister and helper of nature. <margin>Averroes: Physicians are a sea of envy</margin> Averroes, observing his <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a 12th-century Andalusian philosopher whose medical work *Colliget* Peter frequently cites.</note> clever acts, says: "A physician is an inexhaustible sea of envy, an organ of detraction, a perforated <term>clepsydra</term> <note>A water-clock; here used as a metaphor for leaky or hollow ambition</note> of undefended ambition, a talkative contradicter of another’s truth, a most constant non-confessor of his own ignorance, and an inexcusable neglector of the sick."

What science and speculation are, the introductory differences will show. The science of speculation is the knowledge of some two or three demonstrations, or of three ordinary doctrines handed down, as shown in Difference 8. "Necessary" is also spoken of in four ways according to the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*. In one way, that without which it is not possible to be or to live, as food is necessary for an animal. In the second way, that without which a thing cannot go well or be done well, just as for a laboring man it is necessary that he be restored to firm health.

<margin>first reason</margin>
Necessary is also called "forced" or "violent," according to which <note>Evenus of Paros was a Greek poet.</note> Evenus says that "every necessary thing is a sad thing." It is also said of that which is so and cannot be otherwise, which is the necessity of immobile and eternal things, such as God and first principles.

<margin>2nd</margin>
Regarding the second point, it should be known that the school of physicians was threefold. For some were <term>Methodics</term>, that is, unartful, though calling themselves followers of the method. Others were <term>Empirics</term> or experimenters. The third were <term>Logicians</term> or Rationalists. The first group considered only universals, despising particulars and intermediate things; of this school was <note>Thessalus of Tralles, a physician in Nero's time.</note> Thessalus with many others. According to them, the more universal things were, the more necessary they were to medicine. The second group, however, intended only for particulars, spurning universals and intermediates, doing in all ways the opposite of the first. According to them, by law, other sciences would be nothing necessary for the investigation of medicine, since medicine itself is specifically particular—indeed, it is entirely so. The founder of this school was <note>Serapion of Alexandria, an ancient head of the Empiric school.</note> Serapion. The third group, however, observed the middle path of truth, considering particulars as they are contained under universals and receive the power of demonstration from them. Hence they placed the most specific things, with which the first science of speculation is concerned, as necessary for medicine. The founder of this school was Hippocrates, Archigenes, and Galen, with other colleagues. Whence Cornelius Celsus says: the most ancient author Aesculapius (or in Greek, Asclepius) is celebrated, who cultivated the raw and common science of medicine a little more subtly and was received into the number of the gods. Concerning this matter, see the first book of the *Pandects* <note>original: "re. fa." likely referring to the *Digest* or a similar legal/encyclopedic collection</note>, which I translated into Latin. Our first god Aesculapius was of no small renown; his two sons, Podalirius and Machaon, followed the leader Agamemnon to the Trojan war, providing no small help to their own...

...brought to their fellow soldiers. However, Homer showed that they brought no help in pestilence or in various kinds of diseases, but were accustomed to heal in wounds only with iron and medications. After these, indeed, came the most famous Pythagoras, Empedocles, and Democritus—whom some believed Hippocrates <note>original: "Y.", an abbreviation for Ypocras/Hippocrates</note> to be a disciple of, notably distinguished in art and eloquence. After him came Diocles of Carystus, Praxagoras, Chrysippus, and finally Erasistratus. After these came Serapio, who was the first of all to declare that this rational discipline pertained nothing to medicine. For he placed it in use alone and for the sake of experiments. Whom Apollonius and Glaucias followed, and later Heraclides of Taras, men of no small standing, and from that profession they called themselves **Empirics**. Therefore medicine was divided into two parts: the **rational art**, or the other for those claiming **practice** <note>original: "usū," referring to the Empirical school's reliance on experience over theory</note> alone. None of those who were included above accepted anything after them except what they received.

Asclepiades, however, changed the method of healing in great part. From his successors, Themison turned away from it in his old age. Through these men, this salutary profession of ours became known to us. But Galen (Ga.) immediately places Archigenes and his imitators as the first of the <term>Critics</term> <note>original: "creticoꝝ," likely referring to those who judge or distinguish "critical days" in illness</note> against him. Beyond him was Heraclides of Taras, whose knowledge he says was experimental. Above him, indeed, were Phylotimus and Diocles. Before all of these, he perfected that Hippocrates existed as a wonder. For he, a good and kind man, was the first to write what was useful in the medical arts. Galen (Ga.), in the book *On Black Bile*—translated by me—touches upon the end of this Hippocratic production.

But it is hesitated how it is said that Hippocrates wrote first, since it was said that many preceded him, as the physicians who denote those from <term>Assidis</term> <note>original: "Assidis," likely referring to the school of Cnidus or Cos</note> point out. It must be said that this is verified in terms of that which is to "rightly invent," just as Aristotle <note>original: "Au.", here referring to the Author/Aristotle</note> discovered the *Topics* and the *Sophistical Refutations*. But how anyone arrives at knowledge—I mean by the intellect of the habit of principles even within oneself, as soon appears, and in other ways not a few—is seen with this. Whence, in certain <term>Problems</term> attributed to Aristotle, many of the ancient physicians found certain things of medicine scattered about, gathering them from mathematics or the <term>trivium</term> <note>The basic liberal arts: Grammar, Logic, Rhetoric</note>, and by fortune or prophecy or the invocation of demons or certain other ways. Wherefore the Empirics established this art; for others think it appeared from fortuitous revelation and the likeness of benefits.

Whence <note>original: "q̄rto ttia", likely a reference to a specific medical text or chapter</note>, certain people were cured of leprosy by drinking wine into which a viper had fallen with the intention of killing them; or by obeying a dream or vision, as it was commanded to apply urine in a case of a great spleen. According to Galen in the ninth book of the *Method of Healing*, his father was moved and came to the medical art; likewise he praised his own advice in the fourteenth book. Indeed, by the likeness or imitation of a bird, Hippocrates, observing, discovered the <term>enema</term> <note>original: "clistere"</note>. For a certain small bird <note>referring to the Ibis</note>, suffering from a heavy load of little fish it had consumed, lowered its beak into the sea and drew it into its anus so that, by evacuating, the pain ceased. Similarly, Dioscorides found that fennel benefits human eyes by watching serpents emerging from caves rubbing their eyes with it constantly.

<margin>3m</margin>
First, indeed, the annulment of the <term>Practics</term> <note>original: "fȝoꝝ," likely practitioners</note> in the book of benefits and the curative art is apt. Because of the third reason, it must be known that other sciences or liberal arts are necessary in medicine, at least in the manner of the aforementioned practitioners, even if not primarily or fourthly in regards to its principles or the method handed down by any of them. This is shown by authorities and reasons. In the beginning of the *Therapeutic Art*, as the translation <note>likely the Burgundio of Pisa translation</note> writes: if they lack geometry or astronomy or dialectic or any other good doctrine, those who ought to become physicians are in need, just as the disparaged Themison was. For they lack long experience, and thus anyone could easily learn the works of the medical art. Thus, therefore, not only are **astrology** and **logic** necessary for medicine, but also **geometry** and any other good doctrine through which I understand natural science, metaphysics, and the other liberal arts expressed. Whence the translation of Constantine, adhering to the meaning, says the other liberal arts are necessary.

Furthermore, Galen at the end of the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Art of Medicine"</note> testifies that he composed two books on the constitution of the arts, ordering them into the medical discipline. Further, Haly Abbas in the beginning of the *Theoretical* part says it is necessary for the reader of his book—which he called "Complete" and "Royal" <note>the *Liber Regalis*</note>—to be prepared and proved to know all arts. For in his book, all medicine is contained; and therefore he says the reader of this book of medicine does not need to read any other books, since it contains everything necessary for students and experts. For it is necessary to pre-understand the meanings of words so that one can conveniently express one's concepts to others, and understand those pronouncing them.

<margin>What Grammar is according to Al-Farabi</margin>
This, however, is done through **Grammar**, which is the science of the ratio of writing and knowing that which is uttered, according to the sixth book of the *Topics*. And therefore Al-Farabi, in *On the Rise of the Sciences*, called it the science of language, which seems to be nothing other than a certain directing rule of an idiom.

<margin>What Logic is according to Avicenna and how necessary it is</margin>
He also especially needs **Logic**, which according to Avicenna in his *Logic* is the "speculation of things by which one arrives at the knowledge of the unknown." But according to Haly Abbas, it is the "balance of words" and useful to every art. Whence, in the first book of *Complexions*: small falsehoods in those things taught in the principles of logical consideration become the causes of the greatest errors; and it happens that all things operated badly follow from sophisms, both according to all arts and according to all operations of life. Whence Haly Ridwan said: "Galen spoke of the doctrines so that he might invite us to learn the art of dialectic, and to make us know that it is impossible to comprehend the art of medicine without the art of dialectic, unless the man be of excellent nature like Hippocrates." For it is manifest that the truth is not known, nor is anyone saved from error, except through the art of logic. Wherefore Boetius in his commentary on Porphyry said: "It was necessary for Epicurus and others to be deceived, who sought the truth of things while casting aside the science of disputation." Similarly in the first book of the *Physics*: the first ones seeking the truth according to philosophy...

<meta>This page continues the "First Difference" of Peter of Abano’s "Conciliator," moving from a history of medical sects to a detailed argument for why a physician must be trained in the Seven Liberal Arts (the Trivium and Quadrivium) and the higher sciences.</meta>

...and they diverted the nature of things into a certain other path because of weakness—that is, because of a lack of exercise in dialectic <note>The art of logical argument and investigation of truth</note> according to the **Commentator** <note>original: "Cōmētatoremi"; referring to Averroes, the 12th-century philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to medieval science</note>. Hence, it is gathered at the beginning: you should know that no one can stand upon the boundaries of this book, nor understand the greater part of it, unless he has read enough in logic that he can at least recognize the modes of the three demonstrations—namely, of the cause, of being, or of the sign—as will be seen in Difference 8. It is also necessary in another way, because through logic they defend the principles of the particular sciences with probability, as stated in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. Hence, in the first book of the *Topics*: "It has a path to the principles of all methods." And therefore in the *Categories* of the **Simplicities** <note>original: "Simpliciȝ," likely referring to the Simplici or basic logical structures</note>, **Logic** is the organic part of all philosophy, defending us from evils in practical matters and from falsehoods in speculative ones. Oh, how great then is the necessity of logic!

<margin>What Rhetoric is and to whom it is necessary</margin>
Rhetoric is also needed, which according to Cicero <note>original: "Tuliū," referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> is the faculty of speaking appropriately for persuasion, so that a person may know how to decorate the expressions of their concepts so clearly that they are gratefully received by the sick. This leads the patient into a state of confidence, as will be shown in Difference 35. It is also no less necessary because **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note>, the prince of physicians, uses a rhetorical speech inductive of persuasion. Hence **Al-Farabi** <note>original: "Alpharabius," a 10th-century Islamic philosopher</note> in his *Didascalia* regarding Aristotle, seeing in what was set down in many of Galen's books, declared in his explanation of scientific matters that Galen often used rhetorical speech—such as when he says that veins arise from the liver <note>original: "epar"</note> because the thickest part of them is around the liver, and that they become thinner as they move further away from it; and that the ruler of the whole body has his dwelling in the brain, because a king always lives in the most excellent place of a city. And since a human understands through the brain, people say of someone they see suffering a defect in intellect that he is "without a brain." And since strength and fear come from the heart, people say of a fearful man that he "has no heart." There is more on these internal matters in the third part, of which something will be said in Difference 66.

<margin>How Arithmetic is necessary</margin>
**Arithmetic**, the science of numbers, is also necessary—both in itself regarding the "critical days" <note>The specific days during an illness when a "crisis" occurs, determining if the patient lives or dies</note> which medicine deals with, so that through it one may know the composition of numbers, fractions, and their natures; and also in how it is ordered toward other mathematical sciences like music and especially astrology.

<margin>In what way Geometry is necessary</margin>
Medicine also requires **Geometry**, the science of measuring magnitude, so that through it one may know the shapes of wounds. For a round wound is healed more slowly and with more difficulty than others, because the sides are most distant from each other—since a circular figure is the most capacious of all. However, triangular or quadrangular wounds are healed more easily, since the parts are closer together. For where there is an angle, the application of flesh begins generation there more quickly. And for this reason, surgeons make diagonal incisions in wounds.

<margin>Music is necessary according to Difference 83</margin>
It also exists as necessary insofar as it is ordered toward astrology. The necessity of **Music** is sought in Difference 83.

<margin>How much Astrology is necessary to the method</margin>
**Astrology** also stands as necessary to him in no small measure; it is the science of the quantities and movements of celestial bodies, considered both in themselves and in their effects. Physicians use it to choose favorable times when the Moon is more happily tempered by the planets and under suitable configurations. For as appears through **Ptolemy** in his *Centiloquium*: "If anyone undergoes a purging while the Moon is with Jupiter, the effect of the operation will be diminished." Likewise, to touch a limb with iron <note>to perform surgery</note> while the Moon is in the zodiac sign of that limb is a horrible thing. And there are many such things. **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Y."</note> touched upon this necessity vehemently in his book *On Air and Water*, saying: "Those who hold and believe the things we have treated concerning the highest matters should know that astronomy is no small part of medicine." Hence, in the same book of *Prognostication* according to the Moon it is written: "A physician who is ignorant of astrology—no one should put themselves in his hands." He said this at the beginning of the *Prognostics*: "And if there should finally be anything celestial in illnesses..." although the **Commentator** <note>Likely Galen or a later medieval commentator</note>, speaking of the environment surrounding us, explains it differently. This necessity is also shown in the third part of the *Critical Days*. Therefore, Geofar, called **Albumasar** <note>The 9th-century Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar</note>, in his *Introduction*, says: "Physicians necessarily require the science of the stars so that through it they may know the most certain roots of their mastery." It is also necessary for the physician to cure that sick person for whom the astrologer has already provided foresight from the significance of the stars.

<margin>Natural Science is the most necessary method</margin>
**Natural Science** <note>Physics/Biology</note> is also most necessary, and is the only one of these the aforementioned authors did not touch upon [as separate], since it is subordinated to medicine. For the subject is placed under a sub-subject <note>i.e., medicine is a branch of natural science</note>, as Difference 7 will show, which takes its principles from it as if from the books on animals. Hence in *On the Spirit and the Soul*: "Philosophy provides the closest principles concerning health and sickness." And therefore it is gathered at the beginning that for one about to read this book, it is necessary that he be among those who have practiced somewhat in the roots of the natural sciences.

<margin>Metaphysics and where it is necessary</margin>
**Metaphysics** is also necessary to it, as it is to others, since it actually defends the principles of all sciences, as stated in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. And therefore all sciences are finally raised up into it, as **Aristotle** <note>original: "Au."</note> testified to them in the third book. Further, it is proved by reasons: since we have received sciences from existing things in the *Categories*. For as a thing is, so too are the sciences that exist concerning them. Now all things are connected and joined—not only those of one genus or matter, but those of different ones—so that the highest of the lower things reach the lowest of the higher things, according to **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note> in *On the Divine Names*. They are also connected because everything that exists is either a substance or an accident; since this division exhausts the entire nature of being, so all sciences will be either about substance or accident. But those which are about accidents are finally reduced to substance, since an accident has no being except through substance and definition. Again, the principles—at least the universal and mediated ones—are the same for all, as stated in the 13th book of the *Metaphysics*; these either exist as one or depend on each other by a certain necessity. Because of this, Galen in the ninth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." - De Ingenio Sanitatis</note> says: "Immediately from childhood, desiring philosophy, we came to it; then later, prompted by our father through manifest dreams, we came to the exercise of medicine, and through our whole life we have held both sciences in study as works belonging to each other." However, those which belong to medicine are more necessary: Logic, since it is [the science] of all sciences...

<meta>This page continues the "First Difference" of the "Conciliator," focusing on the hierarchical necessity of the sciences for a physician, before transitioning into "Difference II," which examines whether a physician must specifically be a logician.</meta>

...just as salt seasons food. Arithmetic <note>original: "Natalis," referring here to the "nativity" or origin of numbers</note> reveals the principles of its origins, and Astrology <note>this refers to what we would now call astronomy and medical astrology</note> provides the direction for its judgments. Furthermore, all things are essentially ordered; therefore, so too are the sciences that exist concerning them. In things so ordered, a later stage cannot be perfectly attained without knowledge of the prior one. And so **Boethius**, in his *Consolation of Philosophy*, detests those who, with violent hands, tear the garments of Philosophy, thinking that because they have claimed some small part of her for themselves, they contain her in her entirety. Therefore, from all this, it is concluded that a physician must have a discerning knowledge of all good doctrines. And perhaps students of medicine are immediately called "masters" of other arts—namely, not of medicine. It must be noted, however, that it is not necessary for a physician to have an exhaustive and expert knowledge of all the aforementioned sciences; it is sufficient if he has some general grasp of them, as **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Halyabbas," the 10th-century Persian physician Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi</note> finally seems to suggest.

<margin>It is sufficient for a physician to have some general knowledge of all the natural sciences.</margin>

Next, it should be known that a thing can be considered in two ways, as can the general sciences which concern them. Either they are considered in common, as they all have an order to one another; for they arise from the same principles and tend toward the same ultimate end. Whence, **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> says in the first book of the *Metaphysics*: All sciences share in one utility, which is the acquisition of the perfection of the human soul, preparing it in effect for future happiness; and thus one thing needs another and is connected to it, and so it is with science. Or, they are considered as they are particularly distinct in their genera and species. For some have different principles than others, such as the principles of numbers or planes or the soul. And thus one science exists by itself just as another does, since it is not always necessary to seek the ultimate cause, but rather the more immediate one, according to the physical scientists. Furthermore, one should not linger too long in other sciences, especially those that are more universal and concern language. For it is then that one arrives with greater difficulty at the knowledge of the particular things and the senses with which the science of medicine is primarily concerned. For it is necessary to receive the mandates of physicians from childhood and adolescence. In these times, the preservation of knowledge is easier than in old age, which is the "house of oblivion," as stated in the first book of the *Theory*. Indeed, **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note> recounts in the first book of *On the Affected Parts* that when he was nineteen years old, he began to learn medical matters from a certain teacher of Athens <note>original: "Attanei"</note>. Whence it seems better to know how to return from this science to the prior ones thereafter. 

<margin>To the 4th argument</margin>

Regarding these points, one must respond to the fourth argument. 
To the first, it should be said that even if the branches of the sciences had not been invented yet in the time of **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Y." for Ypocrate</note>, nevertheless by a certain goodness of his own nature—he being a diligent student of nature—he used them as if they were already established. This is according to the first book of the *Sophistical Refutations*: even common people use dialectic and testing while attempting to argue. Whence **Boethius** says: "to build the wall of natural genius," though it is done better through art. And so **Haly Abbas** says that **Hippocrates** was born with excellent natural goodness and an abundance of skill, which led him to use the three doctrines <note>likely the branches of logic or the primary medical sects</note> without the formal art of natural dialectic. 

<margin>To the 2nd argument</margin>

To the next, it should be said that things considered particularly are distinct, some from others; however, in common, as has been said, they are the same. It should be said that regarding a certain particular essential knowledge of medicine, other sciences are not necessary; however, regarding a more universal and fuller knowledge of "perfect being," they are necessary.

<margin>To the 3rd argument</margin>

To the other, it should be said that medicine, regarding those things which are proper to itself, needs no other science; yet it needs others insofar as one science is placed under another, as was shown, just as one thing is contained under another. For since there are two things in science—the "suppositions" and the "reasoned conclusions"—as noted in the first book of **Aristotle's** *Metaphysics*: as for the reasoned conclusions, since they are proper to that science in which they are reasoned from proper principles, they do not need others; but as for the suppositions, they need the superior science to declare and defend them through common principles. To the next, a similar response should be given. To the other, it should be said that although every particular science, as has been shown, in some way needs the universal, they do not need it in the same way. For one is more particular, such as that which concerns a particular being, while another is less so. A more universal science does not require administrative aids like grammar or relational logic, as it concerns particular being. Medicine, however, is said to be the most particular of all.

## DIFFERENCE II.

<margin>First reason</margin>

It seems that it is not necessary for a physician to be a logician, because that which is "vain" is not suitable for him. But being a logician is such a thing. Whence in the prologue of *On the Soul*: It is manifest that dialectical definitions are all vain. And thus almost all logical knowledge is vain, since a definition is the "middle term" of a demonstration, or at least the most powerful part of it.

<margin>Second reason</margin>

Furthermore, that which is irrelevant and extraneous a physician does not need to have; but logical discourses are such. Whence the **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note> in the fourth book of the *Physics*: **Aristotle** intends by "extraneous discourses" to mean logical ones, and he calls the philosophy composed of these "extraneous philosophy."

<margin>Third reason</margin>

Again, that which is futile is not necessary for a physician who establishes his goal in useful things. But logic is such a thing. Whence in the third book of the *Lower Parts* <note>original: "infiorū," likely a corrupted reference to Galen's De Locis Affectis</note>: Logically true things are whatever consider things beyond their natural utility. In the first book of the same: it is useless to be persuaded by the investigation of logicians, since nothing helpful is found in it for the diagnosis of passions, nor in healing, nor in prognosis. Wherefore the **Commentator** in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* says: universally, he who is always in a state of argument many times happens to see things extraneous and remote from the nature of the thing. Therefore, in the first book of the *Theory*, **Galen** says in the first book on the knowledge of diseases that the logical investigation of questions is not useful in the art of medicine, since nothing is gained through them regarding the nature of diseases, nor the imposition of causes, nor signs, nor remedies. Furthermore, one science does not seem to need another that is entirely different in kind; but logic and medicine are entirely distinct. Their principles, subjects, means, and ends are different. For the subjects and principles of logic are "beings of reason" and second intentions <note>concepts about concepts, rather than things in the physical world</note>. **Aristotle** in the first book of the *Metaphysics* says the means by which the universal is supported are different; the end, moreover, is to reason perfectly. The subject of medicine, however, is the human body capable of being healed, as will be shown in this "Difference." The means by which individuals are finally affected are sensible things. For a physician does not heal "Man" <note>the universal concept</note> except by accident, but rather heals **Calyas** <note>a traditional name used in logic puzzles, like "Socrates"</note> or perhaps a specific person, as in the prologue of the *Metaphysics*. Similarly, **Haly Abbas** says the speculation of all medicine does not transcend the senses; whence the same says upon the *Quadripartitum*: The art of medicine regards nothing except manifest things by feeling and seeing. Its end is the possession of health, as in the first "Difference." From all of which it is inferred that a physician does not need to be a logician.

<margin>Opposition</margin>

The opposite of this, however, is taken from the "Difference" already brought forward. Furthermore, that through the defect of which a physician might fail...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the necessity of Logic for the physician, moving into the second and third parts of the argument which distinguish between the rational approach of learned physicians and the limited approach of the Empirics.</meta>

...to err stands before him. This [foundation] is **logic**. Whence in the books: The necessity of **Dialectic** <note>Dialectic is the medieval term for the art of logical disputation and reasoning.</note> is great, so that from certain known things one may be led to know something else clearly, and never obey a **sophism** <note>A sophism is a fallacious argument used to deceive.</note>, neither from another nor from himself. And according to the nature of simple medicines: Physicians for whom there is no knowledge through the path of dialectic and its canon err with a very great error, for they pass over their own terms. They also err in their own reasoning, like the error of children who do not begin to learn dialectic except from practice. Furthermore, **Galen** <note>original: "Ga.," referring to the 2nd-century Greek physician Galen of Pergamon</note> with others teaches how to investigate the natures of diseases and to know their causes through reason; this is the work of logic, since it exists as the science of reason. For "Logic" is interpreted as "rational." From these things, therefore, it is concluded that it is the task of the physician to be a logician. In order that the truth of this inquiry may be shown, its terms must first be opened, since for any proposition it is necessary to first know what it signifies by name. For disputes happen over names and not over things when one falls into discrepancy at the beginning of "Refutations" <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Sophistical Refutations*.</note>.

<margin>Response.</margin>
Secondly, it must be seen what several others have felt about this. Thirdly, the truth shall be subjoined. And fourthly, let the arguments finally be addressed. Regarding the first, it must be known that every [definition] of the terms of this distinction was seen in the previous section. Regarding the second, however, it must be known—as became apparent in the case of some **Empiric** <note>The Empirics were a sect of ancient physicians who relied solely on experience and rejected the need for anatomy or hidden causes.</note> physicians—that by setting aside necessary reason and intending only experience, they wished it not to be the task of the physician to possess logic; they believed it imparted nothing useful but rather brought about a loss, since logic is the use of those things which (as stated in the *Book of Heresies*) they are despisers of. But the defect of these men is marked by the present distinction. For it happens to them that they can distinguish no disease or medicinal matter with certainty, since sensory knowledge alone does not suffice, and they especially fail regarding rare occurrences. Whence in the third [book] of "On the Beginnings": Those who observe experience alone without reason are irrational; their use of those things which happen rarely is held as experience. And because these rare emergencies are often derogatory to their general rules, they despise them; thus they do not signify the cures of such things nor the preceding signs, but their knowledge [fails] in the third [book] of "On the Beginnings."

<margin>Thirdly: Dialectic while used according to two modes in the commentary on the 6th [book] of Metaphysics.</margin>
Furthermore, according to the **Commentator** <note>original: "Commentatorem," referring to the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Averroes</note> in the seventh [book] of the *Metaphysics* and the eighth of the *Physics*, it must be known that dialectic is used in two ways. In one way, it is an instrument, and thus it is used in other sciences insofar as that which is declared in it is accepted in them; and this use is in the modes of knowing common to all sciences, handed down in that which I announced previously. And in the other way, it is a speculative science in itself toward another science, and thus **Metaphysics** seems to use it more, since it considers "being" simply. For the propositions of dialectic concern "being" simply, though not in the same way as being is treated in definitions and descriptions and other things said in them. And this mode seems to me somewhat foreign in other sciences, especially in divine science. Thirdly, he also writes that logic is twofold. One kind is used in all sciences, being one of the seven **liberal arts**. For it is said that dialectic itself has a path to the principles of all methods. The other kind is proper to each individual science. The first kind, as shown in the previous distinction, is necessary for the physician. This is further confirmed because every science is with reason, and without it, it is not a science.

**Medicine**, as will be shown, is a science. Now, one ought to know the principles of reason most especially through the science that deals with reason; this is logic, as the name itself—namely "rational"—denounces. For it illuminates and directs the other sciences in their mode of proceeding. It also establishes at least the probable principles of those sciences.

Fourthly, as touched upon before, Metaphysics differs demonstratively from logic in the mode of its excellence. For this reason, the physician needs the more common logic in no small measure. **Galen**, in the first of his [works], mentions that he followed its precepts against the **Atanebic** <note>referring to a follower of a specific rival medical sect</note> opponent, of whom that disciple says: "nourished here in dialectic, he was then filled with contagion." Whence in the third [book] of "On Natural Faculties," he who ought to know what is better than other things must soon know nature and the "first doctrine," that is, the instruction of the sciences which concern speech and logic properly; since it leads all things back to their ends, it differs much from others. This "first" is twofold: one belongs to the science, the other is for the sciences. The first is the mode in the order of proceeding and demonstration observed in this science or that; which **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ar."</note> handed down in the many beginnings of his books, such as the *Topics*, *Physics*, and *Ethics*. **Ptolemy** also in the beginning of the *Quadripartitum* and the *Centiloquium*. And Galen in the exordiums of almost all his books; and Aristotle in the beginning of "On the Substances of Medicine," on the "Discourse on Pulses," and especially on "Urines." And even if all sciences use this logic, they nevertheless enjoy it more [in these specific subjects]. The knowledge of these is received from matter or human acts, just as natural astrology, judicial medicine, and moral science. For because of the diversity of the things from which they are made, one must put forward logic or a "canon" by which they are constrained to some uniformity of knowledge. The second [part] attends to certain dispositions and habits that are more extrinsic to the physician, some of which are taken from the part of the soul, others from the part of the body, because he is a composite being (as in the first [book] "On the Soul"). Those which are considered by reason of the soul are the **morals** which it is expedient for a physician to have. For although a skilled physician may naturally be of rustic morals, he ought to strive through custom and art to acquire praiseworthy ones; and he will be more appreciated when he works against the "markers of his birth" <note>A reference to astrological determinism; the physician should overcome his innate negative traits through reason.</note> with such a bridle of reason. The morals and acts of the physician, as the illustrious ones—**Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Ypo. Ga. & Halyabbas"</note>—testify, are especially those which are denoted by a name of possession, while others are by privation. I say "possession" because he ought first to be a lover of God and to put Him before all his works. For He alone heals illnesses and leads those who stray into the Truth. And he should fear Him, since it is announced as the "beginning of wisdom." From these things, he is made holy and divine, so that things may be revealed to him, which are shown only to sacred men.

And let him be apprehensive, intelligent, fully mindful, and a diligent reader, failing in study neither by day nor by night, and an indefatigable meditator. For meditation is the key that leads to truth. Let him observe the most proven authors. Let his study be especially in medicine; let him be diligent, experienced, truthful, faithful, strong, modest, chaste, gentle, merciful, pious, of long experience, slow [to anger], and [free] from ignominious passions.

<margin>The presence of the republic and the rationale of the good are paramount.</margin>
The wise healer keeps his own counsel; a diligent visitor of the sick, especially of those with **acute** <note>Diseases that come on suddenly and progress rapidly.</note> conditions, he should visit at least in the morning and evening, always assisting in such cases. As an investigator of the host of such infirmities, in which many strange cases arise, he should not be loath to ask the patient about hidden symptoms, not out of ostentation, but so that what the art of medicine does not reveal, interrogation might make manifest. Let his primary intention be health. For the intention of medicine is health, and its end is the possession of it for the patient. He should also make himself familiar with a few friends, especially if he is a famous physician. It is necessary for him to labor at this from youth. For **preservation** <note>original: "custodia"</note> is easier then than in old age, which exists as a house of forgetfulness. If he should be a teacher, let him love and treat fit disciples as his own sons. Let him teach them freely and without any fear, and let him cast out the unworthy. The disciples, in turn, should love and exalt him as a father—and even more so—believing so that they may learn, showing him worthy rewards, and binding his sons to themselves in affection as brothers. He should be quick of tongue and of keen senses when present with his masters, since he is deputed solely to the **office** <note>original: "offō," abbreviation for "officio"</note> of healing. For then everything is done best when it is ordered toward a single end; the contrary, however, is perverse, and he should stand firm in a single, honest life. Those acts or habits which belong to privation and imperfection should be driven away by the same man with the bridle of sobriety; hence he should not be envious, nor greedy, nor a person of unreasonable silence <note>The text suggests he should be communicative enough to be helpful, as silence can be hated by those in need.</note>, which is why he should hate all things that are loathsome. He should not be an avaricious man, nor distrustful, nor lustful, nor a drunkard, nor a detractor, nor even a flatterer. He should not be a worshiper [of idols] or a gambler, or a player of musical instruments <note>In this context, playing music was seen as a distraction from the gravity of medical study.</note>, nor a hypocrite, nor a physician in name only <note>original: "uerbo f[aci]o e[piscop]o," likely a metaphor for a physician who is all talk and no substance, similar to an "overseer" in word only.</note>. He should not be a man ruled by passions like fear or audacity, for the former breeds weakness and the latter breeds lack of skill. He should not be bold or presumptuous, nor headstrong, nor stubborn, nor a "greeter of the city" who wanders about. For some go about the whole city greeting people and following the powerful just to be seen by them. He should not be a buyer of disciples <note>One who "buys" students through favors rather than merit.</note>, nor a poisoner, nor a perpetrator or teacher of abortions on any occasion. For there are the heavens that judge such things, and even what they sow, they shall see in the hereafter. He should not be ambitious or vainglorious, as if established in a single heresy <note>In this sense, "heresy" refers to a narrow-minded medical sect.</note>, nor a talkative orator or abusive, nor litigious, lest a great nature rise up against you in anger. O, in vain does the ungrateful race of mortals die! The sick man dies and does not die, and my fragility is blamed, says <term>Theodorus Priscianus</term> <note>A 4th-century Roman physician who wrote on the ethics and practice of medicine.</note>. Regarding the body, there is a two-fold requirement: first, as to those things they owe to themselves, such as being of moderate habit and stature. He should not be exceedingly beautiful and adorned, like those who procure women while tending the sick, nor so ugly or deformed that nature spits him out in abomination. He should be neither a giant nor a midget, but should maintain a middle ground as a virtue between these two extremes. He should be deliberate in his actions; his breath and sweat should not be foul or smell like a goat or a polyp <note>original: "caprosq[ue] aut polipsosus." A polyp in the nose was historically associated with bad breath.</note>, and his body should not be so greasy that a horrible stench of sexual excess <note>original: "coit[us] fetor"</note> is perceived from him as from a jar. For it is highly expedient that

<margin>The physician should conduct himself cleanly and honestly.</margin>
he conduct himself cleanly and honestly. Either from the part of the body 

---

or from supporting things, such as those called the "goods of fortune," without which it is not possible to be happy. Therefore, he should receive his fee without interruption. For he who wishes to buy and intends to give away is preparing to beg. While the pain lasts, take the fee. For if the pain ceases, the reward for labor will immediately cease, according to that saying: "While there is a place for diseases, the world is promised to the physician. Soon the physician flees from the mind as the disease flees." For when the sick man has progressed well, he thinks more of you and binds himself and his family to fulfill what you command, lest his expenses be lost; he is healed more quickly according to that saying: "Medicine bought at a high price is accustomed to help many. If it is given for free, it offers no utility." For he does not respect or trust you in the same way. Because of this, it does not heal as well, as will be touched upon in <term>difference 35</term> <note>original: "drā," meaning *differentia*, a section or chapter in a scholastic text.</note>. Yet you should not wish to oppress the poor, nor desert the needy, at least out of a sense of piety, since from this a laudable reputation arises. What you have received in abundance, you should wish to share for free with these out of love for goodness. However, never be a rejecter of a gift offered, unless perhaps someone has already brought you enough, especially when you are a junior or middle-ranking physician. Since medicine, and especially the curative part, is written under **Mars** <note>The planet Mars was traditionally associated with strife and unrewarded labor in medieval medical astrology.</note>, which is judged to be more hateful than almost all other planets; here stands the planet of lack of remuneration, of verbal abuse, and of all inequity. Because of this, it is expedient to firm up your business first so that you are not deceived, unless the patient is a magnificent and courtly person. To those still suffering, it seems as though you expend almost nothing of yourself in visiting them. And services of physicians are often lost for one as they are for many. The office should be private and known to few as to its inner workings, not echoing with the footsteps of those treading through, not denoted by insignia of mitres or medical banners, and not proclaimed by bells. Furthermore, it is necessary for the physician to be shrewd and wise, especially in the pronouncement of future outcomes. For nothing should ever be pronounced absolutely, but should be said under a condition, restricting it to what happens in most cases. Whence in the <term>fourth fraction</term>: When bad and fearful signs appear, we shall preface our speech regarding the loss that follows in most cases. For many are saved miraculously and without hope. Therefore, <term>Galen</term> in his <term>sixth Aphorism</term> says: It is necessary for the physician to be studious so that he does not say anything absolutely. For the pronouncements of health or death in diseases—especially acute ones—are not certain in every way. Nor even in chronic ones, at least as to their beginnings. This happens because of the disordered diversity of the matter, as will be shown in <term>difference 38</term>. And therefore, the judgments of the physician, like those of the **astrologer** <note>Medicine and astrology were closely linked; physicians used celestial positions to determine the "critical days" of an illness.</note>, must be continually bound to conditions with multiple meanings, as those who provide pronouncements by their excellence. For example, let it be said: "It is accustomed to happen so in such cases, but not necessarily." For we sometimes see old men with five fingers [on a hand] and with such color and the like. For monstrosities sometimes occur in illnesses just as in nature, as noted in the <term>seventh Colliget</term> <note>Referring to the *Kitab al-Kullyat* by Averroes (Ibn Rushd), a foundational medical encyclopedia.</note>. However, when you lean with a certain hesitation toward the side of death, nevertheless...

...with a certain downcast expression and a feigned sadness. This should not be done out of necessity, as if you wish to seem to disparage the Creator <note>The physician should not blame God for a patient's decline unless death is truly inevitable.</note>, unless there are signs of absolute necessity. In such a case, it must be said that the patient's health can only occur through a divine miracle and not otherwise. Furthermore, after your judgment has turned toward a fatal outcome, you should not wish to repeat it unless those who are present ask. If you do this, you will seem to be doing it so that you may later rejoice in the glory of your own prognosis. Many doctors—vainly seeking glory—when they have predicted a fatal end, practically gape at the patient's death <note>They wait eagerly for the patient to die just to prove they were right.</note>, perhaps not even providing the necessary treatments for health, so that they might be heard by others as having predicted it; through such vainglory, they have even been known to kill those who were about to recover by giving them lethal medicines. Similarly, those standing by are often led astray by such familiarity. 

However, you should **never remove the hope of health from the sick person**, even if you and the patient himself are completely despaired of. For it is known <note>original: "sciēť," likely referring to Galen or Avicenna's Canon</note> how much the confidence of the infirm person in the doctor helps them toward health. You shall pronounce that those who are about to escape death—even when in a state of loss and necessity—have been reasonably saved if they had a diligent doctor. Let the sick person be obedient, the assistants suitable, and the necessary external preparations ready, and let nothing unforeseen happen. Therefore, **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note> testifies that this diligent caution in prognosis should be observed in the third book of *On the Times of Diseases*. He says: "Throughout my entire life I have abstained from bold confessions; and practicing medicine until old age, I have never to this day had to blush <note>He was never embarrassed by a wrong prediction.</note> regarding a cure or a prognosis, unlike other most vainglorious doctors." For they used cautious rules regarding definitive pronouncements, using perfectly "conditioned" <note>Using "if/then" statements rather than absolute certainties.</note> and, as it were, double-toned voices.

<margin>To the 3rd</margin>
<margin>4th To the 1st</margin>
Having seen these things, we must address the arguments. To the first, it must be said that **dialectical definitions** <note>Logic-based definitions used in debate.</note> can be considered in two ways: either regarding the **form** they pass down for defining—and thus they are not vain but necessary—or regarding the **subjects** they are about. Because those subjects are common and external, contributing very little to knowing in other sciences, they are called "vain." Hence the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher who wrote famous commentaries on Aristotle.</note> says: "Every definition fails through which only **accidents** <note>Non-essential qualities, like color or temporary symptoms, rather than the true essence of a thing.</note> are known." Nor is a definition spoken except equivocally, as when something false is gathered in it, or it is composed of remote causes or accidents; such is seen to be a dialectical definition. For it is considered one way by a Logician and another way by a Philosopher, according to the Commentator in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*. Or even by another craftsman in his own way. For the Logician considers it as an instrument leading the intellect to understand the **quiddities** <note>The "what-ness" or essence of a thing.</note> of things. The Philosopher, however, considers it according to the nature of things, and thus concerning another being according to the consideration of his own science. Thus, logic moved in a special science should assume logic's methods, not its objects. 

<margin>To the 2nd</margin>
Regarding the other point, it appears what must be said: that in one's own science, one must proceed from one's own principles when one wishes to generate knowledge, while maintaining the common method of logic. One should not proceed from those things which are in themselves "common," such as "if the proposition is in the proposition, then the opposite is in the opposite," or how often one of the contraries is spoken of alongside the other. For it is necessary for the one who seeks well to be persistent through the primary instances of the **genus** <note>The broad category or classification of a thing.</note>, which is done by considering all the differences of that genus, as noted in the third book of *On the Heavens and the World*. 

<margin>To the 3rd</margin>
Regarding the other point, it has already been seen what **Galen** felt regarding the "Logician." For what he says specifically about one logical question—such as whether a **passion** <note>An ailment or condition.</note> existing in the head caused by fumes rising from the stomach should be called a disease of the head or of the stomach—**Haly Abbas** <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note>, in his discourse on these matters, seems to despise every logical question. Galen wanted this to be handled at least by reason of the method of use, which he also showed by pretending the aforementioned speech. Thus, from such argumentation on either side, it is useless, etc. 

<margin>To the 4th</margin>
To the other point, it must be said that although **logic** stands by itself as a teaching tool and differs from medicine and other sciences, yet by reason of the way it is used, it reaches into all and agrees with all.

***

## DIFFERENCE III.

<margin>1st argument</margin>
It seems that **Medicine is not a science**. First, because science concerns **incorruptible and perpetual things**, according to the first book of the *Posterior Analytics* <note>Aristotle's work on the requirements for true scientific knowledge.</note>. But the things with which medicine is concerned are all corruptible. For the human body, which it treats, along with everything applied to it, is changeable and corruptible. Furthermore, all science is about **abstracts**; but medicine is not about abstracts but about **concretes** <note>Real, physical things rather than mathematical or theoretical concepts.</note>. 

<margin>2nd</margin>
This is shown from its definition: for it is the science of the "healthy, the sick, and the neutral," all of which are concrete states in the body. Again, science is of the **universal**, but medicine is of **particulars**. For no doctor heals "Man" except by accident; rather, he heals **Callias or Socrates** <note>Standard philosophical names for specific individuals.</note>. For the singular individual is what is curable; hence it is said of medical skill: "Medicine is not made for the universal man, but for each individual." 

<margin>3rd</margin>
Furthermore, if medicine is a science, it is either of particulars or universals. Not of particulars, because there is no science of them, only **sense perception**. 

<margin>4th</margin>
Nor of universals, because if there were a science of them, the intellect would have to perceive them, since science is an intellectual **habit**. But if it were comprehended by the intellect, since it is one and singular—and everything that is received is received according to the mode of the receiver and not the thing received—everything that enters into an individual becomes individual. Therefore, these universals would be rendered particular and singular. 

<margin>5th</margin>
Again, for there to be science of something, there must be some **subject** through which a property is proven. This is the definition of a subject. But in the definition of medicine, **accidents** <note>Health and sickness are considered "accidents" because they are states the body inhabits, not the body's essential nature.</note> occur—namely, the healthy, the sick, and the neutral. There is no definition or demonstration of accidents, according to the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*. 

<margin>6th</margin>
Furthermore, that which is not **one** is nothing; because whatever exists, exists because it is one, according to the book *On Being and the One*. But medicine is not one, because there is no single way of knowing its parts; for some things in medicine are known by **reason**, while others are known by **experience**.

<margin>
7th Method
B.
</margin>
It considers even corruptible things as if they were incorruptible, following the reasoning regarding air and water. If they consider matters from the highest perspective, they would know that astronomy is not the smallest part of medicine <note>Medieval physicians believed the positions of planets and stars influenced human health and the "critical days" of an illness.</note>, at least in the rendering of critical days and the contemplation of higher impressions, which do not seem to have a single rationale since they dominate more than the genus of metaphysics—that is, it considers both substance and accident.

Likewise, a science belongs to a single genus of a subject, considering its parts and passions, according to the *First Book of the Posterior Analytics* <note>Aristotle’s "Posterior Analytics" was the standard textbook for defining what makes a study a "science."</note>. But this knowledge [medicine] is not of one thing nor of many, since it theoretically concerns all bodies that exist in the world. For the physician, for the sake of the human body, considers everything that occurs to him in any way. Furthermore, if it were a science, it would be subordinate to some superior science; for this is the nature of a particular subject science. But it is not subordinate to a science, but rather to a mechanical art, since its end is a further health which it confers or introduces through work—or as we see happen in the mechanical arts. From all these points, it is therefore concluded that medicine is neither a science nor a single entity.

<margin>
Opposition
</margin>
In opposition to all these are Hippocrates, Avicenna, Galen, and other distinguished physicians and philosophers who profess that it is a science. Furthermore, science is the comprehension of the truth of an immobile being; medicine is such a thing, as will be declared. Therefore, it is a science.

<margin>
Response
</margin>
So that the truth regarding this question and its related points may be shown, first its terms shall be explained. Second, we shall see what others have felt about this very thing. Third, the truth shall be demonstrated. And fourth, finally, the arguments shall be addressed.

<margin>
First, according to Avicenna.
</margin>
<margin>

</margin>
Regarding the first point, it must be known that "medicine" is named from "mode" <note>original: "medicina dicit a mō [modo]"; a common medieval etymology linking medicine to 'moderation' or 'measure'.</note>. For it provides a healthy measure of living. This term is also accepted in many ways. For sometimes it is taken most broadly, as it is a certain habit caused by its own principles which the soul seeks concerning the object heard. It is also taken generally, as it is the proper administration of the **six non-natural things** <note>These are the six environmental/lifestyle factors: air, food and drink, sleep and waking, motion and rest, evacuation and repletion, and the passions of the mind.</note>, or a potion, or surgery.

In how many ways medicine is defined.
</insert>

It is also taken particularly, according to how it seeks a disease in a particular complexion <note>The unique balance of the four humors in an individual.</note>, or in composition, or in the common nature according to one instrument of medicine; formerly it was called a "medicine" or a "potion." It is taken even more particularly for a laxative drug alone, which is the most common usage today.

<margin>
Medicine has various definitions and notifications; the first is written by Hippocrates.
</margin>
Furthermore, it is found to have many definitions. For it is described in the *Isagoge* <note>The "Isagoge" by Johannitius was the standard introductory text to the Galenic medical system.</note> on the testimony of Hippocrates: **Medicine is addition and subtraction.** "Addition," indeed, of those things which are lacking; "subtraction" of those things which are superfluous. And this description, with its exposition, seems to represent the practical side [of the art] more.

<margin>

3rd in the Book of Sects
4th in his Tegni
5th in the Arabic translation
</margin>
<margin>
And according to Galen.
</margin>
It is also written by **Plato** that medicine is "the science of man so that he may participate in health." In the *Book of Sects* <note>original: "lib' heresū," referring to Galen's "On the Sects for Beginners."</note>, medicine is "the doctrine or discipline of healthy and sickly things." In the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Ars Medica," often called the "Tegni" or "Microtegni."</note> it is said: **Medicine is the science of the healthy, the sick, and the neutral.** <note>The "neutral" state refers to someone who is neither fully healthy nor actively ill, such as the elderly or a recovering patient.</note> The Arabic translation, considering this definition incomplete, adds to it, saying: "Medicine is the science of things pertaining to health, and to sickness, and to a third disposition in which a person is neither healthy nor sick." First, however, theoretically, Galen in the book of the *Small Art* defined...

In the first part of the first *Canon* <note>Avicenna’s "Canon of Medicine," the most influential medical encyclopedia of the Middle Ages.</note>: **Medicine is the science by which the dispositions of the human body are known**, so that health, once possessed, may be preserved, and when lost, may be recovered.
