**Averroes**, however, in the first book of the *Colliget* <note>Averroes' major medical work, the "Kitab al-Kulliyat" (Book of Generalities).</note>: "It is an operative art proceeding from true principles in which the observation of the health of the human body and the removal of its sickness is sought, according to what can be done in each individual body."

<margin>
9th is the same in the Orisusa.
It is the most rational of all.
</margin>
In the sixth book of the same, he defined medicine in the *Orisusa* <note>Possibly a reference to a specific section or commentary on the "Aphorisms."</note> saying that "it is an operative art which was found by experiment and reason, preserving health and removing sickness." And this is the more rational definition which may be found in any book of the authors. I also said at the beginning that **medicine is the science of the human body as it is capable of being cured.**

Next, concerning the genus of medicine, which is "science," it must be known that there are five habits by which the soul speaks the truth by affirming or denying, according to the *Sixth Book of the Ethics* and at the end of the *Posterior Analytics*: **science, art, prudence, wisdom, and intellect.** For by suspicion and opinion one can be deceived. "Science" for the present, as well as "to know," is spoken of in three ways.

<margin>
Science properly.
What "properly" means.
</margin>
There is "to know" or "science" spoken of most properly, such as that which is through proximate and immediate causes, which are the continuous genera leading to a conclusion; such is the science or "knowing" which is defined in the *First Book of the Posterior Analytics* when it says: "We think we know each thing simply, and not in a sophistical way according to accident, when we think we know the cause because of which the thing is, and that it is the cause of that thing, and that it cannot be otherwise." And this science arises from demonstration, or "compositive doctrine" according to Galen.

<margin>
Properly taken.
</margin>
There are things taken "properly" which can be said most properly regarding us, since a way is open to us to proceed from things more known and certain to us into things more known according to the nature of physical principles. For indeed, with effects inherently following their own per se causes in a prior order, one arrives from proximate and immediate things at the cause which one intends to hunt for; or from more remote causes through certain closer intermediaries, a conclusion is deduced into an effect. This science is drawn out through demonstration, which is called "resolutive doctrine." And that which is taken from these two ways is the science called "the habit of the intellect" or that drawn from demonstration. Whence **Isaac Israeli** in the *Book of Definitions*: "True science is true knowledge, which reason and demonstration confirm." By "reasoning," he understands demonstration; and by "demonstration," he specifically means the demonstration of "why" <note>original: "propter quid"; a logical term for a demonstration that explains the underlying cause, not just the fact.</note>, for he calls that "demonstration" properly.

<margin>
Improperly.
</margin>
"Science" and "to know" are accepted thirdly, improperly and very commonly, for the attainment of truth by any mode whatsoever, whether by reason or experience or another way. And thus, science is nothing other than the comprehension of the truth of those things which exist. **Boethius** in his commentary on the *Categories*. Whence Isaac, mentioned before: "Science is absolutely the soul’s comprehension of the truth of things prepared for knowing." Since indeed its utility is the acquisition of happiness.

<margin>
What "Art" means.
</margin>
**Art**, however, is a habit of making with right reason—or the right reason of things to be made. And "art" is said to be a collection of precepts tending toward one end. It occurs when one thing is made from many experimental perceptions.

<summary>This page explores various definitions of medicine, debating whether it is a "science" (theoretical knowledge of causes) or an "art" (practical application). It compiles definitions from major authorities like Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, and Averroes to establish medicine's dual nature as both a causal study of the body and a practical method for healing.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotelian science, definitions of medicine, Galen, Avicenna, Averroes, six non-naturals, neutral state, logic, art vs. science, Isaac Israeli</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the definition of medicine, specifically debating whether it should be classified as a "science" (scientia) or an "art" (ars). It transitions from the previous page's skeptical arguments into a formal reconciliation using Aristotelian and Boethian definitions of knowledge.</meta>

<margin>Why medicine is intended to be an art</margin>

...regarding the ends accepted from the prologue of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle’s "Metaphysics," which discusses the nature of existence and the hierarchy of knowledge.</note>. It must also be known, as has already appeared in the descriptions of medicine previously mentioned, that medicine is sometimes called a **science**, and at other times an **art** and a **work**. Hence, Hippocrates <note>original: "Y." for Ypocras</note> says: *Life is short, but the art is long.* And in his book *On the Law*: *Medicine is the most excellent or most renowned of all arts.* Likewise, at the beginning of *On the Regimen of Acute Diseases*: *The art of medicine has been reduced to a vanity of indications.* However, there appears to be a significant distance between "art" and "science," because "science" seems to consist in *that which has been done* <note>term: "in facto esse" — a state of completed being or established truth</note>, whereas "art" consists more in *the making* <note>term: "in fieri" — the process of becoming or being produced</note>. Hence, at the end of the *Posterior Analytics*: "Art is concerned with the generation [the coming-to-be] of a thing." If it is science, it is already established. In the sixth book of the *Ethics*, it says: *Every art is concerned with generation and the technical and speculative consideration of how something may come to be which is capable of either being or not being.* The principle of these things lies in the maker and not in the thing made. For art is not concerned with things that exist or happen by necessity, nor with things that exist according to nature, for these have their principle within themselves. Hence, in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*: *Art is the principle and the form of that which is made, but it exists in another [the artist].* Nature, however, has the motion within itself, proceeding from another existing nature that possesses the form in actuality. In this way, Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note> expresses this in the *Metaphysics*: *Some things result from our own work; others from the work of nature.* Those are said to be from our work of which we are the authors through our own skill and power. Such things are properly called "artificial," and it is said that art concerns those things involving a certain transformation and choice. Hence, Eustratius <note>A 12th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> at the beginning of the *Ethics* says: *Art is a collection of tested and proven perceptions trained toward some end of those good things which are useful in life.* However, those things from the "work of nature" are produced by nature itself, and we do not consider our own skill or industry to be their authors. These are primarily the things of the three modes: the natural, the mathematical, and the divine <note>These correspond to the three theoretical sciences in the Aristotelian tradition: Physics, Mathematics, and Theology/Metaphysics.</note>, as seen in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*. Regarding these, the word "science" is properly used, since we have received knowledge from things that already exist.

<margin>Art is considered in two ways</margin>

This is a proper distinction. It should be noted, however, that "art" is properly considered in two ways: either as it is a **disposition** <note>term: "habitus" — a stable quality or learned skill residing in the soul</note> acquired in the soul (and in this sense it is "already established" just like science), or as it refers to the "makeable things" while it is in the process of making them. In this second sense, it is said to concern "generation" and "becoming." "Science," however, is spoken of in both ways as being in a state of completed existence. Therefore, since medicine has two parts—namely, the **theoretical** and the **practical**—it can be properly called a "science" in regard to the theoretical part, but it is more an "art" in regard to the practical part. According to Galen, Hippocrates was the inventor of medicine. For among all those known, he was the first and the inventor of the science; he existed more fully in the movement and the doing of it, applying himself first to things by experience, and finally by reason. Since he still held the reason of this disposition as it was conceived and carried in the soul, Hippocrates could rightly name medicine an "art" rather than a science. Others, receiving it from him as something already nearly perfected, were thus able to call it a "science." Furthermore, **Prudence** is a disposition with true...

<margin>What Prudence is</margin>

...reason regarding the operation of human goods. It is also the "right reason of things to be done." **Rhetoric**, properly, is a virtue in the intellect according to which men can take counsel concerning the good and those works leading toward...

<margin>What Wisdom is</margin>

...happiness. **Wisdom**, however, exists in the most certain arts and is the most certain of the sciences, encompassing under itself both "intellect" and "science." For the wise man must not only speak truly from the principles of science, but also regarding the principles themselves. Hence Boethius says in his *Arithmetic*: *Wisdom is the comprehension of the truth of things which possess a state of being that is immutable in itself.*

<margin>What Intellect is</margin>

**Intellect** <note>The Latin "intellectus" here refers to the intuitive grasp of self-evident truths.</note> is the disposition of first principles, whereas science is of the conclusions. Hence, in the sixth book of the *Ethics*: *Intellect is of terms for which there is no further reason [demonstration],* because science is that which is accompanied by a reason for the conclusion. In this way, science is separated from the intellect. This "intellect" is that which is said to always consist of true things. For it is that which is most known and most firm, which comes to the possessor through itself, as noted in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. For we have this intellect insofar as we know terms through the senses. For once it is known what a "whole" is and what a "part" is, we immediately know that *the whole is greater than its part.* This principle is most known in mathematics and most firm; in medicine, however, a similar principle is that *every cure occurs through the contrary.*

<margin>What Opinion is</margin>

**Opinion**, however, is a conception which is reached with the fear that the other side might be true <note>A classic Scholastic definition of "opinio": holding a belief while acknowledging the possibility of being wrong.</note>. For not everyone who thinks something also knows it. Aristotle says in the fifth book *On the Soul*: *It is also called the conception of one part of a contradiction with the fear of the other.* Therefore, regarding the second point, it must be known...

<margin>The second main point: whether medicine is a science according to the opinions of some.</margin>

...that some have not only denied that medicine is a science, but have also denied this of natural science and astrology (especially the judgment of the stars) and similar fields. Furthermore, some have specifically sought to nullify medicine. Regarding this, it must first be known that certain people did not believe science could be had concerning sensible and corruptible things <note>Things that can be perceived by the senses and are subject to decay or change.</note>.

<margin>Heraclitus and his colleague Cratylus wished to deny science regarding sensible and corruptible things; see Metaphysics books 1 and 4.</margin>

These were primarily **Heraclitus** and his colleague **Cratylus**, as argued in the first and fourth books of the *Metaphysics*. They argued as follows: *Nothing can be a science if nothing can be truly asserted about it,* since science is the true comprehension of an immutable being. But concerning the "natural," nothing can be asserted with certainty, because nothing can be truly uttered concerning that which is in a state of continuous motion and transformation. All natural things are of this sort, as the senses demonstrate.

They prove their first point thus: if something were truly asserted of that which is continuously changing, by the time the assertion was made, the thing would have changed and would be in a different disposition than before. They prove their second point by claiming that the very principles of natural beings are changeable. For they posited the first principle to be "vapor," which is more changeable than all other things; therefore, nothing can be truly asserted of them, and thus there can be no science of them, since science must comprehend and assert the truth. Hence, Cratylus reached such a state of insanity that he thought he should not speak at all, but only move his finger. He even rebuked Heraclitus for saying that *one cannot enter the same river twice*; for Cratylus believed one could not do so even *once*, for it passes away immediately and becomes something else.

<margin>Against these men</margin>

But these men erred in both propositions of their argument, as appears in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. For that proposition is false which says: *It is not possible to truly assert anything of that which is in continuous motion and transformation.* For it is either true to assert that it *is* transforming, or that it is *not*, since an affirmation or negation concerning anything must be true.

If, however, it is true that a thing is "not transforming" [in its essence or as a fact of its change], then they deny the very thing they intend to affirm.

<summary>This page explores the definitions of art and science in a medical context, distinguishing between theoretical knowledge (science) and practical application (art). It also refutes the radical skepticism of Heraclitus and Cratylus, arguing that true knowledge is possible even in a world of constant change.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on the nature of medical knowledge, specifically addressing whether a science can exist for things that are constantly changing. It transitions from a general discussion of "art" and "science" into a refutation of ancient philosophies (Heraclitus and Plato) in favor of the Aristotelian "middle way" of abstraction.</meta>

They say indeed that a thing is transformed; if it is true that what has been transformed can be stated, then the proposition is held—that it is possible to state something truly concerning it. It is clear that concerning that which transforms, it is true, according to **Aristotle**, to say at least that it exists; nor does this have any other cause except that it is what it is. He <note>Referring to Heraclitus</note> also errs in his third proposition when he says: all beings are changeable and in continuous motion. For it is necessary that if some things are changeable, others must be unchangeable. In every transformation, it is necessary that something remain fixed and permanent, upon which the mover relies. For every motion relies upon something immobile, according to the book *On the Cause of the Motion of Animals* <note>Aristotle’s "De Motu Animalium."</note>. It is also necessary in every transformation that there be a subject, because everything that is transformed is transformed from something, as from a subject. Either that subject is itself changeable or unchangeable; if it is unchangeable, our point is immediately proven. If it is changeable, then it has another subject around which it transforms, and there will be the same question regarding that. Thus, there would either be a process to infinity in material causes—which is universally against the second book of the *Metaphysics*—or one must grant a primary matter and a subject in transformation. The same is similarly deduced on the part of the efficient cause <note>term: "efficient cause" — the agent or force that brings about a change.</note>, because everything that is transformed is transformed by something, according to the seventh book of the *Physics*. Therefore, that agent is either unchangeable or changeable. Not the former; and thus there will either be a process to infinity, or there will be a first efficient cause that is unchangeable. Therefore, not all beings are changeable, as **Heraclitus** and **Cratylus** wished.

<margin>Plato's opinion</margin>
**Plato**, accustomed to the opinions of **Cratylus** and **Heraclitus** that all sensible things are in flux and that knowledge of them does not exist, later adopted this view. Because of this, **Socrates** occupied himself only with moral matters and nothing concerning natural science, according to the first book of the *Metaphysics*. For he saw that moral matters were not in such continuous motion and transformation as natural things; and in these he sought universals and definitions and what belongs to them. **Plato**, accepting these, thought that the same should be done in natural things. For this reason, he was forced to provide a way in which science could be preserved regarding natural things. For he posited that the natures and <term>quiddities</term> <note>original: "quidditates" — the essence or "whatness" of a thing.</note> of things were separate from the things themselves. For of all individual things, there is one common, synonymous principle. He posited one Idea or common species subsisting by itself for all those things, which he wished to be the principle giving being to all those participating in it, and through which other things are known. Since it is separate and universal in act, it is the reason that some things are known through something particular existing in them; and since everything existing in them is particular and corruptible. But this opinion is refuted in many places, primarily in the first and seventh books of the *Metaphysics*.

<margin>Against Plato</margin>
Mainly because the "separate" and the "not-separate" do not share the same definition <note>original: "unius rationis"</note>, nor do the corruptible and the incorruptible, according to the tenth book of the *Metaphysics*. If, therefore, the Ideas are separate, they cannot be the essences and natures of particular things. Furthermore, he erred in positing that they were self-subsisting and yet also universal, because everything that subsists by itself is numerically one; and such a thing is a singular in the categories. If, therefore, they are self-subsisting, they will be singulars and not universals. Furthermore, nothing that is separated 

from something can be the immediate and sufficient cause of knowing it. For even if a thing can be known through extrinsic causes, it is nonetheless not known immediately and perfectly; rather, it is known immediately and perfectly through something existing within it. Also, universals are either nothing or are posterior to singulars; whence in the prologue of *On the Soul*: "the universal animal is either nothing or it is posterior." Therefore, if Ideas are separate from particulars, they cannot be the immediate cause of knowledge, nor the knowledge of them. Rather, there must be some intrinsic principle of knowledge for them, which is why they are posterior. That is: "Let the species rejoice, if they exist. For they are monsters <note>original: "Monstra" — used here in the Aristotelian sense of "useless fictions" or "aberrations of logic."</note> since they contribute nothing to generation nor to science." The **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher.</note> in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* seems to excuse **Plato** in some respects: those proportions and powers which are created in the elements by the motions of the sun and other stars are what **Plato** regarded 

<margin>Aristotle's opinion</margin>
as forms, and those were his intent. But he looked at them from afar because he called them "forms." **Aristotle**, however, the prince of the Peripatetics, coming after these men, held a middle way, giving a method by which there can be science concerning natural things and universally concerning sensible, corruptible things. For he did not posit that science was about particular sensible things entirely, as some of the Empiricists did; nor about entirely abstract universals, as **Plato** did. Instead, he felt that science was about these things insofar as they are received by the intellect through abstraction into a certain form common to many. And this is what is said in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Ars Medica" or "Microtechne," a foundational medical textbook.</note>: that medicine is a science of generals—that is, of universals accepted by the intellect in one generalizable form, which is born to be in and predicated of individual particulars. Whence, in the third book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio" — referring to Galen's "De Methodo Medendi."</note>, we say there is nothing in medicine that cannot be demonstrated and shown according to its species. For it is not directly about every single individual thing in terms of its actual existence, nor about some while ignoring others (which would be imperfect and unscientific). The <term>agent intellect</term> <note>The "intellectus agens," the active power of the mind that "strips" sensory data of its particularity to find the universal essence.</note>, being of a greater power of nature, performs this abstraction. For the intellect is innate to divide things joined in being into those parts from which they are composed, even if they are not divided in actual existence—just as it divides matter from form and form from the composite. The **Commentator** in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* and first in *On the Soul* says the same: definitions outside the intellect are particular things, but it is the intellect that acts upon them to create universality.

---

And therefore it must be said, according to the mind of **Aristotle**, that natural things and the subjects of nature that are subject to birth and decay can be considered in two ways. Either as they have being in particulars—which is incomprehensible and impossible, for they are infinite, and then they are corruptible, and thus there is no science of them; whence, according to **Plato**, they are to be abandoned since they are indeterminate. And **Haly** <note>Likely Haly Abbas or Haly Rodoan, famous commentators on Galen.</note> says the individuals accepted in medicine are infinite; they are neither comprehended nor contained, nor does one arrive at them, as **Galen** said. Or, they are abstracted from this or that particular sensible matter, whether in terms of the being they have in the intellect already formed, and thus they are...

<summary>This page refutes the Heraclitan idea of total flux and the Platonic theory of separate Ideas, arguing instead for the Aristotelian "middle way." It concludes that medicine is a science because the intellect abstracts stable, universal "species" from infinite, changing particulars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic defense of medicine as a formal science. Having established that knowledge requires stability, the author now addresses how science can exist for "corruptible" (perishable) things and outlines the four specific requirements for any discipline to be considered a true science.</meta>

<margin>
Truly the body of all individuals... <unclear>istud</unclear>
<note>original: "Verum corpus singulariū..." This marginal note is heavily abbreviated and partially lost at the edge of the page, but it appears to discuss the relationship between the individual body and corruption.</note>
</margin>

...things are incorruptible and finite, and concerning them there can be <term>science</term> <note>original: "scientia" — in the medieval sense, this means certain knowledge derived from logic and causes, rather than just "science" in the modern experimental sense</note>, both natural science and others, by considering their nature, their <term>properties</term> <note>original: "passiones" — the attributes or characteristics that naturally belong to a subject</note>, and their causes. Wherefore **Galen**, in his fourth book *To Teucer*, says: **The Art** <note>original: "Ars" — likely referring to the Art of Medicine</note> consists in things that are incomprehensible and infinite only insofar as it pertains to finite genera and species; it measures that which is infinite, and thus they always remain. For example, a "human being" considered in itself is finite; for although a specific person may perish, the nature remains in Plato, and if he perishes, it remains in another, and so on forever. Because of this, in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*, <term>universals</term> <note>original: "universalia" — general concepts like "humanity" as opposed to specific individuals like "Socrates"</note> are said to be always remaining; and thus there is science concerning natural things, not because of something separate from them, but because of something existing within them, which is their <term>quiddity</term> <note>original: "quidditas" — the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</note>. This quiddity does not corrupt in itself, even if it corrupts in a specific individual. Whence in that same seventh book, it is said that the "what-ness" does not perish, but rather the individual thing to which that "what-ness" belongs.

However, whether it might happen that some universal nature perishes when all individuals of that nature are destroyed is a point of doubt for many, since they say that universals are among the number of things that remain, and that science is about universals, and that science is of things that are incorruptible. But where they might find this universal nature when all individuals have perished is something some have doubted. Perhaps, however, this nature remains in the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectu" — the high rational mind</note>, which is common to all, perpetual and incorruptible, as many of **Aristotle’s** commentators have felt; or it remains in the intellect of the <term>Intelligences</term> <note>original: "intelligentiarum" — in medieval philosophy, these are the celestial beings or angels that govern the heavenly spheres</note>.

On account of these things, it should be known that some have denied that medicine is a science or an art, because of the discord among bad physicians. Whence, in the first book of the *Propedeutics* <note>original: "ꝓ petio" — likely referring to the *Isagoge* or an introductory medical text</note>, after posing certain opposing opinions, it is said: "Since the magnitude of this disagreement concerning acute diseases has grown so much among those who treat them, so that what seems beneficial to one sick person seems harmful to another, the art of medicine has been reduced to a lack of truth." Thus, it even appears most clearly to the common people that the art of medicine should be thought not to exist at all. There are also some of such dull and blunt intellect that they believe a physician cannot know anything of the internal parts of the body, and consequently is unable to provide help; they say this especially regarding the two instruments of medicine: diet and specific potions. In the same way, some have detested judicial astrology, as **Abu Ma'shar** mentions in the first book of his *Introduction*. They do, however, accept surgery, since it appears to their senses, though they are far from joining and healing correctly.

But to these people, it must be said—following a certain saying about disease—that they ought not to be blamed by others, since they blame themselves by not knowing how to distinguish the skilled from the unskilled. Nor does this prove a defect in the art, but rather in the practitioner who does not use it as he ought. For it is the business of a dull intellect to be unable to reach a difficult truth; yet one should not estimate that another with a sharp intellect cannot accomplish this. For although the eye of a bat cannot look upon the light of the sun even when it is dimmed, nevertheless the eye of an eagle looks upon its wheeling brilliance.

<margin>
Property of **Abu Ma'shar** <note>original: "Al." / "Albuasar"</note>
</margin>

<margin>
Thirdly, it will be shown that medicine specifically is a science.
</margin>

Regarding the third point, it first seems (as the most subtle thinkers ask) whether medicine is a science; secondly, whether it is one science; and thirdly, whether it is subordinate to natural philosophy. Regarding the first of these, it should be known—as the learned commonly feel—that medicine is a most excellent science or art, because it contains within itself everything required for a science.

Four things, for the present, seem to be required for there to be science of something:
1. First, that the thing is a **being**, because there is no science of a non-being (just as there is no science of the symmetry of a diameter in the *Posteriors* <note>referring to Aristotle's *Posterior Analytics*</note>).
2. Second, that this being is **comprehensible to the intellect**. For science, as has been said, is an intellectual habit; whence, regarding things that cannot be grasped by the human intellect—such as whether the number of stars is even or odd—a science cannot be established, nor even a reasonable opinion, since they are infinite to us.
3. Third, it is required that this being exists **"per se"** <note>in itself</note>, since there is no science of a being by accident <note>original: "per accidens" — things that happen by chance or are not essential</note>, as the physicists say. Whence in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, no science—neither active, nor factual, nor speculative—is concerned with the accidental. For the art of ethics cares nothing for things that are accidental, since they are indeterminate and fortuitous.
4. Fourth, it is required that it is a being about which **properties and attributes** can be proven through a middle term <note>a logical step in a syllogism</note>. According to the saying: Science concerns the parts and contrary properties of a single subject genus.

<margin>
How many things are required so that one may have science of something: 1st, that it be a being.
</margin>

<margin>
2nd, that it be [comprehensible] by the intellect...
</margin>

<margin>
3rd, that it be "per se."
</margin>

<margin>
4th, that properties and attributes can be proven of the subject through middle terms.
</margin>

But in the matters of medicine, these four are found to occur. For there is a **subject** there which is the most noble body of all things in the world: namely, the healable human body. It is grasped by the intellect, for its nature is not hidden from us due to a weak existence (like primary matter) or because it exceeds the power of the intellect (like the things of God and the Intelligences); rather, it is something middle, bordering on and close to the intellect. It is also **subsisting in itself**, having sufficient causes of its own. Fourthly, it has **properties** and parts which are proven of it through middle terms (that is, definitions).

For example: a body, under the attribute of being "healable," is placed as the subject of medicine. From this, "healable" happens to be demonstrated thus:
*Every human body is an animate body, a participant in a rational soul.*
*Moreover, every animate body participating in a rational soul is healable.*
*The human body is such a thing.*
*Therefore, it is healable.*

Thus, such an argument may be constructed for everything that sufficiently possesses the conditions required for a science; therefore, medicine itself will be a science. It should be noted, however, that the knowledge obtained from medical matters is not always supported by certain <term>demonstration</term> <note>logical proof from first principles</note>, but relies in no small part on **conjecture** approaching the truth—very many of which concern the "crisis" and the *Aphorisms* of the ancients <note>Referring to Hippocrates</note>, as is evident in prognostications and in things that are internally hidden and uncertain. We cannot, in such things, arrive at that which is perfectly certain; thus, as the science of **Asclepius** or **Aesculapius** <note>The Greek god of healing</note> would be ours, we approach it through ingenuity as much as we can, trusting that nature will trim away what is superfluous and increase what is diminished. Thus, medicine is a science, and "science" is its genus, though used in a broad sense. Therefore, it is said in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*</note>: "The name of science must be heard in a common, not a strict sense." Whence the **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note> in the fifth book of the *Metaphysics* says: "Science is not the genus of medicine unless 'science' is said in relation to the knower and 'medicine' to the physician." For then, science would be the genus of medicine, and "knower" the genus of physician...

<summary>This page defines medicine as a formal "science" by demonstrating that it meets the four Aristotelian requirements for systematic knowledge: existence, intellectual comprehensibility, essential nature, and provable properties. It defends the field against skeptics who claim medicine is uncertain, comparing the physician's insight to an eagle's vision.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Galen, Abu Ma'shar, Averroes, quiddity, universals, scholasticism, medical theory, human body, logic, conjecture</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the nature of medicine as a science. The previous page established that science deals with universals rather than corruptible individuals; here, the author explores the unity of medicine as a discipline and its hierarchical relationship to other branches of knowledge like logic and natural philosophy.</meta>

If a **species** is not relative, it is not a genus in the reality of the thing, but rather it is added commonly and with a certain extension. Wherefore the same thing—namely, one of two relatives—can exist in one genus, while its relative exists in another: for example, **knowledge** and **the known**. For knowledge is in the category of quality, while the known object is in the category of substance. **Haly** <note>original: "Haly" — referring to Haly Abbas (‘Ali ibn al-‘Abbas al-Majusi), a 10th-century Persian physician whose works were central to medieval European medicine</note> explains this by saying that knowledge is common to three sciences depending on natural principles: namely **agriculture**, **herding**, and **medicine**. It can also be explained that "to know" is used in two ways in the present context: strictly, as that which is held by **demonstration** <note>a logical proof that shows why something must be true based on its causes</note>, as is shown in the doctrine of "propositional" reasoning which proceeds from causes to effects; or commonly, for a demonstration that is "hunted" through a **resolutive** doctrine <note>a method of analysis that works backward from effects to find their causes</note>, or a definitive one, as shown in the eighth distinction. Or he spoke commonly on account of **practice**, which does not have the nature of science in the same way as **theory** (as mentioned in the fourth distinction), which happened to be said previously.

<margin>2nd Question: Is medicine one science?</margin>
On account of this, it must be known that medicine is **one science**. To understand this, it must be known that "one" is currently spoken of in four ways:
1.  **One in number**, such as those things whose matter is one, like Socrates; for the principle of individuation is taken from matter as it exists under a determined quantity. Although **Porphyry** <note>a 3rd-century philosopher whose introduction to Aristotle's logic was a standard textbook</note> probably posited that individuality is caused by a collection of properties.
2.  **One in species**, such as those whose defining logic is one, like "human."
3.  **One in genus**, such as those sharing the same figure of predication, like "substance."
4.  **One by analogy** (or proportion), such as whatever things are spoken of in relation to one thing; for instance, "healthy" is said of a body, a cause, and a sign <note>scholastics argued that a body is "healthy" because it possesses health, medicine is "healthy" because it causes health, and urine is "healthy" because it is a sign of health</note>.

These relate to each other such that whatever are the same by proportion are not necessarily the same by genus; and those by genus are not necessarily the same by species; and those by species are not the same by number. But it does not work the other way around: for the lower level implies the higher level, but the higher does not necessarily imply the lower.

<margin>Unity in four ways: by Number, Species, Genus, and according to Analogy.</margin>
<margin>A certain unity... medicine is called one science... [partially illegible]</margin>

If it is now asked whether medicine is one science, it must be said that it is not one by **numerical unity**; for such unity, as has been said, belongs to individuals, and it has been established that there is no science of individuals since they are infinite in number, and therefore it is testified that they are to be omitted. Nor is it one by unity of species or genus, since the same discipline can deal with contraries <note>e.g., medicine studies both health and sickness</note>. Not everything determined in one science is of the same logic or predication—like Socrates, Plato, the healthy, and the sick. Rather, it is one in the fourth way: namely, by **analogy**. For everything determined in medicine has a certain analogy and attribution to the **healable human body**.

It is true, however, that the more a science pertains to multiple things and the greater its analogy, the less it possesses the strict nature of a "science," as is shown in the study of the categories and problems; for demonstrations proceed according to consequence and continuity, and do not descend from one genus into another. Therefore, although all the things handed down in medicine are very different in themselves, medicine stands as **one science**. This is because the unity of a science is caused by the **unity of its object**. For science is a "habit" <note>an acquired disposition or skill</note> of the intellectual soul; and a habit takes its logic and distinction from its objects (according to *On the Soul*). Thus, it is manifest that the unity of science is taken from the unity of the object...

<margin>From what does the unity of science hold, and what science is.</margin>

---

...according to logic. Such an object, as has been shown, is sufficient for medicine to be one by a certain unity of analogy and attribution.

<margin>3rd Question: In what way is it subordinate to the natural part?</margin>
Regarding the third point, it must be known that **Constantine** <note>Constantine the African (c. 1020–1087), a translator who brought Arabic medical texts to the school of Salerno</note> at the beginning of his "great theft" <note>original: "grandioris furti" — a historical jab at Constantine, who was often accused of passing off the works of others (like Haly Abbas) as his own</note>, which he called the ***Pantegni*** <note>original: "pantegni" — from the Greek meaning "The Whole Art," a massive medical encyclopedia</note> or "The Total Art," wished for medicine to be **subordinated** <note>original: "subalternari" — a logical term where a specific science (like music) takes its principles from a more general one (like arithmetic)</note> to logic, natural philosophy, and moral philosophy. His motive was that a physician must be a practitioner of rational, natural, and non-natural things, as well as moral things. It is certain that all these fall under various thoughts and subjects. 

However, it is **false** that medicine is subordinated to rational science or **logic**, since medicine does not take its principles from logic, nor is the subject of medicine placed under the subject of logic. Nor should it be said that it is subordinated to logic just because the physician reasons; for in that case, every science would be subordinated to logic, since every science reasons. There is a twofold distinction: logic is a science that can be subordinated to none, because it is not common in the way mentioned, nor is it strictly different from medicine, since it is found in every science—unless perhaps one posits (as is said in the distinctions) that logic holds the principles of all methods, but this is also present in other sciences. 

Neither is it simply **moral science**, even though it teaches character and natural virtues directly, while acquired virtues are taught remotely and quite extrinsically. This follows the saying in the first book of *On Genius*: "He who wishes to cure the soul must first cure the body," and in the seventh book of the *Politics*: "The care of the body must necessarily come before the care of the soul." The soul is indeed cured by the virtues of character, and these are considered by the science of absolute morality. 

Perhaps it is better said that medicine is subordinated to **natural science** by reason, which is declared thus: Since there is a twofold mode of subordination of one science under another:
1.  By reason of the **subject**, because one subject is under another subject; in this way we say **astrology** is subject to natural science.
2.  Because it takes its **principles** from a higher science; in this way **astronomy** is subordinated to mathematics (namely arithmetic and geometry), for it takes its proofs from the science of number and measure, as seen in the beginning of the *Almagest*.

In both these ways, medicine is subordinated to **natural science**. First, by reason of the subject: for the **healable human body** which medicine considers is contained within the scope of natural science, which is "mobile being insofar as it is mobile." Or, according to others, it is the "mobile body," which **Aristotle** strives to prove at the beginning of the *De Caelo*. Hence, in the beginning of *On Sense and the Sensible*, the physicist is said to find the first principles of health and sickness. For neither health nor sickness can exist in things lacking life. Therefore, many of the physicists and those physicians who follow the art more like a physicist end their works with medical topics, while those who begin with nature start with medicine. Similarly, medicine is subordinated by reason of its **principles**; for the ultimate conclusions of natural science (as in the books on plants and animals) are the principles assumed and handed down—but not argued for—by the physician. Instead, they are supported and established by natural science. Aristotle concludes this in his first book...

<summary>This page discusses the logical unity of medicine as a science based on "analogy" to the human body and explores its academic hierarchy, arguing that medicine is primarily a sub-discipline of natural philosophy rather than logic or ethics.</summary>
<keywords>Haly Abbas, Constantine the African, Pantegni, subalternation of sciences, analogy, unity of science, natural philosophy, logic, medical theory, Aristotle</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the nature of medicine as a science. Having previously discussed whether knowledge is common to multiple disciplines, the author now addresses specific objections regarding whether medicine can be a "science" if it deals with physical, changing bodies and individual patients.</meta>

<margin>
To the first prepared [objection]:
To the first matter.
</margin>

**Medicine is an operative art** proceeding from **true principles**—that is, natural ones. And for this reason, the definition given in the <term>Tegni<note>original: "tegni" — referring to Galen's 'Ars Medica', often called the 'Technē' or 'Tegni' in the Middle Ages, which served as a foundational medical textbook.</note></term> touches upon this same point, though it does not mention it explicitly; however, this was not necessary, nor do those who provide definitions always do so, since such things ought to be understood implicitly in definitions, as noted in the *fourth book of the First [Prior Analytics]*. Indeed, those who assert that medical science is entirely **practical** mistakenly desire to subordinate it to the **mechanical arts** <note>The 'mechanical arts' (like blacksmithing or weaving) were considered manual crafts, lower in status than the 'liberal arts' or 'sciences' which were based on rational principles.</note>. It remains now to remove four sharp arguments. Regarding the first, it must be said that it has already been shown how medicine, and any other science, can concern **sensible and corruptible things** <note>Physical objects that can be perceived by the senses and eventually decay.</note> insofar as the intellect receives them in a certain **common form**. In this way, they are rendered perpetual and incorruptible; but science is not concerned with them insofar as they exist in their **particular, designated nature** <note>Science studies the 'idea' of a human, not every specific detail of one individual person who will eventually die.</note>.

<margin>
To the 2nd.
What abstraction is:
</margin>

<margin>
Abstraction is a form:
</margin>

To the next point, it must be said that medicine deals with **abstracts**. To **abstract** one thing from another according to the intellect is nothing other than to consider one thing apart from the rest. For the sake of this, it should be known from the *sixth book of the Metaphysics* that abstraction is threefold.

<margin>
2nd
</margin>

<margin>
3rd
</margin>

The first type is abstraction from **matter altogether**, both in terms of its existence and in terms of how it is considered or understood; such is the abstraction of the **metaphysician**, who concerns himself with matter in no way. The second type is abstraction according to **reason only** and not according to existence; this is how the **mathematician** abstracts <note>A mathematician thinks about a perfect circle (reason) even though in the physical world, every circle is made of some material substance (existence).</note>. The third type is not an abstraction from **sensible matter** in general, but from **signified sensible matter**—that is, this or that specific material. This is how the **natural philosopher** and the **physician** abstract, and generally every craftsman who concerns himself with sensible matter. Therefore, those things which medicine concerns are, in some way, abstracted. If someone says, "On the contrary, they are concrete," for those things which are adjectives and dependencies concern a subject—such as **'the healthy'** and **'the sick'**...

<margin>
Abstract is used in two ways: 1st
</margin>

<margin>
2nd
</margin>

...it must be said that "abstract" is spoken of in two ways. In one way, as already seen, it refers to that which is not immersed in **signified matter** <note>Specific, individual matter.</note>, but rather is stripped from it by the power of the intellect; and science is only about things abstracted in this way. In another way, a thing is called "abstract" when it refers to a thing as **subsisting by itself** and not in dependency—such as **'whiteness'** and **'health'**.

<margin>
The concrete: what it is
</margin>

The **concrete**, however, denotes the same thing but with a certain inclination and dependency toward a subject—such as **'white'** and **'healthy'**. Science can certainly be about such concrete things, provided they are abstracted in the aforementioned way. And because "healthy," "sick," and "neutral" <note>Galen's category for those who are neither fully healthy nor fully ill, such as the elderly or convalescing.</note> involve a certain dependency on their subject, **Galen**, when defining medicine, says it is the science of healthy, sick, and neutral **bodies**.

<margin>
To the 3rd
</margin>

To the next point, it must be said that medicine is about **universals**, as has been shown. If you say, "We do not treat the universal, such as 'Man,' but the particular, such as **Callias** or **Socrates**," <note>Standard philosophical names for individual people.</note> it must be said that this act of "treating" is not directly science, but is rather a **particular act and labor**; and of such a thing there is no science. Whence even those who call medicine a **mechanical art** have only looked at it from a distance. If it is said that in this specific act or work the "reason" of medicine is extended because its end is otherwise attained, it must be said that although this eventually concurs, the end is better attained by knowing **scientific knowledge**, and especially the **mode and quality of operating**. For science directs and regulates the act of operating...

---

...upon the particular; and then the end of medicine is perfectly manifested. For when someone hastens to the work while neglecting the mode and quality of operating, he usually does more harm than good, even if he possesses good **experiments** <note>Practical clinical experiences or proven remedies.</note>, because he does not know how to apply those experiments with the proper conclusions, in the right places, and at the right times, according to the *Book of Experiments*. Other sciences also have this mode—for example, **Logic**. For it teaches how to construct a **syllogism**; to actually "syllogize" is eventually a certain practical act, yet a person is said to have attained the end of Logic even when they are not currently syllogizing, provided they know the science.

<margin>
To the 4th
</margin>

To the next point, it must be said that medicine is not about sensible particulars—just as no other science is, as has been shown—but is about **universals**. You might argue it is not, because universals, when they come into the intellect, are reduced to particulars, since the intellect is one in number and particular. It must be said that the **universal** has a twofold existence: one in the **possible intellect** <note>The 'possible intellect' is the human capacity to receive and store universal concepts.</note> when it has been brought into act; the other in itself, insofar as it is a certain **rational form** abstracted from many particulars by the intellect. For the intellect abstracts the species and likenesses of things even from signified particulars and repositions them in the possible intellect—namely, gathering one common nature born to exist in or be said of many. This is according to the word of **Porphyry**: <note>original: "porphirii" — Porphyry was a 3rd-century scholar whose 'Isagoge' introduced the concepts of Genus and Species to the Middle Ages.</note> "by participation in the species, many men are one man." And finally, by casting its light upon the possible intellect, it makes it understand the aforementioned nature. For the intellect relates to the nature as **light relates to colors**. And thus the intellect arises in act and is finally "acquired" or "accommodated." *[Distinction] 57*. That common nature or species joins itself to the intellect; it remains universal, and being perfected by the object, there can be science regarding it. For it seems that the intellectual nature exists in its own genus just as the **Sun** exists in the corporeal genus. We know the Sun to be one in number and an individual, yet the light within it is considered in two ways. If it is considered as it is the "form" of the Sun, it is one in number. If, however, it is taken according to how it flows out from it, then it is **universally illuminating** of all diverse things—both those that are transparent, which it makes actually bright, and those that are not, which it renders colored—and thus it acts upon and does many things. Our intellect, insofar as it is a nature of the soul, is called individual; however, insofar as it emits the actions of understanding, it is noted as **universal** in its power. And in this way, universals are within it, because it is as capable of abstracting and stripping forms as corporeal light is of colors. Therefore, although the intellect is individual insofar as it is the "form" of a human being, nevertheless, according to its power—insofar as it is the power of a **spiritual, universal light**—it is universal. For universals are in the intellect just as form is in matter, or an accident in a subject. For "being in the soul" is more the **intention** <note>A mental representation or concept of a thing.</note> of the thing than the thing itself; and therefore, just as a thing is not individualized physically by the existence it has in corporeal light, nor is it "specified" by the fact that being in light happens to every color insofar as it is an "actual" color, so also the intention of a thing is not specified or individualized by the fact that it is in the incorporeal light.

<summary>This page defends medicine's status as a rigorous science by explaining that while doctors treat individual patients, the science itself is based on universal principles abstracted from matter. It uses the analogy of light and the sun to explain how the human intellect can hold universal truths despite being a single, individual entity.</summary>

It must be said that those who wrongly propose the **unity of the intellect** <note>A reference to the "Monopsychism" associated with Averroes, which argued that all humans share a single, communal intellect. <margin>To the 9th</margin>
To the other [objection], it must be said that **definition** is twofold. One is truly a definition, which belongs only to **substance**. For just as substance alone truly has a "whatness" <term>quiddity<note>The essence of an object; that which makes a thing what it is.</note></term> according to the *seventh book of the Metaphysics*, so too does it have a definition; and this is properly called a **substantial definition**. There is also another, taken improperly, also called a description or notification, which is also twofold. One of these is composed of **accidental properties** <note>Characteristics that are not essential to a thing's nature, such as its color or size.</note> which inseparably accompany the assigned proper genus. The other is not from substantial differences <term>per se<note>original: "per se" — by itself or inherently.</note></term>, but from a gathering of its closest genus, as in **Boethius's** *Topics, book II*. The first will indeed be a definition according to accidents. For just as accidents do not properly have a "whatness," but rather receive it through an addition, since they include the subject in their definition—as "health is the hollow of the nose" <note>This is a variation of a classic Aristotelian example: one cannot define "snubness" without mentioning a "nose." Here, the author applies the logic to "health" being defined by the body it inhabits.</note>—in this way, it properly has a definition. However, this definition can be called **essential**, but not **substantial**, since the latter belongs to substance alone. The second improper definition or notification belongs to substance, which we often use for lack of a substantial one, as appears in the *seventh book of the Metaphysics*. Thus, it must be said that a proper substantial definition does not consist of accidents, but an essential and improper one can.

Furthermore, because accidental things are divided *per se* against "always" or "frequently," no demonstration is made [of them] since they are casual and fortuitous, or even against what is *per se*. However, insofar as they are separated from their substance, as in the sign of mathematics, a demonstration exists.

<margin>To the 6th</margin>
To the other, it must be said that that which in no way participates in unity does not exist. However, all things of medicine are one by a certain unity, such as the unity of **analogy and attribution**. And thus there can be one knowledge of them, which is known by experience and by reason of substance and accident, of the corruptible and the incorruptible.

<margin>To the 8th</margin>
To the other, it has already been said what must be said. To the other, it must be said that the end of medical science is not a partial work or this or that specific health, but **common health**. For it introduces actual health through its virtue. Just as it will be said of the difference of quantity, when one descends into work, so that by health itself, which is a form of the soul, health is introduced as a habit of the body.

# FOURTH DISTINCTION.

<margin>First point</margin>
To the first, it is said that although medicine is shown to be **theoretical**, it is actually **practical**. Since it was said in the preceding distinction that medicine is the "addition of those things that are lacking and the subtraction of those things that are superabundant." And that it is an operative art discovered by experience and reason. That which is such is clearly practical.

<margin>Second point</margin>
Furthermore: it is just for each thing to receive its name from its **end** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "end" (telos) is the purpose or goal of a thing.</note>, as in the *second book of On the Soul*. But the end of theoretical science is **truth**; of practical science, however, it is the **work**, as in the *second book of the Ethics*. The end of medicine is not truth but operation. For the business is not that we may know, but that we may become healthy. For this is the end of medicine, as in the first distinction.

<margin>Third point</margin>
<margin>Now the physicians speak truly and commonly</margin>
<margin>Opposition?</margin>
<margin>Theoretical comes before science</margin>
<margin>Whether it be a part before [something else]</margin>
Again, in the beginning of the *Metaphysics*, **theoretical sciences** are those in which one seeks to perfect the speculative virtue of the soul through the acquisition of the intellect in effect—namely, through the attainment of imagined and believed science concerning things that are not our works or our disposition. For in these, there is the certainty of science and opinion. Hence, in Logic, its end is the perfection of the speculative part, which is nothing but the perfection of the soul so that it may simply know. Therefore, its end is the knowledge of a judgment which is not a work. There are, however, three essential modes of this perfection: **natural, mathematical, and divine**. Medicine, however, is none of these, since its end is the possession of health itself. On account of which medicine will not be speculative, but rather factive or practical.

On the contrary, that it is **theoretical**: That science is theoretical in which the speculative intellect is perfected by itself. Medicine is of this kind, since it has principles and first causes in which the contemplative intellect is perfected—such as the elements and conclusions, among others. And that science is not practical which teaches the mode and quality of operating before it falls into work; and medicine is of this kind, primarily.

Again, **Aristotle** in the beginning of the *Metaphysics*: practical sciences are those in which one seeks to perfect the speculative virtue of the soul through the attainment of imagined and believed science about things that are our works, so that the perfection of the practical virtue in morals may follow secondarily. Hence here in Logic, the end of the practical is the perfection of the soul, not just so it knows, but so it knows what it ought to do and does it. Thus the end of the practical is the knowledge of a judgment that is in the work itself. But medicine is not about things that are our work, but rather nature's, since its subject is the human body, as in the sixth distinction. Hence it does not treat morals unless perhaps natural ones, concerning which it is not moral but rather natural. Wherefore it is inferred that medicine is not practical. Almost everyone feels this is characteristic, placing something theoretical in medicine and something practical.

Furthermore, just as it is in the liberal arts and philosophy, so it is in medicine; since in both is found what belongs to science. But in the arts something theoretical is found, as in grammar: the first knowledge of elements, of syllables, then of words and sentences, and finally the practical joining of one with another. In logic, as in propositions and syllogisms...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into whether medicine should be classified as a theoretical science or a practical art. It follows the previous discussion on definitions, moving now into how medicine is divided and where it sits among the "Mechanical Arts" versus the "Liberal Sciences."</meta>

Theoretical knowledge stands on its own. However, joining these parts into one and syllogizing <note>To "syllogize" here means to apply logical reasoning to reach a specific conclusion.</note> creates a practical act. In simple philosophy, there are three essential modes that are theoretical. Moral philosophy, however, is entirely practical. Generally, the principles possess more of a theoretical character, while the more ultimate conclusions are practical. It will be the same in **medicine**, for in it, one part will be theoretical and another practical.

<margin>The first point</margin>
Regarding the first point, one must know what medicine is, as shown by the prior authorities, and what is theoretical and practical from the arguments. This definition of medicine is attributed more broadly than others, since it appears more evidently in medicine what is theoretical and practical than in other fields. This is a division of parts from a genus into species, or of an integral whole into its parts, such as is found in the definition of the soul in the book *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle’s *De Anima*.</note>. For one part of it is <term>vegetable</term> <note>The basic life force of growth and nutrition.</note>, another <term>sensible</term> <note>The capacity for perception and movement.</note>, and another <term>rational</term>. Inasmuch as medicine is predicated on the theoretical and practical, it takes on the nature of a division of a genus into species, and is separated from that which divides an integral whole into its parts. However, insofar as the whole nature of medicine is not preserved in both the theoretical and practical (as a genus is preserved in each of its species), it differs from the division of a universal whole and connects to the division of a quantitative whole into its parts.

<margin>The second point</margin>
Regarding the second point, it should be known that **Isidore** in the *Etymologies* and **Hugh** in the *Didascalicon* <note>Hugh of Saint Victor (c. 1096–1141), a leading scholar of the medieval period.</note> do not distinguish medicine into theoretical and practical. Instead, they place it absolutely as a whole within the **practical**, locating it among the seven <term>mechanical arts</term> <note>The "Artes Mechanicae" were the manual counterparts to the seven Liberal Arts; they were often seen as "lower" because they involved physical labor.</note>, which are: **weaving, armaments, navigation, agriculture, hunting, theater**, and **medicine**. However, these last three are not as "mechanical" as the others, since they obtain their principle from the intellect, specifically regarding the natural and vegetable soul. These authors seem to have looked only at the surface, considering that a movement takes its mode and species from the end toward which it tends, and that it is just for everything to be named by its purpose. Since they wanted the end of medicine to be the "work" alone (as perhaps perceived in experimental medicine or the practices of old women), they categorized it thus. Also in **Averroes**, in the seventh book of the *Colliget*, medicine is situated among the mechanical arts, because the practitioner often pursues the end in the things themselves, and is sometimes deprived of that end, just as in other mechanical arts. For this reason, I said in the *Arzusa* <note>Likely referring to the *Articella*, a standard collection of medical texts, or a specific commentary.</note> that medicine is a mechanical art, and many marveled at this; but they were ignorant of what was said in the second book of the *Physics* regarding mechanical arts: that here, just as before, medicine seems to be heard only as the crisis and the movement of bodily actions.

<margin>Whether it is science and what the work is</margin>
**Avicenna** also, like others, strives to show—against some like **Haly**—that medicine is divided into theoretical and practical, and that both are **science** <note>Knowledge</note> rather than practical action. For "science" is defined in opposition to "work," because science is something universal conceived in the intellect, while work is something particular situated in motion and change. He asserts that the theoretical is for knowing principles; hence he calls the theoretical part "scientific," which, when we have learned it, gives us knowledge only, so that we do not involve ourselves in the quality of operation. The practical, however, is for knowing the *quality* of operating. This is therefore called "operative science," for it teaches the mode and quality of operating without us being moved or laboring physically. Thus, it would be a particular thing and not a science, since acts and generations concern singular things, as stated in the beginning of the *Metaphysics* and the eighth book of the *Ethics*. **Ptolemy** alludes to this in the beginning of the *Almagest*, saying it was good for the wise who did not deviate that they divided the part of speculation from the part of operation; these are the two parts of wisdom. He therefore calls both "wisdom" and, even more so, "science." **Haly Rodoham**, in the fourth and first parts of his commentary, says that <term>ministries</term> <note>original: "ministeria"; here meaning professional occupations or services.</note> have two parts, one of which is theoretical and the other practical, such as medicine, judicial astronomy, and agriculture; for the wise work through wisdom, not through the things that laborers know by experience.

<margin>
-- Ptolemy: in four [parts] --
These are the ministries in which men may remain:
1. The first is called theoretical; 
2. The second is practical, and it is admonitory;
3. The third is that which completes the works of nature, such as medicine and agriculture;
4. The fourth is directing and fitting, such as carpentry, military service, and the like.
</margin>
And know, according to **Ptolemy** in that same place, that ministries are of four types. The first is **theoretical**, which is to know only, and this is philosophy. The second is **practical**, and this is that through which the habits of the soul are known, and how one ought to direct and govern cities and maintain a household. The third is that which **completes the works of nature**, such as medicine and agriculture. The fourth is **directing and fitting**, such as carpentry, military service, and the like, and universally everything ordained to the office of a king. For one is ordained toward another, as the making of bridles is for the equestrian art, and so on. And therefore, since **Haly** placed it as action, it would not be science.

<margin>
Haly.
Medicine is divided into: science and action.
What science is.
What action is.
</margin>
For he says that medicine is divided into two parts, one of which is **science** and the other **action**. Science, therefore, is the knowledge of the truth of the intention that is proposed, and it is placed in thought, through which there is discernment and management of those things for which we want action. But action is the bringing forth of that thing which was placed in thought into the open view of the senses and the operation of the hands, according as discernment commands. According to him, therefore, the theoretical will be science and a kind of speculation, but the practical will be more like a mechanical art.

<margin>
According to Averroes, medicine is divided into: theoretical and practical.
</margin>
**Averroes** also concludes and coincides with the opinion of **Haly**, not making medicine entirely mechanical as in the seventh book. For he says that of this art, something is **speculative**, and that is its natural science; and something is **practicable**, and the practical part is the art of **anatomy**.

<margin>Theory properly</margin>
But the theoretical is mostly accepted as concerning the causes of health and sickness, and especially from very remote causes, such as the **elements** and similar things. Regarding the third point, it should be known that "theoretical" and "practical" are spoken of in two ways: by reason of the **thing** and by reason of the **intellect** or mode.

<margin>Theoretical on the part of the thing: what it is</margin>
It is theoretical on the part of the **thing** when the thing itself is produced by the work of nature and not by us, so that it is first and superior in being and in knowledge. Such are those things of which the three essential modes of philosophy mentioned before exist.

<margin>Theoretical on the part of the intellect</margin>
By reason of the **intellect**, because the intellect can make a thing speculative however much it can—that is, it strives insofar as it is capable of perceiving it, appearing first from the parts of the science of universals, however much they concern animals. Whence, in the third book of *On the Soul*, the speculative intellect, when it has speculated on something actual or doable, commands nothing...

It highlights the consensus among authorities like Avicenna and Haly that even the practical side of medicine is a form of scientific knowledge (knowing *how* to act) rather than just manual labor.</summary>
