<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on whether medicine is primarily a theoretical or practical science. It builds on the previous page's distinction between the "parts" of medicine by citing various philosophical authorities to define the relationship between the intellect's understanding and physical action.</meta>

...either to pursue or to flee. For often it <note>The "it" refers to the intellect.</note> understands something terrible or delightful, yet it does not command one to fear or be delighted. In this way, the speculative <term>intellect</term> <note>The part of the mind focused on understanding truth for its own sake.</note> can contemplate something practical within itself, and it remains speculative so long as it does not cross over into the act of pursuing or fleeing. And rightly so, for according to **Boethius**, the intellect is of greater power than nature; for it can separate things that are joined and join things that are separate, as with the "prior difference" according to **Averroes**. Thus, the entire science of medicine will be speculative; indeed, even agriculture—according to the aforementioned **Haly**, and as handed down by **Virgil** and **Palladius**—and every art called "mechanical" <note>The "Mechanical Arts" were practical crafts like weaving, smithing, or agriculture, often contrasted with the "Liberal Arts."</note> would be as well. A thing is "practical" on the part of the object when its very nature inclines it toward work or business. The "Ethical" exists so that we may be made good by operating according to virtue, as in *Ethics II* <note>Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics.</note>. The "Medicinal," however, is so that we may finally enjoy health. We seek its <term>praxis</term> <note>Action or practice, as opposed to theory.</note> so that we may preserve health and remove sickness. Hence, in the introduction to *On the Soul*:

<margin>What a practical thing is on the part of the object</margin>
The **Physicist** <note>In the medieval sense, a "Physicus" was a student of nature or a natural philosopher.</note> exists regarding the passions of matter which are not separable; but regarding these, another craftsman—such as a teacher or a physician—does not inquire into them insofar as they are such. And the **Commentator** <note>Commonly referring to Averroes, the primary commentator on Aristotle.</note> says that from these forms and passions, it is to be considered by mechanical craftsmen, like the carpenter and the physician, not through nature but through the will. <margin>What a practical thing is on the part of the intellect.</margin> Indeed, it is "practical" on the part of the intellect when the intellect itself ordains what is to be chosen or fled in an act; just as when a physician chooses a medicine to flee sickness and induce health. However, actual practice is not of the intellect—since even the practical intellect deals with universals—but of the senses, which exist according to the act of particulars. This is in *On the Soul II*, where <term>experience</term> <note>Original: "empeiria".</note> is owed to the senses just as reason is to the intellect. And therefore, according to **Aristotle**, when someone has both theoretical and practical knowledge, they will have attained both the scientific and operative power, even if they have never actually operated; for "practical" is not the action itself, but the teaching of the mode and quality of operating. **Boethius** testifies to this by a similar example regarding music in his first book:
> **He is a musician who, having weighed the reason, takes up the science of singing not by the service of labor, but by the command of speculation.**
And perhaps this is what **Avicenna** wanted to introduce in the *Colliget* <note>Actually a work by Averroes; the author may be conflating or comparing texts.</note>, so that in the first section he says this art was among the mechanical arts in its power. This is indicated by *Problem 30*, for its power teaches the mode and order of operating. For anyone having this power in their soul can actually act by preserving and curing. Truly, from the ninth book of the *Metaphysics*, it is argued thus: **Aristotle** says it seems impossible for there to be a builder who has built nothing, or a zither-player <note>Original: "citharedum".</note> who has never played the zither; for one learning to play the zither learns to play the zither *while playing*. Therefore, according to the second book of the *Method* <note>Likely Galen’s *Method of Medicine*.</note>, those who learn cannot perform perfectly because of the interior soul's knowledge, unless they are exercised in various ways according to those rules. Hence, although all science is in the soul by the power of the intellect originated from things, nevertheless a fuller perfection is received through its operation—finally, from the application of the habit itself to the things from which it drew its origin. Playing the zither remains more in practice than medicine.

---

<margin>The office of the physician is seen through the "canons," according to Alfarabi in "On the Rise of the Sciences."</margin>
Similarly, **Galen** did not deny science, but rather its perfection, which tends toward its ultimate end and common intent. For perfection is twofold: regarding "being" and "well-being." Whence **Alfarabi**, in *On the Rise of the Sciences*, says:
> A physician is not made perfect as a healer except through two virtues: one of which is the "supervised virtue" and the **canon** <note>The "canon" refers to the established rules or textbooks of medicine.</note> which is acquired from the books of medicine; and the other is the virtue which comes through the length of frequent medical actions upon the sick, and study of them through the length of experiment and observation of individual bodies. And through this virtue, the physician can measure medicines and the cure according to each body in every disposition.
From these things, therefore, it appears what **Aristotle** and **Haly** felt: that both parts of medicine exist as theoretical and practical science. **Haly Abbas**, however, considered the theoretical to be the only science, and the practical to be more of an action. **Averroes**, too, as seen, ascribes it more to practice than theory, since he even says it is an "operative" or "working" art; yet he judged it more sweetly as being rational. **Aristotle** posits that each part of medicine has the nature of science in its own way. Regarding the fourth point <note>Referring back to a previous list of arguments.</note> in relation to the first, it must be said that "addition and subtraction" and the "operative art" do not denote motion and act in this context, but rather the **mode** and **quality** of the thing; <margin>Points regarding the 1st argument</margin> otherwise it would not be a most excellent art, as the following difference will declare. Regarding the second point, <margin>To the 2nd</margin> it must be said that the end of theory is truth and nothing else; but for the practical, there is an inclination toward work along with this, since the mode and quality of acting is declared in it, which happens to manifest that business. Regarding the third point, <margin>To the 3rd</margin> it must be said that medicine is one of those things that is reduced to science. For in the third difference <note>A previous section of the text.</note> it follows that if its final goal is to achieve health through work, it is nevertheless a science since it requires physical action or labor to express the quality and mode of operation; and properly, the intent of the one working here is finished regarding that. Simply put, although they are driven to the opposite by the arguments brought forward, it has been shown that the first part of medicine is simply theoretical, and the rest is as declared: even if it is called "practical," it nevertheless observes a certain speculative mode, so that the whole of it can be called speculative.

### DIFFERENCE V.

¶ That medicine is not the most excellent of arts is shown here. From the things shown above, it exists as practice alone, according to the preceding difference.
Furthermore, concerning that which is vain and reduced to the art of divination, it is not the most distinguished of arts, since that denotes uselessness and imperfection; and medicine is of this sort. Whence **Hippocrates** <note>Original: "Y.", a common abbreviation for Ypocras/Hippocrates.</note> in *The Law* says: "The matters of medicine are vain," and at the beginning of the *Aphorisms*: "The art of medicine is reduced to the vanity of divination." Again, that which is servile or ordained toward another thing is not the most excellent; medicine is such a thing. For it serves the "goods of fortune," since those are mostly acquired by it; and it is ordained toward nature, for according to the third difference, it is subordinated to nature. Furthermore, the knowledge of "intelligibles" belongs to separate substances... <note>The text cuts off here, likely discussing the hierarchy of sciences where metaphysics/theology is higher because it deals with non-physical entities.</note>

And the soul is more excellent than those things which belong to the soul, just as the body is more noble than its parts. Among such things is the science of **medicine**, since it concerns the human body as its <term>subject</term> <note>The "subject" of a science is the specific thing it studies—in this case, the healable human body.</note> which can be restored to health. This is seen in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, section ten, where it is taught that the tradition of the soul is the most noble of intelligible things. This is sufficient because all sciences are ultimately reduced to the first <term>Metaphysics</term> <note>The branch of philosophy dealing with the first principles of things, including abstract concepts like being and knowing.</note>, which is called the first distinction. Likewise, if medicine were the most excellent science, that quality would belong to it alone, since "most excellent" is said by way of surplus and can only apply to one thing, as noted in the second book of the *Topics*. But many other sciences are more excellent than medicine, according to **Aristotle** and the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> at the beginning of *On the Soul*; for this reason, medicine is not the most excellent of the arts.

On the contrary: **Hippocrates**, beginning his book *The Law*, says that medicine is the most illustrious of all the arts. Furthermore, that science is the most excellent which protects and distinguishes that which is naturally desired above all else; this is medicine, which stands over the human body so that life may be preserved and maintained unharmed. For every animal strives to protect its health and avoids death and destruction, as stated in the prologue. Thus, in the third distinction of the first part, it is said that it provides us with security regarding two things: namely, the total prohibition of putrefaction and the defense of moisture so that it is not quickly dissolved, and it also preserves us for use without harm. Thus, medicine shall be the most illustrious of the arts.

Regarding the first point, one must know what medicine is and what an art is, and how it may be called a science or an art, as was seen in the third distinction. That is called "most illustrious" which excels the rest in nobility and priority, so that it is to be desired above all. Regarding the second point, one must know that some have looked unfavorably upon this principal science, just as other sciences are disparaged by the aforementioned critics; for any science is exposed to as many enemies as there are people who disparage it, for "nothing is loved unless it is known." Some committed this because they were inexperienced in the senses and clouded in their intellect, unable to reach the things medicine promises. For it teaches one to know not only the exterior dispositions of the body but also the interior ones; and they think it knows not only the present but even the future. To think that what happens to others happens to oneself is no small ridicule. For if the eye of a <term>vicar</term> <note>Likely referring to a substitute or a person with impaired vision here.</note> is unable to gaze upon the light of the sun, it does not mean other animals cannot; their defect is evident when they disparage themselves and not the art itself, as in the third distinction.

Indeed, some thought the art was vain because, considering those who claimed to be practitioners of this art, they found them wandering far from the path of truth. Wherefore **Hippocrates**, saying medicine is the most excellent of arts, added: "on account of the ignorance of those who use it," both in terms of those who practice it and those who judge it in theory. Such vanity and defect exist in medicine more than in all other arts. Hence, in the first book of the *Regimen*, asking how it has now been reduced to this—namely, the experience of doctors in name and justice alone—it seems to be most clearly shown to the common people that the art of medicine is not considered whole. Since what appears beneficial to one sick person appears harmful to another, the art of medicine has been reduced to the vanity of divination. If indeed this person does not favor this art,

---

or this illustrious science, it is because he is an <term>idiot</term> <note>In the medieval sense: an unlearned or unskilled person, rather than a modern insult.</note> who professes himself to be a "pseudo-artisan" of it; and the common people especially are ignorant of how to discern the expert from the unskilled. For one who is devoid of all medical science is judged by them to be most expert. For if someone distinguishes a <term>pestilential syrup</term> <note>A medicinal syrup used during plagues or for "pestilential" fevers.</note> or honey-water, he is considered a doctor by the common people. This was touched upon in the third distinction. And from this, the science of the stars <note>Astrology/Astronomy, which were closely linked to medicine in this period.</note> suffers no small amount, since today very few experts are found in it; for anyone looking into the heavens and noting Saturn or Jupiter is reputed an astrologer by the ignorant commoners.

Regarding the third point, it must first be known that medicine is now among the most noble of the arts. And finally, it was even more so in the past. Regarding this, one must know that its nobility is shown both from the part of that which principally exists within it and from that which is secondary. First, this is argued in a threefold way: by reason of the subject, the mode of proceeding, and the effect of the principle and the end. Since one science is more noble than another by its subject and its mode of proceeding—as in the beginning of *On the Soul*—for this reason, and especially for the sake of the subject, the science of medicine shall be ennobled; for the human body stands as the thing most greatly desired by reason of its <term>disposition</term> <note>The physical makeup or arrangement of the body's qualities.</note>. This is worthier than all other things here, since man is the highest in body and most noble in virtue.

He is highest in body by reason of the mixing or "nexus" of the elements within him, because they are more subtly woven together, and in him, they seek the equality of weight more diligently. The sign of this is the uprightness of the body. According to that passage on transformation in book five of *The Consolation of Philosophy*:
<note>original: "Pronaque cum spectent animalia cetera terram..." This is a famous quote from Ovid's Metamorphoses, though here attributed to or filtered through Boethius.</note>
"While other animals look down toward the earth, He gave to man a sublime face and commanded him to see the heavens and lift his upright countenance to the stars."
For in him, the direction of the senses is simply "upward" or in a living state, which is not found in other animals except in a relative sense, as in distinction forty. This is also due to the similarity of his <term>complexion</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) and qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry).</note>, because nature gave to man a complexion more capable of endurance than any other that could be found in this world, with an equidistance of those powers by which he acts and suffers. Wherefore **Alexander the Physician**, in the book *On Phlegm* translated by me, says the human body has a nature existing in a tempered complexion more than all other animals. And in the first book of the *Theory*, man is made of a more temperate complexion than the complexions of all other animals.

Furthermore, this is shown from the part of his members; for when these are known, the parts of all other animals are most easily known. As appears in the first book of the *Histories* <note>Aristotle’s History of Animals.</note>: just as knowledge is gained from fragments of gold, so the parts of man are like gold proven in the furnace compared to those of the beasts. He also exists as most noble in virtue: namely, that which is intended by nature as the ultimate completion in the order of individual forms. For nature, having progressed this far, ceased, as if having nothing more honorable to provide as a subject for it. **Alexander the Peripatetic** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a Greek commentator on Aristotle.</note> seeks this in the second book of *On the Soul*. Man is the completion of animals and their end.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic defense of medicine's status. ...intended in generation; that which nature could reach, it attained. Man is an animal possessing a speculative and cogitative or intelligible power; in this part alone is man unique, for he perceives the "marrow" or kernel of the fruit. For this power, granted to him from without, investigates the causes and essence of things. Whence **Aristotle** in **On Sense and the Sensible** <note>original: "Au. de sensu & sensato"</note> says: man understands the differences of things and their proper "intentions" <note>In medieval philosophy, an "intention" refers to the mental representation of a thing.</note> which exist in the sensed object, like the marrow within the fruit. Other animals, however, are as if at the exterior rinds of the fruit. A sign of this is that animals are moved by sensible things only insofar as they imply the need for nourishment. For man alone is stirred by song, by geometric shapes, and by colors. And **Aristotle** says in the same place: Only man, it is said, perceives and rejoices in the odors of flowers and other things. And in the **Ethics, Book III**: In other animals there is no delight according to the senses except by accident; nor do dogs rejoice in the scent of hares but in the eating, though the scent alerts the sense. Nor does the lion rejoice in the voice of the ox, but in the eating of it. 

And if the physician does not consider the soul directly, but rather according to its subject <note>The body is considered the "subject" or container that the soul inhabits.</note>, he nevertheless contemplates the soul from the present. As stated in the third distinction: the care of the body is said to precede that of the soul. It also makes medicine not a little clear and decorous because of its method of proceeding, since it is handed down in a most orderly fashion through the standard teachings named in the eighth distinction. It is subordinated to natural science. I know that it takes its mode of demonstration from that which has certain demonstrations... whence the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher.</note> in the **second book of the Metaphysics**: mathematical demonstrations are in the first order of certainty, and natural demonstrations follow them. 

**Medicine** indeed is a certain particular science of nature. Indeed, philosophy and medicine are sisters, according to the **Commentator in the Sects**. Again, its knowledge is great since it concerns the body known to us and things close to it, so that it compensates for something—not only in natural philosophy but even in that which appears first in the parts of divine philosophies. 

By reason of the efficient principle <note>The "efficient principle" is the primary agent that causes something to exist.</note>, since the first to find, teach, and use it was **Asclepius** or **Aesculapius**, who because of the loftiness of his science was received into the number of the gods, as mentioned in the first distinction. Finally, the divine **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Y." or "Ypocras"</note> perfected it and brought it to light, of whom **Aristotle** says in certain problems ascribed to him: God, pitying the human race dissolved by various diseases, incarnating nature, produced **Hippocrates** as one never erring in the perfect tradition of medicine. This is even supported by the <term>Pyrrhonists</term> <note>The Pyrrhonists were ancient skeptics who doubted all certain knowledge.</note>, that is, the "provers," from whom comes a certain Greek book of theirs attacking all science except medicine. To which the aforementioned problems perhaps allude when they say the medical art is not in the life-giving and in honor just like other arts. 

Also from the part of the "end" <note>The "end" is the ultimate goal or purpose of a discipline.</note>, which is health (**Ethics, Book I**), and its possession. This is worthy and most sought-after, so that according to **Ethics, Book I**, one lacking it will desire health above all else; for without it, one cannot exercise human acts. 

From the part of its secondary effects, medicine confers praise and the acquisition of friends. According to the rhetoric of **Hippocrates**—not indeed his own words, but as the translation signifies: Everyone who desires by the study of the medical art to achieve glory or a delightful abundance of friends, attains a wealth of things. And similarly in **Ethics, Book X**, it brings no small common affection. Whence **Ecclesiasticus 38**: honor the physician because of necessity, for the Most High created him. It also confers the acquisition of good fortune. Wherefore the **Commentator on the Sects** says: the art of medicine was found to be a certain good of riches and opportune for our life, through which great utility of goods is added to men. Whence **Mesue** <note>A 9th-century Persian physician.</note> says: the distinguished gifts of the physician are sought after. Similarly, a famous name is better than all riches, according to **Ecclesiasticus 7**: A good name is better than precious ointments. 

Many of these things are touched upon in the first book of the Theory [of Medicine]: the science of the **medical** art is among the more excellent arts, greater in utility than the others, and of greater danger; for it is necessary to all men. Because of this, it must be known that in ancient times, when the most noble speculative sciences were not yet found, this art was already most illustrious. For the others were found later; for many arts were discovered later, some for the necessities of life, others for introduction to the *Metaphysics*. 

The principles of the speculative sciences and many of their findings were discovered by **Hippocrates**. Whence in the first book of **On the Elements**: **Hippocrates** seems to be the first of all to find the elements of the arts and of human nature, and the first to demonstrate them sufficiently. And in the first book of the *Natural [Questions]*: he was the first of all physicians and philosophers we know to have attempted to demonstrate, just as he was the first knowing most certainly the works of nature. And in the second book of the same: **Hippocrates** was the first of all we know who spoke correctly. **Aristotle** indeed was the second to explain in Greek, and deservedly so, because he found and completed three arts: logic, natural philosophy, and metaphysics. 

The **Commentator** in the *Accessus of Philosophers* says: that **Hippocrates** knew the aforesaid things is shown by his discourse on human nature, similar to which **Aristotle** wrote on generation and corruption. <margin>Asclepiades</margin> **Asclepiades** indeed, with other physicians, wrote on the elements. 

That medicine was the most excellent science in ancient times is suggested by **Aristotle** in the sixth book of the **Metaphysics**, where he argues that if there were no other substance besides those consisting in nature, physics would be the first of the sciences. But if there is an immobile substance, this is prior, and "first philosophy" <note>Metaphysics.</note> is thus universal. Whence, since the earlier philosophers were unable to distinguish sense from intellect, they did not posit any entities except bodies, as seen in the first and fourth books of the *Metaphysics* and the third book of *On the Soul*; they were forced to declare natural philosophy the first of all. Therefore, since medicine was found earlier—as touched upon—being more necessary than the others, it was prior and most illustrious. 

Regarding the fourth point: From the first part, it appeared what should be said from the things distinguished in the first section. To the other point, it should be said that it does not strike a blow against the science...

but to those ignorant craftsmen and the unlearned common folk, it seems they cannot discern the expert from the unskilled. 
To the other point it must be said: that medicine is not currently as great as natural philosophy <note>The study of nature and the physical universe.</note> in excellence, since the latter is perfectly handed down and explained with a higher end; however, anciently it stood in a different relation to the sciences. ### DIFFERENCE VI.

<margin>1</margin>
It is demonstrated that the human body is the subject <term>subject (subiectum)|The underlying matter or central theme that a specific science studies and explains.</term> of medicine, because a science belongs to one genus of subject. This is a distinction: but of those things which are considered by the physician, many are different even in genus, as the same touch shows. This is confirmed because "natural things," "non-natural things," and even things "against nature" <note>This is the classic Galenic division: natural things (elements, humors), non-naturals (lifestyle factors like diet and sleep), and things against nature (diseases).</note> are numbered in the first part of the *First Canon* <note>Avicenna’s *Canon of Medicine*, Book 1, Fen 1.</note> of medicine. Furthermore, the subject in a science is that which is determined within it, because the subject and the science are convertible. But many things are treated in medicine, as is apparent, which are not the human body. 
Furthermore, since the "passions" <note>In this context, "passions" refers to the properties or attributes that belong to a subject.</note> are demonstrated concerning the subject through its definition as if through a middle term, as was said before. And the subject must be intelligible, universal, and incorruptible, since it is the object of the intellect according to the book *On the Soul*; however, the human body is not such a thing, since it is sensible <note>Capable of being perceived by the senses.</note> and its consideration is through the senses. Because, <margin>Ardy <note>Likely Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a famous medieval physician and commentator.</note></margin> as appears from the *Tegni* and Haly <note>Galen's *Ars Medica* (Tegni) and the commentator Haly Abbas.</note> expressing it, medical speculation does not transcend the senses. From these points, it is concluded that the human body is not the subject of medicine. 

The opposite of this, however, is testified by many illustrious physicians. Furthermore, the subject in a science is that to which all things determined within it are attributed. But all things determined in medicine are attributed to the human body, and they are defined only by their action upon it. Therefore, it will be the subject of medicine. 
Regarding this inquiry, because of the points touched upon in the arguments, we must pass through them briefly. Regarding the first of these, it must be known that the "subject" in a science is that which the intellect contemplates in it, which is properly called the "object." For a science relates to its subject just as a power relates to its object. 
Truly, the human body is the most noble of all mixed bodies <note>In medieval science, "mixed bodies" are those composed of the four elements (earth, water, air, fire).</note> and the bond of the universe <note>The human body as a "microcosm" that links the physical and spiritual realms.</note>. Just as purified gold relates to other metals, so this body relates to other corruptible bodies in the prior distinction. 

Regarding the second point, it must be known that Galen in the first of the *Aphorisms* and Haly Abbas at the beginning of his book wish for the subject of medicine to be the human body. However, this stated simply is not direct. Since the subject of moral science, or politics, or physiognomy is also the human body; whence, for a brief and healthy understanding of those authors, one must add something, such as (as already touched upon) "this passion: healable." For every subject ought to have its own properties and determined parts. 
Some, however, propose that the subjects of the books are the medical canons handed down with aphoristic brevity, or divisions, or definitions and such. This is said without art, since they say confusedly that the whole science is the subject of the whole, not discerning the subject from its passions, properties, and parts, signifying almost nothing of reason. 

A manifold subject is also distinguished here, which they take from the "Conciliators" <note>The *Conciliator* is the title of Pietro d'Abano's most famous work, which sought to reconcile the "discords" between medicine and philosophy.</note>. Aristotle and Avicenna, in their discord in the *Metaphysics*, propose a triple subject. One indeed by "predication," and thus in metaphysics the subject is *Being*. Another by "radication" and a certain sustenance, and thus it is *Substance*; for in it are founded all things which are determined in it. Another by way of the "end" <note>The final cause or goal.</note>, and thus God is said to be its subject; for all existence ends in God. 
And so in medicine they say there is a triple subject: 
1. The "medical thing" by way of predication; for everything determined in medicine is a medical thing. 
2. By way of the end: the possession of health. 
3. The human body, they testify, is the subject by way of radication and foundation. 

But this distinction, while it does not certify the inquiry itself, also does not remove many errors that lead to indeterminate conclusions. They say that in metaphysics the subject is triple either because it is common (as *Being*), or certain (as *Causes*), or most worthy (as *God*). These types of distinctions are logical and should be abhorred in the "real sciences" <note>Sciences dealing with physical reality rather than abstract logic.</note>, as they lead to many indeterminate errors, though accepted by many of us out of habit, thinking every distinction is a solution. 

Regarding the third point, it must be known that the subject of medicine is the **healable human body**, just as it is said that the subject of natural philosophy is "mobile being" or the "mobile body." This is sufficiently indicated in the first of the *First Canon* when it says: "Since medicine considers the human body from the part where it is healed and removed from health." For since the physician considers the human body affected by these two dispositions—health and sickness—they are sufficiently included in this property, namely "healable." For this can denote its receptive aptitude once sickness is removed. I say "healable," not "healed," since the latter is the end and the form. The former is the matter, and these never coincide, as per *Physics, Book 2*. That this is the subject...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the "subject" of medicine. In the previous section, the author established medicine's nobility based on its end (health). Now, the text moves to a technical definition of what constitutes the "subject" (the primary focus) of a science and specifically argues that the human body is the subject of medicine.</meta>

is shown. First, however, it should be known that "subject" is spoken of in two ways. In one way, it refers to a being in actuality <note>Latin: *entis actu*; a thing that already exists in its own right.</note> that is yet in potential <note>Latin: *in potentia*; having the capacity to become or receive something else.</note> for something else that is seen to come from it. For example, a human being existing in actuality is in potential to be the subject of some accidental property; however, this is not the sense of "subject" used here. 

In another way, "subject" is used in a science, for which four things are seen to be required:
1. First, that it be better known, occurring first to the intellect among all things considered in that science.
2. Second, that from the knowledge of the subject itself, one proceeds to the knowledge of all other things in that science.
3. Third, that "affections" <note>Technical term for the qualities or attributes that can be proven to belong to a subject.</note> and properties are proven of it in that science.
4. Fourth, that all things determined within that science have an attribution to it.

The first point is shown because a science is compared to its subject as a power is to its object. Second, as is apparent in *The Soul* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *De Anima*.</note>: just as the object determines the power—and the nobility of the power comes from the nobility of the object—so the subject determines the science, and the nobility of the science comes from the nobility of the subject. For one science is nobler than another because it concerns a nobler subject. But among all things first apprehended by any power, that which is the primary object of that power is apprehended first. For example, since color is the primary object of the power of sight, that which is first apprehended by sight is color (or the colored thing). Therefore, among all things known in a science, the subject is known first. 

From this follows the second point: that from the knowledge of the subject, one must proceed to the knowledge of other things in that science, since one must proceed from the knowledge of the better known to the knowledge of others. Since the subject is of this kind, one must proceed from it.

The third point is also declared, because the subject in a science must be that of which the "affections" are demonstrated. For through those things that are determined, we only know of the subject *that* it is and *what* it is called by name; for it is assumed to be the foundation of subsequent things. But *what kind* of thing it is, we know through its own proper affections; therefore, affections and properties are demonstrated of the subject in that science.

The fourth point also seems manifest from the meaning of the name: for "subject" seems to imply a foundation or support from which other things determined in the science take their being, and thus are referred back to one thing. Now, the **healable human body** possesses these four conditions:
It is better known than anything else in medicine and occurs first to the intellect. From knowledge of it, other things are made known, just as from its analysis its primary parts are known. It also has parts (which is evident from the aforementioned analysis) and affections, such as being "healable" or being the recipient of health and sickness. Other things determined in medicine are referred back to it and are considered through their attribution to it. It is, therefore, the common subject.

Regarding the fourth point, it must be said to the first objection that although the things considered by a physician are many and differ in kind, they are nonetheless united in a certain unity of analogy or attribution to the unity of the science, just as all things are united in "being" <note>Aristotelian concept: many different things (substances, qualities, etc.) all relate back to the single concept of "being."</note>. For all things considered by the physician, whether closely or remotely, are referred to the body as "healable" through this kind of attribution.
To the other objection, a similar thing must be said: those things which are not the human body are ultimately reduced to it.
To the next, it must be said that the "sensible" <note>Something perceivable by the senses.</note> is twofold: one is the particular, joined to motion and this specific matter, and of such there is no science. The other is abstracted by the intellect from these particulars, yet not in a general way, and of this sensible there is science. And there is also a "presential" motion, such as the natural one, as exists evidently in the previous inquiries; medicine concerns this kind of sensible. The physician also observes such a sense. For he considers universals, the knowledge of which is very close to the sense, since from later and apparent things they arrive at prior things. Medicine also consists greatly in experience, whereas other sciences, though they take their origin from the sense, are mostly abstracted from it.

For Galen <note>Abbreviated as G. in text.</note> sees that by a lesion of the brain or liver, or by a harmful or helpful aid, the animal and natural virtue <note>The "virtues" or powers that govern the body: "animal" (nervous/sensory) and "natural" (nutritive/metabolic).</note> is damaged or perfected; he places the former in the brain and the latter in the liver. And because in the bones and similar parts there is no visible nerve or vein, he simply asserts that they have only innate virtue, even though they receive life and nutritive virtue along with nourishment from the heart and liver. This is proven first by the obstruction of the passages between these and all parts; however, the innate nature is not removed, but rather its preservation, whatever Aristotle <note>Abbreviated as A. in text.</note> may say. This is usually interpreted otherwise, but because it will be discussed sufficiently below, let it be passed over for the present.

### DIFFERENCE VII.

<margin>7</margin>
**That** the aforementioned subject of medicine should not be committed to one but to several physicians is shown: since two people working together are more powerful in acting and understanding. And in the *Politics*, book VIII, it says many judge better than any single person. And in the *Ethics*, according to that saying which you know: "Perhaps what you know, Offellus also knows." <note>A reference to a proverb or perhaps Horace’s Satires, suggesting that wisdom is shared.</note> In a plurality of physicians, there is a "multitude," and not just one. Furthermore, as the sense is to the sensible, so is the intellect to the intelligible (from *The Soul*, book IV); but several senses perceive and discern a sensible better than one. According to the same *Politics*, book IV: "It would perhaps seem inconvenient if someone could perceive better with two eyes and judge with two ears, acting with two feet and hands, than many people could with many." 

Moreover, the prince of physicians, Galen, recounts many cases in which he judged other physicians to be associated with him, whom he himself was seen to accept. From these points, it is concluded that the human body should be committed to more than one physician so that it may be rightly cared for.

To the contrary, Damascenus <note>Referring to the *Aphorisms* of Masawaih (often called Mesue or Damascenus in the West).</note> seems to say in his *Aphorisms*: "the sick person should be committed to one faithful physician," whose error is small due to the distance of the art, because it is never a greater sin than according to the man; however, he who sins less is more skillful than he who sins more. For human nature cannot run a risk, especially in subtle matters, the cause of which he assigns in the former...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into whether medical care should be provided by a single physician or a committee. Having previously defined the "subject" of medicine as the human body, the author now applies Aristotelian political theory to medical practice, weighing the benefits of individual accountability against the collective wisdom of multiple practitioners.</meta>

It is affirmed: for if many consult together, the errors of individuals will be greatly reduced. Furthermore, according to **Aristotle's *Politics***: nature makes nothing in the manner of a "Delphic sword" <note>Latin: *delphicū gladiū*. A cheap, multi-purpose tool that Aristotle used as a metaphor for something that performs many tasks poorly; he argued nature creates specialized organs for specific tasks.</note> for the poor, but rather one thing for one purpose. In this way, each instrument will certainly perform its task best. In the second book of the same work, he says that one task is performed best by one person.

Again, in the second book of the *Politics*, arguing against **Socrates** <note>Aristotle is critiquing the communal living proposed by Socrates in Plato’s *Republic*.</note>, who proposed that women and other things be held in common: a person cares most for their own things, and least for those held in common. Whence the proverb: "The mill of many participants is bound with chains" <note>A variation of the sentiment that "everyone's business is nobody's business."</note>. For as he says there, two things especially make men care and love: what is one's own, and what is dear. But if a treatment is committed to many doctors, the act of care becomes a common responsibility, and the affection for the one being treated is diminished. Therefore, the human body should be committed to only one doctor.

Regarding the first point, it should be known what the subject is, as appeared in the preceding section: what is specific to medicine. Regarding the second, it should be known that some have declared that the human body requires very many doctors for its health, because one helps another in searching for what is beneficial for it. Others, however, taking the opposite view, said it should simply be committed to one alone, supporting themselves with the words of **Damascenus** <note>John of Damascus, an influential theologian and philosopher.</note>. The deficiency of these views will be explained by what is to be said. Regarding the third, it must be said first that by observing the path of medicine, the human body should be committed to several doctors, provided one is ultimately made the principal. Second, we must see what sort of group should gather together. The first point is shown because just as it happens in other forms of government—such as in the governance of a city—so it is in the governing of the human body. For a living being must be thought to consist like a city rightly ruled by laws. Whence the legislative, judicial, executive, and medicinal powers are placed as four parts of the principle of urbanity by **Eustratius in his commentary on the *Ethics*** <note>Eustratius of Nicaea, a 12th-century Byzantine commentator on Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note>. But in a political government, several rulers are ultimately ordered under one supreme ruler, who knows the movements and counsels of all the others below him. This is found in the books of the *Politics* on the Aristocratic state, and also in the 8th book of the *Physics*, the 12th of the *Metaphysics*, and is judged in the *Vision* <note>Latin: *oculatione*.</note> of **Proclus the Platonist**. For every movement is ultimately ordered toward one, just as all the "intelligences" <note>In medieval cosmology, these were celestial beings that moved the planetary spheres.</note> are ordered toward the first. But not only this: the soul is also ultimately enclosed by that one as its end. 

Furthermore, because of the human nature's tendency to fail, one person cannot foresee all things that arise for the human body or provide for all its necessities, since they are nearly infinite. For one person cannot possess all the perfections of even a single thing perfectly, because nature has exposed nothing in a simple genus that is perfect in all its parts, according to the second book of the *Old Rhetoric* <note>Referring to Cicero's *De Inventione*.</note>. For this reason, when **Zeuxis** <note>A famous Greek painter (5th century BCE).</note> was composing a most elegant painting for the **Crotonians**, he chose from among all their most beautiful women whatever supreme beauty was in each, so that he might take up what was most graceful in each one, leaving the opposite behind. Thus, many people can look into the aforementioned matters more perfectly, as they use more senses and intellects. This is confirmed because power united is more infinite than when it is multiplied or dispersed, as stated in *The Book of Causes*, and consequently it is more moving and effective. 

Lest confusion and excessive talk also bring hindrance to the human body—especially a failing one—everything must ultimately rise to one principal doctor who is more prudent, skillful, and more diligent, and who is more beloved by the sick person, and in whom the patient has placed all hope. How much this contributes to health will be discussed in Distinction 135. Under his command, the entire regime shall be ordered, whether it be for preservation or for cure. However, some wealthier people, led by a certain pride, summon many doctors to themselves; I do not praise this unless they are reduced to one in the manner described. Therefore, the human body should be committed to several doctors with one made the principal, especially when he is well-known and familiar. Whence **Cornelius Celsus** <note>A Roman medical encyclopedist from the 1st century AD.</note> says: "While both kinds of knowledge are useful, the doctor who is also a friend is more beneficial than a stranger."

Regarding the second point, it should be known that these doctors ought to be: learned, experienced, equal in rank, or nearly so, diligent, faithful, and benevolent, intending simply the health of the human body—not victory, nor vain glory, nor the acquisition of wealth—lest nature, being agitated, complain about them. For such a plurality can certainly come together as one principal. Those described in the second distinction are those who stand as diligent ministers of nature. 

Yet, nearly the majority of doctors are the opposite of these, in their wicked acts and habits, as the first description of doctors touched upon: namely, they are rivals, detractors, backbiters, arrogant, ambitious, haters of others' knowledge and praise, talkative, negligent, luxurious, violent, gamblers, and greedy for money, vainglory, and pride—treating the worship of God and all things with constant contempt. This is what was commanded to doctors in the **Testament of Hippocrates** <note>Latin: *Y.* stands for *Ypocras* (Hippocrates). The "Testament" likely refers to the Hippocratic Oath or the "Law."</note>, as appears from the *Law* and the beginning of the *Theory*. When such men come together, they do not truly unite; rather, each one desires his own way rather than another's. While the human body should be committed to no such person, a single one can do less harm than many. On account of this, for the health of the patient, one doctor should be had who is adorned with the aforementioned good properties, who chooses a companion from among his more upright peers, or one or two or even three students with whom he may inquire into and accomplish what is beneficial for the subject. These should visit frequently, or one of them should be continuously present. For the truth cannot be judged by the crowd, but by some who are intelligent and possess sense <note>Latin: *quatriptiti t īrto*, likely a corrupted reference to the *Quadripartitum* of Ptolemy.</note>. Here, this **Ptolemaic** <note>Refers to the intellectual tradition of Claudius Ptolemy, often used in medicine for timing treatments by the stars.</note> doctor willingly perceives the movements of those others, granting them what is well said as if it were his own, nor is he ashamed to confess anything to them. Similarly, those others, wishing to appear well before him and not to detract from him, grant all things that seem reasonable. But if they doubt, they inquire unanimously. For this is the way of seeking the truth, according to the second book of *The Heavens and the World* <note>Aristotle’s *De Caelo*.</note>. Whence, in the highest degree, it is more healthful that one...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding whether a patient should be treated by a single physician or a committee. ...the prince should exert his effort, for which he will receive either praise or blame. For the zeal of a leader cools when there are many involved; each person acts for himself, as if he were not entirely responsible for the outcome of the government. Therefore, I am spurred <note>The Latin *piscatus* (fishing) here is likely a metaphorical expression or a scribal variant for being "pulled" or "hooked" into the argument.</note> against my will. It must be known that physicians, for the most part, are often found to have the worst characters. This is partly because they spring from a lowly and sterile origin, eventually becoming puffed up and insulting once they have grown wealthy. It is also because the science of medicine—which is simply curative—is primarily attributed to **Scorpio** and **Mars**, whose properties tend toward harm, as has been mentioned. 

The preservative branch of medicine, however, is more associated with **Taurus** and **Venus**, which incite people toward every kind of ruinous luxury. Nevertheless, those who are exempt from these wicked characters by the stars—despite the dominating power of **Scorpio** and **Mars** in them—become perfect royal physicians due to the power of that attribution. Whence, a naturally honest physician must often be of "bad" morals <note>This is a paradoxical scholastic argument: a "good" doctor might need "harsh" Martian qualities to perform surgery or rigorous cures, even if those qualities are socially considered "bad."</note>. This is also because this science does not define itself by acquired virtues and morals, as many other sciences do, but only by natural things within the *Tegni* <note>term: <term>Tegni</term> (The "Art"): A common title for Galen’s *Ars Medica*, the foundational textbook of medieval medical education.</note>. This is due to an astral alignment that is the opposite of moral character. 

Regarding the fourth point, for those briefly constrained by these things, with reverence and having introduced his <margin>procedure</margin> preceding arguments, the conclusions stand as part of a more extensive grace of teaching. 

<margin>To the 1st.</margin> To the first point, it must be said, as others do, that **Aristotle** speaks of the judgment of the *practical intellect* in matters of action, where many are found to be perfect. Here, however, the discussion is more about the judgment of the *speculative intellect*, in which very few are truly vigorous. Therefore, it is better to agree with one highly vigorous mind than with many who are deficient. Even if many vigorous minds are found, the matter should be committed to one alone, though it may happen otherwise by accident due to the appropriation of wicked morals in physicians, as was touched upon. <margin>It must be said</margin> It must also be said that a large crowd judges better than any single individual. For that one individual can have a flawed judgment, especially in particular cases; but one skilled and experienced individual judges more perfectly in universal matters and in those things which require subtle investigation, compared to many unlearned people, since few are found who know how to judge in such matters.

<margin>To the 2nd.</margin> To the second point, it must be said that many wise people judge better than one, unless they are perverted by love or hatred, which often change the truth of judgment, as noted in the first book of the ***Ethics*** and the ***Centiloquium*** <note>The *Centiloquium* is a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy.</note>. This happens to physicians quite often, since their judgment is not slightly submitted to their passions.

<margin>To the 3rd.</margin> To the third point, it must be said that **Galen** supported other physicians either because of his own virtue and honesty, or so that he might correct them by exposing their errors, as **Aristotle** says in the tenth book of the *Method of Healing* regarding a youth who was fed before a purge <note>original: <note>ante pocismum</note></note> by the observation of the "diatritos" <note>term: <term>Diatritos</term>: A medical term from the Methodist school referring to a three-day period or the third day of an illness used to determine treatment timing.</note>, and who subsequently fainted.

<margin>To the arguments</margin> To the arguments of the other side, it must be said for the first: that a sick person should be committed to one faithful physician, namely the principal one, who may receive the motivations and counsels of several others at once. For if a patient consults many one after the other, and they do not agree, or they agree only with varying degrees of difference, the distracted patient will not know to whom he should entrust his faith. Thus, he might try one medication today and another tomorrow, and finally a third, and so fall into the error of each individual, because the plurality was not reduced to unity. 

To the next point, it must be said that when many physicians, according to the aforementioned manner, come together to care for one body, they are ordered as one toward one goal. For although they are many, they are nonetheless united in species, and species is ordered toward one act of care. This is what **Aristotle** means: that each thing should be ordered toward one act and not many; it does not mean, however, that many things of the same species cannot be ordered toward the same act, since every physician is ordered toward the act of healing. It would be "not one" if, for instance, a physician were ordered toward the act of hunting. 

But on the contrary, at the end of ***On the Soul***, it is said that the tongue is suited for two works of nature: taste and speech; and also that the hand is for grinding, bringing in food, according to the twelfth book of **Avicenna's** *On Animals*. It must be said that although it is ordered toward several acts, it is more principally for one, such as taste. This is apparent because some animals have taste but do not use speech. To the final point, it must be said that many physicians are rendered appropriate by the virtue of that one more principal physician.

### DIFFERENCE VIII.

<margin>Q. 1. do.</margin> Regarding the fact that the number of ordinary teachings is not threefold but appears to be indefinite. Since "ordinary teaching" is named from "order," wherever there is an order to be given, there will also be ordinary teaching. But every teaching observes an order, at least from the predicate to the subject, from the genus to the species, and from the conclusion to the premises. Furthermore, every science is about the "good and the difficult," according to the second book of the <margin>2. Et.</margin> ***Ethics***; but goodness is in things especially because of order, as per the <margin>12. met.</margin> twelfth book of the ***Metaphysics***. 

Furthermore, it seems that there is no ordinary teaching, because it is the "face" of science. But "to know" simply and not by accident is to know through causes, as stated in the beginning of the <margin>1. po.</margin> ***Posterior Analytics***. But causes are unknown to us—namely, the Intelligences and God. For our intellect is related to them <margin>2. met.</margin> as the eye of a bat is to the light of the sun, according to the second book of the ***Metaphysics***. 

Again, they prove by this means that there is only one teaching, since to know is one thing—namely, through causes alone. For ordinary teaching is ordered toward knowing. Furthermore, in the <margin>in teg.</margin> *Tegni*, it is said that all arts consist of **resolution** <note>term: <term>Resolution</term> (resolutio): A logical method of moving from effects back to their causes.</note> according to reason. Therefore, there is no other; if all consist of this one, then any other teaching would be useless. 

Likewise, **composition** <note>term: <term>Composition</term> (compositio): A logical method of moving from causes to their effects.</note> and resolution seem to be the same thing; one seems to be from the effect to the cause, the other from the cause to the effect. But this process is the same, just as the road from Athens <margin>3. phi.</margin> to Thebes is the same as the road from Thebes to Athens, from the third book of the ***Physics***. Furthermore, why are there two? For as **Haly** says, composition is done through demonstration "of the reasoned fact" <note>original: <note>propter quid</note></note>, while resolution is through demonstration "of the fact" <note>original: <note>quia</note></note>. But these are the only two <margin>1. po.</margin> demonstrations placed in the first book of the ***Posterior Analytics***. Finally, definition does not seem to be an ordinary teaching, since ordinary teaching is done through genus and continuation, according to the Arabic translation of the <margin>in teg.</margin> *Tegni* and **Haly**. But the "what a thing is" exists as the object of the intellect.

## DIFFERENCE VIII ##

->**Whether medicine is a science**<-

Following this, let us proceed to the eighth difference, which is: **whether medicine is a science** <note>The Latin *scibilis* refers to "knowability" or the status of a discipline as a "scientia"—a rigorous, demonstrative branch of knowledge.</note>. 

It appears that it is not. For according to **Aristotle** <note>referred to simply as "the Philosopher" in the text</note> in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*, science is only concerned with things that are universal and necessary. Medicine, however, is concerned with particulars—namely, this specific individual, such as Socrates or Plato—and with things that are contingent and changeable, such as health and disease. <margin>Medicine deals with singular things</margin>

Furthermore, the authority **Galen** states in his *Medical Art* <note>original: "Ars Parva," Galen's influential introductory manual</note> that the physician does not grasp the internal causes of the body directly, but only works through signs. Because science requires a certain knowledge of causes, it would seem medicine falls short.

On the contrary, however, is the statement of **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), whose *Canon of Medicine* was the definitive authority for scholastic physicians.</note> at the beginning of the first book of the *Canon*, where he defines medicine as a science by which the dispositions of the human body are known, in order that health may be preserved when present and restored when lost.

To resolve this, it must be understood that "science" is spoken of in two ways. In one way, it is taken strictly as the knowledge of a thing through its necessary and universal cause. In another way, it is taken more broadly as a structured system of knowledge. <insert>Medicine is a science because it considers universal principles, even if it applies them to individuals.</insert> Therefore, medicine is a science insofar as it draws from the principles of natural philosophy, but it is an art insofar as it is practiced upon the individual patient. <margin>Medicine is both science and art</margin>

<meta>This page continues the logical investigation of medicine's status as a science. Having established that medicine relies on certain knowledge, the text now moves into a technical scholastic discussion of "scientific method" (doctrina), categorizing how a physician or scientist moves from observations (effects) to principles (causes) and vice versa.</meta>

...becomes this doctrine: truly ordinary. And what is not:
Second, what **resolutive** and **compositive** doctrine is; third, concerning certain doubts about them; fourth, what **definitive** doctrine is; and how much and in what way they differ from one another, and in what part they are divisive, and how they agree.
Regarding the first of these, it must be known that the aforementioned order, established through essentials, can be considered in three ways: commonly, properly, and most properly.
Indeed, in the most proper sense, there is only one such "ordinary doctrine": the **compositive**, which is exercised through the demonstration of the "why" <note>original: *propter quid*—this refers to demonstrating a fact by starting from its primary cause or reason.</note>. For this is the most perfect of demonstrations, in which the true character of the demonstrative syllogism is preserved, which properly produces knowledge, since it proceeds from an immediate cause to an immediate effect. And therefore, mathematicians <note>original: *doctrinales*, referring to those who teach the 'doctrines' of the mathematical arts</note> out of both types of knowledge, since their demonstrations are in the first degree of certainty; natural scientists follow them.
**The Commentator** <note>Averroes, the 12th-century philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to medieval science.</note> in the second book of the *Metaphysics*, where at the beginning of the philosophy he describes "ordinary doctrine" as being named by excellence <note>original: *antonomasice*—using a title or description to refer to the highest example of a category.</note> or named in itself, touched on only this, saying: "Ordinary doctrine is to begin from the knowledge of the primary causes of the thing to be known perfectly, then to intend toward the knowledge of other remote causes in order, until one arrives at the proximate causes."
But if the aforementioned order is taken "properly," then with this there will also be **resolutive doctrine**, which extends continuously from the effect to the cause, or from the cause to the effect in an interrupted way—that is, skipping some intermediate cause between itself and the effect to be investigated. <note>This refers to the *Posterior Analytics* of Aristotle.</note> And this mode of the demonstrative process is touched upon at the beginning of the *Physics* <note>original: *phi.*</note> when he says: "It is innate to us to proceed from those things more known and certain to us toward things more known and certain according to nature." This is because effects in sensible things are more known to us than causes, since they fall more under the senses, although causes absolutely and in themselves are more known. <margin>All knowledge comes from pre-existing knowledge</margin> And "all doctrine and all intellectual discipline comes from pre-existing knowledge."
If, however, the aforementioned is taken "commonly," then **definitive doctrine** can be called ordinary doctrine, since it follows a certain method itself. For it explains the thing defined and declares it through essentials, since it receives the best limit, which some call "substantial" according to **Galen**. Likewise, it happens through continuity; for the parts in a definition ought to be continuous, denoting the unity of matter with form; for form, in itself—that is, without a medium—comes to the matter, according to the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: *de anima*</note> and the eighth of the *Metaphysics*. And therefore, in true definitions, a "copula of diversity" <note>A logical link that implies separation rather than unity between the words in a definition.</note> should not intervene as a designator, but the whole should be continuous, such as "Man is a rational, mortal animal."

Regarding the second point, it should be known, as written in the beginning of the second book of the *Posterior Analytics*, that the things sought <note>original: *quesita*—the specific questions a researcher asks.</note> are as many in number as the things known; for we know nothing in the end unless it was sought in the beginning. There are four things sought: two simple—namely, **Whether it is** and **What it is**—and two composite—namely, **That it is** and **On account of what (Why) it is**.
The first of the simple ones is whether the thing is found simply according to what the thing is. Of the composite ones, the first is "Whether this is found to be in that" <note>Determining if a specific property belongs to a specific subject.</note>, and "Why this is found to be in that."
In these four inquiries, the seeker intends nothing else than that the finding of the **middle term** <note>The "bridge" in a logical argument that connects the subject and the predicate to prove a conclusion.</note> be shown to him, by which the doubt is certified for him and a conclusion is reached. And therefore the "middle term" is properly called that from which the science of the thing is produced; for the conclusion is properly called the "thing known."
Indeed, the third of these inquiries is for the demonstrative syllogism—namely, that by which it is asked *whether* this is found simply in that—and that by which it is asked *why* it is found in it; and that by which it is asked *whether* it simply is. The fourth, however—namely, that by which it is asked **What a thing is**—is known through **definition** and through the "middle" concluding it. And the knowledge acquired through definition is not the same as that through a syllogism, even if it happens to be one and the same for someone, but not in the same respect.
Since, therefore, in the first three inquiries nothing is sought except the finding of the middle term, it should be known that in each of those where it is asked *whether this is found in that*, and in that where it is asked *whether this is found simply*—if its finding must be through a middle term that is not the cause of the connection, then in both there remains the question of "on account of what" (the why), which is not certified unless the middle term is given which is the *cause* of the finding. Then the question of "why" ceases, because the finding and the cause have already been given.
Nevertheless, as **Aristotle** says in the first book, the demonstration that gives the *cause* of the finding is different from the demonstration that gives the *finding* only. For that is called the **demonstration "on account of what"** (*propter quid*), which corresponds to the inquiry about the "wherefore" <note>the *quare*</note>; and that demonstration is made through things "prior by nature," because the middle term in it is the cause of the thing sought. But that which gives the "finding" only is called **demonstration "that"** (*quia*), which corresponds to the inquiry of *whether this is found* or *whether it is found simply*. For although it may be from immediate and necessary and "in-itself" propositions, the middle term in it is a thing *caused* by the "major" term, as will appear at the end, and thus it is made through things "posterior by nature."
But to that inquiry about the **why** (*quare*), the answer is given through demonstration, which is called demonstration "absolutely," and it is the demonstration "on account of what" (*propter quid*). And this is **compositive doctrine**.
To the other two, however, the answer is given through the demonstration which is not named demonstration "absolutely," as Aristotle wills; and it is the **demonstration "that"** (*quia*), and this doctrine is called **resolutive** through conversion.
Now, however, the process of these doctrines and examples of them are assigned; finally, we shall say how the fourth inquiry <note>What it is</note> is satisfied through definition, from which a third doctrine arises, called **definitive doctrine**.
Let it be said, therefore, that the process of each of the two is as **Haly** <note>Likely Haly Rodoham, an influential commentator on Galen.</note> also wills: that the thing sought is assumed, and one looks toward that which follows from the subject and precedes the predicate. And this is in the "first figure" of syllogisms, which is the most worthy of the figures. For the figure that primarily produces knowledge is the first. In others, however, according to that... for that will be the middle term from which the reasoning is extracted regarding the thing sought; and let it be considered if that middle term... the syllogism through which the sought thing was made a conclusion; if there should be a place of doubt in any of those, because...

<summary>This page defines the three modes of scientific teaching (compositive, resolutive, and definitive) and maps them onto Aristotle's four types of inquiry. It distinguishes between demonstrating a fact from its cause (propter quid) versus discovering a cause from its effects (quia).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical exploration of "resolutive" and "compositive" methods in medical science. Having previously defined these methods in a general sense, the author now provides specific examples—notably a clinical breakdown of a fever—to show how a physician moves from symptoms to causes (resolution) and from causes back to the diagnosis (composition).</meta>

...once a principle known through itself <note>original: *principium per se notum*—a self-evident truth that requires no further proof</note> has been reached in that category, from the knowledge of which the prior knowledge of the quantity is confirmed. Let us now provide an example of both, following **Galen’s** order: first concerning the **resolutive** method, and finally the **compositive**. Indeed, two common examples are found.

One is placed in theory: first, the subject of medicine—the healable human body—is taught to be resolved into its integral parts, and finally composed from those same parts. The other example comes from **Haly** <note>Haly Rodoan (Ali ibn Ridwan), an 11th-century physician and commentator on Galen.</note> concerning the resolution of medicine into its essential parts: namely, the **preservative** and the **curative**; and finally, composing medical practices by beginning from these parts. This theoretical example should not be rejected for his purpose, since he wished to resolve the subject into parts or compose it from them, just as **Haly** himself seems to suggest, saying this does not disagree with **Galen's** opinion. For Galen intends more to perform the resolution of the *science* of medicine than of its *subject*. Nevertheless, both are correct examples in their proper place.

Because these examples are well-known, let us take another example which concerns the eleventh book of the *Art of Healing* <note>original: *Ars Curativa*, referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note>. I take, therefore, according to the **resolutive** doctrine, some quantity in the mind—for instance, a **humoral fever**—and I resolve it into a subject and a predicate: namely, into a **putrid smoke** or **sooty vapor** immediately attacking the heart. For this is the immediate cause of fevers. After this resolution, let a demonstration be made in this way: wherever there is fever, there is putrid smoke immediately attacking the heart; but in this man there is such smoke; therefore, the fever is in him.

Furthermore, resolve this smoke into **putrefaction** and demonstrate consequently: whoever has this putrid smoke has a "source" of putrefaction; such a person has it, etc.

Next, resolve this source of putrefaction into its cause: for instance, into **inhibited transpiration** <note>The blockage of the skin's pores, preventing the body from "breathing" or releasing waste vapors.</note>; and then demonstrate: wherever there is a source of putrefaction, there is inhibited transpiration; but in this case, there is a source of putrefaction. Likewise, resolve inhibited transpiration into its cause, such as an **oppilation** <note>original: *opillatio*—a medical term for a blockage or obstruction in the vessels or organs.</note> or obstruction, demonstrating finally: wherever inhibited transpiration is found, there also is an obstruction; but in such a person, inhibited transpiration is found.

Similarly, resolve the obstruction into its causes, since it occurs either from a vice of the **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that governed health in medieval medicine.</note> or without a vice of the humors. And demonstrate as before: if it is from a vicious humor, resolve it again by dividing it, for that humor is either excessive, or viscous, or thick. Proceed as before: if it is excessive, resolve it into its immediate cause—perhaps because the person eats too much. They eat much because they have a great appetite; and they have a great appetite because the **mouth of the stomach** is cold. For a good stomach is meant for desiring, but a bad one for digesting (according to the second book of the *Tegni* <note>The *Tegni* or *Ars Medica* of Galen, a fundamental textbook.</note>). The mouth of the stomach is cold because of a "cold complexion," whether simple or humoral, or because of the coldness of the air, and so on. In this way, show the whole through a demonstrative syllogism, and then resume the other branches of the division, resolving them either simply or by dividing, and finally demonstrate.

The example of the **compositive** doctrine is now evident. It is, in fact, the conversion of the previous steps, so that it begins from the **ultimate cause** where the resolution stopped.

For example: from a cold complexion or cold humors, the mouth of the stomach is made cold, so that it is demonstrated thus: Whoever has cold humors in the mouth of the stomach has a cold mouth of the stomach; this man has cold humors, etc. Then proceed further by composing: if he has a cold mouth of the stomach, he has a great appetite, so that one says: whoever has a cold mouth of the stomach has a great appetite. If he has a great appetite, he eats much, and it is demonstrated: whoever has a great appetite eats much; but such a person does so, etc. Likewise, if he eats much, many humors become sour, or thick, or viscous; and if they are such, an obstruction is caused; and if there is obstruction, there is inhibited respiration; and if this occurs, there is a source of putrefaction; and if that, there is putrid smoke immediately attacking the heart; and thus there will be **fever**. Let it be demonstrated continuously: wherever there is putrid smoke immediately attacking the heart, there is fever; but in this case, etc.

Thus you see that fever is the **ultimate effect** <note>original: *ultimum causatum*</note> at which you arrived through the **compositive** doctrine, which was the **first effect** in the **resolutive** doctrine. It is also argued from this example that the resolutive doctrine does not only resolve, and the compositive only compose; but the resolutive also returns upon what was resolved and proves it through demonstration, while the compositive does the same for what was composed.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that there are many simple doubts concerning the things said above. First: because some, expressly dishonoring **Haly**, say that the **resolutive** doctrine is a **demonstration of the "why"** <note>original: *propter quid*—demonstrating an effect through its cause.</note>, whereas the **compositive** is a **demonstration of the "fact"** <note>original: *quia*—demonstrating a cause through its observed effect.</note>. They seem moved by many things. First, because **Aristotle** calls the books of the *Prior* and *Posterior Analytics* "analytics"—that is, "resolutive." And it is certain that in these books, and properly in the *Posteriors*, he treats the "demonstration of the why" and the "demonstration of the fact." Therefore, the name of "analysis" or "resolution" more properly belongs to them.

Furthermore, **Galen** says that all arts consist of the **resolutive** method according to reason; such a method seems to be that which is perfected by the "demonstration of the why," since it is absolute and the more worthy demonstration, through which a science-making art ought to proceed. Moreover, **Haly** says that geometricians know this method, and they use the "demonstration of the why." Finally, he adds that the authors of the sciences know this mode of doctrine. And **Aristotle** placed it in the *Analytics*. Again, **Galen** says that the resolutive method stems from the **notion of the end** <note>The goal or final cause of the process.</note>. If, therefore, demonstration were to consist in the "fact" (which proceeds from an unknown effect to a cause), then Galen should have said it stems from *ignorance* of the end, and not from the *notion* of the end. Those who wish for both—namely, the resolutive and compositive—to proceed from the notion of the end, argue that until the known end is reached, the quantity is not extracted by either resolution or composition. They explain it thus: the second is that which comes from the notion of the end—that is, through the end known from the composition of things found according to resolution. But they say the resolutive is especially said to happen from the notion of the end because that which is the end of the resolution is also implicit...

It also discusses scholastic debates over whether these methods constitute "causal" or "factual" demonstrations according to Aristotle and Galen.</summary>
