<meta>The text continues the scholastic investigation into the two primary modes of scientific demonstration: "resolution" (analysis) and "composition" (synthesis). This page specifically addresses the relationship between these methods and the Aristotelian distinction between what is "known to us" versus what is "known by nature."</meta>

...better known [in nature] and better known to us. But it must be said that **Haly** <note>Haly Rodoan, a medieval commentator on Galen.</note> understood this perfectly. It can also be gathered from **Haly’s** words by positing that resolution consists of a **demonstration of the fact** <note>original: *demonstratio quia*—a proof that shows something is true based on its effects, without necessarily explaining why.</note>, in which the process moves from the effect to the cause; while composition consists of a **demonstration of the reason why** <note>original: *demonstratio propter quid*—a proof that shows why something is true based on its primary causes.</note>, in which the process, as has appeared, is reversed.

Whence the Commentator <note>Averroes, the influential 12th-century philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were standard in medieval universities.</note> on the seventh book of the *Metaphysics* says that considering one thing after another occurs according to **dissolution**—namely, by beginning from what is posterior [the effect] and arriving at the principle in thought. But the motion that begins from the last point in dissolution—which is **composition**—is called **action**, proceeding from health. Thus it happens that health which is outside the soul [the physical body] is produced by the health which is in the soul [the doctor's mental concept].

Indeed, health in the soul exists in composition according to the intention of **Aristotle**. Toward the actual being of health outside the soul, it is said that the **principle of operation** is the **end of thought**, and the **principle of thought** is the **end of operation**. This is even suggested by the names of the terms themselves.

In things made by art, which imitate nature, something is said to be **resolved** into another when an effect is resolved into its cause, and the whole is separated into the parts of which it consisted: such as a house being resolved into its roof, walls, and foundation. Something is also said to be **composed** when it is constructed from its established parts: such as a house being built from foundation, walls, and roof.

Furthermore, the **resolutive method** is said to arise from the notion of the **end**, that is, the effect; for "end" and "effect" are the same, according to **Boethius** in his *Topics*. For the end is the "cause of causes" and the "effect of causes." The teaching that begins from the notion of the effect, arriving at the cause, is supported by **demonstration of the fact** in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*.

But against this is what was said: that then they ought to be said to arise from **ignorance** of the effect, since that which is proposed first would be unknown; for if it were known, the seeker would not be seeking it.

And therefore it must be known that something can be "known" and "unknown" in two ways, as stated in the beginning of the *Physics* and the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*: namely, **in relation to us**, and **in relation to nature**. Effects are known to us [through our senses] but unknown to nature; causes, however, are the opposite. Thus it must be said that **resolutive teaching** begins from the notion of the effect, because the effect is known to us, yet unknown to nature (or "simply"). Therefore, one wishing to prove and make it known through resolutive doctrine seeks it until it becomes known simply.

That this is correctly the intent of **Galen** is shown from the Arabic translation of the Greek commentary: thus, the first method is that which occurs by way of **conversion and solution** [resolution]. It is when you establish the thing at which you aim—the knowledge of which you seek in your mind—according to the "end of its fulfillment." Then you consider the most immediate part, and the part most immediate to that end, without which that thing cannot stand or be completed, until you arrive at its **principles**.

But regarding principles, since they are the terms at which one arrives only through effects, this is where **demonstration of the fact** consists; which **Haly** likewise confirms. There are, however, others besides this described mode who interpret the aforesaid sequence correctly; nothing will be said of them at present, since the text does not comment on them. Therefore, we must return to the arguments of those mentioned before, now that the truth has been established.

It must be said regarding the first argument that **Aristotle**, principally in the *Posterior Analytics*, teaches how to construct a **demonstration of the reason why**, and generally a demonstration "of the fact" or "resolutive." Likewise, he constructs the **syllogism** <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> in the *Prior Analytics* using this same method simply. For he takes in his mind a common effect—namely, demonstration itself—and resolves it into its primary and secondary parts, as in demonstrations "of the reason why" and "of the fact," affirmative and negative, and the rest. Similarly for the simple syllogism; therefore, he at least uses **resolutive doctrine** in these matters.

Furthermore, although causes can be said to be "resolved" into effects improperly—in that when causes are applied, they constitute the effects—the term **resolutive** taken broadly can contain both the truly resolutive and the **compositive**. This is shown because, according to **Cicero** and **Boethius**, "resolutive" is the same as "**judgmental**." This, however, as will be said, gathers within itself demonstrations "of the reason why" and "of the fact."

To the other point, it must be said that some say all arts consist of resolution "according to reason," or that this applies to the **first discovery** of the arts, since the discoverer proceeds from the doubtful to the self-evident and stops there; whereas the mode of **teaching** a discovered art is the opposite. But this argument is not valid, because the way of discovery and the way of teaching from sensible things—namely, those better known to us—is the same.

And so it must be said differently, so that the main defect of those opponents appears: **Galen** does not simply say all arts consist of the resolutive method, but adds "according to reason." Because the mode of human teaching handed down by **Aristotle**—contrary to **Plato** and the theologians—is to proceed from confused things and those better known to us. That doctrine which preserves this mode by making a doubtful thing known through better-known things will certainly be "according to reason," since it strives to arrive from the better-known to the unknown. The result proves this.

For we see that almost all sciences, and especially those of sensory things, are handed down in the **resolutive mode**, as appears from **Aristotle’s** books on nature, and perhaps even logic. **Galen** acts similarly now, where he almost always seems to use the **compositive method** except in his *Book of Elements*, following the opinion of **Hippocrates**.

To the other point, it must be said through <note>original abbreviation likely for *per*</note> **Haly** spoke less well, which thrust many of his followers into the pitfalls of ignorance; or rather how he says that **geometers** know the method well, but do not use it. For if they know a **demonstration of the reason why**, they also know the **demonstration of the fact**, since they are connected and are taught in the same part of the art; they do not use only resolution, but the compositive method more. Likewise, when he says that **Aristotle** placed this in the *Analytics*, I will say that he used it more in the *Prior Analytics*, and both taught and used it in the *Posterior*.

Regarding the fourth point, it has already appeared what must be said. Secondly, however, there is doubt concerning the aforesaid, because some wished the **resolutive doctrine** to be the same as the "judgmental" [iudicatica], called ***Analytics*** by the Greeks. The **compositive**, however, they claim is the same as the "inventive," which they call ***Topics***. And since the inventive proceeds through signs and posterior things—for it preserves this mode more than it discovers—similarly the compositive through...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the classification of scientific methods. It specifically addresses whether the "resolutive" (analytical) and "compositive" (synthetic) methods can be mapped onto the classical logical divisions used by Cicero and Boethius.</meta>

They established such things because they had a reason: they wanted to reduce the division of doctrine into **resolutive** and **compositive** to that division used by **Cicero** and **Boethius**, which splits logic into the **judicative** <note>The part of logic concerned with judging the validity of arguments.</note> and the **inventive** <note>The part of logic concerned with the "invention" or discovery of new arguments.</note>.

But it must be said that these methods fall short of that goal, because the division of **Cicero** and **Boethius** is superior and divides the whole of logic, whereas this division into resolutive and compositive concerns only the demonstrative part. For the compositive and resolutive are reduced to the **judicative** part, since a person who judges must bring their judgment forth with proof and diligent examination, so that the judge may be just and the judgment correct, not leaning unjustly toward either side of a dispute.

Likewise, these do not lead to the **inventive** part of any true ordinary doctrines, since that part is "topical" <term>topica (topics): the study of probable arguments based on commonplaces rather than certain demonstration</term>, proceeding from certain external and foreign signs. The resolutive method, however, proceeds from proper signs or meanings that are inseparable and familiar; these generate the "form" of the knowledge especially, rather than the "matter" as others do.

And for this reason, there is a doubt. Some have said that the resolutive doctrine contains the compositive within itself, since some processes eventually involve a "regression." They were moved by the same reasons as the first group, because **Aristotle** <note>abbreviated as Au.</note> teaches the resolutive in the *Posterior Analytics* and teaches the demonstration of the **reason why** <note>original: *propter quid*—a proof showing the cause of a fact</note> to compose principally. This is the method that **Geometers** also use, even though **Haly** <note>Haly Rodoan, a commentator on Galen.</note> says that the resolutive happens through demonstration of the **fact** <note>original: *quia*—a proof showing that something is true based on its effects</note> and the compositive through the **reason why**.

To this they respond, saying that in the resolutive there is a double act: namely, the **resolution** itself, which leads back into the causes, and then the **regression** from those causes back to the thing sought. Thus, regarding the first process, it can be said that in resolutive doctrine there is a "demonstration of the fact" because one moves from the effect to the cause; but regarding the second part, there is a "demonstration of the reason why," because in the regression, the process moves from the cause back to the effect. But because in compositive doctrine one begins from the causes and proceeds to the effect alone, as he says, therefore demonstrations occur in it only of the **reason why**.

And the speech of these men is more **gilded** than **golden** <note>A common medieval idiom meaning the argument looks impressive on the surface but lacks the weight of truth.</note> here and in most cases.

However, a statement by **Haly Abbas** <note>Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi, a famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note> provides a "fantasy" <note>An imaginary or superficial support.</note> for this opinion. Speaking of the resolutive doctrine, he says:

-> "The way of conversion is for one to contemplate what he desires to know, and place it in his imagination from its beginning to its end; then, returning from its end, let him begin by conversion, and he will consider each of its parts from which it is composed, and not without them until he returns to the principle." <-

Therefore, the speech here apparently sounds as if "regression" is intended in the resolutive doctrine, and thus the compositive would be placed under it.

To this it must be said that resolutive and compositive doctrine can never formally coincide. For they are divided by opposition, just as a "demonstration of the fact" and a "demonstration of the reason why" are. Such opposites never coincide; for one opposite species does not help the other to exist, as **Boethius** says in the fourth book of his *Topics*. But perhaps they are the same in "subject"—that is, the process is the same in both, just as the road from **Athens** to **Thebes** is the same as the road from **Thebes** to **Athens**. But that identity is "material"; here, however, we are looking for "formal" identity.

---

...and not of terms. For that distinction leads into knowledge; however, it should not be denied that in traditional science one doctrine can fall into the cause of other ordinary or extraordinary doctrines, as appears in **Galen’s** first text <note>abbreviated as G. 1 tex.</note> where he uses "definitive doctrine" and yet improperly uses "ordinary doctrine" when he strives to prove this principle: *Every cure is performed by its contrary*, through induction and **syllogism** <term>syllogismus (syllogism): a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term>.

Regarding their speech, what must be said is evident from what was said to the first doubters. Regarding the speech of **Haly Abbas**, it must be said that there is a "sophism of the sequence" <note>A logical error in the order of the argument.</note>. For he himself counts several doctrines, and having enumerated them, he resumes and says, "But the way of conversion is..." and finally proposes something common to both doctrines (resolutive and compositive), saying that one should "contemplate what he desires to know," and so on. And proceeding specifically regarding resolutive doctrine, he says, "then returning from its last part," etc. That this is simply the resolutive appears when he says, "nor without them until he returns to the principle."

And then he adds an example, such as the **human body** which is divided into "instrumental members" <note>Complex organs like the hand or eye.</note> and those into "similar parts" <note>Tissues like bone or flesh that are the same throughout.</note>, and so on. And finally, he resumes specifically about the compositive doctrine, saying, "But the way of composition is contrary to this, beginning," etc.

For the fourth point, it must be known that **definition** is threefold according to the *Posterior Analytics*:

1. One is the **principle of demonstration**, such as "thunder is the extinction of fire in a cloud" or "anger is the appetite for vengeance."
2. Another is the **conclusion of a demonstration**, such as "thunder is a continuous sound in a cloud" or "anger is the boiling of blood around the heart."
3. Another is a **demonstration differing only in position**, with the proper arrangement of the figure and modes, such as "thunder is a continuous sound in a cloud because of the extinction of fire in a cloud" or "anger is the boiling of blood around the heart because of the appetite for vengeance."

Indeed, a definition does not differ from the thing defined except as the **explicit** differs from the **implicit**, according to **Eustratius** <note>A 12th-century commentator on Aristotle’s Ethics.</note>. For a definition is the "ratio" <note>The essential account or meaning.</note> which the name signifies, according to the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. However, how a definition is to be "hunted" <note>A technical term for the discovery of a definition through division.</note> is difficult to see in the second book of the *Posteriors*. For it cannot be done by demonstration, because that requires a **syllogism**, and a syllogism works through a "middle term." But the definition of a thing is "convertible" with the thing itself and is predicated of it "in what it is" <note>original: *in quid*—referring to the essential nature of a thing</note>.

Therefore, if someone wants to conclude that the "major extreme" is the definition of the "minor," the "middle" must be convertible with both extremes, so that the middle itself is predicated of the minor as its essence and equal. And the major is predicated of the middle as its essence and equal. Unless these two conditions are present in the syllogism, the major extreme does not follow as the definition of the minor; rather, it follows only that it is found within it. In that case, the middle term would be just as much a definition of the minor as the major extreme is. It would be as if there were two definitions, differing only in their interpretation and the different words used to signify their meaning. If, therefore, through one discovered definition another is seen to be found in the same thing—since one is understood in the other—and they correspond to each other equally in the question of "what is it," it is manifest that it is already shown...

<summary>This page analyzes the logical relationship between the methods of "resolution" (analysis) and "composition" (synthesis), arguing that they are distinct but related processes used to move between effects and causes. It also details the three types of scientific definition—as a principle, a conclusion, or a complete demonstration—using the classical examples of thunder and anger.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into scientific methodology, moving from the distinction between resolutive and compositive methods to a specific inquiry into whether a definition can be formally demonstrated or discovered through logic.</meta>

...the same thing through itself. And thus the first point of inquiry is requested. From these things, therefore, it seems that it is **not possible to demonstrate a definition**. Nor does this seem possible through a **hypothetical syllogism** <note>A form of logic where the conclusion depends on a condition (if A, then B).</note>, as **Aristotle** also says. It is just as we often do when hunting for a definition among contraries: we say that if the definition of health is "the cause producing action," then the definition of sickness will be "the cause harming action." But the definition of health is indeed the former; therefore, the definition of sickness will be the latter. 

However, one who proceeds by this path in finding a definition is **begging the question** <term>petitio principii: a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premises</term>. This is because the discovery of one definition involves the knowledge of the definitions of its contraries, and ignorance works in the same way. Thus, one demonstrates one thing through the very thing that is meant to demonstrate it, which is a "petition" for the definition. And even if perhaps the definition of one contrary were sometimes better known, this would not happen in every case. Because he posits that a definition is found through a definition always and in every place, it follows that he is already assuming the definition he seeks.

Nor, again, can a definition be proven by **induction** <note>The process of reaching a general conclusion from specific examples.</note>. This is because through induction it is shown that a thing is found through a predicative statement. A definition, however, is a statement that elucidates the **substance of a thing** <note>The essential nature or "whatness" of an object.</note>, being conditional and consecutive rather than merely predicative. Furthermore, a definition deals with the general or the totality of universals, whereas induction deals with particulars. Thus, a definition cannot be shown by either a syllogism or by induction in such a way that the definition is concluded from those arguments out of necessity.

It remains now to inquire whether it is possible to find a definition by the **way of division**. Let it be said, therefore, that **Aristotle** says the way of division is not a "perfecting" method for discovering something unknown, much less for finding a definition. For a conclusion ought not to be granted simply as a concession, but must follow by necessity from those things which have been granted. 

For if we wish to show that "man" is a "two-footed walking animal" through division, there is no other way than to say—as appears in the *Prior [Analytics]* <note>Aristotle's work on the structure of syllogisms.</note>—that "man is either an animal or not an animal." And when it is granted to us that he is an animal, we proceed and ask if he is "walking or not walking." And when it is granted that he is walking, I say after that, he is either "two-footed or many-footed." When it is granted that he is two-footed, we aggregate all the things granted to us and say: "**Man is a two-footed walking animal**." But this is nothing other than the things already granted. A conclusion, however, ought to be something different from the premises from which it follows.

In the second book of the *Prior [Analytics]*, it is also said that in division, when we attempt to show something unknown through it, a **petition** <note>A begging of the question.</note> is committed. For instance: "man is either rational or irrational; but he is not irrational; therefore he is rational." He "petitions" because he does not show that man is "not irrational" except by the fact that man is "using reason" and "rational." Therefore, that which he puts in the premise is shown by the conclusion. 

Nevertheless, as **Aristotle** maintains, even if the way of division is not a formal syllogism, it is still **useful within a syllogism**. For when a division is established—that man is either an animal or not an animal, and if an animal...

---

...he does not escape being either walking or not walking; and if walking, either two-footed or many-footed. Then it is shown through a syllogism that he is an animal (and not "not-animal"), and that he is walking, and that he is two-footed (and not "not-walking" or "many-footed"). The definition of man is then aggregated for us from these syllogisms. 

But this does not happen always, but only when the **genera** <note>The broad categories (e.g., 'Animal').</note> being divided are known parts of the thing about which they are predicated. And it happens when a division is made in which no error falls—namely, into **primary differences** and not into differences that are far removed. For example, if one were to say "an animal is either healthy or sick," the definition of man is not found through such a division of the genus. 

Therefore, when it is granted that a divided genus leads to the discovery of the thing whose definition is sought, and one does not err in the division and the transition until reaching the species whose definition is intended, then the definition will be reached by the way of division out of necessity. For this reason, the knowledge arriving from it in this manner is neither from a syllogism nor from a species of knowledge arriving from a syllogism; rather, they are syllogized together in some way, though there is no need to refer to the similarity here. Thus, it seems a definition can be found through division.

**Boethius**, in his book *On Division*, suggests this when he says that the logic of definition and division are occupied with the same thing; for when divisions are joined together, a single definition is composed. **Aristotle** also provides a rule for defining: once a species to be defined is proposed, its genus should be taken and divided by its **primary differences**. One of these differences that is predicated of the species should be joined to the genus, and one must see if it is "equated" <note>Coextensive; if the definition applies to all members of the species and only those members.</note> to the species. If it is equated, this will be its complete definition. If not, then the difference should be divided similarly into its own primary differences, and the one predicated of the species should be added to the previous ones, and one must check again if it is equated. Let this be done repeatedly until they are equated. 

And so it seems that a definition is nothing other than a **composition of divisions**. This is supported by the **Commentator** <note>Original: "commentator". This usually refers to Averroes, the influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher.</note> at the beginning of *On the Soul*: since it is manifest that there is some single mode or common way in which we inquire into what each thing is, we must ask what that is—whether it is from prior things like **demonstration**, or from posterior things like **division** as **Plato** felt, or whether there is some middle way like the **way of composition**, which is the collection of defining elements found through division and their composition, which **Aristotle** gave in the *Posterior [Analytics]*. 

It seems, therefore, that the kind of teaching by which a definition is found and extracted is the way of division itself, along with the collection and aggregation of the divided parts until it is equated to that which one intends to define. 

But although it seems that a definition is extracted better through the way of division than through any other way, a **doubt** still arises in this path, as **Aristotle** says. Because of this doubt, it does not seem that a definition is necessarily extracted from division. For it does not follow that when "animal," "walking," and "two-footed" are predicated of man as separate terms, they are also verified as a **joined predication**, according to the second book of *Perihermenias* <note>Aristotle's *De Interpretatione* (On Interpretation).</note>. For a man is signified separately as being "musical" and being "good," but it does not follow joined together that he is a "**good musician**." There does not remain...

<summary>This page explores whether definitions can be proven through logic, concluding that while formal syllogisms and induction fail, the "way of division" is a useful, if imperfect, method for constructing a definition by aggregating essential differences.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical investigation into whether a definition can be "demonstrated." Having concluded that a definition is not found through syllogisms or induction, the text now explores whether the "definition" itself constitutes a specific method of instruction—a "genus of doctrine"—particularly in the context of medical science.</meta>

<sig>a.ii</sig>
<meta>Double column gothic print; the catchword "e-" at the bottom of column 1 connects to "dicine" at the start of column 2, forming "medicine."</meta>

Therefore, there must be some way by which a **definition** shows something out of necessity, just as it reveals the hidden through the manifest. Consequently, the way of investigating a definition is not another "genus of doctrine" <term>genus doctrinae: a formal method of teaching or organizing knowledge</term> in the ordinary sense, taken strictly and for its own sake. **Galen**, considering this and seeing that a definition is often assumed as a principle in all arts, did not say that there is a genus of doctrine by which a definition is *found*, but rather he called the **exposition and division** of a definition—once it has been assumed—a genus of doctrine. 

And although **Aristotle** did not make mention of this genus of doctrine, he nonetheless clearly used it in many places within his various treatises on specific sciences. He seems to have remained silent on it because this genus of doctrine does not seem to declare something unknown through something known—as a logical conclusion does—or perhaps because it does not seem to be a "hunting" mode of definition. Aristotle stated that such a mode was either **division** or the **composition of divisions**, which is the "compositive" mode of defining. 

For here, he also speaks of the "divisive" mode of definition. Indeed, one takes a definition and divides it into **genus** and **differences** <note>In classical logic, a definition is made of a "genus" (a broad category) and "specific differences" (the traits that make the thing unique within that category).</note>, and then divides each difference into its various meanings, and each meaning into its specific types. This continues until a certain limit is reached, without dividing down to the most specific individuals or following every single detail as far as it might go. Therefore, just as there is a **composition** of a definition from diverse parts, so there is an **exposition** of a definition from parts already composed. Thus, it seems to be one and the same path. 

However, **Galen** posited this—namely, the division of a definition—as a genus of doctrine rather than its investigation and discovery. He did this because since most definitions are assumed in the sciences as starting principles, they do not need to be "found" through investigation, but rather "unpacked" through explanation. Or perhaps he did so because this genus of doctrine is not primarily used to deliver an entire science in a single, simultaneous order. Rather, it is used to list the general chapters of a science so that one might have a sort of mental map of the whole. For once these universal chapters are held, a person has an easy path toward the specific chapters and an easy memory of them. We do not, however, use it to declare specific hidden truths of a science as we do with other methods. 

Because of this, upon subtle inspection, it could be said that we use this method for **remembering**, not for learning or teaching. This is why Aristotle did not list it as a doctrine, even though he used it; for the "middle term" in a demonstration is either the definition of the subject or of the attribute, according to some. **Galen**, speaking more broadly, calls this a "doctrine." Or perhaps it is because we only need this type of doctrine to shorten the great length of the art. This was necessary in **medicine** above all other sciences, because it is longer than the others; and at the same time, there is a need to have it by heart for the sake of the practical work that comes from this teaching. Therefore, it is believable that it is only in medicine that this method is worthy of mention. Furthermore, since the definition that exists as the middle term of a demonstration belongs to the subject (as the more skilled thinkers hold), and since one assumes regarding the subject "what it is" and "what its name says," the same applies to the definition: nothing, therefore, will be proven. 

It remains now to clarify the aforementioned doctrine with an example. It is fitting to take what was right before [Galen's] eyes: which is to take the definition of **medicine**, and divide it as we said above, and explain everything whose understanding is required in each of the parts—in such a way, however, that one does not stray from the general heights.

And it should be divided as we said above, and everything that needs to be understood in each of its parts should be declared, yet in such a way that it does not decline from the general principles. Regarding this genus of doctrine, however, it is possible to have doubts. It seems like a certain **compositive** genus of terms, just as there is a **resolutive** genus of terms, so that they might correspond like "compositive" and "resolutive" doctrine. Some also say that this genus should be reduced to the compositive. 

Others say it is not an "ordinary" method, because the parts of the definition are reached through accidental properties and not through the essential principles of the thing—for those principles, in their own genus, do not have further principles. But I <note>The author/commentator.</note> agree with the more skilled experts that the compositive genus of definition is necessary, but it should not be "touched upon" <note>original: "tangi"</note> but rather "assumed" for two reasons. One is derived from the composition of a thing from its own principles. The other is that a goal is not extracted through just any genus; rather, the definition of medicine which this science intends is not sought, but assumed. And if it were sought, it would be found through the composition of its principles and causes derived from other sciences. For this reason, Galen compared the "definitive" method to the **resolutive**, but not to the **compositive**. 

But if someone were to say that this only holds true for the first thing undertaken—namely, medicine—and not for the things contained under it, it must be said (at least according to Galen's view) that he only pursues the **exposition or explanation** of the definition, not its investigation or discovery. Therefore, it was not his purpose to subject it to the compositive limit. Because of this, it should be known that the "descriptive" and "divisive" doctrine seem to differ from true ordinary doctrine (which is more the definitive-resolutive and especially the compositive). 

Indeed, these doctrines seem to be simple and ordinary because, as it appears, Aristotle and **Boethius** use the divisive method. **Haly Abbas** <note>An influential 10th-century Persian physician known for the 'Liber Regalis'.</note>, however, places both this and the "descriptive" method after the other three. The opposite is said by Haly and hinted at by Galen: that the descriptive and divisive are not "ordinary" because they do not extract the sought-after knowledge through accidental things. It should be said that these are only things as Galen and Haly wish: for whom the "compositive" is more proper, the "definitive" is somehow improper, and the "resolutive" is in the middle. 

How this is so has been declared from what was said before. It should be known, however, that some have wanted to reduce the "descriptive" to the "definitive," and the "divisive" to the "resolutive," saying that Galen only speaks of "ordinary" doctrines in comparison to "un-ordered" ones that are made through middle terms. However, saying this does not taste of the truth or the mind of Galen, since he himself rejects the "descriptive" method because it does not take the "best term" (which some call "substantial"), but instead takes an "accident" <note>In logic, an 'accident' is a property that isn't essential to what a thing is—like a person being tall.</note> from which notions, but not definitions, are made. 

But regarding the "divisive" method, one ought not to judge so simply. Since, according to Haly Abbas, division occurs in seven ways, he mentions one mode of division as being from species into individuals—though this did not please Boethius in his *Book of Divisions*. Accidental division is split into three modes: a subject into its accidents, an accident into its subjects, or an accident into other accidents. "Per se" division, he again separates into three modes: namely, the division...

<meta>This page continues a logical and medical investigation into the methods of instruction (doctrines). The previous page established that while Aristotle did not explicitly name "division" as a primary method of teaching, it is practically used to clarify definitions. This page explores how the four methods—division, resolution, composition, and definition—differ and overlap, particularly in medical diagnosis and scientific proof.</meta>

...of a genus into species, of an integrating whole into its parts, and of an equivocal <note>original: "equoce"; referring to a word with multiple meanings</note> term into its different significations. Among these, the division of a genus into species is an essential form of division. It acts as a certain mode for creating science, as it were—a method that perhaps assists the three previously mentioned doctrines, as will be shown. Regarding the point introduced earlier, it must be said that <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: "Az"; likely referring to the Persian physician Avicenna, whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook</note> holds that the divisive method is not truly an "ordinary" <note>In this context, "ordinary" means a standard, systematic method of teaching a science from start to finish.</note> doctrine. However, how it contributes to the other doctrines will become clear. Similarly, if **Aristotle** or **Boethius** uses it, they do not use it as a primary "ordinary" doctrine. In the same way, when **Haly Abbas** <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician</note> says that the doctrines are "whatever," he does not add the word "ordinary." Or, it may be said that division according to its many parts, and description according to all of them, are not simply ordinary doctrines—unless the division itself is accepted as a true definition—since those parts may remain hidden, as was shown previously.

It remains now to see how the four differ from one another and how they agree: namely, **division** (made through essentials), **composition**, **resolution**, and **definition**. It must be said that the divisive method differs from the resolutive and compositive because those two prove their points through the <term>effect</term> or the <term>cause</term> which they assume. This method [division], however, simply separates a genus into its essential parts without "proving" them; for example, "of animals, one kind is man, another is an ox." Yet they agree when a division is made for its own sake, because the resolutive method sometimes uses the divisive—for instance, when one effect is resolved into several causes, as appeared in the example of the resolution of an <term>opilation</term> <note>A medical term for a blockage or obstruction in the body's vessels or "pores."</note>. For a blockage is sometimes caused by humors, sometimes by a "cold complexion" <note>The "complexion" refers to the balance of qualities—hot, cold, moist, dry—in the body.</note>, and sometimes by a "stipticity" <note>A binding or contracting quality.</note> of the environment, such as mineral-heavy air, sulfurous water, or the like. It is clear that this is a mode of division, since it is the cutting of one thing into many. Similarly, resolution uses the compositive method when a cause is applied to several effects individually. But when one cause produces one effect simply, that is properly called **composition** or (as was said) **resolution**. 

Division also differs from **definition**, though they are related. It differs because a definition explains and makes known the thing defined through several terms joined together. Division, however, manifests what is contained in the thing divided with a certain degree of indeterminacy. But they agree because a definition sometimes uses division for its own sake, as will be shown. Likewise, the **definitive** method differs from the **resolutive** and **compositive** in this: those methods prove the unknown through the known, whereas the definitive method only unfolds into particulars. It agrees with them, however, because the definitive method does not use resolution first, unless there is some primary thing in the mind to be resolved—such as **medicine**—which it then defines. But afterward, it uses resolution when an effect is traced back to a single cause, or it uses composition when a cause produces a single effect. When an effect is traced to several causes (or vice versa), it then uses division. This is apparent when one says that "healthy" <note>original: "sany"</note> is spoken of in three ways: namely, the **body**, the **cause**, and the **sign**; and similarly for "sick" <note>original: "egrum"</note> and "neutral" <note>original: "neuty"; the Galenic state of being neither healthy nor sick.</note>. In this instance, the definitive method uses the doctrine of division. 

Regarding **description**, how it differs from and is related to the others is clear from this: it differs from definition because it often uses many "accidental" differences, and also because its genus or differences are accidental. It agrees, however, because it explains (though in a different way), and because some of its parts, like the genus or differences, can be essential—such as "vision" being the third difference. Thus, only the other three are properly "ordinary" doctrines.

It remains now to address the fourth main point: namely, to remove the objections raised against the determined truth. It must be said regarding the first and second points that the "ordinary" doctrines are best held in a group of three, and that not every science or method of teaching is called "ordinary" unless it is taken in a particular and proper order. To the third point, it must be said that there is such a thing as an ordinary doctrine, as has been shown, yet it is not necessary to know the "First Cause" <note>God</note> of that genus in every case. A superior and immediate cause within that specific genus is sufficient. Hence, the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> proved that one should always seek the highest cause within a specific category, not necessarily in the totality of existence. For example, a man builds because he is a "builder," and he is a builder according to the "art of building." One does not need to seek a cause beyond this; one should stop here. Or perhaps, as many believe, we can know nothing perfectly in this life since we are ignorant of the prior [divine] causes. 

To the next point, it must be said that there is one "ordinary" doctrine if it is taken in its most powerful form, as was declared earlier. Similarly, it has been shown how all arts consist of **resolution** according to reason. To the other point, it must be said that there is a "material identity" which does not make doctrines one or many; rather, it is "formal identity" that does so. The seventh and eighth points have already been clarified. To the eighth, it could also be said that although the definition and the thing defined are the same in subject, one is confused and implicit, while the other is determined and explicit. For a definition is a judgment and exposition of the being of the thing defined, since it is the reasoning <note>original: "ratio"</note> signified by the name.

Regarding the ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth points, what should be said was shown earlier. Specifically, however, it must be said that there are really only two kinds of **demonstration**: "demonstration of the fact" <note>original: "quia"; proving that something is true from its effects</note> and "demonstration of the reasoned fact" <note>original: "propter quid"; proving why something is true from its causes</note>. For these are the same as demonstrations of "cause and being" <note>original: "causae et esse"</note>, just as species are the same as their genus. A "simple" demonstration occurs when the cause and effect are equally well-known, which happens in mathematics but rarely in the natural sciences. Hence, the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, commenting on Aristotle's *Physics*</note> says: "If it happens that what is known to us is also known to nature, then the demonstrations in this science will be of 'cause and being.' But if what is known to us is not known to nature—being posterior in existence rather than prior—then the demonstrations given in that science will be through 'signs' <note>i.e., through effects</note>, and not 'simple' demonstrations." In natural things, the things that are known to us are not the things known simply (i.e., by nature), which is the opposite of how it works in mathematics.

### DIFFERENTIA IX.

<margin>1</margin>
**That human nature has not been weakened from what it was seen to be in ancient times.** First, because whatever is generated is generated either from something finite or infinite. It is not from the infinite, because the infinite cannot be given, as stated in the <term>Physics, Book III</term> <note>original: "pbi. iii."; Aristotle's Physics</note> and in the first book of *On the Heavens and the World*. Thus, in the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*: "Nature flees the infinite." Therefore, it is generated from the finite. This could not happen if nature always proceeded by weakening in the process of generation. For if it did, it would have ceased long ago, according to the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> who assert the eternity of the world; and similarly according to the discourses of the religious laws regarding the world's generation, it would either have ceased entirely or a manifest weakness would now appear, since a great space of time is placed between the world’s generation and now—whether you wish to consider this according to the Indians, or the Persians, or the Jews, or the Christians. Furthermore, if nature were weakened, this would either be on the part of the "superior nature" or the "inferior nature." It is not from the superior nature, because the higher things <note>the celestial bodies</note> are perpetual and incorruptible, possessing an optimal and most perfect life through all eternity, which no external things distract from their order, nor does time cause them to grow old, as stated in the first book of *On the Heavens and the World* and the book *On the World*. Nor is it on the part of the inferior nature—for example, by reason of the parent—for generation does not come from the substance of the parent, but from their "superfluity" <note>referring to semen or reproductive fluid</note>, so that the generator is not destroyed by the emission of their substance and thus generation would turn into nothing.

Again, every natural motion and order of nature is strengthened at its end, as stated in the first book of *On the Heavens*; since it attains its goal more fully, it is more perfect. The life of nature consists in a certain natural motion and order; therefore, it will be strengthened as it tends toward its end. This is also according to the word of the Psalmist: "If in powers there be eighty years, and more of them are labor and sorrow" <note>Psalm 90:10</note>. Therefore, human nature has not been weakened since ancient times. On the contrary, in ancient times men were very long-lived, large in body, most robust in strength, and very beautiful, such as the giants. Hence **Solinus** <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, 3rd-century Roman geographer</note> wonders: "For the succession of our offspring is corrupted by the passage of time through the diminishment of those being born."

Likewise, that which is in the final part of its period or age is weakened. For this is its nature, since its path is toward corruption. But such is the age of the present moment, namely the seventh and last, according to the lawgivers since Christ. Hence the Apostle says: "We are those upon whom the ends of the age have come" <note>1 Corinthians 10:11</note>. Furthermore, this entire lower world is constantly aging and being corrupted; hence in the first book of the *Meteorology*, it is noted that where there is now dry land, there was once sea. But modern human nature is far distant from its principle, even according to those who believe the world was generated—for instance, from Adam or from God. The **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher</note> and Boethius also in *On the Two Natures* accepted nature in four modes:

1.  **Most generally**, for every thing—whether substance or accident—of which this is the definition: "Nature is that which, since it exists, can be grasped by the intellect in any way."
2.  **Commonly**, as it is said of substances alone; and then it is either that which can act or that which can suffer <note>be acted upon</note>; for substance is twofold, corporeal and incorporeal.
3.  **Properly**, for corporeal things, which is the "principle of motion" in itself and not by accident <note>Aristotle's classic definition</note>.
4.  **Most properly**, for the diversity of nature, as we say one nature belongs to gold and another to silver; this is the "specific difference" <term>the essential quality that defines a species</term> in forming a species.

Human nature is indeed denoted by "man," which contains within itself the participation of being human. **Debility** <note>weakness or decline</note>, however, is said to occur when a person departs far from the strengths formerly held for actions, or when a shorter time of life remains. **Antiquity** refers to that which is distant in time from its beginning.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that—as the discourses of the laws and especially the Mosaic laws resonate—human nature has been weakened from what existed in ancient times. A sign of this is that we hear of men from the generation of the world and those produced around that time who were of the longest-lasting life, as is gathered from **Moses** in the book of Genesis. **Adam** lived 930 years. **Methuselah** lived 969 years. **Noah** lived 700 with **Abraham** and others. Conversely, those after that longevity were diminished, such as Moses, David, and Aaron with the Levites, as appears in the same place where it says: "I will not permit my spirit to remain in man, because he is flesh, beyond 120 years."

This is indeed the "natural life" of man, even according to the **astrologers**; for these are the "greater years" of the Sun <note>In medieval astrology, the Sun was assigned a 'great cycle' of 120 years</note>. But now, from that limit, the human age is diminished; it now commonly extends barely to a space of 80 years. And because of this, the natural life would be 35 years <note>referring to the peak of vitality before decline</note>. And so **Muhammad** <note>original: "Machometus"</note> said that the average life is between 60 and 70 years. In the "Time of Grace" <note>the Christian era</note>, the Commentator flourished around the year 1150, as he indicates in the second book of *On the Heavens and the World*.

Furthermore, the same is persuaded by reason. Since human nature could not be saved in the individual, it is saved in the **species** <note>referring to Aristotle's *On the Soul* and *On the Generation of Animals*</note>. However, this safety and permanence is not simple and through itself, but by accident, and mixed with an external corruptible thing, as considered through the use of the **six non-natural things** <term>six factors like diet, sleep, and exercise that physicians believed governed health</term> established in the present life. In the future life, however, it is incorruptible and perpetual, remaining as if in itself without "nectar" <note>likely meaning without need for external sustenance</note> and needing no universal external aid against corruption.

Thus it is that it is much better to be in oneself and in incorruption than to remain in corruption and through another. And so God—whose role it is to dispose all things in a certain order (Metaphysics, Book 12)—produced nature so that the preceding debility might finally end; so that at last, with the corruptible and accidental life left behind, we may enjoy the substantial and perpetual life in the heavens with Him.

And so, as touched upon, since we are those upon whom the "ends of the ages" have come, human nature now rightly exists as weakened according to the laws: both in its strengths and measured by a shorter space of time.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that since he discusses natural things—which He [God] produced with a certain preceding will—nothing should be scrutinized at present regarding His miracles and will, since laws possess only the power of persuasion (Politics, Book 2). The **astronomical** way is divided into three parts. The first is taken from the part of the **fixed stars** existing in the "eighth heaven" <term>the sphere of the stars beyond the planets</term> and the images, almost allegorical, placed there by the **Indians**, with the heavens and zodiacs marked or imagined in them. In this cycle, according to certain **Stoics** and **Pythagoreans**, all things return as they were before. Or whether it moves in 70 years, or 60, as is more commonly held today; or whether one posits what Ptolemy calls the motion in opposition to the ninth [sphere], a certain retardation of the eighth sphere because it does not entirely follow the motion of the "first mover" <term>the outermost sphere that drives all others</term> due to a small distance, as **Alpetragius** <note>al-Bitruji</note> and **Abu Isaac** posited.

I have found, however, in modern times, that the "head of Aries" <note>the vernal equinox point</note> of the mobile [zodiac], and similarly of Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn, [has moved from] the immobile points by 10 degrees and 22 minutes in the **Year of Grace 1303**, in which I, **Peter of Abano**, constructed this book. Because of this, the astronomical judges today, more truly, add 10 degrees and 22 minutes to the motion of the eighth sphere they seek—the true motion in the ninth sphere from the motion previously found by calculation in the eighth—so that by such an act, the heads of the equinoctial and tropical signs of the mobile zodiac occur directly under the heads of the aforementioned immobile zodiac.

Since men then used a proper administration of diet, and foods tending toward a certain "thickness," their natures were strong, their **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health and temperament</note> were compact and resistant to being purged. 

And because of this, Hippocrates was able to use strong medicines or strongly-purging agents for their evacuations, such as **white hellebore**, **black hellebore**, **euphorbium**, **mezereon**, and others <note>These are all potent, often toxic, botanical purgatives</note>. Because of this, it is said in the first book of the *Practica*: In the lands of the Turks, there is a great quantity of the sickness of **scammony** <note>original: "scamonee"; a harsh resinous laxative. But in modern times, because men use a disordered regimen and thin, liquid, and delicate foods, they generate a "sparse" and soluble composition of the body and "fluid" humors. Since their natures are thus weakened and the humors are made easily dissolvable along with the spirits, they do not tolerate such medicines as the stronger people of old did. From this, the meaning of the words of **Serapio**, **Alexander**, and **Mesue** <note>Key authorities in the Greco-Arabic medical tradition</note> becomes clear.

The third cause is taken from the manner of human generation <note>reproduction</note> observed in ancient and modern times. For anciently, male and female were not joined except at a perfect age, when the members of generation were fully integrated. Even now, the **Frisians** <note>original: "friſones"; people of the coastal Netherlands/Germany, often cited in medieval texts as being tall, healthy, and traditionally moral</note> observe this, as they have not yet become (as has been said) "associates of gluttony and lust." This is also demonstrated in the motion of illumination from a candle. Since, therefore, human nature and its order with others is like a certain circle—concerning generation, whence the 17th of the *Problems* <note>Referring to the *Problemata*, a collection of scientific questions attributed to Aristotle; Problem 17 discusses the circularity of human life and generation</note> says human affairs are a circle—it must be said that such motion does not grow stronger at the end, but rather remains in the same disposition, or is altered only slightly, as its causes excite it. Regarding the fourth point, it should be said that that time is not far distant from us; and if it were far distant from the generation of the world, so that a great variety had been introduced, or perhaps not a small one as declared before, this variation has been added to such an extent that the saying of the Psalmist <note>A reference to Psalm 90:10: "The days of our years are threescore years and ten," noting the shortened human lifespan</note> is commonly and everywhere verified today. Thus, let this be said concerning how much can reasonably be understood of this matter according to the cleverness of the wise of the world, without detracting anything from the divine wisdom prescribed above, but rather confirming it through all things, since it alone is the truth and the life. In this matter, however, some perverse men—wishing or rather being unable to hear me—tried to vex me for a long time; from whose hands the aforementioned truth has praise-worthily rescued me, finally even by the arrival of an apostolic command <note>A personal note from the author, likely Roger Bacon, referring to his imprisonment and the eventual protection or mandate he received from Pope Clement IV</note>.

### DIFFERENCE 10

<margin>1</margin>
That a person who is a physician, through the knowledge of <term>astronomy</term><note>In the Middle Ages, "astronomia" and "astrologia" were often used interchangeably to mean both the study of the stars and their influence on Earth</note>, cannot contribute to the health of the sick is shown by **Albubatir** <note>original: "Albubatir"; the Latin name for Abu Bakr al-Hasan ibn al-Khasib (9th century), a Persian astrologer</note> in his *Book of Nativities*, where he says: in any given hour there ascend 23,000 <term>robaoth</term><note>A unit of measure or count, likely derived from the Hebrew or Arabic for 'ten-thousand'</note>, each of which contains 10,000 moments. Every moment has its own color, taste, and nature in its own way; and it is so subtle that it is not within human sense to perceive or investigate it, nor does anyone know it except God alone. If, therefore, celestial motion cannot be perceived by man, its significance cannot be organized for the benefit of the sick. Furthermore, a *robaoth* contains the space of 10,000 stadia. Furthermore, the **Commentator** <note>original: "cōmētator"; referring to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the most famous medieval commentator on Aristotle</note> on the 12th book of the *Metaphysics* says that the astrology of our time is nothing, nor is there any being in it; rather, it is suitable for calculation, not for actual existence. But that which does not exist cannot contribute to the sick. Again, there are three things that fall under the consideration of the physician: the cause, the disposition (or the body), and the sign. Their nature is such that the physician arrives at a knowledge of the three dispositions—health, sickness, and <term>neutrality</term><note>A Galenic concept where a body is neither fully healthy nor diseased, but in an intermediate state</note>—through the cause, as if from prior things; but through the sign, he identifies them as if from later and sensible things. But neither by reason of the cause, nor by reason of the sign, can he benefit the sick. This is shown by the fact that effect and cause are proportional (*Physics*, Book II); likewise, the sign and the thing signified are proportional. This does not seem to happen here in the case of cause and caused, nor in sign and signified; because the cause and the sign <note>the stars</note> are incorruptible, perpetual, and indeterminate like the higher things. But the caused and the signified <note>the human body</note> are like these things and the sick; for the corruptible and the incorruptible differ by more than just their genus (*Metaphysics*, Book X). Furthermore, these things are indeterminate and can never be determined for the health of the sick. For if they were determined—since celestial bodies imprint upon these lower things through motion and light, according to the heavens and the world—it would be either by reason of motion or by reason of light. It is not by motion, because the superior circular motion ceases in the sphere of fire, as noted in the 26th of the *Problems* and in the *Introduction to the Spherical Art*. In the highest places, no winds are created by the mountains, as on Mount Athos or Olympus and such. The sign of this is that those who leave behind ashes from burnt sacrifices find them the following year unchanged, just as they had been before, because wind and rain are not generated in those places. If, therefore, motion ceases in the fire and below it, it cannot be applied again here to anything for the benefit of the sick. Neither can it be determined on the part of light, because celestial bodies are round, having the form of round mirrors, expanding light in every direction. For from any point, infinite rays are carried outward. But those things which gather rays and determine them to a specific place are <term>concave</term><note>original: "p'cauua"; the author argues that because stars are convex/spherical, they scatter light rather than focusing it like a medicinal lens</note>, as the authors on perspective testify. Because of this, proportion and determination cannot occur. Again, if there are some celestial bodies that contribute to the health of the infirm, there are others that harm. For Jupiter and Venus are benign and "fortunes," but Saturn and Mars are "unfortunate," while the others are neutral in nature. Therefore, because he <note>the physician</note> cannot benefit if he is unable to prohibit their effects. And it is confirmed by this: that they dispose the air in this way or that, which we are obliged to use; for we can choose or avoid other materials, but it is impossible to escape from the surrounding air; we must necessarily use it. If, indeed, there is an inevitable necessity, then the ninth point of "Genius" <note>likely referring to a specific technical section or authority</note> applies. Behold, the mobile <term>zodiac</term> has receded from the immobile zodiac by 10 degrees and 23 minutes, as those more expert now testify; this is a difference from the ancients, which some now encounter with the motion of "access and recess" <note>the theory of trepidation, an attempt to explain the precession of the equinoxes</note> of the eighth sphere. When, therefore, an influence flows from the superior things directly into this place, so that the head of a sign of the mobile zodiac is under the head of a sign of the immobile zodiac, and the distance is already so great, in one way it will happen to be beneficial (according to the mobile zodiac), but in the second way (according to the immobile) it will be harmful; especially when two signs of opposing natures exist one after the other. Because of this, it will not benefit more than it harms. Again, the moment of birth cannot be known, since the heavens undergo a great transformation from what they were in nearly a moment of time, as has been said of the first motion. Because of this, a great variety exists in the recipient from what was there before. Similarly, the moment of birth is not known even within a large part of an hour, especially since the birth of the infant is often slow. This is supported by the fact that the stars considered by astrologers are only 1,029; but the others are infinite, which also have being and operation (*Metaphysics*, Book II). Since, therefore, the physician acting as an astrologer does not know these...

...will not be able to contribute. Therefore, a physician who is not an **astrologer** <note>In the medieval period, "astrology" and "astronomy" were often used interchangeably to describe the study of how celestial movements affected the human body and the natural world.</note> will not be able to contribute to the health of the sick. On the opposite side are the opinions of the philosophers, astrologers, and physicians.

As <term>David</term> <note>Likely referring to the *Liber de Causis*, a philosophical text attributed in the Middle Ages to "David the Jew" (Avendauth) or Aristotle.</note> says concerning causes: "The primary cause influences its effect more than the universal secondary cause." But celestial bodies, though entirely separate, are the causes of these lower <note>earthly</note> things, as all the wise agree. Because of this, they work most powerfully. By understanding their operation, a physician who is also an astrologer will be able to contribute twice as much. For a wise man, when he knows how to liken and harmonize superior things to inferior ones, will verify the judgments of the stars in these lower matters—so says <term>Haly Abenragel</term> <note>Al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham or Haly Abenragel, an influential 11th-century Arab astrologer whose works were standard textbooks for European doctors.</note>. Furthermore, whatever can help and remove harm can contribute to the health of the sick. But even an astrologer alone can do this, according to that saying of the **Centiloquium** <note>A famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy.</note>: "An excellent astrologer will be able to prohibit much evil which is to come according to the stars." And a wise soul thus assists the work of nature, just as a **planter** strengthens the natural forces of the earth. How much more so, then, when joined with a physician! Therefore, a physician who is an astrologer contributes to the health of the sick.

Regarding the first point, one must know that when it is asked whether someone "being a physician" etc. [contributes], I understand this as a form inherent specifically to the physician. Indeed, the underlying subject, as indicated by this participle "being," is one in which two forms are inherent: namely, medicine and astrology. This implies both the matter or the composite whole, and not just the form. What a "physician" is has been defined before: whoever knows the science of medicine. However, **astronomy** or **astrology** is the law or reason that considers the celestial figures and motions in themselves and in their effects universally. Some, assigning a difference between them, wish to call "astronomy" the science of motions and "astrology" the science of judgments—though it is not necessary to distinguish them, for they seem to mean the same thing. For astronomy is named from *astron* <note>Greek for "star"</note> and *nomos* <note>Greek for "law"</note>, which means law; while astrology is from *astron* and *logos* <note>Greek for "reason" or "speech"</note>. This description also touches upon the two parts of astrology: one which is called the science of quantities, figures, ordering, and motions of the bodies—the science of the whole through its primary differences—and the second part through its effects and so on.

The other part mentioned is called the **science of judgments** <note>This refers to "judicial astrology," the practice of making specific predictions for individuals or medical cases.</note>, which is twofold: one is the introduction to judgments; the other is called "practice," which is again separated into four parts. One is about **revolutions**; the second is about **nativities** <note>Birth charts calculated for the moment of a person's birth.</note> and their revolutions; the third is about **interrogations** <note>Answering specific questions based on the time the question is asked.</note>; the fourth is about **elections** <note>Choosing the most auspicious time to begin a task, such as performing a surgery or taking a remedy.</note>, to which the science of "images" <note>Astrological talismans.</note> is also subordinate. The part concerning revolutions has three sections: one is about the 120 conjunctions; another is about the revolution of the year considered according to the entry of the Sun into the "head of Aries" <note>The Spring Equinox, the start of the astrological year.</note>, or taken from the preceding conjunction or opposition of the Sun; the third is about the change of times, such as rains. I have previously shown the difference of this as an "illuminator." By "contribute," I mean here to help in any common way—whether that help is in explaining those things said about astrology in medicine, or in applying...

---

...properly the three instruments of medicine to the three aforementioned dispositions, or even by prognosticating in whatever way.

Regarding the second point, one must know, according to **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian scholar and the most famous astrologer of the Middle Ages.</note> in the first book of his *Introduction*, that there was an opinion held by some physicians who boast of their medical science so that they might acquire it without the science of the stars. They claim it contributes nothing universally to the mastery of medicine. This happens to them for four reasons: First, so that they may appear to know everything, providing a consolation for their own ignorance. They become like certain errors in natural philosophy, mocking those powers they are most unable to explain and do not dare to attempt to predict. To others, this happens so they may quiet their own intellects, saying that the science of the stars cannot be understood. These become like **Xenophanes of Colophon** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who speculated on the nature of the Earth.</note>, who posited that the earth rested upon an infinite base downwards so that seekers would not have to trouble themselves looking further into the heavens and the world. Since an infinite thing lacks a perceivable cause, the intellect does not traverse it. Others say this because they have seen so-called astrologers, or those who are both physicians and astrologers, err in their judgments. Because of such people, the science of astrology should not be blamed, for those who judge thus are not astrologers but liars and diviners. To some, this view seemed correct because they felt that the sayings of physicians should always be followed, even when a conflict arises between the judgment of medicine and astrology—not knowing how to bring these apparent differences into harmony. However, those who follow medicine as they ought, and diligently inspect the sayings of their elders, grant that this science of astronomy is not only useful but extremely necessary to medicine. This will be proved in the third part of our discussion, and those first objectors will be refuted in the fourth.

Regarding the third point, it must be known: First, that the celestial bodies act upon these lower things. Second, in how many and what ways. Third, that a physician who is an astrologer can have knowledge of this. Fourth, that astrology contributes to the health of the patient. Fifth, in which specific ways. The first is shown here: because by necessity, this lower and continuous motion is linked to the superior movers, so that all its power is governed from there, as touched on before. This is also what the astrologers said; hence, at the beginning of the **Centiloquium**: <note>original: "Mundanorum mutatio ad hoc & ad illud corporum celestium mutatione est. X ideo causas rerum rimaturus. primo celestia contemplate."</note> "The change of worldly things, in this way and that, is due to the change of the celestial bodies. Therefore, he who would search out the causes of things should first contemplate the heavens." Because of this, the Nine Judges say: "All prediction of worldly birth depends on the planets and their signs, just as iron depends on the magnet stone." Whence **Messahallah** <note>An 8th-century Jewish-Arab astronomer who helped design the city of Baghdad.</note> says in his *Epistle*: "The work of the planets in this world is similar to the magnet stone and iron." This same thing is shown by rational arguments, since (as in the 2nd and 10th books of the *Metaphysics*) whenever a nature is found multiplied in many things while existing according to one uniform reason, it is necessary to trace this back to a cause that is more united and determined, so that at last all multitude may be reduced to a single unity. Now, the nature of heat and cold and the rest is found multiplied...
