<meta>This page continues the scholarly argument for the necessity of astrology in medicine. Having established that celestial bodies are primary causes, the text now details the specific physical mechanisms (motion, light, and "complexion") through which the stars influence the earthly realm and the human body.</meta>

...according to one univocal reason: why it is necessary to trace it back to a further cause. This, however, cannot be unless it is a body and not an intelligence, according to the principles of philosophy, since nature does not commit a leap in its operations. Rather, it proceeds secretly from one extreme to the other through a medium, so that the boundary—that is, the end and the middle—is hidden by continuity, as stated in the seventh book of the **History of Animals** <note>original: "hystoriam vii"; Aristotle’s *History of Animals* was a foundational text for medieval biology.</note>. Furthermore, every sufficient cause that is not impeded in itself impresses its effect, and by necessity upon the subject prone to it. Such a cause is a celestial body, since it is perpetual and incorruptible throughout all eternity, leading a life most sufficient unto itself and never growing old, according to the book **On the Heavens and the World** <note>original: "celi & mundi"; referring to Aristotle's *De Caelo*.</note>. And it is confirmed because the motion of celestial bodies is a divine thing, which no thing in the world can disturb in any way, since it is necessary and cannot be otherwise, according to the **Quadripartitum** <note>original: "quadriptiti"; the *Tetrabiblos* of Ptolemy, the primary textbook for astrology.</note>. And similarly, such a great cause can almost always dispose even an undisposed matter toward itself.

Again, those things which are essentially ordered according to before and after, and cause and effect, necessarily act one upon the other. Such things are, in common, inferior things in relation to superior things; as **Aristotle** <note>original: "az."</note> says, because when the posterior is removed, that which is prior is not taken away, but the reverse is true. Because of this, superior things will impress themselves upon these inferior things. Therefore, according to this, it should be known that superior things are seen to impress upon these inferior things in three ways: one of which is universal, another particular, and the third is intermediate.

The **universal** way is perfected through motion and light; for superior bodies act universally upon these inferior things in these two ways. Hence, according to the second book of **On the Heavens and the World**, heat and light are generated from celestial bodies by the rubbing of the air from their own movement. For motion is naturally suited to ignite both wood and stones and iron, so that lead arrows may melt <note>This was a common medieval scientific belief derived from Aristotle, suggesting that the friction of an arrow moving through the air could generate enough heat to melt lead.</note>. Experience shows that when motion in superior bodies is more frequent and uniformly tending toward one part, it is made effective—such as when the motion of diversity comes with the motion of longitude. This occurs when the planets are "direct," and the air is changed toward heat. However, when the motion of diversity is contrary to the motion of longitude—as when a planet is **retrograde**—because the motion is weakened, it is disposed toward coldness and moisture.

That they also work through **light** is shown by **Aristotle**, since in the conjunction of stars, with their light multiplied at the same time—like many reflecting mirrors according to the inferior region placed beneath them—we perceive the air to be changed toward heat. In their separation, with the light divided, we feel the contrary happen. Because of this, according to the fourth book of **On the Parts of Animals**, the nights of the full moon are warmer because of the light of the moon. For the moon—like a mirror positioned opposite, according to **Haly Abenragel** <note>original: "baly beben ragel"; an influential Arab astrologer.</note>, receiving light from the sun on all sides according to the part exposed to us, and like another sun at that time—transfuses light into these inferior things. Thus, this is verified not only in conjunction, but also in the aspects, and especially in opposition and the trine, since then more rays are sent from one to the other from opposite sides.

The **intermediate** mode of operating is that by which they act through their **complexion** <note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>. For certain stars are said to be cold and dry, such as **Saturn**, regardless of what the **Commentator** <note>original: "commētator"; referring to Averroes, the primary commentator on Aristotle.</note> says in the second book of *On the Heavens and the World*—namely, that the stars do not in truth produce coldness, but rather heats similar to each of the elements. The Commentator says this even more expressly to himself in *The Substance of the Orb*. Certain stars are hot and moist, such as **Jupiter**, etc. And the fixed stars obtain these same complexions along with the planets, according to the *Quadripartitum*. However, I understand "complexion" not as existing in them formally, but effectively; otherwise, they would be composed of contrary elements and thus be corruptible. Hence, in the book *On the Heavens and the World*, **Aristotle** agrees with the ancients who placed the celestial body as a fifth essence <note>The "quintessence" or aether, which was believed to be incorruptible and distinct from the four earthly elements.</note> or a nature existing for itself. And the Commentator says: "We believe what the Chaldeans said, that the heaven is a [divine] nature," for he says that philosophy was perfect in their time, just as in the time of **Aristotle**, since these same opinions return through infinite cycles.

Because it is thus "complexioned," it acts effectively on these inferior things, just as such a motion heats effectively and not formally, and as wine intoxicates, even though the wine itself is neither hot nor drunk. The complexion of all the stars together, as in the *Quadripartitum*, is drawn from the complexion of the planets; it tends toward heat and moisture, or like the human complexion. Since superior things are ordered toward these inferior things, it happens by a certain accidentality and secondary intention, as will be declared in the first chapter of the "Differences." They are indeed more ordered toward man. For according to the first "Difference," from the heat and dryness of the heart, the heat and moisture of the liver, and the coldness and moisture of the brain, a certain "co-alternation" is established; when these are proportioned and weighed against each other, there results a complexion also tending toward heat and moisture, which physicians call the "temperament of justice" <note>A medical term for the ideal, healthy balance of humors in the human body.</note>. So also in superior things, the heat of Jupiter, Mars, and the Sun exceeds the coldness of Saturn; and Venus is tempered in coldness with the Moon, so that heat predominates. Similarly, the great moisture of the Moon and Venus (being near to us) and of Jupiter exceeds the dryness of Saturn, Mars, and the Sun (the Sun not being vehemently dry, since it is the source of the greatest heat and life). For there is no life of living things, after God, except through the Sun and the Moon, as **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer.</note> says in his *Sada*. Similarly, it happens in the fixed stars, since they obtain complexions similar to the planets, as has been said.

---

Thus, therefore, the complexion of all the stars is, in a certain way, ordered toward human nature, so that it tends toward heat and moisture. 

The **particular** mode is a certain stellar influx bestowed upon each individual, almost differently from every other, by their own birth or by the "revolution" of the same. And therefore we see that **Saturn** and **Mars**, although they are simply "malefics" and have the power to take away years from the **Alcocoden** <note>The Alcocoden (or Giver of Life) is the planet that determines the length of a person's life in a natal chart.</note>, nevertheless, when they themselves are the Alcocoden—that is, the givers of the forms of life—they will grant their minor, middle, or major years according to their own fortunateness. This also happens more so in the other planets. And therefore every planet, according to the diversity of the birth and the revolution, exists as a "fortune" for one person and a "malefic" for another. And this mode is so singular and appropriated that even the "medium," since it is not receptive to this impression, is not rendered by the same...

<meta>This page continues the argument for the scientific validity of astrology. Having previously discussed the physical necessity of celestial influence, the author now addresses the epistemological status of astrology—how we can "know" the stars—and the limits of human intellect in interpreting their signs.</meta>

...effect. Just as a torpedo fish <note>original: "torpigo"; an electric ray fish. This is a classical scientific example of "action at a distance" where the fish numbs the fisherman through the rod.</note> numbs the hand of a fisherman and not the net, according to **Alexander the Peripatetic** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> in the first book of his *Meteors*. Regarding the beginning of this, it must be known how one who exists in the world can know these impressions and their modes in these lower realms. For science is an intellectual habit elicited from demonstration; such a habit can be acquired by the intellect from the celestial bodies, since the science of the stars possesses all the conditions sufficiently required for a true science. Indeed, it takes its demonstrations from the science of number and measure, as stated in the first book of the **Almagest** <note>Ptolemy’s foundational work on astronomy.</note>, which is the fourth difference <note>This refers to a specific section or classification within the text.</note>. Its subject matter is also fixed, perpetual, and unalterable, and in a way belongs to those things which are abstracted from matter, yet are entirely sensible. Therefore, **Ptolemy** in the same place prefers this science to natural science, since the latter deals with things that are changing, generated, and corruptible, of which we cannot have certain knowledge; and similarly to metaphysics, since those things are remote from the senses and transcend the power of our intellect. For in this way, the intellect relates to the most manifest things in nature—that is, the Intelligences and God—just as the **eye of a night-owl** relates to the light of the sun <note>A famous Aristotelian metaphor: just as an owl is blinded by the bright sun, the human mind is overwhelmed by the "brightest" or most divine truths.</note>. Furthermore, since science, according to **Galen**, is acquired not only from reason but also from experience—which according to **Aristotle** exists as something sensible received through organic powers—and since the sense of sight makes us know many things regarding astrology, we are able to receive knowledge from it through experience accepted from the senses. This is especially possible because the stars are perpetual and immutable. And even if our senses cannot reach some of them, this flow then ascends to the universal, and the principle of science flourishes by the vigor of the intellect.

### On the Extent of Astrological Knowledge

But further, it must be seen how far the knowledge of these things extends. Regarding this, it should be said that just as 
<margin>G.</margin> 
**Galen** distinguishes in many places that there is a twofold knowledge in medicine—one which is certain, and another which is an artificial conjecture accepted according to judgment and bordering on the truth—so too it happens in **judicial astrology** <note>The branch of astrology concerned with making specific predictions about human affairs and events.</note>. This is because the part of astrology concerning the motions of the stars is more certain than this interpretive part. Therefore, **Abū Ma'shar** <note>original: "Alhuasar"; the influential Persian astrologer Albumasar.</note> in the introduction of his *Introductory Work*, defining the astrologer, says that he shall be wise in the being of the planets and their significance, and a mediator of those things which are done by them from a known time, in his own time, and in future and infinite time. In explaining this, he says that the stars signify every thing that is in this world; yet it is impossible for us to know the whole of it because of the weakness of our intellect. For the stars signify the things of this world in three ways. 

The first of these is subtle and deep, to the extent that it cannot be comprehended by science because of the near infinity of individual things and their signs, such as the natures and specific accidents of all individuals. Because of this, the verification of that which was judged happens in the fourth [place]. In every single hour, twenty-four thousand <unclear>moments</unclear> arise, as stated in the third book *On Ingenuity*, which can neither be made clear nor written in a book, nor spoken by anyone. It is a single thing, namely the true quantity of each particular...

---

The **second mode** is that the astrologer can know the significance over a single species, or over the number of nations of a certain city and similar things; yet he cannot have the precise quality or number and quantity of the significance. 

There is also a **third mode** by which we know the quality and quantity from the significance of things over them, such as genera, species, elements, and their transmutations within themselves and in determined individuals—determined, however, by descending through application. Therefore, the judicial science of things is said to be very difficult; both because of the many things that support it—since one cannot give judgments according to the complexion of the stars unless he well knows the power of the soul and the natural complexion <note>term: <term>complexion</term> (the specific balance of humors—blood, phlegm, bile—in an individual).</note>, as mentioned in the **Centiloquium** <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy.</note>. 

Wherefore **Haly** the commentator <note>Haly Abenragel or Haly Rodan, famous medieval commentators on Ptolemy.</note> says: "This part of the science is better than all the parts contained in this science; the astrologer who knows it well deserves to be called a physician." For this judicial science is comparable and related to the astrology of motions, to natural science, and to medicine. For through the first, the disposition of the heaven and the locations are hunted; through the latter, however, one must know all matter. Furthermore, it is difficult to receive the significations of the conjunction of stars, even when considered internally, and especially when they disagree with one another. Similarly, from the mode of applying the superior and universal to the inferior and particular, it is necessary to bring down that which is universal through due means, having added many circumstances. Also, because of the instability and mutation of the matter upon which judgment is passed, the astrologer at the beginning of the *Centiloquium* ought to put forward a matter not specifically but universally—just like one who looks at a thing from a long distance. For his knowledge is according to matter and not through the form; knowledge of the former is doubtful, but of the form it is certain, since the form is always unvarying in its path, adhering continually to one order. For this reason, **Masha'allah** <note>original: "Mesahalach"; an 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer and astronomer.</note> says not without merit in his epistle: "Know that the science of the stars is very grave, and the most worthy thing that could be known from it is the whole—that is, the universal or the plural—such as the revolutions of the years and the rest." 

Nevertheless, when we have known these universals, we will be able to descend to individualized particulars, just as in other sciences concerning sensible matter. For example, a physician works in medicine by healing not "man" in general, but **Callias** or **Socrates** <note>Standard philosophical names used like "John Doe."</note>. For this reason, although in other sciences a man needs much study, inquiry, and experience above others, in this science he needs an admirable and divine knowledge. 

Next, it should be known that one can know the works done in these lower things in a twofold way by descending properly from the aforementioned universals to the complexions of particulars. First, through a certain universal science: for some of the planets are "fortunes" and happy, such as **Jupiter**, **Venus**, and also the **Moon** and the **Sun** by aspect; others are "unfortunates" and unhappy, such as **Saturn**, **Mars**, and the **Sun** by conjunction. Toward these, **Mercury**, as if indifferent, often inclines further. Therefore, since the fortunes induce prosperous effects in these lower things, and the unfortunates [induce adverse ones]...

It cites major authorities like Ptolemy, Galen, and Abū Ma'shar to explain the three modes of astrological influence and the role of the "fortunate" and "unfortunate" planets.</summary>

...but [the influence] is hers: and the Moon is made the deputy. You have a similarity with the body in its operation. In the **Centiloquium** <note>original: "centilogo"; referring to the *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy.</note> it is therefore said by astrologers that she gives her own disposition to all the planets—that is, she renders herself disposed to receive the impressions of the other planets. If **Saturn** <term>Saturn</term><note>In medieval astrology, Saturn was considered the "Great Infortune," associated with cold, dryness, and chronic illness.</note> opposes her, joined with other infortunes, or looking upon her, or if she is placed in the **combustion of the Sun** <term>combustion</term><note>A planet is "combust" when it is so close to the Sun that its own power is said to be "burnt up" or hidden by the Sun's rays.</note>, or located in "evil" signs, the astrologer can judge a common harm upon any of the sick. This is because a universal cause is not hindered. For sick bodies, because of their nobility and the privation of their own "king" <note>The "king" here refers to the *virtus regitiva* or the body’s internal governing force/vitality, which is weakened during illness.</note>, more readily receive whatever impressions arrive from the outside. 

However, when she is joined with happy planets, or with blessed aspects, and in suitable figures, she promises universal health to the sick. I said "universal" and "in itself" because a fortune <note>A "fortune" refers to a "benefic" planet like Jupiter or Venus.</note> can cause misfortune, and a misfortune can cause fortune, when the quality of the planet is opposite to the quality of the illness. For when the **Moon** is joined to **Mars**, even if Mars is said to harm by reason of its property which it has toward human nature, it nevertheless assists by reason of its quality of heat and dryness for those suffering from a fever caused by **phlegm** <note>Phlegm was one of the four humors, characterized as cold and moist. According to the principle of "contraries cure contraries," the heat of Mars would counteract the coldness of the phlegm.</note>, since from these the feverish matter is "digested" by being heated and dried out; and it is similar with Saturn and others. 

For this reason, it is most beautifully said in the *Centiloquium*: "unless the fortune be contrary to the illness itself," and in the work of **Baly** <note>likely Albohali or Haly Abenragel, famous Arabic astrologers.</note> regarding "similitude." There is also another path of particular knowledge divided into three modes:

1. One is indeed truer and more precious: that which is grasped from the configuration of the **nativity** <term>nativity</term><note>A birth chart or horoscope calculated for the exact moment of a person's birth.</note> of the superiors or from the revolution of the same, as is contained in the scientific part concerning nativities. 
2. There is another held through **interrogation** <term>interrogation</term><note>Also known as "horary astrology," where a chart is cast for the moment a specific question is asked.</note>: for when someone is ignorant of their own birth time, it is conceded to them that they may, with great care and persistence, propose a universal interrogation to the astrologer and receive everything just like a birth figure. For the heavens then are found configured just as they were at the time of birth, or very nearly so. **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a highly influential Persian astrologer.</note> relates this about himself in the *Sadan*, stating that he did not have the configuration of his own birth, but for that reason took up a universal question in which all his conditions were reflected. 
3. A third mode is found: which is through the consideration of the **Lord of the Conjunction** or of the **Prevention** <note>The "Prevention" (praeventio) refers to the full moon or syzygy immediately preceding an event or illness.</note> preceding the illness, and the **ascendants** at the hour of the beginning of the illness and the location of the Moon. For if the Moon was then joined to the fortunes or looked upon by them, it signifies the health of the sick person; but if otherwise, it will signify the opposite.

According to **Baly Heben Ragel** <note>Haly Abenragel (965–1050), author of *The Complete Book on the Judgment of the Stars*.</note>, for the sake of the fourth point, it must be known that astrology is not only useful for practical medicine, but indeed for theoretical medicine and many other sciences. For it assists the science of **metaphysics** because it teaches how to investigate the intended end and subject from things that come after. For through the celestial bodies, we come most powerfully into the knowledge of the first principle; hence the Apostle says in the first chapter of Romans:

> The invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made, from the creation of the world. <note>original: "Inuisibilia dei p ea que facta sunt a creatura mūdi itellecťa cōspiciūt." Romans 1:20.</note>

This is also the opinion of **Aristotle** in the 12th book of his *Metaphysics* when he wished to investigate the first principle and the number of the **Intelligences** <term>Intelligences</term><note>In medieval philosophy, these were the spiritual beings thought to move the celestial spheres.</note>. He turned himself to **Calyppus** and **Eudoxus**, the most famous of the astrologers, and following the number of spheres described by them, he concluded the number of the Intelligences. And therefore he says that the plurality of the motions [of the stars] must be considered from that branch of mathematics which is most properly its own: astrology.

It is also a science which, according to **Ptolemy**, leads us above all others in our character and virtues into the "forms," and into the love and knowledge of the First [Cause], as also appeared before according to that saying of John:

> This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God. <note>original: "hec est uita etna ut cognoscāt te deū uey & unū." John 17:3.</note>

It also supports natural science and theoretical medicine by explaining their books, such as in *On Generation*, *On the Heavens and the World*, in the *Meteorology*, and many others. And **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Ypocras"</note> in his *Epidemics* and in *On Air, Waters, and Places*; and **Galen** in many of his *Aphorisms*, and especially in the third book of *On Critical Days*. These contain discourses that cannot be understood without this [astrology].

That it especially benefits practical medicine, and both types of theory, is shown from the words of Hippocrates in his first "Difference." Again, in the third book of *On Critical Days*: "I return to the matter which I have considered with study and vehement scrutiny: and I have found it certain and true, which does not perish, and it is the thing which the Egyptian astrologers found: and it is that the **Moon** signifies over the days what the disposition of a person is in their illness." For if she is applied to certain stars equal in "blessedness"—that is, the wandering stars—and those are the ones named "fortunes," those days will be favorable to that person. And on the contrary, if she is applied to certain "hesitating" stars departing from equality, those will be days of injury and sadness for the person. This was also felt in the first book of *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "de īgenio sanitatis"; Galen's *De methodo medendi*.</note> regarding **Theatillus**. For he wanted the doctor not only to know medicinal things, but also dialectic, arithmetic, astrology, and to be a master of the **quadrivium** <term>quadrivium</term><note>The four mathematical liberal arts: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy/astrology.</note>.

Furthermore, **Haly Abas** <note>Ali ibn Abbas al-Majusi (died c. 990), author of the *Liber Regalis*.</note> expressly proves at the beginning of his book that it is necessary for a doctor to be a master in all **seven liberal arts**, as was sufficiently declared in the first "Difference." It is likewise shown by reason, since a beneficial effect is seen to be caused by the due and convenient application of the helper to the patient. This can happen in the three modes by which it was said celestial bodies operate in these lower realms:

1. First, it is declared from **motion**. For a doctor who perceives through the science of astronomy that the motion in the superior bodies is becoming faster or slower—and as it was declared, the air is rendered hotter or colder—will strive through the science of medicine to administer a regimen of the **six non-natural things** <term>six non-natural things</term><note>The environmental and lifestyle factors central to Galenic medicine: air, food/drink, sleep/waking, exercise/rest, excretion/retention, and mental passions.</note>, according to similarity in preserving health, but according to the contrary in curing illness. 
2. Similarly, if by the gathered light it is seen that heat is generated in the surrounding air, or by its disposition it becomes cold. 
3. In the same way, according to the **conjunction of planets and their aspects**, which was the second middle mode of the operation of celestial bodies on these lower things, he will proportionately measure out the regimen for both the healthy and the sick.

Thus, finally, by attending to the third particular and appropriated mode of operation; which is also shown by this: that a doctor, through the branch of astronomy, is able to...

...of the **fortunes of the ascendant** <term>ascendant</term><note>The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment; it was considered the most important point for the health of the individual.</note>, the lord of the ascendant, the **Midheaven** <term>Medium Coeli</term><note>The highest point in the sky; in medical astrology, it represents the treatment or the physician.</note>, and the second and seventh houses. The **infortunes** <note>Specifically the "malefic" planets, Saturn and Mars.</note>, however, occupy the sixth house and its lord. Then, by casting an image in which the life-giving celestial light of health is infused, health is drawn forth, just as it appears through the astronomical images of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the most influential ancient astronomer.</note>, **Thabit** <note>Thabit ibn Qurra (c. 826–901), a famous Sabian astronomer and mathematician known for his work on talismans.</note>, **Theben**, **Chorath**, and others.

And I myself have experienced that an **image of a lion** <note>A solar talisman used specifically for healing.</note> impressed in gold—while the **Sun** was in the Midheaven with the **Heart of the Lion** <term>Cor Leonis</term><note>The star Regulus, considered extremely powerful and royal.</note>, and with **Jupiter** or **Venus** looking upon it, and with the "evils" being unfortunate and "falling"—takes away **kidney pain** <note>original: "dolorem renum"</note>. Likewise, a belt made from the leather of a male calf, with a buckle crafted from the bone of a **walrus** <note>original: "rodoarti," likely referring to the walrus or "rosmarus."</note> or a male whale, worn over the skin, [is effective]. And rightly so, for the "faces" of this world are subject to the celestial faces, as stated in the **Centiloquium** <note>A famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms.</note>. This is confirmed by the commentator’s account regarding the **image of a scorpion** impressed during its rising, with the Moon in Scorpio, which heals a sting from the same. Because of this, the science of astronomy contributes to the work of medicine in a twofold way: first, by properly applying these three medical tools to the body: **diet, potion, and surgery**, corresponding to the three dispositions of health, sickness, and neutrality. For the astrologer, foreknowing that the air will change toward heat or cold, or that the paroxysms or continuous exacerbations of fevers will become more intense or more relaxed, will proceed with the proper administration of a regimen for both the healthy and the sick. Furthermore, this is what **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Ypocratis"</note> declares concerning feeding in his **Aphorisms** and the canons on the **Regimen of Acute Diseases**, by considering the strength [of the patient] and when to feed or not to feed. Also, in the administration of a **potion**, one must attend to the judgments [of the stars], as said by **Haly Abenragel** <note>original: "balyabatē"; referring to the Arab astrologer Haly Abenragel.</note>; hence in the *Centiloquium*: "If someone takes a **purgative** <note>A medicine intended to cleanse the bowels or humors.</note> while the Moon is with Jupiter, its work will be shortened and its effect diminished." This is because nature's strength is fortified by the conjunction of the Moon with Jupiter, and the medicine cannot then do its work, since it must overcome the natural virtues to act. Conversely, in the same text: "Take a purgative when the Moon is in **Cancer, Scorpio, or Pisces**." It is also laudable if the lord of the ascendant is joined to a pleasing planet beneath the earth. But if the lord of the ascendant is joined to a planet in the Midheaven, the patient will suffer nausea, vomit the medicine, and it will not stay in him.

It is also necessary when applying the third instrument—namely **surgery**—to attend to the judgment of the sciences, according to that aphorism of the *Centiloquium*: "To touch a limb with iron while the Moon is in the sign of that limb is a danger." Now, the "sign of the limb" is to be understood in this way: since astrologers divided the human body into twelve parts according to the likeness of the **twelve signs** <note>This is the concept of the "Zodiac Man" or "Homo Signorum."</note>, they placed **Aries** to rule over the head, **Taurus** over the neck, **Gemini** over the shoulders and arms, **Cancer** over the shoulder blades, **Leo** over the chest and heart, and so on. Now, when the Moon is in Aries, **phlebotomy** <term>phlebotomia</term><note>Bloodletting, the most common surgical procedure of the Middle Ages.</note> and all surgical work on the head is prohibited, and similarly for the others. Thus, bloodletting of the arms is forbidden when the Moon is in Gemini, and the incision of hemorrhoids and surrounding parts when it is in Scorpio. This is because the Moon, filling the limb with its moisture, [prevents] consolidation in

It also contributes in another way to **prognosis**. However, there remain two other modes of more universal knowledge, by which it is said an astrologer can know the past, present, and future, and consequently can assist in the resolution of the patient's illness. To the second point, it must be said that [Aristotle] said this regarding the **astronomy of motions** <note>Mathematical astronomy.</note> rather than **judicial astrology** <note>The practice of making predictions based on those motions.</note>, because it seemed to him that the latter was built upon false principles, since it posits **eccentrics and epicycles** <term>eccentrics and epicycles</term><note>Mathematical devices used in the Ptolemaic system to explain the varying speeds and retrograde motions of planets, which contradicted Aristotle's requirement for perfect circular motion around the Earth.</note> and proper motions in the planets by which they "cut through" the body of the heavens. These things seem to be contrary to what is determined in *On the Heavens and the World* and the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*. Hence, his opinion—since he said he despaired of this—is not to be valued here. And concerning this, see the *Lucidator* <note>Referring to the *Lucidator Dubitabilium Astronomiae* by Peter of Abano, a famous 13th-century defense of astrology.</note>, fourth distinction: even if eccentrics and epicycles or any other foundations are posited in it, **judicial science** is not condemned because of this, since this does not hinder or divert the work of the stars upon these lower [earthly] things. For this reason, there were three "paths" of astronomy: one which wished to "save all appearances" <note>A technical term in ancient astronomy for creating a mathematical model that matches observed data regardless of physical reality.</note> through a multitude of spheres; for because someone saw a planet moved by so many motions, he concluded it had as many spheres as it was moved by, because he posited the star fixed in the sphere like a nail fixed in a wheel (Metaphysics XII and *On the Heavens*). Another was that which is observed today, founded upon **eccentrics and epicycles**, placing the planets in their own orbits to be moved by their own motions; and they say the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras, often credited with early mathematical models of the cosmos.</note> founded this upon...

<meta>This page continues the technical defense of astrology in medicine, specifically addressing historical astronomical models and the physical nature of how celestial influence reaches the Earth through light and motion.</meta>

...which **Timocharis** <note>An ancient Greek astronomer (c. 320–260 BCE) known for early star catalogs.</note>, **Arsatilis**, **Hipparchus** <note>original: "Abrathā"; Hipparchus was the most significant Greek astronomer before Ptolemy.</note>, **Ptolemy of Pelusium**, and almost all later authors founded. There was also a third theory, much like the first, which **Avempace** <note>Ibn Bajja (d. 1138), an Andalusian polymath.</note> and **Abu Ishaq** <note>original: "ab uisach"; likely refers to Al-Bitruji (Alpetragius).</note> added not long before these times. He arranged all the spheres and **eccentric circles** <term>eccentrics</term><note>A circle whose center is shifted away from the Earth, used to explain the varying speeds of planets.</note> just as he did with **epicycles** <term>epicycles</term><note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used to explain retrograde motion.</note>, or moved by only one simple motor. This was done without disparaging the **Peripatetic** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> view, which posits multiple "motors" [spiritual movers], though they differ in speed and slowness depending on whether the spheres are near or far from the **First Mover** <note>The outermost sphere that sets the rest of the universe in motion.</note>. He also intended to "save the appearances" <note>A phrase meaning to create a mathematical model that matches observed data.</note> through various poles. 

However, both these and the first—as is clear to one considering what I have declared in the *Lucidator* <note>Referring to Peter of Abano's own work, *Lucidator Dubitabilium Astronomiae* (The Elucidator of Astronomical Doubts).</note>—could not stand. Again, the words seem to have been spoken in vain without application to the subjects; for they did not write **canons and tables** <note>Sets of mathematical instructions and data used to calculate planetary positions.</note> by which the defined movement of the heaven and the planets could be grasped, as the second theory did.

Regarding the other point, it must be said that the proposition holds truth in **essential causes** and things ordered by themselves. However, particulars do not essentially reduce themselves to the superior causes of these inferior things. For it happens that from such motion or light, this or that is generated or destroyed, although this entire "inferior" [earthly] world is essentially reduced to those celestial causes. Hence, in the first book of the *Quadripartitum* <note>Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>: "The changes of terrestrial things are variable and convertible, receiving primary qualities from the celestial ones in an accidental manner, with one thing following another."

Similarly, although the celestial motion is circular, it induces a **straight motion** through the rays of the **Sun** and stars falling into these lower regions, such as the air and water, etc. For this reason, one of the *Problems* <note>Referring to the pseudo-Aristotelian *Problemata*, a collection of scientific questions.</note> asks why it is better to hear at night than by day. This is either because the air moves and sounds when heated by the **Sun**, as **Anaxagoras** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher.</note> says, or because sound is heard better through a vacuum than through a full space. For in the day, the air is thickened as it is filled with light and rays, because of those things which descend from the fire itself; and since the rays are **bodies** <note>In medieval physics, light was sometimes debated as having a subtle corporeal nature.</note>, the "body" of the night is thinner and more rarefied.

In the same way, it must be said that although the "mirrors" <note>The reflective or shining surfaces of the stars.</note> of the stars are round, yet since almost all are larger than the earth—for every **fixed star** notable to the sight is larger than the whole earth, according to **Alfraganus** <note>The 9th-century Persian astronomer Al-Farghani.</note>—and especially this **Sun**, whose magnitude is proven by **Ptolemy** to be 166 and 3/8 times larger than the earth. Rays flow from them upwards and sideways, widening as they go; but because of the smallness of the earth, they are narrowed as if to a point, acquiring the shape of a **pyramid**. The "cone" or tip of this pyramid exists at the center of the earth, while its base is in the body of the star. Because of this, the astrologer, by applying the universal light to specific particulars, can direct that light to a sick person, since this is the natural arrangement of the rays.

Similarly, as already shown, it must be said that the astrologer can make **fortunes** <note>Benefic planetary influences.</note> more fortunate and separate **misfortunes** <note>Malefic influences.</note> from a patient, provided he knows how to connect suitable earthly things to the superior ones, applying the action, motion, and specific **hidden virtue** <term>occult virtue</term><note>A natural power or property that is not immediately obvious to the senses, like magnetism or the Moon’s pull on tides.</note> of the celestial conjunction to these lower things.

Regarding the point about the **zodiac**, which the "Calculator" <note>Possibly Richard Swineshead, a 14th-century mathematician, or a general reference to an astronomical calculator.</note> says solves this: if an addition of 10 degrees and 22 minutes is made. For this reason, he posits adding the motion of the **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> to the motion of the **ninth**. But this does not seem valid, because then the judgment would be based on the ninth heaven and not the eighth; nor does it seem that the "Calculator" can change the sign and judgment of the stars through his math alone. And so I say: because a great distance has not yet grown between the **movable zodiac** and the **immovable zodiac**, almost the same judgment is taken from both. However, logic concludes that when a great distance arises between them, it will be necessary to judge by both, and thus establish two meanings: one for the eighth heaven, and another for the ninth. Then one would compare the judgments from both. Today, however, we judge more by the ninth heaven than the eighth. This reasoning indeed seems difficult and is used to turn people away from the science of judgments [astrology].

Regarding the next point, it must be said that the power of other stars is reduced entirely to these: the **fixed stars** of the first magnitude. Their power is reduced to the **seven planets**. And furthermore, the power of all the planets is received by the **Moon**. She gives her "disposition" to all the planets, both because she is similar to a body in her capacity to be affected and because she is closest to us. For she is like a certain **messenger** <note>original: "Algazillus & nuncius"; Peter uses a term for a swift herald.</note> and a swift-running herald of the planets. Therefore, in all parts of applied astrology, it is principally commanded that the **Moon** be observed: her state, her place of conjunction and opposition, her **ascendant**, and her "lord."

Regarding the final point, it must be said that there are three modes of knowing the condition of a sick person:
1. One is general.
2. Another is particular, through **interrogation** <note>A branch of astrology where a chart is cast for the moment a question is asked.</note>.
3. Another is particular, through consideration of the state of the heaven, and especially the **Moon**, at the time the illness began.

And because it further seemed to be proven that because of the swift motion of the heaven, one could barely perceive the exact hour of birth, and even less the hour of conception: it must be said that although a very swift motion occurs at the edge [of the universe], this motion is diminished and dulled in relation to the center—namely, the **Earth**. We experience this: when a solar ray falls through a window into a small amount of water, even a nearly imperceptible movement in the water creates a very great and obvious motion of light reflected on the wall. Therefore, **Albumasar** <note>The influential 9th-century astrologer Abu Ma'shar.</note> says in the first book of the *Introductory*: "An error of one degree does not hinder the astrologer." This is true for most types of judgment. In "prognostications" <note>original: "Indictioibus"; referring to specific timing techniques.</note>, however, it causes errors; especially because an error of one degree results in an error of one year in the technique of **direction** <note>A method used to predict when events in a birth chart will manifest.</note>, as is taught in books on **nativities** <note>Birth charts.</note>. Or the great movement of heaven is changed almost in a moment, even if it diversifies...

<meta>This page transitions from a discussion on astronomical judgment to "Difference XI," which investigates the number and nature of the primary elements. The author, Peter of Abano, shifts from celestial "motors" to the fundamental building blocks of the physical world, citing various ancient and medieval authorities to reconcile differing views on whether there is one element or many.</meta>

...the cognition and judgment of the astrologer, as far as certain most specific details are concerned—of which the word itself cannot fully grasp—though not as far as the universals which it is capable of receiving.

## DIFFERENCE XI.

<margin>1</margin>
**T**hat an element is one is demonstrated by the fact that matter is an element. Whence the **Commentator** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the most influential medieval commentator on Aristotle.</note> in the fifth book of the *Metaphysics* states that an "element" is spoken of in terms of internal causes and, more worthily, as matter. But matter exists as one in number. Furthermore, things which are the same as one and the same thing are also the same as each other, as seen in the *Sophistical Refutations* <note>original: "elencoꝝ p̃rio"; Aristotle’s *De Sophisticis Elenchis*.</note>. But an "element" and a "principle" of nature are the same. Whence in the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*: for which reason nature is both a principle and an element. Yet a principle is only one, as concluded in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*. 

However, it seems there are **two** elements because those things which are the principles and causes of things are elements, as appears in the *Metaphysics*; these are **matter and form**. Whence in the first book of the *Physics*: "Subject matter along with form is the cause of those things that come to be, like a mother." And it is confirmed because elements are ordered toward mixing, and finally toward generation, so that even the superior fire rushes toward it (Difference 15). These things are perfected by action and passion [being acted upon], where at least two things are required: one which is as matter and passive, the other which is as form and effective. 

It is also shown that there are **three** elements, because just as many beginnings of things are posited: **matter, form, and privation** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a form that a subject is naturally suited to have, a necessary condition for change.</note>, according to the first book of the *Physics*. Again, an element of something is that from which it is constituted; but there are three such things: for in every thing there are just as many. In the first book of *On the Heavens and the World* <note>original: "celi & mūdi"</note>, it says that all perfection consists of three. 

That it seems there are **five** or **six** elements: since although there are four material ones, matter does not suffer [undergo change] or cause anything by itself, but rather through an agent, according to the first book of the *Physics*. Whence in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*, matter itself will not move itself, but requires a "divine" power <note>original: "teyoica"; likely a corruption of "theioka" or "theotica" referring to a divine or prime mover.</note>. Therefore it is necessary to submit at least a fifth thing which is the mover itself, leading toward generation. Or a sixth; and therefore **Empedocles** <note>A Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher (c. 490–430 BCE) who posited the four roots (elements).</note>, along with the aforementioned four, introduced **Strife** and **Concord** to move them. 

That **ten** are wondered at, because there are ten primary genera of things called <term>Categories</term> <note>The ten classifications of all things that exist, according to Aristotle.</note>. This is supported by **Pythagoras** <note>original: "Pitagora"</note>, who endeavored to lead all things to the number ten. 

That there seem to be **infinite** elements (∞): because all philosophers, with **Plato** excepted, establish perpetual generation. For only he [Plato] "created time" <note>A reference to the *Timaeus*, where Plato describes the Demiurge creating time alongside the cosmos.</note>, according to the eighth book of the *Physics*. Truly, generation could not be perpetual unless the things from which they are made were infinite. For they would be consumed, and once consumed, they would be gone; otherwise, they would fail in every way. Wherefore **Anaxagoras** <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that all things are made of "seeds" containing every quality.</note> imagined a certain chaos in which he placed infinite "homoeomerous" parts [parts similar to the whole]. **Democritus**, **Leucippus**, and **Epicurus** posited infinite **atoms**. And for that reason, **Empedocles** attempted to posit the elements as unalterable and impassible, or that while the world is generated and corrupted infinitely in its particulars, the elements remain. Therefore, the subjects are various and indeterminate.

In opposition to these are the logicians, physicians, and **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> who posit **four**: namely, **earth, water, air, and fire**. Furthermore, the **humors** <term>humores</term> <note>The four vital fluids of the body believed to determine health and temperament.</note> are certain elements derived from the first ones, according to **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli (c. 850–950), a prominent Jewish physician and philosopher.</note> and **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "balyabatē"; Haly Abbas (d. 982/994), a famous Persian physician.</note>. They write that there are four of these; wherefore **Aurelius** <note>Likely referring to a medieval medical compendium attributed to "Aurelius."</note> says that in all men, illnesses arise from the four humors: by which a man lives, by which the healthy are ruled, and the sick are harmed. Since, therefore, the effect is proportional to and consistent with the cause (as in the first book of the *Physics*), the elements will likewise be four primary ones.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that elements are fourfold. For some are primary and universal, as much of simple bodies as of composite ones—such as **matter and form**, according to the Commentator in the third book of *On the Heavens and the World*. Others are common foundations of composite things only, as those named before [earth, water, air, fire]. Some are proximate and particular, such as the common parts of similar animals. The remaining ones are intermediate, appropriated specifically to animals, such as the mentioned humors: **blood, phlegm, choler, and melancholy** <note>original: "ſanguis fleuma. colera. & melācolia."</note>. According to the first book of the *Theoretical Medicine* <note>original: "theorice p̃rio"</note>: the proximate subject of the human body are the **members** [limbs/organs] and the **spirits**; the remote subject is the humors; and the more remote subject is the four elements. 

The word "element" (or *ylementum*): properly implies a first simple thing, according to the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*. It is also called "indivisible" according to the Commentator there in three ways. First, definitively, as the most general and individual things. Second, in species or form, whether universal or particular, such as the four known elements which are entirely similar. Third, in quantity, such as unity and the point. Elements are also denoted by the qualities of hot, cold, dry, and moist, as **Galen** indicates in many places. This happens perhaps because the word "element" is meant to denote simplicity and indivisibility. The more intense of these are hot and cold; the others are imported through the earth, etc., since the subject and the accidents of matter and form present a composition. Or they are not simple and pure, according to the *Theories of Medicine*, except to the senses and not to the soul or the intellect. Or when elements are referred to action, the qualities are the most and immediately active (Difference 60). Yet some feared to confess that earth, water, etc., were elements, because we neither take anything from the body nor put anything in, which is quite insane according to the *First Principles of Elements*.

This "element" is found to be defined by many who mean almost the same thing. According to the fifth book of the *Metaphysics* and the third book of *On the Heavens*: An element is that from which a thing is first composed, and it is in that thing, and is indivisible in species into another species. In the *Introduction to the Elements*: An element is the smallest particle of that of which it is an element. Also, in the *Theoretical Medicine*: It is that which is simplest in all parts of a composite body and smallest in quantity. **Isaac**, however, says at the start of his *Elements*: An element is a thing from which something is primarily generated, and it exists in the thing generated from it, by power and not by act. According to Aristotle in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*: A corporeal element is that from which, and from something other than itself, a thing is composed, and it is in it essentially, and is not defined by its form. In the *First Principles*: Elements are bodies, namely simple ones, and they are the first parts of the human body and others, which can least of all be divided into bodies of different forms, and from whose mixture the species of diverse generated things are made. And know, that all...

It eventually identifies the four physical elements (earth, water, air, fire) and the four medical humors (blood, phlegm, choler, melancholy) as the foundational subjects of the human body.</summary>

...it further clarifies the definition of an "element" according to the relationship it has to a mixture. It is not distinct according to its own being within the mixture, except as a first principle, and especially when it describes each of the elements individually; for then it certainly touches upon them. However, what an element is according to its nature, and how many ways it may be spoken of, is noted in **Difference 29**, just as the third definition will be mentioned in the discourse on the members <note>The "members" refers to the parts of the body in medieval anatomy.</note>. 

Concerning this second point, three things must be known, just as the elements are posited in a threefold manner. First, it must be known that some have posited other primary elements than those posited by the most skilled physicians and philosophers, diversifying them according to their beings and especially their material nature. For an element is either one or many. If it is one, it is either in the category of substance or accident, such as quantity; and thus **Pythagoras** posits one, which is the principle of number and also the beginning of all things. He did not know how to distinguish between "one" as the principle of number and "one" as a transcendental; for he thought that just as a number is varied by the addition or subtraction of a unit, so too are the species or natures of things. 

If the element is in the category of substance, it is either immobile or mobile. If the first, it is either infinite—as **Melissus**, the most ancient, held—or finite, as **Parmenides** truly held. If it is mobile, as most believe (since all were natural philosophers), it is either one—like **Hesiod** the legislator <note>Hesiod was an early Greek poet, though here Peter of Abano refers to him as a "legislator" or authority</note>, who, according to the <term>Commentator</term> <note>original: "ꝑmētator"; likely a contraction for Commentator (Averroes) on the second book of the Metaphysics</note> on the second book of the *Metaphysics*, posited **earth** as the element of all things—or **water**, as **Thales of Miletus**, the first of the known philosophers; or **air**, as **Diogenes** held; or **vapor**, as **Cratus** and **Eraticus**; or **fire**, as some held, since it is the most subtle and almost incorporeal, qualities which seem to belong to the nature of elements. 

And if there are many elements, they are either from the category of accident—as **Plato** held, wishing the line, the plane, and the solid to be the principles of things—or from the category of substance. These are either finite or infinite. If finite, they are either two, according to the appearance of **Parmenides** (fire and earth), or the remaining three besides earth, as other natural philosophers held. And because earth seems to have the nature of something "elemented" <note>An "elemented" thing (elementatum) is a complex body made of elements, rather than being an element itself.</note> rather than being an element—since it is very dense and compact, and because it is cold and dry—it is contrary to the principles of life. Indeed, none of the philosophers posited earth as a single, simple element. Whence in the first book of *On the Soul*, all elements received an order of priority except for earth. 

Some, however, posited four material elements—but not alone—as **Empedocles** did, joining to the two pairs of elements two formal ones: namely, **Strife** and **Friendship**. And if there are more than four, they are infinite, as **Democritus** and **Leucippus** held, positing infinite **atoms**, by which they claimed alteration occurred through shape, order, and position. Or they posited a middle way among all these, as **Anaxagoras** did with **Anaximander**; for in that he posited a certain **Chaos**, he wanted the element to be one and finite. But in that he perceived that infinite "similar parts" <note>Homoeomeria: Anaxagoras's theory that everything is made of tiny parts that contain the essence of the whole.</note> were contained within it, he posited many and indefinite elements. The defects of all these views are sufficiently eliminated by **Aristotle** in many places, and **Galen** does not do so sparingly in his work *On the Elements*. And therefore, they are omitted for the present, since their defect appears when they say the beginning of things was fated to support this exposition. Whence Aristotle in the first book of the *Metaphysics* says: "We do not comprehend, nor can we understand Melissus and Parmenides, nor do we think they were so unlearned as they seem in their words." 

On account of this second point, it must be known that some also posited one

---

element according to the humor, in their books on human nature and the elements. Some of these say that this humor is **blood**; others, **phlegm**; some, **choler** <note>yellow bile</note>; and the rest, **melancholy** <note>black bile</note>. And they were moved by the fact that they thought they saw death caused only by the flow of one humor, such as by the loss of blood, or by the exit of choler alone, or of phlegm or melancholy. 

**Hippocrates** and **Galen** fight against these views at length by leading them to many inconveniences. For then the body would not undergo alteration, nor would it suffer, feel pain, be healed, nor would it be universally generated or corrupted; since all these things come about from a contrary. For all things are changed and corrupted by their contraries through an unequal distemper. Indeed, alteration and generation occur from opposites. And to feel pain is to perceive a contrary suddenly impressed upon one. Every healing is perfected by a contrariety; on account of which, a human is not constituted from one, but from several humors. 

However, according to the opinion of **Aristotle** and **Avicenna**, along with some physicians, **blood** is the "true" humor, while the rest are rather its superfluities <note>In medieval medicine, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm were often seen as side-products or refinements of blood production.</note>. The distinction in **Difference 30** concerning these humors does not truly exist; for when life fails due to a flow, only one humor flows out. Whence in the book *On the Nature of Man*: "If no one died from superfluous purgations, then only choler would be purged." But first it leads out choler, then phlegm, then melancholy, and finally, at the point of death, blood (Difference 144). For these people were deceived by the "wickedness" of the blood, since in its quantity and color it exceeds and hides the others. 

Because of this, a third thing must be known: that the **homogeneous parts** <note>original: "ptes cōsimiles"; parts that are the same throughout, like bone or flesh, as opposed to organs like the hand.</note> are posited as elements, such as bone, cartilage, ligament, nerve, and the simplest flesh, because they themselves compose and constitute the **instrumental parts** <note>original: "officialia"; organs with a specific office or function.</note>, such as the head, the chest, etc., and consequently the whole body. For there is a **triple composition**: first, of the homogeneous parts from the elements; second, of the instrumental parts from the homogeneous parts; and third, of the whole body from these. This is found in the second book of *On the Parts of Animals* and the first book of *On Diseases*. Some even posited one of these as the principal element, like the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note>; others posited four, namely the brain, heart, liver, and testicles, as did the Platonists and some physicians (Difference 38). 

Regarding the third point, three things must similarly be known. First, that the elements are **four primary ones**, as the present authorities testify. This is supported because the active and passive qualities—namely **heat**, **cold**, **dryness**, and **moisture**—are the four causes of the elements. Whence in the fourth book of the *Meteorology*: "Since the four causes of the elements are determined, each one has one quality essentially inherent to it" (Difference 15). 

Furthermore, from four terms in combination, six pairings arise, of which four are possible:
1. **Heat and Dryness**, which is **Fire**.
2. **Heat and Moisture**, which is **Air**.
3. **Cold and Moisture**, which is **Water**.
4. **Cold and Dryness**, which is **Earth**.

But **Heat and Cold**, and **Dryness and Moisture**, since they are contraries in every way, reject and destroy each other, and thus constitute no elements. Furthermore, one thing is heavy in an absolute sense, which is Earth; another is heavy in a relative sense, which is Water. Similarly, one is light, either simply as Fire, or in a certain respect as Air (from the second book of *On Generation and Corruption*). Finally, everything that comes to be is made from something, as if from matter...

...and by something acting as an agent through form. However, in these two known categories of elements, one type more clearly occupies the place of matter and the passive—namely **earth** and **water**—while the other occupies the place of form and the active—namely **fire** and **air**. Furthermore, multiple signs demonstrate this, such as similarity or figure, generation, and corruption. First, because an effect reflects the nature of its cause; but in things composed of elements, a similarity in substance and quality is found among the effects of the elements. For some are very coarse, some are subtle, and others are in between. These latter are of two kinds: one extreme or the other is more prominent, and some are hot and cold, dry and moist, and likewise heavy and light, either simply or in a certain respect.

**Likewise**, secondly, concerning generation and corruption: from those things which others are generated, they are in turn corrupted into the same; otherwise, they would be consumed and reduced to nothing. Since all these things are finite in actuality—as stated in the *Physics*, book III <note>Aristotle's Physics, a foundational text for medieval natural philosophy.</note>—and every finite body is resolved from a finite body, as stated in the first book of the same. But the generation of anything comes from the four elements, which resolution <note>The process of breaking a compound down into its simplest parts.</note> demonstrates; for a mixture is seen to be resolved into four parts. This is seen either according to nature or in the corruption of an animal; for according to the first theoretical principles and **Isaac** in his book *On Elements* <note>Isaac Israeli (c. 832–932), a Jewish physician and philosopher whose work on elements was highly influential.</note>, those parts which are more solid, such as bone and cartilage, are converted into earth (evidently by its dominance); the moister parts into vapor or water; the spirits into air; and the natural heat into fire—or at least a part of it, as sublimation and especially questioning denotes. For indeed, the senses elicit four diverse substances; therefore, there are four elements. Regarding this second point, it should be known that according to the common opinion of physicians, there are four humors <term>humors|the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to regulate health and temperament</term>, as touched upon before. This is shown by many signs. First and foremost, by the heterogeneity of the blood mass: for if there were only one humor in the blood, then several substances would not be found within it. But this is false, since there is found in it a pure, abundant, purple, and sufficiently "cooked" <note>Medieval medicine used the concept of "coction" (digestion or cooking by internal heat) to explain how the body processes nutrients.</note> substance, which is **blood**; and a substance like a clear, reddish foam, highly cooked, which is **cholera** <note>Yellow bile.</note>; and a viscous, whitish, raw substance, which is **phlegm**; and finally, a thick, dark substance that sits at the bottom, which is less "cooked" than blood, known as **melancholy** <note>Black bile.</note> and liquid wateriness, as noted in the *Differences*, chapter 29.

**Similarly**, pure blood, as it exists potentially, receives diversity in substance, color, and other natures, as is shown by what is found in the heart or the veins. This is also confirmed by the heterogeneity of milk and the way wine is generated from unpressed grapes. In the book *On Natural Things*, folio 30, it is noted that an embryo is formed not from simple substances but from mixtures, such as sperm and menstrual blood, the nature of which is heterogeneous. Furthermore, this is shown by the diversity of the members <note>Body parts or organs.</note>: for some are hard, compact, cold, and dry, such as **bones**; some are subtle, light, hot, and dry, such as the **pulse** <note>Referring to the arterial system or the "vital spirit" it carries.</note>; others are fleshy, manageable, hot, and moist, such as **muscles**. Still others are soft, viscous, cold, and moist, such as the **phlegmatic** parts. These parts would not exist as such unless they were dominated by the four humors within them. Moreover, this is proven by pharmacy; for one medicine draws out blood (according to the book *On Medicines*), or at least a solution of continuity; another draws out phlegm; another yellow bile; and the last black bile. This happens according to age, season, and time. It is concluded, therefore, following **Hippocrates** and **Galen** with **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note>, that four humors exist. However, according to the more skilled and perceptive thinkers, not all of these constitute or nourish the body, but blood alone, or that which is converted into phlegm in time. Regarding this third point—namely the number of members and what should be agreed upon regarding this—it is left to *Difference 38*.

**Regarding** the fourth point, however, it must be said in response to the first that although matter is more properly called an "element" according to **Aristotle** and the **Commentator** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), known in the West simply as "The Commentator" for his work on Aristotle.</note>, here a corporeal element is sought, not an incorporeal one like *hyle* <term>hyle|prime matter; the purely potential, formless "stuff" of the universe</term>. To the next point, it must be said that it would be true if matter were a principle and an element by the same reasoning and not just in its subject; but if it is by another reason, it does not convince, but rather puts forward an accidental property. For a "principle" and an "element" differ from one another: "principle" is said of the agent, while "element" is said of the material. For a principle is one thing that is not an element or a cause, just as a **point** is the principle of a line, yet it is not an element or a cause; for it is disproven in *Physics* VI that a line is composed of points. A principle is also that from which motion is initiated. Furthermore, a principle differs from an element in that a principle is not necessarily homogeneous with the things of which it is the principle; but every element is entirely homogeneous, according to the first book of *On the Elements*. To the other point, the answer is already apparent: since the element sought was said to be a body, matter and form are not such, nor even "privation." Similarly, a principle is the one universal of all things, like the First Cause. There are also many other partial principles ordered toward that one, as stated in *Metaphysics* XII. To the confirmation, it must likewise be said that action and passion do not exist without the four elements, since they occur through the four qualities excited within them. To the next point, the answer is also apparent, since those are incorporeal elements. To the next, it must be said that those three are not the material principles sought here, but others as explained. For according to Aristotle in that same place, the subjects are power and operation, which possess the vigor of form and agent rather than matter—which, according to the **Pythagoreans**, exist as beginning, middle, and end. In the book of *Wisdom* XI, they are "measure, number, and weight"; and according to **Augustine**, they are "mode, order, and species." To the next point, the answer is apparent from those things that Aristotle, along with **Empedocles**, refutes in many places. However, as to what was posited: he correctly said there are four material elements. Yet, because he posited a corruption in most things, and claimed they were unalterable and immutable, he erred (see *On Generation and Corruption*, book I). He also erred by positing that "Strife" and "Discord" generate and corrupt the universe infinitely, unless one listens to these points specifically. It also follows that he claimed "Strife" and "Friendship" congregate and segregate things. To the next point, it must be said that **Pythagoras** does not care for nature, as appears in the third book of the *Criticisms*, attempting to demonstrate all things in nature through mathematics because of his high regard for the "One," positing number as the principle and cause of beings; whence, because the number ten is perfect...

## DIFFERENCE XII.

<margin>1</margin>
That earth is the **primary cold thing** is demonstrated because as much as anything is more distant from the source of heat, so much less is it hot, being mixed with coldness; since everything is weakened by distance from its own principle. Thus says <term>Aristoteles</term> <note>original: "Ay."</note> in **On the Universe** <note>original: "de mūdō"</note>. But the earth is more distant than the other elements: for it recedes from the source of heat—namely the celestial body, which heats by its motion and light—according to **On the Heavens and the World** <note>original: "celi & mūdī"</note>, or it recedes from fire. Furthermore, that which is more compact and coarse seems to be prior: for cold is a motion from the circumferences toward the center, congregating and thickening things, according to the second book of **On Generation and Corruption**. Truly, earth is more compact and coarser than the other elements. Moreover, the motion of the hot is to tend upward, so that the more something is hot, the more it is elevated, like fire; this motion is toward the air. Therefore, the cold, being opposite to it, would seek the lower parts; and the colder it is, the more it tends downward. For just as the simple relates to the simple, so the "more" relates to the "more." This relationship belongs to the earth in comparison to water, even if both are heavy. Conversely, their place and form are prior, and they proceed to the end. For these things made it so: for nature gives as much of place as of form, according to **On the Heavens and the World**. But a higher element like fire obtains a more noble place and a more formal quality. Therefore, that which has a viler place will have a quality opposite to the prior; such a quality is coldness, for it is opposed to heat. Furthermore, secondary qualities are caused by the primary ones. But absolute lightness stands with the highest heat; therefore simple gravity will stand with the ultimate cold; but this is earth. Therefore, earth will be the primary cold thing. The opposite of this is testified to by almost all philosophers and physicians. Furthermore, that element is the coldest which is most opposed to the hottest, since there is the greatest distance between contraries; but here water stands in relation to fire, since they are maximally destructive to each other. Again, that is colder which imprints itself more upon itself, according to the book **On the Parts of Animals** <note>original: "de ptibus aīaliū"</note>; this denotes that water is of such a kind, on account of which water, not earth, will be the primary cold thing.

---

Indeed, this reasoning will appear more clearly in the following extensive section. That the earth is an element, along with its being and number, will appear in the previous and 16th differences. However, there are **three layers** or parts of it. One is lower, around the center; for it is closer to simplicity, so that it may be called **pure earth**. For it is not the earth we tread upon, nor the water we drink; and similarly, the simple air and fire are not found in the primary senses of the elements and simple things, for there is nothing in which one does not seem mixed with another. But they are understood to be so by the mind, according to the first theoretical principles of the elements. Some, however, have felt that in the middle there is simple water of the ocean, as in the following difference. There is also another layer situated above this one, appearing similar to mud, into which the waters flow down. Above this one, moreover, is a third, like the "face of the earth," which is divided into that covered by the sea and that which stands above it. Regarding the latter, <term>Algazel</term> says that it differs in dryness laterally due to the heat of the sun, just as the others differ in moisture. Difference 15 will show what is cold, and the following one will show what is water. Truly, according to the second point, it should be known that from the position of <term>Parmenides</term> <note>original: "pmeidis"</note> it follows that earth is the primary cold thing. For although he said that all things were one in truth proceeding from it, nevertheless, to save the appearances seen in themselves, he posited roughly two principles of things: he called the hot "fire" and the cold "earth," in **Metaphysics**, book 1 <note>original: "metha. i."</note>. <term>Aristoteles</term> sufficiently destroyed this position. There were others who similarly judged earth to be the coldest, though moved by a different logic. For example, Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note> sometimes felt at the end of **On the Heavens and the World** that this is demonstrated by power: since the heaven moves with ultimate velocity, the body existing under it follows its motion, so that it is heated by that motion and also by light. Because of this, it is resolved vehemently, so that dryness falls into it; this is fire. But the body fixed beneath this, being distant, does not attain the motion of the heaven and the light in such a way; thus it is rendered less hot and is less resolved, having parts more contiguous than fire. From this, **air** is made hot and moist by nature. Finally, that which is beneath these, because it is already far distant, the weakness of the motion and light in it is such that coldness imprints a more hidden quality upon it; for it is also constricted and rendered moist; whence **water** is made cold and moist by nature. The fourth body, truly distant from these and entirely from the heaven, is not susceptible to its motion nor its light; it is constricted to the ultimate degree, and **earth** is made cold and dry. Furthermore, earth was made immobile so that the heaven supported above it might be able to move, just as every motion must rely on something immobile, according to **On the Motion of Animals**. For this reason, it was necessary for it to be cold in the ultimate degree, since coldness causes immobility and coarseness. It was also necessary for this to be distant from the heaven in every way, lest by approaching it, it should be heated by its motion and dissolve, not remaining in one place. Therefore, the other elements were placed between the heaven and the earth. Hence, because of such great necessity for earth in the universe, nature seemed to intend its production more than the other elements. Thus, earth will be the primary cold thing.

This same position is also challenged in the **Metaphysics**, book 9, saying that it cannot be proven by syllogistic reasoning.
