<meta>This page continues the investigation into Difference XII, debating whether Earth or Water is the "primary cold thing." It addresses the influence of celestial bodies on elemental qualities and contrasts the views of Aristotle, Plato, and the "Peripatetics" (followers of Aristotle).</meta>

No, this is not true when it is diligently considered; rather, it is otherwise. For the elements are not generated in those celestial bodies, but from four combinations of qualities—four of which can be designated within them. For in the celestial bodies, although there are effectively four combinations of elements, even according to the **astrologers**, these may be assigned qualitatively. For from each of these there flows into matter, fit to receive it, an aptitude for form; this matter, once thus prepared, then receives its form from the **Giver of Forms**. <note>original: "datore formaz"; in medieval philosophy, this is the "Dator Formarum," an external intelligence or principle—often identified with the Agent Intellect—that "pours" specific forms into matter once it is properly prepared.</note> For that whole process was not from one body alone, but there are combinations found there that induce diversity through hidden causes.

However, according to the opinion of the better **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking—peripatos—while teaching.</note> who do not posit a "Giver of Forms," it must be said that the heaven disposes matter through those combinations of qualities and finally receives form from the matter itself; since, according to them, the one who disposes the matter and the one who introduces the form are the same, as was touched upon in point 88.

Furthermore, he added that those who were first did not have any form except a corporeal one to impress; this is not true. For the being of a body is not perfected from the "form of corporeity" alone <note>The basic "form" that makes a thing a physical, three-dimensional object.</note> unless, beyond this dimensioned form, another form is understood. For even by the fact that a body is rarefied by heat or thickened by cold, it becomes another body on account of this motion, even if it is heated by that. That a part of matter also ascends or descends when heat occurs is because of the order of **gravity and levity** in the universe.

To this should be added that nature does not give to anything only in the process of becoming, but also in its completed state, according to how it was fit and proper to receive it. Since there are 22 differences, even an innate **complexion** <note>The specific balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body.</note> can be changed. For not only do the superior bodies [the stars and planets] work through motion and light, but also through **fortune and misfortune** and certain specific appropriated virtues which, without a sensible medium, imprint changes (Difference 10). Whence it follows that it seems to him that he who teaches the generation of the elements has tried to simplify it for someone.

But one coming after him confirmed his saying. The scribe, however, was considering and confusing things, just as when a student depicts what he heard but often does not perfectly grasp the teacher's meaning.

There were also others who distinguished that in the elements there is a **double nature**, as is indicated even in theory: one indeed proper to them, by which water is colder than earth; the other, however, is "adventitious" <note>Added or acquired from the outside.</note>—acquired from the superior bodies—by which they wish earth to be colder than water. This is indeed established from <term>Book 2 of On the Generation of Animals</term> <note>original: "2o de gñatōe aialiu"</note> and the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the "Great Commentator" on Aristotle.</note> on <term>Metaphysics</term> book 12, who posit two heats differing in species: one, namely, elemental heat, and the other truly celestial.

Against these, perhaps someone will go on to explain that the first statement cannot stand—namely, that there is another nature of the elements which was derived for them from a superior power into their matter, whether received in this way or another. This is shown because: as the nature of animals stands in relation to the elements and celestial things, so do the elements stand in relation to the same. But there is no nature in animals—especially in those whose form is drawn out of the potentiality of matter—which is not found in its own way in the elements and in the superior bodies. Therefore, there will not be another nature of elements besides that received from the superior bodies into their matter.

Furthermore, according to **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay."</note>, whenever effects are found in things that share many qualities, it is necessary to trace them back to another cause, since one cannot grant separate principles. The reasoning regarding the parts of animals is this: that finally this inferior nature is reduced to the first superior motion, as has often been touched upon. And therefore those who argue more truly reduce the light of all shining things to the first of shining things, which is the **Sun**, and heat to **Fire**.

Nor is it valid, as has already been shown, to say that there are two heats in the elements such that they are heard as "differing in species." For that is said not in relation to the elements themselves, but only to **compounds** [mixtures], in which is found "fiery heat" as an instrument for preparing nourishment, and "celestial" or "vivifying and informing heat," which is more significant. For an element is simple, but this body here is composed of it and celestial heat.

Regarding the truth, however, it should be known that **earth is not the primary cold thing, but water**, as all who argue by reason and the physicians agree with them. For since each element has one quality in the highest degree, and the other acquired and added: dryness is indeed ascribed to fire, but coldness to water. Whence in <term>Book 2 of On Generation and Corruption</term>, among the four beings, to each belongs one: **Earth** is more of the dry than of the cold; **Water** <note>original: "Az"; likely an abbreviation for Aqua.</note> is more of the cold than of the moist; **Air** is more of the moist than of the hot; and **Fire** is more of the hot than of the dry.

As the Commentator says on the fourth book of the **Metaphysics**: if a mixture is made, it is necessary that one of the two elements be of stronger operation in one of the contrary qualities than its partner. For this reason, it is not necessary that two substantial qualities be found in the extreme in two elements; for if coldness and moistness in water were never tempered and mixed, nothing could be made. And therefore the dryness of fire is not at the extreme, nor is the moistness in water.

That earth is not the primary cold thing is confirmed by a double reason: one from the "prior" things of nature and causes, and the other from "posterior" things, which are prior to us. The first and second rely on a fivefold middle: first, it is shown from the mode of production or governance of the elements. For the "prior" elements, according to **Plato** in the *Timaeus* <note>original: "tbiēi"</note>, were **Fire and Earth**, from which the being of the universe is perfected. For through one of them, namely Fire, the **visible** exists; through the other, indeed, the **tangible**, like Earth. And **Parmenides** here posited these as the principles of sight. Whence in <term>Book 2 of On the Heavens and the World</term>: if earth is granted, fire is also granted of necessity. For if one of two contraries is in nature, so is the other. Thus, since these two were produced or governed first according to the perpetuity of the world, it was necessary that while one [fire] possesses one of the active qualities in the extreme (namely, heat), the other element [earth] should also retain one of the passive qualities in the extreme. But no one will give this to any quality except **dryness**. From these, the other two intermediate elements [Air and Water] and their qualities could finally be generated or governed. For if one were to posit Earth as the "supremely cold" (colder than water), then the order and existence of the passive qualities in these first two elements would by no means be found in the extreme. The reasoning for this will be proved in the second...

<meta>This page continues the cosmological debate from the previous section, moving from general celestial influences to a specific structural analysis of the four elements (Fire, Air, Water, Earth). It draws heavily on the Platonic tradition, specifically citing the "triple bond" that holds the universe together as described by Boethius and Macrobius.</meta>

...from the connection and proportion of the elements and their qualities to one another: for according to the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the origin of the physical world, which was the primary source for Greek cosmology in the Middle Ages.</note> and Macrobius in his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio*, almost all things brought forth are woven together by the **septenary** <note>The number seven, considered by ancient philosophers to be a number of completion and harmony that governs biological and cosmic cycles.</note>, as is introduced there in many places. Here, however, this number is found in the qualities of the elements in relation to the elements themselves. For there are primarily four qualities of the elements, bound together by only three numbers or proportions. This follows what is said in the third book of Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*: *You who bind the elements with numbers.* <note>original: "Qui numeris elementa ligas." This is a famous hymn from Boethius (c. 480–524 AD) describing God’s creation of the world using mathematical ratios.</note> Moreover, a perfect junction and number exists when an active quality in the highest degree attributed to one element is followed by the passive quality of another element, after which another active quality occurs, and finally a passive one. Thus, a triple bond <note>original: "nexus nodo trio." A philosophical metaphor for the mathematical harmony that prevents the opposing elements (like Fire and Water) from flying apart.</note> makes the order of each quality firmer and more stable.

Since, therefore, **Fire** possesses **Heat** in the highest degree—as all agree—it was necessary to place an element after it whose passive quality would be in the highest degree; this was the **Moisture** of **Air**, since it is most receptive and passive toward both <note>i.e., it can be affected by the heat of Fire above it and the cold of Water below it.</note>. From this, an active quality necessarily follows: namely, the **Cold** of **Water** in the highest degree, so that the measure is established in the third position corresponding to Fire. Because of this, among the four elements, **Earth** will possess an extreme **Dryness** proportioned to the Air. For if Earth were placed as extreme Cold, the triple number would fail, and the septenary would fail as well; nor would such a great bond then exist between them. <margin>1</margin>

Thirdly, this is shown from the appropriation of qualities to the elements: for as it has appeared, each element possesses one quality as its property in the highest degree. The reason for this is: since each thing has one form and one being, it likewise has one nature or property corresponding to that being. Therefore, **Fire** will have either extreme Heat, Cold, Dryness, or Moisture. It is not Cold, as the senses indicate and the intellect apprehends, because of the heat acquired from the motion of the celestial sphere in whose concave it exists, and from its light. Nor is it Dry, because the most "formal" quality <note>In medieval science, "formal" means the quality that gives a thing its active, defining character, whereas "material" qualities are more passive.</note> must belong to the most formal of elements. Likewise, it is not Moist, since its location, motion, and light—which cause heat—prevent this.

In the subsequent element, **Air**, there will be either extreme Cold, extreme Dryness, or extreme Moisture. It is not extreme Cold, both because of the heat of the Fire touching it, and because of the opposition between the extremely hot and the extremely cold. For if they were so placed, they would be reduced to a certain middle state, so that the qualities of those elements—Fire and Air—would no longer remain in the highest degree. Nor is it extreme Dryness; for since Fire, on account of its extreme Heat, associates Dryness with itself, if Air also possessed extreme Dryness (which is the sharpening and refining of heat), then with the heat sharpened by these two drynesses, the heat of the Fire would flare up so much that it would totally destroy the balanced temperament of these lower regions, and thus generation would cease.

And therefore **Nature**, whose role is to dispose all things by reason, placed the **Moist** element under the **Hot** one, so that the heat might be tempered by the moisture; it is thus softened and prevented from rushing downward and setting everything on fire. 

---

Under the next element, namely **Water**, either **Dryness** or **Cold** is left in the highest degree. It is not Dryness, because the most moist element touching it—namely Air—would prevent it with its penetrating moisture. Furthermore, two passive qualities would then be joined in the highest degree without a middle term, which the previous demonstration forbade. Thus, it was most reasonably granted to **Water** to be extremely **Cold**, so that it might temper the heat of the two hot elements preceding it. Thus, it is necessarily concluded that **Earth** is, in its essence, extremely **Dry**, but not extremely **Cold**.

Fourthly, this is examined from the "end" or purpose of the elements, which is the generation of living souls, and especially of **Man**, since he is the ultimate intention of Nature. If Earth possessed extreme Cold along with its Dryness—and as proven, it is at the furthest distance from the motion and light of the heavens—then the cold and dryness would prevail so much that generation and life could not be adapted to those dwelling upon it. For extreme cold and dryness are the primary path to **Death**. 

Indeed, we see that generation and life are totally removed under both poles <note>The North and South poles, which medieval thinkers believed were uninhabitable due to the "extreme" nature of their qualities.</note>, where these qualities are pushed to the extreme. Because of this, those things which exceed in these qualities are poisonous, such as **Opium** and **Mandrake** <note>In the medieval "Galenic" system of medicine, opium and mandrake were classified as "Cold in the fourth degree," meaning they were so cold they could extinguish the "innate heat" of the heart, causing death.</note>. This does not happen in Water, because extreme Cold produces Moisture in it, for cold dulls the moisture. Therefore, compositions made from them do not possess an extreme gradual complexion. For Cold joined with Moisture scarcely exceeds the second degree, as stated in Distinction 138.

Fifthly, from the proportionality of the qualities to the elements: it is necessary for a thing to have a proper disposition of its own action configured to its subject. Since some qualities are "formal" and others are "material," just like the elements (of which **Fire** is the most formal and **Earth** the most material), it follows that the formal quality should correspond to the more formal or less material subject. Thus, it is necessary to adapt extreme Cold to a less material subject like **Water**, and not to the most material one (Earth). Thus, from all these previous points, it is clear that Water is "colder" than Earth.

It remains now to show this by another way, through observed effects. First, regarding the substance of Earth and Water—I speak of "substance" in the manner of the **physicians**, meaning a certain quality joined to the substance, such as density and rarity, hardness and softness, and such. Since Earth is dense and hard, and Water is soft and rare, that which is dense and hard (though it receives shapes with difficulty) preserves them well once received. 

In Water, it happens that there is the same proportion of Water to Earth as exists of Air to Water. Therefore, Earth will retain celestial heat better than Water. Because of this, Water has less coldness <note>The author is likely arguing that Earth *feels* colder but Water *is* colder by nature.</note>, especially since the sun continually acting upon the Earth impresses heat into it; and although Earth is indisposed to receive it, an agent—even a weak one—acting upon an indisposed material over a long time produces the same effect as a strong agent acting on a disposed material in a short time. Furthermore, dense and thick things refract rays more strongly than rare and subtle things. Secondly, on the part of its action, if Earth...

<meta>This page continues a cosmological and physical debate regarding the elemental qualities. The previous page discussed the "triple bond" of the elements and how Heat and Cold are distributed. This page specifically investigates why Earth and Water differ in their degree of Coldness and whether Water or Air is the primary "Moist" element.</meta>

...[if the earth] were supremely <term>cold</term> <note>original: "frigida." In medieval science, cold was considered an active quality, not just the absence of heat.</note> and not water, then the active quality would not be properly matched with the passive; instead, they would be separated by a disproportionate gap, which would prevent any action from occurring. This is supported by the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*.

Thirdly, this is seen from the effect. For we observe that water, when left to its own nature—even setting aside its subtle consistency and movement—cools the earth more than the reverse. Furthermore, animals produced on the land possess more <term>blood</term> <note>Blood was associated with the qualities of heat and moisture; hence, more blood indicated a "warmer" constitution.</note> than those generated in the water. Those which have more blood are warmer than the others, according to the first book of *On Complexions*. This is also why, in times of great cold, animals seek the earth to hide themselves within it.

Fourthly, this is argued from the perspective of the quantity of the earth being smaller than the water. For the most powerful cause of heat from the sun's rays is <term>refraction</term> <note>original: "refractio." In this context, it refers to the "breaking back" or reflection of light rays against a solid surface, which medieval physicists believed was the primary cause of atmospheric heat.</note>. To the extent that the rays are initially thickened and condensed, they heat more when reflected. This is found on the earth and not in the water. For rays descend from the higher regions to these lower ones, always tending toward a sharp point and becoming more condensed. Therefore, since the earth has a smaller mass and a greater distance from the upper heavens, the rays will condense upon it more than in the water. For this reason, the earth will be less cold, as it is more affected by heat.

Fifthly, this is argued from the position of the earth and its immobility. Since the earth is the innermost and immobile element, while water is higher and mobile—indeed, according to <note>Alpetragius (Al-Bitruji) was a 12th-century astronomer who argued against Ptolemaic epicycles in favor of a homocentric model.</note> **Alpetragius**, its motion approaches a semi-circle—that which is innermost and immobile receives and preserves an impression better than that which is mobile. For movement in subtle and mobile things seems to cause cooling, as seen in the fifth book of *Problems*, such as what happens when one blows on or moves boiling pots. Thus, due to the movement of the water and the movement of the air and winds generated around it, the heating power of the heavens is not preserved in water as it is in the earth. This leaves water to be colder than the earth.

Regarding the fourth point, to the first argument it should be said that it would be true if the earth received its nature from that heat alone; but it has been said elsewhere that there are combinations of other qualities in the heavens from which the earth receives its nature. Furthermore, one must consider the nature of a thing not only in its becoming but in its completed state, as well as the manner of reception and retention, which exists differently in the earth than in the water, as has been shown.

To the other point, it should be said that it is not necessary for all things: many denser and thicker things are warmer than subtle and rare ones, such as bone compared to hair. Other powers work toward the heat of the earth's thickness and density for the sake of its noble purpose: that by being made immobile, it may be the support for the motion of the celestial sphere. Just as it remains necessary for the sake of the life of perfect animals, as the following distinction will show, the downward motion generally stays more with the <term>dry</term> than with the <term>cold</term>, as many minerals demonstrate.

To the next point, it should be said that the motion of light things upward and downward is not entirely from their qualities, but from the form impressed upon them at their generation. According to the eighth book of *Physics*, that which gives the form also gives the motion and the tendency toward it. Nor are the subsequent qualities derived simply from the first ones, but from the form that impresses them. To the final point, it should be said that location does not follow the qualities, but rather the "fortune" or specific placement of the thing. Something else also prevents the earth from being supremely cold, as has been shown. And by this, the other arguments are similarly answered.

### DIFFERENCE XIII.

<margin>1</margin>
**T**hey demonstrate that **Water** is the first of the moist elements, and not **Air**, because the most proper quality of the earth is <term>dryness</term> and of water is <term>moisture</term>, according to the fourth book of *Meteorology*. That which is most properly a thing is seen to exist as that thing primarily and essentially. Whence the <note>The "Commentator" almost always refers to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the 12th-century philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to medieval university education.</note> **Commentator** says: of the elements, the dry one is earth, and the moist one is water. And from the parts of *Physics*: water is primarily and simply moist.

Again, regarding the first of the elements: I find in water the highest degree of cold and moisture, and in fire heat and dryness. To claim that anything else besides water is supremely moist seems entirely vain. Whence, in the beginning of *On Complexions*: no animal can be supremely hot like fire, or supremely moist like water. That which is supremely such a thing is the primary example of it. For this reason, in the first book of *On Medicines*, water, along with that which it cools, is more moist than all other things.

Furthermore, that which can be separated from something else later and with more difficulty is seen to belong to it more primarily, since it shares more in the essence of the thing. Such is the case with moisture. For it is inseparable from water as long as water remains; it always remains moist no matter how much it is heated by the sun or fire. Conversely, when air is heated and its moisture is consumed, it turns to fire and acquires dryness.

On the other hand, a quality proportionate to the element should belong to the more material and less noble element. Since water is more material and less noble than air, the most fitting quality belongs to it; this is moisture, which is the most passive and "basest" of the qualities. Also, water is proportioned to Winter, and air to Spring. Since cause and effect are proportionate, and winter is moister than spring, [water is moister].

Again, the Commentator in the seventh book of *Metaphysics* says: just as transmutation in substance makes us know that prime matter exists, so does action reveal the form. But the work of water is to moisten more than air, as the senses denote—which are the primary judge in perceiving qualities. Indeed, air seems to fail in this, since it resolves into all sorts of dispositions, as per the first book of *Physics*. Therefore, the moisture of water exists primarily.

The opposite of this was noted in the previous distinction: whence <note>Nicolaus of Damascus, a philosopher whose "On the Philosophy of Aristotle" was used to fill gaps in the Aristotelian corpus.</note> **Nicolaus the Peripatetic** says in his *Problems* that air is moderately hot and moist in the highest degree; for moisture is substantial to it, just as cold is substantial to water, dryness to earth, and heat to fire. Again, if moisture belonged primarily to water, then a quality would not belong to air primarily, the opposite of which was noted before; therefore, moisture belongs primarily to air and not to water.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that water is a simple body whose natural place is to surround the earth and be surrounded by the air. While it remains in its place, it is by nature cold and moist, with a comparative weight. The end of its generation is to give shape to forms, to smooth them, and to temper them. It was said "whose natural place is," because in some parts the earth is found uncovered by water. which, being cold and congealed, the earth was rendered and made 
upon the water; which position Aristotle <note>original: "Ay." likely a shorthand for Aristoteles.</note> condemns in many 
places. There were others also distinguishing that 
moisture is twofold: one kind is subtle, passive, and dissolvable, 
in which air is said to participate more than water; the other 
is almost the opposite of this, in which water rejoices 
more than air. But some say that this is not valid, since 
the distinctions of this are material; and matter 
distinguishes nothing, whence in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, according to Anaxagoras, nothing 
was distinct; for in the foundation of nature 
everything is indistinct, for it is <term>actuality</term> <note>original: "actus." The state of being realized or "in act," as opposed to mere potentiality.</note> that separates and distinguishes; 
from the seventh book of the same: wherefore nature cannot be held here 
between air and water, as if the distinction were present in it primarily. 

---

And others say, 
according to the first proposal, that moisture is twofold: one 
is natural to the air, and the other is accidental 
and wetting, such as that of water. Because of this, 
thirdly, it must be more sweetly said that moisture can be 
considered in two ways: either regarding its essence, 
principally unimpeded, and such is the moisture of air; or regarding 
an apparent manifestation, such as that of water. And this is confirmed 
by the preceding distinction; for since air is most 
changeable and alterable (distinction 16), a quality should be 
proportioned and accommodated to it that is the cause of that: 
such indeed is moisture, since among the passive qualities 
it is the most passive; for otherwise it could not be 
changed and varied easily by our bodies, from which no small 
harm would arise. Nor does heat impede it, since heat 
is weaker than the moisture acquired by it, although it is refining 
and dissolving. It also receives the impressions of the higher 
and lower bodies, which it could not do unless the quality were 
accommodated to it like an instrument. In water, 
however, it happens otherwise, since it is not so changeable 
and alterable, nor so receptive of impressions. And for this 
reason, no pestilential infirmity seems to fall upon 
fish as it often does upon men and other 
walking creatures (from the first book of the *Histories*). For water itself is felt to be 
moister than air, because its moisture is more adhering 
and gathered together; whence, since it is a medium between the totally subtle 
and the thick, then it can certainly moisten more perfectly, 
not only in appearance but in truth, as rain shows. 
Likewise, the elements that contribute most to life possess 
these qualities; these are fire and air; for they 
work toward the generation of spirits and the motion by which 
there is life, since motion is transfused from the heart into the limbs; 
the qualities of this are heat and moisture (distinction 21). 
Furthermore, it is in the nature of the moist to be poorly bounded by its 
own boundary, but perfectly by another's; the dry is the opposite 
(from the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*). But this belongs more to the moisture 
of air, since it is joined to heat, which incites it 
to diffusion and lack of boundaries; and it is equally 
true of the moisture of water, for it is associated with intense cold. 
Understand, then, the moisture of air and water like the heat 
of a flame and that of glowing iron. For although the flame is 
essentially hotter than the iron, the flame nevertheless heats 
 the iron more intensely. Thus also water moistens more than air. 
Therefore, essentially, water is moister than air. 
Regarding the fourth point, it must be said to the first that Aristotle 
does not feel that moisture is present primarily and universally in water, 
but rather in a certain respect, namely, insofar as bodies are [formed] 
by the moisture of water and the dryness of earth, and thus 
otherwise bounded; for the moist is 
unbounded by its own limit, but is easily bounded by an external limit; 
the dry is the opposite. Whence Aristotle, after these things, adds: 
"Because of all these things, bounded bodies consist 
not without earth and water"; the Commentator <note>Usually referring to Averroes, the primary commentator on Aristotle in the Middle Ages.</note> 
states that it is of necessity that bodies are generated 
through moisture with dryness, and the dry element is earth and 
the moist is water; then it is necessary that every generated body 
be a thick substance made from earth and water. And therefore, in the first 
book, the two heavy elements help toward the [composition] of the limbs...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the elements, specifically debating whether the primary qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) are the actual essence—the "substantial form"—of the elements or merely accidents that belong to them. It addresses contradictions between medical authorities like Galen and philosophical ones like Avicenna and Aristotle.</meta>

...their generation and their rest. To the other point, it must be said that **Galen** speaks subtly as a physician, perceiving moisture according to its "clinging" <note>original: "iherētiā" (inhaerentiam). This refers to how moisture sticks to or soaks into things, a practical medical concern.</note>, just as he also writes in that same place. He places the highest heat and dryness in fire, and in water coldness and moisture; however, **Avicenna** more truly feels that a single quality exists primarily for each of the elements <note>Avicenna argued that while each element has two qualities, one is "primary." For example, fire is primarily hot and secondarily dry.</note>, differing from the former view. But perhaps that argument is not valid. Galen, whom Avicenna follows primarily, wished to treat the elements properly not just as a physician, but more as a **natural philosopher** <note>original: "p-hiologū" (physiologum). In the Middle Ages, a "physiologus" was someone who studied the nature of physical things, not just medicine.</note>. Or it should be said that Galen perceived two qualities joined at their highest point, and not a single one existing divided in one of the elements, the contrary of which was nevertheless brought in from Avicenna’s earlier distinction.

Or perhaps this discourse should be explained according to the intention of Avicenna and the **Commentator** <note>The "Commentator" almost always refers to Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note>. To the other point, it must be said that in water, as has appeared, our senses help us; in air, however, it is the intellect. For just as "clinging" moisture cannot be separated from water while the water lasts, neither can "essential" moisture be separated from the air while it remains. To the other point, it must be said that the moisture of air, although it is "material" in respect to fire, is nevertheless "formal" in relation to earth and water, since the two higher elements <note>Fire and air.</note> hold more the place of **form**, and the lower ones <note>Water and earth.</note> the place of **matter**. Whence "material" moisture, which clings, belongs to water since it is of that kind; but the remaining moisture belongs to air. To the other point, it must be said that although **spring** <note>original: "bys," likely a scribal shorthand for "ver" (spring) given the context of seasons.</note> is truly moister, and with an accidental moisture that wets things, it is nevertheless also of an essential, "co-nutritive" moisture; whence also by such moisture we see things are more truly moistened in summer than in winter, which the nature of blood and phlegm demonstrates. To the other point, it must be said that the moistening of water was more an accidental and clinging thing, whereas that of air is properly essential.

$\quad$ But from **Nicholas** <note>Likely Nicholas of Amiens or another scholastic author.</note>, concerning a certain point brought from the opposite side, it happens to be doubted: whether the quality of an element, and especially the one "appropriated" to it, is its **substantial form** <note>The "substantial form" is the deep essence that makes a thing what it is (e.g., what makes fire "fire"), as opposed to an "accidental" quality (like a piece of wood being painted red).</note>, as he seems to know. This is confirmed because the elements—that is, the innate heat of the **prime matter** <note>original: "yle" (hyle). The fundamental, formless "stuff" of the universe that receives forms to become specific elements.</note> of fire—are perfected or generated; and finally earth, water, air, and fire are not from other bodies but are from prime matter and qualities. But that which comes to prime matter is a substantial form and not an accidental one like a quality. And the **Commentator** in *On the Heavens and the Earth* says: Fire is not fire in act except in heat and dryness, which are at their highest. Furthermore, that which is placed in the "definition" <note>original: "rōne" (ratione).</note> of anything is its very substance, since a definition is constituted from the **genus** and the **substantial difference**; but in the definition of the elements themselves, their qualities are placed, as has appeared. Furthermore, that seems to be a certain substance which cannot be separated from it: such indeed is the heat of fire and the moisture of water. Therefore, the qualities of the elements will be their forms. This is what **Aristotle** himself seems to feel in the second book of the *Metaphysics*: "Many who consider themselves wise have thought that some one thing could be both a substance and an accident at the same time according to two different respects." For they said that heat is an accident to a heated body, but to fire in general, it is not an accident—about which we have written enough in the beginning of the *Logic*.

It must be said that the qualities of the elements cannot be their substantial forms, since that which truly is an accident can be so to no substance. For what is a substance in one thing cannot be an accident in another; if, therefore, heat were truly a substance in fire, it could not happen to be an accident in other things—which is false. Wherefore the **Commentator** in the eighth book of the *Metaphysics* says it follows from this as an inconsistency that something could be a quality in itself, and in respect to another, a substance; but "substance" is not said in respect to anything <note>Substance is what a thing is in its own right, not in relation to something else.</note>.

$\quad$ Furthermore, composite or concrete things would have the definitions of fire or another element when they were hot or had another quality. For a "hot composite" is made of substance and quality; or if it were composed of substance and accidents, then one would be "in act" and two "in potentiality." Again, it would be a contradiction at the same time, since it is of the nature of an accident to exist in something else, but of a substance not at all. Furthermore, the substantial form is perceived by the intellect as "what a thing is," for that is its object—as in *On the Soul* <note>original: "ttio de aia" (tractatio de anima).</note>. But the qualities of the elements are received by the senses, whatever the Commentator may feel in *On the Soul*. Again, a substantial form is not generated from another, since nothing is generated except what is in it; but the qualities of the elements are generated from one another. Finally, a substantial form is neither active nor passive; but since the qualities of the elements are of this kind, they are therefore accidents and not substantial forms. From which it also follows that the distinction some make between "heat" or "cold," "dryness" or "moisture" spoken of "simply"—as being the substantial form of fire—and not spoken of simply—as being an active and passive accident—is not valid.

Some, however, have distinguished two kinds of substantial form: one indeed which is constitutive of the essence of a thing, such as the true genus and difference. The other, however, which follows that essence inseparably and convertibly. They do not now place the qualities of the elements as substantial forms in the first way, but perhaps in the second. But even this cannot stand, since that "substantial" thing would be a certain **property**; but properties, according to **Boethius**, flow from the genus of accidents. Then to the first point, it must be said that Nicholas and perhaps Galen were of a disapproved opinion. Or that "substantial" is taken for "essential," at least in terms of inseparable lasting. Or they called qualities "substantial forms" by a certain decorative likeness. For they are better known than the forms, especially those of the elements, since an active property exists in them. Or by "qualities," he understood "substantial," for the form of this quality is its form. Boethius says in the *Categories*: "Indeed, these four qualities will be the causes of the elements." In the fourth book of the *Meteorology*, he understood them more as "instrumental," insofar as they work in the virtue of their substantial forms. To the other point, it must be said that those definitions are not the true and substantial definitions of the elements, but rather certain "descriptions," since the ultimate and completing form of a being is hidden from us—the form which, joined with the genus, would constitute the species. Therefore, in place of those, we have accepted many accidental differences, holding the place of the one ultimate, perfective substantial difference. See the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*: it is clear that the final difference will be the substance and definition of a thing. If it were otherwise, the same difference would often be in definitions...

<meta>This page continues a scholastic debate regarding the elemental qualities. The previous page discussed the views of Galen and Avicenna on whether elements have one or two primary qualities. This page moves into a specific investigation of the element of air, contrasting the views of Lucius Annaeus Seneca—who argued air is naturally cold—with the Aristotelian view that air is naturally hot and moist.</meta>

...take several accidental differences <note>original: "differentias." These are distinguishing characteristics that are not part of a thing's essential nature.</note> to denote the same thing. To the other point, the **Commentator** <note>Averroes (1126–1198), the influential Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were standard in medieval universities.</note> responded: that when fire is removed through the removal of heat, it is not removed primarily or through itself, but rather mediated by the removal of the "form" of fire; just as when the "ability to laugh" is removed, the "human" is removed, but not primarily; rather, it is secondary, as if mediated by the removal of "rationality."

### DIFFERENCE XIV.

<margin>1</margin> **T**hat air is cold by nature is shown through **Seneca** in the second book of his *Natural Questions*, where he says: "Air is cold and dark through itself; light and heat are its food." <note>Seneca, *Naturales Quaestiones*, Book II. Seneca believed air had no light or heat of its own but "borrowed" them from the sun or fire.</note> He further adds: "The nature of air is cold." Again: "The nature of each thing is found purer and more effective in its middle, since its virtue is preserved there more than at the extremes." But the middle region of the air is found to be sensibly cold, as the effects generated in it—such as hail, snow, and frost—indicate. Similarly, the freezing on higher mountains and the great lack of life and sterility found there, since nothing lives without heat, [prove this]. Seneca also says: "That which, when left to its own nature, tends toward coldness, is naturally cold; air is of this sort," as is indicated by its becoming warm in the presence of a heating agent and its absence [of heat] when that agent is away. Likewise: that which is indifferent to heat and coldness does not seem to be hot by nature; for that which is such by nature is determined, since it is from some intrinsic principle of physics and the series of its generation. Such air indeed seems to be. For it quickly receives heat and cold. Its lower part is sufficiently warm as perceived; its upper part is even hotter; yet the middle is cold. Therefore, air is naturally cold, or it determines no nature for itself. 

However, against this view stands **Aristotle** <note>original: "Au." (Auctor), referring to "The Author," Aristotle.</note> in *On Generation and Corruption*, along with other illustrious philosophers and physicians, placing air as naturally hot. Furthermore: that which is changed into water (the first of the elements to be so changed), as has been declared, through the arrival of coldness, is not naturally cold; for such a thing would be meeting itself; but air is clearly such a thing. 

Moreover, in the same *On Generation and Corruption*, from the four primary qualities of the elements, six pairings arise: four are possible, and two (being direct opposites) are impossible. To none but air is it possible to adapt "hot" and "moist"; therefore, air exists as hot by nature. Regarding the first point, however, it must be known that air is a hot and moist element. Whence its primary properties: air is a "simple body" <note>An element not made of other substances.</note> whose natural place is in the concave surface of fire, and its lightness is comparative, and its nature is unimpeded. It is hot and moist, so that it may be preserved in the things generated from it—that they may be rarefied, thinned, lightened, and elevated to higher places. 

Its "interstitial space" or "tunic" <note>Layers of the atmosphere.</note> is also described as triple: one is here [near us], hot and moist, existing from the rays of the sun and stars and the refraction of these against solid bodies; another is the highest [layer], touching the fire, being hot and dry from that contact. There is also the middle [layer], which is sensibly cold and moist compared to the others, due to the aforementioned causes in the very deprivation of heating agents. 

**Algazel** <note>Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a Persian theologian and philosopher.</note> however, separates the air into four tunics, all of which he feels participate in heat:
*   One which is contiguous with the earth, in which there is "smokiness" <note>original: "fumositas."</note> and "wateriness" raised from the earth and water, in which heat is found in some places; for the earth receives the splendor of the sun and becomes warm, whence heat reaches the air near it. 
*   Above this is another layer, free from watery vapor, which is hotter; for the heat of the earth does not reach it because of its distance. 
*   The third is existing as "pure air," which neither heat nor vapor can reach. 
*   Above this is yet another, in which there is smokiness; for the smokiness of the earth is elevated into the air and strives to ascend to the empyrean heaven, namely to the fire. 

What is actually hot will be noted in the following "difference." There is also such a thing in nature that it is inherent to it from the beginning, at least in its intrinsic disposition; and concerning this, the difference appeared in chapter IX. 

Regarding the second point, it should be known that they said air can be considered in two ways: in one way according to what it *is* as air, and thus it is hot by nature; in another way as it is situated in such a place, and thus it stands as cold by nature. This is perhaps false, because air, insofar as it is air, is not "natured" or "qualified," but rather "substantiated." Furthermore, the location follows the form, as do the quality or nature. There were others, as touched upon, such as Seneca, judging the air to be naturally and of itself cold and dark; and that it receives heat and luminosity from the higher bodies, either from their rays as it contains them, or from the proximity of fire and heaven as was said. Whence the middle part of the air, which is affected by neither of these causes, shows its natural coldness: the middle part of the air, therefore, as it is remote from these, remains in its own cold. The cause of this will appear in the third [book] of these sayings. 

Some of the moderns, however, have said that Seneca understood "accidental" coldness, and not that which is potentially in the air; but the fact that he spoke of it as "natural" is clearly indicated by his arguments. Regarding the beginning, it should be known that air is universally hot and moist. According to **Nicolaus the Peripatetic** <note>Likely Nicolaus of Damascus, a 1st-century BC commentator on Aristotle.</note>, it is more properly moist than hot, as seen in differences XII and XIII. 

It must be observed, however, that regarding the being of air and its nature, one may not without merit doubt, because of its mutability and variety; for certain knowledge stands in that which is permanent. It varies easily because of the subtlety of its substance. For a subtle substance receives more of the "passion" of simple things. Similarly, because of its own quality—namely moisture—which is the most "passible" <note>Easily acted upon or changed.</note> of the qualities, being in this regard opposite to heat. Likewise, it varies in heat and cold; whence in the *Problems* [of Aristotle], book XXV, it is said air is apt to be cold and hot, but not moist—meaning the moisture of water. And therefore its nature in "action" was doubted, but not in its "passive" state. Furthermore, by reason of its site, being under fire and above water and earth, it is changed greatly by these and the rays of the stars. This is also confirmed by those who posit that it is agitated by the planets—such as **Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury**—with various motions and "impressions" <note>The astrological or physical influence of planets on the atmosphere.</note> according to their natures and paths, as in difference XVI. I say therefore that...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the elemental nature of air, specifically addressing the conflict between Seneca’s view (that air is cold) and the Aristotelian view (that air is naturally hot and moist). The author explores why the "middle region" of the air appears cold despite air's naturally hot essence.</meta>

Air is hot by nature everywhere, though it is hot by accident in some places: for in the upper layer <note>original: "tunica." Medieval science divided the atmosphere into three "tunicas" or layers.</note> it is more hot by accident than by nature, and similarly dry. However, in the lower layer, it participates in heat both by nature and by accident, and in moisture both by nature and by accident. The ways in which this "accidental heat" operates are manifold: such as the **reflection** <term>refractio: here meaning the "striking back" of solar rays from the earth's surface, which medieval thinkers believed caused the heat of the lower atmosphere.</term> of rays against polished and solid bodies, the heat contained within the earth and water, and finally the exhalations resulting from hot places, or from sulfur mines and fires burning within the earth, such as **Vulcano**, **Apono** <note>The hot springs of Abano Terme, known in Latin as Fons Aponi, famous for volcanic heat.</note>, and many others of this sort. The middle region <note>the "middle region of the air" (media regio aeris) was famously considered the site where clouds, rain, and hail formed.</note>, though being hot by nature, is cold by accident: because it is distant from the motion of the upper spheres and is not heated by the element of fire unless it is very weak; nor can the reflection of rays reach that far. Thus, its heat is merely "potential" based on its position relative to the heavens and the arrangement of the other lower elements, and so it is easily changed by any arriving cold, so much so that its nature is thought to be cold.

This is also confirmed by reasons: because that which is close to the heavens (other than the element of fire) will share in its quality completely, since nature does not permit disorder in its actions, at least according to the seventh book of the *History of Animals*. This [element] is the air. Likewise, no two elements that immediately follow one another in generation are found to be entirely contrary, because of the **harmonic bond** <note>original: "armonicam colligantiam." The idea that elements must share at least one quality to transform into one another.</note> which they have with each other (as seen in Difference XIII). But fire and air immediately follow one another. Fire is hot and dry by nature; therefore, air will not be naturally cold and moist. Furthermore, where natural properties are the same, the things themselves will be the same, since their essence is demonstrated through these properties as if through their own specific "passions." Therefore, if air were naturally cold, being naturally moist, air would certainly be water, since water itself is naturally cold and moist. Again: air by its own lightness moves upward, at least in comparison to earth and water, even if it is heavy relative to fire and within its own sphere; hence in the fourth book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*, it is said that in its own region, all things have weight except fire, including air. But movement away from the center <note>i.e., upward movement.</note> is specifically caused by heat. Furthermore, in all inhabited lands, the air is resolved <note>transformed or broken down</note> in all its dispositions; first, the process of resolution is accomplished by heat. Testimony of this is given by the bodies in which air dominates, for they are hot and moist by nature. This is also indicated by the sense of touch, which feels little cold from the air, but much from the surrounding water and from high mountains that reach the middle interstitial region of the air. From these points, it is concluded that air, according to its whole self, is naturally hot; and if this heat is weak and potential, it is easily altered by any changing force, due to the many causes of change mentioned. And note: this heat of the air is compared rather to the cold elements than to our own bodies. Hence, air is not called "strongly cold" except in comparison to our bodies. To the fourth point:

To the first, it must be said that **Seneca**—a moralist and not a physicist—was in error. To the other, it must be said that it is not true that the middle is always purer and more perfect than the extremes; indeed, sometimes the extreme is better than the middle, as is seen in the pulse between the strong and the weak, for the strong is purer and more perfect than the middle.

---

Or it must be said that this is true if the "middle" is taken by equal distance from the heat, whose properties would then be unimpeded. But that does not happen here. For as is proven in the book *On Twilights* <note>original: "de crepusculis." A work on atmospheric optics often attributed to Alhazen or Gerard of Cremona.</note>, vapors do not rise higher than three miles (or a little less) from the earth; therefore, this "middle" is defined by **negation** <note>meaning it is defined by what it is not—not near the earth and not near the fire—rather than being a true center.</note> and not by equal distance or participation. For clarification, it must be said that the middle region of the air, even if naturally hot, is nonetheless cold by accident, as has appeared. This is partly due to the failure of the sun's rays to reach it, and partly due to its distance from the celestial spheres. Therefore, in the first book of the *Meteorologics*: the region of the air, that is the middle, is not near the hot stars, nor near the rays reflected from the earth, which are prohibited from standing still near the earth because they disperse the substances of heat. For the gathering of clouds happens where the rays cease to be immensely scattered; also, the heat of the element of fire cannot alter the air at such a great distance. This is also helped by the nature of the vapors reaching that place: for though they may be naturally cold, they are hot by accident, and they return to their cold nature. It is like a battle held between their accidental heat and the diminished heat of the air, to which the winds shaking the air also contribute cold. Hence **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay." for Aristoteles.</note> says: "Heat having been extinguished, vapor can be suspended in the air," because higher above the earth the cooled vapor stands firm again, both because of the abandonment of heat and because of the cold place. Some, however, try to destroy this argument because they want to assign a positive cause—and not a privative or violent one—to every positive effect. The previously reduced cause seems privative and violent; therefore, to give a positive cause in the bodies, they look to the upper spheres. Since this movement happens to them by necessity, it is caused by the upper motions (First book of the *Meteorologics*). They say this happens due to the coldness of "cold stars," such as **Saturn**, **Venus**, or the **Moon**. This is not by way of their motion and light (which cause heat), but by way of the "instruments of the upper nature," or through their own effective qualities. But it is perhaps not sound to say this, since the **Commentator** <note>Averroes.</note> says in *On the Heavens and the Earth* regarding **Aristotle** (who suggested some stars might cool and others heat): that in truth they do not act through coldness, but through the specific heats of each of the elements. He says this is manifest in the Moon. But I have spoken of this in Problem XXV and Difference X, which suffices for this matter. And besides Aristotle's cause, since the nature of all things is compensated by mutual trust, it eventually declines toward heat and moisture. Furthermore: they would not only change the middle air so that effects of cold (like rain and such) happen in it, but they would change this air surrounding us similarly. Yet the opposite is seen in the first book of the *Meteorologics*. Nor is it unsuitable for a positive effect to have a privative cause as its immediate one; nor is cold entirely a "privation," since it is perhaps not impossible for something "violent" to be continuous as long as its primary cause remains eternal. Regarding this, the science of meteorology reasons much, which is not suited to the present speculation. To the other point, it must be said that air, when left to its own nature, does not tend toward coldness but rather toward...

<meta>This page continues the technical investigation into the elemental properties of air, specifically debating whether air possesses "gravity" (weight) or "levity" (lightness) when situated within its own natural sphere. It transitions from the discussion of air’s temperature to its physical weight and its role in the Aristotelian "Great Chain" of elements.</meta>

...toward heat. But because it seems to tend toward those qualities by accident, it happens just as it does in all things. However, it appears that when heat recedes, cooling occurs in a similar way. This happens because **air** does not naturally possess such great heat that it remains hot once the source of heating is removed. Regarding the other point, it must be said that air, as has been proven, is naturally disposed toward heat; however, because of its weak heat and its many-sided variations, it seems to possess neither precise heat nor cold within itself.

### Whether Air is Light or Heavy in its Own Sphere

It is asked whether the description of air is eased and elevated toward the higher regions. Does it possess lightness or gravity in its own proper sphere, or within itself? Indeed, it seems here, according to **Aristotle** <note>original: "A." refers to Aristoteles throughout the text.</note>, that it possesses lightness, since its function is to make things light and to lift them. Furthermore, in *Problem 25* of the **Problems** <term>Problemata: a collection of questions and answers on various scientific and philosophical topics attributed to Aristotle.</term>, it is said that air is carried upward. Indeed, it is seen that when a bladder is empty, it is carried downward; when it is inflated, it remains up, because air is carried upward.

Furthermore, it is the nature of heat to be dilated and moved from the center toward the upper circumference in a straight line, as fire demonstrates and as the upright growth of adolescents shows. But air is hot; for its nature has been declared as such. Moreover, whatever things agree according to their location also have proportional forms. As much as nature grants a place to something, it grants just as much to its form, as stated in the fourth book of **On the Heavens and the Earth** <note>original: "celi & mundi" (De Caelo et Mundo).</note>. Likewise, similar properties follow closely related forms, since they originate from them. Now, however, the locations of fire and air coincide closely. But fire is the lightest of bodies, seeking the highest disposition of all; therefore, air follows after it. Again, the **animal spirit** <term>spiritus animalis: in medieval physiology, a subtle, air-like substance that flowed through the nerves to enable movement and sensation.</term> is of the nature of air; for it is released into it when a creature dies. But the spirit seeks the higher regions, since it is the hottest part of the living body. Likewise, when a sharp, hard stone is rubbed and sharpened, the pieces cut from it are seen to seek the heights, even though they are heavy, for the whole stone is heavy. Therefore, air will have lightness in its own region. 

On the contrary, as has been said, in its own region all things have gravity, and air also has gravity, except for fire. Therefore, in *Problem 21*, it is said that air, even if mixed with something, does not make it any lighter; for air has gravity within air. Again, the elements are ordered primarily for generation; thus all who identify them have described them by how they coincide in mixture. With **Aristotle** indeed being an exception, the property of these things is to touch their own place. This is fulfilled even more if it still naturally inclines toward this place, in which almost all things are born and managed. Among these, air—by its heat and moisture being sufficiently tempered relative to others—is ordered most especially for life and its conservation. Fire, however, is devouring and destructive. It seeks the higher moisture, being least receptive to external impressions. How they occur in mixture will be shown in the sixteenth chapter; thus air participates in gravity in itself. 

Regarding the first point, one must know what air is and what its sphere is, as its own description denotes. I hear also that through air, which is sufficiently pure and tempered and the most abundant medium among all, it is possible for a wide

---

magnitude to be fixed through the air in a similar way; for this itself calls to the movement of **The Heavens and the Earth**. There is among these four elements a certain one that is "ultimately light," always seeking the higher regions without hindrance; there it is preserved, like fire. Another is "ultimately heavy," seeking the lower regions by its very nature; and there it is likewise preserved, like earth. Certain others, however, obtain a middle place and nature between these light and heavy things—not simply, but relative to something else. For instance, **water** is light in comparison to earth, but it is extremely heavy in comparison to air and fire. Air itself, however, according to its own nature, has an even greater inclination toward gravity than toward levity, as will be shown. Therefore, that which is born to be carried upward—or away from the center if not hindered—shall be "light." That which is carried downward, or toward the center, shall be "heavy," as in the fourth book of **On the Heavens and the Earth**. Nevertheless, gravity and levity exist in a twofold way according to the **Commentator** <note>likely Averroes, the standard medieval commentator on Aristotle.</note>: one is when something exists in its own place, where there is nothing but the velocity of its motion toward its own "up" or "down" from that which induces violence; the other is "simple," when it is outside its own place.

Regarding the second point, one must know that some have felt that air possesses lightness in its own place, and even that water does not have gravity. **Ptolemy** or **Pytheas** <note>original: "Ptholomeus uel Pitheseus."</note> attempts to show this in the *Book of Weights*. Wherefore **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle.</note> says that he himself, with all the diligence he could muster, found the weight to be the same for bladders full of air and not full. He also says some have written that an uninflated bladder would be of greater weight than an inflated one. Some say this is because of **Aristotle**, who seems to feel the opposite because of the diversity of air—experienced in greater, lesser, or middle moisture, and similarly in thickness, thinness, and medium. 

But others have wanted air to have lightness, and they claim that below a certain point air is heavier than a small lead coin <note>original: "plūbi obolo" (a lead obol).</note>, unless they possess true gravity and levity. Some moderns hold this, such as **Themistius** <note>A 4th-century Greek philosopher and statesman.</note> and his followers; hence he attempted to compel the expressive motive of **Aristotle**, by which he shows that air contains gravity in itself. He wished here for a "talent" of wood <note>A "talent" (talentum) was a massive ancient unit of weight.</note> to be heavier than lead when in the air, and therefore to fall downward faster than it. Yet in water, that wood floats, while the lead is submerged. This is because the wood, existing in the air, is snatched downward by a triple gravity—namely its own, and that of water and earth—while the lead possesses only two of these, since air participates very little in the lead compared to the wood. But it floats upon the water; for in relation to water, the wood is light because of the "dominion" of air in it. Lead, however, is heavy even in respect to water, since earth dominates in it most especially. Indeed, the Arabic and Greek translations for the most part state this in the commentaries. **Themistius** says that the cause given by **Aristotle**—namely that more gravities exist in the wood than in the lead—is not the reason it tends downward faster because of air having gravity in its place; but because the wood, due to its greater bulk, participates more in the gravity of earth and water than a lead of smaller quantity. Thus, the air dominating in it does not hinder its "earthiness" or "wateriness" in itself; but it does hinder it in the water, since it is light in the water. He even introduced **Aristotle** here...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the physical weight (gravity) and lightness (levity) of air. It specifically contrasts the views of Aristotle and the commentator Averroes against the interpretations of Themistius and Alexander of Aphrodisias. It moves from theoretical definitions of "essential" vs "accidental" causes into practical experiments involving falling bodies and heated vessels.</meta>

...to happen. That the elements remain in their own proper places **by force**, or stay in foreign ones, unless they possess **gravity** and **levity** by nature. On this point, the **Commentator** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Western science.</note> fights back, confirming the opinion of **Aristotle**, as will be seen further in the discussion of the third book. For the cause put forward by Aristotle is **essential** and hidden; but for **Themistius** <note>A 4th-century Greek philosopher and statesman who paraphrased Aristotle.</note>, it is **accidental** and apparent. Hence, he took an accidental cause in place of an essential one, and he was in error. The cause of his error was that the accidental cause is manifest in itself, while the essential one handed down by Aristotle is hidden. Since it was concealed, Themistius took up that accidental one and neglected this one. Even his own reasoning is not valid, because "gravity" is spoken of in different ways; it seems to be used equivocally <term>Equivocation: the use of the same word with different meanings, leading to logical confusion.</term> regarding the force an element has within itself versus what it has outside.

Certain people, however, prefiguring the case of **wood** descending faster than **lead**, wanted to assign the **necessity of a vacuum** as the cause. They argued that because the larger mass of wood cuts through more air, it induces a larger "gap," and nature fears a vacuum would occur there unless the wood moved faster through the air. This does not happen in the same way with lead because it is smaller. But this argument is not valid, because if it were true, heavy and light things would not move **naturally**, but rather **by force**. Furthermore, a stronger preventative force would then be required to stop the descent of something larger, appearing lighter, due to the necessity of the vacuum, than for the heavier but smaller lead; nor could it intervene in a vacuum, since air would immediately enter both.

Others, however, said that the wood tends downward faster for this reason: because its greater width of surface area receives the impression of the **movement of the air** more perfectly than the smaller lead. For they assume that air moves continuously, as the **atoms** <note>original: "athomoi," referring to the ancient Greek theory that the world is made of tiny, indivisible particles in constant motion.</note> denote, and similarly that water moves continuously.

But the motion of this air is **wind**; for wind is simply air in motion. In the beginning of the fifth book of the **Problems**, it says the principle of motion even in the blowing of wind is from a higher place, as if from that which is the formal element within it; this is also in the **Meteorology** <note>original: "met hauroruꝝ" refers to Aristotle’s Meteorologica.</note>, books 1 and 3. Therefore, the motion of this air impels the wood thrown down more quickly than the lead. It must be said that this too is not valid, because air—regardless of what **Avempace** <note>Avempace (Ibn Bajja) was a 12th-century Andalusian philosopher who critiqued Aristotelian physics, particularly regarding motion in a vacuum.</note> says—is at rest when left more to its own nature. Likewise, even if it were granted that the motion of air is wind (which is not correctly said, as I declared in that place), the motion of air toward the lower region is not so great that it could cause a body placed in it to be driven downward faster than another because of the air; for we perceive the air not rarely to be at rest, as a feather suspended in it shows. Furthermore, although the flow of wind takes its beginning from above, it does not tend directly downward, but rather **obliquely** or sideways, according to the *Meteorology*, book 3, and the *Problems*, 25 and 26.

Regarding the third point, it must be known that air in its own region has its own **gravity** and inclination, by which it—or whatever is placed in it—moves downward more easily and more quickly, as Aristotle argued. This is proved by reasoning and confirmed by signs. For **earth** naturally always tends downward and **fire** upward, as is handed down; but that which goes upward by force, tends

---

downward. According to Aristotle in the third book [of *On the Heavens*], if the surrounding environment (like water or air) is removed, fire does not ascend, nor does earth descend. **Water** and **air**, being intermediate, participate in both **gravity** and **levity**, but more so in gravity. Thus, the property <note>original: "bonorum," likely referring to the inherent qualities or "goods" of the elements.</note> of gravity is more similar to their natural motion than the act of levity is to forced motion. For if the earth is removed, water naturally descends into that place, as the senses teach us. If, however, air is removed by force, water rushes into that same place. Similarly, if fire is taken away, air will fill its place by force, and not otherwise. But if water or earth recedes naturally, air tends into that place by the inclination of gravity, and not by the **necessity of a vacuum**, as someone might say (this will be confirmed more fully later); however, it moves upward by force when fire is removed.

It is clear that the **inferior place** is owed to that which is material; for such is its nature. But **moisture** (humidity), which is the proper quality of air, is more material than other qualities. Hence, in the 11th book of the *Problems*, the nature of moisture is to move downward. Again, for things that share one surface, one inclines into the other, since they occupy the same region. But there is one surface of air and water—namely, moisture—according to the fourth book of *On the Heavens and the World* and the 25th of the *Problems*, by which these two are bounded. Nothing is bounded by heat or cold. Therefore, although water and earth agree in coldness, they do not share one surface there; wherefore air is not moistened by touching water in the same place.

Therefore, air **naturally descends** toward the water. However, it does not descend into it because it is not heavier than water, but rather it is assisted by the aforementioned shared surface when moved by force. Because of this, through clever devices, one is drawn into the other. This is why Aristotle [explains] that water is drawn into or destroyed in a "fired" vessel. For instance, if a thick glass vessel is formed like a **cupping glass** <note>A "ventosa" or cupping glass was a medical instrument used to create suction on the skin by heating the air inside.</note>, having a narrower mouth than the rest of its rounded body, and a sufficiently lit candle is placed inside: when its orifice has been heated and is then quickly submerged in water so that no air can enter, you will then see the water rise rapidly into the vessel, until it eventually extinguishes the light.

Regarding this, **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a major 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> assigns two causes, which **Themistius** busies himself trying to find fault with. But the **Commentator** [Averroes] repels him with a rebuke, agreeing in some respects with Alexander, which I omit for the sake of brevity as it is not the present business. The Commentator confirms this with many arguments against Themistius, comparing the downward motion of both elements in fire. He concludes that since the cause is essential, it must be verified for both, assuming equal weight. For three causes of gravity will exceed two; on this point, Themistius's cause will not be verified, but perhaps he would deny it. Furthermore, Aristotle [says] that a **bladder** <note>original: "uter," a leather bag or bladder used for storage or experiments.</note> full of air weighs more than an empty one; I have seen by experience that this is so, filling bladders in thinner, warmer, and drier air, and not only with the breath of the mouth, so it could not be said that moisture emitted from the breath was contained within it.
