<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the weight and nature of the elements, specifically air and fire. It concludes the discussion on whether air has gravity in its own sphere and begins "Difference XV" concerning the heat and visibility of the element of fire. It references the ongoing disagreement between Avicenna (Au.), Averroes (the Commentator), and Themistius.</meta>

...heavy. Nor even by weighing bellows; for afterwards, I added a small lead <note>original: "obolo," a small coin used as a unit of weight</note> on top of this downwards when I read [Aristotle’s] *On the Heavens*. However, the **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note> says that the testimony brought forward by **Avicenna** regarding the wineskin was not used by him to prove that air has gravity in its own place, but rather he introduced it as a confirmation. Whence, if it is not granted, it will do no harm, since it is manifest to reason. Also, the leather of the wineskin ought to be dry and thin. Hence, the **Commentator** observes that the wineskin of **Avicenna**, by which he testifies to this, was thinner and drier than that of **Themistius**.

The medium air must also be of a certain substance and quality. Again, we experience that it is easier to push air downwards than upwards, and similarly with water, which denotes **gravity** in themselves. Furthermore, the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>A subtle substance in medieval physiology believed to carry life and sensation through the body.</note> released into the air—although innate heat is present in it—moves downwards; for it moistens. [This matches] Palinurus, which falls into the same problem in book II. Sound is more audible from above downwards than from below upwards. 

But if one says that moisture is drawn out with the voice which ought to make it heavy (as **Avicenna** seems to touch upon in that same place), I would say similarly that heat is also drawn out, which ought to make it light, and this counteracts the weight of the moisture. Also, composite things in which the nature of fire and air flourishes fall downwards, like falling fiery lightning bolts. Therefore, air in its own sphere contains **gravity**. <margin>Note that</margin> in this matter, the necessity of a vacuum makes the question doubtful, as does the instance of the wineskin of **Avicenna** and **Themistius**. 

Regarding the fourth point:
To the first, it must be said that through air, mixed bodies are lightened and brought back to higher places in comparison to earth and water, which are heavy and lead things to the lowest places. For it is said that air is "light" only in comparison to them, not that it actually elevates or lightens mixed bodies within its own sphere. 
To the other, it must be said that **Avicenna** proceeds by way of disputation, not by asserting a definitive conclusion. Whence I said in the glosses there that **Avicenna** is more like one doubting than one teaching. And to **Aristotle**, because he immediately adds the contrary: "But if air lightens upwards and is prohibited from being carried downwards, why then are inflated wineskins heavier?" 
To the other, it must be said that air is only moderately hot unless compared extensively to water and earth; therefore, the moisture truly inherent in it overcomes its heat. For moisture inclines it to sink, as is shown by the animal spirit slipping into the air, since it is a material quality of a place of the lowest quantity.
To the other, it must be said that although air agrees with fire in some things, it agrees more with water, especially in those things where the place is directed downwards, as if there were a certain identity of surface and a common moisture to both. 

Furthermore, in the order of the universe, that which is beneath something is placed at the extremes; it is more similar to the lower common medium than to the similar upper one, as is seen in the following of the inner nature from the upper. For that medium does not seem to be a narrow <term>arithmetic mean</term>, but rather a wider <term>geometric mean</term>. 
To the other, it must be said that the animal spirit is not moved upwards by heat alone, but by the soul with greater power, for the soul exists as the principal agent. Also, although the spirit resolves more into air (because it is a certain subtle body continuous with it), by reason of its heat, it is converted into fire even more. 
To the other, it must be said that although a tiny fragment struck from a stone by friction—having been stirred by a certain heat and motion—seeks higher places at first, it soon seeks lower ones. The shape of the object, which can incite motion, also helps cause this when it is broader.

### DIFFERENCE XV.

-> That fire is not hot is manifest; for if it were <-
-> hot, it would cause heat, and heat would be present in it; <-
-> but according to Algazel, these things are not in it. <-

Furthermore, since it is of the nature of heat to tend upwards (for it moves from the center to the circumference), it would never tend downwards; and thus mixed bodies would not be created from the four elements. But if you say that they seek the bottom by violence, then the mixture will not be natural but violent, and thus not permanent. Likewise, if it were hot—since it is of the nature of heat to shine, to illuminate, and to inflame—fire would be either coal, flame, or light. But then its light would prevent the stars from being seen at night, just as daylight prevents it. Again, if it were hot, and especially since the highest heat would be present in it, it would already corrupt its surroundings, such as the upper orb and the air below; therefore, fire is not hot. 

On the contrary, there are those proving with the Philosopher [Aristotle] that it possesses the highest heat; whence in Difference XIII, to be fire is to have heat and dryness in the highest degree. Furthermore, if one contrary exists in nature, so does the other: as in heaven and the world. But cold is placed in nature primarily in water, as appeared in Differences XII and XIII; therefore, heat will also be in nature. This can be adapted to no element except fire, as seen from the previous differences. Furthermore, the **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note> says regarding *On Generation and Corruption* that when one contrary is in something, the other must be found in it. But "cold" is found in the category of qualities; therefore, so is "hot." Contraries, however, require subjects affected in different ways, yet separately. For they cannot coexist according to all the determinations of opposition. Since, therefore, water is disposed by coldness, heat will affect fire. Therefore fire is hot, which no sane mind denies.

Regarding the first point, however, it must be known that fire is twofold: 
One is **proper**, and this is material fire. Whence in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, that which we call "fire" out of habit is not truly fire; for fire is an excess of heat and like a fervor. 
The other is **spherical**, which is the element of fire, improperly speaking, existing as a <term>simple body</term>. Its natural place exists above all elementary parts, which is the concave surface of heaven <note>The inner boundary of the lunar sphere, according to the Ptolemaic/Aristotelian model.</note>, possessing absolute lightness. Its nature is hot and dry; its function in generated things is to ripen, to thin, to mix, and to subdue the coldness of others. According to **Algazel** <note>Al-Ghazali, the 11th-century Persian philosopher.</note>, this fire is nothing but a single "tunic" or layer; for it is simple and uniform. Nor does it have light according to **Aristotle** in *On the Heavens and the World*, nor color; just as the body of heaven or air does not, though it is thinner than them. For if it had color, it would prohibit the stars from being seen at night, and it would create light upon the earth, just like the fires lit upon it. Whence **Avicenna**...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the elements, shifting from the gravity of air to the specific properties of fire, particularly its visibility, its various forms (coal, flame, light), and the nature of its heat as both an essential and accidental quality.</meta>

**On the Sense and the Sensible**. Fire does not shine unless it is joined with another body, which is also seen in the *On the Generation of Animals*. Fire always appears without possessing its own form, but rather in another body: either in air or smoke, or it appears as something ignited in earth. Moreover, the color of a candle and its light does not occur except from the mixing of clear fire into dark smoke; from these joined together, light and color are made. Otherwise, pure fire has no color. This is shown by the fact that where the fire is strongest in a candle, color is scarcely seen there, so that it appears like a **vacant window** in which there is no <unclear>janitas</unclear> and air. And truly, this fire is the same as that which is there. 

There are three modes of the fire of the other, proper element, as has been judged: namely, **fire**, **coal**, **flame**, and **light**, according to the fifth book of the *Topics*, the second book of *On the Parts [of Animals]*, and the first book of *On Simple [Medicines]*. For it is diversified according to the matter, since true fire and the elements in general can be divided into parts that are of diverse forms. For they are indivisible in species, even if they are divided by quantity or by the reason of their application to matter: for if fire meets with **earthy matter**, "coal fire" arises; if with **watery matter**, "flame"; and if with **airy matter**, "light" is produced. For properly, air is the recipient of light. The reason why he calls it the "species of fire" is because it has no other named name than this, just as there is the named name "ice" and "water"; for if it were unnamed, we would call water "ice."

**Alexander [of Aphrodisias]** in his commentary on the *Meteorology* says the same. **Heat** <note>original: "Calidū"</note>, just like any other quality of the elements, exists in two ways: **essentially** <note>original: "per se"</note> and **accidentally** <note>original: "per accidens"</note>. Essentially, it is either in smoke, such as fire, or relatively; and that is either in act, such as in animals, or in power or virtue, such as in plants growing from the earth. Accidentally, however, it is like the heat of water. 

Regarding the first point, it should be known that some, following appearances and deceived by sophisms, proposed that contradictory things could be true at the same time, so that they even said fire is cold, as **Anaxagoras** <note>original: "az"</note> is detested in the third book of the *Metaphysics*. For these people are like those who testified that Anaxagoras judged that **snow is not white**. They said that it is necessary for a man wise in natural things to exalt his soul from the senses and place it higher than them, and to laugh at his own imaginations. [In the second book of] *On Simples*, it is said that these people should not be insisted upon, since they deny the senses while needing them, and ultimately deny all knowledge.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that fire is hot even in smoke; whence, in *Problem XXV*, it is said: Fire is always hot, and nothing is hotter than it. In the first book of *On Medicines*, it is said there is no mixture if water were contrary to fire, since it exists in the smoke of heat and dryness. Therefore, according to the first book of the *Theory*, a hot substance that is in the ultimate degree of heat is fire. This is proven because that which is placed immediately under a heating agent is a recipient of heat and is made hot by it; this, however, is fire. For it is placed immediately under the celestial sphere, which heats by motion and light, as stated in the second book of *On the Heavens and the World* and the first book of the *Metaphysics*, which is what the ancients said.

Furthermore, that which induces the work of heat is hot, since action makes the form known, just as transmutation reveals the matter. In **Difference XIII**, fire acts in this way: for it heats, it induces evaporation through resolution, it rarefies, it lightens, it aggregates things of the same kind, and segregates diverse things, it digests, and is generated by friction; it seeks higher places, it burns, and such things. Thus, it is hot in this manner. 

It should be known, however, that **heat is more intense** in this material fire than in the formal element of fire, because it is received in a more solid subject. This is shown by fire impressed in steel or tow. Perhaps this was done for the sake of generation, lest elemental fire destroy the remaining elements of a mixture. Whence the **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note> on the second book of *On Generation and Corruption* says: Fire is the burning of the hot and the dry; therefore, nothing is generated from fire, as was also touched upon in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*. Wherefore **Alexander** did not find this except in the fire which is here [on earth]; for the fire which is at the furthest continuity, namely the celestial sphere, is not in the extreme of heat and boiling. This is because several elements are causes of generation. 

But to the contrary: that because of which a thing is such, that thing itself is more so. Because of the fire which is the element, other things are hot and elemental; thus it is with the fire that emerges here. Furthermore, in every genus, one thing stands as the first, which is the cause of subsequent hot things, just as fire is the hottest. For there is another cause of heat here, according to the second book of the *Metaphysics*. This appears to be fire, which is the element, since its being is true. 

It must be said that fire stands as the first of hot things, and that this holds truth in **analogical** <term>analogicis</term> <note>Terms that have different but related meanings, as opposed to univocal terms which mean exactly the same thing in all cases.</note> things, but not in purely **univocal** things. For example, a man is generated by a man; therefore, the generating man is "more" than the generated one—this does not hold. Nor does it hold in purely **equivocal** things, as in a boy and a true man. It is verified in analogical things and in those in which the maker or generator is the total cause of that which is made; which does not happen here, since the heat of fire is fortified because of the matter receiving it, which is signaled by all matter. Similarly, if something is the first and the cause of something, it can exist in it more or less according to the subject, as touched upon regarding reception or in any other way. 

Know also that nature is twofold: **universal** and **particular**. Universal nature, such as that which is roasted and impressing into these lower things, is the **celestial virtue** which adheres to one way and order, as indicated by its motion, from which goodness and perfection are caused in these things. Whence in the second book of the *Cretics* [?]: All good is beautiful, and everything that adheres to one order and way is shown in the traces of wisdom; that is only from above. 

**Particular nature**, however, is the impression in these lowest things, sealed by the prior universal nature; for it is ruled and governed by it. This also emerges as twofold: one is the lowest, the other is the mean between two, such as the nature of living things which, according to "more and less," stands distant from that higher nature, and according to this is more or less ordered—as human nature is most of all, since it approaches it more closely. The lowest are those which are far distant from the first of the elements, being almost opposite; and therefore they least adhere to one order and way, and properly include primary matter and those elements closer to it. Wherefore many things are done according to particular nature, but not universal nature; since particular nature is the cause and mistress of nature. Whence, although **death** is according to the impetus of particular nature, it is not...

...yet universal. And <term>because of this</term> <note>original: "propterea"</note>, in the second book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*, the female sex and every defect and corruption is said to be against nature. According to the second book of the Philosopher <note>The "Philosopher" always refers to Aristotle in this period.</note>, corruption is not outside of nature; for example, growing old happens according to nature. Thus, in one sense, the female is called a "maimed" or "misbegotten" male <note>original: "masculus orbatus uel occasionatus." This reflects the Aristotelian view that nature always intends to produce a "perfect" male, and a female is a deviation caused by external factors.</note>, according to the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*. For "particular nature," which is the specific <term>proper</term> form of an individual, always intends what is perfect and male (since that is more divine). However, "universal nature" also adopts the female, especially <term>because of</term> the necessity of matter and the mixture of deprivation <note>In scholastic physics, "privation" is the absence of a form that should be present.</note>, since without the female, generation could not be preserved, whatever Aristotle may have felt at times.

Similarly, the fact that the water of the sea flows and ebbs exists <term>because of</term> the particular nature of the sea itself, since its more natural state is to be at rest. However, it does not do so through its universal nature, but rather through the motion of the moon moving the sea, according to the way it meets the four corners of the world at differences of 88 and 168 <note>These numbers likely refer to specific degrees or proportions in medieval tidal calculations.</note>. In this same way, fire descends when mixed with light elements, and earth is raised up to the same heights when mixed with heavy ones.

Regarding the fourth point, it must be said in response to the first that fire in its own sphere is not <term>properly</term> said to heat "in itself," since heating implies a transition into external matter that does not exist within that sphere. But where it is joined to the air, it is more truly said to "become hot," since this describes an intrinsic action almost in the manner of desiring and acting. However, this "material fire" here on earth, existing in foreign matter, is <term>properly</term> said to "heat," since it exists in one thing and passes into another.

To the other point, it must be said that fire does not descend downward through its own <term>proper</term> nature, but by the power of universal nature, which governs generation and corruption. Nor is a mixture simply natural, but rather somewhat violent—for instance, because of the inclination of fire to move upward. And <term>for that reason</term>, it can be said that a mixture is in some way "violent," more so by reason of the fire than the other elements. And because a certain violence and opposition is included in mixtures (both by reason of the primary qualities and because the celestial bodies necessitate that a mixture eventually be corrupted), the mixture must eventually fail. To the other point, it must be said that the discussion here concerns fire as an element; you, however, are bringing up "elemented fire" (fire already mixed with matter), as was shown before.

To the final point, it must be said that fire does not corrupt the celestial sphere, nor does it act upon it. Since the acts of agents occur in a patient matter that is disposed to receive them, and this celestial sphere does not receive such impressions (since, according to the Measure <note>Possibly referring to God or a specific astronomical authority.</note>, it does not share matter with the elements). For celestial bodies do not receive foreign impressions, nor does the air corrupt the heat contiguous to it. For the "superior fire," being untouched, is not hot in every way; indeed, its heat is weakened <term>because of</term> its distance from the causes of heating. The celestial sphere also resists fire, along with the other elements that have properties contrary to fire, and <term>because of this</term> it fights against it. In the first book of the *Meteorology*, Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that the sun was a red-hot stone and the heavens were made of ether.</note> posits that everything above this air is full of a glowing, inflamed ether. Since these lower elements would be nothing compared to it, it would entirely corrupt them, so that generation and all motion here would cease. The Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> reject this view in every way.

### SECTION XVI.

> **W**hether elements exist in a mixture "in act" <note>Term: "In act" (*in actu*) means existing as a fully realized, distinct substance, as opposed to "in potentiality."</note>, or whether their substantial forms remain within it, is shown because a thing generated from elements...

...and they are converted into a mixture without their essential forms being corrupted. In the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, Aristotle says that a bodily element exists in a mixture according to its essence. He also suggests this in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*, when he says that most of one element and most of another can interact. However, true contact only happens between bodies. In the ninth book of the *Metaphysics*, it is said that all action comes from that which is "in act"; but elements act and are acted upon within a mixture—otherwise, the mixture would not be corruptible. Furthermore, if the elements do not remain "in act" in the mixture, then it is no longer called a mixture, but rather a corruption, since a mixture presupposes a subject. For a mixture is the union of altered "mixables," according to the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. Truly, "alteration" differs from "generation" in that same place: the subject of alteration exists "in act," while the subject of generation exists "in potentiality."

Likewise, if the substantial form of the mixture is the "act" of the matter, while the forms of the simple bodies (the elements) are excluded, then the simple bodies of the elements would lose their definition. For an element is that from which a thing is first composed, and it is indivisible in species into another species. In the 21st difference, if the substantial forms of the simple bodies were removed, there would be no mixture. Furthermore, if they do not remain "in act," then it seems that since the matter of the mixture would possess no actual form (neither simple nor composite), its privation would be as general as that of prime matter. But prime matter is simple and lacks any form of its own, being the "difference-less" foundation of nature, according to the first book of the *Metaphysics*. Therefore, the matter of a composite would exist entirely outside of reason.

Moreover, if the common matter of a mixture were not made <term>proper</term> to this or that specific matter, the matter would have as many forms as there are composites. Furthermore, that which has the "potentiality" also has the "act," according to the first book of *On Sleep and Wakefulness*. Therefore, if elements are in the mixture potentially, they will also be there "in act," since every being is either potential or actual. They are also the differences of primary qualities, according to the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. Again, wherever one can find the <term>properties</term> and passions of elements, there the elements themselves are found, since passions are inseparable from their subjects, according to the first book of the *Physics* and the first book of *On Generation*. But these are found in a mixture. 

Indeed, Haly Abbas <note>A 10th-century Persian physician and psychologist.</note> and Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus, an influential 10th-century Jewish physician and philosopher.</note> say that in the corruption of an animal, its parts are resolved back into the elements: the spirit into air, the natural heat into fire, the fluids into water, and the bones (and their <term>proportionate</term> parts) into earth. This is apparent regarding the elements. In the second book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*, Theophrastus <note>Successor to Aristotle in the Peripatetic school.</note> recounts that flame can be separated from the eyes of a man. And Megethius, an Alexandrian physician, told me that fire issued from the hip joint of a man from Syria, and in some people, these things happen and the suffering then ceased. Therefore, elements exist in a mixture according to their essential forms or "in act." In contrast, some say they are only there "in potentiality," and they support this with authority and firm it with reason. For in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*, it says the "virtue" (power) of the elements is preserved in the mixture. Likewise, in the book *On the Heavens and the Earth*, it says that in flesh, wood, and every such thing, there is the potentiality of fire and earth. And in the second book of *On the Parts [of Animals]*, it says that a mixture is perhaps a composition of the virtues of the elements—earth, air, water, and fire—not from the elements themselves, but as was said before. For example, the fluid...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into natural philosophy, specifically discussing the definition of elements and the nature of "mixture" (how elements combine to form new substances). It moves from the internal qualities of matter to the external celestial influences of the planets and stars on earthly generation.</meta>

Dry and cold and hot: these are the matter of composite bodies. Whence <term>Galen</term> <note>A famous Greek physician whose works dominated medieval medicine.</note>, regarding the elements, says that <term>Aristotle</term> thinks the elements are fused together in our estimation by the qualities of the sun alone. This teaching is to be chosen for its certainty, because it preserves us from logical inconsistency. And **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a 10th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and physician.</note>, at the beginning of his *Book of Elements*, proving it in many of his books, defined an element as a thing from which, in the first stage of generation, something is generated, and which remains in the thing generated from it, <term>potentially</term> <note>original: "potentia." Having the power to be something, rather than being it currently.</note> and not <term>actually</term> <note>original: "actu." Currently and fully realized.</note>.

Furthermore, from many things that are "actually" beings, one single being does not "actually" emerge through its essence (according to the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*). But elements constitute one "actual" thing, as is agreed. Also, if the forms of the elements remained "actually" in the mixture, that mixture would already possess many forms, which is false; for every single thing has only one single perfected being, as <term>Porphyry</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> feels, following the reasoning of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note>. Again, since every particle, even the smallest, of a mixture is mixed (according to the book *On Generation and Corruption*), then in that same particle there would be four corporeal elements. Thus, in the same smallest of places, many bodies would have their position. This is a contradiction (according to the book *On the Soul* and what is said by the reasoning of the <term>Physicists</term>). Therefore, the elements are in the mixture **potentially**, not **actually**.

Because of this, firstly, it must be known that when a mixture of elements or "mixable things" occurs into one, it follows the truth of the gathering. First, the acts and potencies of the element in the mixture are shown. Second, how mixable things are naturally moved toward the mixture.

Third, we should note what and how many the conditions are concerning the nature of mixture. Regarding this, it must first be known what an element is and in how many ways it is spoken of (shown in distinction 11). However, **mixture** is multiple. One kind is that defined above, in which a new quality results from the qualities of the mixable things being altered and corrupted; it is this kind of mixture that we are speaking of now.

There are other, non-true types of mixture, which are manifold:
*   By **juxtaposition** (side-by-side), like water with oil.
*   According to **mixture**, like barley with wheat.
*   By **adherence**, like one stone to another stone.
*   By **unification and assimilation**, like blood to flesh and marrow to bone.
*   By **nailing/joining**, like wood to wood.
*   By **detention and intertwining**, like one ring to another.

There are certain mixtures that fall in the middle between these and the extremes, such as when one mixable thing is so entwined with another that the flow cannot be discerned, as happens in **honeyed wine** (*mellicratum*) or **vinegar-wine** (*aceticratum*). In these, the nature of the components is changed, so that according to the mixing, they are considered non-existent in truth, according to the substantial nature of elements (as **Alexander** says in his *Problems*). Our mixture is not just for the sake of appearance, nor is it only at the smallest level, but it is **essentially and truly** a mixture of elements.

Now, <term>potency</term> is twofold: one is "remote," distant from the actual state (yet called so because of an aptitude for it). The other is "formal," the form giving being to the thing (also called the "first act"). Similarly, <term>act</term> is twofold: one is the "first act" (the aforementioned potency/form), and the other is the "second act," which is the operation or activity (which contains nothing of potency). Thus, something can be only in potency (like primary matter), or only in act (like an action). Some things are in the middle, such as "formal potency" or "first act." Primary matter is called potency and

simply "potency" with respect to form. The other is called potency in a certain respect, because it relates to the operative act. Conversely, here "act" is taken for the first act or potency, and "formal potency" is taken for "primary potency," which is a certain inclination toward the first act or form (distinction 56). **Substantial or essential form** is that through which a thing has being and is placed within a species; for it is from the form that it receives its species.

Regarding this, we must secondly know that in every action and passion, it is necessary for the **matter** and the **agent** (the mover) to concur actually, driven by the purpose of impressing a form. The matter of the mixture consists of the elements or mixable things. An "element" is like remote, undisposed matter; a "mixable thing" is like near matter. But the **agent** exists in two ways:
1.  The **Unmoved Mover**, who gives motion to all things as the First Cause.
2.  The **power of the celestial sphere**, along with the stars located within it.

These stars are twofold. Some are "erratic," called the **seven wanderers or planets**. Of these:
*   The **Sun** is the fountain of heat; it moves the sphere of fire.
*   The **Moon** is the principle of moisture; it stirs the sphere of water (shown by the motion of its approach and retreat, the tides).
*   The other five stir the **Air**:
    *   **Saturn** disposes it toward cold and death-bearing freezing.
    *   **Jupiter** provides heat and moisture with "temperament" (balance).
    *   **Mars** brings burning heat with dryness.
    *   **Venus** brings cold with measured moisture.
    *   **Mercury** attributes a certain "communicability" and passivity, and thus diverse movements are found in the air.

Other stars are **fixed**, located in the **eighth sphere**. From these (according to **Ptolemy** and **Hipparchus**), 18 images or forms are created without their own physical movements, as noted in the assignment of causes. The motion of this sphere (according to Ptolemy, book 36) is completed in **36,000 years**, assigning 100 years to each degree. Now, however, it is about 70 years per degree (distinction 9, and the treatise I wrote on the *Motion of the Eighth Sphere*). Supported by the motion of the First Cause, it will eventually happen that the Northern signs become Southern, and the habitation of the entire world will be changed in turn. As I declared there (and in *The Meteorologics*, book 3), where there is now dry land, there was once sea, and vice versa. He intends for such permutations to be repeated infinitely.

From this also, marvelous images are imprinted even in the hidden "bowels" of things. The power of the stars descends to the lowest things, and especially the Sun, through its rays, locates and joins its powers to the signs. The fire that exists in a composite body is introduced by the solar rays especially, along with others. This happens not through its natural motion (which is upward), but rather by a "violent" motion induced by universal nature (distinction 1). These also act upon the earth and water, heating the whole and drawing vapors into the middle (the surface of the air), so that a mixture is composed (as discussed in *The Meteorologics*). For although it is according to the nature of "heaviness" for earth and water to seek the lower places, and for the "lightness" of fire to descend [is not natural], it is not against the nature of the **Universal First Mover**.

...and joined in particular. Just as the mover of the heaven <note>The "First Mover" or God, who in Aristotelian physics initiates all motion in the universe.</note> is the primary cause of all transformation; for its motion is like the motion of some wise thing according to **Masha'allah** <note>original: "Me-sahalach." Masha'allah ibn Athari (c. 740–815), a Persian Jewish astrologer and astronomer.</note> in his work *On the Moved Sphere*, to which everything that exists in the elements and things made of elements returns, as seen in the eighth book of the *Physics* and the ninth of the <term>Commentator</term> <note>original: "mentator." This refers to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the preeminent commentator on Aristotle.</note>. 

And so, as is drawn from the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*: the work of nature is an <term>intelligible work</term> <note>A work directed by a guiding intelligence or mind, rather than by blind chance.</note>. The mover here works like a soul, which is the principal cause in living things and is the <term>act</term> <note>The state of being "actual" or fully realized, as opposed to "potential."</note> of everything, according to the third book of *On the Soul* and the fourth of *On the Heavens*. Hence, it is simply the cause of nourishment. 

Fire, in a certain way, is also a cause. For it is the boundary of all things consisting of nature, and the reason for the size and growth of the soul—though not of fire as such. For it sometimes lifts heavy things upward, and at other times brings light things downward, entirely against their <term>mobile inclination</term> <note>The natural tendency of an object to move toward its "natural place" (e.g., heavy things falling).</note>; as has been said concerning bile: for black [bile], being heavy, seeks the mouth of the stomach by tending upward, while red [bile], being light, tends downward toward the intestines. Whence a natural mixture exists that is not a little different from the former. 

Likewise, the "fiery virtue" <note>The inherent power or quality of fire.</note> is led downward in the vapors of rain and dew with which it is mixed; the sign of which is that rain waters and vaporous dews are hot and "digested" <note>In medieval science, "digestion" refers to the process of being matured or refined by heat.</note>. 

Some have said that one of the elements exists in another <term>potentially</term> <note>original: "in potentia." Having the capacity to become something else without currently being it.</note>, as is confirmed from the first book of the Arabic translation of the *Meteorology*. This perhaps is not valid, because mixture is made from elements as they are simple in their own way, and not according to how elements already exist in other elements. 

As stated previously: the element of fire is less hot than this material [earthly] fire. Indeed, many elements are the causes of generation. Miscible things come into the mixture of living beings, and specifically those things born in reality for the sake of perfection: for from these, food is prepared, from which the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health.</note> and seeds are made; and from those finally, by way of origin, living beings are constituted (from the first book of *Elements*). 

The order is as follows: first is <term>primary matter</term> <note>The formless "stuff" that underlies all physical things.</note>, then the elements, then things born in nature; because of that, foods, next the senses, afterward moistures and seeds, then the <term>similar parts</term> <note>Tissues like bone or flesh that are the same throughout.</note>, then the <term>instrumental parts</term> <note>Organs like the hand or eye that perform specific functions.</note>, and finally the embryo or fetus. 

The end is indeed the perfection of the universe and of mixtures—a participation in divine goodness. But the form of the mixture... 

As for the form of mixture itself, it should be known that there are eight or nine conditions required for a mixture. 

The **first** is that the miscible things remain in their essence and are not corrupted into something else; for this is the difference between "mixture" and "generation" <note>Mixture combines things; generation creates a brand new substance by destroying the old ones.</note>. Whence **Averroes** says: Neither do we say that combustible matter, namely fire, is mixed. For it is not mixed when it burns, but fire is generated. So also food will not be "mixed" with the body [but rather transformed into it]. 

Third <note>The author skips "second" or integrates it into the discussion of form.</note>, it is required that the miscible things be bodies; for an <term>accident</term> <note>A quality like "red" or "round" that cannot exist without a physical object.</note> does not undergo mixture with a subject. Hence, a shape does not mix with wax, nor white with color, nor does accident mix with accident—just as a student's learning does not mix with his "whiteness"—because it is necessary for the miscible thing to be able to be separated from the mixture again. For this reason, the intention is sought that they do not always remain joined, but rather that they are sometimes separated from the mixture. 

**Fourth**, that they be of the smallest possible quantity; so that the mixture is not merely on the surface, like barley and millet grains joined together. For in that way, what would be a "mixture" for a human would not be one for a cloth [which has a finer weave]. Although cadmia, verdigris, litharge, and cinnabar <note>These are various minerals and pigments used in alchemy and medicine.</note> may seem to be one and the same when ground and joined together, they are not truly so...

---

...but are many [separate particles], as the first book of *Elements* states. 

It is necessary, **fifth**, that they be <term>homeomerous</term> <note>original: "omiomera." Consisting of parts that are all the same, like water or gold.</note> and homogeneous to themselves. For <term>anhomeomerous</term> or heterogeneous things, such as a nose and an eye, cannot be mixed together at all. 

**Sixth**, that they be "contraries" that act and suffer together while sharing the same matter. 

**Seventh**, that they be sufficiently equal in power and not of every sort; for if one exceeds the other in power, it will not be mixed with it... as with tin. And if it conquers, the whole will be transformed into the dominant thing and not a mixture; whence a single drop of wine will not be "mixed" with a thousand jars of water, since its <term>species</term> <note>Its essential nature or identity as "wine."</note> is dissolved and transformed into the dominant water. 

**Eighth**, that they be well-contained [stable], so that viscosity, fluidity, evaporation, and resolution are removed from them. This happens when the miscible things are applied to one another; for one will receive from the other what was not in itself before. 

It is added, **ninth**, that it is necessary they not be entirely similar, since then no "action" or "passion" <note>In physics, "action" is doing something, "passion" is having something done to you.</note> would occur; nor entirely diverse, for then they would be contraries in the same thing. But the "means" [the intermediate state] between these must also exist as partially corrupted and partially preserved. For their virtue <note>Their power or essential qualities.</note> is preserved regarding human nature, as in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. 

Regarding the second point, it must be known that there have been many opinions on this question, and therefore the definition is difficult to show. The nature of the thing itself indicates its difficulty, since it concerns mixture. Regarding this, there is the act of God and of nature; whence in the first book of *Complexions*: The putting together or mixing of such a thing—not just a confusion of small parts, but a confusion of both throughout the whole—is the work of God and nature. 

For this reason, it is enough to state the truth of such things "probably" <note>In the sense of "provably" or "persuasively" based on observation.</note>, as in the second book of *On the Heavens* and the first of the *Metaphysics*. 

And so, some have posited that the miscible things remain in the mixture <term>actually</term> <note>original: "actu." Currently and fully present.</note> or according to their essential forms. Others, however, say they remain <term>potentially</term> or by "virtue." Some hold a middle way, by an "operative act." 

Of those who posited that they remain in the mixture according to their forms, some wished them to exist actually and entirely whole, like the philosopher **Empedocles** and his colleague the physician **Asclepiades**; just as the philosopher **Democritus** and his imitator **Epicurus** (the Atheist) felt that the tiniest bodies were the compact principles of things. This is very erroneous. Regarding them, it is said: anyone who thinks that the sensible parts of composite bodies occur while the elements remain exactly as they are—merely mixed together like a heap of wheat, barley, and beans—speaks of impossibilities. For in that way, almost no condition of mixture previously mentioned would be preserved; nor would the mixture be certain, but rather a matter of the senses and a fantasy. Nor would one single form arise from it, but only a heap. 

Others, however, said that they are transformed, fused, and altered throughout. Therefore, whoever thinks a sensible thing is made from fire, air, water, and earth being transformed, fused, and altered throughout the whole mixture—even if those parts are not intelligible <note>Meaning they cannot be seen as individual elements anymore.</note>—speaks the truth. 

This seems to have been the position of **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*. He wished the elements to have a double being or act: the first, which they have from their first substantial forms; the second, as they are joined...

nature, as stated in the beginning of the *Histories* <note>Likely referring to Aristotle’s *History of Animals*.</note>; yet fire is not 
fire except through heat and dryness at their highest point. 
And therefore he adds through such things that the lack of exercise 
of **Avicenna** in nature and natural things, and his great confidence 
in his own genius, led him into these errors. 

Some moderns also find fault with the position 
because it becomes impossible for the same matter to 
receive the different forms of the elements. For if, in a mixed body, 
the substantial forms of the elements were saved, it would be necessary for 
them to be in different parts of the matter; 
but for matter to receive different parts is impossible 
unless <term>quantity</term> <note>Physical dimensions or extension in space.</note> is understood beforehand in the matter. For if quantity 
is taken away, substance remains indivisible, as in the first book of the *Physics*. 
From matter existing under quantity, and the substantial 
form arriving, a natural body is constituted. 
Therefore, different parts of the matter of the elements perhaps

subsisting, they take on the nature of many bodies. 
But it has been said that it is impossible for many 
bodies to be in the same place at the same time. 
Therefore, the four elements are not in every part of the mixture, 
for then there would be no true mixture, but only one "to the senses" <note>A "mixture to the senses" is like mixing sand and seeds: they look combined from a distance, but are actually just sitting next to each other.</note>. 
Again, every substantial form in matter 
requires its own disposition, without which it 
cannot stand; hence alteration is the road to generation and 
destruction. But it is impossible for the disposition 
required for the form of fire and the one required 
for the form of water to coincide there; because according to these 
dispositions, fire and water are <term>contraries</term>. 
And it is impossible for contraries to be in the same thing. Thus it is impossible 
that in the same part of the mixture, the substantial forms of fire 
and the others should exist. 

And therefore the **Commentator**, wishing to avoid the 
absurdities that follow from **Avicenna**, and to separate "mixture" 
from "destruction" and keep it safe, proceeded by a middle way. 
For he did not propose that the forms remain pure 
and perfect, nor that they are entirely destroyed; but that they 
remain in part and are destroyed in part, so that they are 
reduced into a certain "middleness." For if they were destroyed in their entirety, 
then the prime matter would receive any forms

are "middle" between "perfect substantial forms" and "accidents,"

the "more" and the "less." He responds to himself that it is not 
inappropriate for forms of this kind, 
since they are most imperfect and diminished from 
perfect substantial forms and are very close to prime matter. 
For their being is a "middle" between 
essential forms and accidents. And therefore he says it would be 
possible for it to be weakened in the mixture and for another 
form to arise from their collection, just as from 
whiteness and blackness many middle colors arise. 

Many follow a similar opinion. 
Firstly, because a "middle" seems to be constructed between substance and accident; 
secondly, because contrariety and the "more and less" are 
attributed to the substantial form. But to say that the forms 
of the elements are middle between substance and accident 
is to place a "middle" between contradictories, which is according to the first book 
of the *Posterior Analytics*. For a contradiction is that which 
by its nature has no middle. For a substantial form is "not being in a subject," 
but the subject and it together constitute something in the 
categories. But the being of an accident—since accidents are not "beings" 
strictly but "of a being" according to the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*—is "being in a subject." 
"Not being in a subject" and "being in a subject" 
import a contradiction. Further, as is proved 
in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*, the middle and the things of which they are a middle—namely, the extremes—
are in the same genus. Hence, in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*: it is necessary 
for the extremes and the middle to be from the same genus. 
But of substance and accident there is no common genus, 
as in **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), whose *Isagoge* was the standard introduction to logic.</note> and in the third book of the *Metaphysics*. 
Since "being," of which it most seems to be a genus, 
is not posited as a genus. Because already the differences would be "of being," 
not "non-being"; but of non-being there are no species nor differences, 
according to the fourth book of the *Topics* and the first book of *On the Parts of Animals*. 
Therefore the forms of the elements will not

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of "mixtures" (chemical or physical compounds). It focuses on the debate between Aristotle, Avicenna, and Averroes regarding whether the substantial forms of the four elements (Fire, Air, Water, Earth) can exist in degrees—being "more" or "less" of themselves—when they combine to form a new substance.</meta>

and the forms of the elements, finally, do not admit of "more" and "less" <note>This refers to the "latitudo formarum," the idea that a quality like 'heat' can be more or less intense, whereas a 'substance' usually just is what it is.</note>. This is because every form that admits of this is divisible, either through itself or by accident—namely, insofar as its subject is able to participate in it "more" or "less." But according to that which is divisible through itself or by accident, it happens that motion is continuous (see **Aristotle’s** *Physics*, Book 5). Change of place, growth, and decay are according to quantity and place, which are divisible through themselves. However, "alteration" is according to quality, receiving "more" and "less," such as "hot" or "white." If, therefore, the forms of the elements were to admit of "more" and "less," their generation and corruption would be a continuous motion. This is impossible, since motion is only found in quantity, quality, and place (see **Aristotle’s** *Physics*, Book 5). And therefore, generation and corruption are "mutations" <note>Instantaneous changes</note> and not "motions" <note>Gradual processes</note>.

Furthermore, they say that every difference according to substantial form varies the species. That which receives "more" and "less" would differ; that which is "more" would differ from that which is "less," and in a certain way, it would depart from itself toward a contrary, like "more white" and "less white." If, therefore, the form of fire or another element were to admit of "more" and "less," becoming "more" or "less" would vary the species; it would not be the same form, but another. And therefore, in **Aristotle’s** *Metaphysics*, Book 8, it is said that just as in numbers the species is varied by the addition or subtraction of a unit, so it is in substances; for substances are positioned like numbers in their limits.

On this point, perhaps the words of these men and similar sayings are what the **Commentator** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198), the Andalusian philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> says, speaking specifically about the opinions of **Aristotle**, namely that they exist truly in substantial form. This perhaps is not valid, since the aforementioned discussions of **Aristotle** are written in universal terms. Thus, these positions appear discordant; some say that in reality, they are one and the same, even if they seem to disagree in words. For they say that **Aristotle** intended for the forms of the elements to be transmuted and blended, and reduced to a certain "middle state"; although **Avicenna** suggests that they could remain whole in their own perfections. I do not believe he [Aristotle] felt this way. For it seems absurd that such a great philosopher could have wanted forms to remain in a mixture as absolutely perfect and unmixed as some of the earlier thinkers wanted, in which the conditions of mixing previously mentioned by **Aristotle** are not preserved.

In this matter, the **Commentator** [Averroes] says they are transmuted, and he wanted them to be brought to a "middle state" through the reception of "more" and "less," just as was said by **Aristotle**, as they claim. But the truth is that **Avicenna** protected the forms of the elements more and made them subsist more than **Aristotle** did. And therefore, here **Aristotle** is seen to hold another position more in harmony with his *On Generation and Corruption*, as will appear in what is to be said later, which the things soon to be said will attest.

There is also a similar position on this very subject among the moderns, which is quite in harmony with the opinion of **Aristotle**. It is, however, a little less articulated and less intelligible to many. For they say that the active and passive qualities of the elements are properly "more" and "less" in relation to each other. From these qualities being altered by one another, a certain middle quality can be constituted, which tastes of the nature of both extremes: just as "orange" is between white and black, or "lukewarm" is between hot and cold. For when the "excellences" <note>The highest intensities</note> of the elementary qualities are relaxed, a certain middle quality is constituted from them, which is

---

the proper quality of a mixed body, just as a simple quality is for bringing forth the form of a simple body <note>A "simple body" is a pure element like Fire; a "mixed body" is a compound like a plant or stone.</note>. In this way, they say the extremes are found in the middle, because it participates in the nature of both: thus also the qualities of simple bodies are found in the proper quality of the mixed body. Because this quality of the simple body is one thing and its substantial form is another, it nevertheless acts by the power of that form; otherwise, heat would only heat, but the substantial form would not, through its actions, bring something into <term>act</term> <note>The state of being fully realized or functioning.</note>, because nothing acts beyond its own species. Thus, the "virtues" <note>Inherent powers or capacities</note> of the substantial forms of simple bodies are saved in mixed bodies—saved in "virtue" indeed, but not in "act." Whence **Aristotle** in the first book of *On Generation* says: the elements do not remain in act as bodies and white things, nor are they corrupted; neither one nor both are destroyed, for their virtue is saved.

Also, in the text of *On the Heavens and the Earth*, regarding the description of a bodily element, **Aristotle** seems to hesitate on this, saying: "let an element then be a body" which is said on account of <term>prime matter</term> <note>The underlying, formless substrate of all physical things.</note>, because "element" is said equivocally of matter itself and of the first simple bodies. The **Commentator** [Averroes] notes this on *On the Heavens and the Earth*. And it is added finally: "into which other bodies are divided, existing either in potentiality or in act." Yet this is still doubtful in both ways—whether it is indivisible into another species.

However, some of the simpler thinkers have said that the elements remain in a mixture in "act" as far as their operations are concerned. For they say that elements can be considered in two ways: one, regarding their substance and distinct being, and in this way they remain in the mixture in "potentiality" and not in act. In the other way, regarding their action, and thus they say they remain in act in the compound. This seems quite absurd, since nothing acts beyond its own species: if therefore they were in potentiality in the mixture, they could not come into the act of operating from such a state of potentiality.

Furthermore, according to the *Metaphysics*, as each thing is related to "being," so it is related to "operating." That which is in potentiality cannot have action, since action is the "act of perfection." Again, each thing operates insofar as it is in act; because of which it seems impossible to place "miscibles" <note>Things that can be mixed</note> in a mixture in potentiality while having an actual operation, since that operation proceeds immediately from the quality. I myself have said elsewhere: that quality can be heard in two ways—either in the *making* of the mixture itself, or in its *already completed* state. If in the former, since in such a "making" action and passion concur, every such subject requires being in act; for only a being in act can act and suffer, while a being in potentiality lacks action entirely; otherwise, act and potentiality would be the same.

Furthermore, the making of a mixture is through "alteration," because a mixture is the union of altered miscibles. This is because alteration is the way toward generation. But alteration, as touched upon, requires a subject in act, while generation requires it in potentiality (see **Aristotle**). Alteration is when, the sensible substance remaining, a change occurs in its passions, either in contraries or in intermediates; but "generation" is when the whole is changed into the whole, with no sensible subject remaining. Wherefore it is entirely necessary that the miscibles remain in the mixture in act. And perhaps this is what **Aristotle** felt, and those who say that the substantial forms of the elements remain in the mixture, though to a lesser or greater degree.

<meta>This page continues the technical debate on the nature of chemical mixtures, specifically addressing whether the four elements (fire, air, water, earth) remain "actual" or "potential" within a new substance. It builds on the previous page's discussion of the "latitude of forms" and whether substantial change is instantaneous or gradual.</meta>

...extremes and separated from their excellences <note>original: "excellentiis," referring to the peak intensity of a quality like pure heat or cold</note>, so that they are led into a middle ground. This is because the motion of alteration of the **miscibles** <term>miscibilia: the individual ingredients or elements that are capable of being mixed together</term> occurs with the alteration in time, receding more or less from the starting point and approaching the end point—namely, **generation**.

If, however, it is explained how much of the element remains in the mixture once it is made and completed, then the elements are said to remain in **potentiality** <note>potentiality (potentia) means they are not currently active but have the capacity to reappear if the mixture is broken down</note> and not in **actuality**, since their forms are corrupted in the principle of the mixture. This is wondered at, because in this way the mixture would simply be that which has been generated. However, this whole process is a transformation of the whole into the whole form. Hence, **Aristotle** says that simple generation and corruption is not a matter of "gathering and separating" <note>Aristotle is arguing against the Atomists here, who thought things just clumped together</note>, but occurs when this whole is transformed into that whole. For since two things exist in the subject of alteration—one according to reason, which is the **form**, and the other according to **matter**—when a total transformation occurs in these, there will be generation and corruption. For the generation of one thing is always the corruption of another.

**Furthermore**, if the elements did not remain in the mixture merely by their power <note>original: "uirtute," meaning virtual presence or efficacy</note> but also in actuality, then the mixture (which is the result of generation) would not differ essentially from the **miscibles** themselves; this is absurd in many ways. Likewise, not every part of the mixture would be a "minimal mixture" <note>meaning the substance wouldn't be uniform down to the smallest particle</note>, as was previously shown from the conditions of mixing. **Proclus** protests that "every cause exists virtually in its effect." Since, therefore, the elements are the efficient cause of the mixture through their active and passive qualities, the qualities of those elements will be in the mixture virtually. And because these qualities do not act except by the power of the **substantial form** of the elements—since it is said that nothing acts beyond its own species, and each thing operates according to how it has its being—the substantial forms will similarly be in the mixture itself by power/virtue. Because of this, one must grant that the miscibles are contained in the mixture (in its completed state) only according to their substantial forms in potentiality or power.

However, so that what has been said may be further declared—and lest the "power" by which the elements are said to remain in the mixture appear to subsist without a subject (since it is posited that substantial forms are corrupted in various ways)—it must be said that when the elements come to a mixture to be within it, and the **miscibles** undergo the process of mixing, then the qualities of the elements act and suffer upon one another. They are led to a certain "middle," which is a quality of the miscibles preparing them for the **form** and **complexion** <term>complexio: the specific balance or "temperament" of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in a body</term> of the mixture. While the action and passion of these qualities can be sustained while the forms of the elements remain uncorrupted, the miscibles remain "in act" in the mixture. 

But when, from the aforementioned action and passion, the substantial forms of the elements are weakened and transformed until they are corrupted, the form of the mixture is generated. This is followed by its **complexion**, arising from the alteration of the primary qualities which were corrupted due to the corruption of the forms. In an instant, the forms of the elements are corrupted, and the form of the mixture is introduced along with its own passion, nature, or complexion. That this is the opinion of **Aristotle** is clear when he posits that simple generation occurs when a sensible subject, along with its passions or accidents, is corrupted into another. It is also said similarly in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption* that **matter** <note>original: "yle," from the Greek hyle</note> is the primary subject of generation and corruption. And in the fourth book of the *Physics*, it is said that matter is not separable; hence in the first book of *On Generation*, it is said that it is never possible for matter to exist without "passion" <note>quality or affection</note> nor without "morphea" <note>shape/form</note>, and the primary elements cannot exist without quality.

Because of this, it is evidently concluded that when one form is corrupted, the matter receives another in an instant—just as the "sensitive" soul is introduced over the "vegetative," and the "intellective" over the "sensitive," as is declared in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*. I understand, therefore, that the elements remain in the mixture in potentiality or power because the **complexion** of the mixture "savors" <note>original: "sapit," meaning it retains the flavor or character of</note> the nature and power of the qualities of the miscibles from which it is drawn out through alteration. Just as blood generated from lettuce can retain the nature of lettuce to some extent, so too the form of the mixture "savors" of the being and power of the substantial forms of the elements from which it was drawn; just as flesh savors of the being and power of the nourishment from which it was generated. **Seneca**, in the fifth book of *Natural Questions*, says the taste of poplars appears in milk, and the power of wine exists in vinegar. Nor should it be granted that the forms of the elements yield entirely into "non-being," since "non-being" and "non-substance" are never constituted from being and substance. A body of such a kind is transformed into such a substance and such a body; yet this whole, by the nature of matter, is transformed into this whole.

But perhaps the first part of the aforementioned distinction regarding mixture, even if it seems acceptable to some, nevertheless opposes the opinion of **Aristotle** and **The Commentator** <note>Averroes</note>; since according to them, a mixture possesses a certain middle ground between alteration and the subject, being "in act" in various ways and only "in potentiality" regarding generation. This is indicated by the conditions and the definition of a mixture. For it is not said to be a union of things undergoing alteration, nor of things corrupted, but of things *that have been* altered. According to this, it is neither a transformation of one of these into another, nor a transformation of them into matter. Therefore, a mixture will be a middle ground between the two extremes, which, if posited, did not preserve the previous premises. However, he did not seem to posit "mixture" in the first sense (from alteration) when the mixture was in the process of becoming, nor in the second sense (from generation) when it was taken as a completed fact.

**Regarding the third point**, it must be said with **Aristotle** and his more diligent interpreters (as touched upon before) that elements, through their active and passive qualities, act and suffer upon one another so that, their extremes being weakened, they are led to a certain prefigured, divisible middle. Hence, in the second book of *On Generation*: those things which are mixed corrupt their intensities upon one another, so that then there is no matter <note>meaning no raw, unformed matter</note>, as happens in the generation of the nature of things where one is simply "in act," as in alteration; but rather a "middle" is formed. And **The Commentator** in the first book of *On Generation* says: "Mixture happens when the miscibles suffer and act equally, so that after them some middle quality comes into being among the secondary qualities—namely, I say, of the hot and cold, and the dry and moist." In this quality, arising from the aforementioned qualities having suffered and been weakened, yet brought into a middle, the power of the miscibles is saved, so that the cause shines forth virtually in its effect. Since, therefore, the miscibles through their qualities immediately produce the mixture, they will exist in it virtually in the resulting quality—that is, one middle quality; or I say perhaps a double one, depending on the resulting complexion...

...simple or composite: and because although every action is perfected by qualities, they themselves do not act except by virtue of the prior substantial form, as will be shown in Difference 60. These qualities also, although they are not the substantial forms of the elements (see Difference 13), nevertheless possess the virtue of those forms. For this reason, heat produces fire by virtue of its substantial form. Then, indeed, it will be naturally preserved in a middle quality, whether single or double—much like a principal agent acting through a secondary one. This is what is indicated by those wonderful things called **automata** <note>original: "automata," referring to mechanical devices that seem to move by themselves</note>, or like the sound of letters within syllables, and syllables within words. Thus, in that middle quality (single or double) which characterizes the form of the mixture, all the first qualities of the elements are present, and even more so than in the forms of those elements themselves. For the qualities are more perfect and powerful in the mixture than in the elements, whereas in the elements the forms are merely broken and diminished. Furthermore, they are receptive to "more or less" and thus allow for division. These [elemental forms], however, are almost destroyed; thus they exist only in potentiality or virtue within the aforementioned middle quality that arises.

According to the saying: "For their virtue is preserved," since the mixed ingredients are neither completely destroyed nor entirely preserved. This is what Galen is said to have estimated: that the elements of the sun would be joined by their qualities. From this, Alexander [of Aphrodisias] in his *Problems* says: they are indeed coupled to themselves by a mixture, as the qualities of the elements or of opposing things have their primary qualities destroyed and others generated. Yet they are powerful enough to be separated and preserved again by nature. And the Commentator <note>The "Commentator" almost always refers to the philosopher Averroes</note> says: the elements are in potentiality in the mixture. However, one should not understand "potentiality" here as prime matter, since the composites that are in potentiality—water, fire, earth, and air—exist in actuality as flesh and bone. Hence, the mixed ingredients are more easily removed from the mixtures than those things which are in matter are removed from it. Nor are they in potentiality in the elements like parts in a continuum, which are parts in potentiality until they are divided and become parts in actuality; rather, a middle way seems to hold between these two.

Thus, let the difficulty of this kind of question be apparent, as well as the probable truth, which the arguments already given support, and which other occurring opinions confirm. Regarding the fourth point: To the first point raised by Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note>, it should be said that this was his opinion, though not currently approved or explained. To the next, it should be said that in the middle quality, as has been shown, the operative act is preserved, since there is no total destruction of those things which belong to the elements. To the next, it should be said that there will be no destruction of opposites, as declared, since the act and form are reserved by the aforementioned quality. To the next, it should be said that the elements do not lose their "reason" <note>original: "rationem," meaning their defining principle or essence</note> entirely, since it has been said they are preserved by virtue in the third thing. To the next, it should be said that the form of the mixture is characterized by the resulting middle quality, and I say the form also contains that quality in its virtue, as has been shown. Nor is it true that the matter of the composite receives as many forms as it does primary qualities, since matter itself is informed by the first form. For it is either confused, or corrupted, or preserved in the middle ground. Similarly, Averroes in *On the Substance of the World* says: indeterminate dimensions assist matter, preceding the arrival of form into the same.

To the other point, it should be said that this would be true in the powers of the soul, in which the question does not stand. For Aristotle <note>original: "Ay."</note> intends to show there that sensing is not a property of the soul alone, nor of the body alone, but of both joined together. Since if the power were the property of the soul alone or the body alone, the act would be likewise, as they are ordered toward each other; for power implies a certain relation and inclination toward the act. To the next, it should be said that just as the ingredients remain, so do their properties and passions; for as some things remain and others strongly so, so too do the properties—not the simple and peak qualities of the elements, but those of the mixtures, as if broken and diminished. To the next, it should be said that elements are not resolved from the parts of a completed mixture like things from a vessel or by simple segregation, but are generated through the corruption of the parts of the mixture. Likewise, the elements remain in it by virtue, as Alexander touched upon. Nor is it true that one body or spirit is resolved into a single element related to it, since every single thing is composed of four elements and is resolved into those things from which it is composed; rather, it is converted into the element that is most proportional to its majority part. And the same should be said to Simplicio. But according to what I once said, the arguments of both proceed within certain limits.

### DIFFERENCE XVII.

<margin>1</margin> That the **complexion** <term>complexio: the specific physiological balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a living thing; often translated as "temperament"</term> is a substance is shown first from *On the Utility of the Parts* [by Galen], which testifies that it is the substance of the body and the nature of the limb. Also, through the secret writings of Monteus, which intimate that this fact makes it the substance of each of the limbs. Hence it is held that in every limb there is a fixed virtue by which it performs its own operation, and the substance of this virtue, according to Galen, is its own complexion—namely, the specific form of the complexion. Furthermore, Aristotle in Book 5 of *On the Soul* says: the complexion of the instruments is specific and natural to them. Again, according to the natural philosophers, it is said that all things become a **mixture** <term>craſim: from the Greek 'krasis', a tempering or blending of qualities</term> according to the opinion of the ancients. Whence in the *Aphorisms*: there is nothing else in animals that works but the innate heat. Nature exists according to the **hypostatic account** <note>original: "yꝓſtaticā rōnē," referring to the underlying essential existence</note> which is this: for it is nothing else that shapes the animal from the beginning, nor again increases or nourishes it to the end, except the innate heat, which is the cause of all natural operations. Such a thing does not seem to be anything other than substance.

***

Moreover, that which constitutes the "being" of anything is its substance; for "being" is given by the substantial form. The complexion is of this nature; hence in the first book of *The Use of Parts*: the "being" of flesh and nerve and each of the others is established by the complexion constructed from the qualities of the four elements. Again: that which, when destroyed, causes another thing to be destroyed, is its substance (see Book 5 of the *Metaphysics*). Such is the complexion; for when it is destroyed, the limb and the animal as a whole are destroyed. Finally: that which is a part and cannot be separated is the substance of that to which it belongs. This, truly, is the complexion.

...constructs the fact of being composite, and it cannot be removed because the <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexio." In medieval medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a person's temperament and health.</note> is inseparable in act.
