Again, that which can be present or absent without the destruction of the subject is an accident; but this is the nature of complexion (Difference 22). Therefore, complexion will be an accident and not a substance. 

However, regarding the first point, it should be known that according to the senses, Galen says that complexion is the factor of the substance of each of the <term>members</term> <note>original: "membro," referring to the organs or parts of the body</note> of an animal; therefore, complexion is the substance of the body and its nature. But Avicenna, in the third book of the *Sufficientia*, says: Complexion is a quality arising from the reciprocal action and passion of contrary qualities in bodies mixed together. And in the third book regarding animals: Complexion will be a thing resulting from the operation of contrary qualities in the smallest particles, dividing and altering them mutually. First, however, it is specifically a quality that comes from the mutual action and passion of the contrary qualities found in the elements, whose parts are reduced to such smallness that most of one part touches most of another. It is also said that complexion is the effect resulting from the alteration of the qualities of the elements in a mixture. 

Complexion can also be considered in three ways: either by reason of substance, or cause, or the order of "before and after." The substance or subject in which complexion is founded (as an accident in its recipient) is the "miscible" <note>the things capable of being mixed</note>; thus, the diversity of the miscible things will diversify the complexion itself. For miscible things exist in a threefold difference: some are equal, others unequal, and some are intermediate. Those that are equal, according to Avicenna, are of two types: for they are such either according to an equal measure—which Galen and Avicenna call a complexion of measure or weight—or as Algazel says, perhaps an intellectual one, or relative to the more noble acts. This complexion, in terms of <term>justice</term> <note>original: "iusticia," here meaning a perfect mathematical or functional proportion</note>, is called "temperate," whether in the whole substance or its totality. This first type can be imagined to occur in two ways: either the quantities and qualities are equal and proportionate in weight and measure of the elements, as in a mixture where none are surpassing or surpassed; and the quality resulting from them would be a middle complexion between all the extremes of simple and composite qualities (such as heat, cold, and the rest—heat, dryness, and others). This is denoted as "equal according to weight." Or, they appear equal in measure but not in weight, and the virtues or qualities of the elements remain equal and proportionate, yet the complexion resulting from them does not stand exactly in the middle, but declines toward one of the extremes of the simple or composite <term>distemperaments</term> <note>an imbalance of the qualities</note> mentioned before. And this second mode is called an unequal complexion according to weight, of which none is found in the nature of things (Difference 18). 

Complexion related to operations, called a temperament of justice, is that which occurs when there is just enough of the measures and qualities of the elements 

---

as is required for the recipient to perform its actions. These follow a rational proportion in every way, according to which a comparison can be made: either to the whole species, or to a part of the species, or to the individual, or to a part of the individual. Each of these is subdivided into two, according to whether this comparison is made externally or internally; and thus eight modes will result. First, the primary ones. 

However, when the miscible things are entirely unequal, they constitute four complexions that are in every way "distempered" in relation to the composite justice, such as hot and dry, along with the other three combinations. Some of these are without <unclear>vice</unclear> and others are with it. This happens in two ways: for either it moistens only the external member, or it penetrates inward. This similarly occurs in two ways, since it appears either in the limbs or organs, which similarly exist in an infinite latitude of "more or less." 

But if the miscible things hold a middle path of moderation, in which there exists neither total equality nor total inequality, then the remaining four simple complexions arise, which are distempered in relation to justice—such as hot and cold, which hold a temperament in the passive qualities, and dry and moist in the active ones. These are distempered in the same manner as the aforementioned simple ones, by reason of the constituting cause; for everything that comes to be does so either by nature, by art, or by <term>perseverance</term> <note>original: "p̃seuano" (perseverantia), here used in the Aristotelian sense of chance or "happening to be"</note> (Metaphysics, Book 7). 

If a variety is observed within nature, it is said that one type is "innate," another "influencing," and another "intermediate." Of the innate, one is "fixed" and the other is "flowing" or "running," which varies according to properties—just as before and after, a person might be hot or moist. For example, the complexion of a child is hot and moist, while that of youth is hot and dry, and so on. They also say there are two types of "fixed" complexion: one is radical and principal, which is acquired from the two primary principles at the start of construction—namely, the seed and the menstrual blood. The other is fixed but secondary, which is that which flows from that prior radical cause. For by the virtue of the innate heat founded in the first principles, the form of masculinity is given, or previously, that of femininity (Difference 28). 

The "influencing" complexion is that which is gradually acquired through the proper administration of the six <term>non-natural things</term> <note>The "Six Non-Naturals" in medieval medicine are environmental factors: air, food/drink, sleep/waking, exercise/rest, excretion/retention, and mental passions.</note>, diversified according to the excess of its decline. The "intermediate" one, which is partly innate and partly influencing, is the complexion of the muscles of the belly and such things. It is "influencing" or "infused" because it flows into them from the heart, brain, and liver; it is partly "innate" because it does not flow from anything outside itself, or because it was endowed as such by the first forming principles. 

But a complexion caused by "perseverance" (chance) arises from an unforeseen cause, such as when someone by chance encounters fire or water or anything else that impresses a bad or different complexion upon them. For health and safety are sometimes the result of fortune, though the design of a house never is (Physics, Book 2). It is also caused by "art," as shown by the complexion of <term>theriac</term> <note>original: "tyriace," a legendary medicinal compound used as an universal antidote</note> by which poison is expelled. Art is not the cause in every way, but because it stands as the principle for applying medicines to one another, from which results the complexion formed by the breaking down of contrary qualities (Difference 184).

<summary>This page defines "complexion" (temperament) as a quality arising from the mixture of elements, debating its status as an accident versus a substance. It categorizes complexions into eight modes and distinguishes between those that are innate (inherited from parents) and those that are influenced by environment and lifestyle.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical ontological investigation into the nature of "complexion," specifically debating its classification as a substance or accident, and refining the definitions of "equality" within medical theory.</meta>

It is diversified indeed by the reasoning of order: because some are primary, such as that of wateriness; of milk, indeed, affected by the curd, it is a cold and moist **complexion** <note>original: "complexio"</note> (Difference 148). Cheese indeed is cold and dry; butter is hot and moist.

The other is secondary, such as that constructed from the whole of the milk, declining toward a temperament (Difference 189 or 193), participating yet more in the cold and moist. And similarly in art: the primary complexion, as in **Theriac** <note>original: "tiriaca," a famous polypharmaceutical "cure-all" and antidote used in medieval medicine.</note>, is the nature of each of the medicines entering into it; the secondary, however, results from the aforementioned through the application of art... by which it expels poison and induces other actions found in none of the medicines that constructed it.

I also hear of an **innate** or **radical** complexion, which first qualifies the principles of generation, namely of sperm and of menstrual blood, in which the complexion of the mixed and living thing is contained and shared. Indeed, there are many degrees of mixture and perfection in the nature of reptiles and especially human nature. And of this sort of complexion, one is in act and the other in potential, as has been touched upon regarding hot and cold (Difference 15).

Regarding this, know that through a part of the discourse, **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."</note> sometimes states that an unequal complexion "to weight" <note>original: "ad pondus"</note> would be unequal regarding "justice" <note>original: "ad iusticiam"</note>. Indeed, they place any complexion whatever, even the simple, as unequal if it departs from the equality of weight. For they argue: given any complexion, it is either equal regarding weight or unequal. It is not equal, because this is impossible to find; therefore, it is unequal. But they speak well and yet against the mind of Avicenna, and therefore their reasoning is sophisticated.

First indeed, he shows that Avicenna suggests that the complexion "to weight" is divided by that which is "from justice," and finally he categorized that of weight into equal and unequal. Therefore, an equal weight cannot be anything other than "from justice," since one species does not help its opposite to exist (Boethius, *Topics*, Book 4).

Furthermore, in the same place: an equal complexion "to weight" is not absolutely the middle of the heavy qualities, but rather always declines, by which he sufficiently suggests that it differs little from a complexion equal in weight, such that it is somewhat a middle between it and the equality "from justice" in its highest measure. Again, he soon adds: that which is considered equal in medicine—namely, as to that which is equal in weight and outside of equality (suppose unequal)—this is not it: that is, equal regarding weight; nor is that thing this: that is, unequal to it. And he confirms this: because he previously said that it exists, but not that it is necessary through a rational distinction, with consideration without any relation to a real thing. And soon he adds that this exists in two ways; yet this consideration remains a fantasy, not found in the nature of things, but rather a thing known; and therefore he wants the discovery of both ways to be impossible. From the opposite indeed it must be supplied: that the complexion "to justice" is through a distinction with consideration related to some existing thing. Therefore, that which is from justice cannot be unequal, nor can any other be "to weight."

But the adversary will rise up, because he says: "But the physician ought to believe the physicist that the equal according to this intention is always..." removing thereafter Avicenna's "equal of weight" from the physician's consideration, he leaves

---

its unequal to be considered by the physician. It must be said that a complexion equal and unequal in weight is "equal" when compared to the equality of justice. And he will rise up no less again when he says that the "equal" of which physicians treat is not named from the equality in which it exists equally with weight, or as before. It must be said—or rather, that the interpretation of the "unequal of weight" removes this, since it posits an equality of the apparent measure of the powers of the **elements** <note>original: "elentorum," likely "elementorum"</note>, and since the complexions resulting from these decline in every way from the middle toward some of the simple or composite complexions.

Regarding that which he brings in, it must be said that some take "unequal to weight" differently than Avicenna; for he himself takes it to differ by a very little (as appeared) from the equal, while they take it by however much. Note also that what stands as unequal in weight according to Avicenna can be a genus and a superior of the sensible complexion; for then a non-being would be a genus and superior of a being since that is not found; this especially, the falsehood of which is in the third book of the *Metaphysics*.

Know also that "equal" and "unequal" are used improperly here, since they imply quantity or relation, while "complexion" implies quality; hence it is more properly called **temperate** and **distempered**.

**Substance** indeed is spoken of in two ways: so that at last it may be of one difference, one being the ultimate "under-subject" which is not predicated of another, such as the individual; for from the principal (there is no predication here, otherwise it would be something here and separable), such is the form and species of each thing (5th book of the *Metaphysics*). And in the *Categories*, another is **primary substance**, which is properly and most principally and especially so called, and which is neither in a subject nor said of a subject, such as "a certain man" and Socrates. The other is **secondary**, such as species and genus, like "man" and "animal," to which the said principal substance belongs. Also according to **Boethius** in the same place, it exists as triple: one called **hypostasis** <note>original: "ypostasis"</note> (that is, matter); another by way of form; and the third "vialis," composed of both, which alone is placed directly in the categories; others are placed on the side and reductively. Here, however, it is received as that which a thing is, or the form.

**Accident** also, insofar as it is present and absent without the corruption of the recipient, and that it is none of the other four predicables (Porphyry); and not according to whether it is a "begetting" or a **symptom** <note>original: "sinthoma"</note> of a disease... like a shadow to a body; thus concerning the accident and concerning the nature.

Regarding the second, it must be known that the previously touched-upon speeches of **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note> appear to sound as if complexion were a substance, and as if the substantial form of the body and even of man, like the human soul. Whence, concerning this type of book of the *Nature of the Soul*, it is nothing other than heat. Wherefore the Commentator <note>Averroes</note> on the *Soul* thought that Galen estimated that the cogitative power was the rational soul. For the place of the people made him err much in this; because since the rational power is appropriated to man, and the cogitative is appropriated, he estimated through the conversion of a universal affirmative that the cogitative was the rational. And one of those who erred in this is **Abelfanus the Babylonian** <note>Possibly a Latinization for an Arabic philosopher, potentially Ibn Tufayl or Al-Farabi.</note>. Some of the moderns also have imputed to Galen that he wants the soul itself to be a **crasis** <note>original: "crasim," from the Greek for "mixture," referring to the tempering of the humors.</note>. Some also have felt this before Avicenna concerning the soul; for some said that the soul is a complexion.

<meta>This page continues the technical ontological investigation into the nature of "complexion," shifting from a classification of its types to a deep philosophical debate over whether complexion (the humoral balance) is the same thing as the soul (anima) or merely its instrument. It draws heavily on Galen, Aristotle, and Boethius to define these terms.</meta>

Because as long as the **complexion** <note>The specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determines a person's health and temperament.</note> remains stable, the health of life will not change. However, what <term>Galen</term> <note>original: "Ga."</note> felt about this in the many places he touches upon it is not yet found to be determined. For he seems to hesitate regarding those in which there are none; whence in the fifth book of *On Accidents*, he says it is inconvenient to say this. If a truly opportune time occurs, he will perhaps dispute it from there, which pertains to rashness and audacity. 

In the fifth book of *On Simple Medicines*, the authors of the "overshadowing" believed that the **spirit** <note>In ancient medicine, "spiritus" or pneuma was a refined substance that circulated through the body to perform vital functions.</note> was the substance of the soul; we, however, have not dared to judge the substance of the soul through anything. Nevertheless, in the eighth book of *On the Usefulness of Parts*, we ought not to report that the intellect is from the "fine" or "subtle," but from the temperance of the animal spirit, albeit instrumentally. 

Concerning liquid motions, he recites many opinions about the soul, after which he says to inquire about the soul: whether its substance is bodily, and whether it never ceases to descend into it when a body happens to be something animal; or is it something continuous with the body which falls away with the body; or is it some virtue and power of the one who forms it; and why do the accidents of the soul coincide with the creation of the body? This he leaves to those who think of themselves as knowing it truly. Similarly, the interior sight of those people is to doubt what <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>original: "ypo."</note> wished to denote by the name of "soul." 

In the exposition of a certain series of these same things, he says: either the soul is a **mixture** <note>original: "crasis," the Greek term for the blending of qualities.</note> of effective qualities, or the soul is altered by their mixture. However, the aforementioned reasoning seems expressly to want the complexion to be something other than the soul, saying that both the moisture and the natural mixture of the body alter the acts of the soul. This has been conceded by the best physicians and philosophers, and has been marveled at by me for a moment: that through the following mixtures of the body, I have demonstrated the virtues of the soul. 

Whence, because in these places it was not the speech of <term>Galen</term> to define the soul, he leaves its business under doubt in that determined place, as is the manner of those writing where he professes it to be something other than the complexion. But so that the intention of the proposition may be held, <term>Galen</term> in the fifth book directly adduces that series from *On the Utility of Parts*, which I have translated from the Greek. For what is commonly held concerning that book is a certain abbreviation in nine tracts, gathering what belongs to it up to the twelfth book; for it contains seventeen books, as also the tract shows which I translated concerning *The Best Composition*. 

It is, however, such as this: There exist indeed primary and greatest complexions. These indeed complete the particular substance of the parts; and since from here they have heat, cold, dryness, and moisture, such are the bodies, and for this reason, they have their nature. For it is such to be for flesh and nerve, and for each of the others here, which is made because of such a complexion from the four mentioned things, insofar as they are natural complexioned bodies: I say "complexioned" and not simple substances or bodies; and he adds: Here, therefore, they exist according to the reasoning of substance. But there follow from necessity flavors, humors, colors, hardness and softness, and other things happen from necessity: position, magnitude, number, and formation. This discourse does not so much press that complexion is a substance, as was touched upon in the prior arguments. Which indeed some, wishing to support, said the complexion...

---

...could be compared to a member in a duplicate way: either as it is **substance** <note>original: "sbā," the fundamental reality or essence of a thing.</note> or the subject in which it exists and which it qualifies, and thus it is an **accident** <note>original: "accñs," a non-essential quality or property that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist.</note>—a quality—since it is the nature of an accident to exist in a thing and to qualify it in this way. Or it is according to how the member stands as an instrument of operation; and thus they say the complexion is a formal shape; for through it the member works and is led into being as an instrument; for it is thus ordered toward the act. 

That this is really impossible is shown in the thirteenth Difference; for thus it would be both an **accident** and a **substance**. Nor can anyone say that it is taken substantially because it is turned substantially into the subject, as "being capable of laughter" distinguishes a human substantially, as appeared in the touched-upon Difference; because, as shown in Difference 22, the innate complexion can be changed. Similarly, even given such a "substantial" status, it is not valid, since it is a certain natural property; but true properties, according to <term>Boethius</term>, emanate from the genus of accidents. 

Regarding the third point, it must be known that complexion can be considered in two ways: one indeed as to the thing itself, the other indeed as to the manner. If the first, it must be said that it is entirely impossible for a complexion to be a formal substance because of the aforementioned inconveniences in Difference 13; but it must be simply said to exist as an **accident**, which is a quality. Complexion does not indeed rise out of the elemental substances, because that which is drawn out of them is elicited through composition; and such, according to <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "A."</note>, is the form of the mixture. Therefore, it is drawn out from qualities because alteration is completed by qualities; for alteration properly exists in qualities of the third kind. 

Furthermore, substance does not come from non-substances in prior things. Therefore, if complexion were a substance, it would not be made from qualities, since they are not substances; but it is made from qualities, as they say. Furthermore, the property of a complexion is to be in a subject according to "more" and "less" <note>This refers to the Aristotelian idea that qualities can have degrees (e.g., more or less hot), but substances (like a human or a stone) cannot.</note>, which is denied to substance in the *Categories*. Therefore, it is impossible for a complexion to be a substance. 

If, however, one imports the manner of substance rather than the reality of it, thus it can certainly be tolerated. Improperly, however, the complexion would be a substance; for according to that by which something is sustained through a substantial form: whence because of that perfection, so in its own way the member is sustained in its being through the complexion and the operation remains. Whence, because that from which the action more immediately seems to come is more manifest to us—such as the instrument or the complexion—than that from which it comes mediately, such as the principal agent or the substantial form; since we arrive at the knowledge of something through its operation. But the production of action and the sustaining seem more manifest from the instrument than to proceed from the principal agent, because of the property which is found equally appropriately; for it proceeds from it immediately, while from the substance upon which this is founded, it is internal (Difference 60). 

Similarly, <term>Galen</term> in many places, and <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: "Ay."</note> in his speech on the parts, as touched upon in Difference 11, name the elements "the hot," "the cold," and "the moist," not as **substances** but as qualities and their instruments. In which same manner the Apostle says to the Hebrews: <quote>Faith is the substance of things hoped for and the evidence of things not seen</quote> <note>A famous quote from Hebrews 11:1 in the Vulgate.</note>: for faith is not really a **substance** but an **accident**; yet by reason of the manner it can be called a substance, because through it, as through a base, it sustains the salvation of the mind; for without faith it is impossible to please God.

The author concludes that while it acts like a substance by sustaining life and health, it is technically an "accident" or quality because it can change in degree.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical ontological investigation into the nature of "complexion," specifically debating whether the humoral balance of the body constitutes its "substance" (what it fundamentally is) or merely an "accident" (a property it has). It moves from these abstract definitions into a new chapter (Difference 18) regarding the physical possibility of a perfectly balanced or "temperate" body.</meta>

Not even the Greek sequence of <term>Galen</term> <note>original: "Ga." - the most influential physician of antiquity.</note> testifies that the **complexion** <note>The specific mixture of the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a person's physical and mental state.</note> is a substance in every way; rather, it states that complexions are primary to other things that follow them. He adds also that the proper complexion of particular parts completes the substance, not as a primary and principal agent, but as an instrumental and secondary one. This is apparent from what he adds: "This, therefore, follows the logic of substance," either because when he defined the complexioned body, it falls into that definition as natural definitions require.

Or, to speak more concisely, he understood "substance" to mean "essence." For the word *ousia* <note>original: "Uſia" - a Latinization of the Greek word for substance or essence.</note> is found in some way even among "accidents" <note>Properties that are not essential to a thing's nature, like color or size.</note> in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle’s work on the nature of being.</note>. For *ousia* implies both substance and essence. 

Phrases of this kind are found frequently; for in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Ars Medica," a foundational textbook of medieval medicine.</note>, within the terms of the definition of medicine, he calls the accidents "substance" and says the definition itself is "substantial," and that certain signs are from inherent things according to the logic of substance. Furthermore, <term>Avenzoar</term> <note>original: "aſſōy" - referring to the Andalusian physician Ibn Zuhr.</note> says that the primary critical signs regarding their first substance are "symptoms." He also says in the same place that a disease is a "substance," and in the seventh book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio [sanitatis]"</note>, where the translation of the <term>Monk</term> <note>likely Constantinus Africanus.</note> refers to the "essence" of the nature of the disease. In the second book of <term>Avenzoar</term>, "virtue" is called both one and a substance; and in the first book on *Fevers*, and the eighth book of the *Theoretical Medicine* <note>original: "theorice"</note>, the opinion of <term>Alexander</term> <note>likely Alexander of Tralles.</note> is that a fever is a substance and that heat is a substance. Even the <term>Commentator</term> <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the famous commentator on Aristotle.</note> in the fourth book of the *Meteors* says the substance of digestion is "temperate." And in the first book of the *Colliget* <note>Averroes' medical encyclopedia.</note>, he says: "This definition is the substance of this book," even though all these things—disease, virtue, fever, digestion, and definition—are truly accidents. 

Because of this, one must say that in such passages, "substance" is used for "essence" by custom, because perhaps they are transferred only to proper things, or the Greek does not distinguish them. Regarding the fourth point: we have already seen what should be said to the first. To the other, it must be said that <term>Haly</term> <note>Haly Abbas, a Persian physician.</note> speaks in the language of <term>Galen</term>, which is apparent because he soon adds, "but according to the opinion of <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Ay." - likely a reference here to the Aristotelian tradition or Avicenna.</note> it is an instrumental complexion," that is, the proper one through which the virtue operates. To the other, it must be said that <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "A."</note> either alluded to <term>Galen</term> or meant "substantial and proper," meaning natural, emanating from internal principles; or perhaps he heard that it followed inseparably. 

To the other second point, it must be said that perhaps <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>original: "Ypo."</note> wanted the soul to be a **mixture** <note>original: "craſim" (krasis) - a Greek term for the blending of humors.</note>, as <term>Galen</term> touched upon, or because complexion arises as the cause of all things, not as a primary principal agent, but as a secondary instrumental one. But because the physician is a craftsman of what is evident, which stands out more in the secondary agent than in the primary non-immediate one, <term>Hippocrates</term> wanted to ascribe the soul to the mixture. Whence the second book of the *Colliget* says: the joined heat, from the "influent" heat sent from the heart and the heat of the complexion of the limb, is the "form" with which it acts and is acted upon. And he adds: "But whether this heat suffices to do this, or whether there is another virtue standing in place of the form for this heat, is not a matter which the physician needs to inquire." 

To the other, it must be said that complexion does not give "quidditative" <note>The "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</note> being, but disposes and prepares for it, just as the action of the primary qualities prepares the matter to receive the form. To the other, it must be said that according to the intention [of the author] in the 13th *Difference*: when "risibility" <note>The ability to laugh, often used by philosophers as a property unique to humans.</note> is taken away, the human is taken away, but not because of the removal of his rationality. Likewise, the complexion is taken away when the substantial form (like the soul) is removed. 

It must also be said that <term>Aristotle</term> speaks here according to the opinion of the <term>Platonists</term>, who posited that numbers were the substances of things, and the point was the substance of the line, and the line of the surface, and that of the body. To the other, it must be said that complexion is not properly "pre-substantial" to the body, but is the "innate complexion" of the same, as has been touched upon in its own way. Thus, in the *Tegni*, signs are said to be "substantial," nor is it the case that even an innate complexion cannot be separated; this will be explained in the 22nd *Difference*, where the aphorism of <term>John Damascene</term> will be expounded.

## DIFFERENCE XVIII.

<margin>1</margin>
He shows that a "balanced" or "temperate" complexion can be found, as in the 5th book of the *Problems*. For this reason, well-proportioned bodies often labor and change easily; or for the same reason, both are "equal" and "commensurate." <term>Galen</term> <note>original: "Palin." - often used to refer back to the authority of Galen in this context.</note> commonly testifies to this with the physicians. 

Reason also demonstrates this. For every motion from one extreme to another is through a middle point; this is seen in the *Physics* and the 4th book of *On the Use of Parts*. A person changes from a hot and dry complexion into a cold and moist one, and similarly from hot and moist into cold and dry (as in the 22nd *Difference*). Therefore, in this motion, a complexion is found between these extreme media, and it is none other than the "temperate" or "equal" one. Therefore, it is possible to find this, even as it is found in justice. 

Furthermore, **Art** can do more than Nature; and therefore it imitates Nature, though it does not always follow it, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "A."</note> labors to show in the 4th book of the *Metaphysics*. But Art can compose a body of temperate complexions; as in the first book of the *Theoretical Medicine*, for when a measured quantity is taken proportionally from hotter and colder bodies—such as boiling water and snow or ice—and from drier and moister ones—such as dust and water—a body arises that is temperate in its whole substance. This is taught in the knowledge of compounding or making medicines. Therefore, Nature is much more capable of constructing such a temperate and equal body. 

Again, "sensation is a certain middle proportion" of the quality that is within it (22nd *Difference*). This could not be unless there were a temperate complexion, especially in man, since he possesses a finer sensitivity than others, and is therefore more prudent than all, according to *On the Soul* and the first book on *Complexions*; he is judged the wisest of animals. 

Furthermore, if one of a pair of contraries exists in nature, the other must also exist. The <term>Commentator</term> <note>Averroes.</note> says in the first book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*: if an "intemperate" <note>Imbalanced.</note> complexion exists in nature, why should not a temperate one also exist, since they are opposites? And it is confirmed: because if there is a "less perfect" thing, there will also be a "perfect" thing by the same reasoning, since they belong to the same category. But the imperfect is found (the intemperate complexion), therefore the perfect must be too. 

Moreover, neither "superior nature" <note>The heavens or divine influence.</note> seems to prohibit a temperament, nor does the "particular inferior nature" of generation, nor the "containing" environment and other supports of nature. Since it is granted that temperate things are found here, for they do not all age and decay entirely and at the same time. 

Likewise, the intellect and science are always of "true things," according to *On the Soul*. But the complexion is in the intellect according to its weight <note>meaning its proportional balance</note>, and <term>Algazel</term> <note>Al-Ghazali, the Persian theologian and philosopher.</note> also hands down the science of identifying and dividing it; because such a thing coexists.

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the "temperate" or perfectly balanced complexion. It moves from the definition of substance toward an inquiry into whether a perfectly balanced mixture of elements (equal weight) is physically possible or merely a theoretical ideal used by physicians and philosophers.</meta>

What does not exist cannot be known, according to the *Posterior Analytics* <note>Aristotle’s treatise on logic and scientific knowledge.</note>. If, therefore, it exists, it is either in the intellect or in science, since these are the ways things are understood. We must also ask whether it is both real and true. Furthermore, if it is a "measured" thing, there must be a "measure," since these are correlatives. A "measured" thing is like a **justicial complexion** <note>A balance of qualities likened to the virtue of justice; not a literal equal weight, but the "correct" proportion for a specific nature.</note> which is tempered, which certainly pertains to the equality of the weight of the mixture according to its primary qualities, and is very close to it. Thus, a tempered mixture is even found in terms of weight. The opposite of this is also found, especially regarding what is perceived of its weight.

<margin>Galen, Avicenna, al-Ghazali</margin>
Galen, in his work on the **complexions** <note>The specific mixture of the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> and on the preservation of health, along with Haly <note>Haly Abbas, a famous Persian physician.</note>, Avicenna, and al-Ghazali, confirms this by reason. For if there were such a mixture of perfectly equal weight, life could not exist in the one possessing it, since it could not stand as a cause. And in Difference 21, it is stated that where heat and moisture are equal, no temperament exists. Furthermore, how could a mixture be made unless one of the **elements** <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> or its causes preceded another, so that the logic of action and passion might be preserved? Again, in all mixtures, earth and water dominate, as stated in the first and fourth books of the *Meteorology*. Therefore, such a perfectly equal temperament does not undergo change.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Furthermore, the Commentator <note>Averroes, the influential 12th-century philosopher who wrote commentaries on Aristotle.</note> on the fourth book of those works says that Aristotle felt that powers are unequal in each of the four elements. For if they were equal, one would not act upon another similar to itself, and then there would be no action of the active virtues upon the passive ones, and thus no effect would proceed from it—the opposite of which our senses show us. Therefore, a tempered complexion, especially one of equal weight, will be found least of all.

Regarding the first point, it must be known what a complexion is and how it is distinguished, especially by the logic of its mixable parts, as was made known previously. However, so that this may be more clearly illuminated, it should be noted that a complexion of weight seems adapted to **moral virtue** and **happiness**. This, indeed, holds the middle point, 

<margin>Ethics</margin>
which is both most difficult and perfectly impossible to attain. Therefore, in the second book of the *Ethics*, virtue is said to exist not simply, but as a "mean" relative to us, which participates in a considerable range. Thus, the specific equality of weight is compared to happiness, which no one can attain permanently in this life. Since nothing in any genus is entirely simple, nature has set this forth in the second book of the *Ancient Rhetoric*. However, an unequal mode of measurement is better adapted to virtue, which participates in a wider range.

<margin>justice</margin>
But the so-called **justicial complexion** is rightly equated with justice, and specifically with natural justice. For one kind is natural, the other political; and of this, one is distributive—such as honors and wealth—and the other is communicative, involving mutual participation. **Justice** is a certain perfect virtue, not simply, but in relation to another. For this reason, it is the most illustrious of virtues, and neither the evening star nor the morning star is so admirable. Truly, such a thing is an equal complexion in terms of justice, as will appear. For it is the equal and the mean however it is taken, and this equal complexion is not simply equal, but relative to another—namely, justice as related to just operations. On the other hand, he calls "unjust" that which happens to be unequal, because it departs more or less from the mean and the equal. Such are the **distempered complexions**: the four composite ones in a major degree, and the four simple ones in a minor degree.

But because the inquiry exists concerning the complexion, which is the combination of the qualities of the elements, an actual quality is sought here; and though it is essential, it is not in the highest degree, because that is the nature of the elements themselves—not like heated water or such things, because that is accidental and not potential, as seen in Difference 15 regarding plants and things born of the earth.

Regarding the second point, it must be known from the principles of complexions that certain of the ancients even omitted the equal complexion without distinction, positing only two complexions: the hot and dry, and the cold and moist. For it seemed to them that the hot could not remain joined with the moist, since heat dries out the moist, continuously turning it into the dry; nor could the cold be associated with the dry, because of the resulting loss of digestion and the generation of raw and watery superfluities.

Against these, others affirmed the four complexions, stating that what they say does not necessarily happen. For heat is proportional to moisture; indeed, nothing exists without heat, according to the fifth book of *The Generation of Animals*. Furthermore, that moisture is condensed and affected by other qualities, not simply as it is, but by predominance. Neither is the cold pure without heat, nor the dry without moisture in the other complexion, such that a pair could not endure for long. 

Without a doubt, however, the complexion of this life is of short duration, both because of the poverty of moisture and because of the increase of extraneous watery humors during indigestion, which more quickly extinguish the innate heat by their bad quality, covering and suffocating it by their quantity. For this reason, 

<margin>Haly</margin>
Haly rightly judges it to consist of a shorter life compared to the others, in Difference 21. Others, positing only the four composite ones, seem to have omitted the equal one entirely, as was common before the opinion of Galen. He, however, strives to distinguish many things; for he says they abandoned the equal complexion, which precedes the others in power and is a most necessary goodness. Without this, one can reason nothing in theory, since it is the rule and measure for directing the others; and 

<margin>Polyclitus</margin>
it is like the **Statue of Polyclitus** <note>A famous Greek sculpture (the Doryphoros) intended to demonstrate the perfect proportions of the human body.</note>. Nor can one reason in practice without it, since every distempered complexion is preserved, restored, or cured by reference to it. And therefore, it is preferred to others in the regime of health, in the *Tegni*, and in *On the Preservation of Health*. For they command that to be heated or cooled is to move toward health from that state. For it is so necessary to have this reference that those denying it would have to affirm it is the same thing.

Some, however, said that this is placed under the hot and moist category. He follows them in the same way, since either this will be tempered (and thus omits the hot and moist), or it will itself be hot and moist, and then there will not be another tempered complexion. Nor can it be placed under the hot and moist, because then contrary things would be in the same subject, such as a distempered and a tempered heat. Furthermore, the cold and dry would be opposed to the tempered, which is a great absurdity. From this contempt, it is concluded that it is necessary to explain the tempered complexion separately from the other four. And although this complexion agrees more with the hot and moist than with the others—because the justicial tempered complexion sought by the physician tends toward the hot and moist, as they say—it differs essentially, and not only by more or less, as...

<meta>This page continues the technical inquiry into whether a perfectly balanced (temperate) complexion—one where all four elements are present in equal measure—can actually exist in nature or if it is merely a mathematical abstraction used by physicians like Galen and Avicenna.</meta>

Firstly, regarding the hot and moist: by grace of the first principle and the second principle, he concludes that it is given by necessity, which **Avicenna** <note>OCR: "Ay."; likely referring to Avicenna (Ibn Sina), the influential Persian polymath.</note> has already conceded, and which reason will affirm.

Know also that **Galen** and **Haly Abbas** <note>OCR: "Ga. cū halyabate"; Haly Abbas was a 10th-century Persian physician whose "Complete Book of the Medical Art" was a standard text.</note> speak somewhat confusingly on the matter of the temperate complexion, so much so that they cause even learned doctors to doubt. There is a great hierarchy of complexions. For the temperate complexion is twofold: one is simple and exists in the universal substance, as in the <term>eucratic balance<note>original: "eucratia"; a Greek medical term for a "well-mixed" or healthy state where humors are in perfect proportion.</note></term> of a human being, or the substance of trees, animals, and the middle state of men. Concerning this, he says: those things are called "temperate" which most certainly come together equally from contraries; and thereafter, it is the middle point in every genus, especially among living substances generated between extremes. And the rule and indication of these was <term>isomeria<note>original: "yfomeria" (isomeria); from the Greek meaning "equal parts."</note></term>, that is, an equal portion; because of this, the mean of all things is called "eucratic" and "commensurate." His discourse on the skin of the hand is similar.

Haly Abbas, however, a more faithful interpreter of Galen, says that a "temperate complexion" is predicated on the truly temperate, whose distance from all extremes is equal; and this is that in which there were equal parts of all elements. Because it is of this sort, it is called "temperate" among all extremes, but also temperate in the totality of its substance. He also speaks of the temperate according to utility and necessity, which seeks what is necessary in the bodies of each. Furthermore, the truly temperate is hardly ever found; in almost all bodies to the very last, except that a human being having a temperate complexion is closest to it—most especially the complexion of the palms of the hands.

**Galen** says: there is another complexion that is temperate according to genus, such as that of trees and animals, when theirs is the best and a middle state—not simply when the equality of the extreme contraries is most certain, but when it results in a commensuration for them according to a "speaking virtue." We say such a thing is a matter of **justice** <note>This refers to the "justicial complexion," where elements are balanced not by weight, but by what is "fair" or appropriate for that creature's function.</note>: not equal in weight and measure, but in opportunity and according to what is fitting. In the second sense, others are judged as <term>eucratic<note>well-balanced</note></term> according to each genus, by the proper acts and utilities of their bodies.

It is also said to be temperate, according to Haly Abbas, in respect to necessity and utility, which seeks what is necessary in any of the bodies, according to which they are said to be tempered. These are the discourses of Galen and Haly Abbas concerning the temperate complexion, which on the surface of their first part seem to portend a complexion of weight and measure, which Galen nevertheless denies. **Avicenna**, his expositor, says that Galen understood the complexion of this thing to be a certain mode of "justicial equality," marvelous in its proximity to a complexion equal in weight. And therefore he compares this to equal mixtures of elements—not that their measures and quantities are simply equal in every way, but rather by comparison to the temperate according to genus in each one. Nor does he compare that former one to foods as he does this one and its utilities, because that one is immediately corrupted and does not remain over time. 

Or perhaps Galen and Haly Abbas do not feel that the complexion will be so existing as equal to the extremes, but rather that it is to be imagined. This was expressed more clearly for the sake of an easier understanding of the real complexion, which he taught to be known by pre-cognition, or estimation, or by the senses, as has already been touched upon—concerning which Avicenna and Galen frequently dispute. Know also that Avicenna, by explaining the complexion in such a way, takes a narrower view regarding "justice"; and as a certain rule for the whole universe, he established it only in man. Galen, however, amplified this and adapted it to every genus of substance. 

Firstly, it must be known that a **complexion of weight** <note>A mixture where elements are balanced by literal mass.</note> is not found realistically in nature. To prove this, one must know that to grant an equal complexion of weight is a fiction scarcely even imagined. Since the weight of fire is the lightest in the extreme, the greater it is, the lighter it becomes; hence it cannot be weighed or associated equally with others. Furthermore, even if it were granted as possible to have weight, if fire were placed in such measure and proportion in a mixture as the others, since it is extremely active, it would immediately or very quickly destroy the other mixable parts. Thus a mixture would either not be made, or if made, it would last for a very short time before being destroyed. 

**Al-Ghazali** <note>OCR: "Algazel"; a major Persian theologian and philosopher.</note> divides the complexion in the intellect into the unequal and the equal (which is perhaps the distinction of complexion by weight). He proves the "equal" to be impossible, because a body possessing it would neither rest nor move. For if it rested on the earth, then earth would prevail in it; similarly if in air or water. If it moved from air to fire, then fire would prevail; if toward the earth, then earth. If it rested in the air, then air itself would prevail. It follows, therefore, that it would neither rest in a place nor move to a place, which is impossible—as the **Commentator** <note>Usually referring to Averroes (Ibn Rushd).</note> says in the first book of *On the Heavens and the World*. If any body were composed equally, it would happen that it would not move at all, but would stand in whatever place it was put. 

Furthermore, it would no longer be "temperate" if it had a place, since it would follow the motion of the element predominating in it, like the rest of mixtures. But perhaps someone will posit that the place of this body is in the middle of the elements, as in the hollow of the sphere of air: here indeed the form of heaviness and lightness seems to be equalized. For if it were placed in the hollow of the orb of the moon, or in the convex of the air, it would tend downward to the aforesaid place, since the form of heaviness would flourish in it. But if it were in the earth, the form of lightness dominating it would move it toward the aforementioned middle.

...human affairs, or at least political ones: such that his life would be non-existent or very short. Again, a **complexion** <note>original: "complexio"; the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that makes up an individual's constitution.</note> is established from the action and passion of contrary qualities and the rest; however, wherever one must assign action and passion, it is necessary for the **agent** <note>The active force.</note> to hold dominance over the **patient** <note>original: "passum"; the subject being acted upon.</note>. This is according to the first book of *On Generation and Corruption* <note>Aristotle’s "De Generatione et Corruptione," a foundational text for medieval science.</note>; for equal proportions are mutually impassive. Indeed, neither action nor passion would intervene unless one of the qualities dominated the other. Where, however, there is a "complexion of weight" <note>A 1:1:1:1 mathematical equality of qualities.</note>, such dominance cannot exist in any way.

Furthermore, in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*, it is stated that human "means" are composites; some have more of this quality, and others have less of that. That which has more or less does not preserve an equal measure of weight. Whence the **Commentator** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the famous 12th-century Islamic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> demonstrates in the same place that it is impossible to find a middle complexion between extremes. As **Galen** says, it is possible to find a composite made from the extremes themselves, without transformation or diminution occurring. Therefore, according to the same book of *On Generation and Corruption*: if the powers were equal, then no form would be created, as is declared in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. 

And since the power of one is not simply dominant, but the dominant overpowers the dominated, a certain "mean" is generated from them, which nevertheless inclines toward the side of the dominant. Therefore, this mean—being that which declines toward one of the two extremes—has a certain **latitude** <note>original: "latitudo"; a technical term meaning a range or spectrum of intensity rather than a single fixed point.</note> that receives "more" and "less." For the "mean" is many things, and not something indivisible. It is to this mean that the elements are transformed and reduced to become **flesh** and such things, according to **Aristotle** in the same place.

From this, it appears to you that it is impossible for any "temperate complexion" to exist as Galen proposed—namely, a temperateness that sits at the very extremes of the species' complexion, which medicine considers. Secondly, however, he concludes by saying that the error he spoke of regarding the temperate complexion is a great one shared with Galen. Mixable things are not found in a mixture except in two ways: 

1. One way is when the measures are equal; this mixture is called "equal from the extremities" by comparison, because it sits in the middle without declining. 
2. The second way is when it is made of unequal measures; and this inequality occurs in many ways, according to which the complexions of various species are diversified and made unequal. 

Again, whatever becomes "one" through **essence** <note>original: "p eēntiā" (per essentiam); a fundamental unity of being.</note> must have one of its components exist by way of **potentiality** <note>original: "p mōm potentie" (per modum potentiae); the capacity to be shaped.</note> and the other by way of **actuality** <note>original: "p mōm act⁹" (per modum actus); the completed or active state.</note>. Because a single essence cannot be constituted from several things that are already fully actualized, except by mere aggregation—like a heap made of many grains. But from mixable things, a single essence is made; therefore, it is necessary that one of them behaves by way of potentiality and the other by way of actuality. That which holds the place of "act" has the character of the dominant over the other. Where this occurs, true equality or "temperament" is not found. Therefore, it is impossible to find a "complexion of weight."

Regarding this, it must be known that although a complexion is commonly conceded according to **justice** <note>original: "iusticiā"; here meaning a "just balance" suited for a specific purpose or species, rather than mathematical equality.</note> in the nature of things, perhaps to show the truth and verify the speeches of the wise, it should not be asserted simply, but with determination. What that might be has already appeared in some way. 

This balance itself appears to exist in three forms:
1. One in which the temperament exists as a "point-like" indivisible thing in the proportions of the measures of mixable qualities, best suited for exercising the operations of the soul.
2. Another with a certain latitude of "more or less," within which a complexion is called "justly balanced," and if one exits this range, it becomes a "distempered" complexion. 
3. A third which is a mean between these.

Regarding the first: it is impossible for it to remain stable over time; some have suspected it to be an "equality of weight," but it exists only for an instant. Such a thing, being almost indivisible, is not "time," nor is it in time, according to the sixth book of the *Physics*. Furthermore, such a temperate complexion would not be lasting, like the human complexion, with its order toward actions; for all these actions are measured by time. Natural forms do not require a point-like and indivisible quantity or complexion, since one can find "minimal flesh" <note>original: "minā carnē"; the smallest possible unit of flesh that still retains its form.</note>, according to the second book of the *Physics*, because there is a limit, a ratio of magnitude and growth, for all things consisting in nature. Thus, they do not have point-like and indivisible actions, since in every action and passion, it is necessary for the power of the agent, the aptitude of the patient, and time to meet.

And one must estimate that Galen touched on this in the first book of *On Preserving Health* <note>original: "de re. sa." (De regimine sanitatis).</note>, according to the abbreviation of the translator: "Simple and perfect health, which has the most certain **eucrasia** <note>original: "eucrasia"; the Greek term for a perfect "good mixture" of humors.</note>, either never was in an animal body, or if it ever was, it did not remain for even an instant in the blink of an eye, being altered in every single moment and not remaining in the same state." 

But according to my translation, which is even word-for-word: "Eucrasia being twofold: one in the intellect or according to the highest degree, as in an animal body; the other being present and appearing in all healthy people." And he adds finally: one must not seek, in such great transformation, a precise and "best" fixed complexion; even if some "best nature" happens to occur, it does not remain certain for an instant. Wherefore, one wonders at the opinion of those men who estimate health and "eucrasia" to be without latitude, and who think that if something is outside this, it is not health. For they do not perceive the consequence of the matter: either they are speaking of things not born in an animal body, or it is no wonder if it does not remain once it is generated. To those dreaming of such health, we have failed to preserve it.

But we have come to the "apparent" things. Whence **Haly** says: the ultimate end of equality is a thing that is perhaps not found, and if it is found, it is hidden from itself. His speech tolerates this, even if he did not understand it by this kind of equality, but rather by the "always healthy body" which runs through all ages, about which Galen and Haly also spoke. This was attacked by those who proposed the dogma that the body is in a state of "perpetual suffering" <note>The idea that life is a slow process of dying or decay.</note>, as if it had no optimal operations, since the **natural heat** <note>The vital force that powers life.</note> continually feeds upon the **radical moisture** <note>original: "huidum radicale"; the innate fluid or "fuel" of life that humans are born with and slowly consume.</note>, and the process of resolution <note>Evaporation or breaking down.</note> brings about a continuous dissolving, according to the same authors. Similarly, the air always resolves some amount of moisture through the celestial rays impressed upon it, according to the first book.

There is also another "just" complexion, possessing a small latitude, which should be called "narrower"...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "temperate complexion," transitioning from the theoretical impossibility of a perfect balance to the rare, almost miraculous instances where such a balance might occur, often linked to celestial events or divine figures.</meta>

It occurs very rarely in nature: for two people possessing this [perfect balance], let alone many, cannot exist at the same time. A great conjunction <note>An astrological event where planets align, believed to cause major shifts in history.</note> seems especially necessary for this—namely, the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter at the beginning of the sign of Aries, along with other factors, and the aspect of all the super-celestial bodies operating by divine command. This occurs just as when a prophet arises under these same signs, imposing a new law and teaching dogmas to the wise and to common men. For such a man is a "middle point" between angels and the wise, let alone ordinary men, according to Isaac Israeli, Avicenna, and Al-Ghazali <note>Three foundational figures in medieval medicine and philosophy: Isaac Israeli (an Egyptian Jewish physician), Avicenna (Ibn Sina), and Al-Ghazali (an influential Persian theologian).</note>. Some have said that Moses was such a man, and the lying followers of Muhammad <note>original: "Marabei"; likely a corruption of "Mahometi" or a reference to a specific sect.</note> said the same of Christ, the son of Mary.

Galen <note>referred to here as "A.", likely for *Auctor* or an abbreviation for a specific work, though the text cites his "On the Best Constitution."</note> also writes about this temperance in his book *On the Best Constitution of the Body*, noting that it is a useful perfection in all things. In this state, nothing is found to be disproportionate, neither in the similar parts <note>The basic tissues, like bone or flesh.</note> nor in the organic parts <note>Complex structures like the hand or eye.</note>. This state is not found continuously, but usually occurs only in long periods of time. You have seen that what is brief falls short of this; I am speaking of a body that is always healthy. This is the **second mode of equality**—the "equality of justice" <note>A proportional balance rather than a strict 1:1:1:1 mathematical ratio.</note>—which was discussed previously. It is a moderate temperament of a broad constitution found even in an individual who is at the peak of equality for their species, but at the peak of inequality compared to others, and at an age when growth has reached its end. In this state, the fourth and sixth modes of equality coincide. 

As the eighth mode relates to internal balance—as Aristotle <note>original: "A."; referring to Aristotle’s "History of Animals."</note> indicates in the twelfth book of *On Animals*—this is temperance in "virtue," which he calls the "complexion of weight." Therefore, true temperance is found only rarely. For this reason, in *On the Best Constitution*, one must be ready to recognize the best arrangement of the body, even if its generation is rare. Perhaps its peak time lasts only two or three years, or even less, if one wishes to define it even more strictly, such as around the age of thirty-three. At this age, writers record that Christ—being most temperate—suffered his Passion.

The **third mode** of balance participates in the "latitude of the many and the few" <note>A range of acceptable health rather than a single point.</note>, which constitutes a body that is simply "healthy." This exists in two ways: one is a body called "always healthy," and the other is "mostly healthy," as found in Galen's *The Art* <note>original: "tegni"; from the Greek "Techne," referring to Galen's "Ars Medica."</note> and *On Preserving Health*. Health is a certain "contemperance" <note>A harmonious blending of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry).</note>. All contemperance is perfected and described in two ways: sometimes reaching the highest and truly temperate state, and other times falling slightly short of it. 

Thus, healthy balance is twofold. One is precise, certain, best, and perfect: I call this the "always healthy body." The other falls short of this, though not so much that the animal suffers; this is the health of the "mostly healthy body," as also appears in *The Art*. That the physician considers this temperament to contain a considerable "latitude" <note>A margin of error or range of variation.</note> is shown by related categories. This is also a logical question, or one concerning the suitability of the craft, since some do not concede that one person can be "healthier" than another, nor that there is a sufficient latitude in the disposition of the body which we call "health." They argue health is a single, perfect thing. However, to us, just as one body appears less white and another more white, so one body is seen to be more or less healthy than another.

The same applies to the "best good-mixture" <note>original: "eucrasia"; a Greek term for the perfect balance of bodily fluids or qualities.</note>. Health is neither narrow nor indivisible, but is seen to be able to extend across a sufficient latitude. This is necessary if the discourse is to be useful to those practicing the medical art—not only to exercise it on rare bodies that serve as a "model of Polykleitos" <note>A reference to the "Canon" of Polykleitos, a famous Greek statue meant to represent the perfect mathematical proportions of the human form.</note>, but also on those who fall short of that ideal. 

Again, regarding the "intention of complexions" <note>The specific goal or nature of a person's constitution.</note>: those who say the body is prone to "eternal suffering" <note>A state of constant physiological decay or imbalance.</note> might find a strong demonstration of this through reason alone, but it has no utility in the practical part of medicine. For we ignore such small sufferings that are, as it were, imperceptible. For this reason, he rejects the opinion of those who placed the body in "eternal suffering," as some dreamed who did not understand *The Art*.

This is the "equality of complexion," which Aristotle divides into eight modes of equality in the twelfth book of *On Animals*, diversified according to comparisons of what is internal and external. 

Furthermore, the temperament of this complexion is distinguished by the ages passing through it over time, as appears in the description of contemperance in *The Art*; for such a state remains during its proper time. To this, he opposes eight complexions of equal imbalance. He shows by arguments why these last two extremes result in imbalance. Because, as Hippocrates <note>original: "Y."; an abbreviation for "Ypocras" (Hippocrates).</note> says in *On Human Nature*: it is necessary that generation does not come from one thing alone. For it cannot be generated from one, nor out of one, unless it is mixed with another. Furthermore, it is necessary that the things being mixed be of the same genus and have the same power; otherwise, they contribute nothing. It is also necessary that the hot and cold, and the dry and moist, be tempered toward each other and be equal. For if one should greatly predominate—as the strongest over the weakest—generation will not occur, but rather a transition into the dominating quality. Whence Aristotle, in the first book of *On Generation*, affirming the ancient sayings, states: "It is not possible to mix one drop of water with a thousand thousand jars of wine." <note>A famous example illustrating that for a mixture to occur, the components must be somewhat balanced; otherwise, the smaller part is simply absorbed and destroyed by the larger.</note>

Therefore, wherever and whenever these dispositions meet each other in this way, they will have a secondary and third temperance joined to them. When the "other-ward" influence is strong, and the active and passive elements are brought close to each other, it is impossible for them not to act. This will occur when they are more or less equalized. Again, since man is the ultimate end and the fulfillment of the universe intended by nature, as stated in the fifth book <note>Of Aristotle's *Metaphysics* or *On the Parts of Animals*.</note>, it was necessary for him to be composed of such things that he could know with certainty and rule over them through genius and wisdom. This occurs if the best temperament of mixable things is placed within him. From these, a most temperate and equal complexion arises, which elicits a sharp spirit. Where that aptitude of mind is present, it follows the saying in the second book of *On the Soul*: "Those with soft flesh are apt of mind, while the hard are inept." From this, men are rendered ingenious or not. Therefore, it is said that man is the most prudent and wise of animals, because he alone among animals is "deliberative," participating in memory and learning, as stated in the first book of the *Histories*. And this is confirmed because...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the "temperate complexion," specifically contrasting the "equality of justice" (the proportion of humors best suited for human life) with the "equality of weight" (an impossible 1:1 ratio of all qualities). It cites Aristotle's views on human nature and the social structure of animals to justify why man requires a specific biological balance.</meta>

Since man is dedicated to many operations, he must cast off the present defects of life to which he is subject. Since human nature is manifold in its service, as stated in the <term>Metaphysics</term> <note>original: "metba."; referring to Aristotle’s work on the nature of being</note>, and in the seventh book of the <term>Politics</term> <note>original: "polliticoy."</note>, the act of living requires many "organs" or instruments. It was necessary for the work itself to be a whole, or at least for its most significant part to exist in a state of balance. 

A <term>temperament</term> <note>A "temperamentum" is the specific mixture of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> occupies the middle ground between extremes. Because this middle state can be extended and adapted to many different things, it is more versatile than any single extreme. For this reason, man possesses a <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexionē"; the specific "weave" or balance of humors in an individual body.</note> that is more balanced than all other beings, as noted in the first book of the *Theory of Medicine*. 

There was also one individual who was the most balanced compared to all others, so that he might be a prince, a leader, and the primary measure for others, according to the aforementioned temperament. We see this also in other species in their own way: for instance, one bee is larger and rules the others through a certain natural prudence, and the others support and follow it. A similar thing happens among ants, and it is possible to find this even in such lowly creatures, let alone in more precious ones. 

Furthermore, this <term>constitution of justice</term> <note>original: "complexio iusticialis"; a proportion that is "just" or "right" for a specific creature's function, rather than a perfect 50/50 split.</note> in man is more balanced than in all others, and is considered worthier and more "simply temperate" since it serves as the rule and measure for all. In other species—such as the horse, the donkey, the fig tree, and the rest—the constitution is only balanced in a certain respect, according to the first books of *Complexions* and *Theory*. 

And therefore <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "A."</note> says that man certainly approaches the <term>equality of weight</term> <note>An absolute, mathematical 1:1 balance of all qualities, which was considered biologically impossible.</note> as closely as possible, since he has attained a mode of temperate complexion following the "truth of justice." And since the process of nature is ordered to move gradually from one extreme through a middle point to the other extreme (as stated in the seventh book of the *History of Animals*), in no way could a constitution be found that serves as a measure or "apparent justice" unless it fell between two distant points, creating not one, but two types of temperance. Thus, the constitution of "simply temperate justice" will be threefold. 

Regarding the fourth point: To the first it must be said that <term>Aristotle</term> and the physicians, when they speak of a "temperate complexion," primarily mean the one concerning justice—especially in its two final modes—and not the one concerning "weight." As has been shown, it is impossible to find a balance of weight in the universe; therefore, it is much less likely to be found as a human constitution, according to <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: "Auic."; the famous Persian physician Ibn Sina.</note>. 

To the next point, it should be said: as has been proven, we must concede that a "constitution of justice" is found, but not one regarding "weight." Indeed, it should be said that all movement and the rest are more truly verified in things that undergo alteration than in others—that is, in movements. Although a real "middle point" is not acquired through the introduction of alteration, a middle point of movement or space is nonetheless acquired. 

Alternatively, one might say that the previous reasoning proceeds from a false imagination. For if a transition occurs from one extreme constitution to another, it happens through a middle constitution found between them, though this is not strictly necessary. According to <term>Aristotle</term>, a thing capable of change remains under the form it is losing until a new form is introduced into it in an instant, whereby the remaining constitution follows once the prior one is corrupted. It is not necessary for this to happen through intermediate forms. For example, whenever air is transformed by fire, it remains under the form of air until the form of fire is introduced in an instant. This is what happens in the present proposal: the mixture remains 

***

under one constitution (such as "hot and dry") until another (such as "cold and moist") is introduced in an instant. It is not necessary for a middle state to be introduced into it. 

Or, it could be conceded that just as a transition is made from one extreme constitution to another (namely from cold and dry) through some middle constitution, it stays there for some time so that this middle constitution can persist within a certain range. Thus, although the changeable thing is altered during the transition, it does not necessarily reach a stable, subsisting middle state. 

To the other point, it should be said that Art can do many things that Nature cannot—such as making a house or a statue—and can make something *look* like a man or a plant. Some things begin from Nature and are perfected by Art, such as health which is assisted by medicine. Other things begin from Art and are perfected by Nature, such as the planting of a seed in the earth. On this, the <term>Commentator</term> <note>original: "gmentator"; referring to Averroes, the influential Andalusian philosopher.</note> in the 30th book of the *Physics*, quoting <term>Alexander</term> <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a Greek commentator on Aristotle.</note>, says: "Nature completes many things which are begun by Art, and Art completes many things which are begun by Nature." 

And as for what is brought up regarding a body constructed by Art: this does not prove a constitution of "weight," but rather a temperament of "justice." This is apparent because the skin is compared to it, and skin has a constitution of temperate justice. Furthermore, such a temperament cannot exist everywhere and always, since the air continuously changes and dissolves it. Who could ever experience such a "mixture of weight" when our senses would fail us there? 

Even if you wish to argue that this "constitution of weight" has been shown, it must be said that although the example is very familiar and close to it, it is not entirely shown to be real. In examples, one does not look for absolute verification, but for an explanation, as the <term>Commentator</term> says in the book *On the Soul* and in the *Prior Analytics*: "We use examples so that what is being said may be perceived." 

To the other point, it should be said that the middle point and temperament of the "constitution of justice" is right for the human constitution so that it may discern the intensities of tangible qualities. For if it were not sensitive to all touchable things, then because of harmful things occurring from without or within, man could not remain alive for long, as he would receive injury from almost all tangible things. 

And therefore, I know of some highly sensitive people who are harmed by the movement of a flea and who are almost continuously sickly. It is not necessary for a man to be only "most sensitive to touch," but he must also be able to resist external and internal occurrences. 

To the other point: "equal according to weight" and "unequal," or "equal according to justice" and "unequal," are not opposites. This is because they do not fall under the same category, just as logic requires for opposites. Non-being is not the opposite of being, since they do not share the same matter or category. 

To the confirmation, it should be said as follows. To the final point: Universal and Particular Nature prohibit the "constitution of weight," as has been shown, for one is ordered within the other. Nature also prohibits the "constitution of justice" as described in the first mode, since it does not persist but is falsified in an instant. Nature never produces anything into being without laboring for its preservation, as stated in the 30th book of *On the Generation of Animals*. And because two constitutions of justice remain noble and active during the time of operation, Nature [produces them...] <note>The text ends with a catchword "pduat et qsu" suggesting "produces and preserves."</note>

Regarding the other point, it must be said that the intellect goes out to its own objects in a dual way. First, there is the **intellect of principles**, which by itself tends toward its own disposition <note>original: "habitum"; a settled state of knowledge</note>. It is said in the fourth book <note>original: "dr. [dicitur] .iiii."; likely referring to Aristotle’s *De Anima* or a similar commentary</note> that this is like a certain light innate to us. It bears witness to the truth, such as the fact that for anything, it must either be or not be, or that the whole is greater than its part. This is sometimes true, as when it understands true things, or false, as when something false is understood about the soul.
