This is because the intellect possesses a greater power than nature. It is said in the fourth book that the intellect has the power to join things never joined and to separate things that are distinct. 

Likewise, concerning the **complexion of weight**, there is no true science of it in itself; rather, it is passed down through principles, accidents, or effects. Instead, it is an "equivocal" or improper science, or a "negative" science. Such a science can be about non-being—calling it "non-existence"—just as there is a science of the infinite or the vacuum. It must also be said that just as a thing has "being," it also has "notability" <note>the capacity to be known</note>, and it possesses both a genus and differences. Similarly, neither a definition nor a description affirms that a thing exists or denies it—since it deals with the "simple" <note>the essence of a thing before it is judged as true or false</note> about which truth or falsehood does not exist, as stated in *On the Soul* <note>original: "itello [intellecto] de anima"</note>. Rather, it simply denotes the "quiddity" <note>The "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</note> of the thing. For a definition differs from the thing defined only in that the name is "implicit" <note>folded in</note> while the definition is "explicit" <note>unfolded</note>, as said in book four.

Regarding the other point, it must be said that a "measure" is a thing in some way—at least according to the idea that the word "thing" [*res*] is derived from the verb "to think" [*reor, reris*] <note>A common medieval etymology suggesting that "things" are objects of thought.</note>. It cannot be said to come from "certainty" [*ratitudine*]. And just as there is "well-being," there is also "measuring." For the passive intellect, such as the imaginative power, has the role of joining things from a simple starting point—just as my own mind might wish to imagine a "mountain of emerald" <note>original: "monte smaragdi"; a classic philosophical example of a thing that can be imagined but does not exist in reality.</note>...

### CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>¶</margin> It is shown that one should not posit a "simple complexion" <note>A complexion made of only one quality, such as pure heat or pure moisture.</note> as existing by itself—whether as hot, cold, dry, or moist. This is because no philosopher or physician, including <term>Galen</term> <note>original: "G."; the influential Greek physician whose theories of the four humors dominated medieval medicine.</note>, posits them, as it would be insufficient to provide such types. Furthermore, <term>Averroes</term> <note>original: "Au."; the Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in his *Colliget* <note>original: "coll. s."; refers to the *Kitab al-Kullyat*, a medical encyclopedia.</note> denies them, saying there are four compound ones that follow. 

Furthermore, everything that participates in the human complexion does so in the same way, since they are all of the same nature. But the complexion itself is composite; for example, it is composed of "hot" and "moist." Therefore, it will always be so, since the lower [the specific instance] always receives the predicate of the higher [the category], for it cannot be separated from it. 

Again, cause and effect are proportional according to the study of nature. Whence in the *Tegni* <note>A textbook of Galenic medicine.</note>, it is attested that the power and beginning of the first principle are reflected in the principles that come from it. But the efficient causes of a complexion—such as the <term>elements</term>—are arranged and preserved through their qualities. Fire, for example, is hot and dry; air is hot and moist; summer is hot and dry; and food is hot and moist, and so on. Similarly, the effects of a complexion are evident, such as... and so on. In the same way, heat is the instrument...

---

...of the complexion and of nature, and it is composite: for it is pronounced "hot and moist" in the *Colliget*. Likewise, the body is composite. Again, a "complexion" is a quality resulting from the action and passion <note>In scholastic terms, "action" is doing and "passion" is being acted upon.</note> of elements, as said in book seventeen. This name "complexion" denotes the same thing as the "joining" or "coupling" of qualities. 

Also, in every nature there is something of **matter** and something of **form**, as discussed in *On the Soul*. The first [matter] is proportional to the passive quality, and the second [form] to the active quality. For "moist" and "dry" are like matter, while "heat" and "cold" are like form, as appears in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. Whence in that same place: "The agent acts through two powers, and the patient suffers through two." The acting powers are heat and cold; the suffering [passive] powers are dry and moist. It is therefore necessary in a complexion for these to coexist. Thus, no complexion exists "simply," but only as a "composite" mixture.

In opposition to this, Galen, in the first book of *On Complexions*, says that many physicians and philosophers recognize four "distempered" <note>unbalanced or extreme</note> compound complexions, but they are ignorant of the four others generated from themselves. I do not know where they failed. 

Again, where there is "more" and "less," there must also be a "middle." Since, therefore, one finds a state very distempered toward heat and dryness, and another very distempered toward cold and moisture, and so on for the others, there must be a middle ground between these extremes. Such a middle will be one of the four "simple" temperaments, but only according to a middle distemper. For when the elements, proportioned in various ways, come to a mixture—the effect of which is a complexion—what prevents the heat of fire from overcoming the coldness of water or equaling it? Likewise, what prevents the moisture of air from equaling the dryness of earth, so that an equal middle emerges between dry and moist? Or that the moist is overcome by the dry, and the cold of water is tempered by the heat of fire? For this reason, some, noticing this, posit four simple complexions.

Regarding the first point, it must first be known what a complexion is, as stated in book seventeen. Among **beings**, some are entirely simple, others are entirely composite, and some are intermediate. 
1. The **Simple** exists in two ways: one is "potential," such as <term>Hyle</term> <note>The Greek term for "Prime Matter," the pure potentiality that has no form of its own.</note>, whose existence is in "possibility." For substance exists through possibility, as Averroes says in *On the Substance of the Orb*, although in the *Physics* he seems to feel that its substance would be destroyed by the removal of its power during generation. The other simple is "actual" only, such as the First Cause. For the First Act is pure and free from all potentiality, according to the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*.
2. Those which are **Intermediate** between these two are composed of form and matter. In all things beneath the First Being, there is a composition of "what it is" and "how it is." As you may understand from the commentary on the *Book of Causes*, nature is composed of "quiddity" and "being." For it possesses both matter and form, and the soul is similar. 
3. The **Composite** in every way is the body, especially the **human body**. For it is more composite than other bodies, since in it are found the grades of all beings, starting from matter...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the "temperate complexion" and the human body as a microcosm. It shifts from pure psychology to the mathematical and physical principles that govern "the mean" (the middle point or balance) in nature and medicine.</meta>

For beginning like other things, this first <note>referring to the primary science or principle under discussion</note> passing through **simple bodies** <note>The four elements: earth, water, air, and fire</note> and those mixed, extends even to **intellectual being**, which is also called the prior difference. Therefore, the physicist will concede in the eighth book <note>of Aristotle’s *Physics*</note> that a **microcosm** <term>microcosm (literally "little world"): the ancient and medieval idea that the human being is a miniature map of the entire universe</term> exists; whence coming to the final composite in the hierarchy of degrees, it is not further ordered into any other animals. For it is the end and the ultimate thing intended here by nature. 

However, the **middle** of these is both simple and composite, according to how it is proportioned to diverse things: for in proportion to the first, it is called composite, but in relation to the last, it is every simple thing which will be greater the closer it approaches to prime matter or the first producer. Whence the elements are composite with respect to prime matter and form; they are, however, simple bodies in relation to mixtures. From these elements, indeed, the **Meteorologica** <note>Aristotle's treatise on natural phenomena and the elements</note> are composed, from which minerals are constituted, and from these, things born of the earth, and so on.

**Difference XVI**
**Which can be called simple or composite by different proportions**

For the sake of what is said about the half or the middle, it must be known that there are ten **means** <note>mathematical averages or proportions</note> in the universe, of which two suffice at present: namely, the **arithmetic mean** and the **geometric mean**. 

The **arithmetic** disposition is that which divides quantities only by equal differences—for example, 1, 2, 3, or 2, 4, 6 <note>where the gap between each number is the same</note>. For in this, the mean is situated as indivisible and true, and therefore it is compared to a **Republic** which is governed by a few. 

The **geometric** mean, indeed, joins terms in equal proportion, which is found in a cubic figure like in a die. For in it there are 6 surfaces, 8 angles, and 12 sides; the paradigm of which is 6, 8, 12 <note>though 6, 8, 12 is technically a harmonic proportion, the author uses it here to discuss geometric relationships</note>, or 1, 2, 4. For in this, the mean is not taken as an equal and indivisible difference in every way, but only as proportions; for 8 is not a mean between 6 and 12 in terms of distance, nor is 2 between 1 and 4. And therefore it is likened more to a **democracy**, in which there is a very broad mean and a certain equality among all citizens and common people. 

**Boethius** in the second book of *Arithmetic* [says]: This equality is twofold: one of equals in quantity, like the arithmetic, and the other of similar things in quality, like what is called the geometric mean; by which that which is just and that which is of virtue is universally called "equal" in the fifth book of the **Ethics** <note>Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics*</note>.

---

On the other hand, in the same place, there are four distempered **complexions** <term>complexions: the specific "recipe" or balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body</term>, of which one refutes and rests against the other, because one theory posited only two complexions: hot-dry and cold-moist. But hot-moist and cold-dry were not accepted at all. 

**Difference XVIII**

This proceeds from an assumed accommodation: hot stands with dry, as in the hot and dry complexion; and it likewise stands with moist, as in the hot and moist, which seems less likely according to the second complexion, because hot and moist are destructive to each other. Therefore it will stand with the middle between moist and dry. Since this middle is closer even to hot than to moist, which is posited to stand. Let the reason be: Cold stands with dry and moist, and so on. 

Therefore there will be a complexion that is only hot and also only cold. In the same way, dry stands with hot, as in hot and dry—as both "heresies" <note>competing medical schools of thought</note> believe—and with cold as the first rejection of the second. Therefore it will also stand with the middle, a tempering between hot and cold; for that which is cold is proper to the dry, so if the dry suffers cold with it, much more so the middle. And similarly for the moist: for it stands with hot and cold. Thus, therefore, there will be two other complexions: dry and moist. So with the first two, they return to four. His speeches also scent the reasoning of this: all motion occurs from extreme to extreme through a middle. Since therefore a transition occurs from a hot-dry complexion to a cold-moist one, and from hot-moist to cold-dry, it happens through a middle, which will be either only hot, only cold, only dry, or only moist. 

To one perhaps wishing to pursue medical truth rather than the apparent probability of **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of antiquity</note>, and not consenting to his persuasion: It is not necessary that if hot stands with dry and with moist, it must therefore stand with their middle. Because in every mixture and middle there is that which is "more," but that is less by way of potency and act. 

**Difference XVIII**

Furthermore, where action and passion concur, the middle is removed, since one has victory over the other. Further, in the extremes—for example in dry and moist—when hot and cold are posited to stand, there is a "latitude" <note>a range of possible states</note>, and because of this, permanence and the acquisition of form; but not in the middle, since it carries more the reason of indivisibility. 

Regarding another point, it must be said that it is not necessary to grant a real permanent middle now introduced, as a new form between the extremes. 

**Difference XVIII**

Or if that passing middle is given, it does not endure even for a moment, being unable to resist the opposing excess; such a middle does not truly constitute a complexion, since we seek a health that is neither narrow nor unperceivable. 

The **Colliget** <note>The *Kullyat*, a famous medical work by the philosopher Averroes</note> in its second book, not only with the ancestors of Galen, posits there to be only four complexions as composites, but by denying the four simple ones which **Galen** confesses to have found. An augmentation of that idea is found from the opinion of **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the famous Persian physician-philosopher</note> in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*, especially thus: Know that in the sum of the two active qualities <note>hot and cold</note>, it follows from the measures of the two passive qualities <note>moist and dry</note>; because proper forms have proper matters under them. As if to say that an active quality existing as a form requires a passive one as matter; for in everything, as has been said, nature seeks something in the place of matter, and something...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic commentary on natural philosophy and the theory of complexions, specifically addressing the relationship between form and matter through the lens of the four primary qualities (heat, cold, moisture, and dryness). ...of form. Excepting **prime matter** <term>prime matter: the most basic, formless substance that underlies all physical things</term> and the ultimate form, form exists even without matter; for form itself is not separated from its *morphe* <note>original: "morphea," the Greek word for shape or essential form</note>. [See] the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. Furthermore, in the same section: every thing which is appropriate to a **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, wet, dry—that determines the nature of a body</term> necessarily belongs to the dominance of an **active quality**, which stands in the place of form; and to the dominance of a **passive quality**, which stands in the place of matter. For if it were not so, the thing so complexioned would not be one in form, but rather two. For this reason, since one cannot provide matter without form, or vice versa.

Therefore, every complexion will be composite, and none will be simple. This is supported by the fourth book of the *Meteorologica* <note>original: "iiii metaph." although cited as Metaphysics, the discussion of the four qualities usually refers to Book 4 of Aristotle's Meteorologica</note>, because that which is a simple and natural generation is a change caused by the **active powers**, namely heat and cold, when it has received a proportion from the underlying matter natural to each. However, these powers are passive, such as dryness and moisture.

But one wishing to defend **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity</note> will say that when a complexion is simply hot or cold, it is not form without matter, since the middle point between dry and moist is the matter of the hot or the cold. Whence in the fourth book of the *Meteorologica*: the thing acted upon is indeed the moist or the dry, or a mixture of these. But because it is more difficult to explain how the moist and the dry can have the character of an agent and of form, while the hot and the cold have that of the patient and of matter; in order that the simple passive qualities (namely the dry and the moist) may be saved, it must be known that all qualities are sometimes called active. Whence he calls all four of these "operative." And **Haly** <note>likely Haly Abbas, the 10th-century Persian physician</note> in that place on Galen, following the opinions of the logicians, named all the qualities active because active and passive qualities are contained in one category of the logicians. 

Whence in the first book of *Natural Powers*, **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay." for Aristoteles</note> sometimes in the books of *On Generation and Corruption* uses these four as all being active when considered individually. But in the books of the *Meteorologica*, the *Problems*, and many other places, he uses only two as active and two as passive. And it is confirmed because even if quantities are in themselves imperfect compared to that which is directed toward action, in theory and in reality, a quality stands as the proper instrument of action; once the quantity is multiplied, the power is also multiplied. And thus, to whatever extent form requires a due quantity in matter—supported by which it emerges in action—the quality is the mediator. Whence the more extended it is, the more the operation is strengthened, since it is beneficial for every agent to be of great quantity. Concerning fire: for fire is most active in as small a quantity as can be, or works least when quantity is minimal. Regarding complexions: the quantity in which a passive quality is supported could be increased so much, and the quantity of the active quality decreased so much, that what proceeds from the passive qualities will have the character of form and agent, and what comes from the active qualities will have the character of the patient and of matter. Thus, the middle point of the hot and cold will exist as the matter of the dry and moist, which are formal and active. So also the matter of a **temperate complexion** will be set as dry and cold; for by the nature of the whole species, it tends toward heat and moisture with its own tempering. For although heat and cold are active qualities by themselves, and dryness and moisture are passive, an accident can occur otherwise in this manner.

A doubt arises because it was said by Galen that Aristotle uses the four qualities as effective [active] in the book *On Generation and Corruption*, even though in the same place he says heat and cold are active, while dryness and moisture are passive, and he explains their acts. Perhaps it should be said that Galen said this noticing that Aristotle speaks of the generation of simple things like **elements** <note>earth, water, air, fire</note>, which achieve their vigor through qualities grounded in substances, as if they were their instruments; so that not only is fire made from air, or water from earth, but also the reverse. Which must happen by moisture and dryness acting as agents. Aristotle also declares there that effects do not only come from the hot and the cold, but from the dry and the moist, as also appears in the book on medicines and in the first book of the *Physics*. For each quality, in respect to the effect proceeding from it, can be called active: for moisture moistens, softens, and smooths; dryness dries, hardens, and roughens, etc. 

Some indeed have said that the passive qualities are also truly called active because of the **resistance** by which they cause a "passion" [an effect] in the agent, according to that principle of physics: everything active is at the same time passive in a physical sense. But Galen’s intention was not so base; it was common. Others have said they act **by accident** <term>by accident (per accidens): an effect produced not by the thing's own nature, but through some secondary or coincidental means</term>, as by the vigor of active qualities; just as the moist moistens not by itself, but through the cold which constricts and thickens the subtle parts, as in the conversion of air into water. But this mode of action is foreign and irrelevant.

From these things, therefore, it is judged and concluded: that even passive qualities sometimes have the character of an agent and of form. Still, Aristotle will reply that such a form would be disproportionate to the matter. Furthermore, it must be known that for such four simple complexions, especially the passive ones, one cannot place the **means** [middle points] according to an **arithmetic mean** <term>arithmetic mean: a middle point calculated by equal distance from extremes, rather than a natural balance or a "true" middle point that can exist in reality</term> consisting in the being of an indivisible and true middle. This is shown because if the hot is placed to exceed the cold, a temperate middle point between the moist and dry could not remain, for two reasons: first, because since heat and cold are active, and dry and moist are passive, and contraries must act upon one another through contact, it is necessary for one to overcome the other. Otherwise, there would be no action and passion. For they will remain equal only for a moment; afterward, one must dominate the other, such as heat over cold, or dry over moist, and thus a composite complexion arises, such as hot-dry or cold-moist. Again: the given exceeding heat will consume the moisture, which together with the dry was making a certain temperate middle; thus the complexion will be rendered hot and dry. Similarly, moisture tempered by dryness cannot endure in a cold complexion so that the complexion remains a simple "cold" one, because of the previously mentioned contrariety of the dry to the moist. Also, the cold given as a middle between the dry and the moist will either make the moist raw or make it drier by freezing it. It will be much less possible by this way to establish a simple complexion that remains for any time, or a formal impossibility in passive things, because heat and cold—the most effective of qualities—do not remain joined together except when one exceeds the other. If the dry is placed to exceed, since it is like a file sharpening the heat, it will stir up the heat placed in the middle toward the other extreme; or if it is very dry, it will reduce that middle to coldness by withdrawing its nourishment, since moisture...

A temperament is formed; but this is of a certain judicial relation <term>judicial relation: a theoretical standard used to judge how far a body has shifted away from a perfect balance of qualities</term> to the mixed. But hard terrestrial particles resist more. 

Likewise, regarding the proximity of the skin, Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note> says it is a certain equality, and Galen <note>original: "G."</note> together with Haly Abbas <note>original: "balyabate," referring to the Persian physician 'Ali ibn al-'Abbas al-Majusi</note> says it is tempered in all of nature, provided it belongs to the most well-tempered <term>eucratissimi: a Greek-derived term for a body with a perfectly healthy and balanced mixture of qualities</term> man and is not calloused. Physicians understand the opposite of this. On the other hand, that medical balance is closer to the supreme temperament, in which the mixture of the aforementioned condition—as noted in *Difference 16*—is more perfectly observed. But this is found in the fixed judicial balance and not the medical one, so that the perfection of actions is finally confirmed.

Furthermore, a temperament is close to a temperament especially when one corresponds to the other, just as a distemper is to a distemper. However, a fixed judicial balance maintains this, but not a medical one. Furthermore, that complexion is more tempered which judges more perfectly concerning any excess, since a judge ought to hold the middle way in every respect and not be inclined toward any part of a contradiction. And thus by the straight we recognize both itself and the crooked, according to the first book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle, *De Anima*</note>; but this belongs to the fixed judicial balance and not the medical, since its law exists in a certain mediocrity of the excellent qualities, as stated in the previous *Difference*. Therefore, the fixed judicial balance is closer to the melancholic weight; for this reason, one must first know what a complexion is, what weight and justice are, and all its distinctions in *Differences 17 and 18*.

Regarding this, however, it must be known that some have said the innate fixed judicial complexion is closer to weight, but not the "influencing" <term>influencing: a quality or power acting upon the body from the outside, as opposed to the "innate" qualities born within it</term> one. For it seemed to them that the innate is more tempered than the influencing, because it is more moderate in heat, whereas the influencing one falls away in faints and especially at the beginnings. But this is not valid, since that one—as will appear in relation to weight—becomes sufficiently distempered. Also, those claiming the fixed judicial balance is a complexion closer to weight, hear this regarding the innate and the influencing. For there is a point where growth reaches its end.

<margin>A</margin> But others have said that it is composed of an equal judicial balance and weight, where every equality of the fixed judicial balance has at least one equality; as those of the fixed judicial balance and any of the others have neither, but some are more similar to the weight of quantities or powers. This can hardly stand, since with absolute reason being inapplicable, they compose something from that which exists and that which does not emerge for itself even by an opposite division, such as a complexion from justice and weight. Furthermore, Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note> is closer to the fixed equality than we previously noted; but he never named such a combined thing, but only the simple; hence it is not a small ridicule. Others said that it is closer to the equality of the weight of quantities, but not closer to the equality of the weight of powers, and vice versa.

But this also does not wish to stand, since the absolute fixed judicial balance is said to approach weight. Furthermore, whatever approaches something, approaches it in both simple respects. Thus it will be shown concerning the fixed judicial balance. And therefore another person stood upon this: that every fixed judicial complexion is close to weight by reason of powers <note>original: "virtutū"</note>, but not by reason of quantities. And similarly in the skin; wishing that by reason of quantities it stands closer to weight, being hot and dry, or hot and moist; because in these, the heavy things exceed less than in the fixed judicial balance. But he strives to show this from many ineffective arguments. But that this does not stand is denoted by the saying about "immediates." Likewise, that which approaches weight in terms of powers does not approach certain equality, but rather the certain judicial balance, since weight in itself, according to proven measures, carries both measures and powers. Also, that any one thing is closer to weight by reason of other measures will manifest as a fallacy.

Others, however, by reason of actions, say the certain judicial balance is close to certain equality. Which also is not valid; for it is not actions that are sought, but the underlying components; nor does the equality of weight participate in actions. You will say perhaps what you have imagined. But finally it must be said therefrom that actions argue for the complexion and the composition just as an effect argues for its cause. Regarding the third point, it must be known, so that the truth of this, which has been hidden until now, may be rendered more known: first, let it be shown what the complexion of weight is, how it is made, and from what it consists; and thus there will be an exposition which was secretly touched upon in the prior differences concerning it. Secondly, it will be shown how the fixed judicial balance is closer to weight in every way above all others. 

Concerning the first of these, it must be known that in every physical action, the agent must run through the motion from the end, and the matter from which the form is made; which may be seen in the whole universe. For some things in it behave by way of matter, like the four primary elements; and others by way of an agent, like the celestial bodies with their movers. Yet of those things which hold the place of matter, some nevertheless preserve that role more than others, like earth and water; while some act as an agent, like air and fire; for they are formal in relation to the others. Just as the power of the higher overcomes quantity and regulates and informs the elements by its power, so also do the two formal elements <note>fire and air</note> relate to the two remaining material elements <note>water and earth</note>. And because the higher things are effective upon the elements at least through motion and light—but also many through specific powers—they cause heat with a certain moisture; for the natures of all of them, when broken down, rise up into heat and moisture through "coalentation" <note>original: "coalētātōe," a blending or growing together</note> as in *Difference 10*. Thus in these, fire overcomes the quantity of water and its coldness by its mass and heat, so that heat obtains over cold and makes the heavy light. And air exceeds the mass of earth and remits its dryness; for although moisture is its vehemently passive quality, it helps with a measured quantity and heat in its melting and glaciating; and also from the humor of water in such a way that the moisture of air with its quantity obtains over the dryness and mass of the earth; for from a handful of earth, four parts of water arise, and from one of those, ten parts of air.

For it is fitting that the universe should incline toward worthier natures, working toward a fuller being and permanence. 

Imagine, therefore, that beings come together with the powers of the higher realms, so that they are marked by both mass and power, since the logic of the whole and the part is the same. [As said] in the first History <note>Aristotle's *History of Animals*</note>, the active vigor should have such power over the passive that action and passion meet, and consequently a mixture can be generated. I say, therefore, that from this a single body necessarily arises, since it stands as a paradigm <note>original: "padygma" (paradigma)</note> of the universe; and this itself will be the fixed judicial temperament <term>judicial temperament: a theoretical standard used to judge how far a living body has shifted away from a perfect balance of qualities</term>. 

But if the measures of the quantities of the elements and their qualities were to be further equalized with each other, then a greater temperament would arise, but it would be as if momentary. If one imagines the elements to be so equalized that their qualities or powers share in total equality—not so much in the true measure of their quantities, but rather in an appearance of equal weight—an unequal nature would be established. 

Or finally, if one imagines it possible for the measures of quantities and qualities to have a most certain and equal composition with each other, thus an equality of weight <term>equality of weight: a literal, mathematical 1:1:1:1 ratio of the four elements (fire, air, water, earth)</term> would arise, as made known in Distinction 18. This mode, along with the one immediately preceding it, is impossible to find in actual existence. It can only be imagined, and even then not easily, since such a state cannot possess generation or life. For these require the active and preserving qualities—namely heat and moisture—which are the primary causes, to prevail over the others, namely coldness and dryness. The measures of the quantities are not entirely equal, but in this state, the earthy and watery parts predominate, since moisture must contain us so that we may perform our proper functions. Therefore, when it concurs with this certain judicial balance in such a way, it can be made in a more perfect mode and endure for some time. 

An instantaneous temperament, located between these extremes, shares somewhat in both natures; so that perhaps it could even be generated into a being, but would endure only for a very brief moment before changing. But after the fixed judicial balance, according to such a measure of the quantities and qualities of the elements, a healthy body is established simply. And then by degrees, after the very healthy, is placed the healthy **sanguine** <term>sanguine: the humor of blood, associated with heat and moisture</term>, then the **choleric**, then the **phlegmatic**, and finally the **melancholic** <note>original: "mlicū" (melancolicum)</note>. This last one recedes far from the "weight" and measure in respect to the others, since it shares less in the heat and moisture hidden in its absolutely imagined temperament, declining instead toward coldness and dryness. 

It also differs very much from it by reason of the measure of quantities, such that the fixed judicial body is distant from the precise weight of that heat and moisture because it participates more in them. The **choleric**, however, contains less of them in respect to the equality of weight. The fixed judicial balance surpasses it by participating more in the equality of measure, such that the **melancholic**, by reason of its heat and moisture, is further from the fixed judicial balance than from the "weight," being located as if on an opposite line to it. Nevertheless, the measures of the quantities were very unequal, yet with these qualities and with heat, moisture, and the form of the species, it can be made and endure for a while. 

After this, the judicial nature considered generally in other species recedes more or less from the "weight" in relation to one another. Thus a pig is very well-tempered <note>original: "porcꝩ tpatillimꝩ" (porcus temperatissimus)</note> within its species and closer to man, or a chicken by nature; yet by reason of life and its species, the chicken, more than others after man, will approach the certain measure or weight. Then the lion, because of the heat and dryness of its species, will be far from it; yet it is pulled back toward balance by the principles of life, which, with their gentle heat and especially moisture, temper the heat and dryness into the measure of the species. A fish, although it approaches the weight on the side of life, nonetheless by reason of its species is far removed, falling much into the cold and moist. A hare or an ant even more so, since they are cold and dry. Attached things and vegetables recede even further from it, and especially those things which lack life, like meteorological phenomena <note>original: "metheologica"</note>, are very remote from the weight and are entirely simple, being like lines ending from the center to the circumference. 

In these things one must also diligently observe the measures of the quantities of the elements. This happens not only in the relation of one species to another, but also within a species itself there is a great and almost infinite distance. For in each species one finds the more tempered and the less, so that the sayings of the experts <note>original: "pitorū" (peritorum)</note> are verified and ordered within the human species. 

Since each of the four degrees is divided into three mansions <term>mansions: sub-divisions used by physicians to measure the intensity of a quality or humor</term> (Distinction 139), the highest and middle temperament outside their mansions will be the imagined equality of weight of the first mode. But in the first portion of the first degree, let there be the fated inequality of the same. In its middle, however, is the instantaneous equality which, remaining for the blink of an eye, is changed. In the first mansion of the second degree, let there be the fixed judicial equality; then the **sanguine**, then the **choleric**, then the **phlegmatic**, and finally the **melancholic**, the worst extreme of the human species; since the fixed judicial balance better endures for some time, as it is not merely momentary. 

And according to this, the saying of the *Universal Diets* <note>original: "dietay uniuerſaliū", likely the dietary text by the 10th-century physician Isaac Israeli</note> can be understood: that human nature is hot and moist, tempered in the second degree. But those tending more intensely from here into the third and fourth degrees become sick and dying bodies. But the double distinction of degrees according to two means will be shown in Distinction 139. And to declare this, the epigraph will generally note: Know that the cause of difficulty here is that it was unknown to them what "weight" implied. As if its distinction is by reason of the mixture, closer to man, then to foods, and to the vine, concerning its nature. Let it be granted, then, that this fixed judicial balance is the most tempered of all...

Avicenna <note>original: "Auic.", the famous Persian polymath Ibn Sina</note>, however, being more certain in this matter, distinguished—as seen in the 17th distinction—the temperament of "weight" from that of "justice," falling into two modes: although their components were not expressly touched upon entirely separately. He also intended that the entire human species should be closer than others to "weight," saying: "When a man has this division," that is, the divided temperament as far as fixed justice is concerned. For above he had introduced the division of temperament into the equality of weight and justice, or the "sequestration" <note>the separation or setting apart</note> of them from their places, and such a portion and such a kind which is suitable for the actions, passions, and dispositions which occur. 

And he adds that what we previously called equality—namely of "weight"—will be very close. And finally he says that fixed "judicial" justice is the midpoint which is found between two widely distant extremes: the temperament of the human species and the individual, which is at the ultimate of equality from the species existing at the limit of equality, and in the age in which growth reaches its end—previously distinguished as something rarely found, and only in longer periods of time. 

And he adds: And this equality also, although it is not the "fixed equality" we named in this chapter—namely of weight—because it is not possible for this to be found, is nevertheless close to it. Yet this closeness is not in every way, because it is not considered in just any organ in itself, but in one alone: such as the skin of fixed justice. For that skin is closer to weight than other organs and beings. Having undergone a moderate "co-alternation" from the breaking down <note>original: "confractione", the mixing or tempering of opposing qualities</note> of the heat of the flesh and blood, and the coldness of the nerves and bones; but specifically of the entire adjunct of organs like the hot, cold, dry, and moist. For these in themselves are remote from this equality. Truly, from the breaking down and co-alternation interchangeably of one of their temperaments with another, such a "fixed justice" results, yet declining from weight toward heat and moisture for the sake of generation and life, as touched upon by Haly Abbas in the 10th book, chapter A, with the collection of Galen <note>original: "lzo", possibly a reference to a specific book or "logos"</note>. 

Just as there is a threefold distinction in a composite body—Distinction 16—so also there is a temperament: one indeed of the general parts, like bones, nerves, etc., which arises from the qualities of the mixables; another of the "official" <term>official organs: organs that perform a specific function or "office," like the heart or liver</term> organs resulting from similar parts; and a third of the whole body from the preponderance and breaking down of these. Know also that this fixed judicial temperament is found simply in a man, but not in a woman, except in relation to others or to the species of others; nor is it found except in one who is perfectly tempered and in a measured household regime. 

Next, he also establishes by reasons that fixed justice is closer to weight in every way. For if we look at two things existing in man—namely the body with its dispositions and the soul—we will find that both are imagined in the body of "weight," and that the whole man is of fixed justice, especially closer than other animals and natures to it. For those elements were like materials, and the powers of the higher realms like formal [causes]: for man, of fixed justice by reason of his mass or measure, approaches those things which are imagined in a composite body more than others. 

For he stands as one <note>original: "extat mundicus", perhaps "little world" or microcosm</note>, which is shown by the composition and site of his parts, and specifically of the fixed judicial man: for "up" in him is simply "up" in the universe. In other animals, however, this is less so, or only in a certain respect, such as toward their head where they receive nourishment. For the name [of the head] seems to come from the act of "taking" and "comprehending," receiving the progress of animals. Wherefore, in the fourth book on Parts <note>Aristotle’s *Parts of Animals*</note>, man is the only animal that is upright, because of his nature and his divine substance, as seen in the 5th distinction. 

Whence Aristotle in the 29th book says man is the wisest of animals because he has a small head in relation to his body. And therefore children, since they are primarily "airy" <note>filled with vapors</note> around their heads, are not able to understand sufficiently; and because quadrupeds are continuously "airy" with heads hanging down, they lacked intellect and reason because of the weight itself. Thus, as heat is diminished and the earthly substance is rendered greater, they become many-footed animals with heads close to the earth, and finally, lacking them, they creep upon the earth or are joined to it. Finally, like plants, they have the part for the head—the roots—directed downwards and fixed in the earth. The figure of the head denotes the image of the heaven and the whole universe, as the three-fold [geometry] bears. 

And according to what is in man in common with others, because he more closely approaches the position of the universe, which the disposition of his parts shows; so also the whole of fixed justice relates to man in respect to the imagined body. This sign would be supported by the "lying Gentile" <note>likely a dismissive reference to non-Christian or pagan philosophers/legends</note>, because he says Elijah <note>original: "Helyam"</note> was so tempered that he could be located in any of them, and thus the elements in him were so proportioned and their contrarieties so quieted that he could remain in almost any [environment]. Nevertheless, they testify that Christ was most perfectly tempered, which the divine acts of the same taught, in as much as his human nature participated.

For by the same reason that it was in one place, it would be moved to another. But a "judicial" body is certainly more fit for motion and for acquiring more locations than the <term>mixed body: an unrefined or poorly balanced mixture of elements</term> in which the heavy elements dominate over the others. 

Also, the more a thing is perfect or tempered, the more rarely it is found, since many things are required for its constitution. Hence, a body that is <term>distempered: unbalanced or out of proportion</term> in regard to justice, yet tempered in other ways, is found more frequently than one that is very healthy or always healthy. This is even truer for the "fixed judicial" balance, and even rarer than the sense of touch; indeed, it is rarest of all because it remains unchanged for almost no moment in time. 

If, therefore, a temperament could exist in the nature of things beyond what is currently possible, it would be even more tempered than this, since they proceed from a very broad temperament to one that is narrow and brief, so that nature cannot suffer a temperament beyond it, nor can it exist universally; just as nothing more perfect has been found beyond the first. Now, however, just as "always healthy" relates to "fixed judicial," and this relates to "momentary health," so that which is mediated by health almost reaches the "imagined weight": if the healthy person is closer to the fixed judicial than the very healthy, then the distempered is much further from it, especially the mixed body. 

From this, the nobility of actions and perfection argues for the temperament and its proximity [to the ideal]. When, however, one makes the form known, every tempered <term>complexio: the specific combination of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body</term> is recognized by its own office. But perfections of the more noble things are far from the fixed judicial than from the mixed body; as in the previous distinction: for he is the giver of the law even if the world were discovered. Thus, it should be certain to a healthy understanding that the fixed judicial is closer to the "weight" than the mixed body or any other thing in the world. 

But concerning the aforesaid, a doubt arises, since it is also said that something is more tempered which is less fixed and determined to a place, and is able to endure more things; such a thing as the **duck**, for it can be located in every element and live for a long time outside the water. Regarding fire, the same is said of the **salamander**. The "fixed judicial" body, however, is by no means able to be adapted to such diverse places; therefore, those creatures would be more tempered than it. 

It must be said that the ability of these or similar things to be located in many places is not because they are tempered themselves, but rather because they are distempered and <term>heterogeneous: made of diverse, non-uniform parts</term>. For the salamander, because it is cold and dry, with a foreign, viscous, and compact humidity, is rendered almost impassive and insensible. Or perhaps someone will say it is false, because we do not find any of the animals living entirely in fire according to the properties of the elements; the truth of which is expressed in the *Account of Complexions*: the salamander suffers nothing from fire for a certain amount of time, but it is burned if it stays in proximity for a longer time.

---

Neither are the parts of the duck and other birds <term>homogeneous: uniform in substance throughout</term> in their temperament, nor is their complexion entirely unified. For the primary parts through which they have their being, by reason of their clearly visible mass, are heavier than those of the "imagined weight" and "judicial" balance; they depart from it in various ways, just as the sense of touch does. Their other parts, however, for the sake of their "well-being," are perhaps drier and lighter in weight, so that they may be carried through the air. 

The **fixed judicial**, however, is a homogeneous temperament throughout everything that is unified; yet, because of the actions and elements dominating in it, it is more firm in earth and water. Regarding the fourth point, it should be known that almost all the previously introduced arguments cease. For they proceeded, as has been shown, from a false root. 

Hence, regarding the first, it must be said that a complexion regarding weight is not one extreme and regarding justice another; rather, that which is of weight is only a "mean," and the fixed judicial is also one of the extremes, although it is less distant from others than weight is. And although both are "medial" (in the middle), they are not equally so, but are ordered separately, one within the other, and one is the extreme to the other. 

The same must be said for the other point, since it proceeds from the same foundation. To the next, it must be said that although the fixed complexion pertains to the hot and moist, it does not therefore recede further from the "mixed" temperament; on the contrary, it approaches it more closely. Since weight does not underlie the melancholic complexion, but rather sits above it, the "mixed" is not a mean between weight and the fixed judicial, but rather one extreme certainly lying below the judicial. For the "mixed" body participates less in the hot and moist than the weight complexion does, which is generated and preserved by greater measures. 

Regarding the fixed judicial, the mixed body is more cold and dry, as shown before. To the other point, it must be said that the fixed judicial is not more alterable than the mixed body. Hence, concerning the **best composition**: because the best composition of the body disposes it perfectly for all actions, it is more "difficultly passible" <note>hard to affect or damage</note> than all others. This happens because of its strength and the continuous homogeneity among its parts. If, however, measured bodies are changed and suffer easily, they nevertheless return and are healed quickly, because that suffering is "extensive" rather than "intensive." Because of their continuous uniformity, one part soon suffers with another; so that when one part suffers, the rest immediately sympathize, and thus the suffering is distributed among many and rendered smaller. Aristotle <note>original: "Ay." or "Ar."</note> says in the same place: likewise, when one part is healed, the others are healed by its help, so that it incurs no strong or lasting suffering. And so, in Aristotle, Galen concurs. 

For this reason, Alexander <note>original: "Alexander in pbleu.", referring to Alexander of Aphrodisias in his *Problems*</note> asks a proportional question: why are fevers and hidden sufferings in brutes harder to heal and more dangerous than in humans? He solves it by saying they are "most difficultly passible"; therefore, they only suffer from major causes rather than from common ones, due to the vigor of that pattern. In diseases, they suffer less [from minor things] than others. To the other point, it must be said that here the nature of the skin is sought as it is "actual" (living), not "potential" (dead).

### DISTINCTION 21.

<margin>1</margin> That a <term>hot and moist temperament: a biological constitution dominated by heat and moisture, which medieval medicine considered the most vital and "life-giving" combination</term> is of a longer life is demonstrated. Because in Book 6 of *The Regiment of Health* <note>original: "vi. de re. sa.", referring to Galen's *De Sanitate Tuenda*</note> it says that those who are most moist and most hot are the longest-lived. Also, Haly Abbas <note>original: "Amp. baly", referring to the 10th-century Persian physician 'Ali ibn 'Abbas al-Majusi</note> says a hot and moist temperament is of a longer life than the others, an opinion which Avicenna <note>original: "Au.", the influential Persian polymath Ibn Sina</note> also strives to affirm, both regarding one's temperament and one's region. For the logic is similar regarding the region and the temperament: those who inhabit a hot and moist region are of a longer life, according to the book *On the Causes of Length and Brevity of Life*. Again, life stands through heat and moisture in that same place. And Damascenus <note>original: "Damasce9", likely referring to the Christian physician and translator John Mesue</note> says in his *Aphorisms*: "such is the temperament of this [life]."

Furthermore, digestion and nutrition, which are the pathways to lives and their length, are perfected by heat and moisture, as seen in Book 6 of *On Accidents* <note>original: "vi. de ac.", likely Galen's *De Symptomatum Causis*</note>. That temperament is indeed such. Again, that temperament in which the moisture is proportioned to the heat will be of a longer life; for from this, the length of life seems to be derived, namely from heat and moisture. This is signaled by the fact that in the first stage, children from infancy until youth exist in a heat that is almost tempered and in a superfluous moisture. This temperament indeed reaches a moderate drying out when youth occurs. Therefore, that temperament will be of a longer life whose moisture is more slowly rendered proportional to the heat <note>Medieval thinkers believed aging was a process of "drying out"; therefore, having more initial moisture delayed the onset of old age</note>. For it is probable that age corresponds to age: if the age of childhood, through heat and moisture, is extended more than the others, so too will be youth, old age, and extreme senility. This is noted more specifically thus: if a tempered constitution with a tempered moisture, removed from the superfluous moisture of childhood, concludes at the end of the 22nd or 23rd year, so that it becomes entirely tempered, this will happen to a hot and moist temperament at the end of the 35th or 36th year. Thus childhood is more extended, and consequently the other ages corresponding to it. Therefore, a hot and moist temperament is of a longer life than the others. The opposite is also true: that temperament is of a shorter life which is most exposed of all to <term>putrefaction: the breaking down or "rotting" of bodily humors, often associated with disease</term>, since that stands as one of the causes of death, and which is prone to every illness from this cause; such indeed is this eighth [temperament] in *On Generation* <note>original: "i ge.", likely referring to Aristotle's *On Generation and Corruption*</note>.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into biological temperaments, transitioning from a general discussion of heat and moisture to a technical debate on which specific physical constitution best preserves life. It follows the previous page's introduction of the hot and moist temperament as a candidate for longevity.</meta>

...as is also indicated by the foul smell of sweat, as well as the rankness <note>original: "egonis", referring to a goat-like scent</note> of those who have a "goat-like" <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determines a person's physical and mental nature</term>. Such is the nature of these people in that place and in the fourth part.

However, that a **hot and dry** constitution is better is shown by the fact that the temperament which most resists the causes of death is the longest-lived. Such is this one, because the most powerful cause of life's destruction is <margin>1st, 2nd, and 3rd reasons</margin> excessive moisture. This kills us in two ways: first, by its own bad quality, it opposes the innate heat; second, by suffocating the ruling power through its excessive quantity. This moisture accumulates least in hot and dry bodies, as noted in the books of the kingdoms and complexions. In such a temperament, the moisture is also less prone to freezing and, because of its compactness, less prone to drying out—which, according to Avicenna <note>original: "Ay."</note>, is the most powerful cause of a longer life. Thus, a hot and dry temperament is longer-lived than the others. 

It also seems that a **cold and dry** temperament would be longer-lived, since death comes to us through <term>putrefaction: the biological breakdown and decay of the body’s matter</term>, which is caused by heat and moisture, according to the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* and the eleventh book of *On Generation*. This temperament is the opposite in both ways. Furthermore, such a body resists both internal and external corrupting causes, since its moisture is the least susceptible to change. Still further, if the principle of life is of a cold and dry temperament, the life derived from it will tend toward a cold and dry constitution. But the principle of life, such as the heart, is cold and dry, which is shown by its hardness, compactness, and resistance to rotting; hence the whole of its nourishment indicates it is indigestible and slow to reach putrefaction. The <term>generative seed: the biological material responsible for reproduction</term> also proclaims this in the fourth book of the *Problems*. Therefore, since it follows the nature of its principles more closely, it will be longer-lived than the others.

That a **cold and moist** temperament is better is shown because death seems to be accelerated by the consumption of moisture by heat. But in such a temperament, the moisture is very resistant to consumption, and the consuming heat is dulled. Furthermore, according to Avicenna, "oily" moisture is the cause of longevity, but oiliness abounds in a cold and moist temperament; therefore, it will have a longer life.

That a **temperate** <note>original: "tempata", meaning a perfectly balanced state between all extremes</note> temperament is best is proven because the temperament which exists first in virtue, power, and the order of intelligence is longer-lived than the others, since life is primarily an order of being. But the temperate state stands first among these temperaments. Again, that in which all things exist in due measure, needing no external measuring, will have a longer life. Only the temperate temperament is like this; for it hungers only for what it can digest well and needs no external dispenser for its governance. Also, it easily expels all wastes through both sensible and insensible pores, and it is least harmed by external alterations according to Galen <note>original: "Ga."</note>. Therefore, the temperate is of a longer life than the rest.

Concerning the first point, it must be known what a temperament is; its definition was seen in Distinction 17. We must now see what life is and what its primary causes are, and then what death is (since it is the opposite of life) and its causes.

Regarding the first, it should be known that "life" is spoken of in three ways: 

First, by the **essence of life**, and this in three ways:
1. According to the more visible way, following the *Commentary on the Book of Causes*:
> Life is a procession proceeding from the eternal, quiet Being, and the first movement, such as that of the intelligences and the heavens, and consequently reaching into these lower things that are born and decay through certain intermediaries from the first cause. 

This is also noted in the book *On the Soul*:
> To live is to be for living things. That is, life is the form and substance of the living being; for by life, each living thing consists in its being.

2. In a less visible and more material way, as when the book *On the Soul* says:
> Life is the consistency maintained through nourishment.

3. Or specifically as it pertains to the more perfect animals, according to **Alfred of Sarashel** <note>original: "Aluredus de cordis motu", a 12th-century English scientist</note> in *On the Movement of the Heart*:
> Life is a continuous motion flowing from the heart into the other members.

Following the words of **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Ypo."</note>:
> Life is short, but art is long.

In another way, life is spoken of as the **mode and measure of living**, according to the principle of the *Metaphysics*: "Man lives by art and reason."

There are three causes of life: namely, universal, specific, and intermediate. One who wishes to investigate the causes of life and its length and brevity must consider all of them. For it is not enough to consider universals unless one also considers the particulars that produce the effect, nor to consider particulars unless one attends to the universals from which they take their being and truth.

The **universal and primary cause** is the heaven, through its motion and light.
The **intermediate causes**, according to the genealogists <note>referring here to astrologers</note>, are two: one of which is proportioned to the matter, or the mother or wife, which is called <term>hyleg: the "giver of life," a specific point in a birth chart used to determine a person's lifespan</term>. The second is the <term>alcocoden: the "giver of years," the planet that rules the hyleg and indicates how many years a person might live</term>, which represents the form, or the father or husband.

The **Hyleg** <note>original: "Yleg"</note> is taken first from the Sun, if possible, in a daytime birth. If that is not possible, it passes to the Moon, and is taken from her first if the birth was at night. If it cannot be taken from her, it returns to the Sun in the degree of the ascendant, and if not from these, then from the one that looks upon the ascendant, then from the Part of Fortune. If it cannot be taken from that, then the degree of the "filling" <note>the Syzygy or previous New/Full moon</note> is considered: if the birth was at the conjunction, or if at the opposition, the Part of Fortune is put before the ascendant, and then whichever degree follows the preceding one. If it cannot be taken from any of these, the person will not live, unless perhaps the luminaries look upon each other with a benevolent aspect, along with a favorable view from the "fortunes" <note>benefic planets like Jupiter or Venus</note.

The **Alcocoden** <note>original: "alcocboden"</note> is the planet looking at the place of the Hyleg with a friendly aspect, and which holds some of the five essential dignities of the planets in that place, or more: such as house, exaltation, triplicity, or term. For the "face" <note>the weakest dignity</note> is usually disregarded because of its low value. This planet, the Alcocoden, according to how it is strengthened or weakened in its five places of power—such as the degrees of the ascendant, the midheaven, and the degree of the Part of Fortune—bestows its years: whether "greater," "middle," or "lesser," or even weeks or days. To this Alcocoden, the "fortunes" <note>benefic planets</note> add years according to their own fortunate state, and the "infortunes" <note>malefic planets like Saturn or Mars</note> subtract from the Alcocoden's years according to their own depraved state. According to **Avicenna**, this is the "containing air" and the period of the Sun and Moon; hence the fourth book on the *Generation of Animals*...

<meta>This page continues the technical investigation into the causes of longevity, transitioning from the debate over hot-dry temperaments to the specific roles of innate heat, radical moisture, and the influence of celestial cycles. It draws heavily on Aristotelian and Avicennian biology to define the "formal" and "material" causes of life and death.</meta>

Concerning the cause of why any animal is long-lived: it must be tempered to the surrounding air and, most especially, to the **periods of the sun and moon**. Reasonably so, for the times of all gestations, births, and lives are intended to be measured according to the natural cycles. According to Aristotle <note>original: "Ar."</note> in the 18th book of *History of Animals*, the causes are not placed solely in the material, but the cause for receiving longevity is an impression from the stars, until life is in harmony with the revolution of a certain star or many stars. From these factors—the cause of life and its length or brevity—astrologers <note>original: "genetalici," those who cast birth charts</note> make their prognostications, as will appear in chapter 113.

The particular and formal causes are twofold: some are primary and mediated, while others are secondary and immediate. 

The primary causes are **heat and moisture**, and their mutual proportion. Thus Aristotle says there are two causes of life: "how much" and "what kind." It is necessary not only for there to be a large amount of moisture, but the proportion must be of a specific quality—namely, that it be hot. It should not be easily congealed into liquid, nor should the moisture be easily dried out. Thus, the proportion of heat to the moisture is seen to be more important for longevity than the simple quantity of moisture. For this reason, Aristotle says that a creature lacking a large quantity of moisture might live longer if it exceeds in "quality"—that is, in its proportion of moisture to heat—than one that is lacking in quantity. 

It is also necessary that this moisture, along with the heat, be "oily" <note>original: "pingue," literally fat or greasy</note> so that it is not easily cooled. Because of its oiliness, it serves as the fuel <note>original: "fomentum"</note> for the heat. Therefore, Avicenna <note>original: "Au."</note> in his treatise on this subject states that an abundance of heat and moisture, and the dominance of the **active virtues** over the **passive** ones, is the cause of long life. The opposite of this will be the cause of brevity of life and the proximity of death. He considers the abundance of heat and moisture to be the primary causes—the "material" cause—while the dominance of the active over the passive is the "formal" cause, which Aristotle also noted.

The secondary and immediate causes are the proportion of the active qualities among themselves, the passive qualities among themselves, and the active to the passive. Likewise, all these things eventually relate to the interior—namely, the **heart**. For the length of life follows universally from the proportional <term>complexion: the specific balance of humors and qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a person's health</term> of the heart. 

Because of this, we see many men whose limbs are strong and healthy and whose virtues are powerful, yet they are struck by mortal illnesses and die before old age. Conversely, we see others who reach old age despite being the opposite, provided they maintain a balanced and consistent <term>regimen: a prescribed way of life, including diet and exercise, to maintain health</term>. From this, it is gathered that it is not impossible to believe that two men of the same temperate complexion, using the same regimen, may reach different ends: one reaches a good end, while in the other, "bad humors" are generated that bring about death. This happens because in a "bad" complexion, there is a fixed predisposition <note>original: "preparatio"</note> that causes this malice to be generated, even if we are ignorant of this predisposition. Ignorance of this predisposition is the cause of the infinite variety of such states. This, I say, is caused by the stars and the "Alchoroden" <note>the "giver of life" in medieval astrology, a planet that determines the length of life</note>, according to how these things are variably associated.

Next, it should be known that some have placed the cause of life and its length in a hot and dry region; others in a multitude of blood; some in the size of the body; and others in the "spirit." They claim the causes of death and brevity of life come from the opposites of these. All these people depart from the truth of Aristotle and his commentators. 

A hot and dry place is not a cause in itself, since life is measured by heat and moisture, and "hot and dry" is scorching and destructive. It only aids longevity "by accident" <note>a secondary, unintentional effect</note> insofar as dryness prevents <term>putrefaction: the biological decay of the body's tissues</term>. 

Nor is a multitude of blood the cause, because an increase in strength does not necessarily follow a multitude of blood, nor does weakness follow its decrease. It is only a cause insofar as blood contains heat and moisture, which is the essential cause of life. Similarly, the size of the body does not cause it in itself, but only "by accident," insofar as a large body contains much heat and moisture. If that were the case, then a horse would live longer than a man.

Nor does it happen because of the <term>spirit: a refined, vaporous substance that carries life and sensation through the body</term> as some have wished to say. They claim a "thick and dark" spirit, being scanty, shortens the lives of many through a lack of nourishment; while a "plentiful and windy" spirit works by great blowing out; and a "subtle and modest" spirit, prone to venting, shortens life like a lamp ready to be extinguished. They also speak of a "moist, turbid, and cold" spirit due to its impure wateriness. But the spirit is not the primary cause; rather, it is the moisture proportioned to the heat, since the spirit is generated from moisture and heat. Specifically, the spirit is generated from the vapors of the humors and their subtlety according to another complexion in which heat and moisture are preserved. As it says in the sixth book of *On the Utility of Parts*: "The spirit is a vapor of tempered blood."

Because of this, it must now be understood in some way what **death** is—the opposite—along with its causes. Death is the extinction of the "innate heat" by the drying out of the moisture or by putrefaction. 

In this description, a twofold death is touched upon: 
1. **Natural death**, through the consumption of the <term>radical moisture: the fundamental, life-sustaining fluid that everyone is born with and that slowly dries out over time</term>. Concerning this, it is said in *On Death and Life* that it happens in extreme old age without sadness. For it is an entirely imperceptible withdrawal of the soul, which is nothing other than the ultimate dominance of coldness and dryness over the natural heat. 
2. **Innatural or violent death**, the principle of which comes from the outside, especially from <term>marcor: a wasting away or withering of the body</term> or some other accident. In this, a great injury of the senses is perceived along with sadness, which is nothing other than the corruption and withering of the moisture and, consequently, the heat. 

Therefore, corruption comes to an individual in two ways: either **naturally**, when the natural heat consumes the natural moisture so that cold and dryness come to dominate; or **accidentally**, as when superfluities <note>wastes or excess fluids</note> accumulate in the body during digestion, through which nature is unable to discern the pure from the impure. From this, infirmities happen to the person, and the passive virtues dominate the active ones, leading finally to a disproportion of the primary principles among themselves and their relation to the heart. It is also seen that, according to Aristotle, both natural and accidental death sometimes follow when the power of the heart and lungs to "vent" <note>breathe/cool the heat</note> fails, which is followed by the extinction of the natural heat. 

Regarding this, it must be known that all agree that a **hot, moist, and temperate complexion** is the longest-lived, since in such people the causes of life are found.

It distinguishes between natural death (the gradual drying of radical moisture) and accidental death (illness or injury).</summary>
