...the more perfect one mentioned before. But they differed as to which of the two would be of longer life. For Haly, along with many of his followers, hearing perhaps the words of Avicenna <note>original: "Au."</note> who suspected that the causes of life are placed in heat and moisture, held that those having this order are longer-lived. As he denotes the degrees of longevity thus: 

The constitution <term>complexio|The specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a living body</term> of the **shortest life** compared to the others is cold and dry. 
Next is cold alone. 
After that, dry alone. 
Next, cold and moist. 
Then hot and dry. 
Next, moist alone. 
After that, the equal <note>temperate</note> constitution. 
And finally, **hot and moist**, provided that heat dominates the moisture and it escapes putrefying diseases. 

And for this reason, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> praised a hot land near the sea for longevity, because of the thinness of the air and its heat. And he praised the hot and moist constitution, which turns out to be twofold: one indeed is natural from the moment of creation and is laudable; the other, however, is accidental and blameworthy, being quick to rot. The invalidation of this position will appear in what follows. 

There were, however, some who held that the **temperate** constitution is longer-lived. Responding to Haly, they say he compares the hot and moist constitution to the imbalanced ones, which has already appeared false from the order of life’s duration assigned by him. 

Regarding the truth of the matter, it must be known that the temperate constitution turns out to be longer-lived than the others—the tempering of which would be according to the second or fourth mode noted before in Distinction 18. I say this one is longer-lived and more opposed to death, not only compared to the other imbalanced ones, but even to the hot and moist one, because it prevents drying out or putrefaction. 

And before he builds this by reason, he first explains the word of Avicenna saying that life consists of heat and moisture. For this reason, note that since heat and moisture are relative—for they are seen to carry a certain relationship—some strive to prove the equal constitution is the primary one, biting at the ancients for omitting it. For as shown in Distinction 18, an imbalanced thing cannot be said to exist or be known except through the temperate, since the "straight is the judge of itself and of the crooked," according to the first book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle, De Anima</note>. 

And therefore, whatever constitution, whether simple or composite, is only perceived in relation to the temperate one, which Avicenna intended to place under "hot and moist," as is more expressly drawn from Avicenna's speech in this treatise. This relationship of heat and moisture refers to the constitution as balanced in weight. This is what falls into the common exposition of those saying life stands in heat and moisture: because everything living stands out as hot and moist compared to the non-living. 

What was sent before is confirmed first from the mixture of elements. For whenever the miscible parts are mixed in a more perfect and equal way, that mixture is of longer life. Because when the active <note>hot and cold</note> and passive <note>moist and dry</note> qualities are truly counter-balanced, the struggle persists equally longer, and consequently, so does life. Such a thing occurs in the temperate constitution, but not so in the hot and moist. For because of the strength of the active heat and the susceptibility of the moist, a more vehement struggle breaks out and victory <note>the exhaustion of the moisture</note> is swifter.

---

Still, let reason be gathered from the harmony of the soul with the body, from which life follows. For according to Plato and Damascenus <note>John of Damascus</note> in the Aphorisms: the constitution of an animated body is 

-> according to the figure of a number, i.e., the proportion or likeness of a harmonic number. <-

Whence musicians like Pythagoras and Timothy called the harmonic motion of the soul with the body "human music." This musical proportion and consonance is found more in the temperate constitution than in others, since the principles of their joining are further removed from the excellence <note>dominance</note> of the joined contraries. 

Again, from the causes of life denoted: because life does not stand by just any moisture and heat, but by moisture proportioned to the heat. For the active qualities have to dominate over the passive ones with an abundance of heat and moisture, and be measured more by quality than quantity, so that the active ones have a proportion over the passive ones among themselves, and the passive ones one to another, and finally both to themselves, and at last, as has been said, to a third, namely the heart. This is found in a more perfect way in the temperate than even in the hot and moist. 

Which is confirmed: because "like joined to like," just as fire in fire, incites to fury, according to the *Problems* <note>Aristotle's Problems</note> and the *Aphorisms* and the *Natural Secrets*. This happens in the hot and moist constitution, but not in the temperate. For in the hot and moist, a manifold excess of moisture and heat grows. And first indeed in the generation of the human constitution, according to the word of Isaac <note>Isaac Israeli</note>, he places the hot and moist in the third degree of such a hot and moist constitution, such as the <term>sanguine|The blood-based temperament, considered naturally hot and moist</term> one, in which the moisture exceeds the heat, since it is proportioned to air which primarily possesses moisture and secondarily heat (Distinction 12). 

For they are "sons of the moisture," according to Balyabates <note>likely Al-Battani</note> and Isaac. Thus, since heat is added triply to heat, and moisture to moisture—and especially since moisture in this constitution exceeds the heat—it will fall into "fury" and be exposed to putrefaction especially, since that is caused by heat and moisture. This is not so found in the temperate constitution, since the moisture is sufficiently proportioned to the heat. 

Furthermore, from the proportion: because in *Problems* V, in a temperate constitution all parts of the body run together in equality, so that when one is healed, the others are healed, and when one is hurt, the others suffer. Because of this, a great harm does not occur to it as easily as to others. Indeed, by injury, life happens to be shortened. 

Likewise from the "habit" <note>body type</note>: because it is best to be "well-fleshed," i.e., moderately so, so that it is neither fat nor thin. For thus it can reach a long old age (Aphorisms, Section 2). This is the temperate constitution in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's Ars Medica</note> and according to Haly and Avicenna. 

Again from the operations: for those that are more perfect, such as the stronger and longer-lasting ones, belong to this constitution. For action made the form known. But such things are found more in the temperate constitution than in others. Which denotes a longer life for this one, because of the more diligent mixing of the miscible parts and the principles of life in the temperate constitution than in others. 

Likewise from the restoration of what is lost: that life is longer which more readily obeys restoration, since everything living here needs it, because of the innate heat continuously consuming the moisture. This is the temperate, and more so than the hot and moist, because in it the regime of restoration is intended either through like or through contrary; not indeed through like as the temperate...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate from the previous page, specifically focusing on the medical and environmental factors—such as "complexion" (the balance of qualities) and geography—that determine a long life. It cites Galen's *Ars Medica* (the Tegni) and *On the Preservation of Health*, as well as Aristotle and Hippocrates, to argue why the temperate complexion is superior to the hot and moist one.</meta>

...for when in the change that occurs according to hot and cold—since these are the most active qualities—fear arises regarding governance through "similars" in Book 6 of *The Preservation of Health*. For they fear lest excessive heat, increased by its own multiplication, should associate itself with cold; likewise with extraneous moisture, especially since one cannot arrive at that which is certain. If it were so, then science would be like that of Asclepius or Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of healing; the author implies a god-like or perfect level of medical certainty</note> in the third book of *On Generation*. For this reason, according to Galen <note>original: "Ga."</note> in the complexions in which heat exceeds cold, whether simply or mixed, whatever he might write as a difficulty in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*, a foundational medical textbook</note>, it is safer to lean toward the side of preservation through contraries <note>The medical principle of *contraria contrariis curantur*, or treating an excess with its opposite</note> than toward the side of likeness through similars. The other guardians of failing health seem to observe this as well in distinction 116. 

Nor can a complexion endure with an extended life through these contraries, because a more violent restoration would be induced by the opposition, since all nourishment is initially contrary to the thing nourished, as stated in the first book of *On Generation*, the second book of *On the Soul*, and the third book of *Complexions*. Because of this restoration, moisture is more quickly rendered "watery," and thus it becomes a cause of death. This does not happen to a nature that is not so imbalanced, because it must be governed through "similars," and because the distance and opposition of the mean <note>the temperate state</note> to the extremes is less than the distance of the extremes to each other. And even if there are many contraries from the mean to the extremes, they are nevertheless less excessive. The mean also stands out as having a stronger virtue in rare cases. 

Furthermore, from the perspective of reduction: for all complexions are judged based on how they deviate from it. Wherefore in the *Tegni* and in *On the Preservation of Health*, they teach that one should be reduced to the temperate state. This is done for no other reason than that they might participate in a longer life. For the science of medicine seems to be primarily ordained for the production of life, as is apparent from Haly <note>Haly Abbas, a Persian physician</note>. 

Again, from the perspective of region: because a temperate region is conducive to longevity of life, as if by touch. This third proposition <note>original: "affōz tētia"</note> is contained between two circular lines, both running directly from East to West. One of these passes toward the South over the island of Hippocrates <note>original: "ypocra."</note>, now called Lango <note>The island of Kos</note>; the other passes over India <note>original: "kindia"</note> toward the North. The distance between these places is about 400 miles. Or it is the region which is under the equality of the day, according to Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note> especially, as distinction 67 shows. The same is true of the complexion and the region. 

Also, from the part of death: that which is more exposed to consumption and extinction is of shorter life. Such is the case with every imbalanced <term>sanguine|The "hot and moist" complexion</term> person, both because of this passivity and the decay of activity; for since more moisture induces extinction and suffocation, it is prone to consumption. The <term>choleric|The "hot and dry" complexion</term> is prone to an excess of heat. The <term>phlegmatic|The "cold and moist" complexion</term> is prone to a deadly extinction by cold; the <term>melancholic|The "cold and dry" complexion</term> also follows these. But these two are the cause of brevity of life; however, nothing of the sort is found in the temperate, as has appeared. 

Again, to a temperate complexion and a natural origin, death ought to be "sweet" and more natural, provided a suitable regimen is followed. This is the death that occurs through consumption <note>natural aging</note>, for it retards those things that are putrefactive and violent more than the others. 

This is proved by the final sensory testimony: for we see that those who are hot and moist, or "sanguine," go gray quickly and rot around the brain, so much so that even when a small imbalance occurs to them, they promptly flow with catarrhs <note>nasal discharge or mucus</note> and head-colds, as is evident from the *Tegni*. This does not happen in a temperate complexion. For the aforementioned people are more exposed to putrefaction because of superfluous moisture, and thus to "violent" death and desiccation. And so they face natural death because of the consumption of this moisture; for this complexion is especially exposed to dissolution, according to distinction 117. 

From these points, it is finally concluded that the temperate complexion—not only compared to the other imbalanced ones, but also to the hot and moist one—is longer-lived. Regarding the first point, it must be said that it is true when comparing these complexions to the remaining imbalanced ones, but not as shown in relation to the temperate one. That this is the opinion of Galen is clear from the continuity of the sixth book of *On the Preservation of Health*. From this, the discourse is taken up: for when he determined the regimen of the temperate complexion, he said he would next determine the regimen of the "failing" ones, which is also clear from the explanation of the complexion which he immediately joins. 

To the second point, it must be said by way of interruption: and if Aristotle <note>original: "Ar."</note> somewhere said that a hot and moist complexion would be of longer life, he either inferred it in relation to the imbalanced ones, or he included the temperate one under the "hot and moist" label according to the custom of the ancients, as seen in distinction 18. And similarly, it must be said regarding a hot and moist region, for which it is true through a balanced hot and moist proportion. 

When it was added that in a hot and moist complexion, heat and moisture flourish more, this must be denied <note>original: "interimēdū"</note>, because the moisture in it was shown to be excessive and disproportionate to the heat, so that it is either quickly dried out or rapidly becomes putrefiable. 

To the other point, it must be said according to some, perhaps, that digestion <note>original: "digō"</note> does not happen from heat and moisture, but through heat and dryness. Whence in Book 13, it is said that digestion is preserved by dryness with heat. But because this seems to repugn the sayings of the wise, it is believed by many that the text might be corrupt, containing dryness only in a small amount. Or perhaps he wished to allude to the speech on accidents in Book 6: "Digestion, if it has a temperate dryness, is such as if the nourishment were moist," whence digestion happens through dryness, namely, a temperate one. For superfluous heat dulls moisture; it is also opposed to the homogeneity of not a few foods, which is most powerful for digestion. And therefore children cannot digest hard things, but young men are able to do so. Digestion also happens through tempered heat and moisture, and in general, as has been shown, digestion shows this. 

To the other point, it must be said that this does not happen in the hot and moist, because although in it the moisture seems to be tempered by heat more slowly, yet in the succeeding time, the heat is restored with virtue by the moisture more than in a temperate complexion. Likewise, as was shown after the age of consistency <note>adulthood</note> and especially in old age, more superfluities grow from the overabundance of moisture in this complexion than in the temperate one. 

To the other point, it must be said that this does not suffice; for it is not, as was seen, that heat and the privation of superfluities alone are present; rather, moisture and a tempered state are necessary. Furthermore, although the moisture of this [complexion] is present, yet it is not from the beginning of birth in sufficient quantity or power to resist the consuming heat, which is sharpened and strengthened by dryness. 

To the other point, it must be said that although cold and dry resist each other...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the nature of the human "complexion" (the balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities). Having previously discussed environmental factors, the text now focuses on the "radical" or innate complexion of specific organs—particularly the heart—and begins a debate (Difference 22) on whether this fundamental constitutional makeup can ever be altered during a person’s lifetime.</meta>

...to putrefaction; however, by accident, as in the digestion of this moisture, the superfluity of putrefaction—which is to say, the cause of death—departs. Furthermore, this complexion resists death by consumption the least; and therefore, according to Haly <note>original: "baly"; likely referring to Haly Abbas (Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi), a famous Persian physician</note>, a shorter life is assigned to it. To the other point, it must be said that this is true in the complexion of a non-living thing; but in that of a living thing, the aforementioned argument does not contain the truth. Regarding the other point, it must be said (as will be seen in distinction 24) that the heart can be considered in two ways. One way is materially: as it is a mixture of elements of a hard and solid composition, so that it can continuously resist the movements and shocks of the pulsations without harm, and so that it may defend the very thin, subtle, and extremely hot spirits within it from dissolving. In this sense, its complexion is cold and dry, which is indicated by its difficult digestion; the semen is also materially cold (distinction 24). In the other way, it is considered according to its formal being, which is by reason of its innate heat and the radical blood <note>A vital fluid thought to be the fuel of life</note> contained within it, as well as the spirit generated in it through motion and agitation; and in this sense, the heart is very hot and slightly dry, as will be shown in distinction 25. To the other point, it must be said that the moisture which directly resists consumption—through which life remains—is more "airy" rather than "watery," such as that of fat or lard. For they are called "moist" equivocally, since one is life-giving, while the other is the opposite, being rather cooling and suffocating. And this is what must be said regarding the rest.

## DIFFERENTIA XXII.

It is shown that the innate or radical complexion cannot be changed. First, because a body according to such a sign or cause remains the same in all ages of life. Furthermore, in the same place: it is in no way possible to make the solid parts of the body—the truly solid and primary parts—more moist. As Damascenus <note>John of Damascus, or perhaps the medical author Mesue the Elder</note> says in his *Aphorisms*: "the natural complexion is separable in terms of its proximity, yet it is inseparable." And in the *First Principles*: "each individual has a proper complexion, in which it is impossible for another to be associated with it." Furthermore, the same author teaches in the *Treatise on Minerals*: "it is not possible for one complexion to be turned into another." Again, by reasons: because that which is naturally and essentially within something cannot have its opposite within it, just as heat is essentially in the nature of fire; hence its opposite [cold] cannot be within it. In the *Categories* and the second book of *Ethics* <note>Referring to Aristotle</note>: "no natural thing becomes accustomed to its opposite." For even if a stone were thrown upward ten thousand times, it would never acquire the habit [of rising], but always falls downward. Such is the case with the innate complexion, as nature itself testifies.

Furthermore, if complexion—according to Galen <note>original: "Ga."</note> in distinction 17—is a substance, substance does not change, since there is no "physical motion" within it (proven in book 5 of the *Physics*), nor does it change according to "more or less." Furthermore, if complexion is a habit or a disposition, in this too there is no motion, but only in "passion" and "passible quality" (proven in book 7 of the *Physics*). Therefore, it cannot be changed by the motion of the heart. Likewise, in the *First Book on Foods*: "If you boil a bean for three days, it is not possible for you to remove its windiness <note>original: "flāmationē"; refers to the gas-producing property of beans</note> from it, because it is in its own proper substance, and not due to a lack of boiling." If, therefore, flatulence cannot be separated from the bean, much less can the natural complexion be separated from other more perfect and elevated things. Furthermore, Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus (Ishak ibn Sulayman al-Isra'ili), a 10th-century physician</note> in the first book of *Fevers*: "natural action is never destroyed except when the separation of soul and body occurs." Therefore, neither is its instrument, such as the innate complexion, destroyed. Again, morals caused by complexion do not seem to undergo change; as told by Haly concerning an old man with a warm heart, who wore the clothes of the righteous and spoke virtuously with strangers, but when he returned home, returning to his natural character, he was as savage as a wolf among his servants and family. Whence the *Proverbs* (chapter 30): "nature always acts as long as it exists"; some are bold there, others are always silent. Therefore, the complexion can least of all be changed. On the contrary, in the 8th book of *On Governance* and in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*</note>, in the chapter on falling: "a dry temperament in the time of the growing age is turned into cold and dry." Furthermore, Damascenus in his *Aphorisms* says that "from the change of the stars in longitude and latitude, both vices and natures and customs change." Likewise, distinction 15: "Complexion is of quality; but in quality, the motion of alteration is located, since it arises from the same." But whatever has motion essentially is moved and changed from one thing into another. Again, if it is possible for a hectic fever to be of the third type, it is possible for the innate complexion to be changed, since that fever lurks in the solid members; but it is both possible and necessary for this to happen sometimes; therefore, the innate complexion can be changed.

Regarding the first point, however, it should be known what a complexion is and what an innate or radical one is, as seen in distinction 17. By "change" of it, I mean the loss of the former and the raising of another in its place, by which the body is disposed and instrumentally governed as a living thing. Regarding the second point, it should be known that three views have been expressed on this question. Many say that the innate complexion can be changed in no way while life remains. Others, directly opposing the former, want it to be changed entirely. Some, however, have chosen a middle path, posing that it is changed according to "act" (which is its operation), but remains according to "essence" or "first act" (which is the form or potentiality); this is to say that the complexion lurks in "habit" when it is unable to come into "act" (which is the operation). Those of the first view strive to prove this with authorities and reasons; it even appears in the speech of Boethius in *The Consolation of Philosophy*: "It is impossible for a natural thing to be separated from the body except in the separation of the soul." Such is the complexion. They also cite the aforementioned statement of Isaac. Again, they affirm it because complexion is caused by a certain and defined proportion of the elements; but this cannot be changed while life remains, since it stands as the sole principal instrument. The defect of these arguments will appear more clearly in the third point to be discussed; nor can their motives stand.

Whence, in response to that point of Boethius, it must be said that a "natural thing" is twofold: for one is that which stands as the subject or an inherent property, and inseparably accompanies the principles of the species of that natural thing—such as the soul and "risibility" <note>The capacity to laugh, often used by scholastics as the defining "property" of humans</note> in a man, and heat in fire—and it is impossible for such a natural thing to be separated, except in the corruption of the subject.

The author explores the "middle path" view that while a person's behavior or health might change, their underlying essential nature remains the same.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the stability and mutability of the "complexion" (the functional balance of qualities) in living beings. The previous page established that while certain organs like the heart have a fixed material nature, their formal or functional qualities might be subject to change. This page explores whether a person's fundamental constitutional type (sanguine, melancholic, etc.) can shift during their lifetime due to age, environment, or habit.</meta>

There is also another natural thing which follows further from material principles, namely **complexion** <term>complexio: the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a person's physical and mental constitution</term>. For it is the form of a mixture, and those things which follow after the **complexion** likewise belong to the same nature. Although a living thing's nature cannot be changed beyond certain defined limits while life remains—such as the human **complexion**—it does nevertheless change within those limits.

Regarding the next point, it must be said that the proportion of the **mixture** <term>mixtio: the blending of the four elements</term> admits a great diversity of "more" and "less," just as the passage of time denotes different ages. Furthermore, the **complexion** that qualifies this specific proportion of the elements of the **mixture** extends so broadly that a variety of extremes can be found within it. For we see a greater distance between the **sanguine** <term>sanguineus: a constitution dominated by blood, characterized by warmth and moisture</term> and the **melancholic** <term>melancholicus: a constitution dominated by black bile, characterized by coldness and dryness</term> in childhood—if we do not wish to deny their outward appearances and functions—than between the state of the same individual in the final stage of decrepit old age compared to their childhood, or from a state of **wasting** <note>original: "marasmate"; referring to marasmus, the natural drying out of the body in old age</note> compared to the same. 

However, those who say that the **complexion** is changed according to its "act" (its current state) but not according to its "potential" or "essence," strive to prove this through the previously cited Damascenus <note>Likely referring to Janus Damascenus, a name associated with the physician Mesue the Elder</note>. He argues that the natural **complexion** is separable in terms of "proximity" but inseparable in "act." They wish to interpret "act" as the primary capacity or the secondary potential—that is, the natural power within the category of quality. They use the analogy of water, saying that its "actual" coldness can be separated from it (by heating it), but its "potential" coldness cannot, since it is naturally inherent to it. 

To these people, it must be said that Damascenus's words must be explained thus: by saying it cannot be separated in "act," he denotes the "latitude" <note>The range or spectrum of health within which a person can vary without dying</note> of the human **complexion** while life remains. Because it is separable according to "proximity"—that is, it comes very close to the extreme limits assigned to the human range—it may cross them, as was said, into a state of "not being healthy." Or perhaps he means that the **complexion** itself exists in "act" through proximity; for its "act" is not perfect and excellent, because it is only a mixture, but rather it is "remiss" or weakened. Yet it is not entirely separated from that excellent "act," but departs from it in relation to the nature of those things being born, whose nature stands out as potential. 

Or it must be said that his opinion, as it sounds on the surface, is not held at present. What they say regarding the "second way" is also not valid, as has already appeared: for a certain degree of **complexion** does not follow the proportion of the **mixture** of elements so inseparably as heat follows fire. This is because it is composed of formal principles, not just material ones, as happens in the **complexion** which emerges as the form of the **mixture**. 

Similarly, when they say the "innate **complexion**" remains in potential, they either mean a "secondary potential" (which is the primary act or form), and thus there would be two **complexions** within one final substantial form—which is absurd, since for every single substantial form of the whole, there is only one **complexion** that mediates and perfects its operations. Or, they mean a "primary potential" entirely separated from "act," like an infant’s potential for military service. And in that case, the innate **complexion** thus changed would not exist in such a potential, nor could any operation ever be performed through it; for what exists only in potential is not a unified **complexion**. Potential is not yet a "being" in the true sense. 

Furthermore, by the same logic that they concede this **complexion** is changed from a "secondary act" and becomes a "primary act," by that same path, through such continuous mutation or alteration, it would eventually be changed from the **complexion** placed above that act until it is entirely destroyed in its subject. Just as we see "whiteness" destroyed and turned into its opposite, "blackness," after many intermediate alterations. 

Regarding the third point, it should be known—though it may seem strange to many—that the innate **complexion** can be entirely changed. For this reason, know that a human **complexion** cannot remain the same. According to some, following <margin>Galen, Book 8</margin>, the result is a set of extremes, of which four are simple: hot, cold, dry, and moist; and four are composite: such as hot and dry, and so on. All of these are "distempered" <note>Out of balance</note>, either absolutely or in some respect. In the middle of these stands the "temperate" state. From these, a person can be changed gradually from one into another through appropriate homogeneous intermediate stages. For example, when a "symbolic" <note>shared</note> quality is found in both, such as moving from **sanguine** to **choleric** <term>colicus: dominated by yellow bile; hot and dry</term>, and from this to **melancholic**, and from **melancholic** to **phlegmatic** <term>flegmaticus: dominated by phlegm; cold and moist</term>. 

But to move from one extreme to the opposite extreme, because of the disproportion of their natures, perhaps it cannot be changed except by passing through the intermediate substances. For that which shares a quality <note>original: "ssymbolum"</note> is much more easily transformed than that which shares little or nothing, as is said in *On Generation and Corruption*. Hence, a **melancholic** person—due to the disproportion and the great distance from the **sanguine** type, and the continuous loss of moisture from the beginning—finds it most difficult to acquire a **sanguine complexion**, especially once childhood has passed. However, changing into a "simple" quality is easier because of the equality of one of the properties, rather than changing into the opposite extreme. 

Subsequently, the opinion of this position is supported by the authorities and reasons of Galen. First, indeed, it is said in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Ars Medica", a foundational medical textbook</note>: when a hot and dry **temperament** <note>original: "crasis"</note> falls, it is converted into cold and dry. Furthermore, in the same place and in Book 6 of *On Simple Medicines*, it is taught that "dyscrasias" <note>original: "discrasias"; bad mixtures or imbalances of humors</note> that have slipped can be reduced to a temperate state. Hence he says that this science corrects innate "dyscrasias"; such teaching would be useless if an innate **complexion** could in no way be changed. 

And Haly <note>Haly Abbas</note> says that the fourfold behaviors and **complexions** of men, and all other virtues, are changed according to any of these things, such as air and region. Again, it is proven by the example of the girl nourished on **aconite** <note>original: "napello"; wolfsbane, a deadly poison</note>, who as an old woman could overcome poison, as noted in Book 4, chapter 10 of the *Regimen of Princes*. And in the book *On Plants*, it is said that a poisonous plant born in **Persia**, when transplanted into **Egypt** and Israel, was made edible. Hence, in the book *On Accidents*: a tree transplanted from **Persia** to **Egypt**, which was deadly while in the soil of the **Persians**, was rendered harmless in **Egypt**. For its bad quality was changed into a good one. The same is said regarding the perfection of nourishment. 

Furthermore, concerning air and water, "Custom is a second nature." An example is given of women who sharpen and lengthen the heads of infants so that they might appear more fierce for war; eventually, nature followed the custom, so that nature now produces such heads in infants by itself. 

It is also shown by logic that the **complexion** varies. For heat feeds upon the **radical moisture** <note>The vital fluid or "lamp oil" of life that we are born with</note> in different ways. Since we were all produced in the ultimate "sliminess" of moisture (as stated in *On Simple Medicines*), the innate heat continuously consumes this moisture by feeding upon it...

...dries out the **moisture** <note>original: "buidū," a common scribal variant or OCR error for "humidum"</note>. From this, it is necessary that even the **radical complexion** <term>radical complexion: the primary balance of qualities one is born with, rooted in the "radical moisture" that fuels life</term> is transformed into a cold and dry state once its principles are changed. This is especially true according to those who argue that this moisture is **unrestorable** <note>medieval physicians often compared radical moisture to the oil in a lamp; once burned, it could not be replaced</note>. For this reason, many deny that an innate state can be changed back and forth; however, what should be said regarding this is shown in the 112th distinction.

Furthermore, we continuously observe a transformation from the action of heat upon the moisture according to the **ages of man**. For age itself is not the cause of this transformation—as some superficial thinkers have estimated—but rather it is the effect created by the proportion of heat relative to the moisture. In this way, the innate, altered complexion is transformed. Indeed, a change in the effect proves a change in the cause. Therefore, it is said to be impossible to return the **solid parts** <term>solid/spermatic parts: the dense tissues of the body, like bone and membrane, believed to be formed from seed and unable to be regrown if destroyed</term> to a more moist state.

Furthermore, if the complexion did not change, then since the **virtue** <note>vital power</note> and the soul do not grow old (as stated in the book *On the Soul*), life could be perpetuated indefinitely, provided that proper administration was maintained. Again, if the complexions of the principal organs did not influence one another through their mutual interactions and preponderance, a total complexion would never result that was different from them—which goes against the teachings of the **First Principle** and **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, the 10th-century Persian physician</note>. Nor could an equal complexion occur in the three types of **hectic fever** <note>an "ethical" or "ethic" fever (febris ethica) was a fever that settled into the solid tissues or "complexion" of the body</note>, which does happen. Hence, in the first book of the *Fevers*, a bad complexion corrupts the principal complexion. And in the *Colliget* <note>The "Book of Generalities" by Averroes</note>, it is said that a total good complexion can be changed by a bad one into something unnatural; otherwise, a diverse or depraved complexion could never be found, all of which would be ridiculous to physicians.

On the other hand, it is absurd to propose that something which is highly alterable or changeable—such as the complexion—should not eventually be altered or changed altogether, continuously and gradually, into another quality. For complexion is a **passion** <note>a state of being acted upon</note> and a passible quality, in which it is proven in the seventh book of the *Physics* that alteration properly exists. It even undergoes "more" and "less," having a contrary, and it is a passion that is continuously altering and casting off from itself.

Likewise, actions and dispositions testify to this. For we perceive the failing dispositions of certain men, not rarely moving away from their original selves, as when those who were **sanguine** become **melancholic** or **phlegmatic**. We see the forms or qualities of the body transformed into one another: such as fleshiness into fatness, or a healthy composition into an emaciated thinness. In the same way, colors and all other things of the body change to such an extent that even **character** <note>mores: habits or moral disposition</note>—which usually follows the formal principles of life—is frequently seen to be transformed. Hence Haly says in his commentary on the first book of the *Quadripartitum*: character becomes manifest in the age of maturity, and when these traits appear fully formed, it is very difficult to change them; however, in childhood, we can change them more easily. Otherwise, the science of ethics, which is ordered toward this goal, would be in vain. All these things demonstrate that the innate complexion necessarily changes. Nor is it only the "flowing" or acquired complexion that changes, but eventually even the truly innate one, since it causes or receives the change of all such things and yields to it.

Regarding the fourth point: to the first argument, it must be said that even when the **six non-natural things** <term>six non-naturals: environmental factors like air, food, sleep, and exercise that doctors managed to maintain health</term> are administered in the most proportional way, a certain continuous natural inclination always remains so that the body might stay as it was formed from its principles, as discussed in the 10th distinction. In this, however, there is a 

---

wide range of gradual **latitude** <note>a "latitude" refers to the span or spectrum within which a quality can vary without changing its fundamental nature</note>. It is found according to "more" and "less." For the innate complexion remains as such even while it is gradually changed according to each age. Therefore, the reasoning includes the opposite no less than the remainder, since the "complexion of an age" is nothing other than the varied transformation of the innate complexion resulting from the proportion of heat to moisture.

If it is said, according to **Hippocrates**, that once a habit of distancing is abandoned, the face finally returns to its original state (as also mentioned by **Boethius** in *The Consolation of Philosophy*), it must be said that either the transformation was not perfectly induced, or that it was caused by the surrounding environment; but once the strong influences that induced the long faces cease, the habit ends.

To the other point, it must be said that although a thing may be dry due to its fixation and the weak impression of the moisture—meaning it cannot be changed back, as has been declared—this does not mean that it cannot be changed into any other complexion. Rather, it is more an illusion of the observer. Hence, it must be said that the **spermatic parts** <note>solid tissues like ligaments and bones</note>, when they have been perfectly dried and hardened as in old age—and this because of the alteration of the complexion and the loss of moisture along with heat—cannot be moistened again, and no regression can occur. Like others, they turn irreversibly into a state of decay. This is why another translation says the dry members of the body that are truly dry and hard cannot by any means be made more moist than they are; it is sufficient only to guard them so they do not dry out too quickly. This will be explained further in the 112th distinction.

To the next point, the answer is already apparent. To the following, it must be said that it would be true in a **punctual complexion** <note>a complexion existing as a single, fixed point</note>, but it has a latitude within itself that is not small and is capable of receiving change. For such a state exists at one time, but in another, it varies continuously, until finally another state close to it arrives. From this, the internal parts would either acquire such a complexion or, conversely, would not die or become firm. However, this does not happen suddenly, for nature does not tolerate sudden mutations. This might occur as will appear further in the following distinction.

Or it might be said that it is possible for the complexion to be changed, yet it is not necessary for every complexion to change completely. For change is twofold: one is indeed "immense," beyond certain denoted specific limits—such as when a **melancholic** changes into a **phlegmatic**—and the other is small, as when a person becomes more or less melancholic within their own limits. The first kind is not necessary but possible when the causes of change are administered. However, there is one necessary transformation: that which tends toward the cold and the dry, toward which everything that lasts long enough must necessarily incline.

To the final point, it must be said that by "complexion," he meant the reason of the substance, or the thing itself along with what the subsequent things indicate. For these things are not perceptible because the **species** <note>the fundamental type</note> changes, but they are **accidents** <note>non-essential qualities</note> and properties. The stripping away of these—such as vapor, color, weight—or at least their diminution, is not impossible, because the form does not consist in these. For complexion is an accident. To the next, it must be said that this is true unless something hinders it, even in those things which are inanimate. But in animate things, and specifically the rational soul...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the nature of the "complexion"—the specific balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—and whether it functions as a stable habit or a temporary quality. It also initiates a new debate (Difference 23) regarding whether two individuals can ever possess the identical physical temperament.</meta>

...the dregs come out. In these, there is no passion or motion derived from the generator, but rather from the **soul** <note>original: "aĩa," abbreviation for anima</note>, which can, through gradual habituation, be changed into a middle or contrary state. For inanimate things do not properly receive "habituation" through action.

Now, regarding the **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific blend of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a person's constitution</term> of which we speak, it exists in inanimate things, but in the soul it is also "discretive" <note>meaning it allows for discernment or is distinct in its operation</note>. A similar thing must be said regarding that which is generated.

Regarding another point, it must be said—as shown in Difference 17—that complexion is not a **habit** <term>habit (habitus): a stable, ingrained quality that is difficult to change, like knowledge or a virtue</term> or a **disposition**, but is rather a **passion** <note>here meaning a "passible quality," something that can be acted upon or changed</note> or a "passible quality." Or, it may be conceded that it is a habit or disposition, such as heat and cold, since they say something exists more in a state of "having been changed" than in the act of "being changed" or altered. It should be said that although in a habit or disposition there is no motion *per se* or primarily, there is nonetheless motion by accident and from the generator.

Regarding another point, it should be said that **Galen** <note>original: "ga."</note> does not mean an impossibility, but rather a difficulty. For if "windiness" <note>gas or flatulence</note> cannot be excluded from beans in a certain amount of time, it might be excluded in another or longer time. For it is difficult, just as it is difficult to change a thin person into a full-blooded one, or a tempered one. Or perhaps "windiness" is more deeply inserted into beans than a complexion is into a body.

Regarding another point, it has already been seen which natural things and actions can be destroyed while life remains, and which cannot. Regarding another point, it must be said that since certain **accidents** <term>accidents: non-essential properties of a thing (e.g., color is an accident of a person, while "rationality" is essential)</term> follow the **matter**—such as the blackness of **Ethiopians**—while others follow the **form**—such as the "ability to laugh"—the former are more permanent. Character traits follow the formal principles more so than the material ones. The complexion, however, consists of principles that are indeed formal and do not change entirely except after corruption <note>death</note>. Hence, the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the famous 12th-century philosopher</note> in the first book of *On the Soul* says:

->The limbs of a lion do not differ from the limbs of a deer, except because of the diversity of the deer's soul from the lion's soul.<-

And this is also manifest in individuals of the same species, and therefore their characters are different. It is also gathered from Book VI that "proper accidents" of the form are the cause of the multitude <note>the diversity of individuals</note> which are recognized in the morality of individual men, because in man many individual species or proportions are found. For man is the ultimate purpose in nature. Hence, in his proportion, he excels all others; for all grades of being are found in him in some way. And for this reason, he is called a **microcosm** <term>microcosm: "little world"; the idea that a human being mirrors the structure and complexity of the entire universe</term>, as recited in the 8th book of the *Physics*.

### DIFFERENCE XXIII.

Whether two or more individuals can have the same complexion is shown here. Because in Difference 21, it is stated that it is not impossible to believe that there are two men of one and the same equally tempered complexion, and so forth. Furthermore, in the first book of the *Canon* <note>the medical encyclopedia of Avicenna</note>, it says that every species on the habitable earth has a complexion proper to itself. **Galen** <note>original: "Palin." likely an OCR error for Galenus</note> says many are sanguine or choleric.

There can be many medicines that are hot or cold in the first or second degree of their primary quality. Likewise, physicians posit equal heat in a child and a youth, even with different dispositions and times. Furthermore, in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Art of Medicine"</note> and in the book *On Preserving Health*, it is taught that distempered complexions should be reduced to tempered ones, which would not be achieved unless they achieved a total likeness to them. Furthermore, take a certain hot liquid and place it in two vessels that are equal in every way; the heat will be identical in both. So it is with complexions. And if someone is of a hot nature for ten years, and then another person of a cold nature reaches old age and becomes cold, while the first reaches a hot youth, they will have similar heat during this transition, as the more intense heat of one is diminished and the more relaxed heat of the other is intended <note>increased</note>.

Furthermore, the causes are the same or similar, and so are the effects, since they are proportional. But the causes and effects of this can be such that they are the same—as the sperm, the blood, and the menses, and in the same place and with the same [astrological] ascendant. **Galen** also says that habits, acts, and later results are the same as the prior ones, because the action of the maker follows the form; and these are sometimes found to be similar.

For **Augustine** recites in *The City of God* that there were two twins, one of whom was happy when the other was sad, one hungry when the other was full, one sick when the other was likewise, and so on. **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Y." or "Ypocra."</note> sought the cause of this and said it existed because they were produced and raised from the same father, a similar womb, the same nourishment, and the same regime. **Posidonius** the astrologer, however, when asked, replied that it happened from the identity of the stars, which answer Augustine took away from him and gave to Hippocrates. Likewise, **Quintilian** mentions twin youths such that when one fell ill, the other became weak, so that the physicians despaired for the health of both; considering them together, they entered into a counsel, deliberating that neither could escape death unless the other were killed—which their father proceeded to do.

From the histories, also in the ninth book: Two twins were seen by us in **Germany** so similar that none of us could recognize one from the other; but whenever we saw them, we were entirely confused as to their names, because we did not know which was which. And they spoke and sang as if with one voice, and loved each other so much that one could not be without the other for long. Therefore, the exact same complexion is found in two people.

The opposite of this is written in the first book of the *Canon*:

->Every individual must have a complexion solely proper to itself, in which it is impossible for another to be associated with it.<-

Furthermore, **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Abraā euēare," a famous Jewish scholar and translator</note>, whom I have ordered into Latin: it is not possible that the complexion of one is not different from the complexion of another by some decrease or increase; for two men cannot be found to be equal in their complexions, operations, and thoughts in every particular. **Galen** <note>original: "Pali baly"</note> says it is manifest that for the health of any body, there is a "latitude" <term>latitude: a range or span within which a quality can vary without changing the thing's nature</term>, which is different from the latitude in another body. For the health of **Zayd** <note>original: "zexdi"</note> is different from the health of **Amr** <note>original: "zambri"</note>; but health is the effect of the complexion, and where effects are different and dissimilar, the causes are as well. Likewise, in the first book of the *Theory*:

The quantities of complexions in bodies are written as infinite, just as if you mix equal parts of **cinnabar** <note>original: "ginnabar," red mercuric sulfide</note>—that is, burnt lead—**ceruse** <note>white lead pigment</note>, **ink**, and **orpiment** <note>a yellow arsenic mineral</note>. A certain color arises from these. If, however, you increase some while diminishing others, the colors perish and others arise. And thus, by mixing in diverse ways, the diversity of the generation of colors extends to infinity; which would occur in complexions as it does in colors. Again, according to **Porphyry**, every individual is said to differ from another by certain properties which are not found in the other.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the "complexion" (the balance of bodily humors), specifically addressing whether any two individuals can ever be truly identical in their physical and spiritual makeup. The text moves from logical definitions of individuality to biological and astrological explanations for human difference.</meta>

### [Column 1]

...is impossible, because there will be only one **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific mixture of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determines a person's physical and mental nature</term>, since it is something unique to the individual. Therefore, several individuals will never possess the exact same total complexion. 

Regarding the first point, it should be known that the **individual** <term>individual: in scholastic logic, the "atom" of being that cannot be further divided without losing its identity</term> is twofold. First, it is the "most specific species" <note>original: "spēs spālissima"</note>; see the 5th book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle’s Metaphysics</note>. It is not possible for a classification to go any further before arriving at individuals. Second, it is the "designated singular," of which **Porphyry** <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher whose "Isagoge" was a standard textbook on logic</note> says: An individual is that which is predicated of only one particular. Or, it is this specific thing in which the essential order of the categories does not descend further, since it is the **primary substance** <term>primary substance: the actual, existing thing (like "this man"), as opposed to the general category ("man")</term> from which no further predication occurs in the categories. 

The reasoning for this individuation is probably described by Porphyry through "prejudiced properties" <note>the unique bundle of accidental traits like height or eye color</note>; for these concern the designated particular. However, it is truer to say, as is elicited from the 5th book of the *Metaphysics*: things are the same in **number** <note>meaning they are the same individual entity</note> when their **matter** is one. For matter itself, existing within larger designated bounds, is the principle of individuation and the reception of form. 

In how many ways "similarity" is spoken of, and how a thing is the same quality despite its differences, will be explained in Difference 116. It should be noted, however, that similarity is twofold. One is **virtual and universal**, such as that of a cause toward its effects—like the **Intelligences** <note>the spiritual beings believed to move the celestial spheres</note> and further, the celestial spheres toward these lower things. For these spheres imprint their powers and perfections upon these things. The other is **real and contracted**, which can exist in four ways, just as the "one and the same" is spoken of in four ways (see Differences 3 and 59): by unity and identity of **analogy, genus, species, and number**. 

Therefore, one type of similarity is **analogical**, in which all things agree; for example, in "the hot and the moist," through which life exists (see Difference 21). More perfect things participate in this more profoundly and more actually, as is said in the *Book of Collections* <note>original: "v. collz," likely referencing the medical Compendium by Rhazes or Serapion</note>: that which is born is said to be more potentially hot. Another type is of **genus**, as it might be said that all humans are tempered compared to other things. In the first mode of equality, justice is served. For man is thus more tempered than all other generated things. Another type is of **species**, which occurs in many ways, since complexion can be more or less intense. Therefore, this similarity is either **broad, narrow, or middle**. 

A **broad** similarity is like one **sanguine** <term>sanguine: a temperament dominated by blood, characterized by being warm, moist, and cheerful</term> person to another, or one **phlegmatic** <term>phlegmatic: a temperament dominated by phlegm, characterized by being cool, moist, and calm</term> to another, in either sex. A **middle** similarity is like that of a sanguine man to another sanguine man, or a phlegmatic female to another phlegmatic female. A **narrow** similarity is when two individuals are not only similar in all these aforementioned things, but even in **accidents** <note>non-essential traits</note>, such as in their physical habits, colors, hair, birthmarks, actions, and morals. This happens most often in **twins**; hence, in the 9th book of the *History of Animals* <note>Aristotle's work on biology</note>, it is said that twins, because of their shared life, are frequently made similar. Upon what this similarity depends will be shown in Differences 37 and 48. Finally, the unity of **numerical similarity** is a certain precise, point-like quality within a precisely received quantity. 

What "complexion" actually is was seen in Difference 17. Regarding the second point, it should be known that some more unlearned people, hearing the first arguments superficially, have claimed that two or more people can have an identical complexion in every way. Their error will be wonderfully revealed in the third and fourth points. Regarding the third point, it must be known that two individuals can **never** possess the exact same complexion in every way, as the cited authorities persuade us. They can, 

### [Column 2]

however, approach this so closely that their habits, actions, and judgments appear to be similar or the same. 

This is built upon several reasons, taken both from those things that **precede generation** and those that **concur in the very act** of being generated and thereafter. First, from the book *On the Soul*: each thing has its own proper species and form. This species is **substantial**, but the form is the "quality-denoting" **complexion**. Unless <note>original: "ne s[econd]mo Ay." referring to Avicenna</note> Avicenna's sixth book [of the *Sextus Naturalium*] provides a superfluous distinction: if the form or species is "proper" (unique), then the complexion is its instrument, appearing immediately. 

Furthermore, the complexion is either the substance of a limb and its maker (as touched upon in Difference 17) or it is the instrument of the soul. If it is the substance, since for each thing there is a unique "being" <note>original: "esse"</note>, the form will also be unique. Thus, each individual will have its own complexion, entirely different from others. If it is the instrument of the soul: since nothing is more "proper" than a complexion, and for one form and one agent there is a single principal appropriated instrument, there will likewise be one proper complexion for each person. 

Furthermore, the principles and causes of different things are different and do not coincide, and thus the preceding conditions will be different. But the causes of complexion are three: one is **inferior**, another is **superior**, and the third is **middle**. 

The **inferior cause** is the sperm and the menses. These cannot be so identical that an entirely similar effect arises in different qualities. Because the **womb** <note>original: "matrix"</note> has two cavities, the sperm will either fall into one entirely or be divided into both, which rarely happens, since nature always intends what is better and distinct. And therefore, "form is that which divides, distinguishes, separates, and differentiates" (7th book of the *Metaphysics*). 

When, therefore, the "form" has been divided into the two cavities of the womb, the **sanguine** parts will begin to attract it to themselves after a space of six or seven days (see Difference 48). If the sperm falls into the **right side**, it is warmer and more vigorous than the left, because of the fuller irradiation of the heart into the liver. Also, movement begins on the right and is supported on the left, according to the book *On the Movement of Animals*. An infinite number of wombs will thus become pregnant. 

Furthermore, even if they were in the same cavity of the womb, one would be closer to the warm parts and the other to the cold, depending on whether it was higher or lower, in front or behind, more to the right or the left. 

The **superior cause** is the celestial aspect. One aspect exists over the right side and another over the left side of the womb, since they possess different **zeniths** <term>zenith: the point in the sky directly above a specific location; used here to show that no two spots on Earth receive the exact same astrological influence</term> on the celestial sphere. Similarly, the celestial influx and aspect will be different even if they were in the same cavity, since for every place and every thing placed, its own zenith and aspect are owed. It is impossible for two bodies to occupy the same place; hence, two needles, however thin, if joined together, have a different zenith and aspect in the heavens. Indeed, even a single grain of sand has its own star, according to **Mercury, Hermes, and Enoch** <note>references to the legendary founders of alchemy and astrology, Hermes Trismegistus and the biblical Enoch</note>. 

Therefore, it is impossible for the birth of one man to be assimilated to the birth of another as if to itself. For the heavens are not standing still in one way, nor will there ever be a single point of an hour that does not remove the proportion that was before it. Hence **Lucan** <note>Roman poet</note> says: "There stand the twin brothers, the glory of their fertile mother, whom the same womb brought forth with different fates." 

The **middle cause** is the "informative virtue" of the intellect...

...is called, having respect for both the lower and higher cause. For it is likened to the celestial powers, even though it is one thing in this person and another in that. Each nature requires its own specific efficient and informing power, and will have a different relationship to the higher and lower cause. One thing will seek an instrument in one way, and another in a different way, just as heat is different in the summer than in the heavens, as will be declared in distinction 48. 

Furthermore, **place** is the "immovable boundary of that which contains," <note>Aristotle, *Physics*, Book 4</note> with a due distance and proportion to the celestial sphere. But as place is, so does nature operate, according to the 10th book of the *Phleumon* <note>likely a reference to a specific medical or natural philosophy commentary</note> and the treatise *On Inspiration and Respiration*. The natures of matter are such as the places in which those beings exist. Hence, concerning the law: our nature is such as our region is. For **place** is a principle of generation, according to **Porphyry**, <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher often studied in medieval universities</note> just as a father is. And as much as nature gives concerning place, it gives just as much concerning the form appearing, as seen in the fourth book of *On the Heavens and the World* <note>Aristotle's *De Caelo*</note>.

But each thing has its own proper place. Since dimensions resist other dimensions, multiple bodies cannot occupy the same place. Therefore, they will have their own proper forms and generating properties, which cannot be found in another individual. 

**Again**, <note>original: "Palin"</note> once the body is organized by the power of the preceding soul and the **complexion**, <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, bile) that defines an individual's health and personality</term> a new, final, and completing form supervenes, such as the **intellective soul** in man, according to the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*. For "the intellect alone arrives from the outside" <note>original: "Solus intellectus de foris aduenit," a famous Aristotelian dictum regarding the human soul</note> at the last. Upon the introduction of this form, a new complexion is generated; not only is it different from the complexion of another individual, but it even supervenes as something diverse from the pre-existing state. 

For matter, along with form, is the cause of those things which come to be as accidents, as in the first book of the *Physics*. In these things, at the arrival of the intellective form—namely the soul—generation is perfected and finished, and a concurrence of accidents occurs. Yet that whole is transformed into another thing in an instant, reaching down even to the matter, so that it expresses the first [cause]. Therefore, why does it assist so many and such diverse things at a specific point in time? 

Furthermore, the complexions and all the body's qualities, as well as those of the soul, are altered and changed at the hour of birth by the present celestial signs, and specifically by the **Ascendant** <term>Ascendant: the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth, believed to govern physical appearance</term> and its lords, and the indicators of life mentioned in distinction 21. From these, the horoscopes provide sufficient indications regarding the stature of the body, its habit, color, and even the dispositions of the soul. 

But in that same hour, however brief, **twins**—about whom there has been much hesitation—cannot be born together, especially when the natural birth has occurred. In an hour, however narrow, it happens that the aspect of the heaven and the impression from it is changed, being one way in the prior moment and another in the posterior, as touched upon in distinction 10. Therefore, at almost any given point, the complexion varies at the time of the proper separation from the womb, when the infant proceeds from the hidden and opaque place into the manifest and the light. For although the variety here may be small, or perceived as minor, it is greatest in the celestial sphere; just as when water in a vessel is moved slightly, the ray of the sun falling upon it and its motion on a wall is moved a great deal. And because there is such a great change in the sphere, those who cast images <note>astrologers</note> strive to choose the most certain hour for the "pouring out" <note>the moment of birth or conception</note>. The individual complexion of someone changes; even for a short time it does not remain in the same point-like disposition. Hence, in the first book of the *Movements of the Heart* <note>original: "prio affōy" / *De motu cordis*</note>, I say the body is flowing and transformed in an instant;

the variation of one to another and the change will be more intense, however much the deceived senses judge them to be identical in complexion. 

Likewise, how could a similar or certainly the same complexion arise in two or more people, given the total diversity of the gradual mixing and the alteration of the complexions of the members and the functional organs—such as the whole body? Regarding the fourth point, however, to the first it must be said: Aristotle did not intend to say simply that two individuals can have the exact same point-by-point complexion, but rather according to sense and appearance. This is because there are so many preparations fixed in matter that we cannot know them through signs, which happens because of the infinity of preparations mentioned in distinction 22 and at the end of the first book. 

To the next point, it must be said: Aristotle speaks of the identity of complexion in terms of genus or species broadly; but this discourse seeks a precise and point-by-point identity. To the next and the one after, it must be said in the same way: for in any degree of quality, there exist infinite "mansions" <note>specific stages or levels</note> varying in more or less, as shown in distinction 139. 

To the other point, it must be said as changed in distinction 27. To the next, it must be said that **Galen** taught to reduce "distempered" states to "temperate" ones by a certain broad reduction, not so that they are made exactly similar, but rather in appearance and broadly. To the next, it must be said: the situation is not like a liquid that has been melted down and then distributed. The complexion of the human body is different, since it arises from the coalenscence of many things, and many degrees of mixing are found—as was touched upon—so that the perfect complexion of a human results. In these, it would be impossible to observe a similarity of all qualities. Nature does not arise like that liquid; or perhaps even the certain similarity of the quantity of the liquid received here and there varies because of the celestial figures impressing themselves in different ways. 

To the next, it must be said: such complexions are not innate, but rather acquired from a certain concurrence of time changed in turn. They are founded in different humors along with different aspects of the celestial sphere; for one of the humors is drier than the other. It would be impossible for two bodies to be equal in heat if one of them is drier, according to the second book of the *Colliger* <note>a medical work by Averroes</note>. 

To the next, it must be said: the causes are not similar except by a certain broad similarity, as touched upon. Similarly, the **Ascendant** [varies] according to the truth; for in any indivisible point of time, it changes, being different now than it was before, although the sense and even the astrologer may fail to discern it. **Geofar** <note>likely Jafar/Abū Maʿshar, the famous Persian astrologer</note> says in the *Introduction* that this is due to the indeterminacy of matter and the infinity of preparations proceeding from it. 

To the next, it must be said: the things mentioned before are not similar in every way and indivisibly, but they seem to approach it enough that the senses judge them to be similar in almost every way. For grieving and rejoicing, being hungry, and the like, are not entirely indivisible things; rather, a great latitude is found in them. Similarly, he did not say of the twins he considered that they spoke and sang simply with one voice, but that they did so with an "indubitable similarity," which allows for a range of difference.

# SECTION XXIII.

<margin>1</margin> **That the brain is hot is shown by Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus, a highly influential 10th-century physician and philosopher</note> **in his *On Diets*, where he testifies it is naturally hot and moist.**
**Furthermore,** since man is a **microcosm** <note>literally "small world"; the medieval belief that the human body is a miniature map of the entire universe</note>, he is produced in the likeness of the universe. In the universe, the higher parts (air and fire) are hot, while the lower parts are the remaining cold elements. The brain is the "superior" or highest part of the body. Since its nature is light <note>original: "leue," meaning low in density or weight</note>, it is proven to be hot, just as gravity indicates coldness. Again, according to **Haly Abbas** <note>a famous Persian physician</note> and the 12th book of *On Animals*, the brain is the marrow of the head. This is also stated in the section on the parts of animals. Furthermore, motion and sensation are produced by heat; for according to *On the Generation of Animals* and the 13th book of the *Problems* and *On the Soul*, nothing is sensitive without heat. But in the brain, many and powerful motions exist, and they proceed from it, since the beginning of the flow [of spirits] remains there at least instrumentally. Coldness, however, makes the **spirits** <note>vital fluids or "pneuma" believed to carry signals through the nerves</note> impure and dulls their motion and flow, making them sluggish, mortifying them, and causing paralysis. Additionally, hot, subtle, and mobile spirits abound in the brain, and these warm it. 
**Furthermore,** <note>original: "Palin." from Greek</note> the **seed** <note>sperm/reproductive fluid</note> drops from the whole body and especially from the brain, according to **Hippocrates** in *On Air and Water* and the 10th book of the *Problems*, which is indicated by the injury to the brain from immoderate sexual intercourse. Since seed is hot (according to the 4th book of the *Problems*), the brain must therefore be hot.

However, almost all philosophers and physicians feel the opposite, positing that the brain is cold and moist by nature; indeed, no one else doubts this. **Additionally,** the fact that it is soft, moist, and whitish testifies to coldness; and the brain is indeed such a thing. **Again,** the natural **complexion** <note>the specific balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> of every organ is similar to that which nourishes it, according to the 6th book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts*. But the brain, according to the greater part of its nutrition, is nourished by **phlegm** <note>one of the four humors, traditionally considered cold and wet</note>, as they say. **Likewise,** nature provides against the excess of any single thing; therefore, since the brain is vehemently heated—partly by the bright, hot spirits, partly by their great motion, and partly by the hot vapors sent up from the heart and the rest of the body—it was necessary for coldness to be present to temper this acquired heat. Therefore, it was necessary for the brain to be cold, so that it might temper that heat. 
**Regarding the first point,** it should be known that the brain is like the marrow of the head situated at the highest point of the body, divided into three or four **ventricles** <note>cavities in the brain</note>, veiled by two **meninges** <note>membranes covering the brain</note>, and is the organic initiator of flow and motion. Whence it is said in the *Introduction to the Theoretical Art*: **The brain** is more honorable and excellent than the other members of the body. For it is the root and, so to speak, the "furnace" of the rational soul, through which there is mind and discernment, and the origin of the [nervous] flows. **Regarding this in the first book of *On the Preservation of Health*:** The brain is a kind of house for the rational soul. According to the manifestation of its operations, it is the principle of the animal virtue <note>the "animating force" responsible for sense and motion</note> and the most honorable part of the body; though according to its essence, the heart is [more honorable]. The brain itself, taken as a whole, is divided into the membrane-like substance, the marrow-like substance, and the ventricles full of spirit. However, the substance described here as "brain" specifically refers to the marrow-like substance. As to whether it is hot or cold, and in what sense, this is discussed in the 15th section. **It is now assumed** that "hot" and "cold" are not used here to describe an absolute abundance of an element, but are used relatively—not as a potentiality, as when things encounter the body, but as an actuality. **This is compared in three ways:** either to the temperate state of its own genus (just as a man is called "temperate" within the genus of animals), or within a species (as Plato might be called "cold" compared to the temperate Socrates, while Aristotle is called "hot"). The brain is likewise called hot or cold in relation to some other temperate thing appearing in the medical art, or to any other circumstance, just as a man is compared to a lion. And here the discussion is about the comparison within the genus, not about the species or any specific circumstance. In this way, one and the same thing could be called both hot and cold. **The question therefore seeks** the true substance of the brain, and its heat or coldness relative to the average state of its kind, like the skin. 
**Regarding the second point, it should be known** that **Isaac** alone dared to pronounce the brain intensely hot. Although the brain is naturally hot and moist because it is of the nature of fats and marrows, it is **accidentally** cold because of the very cold air striking the head and the lack of flesh and fat existing on top of the head. For this reason, some have judged the brain to be naturally cold, saying it is like thick and viscous phlegm. They confirm this from its actions and sufferings, because they say they find that it weighs down the stomach in the digestion of food and weakens the appetite. **Those who seek to confirm their intention** follow the words of **Galen** in the third book of *On Food*: "When you wish to induce vomiting, give the brain [as food] after a meal." **This is also confirmed** by the actions of nature. The brain is the foundation of flow and motion; therefore, they show it to be cold and moist. For if it were hot, since its motion is very frequent, it would overheat and burn up the soul along with it. 
**By Isaac,** these [arguments] are refuted in two ways, both reasonably and through the medical art. **First,** although the brain causes the aforementioned harm to the stomach, it does not do this from coldness, but rather from its fatty, viscous moisture. Indeed, **Galen** interprets it this way: for cold water increases the appetite, while wine diminishes it; it also pushes food downward like air, while heat brings it upward. **By reason it is shown:** for **Aristotle** in his book *On the Natures of Animals* says that since the brain is the foundation of flows and motions, and these come from the power of natural heat, it is impossible for it to be cold. For coldness naturally closes and thickens the flow, puts it to sleep, and resists motion. **Likewise,** if the brain were cold, memory, imagination, and human reason would be taken away, since it is impossible for these to exist with coldness. **This is shown** when phlegm dominates the brain: memory softens, discernment slows, and reason becomes disordered. **From the words of Aristotle,** therefore, it can be well understood: that the brain is temperate hot and moist. Nature, however, strove to give it **accidental** coldness, lest its very frequent motion set it on fire. **In the *Particular Diets*,** some have judged the brain to be accidentally hot, but Aristotle in the book on animals said it was naturally hot and accidentally cold. We say, therefore, that the brain is naturally hot.

<summary>This page debates whether the human brain is naturally hot or cold, weighing the theories of Aristotle and Isaac Judaeus against common medical observations of the time. It concludes that while the brain's substance is naturally hot to support thought and motion, it is "accidentally" cooled by its position and external air to prevent overheating.</summary>
