On account of this, according to the second view, it seems that the more proper quality of the brain is "moist," according to **Galen** in the first book of *Complexions*, and others who place the brain closer to the skin in its degree of coldness than in its degree of moisture—for moisture elevates it more. Likewise, the sense of touch perceives a greater moisture in it than coldness. 

In the fourth discourse, it is said by **Avicenna** that the brain is the coldest body of all the members. Conversely, according to **Aristotle**, the brain is moister, just as the liver is. It must be said that the natural <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> of the brain is cold and moist; whence **Haly Abbas** says the natural complexion is such that heat and dryness are lesser, while cold and moisture are greater, so that they are slightly increased in it; thus the complexion of the brain is called "balanced." 

Some simply assert its preeminent quality to be moisture, and they answer **Avicenna** by saying the brain is colder than all other members in terms of its *effect*—for more <term>superfluities</term> <note>Waste products or excess humors, like phlegm</note> fall from it than from any other member of the body—but not in terms of its *essence*. And this discourse is indeed the talk of the <term>gilded ones</term> <note>original: "deaurantiū"; likely referring to those who offer flashy but superficial arguments</note>, just as the fruit of many other negligent readers is often found; thus they gather common gourds and unripe fruit together. 

Against these, in the 13th and 16th chapters of this work, it is said: for just as something behaves in its essence, so it behaves in its action. Therefore, I say that the more proper quality of the brain is coldness, since the brain is assigned to <term>phlegm</term> <note>The cold, moist humor</note>, and according to the 12th chapter of the first book of *Complexions*, this is what **Aristotle** seems to have felt in the aforementioned senses. 

But so that the solution of these arguments may appear, it must be said that moisture is twofold, as shown in the 12th chapter: one is *essential*, such as that of air, and such is the moisture of the liver; whence **Haly Abbas** says the liver is the source and origin of the moisture of the entire body, just as the heart is of heat. There is another moisture which is, as it were, *accidental* and acquired, like that of water, to which the moisture of the brain is proportioned. For the brain itself is the root and mine of watery moistures, which the aforementioned **Aristotle** touched upon; and touch perceives in it more coldness. For hot vapors and fumes seeking the brain are cooled beneath it; and if it becomes warmer in some parts because of this, yet because its own heat is weak, it remains cold in comparison to those ascending vapors, so much so that it allows them to be cooled and coagulated beneath it, and finally to liquefy into phlegm. Just as an <term>alembic</term> <note>A vessel used in distillation; the author is comparing the skull to a chemist's still where steam turns back to water</note>, though it is hot, yet cools and coagulates the hotter vapors reaching it, as **Haly Abbas** and the vapors carried into the second middle region of the air show. Therefore, it happens by accident that it is judged to be so moist.

Know also for this reason that the *material* complexion of the heart—which it took from the mixture of elements—is cold and dry; and therefore it is of a strong and compact texture, so that it seems to resist fire better than the other parts of the body. To this, moisture also assists, being then compressed into it, which was necessary to withstand movements, strikes, and heat. Because of this, a certain fat was placed upon it (though equivocally so called); it is itself of hard digestion and provides a more <term>melancholic</term> <note>Cold and dry</note> nourishment. Its *formal* complexion, however, is vehemently hot, declining toward a certain dryness on account of the heat of the **spirit** and its motion, although the blood tempers it. For of all the parts of an animal, it is at once the bloodiest and the hottest. For the heart falls little short of the dryness or hardness of the skin. 

The liver, however, according to the first book of *Complexions*, which is touched upon in chapter 21, and also in the *Colliget* <note>The medical encyclopedia by Averroes</note>: if the heart is dry as the physicians say, it seems to me that it declines toward moisture on account of the spirit existing in it; and it is generated from the blood of the arteries alone. The liver, however, is from the <term>menstrual blood</term> <note>In Aristotelian biology, the physical matter of the embryo was thought to come from menstrual blood, while the spirit came from the father</note>, according to the third book of the *Theoretical Medicine*. And it should be known that in the liver and the brain, there is no heat that is proper to their essence, except the heat of their similar parts; rather, the heat with which they perform their arts is of necessity transmitted to them from the heart, which is like matter to them. But the heat which is properly in them is like matter, according to the fourth book of the *Colliget*, and also from the benefit of the pulses. The liver is the primary blood-making organ of the viscera, according to the third book of *On the Parts*. Already indeed its matter is hot and moist, since it exists as coagulated blood, and likewise its form, which its action denotes. It is, however, more hot than moist, for it is further along in the degree of heat than of moisture, since it not only generates blood by its heat, but also other hot and dry things. Likewise, its form stands more in heat than in moisture. Nor is it the source and origin of the body's entire moisture because it is more moist than hot, but it is said to be so because the heart, being hotter than it, is the source and origin of all heat. 

Regarding the fourth point: what was to be said to the first argument has appeared. To the other, it must be said that there is some similarity of the "minor world" <note>The human body as a microcosm</note> to the "greater world" <note>The universe or macrocosm</note>, but it is not manifold. For every similarity does not "walk on four feet" <note>A Latin idiom meaning a metaphor or analogy isn't perfect in every detail</note> according to the Philosopher. Nor are the things above in the universe such as being hot, but bodies lacking quality, like the celestial spheres. Nor does everything light seek the upwards, nor everything heavy seek the downwards, but that which is moved by a generator (as seen in the 8th book of *Physics* and the 4th book of *On the Heavens and the World*), and not that which is moved by a soul. Since otherwise, a heavy thing might be driven upwards, or a light thing downwards. 

To the other point, it must be said that, as seen, the brain is called "marrow" or "fat" equivocally or as a metaphor. To the other: the movement and acts of the brain are perfected by much heat, and that in the brain itself, or in its spirits, there is heat which can suffice for its movements. To the other: here the *proper* complexion of the brain is sought, not that acquired from non-innate spirits, or motion, or other things. To the other: **semen** of itself is cold, since it is a superfluity, unless it is affected by the motion and the primary heats of the members. Whence, in the 4th book of the *Problems*: the seed is cold. Or, sexual intercourse weakens the brain more than other members because the brain is of a weak "weaving" and of a more feeble complexion, being composed of colder and moister qualities.

...it moderates the coldness. It stands as warmth compared to cold; such is the **spinal cord** <term>nucha</term> <note>From the Arabic 'nukha', this term was standard in medieval medicine for the spinal cord</note> in relation to the **brain**. Hence, it is said in the *Book of Parts* that the spinal marrow is continuous with the brain for this reason: so that it might warm it. For nature always devises an aid for the <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities</note> of each thing, placing one part's assistance so that the excess of one might be balanced by the other. 

Thus, in the same place, **Aristotle** says: Some believe the spinal cord is continuous with the brain, and therefore they share one nature. But in this they err, for the marrow of the brain is cold, while the spinal marrow is warm. This is indicated by its fatness <note>In medieval physiology, fatty or oily substances were associated with heat</note>. Moreover, the spinal cord acquired this complexion from the **heart**. Also, that which is the coldest of all particular parts is colder than the spinal cord; such is the brain said to be, according to the previous distinction. 

Furthermore, that which is warm is less cold than the brain—since the brain was previously established as cold—and that thing is the spinal cord, for it is marrow. Whence, among the inner parts, the name "marrow" <term>medulla</term> properly belongs to its substance. According to its nature, this is warm, as stated in the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*, which is also attested by its proximity to the heart.

Again: that which is near to a warm member is itself warm. But the spinal cord, throughout almost its entire length, is closer to the heart than to the brain; and the great arteries pass more through the back, in which a bounty of <term>vital spirits</term> <note>The 'pneuma' or life-force carried in the blood</note> and vital blood is contained. Every part is rendered warmer the closer it is to heat. Furthermore, <term>mucilages</term> <note>Thick, cold fluids or phlegm</note> are not found around it, nor do the flows of <term>rheum</term> <note>Waste fluids thought to be 'distilled' by the cold brain</note> run there as they do around the brain; for these things happen due to the brain's coldness. Because of this, the spinal cord is less overcome by coldness than the brain. **Galen**, **Haly Abbas**, and **Aristotle** seem to hold the opposite view.

Again: just as there is a proportion in things arising from other principal organs, so there will be a twofold proportion in those things coming from the brain. But the arteries, veins, and secretory vessels arising from the heart, liver, and testicles are less warm than their sources. The spinal cord, however, is born from the brain and stands continuous with it. Furthermore, the anterior part of the brain is less cold than the posterior, since the posterior is rarer <note>Less dense</note>, which is shown by the hair and the placement of the warm heart. For the heart lies in the anterior parts, according to the *Book of Parts*; and through the descent from it, the colder, heavier, and impure part of its nature is more inclined to descend. Its coldness is also manifested by its passage through the bone. The brain is located more in the front part, and the spinal cord in the back. Because of this, the spinal cord stands as colder than the brain. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known that the spinal cord is the messenger and deputy of the brain in the course of the back. For from it, the nerves originate laterally, which could not conveniently be born from the brain. 

The word "nucha" is a Greek <note>original: "dictio greca"; the author is mistaken, as the term is Arabic, but medieval scholars often attributed technical terms to Greek</note> word, taken from *nothos*, which means "back" or "spine"; it is also called the **spinal medulla**. Whence, in the *Book of Inner Parts*: That which is properly named "marrow," to which for the sake of distinction "dorsal" is added, just as there is "cervical" and "lumbar." Finally, everyone is accustomed to calling it simply the "dorsal" marrow, which is sent down from the brain through the vertebrae of the back all the way to the anus. For it is like a key or bolt binding the vertebrae. Therefore, in the second book of *On the Parts*, it is said that it alone requires binding because of the divisions; for through a ligament, it is made viscous and sinewy so that it may have tension. Whence **Avicenna** says in the same place: although the marrow is the foundation 

---

of the nerves, it nonetheless serves another purpose: for it is like a helping ligament of the vertebrae. And it is indeed less soft than the brain, especially at its end toward the tail. For the further it is from the brain, the more it hardens. 

Regarding its nourishment: like the brain, it is covered by two <term>membranes</term> <note>The meninges: the dura mater and pia mater</note>. That it differs from the brain was shown previously. Regarding whether it is warm, this is taken from actual observation; and because a comparison involves a standard, the same rule must be observed.

Regarding the second point, it must be known that **Avicenna**, in the place cited above, seems to feel that the spinal cord is not only less cold than the brain, but is actually warm, and of the same nature as the marrow of the bones. But in the second book of *Complexions*, he says the brain is moister and warmer, or less cold, than the spinal cord. Similarly, in the first book of the *Theoretical Medicine*, and in the first of the *Canon*, in the catalog of cold things, the brain is placed as having a more moderate coldness. 

Also, in the *Book of Nourishment*, he places it as having the same complexion as the brain. For it is <term>homogeneous</term> <note>Of the same substance throughout</note> with the brain and of the same nature. Whence, in the discussion of particular parts, the spinal marrow—compared to the marrow of the bones—is already cold and very moist, just like the brain. However, these two authors are speaking of the "potential" complexion in these places. But in the second book of the **Colliget** <note>The 'Kitab al-Kullyat' or 'Generalities of Medicine' by Averroes</note>, where its nature is pronounced, he speaks of the "actual" complexion, just as we spoke of the brain and likewise of the spinal cord. And because the nature of the marrow is from the nature of the brain, their benefits are the same. He held a middle path between **Avicenna** and **Galen**. 

Thus, some have felt it to be less cold than the brain. Others, truly colder. A third group has maintained they are of one and the same nature, because they consider the complexion of the brain and the spinal cord more materially, arising from the mixture of elements, where one stands for the other; or they looked upon them as being very common to each other, as **Avicenna** does briefly. 

Desiring to be associated with the others, I have distinguished them: both the spinal cord and the brain can be considered in two ways. Either as they arose from the elements, and thus the spinal cord is less cold than the brain; or according to how they are affected by some heating agent, such as the <term>spirit</term> or nourishment or something else, and in that way, it is more cold than the brain itself. Some, accepting this, wished to diversify the "innate" and "acquired" complexion, positing that the dorsal marrow is less cold than the brain by reason of its innate complexion. The brain, however, is colder due to the acquired complexion from the vapors and fumes sent to it. 

But this does not hold, since the members here obtain their "actual" nature, not according to their material production from the elements; for in that way, the "potential" complexion is considered. Rather, it is as form, power, and heat are contained within them. For every member, like the whole animal, has an "implanted spirit" which acts as the instrument of its power; otherwise, the heart would be composed of a cold and dry nature, though in its form it is the warmest of all. Also, the brain should be called cold more from its acquired complexion than its innate one, which is shown by the rheums and other cold things, with vapors and fumes cooling beneath it. Furthermore, a similar thing will be said on the part of the spinal cord: that it is colder than the brain from an "acquired" complexion because of its location in a bony, ligamentous, and non-breathable area...

Regarding the third point, it must be known that the **spinal cord** <term>nucha</term> <note>From the Arabic 'nukha', the standard medieval term for the spinal cord</note> is simply colder than the **brain** in terms of total coldness, according to three arguments: 

If its nature is observed more closely, for it participates less in the "heat of the soul" <note>original: 'calore animae'; the vital heat thought to animate living beings</note>. This is shown because that which is more affected by power and spirit is less cold; such is the brain, and not the spinal cord, since the brain is the principle—at least of the manifest animal power—and its furnace. 

Moreover, when a part is located opposite a warmer member, its coldness is reduced by that heat. But the brain is located opposite the **heart**, which is warmer than all other members, so that they might temper each other together, as **Aristotle** <note>original: 'Ax.' or 'Ar.' refers to Aristotle</note> concludes in *On the Parts of Animals*, and **Averroes** <note>original: 'Ax.'; here referring to the commentator Averroes</note> similarly in the *Colliget*, book two. 

Also, movement is perfected by heat, for heat itself is motive—in contrast to the previous distinction, where rest is considered cold of itself. But a more intense, multifaceted, and varied movement comes from the brain than from the spinal cord, since the spinal cord itself is moved by the brain; for the brain is the mover, not the moved, regarding the flow of spirits. 

Again: that member is cold from which many rigors and chills begin, especially in cold people such as women, according to the ancients. But that part is the posterior where the spinal cord is located, and not the superior and anterior part where the brain is; because of this, the spinal cord will be colder than the brain. 

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it must be said that the spinal cord, as formally shown, is not less cold than the brain, but more; nor is its duty to temper the coldness of the brain, but rather that of the heart itself, as stated. 

Regarding the series of arguments **Aristotle** introduces, it should be known that he and **Averroes** seem to argue there that the spinal marrow is not continuous with the brain; and therefore Averroes is explained thus: to many it seems that the brain is marrow and the principle of marrow, because the spinal marrow appears to be and is continuous with the brain. But it is entirely contrary to the brain according to its nature—that is, its <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry)</note>—as was said: that the brain itself should be marrow and its principle, because the brain is the coldest of all parts. 

And similarly, what **Aristotle** says should be explained: so that the phrase "those who err" refers to the idea of the brain and spinal cord being of one nature, and not to the fact of their being physically continuous. To the other argument, while the difference appeared to the author... 

To the other, it must be said that the spinal cord is not "marrow" properly speaking, even if **Averroes** seems to suggest it. For marrow in other bones is warm and moist, but here the term is used **equivocally** <note>original: 'equivoce'; meaning the word is the same but the definition is different</note>. Whence the *Colliget*, book two: The name "marrow" is said equivocally of bone marrow and that which is in the "pot of the head" <note>original: 'olla capitis'; a common medieval metaphor for the skull</note>, i.e., the substance of the brain. 

And we do not call it marrow except because it is so named by the common people. For the nature of the spinal cord, as said, stands apart from the nature of the brain. Whence, in the whole, the marrow found in bones is marrow, and another marrow is found in the spine; and that is the spinal cord, which is harder and drier than bone marrow. 

But hesitation arises about this, since it was said that the spinal cord is properly called marrow according to **Galen**, but according to **Aristotle**, it is named so equivocally. It must be said that "properly" was not applied in relation to true marrow which exists in bones, but by extension, which is why it is ultimately called the "dorsal marrow." 

That this is certainly not said literally but as a metaphor is found in the third book of *On Nutriments*: because the spine is contained by the bones along the back, and being similar in color to marrow, they call it marrow for this reason; and some call the brain itself by the same name. 

To the other, it must be said: although the spinal cord approaches the heart in some places, and even more so according to its physical position, it does not do so according to "virtue" <note>spiritual or functional power</note> like the brain, since the brain stands as the "chimney" of the whole body, receiving all its heats and fumes. Even according to position, the brain is near the heart, more so than the spinal cord in most parts. 

To the other, it must be said that mucilages and **rheums** <note>original: 'reumata'; fluids or catarrhs thought to cause illness</note> abound more in the brain than in the spinal cord, not because it is essentially true, but because it happens "by accident" <note>original: 'per accidens'; a logical term meaning a non-essential or secondary property</note>, as the previously shown difference demonstrates.

...is for the child. Regarding the first point, however, it must be known how much "age" includes: namely, that it is a **living disposition** <note>original: 'dispositio animalis'</note> that remains while the **temperament** <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of the four qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—in the body's members</note> of the limbs is attributed to natural forces, caused by the action of heat upon moisture, and measured in a temporal way by a certain influx. By this process, a person grows until they decrease and manifestly decline. This is indeed a sufficient definition, since it touches upon everything that belongs to the logic of age while excluding other things.

### The Nature of Age

It is well said that age is a "disposition," so as to exclude what some have said—that it is a "space of time"—which would place it in the category of quantity. In fact, age exists as a **quality**, just as the temperament to which it is attached demonstrates. Now, every genus and definition must belong to the same category, as stated in the fourth book of the *Topics*. Other things attached to natural things are joined to the temperament through intermediary means, such as sex, form or quality, and color—to which I also add **habit**, since habit is a kind of "second nature." With the addition of art, it is also called "natural." For the temperament is changed by habit, region, and craft, as noted in the first book of *Theory* <note>Likely referring to the *Ars Medica* of Galen or a similar foundational medical textbook</note>. 

### The Astrological Ages of Man

Finally, the distinction and causes of age are indicated in this description. For age is seen to be caused by a double agent: namely, extrinsic and intrinsic. 
- **Extrinsic causes:** First, regarding the twofold cause, it arises either from the impression of the planets upon the living body, or from the presiding authority, according as a person is suited for these or those civil acts. 

Regarding the first, there happen to be **seven ages**, just as there are **seven planets**. 

1.  **The Moon:** The first age is caused by the Moon. She is the governess of infants in the first four years—called the years of "nutrition." Astrologers first note these from the lordships of the "triplicity of the ascendant" before they judge anything regarding the newborn. This configuration is fitting: since the Moon is the lowest of the planets, and is vehemently moist and mobile, so at this hour the infant is disposed in soul and body. He receives the principle of life from this age, and as if from the Moon, he ascends toward the other planets. In conception, the process begins with Saturn and ends with the Moon. In this stage, the child requires moist and liquid food.

2.  **Mercury:** Above this occurs Mercury, the planet of reason, speech, and science. Therefore, the boy must be handed over to a master when he is **six years old** so that he may be taught. At that time, he easily receives every impression, since he is still like a **blank slate** <term>tabula rasa</term> <note>An Aristotelian concept meaning the mind is born without innate ideas, like a waxed tablet yet to be written upon</note>. Mercury governs the child for **ten years** (which is half of his "minor years").

3.  **Venus:** Then Venus leads. Because she is the planet of this world's delight and cheerfulness—such as gluttony and lust—she thus disposes the youth. Her rule concludes in a space of **eight years**, which is the number of her minor years.

4.  **The Sun:** Afterward, by a certain leadership of its own, the Sun rules in the fourth place, just as it holds the fourth position in the heavenly spheres. Because the Sun is more perfect and worthy than the other planets, the person born at this hour, having dismissed the things of Venus, desires to appear divine, feigning honesty and abstinence. The Sun remains for **nineteen years**, which are its minor years.

5.  **Mars:** Next comes Mars. Because this is the age of pride, magnanimity, and strife, the person is disposed accordingly.

---

For he fights to acquire things by any means, performing great works. In this time, many adverse things happen to those born under it. Mars dominates for **fifteen years**, according to its minor years.

6.  **Jupiter:** And then comes Jupiter, the planet of the future world, of peace and tranquility. Under him, the person repents for the things committed under the leadership of Mars, seeking the things of God and every good work. Jupiter governs for **twelve years**, which are its minor years.

7.  **Saturn:** Finally, Saturn occurs—cold, dry, deceitful, pensive, sad, full of labor and anguish. The person is thus disposed; for then illnesses and sadnesses most especially happen to him. Saturn governs the person according to the number of his minor years, which is **thirty years**. 

Thus, all these years gathered together yield **98 years**; for very few people pass 100 years. If they do pass that mark, they lose all their vital action; as if having surpassed Saturn, they return to the leadership of the Moon—which then leads not for only four years as before, but for **twenty-five years**, which are its "major years" <margin>according to Haly</margin> <note>original: 'baly'; likely referring to the astrologer Haly Abenragel</note>.

### The Legal and Civil Ages of Man

If, however, we look at it another way, as a magistrate joins civil acts, then there are likewise seven ages, according to **Odefredus the Jurist** <note>Odefredus was a famous 13th-century Italian jurist</note>:

- **Infancy** <term>infantia</term>: The first of the ages, defined as **seven years** for both male and female. Within this is the age of the "yearling" <note>original: 'anniculi'</note>, meaning one year old. 
- **Childhood** <term>puerilis</term>: From then until **fourteen years** in the male, and **twelve years** in the female.
- **Adolescence** <term>adolescentia</term>: Reaches up to **twenty-five years**.
- **Youth** <term>iuventus</term>: From then reaching up to **fifty years**.
- **Advanced Age** <term>gradevitas</term>: Extended to **seventy years**, in which men already receive exemptions <note>legal excuses from certain public duties</note>.
- **Old Age** <term>senectus</term>: From seventy onwards, which has no set end, except that the law presumes no one lives beyond **one hundred years**.
- **Dotage** <term>senium</term>: Also called the end of seventy years, lacking a certain term, for it concludes in death.

According to **Oribasius** <gloss>Book 5 of the *Aphorisms*</gloss>, men are at their peak <note>original: 'ptici' / 'practici'</note> mostly from **eighteen years up to thirty-five**, because then they are fit for much exercise—so much so that the **Law of the Romans** <note>original: 'lex rōnoy'</note> calls this the "proven age." For those whom the ancients wished to test for war, they took at eighteen years. From fourteen to eighteen, they were occupied with lighter exercises; from eighteen to thirty-five, they were sent to arms; from thirty-five to sixty, they were **tribunes**; from sixty onwards, they completed their military service and received the dignity of their honor—that is, they were "sent across the little bridge" <note>original: 'per pontem parvum'; a reference to the Roman 'sexagenarios de ponte', meaning men over 60 were excused from voting and public duties</note> and were allowed to do what they wished.

The age caused by intrinsic factors varies in two ways: either it is taken strictly, as the living being tends toward perfection or soon falls away from it into its opposite. Thus, there are two terms for age: the **increasing** <term>augmastica</term> and the **fully grown** <term>paugmastica</term>...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of "age," moving from a general definition to a specific categorization of the life stages. It compares the systems of Aristotle, Galen, and the Hippocratic Aphorisms while debating the "complexion" (the balance of heat and moisture) of children versus youth.</meta>

It is perceived from the beginning; indeed, even in old age, a complete failure of strength does not appear openly. Or rather, it is accepted more broadly, which happens in two ways: either from a natural cause or an unnatural one. If from the former, then four ages stand out, as the previous description of them indicates: **adolescence** or **childhood**, which ends at the 25th or 30th year; and **youth**, which finishes at 35 or 40. **Old age** or **advanced age** is completed at the 55th or 60th year; and from here, empty **senility** <note>original: 'senium'—the final stage of life characterized by decline</note> extends to the end.

The specific ages are separated into five according to **Aristotle** <note>marked as 'A.' in the text</note>: infancy, the planting of teeth, the concussive stage <note>likely referring to the start of vigorous physical movement</note>, the spermatic stage <note>the onset of puberty and fertility</note>, and the age of strength. The third [book] of the <term>Aphorisms</term> <note>the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates, a standard medical authority</note> also mentions these. There is also another age called **consistency** <note>original: 'consistentia'—a stage of peak stability where the body neither grows nor declines</note>, located between youth and old age, of which one is often noted to be contained under the other.

Know also that "adolescence" is found to be used in two ways: one according to the specific properties noted by **Aristotle**, the other for puberty. Hence, in the first book of *Theory* <note>likely the *Ars Medica* of Galen, often called 'Tege' or 'Theorica'</note>, childhood is said to last up to 15 years, and adolescence is said to last up to 30 years—as in the third [book] of the **Aphorisms**. Boys begin to reach puberty at 14 years. Likewise, childhood is twofold in *Theory*: one is universal, lasting up to almost 30 years; the other is partial adolescence, which appears to be named from 15 years onward up to 30. Childhood is also placed between puberty and youth by **Galen** in the third book of the **Aphorisms**; but in *Theory*, it is the third stage. Infancy is placed as extending to the third year; from then to 14, one is a child; and finally, there is adolescence.

Similarly, **consistency** is twofold: one preceding youth, in which growth pauses—the second appearing in the state of health—and the other following youth, in which the body and strength are preserved from falling, at least from the apparent decline already touched upon. I estimate that no small amount of chatter <note>original: 'garrulitatem'—scholastic debate or confusion</note> is brought about by this diversity, perhaps due to a lack of specific names for these stages.

If, however, an unequal age is dispensed by an unnatural cause—such as when it is disposed by certain illnesses or others—then the ages will perhaps be shortened from the previous ones. For **extraneous heat** shortens life; hence, in the sixth book of *On the Preservation of Health* <note>original: 're. sa.' for 'De Sanitate Tuenda' by Galen</note>: whatever bodies have a sickly disposition in their very generation, these never reach old age, or if they do reach it, they eventually have one or another long-lasting illness. Therefore, according to this intention, the third [book] of the **Aphorisms** writes that youth ends in the fifth seven-year period (at 35 years) and old age in the seventh seven-year period (at 49 years).

And know that because heat—whether natural or mixed with the unnatural—affects the moisture of nature in different ways (varied by many natural, unnatural, or extraneous factors), the limit of age should not be announced simply. Hence, in *On the Preservation of Health*, book six, it is said that it is not possible to give certain ages by a fixed number of years as some have done, except by a general range. And therefore, in determining the ages, they said they end in "so many years," or with an addition such as "around" or "almost." This happens because one <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of the four qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—in the body</note> is longer-lived than another, such as the temperate and sanguine ones, and so on. <term>Difference</term> 21. <note>original: 'dra xxi'—referring to a section or chapter in a medical encyclopedia</note>

---

The period of a temperate person is interpreted [as follows]: when it is said that it "grows, stands," and so on, it signifies the previously mentioned fourfold distinction of ages. Now, a child is "agonos" <note>Greek: ἄγονος—sterile or without seed</note>, that is, without the power of generation, as recited in the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*; it is also said in the [book] of *Complexions* that a child is an "imperfect animal," while a youth is its [perfected form]. There is indeed a twofold temperament: one in which the qualities of the elements are combined in the best way; another which can rise to nobler acts, rising from the first. Thus, that which truly is "temperate" is that in which these two exist most perfectly. And because this implies a comparison, the rule of it should be understood as explained in the following <term>Difference</term>.

Regarding the second [point], it must be known that some have said youth is more temperate than childhood regarding the integrity and perfection of form, with more constant strength. However, regarding things external to the body, children are more temperate, since their heat is found to be soothing and sweet, while the heat of youth is unpleasant and harsh. I accept the first of these, but regarding the second—that it could not stand—it will be wondered at in the third and fourth [points]. For this "soothingness" and sweetness of the child's heat exists as a distempered state, not a small one in relation to the balance of reason—as truth compels us to say. <term>Difference</term> 19.

Therefore, others have said these can be referred either to the components or to the acts by which youth are more temperate, since their actions are more perfect, as has been shown. If we look at the spontaneous principles, this happens in two ways: either regarding the first principles of generation, like sperm and blood—and because these are purer in the child than the more natural ones in the youth, children are thus more temperate than youth—or regarding their mixture, in which case children and youth are equal, as physicians feel regarding heat. In passive qualities, however, they differ significantly, because children are vehemently moist, while youth already participate in some dryness. But while the first point is granted to them, it cannot stand: both because (as will be shown) children are sufficiently distempered in moisture regarding the principles of generation, and also in heat; and perhaps those principles are not always purer before than after. <term>Difference</term> 112. Nor is it true that a complexion or composition is more temperate or equal just because it is purer, or that something is never found more in the effect than was in the cause. Since the final principles of generation are caused by the mixture of elements, they cannot be assigned another nature from the elements themselves, since they receive all their power from them; for where one thing exists for the sake of another, the one is in both. How children and youth are equal in their root will be wondered at in the following <term>Difference</term>.

Know also that a defect in understanding arises from listening superficially to the series of **Galen**; for it seems such a listener might prefer children to youth in temperament. Regarding the third point, it must be known simply and without distinction that youth are more temperate than children, as **Aristotle** clearly felt throughout, as has been touched upon. Hence, in the second book of *Complexions*: the state of all animals consists in the middle of extremes, reaching neither the ultimate of dryness like old age, nor the moisture and softness [of childhood].

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on the stages of human life, specifically focusing on the transition from childhood (infantia/pueritia) to youth (iuventus). It expands on the physical and mental peak of "youth," defined here as the age of perfect "temperament" or humoral balance, typically occurring between the ages of 30 and 35.</meta>

...existing as many things do; just as the age of infancy is such, so too is **youth**. This is shown through the operations and occurrences inherent to the substance of the body. And first, indeed, concerning the most similar things: for that body which most closely approaches the highest **temperament** <note>The "temperament" refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which determined a person's health and character.</note> will be more temperate than another. This, however, belongs to the youth and not the boy. For it is certain that the body nears this balanced temperament at the age in which **growth** reaches its end. This is first proven by experience: for this reason youth stands out. Hence, according to the first book of *Theory* <note>original: "theorice"—referring to Galen's *Ars Medica*, a foundational medical textbook</note>: The age that reaches the state of youth is that in which the body's growth is completed and its decline takes its beginning. The status of this age is **35 years**; for the body is in its steady state from the 30th year up to the 35th. This is according to the rhetoricians; but until what time does **Haly** <note>original: "baly"—referring to Haly Abbas (Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi), a famous Persian physician whose works were translated into Latin</note> perceive the parts to be increasing? He agrees with the fourth book of *Theory*, which **Galen** indicates in the previously mentioned first proposition.

But the *Problemata* states that men grow until the 30th year. This is also indicated by experience itself, when it writes that the peak of growth exists around the 30th year. Wherefore, from these combined views, it follows that age cannot be defined by a strictly fixed number of years, as was also touched upon by Galen. Therefore, let those who would correct Haly be silent—those who wish the body to stand simply at the 25th year; their reading of the text is corrupted, though three other versions note the addition of ten years. It is further confirmed because the body in the age of youth, although it closely approaches a perfect temperament, is considered **hot and dry**; nevertheless, it stands apart from the boy’s temperament by declining toward heat and moisture. Since, therefore, the boy is more moist than the youth, he departs further from the aforementioned temperament, at least in his passive qualities. Since, as has been touched upon, he is in a state of prior moisture, he is less temperate than the youth, even if they were equal in heat. Likewise, the total equality or **proportion** of the body is demonstrated by the **complexion** <note>In medieval medicine, the "complexion" was the physical manifestation of the humoral balance in the body's organs and limbs.</note> that is greatly caused by it.

For at that hour when the most perfect and elegant equality of the limbs is found, the same state emerges; but this is at the time of youth, when all the limbs are proportionately extended and completed. According to every four-fold nature of proportion, this is why experience calls it the **age of beauty**. Hence, at the same time, youth is the age of health and completion. This is also seen from the operations of the reproductive and official organs.

Whose operations are more perfect and less impeded, theirs are the more temperate bodies, since their temperament is argued from the actions they produce. Such indeed are the actions of a youth, not a boy. This is shown separately concerning the **soul**: for it is known both in the apprehensive powers—whether external or internal—and in the motive powers. In all these, the youth exceeds the boy and even the old man. But if, perhaps, it is argued that the elderly judge more perfectly than others (according to the seventh book of *Physics* <note>Aristotle's *Physics*, Book VII, which discusses how the soul becomes wise through rest and stability</note>), from which it is understood that the elders/priests <note>original: "presbyteri"—used here both for age and status</note> judge better than youths; on the other hand, the 30th *Problem* states: "Old men have more intellect, but youths, being in a state of motion, are quicker to learn."

To the first point, it must be said that this happens by accident, due to the disordered motion and passions existing in the earlier ages. Hence it is immediately added in the same place: for much perturbation exists regarding their motions. Therefore, no one chooses youths as leaders, because it is not established that they are prudent, as they are subject to passion.

->**PROPORTIO**<- <note>Proportion</note>

To the other point, it may similarly be said that since there are two instruments within us—the **hand**, which is the "instrument of instruments," and the **intellect**—just as we are not immediately powerful with our hands, but later as age proceeds, so the intellect of natural things does not come to us immediately, but most of all in **old age**. For then it profits best, unless it is hindered by something else of nature. For our understanding does not happen without the **phantasia** <note>The "phantasia" or imagination was considered the faculty that processed sensory images so the intellect could understand them.</note> being informed by the "intelligibles" <note>Abstract concepts or ideas</note>; we cannot perfectly acquire a supply of these before old age. Or it must be said that it is different for the intellect than for the other powers of the soul: for all others are weakened by old age, but the intellect alone "grows young," as stated in the third book *On the Soul*. This signifies that it is least tied to a physical organ. Or this instance is not distracted by small things, and it gives the apparent cause there why youths learn more quickly: because they know nothing, in a way. But when we know something, which happens in old age, we no longer seem to learn in the same way. In the same manner, the **vital operations** in a youth are stronger, as the **pulse** shows; for the pulse is more valid in him than in other ages, as stated in the *Introductory to the Pulse*. And according to the strength, so also is the breath.

Similarly, natural acts are more effective in the youth. The **generative power** emerges more vigorously; and if perhaps the adolescent suffices for frequent sexual intercourse, it is because of his softness and the superfluity of his power, which is decided by the acts of a dual virtue: the nutritive and the augmentative. Hence **Damascenus** <note>John of Damascus, an influential theologian and writer often cited for his views on nature and the body</note> says: "In children born to young parents, the primary members are naturally strong and healthy." This also occurs in the **digestive power**, for they are better suited for the digestion of all foods than children. For this reason, in the sixth book of *On Accidents*, it says: "If we wish to make a comparison of digestion in children and youths, we find both are equal regarding moist and liquid foods, but unequal regarding dry ones, because youths digest that which is hard better." If you say this is not by reason of their complexion—that they digest hard things perfectly because such things are not "homogeneous" <note>In this context, foods that match the body's own humoral makeup</note> to them—whereas for youths they are proper to their nature: it must be said they are not homogeneous to children because children are too moist and soft. Youths, being less "remiss" <note>relaxed or weak</note> in their temperament, will be more perfect in the digestion of hard things, aided by their sharpened heat and because their superfluous moisture has been dried out. The **augmentative power**, which is more imperfect in children, brings about the opposite, as will be declared. Again, from the "accidents" <note>In a philosophical sense: outward characteristics or signs</note>: those are the best temperaments which hold the middle ground between hardness and softness, roughness and smoothness, abundance and scarcity of hair, and extreme colors; and in whom all beauty is found in the equal proportion of the whole body and all organs. These are found in youths and not children, since children are superfluously soft and smooth, tending too much toward a white color, and are less decorous in their proportionate appearance since they are still imperfect. This is also noted by the superfluities existing in them, as in their brains; since they are doubly moist, as stated in the second book on the *Movement of the Pulse*, superfluities abound in children...

<meta>This page continues a scholastic medical argument regarding the physical qualities of various ages of life. It specifically addresses the debate over whether childhood or youth (young adulthood) is the most "temperate" (balanced) stage of human existence, citing authorities like Galen and Isaac Judaeus. The text is organized in a two-column scholastic format common in university manuscripts.</meta>

Therefore, they require very large channels <note>original: "fistole"; referring here to the bodily passages or vessels that carry fluids</note>. Their urine also abounds in **sediment** <term>hypostasis (the solid matter that settles at the bottom of a urine sample, used by medieval doctors to diagnose internal balance)</term>. This is not the case with young men. In children, a great deal of "crude" <note>undigested or raw</note> humor collects. The body, however, is measured, as it is written; but no child has a small amount of sediment. Perhaps someone might object that there should be much sediment in them because a single action of the belly cannot sufficiently provide for both nutrition and growth simultaneously, especially regarding the thicker parts. But that argument does not hold, because their food is finally digested in the **third digestion** <note>In medieval medicine, the first digestion happened in the stomach, the second in the liver, and the third in the individual tissues of the body</note>, the waste of which stands out as sediment. Or perhaps one might respond that the preceding digestions cannot correct the final one. 

**Difference XXIX.** But since the urine of young men more closely approaches the urine that denotes a balanced temperament than that of children, this indicates a better **crasis** <term>crasis (the specific mixture or "blend" of the four humors in an individual)</term> and health in the former. This is also taught by the fact that food taken from young plants and animals provides a balanced nourishment. Furthermore, external forces affect a young man less than a child. Even if one or two qualities in children were found to be more "perfect"—which is perhaps impossible in itself—it does not destroy the argument, but rather asserts the comparison: that young men are more temperate than children or any others. For only things of the same kind <note>original: "univoca"</note> are truly comparable. According to the following distinction, the temperament will be judged by the dominant quality. From this, it is concluded that young men are more temperate than children in every way.

However, a doubt arises concerning this. If **youth** is the temperate age, then no age would be both "hot" and "dry," and thus one of the four primary combinations of qualities would be missing. Therefore, some have wanted to raise an objection regarding the temperate age, as **Galen** <term>Ga. (Galen of Pergamon, the most influential physician of antiquity)</term> seems to suggest when he posits a balance of all things. But this is not valid, as will be seen in chapter 66: for that fourfold combination of elements must be maintained equally in all things.

But it must be said that although the age of youth is temperate by reason of "balance of weight," it is nevertheless **hot and dry** compared to childhood, and hot compared to other ages. Just as the skin is temperate when compared to the balance of the whole body, but is cold and moist compared to the heart, and hot and moist compared to bone. 

Regarding the fourth point, and first: it must be said that **Galen** does not intend to say there that the complexion of children is more temperate than that of young men, as many wrongly interpret. For there, comparing a temperate complexion between two extremes to the other distempered ones, he says: "This will be **well-tempered** <note>original: "eucrata" (from the Greek eukratos)</note> according to the state of the times, and not least in its time according to its decline, as is appropriate for them." For the body has its best mixture [crasis] according to the age of children. He says this, therefore, not by comparing this "best" state to young men, but to the unequal complexions of children; because in that state, they have the temperament that children *ought* to have in a temperate complexion, which remains as such in all ages. And he adds: "All others are worse than this," not meaning those according to the state and decline of time (as some falsely understand), but that all other unequal complexions are worse than this equal one.

To the other point, it must be said: **Galen** does not mean that the complexion of children is the "best" in an absolute sense, but in respect to **Spring**, to which it is most closely proportioned among the other seasons. This is because its heat and moisture are moderate, just as Spring is temperate. but this does not prove a temperate complexion in an absolute sense. For if Spring is called "temperate" in relation to our bodies, it is not strictly so in itself, but rather in respect to other seasons which are more distempered, having qualities that are more excessive and foreign to us. 

Or, he called that age "best" by reason of natural actions; for the discussion there is about these, and not about animal actions. For the body is governed by what is similar to it, such as a temperate body. Since the heat of a child is moderate and "blunted" by moisture, whereas the heat of a young man, though more temperate, is more "acute" or sharp, they are not governed entirely by the same things. A body is only preserved by its like if it is temperate. Since we see that cold forces are more effective in bodies, it is safer to use them in times of change than in preservation. **Difference CXVI.**

To the other point, it must be said: for a young man to be "drier" is for him to be more temperate. For "dryness" here does not mean an excess of the quality, but rather a freedom from superfluous moisture. This is because the integrity and perfection of bodily actions flourish when dryness prevails. 

To the other point, it must be said: **Galen**, through these primary discourses, does not labor to show that children are more temperate than young men, but that the quantity of "seminal moisture" <note>original: "humidi disp̄matici"—referring to the vital, radical moisture thought to be the spark of life</note> is more concentrated in their bodies than in young men. Thus they participate more in heat in terms of **quantity**, while young men participate more in terms of **quality**. Hence he adds: there being two types of substance, one having a "delightful" heat and the other an "anxious" heat; infants have the most of the former, while those entering youth have the most of the latter. In proportion to the whole body, a sweet and heavy heat and an innate temperament are further from a "certain" (perfect) temperament than an anxious and biting heat. For the heat of children is weakened too much by the moisture that abounds in them.

To the other point: although they are proportioned to the air, air itself is not close to a "certain" temperament, nor is any element by itself, but only when mixed—of which young men participate the most.

To the other point: those things which are of a temperate nature cannot be in more things. For the fact that children have "augmentative" <note>growth-promoting</note> powers by which they grow more, argues the opposite of the proposition. For in this, they are seen to be on the *way* to perfection but not yet perfect, whereas young men have attained all perfection and have lost none of it yet. Nor, as it appears, is the act of "producing seed" <note>original: "spermatizatio"</note> more frequent in children, nor is it perfect and generative as it is in young men. Similarly, it appears that digestion does not happen with just any heat, but by heat with the moisture pressed out of it. **Difference XXI**: If digestion has a temperate dryness, such is the quality of its nourishment. For young men digest better because, being in the middle state, they are more similar <note>original: "homogenei"</note> to food than children, who are at the extreme.

### DIFFERENCE XXVII.

-> That a boy is hotter than a young man is shown because <-
-> the substance and nature of a hot thing is <-
-> more truly "hot" than that which is so only by quality, since <-

the existence of a quality depends on the substance. A boy is hot by "substance" or nature, while a young man is hot by quality. **Isaac** <term>yfaac (Isaac Judaeus, an influential 10th-century Jewish physician and philosopher)</term> in his book *On Urines* and the fifth book of *On Fevers* says: He is hotter who is closer to the principle and source of heat.

<meta>This page continues a scholastic medical debate regarding the stages of human life. The previous page discussed the "balanced temperament" (crasis) of youth versus childhood. This page specifically investigates the degree of "innate heat" present in each stage, a central question in medieval physiology.</meta>

Since everything weakens as it departs from its origin <note>original: "a eius principio"</note> (Aristotle, *On the Cosmos*), and here we consider the child: as long as a great amount of time has not intervened, in which there was seed, blood, and the spirit of vapor—which are all very hot—it follows that the child is hotter. But the young man is further removed from these. Secondly, and primarily: that which most strengthens a weak **digestion** <term>digestio (the metabolic process of "cooking" food in the stomach to create humors)</term> is that which is most perfected by heat, and which is capable of more natural actions, and whose fuel for heat is more abundant and suitable. Since a sanguine and ruddy person is hotter, and all these things are perfected by sufficient heat, such a person is indeed a child and not a young man. 

Furthermore, in the fifth book of *Simple Medicines* and the thirteenth book of the *Method of Healing*, it is commanded that for a healthy **complexion** <term>complexio (the specific balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile)</term> near to **pollution** <note>original: "pollutiōi"; here likely referring to the release of excess humors or nocturnal emissions</note>, or for a weak stomach, a child should be applied <note>as a heat source</note> and not a young man. Furthermore, the child eats more often due to the softness and relaxation of his body, and his eating—accompanied by good digestion—results in nutrition and growth. The matter of the child is also "airy" and sanguine with a small amount of wateriness, which provides suitable fuel for heat. All these things in the child arise from a more ample heat; however, in the young man, all these things are secondary. 

Likewise, every bodily power is finite (First book of *On the Soul* and book twelve of Aristotle's *Animals*). The heat of these stages is of this kind. That which is such must eventually fail, as it is continually acted upon by its object. But in the young man, it is more finished and "acted upon" than in childhood, since he approaches closer to extinction and death. Therefore, the child stands out as hotter than the young man to those who perceive it. 

**On the contrary:** Because he is hotter who participates in the hottest of elements, namely fire—since fire is the root and principle of all formal heat, existing in him at the highest degree (Difference XV)—all heat is drawn from it (Book II of the *Metaphysics*). This describes the young man, while the child is "son" to the air <note>meaning the child's temperament is dominated by the element of Air, which is hot and moist, whereas the young man is moving toward Fire, which is hot and dry</note>. 

Again, he is hotter whose quality more strongly impresses itself upon the senses. The hairs of a young man are longer, thicker, and coarser; his illnesses and his vomit are **choleric** <term>colericus (related to yellow bile, the hottest and driest humor)</term>. Since all these things are produced by heat, such a person is the young man and not the child, as the senses clearly show. Therefore, the young man stands out as hotter than the child.

¶ Regarding the first point, it must be known what a "child" and a "young man" are, as shown in the previous distinction. "Hot" is also understood in two ways according to Galen: both by the subject (the hot body) and by the quality. It is improperly used in the first sense, since a "concrete" term implies a combination of subject and accident, denoting the accident primarily and the subject secondarily. The Commentator <note>Averroes</note> notes this in Book IV of the *Metaphysics*. 

There is also that which is hot "in act" and another that is hot "in potential." Our discussion concerns the former. Furthermore, "hotter" is said of parts in six ways: 
1. One which heats more by the proximity of its degrees <note>intensity of heat</note>, as Aristotle says: that which heats the touch, like fire. 
2. Another which impresses more upon the sense of touch. 
3. And Aristotle says: that which, when received into the earth, heats it. Regarding this, a falsehood can occur: for because of a state of great sensitivity, the thing touching can impress itself so much that it becomes a cause of pain. 
4. In another way, that which more easily liquefies and burns things that are liquefiable and combustible. 
5. In another way, if one is of a softer mass and the other of a smaller mass...

---

...for that which is of a softer mass is hotter than the smaller. 
6. Additionally, that is called "hotter" which is not quickly but slowly cooled. 

In a certain way, that which is a faster heater or a slower cooler is called "hotter" according to nature. For the same reason, this is truly a property of the long-lasting. In the first, third, and fifth ways, fire is hotter than boiling water; but in the others, the reverse is true. 

Regarding the second point, it must be known that some, with moving arguments, have declared children to be hotter; others, likewise, young men (Second book of *On the Complexions*, first book of the *Theoretical Medicine*). Because children are produced from seed and blood that are extremely hot and concentrated, they remain closer to their origin than young men. The bodies of children are also ruddier than those of young men, participating in much pure and very hot blood.

¶ Again, in children there is an appetite for growth, or an ultimate degree of it in relation to their bodies, along with laudable digestion. Since all these things argue for heat and are perfected by it, children stand out as hotter than young men.

¶ Those who posit that young men are hotter than children are moved by this: that blood is more abundant in them than in children, and hence they not infrequently suffer nosebleeds; and that red bile <note>yellow bile</note> abounds in them. Hence their illnesses and vomits from this humor are multiplied. These things come from hotter blood, since it is a hotter thing of the body's unequal distemper. Also, the strength and intellect of young men are at the ultimate stage of perfection, since the young man is a "perfected animal," whereas the child is "imperfect." Whence it is reasonable that the most efficacious and principal of elements, fire, should dominate in young men. The actions of children clearly fall short of these; they cannot walk, run, or carry weight, nor can they perform any such act perfectly. They are also somnolent, which denotes coldness and moisture, whereas young men are least so. Therefore, they are hotter than children.

Know also that the "heresy" <note>likely referring to a heterodox medical school or a specific "sect" of thinkers</note> of the second sort, as if more bitter than the first, pricked at two points. First, it posited that growth occurs from heat; saying instead that it happens more because of moisture than by the strength of heat. And it claimed that children do not only lack an abundance of digestion, but fall far short of young men. It also attacked the idea that the appetite or the "estimative power" <note>original: "yſtimbre"</note> is good in children; for it says animals do not seek food because of an abundance of heat, but rather because of the coldness of the appetitive parts of the animal. For a cold stomach is good for desiring food, but bad for digesting it. And because the food of children is converted not only into nourishment but into growth, it wants them to require a great deal of food. 

Against this, in defense of the former, Aristotle rises up, saying his speech is false; for moisture is the "matter" of growth and not the "efficient cause." Matter, even though it is the passive part (Second book of *On Generation and Corruption*), is a passive potential that does not act by itself, nor is it hot by itself. Rather, it depends on the operation of the power acting within it, such as the soul or nature, using the proper instrument, which is heat. Whence in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*: "Matter will not move itself, but the craft of the builder will." Neither the tool nor the earth moves themselves, but the seeds and the germs. Again, the saying of this sect is false...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on whether children or young men possess more "innate heat." The previous page argued that children are hotter because they are closer to their origin (the heat of the seed and womb), while this page introduces the counter-arguments and refinements provided by Galen, Haly Abbas, and Avicenna. The scribe uses standard medical abbreviations (Ga. for Galen, A. for Avicenna) common in 13th-15th century university texts.</meta>

...into the first. Because a good appetite or distribution <note>original: "distribre," referring to the movement of nutrients to the limbs</note> is never perfected by cold, since all ordered motions are found there. [Section] 53: Rather, a hunger arises here called **canine appetite** <term>appetitus caninus (an insatiable, "dog-like" hunger, often treated as a medical condition in the Middle Ages)</term>. This shows that in children, there is not only digestion of food for nutrition, but also for **growth** <term>augmentum (the biological process of increasing in size, which requires more heat than mere maintenance)</term>. For they do not suffer from nausea, aversion, or vomiting, except sometimes due to their poor and disordered regimen, because they focus on nothing except eating. 

The Commentator on the *Prognostics* <note>Referring to Galen's commentary on the Hippocratic text "Prognostics"</note> says: Furthermore, Galen, encountering these two "heresies" <note>original: "heresi," referring to competing medical schools or sects of thought</note>, holds that some even add a commonality of heat to both stages of life. He said in part that in these matters one reasons about primary causes based on later results <note>original: "ex posteris"</note>, which is very effective. However, it is not entirely reasonable to place faith in the primary things based on the secondary results, for a correct investigation must be taken from the substance of the thing and its subjects alone, and not from its accidental qualities. 

And therefore, as if looking down upon the disputes of these speakers, he added that the rule of comparison must be observed here: that when any things are compared to each other, a total equality and similarity in all things must be presupposed. One should not compare things that are unique... <margin>The unknown path seems longer.</margin> If we find others having similar traits, only **univocal** <term>univoca (things of the same category and definition that can be logically compared)</term> things are comparable. Therefore, it is necessary to compare a **choleric** <term>colericus (having a temperament dominated by yellow bile, which is hot and dry)</term> boy to a choleric youth, and so on with other natures. One must compare a thin person to a thin one, a fleshy one to a fleshy one, a hardworking one to a hardworking one, a lazy one to a lazy one, a fasting one to a fasting one, and a drunk one to a drunk one—and not otherwise. Generally, there must be an equality and similarity of all natural and pre-natural conditions, even comparing the same person to himself at a different time.

Next, meeting the aforementioned points, Galen says he has diligently investigated many bodies—not only of infants or children, but of adolescents and youths—even those diverse in age. He found neither to be "more truthful" <note>meaning neither group inherently defines "heat" better than the other</note>, nor would he affirm children to be hotter than youths. He found neither to be "simply" or "primarily" hotter than the other, but they differ in the **quality** of their heat. For the heat of children is abundant, soothing, familiar, more evaporable, and pleasant to the touch. But the heat of youths is sparse, anxious, more smoky to the touch, and unpleasant. You can know this from diligent experience in touching many and diverse bodies.

One must begin from the most obvious things. For the air of a **bathhouse** <term>balneum (public baths were the primary laboratory for medieval doctors to study heat and moisture)</term> is sometimes so hot that no one can bear it, but it feels like it will burn; at another time it is so cold that it cannot even induce sweat. Sometimes, however, it is moderate and well-tempered. Similarly, this three-fold disposition can be found in water, whether in the bath or some other body. Since these things are so, you will sometimes say the air and water are proportionally hotter, and sometimes colder, compared to the middle. Yet, well-tempered water and air do not feel entirely the same to the touch, because in one (like air), the touch can perceive diverse things: sometimes it is as if misty and vaporous, sometimes smoky, and sometimes truly pure. This can happen in water as well. Hence, in many and diverse substances, an equality of heat occurs, which clearly deceives those who do not make distinctions.

But those who are not understanding and constantly practicing, as I said, fail to see that a stone can sometimes receive a heat similar to water, yet the stone remains dry while the water is moist. Through these examples, he wants to show that since motion occurs through a middle point from the extremes, youths are the "middle" between children and old men. Youths can sustain themselves and preserve their **radical heat** <term>caliditas radicalis (the vital, "rooted" heat an organism is born with, which slowly "burns out" over a lifetime)</term>, but they cannot increase it. Children can do both; old men can do neither. Therefore, children and youths are similar or equal in their "fourth element" or root heat.

This is also declared by the *Aphorisms* <note>The "Aphorisms of Hippocrates," the foundational text of medieval medicine</note> through simple and composite liquids, both in equal and unequal parts. And it is no wonder how Galen could comprehend such subtle things, difficult even for the intellect: namely, that heat in a youth and a child would be equal. Because according to the fourth element (fire), the "airy" substance with a certain wateriness dominates more in children. In the youth, however, the heat is more "fiery," which Galen shows in the *Aphorisms* from the heat impressed on diverse subjects—one proportioned to children, the other to youths—such as water, oil, bronze, and iron.

It must be said that Galen possessed the most perfect sense of touch, as his reasoning and faithful experience indicate. For by the quality of one's touch, a person is judged to be talented or the opposite, according to the book *On the Soul*. This is also noted in his writings on the pulse <note>original: "fistolis in pulsum," likely referring to Galen's 'De pulsibus'</note> after much inquiry. Regarding this, **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."; the famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> marvels, though he made a firm assertion from the start. **Haly Abbas** <note>an influential 10th-century Persian physician</note>, a more faithful interpreter of Galen, says that heat is equal in children and youths in **quantity**, but diverse in **quality**. The heat of children is vaporous, soft, and pleasant to the touch, while that of youths is intense. Galen gave the example of bathhouse air and hot water: suppose both are at the peak of heat. When touched, they will be found equal in the quantity of heat, but a sharpness and stinging accompanies the air, while the water has more smoothness. Hence, hot water cannot be called "hotter" than the air, nor vice versa; they are equally hot. This is how the heat of the child and the youth relate. The youth's heat is like the hot air of the bath, while the child's heat is like the water. Both, however, agree in the quantity of heat.

**Avicenna**, the eminent clarifier, explaining Galen's position, says: "The heat of the child is equal in its root to that of the youth. But the heat of the child is of a greater quantity and a lesser quality (namely, sharpness)." The youth is the opposite. The explanation is to imagine a single measure of heat penetrating into a very moist substance (like water) and another into a small dry substance (like a stone). The heat of the water will be of greater quantity and lesser quality, while the stone is the opposite. Yet the root of the heat remains the same. This is marvelous: because children were generated from very hot seeds, which have not yet been extinguished, and the child proceeds by continually growing...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding whether children or young men possess more heat. It moves from general observations to citing specific authorities—Galen, Avicenna, and Haly Abbas—to distinguish between different types of heat (innate versus flowing) and the role of "radical moisture" in the body's development.</meta>

In youth, nothing occurs that increases their innate heat; however, nothing yet occurs that extinguishes it, except that the heat in youth maintains a moisture <note>original: "humiditatem," referring to the bodily fluids that fuel life</note> of a smaller quantity. Its quality is gentle and sweet until it reaches the stage of decline. Nevertheless, so great a diminution of moisture has not yet occurred that it would be unable to retain heat. Nor is it such that it cannot achieve **growth** <term>augmentum</term>; previously, the moisture was so great that it could preserve heat and provide growth. Eventually, however, it will reach a point where it can achieve neither, as happens in old age. 

Therefore, since a transition is made from one extreme to the other through a middle point, one of two extremes occurs in that middle: either it can preserve heat but cannot add to growth, or the reverse—which is impossible. For growth always presupposes **nutrition** <term>nutrimētum</term>; since later things in an essentially ordered sequence cannot be separated from the prior things, but are equal to them. Thus, it [the body] will be able to guard the heat, which is the characteristic of the age of youth. 

And know that what **Avicenna** <term>A.</term> calls the "root of heat," **Haly Abbas** <term>balyabas</term> and almost **Galen** <term>Ga.</term> call the quantity of the fourth element, pure fire. And where one divides it into the quantity of heat and its quality (that is, its sharpness), these others divide it into a gentle quality and a sharp quality. This, then, is the abbreviated reasoning of these illustrious physicians.

### Doubts Regarding the Comparison of Heat

But concerning the aforesaid, a doubt arises in two ways. First, that "hot smoke" <note>The "smoky" byproduct of metabolic "burning" in the heart</note> is the cause for the body's grayness and heat, which seems to be assigned against the **rule** <term>cano.</term> of comparison. This is because only things that are "univocal" <note>meaning they belong to the same category or have the same nature</note> are comparable; however, those things which are of different kinds are not comparable, such as the body and a quality. It must be said that these are univocal within each species insofar as they are hot, for in the same way all white things are identical in species. 

Furthermore, it is doubted how equality or a measurement of the "root" <note>the fundamental source of heat</note> or of the "fourth element" <note>Fire</note> is possible in a child and a young man. For the time it has penetrated the body of the child is short, whereas for the young man it is long. Forms are eventually changed according to the variety of their subjects. Since bodies every day, from their first **generation** <note>birth or conception</note>, are rendered drier than they were before, it follows that it is impossible to find two bodies that are equal in heat when one is drier than the other—as **Galen** observes regarding the child and the young man. 

It must be said that **Galen** and **Avicenna** do not intend to say that there is an identical equality of the fourth element or the "root" in the child and the young man, but rather a "latitude" <note>a broad range or general similarity rather than an exact point</note>. For they agree more with each other in heat than they do with the elderly or the decrepit. Both are equal in heat relative to the state of those who are beginning to wither. As if I were to place an equal "fourth element" of fire in both bodies—the young man and the child—so that I might say they are similarly hot. 

Hence, it was expressed earlier: "Always from the first generation, every animal becomes drier every day." Yet it does not necessarily become hotter. In the best composition of bodies, the heat remains constant until the "state" <note>the plateau of adulthood</note> is reached.

### On Celestial and Elementary Heat

The heat of the child and the young man is certainly not the same, or only similar in a broad sense. We have already declared that the heat in children and youth is almost similar. **Avicenna** says the same thing in the chapter on health and medicine. 

Regarding the third point, it must first be known how the multiplicity of heat is touched upon, and then the truth may be drawn from it. First, it must be known that heat is twofold: **celestial** and **elementary**. When these two concur together, they constitute a generated being. Thus, I hear that the "root of heat" or the "fourth element" is a composite of celestial and elementary heat, supported by **radical moisture** <term>humido radicali</term>. 

This moisture is diversified by reason of its subject:
*   In the child, it is more "congealed" and thus more blunt or dull.
*   In the young man, it is sharper.

This heat and moisture can truly be called "innate," planted together in the principles of generation. 

There is also another "flowing" or "running" heat and moisture, which are caused by the power of digestion—especially that of the heart—from food. In the young man, these are greater in quantity and more intense in quality, since his vessels are larger and more fervent. 

Therefore, it must be said that young men are hotter than children, even in primary heat. For although the "root of heat" (and especially the celestial heat) might flourish more in children than in youth—since children possess more and better "matter"—the same species remains, but can be received more or less. In young men, however, the sharpening of this heat, combined with sufficient radical moisture and the "file" of dryness <note>the refining effect of aging</note>, greatly excels the bluntness of childhood heat. Thus, young men are pre-heated compared to children. The heat of those reaching youth is also aided by the "flowing" heat and moisture, in which they certainly surpass children. 

Furthermore, those things are hotter in which the heat begins to overcome its matter, and the matter stands ready to vigorously sustain it. This is found in young men, but not in children. Whence it is said in the *Particular Diets*: "**The natural heat of children** <term>Calor pueroꝝ naturalis</term>, although substantially strong, is not yet in its perfection."
