...abundance of moisture in them. In **youths**, as shown before, all things are present in a more perfect manner; however, this is not the case in **children**, because from infancy until youth they abound in superfluous moisture. Nor is it so in the **elderly**, since, as has been touched upon, the heat in them is not able to preserve its root—which the ignition of wood particularly demonstrates. Also, those who are proportioned with a warmer member are warmer than those with a less warm one. Such are the youths: for they are proportioned to the **heart** <note>The heart was considered the primary source of innate heat in medieval physiology.</note>, which is warmer than the other parts. This is shown by their masculinity, courage, and perseverance. Children, however, are more similar to the **liver**, which is indicated by the greater generation of blood that flows in them than in youths. Therefore, youths are warmer than children.

Regarding the fourth point, it must be said: To the first, that **Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus (c. 832–932), a highly influential Jewish physician and philosopher.</note> understood "warmth" in terms of quantity or softness rather than the heat of substance or nature, since such a thing implies a dependence on the substance, as has been shown, and not that the heat itself exists as the substance. Heat as represented in youths does not carry this dependence, since it refers to its essence more in the abstract. 

To the other point, it must be said: that discourse is to be understood regarding the levels of beings in the universe, and not in any particular being. For it is not forbidden for virtues to become stronger and more powerful from their own principles, because they obtain the matter through which this happens. Hence the power of the extremities of the heart is greater for providing heat than the power of their principles, which are in the seven pairs of nerves <note>original: "septem nervorum." A reference to Galenic anatomy regarding the cranial nerves.</note>. According to **Aristotle** <term>A.</term> in *On the Soul* <note>original: "v. de aia" referring to De Anima, Book 5 (though often cited by medieval authors in different configurations).</note>: since action occurs in time, it is not immediately strengthened by the presence of the agent, which the burning of wood demonstrates. 

To the next point, it must be said that **digestion** <term>digō</term> is perfected not only by heat but also by moisture, which in some way tempers the heat. Youths, however, are more separated from this than children. Nor can a child perform more natural acts than a youth in his vigor, since the growth of children implies a movement toward perfection more than the state of being perfected. Nor do children surpass youths in any natural virtues, since they almost entirely lack the **generative power** <term>generativa</term>. Even the **nutritive power** <term>nutritiva</term> in youths is equal or stronger, because the digestive power is of this kind. In other virtues, it has been shown sufficiently before that children clearly fall short. 

Nor does the airy matter of heat alone strengthen them, though it may be suited for a long-lasting stay when mixed with three-fold qualities, even if the heat is mild. Their blood also is more watery. The redness of children, and specifically of infants, appears more intense by accident, such as through the porousness of the skin which they receive from the heat of the womb along with the thinness of the skin. This happens differently as one grows into youth, and because humors like **choler** <note>Yellow bile, associated with heat and dryness.</note> increase; although the blood is hotter then, it is not more colored, since the blood tints the choler much more with its own color. 

To the other point, it must be said: it is not necessary, as appeared, that something intended to last longer should be more intense; rather, the opposite occurs, since vigor requires a determined disposition of the subject. I concede the arguments of the other side regarding the heat of nature being sharpened and also flowing, since this follows from what was said before. This, therefore, is the truth of these questions in brief, drawn from the previous distinction, with the useless chatter of the moderns regarding this matter being omitted.

->### DIFFERENTIA XXVIII.<-

### Whether every male is warmer and drier than every female.

It is shown that not every male is warmer and drier than every female. For magnitude of body, strength, and vigor are caused by heat and dryness, since they are the more effective qualities. These qualities are found in the females of **insects** <term>enthomoꝝ</term>, small live-bearing fish, quadrupeds, and **birds of prey** <note>original: "auium rapaciū," likely referring to hawks or falcons where females are often larger.</note>, according to the first book of *The Generation of Animals*. Also, the female bear and female leopard are noted to be more vigorous than the male leopard and male bear in the eighth book of the *History of Animals*. 

Furthermore, man is the warmest of animals, according to the tenth book of the *Problems*. But what is said to be "superabundant" belongs to only one, according to the fifth book of the *Topics*. If in birds with curved talons the males are rendered cold and dry because of the conjunction of the heat and dryness of the species with the heat and dryness of the male sex—for this reason "combustion" <term>adustio</term> is caused—in the female, a **temperament** <term>contempamentū</term> arises from her own cold and moist nature of the species, which moderates the heat and dryness. Much more, therefore, in the human species, will combustion happen to the male, so that he is turned toward cold and dry, and finally into accidental moisture. 

Again, if every male were hotter and drier than any female, then "masculine" and "feminine" would seem to be essential accompanying differences of an animal, which is denied in the tenth book of the *Metaphysics* and in its first book. Also, a **choleric** <term>colericus</term> person is hotter than a **phlegmatic** <term>flegmatico</term> one. But a certain woman may be choleric, while a certain man may be phlegmatic. Likewise, a pulse that is clearly larger and stronger argues for more intense heat; such a pulse is sometimes found in females, and the opposite in a man, according to the *Commentary on the Pulses*. 

Furthermore, the pulse and the whole body have as much heat as they have blood. For everything that lacks blood is colder than things with blood, according to the *Commentary on Complexions*. But females, and especially in the human species, participate more in blood, which their periodic flux shows, as does the significant color of the face. Likewise, the body not being harmed by cold denotes heat; but a woman does not seem to be harmed by cold as much as a male, since we see her in colder times wearing fewer clothes than males; she also remains longer in water washing her feet with bare feet. 

Therefore, not every male will be warmer and drier than every female. In the proper sense, men are more warm and dry according to nature; women, however, are moist and cold, as stated in the fourth book of the *Problems*. Also, the male is warmer and drier than the female, as said by the best authorities among philosophers and physicians in the *Commentary on the Pulses*. Therefore, in theory, the male in all animals is warmer and drier in **complexion** <term>complexioē</term> than the female, and the female is colder and moister than the male. This is the opinion in the books *On the Generation of Animals* and the eighth book of the *History of Animals*. 

Furthermore, that one is warmer and drier who acts more perfectly, strongly, and for a longer time; for this is the combination of all the tempered qualities. And this is the male, as appears from his properties by which he is distinguished from the female in the aforementioned eighth book and in the *Commentary on Complexions*. Whence it is gathered: the male complexion is warmer and drier than the female complexion.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic comparison of natural qualities, moving from the ages of man to the physiological differences between the sexes (Differentia 28). Catchword: "teie. fʒo" (likely referring to the third section or feminine principles).</meta>

...which is manifest from their works. Therefore, the **male** is hotter and drier than the **female**. Regarding the first point, it must be known that the male is an animal that has the power to generate into another; the female, however, is that which generates into itself. For the former can do this into that; whereas the latter receives this into itself, at least in perfect animals. Regarding what has been said about <term>insects</term> <note>original: "entho ma"; referring to Aristotle's classification of 'entoma'.</note>, some things differ. And these indeed differ not only by the nature of their definition, but by certain differing organized parts on either side, according to the first book of *The Generation of Animals*. To sum up: the male is an animal participating in a more perfect <term>actuality</term>; the female, truly, in the more imperfect. For a female is, as it were, a "maimed" or "defective" male <note>original: "orbatus masculus seu occasionatus"; a standard Aristotelian view that the female is a male "gone wrong" due to a lack of formative heat.</note>. Hence, in that first book: a woman is like an unproductive male. For the female is in a certain state of potentiality—namely, by chance—because she cannot <term>concoct</term> <note>original: "digerere"; refers to the metabolic transformation of food into seed.</note> sperm from the ultimate nourishment. Wherefore, in the fourth book of this work: the male is able to concoct and cause to stand firm, and to separate the sperm, having the principle of the species; the female, however, is the recipient, unable to make it stand firm or create it. Sex is, moreover, in natural things, one of the things inseparably annexed through a mediating **complexion** <note>In medieval medicine, 'complexion' refers to the unique balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—in an individual.</note>.

Know also that the sexual distinction arises from a part containing within itself the natural principle of heat, such as the **heart** in blooded animals; in others, however, from that which is proportional to it. From this, indeed, the genital organs depend, and not the other way around, as some have thought.

And though some, such as **Anaxagoras**, posited that this distinction exists in the seeds; **Empedocles** in heat and cold simply; and others indeed in the right or left side of the **womb** <note>original: "matricis".</note>. And **Democritus** of Abdera claimed it was obtained by the force of the sperm that arrived from the part.

Against these, especially Empedocles, arguments are made in the fourth book of *The Generation of Animals*. For a **hot complexion** aids in the generation of a male; for when natural heat is present, it aids in digestion/concoction. For when sperm is concocted, its power is rendered complete. Natural or extrinsic coldness, however, prohibits concoction; hence the sperm is rendered unconcocted, raw, and weak. Therefore, the right side of the womb aids in generating a male by its heat, and the left side a female by its coldness. But the assistance of heat or the impediment of cold is not the *essential* cause of this, but rather the equality of the complexion (according to **Aristotle**) rendering the virtue of the heart stronger, or its opposite rendering it weaker.

Regarding the second point, it must be known that **Parmenides** posited that females were hotter than males, and women hotter than men. **Empedocles**, however, in the first book of *On the Parts [of Animals]*, touched upon her movement arising from an abundance of blood, which is shown in the fourth book of the proposed works.

Indeed, this investigation is touched upon in the commentary on **The Pulse** <note>Referring to Galen's 'De Pulsibus'.</note>. For a very similar point is intended there: namely, that the pulse of the male is stronger than that of the female. The sequence of the argument is almost this: because we are not all formed by a complexion in a similar way right from the beginning, and because we do not use study or diets in a similar way, the universal truth of this statement can be corrupted. For it is possible that a woman may sometimes be found with a pulse not smaller, nor small for a man, nor equal, but having a pulse manifestly larger than certain men. It happens that one understands a man to be phlegmatic by nature; for this complexion will be cold and moist compared to a hotter and drier female. Add to this that the man may inhabit the region of **Pontus** <note>A region on the southern coast of the Black Sea, cited here as a cold environment.</note>, which is a very cold region, and he may be raised in the shade, be lazy, and follow a diet of pleasures—perhaps even guarding the gate of a hall <note>A sedentary job.</note>. The female, however, may inhabit **Egypt**, exercise much, and eat a moderate diet. In that case, the pulse of the female will be larger than that of the man. But if they were to follow a diet according to their primary nature and inhabit the same region, not only would the male's pulse be rendered larger, but much larger than the female's. Thus **Galen** intends that, as far as natural complexion is concerned, the male's pulse is always stronger than the female's. But because of the complexion arising from the "six [non-natural] things" <note>The 'six non-naturals' were environmental factors like diet, exercise, and climate that influenced health.</note>—as if the regime of one female were to decline toward heat, while the man's toward cold—a pulse of a certain female could be found stronger than the pulse of a man.

Finally, from this discourse, some have said that male and female can be considered in two ways. First, according to the **principles of generation**—namely, the sperm and blood that constitute the embryo—and in this way, every male is hotter and drier than a woman, since he is produced from hotter and drier principles, and the female the opposite. Second, according to the **acquired complexion** after the aforementioned constitution—whether from the menstrual blood nourishing the embryo, or from any other occurring disposition, or coming upon it entirely after birth. For suppose there are two females: the pregnancy of one results in a male, and the other a female in a temperate region; and subsequently the first goes to Pontus in a sickly state, while the other goes to Egypt, living well with the other aforementioned conditions. It then happens that the one who brings forth a female may be rendered hotter and drier by acquisition. In the third [book], section 21, **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Y." for Ypocras.</note> says: a woman is not colder than every man—namely, in the complexion of her principal members, and her own primary complexion, and the complexion of her healthy seed—unless it happens by an accidental complexion.

But perhaps it will be said here that this does not sufficiently cover all cases, as will appear at the beginning of the discussion. For a female has sometimes been seen having all the virile qualities more than a male, even when they inhabit the same region and use a similar regime. Some have argued more crudely that a female can sometimes foster someone hotter and drier than a male, assuming that every immoderate <term>dyscrasia</term> <note>A bad mixture or imbalance of humors.</note> acts to resolve the substance. For a certain sperm is found to be excessively hot and dry, which is not virtuous because of the evaporation of the spirits; according to **Haly** <note>original: "baly", likely Haly Abbas.</note>, this will generate not a male, but a female. From this, they claim a generated female can be hotter and drier than a male.

This is not valid, among other reasons, because the sperm will be so weakened that the female, after she has been produced, will be very cold. Furthermore, if she were to be hotter and drier than a man, she ought to have been generated from the kind of seed that nature intends to make, at least in particular cases, since it continually intends that which is perfect. Therefore, it should also be known that the causes of the generation of the male and female must first be touched upon, and then applied to the proof of this proposition.

Regarding this subject, it must first be known that these distinctions exist in two ways: some are indeed particular and material concerning the sexes, while others are powers, acting as stabilizing and effective forces. Of these, they depend specifically on the male, the female, and other circumstances. From the male, they depend on his seed; this occurs in many ways due to his power—that is, his natural virtue. For in the generation of males, there is an <term>excess</term> <note>original: "excessus"; referring to an abundance or superior strength.</note> of sperm, while in the female there is weakness. This is according to Hippocrates, in *On the Generation of the Embryo*, chapter 5. By "power," we can understand his <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines an individual’s health and personality.</note>, and no less the divine formative power, about which enough was said in chapters 36 and 48. 

Or it depends on the substance of the seed itself; for the sperm ought to be of moderate consistency, not a runny liquid—lest it spread out like water poured on a mirror—nor thick and viscous, sinking into itself. Rather, it should be of moderate consistency with much <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritu"; refers to "pneuma," the vital heat and airy substance believed to carry the life-force in the seed.</note> floating within it. It ought to be neither cold nor watery, but rather airy and foamy, as stated in *The Generation of Animals*, Book 2, chapter 20. Or it depends on quantity—for it must be sufficient, since it is the principle of many things—or quality, so that it is sufficiently hot in proportion to the passive elements, and of a grand white color because of the spirit enclosed within it; for the abundance of indwelling airy spirits provides that whiteness. 

Or it depends on the part: for it ought to be cast forth from the right testicle and return to the hotter, more favorable liver. From the female, however, it depends on the menstrual blood and her sperm likewise, provided they are marked by these same conditions in their own way; or it depends on the womb being properly purified. It is also required that the cause of the sperm be in the right side of the womb, coming specifically from the right testicle, for from there it exits hotter. Hence, in section 21:

But if it goes from the left into the right, it will be a "masculine female" <note>original: "femina masculina"; often referred to in medieval texts as a "virago," a woman with male physical or temperamental traits.</note>. If, however, the male seed is processed as female, [a female is born]. 

The circumstances include that the age of those coupling should be youth, not childhood or old age. And overall, the one coupling should be like a man of strong body, firm flesh, much sperm, which is sufficiently thick and hot, with large testicles and visible veins, and of immense appetite—such that he is not weakened by intercourse—whose right testicle is also aroused first.

Truly, water and the softened dryness of earth dominate in the female, which touch—along with their actions and other passions—will demonstrate. 

Further, the perfection of qualities ought to be attributed to the combination of perfect things, which comes from their own efficacy. Each individual articulated limb is also found to be more robust by these differences. Similarly, he is more beautiful, and his constitution is more proportionate (*Theoretical Medicine*, Book 1). And ultimately, this can be shown by reason taken from substantially inherent acts and cases, as touched upon in chapter 26. Therefore, the male will be hotter and drier than the female. Although it is more often necessary for nature to generate males than females, universal nature works no less in the production of females, since without them generation cannot be completed and the species saved, whatever may occasionally happen.

From the remaining seed, however, with its strengthened and almost opposite fluid, a male is generated. Whence it seems that in certain years mostly males are generated, and in others mostly females. Regarding the fourth point, it must be said in response to the first: that in certain small, imperfect animals, nature provided for the generation and preservation of the species by producing females larger in stature, stronger, and consequently hotter than males, so that they might better preserve the species through gestation, such as <term>insects</term> <note>original: "enthomoy"; from the Greek 'entoma'.</note> and small fish. In birds of prey, however, the males happen to be weaker, colder, and drier, having become so from a scorching heat because of the combination of the heat of the sex with the heat of the species.

A similar thing happens which one may see <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Ar."</note> perceive in his *Physiognomy*: the female <term>bear</term> is stronger than the male because of her habits; her boldness is estimated to be brief, occurring to the sex especially during the time of nursing cubs, as is also the case with the sow. Yet she does not persevere as long in a fight as the male bear, hence she is not hotter than him. Rather, the lion and the aforementioned birds are hotter in quality. And therefore, as stated in the fourth book of *On the Parts of Animals*, man is the most upright of animals; but quantitative heat does not lead to "burning," whereas sharpened qualitative heat does.

To the other point it must be said: that masculine and feminine are not present in an animal "per se" (in themselves) in the primary mode of being, since they are not its substantial masters. Instead, they are certain natural properties of it, like those mentioned before, and inseparable accidents. For those things which are made by the same agent, and from those things which agree in one form, and from the same matter, and are ordered toward the same end, do not differ in species. Such are the masculine and feminine. For they are made by the active power in the seed; they also agree in form, since there is only one essential form for a single thing. For individuals of any species do not differ in essential form, but in matter marked by a limited quantity. Likewise, the form emerges from the matter undergoing some passive change, according to which it becomes male or female. Therefore, they do not differ in species, but rather in property. As for the statement that the male differs from the female in heat and dryness, it must be said that this varies in many cases, but not in every way as has been declared. For the rules of medicine, and all those that discern flexible matter, are verified as being true for the most part.

## DIFFERENCE XXIX.

<margin>1</margin> **I**t is shown that the humors are generated not all at once, but successively, and how the generation of <term>phlegm</term> <note>Associated with cold and moisture; here described as the first stage of digestion.</note> precedes the generation of the others. For phlegm is the first moisture from undigested food. According to the *Topics*, Book 6: phlegm carries a priority and order in relation to the other humors. Also, according to the *Generation of Animals*: phlegm is the first useful superfluity of nourishment. From these points, a conclusion is drawn: namely, that phlegm is a bloody superfluity or a "diminished" flow, such that it is blood, but not a superfluity that remains as blood after separation from any other humor—as happens with <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile, associated with heat and dryness.</note> and <term>melancholy</term> <note>Black bile, associated with cold and dryness.</note>. Because of this, it is impossible for food to be generated unless <term>phlegmatic</term> superfluities are generated from it. This also seems to be the wisdom of Galen in the third book of *On Acute Diseases* and Theophilus in his *On Urines*. The order removes the possibility of them appearing simultaneously. For from phlegm, blood is made; and from blood, choler and melancholy; and from choler, melancholy. It does not work in reverse. This is found in the third book of *On Acute Diseases* and the first book of the *Theorica*.

<margin>2</margin> Again, things which proceed from a different agent are seen not to be generated at the same time, even when a temporal identity is acquired; but the humors are made by a different agent, such as heat. For the efficient cause of phlegm is diminished heat; of choler, superfluous heat; and of blood and melancholy, temperate heat. These are their specific causes. Also, as the divines show, they are sublimated; from these, in turn, the humors are extracted to which they are proportioned. The first of these is likened to water, the second to choler, the third to blood, and the fourth indeed to melancholy. Again, the imperfect is prior to the perfect, since nature tends gradually and continuously from the imperfect toward the perfected, as noted in the *History [of Animals]*, Book 7. But phlegm is imperfect, as it is blood that is "diminished in its cooking" <note>original: "diminute decoctus"; the medieval concept that digestion was a process of "cooking" or heat-refining food.</note>; whereas blood is perfect. Furthermore, the humors existing as moistures also generate successively. For from its own parts a third is made, and others from the second and third make the fourth, just as Difference 33 shows. According to [Galen] in the fourth book of *On the Use of the Parts*: the proper operation of the innate heat in the blood is in the <term>liver</term> <note>original: "epate"</note>; and after that, another heat more formal than the liver’s heat operates upon it—namely, the heat of the heart. Whence, according to the first book of *Complexions*: blood. Again, the blood itself receives heat from the heart. Likewise in the same place and in the fourth book of the *Theorica*. The liver is generated red so that it might generate something similar to blood, namely red [fluid], according to the fourth book of the *Theorica* and the first book of the *Almansor*. It is written that the liver simply generates blood. From these things, it is concluded that the humors are generated only successively. And that blood is also properly generated in the liver, and no other humor. However, the opposite of these things seems to be the common opinion of authors. Furthermore, whatever things are generated from the same matter according to different parts, and are presented to the same agent at the same time—despite the differences in the matter—and with nature working toward different ends, they are generated as one. This is evident in things boiled in water. A coarse example is usually given of the meat of chickens, castrated goats, pigs, and cows boiled together. In this way, the liquid possesses the aforesaid quality. Also, in the third book of *Natural Things* and the fourth of *On the Use of the Parts*, the generation of the moistures is likened to the generation of wine from trodden <term>must</term> <note>Newly pressed grape juice that has not yet fermented into wine.</note>. In which, whatever exists of the substance exists together as one: one part is soft, light, and foamy, proportioned to choler; another is earthy, heavy, and dreg-filled, proportioned to melancholy; a third is cold and undigested, likened to phlegm; a fourth is the watery part of urine; and the fifth is the pure wine, related to blood. Regarding the first point, one must know the terms of animals. And thereafter a method is inserted by which the humors tend toward generation. Regarding the first of these, it must be known that "humor" is said in many ways, according to the common, the specific, the diverse, and the intermediate. In one way, it is taken commonly for any flowable moisture, as water might be called a humor, according to that line in the *Bucolics*: "A sweet humor, rain, is enough for the ripened crops." <note>original: "Dulcis humor satis maturis frugibus imber." A reference to Virgil's Eclogues.</note> It is also taken for the <term>chyle</term> <note>The milky fluid of digested food.</note> departing from the belly and tending toward the liver through the mesenteric veins; whence the 13th aphorism says: the blood-making power, due to weakness, will not alter that humor which is taken up into the veins of the liver and the mesentery. Therefore, in the same place, the belly draws its own <term>chymus</term> <note>Chyme; the semi-fluid mass of partly digested food.</note> from the food. It is also understood as the primary fourfold humor, and for the secondary humor in a fourfold way—namely, as moisture. Because of this, Aristotle says the humors are bodies which are generated from the proper mixing of foods, and a humor is that which nourishes from what is eaten and drunk. I say also that it is taken properly for a primary humor, whether good or bad. Wherefore the same humor is a liquid, moist body into which the nutrient is first converted—that is, the chyle. But it is better to say that here "humor" is taken for the primary and secondary, because it is said to nourish by itself or with another. It is established, however, that the primary humor does not nourish, as in Difference 33. Also he says: "Which humors we shall name shortly after, and now have named them." Furthermore, Aristotle's order would be very regular if he first touched upon the humors specifically, and finally in common. Nor does it stand in the way that the nutrient is converted first—that is, immediately—into a moist liquid body, since moisture is the respect of this toward the members. Although moistures differ in this more or less, there is no real difference between the nutrient and the member, except that the moist liquid seems to coincide. Finally, "humor" is taken most strictly for the primary and good humor, according to Aristotle in the third book of *Animals*: "A humor is a moist, running body," and it is led toward the good. Thus far also it has appeared that there are primary humors like phlegm, blood, choler, and melancholy; while others are also specified by the name of moistures, as in the wonderful Difference 33. "Generation" is taken in two ways: commonly, insofar as it is placed under motion as a leading from non-being into being, containing within itself the true alteration preceding generation, and its limit in which the substantial form is given in an instant. This is a leading into substance and is an act composed of alteration and natural formation. Generation is also taken properly insofar as it is a certain change and not a motion, as in the *Physics*, Book 5: and it is indeed a change or the limit of the motion of the substantial form produced in an instant. For generations are properly the departures of substances, according to *On Generation and Corruption*. <meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the generation of the humors, shifting from the specific sequence of phlegm to the broader physiological process of digestion and the role of the liver's anatomy in transforming food into blood and other bodily fluids.</meta>

Humors are not distinguished by species, but only by accident—or by matter extended under a certain quantity. Indeed, not only humors, but two individuals are not essentially distinguished. Whence Aristotle, in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, says that singular things of any species, since they are not divided in the intellect of the matter, are one; <note>original: "singularia cuilibet spēi... unū sunt"</note> therefore they must be diverse in their accidents. For this reason, it is difficult to find their true forms, or perhaps impossible, because the forms attributed to them by Aristotle are rather certain "passions" <note>In scholastic philosophy, a "passion" is a property or quality resulting from an action.</note> and true accidents: just as health is a temperate form of decoction <note>The "cooking" or ripening of humors by bodily heat.</note>, phlegm is a diminished decoction, and choler is an excessive one; and likewise for the six "hypostatic" <note>Settling or sedimentary.</note> humors mentioned.

For the forms of these things are seen more in their becoming and altering than in their being and remaining consistent. Thus, physicians follow the opinion of **Avicebron** <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol, an 11th-century philosopher known for his theory of "universal hylomorphism" or graded forms.</note> regarding the gradations of forms, rather than that of Aristotle and the Peripatetics who denote their unity. Likewise, "simultaneity" is said to be found in two ways in the *Postpredicaments*: <note>A section of Aristotle's *Categories*.</note> namely, by nature and by species. This is also twofold: for either things are called "simultaneous by nature" because they require each other in the genus of subsisting—rather, an existing cause allows the other to exist—such as things placed in relation to another, like "double" and "half" which exist simultaneously by nature; or because they divide a genus in opposition to one another, in which way species are said to be contained under a genus. This is logically true, though not necessarily philosophically; for according to truth, one is prior and nobler than the other, since one of the two from which a species is constituted with a genus behaves as a habit or perfection, and the other as a privation or defect. Therefore, in the seventh book of the *Physics*: a genus is not one single thing, but beneath it many things are hidden, such as equivocations. Things are called "simultaneous in time" when their generation occurs at the same time and not successively; this is opposed in some way to that which is called an "instant" or "indivisible now," which occurs if many things are in the same instant.

Because of this, it must be known that food and drink taken by the mouth are led down through the stomach into the belly. If it is earthly and gross, once divided and ground by the teeth, it is made fit for the first <term>digestion</term> <note>The medieval concept of digestion involved four stages: stomach, liver, blood vessels, and tissues.</note> of the belly through this division into the smallest parts; for the division of nourishment into small bits easily facilitates the operation of heat, according to the book *On the Parts of Animals*. To such an extent that some say the beginning of digestion is received in some degree [in the mouth]; finally, once led into the belly and mixed together, it is perfectly digested by it into a mass, or transformed into <term>chyle</term> <note>A milky fluid produced from digested food in the stomach and intestines.</note>. This happens partly due to the heat of the belly—this being the primary factor—and its moisture, and partly due to the many members assisting it, thirdly by the natural power, and first by the primary power. Once digestion is completed, the <term>pileron</term> <note>The pylorus, the opening from the stomach into the small intestine.</note> of the belly opens, and (unless the diet is unhealthy) almost the whole mass slides down into the intestines. Some of the most sensitive people <note>original: "szibilisimoꝝ"</note> testify that they feel this. First it reaches the duodenum, and then it recedes into the jejunum and the rest; then, it is attracted through the <term>mesaraic veins</term> <note>The mesenteric veins, which carry nutrients from the intestines to the liver.</note> from the portal of the liver which branches into it. The mesaraic veins (or those of the intestines) are thin veins fixed to all or most of the intestines and the belly, specifically the jejunum, and are collected at the point of the concavity of the liver; they are joined together into one point like the cords of a tent. And these are, as it were, the hands of the liver.

By the power of the liver, they transform the chyle into the form of <term>chyme</term>, <note>A more processed stage of digested fluid, often used interchangeably with chyle but here representing the transition toward blood.</note> so that even in these veins the liquid assumes a certain reddish coloration. For the **anatomists** <margin>drā xlvii</margin> <note>Referring to "Difference 47" of the text.</note> posit that in the hollow of the liver a vein arises called the <term>milky portal vein</term>, <note>original: "uena lactea porta"; here likely referring to the portal vein system before it was clearly distinguished from the lymphatic lacteals.</note> which is sequestered into five veins. Four of these are divided into the parts of the liver, going from small to the smallest until they become hair-like filaments. One of them, however, extends to the <term>kistim</term> <note>The gall bladder (from the Greek 'kystis').</note> to nourish the bile; finally, toward the back, eight veins are sent out from here to the spleen, stomach, and intestines. Of these eight, six are major and two are minor. How specifically they extend is not part of the present speculation. By these same anatomists, the vein called the <term>vena cava</term> (or the "hollow vein") is said to arise in the <term>gibbo</term> <note>The convex or "humped" part of the liver.</note> of the liver. This vein eventually tends toward small veins like hairs and is directed more into the superior substance of the liver, as noted in Difference 47. When the chyle is attracted through the mesaraic veins and reaches the smallest portal veins, it meets the branches of the liver from the refined vena cava. For the lower branchings and orifices of the vein "drink" and imbibe from the branchlets of the superior vein, so that then "the whole touches the whole." Thus, the digestion is made more effective by contact; for then the humor-making virtue of the liver, with its instrument—namely heat—turns upon the chyle and transforms it into blood, the other three humors, and the urinary watery part (which is necessary for the sake of penetrating into narrow passages).

Regarding this, it must be known that some have simply claimed that humors are generated in an instant and in the liver. This saying is quite vain. For it is not seen "how," since an "instant" is opposed to time and its simultaneity; nor, as will appear, can they all be truly generated in one instant. Nor do they only become humors in the liver, but also in the veins and the heart. Therefore, others have said that the humors are generated simultaneously in time regarding their matter; however, on the part of the agent—namely the heat operating in a greater, lesser, or medium degree—they posited that they are made not simultaneously but successively. But this perhaps cannot stand with that which is quite indistinct, since matter is not the cause of distinction, but rather of indetermination and confusion, according to the act itself which separates and distinguishes (Difference 18). <margin>drā xviii</margin> Whence it is necessary for the agent to be applied to the matter in some way so that a distinct form may be raised from it, retaining something distinct in its being. Regarding the third point, it must be known that humors are generated in different places according to their various definitions: for in the veins of the liver or in other places they are produced by the intention of the soul, by heat, by the part, or by the matter, as will be seen in Difference 32. <margin>drā xxxii</margin> Clearly, they are first made from chyle. It must be considered that those things from which chyle is made are either tempered or distempered in eight ways, or rather according to the four qualities: such as hot, dry, moist, etc. Similarly, the body and the liver specifically are either simply healthy, or slightly lapsed, or greatly lapsed in the eight or four aforementioned ways. Let it also be supposed that in those cases where the body is simply healthy, it makes use of the <term>six non-natural things</term> <note>A standard medical concept: air, food/drink, sleep/wake, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the soul.</note> in a proper manner, so that it may obtain actual health, rather than just a healthy disposition.

<summary>This page details the physiological transformation of food into chyle and then into the four humors, emphasizing the anatomical role of the liver, portal veins, and mesenteric veins. It debates whether these humors are created simultaneously or successively, leaning toward a process driven by the "cooking" action of bodily heat.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the formation of the bodily humors, specifically debating whether they are generated all at once (simultaneously) or in a sequence. It draws upon the anatomical function of the liver and the authority of classical physicians like Galen, Isaac Israeli, and Haly Abbas.</meta>

...and other bodies that are out of balance may use an unsuitable regimen especially. Therefore, I say that regarding the humors—even in a temperate body and with similar food—it is not necessary for all of them to be generated in a single instant. Nevertheless, it can perhaps happen to some people; although the generation of each humor exists by itself in an instant, it does so if it receives a substantial form from that process. This happens because of the great diversity of the matter, the acting force, and the biological "instruments," which are so varied that they do not need to concur into one single effect in one instant. 

The humors also receive diversity from the celestial aspect <note>referring to the influence of stars and planets on bodily fluids</note> during their preparation and generation. Nor are they generated entirely in the same part of the liver. Rather, some are generated more above and near the heart; some more below; others in the middle. And thus, according to these different locations, they are rendered distinct. Nor does the **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid resulting from digested food before it is turned into blood</term>, since it is brought through narrow veins, arrive in the liver all at once. Furthermore, nature’s primary intention is directed toward the production of blood much more than toward the other humors. 

Thus, since it is impossible for such different causes to induce such diverse effects in a single instant, they cannot all be generated together in one indivisible moment. But I say that they can sometimes be made at the same time; however, I cannot define exactly how much time such a "simultaneous" period contains. Natural limits are not perceived with precision, nor is a prescribed time found in which the chyle, once led into the liver, is converted into humors. For instance, in book thirteen, a time is noted in which the stomach completes digestion under a certain lack of determination; yet a meal may take twelve hours up to twenty-two <note>The text suggests a range of 12 to 22 hours for digestion, noting the variability of the process</note>. However, since the liver receives matter for transformation that is more "ready" than that of the stomach, the heat of the liver perhaps becomes more transformative. In a shorter time, it will imprint its effect upon the chyle, translating it into the humor itself. Suppose everything is perfected in a shorter space of time, perhaps taking seven equinoctial hours <note>hours of equal length, as opposed to seasonal hours</note> to complete the whole process. In one of these half-hours, or even less, the four humors might be generated in four successive moments. I say this happens especially when the body or the liver is fundamentally healthy or only slightly declined, and the food is temperate and decently administered in every way.

This is often seen in the teachings of natural philosophers through the example of wine that has not yet been trodden, and in the fourth book of *On the Use of the Parts* <note>Galen's "De iuvamentis membrorum"</note>. When food comes into the liver through the mesenteric veins, it has been prepared so that it is already close to the nature of blood. Then the liver begins its complementary work until it makes it pure blood. Finally, it shows how three superfluities are separated from the food: one which is dreg-like, like the skins of grapes, which departs as excrement <note>original: "stercus"</note>; another which is like the sediment of wine, which descends as melancholy <note>black bile</note>; and the remainder which is a certain frothy substance similar to choler <note>yellow bile</note>. This is also the view of **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a 10th-century physician</note> at the beginning of his work on urines. 

And **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician</note> says that when the substance of the chyle reaches the liver, the liver "cooks" it again and takes from it the four humors. But first, in every decoction <note>the "cooking" or ripening of fluids by body heat</note>—which is simultaneous in this case—there is a thing like froth, which is the over-cooked superfluity called choler; and a thing like sediment, which is melancholy; and a thing that is under-cooked, like phlegm; and the thing that is temperately cooked, which is blood. 

These authors all seem to have found sufficient evidence that the generation of humors in the liver happens in a simultaneous time. They also demonstrate that the actions of agents happen within a patient that is disposed to them. Therefore, although the matter seems to be one, it is nevertheless different because it is composed of different elements. And although the heat is generally one, it varies according to the application of the matter and other factors already mentioned. Thus, within a certain span of time, the heat will be able to imprint effects on matter disposed in different ways, leading to diverse movements. Thus, the humors are created distinct yet together in time, as the aforementioned points most clearly show. 

However, if the food is out of balance toward coldness and moisture, or toward coldness and dryness, and meets a liver that is similarly distempered, then—at least when the body has declined far from the temperance of food—the humors will not be generated at the same time, but successively, unless one extends the definition of "simultaneity" to a very long duration. And perhaps this is what **Galen** intended in the second book of *The Regimen of Acute Diseases*, where he says that phlegm is generated before the other humors, stating that the generation of phlegm always precedes in foods where phlegm is dominant over the generation of blood. Its conversion from food to blood happens with blood acting as a mediator. And we find that this happens not only in bad foods, but even in foods thought to be of the highest quality, such as bread and wheat (which is called *candarusum*) and fish.

In the fourth book of the same work, it is said: crude humors are generally all white and not yet perfectly digested by nature; rather, they are still raw. In the middle of them is blood, between the colors of these fluids and those which are called crude or phlegm. Those that are over-digested become choler; these others are not yet made, because certain humors exist before the food most certainly becomes blood. Some are, as it were, semi-digested, others entirely undigested, and others falling short of the nature of blood. Others, however, are made into blood at the very last. He adds that crude or semi-crude humors, whichever they may be, eventually generate blood. In these discussions, the order of prior and posterior generation of the humors in the liver and veins is expressly shown. Whence **Theophilus** <note>Theophilus Protospatharius, a 7th-century medical writer</note> says: some of these humors are made before the blood, such as phlegm and **ichor** <note>original: "ycor", referring here to watery blood</note>; others are made with the blood, such as red choler and melancholy. Pure, true blood is in the middle of both. And it is confirmed that just as humors exceed each other in generation by reason of greater quantity, so they do in terms of time. For because of a greater aptitude on the part of the matter, and the efficacy of the agent acting upon it, more of one humor is generated sooner than another. This is even seen in cases where no blood or very little is found, but the whole appearance is phlegmatic. In these cases, because the matter tends toward an excess of one imbalance, almost all the heat reaching it is converted into that specific humor. And it is the same when the body is excessively choleric or melancholic.

<summary>This page explores the physiological timing of humor production in the liver, arguing that while humors are produced nearly simultaneously in a healthy body, their generation follows a specific sequence based on heat and the quality of food.</summary>
<keywords>liver, digestion, chyle, blood, phlegm, choler, melancholy, Galen, Haly Abbas, decoction, physiological time</keywords>

...and a very proportionate nourishment, much more and sooner will be generated from a mass of even barley-water <note>ptisan: a medicinal drink made from barley, considered easy to digest</note>, from this than from another, by the proportion of quantity and the simultaneousness of the temperate breakdown; for just as the quantity of the generated humor is prevailing, with the proportion otherwise, so also the priority of the generation of the humor will precede the others. Hence, in the second book of *The Natural Faculties*, Galen states: in young and naturally hot people, honey anticipates becoming **bile** <term>bile: also called "choler," the hot and dry humor</term> rather than blood, which is why the assessment of nourishments is necessary. Honey in hot bodies tends toward turning into bile before it turns into blood; for which reason **Avicenna** also seems to agree when he said that in the liver, once all decoction <term>decoction: the process of "ripening" or "cooking" food into humors via heat</term> has taken place, the matter might perhaps become burnt, or pertain to "adustion" <note>adustion: the harmful "scorching" of humors due to excessive heat</note>, if the decoction has been excessive. If, however, the body is temperate and the nourishment is untempered, or the liver is likewise, then the humors will be generated better in time, though not entirely at the same time, nor very distinctly, but rather more or less according as the excess or equality is greater or lesser.

But if the humors are not generated in the liver, it can happen in two ways: either they are generated before they run into it, or after they have passed through it. Clearly, the first way happens in two manners, either by power—and then before the true humors are generated, the "superfluities" called **phlegmatic** by **Haly Abbas** and **Isaac Israeli** are produced. For all nourishment is converted into a certain sub-phlegmatic mucilaginous substance, and especially in the **mesaraic veins** <term>mesaraic veins: the vessels carrying nutrients from the intestines to the liver</term>, or particularly by the power of the complexion <note>complexion: the specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities</note> or no less by the nourishment itself. Whence **Galen**, in *On Black Bile*, demonstrating to us that the phlegmatic humor is generated from phlegmatic foods according to the first digestion in the stomach, just as the bilious and melancholic humors are transformed in the liver, and in that same digestion, the phlegmatic is turned into blood. Therefore, in the fifth book of *On the Preservation of Health*, he says a cold complexion soon generates phlegm in the stomach. But this does not seem possible because all natural phlegm must be white, according to the seventh book of the *Aphorisms*. Whence Galen in *On Black Bile* says: this humor, whatever it may be, is named phlegm only if it turns out white; but the aforementioned phlegmatic superfluities, at least when they reach the mesaraic veins, are turned into a certain redness. Whence in the fourth book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts*: the veins attracting food from the stomach, before they send it to the liver, prepare and alter it with an alteration close to the liver’s own—namely, into a slight nature of blood. Again, a humor is not a "superfluity" since the body needs it, but phlegm according to Haly is a superfluity. Furthermore, humors are said to be generated only in the liver.

Moreover, **Galen** in the second book of *The Natural Faculties* seems to say that the aforementioned superfluities ought not to be called phlegm, saying finally that one must understand the "indigestion" of phlegm as that which belongs to the second digestion, namely that which occurs in the veins of the liver; for he is accustomed to call the digestion of the liver the "digestion of the veins." For it would not properly be called that which is in the stomach, or if it were not generated according to the principle—namely the liver and its veins—but this humor escapes that, namely when it has not yet come into the liver. Thus, it seems to be generated in the liver and not before. To this, it must be said and first known: that "phlegm" is understood in two ways. One is "proper" phlegm, whose complexion is cold and moist, generated by a diminished decoction in the liver; whence in the second book of *The Natural Faculties*, a certain nourishment is called "semi-digested," whose color also pertains to whiteness, and this is what Galen and others usually mean by the name phlegm. There is another phlegm, "improperly" so-called—namely the **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid of digested food</term> of the stomach and the mesaraic veins mentioned before, because in it are imagined the coldness, moisture, materiality, tenacity, and viscosity of true phlegm. Wherefore in Question 13: that which is found in the stomach, or which is generated in it from the humor, is phlegm. The cause of this is that chyle is truly close to phlegm. And therefore Haly did not call this simply "phlegm," but a "phlegmatic superfluity."

Know also that it is proper for phlegm to be white, or certainly as "gypseous" phlegm <note>gypseous: thick and white like plaster or gypsum</note>; for it is white with its own specific color, namely a bounded or common translucency, like the rest of the phlegms. It is proper for **blood** to always coagulate, and everywhere, whether outside or inside, provided it leaves its proper place. But **bile** is characterized by bitterness.

Wherefore, perhaps according to **Haly** and **Avicenna**, it is not a proper division to split red bile into "natural" and "unnatural," since one should rather call it "bitter." For not all bile is joined to a red color, but to a bitter taste, and therefore it is not distinguished by taste. Nor does red bile have a difference from the difference of black bile, as some wish; since certain biles participate more in the color of melancholy <note>melancholy: the humor associated with black bile</note> than bile, such as "leek-green" and "burnt" bile. Truly, it is proper to black bile to be dark or blackish, along with the fact that it shares with phlegm the property of not coagulating (Galen, *On Black Bile*).

Therefore, regarding the first point, it must be said that although all phlegm is naturally white, it can sometimes be livid <note>livid: a leaden or bluish-gray color</note> from the mixing of other humors, as Galen says in the same place. For not only in the mesaraic veins are phlegmatic superfluities stained with the color of blood, but even the phlegm itself in the liver and veins; for blood, by its greater quantity and its purple-red color, overcomes and obscures all other humors (Haly). Regarding the other point, it should be said that phlegm is a superfluity resulting from a diminished decoction, and not by way of excess or impurity, like bile and melancholy. And this turns out useful, and is preserved for those who are working <note>laborantibus: those exerting themselves or perhaps the sick</note>, as is properly said in *On the Generation of Animals*; and that which is such a superfluity has a necessity. Although it may be a superfluity of the stomach, it is not a superfluity of the liver and the limbs; for it is not inconsistent for something to be a superfluity in respect to one thing, yet a useful and necessary thing in respect to another—just as the bile going to the gallbladder is superfluous to the blood passing through the veins, but not to the chyle and thereafter the intestines; and similarly for the melancholy that falls into the spleen. Regarding the other point, it should be said that although humors, according to the physician, are generated principally in the veins of the liver, they are generated in all other veins by the virtue <note>virtue: the inherent biological power or faculty</note> of the liver itself, as also touched upon in Distinction 91. Whence in the fourth book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts*: in the veins coming to the stomach, and in the veins coming to all the limbs, there flows something of the generative virtue of the blood. Regarding the last point, it has already appeared from what was said. Returning to the point, I say that humors are generated after they have passed the liver, or they receive their generation in the veins or clearly in the heart, by the virtue of the liver, or naturally, and thus it is still generated successively, since they are made from one another; whence Haly says: sometimes the four humors are generated in the veins.

<summary>This page explores the specific locations and stages of humor production, distinguishing between "proper" phlegm created in the liver and "phlegmatic superfluities" found in the stomach and mesenteric veins. It reconciles conflicting classical views on whether humors are defined by their color or their functional utility in different parts of the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical scholastic debate regarding the generation of the humors—blood, phlegm, bile, and melancholy. While the previous page discussed the timing of their creation, this section focuses on the biological "locations" of this process (specifically the heart versus the liver) and the hierarchy of the humors, arguing that blood is the primary and most necessary fluid.</meta>

And in the other members of the body. And the generation of these is sometimes natural, as when **blood** <note>original: "sanguis"</note> is generated from over-cooked **phlegm** <term>phlegm: the cold, moist humor; here viewed as a "raw" or "under-cooked" form of blood</term>, taking the place of blood in nutrition when blood is lacking. For phlegm is blood in potential, being deficient from it only by a shortened decoction <note>"decoction" refers to the metabolic "cooking" or processing of nutrients by bodily heat</note>. For phlegm is blood imperfectly cooked, or it is unnatural, as when they are rendered unnatural: such as **choler** <note>yellow bile</note> produced from subtle blood through over-cooking; **melancholy** <note>black bile</note> from thick blood; and eventually melancholy produced successively from choler. For all eventually turn into the primary matter of the humors, and from there a return is not possible, since what is already scorched or cooked cannot be made raw again: as seen in *Theories*, Book I, *The Colliget* <note>Averroes’ medical encyclopedia</note> Book II and III, and Book II of the *Rules*. This is indicated by the diversity of heat, being more or less expanded, and the transmutability of the adjoining matter, which is continually transformed irreversibly into form and dryness.

If, however, they are generated from the heart, or by its power, they are produced in the liver and also in the veins, since every power ultimately comes from the heart. And then, as has been declared, they are generated either at the same time or successively: and they are properly generated in the right ventricle of the heart itself, as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the preeminent Persian physician</note> wishes throughout his work, and especially in the third book *On the Parts*. Just as in an infant, the humors can be generated, for there blood alone exists in act <note>"in act" means fully realized or functional</note> since it is the only humor that provides nourishment; the others, however, are in him in potentiality <note>"in potentiality" means they exist as possibilities or seeds, but are not yet fully formed</note> according to the difference of quantity. 

That the heart is the generative principle of the humors within itself—the primordial principle—is proved by Avicenna, because the heart is the principle of the veins through which they run: Discourse 47. Furthermore, a greater quantity of blood is found in the heart, as if in a certain fountain-like principle. And therefore he says that no one should consider the liver to be the principle of the whole body, nor of the blood; for the liver does not have the reception of blood within itself in the same way the heart does. This is also demonstrated at length in *The Colliget*, Book II.

Thus, therefore, it appears how the humors are not generated in an infant, and how they are generated at the same time, and how they are not, and in which locations. In this distinction, Discourse 33 will clearly be of help. Know that what is generated from **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid formed in the stomach during digestion before it becomes blood</term> is for the most part simultaneous, but the generation of the humors is successive, as is the case with almost all the matter of the humors. 

Regarding the fourth point, it must be said that the arguments brought forward by Avicenna and **Averroes** <note>Latin: Ax./Axu. - referring to the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher</note> are now apparent, and similarly what was wondered at by **Galen** <note>the 2nd-century Greek physician</note> and **Theophilus**. To the other point, it must be said that the generation of this occurs in the veins and members, in which the processed humor is generated successively. To another point, it must be said that although the agent is varied, it is not excessively so; hence, because of the proportionality of this matter to the agent, different effects can be produced at the same time having a certain breadth. 

To another point, it must be said that it is not entirely the same in things generated by nature—where the heat is soothing and gentle—and in art, where the heat of fire is excessive. For nature is an internal principle sufficient to handle the matter throughout; art, however, is external and insufficient to touch the matter in all its parts: as in *The Generation of Animals* and the second book of *Physics*. For the heat of living things is regulated by the soul, but the quality of art is not of that kind. To another point, it must be said that in the same individual, the imperfect exists first, then the perfect; for an infant changes throughout life. But in those things that differ in number, it is otherwise: *Metaphysics* IX. Or, that each of these is at first imperfect in its own generation, and is then cooked and perfected.

To another point, it must be said that the generation of humors and fluids is similar in one respect, but distinct in another. For while the humors are sometimes generated successively and sometimes simultaneously, the fluids seem to preserve an order of priority and posteriority, such as the order of the stomach in relation to the parts of the liver. 

To another point, it has already been shown what must be said: when the generation is finished and ultimate, the humors are generated in the heart, but the diminished and primary generation occurs more in the liver. To another point, it must be said that **blood** is intentionally generated before the other humors. For blood alone is necessary, while the others are generated more for the "well-being" <note>"well-being" (bene esse) refers to optimal health rather than mere survival</note> and assistance of the generated body. Therefore, nature produced the liver more so that it might be a suitable instrument for the generation of blood than for the other humors; yet they are generated in it, even if blood and choler exceed and color the rest.

To the first point brought in opposition, what must be said was demonstrated before. And to the other points finally brought forward, it must be said that they conclude that the humors are generated at the same time when the body has been sufficiently tempered and the food is provided in a continuous manner.

***

§ Regarding the logic of what was said about the generation of **phlegm**, it likewise happens to be doubted: whether the blood generated from foods is of the same species as that which comes from phlegm. And it seems that it is not; because of different perfectible things, there are different perfections, since each one is separately ordered toward its own end. But phlegm and food are different perfectible things, as they differ in reality. 

Again: when humors are changed from their natural disposition, they are rendered unnatural (**Haly Abbas** <note>a 10th-century Persian physician</note> and Aristotle). But phlegm is a humor that will definitely be altered into a disposition beyond nature, while food is altered into a natural state, purely into blood. Furthermore, phlegm is a colder body, having its own proper complexion, while not a few foods are hot by nature and proportioned to human nature. Those things which differ so much do not seem to result in the same thing. Therefore, blood generated from foods and from phlegm does not exist as the same species.

On the contrary: wherever the true property of something is found, the thing itself is found, since the property follows it inseparably. But in blood generated from phlegm and from foods, the proper property of blood is found—namely, to coagulate (Galen, *On the Black Bile*). Therefore, the blood generated from both will return to the same specific nature. 

Regarding the first, it must be known that the question is heard in its own terms, as in Discourse 61. Regarding the second, it should be known that it is stated uniformly enough, although there is doubt in its proportionality, as will soon appear. Regarding the third, it must be known that blood generated from phlegm and from foods is of the same species, especially if it was generated in the liver. This is shown because the power of the liver, along with its heat, can arrange the materials of food and phlegm—which appear to differ—and prepare them to receive the same form of blood.

<meta>This page continues the technical scholastic investigation into the nature of biological substances. While the previous page focused on the internal hierarchy of humors (blood, phlegm, bile), this section moves into the specific "species" or essence of these fluids and transitions into a major medieval debate: spontaneous generation versus sexual reproduction.</meta>

What is signified by blood generated from monkshood <note>original: "napello"; a poisonous plant also known as wolfsbane</note> or some other foreign substance, and from egg yolk or wine, since from both the substance and its purpose, blood is constituted: <note>distinction 143</note>, appearing as the mistress <note>or "ruling humor"</note>. Furthermore, since the end <term>end: the final cause or ultimate purpose of a thing</term> and the form are the same in number—according to the second book of *Physics*—and the end of blood constructed from both sources is to nourish the body and to generate spirit <note>the "vital spirit" believed to circulate in the arteries to give life</note>. For blood is ordained toward these as its own proper end: <note>distinction 31</note>. Therefore, the blood generated from both is of the same species. The same similarly happens if it is transferred, such as into blood elsewhere than in the liver, because that will be by the power of the liver itself. For it is said in <note>distinction 29</note> that in the veins coming to the stomach and to all the members, there was some blood-generating power. And the truth of this is annexed to the appropriated genus in no small measure. Regarding the first point: although the things presented are diverse, they are the same through the power of the liver and heat, since the same thing disposes the matter and induces the form. And so it must be said to the second: for it separates with those things which possess the power to heat and alter. Regarding the other point, it must be said: that since **phlegm** is diminished and under-cooked blood, it can be altered by measured heat through further digestion, and not into something that is against nature, nor into anything other than being converted into blood. This is not the case with the two types of **choler** <note>yellow bile</note> that precede it in quality or substance: <note>distinction 30</note>.

<margin>B</margin>
On the occasion of this question, a much-hesitated-upon inquiry is introduced: whether those generated from sexual union <note>original: "coitu"</note> or animal combination, and those from **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the medieval theory of "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to arise from decaying matter</term> or by chance, are of the same species. And it seems that they are not. For in the first book of *On Generation*, it says that whichever do not come from animals but from corrupted matter, these generate another kind of animal, and that which is made is neither female nor male. Also, in the sixth book of *History of Animals*: there are many kinds of mice, concerning which a significant question is debated. Furthermore: whichever do not have the same "act" <term>act: the functional expression or biological operation of a species</term> do not fall into one species, for there is one act for the whole species. But those generated by combination and those by chance do not participate in the same act, since the former can most naturally generate, while the latter generate another kind like themselves but in a very minimal way; hence they are called "sordid animals." Whichever precede and are not "orphaned" <note>likely meaning lacking a clear lineage</note>, do not perform spontaneous or casual generation; what power do they have to hold another like themselves, as an animal generates an animal and a plant a plant? Also, in the eighth book of *Metaphysics*: for different matter, there is a different act. And the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the 12th-century philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were standard in universities</note> in the eighth book of *Physics* says: when the matter is diverse, the form will also be diversified. And the same author in the eighth book of *Metaphysics*: In natural beings, any form has its own proper matter; but the menstrual matter from which an animal is generated and putrefied matter are diverse and inappropriate. Again, it would be necessary, if some were made spontaneously, that they be of the same species by some determining natural heat. Likewise, the active power. Neither of these seems to be present, since that heat is celestial and common, as well as putrid, and not an agent that appears to be a partial impression of a form. Furthermore: how, since nothing acts beyond its own species except the heavens, which are incorruptible, can it generate something corruptible by appropriation? Therefore, those generated by sexual union and those by themselves <note>spontaneously</note> do not fall into one species.

On the contrary: if things that seem more distant are of the same species, then so are those that are less distant. But the heavens seem more distant among themselves than those generated by combination and by themselves. This is shown by the diversity of the spheres and stars, and the efficacy of their qualities with the difference of their centers, as shown by the **Lucidator** <note>likely Peter of Abano, a 13th-century scientist/physician</note> in distinction 4. Yet all the heavens are of the same species, according to the Commentator in the first book of *On the Heavens and the World*. Furthermore, since art imitates nature, just as it is in deeds and dispositions, so it is in the beings of nature, according to the second book of *Metaphysics*: but in those, the same species is made by the practical intellect and by chance, as in the acquisition of precious things. **Health** is produced both by nature and by art, as noted in the *Posterior Analytics*, and also in the second book, as being of the same species, as the act denotes. Similarly, therefore, it will be in the beings of nature. They are, therefore, of the same species: those produced by sexual union and those spontaneously. Regarding the first point, it must be known: those generated by combination or sexual union are said to be those that have a determined nature and a universal agent, such as the heavens; they also require a particular agent, such as a human. For "a human and the sun generate a human," according to the second book of *Physics*. Beyond the perfect animals, it is posited that the most universal of beings infuses the soul in the finishing, since only the intellect comes from "those things which are outside," according to the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*. Those generated by chance or spontaneously are those produced without a particular agent. But what "species" means was touched upon in distinction 65: for it is said there that a genus is not one certain thing, but that many things lie hidden around it. For equivocations <term>equivocation: when one word is used for two different things, like "bark" of a tree and "bark" of a dog</term> lie hidden in it, of which some are quite distant, like "dog" as an animal and "dog" as a star; others have some similarity among themselves, like a true human and a painted one; still others are very close in genus or similarity, so that equivocations are not seen in them, although they exist. Just as "body," speaking naturally, is said equivocally of the celestial body and this corruptible body, since both do not have one matter; they agree, however, in the logical genus. By similarity, "master" is said equivocally of a schoolmaster and a master of a household; strictly speaking, here the former is a teacher of students, the latter is the lord of others. Regarding the second point, it must be known: that **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> wished for those generated by sexual union and by putrefaction to be of the same species. And that each individual could come into a species in this double way. For he felt, in the book *On Floods* and the 15th book of *On Animals*, that after the corruption of a whole species by a flood, a plague, or by the will and vigor of the stars and the agent intelligence, the species could be procreated again from the elements. A female would not be required except for the "place" <note>the womb</note>, and thus a **matrix** <term>matrix: the womb or source-material</term> is not sought in generation except so that it might happen better, such as the embryo being nourished more perfectly. And because a perfect place for generation is rarely found in the elements due to their sudden transmutations, there was a little bit of a determined place in a pure matrix, yet without it, there is none. When a tempered place is found in the elements, generation will be perfected. The most profound signs of this are induced: for we see mice generated from putrefaction in some places, and finally lice multiplied; similarly fish and such. Also, **serpents** in tombs are generated more from the hair of women, especially because of their length.
