<meta>This page continues the technical scholastic investigation into the nature of biological substances. Having discussed the composition of blood and humors, the text now pivots to a major medieval scientific debate: spontaneous generation (birth from decaying matter) versus sexual reproduction.</meta>

...they are generated with a viscous humidity and multiplied by repeated mating where male and female are established. Furthermore, in the 15th book of *Animals*, he <note>Avicenna, a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and biology were central to medieval universities</note> says that he created <note>original: "fecit"; likely meaning observed or induced in an experiment</note> scorpions, which then generated other scorpions. Submitting this: you should not think in any way that a thing generated by a **generative power** <term>generative power: the innate biological ability to create life</term> could not also be generated in another way, since generation exists for the preservation of the species, even though the individual is female. He likewise testifies that he believes a certain beaver or "living creature" <note>original: "castorem sive biuarium"</note> was made in the stream of Joceon <note>A reference to a location in Avicenna’s writings</note> when it was there for a short time; it was at too great a distance for it to have traveled there from elsewhere. 

Furthermore, it has been seen that the head of one animal or another part—or even the whole animal—can be generated in the **womb** <note>original: "matrice"</note> of another, even if they differ from each other in size and gestation time, such as a human and a beast. For the stars, and specifically those of **Aries**, can cause monstrous things to be generated; and similarly with fish, just as opposites produce opposites. It has even been seen in some places that stones take on the forms of human parts. This is perhaps the sentiment of the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe</note>, as it is cited in book 1, chapter 10.

The **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the 12th-century Spanish-Islamic philosopher known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle</note>, however, in the 8th book of the *Physics*, goes against these views in five ways, positing that nothing of the same species is generated by both chance and mating.

**First**, regarding the human: he says that if a human were generated from something other than human seed, then that human would be "equivocal" <term>equivocal: a thing that has the same name but a different essential nature</term> compared to one generated from seed. Since the matter would be different, the form would also be different. If matter and form were not specifically appropriate to each other, then anything could be generated from anything, and matter would be idle and superfluous. 

**Again**, if a human were generated from the earth like a **mouse**, it would happen either always, or in most cases, or in few cases. If the first, then humans would not be generated from other humans at all. If the second, then humans would be generated from other humans only rarely and by chance. Thus, the same species would be produced both by nature and by chance, even though these are opposites.

Furthermore, if this were granted, the relationship of cause to effect would be destroyed, and necessity in nature would cease. He adds also that no species is created by chance, though something *similar* to it may be found by chance. In the 8th book of the *Metaphysics*, he says that things found by chance are **monsters**, not natural things. We have said these things because he says denying this would be self-evident. Aristotle says it is possible for a human to be generated from the earth over a long period of time. He adds in the 2nd book of the *Metaphysics* that this would happen more suitably in a womb. And this talk from a man who gives himself to such science is very foolish. 

Aristotle, however, as is more common, will be seen to take a middle path between these views. For not all things can be made by chance, such as "perfect" animals, since they require many things for their production and existence. Similarly, as was touched upon, certain "diminished" and imperfect things—like fish, mice, and the like—can be produced by the power of the stars from **putrefying matter** <term>putrefying matter: decaying organic material believed to be the "seed" for spontaneous life</term> in such a way that both views are partly true. What else will appear from what is to be said?

Someone might also say that both are the same "logical species," but not the same "natural species." The former considers general intentions, while the latter considers specific things. 

Regarding the third point, it should be known that some animals generated from **putrefaction** <note>spontaneous generation</note> are immediately of the same species, while others are generated with an intervening transformation. For there are some whose generation is perfect, such as those in whose generation a specific agent is involved. Others are imperfect, produced only from putrefaction, and they never generate offspring themselves, such as **eels**, earthworms, and the like. <margin>History [of Animals], book 5</margin> 

Others are intermediate. None of these produced by chance are immediately of the same species as those produced by mating, such as mice and snakes. Some are never made the same species as their producers, like **nits** <note>lice eggs</note> produced by lice. 

Others are truly intermediate, returning to the species of the producer through a transformation, like **frogs**. For they produce eggs, from which first come long "little frogs" <note>original: "ranunculi"; tadpoles</note> with a large head and a thin tail, in the manner of gudgeon fish. 

The same is true for **silkworms**. Hence in *History [of Animals]*, book 5: They become what are called *pliche* <gloss>butterflies</gloss> from *campae* <gloss>caterpillars/wrinkled worms</gloss>. In the summer and in standing waters, they are at first smaller than millet; then they become small growing worms. Then in three days they become small caterpillars. When they have grown, they hide and change their form and are called *kirisalides* <gloss>chrysalises</gloss>. These have a hard shell and are shaped like spiders or cocoons. After a long time, they break the shell and fly out as animals called *psiche* <note>Greek for "soul" or "butterfly"</note>. 

Thus, through many intermediate stages, those things which were smaller than millet eventually become *psiche* or **butterflies**. For the investigation of this truth, one must first touch upon the four universal causes for the generation of animals by chance: the decaying elemental matter, the celestial form or "image" from the **48 constellations** <note>The 48 constellations of the Ptolemaic system believed to influence earthly biology</note> acting as a specific material generation, such as for a snake, a scorpion, or similar things. Let the truth of mating be added: I say, therefore, that those born from propagation and those from chance—either immediately or eventually through the stages mentioned—are of the same species. This is shown in the 7th book of the *Metaphysics*. In form, they are from nature; for there, some things are the same whether they are made from seed or without seed. This identity is either numerical, general, or specific. Not the first, because things are numerically the same when their matter is determined by one quantity. Nor the second, for that would be unscientific, since everything participating in a species is an animal. Therefore, the identity will be **specific** <note>belonging to the same species</note>. 

And so Aristotle seems by this discourse to uproot the opinion of **Avicenna**, who said that whatever is made by mating can be produced by chance. **Averroes**, however, added the same, wishing that in no way can things produced by chance and things produced by propagation be united in one species. Also in the *Problems*, it is asked in section 10: Why are some animals produced not only from each other but also by chance, while others only from each other, such as humans and horses?

<meta>This page continues the technical scholastic investigation into the nature of biological substances and the debate surrounding spontaneous generation. The previous page established that some complex animals might be produced both by mating and by specific environmental conditions.</meta>

...that some things come about by chance alone, and others by both chance and purposeful connection. Furthermore, when **sufficient causes** <term>sufficient causes: the full set of conditions required for an effect to occur</term> are present, the identity of the species will be the same for those things whose species are naturally the same. Such cases are found in **spontaneous generation** <term>spontaneous generation: the medieval belief that life could arise from non-living matter like mud or rotting fruit</term> as well as in those produced by mating. This is because in both cases there is an **elemental heat** <note>original: "calidum elementale"</note> that prepares the matter; for it is not entirely something that can be putrefied. There is a distinction to be made here. Similarly, there is a celestial, life-giving illumination that brings living things into being and sustains them, and the power of the **form** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the organizing principle that makes matter into a specific thing, like a dog or a tree</note> is strongly determined in the act of production. 

The environment plays no small part in this, since nature operates according to the place it is in. For example, in places that are consistently warm and temperate, those things generated spontaneously are often more "perfect" than those produced by mating in opposite environments. This is shown by the multitude of both types when they propagate.

->**On Human Intellect and Nature**<-

Even among those beings that have souls, certain men are able by their own power of **intelligence** to join with the **Agent Intellect** <term>Agent Intellect: in medieval philosophy, a shared cosmic mind that allows humans to understand universal truths</term> and discover the middle terms of demonstrations. They are so gifted by the subtlety of their own natural genius—as **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Baly"; a famous Persian physician and psychologist</note> says of **Hippocrates**—that others, even with a teacher and a well-structured education, can never or only with great difficulty grasp what they understand. This is discussed in Aristotle's *On the Soul*; for the powers of the mind are conditioned by circumstances and vary greatly from one person to another. 

Furthermore, things that share the same shape and extension through spontaneous generation are of the same species. Since physical composition follows the **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body</term>—as argued in *Differentia* 63—this proves they have the same form or soul. Since the soul is the proper "instrument" of the body (as noted in *Differentia* 24), it causes the species. If we look at the commentaries on *On the Heavens and the Earth*, it is proven that if one star is round, so is another; therefore, those things which share a shape are of the same specific form. It has already been declared that shape is one of the essential things in celestial bodies because they are **animate** <note>The author refers to the common medieval belief that the stars and planets were moved by living souls or "intelligences"</note>. Just as one star is round because others of the same species are, in the same way, those things produced spontaneously or by mating that have the same shape and extension are entirely the same. This is confirmed because their shapes arise from qualities associated with perfected **substantial forms**. 

Again, things whose purpose and actions are the same are themselves the same, since all things are ordered toward a goal, and action leads us to the form, just as change occurs in matter (referencing *Differentia* 13). Since these appear entirely the same, those generated spontaneously and those by mating are of the same species.

->**Regarding Objections**<-

Regarding the fourth point in relation to the first, it should be said that although one type of generation might happen before the other, they result in the same species through the transformation that occurs in a proximate time. Or, one might say this is verified in certain "imperfect" creatures such as **insects** <note>original: "entcomis/enthomis"</note>. 

To the next point: "genus" is used here improperly to describe the variety of the manner and mode of generation, similar to how the **Parthians** and the **Indians** differ, or as it is said that "the human race lives by art and reason." 

Alternatively, one could say there are many genera of **mice**, extending the name to various kinds: 
*   Some live in trees, such as those called **dormice** <note>original: "nechele"; likely from the Greek for dormouse</note>.
*   Others live under the earth, such as **moles**.
*   Some live under the water on banks with longer tails, called **shrew-mice** <note>original: "da pāogari"; possibly a corruption of a local or Greek name</note>.
*   Some are called the great **Pharaoh's mouse** <note>Usually identified as the mongoose or ichneumon</note>, which have thick hair like an asp.
*   Others live in houses, and others in fields. 

Some of these seem to be of the same species in their nature, while others differ. 

To the other point, according to **Augustine**, it is not true of all spontaneously generated things that they cannot reproduce; rather, this only applies to some, such as the imperfect insects mentioned before. 

To the next point: although the matter of various insects may seem different, they are made the same by the **virtue** <term>virtue: an inherent power or celestial influence</term> that acts upon them. The necessity of the form is not taken entirely from the matter, but rather from the **end** (the purpose), which imposes necessity on the other causes. For the end is the "cause of causes."

To another point: although the heaven is incorruptible in its substance, it is "corrupted" continuously in terms of its position, motion, and light, through which it causes these effects on Earth. Similarly, due to the weakness of matter which cannot fully receive the divine influence, these lowest things are "weak and full of much turmoil," as Aristotle says in *On the Universe*. 

The argument taken from the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the 12th-century philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were standard in universities</note> would not proceed. Aristotle thought celestial bodies were the same in genus but different in species because of the diversity of their motions and the irregularity of their centers. This is also supported by their diverse actions: some are effectively hot, others cold, or moist, or dry; some are masculine and others feminine. The Commentator, however, rejects this, saying the stars do not actually "act" coldness, but rather produce various types of heat, which is clear in the case of the moon. 

But it is truer to say that although they are not formally these things, they are so effectively. Through motion and light, they all induce heat. It is also necessary that there be a balance of hot and cold among the elements, such as in the air, or in a more tempered mixture like the human body. Otherwise, water would not be maximally cold since the earth is, or the heat of some things would be like the coldness of others. Furthermore, their substances appear entirely different, such as the moon compared to others. In the third book of *On the Generation of Animals*, it is said the earth shares in the substance of the fourth element. Similarly, they are not continuous with each other, unlike the parts of an animal which are joined together. 

Therefore, it is perhaps better to say that the higher bodies are the same in genus but differ in species, especially those in different **spheres** <term>spheres: the transparent concentric shells that medieval astronomers believed carried the planets and stars around the Earth</term>. Those in the same sphere, such as the stars in the eighth sphere, were thought by the Commentator to be the same because they are all round. But one might not want to apply specific identity to other round things, because if they were the same in genus and species, they would be composed of different matter and form, and thus would be subject to generation and corruption. They would have to come from something, meaning there would be bodies prior to them, which is impossible. Someone might hinder this by saying celestial bodies have matter, but of a different kind than the matter subject to change here below. For it is said in *On the Heavens and the Earth* that the heaven is a unique thing made of matter, which is verified in three ways, even calling the whole heaven a single unit...

...**Metaphysics** <note>original: "metha."</note> distinguishes a twofold intellectual matter: namely, that which is stable and that which is flexible. Whence **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ax." - a common scribal abbreviation for Aristoteles</note> says that celestial things often do not have matter, or that the term is used equivocally. In the eighth book of his *Metaphysics*, he twice states that it has been declared in **natural science** <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Physics*</note> that the heavens have "local matter" (or matter in regard to "where") and yet do not have matter that can be generated or corrupted. Therefore, we see that the heavens are not composed of **matter which is in potentiality** <term>potentiality: the capacity to become something else</term> and **form which is in act** <term>act: the fully realized state of a thing</term>. This statement is certain according to the distinction of the **reconciler** <note>original: "xificati" - likely referring to a commentator who "reconciles" conflicting texts, possibly Peter of Abano</note>. Concerning this, in the eighth book of Aristotle's *Metaphysics*: in eternal natural things or substances, there is another logic. For perhaps some things do not have matter, or not such matter, but only in terms of movement through a location. And in the twelfth book of the same: all things that are transformed have matter, but of a different kind; and of eternal things, those which are not capable of being generated but are moved by **rotation** <note>original: "latione" - referring to the circular motion of the spheres</note>, do indeed have matter, but not of the generatable kind. But from where? For the truth is that there is one matter of all things considered in itself through the **privation of all form** <term>privation: the absence of a quality that should naturally be present</term>, but it is diversified by logic. Let these things, therefore, which have been said incidentally in the course of the discourse, be sufficient, since the consideration of them is not the proper focus of this work; they have been handed down sufficiently in the tenth part of the **Exposition of Problems** <note>Referring to a commentary on Aristotle's *Problems*</note>.

### Whether the Veins Possess Digestive Power

The cause of what was said—that there is some power of generative blood in the veins—is whether a **common digestion** <term>common digestion: the general processing of nutrients for the whole body, rather than for a specific organ</term> occurs in the veins. And it seems that it does, according to **Galen** in many places; he expresses that a second digestion occurs in the veins. Also, in the text on the **property of health** <note>original: "re sa." - *De regimine sanitatis*</note>: one must hear that the digestive power is not only in the stomach or the veins or according to the liver, but also according to each individual part. And with Aristotle asserting that in them a third digestion is perfected, and a fourth in the individual members. And this is supported because in the first book of the **Prognostics** <note>Referring to Hippocrates' *Prognostics* or a commentary on it</note>: I showed in the book *On Sperm* that blood is often seen in the veins from which a man is nourished, preceding and receiving some mutation toward the generation of sperm; this, however, is perfected by digestion. Furthermore, in the first book of **On Sleep and Wakefulness**: when nourishment enters from the outside into the designated places, evaporation occurs toward the veins; there, however, it is changed and turns into blood, and goes to the primary organ, namely the **heart**; but this conversion does not happen except through digestion.

Furthermore, that which produces a common superfluity also provides a common benefit; but such is the nature of the veins. Whence it is said in the sixth book of **Accidents** <note>original: "de accidenti vi." - likely Galen's *De accidentium causis*</note>: the superfluity of the digestion of the veins is threefold: one is **red bile** <note>original: "colere ru." - cholera rubea</note> or dregs; the second is **black bile** <note>original: "colere nigre"</note>; and the third is wateriness. And it is first said in *On Health*: there is a superfluity of the arteries and veins, just like the whey in curdled milk. Furthermore, digestion is a certain perfection since it is a completion by one's own natural heat. But this is given in the veins, because the veins are the place of the blood (from the first book of *On Sleep and Wakefulness*). Moreover, a place has a **preservative power** <note>original: "uirtutē saluatiuā"</note>, as appears in the fourth book of the *Physics*. Indeed, I saw the principle of generation, as **Porphyry** says: whence nature gives as much of the form as follows from the place (from the fourth book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*). Likewise, that which can do more can also do less; but the veins can generate blood, which seems like more than simply digesting it; for this is to transform it, while the other is to give it form. Whence it was said it was in the veins coming to the stomach and the rest. They also originate from the heart, in which is the root and perfection of digestion alone, as of other actions (from **Difference 38** <note>original: "drā xxxviii"</note>). Also, because phlegm especially passes through the veins with the blood, so that it may supply the defect of the latter when the members lack nourishment. For there is some semi-digested nourishment. This, however, must be perfected by digestion, which does not seem to belong to anything but the veins, since it does not remain afterward in the liver. Thus, there will be a common digestion in the veins.

**On the contrary**, physicians and Aristotle specifically are in agreement, placing only three digestions: namely, of the stomach, of the liver, and of the members. Furthermore, for one member there is a single act (according to **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "baly."</note>), at least a certain and principal one as is sought here, since it proceeds from a being which is unique through the single form of each thing. But the act of the veins is to serve the liver by defending it; whence in the third book of **On the Parts** <note>Aristotle's *De Partibus Animalium*</note>: the veins are the cause of everything that is distributed in the body. Again, digestion—and especially common digestion—is achieved through heat and moisture; but the veins are **cold and dry** <note>In the humoral system, veins were considered "nervous" and thus lacked the active heat of the liver or heart</note>, since they are made of "nerves" <note>In medieval anatomy, "nervous" often meant fibrous or sinewy</term>. Therefore, the veins will not perform common digestion. Regarding the first point, indeed, it should be known what a vein is, or what digestion is, and how many types of it there are, as shown in chapters 47 and 50. However, common digestion is that which is ordained principally toward the proper end of the digester, but naturally toward the nourishment of every part, such as that of the stomach and the liver. For these parts labor for the whole body, though more directly for themselves. **Proper digestion** <note>original: "Propria quide ē."</note> is that which each individual part has, into which common digestions are ordered, either immediately (like that of the liver) or mediately (like that of the stomach). These alone are sufficient in more perfect animals even to transform nourishment into parts; nor can it be perfected without one of them, as **dropsical diseases** <term>dropsy: an old medical term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</term> especially show; for one is sometimes not able to correct the other.

Regarding the second point, it should be known: you will find that there are four digestions, even common ones, as you will find in the first book. You ought to know that blood, and that which flows with it, has a **third digestion** in the veins; and when it is divided into the members, and each one receives its own nourishment, it has a **fourth**. But this opinion is clearly felt in the third book of the **Colliget** <note>The *Colliget*, a medical encyclopedia by Averroes</note> thus: "It seems better to me that a third digestion should not be placed in the veins, as men whom you know propose, for the reason that the blood in them does not pass into another form, as happens in the stomach, liver, and other members." Galen, however, in many places ascribes the second digestion to the liver, yet in some he seems to attribute it to the veins alone. What wonder will arise from these things will appear from what is to be said. Regarding the third point, it must first be shown that no digestion can simply be perfected in the veins as a common one. Secondly, however, how Galen's discourse is to be heard, let it be shown, and from this the act of the veins will appear further. Regarding the first of these, it should be known that the second common digestion happens in the liver, as all physicians feel, and not directly in the veins; whence in the third book of *On the Parts*: "The liver is for the sake of digestion." Which is shown because for digestion, and especially common digestion, two or six things are required. One indeed is that there be a digestive organ having a cavity, in which that which is to be digested may be contained and carried...

<meta>This page continues the transition from the previous discussion on celestial matter to the specific biological mechanisms of the human body. It focuses on the scholastic and Galenic understanding of the "three digestions"—in the stomach, the liver, and the tissues—to explain how food is transformed into living substance.</meta>

For **digestion** <term>digestion: from the Latin *digestio*, referring here to the "cooking" or transformation of food</term> is truly perfected in rest (**Difference 61**) <note>original: "drā lxi" — likely referring to a section in Peter of Abano’s *Conciliator*, a famous medieval medical text</note>. To this process, a power is innate, utilizing qualities, especially heat and moisture. Furthermore, a specific object is determined in a certain operation, and according to the physician, it is essentially transformed. From this determined change, a surplus is produced. Along with this, according to many, the body is nourished more immediately because what is digested is within the organ itself, just as the **stomach** <note>original: "venter"</note> possesses it.

For the stomach is a hollow organ in which the food rests; as a determined object, it is digested by a power implanted in it and by many aids—as has been touched upon—and is essentially transformed. Everyone knows that once the digestion of the **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid of digested food in the stomach and intestines</term> is performed, at least the internal coat of the stomach is nourished by its purer part (**Difference 53**). It also produces a surplus that exits by way of the intestines.

These processes are also found in the **third digestion** <term>third digestion: the final stage where blood is assimilated into the actual tissues/members of the body</term> of the members. For there are parts there possessing cavities and pores in which the food rests; having already been elaborated, it undergoes digestion again. By a twofold power, that which was previously red <note>i.e., the blood</note> passes over into whiteness, being transformed so that it may be rendered similar to the body. It also has surpluses, such as the mucus of the brain, semen, sweat, filth, hair, nails, and that hidden process called **insensible transpiration** <note>original: "transpiratoēʒ" — the release of vapors through the skin</note> by physicians, which is without a specific name.

Because of how it is digested, all agree that the body is nourished more immediately. This is found no less in the **liver** <note>original: "epate"</note>. For the liver itself is an organ possessing cavities and fissures, in which the chyle resides—brought there by the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: "mesaraicis"</note> as a distinct object—and by its own power, it is converted, being transformed in substance and color into blood.

For the substance of the liver is near to the nature of blood. According to the fourth book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts* <note>Referring to Galen's *De usu partium*</note>, as was said before, the liver was created red so that it would be suitable for the generation of blood, just as the breasts and testes were produced white so they might procreate milk and semen. Just as we mentioned with the stomach, the liver also has its surplus: urine, as well as **yellow bile** <term>colera: yellow bile, one of the four humors</term> and **black bile** <term>melancholy: black bile</term>, and the watery part of the urine which nourishes the blood. In this, the liver is said to perform its primary operation, as touched upon in **Difference 33**.

In the veins, however, none or very few of these things are found. For even though they possess a cavity, what is contained in them is not digested there, but rather it is led along for transport. Thus it is said that they serve the liver; nor is there a transforming power within them, as their very substance and **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in an organ</term> denote. They have no other object than the blood from the liver’s digestion. Nor is the blood essentially transformed within them; rather, it remains continually under the nature of blood within them. Whence, in the third book of *On Foods*: "Digestion which occurs in the liver and veins is blood-making."

Nor are the veins nourished by it yet, until the moisture is whitened, since they are **spermatic parts** <term>spermatic parts: tissues believed to be formed from the "seed" (like bone or vessels), which are white and cold</term>. Furthermore, no surplus is assigned to the digestion of the veins themselves. Thus, although **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> claims a common third digestion occurs in the veins, the surpluses of these digestions do not remain there after resolution. Moreover, everything that is generated—at least in univocal generation—comes forth similar to what generated it. For the principles testify to the origins, and the liver is proportioned to the blood since it is essentially congealed blood, generated from menstrual blood (**Theoretical medicine, Book 3**). It has been said that its color is red, just like that of blood. Its great size and marvelous organization also show this, whereas almost nothing of this exists in a vein.

Therefore, a common digestion does not happen in the veins, but only in the liver. Regarding this, it should be known that veins are twofold: some fall into the construction of the liver, while others are outside it. Those that are within are more subtle than the rest, so that the power of the liver can more immediately meet that which is being digested. Whence, in the fourth book of *On Usefulness*: "The body of the liver is the primary instrument for generating blood; the closer the food is to it, the more swiftly it will be altered into its nature." It will better receive the form of blood, and therefore the coats of the veins in the liver are thinner than the coats of the veins in the rest of the body. For these contain what is being digested immediately within themselves by the vigor of the liver, just as a **cauldron** <note>original: "lebes"</note> cooks the pottage. But the act of cooking is often attributed not to the fire that cooks, but to the cauldron itself.

Thus, digestion is often attributed not to the liver as the principal organ, but to the containing instrument. However, those veins which exist outside the substance of the liver are more remote from this action; they have thicker coats because they are far from the substance that generates blood. Nevertheless, by the power of the liver, it is felt that some blood-generating power exists in all veins, especially in the **mesenteric** ones. Whence in Book 3, Chapter 14: "The liver is the member that generates blood, although the mesenterics sometimes convert chyle to blood by some conversion because of the liver’s power within them."

Thus, the mesenteric veins prepare the digestion for the liver, just as **mastication** in the mouth prepares the food for the stomach’s digestion (**On the Parts of Animals**). For the division of food into small parts easily allows the operation of heat. Just as the vessels of the semen, according to **Aristotle**, cooperate in the digestion of the testes. Therefore, the other carrying veins dispose the blood into parts for the third digestion rather than adding anything else to it, especially toward the skin and extremities. **Aristotle** perhaps felt this by placing a common third digestion in them. For what is digested in these parts takes the form of a humor and partakes of moisture. This is indicated by **hectic and putrid fevers** which sometimes occur there (**Difference 93**). Or perhaps Aristotle is moved by the fact that with the blood through the veins, **phlegm** <note>original: "flez̄"</note> is carried, which is placed there to be converted into blood; this conversion, it seems, should happen nowhere else but in the veins. But I say this happens by the contingent power of the liver and not the veins. Or perhaps he posits this common third digestion observing his own method of expanding upon the sayings of others. Thus, digestion only occurs principally in the liver; in the veins, it occurs in no way through their own efficiency.

<meta>This page continues the technical exploration of the "three digestions." Having previously defined the stomach's role, the text now focuses on the liver's blood-making power, the role of the veins, and the critical scholastic question of whether a later stage of digestion can "correct" the failures of an earlier one.</meta>

...the number of **digestions**. However it may be thought that the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritu" — in medieval medicine, a subtle substance that carries life-force</note> enters into it. For since it is of a weak offshoot, as if it were a healthy thing, its substance is coagulated and its color even tints the blood; it is as if something were mixed into it, like a sponge being stained by a dye as the liquid passes through it. Along with this, there is in the **liver** <term>liver: the "epar" or "hepar," considered by Galenists as the site of blood production</term> a transformative and **blood-making power** <term>blood-making power: the "virtus sanguinifica"</term>. Because such a power could not contain a thin liquid within itself, there were many very thin, dispersed venules within it, so that the contact with the **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky, partially digested food from the stomach</term> would be almost immediate. In these vessels, the chyle would be contained. For Nature here, as in other things, balances out the excellence of its commands.

To confirm this, it must be said that this is the series of the Arabic translation, which universally is found to be not rarely distorted and faulty; for this reason, I have translated it directly from the Greek. I have shown, moreover, in the discussion concerning **semen** <note>original: "spermante"</note>, that in the tunics of the vessels which nourish the testes, a transformation of blood into the generation of sperm often appears. For it is not fitting that the tunics of the vessels themselves be nourished by anything else. It appears, therefore, from this sequence, that digestion does not happen in the veins of which we speak, but rather in the "third" digestion of the members, from which the testicles are nourished. Regarding the other point, it must be said that the wateriness of urine is a surplus of the digestion of the veins, as they exist in the liver, and by the liver's own power, as was explained above; for sometimes the digestion of the veins is called **urine**, for it is generated in the liver along with the other humors. Regarding the next point: a place has a "preserving" power and a "being-giving" power. This is not materially from itself—as is the case with the extreme surface of a container—but rather formally, receiving it from a "herb" <note>likely a reference to herbal medicine or a specific botanical analogy</note> according to such an appearance or proportion. So it is with the veins: although they house the material for making blood, they receive the formal power to do so from the liver. Regarding the next point: that which seems to be in the veins regarding the change of blood more truly does not belong to the veins themselves—even the **mesaraic** <term>mesaraic: the mesenteric veins carrying nutrients from the intestines to the liver</term> ones—but is granted to them by the liver, as has been seen. Where one thing exists because of another, it is essentially one in both places. For the nature of the veins is to be "earthy" in their own right; they are like little streams which, being parts of a whole, also assist in some way, though they bear the mark of being lesser. It must also be said that although the veins originate from the heart—in which the principal digestion of blood and spirit is perfected—nonetheless, digestion is not completed in them, but they rather serve as a "delivery" system, as cited from **Avicenna** <note>original: "Ay."</note>. Regarding the final point, the answer is apparent: for if the veins translate **phlegm** into blood in some way, that happens from the power of the liver and not the veins.

<margin>1</margin>Since it was said before that the first "cooking" is in the stomach, or that phlegm is generated from the humors within it (which can eventually be turned into blood by a further digestion), the question arises: can a subsequent digestion **correct** the preceding one? It seems that it can. Again, just as one member relates to another member, so shall one act relate to another act, since they proceed from the same source; but one member can correct and temper another, just as the brain is positioned opposite the heart to temper it (**Difference 25**).

Furthermore, if the liver is a weak member compared to the heart (according to book 7 of *On Generation*), it can work against the heart's heat by 

---

lessening it. Much more, then, can a strong liver (in relation to the belly) stand in the way of the belly's act—namely, digestion—and lead it to a more perfect state, as the dialectical canon confirms. This is valid in the **Tegni** <note>original: "tegnī" — referring to Galen's *Ars Medica*</note>. And it is supported by the fact that the liver is hot and moist by nature, through which all digestion is perfected; thus, it tempers the stomach's digestion, which naturally tends toward coldness and dryness, and strengthens it. Again, when several things are ordered toward a single act, the stronger ones can amend and supply the defect of the weaker ones. This is how the liver and the digestive organs can relate to the stomach; when one has slipped into coldness and dryness, the other can bring it back to heat and moisture. Also, a weak agent can act upon well-disposed matter more strongly than it can upon ill-disposed matter, since every agent requires a certain disposition of the material. But the stomach receives matter that is crude and undisposed. The liver and its members, however, receive what is already disposed. Thus, the following digestion can correct the preceding one. 

However, the opposite of this seems to be the view of **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note> in his *Aphorisms* and *On Aliments*. In his *On Accidents*, he intends that if the operation of digestion is three-fold—in the stomach, the liver, and the members—it is similarly damaged in three ways: by transformation, weakness, and corruption. This is also indicated in the first book of the *Crises* and in many other places. For example, in *On Regimen*: it is impossible for bread that is lacking "breath" <note>likely referring to being unleavened or poorly baked</note>, or meat or legumes that are imperfectly cooked, to be kindly digested in the stomach. The same logic applies to those things which the stomach has processed poorly: those in the veins, which were badly constructed from the beginning, have the same relationship to the food in the stomach as the food in the veins (not rightly digested) has to the food in the flesh. For the stomach does not diligently digest external things, nor the veins those from the stomach, nor the flesh those from the veins, when they have not been well-prepared. Hence **Isaac** <note>original: "Ysaac Israeli," a 10th-century Jewish physician</note> says in his *On Urines*:

> While the food has not been decocted and digested in the stomach and liver, it becomes impossible for it to be digested in the members and assimilated into their substance.

Similarly, if the food is imperfectly digested in the stomach, arriving raw at the liver, it does not receive further cooking there, nor is it changed into healthy blood. Instead, it remains clear, rosy, and raw, so that when it arrives at the members, it cannot be digested by them, nor assimilated into their substance. This is also indicated in the first and third books: although it may happen that much and superfluous nourishment is digested in the stomach, it is rarely digested in the veins; rather, it remains raw in them, stretching and sometimes bursting them. And in the third book, section 14: the weakness of the liver is caused when the stomach sends chyle to it that is not well-digested, but rather weakly or corruptly digested. And as far as I have perceived, no one holds the opposite view. Furthermore, every primary cause flows more strongly into its effect than a secondary cause does; but the digestion of the stomach is primary in respect to that of the liver and members.

It cites major authorities like Galen, Avicenna, and Isaac Israeli to emphasize that each stage of the bodily process relies on the success of the one preceding it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the "three digestions," specifically addressing the scholastic question of whether the liver (the second digestion) can "correct" the errors or deficiencies of the stomach (the first digestion). It builds upon the previously established roles of the stomach and liver in the metabolic process.</meta>

...of the **members** <note>original: "membrorum" — referring to the third stage of digestion occurring in the tissues and organs themselves</note>. Likewise, in things that are essentially ordered, if the first is taken away, the subsequent one is also removed. It is not that the same rules apply to all causes, but there are three digestions of this kind, essentially established so that one is contained in an orderly fashion beneath the other.

For all of them are ultimately ordered toward the restoration of what has been lost. Furthermore, if the stronger agent fails, the mixture becomes even more defective and weak. But let it be supposed that the **stomach** <term>stomach: "venter," literally belly, but here specifically the organ of primary digestion</term> fails, which digests not only by heat and moisture—qualities inherent to its very substance—but also because of the neighboring parts that provide it with a great deal of heat and moisture, as is usually the case. Similarly, since the **liver** <term>liver: "epar," considered the primary organ for making blood</term> is a principal organ, hot and moist, it participates more perfectly than almost all other parts in a more perfect digestion. Therefore, the question is whether a subsequent digestion can correct the preceding one.

Concerning the first point, it must be known before all else what the essence of digestion is, and what nutrition is (as discussed in distinctions 30 and 56). By "to correct," I understand not only when one digestion supports another slightly, but when one more perfectly corrects and amends the other; just as when a sick body is restored to its original nature. Regarding the second point, it should be noted that authorities, as it appears, commonly feel that a subsequent digestion cannot correct a preceding one. This perhaps applies to bodies that are sufficiently healthy, or to those experiencing specific accidents, according to the teachings of **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note>; however, it is rare that such a thing is digested, as will be more fully wondered at from what is to be said.

Regarding the third point, it must be known that a body in which such digestions are observed will either be sufficiently healthy, or in a lapsed state, or **imbalanced** <term>imbalanced: "discrasia," a medical state where the four humors are out of proportion</term>. If it is the first case, I say that a later digestion can in no way correct an earlier one, all other things being equal. For if the act of the first digestion is deficient—which altered the food more for the second stage than the act of chewing did for the first—then the subsequent digestion can do nothing to correct the prior one, as is indicated by the lesson introduced. 

However, if the body is in a lapsed state, it either declines uniformly and proportionately into one of the eight **imbalanced temperaments** <term>complexions: "complexionum," the specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry in an individual</term>, or it declines with a distinct lack of proportion. If the first is true, then this lapse will either be slight, exceeding its healthy temperament by a little, or it will be great. If it is slight—and especially if it tends toward qualities that are not specific to the digestion of that member—then the preceding stages will suffice. But concerning the specific digestive qualities: for instance, if the stomach's digesting power ought to be hot in the middle of the first degree, and the liver is at the start of the second degree, then the digestion of the liver can certainly correct that of the stomach. This is partly because the liver is strengthened by its heat, and partly because with this slight excess in the liver, the **blood-making power** <note>original: "uis sanguifica"</note> is preserved, and also because a stomach that has lapsed only slightly does not weaken digestion so much that it fails to provide the proper disposition for the food, as the prior reasons suggest.

But if the lapse is very great, then I say that the later digestion can by no means correct the preceding one; rather, the preceding one corrupts what is being generated, as taught by **Galen** <note>original: "P.A." — likely referring to Galen of Pergamon</note>. For example, if the stomach's heat is at the lowest level of the first degree, and the liver is intensely hot in the

---

third degree. For you should know that with excessive heat and dryness, the liver cannot sufficiently flourish with its **blood-making power**, since an exceeding imbalance of this kind corrupts the very act of that power. Furthermore, a liver that is too hot draws to itself the meager heat of the stomach—just as a greater force overpowers a lesser—so that the stomach, being under the influence of the liver and deprived of heat, can digest very little. Thus, the stomach will prepare for the liver a very poor **chyle** <term>chyle: "chilus," the milky fluid of digested food before it becomes blood</term> that is raw and corrupt. The overly hot liver will then attract this chyle even before the proper time, so that blockages and weakness arise, as if the liver itself were struck. 

For this reason, one may see many such conditions occur, such as **dropsy** <note>original: "hydrops" — swelling caused by fluid retention</note>, **scabies**, **leprosy** <note>original: "lepra"</note>, and similar defilements. For these bodies are so imbalanced that there is no harmony in their opposition; rather, they incite injury rather than correcting themselves, as the subsequent points persuade us. 

But if the body is unevenly or disproportionately lapsed—as when one of its parts declines toward a temperament similar to its nature, or away from it, beyond what its proper temperament should be, and another part declines toward the opposite—then the lapse is twofold. This is because it declines from its opposite, and also because it does not match or coincide with the other parts in a single shared nature. For example, when the heart is cold or extremely hot, and the brain is hot or very cold, or the liver is drier, or the liver is cold (as mentioned in the **Art of Medicine** <note>original: "tegni" — referring to Galen's *Ars Medica*</note>, book 6, on the preservation of health). 

Then, as was said, if the lapse is slight, it can indeed be corrected. For instance, when the liver is hot in the beginning of the second degree, or a little more, and the stomach is cold and dry in the opposite direction. For a liver that is so potent in its intense digestive heat and moisture can bring about correction for a stomach that is lowered in heat and dryness. In these temperaments, the **chyle-making** and **blood-making** powers are still preserved, especially when the stomach is small (requiring small and frequent meals, as in the *Art of Medicine*), beloved by the liver, and the liver itself is sufficiently large. This has already been argued with no small amount of proof. 

However, if the lapse is great—for example, if the liver is hot and dry in the third degree, while the stomach is cold and dry or moist in the same degree, or even more oppositely disposed—the subsequent digestion will not correct the preceding one, but will instead corrupt it. On the contrary, as shown in the lesson, since these temperaments are adverse and excessive, the transformative powers of the members are not sufficiently preserved. 

What has been said regarding the digestion of the stomach and liver should be heard similarly regarding that of the members; one must judge the intermediate temperaments between these extremes of the organs with moderation. Regarding the fourth point, it must be said that the arguments proceed in their own ways; for they are logical and conclude with some portion of the truth. For **phlegm** <note>original: "flegma"</note> that is natural in the stomach, or carried there, if it is not corrupted, is material suitable to be converted into blood by further digestion. For the digestion of the stomach did not fail entirely regarding it, especially when the fault was on the part of the food, as has been seen. To the other points, it must be said that a member corrects a member, and an act corrects an act, provided there has been no excess.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the "three digestions." ...in final natures, so much so that the act destroys the **virtue** <note>original: "virtutis" — here meaning the functional power or capacity of an organ</note>. To the other point, it appears similarly through this. To another, it must be said that not just any disposition suffices for the digestion of the **liver and members** <note>original: "hepatis & membrorum" — referring to the second and third stages of digestion</note>, but rather one that is proper and proportioned to their actions; this is often lacking, as is seen not rarely. Regarding the authorities of the opposing side, we have also seen what must be said. To the second point, it should be said that the preceding digestion does not fail entirely, but still retains the power to prepare matter for the liver and members. Also, although the primary cause flows more extensively, it is not as intensive or particular as the secondary cause, regarding the action in its broader sense. To the other point, it should be said that the **stomach** <term>stomach: "uenter," referring to the primary digestive cavity</term> works upon matter that is very raw and unprepared, which is not the case for the others.

## DISTINCTION XXX.

<margin>1</margin> **That blood alone does not nourish**, by the authority of almost all physicians. Furthermore, it is seen in general "utilities" <note>likely referring to Galen’s *On the Usefulness of the Parts*</note> that nothing in the body is purely simple; rather, all **members** <term>members: "membra," the various organs, tissues, and parts of the body</term> share in their materials, and all materials are found in all members. These materials are the nutritious **humors** <term>humors: "humores," the four vital fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</term>. Therefore, since nutrition occurs from "like to like," it must come from all of them. Again, concerning human nature and the third [book] of *The Elements*: other humors are found in the blood, as is even seen in **bloodlettings** <note>original: "fleubotomis" — the common medieval medical practice of phlebotomy</note>; these are not placed there in vain. Furthermore, since nourishment is finally transformed into the thing nourished, if blood alone nourished all members in their natures, forms, virtues, and other dispositions, the parts would be similar to one another. But this is false, since a great diversity appears among them. Likewise, nutrition is the assimilation of that which nourishes to that which is nourished, according to the first book of *Natural Philosophy*. Since some members are **choleric** <note>related to yellow bile</note>, others **melancholic** <note>related to black bile</note> or **phlegmatic**, it was necessary for specific humors to be present in their nourishment, besides those nourishing via blood. Moreover, as is commonly felt, the inner lining of the stomach (as discussed in Distinction 53) is nourished immediately from the mass of **chyle** <term>chyle: "chilosa," the milky fluid of digested food before it becomes blood</term>, which is not yet transformed into blood; therefore, it does not seem that blood alone nourishes, and consequently, it does not constitute the embryo alone. On the contrary, **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ar."</note> says in many places that blood alone nourishes, either by itself or simply, immediately, or solely. And **Avicenna** <note>original: "Au."</note> with certain physicians in Distinction 28 says the same. Furthermore, it is a property of a good humor that it alone, or with another, should nourish; but blood is the best of the humors. This distinction belongs to the art [of medicine] and not merely to the force of speech, pertaining to how they join together; hence **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "baly," refers to the Persian physician Haly Abbas</note> in Distinction 33 says: Pure blood is the matter of nourishment for the members. **Etienne** <note>original: "Eti." — likely referring to Stephen of Antioch or a similar commentator</note> says phlegm does not nourish, since it is cold, moist, and only a semi-digested nourishment; for such a task requires heat and moisture, just as life does. Nor do yellow or black bile nourish, because that which truly nourishes must be carried into the veins. But the biles do not reach the veins in which the blood resides, nor does the body nourish itself with them, according to the fifth book of *The Utilities*. Hence, in the book of *Natural Science*, **Erasistratus** <note>an ancient Greek anatomist</note> is mistaken in positing that yellow bile passes through the veins with the blood; therefore, blood alone shall nourish, and the animal shall be sustained by it. **Avicenna**, however, would say that blood alone nourishes the "bloody" members, but not

the others. Regarding the first point, it must be known that blood is a hot and moist humor, sweet in taste, foul in smell, and the least likely to coagulate on its own. One type is in the **arteries**, which is a thin liquid, clear red tending toward yellow; the other is in the **veins**, which is much more red in color. The multiplicity of this will be seen in the present distinction and also in Distinction 33. According to **Galen**, the act of nutrition, or nutrition itself, is the assimilation of that which nourishes into the proper quality and substance of that which is nourished. In this assimilation, **apposition** <note>the placing of nutrients next to the tissue</note> and **union** <note>the final integration into the tissue</note> must precede it, since the later stages cannot be separated from the earlier ones. Nutrition is also the restoration of some similar substance in place of that which was previously emptied. Therefore, its opposite is without natural dimension. Because such an act or effect carries a relationship to its cause—which is the nutritive power—it is also necessary to see what that power is. It is the power that converts the nourisher into the likeness of the nourished, so that through it, the body may receive a restoration of that which is dissolved. This power is dependent and material within time, not only regarding its operation but also as nature regards its substance; therefore, like other such material things, it required a body. It required a twofold matter: one in which it might be sustained as if founded in its own subject, and another upon which it acts. The first is the **members**, by reason of being most similar to it, because this is one of the **natural virtues** <term>natural virtues: "uirtutū naturaliū," the basic biological forces like growth and nutrition</term>. Since natural virtues are material and deeply embedded in those things which cannot be moved to opposites—unlike the **vital** or **animal** virtues—they adhere rather to a single path and a single order. Because of this, these virtues are called "natures," and they required natural subjects proportioned to them, such as the members called the "members of nature"; hence their opposites are called "official members," which are instruments of the soul. Thus we see that this virtue exists in plants because of their materiality and lack of organization, in which the other two [vital and animal virtues] are not found. Finally, the matter in which this virtue exercises its act is the **food** <note>original: "alimentum"</note>. Since all food is initially distinct from the thing it nourishes, it was necessary first to remove its inherent qualities so it could be assimilated to the body; this could not happen unless it was retained in the body for a determined time. Thus, it required preliminary members serving it, as well as virtues and time. It required twofold members: some for the purpose of retaining the food long enough until it is altered through the **three digestions** and finally converted into a substance similar to that which was lost. Thus the mouth was needed to hold the raw food while it was first altered; then, after being sent into the stomach, it required other digestions so that eventually, from that substance, something similar to the bodily substance could be generated. This is attracted by the "hands of the liver," called the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: "mefaraicas" — the veins draining the intestines</note>, which have the form of veins, so that the pure might be sucked out from the impure and digested in the concavity of the liver; in which, and from which, the six substances are generated by the digestive virtue...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the process of nutrition (Distinction XXX). It explores the specific mechanics by which the body purifies and assimilates food, moving from the veins into the various organs and tissues. It introduces the four "ministering virtues" and debates whether blood is the sole source of nourishment.</meta>

In the first of these, health is maintained; namely, that when both excess bile and wateriness are purged, the substance is pushed into the further veins to be digested, so that finally, through digestion in the **fountains of the members** <note>original: "fontibus membrorum" — refers to the internal tissues where the final stage of nutrition occurs</note>, having slipped from the orifices of the veins, it may undertake the restoration of the lost body. And because in every such digestion the surplus was expelled from the nourishment, these parts were also necessary for collecting it, lest the parts be stained by foul surplus; this double cause of purification emerges for the parts. 

First, concerning natural things: There are also certain **virtues** <term>virtues: "uirtutes," the innate functional powers or biological capacities of an organ</term> serving this nutritive power like handmaidens in attracting, digesting, and expurgating the surplus from the nourishment itself. These are the four specific virtues: **attractive, digestive, retentive, and expulsive**, along with **discretion** <note>original: "cum discretia" — the ability to distinguish between useful and waste material</note>, which are called the **ministering virtues**. For these work upon the nourishment like many laborers working upon a single task. 

Time is also required; for in every action, four things must concur: namely, an **agent** capable of acting upon **matter** disposed to it, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in *On the Soul*: *The acts of active things are in the patient and the disposed.* <note>original: "Actus actiuorum sunt in patiente & disposito"</note> Third, it requires **contact**, since all action occurs through contact, according to the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. For it is excited by contrary qualities, bringing things mixed together into action. Fourth, it requires **time** for these things to happen, since power, as has been said, is established within time, in which the agent is in contact with the "patient" <note>the substance being acted upon</note> for as long as is needed to draw out the appropriate effect. 

Supported by these virtues and parts, the nutritive power is seen to work upon nourishment as its end in a twofold way—just as the generative power is also twofold. One is **preparatory** or **transformative**, which works through the heat and **complexion** <term>complexion: "complexio," the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in an organ</term> of the member; the other is **perfective** or **formative**, so that the nourishment enters the members. Of this, there are three works: **to apply, to unite, and finally to assimilate**, as is proved in the first book of the *Natural Virtues*. 

Indeed, it is said to be twofold because the **members** <term>members: "membra," the various organs and parts of the body</term> are, according to physicians, twofold: namely, those generated from **sperm** and those from **blood**. In the **spermatic members** <note>the "solid" parts like bone and nerve, thought to be formed from seed</note>, it works uniformly and irreversibly; because in childhood it restores more than is lost, and therefore growth necessarily follows. In youth, it restores equally, which is why the body's state remains stable. In old age and senility, however, it restores less, which is intellectually understood but even more clearly manifest; from this follows a declining deformity. This order does not finally become reversible from the least to the greatest, or to the middle. In the **sanguineous members** <note>fleshy parts formed from blood</note>, it works nonuniformly and reversibly. This diversity is caused by the variety of complexions according to time and other **non-natural things** <term>non-naturals: "res non naturales," environmental factors like diet, sleep, and air that affect health</term>. This is why we see a bird at one time lose flesh and at another time grow thick again. 

The object of this virtue is threefold nourishment, according to the third book of *Complexions* and the first book of *Natural Virtues*. One is **actual nourishment**, which is truly called nourishment, as that which is applied, united, and assimilated. The other is nourishment that has not yet begun to be applied or united to the part, but is the **beginning of future nourishment**, such as that which is still in the veins or the stomach, already transformed; according to which, food can also be called nourishment in a remote sense. According to the first book of the *Virtues*: *Nourishing starts with mastication.* 

The first of these is positioned against the "outflow" of substance, according to the flow of blood, and also against vomiting and **lientery** <note>original: "liēterie" — a form of diarrhea where food is passed undigested</note>. Concerning the second point, it should be known that in the third book on the *Elements*, Galen considers this question more difficult than those concerning the manner of mixing the elements, and it is probable that there are positions for both sides. For he says: *It is not simply possible to demonstrate whether it is here as in the primary elements.* For each argument has something proper and probable. And he adds after other things: *Therefore, some physicians and philosophers have announced that the animal is nourished by blood alone.* One must praise their opinion as those who recognize what is fitting. 

But in the second book of *Natural Virtues*, concerning the generation, growth, and nourishment of our bodies from the **four humors**: it seemed to Hippocrates to be more natural for bodies to be generated and nourished from the four humors, since transformation and medical observation are better preserved this way. He also attacks those who posit only one element and humor. And therefore some have responded to this inquiry through the distinction of **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a famous Persian physician</note>, saying that the name "blood" is common: for it signifies the aggregation of mixed humors in the veins, as is seen in **phlebotomy** <term>phlebotomy: "fleubotomia," the practice of bloodletting for medical treatment</term>. For there, it is not pure blood, but all the humors exist in it. It is called "blood" because of its dominance in the mixture, because it exceeds the others in its quantity and blends them with its red color; and this mass is called **sanguineous** by physicians. 

The name "blood" also signifies that which is pure and entirely distinct from the others; and this is found rarely or in small amounts, singular and purified, so that no other humor is associated with it. According to the first book of the *Prognostics*: *It seemed to Hippocrates that no humor is pure or sincere, but all are mixed.* Galen also calls the first of these the "humors of the blood." These men say, therefore, that if this statement—"blood alone"—is exclusive, requiring the exclusion of the blood that is the mass aggregated in the veins, the meaning of the proposition is false; for then blood said to be "pure" in that way would nourish. They say this is false: first, because it is not possible to provide a pure humor in the body; and second, because since the members are diverse in their natures, it was necessary for them to be nourished by diverse humors, so that they might maintain a proportional restoration from consumption without harm; and third, because if humors other than blood did not nourish, they would seem to exist in the veins in vain. 

If, however, "alone" is said to exclude the **superfluous bile** tending toward the gallbladder, and **melancholy** <note>black bile</note> toward the spleen, and the **urinal wateriness** tending through the kidneys to the bladder, then they say it is true that blood alone nourishes, which is the same as saying that blood nourishes insofar as it is the carrier of all humors. But what will appear concerning this will be said in the following. 

Regarding the aforesaid, a doubt arises: because it was said that a pure or sincere humor is almost never found in the body, whereas it is said in the first book on *Diseases* that it is rare to find an individual sincere humor. But that which is rare is found sometimes. It must be said that Galen's speech is about particular appearances, and not about the humors of the body... for it is a small thing that many humors are not mixed in the appearance.

It also presents a debate on whether "blood alone" nourishes the body, concluding that blood in the veins is actually a mixture of all four humors tailored to the needs of different organs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the process of nutrition, specifically debating whether blood is the unique and solitary source of nourishment for the body's various parts. It expands on the roles of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—and cites the opinions of Hippocrates, Aristotle, Galen, and Isaac Israeli.</meta>

On account of the third thing to be known: that **blood alone** is able to nourish; this statement also makes an exclusion. Blood is spoken of in the first sense, in which the other **humors** <term>humors: the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to regulate health and temperament</term> are aggregated, including blood in the second sense, namely **pure blood** <note>original: "purum [sanguinem]"</note>. Since "blood alone," understood this way, means the same as "pure," it must be distinguished that "pure" is said in two ways: either as having no mixture at all, like wine with no water mixed in, or that which has received a very small amount of mixture, like wine so slightly mixed with water that it immediately passes through and remains the same. And in this way, it seemed to **Hippocrates** that "pure" nourishment is found in the body. Therefore, I declare that blood nourishes not only the "sanguine" members <note>fleshy parts that look like blood</note>—which even my opponent should not find burdensome—but also the other members, however much they may seem of diverse natures. For since that diversity is not great, it immediately falls into a unity of **complexion** <term>complexion: "complexio," the specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in an organ</term> resulting from their gathering together. For this reason, it was necessary for the nourishment to be common, so that through the internal power of the virtue and further action, that commonality would be specified into the nature of the parts.

That this is true is confirmed by the series of illustrious philosophers and physicians, such as **Aristotle** in *On Animals* and other philosophers and physicians. And this finally seems to have been the opinion of **Galen**. For he says in the second book of *On Natural Faculties*: *That which is sufficiently thick and earthy, refusing perfect transformation, is drawn in the liver toward the spleen.* But that which is moderately thick with its virtues is carried into the blood. For many small parts of the animal's body require a certain thickness of blood, such as in the wide **veinlets** <note>original: "ynulis" / "venulis"</note> for the sake of retention, for they are retentive. Not least, it also needs the **yellow humor** <note>yellow bile</note>, which is not yet fiery but is ultimately made into blood. And its utility will be stated; indeed, in the same book, he [Galen] intends that **choler** <note>yellow bile</note> is not diffused through the veins for the sake of nutrition—understand this—in this opinion he seems to agree in the fourth part of *On the Utility of Parts*, where he simply calls the cholers "superfluities." Hence in the fifth book: *Yellow bile has no utility so that it should go in the veins to the liver, the stomach, and the rest of the body, nor does it nourish any of the members, but it exits to the intestines.* Thus he intends that melancholy and choler pass through with the blood for the sake of utility, but not out of necessity—unless perhaps melancholy in its power. Nevertheless, arterial blood nourishes the spleen, as in the fourth book of *The Utilities*; which necessity, according to him in the second book, and according to **Aristotle** and **Haly Abbas**, finally exists in the act of nourishing.

They also seem to understand this regarding **phlegm**, wishing that it, like pure blood, can nourish all members when it has been converted into blood. For it is like a half-digested nourishment; hence they testify that it is blood that has been insufficiently "cooked" <note>original: "diminute decoctum" — referring to the metabolic "cooking" or digestion process</note>. Furthermore, **Isaac** [Israeli] in the beginning of *On Urines* says: *The heart attracts to itself the better, more praiseworthy, and more temperate part of the blood, from which it comforts and nourishes itself; the remainder is refined, and he cleanses it of choler, phlegm, and other putrefaction, and sends it to the arteries to cleanse the natural heat, and divides it through the whole body, by which the body itself is nourished and lives.* Likewise, in the beginning of *Universal Diets* and *On Fevers*: *Nature, because she held red bile in hatred...*

->---<-

*...on account of its bitterness and sharpness, placed it in the receptacle of the gallbladder, nor did she mix any of it with the blood, except as much as necessity required to excite the **expulsive virtue** through the whole body.* Similarly, she incarcerated the **melancholic humor** in the spleen, lest it be mixed with her blood, except as much as was necessary for the virtue to comfort the **retentive power** in any part of the body. Furthermore, **Alexander** [of Aphrodisias] in his *Problems* says that red bile and even more so black bile are diminished in the body and do not nourish; for red bile is sharp and black bile even more so, because it is an enemy of nature and corrosive to the parts, and properly "burnt" <note>original: "adultum" — referring to scorched or "adust" humors</note>. This finally seems to be the meaning of the third book, when he does not place the utility of choler alongside the others in entering into nourishment.

On account of which, I dare to assert with them: **that blood alone nourishes**, with this addition: that this holds truth in a body located within the "latitude of health" <note>the range of normal healthy function</note>, with the **six non-natural things** <term>six non-naturals: external factors like air, diet, sleep, and exercise that govern health</term> being administered as is due. For it happens in a sick or starving person, forced by the indigence of nature, that they use not only phlegm immediately for nourishment (as Aristotle suggests, without its transformation into blood), but perhaps even the two cholers. For in a time of immense hunger, we see the superfluities and dregs being dried out, because those who are starving draw immensely from the blood, transferring it into the preservation of nourishment. This is confirmed finally by all four causes. First, from the **material recipient**: for the matter of nourishment and the matter of generation are the same, for from the same things we are made, by the same things we are nourished. Hence in *On the Generation of Animals*: *The giver of nourishment and of matter is the same.* But we were made from blood as from matter according to Aristotle throughout the first and second books of *On the Generation of Animals* and the *Natural Books*, saying that vein, artery, nerve, cartilage, fat, membrane, and marrow are generated from blood. This is proven because in the womb there is no actual choler or melancholy. Blood is the one and uniform matter similar to the seed. Galen intends that the embryo is generated and nourished from the purer part of the mother's menstrual blood. Furthermore, if we say that melancholy nourishes some member along with the blood, such as the bones and the like: either it is joined with the blood or separated in the nutrition of such members. Not separated, because Aristotle says it is sent with the blood through the veins to the member. This is also clear because if a member were nourished separately by blood and melancholy, then the member would not exist as a single form of virtue and instrument, which cannot be granted, since each thing has its being through one single form. Nor does melancholy mixed with blood nourish, for melancholy loses its power of mixture when it is present disproportionately (according to my adversaries) in any member. And therefore, the role of the cholers in generation is denied, since they exist only potentially in the menstrual blood. For it is necessary for the act to pre-exist separately, and finally to be in the mixture with others by its virtue. Since they share the same form, virtue, and instrument.
