<meta>This page continues the argument that blood is the primary and sole nutriment of the body. It shifts from general definitions to specific proofs based on the "formal cause" (the nature of sweetness), the essence of the nutritional process, and the principle of natural economy, citing authorities such as Aristotle, Avicenna, and Haly Abbas.</meta>

...namely, that which is warm. Let it be led toward a single actual nature, yet not bringing with itself a potentiality for humors. This same point is clarified regarding the brain, which is more "windy" <note>original: "flantiori," referring to the presence of pneuma or "windy" spirits</note>; nevertheless, it is nourished by true blood and not by wind, as stated in the book *On Sleep and Wakefulness*. Blood is the thinnest and purest; that which is in the head is most thin, as it is in the uppermost parts. This is because it has been in continuous contact with the heart for a long time, making its passage into the brain along with the **vital spirit** <term>vital spirit: "spiritus vitalis," a refined substance believed to carry life-force from the heart through the arteries</term> which exits as the warmest substance. It can also be said that the "windy" substance is made bone-like: because what is "cooked" <note>the process of "coction" or metabolic heat</note> can least of all be made raw again, according to <term>Haly Abbas</term> <note>Latin: "halyabatẽ," a 10th-century Persian physician</note> and **Aristotle**. The marrow of the blood is stopped and distributed at the last stage into the bones, being a digested surplus. But as for the parts: it nourishes the chaste and moist musical bones <note>This likely refers to the "ossicula" or small bones of the ear or delicate structures</note> from within.

<margin>Haly</margin>
The second argument is from the **formal cause** <note>the essential nature or "recipe" of a thing</note>, as found in *On the Generation of Animals* and the fourth book of *Simple Medicines*. Nothing is generated nor nourished except by that which is **sweet**; hence, in the *Universal Diets* <note>A work by Isaac Israeli</note>: "Nothing nourishes unless it is sweet." This is because nutrition occurs through the assimilation of the nourisher to that which is nourished. Now, only sweet things are assimilated to the human nature, because the sweet is warm and moist. Thus, just as the human **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a person</term> is sweet, so only blood is sweet, as **Avicenna** says in the fourth book of his *History* and as all physicians of nature agree. For **yellow bile** <term>colera: yellow bile, one of the four humors, associated with fire and bitterness</term> participates in bitterness and sharpness; **black bile** <term>melancolia: black bile, associated with earth and acidity</term> participates in tartness and sourness; and while **blood** occasionally has an accidental sweetness, **phlegm** is characterized by insipidity. Therefore, only blood remains to nourish. Nor can you argue that only the "sweet" nourishes because it is "friendly" to the body, since no flavor except the sweet is found to be actually amicable to the specific nature of humans. Thus, out of the two biles <note>yellow and black bile</note>, not only is no nourishment made, but even animals like earthworms and intestinal worms are generated from them.

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
This is also declared from the essence of nutrition: for since the food is finally transformed into the nourished part, if any member were actually nourished by yellow or black bile, it would be possible to find their manifest flavors in the nourished parts—which is not the case. For example, the lung is nourished by very choleric blood <note>original: "colericissimo," meaning blood with a high proportion of yellow bile</note>, yet a bitter flavor is not tasted in it. This would likewise be found in the heart, where evaporation of "winds" <note>spirits</note> is not seen. It is also taken from the perspective of the **efficient cause** <note>the agent that brings about a change</note>, since the transformative power acts upon the food through heat and moisture, by which it prepares the matter and induces the form for restoration. From the perspective of heat, action upon the matter is made easy, as heat is the most active quality. From the perspective of moisture, reception is made easy, as the agent requires a well-disposed matter. Because of this, since the agent and the patient <note>the thing being acted upon</note> must be proportional and similar, the patient in this case is blood, as it is naturally warm and moist.

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
Furthermore, it is a fault to do through many things what can be accomplished by fewer; this was indicated by the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note> in the first book. Since all other members can be nourished by blood alone—as the other humors are in it potentially, just as they are in tempered food—there is no need for other sources. Again, and fourthly, from the perspective of the **final cause** <note>the purpose or end goal</note>: generation and nutrition are ordained so that we may be preserved in a divine and excellent state, according to *On the Soul*. This is achieved through that which is best, namely blood; hence **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli</note> in the first book of *On Fevers* called it the "son of nature," and in the second book of *Complexions*, it is said to be most proper to nature. Because nutrition is ordained for the conservation of life, those things which hinder life should never be said to nourish. **Black bile** hinders life because it is cold and dry, which is the disposition of death, as stated in *On Death and Life*; therefore **Haly Abbas** judges those of a melancholic complexion to have shorter lives. Likewise with red cholera <note>yellow bile</note>; hence in the fourth book of *Parts*: "Bile is not proper for nourishment as it is not a purification of any pure substance." And so, some have said the cause of living for a long time is the absence of bile, especially in the liver, as seen in deer and certain other animals and humans. It is also the cause of putrefaction, and because it is destitute of the regime of nature, it is held in hatred by the body. Thus, from these points, it is effectively concluded that **blood alone**—or that which is purely unique—nourishes. This excludes bile entirely and phlegm for the most part, as the latter is a surplus of the first useful nourishment. A sign of this is that when mixed with pure food, it nourishes, and in those who labor, it is consumed and excited, according to the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*. From this, one gathers that **phlegm** is like food prepared for the members, because food is delayed in them; thus it is the "near matter" of blood. This does not happen with the two biles; they are not "near" nor even "remote" matter for the nourishment of the members. Therefore, it is impossible for them to be truly converted into blood. They are, however, in it potentially: for often in the conversion of blood, it suddenly turns into yellow bile, and the thick parts into **black bile**. But they do not turn back into blood or into the body's nourishment, because the heat acting further upon them—being already vehemently hot—seems to thicken and corrupt them, converting them into unnatural humors rather than true nourishment. As for the rest, because their complexion fails, their substance recedes entirely from the nature of blood. Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it must be said that this was the opinion of those <note>the ancients</note> which is not maintained at present. To the next, it must be said that blood itself is not a "simple" <note>unmixed</note> substance, since the other three humors are in it potentially, just as in food. To the next, it must be said that the other humors are not in vain, as they have uses beyond the necessity of nourishing, as **Avicenna** explains. To the other, it must be said that it carries little weight among philosophers who argue precisely, even if it were **Hippocrates** speaking on human nature. **Galen** notes this in his *Theories*. Because the necessity of an effect like nutrition is not taken from the necessity of the matter, but rather from the agent and the form or the end goal, as appears in the *Physics* and the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*, where **Empedocles** is rebuked for wanting to reduce the necessity of effects to the matter. For the members are not diverse because their nourishment is diverse; rather, the diversity of matter follows from the diversity of form or end, and not vice versa. Hence the Commentator <note>Averroes</note> on the first book of *On the Soul* says: The members of a lion do not differ from the members of a deer except because their souls differ. **Galen** felt this in his *On Natural Faculties*, wishing that each thing be generated from the same matter—namely, the blood—on account of its distance...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of blood and humors, specifically debating whether nourishment is derived from the material itself or the "formative power" of the soul, leading into a specific investigation (Difference 31) into whether arterial blood contributes to the body's nutrition.</meta>

...distinguished by the **formative power** <note>the vital force that gives shape and function to organs</note> and not simply from the matter.
<margin>9</margin> Indeed, for many inconveniences follow the aforementioned reasoning if one considers it more subtly. First, because then the power would be frustrated in its purpose; second, because the differentiation in the members would have no basis beyond the diversity of the nutritional matter. Furthermore, it would seem that the change and assimilation of the nourishment into the nourished part would happen solely from the matter. In this way, a member would have to be composed of the parts it is nourished by, according to their theory—all of which is absurd and immature. Hence, in the fourth book of *On the Use of the Parts*: The truer statement of the two is that it was necessary for flesh to exist according to its own being. For instance, a small amount of food was suitable for the **epiploon** <note>the omentum or fatty tissue of the abdomen</note>, the lungs, and the spleen; it is said that the substance of the flesh in each of these becomes similar to the substance of the blood by which it is nourished. Because of this, I believe **Galen**, in the third book of *On the Elements*, was led astray, saying otherwise out of his love for **Hippocrates**. To the other point, it must be said: that nourishment made through blood is made by what is similar in every way, because in the blood, the other **humors** <note>the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> are found in potential. For "corrupted" blood, according to its thinness, is changed into **choler** <note>yellow bile</note>. That which is thick is converted into **melancholy** <note>black bile</note>. From this itself, when it is cooked further, a "windy" humor is drawn out. And so, since blood itself carries the other humors in potential, having been cooked by a higher digestion, it is prepared by the nutritional power to serve the perfecting of nutrition. According to **Avicenna**, it will be able to change not only into bloody members, but truly also into phlegmatic, melancholic, and choleric members, nourishing them in its own way. And rightly so; for in the humors, there exists an irreversible order of conversion of one into another, as seen in the third book of *On the Regulation of Health* and the first book of the *Theoretical Medicine*. For **phlegm**, through its further **coction** <note>internal "cooking" or metabolic processing</note>, is converted into blood; and blood—at least its thick part—is converted by reason of its substance and its thinner part into choler. For this reason, it is not necessary to say that both types of choler pass through the veins with the blood out of a necessity to nourish, but rather for the sake of utility, which **Aristotle** and others have touched upon sufficiently. If it is asked what happens to those humors: it must be said that **red choler**, beyond other expulsions, is expelled in sweat, since sweat is the "wateriness" of the blood to which the choleric bile was previously mixed (according to the third book of the *Canon*), and also through stool, urine, and insensible perspiration. Concerning **melancholy**, it must be said that not much of it passes to the veins with the blood, since its quantity in the body is small. It is also expelled in the expulsions of the third and fourth digestions. Or perhaps some quantity of it, changed somewhat toward whiteness, returns into the **hypostatic matter** <note>sedimentary matter in fluids</note>. What should be said regarding this will be seen in Difference 54.

## DIFFERENCE XXXI.

**I**t is demonstrated that **arterial blood** (or "vital blood") does not nourish. First, because the **liver** is nourished and lives, and yet no branch of the "great artery" <note>the aorta</note> is carried to it. Life, after all, is a consistency maintained through food; yet the liver adheres to the great vein and does not communicate with the artery. Furthermore, in the sections of the liver and spleen, no "aborting" <note>here meaning a large, direct protrusion</note> of a large straight artery is extended. Arterial blood, however, is directed to the parts through the arteries. Furthermore, in the third book of the *Colliget*, **Averroes** knows that blood was not created except for one of two things: either for nourishing, like the blood which is in the liver and the veins (which physicians believe originate from the liver), or to be the vehicle for the **spirit of the heart** <note>pneuma or vital heat</note>, and this is the arterial blood. Therefore, **Avicenna** does not posit that vital blood helps to nourish, but only to carry the heart's spirit. The same is found in the first book of the *Uses [of the Parts]* and the third book of *Theoretical Medicine*. Again, **Isaac Israeli** defines it: "From the blood breaking forth from the liver through the veins to all members, nourishment, power, and constitution are made." Also, from the blood running through the arteries, the vital spirit is nourished, just as fire is nourished by oil—not mentioning the nourishment of the members. Furthermore, in the first book: blood of good essence goes through the great vein from the hump of the liver to the ascending parts, and tends through the veins which separate from it like branches, then into the "vessel-veins," and finally into the veins that are like **capillary branches**. Afterward, the blood, by sweating out of their orifices, glides into the parts by a divine plan. But arterial blood passes through the natural paths only.

Again, in the 11th book of the third part: the heart is nourished by its own natural powers. If, therefore, the power that effects the nourishment of the heart is natural, then its nourishment (like blood) will be natural. Thus, if this is present in the heart, which is the root of the arteries and the vital blood, how much more are other members nourished solely by natural blood. Likewise, nourishment occurs through heat and moisture, which is shown by digestion. Natural blood is warm and moist by nature, whereas arterial blood is warm and dry. Also, giving life and giving nourishment are distinct acts. Since life is given by arterial blood—for it is called "vital"—nourishment must therefore come from natural blood. Therefore, the vital blood does not nourish. Yet the opposite of this is written in *On the Generation of Animals* and the third book of the *Colliget* under the opinion of Avicenna. Furthermore, what can do more can also do less: arterial blood can give life, which is more than providing nourishment; therefore, it should be able to provide nourishment to the parts. And rightly so, since giving life and giving nourishment eventually pertain to the same principle. To understand the first point, however, one must know that blood is twofold in the present context by reason of its container. One is called arterial or vital, originating in the heart and diffused through the whole body by the arteries arising from it. The other is called natural or venous, generated in the liver, from which it is directed through the veins into the whole body. Of these, the one in the veins is redder, while the one in the arteries is more yellow than the other (according to Galen’s book *On Melancholy*). What a vein or an artery is will be shown in Differences 47 and 64. Veins and arteries also agree in name and in fact. First, because sometimes by a common name, arteries are called veins, but not vice versa. For the **Arabs** <note>referring to Islamic medical authorities like Avicenna or Rhazes</note> define this name "vein" more by "pulsating," which they say exists in the artery, and "not pulsating," which is the vein simply so-called. However, by the common name of "veins," that which is one...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the physiological differences between veins and arteries, and whether arterial blood serves a nutritional purpose or merely carries "spirits." It specifically addresses the views of Galen and the Platonists regarding the threefold nature of the soul's power in the body.</meta>

...is surrounded by a **tunic** <term>tunica: the wall or membrane of a vessel</term>. Lacking the movement of dilation and constriction; but in reality, because both are long, hollow, ligamentous bodies, they differ in that veins have only one single tunic—excepting the so-called **arterial vein** <note>original: "uenā artarialē"; the pulmonary artery, which Galen noted had a thick wall like an artery but functioned within the venous system</note> which is in the lung. Arteries, however, have two tunics, with the exception of the **venous artery** <note>original: "artaria uenali"; the pulmonary vein</note> of the lung, in which there is local motion.

They [the arteries] arise with the heart. Veins arise from the liver according to the doctors (Difference 47). As for what nutrition is and its method, the preceding Difference has shown. Regarding the second point, it must be known that the principles of **Galen** and certain philosophers and **Platonists**, whom he often follows, are more wisely understood as follows: that only natural blood nourishes the solid parts of the animal.

Arterial [blood], however, is the matter of the **spirits** <term>spiritus: the vital "pneuma" or breath thought to circulate through the arteries to animate the body</term>, serving as their nourishment and vehicle, as has already appeared in some way. For they posited that the soul is threefold within the body and possesses three principal powers (Difference 18), which also seem to be indicated earlier. Where the difference between the animate and the natural is assigned to an organ, the natural [power] has an act of power innate to itself. Just as a **magnet** has the power by which it attracts iron, so it is with each organ of an animal. Thus, if its power were self-sustaining, it would require neither veins nor arteries. But because it requires nourishment and the preservation of **innate heat** <note>the fundamental warmth believed to be essential to life</note> by generation, for these reasons it had need of veins and arteries.

Thus, he ordains veins solely for blood, but arteries for the innate heat. From his opinion, such a reason seems able to be deduced: those whose souls or powers and instruments are diverse, their operations in the preceding [sections] are diverse; and the aforementioned are indeed diverse. But the operation of the **vital power** with its instrument is to give life; therefore, the **natural power** with its own instrument is to administer nutrition. 

The aforementioned points of Galen do not initially receive the primary arguments. For if the passage between the mouth and the liver were closed, and the mouth had suitable nourishment, its action in that place would be destroyed. Therefore, it does not behave in the same relation as a magnet to iron, which requires no help. However, this instance given by Galen is not valid, nor are others. Because the deprivation of the transport of food from the liver to the mouth does not take away its innateness, but only its permanence and preservation; although, according to Galen's way, this pertains more to probability than to truth. 

Yet, I do not consider it sufficiently stated that only natural blood provides nourishment, as will appear. For here I begin at the very roots. Galen's views are general and medicinal, yet they are apparent; for the natural and animal powers do not relate to the vital power as entirely disparate things, but rather as the lower to the higher. Indeed, these two are founded in the third—the vital power—which emerges as the primary root of all. For such powers can be considered in two ways: either as to their perfect and formal existence—that is, as they are tied to determined organs with spirits related to them to perform their operations manifestly—and thus they maintain the reasoning of disparate things. This Galen thought to be sufficient. Or, they can be considered as to their material existence, and thus there exists only one formal and perfect power: the vital power in the heart. The other two, the **animal** <note>referring to the *anima* or mind/sensation</note> and the **natural**, are imperfect and material within it. Thus they have the relation of the lower to the higher. For the vital power is, as it were, their genus and principle. 

In the heart, indeed, all powers are formed, since it is the first root and mine <note>original: "minera"; a source or treasury</note> in the animal, like the first principle in the universe. However, not all can be manifested in it through works, because here it is effected through a disposed instrument. In the heart, there is only the complete vital instrument; afterward, the vital spirit tending toward the brain through the arteries is refined in the **rete mirabile** <term>rete mirabile: the "wonderful net," a complex of blood vessels at the base of the brain</term> and in the brain, as in an organ assigned to it by nature (Difference 38). 

It also appears that the reasoning introduced by Galen does not conclude the preceding points, because the souls or powers and organs are not entirely diverse; rather, one is contained within the other. Hence, concerning the generation of animals: the form of the liver is in the heart. 

Regarding the third point, it must be said: that arterial blood also has the function of nourishing, and not only natural blood. This is shown both by authorities and by the reasons not only of philosophers but also of doctors. For Galen, in *On Marasmus*: "The heart exists strongly by reason, and all the small parts of the animal have their own nourishment from the heart." Here, however, the blood will be vital [arterial]. Furthermore, in the sixth book of *On the Utility of the Parts*: "In pulsating and non-pulsating veins [arteries and veins], blood and spirit are found. But that which is in pulsating veins [arteries] is a little pure blood, close to the nature of vapor; and that which is in non-pulsating veins [veins] is a little spirit and cloudy." And it is added, as deduced from the prior: that the medicines of the body are communicated to all members, though in unequal quantities. These are not communicated except by the aforesaid blood and spirit; therefore, both bloods nourish, and the spirit will be foamy. 

This can also be gathered specifically from particular members. It is written in the same place: there was a pulsating vein in the lung having a thin covering, similar to the creation of a non-pulsating vein in other members, so that it might give to the lung much of the subtle blood that is in it. This would not be unless it were for the sake of nourishing the same. Hence, according to theory: the vital arterial [vessel], having a single thin and fragile tunic, entered the lung and is divided into many parts within it. It receives air from it, and delivers blood to it by which it may be fed. 

The first principles also agree with these: one of the arteries goes to the lung and is divided within it, so that air may be drawn in, and the blood which nourishes the lung is carried from the heart. That which passes as the nourishment of the lung is to the heart, and from the heart it goes to the lung. It appears, therefore, from this that members are nourished by vital [arterial] blood. 

But someone will immediately rise up and say that the case is not the same for the lung as for other members, so that one could exclude the others because of it; for the disposition of the lung in its veins is contrary to the disposition of other members (*On the Utility of the Parts*, Book 5). For the lung is a hot and dry member, requiring much heat and motion, and needing hotter and more abundant nourishment for three reasons: First, because of the multitude of heat, on account of which its food is made like a vapor and is quickly consumed. Second is the expansion of the lung at the hour of receiving air, for this helps it to attract food from deep and thick places. Third, because the lung alone among all members is fed by the blood of the heart, which the heart digests and makes very subtle; but not so for other parts...

...participate by nature and disposition. It must be said that although it may be deduced from these things that the lung, compared to the other parts, ought to be nourished more by arterial blood, nonetheless others are also nourished by it. For the spleen is nourished from it, being a small organ <note>original: "mēbrū mīcū"; literally "a small member," though the spleen's role was highly debated in medieval medicine</note> concerning which it seems a wonder. Because of this, other parts more closely related to the blood can also be nourished from it. Whence, in the fourth [book] of *The Utility of the Parts* <note>Galen’s *De usu partium*</note>, the aforementioned utility of the pulsating veins <term>脉pulsatile veins: a common medieval term for arteries</term> in the spleen is that they feed and nourish it with that which exudes from them.

So also in the third [chapter] of the fifteenth [book], there are both pulsating and non-pulsating veins in the spleen in which the blood is digested and assimilated into its substance. And therefore, in the fourth [book] of *The Utility of the Parts*, the spleen is nourished by thin black blood, while the liver is nourished by thick red blood. Regarding this, a doubt arises: for in the thirteenth [book] of *The Method of Healing* <note>Galen's *De methodo medendi*</note> it is mentioned that the spleen is nourished by gross blood, which is like the dregs of the purer blood. It must be said that the spleen, like other organs, is nourished by a twofold blood: arterial and venous. And because the arterial blood is ordained more toward its end, even if the blood of the spleen is attracted for nourishment, it is nevertheless digested and thinned before it nourishes, just as was touched upon by the authority of **Avicenna**. Whence this will be fulfilled by **Galen** when both [views] are joined as one.

Wherefore, in the fourth [book] of *The Utility of the Parts*, matter is digested in the spleen before it is transmitted into the stomach. This is aided by the motion of many arteries existing within it, which bring to it the power of the heart, the spirit, and the blood, so that by digestion the blood becomes thin and suitable for its nature. Concerning the nourishment of the kidneys in the fifth [book] of *The Utility of the Parts*, the kidneys do not lack a vein coming to them to feed them, and two coupled vessels suffice for them: namely, a pulsating vein <note>the renal artery</note> which arises from the "great pulsating vein" <note>the aorta</note> which is toward the back, and a non-pulsating vein <note>the renal vein</note> which arises from the "ample vein" <note>the vena cava</note> that originates from the convex part of the liver.

**Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician</note> also says in his [work] on the nutrition of the members, and especially of the heart: we say that we do not mean, by saying the blood of the heart is pure and clean and stripped of humors, the blood which is directed to it from the liver to nourish its body. Rather, we do not mean even the blood proceeding into the arteries to the whole body—which is the vehicle of innate heat and the matter of its own nourishment—from the blood which is transmitted to it from the liver to nourish its own body; they are not separated. For if that were so, it would be deprived of its natural operations.

However, the cause for which the blood of the arteries becomes pure, clean, and stripped of humors and dross, is because nothing goes to the heart from the blood except that which is better and more praiseworthy. Then [the heart] discerns it and takes for its own nourishment and the nourishment of the innate heat <term>calor innatus: the vital warmth believed to be the source of life, centered in the heart</term> that which is better within it. It then transmits what remains of it after that to the members of the chest, the lung, and the head, so that they may be nourished by it; thus the food of these members comes from the superfluity of the heart's food.

But that which is said—that the heart is nourished by the blood of the liver and not by other humors—perhaps does not hold the truth, because the heart, before it is nourished by natural blood, digests it further and converts it into **vital blood** <term>sanguis vitalis: blood enriched with "spirit" or pneuma in the left ventricle</term>. Whence **Isaac** in his book *On Urines* says: the blood is purified of both [dark] colors and of its windiness and wateriness; the heart draws to itself the better and more praiseworthy part, whereby it strengthens and nourishes itself. Thus, therefore, the blood nourishing the heart will be vital, and though it was modified in color in the heart, it was already so in potential.

To **Isaac's** proof, it must be said that the heart is not for this reason deprived of natural powers, since these are in every member specifically and contracted. In the liver, however, they exist in common, according to the doctors especially. These natural powers in the heart are, however, rendered of a different nature than those that were in the liver. He adds after the aforesaid: the residue of the heat thins [the blood], and it is purified of dregs and windiness and other putrefaction through the arteries, sending it to purify the natural heat, so that it may nourish by its richness and be divided through the whole body. For the heart is the foundation of the natural heat, which thus consists of the part it draws to itself for the nourishment of its nature and assimilates into its substance, and the superfluous part which it takes and sends to the members of the chest, nourishing each one and making it similar to its own nature.

**Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> also concludes: You ought to know, if you will, that the food and nourishment of all members is made from two bloods mixed together; and that the blood which is in the liver and non-pulsating veins is like the "matter" of the blood in the arteries of the heart; and that the blood of the arteries is like the "form" of its blood. This is what gives it completion and cooking <note>original: "coctiōz"; decoction or metabolic processing</note> and makes it food close to the actual state [of the tissue]. By this reasoning it is confirmed that we are nourished by the same things from which we are made: as was said before, blood is made from natural and vital blood. For from the vital and natural parts, the sperm and the **menstrual blood** <term>menstruum: considered in Aristotelian biology to be the female material contribution to conception</term> fall away. Whence in the *Theoretical [Medicine]*: the heart is made from arterial blood, but the liver from the menstrual blood, as are all fleshy members. For from both bloods every part is generated and nourished; but some more from the vital, others from the natural. If the vital is removed, nourishment is not easily perfected from the natural blood alone.

And this supports what was assumed: that the embryo is nourished through the umbilical cord according to what is established for its daily growth in the [book] *On the Generation of Animals*. In which there are four vessels: sometimes two, sometimes only one. And of these, two are veins and the others are two arteries, or the remainder, according as the animals are larger, medium, or smaller. Also in the third [book] of the *Theoretical [Medicine]*, two veins and two arteries are placed together reaching from the matrix <note>the uterus</note> to the umbilicus. But when they have passed the umbilicus, then for the most part two veins are gathered into one, and the arteries into one. The veins were born for this: that they might feed the fetus with the menstrual blood contained in them. The arteries, however, [were born] so they might carry spirit and blood. Thus, therefore, the blood attracted through the arteries into the embryo has to nourish it; for it was not given solely for the generation of spirit, since spirit is also attracted from the matrix. For the blood would not be produced in such quantity if spirit were generated from only a little of it; nor can spirit be resolved more quickly, as one might say, because of the more solid container in which it is held. Furthermore, every member that participates in veins also participates in arteries. Since, therefore, nourishment occurs not only through vessels but even through simple confluence and emanation—as in bones and cartilages—it is the role of spirit to restore life, not only through the arteries, but also to assign such things [to the tissues]; but this is because of the **vital blood**, whose nature it is also to nourish. Likewise, nourishment is made from its like: namely, into the member which is nourished...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on whether arterial blood provides nourishment to the body's organs. It focuses on reconciling the anatomical observations of Galen with the theoretical frameworks of Avicenna and Averroes, specifically looking at the liver, heart, and the connections (anastomoses) between veins and arteries.</meta>

Not only is blood of the nature of the natural <note>original: "nature sanguis ut naturalis"; referring to venous blood produced by the liver</note>, but rather it is by itself the nature of life—and especially since each thing is mixed from all others, it is not possible to assign a purely single part within the body. Whence **Avicenna** says: Nourishment must be made from something that is proportional to the matter, such as <term>natural blood: the blood found in the veins, considered "raw" or "undigested" in medieval medicine</term> which is raw, and another of a related form, such as <term>arterial blood: the blood in the arteries, considered "coct" or "cooked" by the heart's heat</term> which is cooked. Therefore, so that the proportion may become more balanced, it is necessary in nutrition for the raw to be mixed with the cooked, so that both may be tempered. Furthermore, everything that nourishes, as he asserts, must be added to the members. But two types of blood meet in the members; therefore, they must be nourished twice. And finally, he adds that **Galen** appears to assert that the upper members are fed by arterial blood. And this is because he ordered the arteries to be cut in the case of <note>original: "emigranea"; migraine</note> and for persistent epilepsy. He also ordered, in the thirteenth [book] of *The Method of Healing*, that the arteries of the temples be cut for diseases of the eyes. And he adds: "Would that I knew what prevents him from believing that this blood of the arteries nourishes the other parts of the body."

From this speech of Galen, however, in the third [book] of the *Internal [Affected] Parts*, it cannot be concluded according to **Avicenna** that it happens this way; it is not because of evacuation for these diseases that arterial blood nourishes the upper members. For I say this is done not for the evacuation of arterial blood, but because through it a different, bad <term>complexion: the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile)</term> is corrected—either a vapor or a blockage. Galen appears in the same place to say that when those things which cause pain are carried to the head, they are diverted elsewhere. Whence, although it is severely noted, it is not justly deduced from the premises. Therefore, it must be concluded as probable that arterial blood nourishes, although its purpose is primarily to be <term>spiritual: related to the "vital spirit" or pneuma carried in the arteries</term> and vegetative.

It must be noted, however, as **Averroes** <note>original: "collz"; referring to the *Colliget*, his medical compendium</note> also feels, that the mixing of vital and natural blood can happen in two ways. One way is that natural blood, proceeding through the vein from the <term>convexity of the liver: the rounded outer surface of the liver, often called the "hump"</term>, ascends into the heart. The other way is through the attraction of the extremities of the <term>capillary arteries: the finest, hair-like endings of the blood vessels</term> from the extremities of the capillary veins. There is an outward distribution of the veins and a meeting of the pulsating vessels with the non-pulsating veins for two reasons: one is to provide support through the membranes covering the non-pulsating veins and binding them with neighboring members; the other is so that there may be a passage from both types of veins to the other, regarding what is contained in them for the benefit of the quantity and the primary nature. Therefore, in the capillary extremities of the veins and arteries, the arterial blood will be associated with the natural blood for nourishment.

But on the contrary, the primary authority says that blood goes through the great vein and ascends from the convexity of the liver. It must be said that the [book] *On the Protection of Animals* says: Blood remains in the convexity, standing there purified in the great vein which divides into two parts, one of which tends downward and the other upward. Note also that there is a certain part of the members which is nourished mostly by natural blood, such as the liver, and especially the upper convex part which lacks arteries. This happens because nourishment is made by like things, and the liver resembles [natural] blood. For blood is the congealed or thickened generator of bones and things related to them. The heart, however, together with the lungs, is nourished by arterial blood. The spleen and the kidneys, commonly, from both.

***

Regarding the benefits, it is written that there is an artery in the liver, yet it is not worse, but rather it is disseminated more through the lower part <note>original: "qcauā"; the concave part or "venerable" side of the liver</note>. For there were pulsating veins in the concave part of the liver and not in the convex part, because the convex part of the liver, which is continuous with the wall, has much motion and its own breathing motion suffices for it; it does not need another "exsufflation" <note>cooling or breathing out</note>. And there were pulsating veins in the concave of the liver because of its necessity for this, since they were sent from the heart to the liver to maintain the temperance of heat.

From this it also appears, according to **Galen**, that it is nourished not only from natural blood. When **Avicenna** seems to want to say this, I say either I do not understand him, or he intended that the artery reaches the spleen and the liver from the <note>original: "abortbi"; likely *aorta*</note>, because this is proven. Or if it does reach them, it is not distributed through the parts of the liver as it has already appeared through Galen, just as it is distributed through the parts of other members. **Avicenna** himself, in the third [book] of his *Histories*, wants no vein to extend to the matrix <note>the uterus</note> from the <term>vena cava: the large vein carrying deoxygenated blood to the heart</term>, but only from an artery—the opposite of which one performing anatomy experiences. Or perhaps Avicenna did not perceive the artery reaching the liver through anatomy because it is small in its lower parts, terminated from the lower part by the artery tending through the back upwards toward the liver.

For it can be said of him what is said of **Parmenides**, as if excusing him in his philosophical speech: "this, however, Parmenides did not see." Whence, according to the *Colliget*, in the time of Avicenna, he did not recognize any benefit of the <term>diaphragm: the muscular partition between the chest and abdomen</term> except for the separation of the spiritual members from the nutritional ones, so that during the time of digestion nothing from that heat would happen to them. He also errs in the speech containing that many hepatic arteries come from the heart—both because it is seen to be false, and because it is worse since he imposes this on Galen, when Galen himself clearly testifies to the opposite of the anatomists. For here he was ignorant of anatomy.

To another point, it must be said that **Avicenna** either speaks according to the opinion of **Galen**, or that the benefit of the arteries is to be a vehicle for the spirit of the heart, because it was primarily born for this. However, it is not taken away because of this that it may also have natural blood. Truly, natural blood primarily has the role of nourishing, while this [arterial blood], as has been said, has the role of vitalizing. And in this manner, it must be said for others, including **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli the Elder</note>. To another point, it must be said that although the speech of **Aristotle** might sound as if natural blood alone nourishes, a sharp-sighted listener will say that the name "vein" also includes "artery." To another point, it must be said that if the heart and its vessels are nourished by natural things, they appear to be of a different order and related almost equivocally to the natural virtues of the liver. Or, although the natural virtue may be in any member, it is varied by the different complexion of the member. For the complexion of flesh is one thing and that of bone is another; because of which, a diversity of nourishment follows. To another point, it must be said that although arterial blood is hot, it is so in proportion to natural blood. It is, however, hot and moist <note>original: "bū." for *humidum*</note>... as **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas</note> says in the tenth [book] of the *Metaphysics*.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the distribution and function of blood. It specifically addresses the paradox of how organs without visible veins (like the brain or bones) receive nourishment, and reconciles the views of Aristotle, Galen, and Haly Abbas regarding the "torcular" or the drainage system of the brain.</meta>

For the heat of arterial blood and its dryness are not so great that they would, for this reason, take away the ability to provide nourishment. To the other point, it should be said that giving life and providing nourishment are not opposites, nor are they separate things where one does not help the other toward the same end. To grant life is, as it were, superior and like a genus to the act of providing nourishment. And that which can do more <note>grant life</note> can certainly also do less <note>nourish</note>.

<margin>§</margin> The reason why it is doubted that blood is contained only in the veins is this: since, according to <margin>at.</margin> **Averroes** <note>original: "Au."; refers to the 12th-century Cordoban philosopher</note> as seen in the previous distinction, blood alone nourishes. The brain—in which, according to the third book of *The History of Animals*, there is no vein, neither large nor small—would not be able to be nourished. Likewise neither the bones and similar parts, nor the kidneys (section 86). Furthermore, in the first book of *On the Properties [of the Elements]*, it says blood flows into the members from the divine part. The extremities, such as the fingertips <note>original: "tactũ carent uenis"; literally "the touch lacks veins"</note>, lack veins. Moreover, since blood flows out immediately when the continuity of the body is broken by something even very subtle—if blood only exited from veins here, then the whole body would be a vein, which is absurd. Therefore, blood is not in the veins alone.

To the opposite is **Averroes** <note>original: "Au."</note> in *On Animals*, who is not infrequently in agreement with physicians on various points: for the veins are twofold, the pulsating [arteries] and the quiet [veins]; they are the locations for blood, serving the heart and the liver. Also, when the veins are emptied, blood is never drawn from any other part of the body. Therefore, it is contained in the veins alone.

Regarding the first point, it must be known what blood is, as touched upon before, and the distinction will be shown. For a threefold distinction exists (section 32): by "vein" I here also mean the artery, in which is contained the "vital blood," and in the veins simply so-called, the "natural blood."

Regarding the second point, it must be known that some, because of what was touched upon before, have felt that blood is not in the veins alone; the truth of which will be shown presently. Regarding the third point, it must be known that blood is only contained in the veins and arteries, and in parts proportioned to them, such as the heart and the "lake" <note>the cisterns of the brain</note>. Blood is received by the first two movements. Whence in the third book of *The History of Animals*: "All blood is in a vessel and in what are called veins; in nothing else except the heart alone." And in the third book of *On the Parts [of Animals]*: "Without a vein there is no blood; the heart itself also contains it in those that have it." Whence in the first book of *On Complexions*: "The heart is the bloodiest of the viscera."

Furthermore, a "lake of blood" or <term>wine-press: the torcular Herophili, a confluence of sinuses in the brain</term> is constructed, according to **Herophilus** <note>original: "Eracleũ"</note>, above the gland from the folding of the covering <note>the dura mater</note>. This is not truly a vein, but because its shape is round and hollow and also curved, blood is found in it just as in veins. Therefore, it is called the "third vein" by **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Halyabate"; 10th-century Persian physician</note>. Wherefore, since it is reduced to a vein in the speech of **Averroes**, the statement of the one saying that blood is found in the veins alone is verified; and in the heart, as he also leads the heart back to the veins. For the heart is like a part of them, according to the third book of *The History of Animals*.

The order of those things which are in the head is as follows: first the bone of the palate; then the "marvelous net" <note>original: "rete mirabile"; a complex of small blood vessels</note> as in wild beasts; then the gland above which is the aforementioned lake of blood; then the dura mater; then the pia mater; then the brain and its ventricles, above the middle of which are two "buttocks" <note>original: "nates"; the colliculi of the brain</note> laterally, and a certain part is in the upper middle, as described in the ninth book of *On the Usefulness [of the Parts]*.

It is proved, however, that blood in the first two modes is contained only in the veins and their equivalents: because where a thing is generated, there alone it is perfected and remains suitable as such; for nature gives form as much as it gives place and other generating factors, as appears in the fourth book of *On the Heavens and the World*. The reason for this is blood; for it is generated in the liver and the heart. Moreover, that thing is only contained in that place where it is preserved; for that place has a preservative power, as proved in the fourth book of *The Physics*. But blood is only preserved in the veins and their equivalents; for if poured out into a "belly" (that is, a cavity), it necessarily putrefies, according to the sixth book of the *Aphorisms*. Whence **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note> writes concerning "black bile" <note>original: "nigra cola"</note> that blood is disturbed/spoiled not only when falling out of the body, but also within it, such as in the lungs or the chest... and so blood is only contained in the veins and their boundaries.

In the third mode, however, blood having exited the veins is located in the members through pores, which is shown when it is ordered toward their nutrition as an end: for it is now assimilated to them, not a little in substance and quality, and especially when it is more fully digested and thickened, and separated from the circuit of the veins. The squeezing of the members also denotes that blood is contained in their sponginess (section 33).

Regarding the fourth point: to the first argument, it should be said as seen before: similarly, although they <note>organs like the brain</note> do not have such [veins], they nevertheless draw blood from nearby veins by a certain contiguity; and it is altered and transmuted into themselves. For the blood of the kidneys is poured through their whole flesh like a vapor, and being continued with it, gradually becomes their food, as in the fifth book of *On the Usefulness [of the Parts]*. To the other point, it should be said as it appeared: that blood, when it flows outside the veins, already becomes the kind of blood which is allowed not to be contained in them. To the other point, it should be said that it is not necessary for the whole body to be a vein, even though it is diffused through the whole (that is, through the greater part of itself). For they <note>the vessels</note> tend to such a point that they are hidden and diminished by the more abundant nourishment that runs through them, like the smallest streams, yet made slow and invisible, by which a garden is irrigated; or like the passages and ways in the leaves of a vine (third book of *On the Parts [of Animals]*), where no veins are manifest. They are hidden, however, especially in decrepit age, as the back of the hand denotes. Since therefore it is carried disseminated first through the body, it becomes thinner in nature and meets none of them; yet by proximity and by the pain of the place drawing it, to which nature also moves with the spirits, soon the blood is led out from the end of the vein along with the humors.

However, blood and <term>m'ie</term>—indeed even the other humors—are produced by the heat of the liver. This heat is one, since it is also its form. For heat is the form of the body... And of one thing there is one form and being. That there is also one heat generative of the humors is suggested in the first book of *On the Properties [of the Elements]*. Furthermore, things which retain the same flavors seem to have the same efficient cause; since one arrives at the knowledge of a thing primarily through flavors (section 145). Thus it happens in blood and <term>m'ie</term>, for the flavor of blood is sweet, and <term>m'ie</term> similarly exists in sweetness and astringency. Since such a thing stands so closely connected to blood. Again, since the generative heat appears simple...

...of humors, either diminished or superfluous, as in the case of the temperate. One cannot say that melancholy <note>original: "m͠ia"; shorthand for *melancolia*</note> is diminished heat, since that belongs to phlegm <note>original: "flāt͠is"; shorthand for *flegmatis*</note>, nor that it is excessive heat, as that is common [to choler]. Therefore, it will be temperate; and this is blood. For you cannot say that the heat of melancholy is of a higher intensity than the heat of blood, for then it would surpass it in quality; nor that it is a lower remission, like that which is in phlegm, because then the melancholy would be insufficiently cooked <note>original: "decocta"; refers to the metabolic "cooking" or digestion of humors</note> due to the shortening of the heat. Thus, by further cooking, it could be converted into blood, which is denied in distinction 29. Therefore, they are produced by the same heat, and the natural efficient cause of blood and melancholy is largely the same.

The opposite of this is felt by [the authors of] *On Natural Things* <note>likely referring to a specific commentary on Aristotle or Galen</note> and the second book of *On Crises*. For the matter and the agent are also diverse; although this may be discussed in any way according to the disposition of the matter, the matter of blood is one thing and that of melancholy is another. Furthermore, the material cause of melancholy is that which, among nutrients, is vehemently thick and of little humidity, and the [metabolic] heat is stronger in it.

Thus, it seems the efficient cause of melancholic heat is elevated, though it is not equal to the heat of blood. Therefore, the efficient cause of melancholy is not the same, but diverse. Regarding the first point, it should be known that melancholy is a cold and dry humor; it exists in a double state: natural and material. Natural melancholy, according to **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."</note>, is the dregs, turbulence, and superfluity of good blood, which possesses a middle taste between sweetness and bitterness. And this humor is properly called "black" according to **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note>.

But unnatural melancholy is black choler, which is a substance [formed] by way of scorching <term>adustio|A medical process where humors are "burnt" or "parched" by excessive heat, changing their properties</term>, ashiness, or the expression and boiling of humidity. This is fourfold by reason of its scorching; for it is produced, as will be shown, for other reasons as well, since any of the four humors, according to **Avicenna** and **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, 10th-century Persian physician</note>, can be turned to ash. For some is made from phlegm by scorching, which is called phlegmatic melancholy; this exists in two forms, depending on whether the phlegm with which the melancholy is mixed was thin or thick—though this happens more rarely because of its resistance to scorching and incineration compared to others. Some comes from the combustion of blood, called sanguineous melancholy; some from the scorching of choler, called colic [choler]; and another from the scorching of melancholy itself, which is twofold depending on whether the substance that scorched it was thinner, which is very evil, fermenting the earth and bubbling like the sharpest vinegar. **Galen** [discusses this] in *On Black Choler*, the fourth book of *Aphorisms*, the second book of *On Natural [Faculties]*, the third of *On Internal Parts*, and the fourteenth of *On the Method of Healing*. In these places, it seems he touches more upon natural melancholy and that which comes from the scorching of humors, which is generated in two ways: by scorching and by putrefaction (from the fourteenth book of *On Method*). We sense that we must flee from this [humor], as do other animals. Or it comes from a thick [matter] which is less efficient in causing [harm], yet it is more difficult to eradicate because of how it is fixed [in the body].

Natural melancholy is multiplied by many causes, both hot and cold and others. And therefore it was not without merit said in the third book of *On Internal Parts* that a thousand things were imagined by him <note>likely Galen</note>; and in the third book [it is noted that] types of fear outside of habit were infinite. First, indeed, if the constitution of the body is melancholic, and specifically of the heart; or because of the heat of the liver; and also according to **Diocles** <note>Diocles of Carystus, 4th-century BCE physician</note>, [the heat] of the intestines, whom they say **Theophilus** <note>Theophilus Protospatharius, 7th-century medical writer</note> calls by the name of the Arabs, or because of the weakness of the spleen in attracting melancholy and cleansing the blood from it, such as through obstructions <note>original: "opilatiōne͠z"</note> and abscesses of the same. Or even because of the mesenteric [veins], or because of vehement cold freezing the liquid and hardening it, so that it passes into a species of melancholy, just as happens to phlegm [becoming] glassy. Or because of a long constriction of any humor and the privation of natural heat; or because of long illnesses, especially in a hot place and in summer. For these eventually turn the humor to ash.

In the *Prognostics*, black humor is [described as] either very evil by superficiality and corrosive, or as being made of thick blood similarly dried out, or by reason of death and fragility. And these occur if the regimen of the "six things" <term>sex res non naturales|The 'six non-natural things' in medieval medicine: air, food/drink, sleep/waking, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the mind</term> declines toward the cold and dry—specifically air, food, and drink—and a superfluity of sadness and fear. It has even seemed to some physicians that melancholy happens because of a demon. To these, **Avicenna** says he does not care to teach whether it happens from a demon or not, since he teaches the cause; though it happens that they say and think such wonderful things that people think it could not happen naturally. For instance, when an illiterate melancholic woman was heard to speak Latin appropriately, but when cured, she ceased to do so, as if it were taken from her.

Regarding the second point, it should be known: first it is written that the cause of blood and melancholy is the same, namely temperate heat. In the second book of *On Natural [Faculties]* and *On Crises*, the contrary seems to be portended: that when food is altered in the veins by innate heat, blood is made from a moderation [of heat]; other humors, however, are made from immoderations. All things that are seen agree with this, because the substance of the humor is different from blood, especially since it is contrary to it in function and nature. What is true regarding this will be seen from what is to be said.

Regarding the third point, so that the contradiction of such great men might not be gathered, since the truth was known to them, let one perceive the interpretation of the other's intellect. It should be known that whoever knows anything of the middle in geometry or arithmetic places it between two extremes. That middle is not truly a single point, as it participates in a "latitude" <note>a range or spectrum</term>, but is rather triple, so that the extremes with the middle result in five points. This happens in the present case: for it is conceded that choler is generated by exceeding heat, and phlegm by diminished heat. That which is between the middle of these, within the latitude of the temperate, either declines more toward the side of one of the extremes (such as exceeding heat), and then blood will be generated, or it declines toward the heat of choler. Or it declines toward the part of the other extreme (diminished heat), and such heat will be procreative of melancholy. Or it will hold the middle and the [perfect] temperament by reason of the center, and from such heat true blood will be generated. **Avicenna** does not intend to say that the heat of blood and melancholy are exactly the same when compared to each other, but rather in respect to phlegm and choler. Just as it is explained that the heat of children and youths is the same in distinction 28; for the heat of melancholy is not diminished like that of phlegm, nor so super-acute as that of choler, but a middle within the latitude between them. <meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on the nature of the four humors. It transitions from a general discussion of their "cooking" (metabolic processing) to a more specific analysis of how different parts of the liver and the quality of raw matter result in different humors, specifically contrasting blood and melancholy.</meta>

The heat diversifies according to their forms. For the form of blood is tempered by a balanced decoction <note>original: "decoctione"; the metabolic "cooking" process that transforms food into humors</note>, while melancholy is indeed hypostatic <note>original: "ypostatica"; referring to a sediment-like or underlying substance that sinks or settles</note>. For if the forms were the same, then these substances would be the same, since it is form that gives being and unity. This is also suggested by the causes of the use of these humors: he placed four qualities in equal measure for blood, but not for melancholy, to generate it—or rather, one quality exceeds the others. Thus, it follows that **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."; refers to Aristotle</note> placed it as a temperate color with a great range, since he said it was the productive cause of blood and melancholy.

**Galen**, however, defines it more narrowly, insofar as that which is truly temperate holds the exact middle between extremes, so that a heat weaker than temperate heat remains a diminished heat, and that which exceeds it is an excessive heat. **Aristotle**, however, placed the aforementioned two humors in a certain middle ground containing them. Blood, therefore, according to **Galen**, is formed by a heat that is simply temperate, though with greater and lesser variations; for from a greater distance from the middle, phlegm <note>original: "fla"; shorthand for *flegma*</note> and choler <note>original: "colera"; yellow bile</note> are caused, but from a lesser distance, melancholy is formed. **Galen** also implies this when he later adds in the same passage that foods hotter by nature produce more choler, while colder foods produce more phlegm, and similarly regarding the stages of life.

Next, it must also be known that the heat that generates the humors can be considered in two ways: either in itself and in common—and thus it stands as one—or particularly and insofar as it refers to something else, which happens in three ways. It refers either to the soul or the intent of nature, or to the parts of the liver <note>original: "hepatis"</note>, or to the matter. Regarding the soul, I say that nature primarily intends blood, then phlegm, and finally the others; and therefore nature uses different heats for their production so that it can also care for the usefulness of their generation at the right time. It also diversifies according to the parts and locations of the liver; for the blood will be purer in its superior part, within the vein close to the heart, where blood is most strongly generated. But in the inferior part, at the furthest line where it is most distant, phlegm or melancholy are generated; whereas in the superior internal prominence, being hotter, more choler is said to be produced. It also varies on account of the matter in which the action occurs and its resistance. For the "aptitude" <note>the inherent suitability or receptivity of the material</note> diversifies the action of the agent for that reason. For some matter is temperate, some is hot, some is cold. Furthermore, some is thin, some is thick, and some is in the middle—as seen in Distinction 29. Reason demonstrates this because an agent varied by application produces something else and does not remain the same, even if it were considered the same in itself, since even accidents in a subject induce a change; such is also the heat that generates the humors by application to diverse things.

<margin>
~
</margin>

Furthermore, cause and effect are proportionate; hence if the effect is singular, the cause is singular. If one is univocal, the other is univocal, as seen in the book of *Physics*. But blood is hot and moist, while melancholy <note>original: "mlie"; shorthand for *melancolia*</note> is a cold and dry sediment. Also, phlegm is of a moderate substance, but melancholy is of a thick substance. Therefore, there will be one cause for one and another for the other in their production. They are of entirely different effects. Things that produce this are produced by at least immediately different causes. Therefore, blood and melancholy will not be precisely the same thing. You should also know that in a natural body, blood exists in the greatest quantity, then phlegm, then choler, and finally a very small amount of melancholy, as stated in Distinction 38—or at least something proportionate in weight. This happens because of the necessities and greater benefits to nature, as they are more or less suitable. **Alexander** <note>likely Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> in his *Problems* says: know that blood, which nourishes the body, abounds in quantity; then phlegm, for it nourishes during hunger; after that, yellow bile is diminished, as it is non-nourishing and sharp. Still more diminished is black bile (melancholy), as it is an enemy to nature. I also hear of this proportion of quantities more by sight than by weight, since melancholy, being earthy, is heavier and more abundant [in weight]; just as in the body, fiery choler indicates a lightness like the nature of agaric <note>a type of fungus used in medicine</note> or lapis lazuli; concerning bitter choler, see the first touch, 91.

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it has already been shown what should be said—namely, that the humors are made from the same heat as the liver in common; even the heat of the whole body can in some way be called one, yet it is greatly diversified as declared by its application. To the other, it must be said that they have the same flavors within a wide range; just as the same heat is said to belong to them in this way. For the flavor of blood is simply sweet; melancholy not only possesses sweetness but also sharpness and bitterness <note>original: "acredine"</note>; for the heat could not perfectly master the thickness of the substance. To the other, it must be said that it happens that the heat of blood and melancholy is not entirely the same, but rather that they have more akin heats than phlegm and choler have to each other. And perhaps melancholy remains mixed with blood much longer than the other humors. Hence, by a concession of heat, both would be the same, but not simply so; nor is melancholy converted into blood by further cooking like phlegm is, because the heat of melancholy remains simply weaker than that of blood, because the thick, earthy substance requires more heat and resists being turned into blood. For a humor to be converted naturally into blood can happen in two ways: either by reason of exceeding heat, like choler, or by reason of substance, like melancholy. Therefore, melancholy is no less a "middle temperament" than choler and melancholy <gloss>this seems to refer to the mixed state</gloss> because of its moisture; also by reason of further heat, it can be converted into blood in times of necessity.

But on the contrary: hard bodies like bones, cartilages, and the like can be converted into blood; therefore, why not melancholy? It must be said that they do not pass through the liver, which is the generator of humors; melancholy, however, has withdrawn from it, nor can it return to it unless it be beneficial. If, however, another path were granted, it would be different; nor is blood truly generated except in the liver and especially the heart, from which the melancholic nature is removed. What parts belong to the other is clear from what has been introduced; nor is the heat of melancholy stronger in its matter, except that it is founded in a thicker subject, by which it is resisted, not being able to overcome it entirely; or it is stronger in that it imprints more strongly upon it, as happens when unnatural melancholy is generated in the liver, as **Avicenna** <note>original: "Auicȳ"</note> believes.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the humors, specifically moving from the general production of blood and melancholy to the specific mechanism of how blood is transformed into the solid tissues of the body. It explores the theory of "secondary humors" (moistures) that bridge the gap between liquid blood and solid flesh.</meta>

It is manifest that for animals possessing blood, blood is the ultimate nourishment. Life exists here in the highest degree throughout all parts of the body. Indeed, it is proven that the embryo is nourished immediately by blood, for in newborns, the marrow is found to be bloody; for it is from blood that the parts of the body are generated. Furthermore, in the governance of the body, such and so much blood must be present in all parts, according to the quality and quantity of what is produced. 

Thirdly, regarding the complexions <term>complexio; the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, wet, dry—within an individual or organ</term>, blood is converted into flesh without any other intermediate transformation. In the first part of the first book <note>original: "prio pria"; likely referring to Avicenna's *Canon of Medicine*, Book 1, Fen 1</note>, it is said that blood, sweating out from the small openings of the veins, glides into the limbs from the divine side <note>original: "ex pte dīna"; this likely refers to the "outer" or "extravasated" portion of the blood once it leaves the vessels</note>. **Palin** <note>likely a corruption of Galen or a specific commentator</note> says the same: blood does not need to be converted many times for the nutrition of certain parts, as flesh does; rather, as soon as the nourishment reaches the part, it is converted into it.

The liver, insofar as it performs such a perfect digestion, acts so that the blood is effective for nourishing that part. Furthermore, in the second collection, it is felt that blood nourishes simply; and many such discourses are found among physicians and physicists. Furthermore, if there were other moistures, fever or pain would clearly arise from them, but not in the limbs; because that would be a hectic fever <term>ethica; a fever that settles into the solid tissues or "moistures" of the organs rather than the fluids</term>. For as stated in the third collection, a hectic fever is an external heat fixed in the substance of a limb. It is unheard of that this should happen in the humors.

Likewise, the matter of nutrition and generation is the same. From whatever things we are composed, by those same things we are nourished. But according to **Aristotle**, **Avicenna**, and the **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note>, we are all nourished by blood, and thus from it we are made. Again, the effect argues for the cause; but flesh, as it is said, is "effected blood." This reason is the explanation: it is clearly indicated by the flesh of the liver, heart, and kidneys especially. Whence, in the first book of *On Natural Things*, in the conversion of blood into flesh, nothing is posited except a certain thickening of the blood into substance, but not a change in color, as when bread is transformed into blood. 

Therefore, these intermediate moistures are minimal. Given this, some say only one exists; for the closer something approaches its end, the more quickly and with fewer intervening steps it reaches it. But blood is closer to the limbs than external food is, which involves one or two intermediate stages—namely, the juice of chyle <term>chilus; the pulpy acidic fluid which passes from the stomach to the small intestine</term> and mastication—along with what the location and accidents indicate generate it. 

Again, since these moistures are made from humors, they are "secondary humors." They will therefore be proportional to the humors. And while there is only one primary humor, which is blood (the others being superfluities), **Palin** says that what is the primary humor is not a moisture but an essence, since it is distinguished from its opposite. But the primary nameless moisture, which can be called "sanguineous," is a humor, because it exists in the veins as it is delivered to their extreme orifices. That which is located in the veins is a humor. 

Also, that which does not contribute simply to nutrition or the binding of the body is not seen as a moisture, since this is its very purpose. Such a second moisture is called **dew** <term>ros; a vaporous moisture that "sprinkles" the tissues like morning dew</term>. For according to **Aristotle**, it is only converted into nourishment when the body lacks food due to some cause; it does not connect the parts of the body, since it is a moist, subtle, and fluid thing. Furthermore, that which is transformed by a perfect transformation and has already become part of a limb is not seen as a moisture but rather as the limb itself, since moistures are humors which, by their principal disposition, are transformed only so far as they are able to pass into the limbs assigned to them. 

Yet they are not completely the parts of any simple limbs; they are effects. In the first book of *On Animals*, **Aristotle** says the reason for this is not the fourth moisture, called **glue** <term>gluten; the "cement" that holds the solid parts of the body together</term>, because that already collects and continues the parts of the body. Upon its dissolution, the body is said to be reduced to ashes. **Palin** says the same thing there, though he posits only three, omitting the first one mentioned. From this, it is elicited that there is either one moisture, or two, or only three.

Against these two opposing views, the general consensus of physicians is held: **Galen**, **Johannitius**, **Haly Abbas**, **Isaac**, and **Avicenna**, with others. These all assert that they exist and remain four in number. Again, nutrition happens by "like by like," but the limbs are thickened and also white. Thus they are nourished by these moistures. Likewise, the moisture receives sensation, as when tender and soft limbs are strongly pressed, like the nose of a hare, and especially in infancy, when the superfluities denote that they are being sent outside imperceptibly. This is also seen in those suddenly beheaded who were giving milk from their veins. 

Furthermore, the moistures ought to be proportioned in number to the things from which they are generated and the humors. But these are four. Therefore, it is probable that they exist as four in number. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known that moistures are twofold: first, blood itself; second, the moistures mentioned, which appear in the arguments to be four in number: **sanguineous moisture**, **dew**, **exchange**, and **glue** <note>original: "ros, cambium, & gluten"</note>. 

1. The first is a humor still in the extremities of the small veins, held near the simple limbs which imbibe and irrigate it, which is appropriated to each limb by alteration. This moisture, according to **Isaac** in his third book on fevers, is found even in vegetables. For this is like the moisture existing in the juices of trees, such as that which comes out of the branches of a vine. 
2. The other is a humor which has not yet passed through the third perfect digestion to become simple limbs, such as **dew** <term>ros</term>, which is ready to be converted into nourishment when the body lacks it, and to moisten the limbs when they have been strongly dried out. This is essential to it, though it does not happen often, just as the water or moisture of trees and growing things, or that which is in grain and grapes not yet ripe. 
3. The third part is the **exchange** <term>cambium; from the Latin for 'change' or 'exchange', referring to the humor that has begun to solidify</term>, which is coagulated and is the true nourishment of the limbs, changed or altered according to the species of the complexion, but not yet reaching completion so as to obtain the hardness and thickness of the limbs themselves. It is like tender flesh that is not yet assimilated into the limbs, similar to the moisture of grain that has begun to coagulate and become flavorful, yet remains soft, or the moisture of grapes beginning to thicken and become sweet but not yet delicate nor turned to hardness. 
4. The fourth is the **glue** <term>gluten</term>, which contains and binds the parts of our body. From the beginning of its construction, it is disseminated in the simple limbs, the very thing that coagulates the ligaments to one another, preserving them and making them one, until they are resolved into dust. Its principle was from the sperm or the matter of the embryo, according to the followers of **Aristotle**. It is like the coagulated moisture of wheat, which is its very substance...

It cites major medical authorities like Galen and Avicenna to explain how the body is nourished and held together by these intermediate substances.</summary>
