...assimilated. That is, you shall keep it from putrefaction; just as the moisture of **raisins** <note>original: "passulay"</note> defends them from corruption.

Regarding the second point, it must be known that certain **sciolists** <term>sciolist; a person who has a superficial knowledge of a subject but pretends to be an expert</term> have denied these moistures entirely—especially the first and the last—claiming that blood is immediately converted into the limbs. Their motivations are based on certain sharp arguments regarding the moistures alone. They reject Galen, Haly Abbas, Isaac, and Avicenna <note>original: "Ax̄"; a common medieval abbreviation for Avicenna</note>. Indeed, they abhor everything as ridiculous, and they accuse Alexander and Serapion <note>Serapion the Elder, a 9th-century physician</note> because they posited these stages. They claim that Avicenna, Haly Abbas, and Galen (in the second book of *On Crises*) do not posit these moistures, nor does Isaac in his *Viaticum*.

How great a ridicule this is! For Avicenna and Haly Abbas do touch upon them. Galen, in the second book of *On Crises*, says nothing about them because he is excusing himself to discuss the signs of hectic fever <note>original: "signis ethice"; a fever associated with the consumption or "drying out" of the body's solid parts</note>, since he follows other fevers for the most part. And it is a marvel that they cite Isaac’s *Viaticum*, for if he had not touched upon them there, he would not be dealing with hectic fever at all. There are many other errors in that same place which it would be vile to touch upon, as it is perhaps foolish to seek out the foolish. 

Hence, woe to those who follow a teacher of such ignorance! They lack the necessary time for the healing art, not just twofold (as Galen says in the seventh book), but many times over. The defects of these men will become clear in the third part of our discussion.

Regarding the third point, it must be known that it is necessary to posit these moistures, and specifically four of them. This is demonstrated both by authorities and by reason.

First, in the seventh book of his *Therapeutics* <note>original: "terapetice"; Galen's *Method of Medicine*</note>, Galen touches on these four when distinguishing four types of dryness. He says that the most certain dryness is that in which the **solid substance** of the similar parts <term>similar parts; "homeomerous" parts like bone, membrane, or fat that are uniform throughout, as opposed to "organic" parts like the hand</term> has become drier. This begins to deprive the body of the **fourth moisture**, called **gluten** <note>original: "gluten"; literally "glue," the moisture that has already been mostly assimilated into the solid tissue</note>. 

Another dryness is that of those things which consist of a moist and coagulated substance, such as fat and the flesh of liquefied parts; this is the deprivation of the **third moisture**. 

The third type of dryness occurs when the "familiar moisture" from which the body is nourished is lost; this moisture is disseminated throughout all the particles of the body in the form of dew. This is the **second moisture**, called **ros** <note>original: "ros"; Latin for "dew," referring to the moisture that has left the vessels and "dewed" the tissues</note>, as is clearly expressed. 

Another dryness is that which exists within the small arteries and veins proper to each part, which is caused by undigested blood; this is opposed to the **first moisture**, which appears as "bloodiness."

Galen also touches on these moistures in the tenth book of his *Therapeutics* and the first book of *On Fevers*, though not as expressly. Similarly, in the second book of *On Marasmus* <note>original: "de tabe"; referring to Galen's work on the wasting of the body</note>—translated by me—he says there is one disposition of thinness when moisture is lost from the solid bodies, which we have said is their proper food and which wears down the soft flesh; another follows the solid bodies themselves, which are called primary and similar parts. In the first book of the *Prognostics*, he also indicates these, saying it will be shown in those things concerning the generation of sperm; for the tunics of the vessels are nourished by nothing else but this blood.

---

Isaac, Haly Abbas, Avicenna, and even Al-Mansur <note>original: "Almanzor"; referring to the famous medical work by Rhazes</note> show this to all who are not foolish. No one can correctly distinguish types of wasting <note>original: "etīcas"; hectic fevers/consumptions</note> unless they posit minor, major, and middle drynesses, to which these moistures are opposites.

Reason confirms this in two ways. First, because **digestion** consists of adding and assimilating the nutrient to the nourished part (as per the first book of *Prognostics*). Nutrition is the same. But everything nourished is thickened and whitened, so that its substance and color are changed significantly from the substance of blood. Furthermore, it is the nature of **innate heat**—being gentle and sweet—to thicken and whiten, as appears in milk and in the seeds produced from blood. This process involves a stripping away and an adding. This is shown because those with poor milk production have watery and yellow milk, and those who cohabit excessively emit blood <note>A medieval belief that semen is highly refined blood, and over-exertion leads to its raw form (blood) being expelled</note>.

Second, according to the *Natural Faculties*, things that have a similar substance happen to transmute into each other. But for things that are far apart, it is unimaginable for them to be assimilated to each other without transformations in the middle. For things that transmute into one another must have a shared symbol (as per the third book of *On Generation and Corruption*). But blood and limbs are very far apart. Therefore, some intermediate must come between them.

Again, **Nature does not make a leap** <note>original: "Palin natura non committit saltum"</note>; rather, it proceeds gradually from one extreme through a medium to the other extreme (as per the seventh book of the *History of Animals*). If the transition from blood to limb were immediate and instantaneous, something false and disordered would happen in nature. Therefore, something must fall in between as a medium.

Furthermore, in the fifth book of *Physics* and the nineteenth book of *Therapeutics*: motion occurs from one extreme through a medium to the other extreme. Since this is a motion from blood into limbs, it will happen by some intermediate occurring—not just a motion, but a change of matter and form.

And what is more: we see these thickened and whitened moistures when **anatomizing** <note>original: "anothomizađo"</note> the solid parts, and especially when they flow from the bones. This is also shown by natural superfluity. These moistures testify to their own usefulness. From this, it is also proven according to Avicenna <note>original: "Aȳ"</note> that a certain medium designated by the name of "moistures" exists between blood and the limbs. 

Finally, the number of these moistures is four. Even if it cannot be shown with such precise harm as has been proven for their existence, I will demonstrate it as far as possible. For it seems similar to the case of efficient and material causes; they depend on the same principle or soul, just as things in the same organ (the body). Among the agents, I see media intervening between their first principle—the soul—and the limb that is immediately acted upon: namely, the virtue, the complexion, the spirits, and the heat. Similarly, between the nourished part and the soul, four media called "moistures" intervene. Each is a necessity because, between things that are far apart and very different, not only a medium but many "medicines" <note>intermediate steps</note> must intervene, as is apparent.

The author uses anatomical observation, the law of "nature makes no leaps," and the authorities of Galen and Avicenna to prove these "secondary humors" exist.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic defense of the four intermediate moistures (humidities) required for nutrition. The previous page established that blood does not turn into flesh instantly but passes through stages, refuting "sciolists" who denied these intermediaries.</meta>

¶ Between the hardest **skull** and the softest **brain**, two membranes intervene in the middle: namely, the **dura mater** and the **pia mater**. Furthermore, because we suspect a certain moisture is inserted into the limbs—to the extent that it appears to be of their very substance—we view it as a fourth thing, more remote [from the limb] and closer to the blood, just like the first moisture. Since these two [the skull and brain] are so distinct, one middle-ground was not sufficient to come between them, but two were needed. Again, it has been shown from four distinct dry states that there are four opposing moistures, since one of a pair of contraries is predicated as often as the other. This is evident from **hectic fever** <term>hectic fever; a fever (Lat. 'ethica') associated with the 'drying out' of the body's solid parts</term> existing in three types. Because the first species (Difference 83) possesses two primary moistures, it is most probably concluded that four moistures exist. Regarding the aforementioned, it happens to be doubted whether the third moisture is caused immediately from the first, or mediately from the second. And it seems that the third is made from the second without an intermediary. For just as is the existence and order of things, so ought their actions to exist; but first is the first, then the second and third; therefore the third will be caused immediately by the second. 

We must say that according to **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note>, for the most part, it is hinted that the third is made from the first. For regularly, when nourishment has been copious for the body, it always generates the third immediately from the first. However, when the first is lacking due to some drying cause, the digesting nature—thereby thickening the second moisture—converts it into the third. For one imagines that from the digestion of the first moisture, in order to convert it into the third, nature elicits a certain subtle dew, like a surplus of itself. Since all digestion, at least in a helpful sense, proceeds by thickening (Difference 1). For a wise nature hides this away in the simple limbs like a **storehouse** <note>original: "promptuariū"</note>, so that in a time of need for the first moisture, it may convert [the storehouse] into the third; just as when a lack of blood, induced by some cause, converts **phlegm** into blood; as the same author [Aristotle] testifies with others, and **Galen** <note>original: "san." likely referring to 'Sanctissimus' or a shorthand for Galen in this context</note> when he digests watery phlegm and at other times moistens it.

¶ However, the discourses of **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note> with others seem to sound more as if the second is produced from the first, and the third from this [the second]. For he said that the particles of the body are nourished by the second; the third, however, is like the moisture of fat and flesh. Whence I do not blame **Aristotle**, who sees a certain instinctual mind implanted in nature, like a providence that prepares a storehouse for itself for future events. What was previously introduced can also be said to satisfy reason: that the act does not always follow the order of production. Although the **heart**, **brain**, and **liver** are truly prior to the others—such as the **mouth**, **stomach**, and such—nonetheless these latter operate upon the food before the former. This is also shown by the nutrition of the **embryo** inside and outside the womb. Further anxiety arises since nature, as has been touched upon, always strives to reach the prefixed end by the shorter path. Moreover, a "sin" is committed by doing with more steps what can be explained with fewer. Since, therefore, nature converts white **chyle** <term>chyle; a milky fluid drafted from food in the intestines</term> into red **chyme** <term>chyme; here referring to the further processed state of food, often used interchangeably with blood in this context</term>, and finally into whitened moistures—which it did not do in non-sanguineous animals and plants, for which there was not such happiness as for perfect animals and especially man. For nature does not work so contingently that, while providing for the base, it despises the precious (Book 30 of *On the Heavens and the Earth*). Therefore, is it in vain, and to what purpose does nature strive to induce so many transmutations? 

It must be said, as appears from the books *On Animals* and the *Ten Problems*, that the more perfect some things are, the more things they require in their production; so much so that some things are generated by a single universal agent alone, with only a small transmutation made regarding the matter—such as those things that persist by putrefaction. But others require a particular agent along with this, and more dispositions and movements—such as perfect things, and especially man. Since the mode of generation does not arise solely from proportion but from the mode of production, they will similarly require more organs and transmutations in their permanence and contraries among themselves; just as it produces from contraries, since it produces one contrary from another by means of a subject (Book 1 of *Physics*).

¶ Also, in the bodies of perfect animals, there is a greater diversity by reason of substance and accidents than in non-sanguineous animals and plants. For some parts of animals are very white, such as **bones**, **nerves**, and the **brain** and its fluids; others, however, proceed toward redness, such as the **liver**, **heart**, and **kidneys**; while others are in the middle, like **muscles**, **lungs**, and **spleen**. And therefore, on account of their diversity, it is necessary for the nourishment to be diversified; so that some are nourished by the whiter [substance], others by that which portends some redness, and some by the middle. Again, in man especially, a natural beauty arises from the variety of colors; for his color ought to be suffused with white and red (from the *Ars Medica* <note>original: "in tegni"; a reference to Galen's 'Techne' or 'Ars Medica'</note>). 

It must be resolved, therefore, that nature, insofar as it can, always intends the end through short means; but on account of producing perfection, it often happens to prolong the way. Similarly, if a liquid can be equally perfected by fewer steps as by many, the fewer should be chosen. But here it is shown that the perfect thing [man] cannot be constructed by nature from fewer steps; and therefore it rather chooses a plurality [of stages] for the sake of perfection in imperfect things. Furthermore, some of the limbs are nourished by blood-like nourishment, such as **flesh**; therefore it was necessary for the nourishment to be changed toward redness. Some, however, are nourished by that which is far removed from it, such as **bones** and such; and therefore it was convenient to cause a transmutation into whiteness. 

But so that the truth may appear more fully, it should be known, as touched upon (Difference 30), that "**blood**" is understood in three ways. In one way, for the blood-mass or the collection of all the humors. In another way, insofar as it is a uniform humor, participating in redness and pure in sweetness—as it is distinguished from the other three [humors] and from wateriness—just as history agrees with the physicians. Or [thirdly] insofar as it already exists thickened, and is stripped of exceeding redness and sweetness; a humor which, being the actual nourishment, lacks all excess. Whence the fourth of the *Aphorisms* says: "Nourishment which simply moistens is without strong quality; for it is neither harsh, nor sharp, nor salty, nor bitter."

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the nourishment of the body's "radical" (permanent) members and the role of the four intermediate moistures. It specifically addresses objections based on the writings of Hippocrates, Galen, and Avicenna, moving from the general nature of blood to the specific coloring and function of organs like the liver and kidneys.</meta>

# On the Transformation of Blood into the Body’s Substance

Wherefore, in the first book of the **Prognostics** <note>original: "prognosticorum"; a work by Hippocrates</note>, it is said to be impossible for the tunics <term>tunics; the enveloping membranes or layers of a vessel or organ</term> of the vessels to be nourished except from this blood. Hence, in the twentieth section of the third book, it is stated that **semen** is the superfluity of the fourth food in the whole body, and it is blood that has been more fully digested. And in the fourth book of the **Colliget** <note>The *Colliget* is a major medical encyclopedia by Averroes</note>, the matter by which the **radical members** <term>radical members; the solid, fundamental parts of the body, like bones and nerves, as opposed to fatty or fleshy parts</term> are nourished is "whitened blood." **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Haly"; a famous 10th-century Persian physician</note> says that pure blood is the material for the nourishment of the members. Impure blood, however, is that which is poured into the veins, being similar to all the other remaining humors; the "hermit" erred by failing to distinguish this when discussing the formation of the embryo.

Regarding the fourth point, to the first objection it must be said that **Avicenna** <note>original: "Av."</note> understood "blood" in the third sense of the word, and not in the other ways. Therefore, many people are quite wrong to think that we are generated and nourished from blood in the second sense. Or perhaps he held the opinion—which he does not maintain at present—that he wished to show this by the fact that even in the newly born, **bloody marrow** <note>original: "medulla sanguinea"</note> is found. Yet someone might say that this does not prove the point, because just as blood must be "whitened" to provide nourishment, so too must the bloody marrow be whitened to nourish the bone.

To the other point regarding **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note>, it should be said in this way: in the third book of **On Complexions**, he adds that blood requires only a minimal transformation to generate **flesh**. To the other point, it should be said that he proceeds by this path: either he took blood as the *immediate* nourishment of the members, or as the *mediate* <note>indirect</note> nourishment, as is clearly seen from his opinion. For we also say that **bread** nourishes during the act of nutrition, and that blood—which is further along the process—does so as well. Nor did **Aristotle** in the thirteenth book of **On Animals** <note>original: ".xiii. animalium"</note> say that blood simply "slips" into the members; rather, he added that it "is imbibed into the members little by little."

To the next point, it should be said that **Avicenna** does not intend to say that blood is instantly converted into flesh when it meets it, but that it requires a small alteration when it is to be converted into flesh—at least compared to the greater alteration it needs when it must be transformed into the **radical members**. For blood is quite similar to flesh in its "complexion" (balance of qualities) and substance. This is what he means: blood does not need to be converted many times over in nutrition, as it does for flesh—as if to say it needs only a small conversion. Hence, in **On Natural Ends** <note>original: "fine naturali"; likely referring to a section of a physical or medical text</note>:

> Flesh and all the viscera and muscles are nourished from blood itself, undergoing a brief alteration. For Nature established intervals and form for members distant from the blood, as is seen in bones, in which nourishment is contained so that it may be converted into them little by little; for because of the distance, many intermediate conversions are required for them to be transformed into themselves. Those things that are closer to blood require less.

To the other point, it should be said that because the nourishment of the **liver** <note>original: "epatis"</note>—at least regarding its truest substance, which is blood—is gradually coagulated and changed in color, it is said to perform its work like a **beech tree** <note>original: "fagus"; perhaps a metaphor for the liver's dense, woody substance or its slow growth/processing</note>. Although it nourishes something, it is nevertheless converted into moistures in its own way; and even granting this, it does not do so simply, but here it only removes the moistures. To the other point regarding **Avicenna**, it has already been seen what should be said.

To the next point, it must be said that these moistures are demonstrated through **hectic fever** <term>hectic fever; Lat. 'ethica', a fever that dries out the body's essential moistures</term>, for the distinction in Difference 98 is founded upon them. And if it is said, according to **Avicenna** and many others, that hectic fever occurs in the "substance of the member," it must be replied that "member" is commonly used to include the moistures themselves, especially those that are already starting to coagulate. And rightly so, because they tend toward and end in the members themselves, and everything takes its name from the "end" toward which it moves, according to the fifth book of **Physics** and the second book of **On the Soul** <note>Aristotle's works</note>. It is just for everything to be named after its end goal. This is shown by the fact that **Avicenna**, in the third book, immediately distinguishes the species of hectic fever according to the three moistures. There are also moistures that cause **abscesses** <note>original: "apostematum"</note>, as the first book feels, and these help the flesh itself; however, they do not appear to be blood because the other humors are blackened by their own quantity and color.

To the other point, it seems what must be said is that we are not made from blood nor nourished by it, unless blood is understood in that "third way." To the next point, it should be said that **flesh is not truly red**, but rather tends more toward white when the blood is thoroughly squeezed out of it and washed away. Or, if some part is red like purple—such as that of the **liver**—this is not in it because of the redness of blood, but rather because of the nature of the liver itself. For the liver was made red so that it might generate red blood, as stated in the fourth book of **On the Use of the Parts** <note>original: "de iuuamentis"; a work by Galen</note> and the third and fourth books of **Therapeutics**.

The **kidneys** <note>original: "renes"</note> perhaps remain red because they cannot perfectly change the redness of the "wateriness" of the blood, since no vein begins to whiten in its extreme ends, except for the **emulgent veins** <note>the renal veins</note>, which however are not spread through them entirely (Differences 87 and 31). To the other point, it should be said that blood is further removed from a member (especially a radical one) than it is from external food. Either this is because movement is intensified at the end—since nature then becomes more industrious, according to the tenth book of **Problems**—for by all ways and means it can, nature busies itself to reach the end by the most expeditious routes. For anyone wishing to reach a destination quickly finds the most numerous and shortest paths.

To the other point, it should be said that the moistures are not called "four" because of four transformations and forms that they take before being truly transferred into the member. For this seems to be the nature of the conversion of nourishment: that it proceeds by always multiplying after it has been changed by digestion in the stomach, until it is assimilated into the member. For first it is converted into feces and **ichor** <term>ichor; a watery discharge or serous fluid</term>; then the ichor is turned into the four humors and wateriness; then the blood into the superfluities and the **four moistures**, and this into their superfluities. Finally, there is the "apposition" <note>placement alongside</note> and "assimilation" <note>becoming similar</note> to the member; and this satisfies the logic of the preceding point.

To the final point, it should be said that the **first moisture** is not simply in the veins, but rather in their extreme orifices that are already contiguous <note>touching</note> with the members. For because of the goal and end toward which it moves, it already tastes more of the nature of the member than of a humor, even if they are commonly called "moistures."

->### CHAPTER 34<-

**Whether semen is shed from the whole body or from all the members.**

It is shown that it is shed from the whole body, because in the book *On Airs, Waters, and Places* <note>original: "de rere & aqua"; a work by Hippocrates</note>, semen is defended as coming from all the members of the body: healthy semen from healthy parts, and diseased semen running from diseased parts. And firstly in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. Furthermore, in the fourth book of the **Problems**: "Why are those engaging in intercourse dissolved and weakened during coitus so frequently?" This is because semen is a purging from all parts. This is confirmed by reasons: since in the emission of seed there is a vehemence of pleasure diffused through the whole body, which does not seem to happen except because of the emission of semen; since it happens in the whole body, it must be emitted from the whole. Likewise, that thing seems to be shed from the whole body whose superfluous emission harms the whole body, when no other cause exists; but this happens in the superfluous emission of semen, as the senses indicate. Again, **mutilated** <note>original: "colobi"</note> or crippled people beget mutilated or crippled children, which would not happen unless the semen was unable to descend from the mutilated part because the body lacks it. Furthermore, the offspring resemble the parents not only according to natural traits, but even according to acquired ones, namely **scars** and **tattoos** <note>original: "stigmata"</note>. For a certain **Chalcedonian** father <note>original: "patre nanq; calcedonico"</note> having a picture <note>a tattoo</note> on his arm that was worn and not clearly articulated, his son contracted a similar mark in the same place. Hence, after the words of Hippocrates regarding *Airs and Waters*, the operations are such that the bald beget the bald, those with gray eyes beget those with gray eyes, and the cross-eyed beget the cross-eyed. Again, every perfect thing begets something like itself, as stated in the fourth book of the **Meteorology** <note>original: "methauroy"</note>. But this does not happen unless the semen is shed from the whole, so that the resemblance happens through every part. Still, it seems reasonable: just as there is something from which the whole first comes to be, similarly there is a particular part for each thing, since the ratio of the whole and the part is the same (*History of Animals*, book 1). Therefore, just as something is shed for the generation of the whole, so something is shed for the generation of the part, since the whole is nothing other than an aggregation of parts, as the **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note> says on the first book of the **Physics**; thus the seed is derived from the whole.

**Avicenna** <note>original: "Ay."</note> feels the opposite of this, along with **Aristotle** in the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*. This is confirmed by reasons: for we see some people emit seed suddenly at the kiss of a woman or at the slightest touch; this could not happen if it were shed from the whole body. Furthermore, one may observe that many mutilated people beget perfect children; but the opposite ought to happen if it came from the whole body. Also, the matter is not shed from the whole like blood, but mostly from the **womb** <note>original: "matrice"</note>; therefore, it is not shed from all members. Regarding the first point, it should be known that although **offspring** <term>offspring; Latin "genitura," the product of generation</term> and **semen** <note>original: "sperma"</note> are commonly heard as synonymous names, they are positioned as distinct in the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*. For one is called "offspring" which comes from the parent, having the first principle of generation to join with the born. "Semen" is also said of that which has its principle from both joined together, as happens in plants and in certain animals. In those where the female is separate from the male, it is even more universally contained as the principle from which motion and matter come. The name "offspring" in more perfect animals implies specifically the cause from which motion comes. For semen or offspring is the **useful superfluity** of the final nourishment distributed to the parts. For although semen seems to come to the surface of the body along with other superfluities, it differs greatly. For it is not a **wasting** <note>original: "tabes"</note> or dissolution as the ancients thought; for such a thing is entirely contrary to nature, but this is most natural. For not every superfluity is useful, since a simple superfluity profits nothing for nature, but is entirely excreted as irrelevant. This, however, is most useful—indeed, entirely necessary for the perfection of the species. Nor is every useful superfluity the same: it is not the first, but the second; because **phlegm** is the useful superfluity of the first nourishment. For there is a first difference of undigested things coming from food (Chapter 29). Wherefore, semen is fittingly described as the useful superfluity of the final nourishment. "Whole," however, is said in two ways: in one way, when none of the parts are missing from which it has its being. and this is threefold: either each of the things contained under it is called one, just as a **universal** contains many in its predication, like "animal"; or it is one from these, such as an **integral whole**. And this is either because...

The first mode can also be understood in two ways. Because of this, there is **assimilation** <note>The process by which the offspring comes to resemble the parent</note>. And therefore, from a diminished or maimed member, a diminished member is sometimes generated—though this happens when the veins do not reach their ultimate goal and the final appetite of the body is not coupled with digestion. It is as if he wants to say that assimilation sometimes fails because the assimilative and completive power lacks seminal matter from the whole body due to its weakness. When the matter of the existing members is undigested, it cannot produce a perfect human likeness and completion; and therefore, it happens that **maimed** <note>original: "colobos," from the Greek for "mutilated"</note> children are born. 

It must be conceded that semen "falls" from the whole in this way, since it is the **useful superfluity** <term>Useful superfluity; Latin "utilis superfluita," the Aristotelian idea that semen is the "leftover" of the highest quality blood that has already nourished the organs</term> of the final blood-like nutrient distributed into the parts. For it is necessary that the semen be derived especially from the more principal parts, because it is in them that the final blood-like nutrient is properly distributed. 

Nor should it be said that semen descends from the **brain** alone; nevertheless, its "ferment" comes from there. For proportionally, one must grant that more semen descends from the brain than from any of the other members, as it has a great similarity [to the brain's substance]. This is also shown by the great harm done to the brain and to the related organs, such as the **eyes**, from frequently repeated coitus, as noted in the *Problems* <note>original: "probleu. iiii."</note>. <meta>This page continues a scholastic investigation into the origins of semen, specifically debating whether it is drawn physically from every part of the body (Pangenesis) or if it is a refined substance carrying a "power" or "blueprint" from the heart.</meta>

The power that produces sperm and carries it during the act of intercourse—namely, the **generative power** <term>Generative power; Latin "uirtus generatiua," the biological faculty responsible for reproduction</term>—flows from all the functional powers of the body toward the testicles. Thus, the sperm contains this power within itself. For at the hour of intercourse, a single spirit <note>original: "spiritus unus." In medieval medicine, "spirits" were subtle vapors that carried life and sensation through the body.</note>, predominantly from the power of the heart and composed of three combined spirits, descends with proportional powers from the three most principal organs of the body. It travels through the arteries, veins, and channels of the whole body to the testicles, or to the "coiled seminal vessels" as Aristotle describes them. Within these vessels, the sperm is perfected and unified, and the generative power is bestowed upon the whole. 

This is also demonstrated by reason, since sperm is the "principle" (the starting point) of generation. Principles are typically smallest in quantity but greatest in power, as seen in logic and biology; such is the nature of sperm when it is drawn off. Furthermore, it is highly reasonable that the **formative power** <term>Formative power; Latin "uirtus informatiua," the active force that shapes the embryo according to its species</term> of generation, which is drawn from the whole, could shape the matter of generation even if it were not physically "cut off" from every part of the body. We see that the celestial power alone <note>A reference to the sun's heat, which was thought to spontaneously generate life from decaying matter.</note>, while remaining continuous and the same, can procreate diverse animals of different species from the same matter. Also, if a seed is so small, how could it be physically "cut off" from a massive tree? By following this logic, all contradictions and impossibilities are removed, as will be apparent to the observer. 

Therefore, it should be concluded from these points that sperm is sent from the whole body—not in terms of its physical mass, but in terms of its **vigor** <note>original: "non quide mole sed uigore"</note>. Regarding the first point from **Hippocrates** <note>original: "ypocratis"</note>, it should be said that he understood this "coming from the whole" as a matter of vigor, or because the material descends from the principal and notable parts. Regarding the other point, it should be said that he speaks according to the opinion of others, or perhaps he refers to all the notable parts, as the appearance of sores on the extremities confirms. 

To the other argument, it should be said that one cannot conclude sperm comes from the whole body just because of the sensation involved. The "itch" or urge in those parts is strong because the spermatic matter, as it passes over the sensitive members, causes a certain titillation from which delight is induced. This is similar to how those with **scabies** <note>A contagious skin disease causing intense itching.</note> feel relief when bathing in warm water. We also see that the pleasure of intercourse often completely exhausts a person, as noted in the first book of *The Generation of Animals* and the ninth book of *The History of Animals*. We also know, according to **Aristotle** <note>original: "Aristotilem"</note>, that young boys who are not yet capable of intercourse still experience pleasure from the emission of "windy spirit" (gas) alone. Therefore, pleasure does not prove that sperm comes from every part of the body.

Regarding the other point about the movement of spirits: even in those with **dropsy** <note>original: "ydropico4" (hydropicorum); an old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid.</note>, water or "corrupt blood" from even one part of the body can suddenly kill the animal, as mentioned in the sixth book of the *Aphorisms*. 

To the next point, it should be said that the opposite often happens, which contradicts the proposal: why a **maimed person** <term>Maimed; Latin "colobus," referring to someone missing a limb or part of the body</term> would beget another maimed person. As for the claim that the offspring must resemble the parents, it should be said that while the fetus usually bears a resemblance, especially in particular features, the formative power sometimes fails to induce a perfect likeness of the parent due to its own weakness or the poor disposition of the matter. Instead, it might produce a distant likeness, such as to a grandfather, a great-grandfather, a paternal uncle, or a maternal uncle, as will be shown in the 37th difference. Furthermore, we see offspring resembling parents in voice, nails, hair, and movement—yet no sperm is "cut off" from these things, since they are superfluities of the body. Similarly, parents sometimes have beards or gray hair which the children lack at birth. Thus, the generation of similarity is a matter of **form and vigor**, not, as has been shown, a matter of **material and mass**. 

This separation of seed and generation occurs not by the logic of the seed's mass, but by the vigor of the formative power rendering it fit for generation. This vigor does not reside in all members equally, but primarily in one—the heart—in which all things meet and which all things serve.

### On the Intensity of Pleasure in Intercourse

Having finished the previous discussion, the question arises: who experiences more pleasure in intercourse, the male or the female? It seems that the female enjoys it more. **Theophrastus** <note>original: "theo.vi"</note> writes that the pleasure a woman derives from intercourse is greater than a man's. For she feels pleasure both in emitting her own "sperm" and in receiving that of the man, whereas the man feels it only in emission. Furthermore, in the ninth book of *Animals*, it is said that the pleasure of females is doubled because they delight not only in the movement of their own sperm and the "suction" of the opening of the womb, but also in the varied movements of the womb itself. I also say they feel no small pleasure from the "strengthening" of the part of the womb's opening located directly opposite the aforementioned parts. Indeed, this part corresponds to the **glans of the penis** <note>original: "balano... uirge"</note>, where great delight flourishes, such that those who copulate frequently find pleasure primarily in that. 

**Tiresias** <note>original: "Therisia"</note>, who was both a man and a woman before being returned to a man, likewise sensed that a woman's pleasure was greater. **Ovid** <note>original: "Ouidius"</note> mentions this in the *Metamorphoses* <note>original: "transfiguratione"</note>. Thus, the woman is more delighted in intercourse than the male. 

On the other hand, it is argued that since pleasure is caused by the proportionate joining of compatible things, and a man has a more "temperate" complexion than a female, the pleasure should be more intense in the man. To this, one must say that in terms of **extension** (duration), the woman is more delighted, for the pleasure lasts longer in her.

...she emits more sperm or fluid; however, she more rarely receives the man's sperm successively. There is a longer duration of movement in the womb with prolonged friction. But the **man** experiences pleasure more **intensely**. For in the brief hour in which he takes delight, his pleasure is more heightened. And it is always continuous when he emits; however, this is not so for the woman, in whom pleasure is more spread out. This is shown because this pleasure consists in the sense of touch; therefore, where touch is more perfect, the intensity will be greater. This is the case in the man, since his **constitution** <term>Constitution; Latin "crasis," referring to the specific balance of bodily humors</term> is of a more tempered touch. Furthermore, the man's sperm is hotter, which induces more "itching" of delight by a certain inciting tickling. Also, the channels through which he emits sperm are longer, narrower, and more winding, so that they may more fully perceive the delight of the sperm passing through them. Moreover, the man's sperm moves more swiftly and suddenly—which induces delight—passing through these expulsive channels to be formed in its being; but in the female, all these things are otherwise. This is also indicated by the man's swift and great exhaustion from excessive intercourse, which results in a consuming depletion. Thus, the man is more intensely delighted in intercourse. ### DIFFERENCE XXXV.

<margin><unclear>from the circle ...</unclear></margin>
That the testicles are not necessary for generation, but exist for the sake of some greater benefit, is shown through the third book of the *History of Animals* and the first book of *On the Generation of Animals* <note>Aristotle's primary biological works.</note>. These testify that the testicles are not strictly necessary but exist for "well-being." Again, in the first and twelfth books of *On Animals*: in the veins—extending from the "hollow vein" <term>Hollow vein; the vena cava</term> and from the kidneys to the testicles—the sperm is digested and turns white, whereas previously it was red, due to the great number of twists and turns in those vessels, and because it also reaches them from the heart. This is indeed shown by reason. Since, if the testicles were necessary, they would exist in all generating beings. However, many things generate while lacking them. Also, their necessity is only posited for the generation of sperm; but this generation occurs in the whole or in the more principal parts of the body. For the generative power seems to be diffused through the whole body, just as the nutritive power is, even though they work upon different objects in a diversified way, as appears in the third book of *On the Soul*. Furthermore, that thing is "necessary" without which a thing cannot exist (from the fifth book of *Metaphysics*). But an animal can exist without testicles, especially since sperm is "decided" <note>original: "decidatur." A technical term meaning the sperm is "cut off" or shed from the body's surplus nourishment.</note> from the more principal parts of the body, and the generative power—as shown in Difference 28—flows from the heart. Therefore, the testes are not necessary. 

The opposite of this was held by almost all physicians and philosophers. Furthermore, a thing is necessary if, when it is removed, the remainder is insufficient; but when the testes are removed, generation is not completed, as will appear. Their necessity is also demonstrated by their composition, shape, and sensation. Therefore, the testicles are necessary. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known that "necessary" is said in several ways, as shown in the first Difference. The testes are certain glandular flesh gathered in a single bony pouch <note>original: "folliculo uno osseo." Likely referring to the scrotum; medieval texts often described the tough, protective skin of the scrotum with terms suggesting a "bony" or hard casing.</note>, created white for the sake of the spermatic moisture. They are like the glandular white flesh of the breasts, established for generating milk, just as the red liver is established for generating the redness of the blood. To these aforementioned testicles, certain channels are continued which are double in nature. For there are some existing between the kidneys and the testicles, called "coiled vessels" by **Avicenna** <term>Avicenna; Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard medieval textbook</term>, in which he posited that sperm is generated, rather than in the testicles themselves. These vessels are so arranged because, on the right side of the body, facing the right kidney, branches originate from the body of the artery and the "chyle vein" <term>Chyle vein; here referring to the vena cava</term> descending through the back. They occur throughout, and very rarely from the emerging veins and arteries tending toward the right kidney. These branches, extended through the body, are widened beneath the kidneys directly at the back, which, penetrating through the <term>sipbac</term> <note>The peritoneum, or the lining of the abdominal cavity.</note>, tend toward the head of the right testicle. Holding a red color within themselves, they pass from one head of the testicle into the other, and finally reflect back toward the head of the testicle mentioned before. In this place, the third book of the *History of Animals* posits that the white spermatic moisture is generated and contained. Here also, the author attempts to show their situation using geometric letters. 

On the left side, however, there are branches of the veins and arteries descending through the back, but mostly from the "emulgent" <note>The renal vein and artery.</note> vein and artery, which then branch out just as was described for the right side. And therefore, as noted in book three, chapter twenty-one, farmers wishing to produce a male offspring tie the left testicle of the bull, so that the projection may come from the right side, which is hotter and stronger. Many times also, a relaxation or a rupture occurs in the channels where they penetrate through the <term>sipbac</term>, so that the <term>zirbus</term> <note>The omentum, a fatty membrane in the abdomen.</note> or the intestines fall into the scrotum, especially on the right side, where the "one-eyed" intestine <note>The cecum.</note> is held, which participates by a small attachment. These coiled vessels are called the *didymi* <note>A term used for the testicles or the spermatic cords.</note> in the twenty-fifth book of *On Animals* and in certain problems ascribed to Avicenna. There are also other channels, called "seminal vessels" by physicians, which, beginning from the heads of the testicles, terminate above the neck of the bladder into the penis; they say these serve the testicles in a "delatory" or carrying service, because they lead the seed from the testes into the penis and finally into the womb. What generation actually is was shown in Difference 28. Regarding the second point, it must be known that it was the opinion of Avicenna in the previously cited places that the testicles were not necessary for generation in the strict sense of the first mode of necessity, but that they exist for the sake of a certain improvement and assistance. For he wanted the testicles to be a kind of "suspenders"...

...which would force the aforementioned channels <note>Latin "meatus"</note> to stay open by pulling them downwards; and therefore they are attached to animals in the same way that weavers adapt stones to their looms. This indeed can be seen among weavers: for they suspend weights from the threads to be woven so that the paths, by being pulled downwards, remain open, allowing the shuttle to be cast through them freely. When these are removed, the channels are blocked. Thus, with the testicles removed, he [Aristotle] believed the pores or channels were retracted inward so that a constricting blockage occurs, and the castrated animal is unable to generate. This position **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay."; a common medieval abbreviation for Aristoteles</note>, like others, strives to support.

First, indeed, because if testicles were simply necessary for all, they would exist in all animals. Yet now, neither fish nor snakes have testicles, and nevertheless they are seen copulating and possessing channels full of sperm. He concluded, therefore, that they exist for the sake of some better purpose <note>i.e., they are an "improvement" rather than a fundamental requirement</note>. Furthermore, he says that a certain **bull**, shortly after being castrated, copulated and impregnated a cow, because the channels had not yet been retracted. Since it then lacked testicles, it appears they do not have a necessity in generation. But what perhaps moved him most of all was that no part of the aforementioned channels terminates in the testicles, but rather they are continuous from the kidneys, leaning upon the testicles, and finally being reflected <note>bent back</note>, they thus pass through to the penis. These things, however—with all reverence shown to the First Teacher <note>Aristotle</note>, though perhaps I do not understand him—seem unable to stand, as will appear more fully in the third part of what is to be said; nor perhaps do those arguments by which he strives to assert this hold up.

First, indeed, it is not valid: for even if testicles are not present in "imperfect" <note>lower</note> animals, it should not be concluded from this that they are not needed in the "more perfect" animals, since they require more in their constitution. Hence they are not simply necessary according to what is common, but they are necessary for the perfection of the species. Regarding what he asserts about the **bull** being castrated—granting him also that the same bull mounted a cow to copulate—this does not prove that testicles are not needed in generation, nor that sperm is therefore generated in the coiled vessels. For the one castrating either cut the scrotum <note>original: "esseum"</note> alone and then violently pulled out the testicles—as castrators commonly do—and because those channels were strongly attached to the testicles, they were snapped, so that the semen coming from the coiled vessels rushed downward to the already divided scrotum. If, however, **Aristotle** were to say that the sperm was contained in the channels existing between the testes and the penis (since in this animal they are very long), the adversary will respond: if that sperm was fertile, it must be so because of the testicles from which it had previously been generated, for it had already passed over them. Hence **Aristotle** does not prove his intent here. Or, the castrator—which does not happen—cuts the membrane of the testicle...

---

...and then the same follows no less than before. Regarding what he said third—that the testicles are not part of the channels—this perhaps does not contain the truth, as it has appeared otherwise to others and to me many times in **sensory anatomy** <note>anatomy learned through direct observation of the senses</note>. It never appeared that sperm falls into the true substance of the testes, which the sperm found in them shows, as does their increase—though commonly, in those animals where they are manifest and in those where they are estimated not to have them, as in partridges and pheasants, as noted in the third book of the *History [of Animals]*. Furthermore, those who cut the seminal vessels see that they are by no means continuous with the upper coiled parts by a reflected force, but rather they arise from the other head of the testicles.

Some indeed, showing reverence to **Aristotle**, have said that testicles can be considered in two ways: either in general, as in the whole scope of animals, and thus they are not necessary since many animals lack them; and because **Aristotle's** discourse was universal, he declared that in all animals they are not absolutely necessary. Or, they are considered in particular, as in the genus of "perfect" animals, and then they assert every such animal has need of them. These people, even if they taste the truth, do not stand as faithful expositors. For the work of a good expositor is not to verify the speech but rather to manifest the intention of the writer, however false it may be (as in the first book of *Prognostics*). For they openly expose things contrary to the intention of **Aristotle**. For he, even introducing this in more perfect animals, wanted the testicles to provide a benefit and not a necessity—namely, to cause a more lingering movement of the spermatic surplus and to keep the pores open, especially in those where the site is external. For he says that in "animal-makers" <note>possibly "procreative animals"</note> such as horses and other such animals, and in humans, they are introduced to preserve the doubling; similarly, the castrated bull is mentioned—all of which are more perfect animals.

And therefore it must be said that in **Aristotle's** time, the science of anatomy was not yet perfected in every way, as shown in Difference 99. **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician</note> also says sperm is generated in the testicles, just as foam is generated in the mouths of horses when they are stimulated, or from the crashing of sea waves. **Galen**, however, said that it is the testicles that generate sperm; but **Aristotle** says it is generated in the coiled veins in the sperm vessels, and its generation is completed in the testicles. That last point which **Aristotle** posits, I do not find in his works. **Nicolaus** <note>Nicolaus Damascenus or a similar scholastic authority</note>, however, in his *Problems*, brought up something ambiguous from **Aristotle's** series, saying: "Nevertheless, the testicles are useful for the digestion of sperm, just as the breasts are for the generation of milk." Now they say milk is generated in the breasts. Because of this third point, one must know that the testes are not only beneficial, but also necessary—either by the first or fourth mode of necessity—since **Aristotle** concedes things similar to this. This is signified by authorities and likewise by reasons.

**Galen**, indeed, in many places, and **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> also in the fifteenth [book] of *On Animals*, treats the opinion of **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay."</note> mentioned before. When the Master first said that the testicles emerge from the paths of the sperm, he did not want it understood that they do nothing for the generation of sperm, but rather that their substance is different from the substance of the paths that are continuous with them. For it is not a single path, but a support for the paths. And he adds: "And it is not a lie that the physician says." What was tangled, he explained in the first part. For he is not rarely ambiguous when speaking of animals. The testicles are necessary for generating sperm, which preserves and aids genealogy; let the complement of the form be given, and let the masculine and feminine complexion be preserved. Hence, in the twenty-first [chapter] of the third [book], he said they would be the principal members in which sperm is generated from the moisture brought to them in the veins. He who is more distressed by these things is **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay."</note>, and **Avenzoar** <note>original: "Az."</note>, his most faithful interpreter and colleague, not holding him back in the second and fourth [sections]. In which he also endeavors to hand down medicine according to the foundations of **Aristotle**. But rather, walking the path of color, he says: The testicles were ordained for the making of sperm, and therefore their flesh was white, like the flesh of the breasts <term>mammae</term>. And for that reason, when blood is converted, it converts to their likeness and makes itself white, just as the liver makes the chyle red, because the power of the agent is to make the patient assimilate to itself. This is indeed confirmed by reasons: because each thing is generated by its like and its fitting match, according to the seventh [book] of *Metaphysics*. Sperm indeed, in substance, complexion, and color, is more assimilated to the flesh of the testicles than to the coiled vessels, since those are nervous, solid, and dry bodies, leaning toward red near their beginning.

Furthermore, the more perfect something is, the more things it requires for its constitution; this appears in the tenth [book] of *Problems on Animals*. For Nature works more and more intensely in the production of the perfect than the imperfect. But man and most quadrupeds are more perfect than others; hence, for them, the spermatic vessels alone did not suffice for the generation of sperm, but the work of the testicles was also present. And because their cutting away <note>castration</note> induces so great a change in the animal, as eunuchs <term>eunuchi</term> demonstrate, it is reasonable that these organs have great power over the sperm.

Moreover, if the testicles were only like hangers pulling the vessels downward, they would not be so continuous and coiled with them, such that the sperm would fall upon the substance of the testicle, but it would instead tend directly through it. The opposite of this is experienced in the **beaver**. If they were only weights <note>original: "Paliti"</note>, the testicles would not be suitable for the generation of sperm, but only helpful by their weight, like stones used by weavers <term>liciatoriis</term>. Then no one would ever be rendered sterile by the application of cold things over them, as occurs with henbane <term>usquiami</term>, mandrake <term>mandragore</term>, and similar things; for such weight would not be diminished by them, nor are the passages so narrowed by cold that they would not later be widened by heat and relaxation. Nor is it similarly said that the coiled vessels are harmed by the application of cold in the same way as the testicles, since the vessels tend further inward where the heat is more intense and hidden. It is a proven fact that the application of cold to the testicles induces sterility. Also, in those animals where the site of the testicles is internal—having a connection firmly adhering to the back, such as in elephants <term>elefantibus</term> and birds <term>uolatilibus</term>—the testicles can provide no widening of the coiled vessels by their weight in the manner of stones hanging on a weaver's loom, since they lack the suspension used in that example.

Perhaps, however, someone will say: the work of weight is not needed when the passages remain open by the heat within. It might also be asked, first, why the testicles of females <note>the ovaries, often called 'female testicles' in medieval anatomy</note> at the time of descent adhere so closely to the womb. Therefore, it is more healthfully concluded that the testicles are necessary for perfections, simply speaking. Know also that although it is said that the necessity of generation and vigor is in the testicles, it is not there principally and primarily, but is infused into them from the heart; for the heart itself is the root and principle of all virtues, not only the vital, but also the natural and animal, according to the thirty-eighth difference. Hence, in the first and fifth [books] of *On the Generation of Animals*: It is not to be suspected, as some already estimate, that the testicles are the meeting point of many principles because they are the cause of great transformations of the body. For it does not happen because of them themselves, but because of the transformation of the heart, with which they have no small community through arteries, nerves, and appearance. For they are more solid flesh, like a mirror reflecting the heat of the heart that has fallen into them back into the whole body. Therefore, it should be said that he does not place the principles as if they were scattered, but rather coordinates all things into one in the twenty-eighth difference. The virtue and spirit of the same are directed from the heart; though the vigor of the heart undergoes a change in the testicles, just as the spirit falling from the heart into the brain is changed by it. Whence it is collected in the twentieth [section]: You ought to know that this member—namely, the testicles—is not the prince of the generative virtue, although the virtue is in it so that it may work. **Galen** says: because that member cannot perform its operation by itself except through the spirit sent to it from the heart, tempered in quantity and quality. Because of which it appears that the cordial virtue—which measures this heat so that it can perform its operations—is the principal generative power. And the virtue that is in this member is its servant; and if it has any dominion in this, it is a particular one. Indeed, because of the fourth [point], the answer to the first has appeared. To the other, it is similarly seen. For that was the opinion of **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay."</note>, which is not held at present. To the other, it should be said that **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> does not understand that sperm is perfectly in those veins.

## DIFFERENCE XXXVI.

<margin>It has [the text]</margin>
That the seed or sperm of the male is not a constitutive part of the embryo is shown [here]. For sperm acts just as those things produced by art;
<margin>It has [the text]</margin>
for it has power by means of its species (see the seventh book of the *Metaphysics* and the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*). For it is not posited there that one thing is made from sperm and menstrual blood, except as a bed is made from wood and a carpenter, or a sphere from wax and a form, or as a healed person comes from the medical art; and universally, as from the mover and the moved. And also because the male provides the seed and the principle of motion, while the female provides the body and the matter, just as in the coagulation of milk. For the milk is the body, but the rennet is the forming agent and the principle that causes the generation. And in the second book of the same work, the female provides the body and the mass, but the male does not; and the body is from the female, but the **soul** <note>original: "anima"</note> truly comes from the male. Furthermore, according to the natural philosopher **Galen**, sperm exists like a craftsman or a soul, while blood is like the wax. And therefore he adds: bone, vein, artery, nerve, cartilage, fat, suet, membrane, and marrow are indeed present in the blood, and are made from the blood. For he agrees more expressly with **Aristotle's** opinion—whatever may be posited elsewhere—that the embryo is constructed from the menstrual blood alone, as if from matter, but from the sperm as if from an agent and the giver of form. For that which is such

is not a part of the physical mass. Whence, regarding the sacred matter, first: Blood and sperm are the principles of our generation. Blood, indeed, acts as a certain proportionate matter, yielding well in all things to the creator. Sperm, however, holds the role of the creator. In the third book [of the *Sentences*], chapter 21: Conception from the male's sperm has the power of an odor <note>Meaning it acts by influence or "vapor" rather than physical mixing.</note> according to the opinion of **Aristotle** in the *History of Animals*. And this is confirmed because in many animals, since they are very small, nothing could be drawn out according to physical mass, for some would be dissolved; they are even joined together in such a short time that no quantity could be shed from them. Also, according to the physician in the tenth book of the *Histories*: "If impregnation is to be completed, there is need for one to project both." When this happens to either one, it will hinder the other from receiving it. Again, "art imitates nature" (the second book of the *Physics*). In art, it happens that the agent does not enter the thing crafted, except by power alone. Furthermore, if the seed were posited to be a material constitutive part of the embryo, since it is also the active part, then the same thing would be both agent and patient, the mover and the moved. Being indistinct in place and subject, the agent would also coincide with the matter, and it would act upon itself first. Similarly, generation would not differ from growth, which is contrary to what is determined in the *Physics* and *On Generation and Corruption*. Therefore, the seed is not a constitutive part of the embryo. On the opposing side, in the second book of *On the Generation of the Embryo*, [the author] wishes not only the male's sperm to enter the constitution of the offspring, but also the woman's. This also seems to be supported by the tenth book of the *Histories*, the first book of the *Aphorisms*, and in many places with the invitation to the book *On Sperm* not yet translated. Similarly, **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."</note> supports this, not only in the *Canon* but sometimes in his treatises on animals. Arguments also bolster this: for I call the "conception" the first mixture from the male and female (from the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*); a mixture does not only consist of bodies (from the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*). Furthermore, it is a failing when something that could be constructed with fewer parts is performed with more, according to the physicist; this appears in the first book, since nature and art always reject what is superfluous, as the study of animals especially denotes. But this happens if, the sperm having been left behind as proportionate, the offspring were constituted from blood—which is less suitable to them—since it would be necessary for the blood first to be transformed into a spermatic nature in the parts where sperm is not needed, since it is already such. Again, diversity in the later parts argues for diversity in the earlier ones, at least the immediate ones, since they are caused by them. Now, however, certain parts are fixed to the sperm, while others to the blood, such as flesh especially; because of this, the birth bears witness to its own integrity of principle. Those parts that are generated will be from the blood, but the rest from the sperm of the same proportion. Therefore, the seed...

...is a constitutive part of the embryo. Regarding the first point, it should be known what the difference is between the "offspring-seed" <note>original: "genitura"</note> and "sperm," as seen in section 34. I mean the constitutive part in a bodily sense, implying more of the material and the mass. The term "embryo" is also used for everything created from the principles of generation in the womb <note>original: "matrice"</note>. Thirdly, however, according to the ancient theory, different names are assigned to this according to the stages of its completion; for it varies across four time periods. 

In the first period, it is found in the form of sperm, and then it is called **spermatic**. In the second, the sperm appears filled with blood, yet the heart, brain, or liver are not yet discerned; however, a distinction of parts begins to appear. At this time, Hippocrates <note>original: ".y." for Ypocras</note> named it the **fetus**. There is a third stage when the formation of the heart, brain, and liver appears more clearly, and the rest of the parts begin to take shape; what is then conceived is called the **embryo**. The fourth period exists when the individual members are distinguished and appear with a completed, equal formation, though still small; then it is called the **conceptus**, because it clearly moves and kicks with its feet.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some—such as Hippocrates and Galen in the second book of *On Natural [Faculties]* <note>original: "naturalium secundo"</note>, where he represents himself as a Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> regarding the utility of parts—have occasionally posited that sperm is the material part and also a constitutive part of the embryo. They are moved to this view by seeing that the so-called "spermatic" members <note>Parts of the body thought to be made of solid, white tissue, like bones or nerves.</note> are white, and the "bloody" members are red; and that some parts can be restored while others cannot, along with other such signs. 

However, this is not necessarily so, since the aforementioned **informative power** <term>informative power</term> <note>The "virtus informativa": an innate biological force believed to "shape" or "inform" raw matter into a specific living structure.</note> existing in the sperm can induce this shaping and likeness by curdling and whitening the menstrual blood <note>original: "menstruo"</note>. Galen here imitates Aristotle’s view on natural things. For the necessity of the thing being generated is not to be taken entirely from the matter, but rather from the agent and the form. This is argued against Empedocles in the fifth book of the *On the Generation of Animals* <note>original: "de ge. animalium v."</note>. To those saying that sperm is the material part of the embryo, many absurdities follow in the demonstrations of natural science. 

Certain followers of Hippocrates and Galen, wishing to avoid the arguments of both sides, said that three things must be considered in the sperm: 
1. A **thick, tenacious part**, which they posit yields the substance of the spermatic members.
2. A **subtle, airy, vaporous part**, which they say is converted into the substance of the spirits <note>In medieval physiology, "spirits" were subtle fluids that carried life and sensation through the body.</note>.
3. A **third part**, namely the **informative power**, acting like an artist. 
The falsehood of this position regarding the first part is manifest from what has been introduced. What should be held regarding the other two will appear in what follows. 

---

There were thirdly others who said that sperm, according to its substance, is in no way a constitutive part of the embryo, but only by its **power** <note>original: "uirtute"</note>. They heard the arguments of Aristotle introduced in the earlier debates. This was also the opinion of Galen in the second book of *On Natural [Faculties]*. For no mass of the sperm, but only its vigor and "odor" <note>Used here to mean a subtle influence or trace, rather than a literal smell.</note>, enters into the constitution of the embryo. Many who explain Aristotle do so incompletely. This position, when understood by Aristotle’s subtle opinion, cannot stand. For it would follow that a vehemently active power would abandon its own proper subject <note>In philosophy, a "power" must usually reside in a physical "subject" or substance.</note>. From this, nature would also seem to work unwisely—and of her wisdom there is no end—if she abandoned a more suitable proper subject to cling to an external and disproportionate one. Furthermore, those animals which are more "perfect" <note>Biologically complex animals.</note> in their kind require not only the power but also the subject. 

Those explaining Aristotle poorly speak against his mind, as will clearly shine forth in the third part of this discussion. To that which is heard on the surface—that Aristotle's words seem to sound as if sperm enters the embryo by vigor alone—it must be said that some understand this power to be the **intellect** <note>original: "intellectum vocatam"</note> mentioned in *On the Generation of Animals*. This does not enter the constitution of the embryo as a power, like the form of an artifact or the likeness existing in the soul of a craftsman that underlies the finished craft (as a person is healed by the discipline of medicine), and certainly not as mass. 

But it should be said more certainly that Aristotle's discourse in the first book of *On the Generation of Animals* stands as a general rule for the nature of all animals. This is shown by the examples of insects <note>original: "entoma"</note> and certain types of fish, from which no spermatic mass is seen to be discharged into the female because of their "imperfection" <note>Simpler biological structure.</note>, nor received by her. Instead, heat and some power, as well as "odor," is sent in, supported by windiness or smoke. For it is the nature of an accident <note>A philosophical term for a property that cannot exist on its own, like "redness."</note> to first remain in its own proper recipient. 

Regarding the third point, it should be known that in perfect animals, the seed enters the embryo not indeed as a material constitutive part, but rather as the **beginning of motion** and the **impressor of form**. And therefore Aristotle, sensing this in such matters, resumes in the second book what he had touched upon more universally in the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*. In this, he shows what happens to the substance of the sperm, and what kind of power it possesses and how it is supported. For he says: *The body of the seed,* etc. He means that with the sperm itself, a power is emitted called "intellect," which is the principle of generation, existing separately from the body. For it does not have an organized member <note>An organ.</note> like other natural powers. For this reason, it is called a **divine and intellectual power** by the Commentator <note>Averroes, the famous commentator on Aristotle.</note> in the 7th book of the *Metaphysics*, section 48. And this power indeed embraces the sperm and proceeds from it in the act of generation.
