<meta>This page continues the scholastic commentary on Aristotelian embryology, specifically focusing on the mechanism by which sperm acts upon maternal matter. It addresses the debate over whether sperm is a material component of the fetus or an efficient "spirituous" agent that organizes the mother's blood, using the famous Aristotelian analogy of rennet curdling milk.</meta>

...of the embryo is awakened and, by the impulse of the motion of the joining <note>Referring to the act of intercourse.</note>, continues until it generates the heart. Finally, through the vigor of that heart, the remaining members are generated. **Difference 38.**
Hence, Aristotle says that the form and species of the liver are in the heart. Wherefore the liver is, as it were, formed from the surplus of the nourishment of the heart. *On Animals*, book nine. Which similarly happens in other things; for from a being in act, that which exists in potentiality is made, whether in nature or in the learned arts. 

It is added afterward that the body of the offspring-seed <note>original: "geniture"</note> is inseparable from the body; indeed, the sperm of the offspring-seed—that is, the action of the principle of generation—is filled with spirit, not having a moist and watery nature. For this reason, he says we should not ask whether the sperm exits the body or whether it is some particular part of the established form; he explains this by saying it is just as rennet <note>original: "coagulum"; the enzyme used to curdle milk into cheese.</note> does not become a physical part of the milk it makes consist. For the rennet is transformed, and no part of it remains in the resulting mass. Thus, the understanding is that the sperm is thinned out and rendered vaporous, converted into the form of spirits which are the makers of the embryo. For the power of the rennet is not impressed upon the milk unless supported by the evaporation of the rennet. As Aristotle says in the same place: 

->And you should not think that Aristotle says that the sperm is dissolved, perishes, and changes as if into nothing.<-

Rather, his reasoning is what I hinted at regarding "new food," as he says in the same book of *On Animals*. And men think that Aristotle believed the male sperm was not a part of the child, nor mixed with its matter. But this was not his intention; rather, his intention stands: that it is involved with the matter itself and penetrates deep into the matter so that it may be the "operator" of the limbs, and that it leads the suitable matter to become limbs. That sperm shall be the matter of the spirit in the creature, and it makes a subtle and capable mixture so that it may pass into spirit. And let us say that the sperm becomes the operator in the menstrual blood without a deep foundation, and it is not the woman's sperm that operates, but rather her matter. Wherefore in book three, section 20: 

The study of the sperm is in the particularity of the spirit of the infant, and it is nothing other than like the rennet acting in milk. Whence in the first book, section one: "That from which children are made is a small amount of sperm and vaporous spirit." The conclusion of these things is consistent with the following: It is not to be believed that sperm provides help through quality alone, but it brings help through "qualitative heat"—as if to say, not only does heat enter in the abstract as a power, but it is heat which is felt to be a body, or "heat in the concrete." By this, he noted that the sperm, dissolved into vapor and spirit, thins the embryo. For by the vigor of the spirit decided from the heart and other principal parts, the "generative spirit" is perfected as one in the testicles. By its power, the evaporating sperm is dissolved into spirits; and yet all of this is generated first in the heart, then the testicles, at section 130. 

The aforesaid is confirmed by reason: for the more perfect things are, the more things they require in their production. **Prior Difference.** This is shown by the manner of the introduction of the human soul; nor are the works of craftsmen any more elegant. Man is the most perfect of animals and possesses more of these qualities. Therefore, how many things do they require in their constitution! Since even imperfect things, as mentioned, emit heat and power, those which are more perfect and more powerful will also provide a support of power. 

Furthermore, when the sperm falls into the womb, a membrane soon consists. *History of Animals*, book nine, or *peryffeton*—that is, "surrounding" or "grains," as noted in *On the Generation of Animals*, book two. That which is thus walled off and affected by the warmth does not have a rite of "turning," <note>original: "querfione" / "versione"</note> but by evaporation into spirit toward resolution. This is indicated regarding the generation of the infant by the sight of six-day-old sperm, contained in a little skin in the manner of the white of an egg. 

Again, every action is perfected by touch; here, however, it is the touch of both bodies. *On Generation*, book one. When the common element of the offspring-seed remains under the nature of corporality, it is saved as something "spiritual-perfecting," as was premised. But if only power or heat entered, it would follow the tenor of art; for art only adorns the matter from the outside, so that one can touch it. Nature, however, fashions everything by extending through the heights and depths. *On Natural Philosophy* <note>The Physics</note>, book two. Otherwise, the similarity between the generation of cheese from rennet and milk, and the embryo from sperm and blood, would not be preserved. Therefore, the offspring-seed enters the constitution of the embryo not by its mass nor by its vigor alone, but by that sperm being resolved into spirits, which method almost holds the middle ground. Because of this, regarding the fourth point: 

What should be said to the first point has appeared from the notes. To the other, it must be said that Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de aīma secundo"</note> intended for odor to change the sense of smell materially, but it is not preserved intentionally. Whence Aristotle will speak twice in *On Generation* regarding the location of bodies. To the other, it must be said that although art is a certain follower of nature, yet art can do what nature cannot, and vice versa. **Differences 18 and 164.** For Nature touches and fashions matter through every part, as if by touch; but art can only do what is extrinsic, and can change it into something else in the generating process which nature cannot do. *Natural Philosophy*, book two. To the other, it must be said that the "drop" of the woman is not then emitted to the outside or to the neck of the womb, preventing the attraction of the male sperm, but rather toward the interior of the womb; it is finally expelled or vanishes when the womb is incited to receive the male sperm. To the other, it must be said that the inconveniences brought into the arguments do not occur. For it is established that the sperm enters the essence of the embryo, yet not as an existing material part, but rather as a formal and efficient part; because the spirit or innate heat stands as the form and mover of the limbs. **Section Two.** Whence in *On the Motion of Animals*: All animals are seen to have a "conplanted spirit" and power by this. That, moreover, by which something can act, exists as its essence.

### DIFFERENCE 37.

Whether the so-called "female sperm," or the whitened humidity, or the "drop," enters into the constitution of the embryo is now shown. This is shown from the ancient book *On the Formation of the Infant*, and by **Galen** in many places outside of his *Natural Faculties*, and by **Haly Abbas** <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician</note> similarly, and by **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> both in *On Animals* and in the *Canon* <note>The scribe may be attributing the "Canon" to Aristotle here, though it is usually Avicenna's work, or referring to a "canonical" rule of Aristotle.</note>. Furthermore, in the tenth book of the *History of Animals*, it says that if a fetus is to be made, it is necessary for both the male and the female to be "commensurate" so as to emit at the same time; for if they are much out of sync, there will be no children.

And similarly in book 23, there **Avicenna** concedes that the woman has sperm. That which is ejected appears to be the sperm of both, since blood is not emitted during the friction of intercourse. Furthermore, curious and attentive women testify when they are impregnated—and physicians also note—that the mouth of the matrix <note>term: "matrix" <gloss>the womb or uterus</gloss></note> and the private parts are found to be dried out after intercourse, indicating that they have conceived here. They also have no small delight in this; but this does not seem to happen otherwise unless the womb attracts and reserves the female "drop" together with the male sperm. Also, women have "testicles" <note>note: Galen and his followers referred to the ovaries as female testicles (testiculos occultatos).</note> hidden next to the two horns of the womb; since none of the natural parts exist in vain, these are surely ordained for the generation of sperm, as in Difference 35. Furthermore, the agent and the patient must be proportioned; and the more similar they are, the more they will effect. (*On Generation and Corruption*, Book 1). But the woman’s "drop" is more analogous to the male sperm than the menstrual blood is, since it agrees with it in its substance and body through further digestion. Again, if the female "drop" does not enter in, then the generation of the parts will be from the menstrual blood alone as the matter. Since, therefore, it is said that any blood-based member lost to age can be restored to what it was before, then every mutilated limb would be regenerated; yet our senses teach the opposite. Therefore, the female "drop" enters the constitution of the embryo.

The opposite of this is maintained by **Avicenna** through the whole collection of animals and the abundance of natural virtues, affirming that the embryo is fashioned <note>original: "spagiari"; likely a corruption of "spagiari" or "fabriari" meaning to be worked or fashioned</note> only from the menstrual blood and the male seed. Likewise, if the female "drop" were to enter, since it would have not only a passive power but also an active one (as **Galen** often forces upon **Aristotle**), and it had the menstrual blood as matter, then a woman could conceive by herself without the help of another agent; which idea of a fetus **Avicenna** mocks. Furthermore, it would coincide with the error in the previous "Difference," since that which is able to be made of fewer things would be constituted of many, as will also appear. But the embryo can be constructed from the male seed as the action and the menstrual blood as the passive matter. For these exist as form and matter coming together. From these, without the others, a single thing arises through its essence. Therefore, the female "drop" shall not enter the constitution of the embryo.

Regarding the first point, it should be known what an embryo is, as was seen in the previous Difference, and what the female "drop" is, along with what will appear further from the things to be said.
Regarding which, it should be known that **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Y."; usually shorthand for Ypocras</note> and **Galen** with their followers felt that the female has sperm that also enters the constitution of the embryo. This is related as the opinion of **Aristotle** in the ninth book of *Animals*, and hence in book 23. According to **Galen** and the physicians, there are two seeds for the male and female at the same time, both of which are called by the name "sperm," not just by a shared name but in a literal sense. For he did not want the female "drop" only to have the power of receiving coagulation <note>term: "coagulation" <gloss>the process of the liquid seeds becoming a solid body; curdling</gloss></note>, but also the power of impressing coagulation. It is, however, weaker than the male vigor in impressing coagulation. In the female drop, the capacity to receive coagulation is more intense. But this is wonderful, and even if it is absurd to say the female has sperm, it is repugnant to what was shown in the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*, where it is held that it does not happen that two "spermatic segregations" are made. For it is manifest that the female does not contribute sperm toward generation. For if there were sperm, there would be no menstrual blood; but now because of this whole process, the rest will not be present. Which he supports with many signs. For many times a female has conceived without any delight occurring to her in intercourse, and similarly, even when delight occurs, nothing happens. Likewise, even when the moisture of the male and female run together equally, nothing is generated unless the commensurate menstrual humor is present. Furthermore, what some think—that the female has sperm because of the pleasure—is not valid, even if it seems similar to males in intercourse, because this is not a spermatic humidity of the whole body, but rather specific to the place, like a surplus of the womb; nor does her pleasure prove the emission of sperm. For it sometimes happens from the emission of "spirit" <note>Referring to "pneuma" or a vital gas</note>, as appears in boys before they are yet capable of intercourse. Again, it happens to some women who are of a white color, but not to others, such as those who are dark and masculine. Furthermore...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate between the Aristotelian and Galenic models of human generation. While the previous page established Aristotle's view of the male as the provider of "form," this page delves into the counterarguments provided by the medical tradition (Galen and Haly Abbas), who argue for a material "female sperm" that helps build the infant's body.</meta>

The quantity of what is emitted is not measured by the emission of the sperm alone; rather, it exceeds it greatly. And it is caused by foods, such as those that are sharp and biting. These indeed make a notable separation of it. Therefore, the female does not have sperm analogous to the man's sperm, but rather the term is used **equivocally** <note>In logic, an "equivocal" term is one word used for two different things, like "bat" meaning both a flying mammal and a sports tool. Aristotle argues "female sperm" is not truly sperm.</note>. Whence in the ninth book of *Animals*, **Aristotle** says that the sperm of the man and the woman are equivocal in the name of "sperm," just as the name "eye" is equivocal when one speaks of the "eye of the sun" and the "eye of a man." This is not recognized in the sperm of the man and woman through a shared nature, but only in name.

Wherefore in book twenty-three: the name of sperm indeed, when said of both, is by community of name. And it is added: the sperm of the man is warm, digested, and thick; the sperm of the female kind is of the **menstrual blood**, little converted, and is not far removed from the power of blood compared to the more refined sperm of the man. And for this reason, the preceding philosophers likened it to the menstrual blood. Whence in the first and fourth books of *On the Generation of Animals*: **Menstrua** <note>menstrual blood</note> are undigested sperm. And therefore Aristotle mostly calls that which belongs to the woman not "sperm," but "drops," and sometimes "water."

Regarding the second point, however, it must be known that **Hippocrates** <note>original: "y."; standard medieval abbreviation for Ypocras</note> and **Galen**, together with **Haly Abbas** <note>A 10th-century Persian physician whose 'Complete Art of Medicine' was a standard textbook</note>, said that the woman's sperm or "drops" enter into the constitution of the embryo. Some of them wanted this to happen not only by way of matter, but as an **agent** <note>The "agent" is the active force that shapes the body, as opposed to the passive "matter" it is made from</note>. As Hippocrates and Galen judge in the third book of *Theorice*, they believe that sperm holds the place of both agent and matter in the generation of the fetus, while the menstrual blood is only matter.

However, **Aristotle**—so that the view of **Galen** is not imposed upon him—strives to build his case in *Animals* with many reasons and signs, though they are less than sufficient. I think [Galen's view] is found in his book *On Sperm*. For first, Galen reproves the one who said that the sperm does not remain in the womb; for there would already be an appetite of the womb toward the sperm if it were to eject it. Rather, the womb retains it, boils it down, and digests it, causing a hard, earthy crust to form around it, just as happens to bread baked in an oven (according to Hippocrates in *On the Generation of the Infant*). And the wombs were made rough so that the sperm might be contained and not slip out.

Furthermore, bones, nerves, veins, and such hard, white things cannot be made from a fluid matter, but must come from a viscous, well-tempered, non-flowing matter, such as the woman’s sperm is, rather than the blood. Likewise, the woman's "drop" communicates more with the **radical members** <note>The fundamental, "root" structures of the body like bones and nerves</note> in quality than the blood does. Since that which is generated must be assimilated to that which generates it, the woman's drop will be a more suitable and closer matter for the generation of parts than the blood. Again, although the sperm is sometimes cast out, it is nevertheless retained when there is a need, just as menstrual blood is sometimes retained and sometimes emitted.

Moreover, for what purpose would there be testicles in the woman and sperm vessels, if they did not contribute to the generation of sperm? They would then be idle. He relates <note>likely Galen</note> that he himself saw in a woman the sperm vessels full of spermatic humidity, although that sperm was... <unclear>his</unclear>... because of [the womb]. He also saw a woman suffer "suffocation" <note>likely referring to "suffocation of the womb," a historical diagnosis for various ailments believed to be caused by a displaced uterus or retained fluids</note> due to the retention of sperm resulting from a husband's absence; she was later healed by the evacuation of it when pleasure occurred. Similarly, the female dreams and takes pleasure and emits sperm. And if the woman's drop does not enter [the embryo], then bones, nerves, and veins would be of the nature of flesh. And thereafter, if they were diminished or broken, they could be restored in every part and disposition. We experience the opposite of this <note>The author argues that because bones do not regrow like flesh, they must be made from the "seed" rather than the "blood."</note>.

Furthermore, a son is assimilated to his mother, but this does not happen because of her blood, since blood is matter, and there is no assimilation to matter; rather, one is assimilated to the **form**. Since a child is assimilated to both father and mother, this must be due to something common to both, which is sperm, and not blood, since the man lacks the menses. Therefore, the woman's sperm enters the embryo just as the man's does.

And finally, **Aristotle** adds that **Galen** thought he had made a great proof with these similar points. Then Galen argues against himself: that the child should always be like the father, since the male's sperm is indeed more effective than the female's. He responds, however, that the woman's sperm is always matured by the menstrual blood, whence its vigor always grows strong. The male's sperm does not have this help. Elsewhere he even said that the woman's sperm makes itself food for the man's sperm. These, then, were Galen's reasonings.

**Haly Abbas**, however, assigns a double cause why the woman's sperm enters the generation: first, so that the woman's sperm would be suitable for the man's sperm. For his is thick and hot in **complexion** <note>The specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a person's health and nature</note>; the woman's, conversely, is subtle and cold. Because of this, one is mixed with the other for the sake of tempering and making a good mixture. There is also a second generation of the covering that surrounds the spermatic matter. For the male sperm cannot extend itself through everything, but is more hidden; for this reason, it required the woman's sperm, so that a membrane might be constructed, and the male sperm might be strengthened by it, so that many spermatic parts could be generated from these two, which could not happen from one alone. Galen's arguments and those similar to Haly Abbas's cannot stand, as Aristotle asserts in the same place.

"We indeed," he says, "marveled at that, because he showed half of the common matter." And he said he knew philosophy [well enough to know] how he stated these rare reasons. Let us see indeed whatever this physician said against **Avicenna**—you think he said something, when he said nothing. Although he knew much of the "branches" <note>practical medical applications</note>, he ignores the "roots" of science <note>natural philosophy</note>. Regarding what Galen said: first, I reprove him because he said the sperm does not stay in the womb, which must be said is not valid, because the member attracts it. When it has fulfilled the utility of this attraction, it expels it, as appears in the attraction of wateriness from the liver and veins, and in members that attract medicines so that their bad complexion may be rectified or the matter dissolved, which they then expel with the help of a potion. It is also written in the ninth book of *Animals*...

...he spoke much on this, stating that the uterus acts upon the seed in the same way that **yeast acts in a loaf of bread**. For although the uterus is very hot, its interior surface is quite moist; therefore, it is not by its own nature forced to create any substance or the chorion <note>The outermost membrane surrounding an embryo.</note> within itself. If this were to happen, then the hot belly and liver would induce a membrane around the things they contain through their heat. In fact, the membrane that forms around the seed is established by the **formative power** <term>Virtus Informativa: The biological "program" or force believed to guide the development of the fetus</term>. For if it can generate bones, it is much more capable of generating the membrane surrounding the seed.

As the logicians say: that which can do the greater can also do the lesser. Nor should it be said, secondly, that the wombs are made rough in order to retain the woman's "drop," but rather the man's seed; and once conceived, they are smoothed by the superfluous flow of moisture. Furthermore, it must not be said that hard parts—like bones and the like—cannot be generated from red, fluid matter. The formative power is indeed capable of generating these from blood. In the second book of *On the Nature of Animals*, it is noted that the necessity of what is generated does not depend solely on the matter, but more so on other causes, especially as seen in the fifth book of *On the Generation of Animals*.

Similarly, one should not say that the "female drop" contributes more to the **radical members** <term>Radical members: The vital, primary organs (like the heart or liver) which, according to medieval medicine, cannot be repaired or replaced if damaged</term>, since this drop is an impure, liquid substance and a superfluity of the uterus, which women of a "cold" complexion <note>In the theory of the four humors, women were categorized as "cold and moist," while men were "hot and dry."</note> possess in no small abundance. And it is not to be said that blood and the female drop are similar, since blood is a necessity without which generation cannot occur, whereas the drop is not. Nor is the argument convincing that the testicles would then be idle; this objection is removed in the second book. For men have breasts, yet they do not possess them for the purpose of producing milk. The testicles provide another utility for this cause: rather than just producing seed for generation, they produce a moisture that incites the desire more suitably for the reception of the male seed. Because of this, neither the testicles nor their moisture are idle.

To the other point, it must be said that he was deceived by a certain broad similarity in color; for that "drop" is more distant from seed than even blood is from seed, as has been shown. The same must be said regarding the arguments about suffocation, and about sound and delight. For children dream while still incapable of the act of sex, and they find delight in the emission of "spirits" without seed. Indeed, women are delighted by the uterus in many ways: in receiving the male seed, in emitting their own moisture, and in the varying movements of the uterus. And similarly, they feel delight in the rubbing particularly around the upper orifice toward the **comb** <note>original: "pecten," referring to the pubic area</note>, so much so that those curious in this matter may lead themselves to a fainting fit. For the delight of this part is proportional to the tip of the male organ. It is also not necessary

---

to posit a female "drop" so that the "spermatic members" (which cannot be restored) may be generated within. It has been shown that the formative power can achieve this from blood. Even the physicians themselves say that at the beginning of generation, blood yields to the nature of the seed, and that the primary parts generated from it—like blood and seed—cannot be restored; this is the wise view.

The argument regarding **assimilation** <note>The physical resemblance of a child to its parents.</note> brought up last is of little value, but the following is more committed to the truth. When a speech is verified in many ways, one arrives at a single simple understanding of it. For one thing, according to Aristotle, can have several causes, as is apparent in the study of color. Therefore, he says that the examples **Galen** introduced are not resolvable by reason into a true form or method, for he brought them forward imperfectly.

Resemblance, as we are saying here, seems to be caused by two things: one is more universal, the other more particular. The **universal** is the intention of the universal species. For universal nature does not only intend generation, but also corruption, since one cannot exist without the other. The corruption of one is the generation of another, and vice versa, as stated in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. Although particular nature always intends generation and conservation—for every animal tries to protect its safety and avoids death and destruction, as stated in the third book of *On Consolation*—similarly, it does not only intend the male, but also the female, since without these two, generation cannot be perfected. Yet, singular nature desires the male continuously; for this reason, in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, it is said that **the female is a displaced male.** Wherefore in the accounts of generation in the **Law of Moses**, it is written that Adam always received two from his Eve, namely a male and a female, so that like doves they could propagate the human race.

Resemblance is also caused by a threefold particular being: namely, by a certain **celestial vigor**, by the intense **imagination** of the female, and by the formative power implanted in the seed. The celestial power consists of celestial forms and images, which the **Indians and Chaldeans** imagined to exist in the eighth sphere of the heavens. Whence **Ptolemy** says in the ninth aphorism of the *Centiloquium*: "The faces of this world are subject to the celestial faces or figurations." And in the ninety-fifth aphorism: "It always happens to the form that that which ascends from the degrees of the stars is similar to that which the newborn seeks." **Haly Rodon** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer.</note> declares this through a long history of a single principle; and rightly so, because the motion of the superior world is the cause of all these inferior motions, so that every power is governed from there, as stated in the first book of *Meteorology*. Resemblance also depends in no small part on the power of the imagination and the forces of the soul; whence in the tenth book of *Problems*, a question is sufficiently answered: "Why is there less resemblance among humans [than among animals]?"

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "formative power" and the causes of resemblance between parents and offspring. Having discussed the physical membranes of the embryo, the text now shifts to the psychological and metaphysical influences on generation, specifically the role of imagination and the Aristotelian theory of "active" versus "passive" principles.</meta>

...the offspring relates to the generator as in other animals. For the human mind is disposed in many ways during intercourse; as the father and mother are disposed at the time of coitus, so the offspring are affected. 

Regarding the **power of the imagination**, much has been said by **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."; refers to Aristotle's 'On the Soul' (De Anima)</note>, especially in the fourth book *On the Soul*, and by his colleague **Algazel** <note>The Latinized name for Al-Ghazali, a 12th-century Persian philosopher whose works on logic and physics were widely read in Latin translation.</note>. They argue that the force of an intense imagination can cause a man to fall into a pit or a camel to fall into a cauldron; that is, it operates not only upon one's own body, but even upon another’s (Difference 134). Therefore, it is no wonder if it can change matter as susceptible as seed and menstrual blood. 

First, thoughts themselves move the **humors** <term>Humors: The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</term>; just as looking at red things moves the blood. Second, it happens that the body suffers due to mental affections. For natural things are often imprinted by chance, such that a child resembles the form imagined at the moment of conception, and its color might be near to the color seen at that time. Those who have not studied the habits of difficult dispositions find such things hard to believe, for they do not love wisdom. 

Third, as some wise men have said (and they are not far from the judgment of possibility), one of the causes of resemblance is that which is made manifest when the disposition of conception is fixed in the mind of the woman or the man by a firm, imagined form.

An example of this resemblance through imagination is found in **Genesis**, regarding how **Jacob** deceived his uncle **Laban**. After a division of the lambs yet to be born was made based on their color, and Laban chose one color, Jacob placed rods of the opposite color in the river where the sheep drank during the time of mating and conception. Through the imagination of such a color, the lambs were born colored in a way that fell to his own lot. 

Indeed, the power of sight is part of the **formative power** <term>Virtus Informativa: The biological "program" or force believed to direct the development of the embryo.</term>, which is a divine principle from the higher realms. According to the second book of *The Generation of Animals*: in whatever thing something divine is apprehended, it is that which is called **Intellect**. Because this power is the most strong and all-encompassing, in one who is perfectly disposed in substance and nature, it will imprint the paternal likeness in every way. 

Thus, a strong-bodied man produces male children. This resemblance is not only according to the species or the radical traits of the individual, but even according to **accidental traits** <note>In medieval philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like scars, hair color, or temporary marks.</note> such as signs and brands. Whence in the first book of *The Generation of Animals*: children are not only like their parents in natural traits, but even in acquired ones. For when parents had scars, the offspring received them in the same places. This was seen in **Chalcedon**, where a father had what is called a **stigma** <note>A mark or brand on the skin.</note> on his arm, and it appeared on the son, though as a blurred and not clearly defined picture. I myself have seen true signs in both at times. Likewise, in the book *On Air and Water*: the bald beget the bald, the gray-eyed beget the gray-eyed, and the cross-eyed beget the cross-eyed. 

However, when the formative power acts contrarily, a resemblance to the "imperfect" or "remote" parent is induced, such as to the mother or the grandfather. 

Know that this is treated in the fourth book of *The Generation of Animals*, where the cause is assigned solely to the motion and vigor of the active principle. Therefore, Aristotle, the **First Master**, notes that this happens frequently: for when the motion is strong, a man is generated, such as a **Socrates**. When it begins to weaken, a [female] human is produced; and if it is further weakened, an animal or a **monster** <note>In this context, a "monster" refers to any birth that deviates from the human form, often viewed as a biological failure.</note> is born. 

From this, it is similarly held that when this motion is stronger, the child will resemble the father; when it is weak, the mother or one of the ancestors. To the extent that the motion of the "Socrates" or the male is saved or corrupted, the resemblance is stronger or weaker. Aristotle says resemblance is both "common" and "proper." 
*   **Common resemblance** is according to species (like in people or Ethiopians). 
*   **Proper resemblance** is according to lineage, as sons properly have their traits from their parents. 

Therefore, when the resemblance is obedient in every part, the offspring is made like the father. If it is obedient to the matter [the mother], it will resemble the mother. If it is not so, it will resemble the grandfather. If it loses the resemblance of the human species, it takes on "humanity" generally; if it loses that, it takes on "animalness," as seen in monstrous things—such as when the son of a man has the head of a ram, or a lamb has the head of a bull. For the power induced in it a form according to the **celestial figures** <note>The astrological alignment of the stars at the moment of conception or birth.</note> which occur and prevail.

But regarding the aforesaid, one might hesitate, because it was assumed that resemblance is given only by the father, yet in many cases, the child is seen to resemble the mother. 

It must be said that resemblance is of two types:
1.  **Individual resemblance**, which follows the outward figure. A child is rarely like the mother in this way.
2.  **Specific resemblance**, which follows the **complexion** <term>Complexion: The internal balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities.</term> rather than the outward figure, and especially the heart. Through this, the form of masculinity or femininity is provided, and thus the conceived child always resembles the parent. For these follow the "radical complexion" of the first seed (Difference 28). 

The female never acts as the primary agent, nor does she imprint her likeness except by a great accident. She "impedes" the agent from imprinting its likeness because she renders the matter ill-disposed. Just as someone wanting to cause a certain effect might be disturbed and turned aside by someone else; even if that person cannot produce the effect themselves, the result will fall according to their interference. Thus, the claims of **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note> appear to have no validity. One must think he wrote those things either following the old masters or during a time when he was still unrefined in the knowledge of nature.

It utilizes Aristotelian biology and biblical examples to argue that the mother is a passive material cause, while the father (and the stars) provide the active form.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the biological mechanics of conception. Having previously discussed the power of the imagination, the author now addresses specific physiological theories from medieval medical authorities like Haly Abbas, Avicenna, and Averroes, focusing on whether women produce a "seed" (sperm) that contributes to the embryo's physical substance.</meta>

->f i<-

...noted in the third book of *Naturalia*. The sayings of **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Halyab"; 10th-century Persian physician Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi, author of the 'Royal Book' of medicine.</note>, his more faithful imitator, are also not difficult to set aside. For the male seed is not so thick that it requires a more liquid substance to melt it with moisture. On the contrary, an initial thickening of the seed is necessary so that it may be strengthened within itself through gathering together. For this reason, the experts in generation <note>original: "genetalici"</note> claim that **Saturn**—being cold and dry—rules over the first stage (Difference 39). Likewise, there is a **formative power** within it, along with spirits that heat and refine it slightly, which is the "half-seed" <note>original: "semis oie"; likely referring to the active principle in the seed.</note>. This work could also be fulfilled by the **menstrual blood**; nor is the seed itself so hot in its **complexion** <term>Complexion: In medieval medicine, the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a person or substance.</term> that it needs a cooling influence, since it is moderately hot and moist, as indicated by its hail-like whiteness and its abundance of spirits.

Furthermore, it is not necessary for the female's moisture to be mixed with the male's for the sake of creating the covering and membrane of the embryo, since this can be accomplished by the male seed alone. As stated in a previous section: when the seed has been received by the **womb** <note>original: "matrice"</note> and has remained inside, a **membrane** <note>original: "ymen"</note> forms around it, just as it does in heated bodily fluids, much like "perixiron" <note>original: "perixiron"; a Greek-derived term meaning "surrounding" or "congealed."</note> around chilled ribs. For just as in that case, surplus matter serves as the nourishment for the compaction of animals before they have drawn nourishment from elsewhere, so too can a membrane—enveloping the seed—be generated from the male seed itself, and the blood eventually perfected.

Regarding the third point, it must be known that **Avicenna** <note>original: "Ay."</note> and his followers believed that the female neither possesses seed nor enters into the physical constitution of the embryo. Experience first demonstrates this. For Avicenna and **Averroes** <note>original: "Ax."</note>—and some women have confessed this to me as well—maintained that impregnation can occur without the provision of their "drop" <note>original: "gutte"; refers to female vaginal lubrication or supposed female seed.</note>. The sign of this is the absence of **pleasure** <note>original: "delectationis"</note>; for pleasure exists only with the emission of this drop. Indeed, some women have been impregnated even though the act of intercourse was displeasing to them. <term>Colliget, book 3</term> <note>The 'Colliget' (Kitab al-Kulliyat) is a famous medical encyclopedia by Averroes.</note>.

In this matter, a solemn testimony is brought forward regarding a certain trustworthy neighbor woman, who swore that she <unclear>had been impregnated by the male seed</unclear>. Averroes admits this to be possible, since the womb attracts the seed by a **specific power**, as **Avempace** <note>original: "Auendadich"; 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Bajja.</note> testifies. However, some attempt to falsify this experience in multiple ways. First, they say the woman does not feel pleasure because she has intercourse so frequently that her sense of pleasure is dulled. <term>History of Animals, book 9</term> <note>A work by Aristotle.</note>. But this argument is not valid, because then the woman's "drop" would not be fit for generation, nor indeed would the male seed be. For the seed of those who have excessive intercourse, the decrepit, the drunk, and those suffering from acute illness, does not generate (Book 20, chapter 3).

The aforementioned experience is also challenged in another way: they say the organs of pleasure are paralyzed or full of moistures. But this likewise does not hold, because then the woman's "drop" would be chilled, and the male seed would be extinguished and suffocated; nor would it be able to be drawn in, and thus generation would cease.

Someone might perhaps bring an objection from **Aristotle's book 15 on Animals**, arguing that even if a woman does not perceive the emission from herself at the hour of intercourse, it nevertheless came out at another time, either before coitus or through expulsion, and entered the womb and was guarded by it until it could provide help. And this happens when the male seed arrives directly to it without any attraction. To this it must be said that Aristotle mentions this with doubt, perhaps as a possibility; he was also of the opposite opinion which he now defends. Indeed, the opposite appeared to be true when Aristotle mistakenly attributed the seed to the blood. Or perhaps that seed could only fall into the womb from the female "testicles" <note>Medieval term for ovaries.</note> through some movement of pleasure; or if it did fall, it was corrupted because of its lack of vigor and the moistures it found in the womb. For just as it is impossible for both bladders to be found empty (as noted in the third book of *Naturalia*), so too for the belly and the womb. Or, if that female "drop" were retained by the womb, it would eventually have to either fall out or the womb would have to close. But if it closed, then the male seed could not enter. This reasoning confirms that it does not enter later, because this "drop" is impure, foul-smelling, and a surplus of the womb similar to urine, as previously mentioned—more worthy of being ejected than received. Since it is excessively liquid in quantity, if it met the male seed, it would suffocate and extinguish it. Furthermore, this is not universal to all women, but occurs more in those who are pale and weak, rather than in those who are dark-complexioned or "viragos" <note>original: "uiraginibus"; women who are physically strong or have masculine qualities.</note>.

Again, the provider of nourishment is the same as the provider of matter, since nourishment turns into matter. Hence, in the <term>third book on the Generation of Animals</term>: "The matter is the same which increases and from which the thing is first constituted." But blood provides the matter of nourishment (Difference 30), not the woman's "drop" which is a surplus of the womb. Moreover, if that drop were to enter [the embryo], the womb would not cast it out as a surplus; yet it does cast it out. Indeed, it is vomited from the womb so that the womb may draw the male seed to itself. It drips from her like saliva from the mouth of a hungry person when they see someone eating. <term>Colliget, book 3</term>. However, the contrary is written in books 20 and 21, which mention the dryness of the generative organs after coitus. But perhaps that happens in time. Nor can it be said that the act of generation is completed partly from the male seed and partly from the female "drop," such that one forms some members and the other forms others; for although there are many members, they are all multiplied from a single principle...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into human generation and the composition of the body. While the previous page addressed the "complexion" of the seed and the role of menstrual blood, this text shifts to a debate over whether the female "drop" (seed) is a formal cause of the embryo and transitions into a medical discussion on "consolidation"—the healing and restoration of different types of bodily tissues.</meta>

...from a beginning, namely the **heart**. For the giver of all members stands forth in its power. Indeed, it must not be said that one thing can be made from the male seed and the female drop, just as **oxymel** <note>original: "oximel"; a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar.</note> is composed of honey and vinegar. This is because something must be present as the established and given form, which is the **formative power** <term>Formative power: *virtus informativa*, the invisible force believed to organize matter into a living body.</term>. In respect to this power, all the ingredients of the embryo's constitution stand as matter. On the other hand, the woman’s drop enters the generation of the embryo either through an active or passive power. It is not active, because the active power enters from the male seed. Nor is it passive, because that role belongs to the "matter," and there is only one matter, as the matter must be proportioned to the form. For a single thing, there is a single form and a single distinct existence. Since the blood is the single matter of the embryo, the female drop cannot also be its matter. Therefore, the female moisture does not enter into the constitution of the embryo.

Regarding the fourth point, it must be said that you do not have to accept the authorities of **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and other physicians when their opinions are opposed to this. To the other point, it should be said that **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ar."; the author refers to Aristotle’s *On the Generation of Animals*.</note> speaks in that same place according to the opinion of physicians, as appears from his words introduced shortly after. For the female drop is not necessary for generation, since generation is completed without it, as has been shown. However, it may contribute as an occasion, often inciting the **womb** to receive the male seed. To the other point, it should be said that it is not valid, as many hold the opposite view to me. Either the female drop follows the attraction and movement of the male seed upward, but it does not follow that it mixes with it into one thing. For the neck of the womb has a great length in respect to the male member.

To the other point, it should be said through the interruption of the assumption, as seen before. To the other point, it must be said that although all members are constituted from blood (as already shown), they cannot all be restored. This is because those parts in which the blood was converted into a **spermatic nature** <term>Spermatic nature: In medieval anatomy, "spermatic members" (like bones, nerves, and tendons) were thought to be formed directly from seed and were considered harder and less capable of healing than "bloody" members (like flesh).</term> at the very beginning of generation cannot be restored, since the formative power has already departed and the matter has hardened. On the occasion of what has been touched upon regarding the restoration of parts, it is doubted whether **spermatic parts** can be restored by a true union once they have been severed.

And it seems that they can. For **Galen** in the 23rd book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio"; referring to *De methodo medendi*.</note> said earlier that perceptible veins are sometimes generated. And in the fourth [chapter] of the fourth book, he says the branches of the veins often stand out and are born just like flesh; but if they are spermatic, they can be glued together by a much more perfect consolidation. And in the fifth book of *On the Method of Healing*, I found a "pulsing vein" <note>An artery.</note> perfectly solidified after the arm had been severed for four days. Furthermore, lost parts are restored in certain animals, such as feet, and in "imperfect" creatures <note>Likely referring to reptiles like lizards or insects.</note>; so in humans and similar beings, severed parts should be refilled or at least reunited most perfectly. For nature does nothing by chance, such that it would care for imperfect and base animals but despise perfect and precious ones, as appears in the second book of *On the Heavens*. Add to this that teeth, which are spermatic, are reborn after falling out, which is even more significant. Again, parts are nourished through everything, and there is a "replacement" <note>original: "cambium"; the metabolic exchange of nutrients into tissue.</note>, even for spermatic parts, which, once thickened and hardened, can be placed in the location of the lost part to unite it. Therefore, severed radical parts can be perfectly united.

The opposite of this is gathered from the 6th book of the **Aphorisms** <note>The *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates.</note>: since when a bone, cartilage, nerve, or thin part of the jaw has been cut, they neither grow back nor conglutinate <note>Heal together.</note>. They are "entangled" <note>original: "inuiscantur"</note> according to the commentator; hence he detests those who claim that fractured bones can neither be consolidated nor repaired when joined. This is shown by the **callus** <note>original: "porus"; the bony bridge that forms during healing.</note> that is generated, which, when closely examined, binds their fracture all around. Furthermore, the fracture of a whole bone, which is a "dissolution of continuity," is incurable in terms of its first confederation <note>i.e., it never returns to its original state</note>, but it is curable according to a certain mode, as will appear. And then there would be no difference between the aforementioned members: that those from seed cannot be restored, while those from blood can. Again, the conglutinated moisture that is dissolved was simply one from the time of generation. That through which reunion must happen is either from now or from that time. Here, however, since the opposite divided parts do not coincide with the whole, severed spermatic parts cannot be coupled.

Regarding the first point, it should be known what a **spermatic member** is and what a **sanguineous member** is, as already seen. There is indeed only a twofold consolidation. One is "certain," so that they return to such a union as they had before; this is called the "first intention of union." The other is a certain application and contact of parts to one another made through **thickened blood**, binding the lips of the wound to each other; hence in the whole. The second is a "contingent binding" that happens through the callus binding the fracture all around.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that the speeches of the superficially wise seem opposed on both sides, as touched upon regarding the fracture of bone before. Whence in the 5th book of *On the Method of Healing*, it is said by certain physicians that wounds in the "pulse" <note>The arteries.</note> cannot be healed. Some think their experience in this is sufficient for them. Some indeed believe in reason, saying that one of the skins of the pulsing veins is hard and cartilaginous, and a hard body cannot be consolidated because solidification only occurs in tender bodies; nor are bones joined according to consolidation, but according to that which is formed and coagulated over them, which physicians call **bony coagulation** <note>original: "offiua coagulatio"; a bone callus.</note>. He adds the opposite of these things, saying: "I say that I have seen pulsing veins solidified and flesh generated around them." This is seen in veins, and in women in the forehead, eyes, sole of the foot, and in the **raseta** <note>An Arabic-derived term for the wrist or tarsus.</note> of the hand. He adds again: "I say..."

<meta>This page continues the medical discussion on "consolidation"—the healing and knitting together of tissues. Having previously discussed the generation of the body from seed and blood, the author now addresses why certain tissues (like arteries and bones) heal differently than others (like flesh), citing the opinions of Galen and Haly Abbas.</meta>

...to show that the nature of the **pulsating vein** <term>Pulsating vein: *vena pulsans*, the medieval term for an artery, distinguished from a "quiet" vein by its pulse.</term> is such that its membranes are hard and difficult to knit together. It is not, however, necessary to think they cannot be healed; therefore, you should not despair of their healing, especially if the wound is small and the body is naturally soft. For we often see pulsating veins that have been cut in children and women knit together because of their softness. Nevertheless, they knit together with more difficulty than other veins. Wherefore, those **primary members** <note>These are the "spermatic members," tissues like bone and nerve believed to be formed directly from the parents' seed during conception.</note> that were first created from the seed do not restore themselves with a certain continuity when they suffer a breach of their continuity—except for a few of them, in few conditions, and during the age of childhood, such as bones and small branches of the veins. This does not occur in large ones, nor in arteries. For when any part of them is severed, nothing grows back in its place; and these are indeed like bones and nerves.

### The Fourth Argument
Reciting the discourse of **Galen**, it says: I say, therefore, that we strive in certain members whose continuity is broken so that their continuity might return as it was, as is the case in **flesh**. And we strive in some of them so that their contact remains preserved, even if their actual continuity does not return, and this is the case in the bones of infants and children. For in them, that return of continuity is sometimes hoped for. 

Concerning **nerves** and **veins**, however, some physicians have said they do not return to continuity; rather, perhaps there remains in them a contact of "gluing" <term>Gluing: *conglutinatio*, a type of healing where tissues are stuck together by a secondary substance rather than regrowing as a single unit.</term> which, by a preservation running over them, joins them together. And some said that this [healing] only occurs in arteries alone. **Galen**, however, has already contradicted them on this point; he said that instead, arteries are sometimes "infleshed" <term>Infleshed: *incarnantur*, the process of a wound filling with new tissue or "flesh" to heal.</term> by the testimony of experience and with the concession of reasoning.

#### By Testimony and Reasoning
By testimony, because we have already seen the artery that is under the **basilic** <note>The basilic vein area of the arm, a common site for bloodletting.</note> and the head of the temporal and leg arteries become infleshed. By the concession of reasoning: because **bone** is the extreme in hardness and is not infleshed except slightly and in infants; and **flesh** is the extreme in softness and is infleshed; but veins and arteries are the midpoint between bones and flesh. Therefore, it is necessary that their disposition be the middle ground between bone and flesh. Thus, they are less receptive to infleshing than flesh, but more easily receive it than bones. They inflesh when the cut is very small and the body is moist and light; and they do not inflesh in a way that is indistinguishable from the original. And this is the theoretical mode of the dispute. But that which is relied upon is **experiment**. And this is indeed the discourse of **Galen** with **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."; likely referring to Avicenna, a major authority in medieval medicine.</note> about which we shall see hereafter.

Regarding the third point, it must be known that if the **spermatic members** are broken by a large or even medium breach—especially in bodies that are already hardened, aged, and poorly disposed, and specifically in those that are more "earthy"—they do not reunite by a true continuation. This is especially true of bones, and consequently cartilages, then ligaments, the heart, the inner tunic of the artery, the nerve, and the membrane; the tunic of the vein and the outer part of the artery do not truly reunite, but rather according to a certain application or contact, so that they appear to be coupled together. 

This is proven perhaps partly because of the abundance of the **formative power** <note>original: "uirtutis informantis"; the life-force that shapes the body in the womb.</note>, for it departs once the fetus is formed (as in difference 48); partly because of the lack of **spermatic matter** from which the member remained united; partly because of the weakness of the power caused in the member by the breach itself; and partly because of the hardness already inherent in it.

Conversely, however, everything that is made from **blood** can be truly reunited. Whence in the **Art** <note>original: "tegni"; referring to Galen's *Ars Medica*, the standard medical textbook of the era.</note>: "When continuity is broken, the intention of the cure is union." This is impossible in **organic parts**, but not impossible in **similar parts**. For in some it is possible, as in fleshy parts where "gluing" is the healing. If the breach of continuity is small, and in infants with a good constitution, the first intention of union will be sufficiently possible—especially in the venous tunics, followed by the membranes, the thin tunics of the heart's artery, ligaments, cartilages, and bones, because of their proximity to the states mentioned before. For some vigor remains in the **principal members** (and especially the heart) in a formative way; there also remains some spermatic matter diffused in the "fountains" of the members. They are also still soft, and the weakness that must be cared for in their breach has not yet intervened. Thus, the truth may shine forth more briefly from these first principles.

Regarding the fourth point: as for what seemed necessary to say to the first [argument], the cutting of a vein can be so modest in a branch so small, and in an infant's body so well-disposed, that it is not only more truly reunited, but it even grows again after its loss. Yet other parts so broken do not. For it is easier for a part to be knitted together than for a lost part to be restored. 

To the other point, it must be said that it is not similar, because in the production of a **perfect animal**, nature exerts its power as one to perfect it from the beginning; but it is not so in the leading out of imperfection. For nature, considering that perfect things could remain for a long time if they had entirely complete parts, made them strong and bounded. But imperfect things [remain] very little, as they often perish; it decreed that in these, it would not expend all its power at first, but would retain some matter for itself. Or, according to **Haly Abbas**, these parts are reborn from "superfluities," nor do they return in the same way or as great as the originals. This is also indicated by **plants**, which are not able to grow together again in a straight line. Therefore, nature did not despise precious, perfect things; rather, it signified that more perfect things [possess] every type of restoration.

For every body is truly such from its generation, as **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas (930–994 AD), a famous Persian physician and psychologist.</note> feels, though some more and some less.

### DISTINCTION XXXVIII.

### That there are several principal members according to the authority of Galen and other physicians, along with the Stoics.

For he says in the *Tegni* <note>The *Tegni* or *Ars Medica* was a foundational textbook by Galen.</note> that the principal members are the **brain**, **heart**, **liver**, and **testicles**. Wherefore the **Commentator** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), known as "The Commentator" for his work on Aristotle.</note> in his work *On the Soul* says: **Avicenna** thinks that the soul acts through diverse powers and unique members—namely, the principal ones—and through diverse principles in those members. These members indeed imply a plurality. Again, according to the unity or plurality of perfections, the "perfectible" things are numbered, for they are ordered toward those perfections as if toward their ends. There are indeed three or four perfections, as he almost everywhere maintained along with the Platonists. **Galen** identifies the "animal" <note>In medieval science, "animal" refers to the *anima* (soul), meaning sensory and motor functions centered in the brain.</note> virtue, the vital virtue, and the natural virtue—the latter being twofold, involving the use of food and the power of generation. He located the first of these in the brain, the second in the heart, the third in the liver, and the fourth in the testicles (as seen in Distinction 47). For he posited, along with the aforementioned thinkers, that the soul is an aggregation of primary substances. Wherefore in the first book *On the Soul*, some say the soul is divisible: one part for understanding and another for desiring. The Commentator indeed agrees with **Plato**, who thinks that the soul is essentially divided in the body according to the division of the members in which it performs its diverse actions; and that it is not shared in any one member, so that the intelligible part is in the brain only, and desire or concupiscence is in the heart only, and the natural part—namely, the nutritive—is in the liver. Furthermore,

---

the same is found in the eighth book of the *Metaphysics*: Just as change makes matter known, so action makes **form** known. We clearly observe three or four actions; therefore, there will be three or four forms. Form here is ordered toward the subject as matter; therefore, there will be three or four subjects. Likewise, a particular being is subject to "Being" and is proportioned to the Universal, but in itself there are several principles, such as matter, form, and privation (from the first book of the *Physics*). This is according to what was stated in the preface to the *Metaphysics*: that three things exist in every single thing. Hence, **Trinity** is attributed to the most noble of divine beings. Therefore, there shall exist more than one principal member.

On the opposite side is **Avicenna** in all his philosophy. Again, regarding the cause of the motion of animals: One must consider the animal to consist like a city well-governed by laws. In this city, one stands at the head, toward whom all things tend, just as is fitting for civil matters. Again, since it is recited in the eighth book of the *Physics* that man is a **microcosm** <term>Microcosm: The idea that the human body is a "little world" that mirrors the structure of the universe (the macrocosm).</term>. Those things in him will be similar to the things in the greater world. In that world, there exists one thing toward which all things are finally ordered as an end (as concluded in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*). Therefore, only one principal member exists.

That the testicles are not a principal member is shown because when they are removed, the remainder of the body persists. But when that which is principal is removed, everything is destroyed. Also, the principal thing is that one in which the organs meet. In other noble parts, this is seen to exist as in the brain, but such a thing is the **heart**. Wherefore in the first book on *Simple Medicines*: "My [vessels] are submerged in the veins of the tongue and are extended from there to the heart." Therefore, there is one principal member.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that "members" are solid bodies which are generated from the first mixing of the **humors**. A member is also a thickened part of the animal, created from moisture and distinguished by the powers of nature. And know that the things integrating the body are called parts or members, or *mele* in Greek. For those things are called "members" which, being whole parts, have other specific parts within themselves—such as the head or the foot, the joints of animals. They are also called the seats of internal principles. Their smaller portions are called "particles." Galen often calls every member a "particle." "Member" is also understood in two ways: properly, as defined above, especially according to the natural power existing within it; and commonly, for every hardened substance ordered toward some office, such as that which is even generated from qualitative superfluities. Wherefore **Haly** says: it is manifest that the hair and nails are included in the number of members. Among these, some are "similar" <note>Meaning homogeneous or made of one substance, like bone or flesh.</note>, simple, primary, and composite; or "homeomerous," of which any sensible part is called by the same name and definition as the whole...

<meta>This page continues the anatomical and physiological categorization of the human body, moving from the specific healing properties of tissues (discussed on the previous page) to a comprehensive classification of all body parts based on their substance and their relationship to the soul's powers. bone, cartilage, nerve, vein, artery, membrane, ligament, sinew, simple flesh—such as that of the liver, lungs, and spleen—fat and grease, skin, hair, and nails. Certain other parts are **instrumental** <term>Officialia: Also known as "instrumental" parts; these are complex organs (like the hand) composed of various simple tissues to perform a specific function.</term>, which are opposite to the former in name and definition, ordained by the soul as instruments for some specific function; these are called heterogeneous, composite, secondary, mixed, or **non-homogeneous** <term>Anomiomera: Greek-derived term for parts whose components are not like the whole (e.g., a hand is made of bone, skin, and flesh, not "smaller hands").</term>. For they are mixed from simple parts, such as the head, the hand, the double foot, the thorax, and the belly. In these seven parts, many **homogeneous** <term>Consimilia: Tissues where every small piece is the same as the whole (e.g., every piece of bone is "bone").</term> components exist. And it should be known that the heart and the rest of the internal organs, as far as their matter is concerned (because they are made of blood and nourished by it), are homogeneous; however, as far as the form of their shape or composition is concerned, they are non-homogeneous. But regarding these parts, nothing is so homogeneous that it cannot also be called instrumental. For in every one of the homogeneous parts, a fourfold nature of composition is found. 

Furthermore, certain members are called **animal** <note>In this context, "animal" refers to the *anima* (soul) and specifically to sensory and cognitive functions.</note> by physicians, some **vital**, and others **natural**; yet they are primarily classified by which of these virtues <note>Virtue (uirtus): The specific power or capacity of an organ to perform its biological function.</note> is most apparent in them. For those "animal" members are assigned to sensation, voluntary motion, and—in man alone—discretion; these are the brain, eyes, organs of smell, nostrils, tongue, nerves, muscles, and the **diaphragm** <note>Original: "diafma" (diafragma).</note>. The "vital" members are those through which life is established and the ventilation of the spirit <note>Spiritus: A subtle substance believed to carry life and heat through the body.</note> is achieved to preserve the natural heat; they perform vital actions, such as the chest, its membranes, the heart, the lungs, the channels of the throat, the diaphragm, and the arteries. The "natural" members are twofold: some exist so that nourishment may be altered through them and converted into the body to restore what has been lost, so that the individual may endure. These are the mouth, teeth, esophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, gall, spleen, kidneys, bladder, the glands near it, and the veins. The others are called the genitals, instituted by nature for the permanence of the species. For individuals could not survive for long. Regarding the soul and the generation of animals, **the Commentator** <note>The Commentator: Standard medieval reference to the philosopher Averroes.</note> says: "Divine care took pity [on the individual] by giving it a power by which it can endure as a species." The members serving this permanence are the matrix <note>Matrix: The womb or uterus.</note>, the penis, both testicles, both spermatic vessels, and the breasts. Of all these parts, some are **principal**, existing as the roots and foundations of the virtues, such as the brain, heart, liver, and testicles. Or, according to **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay."</note> in the 35th Difference, the so-called "enveloped spermatic vessels." The remaining parts are those that provide assistance, some of which serve by carrying [substances], just as the nerves serve the brain, the arteries the heart, the veins the liver, and the seminal vessels the testicles—

---

—constructed from ligament alone joined together, and things of this kind. There are also others that are defensive, such as the membranes and the skull. Some contain superfluity <note>Superfluity: Waste products or excess fluids like urine or feces.</note>, such as the intestines and the bladder; some are for binding, like the ligaments; and some contribute to the aid of digestion, such as the parts of the mouth. Some of these also act by their action alone, such as the heart; others provide help only, like the lungs and their channels; while some provide both, such as the brain and the liver. There are also some that are **spermatic** <term>Spermatic parts: Tissues believed to be formed from the initial seed of the parents (bones, nerves) which were thought to be unable to regenerate if destroyed.</term> and others that are **sanguineous** (blood-based), such as flesh and fat. The rest are from the "seed," as explained in the inquiries about it. The blood-based parts are those that are restored when lost, but the spermatic parts are not (Difference 36). Likewise, the motion of some is natural, such as the womb and the veins, while the motion of others is "animated" <note>Animated motion: Voluntary motion directed by the soul.</note>, such as the muscles. Some have one tunic <note>Tunic: A layer or "coat" of tissue.</note>, like the gallbladder and the bladder (at least apparently), and some have two, like the intestines and the arteries. The origin of all of these is evidently from the **peritoneum** <note>original: "siphac," an Arabic anatomical term for the lining of the abdominal cavity.</note> or the subcostal membrane (Difference 44). A "principal member" is one having the principle of its own power necessarily consisting in the body, so that the individual or the species may endure. 

Regarding the soul, it should be known that according to the unity or diversity of the soul, the parts are either united or diversified, since their reasoning must be taken from their form or their end. It should also be known that there have been many opinions concerning the soul, according to **Avicenna** <note>original: "Av."</note> in his work *On the Soul*. For some thought the soul to be one essence performing its actions through itself, regardless of the diversity of the instruments. Others thought that the soul is wise through itself, knowing all things, and does not act through senses and instruments except to be excited by them toward that which it has naturally within itself. Some even said this happens as if by remembering, for it happens to the soul sometimes to forget. There were several who said the soul is not one, but many, and that the soul which is in one body is a collection of souls—namely, the ruling soul, the apprehending soul, the irascible soul, and the concupiscible soul. Among these was one who said the concupiscible soul is the nutritive soul, and said its place was the heart, to which he attributed both the desire for nourishment and for generation. Similarly, some of these held that the generative power is from a certain power of a part of the soul emanating into the testicles of the male and female. Others held that the soul is one essence from which these powers emanate, each of which has its own action, and that the soul acts nothing except through the mediation of these powers—which seems to have been the opinion of **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay."</note>. Indeed, **the Apostle** <note>original: "ap'le" (Apostolus), likely referring to St. Paul, though in a medical context this might refer to a primary authority.</note> exterminates almost all of these [false] opinions. The position of **Plato** <note>original: "plonis"</note>, and consequently that of **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note>, is sufficiently contested in the first book *On the Soul*.
