<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "principal members" of the body, transitioning from a general classification of tissues to a focused debate on whether the heart, brain, or liver holds ultimate primacy. The author leans heavily on Aristotelian teleology to argue for the heart as the single "sovereign" of the body.</meta>

Therefore, since these matters do not pertain to the current investigation, they shall be suspended for the present. According to this view, it was necessary for Plato and Galen to propose many sensible things, since they established many "perfections" <note>original: "perfectiones"; here referring to the different functional goals or "souls" of the body's organs</note>. However, according to the sentence of Aristotle, who proposes a single substance of the soul—though diversified by its powers—it is fitting to assign only one among the principal members. The rest are secondary and subservient to it. Whence Aristotle, in the first book of his *First Philosophy* <note>Metaphysics</note>, as the physician finally asserts in his definition, states that principal members exist. Thirdly, regarding the permanence of the individual, there is the heart, the brain, and the liver; and fourthly, regarding the durability of the species, as previously mentioned <note>Referring to the reproductive organs</note>. Regarding the third point, it must be shown: first, that there is one principal member; second, which one it is; third, how it can be conceded that many are principal; and fourth, it is finally declared through examples.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that one member is more principal than the others, as Aristotle judged throughout his works. Whence, in the third book of *On the Parts of Animals*, he says that the principle of those things which are in the body must necessarily be one, for where one is possible, it is better than many. This Galen also seems to concede in the fourth book of *On Interior Matters*. This is shown by reason, because in every genus it is necessary at last to provide one primary thing which exists as the cause of all others, and by attribution to which the others have their being, as stated in the 12th book of the *Metaphysics*. For it is necessary to lead every plurality—which contains imperfection and confusion—at last to one supreme regulating thing, since all things by nature seek identity. For they do not wish to be ill-disposed, nor is a plurality of rulers a good thing; "one, therefore, is the prince" <note>original: "unus igitur princeps"; a famous quote from the end of Aristotle’s Metaphysics, Book 12</note>. Thus, in the genus of the animal, making its construction a unity, there exists one primary thing. Furthermore, according to the "Lucidator" <note>Peter of Abano (c. 1257–1316), a famous physician and philosopher known as "the Reconciler" or "Lucidator" for trying to bridge the gap between Greek/Arabic medicine and Aristotelian philosophy</note> in the third distinction of his *Astrological Speculations*: everything that is found in many things through one univocal reason has something prior to them which exists as the cause of them all; just as all heat, according to the skill of Aristotle, is reduced to the first of heats, which is fire. But a diversity of **virtues** <term>Virtutes: In medieval medicine, these are "powers" or "faculties" (vital, natural, and animal) that govern different bodily functions like breathing, nutrition, and thought.</term> is found, both vital as well as natural and animal. It is necessary, therefore, to finally reduce these to one in which they are made univocal. Again, in essentially ordered things, since there is no process to infinity nor a stopping point in many, it is necessary to come to one supreme thing. For it does not happen that many principles and disputes are made from parts; therefore, in the third book of *On the Parts of Animals*, in the genus of animal members, one primary principle stands out, just as in the other parts of the universe.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that such a member is the heart (*cor*), and not the brain or the liver. This is shown by its location; whence in the third book of *On the Parts of Animals*, the position of the heart occupies the principal place, since it sits near the middle, though more toward the upper part than the lower, and more toward the anterior than the posterior. Nature always places the honorable thing in an honorable place, unless something hinders it. But if the point of the heart declines slightly to the left, this happens to temper the coldness of the left side, as stated in the first book of the *History of Animals* and the third of *On the Parts of Animals*. In other animals, the heart exists in the middle of the chest area, but in humans, it is slightly inclined to the left to balance the cooling of the left parts. For more than other animals, man has a cooled left side. I say this also happens regarding the liver's position and its size relative to the body and the mass of the spleen. Therefore, the place of the heart was in the middle because this is the place of the King, so that his kingdom might be equally proportioned to all its surroundings. This also occurs so that it may be diligently guarded. This is also declared by its own proper dwelling, called the "capsule" <note>The pericardium</note>, and its most natural and wonderful construction.

Likewise, that is the principle of the members into which the soul is first inserted and which is moved the most; and this is the heart. For it is the first of all to be quickened and moved, whence the **vital virtue** <term>Virtus Vitalis: The "life force" centered in the heart, responsible for the pulse and the distribution of heat.</term>, the root of all others, is first fixed in it. This is shown by the departure of life, which comes last to the heart, as stated in the 47th and 48th *Differences* <note>Referring to Peter of Abano’s Conciliator</note>. For this reason, in the first book of the *First Philosophy*, the Great One <note>Aristotle</note> said that the member which gives and does not receive is the heart. For it is the first root of all virtues and gives its virtues to all other members, by which they are nourished and live, and by which they perceive and are moved. For the heart does not "receive" in a simple sense. For it does not receive anything that was not first given by it, except in a certain respect, as if it were merely changed. Just as I receive nothing from a goldsmith who restores to me a mass of gold given to him, now struck with the character of coins. Furthermore, the heart is the principle of the **natural virtue** <term>Virtus Naturalis: The power of nutrition, growth, and reproduction, usually associated with the liver, but here argued to originate in the heart.</term>, since it is the first principle, source, and receptacle of the blood (Difference 47). Similarly, it stands as the beginning of the **animal virtue** <term>Virtus Animalis: The power of sensation and voluntary movement, usually associated with the brain.</term>; for the movement of mobile things and universally all sense-perception seems to begin from it and terminate in it, as stated in the same place; whence in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, the "form and species" of the liver is said to be in the heart. Moreover, that is the first of the members in an animal which is first formed and the last to depart, and this is the heart (from the aforementioned Difference). Therefore, the heart is more principal than the other members, which is also shown by its wonderful position.

Know also that some have proposed the liver and the brain as prior and more principal than the heart, as noted in the 21st chapter of the third book. The truth is that the first member created in the body is the heart, although it is said of Hippocrates that he claimed the brain was created first, and the eyes second, as that testimony indicates...

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the "primary member" of the body, moving from theoretical arguments about sovereignty to physiological observations of embryology and the "spirits" that govern life.</meta>

The arrangement of chicks in the egg—for these are the first things that appear so large <note>Aristotle often used the development of a chick inside an egg as a model for all animal development</note>. On account of this, in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, a doubt arises regarding what happens concerning the eyes of animals; for at the beginning they appear the largest in all animals, yet they are the last of the parts to be completed because of the great coldness and humidity of the brain. Similarly, the brain is humid and large in the beginning, yet this later subsides as the humidity is lessened through digestion <note>In this context, "digestion" refers to the metabolic "cooking" or refining of bodily fluids by heat</note>. But it must be said to **Hippocrates** that although the heart may not appear—because it is hidden deeper down—it is nevertheless formed first; whence **Aristotle** says: "The heart, when it is created in the beginning, is not manifest or apparent in every creature." He finally adds those things which follow concerning the liver, in which **Averroes** says that it is more correct that the liver be the first thing created, because the first operation of the body is nutrition, as if it were a thing following its own appetite.

He <note>Aristotle</note> certainly attacks this opinion, saying that this discourse is shown to be corrupt by experience, since those who are studious in this art <note>meaning anatomy and dissection</note> do not testify that the matter is at all as he thought. Similarly, by reason, because nothing is nourished which does not participate in life with natural heat; this heat is given by the heart and not the liver. On account of which it is necessary for the embryo to be created first in a way that heat and the **vital spirit** <term>spiritus vitalis: a subtle substance thought to carry life through the arteries</term> precede the creation of that which nourishes it.

Regarding this, a third thing must be known so that the saying of **Galen** may be verified in some way: that something can be called a "principle" or "origin" of another in two ways: either **radically and primarily**, or **manifestly and secondarily**. In the first way, there is one principal member; in the second way, there are several. In the first way, it is the heart, since according to **Aristotle**, the soul is one—at least insofar as it is the principle of motion and sense—and it is most deeply implanted in the heart; for the soul's entire substance is founded in it. However, not all powers proceed into action within the heart, since it lacks specific instruments, except for the vital power which exists radically, formally, and also manifestly within it.

The **animal power** <term>spiritus animalis: the "spirit" responsible for thought and movement, located in the brain</term> and the **natural power** <term>spiritus naturalis: the "spirit" responsible for nutrition, located in the liver</term> exist in the heart radically only. The animal power is formed and perfected in the brain, and the natural power in the liver. Similarly, according to **Aristotle** in the fifth book of *On the Soul*: The spirit is sent from the heart through the arterial vessels to the brain, which is first digested and refined in a certain folding under the brain called the **wonderful net** <note>original: "rete mirabile"; a complex of blood vessels at the base of the skull thought to "filter" the spirits</note>. And then the animal spirit is made capable of providing life, sense, and motion wherever it is expanded. In the same way, the spirit is sent from the heart into the liver, which is changed in that place into the natural spirit.

However, according to many physicians, the natural spirit is created in the liver alone and does not come from elsewhere, as appears in the fourth book of the *Theory* <note>likely referring to the *Pantegni* or another standard medical textbook</note> and *On Interior Matters*. Whence **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> in his *Problems* says that when blood is digested in the liver and transmitted, a **vaporous spirit** is generated from a proportional heat and humidity. This spirit, ascending with the blood through the hollow vein <note>the vena cava</note> into the heart, is further heated and refined until it becomes "airy." This spirit, returning again through the arterial vessels to the base of the brain and putting aside the immense heat, is made into an **ethereal spirit** by the coldness of the brain. This spirit exists as the organ for action, just as a wild horse is admonished by a bridle. The food of this spirit is made of air. For through inspiration, air entering the heart is refined and ascends through the arteries to the brain.

I certainly grant this nutrition with **Galen** and **Haly Abbas**, even if it displeases **Avicenna** and **Aristotle** in *Differentia 145*. For if the spirit exists as a body, it is shaped to the body. If it is most subtle, pure, and splendid, it is cherished by the rational soul. The spirit, being a sort of "incorporeal body," exists as a **middle binding** between the extremities of substances that have contrary natures <note>meaning the spirit bridges the gap between the physical body and the non-physical soul</note>. This spirit, when well-constituted, allows the soul to operate all things according to reason, depending on the quality or substance of the spirit, as I declared in my edition of *Physiognomy*. However, in these matters I do not hear that the soul is bound to the body by any intermediary; for the form itself meets the matter, as stated in the second book of *On the Soul* and the eighth book of the *Metaphysics*.

Returning therefore, I say that the brain and the liver seem to be related to the heart as the power of sight is to the animal spirit. Whence in the twelfth book of *On Animals*, **Aristotle** said that the sense of touch has its principle in the heart and not in the head; and likewise taste, which is a kind of touch. And he adds: "But although sight, hearing, and smell have their principle in the heart, nevertheless the heart itself neither hears nor smells; rather, the instrument of these operations is the brain." And he said that the instrument of touch is the flesh and the nerve, and both are found in the heart. And he says that some of these powers are completed in their root and some are not; just as physicians say that the brain "feels" by itself but does not "see" by itself.

To the greatest of all philosophers, it seems that the heart exists as the principle of all these powers, but the primary manifestation of their actions exists in the brain, the heart, the liver, and the testicles. For just as the brain, according to physicians, is the principle of sensing and moving, after this, each movement and member has its own proper place in which its action is manifested. For sight or taste is not perfected by the animal spirit in the brain unless it penetrates to the **crystalline lens** <note>the part of the eye then thought to be the seat of vision</note> or to the tongue. So also the actions... <note>text cuts off</note> from the power and spirit; whence in the fourth book of *On the Soul* and in the treatise *On the Physicians of the Heart*, the heart is removed therefrom. The heart is the first principle, and from it emanate powers to the brain, of which some perform their actions...

Archigenes says: I say there is one reason which is more blameworthy than the truth of Archigenes. Truly, in the fourth [book] *On Accidents*: Even if Aristotle was most sufficient at leading a discourse wherever he wished, nevertheless he found nothing persuasive as to why, when the head is filled up [with fluid], the "first sensing" remains at rest, fixed in the heart as he himself suspected. Whence even physicians, by naked experience, object in their cures, providing for the head rather than the heart in cases of lethargy, stupor, and wakefulness. This truth, however, can be declared to some by more sensible fourth-order **paradigms**. 

For the heart is proportioned to a **sea** agitated by winds, from which three great rivers are derived. One of these is diffused through the whole body, carrying the spirit and the blood through the artery called the **aorta**. The second [river] gives life to the lung and draws in air by inspiration, and likewise expels copious vapors by expiration. And there is a river sent out from it tending upward into the brain, like the nerves which are generated from it out of the continuous matter between the matter of the heart and the brain when it is pushed upward. This [river], finding an obstacle above in its expansion,

generates one **lake**, namely the **brain**; from which, indeed, many rivulets originate laterally, one of which stands out as larger, like the **spinal cord** <note>original: "nuca," from the Arabic 'nukha' for spinal marrow</note> with its seven [pairs of nerves], and others no less significant like the seven pairs of [cranial] nerves. For this [the spinal cord], as the vicar and messenger of the brain, is directed through the whole back, from which many nerves emerge laterally on both sides, exiting from the openings of the vertebrae. 

From the aforementioned "sea" there also proceeds, at the right auricle of the heart, a certain great river—namely a vein larger than the small artery—sent to the liver. One part of this vein ascends while the other descends. From these, at last, together with others, the testicles arise. 

Furthermore, another paradigm declares this. Suppose someone has three skills, namely **singing**, **sewing**, and **building**. This man is capable of all three, yet differently; because he is able to sing as soon as he wishes, since the organs for this are located within himself, and therefore this is more proper, more formal, and more perfect to him. In the other two, however, he will not be able to act unless he has acquired the necessary instruments. So it is in the heart: every power exists radically or formally, and the spirit and instrument of one power—namely the **vital power**—is perfectly supported there. In the remaining two [the brain and liver], it is otherwise. Wherefore it is shown that the heart acquires instruments from elsewhere, which are the brain, the liver, or the testicles. 

From these things, therefore, it happens that one may grasp the foundation of **Aristotle** as true, and the "fantasy" of the physicians as probable. Whence, in the first [book] of the *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle's Metaphysics</note>: The discourse of the Philosopher, when it is subtly certified, is more true; but the discourse of the physicians, when one first attends to it, is more manifest. And finally, when they are contrasted as they ought to be and certified, they find the matter to be as it appears to Aristotle, and not as it appears to the physicians. For they [the physicians] find their extracted treatises from "sufficient" (that is, probable) propositions, and not from "true" (that is, necessary) ones, in which they pursue nothing except what appears from the things themselves, just as the aforementioned figures beautifully show. Regarding the fourth point: what ought to be said to the first [objection] has appeared. To the confirmation of the <term>Commentator</term> <note>Averroes</note>, it must be said that Aristotle heard that those diverse members, with their powers, are united in one principal member, namely the **heart**; which is what he meant when he spoke of "unique members," i.e., the principal ones, for otherwise he would fall into the opinion of **Plato**. To the other [objection], it must be said: that the apparent and secondary perfections exist as two or three; but the real and primary perfection is only one. To the other, likewise, it must be said: that the action makes the apparent form known...

## DIFFERENCE 39

-> That the skull is constituted of one bone is shown. <-

Since that is one and continuous whose motion is one in itself and individual (according to the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*), such indeed is the skull; for the joint of the head moved upon the first <term>vertebrae</term> <note>original: "spondilium"</note> of the neck moves the whole head. And it is supported because the upper bone of the head is continuous with the last vertebrae, which is called the "storied skull" <note>likely a reference to the *History of Animals*</note> in the third [book]. Furthermore, if the skull were constructed from many bones, since the brain is a member existing in the extreme of softness, it could not be sufficiently protected; for joints are not made for the sake of defense, but for the sake of motion. Because of this, so that it might be more perfectly fortified, it was necessary for it to be made of a single bone. 

However, that it is [made] of several is shown because the brain, both due to its weak digestion, collects many <term>superfluities</term> <note>waste products or "smoky" vapors believed to be produced by the body's internal heat</note>, and also because it is the **chimney of the whole body**, receiving vapors and fumes that need to be led out; unless they breathed out through the pores, it would be corrupted. And therefore [the skull] is joined by sutures. Those lacking [sutures] in the skull are exposed to pains and universally to diseases of the head more than others. 

Furthermore, since the heart is stronger and harder than the brain, it has more and divided bones, such as the ribs protecting it; and therefore the brain [should have] even more. That it is composed of two is argued because, according to the division of the contents (the brain), the container (the skull) should be divided, since the latter is ordered toward the former; but the brain is divided into two parts along its length, which the <term>dura mater</term> <note>the "hard mother," the tough outermost membrane surrounding the brain</note> shows by cutting through the middle of its length; and similarly the hair falls on either side, to the right and left. 

That it is [made] of three is seen from the bones left by the division of the saw-like sutures; for these are three. Hence, in the first and third [books] of the *Histories*, [it says] men [have] three sutures joined into one. Furthermore, there are three ventricles of the brain, for which the skull is ordered as an end. That it is four or five is shown because, with these three true sutures, physicians commonly add two "untrue" ones; from their extension, four or five bones are left. Thus the skull will be joined from different bones in different ways. On the opposite side, **Averroes** and **Almanzor** <note>likely referring to the Persian physician Al-Razi</note> constitute it from six bones.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that the body is constituted of several bones and parts universally for a sixfold cause of utility. Either for the sake of **motion**, as when it is sometimes necessary to move one without the other, like a small hand without the arms. Or for the sake of the **resolution of vaporous superfluities**; for distinctions and spaces are made in the parts through which they can be emitted to the outside. Or for the sake of **accidents** occurring to the bones; for if it were one, the corruption of one part would result in the harm of the whole. Or for the sake of the **diversity in size** of the parts, for it was necessary for some parts to be large and needing larger bones, and small ones on the contrary. Or for the sake of **strength and stability**, as there was a need for the bones of the upper jaw, lest they should incur harm by moving unsteadily above those noble things contained within them; hence the upper jaw of animals remains still, except for the river crocodile, while the lower jaw is moved. Or for the sake of **lightness of motion**, wherefore some were made hollow so they would be lighter, in the cavities of which is situated the <term>marrow</term> <note>original: "medulla"</note> nourishing them, such as in the arm and hip bones. 

The skull is entirely a round bone, not covered by fleshy skin, [according to] the first book of the *Histories*. Whence in the second book of the *Theory*, the skull is a bone of the head, sharp in shape at the front and back, whose roundness is present both so that it might be further from receiving harms—since a bronze sphere cannot be touched except at a point, [as in] the prologue of *On the Soul*; wherefore <margin>Castellans</margin> build towers round so that a [siege] engine cannot harm them—and also so that it might be made more capacious. For a circular figure, since it stands uniformly distant on all sides from its edges, is the most capacious, [according to] the second book of *On the Heavens and the World*. It is sharp at the front and back so that the <term>nucha</term> <note>the spinal cord, often called the "neck-marrow" in medieval texts</note> might be preserved with the origin of the nerves. The word "skull" is derived from *cranyon*, which in Greek implies "containing," for many things are located [within it].

It also explains the skull's round shape as a defensive and volumetric necessity, comparing it to the construction of medieval towers.</summary>

...hidden beneath it. The term itself is understood in multiple ways. For it is taken most strictly for the part of the crown bounded by the <term>sagittal suture</term> <note>original: "aderez sagittali"; "aderez" is a Latinization of the Arabic word for suture or seam</note>, according to that passage of the first [book] of the first [part]: "the four walls of the head were made harder than the rest of the skull because falls and blows frequently occur to them, and because it was necessary for the skull to be porous in the middle."

It is also taken more specifically for the four walls—front and back, right and left—which become six when including the two bones called the <term>temporal bones</term> <note>original: "supertemporaneis"; literally "above the temples"</note>. According to the second [book] of the *Theory*, the bones of the skull are divided into six; according to the sixth [book] of the same, these are specific to the skull. Or, one might perhaps place the two <term>petrous bones</term> <note>original: "pium ossa" likely referring to the stony or petrous part of the temporal bone</note> among the twelve, even if four truly stand out.

It is further understood properly for all the bones supporting the brain, according to the first [book] of the first [part]: "The utility of all the bones of the skull is that they stand as a shield for the brain, defending it from injuries rising against it." Hence, in the second [book] of the *Theory*: "All the bones in the skull are fifteen," such that the bone called the <term>basilar bone</term> <note>original: "baxilar̄"; the sphenoid or base of the skull</note>, which comprises the base of the brain, is included here.

Fourthly, it is taken commonly for all the bones of the head. According to the first [book] of the *Almansor* <note>The "Almansor" refers to the "Liber ad Almansorem" by the Persian physician Rhazes (al-Razi)</note>: "The bones of the skull, when counted together, will be twenty-four, excluding the teeth." In this sense, the "skull" is denoted more broadly here. The skull also more truly possesses <term>sutures</term> <note>original: "aderez"; from the Arabic "al-darz"</note>, or saw-like seams—five <term>commissures</term> <note>original: "commissuras"; joints or connections</note> or junctions. Three of these are "true" because they penetrate directly from the outside to the inside. One of these is called the **sagittal**, which passes through the crown of the head, separating it into two parts. Another is named the **coronal**, passing from temple to temple across the top toward the front. Indeed, upon this the "crown" is established; when it is joined with the sagittal, this "spring-like" junction arises. There is a third called the **lambdoid** <note>original: "laudalis"; so named for its resemblance to the Greek letter Lambda (Λ)</note>, because it is shaped like the Greek letter or the figure representing seven in <term>algorism</term> <note>original: "algorismo"; the medieval term for the Arabic numeral system</note>, like this: <insert>Λ</insert>. This part is called the **vomer** or **upsilon** in the first [book] of the *Histories*, for it bears some resemblance to it. Its junction with the aforementioned sutures constitutes such a shape.

There are also two other sutures that are "false" or <term>squamous</term> <note>original: "mendose corticales"; literally "faulty/lying" and "bark-like," referring to how these sutures overlap like scales rather than interlocking</note>. For they do not penetrate directly to the interior like the others; these pass on either side near the semicircle from the tear duct to the ear. If these are joined to the first three, a shape like this arises. These six sutures primarily define and set apart the bones in the skull, although there are many others arising from other divisions and seams for no small purposes and benefits. One benefit pertains to the bone itself, and the other to what is contained beneath it. The first is twofold:

One, so that if the skull were injured, the damage would not communicate to the whole through the continuity of the parts; this is the common benefit of having a plurality of parts. The other is because a diversity of perfect hardness and softness, porosity and thickness, thinness and density could not exist in a single bone; for the different dispositions of the brain required these varieties, so that it would not be weighed down by thickness and hardness, nor lose its contents through porosity and thinness.

The second benefit is achieved through the saw-like joints in multiple ways: either so that vapors and fumes may be released from the brain through the sutures; or so that the **dura mater** <note>The "hard mother," the outermost membrane surrounding the brain</note> may be tied to the skull at the sutures so it does not weigh upon the brain, especially during times of swelling, loud shouting, or rage; or so that the filaments of the nerves may exit the brain and the vessels of life and nourishment may enter.

How many and of what sort the figures of the skull and the head are, Difference 98 will teach. **Bone** is a hard, white body, the support and uprightness of the body, generated from "impurer seed" by the action of heat, according to the second [book] of *On Generation*. And know that the preceding discourse is verified for the most part and primarily in natural bodies.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that in this "Difference," the authorities seem to vary significantly, at least in appearance—firstly regarding the bones of the skull, and then regarding those to come. For the first of these, know that the head is composed not of four parts, but of six, according to the third [book] of the *Histories*. Whence *Almansor* says there are six bones proper to the skull; and the *Colliget* <note>The "Colliget" is the medical encyclopedia by Averroes (Ibn Rushd)</note> in the first [book] says that its anatomy is almost the same as that of animals. **Averroes** says the head has five bones. But **Haly Abbas** <note>A 10th-century Persian physician</note> says: "All the bones in the skull are fifteen." Furthermore, *Almansor* says: "All the bones of the skull, when counted together, will be twenty-three, excluding the teeth."

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have a skull of a single bone, such as a dog; this one, however, is composite, as in man and the like. Indeed, the head of **women** has only one suture in a circle, while **men** have three joined into one, in most cases. However, a man's head has been seen having no suture at all, according to the third [book] of the *Histories*; whence Aristotle says in the same place: "In the human head there are many sutures." And **Az.** <note>Possibly a reference to Avenzoar (Ibn Zuhr)</note> has seen a man having no suture in the head, and this often happens to women. Generally, however, physicians distinguish five sutures, as has been introduced, which appear for the most part: three true and two false. The truth of these will be shown in the third [part] of what is to be said. For the third point, let the bones of the skull be enumerated as commonly accepted. And thereafter, this twofold aforementioned discord may be laid to rest. Regarding the first of these, it should be known that the **coronal** bone of the forehead is the first of the bones of the head...

<meta>This page continues the detailed anatomical breakdown of the skull, specifically identifying the individual bones of the crown, the temples, and the base of the head, while reconciling the different counts provided by Greek and Arabic authorities.</meta>

Finally, the <term>lambda bone</term> <note>original: "os laude"; the occipital bone, named for its resemblance to the Greek letter Lambda</note> corresponds to it from the opposite side. Secondly, there are the flat bones, nearly identical on the right and left according to <term>Almansor</term> <note>Rhazes (865–925 AD), a Persian physician</note> and <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: "A."; the Latinized abbreviation for the 11th-century philosopher-physician Ibn Sina</note>. According to <term>Haly Abbas</term> <note>original: "Halyabatem"; a 10th-century Persian physician</note>, these exist as doubles on each side; specifically, the thinner part of each, located laterally around the <term>sagittal suture</term> <note>original: "adreg sagittalem"</note> and being quadrangular in shape, are called the two bones of the crown <note>the parietal bones</note>. 

However, their lower part, which is hard and located around the ears, where it remains thin as it attaches, is called the <term>temporal bones</term>, representing a triangular shape. Each of these is separated into three parts. One of these is solid, like a stone, and is for that reason called the <term>petrous</term> <note>original: "lapidea"; literally "stony"</note> part. In this is located the auditory opening, so that the onset of injuries might be prevented. Another part is a bone extended to a point arising from the first, resembling a <term>nipple</term> <note>original: "mamille"; the mastoid process</note>, which prevents the lower jaw from moving too far outward. The third part is called the <term>squamous</term> <note>original: "cympus"</note> part, which is joined on both sides by the elevated bones of the temples; its solidity is not as great as that of the first two parts. This subdivision differs more by its function than by being a distinct and separate essence—much like the hip bone. According to Avicenna, this is fourfold, but according to Haly Abbas it is threefold, even though it is one continuous bone. Indeed, these six parts seem to be the extremities of the two larger, lower bones on each side, according to the same author.

Then, according to almost everyone, there is the bone called the <term>basilar</term> <note>original: "basillare"; the sphenoid bone</note>, or "algecedi," or "peg," which supports and carries all the bones of the brain, and for that reason is called its base. It similarly appears to be continuous with the lambda bone above. Regarding this, Haly Abbas says: the bone that continues from the bone of the back of the head <note>original: "ossi puppis"</note> was created hard in the place called the base of the head so that it might better support and carry [the brain], and so it does not decay under the waste products where it is located. There are also four unequal bones in the said part: two on the right and just as many on the left. Their purpose is to hide, pair, and protect the nerves that come out from the fifth pair of cerebral nerves. Hence, according to Avicenna, there are only nine of these bones; but according to Haly Abbas, there are fifteen. 

Subsequently, all authors falling into agreement set forty-nine bones of the upper jaw, which are left to be identified from the connections: I believe six for the eyes, two for the cheeks or jawbones, and two for the nose. Behind these, under the former, are two more; indeed, four are found in the nose. There are two in which the teeth are situated on each side. But is there perhaps another one dividing the nose, or is it reduced to the four previous ones, since it arises from them like a <term>partition</term> <note>original: "dyazoma"</note> from the diaphragm and the subcostal membrane? Whence it is annexed to the basilar bone, or exists as one by itself, almost untouched due to its smallness. 

The lower jaw, however, contains two bones which are joined by a strong joint under the chin, so that it appears as only one bone once it has hardened over time. Furthermore, in each jaw, for the most part and especially in ancient times, thirty-two [teeth] are contained; however, now twenty-eight are frequently found. There is a difference, for at the ends of the jaws there are four large molar teeth which arise quite late in the middle of the growth period, around thirty years of age, between the time of youth and full consistency. Therefore, according to Avicenna, these are called the <term>teeth of sense</term> or <term>intellect</term> <note>wisdom teeth</note>. Hence, in the second [book] of the *Histories* <note>Aristotle's *History of Animals*</note>: the last teeth to grow in humans are the <term>gumfei</term> <note>original: "gunfei"; likely from the Arabic 'al-ajmāf' for wisdom teeth</note>, that is, the teeth of sense, around twenty years of age in both men and women. Indeed, in some women of eight years, the wisdom teeth have grown, and similarly in men. This happens to those whose canine teeth did not grow in their youth. 

I myself saw a strong and fleshy soldier who said that in his forty-third year one of these teeth grew, in his forty-fourth another, and in his forty-fifth a third. Likewise, I have seen others who, having lost all their teeth before their fiftieth year, grew them again, though they were smaller and weaker than the first ones. Regarding this, the commentator on the fourth [book] of the *Quadripartitum* <note>Ptolemy's astrological work</note> says: "I hold well that the teeth of life are reborn for those passing the age of Saturn" <note>the age of Saturn was the final stage of life, usually after 60 or 70</note>. The opposite of this is thought in the ninth [book] of the *Theory*: "I have heard of some who said they saw old men whose teeth returned after they had fallen out, and others were produced in their place, but I do not believe it is true. For the matter prepared for the production of teeth is not found in the bodies of the elderly." It must be said that the truth is that they are sometimes reborn, as mentioned, but not equal to the previous ones. And rightly so; for they have certain properties beyond other bones, such as sensation, as will be told. 

And even if <term>Avenzoar</term> <note>12th-century Andalusian physician</note> felt that all bones have sensation, nevertheless, according to Almansor (who seems to omit two smaller paired bones of the skull), there are only forty-five in total. According to Avicenna, who collects them, there are forty-seven. But according to Haly Abbas, who subdivides the temporal bones into six parts, there are sixty-three—always assuming thirty-two teeth. But a woman, because of the dimension of the coronal bone, has one more. The count and proof of these is shown by their action and purpose.

<meta>This page continues a technical debate regarding the number of bones in the skull, citing various authorities like Haly Abbas, Rhazes (Almansor), and Avicenna. ...finally the others. This appears when he subsequently adds four pairs of bones. For taking the <term>cranium</term> in its proper sense, the <term>basilar bone</term> <note>the bone at the base of the skull</note> is included in its constitution. To the other point, one must similarly say that <term>Haly Abbas</term> <note>original: "Halyabas"; a 10th-century Persian physician</note> understood the cranium in its proper sense, which he indicates by concluding: "Therefore, all the bones in the cranium are fifteen, of which six are proper to the cranium." To the next point, it should be said that <term>Almansor</term> <note>Rhazes (865–925 AD)</note>, as it appeared, understood the cranium in a general sense, as the distinction has already established.

Regarding the other point, it should be said that they explain that a woman generally has only one <term>suture</term> <note>original: "futura"; the fibrous joints between skull bones. The text uses the medieval spelling 'futura' for 'sutura'</note>, and that in a circuit. This is because, due to her coldness and humidity, her vapors are rendered cold and viscous, so they are disobedient to the formative power. Thus, it is not only necessary to have one in a circuit, but sometimes every apparent suture in the circuit is lost. According to <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "A."</note>: "It often happens in women that their heads have no suture," since many times a head has been seen without a suture. He seems to mean that the reduction and covering of sutures happens more often in women than in men. For in men, the <term>sagittal suture</term> <note>the seam running down the middle of the top of the head</note> ends at the <term>coronal suture</term> <note>the seam running across the top of the head from ear to ear</note>; but in women, it actually penetrates all the way to the nose, even dividing the bone <note>the frontal bone</note> into two. And therefore, "one in a circuit" is to be explained by the power of the head passing from the sharp <term>lambda</term> <note>original: "trianguli laude"; the lambdoid suture at the back of the head, named for the Greek letter Λ</note> all the way to the nose, along with the two remaining sutures found in man. This is also what the sequence of <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: "Az."</note> suggests: "The cranium of women has three sutures just like men, and of those, one is in a circuit." For nature increased the sutures in her to purge many <term>superfluities</term> <note>waste products or vapors that medieval medicine believed needed to be vented through the skull</note>.

To the other point, it must be said that <term>Avicenna</term> is speaking of <term>certain sutures</term> <note>stable, standard anatomical seams</note>, which are only the three positioned ones, and not the <term>fallacious</term> <note>original: "fallacibus"; non-standard or 'false' sutures that appear in some individuals</note> ones. Or, to speak more perfectly, he does not simply say "three," but adds "mutually coupled and joined." For they join and touch each other as truly described, not like the deceptive <term>cortical</term> <note>superficial or surface-level</note> ones. As for what <term>Avicenna</term> saw—a head without a suture, just as I have sometimes seen—this does not contradict the physician's report. I have observed a skull, more natural than the head of a woman, having seven structures. For internally, from the sharp lambda, a line descended downward, while another divided it across the width.

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it must be said that although the bones of the cranium are not entirely one according to their essence (like a magnet), they are nevertheless one by connection and easy <term>enclavation</term> <note>original: "inclauatione"; a 'nailing' or interlocking, referring to the dovetail-like joints of skull sutures</note>, whether wide, long, or otherwise. This is sufficient to cause a single motion; for any other thing is rendered multiple either by binding (like a load by a strap) or wood by glue. Even a reflected line is called one and continuous, as are individual parts like the shin and the arm. Those things that are continuous by nature are more "one" than those made by art, according to the fourth book of the <term>Metaphysics</term> <note>by Aristotle</note>.

Regarding the support of the explanation, it should be called "continuous," that is, "applied" according to another translation. Or, he used "continuous" improperly for "contiguous," for everything continuous is contiguous, but not vice versa, according to the fourth book of the <term>Topics</term> <note>by Aristotle</note>. However, this contiguity or application does not refer to the parts of the cranium among themselves, but rather to the <term>vertebrae of the neck</term> <note>original: "colli spondiles"</note> upon which the cranium is placed.

To the other point, it should be said by rejecting the former: although the cranium is constructed from many bones, they are nevertheless connected to each other by a firm joint. Thus, their plurality does not result in injury to the brain, but rather provides benefits through the sutures as shown before. The next point is to be conceded.

To the other, with an explanation, it should be said that although the heart is more noble than the brain, it is nevertheless more solid and stronger, located within the protection of a cavity. Furthermore, since the heart is very hot, it requires <term>ventilation</term> <note>original: "euentatione"; the cooling or airing out of vital heat</note>. But it could not be ventilated except through motion, and motion does not exist except through muscles—especially where some act of the will is mixed in. However, the ventilation of this bone [the skull] would impede everything surrounding it. For this reason, it was necessary for muscles to run along with the ribs protecting the heart above, below, and in the middle.

To the other point: although the longitudinal division of the brain is more manifest, there are nevertheless other divisions denoted by the remaining sutures, even if they do not appear as much. This is shown by the separation of the <term>ventricles</term>, which cut across the width and not the length.

To the other: it must be said that there are three sutures mutually coupled, as has been said, but the remaining two are not therefore removed. Or, the ventricles of the brain are not compared to the sutures, since there are five of the latter—and sometimes more, as has been brought up—while there are only three ventricles.

To the other: it must be said that just as lines intersect or do not intersect, more or fewer intermediate spaces result. If they intersect in a <term>crucial</term> <note>cross-shaped</note> manner, four intervals are produced. If, however, they are produced by juxtaposition, four enclosures are produced from five. But the lining of the head is done in both ways, so that from these five, six gaps intervene.

### DIFFERENTIA XL.

> <term>That the head was not created for the sake of the brain, but for the sake of the eyes</term>. This is shown from the eighth book of *On the Usefulness of Parts* <note>original: "de iuuamentis"; a work by Galen</note> and the certain beginning of the third book of the <term>Canon</term> <note>Avicenna's *Canon of Medicine*</note>. Furthermore, if the brain existed for the sake of the eyes, one would not be separated from the other; otherwise, that which comes before the end would be idle. But now, as written in the aforementioned works, the brain in certain animals is found in the chest, while the eyes are in a higher place, as on the horns of some of them. Some also say that the <term>yellow bee</term> <note>original: "apē croceam"</note> has eyes in the front part of its body...

...placed after the belt. Again, since the <term>eye</term> <note>original: "oculus"</note> is like a certain scout watching from afar, it must be situated in a high place—just like the watchmen of ships, the guardians of vineyards, or the scouts of armies. However, this high position is not for the sake of the <term>brain</term> <note>original: "cerebro"; medieval philosophers often debated which organ was the "ruler" of the body</note>, since some animals have the brain around their middle or lower down, according to the fourth book of the *History of Animals*. And <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "A."</note> says elsewhere that what is more principal and worthy ought to be ordered toward the end, since it is more intended than the rest. But the <term>eye</term> is a more principal and noble part than the <term>brain</term>, since it is more "animated" than it. For the eye participates in the vegetative, sensitive, and visual aspects of the soul, from which all nobility arises. Hence, in my edition of the *Physiognomy*, I wrote that the eyes are like the flowers of the soul and the faithful messengers of the heart. The <term>brain</term>, however, possesses only the vegetative power. For <term>Aristotle</term> says in the second book that the sense of touch provides no sensation from those parts; and in the fourth book of *Accidents*, he states that the <term>brain</term> is an insensitive organ created by nature.

Therefore, the <term>head</term> <note>original: "caput"</note> was made for the sake of the eyes, and not for the sake of the brain. The opposite view is gathered from several books on animals. Furthermore, a thing is "made for the sake of" that whose quantity, shape, and covering it represents. Yet the <term>head</term>, as it appears, relates to the <term>brain</term> and not to the eyes. For the <term>brain</term>, since it is soft and easily vulnerable, required a defensive covering; this was the <term>skull</term> <note>original: "craneum"</note> along with the parts placed beneath it. Hence, in the first part of the first book of the *Canon*, it is said: "The benefit of all the bones of the <term>skull</term> is that they are a shield for the brain, covering it and defending it from all evils." Also, the eyes, like the sense of touch, must be situated in the highest part of the body, and this is where the <term>brain</term> is. Thus, in the third book of the *Theoretical Medicine*, it is said that the <term>brain</term> is more excellent than the other members. It is placed within the head, and all other members are subject to it, as I noted in my second book. Therefore, the <term>head</term> was made for the <term>brain</term>, and the brain for the sake of the eyes and other senses, specifically sight, as concluded in the second book.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that the <term>head</term>, according to <term>Plato’s Timaeus</term> <note>original: "Tbimeuz"; referring to the Platonic dialogue discussing the soul and body</note>, is more honorable than the rest of the body due to a certain excellence of the best part, which the remaining members obey and serve by right as subjects. And <term>Cassius Felix</term> <note>a 5th-century Latin medical author</note> says: "The <term>head</term> is the highest citadel of the body, and the honorable and most necessary home of the senses." Now, the <term>head</term> is so called simply from the word "to take" <note>original: "capio"</note>, because food is taken through it by means of an opening; or from the Greek <term>cephale</term> <note>original: "cephali"</note> meaning <term>head</term>, from which comes <term>cephaleon</term> or <term>capim</term>, because the <term>head</term> contains within itself many things in summary, both in power and in action. In some creatures, it is held directly upright, so that "upward" for them is simply the "upward" of the universe, as in humans. In others, the opposite is found, as in plants and <term>shell-skinned animals</term> <note>original: "ostrachadermis"; from the Greek 'ostrakodermos', referring to invertebrates like oysters or snails</note>. Thus, in the fourth book of *Parts of Animals*, it is said that <term>shell-skinned animals</term>, like plants, have their <term>head</term> downward, because they receive nourishment from below.

---

Just as plants receive nourishment through their roots, what they have as "upward" is simply "downward" for us, and vice-versa. Most creatures, however, have a middle position; some of these approach one of the extremes more closely, such as birds and horses approaching the human form, as they do not have a <term>head</term> turned back like other beasts, nor is it upright like a human's. Others approach the state of plants and oysters more closely, such as crawling things and those with many feet. Finally, there are beasts that observe a middle ground between the extremes. And because most <term>animals</term> have a <term>head</term> situated and fixed at the extremity of the body—either simply "upward" or relative to them—therefore both definitions of the <term>head</term> can be heard: that which is situated at such an extremity of the body.

What the <term>brain</term> actually is, is shown by the distinction in chapter twenty-four. This preposition "for the sake of" <note>original: "propter"</note> implies causality. There are four causes: material, formal, efficient, and final, according to the second book of the *Physics*. To these, <term>Galen</term> <note>original: "Ga."</note> associates the "instrumental" cause in the fourth book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts*, though it is reduced to the efficient cause in the third book. For all these causes can be expressed by the preposition "for the sake of." For instance, if one asks "for what sake" the eye is such as it is, assigning the material cause, one says "for the sake of the brain," for from the brain its matter is received, since its origin is in the membranes. Assigning the formal cause, one would give a different reason. The efficient cause would represent the power of the agent with its instruments. But assigning the final cause reduces it more to its action; for the "end" is what is sought in the inquiry, since intentionally it is the "cause of causes," although in practice, according to <term>Boethius</term>, it is their effect.

And this "end" is stated to be threefold in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals* and the sixth book of the *Collectaneum*. One is called the "end for the sake of which," which is that toward which a thing tends and is ordered. Another is called the "absolute end," like the heart in the generation of the members. There are also two other ends for the sake of this: one is called the "end of perfection of being," which is inseparable, just as the "form" is called the end of "matter." For the making is only for the sake of the result; because such things are ordered toward the finished and generated product, just as after the heart, the whole animal follows, finished and perfect. The other is the "useful end," which is the use one makes of finished and completed things; when this end exists, the things that exist through it are present. This is called the "cause of causes," just as use is the end of organic parts. According to <term>Boethius</term>, the "end" is also the shape of the vessels made by it. Furthermore, in the second book of *On the Soul*, the end is said to be twofold: the "of which" and the "for which," representing the species and the individual. Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have pronounced indistinctly that the <term>head</term> was made for the <term>brain</term> in terms of substance, quantity, and shape, but for the sake of the eyes in terms of its position. Their error is apparent, since they separate the later from the former. And let it be...

...for indeed, being founded upon the prior types, it can by no means be divided against them. On the other hand, it will not appear that they reconcile the discordant views. And for this reason, some have said that in <term>perfect animals</term> <note>Aristotle's term for animals that are "complete" in their development, usually meaning those with blood and lungs, like mammals.</note> the head was made for the sake of the <term>brain</term> <note>original: "cerebrum"</note>. In certain <term>imperfect animals</term>, however, it was made for the sake of the <term>eyes</term>, since in such creatures these parts are found without a head and brain. The rejection of this view will be shown subsequently, since the eyes cannot be entirely separated from the aforementioned parts; rather, the opposite happens. Others, however, such as <term>Galen</term> <note>A famous Greek physician whose works dominated Western medicine for 1,300 years.</note> and <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "A."</note>, have said that one ought not to say the head existed for the sake of the brain because it is the instrument that stands as the principle of sense and motion—that is, in all animals—even though it is found in different locations in certain animals. For in some it is in the chest, and therefore one ought not to say that the head was for the sake of the brain, nor for the sake of the <term>mouth</term> <note>original: "orificium"</note>. For the mouth is found in the chest in animals lacking a head; nor is it for the ears or nostrils or other instruments, since these are found in the chest in animals lacking a head.

Wherefore it ought to be said that the head existed for the sake of those members which are not found in the chest of animals lacking a head. For eyes are found in animals lacking a head, positioned upon <gloss>appendages</gloss> <insert>additamenta</insert> similar to long horns. And the motive touched upon before is submitted for this: for the eyes need to be in a high place because their action is to look out and preserve; for they are situated on high like <term>scouts of the roads</term> <note>original: "uiarum exploratores"</note>. Indeed, from such a position they look out into more remote places; and if they are located in this way, they do not suffer from things they encounter, since they are of a hard substance, whereas if they were soft, they would suffer. And therefore, according to <term>Aristotle</term>, it is not necessary to create a head for every eye absolutely, but for the animal having a <term>smooth eye</term> <note>likely referring to the unprotected eyes of vertebrates as opposed to the compound or hard eyes of insects/crustaceans</note>, which needs much caution and the security of its location. For in many animals deprived of a head, two appendages were created, raised up from the body, upon which their eyes were fittingly established. However, that their discourse should not be accepted simply will be shown next, by demonstrating that the eyes are always situated around the head and the brain—or in that place where it would be—and not above extended horns, but rather below them; and that all things with heads are animals. Regarding the third point, it must first be known that other animals participate in having a head, even without eyes, as is shown in the fourth book of the *History of Animals* by running through all things about which doubt seems to exist. Such are the <term>bloodless animals</term> <note>original: "exanguia"; Aristotle’s category for invertebrates</note>, even of four kinds: such as the <term>hard-shelled</term> <note>original: "ostrachaderma", i. duri corii</note>, like <term>snails</term> <note>original: "chochie"</note>, <term>limpets</term> <note>original: "spolete"</note>, <term>whelks</term> <note>original: "uerices"</note>, and the like. Also the <term>soft-shelled</term> <note>original: "Mallacostrata", i. mollis teste</note>, for their beginning was from a soft shell that has now hardened, such as <term>crabs</term>, which lack a <gloss>tail-piece</gloss> <note>original: "urepigio", i. caudali</note>; those alone called <term>shrimp</term> <note>original: "caridi"</note> by the Greeks, which are <term>crayfish</term> <note>original: "gambari"</note>; and <term>sea-locusts</term> <note>original: "carabi", i. locustæ maris"</note>.

---

The <term>soft-bodied</term> <note>original: "Mallachia", i. mollia</note>, such as <term>octopuses</term> <note>original: "pulpi"</note>, <term>cuttlefish</term>, and <term>squid</term> <note>original: "teuthides"</note>. Also the <term>segmented animals</term> <note>original: "Euthomia", i. diuisa</note>, such as wasps, bees, and the like, and many living outside of the waters. Concerning the hard-shelled, <term>Aristotle</term> says: it is unmanifest whether they have anything besides a head, and it happens that the said head and mouth of the <term>sea urchin</term> <note>original: "ericiū"</note> are held downward. And in the fourth book of *Parts of Animals*, all have a head. But regarding the parts of the body other than those for the reception of food, some are unnamed; and concerning their sight and hearing, nothing is firm, nor is it very manifest. However, the <term>spider crab</term> <note>original: "Carcbinum", i. araneam marinam</note>, which is between the hard-shelled and the soft-shelled, he posits as having two subtle red horns, and eyes under these, long and straight—not, however, above the horns, as <term>Galen</term> says along with <term>Aristotle</term>. He also says the soft-shelled have a head and a mouth under the eyes; similarly, in the soft-bodied, the head is between the middle of the belly and the feet, and by nature the head is called to the side by those extending their feet, because it happens that they must look forward while swimming. For the eyes are on the upper side, but the mouth is on the posterior; and further above the mouth are two large eyes. All <term>insects</term> <note>original: "Enthomorum"</note> have eyes, but no other manifest sense-organ, except for a tongue in some. This also <term>Aristotle</term> testifies there; for he is a <gloss>briefer</gloss> <note>original: "breuiator"; meaning he summarizes the observations</note>. This is also confirmed by reason, because that thing has a head which takes and receives food, since the head drew its origin from there; but every animal has this, since life consists in it. Therefore, everything participates in a head, even plants. Or, because man has his head directed upward, and a tree downward, <term>Plato</term> pronounced that man is like a tree turned upside down.

The eyes also, in those that have them, ought to be located around the head and the opening, so that they may perceive and discern the food for those bringing it in. But regarding the fact that the head exists for the sake of the brain, he writes thus in the fourth book of *Parts of Animals*: In <term>blooded animals</term>, the head exists mostly for the sake of the brain, because in those having blood, this part is located opposite the heart, so that it may <term>refrigerate</term> <note>In ancient physiology, the brain was thought to act as a cooling radiator for the "heat" produced by the heart.</note> and temper the heart's heat. For a warm nature, becoming strong, creates growth from the center according to its own movement; for coldness and humidity are opposed to great heat. It was also necessary for the brain to be located above, so that it would be safe because of its weak and exceeding qualities, and to quickly counter its fragility to suffering. Whence in the first and second [books]: if the brain's proper place were not high, a situation would arise from such a manner that it could not tolerate, nor would its power remain with it. Also, among physicians, it is not slightly ordained for the "ventilation" of the heart. For especially because of the motion of the chest and the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: "dyaflāmatis"</note>, the lung now acts like a fan to it, which is shown by the sudden suffocation of <term>apoplectics</term> <note>Those suffering from a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness.</note> and the like regarding their breath.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the primary purpose of the head. ...it cannot reach from the brain to the muscles of the chest. Therefore, regarding the idea that the brain was created for the sake of the eyes, <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Ar."</note> and <term>Albertus Magnus</term> <note>original: "Al."</note> address this purpose more than is strictly necessary. In humans, however, the brain is also a very great manifestation of divinity. 

Thirdly, it is perceived that the head and the brain are the underlying subjects of the eyes. This is discussed in the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*: Hearing and sight are located primarily in the head, and of these, sight is present in all animals. For although fish and similar creatures hear and smell, no distinct sensory organ for these is clearly found in their heads. Yet sight, in all creatures that possess it, is reasonably located around the brain. 

This is proven because the eye is of the nature of water, as stated in *On Sense and the Sensible* and the fifth book of *On the Generation of Animals*. The brain is of this same nature, being cold and moist. Furthermore, the eye must be sufficiently <term>transparent</term> <note>original: "dyaffonū" (diaphanous)</note> so that it may receive and preserve the <term>images of colors</term> <note>original: "colorum species". In medieval science, "species" were the invisible forms or "likenesses" that traveled from an object to the eye.</note>; water provides this quality better than the other elements. The brain is of this same sort. 

Furthermore, if eyes are never found without a head and brain, but heads and brains are found without eyes, then Nature did not create the head for the sake of the eyes, but rather the opposite. As previously noted, all animals have eyes situated around the head and brain; they are not extended out on horns, as <term>Galen</term> <note>original: "G."</note> and Albertus say. It is true that eyes seem to be more extended in <term>shrimp</term> <note>original: "caridis"</note>, <term>crayfish</term> <note>original: "carabis"</note>, and <term>crabs</term> <note>original: "carebamis"</note>. However, as precise anatomy confirms, even in these they are situated in the head of those that possess a head and brain. 

And take note that there are certain creatures of the worm kind that are without eyes, such as <term>blindworms</term> <note>original: "yrūbines"</note>, earthworms, and the like, which at least share in having a head by which they draw in necessary blood and nourishment. The mole, however, has eyes hidden under its skin. 

As for what some say—even those who study philosophy alongside the <term>unlearned</term> <note>original: "ydeotis"</note>—that <term>flies</term> <note>original: "nipbes"</note> or <term>gadflies</term> <note>original: "tauanos"</note> have eyes under their wings because they seem to be blinded when certain parts are removed (since they then fly about in a disordered way), this is ridiculous. This does not happen because they have eyes in that location—since nature does not place eyes in hidden spots, as shown before—but rather because a certain harmony and proportion of their bodies is destroyed, which aids their ventilation. 

Because of this, it is more confidently inferred that the head was made for the sake of the brain more than for the eyes. Nor are the eyes situated anywhere else than in the head or brain. However, someone wishing to agree with the useful points of Galen and Albertus might say that by "head" they understand the extremity situated at the top of the body, shaped as a receptacle for the brain. For things that do not have it shaped this way would not seem to have a head or brain at all, but rather something else in its place. Hence, in the fourth book of *On the Parts of Animals*, it is said that all animals with blood have a head. Among bloodless animals, however, this part is indeterminate in some, such as crabs. 

It can also be said that the "end" or purpose of the eyes is the brain in one sense, but in another sense, it is the opposite. Regarding the fourth point Galen and Albertus made, it has now been addressed. Regarding the next point: as has been shown, the eyes are not separated from the head and brain unless you define these parts by a very specific position and shape. Nor is it true that eyes are found around the chest, as was suggested regarding <term>cephalopods</term> <note>original: "malachiis" (mollusks/squid)</note>; yet they see in their own way from a distance, and it was said they swim sideways so that they may see what is in front of them. Therefore, those that have the head entirely underneath, like <term>shellfish</term> <note>original: "ostracaderma"</note>, lack a head in that specific way.

Regarding another point: even if eyes were located around the middle of the body, they could be positioned sideways or otherwise due to their shape so that they might see ahead and look out for things at a distance. Nor is height alone sought for the eyes, but also safety and a lateral view. If height were the only goal, they would be located on the <term>top of the head</term> <note>original: "bregmate"</note> in many creatures, but they would not be safe there; instead, they are tucked away and protected under the brain and head. 

Regarding another point: it would be true if the body possessed sense of itself, which it does not; but sometimes it receives it, as from the heart or the middle of the brain. But it resides in the brain by virtue, just as heat is in motion or "drunkenness" is in wine—because it heats or intoxicates other things. Because of the great coldness and moisture which the brain must have (the benefit of which has been shown), and its soft, almost fluid substance, the brain could not actually perform the act of sensing by itself. 

The fact that the emotions of the soul and the actions of the heart are visible in the eyes happens because the eyes are like a living mirror. The heart and the brain are hidden and cannot directly show the signs inherent in them; therefore, <term>physiognomists</term> <note>Those who judge a person's character or health from their outward appearance.</note> observe the actions and outward accidents of the eyes. The brain is also the seat of the mind, as it is a more divine power, which the eye is not.

### DIFFERENCE XLI.

That the nerves originate from the brain is shown by the authority of nearly all physicians. Again, in the fifth book of <term>On the Soul</term> <note>Likely a reference to a psychological or anatomical text by Aristotle or a commentator.</note>: lest the source—the heart—be overburdened, the nerves were created in the brain and the veins in the <term>liver</term> <note>original: "epe" (hepar)</note>. Likewise, a thing takes its origin from that which, if destroyed, the thing itself is destroyed. But if the brain is destroyed, the nerve is destroyed in its operation of sense and motion. The proof of this is that if the path from the brain to the limbs is tied or cut, every action provided through the nerves is destroyed; but if the path is preserved, they are invigorated. Furthermore, a thing is seen to be born from that which it is immediately derived from...

<summary>This page argues that the head's primary purpose is to house the brain rather than the eyes, citing the anatomical necessity of the brain's cold, moist nature to facilitate sight. It also establishes the brain as the point of origin for the nervous system, distinguishing its role from that of the heart and liver.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Albertus Magnus, Galen, anatomy, brain, eyes, nervous system, physiognomy, transparency, cephalopods</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the origins of the nervous system, weighing the competing theories of whether the nerves arise from the brain (the view of Galen and physicians) or the heart (the view of Aristotle and certain philosophers). It explores the anatomical nature of nerves, ligaments, and tendons.</meta>

...does not pass through the third part. Thus, however, it is seen through **anatomy** that the nerves relate themselves to the brain. Furthermore, in their whiteness and flexible softness—especially at their exit from the brain—the nerves most closely resemble the brain. Indeed, their origin is attested to be there, as a principle of the brain, rather than the opposite. Hence <term>Seneca</term> says in the third book of *Natural Questions*: "There is no thing which does not reflect the mark of that from which it is born." <note>original: "Nulla res est que non eius quo nascitur notam reddat."</note> Regarding the sense of touch, we see that the nerves at their beginning are most similar to the brain and not the heart. Furthermore, the principle of the nerves must be the starting point for elective <note>voluntary</note> power, which can act in opposite ways; this cannot be in the heart, since its movement is more <term>natural</term> <note>involuntary/automatic</note>, adhering to a single order and path. Therefore, the nerves originate from the brain and not the heart.

The opposite of this is held by <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Ar."</note> in his books *On Animals*, along with <term>Averroes</term> <note>original: "A."</note> and <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: "Av."</note>. And in the fifth book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts*, he says: "The nerve which is one of the three things appropriated to the hollow vein is a strong nerve, and it arises from the right <term>auricle</term> <note>chamber</note> of the heart."

Again in the same place: Nerves exist in the liver and the heart because each of them is the principle of some **virtue** <note>a biological power or faculty</note>. For the liver is the seat of the <term>appetitive</term> <note>desiring</note> faculty, while the heart is the seat of the <term>irascible</term> <note>spirited or emotional</note> faculty. However, regarding what he had said before—that nerves are not found divided at all within the body of the heart—this must be understood to mean not that they are found there in no way at all, but that they are very few in comparison to other members. Thus, when he says they are "not found at all," he means they are not found "universally." For the negative particle "not" does not apply to the universal sign and therefore does not cancel it out entirely. Since, therefore, nerves originate in the heart, which is the principle of the other organs, they draw their origin from there, just as all other things do. Again, the heart is more proportionately similar to the nerves than the brain, since both are a certain hardened substance, just as each is a source of motion; however, they relate differently to the brain, as has already been shown. Therefore, the nerves originate from the heart and not from the brain.

Regarding the first point, one must know what the brain is; this was shown in the 24th Difference. But according to <term>Avenzoar</term> <note>original: "Zoar"</note>, the heart is the principal member whose **virtues** are powerful in the body and whose effects are greatest. For it is woven from hard flesh, the organ of the virtues situated in the middle of the body, like a furnace, divided by a wall into two ventricles and four "doors" <note>valves</note>. Its own dwelling place exists as its own proper home. For it is in the **microcosm** <note>the human body</note> just as the sun is first in the **megacosm** <note>the universe/macrocosm</note>.

Indeed, the name "**nerve**" is understood in three ways according to the second book of *Internal Things* and <term>Haly Abbas</term>:
1. First, for a whitish substance, easy to bend but hard to pull apart, which according to physicians is the organ of sensation and motion. Its origin, according to them, is from the brain or the <term>nucha</term> <note>the spinal cord</note>, concerning which there is some present hesitation. 
2. Second, 

---

for a substance that is more hardened than the first, also whitish and visible, born from the bones, joining and holding them together; it similarly connects the muscle with the rest of the body, and for this reason, it is called a **ligament**. 
3. Third, there is the **corda** <note>tendon</note>, which is born from the muscle at one of its ends, composed of both nerve and ligament.

Furthermore, for something to "originate" from another can now be said in two ways. To be "from" or "out of" can imply either an **efficient cause** <note>the agent that makes it</note> or **matter** <note>the stuff it is made of</note>. First, they are said to be produced sometimes from the celestial body; second, the members are produced from the <term>menstruum</term> <note>the formative material in the womb</note>.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that <term>Plato</term> and <term>Galen</term> <note>original: "G."</note> (who imitated him) frequently felt that the nerves originate from the brain, not just according to **virtue** <note>faculty</note> as many of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>followers of Aristotle</note> believe, but even radically according to their **matter**. For they posited that the soul was a collection of substances distributed equally through three members (as seen in Difference 38). And indeed, there were later scholars who tried to find many ways in which **Aristotle** and **Galen** could be made to agree. <term>Averroes</term> <note>original: "A."</note> and **Haly** attempted this first, as if preferring the opinion of Galen to that which **Avicenna** brought into medicine, wishing to lead physicians who were ignorant of these distinctions away from Avicenna's error.

Likewise, some have said that nerves can be considered in two ways: either regarding their **diaphaneity** <note>transparency/clarity</note>, and thus they originate from the brain because both share that quality; or regarding their **substance**, and thus from the heart. But this cannot stand, at least regarding the first point, because where nerves have become transparent, they are luminous, cold, and dry, and they differ sufficiently from the brain, as shown by the brain's immobility and lack of sensation (Difference 47). Others have said nerves can be considered regarding "perfect" sensation and motion, and thus they are born from the brain, as it is the giver of these to the instruments perfectly; or as "imperfect," and thus from the heart. For their principle in the heart is imperfect and confused.

This also is not valid, as will be seen, since sensation is more perfect and sharp in the heart than in the nerves. This is indicated by the heart's intolerable pains, and because this distinction does not fully resolve the question. Some also wanted nerves to be born from the brain by a **manifest origin** (indicated by their actions), but from the heart by a **hidden origin**, about which more will appear with other points. Some felt that they originate from the heart **virtually** (since it is the first root of all) but from the brain **materially**. These scholars "caught the scent" of Aristotle in the fifth book of *On the Soul*, although they do not explain him perfectly; a fuller exposition will not only support them but clarify the matter. For he intended the principle of the nerves to be in the brain, but their **virtue** is transmitted to them from the heart, since it is not necessary...
