...as in a member which is the principle <note>source or starting point</note> of some power, there reside the primary operations of that power; and as if it were an instrument of action for that power which has been created. This is so that the principle would not be weighed down, because it is possible for an instrument to be created to receive from something else that which it does not receive until after it has been generated. Thus, in the brain, that which is first created is not the principle of sense and motion in actual practice, but it is fit to become a principle for the members that come after it when it has received power from the source. Hence, when the nerves reaching to the heart are created in the brain, the brain receives sense and motion from the heart. And this happens after the brain has been generated as an instrument for receiving from another. Therefore, when the brain is generated from its matter, something reaching to the heart is created. It is indeed distinct from the heart, and through it sensation and motion are transmitted, even though their origin is in the brain <note>according to the physicians</note>. Their arrival at the heart is not so manifest, which led that man <note>referring to Galen or his followers</note> to boldly assume that the origin of the nerves between the brain and the heart goes from the brain to the heart, and not from the heart to the brain.

This is declared by an example, just as the first things are made known first. For just as the brain is the principle of sense and motion according to the **physicians**, it is nevertheless not completed—for example, vision or taste—until the visual power has reached the <term>crystalline lens</term> <note>the lens of the eye</note> or the motive power has reached the muscles for walking. In the same way, the power of the heart itself is not perfected except for the vital power; but when it reaches another instrument, namely the brain, the <term>liver</term> <note>original: "epar"</note>, or the testicles, it becomes complete. Thus, the nerves appear to arise more from the brain, yet they receive their virtual <note>power-based</note> origin from the heart, which is the **primary root** <note>original: "prima radix"</note> of all things. And this occurs through the mediation of nerves whose origin is more from the heart to the brain than the reverse, which is also suggested in the <term>Canon</term> <note>The "Canon of Medicine" by Avicenna</note>. 

Thirdly, however, <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Ar."</note> in his book *On Animals*, agreeing with this, appears somewhat to contradict himself, as will be shown. For he wished for the nerves to arise from the heart substantially in whatever way. Regarding the third point, it must be known that the nerves arise from the heart both in terms of their matter or root, and also in terms of their form and power—either immediately or through a medium. Each of these views is supported by authorities and reasons. For in the third book of the *Histories* <note>Aristotle's *History of Animals*</note>, the principle of the nerves in animals is from the heart; for the heart has nerves within itself in its largest <term>ventricle</term> <note>chamber</note>, and the vessel called the **aorta** <note>original: "adorti"</note> is a nerve-like vein. He says this especially when he speaks of the material cause. Likewise, in the *Parts of Animals* (page 130), he says that the brain has no continuity or path to the sensory parts, as is evident through sight. Furthermore, in the third book of *On Animals*, Aristotle says of the nerve that it is "appropriated" due to its application, and it is not born from the heart insofar as the heart is fleshy, but from a certain hard substance hidden within the substance of the heart. And the nerve

---

was created in the heart, and it does not resemble it, just as a wart or a gland in the flesh. It is not born from the very substance that is visible, but from the matter which is gathered and hidden within it. And if this is the case, then <term>Galen</term> <note>original: "Ga."</note> must not have spoken the truth in his **pledge** <note>a famous wager or challenge</note> which he placed against the "guardian of the altar," where he offered much gold to anyone who could show that the nerves were born from the heart. 

Likewise, in the second book of *On the Soul*: when the principle is in that place, it will be sentient through itself, which is the flesh, just as is the heart. For although the threads of the nerves are separated in the heart, it is not long before they receive sensation from it and return it to a single origin, and from there to the brain and other members. 

This is confirmed by reason in the <term>Paucorizatum</term> <note>a medieval embryological text</note>; for in the ninth and third books of *On Animals*, and in the twenty-first and third books of the *Theory*: When the **seeds** <note>original: "spermata"</note> are collected in the **womb** <note>original: "matrice"</note>, a "blowing out" <note>original: "exsufflatio"; a thermal expansion or vital spirit</note> is found to be entirely pushed to the middle of the moisture so that the place for the heart may be prepared. Finally, on its right side and on its upper side, two rarefied vesicles are formed, touching it as if from it until that hour. Then they are separated from it and distinguished; the first becomes that from which the heart is created, the right one becomes that from which the **liver** <note>original: "epat"</note> is created, and the other is filled with blood turning toward whiteness, from which the brain is co-created. 

Thus, the heart was the first of all things, both radically and truly in the matter from which the heart was first created. By its power, a separation was made: directing downwards to the right when the liver was created, and directing upwards when the brain was produced. The nerves appear to be hidden and to vanish when they extend into the brain from the heart, like a **river** <note>original: "fluuiū"</note> which flows from the sea into a wider, distended lake. Furthermore, when the part of the matter was separated and raised up from the matter of the heart so that the brain might be formed, a certain continuing "offshoot" remained between the matter of the heart and the brain. From this offshoot, the nerve is made, whose path is from the heart to the brain, as is also touched upon in the fifth book of *On the Soul* by <term>Averroes</term> <note>original: "A."</note>. For the heart is bound to the brain through these means, just as when the matter of the liver tends downwards to the right, a vein is made continuously between the heart and the liver (Difference 47). 

This is supported because whatever is the cause of a cause is the cause of the thing caused. Again, in the third book of *On Animals*: where the principle of power is, there also exists the principle of the instrument; for one is ordered toward the other so that the work and the end may finally be reached. But in the heart is the beginning of power, just as it is the root itself. For in every genus, one must place one thing as the first of the others, lest the process go on to infinity (from the second and twelfth books of the *Metaphysics*). Furthermore, the nerve is the organ primarily of sensation and also of motion, as discussed in the following section. But the brain does not feel; hence I know from the study of the parts: the brain produces no sense of touch, just as neither blood nor the "superfluity" of animals does. Rather, the brain exists in animals for the preservation of nature, so that it may temper the heart with its excessive heat...

...would altogether inflame it, and therefore that part which is the coldest of all was placed in opposition to it, so that it might temper this heat. For Nature always contrives a remedy for the excess of any thing in that very place and by its opposite.

The brain indeed did not exist nor move except because of the tempering of the heart's heat and dryness; it required a great deal of coldness and humidity, which in itself and in its <term>pernicity</term> <note>speed or swiftness of action</note> is taken up by the senses. Even if the brain, being of a weak composition, stood in its own nature, it would be so harmed by the rising vapors and other things it encounters that pain and spasms would occur very quickly. Similarly, if it were moved [too much], it would be harmed not a little because of its weak structure. For it is not moved except perhaps by a certain alteration or by the dilation or constriction of its quantity. Since this local movement is perfected by sufficient heat, and because it is much more vigorous than the rest, it requires a stronger constituent.

Therefore, the statement in the fourth book of <term>Accidents</term> <note>Referring to "De interioribus" or "De accidenti et morbo" by Galen</note> might perhaps be criticized, which says the brain is an insensitive organ by nature, but was made the organ of the sensing senses. For it is <term>sensate in potential</term> <note>having the capacity to feel but not actively feeling</note> but not <term>sensible in act</term> <note>not currently perceiving</note>; hence the Monk’s translation <note>Constantine the African, a 11th-century monk who translated Arabic medical texts into Latin</note> says: "The brain was not constituted to be sensible, but to exist as sensate in potential." For its potential is brought into act either through itself or through another. Not indeed through itself first, since it is the coldest of all parts and the most remote from sensation and motion by its nature, which is perfected by heat. If, however, it is through another—such as through the heat of the heart brought to it, as is also declared by Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note>—then it is found to be so by accident. And truly nothing thus brings itself into act unless it is driven by something already existing in act. Therefore, it contributes to sensation and motion through another, as has appeared for the sake of its preservation; for it tempers, refreshes, and quiets the <term>spirits</term> <note>the "vital spirits" believed to carry life through the body</note> that have been dissolved by the heat of labor or other things, by remitting the excess and causing them to rest.

Furthermore, in the heart is the principle of the senses, and consequently of motion, even before the perfect creation of the brain and the nerves. For all plurality is reduced to unity; and everything found in many things is finally drawn together into one thing existing prior to them through a single, unambiguous reason. Such a thing is the heart in the category of genus, sensation, and motion; and sensation also exists within it. This is confirmed because the heart is the principle of the nerves, which are the organs of sense and motion in which these powers are most vigorous. Therefore, from the heart come sleep and waking first. The principal beginning of sense and motion is from the heart; even intolerable pains occur in it, according to Aristotle and Averroes <note>original: "A."</note> in the fifth book on the Soul. It is also the first thing that moves and the last to be stilled. Moreover, in the heart is the species and the form <note>the essential blueprint</note> as in the book "On the Generation of Animals," and for the same reason as the brain. This is also declared in the examples of chapter 48 and 38. Therefore, the heart is the principle of the nerves, and not the brain, as shown in the difference 38, by both modes of beginning and origin. Thus, it appears radically that all nerves are created with the brain from the heart, either more immediately (like the first ones) or

mediately, just as the brain is created with the secondary ones. Regarding the fourth point: as for the first authorities of the physicians, what appeared necessary to say has been said, especially concerning Galen, who either accepts the origin as immediate, or his view is not verified in the origin of all nerves.

To the next point, it must be said that Aristotle did not deny that the principle of the nerves, sense, and motion is from the heart, but rather he denied that all of them draw their origin *immediately* from the heart. To the other point, it should be said that although sensation and motion are lost below a ligature <note>a tied-off part of the body</note> or an incision, it is not because the power flows with the spirit from the brain primarily, but rather from the heart. Or the reasoning concludes that the brain is the *immediate* principle of the nerves because they are implanted in it when they arise from the heart, namely through the brain. Or the previous assumption is not universally true, as shown in chapter 14.

To the next point, it should be said that some of the nerves pass through, as shown, from the heart into the brain; yet within the brain, because of its size and humidity, they are softened and hidden, and are almost converted to its nature. For nerves, when moistened, quickly become softer and are greatly changed, just as the veins are changed when passing through the liver. For there are some that have much thinner tunics <note>coatings or layers</note>, as in the fourth book of "On the Usefulness of Parts." Or the statement about nerves arising from the brain without a medium is verified.

To the next point, it should be said that nerves do not resemble the brain in whiteness as they proceed, although they may resemble it when they first come out of it. Yet they differ just as an <term>indeterminate color</term> <note>a vague or mixed color</note> differs from a <term>determinate</term> one; for the color of the brain is determinate, but that of the nerves is almost indeterminate and very bright. Or, the similarity taken from color does not prove a similarity in substance entirely. And because color is a very spiritual and changeable external thing, as per the 145th difference.

To the next point, it must be said that it was not necessary for every nerve to be the principle of voluntary motion, unless it is constituted as a muscle along with other required things. For the motion of the womb and the veins is natural <note>involuntary/biological</note> first and foremost, and yet there are nerves in them. Similarly, the motion of the heart is reduced to a natural motion, as in difference 48.

To the authority of Galen on the other side, it must be said that either that series of writings is not Galen’s at all, as said in difference 47, or he held a different opinion there from the common one, as in the book of natural things. Or I understand that "origin" to be a certain detection and manifestation of the nerve itself around the right auricle <note>chamber</note> of the heart for the sake of protecting the great vein. Otherwise, he would be contradicting himself in the ninth book, where he posits that all nerves arise from the brain or the <term>nucha</term> <note>spinal cord</note>; and if he grants that some are in the heart, he does not want them to arise from it, but rather to be derived to it from the brain, just like the nerves which he posits arise from the sixth pair of cranial nerves.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate concerning the primary organs of the body. Having previously discussed the brain's role as a cooling agent for the heart, the text now moves to Difference 42, which specifically investigates whether flesh or nerves constitute the organ of the sense of touch, a central question in medieval physiology and Aristotelian science.</meta>

### DIFFERENCE XLII.

<margin>1</margin>
**That flesh is the organ of touch** is the opinion of Aristotle <note>original: "Ay."</note> in many places in his books on animals. Averroes <note>original: "Au."</note> also testifies that Alexander and Themistius <note>commentators on Aristotle</note> maintained the same. He further confirms this by reason, because touch exists in a certain middle proportion of tangible qualities; moreover, this proportion is found most in the flesh, since it is of a warm and moist nature and is more proportioned to the human temperament. The nerve, however, is cold and dry—indeed, cold in many ways, as noted in the third book of the *Colliget* <note>Averroes' medical compendium</note>. Furthermore, this is shown by the difference of the organ from the medium, because the medium receives but does not discern, as could be shown by induction. Flesh, however, receives and discerns the qualities of tangible things, as the sense suggests; therefore, the flesh itself is the organ of touch and not the medium.

The opposite of this opinion is found in the books *On the Soul* and *On the Parts of Animals*. It is likewise supported by reason, because a sensible object placed upon the sense organ itself produces no sensation, just as color placed directly on the eye [cannot be seen], according to the second book of *On the Soul*. However, the sensible qualities of touch occurring to the flesh immediately constitute a sensation. Furthermore, among physicians, no flesh feels except by the admixture of nerves; for they say that flesh is only a certain coagulation of blood. This, by itself, produces no sensation; hence in the first book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts*, it is said that no flesh is essentially sensible in itself. Therefore, flesh is the medium and not the organ.

That the nerve is not the organ of touch is shown from the first book of *On the Soul*: **Whatever things in the bodies of animals are simply earthy, such as bones, nerves, and hair, appear to feel nothing because they are of an earthy nature.** Furthermore, as was said, touch exists in a certain middle proportion of tangibles; however, the nerve lacks this, since it is cold and dry, and therefore it cannot be the organ. Also, Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul* says: if the nerve alone were the sensing thing, it would be necessary for it to be expanded through the whole body like a membrane, and consequently the whole body would be nerve, or touch would not be diffused through all parts. These things are absurd; for the whole body is not nerve, nor is any part entirely insensitive—at least on the outside—since touch extends through the whole animal so that nothing harmful may encounter it unawares. Conversely, a nerve is a "similar member" <note>a part whose smallest pieces are the same as the whole, like bone or skin</note> whose name and definition apply to the whole and the parts as one. But sensing is an operation of the vital power <note>the soul’s ability to interact with the world</note> which is perfected in instrumental members; for the member itself is ordained to most powerfully complete the act of this power. Therefore, the nerve is not the organ of touch.

The opposite of this is held by Galen <note>original: "Ga."</note> together with the physicians, wishing the nerve to be the organ of sense, motion, and the perception occurring from the outside. Furthermore, in *On Sense and the Sensible*, it is said that touch is of an earthy nature, and the nerve is earthy, cold, and dry. Again, an animal exists because of sense, according to Aristotle; for the addition of sense to the vegetable nature constitutes an "animal." Moreover, the existence of animals and universal mixtures consists more of earth and water than of air and fire, according to the fourth book of *Meteorology*; and the nerve is earthy and aquatic.

As to whether flesh and nerve together are the instrument of touch, Aristotle says in the twelfth book of *Animals* that the instrument of touch is not flesh and nerve, even though both are found in the heart and not in the head. However, that neither of these is the organ appears from the books *On Animals* and *On the Parts*; for the organ of touch is said to be "something within." In *On Sense and the Sensible*, he also asserts that the sensorium <note>the seat of sensation</note> of touch and taste is near the heart. This appears from the books *On Sleep and Wakefulness* and the third book of *On the Parts*, in which the movement of delights and sorrows, and totally all sense, is written to begin from the heart and terminate at it; which is especially verified in touch, since it appears as a certain vital form. Therefore, that which is inside, before the heart, will be the sensorium of touch.

The contrary is indicated by the vehement heat and dryness of the heart, which is disproportionate to the equality of tangible things; for vehement heat hinders sense to such a degree that even the breaking of continuity <note>wounds or cuts</note> is not perceived by those who are heated from fighting. Therefore, the heart is not the organ of touch, nor is it that which is inside, since sense appears to be perfected in that which is outside, as in the entire exterior surface of the skin.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that **flesh** is a soft substance determined from the beginning of the animal's creation, and afterwards generated from blood, situated between the bone and the skin. Taken commonly, it is of two kinds: namely, true flesh and that which is similar to flesh. Regarding what flesh is, it is discussed in the 10th and 14th books of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio"</note>, in the *Theory of Complexions*, in the third book of *Almansor*, and the first book of the *Colliget*, where five types are listed:

1.  **Lacertous flesh:** Such as is found in the muscles; for the muscle itself is composed of simple and primary flesh and integrated nerves. Because of these nerves, physicians say this flesh feels, which is called "true flesh."
2.  **Pure flesh:** So called not because no nerves are mixed in it at all, but because very few are present compared to the aforementioned type. Thus they say "pure flesh" is not found [without nerves], but it is found in the gums, around the bones of the back and the nose, and in the <term>glans</term> <note>the head of the penis</note>; and this feels for the same reason as the first.
3.  **Parenchyma:** According to Erasistratus, this is called "infusion" or "poured-in" <note>original: "parēcbima seu ifusa"</note>, such as the internal organs that labor over nourishment, like the liver, spleen, kidneys, and lungs; for they are "poured into" by moisture. And therefore, as Cornelius Celsus suggests, they are called "viscera." Some, hearing the force of the word, call them "confused" <note>original: "gfulā"</note> because they do not appropriate a specific complexion for themselves, but rather that which the parts claim for themselves and mix—for example, the liver is warm and moist, the spleen is cold and dry, and so on.
4.  **Simple flesh:** A certain common flesh in which only the thickening of blood is observed. Hence Galen says the flesh of the liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys is simple in nature. Because it lacks nerves, it is judged insensitive, as the mere curdling of blood provides no sense to it. Therefore, these members are pronounced not to feel.
5.  **Glandular flesh:** This is twofold. One type is ordained for the generation of moisture, either of a liquid or phlegmatic sort, such as the mesentery, the pharynx, and the larynx; or...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of flesh and its role as the organ of touch. ...of a more universal and further digestion, perfected. This exists either for the being of the individual, such as the glandular flesh situated behind the root of the tongue; or for the being of the species, such as the flesh of the testicles which generates sperm, and the maxillary flesh <note>The glands in the jaw or cheeks</note> which produces milk.

There is also another type of flesh ordained for other, more noble purposes: either for receiving superfluities <note>Waste products of the "concoctions" or digestions of the body</note>, such as the flesh of the throat which receives the superfluities of the brain, or that which is under the armpits for the heart, and that of the groin for the liver; or it is assigned for support, like the gland located under the base of the brain, under which is placed the so-called **marvelous net** <note>original: "rete mirabile," a complex of blood vessels at the base of the brain</note>; or ordained for filling empty spaces to provide support, such as the glands of the mesentery; or for conducting <note>as a duct</note>, such as those around the neck of the bladder; or for warming, such as the gland called "mora" <note>likely referring to the thymus or a protective fat pad</note>, for it warms and sits beneath like a cushion for the **vena cava** <note>the large vein carrying deoxygenated blood</note> situated near the right auricle of the heart. It is held that this flesh, and especially the glandular kind, does not possess sensation.

However, that which is "similar to flesh" has a triple origin. First, because it holds the place of flesh in bloodless animals, as in cuttlefish and polyps, which Averroes <note>original: "Au."</note> names "proportionable flesh." Second, because it resembles the quality of the generation of flesh, especially concerning sensation, such as the teeth. For according to the *Commentator on the Sects* <note>Galen</note>, teeth are not bones, or at least not like other bones; hence, according to the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, it happens that teeth do not have the same nature as other bones. For they alone among bones, and especially regarding sensation, "resound" <note>respond to stimuli</note>; for they actually feel, according to Galen <note>original: "Ga."</note> and Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note> in the following discussion. They also grow throughout one's whole life, as is manifest when a tooth is lost, for the opposite tooth grows out since it lacks the resistance of its partner. They also "ebb and flow" <note>change or grow</note> just like flesh, and they even regenerate sometimes in old age (Difference 39). In the third way, something else is called similar to flesh because it is an instrument vehemently tied to it, receiving support and nutrition, such as nerves and similar structures. And this is why sometimes the whole body is divided into "flesh and bones," especially by the common people, who even understand "bone" to include cartilage. Everything else, they confess to be flesh.

An organ or instrument is a part through which a principal power operates. Since the power itself is simple, it cannot reach the matter upon which it acts without a medium, due to a lack of proportion. Therefore, according to the second book of *On the Soul*, the first instrument of the soul is a certain warm body <note>the innate heat or pneuma</note>, and then the rest of the body, qualified by the primary temperament. The medium here is the "interstitial space" in which the sensible object is received before it reaches the organ. The necessity of this is evident in the senses that receive their sensations from a distance.

What touch actually is will appear from what is to be said. Touch is understood in two ways: one is for the **tactile power** fixed in the organ, consisting of a balance of tangible qualities; the other is according to the **act of touch** itself, led into action by its object, which is the formal aspect of it—namely, the actual sensation of touch. Thus, as many contrarieties as there are in the act, there are as many in the sense itself. Previously, however, it was considered only one sense, since its subject is a single thing, namely the heart or the nerve. Yet the unity and plurality of touch is more truly and formally understood from its origin than from its organ.

Furthermore, touch is twofold. One is **natural**, when tangible things encounter the organ without bringing injury, but rather perfection. There is another **unnatural** touch, such as the **solution of continuity** <note>a wound or break in tissue</note> occurring immediately to a heart or nerve, whether from within or without. What the heart or nerve is was made known in the prior section.

According to Aristotle <note>original: "Xo."</note>, it should be known that in the first book of the *History of Animals*, he writes that touch exists in every uniform part <note>homeomerous part</note>, such as in flesh or something similar. In the third book of the same, he says that the skin itself, if cut, is insensitive through itself—that is, without the flesh—and especially the skin on the head, since it is over bone without flesh. In the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*, he writes that the sense of touch is in the flesh for the hot, dry, moist, and cold, and that which is proportionate to it, because it exists as the most complex of the senses. He adds finally that an animal is defined by the sense of its parts; flesh and its proportionate parts are the "sensory." Whence Avicenna <note>original: "Au."</note> in *On Sense and the Sensible* says: **The instrument of touch is flesh.**

In the second book of the *Colliget*, it is said there are two species of flesh: namely, **muscular** <note>original: "lacertosa"</note> and **pure**. And Aristotle says regarding these two that they are the instruments of the sense of touch, properly standing with it just as the eye stands with sight. He demonstrates this because a simple sense is only found in a simple body, and that the nerve is the "servant" of the flesh in this apprehension, in order to temper the spirit of the sense which is sent from the heart. He wished, therefore, that just as the brain exists for the sake of safety—by tempering from its opposite position the heat of the heart and bringing it to a certain proportioned medium for life and sense (as appears in the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*)—so the nerve operates in subservience to the flesh. It is also added later: it is said that flesh is the proper instrument of the sense of touch, because it is the member shared by all animals, just as touch is the sense common to all animals. And in the flesh of perfected animals, there are "dispersed" nerves to temper the generation of the flesh; and because nerves are similar in generation to the brain, they assist in the same manner as the brain.

The contrary of these things is written by Aristotle with the Commentator <note>Averroes</note> in the second book of *On the Soul*. For he asks what the "tangible sensory" is: whether it is flesh (and in others the proportionate part) or not. Answering, he says: "Flesh is the medium, but the primary sensory is something else within." Whence in the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*, where he shows each of the sensations to be double (namely right and left, as in the eyes and ears), he says this is unmanifest in touch. The reason for this is that the primary sensory is not flesh or such a part, but something within. In *On Sense and the Sensible*, he says that perhaps touch is of the "earthy," and taste is a certain species of touch, and therefore their sensory is near the heart.

Thus, it appears that Aristotle and the Commentator seem to contradict themselves. Also, in the second book of *On the Soul*, Aristotle says: "From the properties of touch, it is a natural instrument because it feels; it is nervous flesh or flesh, and the nerve feels from touch, although there is no medium there in any way." Whence Avicenna <note>original: "Au."</note> in *On Sense and the Sensible* says that touch and taste are distinguished by the fact that they do not require an [external] medium. This is no small contradiction to Aristotle writing in the second book of *On the Soul* that a medium in touch is not only...

...internally; but truly also through external intervention.

Identity or the same: if the principle of feeling were in the flesh, it would exist through itself. Although the heart is flesh, as is the heart <note>The author uses 'heart' both as a specific organ and a representative of fleshy substance</note>, even if the threads of the nerves are separated in the heart, they are not far away. Unless they are received by the sensation <note>original: "ssm," abbreviation for 'sensum'</note> and fall back to a single origin, and from that origin are returned to the brain and other members. Therefore, since the sensation of the heart and the sense of touch are the same, the sensation of the heart is greater than that of the brain itself. Hence its pains are intolerable; and thus the heart is the first principle, and from it powers flow to the brain. Galen also, in his letter on vision, posited the nerve to be the primary instrument of the sense of touch. Thus, a great difficulty appears regarding the organ of touch. Because of the third thing to be known, it is necessary first to gather the truth from their diversity and then to reconcile them with one another. Regarding the first thing to be known here, the organ of touch emerges in two ways. One is the radical and primary organ, like the heart; for it is the principle and root of all powers, and it is more of a subject <note>The underlying foundation</note>, since touch is not seen only as a power, but even as a "form" according to some, since an animal has its being through it. And perhaps Averroes <note>original: "Aų.," shorthand for the commentator Averroes</note> felt this when he said the primary organ of touch would be that which is within. Hence Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note>, as it appeared, posited that the flesh of the heart feels through itself.

But another sense of touch exists by means of a certain medium <note>A substance through which a force or sensation is transmitted</note> of the proportion of tangible qualities. For since the heart is separate, it happens continuously from within to without: touch actually intervenes unnaturally. In this, the same thing is receiving and returning; for according to Aristotle, the receiving flesh is different from the flesh of the heart. The flesh is indeed that which receives and returns, and similarly the nerve which he posits as the organ of touch. However, what Averroes says—that touch occurs through a medium—is verified concerning the so-called "natural" sense, since he had to treat that. Because a nerve is inserted mediated by skin and flesh, and by a membrane <note>original: "ymene," referring to the hymen or a thin pellicle</note> or a very subtle, insensible skin extended over the entire surface of the body, following the diameter. Hence in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's "De Anima"</note>: "if someone were to stretch a membrane around the flesh." And perhaps it is not inconvenient for touch to be perfected somewhere without a medium, especially in the skull; since we see nerves and the heart uncovered, touched without flesh, providing sensation and pain. For it is not the same for touch as for other senses, since according to Aristotle in *On Sense and the Sensible* <note>original: "de sszu & sszato"</note>, touch is distinct from the others because of those things it perceives, being constituted of elements; and therefore it does not feel all tangible things in the same way as sight feels all colors and pains, because they are not sufficiently exceeding. In the fourth book of the *Meteors* <note>By Aristotle</note>, Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> says: furthermore, not only as a potential but as a certain form, the power of touch is given to the animal; for an animal is defined by its existence through this. However, some external medium intervenes, such as a liquid, watery or airy, when any two bodies touch each other in water or air, as stated in the second book of *On the Soul*.

There is also another organ, which is indeed secondary and partial, such as the nerve, which can be understood in two ways: either in terms of its origin, as it arises immediately from the brain or mediately from the spinal cord <note><term>nucha</term>: a medieval term for the spinal cord, derived from Arabic</term></note> or the heart. And according to this, perhaps it does not feel, since it is not forbidden for powers to become stronger and more valid outside their principles, because they obtain the materials through which they become such. Hence the extremity of the "cords" <note>tendons or sinews</note> is greater in power for contracting than the power of their principles, which emerges toward the part of the nerves, as in Aristotle's fifth book on *The History of Animals*. And according to this, someone will perhaps verify the speech of Averroes saying: "a sensible thing placed upon the sense produces no sensation." A nerve is also understood in a second way, as it is stretched and separated from the spinal cord and brain, acquiring a "tension" <note>original: "dyasonitatem," likely referring to the vibratory or tense quality of the nerve</note> which is no small cause of feeling, being also mixed with flesh. For it is tempered by it if it is its stimulant; and thus I posit the nerve to be the instrument of unnatural touch—that is, as declared, without a medium—but natural touch with a medium such as flesh, skin, and membrane. That the nerve taken in this way is the organ of touch is felt by Aristotle in the first book of *On the Soul*, besides Galen. He said: Touch is a power diffused through all the skin and flesh, and a force ordained in the nerves of the skin of the whole body and its flesh, for apprehending that which touches it and affects it by a contrary change in the complexion <note>The balance of bodily humors</note> and the affection of the proportion. Hence Algazel <note>The Latinized name of Al-Ghazali</note> says: Touch is a power diffused through all the skin and flesh, mediated by a subtle body which is the vehicle, which is called the spirit <note><term>spiritus</term>: the 'vital spirit,' a subtle gas thought to carry life and sensation through the body</term></note>, and it runs through the branches of the nerves by which, through mediation, it reaches the parts of the skin and flesh. This is sufficiently commented upon in the second book of *On the Soul*: The speech of Averroes gives the instrument of tangibles to animals inside the flesh; and this agrees with what appeared through anatomy <note>original: "anotboia"</note>, namely, that if flesh has an entry into touch and motion. If the parts are nothing: for it has already appeared after Averroes and through Alexander that in animals there are certain bodies called nerves, and they have an entry into sensation and motion. Therefore, what appeared to Averroes by reason is manifest; after the senses, there is nothing to what the later Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy</note> say, that nerves do not have an entry into the sense of touch. For the speech of Averroes is in "proximate potential" <note>Ready to be acted upon</note> and is also sensible.

Thus, it appears that Averroes showed, as the Commentator maintains, the nerve to be the instrument of touch in truth, understanding it as that which is "within." The aforesaid is also indicated by experience; namely, that more vehement pains occur to it <note>the nerve</note> than to the flesh. This is confirmed by this: that a simple sense should belong to a simple thing, so that a proportion happens between them. Likewise, as said before: Touch is the mean proportion of tangible qualities; where, therefore, the mediocrity <note>The balanced middle point</note> of the proportion of tangibles is found, there the instrument of touch will be. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the physiological basis of touch, moving from the heart as the primary source to the specific roles of flesh and nerves as the "media" or instruments of sensation. It addresses contradictions in Aristotle's works caused by the historical development of anatomical knowledge.</meta>

Sensation is tempered almost entirely in dryness and moisture. It is the first of the complexions and is not very cold, like the "flower of the collection" <note>This likely refers to a specific medical or philosophical anthology</note>. The Commentator <note>Averroes, the influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle</note> writes that the moderate coldness of the flesh tempers its heat, so that it almost reaches a state of balance. Therefore, the organ of touch will be the nerve and not the flesh—unless by the name of "flesh" the flesh of the heart is meant, or the term "nerve" is understood more broadly as falling under the category of flesh. This is especially evident since we see that teeth can feel, yet no flesh exists in them. 

Regarding this point, it must be known that this is quite difficult, primarily because Aristotle <note>abbreviated as "Ay." in the text</note> does not seem to have fully understood the nature of the nerve, as all his biological treatises and especially his *History of Animals* show. He writes: "All bones, wherever they touch, are joined together and bound by nerves <note>Aristotle often used the word 'neuron' to mean ligaments or sinews rather than sensory nerves</note>; and around all bones there is a multitude of nerves: but in the head there are none, but the sutures of the bones themselves perform their function." For at that time, the science of dissection <note>original: "scisionis," meaning the anatomical cutting of bodies</note> was not yet perfectly known. Therefore, the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> are divided on this.

This also depends on a prior question in the book *On the Soul*: whether touch is a single sense or several. Hence the Commentator says: "If it were declared that this power were several, it would necessarily follow that the flesh is like a medium <note>A 'medium' is an intermediate substance through which a sense travels, like air for sound</note> and not the actual instrument." The truth is that the sense of touch is either one sense or several unified into one; though Alexander and Themistius <note>Two early commentators on Aristotle</note> seem to have ignored the reasoning for this. He provides a reason: those things are "one" which receive a unified name from a single category, as appears in the *Metaphysics*—for example, white, black, and other intermediate colors are all within the category of "color"; heavy and sharp with other intermediates are within "sound"; and so it is with the other two senses, smell and taste. Therefore, each of those is a single sense.

However, things that do not share a unified name in any of the ten categories are not "one," such as the different types of tangible things. For some of these are in the category of Quality—like hot, cold, dry, and moist—while some are in the category of <term>Substance</term> (the fundamental nature of a thing), like heavy and light. For the power that perceives heavy and light only perceives them through the mediation of movement, because the sense does not perceive "heavy" or "light" unless a heavy or light body moves. Therefore, it seems to be Aristotle's opinion that the sense of touch is more than one sense, and that flesh acts as its medium. Similarly, "rare" and "dense" are appearing in the categories of position. Since there is no single unified term for all these, they cannot be a single sense. 

But as for the fact that heavy and light are regarded as substances, it should be said that the Commentator believes this because they inhere in the qualities of substance more intensely than others. Hence, in the fourth book of *On the Heavens*, heavy and light seem to be the principles of motion themselves—the increase and decrease of these qualities are very close to the substance of their matter. A clear sign of this is that when they are separated from their place, they exist as their own substances; and here, they are the result of the final movements. Hence the Commentator says: the matter of motion in "heavy" and "light" is very close to the matter of the heavy and light thing itself, and thus it approaches substance. But in other accidents, the opposite is true. And so, when

---

it acquires some part of the form of heavy or light, it immediately reaches a place with that part, unless an impediment intervenes. This does not happen in all other movements.

Note also that there will be hesitation regarding this question because Aristotle defines touch as a sense that is perfected through an external medium (like water and air) and an internal medium (like flesh). Regarding the external medium, Themistius, Alexander, and Aristotle did not agree. Lest this external medium alter the tangible things and change the organ, the Commentator was moved to say that animals do not sense the "proper qualities" of the elements—for instance, the cold of air or water—when they are simple and the animal is within them. He also posited that natural coldness cannot be separated from water, nor moisture from air, just as heat cannot be separated from fire. When an animal feels heat or cold in these elements, it only happens because hot or cold bodies foreign to the air and water are mixed with them. This statement—that a "natural place" is similar to the thing placed in it—is criticized by later scholars interpreting this passage, since change properly occurs in the primary qualities, and consequently in the substances they inhabit. We see that both water and air, being closer to simple elements, are more quickly changed by heat and cold.

Note also that Aristotle intended for there to be an external medium in touch as a necessary requirement. Hence, when the Commentator explained the way in which water and air are called "media" in touch, he returned to saying what the medium is in reality for this sense: namely, that it is impossible to sense without it, and that flesh is to touch what water and air are to the other three senses. Thus, according to the Commentator, an external medium in touch is not strictly necessary, especially since the air we feel expresses the contact of solid bodies, though more by accident. 

A similar case is seen when someone is struck while holding a shield. The shield is struck no less than the person; the shield being struck then strikes the person carrying it. The shield itself is not the primary cause of the blow, but rather the striking itself. Because the one with the shield is struck simultaneously, which happens in those things that touch each other in the moisture of water or air. This perhaps is Aristotle's subtle opinion regarding the external medium of touch. An internal medium is generally necessary, while others are not, as in "unnatural touch" like the touch of a primary quality.

Next, it should be known that in the commentary on *On the Soul*, the Commentator—wishing to reconcile Aristotle’s seemingly conflicting statements—says: Aristotle's discourse in *On the Soul* is "colder" <note>original: "frīg ē," likely meaning less vigorous or less certain</note> than his discourse in *On Animals*. This is perhaps because he spoke according to what was apparent at the time: specifically, what he knew of animal anatomy when he published the book *On Animals*. At that time, he did not yet know about nerves, and therefore he said the instrument of touch is the flesh. This statement of the Commentator faces criticism...

<meta>This page continues the debate over whether the "organ" of touch is the flesh or the nerves, specifically addressing contradictions in the works of Avicenna and Averroes by appealing to the developmental nature of their scientific knowledge and the role of the heart as the ultimate source of sensation.</meta>

...receives not a few things. Because, as previously introduced from the books on animals, Avicenna <note>original: "Av."</note> did not only posit the flesh as the organ of touch, but also that which is within, just as he also did in *On the Soul*. It also becomes probable that Avicenna knew the nerves better at the time he constructed his book *On Animals* than when he wrote *On the Soul*, since he was a most prudent man who labored first on general principles before moving to more specific details, as experience is something possessed only after a long time. For this reason, in the first book of the *Ethics*, <note>Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics*</note> it is said that a boy can be a good mathematician, but not a moral philosopher—and consequently, he is even less a natural philosopher or a physician.

Again, Averroes, <note>original: "Au."; referring to the 12th-century philosopher Averroes</note> in his works *On Sense and the Sensible* and his *General Rules of Medicine*, <note>original: "coll3" for *Colliget*, Averroes' medical encyclopedia</note> as has been shown, did not keep to his own legislation. In those works, he posited flesh as the organ of touch, but in *On the Soul*, he said it was that which is within. For this reason, it must be said that either at that time Averroes held that opinion—and especially because he believed the sense of touch was then one and not many, as even the Commentator says—for both of these reasons, Averroes' opinion was famous at that time and afterward. This appears to be so because Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a major 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle</note> posited flesh as the instrument of touch, as did Themistius, his abbreviator. Or, to put it more kindly, when Averroes says that flesh is the organ of touch, he may have meant by "flesh" something flesh-like, such as a nerve, or perhaps that which is within, like the flesh of the heart. But this path cannot be taken by Averroes, especially in the *General Rules of Medicine*, since he explicitly distinguishes between the nerve and the flesh, and posits flesh as the principal instrument of touch rather than the nerve. This is apparent because he says the nerve serves the flesh by <unclear>carrying</unclear>. Indeed, the defect of this view appeared when it was realized that flesh does not feel by itself, nor is it a principal part of the body—unless one understands that "flesh" to be the flesh of the heart. As for Aristotle's statement that "nervous flesh" <term>nervous flesh</term> <note>a compound tissue involving both flesh and nerve fibers</note> would be the instrument of touch, it is not to be understood that this power resides in the flesh itself, except insofar as it is radiated by the power and nature of the nerve, as he touched upon more expressly in the first book of *On the Soul*. From these points, a great concord appears in this apparent discord. And it points toward one conclusion: an animal is an animal because of its senses, and therefore because of that which is most principal in the animal; this is the heart itself, and thus the organ of touch. Regarding the fourth point concerning Averroes and the other discourses, it has appeared what should be said, even if they seemed to hold that flesh was the organ of touch.

To the other point, it must be said—as already seen—that in flesh there is not such a great <term>mean</term> <note>the "mean" or *mediocritas* is the Aristotelian balance of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) necessary for a sense organ to perceive extremes</note> of tangible qualities as there is in the nerve, since the heat and moisture of the flesh are quite prominent and remove it from an absolute balance; whereas the skin, the coldness of the nerve, and its dryness <unclear>maintain</unclear> it. To the other point, it must be said that a "medium" may receive a sensation without discerning it; this is true in an external medium, such as exists in the three [higher] senses, for the sake of well-being. But it is not so for an internal medium, because since that is joined to the sensitive organ, it is irradiated and receives the sensation for the sake of that organ. As for the opposing argument that flesh is a medium because when a sensible object is placed upon it [sensation occurs], it must be said that this is true of touch in a natural state and not an unnatural one, since it is established that it is perfected without an intrinsic medium. To the first of those points that were brought up—that the nerve does not feel according to the speech of Averroes—it must be said that by "nerve," as appeared,

he meant a ligament, since he assigns the cause to the earthiness of its nature. Or, it could be said that the nerve does not feel in its starting principle, since they emerge from the brain or the <term>spinal cord</term> <note>original: "nuca," a term derived from Arabic meaning the spinal marrow</note>; or it feels by reason of a certain diaphaneity <note>transparency or clarity</note> and translucency, for then the <term>spirits</term> <note>the "vital spirits" or *pneuma* believed to carry sensory information through the body</note> can pass through. It is insensitive, however, by reason of that which is earthy and compacted. To the other point, it must be said (as has been shown) that the coldness and dryness of the nerve stand closer to an absolute balance than the complexion of any other member except the skin, unless the spirit meets it, since the spirit here is hot and moist. To the other point, it must be said that it is not necessary, as Aristotle said, for the nerve to be diffused through the whole body in order to be the organ of touch by administering sense to the whole, as in an artery or a vein. For the spirits passing through the nerve alter and assimilate the flesh joined to them, rendering it sensitive; indeed, what is harder to believe is that it is rendered sensitive by the irradiation of the spirit through the nerve itself, without any actual expansion of the nerve into it. And flesh, having been rendered sensitive after this <unclear>depiction</unclear>, differs in its nature. Whence, in the third book of the *General Rules of Medicine*, we see that members feel through the nerve even in places that are not nervous. To the other point, it must be said that although the nerve is a "similar" member <note>a tissue that is the same throughout, like bone or flesh</note>, because a part shares the name and definition of the whole, it is nevertheless a functional, structured member, as the nature of the body's formation requires. For every generated composite has a fourfold nature, though it is not as manifest as an instrument; for it is moved by the form of its shape, as with the parts of the third [book].

To the other points from the third part, it must be said that touch is said to be of "earth" not simply, but in comparison to the other three senses, in which other elements predominate—such as fire in smell, air in hearing, and water in sight, as in *On Sense and the Sensible*. Whence, in the second book of *On the Soul*, touch is not of simple elements but of composites reduced to a certain balance. Indeed, it is written there that the sensitive power is only from two simple elements, such as air and water. For the pupil of the eye consists of water, and hearing of air; but smell is of one of these. Fire either belongs to none or is common to all, since nothing is sensitive without heat. But earth belongs to none, or it is mixed most especially in touch. To the other point, it must be said that the nerve and flesh are the organ of touch according to opinion, place, and time, as they differ in respect to one another—as appeared, one is primary, and the other is secondary and tempering. To the other point, it must be said that it should be conceded that what is within is the first organ of touch—suppose the flesh of the heart or the nerve. To the first point of the other part, it must be said that although the heart, in respect to the universal balance, is hot and dry, nevertheless, by the tempering of life and the excellence of the sensibles meeting it (such as sudden suffocations and the impressions of the sun), it turns out to be located in a certain balance. And therefore, touch is found in the heart not only in the first way mentioned, but also in the second. To the other point, it must be said that the sense found superficially on the outside is caused by the power of the nerve located more internally; whence if one places a membrane under the skin and touches it, it would produce sensation in the second [way].

<summary>This page reconciles conflicting views from Aristotle, Avicenna, and Averroes regarding whether flesh or nerves are the primary organ of touch, concluding that while nerves provide the sensing power through vital spirits, the heart remains the ultimate source of sensation.</summary>

## DIFFERENCE 43.

<margin>1</margin><margin>Whether the skin feels.</margin> Since the *General Rules of Medicine* <note>original: "coll;" referring to Averroes's *Colliget*</note>, in book 2, posits that its benefits are only to defend and to hide; that, however, is not "feeling." Moreover, in *The Generation of Animals*, book 5, it is supposed that the true skin is entirely earthy; and that which is such does not feel. And therefore, in book 3 of *On the Soul*: "With all hairs and these parts, it does not feel, because they are earthy." This is supported because in book 2 of *On Complexions* <note>Galen's *De complexionibus*</note>, it is stated that the skin is exceedingly dry; such a thing does not feel, since sense is a certain middle-point between extremes of qualities, as was demonstrated earlier. Also, that which is present or absent while the subject remains—in the manner of an accident—does not feel, since sense is a characteristic of a certain perfect being. For sense constitutes the animal, as was previously posited, and the skin is such a thing that its disfigurements, inflammations, poisonings, and skin-strippings <note>original: "excoriatione"</note> denote this, and other things of this kind. Again, it was said before that every sense is perfected by a medium; this would not be so if the skin felt, for the sensible object would meet it without a medium. Likewise, if the skin felt, it would need to be naturally stripped of all the qualities of sensible things that it receives; otherwise, it would not receive them. For in the reception of sound, there is a need to be soundless, and for color, to be without color, as stated in book 2 of *On the Soul*. From these things, however, the skin is immediately constituted; therefore, it does not feel.

In opposition, physicians agree, positing the skin as the rule and measure of the senses and of temperament. For just as a temperate complexion of the whole, caused by a certain alternation and refraction, is a state of being tempered <note>original: "tẽpatĩsia"</note> and is most powerfully perceptive of extreme contraries, so too in a single limb, the skin stands out almost by itself. Furthermore, that which is temperate, porous, and <term>transparent</term><note>original: "dyafonĩ" (diaphanous); referring to the medieval belief that certain membranes allowed the "animal spirit" to pass through them like light through glass.</note> feels, since the animal spirit is able to pass through it; and such, as will appear, is the skin. Moreover, in all things very cold, dry, compact, and impure, according to Avenzoar <note>original: "zoar"; the 12th-century physician Ibn Zuhr</note>, there is some sense; but the skin is measured in both these regards. Therefore, the skin feels.

Because of this, it must first be known that the skin or hide is a member woven from nerve and flesh, receiving the whole body as a protection for it, according to book 1 of *On Complexions*. The skin is like a certain "bloody nerve," existing most certainly as a middle between nerve and flesh, being made from a fusion of both. It defends either by hiding what is internal and soft, or by wearing down what is hard, which happens especially in beasts; or by providing sense: for because of the pain of sensory passion, animals flee things that cause them sorrow. The skin is also diversified: for some it is hard and shell-like, as in many bloodless animals; for others it is soft and thin, as in humans; for others it is in between, as in those with blood. For human skin is like an affection of the flesh, while in others it exists as a physical part. It is proven in book 10 <note>of Aristotle's *History of Animals*</note> that human skin, although it is thinner than the rest (as seen in *Generation of Animals* book 5 and *Theory* book 2), stands out as so much thinner and softer that a certain king ordered it to be applied to windows, according to Oribasius <note>a 4th-century Greek medical writer</note> in his *Aphorisms*, because of its porous and <term>transparent</term> substance which does not block the light.

It differs, however, because in some places it is thinner, such as on the face, which the change of color shows: it happens quickly there. In some parts, however, it is thicker, such as on the soles of the feet and the palms of the hands. Then in other places, it is intermediate. Its temperament is that of a tempered person, not of a manual laborer whose hands are rough, such as a helmsman's in the palm, where it is more intense. (See book 4, chapter 7). Finally, the matter of an itch collects between "two skins." Those things which pertain to the rest of the complexions and theory should be sought from the senses; what "to feel" means was made known in the previous part.

Concerning the second point, however, it must be known that in this fifth section the speeches of the wise seem adverse. For in book 3 of the *Histories* <note>Aristotle's *History of Animals*</note>: "The skin when cut by itself—that is, without flesh—is insensitive, especially that which is on the head, because what lies between the skin and the bone is without flesh." Likewise, it should be held according to book 2 thus: The skin is like a covering and a certain innate garment of the animal. It does not deserve credit for the distribution of food, nor blood, nor pulse, nor breathing, nor motion according to impulse, nor does it provide any other act to the animal. Being thus placed on the outside of all things, it reasonably receives the superfluities of the whole body.

To this, the opposite is written in *On Complexions* books 1 and 2: indeed, it feels so much that it perceives all other things that occur, contrary to the first view. Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note> truly in book 3 of *On Animals* says: Avicenna <note>original: "Ay."</note> says that the skin does not have sense unless it were fleshy, and especially the skin of the head. And in truth, the skin that is near the nerves has sense, but that which is on the outer surface does not have sense, because there is no nerve in it. The discussion of these sayings will appear in the third part.

Concerning the third point, which is to be held from what preceded: that the skin feels by itself, being generated from the internal principles of its parts. Hence, Aristotle in book 2 of *On the Soul*: "It is from the properties of touch that the whole skin which surrounds the entire body is sentient through touch, and not just one part of it alone." Since in this way the sense of the natural parts preserves the body from accidents. For the skin stands out as twofold, as was also hinted: for one is not "true" skin, like a <term>membrane</term> <note>original: "ymen" (hymen); used here in the general sense of a thin film or tissue</note>, and an insensitive covering for the whole body, according to the previous statement: "if someone were to extend a membrane around the flesh," according to *On the Soul* book 2. Which is confirmed, because if it were sensible, once lost it would not be restored, since the nerves (in which the principle of sense is manifested) have this from nature. Likewise, nature in the beginning set forth all its power in attributing to itself such a noble virtue. Whence those parts of nobility cannot be compensated for from death, but these are continually restored for those in whom all sorts of things flow away. Again, when pricked <note>original: "pũcta"</note> it returns no sensation of touch. Nature constructed these, as it were, from a certain surplus of nourishment of the inner skin. And perhaps, as was previously posited by Avicenna, that which is internal stands as the medium of touch. Therefore, this outer layer does not feel, but is almost a covering and a safeguard for the preceding skin, and a dulling of touch so that the animal does not suffer too much from the sensible things it encounters. There is also another skin...

...the true spermatic skin, <note>Spermatic skin refers to the "primary" skin formed early in development, believed to be derived from the "sperm" or formative seeds of the parents, making it a fundamental organ rather than a mere covering.</note> which is located beneath the first layer. From these points, it is clear what must be said. <margin>Galen, sermon 3</margin> In book 3: because **Galen** in that discourse on the skin is verified to be speaking of the exterior superficial skin, which he indicated was insensitive since it lacks a connection to the principle of sensation. For its duty is to suffer and receive. It receives things sent to it from the interior nature, as well as exterior things that strike it. Either the spermatic skin properly feels, or the superficial skin receives what is superfluous.

<meta>This page continues the medical and philosophical investigation into the sensitivity of various body parts. Having discussed the skin, the author now addresses the long-standing debate over whether bones and teeth possess the capacity for sensation, weighing the opinions of Aristotle, Galen, Avenzoar, and Isaac Israeli.</meta>

...he found pain in the bones of his face. <note>The author refers to the physician Avenzoar, who famously diagnosed himself with a bone ailment.</note> Likewise, it is true that a child might experience this more than another because they participate more fully in that parent's nature. However, the sense of touch is primarily attributed to the power of the element of earth, as noted in **On Sense and the Sensible**. <note>original: "De sensu et sensato"</note> Therefore, they associate earth with bone, or rather, they align it more closely with bone both by reason of its complexion <term>complexion|the balance of primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</term> and its substance, which provides rest and support. Furthermore, the sensitive soul is a "form," which is proven by the fact that it gives "perfect being"; for it is because of sense that an animal is an animal, as seen in **On the Soul** and **On the Generation of Animals**. It is in the nature of such a form to be diffused throughout the whole, since it provides a simpler state of being. Therefore, it must be present in the bones. Furthermore, the utility of a nerve is the return of sense and motion to all parts of the body, according to **On the Usefulness of Parts**, book 1, and Aristotle’s **On the Soul**, book 2, so that the whole body is rendered capable of feeling through touch, and not just one part. For sense is the nature that preserves the body from harmful accidents above all else. Thirdly, regarding accidents: the harm of touch is felt in the whole body; but bones are a certain part of the body and are contained within the scope of the whole body. Moreover, if ligaments feel, so too do the bones, because they are considered to be born together from the ends of the bones. Their origin, from which they are produced, should be carefully observed in the **Tegni** <note>The *Ars Medica* or "Small Art" of Galen</note>; but ligaments do feel, as stated in the ninth book of the **Pantegni**. <note>original: "theorice nono," referring to the Theoretical section of the *Pantegni* by Haly Abbas/Constantine the African</note> Another cause for the heavy pain in the joints is due to the power of sense, which is in the ligaments and nerves. Again, according to Galen and Aristotle, the teeth feel. In that place, there are bones proper to themselves; for they have the same nature as bones and are made from bones, as noted in **On the Generation of Animals**, book 2. Therefore, bones must feel.

On the opposite side are almost all physicians and philosophers. For in **On the Soul**, books 1 and 3: bones, nerves, hair, and parts of this kind do not feel because they are of an earthy nature; because of this, plants also have no sense. Hence **Alexander the physician** <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle</note> says bone is insensitive. Furthermore, if bones felt, then because of motion, labor, fracture, and the compression of too many touches, pain would be constant, so that an animal could not live long. For no animal could endure it, as pain is destructive; thus, it must be avoided. Likewise, in essentially ordered things, that which is prior is always in the posterior, so that it can be separated from them; but this is seen to be the contrary here. Then, if bones felt and had such sense, life would be more "narrowed" <note>Life would be restricted or overwhelmed by the constant sensory input from the skeleton</note>, since as the intellect relates to sense, so does sense relate to life. But the intellect, having no physical organ in the body, is bound to its operation, yet not to the whole body, but only to the "phantastic" powers <term>phantastic powers|the mental capacity to form and store images/memories</term> represented more fully in the brain. For the bodies of animals are not homogeneous like those of the heavens, so that one and the same soul could vivify the whole in the same way. Therefore, bones feel the least.

Regarding the first question, one must know what bones are (see **On the Differences of Vision**, chapter 39) and what sense is (from the **Prior Analytics**). Regarding the second, one must know that **Avenzoar** <note>original: "Zoar"</note> alone expressed more fully that some sense exists in all bones, having dismissed the aforementioned insufficient arguments, as will appear. **Isaac Israeli**, however, in the beginning of his **Book on the Elements**, along with the fifth book of his **Book on Fevers**, suggests that bones and everything of that kind feel just like plants. For he distinguishes a triple sense:

---

A **natural sense**, which is prior in animals and plants; for they receive and are delighted by suitable nourishment and flee from the opposite. And an **animal sense**, by which bodily pain is perceived and which moves voluntarily. And an **intellectual or spiritual sense**, which is the investigation, discretion, interpretation, and knowledge of truths. After which he adds: The celestial bodies are sensing, but they are not "suffering" <term>suffering|in the Aristotelian sense of being acted upon or changed by an external force</term>, nor are they changeable in their nature and essence, and because of this, they do not feel pain. This was also the opinion in the first book of **On the Heavens and the Earth**, more simply, though some argue with less sufficient movements; this is not part of the present inquiry. Indeed, by this distinction, Isaac even confuses the levels of sense. Furthermore, sense would not only be a passive power, but also an active one. The opposite of this is told in **On the Soul**, where this term is used improperly for any natural reception. Thus, they might say that fire, or any inanimate thing attracting something to itself, "feels." Again, some have brought forward from Avenzoar that sense is twofold: **confused and hidden**, such as that of the bones and similar things; and **determined and manifest**. But what about these? It will be seen in what is said in the third and fourth books.

Regarding the third point, it must first be known that bones do not feel at all. And finally, for the sake of certain arguments mentioned before, it must be shown that teeth do feel in some way. Regarding the first of these, it can be shown in many ways that bones do not feel. First, because sense is a certain "mean" or balance of excellent qualities, as said before; but this is not present in bones, since they are colder and drier than the other members, according to **On Complexions**, books 1 and 2. Likewise, nothing feels without heat, according to **On the Soul**, book 2. They are also harder than the rest and less capable of receiving the "animal spirit" <term>animal spirit|a refined substance thought to travel through nerves to enable sensation and movement</term> which is the organ of this power, because they lack porous transparency. Furthermore, that which has no continuity with the sensing parts does not feel, according to **On the Parts of Animals**, book 2; and in that which is not continuous, the transmission of sensation fails since it lacks an organ; such is the bone. For it is not continuous with the heart or the nerves, nor do they terminate in it. Also, sense was given to the animal for its protection, according to **On the Soul**, book 2, and Aristotle; but bones do not need this protection and safety, since they are buried within and created hard because they are removed from external accidents. Again, it appears more likely that the ligament feels, since the bone is the "son" of the nerve in reason and name <note>A metaphorical way of saying ligaments/nerves and bones are developmentally or functionally related</note>. So much so that a nerve is also called that, as said before, because it is an organ of sense; but it does not feel in the first sense. For in the theoretical part [of the *Pantegni*], book 2, the origin of ligaments is from the extremities of bones, which is why sense is expressed there. Therefore, bones feel in no way. Regarding the second point, one must know that there is disagreement regarding the sense of the teeth. Hence, in the second book of the **Pantegni** (Theory): many physicians say that sense exists in the teeth among the rest of the bones, which also tingle and tremble like the lips; and they give as a sign of this the pain that happens to them, since there is no pain except in that which feels. However, some despise this and say that the pain belongs to the nerves in the gums <note>original: "gigiay" (gingivae)</note>. Also in his ninth book...
