[the author] asserts that they do not feel in that way. It should be known that teeth possess no pain **in themselves** <note>original: "per se"</note>; for they do not truly perceive. The proof of this matter is that when someone breaks a small part of a tooth, the person is not harmed. Pain happens to the teeth due to a **bad complexion** <term>complexion|the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, and dry) in a body part</term>, which happens to the nerves, or from an appearing cause of heat or cold. But the pain is mitigated when the tooth is pulled, because the nerve is no longer stretched; for that place is widened, and the location where the cause was added is removed so that it may be dissolved. Then the medicine is applied to the suffering place and put under it and touches it. 

And this discourse indeed seems to have come from **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (fl. 200 AD), an influential commentator on Aristotle.</note> saying so: some say that pain is in the depths of the tooth, to whom others respond that a tooth is bone, and a bone can be without pain. For bone is insensible, which is shown by applying a file to it. I show this to be without logical and philosophical reason. For when I diligently learned about tooth pain through my own experience—just as I had heard the arguments—I found that not only do teeth ache, but they also constrict and "slaughter" <note>An evocative medieval description of intense, throbbing pain.</note>. Similarly, they suffer from inflammation. Indeed, at one time I had a toothache, and it was manifest that the inflammatory pain was not in the tooth itself, but in the gums. Therefore, those things that are nearby suffer from the pressure; and because the teeth are hard, the pain increases because of the pressure, so that both sensitivities are found in the experience: one in the gums, and the other in the substance of the tooth. 

For I clearly know and bear testimony to those who say teeth ache, because in the nerve which rises into the roots of the teeth and binds them around, there is a small membrane by which they are held. When inflammation arises in these, pain is generated. Thus you may more clearly know that it is not the tooth but the nerve or membrane that aches; for when the tooth-bone is removed, the pain diminishes—not because it is taken away, but because the place that has the inflammation is no longer oppressed. Once it is made free from pressure, the pain ceases. 

Regarding this, **Serapio** <note>Yahya ibn Sarafyun, a 9th-century Syriac Christian physician.</note>, from whom the force of these discourses first emanated, says: "When the sickness is in the nerves and the skins of the gums, many imagine that the pain is in the tooth itself." And this is known from the tooth because it is eradicated; for if any pain remains after the eradication of the tooth, then it signifies that the cause is in the nerve. The lessening of the pain when a molar is pulled occurs because some [nerves] do not extend by an extension of quantity, with which the striking falls; and the injury harms by its continuation with the bone, because of which there is tension and so forth, as said by others besides him. 

Therefore, the teeth do not feel. On the contrary, because first things are first, no official part <note>An "official" or "organic" part is one with a specific function in Galenic anatomy.</note> feels in no way except for the teeth. For **Galen** said that experiment demonstrates to us that they possess sense, about which Nature was concerned. She made them with a power that comes from the brain, so that they might discern between heat and cold. Whence in the third book [of *On the Usefulness of Parts*], chapter 17: "And that you may know that teeth are among the highest of those bones in which sense exists, it is because of that which comes to them from the nerves proceeding from the brain..." And when they ache, they feel that which happens to them from striking and jarring, and sometimes they feel their own friction and their own movement. 

And you should know that teeth ache sometimes because of a painful cause existing in their own substance, and sometimes in the nerve which is in their root, and sometimes in the gum and the rest. Furthermore, in the third book of *On Accident and Disease*: "In the pain of the teeth, the sense of touch seems to suffer." And in the *Problems*, section 22: "Teeth ache quickly." And in section 34: "They feel cold more, and it causes pain." For they are naturally suited to have pores. They also incur a numbing pain, which argues for the subject of sense within them. 

Therefore, the teeth feel these things which have been touched upon by others. It must be said that teeth do feel, both because of the nerves coming to their roots and disseminated into them from the **third pair** <note>The trigeminal nerve, often classified as the "third pair" in medieval anatomical traditions.</note> of cranial nerves, and because of the purpose and care of Nature which depends greatly on it, so that they may be protected from harmful things and select what is suitable for themselves. However, their sense is weak and very dull because of their coldness, dryness, and their hardness, which is necessary for their friction and cutting, lest they break and ache. Yet with a certain translucent "diaphaneity" and porosity, they perceive some things. 

And because their sense is such, they do not feel the distance of continuous touch on the surface especially, or because they minimally perceive the encounters of earthy things. However, they feel the **primary qualities** <note>Heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note>, and especially the most effective ones, because they feel intense things, and those qualities immediately bring pain to them since they are more "spiritual" <note>Meaning subtle or non-material/gaseous in medieval physics.</note> and penetrable; in these, the reason for the action is found because of the contrariety. And because of this, they feel each thing more. Thus, therefore, the teeth feel not of themselves, but by the transmission and irradiation of the **animal power** <term>animal power|the "spiritus animalis" or vital force responsible for sensation and movement</term> coming from the nerves to their roots. This is like flesh generated after an injury, which acquires a numb sense from such an emanation. For a nerve cannot be born if it has been cut away. Nor, because they feel in such a way, should it be said that they do not feel. Flesh does not feel by another; whence in the first book of *On the Usefulness of Parts*: "No flesh is essentially sensitive in itself, for it feels through something else, such as a nerve diffused into it," and then it is said to feel. Unless, perhaps, it is the flesh of the heart. 

And as for the fact that tooth pain seems sharper, it is not of the teeth themselves but of the nerves or the membranes of the gums. This, moreover, is confirmed: for when a tooth was broken for me in the upper prominence, and I touched the deep part with a sharp iron, I clearly perceived pain. From these things, therefore, and more, **Avenzoar**, **Galen**, and **Aristotle** agree that it appears to the rest that teeth feel, and in what way and by what means. It is also seen that the softening arguments of others—that they do not feel or they pretend they do not feel—refer to the teeth not feeling **by themselves**, just as flesh does not feel without membranes or such things, or those parts most suited for sense. This I grant, as flesh can be generated after a cutting. 

Regarding the fourth point, however, what should be said to the first [argument of] **Avenzoar** <note>original: "Zoar az"</note>? For thus life was extinguished, not because he held it as an absolute truth in every way; whence at the end of his inquiry: "This is among the things in which doubt remained with me." To the other argument, it must be said that it is not similar; for the nature of bone requires natural power, and even more, vital power, but not "animal" <note>sensory</note> power. For it would rot...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the anatomy of the human body, moving from the properties of bones to a detailed "Distinction" (section) on the nature and function of membranes. It draws heavily on Galen’s medical works and Aristotle’s philosophy to define how these thin tissues provide sensation and protection to the internal organs.</meta>

...is simple and uncomposed. On the contrary, in the first section of the <note>original: "propria"</note>, a **membrane** <term>panniculus|A thin, sheet-like tissue layer; the term from which we get 'pannicle' or 'panniculus'</term> is composed of **nerve** and **ligament**. Furthermore, if it were composed solely of nerve, its constitution would induce a spasm, just as it does in nerves; but this is not the case. It is truly composed of nerve or cord, according to that passage in the *Tegni* <note>original: "tegni"; referring to Galen's *Ars Medica*, the standard medical textbook of the Middle Ages</note>. Indeed, nerves and tendons <note>original: "tenantes"</note>... That which binds and provides sensation is constituted from a binding of nerves. 

Such indeed is the membrane; for it is seen to prevail, as in the kidneys, which, when connected with the back and with essentially insensitive members, are provided with sensation. Therefore, a membrane is constituted of nerve and ligament. 

Regarding this, it must first be known that a membrane is a thin, expanded body woven from nervous fibers not perceived by the senses. It is also called a covering, a **hymen** <note>original: "ymen"; used here as a general term for a thin membrane</note>, a **meninx** <note>original: "miringa"</note>, a **web** <note>original: "tela"</note>, or a **membrane** <note>original: "membrana"</note>. This nature must be strong so that it may defend; not fleshy so that it may attract; nor should it have moisture or such thinness that, being light, it would create no weight. Indeed, it is stronger around the more noble members, for they require guardianship, such as the heart and the brain. 

Concerning the opposites, the benefits of the membrane are many:
1. One is so that it may preserve the incision or figure of the members so they do not slip. 
2. Another is so that it may suspend and connect bodies to one another, just as the kidneys are connected to the back; for the membranes alone join them. 
3. Some allow members lacking sensation to receive it through the membrane, such as the **lung**, **liver**, **kidneys**, and **spleen**. 
4. Another is so that one muscle <note>original: "lacertum"</note> may be separated from another. 
5. The remaining reason is so that if harm ever happens to one, it does not become common to others, and so that a muscle is not affected by the movement of another. 

It is also the membrane's benefit to constrain a simple member, like the **gallbladder** <term>kistim fellis|The gallbladder</term>, or a composite one such as the **cornea**, the **intestine**, and the **bladder**. 

Know also from theory that two principal membranes are established: the one covering the ribs inside the chest <note>the pleura</note>, from which all membranous and membrane-wrapped organs originate, and the membrane called the **siphac** <term>siphac|The peritoneum, the lining of the abdominal cavity</term> or *pyteineon*, which covers the internal muscles of the belly. From this, as from the first, the membranous and wrapped parts originate, especially regarding their outer tunic. For the interior tunic of the bladder is described in the first book on natural things <note>likely Aristotle’s *Physica* or a similar commentary</note> as having its own proper constitution. But the exterior is said to be created from the omentum or the *siphac*. In the third book <note>original: "tertio uero xiii"</note> it is said that all membranous members and those wrapped in membranes derive their origin from the membrane covering the muscles of the belly from within. This perhaps occurs because it is greater than the former; for this origin appears more to the senses than being strictly bound to the truth. What a nerve and a ligament are is discussed in section forty-one.

Regarding sensation, it should be known that in this distinction, contrary opinions are found, especially those of Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note>. For he expresses in his first writings that the membrane of these... in the third [it is said] that the internal membrane of the lungs is constructed on the outside from two very small nerves coming from the **sixth conjugation** of the brain <note>In historical anatomy, the 'sixth conjugation' refers to the group containing the Vagus nerve</note>. 

What will be made manifest about this follows from what is to be said. Regarding the beginning, it should be known that as a mixture, a membrane is composed of nerve and ligament; there, only the part of the nerve often exceeds that of the ligament, though perhaps in some places the membrane exists only as a dilated nerve. I said "often," because there is some membrane in which the nature of the ligament perhaps prevails over the nerve, since its primary purpose is to bind, such as the membrane binding the bones of the fingers together. Hence, in the first section, the joints of the fingers are understood to include ligaments and forms that meet with cartilaginous membranes which participate not a little in the nature of ligaments.

Or perhaps some membrane consists of ligament alone, as around the joints, for the sake of binding and not causing pain. Regarding this, it is shown that according to the first complexion, the cords are located in coldness because of the ligament. Then comes the membrane, and after that the nerve, because the ligament arises simply from the cold bone, and is therefore cold. Then the cord follows it, since in it there is no small portion of the binding; then the membrane, and finally the nerve. This order notes that the membrane participates in both nerve and ligament, but more in the nerve, as has been stated. If the membrane were only an expanded nerve, it would not be placed before the nerve. 

Furthermore, that which has the benefit of binding, suspending, and contracting is considered cold, and since these belong to the nature of the ligament, the membrane participates in this. Again, toward the muscle, a nerve and a ligament are transmitted as its beginning. Around their middle, nothing is manifest except a thin, dilated body; such a thing is said to be a membrane. Therefore, insofar as a membrane is woven from nerve and ligament, reason persuades us that nature protects the most sensitive parts because of their purpose. 

Such a part is the **heart**. Aristotle says in the fifth book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "quinto de aia"</note> that the sense of touch in the heart is greater than in the brain itself, which is why its pains are intolerable. Therefore, in the third book of *On the Parts of Animals*, it is said that the heart sustains no heavy passion. This is supported because the heart has a membrane at its extremity, and finally its **capsule** <note>the pericardium</note> or membranous sheath, which recedes from the heart itself after the base. Such membranes, especially the first, participate very little in the ligament, since ligaments originate from bone. But the heart, with its membrane, was produced before any bone. Likewise, the membrane of the capsule precedes the generation of the heart. For just as when seed falls into the womb, a hymen immediately surrounds it, so when the heart is generated (which is the beginning), the membrane of that capsule exists before the generation of bone. 

The **mouth of the stomach** <note>the cardia</note> is also most sensitive, which the nerves of the sixth pair of the brain denote, piercing into it and providing it with a soul-driven sense especially above other parts, so that it can feel hunger and desire more than other parts. To this, even if they lack the sense of the eyes, the conjunctivae <note>original: "coniūnctiue"</note> approach, since the eye is...

To the first, it must be said that "simple" and "uncomposed" are spoken of in two ways: either something that has no composition at all according to truth—and thus a membrane is not simple, nor is any part of the body, since they are at least composed of the principles of generation, matter, and form—or that which is not perceptible to the senses. Yet a tendon is composed of nerve and ligament, as they coincide; and flesh is composed of the true matter of flesh, such as thickened blood and the fibers of nerves, which Distinction 57 will explain more fully.

To the other point, it appears evident that the definition of a "simple part" is given based on how it appears to the sense, and not as it truly exists. To the next, it should be said similarly that **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note> enumerates the tendon and flesh as simple, though they are no less composed than a membrane. To the other, it must be said that for the most part, a membrane exists not only for the sake of providing sensation, but for other aforementioned benefits. To the next, it must be said that it is not valid, because where a portion of ligaments concurs in a membrane, it is not so great that it utterly perverts its sensation; just as when a part encounters an imperceptible softness, and therefore pain does not occur there. Truly, as was said, it is a "stinging" pain. To those things said of the other part: that a membrane is composed of nerve and ligament, though sometimes from nerve alone. To the other, it must be said that the reason why a puncture of a membrane does not induce a spasm is not because it is made only of ligament, or that ligament is its most powerful part. Rather, it is the diversity of the body's texture, the thickness or thinness of the substance. For the nervous fibers in a tendon extend directly along its length, so that a **terrible vapor** <note>original: "vapor horribilis"; in medieval medicine, "vapors" or "spirits" were thought to carry sensations or morbid influences through the nerves</note> from its puncture seeks the brain most directly. In a membrane, however, the fibers extend in every dimension, so that this elevated vapor is prevented from reaching the brain by being dispersed. Furthermore, a tendon is thick and hard, not yielding much to what strikes it, and it even preserves the injury inflicted. In it, the sensation is more unified; but a membrane is light and thin, yielding easily to pressure, and sensation in it is not unified as in a tendon. For this reason, pain is not as intense in it as in a tendon, and its puncture does not cause a spasm in the same way. 

Another point follows, as much as was concluded previously:

## DISTINCTION XLV.

<margin>1</margin>
That the nostrils are the organ of smell, and not the **caruncles** <term>carunculae|Small, fleshy growths; here referring to the olfactory bulbs</term> or the nipple-like additions, is shown. First, from the *History of Animals* <note>Aristotle's *Historia Animalium*</note>: smell occurs through this part, namely the nostrils; and this is the sense of smell. Likewise, in the fourth book of the same: some animals have nostrils, others have pores through which they smell. Again, in the fourth book of *On Accidents*: I have named the nostrils which are below for two functions, just as the tongue is for smell <note>This may be a scribal error in the original text, as the tongue is typically associated with taste</note>, so the nostrils are for smelling and breathing. Further, from the second book of *On the Soul*: It is manifest that the instrument of smell is the nose. The same is found in *On Sense and the Sensible*. More rarely, it is said that air is placed within the nose. Again, by a firm reason: because a defect in the utility of the nose affects both nostrils. That larger part of the nerve which comes to the "little ears" <note>original: "auriculas"; likely referring to the ear-like shapes of the olfactory bulbs</note>; since therefore the nerve is the instrument of all other senses, it will be the instrument of smell. Also, the **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note> on the second book of *On the Soul*: in what **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay."</note> said, "The veins and passages are widened," he demonstrates that the nose exists by necessity, and not just for the sake of what is "better." That which exists by necessity is the primary organ of that for which it is ordained, and not merely a subservient part for the sake of improvement. Furthermore, that which is cold and moist cannot be the primary organ of any sense, since coldness is mortifying and causes paralysis, while moisture softens and dulls. The brain, however, is the coldest and moistest of the parts of the body, as per Distinction 24. Also: that which is the organ of any power must have that power actually existing within it; otherwise it cannot proceed into operation, which the paralysis of nerves shows. The brain itself lacks the power of sensation; for touch produces no sensation there, just as neither does phlegm or other superfluities of animals, as the aforementioned Distinction and experience teach. Furthermore, a sensible object placed directly upon the sense produces no sensation, according to *On the Soul*; since every sense is perfected by a medium. But an odorous thing placed upon the nostrils as if inside is not smelled. Again, it seems that to be the sense-organ of an object, it must receive an impression from it. It is the nature of objects to bring the pores bound to the organs from rest into action. But an impression is made in the nostrils during smelling—namely, a certain extension and tickling. The nostrils, therefore, are the sensing organs of smell, and not the aforementioned additions similar to the heads of nipples. Almost all doctors feel the opposite: that the aforementioned nipple-like heads are the organs of smell, and not the nostrils. Again, others say: all senses must be derived from the brain, which is also established here; similarly from the same: nor does there appear to be an organization in the nostrils such that they would be the instruments of smell, since they have other proper operations, and it belongs to one member...

...unique according to **Haly Abbas's** <note>original: "Haly"; a 10th-century Persian physician famous for the *Liber Regalis*</note> own opinion. And the organ of a faculty is located where it happens that the faculty primarily experiences and is shaped by its object. However, the impairment of smell is not an affection of the nasal passage, but of the anterior ventricles of the brain—specifically the third of the internal parts. It also strengthens the womb <note>Smell was historically believed to have a direct physiological effect on the uterus</note>. Therefore, the **mammillary processes** <term>capita mammillaria|The olfactory bulbs, named for their resemblance to small breasts or nipples</term> are the organs of smell.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that a sensory organ or instrument is the subject in which a faculty is fixed or toward which it tends. For the sense of smell is a power arranged in two caruncles <note>small fleshy growths</note> of the anterior part of the brain, similar to the tips of breasts. These are meant to apprehend what is offered by the air drawn in, which contains odor mixed into vapor, or from an odor impressed upon the air by a change caused by an odorous body, according to **Aristotle** in the first book of *On the Soul*.

From this, it also becomes apparent what these aforementioned "additions" are. For directly opposite them and above them, a wider bone projects on both sides, connected on the outside. Toward the interior, however, it is concave, and the brain descends into this on both sides. It is formed within the **dura mater** <term>dura mater|The tough, outermost membrane surrounding the brain</term> in the shape of breasts, and it hardens slightly from the substance of the brain, much like the tip of a breast or the hard part that stands out on a nipple. Whence **Aristotle** says in book 12 of *On Animals* that in the anterior part there grow additions similar to breasts, through which smell occurs. They are distinguished from the softness of the motor-brain, yet they are not as hard as a nerve.

Also, at the beginning of the "third flesh" in the anterior brain, there arise two mammillary additions by which smelling occurs. At first, they differ little from the softness of the brain, but afterward, they take on the hardness of nerves. The attraction of air and odor through the nostrils occurs toward these additions or caruncles. For the composite bone is perforated by two manifest openings; first between these, and finally it is perforated above by many small canals, being made like a **sponge** <note>Referring to the ethmoid bone's cribriform plate</note> so that it may diminish the intense coldness of the air during breathing, lest it proceed unaltered to the brain.

This is situated under the dura mater. It is itself perforated with holes like a **sieve** <note>original: "clepsedra"; literally a water-clock, but here describing a perforated vessel</note>, according to book eight of *On the Usefulness of Parts*. The nostrils are the instruments for conveying air to the lungs and odor to the aforementioned caruncles; they are composed of several bones and cartilages. There is also a passage coming from the palate into the nostrils and these caruncles.

The benefits of these are many: through them, as prescribed, the fumy evaporation reaches the aforementioned additions and air is sent to the lungs; it also tempers the heat in the brain. They help in "cutting" the air so that speech may be properly articulated. They also expel superfluities from the brain and hide them from sight. For it would be foul to see the discharge flowing from those holes; they also assist in shaking out and expelling such things with the hands.

Note also that man has a worse sense of smell than other animals—at least in terms of intensity, according to *On the Soul*. However, in terms of "extension" (discrimination), man's sense is more certain/accurate, whereas many other animals are overwhelmed by odors. Whence in a dog, according to **Alexander** in his *Problems*, smell is more intense than in man. In an eagle, sight is superior; in the animal first called "the one who tastes beforehand" <note>likely a reference to a monkey or a specific species noted for tasting</note>, taste is superior. According to the example of spiders and some birds, touch is superior—at least regarding the subtle encounter with an object, though not regarding the discernment of the quality of the thing touched. For in this latter respect, man's touch is more perfect than all others, and therefore he is the most "prudent" of animals according to *On the Soul*. In boars, truly, hearing is superior.

Regarding the sense itself, it should be known that **Aristotle**, in the *Collection on Sense*, intended the nostrils to be the proper instruments of smell. For he says, according to **Avicenna**, that this sense occurs in the two passages in the nose. However, according to **Galen**, it occurs in the two caruncles similar to the heads of breasts; he says that because of the distance of this location, it required the attraction of air.

**Aristotle** then attacks **Galen**, saying: "If it were as Galen says, then we would be able to smell even if our nostrils were blocked, because we can draw air through the palate." For a hole exists in the palate, as said, which connects with the nasal passage leading to the aforementioned caruncles. And he adds what **Avenzoar** <note>original: "Auenafor"; 12th-century Andalusian physician</note> says: "We would smell the odor of foods beginning to digest in the stomach even with the nostrils blocked," etc. Likewise, if smell occurred through those two caruncles, non-breathing animals—which are seen to smell—would not be able to smell. For they perceive odor with few sensory differences, as noted in *On Sense and the Sensible*.

Man distinguishes the differences of olfactory sensations better than other animals; and yet many animals perceive odors more strongly from a distance. Therefore, in book five of *On the Generation of Animals*, it is said that man has the least certainty of the senses from a distance relative to the size of animals. But concerning the differences between odors, he has the most. For regarding smell, man is of greater talent in smelling than all animals, and in manifesting hidden odors by rubbing them <note>likely referring to crushing herbs to release scent</note>, which other animals cannot do. **Aristotle** therefore says in book five: "Man alone among the animals enjoys flowers and other odors." Whence in *Problems*, section 10: man is more expertly smelling than other animals. Therefore, smell is not located in those two caruncles.

However, this position cannot stand, as will be shown in the third part of this discussion. It is also necessary to remove the supports of that argument. What must be said to the argument of **Aristotle** will be seen in the third and fourth sections. Regarding the other point, it must be said that it is not valid, because according to *On the Soul*, smell is perfected only when the "lid" is removed—just as sight occurs when the eyelids are opened. This happens to us when we breathe, enlarging the passages and pores. But this cannot happen unless the smellable thing is drawn in through the nostrils. For this does not happen if someone holding their breath wants to draw it in through an open mouth. Still more, the smellable thing mixed with air would be carried into the lungs and stomach rather than ascending upward through the "strainer" <note>the ethmoid bone</note>. Therefore, the reason rather supports the opposite of the proposition...

...and with healthy nostrils. The sense of smell is also harmed by foul-smelling collections <note>likely referring to abscesses or buildup of phlegm</note> perceived in the front part of the brain, and many cases of **head colds** <note>original: "corize"; a common cold or nasal catarrh</note> show no injury to the nostrils themselves. Therefore, the pre-formed **caruncles** <note>the mammary-shaped olfactory bulbs at the base of the brain</note> are the organs of smell, and not the nostrils.

Know also from the second book of **Aristotle's** *On the Soul* that an **instrument** <term>instrumentum: a physical organ or tool of the body</term> is double. One type merely serves as a medium and a subsidiary, such as the **optic nerve** <term>nervus opticus: the nerve of sight</term> is to the crystalline humor <note>the lens of the eye</note>, or the seminal vessels wrapped around the testicles. The other type is purely perceiving, which is the principal and perfecting part, such as the crystalline humor of the eye or the testicles in the generation of seed. Some organs both provide a medium and receive, such as the nerve of touch, and even the flesh of the heart, for it feels by itself (see Difference 42). Thus, in the present case, the nostrils are only the medium-providing organs, while the aforementioned caruncles are purely the receivers. For it was necessary that there be prior passages and structures so that this sense—which is bound to us with difficulty due to the mentioned hardness and immeasurable humidity of the brain—might be perfected.

Regarding the first point proceeding from **Avicenna's** <note>original: "Āu."</note> statement, it has become clear what must be said: either he did not want the nostrils to be the principal and receiving organ of smell, but only the carrier and subsidiary, just as the "second philosopher" <note>Aristotle</note> defined the nostrils as the "bringing-in" of odors. Or perhaps **Avicenna's** discourse was from a time when the science of **dissection** <term>incisio: the practice of anatomical cutting/dissection</term> had not yet been perfectly handed down (see Difference 99). Regarding the other point, it must be said that it appears the nostrils are in some way **instruments** of smell, for they serve and carry to the proper instruments. And because they do not have this benefit alone, but many others as mentioned, **Galen** wished to compare them to the tongue; while the tongue's own act is tasting, it also serves as a subsidiary in speech. It is also like the hand of a miller in rolling the food under the teeth. More certainly, in the thirteenth book of *On Animals*, **Aristotle** said the nostrils were the **instruments** of smelling and breathing. Regarding the other point of **Avicenna**, it is already clear that it does not hold now. Regarding the next point, it must be said that the air placed in the nose is called an "instrument of smell" because it contributes most to the act of smelling being perfected; for the same reason, he placed there that the air in the ear was the **instrument** of hearing. For here, the necessity of the sense is most apparent from the book *On the Soul*. Regarding the next point, it must be said that that part of the nerve is not the part that is sensitive to smell, but to touch. For this arises and branches out from the third pair of nerves originating from the brain. Regarding the other point, I do not accept **Avicenna's** speech or its exposition here, since it was of the opposite opinion. Regarding the next point, it must be said that it notes a difficulty; for it only proves that man has a worse sense of smell than other animals. Nor is the **brain** <term>cerebrum</term> only cold and humid; rather, it is warm and tempered in its own way, but it is "cold" in respect to the heart and liver, and "humid" in respect to its own bones. And because the **brain** was so cold, smell was attributed to fire so that a sort of balance might be shown. This sense also has an ingenuity in smelling, like touch, by which the odorous thing easily acts to reach the organ. Regarding the other point, it must be said that the power in the caruncles is found in act, at least as far as its form is noted.

Nor is the organ of smell removed from around the **brain** because the brain itself lacks sensory power; for it is not properly in the substance of the brain, as has been declared, but in the pre-formed additions—and because they differ in substance from the part of the brain, the reasoning concludes a difficulty and not an impossibility of smelling. If the words of **Galen** sometimes sound as if the instrument of smell were in the brain or the two anterior ventricles, it should be explained as being "around the **brain**" and its membranes. For that which is annexed to a natural thing is often called by its name; just as the heart is called an artery in the third book of *Histories* <note>Aristotle's *History of Animals*</note>: "The heart is like a part of the artery." And at the beginning of the third *Canon* <note>of Avicenna</note>: "The **brain** is divided into membrane-covered medullary substance and ventricles full of spirit." Regarding the other point (shown in Difference 42): from the fact that an odorous thing placed deep inside the nostrils is not sensed, it is argued there that it is the proper organ of smell. But this happens because, since smelling consists of an effective evaporation aided by inhalation, the evaporation cannot reach the aforementioned caruncles if blocked. This is shown: for if what is placed inside the nostrils is of a small quantity, so that the vaporous evaporation is not prohibited from passing through, the odor will still be perceived. Regarding the other point: it must be said that not every change proves a "proper" sensory organ; just as a nerve is the **instrument** of touch (as shown in Difference 42), yet the flesh is changed by its object. This proves it is not the principal instrument, but rather an accessory and a carrier.

<meta>This page continues the anatomical and physiological investigation into the body's "instruments," moving from the organs of sense to the structure of the arteries, the esophagus (meri), and the intestines. The text focuses on the "villi" (fibers) that make up the different layers of these organs and how their orientation determines their function.</meta>

...soon, as if through the arteries with the help of the **spirit** <term>spiritus: the vital force or "pneuma" believed to circulate through the arteries to sustain life</term>, it is carried into the heart. This is completed by the **expulsion** <note>the act of pushing something out or along</note> performed by the inner **tunic** <term>tunica: a layer or "coat" of tissue forming the wall of an organ</term> of the artery, using the **latitudinal fibers** <note>original: "uillis latitudinis"; horizontal fibers wrapping around the vessel</note> placed within it. Indeed, the latitudinal fibers would hinder the process if they were pulling inward. Furthermore, the longitudinal fibers, being situated on the outer side, are closer to the air than those situated on the inside, and thus they can more easily draw in the airy substance. Therefore, the latitudinal fibers are found in the inner tunic of the artery.

Regarding this, it must first be known that an **artery** is a nervous member arising from the left ventricle of the heart, organized for its support by a motion contrary to the heart's own. It is extended as a long and round vessel, covered by a double tunic. It carries life by means of the blood and spirit to the rest of the body. Of this double tunic, the inner one is of great thickness and hardness. The outer one, however, is soft, thin, and porous, with threads like those of a non-pulsating vein (see the sixth book of *On the Use of the Parts* <note>Galen’s "De juvamentis membrorum"</note> and the *Theoretical Medicine* <note>Haly Abbas’s "Liber Regalis"</note>).

The inner tunic is five times thicker than the outer one. Because of this, **Abrucas** <note>possibly a corruption of a name like Archigenes or a reference to a specific teacher of Galen</note>, the master of **Galen**, who measured this well, maintained that an artery should be six times the thickness of a vein. They possess two tunics so that they are not split by the force of the pulse, and so that the spirits are not dissolved through their porosity. They pulse in order to temper the vital heat and so that the spirit may be carried with the blood to the parts of the body, and so they themselves may draw blood from the veins into them.

A **fiber** <note>original: "uillus" or "ynulus"</note> is a thread or a very thin, extended nervous member, ordained for the motion of a common action. For those members which act only for themselves did not require fibers, since their action is small. For them, natural heat suffices in place of a fiber, such as in bone, cartilage, and similar things. However, those which work for the sake of the whole body required them, since their action is more violent—such as the stomach, the artery, and the like. This fiber is threefold, corresponding to the three dimensions: **longitudinal**, **latitudinal**, and **diagonal**.

The arteries also operate through these means. For in them are four virtues <note>or "powers"</note>: some which dilate, others which constrict, some which retain, and some which cause dilation after a period of rest, and others which retain and cause constriction after rest. All these operate by their own specific fibers, according to **Haly Abbas**. Because there was doubt about which fibers act and how, he was afraid to assign them specifically to parts of the artery. Therefore, I will first set forth what the predecessors felt about this, and then touch upon the disagreements among the wise concerning these fibers.

Regarding this first point, it should be known that in the third book of the *Naturalia* <note>likely referring to Aristotle’s "On the Parts of Animals"</note>, it is written thus: The tunics of the artery are composed of round fibers on the outside, but on the inside, they are composed of many straight fibers and a few oblique ones. I call "round" the **latitudinal** and "oblique" the **transverse**. This is supported because the arteries are said to be similar to the stomach. To these things, it also seems that the first book of the *Therapeutics* <note>Galen's "Megategni"</note> agrees: In members having two tunics, the latitudinal fibers are always in their outer tunic, and the other two are in the inner tunic, so that the longitudinal fibers incline more toward the inner surface than the transverse ones. According to this, therefore, the longitudinal fibers are found in the inner tunic.

On the contrary, in the sixth book of *On the Use of the Parts*, it says: The inner tunic of the artery is dissolved into threads according to their breadth <note>latitudinal</note>. Whence, in the *Theoretical Medicine*, the opposite of the third book of the *Naturalia* is stated: The inner tunic of the artery is fibrous and oriented in breadth, but the fibers of the outer tunic are longitudinal, and in it are a few transverse ones. The **Colliget** <note>Averroes’ medical compendium</note> says in the first book: The texture of the inner artery tends toward breadth, and the outer toward length.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> in his *Problems* writes thus: Straight fibers in the stomach—that is, the **esophagus** <term>ysophagus: the tube leading from the throat to the stomach; here called "meri" or "stomacus"</term>—attract, but the oblique ones expel. In other parts, however, the oblique fibers retain, as in the matrix <note>the uterus</note>. Third, in the thirteenth book, the **esophagus** <note>original: "Meri"</note> is said to be deprived of transverse fibers since it is not meant for retention. This is agreed upon by the *Colliget* where only the long and broad fibers are explained, but not the transverse.

However, in the third book of the *Theoretical Medicine*: The esophagus is composed of two tunics; the outer one is fleshy, whose fibers run in breadth, while the other, the inner one, is nervous, and its fibers are extended in length, with a few transverse ones drawn through it. This is also hinted at in the third book of the *Naturalia*. Also, the motion of swallowing is composite; for it happens through specific fibers by way of their position in length, breadth, and transversality. But this is the motion of the esophagus. It appears, therefore, that these authors contradict each other in two ways: first, because Alexander placed transverse fibers in the stomach or esophagus along with Haly Abbas, and then he made the transverse fibers expel in the stomach, whereas elsewhere they are said to retain.

Furthermore, according to the *Colliget* concerning the stomach: Retention and expulsion are performed by the tunic that proceeds by breadth. Almost all others, however, testify that expulsion is performed by the tunic dissolved into fibers of breadth, and retention by that of transversality. In the third book of the *Naturalia*, the stomach has oblique fibers for the sake of contraction.

Furthermore, there is disagreement concerning the fibers of the **intestines**, not only compared to other organs but even among themselves. Whence, in the third book of the *Naturalia*: For each of the intestines, there are round fibers according to one or the other of the tunics; for they only draw together <note>constrict</note>, but they attract nothing. In the fourth book of *On the Use of the Parts*: Since the intestines do not lack attractive power, they have threads through which it would be possible for them only to expel. In the third book of the *Theoretical Medicine*: The intestines are composed of two fibrous tunics, and the fibers of each tunic are rounded in breadth. In the sixteenth book: That which prevails over the two tunics of the intestine is the fiber tending according to breadth.

The *Colliget*, however, says in the first book: The intestines are composed of two tunics and have a texture tending toward breadth alone. Whence, the power most manifest in them is expulsion, not attraction. To this, the third book of the *Naturalia* agrees: Of all the organs made from tunics and threads, only the intestines have oblique fibers in both. Haly Abbas also says the intestine expels...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the body's mechanical functions, specifically how the "villi" or fibers within the organs facilitate the movement of substances. It bridges the transition from general fiber theory to the specific anatomy of the arteries and the respiratory system, addressing debates between classical authorities like Galen and Avicenna.</meta>

...immediately what it gathers from the self into itself, and it attracts to itself something else from the surpluses. First, however, it is better for the intestines that the **fibers** <term>villi: in medieval anatomy, these refer to the structural fibers or "grains" of a tissue rather than the microscopic protrusions known as villi today</term> for attracting and retaining should not be situated there, but rather supplied separately through the **tunics** <note>layers of tissue</note>. For they do not require much retention, but rather attraction and expulsion. Thus, long and wide fibers will be within them. This is confirmed: for it is stated that sometimes a member has two tunics so that its attraction and expulsion may occur with powerful motion, whereby one of the two functions is performed individually by each tunic.

Therefore, **Galen** and **Avicenna** almost contradict not only others but even themselves regarding the third point. Therefore, the truth of the question should be explained first; thereafter, the disputes regarding the previously introduced difficulties may be laid to rest. Regarding this, it must first be known—according to the sixth book of *On the Use of the Parts*, **Haly Abbas**, and **Avicenna**—that the inner tunic of an artery is composed of wide fibers. The outer tunic, however, is composed mostly of longitudinal fibers, with a few transverse ones. 

Experience shows this more clearly: when someone takes a large artery and boils it, as if peeling it, the layers will appear to separate, showing that it peels more easily along its width or circumference. This is also confirmed by reason. It is first assumed, however, that **inspiration** <note>breathing in</note> precedes **expiration** <note>breathing out</note>; hence in the book *On the Pulse*, dying things expire, which is why it is necessary for inspiration to be first. And in the sixth book of *On the Use of the Parts*: the principle of all these motions is one, and it is the expansion of the heart, which is stronger than its contraction. Furthermore, when the heart dilates, the arteries are constricted, and vice versa (see Distinction 80), and the arteries, as stated, exist at the service of the heart. Furthermore, attraction occurs through **dilatation** <note>widening/expansion</note>, while expulsion occurs through **constriction** <note>narrowing</note>. Again, long fibers attract, wide ones expel, and transverse ones retain.

Furthermore, it is necessary for the instrument of expulsion to be located on the inside, as it is closer to the "agent" or force acting upon it. Hence in the thirteenth book, the expulsive fibers were not placed on the outside of the belly and the longitudinal ones on the inside, except because attraction is the first of its operations and is closer; thereafter, expulsion follows. 

This is clearly shown by the **intercostal muscles** <term>mesopleuri: the muscles between the ribs</term> which dilate the chest and constrict it at once, receiving fibers from four directions. Therefore, according to **Al-Mansur** and **Avicenna**, each one is double. However, according to Galen and Haly Abbas, they are single; thus there are 88 or 22 of their fibers. Indeed, those that dilate expand more toward the outer part to more fitly attract the air that comes from outside. Those that constrict do so on the inside, so they may more freely expel the **sooty smoke** <note>original: "fumum vaporosum"; the waste products of "internal combustion" or metabolism</note> toward the outside. 

With these things assumed, let us proceed: if the first inspiration occurs through expiration and the expansion of the heart, the heart first dilates the **venous artery** <term>artariam uenalem: the pulmonary vein, which medieval doctors believed carried air from the lungs to the heart</term> by drawing air into itself for its own cooling from the lungs. And because the artery serves the heart, it is constricted by it; for when one member dilates to attract, the other constricts to expel (see the third book of *On Natural Faculties*). 

Since expulsion is more necessary than attraction, it is performed by the wide fibers placed on the inside, because they are thus closer to the acting force. Subsequently, in this expansion of the heart, if the great artery must be constricted to serve the heart, it is so that the blood might be expelled from it, having been cooled in the heart's heat. This is also to prevent it from over-expanding during dilatation. However, when the heart narrows, the arteries dilate, such that in the great artery, constriction precedes dilatation, but in the venous artery, it is the opposite. 

Again, the expulsion of the artery is a stronger movement and more necessary than attraction, because through it, the sooty vapor mixed with the air previously introduced is expelled. Because of its "inflamed" nature, this vapor has become harmful to nature; therefore, the body strives to propel the excretions through the pulse, while it introduces air for cooling with a more moderate motion. This is because that air, however warm it may be, is cold in comparison to the **vital spirits** <note>original: "spirituum"; the refined substances that sustain life</note>. Furthermore, the vapor is thicker and thus requires a stronger impulse, while the air is more subtle and a weaker motion suffices for it. 

For a stronger and more necessary act, it is assumed that the instrument must be internal and close by. And it is supported by the fact that fibers arranged this way, being exposed closer to the air, can attract it more perfectly than if they were on the inside. A few transverse fibers are associated with these. Longitudinal fibers are always accompanied by them because their very strong attractive motion requires additional support. Therefore, the wide fibers will be in the inner tunic, and the long ones in the outer tunic. 

Regarding this, it must be known that fibers sometimes operate by themselves—and thus, as said, the long ones attract, and so on—but sometimes they operate by **accident** <note>an indirect or secondary effect</note>, and thus perform a work opposite to this. For in this way, not only the transverse but also the wide fibers retain. It is also true that those which run according to width provide help in the **retentive faculty** <note>the body's ability to hold onto nutrients or substances</note>. Hence, regarding **Alexander's** position that transverse fibers in the stomach expel, it must be said that this occurs "by accident" or not in all cases; they retain most strongly by finally constricting the "appetite" <note>the drawing-in force</note>, which results in the expulsion of what is contained in the stomach. Since the stomach is long and somewhat round, it is said that they retain of their own accord. But when some part of the transverse fibers operates, it can retain and provide rest, so that the attraction, leaning on this support, may perfectly draw things in, especially when the appetite is not immense.

To the other point—that Avicenna and Aristotle do not place transverse fibers in the stomach, while Alexander and Haly Abbas confirm them—it must be said that the former omitted them as being less necessary and obvious. For the action of the stomach is a powerful attraction in which very little rest is perceived. Those who considered a certain delay in the attraction of the nerves, and because transverse fibers are always associated with long ones in other parts, argued that the stomach also enjoys them. To the other point, it must be said that in the belly, expulsion is performed by the wide fibers themselves, especially when...

Regarding the other point, it should be said that the text of **Galen** is perhaps corrupted by translation. For in the Greek it was *egcarsion* <note>original: *egcarſion*, from the Greek ἐγκάρσιος, meaning "transverse" or "crosswise"</note>. This term, as Galen says in the thirteenth book of *On the Use of the Parts*, is the opposite of "straight," which is "round." It is also commonly called *egcarsion* or *plagion* <note>original: *plagion*, from πλάγιος, meaning "oblique" or "slanting"</note>, that is, "oblique." Hence the translator was deceived by the multiplicity of the name; whereas he ought to have translated *egcarsion* as "round" or "wide," he translated it as "oblique."

And so regarding the other point: it must be said that he erred previously by the logic of the translation when he translated the third book of *On the Natural Faculties*: "Of all the organs, only those made of tunics have both oblique layers," when he should have said "round." Or it must be said that "oblique" is an equivocal term for "wide" and "transverse," as Galen was previously seen to suggest.

Regarding the other point: it should be said that **Aristotle** <note>referred to as 'A.' in the text</note> opposes others who state simply that the intestines have wide **fibers** <term>villi: structural fibers or grains of tissue</term> in both tunics. Or it should be said that Aristotle understood the upper intestines, while others understood the lower ones. Or perhaps, although the five upper intestines have only wide fibers, the last one, such as the **rectum**, and especially its extremity, also has long ones. Hence in the sixteenth book: "In the rectum, very long fibers already appear," because it is the part of the intestines with greater operation, needing to attract that which is above it. Or someone might say that these longitudinal fibers are not from the substance of the rectum itself, but from the two longitudinal muscles that are in it. But if Aristotle says that attraction in the intestines happens by a violent motion, either I do not hear him, or perhaps it is by something other than longitudinal fibers; or he will assign attraction to the stomach and expulsion to the intestines. This, indeed, would not be interpreted correctly against the mind of the reporter. For if there were no cause for the doubling of the tunics, why would I say the tunics of the intestines exist as doubles for a common benefit? It is so that if an injury happens to one, it does not communicate it to the other. For if anyone attends diligently, he will find two nervous tunics in all members containing something foreign to their own substance, except for the veins, or perhaps the sheath of the heart; thus even the **frenes** <note>likely referring to the membranes such as the pleura or diaphragm</note> are double, as stated in the tenth book.

Regarding the fourth point: it must be said that this was at a time when he did not yet know perfect **anatomy**; for it is testified in the ninth book of his own works that Galen said: "It will not be impossible to find in the art of medicine that which has not been found by him." Regarding **Avicenna**, it must be said either that he followed Galen there, or his speech is regarding the male parts having two tunics; the truth of this for one part does not perish by being endangered, since for the logic of science itself, it suffices as it is for the most part, according to the second book of the *Physics* and the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*.

Regarding the other point, what should be said will appear. For it is granted that in other arteries, aside from the one of a single tunic, constriction precedes from the passion on account of the service they provide to the heart. Regarding the other point: it should be said that although breath and pulse are proportional by a broad proportion or similarity, they are not truly so. For similarity is twofold: one according to truth, and another not; as when something is compared to another by a more distant similarity, according to **Haly**. For although breath and pulse agree in almost the same number of species and in three causes—namely power, instrument, and necessity—they differ in many more; and specifically, the brain then works in opposition to the heart.

Regarding the other point: it should be said that by the vigor of the heart all things are rendered alive in the beginning, which are then preserved in being by the due flow from the heart to them according to dilation and constriction. But in this, as was shown, the constriction of the arteries works toward dilation even more; nor is it necessary for the arteries to have fibers. Or perhaps it is because of its particular act of nutrition, since, as has been touched upon, heat as an instrument is sufficient for nature. Regarding the other point: it should be said that because of the necessity of the near-vacuum that follows upon constriction, attraction follows immediately, as in the eighty-first book. And because of the subtlety of the air and the necessity of its motion with respect to ventilation, it does not prevent wide fibers from existing within, but forces them to be placed underneath.

## DIFFERENCE XLVII.

<margin>1 <unclear>...</unclear></margin> That the veins originate from the **liver** <term>hepar: the liver</term> as shown by the whole of Galen and in not a few other places. Aristotle says this in the fifth book of *On the Soul*. and almost all physicians; hence in the first book of the *Collectio*: "It is found by way of signs that the veins branch out from the liver." Furthermore, if they originated from the heart, they would move when it moves, since the motion of the whole and the part is the same, like the whole earth and a single clod of earth, as in the first book of *On the Heavens*. Since the consequence is false, the antecedent will also be false. Again, if the veins originated from the heart, since they are ordered toward the end of blood—so that by its delivery through them the body might be nourished—then the heart would be the principle of the blood, giving it form. And thus all the blood would have to fall into the heart; but this seems impossible. For since between the liver and the heart there is only one passage, namely the **vena cava**, it would be necessary for all the blood to ascend through it at once, and for the part of it that will nourish the lower parts—the smaller and larger ones below—to descend through that same vein. This, however, seems impossible, since the movements would thus occur in opposition through the same path, resisting each other in the intermediate place between the heart and the liver.

In the tenth book of the *Metaphysics*: the smallest thing in any genus is the principle in it, since it is the measure or meter. But the smallest veins are in the liver, not in the heart. Likewise, the veins seem to take their origin from that which they more closely resemble; this is the liver, and especially as to its membrane, not the heart, since it is of a hard and solid substance. And the principle of the blood exists as the principle of the veins, since these are ordered toward it; the liver exists as the principle of the blood.

<meta>This page continues the anatomical and philosophical debate regarding the primary organ of the body. Having previously discussed the structure of fibers and the errors of translators, the text now focuses on whether the veins originate in the liver, the brain, or the heart, citing authorities like Haly Abbas, Aristotle, and Galen.</meta>

Since it is hot and moist, and kindred to it in color; wherefore, concerning the "benefits" <note>This refers to Galen’s *On the Use of the Parts* (De juvamentis membrorum)</note> and in agreement with **Haly Abbas** <note>original: *Haliabate*; refers to the 10th-century Persian physician Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi</note>, the liver itself is purple so that it may generate purple blood. Hence, both the form of the blood and its entire disposition are given in the liver. The liver, therefore, is the principle of the veins.

Conversely, it is shown that the veins arise from the brain or the bones, because a vein is constructed from a **membrane** <term>panniculus: a thin sheet or layer of tissue; a membrane</term>. A membrane, moreover, as is widely agreed, is composed of nerve and ligament. Difference 44. But these take their origin from the brain and the bones.

As for the view that it arises from a membrane, this is because (according to the second book of the *Theory* and the first book of the *Practice*) all membranous members, or those wrapped in membranes, arise from the membrane covering the ribs internally <note>The pleura</note> and the membrane lying beneath the muscles of the belly, called the **siphac** <term>siphac: an Arabic-derived term for the peritoneum, the lining of the abdominal cavity</term>. Furthermore, in the third book, chapters 13 and 22, he also writes that the membrane surrounding the chest internally, along with all the others mentioned, originates from this membrane, as touched upon in Difference 44. Since, therefore, the veins are membranous, they will derive their origin from that membrane.

**Aristotle** <note>original: *Aų.*</note> holds the opposite of this in his books *On Animals*, and most especially in the first and third books, which he endeavors to establish with no few reasons. Furthermore, in the sixth book of *On the Use of the Parts*, the origin of the non-pulsating vein <note>The vena cava or portal vein</note> coming to the lung was from the same place from which the pulsating vein <note>The artery</note> arises from the heart. Also, because of the differences between the webs of these veins, there was an origin of vessels that have a single, soft, thin tunic from the thinner part of the heart. And the origin of those that have two thick, hard tunics is from the thicker and harder of its parts. These, moreover, are the right and left sides of the heart.

Clearly, in the third book of *On Natural Faculties*: if indeed the vein that leads to the lung is only so much larger than that which is born in the heart, namely [the artery]. Furthermore, in the third book of *On Animals*, **Aristotle** easily proves that the heart is the principle of the veins and the nerves. Again, the veins arise from that in which life is first and last perceived, since they are ordained for the purpose of nutrition; but this is in the heart, and specifically in the right ventricle near its right auricle, where the vein of the belly <note>The vena cava</note> is continued to the heart. 

Indeed, I have noted many things by sight while **dissecting** <term>arthotōzans: a corruption of *anatomisans*, referring to the act of performing an anatomy or dissection</term>: that when the motion of the heart ceases, and consequently life, while the motion in the left ventricle stops gradually and in an orderly fashion, it remains in the right until it finally reaches the middle of the **concave vein** <note>The vena cava</note> attached to the heart. For there, at last, all the vital motions of the same appear to cease.

Likewise, the principle of the veins and others ought to be in a more noble place, so that, supported by it, it may be able to rule; for as the place is, so nature works (from the tenth book of *Problems*). Such a place is the **chamber** <note>original: *collō lzo*, likely a corruption of *collocatio* or a specific anatomical chamber</note> of the heart. For it is situated in the middle, though declining slightly to the left, at least as far as its apex. For in all animals the heart is in the middle of the place of the chest; but in humans it declines slightly to the left, to balance the coldness of the left side (from the first book of the *Histories* and the third book of *On the Parts*). Therefore, the heart, and not the liver, will be the principle of the veins, since it descends into the right side, having the spleen opposite to it. Nor [does it arise from] any other [organ].

Regarding the first point, it must be known that a vein is an oblong, round, membranous body consisting of one tunic, containing natural blood for nutrition. Moreover, the liver is thickened blood and the first instrument or organ of its generation. I say "first" specifically because of the heart, which is its organ, but it [the blood] exits [from the heart] as a principal thing. What the brain is, and what it is to arise from bone, or what the heart and membrane are, is discussed in Differences 24, 39, 40, and 44.

Regarding the second point, it must be known that some have said the veins arise from the brain (from the third book of *On the Parts*). **Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician</note> also seems to have been of this opinion in his *Book of Urines*. Their motive was perhaps taken from the previously mentioned texture of the membranes being derived from nerves. But the defect of these views will appear in the third and fourth books of the *Declarations*. 

This opinion—along with those who positioned the veins to arise from the liver (third book of *On the Parts*)—the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> rejects through these primary points: for they create many and scattered principles, whereas in every genus and also in the whole universe, it is necessary for there to be **one single principle** to which all things are finally reduced and by which they are governed. Hence at the end of the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*: "Beings do not wish to be ill-disposed, nor is a plurality of princedoms good; therefore, let there be one prince." For from the order of the universe, perfection in beings tends toward one. Since, therefore, an animal (and especially man) is a **microcosm** <term>microcosmus: "little world," the idea that the human body reflects the structure of the universe</term> (as recited in the eighth book of the *Physics*), there will be some one member in it from which the others take their origin and are governed. 

An animal is also to be considered to consist like a city well-regulated by laws (from *On the Cause of the Motion of Animals*). In this, all things are derived from and tend toward one prince; for which reason, in the body of an animal, there will be one such thing, like the heart or something in its place.

Furthermore, the veins do not originate from that which is the coldest of the body's members, since they are ordained for the end of carrying heat. But the brain is of this sort; for it stands as the coldest and most moist of all parts of the body (Differences 24 and 25). Also, veins proceed through other members, passing through all of them; but none pass through the heart. For that which passes through all things from something else cannot be the principle of those things. 

Furthermore, the heart is proportioned to the veins, since it is a thick, solid body and contains only blood, apart from the arteries and veins. Again, anatomy and the generation of the animal indicate that the heart is the first thing created, and blood is first in it. Furthermore, the motions of things desirable and saddening—and indeed all motions—appear to begin in the generation of the animal from the heart and to be terminated in the same. 

Still further, its middle location and the site itself, so skillfully arranged, show the heart to be the principle of the veins and other things. Likewise, that which is bloodless, having no heat, is not the principle of the veins. But the brain is such a thing. It is the most bloodless of all, and neither a small nor a large vein terminates in it (from the third book of the *Histories*). It also possesses no sense of touch, just as neither blood nor the superfluities of animals do (from the third book of *On the Parts*). Therefore, the heart is the principle of the veins.

...and not the brain, the liver, or another organ. There were also others, such as **Galen** with his followers, as it appeared, who posited that the veins arise from the liver. They asserted this most strongly because the veins originate from it, branch out, and draw nourishment, just like the roots of plants from the earth. This, as will be seen, cannot stand; for although the veins fixed in the liver bring nourishment to the heart through its mediation—and in this they have a similarity to certain plants—they do not, however, originate from there. This is because their larger sections continually pass through the entire substance of the liver, which does not happen in something that is born from another, as with plants born from the earth, provided they are in their own place and not enclosed in a vessel. Nor do all plants branch out in the earth merely to draw nourishment, but also to be supported, so they do not fall from impacts and winds; and thus one may see many plants having only a single root.

Furthermore, they argue that the form of the blood is provided in the liver because a transformation into redness occurs in it, though it seems this power is sensed accidentally from the heart. Yet, it should not be said because of this that the form of the blood is primarily given in the liver; rather, it is diminished there. For some change of the **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid of digested food</term> toward redness is introduced in the **mesenteric veins** <term>meseraics: the veins of the mesentery that carry nutrients from the intestines</term>, in which, however, it is not said to be generated for this reason in any way. Since, therefore, the blood in the liver is in the process of reaching perfection, and since its nature does not vary between the more and the less perfected states, there will be one agent of the fully induced form. For things that are of one species are introduced by one agent; that agent will be the heart and not the liver, since the heart is the most formal <note>meaning: the most essential or life-giving</note> of all the parts. Therefore, the heart will be the principle of the blood and the veins.

The followers of **Galen** are also moved by subtle arguments, whose deficiency will be noted in the fourth of the proposed points, and in the third, chapter 14. The discourse on this remains ambiguous, inciting the question: does such a vein continuing between the heart and the liver descend from the heart to the liver itself, or does it ascend from the liver to the heart, or is it according to both intentions? To ascend or descend in such a way is nothing other than to originate from the heart or the liver, or independently from both. There were, however, some contemporaries saying that the veins could be considered in a twofold manner: by reason of the liquid matter or the containing vessel. In one way, they say they undoubtedly originate from the heart. Or they consider that which is carried through them, namely the blood; and because this is twofold—imperfect from the liver and perfected from the heart—they say the veins according to this contract a dual origin: of imperfection from the liver, and of perfection from the heart. But these people, though they may savor the truth regarding the first part, are foolish regarding the second, since here we are not asking about the origin of the content, but only of the container. Furthermore, it was stated before that perfection and imperfection are introduced by the same specific agent. There were also others positing that the veins originate from the heart as if from a primary mediated principle, but from the liver as if from an immediate and secondary one. This also cannot stand, because it will be noted clearly that the heart exists as the principle and immediate source of the veins.

### The Truth of the Matter

Regarding the third point, the truth is first explained... and thereafter it is shown that the heart is more noble than the ventricles. <note>original: "uētriculoꝙ cordis sit nobilior"</note> Regarding the first, it is well to be known that the heart is the principle of the veins, just as the **Peripatetics** <note>original: "pypathetici"; the followers of Aristotle</note> understand, not only in power but also in matter; and this will be shown in Difference 38. And it is noted by reason no less, for in **Aristotle's** *On Animals*, book 9, and book 3, chapter 21, along with the third book of the *Theory*: when the womb conceives the seed, finally, as is said in Difference 41, by the vigor of heat and the informative power, three vesicles are formed from the foaming seed. Of these, the first and most principal is the matter of the heart; the others are the ascending matter of the brain, and the third, descending on the right, the matter of the liver, such that this is separated from that of the heart, yet both are joined by a certain intermediate. This intermediate is nothing other than the matter of the **great vein** <note>the vena cava</note>, since nothing else exists between these two to continue them. This is confirmed because in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, the form and species of the liver are in the heart. Moreover, this vein is the principle and origin of the other veins, as its branching indicates.

Anatomy also shows this, since part of this vein called the **chyle** <note>here referring to the "vena chilis", a medieval name for the vena cava</note> is continuous with the liver, passing through one part to the other, descending entirely into the opposite parts, into both of which it sends out the aforementioned emerging veins. Similarly, the branches of the vein called the **portal vein** <term>vena porta: the vein that carries blood from the digestive organs to the liver</term> are said to branch in the concavity of the liver, being continued with the branches of the **vena cava** <term>vena cava: the large vein that returns blood to the heart from the body</term> originating from the heart, which branch from the hump of the liver to the middle. Although, because of the smallness of the passages, one cannot discern this with diligence. Whence in the fourth book *On the Parts of Animals*, what is called the "unfelt membrane" <note>original: "insentierū ymen"</note> is stretched continuously from the protrusion of the intestines to the great vein, and to a region full of many and thick veins tending from the intestines toward them. Nor should it be said that the continuation of the liver with the heart is only from an artery and not from the aforesaid vein, since the vein is more noble, as will be noted, even than the artery, and it is also incomparably larger than it. For this artery which is directed to the liver is very small, and from the lower part of the very large artery they pass, namely, branched through the back, it meets the concavity of the liver: both on account of its smallness and also on account of its hiddenness. **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay."</note> in many places in *On Animals* did not know of it, testifying that no vein tends to the liver in a circle, just as many performing anatomy do not know how to find it. Wherefore also perversely **Averroes** <note>original: "Ax̄."; referring to the second book of his "Colliget"</note> wanted many arteries to come to the liver. Regarding this artery, **Galen**, the prince of anatomy, knowing it better, testifies in the fifth book of *On the Use of the Parts* that it vivifies only the lower part of the liver. For the upper, hump-like part is vitalized by the mediation of the motion of dilation and constriction of the heart.

This is also discussed in Difference 31. And if this mode of demonstration should be noted in Difference 41, it declares that the nerves originate from the heart, and even more so that the veins are born from the same, since the nerves do not pass through the substance of the brain in the same way, nor do they appear so continuously to the heart as the veins do. Furthermore, the origin is attempted by its principle of production in the embryo. The vein, however, does not bear witness to the liver, since it is nothing but the congealed substance of animals. Nor as some of the unlearned say, that they originate from the liver because they have a similarity with its **membrane** <term>panniculo: the thin protective layer of an organ</term>...

It utilizes embryonic development and anatomical observations of the vena cava and portal vein to support the heart's primacy in the body's hierarchy.</summary>
