<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the origin of the vascular system. While the previous page argued against the liver as the source of the veins (countering the Galenic view), this page reinforces the Aristotelian position that the heart, specifically the right ventricle, is the true principle of the veins, blood, and life itself.</meta>

...because by the same reasoning they would be born from the lung or the spleen. Furthermore, to be born in this way would not be to arise from the **liver** <note>original: "epate"</note> nor from its membrane. Also, they would not pass through into the liver by totally piercing the substance of the membrane, just as the arteries do not penetrate the heart. Likewise, the membrane of the liver is not truly part of its constitution. The veins, however, attest to the heart, and especially to its right ventricle, both by reason of its corporeality and its capacity, as well as its content, since blood is found in both alone. 

Furthermore, that which is the principle of the blood is the principle of the veins; for the veins are ordained for the blood. But blood originates in the heart, since the heart is "salty and humid," as stated in the second book of the *Collection*; <note>likely referring to a collection of medical aphorisms or Galenic commentaries</note> whence it is the first of the complexions. The heart is by nature the most "bloody" <note>original: "sanguinitimum"</note> and the purest of all the internal organs of animals. When this occurs, the blood will be the principle of the heart, both perfect and imperfect, since they are ultimately of the same nature. 

Again, life consists of nourishment, as stated in the second book of *On the Soul*. <note>Aristotle, De Anima</note> But nourishment is primarily in the heart, as seen in the third book of *On the Parts of Animals* and the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*. Nor should it be said, as some "little scholars" <note>original: "scioli" — a dismissive term for those with superficial knowledge</note> claim, that the proper nourishment for the heart's nutrition comes from the womb; <note>original: "matrice"</note> rather, it must first be changed by the heart so that through digestion it is made similar to itself. Since the heart is the principle of this blood, it will also be the principle of the **veins** <note>specifically referring here to the "vena cava"</note> and the arteries. 

Because of this, it should be known that because the vein arises from the right ventricle of the heart, it is more noble than the artery, just as **Galen** signifies the former over the latter. For he maintains that the right ventricle is nobler and more vital than the left; furthermore, just as the noble and primary is in the "front" rather than the "back," and "above" rather than "below," so the "right" is over the "left." These qualities belong to the right ventricle, while the others belong to the left. 

This is particularly remarkable because the heart indicates the principle of the whole body, since motion and life are first found in it and last to leave it, as stated in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*. Now, since the same reasoning applies to the whole and the part—at the beginning of the *Histories* <note>Aristotle, History of Animals</note>—the principle stands to the part as the whole to the whole. In that part where motion and life cease last, that part will be nobler and prior. This is the right side. For when motion and life cease in the left ventricle, it is perceived for a little hour <note>a short duration</note> in the right. For when it tends toward death—as I have often observed at the beginning—the left side ceases to move, moving toward the right, always establishing itself toward that which moves and toward the immobile center of motion, until it reaches the place where this vein is born from the heart. Once this immobile center is established, motion is perceived around it for a modest time, until finally all motion and life cease here. Thus, the vein is intended to arise more from the heart than the artery; whence in the thirteenth book of *On Animals*: 

->**The better and nobler part of the two parts of the heart is on the right, and from that side much of its power emanates.**<-

But perhaps someone following **Galen** might disagree. For he expressly feels the opposite in the sixth book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts*, where it is written that the right ventricle of the heart was made for the sake of the lung, so that it might grant it nourishment. He says the reflected motion of the heart is composed of two motions and two rests, or like that of the pulse. In such a motion, since a rest always intervenes in the middle—according to the *Physics*—one must establish a certain immobile part in the heart itself. For it is proven in *On the Cause of Motion in Animals* that all motion must lean and be supported by something immobile. 

A certain part of this exists in the heart, and especially in those having two ventricles. Therefore, when the power fails in such a state, the aforementioned motion of the heart cannot exist in the left ventricle alone, which is solid and thick. For parts that are so thick and solid are disobedient to motion; they cannot move laterally in the manner of dilation and constriction toward a single established immobile wall. As the power of the pulse fails, this motion arrives at the right side of the heart, where the parts are softer, and especially at the place where the "great vein" <note>the vena cava</note> continues with the heart. For there, the pulsating power, aided by the flexibility of the parts for motion, can establish one immobile part... the motion will arrive at the first side. 

Therefore, the right ventricle will not be nobler than the left here. To which it must be said that the argument brought forward is not valid, because organs are ordained toward their actions as their own end, and not vice versa. For flutes are provided for the flute-player, and not the flute-player for the flutes, as stated in the fourth book of *On the Parts of Animals*. Whence, since nature produced such organs on the right side in which, as was remarked, motion and life can endure until the end (but not in the left), it must be concluded simply that the right side is nobler than the left. For nature would have ordained the aforementioned things in the left if it were as noble as the right. 

One might see a sign of this in the fact that the "fifth part of the lung" <note>the accessory lobe of the right lung</note> which is between the two, reaches toward the right side... **Galen**, however, perhaps reasons that this part of the lung does not consist of the principal part. Or perhaps its magnitude indicates this. **Galen** would also insist that the left ventricle has other utilities for which it was made denser than the right. But this also is not valid, because the principal act of the heart is to provide "vegetative" life <note>growth and nutrition</note>, toward which all its most powerful organs are ordained. 

Again, I have perceived some people having a pulse—not a small one—notably stronger in the left than the right due to nature or disease; yet as they approached death, it was the opposite. But as they resumed their strength, they returned to how they were before. Furthermore, in suffocated animals, all the blood is found in the veins and none in the arteries. This does not happen except because the "governing power" <note>virtus regitiva</note>, with all the spirits and blood exiting the arteries at the time of strangulation, runs together to the heart as if to a citadel. They pass through the perforated wall <note>the septum</note> as much as possible, as shown in the third book of *On Natural Things*, into the right side as if into their greater refuge. Nor should it be said that the spirit existing in the left ventricle is nobler than that in the right. For that spirit exceeds both in heat and dryness because of the motion necessary for life. For life consists in motion.

The author uses observations of the dying and suffocated animals to show that life and blood retreat to the right side of the heart as a final "citadel."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate from the previous page regarding whether the veins and blood originate in the heart or the liver. The author is reconciling the views of Aristotle (who favored the heart) and Galen (who favored the liver), ultimately supporting the Aristotelian position while explaining the medical utility of Galen's observations.</meta>

...and nourishment. Its form is more firmly established in the **right ventricle** <note>original: "dextro uentre"</note>, since spirit and blood are most abundant and quantitative there, and not as qualitative as in the left ventricle. For there must be a proportion of those things in the right to those in the left, just as the blood of the "blood-maker" is to the **choler** <note>original: "colticum," referring to yellow bile or the choleric humor</note>. I posit that the right ventricle of the heart exists principally so that it might be the principle of the blood itself; the left, however, exists more so that life might be impelled into the rest of the body, from which benefit eventually comes back to the heart. 

Against this, Galen argues. Regarding his first point, it should be said that Galen and his many followers held another opinion, which is not maintained in the present case; or perhaps they spoke with "probability," as physicians do, whose speeches are concerned with appearances. 

Regarding Aristotle, it must be said that he spoke both properly and [comprehensively]. First: When he described anatomy there, he was following the soul from the outside. This is shown by the fact that he spoke of the path of the **flow** <note>original: "ffzus," likely "fluxus"</note> and the branching of the veins from the liver; which he perhaps hinted at in the *The Art of Medicine* <note>original: "tegni," referring to Galen's *Ars Medica*</note>, that they come from the liver as if from a beginning of the veins, but they do not truly "arise" there. 

To the other point, it must be said that motion is twofold, as appearing in the eighth book of the *Physics*. One kind is from an impressed form that generates it; this is always determined to a specific place by the generator. For as nature provides the form, so it also provides the place, since the place is the preserver of the form, as stated in the fourth book of the *Physics* and in *On the Heavens and the Earth*. This motion exists in the being of the elements, in that they follow the motion of the element that predominates in them, as stated in the fourth book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*; in this genus of motion, the whole moves, and the parts move in a similar manner. 

There is another motion from a form, such as the soul induced by **leaping powers** <note>original: "salibus," likely "salitibus" or "virtutibus salientibus"</note>, which many times does not follow the motion of the predominating element. This is apparent in heavy terrestrial matter, which by the vigor of the soul tends upwards to excite the appetite of the mouth of the stomach; whereas light, igneous **bile** <note>original: "cola"</note> tends downwards to stimulate the intestines, so that they may eject the superfluity contained within them. Therefore, [Aristotle] in the first book of *On the Parts of Animals*, considering this motion so contrary to the prior natural order, gave thanks to God, the best of all makers. If the veins moved in that former way, they would move with a motion different from the whole, just as the motion of the heart and the arteries is distinct (Difference 80). In the first kind of motion, the veins could not be moved very far, since they are soft and flexible, not strong enough to follow the motion of the heart. 

To the other point, it should be said: it is not necessary for all the blood to pass into the heart to acquire its form, since natural blood can be rendered vital by the attraction of the extreme arteries from the extremities of the veins and vice versa (Difference 31). For there occurs a mutual meeting of these; there is a "breathing together" and a confluence of all things in existence through the same natural pores, as stated in the third book [of the *Physics*]. From this it also appears that it is not inconvenient for blood to both ascend and descend laterally through the **vena cava** <note>the "hollow vein," the main vein returning blood to the heart</note>. For as the motions of nature are ordered, there are certain attractive and expulsive powers determined there, just as the **blind intestine** <note>the cecum</note> has only one opening through which nourishment enters as dregs, and eventually, after greater desiccation, exits from the same place. 

To the other point, it should be said that it is not enough for something to be a principle simply by being the smallest in quantity; it must instead be the greatest in power. For this, according to Aristotle, is the principle of reason in his works on *Sophistical Refutations* and the *History of Animals*. 

The veins that are in the liver, although they are smallest in quantity, are not greatest in vigor, since they are not in themselves the principles of any great actions, but operate by the power of the heart. Furthermore, those veins of the liver are even smaller in the simple, branched members, concerning which it is written in the third book of *On the Parts of Animals* that their passages are smaller than the thickness of the blood which is transmitted through them. Therefore, it is said in the first book [of the *History of Animals*] that the blood flows from these into the members from the divine part. Even if these veins are so small, no one considers them to be the principles of the great veins, but rather things derived from a principle. 

To the other point, it should be said: the veins do not "testify" to the liver or its membrane as having been declared the source, any more than to the heart; in fact, they testify to it less. 

To the other point, it should be said: although the **liver** <note>original: "epar"</note> is hot and humid and has a purple color, it does not appear to be the giver of the blood's form, but rather the **preparation** <note>original: "prepatium"</note>. Just as the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: "mefaraice," from *mesaraic*</note> are called "internal livers" by Galen, they prepare the chyle by transforming it into a certain reddish humor. The principle of the form of blood, simply speaking, was shown to be the heart first. 

To the other point, it should be said: it was shown that the veins are born from the brain because they belong to its membrane. The heart does not have a membrane from which they are born that contains them so vehemently; as the text shows, what is attached to it is a certain continuation of its own strong texture, which is of a different nature than a membrane, being woven together like nerves and ligaments (Difference 44). Even nerves, along with membranes, originate from the heart (Difference 41). 

To the other point, it should be said: their speech is largely "apparent" or probable medical talk, but not exquisitely certain, as is seen in Difference 44. For it is said in the first book of *Natural Things* that the interior tunic of a vein is more than double the exterior one. Regarding Galen, I say that in another part, in *On the Use of the Parts*, he was of the opposite opinion to the physicians, being then of another opinion just as in his books on natural science he follows the Aristotelian view—and in *On the Use of the Parts* not a little. Or perhaps it is an error of the scribe, since in the first, fourth, and fifth books, it is already stated that the veins arise from the heart. For what is contained in this book is a certain abbreviation, as the books in Greek contain seventeen volumes; thus the Greek series of the same text says: "The veins indeed begin from the liver," as is said in the dogmas which are shown according to Hippocrates and Plato. And all things are consistent and testify to the truth. 

To the other point, it should be said: he speaks according to the position of Aristotle, who holds that the veins are seen to be born from the heart according to the natural way. I recognize the dogmas of the **Peripatetics** <note>the followers of Aristotle</note>, but not the others, at least not as closely. Or it should be said that whatever he said there, as appears in the third book of *Natural Things*, he did not want the veins to "arise" from the heart in the sense of being "born." To be "born" is to arise. To be "implanted," however, is to be set directly into something else, just as "to be born out of" or "to be transplanted" is to be set laterally into something else rather than being struck into it. Whence in that same place: "The vein tending into the lung is said to be transplanted into it," just as the veins emerging into the kidneys do in that manner.

<meta>This page transitions from a discussion on anatomy to a scholastic biological debate regarding the "soul" of sperm. It specifically addresses whether the reproductive seed, once separated from the body, is "animate" (living) or merely has the potential for life. The text heavily references Aristotle’s *On the Generation of Animals* and *On the Soul*.</meta>

# DIFFERENCE 48.

<margin>q</margin> It is shown that separated **sperm** <note>original: "spma"</note> is not animate, because that which is becoming animate is not yet animate.

<margin>☛</margin> For that which is "becoming" among permanent things does not yet exist. But sperm is becoming each of the individual parts and the animate whole (according to the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*). Furthermore, everything here that is animate is nourished; for it is living through a soul. Life indeed is sustained by nourishment. But sperm does not seem to be nourished, since it does not yet have the organs or the actions of nutrition.

Moreover, no **superfluity** <term>superfluity (original: superfluītas): in medieval biology, a byproduct or "leftover" substance from the process of digestion and refinement, rather than a primary organ or tissue</term> is animate, since everything animate is necessary and helpful. But sperm is a superfluity (see Difference 34); therefore, these are to be cast off. Again, everything animate participates in the soul, since it receives its reality and its name from it. But sperm does not participate in it; if it did, it would be a plant or an animal, for these alone participate in the soul here, the acts of which denote an animate thing.

Alternatively, the soul will be in the animate thing from the sperm from which it came, or from the soul of the one coupling. Not the first, since it is a superfluity. Nor the second, because the soul is in the parts, or it is one of the other forms; hence the soul cannot be separated from the coupling partner according to a part. Therefore, separated sperm is not animate.

**To the contrary:** Aristotle in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*. Also, that which does not cast off the soul—indeed, which contains it within its scope—is animate. This is for the purpose of it being something animate. Sperm is truly of this kind; for it does not cast off the soul as if it were a being with the potential to live, but it is something that has it, like a seed and a fruit (according to the second book of *On the Soul*).

Likewise, that is animate in which the act of the soul is shown, since acts lead us to the knowledge of the powers of the soul (according to the second book of the same). In sperm, a marvelous action of the soul is found, since it not only preserves the whole but leads to that which is apparent. For as soon as it falls into the **womb** <note>original: "mricē," likely *matrice*</note>, a membrane surrounds it (Difference 36). Then it draws blood to itself and so on, as will be shown from what follows.

Furthermore, that is animate in nature which works like things made by art; since just as art works through a certain principle, so does nature. It differs, however, because the principle of art is from without, while that of nature is from within (*On the Generation of Animals* and the *Lessons on Nature*). But sperm is such a thing, for it acts like things made by art (Difference 36). Therefore, separated sperm is animate.

Regarding the first, it must be known what sperm is (Difference 33). An **animate** <term>animate (original: aiatū): possessing an *anima* or soul; in this context, it refers to biological life and the capacity for growth and sensation</term> body is one participating in the soul in a certain way, which is the substance or form of a physical body having the potential for life, or the principle of living, sensing, moving, and understanding (second book of *On the Soul*). Sperm is called "separated" when it has been separated from the one coupling and received in a suitable place, supported by the principal spirits, and possessed by the formative power.

Regarding the second, it must be known that certain of the ancients, positing that sperm is substantially "cut" from the whole body, are forced to confess that it is animate not only in potential but also in act. Hence, in the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*: if the parts are dispersed in the seed, how do they live? As if he were saying it would be impossible. For those things that live must be united. If they were continuous, then the seed would be a certain small, continuous animal. Which is also ridiculous. For it would happen that the soul of the generated thing would be fragmented, and its substance would cease immediately upon generation, or it would have been annihilated long ago (Difference 24).

Again, if the seed were an existing animal, it would have sensation; for by this an animate thing is distinguished from an inanimate one (*On the Soul*, book 1). But it does not sense. For it does not contract when pricked; because of which, sperm will not be actually animate.

Regarding the third, it must be known first that sperm is animate in potential and not yet in act. This division of the whole nature of being holds in these matters. Finally, it must be seen what kind of potentiality this is, and afterwards how it progresses into act, and fourthly, what happens regarding the principle moving it.

Regarding the first of these, it must be known that just as in vegetables there is first an inherent potential before the seed and root are emitted, so also in the fetus, in a certain way, while all the parts are potentially inherent, the principle exists most especially in readiness. Because of this, the heart is the first part separated in act. And indeed, the sperm and the fetus have the **nutritive soul** <note>original: "nutritiuā aīā"</note> as separable, though they are now joined. Hence, all things must be posited in power/virtue, but they do not have them in act before they are separated and perform the work of the soul (*On the Generation of Animals*, book 2).

Furthermore, that is in "potential" which is led into "act" unless something hinders it. Such a thing is sperm; for it inclines naturally from potential into act, like something impressed toward perfection. If it is said that every potential is led into act, because it would be idle unless it reached it, and nothing in the nature of things is frustrated in its proper end—it must be said that not every potential possesses the aforementioned truth, but only the most proximate one, which holds itself in the manner of a "habit," which emerges like a certain necessity, as its distinction will show.

Or perhaps someone might hinder this by showing that this potentiality does not yet exist in the nature of things. The principal question is also solved in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, which places a nature in the seed that is midway between that which has being "univocally pure" and "equivocally." For it does not have a soul in act like a perfect animal, nor is it deprived of it like a dead thing. But it has it in "virtue"—and that from afar. For it is like a **sleeping geometer** <note>original: "dormiens geometra," a classic Aristotelian example: a mathematician who is asleep has the knowledge (potentiality) to do math, but is not currently doing it (actuality)</note>, who geometrizes by his potential or "first act"; whereas one who is awake is more "proximate," like one geometrizing in act.

Regarding the second of these, it must be known that potential is spoken of in three ways according to "before" and "after" (*On the Soul*, book 1). One is an absolute aptitude, from which nothing goes out into act; for nothing is yet in it because of which it might go out into act. And this is called "absolutely material potential," having no form, like matter. Such is the potential in a newborn infant for writing, or the matter of the sperm when it still lies buried in the sources of the limbs. Another is an aptitude more ready for act, but which cannot reach it without a medium and alteration; this potential is called "potentiality," like that of a boy for writing when he has already learned the instruments of writing; or of the sperm when the seed is in the testes; and this potential is between God and...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the nature of sperm, moving from its "animate" status to the physical process of conception and early embryonic development. There is also a third type [of potentiality], which is an **aptitude** joined to the act without alteration. For it is not correct to say a wise man is "altered" when he acts wisely, just as a builder is not altered when he builds. Specifically concerning the **soul** <note>original: "anima"</note>, this potentiality is called **perfection** <term>perfection (original: perfectio): a translation of the Greek term *entelecheia*, referring to the state of a thing having reached its full purpose or "actualized" its potential</term>, like the potential of a writer when he is not actually writing; he is able to write whenever he wishes, provided he is not hindered. 

This same potentiality exists in the **sperm** <note>original: "sperma"</note> injected into the **womb** <note>original: "matrice"</note>, which is set in motion by the act of coupling and participates in a certain excited state of action, as will be explained further. This [potentiality] can be of two kinds, depending on whether it is more or less close to the final form: one potentiality is called a "habitual state" (*habitudinis*) and the other a "habit" (*habitus*). (Distinction 67).

But in every discussion concerning the soul, only a two-fold potentiality is distinguished. The first contains the two previously mentioned; the second is the **first act** and "perfection" or "form." **Action** <note>original: "actus"</note> is also two-fold in reality: the first is the potentiality already mentioned, and the second is the actual operation or action itself. (Distinction 17).

Regarding the third point of this study, it should be known that the perfected sperm is first propelled into the womb by the one coupling. It moves by a power held within it, just as in **automata** <term>automata: mechanical devices that appear to move by themselves; scholastic writers often used the gears or "successive motions" of machines as a metaphor for biological processes</term> (that is, things that move by an internal cause), a most wonderful thing happens: from the first touch, they move in a certain order of succession, and the remaining parts continue to move as long as the power of the initial touch lasts. This is seen in the third book of *On Accidents*, like pebbles or bricks arranged in a row; when the first is touched, it hits the next, and so they all fall in turn. This is similarly shown by machines and mills. (Whence, from book 2 of *On the Generation of Animals*).

It happens that one part moves while another does not, like the wonder of automata. For the parts at rest, being arranged in a certain way, possess potentiality; when something external moves them, that which was in a "habitual state" immediately becomes "in act." In these cases, the mover is not touching the object now, but it had touched it before. 

It happens similarly regarding sperm; although the mover is not touching it now, a motion was previously initiated within it. For just as the art of building constructs a house, so the sperm is aided by the womb. Once the womb has received the sperm, its opening <note>the cervix</note> narrows so much that even the point of a needle could not enter. (From the third book of *Natural Philosophy*). 

The first thing that appears in the sperm thus received is a certain **vaporous foaminess** <note>original: "spumositas"</note> caused by its internal heat. (Whence, in Distinction 21): The first disposition of the sperm enclosed in the womb is its foaminess, which results from the operation of the **formative power** <term>formative power (original: virtus informativa): the biological force believed to organize matter into the specific shapes and organs of a living being</term>, mediated by heat. At that time, a thin skin from the womb, like the membrane inside an egg, surrounds the sperm.

<margin>
**Hippocrates** on the formation of the embryo.
Whence, book 9 of *The History of Animals*.
</margin>

When the sperm has been received by the womb and remained there for a time, it is encircled by a **membrane** <note>original: "ymen"</note>, which surrounds it just as a skin forms on moist bodies when they are heated and then cooled. (From book 2 of *On the Generation of Animals*), as is seen in lungs that have cooled. This sperm derives from a certain inner and more liquid part of itself the nourishment of a purer sustenance, just like the seed of plants cast into the earth. 

<margin>
**Avicenna**
</margin>

Just as in the seeds of plants there is immediately a "first milk," so too in the matter of animals: the "superfluity" resulting from the compaction of the pure with the impure serves as nourishment for the purer part, which has been "foamed out" into the sperm. The power by which the embryo is nourished is derived from the father, until it finally fades and another more noble power arrives. 

<margin>
**Aristotle**
</margin>

(Book 16 of *Animals*): Another power follows the "acquired" nutritive power that comes from the father. For it is believed that the nutritive power coming from the father grows old, until the **complexion** <term>complexion (original: complexio): the specific balance of the four "humors" or qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a person's health and nature</term> changes through transformation. With that new complexion, a nutritive power proper to the individual continues after the old one has faded. 

Thus, that which is acquired from the father cannot suffice for the governance of the body until the end; it must be assisted by another, stronger nutritive power that nourishes in a different way than the first power held from the father. On account of which (Distinction 22): The formative power does not require external nourishment during the stage of formation, provided no perceptible dissolution or harm occurs. Nor should it be said that the male seed is mixed with the female sperm as nourishment, since it does not enter into the physical constitution of the fetus. (Distinction 37).

Finally, with the sperm thus supported by itself, the vaporous foaminess swells up. This foaminess shifts from the center of the sperm toward the outer edges by the power of heat. This motion belongs to the heat itself; when it meets the obstacle of the surrounding membrane, it is refracted back into the center, where it settles and establishes a foundation. (Whence, in Distinction 22): The entire "blowing-out" <note>the expansion of gas/spirit</note> is pushed back by the membrane toward the center of the moisture, so that the **place for the heart** may be prepared.

That this is produced from this spermatic foaminess through heat and the work of the formative power is shown by the swelling and whiteness of the formed seed. 

<margin>
**Avicenna**
</margin>

The **spirit** <term>spirit (original: spiritus): a subtle, airy substance thought to circulate through the body to carry heat and life-force</term> makes the mixture of sperm soft and illuminates it with whiteness. This is why seeds appear white, unless they have been "over-cooked" by excessive heat, like pepper. These qualities are caused by the subtle, airy foam, as snow and soap-bubbles indicate. This designates the substance of the "spermatic spirit." 

When it is first formed by the heat of the body and nature, it is excited and soon dissolves the viscous moisture. This moisture is carried to the outer parts and begins to settle as it cools due to its distance from the source of heat. This spirit, pulsing within the moist parts, distends the moisture by the power of heat so that the shapes of the limbs can be received. 

(Aristotle): The seed is divided into three **vesicles** <note>bubbles or small sacs</note>, of which the primary and middle one is for the constitution of the **heart**. The one ascending directly is for the **brain**, while the one on the right descending is for the **liver**. These vesicles fill up, and the first develops bloody threads like veins, by which they draw the matter of blood from the womb. Finally, the heart begins to form, along with the other two members.

...and the **navel** <margin>navel</margin>; for although the principle of their creation precedes the creation of the navel, nevertheless the completion of those three and especially the two comes before it. Now, the power behind this so divine a work is called the **formative power** <margin>formative power</margin>, separated from the soul of the parent, and stirred into action by the impulse of those coming together in copulation. This power **Galen** <note>original: "Ga." — Galen of Pergamon, the influential 2nd-century physician</note>, in his work *On Natural Faculties*, calls the supreme presiding art and a divinely implanted force, as **Haly** <margin>Haly</margin> <note>original: "Haly" — Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician</note> ascribed to it. 

But **Avicenna** <margin>Avicenna's intellect</margin> <note>original: "Ay." — the Persian philosopher and physician Ibn Sina</note> named it the **"called intellect,"** to distinguish it from the potential and active intellect, as an output of the intellectual soul. As he says in the third book *On the Soul*: "I call it the **intellect** <margin>intellect</margin> by which the soul forms opinions and gains wisdom." This is to distinguish it from the intellect which **Anaxagoras** <margin>Anaxagoras</margin> <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</note> proposed as a god of **chaos** <term>chaos: the formless matter from which the universe was organized</term>, separating like parts from it. 

And therefore, the **erroneous** <margin>erroneous</margin> understanding of the **Jacobites** <note>likely referring to a contemporary theological or philosophical faction accusing the author of heresy</note> who persecute me becomes apparent here, **as if I had claimed** <margin>as if I claimed</margin> that the intellectual soul is drawn out from the potentiality of matter. This and fifty-four other errors were attributed to me in Distinction IX. From their hands, by the grace of God and the apostolic [authority] acting as mediator, I have praise-worthily escaped <margin>Book IV</margin>. 

Concerning this power, in the 16th book *On Animals*, **Aristotle** <margin>Aristotle's power</margin> <note>original: "Ar."</note> says: the formative power is that which gives life, and it is **proportional** <margin>proportional</margin> to the power of the celestial [bodies]. And this power makes things similar to the celestial powers, as far as it is possible to receive that life. It is distinct throughout the **substance of the body** <margin>substance of the body</margin>, whether it be wet or dry. In the sperm, the substance is the potentiality capable of receiving this power; and it is the **spirit** <margin>spirit</margin> <term>spirit (original: spiritus): a subtle, airy substance thought to carry life and heat through the body</term> which is the first carrier of **celestial heat**; and it is the cause of all formed parts. 

This power is abstracted from the body; receiving this from Avicenna, the **Commentator** <margin>Avicenna, Commentator</margin> <note>"The Commentator" usually refers to Averroes, the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher, who provided the standard commentaries on Aristotle</note>, in his commentary on the 7th book of Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, said in the book *On Animals* that it is similar to the **intellect** <margin>intellect</margin> in this: that it does not act through a bodily instrument or a specific organ, unlike other natural powers. For the other powers do not perform the action of an operative intellect, but rather work through specific limits and organs. 

Therefore **Galen** <margin>Galen</margin> doubts regarding it, saying: "I do not know whether this power is the creator or not." And in another of his books, Galen compares it to an **adamant** <margin>adamant</margin> <term>adamant: a legendary rock or crystal of extreme hardness, often associated with magnets</term> and comes to see it [this way]. In the second book of *On Natural Faculties*, he posits that the power is a certain attraction without a mind, just as a **magnet** <margin>magnet</margin> <term>magnet (original: magnes): a lodestone</term> has the power of attracting iron. 

But ultimately it does not act at all except through the **heat** <margin>heat</margin> which is in itself. It is not a form within the heat in the way the soul is enclosed in celestial bodies. Therefore, **Aristotle** <margin>Aristotle</margin> praises this power and attributes it to divine principles, not natural ones. In the second book of *On the Generation of Animals* <margin>generation</margin>, he says of it: "The body of the semen into which the principle of the soul goes out, and this is indeed **separable** <margin>separable</margin> from the body in whichever things something divine is perceived; and such a thing is what is called **intellect** <margin>intellect</margin>." 

Considering therefore that it does not yet have a shaped organ in the spermatic mass, Aristotle called it "separable." However, its separability is different from that of the intellect, and far lesser, for the intellect is entirely separable. This divine practical power, more noble than other powers of **generation**, since it is simple and almost immaterial, does not immediately touch the matter. It required a more distinct subject to carry it (*vehiculate*) to give the appropriate shapes and forms to the limbs. This [carrier] was the **spirit** <term>spirit (original: spiritus)</term>: for it is a subtle body, the vehicle of the power. Since it is simple, it also required an instrument, just as other mixed powers do. 

Now, there are two instruments of this power. One is **celestial heat** <term>celestial heat (original: calor celeste): the life-giving warmth associated with the sun and stars</term>, which is continually life-giving, never failing, making animate things reach toward a certain celestial strength. For it works toward the consistency and containment of things, just as all celestial power causes substances to be constituted and contained in being. This is the more worthy of the instruments, through which the power performs its more noble acts.

There is also for it another secondary instrument, namely **elemental heat**, which does not have the power to give life in every way, but rather tends to corrupt unless it is governed by celestial heat. By this heat, matter and nourishment are attracted and prepared by the formative power, separating them from opposing conditions, digesting and changing them; for it scatters heterogeneous things and brings together homogeneous things. In the second book of *On Generation and Corruption*, nature prepares the matter for shaping just as **fire and water** (according to Aristotle) prepare **iron** for making a sword, softening the hard parts and hardening the soft. Finally, with the "idea" existing in the soul, the form of the sword is introduced into the iron. This dual heat is also distinguished in the ripening of fruit. 

The physicians call this formative power, thus prepared, the "first transformative power," to distinguish it from the transformative power of nourishment in the third digestion, so that the formative power may shape it and make it stay in the place of lost parts; these latter are the nutritional powers. 

The matter upon which the formative power works with these instruments is **menstrual blood** <term>menstrual blood (original: sanguis menstruus)</term>, drawn from the womb into the place of generation, which receives the proper forms of the limbs, and finally guards them through nourishment and growth. Whence Aristotle says: In all sperm there is that which makes the sperm fertile, namely celestial heat. This is not fire, nor such a power, but a certain spirit contained in the sperm and its foam, and in the **spirit** <margin>spirit</margin> is a nature proportional to the order of the stars. As Aristotle says in the book *On the Heart*: **Spirit** is a bodily substance generated from the mixture of elements and acting in the likeness of the super-celestial bodies. In the fourth book *On the Soul*, he says: "It fashions its own vessels into the likeness of celestial bodies." For this reason, fire does not generate many animals, nor does anything consist in fire or dryness; but only the warmth of the sun and of animals generates. For "man and the sun generate man," as stated in the second book of *Physics*. In the aforementioned spirit, the power first receives the vital principle. Therefore, the vital power is the primary power that moves this spirit...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of embryology, specifically focusing on the "spirit" (the refined vapor that carries life) and the "formative power" (the intelligence that shapes the body). ...when it proceeds from the **refinement** of the moistures existing in the mass of generation. For the **spirit** <term>spirit: in medieval medicine, a subtle, airy substance that acted as a bridge between the soul and the physical body</term> is generated from the refinement of the humors. This, however, will be the **innate, implanted spirit**. Finally, according to **Avicenna** <note>original: "Ay." — Ibn Sina</note>, the spirit receives its first principle through this power, and it is the first [power] of **souls**, in whose strength the **heart** is created; then, from the motion of the heart and the arteries, a **second spirit** is generated: a material, flowing spirit. In the sixth book of *On Animals* <note>Aristotle's "De Animalibus"</note>, he says the same: in the **sperm** is the primary substance capable of receiving this power—namely the **vital power**—and the first spirit carrying this heat is the cause of all parts of the sperm. This heat, I say, is **celestial**; whence he says in the same place that because this heat coming from the super-celestial regions has an effect in its power which the heat of a fire could not have.

Indeed, this spirit is seen to exercise **four acts** regarding the beginning of generation:

1.  The first is to **dissolve and extend** the moisture by its own heat-power joined to it, so that it may become receptive to **forms**.
2.  The second is to **strike and beat** powerfully throughout the whole moisture, by which the passages, holes, and cavities are established, such as the heart and the arteries, forming the vessels themselves.
3.  The third is to carry the **formative power** presiding over this work to all the formations of the limbs; for this is the specific office of the spirit.
4.  The fourth is to **separate its own paths** from the paths of the moisture; for the spirit could not pass quickly through the moisture’s paths because of its thickness and density, whereas the spirit must swiftly illuminate the whole body, like a **candle** lighting up a house. For a long time, the path of the spirit was joined to the path of the **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: the essential fluid believed to be the basis of life and longevity</term>.

And these indeed are the **natural operations** of the spirit implanted in the seed. That this is so is clear, for everything that is moved must have a **motor** appropriate to itself. From those things said in [Aristotle's] *Physics*: since we see the material principles of generation moved specifically to transform themselves into the proper forms and figures of living things, a **motor** must be present. This motor can be nothing other than the **formative power**, and therefore it is sometimes called the **soul** by physicians. But because this power, being formal and simple, cannot inform diverse things by itself, it required an **instrument** <note>the "spirit"</note> which might introduce the diversity of shapes. It would be unworthy for the soul to be the substance that carries these out, which is why it assumed an instrument through reason. Furthermore, just as the **ideal form** in the mind of a craftsman needs tools because it does not immediately touch the material, so too does this power of formation require them.

With these principles of generation thus acting and being acted upon by one another, the **heart** is formed along with the other parts. By the vigor of the formative power and its other principles, the aforementioned **flowing spirit** is generated from the **menstrual matter** <note>The material provided by the mother, according to the science of the time</note> through the power of the earlier spirit and the heat inhering in the heart. This happens through the motion of the heart and the arteries and the friction of the vapors of that matter, which helps the earlier "son" of spirits and the heat in extending and attracting matter to complete the **figuring of all members**, and to prepare and **cook** the menstrual matter so that it may pass not only into the formation of the limbs but also into their **nutrition**, and especially that of the heart, since it finishes those parts first.

Thus, this spirit is seen to do two things in the menstrual matter, and it differs from the aforementioned spirit in that it is **not the cause of the heart's formation**, but rather is formed **by** that body which is already organized and divine. This spirit clearly seems only to carry the **vital power** through the whole body, and to give it the power of living and nourishing. To this spirit, as to the first, **four operations** are assigned:

1.  The first and primary is that it is **vivifying** (giving life), which it acquired from its motor, which is the **soul**.
2.  The second is that it is **heating**, which is derived from the heart, the source of heat.
3.  The third is that it **ventilates** <note>or "airs out"</note>, by which it dissolves and, as if by beating and pulsing, refines those things which are viscous in the body’s nutrition; it obtains this from its own proper motion.
4.  The fourth operation is, as is commonly said, that it dispatches every power of the soul to its essential and proper operations.

These spirits are both drawn out from the formation of the **fetus**. **Hippocrates**, concerning which double spirit and heat he will speak, also in the 59th [section]. Thus it appears how and by what means the potential of the sperm is led into act, so that a living creature is constituted.

Regarding the fourth point of this science, it must be known whether the **intrinsic moving principle** (called the **formative power** or the "called intellect") perishes. **Avicenna** seems to say it does not perish, saying: "If it were corrupted, what would be making the parts?" But it must be said that the **formative power does corrupt** (cease) once it has fashioned the **embryo**, just as the nutritive power from the father grows old. Its permanence is in vain after its act is perfected, as is seen in the **augmentative power** (the power of growth). This is shown because, according to **Aristotle**, it is something "separable" existing from the body, in which it apprehends something **divine**. This is because it does not have—as has been touched upon—any specific limb assigned to it as an instrument <note>unlike sight which has the eye, the formative power acts on the whole</note>, and thus it was likened to the **celestial powers**. This would not be the case if it endured in the already organized body; for then it would be joined to an organ, and the power would be simply natural. Therefore, it is abolished once the body is formed. Its "corruption" (end of activity) occurs at about **35 days** in males, and in females at about **45 days** (though some say 49). For embryos are formed around these times. Some have said that it perishes when the **intellective soul** is introduced, so that all operations of the embryo belong to the soul itself, which they try to persuade from **Aristotle's** book *On the Generation of Animals*.

...appears from what has been said before. Or rather, that it [the formative power] is resisted in many ways, since life first lives in the **embryo** <term>embryo: the earliest stage of development in the womb</term> as a plant (the **vegetative soul**), then as an animal (the **sensitive soul**), and finally as an **intellective soul** <term>intellective soul: the rational part of the human soul capable of reason and thought</term>. For the "formative" power, as the name itself shows, does not do this [permanently]; rather, it only exercises the act of formation along with other helping factors. 

Because of this, the common authorities have said that while the formative power is present, the **nutritive power** <term>nutritive power: the faculty that allows a living thing to absorb food and grow</term> is also present, as was shown from **Avicenna** <note>original: "Au." — Ibn Sina</note>. When this formative power recedes and the embryo is reduced to **prime matter** <term>prime matter: the most basic, formless substance from which all things are made</term>, the prior soul is destroyed and a new one follows, having the power of growing and nourishing. Finally, just as the first soul was reduced to prime matter due to preceding alterations, the prior soul is abolished and the **intellective soul** is introduced, supported by the two aforementioned powers. 

Regarding these things, **Avicenna** <note>original: "Au."</note> in the sixth book of *On Animals* agrees and denotes the time when it is sent in, saying: "When the heart and brain are found, the **rational soul** <note>the human soul capable of logic</note> is joined with them." According to the experts on birth, this happens in the **fourth month**, for the **Sun** then holds dominion over the embryo and denotes the soul of reason. He adds: "And the **natural sensitive soul** <note>the soul responsible for the five senses</note> is separated from it, which will sometimes be material and sometimes not; however, it will not yet be distinct, but rather like that in a drunk or an **epileptic** <note>original: "epylētico"</note>, but is completed by the intellect which provides from the outside." The rest of the powers are completed by the body and bodily things.

But concerning the predicted things, it happens to be doubted: why is the **intellective soul** not introduced from the very beginning, so that nature might proceed by a shorter path and avoid the "sin of plurality" <note>the philosophical problem of having multiple overlapping forms or souls in one body</note> of time? Furthermore, if the embryo is reduced twice (as was given) to **prime matter** and is corrupted, this looks more like a mode of **corruption** <note>death or breakdown</note> than of **generation** <note>creation or birth</note>. And the dispositions preceding the introduction of **form** into matter would seem to weaken and destroy it first, leading it to corruption, just as when someone born for death approaches it first through weakness and then is corrupted. This is not perceived here; rather, the embryo is seen to be continuously strengthened as it grows. 

It must be said that nature always works that which is better and through short ways, since there is no end to its wisdom. To the first of these, therefore, it must be said that nature tends from imperfect things to those that are perfect, gradually and secretly. And that **form** (according to **Plato**) is not imprinted except according to the disposition and merit of the matter. Since, therefore, the matter was not first disposed for the reception of the **intellective soul**, nor did it need it, it did not receive it, but was altered. Nature, having been taught, is seen to observe this order in corporeal things: for first it produces [milk] teeth, then, when they have served their purpose and are cast out, it supplies stronger ones. To the other point, it must be said that because it happens in an **instant** <note>the moment of transition from one state to another</note>, it is not perceived, since it is introduced by "change" and not by "motion" (as per the fifth book of the *Physics*). This also seems to be felt by **Avicenna** in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*, when he wants it to happen by itself, since "this whole is transmuted into that whole."

This would not be unless it reached **prime matter**; otherwise, it would not be a "generation" but rather a "substantive alteration" while the subject remained the same. Furthermore, unless the first form were corrupted, a second would come to a thing already existing in act; but what happens this way is an "accident" <note>a non-essential quality</note>. Similarly, since being comes from a **substantial form**, a thing having many forms would have many "beings," so that nothing here would truly exist as one thing. It must also be said that the preceding dispositions prepare for the reception of a more perfect form, and even if the preceding one is corrupted, it does not cause weakness even given the time. Nor is it like the corruption mentioned of one already born, because the dispositions preceding such corruption simply dispose it toward that, and not toward the reception of the forms of the embryo which perfect it further. 

To the first of the points introduced, it must be said that some, perverting the speech in many ways, want to take an argument from **Avicenna** <note>original: "Au."</note>: that if the formative power remained, the forms would be assigned by degrees. For example, **Avicebron** <note>Ibn Gabirol, a Jewish philosopher</note> in the treatise *The Fountain of Life*. But what they assume proceeds from a perverse understanding of him. For he does not proceed there by determining the truth, but by posing an opposition, as appears from his final determination. It must also be said that this power is saved within: while it informs all the parts, whether it informs some first and others later. For as he says, some have proposed that all parts are made at the same time, others that they are made one after the other, as the verses called those of **Orpheus** <note>legendary Greek poet/prophet</note> say. Know also that many things collected in this section are written specifically in other places. 

Concerning the fourth point of the first part, it must be said that the **sperm** <note>original: "spma"</note> is made animate in act, but not in potentiality, since it possesses that sufficient act nearby. To the other point, the answer has appeared. To the other, it must be said that no "superfluity" <note>waste or excess byproduct</note> is simply animate in quantity and quality. Sperm, however, is a superfluity not of quality but of quantity. Furthermore, it is not a superfluity of the species, but rather necessary—not only helping but necessary for the individual. To the other, it must be said that sperm is animate as was stated: for it participates in the soul potentially (as was declared) and not in act; whence the animal comes forth potentially. To the other, it must be said that it has now been shown how a superfluity exists as animate and in what way it does not; nor does the soul perish but it recedes: rather, a certain power falls away with the seed, just as a pusher grants power to the thing pushed. However, it is not from this that any "natural form" is implanted in it (from the third book of the *Ethics*).

## DIFFERENCE XLIX.

<margin>q</margin> That what is born in the **eighth month** <note>original: "octimensis"</note> lives is shown from the ninth book of the *History of Animals*, and the fourth book of *On the Generation of Animals*, and the tenth book of the *Problems*. It also comes from **Avicenna** in the ninth book of *On Animals* and the twenty-first book. Again, if what is seen less in a series [lives], then that which is seen more should live. It seems that an eight-month-old ought to live more than a **seven-month-old**, since by remaining longer in the womb, it possesses more vigor and growth for life...

It also begins an inquiry into why infants born in the eighth month were traditionally thought to have lower survival rates than those born in the seventh.</summary>

...can be received more fully. But as they agree, a **seven-month-old** <term>seven-month-old: an infant born in the seventh month of pregnancy</term> lives. Furthermore, the time of formation and movement in a female is delayed more than in a male by about six days, as they write, or thereabouts. Therefore, when the time of formation and movement is tripled, so that the time of birth is obtained according to the ingenuity of **Hippocrates** <note>original: "ypocratis"</note> and **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Halyab" — Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi, a famous Persian physician</note> in the third book of the *Theoretical Medicine*. 

But a female will be born in the ninth month, which happens perfectly. A male, however, anticipating the time, will be born in the eighth month at the most, and then he will live as if perfect; otherwise, nature would be working on something imperfect and not toward a finished end, which is absurd. For nothing imperfect is made by nature, neither regarding the time of fertility, nor according to the shaping and generation. This is from the *Problems* of **Alexander** <note>original: "Alex." — likely referring to the pseudo-Aristotelian Problems or Alexander of Aphrodisias</note>.

On the other hand, one born [in the eighth month] is likely to die because of the conflict of qualities that destroy nature, being entirely adverse to it. For this reason, the **astrologers** <term>astrologers: specifically "genetalici," those who cast birth charts</term> posit that one born under the power of **Saturn** <note>In medieval astrology, Saturn was the "Greater Malefic," associated with cold, death, and restriction.</note> does not live, as will be shown. But now suppose a movement happens where one is born in a time of most vehement frost; an eight-month-old, however, born in a warm time, will be so tempered that he will live no less than a nine-month-old. Perhaps in **Egypt** an eight-month-old will live, assisted by the heat of the region. And just as differences occur in other men—for in some places they live longer, and in others it happens differently—so it will also happen regarding the eighth month. Therefore, some born in the eighth month will live. Concerning this, **Haly Abbas**, **Alexander**, and other astrologers have made findings which experience shows us to be true. Furthermore, if those born in the eighth month are in danger, they are much more so [than others] because they are stronger in themselves; but they are in danger, according to the ninth book of the *Histories* <note>Aristotle's "History of Animals"</note>. 

Again, regarding the delay of the birth matured in the womb, the astrologers posit only three lengths: one which is called "minor," containing 268 days (which is 8 months and 18 days); another "middle" one having 274 days (which rises into 9 months and 3 days); and a third "major" one containing 289 days (from which arise 9 months and 18 days). Therefore, since none of these fall exactly into the eighth month, it seems no one is born in it, and consequently, no one lives in it. For one is not born in it unless they can be nourished, since nature never produces anything unless it is concerned with preserving it, according to the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*.

Therefore, an eight-month-old will not live. First, it should be known what a month is, and how many days it is said to have. A month here, according to **Haly Abbas**, is understood to be **lunar**. But according to **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> and commonly speaking, "month" is used for that which is accepted as **solar**. Yet it does not matter much, since nine lunar months do not fall short of nine solar months except by four or six days; the lunar month containing 29 and a half days, and the solar 30 at most. As written in the ninth book of the *Histories*: "Other animals indeed produce their offspring at a single time of perfection—for one determined time of birth exists for all of them—but for man alone of all animals there are many. For there are births of seven months, eight months, and nine months, and ten months is the most common." Some even accept a birth in the tenth month, according to the tenth book of the *Problems*: "Man alone among such animals has many times of generation, for births occur at seven, eight, and ten months, while for others there is only one time of perfection." 

**Avicenna** <note>original: "Auicē."</note> accepted this same thing in the ninth book of *On Animals*, connecting these things in succession. "A faithful man once told me that a woman gave birth after 14 months and [the child] lived well." Also, the birth of those born early is threefold: for there is the "natural and customary," such as those of nine months with some ten days; another is "unnatural and entirely foreign," like those of eight months; and the remaining is "intermediate." This intermediate type is also threefold: either it is entirely in the middle, like those of seven months, or it leans toward the natural and customary side, like those of ten months, or toward the side of its opposite, like those of eleven or thirteen months. 

According to the definitions of births by **Omar of Tiberias** <note>original: "Omar tyberindī" — Abu Hafs Umar ibn al-Farrukhan al-Tabari, an 8th-century Persian astrologer and architect</note>, there are four types regarding nutrition: 
1. Those who do not taste food, for with them there is no life. 
2. Those who taste food but are not nourished. 
3. Those who taste and are nourished, yet do not achieve a long life. 
4. Those who taste food, are nourished, and reach final old age. 

Among the astrologers, "nutrition" is a space of time of four years, so that the overcome [infant] may pass through all four elements of nature. For some ascribe to **Ptolemy** <note>original: "P̄bolemeo"</note> that the space of nutrition contains one year according to the motion of the sun. **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, the commentator on Ptolemy</note> rejects this in the fourth book of the *Quadripartitum*, confirming that others wanted nutrition to contain four years. Therefore, according to the third and fourth parts of the aforementioned distinction, one can live, but not according to the first and second. 

Secondly, it should be known that this author seems to openly contradict himself. For **Alexander**, in his *Problems*, simply asserts that an eight-month-old birth will not be viable, asking why seven-month-old infants are viable but eight-month-olds are not at all. **Haly Abbas**, in the third book of the *Theoretical Medicine*, asks: "If anyone should ask why a boy born in the eighth month does not live?" Similarly, **Al-Qabisi** <note>original: "Alchabici" — also known as Alcabitius, a 10th-century Arab astrologer</note> in his book on births: "If anyone is born in the eighth month, it happens because of a cause that prevents nature, occurring either on the part of the body, like a disease, or the soul, like a sudden fear; hence if he comes out in this month, he and his mother will die." 

The opposite of this is felt in the ninth book of the *Histories* and the tenth book of the *Problems*: "Thus, eight-month births in Egypt and in certain places where women carry well and easily give birth to many, the children can live; even if they are born monstrous, these eight-month-olds live and are brought up." This surely agrees with **Aristotle** in the ninth and twenty-first books of *On Animals*. 

Thirdly, it should be known: first, that an eight-month birth is rare, and for the most part does not live. Second, because it lives only in particular and more foreign cases, or in very few, since it is something "monstrous" <note>In this context, "monstrous" means a deviation from the natural rule, not necessarily a physical deformity.</note>. This is rarely permitted by nature. Regarding the first part of this, it should be known that this contains the truth with its modification, as the experience of almost all places teaches.

And therefore he adds: **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> in the fourth book [of the *History of Animals*]: "Following the aforementioned sequence, in the regions around Greece, in the eighth month, very few survive, but many indeed perish." How much more, then, will they not live in other intemperate regions? For the land of the **Greeks** is considered more temperate than others by **Aristotle**, and especially the land of **Hippocrates** <note>original: "ypocratis"</note> as gathered in the thirtieth [section]. Furthermore, what was stated before is confirmed by a triple reason. One of these is taken from the science of medicine or nature. Another from that of number. The third, however, takes its beginning from the judgment of those skilled in **astrology** <term>astrology: here refers to the medieval belief that planetary influences dictated the physical development and viability of the fetus</term>.

Regarding the first reason, it must be known according to **Hippocrates** in the sixth book of the *Epidemics* <note>original: "sexto epidimie"</note>, the third book of the *Theories*, and the ninth book of the *Animals* by **Aristotle**, and the third and twenty-first books with **Avicenna** <note>original: "Au."</note> in his books on animals: that after the collection of the seed in the **womb** <term>womb: "matrix" in the original, the common medieval term for the uterus</term>, it is soon surrounded by a membrane or thin skin, containing and nourishing it, as was written before. This was also shown by the seed of six days falling from a girl at the command of **Hippocrates**, who jumped backward seven times, she whom it was not fitting to conceive in the womb. That which was seen fallen upon the ground was like the white of an egg wrapped in a thin skin. Some indeed say it remains in this state not only for six, but even for seven days. 

When it has been thus, as noted, the formative power seeks nothing yet from the womb, as **Aristotle** confesses along with **Avicenna**. Then, after a space of three days, by the beginning of points and lines, it is led into a mass of seed. Then after a delay of six days, which together with the previous ones make fifteen, the quality of blood penetrates it entirely. And that occurs from which [the fetus] is caused; and sometimes it precedes or follows by one or two days. Next, from this point for twelve days, the moisture becomes flesh, and the fleshly parts begin to be distinguished in a large mass, and the three principal members <note>The heart, liver, and brain were considered the "tripod of life" in medieval medicine.</note> are manifested; and now indeed some are separated from contact with others, and the moisture extends itself; this also precedes or follows by two or three days. Finally, after nine days, the head is separated from the shoulders, and the extremities from the sides and belly, so that it may be discerned in some of them. In some, however, it is hidden; and the space now contains thirty-five days, so that if four are added in which the hiding occurred, the entire space in which the embryo is formed will be forty days. 

And this indeed is the triple common measure of formation <note>original: "plasmationis"</note>; for sometimes it is formed in thirty days, which is earlier; sometimes in fifty, and specifically the **female**; for her formation and movement are delayed. There is also another space of thirty-five days, and another of sixty-five, and so on here and there according to the diversity of the heavens and the surrounding air and the proper matter, with the formative power ruling more or less; and therefore it was said by **Aristotle** that the time of human birth is extremely varied. They also say, as **Aristotle** asserts—and here he seems to have been with **Hippocrates** and **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Halyabate"</note> in the seventh part of the sixth book of the *Epidemics*—that if the time of formation is doubled, the time of movement will arise from it. If, however, this is tripled, the time of the double will give the birth. Wherefore, one formed in thirty days will move in sixty, and will be born in one hundred and eighty, which are six full months of thirty days each. 

---

One fashioned <note>original: "plasmatus"</note> in thirty-five days will move in seventy and be born in two hundred and ten, which are seven months. One formed in forty days, movement will be present for it in eighty, and born in two hundred and forty, which are eight months; and because such a one very rarely lives, and **Aristotle** places the common formation in forty days, he therefore reports the rule of the aforementioned under the opinion of others. One fashioned in forty-five days moves in ninety and is born in two hundred and seventy; and these constitute nine months. He who is formed in fifty days moves in one hundred and is born in three hundred, which will be ten months. Wherefore from this sixth book of the *Epidemics*, the seventh part: labors in the periods which move in seventy days are finished in triples; and those which move in eighty are ended in triplicity. This, therefore, is the manner of the termination and birth of the embryo.

Furthermore, it should be known that birth does not happen except through the womb being distended further with the weight of a swelling. Or by irritation, as when its moisture, having become serous and sharp, stretches the membranes in which they were contained so that they occur by the force of the womb, in the third book of *On Natural Faculties*. Or because of that which is contained, as because it struggles to go out due to a lack of nourishment according to **Hippocrates**; then indeed it kicks, breaks the membranes, and seeks an exit. According to **Aristotle**, another not small cause is added: the need for ventilation and the attraction of air along with the narrowness of the place. Therefore, when the fetus is strong and the womb weak and narrow, then the child in the seventh month, being perfect in every way—at least regarding the quality of the body—and as if needing air, space, and more food, moves and kicks so that an exit may be opened for itself. If it attains this, it is perfect so that it can thus live; whence **Alexander** <note>original: "Alex."</note> says: a seven-month child is generated because of the formative power existing very strongly in the womb, and finding useful and commensurate blood, and therefore it quickly perfects the work. 

That the power of the embryo and the disposition of the womb are to be considered, **Hippocrates** testifies thus: "These things always happen, and in the nature of the fetus I have seen the same regarding the kinds of wombs." And because first-time mothers have moist and manageable blood, but a small and weak womb, they for the most part give birth like others in the seventh month. If indeed in the seventh month an exit is not opened, being fatigued and even weakened by the movement of formation and the desirable effort of egress, it rests in the eighth month, so that the preceding labor may be cut off and its vigor may increase with the body's growth. And therefore it stays until the ninth month, in which it may indeed go out; because having been refreshed, strengthened, and advanced, it will be a most natural birth, according to the third book of *On Natural Faculties*, and it will live above others. For it goes out by its own strong power, with the womb having nourished it more completely for a longer time, and then expelling it. If, however, it goes out in the eighth month, it exits weak and fatigued, and not by the power making it to be born, but rather from a symptomatic cause driving it out. This, according to **Alexander**, is an imperfect thing according to an excess and disorder of matter, fashioned in another form. **Haly Abbas** also says that because there is in it a condition of disturbance, languor, and weakness, it does not live; for there is not within it...
