...the power of nutrition and growth. A sign of this is that in the seventh month there is a disturbance and sickness for the fetus, and a poor condition and heaviness for pregnant women occurs in the eighth month, since the condition of the pregnant woman follows the condition of the fetus. Hence, in the ninth book of the *History of Animals* <note>original: "historiarũ nono"</note>, it is said: women suffer most in the fourth and eighth months. And if a miscarriage occurs in the fourth or eighth month, the women themselves are frequently in danger. For this reason, not only do those born at eight months not live, but those giving birth are also at risk. And therefore, wayward women <note>original: "adulterantes meretricule," a harsh medieval reference to women seeking to hide pregnancies</note> should be especially wary of themselves if they attempt to procure an abortion in those months. For many have already been killed in this way. If, therefore, as was judged before, the one carrying the child—who is full-grown and robust—is at risk, how much more so is the fetus.

That a miscarriage occurs in the fourth month happens because the embryo then begins to draw the mother's blood and to be more forcefully bound and attached to the **womb** <term>womb: "matrix" in the original Latin; medieval anatomy often viewed the uterus as an active, almost independent organ</term>. Just as fruit in the middle of its season is gathered from the tree, as seen in the image of the fourth book of the *Aphorisms*. In the eighth month, they are also greatly burdened because of the labor they endure and the **dyscrasia** <term>dyscrasia: a medical term for an imbalance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile</term> they incur. Likewise, a great flow of blood follows from an unnatural solution <note>likely referring to a placental abruption or rupture</note>, so that they more often miscarry. 

But if the child is not born in the ninth month, but reaches the tenth or beyond, **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> says his judgment is that the child is born infirm and weak. For the one who first desired to be born in the ninth month but could not, is born in the tenth, and to him happens what almost happens to one born in the eighth. For it signifies the weakness of his own vital power; this, therefore, is the probable reason that doctors along with natural philosophers can bring forward to assign the cause of the question.

But regarding the aforesaid, it happens that one may doubt why any time is more vital than the seventh month. For here the fetus is exhausted by movement and kicking and exits. It is also constricted and harmed in birth. Likewise, it comes into the air, in which everything is harmful and foreign to it, as appears in the third book of the *Aphorisms*. However, another staying until the eighth month, not so exhausted, nor so constricted, nor led out into the external air, is freed from exhaustion in a space of twenty or twenty-five days or the like, and is magnified and strengthened. Therefore, why is the seventh-month child more vital? Indeed, according to the third book of the *Theories*, the dispositions occurring to the fetus in the seventh month and thereafter in the eighth—a space of nearly forty continuous days—are like a turning point of an acute illness which reaches its **crisis** <term>crisis: in medieval medicine, the "criticat" or "crisis" was the turning point of a disease where the patient either begins to recover or declines toward death</term> in forty days. Hence it is said these dispositions cease for the fetuses at about forty days; for these days coincide with the ninth month, which is why the child then becomes vital. And there is an astrological cause to be added to this. 

<margin>Every crisis is itself healthy unless it is pestilential</margin>

Again, it is doubted because every crisis is more health-giving than deadly, unless the disease was pestilential <note>original: "pestilẽs"</note>, according to the second section of the *Aphorisms*. But birth is a mode of crisis. Someone born in these conditions would therefore be, for the most part, vital. It must be said that he will not be able to live because he is harmed first, and also in birth. He is also harmed sometimes by external things and those things occurring to him. It is also pestilential and monstrous, which is why he will not be able to remain in life.

There is also a second deduction, which is arithmetic, touched upon by **Alexander** <note>likely Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> in the dissolution of this question. For he says seven is a perfect number, as **Pythagoras** and the arithmeticians and musicians testify, but eight is imperfect. That seven is perfect is proven in many ways: because many principles, and especially those of man, are constituted by the number seven. For God governs the world with seven stars <note>the seven classical "planets": Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>. Infants born at seven months produce teeth; at seven years they lose them. In twice seven years <note>fourteen</note> they reach puberty; in thrice seven <note>twenty-one</note> they become men. Diseases are also judged proportionally by the number seven. The moon likewise is figured by such a number in its weekly phases. And the week <note>original: "edomoda"</note> consists of seven days. Likewise, there are seven vowels among the Greeks, though according to the Latins there are only five, and the others are regrouped. For although the Greek varies the figure by adding two, the sound remains the same; however many are placed in Greek—suppose the third simple letter *i* <note>iota</note>, the *u* or *y* <note>upsilon</note>, and two compounds or diphthongs like *ei* and *oy*, and the two O's, namely the small <note>omicron</note> and the large <note>omega</note>—they have a single continuous sound. The Greek, being a more curious imitator of nature, wished to adapt seven vowels to the seven planets, just as he established twenty-four elements of writing, imitating the twenty-four hours of a natural day. 

**Macrobius** also, in his exposition of **Tully's** <note>Cicero's</note> *Dream of Scipio*, tries to persuade us of this same thing through many examples, stating that almost all things are numbered by seven, and especially those of man. For he says the month arises from the first cube of even numbers, which is eight, and the first of the odd numbers, which is twenty-seven. Now eight and twenty-seven constitute thirty-five, which, when multiplied by six—the first of the perfect numbers—results in 210 days, exactly constituting seven months of thirty days. Whence he concludes that this number is so fertile in nature that it completes the first perfection of human birth as a sort of judge of maturity. A number is called a "cube" when it is led into itself twice, such as two times two [times two], which is eight; or three times three [times three], which is twenty-seven. 

It is clearly shown by reason that seven is an odd number and all such are perfect, for it emerges as a form containing both even and odd within itself. It also rises from the number three according to its parts, in which perfection is found, as in the edition of the *Sermons of the Masters*. For six and one make seven; two and five; and three and four return seven. Nine is likewise a perfect number, for it is attributed to the order of the Intelligences <note>angels</note>, which the divine commentators place as nine, such as the Cherubim and Seraphim and those following. There are also nine celestial spheres, as astrologers commonly testify today... That this number is perfect is similarly argued since it is itself an odd number. Furthermore, the parts constituting it recommend it. For it arises from three, one of which is proportioned to the most perfect number three...

### The Odd Number is More Perfect

Three times three is nine: for here are three triplets <note>original: "tres trinarii"</note>, each of which arises from three. Thus, in this number nine, the perfection of the trinity is most powerfully gathered. There are also in this number other [combinations], such as four and three, five and four; these four are indeed proportional even with their intervals. Thus, in this number, perfection will be most natural. The number ten <note>original: "denarius"</note> also exists as a natural number after this one. For it stands as a perfect number, as seen in the fifteenth of the *Problems* <note>Referring to the *Problems* attributed to Aristotle</note>. Whence Alexander says: The number ten is perfect because every number is constituted through ten according to a cycle. And therefore Aristotle, in the third book of the *Physics* <note>original: "Ar. philicos tertio"</note>, says that Plato made numbers only up to ten. Pythagoras also emphasized the significance of this number. He established two orders of things: one perfect and the other imperfect, each consisting of ten categories, wishing them to be the principles of the aforementioned correlation. In the first category he placed:
->**the finite, the odd, the singular, the right, the male, the resting, the straight, the light, the good, and the square.**<-
In the other, he placed their opposites:
->**the infinite, the even, the plural, the left, the female, the moving, the curved, the darkness, the evil, and the oblong.**<-
Furthermore, the Pythagoreans make ten spheres out of the nine manifest ones and the tenth, the *antikhthon* <term>antikhthon: the "Counter-Earth," a hypothetical celestial body in the Pythagorean astronomical system that was always invisible from Earth</term>, which moves or exists in opposition, as described in the *Metaphysics*.

<margin>it is above</margin>
The eleventh number, however, possesses little perfection in these matters, and therefore a fetus is rarely born in it. But the sixth, eighth, and twelfth are clearly imperfect among the even numbers; and therefore, a child born in the eighth month does not live. For it is even, as are the other two. It is also more greatly diminished in its imperfection, as will be seen below; for which reason a child born in it shall not live. In the others, however, such as the twelfth and the sixth, the child either is not born or a miscarriage <note>original: "iuitialis" - likely referring to an early or "initial" death</note> occurs. For these numbers are the opposites of the aforementioned perfect numbers, especially the eighth and twelfth. As said in the first book of the *Cretan* <note>Likely referring to a work by Galen or Hippocrates</note>: "I have never seen anyone judged [fit to live] on the twelfth day, nor likewise in the eighth; it happens rarely and ends badly." Note also that the **arithmeticians** <term>arithmetras: scholars of the medieval "quadrivium" who studied the mystical and mathematical properties of numbers</term> prefer the odd number over the even, because the former has the quality of perfection and **form** <term>form: in the Aristotelian sense, "form" is the active principle that gives a thing its identity and purpose, whereas "matter" is passive</term>. The even number, however, relates to imperfection and matter. Whence even God, according to Virgil, "rejoices in the odd number." And for this reason, the Pythagoreans offered the first actual odd number, the triplet, for the significations of the gods, as noted in the first book of *On the Heavens and the World* <note>original: "primo ce. & m." for Aristotle's *De Caelo et Mundo*</note>. From this they also assigned the reason why a custom grew: that pills should be given in an odd number for a laxative effect. For they ought to act; and the principle of action is taken from the form, as from that which is its sustaining principle, and not from matter. The odd number has the quality of form, while the even has that of matter.

Regarding the aforementioned things, one might hesitate, because in the ninth book of Euclid it is said that a number is called "perfect" when it is equal to all the parts by which it is counted. And in the third book of Boethius’s *Arithmetic*, such a number is six, below ten; for there are three parts from which it arises: a half, which is three; a third, which is two; and a sixth, which is one. For three, two, and one constitute the number six. Below one hundred, however, the perfect number is twenty-eight. Below one thousand, four hundred and ninety-six. And below ten thousand, eight thousand one hundred and twenty-eight. There is also the "abundant" number, which is larger than all the parts by which it is counted, such as twelve; for its half is six, its third is four, its fourth is three, its sixth is two, and its twelfth is one—which, if counted together, grow to the number eighteen.

A "diminished" number, however, is found to be smaller than all its counting parts. Such as eight: its half is four, its fourth is two, and its eighth is one; which, collected together, only rise to seven. Thus, the imperfection of the number eight appears here as well. It is concluded that seven, nine, and ten are not "perfect" numbers [in this mathematical sense]. To this it must be said that a "perfect number" is currently spoken of in three ways. First, because all its parts taken together return exactly to the whole, as was said before regarding six and twenty-eight; this is not the kind of perfection sought here, which is more of a material perfection, for parts are the matter of the whole, according to the third book of the *Physics*. Perfection is also spoken of in the manner of form and giving essence, which is the quality of the odd number; and because the triplet is the first of such, it is indicated in the first book of *On the Heavens and the World* to be perfect. For of it, it is first said that "all" and "whole" and "perfect" are the same in kind. A number is also called perfect by reason of a certain finality and recirculation which is observed in it, and thus the number ten is called perfect. And these latter perfections are more real than the first.

This reasoning, although pleasing and accepted by the Pythagoreans and seemingly by the arithmeticians—who posited numbers to be the substances and causes of things—failed because they did not know how to distinguish between the "One" which is equated with Being, and the "One" which stands as the principle of number. They thought that just as it is the principle of number and varies it, so too it varies Being. The school of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle</note>, however, does not agree with these speeches in the third book of the *Cretan*; rather, they estimate them to be more accidental and estranged from the truth, seeking a proper and natural reason in each genus. Nevertheless, they clothe their words with a certain probability through the assimilation of numbers to things.

A third reason is taken from the general practice of the part of astrology seen in the movements of the upper bodies, which assigns the causes of all lower things. According to that opening of the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note>: "He who is about to investigate the causes of things must first contemplate the heavenly bodies." For the change of worldly things happens because of the change of the heavenly bodies. So that a cause might be given for this effect—for instance, why an eight-month-old fetus does not live—the order and movement of the planets is considered as a guide in the embryos, each dominating in its month. For it is posited that in the first month after conception, **Saturn** dominates, who is firm and dry. For then the seed, being watery and fluid, required something that would stop, constrain, and fix it, and something that would invigorate its heat with life-giving force, which is the nature of the cold and dryness of Saturn. For he is the origin of the retentive virtue in the *Centiloquium*. Also, in the second month...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of human gestation, moving from the philosophical properties of numbers to the specific astrological influences of the seven planets on each month of pregnancy. The author, Petrus de Abano, uses this framework to explain why some infants survive birth at seven or nine months while those born in the eighth month often perish, eventually citing his own birth data as evidence.</meta>

Over the embryo, **Jupiter** rules, being hot and moist in form and an augmenter <note>original: "augmentativus"</note>. For he is the origin of growing virtue; at that time, the conceptus requires a heat that dilates its matter and a moisture for the extension and dilation of its growth, the drawing out of lines and points, and finally for its formation. This also serves to repress the coldness and dryness of Saturn. In the next month, **Mars** occurs, who by his heat warms the now-forming embryo, dries up its superfluous moistures, and incites it to movement. For then it is commanded to move, since heat and dryness greatly provoke motion.

In the **fourth month**, the **Sun** supervenes, the prince of the heart of heaven and the world. By his life-giving heat, he perfects the embryo to such an extent that the rational spirit enters into it, as appeared previously. For he is the origin and furnace of the virtue of life. In the **fifth month**, **Venus** occurs in order, tempering with coldness and moisture the heat of Mars and the Sun; she increases the flesh and prepares all the limbs, shaping them with a decorous form. In the next month, **Mercury** arrives, drying up superfluous moistures, inducing a tempering influence, and acting toward the movement that separates the smaller external parts especially, distinguishing and equalizing the whole.

The **Moon** is added in the **seventh month**, nourishing and increasing the infant with her moisture, providing flesh and fat, since she is the origin of natural virtue. She also moistens the parts of the womb. Because the infant is then perfected in every way, having now received the benefit of all the planets, and because it is born under the power of the Moon, its exit is saved, since she is a cause of fortune and life. Whence Alualar <note>likely referring to Al-Andaluzi or another Arabic astronomical source</note> says in the *Fadan*: "The life of living things, after God, is the Sun and the Moon." Therefore, Ptolemy dignifies these two greatly in his judgments.

Finally, in the **eighth month**, **Saturn** returns in a fortune of cold and dry, who chills the infant and constricts it, forcing it to remain in the womb. If it should exit then, being harmed by other external factors, it will not be able to tolerate the malice of Saturn. For Saturn plots destruction not only through his quality <note>cold and dryness</note>, but also through a certain hidden malevolent impression of his, as was declared in Distinction X.

Then in the **ninth month**, **Jupiter** supervenes in order, a fortune hot and moderately moist. Since he is the "father of gods and men" (according to the third book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*</note> and the first book of the *Politics*), the living parts are greatest under his dominion. If, however, the infant remains in the womb into the **tenth month**, it will be born under the dominion of Mars; and because Mars moves with laborious motions, this child is agitated when it emerges. Because Mars is an "infortune," hot and dry, Abraham Avenezra <note>original: "Abraam euenare"</note> posits that those born under him live but a short time.

->**The Author’s Birth**<-

I, however, being in my **53rd year**, was able to understand from my most diligent mother—and through the investigation of the hidden degree of the ascending birth by the *Balance of Hermes* <term>Trutina Hermetis: A traditional astrological method used to calculate the exact moment of conception or the birth ascendant</term>—I found that I had contracted a stay in the womb of nine months and fourteen days. 

If a child is born in the **eleventh month**, it returns to the power of the **Sun**. Such a child can live, since the Sun (as said before) is a cause of life after God along with the Moon; however, the birth will not be entirely natural.

Regarding the aforementioned things, a doubt arises: since the astrologers hand down that **Saturn** signifies the end of things, antiquity, and old age, he does not seem suited to signify the beginning and novelty of impregnation. Nor does the **Moon** seem suited to the end of impregnation (as ascribed to the seventh month), since she signifies beginnings, innovations, and motions. This is supported by the fact that she denotes the first four years of the person born, as in Distinction XXVI. 

It must be said that these attributions of the planets to the conditions of bodies are made according to certain similarities and properties. In the generation of the embryo, they looked at the property of Saturn, which is to constrict and hide by its coldness and dryness. For, as was said, the seed required this in the beginning; therefore, they attributed Saturn to it first, and the others in succession as mentioned. But considering the slowness of motion and operation that comes to the person in old age—as well as the coldness and dryness of that age, and the impediments of body and soul such as diseases, sadness, and death—they ascribed Saturn to old age for those reasons. From these points, it appears what should be said.

Therefore, from these three [factors], it is concluded that a child born in the eighth month regularly and almost always does not live. According to this science, it must be known that it can live only rarely, as is said of certain places in Egypt, provided the cases do not exceed the first [month], where there are "thrice-strong" <note>original: "triragines," likely meaning exceptionally robust or prolific</note> women who are well-bearing, and many tempered by the heat of the region. Thus, in places that do not conform to these reasons, they do not survive at all. This is not for the strength of the fetus, nor the size of the body acquired from the mother and father providing warm blood and sufficient seed. It also fails there because the one born in the eighth month lives there in perfection, yet it is perfected somewhat through the "mediastinal affinity" <note>an astrological proximity</note> which it has with the seventh and ninth months, which are declared most perfect. 

It is also not a small help if, because of innate heat, vigor, and perfection which the infant contracted from its mother and father and the heat of the region, the hidden malice of Saturn and its coldness and dryness can be countered. This is supported by the fact that such births are "monsters of nature," since they happen rarely and outside her intention. Truly, the things mentioned before are parts of nature which sometimes fail—just as the whole genus of mules is sterile, yet a mule once conceived, though it did not nourish the fetus to the end (from *On the Generation of Animals*, Book II). That people in these regions fear that someone born in the eighth month cannot possess life happens because the beginning of a woman’s conception is often hidden. For they frequently retain menses and are inflated with foamy winds, and then they believe they are pregnant, when in fact they become impregnated later during intercourse.

...to have [gestation] for ten months. For I have already heard this many times. But I will say how this happens: For she has poorly conceived the beginning of pregnancy in this way: When the **wombs** are filled with a certain windy spirit <note>original: "spiritu quodam uentoso"</note>, women think they are already pregnant, because they also retain the menses descending into the wombs. Then, when the menses break out of their own accord, or come out because other things meet them, these [menses] and the earlier spirituous winds exit together. And finally, being thus purged, they approach men and, by copulating, they are impregnated then or shortly after. And therefore, women think they will sometimes be seven-month, eight-month, nine-month, ten-month, or even eleven-month [pregnant]. But if it is indeed posited that they are impregnated without the eruption of the menses, which seems more probable to some, then if they menstruate while copulating, they are not actually pregnant.

Regarding the fourth point: what should be said to the first [objection] has appeared. To the other, it should be said that an eight-month-old does not seem more vital than a seven-month-old, as has been sufficiently shown; indeed, it is much less so. For not every delay of time increases and strengthens the fetus, but rather a determined delay with the appropriate dispositions shown to be operating toward that end. To the other, it should be said that although the formation or movement [of the male] precedes that of the female, nevertheless a delay and equality in the time of birth can occur; this is because perhaps these times are not always proportional, as seen in the rule of doubling and tripling. The opinion of others confirms what was stated. Or it should be said that the ninth month has a great breadth, which the beginning of the tenth follows, so that a male is born around the beginning and no further, but a female is born around the end or the beginning of the tenth. To the other, it should be said that one perishes in the eighth month not only because of the primary qualities <note>The primary qualities are hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> acting excessively upon it, but also because of weakness and impotence; for when it arises, impotence and languor occur. Nor does **Saturn** crush it by his severity and dryness alone, but also by a certain hidden power implanted in him, as was said in Distinction 10, which operates without the change of a medium. To the other: what should be said has appeared, for it is granted that it is rarer, yet nature erring makes this diversity—namely, to live in the eighth month—and at other times it has been found to happen occasionally. As for how much the authorities argue against this part, it has appeared before. To the other, it should be said that it is very rare for those born in the eighth month not to be precipitated; but such a fetus is not destroyed when it happens properly and in a particular place. To the other, it should be said that the "genetalici" <note>An astrological term for those who cast birth charts.</note> distinguished the delays only falling in the ninth month or thereabouts, since that is how it happens for most. That they might be born at another time is not prohibited, but it happens more rarely, as **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Abraam euenare"</note> testifies; whence the **Balance of Hermes** <term>trutina Hermetis: an astrological method used to calculate the exact moment of conception by looking at the position of the Moon at birth</term> or other modes of finding the hidden degree of birth do not extend at all beyond the ninth month, as indicated by the habits of fetuses remaining in the womb. Know also that one should not provide precise and usual limits of months in this kind of matter for any art concerning sensible things, because of its wandering and indeterminate nature, as was touched upon in Distinction 26.

### ->DIFFERENTIA L<-

**W**hether the digestive virtue proceeds by **thinning** <note>original: "subtiliando"</note> seems to be the case, because the thing contained is proportioned to the container and disposed according to its disposition; it changes itself into its own temperament and likeness. But the container, such as the vessels through which that which is being digested is sent to the limbs—as is apparent—proceeds by thinning. For there is a path from the largest veins to the capillaries <note>original: "capillares"</note>, from which blood glides into the limbs, as is shown in the prior section. And rightly so, because the veins proceed from larger to smaller until the passages become so small that the thickness of the blood [is removed] in the third stage. Furthermore, that which has to penetrate into narrower parts penetrates better if it proceeds by thinning, since it is more exposed to such motion; and such is the nature of what is digested. Further, **chyle** <term>chilus: the semi-fluid mass of partly digested food</term> is a liquid substance, similar in thickness to barley water, which is then led further, by means of the **ichor** <note>original: "ycore"; here referring to a serous or watery fluid</note> generated in the mesenteric veins, into blood by the liver; this blood is thicker, as previously indicated, than the ichor and the blood [at later stages]. Similarly, blood generated from phlegm through digestion appears thinner than it, since phlegm is thicker than blood. Also, the dew <note>original: "ros"; in medieval physiology, one of the humors that nourishes the tissues</note> of the diet shows a thinner moisture than the blood.

Also, **arterial blood** is thinner than venous blood, from which it is generated. Likewise, the vaporous **spirit** of the heart, digested and altered in the **rete mirabile** <note>term: "rete mirabile" - a "wonderful net" of blood vessels at the base of the brain once thought to refine the vital spirit into the animal spirit</note>, is rendered thinner; so too the vaporous spirit, which is thus matter contained in empty places like the arteries and the heart, is converted by digestion into the innate spirit in all limbs. It is, however, proportionally contained in these, which is finally rendered more porous and innate in its quality, whereas before it was vaporous as matter, being simpler. Again, that which is cast off from something testifies to it, as in the *Tegni* <note>A work by Galen</note>; but the superfluities of digestion proceed by thinning. For the excretions of urine are thicker than sweats and transpirations, which are hidden. Conversely, the *Aphorisms* <note>of Hippocrates</note> posit that undigested humors are only thick and viscous; these, in their digestion, require thinning and "cutting" <note>original: "icisiōe" [incisitione]; the breaking down of thick humors</note>, which similarly implies thinning.

Therefore, digestion proceeds by thinning. The **opposite** of this seems to be true according to the *Meteorology* <note>of Aristotle</note>: "All things digested are by nature born to be thickened." Whence **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle</note> says in the same place: "All digested things first consist and become thick." And in the fourth book of the same: "It happens that digested things are thicker and hotter." From spirituous or spiritual things come watery things; from such things, those that consist of earth. Also in the fifth book: "Digestion cooks, unites, and thickens everything." Furthermore, according to the *Prognostics*: "It is of the nature of digestion that it should thicken," not the urine indeed, but the excrement, and in those things that receive digestion in the stomach; also the sputum in one who has **pleurisy** <note>original: "pleuresim"</note> or pneumonia, and the moisture descending from the nose, and the **coryza** <note>original: "corizā"; the common cold or nasal congestion</note>, and bleary eyes.

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of human gestation to a detailed medical and philosophical treatise on digestion (concoction). It draws heavily on Aristotle's IV Meteorology and various medical authorities like Haly Abbas and Hippocrates to categorize how the body processes both helpful nutrients and harmful humors.</meta>

...in the disease of ophthalmia <note>an inflammation of the eye</note> and in the pus of ulcers. Whence, in the fourth book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "metahaurorum", referring to Aristotle's work on the elements and transformations</note>, it is said that things which consist of growths are such as those found in ophthalmia—namely, tears—when they have become mud or rheum <note>original: "lippitudo", a thick discharge from the eyes</note>.

Furthermore, ichor <note>a thin watery discharge</note> is thinner than blood and the humors of the blood; it exists in the members into which they are finally converted. In its thin state, it requires a thickening <term>ingrossatio [thickening of thin fluids to prepare them for expulsion]</term>, which digestion provides, so that once it is gripped by the expulsive faculty, it may be more freely secreted. Thus, digestion precedes by thickening.

### The Nature and Types of Digestion

Regarding the first point, it must be known that **digestion** is the perfection or completion [of a substance] by natural heat and proportion from opposing passive qualities or contrary passions. Therefore, digestion performed by heat is of three types:

1.  One is called **pepansis** <note>Greek: πέπανσις, ripening or maturation</note>, which is observed in fruits and is utilized in the seeds of animals.
2.  Another is **ephesis** <note>Greek: ἕψησις, boiling or decoction</note>, found in boiled things and in all the humors of animals.
3.  The third is **optesis** <note>Greek: ὄπτησις, roasting</note>, found in roasted things; it is used in bones and more solid parts. For roasting is done by heat, like a tile in a furnace, according to the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*.

Conversely, the "indigestion" or failure of cold is also threefold, namely: **omotes** <note>rawness</note>, **molynsis** <note>tainting or softening</note>, and **stathmeusis** <note>stalling or stagnation</note>, according to the fourth book of the *Meteorology*.

### The Purpose of Digestion

This digestion is twofold in its outcome. For one type is for **benefit**, which is the change or transmutation of that which nourishes into the proper quality and essence of that which is being nourished, according to Aristotle in the first book of *Elements*, the third book of *Complexions*, and according to the *Physics*. This is nothing other than the refinement of food to such an extent that the nutritive faculty makes it stay in the place of what has been lost [to the body].

However, digestion in **harmful substances** <note>original: "nocitiuo"</note> is also twofold. Either the substance is not so harmful that it cannot be reduced to a benign state—such as sweet phlegm, which according to Haly is changed into blood, just as wine on its way to changing can be reduced to vinegar—and then at least by reason of the end point it reaches, it is called digestion. Or, the substance is superfluous and harmful to such an extent that it can never be corrected, such as completely acidified phlegm or wine perfectly turned into vinegar. In that case, the digestion owed to it is **preparation**, so that it may be easily expelled once conquered by our nature, according to the first part of the fourth book [of the Canon or similar text]. 

### Preparation for Expulsion

The intention in "digesting" [harmful matter] is to balance the substance of the matter so that it is prepared for easy expulsion. This is according to the second *Aphorism*, the eleventh of the *Therapeutics*, and according to Haly. Now, the lack of preparation <note>indispositio</note> of a "bad humor" <note>original: "bon oris", likely a scribal error for "bad humor" or "matter"</note> so that it cannot be conquered and expelled by nature can happen in three ways:

*   **By reason of its substance:** For example, if it is **thick** <note>grossus</note>. For such matter, being wedged and enclosed, blocks the passages and cannot be expelled; whence it must first be thinned <note>subtiliare</note>. 
*   **If it is viscous:** Due to its stickiness, it cannot be led out; therefore, it must first be "cut" <term>incidere [to break up thick, sticky humors with medicine]</term.
*   **If it is too thin:** For such matter is absorbed and inserted into the members so that nature cannot grip and lead it out in expulsion. Therefore, it must first be **thickened** <note>igrossare</note>. For not all digestion in harmful matter proceeds by thinning, as some argue.

Humors indeed require digestion and excretion for a praiseworthy **crisis** <note>the turning point of a disease</note>, according to the fourth *Aphorism*.

### Quantity and Quality in Digestion

This [failure to digest] may also be by reason of **quantity**. When a humor is present in great quantity, it cannot be digested all at once. Therefore, especially when the [bodily] virtue is weak, it is necessary to evacuate it gradually at intervals, and thus "digest" it as it were. 

Or, it may be by reason of **quality**, which happens in two ways:
1.  **Primary qualities:** If it is too hot or too cold, or too hot and dry, etc. Then it must be brought to a moderate state by its contrary.
2.  **Subsequent qualities:** Such as when it becomes putrid, or biting and sharp. Then it must be rectified and purged with cleansing and purifying agents. If it is poisonous, it must be corrected with those things which, by their own power, resist poisons.

### The Role of Nature and Art

Know also that each of these digestions—whether for benefit, for harm, or the middle state—is performed either entirely by **Nature**, or is initiated and perfected by **Art** <note>medicine</note>. 

*   **Benefit by Nature:** In one who has perfect digestion, such as a healthy youth.
*   **Benefit by Art:** When digestion is weak, such as in an elderly person. For them, electuaries <note>medicinal pastes</note> and ointments are administered, along with warming regimens. To enter warm places and to have elevated pillows are among the things that help digestion. Such an operation of art is necessary when it reduces a "semi-bad" state to a benign one.

Similarly, even in simply harmful cases, some are perfected by nature alone when nature is powerful enough to digest the matter without a doctor's help and expel it. Often, nature is helped by art, especially when it is weak. Then it is necessary to ripen and digest with foods, drinks, and medicines, such as syrups, electuaries, rubbing, and exercises.

It should be known that digestion for simple benefit is ordered toward the restoration of:
1.  **Thick substance:** Such as bones.
2.  **Thin substance:** For easy penetration, such as the spirits.
3.  **Medium substance:** Such as flesh.

Digestion which results in superfluities <note>waste products</note> varies in two ways: for such harm is either throughout the body itself, or within the veins, or outside them, or collected in a place like an **aposteme** <note>an abscess or swelling</note>. This happens in two ways: either the matter of the abscess is hot in its essence (like blood or choler), or through putrefaction (like **cancer**), or because its nature is opposed to movement (like **scrofula** <note>swelling of the lymph nodes</note> and nodes). 

There is also a third digestion regarding the middle ground between these two, which occurs either because the superfluity is natural, or it is a humor prone to corruption which is being reduced to a benign state. Furthermore, one must consider the causes of digestion, because the cause of that which is simply for benefit...

<meta>This page continues the analysis of digestion (concoction), moving from the definitions of its types—ripening, boiling, and roasting—to a systematic investigation of its four causes (material, formal, final, and efficient) and a debate over whether digestion primarily thins or thickens bodily humors. It maintains the scholastic style of citing Aristotle and Galen to resolve medical contradictions.</meta>

But as for the composition and heat that exists in the limbs, [this is discussed] in the books of natural science and in the first book of the *Canon* <note>original: "prima", referring to Book 1 of Avicenna's Canon of Medicine</note>. Indeed, the causes of digestion in harmful matter can be absolutely designated as three, or perhaps four. Because digestion, since it is an **accident** <note>a philosophical term for a property that exists in a subject but is not part of its essential nature</note>, does not have "matter from which" it is made, but rather "matter in which" it exists, according to the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*.

Whence the **material cause** is not properly in the digestion itself, but in that matter in which it is grounded. The **formal cause** will be a sufficient decoction <note>a "cooking" or processing of humors by bodily heat</note> proportioned for digesting. The **final cause** is the orderly arrangement for expulsion through this digestion. The **efficient cause** is also twofold: one is the principal cause, which is like the master craftsman, the governing power of the whole; the other is instrumental and secondary, which is itself double:

Internal, and this is twofold: one is simple and incorporeal, such as the **complexion** <note>the specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in an individual</note>; the other is opposite to this, such as the innate heat in a specific member. And the external [cause] is also twofold: one which regards the governing power more, such as **diet**; and another which regards the cause and disposition, such as **medicines**. For in sickness, when the governing power is inspected, food and drink are suitable for the cold and the sick, and similarly medicines in their own way. I say this because in medicines there is more of a "contrary" opposition to be observed than in diet. For diet seeks more to be administered in a way similar [to the body], whereas medicine acts through contraries.

Now, "thick" and "thin" are certain material qualities, just as "dry" and "moist" are more fundamental witnesses. In a thick substance, the parts are gathered together and densified; in a thin substance, it is the opposite. Regarding this, it should be known that someone said that digestion proceeds by **thinning** <term>subtiliando [the process of making a substance finer or thinner]</term>, according to the fourth book of the *First* <note>Avicenna's Canon, Book 1</note>. The motive for this might have been that he happened upon experiments which led him to this conclusion. But because these were not according to the rules <note>original: "canones", likely referring to established medical principles</note>, they are not valid, nor is any one of them sufficient to demonstrate this. For perhaps he gave a hot medicine to someone with thin matter, which, by opening the pores and dissolving the matter into vapors and thinning it further, cured the patient.

He might also have been persuaded by a frivolous reason: because it is said that the nature of heat is to thin, dissolve, liquefy, and penetrate. Since digestion is properly perfected by heat—and more absolutely so in the case of harmful matter—they concluded that digestion proceeds by thinning. This position, however, is false in itself for the most part, since in many cases, as will be shown, digestion proceeds by **thickening** <term>ingrossando [the process of making a substance denser or thicker]</term>. 

For many inconveniences follow from that [thinning] theory: because according to it, nature would immediately evacuate at the beginning of illnesses where there is this thinness, since it would already be prepared by digestion. And the medical art, which imitates nature, would also radically evacuate at the beginning of such illnesses; yet the artistic precept is to **medicate digested things** <note>a classic medical rule: do not attempt to purge humors until they have been "cooked" or thickened by the body's heat</note>. Furthermore, thin matter would never be disobedient to evacuation, but the flow [of illness] often indicates the contrary. The falsity of that position will appear more clearly in the third discussion.

The arguments for that position are not valid because in those experiments the effect was accidental, as Avicenna <note>original: "A."</note> suggests. Whence one must be careful lest an accidental impression deceive you. For sometimes one is seen to be cured of a fever because of some hot things disturbing nature and inciting it to the nearest [crisis]; yet this is accidental, caused by the irritation of nature into a fight. When the matter is undigested, it is not to be imitated as an "artistic" method. For if they thinned hot matter in someone so much that they resolved it, after which the disease ceased, in others they could lead the parts to intensity, inflammation, and consumption.

To the other argument, it must be said that heat thins, resolves, and liquefies things that are of the same kind. But in those things which are of three different kinds, it works the opposite, as in *On Generation and Corruption*. Digested matter is rendered uniform in a twofold way: for it is the nature of a good digestion to make every thing smooth and to place it in whatever way is needed. It has also been said that digestion is perfected not only by heat as an instrument, but by the governing nature as the craftsman.

There were also some who held the entirely opposite position, wanting all digestion to proceed by thickening. They perhaps took their motive from the speech of Aristotle and Galen in the sharp arguments already premised. Furthermore, heat, by warming, opens the pores; it liquefies, evaporates, and resolves that which is thin in the matter. That which is then left behind is thickened. For a passion more strongly made casts off from the substance. That which is thin is more easily cast off. But digestion is said to be perfected more by heat, because of which it seems that digestion always proceeds by thickening.

It must be said that although this position contains more truth than the preceding one—as for the most part that which is digested grows thick—nevertheless it suffers no small criticism, both in itself and in its arguments. For as in the previous rejection, it would mean that nature and art would need to radically evacuate thick and viscous humors from the very beginning, since by their thickness they would already be "digested." Similarly, thick and viscous matter would be fit for evacuation and would lack any impediment, the falsity of which the senses denote. 

The arguments they take from Aristotle and Galen are not valid, as will be remarked in the fourth [chapter] of the proposed topics. It also appears what should be said to their reason: because digestion is not only perfected by heat, but even more by the governing power presiding over it and ordering it to an end. For that power removes everything from the humor, when it is able, into a [proper] disposition, because it was unfit for evacuation. And although it may evaporate and resolve something, that which remains does not always become more solid; rather, the thick, trapped fluid, when resting, thins as it is liquefied, just as appears in the melting of ice.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that digestion for the most part tends toward thickening, but in other cases toward thinning. For digestion in a simply beneficial sense—which is ordered toward the restoration of thick matter that has been lost—always proceeds by thickening, as Aristotle clearly notes. For it is necessary that it becomes "earthy" [solid] by which we are nourished, that is, thickened. Whence **Damascene** <note>John of Damascus, an influential theologian and philosopher</note> says we are nourished by the cold and the dry, that is, by the thickened earthly substance. This is clearly...

It refutes the idea that digestion is merely thinning, arguing instead that nature and medicine usually require humors to be "processed" or thickened before they can be safely expelled.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the mechanics of digestion (also known as concoction), specifically debating whether it works by thickening or thinning the humors. It builds on the previous page's discussion of causes by applying them to clinical observations of bodily fluids and diseases like pleurisy.</meta>

It is apparent in the transformation of **chyle** <note>original: "ycoris", likely a variant of "chyli", the milky fluid produced from digested food</note> into blood, and of blood into moisture, and finally into the limbs, which is also asserted by reason. For those things which lead toward an end are disposed proportionally to that end, since the end imposes necessity upon the things leading to it (according to the third book of the **Physics** <note>Aristotle’s *Physics*, a foundational text for medieval natural science</note>). But the end of digestion is that thick matter lost by the body should be restored. This restoration must be made as similar as possible; therefore, the things preceding that end must also be thickened to attain it. However, they thicken from what was previously thin. Furthermore, every movement and change occurs between opposite endpoints (according to the fifth book of the **Physics**). But movement exists within digestion, as it occurs through a certain alteration or even local movement that eventually intervenes. Since what moves (as is clear in the same source) starts in the starting point and ends in the destination, it is always casting off what it had from the starting point and acquiring what belongs to the destination. Therefore, that which is digested will first be in one of the endpoints, namely the thin state, and finally, by acquiring what belongs to the destination, it will gradually be made thick. Wherefore it is proved that digestion proceeds by continuous thickening until it produces the thick state.

If, however, digestion is "simply helpful"—as it clearly is when it restores thin things that were lost, or so that movement may proceed from it, such as the digestion of **spirit** <note>In medieval medicine, "spirit" refers to a refined substance—vital, animal, or natural—that carries life and function through the body like a vapor</note>—then I concede that digestion proceeds by thinning, as was touched upon in the arguments. For it thins the humors by digestion and transforms them into vapors, from which the spirit is finally created. This is even more clearly evident when the vital spirit, having been digested in the **miraculous network** <note>original: "rete scdno", referring to the *rete mirabile*, a complex of blood vessels at the base of the brain where spirits were thought to be refined</note>, passes further into the animal spirit, and from the material into the formal and natural. That this is so can be demonstrated by those same reasons, with the terms transposed, by which it was shown that digestion helps in the restoration of lost thick matter by proceeding through thickening.

If, however, digestion is considered in matter that is "simply harmful," according to whether the spirit <note>here meaning a vapor or humor</note> has been throughout almost the whole body within the veins or outside them, or in a specific part such as an accumulation in the liver: then it must be said that since such digestion is nothing but a certain preparation and enabling of the **expulsive power** <note>the body's natural ability to rid itself of harmful substances</note>, and if the humor should be disobedient to nature—either because of thickness and viscosity or because of thinness—there is a need to thin it, to cut the viscous, and to thicken the thin. Because of this, it is sometimes necessary to thin and sometimes to thicken, according to what the disposition requires to prevent the evacuation of the humor; and this is established by everyone, with one exception.

If, however, digestion occurs in harmful matter of the third kind, either that accumulation is hot (either of itself, like choler and blood, or through putrefaction, like windiness and phlegm), or it is cold. If the former, it also happens in two ways: for it either matures or it reaches a crisis through resolution. For **abscesses** <note>original: "apa", abbreviation for *apostemata*, any inflammatory swelling</note> are terminated in three ways: for sometimes they are resolved, sometimes they are turned to pus, and sometimes they are changed into hardness from an unequal disorder. If it turns to pus, it is attested that the digestion itself is thickened, as we asserted before. For if there is an abscess along the outer skin, certain thin liquids sweat out at the beginning; then, by digestion, they become thicker according to whether they are more or less digested, just as happens in fluids of the mouth and eyes, and in those occurring in each specific part.

Similarly, it happens in **pleurisy** <note>original: "pfesibus", referring to *pleuresibus*, an inflammation of the lungs or chest</note>; for first there is indigestion, as when nothing is spat out, then they produce thin liquids, which become thicker as they reach the end of digestion. Whence, in the third book of the **Aphorisms** <note>referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates</note>, it is said that the nature of digestion is to thicken the sputum in one who has pleurisy or peripneumonia. Reason demonstrates this because these abscesses are formed through the path of the pores by **revulsion** <note>a medical technique or process of drawing humors from one part of the body to another to relieve a condition</note>. That which is "revulsed" or drawn away comes out thin; otherwise, it could not run so quickly into the sponginess of similar parts, exiting the smallest veins—which is the manner of the generation of abscesses given in the **Tegni** <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*, a standard textbook</note> (on unequal disorder) and the fourteenth book of **On Method** <note>original: "de ingenio", referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi* or *On the Method of Healing*</note>. Therefore, that which is thin must, by the contrary, be cured by thickening, which usually happens first.

Sometimes, however, when the matter is thin and the power for resolution is strong, the digestion of the abscess (which is ordered toward its diminishment) is completed more by thinning. If, however, it is cold in essence and by accident, and hardened, then its digestion will proceed by thinning, since every cure of a contrary is completed by reason [of its opposite]. Whence in scrofulous nodes and such cold abscesses, one should first administer maturing and thinning agents with moisture, and finally add hotter and dryer things, so that once softened and thinned, they may be resolved into vapor and smoke, following this method until the whole matter vanishes.

If, however, the digestion is in the middle of these, as when a humor is putrefied in the liver (like sweet windiness), or if crude matter is converted to a healthy state, it is judged similarly: as being "simply helpful," it proceeds by thickening. If it is in the natural superfluities, it is the same way, as seen in many places, which reason also confirms. For a material superfluity tastes of the nature of that from which it falls away, for the thing falling away is proportioned to the thing it fell from; which is shown by urine, sweat, saliva, nasal discharge, and the discharge of the eyes or bleariness, according to **Aristotle** and **Galen**.

But regarding the aforesaid things, a doubt happens to arise; for it does not seem that digestion proceeds mostly by thickening and sometimes by thinning, since digestion is completed by a certain **natural power**; but this power, being irrational, is not capable of opposites, but only a rational power is (according to the eleventh book of the **Metaphysics**). Whence, according to the first book of **On the Soul**, natural powers do not arise from will, which is why they are not [capable of opposites]. To this, it must be said that although the digestive power is one in general, it is not so in specific instances. For it is diversified by the **complexion** <note>the specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in an individual</note>, the heat, and the parts upon which it depends; whence I say that for all identical things, it is not capable of opposites, but rather when they are varied in many ways. Or it is said that they are clearly the acts of a natural power like any other. Regarding the fourth objection, however, to the first point it must be said: it is not true that the vessels always proceed by narrowing; rather, sometimes it is one way, sometimes another, as appears in the esophagus, the stomach, the mesenteric veins, and those which are in the substance of the liver, being narrow...

Whether attraction which is caused by heat can be reduced to that which is shown to be caused by a **vacuum**. 

Because a positive cause does not lead to a **privation** <note>A "privation" is the absence of something; here, the author argues that "heat" (a real thing) cannot be explained by a "vacuum" (which is the absence of matter).</note>, since the prior state coincides with a "habit" <note>A positive quality.</note> rather than the reverse. But the attraction of heat imports something positive, whereas that of a vacuum imports something privative, as will appear. Furthermore, attraction is an **action**, since according to it, something is said to be acted upon in that which is subjected to it. Moreover, every qualitative change is perfected by contrariety, and most properly by heat, since it is the most effective of qualities and quick in motion (Difference 60). In a vacuum, however, there is neither action nor contrariety nor quality, since it is "non-being." 

Again, proof is provided by presence: much fire drags a small amount to itself, as is shown by the light of a candle to which a wax taper is brought near. And likewise, a light just extinguished receives light from a burning one by being placed next to it, even from below. You cannot feign that such things happen because of a vacuum, since the surrounding air is copious and fills the place thinned by the heat. And thus, since attraction occurs by something similar to a flame (according to the third book of *On Simple Medicines*), fire is proportional to fire, but not to a vacuum. 

Signs still bear witness to this. For what necessity or fear of a vacuum is there when the vapors of celestial rays rise into the air by their own indwelling heat? And why, under the mountain of **Custodia** <note>Likely referring to a specific cave or mountain known for natural drafts, possibly the Grotto di Custozza.</note> in the vaulted hollow called the "cupola," does the wind move from the inside to the outside in summer, but the opposite in winter, if not because of the heat being outside at one time and inside at another? Or why do **pellitory** <note>original: "piretrū", a medicinal plant used to stimulate saliva.</note>, **mastic**, and similar hot things, when placed between the teeth, attract fluids by liquefying them, while cold things do not? 

Therefore, attraction caused by heat is not reduced to that caused by a vacuum, but rather the reverse. On the contrary, in the third book of *Natural Hearing* <note>Aristotle's *Physics*.</note>, they only posit two modes of attraction: that from a vacuum and that from the property of a quality. You will find that the attraction from heat is reduced to that from a vacuum, since it is not possible to assign a failure there. This is expressed in the first book of the *Prior Analytics*. Again, if there is a vacuum, there is no motion, because every moving thing must be supported and lean upon something immobile (from *On the Motion of Animals*), which is not available in a vacuum. If, however, there is no motion, there is no heat, because heat is caused by motion and light. Therefore, so that there may finally be an effect, it is necessary that a vacuum does not exist. 

Furthermore, Nature, intending that which is better and more perfect, orders whatever things exist toward that cause, removing the opposite. This, however, is the "full," while the other is the "vacuum," which imports defect and privation, on account of which heat exists so that a vacuum does not occur in nature. Again, heat dissolves and consumes; in response to which, it is necessary for another thing to take its place. Otherwise, non-being would be mixed with being, which is impossible for contrary beings. Therefore, the attraction that comes from heat will be led to that of a vacuum. 

Regarding the first point, one must know that attraction is a certain motion. Motion itself is the act of a being in potentiality, according to what it has, or the movable insofar as it is movable (third book of the *Physics*). These things happen because the "mover" is twofold: one kind is that for the sake of which, or for the sake of an end, which is distant from the thing moved. Just as a separate thing, in itself, attracts what is situated near it—as the "beloved" attracts the "lover." The other kind of mover is that which is the beginning of the motion, existing simultaneously with that which is moved, as appears in **rotation** and **attraction** proper. And everything that is moved is moved either by itself or by another. By itself, when the mover and the moved coincide without a medium.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into physical forces, specifically transitioning from the discussion of digestion and the movement of humors to the broader mechanical and natural definitions of "Attraction." It builds on the previous page's mention of how heat pulls substances, now categorizing attraction within the framework of Aristotelian physics and medical theory.</meta>

Although it is **proclaimed** <term>p̃nuntiatū: announced or established as a principle</term> that "everything that is moved is moved by another"—either by some first moving **principle** <term>principiū</term> within itself, or by a superior source according to the order of the universe—that which is **carried** <term>fert̃: from 'fertur', moved or borne</term> by another is moved in four ways. For there are four types of motion caused by another, or "violent" motions: **pushing** <term>pulsio</term>, **pulling** <term>tractio</term>, **carrying** <term>uectio</term>, and **turning** <term>uertigo</term>. Any other types of motion that might exist are reduced to these four.

Leaving those aside for the **present** <term>p̃ntiaꝝ: 'presentia'</term>, let us focus only on **attraction** <term>attractione</term>. This occurs when the motion of the puller toward itself or toward another becomes faster than the motion of the thing being attracted, and the puller is not separated from the attracted object. Therefore, take note of the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher who wrote famous commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in that same passage, who says that attraction is twofold. One type is "true" attraction, in which the attractor moves along with the thing attracted, and the motion of the attractor is faster than that of the attracted. This is found in the voluntary powers and in the **parts** <term>p̃tis: 'partibus'</term> of nature; **therefore** <term>iō: 'ideo'</term>, in **living beings** <term>aīalibus</term>, there are certain conditions by which an action is **perfected** <term>pficit</term>.

The other type of attraction is "not true," in which the thing that attracts is what **perfects** <note>Completes or fulfills the action.</note> the process; that which is attracted moves so that it may be perfected by the mover. Examples include a stone moving downward, fire moving upward, iron moving toward a **magnet** <term>magnetē</term>, and nourishment moving toward the **parts** <term>ptes</term> of the body with health, tending toward the upper regions of the body. There remains, **however** <term>tñ: 'tamen'</term>, a **difference** <term>dīa: 'differentia'</term> between these things and those which move to their **proper** <term>ꝓpriū</term> place as if toward their end. For those things move toward that place whether it is **near** <term>ꝓpīqꝝ</term> or distant from **them** <term>eisdē</term>. But these things—like nourishment—do not move to provide nutrition even if they are sufficiently **close** <term>ꝓxima</term> unless they are **strengthened** <term>fīr: 'firmentur'</term>. Similarly, iron is not attracted unless a complete disposition between the active and passive elements is found between them. For if a **magnet** is rubbed with garlic, it will not attract iron. <note>This was a common medieval belief, often cited to show how specific substances could 'bind' or inhibit natural powers.</note> This is **likewise** <term>etiā</term> a **primary** <term>prīo</term> fourfold rule. Which, to be sure, is not **found** <term>repī: 'reperitur'</term> regarding [goat] blood, unless perhaps I were to dip it in the blood of a male goat for one day. <note>Refers to the ancient alchemical belief that goat's blood could soften diamonds or affect magnetic properties.</note> 

It **likewise** <term>etiā</term> requires a due distance; for when the distance is great, it will not attract unless the magnet is very large, since the medium between them is not strong enough to be changed. **Similarly** <term>Si l̃r: 'Similiter'</term>, a **joining** <term>cōiūctio</term> is required, and a prior **rubbing** <term>cōfricatio</term> of the iron with it. **Whence** <term>uñ: 'unde'</term> amber, when **warmed** <term>calefc̃m</term> by **rubbing** <term>cōfricatione</term>, more **perfectly** <term>p̃fcius</term> snatches up bits of straw. **For heat** <term>Caliditas nanq̄</term> strongly initiates and invigorates attraction, just as the **highly** <term>uehemēt</term> hot dissolving agents show, and the **mixing** <term>cōmixtio</term> of elephant-medicine. Whence, in the third book of *On Natural Things*: those **kinds** <term>gña: 'generis'</term> of things that are spread out can attract from a distance, but those with a **familiar** <term>failiari</term> quality can only do so from close by. For a siphon can pull water from a very long distance, but iron is **withdrawn** <term>abducitū</term> no further from a lodestone, nor can grain be pulled from a shell. Know **that** <term>q̄</term> a **magnet** <term>magnes</term> is found which attracts iron with one side and repels it with the other. I **certainly** <term>quide</term> have an iron knife that attracts iron more **vehemently** <term>uehem̃tius</term> than a magnet. A certain magnet even pulls human flesh; and when a large **piece** <term>frustrū</term> of pure iron is **taken** <term>accipit̃</term> and applied from the **opposite** <term>oppofito</term> side, it pulls the **same** <term>eandē</term> way. Many magicians **also** <term>etia</term> **use** <term>utun̄</term> it. But what the **difference** <term>dīa</term> of heat is was made known in book 15.

A **vacuum** <term>Vacuū</term> **also** <term>quoq̄</term> **can** <term>pōt</term> be understood in two ways: either in terms of motion, the **reason** <term>rō: 'ratio'</term> for which is that a **vacuum** <term>uacuū</term> is a place **deprived** <term>priuatꝝ</term> of a body but capable of being **filled** <term>replŕi</term>. As the **Philosopher** <term>phi.: Aristotle</term> says in the fourth book [of the Physics]: for the common people

say that the **vacuum** <term>uacuū</term> and that which is full of air are the same thing. In the seventh book of the *Topics*, **clearly** <term>liquidē</term> a **definition** <term>diffinitio</term> of **this kind** <term>huiōi</term> is the explanation **which** <term>quā</term> the **name** <term>nomē</term> **signifies** <term>fignat</term>. Whence it lacks a **limit** <term>termīo</term> in this way, which **entirely** <term>oīo</term> goes out **signifying** <term>fignās</term> "what the thing is." **Cold** <term>Frīm: 'Frigidum'</term>, **however** <term>autē</term>, if it attracts, does so more by **compressing** <term>coangustādō</term> **everything** <term>oīa</term> within itself and **staying** <term>stādō</term> **immobile** <term>imobili</term>. **Moreover** <term>autē</term>, attraction is a certain action; but **all** <term>omīs</term> actions are **perfected** <term>pficiū</term> by a **contrariety** <term>cōtrarietate</term> of powers, since an action does **not** <term>nō</term> **proceed** <term>pueniat</term> **immediately** <term>imēdiate</term> from a **substance** <term>s̃bā</term>. **Indeed** <term>siquidē</term>, Alexander the Physician in his *Problems* says: **Attraction** <term>Attractio</term> **also** <term>quoq̄</term> occurs through fear of a **vacuum** <term>uacui</term>, **just as** <term>uelat</term> that which is **pulled** <term>trahit̃</term> by a siphon and a **syringe** <term>firīge</term>; and by heat, as in **heat-treatments** <term>tapfie: 'thapsia' or similar</term>; and by use; and the weak by the strong; and by property, as **iron** <term>ferrū</term> **from a magnet** <term>amagnete</term>; and by the **particles** <term>pticulis</term> of health. <meta>This page continues the physical and philosophical investigation of "attraction," moving from the general definitions of motion on the previous page to specific mechanical and medical examples. It focuses on the debate over the "vacuum" (void) and whether heat is the primary cause of all attractive forces, citing major authorities like Avicenna, Galen, and Philo of Byzantium.</meta>

...least: unless the motion begins from that which has first descended from above. As much as it returns, it is increased by the **impulse** <term>impulsione: a driving force or push</term>. For when a **tube** <term>fistula: often referring to a siphon or pipe</term> draws liquid upward by its mouth, no vacuum occurs because the motion of what is evacuated exits faster than the descending air pushes in. However, when the instrument is held lower and at an angle, such motion of the liquid downward will be faster and stronger than the air moving upward. And therefore, no vacuum occurs. 

Know that a moist substance moved upward because of its descent from on high—the denser and more **congealed** <term>congelatū: thickened or solidified</term> it is, the more it is projected upward; and the rarer it is, the less it moves, because of the more vehement or relaxed impulse caused by the thick or the subtle. This is shown by springs drawn by art in cold and hot times, and similarly by night and day. 

**Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the 11th-century Persian physician and philosopher.</note>, although he gave three other causes of attraction to others, finally asserted that attraction which occurs through heat must necessarily be reduced by certain observers to the "filling of a vacuum"; indeed, he claims it is the same thing. He perhaps looked more closely at the books on *Natural Philosophy*, where the definitive teaching is handed down, since he shows himself there to know only the doctrines of the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>. 

Regarding this, it must be known that if attraction is an existing motion, it happens for the sake of an **end** <term>finē: a goal or purpose in Aristotelian physics</term>. The attraction caused by heat, as well as that caused by an "attractive power," is reduced to that which is caused by a **vacuum** <term>uacuo</term>—that is, so that a vacuum does not occur in nature. For nature holds the vacuum in hatred and utter contempt. Every body endeavors to move even against its own natural inclination so that it may fill every empty place, having utterly driven out the void. It would sooner cause the **heavens to sink down** <note>A common medieval phrasing of the "horror vacui" principle—that the structure of the universe would collapse before nature would allow an empty space to exist.</note> to fill that space than permit a vacuum to arrive, as they ascribed to Avicenna. This is perhaps what he meant when he said: "Indeed, it is the same thing." 

For the vacuum rightly has the power to fight against nature, since destruction and disorder would follow in the universe; for it brings about deprivation and imperfection. Furthermore, if there were a vacuum, it would be a place without a body, and there would be neither rest nor motion, since there is a need for support; nor would there be boundaries of motion or direction. Nor, if motion did occur, would it happen in **time**, but in an **instant** <note>Aristotle argued in his *Physics* that since speed is relative to the resistance of the medium, a vacuum (having zero resistance) would result in infinite speed, which he considered an absurdity.</note>, because there would be no medium to resist it. Also, a sealed vessel would sink in liquid, which does not happen, because it is full of air. And therefore **Philo** <note>Philo of Byzantium, a 3rd-century BCE engineer known for his work on pneumatics.</note>, along with others, strives to prove that air is a body—something which those ignorant of these matters thought was a vacuum.

Many other inconveniences would follow, as noted in the fourth book of the *Physics*. But if motion is considered as it happens from a **principle** <term>principio: the starting point or agent</term>—that is, from the agent which exists simultaneously with the motion, and not from the "end"—it must be said that all action universally and initially happens because of **heat** <term>calido</term>. And generally, all attraction, however it happens, does not occur except through heat; for attraction, insofar as it is attraction, is appropriated to heat. This is what was intended by Avicenna. 

For the attraction that follows from a vacuum likewise follows that which is from heat. In the **siphon** <term>azaracha: a medieval Latin term derived from Arabic, referring to a water-lifting device or siphon</term> and in tubes, which are said to compel attraction by a vacuum, the process is initiated by the heat of the containing vessel; and lest a vacuum intervene, the moisture that is drawn remains **uncongealed** <term>in cōgelatū</term> by the heat. For if it were vehemently cooled, it would congeal, so that what is evacuated could not be drawn out. Where the moisture remains liquid because of heat, one part pushes another upward and follows it. 

Motion is similarly caused by heat in the siphon. For the moving power inherent in heat, which consists in its concavity when the air is drawn upward, finally pulls the moisture along. This happens in the same way in **bellows** <term>follibus</term>. **Cupping glasses** <term>uentose: medical jars used to create suction on the skin</term> are also applied with fire or hot breath. Whence attraction, rather than being reduced to a vacuum, is reduced to that of heat; and much more so that which is initiated by a specific property or form through heat. 

As it comes from other things in common, and primarily from the **complexion** <term>cōplexione: the balance of qualities in a body</term> or from an instrument, Galen shows this property of quality. In the fifth book of *Simple Medicines*, he says: an "attractive medicine" is one which pulls from the depth of the body by attraction. Its substance is subtle, and this is twofold: one is such according to nature, like **pennyroyal** <term>pulegiū</term>, the dregs of the beehive, or **ferapinum** <unclear>ferapinū</unclear> and the like. The other is by accident, such as by **putrefaction**, like the ferment of dung and specifically **pigeon dung** <term>colūbinū</term>. 

There is another attraction by the property of its quality, by which the members of the body seize for themselves suitable nourishment. It is necessary that every such medicine of this property be **hot**. Whence that which stands out with more vehement heat attracts more—not because of the heat alone, but because it is aided by that heat; then it works for a twofold cause. All **purgative drugs** <term>purgatiua farmaca</term> are hot to the nutrients. If they are not such by themselves, they are ordered to be mixed with warm species. 

When a **magnet** <term>magnes</term> attracts iron, or as **amber** <term>karabe: from the Arabic 'kahraba'</term> attracts straws, or as the **anastach** <note>Possibly a reference to a plant or substance like "anagallis" or a specific stone described in lapidaries.</note> attracts fire, the medium is first changed by the primary qualities and altered. Indeed, alteration is proper to these. And although every action is ultimately and primarily caused by heat, such attraction is nevertheless perfected by a vacuum or by power. Though attraction, insofar as it is attraction, is appropriated to heat, the magnet does not attract iron because of "absolute attraction," but because of such specific attraction. 

Thus one should listen to **Alexander** <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle.</note> when he says that the **siphon** <term>firingā: likely a variant of 'syringa' or 'siringa', meaning a tube or syringe</term> does not attract by heat or property [alone]. But because ultimately all attraction is initially and absolutely caused by heat, and is reduced to it, it is a marvel; because everything found in many things through one univocal reason is in something prior to them, which is the cause of all those things. Just as every hot thing is reduced to the "first heat," which is fire. Also in the tenth book of the *Metaphysics*, it is said that it is necessary to reduce every multitude to some unity, so that infinity and disorder may be removed. For this reason, it is necessary to return all various attractions into one; but not into that which is from a vacuum, nor from a power...

<summary>This page argues that while nature's abhorrence of a vacuum (horror vacui) explains why substances move to fill empty spaces, the primary physical agent behind all attraction is heat. It reconciles mechanical devices like siphons and bellows with medical theories of how drugs and body parts draw in substances.</summary>
