<meta>This page continues the physiological examination of human hair, building on the previous discussion of the head as the "chimney" of the body's heat. It explores the causes of baldness, the variety of hair textures across different peoples, and the biological origins of graying hair.</meta>

...especially: And it stands out in men almost everywhere, and especially because it stands out more than the laws of other [animals]. For they **defend the head** from rains, heat <note>original: "caumatibus"; referring to intense solar heat</note>, and other harmful things rising from the outside. Furthermore, they adorn the head and the chin according to the Apostle <note>A reference to St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 11, discussing hair as a natural covering</note>, and women. Women's hair also provides protection instead of [the armor used by] men, either because their moisture is more susceptible and extensible. And they lack a beard, as was said. Again, for men, the cutting of hair happens by accident; for a woman, however, it is a disgrace <note>original: "taf̄" / "turpitudinem"</note>.

### The Conditions of the Hair

The hairs receive conditions from the head, specifically in their **substance** and in their **accidental qualities**. 

In **substance**, they are sometimes entirely cut off in the place called **baldness** <term>baldness: "calvities," derived here from "calx" (lime/dryness)</term>, on account of the extreme dryness of their composition. And because, due to thinness and dryness, the brain stands apart from the skull, so that it cannot be easily moistened by the dewy sprinkling of the head. This does not happen to women or eunuchs <note>In Aristotelian biology, women and eunuchs were considered "cold and moist," which supposedly prevented the "burning" of the hair roots that caused baldness</note> because of their great coldness and moisture. 

Why then do men, more than other animals, incur baldness since the brain is the coldest and moistest of all bodily members? It must be said that this happens because of its **location**, as it is a receiver of burnt vapors rising directly upward, where the skull is very dry. And because there are more movements of the **animal spirits** <term>animal spirits: "spiritus animales," the subtle fluids medieval doctors believed traveled through nerves to control movement and thought</term> due to various necessary acts of life, or because of the luxury of the mind. For these causes are all eventually heating and drying.

### Varieties of Texture and Curl

There are also some hairs that are thick, others thin, others medium, and some soft; others are rough and shaggy, while some are moderate. In their **accidental qualities**, they vary in shape: for some are straight, sometimes curly, and sometimes in between. **Curly hair** is produced by great heat, as in the Ethiopians, in whom the hair is so wrinkled that it becomes like peppercorns <note>A common medieval trope describing tightly coiled hair</note>. For, lacking moisture, they cannot remain extended, but like leather straps exposed to fire, they contract; or it is due to the twistiness of the pores from which they emerge. For the exterior is so arranged that the passages through which they pass are twisted; for this reason, one can sometimes see curly hair on the forehead and shoulders. 

Narrowness of the pores also sometimes causes this: for the rising vapor is so thin that when it thickens into hair on the outside, it cannot contain itself but folds and twists back, just as when a thread is suddenly pulled out of a narrow hole. This is the second and more moderate type of curliness and has very little hairiness. From opposite causes, hair is rendered straight, and from middle causes, it is intermediate between straight and curly. They also vary in quantity, either by reason of the places where they arise (as touched upon before) or by reason of age, such as youth, sex, or other regimens concerning non-natural things.

### The Color and Graying of Hair

They also diversify in color: some are white, some black, some intermediate, and these are the most numerous. Whether this happens from birth or by accident—such as from excessive burning or a dye—many are made black. The material of the hair itself, turned toward a kind of rot or decay near old age because of the inability to digest heat, occurs especially in humans and horses; this white color is called **grayness** <note>original: "canicies"</note>. (See *On the Generation of Animals*, Book 5). 

This happens first at the **temples**, mostly because of the windy moisture intercepted in the muscles of the temples, moistening them. And therefore **Homer** called men "temple-gray" <note>original: "temporitanos"</note>, as Alexander says in the first of his *Problems*. 

And know that the cause of grayness, according to Aristotle, is a change toward the heat of the internal vapor. And according to Galen, it is *athacoruga* <note>original: "athacorū gī"; likely a corruption of a Greek term for a scalp condition or "moldiness"</note> which accompanies the nourishment that comes to the hair when it is cold and its time of movement and penetration into its pores has passed. But so that the truth of this may appear, the following agreement between both authors is set down.

Grayness is indeed a **putrefaction** of water and earth in such bodies; for a terrestrial vapor (like the aforementioned "decoction") is a putrefaction of terrestrial vapor. Therefore, such undigested nourishment existing in the hairs putrefies and becomes what is called grayness. It is white because the putrid vapor is released, which is white. The reason for this is that it contains much air. In the second of the *Problems*: hairs become weak and white, which they call "gray." They are weak due to a lack of proper nourishment; they are white just as wood is nourished by a kind of "caries" <term>caries: properly the rot or decay of wood</term> in the time of putrefaction. Whence **Ovid** says:

->*It turns into rotten decay and gapes with cracks.*<-

From these sequences introduced here, it is clearly seen whatever may be said. Aristotle speaks of the nourishment accompanying the decay, which is the same cause Galen assigns, and also Aristotle, for grayness. Therefore, he added: when you consider their two sayings, you will find them to be certain. For the cause of the whiteness of the vapor's color and the cause of the whiteness of the *athacoruga* is one. And perhaps the errors of the Arabic translations led to this.

It has also been seen that grayness sometimes occurs from the **contraction of spirits** due to a sudden fear, just as death overtakes those expecting it suddenly. And it is said *a priori* that the former begins from the roots of the hairs, but the latter from their ends, like the whiteness in plants beginning to dry out.

### Other Bodily Hair

There is also another use for hairs on external parts, as a protection as mentioned before. Galen says this happens from the necessity of the condition: because heat exists, the matter is propelled into the hairs. Haly Abbas <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician</note> asserts this happens by accident. In our bodies, they serve one purpose; in others [animals], they provide the benefit of clothing and protective armor. And if they say these arise in us by necessity or by accident, nevertheless, a use is assigned to all external hairs, such as those around the private parts, the abdomen, and the armpits. For those were produced for the sake of covering and hiding the shameful parts, and similarly to protect and warm them from the outside. Those around the penis likewise protect and warm, which was very advantageous for humans and wild creatures, since they do not have, as we do, the art of preparing warmth and defense for themselves. And therefore nature, which applies ingenuity to the excess of each part, labored so that more and longer hairs would extend there. 

Concerning this art, it should be known that the **nail** is a body...

<meta>This page continues the physiological discussion of the body's appendages, transitioning from the hair of the head to the nature and function of the fingernails, comparing their growth and nourishment to that of hair.</meta>

The **nail** is an expanded plate <note>original: "petale"; likely referring to the thin, leaf-like structure of the nail</note> produced from residues <term>residues: "superfluitates," the materials left over after the body's primary digestion</term>, hardened and situated upon the extremities of the fingers for protection. Indeed, it is a leaf-like part located at the ends of the fingers of the hands or feet, just as hair is in the skin, a peripheral part of the body. Whence, if any of the small bones at the tips of the hands or feet are lost, the nails do not grow there; just as hair is lost in us when the skin is destroyed, which is why they do not grow in scars. Whence in the *Problems*, book 10 <note>A reference to the *Problemata*, a collection of scientific questions attributed to Aristotle</note>, it is asked why hair grows in the scars of horses and donkeys, but not in humans. This is either because in those animals the hide is like a part of the flesh, whereas in us the skin is not like a part of the flesh, but rather an "affection" <note>original: "passio"; in this context, a secondary condition or covering</note> of the body. 

The mode of their origin is proportional to the production of hair, though they are generated from thicker residues that are not so "burnt" <note>original: "adustis"; referring to the internal heat that dries out bodily fluids</note>, as their relative softness indicates. They are also diversified in many ways, both by reason of their substance and their accidents <term>accidents: "accidentia," the observable qualities like color and texture that do not change the essential nature of the thing</term>. For some are thick, rough, and hard; others are thin, smooth, and softer. Some are more expanded; some small and sharp. Indeed, some are flatter and straight; others are hooked and curved back. Some are clear and shining; others obscure and dark. Some are white; others dark; and some are a mixture of white and red, being more vivid and bright. I have sufficiently demonstrated the significance of these variations in the treatise I composed on **Physiognomy** <note>The medieval science of judging a person's character from their physical features</note>. 

For nails participate more in the governance of nature than many types of hair, since not a few are thought to be produced from the residues of the heart. And therefore, they are proportional to the hair of the eyelids, eyebrows, and the head, according to the first principle. In certain animals, however, they are so helpful that they exist as the very limits of necessity.

   Furthermore, there is the utility which they bring to the inner parts, as is shown by the fourfold benefit they exhibit externally. One, indeed, is that they are like a defense and protection for the flesh of the fingers, so that they are not harmed when pressed against a hard thing; they preserve the ends like the iron tip of a spear. Another is that with them, the fingers can pick up very small things and hold them more firmly. 

   Third, because with them one can scratch and groom. Another is because they are sometimes used as weapons for defense, which happens more in other animals than in man. Beyond this, they make the extremities of the fingers more beautiful to the sight, just as happens in artificial things where gold or ivory is inlaid. 

As for what their nourishment is, and how many differences are spoken of, book 30 shows. Regarding this, it must be known that some have argued indifferently that nails and hair are nourished in truth, and not merely in appearance. But both sides of this argument are discussed unscientifically. For, as will be declared, they are nourished very little. Furthermore, if they were nourished, how could it escape our notice over such a long span of time? Whence the masters of ideas follow Plato; against whom Aristotle writes in the *Metaphysics*. It is a marvel how this remains hidden to those possessing the highest knowledge. It is astounding, therefore, how—if hair and nails have a perfect nutritive power implanted in them—it should escape us unperceived. And yet it appears that hair and nails are nourished and grow more than even the principal members, since we see their extension happening so continually that they require cutting; and because of this, they manifest themselves more clearly.

Therefore, there were others who argued more probably that hair and nails can be considered in two ways. Either as they are residues expelled by nature to the outside; and thus, since they are not members <note>i.e., vital organs or living parts of the body</note>, they do not enjoy nourishment. Or, in the sense that these residues are condensed into a specific part from which some benefit comes to the body; and thus, because they acquire the character of a "member" in some way, they can perhaps be nourished. But even this perhaps cannot stand, since as it has been shown, some hairs and nails are not produced from residues in every way, nor do they seem to exist outside the intention of nature. Nor does the condensation of residues into a solid part constitute a "member" such that it uses nourishment. 

Since the power [of nourishment] fails, as will be shown, we must speak of this with a fuller determination. **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd, the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher</note> in the *Colliget* <note>original: "coll’3"; his medical encyclopedia, *Kitab al-Kulliyat fi al-Tibb*</note>, following the aforementioned, seems to go against **Galen** <note>The 2nd-century Greek physician whose work dominated medieval medicine</note>. Galen wanted hair to be generated from a continuous emission of smoke to the skin, saying that certain types of hair are generated by the necessity of matter, such as in the armpits and chest and other parts. For hair, according to Galen, is generated from a certain smoky, burnt vapor. This requires investigation. It flows into a detestation of Galen's view that hair is a dry, extensible body; and such is the residue of dry food when it is cooked while fat is mixed in it. And finally, he concludes: therefore it is not that vapor whose parts are aggregated, but it is a continuous body of strong extension growing in length. 

He [Averroes] wishes, therefore, that since hair is a continuous body, it is not generated by a mere mode of emission, but rather as a permanent thing, it receives suitable nourishment. To this, the *Problems*, book 10, lends support by asking why the hair of sheep becomes harder the more it extends, while the hair of humans becomes softer. The answer given is that the hair of sheep originates from the surface of the body, whereas that of man comes from the depths. Therefore, the nourishment for sheep's hair is meager, while for man's it is the opposite. Thus, when the nourishment is meager, as he says, it makes them softer. The hair of sheep at the beginning is rendered soft, but as it proceeds further toward the end, the moisture is exported and dried out, rendering them harder. But in human hair, since at first the nourishment is meager <note>because it is being used to form the root</note>, the hair is hardened; but when it is extended, it is digested and made moist to the point that the hair softens toward the ends.

From these points, therefore, it is clear that as long as the hair remains, nourishment is carried through it, and does not only reach the roots. Therefore, hair does not exist solely from a continuous, successive steaming out to the exterior, as it seemed to Galen. To this, it must be said that in the hair of the eyelids and eyebrows, the growth proceeds simply, since a limit to their extension is seen. But in other hairs and nails which seem to extend continually, it should not be said absolutely. For they seem to be lengthened more by a continuous evaporation than by the assumption of nourishment throughout the whole. Thus, in these, it must be posited that their extension occurs primarily from a continuous submission of matter. Nevertheless, some moisture can be distributed into those parts already condensed, from which they retain some humidity.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of bodily appendages, specifically addressing the mechanical and physiological differences between the hair of humans and animals, and transitioning into the specific growth patterns of fingernails. It references the catchword "nutricatō" from the previous page, indicating a continued focus on the nourishment of these parts.</meta>

...they acquire. And especially when the moisture has been subtle, watery, and the vaporous member <note>In medieval physiology, "vaporous" refers to parts formed from the rising heat and moisture of the body's internal "cooking" or digestion.</note>, so that it may be burned very little. And this is why we see the hair of some people almost continually moistened by ichor <term>ichor: "ycore," a thin, watery discharge or serous fluid</term>, and especially when it has been thickened. 

And to this, **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a prominent Andalusian philosopher and physician whose commentaries on Aristotle and Galen were foundational to medieval medicine.</note> would say that hair is an extensible, dry body of strong continuity, once it has been hardened from the outside by the air—but not when it is remaining in the pores or under its own nature, where addition is made to the same. Hence, he wrongly asserts here that the vapor would not be an aggregation of part upon part, but rather a continuous body of strong continuity receiving increase in length.

But **Galen** <note>The influential 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years.</note> could respond that the aforementioned density in the hair of sheep and cattle does not occur because of the nutritive moisture flowing through them, but rather because of the coldness of the air. Or else, it is due to the density of the material hardening. For when the hair of sheep proceeds from the skin, it still participates in sufficient moisture; and because they have been in the air for only a short time, they still emerge soft. However, when they have remained longer, they are dried out and hardened by it. In the hair of cattle, however, there is immediately a thick, viscous moisture with sufficient expulsive heat hardening them; but when it has remained in the air, they will be inspired by it, thinned, and digested by the strengthened heat, tinted more by the cold than if it had condensed and hardened them, since its heat is repugnant to it so that some temperament arises.

Or perhaps it is better to concede, as given before, that a certain moisture is differentiated in the permanence of the hair, with a continuous emission of "effluence" <note>The outward flow of waste or surplus materials.</note>. Regarding the fingernails, it should be known that the truth of the question can be known from the things already mentioned, as will be said regarding their utility. **Nails** do not stop growing immediately because of the practice of scratching or abrasion and other operations; therefore, they are suited to receive increase in all times. But their increase is not in all dimensions—that is, in length, width, and depth as in other members—but in length only, just like the increase of hair. For when the moisture is plentiful, the exit easy, and the "burning" <note>original: "adustio"; the metabolic heat that dries out fluids</note> weak, they become well-augmented and thick by a moderate abundance of the superfluities nourishing them.

Whence **Haly Abbas** <note>’Ali ibn al-’Abbas al-Majusi (10th century), a Persian physician famous for the *Kitab al-Malaki* or "Royal Book" of medicine.</note> says: nerves and arteries tend toward the nails from nearby, to which they bring food by which they are quickened; except that their food does not increase them and make them grow in a wide and deep place as other members do, but it only extends them in length, as was shown in the hair. To make this truth shine more clearly, it should be known that **nutrition** occurs in two ways:

1.  One is by **preservation**, such as when the food is transformed and takes the form of the member in every designated part. This is how nourishment works in members we call "true" <note>Members like the heart or liver that assimilate food into their own living substance.</note>, since they have four serving virtues: the digestive, the transformative, the seductive (of nourishment), and the informative (which shapes the nourishment into the member's likeness).
2.  The other is **nutrition by juxtaposition** <term>juxtaposition: "iuxta positio," growth by adding material alongside or on top of existing parts, like stacking bricks, rather than absorbing it into the structure.</term>, as when the nourishment is placed alongside certain parts of the member. Some have said these members are not "nourished" at all; indeed, there is a certain undeniable difference in this in Chapter 12. 

Nevertheless, it must be stated that members taken commonly are nourished, like parts of the hair and the nails. For to the roots of these existing parts, a "burnt" vapor comes and pushes them forward. It also emits moisture into them, which is carried into the hair and nails by a natural expelling force—or, according to **Averroes**, by a certain attraction, specifically in the hair of the eyelids and eyebrows. For nourishment is not transformed through every primary part in them, but the material is pushed outward through a certain juxtaposition. And with this distinction sufficiently understood, the rest of the arguments for both sides can be addressed.

But a doubt arises regarding the above: for in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica* (The Art of Medicine), often called "Tegni" in the Middle Ages.</note> it seems that true nutrition also occurs through juxtaposition, when it is written that in members having similar parts, their own nourishment is made from "apposition" <note>The placing of one thing next to another.</note>. This apposition seems to imply a kind of juxtaposition, since every nourishing thing must be applied to the nourishment. It must be said that Galen does not intend to say that all parts are nourished this way, as appears more fully in the *On the Nature of Animals* and *On the Generation of Animals*, but rather he invites a distinction of nourishment based on the "hypostatic" difference <note>original: "ypostatica"; referring to the underlying substance or essence of the nourishment.</note>.

That is: one kind of nourishment is "true," which is apposed, united, and assimilated to the part; another is "future" nourishment or the humor existing in the veins which is not yet apposed. But to open this speech more fully, it should be known that **governance** <term>governance: "regimen," the way a part of the body is controlled or maintained by the soul or natural forces.</term> is twofold. One is of members generated from pure matter; another is of those produced from superfluities <note>Residues or waste products.</note>. The first is fourfold:
1.  Some have a governance so principal that many members are ruled by them, such as the four **principal members** <note>Usually the heart, brain, liver, and testicles.</note>.
2.  Some have a governance by which they serve those principal ones.
3.  Some have a governance through an innate and "influenced" <note>flowing from the principals</note> power.
4.  Some have a "vile" <note>lowly or secondary</note> governance, because they have only an innate power instilled in their generation by nature. This nature is primary and exists like a basis in which the member is placed in its being.

Although the three aforementioned differences of members participate in this power or nature, they are placed in their specific being by nobler virtues. Just as a human is established in the being of his species by "rationality" <term>rationality: "rōnale," the defining characteristic of humans in Aristotelian logic</term>, and not merely by being an "animal" or a "body." And because members commonly called "vile" do not participate in true governance—except perhaps the hair of the eyelids and eyebrows, which are almost like the larger feathers in birds—they are not "certain" members <note>Meaning they are not definitive organs with complex functions.</note>. Yet, imperfectly, they can be said to enjoy governance; although nails and the hair of the head do so far less than other parts. 

Considering therefore that their governance is "improper" <note>not in the strict sense</note> and taken only by similarity, **Galen** says that hair and nails do not have governance, and consequently neither "nutrition," nor "increase," nor "generation" in the true sense—even if in common speech one might say they do. This is shown because it falls outside the definition of a "truly nourished part," which would be generated all at once in time, and not successively and little by little, and which would have a fixed limit to its growth through transformation, and not merely through apposition.

It ranks bodily members by their level of "governance," placing hair and nails at the lowest, most "vile" level of the biological hierarchy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding whether hair and nails are "true" parts of the body and how they receive nourishment. It then transitions into Difference 55, a systematic classification of the three vegetative powers: nutrition, growth, and generation.</meta>

Furthermore, it appears that their own dissolution <note original: "resolutio">The process of breaking down or wearing away of bodily tissue.</note> is possible. Since, therefore, hair and nails participate in none of these [nutritive processes], or only a few, they truly lack the act of nutrition. Hair, however—especially the eyelashes—is brief in its growth. For almost from the beginning of their generation, they have a limit to their increase, which teeth do not have, for a specific purpose <note original: "propter finem">The "final cause" or biological purpose.</note>: so that they are not lost by continuous wear. Also, their nourishment occurs more through transubstantiation <term>transubstantiation: here, the biological process where food is fully converted into the substance of the organ</term>. Fourthly, it is said that a man may lack them; hence **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in medieval Europe.</note> says in certain "Problems" that they do not turn grey. Such are the aforementioned hairs, and almost all nails and beaks in other animals. Other nails and hair, however, have none of these qualities, except perhaps a more manifest dissolution or loss. Because of this, they participate in nature or nourishment in a very particular, restricted way. 

Because of this, regarding the previous authorities, it must be said that "nutrition" and "nourishment" were used improperly, or that they were not nourished through transubstantiation but rather through juxtaposition <term>juxtaposition: the addition of new matter to the end or surface of a part, rather than through its entire substance</term>. For all hair and nails are not "members" <note original: "membra">True organs or functional parts of the body.</note> unless the name is extended, as **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas (died c. 982), a famous Persian physician.</note> did here by calling them members. To the other point, it must be said that just as their increase is not "true" [growth], so their nourishment is not "true" nourishment. Hence, in the fourteenth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note original: "de ingenio," referring to Galen's "De Methodo Medendi"></note>, where I supplied the lack of thickness: as much of the transpiring humors as is muddy generates hair right from the start, and the rest increases according to the substance. For he does not speak simply, but is speaking about the decrease [of humors]. For true growth is an extension according to three dimensions: length, width, and depth. 

To the other point, it must be said that "generation" is taken commonly for any giving of substantial form in whatever way. Thus, the generation of this kind is caused by an expulsive act <note>The body "pushing out" waste matter which then hardens into hair or nails.</note>; for true generation is preceded by a mixing in which action and passion occur according to all parts, and not just some. It is not as if the whole that is generated arises almost at once; yet I do not prohibit a substantial form from being impressed in an instant. To the other point, it must be said that it could be granted for both the hair of the eyelids and the eyebrows, but for other hair and nails, not at all. For nature produces many things not simply for the sake of "being," but rather for the sake of "well-being," such as nails and other hair. To the other point, it must be said that it does not conclude concerning nourishment made through transubstantiation, but rather through juxtaposition, as was said above. The arguments brought from the other side concerning nourishment conclude regarding transubstantiation and the virtuous governance [of the body].

-># DIFFERENCE 55.<-

**Whether the power of growth is entirely different from the power of nutrition.** Since the vegetative [soul], which is the natural power, has two works—to generate and to be maintained by food—as stated in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's "De Anima," the foundational text for medieval psychology.</note>, there are therefore two acts and two forms, namely the nutritive and the generative, since every work is led into its own being by a power. Again, those whose substance, subject, object, and work are the same, seem to be the same form. So it is with the nutritive and the augmentative [growth] powers. For they are the same in substance. For the division of the soul into its parts is like a fruit divided into its smell, taste, and color, as stated in the first book of *On the Soul*. The subject is also the same, such as the member and the instrument; likewise, the food is the single object of both, and they share a common work, such as apposition, union, and assimilation. Also, the nutritive power sometimes brings in more than it dissolves, sometimes 

---

the same, and sometimes less. Therefore, when more is added, that work of "increasing" will belong to the nutritive power. Or, if it is assigned to the augmentative power for the same reason, one would also have to posit an "equating" power and a "diminishing" power—and especially an "equating" power since its work is to bring things to perfection. Furthermore, it would at least seem that the augmentative power is the effect of the nutritive, and not something distinct or opposite to it. Therefore, the "increasing" power would be the same as the nutritive power. 

The opposite is held by both philosophers and physicians. Clearly, those things are not the same if one can be destroyed without the other being destroyed, since the whole remains even with the destruction of one part. This is how it is with the nutritive and the augmentative powers. For the latter is destroyed while the nutritive power remains, since animals are always nourished but do not always grow, as stated in the *Topics* and the second book of *On the Soul*. Therefore, the nutritive power is distinct from the increasing power. 

Regarding this, it must first be known that the vegetative soul or power (called "nature" by physicians) is the proper perfection of a natural, instrumental body. It has three powers: **The nutritive power**, which is the power converting a body from the state it was in into the likeness of the body in which it exists, and it applies, unites, and assimilates it to restore that which was dissolved from it. And **the augmentative power** is the power increasing the body in which it exists from the body which it assimilates to it, by a proportional increase in all its dimensions, which are length, width, and thickness, in order to lead the thing to perfection. **The generative power** is the power which takes from the body in which it exists a part similar to it in potentiality, and works in it by the attraction of other bodies which it assimilates to it, to be generated and mixed, and converts them into its own likeness in effect, as stated in the first book of *On the Soul*. 

In the first book of *On Natural Things*, the acts of these powers are described. **Nutrition** is the addition to solid parts without increase in dimension from the particles. **Augmentation** [growth], however, is the addition of dimensions according to length, width, and depth in those same parts. **Generation** is the leading forth of a substance, or the progress from non-being to being through a substantial form. For that form is acquired and comes upon the matter. These three powers differ in many ways, because the nutritive is more useful than the other two and lasts longer in time, since it remains almost always as long as life remains. One says "almost," because sometimes an animal is not nourished, such as by accident or for a brief hour. But the augmentative power lasts until the body reaches its [adult] state and then ceases. The generative power is more restricted than the nutritive, and more useful than the increasing power. For starting around the 14th year, it extends to the 85th, or further. The increasing power, however, lasts only until about the 35th year, a difference of 21 years. These also have an order of priority and service to one another: the nutritive is ordered toward the increasing, and the increasing toward the generative, as if toward the end of the natural powers. They also differ in their "instrument," namely heat. For the nutritive uses a different heat than the augmentative, because the latter is stronger and more extensive. And these differ from the generative, because it is more spirituous and more complex than those two heats, since three spirits constitute one. They also differ in their object, because food exists as the object of the nutritive power as a "certain something" and substance, but for the augmentative, it is not just as a substance but as a "quantity."

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the vegetative soul, specifically moving from the unique growth of hair and nails into a broader debate on whether the powers of nutrition and growth are distinct or identical. It follows the previous page's distinction between simple nourishment and the addition of mass.</meta>

### DIFFERENCE LVI.

In the second book of *On the Soul* <note original: "de aia s30">Aristotle, De Anima, Book II.</note>, it is discussed regarding generation. Likewise, in the actual process, the nutritive power unites nourishment according to the measure it possesses, either equally or nearly so, producing growth in terms of thickness; but the augmentative power <term>augmentative power: the biological force responsible for increasing the physical dimensions of the body</term> increases the body across every diameter, and more so in length. This is more difficult to achieve since it occurs in the "spermatic" members <note>In medieval physiology, these are the primary, hard parts like bones and nerves, believed to originate from the reproductive fluid.</note> which are hard, unlike growth in width and depth or general thickness. And so it happens that certain members are sometimes large at the beginning of generation—especially the upper parts in men—while others, like the lower parts, are small, a condition that does not always persist. Therefore, this is not the work of the nutritive power alone, for then growth would occur in equal proportion. Rather, the augmentative power performs this because it almost always unites matter [to the frame]. Its end goal is also different, as indicated in the previously mentioned definitions.

The same is also addressed here regarding how many powers are ascribed to the soul. Whenever a distinction is made, it is shown in the third part.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have posited that the nutritive and the "crescitive" <term>crescitive: a synonym for the augmentative or growth power</term> powers are one and the same. They held that they differ only by reason, just as they believed of the other powers of the soul. For they wanted the powers of the soul to differ only by conceptual distinction (Difference 38). Augustine the Monk <note>Likely referring to Agostino Triumphus (1243–1328), an Augustinian theologian who wrote extensively on the soul.</note> also held this view. Their opinions will be shown from what follows, as far as is sufficient for this topic.

Regarding the third point, it must be said that these two powers belong to a single part of the soul. Although they are very closely related, they are not actually identical, as the physicians have held alongside the natural philosophers. This is apparent because just as the soul needs the nutritive power for its existence—since life consists of persistence through food—it also needs growth from food introduced through the crescitive power, since it was produced from a small amount of initial matter. For it could not perform its proper acts unless it received an increase. Whence in this matter it is necessary to posit a double virtue, just as in generation there are both the proximate transformative and the informative powers (Difference 48). Furthermore, their definitions differ and they are distinct in themselves. But the definitions, as proposed, are different for generation and augmentation. Also, when the instrument, the object, the time, the manner, and the end are not the same, the essence is not the same. It is through these things that we come to know the two: the nutritive, as shown, and the augmentative. Thus, the nutritive is distinct from the crescitive. It should be known, however, that these two powers are very closely related since they concern the same subject, namely the whole body, just as the generative power is related to the crescitive. Whence it is gathered in the second book [of *On the Soul*]: the augmentative power does not have its own specific members, but they are the same as those used for growth. Therefore, the generative power can be separated from growth, but not from nutrition. And since it has a subject given at least in form, such as the testicles <margin>the testicles</margin>—though not in terms of matter, as the whole body is the matter—neither can depart from the nutritive power, as it is their principle and root.

Regarding the fourth point, it must be said that Avicenna <note original: "Au.">Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath.</note> in his *Breviloquium* included both the nutritive and augmentative powers under "nourishment," as the Commentator <note>Typically refers to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the preeminent commentator on Aristotle.</note> expressed. This is also apparent because they are finally distinguished by their objects, as has been shown.

Regarding the next point, it must be said that although certain things seem to be the same, they are only identical in a general sense, not in their specific properties. For the great affinity between these powers mentioned before creates the appearance of identity and thus leads to this deception. Regarding the other point, it must be said that the case is different for the other works of the nutritive power; the crescitive power adds more matter than that which it works upon, whereas nutrition merely restores what has been lost. The power of growth implies perfection, while loss implies imperfection. For diminishing is not a power, but rather a failure and an imperfection. Nor is a "power of equalization" to be assigned to the proportional restoration of loss, since the power is needed so that the individual or the species may be perfected over a longer time. And this does not happen when such restoration lasts for only a very short time. Furthermore, no work of the soul would be shown beyond mere nutrition and existing through food. Regarding the last point, it must be said that the crescitive is not an effect of the nutritive, but rather a power standing by itself, separate from it as shown, though it must exist in a very similar form. Thus, all powers, even of different types, naturally serve one another by preparing suitable matter from which the other finally works to induce growth. That more is sometimes added is not due to the vigor of the nutritive power, but of the augmentative.

### DIFFERENCE LVI.

THAT augmentation occurs according to the material parts <term>material parts: the physical matter that flows in and out of the body</term> and not the formal parts <term>formal parts: the structural "blueprint" or soul-guided shape that remains constant</term> is shown by the fact that the "official parts" <term>official parts: heterogeneous organs with specific functions, like a hand or eye</term> are increased because the "similar parts" <term>similar parts: homogeneous tissues like flesh, bone, or blood</term> are increased. Whence in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption* <note original: "de ge. & cor.">Aristotle's treatise on the coming-to-be and passing-away of things.</note>: the *anomiomera* <note original: "Anomiomera">Heterogeneous parts made of different tissues (e.g., a finger).</note> grow when the *omiomera* <note original: "omiomera">Homogeneous parts where every piece is the same as the whole (e.g., flesh).</note> grow. But the *omiomera* are like matter. For the *anomiomera* are composed of them (Metaphysics, Book 4, and *On the Parts of Animals*, Book 2). Growth, therefore, occurs through similar parts and not official ones. Again, quantity follows the substance composed of the material part; quality, however, follows more from the formal part. But growth seems to imply quantity, since it is an addition to pre-existing quantity (*On Generation and Corruption*, Book 1).

Furthermore, that which is increased must by its nature be capable of extension; such is matter, not form, since form occurs as simple and indivisible, according to the *Six Principles* <note>The *Liber de Sex Principiis*, a medieval logic text attributed to Gilbert de la Porrée.</note>.

On the other hand, if every small particle of the thing grown is increased—as is assumed in the growth of homogeneous parts—then given the smallest of particles, the homogeneous parts will be increased from a minimum of nourishment. Because of this, it follows that growth would happen by doubling, then quadrupling, then a hundredfold, and so on unto infinity. Therefore, either not every particle of the grown thing is increased, or the thing capable of growth would be increased to infinity. Since these are absurd, either there would be no growth, or it must be according to the fluid material part and not the formal and permanent part. Therefore, the material part is increased, and not the formal. To the contrary, in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*, it says that whatever part is increased by something arriving, it happens according to the species; which "species" is nothing other than form, and least of all according to matter. And it is necessary that growth occurs upon a firm, standing thing. Alexander the Peripatetic <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, the 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> [says this] in his little treatise *On Growth*. For that which flows cannot be increased, since it cannot be joined to pre-existing quantity; thus the said reason testifies to growth. It is manifest that matter does not stand still but flows in and out. Whence Avicenna: this material part flows away, while this other arrives; but the form and species of anything [remains].

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the nature of biological growth. It transitions from the simple distinction between nutrition and growth into a complex debate about whether growth occurs in the "matter" of a body or its "form," citing the heavyweight authorities of the Middle Ages: Aristotle, Averroes, and Galen.</meta>

...the parts remain. Furthermore, growth is one of the four types of motion <note original: "motuū">The four Aristotelian motions are: change in substance, quality, quantity (growth), and place.</note>. However, motion only occurs upon a stable, existing part, because every motion relies on something immovable, as is clear from the cause of the motion of animals. For this reason, growth occurs according to the parts **formally** and not **materially**.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that growth and diminution, according to the Commentator <note original: "cōntatorē">Averroes (1126–1198), the Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to medieval science.</note> in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*, is a motion. But this is either:
1.  **True growth and diminution**, which occurs only in plants and animals.
2.  **Alteration**, as happens with water and air; for when they are thickened, they become of lesser quantity, but when they are rarefied, they become greater. This is frequently found in the bodies of natural things, as happens in the addition to a mixture.
3.  **Accidental growth**, which is found in composite, standing bodies like minerals. In these, growth occurs when some extrinsic thing is added and remains with the original substance; in this sense, it is said that "fire grows" from the things mentioned.

Commonly, it is also said that growth is understood in two ways:
Either **generally**, through any addition of any amount, whether in animate or inanimate things, or across all three dimensions, or just two or one. This is defined by Aristotle <note original: "Au.">Aristotle, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" or "Au." for Autor/Authoritas.</note> as "the addition of magnitude to a pre-existing thing."
The Commentator says that growth is nothing other than "quantity insofar as it retains form."
Or, **more properly**, as it is found only in animate bodies, extending across the three known dimensions. This is observed solely in the **spermatic members** <term>spermatic members: the primary, solid parts of the body (like bone and nerve) that medieval doctors believed were formed from the reproductive "seed."</term> in the beginning of natural life, as is manifest from the swelling of a bladder. Therefore, "fattening up" through a lack of leanness in the stable years of life, although it generates bulk, is not strictly "growth" <note original: "crefcētia">Crescentia: true biological development.</note> because it does not occur according to a natural proportion across the three diameters. Extension, however, as touched upon earlier, is made greater in the upward and downward directions than in the right and left; and there is even a minimum of these dimensions in the front and back, more generally in length than in width, and finally in depth.

According to Galen <note original: "Ga.">Galen of Pergamon (129–c.210 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note>: "Growth is the addition of dimensions in length, depth, and width of the solid parts of an animal, of which the formation was also original."
Thus, growth is threefold:
- Either **commonly**, through the addition of any thing to another thing.
- Or **properly**, through that which occurs in the "bloody parts" at any time.
- Or **most properly**, according to that which occurs only in the members of the "seed" <note original: "mēbr̄ē solū ſpmatis">The spermatic members, which were thought to be the only parts capable of true growth in size.</note> through extension in every dimension.

In growth of this kind, parts are found according to **matter** and according to **form**, both being double in nature, as suggested in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*, the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*, and in the book *On the Parts of Animals*. For some parts are more noticeable and, as it were, prior; others are more hidden and, as it were, final, with the first parts holding a certain middle ground with the others.

There are parts which, according to matter, reflect the form weakly in relation to the act of the **vegetative soul** <term>vegetative soul: the lowest level of the soul responsible for basic biological functions like nutrition, growth, and reproduction.</term> and are more discussed as "homeomerous" <note original: "omiomere">Homeomerous: parts that are uniform throughout, like flesh, where every piece of flesh is still just "flesh."</note> parts. In one of these—take flesh, for instance—sensation can exist, as seen in the first book of the *History of Animals* and the book *On the Parts of Animals*, from which also come fat and general greasiness.
There are other parts which, according to form, contain the matter within themselves for the act of the soul or its ordered power, such as the **instrumental parts** <term>instrumental parts: complex organs like the hand or eye, made of various tissues working together.</term>. For these fulfill the motions and works of the soul manifestively, at least regarding the distinction between this and the sensation of flesh.

Between these, three types of "middle parts" exist:
Some hold more toward the **material parts**, such as bone and cartilage, which are the basis and protection of the body.
Others hold more toward the **formal parts**, such as the nerves, membranes <note original: "pānniculi">Panniculi: thin layers of tissue or membranes.</note>, ligaments, veins, and arteries, along with the seminal vessels serving the principal members in which the nature of formality resides.
Still others hold a middle position, being equally distant from both extremes, such as a **muscle**, which is composed of simple flesh (as its material part) and nerve, ligament, membrane, and cord (as its formal parts).

The parts according to matter, being more hidden and final, are also contained within the homeomerous parts; for flesh and bone and each of such things are spoken of in two ways: one according to **form**, and the other according to **matter**, from which the principal existence arises.
A part is said to be "according to form" if it retains its proper shape in the composition, being capable of its own operation. For this reason, it requires a specific quantity in the matter; since there are "minimums of flesh" to be found in the first book of the *Physics*, which, if divided further, do not remain "natural flesh" but are changed into something mathematical, since they no longer possess their proper form and act in the matter.
A part is said to be "according to matter" which cannot, by itself, perform its own proper act, but is an aid to another; such as matter that is opposed to the prior act. For matter will not move itself, but "the art of building" <note original: "tectonica">Tectonica: the craft or formal principle of construction.</note> moves it, as in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*. It is clear that not every part, however small, is a part "according to form," since it may lack total action and be a part only according to matter and quantity.

Thus, according to Aristotle, there are double parts—according to form and according to matter—in a single thing, like a **hand**. For there is a part in it more notable, like the general proportionality arising from its components: bone, cartilage, nerve, ligament, membrane, cord, veins with arteries, and skin. These parts stand as the "matter" of the aforementioned form. The remaining part exists according to form and matter insofar as each of the aforementioned simple organic components is double: one part according to form, the other according to matter.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some of the more unrefined scholars—who only listen to Aristotle saying that growth happens according to **species** (form) and not according to **matter**—have claimed that growth occurs only in the formal parts and not the material ones. This is nothing other than separating form from matter in things that are subject to generation and corruption. From this, it would follow that all things are generated in this way; but as only the composite is generated and corrupted (according to the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*), so also does it nourish and grow, since that is the manner of its production and preservation. The truth of this difficult matter will appear more clearly from what follows.

There was also the opinion of **Alexander** <note original: "Alexādri">Alexander of Aphrodisias (fl. 200 AD), a famous Greek commentator on Aristotle.</note> which was opposite to this, positing that growth happens according to matter and not according to form, as the Commentator [Averroes] reports in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. For Alexander said that Aristotle's statement on this question was not made by the force of proofs, but because he rested in such thoughts. For matter does not entirely dissolve, as Alexander wishes, but a certain thing remains fixed in it. If it were otherwise, it would happen either that form is separated, or that it underlies many matters. Since these are absurd, he [Alexander] posited that the fixed part in the matter must necessarily grow and diminish, having been grown anew...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on whether biological growth (augmentum) occurs in the matter or the form of a living being. It addresses the views of Aristotle (the "First Master"), Averroes (the "Commentator"), and Alexander of Aphrodisias, using the classic analogy of a vessel and flowing water to explain how a body can change its substance while maintaining its identity.</meta>

...from the moistures of food coming to that matter or receding from it, according to all its parts. And nature is the preserver of the shape of the limb at the time of growth and diminution. 

And he <note>Likely referring to Averroes or a contemporary commentator.</note> adds that if it be true that the **First Master** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE), often called the "First Master" or "The Philosopher" in medieval texts.</note> granted these things without proof, he is never believed to have said anything without strong proof.

I say, however, regarding the support for Aristotle, that although he possesses proof, he does not bring much forward here. Yet, from his words in several places, a double reason for this may be assigned. For that thing grows in which the principle of the motion of **alteration** <term>alteratio: qualitative change, such as water turning hot</term> and **growth** exists. For the first principle of motion, which is neither increased nor altered, is in the principle of motion that is first increased, because it holds within itself power obtained from the primary principle. However, the power of quantity, alteration, and growth—and other such powers—are in the **heterogeneous** <note original: "anomiomera">Parts made of different substances, like a hand or an eye, as opposed to "homoeomera" like flesh or bone.</note> or **formal** part, as appears in the relevant sections on animals.

Again, every act is from the form, because the form and the act are the same. Everything acts insofar as it is "in act"; whereas it is acted upon (passive) by matter. Matter, however, does not suffer by itself, nor is it created as its own thing; for it is said that matter does not move itself, but rather the "architectural" force <note original: "tectonicam">Derived from the Greek *tektonikos*, referring to the constructive or formative power of nature.</note> moves it.

Growth, however, is the act of the "increaseable" part of natural things. For this reason, logic concludes that growth comes to the increaseable thing by reason of its **form**, and not its **matter**. 

The **Commentator** <note>Averroes (1126–1198).</note> indeed refutes **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (fl. 200 CE), a major Greek commentator on Aristotle whose works often sparked medieval debates.</note>, who says that growth happens according to matter. For then it would follow that growth happens either by **accumulation** (for example, by placing one part next to another) or by the subtraction of what comes in to that which leaves, and that which comes in is received. These ideas are sufficiently absurd, since mixed substances do not yield to the underlying parts equally, nor are they united to them except insofar as they have a determined form. In such a case, it would be possible for all things to be mixed together, which does not happen unless the power and form are present, cooperating through the mixture.

Again, Alexander—according to the Commentator—does not solve the question but rather changes it. For it still remains to be asked how things grow from moisture <note>Refers to the liquid stage of digested food, or "chyle."</note> occurring in all parts if an augmenting power and form are not presupposed. Also, Alexander would not be able to explain how the shape, position, and other dispositions of an **organic limb** <term>membri officialis: a limb that performs a specific function or "office," like a hand.</term> grow, since they are not merely material mixtures, but are more formal in nature. 

And therefore, he concludes with Aristotle, as will appear. For the cause and manner of growth is found in things that are mixed and their opposites. Alexander, however, only sees it in mixed things. Because of the third point of the first [book], according to Aristotle and the Commentator, the truth is added in the fourth. Finally, the method of growth should be considered.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that growth happens according to the **form**, but not as the form exists on its own. For then every form would be increased. Rather, it happens in that which is a specific quantity having a form. It does not happen according to the **matter**, because matter **flows and ebbs** <note>This is the famous "Fountain Analogy": like a fountain where the water (matter) is constantly changing but the shape of the spray (form) remains the same.</note>, not observing the same disposition as before. Growth, however, must occur upon a fixed, standing thing, which is the form. 

Yet, it is not to be understood that growth happens in matter without form, as is attributed to Alexander. Whence, in this short treatise on growth ascribed to him, let us say that the form of the thing and its **hyle** <term>hyle: the Greek word for "matter," used here to denote primordial, unformed substance.</term> grow together, and that the matter assimilates to the quantity, and the form to the quality. For quantity changes and is altered, and is not fixed according to its own disposition; but its quality, which is the form itself, is fixed, remaining according to its own disposition without change.

Aristotle declares this through an analogy: If the same measure—for example, a **flagon** <note original: "lagena">A large jar or bottle.</note>—measures water, and different water is measured at different times, the measure (the flagon) remains, observing its own form unshaken. In this, the water corresponds to the material part, while the measure (the flagon) corresponds to the formal part.

This density or difference is more apparent in heterogeneous parts than in **homogeneous** <note original: "omiomere">Parts made of a single substance, like pure fat or blood.</note> ones; for the ambiguity is more hidden in them than in the heterogeneous. For a dead hand or a dead head possess the "reason" <note>In the sense of "defining essence."</note> of a hand or head far less than dead flesh or bone do, as stated in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption* and the fourth book of *Metaphysics*.

Thus, since Aristotle saw that the formal part remains and the material part arrives and recedes successively, he established that growth is primarily perfected by the **form**, as it is that in which the essence of growth is especially preserved. It happens through the matter of food, however, as the medium through which growth is completed. It happens through the matter of the limb as that into which growth is introduced by the formal part, so that a part can be made according to the form. 

Whatever may be attributed to Alexander in the treatise prepared for him, he seems to think entirely as Aristotle does. Whence the Commentator, as he testifies in the third book of *On the Soul*, not having seen Alexander's books, perhaps received his words poorly. He supports the same idea because growth is only upon a standing, fixed thing; this is the form and not the matter, since matter flows and ebbs. For this reason, in the *Metaphysics*, matter must be imagined in the thing moved, but the form remains invariable, falling least under corruption.

Furthermore, it is said that every perfection of a thing comes by reason of the more perfect entity within it. Growth is indeed a certain perfection of the thing, since nothing can be perfect in its original smallness. Therefore, growth will occur according to the form and not the matter. I hear, however, that growth is of the formal part through the form, but not that the form increases by itself; just as it is not generated by itself, as touched on before, but as that by which the form is the reason that growth is effected. For nothing grows except the **composite** <term>compositum: the whole being made of both matter and form.</term>, just as nothing is generated except the composite. As Alexander says: "The growing thing grows with its matter and its form," yet not by reason of the matter (since it is not fixed), but of the form. 

Wherefore, in those things which grow, such as the **soul** or the **animated being**, the form holds the reason of the formal and efficient cause of growth. Also, the whole composite acts through the form, as Aristotle says in the first book of *On the Soul*. And the form or matter—such as the soul—is not what is understood, nor is it the body; rather, it is the human who understands through the soul.

Regarding the second point, it must be known that three conditions of growth are set by Aristotle:
1. Every part of the increaseable thing must be increased, thus being rendered larger.
2. Growth is perfected by something external coming in.
3. That which grows must preserve its own form.

Furthermore, know that according to the Commentator, when the limbs are already extended in every dimension, a certain moist food meets them, which is distributed through all the smallest parts and pores. These indeed extend the pores and are condensed into parts, and are transmuted into the smallest fleshy parts, thus increasing the aforementioned limbs. Furthermore, in those parts of the flesh, small pores are left where the moisture...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of biological growth, moving from the philosophical definitions of form and matter to the specific physiological mechanisms described by Galen. It then transitions into "Difference 57," a new section debating the distinction between the vital, natural, and animal powers of the soul.</meta>

...again filled with food, and at last changed into parts of flesh, it again effects extension and growth. Likewise, in the third and fourth steps and thereafter, there will be such a transformation and subsequent growth, perfected by the **natural power** <term>virtus naturalis: the innate force in living things that governs growth and nutrition</term> of the limb. This occurs through the transformation of the food's moisture into parts of the body, which continues as long as these conditions remain. Therefore, growth exists only according to this kind of power through which that which is increased possesses form; this is what **Averroes** <note original: "Au."> intended when he said that growth happens according to form, and not according to matter. For if this power did not exist, it would be impossible for growth to occur in all sensible parts unless one body penetrated another, or it happened merely by accumulation <note>The author argues that growth is a biological integration, not just piling stuff on top.</note>.

**Galen**, in the first book of *On Natural Faculties*, asking how things grow from all sides—extending and nourishing the fibers appropriately—replies that this is best understood if one calls to memory what was said regarding the extension of the bladder. And from this, he now says: let the heart be imagined at its beginning to be so small that it does not differ from a millet seed or a bean. And it is asked: how can it become large without being nourished and extended from all sides? For it is through the whole that the nourished body will grow.

Promising the mode of nutrition, he does not give it <note>Perhaps implying a missing text or a failed explanation in the source being critiqued.</note>. Regarding the fourth point said to the first, this growth proceeds equivocally; for the parts, as has been said, are not only called such according to matter but also according to form. Since each thing is spoken of in a double sense, the parts are shown to be double: according to matter and similarly according to form.

To the other point, it must be said that growth "imports quantity" in the common sense of the word, but not in the proper sense in which we are primarily speaking; for as it appears from reason, according to **Galen**, the growth of things is an increase in size.

Or, although growth regards matter as that by which something is increased, it nevertheless regards the form even more, for the sake of which it is increased by reason. To the other point, it must be said that to be extended and to be increased does not belong to matter, since its substance is in potentiality; and such a thing lacks "act" except through the nature of form. For it is said that matter, by itself, neither suffers nor is created.

Form also, although in itself simple, inextensible, and indivisible, is yet bestowed with a designated quantity by the matter.

<margin>Asclepiades</margin>
To the other point, it does not follow what is introduced concerning the consumption or the loss previously made, into which the incoming nourishment succeeds. Nor does a vacuum occur in animals because of this, since their parts are soft and able to collapse and extend, as **Asclepiades** <note>Asclepiades of Bithynia (c. 124–40 BCE), a physician who famously disagreed with the theory of "natural faculties."</note> says against **Erasistratus** <note>Erasistratus of Ceos (c. 304–250 BCE), a Greek anatomist.</note> in the book on *Natural Faculties*. Nor does it follow that growth happens according to a double proportion of the nourishment, as nature requires for the thing to be increased. For example, if one **mina** <term>mina: an ancient unit of weight</term> is lost from the whole body, then for the sake of nutrition, one mina and twenty <note original: ".xx."> will be necessary for a single nutrition. Or it is said that what is added does not retain its own quantity, but takes on the quantity of the limb to which it is added; it possesses this quantity in potentiality and not in act. Because of this, that which arrives does not bring its own quantity with it—neither as equal, nor as greater, nor as lesser—to the thing to which it is added. Rather, it acts like matter poured into a vessel, which exceeds or is less in proportion to the flow. But it is not as some have felt: that the moist exists under a greater quantity than the dry. For when the smallest moisture is converted into the smallest dry part, the dissolved and liquid moisture will be condensed into the dry part by firming itself. Thus, it will not constitute more, but less than the dry part. If it were otherwise, it would follow that what grows would increase by a tenfold or sixfold proportion, which is absurd; or a great vacuum would intercede in the bodies being increased, as in ash that receives no less water <note>A classic scientific riddle: why does a bowl of ash still hold a full bowl of water? Medieval thinkers used this to debate the existence of "pores" or "voids."</note>.

### DIFFERENCE LVII.

-> That the **vital power** is not different <-
-> from the **natural** and **animal** powers, shown <-
-> by **Galen** at the beginning of *Natural Faculties*, <-
-> in the third book of *On Accidents*, and the fourth of *Theories*. <-

Furthermore, powers are distinguished and numbered according to the subjects in which they are founded. These are the **soul** and **nature**, as in the first book of *Natural Faculties*. Moreover, there are many things possessing life that lack the **vital power**; for though they have life, they do not have a heart <note>This likely refers to plants or "lower" animals in the Aristotelian hierarchy.</note>.

Again, those things are the same which have the same specific form. Since "being this" and "being such" are the same, not all powers are the same. Since all individuals of the same species have one form according to the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, they do not differ except by accident. For all men are one "Man" by participation in the species. And the **vital power** seems the same as the **natural power** because it gives life; and that is the consistency through nourishment which issues as vital. Likewise, it is the same as the **animal power** because the "motive power" is contained under the animal; the vital, however, like the "irascible" <note>the capacity for anger/spirit</note> and "concupiscible" <note>the capacity for desire</note> powers, is known to be moved, as in the first book of *On the Soul*. Therefore, the vital substance is not different from any of these.

To which opposition the physicians commonly agree. Furthermore, there are three principal members: the **heart**, **brain**, and **liver**. The powers are ordered to them as to bases or roots. Again, those powers are not the same which are distinct and where one is separated from the other. For when the liver is not yet existing or is dead (where the natural power is the principle), the vital power still stands, as will be shown. Therefore, the vital is distinct from the others.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that **power** <term>virtus: also 'virtue' or 'faculty'</term> is the efficient cause of medicines, and the beginning of every work. This power is found to be taken in four ways by **Aristotle**. One is for "quality," since every natural operation proceeds from it. And the elements act and suffer by their powers. In another way, it is for the "ultimate limit of a capacity." Power is an excellence... its parts are soft and able to collapse... which is a habit and a state immediately existing for us, determined by reason as a wise man would determine it (from the *Ethics*). It is also taken for the "powers of the soul" according to which Aristotle divided it into the **vegetative**, **sensitive**, and **rational**.

What the vegetative or natural power is, and what the nutritive and generative are, along with their parts, will be shown. And this power is twofold: **ministering** and **ministered**. And these pertain either to the "being of the species" and are thus **generative**—one of which is universal, generating seed in the testes of the male and female—and the other is particular. And that is twofold: one called "altering," which changes the principles of generation without giving form; and this is twofold: one common, working on the principle of generation as a secondary altering power in the liver; the other particular, which prepares the formation in the members from the heart by "plasmation" <term>plasmation: the act of giving shape or form to biological matter</term>, and thus it is "altering."

Galen, On Natural [Faculties]
