...of each of the individual parts. And the other, participating more fully in the aforementioned divine <note original: "informatione">forming power</note>, is called the **natural power** <note original: "natā drā.xlviii.">difference 48</note>. This serves either to create an individual, which is twofold: either to perfect the divine existence from birth—and thus it is **augmentative**—or to preserve it, and thus it is **nutritive**. Just as the **generative power** is specifically concerned with parts, there is a twofold transformation: the first alters the nourishment and transforms it; the second provides form, shaping it in every way to replace what was lost—which is called "touch" in the aforementioned passage. There are two "servant" powers: one that attracts nourishment from a distance to be added to the body, called the **attractive power**; and another that is contrary and different from the body, whose work is preparation so that the food is made similar to the body, which the **digestive power** performs. But because this takes time, the **retentive power** was necessary, which remains at rest for as long as needed until the transformation completes its action. However, because nourishment cannot be totally assimilated into the thing nourished, there are two types of waste: moist/foul and smoky/bitter. Thus, the **expulsive power** was necessary to secrete these outward. Therefore, it is gathered that **Avicenna** <note original: "Vane."> adds a **discretionary power**, though he places it under both the expulsive and attractive powers. For in many cases, when it attracts one part, it expels the rest, from which "discretion" or sorting occurs. And here arises the necessity of parts having a likeness to their natural origins. These four <term>virtutibus</term> <note>powers or faculties</note> serve as the foundation for all others, using the four primary qualities: heat, cold, dryness, and moisture.

The **animal power** <term>vireȝ</term> <note>or "soul-force"</note>, or the soul, is the perfection of an organic body according to which it perceives and moves by appetite. It exists as a twofold power: **motive** and **comprehensive**. And the motive power is twofold: one moves because it commands the motion, and the other because it effects the motion. The first is the **appetitive** or desiring power of the heart <note original: "cordi. xxxviii.">difference 38</note>, which is also twofold. One is the **concupiscible power** <note>the faculty of desiring what is pleasurable or suitable</note> which commands movement to acquire what is fitting. The other is the **irascible power** <note>the faculty of resisting or repelling what is harmful</note> which commands movement to repel what is harmful. The **motive power** that effects movement through the nerves and muscles is the tool that binds and relaxes the cords and ligaments, by which the limbs are moved and hardened through expansion and fixation.

The movement of this power differs according to how it is commanded to move by the desiring existence. The **comprehensive power** is also twofold: one is **manifest** <note>the external senses</note>, which is divided into five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. This last sense is multifaceted according to various opposites, for it perceives heat, cold, dryness, moisture, hardness, softness, roughness, smoothness, and wetness. Because these are all fixed in one organ, this <term>virtus</term> <note>power</note> is considered in a certain way to be a single common sense, one in essence, and of this it is called "vision" <note original: "uisū. xlii.">difference 42</note>.

The other power is **occult** <note>internal or hidden senses</note>, and it is twofold because it deals either with "form" or "intention." If the first, it works with a simple form in three ways: either by perceiving it—which is the **common sense**; or by preserving and retaining it—which is the **imagination** or **phantasia**, which according to **Algazel** <note>Al-Ghazali, the Persian philosopher</note> is the "storehouse of forms"; or by composing them. For it composes and divides forms, and thus it is the **imaginative power** <term>virtus</term> in animals, or the **rational cogitative power** in humans. If it exercises itself concerning the "intention" <note>the deeper meaning or instinctual significance of a thing, like a sheep sensing a wolf's danger</note>, it does so by abstracting it from the form, along with the attachments of matter like "here" and "now," or even more universally.

If the first, it is twofold: either by stripping the intention from the form individually, which is the **estimative power**, or by retaining it. This is done in three ways: either without any interruption of the thing or the time (regardless of distance), which is called **preservative**; or externally, which is **reminiscence** (which is like a thread); or in a middle way, which is **memory**. Memory is more common, as it exists in all "perfect" animals, whereas reminiscence exists in man alone, for he alone "threads" his thoughts. If the power is independent of these, it is the **rational or human power**, which is the perfection of the aforementioned organic body, receiving universal truths through deliberation and meditation. This is twofold: **speculative** and **active**. The active is the principle that moves one to the patterns of thought. The **active power** is twofold: either the action begins in external matter—this is **Art**, which is defined as "the right reason of things to be made" <note original: "drā. iii. in. vii.">Difference 3, in 7 parts</note>, distributed into the **mechanical arts**; or it operates within itself, considering what is good—this is **Prudence**, which is "the right reason of things to be acted upon." This is multifaceted: concerning oneself it is **monastic** <note>ethics for the individual</note>, which is taught in the *Ethics*; or it dispenses for the family, called **economics** <term>yconomica</term>; or for the city, called **politics** <term>politica</term>. The **speculative power** is the <term>virtus</term> <note>virtue/power</note> which is formed by the universal form, stripped of matter. This exists as both **potential** and **actual**.

**Potential** is also threefold. One is absolutely remote, not yet ready for action, called **material potential**—like an infant's potential to write. There is another less distant from action, called **potentialized**, like a child’s potential to write when he already knows the letters of the script. The third is even closer to the act of perfection, called "ready," as when a writer is not currently writing <note original: "tactū. xlviii.">Difference 48</note>. To these potentials, a threefold **intellect** corresponds. The **material intellect** has no forms of its own but is the subject for all of them; this is the first potential. There is also an intellect related to the second potential, as when the material intellect possesses "self-evident" concepts from which it can reach further knowledge. These primary concepts are the "prior propositions" that come to one naturally—as mentioned in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*—such as "everything must either be or not be," and "the whole is greater than its part." This is called the **potential intellect**. The third is called the **intellect in perfection**, which can act whenever it wishes to understand. This is what **Aristotle** <note original: "Ar."> calls the potential intellect in three ways. But when it understands in act, and understands that it understands, it is called the **intellect in effect**. Then there is joined and united to it what is called the **acquired intellect**, which comes from outside, as stated in the first book of *On the Soul*. Or it is acquired from the "intelligence" which the *Metaphysics* (book 9) posits as the **agent intellect**. Thus, he did not place the agent intellect as a different part of the soul, unlike **Plato**, who posited that these exist as self-subsisting essences. The **intellect**, which by its nature performs actions according to Aristotle, is the "agent" part of the human soul, standing in relation to the potential intellect as light stands to colors. For the intellect itself, though immersed in matter and joined to individual conditions, extracts the "species" (essences) of things and places them into the potential intellect; by casting light upon them, it makes them "understandable in act." The **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note>, in the third book of *On the Soul*, wanting to show the way we are joined with "separate substances" <note>divine or non-material beings</note> so that we may understand them, posits that the things understood are within us...

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of the soul's powers, moving from the physical growth of organs into the psychological and intellectual faculties as understood by medieval Aristotelian and Galenic traditions. It specifically bridges the gap between the physical organs (liver, heart, brain) and the intellectual operations of the mind.</meta>

<margin>
Commentary 3 on *On the Soul* <note original: "d̄ Ana">Aristotle's *De Anima*</note>: Propositions [acquired] through the means of the natural intellect.
</margin>

¶ Understandings—or proper propositions—are twofold: either natural—that is, the **intellect in habit**—or voluntary, which are the understandings acquired from those first propositions. The first kind of understandings are produced by the **agent intellect** <note>The "Agent Intellect" was thought to be the active force that allows the human mind to grasp universal truths.</note>, while the acquired understandings are formed in us from the agent intellect and the propositions of the primary understandings. From these rises the **speculative intellect**, which is created voluntarily from the first propositions and the agent. In this action involving these two intellects, the **intellect in habit** <note>The state where the mind possesses knowledge but is not currently using it.</note> acts as the matter or instrument, while the agent acts as the form or efficient cause. 

Therefore, when the **material intellect** is formed by the speculative and the agent, it finally becomes the **intellect in act**, separate and continuous; this occurs properly when all speculative understandings have been formed within us. When it has reached this state, it understands all beings. In this way, as **Themistius** <note>Themistius was a 4th-century philosopher famous for explaining Aristotle's complex ideas.</note> says, man becomes like God in that he is, in a certain way, all beings and perceives them all. Oh, how wonderful is this order! And how extraordinary is this mode of being! I have declared this more at length in my edition of these discourses.

From these things, for one who calculates diligently, it appears that the "chain" of the soul's powers consists of 33 or 35 rings <note>The author uses the metaphor of a chain to describe how the different functions of life and mind are linked together.</note>: specifically, four qualities, four servant **natural powers**, six dominant powers, two **vital powers**, and one general **motive power**—which is divided according to the 529 muscles <note original: "dxxxix.">The traditional Galenic count of muscles in the human body.</note> through which they operate—five manifest **apprehending powers** <note>The five external senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch.</note>, seven hidden perceiving powers, and five or six active powers. Among these rings, the **intellect in act** (or the "borrowed" or "acquired" intellect) stands as the participant and the overseer of all. There are also four qualities that are entirely servant and dominant. Those in the middle maintain a moderate state. These are the categories of God's work, so that the entire number of the soul's virtues might be understood here. The Physician <note>Likely referring to Galen.</note>, as a craftsman of specific details, divided these powers into the **natural**, **vital**, and **animal**, since three or four members manifest themselves as the principles: the heart, the brain, and the liver along with the testicles.

The **natural power** <term>virtus naturalis</term> is that whose seat is the liver <term>epar</term>; starting from there, it extends with the blood and the "natural spirit" <note>The *spiritus* was a subtle substance thought to carry life through the body.</note> through the veins into all parts of the body to nourish them. The **vital power** is the power through which there is life; its foundation, origin, and furnace is the heart. Starting from the heart, it is sent to all members of the body through the arteries and administers life. 

The **animal power** <note original: "virtus animalis">In medieval terms, "animal" refers to the *anima* (soul) and specifically to functions like sensation and movement, not "animalistic" behavior.</note> is the power which, once received in the limbs, prepares them to receive the power of sense and the operation of the "senses of life," into which the motions of fear and anger are also mixed. This power is twofold: one is active or operative, which alternately expands and contracts the heart and the arteries; the other is passive, or the result of these operations, from which the "passions" or "accidents of the soul" arise—such as anger, fear, joy, sadness, and the like. These are the powers discussed in the section on "differentiation," under which the "irascible" <note>The drive toward anger or courage.</note> and "concupiscible" <note>The drive toward desire or pleasure.</note> powers are contained. The seat and furnace of the **animal power** is assigned to the brain, as was touched upon in section 38. Regarding this, it should be known that discourses find greater disagreements in this fifth part.

For some writers, in various places, describe three distinct powers that rule as overseers, such as **Galen**, **Johannitius** <note>Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a famous 9th-century translator and physician.</note>, and **Aristotle**.

---

Thus, in the ninth book of the *Introduction*, it is said (referencing the book on the teachings of **Hippocrates** and **Plato**) that the animal soul dispenses three powers of a higher genus to one another. These are distributed to its own body as if from a fountain, which Plato called "souls," finding a proper substance for each. 

1. One is connected to the nutrition of animals and plants; it is common to both. Its fountain is placed in the liver, and its rivers are the veins spread throughout the entire body. These are called the "concupiscible," "nutritive," "natural," or "animal" power.
2. Another exists only in animals; it is located in the heart as the fountain of innate heat. Its rivers are the arteries. This is called "life," the "irascible power," and the **vital soul**.
3. The third soul is located in the brain to assist the "thinking power" <term>excogitatiua</term>, which operates by choice through the senses. Its little rivers are the nerves, through which it provides sensation and motion to the animal.

Some, however, place the **vital power** under the **natural power**. This is why they claim the substance of the brain, the thin membranes, the spinal marrow, the diaphragm, and the nervous parts are primarily strengthened by a sound mind. Thus, those parts are denoted as healthy which, according to the belly and the liver and the heart itself, are ready to receive food; this seems to belong to the **natural power**. 

In the section on "accidents," there is also a reason given: they write that the pulse is an accident of the natural [faculties]. Furthermore, the vital power should be placed under the natural rather than the animal. The reason is this: the "pulsatile power" <note>The power that causes the heart to beat.</note> is by necessity a gathering, dividing, and principal power; for since it gives heat from the heart to the other members, it serves the principal nutritive power, because it is preserved by it. Thus, it is not necessary to make it a single power like the other five—namely, the **attractive**, **digestive**, **retentive**, **expulsive**, and **discretionary** powers—even though the pulse is more closely associated with life because of the great heat within it. Some call this the "plant-like" or **vegetative power**. 

Perhaps physicians only called this the "vital power" because it is more associated with life, even though it belongs to the genus of the nutritive power. This is confirmed because if an action is natural, it argues that the power itself is natural. But the vital pulse is a natural action; as we know from the section on "accidents," the pulse is moved naturally. And in the thirteenth [book], the motion of the pulse is purely natural. Also, in book six of *On the Use of Parts*, the operation of the heart is natural. Therefore, the vital power is natural.

Others, however, place the vital power under the animal power, as at the beginning of the "natural" sections, where it is said that some works are of nature (those common to plants and animals), while others are of the soul (those proper to animals). It is added that if anyone says a soul exists in plants, then the divider will not call it a "plant soul," but a third kind of soul. This suggests that the vital power is contained under the animal power since it exists alongside sensation. This also seems to be the view in the section on "accidents," stating the action of the soul is of the soul, and others are of nature; and of the soul, one part feels, another moves, another rules and orders. But the powers of nature are called the **attractive**, **digestive**, **retentive**, and **expulsive**. Hence, in the fourth book of *Theory*: "It is necessary for the powers of nature and the soul to be those through which they can perform their actions." The actions of nature are to generate, to increase, and to nourish. The actions of the soul are...

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of the soul's faculties, moving from the intellectual operations discussed on the previous page to the physiological foundations of life: the vital, natural, and animal powers. It focuses on the heart as the primary organ of life and the source of motion.</meta>

Life consists in the expansion of the heart—namely, the pulsation of the veins—and inspiration and contraction. Some of these motions are those by which the soul <note original: "animus">The mind or rational soul</note> exercises discernment and voluntary movement. **Aristotle** <note original: ".A.">Standard abbreviation for Aristotle</note> also perceived this, previously dividing motions into those which the soul commands, such as the **desirative power** <note original: "desideratiuā">The faculty of wanting or seeking</note>, under which are placed the **concupiscible** <note original: "gcupiscibilis">The drive for pleasure or basic needs</note> and the **irascible** <note original: "irascibilis">The drive to overcome obstacles or anger</note>. From the virtue of this, he calls the sensible power the **vital power**.

And **Damascene** <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian influential in medieval philosophy.</note> says the same when he speaks of the natural and spiritual powers; by "spiritual," he understood the **animal powers** <term>Animal power: From the Latin 'anima' (soul); the faculties responsible for sensation and voluntary motion, centered in the brain.</term> as they also contain the vital powers within them. Even if **John** <note>Likely referring again to John of Damascus</note> calls the vital power a "spiritual" faculty, some have claimed that the vital power is essentially the same as the natural power, though they appear different. The error of these people will appear in what follows, where it will be proved that they differ most certainly from the natural, not only in essence but also in appearance.

Regarding this third point, it must first be known that the "vital" can be called "natural," and the "animal" is also distinguished from it. Second, it must be known that the vital faculty is a proper and principal animal faculty, essentially different from the others. Third, from these points, the difficulties introduced by **Sopianus** <note>Likely a reference to a specific commentator or a corruption of a name like Sosigenes or Simplicius</note> will appear. 

First, it must be known that "nature" can be understood in two ways. Either generally, as it is distinguished from **art**; for there are two principles of things, **nature** and **art**, according to the second book of the *Physics*. Nature is the principle of motion and rest in that in which it exists primarily and by its own essence, and not by accident. Hence, in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*: Nature is that which possesses the principle of motion in itself from another nature which possesses the species in act. **Art**, however, is the principle and species of that which is made in another. And so, since all three of these powers arise from an internal principle, they shall be called "natural."

Or nature is taken properly, as a certain ordered path adhering to a single way and order, such as that of the celestial bodies. There is another nature entirely opposite to this, subject to variation and diversity in many ways, such as the nature of the elements, which differs greatly from the order of the superior nature. There remains a middle nature, such as that of mixed bodies. Of these, one is ordered, like that of man; another is less so, as in some imperfect beings which are mediocre, according to whether they have a greater or lesser access to the higher or lower states. For all things are ordered by a higher nature, just as they are rendered disordered by the lowest; because every good and beautiful thing, which adheres to one order and path and shows in itself a "footprint of wisdom," is nothing other than that which flows from the supreme nature—namely, the ordered, immutable, and incorruptible. 

Now, therefore, the **natural power**, since it adheres to one order and a determined path continuously, perfects the acts of that nature by a certain instinct; thus, its work is more the work of intelligence than of the soul's faculty. The **animal power**, however, since its acts are varied in every way and do not adhere to one path—especially in a being possessing reason—is different. For rational powers are capable of opposite effects. Thus, the natural power is proportioned to the lowest level, and the vital power to the middle, reducing them to a middle substance. For it performs various works, such as dilating and contracting at the same time, and thus separates from the natural. But because it preserves order in this diversity, it agrees with the natural and is distinguished from the animal. It appears, therefore, that the name and definition are not said univocally of these three, but rather **analogically**.

Similarly, the **animal power** can be understood in different ways: either as it is said of the soul <note original: "ab aīa">From the anima</note> insofar as it is the act or principle of perceiving and moving, arising from some voluntary apprehension. And the **natural** is the beginning of the operations of the faculty which occur in the body itself; and thus it will be "animate," different from the natural and the same as the vital. But if the natural power is taken as that which works regarding nourishment for the health of the individual or the species, and the **vital** as that which works principally for the life of the individual, then it will be distinct from the natural.

Furthermore, it should be known how much this can be referred to the whole genus of living things, or specifically to the animal and especially the "perfect" animal <note>In Aristotelian terms, "perfect" animals are those that are fully developed, usually meaning red-blooded vertebrates.</note>. And likewise, know that the division of the soul into its powers is a division of a subject into its accidents (like an apple into its color, flavor, and smell) and not a genus into species, according to the **Commentator** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the "Great Commentator" on Aristotle.</note> in the second book of *On the Soul*. However, **Boethius**, in his *Book of Divisions*, considering common intentions and predications, says the division of the soul is common to the division of a genus into species and a whole into its parts. For in that any part of the soul receives the predication of the soul itself, it belongs to the division of a genus. But because not every soul is joined to all parts, it must be referred to the nature of the whole; for the whole definition of the soul is not saved in every part of the soul.

Regarding the second point, it must be known that the **vital power** is the root of all and the first of all, not only in nature but also in time; although in the seed at the beginning all are confused and not "prior" or "posterior." Nevertheless, it acts first and manifests itself to the others as the substrate on which they lean, namely the **heart**.

<margin>Difficulty</margin>

It is asked in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals* whether the spermatic power nourishes the womb, since it cannot have nourishment from the outside. The solution is that it is not true that nourishment must always come from the outside, since it is found internally within itself. For just as in the seeds of plants there is found something like milk, which it can use for nourishment before it can take nourishment from the surrounding earth—using that "milky" superfluity to nourish the germ—so too in the matter of animals there is a "superfluity of the composition" which serves as nourishment. Hence **Aristotle** says in that place: The proper creatures, like the heart, have their nourishment near to them, and after this, it nourishes itself from external bodies. 

Furthermore, **Averroes** in his commentary says: in the heart is the form and the species of the seed. And Aristotle in the ninth book of *Animals*: Since the **spirit** <note original: "sp̄us">Pneuma; the thin, vaporous substance that carries the soul's powers through the body.</note> is the carrier of the soul, and the soul is one, then the seed will be as if from the superfluity of the nourishment of the heart, and then the heart will be the principle of the generation of the seed. And this "superfluity of the nourishment of the heart" from which the seed is said to be made is what Averroes called the "superfluity of the composition."

First, therefore: the **vital power** is the first which arrives in it, since the spirit proceeds from the heat of the subtle parts; then the spirit, according to **Averroes**, receives through itself the first principle and the first soul, from which the other powers flow—namely the natural and the animal.

Third: the truth is that the first member created is the **heart**, although it is said of **Hippocrates** <note original: "Ypocrate">The famous Greek physician.</note> that he first said the brain and the eyes were created, as appears in his *Book of Infants*. But he is deceived, because when the heart is created, it does not appear clearly at first. It also seems to some that the liver is generated first, because the first operation of the body is nourishment. But that is found through diligent experiment in the art [of medicine] not to be so. And by reason: for a member is not nourished in which there is no sustenance of life with its proper **natural heat**, which is why...

If that which prepares the body to receive other powers of sense, motion, and the operation of life is "prior," then the vital power is strictly the prior one. But that which the "Givers of Forms" <note>A philosophical term for the divine or celestial influences that bestow specific natures upon matter.</note> grant, while it remains pre-existing, does not generate. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the physiological foundations of movement and the soul's faculties. It follows the previous discussion on the heart as the source of vital power, now transitioning into "Difference 58," which explores whether the command for motion begins in the nerves or the muscles, and how the "internal senses" (like imagination and estimation) trigger physical action.</meta>

<margin>
Still [Difference] 58
Averroes
</margin>

The magnitudes will be most proper, but least of all in a subtle nerve or body. <note>The author is discussing how the physical size or density of a body part relates to its ability to transmit or execute the soul's commands.</note> **Again**, according to **Averroes**, for a single part there is a single action, since it arises from a form that is ultimately one for each thing; but a nerve has one operation because it perceives a difference. (Section 47). Therefore, the **moving power** is immediately bestowed in the muscle rather than the nerve. In opposition to this, it is claimed that the moving power resides first in the nerve, for the nerve delivers the **animal power** <term>Animal power: From the Latin 'anima' (soul), this refers to the functions of the brain, including sensation and voluntary movement.</term> from the brain. The utility of the nerve is the induction of sensation and motion to all parts of the body, as stated in the *Book of Benefits* <note original: "de iuvantiis">Refers to Galen's 'On the Usefulness of the Parts of the Body'.</note> in the first part and its specific sections. Frequently, the principle of sensation and motion is a single nerve. And in the same place: "Similarly, the penetration of the moving power is in the nerves which are continuous with the muscles."

Regarding the clear movements, diligent physicians have carefully investigated whether nerves derive their utility for movement from their own substance and nature, or whether there is some member above the nerves that grants them this power, just as muscles display strength. Those who observe every part below an incision in a nerve see that sensation and movement are taken away from where it proceeded from that nerve; this is declared in the origin of the nerves from the brain and the spinal cord <note original: "nucha">A medieval term for the spinal cord, derived from Arabic.</note>. From these long discourses touched upon there, a brief reasoning arises: everything which, when removed, takes away what remains, was the cause of that thing. But when a nerve is removed or greatly injured, sensation and motion are taken away (Section 4). Therefore, the **nerve** will be the principle of motion and the first "irradiation" <note>The "shining forth" or transmission of the soul's power into the body.</note> from the soul, and not the muscle, because when the muscle itself is removed, sensation and motion still remain in the part situated above the cut. Therefore, the moving power first irradiates the nerve rather than the muscle.

Regarding the first point, however, it must be known what the moving power is, as its difference from its companions was made known previously. Its mode of moving is brief: first, the **species** <term>Species: In medieval psychology, these are the "mental images" or "sensory data" perceived from the outside world.</term> of something sought or something distressing changes the air, which then changes the particular sense, and finally the **common sense** <note>The faculty that pools data from the five individual senses.</note>; the **phantasy** or **imagination** receives and preserves this impression. Then, the received species changes the **cogitative faculty**, and this changes the **estimative faculty** <note>The faculty that allows an animal to perceive 'intentions' like danger or utility, such as a sheep fearing a wolf.</note>, which is sometimes located in the memory with others. The estimative faculty then changes the heart's active or operative power, making it passive so that it acts upon this; then it is commanded in the **irascible** or **concupiscent** <note>The 'irascible' faculty deals with anger and aggression; the 'concupiscent' with desire and lust.</note> faculties, according to whether the apprehended species is to be fled from or pursued. Finally, it commands the moving power fixed in the muscles, moving through its different muscles; for there are **529** of them, according to **Galen** (Section 1). From this it is also clear that the moving power can be called both an **animal power** and a **vital power**, according to whether this or that faculty commands it. (Section 135). What a nerve is and how many types are spoken of was made known in Section 41. What a muscle is and the necessity of its intention will appear in what follows.

Briefly, the "first mobile" <note original: "mobile primum">The first thing that is moved in a sequence.</note> is that which first receives the moving power before it generates the motion that subsequently moves other things. According to **Averroes**, this is the **soul**, for it acts as a form that diffuses its power through the natural matter determined for it; however, as a "motor" (mover), it is most closely bound to the **heart**. Whence the *Commentator* <note>Averroes, known as 'The Commentator' on Aristotle.</note> on the eighth book of the *Physics*: "A muscle is that which has motion in itself and is composed of three things: the flesh of the muscle (which is the last thing moved), the **natural heat** (which is the mover and the motion that passes into the nerves), and the **soul** (which moves as the form within that natural heat)."

However, among physicians—and especially **Galen**, who is more concerned with sensible craftsmanship—the "first mover" in voluntary motion is the **brain**, as stated in *On Manifest Movements*: "The first and chief mover, moving all the animal members with voluntary motion, is the brain." Those parts which are extreme, such as the hands and feet, are only moved. In the middle, each thing both moves and is moved, such as the nerves, muscles, the heart, and so on.

Motion is also manifold. **Natural motion** is that whose principle is from within, whether it be passive (as with heavy and light objects) or celestial. For these do not properly have an active principle of motion within them, but rather one bestowed from without. For the "generator" bestows the motion on heavy and light things that remains within them; for just as other accidents follow the substantial form, so too do place and being moved toward a place. For motion exists for the sake of place; yet the natural form is not the "motor" except in the sense that the form impressed a nature toward which such motion follows. **Celestial bodies** are also moved by a separate principle, which is discussed in the *Substance of the Orb* <note>A work by Averroes on the nature of the heavens.</note>. For it is separate from them but essentially joined by power and situated within them, in which way perhaps the heaven is animated by the soul of the heaven and the world. Or, according to most, it is by its soul into which an exterior Intelligence flows by its power, in which way the Commentator thought in certain books that a separate intelligence flows into the **cogitative faculty** of man.

The **active principle of motion** in animals, however, comes from within, and this motion can also be called **voluntary** if it proceeds from a mover using reason, whose power is directed toward opposites (Section 1). Opposite to this is **violent motion**, whose principle exists from without. For motion is "violent" when the principle is from the outside and the subject contributing the force does not participate in the natural form (Ethics, book 3); whence in the *Great Morals*: "it is when the principle is from without and from which one is compelled to act." There is also a **middle ground** between natural and violent motion, such as an animal walking upward. By reason of its form or soul, the motion is natural, as is said in the second book of the *Physics*; however, on the part of its physical mass, it is violent.

Regarding the second point, it should be known according to the second collection: it is expressly written that the first thing moved by the soul or the **natural heat** is the muscle, so that the muscle is the first mobile thing from the natural heat, as if placed there by instinct. For the soul moves through these intervening media, both incorporeal and corporeal: namely, by the power of its situation and action, then by the innate qualified complexion, by heat, and by the warming **spirit**, and by the power carrying them to the act, and by the member sustaining all these things. For since the soul is far removed from the more corporeal organ in which the mixed action is seen to be manifested, it was necessary for proportionate things to intervene, so that nature at least does not leap, but proceeds very gradually and orderly from one extreme to the other through intermediates, so much so that its continuous continuity is hidden.

**Averroes** also fortifies this position with reason. For it is fitting that the mover be proportioned to the thing moved. **Heat** is hot and moist, and the **muscle** is similar because of its composition. For it is composed, as he says, of simple flesh and nervosity, and is born from the heart. A **nerve**, however, is only cold and dry, not having much similarity with the natural heat.

<meta>This page continues the debate between the views of Galen and Averroes regarding the physiological origins of voluntary motion. The previous page established the conflict: does the power of movement reside primarily in the nerves or the muscles? This text examines Averroes’ logical critiques of Galen and introduces the "sleeping nerves" (carotids) as evidence.</meta>

For it is said that the vein or artery is first [moved] by **innate heat** <term>Innate heat: In medieval medicine, the natural internal warmth of a living being, centered in the heart, which fuels all bodily functions.</term> of motion, since the vein arises from a member that is not primary. He also adds that it is not reasonable that the instrument which provides nourishment should also be the instrument of motion. Indeed, it is more fitting that nutrition occurs through an instrument of rest. Nor also is the artery—since it is the same path for another active gift, namely acting as the worker of **pulsations**—suitable for voluntary motion, which does not seek rest. From this, he concludes that the **primary subject of motion** <note original: "primum mobile">The first physical part that receives the command to move.</note> would be the muscle and not the nerve. 

Upon this he relies, and not long after, he shamefully attacks **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–210 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note> and perhaps, using sophistry, assumes the force of reason in the sharp arguments mentioned before. [He argues:] If there is voluntary motion, there is a nerve. But if the nerve is not there (its severance having been posited), then by the destruction of the consequent <note original: "destructiōe gñtis">A logical term referring to the second part of a conditional statement.</note>, he concludes the destruction of the antecedent <note original: "destructiōē añtis">The first part of a conditional statement.</note>—namely, that there is no voluntary motion. Therefore, voluntary motion will be in the nerve. 

Indeed, he says this fallacy is a fallacy in principles and corrupt in its figure, such that it errs in both matter and form. Since when one predicate <term>Predicate: A property or characteristic attributed to a subject.</term> of a thing is removed from a subject, it does not always follow that the subject must be removed from that from which it was removed. And those who hold this opinion are bound to believe that with the negation of the opposite antecedent, the negation of the opposite consequent follows in all matters. Therefore, these words are not worthy to be heard. And this is one way in which it is manifest that Galen did not have a **true root in logic**. For if some motion is removed by the removal of a nerve, it does not necessarily follow that when the nerve is present, it is called the proper cause in this matter.

This, therefore, seems to be the opinion of **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a famous Islamic philosopher and physician known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note>. However, he warns that the foreign arguments of Galen allow for a deception of the "how much" <note original: "deceptiōē q̃ntis">Likely referring to a logical error regarding the quantity or scope of a premise.</note> from a proposition that is only valid in one direction. Where terms are not convertible <note>In logic, terms are "convertible" if "All A is B" also means "All B is A."</note>, the common grace of the matter might hold, but not by reason of its form. For it is not given that "if there is pain, there is an injury to an unequal part"; this is not found in such a way, nor is the pain always from a bad constitution.

<margin>
Difference 76
</margin>

Finally, he adds the same in support of his position: that men have already been seen who were struck against the **sleeping nerves** <term>Sleeping nerves: The carotid arteries. Ancient and medieval physicians often grouped them with nerves because pressure on them causes unconsciousness (the name 'carotid' comes from the Greek 'karoun,' to stupefy).</term> branching out from the fifth pair of brain nerves, brought outside the cranium under the coverings of the paired bones; and then all voluntary operations were taken from them, and for that reason, they are called "sleeping." 

Wherefore he adds that **Rhazes** <note>Al-Razi (865–925 AD), a Persian polymath and physician.</note> says that when the King of India wished to kill certain nobles, he killed them through this method. And he seems to be able to say this because all voluntary motions are attached to these two pairs of nerves. This, therefore, is the discourse of Averroes. 

However, because this position perhaps cannot stand, it will appear in the following. Now, however, someone might show the defect of his argument against Galen in this way: For what he says first—that **innate heat** seeks the muscle because both are hot—is perhaps not true. Because in motion, not only is heat required to perform it, but also cold by which it is tempered, so that the parts may be thickened and supported. Furthermore, the power to be moved is in it through the nerve, as will be shown first. Moreover, how is the muscle born from the heart unless by the same power as other things? For he asserts regarding the nature of the muscle that very thing which he denies in the eleventh section, and that its motion is voluntary, which is ridiculous. But what he says about the nerve being very cold—

---

—this clearly contradicts the truth and the discourse of Galen on the theory of complexions <term>Complexion: The balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a person or organ.</term> and in the first book. For he writes well that the nerves are of little coldness, wherefore they are situated near the skin. It seems even more can be concluded from his words: that the nerve is the **primary subject of motion**, since it has little coldness and is heated by innate heat, by which tempering it is rendered more fit for motion and support than the muscle. Nevertheless, I say the mass of the body is also required, which is found more in the muscle than in the nerve. And therefore, motion is manifested more in the muscle than in the nerve—and indeed even more in the heart. 

Whence the primary proper movements are described by them; for those moved the common man <note original: "ydiota">In this context, an unlearned person or non-specialist.</note>, but not the muscles in that way. As for his saying that the vein is born from a non-primary member, it seems a light movement not preserving the position of the Master **Avicenna**, who wishes the veins to be born immediately from the heart (Difference 47). He also attacks Galen unjustly, since the muscle has nothing in itself that manifests motion primarily except through its principal principle, the nerve, just as it is for other things that move voluntarily. For voluntary motion can never be separated from the nerve. Thus the earth would have a gift <note unclear>Latin "g̃dato" is abbreviated; possibly 'gradu' or 'fundato'</note>, since no voluntary motion is granted to the muscle except through the nerve. Therefore, if the nerve is cut, it follows well that motion is removed from the muscle, since its whole is not receiving from elsewhere; thus an accident does not permit itself to be in it [the muscle] as it is in Galen. 

In the nerve, however, since it is a common flowing path, motion is not manifested in the same way, since it is thin and flexible. But motion requires a fixedness which the nerve cannot provide, although it can exhibit a foundation. For it is more difficult to move than to feel, since the former is to act and the latter is to be acted upon. To act, however, requires more vigor than to be acted upon (from the fourth [book] of *Accidents* and the first [book] of *Principles*). Nor also is what Averroes brings forward about the **sleeping nerves** valid, since death can happen from something else rather than because of the striking of those nerves; and likewise, voluntary motion can in no way be perfected without the nerve. 

The discourse of Averroes, though to be preferred in truth, can perhaps be admitted, but it is not drawn from sufficient evidence—such as that the muscle is the primary subject of motion from innate heat, as mentioned before regarding the manifestation of the spirit. For motion is represented more in the muscle because it can possess more sufficiently those things necessary for motion mentioned before, which the nerve might lack. 

Thirdly, it must be known that the moving power radiates most immediately upon the nerve and is sent into it; it is then directed into the muscle as something composed of the nerve and other things. Whence in the first book: No nerve is itself, by itself, operating in the parts of the animal in such acts; but through the medium of the muscles, all voluntary choices called "motions" are perfected. Sometimes the muscles themselves are clearly seen to move the parts, and sometimes through a medium—

And likewise, other roots of nerves are known by physicians which move the muscles, providing the foundation for the hand from the roots of the nerves in the skin. Whence in the first book of *Liquid Motions*: After the motion of the muscles is observed in the arteries and veins being constricted, it is led to a standstill, and if the nerves are constricted, the motion is hindered.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the physiological relationship between nerves and muscles, specifically addressing whether the nerve or the muscle is the "primary instrument" of voluntary motion. It resolves the conflict by defining the muscle as a composite structure while the nerve remains the essential conductor of the soul's power.</meta>

That with respect to the muscles, indeed, they judged that some **power** <term>Power: (Virtus) In medieval physiology, an active force or faculty of the soul that governs specific bodily functions.</term> is directed from the nerves through which their action occurs. No, it transmits the ordering power through the nerves from the brain to the muscles; wherefore, in the first distinction, the thinking power located in the brain uses parts like certain streams—the nerves—sending sense and motion through them to every animal.

In the fourth book of the *Theoretical Medicine*, however: The power moving the limbs voluntarily proceeds from the brain and is sent through the nerves arising from it, and from the **spinal cord** <note original: "nucha">The medieval term *nucha* specifically refers to the spinal cord, viewed as an extension of the brain.</note> it reaches the muscles, giving them voluntary motion. Also in the first book of the *Practical Medicine*: Where the necessity of the muscle is given, it is said that voluntary motion in the limbs is not completed except by the power arriving at them from the brain via the mediating nerves.

For it was not fitting for the nerves to be continuous with the bones lest they be injured by their hardness; therefore, a substance similar to a nerve emerged from the extremity of the bones called a **ligament**, which was joined to the nerve and made one thing with it. And because this substance thus composed was still too thin and weak, it could not be extended much unless it were supported by something else, especially when it arises from the brain or the upper spinal cord; and specifically when this substance is divided into many parts, for that reason simple flesh was mixed with it, which, being joined to it, would support it and fill the voids. And because these substances were joined together, the nerve and ligament were thinned and divided into threads, and from them a **membranous** <term>Panniculus: A thin, film-like tissue or membrane; here described as a protective wrapping woven from nerve and ligament fibers.</term> substance was woven, then collecting and containing the aforementioned adjuncts and separating them where necessary and distinguishing them. 

The part of this composite substance also which tends toward the limb to be moved is collectively thinned and hardened so that, assuming the likeness of a small rope, it is called a **cord** <note original: "corda">Here meaning a tendon.</note>. For it is composed of nerve and ligament because the flesh ceases, extending only through the tendon, and the membrane hardens into nerve and the ligament into a cord as they pass through. And this substance composed of these four parts is called a **muscle** or **lacertus** <margin>in flow</margin> <note>The marginal note "in flow" refers to the fluid-like transmission of the motive spirit through the muscle fibers.</note>, which does not imply a real distinction in dignity. 

From these series of arguments recently heard, it follows that the motive power enters primarily into the nerve rather than the muscle. The necessity of the muscle and its essence also appear, and why it will be the "first movable thing" or immediate instrument, since in it the reason for motion and support is more aptly found, though only by the power of the nerve itself. For the nerve is thus a **uniform part** <term>Uniform part: (Pars consimilis) A tissue that is the same throughout its structure, like bone or nerve, as opposed to an "organic" part like a hand or eye.</term>, the principal instrument of the muscle. Now, however, let the conclusions be confirmed by reason.

For there must be a proportion between the thing moved and the mover, as between the intelligible and the intellect, as that which is taught in the *Physics* <note>Aristotle's *Physics*, a foundational text for medieval natural science.</note>. But the nerve, since it is simple, is more proportioned to a simple power and being than to a composite muscle, at least in its particular composition. The chest and these things are constructed according to a general theoretical intention, and specifically where they are located in the anatomy of composite parts. Furthermore, since this power requires a subject through which it is carried and without which it would never move of itself—since nothing moves thus unless it is a body (*Physics*, book 6)—that subject will be nothing but the nerve, because it arises immediately from the brain or spinal cord, as is manifest. 

The muscle, however, does not extend so far as to touch the brain or spinal cord as something underlying sensation. The nerve is also bright, or rather porous, and as such it deserves to be the first recipient of the **animal power** <term>Animal power: (Virtus animalis) The faculty of the soul responsible for sensation and voluntary movement, traditionally located in the brain.</term> via the mediation of the spirit; these things, however, are not in the muscle except perhaps through the nerve. And therefore in the **blockage** <note original: "opilationem">A medical term for a physical obstruction or clogging of the vessels or channels of the body.</note> and obstruction of the nerves we see paralysis and similar conditions, but not so in those of the muscle. 

Furthermore, in each of the functional limbs there is a "uniform" part which primarily governs the action; other parts are for the sake of well-being (Distinction 63). Such a part, rightly considered, will be the nerve and not the ligament, since the ligament does not feel, nor is it bound to the source. It is also made to assist the more principal nerve, as appeared from the composition of the muscle. Neither is it the membrane, since that is a separation, nor the flesh, because it is not principal but formed from blood according to the flow and reflux of life; nor even the whole muscle, since motion is in the whole through the part, according to *Physics*, book 8. 

Moreover, experience teaches us this because we see motion and sensation cease when a nerve is cut, but not when a muscle is cut; yet motion then is not in the nerve (except perhaps that of contraction or spasm) but rather in the muscle, yet sensation is beyond the muscle, or is manifest there. Thus, therefore, let it be sufficiently concluded that the nerve is that which immediately and principally receives the vigor of the animal power—namely of motion and sensation. And that which is said <margin>to the works</margin> is manifested in the muscle. 

Because of which, all the primary authorities agree that the power moves the muscle, but not that the power is primarily received in it; rather it is received in the nerve, just as the principle of the operation of sight is placed in the **crystalline lens** <note>The lens of the eye, which medieval anatomists believed was the actual organ of sight.</note> yet is manifested more in the adjacent parts (Distinction 63). To the other point it must be said that parts do not function there "organically" in the sense that "organic" and "uniform" are opposed, but "organic" is said in relation to the simple concepts of the soul. Either this is verified in motion, as was said, or in the manifestation at the principle that first receives the mover. 

The reason for the other point appears from what was said before. To the last, it must be said that the nerve, by reason of its connection and substance, provides more support to the muscle, yet the mass found in the muscle is lacking in the nerve. Or as much as the organ requires into which the motive power is first sent, and not that in which the appearance or more immense manifestation of the power stands. 

To the other it must be said that it is true when that limb is one in every way. But a nerve is often both sensing and moving. Or let us not consider it in only one way even with a given nerve. For in itself it is possible to find [a degree of] coldness and less dryness and softness, and thus it will be an organ fit for sensation. And one can find the aforesaid qualities in it, along with intensities of greater transparency and porosity, by which the instrument is rendered more fit for motion.

Since it was said that the utility of the nerve is the distribution of sensation and motion to all parts, the question arises: can one single nerve be the source of both sensation and motion? Because the power is one thing, the substance another, and the end or operation another, they will not coincide in the same principle. Such indeed is the nerve, both sensing and moving, since the sensing power is ordered toward the sensory, and the motive power toward the motor; and let the motor nerve be drier and harder than the sensory, according to the first books of the *Theoretical Medicine*. The end of the sensory is to provide sensation, while that of the motive is motion. Furthermore, those things do not coincide in one principle whose being is generated from different origins. Since the coordinations of the **predicaments** <term>Predicaments: (Praedicamenta) The Aristotelian categories of being, such as substance, quality, or passion.</term> are unmixed (Posterior Analytics, book 1). But that which belongs to the sensory is in the category of passion...

It defines the four components of a muscle—nerve, ligament, flesh, and membrane—and explores the anatomical reasons why nerves are better suited to receive the "animal power."</summary>

falls outside of motion or into that which is the action of perception. For **to feel** is to be acted upon in some way, whereas **to move** is to act, as stated in the fourth book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"; refers to Aristotle’s treatise on the animating principle of life</note> and in the first book of *On Internal Matters* <note>original: "de interioribus"; likely referring to Galen's work on the functions of internal organs</note>. And this is supported because in that context, feeling receives an action from another, such as from a **sensible object** <term>Sensible object: (Sensibile) A physical thing that can be perceived by the senses, such as a color, sound, or texture.</term> which stands toward it as something to be suffered. Motion, however, is not of that nature; rather, it more likely causes action in something else. And if there is one nerve perceiving both sense and motion, then there will only be one act corresponding to it, since it belongs to that which is distinct and also to the rest of the motor functions.

Again, in the *Tegni* <note>original: "tegui"; refers to Galen's *Ars Medica*, a foundational medical textbook</note> it is said that for the most part, sensory nerves arise from the anterior [front] part of the brain, while motor nerves arise from the posterior [back]. Likewise, for what reason would there be a specific nerve for perceiving sense and another for motion? For one would seem to suffice; therefore, one nerve cannot be the principle of both sense and motion.

The opposite, however, is the common opinion of physicians. Furthermore, as it is in the first and second parts of this work, so it shall be in the beginning—namely, in the brain, the **spinal cord** <note original: "nucha">The medieval term for the spinal cord, viewed as an extension of the brain's substance.</note>, and the nerve. But each of these, being one, initiates both sense and motion. Again, those whose name and definition are the same, their principle of action will be one since they have the same nature; such is the case with the sensory and motor nerve. For both are one, and it is a flexible, thin, stretched, white-colored cord produced from the brain and spinal cord. Therefore, one nerve can be the principle of both sense and motion.

Regarding the first point, it should be known how many ways "one" is said... "One" here implies a numerical unity. What, then, is a nerve? Distinction 41. What is sense? Distinction 42. But motion is in Distinction 50, with their multiplicity. Principles, however, are spoken of in many ways. First, that from which a motion begins, as in a distance, where one end is the start and its opposite the limit. Second, that from which any thing is best made, as in teaching, one must not begin from the absolute beginning of the matter, but from where it is most easily learned. Third, that which is first produced or generated in an existing thing, like the foundation in a house or the heart in an animal. Further, that from which motion first initiates, as a father and mother are the principles of children, and a dispute is the principle of war; or someone moving and changing another according to will and impulse, such as a prince or a tyrant, or the master-builder of the arts. Sixth, that from which a thing is first known, such as suppositions and prior axioms are the principles of knowing conclusions. Here, "principle" is understood in the fourth sense.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that **Avicenna** <note original: "Ay.">Abbreviation for Avicenna (Ibn Sina), whose *Canon of Medicine* is the subject of this commentary.</note>, as touched upon in distinction 42, perhaps not knowing the precise nature of the nerve, positioned its duties as diverse and different; primarily as a way to bind bones and connect them to each other, especially in the skull where there is a suture or saw-like coupling. And this is not truly a nerve except equivocally, but rather a ligament. And regarding sense, he provides it so that it is not absent, for **numbness** <term>Numbness: (Stupor) A medical condition defined by the loss of sensation or the inability to feel touch and pain.</term> does not occur where there is no nerve in the body. Most nerves are around the feet, hands, ribs, neck, and arms.

Numbness, however, is a passion of the sense, as in distinction 73. Nevertheless, in the second part, Avicenna suggests that he wanted the nerve only to temper the flesh of the ribs with its coldness, being unable to be felt by the excellence of heat. For he says it appears from Avicenna's opinion that the nerve exists only to temper internal heat so that it may give the **power of feeling** <term>Power: (Virtus) The functional ability or faculty of an organ provided by the soul.</term> to the flesh, as he adds after many points. And this opinion is followed more in the context of the benefit of the brain. But perhaps Avicenna’s view cannot stand,

---

since nowhere will you find such a nerve-benefit when you search diligently, as these temperaments are caused by the brain sufficiently for the parts in the second section. Furthermore, the flesh of the heart, the most fleshy of all parts, is said to feel in distinction 42. Where hesitation appeared concerning the nature of the powers, likewise for Avicenna.

Regarding the beginning, it should be known that one and the same nerve can not rarely be the beginning of sense and motion; this is testified in the fourth book of *Accidents*, the first book of *Internal Matters*, on manifest motions, and in the sixth book of *Theories*. For they wish that many times sense and motion are given through one nerve, and frequently that one of the nerves provides sense individually and another motion. Then the doubt will not coincide if sense can exist without motion or vice versa, as in the tongue and the eye, but rather when the same nerve serves both.

The truth, however, is more famous: that wherever there is sense, there is not necessarily motion, since to move is to act, but to feel is to be acted upon. To act requires more power and heat; to be acted upon, a moderate amount is sufficient. Where motion is found, by contrast, sense is also found, provided a sensible object meets it. I say this because some nerves are the principle of moving and not of feeling—not because they *cannot* feel, but because they are buried deep and the external sensible nature cannot reach them; whence the first book of *De Partibus* <note>Aristotle's *On the Parts of Animals*</note>.

Of the mobile sensing members, for the most part, one nerve is the principle of both sense and motion, though they are often separate, and a nerve will be the principle of one or the other power. To understand this more fully, it should be known that the nerve is not the *primary* principle of sense and motion, but rather the heart or the brain with the spinal cord—more like a treasury with respect to the flesh, membranes, muscles, and cords—just as the spinal cord relates to the brain and the nerves.

Moreover, the nerve stands more as a principle of sense than of motion. For it feels in itself and makes other things feel over which it is spread, such as the membranes and cords it weaves together. But the beginning of motion is not an act of the sensory power. For it cannot move itself locally unless a natural act is brought into the muscle’s joining, of which the nerve is a significant part (since a muscle is made of nerve and simple flesh); it contributes to motion. And because it is the organ that carries power and natural heat into the muscle, it is the organ of motion, either carrying it or delivering sense—not only because it has the power, but because it perceives or judges more. This is how it is with the optic nerves and the crystalline lens, distinction 45.

The proposition is confirmed by reason: because in those things where one is ordered toward the other, that which can do the greater can also do the lesser. Such is motion in relation to sense; for motion is for the sake of perception, and sense is for the safety of the animal. For it is deficient if it does not move toward what is apprehended. Thus, a nerve that moves (since moving is acting, which requires much power) will also be able to feel, since being acted upon requires only a small amount of power. Furthermore, since the act of the soul and natural heat are vigorous according to whether they inhabit an organ more or less, one organ can perform diverse tasks—for example, running and standing in an animal—where one requires more power and the rest less. Indeed, the nerve is the organ with respect to natural heat and power; for much of these is sent into the nerve for motion.

Again, since the composition differs only slightly in its helpfulness, one thing will be able to act upon the sense in such a way that it is naturally affected by heat and by such a power. The **reason** <note>original: "Ratio"; often used here to mean the underlying principle or defining logic</note> for the nerve is that while it is cold and dry in a measured way, once those sensations are received, it relaxes the cold and likewise the dryness.

**The Reason:** It is not enough for the **innate heat** <term>Innate heat: (Calor innatus) In medieval medicine, the natural vital heat present in a living body from birth, centered in the heart.</term> to operate unless there occurs an **influent power** <term>Influent power: (Virtus influens) A power or "spirit" sent from a primary organ (like the brain or heart) to a secondary organ to enable a specific function like movement.</term> which renders to it something else, like a formal heat. Also, from the organ, because the substance exists in whatever way, this occurs so that the agent is varied by touch; however, the principal effect can be preserved.

But this is the substance of the nerve: in it, one must consider either its **transparency** <note>original: "dyaponeitatē" for "diaphaneitatem"</note> or its smallness according to its sounding nature. Since the spirit is mostly in this, it happens that it has an earthiness and hardness by which the nerve is made conformable to motion, since motion strongly requires a subject for action, and hardness provides the support for rest. Likewise, one and the same thing in number can be used for two different purposes, like the tongue for taste and for speech, as noted in the book *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle, *De Anima*</note>. There is a difference, however, because it serves one principally, namely taste, and the other insofar as it is for speech; for even if the tongue exists as one substance, it is nonetheless for a different reason. For it tastes by means of the nerves descending to it from the **third pair** of cranial nerves. It articulates speech, however, by means of those from the **seventh pair**.

Thus, there is a double nature in the nerve: by reason of its substance, it is principally ordered toward sensation since it actually receives a sensible object when it occurs, but it does not initiate motion except by its power. Therefore, a nerve can initiate both motion and sensation. However, because it sometimes requires a simple and intense sense, not distracted into many things, nature added a nerve here simply for sensation; and when it requires motion alone, it then constitutes a nerve for absolute motion, such as those of the **extremities** <note>original: "sepultorum"; likely a scribal error or variant for "extremorum"</note> like the hands and feet. Yet it never participates in both unless it needs to be in the third and fourth pairs produced from the brain.

Regarding the fourth point, it must be said to the first that although these are dissonant in their specific types, they agree in common such that the soul, with the innate heat brought into that organ, can impress that diverse effect upon it. To the other point, it must be said that although the "patient" (which is the nerve) is for sensation and the "agent" (which is for motion) are of different kinds, nothing prevents them from being the same in substance; just as a thing is said to be generated by reason, being placed in a genus toward something else. For the **Reason** <note>Ratio</note> subsists in itself in the category of substance. Similarly, regarding the nerve, different things are found in it and impressed upon it. Everything that is simultaneously active and passive, and moving physically, will be physically mobile in its intention.

To the other reason, it appears similarly from many examples. To the next, it must be said that the power is one in common, yet it is diversified in specific organs. An organ like the sight, which has another nature and reception, can be similarly diversified. To the next, it must be said that nothing prevents a nerve from being the beginning of both sensation and motion, as has been declared; although simpler sensory nerves proceed more from the **anterior** [front] part and motor nerves from the **posterior** [back] part. To the other point, the answer is already apparent. And to those things of the other part, it also now appears sufficiently.

### On the occasion of what has been said, that muscles have only innate virtue, it is finally hesitated:

---

Whether, indeed, a muscle does not have only this innate power, or also an influent one, since **John** <note>likely referring to Johannes Mesue or another medical authority</note> enumerates it among the members possessing both innate and influent power, as do all three types of muscles. This is hinted at in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*</note> where, having enumerated the principal parts and their servants, and those having innate power alone (in which he does not place the muscle), he finally says: "All other common parts have their own governance and require nerves." Under these, the muscle seems to be located. Also, no **official member** <term>Official member: (Membrum officiale) An organ with a specific function or "office" in the body, such as the heart, liver, or a muscle.</term> has innate power alone, but also influent power with it, and is thus a composite. That which receives from a simple thing is itself simple; the muscle, however, is an official part, according to the theorists, since it is an instrument of the **animal power** <term>Animal power: (Virtus animalis) The power of the soul, governed by the brain, responsible for sensation and voluntary movement.</term>. And this is confirmed because it receives sensation and motion from the brain (Distinction 58).

Furthermore, things having innate power alone are bones and flesh, which do not feel; a muscle, however, certainly feels. Therefore, a muscle has both innate and influent power, and not only innate.

**On the opposite side:** The same John <note>Johannes Mesue</note> had grouped the muscle among those things that have innate power only. And in the *Tegni*, where he deals with the parts that have innate power and treats their disposition, he considers the muscle as part of their construction and nature. Furthermore, if the components of a muscle have innate power only, then the muscle itself must too, since the whole arises from its parts. These parts are the proper and simple flesh, since it is compressed blood. And the nerves through which it does not receive <note>unclear/contradictory in text</note> sensation. For they are of an earthy nature, and such things do not feel (Book 1 of *On the Soul*). Nor do they have motion (Distinction 58). The ligament also is part of its constitution, according to **Almanzor** <note>The Latinized name for Rhazes (Al-Razi)</note> in the first books. And therefore, on this point, **Haly Rodoan** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an Egyptian physician and commentator on Galen</note> is said to have failed, separating the ligament into its own category and the membrane from the muscle, as if it did not enter into its constitution. And it is confirmed, because it is more often said (Distinction 58) that a muscle is composed of flesh, its own innate heat, and the soul. Flesh, however, has only innate power.

Again, a thing is said to act because it has motion from itself (Book 1 of *On Internal Matters*). Such a muscle is concluded to be in the genus of motion (Book 1 of the *Physics* and Book 8 of the *Physics*). Therefore, the muscle has innate power only.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that what is called a muscle or **lacertus** <note>A classical term for a muscle, especially of the arm</note> (Distinction 58) has innate power only as one of the four types of parts. This can be understood in three ways. Either something has innate power only—that is, a natural power given at birth (Distinction 58)—which is a principle more internally inherent to its path, and thus certain natural members assigned to animals have their origin from forms and have mostly innate power alone.

Others are said to be members having innate power that is sufficient for themselves, needing nothing simple from another, nor receiving from it absolutely. Rather, it contributes its own internal power to the others in the manner of the "first" in the universe; such is the **heart**, which stands as the explicit opinion of Aristotle. Or, something possesses innate power alone because it was so given to it at the beginning of its generation, because it is the proper root and principle of the others. For it arrives before and recedes last; it begins before the others and is completed before them. For although parts are generated at the same time, the superior ones are made before the inferior, and the younger before...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the physiological origins of bodily power, specifically transitioning from the general influence of the heart to the specific composition and naming of muscles. It reconciles the views of Galen, Avicenna, and Johannitius concerning whether organs possess their own internal "innate" power or rely entirely on "influent" power from the brain and heart.</meta>
