...principal external factors which follow. And also in chapter 49, it is therefore said in the book *On the Generation of Animals* <note>original: "de ge. aialiu"; Aristotle’s "De Generatione Animalium"</note> where it appears that every form pre-exists in the heart. Thus, no member will have an innate virtue <note>original: "uirtutē"; refers to a functional power or faculty</note> derived from the heart, since all are seen to depend on it in some way, as also appears in the joints. And that is a certain truth, or at least a likely image, that from the pre-existing spermatic mass of generation, each of the parts receives what is its own, not through the power of one or by some succession as before. And so the physicist Galen estimated that a pre-existing innate power only obtains. Since it appears in the parts themselves, he did not perceive an artery, vein, or nerve to be carried there, whereas bone, cartilage, ligament, and fat are shown. Therefore, the speech of Galen was more beautiful in appearance, but that of Avicenna <note>original: "Ay." for Avicenna (Ibn Sina)</note> was more profound in its coexistence.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that according to Avicenna, a muscle is said to have an innate power insofar as it is rendered hot, cold, dry, fat, or thin, hairy or the opposite, or situated in this or that way. Insofar as motion is perfected by it, its sense has both an innate and an **influent power** <term>Influent power: (Virtus influens) A vital force or "spirit" sent from a primary organ, like the brain or heart, to a secondary part to enable functions like movement or sensation.</term>.

But those saying this do not put to rest the doubters, since they do not assign the method and cause, nor do they open up the difficulty.

Furthermore, some have wanted to call a "muscle" by another name, or a "lacertus" <note>original: "lacertū"; literally "lizard," a common anatomical term for a muscle</note>, attempting to establish this from Johannitius <note>original: "Iohannitio"; Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a famous translator and physician</note> in his *Isagoge*. But this is not valid, as the names are more synonymous, having been used more through translation than by nature. One may therefore be used indifferently for the other. However, "muscle" <note>original: "musculus"</note> is seen to be transformed from the Greek. For "Mus" <note>original: "mus" (μῦς)</note> among them signifies both a **mouse** and a muscle, which is also said in the *Xitrio*. A "lacertus" is so called as if it were a "little lizard" <note>original: "lacertulus"</note>, because in the manner of a mouse or lizard, they spread through the body from the sides. Although it may imply a muscle, it specifically refers to those of the arms and shoulders. Wherefore the poets also denote the arms as **lacertos** <note>In Latin poetry, "lacerti" is frequently used to describe the muscular upper arms.</note>. Regarding the third point, it should be known that a muscle or "lacertus" is supported by a worthy flowing power and an innate one, as they noted here, since its birth supports animals in their natural functions, such as flux and motion. For veins and arteries are not of the presiding essence of the muscle, but rather act as conduits by which life is preserved and nourishment is carried to it. Consequently, by innate power alone, it is shown that the flesh of the muscle is like thickened blood; and by motion, it lacks sense until it is perfected by the muscle and nerve. Hence it was said by Aristotle: "bones and flesh are not sentient," yet in their composition falls the ligament, regardless of what Haly <note>original: "Haly"; likely the physician Haly Abbas</note> said regarding a member having only innate power. However, the nerve falling into the construction of the muscle, besides what it has, can provide sensation and motion, and it may be found otherwise, namely by reason of its earthiness rather than its deformity, and insofar as it is dissolved into threads of simple flesh binding them together, as it could not otherwise remain; thus it takes on the action of a ligament when that was not sufficient. And so some, not hearing this, said the muscle was a part of them like flesh. But an anxiety arises concerning this, since it is written in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Ars Medica"</note> that members having innate power only rule themselves, so that they neither dominate others nor are dominated by others. Johannitius says they rule by their own good innate powers.

<margin>
DIFFERENCE 59.
</margin>

Which rule and show their quality. On the contrary, these members are natural; for of these it is written in the first book of the *Physics* that a power is granted to them in which they perfect their act, just as a **magnet** <note>original: "magnes"</note> draws iron by a power placed within it. If they were to remain as they are, they would eventually need nothing, neither arteries nor veins. But because they require nutrition and the protection of measured heat, they needed them. Therefore, they receive power from elsewhere, not having it only innately. It should be said that they receive it not to acquire vitality (which they received at the beginning of their production), but for the preservation of the vitality previously received, as the expositor made manifest. Galen, when he was in the *Tegni*, was brief, as was Johannitius. And Aristotle remains silent, saying that if the way between the head and the bone were closed, and it had suitable nutrition, its act would be destroyed. For this does not take away vitality, but rather its conservation, which Galen has already granted. Regarding the third point, following the first and second, it should be said from the premises: a muscle flourishes by both powers, as shown. To the other, it should be said that it is constructed of simples, having the reason of a member with innate power only; but as a composite, it participates in both powers, for a muscle is an **official** <term>Official member: (Membrum officiale) In medieval anatomy, an organ or body part composed of various tissues (like a muscle) that performs a specific function, as opposed to a "simple" tissue.</term> and composite member. It is not like the head, but rather occupies a middle ground between simple and composite parts. To the other, it appears that the flesh is the greater part of the muscle in anatomy. The flesh of animals is the greatest part of the muscles, which, when bound with ligaments and nerves, creates the muscle. Although it lacks sensation and motion by itself, it receives them through the vigor descending from the brain through the nerve. As for those things which are higher, it is seen that Galen, considering with Johannitius what is most represented in the muscle, placed organs enjoying innate power only; for in it is flesh and ligament, and both are reduced more to flesh. For it involves and surrounds bone and cartilage, all of which exist by a good innate power alone; and the nerve thus binding and containing the fleshy parts takes on this reason, and by its kind, the **panniculus** <note>original: "paniculū"; a thin membrane or tissue layer</note>, since it is constituted from ligament and nerve. Flesh is also sometimes found throughout the structure down to the bone and cartilages, as here when the muscle is composed of flesh.

-> That heat and spirit are the same is shown from the fifth book of *Medicines* <note>original: "farmacoy"</note>. Hippocrates saying that **innate heat** is spirit. Furthermore, by reason: whatever things have the same agent and are produced from the same matter and at the same time are seen to be the same, since these are the causes of identity. Both heat and spirit have these. For they are made by the heart from the subtleties of the humors as their vaporousness, and at the same time. Further, those things whose operation and property are the same, are themselves the same. For these... <-

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the physiological principles of life, specifically the relationship between natural heat and the "spirit." It transitions from the general powers of the organs to the specific definitions used by Isaac Israeli and Avicenna regarding how the body is animated and warmed.</meta>

...made known through form or the transformation of matter. However, **heat** is dissolvable or subtle and highly mobile, as is the spirit from the distance of the liver <note>original: "ieglis," likely a contraction for *iecoris*</note>. And if heat and spirit were the masters, since heat is a body, as will be seen, it would be diffused through the whole body; and if the spirit were also a body, two bodies would occupy the same place, which is impossible. Likewise, since heat is not a "non-natural" thing <note>In Galenic medicine, "non-naturals" are external factors like air, diet, and sleep; "naturals" are internal components of the body.</note>, nor even against nature, but is natural, the "natural things" would become eight. However, a consensus given by the learned puts them at seven. Therefore, heat and spirit would be the same. 

To the contrary: because they are noted at a distance from one another, they present heat as distinct from the spirit. Whence, regarding the cause of the motion of animals, the same can become greater or lesser in others because of both heat and spirit and solidity. And primarily, the **brain** and the **liver** receive both natural heat and spirit from the heart by their own power. And let it be that the spirits exist: just as the external parts have spirit, blood, and heat, so do the internal. And therefore, many such expressions are found. 

### The Definition of Natural Heat

Furthermore, **natural heat** is described as temperate, nourishing, and mild—the primary of the affections. **Spirit**, however, is the "vessel" <note>original: "catio," likely *vas* or *vehiculum*</note> of the body's powers, the first among the primary things. Moreover, those things are said to be distinct whose locations are distinct, since a natural location preserves that which it contains in the likeness of its form. For as much as nature gives to the form, so much does it give to the location, as seen in *The Heavens* and *Physics* book four. 

<margin>Spirit</margin>

The location of heat, according to the *Book of Definitions*, is within the tunics of the **arteries**; the spirit, however, is between tunic and tunic. Because of this, heat is not the same as spirit. However, regarding the first point, it should be known that a twofold distinction of heat is currently given: one is taken from its preceding principle, the other from its very being. According to the first, heat is twofold: one indeed is **simple** (unmixed), the other is **composite** and mixed. 

1.  **Simple heat** is found to be twofold: 
    *   **Elementary heat**, which is the proper quality of fire, so inseparable from its form that many of the ancients thought it to be its essential form. This is refuted in chapter 13. This heat is least present in the generation of living things. For the heat of vegetables is not fire, nor does it take its principle from it. It contributes, however, to the preparation of matter by altering and transforming it so that a form may be introduced into it. Just as heat and solidity work toward the reception of a form by the soul of the swordsmith. 
    *   **Celestial heat**, which is life-giving and preserves the seeds of all living things in being, never inducing consumption or destruction; this is called "warmth" <note>original: "calūm," likely *calidum*</note> which exists in the semen of all things. From this comes the immediate instrument upon which the soul relies in its being and operations, as said in chapter 48.

2.  **Composite heat** is composed of these two aforesaid types, and it is the heat of both animals and plants. For it belongs to the soul. Of these, one type goes out for the preparation of matter, while the other is given for the form. 

### The Dual Nature of Innate Heat

Indeed, this heat is twofold by reason: **heat of generation**, which is diffused and found in all members and most especially in the **heart**, and is called **innate heat**. By the virtue of this heat supported in the heart, another heat is generated, which is "influent" <term>Influent heat: (Calor influens) A secondary heat that flows from the heart through the blood to the rest of the body.</term> and runs down to the members. From this and the previously mentioned heat, a compound is made in those parts which goes out as the form of the members; through its mediation and the virtue of the soul (as the more principal part), every member perfects its due composition, assuming action and passion. This is also touched upon regarding the utility of the **pulse**. 

The heat of the heart is preserved by **respiration**; that which is in the remaining parts is preserved by this and by the transmission of heat from the heart to them. Avicenna touched upon these types of heat in many places of the *Canon*, saying: "The innate heat which goes out in us or is within us, by which innate heat is indicated, is called 'influent' in three ways." He also frequently calls this heat not just "innate" but "natural." 

What innate heat actually is has now appeared. It is a more specific drawing-out of the "natural." For according to some, as it is more common, it implies both innate and influent heat, as if derived from nature's governance. **Isaac**, however, in the first book of *On Fevers*, calls that heat "natural" which is sent down from the heart through the arteries into the body. He says its foundation is the **vital spirit**, which also travels through the arteries. **Avicenna** calls the "body" of this heat the vaporous substance sent from the heart into the members through the arteries. 

### The Various Meanings of Spirit

There is also another distinction for the spirit. For it is understood in two ways: properly by its quality, and improperly by the compound of the body and heat. Spirit is spoken of in many ways: 
*   For one of the three Divine Persons (The Holy Spirit), according to the Gospel of **John**: *"The Spirit breathes where it wills."*
*   For demonic substances, whether graced or depraved.
*   For the soul, according to the Gospel: *"The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."*
*   For the wind (meteorological).
*   For the subtle bodies in **alchemy** which transmute metals, from which the elixir is constructed. 
*   For the subtle, airy body that is the carrier of virtues, which is twofold: **innate** (properly the bodily substance generated from the mixture of elements) and **influent** (the vapor of tempered blood). 

Regarding the latter, the ancients agreed: **Spirit is a subtle body proceeding from the heart into the arteries to the whole body, making it have life and breath through the lungs; it ascends to the brain, and proceeds from it into the nerves through the whole body, creating the 'animal spirit' which possesses sense and motion.** 

From these things, it seems "spirit" is properly said to be innate; the reasons for calling it "spirit" (as the name sounds) are its subtleness and quick mobility. Know also that, speaking properly, there are only two spirits: the **vital** and the **animal**. Hence it is gathered: there are two spirits—the spirit appearing in the heart and the spirit appearing in the brain. But in the liver, there is no apparent spirit. This is what Isaac suggests in his *Definitions*, noting that when combined with blood, it is called the vital and animal spirit, never mentioning a "natural" spirit there. If, however, there is any natural spirit, it is generated there. The **Physician**, extending the name of spirit, many times expresses a "natural spirit" originating from the liver alone, which is a vaporous and turbid body.

It also categorizes the multiple meanings of "spirit," ranging from the theological and alchemical to the medical "vital" and "animal" spirits.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the biological relationship between "innate heat" and the "spirit" (the vaporous substance believed to carry life through the body). It draws heavily on classical and Islamic authorities to determine if these are two names for the same thing or two distinct physical substances.</meta>

...be spoken of. There is a distinction in vision and appetite as well. 

Regarding this, it must be known that **Galen**, in the fifth book <note>original: "qntō," referring to the fifth book of *On Simple Medicines*</note>, attributes to **Hippocrates** the idea that heat and spirit are the same thing, not only by accident but also by their natural essence. This is the sequence of the argument. It is necessary for us not to err in understanding the intention of his speech. We should know that he did not mean by his statement that **innate heat** is nothing other than what we, in our terms, call the **spirit**, which is fixed in the body of any animal. **Avicenna** also said this again in his own book. 

Furthermore, there is nothing to prevent us from understanding from **Hippocrates** that he implies by the term "innate heat" the substance of the blood and the substance of the **seed** <note>original: "spmatis," referring to reproductive "sperm" or "seed"</note> along with the spirit, since this innate, natural heat belongs to each of these substances. This is what **Galen** often seems to assert in his *Prognostics* and his *Commentary on the Nature of Man* <note>original: "nataliū sʒo."</note> alongside **Hippocrates**, wishing that this innate heat alone performs all functions in the animal, and that the substance of our generation is completed by three things: namely, seed, blood, and airy humidity.

### The Ambiguity of the Terms

The discourse repeats an ambiguous point: that heat is the same as the spirit and [yet] something else. This perhaps happens through an error of the monk <note>A likely reference to a translator or scribe, possibly Constantine the African</note>. Indeed, **Averroës** perhaps felt this in the *Colliget*, saying: "It is necessary to speculate on what is the first body that is moved," and it appears that this is the **natural heat** which is in us. And this is perhaps that vaporous heat-body found in the **heart**, which is sent from it to the other members through the pathways of the **arteries**. 

But what should be said of this will be seen in the third and fourth sections. However, although they may say heat and spirit are the same thing in reality, they nevertheless differ in reason. For **Heat** is so called because it warms, thins, digests, and matures; it gathers homogeneous things and separates heterogeneous things, and other such actions. **Spirit**, however, is named from that which breathes, pulses, illuminates, and carries the [vital] power to perform its actions.

### Differing Opinions of the Masters

**Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Haly," the Latin name for the Persian physician 'Ali ibn al-'Abbas al-Magusi</note> was of the opinion that spirit and innate heat are two natural vapors in the body—namely, subtle airy bodies—between which a difference exists because the spirit is more subtle <note>In medieval science, "subtle" means refined, thin, or gas-like</note> than the innate heat, and the innate heat is thicker and possesses more humidity. 

This position, as it sounds, cannot stand. For it is contrary to those who place the animal in incorruption, comparing its heat in its subtlety to **fire**, but the spirit to **air**, as in the first book of the *Pantegni* <note>original: "prīo theori."</note> and **Isaac Israeli** in many places. Even the name "heat" indicates this, since it is that which descends from fire, the most subtle and lightest of bodies. 

Furthermore, one cannot be separated from the other, just as an effect is continually inherent to its cause and accompanies it inseparably, like light accompanies that which illuminates. There is, perhaps, another way of speaking according to **Isaac**, who posits that heat passes with the blood through the middle of the inner **tunic** <note>An artery was thought to have two "tunics" or layers</note> of the artery, but the spirit [passes] between one tunic and the other, lest the spirit's motion be hindered by the blood if it passed through the interior tunic. For he wants the spirit to be suddenly diffused through the whole body, like light through a house. 

This statement, although it may seem plausible, cannot stand, since it would be more hindered passing between one tunic of the artery and the other because of their connection to each other. Furthermore, it would not be hindered on the inside since the artery is not entirely filled with blood. Again, since that innate heat which passes through the arteries is like the spirit...

---

...and the spirit passing between the tunics of the artery is joined to the heat, for it moves. Nothing moves, after all, unless by heat. If heat does not possess a different location from the spirit—unless perhaps by some addition or subtraction—then some spirits are affected by more heat and others by less. There were others who said that **natural heat** and **natural spirit** are the same, but the **vital** and **animal** [spirits] differ. Those speaking thus wish to attribute the "natural" only to the power situated in the **liver**, according to the physicians. 

This was perhaps motivated by the words of **Hippocrates** and **Galen**, who intended that heat felt in the limbs is the cause of natural operations. However, this goes against many determinations. For they understand "natural heat" as that which rules nature, namely as an instrument of the liver. Nor is the spirit properly called "natural" when it carries within it the qualities of breathing, pulsing, carrying, and vehement motion. 

### On the Term "Pneuma"

"Spirit" is called **pneuma** in Greek, which is said to be "breathing" <note>original: "baheli," likely a corruption of the Greek *pnoe* or *emphysesis*</note>, or inspiration or expiration, which carries a fast and great motion of attraction and expulsion. 

Because of this, it must be known that heat and spirit are neither identical in reality while differing only in reason, nor are they two different bodies, nor is natural heat the same as the natural spirit. Rather, I testify that they are the same only in **substance**; they do not differ except according to the requirements of the subject and the mode of speaking, assumed from their properties and from their modes of being. For the mode of signifying arises from the mode of being. It is called **Heat** with regard to its essence, or "innate heat" or "natural heat." For an added term never changes the primary and principal thing signified. By whatever properties heat is varied, its essence is always located in the **category of quality**. 

That it is the same only in substance—just as a quality is the same as its subject—is distinguished by opinions and confirmed by reason. For heat adheres more immediately to the **soul** than the spirit does, and the spirit in turn has its being and operation from these. Just as the heat of a fire is sustained in it from the air generated by the fire, so the animal heat, from the vigor of the formative power or the soul, produces spirits from the seed. 

What does **Aristotle** <note>original: "y." usually an abbreviation for *Ystoria* or *Philosophus* (Aristotle)</note> think about the formation of the embryo? He says the seed is collected and, being thickened, it is warmed, and the substance of spirits exists in the heat; and the spirit extends outward through the heat existing in the seed. He also says that warmed moisture constitutes spirit, and the seed warmed in the womb has and emits spirit. 

**Life** is the primary power that reaches the spirit, since the spirit proceeds from the subtlety of the humors; these however are caused by heat. For its nature, as was said, is to subtilize. From this, therefore, it appears that heat precedes the spirit, being supported by a substance, and it causes the spirit as an effect causes a cause—here, however, it exists as a quality. Furthermore, in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, he thinks that the seed is "spirited" and moved by heat. Seed goes out from the inside joined together—that is, its spirit is united—and it is white because of the internal heat and having much warm spirit. But when it has gone out and the heat has exhaled and the air cools it, it becomes moist and black from the air. That the spirit is something other than heat appears plainly in the second book of *On the Nature of Man*. For it [heat] is the cause of digestion. That heat is an accident and a quality of the blood, and not only of the spirit...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the relationship between innate heat and the spirit. The previous page established that while some authorities (like Hippocrates and Galen) seem to conflate the two, there is a technical distinction to be made between the "substance" of the spirit and the "quality" of heat. This page cites Averroes and Isaac Judaeus to refine this distinction and then begins a new inquiry into whether the spirit is a permanent substance or a constantly fluxing one.</meta>

The Commentator <note>Referring to Averroes, the influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note> testifies to this same thing in the second section of the *Aphorisms* as follows: In the beginning [of illnesses], we command those who are suffering to stay awake, ordering those things which, through wakefulness, draw the **spirit** and **blood** and their heat outward. However, this mode of being is nothing other than that of a **form** in a **subject**, and is properly **accidental** <note>In scholastic philosophy, an "accident" is a property (like heat) that exists within a "subject" (like the spirit) but is not the substance itself.</note>. Whence in the first book [it says]: "Let it remind you of the great heat around the body of an animal; the fire of the spirit is that nature without which it is impossible for life to stand, and air moves mostly with it, or fire." 

Thus, since heat is principally attributed to fire and spirit to air, they must be distinct from one another. And because the spirit is primarily of the nature of air, while heat is of the nature of fire, heat will be a quality of the spirit. This is also what **Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus (c. 832–932), a Jewish physician and philosopher whose work "On Fevers" was a standard medical textbook.</note> felt in his book *On Fevers*, saying that the foundation of natural heat is the **vital spirit** within the arteries; but that accidents <note>The physical symptoms or properties.</note> are founded within a subject. 

This is also confirmed by reason, for the arrangements of the **Categories** <note>Aristotle’s *Categories*, which organized all things into ten classes such as Substance, Quality, and Quantity.</note> are unmixed. The prior cannot pass into the posterior, such that one category cannot transform into another, since they are divided by opposition. Most importantly, an **accident** cannot be a **substance**, as shown in distinctions thirteen and sixteen. Therefore, since innate or natural heat is a quality of the third species <note>A technical classification of qualities in Aristotelian logic.</note>, it is no wonder that the spirit—which is a **corporeal substance** generated in the heart from the refinement of humors or their vapors according to a certain complexion—cannot be the same as heat, which is its quality. 

Furthermore, whatever things relate to each other as **cause** and **effect**, or prior and posterior (like an accident and its subject), are not truly the same. As has been declared, heat relates to the spirit in this way. For it is that which first comes to bodies, whether they are simple and corruptible or incorruptible. Yet this specific heat belongs to this kind of spiritual power in which it is primarily founded. Again, those things are not the same in essence where one acts as the **mover** and the other as the **moved**. In this way, heat relates to the spirit: for innate heat moves the spirit and impels it into external vapors. And the unnatural heat [moves] toward the resolving and destroying of them. Their natures and real properties are different and stand apart. From such things, we are led to the knowledge of hidden things from their effects. These are the natures and properties of heat and spirit as touched upon before, and thus they are distinct.

Thus, from these points, it appears that heat and spirit differ **really** <note>i.e., they are different things in reality, not just different names.</note>, though they are the same in terms of their subject. It also appears that heat is the more immediate instrument of the soul. Perhaps someone will oppose this by citing **Aristotle**, taking the origin from what is said about the medicines of the heart: that the **spirit** is the first appendage of the powers of the soul, and that the secondary emanation into the members of the body occurs through its mediation. To this, it must be said that Aristotle there takes "spirit" to mean that which is qualified and informed by primary heat, which is clear from the attribution of the operations of heat denoted there under the name of "spirit." 

For this is the order of the soul's progression into the limbs, so that it may vivify, govern, and cause the proper operations to arise from them: first, the soul immediately joins its organized matter, giving it its first substantial being (as seen in the second book *On the Soul* and the eighth book of the *Metaphysics*). Then it distributes its powers into the members by seizing them, which is done through formal **complexion** and heat generated from two types of heat. Afterward, this association is received in the spirit. The spirit is moved by the **heart** and moves it in turn; by these two, it effectively moves the **brain** and the **spinal cord** <note>original: "nucha," a term used in medieval anatomy for the spinal cord.</note>, from which motion rises into the **nerves**, from the nerves into the **muscles**, and from the muscles it finally proceeds to the **tendons** and at last to the limb that is moved—such as a finger of the hand or foot. Of the members, some are only movers (like the brain and spinal cord), some are only moved (like the extreme parts), and some are both moved and moving (like the muscles, for they are moved by the brain and then move the extreme parts).

Regarding the fourth point [of the debate], it has already appeared what should be said to the first and second points. By allowing for improper usage in speech, heat (that is, the heat of the body) and spirit are "really" the same, yet they differ in terms of their rational definition. The impropriety of the speech is clear because the name of the concrete thing names the accident rather than the subject. See the Commentator on the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*.

To the other point, it must be said that these do not behave in the same way, but differ very particularly; nor do they have the same end, as was shown by the properties of heat and spirit. To the other [objection], what has been said is sufficient. To the other, it must be said that this would only be true if heat and spirit were different bodies based on thickness and subtlety, as was argued against **Haly** <note>Likely Haly Abbas, the Persian physician.</note>. To the last point, it must be said that the "natural things" are only seven <note>A reference to the "seven naturals" in medieval medicine: elements, complexions, humors, members, virtues, operations, and spirits.</note>; for heat is reduced to the spirit as a composite of heat and the body of vapors. As for the arguments of the opposing side, although they are probable, let them now be dismissed unharmed. However, the corrupt translation of the **monk** <note>Referencing the previous page's note on a translation error by a monastic scholar.</note> deviates from the truth of the other.

### On whether the spirit remains the same throughout life

It now happens to stand around the aforesaid: whether the **spirit** remains numerically the same throughout the whole life of the animal. Since it is posited that the spirit is "innate" and "implanted," it would seem to endure for that reason, and because the spirit is the warmest thing in the body. This is testified regarding fire especially, as its nature stands out. 

But it [the spirit] does not remain the same. Rather, it is soon generated from other matter, and then other matter again, as seen in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption* and the second book of *Meteorology*. Whence in *On Youth and Old Age*: "Fire remains always made and flowing, **like a river** <note>A classic Heraclitean image used by Aristotle to describe constant flux.</note>, but it is hidden because of its velocity." Furthermore, that which is most altered with another thing is on the road to corruption, and a subtle thing does not endure long; but the substance of the spirit is the most subtle and most subject to alteration because it is the finest. 

Again: blood, and even the substance of the flesh (according to the eleventh book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de īgeīo xiade," referring to Galen's *Megatechne* or *De Ingenio Sanitatis*</note>), which seem more likely to endure because they are thicker than spirit, do not remain the same; they are changed in turn. For if that which is greater does not endure, much less does that which is lesser. Also, every passion <note>In the sense of an "undergoing" or change.</note> once completed casts out the substance (from the fourth book of the *Topics*). Such is the nature of the spirit; whence in the eleventh book of *On the Method of Healing*...

It also introduces a new debate on the "flow" of the spirit, arguing that it is not permanent but constantly renewed like a river.</summary>

Its **substance** becomes larger or smaller according to almost every reception. **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–210 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity; his works formed the basis of medieval medicine.</note> shows this further on account of the dissipation of the spirit in *On Safeguarding Health* <note>original: "De Sanitate Tuenda"</note>, chapter 108. Therefore, the **spirit** does not remain **numerically the same** <note>A philosophical term meaning the exact same individual entity, rather than just something of the same type.</note> throughout the whole of a human's life. 

On the contrary: if it did not remain, it would be destroyed; but it cannot be destroyed because everything that dies or is destroyed is ruined by its **contrary** through an unequal imbalance <note>original: "discrasia," a medical term for an imbalance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile).</note>. However, nothing is contrary to the spirit since it is a **substance**. And this is confirmed because everything is destroyed either in itself or by the destruction of its subject, just as knowledge is destroyed by ignorance, and health by the sickness of the animal. This is understood from the causes of the "length and shortness of life." 

But this does not happen, because nothing occurs in the body so cold that it could overcome the immense heat of the spirit mentioned before, since perhaps nothing is actually cold within it. Nor is it destroyed for this reason, since it would rather preserve its own vessel or receptacle; otherwise, it would strive for its own softening and destruction, which no **nature** intends or works toward. 

Furthermore, since there is a double spirit—the **implanted** <note>original: "prolantatus," likely a variant of "plantatus," referring to the innate pneuma fixed in the organs.</note> and the **flowing**—the first indeed lasts as the same continuous thing, as its name shows. For the spirit ought to be a symbol and proportional to the thing: regarding the breather and the breathed. Likewise, the second is active and in motion, and it is what most excites the implanted spirit into action. Thus, the spirit remains **numerically the same** throughout the entire permanence of the animal. 

Regarding the first point, one must know what the spirit is, how often it is spoken of, and that it is similarly numerically the same, as seen previously in chapter 48. From which chapter 56 depends as a consequence. Regarding the second point, one must know that some have wished the spirit to remain numerically the same, since the permanence of the animal is caused by that same thing. Others believe it is changed and altered continuously every hour, or in a shorter time. Some, however, omit this under doubt, as in *On the Cause of the Motion of Animals*: whether it is always the same or always another. It is "another," according to the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*; but what is to be felt about this will be seen in the third and fourth parts of what is to be said. 

Regarding the third point, it must be known that the **innate implanted spirit**, principally in the heart and its other parts, remains continuously one and the same in number. For it is shaped by the more formal and "spermatic" parts <note>In medieval embryology, "spermatic" parts were the solid tissues (nerves, bones, vessels) believed to be formed from the father's seed, which did not change after birth.</note>; although it is altered and transmuted, it remains no less itself. 

The **flowing** or **running** spirit, however, as the name denotes, does not remain always the same. It is made different, and for a not very long time, it is proportioned to the material and bloody particles. How the innate spirit is brought into being with the seed, and from it before the construction of the heart, and how the flowing spirit is generated from the heart by their actions, is seen in chapter 48. 

That the innate spirit remains continuously the same in number is supported by reason. For three bodies around the beginning of our generation complete the substance of the spirit: the **blood**, and the **airy moisture**—from which, according to the principles in the *Book on the Seed*, is the generation of the animal's particles—and the **primary aphorism**. Therefore, the spirit remains then. Likewise, the blood, when it is turned into the spermatic substance of the solid members, as in chapters 36 and 37. And all seed, especially by dissolving and expanding, will assist the heat of the **complexion** <note>The specific balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in an individual.</note> in the construction of the innate spirit. For this spirit is one in number, first in generation; and many things can be generated from it, just as one member is first in generation, namely the **heart**, but many members are generated from it, as in *On the Medicines of the Heart*. 

Furthermore, the **soul** remains one and the same continuously; but this spirit was created as the first appendage of the powers of the soul, and its emanation into the members of the body is achieved through it, namely by the flowing spirit. 

Again, if that in which something is inseparably founded remains, then that thing also remains, as are **matter** and **form**. But the **radical moisture** <note>The vital fluid believed to be the fuel of life; its exhaustion led to old age and death.</note> is restored; or according to the first principles, it remains numerically the same and unrestored. The innate spirit completes and informs it. Likewise, that which holds itself proportionally as a formal and solid part remains numerically the same continuously, as seen in chapter 56. But the spirit is such, as has been touched upon. Whence, after the premises from *On the Cause of the Motion of Animals*, it is added: "For it is the same concerning other parts," that is, there is a similar doubt whether they remain always the same in number or are made into others. 

Furthermore, that which is **nourished** always remains the same in number. For **nutrition** is ordained for the permanence of the animal; but the innate spirit is nourished by the flowing spirit, as in chapter 155. Therefore, the innate implanted spirit remains always the same in number, is nourished, and grows, as shown regarding the formal parts in chapter 56. 

However, that the **running spirit** does not remain the same in number continuously is demonstrated by the opposite. And it is confirmed separately, because that which is like matter is by its nature dissolvable; it is greatly ordered for the aid of another and never stands continuously in its life. Such is the flowing spirit. For it is generated, as was touched upon, from the **vapor of the blood** or its refinement; and this is most especially alterable and corruptible. 

Whence **Heraclitus** and **Cratylus** <note>Presocratic philosophers known for the doctrine of universal flux ("you cannot step into the same river twice").</note>, positing vapor as the principle of all things, said that nothing could be verified because of its sudden change (chapter 3). It is also ordained for the nourishment and excitation of the implanted spirit, and its power is almost brought into act by its virtue; since flowing qualities are more apt than innate ones. Nor is it fixed in moisture and pervasively as in the implanted spirit, but it rests in empty places, which in us are simple, such as in the **heart**, the **arteries**, and to some extent in the **veins**. 

To this, it is proportioned to the blood and to the flesh-like substance, and like material parts that endure the least but flow out continuously. Therefore, the flowing spirit does not remain always the same in number, but it slips away greatly, both by reason of its substance and its complexion. That which remains for a shorter time is the animal spirit, since it is thinner, more dissolvable, and most especially because it is motive and more corrosive. And finally, it is least resolved; therefore, these will be explained by comparison, if anything is natural with the reason of a fatter substance, a lower complexion of heat, and a motion that is not laborious. 

Regarding the fourth point, it should be said—and if it appears at first—that it concludes regarding the running spirit that it remains for a short time; yet not in a total lapse like fire, since it is something mixed with gross fire. To the other point, it should similarly be said: for it alters and suffers as much as possible, nor does anything in its ordered permanence subsist like the un-implanted spirit itself. To the other point, what should be said soon appears: for the **blood** and the flesh-like substance also flow out...

It uses Aristotelian and Galenic principles to argue that the innate spirit must remain numerically the same to preserve the animal's identity and life.</summary>

...regarding the flowing spirit, where it is more clearly defined in the path by which it is ordered toward something else; just as **blood** is ordered toward nourishment and the **spirit**. **Flesh**, however, is not the primary intention of nature, especially since its material—namely blood—is always found prepared in the body. But the **innate spirit** remains the same in number <note>In scholastic philosophy, "numerically the same" means the exact same individual entity over time, rather than just something similar in kind.</note> as a most necessary foundation. Hence, the "flesh-like" substance seen with the blood appears to hold a certain middle ground between these two spirits. And because of this, it subsequently appears directed toward something else. For the "running" spirit suffers from obstacles so greatly that it is not infrequently corrupted. The **innate spirit**, however, is not so, since it is defended by its own vigor and nourishment; it is not, like the other, subtly and shiftily agitated, but rather remains almost quiet and certain. This is also apparent in another way: for the "running" spirit extends itself more broadly when it expands from the center to the circumference and beyond, as is seen in the act of **vision**. Regarding those things that appear in other parts, it must be said that they are more overcome by the "implanted" spirit. 

Nevertheless, it must be said in response to the first point that although nothing is **contrary** <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "contrary" is an opposite that can destroy its partner (like heat and cold). Substances (like "spirit" or "gold") were thought to have no contraries—only their qualities do.</note> to the spirit insofar as it is a substance subsisting through itself, it is nonetheless affected by many passions insofar as it is a substance of such a kind. Indeed, it is through its primary and secondary qualities that it is altered and finally corrupted. But from where does this contrariety arise? This is a question for another discourse, since all of this originates from the substance of the present consideration. 

As a further support, it should be said that the spirit is destroyed by its contrary, such as by extreme cold <note>original: "frostatico," likely referring to an icy or freezing quality.</note>, and especially by "glassy" or "crumbly" <note>original: "vitreo uel mico." In medieval medicine, "glassy phlegm" was a cold, thick humor that could extinguish the vital spirit.</note> states, since the heat of the innate spirit does not exceed a well-tempered limit. Similarly, many other things corrupt the spirit, such as excessive strain and violent movements, as well as those things that dissolve it—especially **pain**. This is introduced by a specific contrariety, and rightly so, for it exists as a most passive substance, particularly susceptible to fluctuations. It is also corrupted when its foundation or support is struck, even if a secondary difference occurs. For the spirit strives to sustain itself within that which affects it with its "pasturing" quality <note>original: "qualitate pabulatiā." Pneuma was often described as "feeding" on certain vapors or blood.</note> and consumption; by its own nature, the innate spirit continually intends and endeavors to preserve itself. To the other point, it must be said that one must proceed from the innate spirit; however, regarding the flowing spirit, its sharpness and the evidence of its perfection are not located within itself, but are ordered by the innate, "implanted" spirit and the **heart**, which serves as a kind of fuel and a certain awakening for it.

## DIFFERENCE LX.

-> Whether all action arises from quality alone. <-

It seems that all action occurs from **quality** alone, because the four defined qualities in the book *On Generation and Corruption* <note>Aristotle's "De Generatione et Corruptione," which discusses how things are born and decay through the mixing of Hot, Cold, Wet, and Dry.</note> are the causes of things; so says the fourth book of the *Meteorology*. If this is true of things that are becoming, it is even more true of things already established. And because simple and natural change arises from these virtues <note>In this context, "virtue" means an inherent power or property.</note> in that same place. Furthermore, a specific cause is assigned to the resolution of medicines for either the upper or lower part, or for both, based solely on the qualities predominating in them. For **White Hellebore**, because it is hot and light, purges the upper parts <note>i.e., it causes vomiting.</note>. **Scammony** <note>A plant resin used as a harsh laxative.</note>, because it lacks both [heavy and light qualities] in equal measure, purges in another way. Hence, **Oribasius** <note>Oribasius (c. 320–403 AD) was a Greek medical compiler and personal physician to the Emperor Julian.</note> says in the fourth book of his *Aphorisms* that because white hellebore is light, it causes vomiting, purges light matters, and seeks the upper parts. **Black Hellebore**, however, is heavier, and the heavier it is, the more it seeks the lower parts; for heavy things always seek the bottom. Again, every action comes from a **contrary**, as stated in *On Generation and Corruption*. But contrariety is properly found in quality, since in quality there is truly the greatest distance between the natures of the **active** and the **passive**. However, the **Commentator** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the 12th-century Islamic philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in the 8th and 10th books of the *Metaphysics* wished that contrariety be found in **position** because of the greatest distance, such as from the center to the circumference. For contraries are those things which, placed under the same genus, are most distant from one another (Difference 72). Moreover, every action of this kind issues through **motion**, or at least begins with it, and to be in motion is the very essence of action (from the *Six Principles*). Since all motion arises from a contrary, it follows that all action arises from quality.
<margin>Opposite</margin>
The **opposite** is shown because, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says, no operation arrives except from a **virtue** (power). And in the same place, he writes that a "secondary action" arises from the matter and from the **specific virtue** or **form**. This is also what **Galen** feels in his books. Likewise, action may come from something other than quality, such as from **substance**. For the Commentator in the 7th and 12th books of the *Metaphysics* says that qualities are the "instruments" of the substantial forms, so that the substance is the principal beginning of the operation. Again, Aristotle argues against certain people in *On the Soul* that **fire** is not the cause of nutrition and growth, but rather the **soul**—though fire may be a contributing cause. Since the soul is a substance, action must proceed from substance. Furthermore, that which gives "being" in a simple sense also gives the action that follows it; but the substance gives being in a simple sense, whereas accidents <note>Non-essential qualities like color or size.</note> are not "beings" but only "of a being" (7th book of the *Metaphysics*). 

Moreover, it seems that action may arise from a certain **occult power** called a **specific form** or **property**. For if every action arose from a quality, then one would always find the nature and property of that quality in the action. But now certain operations are found which can in no way be attributed to the [four] qualities, such as the **attraction of medicines**. For some heavy things purge upwards, like **Lapis Lazuli**, and some light things purge downwards, like the pulp of **Colocynth** <note>Also known as bitter apple, a powerful purgative.</note>. Similarly, in the invention of the "instrument of birds" <note>Possibly a reference to a specialized medical tool or a biological observation.</note>, it was found to be lessened, which does not happen from fire's heat. We also find that a **needle**, having been touched at its tip by a **magnet**, turns toward the Arctic pole. It is also shown in the fourth place that action may arise from **quantity**. For physicians state that some humors and illnesses corrupt and induce death by their **quality**, but others by their **quantity**, as appears in the necessity of evacuation for **athletes**. Pliny <note>Or possibly Paul of Aegina.</note> certainly says that one who is "temperate in his quality" may yet have his veins burst by his "quantity" <note>A reference to "plethora," or an overabundance of blood.</note>, and a temperate liquid is seen to sometimes corrupt its vessel. Again, since everything that is made is determined by its own form, virtue, end, and quantity (4th book of the *Meteorology*), if quantity lacked these, its action would seem to be in vain. But in nature, nothing is found to be idle or in vain (*On the Heavens* and the 3rd book of *On the Soul*). Therefore, not all action is performed by quality, but by substance, property, and quantity alike. Regarding the first point, it must be known that action is that according to which the subject is said to "act" (Difference follows). **Quality**, however, is that according to which we are said to be "of a certain sort" (in the *Categories*), which issues in a threefold way as will appear below.

<summary>This page explores the distinction between the "running" spirit (mobile pneuma) and the "innate" spirit, arguing the latter is the stable foundation of life. It then begins a scholastic debate on whether physical actions are caused solely by the four qualities (heat, cold, etc.) or by a thing's essential substance, quantity, or hidden "specific forms" like magnetism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of physical and spiritual actions. It addresses Difference 71, moving from the specific discussion of the "spirit" into a broader scholastic debate on whether the four qualities (heat, cold, moisture, and dryness) are the sole causes of all natural actions, or if higher "specific forms" are required.</meta>

It must indeed be known that many of the ancients posited that every action occurs through the four qualities of the <term>elements<note>original: "eloꝝ" (elementorum). The four basic components of matter: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note></term> alone, such that they attempted to reduce the nature of even those actions proceeding from hidden "specific forms" to the power of the elements.

The position of <term>Aristotle<note>original: "Au." or "Ax." in this manuscript often refers to Aristotle (Aristoteles).</note></term> also seems to lean this way in Difference 71, which <term>Alexander the Peripatetic<note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (fl. c. 200 AD), a famous commentator on Aristotle who argued that the human soul was a physical byproduct of the body's elemental mixture.</note></term>, the most excellent expounder of Aristotle, strives to defend. He wishes for all forms to be raised up from the mixture of the elements along with their qualities. He relies so heavily on this position that he even wanted the <term>possible intellect<note>The "possible" or "passive" intellect is the capacity of the human mind to receive knowledge and concepts. Medieval scholars debated whether this was an immortal part of the soul or a physical faculty that died with the body.</note></term> to be drawn out from the potentiality of matter through the action of the qualities. And therefore, alone among the other Peripatetics, he posited that this intellect is corrupted <note>meaning it is mortal and perishes with the body</note>, as appears in his own treatise and in the <term>Commentator's<note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), known simply as "The Commentator" in medieval scholasticism.</note></term> work on *The Soul*. In persuasion of this position, he leads us into an admiration for the mixture of the elements. For he says that from simple elements, or from those not undergoing a high degree of mixture, the noble forms capable of worthy actions and virtues can least of all emerge. However, when elements are placed together and altered by one another in a mixture, they receive a higher and nobler degree of mixture; because of their "cooking" and purification, noble forms emerge with marvelous actions, far beyond anything that was tempered in any of the simple elements.

He strives to show this from <term>alchemical species<note>original: "spibus alcibis" likely a corruption of "speciebus alchymiae."</note></term>. For we see that when these have been simple, or not prepared through art and subtle ingenuity—neither cooked nor purified—they have no great effect in the conversion of metals. But when they are prepared and joined together with one another, marvelous actions proceed from them by their excellent transformation, far beyond what exists in simple elements or those poorly prepared.

But this position, even if it seems to have a certain probability at first glance, is nevertheless against the truth and the opinion of Aristotle, especially regarding the possible intellect. This is also shown by reason: for any simple or mixed heat, although it may have different operations in particular, they nevertheless agree in their <term>genus<note>The general category or class to which a thing belongs.</note></term>. For all heat is said to "aggregate things of the same kind and disintegrate things of different kinds," according to the second book of *On Generation and Corruption* and the fourth book of *Meteorologica*. The same is true of cold, dryness, and moisture in their actions. Now, however, we perceive many actions (as will be declared in what follows) which agree with the qualities of the elements neither in genus nor even in species. Because of this, it is not to be granted that every action is produced by quality alone.

Furthermore, it is highly insufficient to direct or inform the qualities of the elements only through the mixture itself and the <term>complexion<note>The specific balance or "temperament" of the four qualities in a body.</note></term>. For in this way, there would be no species or other form except the "complexion," which is entirely false. For then no <term>generation<note>The Aristotelian process of a new substance coming into being.</note></term> would occur, or only an accident would be generated. Again, the virtues predisposing toward generation and the reception of subtle forms would seem to be idle. Moreover, nothing acts beyond its own species and form; because as a thing possesses being, so it acts and operates, according to the *Metaphysics*. Yet we see many actions, especially in mixed bodies, which (as will appear) visibly transcend the natures of the qualities of the elements. Therefore, action proceeds from something other than qualities, as will also be seen in Difference 71. Regarding this, let it first be shown in which action it is most verified that it is accomplished by quality.

---

Secondly, let it be demonstrated how any action whatsoever can, in some way, be said to be accomplished by quality. Regarding the first point, it must be known that action is twofold: for indeed, some is corporeal, and another is incorporeal, as in the *Six Principles*. Now, I understand "corporeal action" to be that which occurs by means of a body with motion and transformation. "Incorporeal" action, however, is that which occurs without these, such as the action of the <term>intelligences<note>The celestial beings or "angels" believed to move the planetary spheres.</note></term> and of God—if it can be called "action," which is more truly called "operation," according to the *Book of Causes*.

Corporeal action, however, turns out to be twofold. One is "non-reciprocal," such that the agent imprints its action upon the patient without any "re-passing" or reaction upon the agent; such is the action of the <term>celestial body<note>The stars and planets.</note></term> upon these lower things. For since the higher and lower things do not agree in matter except <term>equivocally<note>In name only; they do not share the same physical substance.</note></term>, they will not act and suffer from one another in turn, since nature has placed the celestial body as unalterable, perpetual, and incorruptible, exempt from contrarieties, and not susceptible to the impressions of neighboring things.

There is also another "reciprocal" action, such that the agent is acted upon in return by the patient, and they act alternately. Such is the action of these lower things—those that are generated and corrupted—which share in common matter, as discussed in the third book of the *Physics*. Everything that is simultaneously active and passive and moving will be physically mobile. This happens by reason of their shared communication in matter with <term>contrarieties<note>Opposing qualities, like hot and cold, which fight for dominance in a material body.</note></term>; and therefore, in the first book of *On Generation*, it is said that "whiteness does not suffer from a foreign thing" when their matters are different.

Therefore, if it is asked whether all action occurs from quality, it is manifest that this is most verified in "reciprocal" corporeal action. Whence the Commentator says in the eighth book of the *Metaphysics*: "It appears that elements neither suffer nor act except through qualities, and not through substantial forms." For material <term>substantial forms<note>The essential nature of a thing that makes it what it is (e.g., the "human-ness" of a human).</note></term> are neither active nor passive; for qualities are the primary things that are passive and active. Aristotle seems to have felt this in the first book of *On Generation* and the fourth of the *Meteorologica*. Whence, in *On the Cause of the Motion of Animals*, the cause of such motions (namely those in which there are passions altering the imagination and appetite) are heat and cold, which exist naturally from without and from within. Wherefore he seems to feel that even in the apprehensions of the soul, there is some motivating quality that moves the agent to operate toward the "good" or that which desires the good.

Nor can it be said that action proceeds principally from **quantity**, since all action is with motion. Mathematical things, however, are [treated as] immobile, according to the third book of the *Metaphysics*. In immobile things, the principle of motion cannot exist. And therefore it is written there that in mathematics there will be no explanation of the purpose or the "good." For in them, there is neither "worse" nor "better." This is also bolstered by reason: because all contraries are in the same genus. All action is through a contrary. Quality, however, possesses contrariety through itself, which is found neither in substance nor in quantity, as stated in the *Categories*. This is affirmed because like meeting like not only fails to induce action, but not even passion—consider, for instance, "to sense," which is a kind of being-acted-upon, as is shown when two bodies similar to each other touch one another.

Because of this, action primarily proceeds by reason of quality, and not of substance nor of quantity. It should also be known, as appears in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption* and the seventh of the *Metaphysics* by the Commentator, that qualities are twofold: namely, the primary ones, which are heat, cold, dry...

<keywords>Aristotle, Alexander of Aphrodisias, Averroes, four qualities, possible intellect, alchemy, substantial form, reciprocal action, celestial bodies, generation and corruption</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on whether the four elemental qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) are the sole drivers of natural change. It moves from a general discussion of Aristotle’s views to specific examples of "occult" or hidden powers—such as the properties of amber and the digestion of an ostrich—that seem to exceed simple elemental physics. It concludes by attempting to reconcile Aristotle's focus on the elements with later theories of "specific forms" and celestial influences.</meta>

Moreover, the secondary qualities—as is apparent from the books of the *Categories* <note>original: "sbis q̄zuū" refers to Aristotle's *Praedicamenta* or *Categories*.</note>—such as hardness, softness, and the rest, [behave in this way]. There are also the fourth species [of quality], such as whiteness, blackness, sweetness, bitterness, sound, and the like; just as these have their being through the primary qualities, so too do they act through them, since the disposition of a thing in its being is similar to its disposition in its operation. For these secondary and tertiary qualities are reduced to the primary ones because in them the principle of contrariety is primarily preserved, according to the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*.

But if we speak of physical action that is not transformative <note>meaning an action that does not change the basic nature or "form" of the substance</note>, it must be said more properly that not every action comes from these [four] qualities; for it has been shown that besides these, there are either other qualities or a certain manner of possessing qualities. Indeed, we see certain hidden <term>occult<note>In this context, "occult" simply means "hidden from the senses" or "not explained by the four basic qualities," rather than anything supernatural.</note></term> actions which cannot be denied to arise from things other than the sensible, transformative qualities. 

This is apparent, for example, regarding gold taken into the body of an ostrich; it was found to be immediately diminished upon being extracted, which does not happen from fire, as has been observed. We also see that precious stones and medicines possess wonderful and hidden powers which cannot arise from the qualities and natures of the <term>elements<note>original: "etoy" (elementorum). The four basic components: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note></term>, since nothing acts beyond its own species, and every agent introduces into matter an effect proportional to itself. And therefore **Galen** felt rightly in the third book of *Simple Medicines* that these actions cannot be investigated through reasoning derived from the qualities of the elements, but rather through experience, since they proceed from another, higher nature toward the goal—namely, a celestial nature.

For this reason, besides action from a transformative quality, it is necessary to add another, which is called the action of a hidden property, or of a "specific form," or of the "form of the whole." And perhaps **Aristotle's** statement in the *Physics* is verified in these things, at least in that a certain qualitative action or affection and disposition precedes every action of a hidden power. Hence, in the third book of *Simple Medicines*: "Every medicine similar in substance which is of a more vehement quality is more attractive." 

For quality assists that which it does through similarity. Therefore, it attracts for a twofold reason. First, concerning **Wolfsbane** <note>original: "Napellz" (napellus), a highly toxic plant.</note> and other poisons which operate by a hidden power, they act through some transformation in their quality. But the venom of a serpent is said to act there by its very encounter, because it possesses actual heat—since it is animal heat—in excess, which you do not find in inanimate things, since they are only such things in potential.

It is evident, therefore, that by extending the name of "quality" in a certain way, it is verified both in non-transformative physical action and in non-physical action. This is because every action seems to depend on the principal agent through certain means, like instruments, in the manner of "quality-bearing" means. Through these, the First Cause is said to act through the intellect by the mediation of certain species or Ideas—as **Plato** perhaps seems to have held—looking upon which, the Lord produces the species of things. For although He [the First Cause] always remains one and the same, entirely lacking real change, He is nevertheless posited to be differentiated through these ideal species. Through these, even the <term>Intelligences<note>Spiritual beings believed to move the celestial spheres.</note></term> are posited to exercise their action—which is to understand and to move—according to their own manner and measure.

Similarly, one can reduce non-transformative physical action to qualitative action. For the superior bodies [the stars and planets], in which it was said this action resides, act upon these inferior things through the mediation of light and motion. Now, light is categorized under the predicament of Quality. Likewise, motion, considered in terms of the perfection toward which it tends and its limit, differing only by "more or less," will be found in substance, quantity, quality, and place. For there are as many species of motion and change as there are of being—namely, these categories. Or perhaps, for every category of being, there is a way to assign perfection and imperfection within it. But that which is rather on the path toward the aforementioned perfection is in the category of Passion, according to the third book of the *Physics* and the <term>Commentator<note>Averroes, the influential 12th-century philosopher.</note></term> therein. 

<margin>According to these things, it should be known that an action proceeding from something can happen in two ways: either because that thing is like the first principle and foundation of the action itself, in which the principle of contrariety is sustained—and thus even substantial forms are active and passive, though not essentially, according to the Commentator in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*, since in them there is no principle of contrariety.</margin>

This also seems to be Aristotle's meaning in the second book of *On the Soul*, where against certain people he has already posited that the soul—which is the substance of an organized physical body—is the cause of nutrition, and not fire; fire is rather a "concomitant cause," as has been touched upon in a certain way. And in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, he writes that heat and cold soften hard things and make viscous things fragile, yet these do not act according to the logic and form by which this thing is now flesh and that thing is bone. Rather, this is done by the motion that proceeds from the operator—for example, the so-called intellect or the power called "informative" by physicians. 

An action can also proceed from something because it is the first and immediate source from which the action comes, although it may seem to do this more by way of instrument and matter than by the manner of a principal agent sustaining the action, as is evident from the Commentator in the second book of *On the Soul*. Thus, it seems more worthy to attribute the action to the form, which is the soul, than to fire, which is the instrument and matter. Hence, when the decoction <note>The process of "cooking" or breaking down nutrients.</note> of food is performed by the heat that is in the one being fed, the heat is not the primary mover in this matter, but the nutritive soul. For it is the soul that ordains and determines the process toward a single end, and not the fire, according to the second book of *On the Soul*. 

And therefore Aristotle, in the book *On Generation and Corruption*, strives to disprove those who, by removing the source from which the principle of motion comes, see all action as arising only from qualities. Thus, it has been briefly declared how every action may come from a quality and how it may not, and how quality can be understood differently. I testify, however, that Aristotle says every action is completed by quality, at least initially; this is shown by attractive heat being secreted, and attraction being improved by heating—just as **amber** <note>original: "karabe," from Arabic kahrabā.</note>, in seizing straws, indicates its heating by friction. 

Regarding the fourth point, however, it must be said first that Aristotle is speaking of transformative physical action, all of which is completed by quality, as has been declared. To the other point, it must be said that perhaps Aristotle did not yet see this, just as he says something similar regarding **Parmenides** in the first book of the *Physics*. For Aristotle seems to have posited no action in these inferior things unless it proceeded from the powers of the elements. Later philosophers, however, discovered a dependent action besides this one—as has been declared—arising from superior, hidden powers, from the "whole species" or specific form. Or it must be said that every action comes from a quality, either essentially or initially and cooperatively. For the powers...
