<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the origins of natural action, specifically exploring whether the "properties" of things arise from their material composition or their essential substance. It follows a discussion on the primary qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) and moves into the role of quantity and hidden powers in medicine and physics.</meta>

...they help secretly in their action through their qualities, such as touch. For just as it appears more clearly in animals, the first distinction is the **substance** of a thing; then its **power**, in which hidden things reside; and finally its **composition**, so that at last the action here proceeds from the <term>complexion<note>The specific balance of the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines the nature of a body.</note></term>. 

Regarding another point, it must be said that there is a single type of transformative bodily action among these things subject to growth and decay, concerning which there is a discussion in *On Generation and Corruption* <note>original: "de ge. & cor." referring to Aristotle's *De Generatione et Corruptione*</note>. However, there are other actions that arise from a specific **property**. Alternatively, "property" is used equivocally in these cases, if someone were to say that these actions arise from properties just as "quality" was used equivocally in the same context. 

Regarding another point, the same must be said since motion exists in such qualitative action. For in many actions, motion is not found, as in the case of indivisible beings. Regarding those things that undergo alteration, it must first be said that the quality of a thing is a certain **power** (as per the distinction in *Book 7* <note>likely Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, Book VII</note>). Those who consider the matter subtly see that action is reduced from matter and substance to action through quality. In certain actions, qualities alone are altered while the substance remains—and this they call action from quality. In others, however, the substance and the matter are also corrupted. Yet, this is improperly called "action"; for strictly speaking, action proceeds from quality and the <term>form of the species<note>The "substantial form" that makes a thing what it is (e.g., what makes a tree a tree).</note></term>.

Regarding another point, as has already appeared, it must be said how action arises from quality, and how it arises from substance as if from that which sustains and carries the subject of properties, through which something operates first and mediately. From qualities, however, action proceeds more directly and immediately; they may be seen to have a certain **instrumental** character in respect to the substantial forms. 

Regarding another point, it must be said that just as many things arise in a composite from the construction of matter with form—things which were in neither of the components—so it happens in its own way from the application of an <term>accident<note>A non-essential characteristic, like color or size, that "happens" to a substance.</note></term> to a substance. Although substance is the cause of sustenance and the subject for accidents, it is not the immediate cause of the action of a property. 

Regarding another point, this conclusion would hold if one were to totally exclude the "whatness" and the principle from which motion begins from action, as is argued against certain people in *On Generation and Corruption*, Book I. Regarding the other point, it must be conceded as has already appeared. For it is necessary to posit this second necessary primary action if we do not wish to contradict the senses and to reasonably trace effects back to their own specific causes.

Regarding another point, it must be said that no action occurs from **quantity** insofar as it is quantity, separated from sensible qualities. This is because mathematical objects, which concern quantity, are immobile <note>original: "imobilia", meaning they do not change or move on their own</note>, according to the *Metaphysics*. That which does not have such action [is immobile], since it was said that every action exists with motion, as does place; hence in the fourth book of the *Physics*. Mathematical objects also show that they are not in a place. But if they are said to have a place, such as right and left etc., this arises in relation to us, according to the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*, where it is said that "touch" and "place" must be granted to mathematical objects. However, things that do not have a place do not undergo action, because nature operates just as place is; as in the tenth book of the *Ethics* <note>original: "x. pbi." likely referring to the *Ethica Nicomachea* or *Problemata*</note>. 

Hence, if doctors say that certain actions arise from these qualities, and some from quantities, it must be said that this is according to sensible judgment, since according to **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a famous 10th-century Persian physician</note>, medical speculation does not transcend this level. Indeed, he discusses the most diligent subtlety of **fevers** in the second book. For seeing certain people unrestrained by these sensible qualities, they claim these people "sin" <note>in the medical sense of having a pathological excess</note> in quality; others, however, who are milder in the same qualities—as is often the case with blood—they say are destroyed by a **quantitative action**. Yet, to those considering subtly, as has appeared, it is necessary that this action exists from quality. It is helped, however, by quantity to the highest degree, since every agent operates by means of quantity. For the powers of bodies are according to their magnitudes, as the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the "Great Commentator" on Aristotle</note> says in the first book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*. 

Regarding another point, it must be said by way of objection: for from this super-excellent quantity, a bad quality already associated with it emerges, even if it seems imperceptible. And therefore they say that <term>repletion<note>A medical condition of being "over-full," usually with blood or humors (plethora).</note></term> in regard to the vessels does not remain for long without associating with itself repletion in regard to the power. Regarding another point, it must be said that **Avicenna** is speaking of the being of these things subject to growth and decay in which transformative action is placed. Quantity, however, as shown, has no action unless "action" is extended very equivocally and improperly, since it is placed in the same category as contraries.

<margin> ¶ </margin> Again, it is shown that the harm of some disease may occur through the **quantity** of the humors, although it was indicated that there is a difference in the ninth [book?]. As in the first of the **Aphorisms** <note>of Hippocrates</note>: some **athletes**, arriving at the ultimate repletion, perished suddenly, or their vessels were ruptured in them; but immeasurable repletion refers to quantity likewise. Hippocrates <note>original: "y." for Ypocras</note> says: whenever nourishment enters more than nature can handle, this causes sickness. But "more" is a property of **quantity**; wherefore the Commentator [Averroes] says it is manifest that sickness comes through the multitude of nourishment. And he confirms that first, the second repletion bursts the veins, and a flow occurs leading to suffocation; and there occurs suffocation, or **apoplexy**, or **epilepsy**. The cure for this is that relief be given quickly through **bloodletting** <note>original: "minutione"</note>, on account of the quantity. 

Wherefore **Averroes** in the third book of the *Colliget* says: there are two species of blood fever. One occurs on account of the increase of quantity alone. He also says that humors are sometimes extinguished by heat on account of quantity. Likewise in the thirteenth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de igeio." for Galen's *De Ingenio Sanitatis*</note>: in tumors that are against nature according to magnitude, the members cease from that which is according to nature.

Furthermore, if **phlebotomy** <note>bloodletting</note> is appropriate for a certain disease, that disease harms by quantity; for phlebotomy is an evacuation of a multitude of humors, from the books on pharmacy and the fourth book [of the *Method of Healing*]. This same treatment is appropriate for it, as the manifest cure shows. Again, there is the case of providing a tempered humor, such as blood; this can burst the veins (as the discussion on "the handful" shows), not by reason of quality, since it is tempered, but it will work a rupture by **quantity**, just as a great deal of tempered air trapped in the belly [causes pain]. Therefore, some diseases will cause harm by quantity. 

On the contrary: because if any disease harmed by quantity, then since that is a certain action, it would already be performed by quantity itself and not by quality alone, as the distinction showed. Also, every action is with motion, according to the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*. The characteristic of action is to be in motion; but in quantity there is no motion, which mathematical objects (the subtleties of quantity) show; for they are separated from motion and from all sensible qualities. Wherefore in the eleventh book of the *Metaphysics*, the mathematician treats those things which he has made by abstraction, removing all sensible things...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into how things act upon the body. Having previously discussed whether actions arise from "hidden properties" or the primary qualities, the text now shifts to a rigorous definition of "Quantity" versus "Quality" and how these categories relate to the manifest injury of disease.</meta>

One considers, for example, heaviness and lightness, hardness and softness, and also heat and cold and other sensible qualities; yet one leaves aside only quantity and the <term>continuous<note>In Aristotelian physics, a "continuous" thing is something that can be divided infinitely, like a line or a body, as opposed to "discrete" things like numbers.</note></term>. Again, this does not harm that which has the nature of matter, since it acts very little; for matter itself, insofar as it is matter, is passive, as stated in *On Generation and Corruption* <note>original: "prīo de ge. & cor." referring to Aristotle's *De Generatione et Corruptione*, Book I</note>. Therefore, a disease does not act simply through quantity. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known that for diseases to harm and consume the body is to cause sensible damage and finally to destroy it. For the definition of disease itself is a "manifest injury to the operations of the body," as seen in the *Differences of Diseases*, Chapter 72 <note>original: "drā maxie lxxii" likely referring to Galen's *De differentia morborum*</note>. 

**Quantity**, on the other hand, or the "how much," is called one of the ten categories of being. It is that which is divisible into those things which are within it, of which either or both are a "this" or "something" naturally born to be. Quantity exists as a double entity. For one type is **discrete**, such as number and speech; the other is **continuous**, such as a line, a surface, and a body, and with these are place and time. 

Likewise, either of these can be quantity *per se* (by itself) or *per accidens* (by happenstance). Quantity *per se* is according to substance—for example, a line, a surface, and a body—or according to a "passion" or state. This might be a passion of discrete quantity, like number (where we find "much" and "few"), or of continuous quantity (where we find "large" and "small"). Regarding a line, this is "long" and "short"; regarding a surface, "wide" and "narrow"; or regarding a body, "high" and "deep." 

One might also include "heavy" and "light" here, which, if they relate to quantity, do so less directly; for these are numbered among the accidents of quantity in a secondary sense. For "heaviness" and "lightness" are divided by the same distinction as magnitude. In a greater quantity, there is a greater proportion of heaviness, but the opposite is true for the reverse. Quantity *per accidens* is that which has the nature of magnitude because of the thing it adheres to (like a "white" thing or a "musical" thing). For their subjects are certain quantities, just as the motion of the "first mover" <note>The outermost sphere of the heavens in medieval cosmology</note> has the nature of magnitude, from which "how much" and "time" are caused by motion alone. 

Note that "large" and "small," or "much" and "few," when they are taken as essential dispositions in quantities, are called "passions" and accidents of quantity; but when they are considered in relation to one another, they are placed in the category of **Relation**. For Relation happens to quantity and the other categories, as stated by Augustine in the *Categories*, in Book 5 of the *Metaphysics*, and by the <margin>The Commentator</margin><term>Commentator<note>The "Commentator" almost always refers to the 12th-century philosopher Averroes, whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to medieval science.</term></note>.

Furthermore, so that this "quantity" may be investigated more diligently, it should be known that quantity can be understood in two ways: either simply or in a certain respect. If it is "simply," it is either according to a common nature or a more particular one. If common, it is either as an "intentional" concept—concluding that a lower quantity is both a subject and a predicate, which is the concern of the **Logician**—or according to its real existence as a "being," which is what the **Metaphysician** contemplates. For he contemplates "being insofar as it is being" (*Metaphysics*, Book 6). 

If, however, the nature is inspected more particularly but still as a reality—for example, as something that can be multiplied by units—it is **discrete quantity**. Or if it is measurable by a point, like a line or surface, it falls under the consideration of the **Mathematician**, for he busies himself with such quantity. But if the quantity is "moved"—that is, as it is the limit and measure of physical bodies and generally of finished quantities—then it is the business of the **Physicist** (the natural philosopher). 

Regarding the second point, it should be known that a common conclusion has been made, as appears from the arguments of the physicians, that some diseases harm by **quality** and some by **quantity**. This is shown by the fact that if health is to be present, all humors <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> must be determined by a measure of quantity and proportioned by quality. Since the natures of opposites are themselves opposite, let the discourse of the physicians be clear. They introduce that which is then proven not to be obvious, the truth of which will be seen in the following.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that from quantity "simply" and *per se*, no injury of disease—and generally no action—proceeds. Rather, it happens more by way of contrariety or as an aid. The first is shown because "to harm" is a type of "acting." To act is said of that which is done to a subject; but all "acting" or "action" is perfected by a contrary. But in the Categories, nothing is contrary to quantity. 

Furthermore, nothing acts principally and *per se* beyond its own species. For as a thing relates to its being, so it relates to its operation (*Metaphysics*, Book 9). But if a disease were to harm by quantity, it would simply be a qualitative difference. Likewise, that which is "absolute" from the sensible qualities (upon which injury and all action depend) does not harm or act. Quantity is such a thing, since it is prior to quality, and a prior thing can be separated from its posteriors. To quantity there belongs no place, motion, or time, nor touch, and therefore it does not have the nature of an "apparent good" (*Metaphysics*, Book 3), unless perhaps by accident and in relation to us.

Again, whatever belongs to one thing in a species by reason of a higher category belongs also to another; but in the disease of "unhealthiness," some things harm by quality—for example, by heat—even if it seems to involve a smaller amount, as shown in the ethics of simple things and the ethics of old age. This, however, is countered by the "disease of repletion" <note>Repletio: an excess of humors, literally "over-fullness."</note>. This is confirmed because "more" and "less" lead back to the same differences of health. Therefore, quantity "simply" and *per se* does not cause harm.

It is also declared that this happens *per accidens* and as an aid, because a "natural form" requires a proper quantity in matter so that it may exist and operate; thus, in a greater extension, it acts more. This is according to the **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note> in Book 1: "The powers and the body follow the magnitudes which are in them." And for this reason, every acting work must exist in a large quantity. In a smaller quantity, it acts less, so that the most active fire, if received in a very tiny quantity, will not be felt, let alone cause harm. This is also shown by poisons taken in the smallest quantity. For there is a "minimum amount of flesh" to be found which, if divided further, will no longer retain the form of flesh (*Physics*, Book 1). 

Therefore, a disease harms "in a certain way" by quantity, and generally acts through it. For in quantity, the intensity or remission of an action is most clearly manifested. And so, because the physician is a craftsman of what is sensible and evident, he not without merit claimed that some diseases harm—and acts generally are performed—by quantity. 

Regarding these things, it is right to doubt, for we said that nothing is contrary to quantity and that motion is not contained within it; yet generally, everything comes from a contrary into a middle (*Physics*, Book 5), while the same author writes the opposite: that motion exists only in quality, quantity, and place. For in each of these, there is contrariety. It must be said, therefore, that to quantity "simply"...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the nature of movement, change, and physical action. Building on the previous discussion of how diseases affect the body, the author now distinguishes between the roles of Quantity and Quality, drawing heavily on Aristotelian physics and the medical theories of Galen and Avicenna.</meta>

Consider that among the logician, the metaphysician, and the mathematician, nothing stands outside of a <term>genus<note>In scholastic philosophy, a "genus" is a broad category used to classify types of being or things.</note></term>. This is shown because contraries that are placed under the same genus and are at a maximum distance from one another will expel each other from a subject in turn. <margin>Metaphysics, Book 10</margin> Hence, in the <term>Categories<note>original: "predicamētis"; referring to Aristotle’s work *Categories*, which defines the ten ways things can be described (substance, quality, quantity, etc.).</note></term>, when something exists in a susceptible genus, it is possible for a transformation into the other to occur, unless one exists by nature, such as heat in fire. However, this reasoning regarding contraries applies more strictly to **quality**, since all the aforementioned things exist in it more fully than in "where" (place) or in "quantity." For in the category of "where," opposites do not mutually expel each other from a subject; for that which is "up" in the universe can never be "down," or even that from which the <term>Commentator<note>In the Middle Ages, "The Commentator" almost always refers to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the influential Islamic philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note></term>, as if from a prior principle in the 8th and 10th books of the *Metaphysics*, proposed that changeability emanated into other genera. This I do not approve of. The author of the *Six Principles* <note>original: "vi. pricipioy"; a standard medieval logic textbook attributed to Gilbert de la Porrée.</note> confirms this, removing changeability from "place" in the same way that **Aristotle** removes it from quantity. Whatever generates these things tries to say something by way of proof. For perhaps changeability is not woven into them essentially and primarily, but perhaps more by accident—for instance, by reason of a quality such as heaviness or lightness; for one of these leads to the place "down" (like the earth), while the other leads to the place "up." Similarly, in quantity, contrariety exists according to how it is used and generated, but it exists principally in quality. For when some things reach a complete magnitude through growth, they are "perfected"; when they exist around that state, they are "imperfect" and "diminished." Thus, perfection and imperfection regarding quantity occur around the same thing in physical matters; for this reason, contrariety enters into quantity. Hence, just as contrariety exists more in a genus like quality, so too does it have more power to harm or to act universally. For only in quality is there motion. Every quality is sensible. The Commentator says in the 3rd book of the *Metaphysics* that although mathematical things are in a moved thing, they are not themselves moved except by accident. This truth is indicated in the second book of the *Critical Days*. For those things which are in themselves do not do anything, but they follow the foundations which act for the good in some things.

Know that the motion which most fully inheres in a thing is in "where" (place), since it is by heaviness and lightness, which perfect substances more than those things which are moved in quality or quantity. Thus, the Commentator in his work <note>original: "de aīa"; Aristotle’s *De Anima* (On the Soul).</note> *On the Soul* says that "heavy" and "light" exist as substances, though they are more truly qualities <margin>Metaphysics, Book 5</margin> or quantities, as has been touched upon there. For "translation" (local motion) is the movement of perfected things after they have been perfected by generation. For they follow a form that is more than substantial. Hence, heavy and light things have the principle of motion in themselves and can be hindered only slightly from the outside, which does not happen in the same way with things that are capable of growth or alteration. For a "healable" thing comes into health from itself, as when it is not aided by the art of medicine, it is often relieved by its own help, as noted in *On the Heavens and the Earth*, Book 4 <note>original: "ce.&.m.iiiii."; Aristotle’s *De Caelo*.</note>. Thus, motion in "where" is more perfect than others, as it reaches substance more fully and is, as it were, the effect of alteration and somehow of growth and decrease. For in those things which are generated and corrupted, that motion (local motion) emerges prior to the other natural motions. In the universe, however, it is proved in the eighth book of the *Physics* that local motion is the first of motions. Therefore, regarding the fourth point—even if what has already been said appears clear—nevertheless, for the sake of more perfect instruction, let us respond to the arguments of both sides. To the first, it must be said that repletion or an excess of nutriment or a multitude of humors harms 

by suffocating, or by rupturing vessels, or by inducing apoplexy or another sickness from the multitude of humors. This is not strictly due to **quantity** as if it were "how much," but rather according to its natural quality. This happens more because of a quality, for instance, by heat stirring up the excess movement of athletes, or by cold constricting, as if by exercising dominion over them or by being viscous, thick, hard, or soft and such. Hence, it is gathered in the third book of <note>original: "Ga."; Galen, the 2nd-century Greek physician whose works dominated medieval medicine.</note> **Galen**'s *On the Affected Parts* that it is seen that every disease of the parts is caused by qualities; for it is not only by these that one must solve the problem of hardness and softness. This is confirmed because in the discussion of the "repletion of blood," it is added that it harms more by reason of fever and quality than by quantity; since fever is a bad condition that is hot and dry. If **Avicenna** <note>original: "Auẽx."; Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath and author of *The Canon of Medicine*.</note> says that this happens solely because of quantity, it must be said that this occurs according to medicinal appearance, yet quality—being prior to it, as has been touched upon—stirs the matter into that opinion. For a "thick" and "viscous" thing has more of the cause of blockage by reason of quality. And thus, concerning the arguments introduced, that which was said holds.

To the other point, it must be said that <term>bloodletting<note>original: "flōia"; short for phlebotomia.</note></term> does not simply evacuate quantity, but more the natural quality; for when **Aristotle** says that in it the multitude of blood is evacuated, he sometimes means the "malice" (badness) of the blood itself, and sometimes both. To the other argument, although the temperament of the humors seems to be in them, it nevertheless exceeds certain qualities according to their power. Regarding the first of those things which were touched upon earlier, it must be said that injury or action does not happen from quantity *per se*, as was shown, but is said to come from quality alone (Book 9), according to how it happens in a genus. To the other, it must be said that mathematical things are "how much" as absolute things, and those about which mathematics is concerned are separated from motion, time, contact, and act simply, as if seen to be separated from place—which belongs only to natural things—by the mind which abstracts them. Hence the Commentator in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption* says: it is impossible for mathematical things to be abstracted from place as mathematicians abstract them from other accidents; nevertheless, a body is not in a place except through its dimensions, not through other accidents. To the other, it must be said that quantity as quantity does not harm or act insofar as it follows the matter, but rather quality does. For quality is, as it were, the reason by which an action is perfected and its immediate instrument, found primarily by reason of its nature. <margin>st...</margin> Substance, on the other hand, is like the base and the primary and immediate support of the act. Quantity is like a certain helper; for it is through quantity that the active quality is extended. For however large a surface is, so much "white" will you say it is in the *Categories*. Therefore, the whole composite acts, but truly by its quality more fully.

It is shown that **coldness** does not enter into the operation of nature essentially, but by accident; as is seen in the fourth book of the *Meteorology*. For an agent acts either to corrupt or as if by accident. Furthermore, in the sixth book of *Accidents*, I say that the increase of heat is useful if it does not proceed to the extreme so as to dissolve the members and liquefy them; coldness, however, confers no help in action.

<meta>The previous page established that contraries (like heat and cold) within the same category (Quality) expel one another. This page continues that inquiry, specifically looking at the role of Coldness—not as a primary life force, but as an instrument used by the soul to shape the body.</meta>

Coldness <note>original: "fritas," an abbreviation for *frigiditas*</note> does not hold a primary place among the powers that serve our natural appetites, except perhaps as a servant to the generating force. This is shown through reason, because the operations of all <term>powers<note>The "virtues" or "faculties" of the soul, such as the power to digest or the power to grow.</note></term> exist through motion, and here it is heat that brings things to completion. This is why it is said in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals* and in the *Problems* (Section 13) that heat is associated with motion, while cold is associated with <term>permanence<note>original: "pmanſuū" (*permansuum*); suggesting a state of rest or lack of movement.</note></term>.

Indeed, coldness—by causing paralysis and deadening—is the opposite of motion, just as one contrary opposes another. For contraries mutually expel each other from a subject when their underlying logic exists at the maximum distance. This is explained in the *Differences* <note>Referring to a common medieval textbook on logic and natural philosophy.</note>, section 154: it is essential for heat to involve itself in operation because to be hot is to move things.

Furthermore, biological operation proceeds through <term>generation<note>The process of creating or sustaining life.</note></term> as if using the instruments of nature. However, the human <term>complexion<note>The specific balance of the four primary qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) in an individual body.</note></term> leans mostly toward heat and moisture, which are necessary for generation. Therefore, coldness is held in check by heat. It is affirmed that heat in the body is twofold: one is the heat generated within each specific organ <note>original: "mēbri"</note> which serves as the "material" heat, and the other is the heat sent to each organ from the heart. From these two heats, a single heat is produced that acts as the "form" of the organ. These two heats, when increased, do not essentially allow coldness to interfere with the operations of nature. Therefore, coldness does not enter into nature's work essentially, but only by <term>accident<note>In Aristotelian terms, an "accident" is a property that isn't part of the essential nature of a thing (e.g., the color of a shirt is an accident, while being clothing is its essence).</note></term>.

On the other hand, in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, we see that hard, soft, viscous, and brittle parts of animals arise from these qualities. Heat and coldness certainly produce them. Thus, from the food provided, the power of the nutritive soul causes growth, using heat and cold as its instruments. Moreover, it is added that motion arises in these things, and in the things that are created, heat and cold act to create each part—this part becomes soft flesh, and so on. Again, in the fourth book of the *Meteorology*, it is said that heat and cold master the matter, and in the end, parts are formed by these qualities and the motions resulting from them, becoming coagulated. So it is with silver: heat, cold, and motion are all involved.

Likewise, the same is felt regarding natural things. When the seed is submitted to the womb <note>original: "m̄rice" (*matrice*)</note>, nothing is given to the passing time until its particles are constituted by dryness, heat, cold, and moisture. Hence, in the first book of *On the Use of the Parts*, it is said: "The complexion is the operation of any of the members through heat, cold, dryness, and moisture." And in the third book: "The operations of the mouth and stomach are helped and prolonged by a temperate coldness."

Furthermore, reasoning leads to the same conclusion. That which is a natural work enters essentially into nature's operation. Such is the case with coldness. Hence in the fourth book of the *Meteorology*: "Each perfection is determined by natural heat and cold." Again, that which essentially contributes to a thing being created must essentially enter into the work of nature. But coldness essentially contributes to things being created, as is apparent in snow, ice, crystal, many metals, and specifically in glass. Perhaps this also occurs in animal bodies. Therefore, coldness essentially enters into the work of nature.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that coldness is a natural <term>passive quality<note>In medieval physics, heat and cold were "active" qualities, while moisture and dryness were "passive," though here the author is debating the active role of coldness in formation.</note></term> or property inherent to it by birth.

---

Earth and water specifically [possess this]. For each element preserves one quality in the highest degree, from which it acquires another. How many times is it said in the *Differences* that this quality was repressed by actual coldness? This quality enters into another in multiple ways. Either as essential parts (defined by their nature) or as integral parts (like organs making up a body). Or, an accident enters the constitution of a subject... as an instrument. This instrument, if it is bodily and acted upon by a principal mover, will have its entry into the body according to its essence, since it contributes to motion and thus to form and being, as we see in mixed qualities.

Furthermore, "operation," "action," and "making" <note>original: "opatio actio & factio"</note>, though they seem to agree, differ in ways that will appear from their definitions.

<margin>Operation</margin> **Operation** is that in which the "form" of the work vanishes and is destroyed once the doer rests. As noted in the *Book of Definitions*, examples are walking or speaking; these vanish and no trace of them is found after the walker or speaker stops.

<margin>Action</margin> **Action**, however, is the immediate effect of a power. In the *Six Principles*, **Action** is that according to which we are said to act upon a subject. In the fourth book of the *Pantegni* <note>A famous medical encyclopedia by Haly Abbas, translated by Constantine the African.</note>, action is nothing other than a certain movement of power toward that which is being produced. I do not say that action *is* essentially motion; however, action exists along with motion. For it is the property of action to be in motion, and motion is fixed in action. According to Haly Abbas, the motions of individual actions are the agents moving them.

<margin>ART, Prudence</margin> **Making** <note>original: "factio"</note> relates to the things of art, just as action relates to the things of morals. As the third book of *Differences* says: **Art** is the right reasoning of things to be made; **Prudence** is the right reasoning of things to be done.

To the subtle observer, "operation" is closer to these two, although one is often taken for the other. Action requires an external matter to act upon, although action is twofold: of the body and of the soul. Operation also requires something to act upon, whether external (like cutting or burning) or internal (like understanding). For there is a "transient" operation, like burning and cutting, and another "remaining" within the operator, like understanding and willing.

Again, every action is inseparable from motion, as if from its nature and property. But **operation** occurs both with motion and without motion (as in divine things). Hence in the seventh book of the *Ethics*: "Operation is not only of motion, but also of immobility."

<margin>7th [Book of] Ethics</margin> It is shown that operation can exist without motion in the case of <term>retention<note>The body's ability to hold onto nutrients or humors.</note></term>. What "nature" is, is explained in the ninth book. Here it is through the governing and natural power. "Essentially" <note>original: "Eſſentialr̄"</note> takes its name from "essence." Essence or "quiddity" is made of formal parts. Furthermore, it denotes that which indicates the "what-it-is" of a thing, as in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*.

<summary>This page explores the physical and philosophical role of coldness in biological life, arguing that while heat is the primary driver of motion, coldness is an essential "instrument" for the formation and stabilization of the body's parts. It also provides precise scholastic definitions for "operation," "action," and "art."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on the qualities of heat and cold within the body. It specifically addresses whether coldness is an "essential" or merely "accidental" participant in biological functions. The previous page suggested that heat is the primary driver of life's motion, while coldness acts as a stabilizer or servant.</meta>

...it is inherent and is spoken of concerning everything, both in itself, universally, and according to what it carries. To each essential thing, there exists an opposite that emerges accidentally. This is recognized in the notification of contraries. 

It should be noted that a "pre-accident" <note>original: "p̄acēs" (*praeaccidens*); something that happens as a prerequisite accident</note> is found in things that are essentially ordered, and in their opposites, and in both in two ways. First, according to how the primary thing is divided. For example, regarding the benefit of the nerves: some are essential, such as providing sensation and motion; others are "by accident," <note>original: "p̄accñs" (*per accidens*)</note> such as strengthening the flesh and fortifying the body, which are more common here. Or, something might happen not immediately or principally from heat and cold, but accidentally—that is, through something else. In contraries, this also happens in two ways: either against what happens usually and in most cases (as something casual or fortuitous) or against that which is essential, such as coldness entering to make heat act, or heat making things cold.

Regarding this, it should be known that **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician.</note> and **Avicenna** (in the first and sixth books of the *Naturalis*) strive to show that coldness does not have an entry into natural operation or the order of its powers. They suppose that all operations and <term>faculties<note>original: "tuz" (*virtutum*); the biological "powers" or "virtues" of the soul.</note></term> exist through motion. Coldness, however, takes away motion—as seen in paralysis or "mortification" <note>The death of tissue or loss of vitality.</note>—making the subject immobile. 

Therefore, they conclude that the operation of the faculties that serve the natural appetites does not essentially include coldness because coldness removes the motion that falls under the logic of operation. Instead, coldness acts "by accident" by preparing an "inflow"—for example, by thickening a substance to help the spirit or wind expel it. 

However, there is a defect in the intention of this position. Their view of motion perhaps lacks strength. For **Avicenna** elsewhere posits that motion consists not only of heat but also of coldness, and that the parts of animals receive their "coagulation" <note>The process of becoming solid or firm.</note> from both heat and cold and their motions. 

Furthermore, all "slowness," which belongs to coldness, moves things from the circumference to the center by contracting them. By contracting, it gathers things that are of the same kind and things that are different. This is discussed in the *Generation and Corruption* and the fourth book of the *Meteorology*. 

Heat also has a motion, but unlike coldness, it only gathers homogeneous things and expels heterogeneous ones. Similarly, in the primary principles of nature: the veins and each of the other organs operate through a specific proportion derived from the four qualities. 

Thirdly, consider the <term>Matrices<note>original: "matrices"; referring to the womb or uterus.</note></term>. In most women, the womb remains closed for nine months to contain the fetus. This "permanence" and "construction" is perfected by coldness, as noted in the *Problems* (Section 13). 

**Aristotle** <note>original: "Aet"; likely referring to Aristotle.</note>, wanting to prove that the "retentive faculty" uses motion in its operation, did not reason justly. He said: "The retentive faculty operates by moving the transverse fibers <note>original: "uillos trāsuer s̃os" (*villos transversos*)</note> according to the shape of a well-made grip." If local motion is attributed to retention, then attraction and expulsion would also be accidental. I would say this is true when the instrument itself contracts upon that which it will eventually operate on, either for digestion or generation. When the instrument has contracted and the shape of a good "grip" is achieved, the motion of the grip ceases. Correcting himself, he adds: "Those things moved locally and those retained..."—which the name itself implies. Thus, the operation of the retentive faculty emerges without motion, even though he previously supposed every operation is perfected by motion, like touch. 

Indeed, the time of this retention is very long compared to the time it takes to shape the fibers into a good form. If anyone says there is a "commotion of the spirits" <note>The movement of the "vital breaths" or "pneumata" within the body.</note> there, as some have said, it would not be for the purpose of retention. Similarly, in <term>digestion<note>original: "digōne" (*digestione*)</note></term>, there is no local motion except "by generation" and "by accident," as in the mixing of parts. In the fourth book of *Accidents*, it says that in conversion, it is not necessary to be moved by local change, for it is perfected in the cavity and not in the small parts.

Thus, not all motion is from heat in every way. Nor is every operation preceded by motion as its essential outcome, though it may happen as in touch. 

Some "gilders" <note>original: "deauratiū" (*deauratium*); likely a metaphor for those who try to make a weak argument look good.</note> wishing to take up arms in defense of **Avicenna**, said that coldness essentially enters the first proposition of a "mixture" because all things consist of the elements. But they say that regarding "operation," it does not enter essentially, but rather accidentally, by sustaining the fibers, thickening winds and vapors, and preventing their dissolution. 

This is a great ridicule! For those who say this make nature act in vain without a purpose. They accept what leads to the end but cut off the end itself. 

To understand this, it must first be shown that coldness *does* essentially enter into operation, and not only by accident. However, coldness does not remain as "elevated" <note>original: "elata"; dominant or high-intensity.</note> in animals (and especially in us) as heat does. 

First, it should be known that coldness essentially enters natural operation in whatever way it preserves nature. It is clear that if nature is taken generally, coldness enters operation almost equally with heat. This is seen not only in things that are "generable and corruptible" <note>Things on Earth that are born and die.</note> but also in those that are perpetual and incorruptible—namely, the celestial bodies. For **Saturn**, **Venus**, and the **Moon**, along with other fixed stars of the same nature, produce the power of coldness here by their own essence. Whatever the Commentator <note>Averroes, the "Great Commentator" on Aristotle.</note> may say in the third book of the *Heaven and Earth*, all that is multiple and deformed must eventually be reduced to a single, uniform first principle, as noted in the third book of the *Lucidator* <note>The *Lucidator dubitabilium astronomiae* by Peter of Abano.</note>. 

Even in this lower nature, whenever coldness is "remitted" <note>Moderate or weakened.</note>, it essentially obtains entry into its work. This is proven by both authority and reason. **Avicenna** says in the *Generation of Animals*: "Flesh and such things are made proportionally, and with coldness accompanying it, they are dissolved by fire." The rule of the fourth book of the *Meteorology* is that whatever is made by cold is dissolved by heat. This is especially true for things not made by the soul. 

It is false to say coldness doesn't enter operation because it removes motion. Regarding the motion of animals: the causes of motion are heat and coldness, which exist as natural forces from without and within. Every motion requires a stable, immobile beginning, and this "stability" comes from coldness, just as the motion comes from heat. Therefore, motion requires coldness. 

Again, in the generation of fat <note>original: "piguedieʒ" (*pinguedinem*)</note>, it is said that coldness causes the membranes to be generated. Fat is coagulated by coldness. Coldness and heat together are the causes of the generation of the <term>humors<note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note></term>. Similarly, outside the bodies of animals, things are properly formed by coldness, as seen in snow, ice, crystal, and certain metals. Indeed, coldness even helps generate substances within our bodies, as in a bladder. 

Furthermore, reason dictates: everything has its being in the same way it has its...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the role of primary qualities—specifically coldness (frigiditas) and heat (caliditas)—in biological functions and the preservation of health. It builds on the previous discussion of how these qualities interact within a "mixed" body.</meta>

To act, as previously stated, is that which begins to move toward an actual effect. For just as the disposition of a thing exists in its being, truth, and operation, according to the second book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book II</note>. Coldness, however, along with other qualities as shown in chapter 16, exists essentially with the substances of those things to create a mixture; because of this, they also enter essentially into the operation. For in the same way that a subject holds itself, so too does the passion or natural property derived from it. Likewise, unless coldness entered essentially into the operation of the natural constitution, an excess would destroy the composite body. Therefore, it requires coldness, at least for the sake of tempering.

Clearly, health arises directly from the operation of nature, just as it does from the due proportion of the generation and composition of the limbs, both the simple and the official <note>In medieval medicine, "official" members are organs with a specific function, like the heart or liver</note> acting together. Thus, coldness, by extinguishing the quality opposing it—such as a febrile heat—reduces the body to a proper temperament and health. This, however, would not happen unless the [vital] power used it in its act.

If Aristotle <note>Abbreviated as 'A.' in text</note> says that intense coldness does not enter the work of nature, but only weak coldness does: this is of little weight, because even heat only enters essentially into the constitution and operation of the composite when it is weakened and tempered by coldness. For in natural things, it enters the governing assembly of powers, as appeared in the retentive and expulsive powers, which are natural beings. Also on the part of animals, namely the powers that perceive hidden things in the preservative and meditative [faculties]. As far as vital powers are concerned, this is seen in the motion of the lateral parts of the heart itself. For every motion relies on something immobile. This is also clearly seen in the nature of the elements and their form or composition, which depends on the nature of the elements; hence the first of the complexions. The formation perhaps follows the good-mixture <term>eucrasia</term> <note>A state of healthy balance of the four humors</note> of the four elements, or some divine principle from above from the higher spheres. For the formation, because of the first [cause], is not a small thing to exist; it gathers them and retains them in being, not only the homogeneous parts but also the heterogeneous. Heat aggregates homogeneous things but disperses and separates heterogeneous things; hence Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>De Anima</note>. The primary instrument of the nutritive power is natural heat. For heat is apt for moving matter; because of this, coldness follows to make them rest in their created perfections.

This same thing which was said is verified in other natural things. In nature, it is by custom of the goddess <note>A metaphorical reference to Nature as a guiding force</note>, since she is a certain governing force, and also in nature according to the physicians, it is attributed to the primordial principle or foundation. In that place alone, Aristotle denied that coldness had an essential entry into natural operation. However, the contrary is given regarding the retentive and expulsive power. It was also shown that motion is not only from heat but also from cold, and that not every operation is with motion; rather, some are with rest. From these things it is also concluded that Mesue and Isaac the Israelite <note>Famous medieval medical authorities</note>—according to what Haly <note>Haly Abbas</note> imposes on them as an error, as well as the Lebanese and Baliab—do not fall into error by positing that the retentive power works through cold and dryness, and the expulsive through cold and moisture. Because of this, it should be known that in the bodies of animals, and especially in ours, heat is less weakened in the constitution of the work of nature and their operation, because the coldness of our complexion declines toward heat and moisture (Difference 20). And therefore, although I posit that coldness essentially enters the operation of nature, it is more in a weakened state, namely by reducing the heat under a smaller excess.

<column-break/>

<margin>a.</margin> It enters [more] than heat. Hence, Galen in *On Types* says a mixture consists of heat and cold, although heat itself is principally of the intention of nature because through it the motions and operations of nature are made, to which the contrary is repugnant. Nevertheless, coldness exhibits a great help, and this because since it is of the nature of heat only to move upward and draw toward the opposite, if coldness did not impede it, it would hasten to a very long distance; but it impedes it so that it does not allow it to be dispersed quickly. Wherefore Averroes in the third book of the *Colliget*: The members do not act and suffer except with a certain tempered heat from a coldness proportional to it. For it has been shown in natural philosophy that coldness is in the body like an instrument tempering the natural heat. The same is also true of the causes of the length and shortness of life. Heat infused with cold gives generation and the proper natural form. You, however, understand from this that equality and health are more pleasing to heat than to cold. And by the same force, heat is more quiet to heat than cold is. Still, in the third [book] of the *Firsts*, heat is quiet to the powers when tempered by cold, and therefore it can follow the debility and destruction of the operation, the cause being coldness, but not heat unless it is vehemently exceeding. Third, in chapter 13, not following the legislation of the first [book], he says: Retention, as is generally known according to the philosopher, is through dryness with a decline toward coldness. Expulsion is with moisture and coldness. This is supported because that which is more elevated in something, as in a mixture, contributes more to the being and operation of its opposites, such that coldness in relation to heat denotes the impression of form and motion. For this is formal, while coldness is more material, so that heat stands more intense than coldness in the mixture.

Because of this, as to the first point, it must be said that Avicenna <note>Abbreviated as 'Ay.'</note> did not say that coldness always operates accidentally, but that it operates less by itself toward being because it only applies by tempering (Difference 48). Substantially, however, it works toward the corruption of generations (the Commentator <note>Averroes</note> in the same place), but accidentally toward their being. Or that discourse is about cold in general preparing the mixture, while here it is in particular as it is ordered toward animals. To the other point, it must be said that Galen speaks toward the end, not that the operation or coldness provides no help in action, but it is ultimate; however, coldness is remitted more than heat, as was said, and this perhaps he understood, or the help by which a cure is made. And if you read further, Galen immediately adds a discourse saying that in other actions moisture is of no value except in nutrition and augmentation especially; or that was an opinion which I do not approve of in the present. And so says Haly and Aristotle. To the other point, it must be said that it is not true that every operation exists through motion, but some happen more through rest, as in the divisions. Which also appeared in the retentive [power] in act. For not all coldness, as shown, renders one paralytic and deathly. Rather, tempered coldness allows for motion with it, as appeared in many acts. To the other point, it must be said by conceding it to be true that the power enters through their nature and not through the nature of a superior genus, just as in white and black it is inherent to be seen through the nature of color. It must also be said that health does not enter the operation of nature through a nature proper to itself.

<meta>This page continues a scholastic investigation into the physical qualities of the body, specifically transitioning from the nature of heat to the role of cold in the biological process of digestion.</meta>

...which is opposed to cold; for through heat, [the body] is more superior and heavenly, along with its celestial heat and form, as appears from the distinction of the stars' origins. Or it should be said that heat creates a temperate coldness in our bodies, for as the Commentator <note>Averroes, the 12th-century philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> says in the fourth book of the *Meteorology*, it prevents roasting. Regarding the other point, it should be said that when associated with human heat, cold does not exceed it, but rather moderates it; therefore, in us, cold is more moderated than it is in a mixture where there is an excess of heat. And this must be said regarding the other question.

### DISTINCTION 62.

That digestion may be produced by cold is shown from the work of physicians. For when they wish to digest <term>hot foods</term><note>In medieval medicine, foods were classified as hot, cold, moist, or dry; "hot" foods required cooling agents to be processed by the body.</note> and drinks, they provide cold medicines such as <term>oxysaccharum</term><note>A medicinal syrup made of vinegar and sugar.</note>, syrup of roses, violet sugar, and confections of "three-sandalwoods." Furthermore, digestion is a kind of generation, just as putrefaction is a kind of corruption, according to the fourth book of the *Meteorology*. But generation is produced by cold, as can be seen in many things; for instance, a worm is born in the snow, as noted in the fifth book of the *History of Animals*. Again, that which is natural can cause digestion; for cold is of such a nature, as was said before regarding every perfection concerning those things which are determined by natural heat and cold.

Again, that which contributes to being also contributes to operation. For [the quality] is ordered toward that end. But cold contributes to being since it enters into the mixture of qualities, as per the previous distinction. From this mixture, a result finally emerges; therefore, it will contribute to the operation. But digestion is the operation of the digestive power. Furthermore, digestion is called the preparation of matter so that excrement may be more freely expelled by the [natural] power. But cold works on hot matter by inward-turning <note>original: "insirando," likely referring to the thickening or condensing of matter.</note> and by removing the thinness that hinders expulsion; at the very least, it must digest the matter in this way. Hence, Haly <note>Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician.</note> says that what is turned inward and moistened prevents digestion, except in hot and dry "causic" <note>likely "caustic" or "choleric"</note> matters—namely, yellow bile alone. Therefore, cold induces digestion.

To the contrary, the fourth book of the *Meteorology* says that indigestion is caused by cold. Hence Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a Greek commentator on Aristotle.</note> says there: "No digestion is produced by cold; rather, digestion is caused by heat." And the Commentator says: "The work of cold prevents digestion," which is itself operated by natural heat in every way. Therefore, in the first book of the *Prognostics*, it is said that maturation is not completed except through heat. Furthermore, digestion is a completion by the natural and proper heat. Indigestion, however, is an imperfection due to the lack of proper heat, as the distinction says; hence, in *On the Generation of Animals*, the reasoning is: "Digestion is a certain heat." And in the fourth book [of the *Meteorology*]: "All digestion is worked by heat." For this reason, digestion will not be produced by cold. Regarding the first point, it should be known that it is sufficiently clear from the distinction and the premise.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that Aristotle would by himself deny that cold induces digestion, since that is a work of nature. But cold, according to him, does not have a primary role or order in the powers of nature, as stated in the previous distinction. But what should be seen concerning this will be sought later. Regarding the third point, it should be known that under the double distinction of digestion—as either helpful or harmful—cold causes both in a certain way. For it can induce digestion in two ways: either <term>essentially</term><note>original: "per se"</note> or <term>accidentally</term><note>original: "per accidens"</note>.

Accidentally, it contributes to helpful digestion because, by closing the pores of the body on all sides, it drives the internal natural heat inward, gathering and strengthening it, according to that saying of Hippocrates: "The stomachs are naturally hottest in winter and spring," and when this happens, digestion is intensified. It also contributes to harmful digestion in that it cures a <term>material disease</term><note>A disease caused by an excess or corruption of physical matter/humors.</note>; it induces digestion since the cure of the disease must (if nothing hinders it) precede digestion, according to the old saying: "Treat and move things that are digested, not those that are raw." But cold induces the cure; hence the fifth book of the *Aphorisms* says: "Where there is tetanus without a wound in a well-fleshed young man in the middle of summer, the pouring on of much cold water causes a return of heat." This heat then liberates [the patient]. For the cold heats by a certain kind of generation and by hiding [the heat] within, as noted in the eighth book of the *Physics*. Thus, it is shown that cold somehow leads to digestion accidentally in both ways.

<margin>the matter is not</margin>

Essentially, however, I say that cold causes digestion to be sufficiently intense when it is present with other qualities, as in a single generation. For from all the qualities of a mixture, its generation results. Thus, for some digestion to be hot and dry, or moist, it is because those qualities exceed in it; nevertheless, there is no generation in which cold and moisture are not involved. For that which digests must be constituted from the four natures, and that which is digested likewise. Hence, the fourth book of the *Meteorology* says: "The moist itself, by itself, undergoes ripening and is matured without the dry." However, cold contributes very differently to digestion than heat and moisture, since digestion begins and is perfected by heat and then by moisture. Hence Haly says: "Digestive heat is increased and moisture is tempered." 

Therefore, primarily, digestion is that which requires heat and does not require cold—concerning which one should be careful—but it does require moisture. Hence the third discourse, chapter 13, in the inscription says that corruption having digestion occurs through dryness joined with heat; for it is the same as saying through moisture with heat. Or perhaps you would say that he wants dryness to work toward digestion, according to the sixth book of *On Accidents*: "Digestion having tempered moisture and dryness is such as it would be if it were nourishment." Cold also seems to contribute to digestion because it tempers the heat joined to it, which might otherwise be excessively sharp, and it renders it with a quantity of moisture. For it gathers the parts of the limbs and makes them more powerful in retaining heat and invigorating it; as was said before, heat is suitable to the powers when tempered by cold. Thus, digestion is perfected principally by heat, then by moisture, and thirdly by dryness and cold.

This can be shown by the reasons that cold is essentially necessary for the work of nature in a mixture and has its entry as per the predicted distinction. But as for the claim that cold does not cause digestion, this should be understood as meaning it is not the *dominant* quality; for digestion is most powerfully perfected by heat and moisture. Nevertheless, it is considered alongside the other qualities. Thus we say one nature is choleric and another phlegmatic, yet each is composed of the same elements, only in a different manner. As for the second point, that cold procures harmful digestion in hot diseases, this is indicated by the practice of physicians. Thus, in brief, let it be shown how cold stands in relation to digestion, on account of many other things declared in other distinctions.

Regarding the fourth point, it should be said to the first that physicians do not always provide cold things for the sake of digesting the matter, but rather on account of a <term>feverish disharmony</term><note>original: "febrilem discrasiam." A state where the humors are out of balance, typically causing fever.</note>, unless we wish to reduce such disharmony to the digestion of the matter, as happens in fevers, which...

...matter is not the cause. In colics or the cold of fevers, they certainly alter and digest matter by thickening it; and they are not much <note>The text suggests that cold helps digestion by "thickening" or condensing matter so that heat can work on it more effectively.</note> removed from the cold of colic fevers by comparison. ## DISTINCTION 63.

Whether action commonly attributed to the **official members** <term>official members</term><note>In medieval anatomy, "official" members (membra officialia) are organs with a specific function or "office," like the heart, hand, or eye.</note> depends on their composition, as it is innate to official members. First, from the *History of Animals*: Touch occurs in a uniform part <note>original: "omiomera"; tissues like flesh or bone where every piece is the same as the whole.</note>, but certain powers exist in non-uniform parts <note>original: "anomiomera"; complex organs made of different tissues, like a hand or eye.</note>, such as the separation of food in the mouth. Movement in a specific place is by the feet or other proportional parts; hence it is said of the parts: Uniform parts are the types of non-uniform parts. For their works and operations stand out, such as those of the eye, the nose, the whole face, the finger, the hand, and the whole arm. He adds elsewhere: Sense belongs to the uniform parts, but its operation emerges through the non-uniform parts. Also from the *Generation of Animals*: official parts do something by themselves, like the tongue and the hand.

It is also said at the beginning of the *Metaphysics* that the sense of sight occurs through the eyes. Furthermore, in the book *On Sense and the Sensible*: to see is for the eyes, to hear for the ears. And thereafter: I say sight is the action of the eyes, speech of the tongue, and walking of the feet. Moreover, in the *Tegni* <note>A common medieval name for Galen’s "Ars Medica."</note>: and of those things inherent to the official members, such as the effect and the power.

Likewise, in the first book of *On the Rescue of the Healthy* <note>Likely referring to Galen's "De sanitate tuenda."</note>: Action necessarily follows favorable compositions without complaint. And he adds: Form, position, number, and quantity are the causes of all things. All doctors seem to agree on this. Again, the members to which composition is owed are the "official" ones; these are ordered toward movements and operations to be perfected. And if one is destroyed, the thing becomes more equivocal and imperfect than if another were. In that member, the nature of the thing will flourish more than in the rest. For thus it seems to be in the class of things attributed to the constituent members and the official composition. For a severed hand is called a "hand" only equivocally, more so than bone or flesh, as in the fourth book of the *Meteorology* and the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. This would not happen unless the unity of the member was preserved more in the nature of its composition than in its material mixture <term>complexio</term><note>The "complexio" (complexion) refers to the chemical/elemental balance, while "compositio" refers to the anatomical structure.</note>. Likewise, if composition is the cause of actions...

<margin>Note: 9. Metaphysics</margin>

...much more will it be the cause of its own operations. For everything has more power in itself than in another; but operations are made by the composition of the constituents. Because a nerve is a part, but it is long and situated in such a way that its structure perfects its work; and so it is with bone. The digestive power, which is mostly in the flesh of the belly, fulfills its operation by its hollowness and roundness, or such a shape, more than by attraction and expulsion. Again, movement is made by the muscle <note>original: "lacertum"; refers to the upper arm or muscle in general.</note>, which is an official member in all theory. For it is composed of simple flesh, nerve, ligament, membrane, and even cord. If we look at the others, inducing the senses, both external and internal, they will be seen to be exercised through the official members. For such are the internal senses. Again, that action must come from both and not from just one or the other, as in the first book of *On the Soul*: for the whole composite acts, not just one part. Hence it is said that the soul is angry, or that it is the soul that weaves or builds. Also, because it comes from neither primarily: because according to Aristotle, they are in potentiality in the whole; but that which is in potentiality does not act, since every operation is done by an existing act, according to the ninth book of the *Metaphysics*. For that which is in potentiality is non-being. Therefore, it is concluded that the operations of official members are attributed to the composition and not the material mixture, and not to one of these but to both, or neither. The opposite of this often seems to be true. Galen, in his *Book of Places* <note>original: "questibus locorum"; likely referring to "De Locis Affectis."</note>, wishing that the act of a member—no matter how much an official one—be perfected by a single particle of the material mixture existing in it. Hence in the first book *On Disease*: from uniform parts are made the utilities for other parts; the act is not. Wherefore, in the first book *On the Parts of Animals*, actions are made by all uniform parts. Furthermore, that which is prior and simpler holds itself in the manner of a cause; but the opposite is true by way of effect. Such is the composite when it is the cause of a greater composition rather than simplicity... Moreover, the muscle, according to Galen and Aristotle, stands as a constituent member when he treats the anatomy of the constituents, as was sent in the preface; and yet through it, movements and the most immediate operations are perfected. Also, the act emerges from the primary substance of the particle, not from the composition... This implies the nature of being "official." Therefore, the operations of official members are attributed to the material mixture and not the composition. Regarding the first, it must be known what is action, what is effect, and what is operation, and how they agree and differ... Next, it should be known, as appears in the *History of Animals* and the second book *On the Parts of Animals*, that some members are uniform (*omiomera*), which are called homogeneous, constituent, simple, and uncomposed; others are non-uniform (*anomiomera*), or heterogeneous, official, instrumental, or organic, which are composite and secondary. According to the first, and Galen, they are constituent members of which any sensible part you take will share the name and definition of the whole, like bone. For any part of a bone is bone, and it is a hardened white substance produced from the superfluities of the principles of generation. Such things are bone, cartilage, nerve, ligament, cord, membrane, fat, grease, flesh, nails, and hair, if one wishes to extend the name of "member." Official members will be the opposite, of which any sensible part you take is not the same as the whole.

**...will coincide** in name and definition, as the part is greater than, say, the finger. For the hand is not simply a part, but is the "instrument of instruments." This is indeed the reasoning regarding the hand in the third book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle, *De Anima* III.8, where he famously describes the hand as the "tool of tools" because it can grasp other tools.</note>, in the fourth book of *On the Parts of Animals*, and in the first book of *On the Use of the Parts*. Positively, from the aforementioned points, we define the "composite members" <note>Also known as "official members" or organs.</note> as those which are established for the performance of motion and the operations of the soul. These are: the heart, brain, liver, testes, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, lung, windpipe, stomach, intestines, spleen, gall [bladder], kidneys, bladder, hand, feet, neck, chest, back, and thigh, as mentioned in the 38th distinction.

**It must be noted**, however, that some of these are purely similar <note>original: "consimilia"; tissues that are uniform throughout, like bone or fat.</note> which exist as primary and simple, such as bone, cartilage, nerve, ligament, fat, suet, flesh, and the substance of the spleen and kidneys. These are of a simple nature and similar, as is the lung, whose flesh exists without any admixture of other bodies. There are others that are purely official <note>original: "officialia"; organs with a specific function or "office," like the hand.</note>, such as the hand, the foot, the chest, and others which receive a great diversity within themselves. Indeed, these are more composite than the heart, brain, liver, and the like. For in the hand or the large foot, especially concerning the disproportionate temperament, there is a manifold composition. For it is composed of the forearm—namely the two bones, the ulna and the radius <note>original: "adiutorio ulmis duabus seu focilibus"; "focile" was a medieval term for the radius or ulna.</note>—and the part called the hand, which consists of the fingers, the metacarpus <note>original: "pectine"</note>, and the wrist <note>original: "raseta"</note>, all of which are composite. Each of these three is constituted from more "similar" parts, such as bone, cartilage, nerve, ligament, tendon, flesh, fat, vein, membrane, fingers, and nail.

**Certain** parts exist in the middle, between the two extremes mentioned above, and these are also simple. Some of these lean more toward the side of the "official" members, such as the muscle. For the muscle itself is composed by a particular arrangement, whereas the aforementioned official members are universal. In the third book of the *Theory of Medicine*, it is said that an artery is a dual membrane and a woven power. Certain other parts lean more toward the side of the "similar" members, such as the membrane and the skin; then the tendon; finally pure flesh; others are truly in the middle, like a vein filled with hairy threads. It must be considered that although some speak of "simple members," these are nevertheless composed of their own priors—not indeed from things of the same nature as themselves, and therefore in the genus of members they are called "simple" and "primary." For there is a threefold composition in the body: first, regarding the parts and elements and the primary disease; one is that which is called "similar," composed of elements; the second is that which is called "official," composed of the similar parts; the third is that by which the whole body is constituted from these. However, the composition of the first is from the seeds <note>The reproductive "spermatic" matter believed to form the basic tissues.</note>, or rather from foods, and foods from things growing from the earth; these arise from the universal elements, and these [elements] arise from matter <note>original: "yle"; from the Greek 'hyle', meaning primary matter.</note> and quality or form. I have said this so it may be noted that there is no member so uniform that it cannot in some way be called "official" under another reasoning. For all things, insofar as they participate in form, quantity, number, position, and unity, are both similar and, properly according to Averroes, <term>consimilia</term> <note>Similar or homogeneous parts where every piece is the same as the whole (e.g., a piece of bone is still bone).</note>. **...threefold** it consists: namely, one is the primary similarity; the second is the composition of these arising from the alternation of the primary generations; the third is the generation of the whole body arising from the co-alternation and contraction of these generations into a third. Hence, according to Haly <note>Haly Abbas, a famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note>, the generation of any of the composite members is composed of the generation of the similar members from which it is composed. And each composition possesses four natures of "equalization" <note>original: "coequallitatis"; referring to the balanced mixture of qualities.</note>, as will be said in the second and third [sections], so that it may flourish more in the composition. Composition, or equalization, or "plasma" <note>The formative power or the resulting structure.</note>, is a certain disposition or ordination attributed to the official members, arising perhaps from above, from the higher divine principles of generation; this is either an informative [power] or a certain stellar influx. These are distributed into four natures: form, quantity, number, and site or position, each of which is divided into its own types, which is not the subject of the present speculation. Regarding this, it should be known that the speeches of some seem to sound as if the operations of these members are attributed to the "composition" <note>original: "symposio" or "sponi"; likely referring to the structural arrangement.</note>, which perhaps happens to many because they accept common, unexplained expressions. There are others supporting the same by reasoning: that since the soul corresponds to the [animal] power, and organization alone is the composition of the members, this is perfected by composition. Therefore, the power in animals will operate through composition alone. Furthermore, the similar members, to which generation is due, are like matter and are ordered toward the official members as toward the form to which composition is attributed. Act, however, is reduced to form, not to matter. It is concluded, therefore, that the operations of the members are reduced to the "composition." But this position, as it sounds, cannot stand, as the following opinion will marvel. For they dream that the "composition" is a certain nature separate from generation, which is indeed absurd. For the nature of the body is not predicated of these two as a genus is of a species, but rather imports an order of cause and effect. For composition is the position of the things being composed; for their own motion, as will be seen, is sufficient. Although one should speak as the many do, one should judge as the few, as in the *Topics*. For it is not true that organization alone corresponds to the animal power. Indeed, even the "complexion" <note>original: "complexio"; the specific balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note>, since it is the instrument through which the said informative power fashions the body's "plasma." Hence, **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of antiquity.</note>, by diligently observing the official members, teaches in the **Tegni** <note>Galen's 'Ars Medica', a foundational textbook in medieval universities.</note> to recognize them more by their "generation" than by their "composition," since generation is the most powerful cause producing composition. To the other point, it must be said that while similar members are ordered toward official ones like matter toward form, generation is not merely for their composition; this applies not only to the primary similar members but also to those already composed by their power, since it has been shown that composition is manifold. For those parts have the reasoning of matter in every way, and these have the reasoning of form. Regarding the final point, it should be known that the operations of the official members are ascribed not only to the radical and primary "generation" of the similar members, but also and demonstratively to the "composition." For it is like the order and a certain habilitation of the parts so that they may perform their operations freely. Thus also, the action of the similar parts manifests through the organs. ...they attribute these [functions] not to the principal agents and fathers, but rather to the instrumental and secondary ones. In the seventeenth book of the *Prior Analytics* <note>original: "priorum"; likely referring to Aristotle's logical or natural works</note>, this power and the soul itself are discussed alongside their subject. For the soul, being immaterial, if it is to proceed into operations that pass into external matter, must descend into these through many mediators. And therefore, after the soul, its virtue or power follows, which is bound to specific parts as the principal agent; then there were multiple instruments. Some of these were corporeal, such as the spirits <note>term: "spirits" (spiritus) — In medieval medicine, these were subtle vapors that carried life and sensation through the body.</note> and the ultimate material organ; others were incorporeal, such as a "power" which is more immediately coherent to the soul or its virtues. In the fifth [book] of the *Problems*, he also shows that walking is perfected by the muscles and nerves.
