Those who have tension perform the stride with the muscles and nerves, creating a violence in them that facilitates or hinders the action. Furthermore, concerning the best complexion, he speaks specifically about disease, the second [book] of the *Art of Medicine*, the eighth, and in other places: that in a few things, whatever official member it may be, they have one particular quality through which they principally perform their task. Other parts are, as it were, helpful and improving, like the **crystalline lens** in the eye, certain larger muscles in the leg, the flesh in the liver, the "pleat" <note>original: "plex"</note> in the heart; or in the heart, the place where the hollow vein arises. Hence he says specifically regarding talent: the crystalline lens, which necessarily changes color according to external things, must be most lucid and clear so that it may see. This would not be so unless its **complexion** existed in such a state. However, some have erroneously said that there are ventricles in the heart full of spirits, though they do not give the heart its own specific part. This also seems to be the case when he spoke of the complexion of the base of a member and the maker of its form in *On the Use of Parts* and *On Secrets*. In these places, he seems to extol the complexion so that it even provides the soul and the form of the human body. Whence Haly <note>Haly Abbas, a Persian physician.</note> says that in every member there is a fixed power by which it performs its own operation. And the substance has power according to the opinion of Galen: it is the primary "form" of the member, namely its own specific complexion. 

But according to Aristotle, the soul is in the heart, or rather the specific power by which the virtue operates. In the second book of *On Natural Things*, the qualitative "crasi" <note>original: "crasiȝ"; from the Greek "krasis," meaning a mixture or temperament.</note> is felt, and according to the opinion of Hippocrates, all things are perfected. And his own statement: "nature is nothing other than the innate heat that operates in animals." According to the Hippocratic reasoning, which is reinforced here, this is given most fully. Furthermore, Aristotle in the fifth book of *On the Soul* says: "The power of the apprehensible virtues is fatigued by the movement of waking and is destroyed because that which is natural and substantial to them [is worn out]," and these are the official members. This is apparent through his induction regarding each of the particular senses.

...of the same reason and nature. But in the first place, it is such that an operation is not made except by a composite thing; yet it is through one of the parts principally, as if it were that by which the act is done, just as the soul is in the respect of the body. For a human properly understands and operates through the soul. Likewise, although operations are composed of both—namely, **composition** and **complexion**—they are nevertheless primarily ascribed to complexion, since it is the instrument more immediately touching the powers of the soul. Furthermore, every action is made by a quality because of the reason of contrariety <note>In Aristotelian physics, change and action only occur between opposite qualities, like hot acting on cold.</note>; it is said to be almost the only immediate and true difference. But complexion is immediately from the quality of those things. **Composition**, however, is not made of primary or secondary qualities, but mostly of the "last" qualities, as Galen says: the specific qualities and those which follow complexion by necessity, such as flavors, humors, colors, hardness, and softness, and other accidental things by necessity, such as position, magnitude, number, and **shaping** <note>original: "plasmatio".</note>. It is a certain "improper" quality, such as in continuous or discrete quantity, or figure, or position, in which there is no true contrariety, but by accident it is said to be a difference; and therefore it does not lead to action or passion. 

Furthermore, since natural heat is the instrument of nature by which other acts are perfected, to whichever it is more closely allied, it will contribute more to its operations. This is **complexion**, since it qualifies the thing, but not **composition**. 

<margin>Note</margin> 

Again, the accidents of the official members ought to be ascribed to the more principal cause existing in the same genus, and not the secondary. This is complexion, since it is always the cause of the composition itself. For whatever is the cause of the cause is also the cause of the thing caused. For it follows that there is perhaps a certain more divine principle from above, as touched upon before, which is changed through the specific complexion. Likewise, if the complexion in a member is destroyed, even if it is perfectly "organized" (structured), the action is immediately taken away. But it is not so when other parts of the composition are greatly damaged; action can still occur, as seen in **mutilated people** who, using hooks that resemble the form of hands, attempt to exercise the operations of true hands. Whence I also saw a woman lacking hands who could spin with her feet, even though the perfect composition for exercising such an act was lacking. It is proved, therefore, that the acts of the official members fundamentally and primarily consist in the **complexion**. 

From what has been said, it also appears that, secondarily and manifestively, **composition** contributes to the operations of the official members as the ultimate instrument, since it is a certain "enabling" for operations. And therefore, one can see that the more imperfect animals, which require few operations in life, have little "dearticulation" <note>structural complexity or distinct joints</note> in their parts. But those which are more perfect, such as **Man**, who is the most elevated and most composite of all animals, have a more curious dearticulation. This is because, for the many acts necessary for life, the living being requires many organs.

<margin>Note</margin>
Perhaps the first physicians, seeing that **composition** <note>original: "compositio"; the structural arrangement of an organ</note> falls short just as **generation** <note>original: "generatio"; the natural process of growth and formation</note> does, expressed the composition of natural things very little. Regarding the fourth point concerning the first authority, **Avicenna**, it should first be said that he did not deny that the acts of the **official members** <note>term: "official members" (officialia membra) — Organs designed for a specific task, like the hand or the eye.</note> proceed more radically and primarily from **complexion** <note>term: "complexion" (complexio) — The specific mix of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in a tissue.</note>; rather, he intended that they occur necessarily and manifest through composition. However, by virtue of the generation of a single **similar part** <note>term: "similar part" (consimilis) — Tissues that are uniform throughout, like bone, fat, or flesh, as opposed to complex organs.</note>, as it appeared both to him and in the opinion above, the words of **Aristotle** seem to sound as if the operations of the official members proceed from generation. Thus, regarding the inquiry of Aristotle and **Galen**, it should be said that they spoke either as those who, when a fault is thus placed, transgress common figures of speech. For almost all people both speak and begin their sentences saying "the eye sees," "the ear hears," or "the sense of smell perceives," even though these powers belong to the passive distinctions discussed later. For they are located under the sensitive power, which, although the soul designates it as passive, is nonetheless described by an active name because the act is attributed to them. Hence the sensitive power acts in a certain way in that it judges its object to be this or that—such as the sight distinguishing white from black.

Or it should be said that, at least with the same priority regarding generation, concluding that the eyes are the instruments whose action is sight, he immediately corrects the speech by adding that the "primary instrument" of this is the **crystalline lens**. <note>original: "cristallina"; in medieval medicine, this was thought to be the central organ of vision.</note> Regarding another point, it should be said that in the brevity of his *Tegni* <note>A foundational medical text by Galen</note>, he followed the common way of speaking without distinction.

The same should be said for the next point. To another, it should be said that they are called "instruments of the soul" rather than "natural instruments" because the operation of the soul appears more manifest in them. And therefore, in the 33rd *Problem*, he says the head is "most divine" because of the things that exist around us. For the brain is a divine member and the soul is its inhabitant. But as for why the operations of the soul's members are manifested in the official parts and not entirely completed, perhaps Aristotle meant this when he said they exist only to fulfill movements and operations, here denoting "help" rather than "necessity." For it happens as in all other universal acts: for the action of a physical principle is least compared to the heavens, and least of all compared to the Intelligences and God, even if it stands more powerful and prior to the rest. To another point, it should be said that not only is composition destroyed, but rather generation is more actual, since it requires this in the act itself. **Composition** or **organization** seems to remain, at least according to appearance. For nature is supported more in generation than in composition. As for why they are called "instrumental" in a life deprived of its primary state, this happens from a defect of the manifestation of operations which were fulfilled by generation. To another point, it should be said that composition is not the cause of planned operations except in a very remote and cooperative way, like an external occasion; but generation is their essential cause. Composition, however, is the cause of the organs themselves, because the acts belong to the whole and not just the part. To another, it should be said that the **muscle** <note>original: "lacertus"</note>, because it holds the middle ground between similar parts and official parts, can be called both an official and a similar member in different ways. Since middle things are sometimes designated by the names of their extremes, the middle, compared to one extreme, seems to be a different thing from the other. For when it is compared to the head, which is the most powerful official member, it is considered a middle part and is judged as similar. But when compared to the bone or the official power, it is called official. And therefore some physicians place the muscle under the category of similar parts, while others place it under official parts. To another point, it has long been known what should be said: although the act belongs to the composing whole, one of the components is more principal than the other, and is the reason why the act is properly effected, while the rest assists and improves it. To another, it should be said that the parts are not powers in themselves, but in respect to the whole. And therefore the whole acts more principally, as in the case of touch; yet nothing prohibits a part from operating by the vigor of the whole, as is mentioned in the eighth book of the *Physics*: the whole is moved by some of its parts. Hence, assuming that the whole acts more directly, it is doubted whether this is due more to generation or composition.

# DIFFERENCE LXIIII.

Whether sight occurs by **emitting** [rays] and not by **receiving** [them] inward is shown by many authorities.
First, indeed, that of **Plato**, as will be declared from the *Timaeus*. And **Aristotle** in the 33rd *Problem*, saying: With the visual spirit exiting and cooperating, things are seen more when it is expanded, but they are severed from the eye. And in the same place: Sight is more unified when it exits through a small opening, and it is not immediately scattered as when exiting in an expanded way. Furthermore, from the *Meteorology*: A certain passion happens to one seeing weakly, so that he always saw his own **image** <note>original: "idolum"</note> walking before him; this happened because his sight was reflected back to him. For his sight was so weak and thin that it could not push and divide the air. And this, according to **Alexander the Peripatetic**, as Aristotle said elsewhere, was "Antipheron"—which he interprets by saying that because the air is thick, the emitted rays cannot pass through it but are refracted. **Boethius** also in the fifth book of *The Consolation*: Sight, remaining as a whole, beholds by its innate rays.
Physicians also wish to perceive this for the sake of the theory of **intromission**. <note>The theory that sight happens by light entering the eye, rather than rays leaving it.</note> Hence, in the first book of the *Prognostics*: Visible light penetrates from the pupil to the external air, with which it is continued in a subtle, clear moisture. This is denoted in the fourth book of *Accident and Sense*: a visual spirit, abundant and clear, going outside, seems to see and discern near and remote things well. The opposite happens in the opposite case: clear but sparse spirit sees and discerns near things well, but not from afar. Indeed, much and turbid spirit sees from afar, but not from near. This is why the elderly move things further away to see clearly. **Alexander of Aphrodisias**, the physician, in his *Problems*: The visible spirit, being subtle and pure, when going further out, is dissolved and not firmly fixed. **Isaac Judaeus** <note>original: "Ysaac... salamonis"; a famous Jewish physician and philosopher</note> also in his *Universal Dicta*: Visual splendor, when it has exited the eyelids, is extended into the air and apprehends the things to be seen. Fourth, in the *Theology*: This opinion is more manifest to you, that the nature of the seer's spirit is of illuminated fiery air, which, when it reaches the crystalline lens, goes outside and is continued and united to the diurnal illuminated air because of the configuration that exists between both; for each of these is easily changed and altered, and the external air is easily and quickly altered into colors. The spirit also, having exited and being continued and united to the air, is altered into that color into which the air was first altered, and brings that same color back to the eye...

### [Left Column]

It brings about a change, and the **crystalline humor** <note>term: crystalline humor — The lens of the eye. Medieval scholars believed this was the actual organ of sight, rather than the retina.</note> undergoes this change, as it is easily susceptible to alteration. **Augustine** says the same in his book *On Free Will*. Furthermore, reason supports this because color is not an **active quality** <note>In Aristotelian physics, "active" qualities like heat change things, while "passive" qualities like color were thought to require an external force to act upon the sense organ.</note> and cannot, by itself, change a body; therefore, it cannot cause a change in the eye. For this reason, it is necessary for the eye to be changed by the color. It is also established that while other senses receive their objects through a certain motion, sight does so least of all. Furthermore, if vision were perfected by receiving, then the eye would dilate upon diligent inspection, as it would be more fit to receive, as seen in other things. However, the opposite occurs: the eye contracts and narrows when looking intensely.

Again, one who looks into another's pupil sees an **image** <note>original: "ydolū"; from the Greek "eidolon," referring to the reflected miniature image of the observer seen in the pupil.</note> in it, seen and caused by the observer, but it is not imprinted by the one in whose pupil it appears. If, therefore, vision were perfected by receiving, that image would be perceived more strongly in the pupil itself than by anyone else. Likewise, anyone standing opposite a mirror sees themselves as an image rising within it. This seems to happen because of the emission of rays reaching it and being **refracted** <note>term: refraction — the bending of light or rays as they pass from one medium (like air) to another (like water or a mirror).</note> from it, just as solar rays causing a **rainbow** <note>original: "yridē"</note> are refracted by a watery cloud. Furthermore, what is received within is either a substance or an accident. It is certainly not a substance, for then it would be poured into the pupil, destroying it and sight itself. Nor is it an accident, since a subject is not changed by it. For according to **Boethius**, accidents follow the nature of the thing that produces them; the first kind can be changed, the latter least of all. Even if vision occurs by receiving within, this would be, according to **Alhazen** <note>note: "Az." here refers to Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), the most influential medieval authority on optics.</note>, according to the **intentional species** <note>term: intentional species — A philosophical concept describing the "form" or "likeness" of an object traveling through the air to the eye without the physical matter of the object.</note> of the color. Since an intentional form faces no obstacle, sight would occur regardless of the **glaucoma** <note>original: "glauceſīz"; here used generally to refer to a clouding or opacity of the eye.</note> which happens chiefly in the cornea due to excessive dryness and density. It was made porous so that something might emanate from the eye. Again, if it were by receiving, then sight, like other senses, would receive from every part, even from behind itself, which is not the case. Furthermore, the color that is received is that which is "without color," according to the second book of *On the Soul*. But they say the eye is colored in the third or fourth degree.

This very thing is denoted and signaled. For light not rarely descends from the eye and flickers upon the nose, especially when someone has been in the dark. Similarly, one perceives this in the morning upon waking. Furthermore, certain animals emit such rays from their eyes that they suffice to illuminate the medium, such as lions, wolves, cats, and serpents; this is necessary for the hunting they do at night. Again, when a woman who is menstruating looks into a polished mirror, she induces a bloody cloud in it that is difficult to wipe away, according to the second book of *On Sleep and Waking* <note>note: This was a common medieval scientific belief, originating in Aristotle’s "On Dreams," used to prove that the eye exerts an outward influence.</note>. Furthermore, the pupil of one eye is filled and magnified when the other is closed, because the whole **spirit** <note>term: spirit (spiritus) — In medieval medicine, a refined "vapor" that traveled through the nerves to carry out bodily functions.</note> wishing to exit is carried into it. They also say the **basilisk** <note>note: A mythical serpent said to kill with its gaze.</note> kills by sight alone. Likewise, it is said "the sight sees." This seems to imply an action and an emission outward. Receiving would imply a passion or being acted upon. Furthermore, sorcerers instruct that when someone wishes to provoke love or destruction in another, they should look intently with a certain gaze, as if the spirit of love or hate
<margin>Venus <note>The goddess of love; here referring to erotic influence.</note></margin>

### [Right Column]

is directed from the eyes into the other person, as **Alexander** <note>note: Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a commentator on Aristotle.</note> indicates in his preface. From these points, it is concluded that vision is perfected by emission.
<margin>Opposite</margin>
On the other hand, **Alhazen** <note>note: "Az." here refers to Alhazen, who famously refuted the emission theory in favor of intromission (light entering the eye).</note> holds the opposite view regarding sight, as do the rest of the **Peripatetics** <note>term: Peripatetics — Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>. They support this with reasons: according to **Avicenna**, if something were emitted for vision, it would be possible to see in the dark just as in the light, nor would a medium like light be needed, nor the **retina** <note>original: "retibg" / "retiform"; referring to the tunics of the eye.</note>; yet if any of these are destroyed, sight is destroyed. Furthermore, if this exit of rays occurred, then things seen from far and near would be apprehended in the same way, and under the same dimensions and figures. Again, **Algazel** <note>note: Al-Ghazali, an influential Persian philosopher.</note> in his writings *On the Soul* says: many people standing together would see better, and a weak-sighted person would see more perfectly along with them, since they would illuminate the medium. We experience the opposite of all these things. Furthermore, in windy weather, we would see the emitted rays being agitated, and especially we would see them in a triangular or **pyramidal** <note>term: pyramid of vision — The geometric cone of light rays with the object as the base and the eye as the vertex.</note> shape.

Furthermore, since the ray or light which is emitted would be a **body**, it would happen that two bodies would be in the same place, namely the emission and the air. The effect of sight would then be like touch, without an external medium. The base of the emission would be at the eye and the point at the thing seen. For such is the emission of a body, as the pyramidal form of fire denotes, the theory of which the **perspectivists** <note>term: perspectivists — Medieval scientists who studied optics (perspectiva).</note> hand down. It would also destroy the one seeing to emit so much towards the stars. Neither is air emitted, as there is plenty outside; nor fire, for then one could not see in water, which would extinguish it. Nor does fire move except upward, and not to every different location. Therefore, sight happens by receiving within and not by emitting outward. I will remain silent regarding the arguments taken from the books of geometers and perspectivists, such as **Euclid**, **Alhazen**, and others, denoted by the letters of the alphabet, as they are not familiar to those for whom this is written. Primarily, vision is the reception of the "species" of color through the pupil by means of light in the medium; hence, in the fifth book of *On Generation*, vision is the motion of the eye according to the **diaphanous** <note>term: diaphanous — Transparent, like air or water.</note>. One must know what the pupil is, what light and color are, and their counterparts. The **pupil**, then, is the opening of the **uvea** <note>term: uvea — The pigmented middle layer of the eye; here specifically the iris and its central opening.</note> tunic, according to the fourth book of *On Accidents*.

</margin>

The eye, moreover, is the instrument of seeing, watery in nature, round with a certain frontal flatness, located in the uppermost part of the head. It is composed of **seven tunics** and **three humors**, moved by six muscles, and supported by one, two, or three. Both physicians and perspectivists write about the particular composition of the eye. For they say that two nerves proceed from the brain, which are hollow inside, according to the fourth book of *On Accidents*. These cross before exiting the cranium, with the right nerve finally returning to the right and the left to the left, so that there is one carrying path... from the membranes of the **dura mater** and **pia mater** <note>term: dura mater and pia mater — The tough outer and delicate inner membranes surrounding the brain and optic nerves.</note> through which they pass. When they reach the orbit through this crossing, they take the shape of a hemisphere outside the cranium. A thick membrane is separated from the dura mater, which is called the **sclerotica** tunic, located in the hollowed upper hemisphere.

After some membrane of the pia mater is separated from the nerve, it is called the **secundina** <note>term: secundina — Now known as the choroid; the vascular layer of the eye.</note> and is located above the former. And finally, the nerve is led forward into the **crystalline humor**, whose substance is dilated into a membrane, constituting the tunic...

...located above the previous ones is the **retina**. Within its capacity is located the **vitreous humor** <note>original: "humor vitreus"; a clear, gel-like substance that fills the space between the lens and the retina.</note>, which is similar to molten glass. In front of this, the **crystalline** or **glacial humor** is situated. Over this is placed a tunic called the **aranea** <note>original: "tela aranea"; literally "spiderweb." This refers to the lens capsule or the arachnoid membrane, thought to separate the humors.</note> like a web, so that it may distinguish between the primary and secondary, the nourished and its surplus. For the crystalline humor is nourished by the vitreous, and its surplus becomes the **albuginous humor** <note>term: albuginous humor — The aqueous humor, compared by medieval authors to the white of an egg ("albugo").</note>, which stands forth; this indeed arises from the retina, extending through the hemisphere. Behind this is located the albuginous humor, compared to the white of an egg. Next is the tunic called the **uvea** <note>term: uvea — The pigmented layer of the eye, including the iris; named for its resemblance to a grape skin ("uva").</note>, which is colored with a very similar hue and originates from the **secundina** <note>The choroid membrane.</note>, being perforated. Its opening is the **pupil**, so that the act of seeing is not hindered by its own color. For that which receives color must be without color itself, just as that which receives sound must be soundless, according to *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle, *De Anima*, Book 2.</note>. Above this is situated the **cornea**, which is bright and porous, and therefore it was not necessary for it to be perforated to appear clear. In truth, although it is not thin, it is fourfold and originates from the **sclerotica** <note>The tough white outer layer of the eyeball.</note>, so that all the substantial tunics of the eye are only three in total. Next, from the membrane—that is, from the membrane of the cranium—emerges the **conjunctiva** or **consolidativa**, binding the eye and compelling it to stay in its orbit with muscles, of which six are for movement and one, two, or three are for support.

The upper **eyelid** <note>original: "palpebra"</note>, however, is the only one that moves, so that it may regulate and protect the eye in its function. It possesses three muscles: two at the tear ducts for pulling downwards and thus closing the eye, and one higher up near the middle of the eyelid for raising and opening it. But concerning the aforementioned, a doubt arises, because it was said that after the **crossing** <note>term: crossing — The optic chiasm, where the optic nerves intersect.</note> of both nerves, each returns to its own side, right or left, from which it proceeded; however, **Stephanus** <note>Likely Stephanus of Athens, a 6th-7th century medical commentator.</note> translates the opposite in his *Theology* <note>original: "theoỹ" (Greek: theologia)</note>, saying: "These two nerves having been extended to the eyes, that which arose from the left side of the brain goes to the right eye, and that from the right side to the left."

And this is confirmed because when the **meninges** <note>The membranes covering the brain.</note> are punctured on the right side of the head, the left side is paralyzed, and vice versa. This is because the nerves arising from the right side of the head are carried to the left, and so on. For although they are cross-wise, they suffer together in their afflictions.

However, the monk **Stephanus** translated the contrary. And therefore, regarding the former: Someone who is not **Galen** <note>A reference to a pseudo-Galenic text or a disputed attribution.</note> said that they penetrate through the cross-shaped junction without reflecting back. He says "someone who is not Galen" so that it would not be thought that this was his speech, since **Haly Abbas** <note>term: Haly Abbas — ‘Ali ibn al-‘Abbas al-Majusi, a famous Persian physician whose "Complete Book of the Medical Art" was a standard medieval textbook.</note> was a more diligent imitator of him. The prior statement should be given with approval, unless he intended that the nerve does not return to the side where it began. Haly Abbas wished to hear this whenever he closes his eyes, which the sequence of the matter allows. This is confirmed because everything that arises and is received from something is more worthy to extend toward the side from which it directly proceeds, since it receives more perfectly from its perfecter; this can be seen in all things. Thus, the right side relates to the right, and the left to the left. Therefore, the right nerve becomes the left, and the left, having crossed over, finally becomes the right. I respond also to **Cassius** <note>Possibly Cassius Iatrosophista.</note> that it is not that the part opposite to a blow is softened because the position of the nerves tends toward the opposite of where they arose; rather, it is because of a greater and sharper lesion which, from that very impression, passes into the part opposite to the part struck. A wound there is said to be "strict" and cannot be purged like the rest.

The eye is composed of a watery substance... for water is more predominant in it than other elements. For whatever has more potential according to its nature, as in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. This shows that water is receptive and retentive of impressions, which the "perforation" of the eye also indicates. For no other humor is so powerful here as the aqueous, nor is it so airy that the visual power would then be at the extreme edge of the eye, but rather it is further within, which the crystalline humor denotes. That it is not made of fire is because fire is moved too much and dissolves easily, retaining nothing. Yet some posited this, deceived by the sign that when the eye is moved, it seems to shine; the cause of this fallacy will be opened in the discussion of the fourth book. But if **Aristotle** <note>original: "Aỹ."; referring to the philosopher's works on nature.</note> says in Book 31 that it is of fire, it must be said that he was speaking according to another flowing opinion, which happens many times in that book. Or it must be said that as far as the eye's own nature is concerned, it possesses the nature of fire, yet water always predominates in it. For there being five senses: touch and taste (being a kind of touch) belong to earth; the eye to water; hearing to air; and smell to fire.

<margin>Light.</margin>
For it arises from a formal vaporization which is perfected by fire. Light is the act or perfection of the **diaphanous** <note>term: diaphanous — A transparent medium, like air or water, that allows light to pass through.</note> medium insofar as it is diaphanous, according to *On the Soul*, Book 2. It is also that which creates a shadow in an opaque body, as noted in the sixth book of the *Births*. It is a quality which, from its essence, is the perfection of the translucent insofar as it is translucent. **Lumen**, however, is the quality which a
<margin>Lumen</margin>
non-translucent body borrows from a luminous one, and it makes that body translucent in act. It is called *lumen* from *lux* (light) because *lux* is in a body that is luminous by itself, like the sun or fire; *lumen*, however, is that which is received from light in the medium. For it belongs to a body possessing light. A **ray**
<margin>Rays</margin>
is also called a rectilinear *lumen* sent from a luminous point into a diaphanous medium. Whence the ray of *lumen* stands forth and not the other way around, since *lumen* is caused by refraction. **Splendor**,
<margin>Splendor</margin>
however, or "radiosity," is a quality from the refraction of a luminous thing toward some polished surface in the medium, just as when solar rays are refracted by mirrors, especially concave ones.

<margin>Color</margin>
The diaphanous is a small translucent body, not visible by itself, but receptive of light and darkness in turn, such as air and water. Color is the "motive of sight" according to the act of the diaphanous, from *On the Soul*, Book 2. Also, from *On Sense and the Sensate*, it is the "extremity of the perspicuous in a bounded body," as the Commentator <note>Averroes, the primary commentator on Aristotle.</note> says. Color is the ultimate part of the bounded diaphanous; in the sixth book of *Births*, it is a quality which is perfected by light and usually places a body between the source of light and itself, preventing the light's influence. For color is perfected by light, as Aristotle says; hence the saying that "colors exist in the dark only in potential." Some have attributed this to him, but I would say it is true not by reason of color as color, but because it is not seen in act.

Concerning light, there have been many opinions. For some of the most ancient, like **Empedocles**, said it was a body. Whence **Augustine** says in *On Free Will*: "Light holds the first place among bodies." Others wished light to be a corporeal substance in a shining body, received in illumination. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of vision, specifically moving from the anatomy of the eye's layers to the competing philosophical theories on how light and color are perceived by the soul.</meta>

...with a certain evidence or manifestation of color, as if it were a more formal and noble color among colors, which **Avempace** <note>Ibn Bajja (c. 1085–1138), an Andalusian philosopher who wrote on optics and the soul.</note> is said to have perceived. Some others, likely because light does not have a fixed existence in nature but is only intentional or spiritual, have said that light is the "intention" <note>term: intention — in medieval philosophy, this refers to the mental or representational existence of an object, rather than its physical matter.</note> of the form of a luminous body generated spiritually in a transparent medium. However, the truer **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> posit that light or brightness is a real quality. The refutation or approval of these opinions is not the subject of the present inquiry, as I have treated them in the eleventh book of the *Philosophia*. Indeed, "to send out" is said when something is produced from the eye into the medium. Conversely, "to take in" is when something is received from those things that are outside.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that three positions are found. For certain earlier thinkers said that vision is perfected by **extramission** <note>term: extramission — the theory that the eye sends out rays to "touch" objects in order to see them.</note>; others among the ancients by **intromission** <note>term: intromission — the theory that objects send images or "species" into the eye.</note>. Others among the moderns have collected both into one. The first group, while agreeing in general, differed in many particulars. For some of them, such as **Empedocles** <note>A Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher.</note> (whom **Al-Kindi** <note>An influential Arab philosopher and scientist (d. 873 AD).</note> supports in his *On the Diversity of Aspects*), posited that light or a corporeal ray in the form of a pyramid—having its point in the eye and its round base on the thing seen—is directed through the medium, and in this way vision is perfected. They held that these rays emerge from the tunics of the eye just as light passes through a thin membrane. 

Certain others, like **Timaeus** <note>A character in Plato's dialogues representing Pythagorean views.</note>, noting that such a great body would quickly dissolve if it were a corporeal emission from the stars of the eyes, wished for a "gentle fire" related to us to go out into the medium. There, adhering to the light of the exterior air, it would spread out so as to reach the object in a pyramidal form, for the sight would otherwise be too weak on its own. Because of this, he said that things are not seen in the darkness. For the light of the eyes is extinguished in the dark, wherefore it needs to be helped by external light. It is helped in such a way that, having received the "species" <note>term: species — a likeness, image, or "form" of an object that travels through the air.</note> of the color, it is struck back to the eyes by a certain return, and thus the act which is called sight is perfected.

Others, such as **Euclid** <note>The famous Greek mathematician; his "Optics" treated vision as a matter of geometry.</note> with his companions in perspective, posited only lines exiting from the eye and constituting triangles. The "catheti" <note>term: catheti — perpendicular lines in a right-angled triangle.</note> represent the quantity of the thing seen; the **hypotenuse** <note>original: "ypotheiia"; the slanted side of the triangle.</note> of the rays or the line touches the upper part of the visible thing; the base ray or line touches the inferior part. The diameter is mobile over the parts of the thing seen, where more certain vision occurs in the mobile diameter (as in an arrow). In the hypotenuse and the base, vision is weakened because it comes from the body of the eye to the base at the edges of the view. 

The second group, saying that vision is perfected by internal reception, are also divided. For some, like **Democritus**, and indeed **Aristotle**, said that the eye is of a watery nature and that vision exists as a certain "receptive opening." He did not speak without reason. For he estimated that the visible form would be a certain discourse of the visible thing to the eyes, so that something material would be involved...

---

...from the thing seen and come to the eyes; and yet nothing of the divine thing itself is lost, since the image lacks all thickness. He also wished for vision to be perfected from the painting of a "species" image running from the object into the cornea, which is wiped clean and polished like a mirror in water. He sensed this to be the case for sight when he said the eye is an **animated mirror**. This motion occurs because no notice of a thing is made except through something of it. Sight is the "noticing" of that which brings something to the viewer. A third group, wishing to hold the middle ground, said that vision occurs through both the emission of something outward and the reception of species inward; but what must be said of these third and fourth views is sought hereafter. 

Regarding the third point, it should be known that it was the opinion of **Aristotle** and other Peripatetics that color multiplies its species intentionally or spiritually in a medium affected by light—such as air or water—and this medium carries the received species to the eye. For the air, having first received the light, receives the species of things, and then gives them back to the external net <note>Refers to the surface of the eye or cornea.</note> such as the cornea; and this gives them back until their motion reaches the final "net" <note>The retina.</note>. In the middle of these nets of humors exists the **crystalline** <note>original: "grandinosus"; literally "hail-like," referring to the crystalline lens.</note>, which grasps and judges the species of color, because it holds a middle nature between air and water. For its nature is common to these two natures. From here, through the **optic nerves**, the species is carried as far as the [brain], where it is rendered more spiritual. 

For forms have three or four orders of their degrees: one of which is material (which they maintain in nature); another in the **common sense** <note>term: common sense — the faculty that binds different sensory inputs (sight, sound, etc.) into one perception.</note> which is more spiritual; a third is even more spiritual, made in the **estimative virtue**; and finally it becomes more spiritual still until it is led into the **intellect**, where it is super-spiritual and universal. For it is the intellect that renders particular things into universals. 

It should be known that in seeing we use certain "intentional lines," whereof **Averroes** speaks in the third book of the *Colliget* <note>A medical encyclopedia by the philosopher Averroes (Ibn Rushd).</note> and in *On the Sense and the Sensible*. The discovery of these lines does not have an intention according to the sense, but according to the intellect; as if they are understood to exit from the eye. To see perfectly, and what happens from it, is not perfected except through the intention of these lines and pyramids in ever-new figures. Yet they have no subject except the transparent medium. For the medium has it from its own nature to receive light, and it has the reception of color. 

That vision happens by receiving [images] inward is proved in two ways, directly and by consequence: first, by inferring that to receive inside is a "passion" <note>term: passion — in the philosophical sense, an "undergoing" or being acted upon.</note>. To send out, conversely, is to act. To sense and to understand are held to be [passions] in *On the Soul*. The visual virtue is passive, since it is subject to the sensitive faculty, which is generally passive.

<margin>Species or Form</margin>

Furthermore, since color is affected by light, which is active, if vision were perfected by extramission, the visual virtue would then be active; and thus it would be both "act" and "potency" with respect to the same thing. For in vision, one would be active and the other passive, but both would be more active; yet it is written in the third book of *On the Soul* that in every nature there is something which is as matter and potency, and another as form and act.

Others also conclude that sight is perfected in receiving and not by sending anything out from itself. From the general [consensus] of these in proving that vision happens through some...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding how we see. Having introduced the theories of extramission (rays going out) and intromission (images coming in), the author now systematically dismantles the idea that the eye sends out a physical or accidental substance to "touch" distant objects like stars.</meta>

...by the sending out of something, because that which is emitted will either be a corporeal substance or an **accident** <note>term: accident — in Aristotelian philosophy, a quality or property (like color or heat) that cannot exist on its own but must belong to a "substance" like an object or person.</note>. It is not as if that substance is somehow composed of both the viewer and the thing seen, or is separated from both.

This can happen in four ways:
1. It is joined with the vision and the viewer.
2. It is separated from the viewer but joined to the thing seen.
3. It is joined with one part of the thing seen and not with another.
4. In whatever way its disposition is with the viewer, it is separated from both the vision and the viewer.

The **first** cannot be the case. Since we can open, close, and reopen our eyes at will almost infinitely many times a day while looking at the stars, if the eye were as large as the celestial sphere <note>The author argues that if our eyes "sent out" a physical substance to reach the stars, the volume of that substance would have to be as vast as the universe itself every time we blinked.</note>, it would have to be animated and then dissolved. Nor can you say that when the eye is closed, that which was emitted from it returns back into it, since it is impossible for such a reduction to occur. Furthermore, an object would always appear in the same shape and size no matter the distance, just as it appears from up close. 

Additionally, according to **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a prominent Andalusian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note>, it would result in vision taking place over a duration of time, specifically when the object seen is remote; for it is proven in the sixth book of the *Physics* that a body must move through time. Although **Aristotle** <note>original: "A.d." (Aristoteles de...)</note> does not seem to emphasize this reason, perhaps **Avicenna** <note>original: "au." (Avicenna)</note>, who posits that vision occurs by receiving images internally, reasons against **Averroes** regarding the linear ray, not knowing that this argument against them is frivolous. For the followers of **Avicenna** can claim that the ray moves in time, but the duration is so brief as to be instantaneous, even when the ray travels to the fixed stars. Indeed, they wish for "looking" and illumination to happen in an imperceptible amount of time; thus, astronomers prove that the Earth has no significant size when compared to the furthest celestial spheres.

And if it truly possessed physical size, that would go against **Avicenna**, who says in the third book of *On the Soul* that it exits by reason... and that the illumination occurring over time in such a vast space (from East to West) is hidden from us. In a small space, it could perhaps remain hidden.

Furthermore, the visual power exists within heat—for no body serves as their substance except natural heat—which, if it were separated from the eye while traveling toward the thing seen, would cool down immediately and its action would be annihilated. It cannot be said that the thing exiting the eye is separated from the viewer and joined to the thing seen (such as the stars) when no continuous connection exists between the thing seen and the viewer. If that were so, it would be as if one said someone could touch something with a severed hand, or like the tail of a serpent which still moves after being cut off.

Similarly, the **third** path is destroyed: namely, that the ray is continuous with one part of the thing seen and not another. If this were true, one would not see the whole object, but only that part which was "struck" or touched. And even if the nature of the medium did not change into the nature of the outgoing ray to become one... for then, when we looked at the heaven, we would have to say the heaven itself is transformed into the nature of the outgoing ray so that it becomes "sentient" with it. It would have to become a single thing so that it strikes or touches the star of Saturn or Jupiter and sees it in its entirety, the falsity of which is obvious.

The **fourth** possibility also cannot be posited—that the thing exiting has no connection to the viewer or the thing seen—because no action can occur when nothing is connected, according to **Avicenna** and the **Commentator** <note>Averroes is frequently called "The Commentator" in medieval texts for his work on Aristotle.</note>. Otherwise, how would the form of the thing seen be carried to the eye, or what would facilitate the union with it? Therefore, that which is emitted from the eye cannot be a body. 

Now, it also cannot be an **accident** existing in that which is between the viewer and the visible object, such as the air. If something is emitted from the eye into the air, it would be either a medium or an instrument. If it is an instrument, it is either "sensing" or "returning" [information]. It cannot be sensing, such that the air "feels" the stars and then returns to the sight what it felt. Furthermore, the air does not touch everything seen, such as the fixed stars. Again, it would require light to be a body dispersed in the air and the heavens, united with our visual organs. It is absurd to say that the heavens are "acted upon" by our sight so that the air becomes their sensitive instrument. 

**Averroes** charges **Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician and philosopher (c. 129–216 AD).</note> with this great crime. **Galen** is so committed to this error that he claimed the air itself becomes sentient. His speech in his first book seems to sound almost like this; for he says he showed in his book *On Vision* that the bright air, with which visible light is continuous, stands in the place of a "natural instrument," because its power is similar to the power of the nerves in the body. But if the air were a "returning" or "carrying" instrument, then the entire air would frequently receive sensory power from us and many times lose it—and not just here, but the entire heaven. Thus, the nature of the heavens would be transformed by a great change every time a sensing being turned their gaze toward them, which is absurd. 

It is not as a medium that is first "acted upon" by the sight and afterwards perfected to become a medium. For what power would it receive from the sight? Not something that illuminates it, since the medium is already simple. It does not "sense" it, for that was disproven before. It does not acquire any property from the eye, since the sun is more effective in this regard. Not light, because light is the medium by which (it is said) vision is perfected. Nor heat <margin>soul</margin> or cold; for if there were heat in the medium while it was cold, there would be no vision, or if there were cold while heat remained. Nor can it be anything "unnamed," because whatever happens to be known can be signified.

According to **Averroes**, an accident cannot be emitted because the substance of the soul is substance only. The soul is not placed in that light, but remains within the eye; it could not comprehend sensible things since it would not "touch" them, and all action and passion <note>term: action and passion — the basic relationship where one thing acts and another is acted upon.</note> occurs through contact. Furthermore, light is not in the eye by the eye's own nature, but enters it from the outside; if it were part of its nature, we would see in the dark. This is why those who close and open their eyes repeatedly do not see clearly until after the eye has been illuminated. These thinkers were deceived because they mistook the "spirit" through which vision occurs (which is compatible with light) for light itself, believing light to be a body.

Many were also deceived by optical illusions. Of these, the greatest mentioned by **Aristotle** <note>original: "A. maxima"</note> is that when one eye is pressed, one thing appears as two. Regarding the discourse that every action occurs through physical "striking" or contact, **Aristotle** does not seem to entirely agree. He says it is not self-evident or entirely manifest that every active body must "strike" the one being acted upon, even though this is found to be true in most bodies through induction. It is not necessary that every action and passion occurs through striking and contact. For it is possible for the actions of some things to happen without striking; thus it is possible for a non-body to act upon another body without striking, as if untouched.

Therefore, if some bodies act by touching others, while others do not, no one can prove this to be impossible; that despite the distance and position between two bodies, one can operate upon another without striking. Because, however, operating through contact in physical things...

<meta>This page continues the systematic scholastic investigation into the physics of sight. After dismissing the idea that the eye "shoots out" rays like a physical substance, the author now refutes older theories from Plato and Empedocles while attempting to harmonize Aristotle's philosophical certainty with the practical observations of medical authorities like Galen.</meta>

It follows that a sense of wonder arises as to how vision occurs through contact. For if it were reported that an action could happen without contact, the opposite reaction—total amazement—would arise. This is the very reasoning that emboldens necromancers <note>Historical practitioners of "black magic" who claimed to influence objects or people from a distance without physical touch.</note> and sorcerers, although the earlier opinion of **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay." (Aristoteles)</note> is the truer one. For he wishes to show that nothing acts unless it is close to what it acts upon; hence, in his book *On Generation and Corruption*, he states that it is impossible for an animal to move something without touching it.

Furthermore, according to **Al-Ghazali** <note>original: "Algazelē"; an influential 11th-century Persian philosopher and theologian.</note>, if that which is emitted from the eye were an **accident** <note>term: accident — a philosophical term for a property (like color or warmth) that cannot exist on its own without a physical body.</note>, it would be impossible for it to move, since nothing is moved unless it is a physical body. This is the reasoning of **Aristotle** and others, summarized from their lengthy treatises. From all these points, let it be concluded that vision occurs by receiving something, not by sending something out. For if it occurred by receiving physical matter—as **Democritus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who proposed that physical films or "atoms" shed from objects and flew into the eye.</note> believed—then different bodies would be consumed by the flow coming from them, which is not the case. Moreover, the instrument of vision would be damaged by the continuous diffusion of this reception. Or, a thing would only be seen in its entirety according to the size that the pupil was able to receive. His reasoning in the book *On the Soul* also removes and corrects these errors.

The position of the moderns, which is composed of two conflicting ideas, is attacked just like the previous ones. For they agree with the idea of "extramission" <note>term: extramission — the theory that the eye sends out rays or "visual spirits" to touch objects.</note>, similar to the view of **Plato**, who claimed that a spirit is sent out and then reflected back again to the eye. This is not so much a "modern" opinion as it is insanity. For the sake of brevity, it is enough that these opinions are generally destroyed in this manner.

Regarding the fourth point, it must first be said that it was the opinion of **Plato** and **Empedocles** that vision occurs by sending something out; **Aristotle** attacks them in his book *On the Sense and the Sensible*. As for **Empedocles**, how could vision extend all the way to the stars if it is a physical body being emitted from the eyes? This is as impossible as what was mentioned before. Regarding **Plato**, it would have been better to say at the start that the air is already joined to the light of the eye, thus sparing them the labor of imagining something being carried out into the space of the air. Nor is there a way to explain how light is "joined" to light, for joining or separating is properly for physical bodies, and not for a quality such as light. Furthermore, light would join to anything it met, even if it were not of the same nature. Additionally, the eye would then fall between two lights, preventing them from coupling. Nor is his claim valid that light is extinguished by the darkness of night, and thus vision does not occur. Light is not extinguished by heat, nor by cold, nor by dryness or moisture, because vision occurs in these conditions as long as they are illuminated.

To the other points, it must be said with **Aristotle** and **Alexander** <note>Probably Alexander of Aphrodisias, a major commentator on Aristotle.</note> that he speaks according to the aforementioned opinion while he has not yet disproven it. This is indicated by the order of the books on nature and his method, which was to entertain other opinions before they were disproven. Or, it must be said regarding the second point that the **image** <note>term: idolum — a technical term for the visual "species" or reflection of an object.</note> does not exist in its own right in the external air, but rather in the moisture of the **albuginous humor** <note>The watery fluid (aqueous humor) in the front of the eye, described here as "egg-white-like."</note> which is proportional to the external medium, and which the **crystalline lens** <note>The "crystalline" was considered by medieval scholars to be the primary organ of sight where the image is actually perceived.</note> irradiates. This is apparent in the images seen by those suffering from "frenzy," melancholy, or fevers; the things they think they see outside are actually coming from within their own eyes, as **Galen** says in his *Prognostics*. To the other arguments brought forward, it must be said that those who held that opinion agreed with it because the idea that vision occurs by sending something out seemed more "probable" at first glance, and the cause of the various afflictions of the eye is more easily assigned this way.

<margin>The image in the mirror</margin>

Therefore, the physician, being practical, adopts this opinion. However, vision occurring by receiving inward is the "truer" and more "hidden" explanation. Thus, the relationship is this: **Aristotle's** view and the medical view differ because the former is intellectually certain, while the latter is called "probable science." The same is true for the opinion regarding the unity of form and its degrees. To the other reason, it must be said that color is an "active quality," as is known from other sciences. Some have wished to claim a certain common movement of the sensible object; or if not that, it would at least be rendered by the power of the illuminated medium, so it is said that color is the "mover" of sight through the act of light. For if a visible object touched the eye directly, no vision would occur. Indeed, a twofold medium must intervene: one active, which is the light acting upon colors to make them visible in a spiritual <note>In this context, "spiritual" means "non-material" or "informational," referring to how an image can exist in the air without being a physical object.</note> way; the other **diaphanous** <note>term: diaphanous — transparent, like air, water, or glass.</note>, acting as the carrier. This does not proceed from the eye, because the eye never finds a passive power to act upon its own active form; rather, light perfects the transparency of the medium. Nor does this happen through physical movement, but rather through a "change" <note>The author distinguishes between local motion (moving from A to B) and "instantaneous" change in the medium.</note>.

To the other point, it must be said that the eye does not contract in sharp vision because light is being "squeezed out" of it, but rather so that the visual power may be united with the **spirit** <note>term: spiritus — the "visual spirit" or pneuma, a subtle vapor believed to flow through the nerves to facilitate sensation.</note> around the crystalline lens, by which the sight is strengthened. For every power is more vigorous when united than when diffused and multiplied. From this strengthening, the pupil is rendered more fit for receiving. Hence, those wishing to see more sharply shade their eyes with their hands; and thus small, deep-set eyes are praised as being more piercing. This is also why the **Tartars** <note>A reference to the people of Central Asia/Mongolia, often cited in medieval texts for their legendary long-distance eyesight.</note> excel at this. The visual spirit is fortified—specifically the "thick" spirit—by movement and constriction, so that it sees further. Among those who say the pupil carries the forms of seeing, it is also said that the movement of the crystalline lens is strong when it sees something far away. This is because the thick spirit dwelling within is refined, and the visual spirit is resolved.

To the other point, it must be said that what is seen is the **species** <note>term: species — the "form" or "likeness" of an object that travels through the air to the eye without the object's physical matter.</note> of the color carried through the medium to the crystalline lens. However, the **image** <note>original: "ydolū"</note> in the cornea of the person looking is not something received by the visual power as a "visible thing," but rather because the eye is a small, polished body acting like a mirror. This is what **Democritus** meant, though it is more of an "intentional" change of the medium and the organ—causing it spiritually or intentionally, not really or materially. For the image does not "remain" in the mirror, but is continuously produced by the movement of the onlooker; as one image is corrupted, another is formed. Nor is it necessary for "spiritual rays" to be emitted from a luminous body to a mirror, just as they are sent into a rainbow far from the sun. Even a weak light in the medium is enough to represent an image in a mirror. To the other point, it must be said that it is an intentional and internal accident...

The eye receives what we call the **species** <note>In medieval science, a "species" is not a biological category but a "likeness" or "form" of an object that travels through the air to the senses.</note> of color, which is able to multiply itself through the medium of the air until it meets the **crystalline lens** <note>The lens of the eye, which medieval scholars believed was the primary organ of sight.</note> as was declared previously. Although a thing's nature does not change its location, it can nonetheless multiply its likeness into the medium, just as the heat from a fire is sent into the air, successively altering it. To the next point, it must be said that as it appeared that the species of color is received in the illuminated air, the eye—by the illumination of the medium—receives that species through the medium of the air, provided the **cornea** <note>The transparent front part of the eye.</note> is porous and transparent. This would not happen if the cornea were dry, intemperate, or thickened. 

To the next point, it must be said that sight differs from the other senses in this regard. For in the other senses, the sensitive power expands outward from the center, as is seen in smell, hearing, taste, and touch. But the organ of **sight** <term>v°</term> <note>original: "visus"</note> is constricted. Indeed, the opening of the **uvea** <note>The middle layer of the eye, including the iris; the "opening" refers to the pupil.</note> is narrow. Likewise, the eyelids also compress it, as **Timaeus** <note>A reference to Plato’s dialogue *Timaeus*, which discusses the creation of the world and human anatomy.</note> writes, so that it does not receive light from every side but more directly. Sight also requires "subterranean" pores that correspond to each other in a straight line, whereas hearing does not, as it can perceive through various paths. To the next point, which must be said about the sensory appendage, we shall see later. 

Regarding the signs, it must first be said that the light appearing before the eyes is either, as mentioned, within the "albuginous" humidity <note>The aqueous humor, or the clear fluid in the front of the eye.</note>, or it is not actually emitted from the eye as a benefit to vision, but rather because the cornea is polished and reflective like other smooth surfaces.

To the next point, **Aristotle** <note>original: "A." or "Ar." (Aristoteles)</note> responds that the pupil is among those things that shine and illuminate at night, casting rays upon what is opposite to it. These are the eyes of many animals, as previously stated, in which a light thrives due to the heat of their brains, so that at night they can illuminate the medium with light proceeding from their eyes by the power of their spirits. Some, however, simply say this light proceeds from the eye and illuminates in the same way as "night-lights," such as fish scales, rotting wood, and similar things which do not rest at all. **Aristotle** says that if they truly emitted light, the medium would be so illuminated that it would show color to us. This is not a very compelling argument, because something might appear to them that does not appear to us, since their visual power differs greatly from ours. However, if such an emission exists, it does not prove that vision is completed by sending something out, but rather that it prepares the medium to receive the species of color. As for the claim that "rays are thrown," we must look at the **Truth** <term>Veritatem</term>. This is not quite right, as if a ray were a physical body. For that which is "thrown" or "moved" is a body. 

Those who study perspective show that a ray "hits" something, "touches" it, "descends," or "refracts." To these, **Aristotle** responds that such arguments are false because the aforementioned terms concerning "rays" are not their proper names, but are used metaphorically. **Aristotle** holds nothing of these as literal; for because it approaches from another thing, it is "thought" to descend. Therefore, since a ray is not a moving body, it does not possess motion, but rather a "mutation" that occurs in an instant, just like illumination and vision.

To the next point, it must be said that although one eye becomes larger when the other is closed, it is not because something is being emitted from it, but rather so that it may be strengthened and illuminated by the "spirits" gathering to receive what occurs from the outside. To the next two points, it must be said that what is emitted from the eyes of a menstruating woman and a

**basilisk** <note>A mythical serpent said to kill with its gaze; in the Middle Ages, this was often discussed as a "natural" but poisonous phenomenon.</note> is not for the purpose of completing their vision by emission, but rather they are certain corrupt and poisonous vapors. Because of their cloudy thickness, they appear in a mirror like a bloody cloud. These spirits would actually be more of a hindrance to vision. To the next point, it must be said that although the receptions and perfections of the visual organs are expressed with active verbs, they are to be understood passively. Hence, in such cases, the speech is proper in that an active verb <term>v°</term> denotes a "passion" (a being-acted-upon) and a passive verb often denotes an action, following the Greek custom.

Or, in the sensory power, such as sight, there is first a passive reception and then an act of judging the thing colored. This perhaps is what is meant in *On Sleep and Wakefulness*. Just as sight "suffers" (receives an impression), so also it acts—or rather, it acts more forcefully, like the eye of a menstruating woman or a basilisk infected with a smoky vapor, as the preceding arguments touched upon. To the next point, it must be said that the aforementioned "sending in" that a lover directs at the beloved, or one who hates at the hated, contributes nothing to vision, as they say. Rather, a certain **intentional mutation** <note>A change in the "intentio" or mental/spiritual image, rather than a physical change.</note> occurs, which perhaps causes an impression in the "phantastic" powers <note>The imagination or the part of the brain that processes images.</note> of the one it is directed toward. 

It should be known that some, interpreting the speeches of the wise regarding **images** <note>Here referring to talismans or astrological charms.</note>, say that these images have an efficacy comparable to how "Art" is moved by our world, which is ordered toward the higher principles. For when something good or bad should happen to someone due to the alignment of their birth, this incites the "Art" to construct images or similar things, so that this grace might occur in the present. But because this seems to come from the heat of the "spirits" of the Art and does nothing on its own—since we see such images often fail—the theologians have said this happens more through the power of **demons** who involve themselves in such acts. They say these effects arise more among the simple-minded and especially among "little women" <note>original: "mulierculis"; a dismissive term often used by medieval scholars to describe uneducated women believed to be prone to superstition.</note> than among the prudent, for the demons are more able to deceive the less cunning. 

However, since this persuasion regarding spirits is not the method of the present study, it should perhaps be said instead that the material, having been received and melted in proportion to the stars, is shaped at a favorable time. The celestial light—which is like the instrument of the **Intelligences** <note>The angelic or spiritual beings believed to move the celestial spheres.</note> through motion and rays—imprints upon this disposed matter so that a certain power falls "intentionally" or "spiritually" upon the thing. This intention, raised by the light of the stars and the Intelligences, moves the recipient toward love or incites them to hate. Hence, these works are done more by night than by day, lest the rays of the sun or other celestial bodies darken and dissolve the power. They also try to make the rays fall directly upon the object. And if the simple-minded achieve the effect more than others, it perhaps happens because they believe more firmly in these things; and therefore, the powers can more easily alter and change them. As a general cause, I agree more that whatever happens naturally to a human is a work...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how the soul and celestial influences interact, specifically addressing how a "poisonous" or powerful gaze might be rooted in a person's birth chart (nativity). ...magic is arranged from these things through a certain co-astrality <note>A shared alignment of the stars affecting multiple people at once.</note> in whatever way it arises, yet it is assisted by art. For according to **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the influential 2nd-century astronomer and astrologer.</note>, a wise soul assists the work of the stars just as a sower assists the strengths of the seeds at birth. Or perhaps a person was a "poisoner" from their very birth so that they might obtain such an effect. Thus, when by the co-astrality of a prince, almost infinite numbers fall in war—which was not necessarily going to happen to such a great multitude from their individual births—it often happens there through a very small <margin>‡</margin> inclination. **Aristotle** and **Algazel** <note>Al-Ghazali, a Persian polymath who influenced Western scholasticism.</note> posit that such things happen by the power of the soul, such as that which belongs to prophets. ### And concerning the aforementioned things of this last reason, one might doubt concerning colors in a ruptured eye.
<margin>‡</margin> For if they are to perfectly complete the sight by receiving it, then the eye will be without color, since an inherent color would prevent others from being seen, as appears in the beginning of *On the Soul*. For a color appearing inside will prohibit another, and obstruct it. Furthermore, the eye is transparent and permeable, specifically the **cornea** <term>cornea</term>, which they say varies in color; but the transparent is without color of its own, according to **Isidore** <note>Isidore of Seville, an early medieval encyclopedist.</note>. Furthermore, as touched upon before, color is the limit or the end of a bounded transparent thing, but the transparency of the eye is its beginning, since it is a transparent passage, specifically regarding the cornea. Therefore, the eye is not colored. 

On the opposite side are the **philosophers and physicians** who posit eight, three, or four colors. According to the book *On Sense and the Sensible*, all bodies participate in color; the eye is a body, therefore it will be colored. Regarding the first point, one must know how color is spoken of, for what it is that makes a thing seen, and thereafter how it is caused. For the sake of the former, it must be known that "color" is understood in two ways. One way is common and extended, insofar as it is the same as that which is "visible." This is "color" according to what has been said: that color is the motive force of sight according to the act of the transparent; <margin>}</margin> and in this way, the eye is indeed colored—even the super-celestial things are called colored. Whence **Aristotle** says in *On Colors*: "Air and water are by their own nature white. Fire and the Sun are reddish. Earth is naturally white, but because of staining it is called multi-colored." This is supported because that which is seen is "colored," for the proper object of sight is color, according to the book *On the Soul*. But the eye is seen to be colored along with other things; therefore, it will be so in this manner. 

They also understand "color" properly and strictly, insofar as it is less seen to have that which is visible, according to what has been said: that it is the extremity or the limit of the transparent in a bounded body. For regarding the nature of color, two things are seen: one, that it is in a bounded body and not a transparent one, since the latter is rather the medium of color carried into the organ; the other, that it exists only in mixed things. For color is like sound, smell, and flavor: a quality of the three things caused by the mediating principles through which movement goes out. And as taste and touch go out, so does sight. 

Here, however, according to this, color is caused from a mixing of the luminous transparent in a body that is not clear or is bounded; thus, this or that color will be caused according to such or such a proportion of the mixture. Wherefore <margin>}</margin> **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd, the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher.</note> in *On Sense and the Sensible* says: "White color is made from the admixture of bright fire or light with a maximally transparent element, such as air." Wherefore in *On the Generation of Animals*, book 5: "Vaporous air exhibits white included in all things." Blackness, however, is caused from the mixture of fire therein with a minimally transparent element, such as earth. A middle color is produced from these causes according to a middle-state. And because colors can be varied in many ways, they will be many and almost infinite in theory, although they are called a defined number. 

Regarding the second point, it must be known that the colors <margin>colors of the eyes</margin> <margin>}</margin> of the eyes are found expressed in different ways. For some have posited three. In *Problems*, section 10, and in the beginning of his theories, it is written: **black**, **sub-black** <note>Likely a dark brown or hazel.</note>, and **glaucous** <note>original: "glaucus"; a blue-gray or sea-green color.</note>. And in the fifth book of *On Generation*: **black**, **glaucous**, and **variegated**. In the *Tegni*, section 11: **glaucous**, **black**, and **middle**. Finally, **Avicenna**: **green**, **variegated**, and **black**. Some, however, posit four, such as **Iohannitius** <note>Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a translator and physician in Baghdad.</note>, namely **off-white**, **glaucous**, **variegated**, and **black**. **Avicenna** also lists **red**, **yellow**, **leaden**, and **tawny**. But **Averroes** lists **red**, **off-white**, **black**, and **variegated**. 

Although these seem to disagree, they can nonetheless be sufficiently reduced into one. For **Aristotle** first and **Haly Abbas** <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note> understood by the color "sub-black" that color which **Galen** calls "middle." But Aristotle later understood by "variegated" the middle or sub-black. **Avicenna**, however, understood "glaucous" by "green," and "middle" or "sub-black" by "variegated," so that they agree very well, not only in number but also in form. **Iohannitius**, however, positing four, placed "glaucous"—which the others called an extreme—in the middle, placing "off-white" as one of the extremes. He explained the middle color in two parts for the sake of introduction. Those colors prescribed by **Avicenna** seem to many to disagree with the previously noted ones in number and quality. It can be said that **leaden** and **tawny** are reduced to **black**, and **yellow** to **glaucous**, and **red** to **middle** or **sub-black** or **variegated**. 

Or better: these colors are not of the substance of the eyes—such as the cornea—but rather of the humors representing themselves more fully in the conjunctival veins. <margin>}</margin> As **Avicenna** says: "Color signifies the dominant humor proportionally." For **red** shows the dominance of **blood**; **yellow** shows **choler**; **leaden** shows **phlegm**; and **tawny** shows **melancholy**. **Averroes**, however, as another, posits four colors and sees more clearly that they are in the conjunctival veins, placing them as signs of the "complexion" <note>The physical and mental temperament determined by the balance of humors.</note> of the brain. This will be true if the whole head is uniformly complexioned. And they are: **red**, as the eyes have red veins, which signifies a hot complexion of the brain. And **off-white**, which notes coldness, and **black** which notes heat. And the **middle** of these two, such as **variegated**, shows a balanced temperament. 

Regarding the beginning, it should be known that **Empedocles** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed the theory of the four elements.</note> wanted to ascribe the cause of the color of the eyes to fire and water, thinking that **glaucous** eyes have more fire and less water, and therefore they do not see sharply by day because of the lack of water. **Black** eyes are the opposite, and because of this they do not see perfectly at night because of the penury of fire. The **variegated** eye is the middle between these. But **Aristotle**, coming upon this, attacks it, supposing that the primary part of the eye is not fire but water, and therefore the cause of the eye's color should be assigned to the air. For some eyes have much aqueous humor in proportion; these are **black**. Some have it in moderate proportion. Those having more humor are black because it is not easily rendered clear. If, however, they have a small amount, they will be the opposite. Those having a middle amount will be middle between these. This is shown by the water of the sea. For when it is deep...
