...appears black. But when it is expanded, it appears somewhat whitish; yet in the middle, it is moderate or brownish. This indeed is the cause of color in healthy [eyes] concerning the generation of animals. More specifically, however, it is stated in the *Tegni* <note>The *Tegni* or *Ars Medica* was a fundamental medical textbook by Galen used in medieval universities.</note> that whatever cause is taken from the part of the **crystalline** and **albuminous** humors <term>humors: the vital fluids of the body; here referring to the lens (crystalline) and the watery fluid (aqueous/albuminous) of the eye</term>. For if the crystalline humor is abundant, or reddish-bright and splendid, or is located more prominently (that is, positioned further outward), and the albuminous humor is either small in quantity or pure, it will render the eye grey-blue; indeed, it will be extremely grey-blue when all these factors occur together.

On the other hand, if the crystalline humor is small, somewhat turbid, and situated deep within the eye, while there is a multitude of albuminous humor, it will result in the darkest black. From these causes, when they occur in a moderate balance, a medium eye color arises. **Johannitius** <note>Johannitius (Hunayn ibn Ishaq) was a 9th-century Nestorian Christian physician who translated Greek medical works into Arabic, which were later translated into Latin.</note> expanded these into seven causes, adding two from the perspective of the "visible species" <note>In medieval optics, "species" were the forms or images emitted by objects that traveled through the air to the eye.</note>—such as its abundance and its opposite—and one from the quality of the uvea humor, whether intense or relaxed. He omitted, however, the cause that had been taken by **Galen** from the reddish-brightness of the crystalline humor and its opposite.

Regarding the fourth point, it appears that what should have been said was introduced by pathways that have been put to rest. From this, what should be said to the first point is known: the eye is not "colored" with a permanent color (which belongs to a bounded body), for such a color would prevent its recipient from receiving another color. Rather, it possesses an "improper" and extended color, just as any transparent thing—and generally any visible thing—is judged by the name of color. To the other two points, it should be said subsequently: for they conclude regarding color in its proper sense. Regarding those things introduced by the other party, what should be said has been seen. They agree generally concerning color as the visible stimulus that moves the sight.

# DIFFERENCE LXV.

<margin>1</margin>
Whether health is an "intermediate species" <term>species subalterna: a category that sits in the middle of a hierarchy, acting as a species of a higher genus but a genus to lower species</term> just as disease is, so that an interposed mark of distinction ought to be defined, just as disease is shown to be. Since health is a certain proportion of the hot and the cold, or of those things which are within or related to the physical container—see **Aristotle’s** *Physics*, Book VII. Therefore, since a mark of "either/or" <note>Latin: *aut*</note> is interposed, denoting separation and diversity, it will not be the "most specific species" <term>species specialissima: the lowest level of classification that cannot be divided into further species</term>. Again, regarding these things, nothing is more healthy or more sickly according to nature or outside of it. It is therefore spoken of equally. For if health were the most specific species and disease were an intermediate species, then "healing" (derived from health) would certainly be spoken of more according to nature—since it would embrace all its aspects conjunctively—than "falling ill" (named from disease) according to nature. Furthermore, in the *Tegni*: since they refer to the whole genus of health, etc. But "genus" is spoken of in relation to species.

**Johannitius** says in the same place: the "genera of lapses" <note>Medical "lapses" or "declines" from a healthy state.</note> are the same. That is, they are either from those things that complete their power, or perhaps they are the same in genus. But the genera of lapses are three: of proportion, of composition, and of common nature. Therefore, there are also three existing genera of healthy consistency. Furthermore, in **Aristotle’s** *Metaphysics*, Book X, only one thing is opposite to one thing. If, therefore, health were the most specific species and disease were an intermediate species, one would be opposed to many—as if one health were opposed to many diseases.

---

Likewise, as often as one is said to be many, so is the other (from the *Topics*). And there are many accounts and causes of many kinds—see *On Generation and Corruption* and *Metaphysics*, Book IV. Health and disease are genera when they are most distant from each other. Since, therefore, disease is manifold, health will also be manifold. Health is therefore an intermediate species and not the most specific. On the opposite side, concerning human nature: a body is healthy when it has those things which constitute it and its power in moderation toward one another, and especially when they are well-mixed. But it suffers when any of these is more or less in the body, or departs and becomes unmixed with the others. Hence Galen says on this in his work *On Black Bile*. Therefore, it is not simply that it is healthy when it has these things tempered toward each other. A person is sick either when there is some abundance throughout the whole body (i.e., in all the vessels), or if it is generated in one particular part—as anyone would say is verified by the works of **Hippocrates**.

He wishes, therefore, that health be one "coupled" or unified state, while disease is manifold. Wherefore, in the *Tegni*, when defining health or a healthy body, he does not denote a distinction within it, but rather a "coupling," suggesting it to be a **eucrasia** <term>eucrasia: a perfect or "good" mixture of the four humors</term> from its generation in the simple and primary parts. It is equal to those things which are composed of these organs. But when defining a simply sick body, he adds a mark of distinction, saying it is either from its generation "distempered" in those parts that have similar characteristics, or "not equal" in the organs, or both. Which is to say that in natural things, a "eucrasia" (good mixture) is always the best, while a **dyscrasia** <term>dyscrasia: a "bad" mixture or imbalance of the humors</term> is that which is worse.

Likewise in the *Tegni*: in healthy people, all things are according to nature; but in the sick, they are against nature insofar as they are sick. Since, therefore, he does not repeat "all things" for the sick, but adds "insofar as they are sick," he indicates that a portion of health exists simultaneously with the disease. And thus health will be one, simple and perfect, while disease is manifold.

Also in the first book of the *Ethics*: health is a disposition or habit through which the human body, in its constitution and composition, turns out such that all operations proceed from it unharmed. Disease, however, is a non-natural disposition in the human body from which harm essentially results in operation at its first onset. And it is either a non-natural complexion <note>The overall balance of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) in a person.</note> or a non-natural composition.

Furthermore, health has the logic of the "whole" and the "perfect," while disease has the logic of the opposite. That which is such, however, is indivisible and simple—see the *Ethics*, Book II, and the *Magna Moralia*, Book I. For evil and the imperfect have the logic of the infinite, while the good has the logic of the finite, as the **Pythagoreans** said. Health, therefore, is the most specific species. Regarding the first point, it should be known what health is and what disease is; this is shown here in section 72. A "species" is also that which is placed under an assigned genus. Of which a certain type is called "subaltern" (intermediate), having the nature of both a genus and a species; hence the logician says it obtains the nature of a genus and a species. It is a genus insofar as it is compared to lower things; it is a species insofar as it is compared to higher things. The reason for this is that it is predicated as one thing over many things that differ not only in number but also in species.

<meta>This page continues the technical philosophical and medical investigation from the previous page, shifting from the optics of the eye to a scholastic definition of "species" and "genus" as applied to the concepts of health and sickness. It draws heavily on Aristotelian logic and the medical authorities Galen, Avicenna, and Averroes.</meta>

**Species**, also known as the **most specific species** <term>species specialissima: the lowest level in a hierarchy of classification, such as "human," which cannot be further divided into smaller groups, only individuals</term>, is like an atom or an indivisible unit. Although it is divided by essential differences, its definition is such that it is only a species and in no way a genus. Whence **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a philosopher whose "Isagoge" served as the standard introduction to logic in the Middle Ages.</note> says it is predicated of many things differing in number in answer to the question "What is it?" A species arises—since it is a "being of reason" <term>ens rationis: a concept that exists in the mind rather than a physical object in the world</term>—from real, natural existence.

For all **Logic**, under which the consideration of species falls, considers **intentions** <term>intentions: in medieval logic, "first intentions" are concepts of real things, while "second intentions" are concepts of those concepts (like "genus" or "species")</term> or concepts as they are applied to primary things. As **Aristotle** says at the beginning of the *Metaphysics*: the subject of logic, as you have learned, consists of "second intentions" of the intellect which are applied to the primary intentions understood by the intellect. This is done so that one may proceed from the known to the unknown, not insofar as they are understood and have an intelligible existence—which in no way depends on matter—but rather as non-corporeal forms. Just as a real natural being, as previously stated, is composed of matter and form, so too a **Species** consists of a **Genus** (taking the place of matter) and a **Difference** (acting as the form of the letters). Each of these expresses the whole, though only in the manner of a part.

It is a property of the species that it alone can be defined. For a **Genus**, insofar as it is a genus, lacks a higher genus and thus cannot be strictly defined. Nor can an **Individual** be defined, as it lacks an essential difference; thus, individuals are indivisible. <insert>Note 11</insert>. Indeed, one must know that genus and species differ not only as the "more general" and the "determined," but also in that they do not possess the same kind of nature or existence. For a genus is not "one thing" according to the *Physics*, book 7.

A **Species**, however, stands as a single nature because it is derived from the "ultimate completive form," which is simply one being in nature. But a genus is not derived from any single thing in reality, but rather by reason alone. For there is no single form by which a human is an "animal" separate from the form by which he is a "human." All humans, who are of one species, agree in the constitutive form of that species. For each has a rational soul; there is no common "animal soul" in a human, a donkey, and a horse that exists apart from the soul that makes them specifically a human, a donkey, or a horse. If such a thing existed, the genus would be a single comparable nature like a species; but the form of the genus is only grasped in contemplation through the abstraction of the intellect from specific differences. And so, a genus is "one" in Logic, but not in Physics. And this is what is touched upon in Note 29.

But because he does not intend to speak of **health** and **sickness** simply as concepts or logical bases, but rather as "primary things" and natural forms concerning a particular subject:

It should be known from this that **health** can be compared to three things: to its causes or subject, or to its operations.

The first comparison (to causes) is twofold. For it is either compared to primary, mediate causes—such as those causing health from "simple generation" <note>Generation refers to the biological process of coming into being or the maintenance of the body's constitution.</note> or from generation in the present time. For one kind of health is implicit and another is "as of now," and yet both come from generation. One is always continuous, such as that of a body that is always healthy; the other is somewhat deficient, such as a body that has contracted much so that it is healthy only for now or for a short hour. This was the mind of **Galen**, as **Haly Abbas** <note>Haly Abbas (925–994 AD) was a famous Persian physician; his "Liber Regalis" was a major medical text.</note> correctly understood—not as it is commonly explained regarding health caused by the timely or customary administration of the "six non-natural things." <term>six non-naturals: factors like air, diet, sleep, and exercise that doctors believed governed health</term>.

---

...making **Galen** appear disorganized in the *Tegni* <note>The *Tegni* or *Ars Medica* was Galen's foundational textbook.</note>. Alternatively, health is compared to secondary and immediate causes, such as "composition" and the common nature arising from both. If the comparison is made to the **subject**, this also happens in two ways: either according to a part of the subject—such as the health that resides in a specific member like the health of a bone, flesh, or the eye—or according to the whole, distinguishing by degrees. Regarding this, bodies are said to be healthy in three ways: "always," "mostly," and "as of now." Or, the comparison is made to the **operations** of health, according to whether they are performed better or worse.

The antecedent cause of health is the **complexion** <term>complexion: the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile)</term> and the composition of similar parts. The "official" composition is the conjoined cause, but the measured proportion of these is the health of the whole body. The same applies to sickness and the "neutral" state in their own way. Regarding this science, **Avicenna** in the fifth book of the *Physics* seems to feel that health is a **subalternate species** <term>subalternate species: a category that acts as a species to the thing above it and a genus to the thing below it</term>. Moving on to this question, he says: "What is said by Avicenna is estimated not to follow," because even if an infirmity consists of many species, it is estimated that it does not follow that there are contrary species of health, since health is one and sicknesses are many. Responding, he says that perhaps it seems that one "health" contains many particular healths opposed to those many sicknesses, but they do not have names and therefore remain hidden.

Thirdly, he gathers and confirms this opinion by a great argument: the number of species of sickness is the same as the number of species of health. From the knowledge of health, sickness is known, although some think that the species of sickness are better known than the species of health because many sicknesses have names while the healths opposite to them do not.

<margin>Averroes</margin>
The Logicians also coincide with this position in the subtleties of their words, considering "intentions" not slightly separated from their essences. Whence I think **Avicenna** fell into this opinion more so that he might disagree with his predecessors, as was his custom. I and others have dogmatized that health can be referred to two things: to the **subject** (which it disposes), and in this way it is a subalternate species, which I think was Avicenna's intention. This is shown because in the *Colliget* <note>The *Colliget* (Kitab al-Kulyat) was the major medical work of Averroes (Ibn Rushd).</note>, he defines health not in general (as it pertains to the whole body like others do), but rather according to what is owed to each part, calling it the "good disposition in a member by which it performs the action it has by its nature or undergoes the passion it must undergo." Regarding what was said before, healths are very numerous. But that is not sufficient, because just as one complexion of the whole finally arises from the alternation of the parts of the members, and one universal composition in the whole arises from the partial compositions (as he also wished in the *Colliget*), so besides the individual healths of the members, one must posit one health of the whole arising from the partial kinds and compositions, which will be the **most specific species**. Or, health is considered according to its relation to **operations**, and in this way, it is not a subalternate species. But what is to be said of these things will appear by reasoning in the fourth part.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on the logical classification of "health." Having previously defined "species," the author now argues that health is a "most specific species" (a fundamental, indivisible unit of classification) rather than a "subalternate species" (a broader category that contains other sub-types).</meta>

Now it should be known that health can in no way more truly be called a **subalternate species** <term>subalternate species: a category that sits in the middle of a hierarchy, acting as a species to the level above it and a genus to the level below it</term>. This is apparent if one examines the parts of the distinction provided, regarding how health is constituted as a specific entity. For to an observer, it will be seen that health—as it is compared to the subject it qualifies—cannot pass into a plurality of "species of health" based on the diversity of individual limbs. In this way, health is not differentiated from health by such a distinction; a subalternate species is not constituted here, just as **whiteness** in a wall and in snow does not differ in species, since all white things are indistinguishable in species according to the fourth book of the *Topics* <note>Aristotle's *Topics*, a treatise on the art of reaching conclusions from probable premises.</note>. Furthermore, the specific and final difference is lacking, such as the **integrity of operations** <note>In medieval medicine, health was defined not just by the body's structure, but by whether its "operations" (functions like digestion or breathing) worked perfectly.</note>; nor does the degree of "more or less" health in a subject vary the species, since "more" and "less" do not change a species. Nor is it varied by the nature of its primary causes. Because health results from a simple generation, health exists as a single species, since operations can coincide sufficiently into the same thing, which argues for a single form and species. Therefore, a subalternate species of health cannot be found in these things.

It remains, then, finally to look at what constitutes the species which, according to **Boethius** <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), a philosopher whose works on logic were foundational to medieval education.</note>, alone defines and constitutes the "quiddity" <term>quiddity: the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term> of a thing in being. This will be easy if one pays attention to the remaining parts of the aforementioned distinction, such as the immediate and contrary causes, and the operations proceeding from health. For since the definition of the "ultimate species" is constituted from the **proximate genus** and the **ultimate difference** <note>In logic, you define a thing by its general group (genus) and the specific trait that sets it apart (difference).</note> which is convertible and completive with that of which it is the difference, it will be correct to say that health is the **most specific species**. Because the complexion, composition, and nature <margin>}</margin> <note>These three—complexion (balance of humors), composition (arrangement of parts), and nature—were the Galenic pillars of health.</note> are a third common difference in the genus of "disposition" or "habit," which is the genus where health is located, thus identifying it through health. **Perfect operations** are also the completive difference, constituting health in its being as something formal. This is especially true because health and sickness are perfectly defined by their "act" <note>The actual functioning or performance of the body.</note>, as is first seen in the book *On Disease*. Full operations cannot exist unless they arise from both natures, namely the complexion and the composition, and finally from the entire disposition, since a subalternate species expresses the whole being of individuals. Thus, it is concluded that health is the **most specific species**, and not a subalternate one.

The **Logicians**, however, wishing to abstract a certain common concept from the two or three things mentioned above, say that health is a subalternate species. Yet they do not consider **operation**, which is the more formal difference of health, and by which health is named as if by its purpose. This can be considered further by authority and reason. **Avicenna** says in the first book of the *Great Morals*: "Evil is indeed multiform, but good is uniform." For example, health is simple, but disease is multiform. This is also the opinion expressed in the second book of the *Ethics*. The same view is found in the fourth book of the *Topics*, although many logicians, ignorant of the truth, explain it differently. For it is intended that if there is something contrary to a genus, it is contrary to both the genus and the species. Just as vice is opposed to virtue, so is injustice to justice. However, there will be something contrary to a genus that is not contrary to a species. An instance of this is found in health and sickness, because health is simply...

...true and perfect, the essence of which consists in the joining together of complexion, composition, and a common nature. **Sickness** is its contrary, because it can be of a threefold nature involving a lapse in those same three joined things. But a certain sickness—when it is a species of sickness, such as one of complexion or composition or both—is contrary to nothing, because it cannot be directly opposed to health, since health consists in the union of all three. It is opposed, however, in a certain way, as a middle ground between extremes. For example, a **fever**, which is a sickness in the complexion, is not properly contrary to true health; nor is it even "obliquely" so, as in the conjunctive sense. For an organic disease <margin>}</margin> is a distinct difference. <note>In Galenic medicine, diseases were categorized as "similary" (affecting humors/tissues) or "organic" (affecting the structure of organs).</note>

**Avicenna**, however, explains that nothing is contrary to health, noting this "obliquely." Others note it under one name, as happens with vice and virtue, or justice and injustice.

Furthermore, in the sixth book of *On the Preservation of Health* <note>Referring to Galen's "De Sanitate Tuenda."</note>: "The best in every genus of things is one." It is clearly manifest that evil things are many. Health, however, is something "best." For it is a **good disposition** through which an animal performs its actions and undergoes its natural passions. Sickness is the opposite. Therefore, all health is one. Such a thing is "atomic" <note>In the sense of being an indivisible unit of classification.</note> and deprived of division into essential parts. Furthermore, that which has one cause—whether simple, proximate, or immediate—is also one in its effect, since cause and effect must exist in total proportion. Such is the proper proportion of cold, dry, and moist qualities <margin>}</margin> toward each other, which regards the complexion and the similar members. From this cause, according to **Galen**, everything is caused, since it exists as the substance and form of the members. The "composition," called the **official nature** <term>official nature: relating to the "official" organs (like the heart or liver) which have specific duties or "offices" in the body</term>, or the unity of the common nature, is rather a certain effect resulting from the complexion, just as "official parts" are constituted from "similar parts." And parts are the matter of the whole, according to the second book of the *Physics*. Again, operation is an effect resulting from the aforementioned natures as if from instruments, caused by the "virtue" or the "soul" as the principal cause. But operation is a single common thing; therefore, the cause of health will be one. For health is the cause of natural operation, according to the first book of *On Disease*. For if someone is healthy in their complexion but not healthy in their composition, or vice versa, he should not be called healthy, but rather "neutral" or "incomplete." Furthermore, more things are required for the constitution and especially the perfection of a thing than for its destruction. Indeed, if any one of those things is destroyed, the whole is largely destroyed, as is apparent regarding the voice and speech. But health is something "made"; for according to Galen, it is the construction of all particular parts of the body according to nature. Sickness, however, is a certain imperfection and a defect of health. Just as it is in art, so it is in nature, since art imitates nature. In art, a crafted object does not have the "being" of that crafted thing unless it has all its parts integrally. For example, in a **house**, the perfection of which requires the foundation, wall, and roof to exist together; by the removal of all of them, or two, or even just one, the "being" of the house is destroyed. So it will also be in nature regarding health and sickness, which exist primarily as natural forms. And indeed, one reads...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the nature of health and illness, building on the previous discussion of whether health is a specific or subalternate species. ...that if health exists according to proportion or in composition, it is because health is present in the body simply, since they [the parts] better understand the nature of the integral whole than the nature of the universal whole. In illness, however, it is the opposite, since from a lapse in any one part, the nature of the operation in the whole is entirely harmed. Furthermore, matters of reason, when they are taken from things of nature, are proportioned to them; but in matters of reason—take for example a **definition**—all parts are required together so that it may be a perfect definition. An infinite thing, however, [is created] through the loss of one small part, such as a **genus** or a specific **difference** <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "difference" is the specific characteristic that distinguishes one species from others in the same genus.</note>, according to the seventh book of the *Topics*. Thus, it will be the same in the things of nature, such as in health and illness: for health is like something finite and determined, while illness is like something wandering and indeterminate. For illness speaks rather of a defect of perfection (which is health) rather than positing any nature of reality. Therefore, health is a **most specific species** and not a subalternate one.

Regarding the fourth point, it must be said in response to the first that health is essentially and absolutely the **commensuration** <term>commensuration: the proper balance or "measuring out" of the primary qualities</term> of the hot, the cold, and so on. But what is added—either "above" or "below" or "to the boundaries"—does not describe the essence of illness, but rather the subject in which it is founded, or the remote cause from which it can be caused. Or, **Averroes** <note>Original: "Au."; referring to the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known as "The Commentator."</note> speaks by way of example where a manifestation and not the absolute truth is sought. To the other point, it must be said that he errs through the fallacy of composition and division. For it is not the intention of Averroes to say separately that health is "according to nature" and illness "beyond nature" equally, but rather jointly: that health is no more according to nature or outside it than illness is. This appears in what follows, for he says that generation is not according to nature and corruption is equally against nature; now, both are according to nature—for growing old is according to nature. Nor do we see one generation according to nature and another truly beyond nature, when nature is taken generally as the "principle of motion from within." To the other point, it must be said that there "genus" is taken commonly and improperly for some higher reversible term. For not everything that follows and does not reverse is a genus, although it is difficult to separate them in the fourth book of the *Topics*. That which is common to the whole "being" of health is not a common "true genus" according to which it is separated into its own specific differences from which the species arises; rather, it is a commonality of **latitude** <term>latitude: a range or span of degrees within which a quality like health can exist</term> among subjects, according to which health is found in a body that is "always healthy," "very healthy," and even "simply sick" or "in the middle," according to **Galen** <note>Original: "Ga."; the influential Greek physician of the 2nd century.</note>. For there is a great latitude of health in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Ars Medica," a fundamental textbook of medieval medicine.</note> and regarding the beginning of disease, just as it was said in the first book of *On the Preservation of Health* that "healths are very many." To the other point, it must be said that although the types of "lapses" are equal, they are not ordered in the same way toward the constitution of health and illness. For in the constitution of health, as has been declared, all the natures of the body must be joined together; but in the constitution of illness, it is not required that they be present cumulatively, but it suffices that they be present disjunctively.

To the other point, it must be said that only one thing is the opposite of one thing in the same genus of opposition and in a direct line. Either health, as a most specific species, is opposed to the species of illness just as one extreme is opposed to another extreme, or an extreme to a middle. For directly, as has appeared, health is opposed to illness...

...and it exists as the least deadly, being temperate. For because of **temperament** <note>The "temperament" or *complexio* is the specific balance of the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines the nature of a thing.</note>, health and life consist. This, however, is the true definition. Furthermore, there is a goodness of disposition and a strength of virtue in the temperament of the stars. These, however, occur in Spring more than in other seasons. Again, generation exists in a certain temperament; but this occurs most powerfully in Spring, for then animals are moved to copulation. The sun also causes and determines this, consisting in its own **exaltation** <note>In astrology, an "exaltation" is a sign of the zodiac where a planet is thought to have its most harmonious and powerful influence. For the Sun, this is Aries, the sign associated with the start of Spring.</note>, as the astrologers say, in the sign of Aries with a sufficient tempering. Similarly, it exists for us in a disposition that is not untempered; for it is neither as close as in summer, nor very far distant as in winter, but in Spring it works in a disposed and moderate way. Therefore, Spring exists as temperate. 

Regarding the first point, it should be known what Spring is and how it is caused; the 115th distinction will show this. The "temperate" quality which is sought here, as in other things, is that which belongs to **justice** and not to **weight**, since there is a difference between these—it is impossible to find [the latter] <note>The author distinguishes between "justice" (a relative, healthy balance for a specific organism) and "weight" (an absolute, equal measurement of qualities). In medicine, balance is relative to the needs of the body, not a 50/50 mathematical split.</note>. However, the temperament that is found by "justice" declines toward the hot and the moist, presupposing that Spring remains in its own natural state. 

Regarding the second point, it should be known that **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (c. 129–216 AD), the most influential physician and medical philosopher of antiquity.</note> in the first book of *On Temperaments* strives to show that Spring is temperate, against certain others who say it is hot and moist, following the firm opinion of **Aristotle**, **Theophrastus**, and the **Stoics**, and others. First, he touches upon their motives; for they think, he says, that **eucrasia** <term>eucrasia: a state of "good mixture" or perfect health where all bodily humors are in balance</term> results from strong natural acts. They claim that death leads the animal toward coldness and dryness. They also say that life consists of the moist and the hot, while death is outside of these; therefore, it is necessary to bring this into a proportional comparison of the seasons. One of these qualities is adapted to Spring, and the other to Autumn. 

From this they further prove that the disposition of Spring is the best and most temperate, because it is hot and moist; for they say it is not like winter (cold and moist) nor like summer (hot and dry); wherefore they wish to conclude it is a "temperament." And they adapt the four combinations of the four elements to the four seasons. He [Galen] says these people are doubly deceived. First, because they attempt to find a fourth conjugation in the seasons of the year. Second, because they think Spring is hotter than winter and moister than summer. But if this were so, he says, since Spring would be moister than summer and drier than winter, then it would be both moist and dry. Whence he adds that it is necessary to take the difference from both, not by half, but in its entirety. For it will be hot and dry if it is compared to winter, but cold and moist if compared to summer. Therefore, according to neither comparison made in its entirety will it be "hot and moist," because of which it is necessary to examine it by itself and not only in relation to other seasons. 

Furthermore, according to this comparison, Autumn could also be called temperate, since it is not cold or moist like winter, nor hot and dry like summer; wherefore they rightly prove that Spring is hot and moist by a comparison made to the other seasons. But a great number of people attack the reasoning of the four combinations in the seasons. For it does not follow that if there are four conjugations of dispositions, they must all be distributed unmeasured to the four seasons. This is shown more by persuasion than by demonstration, as follows: If there is a state of **eucrasia** in the world and all things are ordered according to the better and not the worse, it was more probable that the seasons would be measured and only one of them would become untempered. These others, however, study to demonstrate the opposite: that none of the seasons is temperate, since in them there rules now cold, now hot, and again now dry, then moist. He also adds a reason constructed at length from the words of **Hippocrates**, which is this: That time which is prone to **putrefaction** <note>In medieval medicine, putrefaction (rotting) was thought to be caused by excessive heat and moisture acting upon a body.</note> and, to speak of one thing, to **pestilence**, is not temperate; such is the hot and moist, as he brings forth from the *Epidemics* of Hippocrates. This reasoning is also introduced in the fifth book of the *Theorems*. 

This is the abbreviated discourse of Galen. <margin>2 <unclear>??</unclear></margin> But perhaps it will not convince an adversary wishing to attack the previously induced points. First, because when some things are compared to others, even if they are not entirely like those to which they are compared, they can nevertheless be more or less similar or diverse to them. For Spring, compared to winter, is hot with much heat; but compared to summer, it is a little cold. Similarly, compared to summer, it exists as dry; compared to winter, however, it is moderately [moist?], because of which it is left as hot and moist. Nor will Spring be simultaneously moist and dry, since this is an impossible combination, but only relatively so. And thus it must be said of Autumn, since when compared to summer it is more cold, but a little dry; compared to winter, it is cold and dry. 

The truth will also be known in itself, or at least by comparison to the other half. Also, he to whom Galen’s combinations were breaking down will say that the adversary’s point is not valid, since these things are found in the summer and are used in others. For later things cannot ever be separated from prior things. Furthermore, the temperament given in beings, since it is "judicial" <note>i.e., balanced for the sake of health</note>, exists with the hot and the moist; and because of this, our nature, for human nature, declines toward the hot and the moist more than the others. Whence, since the hot and the moist possess a great latitude, it can be brought to that temperament. This is what almost everyone before Galen felt.

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the "temperament" of Spring. ...accidental humidity, and this is blameworthy because it is quick to putrefy; and the other is innate from the beginning of creation. Indeed, the accidental is likened to a spring that is very hot and moist, whereas the natural is that which is measured in its moisture and heat. And therefore, someone might wonder about **Galen** <note>original: "Ga." — Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note>, for in the destruction of another’s position and the confirmation of his own, he does not use a <unclear>demonstrative</unclear> argument. For his discourse here seems to be more probable or persuasive than certain. Hence **Al-Farabi** <note>original: "Alfarabius" — A renowned 10th-century Islamic philosopher and logician.</note> in the *Didascalia* on the *Rhetoric* of **Aristotle** <note>original: "Au." — Likely referring to Aristotle (Author), though sometimes used for Averroes.</note> says: "Emotional and moral speeches and those intended to strengthen the authority of the teacher do not belong to the sciences in any way, nor is it appropriate for anyone to use them, as they cause error." And you will find all these things in the books of Galen concerning this; for what he confirms or proves in most of his books, he intends to strengthen or invigorate his own powers through the honors and reverence shown to him by men on account of the experience of his fairness and justice, and then through the boasting of himself and the depression of other physicians.

Accordingly, the Commentator <note>Likely Averroes or a similar scholastic authority.</note> took up this discourse, first making it not simple but modified: the nature of spring draws toward equality in moisture and dryness, and thus it is a temperament between heat and moisture. Although we do not forbid that the beginning of spring should draw toward a certain moisture, nevertheless it is not far from equality as is the dryness of autumn. Similarly, it must be said that its end draws toward heat. Whence the **Aphorisms** <note>original: "affōy." — Refers to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates.</note> say: "Spring in its beginning is more like the mixture of winter, but in its end like summer, and in its middle it exists as more temperate." Hence, the commentator on the second book of *The Pulses* says: "In the middle of Spring, there is the most well-tempered constitution of the surrounding air, which is why bodies are healthy." But according to **Avicenna** <note>original: "Auic." — Ibn Sina (980–1037 AD), the Persian "Prince of Physicians."</note>, the whole season leans toward a subtle, slightly dormant heat and natural moisture.

Certain people, however, wishing to reconcile Galen with his predecessors, said that Spring can be considered in two ways: either according to its **effect** (that is, in itself) or by the result it produces in the body. Formally, they declare it temperate; effectively, however, they call it hot and moist. But these people fail, both because they disparage Galen (since he asserted it was simply temperate, wishing "temperate" to be opposed to "hot and moist"), and also because what a thing is formally, it produces effectively, since a thing operates according to how it has received its being. But formally Spring is temperate, as they say, because of which its action will be formal and not merely effective. Furthermore, such an effect must proceed from the **form** <note>In scholastic philosophy, the "form" is the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing that determines its properties.</note>, since every operation originally arises in it, especially in those things in which the agent always goes out into act, whereas a potentiality is aroused to act by something external. This was said regarding drunkenness from the pure effect <note>A common scholastic analogy: wine is formally temperate or cold in some theories but "effectively" intoxicatingly hot.</note>.

Moreover, it would be more tolerable to say that the necessities—namely, "hot" and "moist"—exist formally, and "temperate" exists effectively. The Commentator on the first book of the **Tetrabiblos** <note>original: "quadriptiti" — Ptolemy’s fundamental work on astrology.</note>, where he says Galen contradicts **Ptolemy** on this, says: "We wish to place a recorded agreement between these two wise men by this reasoning." For Ptolemy holds that the heat of spring is such as the heat and moisture of **Jupiter** <note>In medieval medical astrology, the planet Jupiter was considered "temperate" and "sanative," specifically hot and moist.</note>, which is of a balanced temperament. Here, he wished rather to follow the more famous opinions: that a temperate mixture, which is suitable for life and growth, tends more toward heat and moisture, and because of this, there is no contradiction between these two wise men.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that when the sun arrives near the line of equality <note>The celestial equator/equinox.</note>, by its effective heat it renders the air hot, and by heating it, causes the superfluous moisture of winter to evaporate, so that the accidental watery moisture exhales and the natural aerial moisture remains. Therefore, it is rendered less moist than in winter. And because heat will first cause warming, then cause evaporation and drying, spring is further removed from winter by heat than by moisture. But when the sun arrives near the beginning of **Cancer** <note>The Summer Solstice.</note>, further heating the predisposed matter, it dries it so much that the season is rendered hot and dry, which is Summer. Finally, as the sun begins to recede from us, it turns toward a certain coldness; the air is changed slightly in dryness compared to summer, since any heat dries, but not any coldness moistens (as stated in the first book). When the sun has entirely receded from us, then coldness is intensified in the air; for the rays do not meet each other in a thickened way (which is the greatest cause of heat, according to the first book of the **Meteorology** <note>original: "methaur." — Aristotle’s work on atmospheric phenomena.</note>), nor does a delay of coldness intervene. By the intensity of the cold, the moisture is not thinned but remains watery vapor. Similarly, the vaporous fumes from the "eyes of the earth" and the waters, being minimally resolved by the surrounding air, moisten the air, which is why winter is rendered cold and moist.

However, so that the truth may be more fully known, it must be observed that Spring can be considered in two ways, as it appears regarding the hot, cold, dry, and moist (as stated in the first book). For either it is considered as one of the four seasons distinct from the others, and thus it is hot and moist, yet with a temperament that is proportioned to the air. For its heat is not as great as that of summer, nor its moisture as great as that of winter; for it is proportioned to the air, which is indicated by its relationship to human nature. Especially according to the year, Spring is moist and hot. Or it is considered in relation to our body, and thus it is **temperate**. For it is more proportionable to the body than any other season, both in its nature in itself and in the relation of the action it performs in the body, since it is temperate. Thus, even Spring is called "temperate" in its own way.

<margin>3</margin> Whence it is gathered in the second book [of the Pulses] that the pulse of spring is [large] because of heat and moisture. But although it can be said that it is a temperate time in comparison to the human body, it is not, however, a temperament by an equality of qualities in weight. Similarly, there is a sophistical distinction regarding Spring that can be made concerning **blood** in relation to the other humors. For blood can be considered as it is one of the humors distinct from the others, and thus it is hot and moist. It is also such in relation to a "just" temperament <note>A balance that serves a purpose, like the skin or a specific organ.</note>, for example, of the flesh and skin. Or as it relates to the body, and thus it exists as temperate, since it is most loved by nature and is, as it were, its "proper son." This is most clearly shown by **Isaac** <note>original: "Ysaac" — Isaac Israeli (c. 832–932), a Jewish physician and philosopher whose work on fevers was a standard textbook.</note> <margin>2</margin> in the fifth book of *On Fevers* and in the following [book] on *Elements*. ...so that later things are never detached from the prior ones, since they essentially depend upon them and not the other way around. And it is confirmed because nature

To the other two, it is clear what must be said. For the truth concludes that air is considered as it relates to the natures of other seasons. To the other, it must be said that Spring, since it is hot and moist, can be called a "temperate body" <note>The author is balancing the technical definition of "hot and moist" with the medical definition of "temperate" (ideal for health).</note> which carries both heat and moisture. To the other, it must be said that this would be true if it happened of itself; for by accident, or through <term>plethora</term> <note>original: "plectora" — An excess of bodily fluids, particularly blood.</note>, or through an acquired weakness of virtue, it can happen otherwise. Regarding the arguments of the other side, it has been shown in common what must be said and how the speech of **Galen** is verified, and how much his reasons conclude. To the other, it must be said that "temperate" and "distemperate" are not directly contrary, since there is not that maximum distance between them which is the nature of contraries (Difference 72). To the other, it must be said that it is true by relation to the body, but not to the seasons, unless "hot and moist" is broadly called temperate. This is because heat does not flee from moisture, since it is the cause of life, and this ought to be the cause of generation, since generation is ordered toward life. And what should similarly be said to the other has appeared. Yet all can be fitted into one single distinction.

<margin>{</margin> Regarding the aforementioned, a hesitation occurred. For it was indicated that **Autumn** is distemperate—namely cold and dry—which does not seem to be the case since **Philaretus** <note>original: "Philaretus" — Likely referring to the author of a popular medieval Byzantine medical text on pulses.</note> writes that Spring and Autumn are temperate seasons. Also in the seventh *Theorem*: of Spring and Autumn 
the property is temperate in heat and cold. 
But if we have judged that in Autumn there is a strong equality between heat and cold, it will not be far from equality. Again, whatever causes and effects are temperate, the thing itself is temperate, since one causes and the other demonstrates it. But this is achieved in Autumn in a middle proportion of proximity and distance to us, just as in Spring when it begins around the entry of the Sun into **Libra**, just as the other starts in **Aries** <note>These are the two equinoxes (Autumn and Spring), where day and night are equal.</note>. The pulse also, which is the more powerful act of nature, is written to be large and strong in Spring and Autumn (Theorem 7), since the temperance of the person increases and preserves virtue. Hence **Galen** to the **Theurgist** <note>original: "theurcũ"</note>: according to the middle hours of Spring, the pulses are greatest and most vehement, being moderated in speed and thickness. Similarly, the middle of Autumn. Therefore, Autumn is temperate.

The opposite is argued because Autumn is a time of life contrary to the former. It is the beginning of acute and mortal diseases and the generation of <unclear>afflictions</unclear>. From which it is gathered in the fourth [book]: Autumn is likened to the age of old age, which is the path to death; because such a thing is most distemperate. Furthermore, "temperate" implies a sufficient middle-ground of all qualities. But Autumn is itself the driest, almost equal to Summer; for Autumn is measured as drier than Summer. I hear, however, that this happens more by accident than by its own nature, since it follows from the earth. Thus Autumn is rather distemperate. 

Regarding the first and second points, it must be said that the first became known from its own properties, and the second from arguments. For among these four, there were suspecting opinions. Regarding the third point, it must be known that Autumn is distemperate most of all, both in active and passive qualities. First, because although the cold is not as intense as in Winter, nor the heat as in Summer, the **sudden change** that exists in it within the same natural day—now toward cold, then suddenly toward heat—alters and changes the body more wickedly than a long-lasting mild cold or intense heat. For nature 
<margin>}</margin> does not tolerate that which is sudden. The cause of this inequality is the immense resolution and subtlety of the air due to the preceding heat of Summer and also Spring. For a subtle substance accepts alteration and incurs passion (Difference 14). 

That it is distemperate in passive qualities appeared from the arguments concerning the aforementioned cause of heat. This is confirmed because the Sun in Autumn reaches **Libra**, where it "falls," and especially in the **Combust Way** <note>original: "uia cõbufta" — In astrology, a specific stretch of the zodiac (late Libra to early Scorpio) considered unlucky or debilitating for the planets.</note> before its 19th degree unto the 3rd of **Scorpio**, just as it is exalted in Aries and specifically in the opposition of the Combust place. In that place, all planets, and especially the Sun and Moon, suffer detriment, unless perhaps **Saturn**, since he is exalted in Libra and specifically at the 21st degree, so that there are no planets from which they may preserve life as they do when in other parts of the signs. For it is often perceived that very cloudy weather is rendered serene when it reaches the 19th degree of Aries, where according to **Hermes** <note>original: "Hermetẽ" — Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and astrology.</note> it is specifically exalted. The opposite happens when it occurs at the degree of Libra... just as the Moon is honored in the third of **Taurus**.

<meta>This page transitions from a medical discussion on the "temperament" (biological balance) of the seasons to a geographical and astronomical debate regarding the habitability of the Earth's equator. It continues the previous page's scrutiny of Autumn's qualities before introducing "Difference LXVII."</meta>

...but it depresses in its opposite. Therefore, it is not on account of the sun—as some have felt—that Autumn is temperate, since the sun does not impress itself similarly in Spring and Autumn. Wherefore, this season is altogether distemperate <note>imbalanced in its primary qualities</note>. Regarding the fourth point, something must be said. To the first, therefore, it should be said that **Philaretus** <note>original: "Philaretus" — likely the 7th-century Byzantine physician whose works were standard medieval textbooks</note>, as it is said, wished Autumn to be temperate by reason of the sun’s position relative to us. But it has been shown that this cannot stand. Either he felt Autumn was "temperate" improperly, because there is not as much heat or cold in it as in Summer and Winter; or, as I have said properly, because such a temperament is not truly a balanced mixture, but rather is caused by a certain sensible position of more ample temperament. To the other point, something similar must be said: either that he did not wish the pulse <note>the arterial rhythm used for diagnosis</note> of Spring and Autumn to be entirely assimilated, but only somewhat more so. For there is a greater similarity in the motion and rest of the pulse, but not in its quantity or the tenor of its strength. Regarding the other point, what should be said appeared: since even the distance of the sun does not impress itself in the same way in Spring and Autumn. And therefore **Averroes** <note>original: "Auēſ." — referring to the Andalusian polymath Averroes (Ibn Rushd)</note>, detesting those who posit similar pulses in these two seasons, says they err completely. For in Autumn, the virtues are diminished on account of the little heat of the spirits; for the pulse in it is, as it were, similar to the pulse of old age. This is shown by the vegetation, which grows old through dryness.

## DIFFERENCE LXVII.

-> That under the equator, or the equinoctial line, <-
-> habitation may not be possible, can be shown. <-

<margin>1</margin>
As previously felt by those following the second book of *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle's "Meteorologica"</note> and many others, as will appear elsewhere. This is still supported by not a few reasons and signs; for if that place were habitable, someone from there would have already reached our regions, or one of us would have been to them and finally returned to us; but nothing of these things has yet been seen.

<margin>2</margin>
**Ptolemy** and **Albategni** <note>Al-Battani, a 9th-century astronomer</note>. Again here, in the *Quadripartitum*, **Alfraganus** <note>Al-Farghani, an astronomer who calculated the Earth's circumference</note> with the rest of the astrologers, sufficiently distinguishing the climates and the habitations of men, begin the first climate <note>a latitudinal zone</note> on this side of the line of equality at 12 degrees and three-quarters. Furthermore, where many causes of heat are gathered together in a stronger way, it will increase to such an extent that habitation cannot exist there, since life consists in a temperate habitation and disposition, especially for humans. But this is the case under the equator. For since there are three chief causes of heat—directness, proximity, and duration—they are found here most strongly. For there is directness, since the sun twice a year passes over their zenith <note>the point directly overhead</note>, such as when it is in the first minute of **Aries** and **Libra**, and when it is in other signs it is always distant by less than 24 degrees, since the maximum declination of the sun is within this, namely 23 degrees and 33 minutes. There is also great proximity because, since the earth is round, and the part around the upper and middle portion is more elevated, the earth will be more elevated there and closer to the sun. This is also confirmed by the eccentricity of the sun's circle, as appears in the third book of the *Almagest* <note>Ptolemy's foundational astronomical work</note>, leaf [n].

<margin>3</margin>
<margin>Solar Apogee</margin>
The sun now holds its **apogee** <note>original: "augē" from the Arabic 'awj' — the point in orbit furthest from Earth</note> or its longest distance from the earth in the 29th degree of **Gemini**, where the eccentricity is two and a half degrees. The opposite of the apogee is in the 29th degree of **Sagittarius**, being closer to the earth by two and a half degrees likewise. Because of this proximity, certain mathematicians pronounced the zone intercepted between the circle of the **Tropic of Capricorn** and the small **Antarctic Circle** to be uninhabitable, as will be seen in what follows. Thus, it appears that the sun in **Aries** and **Libra** is closer to the earth than when passing through **Gemini** and **Cancer**, because of which it will heat more. Similarly, its duration happens alongside the other causes, since the days are always equal to the nights; however, this does not intervene as much as the two previously mentioned causes. Again, under the **Tropic of Cancer**, about which more will be seen, there is either no habitation or it is poor and rare in water; the sun, as was said, is distant in respect to those living under the equator and only passes once over their heads in a year, such as when it is in the beginning of **Cancer**. Therefore, under the equinoctial line, since the sun is closer to the inhabitants and passes twice over their heads in a year, it will cause unhabitability there through heat.

<margin>EQUATOR</margin>
Likewise, the rays falling straight and axially toward the earth on account of the predicted directness are reflected back upon themselves, whence they are greatly thickened and strengthened in the first region. They will heat the air so much that it is contrary to a temperate human life. Furthermore, one finds the earth uninhabitable on account of its too great removal from the sun, such as that existing under the poles. Therefore, one will find it uninhabitable on account of its too great proximity to the sun, since hot and cold are contraries, and of contrary reasons, both will be oppositely distemperate. Because of this, since the earth placed under the equinoctial line is closest to the sun, it seems to be made uninhabitable.

<margin>The City of ARIM</margin>
The opposite is shown by the common fame of those composing astronomical tables regarding the city of **Arim** <note>original: "arym" — a legendary geographical center of the world, often identified with Ujjain in India</note>, which is preached to be exactly in the middle of the world, distant from each of the four corners of the world—namely East, West, South, and North—by 90 degrees.

<margin>NIMROD
ECONOMUS
Ptolemy
Albategni
Albumazar
Algorismus</margin>
The composers of the tables for the aforementioned city—as is said in the *Theorica* of **Al-Bitruji** <note>original: "p̄lay byſpalenſis" — referring to Al-Bitruji (Alpetragius), an astronomer from Seville</note>—were **Nimrod the Giant** <note>a legendary figure often associated with early astronomy/astrology</note>, **Economus**, **Ptolemy**, **Albategni**, **Albumazar** <note>Abu Ma'shar</note>, and **Algorismus** <note>Al-Khwarizmi</note>. Furthermore, the equinoctial place is the middle, distant equally from either pole. But the middle is more virtuous, more perfect, and more temperate than the extremes. Since, therefore, there is habitation and temperament toward the extremes, so much more will there be in the middle, such as the place which is under the equator; therefore, it will be habitable. Regarding the first point: it is in passing from the East to the West into two equal parts, equally distant from either of the poles, intersecting the **Zodiac** at the beginning of **Aries** and **Libra**; and therefore it is called the **equator** because when the sun is in these two signs, the night is made equal to the day in the whole earth. Also, the part of the earth placed under this circle is noted to be under the equator.

<meta>This page transitions from the medical debate regarding the temperament of seasons to a geographical and astronomical investigation into the Earth’s climatic zones. It explores the habitability of different regions based on the position of the sun and the celestial circles, moving from the physician’s focus on the human body to the cosmographer's focus on the globe.</meta>

->Cura dei<-
<note>Latin: "The Care of God." This likely serves as a header or a pious invocation common in medieval manuscripts.</note>

<margin>Ovid</margin>
In order that the distinction of the zones or regions may appear, it must be known that there are four parallel circles of the equinoctial pole. Two are toward the south—namely, the Antarctic circle and the circle of the winter tropic <note>the Tropic of Capricorn</note>—and two are toward the north, such as the Arctic circle and the circle of the summer tropic <note>the Tropic of Cancer</note>. These denote five zones in the heavens, and consequently distinguish five others opposite them on the Earth, according to that saying of **Ovid the Elder**: *as many regions are placed—that is, impressed—upon the earth.* Furthermore, these parallels are called "equidistant," not because the first is as distant from the second as the third is from the fourth, but because they are equidistant at every point, one not approaching another more closely than elsewhere. This appears through their distances found in every direction: for from the Arctic pole to the Arctic circle (or the pole of the zodiac), 23 degrees and 32 minutes are found. From this circle to the Tropic of Cancer, 23 degrees and 54 minutes fall between. From there to the equator, 23 degrees and 32 minutes remain. And from there to the Tropic of Capricorn, 23 degrees and 33 minutes. These together make 47 degrees and six minutes; and the distance of the other parallels to each other is as great as the distance from the pole of the world to the pole of the zodiac; and so finally to the Tropic of Capricorn.

Habitation is also twofold. One kind is "good" or somewhat temperate, which is simply called habitation. The other is "evil" or greatly distemperate, either because of cold—such as the two parts approaching the poles—or because of heat—such as the places situated under the tropics—so much so that some of these habitations are declared uninhabitable due to their lack of balance. In this sense, a person having deformed or "evil" feet is said to "have no feet" according to the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*. Because of this, it should be known that some have doubted whether there is habitation under the line of equality <note>the Equator</note> or not. Among their number, **Ptolemy** <note>original: "Ptolomeus" — the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer</note> seems to have been of this opinion in the *Almagest*. He says: "Indeed, some say it is possible that the part of the earth under the equidistant line is habitable, because its climate is very good, for the sun’s shadow does not linger over the zenith of their heads because of the speed of its declination in latitude from the equator of the day." Because of this, summer and winter are of good proportion due to the short duration of the sun at the summit of their heads in both tropics. And he adds that what we say is based on estimation. But as to whether that which is under this line is inhabited, we have no knowledge of it, nor have we proven it, because no one from our habitable regions has reached it up to our day. Wherefore **Al-Battani** <note>original: "Albategni" — a 9th-century Arab astronomer</note> says in his 130th chapter: "Habitation of the equinoctial line is not perceived. We know of no one in our time who confesses to have seen it." We find that Ptolemy made no mention of it in his book. **Al-Farghani** <note>original: "Alfraganus" — a 9th-century astronomer whose work "On the Science of the Stars" was a major source for medieval Europe</note> also seems to imitate these views, saying: "Let us now begin to remember the habitable places of the earth according to what we know and what has reached us." Wherefore, after some parts, we find the latitude of the inhabited place according to what we have grasped and what has reached us.

<margin>Meteorologica</margin>
Others, however, have taken the opposite side, asserting without ambiguity that the places under the equator are not inhabited. Thus, in the second book of the *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle’s work on natural phenomena</note>, regarding two possible habitable regions: this one toward the upper pole which is according to us, and another toward the other pole and the south. These two alone are possible to be inhabited, and not beyond the "turnings"—that is, the tropics. For the shadow does not always go toward the north, but places become uninhabitable before the shadow fails or changes toward the south. Whatever is under the Bear—that is, under the Arctic pole—is uninhabitable from cold. And he finally adds: "And indeed, we know the inhabited world as far as its latitude reaches the uninhabitable." For these parts are not inhabited due to cold, and those others due to heat. Wherefore, those regions beyond the Indian Sea (such as in the east) and the Pillars of Hercules <note>the Strait of Gibraltar</note> (as in the west) seem to be joined by the sea, so that the entire habitable world is continuous. Thus he feels that two regions of the earth—lying between the Arctic circle and the Tropic of Cancer, and that intercepted between the Tropic of Capricorn and the Antarctic circle—are inhabited due to the temperament caused by heat and cold. The middle region intercepted between the two tropics is least inhabited by men; likewise, the two extremes are least inhabited because of the frost.

<margin>Tullius</margin>
**Tullius** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> also agrees with all these points in the *Dream of Scipio*, with his interpreter **Macrobius**. He says: 
> "You see the same earth as if bound and surrounded by circles. Of these, you see that two—most distant from each other and supported on both sides by the very poles of the heavens—have grown stiff with frost; but that middle and largest one is scorched by the heat of the sun. Two are habitable, of which the southern one—in which those people stand with their feet opposite to ours—has nothing to do with our race; but this other one, subject to the north wind, is the one you inhabit."

<margin>Macrobius</margin>
Wherefore his interpreter Macrobius explains that both these habitations are habitable, because that glacial numbness provides life neither to animal nor to crop. For in that air, the body lacks the food by which life is nourished. Also, the middle belt—the expositor says—and the greatest of all, by the eternal blast of continuous heat, makes the space which it occupies in its wide circuit uninhabitable to those who would see it because of the excess of heat. Between the extremes and the middle, the two larger than the ends but smaller than the middle are tempered by the lack of balance in their neighbors on both sides. In these alone nature has given the inhabitants the ability to take in the vital air. **Virgil**, who according to Macrobius was a scholar of all knowledge, says of these in the *Georgics*:
<margin>Virgil</margin>
> "Five zones possess the sky; of which one is always red with the flashing sun and always torrid from fire. Around which, on the far right and left, two extend, frozen with blue ice and black storms. Between these and the middle one, two were granted to weary mortals by the gift of the gods, and a path was cut between them where the slanted order of the signs <note>the Zodiac</note> might turn."

Wherefore his contemporary, that wondrous truth-teller **Ovid**, says at the beginning of the *Metamorphoses*: 
<margin>Ovid</margin>
> "And as two zones cut the sky on the right and as many on the left part, and the fifth is hotter than those, so the mass enclosed was distinguished by the same number."

God's care placed as many regions upon the earth. Of these, the
middle one is not habitable due to the heat; deep snow covers two;
between both he placed as many. And he gave a temperate climate
mixed with heat and cold. In this matter, as will appear, the opinion

uninhabitable for two reasons. For some, on account of
the immense and scorching heat of the sun in those places,

<margin>Belenus the Architect</margin>
of the ancient philosophers, of whom one was **Belenus**

at four thousand and five cubits per mile, according to

**Averroes** judges to be most habitable

He also reported that he saw the Antarctic Pole elevated above the earth by the length of a long soldier’s lance in appearance, while the Arctic Pole was hidden. From there, he also announced that camphor, aloe wood, and brazilwood <note>original: "verzi"; a red dye-wood highly valued in the Middle Ages, long before the discovery of the country Brazil.</note> are exported to us. He testifies that there is intense heat there and few dwellings. Indeed, he saw these things on a certain island which he reached by sea. He says also that there are men there, and very large rams having thick, hard wool like the bristles of our pigs. He notes that there is no access to these places except by sea. To this, Belenus <note>a legendary figure often associated with Apollonius of Tyana in medieval Arabic-Latin translations.</note> agrees in the second part of his *Quadripartitum*. And some say that at both ends of the world—in the north as well as the south—there are men who eat other men, and these people have deformed and hairy faces. And I have seen men among those who travel the world who said they had seen this themselves. And Hermes said in the *Book of Latitude* that at the edges of the north and south dwell spirits, devils, and beasts that harm others. 

As to whether there are men who destroy others under the Arctic Pole, this has been reported to me, <term>Pietro d'Abano</term> <note>original: "Petro padubanensi"; a famous 13th-century Italian philosopher and astrologer known for reconciling Greek and Arabic science with Christian thought.</note>, by men worthy of faith in Pisa. Similarly, while I was in the regions of Gaul, I heard from a most faithful companion that in the reaches of Norway there are spirits whom men expel by the sign of the cross; these spirits construct side-paths from which various sights are vanished. From these testimonies, therefore, he judges that the equatorial line must be habitable, and that some have gone there and returned again, since the passage is made from this inhabited region to that in which the Antarctic Pole appears elevated. This could in no way happen except by crossing under the equator, since the whole world lies spread out from east to west.

All the aforementioned is also proven by many reasons, because between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn there is also habitation where the sun passes twice a year over their heads (at the zenith), and for a small space of time—say, one, two, three, or four months. There is also habitation under the Tropic of Cancer where the sun reaches the zenith only once a year, remaining there for a long time, according to that line of Lucan: "<term>Syene</term> which never casts a shadow" <note>original: "Nusquam flectentem Syene". Syene (modern Aswan, Egypt) was famous in antiquity because at the summer solstice, the sun is directly overhead and vertical objects cast no shadow.</note>. For it is a city established under the Tropic of Cancer in which, when the sun reaches the first minute of Cancer on one day of the year at noon, it has a straight shadow within itself and deflected to no side. Therefore, it will be much better under the equinoctial line <note>the Equator</note>, since the space of one passage of the sun over the zenith of those living there is separated from the other passage by a space of six months; and as will be shown, the sun passing over them does not linger at the zenith of their heads. 

That the aforementioned places are inhabited is also testified by <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian authority on geography and astronomy.</note> in the second part of the *Quadripartitum*, and by <term>Alfraganus</term> <note>original: "Alfa granus"; a 9th-century Persian astronomer whose works were foundational to medieval European science.</note> along with others in their distinctions of the climates. Regarding these people living in these climates in almost our own days, Friar John the <term>Cordelier</term> <note>likely referring to John of Montecorvino, a Franciscan missionary to the East.</note> wrote a letter from the region of Ma'bar <note>original: "mobabar"; the Coromandel Coast of South India</note> in India, in the shores where the body of the Apostle Thomas lies, saying that in India it is always summer and never scorching heat, because there are usually winds which temper the heat. There is no winter there because the sun, which always passes directly over the heads of those living there, declines very little 

to the south or the north. Whence, on the 24th day of August, I saw with my own eyes and proved that the ray of the sun fell so directly upon the heads of the inhabitants that it made no shadow in any direction. And the same happens near the end of the month of March. Thus, therefore, it seems that the parallel circle in which the zenith of their heads is figured passes through the seventh or eighth degree of Virgo; for then, on the 22nd day of August, the sun was there, and through the 22nd or 23rd degree of Aries. Because of this, they do not seem to be distant from the invisibility of the equator except by a space of eight degrees and forty minutes of latitudinal distance. He also testifies that the star called "Tramontana" <note>the North Star (Polaris)</note> appeared so low there that it could hardly be seen. Because of this, he thought that from some high place another "Tramontana" <note>a south polar star</note> might be seen toward the south. This, however, is not the case if—as astrologers prove—the earth is of no size compared to the heaven, provided that in a low place there was nothing hindering the vision. He says also that he saw signs revolving around the parts of the other "Tramontana," yet he did not see the star itself. And he reports this to be on account of many vapors ascending around those parts. 

Therefore, the stated assumption of the reasoning appears clear, from which a conclusion will necessarily be inferred. Even if the sun lingers little over the zenith of their heads, indeed it passes quickly; whence <term>Ptolemy</term> in the aforementioned book compared to him, in the first and second parts, says: "The speech should be believed that the land which is under the equinoctial is approximately temperate." For there is one heating cause, which is the opposition of the sun to the heads, which alone does not make a great impression; but what brings a great impression is the long duration of the opposition. And therefore we see at the beginning of autumn and around the ninth hour, because of the longer delay, greater heat is generated than in summer and at noon, even if then the opposition is more direct. For on the land situated under the equinoctial line, the sun is not at the zenith of the inhabitants' heads except for a few days, and then it quickly moves away. But when the sun reaches the Tropic of Cancer or Capricorn, by the same path approaching and receding, it stays a long time over the zenith of their heads. For in the space of five days or more, it does not appear removed from there, because of which it heats them incessantly. And therefore, the land situated under the equinoctial line will be temperate. However, those situated under the tropics are distempered by heat especially; for under the tropics, there occurs the lingering, the proximity of the vertical ray, and the proximity of the sun's power. This does not happen under the line of the equator. Because of this, <term>Ptolemy</term> says it is necessary that this place be uninhabitable on account of the excess of heat—or if it is inhabited, then it is with some labor and not continuous habitation. However, the movement of the sun over the equator of the day and its change from it occurs with velocity. It is necessary, therefore, from this that the places of habitation which are under the equator of the day are temperate. Furthermore, under the line of equality, since the hot day always equals the night, one will always temper the other—namely, the cold and the hot—so much so that the habitation is a prolongation of temperance.
