<meta>This page continues the discussion on the habitability of the Earth's regions, specifically addressing the theory that the equator is the most temperate and habitable zone, countering the traditional view that it was a "torrid" and uninhabitable wasteland.</meta>

This does not happen among those who live near the stationary points or under the **Tropic of Cancer** or the **Tropic of Capricorn**. Furthermore, it is clear from many "distempered" <note>original: "distemperatis"; meaning regions with extreme or unbalanced qualities of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness.</note> and brief conditions that a single temperateness arises. This happens under the **equinoctial line** <note>The Equator.</note>. Indeed, it is said that all seasons of the year exist there simultaneously, and none of those seasons exceeds the others in any quality, unlike our own. Likewise, where winds blow frequently, cooling the air and preventing the direct refraction of solar rays, and where many vapors rise from the seas, rivers, and lakes, the heat is rendered temperate. 

But this happens under the equator because the same occurs between the equator and the **Tropic of Cancer**, for instance in **India**, as I have brought forward from the account of the **Cordeliers** <margin>under whom Damascene and the Cordeliers</margin> <note>The Cordeliers were Franciscan friars, so named for the knotted cord they wore as belts.</note>, where the intense heat is mitigated into a temperate state. Again, regarding the received rays: because under the equator they reach the peak of the earth's curve, they cannot be reflected in the same way as those hitting a flat or concave surface—as the experts in optics <note>original: "perspectivi"; scholars of medieval optics</note> also perceive—which does not happen in other places. Furthermore, where there is a great reflection and meeting of the rays of celestial bodies, habitation there is possible and temperate. Since the nature of the higher bodies, by their proximity to one another, contributes to a proportionate balance of heat and moisture, as was declared in chapter ten. Similarly, the sun, along with the other planets, is the cause of generation and life through its approach to us, and the cause of corruption and death through its retreat. Since this occurs in the best possible way under the equator, that place will be habitable and temperate. 

As for the argument some use—that fruit brought recently around the time of Christ’s Nativity was ripe—it is not valid; for he could have brought it from India, in which fresh fruits are good at all times, as **Damascene** and the **Cordelier** testify. Regarding this and similar points, it must be concluded that there is habitation under the equinoctial line and it is temperate, so much so that according to **Aristotle**, in this place, there will be a <term>justicial temperateness</term> <note>An "absolute" or "mathematical" balance of qualities, like legal justice.</note>, and also a "relative" one. 

However, near the extremes of the **fourth climate** and beyond, there will be a temperateness relative to any of the four simple distempered complexions, which are partly tempered. In the **first** and **second climate**, at the beginning of the **third**, and in the **sixth** and **seventh**, there will be a lack of temperateness relative to the four completely distempered composite complexions. Nor should it be said that temperateness is removed from the equator because of the heat, because our life even stands with quite extensive heat, but not so with cold. This also appears through the first of the *Aphorisms*, where it is said that air, however hot it may be, is cold compared to our body and especially to our spirits. Therefore, the air there, though much hotter than ours, will be well-suited to our body. 

Regarding the aforementioned things, a doubt arises because **Galen**, in the third part of the *Aphorisms* and elsewhere, seems to place the temperate region in a different place. <margin>Doubt?</margin> He claims that the truly and most certainly well-mixed and middle zone of the world is the East and the West, which is through **Kindia** and **Cos**, and through regions that do not depart much from these either toward the North or the South. 

---

But you must consider which regions **Hippocrates** mentioned: namely, the regions to the East and West stretched along a certain straight line, which those who are skilled in such matters understand most certainly as the "well-mixed zone" <note>original: "eucratam zonam"; from the Greek "eukratos," meaning well-blended or temperate.</note>. He wishes, therefore, the more temperate habitation to be contained by two lines extended from East to West, one of which passes <margin>Kindia, Constantinople</margin> through **Kindia**, which is a place situated opposite **Constantinople** toward the East, and the other through **Cos**, known today as the island of **Lango**, the land of **Hippocrates**. The distance between these in latitude is about 300 miles. These lines contain some of the **fifth climate** and a large part of the **fourth**. Whence, in the first book of *Theory*: 

-> **Temperate Regions** <-

Temperate regions are those placed under a straight line from East to West, and those which are closest and bordering them, such as those inhabiting the **fourth climate**, which are in the middle between the two extremes of heat and cold. **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, an Arab astrologer.</note> also approves of the temperateness of the middle of the **fourth climate** and the **third**, declining toward the Salt Sea. Furthermore, **Albumasar** says in the third book of his *Introduction* that the land of prophets and wise men is located there, just as it also appears in the second book of the *Quadripartitum*. **Averroes** also, in the second book of his *Colliget*, says his son **Licho** praises the **fifth [climate]** beyond others, which perhaps happens because he wished to improve the status of his own region. For everyone naturally loves their own place, since it contributes to their generation and preservation. 

None of these places is under the equator; because of this, since one should not grant such great men to be insufficient by neglecting the temperateness of the equinoctial line, it seems that it does not exist. He adds also: "Under the <term>scale of the day</term> <note>original: "sub lance diei"; a technical term for the equator, referring to the balance of day and night.</note> the weather is not temperate, as many people think," and he says this had been declared elsewhere. 

To the first point, it must be said that the aforementioned opinion remains unshaken: that these physicians, acting based on what is sensible and apparent (since the investigation of physicians does not transcend the senses), consider what happens in the majority of cases. However, the temperateness of the equator was unknown to most, as has been and will be touched upon, and so they kept silent. For the things they consider in medicine, they perceive through the most sensible experiments. As for **Averroes**, I do not hold with him here, since he rendered himself suspect in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* regarding things subject to the consideration of astrology, whatever he might have promised as a young man in the second book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*. Or perhaps "under the scale of the day"—that is, under the equator—where the ray is direct and sharpened like a <term>lance</term> <note>The author is playing on the Latin words "lancea" (lance/spear) and "lances" (scales of a balance).</note>, or like the pans of a scale, as it appeared to Aristotle. For his concern was foremost in contradicting that view above others. 

Therefore, according <margin>No</margin> to the second point, it should be known that some mathematicians have said the region intercepted between the **Tropic of Capricorn** and the **Antarctic Circle** is not inhabited, both because of the eccentricity of the sun's circle (proved by **Ptolemy** in the third book of the *Almagest*) and thus because of proximity, and because of the directness [of the rays], and because of the duration [of the sun's stay]. For these three causes of heat are seen under the **Tropic of Capricorn**.

Regarding the fourth point, in response to the primary authorities of **Aristotle** and others, it must be said either that they held that opinion which I do not now approve, or they understood the "Torrid Zone" to be those parts near the tropics which are uninhabitable due to immense heat. However, a statement is left by **Aristotle** that there is no habitation beyond the **Tropic of Cancer**, which appears from his claim that the shadow will always fall toward the north, and habitation would fail before the shadow could change toward the south. To these, he responds that if these parts are inhabited—and based on those speaking of these things and those who think they can refute **Aristotle**—it is believed by the troublesome <note>Those who find the heat unbearable.</note> that these parts would be uninhabitable because of the burning heat. For **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the famous Persian polymath.</note> says they stay in water for the most part and live in a certain way against nature. Or they are those living under the tropics or at a short distance from them. Indeed, the regions further beyond the tropics are habitable despite the burning heat.

The first part of this discourse also touches upon **Alexander**, who posited that the **equinoctial line** <note>The Equator.</note> was temperate.

However, he makes himself suspect since it has been shown that heat is more intense under the tropics, and that by moving away from the tropics toward the equinoctial line, the heat is continually lessened and acquires temperateness. Nor can **Aristotle** be saved <note>In the sense of his argument being preserved as true.</note> as was shown before. For it is not inconsistent that the same man might perceive opposite things at different times. Some, however, say that the passage from here to there or vice versa cannot be completed because there are mountains there which have a nature that draws men to them, just as a magnet attracts iron. For they say that they laugh while they are being drawn, and once drawn, they are held fast.

There, he says, 'we saw two rocks from which a huge force of the river fell out, but whether that is the source or an addition to the Nile, or whether it is born there in the earth or returns from a previous hidden course, is unknown.'" Some report that there is such a great desert and sandy place, full of serpents and poisonous animals and fresh waters, that no one can easily pass through there.

However, what happened to them has remained unknown for almost thirty years now. Nevertheless, a passage is now open by going through the **Great Tartars** <note>The Mongol Empire.</note> toward the north, then circling around toward the east and south.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the habitability of the Earth's equatorial regions. While previous pages focused on the "Torrid Zone" as a potential barrier, this page refines the argument by comparing the climate at the Equator (the "line of equality") with the climate at the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. It also introduces the medieval scientific theory of winds, blending physics with astrology.</meta>

...so that it rises up to the lunar globe. Anyone who claims that the sphere of fire <note>In the medieval geocentric model, a layer of fire existed between the atmosphere and the moon.</note> runs into the truth does not hold a clear vision, but possesses a <term>waxy nose</term> <note>original: "naso cereo"; a medieval idiom for an argument or text that is easily manipulated or twisted to suit any purpose</note> that is subjugated by whatever hollow thing it encounters. Also, in maps and descriptions of the earth, it is written that there will be a place conspicuous for the pleasantness of all things, but uninhabitable for humans, surrounded by a fiery wall reaching all the way to heaven. Within this place, the Tree of Life remains, along with many other things, as the commentators on the Book of Genesis declare. However, the martyrs who were brought before this reality testify unanimously that they felt nothing of this Paradise. 

Regarding another point already shown, what must be said according to the previously noted and very frequent occurrences is this: it must be stated that under the <term>line of equality</term> <note>The Equator.</note>, the primary causes of heat do not converge. For the "delay" <note>original: "mora"; referring to how long the sun's rays linger over a specific point.</note>, which is the most powerful cause of heat, is found to be minimal there, as has been said. There is also the effect of the direction of the rays—namely, the reflection into a straight line and the axis—where the rays are dispersed and removed, partly because of the "round summit of smoke" <note>original: "apicem fumuz rotundū"</note> in that place, and partly because of the winds and vapors moved there.

Nor is the proximity there rendered so much greater that an opposing effect does not occur because of the speed of the motion in those same places, as was shown previously.

Regarding another point, it must be said that the sun's passage once a year over the <term>zenith</term> <note>The point directly overhead.</note> of the heads of those living under the **Tropic of Cancer** or **Capricorn** inflames that place much more—as has been declared—than the two passages that occur over the heads of those living under the line of equality. This is because at the equator, night is continuously equal to day, and no "delay" of the sun intervenes to build up heat.

Regarding the other point, it has already appeared how the rays are rendered scattered and powerless. For under the line of equality, they fall upon a convex surface rather than a concave one; and as is plain to those who study <term>perspectives</term> <note>The medieval science of optics.</note>, such rays heat very little, for they temper themselves.

Regarding another point, it must be said that it is not a similar case. For life persists better with a greater elevation in the sky—as shown in section 61—than with cold, because heat is a friend to nature, while cold is paralyzing and "mortifying" <note>original: "mortificū"; meaning death-dealing or deadening.</note> in that place.

Furthermore, this reasoning does not prove that exceeding heat exists under the Equator, as has appeared, but rather elsewhere, such as under the two aforementioned Tropics. Regarding the other point, it must be said that there is indeed an uninhabitable place due to heat, just as there is one due to cold; but this is under the **Tropic of Cancer** and **Capricorn**, not under the designated Equinoctial line.

### Concerning the Nature of Wind

Next, concerning what was said about the winds tempering the air, there is a doubt. For every wind is cold, according to Book 2, Chapter 5 of the *Meteorologica*. Furthermore, a wind is made from a dry <term>exhalation</term> <note>Medieval science taught that "exhalations" rose from the earth to form wind, while "vapors" rose from water to form rain.</note> so that it flows, driven by the cold of the world. But such a thing does not temper the air; rather, it cools it further. Additionally, wind is caused by the motion of the air, for it is properly an "affection" or property of the air itself. Such motion cools, for motion creates coldness. A sign of this is that things being moved cool down hot things, as seen in Book 25 <note>Likely referring to Aristotle’s *Problems*.</note>. And as happens in plants and with moving pots that are boiling—as noted in Book 5—the water is cooled when moved. Furthermore, that which creates heat does not temper it; and yet wind, since it is in motion, creates heat, as was touched upon. For all motion creates heat. Therefore, according to Book 14 of *On the Generation of Animals*, section 30, heat is a motive force. Hence, in Book 26, it is asked why winds, which are cold, exist because of hot motion. Furthermore, they do not temper the air because of the very humid air, which is an impediment. Likewise, because it was said that winds are caused by dry exhalations, they therefore do not temper the air. 

To the contrary: that which purifies, clarifies, and thins the air tempers it, preventing its alteration and corruption; such is the nature of wind, as is also shown by moving water. Regarding the first point, it must first be known what wind is, from where it is caused, and how. Second, how many there are and of what kind. Third, their descriptive "pygraphia" <note>A likely corruption of "paragraphia" or "geographia," referring to the mapping or description of the winds.</note> should be set forth so that the arguments finally become clear.

<margin>WIND</margin>
Regarding the first point, it must be known that wind is air moved from a determined place by a multitude of dry, smoky exhalations, according to the *Meteorologica*. Some, however, have said that winds are simply the air in motion, a view which is rejected in Book 6 of the *Topics* and Book 2, section 30 of the *Meteorologica*. For not every movement of air causes a wind, just as not every movement of water causes a river; rather, it only occurs when the source is from an original fountain from which a multitude of water continually flows. This is confirmed because that which is humid by its nature is not the same as that which is dry; but air is naturally humid. For humidity is primarily present in it, as seen in distinction 12. Wind, however, is dry, since it is a dry, smoky exhalation. Likewise, it would follow that all winds would be continuous and a single wind, just as the air is one.

Furthermore, they would all blow at the same time if all parts of the air were moved together, which is contrary to the *Meteorologica*, which holds that two contrary winds cannot blow at the same time; I have shown more on this in *Problem* 25.

In the book *On the World*, it is said that wind is "air flowing greatly and suddenly." **Seneca**, in the fourth book of his *Natural Questions*, says it is "air agitated in one direction." 
<margin>SENECA</margin>
In the fifth book of the same, he says: "It is a dry vapor resolved from the body of the earth." Indeed, these descriptions can be criticized, except for the first one.

Regarding the second point, it must be known that its cause is twofold. One is "material," namely the dry, smoky exhalation resolved mostly from the earth, though more or less diversified, as already indicated. The other is "efficient," such as the **Sun**, most especially by its motion and heat, and also in conjunction with the other planets and signs. For **Saturn**, when moving with it, stirs up the Eastern winds; **Venus**, the Southern winds; the **Moon** with **Mars**, the Western winds; and **Jupiter** with **Mercury**, the Northern winds.

<margin>The Triplicity of the Signs</margin>
The **Fiery Triplicity**—namely **Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius**—stirs up the Eastern winds. The **Earthen**—such as **Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn**—the Southern. The **Airy**—**Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius**—the Western. But the **Watery**—such as **Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces**—the Northern.

The fifteen fixed stars of the first magnitude also move the winds by their rising and setting, according to the first book of the *Skeptic Art* of **Ptolemy**, and his work *On Air and Water*, along with the *Aphorisms*. This happens because of the heat trapped within the pores...

<meta>This page transitions from the general climate of the equatorial regions to a specific technical discussion of "Meteorology"—the science of the atmosphere. It focuses on the classification, origin, and physical qualities of the winds, bridging Aristotelian physics with practical navigation and geography.</meta>

<meta>Two columns of text. Humanistic cursive hand with frequent abbreviations.</meta>

<sig>A 1 z. p.</sig>

The exhalation of the air causes a dry vapor, which by its own power is led directly upward until it reaches the middle region of the air. There, it is first refracted laterally and obliquely, blowing downward. Thus, in the third book of <term>Meteorology</term> <note>original: "methauron s3o"; referring to Aristotle's treatise on natural phenomena</note>, the motion of the wind is described as beginning from above, though the source of its material generation is from below; its path is oblique because it blows around the earth. In that same third book, although the primary source of the winds' material is from the lower regions, the start of the motions, blasts, and whirlwinds is from the upper regions. This is the common judgment according to <term>the Philosopher</term> <note>Aristotle was almost always referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance science.</note>.

Regarding this, it should be known that there are twelve winds noted in our inhabited region, just as there are twelve points from which they draw their origin, corresponding to the twelve signs used by astrologers. 

The first point is that which is proportioned to the location of the equator in the East, where the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>The path the sun follows across the sky.</note> intersects the immobile circle, or where the equinoctial sun rises; it is called **Apeliotes** or **Solanus**, and by others, **Eurus**. There are two others collateral to this one: to the left is the proper **Eurus**, and to the right is **Caecias** or **Vulturnus**. The first of these is marked at the point of the parallel of the Tropic of Capricorn (the winter sunrise), while the other is at the point proportioned to the parallel of Cancer (the summer sunrise). 

In the Southern region, under the Tropic of Cancer, a point is noted from which **Auster** or **Notus** is born. If located to the right, it is **Phoenicias** (also called **Euro-auster** or **Euro-nothus**), placed between Eurus and Auster. To the left, from point M, no wind is said to blow in the third book of <term>Meteorology</term>. However, in the book <term>On the Universe</term> <note>original: "de mundo"; a text often attributed to Aristotle in this period</note>, it is said that between **Libonotus** and **Notus**, some call it **Libanotun**, and others **Libaphyntha**. Commonly, it is called **Austro-africus**. 

From the point proportioned to the immobile section of the Zodiac at the equator (the equinoctial sunset), directly opposite the **Subsolanus**, rises **Zephyrus** or **Favonius**. To its right, corresponding to the point of the Tropic of Capricorn (the winter sunset), is **Lips** or **Africus**. To the left, at the parallel of the Tropic of Cancer (the summer sunset), is situated **Argestes**, also called **Olimpia**, **Iapyx**, **Phyrozona**, or **Chorus**. 

But at the point of the North, around the Arctic pole, is born **Aparktias**, **Boreas**, or **Septentrio**. Its right collateral wind is **Thrakias** or **Circius**, while the left is **Meses** or **Aquilo**. 

<margin>VARRO, SENECA, ISIDORE</margin>
This arrangement of the winds is taken mostly from the third book of <term>Meteorology</term>. **Varro**, **Seneca** in his *Natural Questions*, and **Isidore** in his *Etymologies* imitate this. **Haly Abbas** <note>A famous Persian physician and psychologist (died c. 982–994 AD).</note>, however, in the fifth part of his *Theoretica*, departs from them, for he writes **Chorus** where the others place **Circius**. In all other things, he coincides with the rest. Because of this, the common saying seems to deviate somewhat from these, as the poets say: 

->**Subsolanus**, **Vulturnus**, and **Eurus** belong to the Dawn.<-
->And at midday, **Notus** clings to **Africus** and **Auster**.<-
->**Circius**, **Zephyrus**, and **Favonius** blow from the sunset.<-
->**Aquilo**, **Boreas**, and **Chorus** come down from the North.<-

There are four principal winds, coming from the four points denoted: East, South, West, and North. These are also attributed to four signs: Aries, Capricorn, Libra, and Cancer. There are also eight collateral companions. However, sailors alone posit sixteen winds, for they are the ones governing their ships upon the sea; of these, eight are called principal and eight are "middle-men" situated on either side between them. 

I said there would be twelve in "our region" because in the region proportioned to this one, located between the Tropic of Cancer and the Antarctic parallel (which is also habitable according to the third book of <term>Meteorology</term>), there are twelve winds arranged in the same way, and thus there would be twenty-four. Among the **Antipodes** <note>People living on the opposite side of the Earth.</note>—those who dwell with their feet opposite ours, according to **Ptolemy** in the *Spica*—there will also be twenty-four. For according to the twofold upper habitation mentioned before, there will be a twofold lower one, making forty-eight winds in the whole universe. Some say the winds in the upper hemisphere originate from those in the lower, because those that are Eastern in the upper are Western in the lower, and vice versa, as appears here in the <term>Problemata</term> <note>Another work by Aristotle.</note> and in the third book of <term>Meteorology</term>. 

**Oribasius** <note>A Greek medical writer and personal physician to the Emperor Julian.</note>, however, says in his tenth book that some have posited only two winds because of East and West. Others four, because of the four quarters of the world. Others twelve, because of the four seasons, dividing each into three months. 

The quality and nature of every wind, by reason of its matter, is mostly dry and also cold. But it is diversified by its form according to the places through which it passes, influenced both by the sun and the local material. For Eastern winds, because they are born under the rays of the sun (though when the sun is not yet at its full strength nor have they been under it for long), are moderately hot. Because they pass over high, dry places with little water, they take on a certain dryness. 

Southern winds (**Nothi**), because they come from under the sun when it is in its full power and stay with it for a long time—and because they travel through seas and watery marshes—are distemperately hot and moist. 

Western winds (**Zephyri**), because they blow as the sun is receding and losing its vigor, are somewhat cold; and because they travel over very watery places (as noted in the 26th book of the <term>Problemata</term>, the magnitude and depth of the sea is toward the West), they are rendered more moist. 

Northern winds, however, because they are far from the sun's path and pass over arid and frozen places, are very cold and dry. 

Therefore, the Eastern winds are naturally healthy; then the Western; while the others are "distempered" (unbalanced). Of these, the Eastern are the healthiest in themselves. The Northern are healthy by accident <note>meaning their healthiness is a side-effect, such as by clearing the air of pestilence through cold</note>, the Southern are worse, and the Western are, as it were, in the middle. This is verified according to the local disposition; for the arrangement of the sea, mountains, and burnt desert places changes the winds, as the first part of the third book of <term>Meteorology</term> shows. 

Regarding the third point, it should be known that the description of the winds is commonly represented in a circular figure, like the "drums" of maps <note>original: "tympana"; refers to the circular wind roses found on portolan charts</note>, which is better for understanding since the human habitation is Earthly according to **Aly** <note>Likely referring again to Haly Abbas.</note>. Let a figure therefore be described with circular lines, points, and winds as is appropriate. This is its representation: /

Regarding the fourth point, it must be said that every wind is cold, as is evident by the nature of its matter. Or rather, it is better to say here that a wind is cold because, by pushing away the air immediately surrounding us—which has been warmed by our own body heat—it causes the cold to be felt. Whence <term>the Philosopher</term> <note>Aristotle</note> says in the fifth book of *Physics*: "Our own body always emits a certain warm vapor from itself which heats the nearby air, just like a glowing ember." Regarding the next point to be discussed: a wind is indeed very dry and cold by reason of its material. To the next point, it should be said that motion, as motion, does not cool; rather, it heats in whatever disposition. It seems, however, to cool in subtle things like air and even water for the reasons declared in the previous argument's solution. Or, it is because motion removes another cause that was a more powerful perceived cause of cooling than the wind was a cause of heating—as seen when blowing on or stirring pots. This occurs because of the air they push into the pots, the division of the boiling liquid (which, by exhaling heat, is reduced), and the prevention of the refraction of the sun's rays by the motion of the water occurring in it, especially when moving faster, as <term>the Philosopher</term> <note>Aristotle</note> declared in the fifth book. To the next point that appears to be discussed: motion itself heats, but it cools only by accident, as shown below. To the final point, it should be said that although air is moist, wind is not; for such a quality is not inherent to the air itself, but is rather acquired from the dry, smoky exhalation and the motion of the sun. Similarly, it appears that the next point should be addressed.

## DIFFERENCE LXVIII.

That the flesh of snails is of more excellent nourishment than others is shown by the fact that they are served to <term>consumptives</term> <note>original: "ethicis"; referring to those suffering from 'hectic' fever or wasting diseases like tuberculosis.</note>. Similarly, the flesh of crabs is given to those lacking excellent nourishment, as indicated by their emaciation and extreme weakness. It also appears that some fish are superior; for one of the conditions of excellent food is that it be easily digestible, and these fish—being soft—demonstrate this by how quickly they are cooked. For this reason, the flesh of snails and fish is more excellent than others. However, many hold the opposite view, preferring the meat of beasts, as shall be shown. But that the meat of quadrupeds is better than others is shown by the fact that the principle of nutrition is perfected by similarity. For nutrition is the perfected assimilation of the nutrient into the thing being nourished. Such animals are more similar to us, as noted by their forms, figures, and the dispositions of their entire bodies. And therefore, it is deduced that human flesh would be more excellent than all others as it is the most proportional. This is shown by the goodness of human milk compared to that of others. For this reason, <term>Galen</term> <note>The most influential Greek physician of antiquity, whose works dominated medieval medicine.</note> in the seventh book of *On the Method of Healing* prefers pork to all others for nourishment, since he indicates that pigs are more similar to us than the rest. Whence in the third book of *On Foods*: "The similarity of pork can be learned from the fact that certain people once ate human flesh thinking it was pork, having no suspicion based on its taste or smell." For it was discovered through evil innkeepers and others that it had been hidden until human fingers were found in the dishes. <note>This "cannibal innkeeper" story was a common trope in medieval medical texts used to prove the biological similarity between humans and pigs.</note> This actually occurred in the Florentine Alps by a wicked host who, beheading and robbing travelers, sold them as pork; people were moved to eat it greedily because of the flavor. Furthermore,

Frogs.

it seems that the flesh of turtles, porcupines, and hedgehogs is more excellent because they expel their "superfluities" into their shells and spines, just as fish with more scales are praised; for this reason, these are considered more choice. On the contrary, the meat of birds—and especially of chickens—is shown to be superior, since they are temperate and more akin to human food, except for the <term>necks</term> <note>original: "collis"; Galenic medicine often categorized specific parts of animals as having different nutritional qualities.</note>. They are also of a softer and more porous substance. Because of this, they are more obedient to digestion and penetration, and finally, they provide the fastest nutrition. Therefore, these merits surpass the others. Regarding the first point, it must be known what meat is in terms of its composition...

<meta>This page continues the medical and dietary discourse, shifting from the elemental properties of air and wind to the nutritional science of foods, specifically focusing on the qualities of different meats, the process of digestion, and the specific benefits of pork and various fish according to classical authorities like Galen and Aristotle.</meta>

The actual difference has been sufficiently shown in **Difference 42**. For although "flesh" is properly called a body that is hot, moist, and soft—generated from blood and thus belonging only to animals—it can nevertheless be called so metaphorically in those creatures lacking blood, because they have something proportional to flesh. What nutrition actually is, and how often it is discussed, is shown in **Difference 53**. 

Here, however, "sustenance" is understood as that which exists most remotely outside the body, according to the principle of the first book: <note>original: "Nutriens masticatione"</note> "That which nourishes through chewing." Praise be to Christ! Nutrition is considered based on whether it is easily digestible, not viscous or coarse, having little waste, yet not so subtle that it quickly evaporates from the limbs; it must also possess a power that is familiar and innate to the one being nourished. This is seen in the seventh book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>Galen’s *De Ingenio Sanitatis*</note> and the book *On Foods*. 

**Folio 30**

For some things provide much nutrition and are close to human nature, yet they are hard to digest and slow to pass through the parts of the body, such as the flesh of pigs, since they are viscous and full of superfluities. Others, however, are digested quickly and are not viscous, but because they evaporate more rapidly, they give little and non-lasting nourishment to the body, such as the meat of small birds. The preference for meats is also diversified according to the elements dominant in them: for some are terrestrial <note>land-based</note>, some are aquatic, and some are aerial, even though all are composed of the four elements. These are also diversified by reason of their origin, location, season, life, and exercise, as the books *On Foods* and *On Diets* show. This inquiry has such a long output that a significant treatise could be composed on it, both because of the nature of the matter and because of the evident disagreement among those speaking on it. Briefly, however, the truth of the matter will be investigated.

Truly, terrestrial and aerial animals provide more praiseworthy and better nourishment than aquatic ones; and those of the earth more than those of the air, though the latter are still praiseworthy. Nutrition is also diversified in three ways:
1. By reason of the food itself, because it possesses the aforementioned praiseworthy qualities.
2. On the part of the one being nourished; for that which tastes good is more nutritious and praiseworthy, according to that ancient saying: <note>original: "Pay deterior cibus & poty"</note> "Better is a food and drink that pleases." Whence <term>Haly Abbas</term> <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician</note> says: "Good food [sometimes] generates bad blood, and bad food generates good." 
3. On the part of both, as there is a certain hidden power between them. 

For although a specific food is ascribed to definite species in the seventh book of the *History of Animals* <note>Aristotle's work</note>—such as bitter vetch for oxen or acorns for pigs—it is also attributed to the individual and even to the specific limb. And so we see some people adopt one specific food and are healthily nourished by it, while it is different for others. Just as I myself, though seeing someone enjoying eating milk and especially mixing it with bread, am soon moved to vomit, even though that food is pleasant to most. The <term>Centiloquium</term> <note>A collection of 100 aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note> attempts to assign a cause for this. Whence, in the seventh book of *Method of Healing*: "The intent of fitness for foods is twofold: one is the nature of the food itself, the other is the familiar and innate power of nourishing." 

And this discourse must be heard even more regarding the measured body. Whence in the third book of *On Foods*: "I have indicated that one must always refer the discourse to a proportionate constitution, according to all my treatises and especially in the healing regimen." Similarly, in the <term>Canon</term> <note>The *Canon of Medicine* by Avicenna</note> regarding comparison:

The previous point was shown in **Difference 22**. Therefore, in that same third book: "When you hear me comparing the species of animals to one another, inquire, discern, and discuss the discourse; even experience shows that a species does not nourish well if it is not fat, lean, or fed properly, nor if it is too young or too old; for such a comparison would be perverse and unjust." 

Regarding the second point, it should be known that although fish are sought after by many nations (and the Italians have better ones and use them more), no one has ever uniformly preferred their nutrition to that of terrestrial animals and birds. Yet <term>Galen</term> praises marine fish above others. For some are born in the sea and remain there; others come from there to fresh waters. Some are born in fresh water and usually feed there, rarely approaching the salt water. Others are born and eat in both; all of these are diversified, as touched upon, by reason of species, place, and exercise. Specifically, he commends "fortified" fish along with others for their goodness: the viscous ones, <term>sole</term> <note>Latin: *buglossas*, literally 'ox-tongue'</note>, <term>torpedo rays</term>, <term>parrotfish</term>, <term>sturgeon</term>, <term>mullet</term>, <term>open-sea fish</term>, <term>gray mullet</term>, <term>gobies</term>, <term>sticklebacks</term>, and the like. <margin>It is agreed</margin> Among the quadrupeds, however, he prefers not a little the flesh of pigs, saying it nourishes the most. Whence <term>Democritus</term> says: "Pork, when it has been well digested, nourishes the best blood." For we find nothing better for the nutrition of the body, as we see in those of greater age. 

Therefore, in the third book of *On Foods*: "Of all edibles, the flesh of pigs is the most nutritious," of which athletes have the most evident experience. And in the eighth book of *On the Method of Healing*: "The better pork is that from the mountains, and thereafter those raised upon them." And in the fifth book of *Theoretical Medicine*: "Of quadrupeds, pork is the most praiseworthy, being temperate in heat and moisture; its food is most excellent and the blood generated from it is better than all other blood." Whence the <term>Canon</term> <note>Avicenna</note>, folio 30: "The Christians say, and those who imitate them, that the best meat is the meat of the wild boar." Yet <term>Aristotle</term> <note>referred to as 'A.'</note> imposes a choice in the fifth book of *Animals*, saying: "The best of meats is pork," and he feels that this meat is, as it were, more natural to humans than the meat of other walking animals, and experience teaches this. And these thinkers have respected these meats more because they provide the most nourishment and are most similar to our bodies. This is shown by convalescents, who are restored more quickly by it. They are, however, difficult to digest and provide viscous nourishment unless location, exercise, and a vigorous life mitigate them. 

Whence in the seventh book of *Method of Healing*: "If food could digest and assimilate itself to the one being nourished, then one would only need the most nutritious foods. But because that which nourishes is not the same as that which performs the digestion, one must choose not only the food that is most nutritious in itself, but that which can be digested quickly." It also exhibits a temperate nourishment in every way. For that which is most nutritious cannot [always] be the most easily digestible. Also, in the third book of the <term>Almansor</term> <note>The *Liber ad Almansorem* by the physician Rhazes</note>: "It is preferred as an edible; for it is temperate, having no admixture of malice in it." Whence in *On Particular Diets*, the suckling kids of goats are better than other animals in flavor, namely in nutrition, digestion, and the generation of good blood. <margin>thirst</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nutritional properties of different meats, specifically comparing domestic livestock, wild game, and various species of birds according to classical and Arabic medical authorities.</meta>

According to Oribasius, kid meat <note>young goat</note> is worthy of praise, as is the meat of lambs, regarding which he notes certain points. The majority of doctors, however, detest the meat of lambs because an excessive moisture dominates them; instead, they praise the meat of young rams. It is appropriate to say that lamb meat is good because of the overall quality of edible meats. Rhazes holds this opinion as well, along with Avicenna and Al-Abbas <note>Haly Abbas, a famous Persian physician</note>.

Among wild animals, those of the roe deer are most praised, as noted by Almansor <note>Rhazes' book dedicated to Al-Mansur</note> and Avicenna. Gazelle meat is considered the best among wild meats because of its inclination toward moderate qualities; for this reason, the meat of young ones should be chosen. Regarding this, in the books on dietetics, it is said that all wild animals are neither as flavorful nor as nutritious as domestic ones, except for roe deer, which are more flavorful, more nutritious, and more praiseworthy when wild. This is because, through excessive movement and labor, their blood is refined, their pores are opened, and their superfluities <note>waste products or excess humors</note> are expelled. 

There is an even greater disagreement regarding birds. According to Galen's reasoning on food, the meat of birds is more digestible, especially that of partridges, francolins, pigeons, hens, cocks, thrushes, blackbirds, peacocks, and sparrows. Among these are turtledoves, which are harder than the others, and even more so are the meat of the duck and the goose. Similar to the meat of cocks and pheasants in terms of digestion and nourishment are those which provide a similar delight to the palate. However, the meat of peacocks is harder, difficult to digest, and more suitable for those with strong constitutions. In the eighth book of *On the Method of Healing*, it is said that among birds, the best are indeed partridges, along with all mountain sparrows, followed by hens, pheasants, and young pigeons—provided they are not kept cooped up inside. Such birds collect all sorts of superfluities because they are unexercised; this is also why birds from stagnant and marshy areas are less desirable. Regarding the aforementioned "sparrows," I understand this to mean small birds in general, not strictly the common sparrow. For they are very hot and incite lust. Isaac Judaeus and Almansor recommend the grey partridge <term>starna<span>The grey partridge, prized in medieval diets for its light, balanced nature.</span></term> above all others. The meat of the *starna* is lighter than all other bird meat and is beneficial for those who wish to maintain a refined health regimen; next to it in quality is the meat of the quail. After these, the meat of young chicks is ranked.

<margin>quail</margin>
However, the meat of the quail <note>original: "coturnix"</note> generates better blood and increases sperm. Because its meat is thicker than the previously mentioned birds, it binds the bowels and provides much nourishment.

...having a balance in temperament and humors. The broth of such birds is the best medicine for lepers. According to Avicenna, bird meat is better if it is lean, such as that of the turtledove and the hen; their meat is more subtle and does not have the heavy nutrition of other types. Finally, regarding the *duraga* <note>an Arabic term for a type of turtledove or francolin</note>: the meat of the *duraga* is perhaps better than chick meat because it provides more nourishment.

### The Turtledove <note>original: "Durac s. Turtur"</note>

There is, therefore, much diversity—and perhaps not a little else—found among authors on this subject. For meats are praised variously according to different properties of the most commendable nutrition, or according to the goal of health or strength for the person being nourished. Whence Galen, looking at the easy transformation and subtlety in the meats of partridges and sparrows, preferred them. For this reason, Avicenna says the meat of the *alcubugi* <note>likely the crested lark</note> is among the more subtle meats. Almansor, along with Isaac, preferred the *starna* for its subtlety and lightness. By *starna*, one may understand either a large bird like a grey or ash-colored goose, whose meat is highly praised by Almansor (especially when young), or a variety of small partridge known to the Tuscans, which Moses <note>likely Maimonides</note> seems to suggest to the Jews. These *starna* do not seem to be preferred by our masters because they constrict the belly. However, others attribute this property to partridges. 

But because Almansor placed the quail <note>original: "coturnice"</note> after the *starna*, there is some doubt; for by this he either means a bird larger than a partridge, of almost the same color but with red feet and beak and a more delightful flavor, called *coturnix* in the Italian tongue—and this is how his words should be heard—or he means the *ortigo* <note>the common quail</note>. If the latter, I do not accept it, since that is almost the worst of bird meats, even if it is flavorful. Whence it is said in the third book of the *Canon*: from the eating of quail meat, tetanus and spasms are feared, not because of what they eat, but because this quality exists in their very substance. Isaac also says: quails are worse than others, being neither commendable for nourishment nor digestion. I myself have sometimes perceived spasmodic accidents from eating them, as have others with sensitive constitutions. Isaac also praised various birds according to different medicinal intentions. Similarly, there is diversity regarding hens. Avicenna, however, seems to depart from the others the most since he praises the meat of turtledoves so highly. Perhaps in his lands, they are of such great quality compared to others. Or perhaps he is looking at the property by which they strengthen the intellect. Nevertheless, according to Galen, they are placed behind many others. According to Avicenna or even Moses, they tend toward heat and dryness; nevertheless, they are more praiseworthy than pigeons. Regarding the third point, it should be known as a general rule that the meat of bloodless animals and aquatic animals is generally less commendable than the rest. And the meat of birds is more commendable than that of land animals, although it may provide less extensive nourishment and strength. Similarly, one might say that those which tend toward growth are better than others. Those that are dry in composition, like kids <note>young goats</note>, are more suitable for small children. However, older goat meat is not good. Every offspring...

Regarding the moisture of an older animal, the closer it is to birth, the worse it is; and the proportionally further away it is, the more praiseworthy it becomes. In dry meat, however, the opposite is true. Furthermore, the meat of males is more praiseworthy than that of females. On this point, **Haly Abbas** <note>Persian physician Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi (d. 982)</note> says that all female meat generates bad blood. **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli (d. c. 932), a Jewish physician and philosopher</note>, however, makes an exception for goats; for he wishes them to be less blameworthy than the meat of he-goats <note>original: "yrcis"</note> for nourishment. Furthermore, according to **Oribasius** <note>Greek physician to Emperor Julian</note>, the meat of all animals that are still growing is better digested than the meat of those that are declining in age.

## On those of middle constitution, between fatness and thinness, older animals, and those that are castrated
Those of a middle constitution between fatness and thinness are more select than others, as are older animals and castrated ones. Furthermore, the meat of black animals is healthier and lighter than others, especially white ones. Likewise, those that are exercised with sufficient movement are more suitable than their opposites. Next, it must be said specifically that crabs <note>or crayfish</note> found in springs, which are soft in form and called "granci" <note>likely an Italianate vernacular term for crab/crayfish</note>, are praiseworthy; since they come from springs, they have a quality similar to fish meat. Therefore, they are effective for those with wasting diseases <note>original: "ethicis," referring to hectic fever or consumption</note> and those who are emaciated, since they are moist, soft, easily converted, and fattening, as they temper the heat and dryness of the aforementioned conditions. These are properly called crabs; wherefore in the *History of Animals* <note>Aristotle's work</note>, in the fourth and first books, the crab alone among such creatures is described as having a "tail-less" <note>original: "urepigto," a corruption of the Greek 'opistographos' or similar</note> form. One must listen regarding these when they are ordered to be given to those with wasting diseases; when taken, they are not harmful at all, although they are harder to digest unless they happen to be of the soft-shelled variety.

## Fish praised among us are sea fish
These include sea bream, gilt-head, mullet, sole, and red mullet. Regarding fresh water, the perch is praised, which **Galen** also commends, as well as the small stone-perch <note>original: "petritinalis"</note>, carp, pike, and trout, especially the "golden" trout which is bony. The tastiest of fish is the salmon, while the pike <note>original: "esox"</note> truly takes on the thickness of land meat. Among domestic quadrupeds, I especially prefer the sucking kid <note>young goat</note> of the Paduans. I say this because in hot and dry regions, it is valued less than the lamb. Then comes the year-old lamb, and after that the sucking calf, and then the pig. Among wild animals, the roe deer is to be preferred, specifically the suckling. For its meat, because it is crumbly and digestible, is not offensive in its fatness, having a quiet flavor according to **Isaac**; then the wild boar, deer, hare, rabbit, hedgehog, bear, and so forth.

## Regarding birds
The meat of capons and young hens is more praiseworthy. This is shown by the care taken with the testicles of the roosters, especially those that can walk about and are not kept confined indoors; and finally, young pigeons, geese, and ducks. Among wild birds, pheasants are more praiseworthy for both health and strength. Perhaps they are even better than domestic birds, as they are very close to hens and of almost the same species, but they enjoy drier air and food, and more exercise. After these are partridges, grey partridges, quails, larger larks, finches, turtledoves, pigeons, thrushes, blackbirds, and finally peacocks, cranes, and so on. But there is a doubt regarding the aforementioned, because 

<margin>vi. On the Regulation of Health</margin> they place quails <note>original: "qualie"</note> before partridges thus: "The best meat for such dispositions is that of quails, partridges, and francolins." Yet these same quails are elsewhere disparaged. It must be said that the writer or translator corrupted the text; for where he wrote "quails" <note>original: "qualeay"</note>, he should have written "mountain birds" <note>original: "montanaų"</note>. Just as it says in the Greek *orinon* <note>meaning mountain</note>, which appears because [the scribe] wrote "of mountain birds" <note>original: "origiorū"</note> in place of "of quails" <note>original: "orinō"</note> in Greek, wishing to adopt a Latin form.

## Which is proven, even if it is already known
For the most praised capons, when they are fat, are loathed in the treatment of a body that is dry and prone to kidney stones <note>original: "calculosa"</note>. Therefore, they are especially disparaged when they are fat and offensive. Furthermore, it speaks of "quails" without a conjunction; from which it appears it does not denote diversity but uniformity. For the Greeks, and especially **Galen**, always use a conjunction in dense lists and not a punctuation mark in its place. Since the cause and support of these arrangements are found in the aforementioned, a diligent person, for the sake of brevity, will be able to assign the meaning to those things which are said in praise of nourishment. Meat is also praised or disparaged by its parts: those from the right side are more praiseworthy. Also those around the bones and the middle of the muscles, or those of this or that specific limb, as seen in the study of nutrients and in the diets of the sick. Likewise, the meat of domestic animals is more useful by nature than that of wild ones because of the air, life, and leisure; for the opposite is true of the latter, especially those from the mountains. For their meat is less prone to rot, having better food and few superfluities. These things are confirmed by experience, and then by the similarity or contrary nature of these things to the bodies being nourished; and from their nature, according to whether they are easily changed and crumbly, or difficult, and whether they are penetrated quickly or slowly, as the discourse on nutrients shows. Regarding the fourth and first books [of Aristotle], it must be said that [snails] are given to those who have been exhausted because they nourish greatly. Their nourishment is sticking, yet they are difficult to digest. Thus, in the study of nutrients: all Greeks eat snails <note>original: "cochias"</note> daily; they have hard meat and for this reason are indigestible, but if they are digested, they are highly nutritious. Regarding the other point about crabs, it appears it must be said that they provide praiseworthy nourishment in their own kind for those who have taken them, though not simply more than others. To the other point, it must be said that fish are not simply easy to digest since they are cold and watery; nor is their softness airy and light, suited for digestion, but rather watery and fragile; yet the aforementioned fish of "middle meat" are to be praised in their own way. For those of very soft or very hard meat are least praised in the study of nutrients. To the other, it must be said that although quadrupeds may be available to us in act, they are not so in virtue as is required in this inquiry. For as it was said, nourishment does not immerse itself into the body, but does so by a virtue that digests, transports, and applies it. This does not happen in them because of the hardness and viscosity of their meat, since they are very intemperate in relation to the human composition and substance. Indeed, human meat would be of more praiseworthy nourishment than any other animal meat by its proportion to the human mode, were it not for the horror <note>original: "abbomiatio"</note> that falls between them. Perhaps also, because it would nourish so easily and abundantly, it would cause illness more quickly and carelessly. However, certain of the brutes...

...living under either pole, who kill and eat other men <note>A reference to legendary accounts of cannibalism in distant geographical regions</note>, as described in Difference 67. And if it appears that something should be said regarding the meat of pigs: their thinness of digestion and the viscosity of their nourishment hinders that specific firmness. Regarding another point, it appears that turtles, because of the superfluities they expel outward, are rendered of more praiseworthy nourishment, yet not so much as many other things, since their own nourishment is very oily and abominable; although **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a 10th-century physician</note> places them as coming from matter in which the four elements—the heavy and the light—are mixed equally. However, this mixture is not a "true" mixture like that of the human body (where the smallest part of one element touches the smallest part of another), but rather it is a mixture almost by juxtaposition.

Similarly, according to **Isaac**, it is the same for hedgehogs <note>original: "ericii"</note> and porcupines with them; because many superfluities fall away from them, the remaining nourishment is still poor and more medicinal than food-like. Indeed, the meat of the hedgehog provokes urine and loosens the bowels, especially during the time of mating, and particularly the meat of the female. ### DIFFERENCE .LXIX.

That the white of the egg <term>albumen<gloss>the clear part of the egg</gloss></term> is hot and the yolk <term>vitellus<gloss>the yellow/red part of the egg</gloss></term> is cold is shown from the beginning of *On the Generation of Animals* <note>Aristotle's work on biology</note>. Furthermore, that in which the principle of the animal resides is hot. In the <unclear>embryo</unclear>, the animal principle is there, since soul and life are sustained in bodies through heat. This is the white part, since it is assimilated to the sperm and is that from which the chick is formed. The red part (the yolk), however, is terrestrial and thick, from which the chick is nourished, and is thus cold. Furthermore, in marsh birds, the yolk superabounds but is less red and more humid, and the white is diminished. In field birds, however, it is the opposite; but those [marsh birds] are colder and more humid by nature than the field birds. In the same way, the white and the yolk of the egg are parts cut off from those birds, and they will retain the nature of those that produced them, since the product always retains the mark of its producer.

Again, the fact that the white is separated circularly from the red part by a movement of boiling or bubbling indicates it is hot, since this is its nature. Thus, the white, although it was previously united to the red (as will be shown), is sequestered from it, with the red sinking inside as something terrestrial. This is shown by eggs broken in a pan when they encounter the movement of the fire: the white is seen to stand circularly around the red. And that which attracts and that which transforms is hot; the white induces such an action in the red, attracting it and transforming it into nourishment for the chick. Indeed, it is like rennet acting upon milk.

Again, the white is proportioned to the red or the blood in useful diets. Just as blood and sperm are the matter and nourishment for walking animals <note>land animals</note>, so eggs are the matter and nourishment for flying ones. Sperm, however, is denoted as hotter than blood. Therefore, the white is hot and the red is cold. Opposed to this is the whole crowd of doctors, who posit that the whole egg attains an equality <note>a balance of humors</note>, yet the white pertains to coldness in some way, and therefore it is thick and difficult to digest (according to the 12th book of *On Medical Method*). The yolk, however, pertains to heat. Therefore, they testify that the opposite properties are present.

Again, that which is tasteless is cold; that which is sweet is hot. Such are the white and the red. Furthermore, that which 

---

is quickly digested and transformed into the human body is hot and <unclear>healthful</unclear>; such is the nature of the egg. But they say this is true of the yolk and not the white. Also, the red color of the yolk testifies to heat, while the white color of the albumen testifies to coldness. Whence **Avicenna** <note>original: "Ay." - Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath</note> in certain problems attributed to him says: the shell of the egg is terrestrial, cold, and dry; its moisture is watery; but the spirit which is in it is moist and hot and temperately dry. Indeed, this egg seems to be an image of the world. It is also apparent that its white is proportioned to milk, and the red to blood; yet here the red comes out hotter than the milk. Again, that which benefits diseases of heat is cold, since benefit in these cases is achieved by the opposite. This is the white; whence in the 13th book of *On Medical Method*: "It seems to me the ancients, with much investigation, arrived at the moisture of eggs as something very non-irritating and viscous, choosing it for this reason." Wherefore **Dioscorides** <note>Ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> says: the white of the egg is used as medicine for various conditions. Therefore, the white is cold and the yolk is hot.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that the egg is an animal in potential <note>the capacity to become a living creature</note>, produced from the superfluity of egg-making. For because of its imperfection, the bird cannot immediately produce an animal within itself as a perfect being, but rather does so through the medium of an egg. It consists of the superfluity of the animal, for if it were from the substance of the parent, the parent would have ceased to exist long ago, as in Difference 34. This superfluity from which it is constituted is proportioned to menstrual blood, which thickens into a reddish color, in which the matter of the whiteness is still contained. Finally, in the hotter egg-layers, through a path of "boiling" (as touched upon before), the white is segregated and, standing all around, causes the red to remain in the middle of the white, just as the earth remains in the middle of water and air. According to **Aristotle, On Animals, Book XVII**: in those egg-layers that are colder, the whole internal egg remains indistinct. For in those, the white and the red are confused together so that they appear as one single color. In birds, too, the egg is bound to the matrix <note>the uterus</note> by its sharp end, through which it draws nourishment to itself until its perfection is finished; for it is expelled so that nothing of the connection appears when it comes out, like a navel. The shell also, being somewhat soft while the egg is still inside and finished, hardens quickly when it is brought outside, as its moisture evaporates and is reduced, leaving behind the terrestrial part.

<margin>The Egg</margin>
Indeed, eggs are diversified by those things that are inherent in them and by things occurring from elsewhere. First, in many ways: either by reason of those by whom they are produced, since some are of the worst juices <term>chimi<gloss>humors or digestive juices</gloss></term>—such as those of marsh birds—while some are of the best, like most field birds such as hens, pheasants, and partridges. Others are in the middle, but declining much from these, such as geese and ducks. Or on the part of their generation, because some are from temperate animals with praiseworthy nourishment, while some are from intemperate ones falling not a little into excess, the opposite of the former. Or by grace of age, since some are from adolescent birds, others from young ones, and some from decrepit ones, of which the middle ones are more praiseworthy. Or on the part of their condition, since they are either from fat birds, or thin ones, or those of a middle state, which are more perfect than the others. Or by reason of the manner of their production...

# EGGS.

Because those eggs which have been trodden <note>fertilized by a rooster</note> are more delightful, being more thoroughly "digested" <note>In medieval science, "digestion" or "concoction" refers to the process by which heat matures or refines a substance</note>. For in all things, that which is digested is sweeter, according to *On the Generation of Animals*. Conversely, eggs that are not trodden are called "wind eggs" <note>original: "yperieia siue zephiriā"</note>; these are the opposite of the aforementioned, though they can still be perfected by a cock mounting the hen as long as the distinction between the white and the yolk has not yet occurred—so much so that a cock of even a different species, by treading, may impress its form upon any egg.

Alternatively, quality varies by region, for as the location is, so nature operates. Eggs produced in regions that are too hot or too cold possess poor and tasteless humors. However, those in temperate regions are praiseworthy and flavorful, since moderate flavors—such as oily and sweet—arise from balanced causes. Egg quality also depends on external factors like timing; some are near to birth, others remote, and some in the middle. The first are the best, while their opposites are the worst, with the middle ones judged to be in between.

<margin>Many ways of preparing eggs.</margin>
Or the quality varies by the skill of their cooking, which differs in two ways: by the method of cooking or by the duration. Firstly, some are cooked under ashes, while others are fried in pans <note>original: "tyganis"</note>; both of these methods are poor. Others, however, are broken and beaten with oil, <term>garum<gloss>a fermented fish sauce used as a salty seasoning</gloss></term>, and a little wine; these are mixed and placed in a sealed vessel set in a cauldron where water boils until they reach a moderate consistency. Similar to these are eggs broken over boiling water in a pan or kettle. Fifthly, eggs broken and cooked with oil and vinegar until they become <insert>tremulous</insert> <note>likely referring to the wobbling texture of a poached or soft-set egg</note> are very good. Indeed, cooking with oil improves them, especially fresh oil, because it is tempered to the heat of the fire; it fattens the liver and increases its substance. For this reason, religious people <note>monks or those under dietary vows</note> who use oil are often fat and round. These methods of preparation are more praiseworthy.

Some eggs are roasted whole in the fire; some are boiled in water; others are stuffed with meat and herbs. Still others are cooked in water with oil, salt, and seasonings such as onion and <term>cinnamon<gloss>original: "cinamomo"</gloss></term>, and similar things; these are judged to be a middle ground between the aforementioned methods. Regarding the duration of cooking, some are cooked less, some more, and some moderately; the first are more praiseworthy, while the others are less so. Even if the middle-cooked eggs provide more nourishment to the body, the others remain longer in the stomach.

As for what "hot" and "cold" signify, see Difference 15. Regarding the third point, it should be known that some have said the white <term>albumen<gloss>the clear part of the egg</gloss></term> is hotter than the red <term>vitellus<gloss>the yolk</gloss></term> specifically at its pointed end where the "cock's head" <note>the germinal disc or embryo</note> is located; but regarding its other parts, they say it is not hotter at all. This view cannot stand. For just as the part around the cock's head relates to one part of the yolk, so do the other parts relate to one another. However, the part placed around the cock's head *is* hotter than the red, and rightly so, because the entire white must be heated and formed by the cock's head; it is produced through a kind of boiling and the rising of what is hotter and lighter on all sides. Similarly, **Avicenna** <note>the 11th-century Persian physician</note> pronounced absolutely that the white consists of more heat than the red.

Others, interpreting **Aristotle**, said that the white is hotter than the red in "actual" heat, while wanting physicians to hear that the yolk is hotter than the white in "potential" heat. This also is invalid. For as act relates to act, so potential relates to potential. For example, a living lion or duck is hotter than a living hen or partridge; likewise, once dead, their "potential" heat as nourishment for the body is higher. This is similarly found in vegetables, though the difference is not as manifest, because their heat is more in potential than in act.

Furthermore, an egg that has been quickened with life cools down so that its actual heat may fly away <note>an observation that the physical temperature drops as the life force is concentrated</note>. Therefore, one does not escape the problem by speaking thus. Regarding the third point, it should be known that "hot" can be understood in two ways (as in Difference 26). One is the life-giving, airy, and somewhat watery heat—gentle, delightful, and endowed with much heat from the heavens, which makes the <term>seed<gloss>spermata</gloss></term> fertile (Difference 36). In this sense, the white is hotter than the yolk. This is the view in *On the Generation of Animals*, Book 3: the animal takes its beginning of generation from the white. For the principle of the animal is in the heat, and nature has a life-giving heat in the white, which is moist by nature. 

There is another kind of heat: a consuming, fiery substance embedded in earthy matter, which is helpful and flows into the "heavenly" heat. In this sense, the yolk is hotter than the white, as indicated when it says: everything earthy and made of thick parts is not the principle of generation, but is rather proportioned as nourishment—much like blood—whereas the white is like the seed. This is shown by the "passions" <note>physical reactions</note> of heat and cold, which are similar in some and opposite in others. Hence, in *On Animals*, Book 17: the white of the egg is very watery and contains much air, in which the active heat separates it from the yolk, as the yolk is earthy and dry. The heat of the yolk is like that of earthy bodies, while the white's heat is like that of airy and somewhat watery bodies. Therefore, the white is more suitable for forming the radical parts of the body, and the yolk serves as nourishment, being like blood changed into the substance of seed, though incomplete.

<margin>Judgment on the question.</margin>
That the white appears hotter than the yolk is because it participates more in the principles of the soul, using heat as nature's primary instrument. This is shown by the "cock's head" represented in the pointed end of the egg. The yolk, by contrast, is hotter in a fiery sense because its earthy, thick parts hold heat more vehemently. Heat in these two is like heat impressed into a liquid versus heat impressed into a stone. Thus, the white is hotter in one way, and the red yolk in the other. Note however...

...that the yolk, when related to the human body <note>in terms of nutrition</note>, is hotter than before the generation of the chick; this is how physicians understand the reasoning: it is hotter than the white because of the strong heat inherent in it, supported by its more earthy substance. This is also due to its sweet flavor and its <term>heterogeneity</term> <note>composition of different parts</note>, which is more similar to the human body than the egg white is. However, the opposite occurs within the white itself. Furthermore, a substance that is less hot in potential can be raised to a higher actual state of heat by something else that is hotter; because of the heat of the body, it is animated in every way so that all its potential heat is elevated almost beyond the state of heat itself. For duck meat reaches a higher degree of heat when cooked in a pot than when roasted on a spit, or when it is desired strongly or minimally. Also, the "airy heat" evaporates quickly from the white, which is shown by its shrinking when it remains for a time after being laid. Let the remaining matters be taken from Difference 26.

But concerning the aforementioned things, a doubt arises. Because in the generation of chicks from eggs, it was first said that the principle begins at the edge of the white, especially situated near the "cock's head" <note>the germinal disc or the spot where the embryo begins to form</note>; this seems poorly ordered, since it ought to be located in the middle so as to be protected, as is the case in other living beings and those generated by chance. For the principle of generation, whatever it may be, always occupies the middle position, according to the third book of *On the Generation of Animals*.

It must be said, however, that the generation of these animals and chicks is not similar in every way, since in live-bearing animals, the <term>matrix</term> <note>womb</note> is within the mother; but in eggs, it is situated outside the mother in the same womb-like structure. For the "red" <note>the yolk</note> is situated like a mother under a thin membrane containing the egg on all sides, which exists as a sort of womb. Or it should be said: The generation of the chick is not at the extreme edge of the white color, but rather at the lower part where it touches the red yolk. Whence in the book *On Animals*, it is said: The chick is made from the part of the yolk which is drawn into the substance of the white, and therefore the creature is found between the white and the yolk. Therefore, what should be said regarding the first point is clear. For Avicenna <note>original: "Au."</note> speaks of the first life-giving principle, but the Physician <note>Galen</note> speaks of the refined substance.

Regarding the other point, it must be stayed. To the other, it must be said that not only because of the cold do the eggs of such birds participate more in the yolk, but also because of the thickness and the <term>heterogeneity</term> of its parts. It has been said that the heat exhales when the white has been formed into an egg. To the other, it must be said that the separation of the white from the red does not happen by the elevation of heat alone, but furthermore because of the lightness of its parts combined with viscosity. For the red yolk has been declared "earthy." Someone might perhaps say the parts of the white are viscous with a certain lightness, so that the heat reaching them and being unable to separate them lifts them up; this similarly happens in eggs that are lightly fried. As is shown in the boiling of a cauldron, from which the viscous but not heavy material flows out faster than the water. To the other, it appears what should be said: the discourse is about the primary heat, aided by the external heat of the incubating bird.

To the other, it must be said that although life-giving sperm may be hotter than blood through its vital heat, nevertheless, through sharp, "earthy" heat, blood can be hotter than it. Regarding what was asked of the other part, the answer to the first point is now clear. To the other two, it similarly appears that since the airy heat of the white is mixed with it, the wateriness dulls it. It was also said that its heat exhales. It was also shown that the red yolk is more proportionally suited to the body than the white. To the other, it must be said that the redness in the yolk is not there only because of heat, but even more because of nature, like the blood from which it is generated—just as flesh is redder than other parts because of blood. Nor should it be said that the white is assimilated to milk, even if men think so, deceived by the similarity of color. For every sensitive person perceives that the red yolk corresponds to milk, since it is the food for the chicks, according to the third book of *On the Generation of Animals*. To the other, it must be said that when the white is broken, the heat escapes, but not so from the red yolk. Furthermore, it is not only placed here to benefit because of coldness, but also because of the viscosity through which it participates in adherence without "biting" <note>irritation</note>. Whence Galen says that a viscous substance without biting, when it is moderately warm, is the most painless thing that exists.

# DIFFERENCE 70.

-> It is shown that Wine is hot and dry. <-
-> Since the <term>complexion</term> of pure wine is visibly hot <-
-> and dry according to theory. Moreover, pure wine is <-
according to this the wine of grapes and clusters. Furthermore, that which is suitable for "windy" <note>flatulent</note> people ought to be hot and dry, since it includes the nature of "contrariety" to the gas. Wine is suitable for the flatulent both because it mitigates their coldness and because phlegm is digested and thinned by it; and that which does such things is hot and dry. Also, that which has the power to resolve, to dry, to heal ulcers, and to wipe them clean is hot and dry; wine is used for this therapeutically in the third degree. Again, that which induces the accidents <note>symptoms</note> of heat and dryness is seen to be hot and dry, since the effect and the cause are proportional. Now, wine is seen to cause thirst and dryness, as denoted by the drinkers of Padua seeking out the taverns before daybreak; and it causes hot and dry illnesses such as persistent wakefulness, frenetic fevers, and "consuming" spasms and delusions of the mind and body. Conversely, it cures the "canine appetite" <note>extreme, ravenous hunger</note> occurring from simple coldness or from a cold, acidic humor of the mind and body; that which does this is hot and dry, since healing is perfected by the contrary. Therefore, wine will be hot and dry.

Again, some say it is hot and moist according to nature; so says the third book of the *Problems*. Furthermore, that which is vaporous, windy, and sleep-inducing is hot and moist. For these are caused by heat acting upon moisture; but wine is such a thing, according to the first book of *On Sleep and Wakefulness*. Again, that which heats and moistens is hot and moist; such indeed is wine according to the fourth book of the first part <note>of Avicenna's Canon</note>. It also thrives in hot and moist temperate lands. Therefore, it is hot and moist. But some say it is cold and moist...
