# ON WINE

<margin>Wine from grapes.</margin>

They distinguish French wines, and if they are firm and dry, English ones. Regarding the first point, it should be known that wine can be made from many things, as appears in the works of <term>Dioscorides</term> <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, an ancient Greek physician and botanist</note>; however, it is most especially expressed from the juice of grapes, which is a liquid best suited to human nature. Indeed, nature delights in it greatly because of its great proportion to the same, concerning which this present inquiry stands. This can be considered in two ways: either regarding those things which are more intrinsic to it, or those which come to it from the outside. First, one can consider five things in wine: its liquor or substance, its potency, its smell, its taste, and its color. Third, theoretically, the specific properties of wine are discussed. By reason of its liquor, wine gathers diversity: for some is thin, some thick, another is medium, some dense and turbid, some thin and clear, and another medium, and so on. Also, on the part of its potency, some is powerful and strong, another weak, and another medium, according to the diversity of its generation.

<margin>By reason of its substance.</margin>
<margin>By reason of its potency.</margin>

It is diversified by reason of almost every kind of flavor. For some is tasteless, almost like water; some is <term>styptic</term> <note>astringent or mouth-puckering</note> or harsh; some is acidic, some truly sweet; and some pertains to bitterness and sharpness, such as older wines or those artificially treated with medicinal pitch, which are not nutritious, as gathered from the fifth and seventh books <note>likely referring to Galen’s medical texts</note>.

<margin>By reason of flavor.</margin>

Another kind pertains to saltiness, such as wine mixed with seawater, as noted in the twelfth book of *On Ingenuity*. Fourthly, wine takes its diversity from its smell; for some is aromatic—which according to <term>Haly Abbas</term> <note>an 11th-century Persian physician</note> is delightful to the senses—while some has a horrible and unpleasant odor, generating bad blood and inducing headaches; another is medium between these; and some has a "deadened" smell, like water.

<margin>By reason of smell.</margin>

Finally, wine varies by reason of its color, which exists in many forms according to the colors found in it. For some is white, close to water in potency, color, and taste; some is pale; another is citron or yellow; some is rose-colored; some is red; and another participates in redness but turns toward a blackish hue.

<margin>By reason of color.</margin>

However, the differences in wine taken by reason of substance, potency, and flavor are more characteristic than those of smell and color. If wine is considered according to external factors, this can happen in four ways: by reason of the intention of the person taking it, or by some foreign mixture, or by its origin, or by the time. If the first, it is twofold: either on the part of the wine itself, or in relation to the person receiving it. First, it can vary in three ways: for it is either food and drink together, or drink only, or it occupies a middle place. Wine by nature fulfills the role of food and drink because it is offered for the sake of restoring what has been lost—which is the office of food—or it carries nutrition through the body, which is the nature of drink. This is against certain physicians who wish to call wine not a food, but rather just a drink.

---

Wine is also sometimes offered under the definition of drink only, for the purpose of carrying nourishment through the body, such as the drink called "the three carriers," which is given when the digestion of the stomach is complete and that of the liver is nearly half-done. For there are three types of drink: the "mixed," the "carrying," and the "altering." Wine is also taken for the sake of medicine or as an "altering" drink, such as that which is given to aid the digestion of cold things, to open the pathways <note>the "vessels" or "pores" of the body</note>, and for the relief of <term>syncope</term> <note>fainting or loss of consciousness</note>.

The nature of wine is also greatly diversified by reason of the person taking it, whether by quality, quantity, or age. For the person may be of a balanced <term>complexion</term> <note>humoral makeup</note> or a choleric one, and so on; or strong, weak, or medium; and they may drink a large quantity, a small one, or a medium one, according to which the effect of the wine is rendered diverse. For wine, when occupying those who are "chilled," at first makes them quiet and sober; if drunk a little more, it makes them talkative; taken even more, it makes them rhetorical and bold; more still, it makes them injurious; then manic; and finally, taken in great excess, it makes them stupid and <term>epileptic</term> <note>meaning here: prone to seizures or loss of motor control</note>. Hence <term>Isaac Judaeus</term> <note>a 10th-century Jewish physician and philosopher</note> says that wine is likened to a "great theriac" <note>a universal antidote or wonder-drug</note> because it is contrary to various natures: it warms the chilled, cools those who are overheated, moistens the parched, and dries the over-moist. Regarding age: wine is not recommended for children nor for nursing mothers, as it affects sleep and wakefulness. To give wine to children is like "adding fire to fire with weak wood." But to the elderly, it is given as much as they can tolerate; to youths, give it temperately. It helps them by purging bile into the urine and by moistening what is dried out. For the elderly, it is good because it warms and moistens, provokes urine along with superfluities, and strengthens their virtue. For the strengthening of virtue is common to all wines, though none of these benefits suit children. Therefore, just as wine is most contrary to children, it is most useful to the elderly.

If some foreign substance is mixed with wine, its nature is changed, as with pitch; for it is led toward sharpness and bitterness, becoming drier and non-nutritive. Or if roses are mixed in, it is converted to a temperate coldness; or sage, and thus it is changed to heat with <term>stypticity</term>. Or wormwood is added, as the Gauls do, and with these it acquires a sub-bitterness. Also, "alapangine" species, sugar, or honey are mixed in. And an artificial wine is made which they call <term>claret</term> or *steladia*. From many herbs and other things mixed in, Dioscorides constructs wine. Water is also mixed with it during boiling, which is healthier, and sometimes after. If the wine is strong and the water is only a small amount, it intoxicates more quickly. But if much water is mixed in, especially "bora" <note>possibly referring to a specific type of water or mineral</note>, it weakens the stomach and intestines and causes windy pain. Therefore, watered wine weakens both "stomachs" <note>likely referring to the upper and lower digestive tracts</note>.

...and it generates windiness <note>original: "uentofitatē"; gas or flatulence</note> in the intestines, especially when it is consumed very cold in the summer. And therefore, practitioners first order it to be tempered with water six hours before it is taken.

Wine is also diversified by reason of its origin, and this is either by reason of the region—since some regions are hot, some cold, and others temperate. Indeed, in cold regions, the wine produced is cold and lacking in vigor, unless by reason of the accidental heat of rising vapors. Alexander <note>likely Alexander of Tralles, a 6th-century physician</note> in his first book, as even the Commentator <note>likely Averroes, the "Great Commentator" on Aristotle and medical texts</note> suggests in the third book on the *Art of Medicine*, shows that it is easily corrupted. In hot regions, however, wine is hot in itself and powerful and strong, as happens to the Egyptians. In temperate regions, it is temperate. This can also be by reason of the altitude, depth, or temperate nature of the region; for in a high region exposed to winds, the wine produced will be somewhat cold and weak. In a hollow or low region, the opposite is true. In a temperate region, it is temperate. Or it is diversified by the soil; for in cold, dry, sandy soil, the wine produced will be weak and lacking in heat. In stony, clayey, or chalky soil, the results differ; thus, with many factors varying in the middle, a great diversity of wines will be found. Indeed, plants more than other things take on a great diversity from the soil, as if the soil were their womb, as stated in the book *On Plants*. And rightly so, for nature operates according to the location. And by the law of nature, our constitution follows the region; therefore, it is said that the things which are easily generated in one region may not be in another.

Or it is diversified by reason of time. For some wine is new, another is old, and another is medium between the two, according to the seventh book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge."; Galen's *De Ingenio Sanitatis*</note> and Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician</note> in his *Particular Diets*. According to him, new wine is so called from the pressing of the vat until a year or a little more; this wine leans toward coldness and moisture. Old wine is that after four years up to seven, being hot and dry in the third degree <note>Medieval medicine graded qualities like "heat" on a scale from 1 to 4</note>. Medium wine is from two years up to four, being hot and dry in the second degree. Thus, it becomes clear that wine is diverse.

<margin>
qualities
of wine
</margin>

Whether wine is hot and dry or cold and so on is determined by its potential or virtue <note>its "spirit" or inherent power</note>; that is, when its potential is brought into action by natural heat, it will heat, dry, or cool according to its operation. It is not necessarily what it appears to be actually or by accident <note>e.g., wine served cold is still "hot" in its medical nature</note>. Many times an error is made regarding this based on accidental impressions, according to Galen; for sometimes that which is hot might cool, and that which is cold might heat. Therefore, it should be known that although common opinion pronounces wine to be hot and dry, this is either a poor understanding of the matter or refers to old medicinal wine rather than wine used as nourishment.

<margin>
wine
mature
grapes
</margin>

Isaac indeed feels that wine is hot and dry by nature, but cold and moist by accident, because by its subtlety and its ability to penetrate, it carries water through the limbs, cooling and moistening them. This is said very simply and strangely, for their failure usually arises from a lack of heat.

Therefore, it should also be known that according to what is simply stated in the significance of taking it as a drink, wine when taken will be of a hot and moist complexion; that is, considering its temperate nature and its presence as a medium in age. For this reason, supported by authorities such as Avicenna and Galen, the leader of physicians, and others—with convincing proofs added—wine is held to be hot and moist, especially when it serves as food and drink. Thus the Commentator in the third book of the *Introduction to the Pulse* says: those things which are added by wine are quickly applied because it is moist and hot.

And when the *Regimen of Health* <note>a famous medieval health manual</note> instructs an elderly person wishing to be moistened to use a good wine suited to heating and moistening, it soon shows the same: he said that a warm bath of sweet waters and the drinking of wine would be useful for the elderly because these things moisten them and moderately move their sleep. Because of this, it is said in the third book of *On the Natural Faculties* that wine generates very little melancholy <note>the "cold and dry" humor</note>. This is also sufficiently drawn from the third book of the *Aphorisms* and from the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*</note>.

Isaac also felt this in his *Particular Diets* concerning new wine—included here—that its heat is in the first degree. Whence it is compared to coldness and moisture in relation to the two other kinds of wine, and therefore it is more nourishing than the others. Haly Abbas <note>Ali ibn Abbas al-Majusi, a 10th-century Persian physician</note>, agreeing with these views, says that wine is suited to temper black bile <note>melancholy</note> by its heating and moistening, to soften the nature, and to moisten the principal members. Wherefore in the ninth book of the *Almansor* <note>the *Liber ad Almansorem* by Rhazes</note>, he orders thin, clear, and well-scented wine to be given as a specific cure for melancholy. It is also gathered in the sixth book that wine consists of many properties from its whole species. Third, just as a composition of coldness and dryness is the contrary that weakens a body, so a composition of heat and moisture, like that of wine, is comforting and suitable. And fourth, it moistens and heats.

This which has been said is confirmed by reasons: because nourishment is hot and moist, and its digestion is celebrated by heat and moisture. Wine is more nourishing than other things; this is because wine, along with egg yolks and meat broth, is numbered among the most nourishing things, and it is more nourishing for them because it is more penetrating and proportional to the spirits, and therefore those using it temperately grow fat.

Furthermore, because it restores the spirits and expands the soul, it is hot and moist; for these spirits, more than other nourishments, are comforted by wine, and it induces joy and alacrity. Third, wine is consistent and suitable to the innate heat. This is clear from the fourth book of the *Almansor* and from the tenth book of the *Colliget* <note>by Averroes</note>, which testifies that wine is the greatest relief for syncope <note>fainting</note>. So much so that even Saracens <note>Muslims, for whom alcohol is usually forbidden</note> are allowed to take it in such a case. Thus, wine has the power by its essence to be converted into spirit. Wine is more the nourishment of the spirit. It would be the spirit: and indeed it is safe in heat and moisture. For the spirit is placed there as hot and moist. From it and the virtues, human nature is joined together with others as if from more formal things which are hot and moist. Likewise, the wine considered here is drawn from mature grapes sweetened by celestial heat, which indeed is said theoretically to be hot and moist, as indicated by its flavor and the abundance of nutrition it provides. For the guardians of vineyards, eating grapes and placing a small amount of bread between them, grow sufficiently fat from this food. Moreover, the wine produced from something retains the nature of that from which it is drawn. Furthermore, this flavorful and friendly wine partakes in sweetness, because of which it is said in the first book of the *Problems*: it is drinkable, not a foe of wine.

...is seen to be sweet. Moreover, that this is hot and moist is shown by many different effects on those who drink wine compared to others; for those who drink it are seen to be fleshier, more robust in body <note>original: "somatitiores"; likely from the Greek 'soma' for body</note>, more inclined to procreation, more cheerful, and better colored. Secondly, the opposite is true [for those who abstain]. All of these similar signs indicate heat and moisture. 

Furthermore, the heat and moisture of wine are shown by its quick conversion into fire. For such a thing is the greatest fuel for fire; for fire is nourished by moisture, as is shown by a candle or a boiling vessel. When wine is touched, especially when it is sweet and red, it responds to the heat. Salt works upon it when cast in, causing it to evaporate by its "cutting" action and producing a searching flame. 

It also bends back <note>meaning: counteracts or neutralizes</note> the harm of choler <note>original: "cole ri"; yellow bile, one of the four humors</note> because of the contrast of heat and moisture, since choler is cold and dry <note>note: while choler is traditionally hot and dry, the text here contrasts it with the "hot and moist" nature of wine to explain the medicinal "bending" or correction of the humor</note>. Every "bending" or destruction of a harmful state is achieved by contraries; such is the case with wine in its primary and third qualities. 

Therefore, wine is said to be hot and moist. Regarding the fourth point against the first: although pure wine is hot and moist by nature, when compared to other drinks, it is actually hot and dry. It is compared to wines made from raisins, honey, dates, or beer <note>original: "ceruisiā"</note>, and moisture in general. Perhaps this is the reason for the distinction. 

Regarding the other point, one must proceed by way of reduction and preservation, not just conservation. But when it is said that wine is suitable for "windiness" <note>original: "flaticis"; refers to gas or flatulence</note>, it is suitable insofar as it is hot, for the sake of reduction or preservation (which is measured by the contrary), or because its moisture acts as a cause of conservation. For windiness is more a product of cold than of moisture. Or it must be said that a proportionate amount of wine is suitable for windiness not only as food and drink, but rather as medicine. 

Regarding the other point, this should be understood of wine as a medicine, not as the food and drink discussed here. Regarding another point: this happens by accident from the wine understood here, because when a great quantity is consumed, it is not digested, but rather corrupted into sub-acid and nitre-like <note>original: "nitrosos"; salty or alkaline</note> humors that bring about rot, just as the digestion of corrupted fish shows. Wine also has a very passive moisture which, if the digestion is unfortunate and the movement of the spirits is overheated, leads almost to a state of dryness. 

Or it is better said that wine is a powerful medicine, such as that which cures "canine appetite" <note>an excessive, ravenous hunger</note>. Whence Galen <note>original: "Ga."</note> says it is because they sufficiently heat the body. And through this, the other point is addressed. To the others, it must be said that they are touching upon wine here not as nourishment, but rather as medicine. For some wine is hot and moist, some hot and dry, another firm and moist, but never cold and dry when related to the balance of justice <note>meaning: a perfectly healthy physiological balance</note>, etc.

<margin>❦</margin>
Next, it is questioned **whether wine is suitable for children**, since it has been said to be harmful to them. And it is asked because preservation is achieved by a similar quality; but children are hot and moist, and wine is likewise hot and moist. Furthermore, children need more nourishment because much is resolved <note>dissipated or used up</note> from them by their natural heat. They also need growth since they are imperfect; and wine is the greatest nourishment. Furthermore, these things are most perfectly achieved with the spirits of the blood. For nature rejoices in this and is nourished by it, since it is the most proper food of the elements. And wine, especially red wine, is proportionate to blood, having the same indicative nature of taste, smell, and color. 

Furthermore, that which relieves superfluities and especially "windiness" <note>gas</note> is beneficial for children, as these abound in them. For they are in a state of excessive moisture. Likewise, that which digests raw humors (which they have in excess due to their greediness) is suitable; and such a thing is wine. For it moves all excretions, as stated in the eleventh book *On Digestion*. It matures humors that are windy and raw. Therefore, wine is suitable for children.

**To the contrary**, as seen in the views of Avicenna <note>original: "Ay."</note>, Galen, and Averroes <note>original: "A."</note> with others. Moreover, the wine that would be given would be either strong and hot—and then it would inflame the substance of their subtle heat and dry out their moisture, since it is very passive and easily consumed—or it would be weak and thus would coagulate their excessive moisture. Furthermore, one must yield to natural appetite, since natural things ought to be imitated; but children, whose natural appetite is healthy, do not desire wine. Whence it is proven that children, being hot, are not lovers of wine. Whereas strong men, also being hot, are lovers of wine. Therefore, wine is not suitable for children.

Regarding the first point, it must be known what a "Child" is; and that childhood is defined in five ways. As for what wine is, its essence has already been shown; and wine here is understood as wine in the absolute sense of nourishment. Regarding the second point, it must be known that some, through sharp excitement, have said that absolute wine is suitable for children, or a medium of circumstances—nourishing and strong—but hot wine is least suitable, the defects of which will appear from what has been said.

<margin>}</margin>
Regarding the third point, it must be said that wine taken as food, in sufficient quantity and quality along with other things, is **not suitable for children**, and especially not for those still nursing. This is what Avicenna meant when he said that wine should not be offered to children nor to their nurses; and especially not to those whose teeth are planting <note>teething</note>, nor later to those who are growing. And eventually not until they are pubescent and strong in age, at which point youth approaches and wine is least harmful. 

And this is the opinion of Avicenna, Averroes, and Galen. In the *Regimen of Health* <note>original: "re. fa."; likely the 'Regimen Sanitatis Salernitanum', a famous medieval health poem</note>, the sequence is as follows: *A child should not taste wine for a long time. For it heats and moistens a body that has already been drunk* etc. And it adds: *Children, like those who do not aggregate any of such humors as the melancholic (like youths) or the phlegmatic (like the elderly), having a great deal of moisture, do not need any of the good things brought about by wine; they only receive injury from it.* 

Whence the practice: *Wine should not be given to children to drink, nor should they become accustomed to it.* For it is profoundly hot and moist. For bodies that are hot and moist suffer an acceleration of the "putrefaction" of the humors and wicked habits; it corrupts the mind. It does the same to children who have already grown. Sixthly, it is concluded: *Know that wine and beer <note>original: "ceruisiā"</note> are bad for children, because they fill their heads and heat them with a "bad heat," and they disturb their minds.* This is confirmed by the fact that whatever fills the head by carrying vapors upward, and then descending and constricting the veins and pores through which the breath is perfected, prepares the body for putrefaction.

...since it is hot and moist, and since it is hotter and more moist than children, it is superfluous for them. It is harmful to the nerves because they are soft, by overfilling and soaking them. Hence Haly Abbas <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note>, along with those mentioned before, says: Let a little wine be given to children so that it provokes urine and reduces their superfluities and moistens the dryness that happens to them from labor <note>In medieval medicine, "labor" often refers to the general physical exertion of growth or movement.</note>, and brings other benefits; however, do not allow them to take a large amount.

And similarly for the other points already addressed. For the last point, it must be said that this is for the sake of medicine, which is granted to be suitable in such a way.

# DIFFERENCE LXXI.

<margin>
Value for
...
</margin>
**Whether the "specific form," called the "whole substance" of a thing, is seen to be the substance.**

Because there are three kinds [of nature], Galen calls this nature the "universal substance," whereas the "complexion" is that which arises from the four elements. And Moses <note>Referring to Maimonides, the Jewish philosopher and physician.</note> in his *Letter on Health* says: The specific form is the whole essence, that is, the substance, not a simple quality. Furthermore, often the specific form and the "whole substance" are said to be the same, since "words are signs of the passions in the soul," as is clear from the *Perihermenias* <note>Aristotle’s "On Interpretation."</note> and the book *On the Soul*. Moreover, substantial forms are grasped by the intellect alone, because "that which a thing is" is the object of the intellect. Accidental forms, however, are grasped by the senses, from which comes experience. But this [specific] form is not perceived by the senses. For it is either the soul or another form not among those perceived by the proper senses. Also, the specific form is the essence of a simple thing, and (13) in *On Ingenuity* <note>Galen's *De Ingenio Sanitatis*.</note>, it is not demonstrable by reason. What cannot be demonstrated is the "whatness" and the substance... for only a "passion" or property is demonstrable through a medium from that undemonstrable subject. Again, that which is not destroyed when an accident is destroyed is the substance, since the definition of an accident is that it comes and goes without the corruption of the subject. Such is the specific form; for when a bull <note>original: "tyro"; likely *tauro*</note> is dead, there still remains in the substance of its flesh a form that is destructive to many animals <note>This refers to the belief that the "essence" of a species (like a bull) remains in its meat or parts even after death, retaining specific powers.</note>. Therefore, it is substance and not accident.

<margin>
"That which is"
is not derived.
</margin>
The contrary of this is shown from many sayings. Third, in the *Natural Books*, it is said that attraction occurs by the property of a quality. And specifically, attraction occurs by an "attractive virtue." And in the book *On the Senses*: Purslane <term>Portulaca: a common succulent plant</term> eradicates
<margin>
Warts
</margin>
warts when rubbed on them, by its own property and not by a quality.
<margin>
Truth of metaphysics
</margin>
But these are accidents. Again, the reasoning of simple things is that attraction occurs through the similarity of the attractor to the attracted. But similarity in every genus is located in the category of "quality," since it is a property to be called "similar" or "dissimilar," according to the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*. Furthermore, that which follows the "complexion" is an accident, because it arrives when the being is already in act; but that which arrives in this way is by nature an accident. But the specific form occurs following the complexion, according to Aristotle; therefore, it will be an accident.

It is shown likewise to be substance and accident in the [book on] *Collections*, witnessing that the womb attracts the seed through a specific power which it has from the specific form or from the whole species.

Furthermore, it is shown that it is not substance, nor does operation come from it, because it was posited that operation finally proceeds from quality (Difference 60). Regarding the first, it should be known what is meant by "specific form" or "whole species." What substance is, and what an accident is, was seen in Difference 17.

Regarding the second, it should be known that some have denied these specific forms or "occult virtues" because it seemed to them that every operation proceeded from their qualities (Difference 60), not raising their intellect to formal principles and a higher nature. They also denied them in minerals, because they did not seem to be found there as they are in the perfections of animals. Others denied them because they could not achieve the experienced effects attributed to them. This is clearly repugnant to truth and the senses. For it is manifest that the magnet attracts iron, and that it is prevented from attracting by the diamond <note>A common medieval scientific belief: that a diamond's presence could "bind" or neutralize a magnet's power.</note>. It has also often been seen that the sapphire <note>original: "zaphiū"</note> draws out a carbuncle <note>An "anthrax" or inflammatory skin tumor.</note>. Gold gladdens the heart, and Jasper checks the flow of blood from any source, and chicory checks the nostrils. Since these things have been seen by almost everyone, it is impossible that the truth is not for the most part contained in them, nor can such things be ascribed to [elemental] qualities (Difference 60). Nor can it be said that wonderful operations do not come from specific forms—since they are the end and the complement of nature—on the grounds that operations proceed from qualities, as they assert.

<meta>This page explores the nature of "occult virtues"—hidden powers in nature that go beyond the basic qualities of hot, cold, wet, and dry. It debates whether these powers belong to the essential "form" of a substance or are "accidental" properties, using examples from medicine, mineralogy, and the human body. It continues the previous discussion on how natural substances interact with the human constitution.</meta>

...in cheaper things and those less intended by nature. As for why **occult virtues** <note>occult virtues: hidden natural powers that cannot be explained by the four basic elements of hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> are not as manifest in animals as they are in minerals: it is said that they exist according to what tradition teaches. For those who consider birthdays, magic, and the marvelous virtues existing in plants and animal parts, these things would work if they were understood, according to **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure associated with alchemy and the "hermetic" arts</note>; whatever is perfected by the magical art is found in **peony**, **scammony**, and other such vegetables. They show this in cases of **epilepsy** <term>epilepsy: often called the "falling sickness" in medieval texts</term> and colic. In the human skull, too, there is a virtue against epilepsy in its own right. In all the diseases of the joints, a great virtue is found. Thus, in the 22nd book, certain experts have extracted things that they do not entirely dislike, such as the burnt bones of a human tooth in a drink; and already some presumptuous people have used these and were entirely healed of **gout** <term>gout: a painful inflammation of the joints</term> and joint pains. 

Or it might be said that because these hidden virtues in animals lie hidden, it is because nature in them is intent upon greater and nobler things, just as the soul in man, which works upon future events and prognostications through the operations of reason, does not perceive the lowest things as the brutes do. In man, there is a total power of the soul operating so vehemently in one direction—as in deep thought—that the external sensory, auditory, or visual power fails. Or perhaps these virtues do not endure with such impression as they do in minerals. But what should be said to those who fail in experience and therefore deny that specific operations exist? This will appear in the third point to be discussed.

Regarding the third point, it must be known that we should first see whether it is a substance or an **accident** <term>accident: a property that a thing can lose without ceasing to be what it is, like being tan or tall</term>, and what it is. Second, how its introduction is manifested. Third, whether it is found in all things. And fourth, how its preservation and durability are shown.

Regarding the first, it should be known from the various discourses of philosophers and physicians that the "form of the species," or the "total substance," or that which operates, can be understood in two ways. In one way, it is through the substantial form coming to the matter by itself, from which the composite thing arises. For matter with form is the cause of all accidents and properties, as stated in the first book of the *Physics*. And since through this form a thing is made simple and its species is produced, it is rightly called its form and its total substance. This, according to **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note>, is that by which a thing is what it is, because through its form a thing has the being that it is.

Finally, considering the "form of the species" insofar as operation comes immediately from it, as will soon appear more fully; and since no action comes immediately from a substance according to the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the influential 12th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> in the 8th book of the *Metaphysics* due to the absence of a mediating property, it must be an accident. Therefore, Aristotle's statement must be supplemented: the specific form is that by which a thing is what it is in its operations alone—namely, its power—wishing to observe all the premises. For the same thing that is eaten and drunk is seen to operate in the human body in three ways. The first is demonstrated by reason: that there is some form through which a thing has its being and is distinct from others. For "act" gives being and separates and distinguishes, according to the 7th book of the *Metaphysics*. Such, as it appeared, is the form of the species. Furthermore, the Commentator in the 8th book of the *Metaphysics* says: "Action makes the form known, just as change makes the matter known." Therefore, since we see certain operations that are marvelous and hidden to us, they indicate that these forms exist, being causative primarily and through a medium.

---

Therefore, we see the organ in which a specific virtue exists attract its own proper nourishment, which physicians know comes from the "total substance" or the species itself. Thus, it will be a substance. Considered in the second way, insofar as action proceeds from it immediately and necessarily, the form must be called "accidental," like a power or a certain property, as the modes of speech of the wise show. **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> suggests this duality. When we say that something is not changed by the body because it is already an absolute poison, we do not mean that it is not heated by the operation of innate heat; rather, we mean it is not changed in its natural form. Indeed, they do not cease from their operation, their power and form remaining, until they corrupt the body. Thus, he calls it power and form. This power or property is placed in the category of quality. 

This is not without reason. For an accident of quality is that which can be more or less; and this is found here. For in the same species, a certain individual may have a stronger and nobler operation than another. Furthermore, that which is found intensified in a thing is not its substantial form, since for one thing there is only one specific form impressing its being. But such a form, thus considered, receives no small intensification. For one thing can have these hidden properties. In the **magnet** <note>original: "magnete"</note>, for instance, there is the power of attracting iron; the property by which it is bound by a diamond; it brings on fantastical illusions; and it is even found to cure **dropsy** <term>dropsy: an old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention</term>. Indeed, infinite things are gathered here. Moreover, that which can be destroyed without destroying the natural substance is an accident; such is this form. For if the power in **scammony** <note>scammony: a plant used as a potent laxative</note> to attract bile is destroyed, or the power in gold to gladden the heart is lost, the forms of these things still remain in some way, as will appear more clearly later. Therefore, it is an accident when taken in this way. 

This is described in the first book of the *Medicines of the Heart*: "Property is a nature found in mixed bodies, proceeding in them from a higher and most full influence through their own generation, which they acquire through a particular and proper disposition." He calls this property a "virtue" found in mixed bodies; hence it belongs to the category of accidents. 

It should be noted, however, that among accidents in which specific forms are found, their primary essence and the mediated principle of operation is an accident, and thus it is called the "secondary form" and the immediate principle of operation. In these, the distinction does not so coincide <unclear>perreta-pera</unclear>. That a specific form is considered among accidents is testified by **Aristotle**, who says it can be a color or an odor, which is shown by their operation. For it matters first and foremost: seeing the color red can excite the flow of blood. And in the 15th book, it is said that patients are helped by considering yellow things. For that moves the nature to expel yellow matter toward the skin. Similarly, the **womb** <note>original: "matrix"</note>, by its specific form or natural property, is delighted by sweet odors and agitated by foul ones. Indeed, in this, the animal nature emerges, on the authority of **Plato**. The aforesaid distinction, among other things, is sufficiently suggested and gathered from the arguments already introduced. Thus, the soul, which in this context is the form of its species...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the origins of specific forms and occult virtues. Having established that animals and plants possess these powers, the author now debates whether these qualities arise simply from the mixture of the four elements or from higher, external sources like the stars, Platonic Ideas, or a Divine Intelligence.</meta>

...constitutive, and the first principle of operation emerges as the **substantial form** <term>substantial form: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is</term>. That which inheres in it, being the immediate principle of operation, is accidental. In accidental things, both are accidental, although the first can be called essential in the manner of a prior, truly substantial form.

Regarding this fact, it must first be known that some of the ancients posited that these **specific forms** <term>specific forms: the unique powers of a species that go beyond the basic qualities of hot, cold, wet, or dry</term> with their **hidden properties** were derived solely from the **elements** <term>elements: the four building blocks of matter—earth, air, fire, and water</term> and their qualities. This perhaps was the view of **Avicenna** <note>original: "Av."</note> in the first book of his *Philosophy*, distinction 60. **Johannes Serapion** <note>a famous 9th-century Syrian Christian physician</note> also seems to have fallen into this opinion in his great *Antidotary*. He claims that the similarity by which a thing attracts is nothing other than a quality arising from the generation of the elements. With these, **Averroes** <note>original: "Auē."</note> also seems to agree in the fifth book of his *Colliget*, wishing that the "attractor," the "attracted," and the "attractability" be found in both through proportion and harmony, which emerges only from the measure of the elements in the mixture—that is, in the attractor and the attracted—which follows the qualities of the elements almost by accident. For these qualities are infused into the things that possess this property. This opinion, however, was revived by **Alexander the Peripatetic** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle</note>, who even posited that the human soul arises from the mixture of elements, as stated in the first book of the *Problems*, distinction 60.

<margin>Great contradictions remain.</margin>

Furthermore, it can be shown by reasons and signs that these specific forms and their virtues are caused by something other than the mixture of elements. Since everything is endowed with a double virtue—namely, the elementary and the celestial—one is common, the other is specific, according to the first book on the *Consolation of Medicines*.

Furthermore, if these operations arrived from the nature of the elements, it would follow that whatever is fiery would tend upwards. Thus, every "dissolving" medicine that is fiery and light would be expelled through vomiting; likewise, every heavy and weighty medicine would be expelled through the bowels. We clearly experience the opposite of this. For **agaric** <note>a medicinal fungus used as a laxative</note> and the pulp of **colocynth** <note>the "bitter apple," a powerful purgative</note> are hot and light, yet they move downwards. Conversely, **lapis lazuli** is earthy and heavy, yet it induces vomiting <note>it moves "upwards" against its heavy nature</note>, as noted in distinction 60. Also, the **magnet**, though it is not hot, attracts iron from a distance. A magnet has even been found that attracted iron with one end and repelled it with the other. Similarly, there was one that did not attract iron, but was instead attracted by it. Again, in certain stones, wonderful figures are found that testify to all the various shapes of the **celestial bodies** and not just the lower ones, as seen in stones found in the form and roundness of a tortoise. In these, stars are found figured with five rays extending at equal distances from the middle, carved with such miraculous sculpture that no human intellect could construct such things by art. Some estimate that these were previously living animals turned into stone by a mineral virtue, as mentioned in the fourth book of **Aristotle's** *Meteorology*. This is what **Aristotle** says, though perhaps it carries little weight, as I have shown in my exposition on the *Problems*. For experts report that **scammony** <note>a plant resin used as a purge</note> is hotter and yet draws downwards, while **hellebore** <note>original: "elīm"</note> draws upwards. Similarly, **elaterium** <note>a juice from the squirting cucumber</note> and the gum of **rue** are hotter than those previously mentioned, yet both draw downwards. Thus, it appears that beyond this power born of the mixture, there is another power appropriated to the thing. And therefore there were others who, beyond the mixture of elements, posited another external principle for the specific form and its caused virtues, about which they received no small diversity among themselves. 

---

<margin>Plato's Ideas</margin>

**Plato** posited separate substances which he called **Ideas**, which cause these forms and provide all nature and knowledge, seeing that particular things are in a constant state of transmutation and flux, according to the first book of the *Metaphysics*. This position, understood in this way, is found to be annulled by **Aristotle** in many places, although the **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note> in the 12th book of the *Metaphysics* labors to sustain it somewhat by interpreting "Ideas" as the impressions made by higher things upon these lower things through motion and light. Nevertheless, as it is presented, it cannot stand, because everything is generated by something similar and suited to itself, according to the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*. That which exists in natural things is neither the form nor its likeness alone, but a composite of matter and form. For a thing to be "subsisting," it must be a composite. 

<margin>Form is not generated, but the composite is.</margin>

A natural form is not "subsisting" by itself, but is that by which something subsists. Hence, the form is not properly that which is generated, but the composite is generated by it. According to the seventh book, the thing that creates natural things is not just the form, but also the matter. Likewise, these Ideas are immobile, whereas motion is the "act of a being in potentiality," according to the third book of the *Physics*, which requires both matter and form. Because of this, it would be necessary for them to always behave in the same way. From a cause that always behaves the same way, forms would proceed uniformly. This does not appear to be the case in the forms of lower bodies, because of their generation and corruption. Furthermore, assuming these Ideas existed, they would be useless in the production of forms, as seen in the third book of the *De Anima*, because they are not proportioned to matter, nor would they touch it or transmute it, since all such forms are seen to be in matter and inseparable from it. It remains, therefore, that the principles of the forms of these corruptible bodies are something other than the Ideas. There were others, like 

<margin>HERMES, the head of the wise</margin>

**Hermes Abadimom**, the "Head of the Wise," who said these specific forms with their properties are caused by the **celestial bodies** <term>celestial bodies: the stars and planets</term>, because of the different images and figures in them, through the motion of access and recess according to the delay in the eighth sphere. This is also felt in another way regarding motion in the *Centiloquium*: "The faces of this world"—that is, the species of minerals, plants, and animals—"are seen to be subject to the celestial faces." For it always happens to a form or image that it desires the nature of that which ascends from its own parts. This position is "sweeter" than the others and more sufficient in **astrology** and the art of **images** <note>likely referring to the creation of talismans</note>. In physics and medicine, however, in which it is necessary to determine how the form comes to a specific and disposed matter, it is not entirely sufficient, since they consider these forms within matter—they do not abstract them from sensible matter in general, according to the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*. 

<margin>Avicenna, 9th Metaphysics</margin>

**Avicenna** also appears to have thought differently in various places. In the ninth book of the *Metaphysics*, he posits that every form and this whole inferior nature is given by an **Intelligence** which he calls the "Agent" <note>the "Agent Intellect" or Dator Formarum (Giver of Forms)</note>. He posited a certain governing Intelligence below the lunar orb for species, actions, and passions. This position, along with its annulment, appears in the exposition of the tenth part of the *Physics*. In certain of his **alchemical** and **magical** secrets, he also seemed to think these forms were imprinted from the imagination and apprehension of the higher movers. For he wished that the movers could not intend this or that particular motion according to location, except through the apprehension of some particulars, which imagination...

...calls it: he uses the term equivocally, yet toward those things which through themselves emerge as feasible to the soul. For he wished that matter capable of being generated and corrupted would obey the mover of the celestial spheres just as our body obeys the soul.

However, this position cannot stand because one cannot adapt imagination or apprehension to the movers of the spheres, since their motion is entirely orderly, adhering to a single path and order <note>The author is arguing that planets don't "think" like humans; they follow a fixed divine geometry</note> according to the second book of the *Criticisms* <note>original: "creticorum szo." likely referring to a specific commentary or a misspelling of a logical text</note>. This is also manifest in the works of nature, which are so orderly and yet operate without deliberation, being subject to those movers and directed by them. Since nature lacks a mind and an intellect capable of scrutinizing better things, it is directed by an **Intelligence** <term>Intelligence: in medieval philosophy, these were non-physical, angelic beings that managed the movement of the planets and the patterns of the world</term>. And therefore, in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*, it is elicited that the work of nature is the work of an Intelligence. Whence the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher</note> says: "Nature does something orderly and perfectly even if it does not understand it," because it is a reminder of those more noble active virtues which are called Intelligences. In the book *On Medicines for the Heart* <note>likely Arnold of Villanova's *De medicinis cordialibus*</note>, it is said that the aforementioned specific forms come from active principles whose cause is God the Blessed.

One must lead this "light philosophy" <note>original: "leue phiaz"</note> from one extreme through the middle to the other extreme, namely to God the Blessed, toward whom all things tend. Regarding this, it must be known—so that the truth may be held more clearly than a mere mixture—that a certain and impressing agent concurs from the outside so that the **form** <term>form: the essential "blueprint" or "identity" of a substance</term> is introduced into the recipient. This happens along with its **hidden virtues** <term>hidden virtues: "occult" properties, like a magnet's pull, that cannot be explained by simple heat or moisture</term> by merit of a good, well-prepared proportion. The things to be mixed are perfected for the reception of the form itself, according to the second book of *On the Soul* and the book *On Medicines for the Heart*. Thus, the more perfect the mixture is (on account of the good proportion of the things to be mixed and a better temperament), the nobler and more virtuous a form will be introduced. Indeed, in the mixture of a human being, because of its nobility and the temperament of its proportion, the form is introduced "from without." For God gave to man the most temperate proportion possible to be found in this world, according to the first book of the *Prior Analytics* <note>original: "prio pria."</note>. This is indicated by man's most temperate sense of touch and the upright posture of his body. For the elements, when they come together in his mixture, are more purified and sequestered from the filth or stain of their individual properties. They are, in comparison to other mixtures, like gold examined in a furnace compared to other metals, according to the first book [of *On the Soul*] and the second book of the *History of Animals*. And therefore, man deserves to receive a form not only raised from the elements through celestial virtue, but also from the outside; for the "intellect alone comes from the outside," according to the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, and from the most noble agent, such as the glorious and supreme God. It is also the most noble of all forms, participating in His divinity most excellently; hence the light of the Psalmist: *You have made him a little lower than the angels* <note>Psalm 8:5</note>. Whence **Algazel** <note>Al-Ghazali, a Persian philosopher</note> says in his *Summa* on the soul: "When the mixing of the elements reaches a more beautiful and perfect equality, such that nothing more subtle or beautiful can be found (as is the case in human seed), then it becomes ready to receive from the **Giver of Forms** <term>Giver of Forms: the 'Dator Formarum,' a philosophical concept of a bridge between God and the physical world that provides every object with its essential nature</term> forms more beautiful than other forms," which is the human soul. This is also stated in the fifth book. He calls this "Giver of Forms" the "Agent Intelligence" mentioned before. Thus, in almost all things, the form of the species, with its hidden properties, is raised from the potentiality of matter by the virtue of the super-celestial bodies, as **Ptolemy** and **Messue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a Persian physician</note> felt, along with **Hermes**; and finally by the power of the Intelligence and God the supreme creator. 

Regarding the aforementioned points, a doubt happens to arise in what was said <margin>(flourish)</margin> that from the temperament of the proportion, the mixture is perfected and regulates the form

and its virtues, or the specific form in the matter. Because every proportion ought to be so corrupted by its property that it would seem impossible to happen. Since it is said in the books *On Generation and Corruption* and on the "inequal distemperament," that all distemperament and corruption comes from contraries. But it seems that nothing is contrary to a pre-existing proportion.

To this, it must be said that once the mixture is prepared by the goodness of the proportion, the specific form (as was said) with its specific properties is raised from matter by an external principle. A new proportion and other substantial virtues follow this form. For when a new substantial form arrives, the previous ones being corrupted, all else is innovated. For the form is annexed to matter without any medium, according to the second book of *On the Soul* and the eighth book of the *Metaphysics*; from which connection all accidents proceed. It must be said, therefore, that corruption is twofold. One is induced directly by a contrary, by which the pre-existing thing is improperly corrupted. The other is the corruption caused by the form or the substantial accident, by which it is corrupted so that a more perfect reception may occur, and thus a more perfect form arrives, which follows from the book *On the Causes of the Length and Shortness of Life*. 

Because of this reasoning, a doubt arises first in that it seems this form (with its appendages) is marked by some celestial virtue and caused under a determined distance; and therefore perhaps it is called "specific" and "hidden." And according to the second book of the *Physics*, "man and the sun generate man." Because of these things, this specific form seems no less a "common form" than an elementary one, and not strictly "contracted," as Messue testified.

Because of this, it must be said that as the distinction appeared in the tenth book, the impression of the superior things upon these inferior things is twofold. One is universal to all things and common through motion and light, by which all inferior things are governed in common. Thus also the elements, according to their distance or proximity. But there is another particular impression without motion and light, received properly without the alteration of a medium, impressed by some particular virtue of the stars and caused by their position. The common attraction of iron by a **magnet** <term>magnet: cited here as a classic example of an 'occult' or 'specific' virtue—a power that doesn't rely on heating or cooling something</term> comes from the North Pole as is experienced and derived. Those specific forms with their virtues follow this power. And therefore, because a regulated and good mixture (placed in elements by proportion or qualities) does not exist in a singular form, this specific form does not arrive unless it has noble and hidden virtues beyond the qualities of the elements. Whence the author of *On Medicines for the Heart* writes that this wonderful and hidden virtue cannot be found in "simples" <note>Simples are single medicinal herbs or minerals, as opposed to compound medicines</note> since it is given from the goodness of a mixture's proportion that is optimally regulated. And for that reason, one can see that in the mixture of the elements—from which a result emerges that declines toward the side of heat and also dryness—this form is found more often. <meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into "specific forms" and "occult virtues"—the hidden powers of natural objects like herbs, stones, and animals that cannot be explained by simple heat or cold. The author explores why these powers vary between individuals and why they seem to fade over time or when removed from their place of origin.</meta>

...the wind carries away the chaff. Also, in things of vehement coldness <note>original: "vehementer frigidis"</note>, perhaps they do not pursue wonderful operations according to their specific form because of an ignoble **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four humors (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a thing's nature</term> of the mixture, which digests and terminates the mixable parts poorly, unless they are animals like the **scorpion** <note>Scorpions were often cited as examples of creatures whose "specific form" granted them venomous powers despite being physically small or "cold"</note> which is raised by the principles of life. And therefore, in the second book on **pharmacology** <note>original: "pharmacorũ"</note>, regarding physicians who infect others by their coldness, it is not placed as something infecting from the whole species; rather, it does not infect except through its own qualities. In the fourth and sixth books, the same thing is seen to be felt. For they posit that poisons operate by their "complexional" quality, just as **opium**, **mandrake**, **henbane** <note>original: "iusqamus"</note>, etc., although in the first book of the *Examples*, the specific virtue seems more adapted to henbane.

Because of this, it must be known hereafter, according to the second book, that these forms are given to the species along with their appetites, and in the individual; whence it is called the "form of the species." And because the species does not receive "more" or "less" according to its essence, yet according to the existence of individuals and the principle of action, one individual participates more and another less, by being closer or further from the form or the matter. For we see that from certain individuals of a species, more noble operations proceed, such as from a **temperate man** or from **Socotrine aloe** <note>A high-quality medicinal aloe from the island of Socotra</note>; from others, however, they are more base, as from a **fool** <note>original: "morione"</note>. For this person, even if he seems to have a human figure, participates very little in the operations of humanity, just as Arabic aloe does within its own species.

The nobility and imperfection of a thing can also happen because of the homogeneity of the matter and a good proportion of the complexion to it. And it can happen because of the confusion of matter and an improper proportion to the complexion. Or it can be because of the virtues or the **soul** from which the specific forms are introduced, because the matter is either optimally configured or poorly configured, according to "more" or "less." And therefore, we sometimes see certain monstrous animals tend toward the human form, yet they are less [human] according to their virtue and power. 

Because of this, fourthly, it must be known that these **occult virtues** <term>occult virtues: "hidden" powers that are not immediately obvious to the senses, such as a magnet's pull or a plant's healing property</term> do not always follow their forms inseparably; rather, while the forms remain, the virtues themselves frequently perish. This can happen either because of the disposition of the matter with a distempered complexion in which the forms were received and upon which they relied, or on the part of the location, if they are moved from the places in which they were produced and preserved. For one's **homeland** <note>original: "patria"</note> is a principle of generation just as a father is. Whence, in the first book, the "Indian body" <note>likely referring to a body from a hot climate</note> will either become weak or die according to the complexion of its origin if moved. For a place <margin>{</margin> has a power that is connective and preservative of the thing located within it, according to the fourth book of the *Physics*. And therefore, in the tenth book of the *Philosopher* <note>Aristotle</note>, "Place makes the thing born as it is." Whence the law: "Our nature is as the region is." 

Or this can happen on the part of those things by which that form is imprinted along with its virtues. For since everything is measured by a fixed **period** <note>original: "pyodo," meaning a cyclical span of time or an astrological era</note>, just as is seen in births, the virtues of the heavens are sustained in the whole and in the matter for a determined time. This is the light of Wisdom: **"You have produced all things in number, weight, and measure"** <note>Wisdom 11:20</note>. And therefore, the failure of the experience of those who test these occult virtues often arises because they do not observe the designated time. For finding the substance and the object, they think they will also find the occult virtue there. For the form in the composite—the figure and color—remains longer than the wonderful occult virtue. Since this follows a determined period of time, it excels more in the **balance of the complexion** <note>original: "eucrafia"</note>. 

Wherefore we see today many stones lacking the virtues formerly attributed to them, <margin>NOTE</margin> partly because of their separation from their places, <margin>{</margin> and partly because of the antiquity of time. This is also true in the virtues of **images** <note>astrological talismans or amulets</note> impressed by art. For images still exist that nevertheless lack their virtues, as I have now proven to be the case in the city of **Constantinople**, and as a decrepit man shows in those things which belong to humanity. 

<margin>{</margin> Furthermore, as to why specific virtues—both natural ones and those induced by the **magical art**—do not have such great efficacy today as the ancients wrote, it may happen either because of another generation or another movement, such as the movement of the **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars; its slow "precession" was believed to change how celestial power reached Earth over centuries</note>, which is not the same now as it was once sung of old. Or it is because the specific movement is now ignored under which determined **characters and figures** <note>the symbols engraved on talismans</note> are imprinted. 

In a form given from the outside in such a way that it is not raised up from the potentiality of matter—as all testify that such forms are incorruptible and perpetual—nevertheless, its specific virtue is corruptible and measured by time. 

Furthermore, it should be noted that men wonder more at the operations of occult virtues than at the operation of simple virtues or appetites, even though the latter are not a little wonderful. The cause of this can happen because men do not wonder at things that are common, but at those things which happen rarely and are more internal. Whence, as has been made manifest by a mother not seen as an example; whence regarding the physicians of the heart: **"Admiration falls away from familiar things"** <note>A common medieval proverb: familiarity breeds contempt, or at least a lack of wonder</note>, and the soul neglects to seek the reason for them. And yet, their virtue can be very wonderful, as is seen in the stupendous operation of **fire**. For by its virtue, it leads something from potentiality into act; it prevents itself from being touched and ascends upward, and makes the things it overcomes ascend. For it grows, according to **Aristotle** <note>original: "Aris."</note>, in a multiplied analogy almost to infinity, and is corrupted and transmuted into its own substance, which it encounters; for it lives as long as it is fed by it. These and such things are more wonderful than the attraction of iron by a **magnet** and other such things. Yet because they are common and continually appearing to us, we do not wonder at them. But because the operation of the magnet and others is rare and foreign, it leads us into wonder and the investigation of the cause. For **"because of wonder, men now and at first began to philosophize"** <note>A famous quote from Aristotle's Metaphysics</note>.

The cause of this can also be the difficulty of knowing the **proportion of the mixture** in which the specific form is received with its virtue. For we are ignorant of the proportion of the simple elements causing the mixture as long as we live in this world. Whence the *Collector* <note>likely referring to the medical text "Colliget" by Averroes</note> says: It is impossible to know by judgment the measure of the mixture through which a specific operation occurs in a being. For the mixing of the whole of two things with a third is from the work of God, blessed and supreme, in the work of nature concerning complexions. 

There is also another difficulty and wonder arising from the ignorance of the principles from which the occult virtue proceeds, since it is not drawn out entirely from the potentiality of matter, but an external agent works toward this, such as a celestial body, or an **Intelligence of God** <note>an angelic being</note> full of forms, and finally the First Blessed One [God]. 

Regarding the fourth point, however, as to the first and second, it must be said that a specific form, as has already appeared, is a substance insofar as it is immediately united to the matter constituting the object. To the other point, it must be said that as it is a substance, it is grasped by the **intellect alone**, just as the soul or another substantial form is not perceived [by the senses]. But as it is a virtue and a property of a substance, or a property itself like the color or odor of a thing, it is said to be grasped through **experience**.

To another point, it must be said that for so much Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note> says that it [the hidden power] would not be demonstrable by reason, and therefore remains hidden, since it surpasses the natural qualities by which physicians undertake demonstrations through touch, taste, smell, and color—as well as the substance, such as whether it is hard, soft, rough, smooth, etc., which the physician calls the "substance." The specific form itself, insofar as it is a certain property, will be demonstrated just as others are. However, when Galen understood it as not demonstrable, he meant that this proceeds from ignorance; for the predicted qualities of reason cannot lead us into a knowledge of their essences and forms. To another point, it must be said that just as an accident is corrupted in the genus of substances, so too is the form. Just as when a cheese dies <note>A metaphor for fermentation or the loss of a substance's original nature.</note>, it is reduced into this or that other form with properties generating that specific form of the corrupted thing; just as in the generation of fire from air, where a quality proportional to fire is introduced, the essence or species either remains in potency or is no longer present as it was in act. Let it be said for the present regarding this difficulty that it touches on no small matter. To the arguments of the other part, it must be proceeded according to Galen, Avicenna, and others saying that the form has a property, virtue, and quality in the manner now exposed.

To another point, it must be said that **similarity** <note>original: "similitudinem"</note> is twofold. One is that which is of respect and proportion. For example, the attraction of the thing being drawn to the attractor is founded upon superior specific forms, which is a quality; and from this, as shown, the action of such virtues does not principally occur. It helps, however, if there is a similarity of heat to heat. There is also another, more properly called "congruence" or "homogeneity" of the specific form of one thing to another, toward which the virtues by which one acts upon another are directed. And Galen understood this similarity when he said the types of attraction exist only through the similarity of substances to substances. 

To another point, it must be said that although the specific form follows generation, it arrives at a being already in act; yet when it occurs, the pre-existing actuality is corrupted, and in an instant a new form is introduced with the dispositions following it, as declared previously. To another point, what must be said is apparent. For it implies that the form, insofar as it is given, is simply the first principle of operation in the substance. But insofar as it is a certain form in the genus of substance, the immediate principle of operation is a certain "hidden property," an occult virtue and natural power. <note>The marginal 'q' likely stands for "Quaestio" (Question) or the start of "Quod" (That).</note> **That a middle state occurs between the healthy and the sick** is shown from the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Ars Medica," known in the Middle Ages as the *Tegni*.</note> and from the first book of the *Theorica* of **Haly Abbas** <note>Haly Abbas (930–994 AD), a famous Persian physician; his "Complete Art of Medicine" was a standard textbook.</note>, which says that medicine is the science of the healthy, the sick, and the **neutrals** <term>neutrals: a state of the body that is neither perfectly healthy nor clearly diseased, such as in the elderly or those recovering from illness</term>. This middle state is felt by **Joannitius** <note>Hunayn ibn Ishaq (809–873 AD), who translated Greek works into Arabic and authored the "Isagoge," a foundational medical primer.</note> and in the fourth book of the *Theorica*. This is also proven by reason: for in the "predicaments" <note>Aristotle's categories of being.</note>, there are "mediated" properties which do not necessarily require one or the other in a susceptible subject. Health and sickness are of this kind.

---

For if it is said that "whiteness is in this," it does not follow that it must be called "white," and the same for blackness. For it is a doubt whether they exist simply or according to a certain respect, as in the third book of the *Topics*. So it shall be in the healthy and the sick: for they can be so according to a part, and simply not be so.

Again, every motion is from one extreme to another through a middle, which is neutral to the extremes. According to **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay." for Aristoteles</note> and Galen, motion is from health to sickness and vice versa. Furthermore, the animated body is changed from sickness into health and back according to nature; but no natural transmutation is sudden. For it does not sustain sudden changes in the *Tegni*. Whence in the seventh book of the *Histories*, Nature proceeds little by little and in an orderly way, so that by continuity the dual states and the middle are hidden. This would not be the case if the transition from one extreme to the other happened suddenly and immediately. Also, since two natures constitute the body—the "compositional" and the "proportional"—there can be three differences of unity from these. For it will be possible for a "temperate" <term>temperate: the ideal balance of humors (complexion) for a specific individual</term> state to exist in generation, but a "distemperate" state in proportion, and vice versa. Or a temperate state in the active qualities and a distemperate state in the passive ones. And similarly, it is described according to its fourfold nature, and in the same way in unity, which can happen from the variety of the causes themselves. For it does not only follow generation; rather, it follows a divine thing from above, from the higher principles of generation. For this reason, the middle state is called "neutral," or a "neutral disposition" falling between the healthy and the sick.

The opposite of these is shown with no less authority and firm reason. For in the "predicaments," the healthy and the sick are placed as "immediate" <note>Meaning there is no gap or third option between them; you are either one or the other.</note> because one or the other naturally exists in its susceptible subject, just like "even" and "odd" in number, as in the fourth book of the *Topics*. Between health and sickness there is no middle; but between good and evil, there is. <margin>Haly Abbas, book 7, on manners.</margin> Furthermore, Galen seems to reject the "neutral" in his *On the Sects*. For he says the ancient discourse of medicine is the doctrine of the "health-giving" and the "sick-making." Furthermore, in the books on the causes and accidents of diseases, and especially in his own work, and in the first and second books on *Elements*, in which he investigates the nature and essence of sickness and health, he never makes mention of a middle between them. For all men, when the actions of the parts of the body serve the functions of life blamelessly, believe themselves to be healthy. For from the exit of the "temperate" state until someone falls into a disease, they are considered healthy. However, whichever part is harmful is estimated to be sick. For it seems that when someone exits the temperate state, they fall into **intemperance** <note>original: "intemperantiũ"</note> and vice versa. Whence he says: "those whose health is moderation, their sickness is immoderation." His faithful imitator Haly Abbas follows this in the sixth book of the *Theorica* where he deals with diseases and their causes; those places are not of insufficient weight.

Also, it is specific. We shall say how between two dispositions—between which there is undoubtedly no middle—a "middle" is called. As in the third book of the *Colliget* <note>A medical work by Averroes.</note>, I still do not attend to that which they said, because it is neither healthy nor sick, which is declared as will be said in the following. This is also conquered by reason, since health is a certain "natural good," while sickness is its opposite, like "evil." Between a natural good and evil, there does not fall any "nature" properly called, but only the **privation** <term>privation: the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present</term> of the good and a defect. Whence it has a "deficient cause," namely, falling away from the good. Between a privation and a habit, as will be declared, no middle falls.
