<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of substances, moving from the "hidden powers" of things to a logical and medical debate: is there a neutral state between health and sickness? This was a major point of contention among medieval scholars following the traditions of Aristotle, Galen, and Avicenna.</meta>

I have said before that between the "good" and "evil" of moral habits and politics, there falls a **middle**—for example, the hermit, who is neither good nor bad in regards to performing political acts, according to the Commentator <note>original: "Cōmentator". This refers to Averroes (1126–1198), the influential Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in the tenth book of the *Metaphysics*. Furthermore, those who claim that **health** consists in a single point—as if it were a perfect and indivisible balance—argue that whatever departs from that point immediately falls into imbalance and sickness. Since one falls away from that precise "point" of balance, they argue that no "middle" state falls between the healthy and the sick.

Regarding this, it must first be known that **health** is the composition of all particular parts according to nature. Or, as the author of *On Diseases and Symptoms* <note>Galen.</note> says: Health is a disposition according to nature that perfects the accustomed acts of each individual. Hence, Johannitius <note>Johannitius is the Latin name for Hunayn ibn Ishaq (809–873), a key translator of Greek medical texts into Arabic.</note> says in his nineteenth chapter: "Health is a temperament perfecting natural things according to the course of nature." At the beginning of the *Canon* <note>The *Canon of Medicine* by Avicenna (Ibn Sina), the standard medical textbook of the medieval world.</note>, it is described as a disposition or habit from which healthy operations proceed. Likewise, in the third book of the *Colliget* <note>A medical encyclopedia by Averroes.</note>, it is placed as a "good disposition in a limb which enables it to perform the operation it possesses or to receive the sensation it possesses." **Sickness**, however, is the opposite: a disposition of the body contrary to nature, which immediately causes harm. Or, it is an imbalance outside the course of nature, from which the effect of injury arises.

In the first book of the *Canon*, it is defined as a non-natural disposition in the human body from which harm in operation proceeds. 

In the third book of the *Colliget*, it is a disposition in a limb through which it acts or suffers contrary to nature. However, because "healthy" and "sick" are **contraries** <term>contraries: two opposite qualities, like hot and cold, that can exist on a spectrum</term>, and because these species of opposites must be discussed first, we shall speak of them and then the others. Also, in the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*, things are called **opposites** when they cannot both exist in the same subject at the same time. Hence, in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*: "Whatever things do not come together in one subject and at one time are called opposites." There are four modes of these opposites, as placed in the *Categories* and the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*: **Contradictories**, **Privatives**, **Contraries**, and **Relatives**. 

Some of these, according to Aristotle, do not determine a specific subject or genus for themselves; such are **contradictories**. For they oppose each other as affirmation and negation. For a **contradiction** is that which has no middle in its own right, as noted in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*; such things occur regarding every subject. For of anything, it is true to say it either "is" or "is not," as per the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. Nor do they belong to a genus, since "non-being" is in no genus; indeed, even "being" is not a genus, as is proven in Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–c. 305 AD), whose *Isagoge* was the standard introduction to logic.</note> and the third book of the *Metaphysics*. 

Some opposites do determine a subject and a genus for themselves, such as <margin>**Contraries**</margin> **contraries**. For they are placed under the same genus and are maximally distant from one another, as described in the *Categories* and the fifth and fourth books of the *Metaphysics*. Thus, "odd" and "even" belong to the genus of number and the genus of discrete quantity; and "whiteness" and "blackness" belong to the genus of color and surface—for it is the property of a surface to be colored. **Relatives** also determine their genus and subject for themselves, sometimes in different subjects and sometimes in one. For the same person can be both a father and a son to different people. They also share a genus. For some are those whose being consists in how they relate to another, such as relatives by essence—like habit, disposition, and discipline. Others are those whose being is said and referred to another, like "great" and "small," "similar" and "dissimilar," or "knowledge" and the "knowable."

There are also others called **privations** <term>privation: the lack of a quality that should naturally be present, such as blindness in a creature that normally sees</term> which determine their subject and genus in one way, but not in another. Such are those in which there can be no "return" from the lack (the privation) to the possession (the habit), as in sight and blindness, or light and darkness. For the subject of blindness and sight is the eye; 
<margin>at Book 6 of the Metaphysics</margin>
and the subject of darkness and light is the air. However, a genus is not determined because a privation is a negation within a subject, according to the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. Whence Aristotle says: "Habit and privation are affirmation and negation restricted to a genus or subject at a specific time and disposition." He says "about a genus" because a privation can in some way concern a genus, just as it concerns a subject—for instance, regarding the sight of puppies or the proper time when one is expected to see. 

Next, it must be noted that a **middle** is called 
<margin>The three-fold middle</margin>
that which is located between two extremes, which is usually distinguished in three ways by those speaking in general terms: namely, a middle according to **subject**, according to **time**, and according to **form** or disposition. 

It is called a **middle according to subject** when the subject itself is not a recipient of either opposite; thus a stone is a "middle" between the healthy and the sick, for neither "healthy" nor "sick" can be said of it. 

A **middle by reason of time** is said to exist when there is a time in which neither opposite belongs to the subject; thus, for a puppy or a young vulture <note>original: "uspiculi", likely referring to a young bird or a specific animal known for being born with eyes closed.</note>, there is a middle time between "seeing" and "blindness." For before nine days, it is called neither blind nor seeing. For a **privation** is properly so-called when a subject is naturally fit to have a quality but does not have it. For blindness is a certain privation, but one is not called "blind" at all times, but only when it is natural to have sight and one does not have it, according to the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*. 

There is also a 
<margin>According to form</margin>
**middle according to form** when a single middle form, composed of the extremes, is inherent in the subject—such as "pale" or "red," which are composed of white and black. 

If you ask, therefore, what kind of middle exists between the aforementioned opposites: first, regarding **contradictories**, it must be answered that there is no middle at all. For no one perceives a middle between "is" and "is not." Of anything, it is true to say in any subject and at any time that it either "sees" or "does not see." Much less is there a middle disposition between them. 

In **privatives**, however, there is a middle of subject and of time. For there is a subject (like a stone) of which neither blindness nor sight is true. And there is a subject of which these are true only in relation to time, like a dog after nine days and not before. Regarding some things, there seems to be a middle of subject and time according to different parts of the relationship and form. For the same person, by different reasons, can be both a father and a son.

In **contraries**, there is a middle of subject, as has already appeared, but not of time. For at any time, it can be said that one of the contraries exists in the subject. A **middle according to form** is that which is principally sought here, and the previous things were discussed for the sake of explanation. In some contraries, a middle is found, as in those called "mediated contraries," such as "red" between white and black. Sometimes this middle is named with a single word denoting the form, such as "red" or "pale," or "lukewarm" between hot and cold. At other times, it lacks a name and is named by the negation of the extremes, just as that which is "neither just nor unjust" is the middle between the just and the unjust; or "neither good nor evil" is the middle of good and evil.

In some contraries, however, no middle is found in any way mentioned. Because of this, these are called **immediate contraries**, such as "even" and "odd" in number, or "healthy" and "sick" in the body, according to Avicenna.

Finally, it must be known that in some contraries, there is a mutual change from one to the other, as from healthy to sick and back. In others, however, there is not; rather, one appears to be naturally inserted into the subject—for instance, "odd" in the number three, "even" in quantity, and "heat" in fire.

<summary>This page analyzes the definitions of health and illness through the lens of Aristotelian logic, categorizing them as "immediate contraries" that leave no room for a neutral middle state, while explaining various types of philosophical opposition.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the definition of health and sickness, specifically addressing whether there is a middle ground between the two states—a concept known in medieval medicine as the "neutral" state.</meta>

Furthermore, a <term>state</term> <note>original: "gratia". In this scholastic context, it refers to a specific condition or quality of being.</note> seems to be entirely opposed and mutually exclusive from its subject, so that one is found completely without the other. This does not seem to fit entirely with the healthy and the sick for some people. For one necessarily suffers the other, because it is impossible for health or sickness to occur in things lacking life, motion, and sensation. Indeed, life persists, however poor and meager, through some portion of balance and health. Therefore, according to these thinkers, sickness will always be located within health, which is not found to be the case in other states. 

Regarding the aforementioned, there is a doubt: for it seems, as they say, that to be sick is to exist in effect with the healthy. Since **Galen**, in his writings *On the Art of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." refers to *De Ingenio Sanitatis*, also known as *Methodus Medendi*.</note>, wishes for the sick to be "not preserved" <note>Meaning they are in a state of decay rather than maintenance.</note>. However, this must be owed to a body participating in health. It is also said in [aphorism] 65: In the healthy, all things are according to nature; in the sick, they are beyond nature insofar as they are sick. Because, therefore, it is said of the sick that "everything is absent" and yet "insofar as he is sick" is found at the same time, health is seen to exist within the sick. 

Again, in the *Colliget* <note>Averroes' medical encyclopedia.</note>: Fever is natural heat mixed with a sickly or foreign heat. Likewise, that which is suffering from a "burning fever" <note>original: "causonisans", from the Greek *kausos*.</note> is healed. Since everything is led from potentiality into act by something already existing in act, it is therefore necessary for health to exist in act within the sick person. 

Are they therefore [opposites]? In these states, they are contraries and "immediate" <note>Logic term: opposites with no middle ground.</note>, whose definition stands at the greatest distance so that they cannot be one. Therefore, the sick person should not walk according to the healthy, nor vice versa. Concerning this, as appeared just now, some have said that no body is so sick that some health does not remain in it in effect. For "health creates health," or a part of health, as stated in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, Book VII, discussing how forms are generated.</note>, so that in the sickest body there is actual health which, through every effort, is finally brought back into effect. 

But because sickness and health are something other than life—which here do not seem to be separated—he shows that **Health** is opposed to sickness, while death is opposed to life. For while life remains, health and sickness are changed in turn around their subject. Hence, from the causes of the length and shortness of life, health and sickness occur in those capable of receiving them. Because of this, it must be said, secondly, that in sickness—no matter how severe—health is preserved in some part of the heart as a "habit" or "potency," or in its own act. For it remains dormant, just as life remains in the seed received by the womb, which, being a "habit," is soon brought into "act" by the generator (aphorism 48). 

Hence, the **Commentator** <note>Averroes.</note> in the fourth book of *On the Heavens and the World* says: The heart is what alters the sick member toward health; the sick member is that which can be altered. It leads this potency or habit into act easily, since it stands but a short distance from it. That which brings such potency into act is "celestial vigor," as when the Moon is joined to some benevolent planet or looks upon it (distinction 10 and 104). Or, it is the "form of health" existing in the soul of the physician, through which necessary healing things are applied to the subject. For in this way, health is made from health, just as a house is made from a "house" existing in the mind of the builder, as touched upon in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*. 

From this, it appears that when a sick person is "in effect," health will not be in them in its own potential as it is in other contraries, nor in its own act. The habit, therefore, has a different nature from other contraries. And through that, what was to be said becomes clear.

Between health and sickness, **Galen** was seen to place a middle ground according to form or disposition: calling it the **neutral** state or neutral disposition. He distinguished this "middle" into three types:

<margin>The first Neutral</margin>

First, the forms of health and sickness are broken down together into a third state, and thus they constitute the first "neutral" meaning, which he says is the true middle between a very healthy body and a very sick one. In this category, they place children, the elderly, and those first recovering (convalescents), with whom those "falling" <note>into sickness</note> are associated. 

Second, because the aforementioned forms are at one time equally joined in the members, as in the body of a paralytic, or by participating unequally, as in the body of a blind man. Hence **Avicenna** says: just as when someone is healthy in their "general state" <note>original: "gōne" likely *generalone*</note> and sick in a "particular part" <note>original: "gpone" likely *proportione* or *partione*</note>. Or healthy in active qualities and sick in passive ones, or vice-versa. Or sick in "quantity" (languid) and [healthy] in form. 

Third, it will be by relation to ages and times, such as a "phlegmatic" person who is sick in childhood and becomes healthy in youth. A "colic" person, on the contrary, is called neutral. Or a child who is healthy in summer and sick in winter; for youths, it is the opposite. 

It should also be known, according to **Galen**, that the "neutral" in the first sense is a certain and real middle between health and sickness. The other two middles, especially the third, are based on reason and relation. For viewed from the outside, they depart into health and sickness. But the intellect—comparing one thing to another in the convention of meanings—constitutes a middle and a neutrality according as it is gathered into one from different parts or dispositions. Know, therefore, that the first meaning implies a unity of the subject according to the unity of time and diversity of parts; the third is the opposite of this. 

Regarding the second, it should be known that **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, 10th-century Persian physician.</note>, moving this doubt, strives with a certain distinction to reconcile **Avicenna** and **Galen**, as if there were not a real but rather a verbal dissonance between them. For he says **Avicenna** wished it to be impossible for health and sickness to be removed from the body at the same time to create a third disposition having no part of health or sickness. Thus, **Haly** wants to understand **Avicenna** as saying there is no "middle ground" that does not participate in the extremes (which is called a middle by negation of the extremes). Just as that which is neither just nor [unjust] would be called a middle between the just and the unjust. 

But he says **Galen** wishes, through the "disposition which is neither health nor sickness," for a disposition of the body in which health and sickness are found together: so that either one is in one part and the other in another, or a portion of each is in each. Or, according to the path of mixing or neighborliness. For according to these three, as appeared, **Galen** distinguishes a threefold meaning of the neutral. Thus, **Avicenna** denies a middle that is a third thing separate from the extremes. **Galen** wants the middle to be "good by participation." 

But perhaps this cannot stand alone, as it seems to oppose the mind of **Avicenna**, who is [usually] in agreement with **Galen**. For if **Avicenna** does not deny a middle between the predicted dispositions except for that which does not participate in the extremes, then by similar reasoning he would deny a middle between all immediate contraries. For in them there is no middle except by participation of the extremes (as appears in motion and sensation). Just as lukewarm is constructed by the participation of hot and cold; and red, gray, and green and other colors are made from white and black. And therefore, in the fifth book of the *Physics*: A middle compared to one of the extremes will seem to be the other. Because of this, according to **Avicenna**, all contraries would be immediate, even though he himself distinguished them by "mediated" and "immediate." But someone in **Haly**... [claims] **Avicenna** [wished] between healthy and sick...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the "neutral state" (medium) between health and sickness, specifically critiquing the views of Haly Abbas and reconciling the theories of Galen, Avicenna, and Averroes.</meta>

...that there is no middle state designated by a single name, just as there are intermediate colors between white and black. However, saying this does not remedy the defect in **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician.</note>, since **Avicenna** expressly intended that the middle state between the healthy and the sick does not occur in just any way they are introduced, but in ways that clearly precede it. For **Galen** also explains well with what intention he places a middle between the healthy and the sick. Properly, in the first [book], he signifies the initial meaning in which this appears most difficult—whether it occurs through a path of transformation or alteration, or in what manner. And for this reason, perhaps, many of the moderns have agreed, many of whom, though they seem to disagree in words, actually coincide in their opinion. 

They say, in fact, that health and sickness can be considered in two ways. Either in regard to their **causes**, and in this way no middle state occurs, because since the causes are immediate, the effect will also be immediate. For the causes of health and sickness are called "equal" and "unequal," <note>Referring to the balance or imbalance of the four bodily humors.</note> between which no middle exists. Or, they are considered in regard to **operations** <note>The functional activities of the body, like digestion or breathing.</note>, according to which a healthy body is said to exercise its actions duly and without distress. The sick body, on the other hand, performs them poorly, between which they say a middle state falls. 

And therefore, some of them testify that **Galen** defined disease as a "disposition or habit contrary to nature, sensibly harming operations." And that health is a "disposition or habit according to nature, perfecting them." Between the perfection of operations and their sensible injury, a middle state falls, namely, an <term>insensible injury</term> <note>A functional problem that exists but cannot yet be felt by the patient or seen by the doctor.</note> in operation, which they wish to be the "neutral" disposition. However, this position cannot stand, neither in its first part nor its second. For regarding the first part, "equal" and "unequal" cannot properly be the causes of health and sickness, since the most proximate and immediate cause ought to be of the same coordination and nature as the effect. This is clear because Galen defines it through them, or many of them define it through natural causes. A definition and the thing defined must belong to the same category and coordination, according to the *Topics* [of Aristotle], book six and likewise book four. But "equal" and "unequal" are properties of **Quantity**, or are placed more in the category of **Relation**. Health and sickness, however, are in the category of **Disposition** or **Habit**, which is the first kind of **Quality**. Because of this, equal and unequal will not be the causes of health and sickness. 

Yet, because many of the great authorities have said this, I say they mean "equal" to signify temperament or proportion, and "unequal" to signify distemper or inequality, primarily regarding disease. <margin>Opinion of Averroes</margin> In the second part of this distinction, **Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician.</note> first collects his thoughts, rejecting the "neutral" state and spurning such a disposition. There is not a middle between the harm of sensible operations and their benefit, nor is there any variation except according to "more and less." And there is no middle between two contraries, such that one of them is in a part without the part in which the other resides. And through this, he denies a neutral meaning in essence, nor does it exist in time without a time in which it is the other, regarding its essential meaning. He says this is manifest from speculative science. If, therefore, there is no variation between these except in "more and less," since these do not differ in species and nature (according to the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* and **Haly**), then there will be no middle state to consider regarding operations.

There were others saying that "healthy" and "sick" can be considered in two ways. Either according to nature, or according to the judgment of the intellect (which tends toward the same thing). And so they said that no middle falls between the healthy and the sick. For since temperament and health, as they say, consist in an **indivisible point**, as soon as something slips from that indivisible point in which health consists, it immediately falls into the divisible and into distemper. Which they later wish to separate into the "neutral" and the "sick." And they testify that **Avicenna** held this consideration. 

Or, they can be considered according to the judgment of the **senses**; and this will be the physician's consideration of them, which **Haly** does not transcend. Whence he says in the fourth book of the *Quadripartitum* <note>Ptolemy's work on astrology, frequently commented on in medical contexts.</note>: A physician does not look except at things manifest to sensing and seeing. Yet this and other opinions can be challenged, because health is not a simple, absolute, and abstract form, but is concrete and related to an insensible natural quantity, as will appear in the following discussion. For a middle state would not differ from a natural philosopher in this way, since both consider beings as they are founded in insensible matter, which is the intention of the *Physics*. But the physician considers the universal and the particular for different ends. Likewise, the intuition of the senses is founded upon the thing. For the sense is informed by the thing or by its accidents, which are said not to deceive concerning their proper object, according to [Aristotle's] *On the Soul*.

There were also others saying that "healthy" and "sick" can be referred to two things. Either to the **speculative physician**, and thus there will be a middle between healthy and sick called "neutral," since the speculator observes motion occurring in the alteration from health into sickness and from sickness into health. Between all such motions, a middle nature falls, as was said before; for which reason a middle will be placed between the healthy and the sick. 

Or they can be referred to the **practical physician**. And because practice is twofold—namely **preservative** and **curative**—insofar as he perceives that a body is in this middle state between health and sickness, it is managed by those things which are owed to the healthy (as preservation through similar things, and by leading it so that it does not slip into their contraries). Insofar as he perceives sickness, he governs with a curative regimen through total contraries. And this is indeed what some say was the intention of **Avicenna** when he said there is no middle between dispositions. 

But this is not valid, because **Avicenna** says there "seems" to be no middle. Which he indicates by saying there is "without doubt" no middle. This is clear because he speaks of the neutral state in the first and second parts, protesting the opinion of **Galen**. This, however, does not seem to be valid; for since theory is ordered toward practice, as a means to its end, one cannot grant that something is considered in theory (as that which is before the end) which is not ultimately ordered toward the end. If, therefore, the practical physician does not deal with the neutral state, neither does the theoretical physician. <margin>[flourish]</margin>

If this opinion is adapted to the aforementioned ones, it probably establishes that there is no middle regarding the causes or nature of the thing, or the intellect (which is considered by the theorist in stable things), but there is a middle regarding operations and the senses, which are primarily attended to by the practitioner. There is also another opinion which **Avicenna** also accepted: that health is taken strictly as it consists in the equality of the hot, cold, dry, and moist—not absolutely, but in regard to operation. Sickness, however, he assumed to be in the inequality of these. Between these, as has been said, no middle occurs. But **Galen** took "health" and "sickness" as broader terms, extending them to two points between which a space is understood. But here, the aforementioned points and those to be said below destroy this view, as he is seen to weaken his own words...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into whether a "neutral" state exists between health and sickness. The author explores the differing definitions used by Avicenna and Galen, reconciling them through Aristotelian physics and the concept of "qualities."</meta>

<margin>and other modes</margin>

You should not place a **middle state** between those things whose consideration is narrow, such as health and sickness according to **Avicenna**; but rather in those things whose consideration is broad, such as health and sickness considered by **Galen**. This is because a middle must necessarily fall between all extreme boundaries. However, this is not the case between "broad" boundaries because one of the boundaries contains the limit or extreme, and not the truth, and likewise for the other. Thus, that which was the "middle" for boundaries accepted strictly is located beneath both. There are many other discourses agreeing with this opinion in spirit, if not in words, and therefore they are omitted.

Regarding the third point, it should be noted that **Avicenna** <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, d. 1037) was a Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard medical textbook in medieval Europe.</note> accepted health and sickness as existing under a wider range than **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (d. c. 210 AD) was the foundational authority of Roman and medieval medicine.</note> did. This is shown because health and sickness are opposites by their very nature. Therefore, since the definitions of opposites are themselves opposites, as often as one opposite is used, so is the other (as appears in the *Topics* <note>Aristotle's "Topics," a treatise on logical argumentation.</note>). If "healthy" were simple, equal, and unified, then "sick" would be as well. But "sickness" is multiple and broad, as most physicians and **Avicenna** maintain; therefore, "health" must be so as well. And this is what **Galen** meant in his works on the composition of bodies, where he posits four types of bodies, two of which are healthy and two of which are infirm. And lest I seem to say this without proof, let his own sequence be introduced:

He sees the best body as existing as "well," which **Galen** calls "always healthy," preserving a perfect health without the help of medicine. And he adds: "very close to this 'always healthy' is one that achieves health through a few means—namely, the action of medicine alone." For it requires only moderation, as he says, so that its health may be preserved; and this will be the body that **Galen** calls "largely healthy" and very close to the first. Thus, there are two healthy bodies. Next, he added the sick bodies themselves, dividing them into two parts, saying: "That which is further from these previously mentioned healthy bodies must be reduced to health through many medical actions." For it requires healing through "running, wrestling, and fighting" <note>This refers to the "gymnastic" or strenuous physical regimens prescribed to restore a weakened constitution.</note>. Then he added a fourth, which—no matter how much effort is applied to the other bodies—would not yet emerge as "good" (that is, healthy). For it cannot acquire a certain health, but remains "something else" (that is, continually sick). I maintain, however, that all these are such by their very nature from birth.

Those who understand **Avicenna** less well explain this differently, wishing to find a "middle" between the healthy and the sick by using the second or third body types, understanding the first body as "health" and the fourth as "sickness." But perhaps these people have not yet read what he wrote in the *Categories* or the *Topics*, nor do they understand his foundations in the seventh book of the *Physics*.

Furthermore, in that same place, **health** is a certain "commensuration" <note>The balanced proportion of the bodily qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry).</note> of hot and cold things in comparison to those things which are within (that is, the fluids from which the body is composed) or in relation to the "containing environment" (that is, the air surrounding us), according to **The Commentator** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the 12th-century philosopher known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note>. For these are the causes of health. According to some, it is in relation to the "container" (that is, the whole body). It appears, therefore, through this expression—which denotes a reduction and smallness—that health is described in relation to something that is not a simple or absolute "narrow" form, but rather a composite one.

That **Galen** extended health and, consequently, sickness more strictly is shown by **Aristotle** <note>Abbreviated as "A." in the text.</note>, who says that [the definition] of health belongs to the "living" (that is, the physicians: **Galen** and his followers), and not to "natural philosophers," as some have perversely explained. As appears from what he immediately added: they did not place in the definition of health (which is a **habit** or **disposition** from which the operations of a healthy person proceed) that a "third disposition" (neutrality) is provided, unless they defined health just as it is "refined" (that is, they determined health punctually and strictly). They placed in the definition of health an addition that is not needed (that is, a distinction by which health is separated and distinguished from a third disposition), by taking health in every way, or entirely strictly and truly. And finally, he adds: "Moreover, we shall not quarrel with the physicians on this point regarding the living." He speaks, therefore, against the physicians, and not to the natural philosophers. 

And so it appears that **Galen** wished to take health in a narrow sense, insofar as a "neutral disposition" is located between it and sickness. Next, the opinion of **Avicenna** and the Truth is revealed more fully. I say, therefore, that **Avicenna** in no way wished for a "middle" to fall between healthy and sick, just as "motion" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "motion" (motus) is a gradual, continuous change over time, whereas "mutation" (mutatio) is an instantaneous change.</note> does not exist between them. This is because he located health and sickness in the first species of **Quality**. In the seventh book of the *Physics*, it is proved that the motion of "alteration" only occurs in the third species of quality, which is "passion" and "passible quality." For health or sickness are only caused by a preceding alteration in the primary sensible qualities: heat, cold, dryness, and moisture. Similarly, shape or figure is acquired by a limb because the matter is disposed by some of the sensible qualities existing in the third species of quality; for because matter is made dense or rare, such a shape or another follows. 

It also appears sufficiently that in the third species of quality, the motion of alteration would not exist, as **Avicenna** passed over it as being manifest. This is because natural power or impotence (which is located in the second genus of quality) is not brought in or removed except through an alteration in the preceding basic qualities, and finally, through their generation or corruption, it is given or removed. Whence **The Commentator** in the fifth book of the *Metaphysics* says that natural powers and impotences are "preparations" and "potentialities," not qualities in act. And these preparations follow substantial qualities. And since they are preparations, they are "privations" <note>The absence of a quality that should naturally be present.</note>. And therefore, they were not investigated in the seventh book of the *Physics* as to whether there is motion in them or not.

Since, therefore, health and sickness are "habits" and "dispositions," and these are "relative" <note>The term "ad aliquid" refers to the Aristotelian category of Relation.</note>, they will consequently be spoken of as such. In such things, there is no motion, as shown in the fifth book of the *Physics* and the eleventh book of the *Metaphysics*: motion exists only in three categories: Quantity, Quality, and Place. Therefore, in habit and disposition, there is only **mutation**, which is found in "substance" and finally in all other categories other than those previously mentioned. Thus, in health and sickness, there will be "mutation" and not "motion." Therefore, there will not be a middle between healthy and sick, just as there is not in "substances," since this is acquired through a temporal and successive "motion of alteration" and not through a "mutation" which introduces opposite forms into the instance without a middle. Thus it appears when one element is generated from another: no intermediate form precedes the form introduced into the matter. Also, cause and effect are proportioned to each other; they are "proximate" and "immediate" causes and effects. But the proximate and immediate cause of health is "temperament" and "moderation" (or commensuration). The cause of sickness, however, is "intemperance" or "immoderation," as in the first book on disease. Here they are opposed...

It is a form added to the figure of health. Whether it precedes reason or is given by nature, it prepares the proportions. Whether they are or are not. When Galen responds to these things, he says that in such things, as said before, it is in the boundaries. ...as privation and possession. In a state of privation, a middle state does not exist concerning the thing being sought; however, a middle state of the subject or of time may appear in certain cases. From these points, whoever notices the subtle intellect of **Avicenna** <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, d. 1037) was a Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was the foundational medical textbook for centuries.</note> will see that a middle state falls between the healthy and the sick. However, what **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (d. 210 AD) was the chief authority of Roman medicine; his works dominated medieval medical theory.</note> asserts in the *Tegni* <note>original: "tegni"; referring to the *Ars Medica* (The Art of Medicine), often called the *Tegni* in the Middle Ages.</note> especially concerns observing a middle between the healthy and the sick. He either accepted "motion" generally through change, as in the beginning of natural [philosophy], or he placed the motion of alteration in other species of quality, and not only in "passion" <note>In this context, "passion" refers to a state of being acted upon or a passive quality of the body.</note> and passible quality. This clarifies the matter and it seems to be seen thus: **Avicenna** feels it in sufficiency. I also say that **Galen** in the *Tegni* intended the "middle" between healthy and sick to be local motion, and not in all other places, so that his defining doctrine—which he testified at the beginning of his book to be brief—might be amplified and rendered orderly. He separates these into three meanings, even sub-divided.

Regarding the fourth point, as to what appeared first as the middle, **Galen** was also following the opinions of **Heracleius** and **Herophilus** <note>Herophilus (c. 335–280 BC) was a Greek physician often called the father of anatomy.</note>. Hence, in the fourth book of *On Preserving Health*, some call the middle of health and sickness "neutrality," regarding which no small question exists for the judge to decide if those who propose this are to be held in contempt. Wherefore, in the sixth book of the same: "You remember those things which were demonstrated concerning health, how great its latitude is." This is a certain third disposition of the body which those around **Herophilus** call "neutral." **Haly Abbas** <note>Haly Abbas (d. 994 AD) was a famous Persian physician known for the "Complete Art of Medicine."</note>, in the fourth book of his *Theorica*, touched upon this neutral state lest he seem to diminish the discourse of **Galen**, since he stood as a more faithful reciter, never naming it elsewhere as seriously as **Galen** did exemplarily in the fourth book of *Accidents*. **Johannitius** <note>Johannitius (Hunayn ibn Ishaq, d. 873 AD) was a prolific translator of Greek medical texts into Arabic, which were later translated into Latin.</note> likewise followed **Galen** in the *Tegni*, so that all three proceed from one root.

To the other point, it must be said that health and sickness follow the principles of generation and are vegetatively and uniformly more inherent than color. Since they are generated from more immediate and uniform qualities, the name is therefore diffused through the law of the same. Color, however, is more spiritual and superficial. It is, after all, the extremity of a non-transparent body. Whence the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who held specific mystical and mathematical views on the nature of the physical world.</note> called color a certain "epiphany" <note>original: "epyphariā"; likely a corruption of "epiphania," meaning surface appearance.</note>. To the other point, it must be said that as shown regarding health and sickness, it is not motion but a "change" through which no middle is acquired over time; rather, the opposite form is introduced in an instant. The major difference of the argument is also sufficiently explained in Difference 18. To the other point, it must be said that no transformation of nature is sudden, assuming the thing already exists. For it is said in the *Tegni* that nature does not sustain sudden changes in a conservative regime. Nevertheless, either the thing itself or its subject is introduced through a sudden change.

To the confirmation by **Avicenna**, it must be said that his speech is about the general grades of being, where one extreme is the matter called *hyle* <note>Greek term for "prime matter."</note> and the other is the primary cause, which do not coincide in middle states, except in certain particular contraries. To the other point, it must be said that this being granted, it does not follow that there must be a middle state separate from the extremes. For just as one nature overcomes another in health or sickness, it will be called healthy or sick from the dominant part in the mixture, as **Anaxagoras** <note>Greek philosopher who proposed that "everything is in everything."</note> used to say regarding the distinction of things.

### DIFFERENCE 73.

<margin> <note>A hand-drawn profile of a man's face, likely a "manicule" or marker used by a student or reader to flag this new section.</note> </margin>

> **I**t is shown that pain cannot be a disease.
> Because that which denotes a disease is not the disease itself,
> since the sign and the thing signified can be the same in 
subject, but never in "reason" <note>i.e., by logical definition.</note>. To the physician, pain is a sign; it shows a sudden alteration, which is a disease in the composition, or a solution of continuity <note>A "solution of continuity" is a classic medical term for a physical break in the tissues, like a wound or fracture.</note>, which is a disease in the union, as per the *Tegni*.

Furthermore, according to **Galen**, pain is "impaired action" (*actio laesa*); a disease, however, is "the action that impairs" (*actio laedens*). These are related as the active and the passive.

Moreover, pain is a certain "alteration," according to the fourth book of the *Theorica*. This is a motion. Disease, however, is not a motion, since it is something stable and already fixed, according to the book on *Accidents*. It is, in fact, a habit or a disposition in which motion is proven not to exist, according to the prior Difference.

Again, those things which are divided as opposites cannot one become the other, since one of the opposites does not help the other toward being (**Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works on logic were standard in medieval schools.</note>, in the fourth book of the *Topics*). But disease and "accident" and "cause" are divided as opposites. Pain, as has been said, is an accident accompanying certain diseases. And it is fixed. For Galen detests spasm and fever, saying they are accidents unless they happen from an apparent cause; and he calls it a disease when it arises from a primary bad composition. Again, that which immediately impairs operations is called a disease, as every definition of disease denotes. But pain does not immediately impair operations; for there are as many types of lapses [in function] as there are [parts], as is clear in the *Tegni*. These are three: composition, structure, and the common nature in which pain is not located.

If it were said that pain could be a disease—not all pain, but that which is lasting—this cannot stand. Because according to **Avicenna**, pain is "to suddenly feel a contrary pressure." But that which is permanent and fixed, like a disease, cannot be sudden in any way. Therefore, pain cannot be a disease if it were to be permanent. The opposite holds for disease in the opinion of the fathers. Furthermore, that which impairs operations without a middle is a disease; but pain cannot be such, since if its subject as a disease were to recede, the pain would remain. And an "accident" is not distinguished from a "primary disease" except by being in motion and alteration, rather than in remaining and being fixed. But that which is changed and altered can be generated and fixed, like "whitening" when it comes to the boundary of its perfection. Therefore, pain can [seem to] be a disease. Regarding the first point, it should be known that the boundaries of quality appeared first, and regarding these, see Difference 76. Things "contrary to nature," although many others are posited, are usually reduced to three: cause, disease, and accident. At the beginning of the *De Ingenio* [On the Method of Healing], four things are said to supervene outside of nature: the corruption of action, the corruption of the composition performing the action, the cause of the composition, and the accidents accompanying the operations. The corruption of action and composition are reduced to the same thing, namely disease, so that there remain three, just as there are three things in nature: matter, form, and the composite of these, as well as the generating dispositions. With these three, the particular terms "passion," "pain," and "harm" are expressed. All these in this...

<meta>This page continues the technical differentiation between health, disease, and the "neutral" state. It focuses on the specific definitions of "disease" (morbus), "accident" or symptom (accidens), and "passion" (passio), drawing heavily on the terminology of Haly Abbas, Aristotle, and Galen.</meta>

They coincide because they are qualities. They differ, however, in disposition and habit, in passion and passible quality. And all of these are also against nature, except that "passion" in one of its senses is named as [following] nature, as will be shown. A cause is a disposition or habit from which an injury arises mediately. In this, indeed, they differ from a **disease**, because the impression of the latter is immediate. Causes with a middle [an intervening step] are either that which is first and from which the discovery of some disposition in the human body comes, or its first fixation. And this is threefold: primitive, antecedent, and conjunct (or manifest, preceding, and inherent).

**Haly Abbas** <note>Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi (d. 982), a Persian physician whose "Royal Book" was a major medical text.</note> also says that a cause is distinguished from others as a primitive agent from those things produced by it. For just as when stones or bricks are arranged together, they move with one motion until the last, just as one can see in miraculous automata <note>original: "anthomatibus"; refers to self-moving mechanical devices, a common medieval metaphor for chains of causality.</note>. So, when a cause is set—especially a conjunct or primitive one—a disease is established. Once established, an **accident** <note>original: "accidens"; in this context, it refers to a symptom or a secondary effect, not an unexpected event.</note>, injury, passion, and pain follow in their own way. 

For a disease differs from an accident because a disease is something that injures principally and is, as it were, the subject. An accident, however, does not injure directly but secondarily and as something following. Hence it is called a <term>symptom</term> <note>original: "sinthoma"; from the Greek "symptoma," meaning a "falling together" or coincidence.</note>, that is, a "co-falling," or an "offspring," or a "consequence," so that ambiguity is removed; just as an accident qualifies the subject and accompanies the disease, so is the reasoning concerning the accident. 

Furthermore, a disease, since it is a disposition, is said to be "in a state of completion" <note>original: "in facto esse"; a state that has already been reached and is now stable.</note> as in a disposition or habit. An accident, however, since it is an alteration against nature—and generally a passion and a passible quality outside of nature—exists "in a state of becoming" <note>original: "in fieri"; a process currently happening.</note> and changing. And sometimes, as will appear, it can also be in a state of completion. And because a disease is proportional and properly a simple vice lacking humors, it is said more than the others to be "in a state of completion," as in <term>marasmus</term> <note>A wasting away of the body.</note>; properly, the definition of disease is more truly owed to it since it is fixed and more fully at rest. 

It is also a condition more worthy than other natures. This, more than the others, is declared to be "in a state of completion" since no alteration is there by reason of a cause, for it has departed. But still, in the subject, a small alteration occurs in the disposition, so that one having a <term>hectic</term> <note>original: "ethicaz"; referring to a "hectic fever," one that has become part of the body's "habit" or "constitution."</note> does not perceive it from the unequal distemper. In other diseases, however, 
<margin>3</margin> 
the subject is altered not a little. Hence the seventh book of the *Aphorisms*: "Sickness is indeed motion; health, however, is rest." Nevertheless, the cause is somehow fixed and at rest when it is properly conjunct. Disease, accident, and cause agree in that they are against nature. 

For the sake of clarity, know that a "completed sickness" is spoken of in three ways: either properly, when it has no internal cause, such as a hectic fever; or more commonly, when the entire preceding cause is placed underneath, as in the final paroxysm of a fever. Hence the fourth book of *Aphorisms* and the first of *Internal Affections*. The third species of dysentery is called a "completed and constructed sickness," and properly so in respect to the two preceding ones which are more "in the process of becoming."

<margin>{</margin> 
"Passion" clearly sounds like something "in the process of becoming" and changing, which is spoken of in many ways in the *Metaphysics*. In one way, it is a quality according to which the subject happens to be altered, such as becoming white or black; and such a passion can be according to nature. For to sense is a kind of "undergoing" <note>original: "pati"; the root of "passion," meaning to be acted upon.</note> according to the book on *Accidents* and the second book *On the Soul*; and similarly to understand, in the third book of that work. Such a passion is not corruptive but rather the health and perfection of the one undergoing it. 

<margin>2</margin> 
Passion is also said to be that which acts against nature and continually casts something away from it. Hence in the sixth book of the *Topics*: "Every passion, having been made, casts away from the substance." Similarly, harmful alterations are especially those of sadness, and great calamities are called "passions." Passion differs, as is clear from these points and as **Galen** testifies, from disease in that disease is said to be "in a state of completion," whereas passion is always "in the process of becoming." 

Furthermore, passion is sometimes against nature and sometimes according to nature; disease, however, is only against nature. 

This also differs from an "accident," since passion is entirely in motion and sometimes according to nature. An accident, however, is not in motion alone, but sometimes in habit or form when it receives fixation, and it is entirely against nature. 

"Injury" <note>original: "nocumentum"</note>, however, is the cutting off or the lesion caused by the action of the disease. For "injury of action" is an animal symptom, according to **Galen**. The injury itself, or lesion, is like a genus to a passion against nature and to an accident. For an accident is an injury of action, according to the sixth book of the *Theory* and the third book of the *First Canon*. The second is a lesion in the members of the head.

Regarding the aforesaid, it happens to be doubted: because it was said an accident would sometimes be in "habit or form," which does not seem right. Because in the third book of *Accidents*: "An accident is an alteration of that which is according to nature," which is properly called its highest reason. But although a disease is an alteration, it is not so simply, but in a certain respect. For it is an alteration in the dispositions of that which is according to nature, so that a disease is in a disposition or quality. And because it consists in a certain fixation and habit. An accident, however, is not in a disposition but only in alteration. 

Because of this, it must be said that an accident is never in habit or form, but only in alteration and motion, as the logic dictates. But an accident—that which is an accident—can, when it is fixed in a disposition or made into a quality, show in this way that "pain" is a disease, which would be a wonder. But then, to the contrary, it will be said that this distinction can also be adapted to passion.

Because of this, perhaps it should be said that **Galen's** text said an accident would be in "habit or form" sometimes so that a middle point might be noted between passion (which is entirely in changing and becoming) and disease (which is in a state of completion and alteration). Thus, some of the accidents have a no small affinity for it, as indicated in the first book of the *Internal Affections*. 

Furthermore, it is doubted: because in that same place, disease is nothing other than "motion outside of nature." But an accident is also a motion existing against nature; hence it seems that every accident is a disease. It must be replied, as is written there, that alteration or motion is twofold. One is when it has come into a first fixable disposition, and such a sickness emerges. Hence we say that sickness is motion and health is rest. For from that slight change coinciding in the thing itself, it can somehow be called "motion" only with confusion. For soon that slight alteration is fixed, essentially injuring the actions. 

There is also another motion which remains entirely in the change of alteration, not yet becoming a habit and not fixing anything; such a motion is an accident, just as "becoming white" is.

...so that a great motion of whitening <note>original: "dealbatis"; likely referring to the development of skin conditions like leukoderma or leprosy.</note> which is like a disease is compared to a fixed sickness. In another way, when something is in the middle of changing—as in the process of whitening—it was not originally in the person, but it is still occurring and is "on the way" <note>original: "in uia"; a scholastic term for a process that has not yet reached its final state.</note> so that they are more fully whitened; and such a disease is "in the becoming." The remaining type is that which has never yet arrived at a fixed state but exists always in alteration and in the process of being made. And such a thing is an **accident** <note>In medieval medicine, an "accident" refers to a symptom or secondary effect that "falls upon" the patient, rather than the underlying essence of the disease.</note>. Thus, one type of motion is a disease, and another is an accident. 

**Passion** <note>original: "passio"; here meaning a state of being acted upon or suffering an external influence.</note> is similarly of this motion. For passion is an alteration which is still occurring in the matter or the motion. However, an alteration that remains fixed is a disposition or a sickness. An **accident**, on the other hand, is that which happens to a living being beyond its natural state. 

Regarding this, one must know that **Eulimicus** <note>A likely reference to an ancient medical authority, possibly a corruption of a name like Eudemus or a specific commentator on Aristotle.</note> said in his first book on origins that **pain** is a **disease**. Thus, here pain would be a certain change of the body leading away from natural qualities to those outside of nature. He also said that sometimes disease happens because of pain. 

**Galen** <note>The most influential physician of antiquity (2nd century AD), whose works formed the backbone of medieval medicine.</note> derides this view for many reasons. However, he and **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."; likely referring to the Philosopher.</note> seem to respond to this question with the distinction mentioned before, distinguishing between two types of pain: lingering (fixed) pain and its opposite. They say the first (fixed pain) can be a disease, but the second (fleeting pain) cannot, since it consists entirely of alteration and is still "in the process." 

I, for my part, say that the parts of the body "suffer" only when they are not yet in a lasting disposition—as in a headache caused by humors contained in the stomach. If anyone wishes to argue about names, the head is properly said to "suffer" while the stomach is the one that is actually diseased. But a part is truly "sick" when it suffers by itself and for itself. Whence, in the first book on disease according to **Constantinus the Monk** <note>Constantinus Africanus (d. 1087), a translator who brought Arabic medical science to the Latin West.</note>: "The first species of disease is that which I described, and also pain, when it remains in the body from the heat of the sun or fire." 

Frequently, also, an accident itself becomes a sickness, just as a headache which happens from a fever; when it becomes fixed and remains for a long time, it becomes a sickness even after the fever has receded and the pain has remained. For then it puts on the nature of a consequence and a shadow, and takes on the nature of a self-standing thing. 

Because of this, it should be known that the same thing can be both a **disease** and **pain** in different ways, just as the same thing can be a **passion** and a **symptom** <note>original: "sinthoma"; from the Greek "symptoma," meaning an occurrence or a sign of disease.</note> depending on the reasoning used. Hence, in the third book on accidents: "It happens sometimes that the same thing is called both a passion and a symptom, though their meanings are different according to one or another rationale." 

**Pain** can be understood in two ways: formally (as pain itself) and materially (the thing which is the pain). 
1. In the first way, pain can in no way be a disease, since it is entirely in alteration and has never achieved permanence or stability. Whence, in the fourth book on accidents: "Pain does not exist after the cut or tear is made, but only as long as the incisions and tears are occurring in the passion itself." Even if someone says a disease is a motion against nature, a disease has still achieved stability or permanence. 
2. In the second way, pain can be a disease when it acquires a certain permanence and does not exist in a state of total alteration. Properly, when its subject is fixed in a part of the body, it then becomes a disease because it hinders the body's operations by itself.

The explanation of this is as follows: pain, as first understood, is a certain "passion" and a "passible quality" <note>Terms from Aristotle’s "Categories." A passible quality is a temporary state resulting from an external action.</note> against nature. In these things, there is properly and immediately "motion," that is, alteration. For in this species of quality are placed qualities and intentions that remain in a state of total alteration and constant change. Therefore, pain—being made of these things—can never have the rationale of a **disease**, which implies a certain permanence. 

However, pain received in another way, when it has taken on a certain fixation and permanence, is no longer in that state, but is rather placed in the first species of quality <note>In Aristotelian logic, "Habit" or "Disposition."</note> in which there is no motion except by accident. And so, since disease and cause imply a certain permanence and fixation, one of them is a "habit" and the other a "disposition," as **Avicenna** <note>original: "Ay."; Ibn Sina (d. 1037), the great Persian physician-philosopher.</note> placed them in the mode of quality. Therefore, when pain has achieved such stability and lack of change, it is not unfitting that it can become a disease. 

**Galen** sensed this more subtle opinion, though he did not express it clearly. I maintain, therefore, that in a disease there is no motion properly speaking—at least regarding the cause of the alteration—but it is something already finished. In pain, however, there is no such state unless it becomes fixed in a limb. And so, when it is fixed, although the greater part of the alteration is gone, the person still feels it; it is no longer a caused effect but is now a "bad composition" of the body. 

This can be explained by a more sensible example: imagine heat applied to the body. When the heat is being applied but has not yet fully impressed itself, it is still in a state of "alteration" and "becoming," which is proportional to pain as something distinct from disease (the way a shadow is distinct from a body). But one must also understand that the heat can be so impressed on the body that even when the source of heat is removed, the heat remains in the body—as in those suffering from "hectic" or "ephemeral" fevers <note>Medieval medical terms for fevers that last a short time or consume the body's moisture.</note>. Even when the cause ceases, the heat remains in the part as a quality. Pain conforms to this opinion: when its duration and its inheritance in the subject become fixed, even when the cause is removed, it becomes a disease. 

And this pain will be caused more by a sudden alteration. For pain that comes from a "solution of continuity" <note>original: "gtinuitatis sōiōe"; a medical term for a wound, break, or tear in the flesh.</note> can hardly be fixed or made lingering, since it consists in an ongoing alteration. However, it should be noted by considering subtly that a pre-existing pain and one that has been made lingering are not the same thing, since the subject in which it is fixed is different, as is the time of its fixation—just as the heat of a fire is different from the heat impressed into iron. This [lingering pain] is generated from the former. Or, as it is not the same thing to be "in the process of whitening" as it is to be "the result of whitening" when the preceding alteration is finished. To understand this more fully, consider the ninth chapter. 

Regarding the four points, we must first say that pain—insofar as it merely points to a sickness—could never be a disease, since it consists in a total alteration. But it becomes a disease when it "rests" in some way. Secondly, insofar as pain is an accident, it is entirely an "injured action." Insofar as it takes on the nature of a disease, it becomes the thing that "injures" the action. Thirdly, we have seen how pain is an alteration and how it is not. Fourthly, although these things are divided into opposites, one can become the other. For a thing that is one in its underlying subject can become different according to its various levels of reality—for pain exists both in alteration and in a state of rest...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on the classification of medical conditions. ...almost by a certain permanence, it is made into one thing and then another.
<margin>In book 4 of *On Accidents*</margin> Regarding the affirmation, it must be said that those thinkers perhaps proposed that disease and accident <note>The term "accident" in scholastic medicine refers to a symptom or secondary effect that follows a primary disease.</note> were the same according to the same criteria, not distinguishing between them at all. Or, whichever fever it is, it has more the character of a disease than an accident. Regarding this, focus on the beginning of the fourth section. Concerning the other point, pain also appears; for pain, insofar as it is an accident, does not harm actions since it is itself a "harmed action" <note>A technical term meaning the function of the organ is already impaired.</note>, but rather insofar as it is a disease in itself. And because the proper definition of pain is that it be an accident and not a disease, it is therefore assigned under the category of accident and not disease.

To the other point, it must be said that if pain were entirely fixed and habitual, it would now lose almost the entire definition of pain. However, it is not said to be "fixed" because that arrives entirely on its own, although the cause for why it is fixed is something else; nevertheless, it remains in a certain alteration, yet not similar to the previous one. Therefore, it does not have as much power to inflict injury on the senses when it reaches an equal bad complexion <note>An imbalance of the four bodily humors.</note>.

On the occasion of this subsequent question, it is doubted: **Whether stupor is a disposition or an accident**, such as pain. For it seems to be a disposition, according to the second section. Whence the Wise One says: "The winner in this sickness is the colder one." And in the third section: "Stupor is an organic disease" <note>original: "morbus officialis"; a disease affecting the "offices" or functional parts of the body.</note>. Galen, against Archigenes <note>A 1st-century Greek physician.</note>, tries to show in the great interpretations that the relationship is like that of an ulcer and an aposteme <note>A swelling or abscess.</note>, so is it with pain and torpor. But an aposteme is not a different kind of ulcer, rather it is another disease, like an ulcer and the loss of flesh in the skin. Therefore, torpor will not be the cause of pain, since it is a certain great coldness, but rather something distinct from it. Again, that which cures pain is not pain. For the same thing does not suppress itself. But stupor cures pain; whence the Aphorism says: "Moderate stupor diminishes pain." Furthermore, a disease can be caused by a primary cause; but stupor is caused by vehement cold, as appears in those traveling in a time of most intense frost. Again, stupor is caused by constriction and by the touch of a "torpedo fish" <note>An electric ray; ancient and medieval doctors used its shock to treat pain.</note> while still living, and similar things which seem to cause a blockage. Furthermore, if stupor were pain, those suffering from numbness would be in continuous pain. But they do not feel pain; rather they feel the passion only when they move. Galen concludes from these points that stupor is a disease and not an accident or pain. However, that it is an accident is written in the fourth book of *Accidents*, as it is proper to the sense of touch; and in the fifth book of the same, and also in the book *On Types*. Whence Haly <note>Haly Abbas, a Persian physician.</note> says: "Epilepsy, spasm, stupor, tremor, and jumping are accidents following sickness." For which reason he places stupor as one species of pain in the first section. Also in the *Internal Parts*: "In the teeth and gums there occurs a certain passion which we call stupor," but passion is an accident in the third book of *Accidents*. Again, in the fourth book of the same: "Torpor is composed of difficult sensibility and mobility." These are caused by a cold imbalance <note>original: "discrasia"; a lack of harmony in the humors.</note>, which seems to make the animal acts entirely sluggish. But this was previously placed by Galen as a disposition, and from it, the accident follows. Therefore, torpor will be an accident and not a disease. Because of the first point indeed—

***

—it should be known that torpor, stupor, "falling asleep" <note>original: "obdormitatio"; the tingling "pins and needles" sensation.</note>, or freezing is a corrupted quality caused by a lack of the delivery of the sensory spirits <note>In this period, "spirits" were believed to be subtle vapors that traveled through nerves to allow sensation and movement.</note> into the body. It is called a "corrupted quality" because this is common to everything outside of nature. It has not yet been shown whether it is a disease or an accident.

It is also called "lack," because when the spirit sufficiently illuminates the sensitive body, health exists. But when it is entirely prohibited, insensibility is caused; when it finds a middle ground, it produces stupor. It is said to be of the "sensory spirits" because stupor works against sensation, and tremor against proper motion. It is a "lesion of the sensory spirits" because stupor works against the immense. And therefore it is said to be composed of difficult sensibility and mobility. Wherefore in the third section: **Stupor is an organic disease** causing harm to occur in the sense of touch, namely, either destruction or diminution with tremor if it is weak, or with softening if it is established. Because not only is the sensory power prohibited from penetration, but also the motor power. It is sometimes called "stupor of admiration" <note>The root of the word "stupid" or "stupefied" refers to both physical numbness and mental wonder.</note> when it affects the soul more, since it is a certain passion of the soul, according to that saying: "The Pope, the wonder of the world" <note>original: "Papa stupor mundi"; a common medieval epithet for Pope Innocent III.</note>. Not infrequently, however, it affects the body more, and this either throughout the whole body when the lesion is in the brain—and especially in the anterior part—or according to several parts, for instance when it is in the nape of the neck, or according to some specific part, as when it is in some nerve, or attributed to the teeth from the eating of acidic and tart things. 

There is a difference between common stupor and **epilepsy, apoplexy, and catalepsy** <note>original: "cathelenfim"; likely catalepsy.</note>, because the former occurs in the anterior part of the brain from coldness or heat and humidity, and the patient lies with eyes closed and seems to bring on a heavy sleep. Apoplexy and epilepsy happen more in the middle of the brain from a maximum of cold and humid humor. Catalepsy indeed arises from coldness or dryness mixed [with other humors], while lying with the eyes open. For by its quality, the eyelids are dilated and prevented from closing, as in the fourth book of *Internal Parts*. The cause of stupor is manifold. For sometimes it is induced by a constricting coldness that semi-mortifies the sensory power, or by heat that dissolves the spirit, according to the Aphorism: "Harmful heat frequently used induces stupor of the mind." Or it comes from excessive dryness and humidity, or from a humoral or windy fullness, or from some occult power like the torpedo fish, and similarly by hot or cold poison, or by a very tight bandage. What constitutes a disposition, disease, accident, and pain is written in chapters 72 and 73.
