<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into medical terminology, specifically focusing on whether "stupor" (numbness) is a disease or a symptom. It transitions from a general discussion of bodily sensations into a formal "Difference" (chapter) regarding the classification of diseases of composition or structure.</meta>

...must be said. Regarding the third point, it should be known that **stupor** <note>numbness or insensibility</note> can be understood in two ways: either by a blockage of the pores <note>original: "opilatione pororum"</note> that is thinning or constricting, occurring in the nerve that carries the sensory spirit, or by an excessive looseness of them. In this way, stupor is an <term>official disease</term> <note>A disease of the "organs" or "instruments" of the body, rather than a general imbalance of fluids.</note> since it happens in a pore located beneath the structure of the part. This is perhaps what **Avicenna** perceived when he said it would be an official disease, or because in it there occurs a distorted shape of the parts characterized by trembling, according to **Galen** and **Avicenna**. For a blockage, a looseness, or a distorted shape is a disease, and such is the nature of stupor. 

Indeed, several causes induce a blockage; some others induce a dilation (such as those related to heat), or a distortion (such as in the sense of touch or the shape). Therefore, it is an official disease. But wait—it was said above by **Galen** that stupor is a certain "great coldness." It must be said that this coldness can be considered in two ways: either in itself as it is impressed upon a part, thereby harming the sensory operations (and thus it is a disease of the <term>complexion</term> <note>An imbalance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, wet, dry.</note>), or according to the blockage it causes in the limb where it occurs (such as in the sense of touch), and in that way it is an official disease. This is written at the beginning of the book *On Interior Diseases* <note>original: "De interioribus"</note> regarding thick, abundant humors; sometimes they harm as organic particles, other times as similar parts. For according to the obstruction of the pores, they are organic; according to the alteration of the temperament, they are a disease of the similar parts.

However, if stupor is considered as a certain difficulty of sensation caused by the aforementioned causes or diseases—whether constricting or dilating—then it is an **accident** <note>In this context, an "accident" is a symptom or secondary effect that follows a primary disease.</note>, since it follows them "like a shadow follows a body." And it is more true and proper to say that it is an accident rather than a disease. This is shown by its mode of being, which consists in being in a state of flux and transformation. For when the animal spirit passes freely through the body, there is health, because it exists in a certain completed and continuous state. When it passes through in no way at all, by the same logic, there is sickness. But when it is in the middle of these two, in the act of departing and changing, then **torpor** <note>sluggishness or partial numbness</note> is produced, which is shown by the compression of the limb. It is, therefore, an accident that is a kind of moderate pain, whether it occurs in limbs that naturally have little sensation (as is said of the teeth in Difference 42) or because the sensory spirit is prevented from passing freely. Thus, I agree more with **Archigenes** and many others that torpor is a varying accident, and that it is a pain that is properly called a "disposition."

Regarding the fourth point, what needs to be said appears from what preceded; for they follow the paths already heard in the previous sections. However, for the sake of a fuller teaching, one might wish to address Galen’s arguments. Responding to the first, he hints at a similarity which he introduces simply without proof, the intention of which has already been seen; he will not concede that stupor is a "certain great coldness," but rather an accident of it, as is seen not insignificantly in the books *On Accidents* and *Interior Diseases*. To the other point, it must be said that pain and torpor can cure pain and torpor, yet they differ as shown in Difference 154. The same thing can also suppress itself by accident. To the other point, it must be said that the cause immediately induces a distorted disposition in the part, from which stupor is finally caused, as was seen. To the other, it is clear from the text, because it was conceded (though improperly) that stupor would be the aforementioned blockage. To the other, it must be said that when stupor intensifies, a pain is perceived to some extent even without movement, along with a certain biting "creeping" sensation <note>original: "formicatione," a sensation like ants crawling on the skin.</note>. And furthermore, Galen speaks as one desiring to obtain victory, grasping at everything. To those things which...

---

...is said of a higher part, provided it is more fully conceded. But nevertheless, to the second point, it must be said that a "passion" <note>A state of being acted upon or suffering an effect.</note> sometimes serves properly when it is in the process of becoming and being transformed, either according to nature or against nature. Sometimes, however, it is used improperly for a disease, as is said in Difference 73. Other reasons justly prove more strongly that stupor is an accident.

## DIFFERENCE 74.

<margin>1</margin> That it is not a disease of **composition** <note>A disease affecting the structure, arrangement, or number of parts in an organ.</note> is shown because a disease is only that which centrally harms actions. However, by "composition" <note>The structural arrangement</note>, actions are not performed, since they are perfected through the part; consider that "composition" is the nature but "assistance" constitutes the function, as in Difference 63. Likewise, every disease is thought to be of composition or of "effectuation," since it is seen to depend on the thing itself as an effect from a cause, since composition is the "forming" of the limb, as in Difference 17. Furthermore, if it were a disease in composition, since it is divided into structure <note>original: "plasma"</note>, quantity, number, and position or site, then the disease would no longer be in the category of **quality**, nor could it be cured (at least those in number and quantity), since nothing is contrary to them. <margin>structure</margin> For "structure" is divided into form, pores or pathways, and the receptacle (such as a cavity and a surface). In form (at least the essential kind), no contrariety is found, nor in the surface, since it stands as a mode of quantity. Number also, and quantity or magnitude, belong to the category of quantity; and position is similarly a genus distinct from quality. Further, this disease would seem to be a disease of the surface, since it is a matter of roughness and smoothness, which are noted to involve "positions" in the categories. Again, position is a species of quantity, but disease is not; rather, it is a quality. Therefore, it is not a disease in composition.

The opposing view is held by the physicians. Galen says in the *Tegni*: "The kinds of failures are the same as those things which display excellence." Since composition is one of the things that perfect excellence, its destruction is also shown in them. Because of this, it will also be a different disease. Regarding the first point, it should be known what a disease is and what a "disposition" is, as shown in Differences 72 and 73.

<margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;/ DISEASE
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Y | Of Composition
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;\ Composite Disease
</margin>

It should be known, moreover, that a "disease of composition" (or of "equalization") is different from a "composite disease." For it is called "of composition" when it is innate and assigned to the organic limbs. It is "composite," however, when many things concur into one. And this is also manifold: either because three types of diseases are composed in it (namely, of composition, of disposition, and of common nature, as in the proper Difference), or because several diseases are composed with one another, remaining distinct according to their form, like a heap of stones forming one disease from prior diseases, as will appear in the appendix to this and in Difference 72. 

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some, moved by common opinions, have somewhat departed from the truth, thinking that diseases occur only in composition because of the "origin" mentioned above in Difference 63 regarding composition. Some even estimated that only a "material fever" <note>A fever caused by the corruption of physical humors.</note> was an illness of the affections, but not of the parts. Others, however, as will be seen, thought that composition alone was disease. But what is to be thought of this will appear in the third part. Regarding this, it should be known that disease is found in composition. For a disease is a disposition or habit by which actions are actually destroyed; such is that which is in composition. For if an operation must be perfected, not only is a temperament <note>original: "complexio"</note> required as the principal instrument, but there must also be a "composition" through which the act is brought into being more perfectly in the power of the similar part, as in Difference 63. It should also be noted: that while every disease is a quality (whether as a disposition or a habit, as in Difference 72), some are nevertheless founded in other categories.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic classification of medical conditions, transitioning from the specific symptom of "stupor" to a broader philosophical discussion on how "Position" and "Composition" define the nature of disease.</meta>

->**Position**<-

Just as "relation" is founded upon other categories, so too is position. For a disease of the formed structure <note>original: "plasmatis"</note> is a quality and is founded within it. Indeed, form and the shape standing around something is the fourth kind of **quality** <term>Quality</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, Quality is one of the ten categories; the "fourth genus" specifically refers to form or external shape.</note>. However, a disease of the surface brings with it smoothness and roughness, which are certain qualities existing around a position. For from the fact that parts are so disposed—either as some protruding beyond others or lying equally in a plane—such a disposition is left upon the surface. But a disease of number and quantity, as well as of continuity and position, is a quality founded in quantity or position.

<margin>Health is found in several properties and in the composition.</margin>

## General Union
In the **official members** <term>Official members</term> <note>Also called "instrumental members," these are complex organs like the heart or hand, as opposed to "simple" parts like flesh or bone.</note>, disease is found in quality and in the quality which is in quantity. And it is added that it exists in position and connection. For number, quantity, or position is not the disease itself, but rather the "bad quality" founded within them; just as a stone <note>such as a kidney or gallstone</note> or a worm are not the diseases in their own right, but rather the malice of the disposition is the disease, as their essence is found to be harmful.

## So that it may shine more clearly
It should be known that the powers of the primary qualities are necessary, in which their "scent" <note>metaphorical for their essential nature</note> is preserved. In the qualities, this is pre-informed; by a regulating power, it is formed—that is, articulated. It reaches into quantity and position so that the resulting quality is either **health** or **sickness**, which is found in several **predicaments** <term>Predicaments</term> <note>The ten fundamental categories of being (Substance, Quality, Quantity, etc.) used to organize all knowledge.</note>. For illness is found in the first type of quality, as a disposition or a state of the sense of touch. It is also supported in the fourth type, which consists of form and the shape surrounding a thing: straightness, crookedness, and such qualities as are found in the limbs—most especially when some are straight that should be twisted, or the twisting of what should be straight, or the roundness of the square and the squareness of the round. And this is called "disease of form" in the formed structure, according to which the actual function is realistically harmed. Quality is also found in **continuous quantity** <note>Measurements like size, length, or volume.</note>, namely in greatness and smallness, insofar as the action of touch is essentially harmed by these. Or even in **discrete quantity** <note>Measurements involving distinct numbers, like the number of fingers.</note>, such as in number as it is founded in site or position. Which is certainly accepted generally by the physician as "Place" or "Where," and as "Association" or "Connection," or even the "Predicament of State" <note>original: "habitus"</note>. Thus, disease is found in five predicaments: namely **Quantity, Quality, Position**, and finally **Where** and **State**. In "Position," it appears in a twofold way. In the category of "When," however, there is properly no disease, except perhaps regarding "priority" and "posteriority," as in the primary and passive stages of an illness. It is not located in "Substance," since disease is an **accident** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist; you can be sick or healthy and still be a human.</note>. Nor does it exist in "Relation" <note>original: "ad aliquid"</note>, since it describes the thing itself simply without respect to another, unless perhaps generally. Nor is it in "Passion" <note>The category of being acted upon</note>, nor is it distinguished by "Action," for when a disease is present, the action is the thing causing the harm, just as the action itself is what is harmed. Because only four modes of articulation are apparent, there are only four diseases in "composition" <note>structure</note> that should be heard of in their own way. And know that "position" is used in many ways: one as a difference of continuous quantity.

<margin>Diseases in composition are only four.</margin>

## For one quantity consists
of parts having position, while another does not. The latter is "discrete," while the former is "continuous." Parts of the continuous have position, but not those of the discrete in the predicaments. This position is the ordering of parts toward some common boundary.

## Position is also taken
as one of the ten genera of things: a certain "site" of the parts and an ordering of their generation. This mode (and not the first) fits more fully with the "position" that the physician feels to be the fourth nature of composition or co-equality, insofar as it implies site or place. For he says "Place" and "Association" or "Community" or "Connection" is proper to disease, according to which mode the predicament of "State" <note>original: "habitus"</note> is said to enter the third collection. Nevertheless, for a physician who does not require such a piercingly deep investigation, it is sufficient to place these two modes within "Position," since in both cases a certain site of the parts is observed, and an order is introduced between their couplings. Thus, in composition, disease is established as an existing disposition or state which is located in three genera: Quality, Quantity, and Position.

**Averroes**, however, whose view always seems to stand out above others, excludes three genera of sickness from entering five predicaments—namely Quality, Quality-in-Quantity, and Position-in-Quality, discrete and continuous Quantity, Where, and State. And partly he finds the matter well-placed in "When," that is, through priority and posteriority. But he argues that the ordering of the official members and priority and posteriority should rather be placed in the six subsequent predicaments. Regarding the fourth point, it must be said to the first that operations do not primarily occur because of "position," but rather they receive "assistance" from it. Nevertheless, it does not happen that way in their destruction; for when a major injury occurs in the position, the disease is first corrupted <note>i.e., the condition changes</note>, since more things are required for the constitution of something than for its destruction. To the other point, it must be said that a disease of composition is a **quality**, even if it is founded elsewhere in other predicaments; and it can be cured because "contrariety" <note>The medical principle that opposites cure opposites</note> is truly found in Quality. Furthermore, the physician does not attempt to grasp "contrariety" in a narrow sense, and it is true when he says every cure is perfected by its own contrary. Similarly, it is clear how disease is founded in position. What must be said to the other point is now apparent. But here, a diversity arises between the "Predicaments" and the "Six Principles." In the Predicaments, it is said that "hard" and "soft," "rough" and "smooth," and similar things are considered foreign to the definition of Quality. From the "Six Principles," it is induced that these are not positions, but rather qualities existing around a site. It must be said that they are somewhat "middle" things existing in both predicaments. For it is not stated simply that they are positions, but that they are "thought of" as such and vary in a certain way. Similarly, it is not written that they are absolutely qualities, but "qualities existing around a site." For insofar as they bring about some "passion" <note>an effect or sensation</note> in the surface by which we are called "such-and-such," they can be called qualities; but insofar as the superficial parts of the thing are situated this way or that, they have positions.

It reconciles medical practice with Aristotelian philosophy, specifically examining how organ structure (official members) relates to the categories of Quality and Position.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic classification of medical conditions, transitioning from the specific symptom of "stupor" to a broader philosophical discussion on how "Position" and "Composition" define the nature of disease. It specifically addresses the categorization of diseases according to the "Categories" of Aristotle and Boethius, leading into a debate on the number of "general diseases."</meta>

...to signify. It should be noted that a single entity can be counted in various categories according to different logical reasons. **Boethius**, in his commentary on the *Categories* <note>original: "predicamētis"; refers to Aristotle’s work on the classification of beings</note>, explains this. For the term "Father" signifies both a substance <note>the man himself</note> and a relation <note>his role relative to a child</note>. Hence, in the categories, the "position" of the whole is commonly understood as any situation of parts and their figuration. Thus, roughness and smoothness signify a certain position due to the distance and arrangement of the parts. 

Physicians seem to perceive this when they categorize a disease within the "plasma" <note>original: "plasmate"; the formed structure or "mold" of the body</note> or the figuration and form of the members—such as a disease of the surface being smooth or rough—treating it as a natural quality rather than a mathematical quantity. In the *Six Principles* <term>Six Principles</term> <note>A medieval logical textbook that expanded on Aristotle's categories, often attributed to Gilbert de la Porrée.</note>, "narrowness" is considered a position, just as the situation and order of parts defines whether a limb is in a state of flexion or standing. Therefore, "rare" and "dense," or "rough" and "smooth," do not seem to signify a disposition in the same way. But because "position" according to the *Six Principles* is more perceptible to the senses, physicians have classified diseases of "position" by these changes. They differ from the logicians, however, because logicians say "position" is a natural and stable situation of parts in the whole, whereas physicians consider it to be not only natural but also acquired and quickly changeable.

<margin>
A doubt arises concerning the number of general diseases. For it does not seem that there are 16, as is posited, according to the cause given by **Johannitius** <note>Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a famous translator and physician</note> and **Avicenna**.
</margin>

And because of certain points argued previously, a doubt arises concerning the number of general diseases. For it does not seem that there are sixteen, as is usually posited by **Johannitius** and **Avicenna** <note>original: "Au."</note>. Since the four simple qualities <note>heat, cold, moisture, dryness</note> do not seem to be states in which a "simple" quality alone offends, for it must be intensified at least to a third degree before it begins to cause harm. Indeed, a body can remain healthy even with an excess of a quality. However, once a quality is so intensified, it soon associates itself with another quality, and thus a "compound" disease arises. This is confirmed because these simple qualities do not remain alone for long without associating with others, even within the range of health. For a heat greater than what is proper renders the body dry. 

Furthermore, a disease in a simple quality does not seem possible when "matter" <note>bodily substance or fluids</note> is involved, since every humor participates in two qualities. Nor does a simple quality appear in the evil complexions of the brain. Therefore, a compound disease arises from two qualities without the fault of the humor; for by their conjunction, they strengthen themselves and associate with a humor. Hence, in the *Sixth Book of Theory* <note>likely referring to a work by Galen or Haly Abbas</note>, it is said: "A compound disease will not be void of matter." Only four diseases, therefore, are left as "compounds" by reason of quality and matter, such as the sanguine or the choleric.

Hence, even if there were more than sixteen—such as hot, cold, dry, and humors—it follows from the cause that contrary dispositions often exist together, which is thought to be impossible, such as being hot and cold at the same time. This occurs when the same body is affected by nature and yet also by an "anomalous dyscrasia" <term>Dyscrasia</term> <note>A term from Greek medicine meaning a "bad mixture" of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile).</note>. This is what produces an "epial" fever <note>a type of fever where the patient feels hot and cold simultaneously</note>. 

However, physicians write the opposite. Regarding the first point, it should be known that this is sufficiently well-known from many sources. Regarding the second, it should be known that **Democritus**, **Epicurus**, **Empedocles**, and **Asclepiades**, who posited that material principles were impassible and unalterable (such as atoms or the four elements), did not place disease in the "genus" or nature of a quality; they believed it consisted instead in the "composition," such as the dilation of pores and the narrowing or gathering and dispersing of them. But because "composition" exists in similar parts, they placed disease in compound parts. **Avicenna** argued against them at length, as did **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note>. 

Regarding the third point, it should be known that there are sixteen common and well-known general diseases. Their more exquisite distinction arises when matter penetrates into a member or remains on the outside, merely moistening it. Most often, the four compound diseases—either in themselves or with a humor—are those that occur and are most suitable for study. It is also known that "mixture" or "composition" is of two types. One is "true mixture," where the things mixed concur into a third new thing. The other is a "flexible" or "apparent" mixture, where the mixed things are merely placed next to each other without a single new result. **Isaac Judaeus** <note>original: "Ysaac"; a 10th-century Jewish physician</note> calls this a "mixture by vicinity" in his work on urines, such as the mixing of blood and phlegm, or wind and bile. For they are entirely opposed in qualities, and not a little in substance. Blood, however, forms a "true mixture" with phlegm, since they are not opposed in every way. 

Sixteen examples of famous general diseases are listed below:

<margin>
The 16 General Diseases
</margin>

1. **Simple Heat:** According to **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Hayab."; a Persian physician</note> and **Johannitius**, this is a "Hectic" fever <term>Hectic</term> <note>original: "ethica"; a persistent fever that "consumes" the solid parts of the body</note>, or an evil state caused by fire or very hot air.
2. **Heat with Humor:** Such as a putrid fever.
3. **Simple Cold:** Such as numbness or a spasm caused in the members, where the spasm is an accident or an "official" <note>organ-based</note> illness rather than a systemic one.
4. **Cold with Humors:** Such as paralysis, epilepsy, and apoplexy.
5. **Dryness without Humor:** Such as a "spasm of inanition" <note>cramping caused by emptiness or dehydration</note> and similarly "dry wasting" <note>original: "tabes sicca"</note>, like the marasmus <term>Marasmus</term> <note>Severe wasting of the body.</note> of old age.
6. **Dryness with Matter:** Such as cancer and elephantiasis.
7. **Simple Humidity:** Such as a loss of vision or a very foul wasting.
8. **Humidity with Matter:** Such as the inflated flesh of those with dropsy <term>Dropsy</term> <note>original: "ydropicy"; an old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid.</note>, which is torpid and hollow, and the humidity of a body that has "swollen enervation." 

This occurs in "hyposarca" dropsy <note>edema under the skin</note>, where there is a humidity adhering to the members. If it is said that dropsy is a material illness, it must be said that this refers to "ascites" <note>fluid in the abdomen</note>, or that the term "matter" is used commonly for the four humors. Some here understand the body of a dropsical person to be filled with water. But then it is a compound illness—cold and moist with humor. Because, in truth, a disease that is declared to be of a "simple quality" but exists "with humor" is actually affected by a double quality. For that is how every humor is disposed. This is proven because in putrid fever, paralysis, and such things, a double quality exists. It is better to say that with a single humor, this cannot be shown except when a "composition" is understood, such as when blood and bile are mixed, which results in a prevailing "evil heat."

<meta>This page continues the scholastic classification of medical conditions, moving from the definitions of simple qualities (hot, cold, dry, moist) into a discussion of how these qualities combine to form specific diseases like hectic fever and consumption. It then transitions into "Difference 75," which explores the concept of a "common disease"—a category that affects both the simple tissues and the organized limbs of the body.</meta>

...of some humor. A "cold" disease is established when the cold quality joins with the matter of **phlegm**. It is "dry" when it joins with **melancholy** <note>original: "cosa mlia"; likely referring to melancholic matter</note>. Both of these are dry and, by reason of their contrariety, are tempered in their actions. However, a disease is "hot and moist" when blood is mixed with phlegm. Now, indeed, examples should be provided for when two simple qualities are associated, although **Haly Abbas** <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician</note> says that such diseases do not occur. Indeed, a composite disease will not be void of matter. In such a case, a disease that is "hot and dry" would be **hectic fever** <term>ethica</term> <note>a fever associated with the wasting of the body's tissues</note> and **consumption** <term>tabes</term>, since the intensity of the heat dissolves that which is associated with it in its composition; more truly, it is called a "hot disease" alone, as he writes. However, a "dry and cold" disease is what is called a **spasm of inanition** <note>a cramp or seizure caused by extreme depletion of the body's fluids</note>, or more certainly, its cause. To be sure, he writes that this is simple, as is the hectic fever of old age. It is difficult to imagine a "hot and moist" or a "cold and moist" sickness without matter in a collection of thoughts.

I say, however, that this can arise in two ways: either from a primitive cause, such as a hot and moist bath, or from within, such as when someone of a sanguine temperament is greatly diminished, yet heat and moisture are not separated from the parts. A "cold and moist" state is likewise twofold: either from air or water and such things, or when a **dropsical** <note>suffering from edema or fluid retention</note> person is understood to be cured of the water.

Examples also appear clearly in material fevers and **abscesses** <term>apostematibus</term> when two qualities affect the humors. Regarding the first point to be said, the preceding **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of antiquity</note> did not place simple diseases—those erring in only one quality—without matter, nor did he distinguish them in the 19th chapter. But it can be said that they begin as such and soon associate another quality with themselves. Because the dominant quality does not dominate the other opposite quality, it remains hidden, just as it does in those natural **dyscrasias** <note>an imbalance of the four humors</note>. Yet it is called a "simple quality" because the quality it acquires does not immediately equal the first. And because diseases of this kind do not occur often, or only rarely, it is said that diseases consisting of a single imbalance of qualities are rarer and difficult to understand, unless a great conversion to a contrary nature occurs in some part.

Regarding the other point, it has already appeared how the humors can be composed. For these aforementioned diseases do not arise from two singular entities. Therefore, the examples from **Haly Abbas** and **Johannitius** <note>The Latin name for the 9th-century scholar Hunayn ibn Ishaq</note> are not sufficient paradigms, even if the author does not explain them here. He does, however, imply them, adding them elsewhere. To the other point, it must be said that those joined qualities, even if they are effective, nevertheless have a subject member in which they act, and they do not bring any moisture unless perhaps by accident of indigence. Regarding **Haly Abbas's** view, it has appeared what should be said, since more joined paradigms of those diseases are given.

Regarding the other point, it has appeared that the composition of diseases is more truly a mixture. However, these two which **Galen** added are composed by a certain sensible proximity, just as when a pain seen from a distance seems simple, but from near it appears composite. This is shown by the illusion of vision when the paintings of bowls and such hollows appear on walls, which happens by the layering of colors. **Alexander** <note>likely Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> in his *Problems* says: between white and white, they lead in dark brown, so that the white, representing itself more strongly to the sight from every side, appears to stand out, while the brown, being more weakly perceived, seems to sink. Similarly, the sense of touch is deceived when judging coldness and heat in one indivisible part, when it is actually divisible. Truly, these are "phantasms of touch" as noted in Distinction 81.

## DIFFERENCE LXXV.

<margin>1</margin>
It is shown why there is no "common disease." A **common disease** <note>a disease that affects both the simple tissues like flesh and the organic parts like a finger</note> exists only by a **break in continuity** <note>original: "solo gtinuitatis"; a wound or ulcer</note>. A disease is a certain composition or construction against nature by which the primary act opposite to it is harmed. Furthermore, things that are divided from each other as opposites—where one is present, the other cannot be—since one opposite species does not lead the other into being. But a bad constitution and a depraved composition are divided as opposites. Therefore, nothing "common" will be in them such that it could be called a common disease. Also, every disease from which it is possible to escape has four times: the **beginning**, the **increase**, the **peak**, and the **decline** of the crisis. Therefore, there is no common disease.

<margin>2</margin>
The opposite is held by almost everyone. Still, a disease is called "common" because it harms the action of both the simple tissues and the official organs without distinction. Such a disease is a "break of the joint," since both maintain a certain continuity, because of which the disease exits. For the first point, it should be known that this "common disease" is spoken of in two ways: either spiritually, because the whole body is affected together, or it happens to its parts without distinction, such as fever, abscess, and the others mentioned in the fourth book of the *Canon*. Alternatively, it happens in nature from composition and the resulting composition, which is called a "disruption of unequal continuity" or a "joint."

<margin>3</margin>
Know also that although there are three simple diseases, they can be composed in many ways among themselves and with others. For between them, two genera are composed, such as hot and moist, or hot and dry. Sometimes an organic disease is composed with another organic disease, such as an abscess causing a blockage and a narrowing. Other times it is organic and general, like an abscess of the head with a fever. Sometimes it is general with a common disease, as in a wound with a fever, in which two diseases exist: the fever and the **break in continuity**. Sometimes it is constructed from an official organ and a common disease, like the cutting off of a finger. For there is a disease in number and a common disease in the breaking of the joint. Other times there are three, like an abscess with a wound and a fever.

Sometimes all modes of diseases are joined together, as in **ophthalmia** <note>severe inflammation of the eye</note> with an ulcer, in which the **uvea** <note>the middle layer of the eye</note> protrudes sharply, water descends into the eye, and an **ungula** <note>original: "ungula"; a claw-like growth or pterygium on the eye</note> is produced. Here, indeed, six diseases are present: 
1. **Ophthalmia**, which is a hot abscess—a disease of composition in quantity where the heat is the disease. 
2. The **ulcer**, which exists only as a break in the joint. 
3. The sharp point or protrusion of the **uvea**, a disease of quantity. 
4. The disturbance of the **pupil** from its place, which is a disease of position. 
5. The **water**, which creates a disease of blockage. 
6. The **ungula**, which is a disease in number <note>meaning an extra growth or addition of substance</note>.

Regarding this, it should truly be known that according to **Democritus** and **Epicurus**, no such "common disease" can properly be placed, since the body is constituted of simple and official parts. Although they consider the whole, they do not place a common part with the other. For a composite thing is corrupted when its other part is destroyed. Considering, however, that nature preserves these things which it has composed, a common disease is placed here according to them. Therefore, omitting those more rustic views, it should be known that a triple probable opinion appears regarding this.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the classification of ailments. Having previously discussed simple and composite diseases based on the four humors, the text now focuses on the "common disease" (morbus communis), a category that affects both simple tissues—what the text calls "similar parts"—and complex organs, referred to as "official" or "instrumental parts."</meta>

**Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–210 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity, whose works formed the basis of medieval medicine</note> indeed feels that a **common disease** is one that occurs in a certain nature when a limb is harmed in its consistency and its organic structure—for example, if a ligament or an artery is torn away.

One might call it a "common disease" of the whole organ and its similar particles <note>similar particles refers to uniform tissues like bone, flesh, or nerve</note>. In both cases, the continuity is dissolved. That which is torn away does not remain one thing, but is made into two. If, however, the particle is not totally torn away but only in some part, it will not be a disease of the whole organ except by accident <note>a secondary consequence rather than a primary cause</note>, because only one constituent particle has suffered what is properly called a disease. Therefore, a disease is called "common" according to this: it occurs in a common nature in which both the coordinating and the **official parts** <note>complex organs with specific functions, like the heart or stomach</note> meet—for example, in a certain joint and their connection.

Some thinkers, however, have wanted a common disease to be identified in both similar and official parts, but they claim it only touches them when one part is primarily affected and not another—a point to be supplemented regarding the cure. Thus, in the seventeenth book of *On Diseases*, it is said: A common disease happens to similar and instrumental parts; it is said to be instrumental so that it does not happen to them merely because of an accident occurring to the similar parts. For it often happens to a joint primarily so that it does not occur in any way to the similar parts <note>original: "similibus partibus"</note>. It should be understood that this also requires a cure. While Galen proposes that a dislocated limb is an **organic disease** <note>affecting the structure of an organ</note> because the joint was displaced, he often adds that it happens to a nerve or a bone as a "split." Other matters should be investigated and differentiated alongside these.

Therefore, according to the sixth theory: A common disease affects both similar parts and their organic members through **separation** <term>separatio</term> and loss of connection. A disease is called "common" because it occurs differently in bone than in flesh, and sometimes in other similar members. Occasionally it occurs in the whole hand or foot, or other major members, and in all similar parts common to that member. According to this, therefore, a disease is called common because it indiscriminately strikes now the similar parts, now the official ones. Perhaps this was the opinion of **Aristotle** <note>abbreviated as "A." in the text</note>, for if a solution of continuity <note>a break in the physical unity of a tissue, such as a cut or fracture</note> happens at the same time to similar and official parts, it would then be a disease as clearly shown in both, since he distinguished this from a "simple disease."

**Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the Andalusian philosopher and physician known for his "Colliget"</note> however, in the third book of his *Colliget* <note>original: "collyz"; his major medical compendium</note> felt that **continuity** properly belongs to similar members. In official members, this property exists improperly, or rather by contact. Thus, a common disease would properly belong to the similar members. As he says: A common disease is twofold. One is a **solution** <term>solutio</term> <note>a "solution of continuity" or a break</note> in the true sense, such as a break between one similar part and another; this is attributed more to similar members than to official ones. For the "solution" only happens to a member in terms of the part that is composed of similar tissues, not in terms of its status as an "official" organ. The other type is "separation," which is a change in contiguity. This is not strictly called a solution of continuity, because continuity behaves more like a joining of one part to another. Such a solution must be placed among the ailments of official parts, such as a dislocation or separation where some connection exists.

For just as I might say of a wall, a twofold joining is found: one is true, like stones joined by their own substance; the other is not "true," but is like one stone being joined to another by glue or lime. So it is in the animal body. One is "true," which belongs to similar members; the other is "untrue," according to which official organs are generated from similar ones. Finally, in both of these, a single "common nature" results, such as a wall or an animal body. Therefore, it should be known that...

---

...the received opinions regarding these beings, especially since they sound almost the same when considered diligently. It must be said that a common disease principally affects the composite member. This is indicated when it is said that the universal sickness of all simple members is either a **dyscrasia** <term>discrasia</term> <note>an imbalance of the four humors</note> or a solution of the parts' continuity. This general category belongs to the official organs and not only to the similar parts. And perhaps it can never happen to the organs without also occurring in the similar tissues.

<margin>👉</margin> Note also that a **solution of continuity** that hinders the senses of the whole or a major part is the disease of those parts. If, however, some small particle has a minor solution, such a disease is no longer of the whole, but only of that part—like a small cut on a finger. It does not hinder the natural functions, even if a natural benefit follows, such as the opening of a vein for **hemorrhoids** <note>original: "emororice"; bloodletting was sometimes used to treat or mimic the "purging" effect of hemorrhoids</note>.

Regarding the fourth point, it must be said that Galen understood "proposition" or "obstruction" as a disposition or a habit. When he adds that if I have called a certain disposition "contrary to nature" by which an action is harmed, he shows the same thing everywhere. To another point, it must be said that the division of members into similar and official—or the division of nature into similar, official, and common—is not a contradiction, since one is higher and ordered toward the other. It is shown that what is of a common nature comes before the genus and is in the proposition.

Finally, concerning the "solution" <note>the break in tissue</note>, since it is an action and occurs in time, there will be a progression from part to part. Even if it seems instantaneous due to the brevity of time, it exists. Such is the case with an inflammatory swelling <note>original: "fimocha"; likely a phymosis or abscess</note> in the beginning, leading toward **syncope** <term>syncopis</term> <note>fainting or loss of consciousness</note>; the removal of the part increases the benefit when the **phlebotomy** <term>flobotomum</term> <note>the surgical opening of a vein to draw blood</note> strikes the vein. Even when the patient faints or approaches it, the process has a beginning. According to Galen's method, this has a "habit" in diseases that occur spontaneously, which reach their end by changing the movement of nature. Thus, art will never cure at the very beginning when nature is not yet acting. Or it must be said that when this "solution" is induced, it has a beginning, then an increase as the humors flow and the symptoms intensify, then a peak when all things reach their state, and the remaining stage will be the decline.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the classification of diseases. While the previous page discussed "common diseases" that affect both simple tissues and complex organs, this page focuses specifically on the nature of the "apema" (an inflammatory swelling or abscess) and the fundamental causes of pain.</meta>

Concerning the aforementioned things, it is doubted what kind of disease an <term>apema</term> <note>original: "apā"; a Greek-derived term used in medieval medicine to describe an inflammatory swelling or abscess</note> is: whether it is simple or composite. And it seems to be simple, because it is said to be an organic disease by <term>Haly Abbas</term> <note>Haly Abbas (died c. 982) was a famous Persian physician whose "Complete Book of the Medical Art" was a standard textbook</note> in the sixth book [of the *Pantegni*]... for quantity is what is at fault in it, and quantity itself is a simple category. Furthermore, in the first book *On Disease*: an <term>apema</term> is a disease found in any of the members. Thirdly, in the thirteenth [book]: **apemas** happen to the lungs, appropriated to members of **similar parts** <note>tissues that are uniform throughout, like flesh or bone</note>. A disease that happens to similar parts is itself a "similar" disease, for a suffering is characterized by the subject it affects. These things cause one to doubt whether an <term>apema</term> is an organic disease or a "similar" one. 

That it is composite, however, is proven first by its nature. For in it there is a **bad complexion** <note>an imbalance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile)</note>, a diverse and inept composition, and a **solution of continuity** <note>a physical break or tear in the body's tissues</note>.

<margin>Apema</margin>
Regarding the first point, it should be known that <term>apema</term> is defined in two ways. One way is through its essentials: an <term>apema</term> is a composite disease of the three-fold nature of the body, which essentially harms its action. In another way, it is defined by its "accidents" <note>secondary symptoms or characteristics</note>: thus an <term>apema</term> is a **tumor** or a thickness beyond nature. This latter definition does not capture the essence of the <term>apema</term>, since a tumor is a secondary consequence of the composition or the quantity. For a tumor is not always a disease; as stated in the first book *On Disease*, a tumor only makes the members desist from their natural state when it rises to such a magnitude that it harms some action—only then is it understood as an actual illness. Otherwise, tumors are merely symptoms and "sufferings," just as pain is. It is also said in the first book *On Ingredients* that a tumor beyond nature is an accident of the <term>apema</term> following its character.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that various opinions have appeared from these arguments. According to <term>Aristotle</term> <note>often abbreviated as "A." in these manuscripts</note>, an <term>apema</term> is more of a composite disease related to a true mixing of humors. But according to **Galen**, it is perceived more through the senses and the imagination. In every <term>apema</term>, there is a break in continuity, at least a hidden one. According to **Galen**, this break is sometimes manifest, as in an ulcer or in **erysipelas** <note>a bacterial skin infection</note>. At other times, it is deep or hidden, as in a **carbuncle** <note>a cluster of boils</note>; and sometimes it is in both ways, as in **herpes** and **cancer**.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that ancient writers commonly called an **edema** a composite disease of a triple nature, as mentioned before. This is because the fault lies principally in the quantity, the union, and properly in the similarity of the parts. Hence, in the first book *On Disease*: some illnesses belong to the primary "similar" bodies, others to the organic and composite ones. An <term>apema</term> occurring in a similar part—for instance, in the flesh—is a "similar" disease by accident and an "official" <note>organic/complex</note> disease secondarily. Likewise, the dislocation of a joint is primarily an official disease, and the <term>apema</term> happening there is secondary. Know also that every disease exists more radically and primarily due to a defect of the "complexion" <note>the balance of qualities like hot or cold</note>. According to medical appearance, some diseases are principally "similar" and accidentally "official," while others are as described above. Thus, a disease can be called both simple and composite, and likewise "official," depending on which nature it harms more.

From these things, it appears in the fourth part how each individual case proceeds along the path of truth. Furthermore, since an <term>apema</term> is a tumor beyond nature, it harms the composition more visibly than it harms other natures.

<margin>To that extent, it can be called an organic disease, etc.</margin>
# DIFFERENTIA LXXVI.

> That there may be only one cause of pain: namely, a sudden alteration. This conclusion is gathered here, placing this as the sole cause of pain and not the **solution of continuity**.

Again, in the sixth book of *Theories*: pain is an alteration from a natural state into a non-natural habit. This, however, only exists in qualities, and especially in the third species of quality. Furthermore, since a **solution of continuity** <note>a physical tear</note> does not exist in quality but rather in quantity, it happens to members insofar as they possess quantity or position. Furthermore, every action is perfected by quality, according to the sixtieth distinction; the reason is that action arises from contrariety, and quality is the proper recipient of contrariety. Pain, moreover, is a certain action [or passion], since it consists in "becoming," as in the fourth book *On Accidents* and concerning unequal distemperance. It is also in motion, which is proper to action. Therefore, pain happens from a sudden alteration and not from a solution of continuity.

That only the solution of continuity causes pain is shown by **Galen** speaking on unequal distemperance. **Hippocrates** held that all diseases were **ulcers**, since an ulcer includes a solution of continuity; for an ulcer is a deep wound. Likewise, in the sixth book *On Accidents*, as **Aristotle** posits and **Galen** declares, a solution of continuity induces pain not only in the sense of touch but in all senses, because by extending the parts in a fall or contracting them in a spasm, a sudden alteration occurs. Therefore, only the solution of continuity causes pain.

Again, in the first book: **Pain is the sudden sensation of something distressing.** But a sudden alteration does not seem to be able to bring on pain immediately, since it is necessary that it be altered and changed gradually over time first. Therefore, only the solution of continuity causes pain. Furthermore, it is shown that neither of these two causes induces pain [on its own]. For according to *On the Soul*: **The sense is the recipient of species without matter.** Hence **Aristotle** says: "To perceive is to receive the form of a thing stripped of its matter." But this intentional reception does not properly induce pain, since it acts nothing beyond its own species. Therefore, neither of these two will be the cause of pain.

There is also a middle view: that there is only one cause. For in every genus, there is one primary thing which is the cause of all things in that genus—like fire in the genus of heat. Therefore, there should be one in the genus of pain. Yet others say there are three, corresponding to the three things in which bodily delight consists: generation, composition, and natural state. Consequently, there are three things that corrupt these and induce pain. Pain seems to be caused by a sudden change of composition, just as it is by the natural state. **Palin** shows that four causes exist, since every cause of pain is a change of complexion, or its diversity, or a solution of continuity, or a combination of both. 

**Aristotle** on <term>soda</term> <note>original: "soda"; a medieval term for a headache, often thought to be caused by vapors rising to the head</note>: as for the many species of pain, each is constituted from its own causes. There are fifteen species of pain, as touched upon before and in the first book of the *Pantegni*. The opposite of all these views seems to be held by the most illustrious physicians, who posit only two causes of pain: sudden alteration and the solution of continuity. Moreover, just as there are two principal natures in the body, so too there are two causes of pain...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the nature of disease and suffering. While the previous page examined the definition of an "apema" (an inflammatory swelling), this page transitions into a deep philosophical and medical analysis of "dolor" (pain)—the primary symptom of such conditions. The text navigates a classic medieval debate: is pain caused by a sudden change in qualities (like heat or cold) or by the physical tearing of tissues (solution of continuity)? The author attempts to reconcile the seemingly conflicting views of Aristotle, Galen, and Averroes.</meta>

<margin>sensation</margin>
## Regarding the first point, it should be known what "sensation" is first,
since pain is included within its definition. Now, sensation is a certain intermediate ratio <note>original: "ratio"; here meaning a balanced proportion or relationship</note> or proportion of that which exists in sensible properties and qualities—namely, of the <term>similar parts</term> <note>tissues like flesh or bone that are uniform throughout</note>. This is discussed in the 42nd distinction. And because human nature possesses a greater proportion of equality <note>balance of the four humors</note> than other qualities, the perfection of sensation in humans excels that of other animals, as indicated in the second book of *On the Soul* and the first book of the *History of Animals* <note>References to works by Aristotle</note>. And because pain implies a certain privation and defect, and a privation is known through its opposite habit, let us first state what the opposite of pain is. This is sometimes called <term>delicia</term> <note>original: "delicia"; sensory delight or physical pleasure</note>, by others <term>leticia</term> <note>joy</note>, and occasionally <term>delectatio</term> <note>pleasure</note>. It is a passion <note>an experience or state acted upon the body</note> by which we are suddenly led back from a state contrary to nature to our natural state. For he who defines well links contraries together, as seen in the seventh book of the *Topics*. In the second book of *On the Internal Senses*, "joy" is defined as a "cheerful sensation," while "pain" is a "sad sensation." In the sixth book of the *Theology* <note>likely referring to a pseudo-Aristotelian or Neo-Platonic source</note>, "delight" is the alteration from a non-natural state to a natural state. I understand, however, that this description denotes the cause rather than the form; for strictly speaking, pleasure or pain is not the alteration itself, but is caused by the alteration.

<margin>what pain is</margin>
## In the first sentence: Pain is the sensing of a contrary thing occurring suddenly.
And therefore he adds finally that pain is nothing other than sensing a sudden "contrary impression." The rest is noted. Regarding the second point, it should be known that the illustrious among physicians differ regarding what it is that causes pain. For in the third book of the *Colliget* <note>The "General Rules of Medicine" by Averroes</note>, it is pronounced that "sudden alteration" alone is the cause of pain. He strives to show this through reasoning, arguing that a <term>solution of continuity</term> <note>original: "solutio continuitatis"; a physical break, tear, or cut in the body's tissues</note> is not the cause of pain, as <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity</note> says, but rather it is the cause of the "becoming" <note>the process</note> that makes the pain. For a solution of continuity is only coupled with a "bad movement" and it is because of such movement that the bad suffering follows. Nor are there two causes of pain—namely solution of continuity and heat or cold—as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "A."; the text refers to him as "errant" here</note> says in error. Galen finally builds his argument by saying it was declared in the book *On the Soul* that this sense—namely touch—perceives all four primary qualities: hot, cold, dry, and moist. Therefore, pains will not be made nor felt by that sense unless they greatly exceed their proper temperate balance, just as happens with the other senses.

## Likewise, he adds that if pain happened to this sense of touch
because of a solution of continuity, then the "solution" itself would be its own proper object of sensation. But a solution of continuity—nor its opposite—is not placed in the second book of *On the Soul* where the objects of this sense are treated; rather, the objects are hot, cold, moist, dry, rough, smooth, hard, and soft. And therefore in the first book of the *Sentence* and in the sixth book of *Natural Philosophy*, this sense is said to be fourfold according to these enumerated objects or properties. <term>Averroes</term> adds also that the "sensible soul" exists only for qualities, which Galen also testifies to, saying he does not want the hand to have been made in the perfection of temperance except to perceive contraries. And so it appears that the "superfluity of contraries" <note>an excess of heat, cold, etc.</note> is the cause of pain which occurs in this sense, because the small and the great necessarily fall under the same genus. What should be known about this will appear in the third part.

## Galen, whose opinion is verified,
seems to feel that pain finally happens from a solution of continuity, as he demonstrates in the fourth book of *On Accidents* by examining all the senses. On this point, Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note> attacks him, assigning him weak reasons, and showing that there are two causes of pain: namely, sudden alteration and the separation of parts. However, the adversary <note>Averroes</note> might be making a "begging of the question" <note>a logical fallacy</note> which will be noted at the beginning, even if it concludes with the truth. And in his second book *On the Soul*, some men have already thought that no qualities are felt except by means of what happens from a solution of continuity; but it is not so. It is truly worthy of wonder how Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note> dares to note Galen with such "rage" <note>or "madness"</note> when Galen himself says in that same fourth book that pain happens because of heat or the sharpness of humors. In many places, Galen expressly felt there were two causes of pain, as noted in the *Tegni*, *On Maltemperament*, and the 12th and 13th books of *On the Method of Healing*. He proves this in the second book of *Internal Senses* by the example of the sudden exposure to fire of limbs that have been extremely chilled. Aristotle, perhaps not understanding Galen, is distressed; for Galen does not mean that sudden alteration is *not* a cause of pain and only solution of continuity is. Rather, he anticipates the doubt, wanting to show that the more effective qualities like heat and cold cause pain not only by alteration, but also by a resulting separation of parts. This is sufficient regarding "unequal distemper," where he concludes that after the pain resulting from sudden alteration, it happens because of the separation of parts. This discourse follows what <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>original: "Ypocras"; the ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</note> says in some places, stating that "all diseases are ulcers" <note>meaning all disease involves a physical break or wound</note>. Let Aristotle cease, therefore, here and elsewhere, to bite at Galen when he perhaps does not understand him, as seen in the 89th distinction. Galen is found to be a sufficient expander of the speeches of others, while his attacker is a vain and dissonant reciter.

<margin>Note Aristotle and Averroes</margin>
<margin>Cause of pain</margin>
## Regarding the third point, first the truth is established,
and thereafter the ideas of Averroes are modified. Concerning this, it should first be known that the "radical" and primary cause of pain is a "violent disproportion" occurring suddenly to a sensitive member; just as delight is a "great proportion" that is also sudden. That the aforesaid is the cause of pain is suggested by the similarity of the opinion of Averroes and by reason. For in the sixth book of the *Topics*, one must consider if a defined passion or disposition is not susceptible to that which it is said to be—if it is not, a mistake is made. For example, if it is claimed that "pain is a distance created between natural parts with violence," an error is committed because it would follow that inanimate things could feel pain, as they also have natural parts that can be separated. Therefore, one must place this "separation of natural parts" within the category of "sensation." This will happen if, instead of "natural parts," one writes "sensible parts."

## He adds also that a mistake is made
by expressing the definition of pain through its effects rather than its form. For pain is not the "distance" of parts itself; rather, pain is *produced* from such a distance of parts. Thus, after the correction of the ancient definition of pain, it remains that the distance between sensible parts is the cause of pain. Which, indeed, is nothing other than a disproportion...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the nature of "dolor" (pain). Having previously defined sensation as a balanced proportion, the author now seeks the specific causes that disrupt this balance. He relies heavily on the "Old Logic" and the physics of Aristotle and Euclid to argue that all types of pain must be reducible to a single primary cause.</meta>

The aforementioned vehement <note>original: "vehemens"; meaning intense or forceful</note> thing suddenly occurring to a sensible member is perceived. For in distance there is an imbalance in hearing, according to that [proposition] in the fifth book of the *Problems* <note>A work attributed to Aristotle</note>. "The thighs ache most due to a distance of continuity" <note>This refers to the physical stretching or separation of tissues</note>. For whatever is distant or differs in any way is entirely out of proportion. By what is added regarding the soul, he understands what is implied by that which is intense and sudden. For everything violent is sudden and great. Furthermore, through that which is said regarding the "sensible part," the subject of the passion is denoted as a recipient at rest. 

This is finally confirmed by reason: whenever one common passion is found in many things, it is necessary to trace those passions back to some higher and primary cause through the senses, as shown in the *Posterior Analytics* <note>Aristotle’s work on logic and demonstration</note>. This is like the passion in the 32nd <note>The text says "xxxi i," likely referring to Proposition 32</note> proposition of the first book of Euclid: "a triangle contains three angles in its circuit equivalent to two right angles." This property belongs primarily to the triangle in general before it belongs to any specific type of triangle. But this common passion, like pain, as the experts say and as will be shown, is found in two things: namely, in **sudden alteration** and in the **sudden disruption of continuity** <note>original: "solutio continuitatis"; a medical term for a wound, break, or tear in the flesh</note>. Therefore, before these two separate causes, one must subjoin a third. This aforementioned [primary cause] appears to be fitting. 

Again, it is necessary to reduce every effect to one primary cause according to the opinion of Aristotle, and to stop there, since a process into infinity is denied in the *Metaphysics*. Pain is one common effect caused by these two causes; however, they differ in "more or less," as will be shown. Thus, it is necessary to place a cause before these two, especially since every multitude must return to the unity from which it issued, according to the 12th book of the *Metaphysics*. Furthermore, nature does not permit a "leap" in its operations <note>The principle that nature acts continuously, not in sudden jumps</note>. Likewise, whenever one finds something existing in many things according to a single definition, it is necessary to reduce them to something prior which is their cause, just as all hot things are reduced to fire, and all bright things to the sun, according to the *Metaphysics*.

<margin>
And two [causes]
Cause of pain
</margin>

Since, therefore, pain arises from the disruption of continuity and sudden alteration—at least according to the logic of the situation—and since in both cases there is a sensation of a harmful thing suddenly occurring, it will finally be necessary to reduce pain and its immediate causes to a higher and primary cause: namely, an intense **imbalance** <note>original: "inproportio"</note>. 

However, this higher and radical cause is divided into two intermediate causes which nevertheless hold an order between themselves: **sudden alteration** and the **disruption of a joint**. This is shown from the many things constituting the body and the habitual causes of pain, as if from opposites. For there are two primordial natures constituting the body, as seen in the first book of *On Generation* <note>Aristotle's "On Generation and Corruption"</note>. For according to the opinion of Hippocrates and Aristotle, the body arises from the mixing of the <term>elements</term>, in which two things are observed: namely, the qualities and the substances affected by those distinct qualities. 

From the qualities, according to a certain mode of union, there results a nature which is called the <term>similar members</term> <note>original: "membra consimilia"; simple tissues like flesh, bone, or nerves that are the same throughout</note>. But from the composition of the substances found in the elements, there results—according to a certain mode of joining unity with the aforementioned "complexion"—a certain form for the members, such as the <term>official members</term> <note>original: "membra officialia"; complex organs like the hand or the heart that perform a specific "office" or function</note> attributed to the <term>organic</term> parts through the mediation of the complexion.

In the first nature, belonging to the "similar members," sensation exists inherently, according to the first book of the *History [of Animals]* and the second book of *On the Parts [of Animals]*. In the second nature, attributed to the organic members, [sensation exists] as declared in [chapter] 63. However, the second nature receives its being through the first, just as a whole is constituted in its being by its parts. For organic members arise from similar parts, according to the second book of *On the Parts* and the first book of *On Generation*. Perhaps the "plasma" <note>The formative material of the body</note> follows the <term>eucrasia</term> <note>A healthy, balanced mixture of humors</note> of the four elements, or perhaps it has some more divine principle from above, as mentioned in chapters 63 and 74. 

Therefore, according to these two natures, two types of "delights" follow the body, according to which the sense is disposed by its object in proportion to the subject. Pain, on the other hand, arises from the opposite of these, occurring through an imbalance. Thus, these things being supposed, I assert that there are two causes after the primary cause of pain: **sudden alteration of the complexion** and **disruption [of continuity]**. 

And if pain occurs properly in sensible bodies when a great alteration happens to them, it suddenly drags them out of their natural disposition. This happens in two ways: either by a sudden violent change of quality, or by a breaking of continuity. For regarding the nature of pain, as appears from its descriptions, there are two factors: namely, the sensation and the sudden impression of a contrary thing. Both are causes of pain through sudden change. First, the sense is affected because a proportion of contrary qualities is found in the sensible member. There is also a contrary impression occurring suddenly because of a sudden alteration of that same kind. Thus, sudden alteration is itself a primary and sufficient cause of pain. 

In the breaking of a joint, even if the impression occurs more suddenly than in a change of complexion (for a harmful thing is seen to be a sudden and violent transformation), the other factor—sensation—is not changed in the same way. For the disruption of continuity is felt through the sudden alteration of the complexion. If the disruption were perceived through itself, then pain would be present even in those [wounds] of sensible parts [where the qualities are balanced]. But in a sudden change of complexion, what is perceived is the "alterant" which suddenly affects the primary qualities from which the sense is constituted. 

Therefore, the disruption of a joint is perceived **accidentally**, insofar as it exists within that [alteration]. This is evident: for it is seen that if a disruption of continuity occurs in a member that has an indisposed sense—either because of [extreme] heat or [extreme] cold—it is hardly perceived. This would not happen if the disruption of continuity were felt through itself. Therefore, the disruption of continuity is not a sufficient cause by itself unless a sensation perceiving it on the part of the complexion is present. As for why a separation of a joint seems to provide greater pain than a sudden alteration, this happens to it because of the violent and sudden occurrence from without or within, or perhaps because another cause of pain—namely, sudden alteration—gathers following the disruption of continuity.

<summary>This page argues that while pain is triggered by sudden physical wounds or temperature changes, its primary philosophical cause is a "vehement imbalance" that disrupts the body's natural proportion. The author concludes that tissue damage is only painful because it causes a sudden, violent alteration in the sensory qualities of the body's tissues.</summary>
