<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the causes of pain, specifically focusing on the physical mechanics of "sudden alteration" and the role of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, dry, moist) in causing physical distress.</meta>

These things are held in this order: since a sudden alteration of disposition <note>original: "subitā alt̃atio gōnīs" (dispositionis); referring to the physical state or arrangement of the body</note> by itself causes pain and is perceived from the joining of qualities. Because an alteration that is not sudden is not considered "violent" <note>In medieval science, "violent" refers to a force acting against the natural inclination of an object</note> in the same way, as it occurs over a span of time, not as much pain is caused by a sudden alteration as by a separation of the joining—unless, finally, the separation of the joining follows from a forceful, sudden alteration. Although that alteration may be forceful and impression-making, it is not perceived as pain unless it is felt by the subject. At that point, a sudden alteration follows, and finally, a separation of the joining is linked to this. Thus, there are three existing causes of pain: two involving the dissolution of the joining <note>original: "iūcture solutiōes"; the breaking of physical continuity in tissues</note> and one being the sudden alteration.

However, I do not mean that when a sudden and forceful impression occurs, a "bad disposition" is instantaneously induced in the limb. This is impossible, since this alteration must happen over time. Alteration determines a specific time for itself, according to the fifth book of the *Physics* <note>referring to Aristotle's "Physics," which discusses the nature of motion and change</note>. But that which is perceived occurs as a "flow" <note>original: "fluxu"</note> not yet in the altered limb. For when it begins to be altered, we see the pain from the dissolution of continuity increase, while the previous state ceases. And therefore, when it is said that the cause inducing pain must be a sudden alteration of disposition or a repentant <note>meaning "unforeseen" or "abrupt"</note> separation of the joining, it is not to be understood that this happens instantaneously in every respect; for if it did, it would be perceived the least. 

Indeed, we experience that when someone is cut by something extremely sharp and entirely suddenly, little or no pain is felt. This is because not only alteration, but indeed any other passion <note>original: "patio" (passio); meaning a physical effect or suffering acted upon the body</note> requires sufficient time in which the sensible object can make an impression on the sense. This perhaps also occurs in the flow of sight in the thirteenth book <note>likely referencing Galen's "De Usu Partium" or a similar optical treatise</note>. That sudden alteration and the dissolution of continuity are the causes of pain can be deduced by brief reasons.

It should be known, however, from the first section, that **heat** and **cold** are causes of pain by themselves <term>per se<explanation>essentially or directly</explanation></term>. **Dryness**, however, is a cause by accident <term>per accidens<explanation>indirectly or as a side effect</explanation></term>. **Moisture** <note>original: "humidū"</note>, however, is a cause in no way at all. Hence, in the fourth book of *Accident and Cause* <note>A work by Galen</note>: in the sense of touch, a change of its nature happens because of the strength of heat or cold. Because a moist or dry body falling upon another body will not cause harm unless it suddenly heats or cools it. For this reason, in the thirteenth book of *The Art of Healing* <note>original: "de īge." (De Ingenio Sanitatis)</note>, only heat and cold are named. 

For since there is a double act of heat and cold: the first and essential act is to heat and to cool. The second act, however, is to extend and dilate, or to contract and narrow, from which finally follows the division of the joining. Heat and cold, since they are the more effective qualities, will induce pain by themselves in their first act by sudden alteration, and by accident in their second act they will cause the same by the separation of the joining. But because one of the passive qualities is stronger, such as dryness, even if it cannot impress pain in its first act (since it is generally passive), it will nevertheless cause it. Hence, Aristotle says: **Dryness** induces pain by accident when a cause of another kind follows it, such as the dissolution of the joining. This is because, due to the strength of its constriction, it becomes the cause of the breaking of the joint.

**Moisture**, however, because of its material passivity, causes pain neither in its first act nor its second; moisture, by softening or relaxing, can provide pain neither by itself nor by accident. Nevertheless, by reason 

<margin>Mesue</margin>
of a great quantity of matter, Mesue <note>A famous Persian Christian physician</note> says in his work on pharmaceuticals: "We do not find moisture, insofar as it is moisture, to be a cause of pain, except insofar as it can be present with matter which, by its quantity, moves toward the dissolution of continuity." This is also what Rasis <note>Rhazes, the influential Persian physician and polymath</note> 
<margin>Rasis as quoted by Alexander</margin>
writes in his "Dispositions." Alexander <note>likely Alexander of Aphrodisias or Alexander of Tralles</note> says that if headaches are stronger according to the operative qualities, they come especially from **heat**. From **dryness**, they are not made vehement. **Moist** qualities, however, which come from moisture itself, in no way inflict pain, unless perhaps the moistening is mixed with heat, cold, a fullness of humors, or sharpness. 

Furthermore, moisture makes pain either by evaporation or by windiness <note>original: "uentositate"; gas or "pneuma" trapped in the body</note> which dissolves the joints. Avicenna <note>The great philosopher-physician Ibn Sina</note> 
<margin>Avicenna, Avenzoar</margin>
and others, besides Avenzoar <note>Ibn Zuhr, the Almohad-era physician</note>, said it causes nausea, as gathered from the fourth book of *The Art of Healing*. A moist or dry complexion does not cause pain except in part; when it is moisture alone, then only **heaviness** <note>original: "grauitas"</note> is felt. This can also be declared in another way: moisture is either "simple" (and thus it is minimally active since it is the most passive of qualities) or it is joined with heat, and then the suffering is attributed more to the more active heat if it exceeds its proper measure. Thus, such a moistening would be more due to the heat causing evaporation and dissolving the moisture. Or, it will be coupled with cold, and thus it will barely exceed its measure. 

Hence Mesue says in the same place: cold things joined with moisture do not rise above their measure, just as Hippocrates <note>original: "Ypocras"</note> says in the *Epidemics*. According to Galen, a moist thing does not cross the boundary to which the regimen of a human can be extended. Those things which are in the "second degree" <note>The medieval system of grading the intensity of medicines and qualities from 1 to 4</note> do not operate by heating, cooling, drying, or moistening in a clearly harmful way. Hence, things in the second degree do not reach the point of impeding manifest operations, nor do they change their natural course except by accident (such as if they are many or often repeated). 

But a painful thing impedes and changes manifest operations to such an extent that it seems more troublesome than other harmful things. Because of this, moisture, insofar as it is moisture, cannot cause pain. But on the contrary, it seems that moisture does sometimes induce pain. Pains, according to the place where they rest, show either a dissolution of continuity or sudden alterations. And it is added: 
<margin>78</margin>
it is altered indeed by sudden heat, cold, dryness, and moisture. Also, in the second book, it is said: Pain occurs in sensible bodies when a great alteration happens in them by active agents, when they are heated, cooled, dried, or moistened. Therefore, moisture is a cause of pain by itself. 

It must be said that Galen either understands moisture not by itself, but as a moist *body* (which is an alteration or a quality associated with something else, as explained by Alexander). Or, because he is speaking specifically about dryness and moisture, and his discourse is of a general nature. They show now that sudden alteration induces pain by itself because it is possible...

It is proved again that the dissolution of continuity is a cause of pain, because if sudden alteration alone were the cause, the pain felt would always be of exactly the same disposition as the quality that is suddenly altering it, the sensation of which we perceive to occur.

This is explained in the third book of *Internal Affections* <note>referring to Galen's medical work "De Locis Affectis"</note> concerning Galen suffering from colic due to wind <note>original: "flate"; intestinal gas or "pneuma" trapped in the gut</note>, which Praxagoras called "glassy" [phlegm], saying that he felt a pain so vehement that it seemed as if his intestines were being bored through with a drill. For although that which has to induce pain because of a sudden alteration of disposition may be felt soon, it is not felt as suddenly painful as that which is induced by a sudden dissolution of continuity. For alteration in disposition happens more swiftly so that it may perceive pain. Therefore, the separation of a joint is another cause of pain, distinct from the sudden permutation of disposition. Because of this, it must be said according to the second [point] that Avicenna, considering that every perception of pain occurs by means of a disposition, wanted that alone to be the cause of pain. Regarding the fourth point, however, it should be said to the first by way of the intention or explanation of a certain reduction of one cause to the other, such as touch. To the second, it should be said that pain is not an alteration, but more truly, alteration is the cause of pain. To the other two points, it should be said that they do not understand sudden alteration as not being the primary cause of pain, but that it eventually follows the dissolution of continuity, so that ultimately the pain is felt more vehemently when, as explained, two causes of pain exist. To the other point, it should be said through the intention assumed above: either because "suddenly" imports a bit of time, for a greater suddenness happens in the dissolution of continuity than in the alteration of disposition; and therefore, the pain of the separation of a joint is more internal and more sudden than the pain of a sudden alteration. To the other point, it should be said that pain in the sense does not happen from the perception of a sensible species or object, but from the medium touching the organ. Since every sense occurs through a medium (*On the Soul*, book III), a medium sometimes exceeding the proportion of the sensory power causes it to feel pain. Whence Aristotle says in the third book of *On the Soul*: "The disposition of hearing and sight does not feel pain because it sees or hears, but because it is touched; tactile pain happens to it." This is evident in the reception of the species of the sun: because of its brightness touching the pupil, it provides pain and corruption. To the other point, as has already appeared, there are only two proper natures: one which follows the alteration of the quality of the elements, and another which follows the form resulting from their substances. For the unity of the body, which contributes to its constitution, belongs to the limbs first and then to the organic parts. For that union or common nature of the limbs and organs is more of a certain order of parts and decoration than a true common unity and nature.

Labor [considered] in multiple ways.

First, it appears for injury or pain, according to that [saying] of the ancient one <note>Hippocrates</note>: "In which disease sound provides a mortal labor." From the *Aphorisms*, also for fatigue, according to that same source: "Where hunger is, one should not labor," and in the sixth book of *Epidemics*: "Labors should be predisposed by foods."

<margin>
Ulcerous labor
<note>Manicule</note>

**Ulcerous labor** <note>original: "labor ulcerosus"</note> is a disposition in which is found on the surface of the skin and in its depths a likeness of ulcers that stimulate, bite, and prick. For those suffering from this labor imagine that sharp things are fixed in their muscles, especially when they move. The cause is indeed a plurality of sharp and thin excesses that are poured out, or the melting of fat or soft flesh; if this reaches the veins, sometimes the good blood contained in them is corrupted, from which shivering and rigor finally come, and a general fever, especially when the patients are further agitated in soul or body.

Tensive

Apostematous

Its cause is repletion and **cachochymia** <term>cachochymia: an unhealthy state of the bodily fluids or humors</term>, and this labor is indeed the worst.

Withering
</margin>
That which is likened to labors, even if it is not considered as such, is the **withering** <note>original: "arefactiuus"</note> disposition, in which the patient imagines himself to be dried up, withered, and contracted; this happens in well-humored bodies from the immoderate heat of things that resolve the humors, when they have been poorly treated.

Constipation
Rareness
</margin>
The dispositions near to these and generating them are such as **constipation** and the **rareness** of the pores. **Constipation** is a disposition properly occurring in the pores of the skin which happens by blockage or density, called the obstruction of the pores. **Rareness** <note>porosity</note> on the other hand is the disposition opposite to this, which occurs to the body from little friction and bathing, and generally from all things that are "opening" and "pore-making."

15th combination.

Indeed, these labors occur from a twofold cause: either from excessive exercise, and then perhaps they are properly called **lassitudes**; or from themselves spontaneously without an external cause, and these are worse than the former and require more diligent reasoning. Furthermore, some of these labors are entirely simple, such as the ulcerous, tensive, and withering. Another is composite in every way by the twofold composition mentioned before, such as that which is like the washing of meat, simultaneously oily and crimson, or ash-colored; which painters also show by the mixing of colors, to which other mixed labors are compared. 

But some are intermediate and composite by a certain mixture, such as yellow, red, green, and the like, to which indeed apostematous labor is adapted. Therefore, it agrees with the ulcerous and tensive more than the simple types do among themselves; yet it differs essentially from those of which it is composed, just as an intermediate color made from black and white [is distinct]. This is confirmed because those things whose causes and effects are different are themselves different. But the causes of the ulcerous and tensive are different from the apostematous. For the causes of the former are simple, while the causes of the latter are composite. For composite things act differently than simple ones, as the **alchemical art** <term>alchemical art: medieval chemistry focused on the transformation of matter and the properties of compounds</term> designates.
    Likewise, those things whose properties, accidents, and indications of treatment are different are themselves distant from one another, since each of such things is sufficiently determined by these. 

---

But these differ: since it is proper to apostematous labor for the body to swell and for the very innermost nerves to seem shattered and bruised even to the bones, which is not the case for the ulcerous and tensive, which are rather a stinging and a stretching.
  Similarly, in the apostematous type, every movement is dreaded in an expanded and uniform way; but not so in the ulcerous and tensive. The harm is also imagined to be felt more immensely since its cause is twofold: namely, **plethoric** <term>plethoric: an excess of blood or bodily humors</term> and **cacochymic** <term>cacochymic: an imbalance of bad or "corrupt" humors</term>. One of these seems to dissolve what is continuous, and the other to alter what is well-tempered. The indication of treatment is also different: because that which is attended to in the apostematous type regards the strength of the indication and its dignity. But that which is in the ulcerous and tensive regards the substance. For it is necessary to vary the treatment in many or fewer ways according to these, by insisting more on one—without abandoning the other—against that which seems to plot a greater evil. Therefore, apostematous labor is another thing by a specific difference, even from the tensive and ulcerous, although it coincides with them in common, just as a middle point with extremes. For they are more distant from each other than the middle is from them, as is denoted by the colors. Regarding the fourth point, it should be said to the first that it is already known that it is not similar concerning the fifteenth combination of labor and many composites of sensible things; it is an apparent composition, certain and existing, such as has been declared for apostematous labor. To the other point, it should be said, as has been shown, that **withering labor** <note>original: "arefactiuus labor"</note> is not truly a labor, even if it is likened to one. Whence **Galen** says: "There is also a certain other disposition deceiving someone as labor," and finally another which is similar to labor but is not labor; because it has neither an ulcerous, nor tensive, nor phlegmonous disposition. But neither does it refer to any error or pain, nor to a movement of blood similar to labors, but rather possessing thinness with dryness. For labor is seen to portend a material disease, which the withering type is not, since the sign and the thing signified must be proportional. It remains, therefore, that among these, the third labor will be the apostematous and not the withering. To the other point, it should be said to be true as long as those separate parts maintain the reason of parts and exist as if imperfect in the whole. But if, being disjoined from it, they still observe the reason of the whole in themselves and not of parts, it is not necessary, as the extreme colors show. Or the whole material thing exists as the same with its parts, but not formally, since they have one form and another when separate versus when joined. For in the whole it exists in potentiality, yet in the sequestered state it exists in act. To the other point, it should be said that everything produced by something obtains a certain nature of it—univocal, virtual, or a middle difference—as is seen in how apostematous labor relates to the ulcerous and tensive; for it is likened to them, yet is essentially another.
   Nor is every division made through altogether opposite things.

direct opposites, looking at them as immediate, such as animate and inanimate, rational and irrational, and the like. Just as they arise from such a division, one does not help the other to exist. This does not happen in colors or in **labors** <note>original: "laboribus"; referring to the specific categories of physical distress discussed on the previous page</note> and as it is in intermediate opposites. And thus, from the book of *Divisions*: every division is either two-membered or reducible to the same. Similarly, although cause and effect exist simultaneously in act and reality, they are nonetheless spoken of as prior and posterior, perfect and imperfect. For although something is produced by another, it is not nonetheless the same in every way, but rather in species or likeness, but not in number. Regarding those things that appear on the other side, it must be said: because **apostematous** <term>apostematous: pain resulting from an inflammatory swelling or abscess</term> labor is not as distant from its components as they are from each other. Nor, likewise, are the treatments entirely different; for they differ in the specific, but not in the general, since in both cases there ought to be an "extraction" and "alteration."

->### DIFFERENCE LXXVII.<-

It seems that pain is not sensed. For a sense is for nothing other than qualities <margin>Sign</margin> <margin>2.</margin> as distinguished previously; but pain is not a quality, but rather a relation. For it was said earlier that the sense of pain is "sad." Furthermore, pain is a sense; but a sense is not sensed. For it would be sensed either by itself or by another. Not the first, because a sense does not apprehend itself nor its own instrument. **Algazel** <note>Al-Ghazali (1058–1111), a Persian philosopher whose works on the soul were influential in Latin translation</note> in *On the Soul* says that because a sense is a material power, such a thing does not reflect upon itself, but only that which goes out in an immaterial way. And therefore the intellect understands itself (as in the third book of *On the Soul*), but not by another [sense]; because, as some argue, that would be another sense, and that one would have another sense, and so it would proceed to infinity, which nature rejects in the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*. Again, they argue: if pain is sensed, then touch is perceived by the sense because it is the sense that comprehends sensibles. But none of the philosophers ever placed pain among the "sensibles" <note>the standard objects of sense perception like color, sound, or smell</note>. Also, a "sensible" perfects the sense, leading that which was in potentiality into act, just as the "intelligible" perfects the intellect. Pain, however, does not perfect the sensitive power; on the contrary, among other things that harm, it corrupts it. **Galen** confirms this, because that which is a contrary corrupts, since it is in the nature of contraries to be mutually destructive. But pain is the contrary of sense, since sense is a certain moderation of primary and even excellent qualities, as distinguished before. Pain, however, is a vehement "passion" <note>original: "passio"; in the sense of a suffering or an affection acted upon the subject</note> occurring suddenly by force. Furthermore, pain is an "accident." That is, it is a "damaged action" <note>original: "actio lesa"; a classic medical definition of a symptom</note>. That which the sense perceives is perfected by "alteration," since sensing is a kind of "being acted upon" which consists in alteration. But because this action is damaged as if already done, it seems to withdraw from the process of alteration. Therefore, pain is not sensed at all. 

**The Opposite View.** Whosoever are in pain in some part of the body do not sense much of the rest, etc. Again, it was said before by **Aristotle** that pain happens when one suddenly senses a contrary impression.

<margin>Love and <unclear>nature</unclear></margin>
Furthermore, that which is a sign is sensed; because a sign is that which, by offering itself to the sense, leaves something else in the intellect. But pain is a sign; hence in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*, a foundational medical textbook</note>: pains, according to the place where they press, show either a sudden alteration or a "solution of continuity" <note>original: "solutionem continuitatis"; a medical term for a wound, break, or tearing of tissue</note>. Again, that which makes power fail and destroys it is sensed, unless the mind is diseased. For sense was given to the animal, according to Aristotle's *On the Soul*, so that it might perceive helpful things and harmful things—choosing the former and spurning the latter. Pain performs this function primarily. Therefore, pain is sensed. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known what sense and pain are, as seen before. Regarding the second, it must be known that some wished to reduce all tangible qualities to "hot" and "cold," which is argued against by Aristotle in *On the Soul*; for the other sensibles are perceived by hot and cold without their mediation, whether of taste or smell or others, although hot and cold are virtually within them, since the primary "second qualities" <note>complex qualities derived from the four primary elements</note> are composed of them. Hence, in *On Generation and Corruption*: it is manifest that all other tactile differences are reduced to the first four. These, however, are not further reduced into smaller ones. Yet "hot" is not "dry," nor is it "moist," and so on for the others. Nor do they exist under one another, as if under "hot" and "moist." <margin>3.</margin> Hence, from these points, some have taken up the cause of error, wishing to reduce pain and pleasure to the primary qualities, which is not the case. Because if these were traced back to the first qualities because they are caused by them, then the sensibles of the other four senses would also be reduced to touch, since they are caused by them, as are intermediate color and taste. And thus the objects of the other senses would not be intermediates, but only extremes, since they are composed from them. The falsehood of this is apparent.

Furthermore, it should be known that Aristotle posits there that pain is one of the "tactile sensibles," saying: "There is another mode concerning it," and so on as before. After which he adds: "Pain and the remedy for pain are among the tactile sensibles." <margin>3.</margin> This is also the view of Galen in the fourth book of *On the Causes of Symptoms*. To be glad, to be sad, and to feel pain occurs in the senses, which he declares in all the senses in order, beginning with sight. This is also shown by his discourse on the pleasure of the genitals and its opposite. Others, however, have claimed that two things enter into the essence of pain according to sense: and the proof they say is clear from the definition of pain, since it is a "harmful sensation." Because of this, they say that insofar as it is a sensation, it is not sensed at all; but rather insofar as it is harmful. They hold a similar view regarding pleasure: for it is not sensed insofar as it is a sensation, but in that it is helpful. But this cannot stand, because pain is by no means the sensation itself, as they indicate, but rather it stands as its "passion" <note>affection or suffering</note>. For sensation is a "passion" occurring suddenly, which is its reception. For just as other tangible things are not the sensation itself (as will be declared), so it is not pain. If it is said that sometimes pain exists as "sad sensation" or "harmful," it must be said that such is not pain itself, but rather a certain famous notification or the aforementioned...

<meta>This page continues the logical inquiry into the nature of pain (Difference 77), specifically whether pain is a sense in itself or a "passion" (an experience acted upon the sense). It references Boethius's *Categories* to distinguish between temporary dispositions and stable habits. The author also provides a personal anecdote about a shoulder pain to illustrate his point.</meta>

<margin>Boethius in the Categories</margin>
...further to include its perfect reasoning. For it is not valid to say that pain is a "sad sense." Therefore, it is a sense, as they say. For phlegm is blood <note>original: "san." for "sanguis"</note> that is diminished or under-cooked, yet it is not blood simply, but the whole thing together. So also in the *Meteorology*, Book 1: Dew is small rain, and rain is more than dew; yet rain is not simply dew, nor is dew rain, just as a habit <term>habit: a stable, long-lasting internal state</term> and a disposition <term>disposition: a temporary or easily changed state</term> are not the same. Although Boethius writes in the *Categories* <note>original: "Praedicamentis"</note> that a disposition is a weak state, while a habit is a stable one. Thus, pain is not a sense in an absolute sense, but is "sad" or "harmful" when joined together. This is nothing other than a passion of the sense and its object. Similarly, delight is not a sense, but a "cheerful passion" and an object by which we are soon restored to our natural state. 

Regarding the third point, <margin>Objects of touch</margin> it must first be known that the objects of touch are multiple, since it is the primary perceiver of many more contrarieties than exist in the other senses; for there are forty-two differences of touch. For a sense takes its definition from its object, just as a science does from its subject. For the sensitive power is materially one in its organ, but formally it is many because of the objects that bring it into action. Thus, the sense will be twofold: material, as the sensitive power bound to the organ; and formal, when that power comes into action through the object. Furthermore, in the book *On Generation and Corruption*, the differences of touch are listed many times: namely, hot and cold, dry and moist, heavy and light, hard and soft, viscous and fragile, rough and smooth, thick and thin. These are found in the origins and helps of the parents. From the sperm sent into the womb <note>original: "matrice"</note> or the earth, at a predetermined time, the parts of that which is generated are sown with many qualities of dryness, moisture, heat, and cold, and any others that follow these differences, which you will know from the discourse on generation. These primary qualities are especially followed by the remaining tangible differences, after which come those that can be tasted, smelled, and seen. Therefore, hardness and softness, slipperiness and dryness, lightness and heaviness, density and rarity, smoothness and roughness, thickness and thinness are these tangible differences. 

This is also confirmed by reason. For according to the aforementioned, every contrary disposition of the body is felt by a change that suddenly alters it. For that which occurs in an orderly and gradual way is not perceived by the senses, nor is that which has already ceased from its change. Since every "passion" <note>the experience of being acted upon</note> and even the act of sensing consist in a state of becoming and of being altered in the third kind of accident. For in residing and resting, there is no "passion." For this reason, according to the author A., the heat of those with hectic fever <note>original: "ethicoy"; a chronic, wasting fever</note>, although it is more intense than the heat of those with tertian fever <note>a fever recurring every third day, common in malaria</note>, is not perceived by them through touch. Such a disposition is pain, and especially since it is more contrary to nature than others. Furthermore, that thing is perceived by touch on its own which is discerned from other sensible things existing with it, or which perceives nothing else but that very thing. But such a thing is pain. 

<margin>Note</margin>
For often a sad passion is perceived in a part of the body together with heat or cold. Likewise, when the aforementioned passion is present, it is not rarely felt without any primary or secondary quality. **For this reason, while I was writing this, a pain came upon me in my shoulder blade, and in that perceptible event, I could perceive no primary or secondary sensible qualities mentioned before, except for the "sad passion."** Again, in sexual intercourse <note>original: "coitu"</note>, what primary or secondary quality is perceived except only the joining of the suitable with the suitable, which is delight? The opposite of this is felt in its contrary, as in the fourth book of *On Accidents*. For the reasons of contraries are contrary. Again, that which is the cause of sensing the rest is what is most sensed. For because of one thing, each other thing is also sensed, and that thing even more so. But because of pain, sudden alteration and the loss of continuity <note>original: "solutio continui"; a medical term for a wound or break in tissue</note> are sensed. 

Perhaps someone using logic will want to challenge this reasoning. Yet it seems absurd to say that the most sensible thing, occurring suddenly in nature, would not be perceived by the sensitive power, such as pain and its opposite. Therefore, pain is also sensed on its own, being one of the sensible things. Regarding the fourth point, it must be said in response to the first that pain and delight are types of qualities. For they are placed in the category of "passion" and "passible quality." If, however, Avicenna intends only the primary or secondary qualities commonly expressed, then I do not disagree. Since pain is perceived by them in one way or another. Nor would this be an obstacle even assuming pain were related to something else, because primary qualities are placed directly in the genus of quality; heavy and light in the predicament of substance; rough and smooth in the genus of position—forty-two differences according to Aristotle and the Commentator <note>Averroes</note>—and yet they are objects of one sense, namely touch. 

To the other point, it must be said that, as it appeared, pain is not the sense itself, but rather the object and the "passion" of it; therefore the deduction is not valid. There is also one common sense that does not proceed to infinity among sensible things, distinguishing between the objects of different senses, as appears in the book *On the Soul*. To the other point, it must be said that some philosophers, like Galen and Aristotle, expressly placed pain and its remedy among the sensible qualities, which is proved to be necessary. For these same wise men sometimes list many tangible qualities, and other times fewer. For in the book *On the Soul*, they express only hot, cold, dry, moist, hard, and soft. And the Commentator explains heavy and light. And the parents of such things are those announced above. Also, in the first place, they find only four contrarieties to be in touch, though there are eight senses according to those who posit multiple types of touch. These are expressed by Haly as, along with the former: hard and soft, rough and smooth. In the book *On the Soul* by Aristotle, many more are explained. 

To the other point, it must be said that a sensible object perfects the sense and invigorates it when it is proportional and suitable, but not when it is disproportionate and contrary. For the excesses of sensible things destroy the sense, according to the book *On the Soul*. For the likeness of the sense to the intellect is not in every respect, because the greatest of sensible things overwhelm the sensitive powers. Intellectual things, however, when they are greatest, corroborate the intellect, according to the third book of *On the Soul*. To the other point, it must be said that although one of the contraries destroys the other, the action is not nonetheless removed among them, but is rather made more unstable. For a thing is said to "be destroyed" in the process of becoming, but not in the completed state. For if the sensible thing, such as pain, already destroyed the sense, nothing else of the sensible things would be perceived, since it has been said that sensing consists in the process of becoming and being altered. To the other point, it must be said that an accident and pain are called a "damaged action" in respect to the disease, which is the "damaging action." Yet the damaged action of the accident or pain is more in the state of becoming than the damaging action of the disease, as declared in difference seventy-two.

<meta>This page transitions from a general discussion on the nature of sensation and pain (Difference 77) to a specific medical debate concerning diagnostic signs, specifically jaundice and its timing during a fever (Difference 78). It applies the philosophical definitions of "accidents" and "dispositions" discussed previously to the practical observation of a patient’s symptoms.</meta>

### DIFFERENCE 78.

That jaundice occurring before the seventh day is a good sign is shown from the fourth book of **Rhazes** <note>original: "re. a." likely referring to the Liber Almansoris of Rhazes</note>, as follows: In a choleric fever, a jaundice that appears before the seventh day breaks the fever. Both **Avenzoar** <note>original: "Zoar"</note> and **Avicenna** <note>original: "Ax."</note> testify to this. Furthermore, it seems more or less certain that phlegmatic or sanguine matter finishes its course before the seventh day, since it is earlier and thicker, and choler moves less. This is seen in cases of apoplexy <term>apoplexy: a sudden loss of consciousness, similar to a stroke</term> which ends in paralysis, and in fevers of the blood by a nosebleed, as well as in the appearance of pustules <note>original: "uariolas," likely referring to smallpox or similar eruptive fevers</note> on the fourth day or before. Again, just as choleric matter can be evacuated before the seventh day through vomiting or bowel movements, it likewise appears through the skin, since choler is a subtle <term>subtle: thin or refined in consistency</term> substance, capable of moving from the center of the body to the circumference. This is shown by the fact that a crisis <term>crisis: the turning point of a disease where the patient either recovers or declines</term> mostly occurs through sweat, in which the dregs of choler are mixed; for sweat is an excess of blood mixed with watery, choleric dregs. And this is confirmed because the fourth day is the strongest indicator. Sweats are judged to be good if they begin on the third, fifth, or seventh day, etc. **Palladius** in the third [book], chapter 15: If choler putrefies within the vessels, it produces a tertian fever <term>tertian fever: a fever that spikes every other day</term>; but if it does not, it produces jaundice. But a tertian fever can be ended for the better before the seventh day, such as on the fifth; for then its movement lasts until the day in which the choler, through subtle putrefaction, is rendered thicker and un-putrefied. Therefore, jaundice before the seventh day can be a praiseworthy sign.

<margin>Opposition.</margin>
On the contrary, there is a group of physicians [who disagree]; hence **Isaac [Judaeus]** in the fourth book of *On Fevers*: Jaundice before the seventh day undoubtedly invites fear. Again, jaundice is placed under the crisis of change appearing on the fourth day, but such a thing does not happen before the seventh, nor universally in an acute disease and subtle matter, but rather in a chronic and thick matter accompanied by a weakness of virtue <term>virtue: the body's natural strength or healing power</term>. Furthermore, a praiseworthy crisis requires an indication equally distant from the start of the disease and the crisis itself, as Isaac says in the fourth book of *Fevers*. But no such day exists before the seventh except the fourth, which stands as a certain indicator of them, as the movement of the moon denotes. Therefore, jaundice before the seventh day will not be a praiseworthy sign. For this reason, first, since the inquiry into the sign is not yet complete, it must be known that a sign is a sensible thing which, offering itself to the sense, leaves something behind for the intellect.

For memory arises from many observations, from which experience is drawn, and from that finally comes a universal principle, which is the beginning of art and science, as stated in the *Posterior Analytics* and the preface to the *Metaphysics*. From this, it is hinted that since a "sign" is a relative term, its meaning is twofold: one is immediate, with which it exists essentially, such as touch. When it says "offering itself to the sense," another is mediated, with which it does not always exist, when it is added "leaving something in the intellect," which is called a prognostic sign. There are, however, three things: the **sign**, the **signification**, and the **accident** <term>accident: a symptom or non-essential quality of a disease</term>. This is not used here as it is divided against "substance," but rather as that which follows the disease or the disposition, like the shadow of a body, which is properly called a consequence or a child of the disease. But mostly, these are the same in subject, though different in their reasoning.

<margin>
Signification.
What a sign is.
In what way it is spoken of.
</margin>

For although "sign" is commonly taken for "signification," a difference is nevertheless seen to be granted in the third book of the *Prognostics*. One difference is that a "signification" is of necessary things, while a "sign" is of those things that happen for the most part. The other is that signification is grasped by reason, while the sign is grasped by experience. For "signification," being an abstract term, denotes its nature in a memorial way, whereas "sign" is concrete, as if it were a being, since it is said to be an "accident" first and then a "subject." The **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note> in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*, although he suggests the contrary, seems to say that a certain signified thing is seen by the sense and is held to be in the manner of an act of reason. Therefore, it ought to belong primarily to the natures and passions <term>passions: conditions or experiences acting upon a body part</term> of the internal members. This is why the book is inscribed *On the Significations of Internal Passions*. A "sign," however, denotes something simple and more apparent to the senses among those things that occur externally, since it falls immediately upon the senses. A sign or a signification is called an "accident," for both exist in the same subject. However, as it is often said, some things are a sign but not an accident, such as a prognostic sign that does not yet exist. For nothing is a "damaged action" unless it exists. On the other hand, something is an accident but not a sign, such as something not perceived by the physician. And therefore, **Joannitius** <note>Hunayn ibn Ishaq</note> says the division among them is one of overlap; for they relate to each other as the exceeding and the exceeded.

But they differ in their reasoning in every way, even if they share the same subject for the most part. For what is an accident to a weak physician is a sign to a skilled one. For an accident is a thing according to its essence, such as a "damaged action" or the preparation of the infirmity, to which something happens that is also called a "symptom" or a "concurrence." But "signification" is the thing in respect to the consideration of the physician, as he proceeds to know the nature of the sickness. Sometimes the "signification" of the sick person can be spoken of, not as he is sick, but insofar as he acts in the place of the physician by describing his own accident; for a certain sign is taken from the indications of the patient, as Joannitius says.

<margin>
See also
Difference 73.
</margin>

What an accident is, and how it differs from other things contrary to nature, was shown in Difference 73. Indeed, there is a manifold variety of signs: for some are considered by reason of their essence, and thus some are a **changed quality**, such as jaundice; others are a **damaged operation**, which happens in three ways: because the action is harmed either slightly (which is properly called "changed"), or moderately, or is taken away entirely.

<margin>A sign is an action slightly [changed], or mostly changed.</margin>

The rest is drawn from the body, which is sometimes perceived by sound, and sometimes without it. That which signifies by quantity, or jaundice, or by quality, such as black urine; or by both, such as a flow of blood; or by reason of what is signified, where one sign is **healthy**, another is **sick**, and the rest are **neutral** according to the *Ars Medica* <note>original: "tegni," referring to Galen's Techni/Ars Medica</note>. Each of these is spoken of according to the body as such, or at least for the most part, as it is now. The "neutral" sign is subdivided into three modes in Difference 72. Of the signs of the sick, some are "familiar" (concurring with the disease), others are "supervening" (occurring later); some indicate digestion, others indigestion; some are contrary to digestion, some are "critic" <note>indicating a crisis</note>, others indicate health, and some indicate death. Or they are observed by the manner of their signifying, which also happens in three ways: as they refer to the one who knows, or to the power...

<meta>This page continues the medical discourse on diagnostics, moving from specific symptoms like jaundice to a systematic classification of "signs" (semiotics). It categorizes signs based on the "animal," "vital," and "natural" faculties, drawing heavily on Aristotelian psychology and the medical authorities Galen, Averroes, and Rhazes.</meta>

### Animal [faculty].
And this is done in a two-fold or three-fold way regarding movement; thus, a sign might be different from the movement itself. This occurs either naturally, such as a **shudder** <note>original: "horror," referring to the chills accompanying a fever</note>, or voluntarily, such as **yawning** and **rolling** [of the eyes], or both, such as a **cough**, in which nature overcomes the will, or similarly in defecation and urination, where the opposite occurs. Or the sign may arise from rest, as in **apoplexy** <term>apoplexy: a sudden loss of consciousness or paralysis, often a stroke</term>, **epilepsy**, and **syncope** <term>syncope: fainting or a sudden loss of consciousness</term>. 

Alternatively, it arises from the apprehensive faculty, which is two-fold: either external or internal. The external is further divided: first, regarding the **common sensibles**—as the Commentator <note>Averroes, the influential 12th-century philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> says in the third book of *On the Soul*—which are:

<margin>Common sensibles</margin>
**motion, rest, number, magnitude, and figure.** In the fourth book of *On the Soul*, **position** is added to these. According to the Commentator, the first three are common to all senses, while the remaining two belong only to touch and sight. Beyond this, meaning is signified by the signs taken from them, according to how they are numbered or shaped. 

Second, it relates to the **proper sensibles**, which occur in five ways: either through the sense called **touch**, such as hot and cold; or **taste**, such as bitter and sweet; or **smell**, such as in the case of a polyp; or **sight**, as in jaundice. Regarding how **hearing** and **touch** signify in those matters, they are primary in what they discern from the body. 

Regarding the **internal [senses]**, a sign denotes a directed action or the mind, and this is manifold: namely, the powers of **imagination**, **phantasy**, **thought** <note>original: "cogitativa," the faculty that combines or divides images</note>, and **memory**. Sometimes one is corrupted while the other two remain, as described in the third and fourth books of *On Accidents*. 

Or the distinction is based on the mode of inherence between the sign and what is signified. Thus, some signs are taken from **substantial inherences**, which are necessary; for an operation or effect always exists necessarily and closely to its cause. This appears to be the truth, whereas others are based on **accidental things**, which follow only by chance and contain neither of the aforementioned [necessities]. However, those that lie are rarer. There is also a sign that is enduring and primary, taken from the disposition of operations. Another is primary but not enduring, such as that taken from excretions.

<margin>Another distinction.</margin>

<margin>Another distinction.</margin>
The remaining signs are neither, being common or extrinsic. Or, by reason of **time**, some are **rememorative** [past-oriented] regarding the sick person; these have small utility, serving only the physician immediately. Others are **demonstrative** [present-oriented], which benefit the sick person only as a **prognostic** <term>prognostic: a forecast of the likely course of a disease</term>, which according to Baly <note>likely Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician</note> serves both the physician—since it pertains to the terms of his fee—and the sick person, because through this he knows how he must be managed, for his affairs are known by it. 

From these, finally, a two-membered distinction of the sign can be formed: one is

<margin>Two-membered distinction.</margin>
**common**, noting the **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) in an individual</term> and composition, and everything regarding nature and disposition. The other is **particular**, signifying a hidden lesion, which is more properly called an internal signified sign. 

The first [common signs] are manifold. Some are given by **touch**, as it discerns hardness and softness especially; others from the flesh and fat, according to variations in quantity, quality, and their types. Others come from the **form of the limbs**: for instance, the width of the chest and the extension of the extremities denote **heat**, while the opposite denotes **cold**. Others are taken from **operations**, either **natural**, such as the excretion of superfluities, or **vital**, such as the pulse, or **animal** <term>animal: in this context, relating to the "anima" (soul) or brain-centered functions like movement and sensation</term>. And this is twofold: internal and external, according to

---

### fully completed.
...either by generation or from those vital functions, such as what is perceived from the **breath**, for both work toward it. Others come from the **ease or difficulty of suffering**; for that which is quickly heated is hot and dry, while that which is quickly cooled is the opposite, unless the rarity or density of the internal muscles varies this. 

Others come from the **hair**, as they are distinguished by the speed or slowness of their growth, color, shape, quantity, scarcity, or absence. The last are taken from the **color of the skin**, which is rendered such by nature or by accident. For **whiteness** signifies a lack of blood with a dominance of **phlegm**; **redness** signifies the opposite; **yellow** [citrine] signifies **choler**; **lividity** <note>original: "suscedo," likely "fuscedo" or "subcedo," meaning a dark or dusky hue</note> signifies melancholy; and **blackness** signifies black jaundice. This is caused by **adustion** <term>adustion: the "scorching" of humors through excessive heat, making them toxic</term> or by extreme external factors, as with the Ethiopians, or whiteness from the cold, as with the Scots.

### More Particularly
<margin>2 2 1</margin>
the sign is understood in two ways. One is from the **sense of anatomy**; for those who wish to discern internal sufferings in anatomy should be practiced in the internal parts. Through these, the four-fold composition of the limbs is diagnosed, along with their substance and even their complexion.

### Another
is the signified sign proper, which proceeds like a rule in the knowledge of the aforementioned things, taken from four or six things, such as from a **visible lesion of actions**. This is demonstrated in three ways: for the action is either **changed**, or becomes **weak**, or is

<margin>excretions</margin>
**destroyed** entirely. Or it is taken from that which is **evacuated**; for sometimes that which is natural is sufficiently drawn out, but at other times the opposite occurs, such as when substance from the limbs [is expelled]. And sometimes it is varied by quantity, quality, and mode. 

Or it is taken from **pain**, which is signified by its **location** (whether it is on the right or left side) or its **essence** (whether it is a heavy or acute pain). Or from an **aposteme** <term>aposteme: a swelling, tumor, or abscess</term>, which similarly signifies by its location, substance, and shape. **Position** is also added, whether it indicates the place or the association of the patient, according to **Galen** and the judgment of **Lobicium**. 

According to **accidents** that are manifest and prepared, their significance is attested; for they are neither primary nor enduring. Such signs are **common and extrinsic**, and their significance remains somewhat conjectural. The remaining are **essential**, inseparably accompanying their signified meanings, through which perfect knowledge is obtained, as shown in Difference 84. 

"Good" and "bad" are not said uniformly or 

<margin>Not</margin>
absolutely, but are said in relation to something. For perhaps one **bad sign** outweighs many laudable ones, and one strong laudable sign outweighs many bad ones, as noted in the first book of *On Crises* and the third book of *Prognostics*, such as the constancy of virtue and its opposite. Therefore, it is necessary to establish an order among them, as the writings of the ancients suggest. For sometimes a sign is called "not bad," or "not good," sometimes "benign" or "crafty," sometimes "salutary" or "mortal," or "pernicious," or "worst" and "best," or "most faithful." Whence in the tenth book of the **Almansor** <note>The *Liber Almansoris* by the Persian physician Rhazes</note>, a word must be placed with each sign to denote the quantity of its strength. For that which is a weaker sign is called "not good," while that which is stronger...

<margin>jaundice</margin>
<margin>Warning ⁒</margin>
...an evil [sign] and one that is most strongly mortal, or very mortal. Similarly, it is to be understood regarding the signs that are praised. This is, therefore, a concise collection of the variety of common signs. **Jaundice** is an alteration of the color of the skin tending toward yellowness or blackness, arising from the encounter of yellow or black bile at the skin, and those things which follow it without **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the decomposition of humors, which medieval doctors believed caused fevers</term>; for if it were to putrefy, it would cause a **tertian fever** <term>tertian fever: a fever that spikes every third day, associated with yellow bile</term> in the case of yellow [bile], and a **quartan fever** <term>quartan fever: a fever that spikes every fourth day, associated with black bile</term> in the case of black [bile]. Third book, chapter fifteen. 

According to the *Viaticum* <note>original: "Viaticus"; a popular 11th-century medical manual for travelers</note>, jaundice is a mixture of red bile with the blood, spreading itself over all the members of the body and appearing on the surface of the body. Whence in the fourth book of *Accidents* [it says]: all things appear yellow to those with jaundice. In the fourth book on fevers, Isaac and the *Viaticum* say the name of jaundice is derived from a bird having a yellow color which is called a **galberg** <note>original: "galberg"; likely referring to the Golden Oriole or Yellowhammer</note>; by some, it is called the *apsdiluca*. It hangs its nest in a magnificent way under the branch of a nut tree. It is called *icteris* <note>original: "ycteris"; the Greek word for jaundice and the bird believed to cure it</note> according to the saying: "Traveler, take your path; upon the tree the *icterus* sings." The derivation of this name is indicated at the end of the sixth book of *Accidents*.

A harm to the **transformative power** <term>transformative power: the biological faculty responsible for changing nutrients into blood and tissues</term> occurs, happening to the humors that differ from blood; whence a change of color necessarily follows. One of these is called jaundice. The type which arises from **melancholy** <term>melancholy: black bile</term> remains unnamed [by some]. In the *Passionarium*, however, it is written that the Greeks call this *melanchion*, that is, **"black dog."** Others write *melanchiron*, that is, "blackening the hand." Those suffering from this passion are said to be **arcuati** <note>original: "arcuati"; from "arcus" (rainbow), referring to the skin's varied discolorations</note> from *arcus*, that is, the rainbow; or they are said to have the **"royal"** or **"golden"** passion. 

Two common modes are noted: **yellow** and **black**. They also add **green**, and another which they name **agriaca**, that is, "wild," because the wild polecat <note>original: "mustela"; literally weasel, but here used for a wild animal associated with bitter bile</note> is called *capre cri solonca*. In the *Viaticum*, another is called *agriaca pegaseleontos*. The cause of the yellow kind is the dregs of bile, which is mixed with the blood and diffused through the exterior parts of the body, staining them.

This occurs either through the action of nature, as when it is judged on a **critical day** <term>critical day: a specific day in a disease's progress when a turning point occurs</term>, or it is not by the action of nature but rather occurs as a **symptom**. This happens in two ways: either from external causes, such as the puncture of a serpent, the sting of heavy insects <note>original: "pediclorum"; likely referring to lice or stinging parasites</note>, or the consumption of **leopard's gall** or viper [venom], from which jaundice arises quickly. Or it arises from internal causes, which most often happen in the liver and gallbladder, and sometimes from the heat of the entire body—and specifically of the vessels—but very rarely from the intestines. 

From the gallbladder, it also happens in two ways: either from a thick, viscous humor causing an **obstruction** <term>obstruction: "opilatio," a blockage in the body's channels or "pores"</term> in its ducts, of which there are two, the second of which passes toward the intestines... or from a passion of the substance of the gallbladder, which happens either from an intense heat burning the liver and the whole body so that the blood seeps into the bile, or from a weakness of the gallbladder itself, so that its **attractive power** is feeble in drawing [bile], or it fails in its **expulsive power** due to dryness, or an abscess or obstruction occurring in the aforementioned ducts. 

That which arises from the liver happens in the two ways mentioned before. It occurs from the intestines very rarely, when [bile] descends into the colon and, finding an obstacle,

<margin>Aghia. . 91 . distinction</margin>
<margin>Soap</margin>
refuses to pass through; whence the bile contained in the gallbladder lacks a place to which it may be diverted. 

**Black [jaundice]** also sometimes occurs by the vigor of nature as a **crisis** for a disease of the spleen. More often, however, it is a symptom, such as from a weakness of the spleen, or from the humors being scorched by the heat of the liver, or from an inflammation of the whole body. And it can happen for those reasons in its own way, just as with the gallbladder and liver. Some have wanted **agriacal jaundice** <note>original: "agriacam"; the "wild" or most severe form</note> to arise from leek-green or rust-colored bile, the opposite of which is shown in the 91st distinction. But one should agree with **Serapion** that it is caused rather by a malignant gallbladder, or the liver and spleen. For he says: if during the cleansing of yellow bile any "cleansing" disease occurs, and if jaundice occurs mixed from yellow and black bile, that color turns toward green. This is another species of jaundice which is composed of yellow bile and melancholy, and it happens when the liver and spleen are similarly injured. The color rendered from these is green. He also holds that when the blackness is light, it comes from the liver; if it is intense, it comes from the spleen.

<margin>Avenzoar.</margin>
<margin>4th of the *Colliget*</margin>
Regarding the prognosis, it should be known that he who fixed himself to **Hippocrates** <note>original: "ypocrate"</note> in the fourth book... wrote with a certain condition regarding the onset of jaundice, namely that it is determined by a **rigor** <term>rigor: a sudden chill or shivering fit</term>, perhaps alluding to what is said: "A rigor coming upon a burning fever," etc. Galen, in the same place, does not admit this determination of rigor. 

**Avenzoar** <note>original: "3oar"; the 12th-century physician Ibn Zuhr</note> simply seems to concede that jaundice appearing before the seventh day can be a great and **laudable sign**. Physicians generally condemn jaundice at the beginning of a sickness because it emerges before the **maturation** <term>maturation: "decoction," the process where the body "cooks" or prepares humors for expulsion</term> of the humors. But I say: because jaundice is an acute disease and its movement is swift in the agent and the patient, we will not deny that maturation can occur on the second day of its generation, and especially on the fourth day, particularly in the prime of youth, in the time of summer, in a hot region, and in eastern or southern places. In such cases, maturation and decoction are accelerated. 

In the fourth book of the *Colliget* <note>The "General Principles of Medicine" by Averroes</note> it is said: if jaundice comes upon acute fevers before the seventh day, it is evil; this has been rejected by experience in all our lands. And if it comes on the fifth day, it is very laudable for one reason, and especially in hot bodies and in hot weather; and this is the opinion of all the colleges of famous physicians and of **Greater India** and for the most part those of **Andalusia**. The others felt the opposite, following the word of the ancients entirely; whence [it is said] in the fourth book, second part: "At the last, jaundice before the seventh day is not laudable." 

The defect of the aforesaid [ancient] sayings will appear manifest, even if both their specific arguments are treated individually. For perhaps someone will accuse **Avenzoar**, saying that jaundice is a disease when it is more of an accident and an injured action—namely, a foul alteration of color. However, that it can appear "benignly" on the second day is clearly false.

Thus, the experiences he had upon this are approved as being asserted, but not falsely believed by open reason. 

Indeed, Avicenna was rustic <note>meaning unrefined or blunt</note> in his judgment. For what he says regarding the **monstrosity** <note>a term for a highly irregular case</note> of Hippocrates is proved false by experience and is uncivil, since it is against the canons of the art and the rest. However, the specific discourse of Avicenna is almost never proven. He does not refute Hippocrates since, in the sixth book of **Aphorisms**, the occurrence is rare and does not make Hippocrates a liar in most cases of evacuation. Similarly, neither in the fourth day of praiseworthy diseases does he judge jaundice [a good sign], since choler is thicker than this, as if six times over, and can hardly be **digested** <term>digested: in medieval medicine, "coction" or the ripening of humors so the body can expel them</term> in such a short time. 

Truly, the dregs of the matter itself, which the thicker tint of jaundice shows, are prohibited from penetrating, but not the sweat, since the **cholerous pus** <note>original: "pus colicum"</note> is also mixed with it. Nor did any aspect of the moon then intervene. Furthermore, let him notice for himself when he says this is verified in a hot time and consequently in a hot region. Why is the judgment the same for those [others], since he adds that this is similar to all <note>meaning it applies generally</note> like the Persian physicians? But **Persia** is colder and much more similar to **Greece** because of the rigor of the poles, if one truly hears the location of Persia. Its king was **Darius**, and today the **Tarts** <note>Tatars</note> occupy it. And therefore, one must not yield to his experience or reason, since **Hippocrates** is a more faithful witness that he had experience not only in Greece but in **Libya**, **India**, and **Ethiopia** <note>original: "subacia", likely a corruption of Sub-Aethiopia</note>. 

This is also what Avicenna sanctifies: if it happens by accident, it is more [deadly]. Or perhaps because of some crisis associated with it, and not regularly or by itself; or by a double **obstruction** <term>obstruction: or 'oppilation', a blockage in the vessels or organs</term> or by the way they are deceived by appearances. Or it must be said that jaundice seen to be not for evil before the seventh day is not "true" jaundice, but rather a moderate **sub-citrine** <note>lemon-yellowish</note> color especially around the eyes and face from an inflation of the **cataract** <note>likely referring to a facial swelling or specific ocular condition</note>, as was seen. 

Therefore, others have said that a crisis before the seventh can be benign if a flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note> assists it. That, however, requires determination, because this flux is either mixed choler boiling over, with the exit of sticking foamy materials—and thus its significance is bad, so much so that one fears for the sick man, especially with a weakness of strength—or the flux of the belly is vehemently **mordicant** <term>mordicant: stinging or biting, often used to describe corrosive humors</term>, or even a common exuberant sweat and a strong **pulse** <note>original: "xp̃tus", abbreviation for pulsus</note>, and thus it is praiseworthy since the relief of the patient occurs more quickly on the fourth. And this is according to the fourth book of Aphorisms. Because of which a third thing is to be known: that jaundice regularly and by itself before the seventh day—as the others testify, except for two—is an evil sign. This shows that if anything ought to be benignly and swiftly expelled by nature, it must be fit for it.

**Digestion** <note>coction</note> is required so that the material is rendered into a uniform substance in quality, sequestered from the walls of the members, and that the ways and ducts for the same are prepared and fit so that it can be propelled outward. And therefore, since they more greatly redound into the **hemorrhoids**—whether of the matrix, the anus, or the nostrils—the evacuations of the belly and intestines are more praiseworthy here on the fourth [day], [such as] the flux of blood, stool, and vomiting. However, those of sweat are of lesser praise than the others. Since the material lacks the ducts for those which are carried, it is judged to be benign only by its thinness, penetrating through hidden pores to the skin as sweat. 

Because, as is supposed, digestion and the separation of sticking matter must precede the crisis; but that cannot happen before the seventh day according to **Galen**. Likewise, it cannot happen when the choler is disobedient and the passages are unprepared. Again, for a perfect crisis, the digestion of the material is required, which cannot be unless a sufficient space of time intervenes, and especially when the exit lacks an opening. It requires then the **aspect of the moon**; but this cannot be present before the seventh. First, because the time in the illness is not sufficient, and second, because the aid of the moon is not found. Not even in the fourth, because even if some operation exists in it, the "breath" <note>influence</note> of the moon does not exist. 

Similarly, crises are always in the worse [days] according to Galen, if we are able [to judge]. Not in the fifth, although nature may move, because the time for the disposition of the material and the ducts does not yet occur sufficiently, nor does any aspect of the moon. Also, because of the work, it is necessary to wait for the seventh; or if it does not happen, it happens more by reason of the time in which nature was able to work longer than by the inciting of the moon. 

Furthermore, a **burning fever** <term>causon: a severe, acute fever associated with yellow bile</term> whose choleric material is mostly situated in the very thin areas near the heart, is scarcely terminated before the seventh, even if it can be by sweat. Since, therefore, jaundice happens from a thicker material of sweat than choler (according to **Isaac** [Israeli] even next to the blood), it cannot be terminated for the better before the seventh. Because of which it is necessary to reach a crisis on at least the seventh, ninth, eleventh, or fourteenth, since a longer time then intervenes in which nature can perfect the digestion, and a similar incitement of the moon often intervenes. 

For if it [jaundice] supervenes before the seventh, it is evil. Because according to Galen, it happens from an appearance or obstruction of the **liver** <note>original: "epatis"</note>, which is subtle. On the seventh or after, it is not simply praiseworthy if the right **hypochondrium** <note>the upper region of the abdomen</note> does not become hard according to the ancients. This can happen from an obstruction and a hard appearance when it does not happen immediately. For fevers are judged in those same days according to the number from which men escape and from which they perish, in the third book of the *Prognostics*.

Jaundice supervenes either because of a symptom of the liver or because nature, attempting to expel the choler through the skin, ultimately cannot, as is accustomed in appearances, with everything returning to the Aphorisms in which it is hinted that the truth is contained. ...as has already been seen. Regarding the other point, it must be said that the termination of **apoplexy** <term>apoplexy: a sudden loss of consciousness, similar to a stroke</term> into **paralysis** <note>original: "palisim"</note> is likewise bad for some, while for others it is good. It is not similar because nature is more troubled by the quantity of the matter in apoplexy than by its sharpness; hence, it forces a **crisis** <term>crisis: the turning point of a disease</term> to happen before its time, and thus it remains imperfect. Similarly, nature is more troubled by the matter of the various **poxes** <note>original: "variorum," likely referring to smallpox or similar eruptive diseases</note>; they even arise from the boiling and corruption of the blood, whose crisis nature usually receives on the fourth day, since it moves continuously. Also, nature is accustomed to expel the matter of this disease to the skin continuously, but it does not do so with the **choler** <term>choler: yellow bile, one of the four bodily humors</term> that induces jaundice, even though it follows the other paths of the critical days. 

To the other point, it should be said that the matter appeared to have more suitable paths through the belly and intestines than toward the skin. And as a confirmation, it must be said that the matter producing sweat is not the same as that producing jaundice, since the matter of jaundice is more subtle than that of sweat. For what pure thing mixes with choler in sweat, given the watery and subtle nature of the blood mass? To the other point, it must be said that jaundice acting as a crisis cannot appear favorably before the seventh day, as has been shown. However, according to **Galen** <note>the famous Greek physician whose works dominated medieval medicine</note>, it is possible for it to arrive soon after an obstruction or a warm swelling; but there is doubt concerning the former, not the latter. 

Regarding the other part, it must be said that jaundice is not properly placed under a "crisis of permutation" <note>a change in the state of the disease</note> but rather under one of "evacuation." For in both cases, just as sweat is expelled through the pores, so is the choler; and because it is thicker and colored with a formal hue, a small amount of it tints the skin, just as a little saffron colors a large part when it is dissolved. That this has the character of a crisis is suggested by the fourth [book of the] *Aphorisms*. Regarding the types of "permutation," there are those that do not lead to an exit or eruption, but instead cause a twisting, a spasm, a softening, or pain in the hips, back, testicles, and knees, as well as jaundice, elephantiasis, and varicose veins. For that is properly called a crisis of permutation in which eruptions are formed, such as **carbuncles** <term>carbuncle: a severe abscess or cluster of boils</term>, white "dubellet" <unclear>dubellet</unclear>, "ants" <note>original: "formica," a term for a creeping skin eruption like herpes</note>, **erysipelas** <term>erysipelas: a bacterial skin infection characterized by large red patches</term>, Saint Anthony's fire, poxes, and similar ulcers. Thus, one type is properly a crisis of permutation, and the other is improper, and some are mentioned in another way.

## DIFFERENCE LXXIX.

### That a small head is better than a large one

This is shown from the 30th book of the *Problems* <note>referring to Aristotle's "Problems"</note>, which suggests this wisdom. Again, according to the *Topics*: if the premise is in the premise, then the opposite is in the opposite. Small and large heads are opposites. But a large head is a bad sign in a kingdom; therefore, a small one will sometimes be good. Furthermore, the origin of things born upon them testifies to this; for the eyes originate from the head, and a small eye <note>original: "pug," likely pugillus or a similar term for small/fist-sized</note> is also praised there. But because you might say the similarity of the origins to the principal parts does not hold, it must be shown that this is valid in all principal parts, such as the heart. Its smallness is praised in the third book of *On the Parts [of Animals]*, for the **spirit** <term>spirit: the vital force or "pneuma" believed to animate the body</term> is unified in a small space and fortified. In a large space, however, it is dispersed and weakened, just as fire shows when contained in a small versus a large dwelling. Hence, animals with larger hearts, such as the deer, the hare, the donkey, and such, are weak and timid. Furthermore, a unified power is stronger than a dispersed version of itself, as **Proclus** <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says: "All power remaining in parts is greater, but when divided it is smaller." This also appears in the seventh book of the *Physics*. In a small brain, the power is unified; in a large one, it is dissolved. 

Additionally, since the brain is the coldest of all the parts of the body according to **Avicenna**, in many cases its great size renders it so cold that the movements and universal actions of the soul are dulled; but they will be fortified by smallness, as the heat is almost stirred up by it. And therefore, we see that those with large heads are dull, senseless, and full of catarrhs and colds. This is confirmed because, since the brain is cold and moist, and the other parts of the head are cold and dry, earthy, and heavy, their mass will pull the whole body downward. This is contrary to the natural position of man, since he is an animal of upright stature, standing upward in the universe—which is the "fifth difference" <note>referring to man's unique upright orientation compared to other animals</note>.

<margin>A small head is [better].</margin>
Therefore, a small head is more praiseworthy for operations—especially human ones—than a large one. To this, the contrary is often presented to us by the senses. This is still the opinion of **Galen** <note>original: "integni," likely referring to Galen's "Tegni" or Art of Medicine</note> and other physicians who follow him. Furthermore, a broad chest is praised, while its opposite is criticized. But this occurs when the head is large, since the brain is then made large. For the skull is proportioned to the head; if it is large, the nape of the neck will be large, the nerves and vertebrae great, and universally the whole body.

<margin>Head.</margin>
Furthermore, a large head is like a "habit" <note>original: "habitus," meaning a positive possession or state</note>, while a small one is like a "privation." Since one of the opposites has the nature of a habit and the other of a privation, and a habit is judged more perfect than a privation, a large head is therefore more praiseworthy than a small one.

<margin>Brain.</margin>
Regarding this, it must first be known that the head is a divine member situated in the superior parts of the body, distinguished by all powers. That it is something divine is indicated in the 34th *Problem*: "Among the three locations—the head, the chest, and the lower belly—the head is the most divine." Since its inhabitant is the soul, as stated in the first book of *On the Health of the State*: "The brain is a certain rational house of the soul," which was also touched upon in the 24th Difference. It is located in the upper part because "upward" in us is "upward" simply and in the universe, both because of our great heat (for man is the warmest of animals, according to the 4th *Problem*) and because of its parts. For its upper parts are small at the end or large, so that it may be in its proper order at the end—namely, for the contemplation of higher things. Other animals, however, have a lowered countenance (the "fifth difference") along with many other distinctions.

<margin>Essential parts of the head.</margin>
The head is composed of many parts according to **Aristotle**. Indeed, the essential parts of the head and those that follow them are eleven: namely, the hair, the skin, the flesh, the **pericranium** <note>the membrane covering the skull</note>, the skull, the hard membrane called the **dura mater**, the subtle membrane called the **pia mater** (or the "secundina"), the substance of the brain with its **ventricles** <term>ventricles: the cavities within the brain</term> and the things located in them...
