...with spirits, there are two membranes <note>original: "panniculi," likely referring to the dura mater and pia mater</note>, the **wonderful net** <term>wonderful net: the "rete mirabile," a complex of blood vessels at the base of the brain once thought to refine "animal spirits"</term>, and the bone that is the base of the brain. Within this, many distinct powers are established, such as the **motive power** <note>the ability to initiate movement</note>, which is perfected through the muscles and the heart; and the **sensitive power**, which is twofold. First is the external type, namely the five senses, four of which are located in the head: sight, hearing, smell, and taste; and likewise touch, although it is diffused through every part of the sensible body. According to **Aristotle**, touch is centered in the heart <note>Aristotle famously believed the heart, not the brain, was the seat of intelligence and sensation</note>, though a distinction is made in the twenty-fourth chapter: the organ of every sense is known except for touch. For touch itself is common to the whole body, as stated in the fourth book of *On Accidents*.

¶ A more divine, internal power is located in its three **ventricles** <term>ventricles: cavities in the brain where medieval scholars believed the soul's faculties—like imagination and memory—resided</term>: namely **imagination**, **thought**, and **memory**; as well as **estimation**, **reminiscence**, and the **intellect**, which operates above these others and is situated as their subject. Through these mediating powers, man is mostly joined to celestial things, receiving their marvelous impressions. Regarding the shapes of the head, in the ninth book of *The Utility of the Parts* under the authority of **Hippocrates**, there are four. The first is the natural shape, which is taught to be imagined in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Ars Medica," a standard medical textbook</note>: it is like a wax sphere that has been lightly compressed by the hands. In this shape, the front is somewhat elongated and flat, the back is bulging or "gibbous," and the sides are flat and straight. There are three unnatural shapes: the first simple one is where the prominence of the frontal crown is diminished; the second is where the rear or "laudable" part is depressed; the third is a composite where both are diminished. The fourth shape cannot exist while life remains: namely, where the dimension from right to left is greater than from front to back.

<margin>Note</margin> However, in a certain monstrous infant and another nearly similar to it, I measured the distance from temple to temple to be greater than from the back of the head to the forehead. Thus, it seemed that this fourth shape of the head was held as unnatural. But such monsters are rare and, as it were, not viable for life. Or, perhaps in these cases, the distance from right to left did not so greatly exceed that of front to back as to be impossible. This should be understood according to the discourse of **Hippocrates** regarding the four shapes. Furthermore, the neck, the nerves, and those things arising from the head, as well as its shape, must be observed; for when these are "laudable" <note>well-formed or healthy</note>, they add to its perfection, but when "unlaudable," they diminish it. Whether the head be large or small—as stated in the third book of the *Prima* <note>Avicenna's Canon of Medicine</note>—if there is a scarcity of matter in the head but the primary formative power is strong, it will be of good form. It is less of an evil than when a bad shape is joined to smallness in a creature, which signifies a weakness of power. Finally, since the operation depends on quantity—for "large" and "small" seem to involve a certain relation in the categories—it is necessary to establish a medium to which this refers. This head shall be called "commensurate." I understand such a head to be one that, in a well-proportioned man, is balanced with the other parts. Large and small are determined by their deviation from this equality.

---

Supposing all other parts are consistent according to the canon of complexions, it is debated in the second book—which must be observed in all things—whether a large or a small brain is worse or better for human actions. Regarding the second point, it should be known that I have not yet seen any writers who did not pass over this question, omitting the apparent contradiction between **Galen** and **Aristotle**, which is the primary cause of difficulty here. Among those who do speak, some "dream" <note>the author's way of saying "falsely claim"</note> that **Avicenna** wanted a small head to be good for moral virtues and matters of prudence. They claim **Aristotle** suggests here that among animals, man is the most prudent, yet possesses a head that is small—which they interpret as meaning a small head is excellent for intellectual virtues. They affirm that **Galen** intends the same, pointing to women, who, despite having small heads compared to men, are more prudent and shrewd than men. 

But these people neither interpret the mind of **Aristotle** correctly, nor do they speak the truth, since the opposite is actually true. They do not know the mind of **Aristotle**, who in the fourth book of *On the Parts of Animals* not only praises a small head for moral virtues, but indeed for intellectual ones, saying that the substance of man is divine. The most divine work is to understand and to be wise, which comes to him because he does not have weight and mass in the upper part of his body. For his head, compared to others, is without flesh, as stated in *On the Parts*. Furthermore, experience shows that some with small heads—influenced by **Mercury** <note>in astrology, Mercury governs the intellect and communication</note>—possess a sufficiently sharp genius for speculation. However, they are inept and headstrong in matters of moral virtue. The reason for this defect is apparent: the spirits of speculation require a more vehement movement and a more intense gathering to perceive the subtleties in nature. But for moral virtues, the spirits must be quiet, with discerning foresight, and slow enough to perceive everything as it occurs. In morals and moral acts, many contingent diversities occur. 

The evidence they bring concerning women is also invalid. For the virtue of reason—which strikes a middle path between extremes—is not in them. They do not do what they do out of **prudence**, which is the "right reason of things to be done," but rather they operate more out of a certain instinct prone to evil. 

<margin>Because women's pity excludes [them from the argument]</margin> 

This is apparent because subtle craftiness and ingenuity occur to them suddenly; but they never act through a meditative middle path, since they participate in none of the goodness of men except for pity, as stated in the eighth book of *Histories*. But these virtues are more present in men.

¶ The great masters, **Aristotle** and **Galen**, were apparently opposed on this question. For **Aristotle**, asking why man is the most prudent of animals, says in solution: Is it because he has a small head in proportion to his body? Having posed the question more for the sake of inquiry, he adds the truer reason: or is it because man is unequally the smallest...

For because of this, those with a small head and such types are more prudent than those who have a large head. **Galen**, however, appearing to hold the opposite view, says that a small head is a specific sign of a poor composition of the brain; he says that other later physicians simply accept this discourse. One way is by reason of capacity, such as the container or the skull; and such smallness is necessarily criticized, since the brain follows it by being small and narrow. Indeed, the largeness of this [the skull] is not entirely praised, since it can sometimes occur without the strength of virtue <note>original: "virtutis," meaning the functional power or "faculty" of the organ</note>. Regarding this type of largeness and smallness, **Galen** and all other physicians hold a common discourse. The detestation of this [small skull size] appears in all behaviors and actions. 

There is another smallness and largeness of the head considered by reason of having little flesh or much mass existing in a circle upon the skull, and especially in the anterior <note>front</note> parts. In other animals which are "lower," the upper parts are large and the lower parts small. In humans, and especially adults, the opposite occurs, whereas in children the upper parts are large and the lower parts small; because of this, they crawl but are not able to walk. Children are jaw-heavy. This is not only present in quadrupeds, but also in the kinds of birds and fish, and all things having blood are jaw-heavy. And he concludes from this that all animals are less prudent than humans.

<margin>In the first age [of life].</margin>

From this, for instance, because it [the human head] does not participate less in weight, it is carried downwards. **Aristotle** concludes that the head, consisting of itself without [excess] flesh in comparison to others, belongs to a body that stands upright and participates in the divine substance of others through prudence and intellect alone. This is also proven by reason: that head which dulls operations and eventually corrupts them is worse than its opposite. Such is the head large with a mass of fleshiness, which, with a certain weight, forces its own position to incline in opposition to itself, as if downward. Furthermore, by the mass of fleshiness and moisture, the spirits of the brain are softened, and thus they acquire slower movements. Also, the animal spirits, lacking luminosity, are overshadowed by the moisture and evaporation which ascends in great quantity into such a head. 

But a small head, by the smallness of its container <note>the skull</note>, is bad in itself and worse than a large one that has exceeded the measured proportion. For that head is worse which is created with a scarcity of matter and weakness of virtue, or which has one of these; such a head is [too] small. **Galen** says it is not so with a large one. Again, that head which makes the whole body small and weak is worse than its opposite; such is the small head, and not the large one. For if the head is small, the brain is small, according to **Haly Abbas**, since the brain is proportional to the skull. And if the brain is small, the spinal cord <term>spinal cord: "nucha," a term used in medieval medicine for the spinal marrow</term> is rendered small, and eventually the nerves and the vertebrae are similarly small, and the whole chest is entirely nervous and bony, no matter how much the heart strives to work to the contrary. For it [the heart] cannot cause the body to be as large as it would be if the head had been large first. With these parts thus diminished, the whole body will be unprotected. It also follows that with a small brain, the ventricles <note>cavities in the brain</note> are diminished, which leads to a narrowing of the spirits and sudden, disordered movement. For when subtle things are compressed, they acquire a rapid motion, as is seen in water and air. But from the movement of the spirit, they become overheated, and from the narrowing, they are rendered dark. For subtle and distinct things, when they are narrowed, acquire a certain darkness; and when they become dark, they depart from their own nature as "animal" spirits, since the spirit is either light or retains the form of light.

<margin>Spirit is Light.</margin>

In the fourth [book] of *On the Soul* by **Aristotle**, it is said that once this happens, the operations of the head are rendered imperfect; these defects will not be present in a large brain in the same way. Again, that which is placed opposite a more noble and stronger member, so that it may temper it by resisting it, ought to be of sufficient quantity. This is the brain; for it makes the heat and fervor in the heart well-tempered... [it is placed] in opposition to it, as the coldest of all members, so that it might restrain it in its frenzy. And rightly so, because nature is devised [to balance] the excess of each thing there. But a small brain cannot temper this, and therefore we see those having small heads [by smallness of capacity] to be unstable, dull-witted, and ecstatic <note>mad or prone to fits</note>. It is thus proven that a small head is worse than a large one, and more so than one of measured size. For in [the large head] there is perhaps a threefold virtue <note>power</note> by which, for instance, in the intellectual powers, it could be more perfect than a measured one; for nothing prohibits a body that has fallen away from smallness from having certain actions more perfect than a temperate one.

As for the acts of the body, such as strength, I have perceived that those with smaller heads are stronger, especially with a broad chest. This is shown by brute animals, which, having little brain matter, are robust; nor are their nerves softened by a mass of the same [brain matter], as is clear in the horse. ...it appeared necessary to say. Regarding the other point, it must be said that that proportion is verified in those things which are truly opposite. For a large head [signifies] a multitude of matter, while a small head [signifies] the vigor of virtue <note>original: "virtutis," referring to the functional power or "faculty" of the organ</note>; these are opposed by a defect. Since, according to the tenth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle's work on the nature of existence</note>, the nature of contraries involves the greatest distance. However, a large head is not opposed to a small one simply by a weakness of virtue and a mass of matter, where either is caused by scarcity or weakness, since both [extremes] are bad.

<margin>No.</margin>
For opposition is taken from the form, not from the matter. Just as health and sickness in every triple nature (as noted in Difference 65) are directly opposed. And therefore **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician</note> says that **Galen**, not by dismissing the idea but by moving his own argument, suggests that a large head might be a good sign just as a small one is a bad sign; rather, he says with a qualification that a large head is not necessarily a sign of a good composition. 

Regarding the other point, it must be said that the situation is not the same for the branches as it is for the principal part everywhere, nor for the eye as it is for the brain. Wherefore **Haly** made a distinction between **Galen’s** discourse on the eyes and his discourse on the brain. For **Galen** criticized a small brain regardless of whatever form it was made in, but he did not criticize small eyes in every disposition. The cause for criticizing smallness was touched on before: for the brain is the root and principle of others, such as the <term>nuchae</term> <note>the spinal cord</note> of the nerves and the <term>spondilium</term> <note>the vertebrae</note>, and it is the source of the "animal spirit" <note>the vital force responsible for sensation and movement</note>. The eyes, however, are branches and not roots; also, the spirits of the eyes are subtler and clearer than those of the brain, and more exposed to the outside. Therefore, so that they would not be dispersed and dissolved, it was good for them to be sufficiently placed in a narrower location. 

Regarding the confirmation of this, it must be said in two ways: either that a small heart is not praised at all in stronger animals—wherefore in the third book [chapter] 11, as if **Aristotle** were opposing this, he says: "Animals that are most bold are those that possess a large heart." But it must be explained by **Aristotle** that every bold animal is of a larger heart the bolder it is (from the 13th book of *On Animals*). This is apparent, for **Aristotle** adds that in larger cavities, the spirit is more abundant and grows stronger. And therefore, none of those animals which have large cavities and veins are "fat" in terms of flesh. 

Or it must be said that there is still no comparison between the heart and the brain, although the heart is the most principal of the members. This is because the heart is in violent motion; the spirits in it are hot and boiling, and they are the principles of the others. Wherefore it was necessary for them to be contained in a very confined place, lest they be weakened and dispersed by its width, being unable to heat and radiate perfectly if the heart were large—just as a small fire cannot heat a large house. In the brain, however, it is different, because its spirits are not in such motion and agitation; they are also mildly warm, which is why they are not consumed in their dissolution, being tempered by its coldness. 

Or it must be said that perhaps formally the brain—apparently according to the physicians—has more origins <note>meaning more branching nerves or connections</note> than the heart. And therefore, it was necessary for it to be proportionally larger than the heart so that it could perfectly temper the heart’s heat. For there are two members in us which are largest in comparison to others: namely, the brain and the liver, according to **Aristotle** in *On the Parts of Animals*. 

Similarly, it appeared how this should be explained here. Regarding the other point, it must be said that the unification of things is twofold: one is "virtuous," when operations are made stronger, as when the ranks in an army are unified in a measured way, or fire in a hearth. The other is "vicious," ultimately destructive to the operations and the subjects, as when it is constricted so much that it loses its own action, or fire is smothered by a covering. This latter kind exists in a small head, but not the first kind, which exists in a well-proportioned or considerably large head. 

To the other point, **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a 10th-century physician and philosopher</note> responds in his *Universal Diets* that the brain is hot and moist, and therefore it does not dull things in the way the heart's heat is said to. Or, because I do not hold this view (Difference 24), it must be said that although the brain may dull the heart's excessive heat, this is not harmful to actions, as a small brain would be, being unable to restrain the heart's heat. For a large brain is heated by the blood of the arteries passed through the <term>rete mirabili</term> <note>original: "wonderful net," a complex system of blood vessels at the base of the brain</note>, and by the spirits and their motion, and by the vapors carried upward, and by those things encountered from the outside, so that it does not excessively reduce the heat of the heart. For the brain, according to **Aristotle**, is only cold. Nor is there yet a weight added to this head which would make it inclined to fall, since it is continually overheated and dried out as age advances. And let the arguments induced for the other side be admitted insofar as they remain for a small head by reason of its smallness of capacity or containment, and not by its mass of fleshiness or burtensome bone.

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the physiology of the heart and the arteries. The previous page discussed the proportions of the brain and heart; here, the author explores whether the heart and arteries expand and contract in unison or in opposition, reconciling the views of Galen and Haly Abbas.</meta>

It is natural since it stands from an intrinsic principle. Such a movement is unique and uniform; for the movements of nature are ordered, according to the book *On Crises* <note>original: "de creticis," referring to Galen's *De diebus decretoriis*</note>, which the movement of automata <note>self-moving machines or mechanical puppets used as a metaphor for biological systems</note> shows. In the same place, by the dilation of the heart, the natural heat of the body is vented. If, however, the arteries were then constricted, they would not draw in what must be led out from the heart, but they would instead expel it, so that the innate heat could not be vented. Furthermore, it is the same thing that arises from the same source and end. But the pulsative power is one and the same and exists for this same end: namely, it is ordered for the cooling of the heat of the heart and arteries. Thus, when the heart is dilated, the arteries are dilated at the same time, and by its constriction, they are constricted. 

The opposite of this, truly, is shown by the sensible sign of incision <note>referring to evidence found during dissection</note>. Also, in the first part of the *First Power* <note>likely referring to Galen's *On the Natural Faculties*</note>, the vital power simultaneously dilates and constricts; but this could not be unless it were according to different parts, since contraries cannot be joined in the same thing at the same time. Furthermore, when the heart is dilated, it is shortened while being expanded on all sides, as the sixth book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts* shows regarding its inflation. When this happens, it is necessary that the same thing follows for the arteries since they are contiguous to it; because of which it is necessary for them to be elongated, which results in their narrowing. Therefore, from the dilation of the heart follows the constriction of the arteries, and from its constriction follows their dilation, and vice versa. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known what the heart is (as noted in Difference 41) and what an artery is (Difference 36). Now, dilation is the local expansion of a part made from the center toward the circumference, just as when a bellows draws in air; constriction, truly, is the opposite. For the movement occurs from the extremities toward the center, so much so that the ends of the boundaries almost meet each other, just as when air is pushed out of a bellows, as seen in the following difference. 

Know also that this sought-after truth is verified while the animal remains in its natural disposition, according to **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas</note>. He wished his opinion on this to be verified while the body remains in a state of health, or in that state in which sickness does not change the disposition of the arteries. For when there is an aposteme <note>a swelling or abscess</note> near the arteries, their dilation and constriction will be faster and thicker than those of the heart. Indeed, this also applies to the arteries of the genitals when one is prepared for the act of intercourse. 

Regarding the second point, it must be known that **Galen** seems to contradict himself on this difference. For he says in his *Introductory Book on the Pulse* <note>original: "ad teucrum," likely a corruption of *Ad Tyrones*</note>: "All arteries indeed pulse at the same time and alternately with each other and the heart, so that from one of them a similar conclusion and argument can be made about all." In *On the Utility of the Pulse*: "The arteries move after the likeness of the heart." Whence in the seventh book of the *Theoretical Medicine*: "The heart and the pulsatile veins <note>technical term for arteries in this context</note> move with one movement in every way at one time; the movement of one is equal to the other, nor does one movement precede another in all conditions, so much so that from one of them knowledge may be grasped for all by comparison." **Haly** also expresses this more clearly.

<margin>
Dilation
Constriction
</margin>

When the heart is dilated, all the arteries of the body are dilated simultaneously; and when it is constricted, they are all constricted simultaneously. **Galen** held the opposite view in his *Compendium of Pulses* and in the fourth book of the *Theoretical Medicine*, as will be shown hereafter. And the truth of this discord will be shown in the third part of what is to be said. Some, wishing to smooth over this contradiction, said that when the heart is dilated, the arteries are dilated, and when constricted, they are constricted, [only] according to judgment and the most sensible perception, but not according to intellectual understanding; because through the dilation of the heart, the dilation of the artery is known, and vice versa. This is confirmed by that aforementioned passage of **Galen**, "so that from one of them," etc. But it must be said that although they appear to move thus, **Galen** does not correctly explain his mind here, since on this matter, as will appear, he held a double opinion. 

Regarding the third point, let it first be shown from the *Introduction to Pulses* that when the heart is dilated, the arteries are constricted, and upon its constriction, they are dilated. And secondly, let it be confirmed by reason. And thirdly, let it be addressed by the authorities previously mentioned to the contrary. 

<margin>
How the
pulse occurs
</margin>

The pulse, according to **Galen**, occurs when the heart has drawn the spirit <note>original: *spiritum*, referring to 'pneuma' or vital air</note> from the lung; for first, when it receives it into its left ventricle, it eventually grants it to the arteries. For it happens that when the heart is emptied and the arteries are filled, the pulse or diastole <note>term for the expansion of the artery</note> occurs; but when the arteries are emptied, systole <note>term for the contraction of the artery</note> occurs. For the pulse consists of diastole and systole. Then, removing the false estimation by which one might think the heart and arteries pulse together, he adds that because the heart and arteries seem to perform the pulse or diastole at the same time, almost everyone reckons that the pulse or diastole occurs with both heart and arteries filled or dilated; I wish to expose their error. For it is manifest that the heart and arteries cause the pulse at unequal times, because it happens when the arteries are filled but the heart is emptied. 

In the declaration of which I intended to refer to anatomy; however, lest I seem envious, I will represent it in a few words. For the heart is of a pyramidal shape, whose broad part, in which are the mouths of its ventricles, is joined to the lung, so that in the middle of it lie four small flaps [valves], and a fifth, like a cushion. The pointed part of the heart tends both downward and to the left. Therefore, when the heart has drawn the spirit from the lung and has been filled, it tends downward and laterally so that it moves away from the chest quite a bit. But when the spirit drawn in has subsequently collapsed into itself and the heart, having been emptied, returns to its natural shape, returning upward, it then strikes the chest and completes the percussion, and thus collapsing, it constitutes the pulse. Thus, he maintains that when the heart is dilated, the arteries are constricted, and when it is constricted, they are dilated, and vice versa; whence in the first book...

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the physiology of the heart and the arteries. ...the pulse on one side might be of a warm complexion and on the other cold. From this, it is known that the pulse in its <term>diastole</term> <note>dilation or expansion</note> and <term>systole</term> <note>contraction</note> does not follow the manner of the heart’s own approaching and retreating. Rather, it follows the manner of the diastole and systole of the arteries of the body themselves.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that the arteries serve the heart through dilation; for they draw blood from it and air from the outside. Through constriction, however, they expel both the tempered air and the smoky vapor into the surroundings with a resulting difference. The heart also—as is known by touch— 

<margin>The heart has four orifices</margin>

sometimes has four orifices (according to the sixth book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts* <note>original: "de iuumentis"</note>), such as the great vein <note>the vena cava</note>, the arterial vein <note>the pulmonary artery</note>, the greater artery or <term>aorta</term> <note>original: "adorti"</note>, and the venal artery <note>the pulmonary vein</note>. Through two of these it draws in, just as it does through the hollow vein and the venal artery. For this reason, coverings and closing <term>panicles</term> <note>membranous valve flaps; original: "panniculi"</note> were created, which move from the outside to the inside. There are three orifices for the major vein, but only two for the arterial vein. The other two are orifices for emitting from the heart to other parts, such as those of the aorta and the arterial vein. Over each of these are three closing flaps which tend from the inside toward the outside. 

Therefore, when the heart draws in, it is dilated. But if the arteries were dilated at that same time, they would not draw from the heart, thereby hindering the attraction, because it is necessary for them to be constricted to create the proper flow. Similarly, when the heart is constricted, it expels; if the arteries were also constricted at that moment, the heart could not expel anything, since there would be no empty space into which the discharge could be received. It is therefore necessary for the arteries to be constricted if the heart is to assist them. In the same way is the relationship of the arteries to the heart: if, when they constrict to expel, the heart were also constricted, it would not be able to receive what was sent. Similarly, if they are dilated to draw from the heart, then the heart must be constricted; otherwise, they could not pull what is inside it. Since the heart is the strongest of the members, the arteries could not take anything from it if it were also dilated.

Furthermore, from the third book of *On Natural Faculties* <note>original: "naturalium tertio"</note>: when one member expels, the other attracts, as even the mechanical arts show. For when the belly expels <term>chyle</term> <note>the milky fluid of digested food</note>, the <term>mesaraic</term> <note>mesenteric</note> vessels attract it. When the veins push, the liver pulls; and when the veins and heart push, finally the smaller branches of the veins push until it reaches the simple members and the skin, which pulls in such a way that it never expels to another. Therefore, since the arteries are ordered (as touched upon) in service to the heart, and the heart and its actions are prior to them: when the heart expels, the arteries attract. And from the third book of *On Natural Faculties*: at different times, attraction and excretion happen through the same pore, for all things seem to be drawn from everything and distributed to everything, and there is a "confluence and conspiracy" of all things, as noted in the sixth book of *Epidemics* <note>original: "epydimie sexto," a work by Hippocrates</note>. The flesh draws both from the belly within and from the outside. This is shown by the additions situated upon the base of the heart called its **auricles** <note>the "ears" or upper chambers of the heart</note>; for they follow the movement of the heart in opposition:

->when the heart dilates, these are constricted, and vice versa.<-

The art of the physician stands as an imitator of nature. In art, it also happens that when one mechanism expels, another attracts, and so on in succession until the works reach their intended end, as the art of shipbuilding demonstrates. Therefore, when the heart dilates, the arteries are constricted; and when the heart is constricted, the arteries are dilated, and vice versa. 

Regarding the third point, it should be said that **Galen** and **Avicenna** were perhaps of that opinion in their introduction to the pulses and their utility; for as the same author suggests, there was a double opinion on this. One view seems probable and introductory, but not demonstrative and true, since nothing prohibits some things from being more "probable" than certain truths (from the first book of the *Topics* <note>Aristotle's work on logic and probability</note>). This "probable" view was expressed by **Haly Abbas** <note>the Persian physician 'Ali ibn al-'Abbas al-Majusi</note> and **Haly** <note>likely the commentator Haly Rodoham</note>. However, through that introductory series, the theory is better adapted to the opinion that says the arteries and heart pulse alternately, so that an ordered change is heard through the opposite; for instance, when the heart dilates, the arteries are constricted, and so forth, creating a certain contrary containment. He brought forth a similar ambiguous discourse in the third book of *On Natural Faculties*: with the arteries, heart, thorax, and lungs all pulled and stretched alternately, it becomes necessary for what was drawn in before to be cast out afterward.

Regarding the first point, what should be said will soon appear. Regarding the other, what should be said is similarly deceptive; for that empirical evidence of **Galen** stands: when the heart is touched, contraction is felt, but not dilation. For when it is moved into itself, it thickens at the base of the chest and thus meets the touch; but when it is dilated, it extends according to its direction almost straight downwards, so that it is then felt least by the chest. However, one perceives the dilation of the artery's own pulse. 

To the other point, it should be said that it is different for those paths and passages crossing from one part of the heart to the rest compared to those distant from it. Indeed, a healthy understanding of the discourse is the support of this: for the paths that are in the heart are dilated with its dilation, but then those which are along the length of the heart—that is, the arteries—are constricted. This is shown by the action of the arteries according to distance and proximity; for those near the heart draw from it, while those extending to the skin draw from the air outside. Those that occupy the middle draw the more subtle part of the blood from the mouths of the veins (from the third book of *On Natural Faculties* and the fourth of the *Theorics*). Because of these paths and the association of the ends of the veins and arteries, when an animal is decapitated, no blood is found in the arteries, but only in the heart. You will find all this concerning the utility of the pulses; and therefore the third book of *On Natural Faculties* concludes that nature did not construct these causes in vain.

This downward flow occurs from the arteries into the veins at the third interval because of the downward course of the spirits and blood into the right ventricle of the heart, as if into a citadel from which they originate. For that [ventricle] stands as more worthy than the left, as noted in **Difference 47**. Regarding the other point, it must be said that it is true in those things moved by a generator through the form instilled in them (as stated in the eighth book of <term>the Physics</term> <note>Aristotle’s *Physics*, a foundational text for medieval science</note>), just as light things move upward and heavy things downward. However, this is not the case for those things whose motion is from the soul, especially since the <term>vital power</term> <note>the force believed to sustain life and movement</note> is sufficiently related to the animal nature (as noted in **Difference 57**), since the motion of the soul can act toward opposites. For by this power it happens that light, sharp bile bursts downward, while heavy matter tends upward; and therefore, first and foremost, praise is offered to the better Creator of all things. Regarding the other point, it is said that natural motion is called unique and uniform in respect to the will. "Natural" can also be understood in two ways: either because it arises from some intrinsic principle, as here from the "sprouting" soul being a certain form—for "nature" is spoken of regarding both matter and form in the second book of the *Physics*—or because it comes from a determined, handed-down principle, such as from a generator. In this latter sense, the motion of the heart is not strictly "natural," but rather "animal" <note>meaning "animated" or "from the soul"</note>, per **Difference 57**. In this motion, even if diversity is seen, it is nonetheless fixed and reduced to a single order. Hence, although it has been said that the vital power constricts and dilates at the same time, that same holy period <note>the rhythm of the heartbeat</note> preserves it entirely. For although the motion of <term>automata</term> <note>self-moving machines, often used as a metaphor for biological systems</note> is a single primary movement, many things subsequently flow from it according to order, which is what happens in the motion of the heart. Regarding the other point, although the pulsative power is one in common, it is nevertheless different and diverse in its specifics. For power is one in substance according to its genus, yet it has many species, as noted in the second book of the *Aphorisms*. Or it should be said that although the acting power and the end goal are the same, they are not so for the same reason. There are also diverse instruments that serve to vary the operation; for one and the same power works one way or another according to the variety of the instruments. From this it appears that the motion of the heart and arteries is produced by the vital power, and not—as <term>Erasistratus</term> <note>an ancient Greek physician who believed arteries were normally filled with air, not blood</note> wished—as a consequence of emptying, as he stated in his discourse on natural matters in the fourth book of *Theory*. Nor is the motion of the heart and arteries due to the air, in the way that wind and air move. For some physicians have thought this; rather, their motion is due to the attractive power of the drawn-in air, just as the exit and entry of air in a bellows is due to the action of the craftsman. Regarding the other point, it should be said that by the dilation of the heart, the natural heat is <term>ventilated</term> <note>original: "eventat," referring to the cooling or airing out of the heart's innate heat</note> through the "venal artery" <note>the pulmonary vein</note> sent down into the lung. Through the artery called the <term>aorta</term> <note>original: "adorthē"</note>, however, nothing or very little is ventilated, as <term>Galen</term> <note>original: "G."</note> and several others have bound all his arteries regarding the utility of the pulses; and yet life remained with the ventilation of the heart, which difference will appear more fully in what follows. Or, even if it is not ventilated then, it will be so immediately afterward, which is sufficient.

## DIFFERENCE 81.

<margin>It occurs</margin>
That expulsion occurs by the dilation of the arteries, and attraction by their constriction, is shown by this: because it is necessary that what is expelled has an open path. But in dilation, the pores of the arteries are opened, since in that state they expand across their whole diameter. That which is attracted and drawn in, however, requires constriction; for this occurs through it. Furthermore, a body that is stronger and more resistant drives its motion further against one that is weaker and more yielding, rather than allowing itself to be met; but in dilation, blood is driven to every part of it, meeting the air and the rest of the body able to enter. Likewise, since an artery cannot be empty, but air would chiefly enter during dilation when the blood then swells within it, two bodies would then be in the same place, which is impossible due to the resistance of their mutual placement. Similarly, it could not expel by constriction since that action starts from a full state. At that time, however, the artery remains compressed and as if emptied. Again, as they say, expulsion flourishes through moisture, but attraction through dryness; but by dilation, the artery is moistened when blood overflows everywhere. In <margin>Not</margin> constriction, however, it is as if dried out by contrast. Furthermore, the dying breathe their last out of inspiration and respiration; but then dilation must occur, since this is the final movement of the soul, otherwise the spirit could not exhale at the last. Thus, by the dilation of the artery, expulsion occurs, and in constriction, attraction occurs. <margin>Opposite</margin> Almost all physicians feel the **opposite** of this. Also, if something must be attracted, the orifice of the attracted thing must be [open] to the thing that will attract it. This happens in dilation. That which must be expelled needs constriction to be accomplished, as appears in things squeezed out from between the fingers, and as demonstrated by a compressed sponge. For in liquids, they attract when dilated, but when squeezed, they press out what was taken in. Therefore, attraction will be accomplished by dilation, and expulsion by constriction. Regarding the first point, it should be known that respiration is the motive action of the organs of respiration, alternating for the preservation of the animal's natural heat. <margin>Respiration.</margin> Indeed, its effects are twofold: <term>ventilation</term> and <term>cleansing</term>. <margin>Ventilation.</margin> Ventilation is the introduction of cold air through openings or pores. Cleansing is the re-expulsion of the same through them. Dilation is the expansion of that which is dilated across its whole diameter. Constriction is the bringing together of everything into one. Breathing is accomplished in two ways: sometimes through openings subject to the senses, and sometimes through hidden ones. <margin>Expiration.</margin> The first occurs in three ways: either by the mouth or the nostrils, just as those having lungs are more warm and—

...larger [animals], both terrestrial as well as aquatic. For instance, **cetaceans** <note>original: "cetodea"; referring to whales and large sea mammals</note> introduce air through the **trachea** <note>the windpipe</note>, or by gills as fish do, for their heat is well-tempered by the water. Or they breathe by suction, like <term>insects</term> <note>original: "entboã" (entoma); literally "divided" or "segmented" creatures</note>, such as bees and other sounding [creatures], like gadflies and the like, concerning inspiration. For it is said that fish use water in their intake, while the other two types use air.

<margin>Pores.</margin>
That [respiration] which is performed through **pores** invisible to the senses is completed, as they write, at the surface of the arteries and the flesh in many places; for every body, and especially a warm one, is distinguished by insensible openings. This is denoted by sweat and other things that exit the body, which is the primary subject of inquiry regarding this type of respiration. Regarding the second point, it should be known that **Aristotle** <note>original: "Aψ"; a standard abbreviation for Aristoteles</note>, in his work *On Inspiration and Respiration*, seems to omit this mode of respiration as if it were useless, as will appear more clearly later, referring himself only to the three-fold manifest transpiration mentioned before. **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note> also seemed to follow this initially in his work *On the Utility of the Pulse*, proving that the dilation and constriction of the arteries would be of little or no utility; for if all arteries are tied so that no pulsation is perceived, the body loses nothing of voluntary motion or sense, and incurs no harm. But when we are deprived of **breath** <note>original: "ahelitu" (halitus)</note>, death follows immediately. Because of this, he adds that if the pulsating vessels suffer a lesion, no deep harm occurs. It is therefore clear to all men that no utility follows from them [the arteries] when the body is preserved in its health, which seems to be granted, especially when the body is not in a feverish state.

<margin>Note.</margin>
Gradually moving away from this opinion, he thereafter agrees with the other physicians that by the strong heat of a bath, exercise, or other causes, the animal is helped by the breathing of the arteries. He finally says that the arteries, with their orifices touching the skin, "vomit out" and cast forth all the **smoky waste** <note>original: "superfluitalẽ fumosam"; the metabolic "soot" or waste believed to be produced by bodily heat</note> generated in them, and take in a significant part from the surrounding air. 

<margin>ISAAC</margin>
**Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli the Elder, a highly influential 10th-century physician</note> also felt this when he said: "The body exists in inspiration and expiration." For the confluence or "breathing-together" of the whole is through the whole. If respiration through the arteries were considered useless, to what end would they pulse? For they would seem to be idle. Or it must be said that they have a nobler end than the one previously given; for by their motion, the <term>vital spirit</term> <note>the refined substance believed to carry life and heat from the heart to the rest of the body</note> is purified and perfected, and it impels the spirit toward the limbs to bring them life. 

<margin>Another utility of the pulse.</margin>
They also draw blood from the veins, and the veins from the arteries. For the **rarefaction** <note>the thinning or expansion</note> of the arteries occurs alongside the veins to a great degree. This can happen for two reasons: one, that the arteries are bound to neighboring members; the other, that a transmission occurs from the artery to the vein and vice-versa, according to what is contained in them regarding their benefits. From this, utility follows for the veins from the pulse, which takes the place of breath; hence even the <term>natural spirit</term> <note>the spirit associated with nutrition and growth, centered in the liver</note> can become "vital" if it does not reach the heart. By the commonality of these [vessels], the color of the veins is given life. In a twofold way, the color of all members is preserved: one by the respiration of breath, the other by that which overflows from the heart, flowing down from the heart to the members. 

<margin>Note: The Heart</margin>
For the heart is distinguished from other members in two ways: first, because it requires much heat while the others do not; and second, because no heat flows into the heart from elsewhere, but rather heat runs from it to the other members. Because of this, ailments of the heart are ruinous, since the heart is the first to meet all harms coming to the body, and it has no source from which to receive support, since it holds the sovereignty in the animal like a **King in a kingdom**. 

<margin>Timaeus</margin>
**Timaeus** <note>referring to the Platonic dialogue "Timaeus"</note> also, as Aristotle ascribes to him, says that the respiration of the lung happens in this way: When warm, smoky air exits through the mouth, the surrounding exterior air enters through the pores of the flesh into the same place from which that warm air exited the mouth. Because no space can be empty, they undergo <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>original: "antipersista\int im"; the ancient physical theory that as one substance moves, another must immediately move to take its place to prevent a vacuum</note> with one another; thus, as the warm air exits, the exterior air is forced to enter. Then, when that air is warmed and exits again through the mouth, the exterior air is forced to enter through the pores of the flesh. Aristotle, examining this opinion, says that according to this, expiration would have to exist before inspiration. And he argues that nothing expels unless it is first drawn in; just as ventilation must come before cleaning. Furthermore, Timaeus is challenged for thinking that the warm air exiting the mouth returns again into the body and that we do not notice it; for we do not perceive this. Likewise, expired air ought to be "empty" <note>or spent</note>, while inspired air should be cold. Timaeus testified to the opposite. Therefore, Aristotle says that this model is fictional.

There were others speaking of "hidden" breathing, claiming that by the dilation of the arteries, expulsion occurs, and by constriction, attraction occurs—such as **Empedocles**. He says that respiration and expiration happen through certain veins that contain blood, yet are not full of it. These have pores to the exterior air that are smaller than the parts of the body but larger than the parts of air, which is why blood is naturally moved up and down. For when the blood is carried downward, air flows in and respiration is completed. But when it tends upward, the air is cast out and expiration occurs. To demonstrate this, he compares it to what happens in <term>clepsydras</term> <note>water-clocks or vessels used to transfer liquids</note>. These are instruments having small holes at the bottom and one large hole at the top, so skillfully constructed that when a beautiful girl closes the upper hole with her hand, the water does not flow out of the lower holes. But when it is not closed, it pours through them. In this way...

<sig>N 3</sig>

He intended that when the **arteries** <note>the pulse-carrying vessels</note> are dilated, then—as if the obstacle were removed—the inward-flowing air is received into them; but when they are constricted, they block the exterior so that the air drawn back is spread through the interior. **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ar."</note> also attacks **Empedocles** <note>a Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher</note> in the same place, reducing his discourse to manifest respiration <note>visible breathing</note>, though it seems here that he rather touched upon **hidden respiration** <note>original: "imanifestā"; the subtle exchange of gases through the skin or tissues</note>. For Aristotle did not deign to say anything concerning hidden respiration, saying that creatures which manifestly breathe do so through the artery <note>the trachea</note>, which indeed seems to be the opposite of what Empedocles felt. For animals breathe by elevating the area, not by blocking it, and they exhale by lowering and compressing it like **bellows** <note>original: "folles"</note>. It is said, however, in these cases that air is taken in at one place and emitted in the same way. But in animals, it is through the same [opening].

And **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note> fell into this opinion, likening the filling to the inflation of blacksmiths' bellows, and not to that of a **wineskin** <note>original: "utrīū"</note> when it is filled with some liquid. Again, if Empedocles understood only that breathing of the nostrils, he erred greatly since this is not the specific [pathway]; rather, it is diffused into the canal of the **tracheal artery** <note>original: "tracee... artarie"; the windpipe</note>, for the nostrils rather fall into the mouth through the palate. This, therefore, is the Aristotelian nullification of Empedocles' discourse. Perhaps his direct intention is not reached because the mode of both types of breathing—namely, the manifest and the hidden—exists almost as the same, as will be shown; and conversely, that which was introduced proceeds. In the same opinion concerning the utility of the pulses, **Archigenes** <note>a Greek physician of the 1st/2nd century</note> is placed as coinciding with Empedocles. For the sect of Archigenes and some before him estimated that the arteries are filled by contraction, but are emptied by dilation.

<margin>Galen</margin>
Of these movements, because at the time of inspiration and the attraction of air, the lips are drawn out and constricted, as well as the opening of the nostrils; whence in the fourth [book] of the *Internal [Discovery]* <note>likely referring to Galen's "De Locis Affectis" or a similar anatomical work</note> on the dilation of the chest, you will find the wings of the nose contracting. To which indeed Galen responds in two ways: either because this investigation and its like should be observed in natural motion, not in violent motion; for in a healthy and properly moved body this does not happen, but only in one that is weak or vehemently exercised. Or it must be said

<margin>saying in</margin>
that it is conceded to them that where this happens, they nevertheless infer nothing from it. For they do not rightly say that the arteries are like the lips and nostrils. But that the pathways of the breath are like the arteries between the nostrils and the lips, which is one of the extremities, and the heart is the other. For the lips and the wings of the nose are seen to be contracted by an accident; for because of the very great dilation within, they are constricted and curved back outward in some way. Know also that the arteries draw out diverse bodies according to how they are diversely situated. For those that terminate in the skin attract air from the outside by dilation, but those that are coupled to the orifices of the veins draw to themselves that which is more subtle of the blood and more capable of evaporation.

---

But whichever ones run near the heart attract from the same, according to the third [book] of *Natural [Faculties]*. Regarding the third point, it should be known that Galen, in [his work] *On Breath* and in many other places, feels that by the dilation of the arteries, the attraction of the same occurs, and by their narrowing, expulsion occurs; whence in the same place: just as when the body is dilated, it attracts to itself that which is closest to its openings, and when it is constricted, it compresses and vomits out what is in it, so also the arteries, when they are dilated, attract to themselves, but when they are constricted, they vomit out what is contained in them. Also in the seventh [book] of the *Theory* <note>The "Theorica" of the *Liber Regalis*</note> with **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician</note>. This is confirmed by the supposition that in dilation and constriction there are three things: the beginning of motion, its middle, and its end. When finally the artery performs **diastole** <note>dilation</note>, it is extended according to every dimension: of length, width, and depth. For every body has three dimensions; whence concerning their differences, it is necessary that a certain quantity of dilation and contraction occurs according to each and every dimension.

<margin>Attraction happens by dilation.</margin>
Also in the fourth [book] of the *Theory*: the dilation of the heart and the arteries is a local motion, moving them from the center toward their extremities and the heads of those terms, just as a blacksmith's bellows moves. But their constriction is the opposite of this; for they are moved from the extremities to the center, so that the heads of their terms meet each other. For in such a dilation, it is spread to the lateral interior parts of the artery, lest a **vacuum** <note>original: "uacuun"</note> intervene, which nature fears above all things, resisting the same in every way; so that even the heavens would rather collapse than allow this. Through indeed insensible **pores**, air is attracted into the artery. This happens because that which is contained in it remains constant. For even as Empedocles said, it remains full, which happens most in the middle and the end of dilation. In which way also, when the lung is dilated because of [lacuna], since it has no proper motion <note>referring to the debate on whether lungs move themselves or are moved by the chest</note>... and finally is expelled by a cough. Conversely, expulsion occurs by constriction, which indeed appears when containing vessels squeeze out liquid, and specifically when, after dilation, the pores are not immediately made constricted but still remain dilated, so that the copious superfluity entering them may be expelled by a more perfect constriction. Furthermore, the arteries serve the heart so that by their dilation, the constriction of the heart occurs, and by their constriction, the dilation [of the heart] occurs, according to the prior difference. Therefore, when the heart is narrowed so that it may expel—for otherwise it would never be squeezed out—so that it may receive, the arteries will be dilated. Similarly, to the dilation of the heart follows attraction, and the constriction of the arteries, and consequently expulsion. Therefore, by the dilation of the arteries, attraction will occur, and by constriction, expulsion. It is nevertheless to be understood that a twofold attraction and expulsion is found existing...

Regarding the fourth point against the first, it must be said that it is true when the movement of the heart and arteries is simultaneous, and both are like a **wineskin** <note>original: "utrīū"; a skin bag used for liquids</note> being inflated, and not like **bellows** <note>original: "folliū"</note>; but it has been shown that they are similar to the action of bellows. Indeed, by that **sophism** <note>a fallacious argument</note>, **Erasistratus** <note>a Greek anatomist and royal physician</note> wished to deny the restoration of nourishment to the parts, since he argued it would lead to one of two impossibilities: either that a vacuum would suddenly be created, or that a continuous overflow would follow that which empties without being refilled. Considering this, **Asclepiades** <note>a Greek physician who practiced in Rome</note> said it was not necessary for only one of two things to happen, but one of three; for besides the two premises, the vessel happens to contract within itself, as noted in the second book of *On Natural Faculties*. Regarding the other point, it must be said that it is true concerning the action and expulsion of the **simple natural virtue** <note>original: "uirtutis simpliciter naturalis"; the innate biological power of the body</note>, which is similar to the inflation of a wineskin; but it is not so, as has been shown, regarding the attraction and expulsion of the **vital virtue** <note>original: "uirtutis uitalis"; the power associated with the heart and spirit</note>, which resembles bellows; rather, it seems to consist somewhat differently. Regarding the other point, it must be said that this final expiration does not happen while the soul or virtue remains within, but rather as it exhales with the spirit, about which this discourse is not concerned, but rather with the former.

# DIFFERENCE LXXXII.

<margin>+</margin>
**T**hat there is only one genus of pulses is shown here. Since the pulse is a movement according to only one genus, the pulse was derived from movement, specifically from the time of movement. Therefore, there is only that one genus of pulse. And by this, it is shown that there is no genus of pulses taken from rest. Furthermore, there seem to be only three: because so many things are to be observed in movement—namely the mover, the mobile, and the magnitude over which the movement occurs—as shown in the *Physics*. The pulse, however, is a movement. And it is supported because there are three things that complete a pulse: **virtue** <note>the driving power</note>, the **instrument** <note>the vessel</note>, and **necessity** <note>the physiological need</note>; therefore, the genus of pulses is only threefold so that it might be in proportion to those. Again, it is shown to be fourfold: because since the pulse is movement, where movement is not found, neither is the pulse; but in a pulse that is large, strong,

---

fast, and thick—along with their opposites and intermediates—movement is found. But in a hard or soft pulse, and in others, it is least found; whence **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note>, noting the difference of pulses in his *Introduction*, says that among the aforementioned genera of pulses, both the hard and the soft occur with the movement of the artery. But the difference of a hard and soft pulse is not properly the movement itself. For a soft or hard body does not need movement to become warm. Furthermore, the genera of pulses which are founded upon the prior ones do not have to be divided against them or placed in their order. But the equal pulse and the unequal—ordered differently and disordered differently—along with that which is founded upon weight, make seven genera; and most especially above whatever four there seem to be. Again, it is gathered that only seven genera of pulses are truly established, since the three that were accustomed to be joined to these seven—one of which is taken from what is in the arteries, namely quantity; the second from the quality of the artery itself; the third from the disposition of the substance of the artery—are not proper to the pulse insofar as it is a pulse, because the pulse insofar as it is a pulse does not exist except through movement and rest.
<margin>Δ</margin>
Which is confirmed because the pulse and **breathing** <note>original: "anbelitus"</note> are proportional, according to the tenth [book]. And the integrity appears. But there are seven genera of breathing in the same place. Furthermore, in the *Introduction to Pulses*, no mention is made of hot and cold, which would have been made if it clearly constituted a genus of pulses; nor of full and empty, or the pulse of weight. Similarly, in the tenth book of the **Almansor** <note>original: "Almanforis"; referring to the medical work by the Persian physician Rhazes</note>, no genus of pulses is placed as being taken from the time of rest. Also, in the first [book], the second ordered differently and disordered differently seem finally to be placed under the unequal. However, it is shown that there are more genera of pulses, either nine or ten; for by the same reason that a genus is established for hard and soft, a genus ought to be established for dry and moist, and composites such as hot and dry, and so on; and a genus for rough and smooth, dense and rare, by reason of the body of the artery and whatever qualities of this sort are tangible differences, and especially the primary and secondary ones, according to the second book of *On Generation and Corruption* and the first of the *Physics*. Similarly, they seem to be diversified according to sight, since sight can perceive the movement of the arteries. Because of this, it is concluded that the genera of pulses exist in multiple numbers, so much so that they are commonly recorded as varied. However, Galen seems to feel the opposite of all these. For when the intellect gathers all these from the sources, it appears to confirm ten genera of pulses. To which the seventh book of the *Theory* <note>likely referring to a standard medical curriculum text</note> and likewise the first and second agree. Regarding the first point, it must be seen what the pulse is, with some explanation of it. But because it is a movement, let it be seen what kind. Regarding the first,
<margin>α β</margin>
it should be known that the pulse is identified in two ways: namely through its **essence** <note>what it is fundamentally</note> and its **accidentals** <note>its observable characteristics</note>, according to the seventh book of the *Theory*. For its essential definition is the **local motion** <note>movement from place to place</note> by which the heart and the pulsatile veins <note>arteries</note> are moved by dilation and reduction for the preservation of heat.

<margin>Pulse</margin>
...natural and vital imbalance; the increase and generation of the **animal spirit** <note>The "spiritus animalis," believed to be the refined substance responsible for nerve function and sensation</note>. First, however, is the second [aspect], which is the movement of the spirit's receptacles, composed of **diastole** and **systole** <note>expansion and contraction</note> to regulate the spirit through the air drawn in. With these two, the explanatory reasoning also coincides. The **pulse** is the motion of the heart and arteries according to **diastole** and **systole** for the cooling of the **innate heat** <note>the fundamental life-warmth of the body</note> and the expulsion of smoky superfluities <note>metabolic waste products compared to soot from a fire</note>. Furthermore, **diastole** and **systole** signify dilation and constriction, or elevation and lowering. The accidental notification of the pulse is a messenger and herald that makes known and narrates hidden things through movements—both contrary and manifest—in theory. 

For they are contraries, because the vital power that causes the pulse simultaneously dilates and constricts in the first [mode] of the first. Furthermore, sometimes they are called "genera" of pulses, sometimes "differences," and occasionally "species." They are called **genera** because they contain species beneath them, as division shows; **differences** because they define and create distinctions; and **species** insofar as they are contained within a higher genus. Indeed, there are subaltern categories which, according to the logician, are species in relation to those above them, but genera in relation to those below. Here, as will appear, "genus" is taken commonly as it is predicated by the logician: of species univocally according to nature, or rather more analogically. For many things lie hidden within genera, as stated in the seventh book of the *Physics* <note>Aristotle's Physics, Book VII</note>. 

It should also be noted that the pulse is primarily the motion of the heart, and consequently of the arteries; hence some explain the pulse to be the motion of the heart and arteries—that is, from the heart into the arteries. This pulsation of the heart and arteries is twofold, as its primary cause is both efficient and final. The **efficient cause** is likewise twofold: the primordial one is the soul in the heart, as it is primarily implanted there. For it perfects the pulse through the mediation of the vital power. The instrumental cause is also twofold: one is simple and incorporeal, such as the **complexion** <note>The balance of the four humors/qualities</note>. For when the soul predominates with the pulsative power, it performs the **diastole**, whereas in its [restorative] state it performs the **systole**. The other is corporeal, such as the artery, with the heart acting as its principle. 

The **final cause** <note>The purpose or goal of the action</note> is fourfold: twofold on the side of dilation and twofold on the side of constriction. Regarding dilation: one [purpose] is so that blood and spirit may be drawn in for the nourishment and protection of the heart; the other is so that the drawn-in air may be tempered. Regarding constriction: one is so that blood and spirit may flow out from the heart into the limbs; the other is so that the "smoky" spirit, which has been overheated, may be expelled. This is accomplished by the constriction of the heart and the dilation of the arteries. For when the heart is constricted, the arteries are dilated, and vice versa <margin>Difference 80</margin>. 

It is also to be known that the pulse, as it is felt, is stronger—whatever may be said in theory—on the right side than on the left...

<margin>150</margin>
<margin>Signs of diastole and systole</margin>
<margin>The arteries are felt more</margin>
...even if the artery originates from the left ventricle of the heart and is near to it. Since in humans the heart inclines slightly to the left (from the first book of *Histories* <note>likely Aristotle's History of Animals</note>), this [strength on the right] is due to the right part of the heart having more forceful ventilation and irradiation; also because of the heat of the liver and gall bladder and the movement situated on the right, supported by the left with the coldness of the spleen there. 

Know also that the arteries in which the pulse is most conveniently felt are those of the hand, because they are not far from the heart, nor buried and hidden deep inside like those of the hip, back, or chest; nor are they winding, where the four fingers cannot be applied, like those behind the ears. It is similarly less laborious to touch these, both because of the ease of offering the hand and because it is not necessary—especially for a woman—to uncover oneself, particularly according to the [customs of] the Spanish, lest she be struck by shame. 

Regarding this, it must be known that motion is twofold, or rather threefold (from the first [book of] *On the Heavens and the World*). One is **straight motion**, which is twofold: toward the center (like heavy things) and away from the center (like light things). The other is **circular motion**, like the motion of the heavens. From these extremes, we can confirm a "middle" motion which can be called **reflexed** <note>original: "reflexus"; a back-and-forth movement</note> or **intercepted** motion, which is the kind of motion the heart has. For although it is commonly said to be similar to circular motion, it is more properly called "reflexed." The heart's motion is not "straight," because straight motion is caused by a generator that is determined toward one part, such as up or down; also, its velocity [increases] as it reaches the end, as it approaches closer to its perfection. But the motion of the heart happens in diverse directions through dilation and constriction; it is composed of a pulse and a pull, being continuous unless something intervening perturbs it, and it eventually slows at the end—for instance, when there is excessive intensity of power and it approaches near to ruin. 

Nor is it "circular," because circular motion occurs over a circular and eternal magnitude, as they say. But it is perhaps a composite of straight and circular, pertaining more to the circular. This is shown by the magnitude in which it occurs—the heart—for it is not purely straight, nor purely round, but round with width and a certain lateral shape. Hence its motion is "reflexed," composed of motion and rest. For as is proven in the eighth book of the *Physics*, it is impossible for one motion to be continued to another unless a complete rest falls between them. 

In one pulse, there are two movements—**diastole** and **systole**—and a rest after the systole which is perceived by few. For it is weighed almost exclusively by the learned and the practiced, such as Galen was. There is also a rest after the systole <note>likely meaning the rest after the full cycle</note> which is understood even by the unlearned. Furthermore, since there are different types of motion—one natural, another violent, and the third <margin>Threefold motion: natural, violent, voluntary</margin> voluntary—it should be known that the movement of the heart is not "violent," since it arises from an internal principle.

For that which is **forced** <note>original: "violentum"; in Aristotelian physics, this refers to motion caused by an external force rather than an object's internal nature</note> is that whose principle is from the outside, where the thing affected contributes no force—that is, it does not imprint any natural inclination. Alternatively, it is that whose motion is from without, by which cause it is compelled to act, as stated in the third book of the *Ethics* and the second of the *Greater Morals* <note>Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Magna Moralia</note>. Yet this is not **voluntary**, because the latter proceeds from a certain mental apprehension, not adhering to a single way or order. Indeed, the voluntary can move toward opposites since it proceeds from a rational power. 

However, the movement of the heart occurs without any deliberation and is fixed to a single order. For although the **vital power** <note>the force responsible for life and breath</note> by itself simultaneously constricts and dilates, it nevertheless keeps this order immediately unharmed. It is therefore **natural**, but not in the same way as the movement which follows the "form" caused by a generator. For a generator, in giving form, gives also a location (as in the fourth book of the *Physics* and *On the Heavens*) and consequently gives motion; for a location is acquired through motion, being given for the sake of that location. And for this reason, such things tend naturally to their own places—light things upward, heavy things downward—and when they are there, they rest as if they had achieved their perfection and end. 

But this movement is natural from the **soul**, which is the "form" of which nature is predicated, more so than of matter (as in the second book of the *Physics*). For in the heart is situated the **pulsative soul**. It moves the heart continuously through the pulse, with a small period of rest intervening. Since every agent here must necessarily fail from continuous action—as is apparent with the eye in seeing, or regarding sound and wakefulness in the first book of *On Sleep and Waking*—similarly, everything that moves must necessarily be supported by something immobile, as explained in the *Movement of Animals*. In the heart, this is the intermediate wall of its two ventricles. In larger animals, there exists a **cartilaginous bone** <note>Aristotle and later medieval anatomists believed large animals like stags or oxen had a small bone in the heart to act as a structural anchor</note> in these parts; for this part rests by itself, even if it is moved by accident. 

From these things it also appears that the movement of an animal downward is agile, since it is doubly natural. However, moving upward is partly natural (from the soul) and partly unnatural (as it goes against the form imprinted by the generator), and therefore an animal is more fatigued by tending upward than downward, unless the motion of the predominant element is governed by another. Hence the thighs labor so much, as noted in the fifth book of the *Problems*.
