There is, however, a certain order of **weight** <note>original: "pondus"; in this context, it refers to the rhythmic proportion or "beat" of the pulse relative to the patient's age</note> and measure in which musical proportions are observed. Of this weight, there is a twofold mode: for one is the pulse of "good weight," called **eurythmic** <note>original: "eurithidis"; from the Greek for "well-rhythmic"</note>, which is well-numbered or measured. Hence, <term>Haly Abbas</term> <note>a famous 10th-century Persian physician</note> says a pulse of good weight and suitable measure is one in which there is a similar relationship and good configuration between the pulse and its "masters" <note>likely referring to the governing factors of the body like age or temperament</note>, such as when a child's pulse is configured to a child’s age. There is also a pulse of "bad weight," or the **arythmic** <note>original: "arithique"</note>, which exists in three forms. First is the <term>pararythmic</term>, which is "near to" the rhythm and measure of a suitable pulse, observing the rhythm of an age close to its own—as when a child's pulse resembles that of a youth. Second is the <term>heterorythmic</term>, which is of a "different" rhythm, as when someone has the rhythm of an age distant from their own—for instance, when a child’s pulse has the weight of an old man's. There is also a third called <term>ecrythmic</term>, which observes the weight of no determined age, as when a child's pulse sometimes runs with the weight of an old man's and then takes on that of a youth, which Aristotle calls a "wild" pulse.

If the pulse is situated above all differences or many of them, this can happen in two ways: either generally, and thus it is **equal** or **unequal**. The unequal is divided into the "absolutely unequal" and the "unequal in a certain respect." It is absolute when all the differences of equality or inequality are observed across the categories of pulses—five, seven, or eight according to Aristotle—and perhaps poorly because of the pulse's weight. It is called equal or unequal **in a certain respect** <note>original: "secundum quid"</note> when one specific difference is observed among others, such as two or three, and so on in various combinations. Or it is situated specifically, and then it is a category of pulses that are "differently ordered" or "differently disordered," which is divided just as its primary category was. For this is placed under the "unequal" as a species under a genus. And know that there are ten categories of pulses ordered in different ways. For some authors place one before the other, while others put them after. But how they are to be ordered will be shown in what follows. 

And again, in all ten categories of pulses, a "middle" or mean state is properly found, except in the pulses of "equal" and "weight." This mean is natural in all cases except in the **strong** and the **weak**. For a strong pulse is natural and tempered, as is every pulse in which the constancy of the **vital power** <note>the "virtus," or the force driving the heart</note> stands out. In others, the equal and well-weighted pulse is considered ordered. And to these differences of pulses are reduced the species of certain "composite" pulses which have specific names, such as <term>caprizans</term> <note>the "goat-leap" pulse, which feels like a double beat where the second part is faster</note>, interrupted, <term>hammer-like</term> <note>original: "martelinus"</note>, wild, <term>wave-like</term> <note>original: "undosus"</note>, <term>formicating</term> <note>original: "formicans"; a pulse that feels like ants crawling</note>, <term>worm-like</term> <note>original: "uermiculosus"</note>, <term>spasmodic</term> <note>original: "spalmosus"</note>, trembling, twisted, cord-like, and similar types. This, therefore, is a sufficient account of pulses taken in a general sense. Regarding the third point, it should be known that "pulse" can be understood in three ways: commonly, properly, and most properly. If taken in the last sense, then 

---

only those categories of pulses should be posited in which the logic of motion is preserved—these are the four appearing in the introduction. These are the categories taken from the **quantity of dimensions**, from the **center of power**, from the **time of motion**, and from the **time of rest**. And further, it is taken "properly" from the time of rest and motion. And "most properly" from the time of motion, since the <term>systole</term> <note>original: "fistoles"; the contraction of the heart</note> and its rest are perceived in pulses by few people, and by researchers only rarely; hence <term>Philotheus</term> <note>a 7th-century Byzantine medical writer</note> says that the "proper" differences of those things which are in motion are **velocity** and **slowness**. 

If, however, it is taken "properly," then the categories of pulses will be founded upon the primary differences mentioned above, such as the equal and unequal pulse and its species, the differently ordered, the differently disordered, and the rhythmic. For in these, for their own sake, the logic of the pulsation is observed. But with "pulse" taken in the common sense—as a physician comes to know it through any kind of motion—there remain the three other mentioned categories of pulses, along with those understood to be reduced to them, which are the **soft**, **hard**, and **full** <note>original: "mollis casus et plenus"</note> with their companions. Thus, although pulses may be infinite in terms of "more or less" (just as temperaments are), physicians have nonetheless reduced them to ten categories, taking "pulse" in the common sense in every way. For the number ten is a certain "perfect" number, as in <term>Problem XV</term> <note>referring to Aristotle's "Problems," specifically Book 15</note>. Yet all of these can be reduced to the category of pulses based on **time** or **motion**, since every plurality is eventually reduced to a unity, which stands as the difference of that entire whole [index 76]. Of this, then, is the pulse understood from the time of motion, since it adheres most closely to motion; and finally, that from the time of rest. For the pulse is a reflected motion composed of a little movement and a rest. 

Next in order is the pulse taken from the **quantity of the diameters**, and finally that which comes from the **tenor of the power**. After that, the pulse of weight, and then the equal and unequal with its diversified species. And finally, the hard, the soft, the full, the empty, the falling, and the rising. 
<margin>According to Aaron [?]</margin>
Concerning the differences of pulses, it is said: It seemed persuasive to some that such a category of composite pulses is one that is received according to another part. For we speak according to the location of the artery and specifically <note>note: lines 40-42 appear to be an interlineated or misplaced observation about diagnostic signs</note> the "ethical" <note>likely referring to "hectic" fevers</note> knowledge of fever is more manifest through heat than it is numbered by other things, through which one knows the quality of color. Regarding the fourth point: as for the first thing to be said, it has already been seen that in the category of pulses taken from the time of motion, it is granted that the nature of pulses is more truly preserved. How should one respond to the other point? It must be said that the **pulse** is commonly understood as a form of "touch," not in the way its types are categorized in a single sense, but rather analogically. To the next point, it must be said that <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: "Ax."; refers to the 11th-century physician Ibn Sina, a primary authority for medieval medicine</note> accepted that the pulse is truly where motion is found in nature, though according to a "before" and "after." Regarding the confirmation, it must be said that pulse and **breathing** <note>original: "ambelitus," a variant of "anhelitus"</note> are not always proportioned in the same way, since the pulse is a simple act of the heart and arteries, whereas breathing is composite. To the other point, it has already appeared that the hot pulse and the cold pulse are placed as a more extensive genus of pulses, since heat is perceived in other places besides the arteries. To the next point, it must be said that either the category of pulses taken from the "time of rest" was omitted there by the scribe, or it is placed under the category of pulses taken from the "time of motion." To the next point, it must be said that ordered, varied, and disordered pulses are types of **unequal pulse**, according to <term>Avicenna</term>. And therefore, those who say the pulse is only what is equal and ordered are in error. However, so that they might lead it to the number **ten**—and especially according to the <term>sysiticias</term> <note>likely "syzygies" or "pairings"</note> or orders of the ten of the **Pythagoreans**—it appears in the first book of the *Metaphysics* that they placed it as the tenth genus. Furthermore, because these are improper differences of the pulse, if any other improper ones are found, they should not be calculated separately under the genera of pulses. Rather, if any knowledge is needed of them, it should be reduced through these categories. To the final point, it must be said that the pulse is not properly perceived by **sight**, since sight only perceives color. If it were perceived, it would be by reason of a "common sensible" <note>a quality like motion or shape perceivable by more than one sense</note>. From which an imperfect knowledge is received. And likewise, it is reduced to the pulse which consists of the quantity of dimensions, such as "height," which sight also perceives in a diminished way; however, it does not comprehend the **systole** <note>original: "fistolem," an OCR error for "systolem," the contraction phase of the heartbeat</note>, whereas a more diligent touch can perceive it in certain states, such as in a pulse that is strong, large, hard, and slow.

## DIFFERENCE LXXXIII.

It is shown that **musical consonance** <note>harmony or pleasing ratios</note> is not perceived in the pulse. First, because for different genera that are not subordinate to one another, there are different species and differences in the categories. But <term>Music</term>—whose role is to observe consonances—and <term>Medicine</term>—which provides knowledge of the pulses—are different genera and are not subordinate, since they seem to have nothing in common; therefore, their species and differences differ and thus cannot be ordered into one. Furthermore, Music is a certain **quantity**, since it is commonly numbered among the mathematical sciences. Medicine, however, is a certain **natural science** concerning qualities—namely health and its opposite. Moreover, those things whose <margin>Ba</margin> substance differs also have distant "passions" <note>properties or attributes</note>, since science is determined by its subject, just as a power is determined by its object (Sixth Difference). The subject of music is **sonorous number**; the subject of medicine is the **healable human body** (previously cited difference). Also, consonance is the concord of dissimilar voices brought into relationship with each other, according to **Boethius** in the first book of *Music*. <margin>Boethius</margin> The pulse, however, is not this, but is the motion of the heart and arteries consisting of **systole** <note>contraction</note> and **diastole** <note>expansion</note>. Therefore, the treatment of them will not be the same. Likewise, music is joined not only to speculation but also to **morality**, according to the first book of Boethius’s *Music*. But medicine is not joined to morality, since it does not deal with the instruction of morals, even if it negotiates something regarding natural matters. Therefore, musical consonance is found in the pulse not at all. Yet many **metric** patterns are found in the pulse. For there, the pulse of infants is "irrational" and proportioned to the rhythm of <term>trochees</term> <note>a long beat followed by a short beat</note>; that of those in their prime to <term>spondees</term> <note>two long beats</note>; and that of the elderly to <term>iambs</term> <note>a short beat followed by a long beat</note> or trochees. Regarding the differences of the pulses, it is written: A **rhythmic pulse** consists of an equal or unequal ratio or proportion. Sometimes it is in an odd ratio. First, when the time of the diastole is equal to the time of the systole. But it is unequal when one time exceeds the other. This happens in two ways: for sometimes it abounds in ways that can be described, and sometimes in ways that cannot be described. And the first happens in two ways: either in a multiple proportion, which is double, triple, or quadruple, or any of those that follow, according to which an "improper proportion" <note>original: "interproportio"</note> exists—such as the <term>diapason</term> <note>the octave</note>, the <term>diapente</term> <note>the fifth</note>, or the double diapason—yet it is not a proportion. But <term>Avicenna</term> in his second book, section eight, says: "You ought to know that the nature of music is found in the pulse." <meta>This page transitions from the medical discussion of the pulse to a foundational treatise on music theory. ...the terms may be explained. And finally, the **monochord** <note>A single-stringed instrument used by medieval theorists to demonstrate mathematical proportions in music.</note> is arranged. Regarding this, it must first be known
<margin>Music</margin>
that **music** is the science of modulating well, or the science of moving well. For anything can be said to be "moved well" if it is moved while preserving the numerical values of the timing and the measurements of the intervals.

According to **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the standard textbook for music theory in the Middle Ages.</note> in the fifth book of his *Music*: Harmony or music is the power and effective faculty that judges the differences in sounds by the operation of the senses. For the senses and reason are, as it were, the instruments of the faculty of harmony. The sense perceives a certain confused thing that is very close to the thing it feels. But **reason** judges and follows the deepest differences. Thus, the sense finds things that are confused and close to the truth, while reason judges them. 

It is as if someone were to draw a circle by hand; the eye itself judges that shape to be a true circle. Reason, however, in no way understands that which is merely an imitation to be the truth. This happens because the sense is focused on matter and perceives the form within it as something flowing, existing, and imperfect. **Intellect**, however, works otherwise. **Guido the monk** <note>Guido d'Arezzo (c. 991–1033), the inventor of modern musical notation.</note> also put forward that music is the distinct movement of voices.

Music is also threefold. One type is **Worldly Music** <note>original: "musica mundana"</note>, existing in the heavens and their structure or the variety of the seasons.
<margin>Worldly</margin>
For musicians say that the harmonic sound in the heaven exists, in the highest and most proper sense according to the **Pythagoreans**, through the motion and contact of the spheres. This sound, however, cannot reach our ears due to the intervening great distance; or, secondly, it is disputed [in other texts]. 

The second type is **Human Music** <note>original: "musica humana"</note>, which is observed in the connection of our **body and soul** and their elements. 
<margin>Human</margin>

The third type is **Instrumental Music** expressed through instruments. Some of these are natural, such as the vocal organs, and
<margin>Artificial</margin>
some are artificial, such as the organ, the **psaltery** <note>A stringed instrument similar to a harp or zither.</note>, and those of that kind. 

Now, as has been touched upon, **consonance** is the concord of different voices brought together into one. **Dissonance**, however, is the harsh and unpleasant striking of two mixed sounds reaching the ear. 

Of this consonance, there is a certain **proportion**, which is the relationship of one to another between any two quantities of the same kind. This proportion is observed in **arithmetic** regarding numbers. In music, which is subordinate to arithmetic, it is observed in sounds. Therefore, for those wishing to know the consonances, it is helpful to first consider the arithmetic proportions. 

There are five of these: three are simple and two are composite; all of them are situated in unequal quantity. 

The first simple one is called the **Multiple** and sub-multiple proportion. 
<margin>Multiple</margin>
It occurs when the larger number contains the smaller number within itself exactly twice, or three times, or four times, and so on. Its types are the **double**, **quadruple**, **sub-double**, **sub-quadruple**, and the rest. 

The second is called **Superparticular**. 
<margin>Superparticular</margin>
This is when the larger number contains the smaller number entirely plus one part of it—either a half (as three is to two, which is called the **sesquialtera** proportion) or a third (as four is to three, which is called the **sesquitertia**), and so on. And similarly, the sub-sesquialtera and sub-sesquitertia. 

The third is called **Superpartient** and sub-superpartient. 
<margin>Superpartient</margin>
This is when the larger number contains the smaller number entirely plus some parts of it. If it contains two parts, it is called the **superbipartient** (as five is to three). If it contains three parts, it is **supertripartient** (as seven is to four). And so on, and conversely in its correlates.

The fourth is the first of the composites, joined from the **Multiple** and the **Superparticular**. 
<margin>Multiple Superparticular</margin>
This is when the larger number contains the smaller number twice or three times, or any number of times, plus one certain part. If it contains it twice and its half, it is called **duple sesquialtera** (as five is to two). If the smaller is contained twice plus a third of it, it is called **duple sesquitertia** (as seven is to three). If three times plus a half part, it is called **triple sesquiquarta**, and so on. 

The fifth is called **Multiple Superpartient**. 
<margin>Multiple Superpartient</margin>
This is when the larger number contains the smaller number entirely more than once, plus some of its parts. If the larger contains the smaller twice plus two of its parts, it is called **duple superbipartient** (as eight is to three). And again, for its correlates, the reverse. 

Note that the last two composite proportions are not assigned to musical consonances, but only the first three simple ones. 
<margin>3</margin>
Of these, the **Multiple** proportion produces the better consonance, and after that the **Superparticular**. 
<margin>2</margin>
The **Superpartient** is excluded from the consonances of harmony by everyone except for **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century mathematician who argued for more complex ratios in music than the Pythagoreans allowed.</note>. 

Finally, it must be said that musical consonances are derived from the aforementioned two or three numerical proportions. Beneath these, six differences of numbers are found: namely, the **epitrita** (or sesquitertia), the **hemiola** (or sesquialtera), the **duple**, the **triple**, the **quadruple**, and the **epogdoa** (or sesquioctave). 

The **epitrita** is when the larger number contains the smaller plus a third part of it (as four stands to three). In four, three is contained plus a third part, which is one. From this numerical difference arises the musical consonance of the **diatessaron** <note>original: "dyatessaron"; the interval of a Fourth.</note>, which means "through four." 

The **hemiola** occurs when the larger number contains the smaller plus its half (as three stands to two). In three, two is contained plus their half, which is one. From this symphony is born the **diapente** <note>original: "dyapente"; the interval of a Fifth.</note>, which is named "through five." 
<margin>Diapente</margin>

The **duple** occurs when the larger of the numbers contains the smaller twice (as four contains two). From this arises the **diapason** <note>original: "dyapason"; the interval of an Octave.</note>, which means "through all"...

...or called the whole. **Triple proportion** also occurs when the larger number contains the smaller number three times, such as three to one. From this, a composite symphony arises called the **diapente-diapason** <note>original: "dyapente dyapason"; this is an interval of a twelfth, combining an octave (diapason) and a fifth (diapente).</note>. There is also **quadruple proportion** when the larger number contains the smaller four times, as four relates to one. From this arises the composite symphony called the **bis-diapason** <note>A double octave.</note>. Thus, some consonances are simple, like the first and second, while others are truly composite, like the last two. The **diapason** <note>The octave.</note>, however, is, as it were, in the middle—simple in name but composite in reality. 

**Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), an astronomer and music theorist who refined the Pythagorean system.</note>, however, added a sixth composite consonance against the opinion of **Pythagoras**, consisting of the **diatesseron** <note>The interval of a fourth.</note> and the **diapason**; and thus it is placed under the "super-particular" proportion. **Boethius** in his fifth book says: **Sesquioctave** <note>original: "Epogdasiu"; the ratio of 9:8.</note> is when the larger number contains the whole smaller number within itself plus its eighth part, as nine relates to eight. For in nine there is eight plus one unit, which is the eighth part of eight. 

From this also arises the sound which is called a **tone**. This is divided into two unequal parts, for it cannot be divided into equal parts, just as vowels cannot. One of these parts, the larger, they called the **major semitone**; the other, the smaller, they called the **minor semitone**, which is called the **diesis** <note>A term for a small melodic interval, often a quarter-tone or a small semitone.</note> by the Pythagoreans. **Verso** <note>Likely referring to a specific authority or "on the other hand."</note> nevertheless asserts the minor semitone is the diesis, which **Plato** called the **limma**. Whence Boethius says in his first book: A tone is never divided into two equal parts. 

To demonstrate this, let the **sesquioctave proportion** be eight and nine. Between these no middle number falls. But if we multiply them by two, they become twice eight (16) and twice nine (18). Between 16 and 18, one number naturally falls: 17. Thus, 16 compared to 18 retains the sesquioctave proportion and therefore the tone. According to this proportion, the middle number 17 does not divide them into equal parts because, compared to 16, it contains the whole and its sixteenth part (the unit). However, if 17 is compared to 18, then 18 will contain it [17] and its seventeenth part. Therefore, 17 does not exceed 16 by the same parts that it is exceeded by 18. Both are called **semitones**. Not because they are exactly half, but "semi" is used to mean it does not reach full integrity. 

Between these, one is called the **major semitone** and the other the **minor semitone**, which relate to each other as 243 to 256 <note>The "Pythagorean limma," the mathematical ratio for a minor semitone.</note>, containing two voices, for example, like the step from *mi*. There is also the **ditone** <note>A major third.</note> arising from two whole tones. And the semitone which arises from non-integers. From these tones and semitones, the musical symphonies are composed. For the **diatesseron** (the fourth), which is the fourth consonance of voices, consists of three intervals—as the marking of the **monochord** <term>monochord: a single-stringed instrument used to measure the mathematical ratios of musical intervals</term> will show—and consists of two tones and a minor (or non-whole) semitone. 

An interval is the distance between a high and a low sound. But the **diapente** (the fifth) is the fifth consonance of voices, consisting of four intervals, three tones, and a minor semitone. The **diapason** (the octave) is the eighth consonance of voices. For one [voice] is repeated from the first seven, through seven intervals, and consists of five tones and two minor semitones. And thus it is said that the diapason consists of the diatesseron and the diapente. This is because the tones and semitones of these two symphonies are collected into one. 

But the **diapente-diapason** is [a consonance] of twelve voices and eleven intervals, and consists of nine tones and a minor semitone. The **bis-diapason** will then be a consonance of sixteen voices and fifteen intervals, and is perfected by twelve tones. The **diatesseron and diapason** <note>The eleventh.</note>, according to Ptolemy, is a consonance established beyond the Pythagoreans; it will be thirteen voices, just as there were seven primary ordered voices. For voices and letters are repeated, just as happens with the days of another week. 

Indeed, of the voices, four are "low" and three are "high." Because of this, it should be known that according to **Pythagoras**, he invented a certain instrument of one string called the **monochord**, in which all musical symphonies are found. By this, the unlearned are first taught to perceive simple voices, so that from there the composite voices of many strings may be more easily understood. 

The first description of this simple [instrument] is set down below. It is a long, four-sided piece of wood, sharpened at both ends like a **spindle** <note>original: "fandois" / "fusi"; likely describing the tapering shape.</note>, hollow inside, over which a string is placed. By its sound, the varieties of voices are easily understood. This is its form in the **double proportion** (or diapason), so that through this, it may be understood in others. Music is not being "taught" here in detail, but only enough is said to clarify the matter at hand. 

The description of the more complex monochord, in which the voices follow with others, is as follows: first, according to the moderns, the Greek letter **Gamma** is inscribed, or the "eight," of which this is the figure: **Γ**. And thereafter, the seven Latin letters are placed in order from the beginning as the "low" notes; therefore they are denoted by larger figures. After these, the aforementioned seven are repeated as the "high" notes; whence they are depicted with smaller characters, in which a double **b** is placed: the first is "round" <note>The "soft" b, which became our flat symbol (♭).</note>, while the other is "square" <note>The "hard" b, which became our natural (♮) and sharp (♯) symbols.</note>. Some also add to the predicted various tetrachords the figures of the "super-high" notes, in which *a* and *b* are similarly repeated. **Boethius**, however, along with the ancients, omitted the Greek Gamma. 

The paradigms of the ten letters of this monochord's extent are:

Or if they are found, they say no one can reach an understanding of them. To whom it must be said—according to the first book of *On Diseases* <note>Likely referring to the Hippocratic or Galenic medical corpus.</note>—that there is no need for good work to be censured by others when they censure themselves, wishing to obtain solace for their own ignorance according to **Priscian** <note>A famous Latin grammarian.</note>. 

In the fourth collection, a discourse on these proportions of **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity, who wrote extensively on the "music of the pulse."</note> is recited, where it is said that if it is as he says, it is marvelous. But it is difficult to grasp these comparisons, because many men grasp them in music because musical notes have a superfluous extension, so that the smaller dimension of them can be understood by example; and it is that which multiplies one part out of thirty-six parts, and this would be a minor **semitone** or perhaps a **diesis** <note>A very small musical interval, smaller than a semitone.</note>. But in **Ptolemy**, **Galen**, and **Aristotle**, after a proportion adding a **fourth**, sensory discernment does not intervene. And it is added that these words belong to another opinion which is only slightly necessary to this one by accident. Aristotle also marvels at this, saying: "I wonder how these proportions can be discerned through the senses." And finally, Galen provides a way by which one might attain these proportions such as: I say that it is easy—that is, possible—for him who is accustomed to the degree of touching and [can recognize] proportionate sounds after he has been given the power of knowing music.

For when one applies their attention entirely to the pulse, they will be able to discern these proportions through the senses. What appears regarding this follows below.

Regarding the third point, it must first be known that musical **consonance** <note>The pleasing harmony produced by specific mathematical ratios.</note> can be found in the pulse. Second, the sequence of this should be explained. **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."; refers to the Persian physician Ibn Sina, whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard university textbook.</note>. Regarding the first part of this, it must be known that **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."; the famous 2nd-century Greek physician.</note> and Avicenna testify that musical harmony can be found in the pulse, as has been introduced. This is confirmed because, as stated, musical consonance is a certain proportion, and this proportion is found in all quantities of every kind.

In the pulse, as they say, it is necessary to designate quantity, especially because one genus of pulses is derived from the quantities of three diameters <note>Medieval physicians measured the pulse in three dimensions: length, width, and depth.</note>. Furthermore, if it is found in these, the primary and principal part will be instrumental, and the secondary will be discovered, since all these things operate through certain organs. But music is primarily and first innate in us, as the human soul demonstrates. For the human soul connects to the body with such a bond, as **Socrates** judged among many others in the *Timaeus* <note>original: "ebimeo"; a corruption of "Timaeo," Plato's dialogue where the soul is described as being composed of musical ratios.</note>. <margin>John of Damascus in the *Aphorisms*, 9</margin> Whence **John of Damascus** says in his *Aphorisms*: "The binding of the body and the soul is made according to the order of a consonant number so that it may persist." He even says that the constitution of the living body, and specifically ours, exists according to the pattern of a consonant number. For this reason, some have posited that the soul is a kind of harmony. <margin>On the Soul, book 1</margin> In the first book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's "De Anima," where he discusses and eventually rejects the theory that the soul is a "harmony."</note>. Because of this, "organic" music <note>The music produced by the body's internal organs.</note> will be within us, even though it depends on the soul. Through the path of cognition and effect, the music of the organs depends on the music of the pulse. In the path of the cause, however, the opposite occurs. Thus, musical harmony is found in the pulse, and similarly in the breath as well.

Finally, someone with a very balanced and sharp sense of touch can arrive at a knowledge of the pulse's consonance. As **Galen** testifies concerning himself, this happened regarding the **systole** <note>The contraction phase of the heartbeat.</note> of the pulse. Although he had not perceived it for a long time, he finally perceived and understood it through continuous practice in feeling the arteries, so that the "gates of the pulses" were then opened to him. <note>original: "primo. secunda."; likely referring to books 1 and 2 of Galen's "De pulsibus."</note> This is also supported by **Haly** <note>Haly Heben Rodan (Ali ibn Ridwan), a commentator on medical texts.</note> in the fourth book of the *Quadripartitum*. For that can be known and finally perceived of which we have a likeness within us, especially since our soul understands by the mediation of a **phantasm** <note>A mental image or representation used in the process of thought.</note>. But we have a likeness of the proportion or consonance of the pulse—

---

namely, musical consonance—as has been shown. Again, that which is perceived by a more certain sense can be known. In this case, it is touch; for where other senses are deceived, touch provides certainty, except perhaps in the variations of the fingers, and especially since we have a more certain sense of touch than other animals. <note>original: "secundo de anima"; Aristotle's "On the Soul," Book 2.</note> For our composition reaches more fully into moderation and temperament. Thus, we can gain this knowledge, even though it may be difficult due to the brief duration of the movement, since the soul perceives nothing without time and the continuity of memory and recollection.

Regarding the second part of this, it must be known that **Avicenna** says there: "The genus that comes from weight" reveals the tenth genus of pulses according to his order, which **Galen** and **Haly Abbas** <note>Another prominent Persian physician.</note> placed as the eighth. He says that the genus of pulses taken from "weight" <note>original: "pondere"; in this context, it refers to the "rhythm" or the ratio between motion and rest in the pulse.</note> is determined by comparing the proportion of the four proportional "times" to each other: namely, the two movements and the two rests. And although the senses cannot discern all of this, it can be done by comparing the proportion of the times of the **diastole** <note>The expansion phase of the heartbeat.</note> to the time between two diastoles, since then three times intervene: the motion toward the **systole**, the rest, and the motion toward the next diastole.

At the most basic level, one compares the time in which there is motion to the time in which there is rest, or vice versa. For motion is perceived more clearly through its opposite, rest, than motion is perceived through motion or rest through rest, since they are opposites and gather more time. Therefore, those who compare the time of motion to motion, and rest to rest, place "chapter within chapter" <note>A metaphor for overlapping or redundant classification.</note>. And this is found in the seventh book of the *Theory* <note>Likely the "Liber Pantegni" or a similar theoretical medical compendium.</note> with Galen; that is, moving from the sensory knowledge of the local pulse into intellectual action. For there are two "chapters" or principles of knowledge: sense and intellect, however much they may be opposites. And although the loss of this [intellectual knowledge] is tolerable and not unsuitable, it is not good or useful because it cannot reach into sense and experience, as the study of medicine requires.

Next, he shows what "weight" or "measure" is, saying it is that in which musical proportions are considered. This appears to be speed and slowness, or density and thinness, primarily by reason of the time in which they consist; consequently, it involves magnitude and smallness, strength and weakness. It is upon these differences that the proportions of the pulses properly seem to be considered. Therefore, since the parts of one pulse—or one pulse itself—according to the aforementioned rule of proportions or consonances, relate to another in four or five main differences: namely, magnitude and smallness, strength...

...and weakness, speed and slowness, density and rarity, or even hardness and softness. Just as four to three constitutes the pulse-consonance of the **fourth** <term>fourth: original Latin *dyatesseron*; a musical interval where the frequency ratio is 4:3</term> related to musical consonance. If indeed they relate as three to two, then there arises the proportion of the **fifth** <term>fifth: original Latin *dyapente*; a musical interval with a 3:2 ratio</term>. But if as four to two, that very proportion is an **octave** <term>octave: original Latin *diapason*; a 2:1 ratio representing the most fundamental consonance</term>, and likewise for other combined proportions.

I proceed, therefore, further into the explanation of **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."; the text uses an abbreviation for the Persian physician Ibn Sina</note>, who, in giving his intention, says: "Know that in the pulse, the nature and power of music is found." He declares this in the equal and unequal pulse, and in the **pulse of weight** <note>original: *pulsu ponderis*; in medieval medicine, "weight" refers to the rhythm or musical meter of the heartbeat</note>, in which the nature of music is most observed. Secondly, he exemplifies the proportions which we can observe in the pulse there. **Galen** <note>original: "Galienus"; the 2nd-century Greek physician whose work on pulses was foundational</note> truly showed this first in the equal and unequal pulse; secondly in the pulse that is unequally ordered and unequally disordered, and in the pulse of weight. And just as he proposes a certain similarity, he says:

> Just as the science of music is perfected from the joining of sounds to one another according to the proportion of the times following them in highness and lowness—which are the differences of the voice—through certain circular paths, now descending with the voice and then raising it, which exist between their strikes. For there they constitute something like circles, beginning from one of the **seven voices** <note>Refers to the seven notes of the medieval musical scale</note> and, passing through the others, they return.

Then, adapting the aforementioned points to the two things proposed, he says it is similar in the pulse. This is because the proportion of the times of the pulses—in which proportion is principally observed in speed and density, and likewise in rarity and slowness—is just like the proportion of musical sounds in such things. Furthermore, the proportion of the dispositions of the pulses in strength and weakness, and in magnitude and **smallness** <note>original: *pūitate*, likely a scribe's error or contraction for *parvitate*</note>, is like the proportion of the joining or composition of musical sounds, through which it happens that sounds vary according to speed, slowness, and so forth.

Next, he also declares this in the pulse of weight and in the diversely ordered and disordered pulse, first positing two parts of the similarity and then adapting them to the proposition. **And the proportion**: he says that just as the time of striking may be long or short, and the quantity of the extension of sounds is sometimes suitably proportional—as in **war trumpets**, or in chambers the **psaltery** and the **viola** <note>The author uses familiar medieval instruments (trumpet, psaltery, and viola) to explain how rhythm and "weight" create harmony or discord</note>—and sometimes unsuitable and disproportionate to the place, like the example given to the contrary. And this relates to the pulse of weight. Similarly, it happens sometimes that the diversities are ordered in five or more things, and sometimes they are unordered, indifferently corrupting the order. This pertains to the diversely ordered and disordered pulse.

Then, with the phrase **And the proportion**, he applies these two parts of the similarity very succinctly and somewhat obscurely, saying: "So the proportion of the disposition of the pulse in strength and weakness, and in quantity, in magnitude and smallness and similar things for both types of pulses (though it speaks of the pulse of weight), happens to be suitable," and so forth. He adds that this emerges from the genus of pulse in which order—or its opposite—is considered, which is why the pulse enters into "weight." For in it, the proper pulse-consonance is preserved because it is taken from the time of movement where quantity is found.

Then, **Galen** expresses the pulse-proportions according to how they are adapted to musical consonances, saying that it seemed to Galen that what can be perceived from the proportions of the pulse of weight is according to one musical proportion called the "proportion of the whole" (that is, the double) and "five," which is called the triple proportion. Explaining this, he adds that this is the double proportion joined to the proportion that adds a half, because it contains a whole and its half. This is the proportion composed of the **fifth and the octave** <note>original: *dyapente dyapason*; a compound interval resulting in a 3:1 ratio (triple)</note>, and is so called because it contains something twice the whole and its half. Thus, when one pulse relates to another in speed and slowness and the other differences mentioned—whether in numbers or voices—as three to one, a proportion similar to the one predicted will coincide in the pulse. And the same must be said for other proportions of pulses in their own way.

The second proportion observed in the pulse is according to the musical proportion called "through the whole," which is the property of the double, and this is the **octave** <note>original: *consonantia dyapason*</note> consonance. It is called "through the whole" or the "mean," since it is terminated in the whole or the perfect, for instance at the end of the **monochord** <note>A single-stringed instrument used for demonstrating the mathematical ratios of musical intervals</note> as in eight. For "all" and "whole" and "perfect" do not differ from one another in kind (according to the first book of *On the Heavens and the World*). It is also named so because it obtains all the voices. In ancient times, as it appeared, **citharas** <note>A type of ancient lyre</note> consisted of eight strings, and because it is constituted of eight voices.

The third proportion considered here is that which is called "**through five**," which adds a half, just as when something contains another whole and its half; as three relates to two. This proportion is called the **fifth** <note>original: *dyapente*</note>, because it terminates in the fifth place of the monochord, obtaining five voices.

Also, the fourth proportion which is said to be found in the pulse is taken according to the proportion which is "**through four**," adding a third part. For it contains a whole and a third part on top of it, just as four relates to three. This is called the **fourth** <note>original: *dyatesseron*</note>, because being consisting of four voices, it falls in the fourth place of the instrument.

There is also a fifth proportion observed in the pulse, which is taken according to the proportion of five, which adds a fourth part, in which proportion five relates to four. Since it has the whole and one part which is its fourth. This proportion is not properly musical, since...

...only five or six extend. <margin>Mö</margin> For the smallest of musical proportions is the **fourth** <term>fourth: *dyatesseron*; a musical interval with a 4:3 ratio</term>. The largest truly is the **double octave** <term>double octave: *bis dyapason*; a 4:1 ratio</term>. Some, however, prevaricating here and being ignorant of the principles of music, think this musical proportion is distinct from the others, even claiming there are seven proportions since they place the **whole tone** <term>whole tone: *dyatonum*; the interval between two notes</term> among them. Then it is added that afterwards, in pulses, no moderate proportion is perceived when a small amount of time intervenes between two comparable distances—such as the proportion of five to six, or seven to six—and so on; it is perceived much less. It is doubted why the musical proportion of the **double octave** <note>original: *bis dyapason*</note> is not numbered by **Avicenna** <note>original: ".A."; the Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> since it can be found in pulses just as it is found in other things. Or perhaps it should be said that such a great distance does not occur between the parts of the pulse. Or perhaps he left a note regarding the **fifth** <note>original: *dyapente*</note> and the **octave** <note>original: *dyapason*</note> approaching it. Thus the truth of this appears difficult to the admirer, since it concerns pulses, the knowledge of which is arduous. <margin>1</margin>
The science of pulses is heavy and difficult, and its recognition is undertaken with great difficulty for a threefold cause. First, because it is not easy to become accustomed to the sensation of the veins so that one can recognize the slight alteration that occurs in the 

<margin>2</margin>
pulse. Second, because it is necessary in a very short time to recognize all ten types of pulses, since one has a relation to the others. 

<margin>3</margin>
Third, because nothing more common is found externally to which the pulse can be compared—as, for example, the pulse can be compared to **urine** <note>original: *urina*</note>. I add a fourth: because the pulse is a motion of a hundredfold variety, and the knowledge of motion is difficult since it is material, potential, not permanent, but successive, as the discourse of **natural philosophy** <note>original: *phisico*</note> shows to the listener. 

Regarding the fourth point, but [returning] to the first, it must be said that some say proportions are taken equivocally here and there—for instance, in music and the pulse. This is false, as seen from what has been said, since it has been shown that at least **human music** <note>original: *musicam humanam*; the medieval concept that the human body's ratios are a form of silent music</note> is found in the pulse. And music is predicated as a genus, either univocally or at least analogically, as being the three particular types of music noted above. Whence it should be said that some species and differences are placed under others, because the proportions of sounds are contained under those that naturally contain the pulse—especially if we wish to observe **human music** in the pulse itself and **instrumental music** <term>instrumental music: *musica organica*; music produced by instruments</term> in sounds, then the former is contained in the latter like a part in the whole. 

If, however, the proportions of pulses are considered as unmanifest, the proportions of sounds are known as something manifest, and thus they are proven to be subject to the proportions of **instrumental music**. Or it can be said that the proportions of pulses were transferred by a certain similarity—by which all things are transferred in the sixth [book] of the *Topics*—from the proportions of instrumental music, which transfer appeared long ago. To another point, it must be said that just as instrumental music concerns the quantity of time, so also does the music observed in the pulse, as seen in the exposition of the series of **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."</note>. To another, it must be said that they do not differ much in substance, since the number of sound is adapted to man according to his most natural instruments, just as the pulse is in its own order. To another, it must be said that although in one, the consonance of voices is attended to, and in the other, the consonance of pulses, these are so far apart (as has already been declared) that they relate to each other by proportions through which a similarity is grasped. To another, it must be said that just as instrumental music quiets souls and leads to more praiseworthy character, so consequently **medicine** <note>original: *medicina*</note> preserves a perfect habit in the body or induces health; for when the body is not at peace, the soul and character do not arise distinguished. Whence in the first [book] *On Ingenuity*: "He who wishes to heal the soul should first heal the body," and so forth.

Again, that which shows the vigor of nature is good; of this kind is the variety of color, since it shows nature's power over many humors that must be expelled. Therefore, the variety of color in excrement is praiseworthy.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the musical proportions found in the human pulse, shifting now into the diagnostic signs found in the appearance and nature of human waste (excrement), which was a standard part of medieval medical examination.</meta>

<margin>Regarding the color in the excretion</margin>
However, so that it may be visible, the natural color of the **stool** <term>stool: *egestio*; the waste product of digestion</term> tends toward a **pale yellow** <note>original: *subcitrinum*</note>. Any variety that deviates from this is diverse and complex. Therefore, a variety of color is considered unfavorable. Regarding the first point, it should be known that "excretion" is understood in two ways: first, generally, as the removal of all waste products. This follows the second [book] of the **Aphorisms** <note>The *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates, a foundational medical text</note>: one ought to consider the **excretions** <note>original: *egestiones*</note> that are properly called **waste** <note>original: *excretiones*</note>. Otherwise, it is specifically the waste of the first digestion caused in the lower intestines, and especially in the **caecum** <term>caecum: *monoculum*; literally the "one-eyed" or blind-ended start of the large intestine</term>. For in that place, when the diet and the quantity of food are blameless, the dung is separated; with this, **bile** <note>original: *colera*</note> is mixed, brought down from the **gallbladder** <note>original: *chisti felle*</note>. This itself can be considered in four ways: by its quantity, its quality, the time of its exit, or the manner in which it comes out.

In **quantity**, it varies in two ways: either absolutely, or according to its quality-within-quantity. First, it varies between much, little, and a middle amount. This happens either because of the food consumed or the nature of the person receiving it. A large amount denotes many foods. If it is little, it indicates few foods, or a specific medical arrangement or condition. A middle amount indicates moderate food and the sufficiently healthy state of the body parts working upon it. Second, if there is a strength in the expulsive power combined with a weakness in the **mesenteric** <term>mesenteric: *mesaraicaz*; the veins or tissues connecting the intestines to the liver</term> attraction—for instance, a manifold flow of bile into the intestines—it causes excessive movement. A small amount is produced by the opposite causes: a weakness in the digestive power and a serving retention.

Regarding **quality in quantity**, this is in respect to whether more of the food is sent into the body than is transferred into the waste. For example, nuts (as seen in the seventh book of **Medical Theory** <note>The *Liber Regalis* by Haly Abbas</note>) and especially wine, or the testicles of fattened roosters, or the broth of praised meats (difference sixty-eight). Or it is the opposite, such as with **parsnips** <note>original: *baucia*</note>, turnips, cabbage, and things of this sort. Or it holds a middle ground, like bread (according to **Avicenna** <note>original: *Al.*</note> and **Galen** <note>original: *galei*</note>), meat from a year-old lamb, or kid goat. And these likewise vary according to the bodies fit to receive them in one way or another.

<margin>The substance of the excretion</margin>
By reason of **quality**, it is also three-fold: the liquid or substance is often noted by physicians in terms of heat and odor. Regarding the liquid, one is moist, another dry, and some are in the middle. The moist kind denotes that the juiciness of the food was minimally sent to the liver, or that there is a downward flow of **humors** <term>humors: *humōy*; the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health</term> into the belly and intestines. This is discerned by the color of the food or the humors. The dry kind signifies a lack of these causes and a heat in the digestive parts along with a strong liver. The arrangement of foods works similarly toward this. The middle state arises from middle causes.

<margin>Colors of...</margin>
Regarding **color**, many things are signified, just as many colors exist; they can be simple or mixed. For one is off-white, another

---

chalky, yellow, fiery, saffron-colored, rust-colored, green, indigo, bluish-livid, and black. Of these, **off-white** denotes an abundance of "gypsum-like" **phlegm** <note>original: *flegma*</note> or a dominance of coldness. **Chalky** signifies a lack of bile descending into the intestines. **Yellow**—specifically a mild yellow—denotes a natural excretion as such. **Fiery** signifies that red bile is being sent into the intestines in abundance. **Saffron** is even more so than that. **Rust-colored** signifies that kind of bile, just as **green** signifies green bile and sometimes coldness. **Indigo**, **livid**, and **black** denote the "death" of heat, or **scorching** <term>scorching: *adustionē*; the "burning" of humors through excessive heat, making them toxic</term>, or scorched bile, or wicked black bile, to a greater or lesser degree. The significance of this last one is the worst, unless it is perhaps evacuated little by little. There are also many **composite colors**; some tend more toward the side of naturalness, like the former ones, while others tend toward the opposite, like the latter ones, whose wickedness is more intense.

<margin>Odor from... stench</margin>
Regarding **odor**: one type is deprived of odor, which signifies great coldness or a dominance of phlegm. Another is an odor pulling toward sourness or bitterness, like that of **melancholy** <term>melancholy: *melancolię*; black bile</term>. Some tend toward a salty-sharpness like that of yellow bile. Or it will be very stinking, which signifies a rotting of the humors or a corruption of digestion. This sometimes happens from foods, such as the growth of trees, **asafoetida** <note>original: *gumi ase*; a pungent resin used in medicine</note>, leeks, garlic, **arugula** <note>original: *eruca*</note>, and such things. Or it is a middle ground between having a stench and not, which denotes perfect and natural digestion.

By reason of the **time** of excretion, it is diversified: some are quick, others slow, and some in the middle. This happens from the diversity of the foods themselves and their order, or a weakness in the attractive power with a strength in the expulsive power, or excessive sensitivity of the digestive parts, or an ulcer, or a flow of humors—or from the opposite of these, or their middle ground.

Regarding the **manner** <note>original: *habitudine*</note>: it may come out with sound, or windiness, or foam, or oiliness, or blood, or pus. That which comes out with **sound** denotes that windiness is mixed with the moisture, and a coldness of the intestines, or a narrowing of the "instruments" <note>the intestinal passages</note>, which is caused in no small part by windy foods; the significance of this in patients who are bashful is bad. That which comes out with **windiness** [without sound] is less than the aforementioned, and less evil, being caused by heat or movement, or both. **Foamy** stool shows a strong heat that is melting things down (as in those with wasting diseases) or a mixture of windiness. **Oily** stool signifies the melting of fat and grease, and the moisture of the principal organs; when it is light and viscous, it is "light" in the sense that it floats on water. Just as **cow dung** [consistency] demonstrates no small amount of windiness, as in those with **colic** <note>original: *colicis*</note>. **Bloody** stool comes out either from the whole body or from a specific part, such as the liver, the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: *mesaraica*</note>, the spleen, or the intestines, and so on.

There is here a diverse variety in the perception of colors in the stool; also, the term **praiseworthy** <note>original: *laudabile*</note> now carries a significant meaning. For something is praiseworthy, another unpraiseworthy, and some indeed are in the middle. The praiseworthy is also manifold: either because of very little goodness (and thus it is a "not-bad" sign), or of more (and thus "good"), or still more intense (and that is "better"). And so it goes on to "best" and "very best" or "most healthy." Similarly, the unpraiseworthy will be of little malice and even a "not-good" sign; or of greater malice, and that is "bad"; or thereafter, and then "worst" and "most worst" or "most deadly." On account of the second point, it should be known that the assembly of living physicians commonly condemns variety in the color of the stool. Also in the first [book] of **Crises**: a varied stool shows the body to be possessed by varied dispositions, and for that reason it is long-lasting and malicious. For many dispositions need a longer time for digestion and bring danger to the body's stability. The contrary of which is found in the fourth [book]; let it be stated thus in the second: diversity of color in that which comes out in the stool is **praiseworthy** in two hours [occasions], and not elsewhere. One of these is a **critical diversity** <note>original: *diversitas cretica*</note> after digestion on a **critical day** <term>critical day: a day when the disease is expected to reach its turning point</term> and with a critical sign. The other is after a strong laxative potion has passed through; for in these two dispositions, it signifies the expected cleansing. But in others, it signifies burning, liquefaction, and a multitude of corrupt humors. Hence in the third [book], fourteenth [chapter]: there is sometimes lightness in the expulsions of diverse colors. What follows from this will appear later.

On account of the third of these, it should be known that the diversity of color in the stool either comes from art through **medicine** <term>medicine: *farmacun*; from the Greek *pharmakon*</term> or spontaneously. If the first, the medicine is either unrestrained or not. If indeed it is unrestrained, it is bad, for it causes a wicked disposition in the body. If however it is not unrestrained, then either the medicine must evacuate several humors and consequently several colors together, and that is good, provided that it is necessary to evacuate. If indeed it is meant to lead out only one humor but evacuates many, it is not good, at least significantly so, as it denotes mixed humors in the body which nature, not being able to govern, emits almost spontaneously.

If, however, these colors flow spontaneously with the humors, they are either entirely wicked and corrupt, or they are not such, but still pertain somewhat to a natural state. And then they are either expelled in the beginning, when the signs of digestion have not yet appeared, or in the [later] state when they have already appeared. If earlier, the strength is either strong or weak. If indeed it is weak, it denotes evil and death. If it is robust, it indicates the length of the disease. For sometimes the strength is perceptibly strong, and being intolerant, it expels the undigested matter in the beginning—or with it, the digested matter during the increase [of the disease]—since the preceding signs of digestion are always indicative. If however it is the second [the later state], then either the crisis will be perfect, and thus such digestion can occur in the variety of the stool's color with its substance, so that not only itself but the color is changed, and that is shown to be the best. If indeed the crisis is diminished, then the colors change for the better but do not lose their variety entirely; and that becomes praiseworthy in respect to the evacuation performed in the beginning...

...however, those which are perfected in the final **temperament** <term>temperament: *crasi*; the balance or "mixture" of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</term>. Truly, they are not always indicative of health unless they are preceded by signs of digestion. I said "in themselves" because the matter can be digested without health following, precisely because the **expulsive power** <note>original: *uirtus excretiua*; the natural faculty of the body to push out waste</note> was unable to lead it out, such as **pus** <note>original: *sanie*</note> contained in the chest, as mentioned in the second book of the *Prognostics* and the fourth book of *Internal Affections*. And rightly so, since one is the natural power that digests, while the power that expels is further part of the animal faculty. 

If, however, humors of this sort exist in entirely unnatural colors, then not only are several colors judged poorly, but even one is judged as the worst by the ancients; hence it is added: *In whatever diseases beginning with **black bile** <note>original: *colera ni.* (colera nigra)</note>, if it emerges upwards or downwards, it is fatal.* This is because every praiseworthy evacuation must be preceded by digestion, followed by the separation of the matter from the parts, and then finally the evacuation itself. 

The **Commentator** <note>likely Galen, commenting on Hippocrates</note> says in the same place: If it comes out in a stable state where signs of digestion have already appeared, even if it does not lose its variety of colors in every way, it can be converted from an ill-omened sign through the constancy of the body's power. Since nature cannot change them due to their extreme badness, they are nevertheless changed for the better, shifting into colors opposite to their nature. Hence the Commentator says: *Because we have seen many such excretions in long, pestilential diseases in those who were in danger and those who were to be saved.* Yet these did not appear at the beginning of the diseases or during their increase; rather, yellow-colored **dissolutions** <note>original: *colliquationes*; the "melting" or breaking down of body tissues into fluid</note> were present when they emerged, whose color afterwards appeared black, like the dregs of blood. 

Wherefore, in the first book of *Theory*, [it is said]: I saw some discharging this species of melancholy as black who perished quickly. I also saw some of them discharging this, and after two days the excretion gradually became **pale yellow** <note>original: *citrina*</note>, and they were liberated from the disease. I indeed saw one in whose skin a violet color appeared, and he was liberated after a short time because the melancholy was altered, and after a little while a yellow color appeared in their excretion. I myself also observed a black, melancholic, odorless, and shimmering excretion, like **purging cassia** <term>purging cassia: *cassia fistula*; a medicinal plant whose dark, sticky fruit pulp was used as a laxative; here used to describe the appearance of the stool</term>, in a young man; it remained for five days and then returned to a final state. And in him, traces of **leprosy** <note>original: *lepre*</note> were already showing in his face. And this kind is indeed the worst, since it was not through the proper way of purging. 

Hence in the first [book], second [section], chapter eight: Melancholic humors purged at the end are mostly lethal when they emerge; that is, it is a sign of death. However, the discharge of a black exit like black blood often brings relief. Such **black bile** <note>original: *colera nigra*</note> is generated either from the black humor itself or from that which is not certainly black, which is the dregs of blood through the process of **combustion** <term>combustion: *adustionis*; the "burning" or overheating of humors, which was thought to turn them black and toxic</term> or putrefaction.

For when the **spleen** <note>original: *splen*</note> is weak and unable to draw in the natural black humor or melancholy, it remains in the liver and the vessels with the blood; through corruption in such a place, it is transformed into something so wicked that it induces the worse types of leprosy, **cancers**, **herpes**, and the like. In the thirty-second distinction: Indeed, black humor differs in three ways from black excretion. However, someone might say it is "unpraiseworthy" by way of being a sign, because it shows the great malice of the excretion and how far it has moved from its natural state. Of all these things, there is evident confirmation from the nature of any matter: that in every good evacuation, digestion must precede and expulsion must follow, as the medical art shows.

Regarding the fourth point, it seems necessary to speak on the first. It is, however, good in a certain respect, such as in relation to that which occurs at the beginning. So too, that which is done according to the medical art at the beginning is somewhat praiseworthy compared to that which happens spontaneously, provided that the art evacuates for some time before nature does. For if it evacuates on one day, and nature would have evacuated under compulsion on that same day or the following, this varied excretion would not be less bad than that which occurred spontaneously. Indeed, it might be worse, since the body's power would have been fatigued by the **drug** <note>original: *farmaco*</note>.

<meta>This page continues a scholastic medical debate regarding the diagnostic value of bodily excretions. It concludes a discussion on the variety of colors in stool (egestio) and begins a new "distinction" (Difference 85) concerning whether the color or the substance (thickness/consistency) of urine is the primary indicator of the body's digestive state.</meta>

V-

To the other point, it must be said that it is not valid, because this discussion concerns an unnatural variety of **excrement** <term>excrement: *egestio*; the waste product of the "third digestion" in the bowels</term>. However, an objection is raised concerning **urine** that is partly supernatural and partly natural. For it would be said of the excrement that if it were partly natural and partly unnatural, it would be less an evil than if it were entirely unnatural.

To the other point, it must be said that a variety of many colors in excrement is not praised simply in itself; however, according to the medical art, it would be praiseworthy if it were a single, simple color. But this is said in comparison to those things which are of diverse colors by their own nature. Furthermore, some things can be achieved through **art** <note>original: *artem*; here meaning medical skill or human intervention</note> which cannot be achieved by nature, and vice versa. Although art generally imitates nature, it does not, however, reach it. 
<margin>Aristotle, Book 4 of the Metaphysics. Art.</margin>
Hence, Aristotle says in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*: "Art is weaker than nature, nor does it overtake it, though it labors much." For art always follows nature when it is operating rightly. If, however, nature is not operating rightly, art does not oppose it but rather corrects it. 

To the other point, it must be said that the variety of colors in excrements does not simply show the vigor of nature, but rather the opposite, as has been shown. For nature never completes a good evacuation unless a **preparation** <note>original: *preparatio*; the "cooking" or ripening of humors known as coction</note> precedes it, no matter how strong nature itself may be. For it is not as if one is supported to conquer their enemy by joining with them entirely, but it is necessary that they stand at a distance to be supported outside of the enemy. To the other points belonging to the other side, as to the first, what should be said has now appeared throughout. 

To the other point, it must be said that this is verified in a **crisis** <term>crisis: a turning point in a disease when the body's nature "battles" the sickness</term>, assuming all its praiseworthy conditions are first met, as touched upon in the first book of the *On Critical Days* and the *Aphorisms*. 

To the other point, it must be said: since **sputum** <note>original: *sputum*; phlegm or spit</note> is a waste product of more "homogeneous" parts, or since **vomit** is like excrement that occurs in more principal and warmer places: the situation with these is not entirely the same as with bowel excrement. 

To the other point, it must be said that the color of natural excrement tends toward a yellowish-orange (citrine), as has been noted; however, this variety of color is praiseworthy in a specific case and not simply as a natural state, but according to specific conditions, as has been shown, and only imperfectly.

### DISTINCTION LXXXV.

Whether the color of urine is produced before its **substance** <term>substance: *substantia*; in uroscopy, this refers to the consistency, thickness, or "body" of the urine</term> is shown by the testimonies of **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a foundational 10th-century physician</note> and **Theophilus** <note>Theophilus Protospatharius, author of a standard medieval text on urine</note>. 

Furthermore, nature proceeds gradually from diminished things to more perfect things, and from easier things it arrives at more difficult things, as is apparent in animals. But color is something "diminished" and more easily received in respect to substance, as the aforementioned authors know. Moreover, that which is given by a stronger agent is given more lightly and earlier; but the color is of this sort in relation to the substance. For color itself, according to Isaac, is caused more by the **active qualities** <note>heat and cold</note>, while substance is caused by the **passive qualities** <note>moisture and dryness</note>. 

Again, that which follows and is not reversible is "prior" in the categories; hence if there are two things, one exists [first] and not vice versa. But if the substance is present, color is immediately present, since such a substance is always qualified by accidents. But if color is present, it does not mean for that reason that the substance [of digestion] will be present, because certain urines, according to **Avicenna**, do not have substance and yet they participate in colors. 

Furthermore, as the **sediment** <term>sediment: *ypostasis*; the material that settles at the bottom of a urine flask</term> relates to the substance, so the substance relates to the color, as the order of digestion shows. But sediment is given after substance; therefore, color will be given even later. 

Furthermore, in the first book of the *Problems* [of Aristotle]: "Why is it necessary to look at the signs around urine?" The answer is: because it is a sign of being digestive if it is reddish. For Aristotle shifted his focus to the color and not to the substance as the primary and more revealing indicator of digestion. Thus, the digestive power will provide the color before the substance.

**The Opposite View**
The opposite seems to be felt in the first [book] of the *Second Analytics*. **Substance** <note>here used in the philosophical sense of "subject"</note> is prior to the accident in definition, in knowledge, and in time, according to the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*. Truly, color is an accident, while the liquid is the substance. 

Again, that which can exist without the other is given first. Such is the substance in respect to color, since color is an accident, and it is the nature of an accident to "be in" something. 

Also, that which is more intended by nature will be given first, since the imperfect always strives to reach the limit by the shortest path. But digestion shows a more vehement perfection and goodness in the substance than in the color, according to Avicenna. 

Likewise, in the same number, something is prior in **potentiality** before it is in **actuality** <note>referring to Aristotle's concepts of *potentia* and *actus*</note>, as per the ninth book of the *Metaphysics*. But substance is given by the passive qualities which are potential, since they are more material; color truly comes from the active, actual, and formal qualities. Therefore, substance will be given before color. 

Furthermore, it is shown that the generation of a man and a "white man" exist at the same time—that is, the substance and the accident—in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. But the liquid of the urine is the substance, while the color is the accident. 

Furthermore, in the fourth book of the *Aphorisms*: "If the disease be very acute, the change of color or liquid alone suffices for a future crisis." Therefore, they seem to appear indifferently. 

Again, an accident is produced at the same time as its subject, and the effect is at the same time as its cause, according to the second book of the *Physics*. But the substance seems to be the subject and cause of the color, while color is the accident and effect. Because of these things, it is proven that both are given at the same time by digestion. 

Regarding the first point, one must first know what 
<margin>Urine</margin>
**urine** is; secondly, where it is formed and how; thirdly, how many things are observed in it; and finally, what is meant by the terms "prior" and "at the same time" in relation to it. Regarding the first of these, it must be known that urine is the **strainings** <note>original: *colamentum*</note> of the blood coming from the liver to the bladder, according to the fourth book of the *Aphorisms*. By "blood," or the "bloody mass," all carrying humors are understood, for blood is taken to represent them, as in Distinction 30. And it is so accepted by Isaac, who says...
