<meta>This page continues the discussion from Distinction 58 regarding the definition and essential nature of fever, transitioning from the theoretical debate of "heat as a body" to specific definitions provided by authorities like Isaac Judaeus and Avicenna.</meta>

<margin>Isaac</margin>
<margin>Avicenna</margin>
<margin>Distinction 58</margin>
...affected in meaning and cause. The action of a fever is to heat excessively or beyond nature so that all actions and passions are harmed, because a fever will essentially be **heat** and **beyond nature**.
Regarding this, it must be known that this extraneous heat is something that exists of itself. It is a certain overwhelming, terrifying quality that overcomes natural heat, changing it from its natural disposition into its opposite; it is not, however, a body. Hence **Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus (c. 832–932), a highly influential Jewish physician and philosopher whose "Book on Fevers" was a standard medieval textbook.</note> [says]: "With extraneous heat approaching the heart, the natural heat departs from its temperament. Since it is divided through all parts of the body to grant them life, when it departs from its temperament, it is necessary that the members receive it in that quality which heats and burns them, generating a fever that suddenly harms every natural action." In this opinion, **Avicenna** concurs, thus: "Fever is natural heat mixed with some quality of putrid heat." In this way, extraneous heat affects natural heat.

Here, however, in Distinction 59, it qualifies the **spirit**; if it affects it vehemently and reaches the heart, departing from there, it generates an <term>ephemeral</term> <note>original: "effiera" (ephemera). A one-day fever believed to affect only the spirits or pneuma, not the humors or tissues.</note> fever. But if these three alter and corrupt the humor, a **putrid** fever is induced. If, however, they affect the members <note>The "members" refers to the solid parts or organs of the body.</note>, it is a **hectic** <note>original: "ethica." A chronic fever affecting the solid tissues, often associated with consumption/tuberculosis.</note> fever. That this heat is a quality is shown by the signs [which] signify a bad hot and dry **complexion** <note>A person's "complexion" was their specific balance of the four humors and qualities.</note>. Know also that although this heat is said to be extraneous or beyond nature, it is not so in every way, such as the heat found in dead bodies (as Avicenna notes), but rather it is an affection of the natural heat, yet, as was said, with a putrid quality. Since it is a mean between natural heat and that which is beyond nature—just as semi-putrefaction is a mean between healthy fluid and pus (which is simply good in its kind) and putridity (which is altogether bad)—so it is with all primary fevers. For means, since they are composed of extremes, taste of their nature, so that when compared to one extreme they seem like the other, according to the *Physics* <note>Aristotle's *Physics*.</note>, in proportion to how much of the nature of each extreme they possess. For this reason, they are denoted by the names of the extremes in the *Aphorisms* <note>The *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates.</note>, book four. And therefore Avicenna, referring this mean to one of the extremes (which is less deceptive in fever), called it "natural heat qualified by a putrid quality." And another definition: "Fever is the turning of innate heat into something fiery."

<margin>
First [book of] Aphorisms.
Fever.
</margin>
Others, however, seeing how fever declines toward the worse of the extremes, have said it is "extraneous heat" or "extra-natural heat" or "beyond nature."
Fever is, therefore, a certain compound heat composed of natural heat and extraneous putrid heat, seeking the heart and from it—with the spirit and humors as intermediaries—conveyed through the vessels into the lesions of the actions of the whole body.

<margin>
To the fourth [point](?).
Not opposed.
</margin>
Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it is said that fever, as shown, is not heat that is a body, since heat is a quality and not a body, unless the word "heat" is used very improperly to mean a "hot body." Even assuming it were a body, it has been shown how two bodies would then be in the same place, and how both would be the agent and the patient simultaneously, though they are distinct in place and subject. Heat will therefore be an **accident** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not belong to the essence of a thing—like the color of a shirt.</note> as a quality, and thus the thing defined and its genus will be from the same category of the Predicaments.
But if **Galen**, with **Haly Abbas**, says that the substance of fevers is in the genus of heat which is beyond

nature, he takes "substance" to mean "essence," as when he says: "Complexion is a substance" and "Sickness is a substance." Distinction 17. For in accidents, essence is found at least by addition, as in the 7th book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>, and not substance. And next it must be said that although fever does not move nor proceed by itself, it is moved by accident—namely, by means of the spirit and the blood, which are bodies, just as it is touched upon in the definition of fever. This is what **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Halia." Latinized name for the 10th-century Persian physician 'Ali ibn al-'Abbas al-Majusi.</note> meant when he said, "sent from the heart." And Avicenna: "proceeding from the heart by means of the spirit and blood." To the other point, what should be said is apparent: for fever is heat, where here "heat" is the effect of heat, which comes forth as a passion and a passible quality.
To the other points, it must be said that those are not strictly definitions of fever, but certain common descriptions. Either "superabundance," "turning," "mutation," or "declination"—by reason of their heat being determined—can be reduced to a quality. Or "superabundance," although by reason of the respect it carries it is "toward something," yet on the part of that which it regards (like heat), it is located in "quality"; and thus motion and declination can in some way imply quality. To the other point, it is said that no fevers are cold of themselves as they actually exist, but by reason of their **shivering** <term>typus</term> <note>original: "typus." Refers to the periodic cycle or paroxysm of a fever, specifically the cold or shivering stage.</note>. However, it is not by the nature of fevers (at least those currently occurring due to a lax lifestyle, as appears from the symptoms). The reason for this also arises from the refraction of heat from the heart into the rest of the body (Aphorisms, book 7), whence regarding fevers: "They are cold, having rigor or shivering," as he adds. Or because of a <unclear>fantasized(?)</unclear> matter itself upon the sensible members. Just as happens in **empyema** <note>A collection of pus in a body cavity, usually the lungs.</note>, in which the external parts are hot and the internal parts grow cold, or vice versa, as happens in **lipparia** <note>A "leipyria" fever, where the patient's internal organs feel as if they are burning while their limbs feel cold.</note> and in the fevers of pernicious internal tumors, in which—because of the heat attracting like a cupping glass—they burn within and the exterior parts grow cold; hence when someone has this with that, [the Aphorisms, book 4] pronounces it fatal. It also happens sometimes due to the weakness of the natural heat, not being able to expand itself through the whole. To the other point, what should be said has partly appeared. For it has been declared how, in different respects, fever can be called "natural heat," yet not simply so, but "as if natural" or "extraneous." Nor is it inconvenient among some [philosophers] for two contraries to exist simultaneously. Indeed, in some things it is necessary, as with health and sickness, since the latter cannot exist without health (Distinction 72), where natural and unnatural heat are seen to be such. Or although one of the contraries eventually expels and corrupts the other, they remain together during the struggle between them, just as the elements do in a mixture, until finally natural heat overcomes the extraneous heat when health is introduced, or vice-versa when death occurs; nor is it that febrile heat is always so corruptive as to destroy all actions. To the other point, which is a fallacy of some by which they try to prove a bad disposition is not a disease: I say that a "good disposition" is health, not simply and totally, because that consists of the tempered proportion of qualities and the elegant composition of the instrumental parts, and nature participates in both. But a "good complexion" is indeed the health of the parts, and "just composition" that of the organs. And so a bad disposition or fever is a disease and an extraneous heat.
This dissolution is based upon what was shown in Distinction 65: that health exists in the most specific species, but sickness is a substance.

### DISTINCTION 88.

<margin>
3rd Book of Meteorology, 21.
Page 20. Concerning critical days.
</margin>

It is argued that the humors cannot flow periodically. This is because such a flow would have to come from something either intrinsic or extrinsic to them. But it can be neither. It is certainly not the first, since blood—the most principal of the humors—does not flow periodically but is moved constantly by putrefaction or inflammation, though it is seen to flow more abundantly than the others. Indeed, it is more multifaceted and deeper than the rest regarding its cooperation in <term>confluence</term> <note>original: "confluxio." In medieval medicine, this refers to the gathering or movement of humors toward a specific point, often the heart or a site of disease.</note>. According to Geofar <note>Likely referring to the astronomer Albumasar (Abu Ma'shar), whose works on tides and planetary influence were standard in the Middle Ages.</note> in his third book, it is introduced thus: either they are elements from which they derive a straight motion—yet here the flow is a reflection—or they are moved by super-celestial bodies. But it is not from these either, since the flow of the humors cannot be made to fit their cycles; for the eighth sphere, according to Ptolemy, completes its course in 36,000 years, Saturn in 30 years, Jupiter in 12, Mars in 2, the Sun, Venus, and Mercury in 1, and the Moon in approximately 27 days and 8 hours. However, the period of the humors is, for the most part, three days. Furthermore, it must be from either a superior or inferior nature. Certainly not the latter, because the inferior nature is governed by the superior: all motion of the former is governed from there. Hence, concerning the <term>critical days</term> <note>original: "creticoꝝ" (criticorum). These were specific days in an illness (like the 7th or 14th) when a physician expected a "crisis" or decisive change in the patient's condition.</note>: everything good is beautiful, and everything which adheres to the order of the universe and its path shows a trace of wisdom in it—which is only from above. Nor is it from a superior nature, because agents and patients must share in the same matter, according to the first book of *On Generation*. But the inferior nature does not share matter with the superior nature, since the heavens, according to the Commentator <note>Averroes, the "Commentator" on Aristotle.</note>, consist of a different matter than these things here below. Furthermore, that which is as matter and participates in being through form does not flow periodically; for it is said to stand most firmly when it is fully formed. Such are the humors in relation to the formation of the body's soul. Even if one were to ask, since there is a certain motion and all motion comes from heat and spirit, whether heat and "windiness" are required—for according to Albumasar they work toward the flow—then <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile, characterized as hot and dry.</note> and <term>melancholy</term> <note>Black bile, characterized as cold and dry.</note> would flow more than <term>phlegm</term> <note>Characterized as cold and moist.</note>, since melancholy is "windy," according to the 30th book of *Problems*. And choler is hot, yet we experience the opposite. On the contrary, melancholy does not flow, as it is "frozen" by the earth, which stands immobile. According to *On the Motion of Animals*, choler, being hot and dry, is opposite to the nature of water, from which flow, or "accession and recession" <note>An analogy to the high and low tides of the sea.</note>, is found. Therefore, the humors cannot flow periodically.

<margin>
Confluence
</margin>
The opposite of this is experienced by the senses. Furthermore, that is said to flow periodically which is moved at certain hours from the circumference to the center or vice versa. But the humors are of this kind, since they are running liquids. For they are driven by internal cold and, following the motion of heat, they are expanded outward by that expansion. This is denoted by the event of an unexpected disease; for the process begins first from the "mine" of putrefaction toward the heart, and from there to the remaining parts of the body. Therefore, the humors are able to flow periodically. Regarding the first point, one must know what a humor is and how they are distinguished, as shown in Distinction 29. <term>Confluence</term> is the motion by which nature, with heat and moisture, is drawn back from the circumferences into the center, and finally expands from the center back into the circumferences. This is sufficiently likened to the accession and recession caused by the moon in the water. For the moon expands it from the middle toward the outside. And it happens when the moon proceeds from the point of the east into the mid-heaven; and then it is restricted inward until it reaches the angle

---

of the setting sun. And from here it returns to expansion as if by nature, until it reaches the angle of the earth; from which, as before, it is led back into itself in that central place. The moistures of bodies "approach" in the first quadrant, "recede" in the second, and so on proportionally in the others, as will be declared in Distinction 168. To this accession and recession, according to the third book of Geofar's *Introductory*, three things must concur: namely water, depth, length, and width, provided by high mountains from above, and windiness. Also, when the quantity of water is great, not poured out by new rivers, but gathered over a long, extensive time, it becomes thick and salty or bitter, and vapors and winds are born there. Where the place and the water are opposite to this, they receive the influx and reflux minimally. There are also some waters that move by their own nature. For when they are outside their proper place, they seek it by their own weight, as through rivers. And it is necessary that the moon intervenes in the third place, for it has dominion over moist things, such as the moistures of the brain, the spinal cord, fats, and marrow, according to the books on critical days and the third book of the *Introductory*. For the moon is ascribed to water just as the sun is to fire, as seen in Distinction 16. According to the diversity of its motion, water especially undergoes change; for the greater parts of the waters are thus moved, attracted by the moon. In this way, many things naturally excite and attract one another. For the **magnet** pulls iron to itself; **Alnapth** <note>A term for white bitumen or naphtha.</note>, a certain Judean white bitumen, pulls fire from a great distance, so that wicked priests may deceive the common people with it. And there is a stone that pulls vinegar without contact, another like an olive pulls oil, and **amber** <note>original: "karabe." From the Arabic "kahraba," meaning amber, known for its static attraction.</note> pulls straws. It has been sufficiently stated concerning the starting point and the destination; it is said here that this differs from the flow of water: for when humors begin to move, they tend more from the circumferences toward the center, and from the center back to the same. A **period** is a completed circuit which has begun; of which there are two parts here, namely the *proximus* <note>original: "poxīm⁹" (paroxysm). The period of the onset or intensification of symptoms.</note> and the *declinatio* (decline). Whence, regarding the movement of paroxysms, you ought to understand that it determines a portion of the whole period, from the first onset until the "state" (peak), just as the remainder belongs to the decline, which is better. And one kind of period is "fixed," beginning and ending at the same hour; another takes some time beforehand and another postpones the rest. This properly occurs in fevers in which an exacerbation is found, followed by a manifest rest. It occurs improperly in those which undergo an "increase" and "decrease" of the paroxysm. It occurs most improperly in the opposites of these, such as in a blood-fever <note>A "continual" fever believed to be caused by the blood itself rather than other humors.</note>, or in certain burning fevers, unless one wishes to call the entire sickness one "period," since it begins from health and finally terminates at it. And therefore, some place fevers among the "continual" and others among the "periodic." Here, however, a period does not occur, or is hardly perceived, in healthy bodies. Regarding the second point, it must be known that what is sought is difficult. Whence, in the third book on *Critical Days*, [it is asked] why in acute diseases the paroxysms come every third day for the most part. In long-lasting diseases, however, it is not easy to find them either every day or every third day. Moreover, finding no modern writer on this question, I turn to the ancients, and I find them to be somewhat discordant, touching upon the cause of it more from the dispositions of the matter than from the acting form and the end, although all correctly assign the cause.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the cycles of humors and fevers, moving from the astronomical influences discussed previously to the specific physiological mechanisms of natural heat and putrefaction.</meta>

<margin>The cause of the cycles of fevers.</margin>
<margin>Variety of reasons.</margin>
...it must be strictly followed. For necessity arises from other causes and not simply from the material of a thing, as seen in the second book of the *Physics* and the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*, where Empedocles <note>Empedocles (c. 490–430 BCE) was a Greek philosopher who proposed the theory of the four elements. The author here refers to Aristotle's critiques of his materialist views.</note> is refuted. Some assign the cause of these cycles to the substance of the humors—their quantity and quality. Others assign it to the location. Some attribute it to <term>natural heat</term> <note>original: "calore naturali." In medieval medicine, this is the innate warmth of a living body that drives digestion and life processes.</note>, while others attribute it to an extrinsic or "alien" heat.

Whence Averroes <note>original: "Auar." refers to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), specifically his medical encyclopedia *al-Kulliyat* (The Colliget).</note> concludes in the fourth book of the *Colliget*: the reason why fevers have cycles is that the humor which is meant to putrefy does not do so all at once. This is because the preparation for putrefaction in that humor is not completed instantly but proceeds gradually. This follows a specific mode of organization, because this operation is, in a way, natural; nature maintains a regime over it, as it is a "putrefaction with digestion." Therefore, a variation in the order of these cycles is a bad sign.

<margin>Averroes, 4th [book of] the Colliget.</margin>
Furthermore, this operation is not to be attributed substantially to the "putrefactive heat," but rather to natural heat. This is because it operates on matter that is "non-natural," as is found in many of nature's pathways. The foundations of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 210 CE), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note>, by which he attempts to attribute the order of cycles substantially to putrefactive heat, are weakened here. Therefore, our opinion in this matter is that nature performs these cycles using a heat that "makes tender" <note>original: "calore tenrifico."</note>, even if something unnatural in quantity or quality has been added to this heat—acting upon non-natural matter, such as a humor that is causing illness.

These orders of cycles are diversified according to the nature and quantity of the humor. And while this discourse fits the common understanding of <term>periodic</term> <note>original: "periodice." Referring to the regular intervals at which a fever returns.</note> cycles, it perhaps suffers from criticism in several points.

<margin>Common authority.</margin>
First, because natural heat would not be the cause of the period, as it is a mover that preserves rather than incites. Furthermore, nature does not move unless it perceives something harmful. And since <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile.</note> is more parching and hateful to nature—and <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "Colera nigra."</note> according to Alexander <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a commentator on Aristotle.</note> is an enemy—these ought to flow more rapidly than phlegm. Again, digestion does not always follow putrefaction; rather, there is often a greater "choking" or immense corruption.

Conversely, a variation in the order of the cycles is approved when its opposite is detested. Whence in the fourth book of the *Aphorisms* [of Hippocrates]: "To whomever <term>paroxysms</term> <note>The periodic peak or 'attack' of a fever.</note> occur, whichever fever leaves on the next day at a different hour," unless the variation in the order of the cycles arises from the weakness of nature. This is in accordance with that same fourth book: "If a shivering fit occurs while the fever is not subsiding and the strength is already weak, it is fatal."

Yet, however true that may be, his position does not allow for it. The saying of Galen—which he takes from the second book of *On Fevers*—is more valid when the putrefactive heat, remaining as a "habit" in the matter of the putridity generated from food in a previous paroxysm, is suddenly made active (as heat dormant in lime rises up when water is sprinkled on it) with a difference in the time of exacerbation and rest.

<margin>Note</margin>
And thirdly, more precisely, I shall show as far as possible why this humor moves continuously, while that one moves daily, or another at a certain fixed time. Regarding this, one must first know that since every effect arises from the action of an agent upon matter, a gathering <note>original: "confluxus."</note> will be ainsi excited in the humors. He who considers the matter but ignores the "agent" (the force acting upon it), or considers the agent while neglecting the matter, is insufficient; matter does not bring itself into action, nor does an agent act upon itself, since action falls upon external matter. This is like a merchant dealing with the body while neglecting the soul, or vice-versa, as Aristotle <note>original: "Aru." abbreviation for Aristoteles.</note> rebukes some in the first book of *On the Soul*.

The matter in which the periodic gathering is founded consists of the humors, marked by various properties. The agent, however, is the celestial body, acting through the mediation of elementary nature. Whence in the fourth book of *On the Generation of Animals*: "Thus in the air we see the nature of all moist things standing and changing according to the motion and standing of the winds, and the air changing according to the periods of the Sun and Moon." So too must the things composed of these necessarily follow; for it is necessary to follow the periods of those things which are more principal. For life is a certain "time," as are generation and decay.

Therefore, since the humor is governed by the Sun and Moon as more principal forces, their gathering follows the periods of the Sun and Moon, and generally the periods of the stars. Just as in the air, every liquid and the air itself receives its standing or changing nature from these. This motion of the world is continuous with the superior rotations by necessity, so that all the power of this world is governed from there.

<margin>First cause of the flow.</margin>
This is from the beginning of the *Metaphysics*. Whence Messahallah <note>A famous 8th-century Jewish-Persian astronomer and astrologer.</note> says: "The likeness of the planets in this world is as the magnet and the iron." And the "Ten Judges" <note>A famous medieval astrological compendium.</note> say: "The condition of every human birth is from the planets and their signs," just as the earth depends on the magnet stone.

Furthermore, know the certain periods of the intermittent humors: for the **phlegmatic** fever afflicts for 18 hours and cools for 6. The **Tertian** fever rests for 12 and 36 hours. The **Quartan** fever has a paroxysm for 24 hours and an interval of 48. But in those that do not fail, they sometimes afflict for a longer time than predicted, and sometimes less.

There is a triple cause for this lack of determination:
1. The **humor**, which is sometimes larger or smaller, thicker or thinner, hotter or colder.
2. The **virtue** (strength), which is sometimes strong and sometimes weak.
3. The **construction of the body**, which is sometimes "rare" (porous) and easily permeable, and sometimes the opposite.

In these, a balanced middle ground is found. If these three factors agree, it will produce the primary period. In the other three opposite conditions, the result will be different, as noted in the second book of *Fevers* and the eighth book of *Therapeutics*.

Again, it should be noted that the humor is governed by its own "form" just as every soul is, when the body is in a natural disposition. Sometimes, however, the "supernal virtue" (celestial power) is shown more clearly, as when there is a <term>dyscrasia</term> <note>An imbalance of the four bodily humors.</note>; then the body is not perfectly governed by the soul, but is agitated by the motion of the superior bodies and elements. This is indicated by the "best bodies," in which no [imbalance is found]...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how humors (the body's primary fluids) trigger different types of fevers. It moves from general principles to specific classifications based on the physical properties of these fluids—their thickness, temperature, and location in the body—drawing on major medical authorities like Haly Abbas and Isaac Judaeus.</meta>

A slight impression results from this cause. In the healthy, this is not visible in every way, but in the sick, it is completely apparent. As it is said regarding the soul according to Geoffrey <note>Likely Geoffrey of Auxerre or a similar scholastic commentator.</note>, some things do not flow at all, or very little; others appear slightly; and a third type is manifest everywhere. Nor is this contrary to what was said: that moisture arrives in the first quarter and the rest follows; for this happens according to what is possible, as if the subject were already adapted to it. Then, the action of the agent occurs upon the subject itself. 

Regarding this, one should know that the humors can be separated into two categories: either by their **intrinsic** factors or their **extrinsic** factors. In the first case, this happens in four ways according to what is found in them: 
1. **Substance** <note>The physical consistency, such as thickness or thinness.</note>
2. **Quantity**
3. **Quality** <note>The primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, or dry.</note>
4. **Location**

From these—according to Haly Abbas <note>original: "Halyab."; referring to the 10th-century Persian physician Haly Abbas and his work *The Complete Art of Medicine*.</note> in the eighth book of the *Theorica*, and Isaac Judaeus in the fifth book of *On Fevers*—there arises the speed or slowness of the humor's gathering, its <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putredo." In medieval medicine, fevers were often thought to be caused by a "rotting" or "fermentation" of humors when they became stagnant or overheated.</note>, the ease or difficulty of that putrefaction, and the acceleration or delay of its evacuation.

If, for instance, a humor is moderate in substance, large in quantity, hot and moist, and stays inside the <term>vessels</term> <note>The veins and arteries.</note> so that it must necessarily move through those locations, it will not flow moderately but will flow more continuously, much like blood. Indeed, all these factors coincide in the first type. Because its substance is fluid, abundant, hot, and moist, it is ready for putrefaction; and especially because of its internal location, it will afflict the body continuously and uniformly, so that no increase or delay is perceived in it. This is because all matter acts universally when it is situated in the innermost parts of the heart.

<margin>Burning fever. Putrid soot.</margin>
As the <term>causon</term> <note>original: "causon"; a Greek medical term for a highly acute, "burning" inflammatory fever.</note> shows, this even occurs with the phlegmatic humor. For putrid **soot** <note>original: "fuligo"; the "smoky" waste products produced by the burning of humors by internal heat.</note> seeks the heart directly and, being unable to breathe out through the aforementioned obstacles, it afflicts the body constantly. Therefore, in such cases, the sweat typical of periodic fevers is not expected, since that which is inflamed and putrefied resides in one part and affects the body continuously. These fevers will be brief and generally terminate within eight days for two reasons: first, because the material easily obeys the process of <term>coction</term> <note>The "cooking" or ripening of a disease-causing humor so the body can expel it.</note>; and second, because of its thinness and sharpness. Avicenna added to this that the body does not feel what is dissolved from the sensible members. 

When, however, the matter is **outside the vessels**, the movement is not continuous.

<margin>Intermittent fever.</margin>
Instead, a remission <note>original: "anesis"; a temporary lessening of fever symptoms.</note> occurs through the opposite of what was just described, where an interruption happens. For when the heat finishes moving the matter toward putrefaction, since it is not contained within the vessels, it forces the thin part that remains to breathe out as "incinerated" or earthy matter. This earthy matter does not carry heat or fever. This is similar to what appears in heaps of dung when they ignite. But when the cause arising from food is not entirely overcome, it returns to the "mine" or source of the putrefaction, finding the remaining heat. It then inflames again from the preceding putrefaction. This is like lime or gypsum when water is added. This lasts as long as the cause persists at the source of putrefaction, where you will find sufficient traces of the preceding heat, as seen in the works of Galen and in the fourth book. 

Now, as to why **phlegm** is added after

<margin>Phlegm.</margin>
blood: it is because it is moist, slightly cold, and—according to Alexander <note>Likely Alexander of Trallies, a 6th-century medical writer.</note>—viscous in its physical expansion, and it occupies a location outside the blood. This makes it more prone to putrefaction than others. Because of its quantity and moisture—according to Alexander—the **daily fever** <note>original: "quotidiana"; a fever that recurs every day, traditionally associated with phlegm.</note> has an abundant, thick, and viscous material, and it gathers for putrefaction more easily. Because of its viscosity, the putrefaction lasts longer. It cannot be resolved as easily as others. But because of its slight coldness and its external location, it stops putrefying for a short time, so that the time of its putrefaction is longer than the hour of rest.

<margin>Melancholy.</margin>
**Melancholy** <note>Black bile.</note> also, because it is thick, scarce, cold, and dry, is subject to putrefaction more slowly than the others. Nevertheless, because it is a moist, liquid, or flowing body—for it is a humor, and such things are prone to putrefaction, especially when they receive external heat—once it is set in motion, its worsening lasts a long time. This is due to the impression made on its "earthy" subject, just as heat lasts longer in a stone than in other things, so that it takes a longer time to subside than it took to reach its peak.

<margin>Choler.</margin>
**Choler** <note>Yellow bile.</note>, being thin, holds a middle ground among these humors. It is not as prone to putrefaction as phlegm, nor as ill-disposed as melancholy. It exists in a smaller quantity than phlegm but a larger quantity than melancholy, as shown in distinction thirty-two. 

And because it is hot and thin, it receives "passion" <note>In the sense of "being acted upon" or affected.</note> more readily. In the first book of *Fevers*, it is said to gather for putrefaction more quickly than melancholy. But because it is dry and bitter, it resists putrefaction; and because it is thin, it dissolves more quickly, so its peak does not remain for long. For an impression made on a thin subject is quickly received and quickly lost, just as the autumn air shows. Thus, it afflicts the patient for a shorter time and pauses for a shorter time than the <term>quartan</term> <note>A fever that recurs every third day (four days by inclusive counting).</note>. 

Beyond these humoral factors, one must also consider the **strength of the virtue** <note>The "vital force" or "natural power" of the patient's body to fight disease.</note> and its opposite, along with the "habit" of the body (whether it is porous or dense). One must also consider the disposition of the specific body part that is sending or receiving the fever. From these things, the diversity of the peaks and the rest periods of intermittent fevers can be gathered. 

But concerning the aforementioned, a 

<margin>Strength of the Virtue.</margin>
<margin>Doubt.</margin>
**doubt** arises: for it is said that a great quantity of matter disposes one toward putrefaction, and that things which move are more likely to putrefy. However, the fourth book of the *Meteors* <note>Aristotle's *Meteorology*.</note> contains the contrary: that a large amount putrefies much less than a small amount. Similarly, that which moves and flows putrefies less than that which is stationary. It must be said that both are true. If the matter is abundant and moving, it may allow for **transpiration** <note>Breathing out vapors through the skin.</note>, because in such cases a more intense "preservative virtue" exists. If, however, they lack ventilation, the opposite happens. Similarly, it is true when large and small amounts, or moving and stationary things, are equally disposed or ill-disposed to putrefy—as blood and melancholy demonstrate. If, however, the humor is compared to **extrinsic** factors, it happens in two ways. For they either act as principal agents—such as the celestial bodies—or as instruments, such as the elements. These are assigned in two ways: either by reason of substance or accident. And that is either by quality, quantity, or action. Regarding quality, it must be said that since blood is attributed to the truth, in which heat and moisture reside...

...and these qualities are the cause of movement and flow, especially...

...expanding itself steadily from the center to the circumferences. For heat moves moisture, and because it passes through it as a fast-moving <term>passible</term> <note>Something capable of being acted upon or changed by an external force, in this case, the moisture being affected by heat.</note> substance, it dilates with it and expands toward the exterior parts, so that this motion continues without period until the end. And because 
<margin>Phlegm is cold and moist</margin>
coldness in phlegm is joined to moisture, it hinders its expansive motion for the reasons aforementioned. Yet, because it is a large quantity and susceptible to heat by accident—as in the obstruction it causes—even though its motion is inward, it causes a fever placed at intervals. But because in **choler**, heat is joined with dryness, it must move outward. Dryness, however, hinders the outward motion of the heat, so that a greater interval intervenes than occurs in 
<margin>Melancholy is cold and dry</margin>
phlegm. But because in **melancholy**, coldness is mixed with dryness, since both constrict and draw back toward the internal parts, its flow is slowed so that the rest is greater than the exacerbation; it also lasts longer than the qualities would suggest because of the <term>terrestrial substance</term> <note>The "earthy" nature of melancholy, which makes it heavy and slow to move.</note> in which the impression was made. Just as in choler the duration is less than one might seek, due to the substance being opposite to this. For in this way, such qualities are seen to operate in a living body. If one considers the 
<margin>Motion of the elements</margin>
motion of the elements, the humors will be found to correspond to them in some way. For fire is agitated in its upper part by the motion of the celestial sphere—though not in its entirety, as shown by the ash remaining from a sacrifice found in the following year (referencing the 26th <term>Problem</term> <note>A reference to Aristotle’s *Problems*, specifically Book 26, which discusses wind and weather; the "ash" story refers to altars on high mountains where the air was thought to be so still or the celestial motion so specific that ashes remained undisturbed.</note>). Thus also **choler**, which is attributed to fire, moves for a shorter time than it rests, which is a longer period. And because air exists in continuous motion and agitation—as denoted by the atoms <note>original: "athomi"; referring to dust motes visible in a sunbeam, often used in medieval texts to illustrate the constant movement of air.</note> contained within it—**blood**, which is appropriated to it, will be similarly agitated once it begins to move, until it ceases altogether.

But since water moves less—for it has a motion of ebb and flow, of access and recess, in which a period of rest intervenes (according to the eighth book of the *Physics*)—**phlegm**, which is assigned to it, will move for a longer time through the periods of the ages. And because **melancholy** is proportioned to earth, which moves the least 
as a whole, but rather moves in its parts; whence the 
<margin>The Commentator on the Physics</margin>
**Commentator** <note>original: "Co.dr"; referring to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), known in the West simply as "The Commentator" for his work on Aristotle.</note> on the first book of the *Physics* asks whether the parts near the center of the earth can be moved or not; it will move with difficulty and for a longer time than the other motions, yet its long-lasting motion endures. By reason of its attribution in substance, this is persuasive, because the subtler a humor is, the more mobile it will be—as choler, which does not retain an impression—and the thicker it is, the more resistant to motion, as melancholy demonstrates. This occurs in the elements just as with fire, which, by the subtlety of its substance, follows the motion of the celestial sphere. Regarding the quantity of the humors, this does not admit an exception: for the more they increase, the more mobile and outward-tending they become. In the elements, however, this is due to what was said about fire. But if the humors are reduced simply to the celestial bodies—either to the Moon, with the elemental matter attributed to it, or the 
<margin>If assigned to the celestial bodies / Melancholy to Saturn</margin>
planets—it might then be said to someone that **melancholy** is proportioned to **Saturn** by reason of coldness and dryness and its slow motion. For as the astrologers testify, he moves slowly according to the motion of longitude, which is more natural to him in the East, and similarly according to 

retrograde motion, which is more unnatural to him, for he seems to stay under it for a long time. Thus also melancholy has a long interval even in its proximity. **Choler**, however, is given to **Mars**, who is hot 
and dry, and least of all to the slow Saturn. In Mars, the 
<margin>Comparison of Melancholy / Motion / Choler</margin>
natural motion of longitude is longer, but the retrograde motion is shorter than even in the rest periods of melancholy. **Phlegm** is ascribed to the **Moon**, which is more changeable, cold, and moist. Its motion is precipitate and laborious with little rest, as will be declared in conjunction; therefore, it moves for a longer time through the periods of the ages. **Blood** is principally ascribed to **Jupiter**, who is hot and moist, and to the other planets, since it is the source of life, nourishment, and all nature. And because its motion is continuous—for the Sun never goes retrograde, nor any other like it—its motion stands as continuous. Regarding these three, and the other part of the distinction immediately preceding, 
<margin>Humors similarly also</margin>
it should be known that the humors which are pronounced from the complexional nature of the "sons" <note>This likely refers to the "sons" or "children" of the planets, a common astrological concept where people's temperaments are governed by a dominant planet.</note> by **Haly Abbas** and **Isaac**, are ascribed the qualities of the elements: such as choler being hot and dry, 
proportioned to fire. Yet their substance is adapted more to water, which the resolution of the body shows. For moistures are thinned and become vapors (according to the first book of the *Theorica*); a vapor is moisture cut into tiny pieces of water (according to the first book of *On Simples*). And in the fifth book of Isaac's *On Fevers*, humors are turned into water. Since therefore **phlegm** is 
<margin>Motion of phlegm</margin>
properly water, and the Moon is ascribed to it, it will proportionately have a flow like water. And because in this there coincides rest, access, and recess (as previously noted regarding motion and ebb), in which a mean rest intervenes: for those two direct motions cannot be joined. A similar thing happens in phlegm, for its motion is mostly like 
eighteen hours, while the rest is small, like seven hours. This is explained in detail: for just as in the **Moon**, because of the smallness of its <term>epicycle</term> <note>In the Ptolemaic system, a small circle the planet moves around, while the center of that circle moves around a larger circle (the deferent). This was used to explain complex planetary movements.</note> 
<margin>Note</margin>
and the speed of the Moon's motion within it, stationary points, direction, and retrogradation are not perceived, but rather velocity; yet when it is in the lower part of the epicycle, there is slowness, and in the upper part, speed. Thus also in phlegm, a small and false pause is felt; whence in the first part of the fourth book: "Phlegmatic [fever] is not eradicated, for hidden remnants remain there," which is why in the book *On Fevers* it is not finally purged in the next decline. There are, however, six such hours of rest, because the floods 
of water and moist things universally (as will be shown in Chapter 178) last for such a space. For in the space of six hours, the heavens complete one quarter of their journey. And because phlegm could not follow the motion of the Moon and water entirely in one rotation of the lunar heaven—which is completed in the shorter time of 24 equinoctial hours—it falls short of that motion by almost six hours. For the Moon traverses the sphere by its own motion faster than the Sun itself, and therefore arrives more quickly at the prefixed point. And 
because **melancholy** is least similar to water and the Moon, it

imitates their motion the least. Since it is indisposed to motion and to receiving an impression because of its thick substance and qualities opposed to motion, it requires not only one circulation of the lunar heaven to pass before it is agitated, but two; so that finally, having been long affected by the resolution of the Moon, it is moved in its third circuit.

It is not detained for only six hours like phlegm, nor for forty-eight like melancholy, but occupies a <term>geometric mean</term> <note>A mathematical average. For being subtle, it quickly abandons the impression once it has begun. 

Know indeed that in such matters it is not expedient to investigate entirely precise limits; whence it is said in the third book of *Fevers*: "The most diligent subtlety seems inappropriate." <note>A warning against over-calculating biological processes that have natural variation.</note> Since even water is not more precisely excited by the moon. For motions and conjunctions induce their effect over a longer time, especially those of the superior spheres and planets.

Movement of choler.

For a cause is always joined in time to its effect. Some causes are very distant from the effect, such as a progenitor from the one being generated. Others accompany the effect instantaneously, like illumination accompanies the light-bringer; and some occupy a middle ground, like a sufficient cause that heats something. Upon the removal of such a cause, the heat remains for some time; such is the influence of the moon, the exciter of humors and also of the tides. What supports this even further is the belief that the flux <note>The "flow" or active period of a humor during a fever.</note> and the pause of humors follows the period of the moon—whether 18, 6, 36, 12, 48, or 32 hours—for the six-hour delay of the lunar quarter is always preserved intact. 

Thus it is that the motion of **phlegm** compared to its rest, and the rest of **choler** compared to its motion, preserve a "triple" proportion, just as a <term>diapente diapason</term> <note>An interval in music theory equivalent to an octave plus a fifth (a 3:1 ratio). The author is linking the rhythm of disease to the mathematical "Music of the Spheres."</note> is arranged—though in an inverse manner. For in phlegm, the hours of motion are triple those of rest, while in choler, it is the reverse. The motion of **melancholy** compared to its delay establishes a "double" proportion, from which arises the <term>diapason</term> <note>An octave (a 2:1 ratio).</note> harmony. (Difference 83). 

Since, however, the aforesaid motions do not coincide exactly as defined, it happens because they do not directly follow the motion of the moon, nor are they proportioned to waters that have a manifest flux, but to others. But because **blood** is proportioned to the flux of water, it therefore exists in constant motion, like water, not receiving a distinct period of rest. This is also suited to the air, which exists in great turbulence, both because of the many planets exciting it and because its substance and quality are vehemently <term>passible</term> <note>Sensitive or easily affected by external influences.</note>. This makes it difficult to judge: whence in the third book of *Crises* <note>Referring to Galen’s work on the "critical days" of an illness.</note> it is said that it is not easy to assign a cause why in acute diseases the crisis is usually near every third day, but in chronic ones every day or on the fourth. 

But a doubt emerges in these premises, because the Commentator <note>Likely Averroes, the primary commentator on Aristotle.</note> in the first and third books, and Aristotle <note>Abbreviated as "Au." for "Autor" or "Auctoritas," usually referring to Aristotle.</note> in the *Book of Animals*, said that the nature of the moon communicates with the nature of the earth because of the defect of light within itself.

It should be said that the moon relates to both, yet water is proportioned to it perhaps more by nature and motion (as its actions show), while earth is proportioned to it by opacity, but not so much by action. 

Regarding the fourth point: To the first it should be said that although blood does not flow periodically, nevertheless other humors can flow intermittently. For there is a particular cause why blood cannot flow in this way, even though blood is plentiful; yet when it "sins" <note>An old medical term for a humor being out of balance or "corrupted."</note>, nature is more angry against it, since the offense is graver the closer the offender is to the heart. Nor is the place of the blood wide enough to allow for the flux required according to Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a famous Persian astrologer.</note>, even if it is deep and long. Or perhaps someone will sense that blood *does* have a period, but it is not perceived because of its greater motion; for small motions are hidden by larger ones. As noted in *On Sleep and Waking* and *On the Sense and the Sensible*: a greater motion always drives out a smaller one. 

It should also be said that the motion of a humor here is not proportioned to the elements as they received them from their "generator," but from some

According to Albabricius <note>Likely Al-Battani (c. 858–929), the astronomer.</note>, the moon gives its disposition to all other planets—that is, it renders itself ready to receive the power of all planets. Saturn, however, is opposed to the moon in this. Humors also, as shown, resemble in some way the apparent particular motions, rests, and natures of the planets. 

And know that such flux and motion is "natural" by a more universal nature (such as the moon), although it implies a certain "violence" or disruption to the particular nature of the water or the humors themselves, as appeared in Distinction 15.

To the other objection, it should be said that the impulse comes from the "inferior" nature of the body, which is disposed to receive the power of the "superior" celestial bodies; the planets act as the primordial cause impressing that power. The superior bodies do not act formally, but "effectively." To the other point, it should be said that when someone is sick, the humors and the "complexion" <note>The specific balance of humors in an individual.</note> which serve as the instrument of the soul are so distracted that they do not obey the principal agent (the soul). Instead, they withdraw from its rule of their own accord and are subjected to another, superior nature. 

To the other point, it should be said that not only heat and windiness are required for motion, but also many other factors involving both the medium and the agent. <meta>This page continues the scholastic medical debate regarding the nature of humors and their movements. This page transitions into a specific "Distinction" regarding the fevers generated by blood.</meta>

...only so much as to place it under the nature of a humor. For the human body is a fluid thing. Similarly, if it does not move according to the whole earth or the parts near the center, other distant parts nevertheless move successively by the motion of the **eighth sphere** <note>In medieval cosmology, the eighth sphere was the "Firmament" or the sphere of the fixed stars, which influenced the cycles of the earthly world.</note>, as was said in Distinction 16. Neither is choler <note>original: "colera," referring to yellow bile</note> opposed to it by reason of the substance of water, as is clearly declared.

### DISTINCTION LXXXIX.

<margin>1</margin>
**Hippocrates**, in the fourth part of the first book, shows—against the introduction of **Galen**—that putrefying blood generates a **sanguine fever** and not a choleric or any other kind. Again, according to **Johannicius** <note>Johannicius (Hunayn ibn Ishaq) was a 9th-century scholar whose "Isagoge" was a fundamental medical textbook.</note>, there are four simple and singular modes of putrefaction. The first occurs from the putrefaction of blood, burning both the interior and exterior parts, such as is the case with *synochus* <note>original: "synochus," a technical term for a continuous fever caused by putrefying blood.</note>; the second, and so forth. Furthermore, others state that the species of fevers arising from corrupted humors are four: *sinocha* <note>a fever caused by blood overheating without putrefying</note>, *amfimeria* <note>a daily fever caused by phlegm</note>, *tritea* <note>a tertian or every-other-day fever caused by choler</note>, and *tetratea* <note>a quartan fever occurring every three days, caused by melancholy</note>. However, the humors are only four.

<margin>2</margin>
Likewise, in the third book on Crises: A fever is concluded which the Greeks name *sinochus*; it is that which remains from its beginning until the hour of the **crisis** <note>The "crisis" was the turning point of a disease, where the body's nature either overcame the illness or succumbed to it.</note>, according to the likeness of a single disposition, in which there is no apparent increase or decrease, but it remains equal through all days. But if the blood were to turn into choler, there would be a manifest increase and decrease, because choler moves in a tertian cycle <note>occurring every third day</note>, even if it produces a continuous fever—except perhaps in the case of a *causon* <note>a "burning fever" associated with intense heat and bile</note>, which is not a fever of this kind. Furthermore, putrefying blood generates either a sanguine fever (which is the intent here) or some other kind, but certainly not a **phlegmatic** one,
<margin>3</margin>
since blood does not turn into phlegm. For that which is cooked or roasted cannot become raw again <note>A common scholastic analogy: phlegm was considered "raw" or "undigested" blood, while blood was "cooked" humor. Just as you cannot un-cook meat, blood cannot revert to phlegm.</note>, as stated in the first book of *Theory* and the third of the *Collections*. Nor does it generate a **quartan fever**, because that is caused by the "incineration" <note>the drying out or "burning to ash"</note> of the humors left behind after putrefaction, even when extraneous moisture arrives. Indeed, the inquiry into putrefaction implies this. Similarly, it does not generate a **choleric** fever, such as a tertian; for in this case, the blood would change into choler, either through an excessive "decoction" of blood in the liver—which does not induce a fever in this way—or through putrefaction generated from blood. But since putrefaction precedes this kind of generation and is joined and immediate to the fever itself, the fever will be sanguine before the blood turns into choler.
<margin>First, general</margin>
And as for the choleric fever, **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> says: Putrefaction does not have a fixed time, and the turning of blood into choler does not happen except in time. Furthermore, when choler is formed, that motion and transition into another state—inducing a change by its heat and sustaining it with dryness—suggests that its putrefaction would not generate a choleric fever, but rather a **melancholic** one. Therefore, if that which seems less likely is present, that which is more likely is also present. But choler, being agile and changeable, produces a tertian fever and not a melancholic one. And putrefying blood will generate a continuous sanguine fever and not a choleric one. Furthermore, that fever is seen to be sanguine for which the cure is applied as for a sanguine sickness, in the book inscribed **To Glaucon** <note>Galen’s *Ad Glauconem de medendi methodo*, a famous therapeutic manual.</note>, which distinguishes the species of *sinocha* under all existing conditions. To evacuate the multitude of blood, he prescribes a great evacuation of blood, taken especially according to strength and age.

---

Indeed, in the ninth book of the *Therapeutics*, two young freemen and a servant are introduced, one of whom suffered from an inflammatory *sinocha* without putrefaction, and the other from a *synochus* with putrefaction; for both, he ordered blood to be evacuated until **syncope** <note>original: "lypotomia," meaning fainting from bloodletting. This was a radical but standard treatment to "reset" the body's heat.</note>. Since, therefore, such a great extraction is proper to a sanguine disease—for it is not so expedient in a choleric, melancholic, or phlegmatic disease to extract blood, let alone so much—it follows that putrefying blood produces a sanguine fever and no other.
<margin>4</margin>
The opposite of this is also found in the *Book of Crises* and the *Book of Fevers*. **Avenzoar** <note>original: "Az." (Ibn Zuhr), a famous Arab physician.</note> says that when blood putrefies sufficiently, its subtle part turns into choler, from which a choleric fever is generated and not a sanguine one. The gross part, however, turns into melancholy. For when something putrefies, two parts arise in it: the gross and the subtle. Blood especially splits when it putrefies;
<margin><unclear>symbol</unclear></margin>
here indeed red choler is made, and there black bile, according to the *Book of Fevers*. And this is confirmed, for in the aforementioned *Book of Crises* it is necessary to add to the discourses that there are three universal kinds of fevers which are kindled in putrefied matters. For some consist in **red choler** (and these are very many), some in **black bile**, and others in **phlegm**. Again, humors are the "children" of the elements. Since blood is the "child" and proportioned to **air**—and air, among the other elements, is the most alterable and changeable (Distinctions 14 and 16)—blood, being more changeable than other humors, will not remain within its own limits when putrefying, but will rather turn into other humors. And this is confirmed because blood among the humors is the only one that is sweet. But that which is of this kind, when it overheats and inflames, quickly changes into choler. And for this reason, they forbid giving sweets in fevers, especially choleric ones. Furthermore, if putrefying blood remained blood and did not turn into choler, its sickness could not be cured, since we lack a medicine that specifically "evacuates" blood <note>Blood could be removed by bleeding (surgery), but there was no internal drug (pharmacy) that specifically purged blood like there were purges for bile.</note>. For **Galen** relates in his book on pharmacy that he brought in a presiding judge with his eyes bound—lest he reveal it to others—to hang a man who knew a medicine for evacuating blood. For this reason, putrefying blood will generate another sickness or fever and not a sanguine one. Regarding this, one must first know what blood is made of with other humors (shown in Distinctions 33 and 34), and what putrefaction and fever are (Distinctions 159 and 187).
<margin>5</margin>
A fever of blood, whether it arises from inflammation (like *sinocha*) or from putrefaction (like *synochus*),
<margin>6</margin>
has three modes, according to the ninth book on the *Nature of Fevers* and the seventh of the *Collections*. One is "equal," called *homotenos* in Greek; just as it begins, so it remains until its stationary period, since it is resolved equally to that which boiled over and putrefied. This is the greatest and most dangerous, as stated in the first book **To Glaucon**. Another is "augmatic" or "increasing," growing continuously from the beginning to its peak. For it evaporates less in smoke than it inflames and putrefies. And the third is "paugmatic" or "decreasing," the opposite of the middle case. Generally, however, these are adapted to the *synochus* made from the putrefaction of blood, which according to **Galen** is the *synoche* that is now generated, as well as the other putrid fevers according to **Johannicius**.

<meta>This page continues a detailed scholastic debate on humoral pathology, specifically focusing on whether blood can cause a fever through putrefaction. It follows the previous page's introduction of fevers like synochus and the classification of humors, now moving into a direct confrontation between the theories of Galen and Avicenna.</meta>

And so I perceived. Truly, to understand this matter, one must first know what the moderns have said about it, and thereafter the ancients. For the sake of the first part, know that several thinkers on both sides of the question have hesitated to assign a response because of the "crime" <note>likely referring to a scholarly error or a controversial stance</note> of **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."</note> himself or **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note>, perhaps not knowing the way of truth. Or perhaps they did not dare to choose a side concerning that which has hitherto been considered difficult, but rather excused themselves, saying it is not the place of literate men to settle disputes, but rather to quiet them and bury them with honor. Others, however, declared that they themselves were not judges between **Galen** and **Avicenna**, nor did they wish to take a side, but rather that it was sufficient to present what had been brought forward for each side. 

Concerning this matter, it should be known that the speeches of almost all physicians agree indistinctly that putrefying blood generates a sanguine fever. These include **Serapion**, **Rhazes**, **Haly Abbas**, **Alexander [Trallianus]**, **Isaac [Israeli]**, and especially **Avicenna**. **Galen** also felt this in the ninth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." referring to Galen's 'De Methodo Medendi'</note>, saying that in a young man suffering from a fever during the night, a *synochus* <note>a continuous fever caused by blood</note> was made from the putrefaction of blood on the third night; nor in others was it made more severe on the third night, although it was less than the first, with the fever being in a paroxysmal <note>original: "paumastica," referring to the peak of the fever</note> or declining state. Therefore, the blood was not turned into choler <note>yellow bile</note>, causing a choleric fever and not a sanguine one. **Avicenna**, however, passes over **Galen** here for free; for it is not enough for him to reasonably rebuke him, but he even claims his speech contains a lie. And he brings up a similar point in the ninth book on *Animals* <note>likely referring to Aristotle's 'History of Animals' as commented on by medieval scholars</note>, saying that he [Galen] did half-work for everything, and that he knew much about the branches but was ignorant of the roots of science. This sequence begins in the fourth book.

<margin>p. 4</margin>
**Galen's** opinion is that a fever of blood does not happen from its putrefaction, because when blood putrefies, it becomes choler, and it does not remain blood. Thus, it becomes a choleric fever and not a sanguine one. It becomes *causos* <note>a "burning fever" associated with yellow bile</note> and a tertian fever <note>a fever that peaks every third day/every other day</note>, and he treats it with the cure for *causos* and tertian fever. Thereafter, **Avicenna**, attacking this speech, says it is contrary to **Hippocrates** <note>original: "ypocrate"</note> and does not agree with the truth. For he assumes this opinion: "When blood putrefies, it becomes choler." And he says that a double understanding can be taken from this. One is that after the putrefaction has already happened, the blood turns into choler. The other is that this happens within the very process of putrefaction, as the name implies here more an alteration and a putrefying. However, he attacks this double understanding of the aforementioned opinion in multiple ways: the first in three ways. Since when blood putrefies, the conversion is not only into choler, but its thick part turns into melancholy <note>black bile</note>; therefore, it would not only become a choleric fever but also a melancholic one. Furthermore, the consideration we intend is in the *becoming* of putrefaction, not in the *already being* of it, which happens after the process is finished. For putrefaction in its *becoming* is the cause of fever, not in its *finished state*. Also, it is not necessary that if choler is made after the putrefaction of blood, that it is [already] putrefied and causes fever; since from a putrid thing, something is generated that is not putrid, as appears in the generation of worms from dung <note>a common medieval belief in spontaneous generation used here as a logical analogy</note>. Thus, the understanding is false which denotes that blood, when it putrefies, that is—

<margin>From a putrid thing is generated that which is not putrid, or worms from dung.</margin>

---

—after the putrefaction has occurred, is converted into choler. I say
<margin>Saving Galen.</margin>
also that **Galen** himself held this understanding, since fever is a sickness that is in the process of becoming putrid, not one already completed. Nor should it be said, as for the first point, that the thick earthly part is naturally suited to produce a melancholic fever just as the subtle fiery part produces a choleric one; for there is little of the humors that becomes earthly. This is shown by the burning of wood, where most of it evaporates and only a little subsides at the end of the fevers. The earthly part is also small in relation to that which smokes off and turns into choler; for choler is much further removed from melancholy than the latter is from blood. Truly, the second understanding—that in the very process of putrefying, blood converts into choler—he [Avicenna] similarly devalues in three ways. First, **Hippocrates** says that the fever of blood arises from its putrefaction, and this truth is sound. Again, putrefaction is a path toward corruption, but putrefaction does not have "time" <note>in the Aristotelian sense of a duration of change</note>. But the conversion of blood into choler happens in time. He wishes to hold, therefore, that since putrefaction precedes the conversion of blood into choler and is itself the immediate and perfect cause of fever, that before the conversion of blood into choler, the fever will be sanguine. Furthermore, it is similar for blood and other humors; for other humors, when they putrefy, remain the same, and generate fevers proportional to themselves. For example, putrefied phlegm is called phlegm and induces a phlegmatic fever. And so it is with choler and melancholy. Nor do they turn into one another except after the completion of putrefaction. For which reason, blood is also putrefied, and it will be blood, and it will cause a sanguine fever. A subtle supporter of **Galen** and **Avicenna** here, whoever considers the understanding and attends more to the truth, will be able to briefly remove the arguments introduced by **Avicenna** for the destruction of the second understanding of the premise. And first, regarding the authority of **Hippocrates**, what must be said
<margin>Solution of the article by me...</margin>
will appear in the response. To the other point, which says that putrefaction does not have time, but the conversion of blood into choler does, the adversary will say that this does not contain the truth, according to the perceptive understanding of **Avicenna**: because putrefaction or "putrefying" is a certain alteration, just as the name indicates an action. Alteration and action, while the subject remains, occur in time, according to the fifth book of the *Physics* and the first book of *On Generation* <note>Aristotelian texts fundamental to medieval science</note>. 
<margin>(manicule symbol)</margin>
Nor will the antagonist say that the conversion of blood into choler has time, but rather happens in an instant, because that is "generation" <note>the technical term for a sudden change of form</note>; and generation happens in an instant according to the same texts, since it is the giving of a substantial form. For a substantial form is indivisible, and everything that moves and alters is divisible. In this, indeed, alteration differs from generation: because alteration happens in time while the subject remains. Generation, however, happens in an instant, a total transformation of this whole into that whole, according to the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. This, too, any supporter of **Avicenna** cannot truly prohibit, unless **Avicenna** says that he takes "alteration" improperly, so that he calls the short time preceding it "generation" and says it does not have time. Because that which is temperate is reduced to a nearly point-like state due to the homogeneity of its parts, and because of the contrariety it has with the extremes, it is more liable and quicker to be changed. I testify also that Avicenna <note>original: "A."</note> did not sufficiently consider these things, and he found Galen’s <note>original: "Ga."</note> speech suspicious, and therefore more readily condemned it. So that this may be apparent, let his words finally be brought forward so that his intention and understanding may be had more clearly. 

In the Second Book on Fevers, no investigation is worse than this: whether, just as in other humors fevers arise from putrefaction, it is also so in putrefied blood. In such dispositions, blood is corrupted for a twofold reason: first, because it does not transpire <note>breathe out/evaporate</note>; and second, because it is not retained by nature—that is, in its proper place; for just as the place is, so does nature operate. Things that contain these two conditions within themselves must necessarily be corrupted, as appears most especially in fruits and seeds, and in blood situated outside its own place. # Distinction 6a

<margin>Galen, *On Fevers*, Books 3, 4, and at the end.</margin>
...there is only one cause of putrefaction <note>the process of humors decaying or "rotting" within the body to produce heat</note>: namely, prohibited transpiration <note>the inability of the body to release vapors through the skin</note>. For in this case, the blood remains in its own place because it does not strike out vehemently toward inflammation and putrefaction. It can putrefy moderately for some time and generate a sanguine fever <note>a fever caused by blood</note> without being immediately transformed into choler <note>yellow bile</note>; hence the origin of these fevers. In any case, without paroxysms <note>the periodic "attacks" or peaks of a fever</note>, no specific part of the body is particularly affected in these patients. But the humors that are found throughout the arteries and veins—especially those in the largest and hottest vessels—ignite into fevers either due to some other cause (such as an external factor) or due to bubbling putrefaction. These produce a single *synocha* <note>a continuous, non-intermittent fever</note> that does not cease from beginning to end, remaining and burning the person until the humors generating the fever are consumed, digested, or both. It appears, therefore, from this sequence that the author did not believe blood must always be corrupted into choler, as was suggested in the previous arguments. This is shown because in such cases, signs of putrefaction appeared on the first day of recognition; sometimes on the third, and occasionally on the fourth, according to the ninth book of Galen’s *Therapeutics* <note>original: "nono terapētice"</note>. And thus, the blood remains for a long time under the state of fever before it converts into a choleric state. Indeed, this lasts throughout the illness if signs of putrefaction do not appear, until the fourth day or

at most, until it terminates on the fourth day. Thus, I propose that in this disposition—for example, in a fever that ought to terminate on the seventh day—for three or four days, that putrefying blood will remain largely under the form of blood and will induce a sanguine fever. In the following days, however, as it becomes more overheated and putrid, it gradually converts into choler and generates a choleric fever. If, perhaps, the characteristic movements of "tertian" choler <note>a fever that peaks every third day, associated with yellow bile</note> are not perceived, it happens because the

it is no wonder if the movement is continuous. But if the putrefying blood is contained *outside* the veins, then two causes of putrefaction occur: namely, prohibited transpiration and the fact that it is not being retained by nature in its proper place, but is instead poured out into the "belly" <note>likely referring to a body cavity or the core</note>. There, putrefying further and faster, it converts into choler and generates a choleric fever. This mode of the "settling" of blood was seen in the previous sections. Galen seems to have intended this in the second book of *On Fevers*. Hence, in the ninth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "ix. de i'ge." (De Ingenio Sanitatis)</note>: if putrefaction

<margin>...on the Method of Healing.</margin>
is present either from the very beginning or shortly thereafter throughout the universal veins—and especially the large ones—the putrefaction generates *synoche*, that is, continuous fevers. In these, no distinct increase or decrease of the exacerbation <note>the peak of the fever</note> appears, which is a specific property of blood. For phlegm moves every day; choler from the third day to the third day; and melancholy <note>black bile</note> from the fourth day to the fourth day. But blood moves continuously and uniformly because of its containment within the veins and its large quantity

which seeks the heart continuously. He adds again: if blood is located in a single part of the animal, it produces those fevers that are exacerbated according to a certain paroxysm, such as the tertian fever. In such a case, the blood—due to the aforementioned causes—converts more easily and quickly into choler. Being situated in such a disposition, after putrefying for the first day (or a little more or less), it converts into choler and finally causes a tertian fever. And because Galen, as introduced before, was speaking more with this understanding, he said that overheated blood beginning to putrefy is transformed into "instant" choler. However, he does not deny that a sanguine fever can be generated in such a state at the very beginning of the putrefaction.

<margin>HALY ABBAS, *Theoretical Medicine*, Book 8</margin>
That he wished a sanguine fever to arise from the putrefaction of blood is confirmed by his most faithful interpreter, Haly Abbas <note>an influential 10th-century Persian physician</note>, in the eighth book of his *Theoretical Medicine*. For Haly Abbas, along with Johannitius <note>the Latin name for Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a famous translator and physician</note>, also says that there are four putrid fevers made from the putrefaction of the four humors: namely, that the continuous sanguine fever called *synocha* is made from the putrefaction of blood. This shows that just as a putrid fever is categorized according to its beginning and its starting point, and a "hectic" fever <note>a chronic fever affecting the solid parts of the body</note> according to its end point (which are fevers differing in kind), much more so can fevers that share the same genus consist of the same humor. Thus, by another way, there is permutation and transduction <note>transformation</note>. Thus, considering subtly Galen's *On Fevers*, in both the disposition and the location of the blood, it does not remain blood for long, but is changed into choler. Because a "pure" and "true" sanguine fever does not persist, he finally said that putrefying blood is converted into choler and its [subsequent] fever. Thus is the correct intention of Galen explained, which Avicenna <note>original: "Au."</note> imitates. And afterwards, Avicenna is criticized, who perhaps with his "satirical" <note>sharp or biting</note> understanding looked only at one side: wishing with his

<margin>Against Avicenna.</margin>
"lion's tooth" <note>a metaphor for a sharp, aggressive critique</note> to tear apart the truth-telling Galen, even though in many places he confesses himself to be Galen's interpreter. A contradiction is thus committed. Regarding the fourth point: to the authority

To the other point, it must be said: just as a *causon* fever does not perceptibly receive decrease or increase because the matter is situated in places near the heart, so it is with *synocha*, due to the quantity of its power, the weight of the humor, and the great amount of putrid smoke <note>vapors believed to rise from rotting humors</note> continuously seeking the heart, so that the diversity in it is minimally manifest. To the other point, it must be said that putrefying blood indeed generates a sanguine fever, as has appeared elsewhere. For putrefying matter can be considered in three ways: either at the very beginning of putrefaction, and thus it generates a sanguine fever; or in the middle of putrefaction, and then it makes a choleric fever (as held previously); or finally at the end, and thus it induces a quartan fever <note>a fever peaking every fourth day, associated with melancholy</note>.
