<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of blood and its role in generating fevers. It specifically addresses the debate over whether bloodletting (phlebotomy) is performed solely to remove excess blood or to clear out other corrupted humors that have mixed with it. It also begins a new "Distinction" (Distinction 90) concerning the "composition" or mixing of different types of fevers within a single patient.</meta>

...toward motion, and especially local motion, because blood, by its own lightness and heat, is inclined toward the motion of alteration—namely, toward putrefaction <note>the process where a humor "decays" and generates unnatural heat</note>. For as long as it remains blood, it is more prone to change than other humors, since putrefaction thrives on the hot and the moist, which is the very nature of blood. Furthermore, when blood changes toward choler <note>yellow bile</note>, it approaches the nature of fever; but when it retreats toward melancholy <note>black bile</note>, it moves away from that nature. 

Regarding another point, it must be said that although [the previous argument] brings much truth, it nonetheless includes some falsehood. For phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> is not sought solely because of the blood itself, but also sometimes because of other humors that are abundant alongside the blood, as appears in the eighth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." refers to Galen’s *De Ingenio Sanitatis* or *Methodus Medendi*</note>, in the third part of the first chapter. Nevertheless, a "evacuation" <note>the removal of humors</note> is not sought as much in these cases as it is when blood alone, or primarily blood, is at fault. Regarding the authorities of Galen brought to the contrary, it has already been shown how they are to be understood. 

Indeed, I grant the subsequent reasoning and its confirmation with them. For it is certain that blood, due to its great aptitude for putrefaction, can eventually be converted into choler and be transformed into a tertian fever <note>a fever that peaks every third day, typically associated with yellow bile</note>. Or it must be said that there are three types of simple fevers subdivided into continuous and intermittent; hence in the second book on *Crises*: there are three types of simple fevers, each of which first falls into two differences: they will either be continuous or intermittent. However, in this subdivision of fevers, blood—since it is always continuous—does not admit to every division. Also, because it possesses the larger veins, it cannot be associated with those three types [of intermittent fevers]. And for this reason, Galen did not provide the signs for recognizing sanguine fevers <note>fevers caused by blood</note> there. 

Or, better yet: his intention there was not, as he says, to show many and unmanifest <note>hidden or hard to detect</note> intentions of fevers, but rather a few manifest ones for the sake of practice. Indeed, the intentions of sanguine fevers were of very difficult recognition; hence in the second book of *On Fevers*: "In the remaining matters, there was certainly no investigation worse than this one." This also appears in the books on *Internal Fevers* and *On the Parts of Fever Types* regarding crises. 

To the final point, it must be said: although one might try to conclude the proposal, it could nonetheless be challenged in some way, even granted that bloodletting is a known medicine among some, yet it is performed among others—or will be known—in Distinction 144. Or, to speak more kindly, phlebotomy is owed not only to a "sin of quantity" <note>having too much blood</note> but also to a "sin of quality"—namely, the malice or corruption of the blood—or both, although not as properly as to the sin of quantity. This is also sufficiently hinted at in the ninth book of *On the Method of Healing*, Distinction 175.

...for their forms are similar. But a sanguine abscess <note>original: "apā," likely *apostema*</note> is composed with others, such as with a choleric one and others, according to the [book on] *Crises* and the 14th book of *On the Method of Healing*. Again, if it causes a sickness or fever, that which is less inclined by nature to do this—namely blood, which is described by Galen and Isaac as "familiar" and a "son of nature"—will be much more likely to cause that which nature does not love as much. For a humor does not putrefy unless it is abandoned by the governance of nature, according to the first and second books of *On Fevers*. Therefore, when it has putrefied and caused a fever, the other humors that were ruled by it will also putrefy and cause a fever. 
<note>The scribe repetitively writes about the putrefaction of choler and humors.</note>
Thus, a sanguine fever is composed <note>mixed</note> with other fevers. 

The opposite of this is also shown: that in almost none of the authors is a sanguine fever found to be composed with other fevers. Furthermore, such a composition would be either by composition or by mixture, which cannot be. For just as blood covers, colors, and magnifies other similar humors, so also its putrefaction will attract to itself that which is of putrefaction or of the strangeness of other humors. Or, regarding "vicinity" <note>proximity</note>, they are not placed together according to the book *On Crises* and the 8th book of the *Theoretical Medicine*, except in these two ways; but this cannot happen here. For there, and in the second book of *On Fevers*, it is said that they are not composed except a quotidian <note>daily</note> with a tertian, or with a quartan, or in whatever other way they are joined together. Therefore, since it is not stated that a sanguine fever is composed with other fevers, and that it is sufficient to give itself [as a cause], a sanguine fever will not be composed with others.

<margin>Opposition.</margin>
<margin>Part 4.</margin>

Regarding the first point, it must be known what a fever is, and what a sanguine fever is, and of what sort; the aforementioned question has taught this. The composition of fevers is explained first in reality and then by name. In the fourth part and Distinction 87, the composition of fevers exists in three ways: one in a "remote genus," another in "proximity," and the third in "species." In the "remote genus," for example, a hectic fever is composed with a putrid one. In "proximity," for example, when fevers caused by different humors are composed with one another, such as a quotidian with a tertian or with a quartan. In "species," such as when one tertian is composed with another, or a quartan with a quartan, or a phlegmatic with a phlegmatic. And such a composition of these last two modes—although this happens most in the second [book]—will be either by mixture or by vicinity and affinity, as touched upon by Galen and Haly Abbas, with Avicenna. 

I call it "composition by mixture" when two different materials causing a fever are composed into one. This can be "much," such as phlegm with choler or melancholy; or "less," such as one species of choler with another (like "citrine" yellow bile with "vitelline" egg-yolk bile), or sweet phlegm with sour or tasteless phlegm, and the like. And such a composition will be either inside the vessels, as in two continuous fevers, or outside, as in intermittent ones. "Composition by vicinity," however, is when two different materials (according to the [second] mode) or the same (according to the third) are composed inside the vessels and outside, causing fevers so that one causes a continuous fever and the other an intermittent one.

# Other [discussions] concerning composite fevers according to seven modes

<margin>Communicating, subintrane, coalternating.</margin>
**Furthermore**, the mode of composition of these fevers is threefold. Either one fever is mixed with another in a **communicating** way, a **subintrane** way, or a **coalternating** way. It is called *communicating* when two or more fevers begin at the same time. It is *subintrane* <note>from the Latin 'subintrare', meaning to enter under or overlap</note> when one arrives before the previous one has separated from the patient. It is *coalternating* when another arrives after the preceding one has been eradicated, as soon as the first is gone. Finally, according to this distinction, one must note that some of the aforementioned compositions have specific names, while others lack names. Some are named by their general class—such as a composition of a hectic fever <note>a chronic, wasting fever</note> with a putrid fever—and others by their proximity, such as a phlegmatic fever with a quartan <note>a fever recurring every third day, associated with melancholy</note>. Likewise, some are named by their species, such as phlegm with phlegm, or choler <note>yellow bile</note> with choler. 

According to their specific character, one is called the **semitertian** fever <note>original: "emitritea," a hybrid fever involving both a continuous and an intermittent cycle</note>. Regarding this name, writers have varied. Indeed, some of the more unlearned have said the semitertian is a fever whose material is phlegm putrefying both inside and outside the vessels. This contradicts the very logic of the name, since "semitertian" denotes a "half-tertian," from *emis* <note>Greek: hemi</note> which is "half" and *triteus* which is "third," which is not found in the aforementioned phlegmatic definition. <margin>Agathinus? Azarain?</margin> **Agathinus** <note>a 1st-century Greek physician</note>, however, seems to call all fevers that exceed tertians "semitertians," so that he admits the semitertian is of the same genus as the tertian, and they differ only in the magnitude of their proximity. Therefore, because he does not preserve the logic of the name as the earlier authors did, he is in error. And since such qualities of names are better known than the things themselves, **Galen** says: "I disdain to linger on them." 

<margin>Minor, medium, major.</margin> There are others saying there are three types of semitertian: the minor, the medium, and the major. They claim the minor occurs when phlegm putrefies internally and choler putrefies externally. <margin>semitertian... phlegm</margin> The medium is external, while the minor is when melancholy putrefies internally and <margin>phlegm</margin> choler putrefies externally. According to these authors, the semitertian requires phlegm in the vessels and choler outside. Better than that, or rather the opposite: the worst humor is the larger one that cooks on the outside.

Others, however, moved by the words of **Galen** and **Aurelius**, say there are three modes of semitertian: namely the medium, the major, and the minor. The medium is that which is joined to a tertian; the major is joined to a quartan; and the minor to a quotidian <note>a fever recurring daily</note>. There are others who call themselves "moderns" who agree with these in number but differ entirely in the manner of their explanation. For they claim a minor semitertian occurs when the choler is inside the vessels and the phlegm is outside; the medium is the reverse; and the major is when the choler is inside and melancholy is outside. These people, trying to uphold the aforementioned motions, strive to build their argument on certain probabilities. But because they draw these from many sources perhaps not correctly ascribed to the wise men and Galen, and since such a dispute concerns names rather than things, it should be set aside as foolish. The more illustrious of the physicians—among whom stand **Galen**, **Serapion**, and **Haly Abbas**, and both **Avicenna** and **Isaac**—seem to posit only two species of semitertian: the pure (or certain) and the non-pure. They call it "pure" when it is made of phlegm putrefying within and choler without. The "non-pure" is, according to Serapion, the opposite; or according to some, when phlegm remains outside and choler inside.

<margin>Semitertian which is similarly made of blood</margin>
...or both are outside, or both inside, which is false. For a semitertian is a continuous and "horrid" fever—that is, one in which for the most part "horrors" <note>shivers or tremors</note> are present, mixed from cold and rigor. According to the first book of *Epidemics*, the first type is not found when both are outside, nor according to him when both are inside the fevers. Thus, there is a composition according to proximity, in which the composition of crises and fevers is placed fourfold: namely, when choler and phlegm are both inside or both outside, or with choler inside and phlegm outside, or vice versa. This can happen in three ways in these last two modes: either the choler and phlegm are equal (and thus it is a certain semitertian), or the choler exceeds the phlegm (and thus it is uncertain). <margin>Choler with Melancholy</margin> Choler also composes with melancholy in eight modes of composition, two of which will naturally have the nature of the triple semitertian. Additionally, phlegm and melancholy can be coupled in the four aforementioned modes, yet none of these will constitute a semitertian, since it requires at least a tertian arising from choler. Because of this, they remain silent on that point. There are others who call every composite fever a semitertian, though improperly and commonly. But the proper and truer view to be held is what those last mentioned said. And because such an investigation is more about the name than the thing, **Avicenna** says with **Galen** that this is not among those matters in which one should be vehemently occupied.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some superficial writers said that a fever of blood <note>sanguine fever</note> is composed indifferently with other fevers from putrefaction, whether inside the vessels or outside. They were moved by this because it seemed to them that other humors have an affinity with blood, just as others putrefy in turn, and especially because blood is most prepared for putrefaction. Furthermore, they think the same happens in fevers as happens in abscesses, for abscesses are composed of blood with others. This composition is quite erroneous and unarticulated, nor does their validity appear in the following reasoning. There were others saying similar things, but adding that a fever of other humors is hidden by a sanguine fever. They try to confirm this from **Isaac** at the end of his book on fevers. In saying this, they fail just as the first ones did, perhaps even if they are wise, because they split the eternal teaching on suffering. Furthermore, there is no disease or fever that does not sensibly harm the [bodily] operations, since this is of the very nature of disease and fever; whence **Johannitius** <note>the Latinized name of Hunayn ibn Ishaq</note> says: "It harms by its effect." And **Avicenna** says: "It hinders operation so that it is restrained." For just as a little water mixed with much wine should not be called water, nor a mixture of both, but wine—and is even called "pure" because it has such a small mixture—similarly, according to the *Prognostics*, other fevers will not be permanent when they occur with a sanguine fever. <margin>Not another [type] here, a mode of composition by name and foreign</margin> There are other modern writers expressing that a fever of blood is composed only with a fever of choler. And they do not see how to adapt it to others. They posit a threefold mode of composition and a triple name, according to what is said in the fourteenth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio," referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note> regarding abscesses mixed from choler and...

However, their discourse, because it is not fully explained, can have a double interpretation: either that this composition of fever—blood with a choler fever—arises from choler pre-existing with the blood (which I think they mean), or from choler generated from the blood through its **putrefaction** <note>the medieval medical theory that fevers are caused by humors "rotting" or breaking down</note>, since it was said previously that blood is converted into choler when it putrefies. The first interpretation, however, cannot stand, as will be shown in the third part of the discussion.

Furthermore, either the putrefaction of the choler precedes, and thus it increases over the putrefaction of the blood; and since the putrefying blood is converted into choler, then the conversion into choler will happen mostly because of the choler. And thus, it would be a fever of choler and not of blood. Or, the blood precedes and its putrefaction increases over the putrefaction of the choler, and then the putrefaction of the blood will draw everything to itself, which is the putrefaction of the choler; especially since choler is easily moved. Nor can an equal composition of blood and choler stand, since blood greatly surpasses choler. Also, humors are very quickly

**Note on the pulse.**
</margin>

changeable. Regarding the third point, it must first be known that almost no **Greek** or **Arab** author has stated that a fever of blood is coupled with others. This also appeared through their words introduced concerning the composition of fevers. **Galen**, in the third book of *On Fevers*, says: "The fever which consists in the blood is simpler than those which are in the other humors." He adds finally that it is not possible for a putrefaction of blood to occur according to one part and something else according to another, unless an inflammation <note>original: "flegmon," from the Greek *phlegmonē*</note> collecting there determines the humor beginning to putrefy. 

However, in the fourth book, Galen offered a certain discourse on this composition as if in flight: "It seems," says Galen, "that a fever of blood is not composed with the remaining fevers, because when putrefaction is in the blood, it is common to all humors." And in this, there is a contradiction to some of his own intentions, in which it is not necessary for us to lengthen our discourse, because it does not help with common usage; since he himself observes what are the senses, but here elsewhere he does not perceive blood to be mixed with fevers, even if the intellect perhaps perceives it. 

<margin>
**Galen, 2nd leaf.**
</margin>

That contradiction of Galen's is perhaps what he stated in the third book of *On Fevers*: "If the virtue <note>the body's vital power or strength</note> is weak, it will be the cause so that not only superfluities, but even the blood itself is corrupted and putrefies and kindles a fever. And then another principle will effect the periods of the paroxysms <note>the cycles of fever fits</note>; and if the predicted heat is preserved, there will be a double species of fevers complicated with each other." And this contradiction will appear in the following propositions from the intention of Galen. 

<margin>
**Isaac.**
</margin>

**Isaac Israeli** <note>a famous 10th-century physician and philosopher</note> indeed says at the end of his work on fevers: "It is impossible for four fevers to be joined unless two are of one matter and two of another; for example, if there were two fevers from choler and two 

---

from **phlegm**, or two from phlegm, a third from choler, and a fourth from **melancholy** <note>black bile</note>." But the signs of blood: it is impossible for them to appear with the signs of others. For blood is more abundant in the whole body than all the other humors. If it putrefies and generates a fever, it covers all the fevers that are mixed with it because of the multitude of its quantity, and it obscures their significations, 

<margin>
**For strong things darken the weak, and the much darkens the little.**
</margin>

just as it appears in the sun darkening the splendor of a fire. Whence, in the first book of the *Aphorisms*: "Of two pains occurring at the same time, the greater obscures the lesser." <note>A famous medical rule: a major symptom hides a minor one</note>. It is manifest, therefore, that blood obscures the other humors if they are mixed with it. Thus he intended that a fever of blood is not composed with other fevers so as to be a fever named by a physician, since their significations do not appear, nor do the manifest cycles which it ought to induce. 

<margin>
**Note on the pulse.**
</margin>

From these points it is shown in order that a fever from blood putrefaction cannot, by its nature, endure while being composed with other fevers. However, an **accidental fever** can. I say a fever *per se* is without an inflammation; but an accidental one is that which arises because of an inflammation. In this also from putrefaction: because a fever from the inflammation of blood cannot be composed with other fevers while it remains. Whence Isaac says: "Nor is blood the cause of another fever although it may be heated, nor does it heat the other humors. For its temperament is close to balance. Therefore, if it is heated and putrefies, it does not depart much from balance." 

<margin>
**Chapter 3.**
</margin>

That a putrid fever of blood is not composed with other fevers is shown by reason: since either a fever of blood would be composed with a choleric, melancholic, or phlegmatic fever—since there are no more fevers of the humors—and these are either inside the veins or outside. Not inside: because blood, dominating in heat and fitness for putrefaction of all humors, would draw them to itself. 

<margin>
**Galen.**
</margin>

Which is confirmed: because a greater motion dispels a lesser one and hides it, as seen in *On the Senses and the Sensible*, *On Sleep and Waking*, and the third and fifth books of *On the Generation of Animals* <note>References to Aristotle’s natural philosophy</note>. Moreover, the motion and quantity of blood is greater—indeed, the greatest. Furthermore, in *On the Cause of the Length and Shortness of Life*: a smaller flame is burned up by a large one by suddenly stealing its fuel or nourishment. Similarly, a smaller fire 

<margin>
**Chapter 3.**
</margin>

is corrupted by a greater, as in the third book of *On the Heavens* and the first book of *On Complexions*. A large amount of fire draws a small amount to itself. Since, therefore, a fever of blood is like a greater flame in respect to others, and a great and much fire, it will burn up all others and draw them to itself. For a fever of blood thus weakens and blunts others according to Isaac, as a greater pain hides a lesser one in the same part; since the whole sensitive power runs to the more vehement pain. So also here with the putrefactive power. Nor can it be composed with **interpolated** <note>intermittent</note> fevers—neither with phlegm nor melancholy—partly because these materials are not ready for putrefaction when blood putrefies, and partly because the heat and moisture that putrefies those materials is drawn into and runs together with that which is the putrefaction in the blood. However, that the matter of melancholy is ill-disposed...

Using the logic of Galen, Isaac Israeli, and Aristotle, the author argues that because blood is the most abundant and naturally warm humor, its putrefaction (fever) effectively "consumes" or "obscures" the signs of any other simultaneous fevers, much like the sun's light hides the glow of a small fire.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether a fever caused by blood can be combined with fevers caused by other humors. It specifically addresses the quartan fever (linked to black bile) and the conditions under which blood might interact with choler (yellow bile) or phlegm, particularly when localized in an abscess or inflammation.</meta>

...shows that in those conditions, a **quartan fever** <note>a fever that recurs every fourth day, traditionally associated with black bile</note> rarely occurs at the beginning; rather, it starts on the fourth day. The quartan fever most often occurs in a succession of putrid diseases, and this is what we are focusing on. It cannot be anything else when it follows the putrefaction <note>the breakdown or "rotting" of humors, believed to release heat and cause fever</note> of other humors. Therefore, if it rarely occurs by itself even in a melancholic body, it will certainly never occur in the **blood**, where the putrefaction of blood is naturally meant to happen. Hence, it is said in the ninth book of *On the Therapeutic Method* <note>original: "nono d. ingenio," referring to Galen’s "Methodus Medendi"</note>: the nature of blood fevers is neutral in the lean—namely, regarding the **melancholic**—and in the cold—regarding the **phlegmatic**. It prefers to exist mostly in those who have much blood and much flesh; that is where they are generated. In a similar way, it is shown that **phlegmatic** matter is not fit to putrefy along with blood, since phlegm does not increase in the bodies where this occurs.

<margin>
17, distinction 8, *On the Therapeutic Method*.
</margin>
<margin>
Note: When they are internal, they can produce a single fever, or putrefy... melancholy.
</margin>

Furthermore, it does not happen on the part of the cause of putrefaction, since such a cause removes putridity from the phlegm. By itself, it heats the blood and dries out the phlegmatic matter, which was cold, moist, and blocked—the very things that were the causes of putrefaction. Likewise, this occurs in the matter of a quartan fever especially, according to its other quality, namely coldness. Its thickness is also thinned when affected by heat. Therefore, a putrid blood fever is not joined with a fever of phlegm or melancholy in any way.

<margin>
Not so common that a fever is composed in the blood.
</margin>

Even less so with a fever of **choler** <note>yellow bile</note>. For choler, by its own heat, thinness, and agility of movement, very quickly leads the blood into the causes of putrefaction. For since choler is naturally mobile and changeable—for instance, it can be transformed into melancholy—it will do so much more when it possesses something boiling and attractive, such as the heat of putrefying blood.

<margin>
No.
</margin>

However, if the fever occurs by "accident"—such as one arising from an **abscess** <note>original: "apantis," likely a contraction for "apostematis," an inflammatory swelling</note>—then a blood fever could be complicated with others, and especially with a choleric one. And this is perhaps what **Galen** means when he seems to contradict himself in other places. This can happen in two ways. Either more obviously, as when there are two abscesses: one from choler in the stomach or diaphragm, and another from blood in the liver or lung. When these two matters putrefy, two putrid vapors will rise at the same time, seeking the heart. This can certainly happen, since the "furnace" and origin of each remains separate from the other, even if some joining occurs during the process. Or it happens less obviously, as when an abscess is composed of both choler and blood in equal measure. For just as the matters are combined, so the putrid fumes will be combined. However, the distinction will not be as clear as in the previous case. And therefore, perhaps someone might not without merit consider it one composite fever rather than two. And such fevers composed from abscesses, especially the obvious ones, last for quite a long time. This is shown not a little by the **crisis** <note>the turning point of a disease</note> in this way: sometimes an abscess occurs in two different organs, such as the spleen and the liver, and each causes its own fever, which is different from the fever that usually occurs. And sometimes a composite abscess occurs in one organ, such as from blood, when the abscess is called a **phlegmon** <note>a localized inflammation of soft tissue</note>, and from choler, which is called **erysipelas** <note>a skin infection characterized by large red patches</note>. And he adds a little later: the fever that occurs from an abscess of blood, in whichever organ it may be, is a specific fever, just as that which occurs from a choleric abscess. Hence, according to the touch of the fevers, it is not possible for putrefaction to occur in one part while another part remains, as if a phlegmon were collecting and holding back a humor beginning to putrefy. If, however, there is putrefaction in both parts, just as they differ in place and matter, so will the fever. Because of this, a blood fever could exist with another fever in such a lasting composition.

Regarding the first point, it should be said that although two fevers are found together continuously, it is not concluded from this that one of them is a "sanguine" <note>blood-based</note> fever, since it has been shown that it cannot be combined with other fevers in its usual way. This is what the Master <note>likely Galen or Avicenna</note> suggested when he posited two continuous fevers joined together; thereafter, the judgments of vehemence and interpolation <note>the gaps between fever spikes</note> follow. This does not happen in a blood fever by itself, since it is truly continuous. Regarding the other point, it should be said that although fevers of different kinds are combined, they are not necessarily of "proximate" <note>closely related</note> kinds. Because fevers of "remote" kinds exist in very different substances, they are not like those that are immediate, such as fevers in proximate substances; just as nearby fires hinder and destroy each other more, especially when they are diverse in quantity, than those that are distant. A blood fever, however, hinders all other fevers, as has been declared. Regarding the other point, it should be said that it is not entirely the same for fevers and abscesses; in abscesses, the remnants of putrefaction are more lasting and distinct than in fevers. It is also granted that a fever from a sanguine abscess can be combined with others. Regarding the next point, although blood is less prone to putrefy by reason of its "kinship" and the "love" nature has for it, yet by reason of its hot and moist **complexion** <note>the balance of qualities in a person or substance</note>, it is more prepared to putrefy. And when its putrefaction begins, as shown, the aptitude for putrefaction of all other humors is converted toward it and into an effective act.

<margin>
14, distinction 8.
Arrangement of composite fevers.
</margin>

Regarding the final point, although **choler**, by reason of its quality, is not as prone to putrefy as blood, yet by reason of the "hatred" that nature has for it, it is more putrescible. Blood, by contrast, is loved and is a "friend." Furthermore, choler is not of such great quantity that it can draw all humors to itself and hide them as blood does.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how humors interact to produce fevers, moving from a general discussion of blood and phlegm to a specific classification of the various types of choler (yellow bile) and their capacity to cause disease through putrefaction or "adustion" (scorching).</meta>

## 14. On Therapeutics.

Therefore, since cholers <note>yellow bile</note> of this kind do not seem to be so fierce, or they are seen to induce tertian fevers <note>original: "fettitātes," likely a transcription error for "tertianitates," fevers that recur every other day</note>, especially because fever is a sickness appropriate to humans according to the seventh book of the *History of Animals* <note>Aristotle's work on biology</note>. Furthermore, a humor does not putrefy—according to the first and second books of *On Fevers*—unless it is abandoned by the governance of nature. These two types [of choler] indeed seem to be entirely abandoned by it, since their state is depraved, and they are returned to nature like a poison opposed to the human state. Also, the smoke <note>vapors or "fumes"</note> of a humor generated in the veins can seek the heart and induce a fever. But leek-green choler <note>original: "colera prassia," a toxic, greenish bile</note>, as shown in the second book of the *Prognostics*, is generated in the veins and shown to be able to putrefy; it can therefore tend toward the heart by its own putrefaction. Moreover, since these are hot and dry, they have a proportion with fever. But for those things that have a proportion and a shared quality, the transition is easier. According to the second book of *On Generation* and the heart [?], and first in the category of proportional things, the transmutation is easier and supported. Because the human body is heated by the cause of leek-green choler in the first degree, this will especially happen when it putrefies.

Again, those things which are contrary to the whole of human nature—such as the venom of a scorpion and the like—induce the worst fevers. Therefore, despite the malice of these types of choler, since they are not as great as such poisons, they will not cease from the induction of fever. Likewise, in the first book of the *Prognostics*: "If there is an anthrax or a carbuncle in the sick body, and if because of dryness it displays a green, lemon, or livid color, etc." <note>referring to the color of infected skin or pustules</note>. Indeed, the green and livid color in these cases testifies to the presence of choler. From these things it is concluded that a disease or fever is caused by such cholers. The opposite of this was expressed more clearly by Isaac in the fifth book of *On Fevers*. Up to now, I have found no one who claims that the two aforementioned types [of green choler] do not express sicknesses, let alone fevers, as being caused by humors that are so depraved. Furthermore, that which is most troublesome to nature is continually expelled; and it does not generate a great fever because its generation occurs in time <note>i.e., it is expelled before it can cause a long-term fever</note>; but cholers of this kind are well-known, and we see them expelled by vomiting nearby. For this reason, leek-green and verdigris-green <note>original: "eruginosa," colored like the rust of copper</note> choler will not induce fever.

Regarding the first point to be distinguished in choler: first and foremost, the place of generation and its location should be observed. For this, it must first be known that I find choler is understood in three ways. Sometimes it is used commonly for every humor, according to that saying in the seventh book of the *Aphorisms*: "If he does not have a fever from choler," and conversely, since this fever is not humoral but ephemeral, founded in the spirits. Wherefore it is made from raw humors of the genus of choler that they attract. It is also accepted properly for the choler called "red" and "melancholy" <note>black bile</note>, regarding which see the first book. Two types of choler are phlegmatic, and so on. It is also accepted more strictly for the bitter humor; hence in the fourth book of *The Therapeutic Method*: "When someone says 'choler' simply, it is manifest that it is the bitter kind." And in the third book of *On the Use of the Parts* by Galen: "It is the custom of physicians to denote 'choler' simply, without the addition of that which pertains to the types of choler." This choler is a hot and dry humor.

<margin>5 species of choler.</margin>
Since its species have been set down by all the ancestors as only five: There is indeed one that is natural, which is the "froth of the blood" <note>a traditional description of yellow bile</note>; its color is a clear red, light, and sharp. It is called clear red, and russet, and yellow, and sometimes lemon-colored. And there is another unnatural kind, which is fourfold. One is called lemon-colored or saffron choler. And "pale," which arises from the mixing of natural clear red choler and watery phlegm. <margin>4 species of unnatural choler.</margin> And the rest is called "yolk-like" <note>original: "uitellina"</note> because it is known to resemble the yolks of eggs, arising from the mixing of the <term>aforementioned natural choler</term> <note>red bile</note> and coagulated or thick phlegm. Galen discusses "black choler" which is generated in the vessels or even in the liver simply, according to him and Haly Abbas. But according to Avicenna, it is with more addition. It is found, however, that according to the naturalists, "burnt" yolk-like choler is named as such. And from the natural and this kind of mixture, all the other types are made. In this, Galen is preferred over others in the second book of *On the Elements*. Indeed, "yellow" choler and "yolk-like" are less hot than the natural. But as was said regarding "black" choler, it touches upon the others whether it proceeds outward or not. Hence Galen in the second book of *Prognostics*: "Sometimes one properly sees thick yellow bile, and diligently yellow bile vomited up and proceeding downward, which some indeed call yolk-like; but many times it is more moist and less yellow, which is properly named lemon-colored, having through its whole mixture a subtle or watery phlegmatic humor, which is superfluous." In the first book of *On Aliments*: "These cholers are some *xanthic* <note>yellow</note> and some *ochre* <note>pale/yolk-colored</note>." And according to the "more and less," both are obtained in multiplicity, so that I may pass over the other cholers that appear in bodies already sick. In the fifth book of *On Internal Diseases*: "He vomits pure choler, like the yolk of an egg; but afterwards he shows it as green." Thus, one is seen to be different from the "burnt" <note>original: "adusta," scorched by heat</note> kind.

One can, however, respond to Avicenna that yolk-like choler is called "burnt" by Galen, yet not with such a burning that the humors are incinerated and turn black, but such a state is rather to be called a kind of "over-cooking" or "passing the limit." For although a strong heat would induce burning, the matter resists it with phlegmatic coldness, according to that passage in the second book of *Prognostics*: "that the white, viscous, round sputum happens from burnt phlegm." And therefore it remains moist and viscous, even though burning has proceeded within it. Because of this, one does not have to bite <note>criticize</note> Avicenna on this point. Nor similarly because lemon-colored choler is more intense in color; therefore it is hotter than the other. It should also be said that this is not valid, because color is not given by quality alone, but the substance—whether rare or dense—also works toward this. For a subtle substance intensifies the color less, but a thicker one more, as yellow, lemon-colored, and yolk-like choler show in the blood. Another species of choler is found called "leek-green" <note>original: "prassia," from the leek, porrum</note>, which reflects the color of leek leaves and is even generated from them. And there is another called "verdigris-green" <note>original: "eruginosa" or "zinaria"</note> because of the similarity it has to the color of the rust on copper. And also because it has a similar quality, such as being sharp and corrosive; for it burns in the manner of a poison when it is born from excessive scorching. And these two types destroy the specific form of natural heat. Just as they are of the genus of poisons, according to the third book of *On the Elements*, along with the others whose origin exists more in the stomach. Haly, however, adds one having an unnatural mode, namely the color of indigo <note>dark blue/purple</note>; which indeed is his explanation of what he had called leek-green. Or perhaps it arises by the mode of the burning of blood, as will appear through Avicenna.

Consequently, as a most proficient medical compiler, he sets down seven species of unnatural choler <note>term: choler; the humor known as "yellow bile," associated with a hot and dry temperament</note>. For he did not describe only the famous ones, but also the less known.

For unnatural choler is produced either when a foreign substance is mixed with it, or when it acquires a cause of unnaturalness within itself. And the first type is twofold. That which is corrupted from within itself is also twofold: for one kind is generated more by the liver, which is the thin substance generated from the scorching of the blood. Its thick part stands as black choler.

The other type takes its generation more from the stomach. This is again divided into **leek-green** <note>original: "prassinā"; a pale green like a leek leaf</note> and **verdigris-green** <note>original: "erugo"; like the rust or patina on copper</note>, as shown before. These, although they are hateful to all natures, even to the natural state, were for this reason—according to Isaac in the *Book of Universal Diets*—located by nature in the gallbladder <note>original: "kisti"; from the Greek "kystis" for bladder</note>. They are extended in heat and dryness, but more or less so. For the worst and hottest of all is the **verdigris-green**; then the **leek-green**; then that which comes from the scorching of what was in the blood; then the hottest and worst natural clear red; then the worse and hotter one made from a mixture of melancholy; then the **lemon-colored**. Finally, the **yolk-colored** is the least hot of all. In terms of malice, it exceeds and stands in excess of the lemon-colored, diversified by the reasoning of its extension and intensity. Regarding this, it should be known that the place and manner of generation of the leek-green and verdigris-green are assigned in multiple ways. For Galen, in the book on *Prognostics*, states that leek-green is generated in the stomach; and perhaps you will find this.

Many others, however, say—agreeing with those who think leek-green and verdigris-green come mostly from the stomach—that its Greek series <note>referring to the sequence of humoral development</note> is thus: Just as natural yellow choler exists in the body, so there is another "accidental" one against nature. And it is seen many times to be generated in the bellies of some during the digestion of foods or oils, such as beets, onions, and cabbage. By reason of appearance, you find this kind of thing also generated by reason of disease in the veins and flowing back into either the upper or lower belly, as a sign of heat in the body against nature. And again in the same place: If a yellow humor is thinned by serous <note>watery</note> humidity and mixed, it appears green; if more intense, the choler appears like verdigris. In the *Summary of Complexions*, he states that leek-green choler is simply generated in the belly. Because the complexion in the belly is hotter, a choleric superfluity is generated that looks like a leek. Red or pale bile is entirely that which comes out of the liver and in those who digest very quickly. Those in whom this leek-like substance is generated must not have eaten

bread or pork, or anything similar; but something hotter than these, and it is generated only in those with poor digestion in the belly. Regarding **black choler**, as touched upon somewhat: thus the mixture of thin humidity and yellow choler becomes paler in color and more liquid in substance. So when this has evaporated quite a bit, it resembles the property of raw eggs, and for this reason, it is called **yolk-colored**. This choler, whether it appears pale or yellow or yolk-colored, has its generation in the vessels. But the leek-green choler that the belly generates, they call "acoloe4" <note>unclear: possibly a corrupted Greek term for "colorless" or "bile-less"</note> after the leek, or "virulent" from *virus* <note>original: "uirulentā a uiru"; here meaning "poisonous" or "foul-smelling"</note>, that is, verdigris-green. Isaac also, in the fifth book of *Fevers* and in *Universal Diets*, maintains that all besides natural and clear red bile are generated in the stomach. Natural reddish bile lives in the gallbladder, and its power is in the liver. Unnatural bile is in the stomach; it is diverse: yolk-colored, saffron-colored, leek-green, and verdigris-green. The cause of these is when natural choler, coming to the stomach, mixes with the humors existing in the stomach. If these were healthy and generated from temperate food in the liver, the reddish choler is changed into saffron-colored choler, being close to the natural. If the humors with which the choler is mixed pertain to coldness and moisture, the choler is turned into **yolk-colored**. But if the humors in the stomach were hot and sharp, such as those generated from pepper, ginger, leeks, garlic, and similar things, the heat is increased and it returns a leek-green color. If this choler remains in its sharpness and external heat warms it, such as the heat of the season or other things, it is intensified and becomes **verdigris-green**.

As for the yolk-colored and lemon-colored, which he asserts—against others who place them in the liver—are generated in the stomach, this does not seem to hold the truth; since not shortly after he adds: "If the matter of a fever is true choler (that is, reddish), a **burning fever** <note>term: causon; a high-grade, acute fever</note> is generated; if it is saffron-colored, it becomes a **tertian fever** <note>term: tertian; a fever that peaks every 48 hours</note>; but if it is yolk-colored, a **semitertian** <note>original: "emitriturus"; a dangerous combination of a continuous and intermittent fever</note> is born." Since, therefore, the matter existing in the veins induces a continuous fever, and not that which is outside, then no continuous fever would happen from choler, except perhaps the burning fever. I say "perhaps," because he seems to locate even red choler only in the gallbladder. Nor would the semitertian ever be certain or "true" according to him, since it arises from the putrefaction of choler inside the veins and phlegm outside. Nor should these cholers be understood to be generated in the stomach—that is, in its veins—but rather in its cavities. And therefore perhaps he says saffron-colored is sometimes generated in the liver when the blood is more moist than it ought to be. Avicenna, however, agrees with him regarding the generation of leek-green and verdigris-green in some way. For he says generally that the cause of their generation is when choler departs from its nature in heat and dryness because of that spreading to the stomach, and it then mixes with other humors, specifically with melancholy; and there it receives some species of putrefaction and arrives at such a complexion, and in this, it differs from the others. For perhaps he places these by way of putrefaction and not by scorching <note>adustion</note> as others do for the causes. Nor do they think choler is thus in the stomach...

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the generation and movement of specific types of bile (cholers), specifically addressing whether leek-green and verdigris bile are produced in the stomach or the liver, and their clinical consequences according to Galen, Haly Abbas, and Avenzoar.</meta>

ignited. And thus it is more subtle <note>In medieval medicine, "subtle" (subtilis) refers to a substance that is thin, refined, or composed of very small particles, allowing it to penetrate tissues easily.</note> and less subtle than what the blood requires. Conversely, melancholy <note>black bile</note> moves with the blood when it is less thick, specifically that which tends toward the spleen. For "subtle" and "thick" imply an excess. But as for that which moves with the blood, the work of the covering <note>likely referring to the membranes or vascular tunics</note> bears witness to it. 

To the first point, therefore, it must be said that choler <note>yellow bile</note> does not descend to the intestines of its own accord, but is rather guided by a propelling force, just as melancholy is moved upward by its own nature. 

To the next point, it must be said that this is not the true substance of choler which appears in that supernatant foam <note>the "scum" or froth that rises to the top of a liquid</note>, but something generated from evaporation or rather from its own effusing. This means that the waste of choler evaporates out of the veins. 

To the next, it must be said that blood does not require such great thinness that a less subtle choler would be unable to thin it, provided it does not cause harm; just as the other members for which they are ordained are also thick and sufficient.

<margin>He doubts.</margin> It is further doubted, since it does not seem these types of choler can be generated in the stomach, but rather in the liver, since it is a humor. For the stomach is ordered toward the digestion of food and its conversion into **chyle** <note>original: "chilum"; the milky fluid of digested food before it reaches the liver</note>. But the liver is for the conversion of chyle into **chyme** <note>original: "chimum"; here meaning the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>; hence the conclusion is gathered. That which is generated naturally is generated [there], and also the unnatural when its temperament is corrupted. Since, therefore, the stomach does not have the power to generate a natural humor, it will not generate an unnatural one either. 

Furthermore, since these cholers are extremely hot, they must be generated by an extremely hot agent. But the stomach is not such an agent, as it is cold and dry by nature; it is nervous <note>composed of "nerve-like" or sinewy tissue</note> and has very little blood. The liver, however, is hot and bloody; and as much blood as a member has, so much heat does it possess, according to the first book of *Complexions* and as is apparent from its parts. Therefore, they will be generated in the liver and not in the stomach, which no one has said. 

It must be said, however, that they are generated in the stomach and not in the liver, because by their sharpness and malice they would corrupt the very tender substance of the liver, which Nature does not allow. Furthermore, the liver's moisture is great. For it is the "fountain of moisture" according to **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Baly"; a famous 10th-century Persian physician</note>, which prohibits the generation of these cholers since they are extremely dry; and everything is generated in a place akin to itself. 

To the first argument, therefore, it must be said that generation is twofold. One is true and **univocal**; and in this way the stomach produces the "pultaceous mass" and the liver produces the humors. 

<margin>Univocal</margin> The other is specifically **equivocal**. And in this way, these two cholers could be said to be generated in the stomach. **Univocal** generation of a genus occurs when the whole is transmuted into the whole (according to the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*), so that the transformation occurs not only in accidents but also in substance. For the substance does not remain the same in essence, being changed only in its accidents. 

**Equivocal** generation is defined by the opposite; for instance, that these types of choler are generated in the stomach because they acquire their greenness in it from the effusion of sharp points, or because choler coming from the liver to the stomach puts on other accidental forms, such as color, thickness, hardness, and the like. And thus perhaps those who say they are generated more by the stomach understand it this way: because they acquire such a form in the stomach, even though they received the matter from the liver, remaining the same in substance but transformed by their qualities. And in this way the modes and also the places of their generation proceed as mentioned before, even if they might seem perhaps suspiciously different. 

Or it should be said that they are formed more by the stomach and specifically by the aforementioned process, though **Galen** says they are sometimes generated in the veins on account of some sickness and are finally poured out into the stomach. 

To the second point, it should be said that heat is twofold: innate/natural and acquired. The liver is the specific home of natural heat, for it is hot and moist by nature. But the stomach, although its indwelling nature is more cold and dry, has many things that concur to heat it (according to the third book of *On Naturals*). The **Heart** is above it, heating it by means of the diaphragm; from the back run the spine and its muscles; in the front is the fatty **Omentum** <note>the "apron" of fat covering the abdominal organs</note> with the muscles. To the right is the **Liver** with the gall bladder. To the left is the **Spleen**, on account of the venous and arterial blood contained within it. All these surrounding parts gather an "adventitious" <note>external or added</note> heat around the stomach, whereby it can generate humors that are scorched and burnt. The liver, however, by its innate heat and moisture, resists the generation of such humors, though it does generate their material—namely, yolk-colored or other choler. 

Likewise it is doubted: since according to **Galen** it is said that leek-green choler is sometimes generated in the veins, it could similarly be generated in the liver, because there are veins in it in which the humor is contained, and not in the substance of the organ itself. 

<margin>Doubt.</margin> For often **Galen** calls the digestion of the veins that which belongs to the liver, so that the generation of such cholers would not be lacking in it, as was said, because their malice would corrupt that tender part. 

<margin>Response.</margin> It must be said that, as it appears, it does not happen that the aforementioned cholers are generated in the liver. In the veins, however, it can happen on account of the heat of certain parching illnesses. Nor is it the same for the veins that are in the body of the liver as for those which extend from it. For the membranes of the veins existing in the liver are thinner than the membranes of other veins in the whole body (according to the fourth book of *On the Utility of Parts*), so that the digestion by the liver may be more perfect. For the closer the food is to the substance of the fleshy liver, the more swiftly it is rendered to alteration and better receives the species of blood. But when they extend away from the liver, the tunics of the veins thicken and strengthen. Hence **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> in the fifth book of *On Animals*: "It is not forbidden for powers to become stronger and more valid outside of their origins." This is because they take on stronger materials through which they are made, as is clearly apparent in the origin of the nerves and finally in their progression. 

Finally, it should be known that I have not yet found anyone, searching diligently, who posits that a sickness arises from the two aforementioned cholers; rather, they are either expelled by vomiting or they bring about death itself—except for **Avenzoar** <note>original: "Hebē soir"</note> and his colleague **Avicenna** <note>original: "Aū."</note>. For he says: "A fever which results from the transition of an ephemeral fever to a choleric fever, if it is of the leek-green or verdigris kind, will have more fraudulent symptoms, and one can scarcely escape from it." And if one does escape, it will persist for a long time. And he adds the signs of it, saying that its paroxysm <note>the peak of the fever</note> is long-lasting, and the end of the sickness likewise. And there are few who escape from this infirmity, and if they do, it will be through much effort and a prolongation of the illness. And it is possible for bad and fraudulent accidents to remain with them.

Third, it is gathered that the **illnesses** which arise from these types of choler <note>yellow bile</note>—namely the **leek-green** <term>prassina</term> <note>A type of bile named for its resemblance to the color of leeks, considered highly "burnt" and pathological.</note> and the **verdigris** <term>eruginosa</term> <note>A type of bile resembling the green rust of copper (verdigris), considered the most extreme and toxic form of "burnt" bile.</note>—are incurable. He also says a burning fever, contrary to what others say, would be impossible to arise from natural choler. 

These indeed are the discourses of those great men, which if anyone considers them diligently, they are not only discordant with others, but even dissent enough among themselves. For **Avenzoar** <note>original: "Zoar"; a 12th-century Arab physician from Al-Andalus.</note> posits that it is possible, though with some great difficulty, for a man to escape from a fever of the aforementioned biles. **Avicenna** <note>original: "Au."; refers to the Persian physician Ibn Sina.</note>, however, says something contrary to this: that it seems impossible to him that anyone should escape from a fever arising from verdigris choler.

Furthermore, if these biles are as wicked as they themselves testify, how is the fever from them prolonged, and also the paroxysm? Why also, according to Avicenna, do they induce a burning fever <note>causon</note>, since that is a continuous fever without paroxysms, yet these biles have paroxysms? Or how is a burning fever generated if it is not from natural choler? For it will not be made from citron-colored bile nor from yolk-like bile that is not burnt, since these are colder than the natural kind; nor even from the yolk-like bile which he called "burnt" in the third book, because in the seventh book he argues that natural yolk-like bile is colder. How then shall yolk-like bile create a burning fever if it is colder than the natural? Or perhaps he now accepts yolk-like bile commonly with the others, not observing what Galen presumed to affirm and impose in the third book. Or if burnt yolk-like bile is distinct from the leek-green and verdigris types, distinguish them for us, **Teacher**! For what these men say is very strange and unusual, which is why I do not fully comprehend these and similar discourses of Avicenna.

<margin>decorative mark</margin> It must be said, therefore, that outside of itself, yolk-like choler is made in two ways: one by the aforementioned mixing, which retains more of its nature; the other through "burning" and the thickening of its substance, which is what **Galen** commonly intends. Therefore, assigning the generation of humors more briefly than in the natural way—since he touched upon it in other treatises—he explained only two types of choler: the natural and the unnatural. By yolk-like choler, he means something more perfect than the others; hearing all unnatural choler is generated in the two ways touched upon. 

Regarding the third point, I say with others that from properly **verdigris choler**, neither fever nor any illness can arise; instead, it is either cast out by **vomiting**, or it brings about **sudden death**. In the case of leek-green bile, it is somewhat doubtful. But as for why

fever does not arise from verdigris, nor from leek-green, I find no other illness assigned to these biles by others. The *Vatican* <note>original: "Vsa"; likely a reference to a specific medical authority or text, possibly the 'Viaticum' of Constantine the African.</note> and the *Fifth [Book] on Fevers* offers such a discourse in common regarding them: It is impossible for leek-green bile to be generated in the **liver**, nor does it pass from the stomach, nor does it generate fever, because it does not remain in the body long enough to putrefy and generate fever. For **nature always assists itself** in expelling it from the body because of its malignity. But if nature fails, being unable to expel it, it sets the body on fire, and the man dies. He adds: Therefore, if such things happen regarding leek-green bile, how much greater and more certain will they be regarding the verdigris type? 

<margin>3</margin> And it is confirmed because in the third book of *On Foods*, all other biles are seen to be evacuated with difficulty, except for the "green" when the body is sick. Whence in the *Universal Diets*: Verdigris is worse and more corruptible than leek-green, which is why it swiftly destroys and kills. This is also confirmed by the reasons placed before: such as that nature is not moved unless a harm is perceived. And because biles of this kind have the worst, sharp, and biting qualities. Also, they are produced in the **stomach**, especially the verdigris. And because the stomach is the most sensitive of members, and especially its "mouth" <note>the cardia or upper opening of the stomach</note>, as said in the fourth book of *Accidents*. For its sensation is even beyond the natural sense of the animal. And that which is contained in the stomach is most easily led out, because its own proper evacuation is through **vomit**. **Constantine** <note>Constantine the African, 11th-century translator and physician.</note> says this of the stomach. The way by which it is led out is short and wide. 

Therefore, let such a discourse now arise: **Nature is not moved unless a harm is perceived.** But from these kinds of choler, a harm is perceived, since they are most sharp and the stomach is most sensitive. Therefore, they are vomited out of the stomach, since they are formed in it before they bring about illness. For just as nature, possessing [natural] choler, has imprisoned it in the **gallbladder** <term>kisti</term> <note>original: "kisti"; from the Greek 'kystis', referring here to the gall bladder.</note>, so it strives to expel these others immediately as much as it can, lest they kill it; and therefore we see them vomited out intermittently. But against this, it does not seem that it would be expelled so quickly from the stomach that it would not generate an illness. Since that which generates green hair—as this happens over a delay of time—could also cause a fever from it. But green hair has been seen, specifically in the temples of a certain person, and these came from this choler, as they themselves testify, which he also vomited out periodically every week. 

It must be said in two ways: either as it will appear, that leek-green can sometimes generate fever; or that although hair might sometimes be made green, nevertheless the leek-green choler did not putrefy so as to cause a fever, because it was continually expelled, just as it was generated without putrefying. However, through many generations of it, it colored the hair with a green color, as the infected vapors were sent upward. Furthermore: whatever causes a **humoral fever** must putrefy and seek the heart, since a putrid vapor seeking the heart is the conjoined cause of fever. But things that are of fire and vehemently ignited do not putrefy. And therefore the other impure elements putrefy, except for fire. Such indeed is properly verdigris choler, since it is most hot and most dry. But against this

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding whether highly "burnt" or pathological biles—specifically leek-green and verdigris-colored bile—can cause fevers through putrefaction, or if they are so poisonous that they kill the patient before a fever can even develop. It picks up from the discussion of whether these substances can be considered "liquid."</meta>

...liquid. But humors of this kind are types of bile. That which is moist and hot is able to putrefy. For putrefaction is caused by these, according to the fourth book of *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle's work on the elements and their interactions</note> and the eleventh book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "xi. de ingenio [sanitatis]"; a work by Galen</note>. 

Furthermore, **melancholy** <note>black bile</note>, which is a drier substance of the body, putrefies and generates fever; and natural bile <note>yellow bile</note>, which is a hotter substance of the body, similarly putrefies from an unequal distemper. Therefore, these will putrefy and generate fever. 

It must be said that these types of bile, and specifically the **verdigris-colored** <term>eruginosa</term>, putrefy the least, since they are excessively fiery and dry. And regarding the statement that the moist and liquid putrefy, it must be said that every such thing putrefies. For Galen says that in a putrefiable moisture, the heat that burns and thickens should not be present, as here moisture is 
<margin>A question is asked / because as stated above</margin>
excluded by intense and smoking heat. 

Wherefore in the first book of the *Particulars*, **zinaria** <note>original: "Ziniaria"; a dark, metallic green bile associated with the oxidation of copper</note> is generated from the **leek-green** <term>prassina</term> when it is burnt so much that its moisture dries up; it remains under the nature of both humors. For these types of bile, specifically the *zinaria*, are like corrosive ulcers, not being capable of putrefying due to their immense heat and apparent dryness. 

Or it must be said that a humor of this kind does not have sufficient time in which it could putrefy, as will soon appear; nor is melancholy drier than this kind of bile, and especially afterwards, since according to physicians, it is the nature of melancholy to nourish, for which reason it must retain some moisture. It is true, however, that some have thought for this reason that melancholy cannot cause a natural **quartan fever** <note>a fever that returns every four days, typically linked to black bile</note>. For the dryness acquired in bile, especially in the verdigris-colored, because it is bile and because of the heat consuming the moisture, is rendered more intense than the dryness of natural black bile. 

Furthermore, for that which causes fever, there must be a sufficient time in which it can be generated, so that it may produce its effect. For three things must concur: a vigorous agent, a disposed subject <note>original: "patiens"; the body or humor being acted upon</note>, and the time in which the agent is applied to the subject. (See Difference 88 and 94). 

But sufficient time is not found in which a fever can be caused specifically from **verdigris bile**, since fever occurs through putrefaction. This requires time, as it is a certain boiling and conversion of the humor. For a fever to be induced, there must be a long transformation. First, the cause must be present... and the putrid smoke resolved from it seeking the heart... then the release of that smoke from the heart into the whole body. For from that point, the fever spreads into the whole subject, unless there is an impediment. 

Therefore, verdigris bile specifically will not cause fever, nor just a lingering illness, but **swift death**, unless it is expelled by vomiting or perhaps by stool. Sometimes such vomiting is followed by pains in the mouth of the stomach so intense that they result in spasms, fainting, cold sweats, and a weak pulse—all according to book 12 of *On the Method of Healing*. 

But concerning this, a doubt may arise. Because it was said that putrefaction requires time, yet the contrary is written in the fourth book of the *Particulars*: "Putrefaction does not have a time." And the conversion of blood into bile does not happen except in time. It must be said that this was insufficiently shown in Difference 89. For [the author] does not intend to say that putrefaction has no time at all, since it is a certain alteration leading to fever; and every alteration, since it is a true motion, happens in time, according to the fifth book of *Physics*. Rather, he wishes to make known that the time is less in which putrefaction occurs from 

blood, than the time in which blood is transformed into bile, since the latter requires more movements and transformations.

***

That this kind of bile, especially the **verdigris** kind as mentioned, is so poisonous is shown because poison is a subtle moisture of a horrible quality, according to Haly Abbas <note>original: "baly"; a famous Persian physician</note>. 
<margin>}</margin> <margin>Whether verdigris bile is a poison / it is not asked.</margin>
And the quality of poison is diverse: for there is one kind which is close to the humors that agree with the body, another which is distant, and another which possesses a wicked poisonous quality. And so, since these biles are of such a nature, it is no wonder if nature tries to expel them, especially by vomiting. 

For by vomiting, many species of humors are drawn out: phlegmatic, choleric, and melancholic. Nor is it a wonder if such a poison generated in the bodies, since it is of great quantity, can induce sudden death, according to the sixth book of *Internal Diseases* <note>original: "sexto interiorum"</note>. Even corrupted menstrual blood, and especially sperm retained in the body, can bring about pernicious diseases and swift death. We see from the very tiny poison of spiders, and especially scorpions, that the most cruel symptoms and death occur in no small measure. Similarly, we see a limb become numb from the mere touch of a **torpedo fish** <note>an electric ray</note> or from the contact of the saliva of a rabid dog. Justly, therefore, menstrual blood and especially corrupted sperm can be reduced to a poison. Whence Haly Abbas says: "Perhaps there is something in sperm similar to poison." 

It will also be possible for any humor to be converted into poison when it is of a violent quality and in a location suitable for it. Regarding **leek-green bile**, it should not be simply stated that a fever cannot be born from it, especially when it is not as condensed as the verdigris kind and can be mixed more with other humors. It is generated not only in the stomach, but as was said, also in the veins. When joined to other humors, it does not become so hateful to nature as the verdigris kind, which is expelled the moment it is perceived. Nor does it resist putrefaction as much. 

This is perhaps what Avicenna <note>original: "A."</note> seems to concede in the fourth book of the *Particulars*, saying: "It is made from very subtle chymes <note>juices/humors</note>, most of which are a bile of intense subtlety; and a poisonous wicked substance is poured out, which then undergoes putrefaction in bodies of a very dry and hot complexion." 

That wicked poisonous substance which is poured out seems for the most part to be leek-green bile, since it is said to be of the genus of poisons. 

**And I saw this fever in a certain young man** of a very dry and very hot complexion, 
<margin>Note on authors' histories</margin>
with symptoms of intense internal heat, thirst, coldness of the extremities, and sometimes fainting. He was afflicted mostly every third day; the fever ceased with a very large flow of watery, leek-green bile from the belly. In that case, although the flow was caused by the strength of nature, there was a restriction <note>of appetite</note>, and he became unable to eat, barely swallowing and taking nothing. Around the **seventh day** from then, being wasted away, he expired. For truly that wicked bile had poisoned his innate spirits and heart.

And since these kinds of biles rarely emerge, authors seem to disagree with one another. Since most of this art is understood by experience rather than by reason, one cannot be certain about things that happen rarely.

...present in the fifth book of the *Internal Affections* <note>original: "iterioꝝ quinto"; a work in the Hippocratic Corpus</note>. However, regarding the fourth point. To the first point, what was said is seen to be correct. To the next, it must be said that that fever was not a true fever, but rather a certain inflammation following from the effort of vomiting and pain. Hence, in the twelfth book of *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "in genio"; referencing Galen's *De methodo medendi*</note>, it is not a fever but only four pre-existing symptoms. Or perhaps the fever existed beforehand from other matter. 

To the other point, it must be said that these biles are worse than **melancholy** <note>black bile</note> because of a subtle, earthy, fermented substance. For they are hotter and sharper. For although that melancholy induces a boiling and fermentation in the earth, it is not hot and sharp in the same way as these; rather, it causes this by a certain biting or sourness of its own, just as vinegar boils and ferments upon the earth, but not so with others; or like the sap of the shrub that bears **spurge** <term>euphorbium</term> <note>a caustic, succulent plant juice</note> when it is not yet condensed into a gum. 

Diseases that arise from this melancholy are not caused by putrefaction, but rather by a certain corrosion. Thus, the humor itself is fit to cause diseases by its minor sharpness and slow penetration, unlike bile, and specifically **verdigris-colored bile** <term>eruginosa</term>, since nature cannot endure it for any time. 

To the other point, it must be said that a humor is abandoned by the "governance of nature" <note>original: "regie nature"; the body's natural self-regulating power</note> in two ways: either because nature does not work upon it to preserve or restore it to a healthy state if it errs—and thus this humor is abandoned by the governance of nature, but not blood or phlegm—or it is said to be abandoned because nature does not care for its expulsion, since it does not bother nature, because its qualities do not have a vehement excess, such as some melancholy and especially a certain phlegm. For these do not move unless a lesion is perceived, appearing to the natural reason. And thus the "good biles" are not abandoned, as has been declared by the governance of nature. On the contrary, nature always strives to turn them away from the body. 

To the other point, it must be said that although **leek-green bile** <term>prassina</term> is sometimes generated in the veins, nature expels it to the stomach if nature is strong. Or it is said that it is not impossible for a small, subtle, "syncope-inducing" fever to be generated from it. 

To the other point, it must be said that although these two biles, as well as the verdigris-colored one, have a proportion with fever, it is not through putrefaction, as has been shown. Or rather, the fever itself is not established from the humors, nor does their heating induce a fever of putrefaction; but a vehement putrefaction in which we are engaged attacks the heart, and its heat does not immediately press down, but spreads itself from there to all the members of the body. 

To the other point, it must be said that many poisons, which are called such from their entire specific form (as appears with the poison of the scorpion and the spider), are nonetheless better endured by nature than this kind of bile. For they are not of such great quantity. They are like poisons taken in great quantity, by which nature, being irritated, soon leads them out through the top by vomiting, or through the bottom, to prevent harm which would have brought death if they were retained. Nor do these have such pernicious and sharp qualities, which is why nature tries to expel them immediately, perceiving the harm from their vehement sharpness. And this is especially true since the stomach is the most sensitive of the organs. 

Similarly, regarding the poisons that are administered: some are mixed with sweet things so that their evil quality is hidden. Thus nature, deceived by the sweetness, draws the poison to itself; because of which it is commanded in the fourth or sixth book that he who fears he might take poison in a drink must guard himself against foods of dominant flavors, such as sourness, sharpness, or sweetness, and dominant odors. There are also treacherous poisons that induce death quickly, mostly of a subtle and liquid nature. 

To the other point, it must be said that that translation is bad; for it does not follow the correct sequence of **Hippocrates** <note>original: "ypocratis"</note>, but only the sense, and even that is sometimes imperfect, as is clear from the Arabic translation. But in that [Arabic version], here and everywhere, the words and meaning savor of Hippocrates. His sequence is: "But an ulcer, or a completed animal..." <note>original: "Vlcus aūt ſiue ꝓfectū zoꝝ"</note>. The Arabic version is consonant with him. "When there is an ulcer in the body of a sick person..." Therefore, Hippocrates is not speaking of **anthrax** or **carbuncles** <note>severe skin infections</note> of the same color, but of an ulcer; nor is this kind of color caused by leek-green or verdigris-colored bile, although it may become green or livid, but it is created from burnt melancholy. For he says that when the melancholic humor overcomes the body, its color is either livid or green.

<margin>Epiala.</margin>
**1.** That in an **epiala** <note>a "chilling" fever where the patient feels cold and hot at the same time</note> there is no internal cold and external heat seems to be shown by Isaac in the fifth book of *On Fevers*, who writes the opposite of this. Furthermore, according to Galen, fever is generated in the body just as fire is from the burning of wood. But in this case, the heat is more in the lowest and deep part of the wood than in the exterior part exposed to the air. Since, therefore, in an *epiala*, the "glassy phlegm" <note>a thick, cold, transparent humor</note> in which it is rooted is in the depths of the body, it will induce heat there, while the exterior will be cold, being unable to be warmed by the fever because of its own coldness. 

Again, an *epiala* fever arises from a colder phlegm, and the putrefaction is deep since it is humoral. Putrefaction, however, is caused by heat. Where it is present, it heats; where it is lacking, it shows cold. Therefore, in an *epiala*, the heat will be internal and the cold external. 

<margin>Lipparia.</margin>
However, it is shown that in a **lipparia** <note>a "burning" fever where the internal organs are hot but the skin is cold</note> there is internal cold and external heat, because it arises from bile alone or joined with glassy phlegm or melancholy. But bile seeks the exterior, heating it; whereas glassy phlegm and melancholy seek the interior. On the other hand, heat is in the part toward which it tends; but this kind is exterior and superficial, since its motion is from the center to the circumference. Therefore, the exterior parts will be heated in it, and the interior parts will be chilled.

The contrary of this is felt in the sixth book of Serapion and in the fourth, which holds the opposite: that in an *epiala*, the internal parts are chilled and the external parts are heated; but in a *lipparia*, it is the opposite. The motion of these things is touched upon. But that such a diversity of heat and cold can exist in neither of these is proved: because fever proceeds from the heart through the arteries and veins into the whole body, as reason itself testifies. When it heats, it heats both parts at the same time, namely the interior and the exterior; and thus the rest. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known what is hot and what is cold, and what is interior and what is exterior, as is clear from many things. Now, *epiala* is called such in Greek "above another" <note>Greek: *epialos*</note>, because the heat is above the coldness. Or both are above the other, because cold is joined with heat everywhere at once, as shown according to Galen and Haly Abbas. For *Epi* in Greek means "above"...
