<meta>This page continues a scholastic medical discussion, transitioning from the properties of corrosive biles to a detailed classification and debate regarding mixed fevers, specifically "epiala" and "lipparia." It synthesizes the views of Galen, Isaac Judaeus, Haly Abbas, and Avicenna regarding how different humors produce simultaneous sensations of heat and cold.</meta>

...carries. And others say another thing—that it is the same as **epiala** <term>epiala</term> <note>From the Greek "epialos," a fever where the patient feels shivering and heat at the same time.</note>. **Lipparia** <term>lipparia</term> <note>From the Greek "leipyria," a "deserting" fever where heat leaves the surface and burns internally.</note>, on the other hand, is so named as if it were "fatty." For *lipparon* <note>original: "Lipparon"; referring to the Greek "liparos" meaning oily or sleek.</note> means fat. Just as fat people become hot internally and grow cold externally—because the trapped heat cannot extend itself to the outer parts, as Galen notes in the eighth book of *On Fevers* <note>original: "p̄bf. viii"; likely referring to "De febribus" or "De crisibus"</note> regarding why fat people grow so intensely cold—the same happens in this fever. For this reason, **Haly Abbas** <note>Ahwazi, a 10th-century Persian physician</note> seems to name it "luxury" <note>original: "luxuria"; perhaps implying the condition of the well-fed or "fatty" body</note>. Thus others have spoken more soundly about it than **Isaac Judaeus** <note>A 10th-century North African physician and philosopher</note>, following this reasoning of the name.

Furthermore, it should be known that in both simple and composite fevers, diverse conditions occur because of the heat or the cause of the matter, which are distinguished by different names. For in certain fevers, there is a great deal of mixed humidity, and it is called **londinis** <note>possibly a corruption of "lyngodes," a fever characterized by hiccups or moisture</note>. When the heat is intensely burning, it is called **causon** <term>causon</term> <note>An "ardent" or "burning" fever usually attributed to yellow bile.</note> or "an incense." When, however, heat and cold are felt simultaneously in both the internal and external parts, it is called **epiala**, generated from **vitreous phlegm** <term>vitreous phlegm</term> <note>A cold, thick humor described as having the clarity and consistency of molten glass.</note>. 

There is also a fever in which immense heat is felt in the internal parts, but a lukewarmness in the external parts. This happens because of the viscosity and thickness of the humor, so that the heat cannot seek the outer surfaces; this is called **lipparia**.

<margin>epiala</margin>
There is also another fever in which heavy cold is felt in the outer parts, which is called **acromidos** <note>likely "akromykos," from the Greek for "cold in the extremities"</note>, that is, "frosty." There is yet another in which the heat is intense and harmful internally, from which very sharp vapors rise, even though the humor is not particularly viscous; this fever is called **tinidos** <note>possibly "typhodes," a smoky or stupor-inducing fever</note> in the eighth book of the *Theoretical Medicine*. 

Regarding this, it must be known that authors have spoken very differently concerning these distinctions. For in the book *On Unequal Distemper* <note>original: "de distempantia i equali"</note>, in the seventh aphorism, in the *Prognostics*, and in others, as well as the eighth book of the *Theoretical Medicine*, it is stated that **epiala** is a fever in which heat and cold are felt together throughout every part of the body. Hence, in the *Book of Fevers*: "Epiala is the proper name for a fever in which patients suffer both the fever-heat and the shivering-rigor, and they feel both at the same time in every small part of the body." The aforementioned etymology of its own name seems to imply this.

Thirdly, in the book *On Simple Medicines*, it is written that this is a fever in which the one having it experiences trembling and hardness in the whole body for one hour. And this fever is the one which **Avicenna** describes by circumlocution, saying: "a fever in which each of two things happens in each of two places." 

But **lipparia** is a fever in which the internal parts grow hot and the external parts grow cold. According to Galen's fourth book of *Aphorisms*, this is even classified among the "pernicious fevers of internal abscesses," by which heat is drawn from the whole body as if by a cupping glass. Also, in the third book of *Simple Medicines*: "Lipparia is a fever in which the inner parts of the belly are set on fire, while its outer parts are cold." This is also mentioned in *On Unequal Distemper*. However, I do not find it determined by Galen from what matter it arises or how it is generated. 

**Isaac Judaeus** and **Avicenna**, along with **Serapion**, seem to disagree quite a bit regarding **epiala** and **lipparia**, not only in the variation of the names, but in the assignment of opposite causes, especially regarding **epiala**. For Isaac says, along with Avicenna in the twenty-seventh book of *On Fevers*, that **epiala** is a fever burning the internal parts and cooling the external parts, the matter of which is thick vitreous phlegm. One part of it is putrefied, but the other part is not. The putrefied part

---

indeed generates the fever. The unputrefied part, by its own nature, causes the freezing. Concerning **lipparia**, he feels that its matter is bilious mixed with vitreous phlegm, or mixed with a melancholic humor. It differs from **epiala** because that one heats the internal parts and cools the external parts and blocks the openings of the pores so that the vapor cannot be dissolved. In **lipparia**, however, all these things are the opposite: the internal parts are cold and the external parts are hot. 

**Avicenna** opposes this, along with **Serapion**, saying that in **epiala** the internal parts are cooled and the external parts are heated. Its matter is vitreous phlegm trapped in a hidden and deep place, which cools where it is. But when putrefaction happens to it, the vapor of that which has putrefied is scattered and dispersed, and it becomes inflamed in the outer parts. For when it was quiet, before putrefaction came upon it, the person did not feel cold or heat in those parts, as it was not yet putrefied. For the matter which is cold internally, being agitated in a place of stronger heat, is made cold <note>The text suggests a paradox where internal agitation paradoxically manifests as external heat</note>, just as the melting of ice is demonstrated. 

However, the vapor led from the putrefying matter is perceived as hotter on the outside. Just as a mixture in a bath signifies heat being returned to the body from the phlegm. He posits that **lipparia** can be made from phlegm or from a certain thick bile. He gives a twofold way for its generation from phlegm: one, because when the phlegm is inflamed internally and putrefies, it heats there; it is not resolved except when it heats the outer parts of the body with a thick, hot vapor. Because of the heat existing internally, it draws the rest to itself with force, so that the external parts grow cold as the heat is withdrawn—especially if the vitreous phlegm blocks the parts and occupies the outer surfaces. 

The other way is because often vapor is resolved from the phlegm that has not putrefied, but is raised up and causes heating; from this, the heat associated with a small space is separated, in the same way that heat recedes when the vapor of water ascends, as is seen in baths. And this is because there was fundamentally an immense amount of coldness before the putrefaction. It also arises from thick bile, because a small amount of it lurking internally putrefies and heats there. And since nothing is resolved from it, what was said in the first mode of phlegmatic **lipparia** occurs. For the heat runs with force from the external parts into the internal ones.

Regarding the things said above, there is a doubt—firstly concerning **epiala**, according to Galen, since he posits that heat and cold are felt together throughout the whole body. This does not seem possible, for these are contraries. Such things cannot be mixed into one at all, since one drives the other away from itself. To the contrary: because, as touched upon, in **epiala** heat and cold are felt in the same place. 

Furthermore, **Avicenna** posits a third fever between **lipparia** and **epiala**, as if composed of these two, which he names by circumlocution, saying "each of two things happens in each of two places." Likewise, there is hesitation regarding **lipparia**, secondly because in the fourth book of *Aphorisms*, **lipparia** is said to arise from an internal phlegmatic abscess or from **erysipelas** <term>erysipelas</term> <note>A skin infection, here used to describe an internal inflammation.</note>. None of the aforementioned authors express this. 

It must be said regarding the first point: that we can understand "the same place" in two ways. Either as a true and indivisible point, and thus heat and cold cannot exist simultaneously...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on the nature of mixed fevers—specifically epiala and lipparia—drawing on the authorities of Galen, Avicenna, Isaac Judaeus, and Serapion. It explores the physiological mechanisms of how cold humors (like vitreous phlegm) interact with heat to produce contradictory sensations in the patient.</meta>

...[heat and cold] cannot exist in it at once; either as a sensible and common thing, and thus they can exist as one. Whence, concerning the distance in equality, it does not happen that one may take a sensible particle in which heat and cold do not both exist. Or rather, that although the sense may judge heat and cold to be present at the same time, the intellect does not. For the judgment of the sense is not as certain as that of the intellect. This is shown by the fact that a circle appears true to the eye when drawn by hand, but not when checked by a compass—as noted in Boethius’s *Music*, book 1 <note>Boethius (c. 480–524 AD) was a foundational philosopher for the Middle Ages; his work on music was part of the mathematical curriculum.</note>. This is also indicated by an image constructed from various colors in miniature; up close they are perceived as diverse, but from afar the image appears as a single thing. Just as concave vessels on a wall appear distant through the superposition of colors. And so it is in the present case.

Regarding the other point, it must be said that **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of antiquity (2nd century AD).</note> with **Haly Abbas** <note>A 10th-century Persian physician.</note> understands **epiala** <term>epiala</term> differently, as it appeared that **Serapion** <note>Referring to Yahya ibn Sarafyun, a 9th-century Syriac Christian physician.</note> and **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (11th century), the "Prince of Physicians."</note> give a broader reason for the name. For what Galen calls "epiala," Avicenna explains by circumlocution as he set forth regarding touch; for he cared little for names. Regarding the other hesitation, it must be said that Avicenna with **Isaac Judaeus** <note>A 10th-century North African physician and philosopher.</note> posits that **lipparia** <term>lipparia</term> occurs without shivering; Galen, however, often says it occurs with it. Yet it has the mode of lipparia according to them especially when the patient burns within and is stiff with cold on the outside. Various, therefore, are the understandings of these fevers. This, then, is the diversity found in these fevers briefly recollected, and specifically between Isaac and Avicenna. Isaac indeed seems, perhaps due to a defect in the translation, to derive his view from others. Yet the practice of the Latins seems to simply imitate things not heard by others.

Regarding the third thing to be known: **vitreous phlegm** <term>vitreous phlegm</term> <note>A thick, cold, transparent humor compared to molten glass.</note> is either of a great or small quantity, and either it putrefies at once or it does not. If it is of small quantity, so that nature can finally putrefy it and master it, then it will heat the interior where the hidden putrefaction is vehement. Thus, this pure vapor being resolved and tending toward the exterior will return to coldness, since its matter was previously very cold; or it occurs according to the diversity of the putrefaction and non-putrefaction of the phlegm, which Isaac seems to believe.

But if it is of great quantity, so that nature cannot putrefy it all at once and master it, that which is moved internally by heat is reduced from "potential cold" into "actual cold"—just as when snow melts when moved by heat, it becomes more intensely cold, both because of the action of opposites and because of its thinning. The vapor resolved by the heat will still retain its nature, so that cold is felt within and heat without. This is the view that Avicenna holds. Galen, however, with Haly Abbas, sensibly feels that in this fever every part of the body is heated and cooled at once, because part of the phlegm putrefies first and part does not at all, which the name was said to denote.

In **lipparia**, however, Isaac and Avicenna are not so opposed, since they do not take the causes from opposites but rather from different sources, as appeared from another cause. Isaac feels it happens as a "rising" and from other things. Avicenna agrees more with the speech of Galen, who wishes for the heat to be hidden vehemently in the interior parts. This is also attested by the son of Serapion. And this I more highly approve.

Furthermore, note that if acidic and vitreous matter moves over the sensible parts, it induces rigor or cold without heat when it barely putrefies. But if it is moved further into a certain moderate putrefaction, it induces **epiala**, in which heat and cold are felt together in every sensible part. If, however, it putrefies further, the cold precedes (as in a daily fever) and the febrile heat supervenes, overcoming it so that it is not perceived in the increase, and especially in the peak of the fever paroxysm. Let this brief discourse suffice here regarding the assigned causes of these involved and, in both ways, probable fevers.

Regarding the fourth point: as for the first thing to be said, it is asserted. Regarding the other: it proceeds in its own way, or it is true unless something hinders it. The "hinderer" is the remaining part of the vitreous phlegm in putridity which moves. Regarding the other: it must be said that although the interior part begins to putrefy, immediately there occurs vitreous phlegm moved in non-putridity, according to Avicenna, which causes cooling. Regarding the other: what should be said about lipparia is also asserted. Regarding the other: it is similarly clear having considered the dominant cause and the mode of generation of lipparia according to Isaac and Avicenna. Regarding the other: it must be said according to Avicenna, who raises this doubt, that in such terms one condition is observed: that there be nothing which prohibits. Just as one defines water as cold and moist when its disposition is according to its nature and there is nothing prohibiting it. Likewise concerning the descent of a heavy object. Here, however, the "prohibitor" is a viscous, cold, enclosed humor, or a heterogeneous matter situated in various ways, as shown from the modes of generation of such fevers.

## Column 1

For then indeed **hectic fever** <term>ethica</term> <note>From the Greek 'hektikos', meaning habitual or deep-seated. In medieval medicine, this was a fever that had settled into the solid parts of the body, often associated with wasting diseases like tuberculosis.</note> will occur at the beginning. Likewise, if it were to occur at the beginning, it would no longer be hectic; since "to begin" refers to what is in a state of **disposition** <term>dispositio</term> <note>A temporary or easily changed state of health.</note>, whereas "hectic" denotes a **habituation** <term>habituatio</term> <note>A fixed, permanent state that is difficult to change.</note>, as will appear in what follows. Therefore, hectic fever least of all occurs at its beginning. **Galen** <note>The primary authority in Roman and medieval medicine (2nd century AD).</note> understands the opposite of this in his *Prose on the Differences of Fevers*, as do **Avenzoar**, **Avicenna**, and all other physicians. This is also confirmed by reason. For since all other illnesses occur from their beginning, for this reason they do not resemble the others.

Furthermore, since it is of the nature of an **accident** <note>In philosophy, an 'accident' is a property that is not essential to the thing’s nature; here, it refers to a symptom or secondary condition.</note> that it follows the disease as a shadow follows the body—as stated in the third book on *Accidents* and the eleventh on the *Internal Organs*—if hectic fever always accompanied other diseases, it would take on the nature of an accident rather than a disease. The reason for this is well known, since there are three types of fever that exist as diseases in themselves. Furthermore, an agent does not act unless the sufferer is able to sustain its action. Since a proportion must intervene between the agent and the sufferer, just as between the mover and the moved, or the thinker and the thought. But the spirits or the humors of the body are not fit to sustain the impression received from a more powerful agent; instead, passing through to the members, the more solid parts sustain it.

<margin>hectic</margin>
Therefore, hectic fever occurs at the beginning. Regarding the first point, it should be known that "hectic" implies something habitual; for *ethicon* in Greek is *habituatun* <note>habitual or ingrained</note> in Latin. Whence in the eighth book on the *Internal Organs*, he calls dispositions that are easily dissolved "habitudinal"—that is, as if they were temporary dispositions. But those that are not so are called "habits." For according to **Boethius** <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose work on logic and categories was a staple of medieval education.</note> in the *Categories*, a habit is a firm disposition, or a disposition is an infirm habit. "Hectic" also implies a habit, either because it is separated with difficulty or impossibility once it remains habitual, or because it reaches a solid subject, namely a limb. From this, once the impression is made, it is removed with difficulty. But hectic fever is placed among several dispositions of **phthisis** <term>phthisis</term> <note>Wasting of the body, usually referring to pulmonary tuberculosis.</note> and even differs from it; for they relate to each other as things that exceed and are excelled. <margin>Isaac on Fevers 130</margin> **Isaac on Fevers 130** <note>Isaac Judaeus (10th century), a highly influential Jewish physician and philosopher.</note> For phthisis is understood in one common way as every consumption emerging from whatever cause, whether contrary to nature or natural—such as the disposition that happens to the decrepit when they approach death. Whence in the fourth book of the **Almansor** <note>The *Liber Almansoris* by the Persian physician Rhazes (10th century).</note>, it is said that for those who maintain such a regimen, it is possible for them to reach a decrepit state and phthisis over a long time. <margin>And he is called phthisical</margin> And this hectic fever is proportional to old age, which indeed occurs not as a result of a specific consuming illness. It is also used for those who are disposed toward it according to the third book of *Aphorisms* <note>Referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates.</note>: for instance, those who have a long neck, a protruding epiglottis, a narrow chest bare of flesh with raised shoulders, and twisted legs. This kind of phthisis extends further than hectic fever. There is also a phthisis that implies corruption: the entire consumption of the body with ulceration of the lung. And in this way indeed, hectic fever exceeds phthisis. For every such phthisical person is subsequently hectic, but the reverse is not true, since many suffer from hectic fever without an ulcer of the lung. Such a hectic fever also follows phthisis as an accident; for when the pus of the lung or chest is not purged, it breathes out freely into the heart itself, inflaming it and inducing hectic fever. There are four humidities of the body, as suggested in the seventh book on the *Internal Organs*, and four distinct drynesses opposite to them. **Serapion** <note>A 9th-century Syriac physician.</note> expresses these in his sixth book, and **Isaac** in his first and 130th on *Fevers*, and in the first and twelfth of his *Basalia* <note>Likely referring to Isaac's medical compendiums.</note>. Or besides this, it may be in the substance of the heart. This is said in the first book on *Fevers*: when indeed the natural complexion of the body is inflamed, and the humidity existing in it does not yet flow together but is shown as a kind of boiling, the first species of hectic arises. <meta>This page continues the technical classification of "hectic fever" (febris ethica). It discusses the progression from simple hectic fever to marasmus (extreme wasting) and debates whether this condition can arise on its own at the start of an illness or if it must always follow another fever. The text cites major authorities: Galen, Avicenna (A.), Isaac Israeli, and Avenzoar (Zoar).</meta>

...in which each **type** <note>original: "spes" (species)</note> occupies a middle ground of knowledge and cure. And this distinction indeed shows the manner of the thing more than the thing itself, because the aforementioned things make it easier to understand. And you should know that **Galen**, in the first book of *On Fevers* and elsewhere, simply names the first stage "hectic." According to the greater part, the second stage and its specific type is when the **moisture of the heart** <note>In medieval physiology, the heart required a specific "radical moisture" to function; its loss was considered life-threatening.</note> is not yet dried out; for when it is dried out, as at the end of the second type and in the third, it is called **consumption** <term>tabes</term>. 

However, according to **Avicenna** <note>The Latin abbreviation "A. adubul" likely refers to Avicenna (Ibn Sina) or possibly Al-Abul, but in this medical context, Avicenna is the standard authority cited alongside Galen.</note>, there is also another type called the hectic of old age, or senility, because it comes upon a person in the hour of old age. This happens at the end of **marasmus** <term>marasmos</term> <note>A clinical term for extreme malnutrition and emaciation, interpreted here as "the total drying of the body."</note>; and this is the dominance of dryness over the whole body without fever. Its cause is most often **coldness** combined with a weakness of the **vital force** <term>uirtutis</term>, whereby the limbs lack nourishment. It is also caused by drinking cold water when the body's disposition is not ready for it. 

Sometimes a physician causes this "marasmic" hectic fever by giving cold water to drink during a hectic fever, or by the application of cold. Regarding this, the physician is deterred from drawing a worse result, as stated in the tenth book of **On the Method of Healing** <note>original: "de ingenio," referring to Galen's *De Methodo Medendi*.</note>: It is better for a person to be transitioned into a different, cold state with a favorable hope of success—even if it is dangerous—than to perish most certainly without hope. For this reason, we provide cooling treatments for all hectic fevers immediately, before they lead to consumption and the patient dies. For we shall not attempt to heal those who are most certainly wasting away once their heat is extinguished. But the remaining dryness of old age allows a man to live for as long as his solid parts can resist until extreme old age.

I understand "hectic at its beginning" to occur when no other fevers have preceded it—neither **one-day fever** <term>effimera</term> nor **putrid fever**, nor any other of those types. First, the primary heat is kindled in the body from some strong cause in the heart. And although all fevers are rooted in the heart, this one is especially fixed in its very substance. 

Secondly, it should be known that some unlearned people, hearing the aforementioned discourse, claimed that **Galen** and **Aristotle** <note>original: "anisitila," likely a scribal error for "Aristotilia."</note> said that hectic fever least of all happens at the beginning. Thus, in the first book of *On Fevers*, some think that this condition cannot happen to anyone except following the diseases just mentioned. They are also deceived by a passage of Galen where he says: Hectic fevers, since they are generated from **procatarctic** <term>pre-existing</term> <note>Initial or triggering causes, such as environmental factors or emotional distress.</note> causes, never attack from the start, but transition from those which arise from putrefaction.

It must be said that this statement is not simple, but rather conditional, as will appear to those who look diligently. The defect of these and other views will be clearly seen.

<margin>To the present point</margin>

Thirdly, it should be known that hectic fever, as a rule, does not occur at the beginning, but rather follows other fevers and illnesses. It rarely happens at the start because its cause rarely occurs on its own. Thus, in the first book of *On Fevers*: Hectic fevers happen in two ways. Sometimes they occur because of **burning fevers** <term>causones</term> <note>A high, acute fever, often associated with bile.</note> which last so long that they consume the moisture of the body and the heart. At other times, while the moisture of the heart still remains, the fevers are kindled like a flame on a lamp wick. 

Hectic fever also arises not infrequently from a **semi-tertian fever** <term>emitriteo</term> <note>A mixed fever pattern that was often considered dangerous or fatal.</note>. Thus, in the fourth book of the *Aphorisms*: The semi-tertian is sometimes among the most lethal of fevers because it leads to hectic fever and to heroic and difficult illnesses. It also arises, as has appeared, from a preceding primary fever, and sometimes from 

**empyema** <note>A collection of pus, usually in the lungs.</note>, and universally from an internal **aposteme** <note>An abscess or swelling.</note> that is mostly hidden, and because of too thin a diet, and the prohibition of cooling (such as drinking water), and because of small attention paid to the "side of the heart" with cooling things from without or within. Many times the necessity of the physician also causes one to fall into it, because of a collapse of the vital force and frequent **fainting** <term>sincopis</term>, when giving wine to drink and meat-water and hot medicines like musk.

It also happens that hectic fever begins as such. Thus Galen says in the same place:
<margin>Note.</margin>
"One generation of hectic fevers has been told to me; the other truly is when they attack from the beginning," which immediately makes the first generation similar to **ephemeral fevers**, caused by sadness, anger, and labor, especially when combined with a scorching heat. 

And in the tenth book of *On the Method of Healing*: Again, from burning fevers it leads into consumption, or from the very beginning, hectic fever happens immediately, leaping over the burning fever stage.
<margin>fevers</margin>
**Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli (c. 850–950), a highly influential Jewish physician and philosopher.</note> also distinguishes this, saying that there is one kind of hectic whose cause is some other disease, and another whose cause is not another disease, which arises from the inflammation of the **humor** existing in the cavity of the veins and arteries of the heart. Summing up, he says: "Because we have distinguished the cause of hectic fever which is due to another disease, but [now] the heart on its own." 

**Avicenna**, having set down the causes by which hectic fever occurs, adds: "It is a very long time before hectic happens at the beginning," because the **radical limbs** <note>The solid, fundamental parts of the body (like the heart) formed at conception.</note> are already inflamed, and the humor or **spirit** <term>spūs</term> <note>The "vital spirit," a subtle substance believed to circulate in the blood to sustain life.</note> is not inflamed before that; rather, it is necessary that those limbs be heated first, and then through the progression of days, the fever heats up, unless a very strong cause occurs. 

**Avenzoar** <note>Ibn Zuhr (1094–1162), a famous physician from Al-Andalus.</note> also takes up the discourse on this: "One type of fever is called hectic, which for the most part does not seize by itself primarily, but follows other chronic fevers that dry out the body while dissipating it." Sometimes it also happens because of "one-day fevers." 

In the fourth book of the **Colliget** <note>The *Kitab al-Kullyat* by Averroes (Ibn Rushd).</note>: Hectic fever rarely happens except after other fevers, such as after an ephemeral fever in bodies prepared for it, or after some putrid fever. However, it occurs by itself in those whose nature is drier and hotter, living in labor, wakefulness, and on a thinner diet. And even more so if, through the disposition of the air and the region, they fall into anger or sadness. 

These are the discourses which have been brought forward concerning the beginning of this fever, whether by itself or after others. Both parts of the argument can be decorated with reasons. For the fact that hectic fever accompanies other diseases in most cases is shown by the fact that every agent, when it acts on matter, introduces a form prepared for it. With many causes introducing heat into the body, the most prepared matter is the "spirit," which is the subject of ephemeral fever, or the humor, which is the subject of putrid fever, rather than the limb in which hectic is fixed; this is because a cause so vehemently impressive rarely occurs to the body. Just as we see in the universe: great and marvelous effects occur more rarely. Furthermore, nature protects the solid part as much as it can—namely the **spermatic limb** <note>The solid parts of the body, thought to be derived from the "seed" of the parents.</note>, which is the subject and support of all things in the animal, and especially the heart, which is the proper subject of hectic fever...

<meta>This page continues the technical debate on "hectic fever" (febris ethica). It addresses the question of whether this fever can be "incipient"—meaning it starts on its own as a primary disease—rather than always following a previous fever like a "putrid" or "ephemeral" fever. The author uses analogies from natural philosophy, such as lightning and the heating of a bathhouse, to explain how heat interacts with different parts of the body.</meta>

<margin>Lightning</margin>
**Truly** <note>original: "uerrū," likely a transcription for "verum"</note> it also happens according to the properties of their own substances. That such a thing should be so is preserved especially by nature with all wisdom and intention. Let it be, therefore, that it does not begin for many. This is indicated by the **Royal Book** <note>original: "Almeliletu," referring to the *Kitab al-Maliki* or "Royal Book" by the Persian physician Haly Abbas.</note>, which for the most part precedes. **But** that it may sometimes happen by beginning <note>i.e., as a primary condition</note> is shown because an agent acts not on just anything, but on a "patient" <note>In medieval philosophy, the "agent" is the thing doing the action, and the "patient" is the thing receiving it.</note> disposed to it. **However**, that a patient might not be disposed can happen in two ways. Either because it is too hard and prepared to resist the action, such as iron, precious stones, and especially **diamond** <term>adamast</term>; or because it is subtle, soft, and yielding, like air or vapor, which cannot withstand the action of the agent, but rather allows a passage into something solid and hard, as is shown in the striking of bodies, where solid bodies are struck while the air does not resist. This can also be seen in the case of **lightning** <note>original: "fulgure"</note>, for not every patient is rendered disposed to it so that it acts upon it, but rather that which is hard, compact, and resisting. As **Al-Ghazali** <note>original: "algazel," the Persian theologian and philosopher.</note> says: **Lightning**, which is a subtle fire, penetrates plants and soft things, but when it strikes hard things, such as iron and gold, it dissolves them, so that it melts the gold in a purse and yet does not burn the purse; and it dissolves the iron in ships and does not burn the men. This happens because those hard things resist, while the others do not. So it is in the matter at hand, where it often happens that the **spirit** <term>spiritus</term> or **humor** <term>humor</term> <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to the vital gases and "humors" to the bodily fluids like blood or bile.</note> is rendered the appropriate patient-matter for fevers, but the solid limb is not. Because of this, hectic fever more frequently occurs after other diseases. But sometimes the spirit or humor is not a suitable subject because of its subtlety and softness, but the hard, solid limb is. And this happens when the cause is as strong as lightning. Because such a thing happens more rarely, it occurs more slowly that a hectic fever should be incipient <note>starting from the beginning</note>. For a moderate impression is induced in the humors and less so in the spirits, because of which heat is fixed in the limbs as a state of **having been heated** <note>original: "in calefactum esse"</note>, and not merely the process of **being heated** <note>original: "in calefieri"</note>, as it is in the spirits and humors.

**Furthermore**, when the matter is highly disposed, even a weak agent can make an impression upon it. But such a disposition is found only in the extreme, such as when both natural and non-natural factors tend toward heat and dryness. For no one is immediately seized by hectic fever from the start who has a moist body at the first sign of fevers, and much less one who is cold. But that a strong agent sometimes occurs has already been seen. Why then is hectic fever primary and not another? Regarding the fourth point to be said against the first: they speak according to what happens in most cases, in which the greatest part of the medical art consists. Hectic fever, however, arrives as an incipient condition in those cases which are rare, as has been shown. For **Galen** <term>Ga.</term>, wishing to excuse himself in his book *On Crises* from giving the signs of hectic fever, says they should be omitted, both because he had treated them in other places (as in the first book *On Fevers*), and because the signs of this fever are taken for the signs of those preceding fevers, since it happens so rarely in this way. But who will doubt that if incipient hectic fever occurs rarely, since there is no science of things that are rare, but only of things that happen always or for the most part (as in the second book of the *Physics*), how can there be science of this fever, given what was said above—that it can rarely happen and then exist for itself without other preceding fevers? It must be said, as it appears...

When their appetite fails, they should be restored to eating; for those among them who act more manfully in this regard and eat by force are delivered and live. **Paulus Aegineta** <note>original: "Palin."</note> says it also occurs in the moistures, but pestilential fever putrefies a certain moisture that surrounds the heart. Thus, Avicenna places pestilential fevers under the genus of hectic fever. 

On the other hand, it seems to be a **putrid fever**, since it happens from putrefaction. For everyone falls into the sickness to which they are most exposed, since the most powerful factor in the generation of sickness is the preparation of the "patient" <note>the body receiving the disease</note>, as stated in the first book on fevers. It should therefore be placed under the genus of putrid fever. 

The opposite of this is shown, however, because a putrid fever is "humoral" <note>based in the fluids</note>. ...the worst quality combined with the substance: for the impression of this air [on the body] by the "agent" <note>the cause of the change</note> seems to depend more on that cause than on the disposition of the matter, as has been explained more fully. Also, thirdly, there is contact: namely, the contact of the air occurring more immediately and externally on all sides, which necessarily involves both interaction and time in every natural process of generation and corruption.

For who can separate their hand from a very active fire so quickly that they do not perceive its heat? Nor can fire operate in any way without the aforementioned causes. The time spent in this impression of the air is significant, especially since such a rotting impression is not easily separated from the air itself. And these things are considered among the primary causes. In the second place, the cause is sought in every physical operation.

<margin>Remote Causes.</margin>

The "agent" causes, supported by these two mediating factors [time and contact] with the "patients" <note>the things being acted upon, like the human body</note>, are twofold: remote [distant] and particular [nearby]. The primary ones are the preceding dispositions from the forms of the heavens or "images," which make it necessary for something to occur whose arrival is unknown to the physician—namely, insofar as these celestial forms cause the air and water to rot.

Decay also occurs in the bowels of the earth due to causes unknown to the physician. This happens especially due to eclipses of the luminaries <note>the sun and moon</note> and the conjunction of planets, particularly **Saturn** and **Mars** with fixed stars, or their gathering in one of the "human" signs of the Zodiac, especially when they prevail in the "house of life" in an evil way. Such a conjunction or aspect, or the revolution of the world-year, brings about wicked constitutions of the seasons, changing the essences and natures of things.

<margin>Particular and nearby causes</margin>

The particular and nearby causes are the corruptions sensible to us here in the air—whether brought by winds, and especially southern winds, from distant parts, as happens in the depths of caves, caverns, and closed-off wells. Or it may be due to the stagnation and constriction of air between walls and roofs when it is rendered immobile, or because of rotten lagoons and stagnant ponds. This includes things like flax <note>The process of "retting" flax in water to separate fibers was famously foul-smelling and considered a source of disease.</note> soaked in them, or because of vegetables—such as cabbage, rocket, and sharp or viscous dairy products. 

Or it may be because of poisonous chasms breathing out a toxic aura, such as those around **Sardis** and **Hierapolis** <note>Cities in modern-day Turkey known in antiquity for "Plutoniums" or openings to the underworld that emitted suffocating gases.</note>, or a large river used for purging a city, or an army of many people being disturbed. It can also be caused by trees of bad "complexions" <note>the balance of their elemental qualities</note>, such as the yew, walnut, or fig trees, which give off rotten odors, and the absence of healthy winds; or because of dung and animal carcasses, or the bodies of men killed in battle and left unburied or unburned. For perhaps from **Ethiopia**, through a continuous flow, certain rotten pollutions reached the **Athenians** <note>A reference to the Plague of Athens (430 BCE) described by Thucydides, which was said to have originated in Ethiopia.</note>, whose bodies were ready to be harmed, becoming the cause of fever. This is noted in the first book of *On the Safeguarding of Health*.

There is also a sort of indirect mode of pestilence: for a "mortality" <note>a mass death event among plants or animals</note> corrupts trees and vegetables, and these in turn corrupt the animals that eat them, and because of this, the humans who eat those animals are corrupted. It also happens according to **Democritus**: when a famine is followed by abundance, or because of weak wheat, herbs, and various foods, which men are forced to eat when the cattle have died during a famine.

<margin>4th book of Meteorology</margin>

This is also recounted by **Avenzoar** <note>original: "3oar"; the Andalusian physician Ibn Zuhr</note> regarding the pestilence in Morocco. When a pestilence comes from the lower regions, physicians advise seeking the higher and open air. But when it comes from the higher regions, they advise seeking the lower, enclosed air. 

Nor is it surprising that air rots, since it is mixed with earthly fumes and vapors, and even the watery rays of the heavenly bodies mix with these things; for air does not remain in its "simplicity." If it did, it would not rot, since nothing that is purely simple can rot. Therefore, since fire remains the simplest of the elements, it rots the least. Whence it says in the fourth book of the **Meteorology**: "All other things rot except fire; for indeed earth, water, and air rot."

Next, we must consider what pestilence is. Since it is a certain change made in the air, we must first know that its change is twofold: one is in its qualities [hot, cold, moist, dry] and the other is more in its substance. However, a change in substance can never be completed without a change in qualities, since every action occurs through quality, though the reverse is not always true. 

A change in quality occurs when air reaches an intolerable state, especially in heat or cold, so that harvests, generation, and life are corrupted. This happens in two ways: either it is a "symbolic" change, such as an excess of summer heat or winter cold; or it is a "reversal," such as the malice of cold in summer or heat in winter. And it is similar with other qualities. For when the air is changed to such an extent, bodies are similarly converted. 

A change of the air itself in substance occurs when it is turned toward "malice"—not that any one of its qualities becomes much stronger by increase or decrease (though this does not happen without their change), and this is called "pestilence" in theory. It is a change of the air into corruption and rotting due to a departure from its proper balance in both substance and quality. According to **Aristotle**, pestilence is a rotting that happens to the air, similar to the rotting of water that has become soft and foul-smelling. For the air thickens and softens just as water does when someone puts flax or hemp or such things into it.

To make it clear what a pestilential disease is, one must know that disease is twofold. One is "particular," meaning it affects individuals separately; for example, at the same time and in the same city, one person has a quartan fever, another a tertian, and some have "frenzy" <note>delirium or inflammation of the brain</note>, and so on. 

There is also "common" disease, which is also twofold. One is familiar and known, called **endemic** or **endemial**, occurring as a habit or contingency due to the location—for example, because of the water, the wind, or the soil. In some cities, kidney disease abounds; in others, **goiter** <term>bocium</term>, which among the Arabs is never or rarely found. In some places, "Medina fever" <note>Guinea worm disease</note> or skin lesions are common, which **Galen** never saw. He discusses such diseases in his book *On Air and Water*. 

The other type is **epidemic**, meaning arriving "upon" or from the outside, to distinguish it from those that arise from the local place. "Epidemia" is often used interchangeably with "pestilence," even if the term itself is more general. ...a manifold and sudden pestilential [fever] [affects] a multitude of people at one and the same time. He indeed called it "manifold" to show the variety of this disease; for only the sickness of pestilence is common to all in this specific way. For there is a certain kind of pestilence from which continuous fevers arise. Sometimes carbuncles <note>clusters of painful, pus-filled boils</note> appear, and at other times it is defined by smallpox or occasionally measles and similar conditions, as he shows in the books on *Epidemics* <note>Referring to the Hippocratic *Epidemics*</note>. It is called "sudden" to distinguish it from endemic disease <note>original: *morbi endimialis*, a disease naturally occurring in a specific region</note>, which comes on gradually from the impression of those things which exist in that specific place.

The remainder which he adds to the description is said to differentiate it from a "proper" disease <note>one specific to an individual</note>. For the same thing does not happen to many people at the same time in most diseases, but rather when it happens from the improper administration of the "six non-natural things" <note>The *sex res non-naturales* were the environmental/lifestyle factors in medieval medicine: air, food/drink, sleep, exercise, evacuations, and emotions</note>, in which people err in various ways. Pestilence and the rotting of the air happen according to themselves and especially at the end of summer and in autumn. **Al-Mansur** <note>likely referring to the work of the Persian physician Rhazes</note> and **Avicenna** [agree].

But there is hesitation regarding the aforementioned points, because it was said that pestilence arises chiefly from the rotting of the air, which does not seem [correct], because in the 25th Problem <note>referring to Aristotle's *Problems*</note>, he asks why water and earth rot [but air does not]. He assigns the cause of this as: every very hot thing becomes non-putrid. For it is necessary to be cooled first [to rot]. Fire is always hot. Air, however, is full of fire <note>In the Aristotelian system, air is hot and moist, sharing the quality of 'heat' with fire</note>. On the contrary, it has been said that all things rot except fire. For indeed, earth, water, and air all rot. All physicians testify to this. It must be said that pure air does not rot, nor does air mixed with fire. For intense heat preserves it from rotting; however, it rots when it is mixed and cooled to some extent.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that some have wanted to reduce this fever to the genus of <term>ephemeral</term> <note>original: *effimere*, fevers lasting only one day</note> fevers. Their motive was based on authority, because a certain pestilence of the air happens on account of a simple quality without the air itself rotting. Indeed, because it comes with the "spirits" <note>vital breaths in the body</note> which are hot and dry, and the sickness happens more readily in a proportional way, they conclude this kind of fever belongs to the genus of the "fever of a day."

But this position cannot stand. For it is quite foreign for this fever to be considered ephemeral, since it has little or no similarity to it. This is shown because an ephemeral fever often terminates in one or more days, and rarely in four; but this [pestilence] extends to more days, according to the disposition of the patient and the strength of the [disease] agent. Furthermore, an ephemeral fever is healthy in itself <note>meaning the patient usually recovers</note>, whereas a pestilential fever is deadly in itself. Hence **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a famous 10th-century physician</note> says that very few are saved from this fever. And **Avicenna** can say that according to himself. This is suggested in the seventh book of the *Aphorisms*: many crises were for health rather than death, unless the disease was pestilential. Thus, because of these and many other things as shall be shown, since this fever differs entirely from ephemeral ones, it should not be said to be placed under that category. Their motive also fails for two reasons: first, because as has been shown, a change in the air's quality, even if extreme, is not properly considered pestilential unless it causes a conversion in the substance [of the body]. Second, because a violently hot and dry disposition of the air does not induce an ephemeral fever, but rather a putrid or <term>hectic</term> <note>original: *ethica*, a fever that consumes the body's moisture</note> one.

---

<margin>g</margin>
Hence, in the fourth [book], he says: accidental fevers caused by dry air become the cause of choleric fevers <note>fevers associated with yellow bile</note>. Therefore, much more would it happen when there is heat; or when that dryness in the air is joined [to heat], it leads to <term>hectic</term> and not ephemeral fever. That it results in hectic and not ephemeral fever is because the "spirit" <note>the vital spirit</note> is a subtle subject that cannot withstand even a slight movement of the air. Hence a transition is made to the humors, because those subjects are thicker and more tolerable once the preceding distance is overcome.

Others, however, wanted to reduce it to the genus of hectic fevers, moved by very sharp authority. This is because, just as in hectic fever one finds dispositions in the sufferers that are almost imperceptible and lukewarm, so it is in this [pestilence]. Furthermore, this also seems to be deeply rooted in hidden, inward parts like hectic fever, for which reason they wanted to reduce it to that. But this is also quite far-fetched—to bring it to the hectic category—because of the great diversity between them. In this [pestilence], evacuations and purging are prescribed, whereas in hectic fever they are used very little. Also, it is terminated by a "crisis" <note>a sudden change in the disease leading to recovery or death</note>, but hectic fever is not. For this reason, it is more correctly reduced to [putrid fever].

Nor are their motives valid, because the dispositions in these [pestilences] are not equal as in hectic fever, but are changed by various mutations. For someone perceives from it heat and strong inflammation, and sometimes coldness, especially in the extremities and outer parts. And at the peak, the internal parts are hot and the external parts are cold, which does not happen in hectic fevers. Furthermore, the position that it is rooted in the interior like a hectic fever is true, yet it does not expand to the exterior in the same way, nor is it in the members <note>solid parts of the body</note>, but in the humors, as will be shown.

Regarding the third [opinion], it should be known that it simply reduces to a "putrid fever." The manner of its reduction [is found in] **Avicenna** with authority. Through this, he touched on the first point, saying: the air rots through the expulsion of the spirit within it, and this rotted [air] reaches the heart. Therefore, it corrupts the spirit of the heart and surrounds it with humidity, and a heat arises that has gone outside of nature and spreads through the body; and thus from there arises the pestilential fever.

He shows this first, because truly pestilential "membranes" <note>original: *meningas*, perhaps referring here to the coverings or the essential nature of the fevers</note> of fevers arise from the rotting of all things. Second, he thus wishes them to arise from rotting. Reason also demonstrates this, taken from the prior cause, since a "putrid fever" is so named because it arises from rotting, and such is the pestilential fever. This is shown through the first [point]... **Galen** testifies concerning this with others in the first book of *Fevers*: A pestilential fever occurs because of humors being fit and ready for rotting, when the animal [the human body] receives some brief occasion from the surrounding [air]. It begins much from respiration, because the air in the vicinity is tainted by a rotting evaporation. The principle of the rotting... Second, he adds also that bodies joined to air in which pestilences consist, which are full of feminine superfluities <note>excess bodily fluids</note>, are already prepared to rot by themselves. Furthermore, in the third book of the *Aphorisms* and the first of *Fevers*, he recites a certain disposition of a pestilential [fever] starting at the beginning, similar to those placed in the *Epidemics*, such as: carbuncles in the cranium and so forth. The cause of these, as he showed there, was rotting. It was also said through...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on the nature of pestilential fevers. A. ...this fever putrefies the moisture of the heart. **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli ben Solomon, a highly influential 10th-century physician and philosopher</note> also falls into this opinion. Furthermore, a putrid fever arises from things that are more hot and moist, since this is the cause of putrefaction. For whatever things are hot and moist rot quickly; such are the humors and the air, for they are hot and moist in relation to the rest of the body. However, the spirit <note>original: *spiritus*; in medieval medicine, this refers to a subtle vapor or "vital breath" that carries life force through the body, rather than the soul</note> and the limbs are not so. Moreover, the signs of a putrid fever are many, and the putrefaction itself changes [the body], since these signs lead us to a knowledge of the disease's existence, especially when they are taken from things substantially inherent to it.

The signs of this fever are situated within it: for in it, there is inordinate heat, a dryness of the tongue, intense thirst, difficulty breathing <note>original: *hannelitus angustia*</note> and a foul odor to that breath, restlessness, nausea, pain at the "mouth of the stomach" <note>the epigastric region or the esophagus</note>, a collapse of strength, a mixing of reason <note>mental confusion or delirium</note>, a pulse that is varied, frequent, small, and sometimes intense, excessive sweating, coldness of the extremities, spasms, *alchubuz* <note>a term likely derived from Arabic, referring to a specific type of swelling or internal pressure</note>, vomiting of bile, [bowel] looseness, gassiness, and such things. These indeed are not present in other types of fevers, but only in the putrid ones. Likewise, it is a putrid fever (or leads to one) if its treatment is the same as for putrid fevers. And such is this case: for in it, bloodletting <note>original: *fleubotomia*</note> is primarily prescribed, along with the purging of the putrefaction, its alteration, and its drying out—the three things to be observed in putrid fevers.

From these points, one concludes that this fever is most properly placed under the category of "putrid." If anyone tries by some comparison to reduce this fever to a hectic fever <note>original: *ethica*; a fever that wastes the body's tissues</note>, and specifically to an ephemeral fever <note>original: *effimera*; a fever lasting only one day, caused by emotional or environmental factors</note>, this would be very foreign and disproportionate. It is not placed in the treatise with other putrid fevers because it does not happen from a specific matter like the others, but rather from the whole.

But if someone objects that this discussion is simply irrelevant, since this fever eventually happens from "superior forms" <note>celestial/astrological influences</note> as was said above, and since these are necessary, who could resist them? What necessity is there, then, for this to be discussed in medicine? Furthermore, assuming it happens from the superior outlook—namely eclipses, the conjunction of stars, and the diversity in the circle of the signs <note>the Zodiac</note>—no one but an **astrologer** could understand and observe it. What does this have to do with the physician?

To the first point, it must be said: although the motion and being of the superior bodies cannot be hindered since it is necessary, and we cannot drive away misfortunes from the sky, we are nevertheless able to turn away their "impressions" <note>the physical effects they exert on the earth</note> by making the matter of our bodies "undisposed" <note>unreceptive or resistant</note> to them. For it has been said that "the acts of active things are received according to the disposition of the receiver." And so, in the *Centiloquium* <note>A famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note>, it is said: "A very good astrologer will be able to prohibit much evil that is coming according to the stars by pre-arming the recipient in such a way that when the influence arrives, the physician <insert>himself</insert> is not affected by it." For if the stars and the heavens bring a certain deadly cold in winter, we are able to avoid it, being protected by foreknowledge.

To the other point, it must be said in many ways: although we do not know the matter and disposition of the heavens, we nevertheless know as physicians which bodies are disposed toward pestilential illnesses, and we can rectify them so they are rendered undisposed to those influences; when this is done, the impression of the heavens does not happen. Or, although we do not know the coming pestilence through superior causes, we know it through "middle causes" and signs—for instance, through the disposition of the air surrounding us. **Galen**, in the first book of the *Prognostics*, understands this as a "divine" or "celestial" sign. In this, the signs of pestilence are declared enough... Or that the physician must have this foreknowledge through the science of **astronomy**, which he ought to have within himself, since astronomy contributes no small thing to medicine. Hence [the book] *On Air and Water* <note>Referring to the Hippocratic text *On Airs, Waters, and Places*</note>...

Regarding the things we have treated from the highest matters... To the first, it must be said that although putrid air arriving at the heart corrupts the complexion <note>the balance of humors</note> of the body, it does not, however, putrefy the spirit. For the spirit does not properly rot, since it is hot, dry, subtle, and in motion; instead, it is inflamed and more easily dissolved. Or, the corruption of the complexion of such a spirit is not in a "state of being," but rather in a "state of becoming." Now, a fever is said to be that which is in a finished state, not in a state of becoming...

<margin>No</margin> To the other point, it must be said: the fever that is in the spirit is in the "influant" spirit, not the "innate" or "implanted" one, which is the more principal root and, as it were, the form and maker of the heart. For in its vigor, the informative power produced the heart, since the male seed is almost totally dissolved into spirits. Thus the spirit receives this from here.

To the next, it must be said: it is not a hectic fever, even if it is placed after it by **A.** <note>likely Aristotle or Avicenna</note>, because **Galen** discusses it after ephemeral fevers and before hectic ones. And **Al-Mansur** <note>Rhazes</note> puts it after fevers of the organs. **Isaac**, however, places it more with the putrid ones, which is not disputed. The cause of this variety could be that this fever is not as "truly" putrid as a colicky or phlegmatic fever. This is apparent from its symptoms, which show a certain deformity <note>irregularity</note> compared to putrid ones. Similarly, there is a diversity in the cause, because other putrid fevers arise more from the disposition of humors being prone to rot than from the strength of the acting agent; but this one is the opposite. **Isaac** supports this, understanding it clearly when he said the fever comes from the "pestilential genus" and not from the "genus of humors"—not because it doesn't happen in putrefied humors, but because a greater cause exists in the putrefaction of the air [predisposing] them to this weakness, rather than from a vice of the humor's own, as in other putrid fevers.

Furthermore, while the rest of the fevers are essentially passions of the heart, this one more so accompanies and afflicts it. For putrefied air, arriving more immediately at the heart than things that are inside it, corrupts and putrefies the moisture... I do not dare to explain this simply. And perhaps this is the reason why physicians have not expressed precisely under which genus of fevers pestilence should be placed. To the other point: although it is cured by the same [remedies], they are not exactly the same, but fewer and smaller. Soon also **Al-Mansur** excludes the bath...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of fevers, specifically focusing on how internal abscesses or swellings (apostemes) generate different types of fever. It bridges the previous discussion of humors and dietary restrictions with a detailed anatomical and pathological classification of internal inflammations.</meta>

Note: The remainder [of this topic] concerns the opposite side. The manner of its generation will be touched upon in what follows. There is also a certain type of **swelling** <note>original: *apātū* / *apostema*; a localized inflammation or abscess</note> that is external, which is subject to the senses such as touch and sight; for these clearly and immediately grasp its boundaries. 

The internal [swelling], however, is its opposite, which is reached only by the senses through signs accepted and deduced. This is generated either in the interior members—wherever they may be, such as the throat, the lungs, the **capsule of the heart** <note>original: *cassula cordis*; the pericardium</note>, the stomach with the **esophagus** <note>original: *meri*</note>, the liver, the spleen, the intestines, the kidneys, the womb, and the bladder—or in the **membranes** <note>original: *pāniculis*</note> surrounding them, whether they divide them along their length, width, or depth.

Regarding why it is called a "fever" and an "acute" one, see section 87. Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have stated without distinction that an internal swelling simply causes a **continuous fever**; others, however, have shown through sharp arguments that it is not rarely an **intermittent fever** <note>original: *interpolatā*; a fever that breaks and returns</note>.

But let us see what must be said regarding this third point. Concerning the third, it should be known that a certain internal swelling can induce an intermittent fever. For the sake of this, it must first be noted on the part of the **matter** <note>the physical substance or humors causing the disease</note> that the cause of fever is twofold. One is **essential and primary**; the other is, as it were, **accidental and secondary**. 

Of the primary causes, one is "mediated"—namely, the one called "antecedent." Another is "immediate," which can properly be called the "conjoined cause," because it changes and is joined with the disease itself. Such is the **putrid soot** <note>original: *fuligo putrida*; according to Galenic theory, "sooty" vapors produced by the overheating of humors</note> or the horrible, thin, putrid smoke rising from the source of the putrefaction. If this is located primarily in the vessels or outside them, as long as its continuation reaches the heart, a fever will be generated—either continuous or intermittent—depending on whether it reaches the heart continuously or successively, as was said in section 87 and others.

But regarding the cause as "accidental" and "secondary," some help to ignite [the fever] by reason of the matter of the swelling itself. Others do so by part of the quality of the member in which it exists. In the first way, it is diversified in multiple ways. Since some swellings are made from **hot matter**, such as from blood and **choler** <note>yellow bile</note>, these are called **phlegmons** <note>original: *ffones* / *phlegmones*</note> from the term for inflammation. Others, however, are made from matter that is cold, hard, soft, watery, or windy. 

The first [hot] types are significant and worthy of bringing on a continuous fever, since they have a greater homogeneity with the heart. For things that are of this nature have a more certain passage according to [the theories of] Avicenna. Thus, they are primary and secondary. The continuous fever accompanying them demonstrates the heat of these hidden swellings. 

Those that are **cold**, however, act more slowly and can therefore cause an intermittent fever more easily, because the smoke proceeding and resulting from the source of putridity is rendered insufficient by itself to be continued to the heart. Rather, the motion of its source waits for the agitation from above, as said in section 88; such is the motion of **melancholy** <note>black bile</note> every fourth day, of choler every third day, and of **phlegm** daily. 

Truly, because the motion of phlegm fatigues the sufferer for eighteen hours and is scarcely moderated by water, if an internal swelling arises from phlegm, it is added to its motion for the sake of the continuity of the fever. Inasmuch as it might strongly induce a fever, it will be fixed as a continuous one. This is why in the first book of the fourth [canon], it is posited that swellings of the kidneys cause fevers mixed from **tertian, quartan, quintan, and sextan** fevers <note>fevers recurring every 3rd, 4th, 5th, or 6th day</note>, but not daily ones. 

The matter is also divided by reason of **quantity**—between a large amount and a small amount. Primarily, this diversity arises from quality, just like almost everything else, because a great deal of matter, filling and extending the continuous space, will induce a "solution of continuity" <note>a physical tear or separation in the tissue</note> most of all. If this occurs in more sensitive places, it will cause a continuous fever; its opposite will be able to cause an intermittent one. 

Similarly, the nature of the swelling varies in causing a continuous or intermittent fever (or inducing none at all) by reason of the **disposition of the matter**. For it happens when the matter of a swelling **suppurates** <note>turns into pus</note>, so that its thin part flows out while its thick part remains burned or "incinerated." In such cases, an intermittent fever is caused, or none at all, as appears sometimes in the "sclerosities" (hardenings) of the liver, spleen, and kidneys.

This can also be varied by reason of the **location** of the matter. Because those swellings located in places near the heart—and especially in those that have a great affinity with the heart—will bring about a continuous fever. Others will bring about an intermittent one.

The fever is likewise diversified in many ways by reason of the **part** in which the internal swelling occurs. For either that part will be **nervous** (full of nerves) and of great sensitivity, prone to being inflamed through the stimulation of "rheum" <note>flowing waste fluids</note> due to the pain of the spirits, and thus induce a continuous fever. Or it is due to the presence of many **arteries** in the member; for through them, it has a greater continuity to the heart, and the spirits and blood contained within are more fervent. There is also **pulsation** in them, all of which testify to the heat and the generation of a continuous fever. Or it is due to the **fleshy nature** of the part; for fleshy members are moister, more porous, and contain more matter. Or it is by reason of the **size of the members**; for larger members receive more matter and are more closely associated with the heart. Therefore, internal swellings in these cause more continuous fevers. In the others with the opposite dispositions, an intermittent fever will arise more often.

The use of the **Six Non-Natural Things** <note>the fundamental environmental and lifestyle factors in medieval medicine: air, food/drink, sleep/wake, motion/rest, evacuation/repletion, and passions of the mind</note> also helps—either through contraries or similarities—to measure the generation of continuous or intermittent fevers. In these, one must consider age, strength, the season, the region, and other such things. These are well-known due to their fame, and for the sake of brevity, they will not be expanded upon further at present. 

From these points, a brief demonstration can be gathered: namely, that an internal swelling more often causes a continuous fever, and sometimes an intermittent one. It appears, therefore, by deducing from the logic of physicians, that an internal swelling can sometimes induce an intermittent fever—such as when the member is "ignoble" <note>less vital or non-essential</note>, distant from a "noble" <note>vital</note> member, not clearly joined to it, and has little or no sensation. And let its matter be colder or small in quantity. Through the opposite conditions, a continuous fever will arise. This can be reasoned and is apparent.

Know that a fever arising from an internal swelling is **not an ephemeral fever** <note>a one-day fever caused by temporary factors like heat or anger</note>, as some think. Rather, it is of the genus of **putrid fevers**. Thus, according to the fourth book: fevers that cause internal swellings perhaps do not arise from the application of heat to the heart, or from putrefaction that induces an ephemeral fever. This...

Regarding the fourth point: To the first argument, it should be said that a **phlegmon** <note>original: *fleumō*; an inflammatory swelling</note> of this kind exists. When it must be generated from bloody and choleric matter with inflammation, it will induce a **continuous fever**. However, it is not concluded from this that other swellings cannot cause an **intermittent fever** <note>original: *iterpollatā*; a fever that breaks and returns at intervals</note>, which according to the custom of **Galen** <note>famous 2nd-century Greek physician</note> are not called phlegmons. Indeed, even "hot" swellings in the removing members—no matter how sensible they may be—induce an intermittent fever, such as **cancerous swellings** <note>original: *apāta cācerata*</note>. This is discussed in the eleventh point.

To the other argument, it should be said that it is not always necessary for a fever to be continuous simply because the **spleen** is a cold organ, possesses few fibers, and is receptive to cold, thick matter that is not ready to become putrid. From these factors, the matter is minimally prone to flowing and putrefying. Furthermore, because of its thickness, the putrefied matter cannot enter the **arteries** <note>original: *artarias*</note> so easily as to make its onset continuous. Rather, it requires movement from the evacuation of the **melancholic humor** <note>the "black bile," associated with the spleen and cold, dry qualities</note>. Nor do the arteries of the spleen directly face the heart, since they do not "implant" into it, but rather "explant" from it.

Similarly, it must be said of the **kidneys** as has appeared: that the connection with the heart is quite oblique. For this reason, regarding natural matters against **Erasistratus** <note>an ancient Greek anatomist</note>, the arteries do not "implant" in the kidneys but "explant"; they are not directly positioned under them, unlike the **vena cava** of the liver or the **aorta** of the heart. Furthermore, their fleshiness is compact and lacks fibers; for they do not have sensation except through their **membrane** <note>original: *pāniculū*</note>. Nor is there a vein or artery contained within their substance (Difference 86). Because of this, a swelling of the spleen and kidneys can sometimes cause intermittent fevers.

To the other point, it should be said that **pus** <note>original: *sanies*</note> is not always present in a swelling. Or if it is, it cannot reach the heart, as will be seen elsewhere. To the next point, it should be said that three types of this lesion sometimes induce so slight a lesion—as declared by their causes, both on the part of the matter and the part and location itself—that they will induce not a continuous but an intermittent fever.

To those points regarding the other part, it should also be said that the authority of **Galen** and **Rhazes** <note>Latinized as Rasis, a 9th-century Persian physician</note> agrees, as has been seen. To what **Haly Abbas** <note>Latinized as balyabat/Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician</note> says, it must be said that in **lethargy** <note>original: *litargia*; a disease of the brain</note> there is sometimes no fever at the beginning, or it is so slight as to be unperceived for a time, mostly due to the quantity of the matter and its coldness. What should be said regarding other types has appeared.

To the next point, it should be said that although in swellings the matter is contained outside the veins, it can nonetheless induce a continuous fever: because a "horrible" and acute **vapor** <note>original: *fumg* / *fumus*</note> is resolved from the source of the putrefaction and is able to continuously seek the heart. This vapor is positioned as the conjoined and immediate efficient cause of the fever. The source from which it falls is more of an antecedent and material cause; thus the matter and the efficient cause do not coincide as the same thing (Difference 160). Sometimes, however, the pus is so thick and muddy that the aforementioned vapor cannot be continued to the heart from it, but at last, as the evacuation of the humor ceases, it breathes.

Nor is it the same with matter dispersed throughout the whole body outside the veins, which causes an intermittent fever, and matter collected into a swelling, even though it is also placed

---

outside the veins. For when matter is collected in a swelling, its **virtue** <note>its power or potency</note> is more aggregated; and when united, it is stronger than when dispersed (from *The Book of Causes*). Therefore, poisonous matter that is often disseminated throughout the whole body, when it runs together into a swelling, presses inward, sending poisonous vapors back to the heart. For it is invigorated by its congregation. From this, **cancer** will be an appropriated sickness, more malicious and incurable than even **leprosy** <note>original: *lepra*</note> when it possesses the whole. (Difference 178). Therefore, matter disseminated through the whole body outside the vessels will always induce an intermittent and never a continuous fever as such. To the remaining points, what should be said has been seen.

->DIFFERENCE 86.<-

**Whether the brain and bones can suffer from a swelling.**
It appears through **Serapion** <note>9th-century Syrian physician</note> in his *Breviary* that he first holds this view. Furthermore, if there were any swelling of the brain, this would certainly be **phrenitis** <note>original: *frenefis*; an acute inflammation of the brain</note>. But this is not in the brain itself, but in its membranes. Hence **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a 10th-century physician</note> in the fourth book of *Fevers* says: phrenitis, absolutely speaking, is a hot swelling arising in the membranes of the brain from the boiling of the blood existing in the heart. The same is said in the first book of the *Viaticum*: phrenitis, to define it absolutely, is a hot swelling in certain membranes of the brain.

Furthermore, a swelling is a **tumor** and a thickness beyond nature (Difference 1). But that which is in the extreme of softness, like the brain, or in the extreme of hardness, like the bones, cannot be extended. That which is not extended cannot rise up into a tumor.

Also, a swelling is generated from the flow of matter through the larger veins and arteries into the smaller ones, until it reaches the tiniest capillaries, which escape the perception of the flow; and then they fall into the sponginess of the members. (In the books *On Tumors*, *On Unequal Distemper*, and book 11 of *On Therapeutics*). But in the brain there is no vein, neither large nor small (Difference 24), nor in the bones.

Also, according to **Johannitius** <note>9th-century translator and physician</note>: the causes of this [matter] flowing from one part to another and thus causing a swelling, as they appear according to the four causes existing previously (Difference 5). But causes of this kind are not found in the brain, since the second and sixth are lacking: because they are a noble member, situated in the highest part. In the bones and teeth, the fifth cause is lacking, for there is a narrowness of the passages. Therefore, the brain and bones cannot suffer swellings.

The opposite view, however, is held by **Serapion** regarding lethargy. And **Oribasius** <note>4th-century Greek physician</note> says **erysipelas** <note>a skin/membrane inflammation</note> occurs in the brain. According to **Haly**, the brain or the **nucha** <note>the spinal cord</note> swells many times. (First [book] of the *Technē*, and the third, first, and seventh sections).

Furthermore, **Rhazes** in his *Definitions*: *birs* is what is more correctly called *fyrsē*, which is a swelling happening in the brain, being either hot (namely phrenitis) or cold (like lethargy). Furthermore, **Alexander** <note>likely Alexander of Tralles</note> and Haly Abbas agree that the substance of the brain can suffer a swelling. Again, a bad complexion, bad composition, and solution of continuity can happen to all members, even to the heart (following Difference). These are common sicknesses; but without these, a swelling does not occur. In the first part of the *Technē*, these three types of diseases are contained. Again, **Avenzoar** <note>12th-century Andalusian physician</note> says: it happens to the bones that one part of them becomes thickened. He also says that a bone grew in his own hand with pain.

It then begins a debate on whether the brain and bones can experience abscesses, weighing the definitions of "tumor" against the specific textures of these organs.</summary>
