you will infer. We also observe certain hard **nodosities** <note>original: *nodositates*; bony lumps or knots</note> being separated from the bones, particularly in horses. From all these things, it is proved that the **brain** <note>original: *cerebrum*</note> and **bones** can suffer from **inflammation** <note>original: *apāri* / *apostemari*; the formation of an abscess or inflammatory swelling</note>. 

Regarding the first point, one must know what the brain is, as shown in Difference 24. What an inflammation is, was shown in the preceding Difference. What a bone is, Difference 39 teaches.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that the writings of the wise seem to superficially contradict one another on this question. For **Serapio** <note>a 9th-century Arabic medical authority</note> says: "When an inflammation occurs in the brain, it should not be judged to be in the substance itself, but rather in the hard covering containing it, which is called the **miringa**" <note>original: *miriga*; the meninges, specifically the dura mater</note>. And it is from this membrane that the **uveal tunic** <note>the pigmented layer of the eye</note> and the **sclera** are born. He assigns the cause for this as follows: we know that in every member where **tension** <note>stretching or pressure</note> occurs, inflammation happens; but it is not in the nature of the brain to receive tension, because it is a "flowing liquid" <note>original: *humidum currens*</note>. And similarly, it is not in the nature of bone to receive tension, because it is extremely cold, dry, and hard. Therefore, it must be that tension only occurs in "middle members"—those that fall between the extremes of softness and hardness—such as membranes, ligaments, nerves, muscles, flesh, and similar parts.

However, support for the opposite view is found in the fifth book of *On the Accidents* [by Galen]: "Hot **phrensy** <note>original: *frenesis*; acute inflammation of the brain accompanied by fever and delirium</note> occurs when inflammation is generated in the substance of the brain or in its membranes." And in the eleventh book of *On the Method of Healing*: By the same reasoning, it also occurs in **phlegmons** <note>inflammatory swellings</note> which are in the brain and the meninges. Whence in the third <margin>p. 31.</margin> book it is specifically said: **Karabitus** <note>original: *Karabitus*; a Latinization of the Arabic term for phrenitis/phrensy</note> is a hot inflammation in the thin and thick coverings of the brain without the "body" [the brain tissue] itself being involved, although sometimes inflammation does happen to the body of the brain itself. 

It is not as some doctors estimate, nor is it true that the brain does not inflame. He sets out their reasoning: they claim that what is soft like the brain or hard like bone does not stretch, and what does not stretch does not inflame. But all this is <margin>Note</margin> erroneous. This is because something soft and viscous *does* stretch. Indeed, all parts can inflame, and **Galen** has confessed this.

Furthermore, **Avicenna** <margin>A.</margin> says that specifically a phlegmon of the brain happens from putrid blood inflaming it. Similarly, **erysipelas** <note>a skin infection, here used for a spreading inflammation</note> and **usacra** <note>likely a reference to *uachra*, a type of sore or pustule</note> sometimes occur in the brain itself. And in the third book, seventh section: sometimes types of inflammation happen even to the **teeth**. The reason is universal: since everything that receives nourishment also receives "superfluity" <note>waste or excess matter from digestion</note> along with its expansion; when this waste is retained, the part stretches. Such is the defined reason for an inflammation to exist; therefore, it is concluded that any member—the brain and bones included—can inflame.

Furthermore, **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note> says: "Phrensy, which is a phlegmon of the meninges, sometimes also occurs in the brain." **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Tralles, a 6th-century physician</note> says in his first book: "True phrensy happens from red choler [yellow bile] when it reaches the brain with a burning fever and creates a phlegmon there." They occur in the **miringa**, that is, the membrane. He also says that "true **lethargy**" <note>original: *litargicus*; a disease of the brain characterized by sleepiness and memory loss, believed to be a "cold" inflammation</note> happens just as phrensy does, for it also has its seat in the brain. 

Whence in the ninth book of the *Theorica*: Phrensy happens from a hot inflammation which occurs in the covering of the brain or in the brain itself. With this, **Averroes** <note>noted as 'Au.' or 'Aū.' in the text</note> agrees in the fourth book of the *Colliget*. The specific signs of the dominance of the humor causing the brain to inflame are found in the *Book of Animals*. It says that sometimes the **rete** <note>the *rete mirabile*, a network of blood vessels at the base of the brain</note> of the brain is inflamed.

There are some who listen naively, believing that the brain and bones can inflame [without distinction]. Their lack of understanding will be shown from what follows. Regarding the third point, so that the harmony between such great men might appear, it must be known that inflammation is generated in two ways:

1. In one way through **rheum** <note>original: *reumatis*; a downward flow of fluids</note>, when matter flows down from the veins and arteries into the spongy parts of the members.
2. In another way through **congestion**, that is, from a superfluity of nourishment, which is different from the first.

In the first way (rheum), bones and parts that are truly hard cannot inflame, since they lack the ducts through which humor is sent into the simple parts of the members. But in the second way (congestion), they can inflame; since they receive nourishment and are expanded by it, they consequently swell from that unnatural excess. This waste is retained upon some hardened part of the bone, with more added little by little until a tumor and stretching appears.

In the first way, the brain ought not to inflame, were it not for the fact that it is of weak consistency and is placed in the upper part of the body. It exists like a **chimney**, receptive to vapors and smokes [rising from the stomach]; when these reach it, they are cooled by the brain's coldness, condense, and penetrate it, sometimes creating a collection of fluid.

Furthermore, it must be known—as can be gathered from the words of the authorities Serapio and Avicenna—that inflammation exists in two types. <margin>True Inflammation</margin> One is "true," in which there is a bad **complexion** <note>imbalance of humors</note>, a bad composition, and a breach of continuity; here, a clearly defined tumor exists externally or internally. With such inflammation, only the "middle members" (those between extreme hardness and softness, like muscles) properly inflame. 

And perhaps this was Serapio's intention. <margin>Inflammation not true</margin> There is also another inflammation, not "true" in the strict sense, but rather called so because of a certain tumor-like similarity. Whence Serapio: "If the teeth receive 'greenness' throughout their whole body, it is no wonder if there follows something similar to an inflammation." Some doctors verify this specifically by the fact that teeth are nourished and grow throughout a person's life. Whence it is said: "Furthermore, inflammation happens to soft members." 

And it is also when something similar to an inflammation happens to bones, through which their cavity is thickened and their humidity increased. He also said teeth sometimes receive "species" <note>types or varieties</note> of inflammation—that is, kinds—rather than "simple inflammations." In this way, the brain and bones can inflame.

These authors agree if one understands them carefully. Avicenna also intended that the substance of the brain itself rarely inflames. This is judged from his statement: "Sometimes an inflammation happens to the body [of the brain] itself." Just as they say that **pleurisy** <note>original: *pypleumoīa*; peripneumonia or lung inflammation</note> rarely happens from choler, because the lung, being porous and light, does not sustain it. So the brain, soft and almost fluid, does not retain hot matter, nor even cold. 

Whence, regarding **lethargy**, which is a phlegmatic **sirasis** <note>original: *syrfē*; a hot inflammation or "burning" of the brain</note>, he says that it occurs specifically in the passages of the brain's substance, without affecting the membranes, the ventricles, or the body of the brain. This is because **phlegm** rarely gathers in the membranes due to their hardness, nor in the brain's substance due to its viscosity. 

Thus, the words of other authors are to be understood: that the substance of the brain and its membranes can inflame, but it is not by a "true" inflammation that the substance inflames, or it happens only rarely. The membranes, however, often inflame with a true hot inflammation. Whence, in the fourth book of the *Commentary on Pulses*: the lethargic patient has the disease generated more in the brain itself; while the phrenetic patient has it in the thin membrane and the **diaphragm** <note>likely referring to a cerebral partition or membrane rather than the breathing muscle</note>. And therefore...

<meta>This page continues the technical scholastic debate on whether the brain, bones, and heart can suffer from inflammation (apostema) or injury (dissolution of continuity). ...just as in **empyematous** <note>original: *pypleumaticis*; those suffering from an internal collection of pus, usually in the chest</note> patients the pulse is rarely ever **distorted** <note>original: *distortus*, also known as *bisferiens*; a pulse that feels like a double-hit</note>, because it participates very little in hardness; so too in the **phrenitic** <note>those suffering from *frenesis*, an acute fever with delirium</note> patient, the pulse is very rarely **fluctuating** <note>original: *fluctuosus*; a wave-like pulse associated with moisture</note>, because he participates very little in softness. This truth is evident from the arguments deduced in this form. From these two points, therefore, the truth of this inquiry may appear in another, more extensive investigation.

It should certainly be known that what has been said regarding the **teeth** must also be understood regarding the **bones**; for they possess the same nature as bones and are formed from them, as stated in the *Generation of Animals* <note>Aristotle’s treatise on the biology of reproduction and development</note>.

Regarding the fourth point, however, what appeared necessary to say has already been addressed in the first. Regarding the other point, it should be said that **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a prominent 10th-century physician and philosopher</note> accepted **phrenitis** <note>inflammation of the brain or its membranes</note> as a true inflammation that occurs frequently; and it was said by such an authority that the brain can indeed be inflamed.

Regarding the other point, it is also apparent what should be said: those members which are in the extreme of softness or hardness are rarely inflamed by a **true inflammation** <note>original: *apostemate certo*; a "true" abscess as defined by Galenic medicine</note>, but rather by one that is **metaphorical** <note>original: *similitudinario*; similar in appearance but not in pathological mechanism</note>. Or perhaps the brain and bones are not so soft or hard that they cannot sustain some extension, or at least a metaphorical inflammation. Or perhaps the brain extends the **thin membrane** <note>original: *panniculo subtili*; likely the pia mater</note> which borders it.

Regarding the other point, it should be said that the conclusion is true regarding inflammation happening mostly by way of a **rheum** <note>original: *reumatis*; a flowing of catarrh or waste fluids</note>; this is especially true regarding bones and other hard members. The brain, however, receives this accidentally, as has been shown, sometimes through the collection of a rheum; since its passive moisture allows for a **penetration** and **hardening** <note>original: *perduratōez*; the thickening of fluids into a mass</note> of that which has penetrated into its cavity.

Regarding the other point, it should be said that those causes concur in a **true inflammation** by way of a flux, and often as stated, as appears from the manner of speaking; but not so in those that are not true [inflammations] and are rarely produced. Indeed, some of those causes are sufficient. And similarly, the answer to the other point is apparent, as well as to those points brought forward by the other side. From these things it is also apparent what should be said. It would also be possible for the solution to these things to appear by assuming the three-fold division of the brain in Difference 34.

-> ### DIFFERENCE 97 <-

#### **W**hether the heart can be inflamed or suffer a dissolution of its continuity.

It is argued that the heart can suffer inflammation. Since that which receives **nourishment** also receives **superfluity** <note>original: *superfluity*; metabolic waste or excess fluids</note>, as stated in a previous Difference. When this superfluity is retained, an inflammation and a **dissolution of continuity** <note>original: *continuitatis solutio*; a medical term for a break in the physical wholeness of a part, such as a wound or rupture</note> occur, since these are found in every inflammation.

Furthermore, the heart is neither extremely hard nor supremely soft, but in the middle. It was said previously that such a part can be inflamed, and consequently its physical unity can be dissolved.

Furthermore, **bad complexion** <note>an imbalance of the four bodily humors</note>, disordered composition, and dissolution of continuity are common illnesses, for they are known to happen to all members. The heart is a member—indeed, the primary one.

Again, as appears in the eighth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: *de ingenio [sanitatis]* by Galen</note> and in the first book of **Isaac's** *On Fevers*: "An acute fever is a more troublesome disease." This is shown by the fact that the principal indication for treatment is taken from it; hence in the eighth book of the same work, it says that fever turns us toward itself above all other things, since its magnitude is more properly present. But the heart sustains the **fever**, which is its own proper suffering, since many are healed from it. Therefore, it will tolerate other illnesses. For if that which is "less" exists [the ability to survive fever], then that which is "more" [the ability to sustain inflammation] will also seem to be present.

Conversely, diseases occur in the strong and principal parts, since they happen according to the proportion of the many specific parts. This is shown by the diseases of the brain, the liver, and the stomach. But the heart is the strongest and most principal member; therefore, the strongest disease will occur in it. This disease is inflammation and the dissolution of its parts. Therefore, the heart will be able to be inflamed and tolerate a dissolution of continuity.

<margin>Opposite view</margin> The opposite view is found in the third book of *On the Parts* <note>Aristotle's *De Partibus Animalium*</note>. The heart alone of the viscera, and uniquely among those parts in the body, sustains no **passion** <note>original: *passiōnē*; here meaning a disease state or injury</note>. This is proved because if the **principle** <note>the vital source or starting point</note> is corrupted, nothing remains to bring help to the parts that have arisen from it. In the dissolution of its continuity and in inflammation, the principle is corrupted. For the heart is the first root of all things and is helped by nothing else.

Moreover, it is a sign that it tolerates no chronic passion that in no **sacrificed animals** <note>original: *ymolata... animalia*; animals used in religious or ritual sacrifice</note> has such a passion been seen around the heart as is seen around the other viscera. For the kidneys often appear with **stones** <note>original: *lapidib⁹*; kidney stones</note> and growths and certain other things. And the liver similarly, and the lungs, but especially the **spleen**.

Again, it is not possible for health or sickness to occur in things lacking life. But inflammation and the dissolution of the joint [of the heart] occurring there take away life immediately, because of the disproportion that happens to the principle from the outset. Therefore, the heart cannot be inflamed or dissolved.

Regarding the first point, it should be known what the heart is, as shown in Difference 41. What inflammation is was shown in 95, and the dissolution of continuity in 75.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that in this Difference the wise seem to disagree, some even with themselves, and others following fantasies. For **Galen**, in the fifth book of *On the Affected Parts* <note>original: *interioꝝ*; literally "the interior [parts]"</note>, writes that the heart suffers dissolution of continuity along with inflammation during fevers. We have observed, when the heart was greatly inflamed in a certain man, that a most rapid death followed those things which cut into the heart in another way—that is, by **piercing** <note>original: *scōpizatiue*; a rare term likely referring to a puncture or stabbing wound</note>.

Therefore, if any of those things which perforate should reach as far as a **ventricle**, they die almost immediately, especially when the **left ventricle** happens to be perforated. However, when the perforation does not pass through into the ventricle, but is fixed in the substance of the ventricle, some have lived not only on the same day they were perforated, but even through the following night; death occurred eventually by reason of inflammation, and not purely by the flow of blood. Thus, from this discourse, it is clearly understood that the heart can incur inflammation and dissolution of continuity.

Furthermore, in **dislocations** <note>original: *dīōibus*; likely *dislocationibus* or a similar structural disruption</note>, the inflammation and rupture of the heart, or the corruption of its firm complexion, are not easily cured.

<margin>Likewise Serapio.</margin> Among those that are vehement and kill with speed is the *almestiera* <note>a transliterated Arabic term for a type of lethal inflammation</note>, that is, the **choleric** and **phlegmonous** inflammation <note>phlegmon: a spreading inflammatory mass</note>, but not the **sanguineous** one. In the ninth book of the *Theorica*, the aforementioned opinion is recited by Galen, which he agrees with in the eleventh book.

The fourth book of *On the Affected Parts* writes: "It is impossible for the heart to suffer inflammation." Whence **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a Persian physician</note> says: "It is not possible for the heart to be inflamed, or for an obstruction to occur in it." For while this is possible in the many cavities of the brain, in the heart death precedes it.

In the first book of the *Practica*: "The heart does not tolerate the dissolution of its parts, because death arrives first." Also in the third book, Difference 11: "The heart does not tolerate injury nor inflammation." And it is further from this: that it would tolerate the dissolution of continuity more than inflammation. In the third book of the *Colliget* <note>Averroes' medical compendium</note>: "The heart in its own substance cannot tolerate inflammation because the sick person fails before then." **Mesue** <note>John Mesue, a major pharmacological authority</note> says the same regarding the dissolution of continuity...

<summary>This page explores the medical debate over whether the heart and brain can sustain inflammation or injury without immediate death, citing authorities like Galen, Isaac, and Haly Abbas. It weighs physiological arguments about "middle" hardness versus the fatal consequences of damaging the body's primary "principle."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into whether the heart can sustain an inflammatory abscess or a physical breach of its structure. It follows the previous discussion regarding the brain and bones, applying similar principles of "softness" and "hardness" to the heart's unique role as the center of life.</meta>

The strength of the heart does not permit an **opening** <note>original: *apertionem*; here referring to an abscess or an inflammatory lesion that breaks the surface</note> to occur; rather, such things are the cause of dissolution and death. From these points, therefore, it appears that there is no small diversity among the authors on this question. However, what can be said about this will soon appear. Regarding the third point, it should certainly be known that the heart tolerates neither an **opening** nor a **breach of continuity** <note>original: *solutio continuitatis*; a technical term for a physical injury, wound, or tear in the tissue</note>, even if it is firm and penetrating. And this is reasonable, because that which supports the defects and injuries of all other members must itself be vigorous. The heart is of this kind, for all accidents occurring to the body make their first rush toward the heart, as if toward the **base of life** <note>original: *basi uite*</note> (Mesue).

But when it has been opened, or when it suffers a singular breach, its vigor does not remain, nor can it receive strength from elsewhere, since it is the principle of life and the primary root of all powers. For it is in the animated body what the **hearth** and the **citadel of the city** <note>original: *caminum & arx ciuitatis*</note> are (Difference 35, ii), and it is the first in the universe, like a **leader in an army** <note>original: *dux in exercitu*</note>. While the leader is strong, he removes all the defects of the soldiers and makes up for their failings; but when he fails, the whole army is destroyed. Since the heart is the "first," it cannot be relieved by another.

Furthermore, that which is subject to sudden death by its own suffering cannot be opened or breached; such is the heart. Thus, **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note> says: *The heart suffering according to its own proper passion is far from the care of doctors, for it brings about sudden death.* Furthermore, the greatest pains occur in the heart because of the breach of continuity and the opening. Hence, **Aristotle** says in the fifth book *On the Soul*: *The pains of the heart become intolerable because of the excellence of its own sensation.* For it is that in which the soul first exists, namely the beginning (from the *Parts of Animals*). This pain precedes the **symptoms** <note>original: *syntbomatibū*; likely a corruption of *symptomatibus*</note> that destroy and cast down the vital power (xii. *On Ingenuity*), so that **fainting** <note>original: *sincopis*</note> and sudden death occur here.

The heart, therefore, cannot be opened or breached in the manner previously described. However, it must be understood in a more extensive explanation that an opening of the heart can be diversified in many ways: by reason of the part of the heart affected, the efficient cause, the matter of the opening, and the time of the opening. Similarly, a breach of continuity either penetrates suddenly to the large chambers of the heart—the right, the left, or the middle—or it dissolves the substance of the heart more superficially. 

Regarding the part of the heart: an opening of the **left side** <margin>604</margin> appears more quickly and kills the animal faster than one on the right. This is because life is driven to the parts from this side; in the actual life of the heart itself, it fails more quickly than from a right-sided opening.

By reason of the efficient cause: some openings occur from an internal cause, others from an external one. From an internal cause, such as something generated within it or expelled to it from elsewhere. From an external cause, such as from a **sword-wound** <note>original: *gladiatiōe*</note>. An opening from an internal cause is less likely than one from an external cause to reach the heart, because it usually affects other parts first, or gradually dissolves other things through dissolution. But from an external cause, it is more likely, unless the heart's vigor is quite intense, as if another cause of dissolution preceded it. 

Regarding the matter of the opening: some is **hot**, while some is **cold**. Hot matter kills the moment it opens the heart. Cold matter does so much less. Thus, in the fifth book of *Internal Diseases*: *A passion of the heart beginning to occur according to "stations" or erysipelas <note>a skin infection, here used to describe spreading inflammation</note> corrupts it immediately, before these passions increase in the animal.* And **Aristotle** says: *A hot abscess is immediately fatal; a cold one is among those things that are difficult, yet it happens.*

---

It is rare for hardness or softness to be found in the heart itself. But what is placed there usually happens in its **membrane** <note>original: *panniculo*; refers to the pericardium, the sac surrounding the heart</note>. If a cold opening occurs, it does not kill in the same moment as a hot opening, but it is nevertheless fatal. And since the hardness that occurs in the membrane arises from thick humor, it prolongs the time of death; however, soft humor does not, as it drips with watery humor—like the humors found in the event of a fall or in the cutting of the hearts of **roosters**, **apes**, or **monkeys**. **Galen** says: *In the capsule of a rooster, the humor existed as hard; but in that of a monkey, it was soft and more watery.* (Fifth book of *Internal Diseases*). 

<margin>
Regarding the heart of a rooster, a monkey, and slaughtered animals.
</margin>

Regarding the time of the opening: since an opening of the heart, especially a hot one, is scarcely perceived by the sensing principle, **Avenzoar** <note>original: *Joar*; refers to the 12th-century Andalusian physician Ibn Zuhr</note> says: *It happens that an opening is beginning in the heart, but before it is perceived, death arrives suddenly and without delay.* Similarly, if a breach of continuity soon reaches the great chambers, death occurs continuously. 

Hence **Galen** says: *If that which perforates reaches as far as any chamber of the heart, the person dies immediately due to the flow and evaporation of blood and spirit,* especially when the **left chamber** is perforated. This is also testified by **Haly Abbas** and **Serapio**. Wherefore **Aristotle** says: *When it happens to the body of the heart that a breach penetrates to the chambers, it kills immediately.* But if it does not penetrate the chambers, **Galen** wished that they might not only live through that same day but also through the following night, death occurring by reason of the "flowing." Thus **Aristotle** says: *Even if it does not penetrate, then perhaps death is postponed until the second day.*

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
But there is a doubt concerning the aforementioned things because, in Difference 46, it was shown that the **right chamber** of the heart is more fundamental and longer-lived than the left. Yet here it is said that life fails more quickly because of a penetration reaching into the **left chamber** than the right. 

<margin>Life is twofold.</margin>
It must be said that life is twofold: one is **primary**, and that is the life of the heart itself. The other is **secondary**, sent out from the heart into the parts through the movement of the heart and the descent of the arteries. The primary life is indeed more fundamental and longer-lived in the right chamber than in the left, as shown in the previously cited Difference. But the secondary life, of which we now speak, is shown to be longer-lived in the left chamber. This is because the arteries of the heart originate from that chamber, through which, as has been said, life is directed from the heart into the limbs. By this distinction, the apparent contradictions of the authors are resolved.

<margin>To the 1st and primary point.</margin>
Regarding the third point, in response to the first argument, it must be said that the heart, as shown, suffers both openings and breaches in a certain way. Or rather, it is not necessary that everything which is nourished should undergo an opening, either by way of a "rheum" <note>a flow of waste fluids</note> or from the residue of nourishment, because the matter cannot penetrate into the heart nor be retained there, but is immediately expelled by the heart’s vigor. Therefore, the earlier opinion did not say that the opening simply expels the surplus residue from the nourishment of the limbs, but rather when it has penetrated the heart or occurred within it. To the other point, it should be said that although the heart occupies a middle ground between hard and soft members, that is not a sufficient cause for an opening to occur, since a strong member repels that matter to other places, as the heart specifically does. For it was said earlier that one of the six causes of an opening is the weakness of the receiving part. To the other point, it should be said...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the heart’s vulnerability to physical injury. Having previously established the heart as the "citadel of life," the text now addresses whether the heart can survive a physical wound or an inflammatory abscess, concluding that while it may endure a systemic fever, a direct breach of its tissue is usually fatal. It then transitions into "Difference 88," a new inquiry into how the body habituates to chronic disease versus sudden illness.</meta>

How an **opening** <note>original: *apertio*; referring here to an inflammatory abscess or lesion</note> and a **breach of continuity** <term>breach of continuity<gloss>original: *solutio continuitatis*; a medieval medical term for any physical injury that breaks the tissue, such as a wound, cut, or ulcer</term> might happen to the heart has been shown. Either it fails in this particular instance, or a single universal truth of natural and medical science removes the objection. This is especially true when a fact is verified in the determination of the matter—namely, that they begin at many points, or at least one.

Regarding another point, it must be said that a fever is more troublesome than other ailments in its **extension** (meaning its reach): for as its definition denotes, it contains the whole body. However, it is not more troublesome in **intensity**, as are **syncope** <note>fainting or sudden loss of consciousness</note>, frequent tremors of the heart, and more intense pain. For fever is a specific ailment of the heart, more troublesome to the other parts than the heart itself, since it is expanded from the heart into the whole body, so that the power which was gathered there is rendered weaker when diffused.

Regarding the other point, it should be said that it is true: a sickness cannot exist unless life remains. A most powerful ailment of the heart, however, deprives one of life. Regarding those points on the other side: first, it should be said that the heart sustains no "grave" suffering—that is, a **breach of continuity** and an **opening**. It does, however, sustain a "bad" **complexion** <note>the balance of bodily humors or qualities</note>, such as a fever. This is because a breach of continuity—as has been said—reaches into the chambers of the heart, especially the left one, and an opening there is never fully or properly "hot" <note>referring to the inflammatory process of ripening an abscess</note>. Similarly, when a principle organ like the heart is so corrupted that it cannot impart life to its own parts, it does not "tolerate" the sickness, since the sickness deprives it of life. 

That a breach of continuity penetrating into the chambers acts unequally has been shown; so too has the nature of a conditioned abscess. The extent to which this contains a sign of truth has appeared: that it arises from an internal cause rather than an external one, which is more tolerable in its outcome. Thus, as to the first point, the heart in its very substance does not suffer the confirmation of any abscess, nor any penetrating or curable breach of continuity, whatever some may wish to argue. For the heart can be said "not to tolerate" an abscess or breach because these cannot be healed within it. For when a person escapes from an injury, that is properly called "tolerating" it. Yet it can be said to tolerate the beginning of an abscess and a non-penetrating breach for as long as life still lasts.

### DIFFERENCE 88.

<margin>2nd part, affection 3, 4</margin>
It is shown that an **accustomed** <note>habitual or chronic</note> sickness is worse than an **unaccustomed** <note>sudden or unfamiliar</note> one. Since, according to the ancients, those who have been frequently released <note>likely referring to a release from symptoms or a recurring crisis</note> often die suddenly without a manifest cause. And **Damascenus** <note>John of Damascus, or the medical author Mesue</note> says: "The frequency of sickness in a principal member announces the dissolution of the body." <margin>3rd part</margin> Also, in the first book of the *Aphorisms*, section three: "He to whom a **nightmare** <note>original: *incubus*</note> and **dizziness** <note>original: *scothomia*; vertigo or darkened vision</note> frequently happen is exposed to **epilepsy**." Such accustomed ailments are seen to be worse because they are said to happen many times, from which a "habit" or custom arises. 

Furthermore, a sickness simply causes harm: this is its very nature. Therefore, a greater sickness will harm more, and the greatest will harm the most. An accustomed sickness seems to be of this kind compared to an unaccustomed one. For from many harmful parts, a great harm arises. The body is also rendered more debilitated for suffering, along with a weakening of its virtue. Again, that sickness is worse which is more difficult to eradicate, since its malice lies in its inseparability, as appears in confirmed **leprosy** and **hectic fever** <note>original: *ethica*; a chronic, wasting fever often associated with tuberculosis</note>. Such an accustomed sickness, 

---

having been impressed by occurring many times, is reduced into a **habit**. Likewise, just as many occurrences of health are better than one, so many occurrences of sickness are worse than one; for the reasoning of contraries is contrary (as seen in *On Generation and Corruption*). We also see that those given to habitual and generally excessive labors have shorter lives, even if they are bound to them by custom; the same applies to sicknesses. Therefore, an accustomed disease will be worse than an unaccustomed one. This is also indicated in the medical treatment of the "doubtful wound in the leg of the king" in the book on *Acute Diseases*. <margin>Opposition</margin> The opposite is shown by **Hippocrates**: "Those accustomed to bearing accustomed labors bear them more easily." <margin>3rd / 2nd part</margin> Again, according to certain men who are not at all unproven, nothing prevents the chronically ill from being long-lived, based on the causes of the length and brevity of life. <margin>3rd / 3rd, 4th</margin> Also, in the book *On the Soul*, sickness in a man who is always healthy and who has almost never been ill is fearsome. And in the fourth section: "When the healthy fall ill, and those who fall ill late in life fear the infirmity, it signifies death." In opposites, however, the opposite location occurs. 

Furthermore, sickness harms because of its contrariety and its fight against nature; but this is lesser when the sickness is accustomed. Out of custom, a certain uniform agreement falls into a middle ground, as appears in the meaning of the *Aphorisms*. In an unaccustomed sickness, however, it turns out otherwise. Furthermore, according to Hippocrates and Galen, everything sudden is an enemy to nature, for nature does not sustain these sudden changes; but an unaccustomed sickness is "sudden" compared to an accustomed one. Because of this, it will be worse than an accustomed one. 

Regarding the first, it should be known what constitutes disease 72. <margin>Custom</margin> Custom is a certain **second nature** <note>original: *secunda natura*</note> acquired little by little through use. For it is like a nature derived from air and water. This is clear from those born with elongated heads due to the custom of flattening them, which turned into nature; hence, regarding memory and reminiscence, custom is like nature. That it is a second nature is indicated in the book *On Complexions*, when it says that customs are additions to nature. And in the first book of the *Theoretical Aphorisms*, Hippocrates testifies that "custom is nature." 

Custom arises from frequent use. Use exists as a sort of precursor, leading to the induction of custom. Custom arises from actions, but it is not perfected from one or two acts. As stated in the *Sublimations* (chapter 21): "Custom is doing something many times and continuously." It must also occur little by little and equally with that which arrives many times. For that which happens suddenly and non-uniformly does not grant a "custom" to nature, but rather corrupts it the more it occurs, since sudden transformations corrupt it. 

This is also indicated by **Augustine** and the **girl who used the poison of serpents** <note>A famous medieval medical trope about a girl who was fed poison (aconite) from infancy until her very essence was poisonous to others</note> and used them in an orderly fashion. Because they used them little by little and in an orderly way, especially from the beginning, they subsequently thrived on them as if they were food. From these things, it can be held that custom is a kind of nature, and that it is to be joined to things annexed to the body through the mediation of the **complexion** <note>the bodily balance</note>. Thus, it is one of the things annexed to the five natural things: age, sex, quality, color, and custom.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the nature of disease, specifically transitioning from the heart's vulnerability to a broader debate on "Difference 88": whether a disease the body is used to (habitual) is more or less dangerous than a new, sudden one. It balances classical authorities like Aristotle and Hippocrates.</meta>

## Whether a Habitual Illness is Worse than an Unaccustomed One.

A sickness is said to be worse in two ways: either because it inflicts more troublesome damage through more severe **cutting** <note>original: *concisionibus*; referring to the breakdown of tissue or severe internal distress</note>, or because it is more difficult to eradicate from the body. This is evident in the first section concerning **melancholy** <note>a condition believed to be caused by an excess of black bile, often resulting in sadness or lethargy</note> generated from the **burning** <note>original: *adustione*; a medieval medical term for the "scorching" or overheating of a bodily humor, which changed its properties</note> of either subtle or gross natural melancholy.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some simply prefer to call a habitual illness worse than an unaccustomed one. This is because it happens more frequently, and "every passion that occurs more often takes more away from the subject," as stated in the sixth book of the **Topics** <note>a work by Aristotle on the art of dialectic and logic</note>. Others, however, argue the opposite, claiming without distinction that an unaccustomed illness is worse than a habitual one. They support this by noting that "anything to which one is accustomed becomes less harmful," as seen in the first book of the **Aphorisms**, number 30 <note>referring to Hippocrates' *Aphorisms*, a foundational medical text</note>. This, however, is more true regarding "non-natural" things <note>in medieval medicine, the "six non-naturals" were external factors like diet, sleep, and exercise that affected health</note>, as is clear to anyone who looks closely. They were also moved by points touched upon in subtle arguments. The first group's error will be made manifest in the following discussion, as the statement can be interpreted in multiple ways.

<margin>Regarding the question.</margin>
And therefore, several thinkers have spoken closer to the truth, saying that illness is of two types. One type is **pernicious** <note>destructive or deadly</note>, bringing heavy damage to the principles of life and its instruments [the vital organs]. Such an illness is worse the more it occurs and is rendered "habitual." There is another type that is not so troublesome, nor so deeply embedded in the principles of life and its instruments, but rather occurs in the extremities—such as ailments of the joints or other small complaints. Such a habitual illness is said to be less dreaded than an unaccustomed one. 

Perhaps the first part of this definition could be challenged, because such a severe illness cannot truly become "habitual," since it leads to death quickly and inevitably—which goes against the very definition of a "habit." Regarding the third point, it must be said according to the **Canon of Comparison** <note>referring to Avicenna’s *Canon of Medicine*, the standard medical textbook of the era</note>, Difference 27: <margin>Part 3, Chapter 11</margin> suppose that in a future habitual illness, two things occur. First, there is a flexible harm to the body's operations as long as the illness exists; thus, the more it occurs and is drawn into a habit, the worse it is rendered compared to an unaccustomed one. This is especially true when it follows a certain order, and the harm is greater in terms of damaging the body's **virtue** <note>original: *virtutis*; the internal healing power or life force</note> than the benefit gained from habituation. 

Thirdly, consider cases like **epilepsy** <note>then often called the "falling sickness"</note>, where continuous attacks kill. Similarly, a **relapse** <note>original: *recidiuatio*</note> is worse than its original root, as seen in Difference 11; particularly in cases of **pleurisy** <note>inflammation of the lining of the lungs</note>, **pneumonia** <note>original: *propleurionicus*</note>, and **paralysis** <note>original: *paletico*</note>, the destructiveness of a relapse is evident. This shows that everything which casts down the body's strength—if it arrives many times and becomes habitual—is worse than its opposite, since it always takes something away from the **substance** <note>the fundamental physical makeup of the person</note>. Therefore, a habitual disease of this type brings damage. Thus, in the sixth book of *On Medical Matters*, it is said: "Whatever bodies had a sickly constitution from their first generation never reach old age; but if they do reach it, they will all have one specific illness of their own."

And it is confirmed that not only does a habit of "preternatural" <note>unnatural or diseased</note> things cause harm, but even a habit of "non-natural" things does so. For example, he who digests bad food should not be deceived by the fact that he feels fine; for eventually, bad humors will be generated in him, inducing deadly illnesses. For from even the most benign nourishment, if administered and used habitually over time, the body eventually becomes "watery" <note>original: *aquaticum*; likely referring to edema or a thinning of the blood</note> due to the continuous wear caused by the <meta>Catchword: age</meta>

age of these substances acting upon the body (Difference 12). 

However, if an illness is considered based on the fact that it is habitual—such as when someone suffers from a few bouts of **tertian fever** <note>a malaria-like fever that spikes every third day</note>, or kidney stones, or **arthritic pains** once or twice a year—these are rendered less worse than unaccustomed ones because of the "familiarity" and "affinity" the limbs develop by experiencing such passions many times. <margin>Alexander</margin> As **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle</note> says in his *Problems*: "Why is it that a frequent occurrence of a sickness does not sadden nature as much?" This is especially true when it arises from a smaller amount of matter. Just as habitual foods are received by the stomach or liver with a certain affinity, habitual illnesses act on the limbs in their own way. <margin>Book 4, Problem 16, Chapter 3</margin> For "from that which is habitual, no suffering arises." He who is accustomed to suffering from a **choleric passion** <note>an illness involving bile, often gastrointestinal distress</note> of the body does not fear it as much as one who is unaccustomed to it.

<margin>Alexander</margin> And perhaps it will be said that this is because its symptoms are usually most terrifying at first. This is why Alexander says that habit is a great "armor" that makes a difficult passion easier to bear. Through frequent experience, nature becomes "more learned in fleeing" <note>original: *fagatione doctior*</note>. From frequent use, nature finds a way to meet the illness, whereby it alters the bad **complexion** <note>the balance of the four humors</note> or expels the matter causing the sickness. <margin>Alexander, Problem 16</margin> **Aristotle** also holds this opinion in his *Problems*, Book 21. He means that things encountered or done, and even actions, confer a certain spirit and delight by reason of the habit induced by custom. 

However, on the part of the **repletion** <note>excessive fullness or congestion</note> that arises from continuous consumption and action performed without intermission, damage is induced in the parts that receive it constantly, since our physical powers are not infinite. In this case, the harm exceeds the benefit of the habit. <margin>Note</margin> From these points, it may be concluded that a habitual illness of this kind—due to the benefit acquired from habit—is "less worse" than an unaccustomed one. This is especially true when the benefit of habit is greater than the harm done to the body's strength. 

And know that "habit" properly exists in the actions of the **soul** <note>referring to the animating principle of living things</note>, and especially in the rational soul, since it can choose between opposites. It is found least in those things whose form and motion come only from their generator. <margin>The Bell and the Key. To the Author.</margin> For a stone, if it is thrown upward ten thousand times, still falls downward continuously, acquiring no habit of staying above. Yet in such things, there is a metaphor for habit: according to how they are used, they reach a state of "wear," just as a **bell** or a **key** is affected by long operation. 

Regarding the fourth point, although it already appears what must be said, we should address the first arguments together. Passions that are sudden cannot become "habitual," as was declared, since they arrive unexpectedly and cast down the primary virtues. Regarding the other point, it has been shown: in as much as an illness can become habitual, it harms less than an unaccustomed one. But in as much as it brings the logic of a "lesion" (damage), it is worse. Regarding the other point: a habitual illness, assuming all other things are equal, is worse because it is harder to cure—such as **leprosy** or **pleurisy**. This does not address the original question of which is more "troublesome," but rather which is more persistent. Regarding the other point, it should be said that health and...

Its signs are a tumor perhaps appearing sometimes, a dry cough, pain of the 
side, difficulty of breath, and milder fevers.

The matter of pleurisy consists of the four humors, and 
especially yellow bile, since it is subtle, sharp, and 
penetrating into the membranes. Then blood; but rarely phlegm. 
According to that old saying: "Those with pleurisy rarely have 
acid eructations." Wherefore it very rarely happens from black bile. 
See Book 13 and in those books concerning the Crisis. Among some people, 
indeed, it never occurs, since these two humors are gross and 
viscous, unfit to penetrate into the more solid parts.

<margin>Peripneumonia</margin>
But in <term>peripneumonia</term> it happens the other way around. For it happens 
mostly from phlegm. From yellow bile, however, because of its 
subtlety and resolution, it happens least, as will appear in the 
following difference. Pleurisy, like other abscesses, 
is either resolved, or it suppurates, or it is turned into hardness. 
Which happens very rarely or perhaps never because of

causes syncope <note>fainting or sudden loss of strength</note>. That is called "worse" to which more and 
more intense accidents follow, and generally a greater danger. 
The right and left side will be shown in Difference 183.

# Whether Pleurisy of the right side is worse than that of the left side.

It must be said that one should not simply declare this side or that to be worse, as will appear from what follows. For the right side is more noble than the left according to **Avicenna** <note>original: *Au.*</note>. I say according to **Avicenna**, because **Galen** <note>original: *Ga.*</note> is seen to hold the opposite view. However, it does not follow that pleurisy harms more for this reason, since, as has been shown, it is further removed from the other organs. Nor does the proportion of the individual parts interfere, because the matter corresponds to it, since the right side is more capable of collecting matter than the left. Others, however, have said that the pleurisy of the left is worse since it stands closer to the **heart** <note>original: *cordi*</note>. Although it may be worse in that regard, it is not worse in another way, as will appear. And therefore, the determination requires more to be said. Regarding the first point, it should be known that the truth subdues the space first subtracted by the first canon. And finally, how pleurisy is purged when it becomes an empyema <note>A collection of pus in the space between the lung and the chest wall.</note>. Regarding the first of these, it should be known that a sickness can be called "worse" in two ways: either by reason of its sharpness and the accidents emerging in it, or by reason of the quality of the underlying matter. 
<margin>2.a. 3.q</margin>
As for the first, the pleurisy of the left side appears worse. As for the second, that of the right side. And this is also indicated in the third place. For some maintain that pleurisy of the right side is worse; others, however, that of the left. Truly, the truth is that the one closer to the left side is worse <note>in terms of immediate danger</note>, but it is more suitable for ripening <note>maturation of the infection</note> and receiving resolution, if it is of such a nature as to receive it. And that which is further from the left side is "safer," yet it is more disobedient regarding resolution and ripening. Thus, **Avicenna** seems to mean that the left side is worse because of the intense inflammation proceeding into the side where it comes from the heart, which makes it more fit for resolution and ripening, as he says. In the case of the right side, however, it is constrained differently, and therefore is declared more disobedient to resolution and ripening. Wherefore it should further be known that pleurisy is either terminated by resolution and suppuration—so that what is digested is spat out—and in this way, while the severe accidents can be tolerated, the left side is of a more praiseworthy termination than the right; or it is terminated by a rupture of the abscess <note>original: *apātis*, likely *apostematis*</note> such that the pus <note>original: *sanies*</note> falls into the mediastinum or one of the two cavities of the chest. And in this way, the left is worse, because the pus there is perhaps sharper due to the quality of the heat in that place. Also, the passages by which the purging occurs are narrower and of lesser strength. 

This question can indeed be decided by the difference in the site of the pleurisy; for the heart is inclined toward the left side. Whence in the third book: 
<margin>Pleurisy of the left is worse.</margin>
<margin>Above, regarding the Heart, question 11.</margin>
The heart is placed in the middle of the chest because it is a more temperate place, and it declines more to the left so that it may be distanced from the **liver** <note>original: *epate*</note>, and so the liver may have a large space. Furthermore, because of the heat of the body of the liver and its warming motion, the right side is raised and enlarged, so that it stands further from the heart. That which is further away does not cause as much harm. Wherefore pleurisy of the left will be worse than the right. And if anyone considers the sensitivity <note>original: *p̄picatōrē*, likely *perspicacitatem*</note> of the right side, he will say that pleurisy of that side is worse, since it would tolerate medicines less. However, if the strength remains stronger, it will be able to expel the disease more swiftly. Because of all these things considered equally and diligently, pleurisy of the left side is worse than that of the right, as the material, the location, and the manner of purging show. Although if someone says you have conceded the left side is hotter than the right, which does not seem to be the case because of the spleen being there and its quietude, and because the heart breathes more into the right side where the liver is situated and its motion exists; it must be said that in some part of the right side, say next to the heart, the heat can be stronger, because that qualitative heat is more acute and intense in the left part. In the right, however, there is quantitative heat, but the qualitative heat is diminished; although the whole right is hotter than the whole left because of the liver. 

It should be known generally that pleurisy of the **diaphragm** <note>original: *dyaflamatis*</note> is worse than those others. 
<margin>1. Location: pleurisy which is of the diaphragmatic membrane dividing the chest</margin>
Next, that of the membrane dividing the chest in the middle; then that of the left side; and finally that of the right side. For those of the diaphragm are followed by worse accidents, such as the mixing of reason or **phrenitis** <note>original: *frenesis*; a state of delirium caused by physical inflammation</note> and the rest. Whence it was said by the ancients that *frenes* comes from *freno* or *frenomo*, which is "I know" <note>original: *sapio*</note>; for because of these abscesses, one incurs phrenitis and reason is corrupted, as the internal wisdom disappears. Whence it is said: because the rein <note>original: *frenum*</note> of the intellect and sense is injured, it is called phrenitis, as if they were participating in that which is *frenon*, from "knowing." 
<margin>V. Internal. Part 3. Physiognomy.</margin>
<gloss>Regarding this, see **Assōx**</gloss>
Regarding this, one should also know that when, around the 13th day, the erupted pus falls into the mediastinum of the chest, it transitions into an **empyema** according to the ancients, unless it is cleansed around the 40th day. The manner of cleansing the pus from the chest is posited by **Erasistratus** to be through the entry of the pus into the veins and arteries, and from there finally running down to the lung. 
<margin>Every pleurisy [is purged] through the drawing of the veins and arteries.</margin>
**Galen** fights against this at length in the fifth book on internal matters, wishing that pus should by no means enter the veins or arteries. Rather, by the subtlety of the digestion, it enters the porosities of the lung. And rightly so; because nature, and especially a strong nature according to **Hippocrates** <note>original: *.y.*</note>, can be resisted by nothing in expelling superfluities, even if the matter is thick and the ways are narrow, as in the 7th Aphorism. 
<gloss>7th Aphorism</gloss>
For we see that nature expels the matter of an abscess from certain places even through the bones. 
<margin>Bones are cleansed.</margin>
For it expels that pus through the middle of the bone to the outside. This is the way of it: since the lung, according to **Galen**, has no motion of its own, it is moved by the motion of dilation and constriction of the chest and the diaphragm, as will appear later. 
<margin>No</margin>
For when the chest is enlarged, the lung is dilated so that it may fill the space, otherwise a vacuum would occur in an instant, which is denied in the fourth book of the *Physics*. When the lung is dilated and its pores opened, it follows that the thinned pus enters them to fill the void. But when the chest is constricted, the lung is likewise constricted. By this constriction, the pus that was received is impelled through the branches of the windpipe <note>original: *trachee artarie*</note>, first through the smaller ones and then the larger, in the same way that liquid in a sponge is impelled to the side opposite the pressure when it is lightly squeezed. When the chest later dilates and the lung becomes enlarged again, the remaining part of the pus is taken up, which is then impelled inward by the constriction of these parts...

<margin>cough</margin>
...following as has been said of the lung, and the windpipe <note>original: *trachēa artariā*</note> expels what preceded it. This finally occurs until it expels it outward by a **cough**. For the cough itself is a certain movement of nature and an instrument which propels out what is stuck in the chest. Regarding the fourth point compared to the first, it must be said that although right-side pleurisy collects more matter, that matter is proportional to the side itself, and the vital power <note>original: *uirṭ⁹*</note> is stronger in that place. Or it must be granted, as has appeared, that it is worse by way of suffocation. To the other point, it must be said that empyemic matter <note>Pus-like matter associated with empyema, an infection in the chest cavity.</note> existing in the chest is not purged by entering into the veins, as **Erasistratus** <note>An ancient Greek anatomist (c. 304–250 BCE) who founded a school of anatomy in Alexandria.</note> felt, but by entry into the lung as was declared. Or, according to others, the delivery of the aforementioned vein is also on the right side. To the other point, it appeared what should be said: for it is expelled on account of the harmfulness to the member. To the other point, it must be said that although the movement is on the right, it is not so when someone is working. For the movement of the chest muscles alone is sufficient; for the sick, if they lie in their beds, they move less frequently, unless some necessity to recover urges them. The work of the **brain** is sufficient for actions that follow voluntary motion. But for the sick, respiration alone is required. To the first point of the other part, it must be said that although the progression of pleurisy of the left side [occurs], that of the right is often worse; yet it is not argued entirely in that way, since it was shown in Difference 47 that the right side is more noble than the left. To the other point, according to **Aristotle** <note>original: *A.*</note>, it has appeared what must be said. To the other point also seen: for although the entire left side is less hot than the right, nonetheless nothing prohibits some part of the left from being hotter, as was touched upon regarding the right.

¶ It has already been said that the **lung** has no motion except through the muscles of the chest, and specifically the **diaphragm** <note>original: *dyaflamatis*</note>. It happened to be doubted whether the lung is the proper organ of breath <note>original: *haelitꝙ*</note> or the diaphragm. Since the lung is seen [as the organ], for in the third [book] of *The Parts*: the lung is the organ of respiration, having the principle of motion from the heart. And according to the second [book] of *The Neck*, there is no doubt that the lung is the proper instrument of breath. Further, that appears to be the proper instrument of a thing which is totally ordered toward it; such is the lung, but not the diaphragm; hence the lung alone provides benefit. Also, since breath is a movement of the chest, that member will be its proper organ which is hot and light, and near the most noble part; for these are ordered toward motion, and such a thing is the lung. For it is nourished by hot choleric blood (Difference 31). Its lightness is denoted by its ability to float. It embraces the heart on all sides, and especially when it dilates. The **diaphragm** <margin>diaphragm</margin> indeed is a membrane <note>original: *pānicl⁹*</note> composed from the membrane covering the ribs internally and the **peritoneum** <note>original: *syphac*</note>. It is also cold and of an earthy nature, and like a certain star, hiding the lower parts of the chest on every side. Such a thing does not act for motion, but rather for rest. Again, that which is more greatly appropriated to the movement of the chest is its true organ, since it is necessary for a proportion to intervene between the movement and the thing moved. But the lung is more similar to it than the diaphragm. For its motion is natural, since it occurs in sleep, and even the parts of breath are performed without intention; but the motion of the diaphragm corresponds more to voluntary motion since muscles hold it. Therefore, the lung is the proper instrument <margin>opposite</margin> of breath, rather than the diaphragm. In the opposite direction, it is said in the seventh [book] of *The Benefits [of the Parts]*: the diaphragm is the muscle by which breathing is produced, and it is positioned diagonally; for such diagonality helps the breath with a great benefit. And in the fifth [book] of *Internal [Parts]*, the diaphragm is the organ of respiration. Furthermore, that is the organ of breath whose nature it is to be moved, since it is, as said, a movement of the chest, and also to feel; but such, as will be seen, is the diaphragm, not the lung, since the lung lacks sensation and motion in itself. It follows the movement of the chest. For it does not have movement through itself (Third [book] of *The Theory*). Its flesh is simple in its complexion. Further, in the first [book] of *The Anatomy*, the diaphragm is the principle and root of the operation of the lung in drawing in air. Therefore, the diaphragm will more certainly be the organ of breath. Regarding the first, it must be known that the lung is the boundary <note>original: *tmīꝙ*</note> of natural heat ordered in the ventilation of the heart. For it separates and distinguishes hot animals, such as those that are most terrestrial, from those that are not hot. For the hotter animals require the lung for the ventilation of heat, such as those having blood. For the rest, ventilation either by gills (as in fish) or by suction (as in insects, Difference 81) is sufficient. By its dilation, it draws air to the interior of the heart, and by its constriction, it expels the smoky and overheated vapor. Thus the heat of the heart remains tempered. And the **lung** <margin>lung : mark</margin> itself is composed of simple flesh, branches of the windpipe <note>original: *trachee artarie*</note>, the "arterial vein" <note>the pulmonary artery</note>, and the "venal artery" <note>the pulmonary vein</note> descending to it from the right and left ventricles of the heart, and a membrane with a portion of the small nerve. It has two fringes on each side, right and left, ordered for the ventilation of the heart. But the fifth part, which is in the middle, remains almost at rest, having been made into a support and bedding for the great vein. The **diaphragm** <margin>diaphragm</margin> is a member composed of flesh, as is shown especially around the **sternum** <note>original: *gladiatā*</note>, and from the membrane covering the ribs above and the **peritoneum** <note>original: *syphac*</note> of the belly below. However, according to **Aristotle** <note>original: *A.*</note> in the thirteenth [book], its third middle tunic is placed, which in truth is a cord. And it terminates the entire chest where the ribs extend, so that it meets the twelfth vertebra <note>original: *spōdili*</note> at the back. And in front, it happens to meet the seventh. Circling the false ribs, it is applied to the true ones in front, where the flesh intervenes around the sternum; in the middle of both its membranes, branches of nerves come to it from the sixth pair of cranial nerves, and after the fourth of those of the neck vertebrae from the **nucha** <note>the spinal cord or back of the neck</note>, so that there is also a muscle in those parts. It is one in substance and double in office; they move the chest. For by its motion, it dilates it, and by rest, it narrows it. For certain muscles only dilate the chest, such as the 11 superior ones coming from the neck and the collarbones <note>original: *furculis*</note>; others only constrict it, such as the 8 or 9 inferior ones. Some, however, both dilate and constrict at once, such as those called the intercostals <note>original: *mefopleuri*</note>; this is according to the medical authorities who are placed by **Galen** in *On the Voice* and the 22nd [book] of *The Theory*. For so many distances coincide between the 24 ribs. According to **Al-Mansur** <note>original: *almanforē*; referring to the work of the Persian physician Rhazes.</note>...

# Whether the Lung or the Diaphragm is the Proper Organ of Breathing

<margin>Usefulness of the Diaphragm</margin>
...[Book] 38, since each [muscle] acts in a twofold way according to the principles that occur to them in the four parts between the ribs. Some of these have the function of dilating more toward the outside, and others of narrowing toward the inside. Indeed, the utility of the **diaphragm** <note>The muscular partition separating the chest from the abdomen.</note> is twofold: one is to dilate and contract the chest along with the other muscles that move the chest; the other is to separate and segregate the instruments of the spirit <note>The lungs and heart.</note> from the organs of food. In man, it is thick in proportion to his nature. In the first book of the *History [of Animals]*, it is stated that its position is straight. 

<margin>Breathing through the members</margin>
The members of breathing are several, such as the epiglottis, the trachea, the lung, the chest with its muscles, and the heart with its capsule <note>The pericardium.</note>. 

<margin>What breathing is</margin>
Breathing is indeed a movement of the chest, ordained for the venting and purification for the cooling of the heart. For just as the **pulse** is the movement of the heart and arteries, composed of **diastole** <note>Expansion.</note> and **systole** <note>Contraction.</note>—in which two movements and two rests are observed—so breathing is a movement of the chest composed of dilation, by which air is drawn into the heart, and constriction, by which it is expelled. For the most part, breathing and pulse are proportionate. 

<margin>Heart</margin>
However, it is not the property of a single organ, but belongs more fully and principally to the agent to whom the action is primarily attributed, as the hand is to the ax. Regarding this, it must be known that before the time of **Averroes** <note>An influential 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician.</note> and even during his own time, no benefit of the diaphragm was known except to sequester the spiritual organs from the nutritive ones. Hence, in the section on parts, the **diaphragm** <note>original: *dyacoma* / *dyazoma*</note> is only for the sake of the area around the belly and the area around the heart, so that the principle of the soul remains uninjured and is not quickly overwhelmed by the exhalations from food and the multitude of external heat.

Furthermore, it distinguishes the more honorable [parts] from the lower ones. Whence in the fifth book of the *Internal Parts*, all the ancients called the lower limit of the thorax the **phrenes** <note>Greek term for the diaphragm; hence "phrenic nerve" and "frenzy."</note>, because when they are inflamed, it harms the wisdom <note>original: *sapientia*</note>, as was touched upon; for on account of their greater injury, one incurs **phrensy** <note>A state of delirium or mental confusion believed to be caused by inflammation of the diaphragm.</note> or a hot fever. However, it began to be called the **diaphragm** <note>original: *dyaflā*</note> because of the lung, as it is a dividing membrane. 

<margin>Naming</margin>
It was called "phrenes" by other ancients because they thought its benefit was to sequester the raging soul, which is in the heart, from the concupiscence <note>Desires or appetites.</note> which is according to the liver. **Aristotle** indeed called it the **hypozoan** <note>Greek for "under-girding."</note> or **diazoma** as if it were a sub-girdle, not recognizing the great and most useful action it provides to animals. For it is the organ of respiration. It is also called the "girding veil" and the "great wall." Therefore, no benefit of the diaphragm was recognized except for the separation of the spiritual from the nutritive parts, so that during the time of digestion nothing would happen to them from the heat. Nor should this be counted as a defect in **Aristotle**, because that which is grasped through the way of anatomy is like a thing grasped by the number of circular movements; that science was not complete in the time of **Aristotle**. For even if the art of medicine was truly perfected in the time of **Galen**, he nevertheless says it would not be impossible for someone coming after him to discover things that had not been found by him.

---

But according to **Galen**, as already touched upon, the proper organ of breathing was the diaphragm. Whence in the fourth book of the *Internal Parts*, we say in the work on the *Causes of Respiration* that non-violent breathing is performed by the diaphragm alone; but the action of the **mesopleurus** <note>The intercostal muscles located between the ribs.</note> muscles occurs when we require greater inspiration, just as the action of the superior muscles occurs with the maximum inspiration. Yet we do not act by these alone for the sake of great or maximum respiration. Even when the diaphragm is in its natural state, it is sufficient for the movement. For it does not need the intercostals or any other muscles. When there is a necessity, either because of the weakness of the power, or intense heat, or a narrowing of the paths of the spirit, it needs not only the intercostals but even the superior ones. And I adhere more to these speeches of **Galen** taken from the book *On the Causes of Respiration*, which the Latin world still lacks. If anything is clear regarding these movements, the opinions are arranged thus: The anatomists said that the diaphragm is the primary part of the **oven** <note>original: *clibani*; a common anatomical metaphor for the ribcage/chest cavity which "cooks" or processes vital heat.</note>. Nevertheless, it was not totally thought until the time of our masters that it was the most noble instrument of breathing. But in our time, it became clear from what I declared about its operation, that it moves only the lower parts of the "oven," just as the muscles descending from the neck move the superior parts. However, the muscle lying against the ribs moves the same by dilation and constriction.

<margin>3.3.1</margin>
Whence, adhering to this, he says: the movement of breathing, being equal and natural and removed from harm, completes the movement of the "veil" <note>The diaphragm.</note>. But if it needs an addition of strength, the veil shares this help with all the muscles of the chest. Therefore, it is stated by some that "pure breathing" is only that which completes the movement of the veil. This is not absolutely true; for although sometimes the movement of the veil alone is pure, it is sometimes equal, for here it needs nothing but the movement of the veil when the power is strong. Note that when the muscles dilating the upper chest move so narrowly that the patient seems to move by an elevation of the shoulders, as if he wished to fly, this is a mortal sign. 

What appears from these will soon be spoken of. **Averroes**, not rarely troublesome to the ancients, feels that the lung is the proper organ of respiration rather than the diaphragm, wishing that the movement of breathing be performed by the lung and not the chest. Reciting the speech, he says that **Galen** himself felt the lung had no proper movement in itself, but that its movement followed that of the chest. And this movement is made through the diaphragm. This is shown because when the chest is dilated by the vigor of dilation, the lung is immediately filled with air, as bellows show. This is confirmed because when the chest is wounded, air enters, and the movement of the lung ceases, and thus the person dies of cold. To which **Averroes** clearly responds: it can be said that the movement of the lung ceases here because it is chilled. 

<margin>Note</margin>
<margin>Averroes Troublesome to the Ancients</margin>
But **Galen** removes this reasoning by saying that it ought not to cease so very quickly, because it would not immediately receive such great cold, especially since it was in air that was hot.
