<margin>Coughing.</margin>
¶ Since it was said that the lung has no movement of its own, except through the muscles of the chest and properly through the **diaphragm** <note>Original: "dyaflā." The muscular sheet that separates the heart and lungs from the abdominal organs.</note>, it happens to be doubted whether the lung or the diaphragm is the proper organ of breath. That the lung is seen as such is clear from the third book of *On the Parts of Animals*. The lung is the organ of breathing, having the principle of movement from the heart. And according to the *Colliget* <note>The *Kitab al-Kulyat*, a medical encyclopedia by the Andalusian polymath Averroes.</note>, there is no doubt that the lung is the proper instrument of breath. Furthermore, that seems to be the proper instrument for something which is entirely ordained toward it; such is the lung, not the diaphragm. Whence primarily the lung provides such benefit. Also, since breath is the movement of the chest, that member will be its proper organ which is warm, light, and near the most noble part <note>The heart.</note>; for these are ordained for movement, and such indeed is the lung. For it is nourished by warm, choleric blood (Distinction 31). Its lightness is denoted by the fact that it floats. It embraces the heart on all sides, and especially when it dilates. The **diaphragm**, however, is a membrane composed of the membrane covering the ribs internally and the **siphac** <note>The peritoneum, the lining of the abdominal cavity.</note> placed below. It is also cold, of terrestrial blood, and like a board, it conceals the lower parts of the chest from one another. Such a thing does not contribute to movement, but rather to rest. Again, that which is more appropriate to the movement of the chest is its true organ, since there must be a proportion between the movement and the mobile object. But the lung resembles this more than the diaphragm. For its movement is natural, as it occurs in sleep; 

even breaths are perfected without intention. But the movement of the diaphragm is more proportionate to voluntary movement since muscles possess it. Therefore, the proper instrument of breath is the lung. 

<margin>The Opposite</margin>
On the opposite side, in the seventh book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts*: The diaphragm is the muscle through which breath is made, and it is positioned diagonally; for such diagonality helps breathing with great benefit. And in the fifth book of *On Internal Parts*, the diaphragm is the organ of respiration. Furthermore, that is the organ of breath whose nature it is to be moved, since it is, as said, a movement of the chest, and also to feel. But such a thing, as will be seen, is the diaphragm, not the lung, since the lung lacks sense of itself and movement. It follows the movement of the chest; it does not have it by itself (third book of *Theoretical Medicine*). Its flesh is also simple, according to the second book of *Complexions*. Furthermore, in the first book of the *Secta*, the diaphragm is the principle and root of the operation of the lung in drawing in air. Therefore, the diaphragm will more certainly be the organ of breath. Regarding the first, it should be known that the lung is the tempering of natural heat, ordained for the venting of the heart. For it separates and distinguishes warm animals—such as terrestrial ones—from those that are not warm. For warmer animals require the lung for the venting of heat, as they have blood. For the rest, venting by gills suffices, as in fish, or by suction-holes as in **insects** <note>Original: "enthomis."</note> (Distinction 81). By its dilation, it leads air 

<margin>Lung</margin>
to the inside of the heart, and by its constriction, it expels smoky, overheated vapor. The heat of the heart thus remains tempered. And the lung itself is composed of simple flesh, the branches of the **trachea**, the **arterial vein** <note>The pulmonary artery.</note>, and the **venous artery** <note>The pulmonary vein.</note>, descending from the right and left ventricles of the heart, and a membrane with a small proportion of nerve. Its two fringes, left and right, are ordained for the venting of the heart. The fifth [lobe], which remains in the middle and is larger than the others, rests as a support and bedding for the great vein. 

<margin>Diaphragm</margin>
The **diaphragm** is a member composed of flesh, as is shown especially around the **xiphoid process** <note>Original: "gladiatā," referring to the sword-shaped cartilage at the base of the sternum.</note>, and the membrane covering the ribs above, and the siphac of the belly below. According to **Averroes** in the tenth book, a third middle tunic is placed, which in truth is a cord. It terminates the whole chest, but the ribs extend over it, so that it meets the twelfth vertebrae in the back. In front, the septum falls opposite. Encircling the false ribs, it joins the true ribs in front, where the flesh meets near the xiphoid process in the middle of both its membranes. Branches of nerves come to it from the sixth pair from the brain, and after the fourth of those of the neck vertebrae from the spinal cord, so that it is a notable muscle. It has a double substance and office... moving the chest. By its movement, the chest dilates; by rest, it narrows. For some of the muscles dilate the chest alone, like the 11 upper ones coming from the neck and collarbones; others constrict it alone, like the 8 or 9 lower ones. Some indeed dilate and constrict simultaneously, such as the ones called **intercostals** <note>Original: "meſopleuri."</note>. These are defined by **Galen** in *On the Voice* and the third book of *Theoretical Medicine*. So many distances coincide between the 24 ribs. According to **Almansor** <note>Rhazes (865–925 AD), a Persian physician and author of the *Kitab al-Mansuri*.</note>...

### Whether the Lung is the Proper Organ of Breath, or the Diaphragm

As each thing follows from its own principles, it happens that the four parts, as well as the ribs, have a certain capacity to dilate further toward the exterior and to narrow themselves.

<margin>The utility of the diaphragm</margin>
The utility of the **diaphragm** <note>Original: "dyaflas/dyaslatis." A common medieval spelling for the muscular sheet separating the chest from the abdomen.</note> is indeed twofold. One is to dilate and contract the chest in conjunction with the other muscles that move the breast. The other is to separate the "spiritual" vessels <note>The vital organs like the heart and lungs.</note> and set them apart from the organs of food. It is thick in man according to the reasoning of his nature. In the first book of the *History of Animals* <note>Aristotle's *Historia Animalium*.</note>, it is noted that it is advantageous for this organ to be upright.

<margin>The organs of breath</margin>
The organs of breath are indeed several: namely the **epiglottis**, the **trachea**, the **lung**, the **chest** with its muscles, and the **heart** with its capsule <note>The pericardium, the sac surrounding the heart.</note>.

<margin>What is breath?</margin>
Breath is indeed the movement of the chest, ordained for the ventilation and purification required to cool the heart. For just as the pulse is the movement of the heart and the arteries consisting of their own **diastole** <note>Expansion.</note> and **systole** <note>Contraction.</note>—in which two movements and two rests are observed—so too breath is the movement of the chest, composed of a dilation by which air is drawn into the heart, and a constriction by which it is expelled. Thus, to a great extent, breath and pulse are proportional to one another.

<margin>The heart</margin>
The heart is the proper organ of this type, to which the action primarily adheres, much as an action is attributed to the hand rather than the tool. Regarding this, it should be known that until the time of...

<margin>Three things concerning this</margin>
...**Aristotle** <note>Abbreviated as "Ay." in the text.</note>, as was already indicated, no utility of the diaphragm was recognized other than to separate the spiritual organs from the nutritive ones. Whence in the third book of *On the Parts of Animals*, the **partition** <note>Original: "dyacoma/dyazoma." From the Greek *diazoma*, meaning a waistband or partition.</note> is always the boundary between the parts around the stomach and those around the heart, so that the principle of the soul might remain unharmed and not be quickly overwhelmed by the exhalations from food or the intensity of external heat.

Furthermore, it distinguishes the "honorable" parts (those above) from the "lower" parts. Whence in the fifth book of *On the Internal Parts*, all the ancients called the lower boundary of the thorax the **phrenes** <note>The Greek term for the diaphragm; the root of "frenzy," as they believed it was linked to the mind.</note>, because when they are inflamed, wisdom and touch are harmed. Because of a significant injury to these parts, one incurs **phrenitis** <note>A state of delirium or "brain fever."</note> or a burning liver.

<margin>Difficult breathing</margin>
The diaphragm <note>Original: "Sya" probably referring to the *septum transversum*.</note> began to be called the "divider of the lungs," a membrane which is named the *phrenes*. Other ancients thought its only use was to separate the "furious" part of the soul (which resides in the heart) from the "desiring" part (which is in the liver). Aristotle called it the *hypozoma* or *diazoma*—as if it were a "sub-belt"—not recognizing the great and most useful action it provides to animals. For it is the primary organ of respiration. He did not recognize any utility of the diaphragm except for the separation of the spiritual from the nutritive, so that the heat of digestion would not affect them. Nor should this be considered a defect in Aristotle, for what is understood through the way of anatomy is like something understood from the number of circular movements; that science was not yet complete in the time of Aristotle. For even if in **Galen’s** <note>Abbreviated as "Ga."</note> time the art of medicine was truly perfected, he said it was not impossible for someone to come after him and discover things he had not found. This was the case with Aristotle and **Parmenides**; Aristotle did not yet see this. But according to Galen, as already touched upon, the diaphragm is the proper organ of breath, as seen in the fourth book of *Internal Parts*.

We say in the work *On the Causes of Respiration* that in violent respiration, the action is performed by the diaphragm alone; however, the action of the **intercostal muscles** <note>Original: "mesopleuroy." The muscles between the ribs.</note> occurs when we require a greater inspiration, just as the superior muscles of the neck act during the greatest need. We do not, however, act twice solely for the sake of a large or maximal breath. For the diaphragm by its nature provides sufficient movement on its own. It does not need the intercostal or other muscles unless there is a necessity—either due to weakness of strength, intense heat, or a narrowing of the breath passages—in which case it requires not only the intercostals but also the superior muscles.

I adhere further to these discourses, having received Galen’s book *On the Causes of Respiration*, which the Latin world still lacks. If the opinion on these movements agrees, the anatomists said that the diaphragm is the primary part of the **kiln** <note>Original: "clibani." A common metaphor comparing the ribcage/chest to an oven or furnace.</note>. However, it was not thought until the time of our own masters that it was the more noble instrument of breath. But in our time, it became clear from what I declared concerning its operation: that it moves only the lower parts of the "kiln," while the muscles descending from the neck move the upper parts. Moreover, the muscle attached to the ribs moves them by dilation and constriction, since it has two tunics placed in different positions. I shall speak of this as a discovered necessity.

Whence, adhering to this, Aristotle says: The movement of breath is a natural channel, and when removed from harm, it completes the movement of the membrane. If, however, it requires an addition of strength, the membrane shares this help with all the muscles of the chest.

<margin>Folio 3, Section 1</margin>
Therefore, some later writers claimed that the "primary breath" is that which is completed by the movement of the membrane alone. This is not absolutely true. For although it is sometimes completed by the membrane alone, it is not always equal; it only requires the movement of the membrane when the power is strong. Note that when the muscles dilate the upper chest, they move with such distress that the patient is seen to lift their shoulders as if they wished to fly; this is a fatal sign. More will appear on this shortly in the third section.

**Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician, "Auer."</note>, however, following the ancients, not rarely felt that the lung itself was the proper organ of respiration rather than the diaphragm, wishing the movement of breath to be perfected by the lung and not the chest. Reciting this discourse, Galen says that the lung has no proper movement in itself, but follows the movement of the chest. This movement is performed by the diaphragm. This is shown because when the chest dilates by the vigor of expansion, the lung is immediately filled with air, just as **bellows** show. This is confirmed because if the chest is wounded, air enters, the movement of the lung ceases, and thus death occurs.

<margin>Note</margin>
To which Averroes clearly responds that it could be said the movement of the lung ceases here because it becomes chilled. But...

<margin>Averroes vs. the Ancients: Troublesome.</margin>
...Galen removes this response by saying it ought not to cease so very quickly, because it would not immediately receive such great coldness, especially since there is heat in the air.

It introduces the metaphor of the chest as a "kiln" and explains the mechanics of respiration using the analogy of a bellows.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the physiological investigation into the mechanics of breathing. It appears also that the movement of the heart does not cease immediately but little by little. Furthermore, the cessation of this movement happens to the lung if there is an injury in the **diaphragm** <note>Original: *dyaflante*. The author uses several variations of this word for the diaphragm.</note>, regardless of whether cold air reaches the lung from some poor temperament or humor, or through a wound that does not penetrate deeply but moves along the side. He adds also that it should not be said simply that the movement of the chest is the principal cause of the movement of the lung, because each of these could have movement from itself, like a shared property by which one does not move without the other. 

But **Galen** <note>The influential 2nd-century Greek physician whose works dominated medieval medicine.</note> says this is also insufficient. For the task is to provide the method by which the lung moves and the connection from which this movement is derived. And why do these two parts move in such a way that one is not the cause of the other? It seems impossible to demonstrate this, as the third explanation shows. Furthermore, it will always be necessary to order these movements—one dependent on the other—until the sequence reaches the first cause. He joins to this that the movement of the lung, according to Galen, is "violent" <note>In the Aristotelian sense, meaning moved by an external force rather than by its own internal nature.</note>, in the manner that artificial things are moved. It would likewise be said that the lung possesses a natural receptive power for that which is thrust upon it by the movement of the **thorax** <note>The chest cavity.</note>, and its movement depends on the thorax's movement, just as the movement of the arteries depends on that of the heart. After these things, however, he excuses himself: for **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath and author of *The Canon of Medicine*.</note> wrote that it is possible our principles are not sufficient to reach the truth of many of these investigations. Nevertheless, it remains appropriate that we speak concerning these dispositions according to the aforementioned times.

<margin>Interval and purpose
The instrument of breath.</margin>

Regarding the three propositions, one must first establish that the **diaphragm** <note>Original: *dyafla*.</note> is the certain organ of breath. Secondly, one must know how its movement occurs. Concerning the first, it should be known that the proper instrument of breath is the diaphragm, while the lung is a cooperative organ; it manifests itself much like a blacksmith's bellows, as the introductory speeches of illustrious physicians note. For in the category of members, the first that is moved by a mover is a muscle, so that there exists an order of movers and things moved. 

The heart is indeed a mover, though it is said not to be moved at all by any other part; that is, the power of moving locally is sent into the brain, and then from the brain to the nerves, and finally this received impulse moves the diaphragm and the chest. Thence, movement is caused in the lung because of its aptitude for it, so that when the chest is dilated, the lung is also dilated, and when it is constricted, the lung is narrowed, just as can be seen in the bellows with which a fire is fanned. 

He shows this by reason: because as has been seen, breath is the movement of the chest. Therefore, that member which will be the principal organ moved will be the organ of respiration. Such a thing is the diaphragm, as shown, because it is a muscle; but the lung is not, since it lacks sensation, let alone movement. For no "insensitive" <note>Meaning a part lacking the faculty of sensory perception/nerves.</note> part can be moved, since movement presupposes sensation as a prior condition. 

Furthermore, if the lung moved sufficiently by itself, why then would nature have created so many muscles in the chest, and thus those movements? Moreover, if the movement of respiration were inherent to the lung itself as its own proper instrument, it would not happen to move when it has been so damaged that parts of it are spat out, as appears in **consumptives** <note>Original: *ptisicis* (phthisis), referring to tuberculosis patients.</note>.

<margin>Tuberculosis</margin>
<margin>Regarding breath</margin>

When something of the lung is wasted in such a movement, and even when it is damaged, the action is only slightly corrupted. But the diaphragm cannot tolerate such a great corruption. Experience confirms this for me: for when a perforation of the diaphragm is made, the lung soon collapses like a heavy weight that has been dropped. Furthermore, when a major injury occurs around the diaphragm, I have perceived some people to be suffocated by a spasmed lung, so that the pulse takes on a wonderfully irregular character before death. Therefore, the proper instrument of breath will be the diaphragm and not the lung. 

Regarding the second point, one must know that the movement of breath appears natural, because it is involuntary; for that which is involuntary appears natural. Hence, concerning the cause of the movement of animals, I call those movements involuntary—such as sleep, waking, and respiration—for these are of the breath. It is also said that breath occurs in sleep and without choice very often. Again, the pulse and the breath are proportional, according to Galen. Indeed, Hippocrates often puts breath in the place of pulses; for example, at a time when the members of breath are not diseased, he says it announces the temperament of the heart just as the pulse does. Therefore, the movement of breath is natural. 

On the contrary, **Galen**, as **Avicenna** says, claims that breath is a voluntary movement. He confirms this because that which exists in our power appears voluntary. For rational powers are capable of opposites (according to the *Perihermenias* <note>Aristotle's *On Interpretation*.</note>). But we can breathe when we wish, and hold it for a long time. Furthermore, the movement of breath is perfected by the diaphragm and other muscles when the chest expands; but all this is voluntary, therefore this movement is voluntary. 

It must be said that since movement is threefold—purely natural (like that of the veins and the womb), purely voluntary (like that of the four limbs), and a middle type composed of these two (such as the eyelids, coughing, labor, urination, and the like)—such is breath. For it is composed of voluntary and natural movement, as the preceding points have sufficiently shown. Hence, in the thirteenth book, breath is completed by two movements, between which there are two pauses, just as it is in the pulse; except that the movement of breath is voluntary because it can be altered by the will from its natural course, whereas the pulse is purely natural. Therefore, breath is not simply voluntary, since nature operates within it. And because its "naturalness" can be changed by the will, it is evident. For a person can breathe strongly, frequently, and thickly, or do the opposite, or even restrain it for a time. Finally, one should judge it to be more voluntary than natural. 

**Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known as "The Commentator."</note>, however, held the opposite of this, because in sleep and waking, breath often happens without elective intention. To which it must be said that this does not hold, because animals sleep for less time than they are awake. And many acts are performed by parts in which the movement is simply voluntary without choice or deliberation; hence in the *Physics*, art does not deliberate sometimes—such as the art of weaving or shoemaking, just as the art of medicine and navigation. The Commentator says in the same place: "Know this difficulty concerning movements," touching upon it by saying that it is implicitly operated. He adds soon after: "Here indeed the inquiry belongs more to dialectic than to medicine." Regarding this, it must first be said that Avicenna did not say respiration...

### Is Phlegmatic Pneumonia worse than Choleric?

<margin>Differences of breath</margin>
Breath is an act of almost involuntary movement, yet it is not "involuntary" in the way that a natural, unconscious process is strictly opposed to a voluntary one. It occupies a middle ground between the purely natural and the purely voluntary. This is apparent from what follows regarding the physical faculties: in no human being is the distinction between sleep and respiration simply a matter of imagination or appetite; rather, it is a necessity that the parts of animals are changed by natural alteration. When these parts are altered, their growth and decrease change in turn. However, the movement of the <note>original: "pudendi"</note> private parts stands as involuntary, since it is often moved by something appearing to the senses without the intellect commanding it. To another point, it must be said that breath is not a purely natural movement, but a composite one. To another, it must be said that pulse and the <term>vital breath</term> <note>original: "animalis haelitū". In medieval medicine, "animal" refers to the "anima" or soul/life-force governing voluntary movement.</note> are proportional in healthy and fallen bodies, but not in their opposites, since the brain can operate differently in sickness. Furthermore, there are more varieties of pulse than of breath; for while there are nine or ten types of pulse, there are about five modes of breath—the thirteenth being "large" along with "high" and "long," or "frequent," "swift," "cold," and "fetid," and their opposites. They are proportional in the first three modes most appearing in sickness. Finally, it was said that <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> wrote that breath signifies the <term>complexion</term> <note>The balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that determined a person's health and personality.</note> of the heart, just as the pulse does. As has been said, Hippocrates perhaps did not recognize these things from the pulses, or perhaps he did not think them worthy of a full account and so did not elaborate. Regarding the first point of the other side, it should be said (as appears in the books on liquid movements and by <term>Aristotle</term>) that the movement of breath is composite and not merely voluntary. Regarding the confirmation, it must be said that it is not entirely from the will, although it is mostly so, since we cannot ultimately restrain it in every way. To another, it must be said that not every movement made by <term>muscles</term> <note>original: "lacertos"</note> is simply voluntary. Rather, some are mixed with many other factors. Beyond the will, nature exists, inciting and eventually overcoming the will. This was done wisely for the salvation of the necessary and most helpful parts, so that not only the voluntary "animal" soul would govern, but also the natural soul—as is the case with the heart and the eye. For in their safety is found a divine clemency or instinct, as if this were the nature of the soul and did not exist by choice. Regarding the fourth point about the soul: it must be said that <term>Aristotle</term> had not yet seen this with the earlier thinkers. Likewise with laughter, as <term>Avicenna</term> <note>A significant Persian physician and philosopher (Ibn Sina) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook.</note> suspected. To another, it must be said that the lung provides help only demonstratively or in appearance, and not as a "principal" cause in itself; for because the lung is lowly in respect to the heart, brain, and liver, it is said only to "provide help" and not to perform the primary operation. To another, it must be said that although the aforementioned factors contribute to movement, they are not sufficient, since it is necessary for large nerves to reach the part, which, joined with others, constitute the muscle, which is the soul's primary instrument of motion. There is a difference: these cannot be coupled in the lung because of its weight and weakness.

It must also be said that the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: "dyas̄lā"</note> provides membranes for its constitution and receives the muscle that constitutes the side toward the ribs, with cords <note>tendons</note> stretched from the middle on all sides. It should likewise be said that the lung does not have such gravity or "earthiness" that it cannot have movement, since it is especially membranous and subtle in the middle. It also requires <gloss>[something?]</gloss> for movement, a certain hard support or compaction, since every animal movement necessarily rests upon something immobile. Nor is the lower part so thick and compacted that it cannot be dilated and contracted, since the underlying part is membranous; it is also near the place of heat and moisture, which renders it fit for dilation and narrowing. To the other point, it appeared that the movement of breath is governed by a twofold power: namely, the natural and the vital <note>original: "animali"</note>, so that sometimes the act of one is more manifest than the other, though it always depends on our will. Similarly, the <term>diaphragm</term> and the other muscles of the chest are ordained most powerfully for the safety of the animal. And since they are around the member which is the origin and base of nature—the heart—they will participate in nature's way.

### DIFFERENCE 100

<margin>1</margin>
<margin>Note</margin>
<margin>Death is twofold.</margin>
<margin>Opposition</margin>
<margin>Pneumonia</margin>
**Whether phlegmatic pneumonia** is worse than choleric is now shown. Because a "true" illness is worse than an "untrue" <note>In medieval medicine, a "true" (vera) disease followed the classic textbook symptoms, while a "non-true" or "bastard" version was caused by a different humor or complication.</note> one, as is judged in true and untrue pleurisy. For the true is considered much worse than the untrue. This is proved by reason: for it is the nature of a disease to hinder operations; therefore, a truer disease will hinder operations more than another. But **pneumonia** caused by phlegm <note>The cold, moist humor.</note> is "true," according to the authority of <term>Mesue</term> <note>A likely reference to Masawaih al-Mardini, a famous medieval physician.</note> and <term>Galen</term>. Furthermore, a "disproportionate" illness according to the ancients is worse than a proportionate one; but pneumonia caused by phlegm is disproportionate, since it is contrary to the complexion of the lung. For the lung is hot and dry, being nourished by <term>choleric blood</term> <note>Blood mixed with yellow bile.</note>, according to the sixth book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts*. For the natural complexion of a member is similar to that by which it is nourished. Furthermore, death is twofold: one which is by extinction and the dissolving of moisture, and the other by suffocation, according to *On Death and Life*. That pneumonia will be the worst which induces suffocation; and such is the phlegmatic type. For the lung is also moist, receiving ascending and descending vapors. This matter <note>phlegm</note> is also less prone to resolution <note>breaking down and clearing</note>; so much so that the best termination of the imbalance cannot occur through resolution, whereas thin <term>choler</term> <note>yellow bile</note> is more easily resolved. Furthermore, that disease is worse which more greatly impedes the operation of the member; such is pneumonia from phlegm, since it impedes the movement of the lung by its quantity and weight more than the choleric type. Therefore, phlegmatic pneumonia is worse than choleric. This is also held as the specific opinion of <term>Mesue</term>. Furthermore, by the opposite of the reason just given: a disproportionate disease is worse, and such is the case here, since the lung is cold and moist—which is shown by the nourishment given to it. For they say it cools and moistens. Therefore, choleric is worse than phlegmatic. Regarding the first, it should be known according to <term>Paulus</term> <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note> that pneumonia of the lung is an <term>inflammation</term> <note>original: "ftō n.", abbreviation for Greek *phlegmone*.</note>, frequently caused by severe catarrhs, or quinsy, or pleurisy, or other diseases. Whence <term>Haly Abbas</term> <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note> and Aristotle say it is an abscess of the lung.

However, the heat is not present by its essence, but rather by accident—namely through putrefaction <note>The "accidental" heat refers to the fever generated by the rotting or "putrefaction" of trapped humors, rather than the natural heat of the organ itself.</note>. This is because <term>pneumonia</term> <note>original: "pypleuonía" or "perypleumonia"</note> happens more frequently from "flatus" <note>In medieval medicine, "flatus" or "flatubz" refers to "windy" vapors or gasses trapped in the body.</note> than from <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile, the humor associated with fire: hot and dry.</note>; indeed, they say it rarely happens from the latter. This discourse is approved by the *Breviary* of <term>Serapion</term> <note>Yahya ibn Sarafyun, a 9th-century Christian Syrian physician whose medical encyclopedias were standard university texts.</note>, folio 39, as follows: "Pneumonia is nothing other than an inflammation of the lung; and an inflammation is an <term>abscess</term> <note>original: "flōn" / "apā". Here referring to "phlegmon," a specific type of hot, bloody inflammation or abscess.</note>." Furthermore, the name of this sickness is denoted by the parts of the name itself: for "pleumon" in Greek signifies "lung" in Latin; hence "pneumonia" or "pulmonary" or "pulmonaria."

And this indeed occurs by beginning through the way of <term>congestion</term> <note>original: "ḡgestiōis . í. aggregatōis"</note>—that is, an accumulation of superfluous nourishment—just as other abscesses do. It also occurs more through the way of <term>rheum</term> <note>Catarrh or fluid "running" down from the head.</note>, when the matter descends entirely from the head to the lung, or ascends from almost all the rest of the body, as frequently happens in the succession of symptoms described in the fifth book of the *Aphorisms* <note>Referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates.</note>. And it follows the succession of <term>pleurisy</term> <note>Inflammation of the membranes surrounding the lungs.</note> and its like. For often pleurisy changes into pneumonia. But one must ask why.

According to <term>Mesue</term> <note>Probably Mesue the Younger, an influential but semi-mythical 11th-century Arabic medical author.</note>, one type of pneumonia is "true" and another is not. And <term>Galen</term> said that true pneumonia is that which arises from <term>phlegm</term> <note>The cold, moist humor associated with water.</note>. Its material causes are the humors. For it arises from every humor, but principally from phlegm; and sometimes from blood; then from choler; and perhaps rarely from <term>melancholy</term> <note>The cold, dry humor associated with earth.</note>, due to contrary causes. For just as primary pleurisy arises from choler, so primary pneumonia arises from phlegm. For the subtle, choleric matter can penetrate the solid membranes where pleurisy occurs. But thick, viscous phlegm can do so the least. Conversely, however, phlegm can penetrate a "rare" <note>In this context, "rare" means porous or spongy, like the tissue of the lung.</note> member, such as the lung. But the choleric matter evaporates due to its own thinness.

<margin>3</margin>

Regarding the second point, it must be known that I find all the wiser authorities agree in positing that pneumonia caused by choler is worse than that caused by phlegm. Yet one thing that introduces difficulty in this apparent situation is the judged <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) unique to an organ or person.</note> of the lung. For according to its primary and radical complexion, it is posited as hot and dry; but according to its secondary and accidental complexion, it is cold and moist, as Galen and Avicenna intimate. And because this proportion involves a specific rule, the canon of proportion in such congestions—which is often touched upon—should be observed: such as phlegmatic to phlegmatic, and choleric to choleric. The discourse of <term>Avicenna</term> on this and others of this kind concludes: pneumonia sometimes arises from "red choler," and it is insufficient according to its own sharpness. Mesue also says that phlegmatic pneumonia is not as vehement in its wickedness as the choleric kind. For the choleric kind kills by its sharpness, since it is near the heart.

This is also demonstrated by reasons no less than these: That disease is worse, other things being equal, which arises from worse matter; and such is choleric matter in respect to phlegmatic matter. Whence the third book of *Prognostics* says: the malice of abscesses will be according to the humors generating them. For bloody and "windy" matters are of lesser malice than matters which are of the genus of yellow choler, or those of the genus of black choler. I say this especially by reason of quality, for all such are bad; therefore pneumonia will be worse from choler than from phlegm. 

Furthermore, "extraneous heat" causes harm. But the heat of choleric pneumonia is double: one is essential, for choler is hot in itself; the other is putrefactive. Whereas that of the phlegmatic kind is only through putrefaction. Moreover, choleric matter is more effective in what it does than phlegm. For that which is such and is positioned next to the heart vehemently hinders it. This is because choleric matter collected in the lung is like an abscess, and not at all like "watery" phlegm. Likewise, hot, inflammatory, sharp choler placed next to a hot member—such as the heart—is like fire upon fire. For a similar complexion supervening and increasing the first is most dangerous. Finally, that sickness is worse which is joined to more severe accidents <note>In medieval medicine, "accidents" are the secondary symptoms or complications of a disease.</note>; such is the choleric kind, since there is an instigation of fever, thirst, and more intense "frenzy" <note>Delirium or mental agitation caused by heat affecting the brain.</note>.

Furthermore, they show this same thing from the perspective of medication. For in the case of that which is administered—whether it is a plaster or a drink—in choleric pneumonia, one cannot extinguish its fervor and induce a cure as easily as in the phlegmatic kind. This is not because of what is applied externally, for such a thing ought to be cold in act so that it may be opposed to the choleric inflammation; but this cannot pass through, especially since the place to which it must reach is remote. Hence, one cause for pneumonia being more "malicious" than pleurisy is the distance of the locations—that is, the proximity to which medicines cannot reach, as in pneumonia, unless by a dissolved path.

For this reason, in the *Tegni* <note>The "Techne" or "Ars Medica" of Galen, a fundamental textbook.</note>, it is said that medicine for this must be associated with that which is "subtle in its parts," for this will be able to penetrate into the depths. But in these cases, as heat is added to the heat of the choler itself, it increases; therefore, it cannot be cured by external application. It happens differently in phlegmatic pneumonia: since its matter is cold, its medicine ought to be maturing and resolving. And this indeed will easily reach the site of the sickness while preserving its own virtue. 

In a similar way, they show that those who are cured by drinks cannot be cured if the drink does not reach the site, while the virtue of its cooling power—which Avicenna and Mesue oppose to it—is preserved. For if I take an external cold remedy as a gradual opposite to choleric pneumonia, because of the long distance from the site, it will become over-heated on the way, and the nature of its coldness will be lost; thus, when it reaches the abscess, it will be warm and will do harm. But if it is made extra cold in degree, then such things will be cold at the end of the third or fourth degree <note>The four-degree scale of medicinal intensity used in Galenic pharmacology.</note>. Along with this, an abscess from choler is perhaps even beyond the third degree of heat. Such cold medicines are "oppilative" <note>Blocking or clogging the pores/vessels.</note>, not penetrating the paths; they are also "mortifying" and "narcotic" <note>Meaning they numb the area or "kill" the vital spirit through excessive cold.</note>. 

But if less cold medicines, which are already able to penetrate, are joined twice, then the inconvenience follows with the heat mentioned before. Because of this, it is concluded as given. In this matter, perhaps someone might rise up in two ways: first, that choleric pneumonia, by its great heat and inflation, will open the pores by the "rarity" of the body, so that the power of the medicine could pass through. To this it must be said that because of the distance of the place, before the medicine can reach the site with its coldness, it will block the pores. For when it first finds the superficial pores somewhat open, entering into them, the cold medicine will immediately constipate them...

<summary>This page discusses the pathology and etymology of pneumonia, arguing that cases caused by "choleric" (hot/dry) humors are more dangerous and harder to treat than "phlegmatic" ones due to their proximity to the heart and the difficulty of delivering cooling medicines without blocking the body's pores.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the classification and severity of pneumonia. The previous page established that pneumonia is an inflammation of the lungs often caused by trapped vapors (flatus). This page specifically compares "true" pneumonia—which some authorities associate with phlegm and others with choler—and debates which form is more dangerous based on the quantity and quality of the humors involved.</meta>

-># Whether Phlegmatic Pneumonia is Worse than Choleric<-

In the generation of steps and in the subversion of moisture, on account of the prohibitive ice, as seen in the first book of the *Meteorology* <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Meteorologia*, a foundational text for understanding how heat and cold affect physical matter.</note>. Second, they also argue that <term>choleric pneumonia</term> <note>Pneumonia caused by an excess of yellow bile (choler), which is hot and dry.</note> is less dangerous because its material is small in quantity. Its burning heat is also tempered on account of the <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>Associated with the humor of phlegm: cold and moist.</note> moisture dwelling in the lung. Furthermore, the subtle [matter] evaporates and resolves, since pneumonia is sometimes removed by resolution, and sometimes it turns into <term>empyema</term> <note>A collection of pus in the space between the lung and the chest wall.</note>, and sometimes it hardens, and sometimes it changes into an <term>exitus</term> <note>A discharge or morbid growth.</note>, and at other times into <term>karabitus</term> <note>A medieval term likely referring to a type of acute frenzy or stupor caused by rising vapors.</note>, which is bad; and sometimes it changes into <term>pleurisy</term>. This is the opinion of <term>Rhazes</term>, <term>Avicenna</term>, and <term>Mesue</term> <note>Three of the most influential physicians of the Islamic Golden Age whose Latin-translated works formed the core of European medical education.</note>.

Thus, therefore, it can be resolved, since this is even the best of the terminations of <term>abscesses</term> <note>original: "apaťū" / "apostematum". In this context, an internal swelling or inflammation.</note>. To which it must be said that some are persuaded by this appearance. However, the reasons brought forward against this for the truth are stronger, and they must be followed more. For although, as was introduced, the matter of choleric pneumonia may be of small quantity, it is nonetheless of immense quality and sharpness. And it burns greatly on account of the proximity it has to the source of heat <note>The heart was considered the "source of heat" in the body; the lungs' job was to cool it.</note>. Certainly, much heat draws much moisture to the lung, since the lung is receptive to it, even inducing suffocation.

To the other point, it must be said that the harm the lung receives from the covering and <term>obstruction</term> <note>original: "opilone" / "oppilatione"</note> which the phlegm causes when mixed with choler (by reason of its quantity) is greater than the benefit [of cooling] provided by the quality of the phlegm. For this sickness is rendered even more dangerous on account of the mixture of phlegm, since in itself no sickness is worse than that which is moved by diverse forces. Nor should it be said that on account of an acute accident of nature, one should substitute such a temperament to evacuate the matter, since the matter generated in the lung is properly evacuated through <term>sputum</term> <note>Coughing up phlegm or mucus.</note>. But choleric matter, by its subtlety, remains undigested and is disobedient to evacuation through sputum.

<margin><note>pointing hand</note> Gay.</margin> This is apparent from the *Prognostics* <note>A work by Hippocrates.</note> and the first book of *Crises*. Regarding the third point, it should be known that the movement itself is from the thing itself, since almost all other wise men agree on it. Regarding the fourth, one must answer the first point. And so that its solution may appear, one must first bring forward a certain inquiry concerning the truth of this disease, which <term>Mesue</term> <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a 9th-century physician.</note> brings up here. For it seems that **true pneumonia** is that which comes from choler and not from phlegm, as previously touched upon by <term>Galen</term>. Since a true and proper disease is that which is proportional to the nature of the organ, such as that made from choler, since the nourishment of the lung is testified to be choleric.

The contrary of this is also brought forward by Mesue. And perhaps the reason is according to Galen, because a "true proper" disease is less troublesome than a "noted" one; yet phlegmatic pneumonia is set down as being less troublesome. In the solution of this, it is distinguished that the disease is twofold: "true" and "proper." One is "proper" when it is made from the matter that is prepared and purified for the nourishment of some organ, which causes a disease when it is corrupted. Another is "alien," made from the matter of the "superfluity" of that nourishment. 

<margin><note>pointing hand</note></margin> For according to <term>Avicenna</term>, a "superfluity" is contrary to that which it is a superfluity of—such as urine, the mass of blood, sweat, the humors in the veins, the marrow and nourishment of bones, and things like fat and flesh. Unless it be a "transferred superfluity" of its potentiality from which it is brought, such as sperm.

---

<margin><note>pointing hand</note></margin> And know that the lung, just like other organs, receives a part of the humors appropriated to itself. For that which is like choleric blood is prepared and purified for its nourishment. The superfluity of its nourishment, which is phlegm, is sent into its cavities for known benefits. And then, after this is established, he states the definition: And therefore **Galen** is believed when he says that true pneumonia arises from phlegm, as if from superfluous nourishment. And others are believed when they say it arises from choler, as if from the nourishment that was being purified when corruption happened to it; and this is according to their own intentions.

Thus, therefore, according to different considerations, it can be called "phlegmatic true" and "choleric true." To me, however, two of Mesue’s discourses seem understood in a way that sounds like they suffer from a "reproach" and a "defect." A reproach, indeed, because he says the superfluity of the lung's nourishment is phlegm, even though its nourishment is choleric blood—and the superfluity should match that which it is a superfluity of. Therefore, its superfluity should be choleric and not phlegmatic. They also say that phlegm is generated in the second digestion and sent to the lung for the purpose of utility: so that the lung does not become inflamed by the excessive heat and movement of the heart. And also there occur "ascending" and "descending" phlegms. There is a defect also, because his previous distinction only touches upon that which is generated by way of <term>congestion</term>, but not by way of <term>rheum</term> <note>Catarrh or the "flow" of humors from the head to the lungs.</note>. And the former happens less often, while the latter happens more frequently; wherefore his discourse is perhaps insufficient.

<margin>Conclusion of Mesue</margin>
I say, thirdly, to the argument: that Galen said phlegmatic pneumonia is "true" because it happens more frequently, as was said. For he calls that "true and proper" which always or mostly happens in respect to another. And therefore logicians say that a "true property" is that which happens to all and only and always. Since almost every one of these conditions is called "proper" and "true" in some way. Therefore, **phlegmatic pneumonia** will be called "proper" and "true" more so than choleric pneumonia, because it adheres more to its subject (the lung), while the choleric occurs more rarely.

<margin><note>pointing hand</note> Note</margin> Regarding the figure of the speech, it must be said that a "true" sickness is not always worse than a "non-true" one; indeed, it is the opposite, as is the case in "true tertian" fevers and others. Regarding the proof, it must be said that a sickness is not always called "true" because it hurts more, but because it arises from a purer matter—just as a true tertian fever is made from pure choler. This is similar to pleurisy: there is "true" and "non-true." The true occurs in the membranes and the diaphragm of the chest, while the non-true occurs in its muscles. But pneumonia always happens in the same place, namely the lung.

Finally, it must be said that phlegmatic pneumonia is not an entirely "disproportionate" sickness. For although it is disproportionate by reason of the innate nourishment and complexion, nonetheless, by reason of the acquired "supervening" complexion, it is not disproportionate. For it has already appeared how it is not disproportionate, since many things agree in its generation. To the other point, it must be said that although the matter of phlegmatic pneumonia is of greater quantity than the choleric, it is nonetheless not as terrifying as the choleric, which is of more immense quality...

### DIFFERENCE 101.

-> It seems that worms or intestinal worms cannot be <-
-> generated in the belly called the stomach. <-

Since that which cannot be generated cannot, according to <term>dialectic</term> <note>The formal system of logical argument used in medieval universities.</note>, be generated in the belly. But worms cannot be generated, which is shown because, since they would be generated from <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The process of decay. Medieval science believed many small creatures were "spontaneously generated" from rotting material rather than born from parents.</note>, there must be some active agent existing separately as their cause. But nothing of the sort is seen to exist. For if they were generated by the movements of the <term>higher bodies</term> <note>The stars and planets.</note>, as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> believe, such an active force of generation would be either universal or particular. Not the first, because that would seem to be the Sun, which by its approach to us is the cause of generation and by its retreat the cause of corruption, as stated in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption* <note>Aristotle’s "De Generatione et Corruptione."</note>. Thus, they would be generated in the spring, since then the Sun most approaches us. They would, however, be destroyed in autumn when it retreats. But they are generated in every season, and especially in autumn, according to the reasoning in the 16th and 9th books of the *Theory* <note>Likely referring to the *Theorica* of the *Liber Pantegni* by Haly Abbas.</note>. Nor is it from a particular agent, because that which is generated <term>spontaneously</term> <note>Latin: "anthomatice," from the Greek "automatos."</note> and by itself lacks a singular acting parent; for this reason, it is said to be "generated" [rather than "conceived"]. Furthermore, a more noble thing never intends a viler thing, since everything intends to represent itself in a better way. If, therefore, they are produced by the heavens or intelligence, or any noble superior, then vileness and ignobility would fall into its very intention and act.
<margin>3.xm 31</margin> That they are not generated in the upper belly [the stomach] is known from the fourth book of the *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle's *Meteorologia*.</note> in the thirteenth section. Worms do not harm the stomach except by ascending to it. Again, if worms ought to be generated somewhere, the place must be disposed and suitable. Such a place is not the belly, because of its heat and the surrounding heat adjacent to it.
Difference 29. Things that are hard and difficult to change, it alters and transforms. There is also in the stomach the frequent movement of food and drink, now entering, then exiting when digestion is finished. Also, <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile.</note>, which is an enemy to worms, is poured out there in no small amount. Similarly, by a very perceptible shivering, it is emitted upwards, or the distress itself presses it downwards. Therefore, worms cannot be generated in the upper belly, but perhaps in the lower. A sign of this is that they are often brought out downwards before they are found in the stool.

To those who concede these things, <term>Theodorus Priscianus</term> <note>A 4th-century Roman physician.</note> opposes this: From corrupt things

in the stomach, and from foods often taken without appetite or through illness, intestinal worms are born, which sometimes occupy that same stomach and sometimes the lower parts. Also, worms are made from phlegm with a certain heat proportioned to putrefaction, but phlegm of this kind abounds in the belly; also <term>Isaac</term> <note>Isaac Israeli (c. 832–932), a highly influential Jewish physician and philosopher.</note> posits that it is receptive of it and putrefies there. Furthermore, the cause of generation and preservation seems to be the same; for a place that preserves (according to the fourth book of the *Physics*) is also generative, since it is the principle of generation according to <term>Porphyry</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> as if it were a father. But the belly or stomach preserves worms, for we see some ascend to the mouth and nostrils. And similarly in <term>anatomies</term> <note>Dissections or clinical observations of the body's structure.</note>, they have sometimes been found in the stomach, and they have even perforated it at times. And what is more, it is known that serpents and slugs enter the stomach, and are preserved and grow there, and sometimes frogs. Again, choler flows to the intestines continuously; this is not generative of worms, but rather destructive of those already generated. Again, it is found in certain animals, such as the liver of sheep, that these same things are generated, and in the kidneys, bladders, ears, and nostrils, as has been seen.
In the first section: Worms are born very often in the front of the head above the place that is in the shape of the nostrils. And it is possible that they are born near the membranes [of the brain], even if it happens rarely. A worm is also sometimes generated between the skin and the flesh, going up and down through the whole body, which is perceived by its movement under the skin, which it sometimes breaks through when exiting. The fear of this is greater lest it should reach the eye. And this suffering is called the "bovine passion," because it usually happens to cows.
<term>Albucasis</term> <note>Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (936–1013), a famous surgeon of Islamic Spain.</note>, book 3. The liver, however, along with the aforementioned members, is hotter and nobler, and more remote from superfluities and putrefaction. It is more closely joined to the life of the subject. Regarding the first, the primary causes of their generation must be seen; second, the modes and diversity of them.
Regarding the first, it should be known that the causes of their generation are twofold: primary and secondary. The primary causes are four, just as for all other things: namely, matter, form, efficient [cause], and end. The matter is twofold: one indeed is indisposed, such as <term>phlegm</term>, the matter of which is light, viscous foods, such as wheat, beans, milk, raw meats, watery fruits, and the like. The other is disposed, such as phlegm somewhat putrid from putrefaction, yet not so much as in fevers and <term>apostemes</term> <note>Large inflammations or abscesses.</note>. For animals are made in these things which putrefy, because the natural heat, being segregated, causes the segregated parts to stand together (fourth book of the *Meteorology*). For they are not, as some say, generated from blood, because of its necessity and friendship with nature. Nor does nature send it to the place of their generation. For if it arrived there, it would be quickly expelled, or if retained, it would be turned into an aposteme or into a rot tending toward choler, which is deadly to them. Nor are they generated...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the generation of parasitic worms within the human body. The previous page established that the stomach is a site of debate for such generation; here, the author analyzes the material and efficient causes, drawing on a vast array of Greek, Arabic, and Christian philosophical traditions.</meta>

-> Whether worms can be generated in the stomach. <-

## Whether worms can be generated in the stomach.

...from **cholera** <note>Yellow bile, one of the four humors.</note>, since it is bitter, hot, dry, and fiery. From such a substance, nothing is generated or nourished. Therefore, regarding the *Generation of Animals* and the fourth book of the *Pharmacopeia*: neither are they generated from **melancholy** <note>Black bile.</note>, on account of its coldness and dryness, which is unsuited to the frothy putrefaction required for the material of life and their nourishment, as it appears far removed from their natures. Since they must be made from some matter, and there is no other in the body besides the limbs—from which the senses show they are not made—they must be generated from **phlegm**. Their colors, their feel to the touch, and their life denote no other humor than phlegm. Their *Form* is also a soul <note>In the Aristotelian sense, the "soul" (anima) is the organizing principle of any living thing.</note>, just as with other animals.

Indeed, their *Final Cause* <note>The purpose for which something exists.</note> is the fullness and order of the universe. For the world, to be thus perfect and ordered, governs every species. Otherwise, it would be diminished, and even the lowliest things would be lacking. Individually within the body, however, they provide no benefit, since they exist in the body contrary to nature. <margin>16. z 1.</margin> Nor is it their purpose to "cleanse" the intestines—as some say worms and the like are produced to "cleanse" the putrefactions of the world—because the nature of the intestines is to be the place of expulsion by their very design. It is said, however, by nature, that there is some benefit in their generation when they are few in number and small in size. Yet they are almost always detrimental. It must therefore be said that their end is harmful and useless.

The *Efficient Cause* <note>The agent that brings something into being.</note> is twofold. One is particular: the "spiritual heat" arising from putrefaction. Putrefaction alone is not sufficient to generate an animal; they require sufficient heat. As Serapio says: the proper cause of worms is putrefaction. A sounder way to say this is: the heat from putrefaction, and specifically **celestial heat** <note>The influence of the sun and stars, believed to provide the "vital spark" for spontaneous generation.</note>.

The other power [the universal cause] has been thought of in many ways by many people. Some, like the Platonists, posited that forms are given by the lesser gods, saying that the "God of Gods" <note>The Demiurge or Supreme Creator in Plato's Timaeus.</note> instilled the seeds of generation into the matter. As it says in the *Timaeus*: "I shall make the seed of this universal race and deliver it to you. It is your part to execute the rest, so that you may surround this immortal and celestial nature with a mortal fabric... command them to be born, provide food, and give them growth." And after dissolution, he would receive back that which had been entrusted.

For this reason, in the commentary on the 12th book of the *Metaphysics*, it is said that Plato spoke in obscure words: that the Creator created the angels <margin>Color 12 met.</margin> by his own hand, but commanded them to create other mortal things, while he himself remained at rest without labor. This, however, is not to be understood literally. Others wanted forms to come from the Sun and the "slanting circle" <note>The Ecliptic, or the path of the sun, which governs the seasons and biological cycles.</note>, as Themistius also testifies.

Thus, thinkers are divided on what the "agent" of generation is. Some posited the "hiding of forms" <note>Latitancy: the idea that all forms are already hidden in matter and just need to be "pulled out."</note>, such as Anaxagoras with Empedocles and Democritus—though this was refuted in the fourth book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*. Others posited "creation," and several intermediate views emerged between these. Those who posited the "hiding of forms" claim that anything can be in anything, and that the agent only extracts things and distinguishes them from one another; they say generation is merely the exit of a thing from its hiding place. They say a Divine Intellect operates more by separating all things from a certain "chaos" which they imagine to be spread out.

Those who posit the "creation" of things say the agent creates the whole being anew from nothing, and that there is no matter upon which it acts, but it creates the whole. This "imagination of creation" led men to say that forms are given by a "Giver of Forms." This led to the "Speakers of the Three Laws" <note>A common medieval reference to the three Abrahamic religions: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.</note> who today say something can be made from nothing. And since no such [natural] agent could be perceived, they said the Agent produces all beings without a medium, and that the action of the agent passes in a single instant into infinite similar actions—to the point that they deny that fire burns or water moistens, saying all such things require [continual] creation. <margin>Creation.</margin> Whence they also say bodies do not create, nor do they induce any dispositions; they even say that when a man moves a stone by pushing it, he is not the mover, but the Agent [God] creates that motion. They thus denied the existence of "potentiality." The error of these people is manifest.

<margin>John the Christian</margin> The opinion of **John the Christian** <note>Johannes Philoponus, a 6th-century Christian commentator on Aristotle known for his theories of impetus and creation.</note> is that possibility exists only in the Agent. And this is perhaps what John writes at the beginning [of his Gospel]: *All things were made by Him, and without Him was nothing made.*

The "intermediates" seem to be divided into two opinions, one of which is further divided, making five views in total. All three intermediate views agree on this: that generation and transformation occur in *substance* (unlike Anaxagoras), and that nothing is generated from nothing—that is, a subject [matter] is necessary in generation. And that which is generated is only made by something of its own kind in form. One of these three claims that the agent creates the form and places it in the matter. This agent is found in two modes: abstracted from matter, and sometimes joined to it—just as fire makes fire, and a man generates a man. That which is "abstracted" generates animals and plants that are not like their parents <note>i.e., spontaneous generation of lower life forms from heat and matter.</note>.

<margin>Themistius, Al-Farabi, Avicenna, Al-Ghazali.</margin> This is the opinion of Themistius, and perhaps Al-Farabi, although he hesitates to apply this to those things generated by propagation. There was another opinion: that the agent is not in matter at all, and they call it the **Giver of Forms**. Avicenna was among these, along with Al-Ghazali, as appears in the ninth book of the *Metaphysics*. He took this from the principle of generation: that the same thing remaining the same is always naturally inclined to do the same thing. Either the First Master, who is stable, produces only one thing immediately—so that by understanding Himself, He produces the First Intelligence with the first heaven; then that Intelligence produces the second, and so on. Thus, the Intelligence of the Moon, understanding itself, produces a certain Intelligence called the **Active Intellect** <note>In Arabic Aristotelianism, the 'Active Intellect' was a celestial intelligence that provided the 'forms' to the earthly world.</note> which governs the sphere of active and passive things, of simples and composites.

<margin>Aristotle</margin> The third was the opinion of **Aristotle**, which is to be followed. According to Alexander [of Aphrodisias], it is the least ambiguous of all opinions and most likely to be true, since he says nothing without proof. This view is that the agent does not "make" anything except the composite of matter and form. This is done by moving the matter and transforming it until the form, which exists in the matter as a potentiality, emerges.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the "efficient cause" of worm generation. Having established that worms are made from phlegm (the material cause), the author now explains the mechanism of how life is sparked from that matter. He balances Aristotle’s natural philosophy with Averroes’s commentary and celestial influence, rejecting the idea of direct divine creation in favor of a naturalistic, though star-driven, process.</meta>

<margin>Averroes</margin>
...into actuality. For the agent draws out that which is **in potential** into **act**, and as it were, binds together the potential and the act—that is, matter and form. This is done in such a way that it draws out the potential into act without destroying the subject that receives those potentials.

And then two things result in opposition: matter <term>namely</term> and form. This view is somewhat likened to the Creator, insofar as that which is in potential becomes actual. But it differs from creation, because life does not arrive through a pre-existing form, but from "non-form" into act. Similarly, this view resembles those who posit the "hiding" of forms <note>A theory that all forms already exist hidden in matter and just need to be revealed.</note>. It also resembles all those who speak of a creator, or of "hiding," or of "aggregators" and "segregators" like <term>Empedocles</term> <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who believed the universe was managed by the forces of Love (aggregation) and Strife (segregation).</note>. To whom this view is also somewhat likened in what he intended, though they were not able to reach the truth of the matter.

Therefore, it is the intention of <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Ay.", a common scholastic abbreviation for Aristoteles.</note> that the like is made from the like, or from that which is truly like; and not that matter acts by itself through its own underlying form. Rather, he says that the agent draws out matter from potential into act, and the agent does not introduce something extrinsic <note>Coming from the outside.</note> into the matter. Just as this is found in **substance** and in **accidents**. For heat does not introduce an extrinsic heat into a warm body, but makes the heat that is already there in potential become heat in act. This also applies to quality and local motion: they do not arrive from the outside, but are awakened into act from the potential of the matter, just as fire is generated from motion as it is from fire. And thus, once generated, it draws out what is in the potential of the matter to be born into act, so that it becomes generated in act.

And everything drawing something out from potential into act must have in it, in some way, that which it draws out—not that it is entirely the thing itself. For the powers that are in seeds, which make living things, are not living in act but in potential, just as the house that is in the soul of the builder is a house in potential and not in act. And therefore <term>Aristotle</term>, in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, likened these powers to "divine artificial powers," which are understood to be intelligences. This, therefore, is the opinion of <term>Aristotle</term> alone which accords with the truth, since the impossible conclusions that follow other opinions do not follow from his.

I will briefly point out some of their defects, since they do not stand up to scrutiny. <term>Plato's</term> view on gods impressing forms (attacked in several places in the *Metaphysics* under the name of "Ideas") is one such error. A similar error seems to be held by <term>Themistius</term>—if indeed the Commentator <note>Averroes</note> attributes it to him correctly. I do not think he held a sound understanding with <term>Aristotle</term>, as the Commentator's recitations of his words sound. Those who posit the "hiding" of forms are entirely refuted by <term>Aristotle</term>, since they cannot account for actual generation, making forms emerge from a kind of chaos or indivisibility. Whence in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*, he says that <term>Anaxagoras</term> <note>A Greek philosopher who taught that "everything is in everything."</note>, the teacher of this position, was ignorant of the term, since by positing one subject he made generation no different from mere alteration.

Furthermore, those who posit **Creation**, even if they follow the truest Law <note>The author likely refers to religious scripture/doctrine here.</note>, are nonetheless not to be admitted in the study of philosophy. For that view makes all things too easy and burdens the First Cause <note>God</note> with manifold labors, removing beauty and order. Consequently, it removes the "perfective" quality from the universe, according to the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school.</note>. It also destroys order by making the agent act almost in vain, and it breaks down the specific principles of nature. Such a view even depraves the opinion of <term>Aristotle</term>, since according to him, the same thing disposes the matter and awakens the form from it, as appears in the saying: "Man and the Sun generate man." Nor is the following argument valid: that if the first cause remains really the same, it is nonetheless posited with certain "ideal reasons." It is not inappropriate for the cause to be changed in some way—not that the cause itself undergoes change, but that the *effect* does, as those who treat divine matters alongside philosophers teach.

Thus it must be said according to <term>Aristotle's</term> opinion: that worms are generated like other things produced by **putrefaction**, with elementary heat disposing the matter which putrefies, and by the power of the sun and other stars—the celestial heat cooperating. Regarding this, see tractate 48. Whence the Commentator <note>Averroes</note> says: "Heat is made in the earth from the heat of the sun, mixed with the heat of the other stars." And therefore the sun and stars are the principle of life for every living thing in nature. For the heat of the sun and stars, sent down into water and earth, generates animals born from putrefaction, and indeed all things that are made without seed. This is because a "soul in act" is found in them, derived from the tilted orbit of the heavens and from the sun, as <term>Themistius</term> asserts. And he adds: the heats generated from the bodies of the stars, generating every species of animal, have their own specific measurements of that heat. These measurements come from the quantities of the stars' motions and their dispositions toward each other in proximity and distance. And this "measure" proceeds from an intellectual divine art, which is like a single, primary, universal form under which are many specific arts. According to this, it must be understood that nature acts perfectly and in an orderly way, even if it does not "think," because it is directed by those more noble active powers which are called **Intelligences**.

These proportions and powers which are in the elements due to the motions of the sun and other stars are the very things <term>Plato</term> considered to be "Forms," and which he intended to describe, but he only saw them from afar. For this reason, he called them "Forms." Since, therefore, from matter that is nearly identical in number, we see diverse species of animals arise, what else is it that contracts them into a singular species, if not a universal celestial power and the heat that makes the matter receptive?

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
For this reason, it must be said specifically that the power in higher bodies is twofold. One is more universal, such as that of the celestial spheres and the stars. The other is more "contracted" or specific, such as that of one of the **48 images** <note>The 48 constellations described by Ptolemy.</note>. Without their influence, the different species would not be intended here. Whence <term>Ptolemy</term> in the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy.</note> holds that the animals and plants of this lower world are subject to the higher images in a general way. This is shown by the fact that wise men, when creating images of the planets, observed the "face" or aspect of the heavens. They then worked toward construction or destruction as was expedient.

For there is a celestial **Scorpio**, which corresponds to those called scorpions below, and a celestial Serpent for serpents. Thus, from the form of a serpent, a scorpion, a cancer, or some other such celestial influence—perhaps unknown to us—such slithering things are produced even within the bodies of men. For according to <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of Hermeticism.</note>, <term>Enoch</term>, or <term>Mercury</term> in his *Book of the Sands of the Sea*...
