<header>Whether worms can be born in the stomach.</header>

# Whether worms can be born in the stomach.

The star <note>sydus</note> holds influence over its growth; much more so will there be something to provide for its perfection in these matters. For indeed, from the highest powers, all these things are filled with certain modest gifts and virtues; whence **Aristotle** in *On the Cosmos* says that some of the ancients confessed all these things to be "full of gods." <note>original: "diis plena fore"</note> Thus, the specific causes of worms and the production of other offspring appear. The true causes are those by which different types are produced by reason of the humors and the location from which they are generated. 

For some are generated from humidity upon which the heat of the heart and liver does not dominate <note>meaning the humors are not properly "cooked" or digested by bodily heat</note>, through the attraction of the liver and vehement putrefaction, such as those generated in the upper intestines; these are the **long worms**, sometimes reaching a length of more than a cubit. <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches.</note> Others, however, are generated from a separate humidity, diminished because of the continuous attraction of the liver and putrefaction and a multitude of disturbed feces; these are like those which are in the rectum, very small. The remaining types are from a humidity that is in the middle, such as the "one-eyed" <term>monoculus</term> <note>The medieval term for the cecum, the pouch at the beginning of the large intestine.</note>, and the round ones, and the broad-bodied ones.

According to this science, a **worm** <margin>Worm</margin> is an animal generated from putrefaction in the belly, brought to life by "vivifying heat." There are three named types in their history: the **broad**, the **round**, and thirdly, **ascarides** <note>small pinworms</note>. From these, no other kind exists. Only the broad one adheres to the intestine and appears like the seeds of a colocynth <note>a bitter cucumber-like fruit</note>. They are also commonly placed into three modes: for some are long and round like snakes, similar to the branches of purslane; or "lumbrici" because they grow long in the slender intestines. And the broad ones are like the seeds of a gourd; for this reason, they are also called "cucurbitini" <note>gourd-shaped</note>, primarily because they resemble gourd seeds joined one to another on a thread. These are called **ascarides** and "buffones" according to some, occurring in the thick intestines and spreading through everything, even scurrying up into the **stomach**. This causes a person to become alienated and soon produces a "canine hunger" <note>An insatiable, ravenous appetite (bulimia).</note>. Indeed, they are sometimes of the greatest length when joined together. Thus, someone reported to me that they had passed a cluster of them measuring fifteen feet. There also exist the third kind, small and slender, similar to the worms found in vinegar or cheese, growing in the rectum so that they do not appear to the eyes as a pair. 

**Avicenna**, however, along with **Serapio**, says there are four species: namely, long, broad, round, and the broad ones are ascarides and small. **Galen** also touched on the round ones in the twelfth book of the *Art of Healing*. He himself, when he observes the aforementioned ascarides, notes a third way from the outside. Ascarides are thin worms in the lower part of the thick intestine, whose indigestion is signaled by the stench of the stools. Another genus of worms, which are round, are generated more in the upper intestines, ascending toward the upper belly of the stomach. There are also broad ones, whose generation is often very long, extended through all the intestines.

<margin>Note</margin> However, in the two prior species of worms, the falsity of the interpretation is felt to be entirely "monkish" <note>Likely a critique of translations or commentaries produced in monasteries that the author finds inaccurate.</note>, the opposite of this truth. At the end of the fourteenth book of *On Method*, Galen places the ascarides, the round, and the broad; he feels that the round are killed by lesser medicines, while the broad and ascarides require stronger medicine. **Oribasius**, however, in the *Practice* dedicated to his son **Eustachius**, says: there are three differences of worms: round, those similar to gourd seeds, and ascarides which are small little worms. There are also long ones. But he speaks perversely against the common opinion of all regarding the round and broad or "gourd-like" ones. 

The great **Avicenna**, saying that ascarides are small worms distinct from the others, agrees with Galen as touched upon in the third book of the *Aphorisms*. Wherefore Oribasius, in his own commentary on the *Aphorisms*, says there are three types of worms: ascarides, which are like gourd seeds. Thus he agrees with Avicenna and others, yet contradicts himself and Galen's *Aphorisms*. And he adds: there are also round ones, which are not as he previously placed them (as animals similar to gourd seeds). And he adds: and others are long, which can even be found to be four cubits long. 

The authors are not equal in the naming of worms. However, Serapio and Avicenna seem most familiar to me. Worms also occur more in phlegmatic complexions and in the ages after the teeth have been planted <note>childhood</note>; for the heat in younger infants is not yet sufficient. In those in whom bile abounds in the intestines, and in gluttons and those with poor digestion, and from the coarse phlegmatic foods mentioned before. And more so in autumn, because of the corruption of digestion and the bad quality of food. 

Some of these worms are very prone to exiting; others not at all, and some only a little. Those in the lower intestine exit easily for four reasons. One is the proximity to the exit; the second is the width of the place; the third is the smallness of the animal. For a small thing falls more quickly from a wide place. There is also a fourth: their weakness. In those which exist in the upper intestines, they are found in the feces. In the middle, a middle ground is found. 

Here, however, he understands the "stomach" by an abusive name <note>A rhetorical term meaning the word is being used loosely or incorrectly to refer to the whole abdominal cavity.</note>. In how many ways this is taken was said in the 54th distinction. For the sake of knowing this: some have said that worms are not generated except in the "one-eyed" <term>monoculus</term> and the colon; whence Avicenna says: and perhaps they are not generated except in the monoculus and colon, and then they spread from the side to the stomach and from the side to the anus. And he was moved to say this because in the long intestine, they are unable to be generated due to its straightness, width, and the continuous exit of feces; for the material would be expelled as dung before their generation. Nor are they generated in the upper intestines because of the lack of putrefaction retained there and the vehement drying that occurs there. There were many others besides these, saying that worms are generated in the four lower intestines. In the two upper ones least of all, such as the **jejunum** and **duodenum**, for reasons that are adapted to the stomach in the deprivation of their generation. To the first of these, it must be said: that they occur in the upper intestines and especially in the slender ones and the rectum, as almost everyone testifies, since the aforementioned causes of their generation can be adapted to these places. Nor will the things inciting them impel them so that they absolutely do not occur in such places; but rather that they occur more rarely in the middle of the intestines than in the rectum, especially since the time of bowel movements coincides with the long worms. For they are produced in a short time of delay. Or perhaps they are not separated by the passage of feces, since the small ones are adhering to the surfaces of the intestines, even if the stool is made liquid. For it has been found that medicine for the belly does not lead out all [worms] in a bowel movement. Similarly if the upper parts of the intestines...

<meta>This page continues the medical-philosophical inquiry into the generation of parasites. The author is reconciling the differing opinions of the two great medical authorities, Galen and Avicenna, regarding whether worms can originate in the stomach itself or only in the lower intestines.</meta>

<margin>To point 7</margin>
...they might contain more youthful vigor, and in them, the attraction from the liver may be strong in well-regulated bodies. In others, the opposite can happen, where the food—by the quantity of intake, the quality, the timing, the preparation, and the order—is corrupted. Indeed, some, such as **Avicenna** in the fourth [book of] *Meteorology* <note>original: "metbauro," likely referring to the Meteororum</note>, feel that large worms cannot be generated in the upper belly <note>The "upper belly" usually refers to the stomach and the immediate upper gastrointestinal tract</note>. An animal is not formed in the digestion itself, as some say, but in the putrefactive segregation <note>The separation of waste or "superfluities" from the nutrients</note>, and in the lower belly. From there, the digested material ascends. For it is in the upper belly. Whence **Alexander** <note>likely Alexander of Tralles, a 6th-century physician</note> says that this is why they frequently vomit in illnesses; however, the segregated material putrefies in the lower [belly]. So **Avicenna** accepts the probable cause: that worms are generated from putrefied segregation, as is also declared in the causes of these things. 

But this does not happen in the upper belly but in the lower; for in the upper belly, they digest food and always move it along by the expulsive virtue <term>expulsive virtue</term> <note>the body's natural power to move waste out</note> of the stomach and intestines, and by the attraction of the liver, and the proximity of the mesenteric veins and the noble parts. Furthermore, where much digestive heat flourishes to dry out the moisture, putrefaction cannot happen, nor can worms be generated there, since they are made from putrid things; the sign of this is that they are nourished by them once produced, as appears in flies and similar creatures. From these points previously introduced, it is probably concluded that worms cannot be in the upper belly, nor generated in the intestines immediately attached to it. And specifically since bile is poured into it continually and nearby. 

**Galen**, however, seems to hold the opposite of this, conceding that these are generated in the stomach in this way: Putrefaction alone is not sufficient to generate these, but it also lacks sufficient heat. Therefore, the nourishment is indeed corrupted many times in the belly, and especially in the "cuticbato" <note>likely a corruption of a term for the small intestine or a specific childhood condition</note>, that is, in that which is below in infants. Whence another translation says: "We well understand that in the stomachs of children and in the intestines, food is corrupted and putrefied, from which the matter for worms is made." 

Wherefore **Avicenna** could argue against **Galen** in the opposite way, thus: Worms are generated from putrefaction where enough of it occurs to suffice for generation. But this happens more rarely in the stomach. Furthermore, things are generated in the stomach that are more "beyond nature" <note>unnatural or pathological</note> than worms, such as horrible unnatural bile or abscesses. Thus, animals are sustained there once received. Again, both from a superior complexion <note>the bodily temperament</note> and also from a poor regimen <term>regimen</term> <note>lifestyle, especially diet</note>, or plague. Similarly to the lower or middle intestines, the upper belly can be disposed [to corruption]. Because it will be disposed in the same way, it can have similar effects. From which it is concluded, according to **Galen**, that worms can also be generated in the stomach. 

Regarding the third point, it should be known that I, reconciling <note>The author likely identifies with the school of Peter of Abano, the "Conciliator"</note> these great wise men with one another, say that if we speak of a healthy body, or even one that has slipped [into illness] but in which the operations are not yet openly harmed: in those things which happen more naturally and most frequently in the stomach and the intestines nearest to it, worms are not generated. And the reasons previously introduced for this are sufficient. If, however, the discourse is about a body that has greatly slipped into a sickly state, or any sick person, or regarding those things which happen by accident and rarely, I pronounce that worms can sometimes be generated in the stomach, due to indigestion and other consequent concurring causes. Just as in almost all parts except the vital ones, I find them to be generated sometimes. 

The arguments introduced here for this are sharp and sufficient enough for now. For sometimes those which are the causes of generation in the lower viscera can be adapted to the stomach. Since their opposites do not show impossibility, but rather difficulty. Regarding the fourth point, although it appears from the premises, it must nevertheless be said in response to the arguments. To the first, therefore, it must be said that worms are made both by a universal power and by a particular one, as shown before; and that the sun becomes the cause of generation through its adjunct to us of simple things, this has truth in those things which are generated in the surroundings that need the sun to be fostered by heat. But it is not so in those which are made in places where their heat is always fostered, such as the bodies of animals in which these are generated; although the sun’s arrival to us contributes to all generation. 

The constellation <note>The specific astrological alignment</note> that is the giver of their particular form is not [acting] only sometimes, but as declared, continuously. For the influence of the celestial body always dominates in terrestrial bodies, and if more sometimes, then less at others, according even to the disposition of matter varied in such a way. 

To the other point, it must be said that the more noble by itself and primarily always intends something more noble than itself; but by accident and secondarily, it happens that it seems to intend something viler. For the Heaven and the Intelligence, so that in intending their own primary [goals] they transform themselves into the First Cause, and the First [Cause] itself manifests the highest communication of its goodness, so that other things may be perfected consequently. Which **Aristotle** declares in the ninth book of the *Metaphysics*, saying: "Water cools by its own nature as an act so that it may preserve its own species, not so that it may cool something outside itself, just as fire heats by itself so that it may preserve its own species, not so that it may heat something outside itself." 

Similarly, the appetitive virtue desires to be delighted by intercourse <note>original: "coitu"</note> for the purpose of expelling surplus, and its delight is completed, not so that an offspring <note>original: "filiz," for *filius*</note> may be made from it; since many, according to **Haly Abbas** and **Isaac**, couple for the sake of pleasure and not for the generation of children. So, therefore, something intending its own perfection, by accident intends the perfection of another. Concerning which the Commentator <note>Averroes</note> in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* says: "To say that God is solicitous about every single individual is in some way true, and in some way false." It is true because no individual has its own disposition unless that disposition is found in some way in that species. In this way, it is true to say God is solicitous about individuals. But to be solicitous about an individual in such a way that no one else has a shared connection with it is not the way of Divine Goodness. 

Wherefore the truth of it exists in this: that there is care. And if there are some things without [direct] care, they happen from the necessity of matter, not from a deficiency of the agent. This has led some to say there are two gods, one of whom creates good things and the other evil, which was the error of the **Manichaeans**. Whence the same [author] says in *On the Soul*: "Divine care, since it could not make the animal remain as an individual, had mercy by giving it the virtue by which it can remain as a species."

# Whether hyposarca is worse than other forms of dropsy.

Wherefore, according to the order of the heavens and the world, celestial bodies and divine virtue are nobler than these things. For that which is found for the sake of another is nobler than that which is found in its own intention. For it is declared in divine science <note>referring to Metaphysics or Theology</note> that these things are not found except for their own sake in the primary intention. But that which is found for itself in the primary intention must necessarily be found through another in the secondary intention. Otherwise, there would not be an innate nature there for the sake of bestowing. However, it is necessary in these kinds of things that can be generated and corrupted. For they are themselves in the secondary intention, and not the primary. For the action of a man in the primary intention is for the sake of another, namely for the sake of the existence of superior beings, but not in intention for his own sake. That there is providence regarding the beings here is inferred from the heavens and the world according to the order and from the first principles of **Alexander** <note>likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a commentator on Aristotle</note>. Regarding another point by **Avicenna** <note>original: "Aų." for Avicenna</note>, what ought to be said appeared. Regarding another point, it must be said that although it happens very frequently, both because of the nature of the whole and the coldness of the stomach's complexion and the indigestion of the matter contained in it, and because of the dulling of its strength, as well as the irregularity of eating and the lack of bile, worms <term>lumbrici</term> <note>large intestinal roundworms</note> can eventually be seen to be created in the stomach. A similar reasoning appeared regarding the other points mentioned. For regarding the first point, what was already said was seen.

Regarding the second point, it must be said that although phlegm may abound in the stomach, it rarely generates worms. However, when it does not putrefy so that it might be emitted, or if it is not frequently evacuated and is not stirred, or some other prohibition occurs, they may form. Regarding the other point, it must be said that something is more easily conserved in a certain place than it is generated in that same place, since the power of conservation is broader than the power of generation. For many things are not generated in several places, yet they can still be conserved in them to some extent. Similarly, concerning the worms entering and those to be generated, it is not similar, unless those already brought in were much stronger than those to be generated. If, however, they exit from above through the mouth or nostrils, it happens as they are passing through to that place for the sake of higher nourishment, as **Avicenna** said, not because they are often generated there. These worms sometimes induce such bad accidents in the stomach that they cause heart problems <note>original: "cardiacā," referring to stomach-related heart distress</note> and fainting <term>syncope</term> with anguish, so much so that someone might die suddenly from their biting. **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Tralles, a 6th-century physician</note> confirms this. **Avicenna** also bears witness that some worms have exited the belly through a perforation. Something similar has also been recounted to me. They can also induce epilepsy and cholera. Regarding another point, it must be said that in the intestines, it is not in most cases so earthy and dreg-like, but that in digestion there remains something subtle, moist, capable of putrefaction, spiritual, and life-giving, and specifically in those whose intestines do not have an abundance of excreted bile. And for this reason, it appeared regarding the other point. Regarding the other, it must also be conceded that it happens rarely, just as it is admitted that they can sometimes be generated in the stomach.

### DIFFERENCE 102.

For indeed, the reasoning occurs with a difference between those things that happen, since the outcome of those things resists in disproportion. Just as **burning fever** <note>original: "causon"</note> in old age is first in the fourth degree. And therefore, this will be more troublesome to some and less to others. Distinction 199: However, the sickness that can be cured in more ways is lighter than that which can be cured in fewer. Therefore, the same discharge will be worse in these cases.

Truly, for the first part, it must be known beforehand what dropsy is, and how many are its types. And finally, what are its causes together with the manner of its generation. Regarding this first point, as gathered from the speeches of the physicians: dropsy is a major error of the liver’s digestive power, because of which all the members—seeking fellowship or nourishment—swell up greatly. It is called a "major error" because from a minor error, other illnesses and bad **complexions** <note>the balance of the four bodily humors</note> arise, but not dropsy. Thirdly: in this, however, because it adds that all <unclear>parts</unclear> are touched, it refers to **hyposarca**. When it joins "or of nourishment," it refers to **ascites** <note>fluid accumulation in the abdominal cavity</note> and **tympanites**.

Also, in the fourteenth section: dropsy is a sickness whose cause is an overflowing coldness entering the members, and they grow because of it—either all the manifest members, or the empty spaces of the parts in which the governance of nourishment and the humors exist. Whence **Alexander** <note>likely Alexander of Tralles, a 6th-century physician</note> says: Chronic dropsy is a passion, and it is generated from the coldness of the liver. There is a doubt about this, because he says that its matter is cold, while some place the cause of dropsy in heat occurring lower down. Furthermore, the fourth of the Aphorisms says: **Tympanites** arises from a slight coldness; for no moisture can be transformed into windy air without some heat. Therefore, it does not seem implicit that the matter is cold. It must be said that "cold" refers to that which is destitute of innate, quantitative heat, even though it may have a horrible and sharp qualitative heat, such as is found in all superfluity. Whence also the fourth problem: is the generation cold? <note>original: "an. s."</note> That is, does it affect and agitate from the heat of the innate spirit? Or it should be said that it happens for the most part from the cold. When he later joins "or the spaces <unclear>of the parts</unclear>," he touches upon—as before—**hyposarca** dropsy, and afterwards **ascites** and **tympanites**.

Next, it should be known that regarding the number of the species of dropsy, physicians have differed. For **Oribasius** <note>Greek medical writer and physician to Emperor Julian</note> in his work to **Eustachius**, and **Cassius Felix**, express only two: namely **ascites** and **tympanites**.

The **Salernitans** <note>physicians of the medical school at Salerno</note>, however, posited that there are four, wishing to bring them into line with the four humors or the proposed fourfold combination of qualities. For they said that **leucophlegmatia**, which is interpreted as "white phlegminess"—for *leukon* <note>original: "leucon"</note> means white—is generated from a fault of coldness and moisture. **Hyposarca**, that is, "under the flesh"—for *sarx* <note>original: "sarsym"</note> means flesh—happens from heat and moisture. **Tympanites**, however, whose name is taken from its accident <note>its symptoms</note>, because when the belly is struck, a sound is heard, or as if from a drum <note>original: "tympani"</note>, proceeds from heat and excessive dryness. **Ascites**, truly, that is, "belly-like," or "womb-like"—for *ascos* <note>original: "asces"</note> means a wine-skin <note>original: "uter"</note>—is so called because the belly, when struck, returns the sound of water moving in a wine-skin half-filled with it; from the fourth of the Aphorisms.

Furthermore, in the beginning of the <unclear>internal</unclear> works, it seems to mean the same. The whole body seems to be contained by phlegmatic blood, and according to **Anasarca** <note>generalized swelling</note>, and **leucophlegmatias**, and those named "watery," but through the belly nothing bloody is excreted, neither in these nor in **ascites** and **tympanites**. It must be said that by **Anasarca** and **leucophlegmatias** he understood the same thing as the first. Either he spoke according to the opinions of others, or to avoid a dispute over names, he said it only follows thus: concerning dropsies, let anyone name them however he wishes. This opinion or a similar one is touched upon in the fourth book of *Acute Diseases*. For he says: some write not "under-flesh" but "over-flesh," and by this they understand **hyposarca**. And he adds: not only in the flesh or next to the flesh—as if he were saying that this is not the same as that which is called **hyposarca** and **episarca**—so that according to them, **hyposarca** is the first and **anasarca** the second. These also precede the other two species, namely **ascites** and **tympanites**. Wherefore there are likewise four. And therefore he adds: therefore, according to the group of physicians who say there are four exceeding differences of dropsy, which is fitting—as if he says there are not unless three. And he joins: "But now is not the time to refute them."

That the species of dropsy are only three—**hyposarca** (or **anasarca**, or by whatever name it is called), **ascites**, and **tympanites**—was the opinion not only of **Galen**, but also of all other approved Greeks and Arabs, whom the Latins now follow. For in the *Viaticum* <note>a popular medieval medical handbook</note> it is said that **leucophlegmatia**, **hyposarca**, and **anasarca** are the same. Whence **Alexander** says: the third type, consisting of phlegmatic blood in the whole body, occurs and is called **anasarca leucophlegmatia**. He shows that dropsy does not happen from a fault of heat and moisture, as some have posited. Since dropsy, as was said, happens because of a major error of the liver's digestive power. Truly, heat and moisture either do not exceed in excess—and thus would contribute more to digestion and the prevention of dropsy than to its induction—or they exceed for the most part, and then they generate a putrid sickness rather than dropsy, since heat and moisture, compared to other natures, are prone to putrefaction. In dropsy, however, as far as this is concerned, there is no putrefaction. Furthermore, **hyposarca** and **leucophlegmatia** differ neither in location nor in matter nor in signs. For there is no humoral distinction in the third digestion, but everything is finally united. For which reason one ought not to place those distances apart. Those things which do not differ in these ways ought to be judged as the same by the physician. Moreover, it is a fault to do through many things what can be accomplished by fewer. And therefore, with their illustrious doctors, it must be posited that there are only three modes of dropsy. Those who posit four create more a number of names than of things. Those expressing only two, the shorter and the fuller, have followed what happens. Know that although in the fourth book of *Acute Diseases* it may seem that he touches on only two species of dropsy, there are nonetheless three heard of; but this **ascites** is twofold, namely with **tympanites**. For the similarity of this, it should be known that the causes of dropsy are taken from natural things, and not <unclear>otherwise</unclear>.

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of dropsy, specifically analyzing the physiological mechanisms of its three forms: hyposarca (tissue swelling), ascites (fluid accumulation), and tympanites (gas bloating). It maintains the previous page's focus on the liver as the primary site of digestive failure.</meta>

### Whether hyposarca is worse than other forms of dropsy.

From natural things and things against nature, just as with other illnesses. From **natural things** <note>In medieval medicine, "natural things" refer to the body's innate components like organs and humors; "non-naturals" refer to external factors like diet and environment.</note> indeed, as if from fallen members. For it arises either from the flanks, or from the loins, or the spleen, or the intestine, or the bladder, or the gallbladder, or the lung, or the **diaphragm** <note>original: "dyastante"</note>, or from the liver—according to the second book of *Prognostics* and the third and fourteenth sections. And although dropsy can happen from almost any member, it is not formally established unless a great malice is fixed in the liver. Whence Galen says in the same place: All types of dropsy come from harm to the **power of generating blood** <note>original: "uirtute generatiua sanguis"</note> when it fails in its completion; this power, however, is located by physicians in the liver.

Therefore, the conclusion is that unless the liver is injured, dropsy is not born. Just as there is no fever—wherever it may arise—unless an external heat seeks the heart by means of the arteries (from the first book of *Fevers*). From **non-natural things** <note>The "six non-naturals" include air, food/drink, sleep/waking, movement/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the mind.</note> it arises when they are administered in an improper quality, quantity, time, order, or skill. From those things which are **against nature**, however, it arises as a result of a bad **complexion** <note>the balance of the four humors</note>, or from tumors, or the dissolution of continuity, and from other causes declared in detail, and especially from a depraved disposition of the liver. For although all dropsy arises because of a fault in the digestion and separation of the liver, it is primarily 
<margin>Signs of Lesion</margin> and more heavily injured in **ascites** <note>fluid in the abdomen</note> during the second digestion; in **tympanites** <note>gas in the abdomen</note> during the first digestion; and in **hyposarca** during the third digestion. This is according to Galen in the sixth book of *Accidents and Causes*. There is also a manner of generation for hyposarca: because when in the **third digestion** <note>The final stage of digestion occurring within the tissues and organs themselves.</note> the members ought to incorporate nourishment into themselves through the triple operation of the nutritive power—namely, apposition <note>placing next to</note>, adherence, and union—a defect occurs in the adherence. For although the nourishment is placed next to the parts, it does not adhere like that which was dissolved; rather, it makes the flesh **illusory** <note>original: "fantastica"</note>, thin, and pale. From this, the superfluity that ought to be expelled in the third digestion is not shaken off because of the imperfect digestion of the nutritive power, or even of the two preceding digestions of the stomach and liver. And since this third digestion occurs throughout the whole body and fails in its entirety, hence the members are said to appear to swell up.

<margin>The Manner of Ascites</margin> The manner in which **ascites** dropsy arises is manifold. In this condition, water enters the middle space between the **peritoneum** <note>original: "syphac," the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> and the muscles of the belly on one side, and the **omentum** <note>original: "zirbi," the fatty membrane covering the intestines</note> and the intestines on the other, and the diaphragm on the rest. This happens because nature, in many ways, seeks to expel from itself superfluities and everything harmful. Or, it seeks to transport them to places of less resistance, especially when nature is strong. For it expels corrupted matter through the marrow even of the bones (Aphorisms, books 4, 7, and 14). One way indeed is due to a fissure in some passage, either of the **mesaraic veins** <note>mesenteric veins</note> or of the intestines, through which wateriness penetrates into the aforementioned space before it can be led to the liver. Or, it may be due to vesicles <note>small blisters or cysts</note> that are formed in the liver filled with water; when these have multiplied over a long time and ruptured, the water flows out into the predicted place. This water multiplies until the whole belly there is filled with wateriness. And this is the interpretation of Galen on the seventh book of Aphorisms: "In whomsoever the liver is filled with water and it breaks out into the omentum, in these the belly is filled with water and they die." A third way is because when the **chyle** <note>milky fluid of digested food</note> is drawn to the liver, it ought to be turned into blood within it; remaining watery, whey-like, and sharp because the power is weakened, it is expelled from the liver's edges and appendages, distilling into the aforementioned place. Or fourthly, that the liver may still be of such vigor that it sends such wateriness through the veins for the nourishment of the body. However, it is indistinguishable and unpurified from the urinary moisture. The members, eventually shrinking away from retaining this, send it back again through the same passages inward until it returns to the liver, since a flow and perspiration occurs through the same pores at all times (from the third book of *Natural Faculties*).

There is also a fifth way, which some of the famous ancients touched upon, by way of the lower abdomen and the navel. For as the anatomists say, from the great artery under the kidneys, two arteries branch out which tend toward the bladder; then through the **lower abdomen** <note>original: "sumen"</note> or pubic area, they extend to the navel. Through these, a fetus urinates when it is not yet born, and even after birth if pressure is applied, provided it cannot yet urinate from the penis. Just as in a youth lacking genitals from birth, he would urinate from here. These veins and arteries appear clearly in the unborn, such as in abortions. But in developed bodies, their extremities have already dried up, though their roots remain. Therefore (according to the third book of *Theories*), a small branch arises from each of the two and both pierce into the body of the bladder until they reach the navel; this is to be found in the bodies of fetuses. In completed bodies, however, the part that tends to the navel is withdrawn. When, therefore, this wateriness—on account of the blockage and resistance to expulsion from higher parts—is expelled into these veins until, tending back, it reaches their openings and finds no suitable passage to the navel, they are dilated and opened much more than they were even before. From these, the wateriness then pours back into the space of the belly. This is shown by the fact that some dropsy patients have already emitted it through the navel.

<margin>The Manner of Tympanites</margin> The manner in which **tympanites** <note>bloating caused by gas</note> occurs is already partially explained. For when, from a depraved and windy digestion of the stomach and intestines, the fluid of the food passes through the mesaraic veins—and especially when the liver is hot—it resolves this into a smoky vapor. This vapor, indeed, breathes through the thin pores into the often-mentioned space. In this space, because of the density of the surrounding lateral walls, it can be held irresolvably, just as vaporous air is held under a vault. **Cassius Felix** <note>A 5th-century Latin medical writer.</note>, however, using a certain admirable figure of speech perhaps accepted from the air, says that tympanites happens to arise from a huge, inflating windiness of the lung. This type of dropsy also happens from a lesser cold than that which causes hyposarca or ascites, for it is necessary for heat to be present so that the cold matter may be resolved into smoky vapor.

<margin>Doubt</margin> But concerning the predicted things, a doubt happens to arise, since dropsy seems to be a common sickness like fever, since it was said before that it is appropriated to each thing it begins with, and it does not occur without the loss of the part itself, just as a fever of the heart. And especially since it is written in the sixth book of *Accidents*: "If phlegm dominates the whole body..."

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of dropsy, specifically debating which of its three forms—hyposarca, ascites, or tympanites—is the most dangerous or "malignant." It cites various authorities including Galen, Hippocrates, and Avicenna to weigh different clinical opinions.</meta>

<term>Hyposarca</term> <note>A form of dropsy characterized by generalized swelling of the underlying flesh rather than fluid in a specific cavity.</note> causes either a swelling in a single member or general edema. It therefore affects a specific member principally and, consequently, the whole body. It is thus a **common disease**. It must be said that although it has a determined member, it is nonetheless not diffused through the whole body in the same way as a fever, because it is not found in the bones; since bones are hard, they do not sustain stretching and thus [the swelling] does not truly appear there. This is according to the ninety-sixth <note>likely a reference to a specific section or "distinctio" in a medical textbook</note> [chapter], since dropsy seems to be the same as an appearance [of swelling]. Those parts that swell are the visible muscular parts; hence it was said by **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> that in dropsy, either all members clearly increase in the case of <term>hyposarca</term>, or the empty spaces increase in the other two species.

<margin>Bones are found [infected] in leprosy.</margin>

But what of **leprosy**? Since it is classified as a common disease, it must be said that bones are indeed infected in leprosy everywhere. 

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have placed <term>hyposarca</term> as the worst form. This is seen in the fourth book of the *Rules* <note>original: "re. a."</note> of Hippocrates, where he says there are two species of dropsy, of which this one called hyposarca is "striving to become inescapable, inseparable, and incurable." On this point, with various translations, **Galen** also corrects **Hippocrates**, saying: he did not say this with a [complete] reason—that is, "striving to become inescapable." Truly, he should have written it thus: "It soon infects the person when dropsy has been formed." Because I do not now follow the opinion of this one [Hippocrates] as it seems to sound on the surface, I say that Hippocrates and Galen, by "hyposarca," intended either a swelling or <term>cachexia</term> <note>original: "cachocimiā"; a state of severe weight loss and muscle wasting</note> throughout the whole body, inside and out, with such weakness of the power that, through coldness and obstruction, it happens that the <term>innate heat</term> <note>The vital heat believed to be the source of life and digestion.</note> is soon suffocated and extinguished.

Or perhaps it is verified—and this is observed rightly—if hyposarca, arising from an appearance in the liver or from any greater cause, proceeds toward **ascites** <note>fluid in the abdomen</note> or **tympanites** <note>gas bloating</note> rising from the flanks, loins, or spleen, and the cause of this is lesser. But if the causes are taken uniformly with the dispositions and qualities of the subjects, I would place <term>ascites</term> first as the worst, and <term>tympanites</term> second. This is also suggested by **Aristotle**. 

<margin>The Aggregator</margin>

And concerning <term>hyposarca</term>, which is very bad: this is according to the consideration of the causes making one fall into it. **Gariopontus** <note>original: "Garipetus," an 11th-century medical author</note>, the author of the *Passionarius* <note>A famous medieval medical compilation</note>, seems to place <term>tympanites</term> as the worst. For he says: "The most malignant dropsy of all is tympanites; second is hyposarca; third is ascites; and fourth is <term>leucophlegmatia</term> <note>a pale, phlegmatic swelling</note>, which is not malignant." This opinion also seems to be professed on the surface by the words of **Avicenna** <note>original: "Aū"</note> in the third book of the *Colliget*. But what will be shown regarding this fourth point? That his position cannot stand if the right reasoning of comparable things is observed, as will appear in the statement of truth.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that in the third [book], fourteenth [chapter], another way and order of "worseness" is placed, which seems most in accord with the truth. Indeed, it is reported by reciting the opinions of others on both sides with their motivations. There are some men to whom it seems that <term>hyposarca</term> is worse than the others, because the corruption in it communicates with the liver and all the veins of the body and the flesh, so that the power of digestion is mostly destroyed. And there are those among them to whom it seems that it is lighter than the others—even lighter than <term>tympanites</term>.

Next, he adds the truth: "Truly, it is more worthy that **ascites** be more malignant than all of them; then let **hyposarca** be some which is lighter than all, and let there be another form of it which is very bad." And this is according to the considerations of the causes falling into it. This same thing is proven by experiment and by the manifest disposition in most cases, which makes the experiment necessary: namely, that there are species of <term>hyposarca</term> that are lighter, but it is not necessary that the worst among them be worse than what is in those remaining [species]—namely, I say, <term>ascites</term> and <term>tympanites</term>. 

Thus, finally, the opinion on this stands: that <term>ascites</term> is the worst, then <term>tympanites</term>, then <term>hyposarca</term>—always observing and understanding the rule of comparison remains intact. In this opinion, **Avicenna** also perfectly agrees. For he says that when a bad, hot <term>complexion</term> <note>The balance of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) in an organ.</note> happens to the liver, exceeding only a little, then much bitterness is acquired. But when this bad hot complexion increases so that it exits its natural form, then the operation of the liver will be a non-natural operation; and that operation will come solely from heat in that which is "such heat," and not in that which is [simply] heat. Therefore, when heat of this kind finds an aqueous part, by steaming it out, it induces windiness; and from this comes <term>tympanic</term> dropsy or similar. But if the cause was the removal of natural heat, the hot sickness will be attributed to those removals of hot sickness, and if it was cold, it will be attributed to the cold. 

And for this reason, physicians labor much to give the cause of this species well, because it happens equally from heat as from cold. And therefore, this species is more difficult than the others to cure. But if anyone scrutinizes this subtly, he will find these things were said of <term>ascites</term> and not of <term>tympanites</term>, as is judged in sharp [arguments]. For he wants it that if water is pre-existing, and if heat flourishes so that windiness is generated from it, nonetheless, because the greatest part of the wateriness remains, it is more truly <term>ascites</term> than <term>tympanites</term>; he judged this by saying "or similar."

This is confirmed because he had touched above on the mode of production of <term>tympanites</term>, because it is no less from that; he says it occurs from heat just as from cold, since it is said that <term>tympanites</term> is not completed without heat. For <term>ascites</term> seems to be the matter and foundation of <term>tympanites</term>. In the *Viaticum* <note>A famous medical travel guide by Ibn al-Jazzar</note>, it is written that <term>hyposarca</term> is easy to cure. The cause of its ease is the goodness of the matter, and also its distribution over all the members of the body. For each member has only as much quantity of it as it can bear. 

But that this order of **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."</note> is to be observed as truer, let it be shown by reasons beyond experience. For dropsy [hydrops] is named for *hydor*, which is **water** <note>original: "aqua"</note>. When a name is imposed rationally, its significance is given by the one who imposes it. Since in <term>ascites</term> there is only water, the common name "dropsy" fits it primarily and as the most harmful. For by the definition of disease, there is a sensible injury to operations. Again, that dropsy is worse which is with worse causes and accidents; such a one is <term>ascites</term>. For it often arises from an appearance [of a tumor]. It is accompanied by fever and vehement thirst, and what is worse, by <term>syncope</term> <note>fainting</note> and sudden suffocation through the swelling of the **diaphragm** <note>original: "dyaflatis"</note> upward, narrowing the spiritual [breathing] organs. Or, according to the commentator, it is on account of the vapors.

...passing through, arriving in the lungs. According to that ancient saying: *A dropsical person, if they have a cough, is despaired of.* <note>original: "Ydropicȝ ſi tuſſim habeat deſpatus ẽ." A famous Aphorism of Hippocrates (V, 35).</note> Or, a cough occurring in a dropsical patient is an evil sign. Regarding <term>ascites</term>, **Etios** <note>likely Aëtius of Amida, a 6th-century Byzantine physician</note> says it happens principally from a failure of the **second digestion** <note>In Galenic medicine, the first digestion occurs in the stomach, the second in the liver (creating blood), and the third in the tissues.</note>, the work of which is to generate better [humors]. But a failure in this [second] digestion is worse than a failure in the first or third digestion. This is shown because the first digestion is easily corrected or sufficiently amended, since it is related to a more primary part than the digestion of other members; but the second cannot be so easily adapted, since it occurs in the members that are most apparent, in which there is no base or strength of nature; for they are lowly in respect to the principal organs. 

Furthermore, the matter of <term>ascites</term> passes through and arrives, generating in one place, since it is phlegmatic and heavier than the others. However, the matter of <term>hyposarca</term> <margin>Some say it is said in "On Coughing"</margin> is somewhat disseminated through the whole; and <term>tympanites</term> is not so quickly insoluble. Additionally, since that water is sharp and serous, it is made more so when agitated by hot and dry medicines; for it cannot be resolved and evacuated through the pores as easily as the matter of <term>hyposarca</term>, which approaches the skin from all sides. Nor is it as subtly resolvable as <term>tympanites</term>. Therefore, <term>ascites</term> is the worst; then <term>tympanites</term>, which is more related to it; and finally the least harmful is <term>hyposarca</term>. 

Regarding the fourth point of the first [argument], it must be said that you do not prove but rather accuse. For the reasoning of this opinion is destroyed. Either the causes of <term>hyposarca</term> will be justly compared to the causes of other dropsies, as **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."</note> indicates, or he uses the term <term>hyposarca</term> equivocally. To the other point, it must be said that although <term>hyposarca</term> is worse in its extent, it is not so in its intensity. Indeed, <term>ascites</term>, like an ephemeral [fever], is worse in extent than a quinsy or phrensy or a rupture of continuity in some great [vessel], but not in intensity. Or this reason, as seen according to the *Viaticum* <note>A famous medieval medical handbook by Ibn al-Jazzar, translated by Constantine the African.</note>, argues more for the opposite than for the proposal. 

To the next point, it must be said that this would be true if the failure occurred as much in the third digestion as in the second. But it is not so much, since it has already been moved through the second digestion. And the nutritive power has already operated there in its first operation. To the other, it must be said that although the matter of <term>hyposarca</term> is more distant from the places to which it is drawn, it is nevertheless of smaller quantity and aggregation than <term>ascites</term>. For it does not weigh down the [vital] virtue as has been said. And therefore, a stronger medicine can be applied to it. It can also be better led out through the pores in evaporations. 

Regarding the second question, it must be said that first, according to the authority of **Avicenna**, it already appears what must be judged by one considering it. To the other, it must be said that although it causes more harm to the **spirit** <note>The "pneuma" or vital force circulating in the body.</note> than other dropsies, that is nevertheless more easily remedied due to the subtlety and rarity of the subject. Just as an ephemeral fever is sweated out in the spirits compared to a humoral fever. To the next, it must be said that the mode of expurgating this "windiness" <note>gas in tympanites</note> is manifold; both by evacuating the matter which is its cause and from which the evaporation is produced, and because that which is resolved by its own subtlety through the pores of the body also obeys the powers of impression and dissolution more. Therefore, we do not see diseases of windiness as continuous as those of humors. 

To the argument of the opposing side, it must be said that it concludes the truth regarding <term>ascites</term> but not <term>hyposarca</term>; for although it obeys the agent within it, it is nevertheless aggregated and of great quantity in relation to the matter of <term>hyposarca</term>. It is also in places closer to the noble members, and thus more infestation. To the third question, it must be said that I grant the authorities and arguments showing that <term>ascites</term> is the worst. To the fourth point induced, it must be said that what was previously called the "fourth of the King" <note>likely a reference to the "Liber Regalis" or "Royal Book" of Haly Abbas</note> is not to be received simply. To the other, it must be said that <term>ascites</term> does not happen more often because it arrives with a proportion of particular [factors], but because it happens from more causes than the others. For it happens from heat, as said, as well as from cold, and from many other reaching causes. To the other, it must be said that although there is a medicine of this kind for drawing out wateriness, and it is near the places of evacuation, yet the matter is of great quantity, weighing down the virtue greatly. Thus, a medicine proportioned to it weakens the virtue and increases the evil complexion of the liver; for it cannot be resolved through the skin like the matter of <term>hyposarca</term> and <term>tympanites</term>, on account of its thickness and its disobedience to resolution. To the other, it must be said that that cure is wicked and done with despair, as even those handing it down assert. For it is not done unless other remedies are of minimal profit. Even when done, if the virtue is not strong, the patient does not escape. With a strong virtue, it is better to be cured by diet and potion.

Our nature is accustomed to reside and be quiet at night in most men. I say this according to those having the *Prognostics* <note>of Hippocrates</note>, as **Galen** says in the second [commentary] on the *Aphorisms* and **Oribasius**.

# Crisis

<margin>
Albumasar: The Sun is the source of the life of living things along with the Moon.

The Sun is the origin of vital virtue <note>original: "uirtutis uitalis"; the "vital virtue" or "vital force" was the power believed to sustain life and heat in the body.</note>, from the *Centiloquium*, leaf 80.
</margin>

...it is also worse at night. Furthermore, since a <term>crisis</term> <note>From the Greek *krisis*, meaning "judgment" or "turning point"; the moment a disease decides toward recovery or death.</note> is one of the more difficult actions of nature, the hour in which nature is stronger will produce a more praiseworthy crisis. This, moreover, is in the day, because then the greater luminary <note>The Sun.</note> is above the earth, whose power is manifest by day; for it comforts nature. For indeed, **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a famous Persian astrologer.</note> says that the Sun, after God, is the life of living things along with the Moon; in a word, the *Centiloquium* <note>A famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms, often attributed to Ptolemy in the Middle Ages.</note>, leaf 80, says the Sun is the origin of vital virtue. Several people explain this by citing the statement of **Aristotle** in the third book of *On the Soul*, saying that the intellect in men is such as the "father of men and gods" <note>A reference to Jupiter/Zeus, often used by Homer and quoted by Aristotle to describe the Sun's influence on human life.</note> leads in the day.

<margin>Homer.</margin>
This, then, was the opinion of **Homer** regarding the Jupiter of political matters.

<margin>Oppian</margin>
Therefore, a daytime crisis is more benign than a nighttime one. The opposite view is held because a crisis is better when the "accidents" <note>The symptoms or secondary effects of a disease.</note> are stronger in their own way. And for this reason, they say good crises occur in more vehement <term>paroxysms</term> <note>The period of greatest intensity in a fever or fit.</note>. But stronger accidents, as has been shown, occur at night.

<margin>Alexander.</margin>
Whence **Alexander** <note>likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a commentator on Aristotle</note> explains why pains intensify much more at night. At night, since the air is colder than in the day, the heat is not resolved and the virtue is not dissolved as it is in the day. For no matter how cold the air is in various regions, it must have a power to resolve. Thus, the virtue will then be stronger; and the more vigorous it is, the more perfect the crisis will be. Because of this, a nighttime crisis would be better than a daytime one.

<margin>
<gloss>Main point present</gloss>
What the term "Crisis" signifies
</margin>
Regarding the first point, it must be known that "crisis" in Greek signifies "judgment." For this name has been transferred to the matters of medicine. For it is proper to one who judges in a civil trial regarding death. For just as when one is judged to die, he is greatly disturbed, so too should an observer of common people see it. Oh, what fearful signs appear at the time of a crisis! It is as if nature exclaims that it is judging the life of the laborer <note>the patient</note>. It was not, however, that any of the physicians imposed this name on themselves; see the first book of *On Crises* and the third book. Whence in the fourth section: the intent of a crisis is a "separation in speeches," that is, in civil questions. For when judgment is given, then the altercation and the fight cease, and each of the litigants goes his own way.

<margin>Crisis is considered in two ways.</margin>
"Crisis," however, having been transferred to medicine, is named in many ways and with many strengths, as is found at the beginning of *On Crises*. It is usually taken in two ways: first, for the commotion preceding the crisis, such as when <term>cretic</term> <note>Signs indicating a coming crisis.</note> signs manifest. Second, for the sudden and almost instantaneous alteration properly called a crisis; this is the "apparent crisis" mentioned in the second section. Just as a judge’s sentence is swiftly pronounced, the "cretic movement" of the expulsion of matter follows; this is "crisis" in the improper sense. From this comes the opinion of the *Aphorisms*: A crisis is a sharp, that is, a swift report in a disease, leading either to health or to death.

<margin>What Crisis is according to Galen, 10th [book] of the Theory.</margin>
In the tenth book of the *Theory*, **Galen** says: a crisis is a swift change which happens to the sick person with difficulty of accidents, either toward the side of health or toward the side of sickness.

<margin>In how many ways Crisis is understood.</margin>
There are several modes of "crisis" when taken generally. For the *Aphorisms* and the third book of *Prognostics* set down four. For one is a certain swiftness toward health. Another is a sudden dissolution toward death. Another is a gradual "liquefaction" toward death, also called "consumption." In the third book of *Crises*, two others are added to these, differing by being combinations. First, where two things are joined and it turns toward health; hence the theory:

In the tenth book: this is a change that happens once into a better condition, and thereafter the disease gradually diminishes until it fails and the body is healed. Second, where two things are joined and it turns toward death. This is a change made once into a wicked condition, by which thereafter the virtue of the patient is gradually diminished until they are led to their end. These last two are called "composite crises."

<margin>The truest crisis:</margin>
The truer crisis, however, is that which turns swiftly to health or to death. And the "most proper" is that which immediately turns to health. For such a thing is called a crisis absolutely. That which goes quickly to death is not called a crisis simply, but with a qualifier, such as "a bad crisis"; as is said in the third book of *Crises*.

<margin>3rd condition</margin>
We say that the resolutions of illnesses with great struggle and sharp symptoms are especially called crises, which exist in the hot humors of fevers. For a crisis is said only to exist in a "material" illness. In "immaterial" ones, however, such as in <term>ephemeral</term> <note>A fever lasting only one day.</note> and <term>hectic</term> <note>A long-term wasting fever, here called "ethica."</note> fevers, there is no crisis properly speaking.

<margin>Diocles</margin>
However, **Diocles** <note>Diocles of Carystus, a 4th-century BC Greek physician.</note> posited that an ephemeral fever could have a crisis, which is said quite abusively <note>in the sense of "improper use of language"</note> for any resolution of illnesses, so that even a hectic fever and any illness whatsoever would be said to be "judged." For by the proper definition of a crisis, it should only be seen in an acute illness. It is of the essence of an acute illness to be dangerous and quickly terminable.

<margin>The most just crisis</margin>
Whence the opinion of the *Aphorisms*: Acute illnesses are great and dangerous, and they hasten quickly to their state. An ephemeral fever, though it terminates quickly, is not considered dangerous. A hectic fever, though dangerous, is slower.

<margin>
Note.
The 7 Conditions of a Good Crisis.
</margin>
Henceforth it should be known that by the definition of a "good crisis"—such as one judged on the seventh or fourteenth day—there are seven conditions.
<margin>1st.</margin>
First, that it be complete, so that no remnant of the illness remains.
<margin>2nd.</margin>
Second, certain, which is that it does not relapse.
<margin>3rd.</margin>
Third, safe, so that in the crisis itself it is not terrifying.
<margin>4th.</margin>
Fourth, manifest, such that clear signs or an apparent <term>subsidence</term> <note>The settling of waste in the urine, a sign of recovery.</note> precedes it.
<margin>5th.</margin>
Fifth, judged, such that it is preceded by "indicative days."
<margin>6th.</margin>
Sixth, that it turns toward the good.
<margin>7th.</margin>
Seventh, that it happens on a praiseworthy "critical day."

A bad crisis is known by the opposite of these. In the first book of *On Crises*, these six conditions <note>The author lists 7 above but refers to 6 here, a common discrepancy in medieval technical summaries.</note> are also applied to the *Aphorisms*. The first of these is that the crisis be through evacuation; for that which happens through an abscess is more praiseworthy. Second, that it evacuates the offending humor. Third, that it occurs according to the "rectitude" of the parts. Whence a flow of blood from the right nostril is praised in an abscess of the liver, and from the left for the spleen. The contrary is criticized in the second book of *Crises* and the second of *Prognostics*. Fourth, with a good consistency of the body. Fifth, with digestion preceding it. Sixth, on a critical day.

From these sayings, it is also clear that some illnesses are cured through a notable "expulsion" of matter. Others, however, through "resolution," or "dissolution," or "digestion." Just as in chronic illnesses, in which no crisis is observed; whence they undergo resolution gradually. This is especially true of those governed by the Sun, in which the movement of all things is slowed.

Properly "cretic" <note>capable of having a crisis</note> illnesses are of two kinds. Some are terminated by a manifest evacuation, such as a flow of blood through the nose, or through the menses, or hemorrhoids...

It establishes that a true crisis only occurs in acute, dangerous illnesses and requires specific signs like evacuation or digestion to ensure a safe recovery.</summary>

# Whether a Daytime Crisis is More Praiseworthy than a Nighttime One

...either by vomiting, or sputum <note>original: "sputo"; phlegm or saliva coughed up from the lungs</note>, or bowel movement, or urine, or sweat. Others, however, occur by an "apparent exit" <note>An visible expulsion of fluids</note>; and this kind is weaker than the others, since nature is not able to totally lead the matter out of the body, but instead transfers it to less noble parts by a kind of "demanding" <note>The text suggests nature "shunts" the disease to a safe area if it cannot expel it entirely</note>. It is like when a weak King 

<margin>A nosebleed is a more praiseworthy crisis.</margin>

expels enemies from his capital city <note>original: "metropoli sede"</note>, yet is unable to chase them out of his kingdom entirely. Regarding the rest of the crises, as is commonly said, the best is that which occurs through a flow of blood from the 
nostrils. For by a single expulsion, it casts out everything harmful. Next is that which occurs by bowel movement, because it leads out both thick and abundant matter. After that, the one by vomiting; then by urine; and lastly, by sweat—which perhaps is most praised in illnesses involving yellow bile <note>original: "colericis"</note>, especially when the matter exists outside the veins. And these [outlets] are indeed the 

ears, nostrils, palate, sputum, hemorrhoids, and menstruation. I also understand "goodness of crises" to refer to those which have the praiseworthy conditions mentioned before. And of this, there are not only signs of a crisis, but also its causes.

Certain things are only signs, such as a headache, shortness of breath <note>original: "disnia"; dyspnea</note>, vehement pain at the mouth of the stomach, a painful tension in the <term>hypochondria</term> <note>The upper part of the abdomen, just below the ribs; in medieval medicine, this was often where "vapors" or "humors" gathered.</note>, intense sleeplessness, delirium, a loss of voice, involuntary tears without any injury to the eyes, or a cracked lower lip. Other signs include seeing black things before the eyes, or flashes and lamps of another color, or the cheeks and nose suddenly becoming red. These are the primary preoccupations 

<margin>How "day" is understood.</margin>

and the particular concerns associated with the timing of crises and prognostics. "Day," however, is twofold: the **Artificial Day**, containing the presence of the sun above the earth (which is called the "bringing of the sun above it" in the sixth book of the *Topics*), and the **Natural Day**, which comprises the space of 24 equinoctial hours in which the night is joined with the day. This is the revolution of the "First Mover" <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the *Primum Mobile* was the outermost sphere of the heavens that moved all the others.</note> along with the distance the sun travels in the Zodiac by its own motion. Regarding the first point about crises: when I say "day," I mean the day and the night together. Here, however, "day" is understood as the artificial day. Know also that artificial days and nights vary. For some are "incidental," such as when the sun is in the first minute of **Aries** or **Libra**, which are called the equinoctial signs. This happens twice a year, around the middle of March and September. Other days are the longest and nights the shortest, such as when the sun is in the beginning of **Cancer**, and conversely in the beginning of **Capricorn**, which two signs are called "tropic" (that is, "turning" signs). When the sun moves in our climates from the beginning of Capricorn to the head of Cancer, the days continually increase; from there back to the head of Capricorn, they decrease. Under the line of the Equator, however, the night is always equal to the day.

<margin>According to the Master Philosopher <note>likely Aristotle</note></margin>

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have said a crisis is twofold: one in which the movement is from the center to the circumference <note>i.e., from the internal organs to the skin</note>, as in sweat; and in such a case, a daytime crisis is better than a nighttime one, since the air is warm, drawing [matter] outward and opening the pores. There is another in which the movement is from the circumference to the center, as in vomiting and bowel movements. And this is better in the night than in the day. But this is poorly argued, because a crisis by sweat is weaker in goodness than the others, as was said before. For nothing that is essentially [inferior] is improved above others by something accidental occurring to it. Such is the case with sweat in respect to a nosebleed or a bowel movement; therefore, it cannot be perfected or raised above the aforementioned evacuations by a mere accident of it occurring during the day. Nor is it entirely true that all evacuations other than sweat move from the center to the circumference.

---

<margin>According to the Master Principal</margin>

Regarding the third point, it should be known that in a given space of time, all other things being equal, a nighttime crisis is better than a daytime one. This is shown because when the movements of the illness and its symptoms become more vehement, the crisis is more perfect. But this happens at night, because of the intensity of nature’s occupation in "digesting" the matter. Furthermore, 

<margin>How is it sharper?</margin>

"united virtue is stronger than itself when dispersed." <note>A common medieval scholastic maxim: power is more effective when concentrated than when spread out.</note> Therefore, when the <term>virtue</term> <note>The "vital force" or "natural power" of the body to heal itself.</note> is more united, the crisis becomes better, since a good crisis is ruled by the strength of that virtue. In the night, it is strengthened by this unity. For the movements of the day, which disturb a daytime crisis, are calmed and rest, and conversely, they strengthen the nighttime one. Also, the <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; the subtle, invisible fluids believed to carry life and heat through the body.</note> withdraw to the interior at night, fleeing the darkness of the night so that they may return the actions of nature more strongly. For when nature intends to "judge" <note>original: "creticare"; to reach a crisis</note>, it hides and conceals itself in its center—the heart—which is more convenient; this prevents the operation from being hindered by the distracted wandering of the spirits. Also, in the night, the fluids <note>original: "huiditates"; humors</note> move more, provoking nature into the "fight." This is also indicated by the fact that more crises occur at night, relative to the amount of time, than in the day.

Furthermore, the following distinction says that a crisis is properly attributed to the Moon. Also, the consumption of illnesses that move by the course of the Sun is quieted by a gradual resolution; but the Moon has its power in the night, and it works more strongly toward a crisis then than in the day.

Therefore, a crisis will be more beneficial at night than in the day. Because of this, a doubt arises: why do more people (in proportion to the time) die at night than in the day, when it seems that the opposite should happen? For many 

<margin>Why more die at night than by day...</margin>

die from acute illnesses and fevers. Since these are hot and dry, the coldness and moisture of the night ought to temper them. Since the night is cold and moist, they should not die from them; whereas in the day, the illness should be sharpened and take hold because of the day's similarity to them, as the day is hot and dry.

It must be said that nature works harder at night in "digesting" the matter of the disease than in the day, concealing itself in its center with its **Natural Heat**. This is clear from what has been said. And the matter causing the illness increases the symptoms, so that if the humors making the illness are weak, they are besieged and surrounded in such a way that they cannot be spread out and dilated with their instrument <note>likely the "spirits" or "heat"</note> because of the obstruction, as they are in the day. For, as touched upon, nature is stimulated more sharply in the night. Hence, nights provide more signs regarding "frenzy" <note>original: "desipientiam"; mental wandering or delirium</note> than days. Nature will indeed be moved toward a crisis on the twenty-first day and not the twentieth, since the disease, deprived of its supports, is then stripped of its adversary's help. For this reason, the eighteenth is indicative and the twenty-first critical, and not the seventeenth and twentieth.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the timing of medical crises.
