# The 20th and 17th days are more critical and decisive than the 21st and 18th.

<margin>The way in which the crisis varies based on internal causes.</margin>
The timing can vary. For it is considered either by reason of its substance—regarding its quantity, quality, or position—or by reason of its motion. By "matter" <note>original: "materiam"; here referring to the infected bodily fluids or "humors" causing the disease</note> I mean, following the speech of physicians, a certain substance composed of accidental qualities. Indeed, these same accidents qualify the substance, which is also called "quality" by some.
<margin>How the substance of the humors behaves.</margin>
The substance of this matter is divided into four main categories: for some is subtle <note>thin or refined</note>, some is thick, some is light, and some is heavy; some is viscous, some is fragile or easily split; some is "rare" <note>low density</note>, some is dense or compact, or somewhere in the middle. If, therefore, several or all qualities of one combination come together in one part—such as choler <term>Choler: also known as yellow bile; associated with fire, heat, and dryness</term>—it is subtle, light, fragile, and rare; these will cause the crisis to arrive more quickly. Such conditions are more consistent with the twentieth day than the twenty-first. If, however, the opposite happens—where the matter is thick, heavy, viscous, and compact, such as a "malacia" <note>original: "malencia"; likely referring to a softening or morbid swelling</note>—the crisis will be delayed; thus it will arrive on the twenty-first day rather than the twentieth. But if the qualities are moderate, as in blood and phlegm, they will cause crises moderately proportioned to those mentioned. 

<margin>By reason of quality</margin>
If the matter is considered by reason of its quantity, then some will be much and some will be little. A great amount of matter causes the crisis to be delayed by itself, since much matter requires a long time and a strong "virtue" <term>Virtue: the body's innate healing power</term> for its digestion <note>original: "digestiōe"; the process of the body "cooking" or maturing the humors so they can be expelled</note>. Occasionally, however, it happens by accident that because of the quantity of the matter, the virtue is stimulated and forced to participate in a powerful crisis. If the matter is very little—so little that it does not cause harm to nature—it will be more easily split; yet, because it does not move unless stimulated, the crisis will be delayed. If the matter, despite its smallness, is sufficient to cause harm, nature will be stimulated toward a crisis and will strive to reach it more quickly. Thus, the twentieth day is more suitable for such a crisis.

<margin>By reason of quality</margin>
By reason of quality, the matter is diversified in two ways: either inherently or accidentally. Inherently, because some matter is hot and dry, while other matter is hot and moist. If it is hot and dry, like choler, it will irritate nature more quickly, stimulating it toward a crisis since its motion is hot. As stated in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals* <note>A work by Aristotle</note>: heat is highly mobile, and the dryness joined to it makes the heat sharper by whetting it. Indeed, dryness is like a file and a sharpening stone for heat. But if the matter is cold and dry, the coldness prohibits movement and the dryness thickens it, so that it will delay the movement of nature toward a crisis. Regarding the moderate qualities of matter, one must judge them to be moderate. Similarly, the matter is qualified accidentally by the illness, 
<margin>By reason of position</margin>
sex, habit, time, and region. 

In the fourth place, the crisis varies by the position or location of the matter. For when the matter is located in places that are either hot or cold, the matter contained within them will move toward a crisis more or less quickly, as noted in the *Prognostics* <note>likely referring to the *Prognostic* by Hippocrates</note>. It will be located either on the right side or the left. If it is on the right, the heat of the heart radiates more upon that part, aided also by the liver and the gallbladder; thus the sickness will terminate more quickly, becoming consistent with the twentieth day. On the left side, however, because the heat is less and opposing causes occur, the limit of the sickness will tend toward the twenty-first day as its proportional result. 

<margin>By reason of Motion</margin> 
By reason of motion: for it is either continuous and uniform, like continuous fevers, which are proportional; or it progresses through odd days or through the stimulation of the critical days. 

From the perspective of the "superior cause" <note>astrological influences</note>, the crisis varies in two ways. Either by reason of the planets to which the humors are appropriated and attributed, or by the disposition of a specific planet 
<margin>The disposition of the superior cause when it varies</margin>
such as the Moon, to which the other planets give their disposition, because she herself rules this lower world of generation and corruption. For she has a specific operation similar to the body she influences, as noted in the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms, historically attributed to Ptolemy</note>. 

The first of these is further divided into two: for a humor can be led toward the upper parts of the body in two ways. Either by reason of its quality and substance, or by a certain property unknown to us, from which the humor has gained its motion. Following the first way, it must be said that melancholy <term>Melancholy: black bile; associated with the earth, coldness, and dryness</term> is assigned to Saturn; and since he is cold and dry and slow in motion, melancholy is likewise thick, cold, and dry, and will move slowly toward a crisis. Phlegm is attributed to the Moon, and in a certain way to Venus. Blood is attributed to Jupiter, and choler primarily to Mars and the Sun. And because the motion of Mars is in a certain way disordered and sudden, choler will move more swiftly toward a crisis. If blood seems to move more quickly, it is in proportion to the motion of Jupiter. Or if phlegm moves more slowly with respect to the motion of the Moon, this happens due to the other causes already mentioned or yet to be mentioned. 

By reason of the "occult property" <note>a hidden or spiritual quality that cannot be explained by the four basic elements</note> which the humors have toward the superior bodies: choleric evacuations occur from every third day to every third day. Melancholy from every fourth to every fourth. Phlegm from day to day. Blood, however, is almost continuous <note>original: "dia. lxxxviii"; likely a reference to a specific medical aphorism or duration</note>. This is seen to happen mostly because of its quantity and its position near the internal parts of nature. 

Furthermore, it must be considered that crises vary according to the diversity of the celestial bodies. These bodies—especially the planets in which the power of the fixed stars is received—can vary in two ways: either by their relationship to the signs or to the "cardines" <note>the four pivotal points of the zodiac: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli</note> of the world; or by their epicycles, or by their conjunctions and aspects. For if it happens that a planet is in a "mobile" sign, it shows that nature will be obedient to the matter made for it and will reach a crisis more quickly. If it is in a "fixed" sign, the opposite occurs. In a "common" sign, one should judge it to be moderate. 

Regarding the cardines: when the matter is attributed to an "oriental" <note>eastern</note> planet, which also possesses power in that position disposed by the planet's virtue, it will receive maturation <note>original: "maturationem"; the ripening of a disease toward its resolution</note> more quickly. If it is an "occidental" <note>western</note> planet, the opposite occurs. Likewise, if it is attributed to a "septentrional" <note>northern</note> planet, since its vigor is impressed more directly upon us, it will have a swifter critical point than if it were assigned to a "meridional" <note>southern</note> planet, because of its distance from our zenith. 

Thirdly, the attribution of the matter is diversified by reason of the planet's epicycle. This occurs according to its station, direction, and retrogradation. And it is no wonder that if the planet is "direct," then its motion...

<margin>The aspect and return of the motion of the crisis is twofold and fourfold.</margin>
...velocity. It will quickly incite the matter assigned to it toward the crisis. If, however, it is retrograde <note>original: "retrogradus"; appearing to move backward in the sky</note>, the outcome changes. If it is stationary, it depends on whether that stationing leads toward direct or retrograde motion. Fourthly, the movement of the matter also varies according to the positions and **aspects** <note>The angular relationship between planets, such as 90 or 180 degrees</note> of the planets. For if the Moon happens to be applying to a slow, cold, and unfortunate planet—such as **Saturn**—at the time of a future crisis, it will happen that the crisis is delayed and becomes restricted, unless the quality of the disease’s matter is tempered by a planet of the opposite quality. This is noted in the *Centiloquium* <note>A famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note> and the third book on critical days. If, however, the Moon joins a hot planet that speeds up motion, such as the **Sun** or **Mars**, the matter of the illness is rendered more mobile and will reach the crisis more quickly.

The motion of the matter is also rendered diverse because of the **aspects**, of which there are also four: **quartile** <note>90 degrees</note>, **trine** <note>120 degrees</note>, **sextile** <note>60 degrees</note>, and **opposition** <note>180 degrees</note>, as shown in diagram 168. Of these aspects, some strengthen nature <note>the patient's internal healing power</note>, while others drive out the disease. The first kind are primarily the **trine**, which is an aspect of perfect friendship and goodwill, and the **sextile**, though it is only moderate. For when the Moon looks upon the place of the future crisis and the beginning of the illness with these aspects, it strengthens nature in the middle of the period, just like well-rested guards who are sufficiently strengthened for a fight. The other two aspects—**opposition** and **quartile**—have the power to exterminate the disease by reason of their enmity, combat, and contrariety. The quartile, though moderate, overcomes the matter through this contrariety in a "good" crisis, such as is most common on the twentieth or twenty-first day, leading it toward evacuation. However, these aspects cannot be maintained without harm unless one observes the Moon's entry into the circuit of the zodiac. This must be especially noted, since even in the third book on critical days, the **motion of the Moon**
<margin>The motion of the Moon is most choice.</margin>
works more toward the crisis than the disposition or indisposition of the matter itself. These aspects are also considered according to the Moon's motion from point to point in the circle, and not just the reception of its light, although that can also intervene at times.

From the perspective of a planet such as the Moon, the operation of the higher bodies upon these lower ones occurs through motion and light. Motion, for our present purposes, is found to be of two types: **simple** and **composite**. Simple motion is further divided into three types. One is that by which the Moon moves from one point of the zodiac and returns to the same point; this motion constitutes the month
<margin>The Month of Peragration</margin>
of **peragration** <term>Peragration: The time it takes the Moon to complete one full circuit of the zodiac, roughly 27.3 days</term> (or "proper impression" according to Galen). This is completed in a space of 27 days and approximately eight hours—specifically, seven hours and a third of an hour. In the *Almagest* <note>Ptolemy's foundational 2nd-century work on astronomy</note>, this motion is properly called the "course of longitude." it arises because the center of the Moon’s **epicycle** <term>Epicycle: A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in ancient astronomy to explain planetary orbits</term> moves 13 degrees and 14 minutes every day (or 11 minutes due to the motion of the *Genzahar* <note>The "Dragon," a term for the lunar nodes where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic</note>, the head and tail of the dragon, which is opposite the surface of the eccentric deferent).

There is also another simple motion, which **Ptolemy** calls the "course of diversity" <note>anomalistic motion</note>; this is the motion by which the Moon moves every day by 13 degrees and [certain] minutes. This motion is accelerated, as mentioned before, when the Moon is in the opposite of the "augis" <note>apogee</note> of the epicycle—that is, in the place closest to the Earth <note>perigee</note>. Then it is said to be swift or fast in its course, and

-> When the Moon is fast and when it is slow <-

<margin>Motion of the Moon</margin>
its motion is from west to east. But when it is in the upper part of the epicycle toward the apogee, the aforementioned motion is slowed, and thus it is called "slow in course." This is the opposite of the other five planets; for when they are in these two locations of their epicycles, they are called "fast and direct" near the apogee, but near the opposite <note>perigee</note> they are called "slow and retrograde." In the middle positions, they are "stationary"—except for the Sun, which lacks an epicycle. Therefore, when these two motions (longitude and diversity) concur in the same direction from west to east—contrary to the first motion—the Moon’s velocity is such that it travels about 15 degrees of the zodiac in a natural day. Thus, in six days, it will traverse one quarter <note>90 degrees</note> of the zodiac. According to this, the Moon will move toward a **good crisis** in six days. Because of this, it sometimes happens that the crisis of the fourteenth day is laudably shortened to the thirteenth, or the seventh to the sixth.

If, however, the two aforementioned motions disagree in opposite directions—namely, when the motion of diversity is opposite the motion of longitude from east to west—it happens that the total motion of the Moon from west to east in the zodiac is found to be less than 12 degrees in a natural day. According to this, it will happen that the Moon will traverse one quarter
<margin>If it is not fast</margin>

However, the first manner signifies an external event. This assumes a diligent calculation of the hour of the Moon’s velocity and its joined-opposite slowness.

If it happens that the Moon is found to be in a medium state between fast and slow—or a mixture of both—traveling at 13 degrees and some minutes per day, it will then traverse one quarter in about seven days. Thus, the crisis occurs on the seventh day, which is the most common occurrence, as appears here from the calculations of **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Abraaz Euenare"; a famous 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer</note> regarding the Moon's motion. For this reason, **Galen** and many other physicians, not distinguishing the Moon's motion in this way but speaking simply and confusedly as if it were uniform in their crises, happen to err completely. Perhaps Galen did not see this because in his time, the motions had not yet been perfectly discovered. Therefore, he is least to be blamed, especially since he was a physician, and an astrologer only rarely. Those who came after him are more to blame.

There is also a third mode of the simple motions already mentioned, which is called "common" or "impression" by Galen. This is because the Moon, being at such a distance from the Sun, can impress the light received from it upon these lower things to give them life. This motion is established as follows: they subtract from the month of conjunction <note>the synodic month, approx. 29.5 days</note> the three days before and after the conjunction with the Sun, which is the time of the Moon's occultation <note>disappearance</note> and weakness when deprived of light. That which remains is 26 and a half days.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how the Moon’s cycle dictates the timing of medical "crises"—the decisive turning points in an illness. ### Year 20 and 17 days; the 21st and 28th days become more critical and indicative.

---

<margin>The lunar month</margin>
Regarding the aforementioned conjunctions <note>The alignment of the Moon and Sun</note>. Which, in the number of 28 natural days with a half, is measured. And this is also called the **lunar month** by its common name. Although calculators say one is 30 days and the other is only 29 for the sake of easier calculation. And this indeed arises from the addition of two days and four hours beyond the previously mentioned month in which the Moon reaches the Sun. For it does not find the Sun in the place where it left it, but the Sun has already advanced by almost one zodiacal sign. And yet, this month does not distinguish the **aspects** <note>The angular relationships between the Moon and other planets</note>, nor does it fix the limit of brief illnesses running according to the Moon, since it happens that the Moon sometimes circles the same part of the zodiac twice in this month. The third kind is a composite one which, according to the conception <note>original: "fantasia"; here meaning a theoretical model</note> of **Galen**, is made from the "month of transit"—or the "proper impression"—and the month of "common bringing-in." For these two months are joined together, and from them results a total of 54 days and 20 hours. The half of this is 27 days and 10 hours <note>The OCR reads "l̄ıı. xxu. dıes & uıgıtıduę hore," but the math for a half-month refers to 27 days and 10 hours</note>. And this is what is called the **medicinal month** by Galen.

<margin>The medicinal month</margin>
Which indeed he [Galen] divided into weeks, establishing each one from six days, seventeen hours, and a half. Half of a week consists of three days, eight hours, a half, and a quarter of an hour. A single day is 23 hours and 1/14th of an hour. And according to this, two weeks are found to end in 13 days and 11 hours. Three weeks, however, end in 20 days and 4.5 hours. This was Galen’s conception so that he might show that three weeks are terminated in a space of 20 days and not 21 days at all. Yet he could not be precise in this, even if he labored greatly to find it, since four hours according to his computation extend beyond the 20th day with a half, so that on the 8th day there are 18 hours remaining, and on the 12th day, 27 hours. But for the sake of truth, it should be known that Galen’s mode of
<margin>3rd principle</margin> speaking—already handed down—namely the composition of the so-called medicinal month from the "month of common impression" and the "proper month," cannot stand, since this month is diminished from the true lunar motion of transit, which is the more powerful cause in a **crisis**. Also, according to him, it does not preserve the full degrees of the aspects by which the illness is judged. Furthermore, it is neither a universal method nor is it necessary in illnesses that are terminated before the 14th day, since time is not repeated in them. Or perhaps he would answer that it only applies to the indicative and critical days extending beyond the 14th. Again, it often happens—indeed almost always—that in an illness terminated before the 25th day, there will be no "month of common impression and proper impression" in any way. What most troubles Galen and breaks his composition is that if someone happens to fall ill 8, 4, or 6 days before the conjunction of the Sun and Moon, and the illness extends into the 7th day and beyond, or even if they begin to fall ill at the conjunction and it extends forward, then the "months of common impression" will fail. In the beginning and in the middle, the medicinal month will remain ill-disposed and useless, with its other corresponding part failing. Because of this, there would be a time in which the illness is not governed by the motion of the Moon. Similarly, Galen, wishing to
terminate the 20th day by reason, with such a changeable fraction of about four and a half hours, passed into that which is very close to a day; it contains a sensible part beyond the sixth part, so that the crisis of the 12th day has 27 hours remaining. Still, his statement can be criticized because the variations of motion—namely speed and slowness—are minimally articulated. A.</margin> method he approves within, saying that to add a little to this, as the sixth did, is a transgression. Or rather, this kind of computation and the assignment of the causes of critical days is a transgression because the physician produces it from his own art, when it is rather a matter for the **astrologer** <margin>Conclusion of Aristotle</margin> to consider along with the natural philosopher. But surely, many and greater inconveniences follow this method and Galen’s statement, both because it keeps the aspects less unharmed and because three weeks would end in only 19 days and 21 hours, and not in 20 complete days. Furthermore, it would often happen that there would be an illness governed by no motion of the moon or lunar month, as if introduced by Galen. <margin>3rd principle</margin> Regarding the third thing to be known: with a certain reverence for the elders, this third way of speaking should be chosen instead: so that the motion or month of the Moon’s "proper impression" remains uncorrupted, just as the astrologers believe. In this way, they remain unharmed. And the common limit is held more between the 20th and 21st day, since three weeks thus end at the 20th day and a half. This limit, in its extreme part, is more suited to the crisis, which is the preceding commotion. Because of this, one must not insist too strictly on these terminations, as if the crisis always follows exactly at the completion of the Moon's motion; for it can come earlier or be postponed due to the disposition or indisposition of the matter <note>the bodily humors</note> toward the aforementioned motion, especially in illnesses whose motion is made slowly beyond 14 days. For he says: "around the 20th," "around the 24th," "around the 40th." Because of the length, it happens that in these illnesses which are prolonged, not only in a space of 12 hours or 7.5 hours—in which the discrepancies of the medicinal month and impression are seen—but certainly and often by two or three days, the crisis...

# Whether a universal crisis is stronger on the 14th or the 14th or the 7th day

<margin>6th main point</margin>
From the beginning of the illness up to the very midpoint. The midpoint is the 7th and the 14th, but not the 11th. Although the 14th is closer <note>original: "propinquior"</note> to the beginning of the disease <note>The author likely means the 14th represents a more complete cycle of the humors</note>, the 7th is stronger than the 4th because the matter <note>The "matter" refers to the diseased humors causing the illness</note> is then more mobile. At that time, the moon is already in the beginning of its **quadrature** <note>A 90-degree angle from its starting point, considered a point of tension in medical astrology</note> and not just in the first stage, as happens on the 4th day. Furthermore, that which can achieve more is stronger than that which can achieve less; the 14th day can achieve more, for it brings the most illnesses to a crisis, being called the "absolute critical day." In it also, more types of matter come together for <margin>7th main point</margin> judgment. **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire</note> says: acute illnesses are moved by the motion of the moon, just as chronic ones are moved by the motion of the sun. This is seen in the 4th, the 3rd, and the "hundred-word" <note>original: "centiloquio," likely referring to the *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note> works. But on the 14th day, when the moon has passed through two quadratures, it is in the aspect of **opposition** <note>180 degrees from its starting position; the Full Moon phase</note> from the place where it was at the onset of the disease. This aspect is associated with enmity and battle. On the 7th day, however, when it has traveled through only one quadrature, it reaches an aspect of moderate enmity and contrariety. But where the battle is stronger, a more intense victory is expected. Likewise, however, the 7th is stronger than the 14th because it is closer to the beginning of the illness; thus the 27th is stronger than the 34th, and the 34th than the 40th. This is not said based on the reason of the lunar aspects, as was shown to happen previously. Therefore, the crisis of the 14th is more vigorous than that of the 7th. <margin>Opposition</margin> However, the opposite of this is commonly held. Which is also shown by reason: for the fourth book of *Aphorisms* says that those things which are judged on even days are difficult and prone to troublesome returns <note>original: "amice quersionis," likely referring to a relapse or 'reversion' of the disease</note>. The 7th is an odd day, but the 14th is even. <margin>Note</margin> Likewise, they say a crisis occurs in a more "vehement" <note>Powerful or intense</note> state, but this vehemence is found more in the 7th than in the 14th, because odd days are stronger than even ones. As stated before: in the fourth [book], one must especially fear the odd number, because these days cause sudden changes for those laboring under sickness. Wherefore in the third [book] of *Critical Days*: a crisis happens mostly in acute illnesses on odd days, but in chronic ones on even days. Furthermore, a crisis happens especially by the course of the moon through the signs [of the zodiac]. Its action is grand in a crisis. On the 7th day, every contrariety intervenes, since the moon (as was said) reaches the beginning of the following quadrature, where opposition is found in two qualities. Just as if it were at the beginning of Aries (hot and dry) when the illness began: when it reaches the end of the 7th day, it has run to the start of Cancer (cold and moist). But at the term of the opposite <note>the 14th day</note>, it will reach Libra (hot and moist), which agrees with Aries in its active quality, namely heat. Therefore, the 7th is stronger in bringing a crisis than the 14th.

<margin>1st principal point</margin>
Regarding the first point, one must know what a crisis is, what a day is, and what a critical day is; these were shown in the <margin>2nd principal point</margin> immediately preceding sections. Regarding the second point, it must be known that some have said the crisis of the 7th would be stronger. This is because in it is the **tertian** <note>A fever that peaks every 48 hours, or every 3rd day by inclusive counting</note> fever, which receives a strong crisis due to its vehement motion. And because in the 7th, it is at its most powerful. Other matters, both simple and <margin>Instance/Example</margin> mixed, make for a stronger crisis on the 14th. But this discourse is rendered suspect and poorly articulated <note>original: "articulato"</note> because the **intermittent tertian** <note>A malaria-like fever where the fever comes and goes</note>, such as that which is called the "true tertian," makes its crisis on the 14th day and not on the 7th. Whence **Hippocrates** <note>The text uses "Y." for Ypocras/Hippocrates</note> says: the true tertian is judged at its longest in seven periods; but seven periods lead to 14 days. This is because as much as a continuous fever acts in one day, an intermittent one acts in one period. Furthermore, blood-related fevers, whose crisis is vehement, terminate on the 7th, not a little later. Again, **Avicenna** <note>The text uses "A." for Avicenna, the Persian polymath</note> simply preferred the 7th to be stronger in crisis than the 14th. Some, however, preferred the 14th to be stronger because the moon is seen in the aspect of opposition to the place of the illness's beginning. But what should be said of this <margin>Main principal point</margin> will appear from what is to be said. Regarding the third point, it must first be known that the crisis of the 7th is stronger than that of the 14th. And then the variety of the <margin>A crisis is called "stronger" in two ways.</margin> critical days should be observed. Regarding the first of these, it must be known that we can understand "stronger crisis" in two ways: [first] as a crisis emerging more often on such a day, so that it is called "stronger" because it can do more; and thus perhaps the crisis of the 14th is stronger than the 7th, since it occurs more frequently in it—especially in temperate or colder regions, and in bodies enjoying leisure and abundant food, such as many bodies are today. For natural forces, compared with the "culinary art" <note>The art of cooking or preparing rich foods</note> that devises delight, do not suffice for the present time. Also, the 14th is a middle time in which hot matters are brought to rest with cold ones. This interpretation I do not <margin>2nd way a crisis is called stronger</margin> accept much. But more properly, a crisis is called "stronger" because the six conditions of a perfect crisis—true and complete—are found in it more than in any other. Whence in the first [book] of *Critical Days*: We have seen the crisis happen many times on the 7th, and it was complete, certain, safe, manifest, <margin>$\P$</margin> judged, and changed toward the favorable. And after certain things, he <margin>Not from Girolamo but the opposite</margin> adds: Therefore I said that the 7th is the day that precedes all others. <margin>I doubt the previous [argument] on critical days</margin> And I do not mean this because it is the preceding day in number, nor in the sequence of the order of days. Rather, I mean it because it is the preceding day in **virtue and nobility**; for in it, illnesses are ended with a perfect, certain, laudable, safe, manifest, and judged consumption [of the disease]. And also in the 6th day illnesses are ended, but not as in the 7th; for the 7th is like a King who is indulgent to those he overcomes, while the 6th is like a tyrant rejoicing in the shedding of blood. <margin>$\P$</margin> This preference for the 7th is also recorded in the second <margin>Note that it is not in the flow of blood...</margin> book: The strongest of the days of crisis is the 7th, and the 4th is its indicator. Whence in the 10th [book] of *Theories*: The 7th day is to be preferred above all, and after it the 14th. Furthermore, **Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician and philosopher</note> in the 4th [book] of *Fevers*: We say the 7th and the 14th are the most laudable and certain of days. <margin>3rd Theory</margin> <margin>Isaac, 4th of Fevers</margin> **Avicenna** <note>Marked as ".A."</note> says: The 7th day is a very strong day, and the 4th indicates it. And although the 7th is placed in the superior first <margin>.A.</margin> rank, he further shows by reason that a crisis is stronger <margin>The 2nd of these days is proved by reasons</margin> in which those things required for the strength of a crisis are found beforehand. The 7th day is ultimately hailed as the "King" of critical days due to its association with "noble" and safe resolutions of disease, whereas the 14th is noted for its frequency in modern, well-fed populations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical investigation into the "critical days" of an illness. <margin>The critical days are varied in many ways, according to many authorities.</margin>

This is shown because in that day the power <note>original: "uirtus"</note> is stronger, as is commonly said, since the duration of the disease does not lie exhausted as it does on the 14th day. The matter <note>The "matter" refers to the diseased humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, or black bile—causing the illness.</note> which is moved on the 7th is also greater, hotter, sharper, and more mobile. And the 7th day is closer to the beginning of the sickness than the 14th. For the further the crises are extended from the start of the sickness, the more the powers are weakened by the 14th, as happens in a long illness. This is shown so that a crisis might occur by extension on the 11th or 12th day. The more it is extended, the more the judgment <note>A "judgment" or *iudicium* is the physician's determination of the crisis's outcome.</note> is weakened. 

The influence of the moon is also stronger then, which occurs in two signs that are many times opposed to each other. Or it happens only in one quality, being stronger in the active ones and exiting the passive ones in opposition; for example, **Aries** is opposed to **Cancer** in two qualities. **Taurus** to **Leo** in the active qualities. **Gemini** to **Virgo** in both. But when the moon is in the beginning of the third quadrature <note>A 90-degree angle from the moon's starting position at the onset of illness.</note>, as at the end of the 14th day, there is no opposition of signs except in single qualities, such as the passive ones. For example, **Aries** and **Libra** only arise in the dry and the humid, since both are hot. **Taurus** similarly is opposed to **Scorpio** in passive qualities, but agrees in the active, for both are cold. And it is the same for **Gemini** with **Sagittarius**, and in the others in the same way. 

There is also in the 7th day a quartile aspect <note>An astrological aspect of 90 degrees, often considered difficult or tense in medical prognosis.</note> which is in the middle of enmity and contrariety. But on the 14th day there is the aspect of opposition, which is considered stronger than the quartile, since it represents perfect enmity and combat; for that reason, the crisis of the 14th day ought to be stronger than that of the 7th. But the specific property of the signs found on the 7th, but not in the same way on the 14th—viewed perhaps with the quartile aspect—conquers the aspect of opposition, besides other factors on the part of particular nature and the matter considered. These things are what fortify the crisis on the day it occurs.

Again, that crisis is stronger which more vehemently and for more types of matter terminates and cuts off the sicknesses, as is apparent from what has been said. Of this sort is the 7th day; for tertian fevers, quotidians, and burning fevers <note>original: "caufones," referring to *causus*, a high-intensity "burning" fever.</note> are terminated on it, since the motion is then sharpened, but not on the 14th. Similarly, several intermittent fevers often grow quiet in four paroxysms <note>A sudden attack or increase in symptoms.</note> which occur on the 7th day. Also, a sanguine fever <note>A fever caused by an excess of the blood humor.</note>, when it turns the subtle matter into yellow bile and the gross matter into melancholy, will move on the 7th, since bile is agitated on the third. The quartan fever <note>A fever that returns every four days, associated with black bile.</note> also agitates on the 7th, but not on the 14th, but rather on the 13th. Cold matters are also mixed with hot ones, terminating before the 7th, which, once the cold is dulled, reach a crisis on the 7th. Therefore, one may conclude [the superiority of the 7th] over the crisis of the 14th. 

Regarding the second part of this science, it should be known that the critical days seem to be varied in four ways: first, by reason of the frequency or rarity of their occurrence; second, by what is predicted in them; third, by the quality—

<margin>Days also according to orders / 21 orders</margin>
<margin>of this [it] seems to be / judged / [unclear] / [unclear]</margin>

***

<margin>3. 31. [unclear] / 4. orders</margin>
<margin>Days on which almost no crisis occurs.</margin>
<margin>Days on which a crisis is rare.</margin>

—of their goodness. First, because there are days in which a crisis frequently occurs and which are in the **first order**, such as the 7th and the 14th. Some are in the **second order**, such as the 19th and 21st. Others in the **third**, like the 4th, 17th, and 27th. In the **fourth** are those such as the 9th and 18th. There are none in which a crisis *never* occurs, but in the first "critical" group, on the 12th and 6th days, I have not seen anyone to whom a crisis ever arrived. In some days, it happens but rarely. And this is similarly described in four ways: in the first order is the 12th and 6th. In the second, the 8th. In the third, the 16th. In the fourth, the 19th, according to **Haliabas** <note>Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi, a 10th-century Persian physician.</note>. 

But **Galen** would order them otherwise; for he would put forward the 12th and 16th, and not the 6th or 8th. The middle of all these in frequency and rarity is the 13th, 17th, 24th, and 27th. Hence, regarding the second order of critical days, some hold a superior rank, like the 7th; then the 11th, 14th, 17th, and 20th. Some are "falling in the middle" <note>original: "intercedentes in medio"</note>, like the 8th, 5th, 6th, 13th, and 4th. The 19th and 15th contain four. For on the 3rd and 5th, a crisis does not occur by reason of the moon's motion, but rather because of the 4th. Sometimes a crisis happens on the 3rd or 5th not because of the lunar revolutions, but because a crisis prepared to happen on the 4th day comes early and happens on the 3rd due to the severity of the sickness, or because nature relaxes and does not refine anything on the 4th. For which reason it pauses, then moves on the 5th day. There are also days that are "least critical," which are neither in the first nor second tension: the 10th, 12th, and 19th. 

Regarding the future that is predicted in them: the 4th is the first **indicative day**, announcing health on the 7th if praiseworthy signs preceded it; but if the opposite, it announces death. The 7th indicates a crisis on the 11th, the 14th on the 17th, and the 17th on the 20th. According to the saying: *The seventh manifesteth the fourth.* <note>A medical rule of thumb: the 4th day gives the signs that will be fulfilled on the 7th.</note> 

Regarding the goodness or malice of the crisis: some excel the others in goodness, such as the 7th, which stands as the leader over all. After it the 14th, after which is placed the 11th, and the 20th is located below these; after that the 17th, then the 14th <note>The author repeats the 14th here, possibly referring to a different cycle.</note>, then the 21st, after all of which is placed the 13th. The days in which a bad crisis occurs are the 6th, 8th, 12th, 10th, 16th, and 18th. According to **A** <note>likely Aristotle or Avicenna</note>: The best are the 7th and 14th, after which are the 11th, 17th, and 21st; then the 14th, then the 9th, then the 13th. 

Regarding their strength and weakness: some are calculated by four-day periods, such as the 7th, 4th, 11th, 14th, 17th, and 20th. This extension continues until it reaches the 40th. The four-day cycles are less significant after the 20th; after the 20th, strength is found in the seven-day cycles, like the 27th and 34th, then the 40th. # Whether the Crisis comes. Let it be stronger from the seventh day.

...twenties into the hundred and twentieth. And thereafter the calculation <note>original: "protatio," likely meaning the progression or count of days</note> does not run by days but by months and years. In the thirty-third [and] thirty-fourth [calculation] however, the hundred and twentieth day is counted.

<margin>An error of the infinite [or end] impedes the crisis.</margin>

Know also that there are some days within the twentieth in which the sickness is soon dissolved, and others in which it is later. The first [group] are indeed like the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 9th, 11th, 14th, 18th, and 20th. But in the other [group] are the 8th, 10th, 12th, 16th, and 19th. The 13th belongs to the extremes of the first [group] or the second somehow. The 1st and 2nd are left out as being improperly critical. But in the error of the scribe, it is a wonder why the 15th is omitted, since it is critical or is heard as the middle of these altogether. If, however, the aforesaid things ought to be verified, it is necessary to incur no error in the laboring.

<margin>...as seen in the second [book] of Platearius <note>Johannes Platearius, a 12th-century physician of the Salernitan school.</note></margin>

Concerning the aforesaid, it happens to be doubted concerning the 4th day, because it is placed among the days in which a crisis will often occur. Where the third [book] of *Crises* and the fourth [book] prioritize it, <term>synocha</term> <note>A type of continuous fever thought to be caused by a corruption of the blood.</note> many times produces a crisis on the 4th. The opposite of this is expressed in the third [book] of *Crises* with the forty-second [chapter?]. <margin>Archigenes; Galen in whichever [book]</margin> Archigenes <note>A Greek physician of the 1st/2nd century AD.</note> professes that he saw a crisis occur on the 4th only twice in his whole life. I, however, until now, have seen it once. 

<margin>Synocha: continuous, concluded.</margin>

It must be understood that sicknesses are twofold. For some are "continuous concluded," as they call a synocha. And because such [fevers] do not sharpen by <term>exacerbation</term> <note>The periodic worsening of symptoms.</note> but are entirely at their peak <note>original: "potissima"</note>, and on the 4th they receive a benefit from the moon, many of them reach their crisis on that day. There are others, either continuous or intermittent, incited on the 3rd day, and these only very rarely make a crisis on the 4th, since they are not then at their peak or are not incited in full. For a <term>crisis</term> <note>The decisive "turning point" of a disease.</note>, as has been said, must coincide with a more vehement peak. 

<margin>Note that on the 6th a wicked Crisis occurs.</margin>

It should also be noted that on the 6th day a crisis occurs which is for the most part "wicked" <note>original: "praua," meaning a crisis that indicates a bad outcome or a deceptive recovery.</note>, since this day is compared by Galen to a **tyrant**, just as the 7th is compared to a **king**. It happens either because the moon, swift in its course, reaches the end of its quadrant in the space of six days, or because the movement of the illness proceeds equally so that the hour of the <term>period</term> <note>The scheduled return of a paroxysm in a fever.</note> falls more on the 6th day; not indeed so on the 2nd and 4th, because the strength <note>original: "uirtus"</note> is still strong. Or it may be by participating in the power of the 7th day, when the peak has been [reached], or because nature, being irritated, anticipates [the 7th], or some external error stimulates it. It is nevertheless a crisis for health, just as the 7th is for death, although it follows it more rarely with a perfect outcome.

<margin>To the reason...</margin>

Concerning the 4th indeed, to the first [point] to be said, it was brought forward by Isaac [Judaeus] by way of opposition, where he says, solving it, that although these [even days] are consistent with the natural critical day, even days are accidental to it. For if the crisis is on the 14th—where a crisis will also be computed—it is because the fulfillment of the action shows itself in that day. Similarly in the third [book], 

<margin>According to the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in...</margin>

nature begins its operation in the [third] and finishes it in the 4th. And this is confirmed because a movement takes its name and species from the end to which it tends, as in the fifth [book] of the *Physics* and the second of *On the Soul*: "it is just for everything to be named from its end." For the outcome proves the acts, since it is the cause of causes. Thus, therefore, regarding the 10th: there is not so much vigor of judgment by itself [on that day] but through another, say through the 13th. Whence he adds: the ancients well ordained the critical days, because when they saw an even day was not critical by the "astonishment" <note>Likely "constitution" or "disposition"</note> of nature, but accidentally by the appearance of its operation being completed in it, they sought for the odd [day] and said it was more worthy than the even. 

<margin>ISAAC.</margin>

Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus (c. 832–932), a hugely influential Jewish physician and philosopher.</note> therefore wants odd days to be critical **by themselves** (*per se*), but even days to be so **by accident** (*per accidens*). This he took from the authority of Hippocrates, which he premised: that odd [numbers] are stronger than even. For he felt the odd to be stronger than the even because the odd contains both odd and even within itself. He says Hippocrates showed this in the aforesaid authority. 

<margin>Pythagorean.</margin>

Or he [Isaac] agreed with the Pythagoreans, who wanted the odd to obtain the nature of the **masculine** and of **form**, to which belongs action; but the even to be **feminine** and of **matter**, to which belongs passion <note>In this context, "passion" means being acted upon.</note>. But this saying of Isaac's is seen to suffer no small calumny <note>criticism or objection</note>; for as it appeared, in a crisis there concur both this inferior nature which rules with matter, and the superior circuit, specifically the moon. Now on the 2nd day, since the strength is stronger, it causes a stronger crisis; this indeed happens on the 4th and the 14th. It can often happen to the "queen" <note>The ruling power of the body or perhaps the Moon</note> when a suitable [regimen] is applied. The matter also is for the most part much, agitable, and hot, especially on the 4th. There are also twin or "gelid" sicknesses whose matters move uniformly without sharpening, so they are no more exacerbated on an even day than an odd, such as a "sanguine" fever. Because the moon on the 14th day is in the aspect of opposition, it results in a stronger "criticization" <note>The process of reaching a crisis.</note>. On the 4th indeed, it is above the half-quadrant, according to which the zodiac-bearer <note>The sun or the ecliptic</note> was divided through the angles by the <term>Almuten</term> <note>The planet with the most astrological "dignity" or influence over a certain point.</note>. Since such things occur on the 4th and 14th more than on the 5th, 6th, or 13th, the crisis will be more "by itself" in these than in those. 

<margin>Note that numbers do not always correspond to nature... one indeed finds it is not a small [matter]... as Pythagoras thought.</margin>

And neither is the speech of Hippocrates to be taken as universal, nor as happening in the majority of cases. Nor should natural things be proved through arithmetic numbers, because they [numbers] do not cause those things. As in many places, Aristotle <note>abbreviated here as "Ay."</note> condemns Pythagoras for positing number as the cause of health and other things. This is because he [Pythagoras] was ignorant of distinguishing between the "one" which is sought with being, and the "one" which is the principle of number. For he thought that the "one" which exists as the principle of number was the cause of beings, thinking things were made from it just as number is constituted from unity. Whence in the third [book] of *Crises*: "I often remember Pythagoras and I wonder at him, because he was a wise man, and it pleased him to say that in numbers [things] are made from their own power." But this is not the place for disputing with one who is foolish. 

<margin>To the 2nd.</margin>

Whence the African <note>likely Constantine the African</note> said, as if by intention, that the sophists in their questioning suppose a fallacy, since it has been shown that the 7th will be stronger than the 14th. To another [point] to be said: through Aristotle, the 14th day is compared to the other days [resulting] from the 7th, and especially to those following it; which is clear because he had already spoken of the 7th. Either because he understood the 14th to be stronger, because more crises happen in it, specifically in the aforesaid places and bodies. Or perhaps he had respect to the aspect of opposition coinciding on the 14th, which is stronger than the [square aspect] falling on the 7th. 

<margin>To the 3rd.</margin>

To the other point to be said: that the peak of the 7th does not decline...

<margin>To the 4th</margin> To the fourth [point], it is said that the fourteenth is simply the most powerful. Indeed, it is extolled above the rest. But <term>in a certain respect</term> <note>original: "secundum quid"</note>, as in a concluded sickness in which no exacerbation is perceived. To the other [point], it must be said that the matter <note>the "materia" or humoral substance causing the disease</note> is not more disposed [to resolve] on the fourteenth than on the seventh, considering that the matter of the seventh day is light and easily adaptable, whereas the matter of the fourteenth is difficult and resists greatly. Furthermore, the [vital] power is commonly found to be stronger on the seventh than on the fourteenth. As for other points declared: perhaps an agent acting in a short time does what a weak one does in a long time.

Others are truly <term>indicative</term> <note>days that provide signs of a coming crisis</note>, such as the 4th, 11th, 17th, or 18th, as appears in the third [book] of *Crises* and in the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note>.

If the matter is thicker and heavier, the <term>indication</term> should be expected on the 7th, and the <term>crisis</term> on the 14th. <margin>Golden verse</margin>

The Moon, according to its quarters, does not properly have the role of indicating, but rather of judging; yet it can be said to indicate to itself according to the midpoints of the quarters.

And the quartile aspect excels the aspect of opposition on the 14th, because the diversity in the signs is more vehement there. There are other things previously shown here: that the crisis of the 7th is more vigorous. 

To the other, it must be said that it is one way up to the 20th and another beyond that up to the 40th. For up to the 20th, the computation is done by fours <note>referring to the lunar quarters</note>. But beyond that, it is done by sevens and the others previously shown. To which it must be said that the 7th is stronger, because as declared, all the causes of the strength of a crisis concur in it more than in the others; nor is it sufficient to infer from one cause alone. 

What should be said to the other side has also appeared. Regarding the second, however, it must be said according to Galen that this aphorism is false and not Hippocratic, since he wrote the opposite in the *Prognostics* and his *Epistle*.

### DIFFERENCE VI.

Whether the critical computation should be made not from the day of birth, but from the beginning of the fever, is shown in what follows; for if it is not computed from the fever but only from the birth, that is an error. Furthermore, the beginning of the computation must be taken from the beginning of the disease for which the crisis is expected, which is the fever. But on the day of birth, there is not yet sickness or fever, since the antecedent cause has not yet transitioned into the joined [state]. 

Again, the beginning of the computation should not be taken from that which is natural, but from that which is not natural, when something already exists that causes disease. Birth, however, is natural, which is shown by its natural end, which is that the fetus has been generated; for that is natural whose end and limit are natural. Moreover, in birth, there does not seem to be sickness, since the operations of those giving birth are not hindered... as is especially found among the Tartars. 

Thus, birth seems to relate to the sickness that supervenes after its time as a <term>disposition</term> <note>a physical state making one susceptible to disease, but not yet the disease itself</note>. Fifthly, the signs preceding the fever and the first of the critical days are those in which there is looseness, headache, wandering, yawning, nausea, and the like; but the computation of the beginning of the sickness is not set from this preceding disposition, but from the fever. 

And this is confirmed by Galen in the third [book] of the *Prognostics*, writing that the inception of the health-loss <note>original: "saniolitatis," likely meaning illness</note> should not be taken from the day on which the patient [first] feels ill, but from the day on which it happens with a rigor <note>a sudden chill or shivering</note> of fever; namely, in which the fever itself is made more manifest and stronger than before; and similarly, when gravity happens to the patient through pain. If therefore in the loss of health it is so, then much more so when these things are more coming upon the fever and its sharpening with rigor. Therefore, the beginning shall not be computed from the day of birth, but from the fever only. 

The contrary of this also seems to be felt in the third [book] of the *Prognostics*, the tenth of the *Theory*, and the fourth of the *Collections*. Furthermore, the beginning of the sickness must be taken from the time when the sickness occurs; but this is in birth. For besides other passions to be mentioned, a <term>solution of continuity</term> <note>a surgical/medical term for a break in the tissues</note> or a great separation of the joints occurs. Hence in the 23rd [chapter]: When the fetus is separated, the womb is opened in such a way, the like of which it cannot produce in its similar state. For it is necessary that certain joints be separated and sustained by the help of God the Exalted. 

Furthermore, the beginning of the sickness is taken (in the first [book] of *Crises*) from the time in which the disease begins with a manifest inception, and when the patient is forced to lie down; but this happens in birth. Therefore, the computation should be started from that and not from the fever. Regarding the first, indeed, it should be known that birth is the emission of the fetus from the womb with its cleansing. But the time of this is different for males and females...

# Whether the critical calculation should be made from the day of birth, or
# from the beginning of the fever in a woman giving birth?

## The time of purgation after birth for a woman.

<margin>12. Wherefore.</margin> For it is not extended in males beyond thirty [days], but in females truly beyond forty days, and frequently a little more. <margin><gloss>The time of the fetus, both male and female.</gloss></margin> The time of <term>purgation</term> <note>Postpartum bleeding or lochia, viewed by medieval doctors as a necessary cleansing of the body.</note> for a female is set at forty-two days; they say both the male and female <term>embryo</term> are likewise formed in that much time. From which it is clear that birth is not only the exit of the offspring, but also the cleansing of the womb. And therefore many laws commanded that a woman after birth, since she is unclean, should not enter the temple lest she defile the sacred things, until a cleansing has been performed. <margin>2.</margin> And because she is rendered more "unclean" by a female birth <margin>3.</margin> than a male one—as is also understood—Moses, <margin>Moses the lawgiver.</margin> the lawgiver of the Jews, commanded in the <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible (specifically Leviticus 12).</note> that a woman giving birth to a female should not enter the temple until after 80 days, but for a male only after 40. This is not for 30 days, because by a natural law, due to the semblance of menstruation, she is rendered unclean; and therefore it passes to 40, in which she is made entirely cleansed. 

And birth is twofold: one indeed is natural, where easier circumstances occur in the act of labor itself, in which a sufficient purgation is also rendered, and the mother is led back into her original nature. The other is the opposite of this, which opposite circumstances follow: such as a flow of blood, which is followed by weakness, or the retention of that flow, which is accompanied by bad <term>apostemes</term> <note>Swellings or abscesses.</note> and fevers; and many times from this there usually follows an egress, an inflation of the belly, and sometimes death. And concerning such a birth, a doubt is proposed. 

<margin>The beginning is twofold.</margin> The "beginning," however, as gathered from the books of Crises and Critical Days, is twofold: one indeed is like an indivisible point, called the "now" or the "instant" <note>original: "nunc vel instans"</note> by the philosophers. This does not fall under the consideration of physicians, who shrink from the dogma that a perpetual passion seizes the body. This kind of "beginning" is perceived only by thought or estimation. 

There is another "beginning" signifying a space or particle of time. This is also twofold. One indeed is of a small time, such as for one hour only or less, provided it includes sufficient time for action and passion. The other is a beginning <margin>Of the most perceptive physicians.</margin> signifying a wider time, which is also twofold. One is as if there were not one <margin>Times of disease.</margin> but four times of a disease: namely, they say a health-bringing sickness is manifested in the **beginning**, the **state** <note>The peak or "acme" of the illness.</note>, the **increase**, and the **decline**; and this is called the "immediate beginning." There is also a "beginning" as it signifies a space of days. <margin>A space of two days, or one beginning.</margin> Indeed, two beginnings of this sort relate to each other as exceeding and exceeded. <margin>2.</margin> For one is called the "beginning of the time of sickness" which covers a space of three days and beyond. 

Next, it must be noted in the investigation of a beginning signifying a duration of time, that sicknesses are twofold. For there are some in which a disposition precedes called <term>almelila</term> <note>An Arabic-derived term (al-maliila) referring to a premonition of fever or a "sub-febrile" state.</note>, and in these it is more difficult to establish the beginning of the sickness, both because of the <term>accidental symptoms</term> <note>original: "accidentia synthomata"</note> hiding the true inception of the beginning, and because of the various dispositions and occupations of the sick. For we cannot, in such cases, take the start from the time they took to bed. For some, being strong or hindered by occupations—such as travelers and the like—though they are equally feverish, 

---

do not seek a bed. There are others, soft and delicate, who have external means for sustenance, who cast themselves into bed even before they incur a fever. There are also other sicknesses generated immediately from a feast or from the <term>almelilatic</term> disposition, in which it is easier to take the beginning. In these and in those first ones, the beginning of the sickness is the hour in which the fever began by a manifest inception, until the infirm person is compelled to lie down, according to the first book of *Critical Days*. What a "critical day" is was shown in chapter three. 

<margin>1.</margin> Furthermore, it should be known according to the third book of <margin>2.</margin> *Prognostics* <note>A work by Hippocrates.</note>, that some have placed the beginning of the calculation <margin>3.</margin> from the sickness alone, or from the fever after birth alone. These people deny [counting from birth] in that same place, but simply and without cause. Their defect in the case of an unnatural birth will appear from what is to be said. And it is manifest that a fever of this sort coming upon birth is an "accident" <note>A secondary symptom or complication rather than the primary cause.</note> of it. And a calculation ought not to be made from an accident, nor usually from any non-manifest cause, but from the more principal sickness, because the former follows the latter as a shadow follows a body (Chapter 73). 

I said "in an unnatural birth" because if it happens that a natural fever occurs after birth from a poor regimen, or generally from any manifest cause, the calculation is in no way to be made from the birth, but from the fever alone, <margin>Calculation is made from the day of fever for some.</margin> since it depends in no way upon the birth. For some, however, their words savor of a suspicious understanding: that the calculation should be taken from the birth alone, whence the reasoning of the *Prognostics*. According to this mode, "crises for women after birth occur according to whichever day she gave birth." Wherefore in the tenth book of the *Theory*: "You shall calculate the passions which happen to women after birth from that day on which she celebrates the birth, just as Hippocrates commands." And it is gathered in the fourth book of the *Colliget* <note>A medical encyclopedia by Averroes.</note>: "You ought to know <margin>4. Colliget.</margin> that crises are calculated from the beginning of the sickness; and there is <margin>No.</margin> a time when it is manifestly from the beginning of the fever, except in <margin>10.</margin> a woman giving birth, because in her you ought to begin from the birth itself, even if the sickness began clearly after the twentieth day." 

The speeches of such great men, <note>Referring to the authorities Hippocrates and Averroes.</note> are interpreted in the best part, suggesting that the calculation should be taken not from the birth alone, but also from the fever. When, therefore, as touched upon: if a woman gave birth, and then a fever happens to her, then if it is not calculated from the fever, but only from the birth, that is an error. From which it is left to the intelligent reader—and especially by the virtue of this statement—that one must calculate from the birth and the fever together. 

Indeed, the words of Galen and the Arabic reasoning on the *Prognostics* can especially import such things. <margin>3.</margin> <margin>3. Prognostics.</margin> It is necessary that the calculation of these days in this sickness be made from the first <margin>4.</margin> day on which the woman gave birth, [but] not only from the day, [we] add, on which the fever attacked her. For the fever attacks many of them on the second or third day after birth. And from those days many physicians count and expect the crisis. And that is not correct in this way, but [only] after they also count the days from the day of birth of the woman. In these words, the same is suggested by the force of this word "afterward." Also, from his Greek speech of this kind, I have thus translated: "The beginning of the calculation shall be for you in..."

<margin>No</margin>
Furthermore, concerning the fact that the woman began to fever: hear the solution. For some women begin to fever on the second or third day after birth, from which many calculate the future <term>crisis</term> <note>The "crisis" was the critical point in a disease when a patient would either begin to recover or take a turn for the worse.</note>. Regarding the third point, which must be known with these things: it must be greatly reckoned from the birth and from the fever as one, provided that the birth was <term>unnatural</term> <note>In this medical context, "unnatural" refers to a birth that caused excessive trauma, disruption, or failed to follow a healthy progression, thereby triggering an illness.</note>, from the commotion of which the sickness arises, and not from an error committed in the [medical] regimen or from some other manifest cause. Reason demonstrates this. For the beginning of the calculation must be taken from that time in which the antecedent cause begins to be placed under the junction [of events]. For that is the immediate and causative reason for the sickness. 

<margin><term>manicula</term> <note>A pointing hand symbol used to highlight important text.</note></margin>
But this occurs in childbirth; for already the heralds and messengers of the sickness or fever are present, even if they are not clearly discerned. This happens because of the violent and sudden snatching away of the <term>accidents</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "accidents" are the observable symptoms or non-essential characteristics of a condition.</note> resulting from the great separation of the joints, pain, anxiety, and the like. For a greater motion—following Aristotle—expels and hides a smaller one, just as the light of an old [source is hidden by a brighter one]. 

Two pains [occurring at once] are the reason why nature, concurring with the <term>humors</term> <note>Bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note> and spirits, inflames the body; not a little after the third day, when the aforementioned symptoms are calmed, the fever manifests itself more fully. And this is especially true if its offending humors are <term>phlegmatic</term>. For phlegm moves from day to day. If, however, they are <term>choleric</term>, the fever will appear perceptibly on the third day, since <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile, associated with heat and irritability.</note> is stirred from the third to the third. For not a few clearly begin to fever—it is understood—on the second or third day, according to Galen. But if the humors are <term>melancholic</term>, the fever will manifest itself more on the fourth day, according to the motion of melancholy. 

Furthermore, a fever supervening upon childbirth is like a fever occurring after an <term>aposteme</term> <note>An internal swelling or abscess.</note> which arises from causes and symptoms. It also seems to behave like a fever that remits for four or seven days and afterwards recurs, such as that which terminates on the seventeenth or twentieth day, appearing on the third of the critical days. But in these cases, one must calculate not only from the supervening fever of the aposteme, or from that occurring after its apparent quietness, but from the beginning of the aposteme and the inception of the fever, as Aristotle and Galen feel. 

Again, if the beginning of the sickness—as has been said—is when the sickness invades with respect to the fate or the preceding perceptible "neutrality" <note>A state between health and sickness.</note> in which the infirm person is compelled to lie down, then it will be necessary to take the beginning of the sickness not only from the fever (especially since it is an accident of birth), but also from the birth itself when such things concur in it. Likewise, if it were not calculated from the birth but only from the fever, then the illnesses occurring during birth that cause fevers—such as the retention of blood and the like—would not receive a proper calculation. And if a calculation were similarly not made from the fever, then a more perceptible onset of the sickness would not be accounted for. Since, therefore, these two things are consistent, it is reasonably sufficient for the calculation to be taken from both. 

From which of these the calculation should be more closely observed will appear from the sequence of the fever following closely after birth because of the more violent accidents occurring in it, without a 

---

<margin><term>manicula</term></margin>
subsequent error in the regimen occurring and the distancing of the fever from the birth. For if the first is present, its beginning will be more from the birth than from the fever. But if the second is the case, so that when the fever is much delayed after the birth, the beginning should be taken only slightly from the birth, but mostly from the fever. 

Although the words of Avicenna may superficially suggest that the calculation should be taken from the birth even after the thirtieth day when a sickness supervenes. Perhaps he said this by "scenting" the discourse of Aristotle, who wished the birth [period] to be extended to 30 days in males, but in females up to 40 and beyond. These, therefore, are the probable truths which I have been able to elicit from the discourses of doctors who wish to imitate the sayings of the ancients, though with no small difficulty and hesitation. 

<margin>No</margin>
<margin><term>manicula</term></margin>
For the fuller assertion of this truth, experimental knowledge must be considered. For the rules of the <term>critical days</term> taken from Hippocrates and his faithful interpreter Galen conclude more by probability than by necessity, since we see not a little—as touched upon before—that it happens otherwise. 

Regarding the fourth point, what should be said to the first? As for the third, it should be said according to the intention [of the author] that the fever has already begun in some way. And the antecedent cause was led into the junction [of symptoms], but they did not appear because of the greater passions occurring in the birth. Or it should be said, as appeared according to Avicenna, that crises are to be calculated from the beginning of the sickness when the lesion is clearly manifest at the beginning. This, however, is an exception in a woman giving birth, since in her the beginning of the calculation must be taken from the birth. 

To the other point, when it was said that birth is "natural," this should be dismissed because, as has appeared, the birth of which this discourse treats is "unnatural." And if its end is said to be natural (namely, the offspring being produced), it should be said—as declared regarding the reason of birth—that it is not only the exit of the embryo, but also the cleansing of the womb. Or, even if it is natural for the fetus, it is nevertheless "unnatural" for the woman because of the passions occurring in her. 

To the other point, it should be said that this is perhaps verified in some way in a natural birth, but not in an unnatural one when illnesses follow as narrated before. To the other point, it should be said that a state of "neutrality" does not relate to fever in the same way that birth does. For in birth, the bodily functions are more perceptibly harmed than in that state. And therefore the beginning of the calculation should rather be taken from it, and not from neutrality. 

For the confirmation of this, though it is difficult for me to say, Galen appears at least to oppose the speech of Hippocrates on such a matter. Therefore, one must look toward the beginning of the future "exsanfiation" <note>Likely a technical term for the clearing of a fever or discharge.</note> originating from the day on which the person fevers the most, or when the <term>rigor</term> <note>A sudden feeling of cold with shivering, often marking the start of a fever.</note> invaded him. For when Hippocrates commands us to consider the first day of the fever and the rigor, Galen does not explain it this way, but rather as the day of the intensification of the fever and the rigor and the more perceptible opening. 

Perhaps the speech of Hippocrates is also confirmed because Avicenna, in the thirteenth [book], where he introduces the aforementioned speech of Hippocrates, does not notice this consideration of the intensification of the fever; rather, he simply seems to assert that certain healthy states are rarely terminated on the seventh day, but rather on the twentieth.

# Whether death occurs in the decline of a disease.

On the fortieth and sixtieth days. Furthermore, from Galen's book 30, it is gathered that acute illnesses should be calculated not only from the more manifest onset of fever and shivering but also from the beginning of the day of recovery itself. For this reason, perhaps Galen's discourse in the *Prognostics* <note>Galen's commentary on Hippocrates' *Prognostic*, a fundamental text for predicting disease outcomes.</note> should be supplemented with a specific or adverbial particle, so that he intends both. The authorities and arguments of the opposing side also proceed insofar as they attempt to show that the beginning of the sickness is the proper time to be accepted for calculation. Those points, however, as they have been explained, do not deny that the beginning must be taken from the fever. To the other point, it must be said that although illnesses may happen during birth, they nevertheless manifest and arrive on the day before the third day, especially after it; therefore, the beginning of the calculation must be taken from them. To the other point, it must be said that although it may be proven that the calculation should be accepted from the birth, it does not deny it is from the fever, as it is understood that the fever occurs upon the birth.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the four stages of disease. It focuses specifically on the "declinatio" (decline) and addresses a contradiction in medical authorities: whether a patient can die while the disease is supposedly fading. It reconciles the views of Avicenna, who suggests death can occur in decline, with Galen, who argues it cannot.</meta>

...[happens] in the **onset**, where the heat contracts toward the interior; therefore, it is the <term>onset</term> <note>original: "principium"; the first stage of a disease before symptoms fully manifest.</note>, and the struggle is not yet manifest. Thus it happens especially in the onset. And it is similar in other particular times, proportioned according to their uses. From these things, therefore, it is clear that the <term>decline</term> <note>original: "declinatio"; the final stage where the disease's strength wanes.</note> is twofold: one indeed is **universal**, occurring in the total time of the illness; the other, however, is **particular**, as occurs in specific episodes.

Because of this, it should be known that some have wished to distinguish a twofold decline: one indeed in which it does not happen that one dies; and an **apparent** rather than true decline in which death does occur. But these authors divide the matter too simply. Neither does it happen that one dies in the decline unless by some <term>accident</term> <note>In medieval medicine, an "accident" refers to a secondary symptom or complication not inherent to the disease itself.</note>, such as a medical error, or the onset of another sickness. 

**Avicenna** <note>original: "Au."; refers to the Persian physician Ibn Sina.</note> (or perhaps **Averroes** in the third book of the *Colliget*) <note>The manuscript shorthand "collz" refers to the *Colliget*, a medical encyclopedia by Averroes, though the text attributes the thought to Avicenna.</note> wished for death to be possible even in the decline, saying: "Death happens to some in the onset of the sickness, and this is when the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health.</note> dominate greatly over the natural heat and extinguish it, either because of their quality, quantity, or both. And it happens to others in the **increase** <note>original: "augmentum"; the second stage where symptoms intensify.</note>, or in the **peak** <note>original: "status"; the third stage where the disease is at its most stable and dangerous strength.</note>, or in the decline." 

<margin>
Because of the cause in the sick person. And namely to the first effect... he says according to Al-Mansur... it is found after the peak... of the perceived diseases... unless there be a fault. First indeed... for when with nature... to die. This stands in the peak... in the peak of sickness... in the decline... nor that... and especially... when... it happens... of the disease... of the flowers... of the heart... Death... and... Concerning... your... from... one... prior... to be. Death... from whom. Others... when... they say... more... with... for already... This... to health... from sickness... he overcomes... in many... one concludes... in the universal. For... simply with... why... or... in... from medicine... by reason... of the sick...
