</margin>

He [Avicenna] maintains that in the decline of healthy diseases <note>Diseases that the body is successfully fighting off.</note>, the decline occurs because of the dominance of the [vital] power; therefore, he intends that even in the decline, death may occur when he speaks of sickness in an absolute sense, and not specifically. Others, indeed, agree with him regarding the **particular decline**, but not as it is shown in the **universal**. 

But that this [Avicenna's] position cannot stand can be destroyed by his own supporting arguments. For he had said a little above that when nature is strengthened over the humor and overcomes it, then it is said to be the time of decline. It is also said through **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."; likely referring to the Philosopher’s principles of nature.</note> that in the decline, the natural heat dominates the matter and overcomes it; whence **Haly Abbas** <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note> says that in the decline, the accidents [symptoms] are calmed and begin to diminish. It is seen that the disease is conquered, and the sick person rests until his illness is finished. When such a thing has happened, it is not possible to die. 

Furthermore, "decline" is said of the disease and not of the [vital] power. This is shown because it is opposed to the onset; the onset is spoken of in respect to the disease, and not the power. Therefore, the same is true of the decline, for contraries are naturally suited to happen concerning the same thing. In a **universal decline**, therefore, death cannot happen. 

If anyone wishes to defend **Averroes** here—seeking to appear to follow his word rather than the truth—he might say that the decline is twofold: one indeed is **real and proper**, already described; the other, however, is **extraneous and nominal**, which is when the sickness "fantastically" [deceptively] seems to decline. This happens either because of the weakness of nature and the extinction of the innate heat. And thus, though very improperly, one can say a decline of the disease is present when the power declines along with the heat. Just as it is said that the fever perishes with the feverish person at the moment of death, because it becomes impossible for health or sickness to exist in those lacking life. This seems to have been the understanding of Avicenna when he said the decline would be because of the weakness of the power and not the sickness. 

Alternatively, it happens because of the hiding of the matter, as when it returns to the interior parts. And thus the aforementioned word of Avicenna can be understood: that someone often dies in the decline of **smallpox** <note>original: "variola".</note>. This also happens in poisonous appearances, such as in **anthrax** or a **carbuncle** <note>original: "antrace seu carbunculo"; severe bacterial skin infections.</note>. And these are certainly reputed by "idiots" <note>Unlearned people or those without formal medical training.</note> to be declines. For when the fever seems to be mitigated in any way, or the swelling is hidden, they think then that the diseases are diminished and failing. 

It is similar to what is written in the fourth section: when a man has a burning fever and finds sudden relief and quiet from the heat without a manifest <term>crisis</term> <note>The turning point of a disease, often accompanied by sweating or other discharges.</note>, with an evacuation or change, and without total extinction, and he rests because the pulse is no longer rapid, yet it is found like a "tranquility" [of the pulse]—then it is judged that he will die quickly. 

Regarding the third point, it should be known that no one dies "of itself" in a universal decline of a disease, but certainly sometimes in a particular one. For in any particular time, death can happen. To understand this, one must know that death can happen for two causes: either **of itself** or **by accident** (as in a universal decline, it is said to happen by error). 

Death **of itself** is twofold: 
1. From the essence and sharpness of the disease, and thus death happens mostly and especially at the **peak** (*status*). 
2. By reason of the matter, either because of **quantity**, stifling the innate heat and blocking the passages through which the breath is vented—just as when someone suddenly heaps a great pile of green wood upon a weak flame—or by reason of a **cold or poisonous quality**; and in such cases, death happens specifically in the particular stages. 

In the **increase** (*augmentum*), when it is the middle ground between these, death happens in a middle way. However, **Galen** says it happens there in the same manner as in the peak. 

Furthermore, some illnesses are continuous, in which no addition or diminution is perceptible. In these, death happens at the peak from the essence of the disease, since it is then complete; whence **Apoplexy** <note>original: "cauton"; likely referring to *kausos* (burning fever) or *apoplexia*.</note> and diseases similar to it bring death at the very peak, and the symptoms precede most sharply. For the extraneous heat, overcoming the innate heat and drawing it to itself, extinguishes it, just as a larger flame extinguishes a smaller one. But in the decline, it never happens when it is universal. 

Other diseases have perceptible addition and diminution, whether they be continuous or intermittent. These are the ones that induce death not a little in the **onset**, specifically when their matter is cold; whence in the first section of the fourth book: "Phlegmatic matter brings death especially in the onset." Those which are from hot matters kill preferably at the **peak**. 

What should be said of the **increase** has already been seen. In the **particular decline**, however, death arrives by way of the weakness of the [vital] power and its resolution, as will be declared more fully. 

Thus, death happens:
- Most of all at the **peak** (*status*).
- Then in the **onset** (*principium*).
- Then in the **increase** (*augmentum*).
- Least of all in the **particular decline**.
- **Never** in the **universal decline**, except by error or the occurrence of another sickness.

This is shown because Galen, in the third book on *Crises*, says that no way of death can be imagined in a universal decline except from a fault or error. By reason of the sickness itself, it is never seen here, neither in experience nor by reason. Whence in the fourth section: "In a total decline, no one dies, unless..."

It concludes that death in a true decline is impossible except by medical error, though it may occur in "particular" or deceptive declines where the body's vital power fails.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a scholastic investigation into the stages of illness, specifically addressing a point of contention among medical authorities: whether it is possible for a patient to die during the "decline" (declinatio) of a disease, which is theoretically the period when the body begins to recover.</meta>

# Does Death Occur in the Decline of a Disease?

<margin>Almanfor.</margin>
<margin>Haly Abbas.</margin>
...[happens] because of laborious causes from the outside that overcome the sick person. This occurs when the patient is weak, such as from movement or an emotional upheaval, namely toward anger, or anger itself. And sometimes this happens even in the **first decline**, that is, the <term>particular decline</term> <note>original: "declinatōi pticulari"; a temporary easing of symptoms within a single episode of a recurring fever, rather than the final recovery from the whole illness.</note>. Regarding this death, **Galen** <note>original: "G."</note> says it is preceded by a small amount of viscous sweat. **Al-Mansur** <note>original: "Almanfor"; likely referring to the *Liber Almansoris* by the Persian physician Rhazes.</note>, however, in his tenth book, states: "A sick person in no way dies after the <term>peak</term> <note>original: "statum"; the point where the disease is at its highest intensity.</note> of the illness, unless another sickness comes upon him after that peak which brings about his end." Wherefore **Haly Abbas**, joining these opinions together, says: "In the decline no one dies, unless perhaps a new suffering arises, or a sin <note>In this context, a "sin" or "error" refers to a mistake in the medical treatment or the patient's lifestyle during recovery.</note> is committed in the <term>regimen</term> <note>original: "regimie"; the prescribed diet, environment, and lifestyle for a patient.</note>." This is proved by no small number of reasons. First, indeed, from the defined limit of the decline: for never does it happen that one dies when Nature is winning and expelling its enemy. Yet this is exactly what happens in the decline, as reason itself attests. Furthermore, according to **Galen**: when the peak of the sickness has passed, Nature is already the mistress; and this happens in the decline, for otherwise the sickness would not be called a "decline."

-> **Death is that through which it happens.** <-

Furthermore, if that which most appears to be present is not present, then neither is that which least appears to be so. But it seems more likely that one ought to die during the **increase** or especially at the **peak**; and if he has not died then, why should he die in the decline? Again, death does not occur except either because of the weakness of the <term>vital force</term> <note>original: "uirtutis"; the internal power or energy of the body to sustain life and fight disease.</note>, or the sharpness of the disease, or because of "accidents" <note>Secondary symptoms or external complications.</note>. But none of these are present by themselves in the decline, since the vital force has already begun to rest and be strengthened, having been released from the previous struggles. The disease is also quieted, since its cause is being continually expelled, and consequently the accidents subside. Wherefore **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Ypocras"</note> says: "Around the beginnings and the ends, everything is weaker"—that is, the accidents—"but around the peak they are stronger." Again, health is produced from sickness as if from its opposite. For one of two opposites is produced from the other in the same subject, according to the first book of *Physics*. That which is produced in this way is brought into being through motion. Motion between two extremes is partly in the "point from which" and partly in the "point toward which," according to the fifth book of *Physics*. Some things, however, participate more in the "point from which," such as when one has just recently receded from it; others equally when they are uniformly distant. Sometimes it is in the "point toward which," when it approaches it more closely. And then the motion is more vehement when it reaches closer to its end or perfection. For in the end, it has already conquered its opposite, so that the opposite has little strength left. This is what happens in the decline; for then the motion toward health is almost at its "point toward which," the sickness having been driven out...

<margin>A strong motion at the end.</margin>
...and every natural motion is strengthened at its end, as it approaches its perfection. From these many points, proceeding as if from a single root, it is more firmly concluded that no one is seen to die in the decline by reason of the disease itself. Yet one may die in it **by accident**. This happens in three ways: first, because of another sickness, as some say, coming upon the first. Second, because of a "sin" or error, either committed by the sick person who is unruly and, disobedient to the doctor, follows his own irrational appetites; or by the doctor, if he errs in the regimen (if such a man ought to be called a doctor and not a corrupter of nature's way); or from the attendants leading the sick person to anger or the like by deed or word. This also happens from external things necessary for health being poorly administered.

Thirdly, death occurs because of the weakness of the **expulsive power**, both natural and animal, located in the muscles, such as those of the chest.

<margin>L</margin>
For <term>matter</term> <note>original: "materia"; the harmful humors or substances causing the disease.</note> that is otherwise well-digested is not expelled but instead kills the patient, according to the teachings on *Prognostics* and *Epidemics*, as in the case of <term>empyema</term> <note>original: "ēpiā"; a collection of pus in a cavity, usually the lungs.</note>. But in the **particular decline** of a disease—for example, a <term>paroxysm</term> <note>original: "pocismi"; a sudden attack or increase in symptoms.</note>—death does occur, not only from error but even from the nature of the vital force and the sickness, as in those whose force is weak. For according to **Galen**: "In the particular declines of paroxysms, we have many times seen many people dying." This is not surprising, because the patient's vital force can be sufficient at the beginning, the increase, and the peak, being then concentrated and striving with all its strength. In the decline, however, the opposite happens. For in that stage, the heat moves from the center to the extremities, whence it happens that the bodily state is evaporated and dissolved. For when the vital force, exhausted in the decline, pursues the remnants of the paroxysm driven to the extremities, it dissolves and exhales unto death along with its instrument. This is just as when someone of weak spirit dies from sudden joy, according to **Galen** and **Aristotle**, or as when someone chasing his enemy falls with him into the pit of death. Some indeed die suddenly, so that to those present they seem to fall into a <term>fainting fit</term> <note>original: "lippothomīā"; from the Greek *leipothymia*.</note> and not death. Others, however, perish slowly, which escapes the notice of many who think these patients have reached the peak and are moving quickly into decline. But the distinction of this ambiguity is found in the **pulse**; for in a true decline, the pulse is strengthened and becomes regular, and the febrile heat is suddenly dissolved. In that decline which follows the peak but leads to death, the pulse is fast and thin. Wherefore it is concluded, as previously touched upon, that there are three ways in which someone dies without a <term>crisis</term> <note>original: "crisi"; the turning point of a disease.</note>. The first is in the beginnings of a paroxysm, which often happens from great flows of humors in the principal parts, or from a multitude and viscosity of humors suddenly blocking the inner passages. The second is at the peak, when Nature is already conquered. The third is in the very rare particular decline when the vital force is dissolved. One also dies without a crisis through a gradual dissolution leading to death, such as occurs in those suffering from <term>consumption</term> <note>original: "taboy"; wasting diseases like tuberculosis.</note>.

<margin>When matter not well-digested kills.</margin>

<margin>C</margin>

<margin>In what ways someone can be seen to die without a crisis.</margin>

But regarding the aforesaid, a double doubt arises. For just as someone dies in a particular decline because the vital force was dissolved by preceding times while moving the heat to expel the remaining matter of the paroxysm, so it would seem to happen in the **universal decline**; for there the vital force is fatigued in many ways, both by the motion of digestion and expulsion, and by the long endurance of labor and the pursuit of expelling the matter. For at the same time, it seems that the heat is dissolved and expelled along with the expulsion of the matter, together with the innate force, because of which death happens. It must be said that this is not similar. Because although in a particular decline of a paroxysm the matter is being expelled, it is not all expelled, but it retains a heaviness that will move again. In such a decline, the matter is not strongly on the way to expulsion, nor mostly expelled as it is in the universal decline. In the universal decline, Nature is already victorious, maintaining a measured order in expelling, not suddenly pouring itself out entirely upon the expulsion of the matter. Rather, it kills the motion...

<margin>Doubts.</margin>

...when [nature] appears to weaken itself, as is seen sometimes in a flow of blood from the nostrils, in sweat, or in a continuous discharge, or in the drawing out of water from those with <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "ydropicorum"; a historical term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid in the body.</note> through the navel. For nature, having already considered [the matter], expels it at intervals, as if the attacker were proving it; she overcomes the more powerful [elements] with a small amount [of strength], for she is rather strengthened by the relief she receives once the <term>viscous matter</term> <note>original: "uiꝫa materia"; thick, sticky fluids in the body believed by medieval doctors to cause blockages and disease.</note> is expelled. And if anyone should say that nature is dissolved by the aforementioned symptoms, it must be answered that [the patient] does not die because of the logic of the disease, but rather from a <term>sin</term> <note>original: "peccato"; in this context, a "sin" refers to a medical error, a mistake in treatment, or a failure by the patient to follow the prescribed recovery plan.</note>. For when a physician sees nature failing during a <term>crisis</term> <note>original: "crisi"; the turning point of a disease where the patient either begins to recover or declines toward death.</note> due to fainting or evacuation, he ought to strengthen it with foods of easy digestion and with fragrant scents. For when <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidentibus"; symptoms or secondary complications that occur alongside the main disease.</note> occur that dissolve the [vital] power, food must be granted immediately according to **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."; Galen of Pergamon, the most influential physician of antiquity.</note>. If this is neglected and the patient fails, such a defect will result from that error.

<margin>
A Doubt.
</margin>

It is now doubted, since it seems death in the <term>universal decline</term> <note>original: "declinatõe vli"; the final stage of an entire illness where the patient returns to health.</note> is for the same reason as in the particular [decline]. Because in the universal decline, death comes through error—which is accidental—and not from the force of the disease. But in the <term>particular decline</term> <note>original: "declinatõe iã pticulari"; a temporary easing of symptoms during the course of an illness, such as between bouts of a recurring fever.</note>, it also seems to happen accidentally, because "decline" always implies nature's victory over the matter of the disease. But because it happens by the dissolution of power, and as a consequence of the expulsion of the matter itself, it appears to happen accidentally. Therefore, it seems to happen similarly in both cases. It should be said that either the "sin" [error] is found to occur in such an accident, or that something happens accidentally which more closely follows the intrinsic principles of the thing, such as the matter and the [vital] power. And such a thing happens in the particular decline which is "per se" <note>original: "per se"; by itself or essentially.</note> close to it. There is also another [type of death] which exists from the outside, such as by error. And this kind of accident is far removed from

that which moves "per se," which sometimes happens in the universal decline. Thus, as was seen, death "per se" and directly occurs in the <term>beginning</term>, the <term>growth</term>, and the <term>peak</term> <note>original: "statu"; the "status" or highest point of intensity in a disease.</note> of a disease. Conversely, in the particular decline, it is closely accidental, while in the universal decline, it is remote. Because of this, what should be said regarding the first point has already appeared. To the other point, it should be said that in the universal decline, death does not happen, as shown, except by error or a supervening illness, as some say, just as **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."; refers to the philosopher whose logic underpinned medieval medicine.</note> finally declares. But since it happens "much"—that is, often—in the particular decline, it happens never or in no way "per se" in the universal decline. And similarly, what was seen should be said to that which **Aristotle** added. For although a fever may decline with its accidents, yet smallpox does not, except perhaps fantastically. To the other point, it shall be said as will be seen in chapter 34. To the other, with its confirmation, it should be said that although death may happen in the particular decline, it does not happen in every case, but only in that which is most closely connected to the universal peak, or the beginning, or the growth. To the other point, it should be said that once a crisis has occurred and a healthy state has preceded it, from which the particular nature collapses along with the matter and the universal [nature]—as with the movement of the moon—and finally some evil celestial influence arrives, it will not be able to prostrate the sick person to death, since the matter is entirely indisposed, the cause having already been partly evacuated and the power there strengthened in some way. Or perhaps if they were to die, it would be either from another illness

or an external "sin" [error] would occur. To the last point, it should be said that if it happens that the "victor" dies while the other [the disease] is still active, nature was not perfectly the victor. For she did not have the matter prepared <note>original: "dispositã"; the state of "matter" in the body being ready to be processed or expelled.</note> in which she acts as nature, since the matter would have been <term>digested</term> <note>original: "digesta"; in medieval medicine, "digestion" or "concoction" is the process where the body ripens or prepares harmful humors for expulsion.</note> in its state and afterwards expelled. For if it happened otherwise, it would not be a "decline." Hence, because of this and similar accidents, some think that someone dies in the universal decline. And specifically because some, seeing people warmed by an accidental heat and regarding them as if they were healthy, and not seeing the cause from which they might die, estimate that they die in the universal decline. For when natural heat fails, the accidental heat also fails.

### DIFFERENCE CHAPTER 8

It is shown that sleep is most harmful at the **beginning** [of a disease], more so than at other times of the illness. For that harm is worse which passes through more stages of time. This is confirmed by **Galen** in the first [book] of *The Regimen of Acute Diseases*. Food given at the beginning causes worse harm than at any other time; likewise, harm is done to [the patient] at the beginning, then in the growth. But it happens differently in the decline especially, and generally in the peak. Furthermore, since sleep is at its most potent in the beginning, <term>tympanites</term> <note>original: "tyꝑ"; likely referring to a type of swelling or a specific feverish state.</note> rises and grows strong, <term>rheums</term> <note>original: "reumata"; the flow of excess humors, often thought to cause inflammation or discharge.</note> run together into weak places, fevers intensify, and abscesses increase. Many also fall into delirium, even though they speak while appearing to be in a dream. These things, however, do not happen in the peak or the decline, since the matter has been conquered and is expelled. For in the peak, the matter of the disease is overcome, and in the decline, it remains conquered. Therefore, in the beginning and generally in the growth, the harm of sleep is worse than at other times. That it is worse in the growth is shown because a similar addition is made. For when illnesses intensify along with their harms, a supervening harm from sleep, as previously noted, will then have the greatest power to hurt, and especially when it must pass through the peak in which the aforementioned extremes occur. Furthermore, in the peak, the harm of sleep seems more deterring because sleep is an accident. Accidents, however, intensify in the peak. Furthermore, at that time when the infestation from the illness and its accidents is more vehement, and the [vital] power is fought by the matter—as if fleeing, it hides within—a worse harm of the disease occurs; this happens in the peak and not at other such times, wherefore the harm of sleep is made worse in that stage. That there is less harm in the decline is indicated because in that stage, the power appears to be fortified since the matter of the disease is then expelled. For in the peak, the crisis occurs in which the cause of the disease is expelled. Once that is expelled, the powers are revived and the sick person is healed. When this happens, harm cannot occur in the decline. Again, in the universal decline, death does not occur, nor even great danger, except from an error coming upon the sick person—as stated in the previous [chapter]—therefore it does not happen in the particular decline either. And it is confirmed because a man, and the being of a man, and "whenever a man" are the same thing according to repetitive speech.

# Whether, against the poet Antiphon, sleep should be called "worse" and such
->(In the stages of disease)<-

<margin>Inopportune?</margin>
**In the fourth book of the Metaphysics.** It seems to be a similar case regarding the universal and particular times of the peak [of a disease]. For just as the whole disease is composed of these, so a <term>paroxysm</term> <note>original: "parocifmus"; the period of highest intensity or "peak" of a fever or illness.</note> is composed of them. Therefore, the harm will be less during the decline of the peak. Yet the opposite of all these things is often observed. In the *Canon* of <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: "Ca. affōr sza."; likely referring to the Canon of Medicine by the Persian physician Ibn Sina (Avicenna), specifically the section on Aphorisms.</note> it says: "Again, in which illness sleep brings labor, it is fatal." But experience teaches that this does not happen in the beginning, nor in the fixed state, nor even in the increase of the illness, since many who are sleeping then do not fall into death or ruinous harm, but rather during the decline. Because of this, the harm done in sleep itself will be worse. Regarding the first point, however, it must be established what sleep is, where it comes from, and for whose sake it exists. Also, in how many ways it is spoken of, and how the body is changed by its action.

<margin>What is Sleep?</margin>
<margin>Abano on Sleep</margin>
<margin>☞</margin>
Sleep is, as some say, a reciprocation of the internal and natural heat. It is also the first "chain" or bond of the senses. According to the first book of *On Sleep and Waking*, three things are gathered: Sleep is the deepening of the <term>common flow</term> <note>original: "flzg[us] cōmunis"; the flow of "animal spirits" through the nerves that allows for sensation and movement.</note> from the brain to the heart. In the fourth book of *On the Accidents of the Soul*, it says that it is a resting of the <term>animal virtues</term> <note>original: "uirtutū aīaliū"; the psychological and sensory powers of the soul, such as sight, hearing, and movement.</note> with an intensification of the natural ones. For it mostly happens that the animal virtues, both internal and external, rest within it; and especially when sleep has been deep, affected by a natural disposition. For there are some who dream while sleeping so that they rise and walk, which happens due to the heat of the brain and a powerful, vaporous obstruction. Sleep occurs because vapors from food and drink—and especially resolved vapors mixed with other pre-existing humors—seek the brain. Finding the brain dense and cold, they freeze and thicken, and descending, they block the sensory pathways of the limbs. Thus, the spirits are withdrawn from their instruments [the organs] to the brain and finally descend into the heart. This is a blockage of the middle <term>ventricle of the brain</term> <note>original: "uētriculz̄ cerebri"; medieval anatomy divided the brain into three ventricles or chambers where different mental faculties were housed.</note> above, around the "worm" standing at its apex. For it extends itself so much that two capsules, or "oval additions," are applied, so that the animal spirit cannot pass or go out from the first ventricle into the back. Thus, the animal is then deprived of flow and motion. Because of this, <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Aū."; refers to Aristoteles (Aristotle), the primary authority in medieval science.</note> says in *On Sleep and Waking* that sleep is an impotence of the flow, not an end of the things themselves.

<margin>Two final causes of Sleep.</margin>
<margin>☞</margin>
Sleep occurs for two reasons at present. One is so that nature may lean more freely toward the <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "digestiōni"; the process of "cooking" or refining food and humors within the body.</note> of matter and food. For in sleep, the heat or spirit is drawn from the extremities of the body to the inside and is strengthened. The animal powers rest, which, by operating through the body, were previously dissolving and dispersing that heat. A sign of this is what was said by <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>original: "Ypocrate"; the ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note>: "The bellies are hotter in winter and spring, and sleep is longest then." Consequently, more offerings [of food] must be provided to them. For the heat is strengthened and united in these times, and rest is then present.

<margin>On Sleep and Waking.</margin>
The second reason is so that the spirit may rest and be strengthened within; otherwise, it would be dissolved by continuous motion. Hence, in the fifth book of Aristotle’s *On the Soul*: "The instruments are fatigued by the motion of waking and are destroyed." And therefore, in *On Sleep and Waking*: "Sleep is necessary for every waking thing; otherwise it would languish and perish." Because of this, perhaps, the saying of Aristotle is explained: that "sleep is an impotence," that is, a weakness of the senses. For it happens because of the weakness of nature, which is not able to continually send spirits out from the primary "mine" [the heart or brain]. Therefore, in the first section: "The necessity of sleep in health and life is not an absolute necessity," since it only exists because of some impotence and is a departure from the natural state. However, this departure is "natural," hence it is necessary; since "necessary" is here spoken of in the common sense of "natural." For sleep occurs so that the spirit may be separated from impediments on account of the weariness happening to it, and because it was necessary for it to attend to digestion. It could not perform these two things while waking. And therefore, from a certain impotence, sleep is necessary for it so that it may rest.

<margin>The substance of sleep</margin>
But let us consider the pulse of the commentator, as one hears from the poets saying: "Sleep is the announcement of death," helping only those operations concerning food. All other things are similar to the dying: for instance, not seeing, not hearing, not tasting, not understanding, not speaking—to be cast down, insensible, immobile, and irrational. For sleep seems, according to nature, to be a middle state between living and not living. In the fifth book of *On the Generation of Animals*: "Sleep is indeed a double departure; one is universal, the other particular." The universal is the return of the animal spirit from the instruments of sensation and motion to the beginning [the heart], by which the instruments themselves are deprived of their operation, except those that are necessary for life to remain, such as the instruments of the breath.

<margin>The nature of sleep</margin>
Particular sleep is threefold. For one is natural, another is contrary to nature, and another is almost in the middle.

<margin>Contrary to nature</margin>
<margin>Subeth</margin>
The one contrary to nature is the revocation of the spirit because of a cause that moistens the instruments and disturbs and blocks the substance itself, loosening the substance of the nerves and muscles, as happens to the drunk or those with an overly full stomach. And this sleep is properly called <term>Subeth</term> <note>original: "subeth"; an Arabic-derived medical term used in the Middle Ages to describe a pathological, heavy, coma-like sleep or lethargy.</note>, which is a superfluous and heavy sleep, whose heaviness and excess are in both quantity and quality, so that its duration is prolonged. Thus, the person is barely awakened, nor can they raise themselves except with great difficulty.

<margin>Natural sleep</margin>
<margin>☞</margin>
There is also another natural sleep. And this is twofold. One is called "absolutely natural," which is the return of the vital spirit to the interior so that it may digest food. The other is "not absolutely natural," which is the return of the spirit from the instruments to its beginning because of an excess of its own <term>resolution</term> <note>original: "resolutōis"; the "thinning" or wearing away of the spirits through activity.</note>. For it cannot be sustained due to the dissolution caused by motion and labor, and therefore it must necessarily return to its beginning, such as the brain, and finally to the heart itself from where it first proceeded.

<margin>Middle Sleep</margin>
And there is a third, which is in the middle between these two extremes. It is called "not absolutely natural sleep," which is the return of the animal spirit from the instruments because of a contrary cooling cause in the substance of the spirit, such as from external cold or from cooling medicines. For because of this cooling, the instruments being blocked and narrowed, the vital spirit in them cannot be renewed to expand itself to the instruments in the place of that which was dissolved. In the third section of the first part, and in the commentary on the pulse, it appears that the accidents of sleep in the body vary in two ways.

<summary>This page explores the medieval physiology of sleep, defining it as the retreat of animal spirits and heat from the limbs to the heart and brain to facilitate digestion and rest. It distinguishes between healthy natural sleep and "Subeth," a pathological, heavy lethargy caused by vapors or illness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic discussion on the medical utility and dangers of sleep, specifically within the context of fevers and the stages of disease. It draws heavily on Galen, Hippocrates (referred to as 'Y'), and Avicenna (referred to as 'A') to distinguish between beneficial rest and "fatal" sleep during a disease's peak.</meta>

<margin>Daytime sleep</margin>
**F**rom the quantity of time and the mass and quality of the matter, [sleep varies]. First, indeed, because either sleep is prolonged and especially during the day—and then it unnerves the powers and dissolves the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>original: "animāles"; referring to the 'spiritus animalis' believed to flow through the nerves to control movement and sensation.</note>, relaxes the paths of the heart, cools the body, and moistens it. It increases <term>phlegm</term>, weakens the natural heat, corrupts the color [of the skin], and inhibits movement. However, if it is moderate, it digests food at the proper time, fills out the body, relieves labor, strengthens the soul, lightens all the virtues, and increases the natural heat; it renders the <term>humors</term> <note>original: "bu."; abbreviation for 'humores'.</note> praiseworthy. But if it is made in a time less than sufficient, there arises from it a weakness of nature, an infirmity of digestion, dryness of the body, and the heat is dissolved by a sharp and over-inflamed nature. 

From the matter and measure and quality, sleep similarly varies in three ways. First, if it occurs in a body filled with very cold, viscous foods that are difficult to digest, with much <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>original: "glili"; likely 'gliscenti' or referring to 'pituita' (phlegm).</note> matter pre-existing. Then, if sleep occurs immediately upon this, it almost suffocates the natural heat; for it causes a "boiling up" in these things and disperses them, so that it regurgitates over the heat, extinguishing it. And thus, just as from sleep at the beginning of an onset, a phlegmatic fever usually occurs. Or, if the body is entirely empty, and the person had previously taken light, easily flammable foods, the natural heat—turned toward the moisture of the body—burns and consumes it, weakening and drying the body out. If, however, a middle ground occurs between these, the natural heat, being directed to the interior, ripens the material found in the body and, digesting the food, warms and moistens it, increases the body's substance, and strengthens all the virtues.

<margin>Harm which is said to be "of itself" and is twofold</margin>
Finally, it must be known that "harm" is a certain accident left behind by a disease. According to <term>Galen</term>, this is twofold: namely, constitutional and specific. Constitutional harm is that which always harms, such as the harm of "cold sleep" at the beginning of a <term>paroxysm</term> <note>original: "pocifmo4"; a sudden attack or the peak of a fever.</note> of intermittent fevers; yet this harm does not carry with it "craftiness" <note>original: "uersuciā"; likely meaning a deceptive or sudden fatal turn.</note> or death by itself. The harm of sleep itself is manifold, as touched upon before: the provocation of shivering or cold, and its intensity and duration, the flowing down of <term>rheumatism</term> <note>original: "reuātum"; refers to the flow of excess humors/fluids.</note>, a certain stupor, the sharpening of fevers, and the increase of "apparitions" [hallucinations].

<margin>Specific [harm]</margin>
However, harm is called "specific" when it harms at a particular time of the disease, such as in the decline or even in the "steady state" <note>original: "statu"; the *status* or *acme* is the period when a disease is at its highest point but no longer increasing.</note> continuous with it. And this harm, according to Galen and Hippocrates, is fatal in a decent sleep. Concerning this, the aphorism is verified: "In which disease [sleep brings labor, it is fatal]."

Furthermore, it is distinguished in another way. For one harm is called "extensive," which lasts for a long time but is not vehemently terrifying. Another is called "intensive," which does much harm in a small amount of time. The first occurs in times other than the decline, specifically in the beginning, but most significantly in the "increase" [of the illness]. The other occurs in the decline and in the steady state. Now, a paroxysm is an "exacerbation," which is the worst hour of the entire <term>period</term> <note>original: "pyodi"; from 'periodus', the cycle of a fever.</note> or circuit, just as the rest [of the cycle] is; the first part of the decline is the best. Because of this, it must be known that some have said sleep does not harm of itself, but only because it deprives one of wakefulness, and thus takes away the help provided by being awake. But Galen refutes these people, saying...

---

...that certain harms arise from sleep, as Hippocrates showed in the books of the *Epidemics*. He said that in sleep many were "stupid" [dull/insensible] and alienated, who became such because of the sleep itself. Whence in the sixth book of the *Epidemics*: "Other things which in sleep are <term>comas</term> <note>original: "comata"; from the Greek 'koma', used here to mean deep stupors.</note>, that is, stupors, and those in whom the extremities grow cold and the mind is disturbed," and whatever other such bad things [occur] around sleep; and conversely, those things which are "praiseworthy."

<margin>Chapter on the Signs / from the part above / of Sleep and Waking</margin>
Thus, therefore, sleep harms by itself. Avicenna in the fourth [book] seems to say: "One will see and hear which harm of sleep is worse in the steady state." Daytime sleep is safer when it occurs at the beginning of the illness; but in the steady state of the fever's peaks, it is all worse. At the beginning of the peak, it often happens and does not harm. <term>Galen</term> feels the opposite of this. For he wants it to harm principally with a worse and fatal harm in the decline. To which it must be said that Avicenna does not intend to compare the harm of sleep in the steady state of a peak to the harm at the beginning of the peak, as his speech seems to do at first glance. Rather, he compares the harm at the beginning of the "steady state" to that which occurs at its end. Thus it is interpreted: "And all this—namely, sleeping during the day in whatever manner—is worse in the steady state of the fever's peaks." Truly, [it is worse] at the beginning of it. And it often happens at the end of the steady state, and then it does not harm since it approaches the decline. Whence in the first part of the fourth [book]: "It does not harm, perhaps, during the steady state." He says "perhaps," that is, "sometimes," because at the end of it, it does not harm. Nor did he relate the particular harm in the decline to that done at other times, as seen. Or perhaps one will respond that Galen, in interpreting him, explains his opinion more clearly and does not oppose him; because by "steady state," he did not mean the *status* as one of the four times of a disease, but rather he wanted "decline" to be understood by it. And then Galen's speech will be explained reasonably, since the name "steady state" can imply both. For we say something "stands" when it declines or ceases from its motion or act. 

When Avicenna says that sleep often does not harm in the beginning, it is to be understood as concerning "intensive" or "common" harm, as said by Galen. Or it does not harm, but rather helps nature by working more strongly during the time of the fever's peak, just as Galen himself testifies; so that if nature is afterwards incited to be more powerful than the matter, it will ripen and dissolve it by being more victorious. Yet, it may be found against Avicenna that he says it does not harm in the beginning while Galen says the contrary. For although sleep may not bring death, nor other "crafty" and great harm, it nevertheless seems to bring some harms, as is added—such as has been touched upon many times—because it prolongs the accidents of shivering, rigor, and strong coldness of the extremities. It increases pre-existing <term>inflations</term> <note>original: "Flōnes"; likely 'inflationes' or gas/swelling.</note> around the viscera. And if any humors have flowed into the belly, they are not similarly digested; therefore, those suffering in the beginnings of fever peaks are prohibited from sleeping, but are ordered to stay awake, as the first part of the fourth [book] also indicates. It must be said that a solution of this kind appeared in the explanation of Avicenna's series. Or of "the day" [daytime sleep]. Concerning the third point, it must be known that the question seems to suppose that sleep harms, perhaps because there is doubt about this very thing...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on the medical effects of sleep, moving from general qualities to a specific inquiry regarding the stages of disease (the beginning, the increase, the peak, and the decline).</meta>

->### Whether the harm of sleep is especially worse in the beginning than in other times of disease.<-

**S**ince every action seems to assist nature, and sleep is a natural action—and furthermore, during sleep, heat is drawn inward and strengthened—it follows that sleep does not cause harm.

It must be said that sleep, by its own nature, has the quality of helping, but it harms "by accident" <note>original: "per accidens"; a logical term meaning a property that is not essential to the thing itself, but happens due to external circumstances.</note>. Insofar as it is an action of nature and the heat within is drawn inward and fortified, it remains a source of help. However, it can be harmful when such internal drawing of heat excites rigors or chills, or causes "rheums" <note>original: "reumata"; refers to the flow of harmful humors or catarrh.</note> to flow, and so forth. Or, one might say that natural sleep always provides comfort, while "symptomatic" sleep harms—especially for those who, in the beginnings of an illness, experience an internal movement contrary to the body's most powerful guiding principle.

Furthermore, it should be known that if sleep causes harm at any time, it is a bad sign; however, according to Galen, that harm is not necessarily fatal unless it occurs specifically in the <term>decline</term> <note>original: "declinatio"; the final stage of a disease or fever when the symptoms should be subsiding.</note>. For when heat turns to the interior, it is united and strengthened so that it may digest food and reform the <term>matter</term> <note>original: "materia"; the pathological humors causing the disease.</note> of the disease into something good, and strengthen the spirits along with the <term>virtues</term> <note>original: "virtutibus"; the internal biological powers or "faculties" of the body.</note>, as has been said. If these powers do not prevail over the harm of the sleep, it indicates that the internal cause of the disease is harmful and exceeds the grade of nature—especially in the decline, when there should instead be more alleviation. As it is said, in the decline of diseases, the sick are in less danger. Therefore, the discourse of the tenth [book] of Avicenna's *Theory* <note>original: "decimi A. theorice"; referring to Avicenna's Canon of Medicine.</note> is unarticulated and indiscreet, simply putting forward an aphorism when it should have opened up an explanation. Because of this, it should be known <margin>☞ Note</margin> with Hippocrates and Galen that the worst harm of sleep is that which occurs especially in the decline. This is proven by a fourfold reason: <margin>1.</margin> One from common reason; another taken from <margin>2.</margin> continuity; <margin>3.</margin> a third from nature and habit, as I shall say regarding the sleep of the decline; <margin>4.</margin> and a fourth from the victory of the matter and its expulsion. Indeed, it is gathered that the reasons for contraries are themselves contrary, and contraries are born to occur around the same thing.

Since sleep should help most especially in the decline—as Galen says—it clearly assists the "form" of the breath, <margin>1. 3.</margin> and also in the "increase" stage <note>original: "augmentum"; the stage where a fever is getting worse.</note> it supports the "peak" <note>original: "statu"; the "status" or crisis point where the disease is at its strongest.</note>. But the most manifest of all helps occurs in the decline. For this reason, in the first part [of the text], one should prohibit the sick person from sleep at the beginning of a fever, and specifically when "horripilation" <note>original: "oripilatio"; shivering or goosebumps.</note>, cold, or rigor is present. For these are prolonged [by sleep], and they squeeze the matter—if it is ready—toward certain internal organs and prevent the digestion of the humors. But at the decline, sleep is greatly helpful. Perhaps it does not even harm at the peak. Therefore, by the opposite logic, sleep harms most greatly in the decline. Whence Galen says: the harms from such sleep are not only fever, but the intensification of pain, the creation of rheums, and the increase of "phlegmons" <note>original: "floumones"; inflammatory tumors or swellings.</note>. Some people, following these sleeps, speak "alien" things <note>i.e., they become delirious.</note>, while others are rendered so stupid that they can barely be roused when prodded. 

Furthermore, since harm is understood in relation to the strength of the <term>virtue</term> at the time the harm arrives, if the virtue is weak, the harm will be worse. The virtue is weaker in the decline because it has been more heavily attacked. It has already sustained the battle through three stages of time: in the increase and especially in the peak. Although some fevers—such as those from "cold matter"—cause no small harm in their very beginnings, the body is so vehemently weakened by the time it reaches the decline that even a moderate harm is most vehement. 

---

In the decline, being vehemently weakened, a small harm to the body is very great. And therefore, in the third [book] of *On Crises*, it is said that those whose virtues are weak die especially in the decline. For if, along with the expulsion of the matter, the spirit and life itself exhale, then at that time when one is accustomed to receive help from something, but instead receives an injury, one must despair all the more; for they do not know where to flee for the sake of help. It is as when a son is not helped by the father who supports him by nature and custom. Whence Galen shows that in a situation where every single thing should be helpful, <margin>3.</margin> if it does nothing to help and even causes harm, it points toward a "decent death" <note>meaning an inevitable or predictable death.</note>. In the decline, nature and custom conspire so that sleep usually brings relief. If, therefore, it harms, it is exceedingly pernicious; for it ought to bring relief then, as the virtue is being eased of the matter and the symptoms are being calmed. This is especially true since the body is not then intent and prepared for battle, but rather for rest and recovery. 

Again, because the matter is conquered and expelled, sleep and everything that provides assistance ought reasonably to help; and to induce the opposite is to do harm, especially since the body labors in every way. But this expulsion happens in the decline. Because of this, one concludes from these points: if sleep harms in the decline, its harm will be ruinous; all the matter is too much and too evil, and at an improper hour it overcomes <margin>Relieving things help, but not all</margin> <margin>4.</margin> nature. For on account of sleep, the heat is united internally, and then the inimical matter rises up against nature, thinking that nature wishes to take up arms in its own defense. And so, being moved to battle, the matter inflicts worse damage upon nature than if the person had remained awake with the heat diffused. 

Regarding the <margin>No</margin> <margin>3.</margin> fourth point, and answering the first: it must be said that the harm of sleep in the beginning, as stated, is small in intensity, even if it is great in extension <note>meaning it lasts a long time but isn't immediately fatal.</note>. However, injury is mostly caused by intensity, not by extension, since the virtue still remains strong at the start. This is confirmed by what was seen in distinction 34. And by this, <margin>No</margin> we answer the second: although the harms that occur in the beginning are numerous, they are nevertheless minor, and the virtue, still being valid, will be able to correct them. But this does not happen in the decline. 

To the other point: it must be said that in the "increase" <margin>TO THE OTHERS</margin> stage, the harm is not worse, but it is more powerful in the decline and generally in the peak. For although all things might be "relieving" in the peak, in the increase the virtue does not yet lie fatigued while resisting them, which *does* happen in the decline and at the end of the peak. 

To the remaining point: it must be said that although sleep is an "accident" <note>meaning a non-essential circumstance.</note> insofar as it is distinguished from "substance," it is not an accident of the "peak" stage. Rather, its opposite—wakefulness—is more so. Here, the discourse is not about "accidents" in general, but about the particular things that emerge at the time of the peak. 

To the other point: <margin>Answer twofold</margin> it must be said that although the matter infests the body more at the peak than in the decline or other times, the virtue is stronger during the peak, being more intent on battle and victory. In the decline, it is not so, but is more intent on rest. And if a harm occurs to it then, it will be more terrifying; just as to a fatigued man hoping to rest, labor now seems more difficult than before. 

To the other point: it must be said that the truth is found most especially in the "true decline," in which...

...nature overcomes. However, it is not in that which it overcomes [the matter] that nature wins; even if the **matter** <note>original: "materia"; the pathological humors or substance causing the illness.</note> seems to be expelled and mostly quieted, this is not so much due to the power of nature but rather the cessation of the movement of the humors. This is because the quieting of the movement of the matter toward putrefaction does not last for a longer time—just as a certain **tertian fever** <note>A fever that spikes every third day.</note> does not last beyond 12 or 14 hours; a **quotidian** <note>Daily fever.</note> not beyond 18; and a **quartan** <note>Spiking every fourth day.</note> not beyond 24.

<margin>~</margin>
Indeed, in the "general state" <note>The overall progress of the disease.</note> where a common **crisis** <note>The turning point of a disease when it is decided if the patient will live or die.</note> occurs, it is not always the same as in a "particular state" <note>The state of a specific symptom or part of the body.</note>. Thus, even when a particular state is established, the matter may still be generally un-expelled; and so, staying in the <term>decline</term> <note>The final stage of a disease.</note> can be very harmful. To another point, it must be said that in a general decline, death does not occur except through an error committed by the physician, the patient, those attending them, or due to external factors. This differs from the previous case, where the matter is truly conquered and expelled. However, in a *particular* decline, one can die because the matter remains un-expelled, especially in those who are weak. To prove this, it must be said that the definition of "man" and "a specific man" would not be the same if "man" were defined simply as "man"; rather, one definition adds to the other, just as the definition of "man" adds "rational" to the definition of "animal." It is not entirely the same with the general and particular times of a disease, as will be shown in Chapter 34. Nor are these essential parts of the disease, but rather integral parts. Yet it is similar in this: just as the four stages of a disease constitute the whole life of the illness, so do the particular stages constitute a particular event.

# CHAPTER IX: DIFFERENTIATION

<margin>1</margin>
It is shown here that a **relapse** <note>original: "recidivatio."</note> is one and the same illness as its "root" <note>The original onset of the disease.</note>. Because an illness is seen as one and the same when its matter is one, its duration is the same, and its mode of affliction is the same. Thus, an illness receives its "unity" from these things. A relapse can happen from the same matter as the primary illness, such as from **cholera** <note>original: "colera"; the humor known as yellow bile, not the modern bacterial infection.</note>. For the remnants left behind in diseases are accustomed to causing "subversions" <note>Upsetting the recovery.</note> just as bad matter does; and the whole can be left to the same judicial expulsion or the same critical sense, following the mode of affliction from one third-day interval to the next. Furthermore, if it were not the same, then a quartan fever—and especially quintan, sextan, and similar fevers—would not be the same fevers, since a long period of rest occurs between one spike and another. But they are commonly considered one and the same. Again, an illness is "one" when it is integrated from four stages. Every illness from which one recovers has four stages. Both the primary illness and the relapse are of this kind, as seen in a patient suffering from a painful **pleurisy**. Otherwise, it would be necessary for each of these four stages to have a contrary within them. Also, the appearance of **digestion** <note>The medical process where the body "cooks" or breaks down the harmful humors.</note> indicates this. Therefore, a relapse is one and the same illness as the primary one.

<margin>squiggle</margin>
The opposite view is held by the "Second Critics." When you see illnesses that seem to be resolved and then return, it often happens that the relapse occurs on the day of the crisis, then runs according to the number of days of the crisis, and is later resolved on another day of crisis. Therefore, each of those

---

particular illnesses would be "acute" in itself. When they are aggregated and continued with one another, the result is a **chronic** illness. If each of these is acute, then they are not truly one single illness. Furthermore, the health one has at dawn and the health one has in the evening are not one and the same, according to the fifth book of Aristotle’s *Physics*. Much less, therefore, will an illness be "one" when it is interrupted by health, as happens between a primary illness and a relapse. Furthermore, a primary illness is generated from the thinner, more easily evaporated part of the matter. First, the thin, resolvable part is consumed; finally, the thick matter that resists evaporation remains, from which the relapse arises. These types of matter are different. And in any "interposed" cause that produces a specific spike—which acts as the efficient cause—it is different from the "antecedent" cause which is daily administered and passes into the "conjoined" cause. This is seen especially in those suffering from a quartan fever for 12 years or more. But this is even more true in a primary illness and a relapse. Therefore, the matter of the primary illness and the relapse will not be the same, since they are more distant from each other than one fever spike is from another. Again, things that have different accidents are not the same. But different things happen to a relapse than to the "radical" illness. For a relapse is worse than its root, differing in its origin from that which caused it. Likewise, someone sick with a "choleric" illness could, through a regime of extreme cooling, fall into a **phlegmatic** <note>original: "flegmatica"; an illness caused by the humor phlegm.</note> illness, which is of a different matter and movement than the choleric one. In such conditions, the relapse is entirely different from the primary illness.

<margin>~</margin>
Regarding the first point, it should be known what constitutes a "noted illness" as described in Chapter 72. An illness is called **primary** or **radical** when it first afflicts, as the name indicates. After a period of rest, another affliction follows, which is called a **secondary** illness or a **relapse**. It is a "falling back" after the primary illness. How many times a relapse can be said to occur will be shown later.
<margin>One</margin>
"One" or "the same" is spoken of in two ways. In one way, it is used accidentally, as described in the fifth book of Aristotle's *Metaphysics*. In one sense, it is "one" by continuity, as a string of a bow or a piece of wood joined to another; or by nature, which is a stronger unity, like the parts of an arm. Likewise, something is called "one" in subject or species. It is also called "one" in genus, where the genus is one but the specific differences are opposite. Furthermore, things whose defining rationale is one are called "one." It is also called "one" by indivisibility, like a point or the number one. In another way, "one" is distinguished logically. Some things are "one in number," having the same matter. Some are "one in species," having the same defining rationale. Some are "one in genus," having the same "figure of predication" <note>A logical category.</note>. Others are "one by analogy," referring to one thing according to priority and posteriority.
<margin>3</margin>
Regarding the second point, it should be known that the radical illness and the relapse are one illness in species and in number from the perspective of the **matter** and the **virtue** <note>original: "virtus"; the body's natural healing power or the "strength" of the disease.</note>, but not from the perspective of the essence of the disease. From the perspective of the matter, because the matter of the relapse and the primary illness is the same. Similarly, from the perspective of the virtue, because the virtue performs its operations in an ordered and...

-># Whether a Relapse is the Same Illness as its Root?<-

...continuous regarding the **matter** <note>original: "materia"; the bodily humors or physical substance of a disease.</note> of the recurring and the principal illness. However, by reason of the **essence of the disease**, they are not one illness in number, but only in **species** <note>That is, they are the same *kind* of disease, but not the exact same *instance* of it.</note>. This is because a single quality in number cannot both "not be present" and then "be present" <note>A philosophical rule: once a specific quality (like a single instance of a fever) ceases to exist, it cannot return as the exact same numerical instance; a later fever is a new one.</note>. But since a disease is not the same in number by reason of its matter, neither is it so by reason of its **power** <note>original: "virtus"; the active force or "strength" of the disease.</note>, as shall be shown. For matter is the subject in which the illness—which is a quality—is founded. However, the identity of the subject does not cause the identity of its **accidents** <note>A term from Aristotelian logic: an "accident" is a property (like color or illness) that exists in a subject but is not essential to its nature.</note>. For in one subject, there can be accidents differing not only in species, but also in number—such as the color, odor, and taste in an apple. 

Furthermore, matter of this kind often differs not only in "more or less," but also by its own proper essence; for example, when the primary matter of the illness was **choleric** <note>Yellow bile.</note>, but that of the relapse was **melancholic** generated through "burning." Again: just as one whiteness relates to another whiteness, so does the principal illness relate to the relapse, since a similar quality exists in both. But the first whiteness, once introduced and then destroyed, is a different whiteness from the second whiteness later introduced—even if the thing being whitened and the agent doing the whitening are the same, just as happens in the restoration of a line or a painting. For things that are corrupted do not return as the same in number <note>See Aristotle, *On Generation and Corruption*, Book II.</note>. Similarly, the matter could be composed of choleric and phlegmatic humors, such that when the choleric part ceases, after a time the phlegmatic part rises up and induces a relapse. Therefore, a relapse is different from its principal illness. 

In the same way, it is said that to claim they are the same regarding their power is highly unscientific, since power is not part of the definition of a disease, but rather something that fights against it.

Also, power is diversified by reason of the things upon which it acts, so that diverse actions result. For the sun acts differently upon a thick cloud than upon a thin cloud, inducing different shapes and colors—as is clearly shown in the **rainbow** <note>original: "yride"; Iris.</note>—and yet the power remains one. The sun also blackens the skin, whitens linen, hardens mud, and liquefies wax <note>A common medieval example from Alexander of Aphrodisias to show how one cause can have opposite effects based on the material it acts upon.</note>. Furthermore, the power remains one throughout, uniformly, as the body’s dispensing possibility. If we followed this, one would conclude that every illness occurring to a person would be "one." And therefore, it is quite unscientific to say a relapse and a principal illness are one in number based on the matter and the power of the illness.

How they might be one or another by reason of the essence of the disease can be understood from what follows. Because of this, those who later corrected themselves say the question can be solved better and more briefly, testifying that a disease can be considered in two ways: first, insofar as it has a **successive being**, and in this way the principal is numerically different from the relapse because "rests" <note>Periods of quiet or remission.</note> multiply the succession through interruption. Or second, according to the **qualitative being** it has, which is compared to the matter remaining in the body and is opposed to nature; and in this way, they say the principal illness and the relapse are one in number. 

But now they seem to fail more than before. For when things directed toward an end are natural, they share the same nature as the end. If a disease is a succession toward a qualitative order of **lesion** <note>An injury or functional impairment.</note>, then if the lesion is one, the quality is one; if there are many lesions, there are many qualities. Since, therefore, the "succession" consists of many parts (as they admit), there will also be many qualities in number. Thus, one quality is introduced through the first succession (the principal illness), and another through the succession that the relapse induces. Furthermore, as will be shown, a disease is not simply a "succession," but rather a quality or a primary disposition of that category, as was said in Distinction 73. It is also a formal thing existing in act.

Regarding the third point, it must be known that "disease" can be taken in two ways. One way is **properly**, insofar as its being consists in actually harming the body's operations; and in this sense, a relapse is not the same illness as the principal one. For the first has already ceased its action. Rather, it is another, since a "rest" has intervened between them. This is true even if the matter and power were entirely the same. This is declared because, first, a disease is a movement or alteration against nature once it has arrived at a lasting disposition. This is said on account of the **accident** <note>The symptoms.</note>, which is a movement or alteration against nature before it has reached a lasting state, but remains in succession. To have unity of movement, three things are required: unity of the thing moved, the species of the movement, and the time <note>Aristotle, *Physics*, Book V.</note>. Now, even granted that the thing moved and the species of movement are one, the time will not be one when a preceding movement is interrupted by a rest. This is confirmed because a thing corrupted and then generated never returns as the same in number, but only in species, since they occur at different moments. Therefore, an intermittent illness will not properly be "one," as a continuous illness having a single movement is.

<margin>
Hippocrates, Aphorisms.
</margin>

Perhaps this is what **Hippocrates** meant in the fourth section of the *Aphorisms*: "In whichever fevers rigors occur daily, the fevers are daily resolved." Again: a quality introduced by different movements is different. But a disease is a quality introduced by different movements: namely, the principal and the relapse. Hence the second aphorism: "Nature, in a relapse, necessarily undergoes the same transformation as in putrefaction." Some, however, not only say this but also usefully claim that a difference in time does not prevent identity, since time is not part of the definition of the product. These people wish to preserve the idea that even a "numerical resurrection" <note>A theological/philosophical parallel: the idea of a thing returning as its exact self.</note> is possible. 

From these points, it is concluded that the principal illness and the relapse are **not entirely the same illness in number**. However, if "disease" is taken **improperly**, as referring to its substance—not in act, but in its aptitude and dependence upon that ultimate act of operation—then it can be conceded in some way that the principal and the relapse are one illness. This is because the matter is either one, or nearly one and closely related, and there remains in the limbs a certain "readiness" through which that which is "in habit" suddenly becomes "in act." Because of the small distance between the principal and the relapse, it *seems* to be one illness. Hence, in the second book of the *Physics*, it is said that the intellect regards such small differences as being nothing. And especially, this does not matter to the intellect of the physician, who seeks knowledge sensibly and figuratively regarding almost all things. Thus, let the truth of the present matter appear briefly.

->### Whether a Relapse is Worse than its Root?<-

...of the question. One can subsequently apply the distinction of **Aristotle** <note>original: "Az."; likely referring to the Philosopher, Aristotle.</note> given concerning one and the same proposition. For if we speak of "one" thing that is called "one" by **continuity** in a disease, this is not "continuity" in the proper sense, since continuity belongs to magnitude or quantity. Thus, in motion and time, continuity exists only through celestial magnitude, according to the fourth book of the **Physics** <note>Aristotle’s *Physics*, Book IV, discusses the relationship between time, motion, and magnitude.</note>. However, the principal illness and the relapse have the same "remote subject" <note>The body or the person.</note>, but the "proximate subject" <note>The specific humor or organ affected.</note> is diversified, though not greatly. Similarly, they have a unity of **genus** <note>They belong to the same category of illness.</note>, but not **indivisibility**. For although a quality is indivisible in itself, it is nevertheless divided by quantity. For "however great the surface is, so great will you say the whiteness is," as it says in the **Categories** <note>original: "predicamentis"; Aristotle's *Categories*.</note>. Indeed, the unity of analogy, of genus, and of species is present in the "root" illness and the relapse, but as was shown, proper numerical unity is not. Regarding the aforementioned things, one might **doubt**, because a disease, properly understood, is said to involve an **act** <note>original: "actum"; an active state of being.</note>. And thus, a definition, since it states the true essence of a thing, consists primarily of the "act" which is the **form**, and not that which is the **operation**. For the parts of a definition express a relationship and not the act; thus the definition of a disease is not given through its form, but through that which is **accidental** to it. It must be said that a disease is made known through its act. This is apparent because the boundary and difference between health and sickness is the **noticeable impairment of functions** in the body <note>original: "sensibilis lesio operationum in regni"; a standard Galenic definition of disease.</note>, as stated in the first book *On Disease*. Every noticeable impairment is "in act." For the natural and vital functions never cease from their act in a healthy person. And if the "animal" <note>Mental/voluntary functions.</note> functions sometimes rest, as is shown in **sleep**, this was mentioned before. Here, however, it refers to a certain **potentiality** and **languor** of a healthy body rather than a perfect state of health. For sleep is not "natural" in the proper sense, but is rather called so by a certain commonality of the name. Regarding the reasoning, it must be said that this is true of proper definitions, such as those of **substances**. For they alone properly possess an "essence" or a definition. **Accidents**, however, have them only improperly and through "addition," according to the seventh book of the **Metaphysics** <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, Book VII, discusses how only substance has a primary definition.</note>.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
**It is also doubted** whether a body is healthy or sick during the time of the **intermission** <note>The period between the first bout of illness and the relapse.</note>. To this, some "neutralizers" respond that it is neither. But one must consider whether, from the preceding events, the most powerful operations remain, and especially if the natural ones are sensibly hindered. In this case, it can be called "sick," as most often happens in a **phlegmatic** <note>An illness caused by the humor phlegm.</note> intermittent fever. Or, if they are not manifestly hindered, it is then still placed within the **latitude of health**. And much more time intervenes between the principal and the relapse. Regarding the fourth point and the first, it must be said that the principal and the relapse are not truly one illness in number; and if any illness seems to be the same in number, there is nonetheless no unity of motion and body existing there, which is the most powerful cause of any unity. Regarding the second, something similar has already been said. Regarding the other, it must be said that in time they are not the same in number but in species, since the middle time in which there was no affliction distinguishes between those times. Times are not entirely equal in number, because the principal illness can vanish or be hidden in the beginning, the increase, the peak, and sometimes even in the decline. But a relapse—and especially if one escapes from it—has four distinct stages of disease. For an **anxious** <note>original: "Anxiq"; possibly a proper name or a description of a specific patient case.</note> man properly had a relapse since [the disease] had always remained with him until the 44th day, although the fever and thirst were present at some times and not at others. That was not the principal illness itself, but rather an accident of the underlying condition. The sharp reasoning of the opposite side concludes that the principal and the relapse were not truly one illness. But in a second and improper sense, as has been declared, they can be one illness in whatever way.

### DIFFERENCE 110.

# ## That a relapse is not worse than its root
# ## or the principal illness is shown:

<margin>a.</margin>
Because a primary and universal cause has more influence on its effect than a secondary and particular cause. This is according to **David the Jew** <note>original: "Dauid Iudez"; likely referring to Abraham ibn Daud or the author/translator of the *Liber de Causis*.</note> in *On Causes*. But the "root" cause of the sickness was primary and universal, while the relapse is secondary and particular. Likewise, a cause is more effective than its effect. And the relapse seems to be generated from the principal effect. Furthermore, a relapse harms less than the root illness. For on account of the principal illness, the **matter** <note>The humors causing the disease.</note> is diminished. Since in a sickness, nature always strives to consume and overcome it. When the matter is diminished, the sickness is rendered less severe. Furthermore, a relapse can occur from a slight cause, such as is manifest from a small error [in regimen], which can be quickly corrected by nature or art. Again, it happens that the principal illness is continuous, while the relapse is **intermittent**. Just as it rarely happens that a blood-fever or another continuous fever falls into an intermittent **tertian** or **quartan** fever <note>Fever patterns: tertian (every 3rd day) and quartan (every 4th day).</note>. A continuous fever is worse than an intermittent one of the same type. Also, those accustomed to bearing labors—even if they are weak old men—are harmed less than strong young men, according to the second book of the **Aphorisms** <note>Hippocrates, *Aphorisms*, Book II, aphorism 49: "Those who are accustomed to endure habitual labors, even if they be weak or old, bear them better than strong and young persons who are not accustomed to them."</note>. But someone suffering the principal illness and the relapse suffers less because he is more accustomed to suffering than one suffering only the principal illness. Therefore, a relapse is less severe than its root.

<margin>Question.</margin>
**The opposite** is also shown by the fourth book of the *Aphorisms* and the principle of **critical days**. Furthermore, the principal illness weakens the **virtue** <note>The body's "vital force" or "strength."</note>, and the relapse does similarly. But a lesion added to a lesion prostrates the same [virtue] further. Likewise, a relapse often occurs because the matter was not evacuated in the principal illness; that matter, moved in the relapse, seems to be greater than before. Since from an excess of nourishment, the matter of the disease continually increases. For this reason, a relapse is worse than its root. Regarding the first point, it should be known that it was sufficiently noted in the previous "difference." Know indeed that relapsing happens to many when the illness did not have a **crisis** <note>The turning point of a disease.</note> or its proper end. According to the second book of the *Aphorisms*: "Remains left behind in diseases after a crisis are wont to cause relapses." And especially when the crisis was subcutaneous and weak, such as in **smallpox, jaundice, scabies**, and the like. This relapsing can happen for many reasons. Either on account of the diversity of the matter—as when there is a mixture of **choleric** and **phlegmatic** humors producing the disease; nature is incited first and more strongly against the choleric humor since it is more "unbridled." When that is conquered, the disease seems to cease, because the phlegmatic matter is cold and viscous and not as mobile or sharp. But afterwards—namely, when a "ferment" occurs from an excess of nourishment—the matter is made active and rises up. For bodies that are not pure...

Using Aristotelian logic and Hippocratic aphorisms, the text explores how bodily habituation and the depletion of "matter" (humors) can make a relapse feel less intense, even while the body's overall strength is further compromised.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a scholastic medical and philosophical discussion.
