->### Whether a Relapse is Worse than its Original Root?<-

...the more you nourish [impure bodies], the more you harm them. Or it may be due to the celestial power over the body. For it is evident that the Moon—both on **critical days** <note>Days of a disease when a change or "crisis" is expected.</note> and in the **Centiloquium** <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy.</note>—may be applied to certain fortunate stars at someone's birth, such as Jupiter or Venus. By these, nature is strengthened and the malice of the disease is put to sleep; the sickness seems to be managed and to have reached its end. But when the Moon reaches unfortunate stars, such as Mars and Saturn, or a conjunction, the battle rises up again; hence **relapses** are most frequently found, unless it happens from a glaring error hindering the Moon. This occurs especially from Mars, Saturn, combustion, the **Burned Path** <note>original: "via combusta"; a specific section of the Zodiac considered unlucky.</note>, Scorpio, or an eclipse. 

It can also happen from an error committed by any doctor, the infirm person, or a bystander, or from coinciding external things. On the part of the doctor: when he administers **opiates**, such as the "Royal Phylonium" <note>A famous ancient opiate-based electuary used for pain and sleep.</note> and the like, before the digestion of the matter and some evacuation of it. Some "diverters of nature" act this way to make a paroxysm cease for a time, such as in a **quartan fever** <note>A fever that recurs every four days.</note> or another. For those opiates chill the matter and thicken it, so that the "antecedent cause" cannot be led to the "conjoined" state. Eventually, when the power of these drugs is overcome by natural heat, the antecedent cause rises up again afterward into putrefaction and conjunction. This also happens because of the administration of hot medicines at the time of the disease's intermission, as if to alter the chilled state or restore the appetite; and also in other ways contained under these. 

Diseases more prone to incur a relapse are **acute fevers**, which leave a dormant heat in the viscera. Also diseases of the brain, chest, and specifically **catarrhs**, and of the stomach, liver, spleen, and kidneys. This is because these are either weak or receptive, or because they labor for the whole body. And especially when those recovering from these passions have not truly healed.

<margin>❦</margin> Regarding the **second** point, it must be known that some, moved by the speech and arguments of **Avicenna**, have pronounced absolutely that a relapse is worse than its "root" <note>The original instance of the illness.</note>. But what follows will soon clarify this. 

Regarding the **third** point, it must be known that one kind of relapse is worse than its root, and another is not. For one occurs from an internal, hidden cause, or without an [apparent] cause; and this is worse than its root. Hence at the beginning of the **Critical Days**: a disease that seems to rest without a manifest evacuation—as if neglected by an abscess—will return more severe than it was at the beginning. Wherefore, in the fourth [book] of the **First Canon** <note>A reference to Avicenna's *Canon of Medicine*.</note>, it is said: A relapse is worse and more vehement than its root, because its malice is coming and staying while the **vital force** <note>original: "uirtus"; the body's natural strength or power.</note> is weak, especially when no evacuation preceded it at the start. For sometimes no evacuation precedes, and sometimes only a weak, small one. Thus that disease is said to be worse in which the vital force is found to be weaker. But this is most common in a relapse, since the force has been weakened by the principal illness, so that its injury seems greatest, even if it is not injured simply by itself. And because of this, **Avicenna** said: That relapse is worse which is faster and occurs with a weaker vital force. Therefore his counsel is that one should not begin a cure in such a case until the mode of the disease is manifest, for it is usually severe. 

There is another relapse opposite to this one, happening from a manifest, external, "preserving cause," such as from an error in the four things to be observed in the cure of any disease according to **Hippocrates**. Because it happens later, and with a constancy of the vital force and a preceding evacuation, such a relapse might not become worse than its root. Thus we have seen many relapses less afflictive than their principal [illness]. Hence, **Avicenna** says it is safer for a relapse to happen from an error in the regimen than to happen by itself while the regimen is correct. For a relapse rising from error, since it is more manifest because it happens from external things, can be better helped by someone than if it happened from an internal hidden cause; nor is its malice proportionately as great as that of a hidden internal cause. Let the truth, therefore, shine briefly from these things.

Regarding the **fourth** point, for the first [argument] it must be said: although the primary force (that is, more power) flows into the secondary particular part, it is not therefore more "intense." For the particular part gives a more contracted existence, and specifies the form from the matter... as in the generation of a horse or a man. Or, the primary cause is not more "primary" and universal than the cause of the relapse. For the cause of both is, as shown earlier, truly one principle. 

From this it also appears what should be said to the second. It also happens that a cause works an effect more strongly when it finds this matter more disposed than that. To the other, it must be said that many times the matter of the disease is not diminished in its progress but is increased more; and this if the disease is unhealthful. For matter in a state of recovery is less than at the beginning; but in those about to die, it is otherwise. To the other, what should be said has already been seen. To the next, it should be said that a relapse can be less terrifying than its root, unless it is accompanied by a total debility of the vital force. The distinction has already been seen. Eighty-eight. What was sought by the sharp arguments of the opposite side has appeared from the premises.

<margin>The subject is assumed in every science. Book 1 of the Metaphysics.</margin>
<margin>Opposite: The Commentator [Averroes] on the 2nd book of the Physics. Galen in the Tegni.</margin>

->### Whether a Science Proves Its Own Subject?<-

❦ By the creation of that which has been said—that the **subject** is assumed in a science—it seems to be deduced that **no science proves its own subject**. Rather, it is believed to receive everything from another, superior science. Hence, in the first book of the **Metaphysics**: No science ought to establish that its own subject exists. 

Furthermore, if it did prove it, it would be from things prior to it; but nothing is said to be more primary and known than the subject itself. For one of the sciences would fall into another, and a demonstration would happen to descend from "genus into genus," and a circularity would occur—which **Aristotle** rejects regarding "priors and posteriors." Thus, it would admit into a science something that is not its own. For that reason, all sciences are led one into another, until finally all are elevated in demonstration into **Metaphysics**, since it is more ancient and worthy than the others (Metaphysics, book 3). And into **Logic** probably, since it has the way to the principles of all methods in the **Topics**. Therefore, no science proves its own subject. 

The opposite of these things is seen by **The Commentator** <note>Averroes.</note> in the second book of the **Physics**, and by **Galen** in the **Tegni** <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*, known in the Middle Ages as the *Tegni*.</note>.

# Whether Eggs are Suitable in Fevers

...proving this therapeutic principle by induction and example: that every cure is performed through its own proper means. Regarding the first point, it must be known that what a science is, along with its subject, stands as known from the preceding remarks. However, what a "differentiation of proof" is will be seen in the following. Regarding the second point, it must be known that **Aristotle** <note>Abbreviated as ".A." in text.</note> seems to wish that no science (as has been touched upon) proves its own subject. On this point, the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> charges the aforementioned **Aristotle** with a second "failing": claiming that although a science does not prove its subject through "demonstration," it may do so through a "sign" <note>original: "siue eē aut signi"; referring to the distinction between *demonstratio quia* (of the fact) and *propter quid* (of the cause).</note>. What these differences are will appear in the present discussion. Regarding the third point, it must be known that a science can indeed approve its subject from those things which come after, and declare it to us as things more known to us or to our adversaries. Just as **Avicenna** <note>Abbreviated as ".Ay." in text.</note> defends the first principles against the ignorant and the perverse in the first book of his *Metaphysics*—such as the principle that regarding anything, either an affirmation or a negation is true. And that every whole is greater than its part. And he does this by leading those who deny these appearances into more absurd inconveniences. Similarly, it is proved in the first book of the *Physics* that "prime matter" is neither generated nor corrupted; and in the eighth book of the same, the "first [mover]" is proved from its own properties, such as from primary and uniform motion. For it is not unfitting that what is known to nature but unknown to us should be declared through those things which are known to us, since there is a twofold mode of knowing, as the present distinction will show. This is later confirmed by the speech of **Galen**, who speaks of the "resolutive" method based on the notion of the end goal. Regarding the fourth point, it must be said that the exposition of the previously introduced speech, if heard diligently, has now appeared. He does not deny the proof of a subject by any means at all, but only by "simple demonstration" and by "the reason why" <note>original: "dem̄ostratiōe simplicii & p̄pter quid".</note>. This is perhaps what **Averroes** wanted, being stimulated by the ancient predecessors, as both he and **Avenzoar** <note>An influential 12th-century physician from Al-Andalus.</note> strive to prick **Aristotle** on this point. Regarding the other point, it similarly appeared what must be said: that for those things which belong to any art from its own principles—which are the subjects and causes of the art itself, as has been explained—they should be established. And this also applies to things that appear to another. And properly to that which **Galen** will be seen to say in chapter 52.

<margin>P</margin>
A great many predecessors have hesitated over whether **eggs** are suitable in cases of **fever**. This suitability seems to be felt in the eighth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "d̄ īgenio" (De Ingenio Sanitatis).</note>. In the first book of *On Ardent Fevers* <note>original: "In effer̄is" (De Ephemeris/De Febribus).</note>, as well as those that come from smoke and confinement. And in the books on humors, specifically the fourth, following the path of a "thicker diet," such as a few thin, soft-boiled eggs. Also in the cure of a **tertian fever** <note>A fever that recurs every third day, often associated with yellow bile.</note>: when the intention is to provide moisture, the **yolks of eggs** are given. Similarly, they are granted in a **quartan fever** <note>A fever that recurs every fourth day, often associated with black bile.</note>. **Galen**, indeed, in his work *To Glaucon*, provides eggs in cases of burning fever <note>original: "causone"; an acute, high-grade fever.</note> and tertian fevers. And similarly in the twelfth book of *On the Method of Healing*. In a **fainting fever** <note>original: "febre sincopali".</note> arising from thin humors. In the sixth book of **Serapion** <note>A 9th-century Christian physician from Damascus.</note> on hectic fever <note>original: "ethica".</note>: "Give him a yolk of an egg in the morning." And **Avicenna** similarly provides a soft-boiled egg yolk. In a **pestilential fever**, indeed, in his *Discussions* <note>original: "d̄ ionibḡ".</note>: "Give yolks of eggs."
<margin>3</margin>
This is also confirmed by reason. For a fever is cured by its contrary, just as other ailments are. Since, therefore, the fever itself is a "bad complexion" <note>An imbalance of the four bodily humors.</note> that is hot and dry, it will be cured by eggs as if by contraries. For they are cold and moist. This is shown from the parts that constitute them. For they consist of the very white part—which according to physicians is cold and moist, and watery in 

quantity—as well as the membranes and the shell, which are cold; and the yolk which, as seen before, pertains to the "earthy" element, but according to physicians is held to be temperate. Thus, when all parts of the egg are diligently inspected, they incline toward coldness and a dormant moisture, as was declared concerning milk in chapter 48. Furthermore, according to **Hippocrates** <note>Abbreviated as "Y." (Ypocras).</note> and **Aristotle**: the cure is the vital force or "nature." But eggs are most proportionately suited to nature. Indeed, they are grouped with the testicles of roosters and with wine. They increase the natural heat, which is weak and besieged in fevers. 
Again, eggs tend toward equality. But a febrile nature ascends to the third or fourth degree, since it sensibly hinders or destroys action. However much they are "temperate," they are [relatively] cold, and especially so in respect to someone so high in heat and dryness. Since even lukewarm things reduce heat. This is also shown by lukewarm oil: it is hot to a cold body, and cold to a hot one. Eggs are therefore suitable in fevers. On the opposite side, however: because they are not used by everyone or expressed by the majority.

Again, it is not the task [of the physician] to increase the strength of the sick, but rather to preserve it as it is found—according to the first *Aphorism* <note>Aphorisms of Hippocrates.</note>. But eggs, as touched upon, increase strength greatly. Furthermore, those with fevers have "impure bodies." "The more you nourish such [impure bodies], the more you harm them"—according to the second *Aphorism*. Eggs are indeed primarily nutritious, as has been said. Therefore, they are not suitable in fevers. Regarding the first point, it must be known what a fever is, and what else has been seen regarding it in chapter 87. However, here we should understand "chicken eggs." For a term used in an absolute sense is to be taken in its best form. And know that although **Aristotle** says they tend toward heat, he means they tend toward equality, and the white tends toward coldness and the yolk toward heat. Certainly, as touched upon before, it must be said that they approach coldness and moisture in the first degree; since even for the yolk, 
<margin>Almasor</margin>
**Rhazes** <note>original: "Almasōris"; referring to Abu Bakr al-Razi's *Liber ad Almansorem*.</note> in his third book places it as "temperate." Whence the *Aggregator* <note>Likely referring to the *Aggregator Brixiensis* or a similar medical compendium.</note> says: "The composition of an egg is slightly colder than a temperate body." For it cools with a coldness that is itself temperate. Regarding the second point, it must be known that whatever 
<margin>3</margin>
opinion has been held on this, it is found in the arguments. For this the previous remarks showed. For some commonly provide eggs in fevers. Others, however, avoid them as much as they can. What should be said on this third point will appear. Regarding the third point, it must be known that once the indications for those things given in fevers have been previously noted, it can be diligently judged whether eggs are fitting in fevers. For if we attend to the "virtue" <note>The vital power or life force of the patient.</note> which alone seeks food to be strengthened—and especially when it has become weak—then eggs are suitable. Since they invigorate it, being not a little proportionate to the spirits and the blood. They are also sufficiently digestible, and specifically the yolk provides much nourishment and little waste. And it is better in fevers—and specifically those requiring moistening—that these be given with that intention as the disease progresses. And when the matter has already been digested and lessened more than at the beginning. This is supported because when a disease or its accidents dissolve the vital force, one must soon descend to strengthening that force. This is accomplished by food, according to the first *Aphorism*; for then the indication taken from the vital force overshadows all others, as all things in *The Method of Healing* teach. But if we look at things [against nature]...

# Whether the Menstrual Flow is Natural

...beyond nature, as with a disease or an accident. Thus, it should be said that they [eggs] are by no means simply suitable in all cases of fever. For if they possess a cause, such as when the humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which medieval doctors believed governed health.</note> do not harmonize, they do not alter that cause through an opposite quality, since they exist according to their own temperament, as has been seen. And it has been seen that [nature] never adapts or evacuates those things that are digested unless it happens by a strong force of nature, as seen in the confirmation of the "curer of diseases." But rather, they [eggs] are by their nature easily alterable and corruptible; just as with milk, they are composed of diverse natures and substances (as was touched upon), and they convert more into the material for the growth of whatever they are added to. And specifically, when the wine has been cold and marshy, or hot and odorless juice <note>original: "chanchimis"; likely a variation of 'chyle' or digestive juice</note>. They do not suit a disease like a fever, since they are not simply and directly opposed to it, through which cure is achieved and completed in all things. Likewise, that which is oily, easily flammable and corruptible, and provides much nourishment, is not appropriate in fevers, specifically those involving the humors. Such is the nature of the egg, as its oil shows, as does its heterogeneity. 

<margin>Alchemy.</margin>
As in the secrets of alchemy, which aptly elicits the four elements <note>The theory that eggs contain earth (the shell), water (the white), air (the membrane), and fire (the yolk).</note> from it, its conversion into blood is not insignificant. Thus, in the same way, it is shown that in fevers it does not suit the accident except in part, since they [the fevers] receive their existence and vigor from them, unless perhaps they are considered in terms of their strength and the restoration of the same, as was touched upon. Thus, in fevers, and particularly in those things that are beyond their nature, eggs are simply not rejected; but they are used for the purpose of moistening the parts, specifically at the end of the illness, as **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."; referring to the Greek philosopher and natural scientist.</note> perceived. And they are no less suitable in dry and hectic <term>Hectic fever|A chronic, wasting fever often associated with consumption or dehydration.</term> fevers, either because of their inclination (as has been seen) toward a certain coldness and humidity. However, because the limits of the material are far distant from the direct opposite, and since the matter of the egg is said to be easily inflamed, they perhaps aggravate the fever further, especially when it is intense, as is shown by the excess of yolks in those who cannot support them after a struggle. For coldness acting upon heat is approved [as a cure]; but because of its greater resistance, it eventually congeals the cold things, as stated in the first book of *Meteorologica* <note>Aristotle's work on natural phenomena.</note>. Therefore, eggs are rejected in such an intention in fevers, and not a little strangely.

Regarding the fourth point, it is now clearly stated. For at first, he does not directly offer eggs in the aforementioned fevers. But he says that "pharmacological foods" <note>Foods that act like medicine.</note> are not suitable, but rather those which, along with providing sufficient nourishment, produce little superfluity [waste]; among these, he enumerates eggs along with other things. And it also appeared that he allows eggs for the sake of bodily strength, and not for the fever itself. And therefore he calls them "sippable" <note>original: "sorbilia"; referring to soft-boiled or liquid eggs.</note>, few, and subtle, so that the harm they bring to the disease is minimized. In a tertian fever <note>A fever that spikes every third day, traditionally associated with yellow bile.</note>, he also allows them for the cause of moistening, as was seen; however, he does not offer them immediately, but toward the end, where he adds: "just as one gives them at the end for the extremities," and finally he says: "and the yolks of eggs." In a quartan fever <note>A fever that spikes every fourth day, traditionally associated with black bile.</note>, however, he allows eggs for the purpose of moistening, and then to preserve health through three weeks. But as for **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."; the 2nd-century Roman physician whose work dominated medieval medicine.</note> offering eggs in "causus" <note>A high, acute, burning fever.</note> and in choleric fevers—either "sippable" or without the skin—he perhaps looked to their moistening and the smoothness they induce, specifically in the rough artery <note>term: "aspera artaria"; the trachea or windpipe.</note>. Or because these things, as **Avicenna** <note>original: "Aui."; the 11th-century Persian physician and philosopher.</note> touched upon, are more beneficial at the end.

---

Finally, I do not much approve of the discourse in *To Glaucon* <note>Referring to Galen’s "Ad Glauconem," a therapeutic manual.</note>, nor does the same **Galen** in chapter 64 of the twelfth [book]. Eggs and certain meaty things are for the preservation of strength, which is especially important in the fainting of syncope <note>Fainting or sudden loss of consciousness.</note> mentioned before, as the name itself denotes. But in a hectic fever where the cause is material, they are suitable not because of the fever, but because of the consumption and dryness. For the prostrate strength requires comforting, and the dried body requires moistening. Yolks are also permitted in a pestilential fever for the comforting of the heart; for these invigorate and protect it, as **Avicenna** says in *On the Medicines of the Heart*. Indeed, every fever is properly an affliction of the heart. Regarding the reasons: to the first, it is now said by **Aristotle** that it does not suit the fever directly. To the second, it is said in chapter 53: for it does not cure the nourishment immediately, but by means of fortifying the strength; for by accident it is granted that eggs are most suitable in fevers for the sake of strength. To the other similar point, the answer has appeared. For one contrary... the other so that it may more strongly resist and blunt it; however, that which rises from the opposite (as has been seen) strengthens it further again, as lime and cold water show in chapter 40; which especially happens when the contraries are equal in power. These also appear as opposite parts when one considers the fever simply and not the strength, or the moistening, or the improper opposition.

For a fuller declaration of that which was touched upon concerning the flow of blood, and especially the **menstrual flow**, we must ask: **Whether this flow is natural.** And it seems that it is not natural. Because that is natural which is from an intrinsic principle of cause, according to the *Physics* and *On the Generation of Animals*, book one; and that which is not from any arriving molestation. But this flow is seen to occur not from an intrinsic source, but from an extrinsic one, such as the moon; hence in the third book of the *Crises*, through my translation, the **Moon** governs the pre-established cycles of menstruation in women. 

<margin>The Moon ☽</margin>
It is caused because she is stimulated by nature in quantity, quality, or both; for every act is produced in her by these two. Furthermore, the evacuation of that which is a familiar child of nature is no longer properly natural to it, but entirely beyond nature. Such is the opinion of **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a 10th-century physician and philosopher.</note> in his 30th chapter. Further, the egress of that to which things beyond nature are associated is not natural. Of this kind is the menstrual flow. For it is accompanied by the dissolution of continuity and divisions, such as anxiety, headache, and the like. Furthermore, sweat—which seems even less natural—is against nature according to **Diocles** <note>Diocles of Carystus, a 4th-century BC Greek physician.</note> in his first book, 

<margin>Diocles. ❧</margin>
even though its matter is less friendly to nature than blood. For it is itself not a small part of the choleric humor. Likewise, the same would be ordered toward different ends, such as toward the lack of flow and retention, which is soon ordered for the support of the fetus. Again, such a flow seems more natural in brute animals, since nature thrives more in them than in the "animal of man" [humanity]. But in them, such a flow of blood is not seen to exist. Therefore, this is not natural. On the opposite side is the opinion of the other physicians; hence in the fourth book of *On the Generation of Animals*: Menstruation occurs according to nature when the monthly cycles fail. In the sixth book of *The Theory*: The egress of menstruation is natural. Furthermore, crises and evacuations that help nature are natural; and such is this flow.

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on fevers and the medicinal properties of eggs into a detailed physiological examination of the "menstrual flow." It establishes the natural causes of menstruation, its definitions, and its relationship to the lunar cycle and the female temperament.</meta>

<margin>Menstruation</margin>
**The menstrual flow** is a monthly course, as its retention in those who are not pregnant clearly shows. Furthermore, it is a natural thing, the causes of which are natural. The causes of this type of flow are, for instance, the moon and the natural expulsive force <note>The "expulsive force" was one of the four "natural virtues" in medieval medicine, responsible for ridding the body of waste.</note>.

<margin>2</margin>
It is therefore natural. Regarding the first point, it must be known that "natural" is derived from **nature**. What nature itself is, and how many types there are, is seen in Difference 90. Furthermore, nature by its power adheres to a single path and order. Particular nature is twofold: one is the lowest, which is variable and indeterminate due to its imperfection, failing to observe order and beauty. The other is a medium between these two, or that which belongs to mixed things. This varies in many ways, according to whether it approaches the superior nature more closely, or departs from it according to order and its opposite. For it is directed toward an end and beauty by the superior, but is distracted by the inferior. Whence, in the second book of *The Curer of Diseases*: "Almost everything beautiful—however beautiful, orderly, and skillful it may be here—glides down from above." And the reasoning of the same authors is: "From those things which are in the heavens, all things here are ordered, for their power governs all." Likewise in the first book of the *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle's work on natural phenomena.</note>. Indeed, nature is spoken of in many ways by the physician, as seen in Difference 9. This "middle nature" is what is mostly discussed here, specifically called the **regulative nature**, and also the **complexion** <note>The "complexion" or "temperament" refers to the specific balance of the four humors in an individual.</note>. For the nature itself acts as the principal agent, while the complexion acts as the instrument. *Menstruum* (menstruation), or more beautifully *mensibile*, is named in imitation of the Greek word for "month." For *amen* is a month, and from that comes *minion*, that is, the menstrual flow. Or rather, it is named after *mira*, which is the **moon**. For it flows, as was said, when the lunar months are failing. For the movement of women occurs around the waning moons, as stated in the ninth book of the *History of Animals* <note>Aristotle, *Historia Animalium*.</note>. This menstrual flow is a natural purification appropriate to women, consisting of a "weary blood" <note>original: "sanguis languorosi"; likely referring to blood that is stagnant or surplus.</note> descending from the womb at a certain proportion; through its exit, the woman's body is rendered purified, so that it is afterward better suited for conception.

<margin>3</margin>
It was called "natural" because it is observed in a sufficiently healthy woman who is governed by a more laudable regimen. It exits in the proper quantity and time. For without these, it exits in an unnatural way, as will be touched upon in the twenty-first section. 
<margin>See book 3, i.</margin>
<margin>History, book 6.</margin>
The word "appropriate" was added because other animals also have purifications of this kind, though they are almost invisible and not in the form of blood, but rather a mucilaginous, whitish surplus. Whence, in the sixth book of the *History of Animals*: "In walking animals, purifications of the menses occur, yet not in the same quantity as in women." In the females of other animals, the flow occurs only externally; but in women, it is most manifest. For the woman emits the greatest segregation of all animals, since the female is full of blood and has very long and abundant menses, according to the third book of the *History*. The cause of this is the **coldness** and especially the **humidity** of her complexion; because of these, surplus fluids are generated during digestion which are mostly cold, watery, and prone to flowing. Voracity <note>excessive eating</note> and idleness increase all these in the coldness of the belly. Nor is this surplus blood transmitted to other parts, as it is in other animals to horns, hooves, the emergence of teeth, or thick, long, and dense hair. 

**Empedocles**, however, posited that menstruation happens to a woman because of heat, and that for this reason, she is hotter than a man (Difference 28). But the man lacks menstruation because he is hot and dry, sober, exercised, and more hairy. It was said "to women" because the subject matter of the discourse requires it, although the flows of women extend to other things. "Blood" is understood here as its mass, according to how it stands ready to flow. And therefore it can be called "weary." It was added "from the womb" because the **womb** in the body of the female is like the **bilge in a ship** <note>A common medieval metaphor: the womb acts as a collection point for the body's waste fluids, just as the bilge collects waste water at the bottom of a ship.</note>, receiving all cold and watery superfluities. For all the veins and arteries of the body fall into it. It was said "at a certain proportion" because natural proportions are not entirely defined, but have a wide range, as seen in the twenty-seventh section. According to the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*: "Certainly, a fixed proportion for the menstrual flow is not established for women, but it reasonably happens during the waning months." And therefore something regarding its change was added. A **period** or **circuit** is a revolution returning to the same point from which it started. This circuit exists in three ways: one is the life-span, another is more specific, and there is a middle between them. The first is the entire time in which the menstrual flow begins and ends, discussed in the ninth book of *Theory*. Menses begin in the 10th year (at its completion) and do not exceed the 14th year for their start. They cease in some in the 35th year; in others thereafter until the completion of the 40th. Also in the sixth book of the *Viaticum* <note>A famous medical handbook by Ibn al-Jazzar, translated by Constantine the African.</note>: "Menstruation happens to women when they enter the age of 14 years. However, if it hastens, it starts in the 12th. But the natural removal of menses is after 50 years; in others in the 40th; in some in the 35th, especially in those who are very fat and fleshy." Whence, in the third part of section 21: "The removal of menses is hastened for some women, ending in the 35th or 40th years of their life. And for others it is delayed until they reach 50 years." And I myself have seen a woman still menstruating at sixty. The **middle period** is the time falling between one menstruation and another, concerning which **Hali Abbas** <note>A famous Persian physician (930–994 AD) known in the West as Hali Abbas.</note> says: "The time which is between two circuits is from 20 days and upward, as far as two months; those which happen after this are not natural menses." Whence, in the ninth book of the *History*: "Continuously in each month, menses proceed for a few days." 
<margin>See book 3, i.</margin>
<margin>3</margin>
In the third part of section 21: "The measure of menstruation is such that a woman menstruates every month up to 30 days; and that which is below that, falling on the 15th or 17th day, is not natural." 
<margin>Law</margin>
And therefore the **Law** states: "A woman who is purged twice in a month is not healthy." 
<margin>4</margin>
The **more specific period** is the hour <note>duration</note> during which the natural menses exit. And on this, Hali Abbas says: "The length of the menstrual circuit in a healthy woman lacking vice is two days, and is extended up to seven as a longer duration." That which is more is judged unnatural. Whence, in the ninth book of the *History*: "Those for whom it lasts a short time, two or three days, are changed or purged easily. But those for whom it lasts many..."

<meta>This page continues the physiological discussion from the previous page, specifically addressing the "natural" status of menstruation. It moves from defining the regularity of the cycle to a philosophical and medical defense of why this flow is considered "natural" in women, despite blood loss being "unnatural" in men, and concludes with the influence of the lunar cycle on bodily fluids.</meta>

-> Whether the menstrual flow is natural <-

...and they suffer with difficulty in those days. For if someone insists that these determined periods differ for many women, it must be said, as previously stated, that these times are not sought precisely because of the material being produced continuously, but rather more broadly. For diversity happens in these things to a great degree, such as from the side of the complexion <note>The "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—in an individual.</note>, humor, strength <term>virtutis</term>, and the habits of age, the arrival of region <note>Meaning the climate or geography where the woman lives.</note>, and indeed of all non-natural things. It also seems that **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Halyab."; a famous 10th-century Persian physician</note> allows a wider time for the natural extraction of menses than others. This is indicated by **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."; the most influential medieval medical authority</note> in the chapter on the **Measurement of menstruation**.

Regarding the second point, it must be known that some over-refined people have hesitated whether the menstrual course exists as something natural. Their anxiety will be removed by what is to be said. Regarding the third point, it must be known that the flow of menses is natural just as the output of waste <note>literally "the output of the lower parts," referring to excretion</note> exists. However, so that this may shine forth more fully, and before it was qualitative, it must be known that "natural" can refer to two things. Either to that which is perfect in the human species, as to the masculine gender, or to the imperfect, as to the feminine. If the former: it refers to that which is preordained in its own output, such as a most temperate and most suitably governed body, such as a healthy body always is, and which is just and certain in years 18 and 20. And thus, not only is the flow of blood in these cases against nature, but as **Diocles** <note>An early Greek physician</note> says, so too is sweat and similarly the reliability of urine. For all such superfluity ought to be excreted insensibly by the body's digestive warmth, except for the seed <note>semen</note>, because it is ordained for the species, and the brain's waste, and that which emanates outward into the hair and nails, as seen in the first book of the *Ars Medica* and the *Therapeutics*. Or it refers to a body receding from this temperament, and thus imperfect according to the third degree of "more or less"; and in this way, some flow of blood could exist as natural, since nature is aided by it in various ways. But if the imperfect gender is inspected, then some flow of blood, like that of the menses, has its nature simply. 

So that a certain flow of blood is entirely natural, like that which occurs by condition, or entirely unnatural, like that which is led from the chest <note>i.e., coughing up blood</note>, regarding how much it offends and in what way. However, some hold a middle ground between these two, so that it can be called natural in comparison to the lower, but unnatural compared to the superior. Just as the middle holds itself compared to the extremes, such an order falls between the natural and the unnatural by moving through the middle. First indeed is the menstrual flow; next, the flow of blood from the nostrils; then from hemorrhoids; then blood in the stools, and specifically a periodic one; then similarly that of vomiting; and finally, the spitting of blood from the chest occurs similarly sometimes. For I have seen sometimes certain hemorrhoidal patients aided periodically from there. The sign of which was that they were troubled before. That the menstrual flow is natural is attested by authority and conquered by reason. Whence, in the first book of *The Generation of Animals*: "The hemorrhoidal flow is because of infirmity, but the menstrual flow is natural." Wherefore, in the **sixth book of the Canon**: "All blood flow, except that which flows in the menses of women, exists outside of nature. But that which is in women is not at all outside of nature unless it exceeds quantity."

And therefore you should know that the flow of blood in other cases exists against nature not only in quantity but in its whole kind. This is also confirmed by reason. First, from the part of the individual, since that is natural which is ordained and happens for the health of nature, since that is its end; and the end and those things before the end are proportional. That which is led out is also harmful in quantity and quality. But such is the menstrual flow sought here. Therefore, for the third time, in summary: Menses, temperate in their quantity and quality, and running in their own time according to their natural custom in every space, are the cause of the woman's health and the cleansing of the body from all harm, both in quantity and quality; and they make her acquire chastity and a lack of desire. By reason of the species, since that which is ordained toward an end is most natural to it. But such is the menstrual flow; for it is directed toward the generation of a likeness to the one from whom it falls, which is most natural, according to the second book of *The Soul* and *The Generation of Animals*. For its extraction preserves the woman's body as healthy, as was said, and prepares it for impregnation thereafter. For after the menstrual purging, for three or four days, impregnation happens more often and more laudably. Thus, this kind of flow is natural, and indeed with a double naturalness.

<margin>
Book 11, ch. 31.
Mesue
</margin>

But from the aforesaid things, a doubt happens. Because it was said that menses occur around the waning moons and more as the months are ending: which does not seem right, since then humidities recede according to **Ptolemy in the *Centiloquium***. For that is in the fourth quadrant. And when the moon is changed in its light, the humidities that it governs ought to be lessened. It must be said that humidities and menses run more at the end of the lunation because of the moon's defect <note>The "defect" refers to the waning phase of the moon</note>, as in the second book of the *Posteriors*. Because of this, the **Nile** <margin>Nilus</margin> flows at the end of the month, that is, the lunar month. Because of this, it is answered that the ending month is more wintry <note>In medieval science, "wintry" means colder and wetter, which encourages the movement of fluids.</note>.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>

But why is the end of the month colder? Because of this, it is added that the moon fails. For when it is invigorated in the full moon, it increases humidities and can rule them by giving power to them. When it fails, being weakened, it cannot govern them or check their motion. And they become rebellious; wherefore they run hither and thither inordinately. Nature, being weakened, works not a little toward this through the coldness and humidity of the month near the moon. And then, the humid things having been made more watery and cold, the expulsive force is strengthened and the retentive force is rendered weak. Whence in the fourth book of *The Generation of Animals*: "A colder and more humid time is rendered at the end of the month, because of the diminution and defect of the moon." And in the same second book: "The coincidence of the months, as when the end of one continues with the beginning of another, are cold because of the moon's defect. Because of which the wintry coincidences of the months are greater in their intervals." From these things and from chapter 68, what must be said is clear. Regarding the fourth point, it must be said to the first that although the moon is an exterior essence, it is nonetheless interior to the mixture <term>mixturae</term> <note>The "mixture" refers to the combination of elements and humors within a living body.</note>. Just as many agents hold themselves thus in the production of their effects. In the same way that the heaven is moved by a principle separated in essence, namely that which is in it by power. See *On the Substance of the Orb*. Similarly, although something is moved by a certain...

<summary>This page argues that menstruation is a "natural" process essential for female health and reproduction, distinguishing it from pathological bleeding like hemorrhoids. It further explains how the waning moon's cold and humid properties weaken the body's ability to retain fluids, thus triggering the monthly flow.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the physiological investigation into the nature of the menstrual flow. Having previously discussed its regularity, the author now addresses the specific quality of the blood—whether it is "pure" or "impure"—and how it serves to nourish the fetus. This leads into Chapter 11, which examines the fundamental relationship between "innate heat" and "radical moisture," the two primary elements that medieval science believed sustained human life.</meta>

...is not acting by violence. Nevertheless, that which is stirred in motion is said to be moved naturally and not violently, because such an excitement in motion arises from a natural act and help. Since it is right for anything to be named after its goal, as stated in **On the Soul** <note>original: "scō de aĩa."; referring to Aristotle's *De Anima*</note>. This is also shown by that ancient saying: "The stomachs are naturally warmest in winter and spring" <note>This is a famous medical aphorism from Hippocrates, explaining how internal heat concentrates inside the body during cold seasons.</note>. And the critical points in a child's development <note>original: "p̃cisiones filiũ crises"</note> are even more praiseworthy and natural as they proceed.

To the next point, it must be said that the menstrual blood being discussed here is not entirely familiar or specific to the nature of the woman; rather, it is rendered as a superfluous, full, cold, and watery fluid, and as something unnatural. Nor is it true blood, but it appears more significant in its color and quantity. Even a small amount of it stains a great deal.

However, the opposite seems true, for regarding the formation of the **embryo** <note>original: "ebrioiꝙ"</note>, it is written: "The fetus attracts to itself the sweetest blood from the mother." And **Galen** <note>A Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years.</note> asserts: "It always desires blood for itself that is sweeter, tastier, and subtle." Such blood is not "superfluous" or "full." To show that he is indeed speaking of menstrual blood, he says: "The blood which was separated from the woman at the time of menstruation becomes nourishment." 

It must be said that menstrual blood is superfluous and impure specifically in relation to the blood that nourishes the woman’s own body. For her body is nourished by the purest blood, since her own "attractive power" is stronger than that of the fetus. However, the sweet and subtle blood that nourishes the fetus is of the same kind as that sent to the breasts to be turned into milk; it is distinct from the part that is retained, becomes impure, and is expelled at the time of birth. 

Indeed, menstrual blood is seen to be five-fold:
1. The part that stands as the matter for the organs <note>as described in Chapter 36</note>, for they are made from blood.
2. The part that nourishes them.
3. The part from which flesh, grease, and fat are generated.
4. The part transmitted to the breasts to be converted into milk.
5. The fifth and more impure part, which is finally led out during birth. 

Thus, the fetus is nourished by the purer part of the menstruation in respect to the more impure parts. For not all of it goes toward nourishment, but only that which is purest. 

To the next point, it must be said that the breaking of continuity <note>original: "solutio ꝙtinuitatis"; a medical term for a wound or cut</note> and the "cuttings" are so slight that no overall injury results, just as a small cut on a finger does not destroy the hand. Although a disease might exist in the part where it is located—since at least the natural actions are harmed—the hand itself is not "diseased" if these actions are not sensibly hindered. Or at least it is natural to bear it and bear it well, which follows thereafter. The answers to the other points have now appeared. 

To the next point, it must be said that it is not unsuitable for the same subject to be ordered toward different things for different reasons. Just as a sailor is the cause of the ship’s safety by his presence, his absence is the occasion of its sinking. For menstrual blood flows outward, helping the individual woman in the present, so that eventually both may concur in a single goal <note>the preservation of the species</note>. To the final point, it must be said that other animals have a menstrual flow once, for the sake of starting and "salting" the process, though not as clearly as in humans, for the reasons already shown.

Menstrual blood is impure and superfluous.
</margin>

# DIFFERENTIA. C. XI.

-> Whether the innate heat consumes more of <-
-> the radical moisture than the influencing heat. <-

Because the **innate heat** <term>calidum innatum</term> <note>The internal, life-sustaining heat humans are born with, similar to a "vital spark."</note> which is within us...

---

...helps in the consumption of the **radical moisture** <term>humidum radicale</term> <note>The "oil" in the lamp of life; the finite bodily fluid that sustains the innate heat. Aging was seen as the drying up of this moisture.</note>. It does this even more than the "influencing" <note>extraneous or environmental</note> heat. But because the innate heat is a "running" or active heat, it must perform its work because the disposition of a thing in its being and its operation are similar (according to the second book of **Metaphysics**). 

Now, consuming the radical moisture is a certain action. Furthermore, that which is of more vehement vigor acts more strongly, since every action proceeds from a power. But that is the innate heat, since it is the principal instrument of the soul flowing into the body, and it is more natural to it. Again, that which reaches and embraces the radical moisture more vehemently and for a longer time consumes it more, since every action is perfected by contact and time. And such a heat is the "running" innate heat. This is confirmed by an analogy: just as a vehement flame fed by a wick consumes oil more strongly than the surrounding heat, so in this case, the innate heat adheres more strongly. Therefore, the innate heat consumes more of the radical moisture than the influencing heat.

On the contrary: That which has a more vehement power in altering things changes them more strongly. But "running" heat is actual and more "elevated," as will be seen. Also, that which is foreign and occurs suddenly changes and consumes more than its opposite, since everything sudden is a "robber" of nature. Such is the influencing heat compared to the innate heat in respect to the primary moisture. Therefore, the radical moisture is consumed more by the influencing heat than the innate.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that it is necessary to first ask about the "father" <note>likely referring to the primary cause</note>. Second, because an effect receives its being through a cause, we must see what and how many are the causes of the consumption of radical moisture. 

Regarding the first, it must be known that because innate and flowing heat are founded in moisture as the matter in which and from which they exist (since there is no heat without moisture, according to **On Generation and Corruption** and **On the Soul**), every natural agent requires a subject upon which it acts and from which it produces such things. That moisture is two-fold: the "radical" moisture and the "influencing" or "nutritable" moisture. Thus it is necessary to see what these are, for which purpose we must bring in some points from Chapter 48.

It must be known, therefore, that at the hour of intercourse, the **seed** <note>original: "sperma"</note> is "cut off" from the more powerful members of the body, sustained by the virtues and spirits of the three principal parts. According to **Avicenna** <note>original: "Ay."</note>, it is perfected by further digestion in the coiled vessels, or according to other physicians, it is "re-cooked" in the small testicles. When it is cast into the womb, it is attracted by a certain gradual attraction; the womb embraces and retains it with delight, as was seen in Chapters 36 and 37. Around this, a **membrane** <note>original: "ymen"</note> or skin soon forms (as in **History of Animals** Book 9 and **Generation of Animals** Book 2). Hence, **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Y."</note> in "On the Generation of the Embryo" confesses that he saw seed that had fallen from a womb in which moisture appeared in an inner skin, just as if one were to remove the outer shell of an egg. 

This seed, sheltered by the membrane, operates in the manner of **automata** <note>original: "anthomatũ"</note>, that is, through wondrous internal channels (as in the same book, *On Generation*). In these, once the first part is moved, all subsequent parts are moved in succession toward the goal, as he shows...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the formation of the embryo and the physiology of vital forces. Having previously discussed the role of maternal blood, the author now shifts to the specific mechanism of development: the "informative virtue" within the seed and the interplay between the body's internal heat and its fundamental moisture.</meta>

## Whether **innate heat** or **influent heat** more effectively conjoins with **radical moisture**.

Just as in the removal of an obstruction in a water mill, or in machines, or in the game of tiles played by children, where once the first tile is touched, the third is also moved by accident. The principle of this movement of the seed is the power and impulse of the one performing the coitus. Within this, according to **Avicenna** <note>A Persian physician and philosopher, known as Ibn Sina, whose 'Canon of Medicine' was a standard European textbook.</note>, there is a power primarily called "intellect." For **Haly Abbas** <note>An 11th-century Persian physician.</note> and **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay."; referring to the Greek philosopher</note> felt that at the moment of coitus, an intellectual spark exists within the seed which leads it forward. This is called the **informative virtue** <term>virtus informativa: the biological force believed to shape the physical body of the embryo from the raw material of the seed</term> by physicians, and by others it is called the "idol" or the "paternal likeness." 

This power is one of the most noble and wondrous in existence. According to Avicenna, as recounted by the **Commentator** <note>Usually referring to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the famous Andalusian commentator on Aristotle.</note> in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*, it resembles celestial powers rather than merely natural ones. This is because it is not properly an "organized" power like natural ones are, but rather it is an intellectual power that encompasses the word of power. In the same way that it is soft when joined, it is sequestered from these powers and comes with the birth-forces, of which Avicenna and other expositors speak in the 48th chapter.

However, like all other material forms, this power requires a subject to sustain it, so that it may be carried into its work, and instruments through which it may reach and act upon the matter to produce the resulting effect. Its instruments are twofold: **heat** and **light** <note>original: "elare"; likely referring to 'claritas' or 'aery' light/heat</note>. Through these, the matter is made ready for formation by removing conflicting passions—softening what is hard, gathering things that are alike (**homogeneous**), and separating things that are different (**heterogeneous**). For this purpose, it also uses temperate heat as a third operating instrument. 

There is also another specific instrument called **celestial life-giving heat**, which holds contraries together and prevents them from falling apart. It is by this heat that the power principally works, granting to each of the limbs its proper form. Indeed, it rouses from that nature the essence of the limbs, which allows them to remain even after that heat has departed. This was necessary because "elemental" heat <note>heat from the four elements: earth, air, fire, water</note> is not capable of generating any living thing; rather, according to Aristotle, it is more likely to be destructive. 

And so he says: "In all things there exists within the seed that which makes the seeds **generative** <note>original: "gonima"</note>, which is called heat." This, however, is not fire, nor is it merely a power of the elements, but rather it is something trapped within the seed and the frothy substance—that is, within the foamy seed—a certain **spirit** <term>spiritus: in medieval medicine, a refined substance that carries life and sensation through the body</term> that is "co-planted." For all animals have a co-planted spirit by which they are empowered, as discussed in the *Causes of the Motion of Animals*. 

In this spirit, there is a nature proportionate to the order of the stars. And therefore, in things called divine, there exists an elemental quality. When Avicenna speaks of the soul, he says that this substance would be a bodily substance generated from the mixing of the elements, shaped to the likeness of celestial bodies. In the tenth book of the *Medicines of the Heart*, he says it tends toward the likeness of the super-celestial bodies. For this reason, he judges that the spirit is a **luminous substance**. And thus it is said of the visual power that it is either a ray or light. He also says that the heat of all animals, coming from the super-celestial realms, has an effect on the power that the heat of fire cannot have. This is shown by the fact that less damage is done to the eyes by the heat of the sun than by the heat of a fire.

<margin>Subject by uniform distraction.</margin>

Supported and carried by these instruments to its work, the power draws the purest of the **menses** <note>The menstrual blood, which was believed to provide the physical matter for the fetus.</note> to itself so that it may compose the limbs. Among these, it first begins to construct the **heart** as its foundation, so that it may be further supported, attract the menstrual flow more abundantly, and convert it into the "spermatic nature" called **radical moisture** <term>humidum radicale: the fundamental, finite fluid that acts as the "oil" for the lamp of life; its depletion was thought to cause aging and death</term>. 

In this moisture, the **innate heat** <term>calidum innatum: the natural heat one is born with, distinct from the heat of a fever or fire</term>—composed of both fiery and "celestial" heat—subsists. It encompasses that moisture everywhere, like a form encompassing matter. This radical moisture is seen to exist in three forms: 
1. The first is a subtle, airy moisture which is the immediate subject of the innate heat, and is inseparable from it in every way; for as has been said, there is no heat without moisture. 
2. The second is denser than the first, somewhat watery, and acts as the "fuel" <note>original: "pabulum"</note> for the innate heat (as Aristotle says in *The Generation of Animals*). The innate heat runs through its pores and cracks like light through a transparent medium. When this moisture becomes too dense or impure, the innate heat can no longer use it as fuel, nor can the moisture be irradiated by the heat. Therefore, it eventually becomes impure, like wine mixed with water, and is rendered watery and sluggish. 
3. The third is a viscous, tenacious moisture called **glue** <note>original: "gluten"</note>, which holds the parts of the body together in a mixture so that they do not fall away into ashes. This is not sufficient fuel for the innate heat, as it would extinguish the heat before being consumed.

<margin>Radical moisture is internal.</margin>

There remains also another heat, called **running** or **influent heat**. This is generated specifically in the heart from the things consumed and digested internally, created by its own heat, motion, and friction. From the heart, as if from a mine, it is directed through the **arteries** into the entire body to serve as fuel and support for the innate heat. These two heats—the innate and the natural—are sometimes both called "innate" or "of nature." Aristotle says, "the bellies are warm in winter," and Avicenna also speaks of innate heat being within us, implanted in the primary seeds, and serving as a "curing" heat.

From these, according to Avicenna, a natural heat arises which exists as the "form" of the limbs, as Aristotle also says regarding the utility of pulses. These types of heat are also called **spirits**, as shown by Galen.

<margin><note>Small profile head sketch</note></margin> 

For heat is said to "warm" and to "give life," since it is the chief principle of life. Hence, names have followed this: some call the heat the **soul** <note>original: "aia(m)"; anima</note>, because we are said to "live" on account of heat. In the first book of *On the Soul*, the Greek word for "to live" is *Zin*. When the letter *Eta* <note>original: "id. i. lra. id"</note> is written, it signifies to be hot or to glow. When it is doubled, or when combined with *Iota* or *Upsilon* to form a diphthong, it denotes living. The **spirit**, meanwhile, is said to breathe, to pulse, to penetrate, and to ventilate. Therefore, it is properly found in those who have a heart.

The subject in which the **influent heat** is sustained, acting as its vehicle, is the **nutritive moisture**. This is created from food by the power of the heart and the arteries. How this is converted into the "fuel" of the radical moisture will be shown in the following chapter. For this reason, it must be known that radical moisture can be understood in two ways: as that which acts upon the body, and as that which, when deprived of its operation, gives up its life.

<meta>This page transitions from the formation of life to its inevitable decline and destruction. It distinguishes between violent death (accidental) and natural death (internal decay), drawing heavily on the relationship between the "radical moisture" (the body's fuel) and "innate heat" (the body's engine).</meta>

<margin>
Astrologers
</margin>
...is either consumptive or non-essential. For such a person, a **violent death** <note>Death caused by external force rather than natural aging.</note> will occur, such as freezing, venereal diseases, a ruinous <term>solution of continuity</term> <note>A medical term for a physical wound or break in the body’s tissues, like a cut or fracture.</note>, and generally all external accidents occurring to the body that deprive it of life. And because the art of medicine does not stand over such matters, they should be left to **astrology**. For it is not necessary to use medicine against swords and wild beasts in a kingdom. A physician, as such, does not have the means to prevent these things except perhaps in a general sense, especially since they are accidental. However, after they have occurred, he may be able to remove the damage they caused. But the **astrologer**, since such things are not accidental to him but are necessary or highly likely to happen, is able to prevent the greatest part of them, according to that saying of the *Centiloquium*: <note>A collection of 100 aphorisms once attributed to the astronomer Ptolemy.</note> "The best astrologer will be able to prevent much evil that is destined to come according to the stars." For when he knows the configuration of the region, of the city where one dwells, and the birth chart of the person, he will be able to predict the events that will happen to the newborn. All of this, however, is useless to the physician on his own. 

Alternatively, death results from a **necessary cause**, which natural death follows more closely. This cause is twofold: intrinsic and extrinsic. The extrinsic causes include the **air** and those things that continuously change it, such as the seasons of the year, the rising and setting of stars, the winds, the layout of lands, and watery or smoky elevations <note>Refers to vapors and mists rising from the earth.</note>. 

<margin>
Air
</margin>
Among these, the air—altered by the celestial bodies—most especially changes and transforms our bodies. For however much moisture we have, through the power of the heavens (via motion and light) and through their own received nature, the air continually exhausts our moisture by drying it out. This is consistent with what is said in the fourth book of the *Physics*: <note>Aristotle's 'Physics', a foundational text for natural science.</note> "All things grow old in time and are forgotten; time is the cause of corruption." On this point, **Parmenides** the Pythagorean <note>The text says "Paronides," likely a scribal error for the philosopher Parmenides.</note> declared that time is essentially undisciplined. For motion, of which time is an effect, causes that which exists to drift away.

<margin>
Condition of the internal cause
</margin>
<margin>
Animal Cause
</margin>
Therefore, more specifically, the air surrounding the matter of the body—which is **moisture**—dries it out. And generally, any "non-natural" thing <note>In medieval medicine, the 'six non-naturals' were external factors like diet, sleep, and air that affected health.</note> does this either immediately or eventually. The **interior cause** is also twofold: **animal** and **corporeal**. The animal cause is evident when all the powers, or the form of the body, are seen as finite. This is because none of them can fully satisfy the "appetite" of this matter <note>A philosophical concept: matter 'craves' new forms, leading to the destruction of the current one.</note>, since matter is always subject to "privation," plotting towards ill-fitting states and destruction, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in his first book. For this reason, matter is compelled to abandon its previous form and be led into another in an instant, since it cannot be separated from movements or forms. This does not happen in the heavens, since celestial matter—

<margin>
Averroes
</margin>
—according to **Averroes**, is different from the matter found here, or at least it is not joined with "privation." For the form of the heaven has satisfied the appetite of its matter all at once, since it is a single form containing everything. Therefore, it is judged to be perpetual and incorruptible, as stated in the first book of *On the Heavens*. And an infinite power can never be found in finite matter, according to the eighth book of the *Physics*. Therefore, as the **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note> says in the second book of *On the Heavens and the Earth* and the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*, the **Prime Mover** of the sphere must be infinite in duration.

<margin>
Aristotle's Physics: What is finite is defined; there is no proportion between them.
</margin>
This does not mean infinite in "vigor," because then it would move the sphere in no time at all, since it would exceed all resistance of the movable object out of all proportion. For there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite, as stated in the eighth book of the *Physics*. But **corporeal powers** are finite. For just as with the nature of all stable things, there is a ratio and a limit to their magnitude and growth, according to the second book of *On the Soul*, regarding continuous and discrete quantity. For all things that are born are limited by a finite period, as in the thirteenth chapter of **Job**: <note>Referring to Job 14:5.</note> "You have set limits for man which cannot be passed," because everything generated will eventually be entirely corrupted. 

This is explained more specifically: natural power is likewise finite because, being fatigued by its long action in processing food and by opposing influences, it is unable to restore the moisture in a way that perfectly matches what was consumed. Rather, the restoration is often mismatched in quantity and quality. Thus, life cannot endure forever. This is also indicated by the **vital power**, which moves the heart with a "reflected" motion. This motion is somewhat "violent" <note>In the Aristotelian sense: 'forced' or against the natural resting state of the object.</note> because it stands against the inclination of the movable object, though it observes a certain naturalness for the sake of the form. Even the **instruments** <note>The organs of the body.</note> grow weary as they suffer while acting. Hence, in *On Sleep and Waking*: "Whosoever has a work according to nature, when the time in which they were able to do it has been exceeded, they must necessarily fail." Just as eyes see, these organs fail when their properties are corrupted. According to the sixth book of the *Physics*, instruments are fatigued by waking and movement, and their **complexion** <note>The unique balance of humors (blood, phlegm, etc.) that defines an individual's health.</note>—which is their substantial and natural essence—is destroyed. For this reason, all motion must eventually cease, and thus life is terminated, since the mover is always in its final state of ability to move. This is like the intelligence that moves the celestial spheres; therefore, in the second book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*, they mock the myth-makers who claim the spheres move with labor and pain, requiring an **Atlas** to hold them up.

In the same way, the work of the **animal brain** must eventually fail, however much something immaterial might exist within it. At least regarding its operation—such as intelligence and discernment—it depends on the "phantastic" powers <note>The faculty of imagination and processing sensory images.</note> and ultimately on the physical organs. Thus, in the first book of *On the Soul*: "Understanding and considering wither away when something internal is corrupted," such as the organ of imagination. Furthermore, from this power and the vital power, both mental and physical labors arise, which—according to **Aristotle** and **Haly Abbas**—dry out the **radical moisture** <term>humidum radicale: the innate 'lamp oil' or vital fluid thought to be consumed by the fire of life</term>. Know that the soul or the immaterial power cannot itself grow old or be corrupted, since it is immaterial and perpetual. But this happens to it by reason of its connection to the organ, since "form" itself is neither generated nor corrupted, according to the second book of the *Metaphysics*. Hence, in the first book of *On the Soul*: "If an old man were to receive the eye of a youth, he would see just as the youth does."

<margin>
Corporal Cause
</margin>
The **corporeal cause** is considered both in terms of the radical moisture and the nutritional moisture. Regarding the first, there are two causes for its consumption: one is the **innate heat** which embraces the radical moisture on all sides, continuously and uniformly. Seeking to preserve itself, it consumes itself by accident as the moisture is used up. 

<margin>
Seneca
</margin>
Hence **Seneca** says: "That which rises with me, dies with me; and that which gives me life kills me." <note>A poetic way of describing innate heat, which powers life but also slowly burns away the body's moisture.</note> The heat, as it runs, consumes two things, and does so more intensely...

It explains that life ends because the body's "innate heat" eventually consumes its "radical moisture" and the physical organs wear out.</summary>
