<meta>This page continues the investigation into the body’s decline, moving from the general causes of death (accidental vs. natural) to a specific debate on whether "radical moisture"—the fundamental life-fluid—can be replenished once consumed, and how the body's internal heat interacts with it.</meta>

# Whether Radical Moisture Can Be Restored

Heating the **innate heat** <note>original: "calidū inatū" — the natural vital heat present in a living being from birth</note>, a less intense heat drawing to itself, causes it to wither and corrupts it, just as a larger flame does to a smaller one (as seen in the third book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*). And from the causes of the length and shortness of life, it consumes, and thereafter exhausts the **radical moisture** <note>original: "radicale" — the essential fluid or "oil" that fuels the body's life-lamp</note>. Regarding these two types of heat and such consumption, Galen touches upon this in the *Tegni* <note>original: "tegni" — referring to Galen's *Ars Medica*, a foundational medical textbook</note>, saying: "The innate heat, which is within us, assists in this. To which also the heat of the iron, made from these things, works." Consumption also occurs on the part of the **nutritive moisture** <note>original: "humidū nūm̄talis"</note>, and this is twofold. Either it is in the process of generation—and thus external heats and excessive imbalances found in nourishment, since they are contrary at the beginning, have a double superfluity: one part being watery and moist, the other smoky and dry (as in the third book of *On the Soul*). Or, it occurs as it has already been generated and is entirely watery and impure due to the weakening of the heat during digestion.

This also happens in two ways: either by reason of quality or substance. By quality, it is through its death-bringing coldness and moisture, which, being opposed to the heat, extinguishes its whole. On the part of the substance, it is again twofold: either by putrefaction, such as **consumptive putrid fevers** <note>original: "febres putride 9sūptiue"</note> and other similar things that cause the acceleration of the consumption of the radical moisture. And for this reason, the sick end their lives in a short time. Or, it is because of the thickness and bulkiness of many humors gathered from indigestion, which suffocate the heat of nature like a covering, preventing respiration. Just as a fire is suffocated and extinguished by too much covering (as in the first book of *On the Heavens* and the first book of *On the Soul*, and also in the twelfth book of *On Animals*).

And for three reasons, the animal body is exposed to consumption. First, because of the contrariety of the elements from which it is constructed; second, because of the heat continuously feeding upon the moisture; and third, because of the foreignness of things not necessary to it. For it is necessary that it be altered and changed. This is noted in three places in the *Tegni* and the first book of *On the Heavens*: if the body were impassive and unchangeable, and always remained in the best disposition, it would not stand in need of the art [of medicine]. But because change corrupts and alters it, [medicine] is required.

<margin>
Regarding the second point
</margin>
Regarding the second point, however, it should be known that some mock the question of whether radical moisture is consumed more by the innate heat or by the **flowing heat** <note>original: "calidū ... currēti" — also called "influens," referring to heat derived from nutrition and metabolic processes</note>. Their motives were explained in the previous arguments. Their deficiency will be revealed in what is to be said here and in the fourth [section]. Regarding the third point, it should be known that the radical moisture is consumed more by the **influential heat** than by the innate heat. This is shown because the influential heat exists in actuality, while the innate heat is almost in potential, since the former is sharp and troubling, whereas the latter is soothing and gentle. Action, however, comes from that which is in an excellent state of actuality.

Furthermore, that which participates more in the so-called **celestial heat** consumes less, since that heat, as has been said, contains and vivifies the nature of contraries in being. The heat of this [body] is, as it appeared, innate and not "flowing." Further, that which is more familiar and kindred to its opposite consumes less. Such is the innate heat in relation to the radical moisture, but not the flowing heat, since both of those [innate heat and radical moisture] emerged together and are soothing and mild. The flowing heat, however, is like a stranger and is "horrible," since it is generated daily from food and is of a wilder nature. In it, the qualities remain for a time exceeding themselves. And it is confirmed because the innate heat and radical moisture, since they are of a less contrary nature <note>original: "miuus getaria"</note>, will act and suffer less upon one another... for they are contrary only because the distance of what is taken is far from the contrariety first found in the center to the circumference. <margin>Commentary 8 / 2nd book of Metaphysics</margin> The **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> says this in the eighth and tenth books of the *Metaphysics*. Also, movement induces the most consumption by its persistence; here, however, it is found in the "flowing" heat, as the name shows. For it runs through the body, especially from the heart into the arteries, in almost an instant, just as the light of illumination travels through a house. From these things, it is concluded without doubt that the flowing heat dissipates the radical moisture more than the innate heat does.

Regarding the fourth point [and] the first argument, it should be said that the innate heat which is within is not only innate but also "flowing," as explained. To the other, it should be said that the statement is true when something receives its whole being from another, just as the truth of a whole demonstrative solution depends on the premises, or as all parental love of a nurse exists because of the child. But it does not stand so here, since the influential heat does not receive everything from the innate heat alone, but more from the heart and nourishment...

To the other, it should be said that although innate heat is the primary and immediate instrument of the soul, and thus of a stronger power in soothing contraries and in preserving the mixture and vivifying it, it is nonetheless not stronger in drying out and blowing away, but rather less so, since it participates more in equality and the celestial heat. <margin>3rd book of Tegni, last part</margin> For confirmation, it should be said that there is no comparison between fiery heat and innate heat, as will be shown hereafter. Since this double or triple heat cannot be compared to a lamp, but is one simple and artistic heat. To the other, it should be said that it is not enough to attain more by acting more, if there was not a greater power in acting. As happens, it is shown that innate heat, compared to influential heat, is gentle and pleasing. The latter, however, is almost the opposite. It [the heat] embraces the innate and radical moisture, and because it is sharp, it can consume more of it.

## CHAPTER XII

<margin>
That radical moisture cannot be restored.
</margin>
That radical moisture cannot be restored is demonstrated because, in the *Tegni*, the **solid parts** <note>original: "solidas corporis ptes" — the stable structural components of the body, like bone and membrane.</note> of the body, which are truly solid and primary, can in no way be made more moist; it is enough if one prevents them from drying out too quickly. And in the seventh book of *On the Method of Healing*, it is impossible to correct the dryness of solid bodies, just as it is impossible to correct old age. In *On Wasting*, it is impossible [to restore] the primary elements of the generation of plants and animals. That which truly restores radical moisture would have to moisten, truly co-extend, and alter the principles of generation. Again, in the first book of *On the Heavens* and the twelfth of *On Animals*, by that infinite and supposed power, death is nevertheless...

It concludes that the flowing heat is more destructive and that the solid parts of the body, once dried by age or disease, cannot be restored to their original moist state.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and medical debate regarding the "radical moisture"—the essential fluid that sustains life—asking whether it can be restored once it is consumed by the body's internal heat. It moves from a negative position (it cannot be restored) to an opposing view using Aristotelian logic.</meta>

...necessarily arriving by a defect of restoring the **radical moisture** <note>original: "humiduz radicale" — the vital fluid considered the fuel for life’s flame</note>. Furthermore, in the first place, a defect occurs that never ceases until the end, which is the failure to restore the moisture in the place of that which was dissolved.

Moreover, if radical moisture could be restored, life could be made perpetual, since the **vital power** <note>original: "uirtus" — the inherent capacity of the soul to animate the body</note> never grows old or is corrupted. This differs from the former. Nor would the heat [fail], since it acts infinitely if fuel is present (as stated in the third book of *On the Soul*); this fuel would be present as the **influential moisture** <note>original: "influens humidū" — secondary moisture derived from food and drink, as opposed to the "radical" moisture one is born with</note>.

Likewise, concerning the parts of the body, according to the doctors, some are created from blood; these receive restoration and recover their lost integrity according to the primary intention. But some are created from **sperm** <note>original: "spmate" — in medieval medicine, "spermatic" parts like bones or nerves were thought to be formed at conception and were unrepairable if damaged</note>, which they deny can be received back, not even at any time, since nothing is reborn in the place of what is lost. This would not be the case if such lost moisture could be restored, since that which is made of blood is restored by blood, while that which is "spermatic" [is not].

The **radical moisture** exists simply or from birth. The **influential moisture**, however, from which such restoration would come, exists from a certain time. Those things which are first by nature and those from time are different, since they are opposites. Indeed, they divide the genus into kingdoms; one of the opposites does not help the other to exist (from the fourth book of the *Topics* and from Boethius).

Even if the radical moisture were restored, this would be through "influence" [from food], as said before. But it is not, since it is generated within from the nutrients received inside. Indeed, many animals stay for a long time without eating or any drink, such as bears, snakes, storks, <unclear>vultures</unclear>, cuckoos, and such things hiding in caves in winter (from the first book of *Natural Virtues*, 130, and the sixth book of *Internal Things*). Likewise, certain women have ceased from all consumption of food for a very long time.

Furthermore, if the radical moisture is restored, either two bodies must occupy the same place—that which restores and that which is dissolved—since both are bodies and a body is not made from non-bodies. The contrary of this is found in the fourth book of the *Physics* and the second book of *On the Soul*. For dimensions resist other dimensions. Or, it would happen that a **vacuum** would suddenly occur when bodies are taken up, which is argued against in the fourth book of the same works. Or one body will penetrate another while the former remains uncorrupted, the opposite of which the **Commentator** <note>original: "cēmētator" — referring to Averroes, the influential Islamic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle</note> states in the second book of *On the Soul*. From these points, it is concluded that radical moisture can by no means be restored.

<margin>To the opposite</margin>
On the contrary is Aristotle in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. Also, restoration happens through nutrition. The Commentator says: "This is the perfect assimilation of the nutrient into the thing that is nourished." Therefore, since the radical moisture incurs loss, it will be necessary, if life is to remain, to receive restoration for a time.

Likewise, with substances being twofold, some have more "youthfulness" <note>original: "iuuenescētes"</note> in proportion to the whole body. If they were not restored at all, they would possess not only less substance compared to the original moisture, but almost none, since they are far removed in time. Therefore, radical moisture can be refreshed.

Regarding the first point, it must be known what is radical and influential moisture, and what is the **innate heat** and the **spirit** <note>original: "calidū īnatū" and "spus" — the vital heat and the "pneuma" or vapor that carries life through the body</note>.
<margin>See below</margin>
These appeared in the 48th, 59th, and the preceding [sections].

Regarding the second point, it must be known that modern doctors commonly hold that radical moisture cannot be restored. They say Aristotle feels the same as other doctors, so that they may support their opposite view with his authority, because it exists from the original "sperm." No such thing, according to them, can receive restoration.

For they say that heat can act upon the radical moisture in two ways. Either so that it restores it from the influential moisture—which is impossible—or that it prevents its rapid consumption through the nutritive moisture. Regarding this, they give such an example:

Let **wax** be that which is proportioned to the radical moisture, and **pitch** <note>original: "pix" — a sticky resinous substance</note> to the influential moisture. Let them be exposed to the sun. Let one ounce of wax be consumed in a day, and let an equal amount of pitch be added to it, and so on, according as more or less is lost; let it be restored by the pitch. For it will be restored, but not in such a way as the part which was dissolved <note>This famous analogy explains that while you can add "fuel" (pitch/food), it never truly replaces the original "wick" (wax/radical moisture)</note>. And therefore they say that young people, like all others, must eventually perish. The defect of this position will appear in the third part of what is to be said.

There are others who wish to hold a middle way between those who say it is restored in no way and those affirming its restoration. They testify that radical moisture can be restored "simply" as far as its **substance** is concerned, because since it is indivisible in breadth and not extended like "accidents" <note>In philosophy, "substance" is the essence of a thing, while "accidents" are qualities like color or size</note>, it either receives restoration entirely or not at all. They try to show it is restored entirely.

But as for certain conditions and properties regarding the substance, they say it can sometimes be refreshed and sometimes not. For example, the **quantity** is sometimes restored more, and sometimes less, and sometimes equally. But as for **quality**, they say it cannot be restored to the same prior degree, but within a range, since quality admits of "more" and "less." As for certain properties they call "relative"—which are **radicality** and **priority** <note>the state of being the "original" or "first" moisture</note>—they say truly that it cannot be refreshed in that way.

However, it is demonstrated that this cannot stand: that a substance which is "generatable and corruptible" (the subject of this present study) should receive restoration simply. As for the accidents that accompany it, it is shown thus: because quality and accidents generally depend on the substance. For they are not "beings" but rather "of a being" (from the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*). Because of this, if it is restored simply according to substance, it will be restored simply according to qualities. Likewise, since the end of **alteration** <note>the process of changing qualities</note> is **generation** <note>the creation of a new substance</note>, if it is generated by restoration simply in substance, the quality will also be altered simply, since its alteration is the path into the substance.

Also, if it is restored, it is extended; but extension is only according to quantity, not according to substance. For just as when quantity is taken away, the substance remains indivisible (from the first book of the *Physics*), so the same remains unextended when quantity is removed. And therefore in the *Categories*, you would say that however large the surface is, so much is the "white" thing. Again, by "substance" they mean that which is a "whatness" <note>original: "qd quid est" — the essence or quiddity</note>, which is indivisible and graspable only by the intellect. For that is the object of the intellect (from the third book of *On the Soul*). And since restoration is a physical process, it is entirely impossible for such a substance to be restored. For substance, as such, does not undergo generation...

<meta>Two-column printed text with handwritten marginal annotations.</meta>

# Whether the Radical Moisture Can Be Restored.

Or whether it undergoes corruption. It is not restored [simply] like a loss, since such passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to things that happen to a substance, such as being heated or worn down.</note> are not of the substance itself, but are added through accidents. And therefore **Aristotle** said that only substance is properly generated; regarding substance, it is verified that it is composed and particular, but matter and form are not [generated] except by accident (in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*). This is not [accessible] to the visual or intellectual sense. Or, for the sake of the composed substance, something is distinguished from it based on its qualities and quantities, as the **doctors** <note>Refers to medical authorities like Galen or Avicenna.</note> wish to say; these qualities are: **thick, subtle, viscous, tenacious**, etc. This view cannot stand, since the qualities and quantities which they call absolute properties belong to the substance as a whole and are indivisible. At most, in medicine, they speak not medically but rather mathematically or divinely, so that even a worn-down person does not understand them in the same way. Or perhaps, possessing a healthy intellect, they hesitate to express it.

<margin>Moisture in the Metaphysics, Book 2.</margin>
Regarding the third point, it must be seen that **moisture** is first of all manifold. Then, it should be explained how radical moisture can be restored, and how it cannot. Thirdly, this will be shown by authorities and reasons. Regarding the first of these, it must be known that moisture exists in three ways. For one kind is scattered in the simple members, like **dew** <note>original: "ros" — the finest stage of nutrition, likened to dew on grass</note>; and this moisture is primary and secondary. The remainder is coagulated from the nearest time, as nutrition in effect is called **exchange** <note>original: "cambium" — the stage of nutrition where food-moisture begins to turn into solid tissue</note>, already drawn to the place and restoring what was lost, receiving the form of the member which underwent the loss. There is also another, called **radical** [moisture], which is spoken of in three ways differently from the first. This radical moisture is especially twofold: the first is nourished by the twofold influential moisture <note>Moisture derived from food and drink.</note>. Its radical beginning was from the first seeds, so that it might collect and contain the parts of the members together from the beginning of generation; by the separation of this moisture, the body falls into ashes (Difference 33). But the beginning of the first two [moistures] is from food continuously.

<margin>The threefold moisture of the lamp.</margin>
There is, moreover, a similarity of this triple moisture to extrinsic moistures, as can be seen in a **lamp**. For in a lamp, a threefold moisture is found proportional to it. For there is moisture like the **oil** poured into it, which is likened to the first [influential] moisture. And there is moisture found already absorbed into the **wick** <note>original: "papiro" — the paper or papyrus wick</note>, which is attributed to the second moisture. And there is a third, which keeps the parts of the wick together so that it does not dissolve itself in the fire which is placed in it; and this is proportioned to the final moisture that holds the members together.

<margin>
The moisture of the lamp and the radical moisture are not the same.
A comparison.
</margin>
It must be noted, however, that this fourth point is primary; and among many doctors and philosophers, this comparison of the lamp's moisture to the animal's moisture is widely used, though it holds a certain difference in the likeness. For **igneous heat** is almost simply inanimate in its internal action, consuming the lamp's moisture. But the **heat of animals** is distinct from the external and celestial; it is a mixing and gentle heat, participating in the soul, and it nourishes the nature of the moisture. Furthermore, this combined heat of the radical moisture embraces every dimension, just like heat pressed through the whole body of water in a vessel; but the heat of the lamp is not כך <note>Hebrew: "so" or "in this way"</note> pressed into the moisture through the whole continuous wick, but only at one of its ends. And therefore—

---

—it is not valid, as some wish to show from such a moisture keeping the parts of the wick together, that no poured-in oil can resist its consumption; just so, the heat that is innate in the radical moisture cannot be prohibited from consuming the influential moisture. And therefore **Galen**, noting this in his book *On Marasmus* <note>original: "de tabe" — a wasting disease or consumption</note>, says: "This ratio or proportion of heat—namely natural heat—to the flame of a fire [is used]." Whence it is adopted by almost all the younger doctors and philosophers, though it is not entirely true. In the same way, doctors in the fourth [book] of the *Colliger* <note>A famous medical work by Averroes.</note> bite back against the idea of **inflation after food** in hectic patients; the causes given by other doctors for this are accidental, like the fables of singers. They say that food in the bodies of such patients is like **water upon lime** <note>original: "aqū sup calcē" — a metaphor for a violent reaction; quicklime heats up intensely when water is added</note>. For it is impossible for the nutritive power to be so far removed from the nourishment that it becomes its adversary, as water is found to be to lime. Let each of these things be sufficiently understood.

<margin>
Galen, On Marasmus, book 3, chapter 4.
</margin>
<margin>
Not regarding the hectic patient after a meal.
</margin>
Regarding this second point, it must be known that **radical moisture**, according to its substance—not as something indivisible, but distinguished by quantity, quality, and other things—can be restored, understanding restoration as it occurs in a natural body, corresponding to the consumption made by the combined heat. For when something of the **spermatic members** <note>original: "spmaticoꝫ mēbroꝫ" — tissues like bones or nerves thought to be formed only at conception</note> is lost, it cannot be restored, since it lacks the [formative] agent and the matter. For the **formative power** <note>original: "Virtus informatiua" — the biological force that shapes the body</note> departs once it has formed the parts (according to the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*). Also, the **governing nature** made everything it could from the sperm in the beginning, reserving nothing for fortuitous accidents, except perhaps for the production of **teeth**, keeping a part of it hidden for a time with the blood. This is noted by the teeth of the **cat** or the **star-lizards** <note>original: "felis seu stelle @z dci" — likely referring to the spotted lizard or gecko</note>. Also, the matter that is restored of the radical moisture is the nourishment and the growth itself, insofar as it remains under the nature of moisture and not as it has hardened into a part. For that which remains hardened in a mutilated part is like moisture that then stands as its own radical moisture; it cannot be applied in every way. Even imperfect animals and plants suffer both.

<margin>
The tail of the lizard and the stars.
An object of wonder.
</margin>
As for what is added to the tails of **star-lizards** <note>original: "stellionū" — spotted lizards</note>, **serpents**, and such, it is very little of the lost radical [substance]. It is also a superfluity generated from a certain viscous phlegm, which its substance, heat, and shape demonstrate. But in **plants**, since they are more material, they have their nourishment joined to them, drinking it continually. Nor is the matter in these and in more imperfect animals all [used] in the beginning as it is in nobler ones; it is restored. This is most true for all, not directly but from the side; whence imperfect animals are in the middle of the restoration of these two. I say also that such restoration is diversified by reason of **quantity**. For in **childhood**, more is restored than is lost, and therefore growth occurs. But in **old age**, it is the opposite; whence decline happens. In **youth**, however, the thing happens equally, and therefore the body and soul then stand organically. It is also varied by reason of **quality**. And this in two ways: primarily and secondarily. For sometimes heat is restored to what was lost, as when one strives with a little [heat], or phlegm [is restored] to a tempered complexion.

And whatever something was in potentiality, such it will be in actuality, when it can undergo change from the agent impressing upon it. But when it is not corrupted. Whence he says: "If it can no longer do this" (that is, if the form or nature, with its instruments, cannot transform nourishment and assimilate it to itself). But just as water mixed with wine, if more is always added, in the end it makes the mixture watery, and the water then causes a decrease in quantity. For when the flesh has become watery and impure, it diminishes, and thus growth ceases because it is unable to restore itself. For just as wine, when it is strong, can convert a little water into itself, so that it makes it stronger and more intoxicating; then it can still convert and change it until it begins to weaken. And finally, having become watery in appearance, it is corrupted because of the opposition between them. So it also happens in the radical moisture: that finally, through the extraneous impure moisture flowing into it, it is corrupted. Although the species remains the same until the end, it is necessary that at last the whole becomes watery and is corrupted. Thus the species of life remains as long as the moisture flowing in can be converted into radical moisture. But when it is not corrupted, life is made consistent through nourishment. Fifth, the <term>Colliget: refers to Averroes' medical encyclopedia, the *Kulliyyat*</term> also holds this view. For it is declared in natural science that the members first nourished are the "generative" parts <note>The "generative" or "spermatic" parts were thought to be formed directly from the parents' seed, unlike the "fleshy" parts formed from blood.</note>. Therefore, food is first converted according to the order it held in the body being fed, and into a moisture similar to the moisture fixed in the generative members; it mixes with them in the same way that liquids mix together. For there is no other way through which nature can restore a thing dissolved in all parts of a member, except by the way of mixing. And when it is mixed in this manner, then it will have existence within it. And after this, it will assimilate that to the member; this is because it gives to it a certain coagulation of stability similar to the stability of the member. And it is declared there that this happens through "concoction" <note>Digestion or "cooking" by internal heat.</note>, and concoction happens through the heat which is in the thing being fed. Not that heat is the primary mover in this matter, but rather the **nutritive soul**, since the operations of heat are not determined or ordered toward a single end. For fire acts infinitely upon combustible material. Regarding the soul: for all things established by nature, there is a limit and a rule for magnitude and growth. From this discourse, it is clearly gathered that radical moisture can be restored. And the manner of its restoration exists through transformation or mixing, and not through "juxtaposition" <note>The theory that new material is just placed next to the old, like stones in a wall, rather than blended into it.</note>, as some seem to dream, thinking that radical moisture is not restored but that the juxtaposition of the incoming moisture merely prevents it from being consumed for a long time.

<margin>See Averroes' *Colliget*</margin>
**A**gainst these people, not a few impossibilities follow: such as that nutrition and growth would not occur throughout the whole, as is felt in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption* and the first book of *The Physics*. Furthermore, **Avicenna** says in the same place: food has, through its own power and preparation, the ability to be converted into a moisture similar to the radical moisture which is in the generative member, and into an internal heat similar to the heat which is in the food, so that they are the same in every way. Moreover, the "plasma" <note>The formative fluid or "molding" power of the embryo.</note> would not be preserved from the beginning to the end, just as they seem to remain unharmed.

Again, things generated from superfluities, such as nails and the like, would then be truly nourished. Which is denied in distinction 54, since they could certainly receive [growth] by juxtaposition. Also, the manner of the conservation of the parts ought to be the same as the manner of their generation from their principles. For generation is ordered toward this end. But they were generated through the blending of "miscibles" <note>Substances capable of being mixed.</note> by transforming them into the interior. Thus nourishment is perfected by "transubstantiation" <note>In a biological sense: the changing of one substance (food) into another (flesh).</note> or mixing. And therefore in the first book of *On the Soul*: when food has been coagulated and assimilated to the body, it is perfected, and all quality is lost. Such is certainly called "nourishment." Which does not happen in juxtaposition. If a logic-seeker scents this truth, it seems that <term>Galen and Avicenna</term> wish to say in the *Regimen*: that it is possible for a bone that is soft and youthful to be consolidated.

<margin>☚</margin>
The members are few or small and in few conditions; and in the age of childhood they are thus standing. And the branches of the veins are small; for they are not large, nor are the arteries loosened, but are restored through a certain generativity. If a part of these is joined, nothing is reborn in its place. Which perhaps would not please an adversary, since <term>Haly Abbas</term> testifies to the restoration of the aforementioned parts, and that it occurs because of the proximity of the vigor and power of the sperm and the softness of the member. But it must be said that both offer [this], and it is more distributed to its pre-existing duties. That this is so, **Galen** writes in *On Consumption* <note>Original: *De tabe*.</note> thus: "If it were possible to work upon a moister substance of the body, the heart, or the liver, old age would not happen." If previously there is no sufficient [moisture], the liver cannot make itself moister, nor can the heart; but it is necessary in the following time for each to become drier.

# Whether Radical Moisture can be restored.

<margin>q</margin>
...of them. And not only the viscera, but also the arteries and veins. To prevent old age entirely is indeed impossible, yet it is seen as possible to delay that which seems to come quickly. The moistening of the moisture, or rather the preservation of the humors, is properly maintained by <term>baths: therapeutic bathing was a standard medical treatment for dryness</term>, a soft bed, sleep, and food. Of these, food is the most important; for it alone, through itself, becomes the nourishment of bodies by being assimilated into their very substances. Each thing, however, moistens another by accident—namely, because it prevents similar parts from being dried out by idleness, or because it increases and extends the moisture which, in the intermediate regions of the moistening members, takes on that name and power. In this way, therefore, it is possible for the liver and heart to be moistened, and thus the entire body. However, for nourishment to be assimilated in such a way, it must be converted directly into the substance of the solid members. If this, as a soft and nourishing moisture, were converted into hard substance and made essentially one with them, then all of it would be further converted into the <term>radical moisture: the primary vital fluid thought to be present from birth</term> in the solid members. Nor can you say, as many do, that it merely "sprinkles" and "remollifies" from the outside, since those things mentioned before perform that action and even more. Likewise, for no other reason can a child sustain himself and provide for his own growth, while an old man can do neither, and a young man does the first but not the second, except through the restoration of the radical moisture. Furthermore, when an infant seeks blood, which his own liver generates, this blood fulfills the role of that which was generated from the original blood. Or it must be said that he is neither nourished nor grows after his initial form is established.

<margin>☞</margin>
<margin>g</margin>
<margin>3.p</margin>
The body remains for the time it lasts only because its moisture resists the "resolving heat" <note>The internal heat that "digests" or consumes the body's moisture like a flame consumes oil.</note> of the world and the heat of its own body in its nature, and that which occurs from its movements and other factors. For the causes of moisture are more difficult in their action than the moisture is in its resistance. Nutrition does not make the body stand still, but rather restores that which is resolved from it. The sequence of the intellect is therefore fitting. This is first confirmed by reason: from which you have nourishment. For insofar as the object of life exists, it is itself a resistance through food, which can in no way be otherwise, unless the food—which produces moisture—flows into the radical moisture by restoration. That which is restored becomes one with that which is being restored. Another reason is the identity of nourishment, because the matter of generation and nourishment is the same, as stated in *On the Generation of Animals* <note>original: "de generatōe aīaliũ," likely referring to Aristotle's work</note>. But the matter of generation was the primary radical moisture, whence comes the first assimilation. From the spirit, the blood, and the airy moisture, the generation of the animal parts alone is made; thereafter, growth and nutrition come from these. And then, regarding quantity, because the moisture generated was of a small quantity—as is seen not only in animals but even more in plants, many of which arise from a seed so small it is not a thousandth part of them. They could never assume such great dimensions unless nourishment coming from the outside entered into them...

---

...and sought out, and the fire assumed those dimensions, as with a fir tree and its moisture. Again, if the innate spirit is restored through the conversion of material spirit, it is the same for the moisture; while the nourishment is converted into the radical moisture, as one is ordered toward the other. But the spirit, which is like matter, is converted into the pure innate spirit. Furthermore, the <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four humors</term> could not then be changed by nature, so that every difference might be changed into health; for it would be founded in the radical moisture. Additionally, the teaching of Galen would be useless, in which he busies himself with reducing distempered complexions to a temperate one. Furthermore, since it is a subtle, airy, and proper moisture, the subject of innate heat, it would be easily overcome by those things which are consumed and wasted by heat, such that it would require restoration and true conversion into itself. And just as transformation has dawned in the knowledge of matter, so too has the action of form. But even the actions of nature, in a more noble and perfect way, coexist there. This happens because moisture is restored and affected by heat. In a certain way, the other powers stand out; when the superfluous moisture drawn from birth is already sufficiently bounded. For the power of nature's heat, along with its moisture and the organ upon which the action depends, then stand out as proportionate and vigorous as possible. From these things, therefore, I dare to confidently announce that this radical moisture can be restored and cherished in this way.

<margin>g</margin>
<margin>3</margin>
Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it must be said that almost all physicians, having been misled by this sequence of Galen, think that the <term>spermatic members: the solid parts of the body (bones, nerves) thought to be formed from the initial seed</term> can in no way be nourished as spermatic parts, nor be moistened or restored. They respond to the objections raised regarding moisture by dreaming that the radical moisture is refreshed, saying that members are nourished and increased as far as their moisture and substance is drawn from the menstrual blood, but as far as the "spermatic" parts are concerned, they are neither nourished nor moistened. Nor, even if they are nourished and increased, do they become "moist" (that is, they do not become tender or soft in a visible way). For the bones of children and plants harden as they grow and are nourished, because heat limits the moisture. And these people, perceiving their own defect, note that hard members like bones are resolved by innate heat because of their hardness. Therefore, they respond to objectors that these require very little restoration. Others say that a dried stomach can never become moist in its spermatic parts, but only in its sanguineous parts. They also respond to those saying the spermatic members are nourished like the sanguineous ones: that although the spermatic parts are restored as far as they are composed of blood reduced to the nature of "sperm" <note>In this context, "sperm" refers to the formative biological matter, not just reproductive cells.</note>, they never receive restoration as if they were made from the original spermatic art. Their defect was detected from the very beginning. For to deny that the spermatic parts are nourished, moistened, and restored is a manifest falsehood, as has appeared; since from the beginning they are small, and then grow to great size like other living things—especially those exposed to the "resolution" of animals. And if they are not as solid as those that are more moist, even these, which are generally dried out, can be specifically moistened.

<margin>Anaxagoras</margin>
...as the following points indicate. Neither is the drying out of the organs a duty of childhood, nor is the changing of the <term>platearū: likely referring to the wide pathways or vessels of the humors</term> in those newly born, nor in its opposite. <note>original: "dra. xxvi"</note> Furthermore, if an organ is established from <term>spermatic matter: the "seed" matter believed to form the solid, permanent parts of the body like bones and membranes</term> which constitutes its single essence, it is impossible for one part to be restored without the other. Hence, it is indeed restored according to its proper blood-like nature and according to its spermatic nature; but I perceive that some are ignorant of why they should hear it called "spermatic." For these people encounter defects in the <term>attitis: possibly "attentis," referring to the specific properties of natural things</term> in natures, and this is most especially true in those things handed down concerning the generation of animals. Therefore, a man ought to be amazed that the famous and useful <margin>Anaxagoras</margin> Anaxagoras has consigned his own voice to oblivion in his own mouth. It is also a wonder how <term>Haly: Haly Abbas (Ali ibn Abbas al-Majusi), a famous 10th-century Persian physician</term> deigned either to approve or to find fault with this as a falsehood, when he might have known the truth through inquiry. Because of this, having set those views aside, let the aforementioned sequence be explained. The body's own primary parts—such as the heart along with the other principal organs—are all constructed from the beginning from blood reduced to the matter of the seed; these are truly solid, that is, certainly dried and hardened, and so forth. Hence, regarding the <term>tabes: a wasting disease or consumption of the body's tissues</term> introduced previously, when the moisture that causes growth is dispersed and dissolved, the body of youths is at least rendered more subtle; and that which happens as a vice in the whole body is manifest in those of advanced years, and it truly happens in the heart and liver. Thus, Galen wishes that when the heart has incurred a natural wasting through old age, it cannot be well-nourished so as to return to what it was before. Perhaps it is possible to prohibit old age and the death resulting from it, which is not something to be taken lightly. However, as has been said, he says it is even possible to make bodies more "bountiful," which is more important, in that it simply restores the moistures.

<margin>Haly & Galen</margin>
Moreover, Haly and Galen provide a <term>canon: a medical rule or standard</term> by which a declining complexion can be led back to its own state little by little by means of the moisture substituted in the species of the members; this is done by filling that moisture with things contrary to the departing complexion. For the similar members are nourished by this moisture. For that moisture itself inclines the member toward its own pre-existing proper complexion over a long period of time. Because, according to Galen, each individual member draws the matter of its own nourishment from the veins and stores it in its own empty spaces until it "cooks" <note>original: "decoquat," refers to the metaphorical internal heat of digestion</note> and digests it, converting it into the likeness of its own substance. For it is necessary that this moisture impresses something upon the member and changes it over a long period of time, so that it converts its complexion toward the side of its own complexion. From this discourse, therefore, the contrary of their statement appears: that the members are moistened and restored little by little through almost the entire duration of life. And perhaps those who would inquire into this would deny restoration because it is not the *identical* spermatic matter that vanished which is restored; but then not even that which is blood-like would be restored in that way. Another point appears that must be addressed: regarding the wasting [tabes], it is not always impossible, but it is possible for a time. Whence it is necessary that soon after its peak state, the body must be dried out; thus it flourishes up until its peak, and after that, very little. This he wished to touch upon with a shorter discourse in the <term>Tegni: "Ars Medica," a fundamental textbook by Galen</term>. Another point must be said: although the <margin>power</margin> power is posited as infinite and restores the moisture, death nevertheless intervenes because eventually it would restore it as something watery and impure, and situated in such a way that the moisture of life cannot exist as was shown. It is not that it is restored in no way at all, as the ignorant think, but in a "similar" way. For even a power that is infinite in duration, if it must act, requires a disposed matter; for action in matter requires a disposed subject <note>original: "de anima," likely a reference to Aristotle's 'On the Soul'</note>. Another point must be said: although the power may be incorruptible and perpetual in itself, it is nevertheless limited and corrupted because of its application to corruptible and deficient matter. Nor is the heat of animals a simple, tireless essence like fire, but a composite one, differing from the former; it has two parts, and therefore it is corruptible, for it grows weary and labors. Whence the philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note> proves in the second book [of *On the Soul*] that natural heat, which carries us to our heights, persists only so long as it does not sink to the lower states. Another point appears that must be addressed: for even the flesh which is generated from blood is restored as before. For it is not, as is known <gloss>in use</gloss>, glandular, nor simple and pure, nor muscular. For there are so many types of flesh. <note>original: "dra. xliii"</note> Indeed, glandular flesh is not properly that which is for the sake of generating moisture, since it was previously intended by nature, as much by reason of matter as of form or function. Nor are the other three types, since in them there is an admixture of nervous, spermatic substance. And therefore, lost flesh is not regenerated as it was before, neither in quantity nor even in quality; for a certain creative power subsides when too much of it is lost. Even the former color is not restored, nor is the constitution in it as it was before, so that the text seems to see a specific mode of flesh. For only blood is restored to its former thickness without the mixture of another substance, in which the liver, spleen, and lungs participate. Therefore, that which is least restored is the spermatic parts. On the contrary, that which is most restored is fat and grease; between these is flesh, and especially that which is called "pure." Another point must be said: it is not that such things are not generated, but they are generated according to the primary rational appetites; nevertheless, according to the act, it becomes possible. For a body can now be made equal to a similar healthy state, even if something foreign is present, and yet eventually it can endure for a long time and little by little become connatural to someone, as Haly touched upon. Another point must be said: although the aforementioned animals seem to survive without the external consumption of food, they nevertheless have internal nourishment, such as thick, viscous phlegm, which they digest little by little and are nourished by it. For by this kind of coldness of the mouth of the stomach, they have a great appetite, especially in warm weather, but a weak digestive power in respect to their desire. And their moisture is viscous and the skin is very pressed down, and generally the body is non-porous. Whence, when they do not receive nourishment from the outside, the heat dissolves the nutritable moisture existing around the site of digestion, and alters and changes it into the members. And because it converts only a little, much undigested moisture and great fat remain in them, so much so that they block the vessels, especially in winter; so much so that the weak heat has no place for the moist, smoky elements to evaporate, but returning to the site of digestion, the phlegm multiplies further, obstructing the pathways of nourishment. And so the appetite ceases, as does the external acceptance of food. The moisture which is then evaporating to the brain renders them "drunk" and sleepy, and therefore **they lie** <note>This is the catchword "iacent" for the next page</note>

...immobile. And by the sagacity of nature, they provide for themselves in caves. A sign of their nutrition is indeed that when they emerge from them, they are found to be thin, having consumed the previously mentioned moisture within them. For animals are always being nourished, but they do not always grow, as noted in the <term>Topics: a work by Aristotle on logic and dialectic</term> (Book III) and in *On the Soul* (Book II). The nutritive power operates through every singular time of life, unless perhaps when someone is at the very point of death, as noted in the sixth book of <term>On Accidents: likely referring to a work by the physician Galen</term>.

<margin>Not <unclear>maduon</unclear> a parent</margin>
Furthermore, concerning the fact that certain cold, elderly women in cold regions have existed without the intake of external food, this was certified to me by the faithful companion John of Corcey in Normandy. He, along with many others, stated there was a woman there who, for the space of thirty-six years, consumed nothing. And when she wished to, blood would flow from her mouth and nostrils. One of my acquaintances also reported that he treated a nun in Stendal, Saxony, who for two years received nothing except a single apple, which pleased her very much; after those two years, she grew hungry and took food as she had been accustomed to before. And for this reason <term>The Commentator: the standard medieval title for the philosopher Averroes</term> doubted in *On the Soul* (Book III) whether nutrition matches the definition of the soul, which stands as a complex of demonstration, since it is spoken of as the "first act." For this power is never found in animals except according to their final perfection.

<margin>Frost:</margin>
Solving this, he says: unless someone posits that there is a certain mode for animals that do not nourish at any time, such as those that remain in stones, like great frogs, which gather no treasure but remain all winter in stones; and likewise many serpents. And according to this, it will be a common trait of every sensing and nourishing soul to have the same brief intention. But if not, then the "perfection" accepted in them will be <term>equivocal: meaning the term is used in two different ways for different things</term>. But in whatever way, whether the diversity between them is understood or not, it will not then be harmful to accept this indefinitely in this definition, even if it is otherwise impossible. Regarding the other point, it must be said that nutrition is completed from bodies, and yet two bodies are not in the same place; for as the preceding part is dissolved, the restoring part immediately occurs to meet it. Thus, there is no "intercut" or vacuum, since the arriving part takes the place of the lost part. The members can also be dilated and constricted. <term>G.: Galen</term>, in the third book of *On Natural Faculties*, argues against <term>Erasistratus: a Greek physician who believed nutrition was a mechanical process of filling vacuums</term> for trying to abolish nutrition in this way, or for saying that what arrives is such in "potential" and not in "act."

It also follows that one body does not penetrate another while the penetrated body remains uncorrupted. With one part thus supposed to be arriving and the other transpiring, and with the distension and contraction of the limbs allowed. To the other point, it must be said that <term>A.: Aristotle</term> did not mean what many unlearned people hear in this speech, as others interpret it suspiciously, believing that <term>radical moisture: the vital fluid one is born with</term> cannot be restored. Rather, he agrees more with Aristotle that in the end, moisture is restored entirely impurely, like watered-down wine, so that the <term>species: the essential form or nature</term> is corrupted because of the unsuitability of the organ and the matter to be converted. Hence, in the first book of *On Generation*, a defect occurs that never ceases until the very end, which is the failure to restore moisture in the place of that which was dissolved. Indeed, this failure of restoration is not to be heard as happening at the beginning, but gradually at last when it reaches the end. For they say first that nothing makes a thing stay unless it is that which restores what is dissolved from it, which is the nourishing substance.

# CHAPTER XIII.

> That natural death cannot be delayed by any
> benefit, nor life prolonged by the same.

He shows this. For "You have appointed his bounds that he cannot pass," as it says in Job 14. Further, in the second book of *On Generation*, the time and life of each thing have a number. And this is determined. For the order of all things and every time and life is measured by a <term>period: a set cycle or natural span</term>. <term>Palin: likely a reference to a commentator or a specific passage in Aristotle's "On the Generation of Animals"</term> in the fourth book says: they want the times of all reasonable things, both of gestations and generations and lives, to be measured according to a period. Now, I call a "period" a day, a month, a year, and the times measured by these. If therefore life is measured by a period, and that period ends at a defined point, then life too will be defined. Again, in the first book of *On Heaven*: All that happens by divine command, and what happens in this way, cannot be delayed, since it proceeds from a cause that is in itself infallible. And it is confirmed because the knowledge of God is the cause of things. Truly, things are received from Him. The Commentator says in *Metaphysics* XII: For through His knowledge, He produced all things from eternity, foreseen in their very ideal <term>species: forms or blueprints</term>. But God's foreknowledge cannot be deceived in the least. For it is determined to one outcome. For "indetermination," since it is a certain privative disorder, implies a certain imperfection. Since He Himself is "pure act" and immune to all potentiality and defects (*Metaphysics* XII), He gathers into Himself the perfections and nobilities of all kinds. The Commentator says: He produces all things in a defined way, according to that saying in Wisdom 11: "You have ordered all things in measure, number, and weight."

Furthermore, they say: the measure and the measured are equal and of the same kind. For this continuous motion [of the heavens] exists by necessity from superior rotations, so that its whole power governs from there, as noted at the beginning of the *Meteorology*. But the measure, as a period, ends at a given defined point. Likewise, according to <term>Boethius: a 6th-century philosopher</term> in his *Topics*, a thing can only do as much as its form allows; and the form itself is limited. Again, they add according to Aristotle that the life-giving power is finite, not acting beyond the limit of its finitude. Moreover, that whose parts are determined is itself determined as a whole. Since the same reasoning applies to the whole and the parts, as seen at the beginning of the *Histories*. But the beginning and the "status" <note>original: "stat9", referring to the prime or plateau of life</note> which are parts of life constituting it, are determined, as the physicians write. Therefore, the "decrement" <note>the period of decline and aging</note> will also be determined. Otherwise, astronomy would already be deceitful and idle, which is said to be absurd, since it is a science of no small truth and certainty (beginning of the *Almagest*). And finally, cause and effect are proportional, according to the second book of the *Physics*. But the causes of life, such as the superior [celestial] bodies, are determined and incorruptible, since they are separate from contrariety. It is therefore impossible for death to be delayed.

On the contrary: According to the sixth book of <term>On Preserving Health: a work by Galen</term>, those who are ignorant of a healthy diet are likely to die sooner than the reason of nature dictates. And by the opposite logic, they may therefore live longer. Also, since medicine is ordered toward the prolongation of life by delaying death, if it did not include this, it would be in vain (*Physics* II). This would be a grave thing to say, since all physicians and philosophers testify that it is the duty of necessary things, or those that happen for the most part, to include their end. Furthermore, life consists in a certain proportion of heat and moisture to each other...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether life can be extended. Having previously addressed the physical properties of "radical moisture" and the ability of some creatures (and even humans) to survive long fasts, the author now pivots to the theoretical and astrological principles governing the lifespan.</meta>

For these are the principles of life. But such a proportion can be preserved for a long time, as the physicians teach—either by generating moisture sufficient to sustain the heat and by removing superfluities, or by altering and tempering the body. For this reason, life can be prolonged and death delayed by such a benefit. To understand this, one must first know (beyond what was said in distinction 21) that life is the proportional influence of the "signators" <note>In astrology, "signators" or significators are specific planets or points in a birth chart that "signify" or represent a particular area of life, such as health or longevity.</note> upon the principles of generation, subsisting by the necessary nourishment. Death is the privation of this, since it and life are opposites by way of privation.

In this understanding of life and death, we find a double set of causes or principles: namely, the material and the formal. Each of these is further divided into two types: those that constitute life and those that preserve it. 

The formal "constituting" causes are the <term>Hyleg: the "giver of life," a specific point in a birth chart (often the Sun, Moon, or Ascendant) used to determine a person's vitality</term> (also called the "mother" or "bride") and in place of it the <term>Alchocoden: the planet that has the most dignity at the Hyleg's location; it was used to calculate the actual number of years a person might live</term> (the "father" or "groom"). For the Hyleg is established as the "matter" of life, while the Alchocoden is looked upon as its "form"—especially if it has a benign aspect. If the Alchocoden is strong—both due to its own essential nature and its position in the heavens relative to other planets—it will grant "greater years" of life. Other planets, especially the "fortunes" <note>The "fortunes" or benefics are Jupiter and Venus, planets traditionally associated with good luck and health.</note> when similarly well-disposed, will grant their "lesser years." If the opposite occurs, the reverse happens, as explained in distinction 21. For one must consider all the signators—both the particular ones and the general forces, such as the climate, the homeland, and the specific moment in time.

For example, the Indians inhabiting the first <term>climat: an ancient geographical system that divided the known world into seven horizontal zones based on the length of the longest day</term> are subject to **Saturn** and are very long-lived, so much so that many do not die until they fail from extreme old age. <term>Albumasar: the Latin name for Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</term> notes this in his *Book of Secrets*; Saturn does not harm them as it does others who are foreign to its influence. Also, in ancient times, men lived for much longer periods, as stated in distinction 9.

The formal "preserving" causes—those that confirm life in its permanence—are the astrological "observations" and "fortifications" that an astrologer can perform based on the pre-designated hour of birth or an astrological inquiry. For when someone "fortifies" the Hyleg, its lord, the Ascendant and its lord, the Alchocoden, and the primary signators of life—such as the Ascendant, the Midheaven, the positions of the Sun and Moon, the "Part of Fortune," and the lord of the conjunction or prevention <note>The "conjunction or prevention" refers to the New Moon or Full Moon immediately preceding a person's birth.</note> prior to birth—and when they "weaken" the malevolent planets <note>The "infortunes" or malefics are Mars and Saturn.</note> so that they are in "cadent" <note>A "cadent" house is an astrological position thought to be weak and ineffective.</note> positions, there is no doubt among the experts in nativities and the authors of "images" <note>The "science of images" refers to the creation of astrological talismans or amulets designed to capture the power of the stars.</note> that this can achieve a certain extension of life in the native and bring about a more praiseworthy state of health. Conversely, the opposite conditions induce infirmity and finally death.

This applies not only to individuals but to entire countries, as <term>Thebit: Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century polymath and key figure in the history of astrological magic</term> recounts regarding the "Phidias" <note>The text likely refers to a story from Thabit's "On Images" about a talismanic statue.</note> who constructed an image to protect a region from destruction. In this way, a person can be "fortified" or "weakened" regarding the goods of fortune, honors, and knowledge. Hence, I have perceived that an invocation to God made by me was effective when performed with Jupiter in the Midheaven and the Moon moving toward it. Even the Kings of the Greeks observed this when they wished their petitions to be heard, according to **Albumasar** in his *Sadan*. The methods of "fascination" and "exaltation" confirm this as well.

The material "constituting" principles of an individual are the sperm and the menses, as stated in distinction 31. One of these is purely material (the menses), while the other is the efficient and formal principle (the sperm). Yet, when compared to the principles mentioned above, these are like the matter or the subject. 

The material "preserving" causes consist of the proper administration of the <term>Six Non-Naturals: the external factors in medieval medicine—air, food and drink, sleep and waking, exercise and rest, excretion and retention, and the "passions of the soul" (emotions)</term>. Through these, a physician keeps the body unharmed. This is either because he foresees issues through his science, or because an astrologer predicts them, knowing the person will become sick or die—for instance, from the "direction" of the degree of the **Hyleg** to the degrees of the "malefic" planets, namely Saturn or Mars, or generally to the "place of cutting" <note>The "Anaretic" or killing point in a birth chart.</note> without the help of a good aspect or conjunction.

The formal "constituting" principles were touched upon in the definition of life as a "proportional influence." The material ones were mentioned regarding the "principles of generation." The preserving causes of both are touched upon by the phrase "subsisting by the necessary nourishment." For life, like any other composite thing, requires matter and form to run their course together. For if the signators of life grant 100 years of living, but the moisture and heat are not sufficient, one will not be able to live that long. And even more so, if these physical elements are present but the "influence" of the signators is lacking, the matter can do nothing without the form of the composite. These things are granted even by those small in the astrology of nutrition and especially in the science of images, although these things can hardly be understood by the majority.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that almost everyone responds to this question with a distinction, gathering from the sayings of the philosophers and physicians (distinction 31) that death is twofold:

<margin>Death is twofold: natural and accidental.</margin>

One is **natural**, occurring from the consumption of "radical moisture" and the general extinction of heat. This is what the book *On Death and Life* <note>Likely referring to Aristotle’s "De Juventute et Senectute, De Vita et Morte".</note> calls the "removal of the soul," occurring because the weakened lungs can no longer move. The other is **violent and accidental**, occurring from the improper administration of the "six non-naturals," from which many diseases arise—sometimes in the "complexion" (the balance of humors) and sometimes in the "composition" (the structure of organs)—or from an external chance accident. 

Physicians say that death that emerges accidentally and violently can be delayed, but not "natural" death, since it is established within a fixed limit. Their arguments for this were laid out previously. But because this position cannot stand—as it contradicts both the truth and the opinion of the physicians—I will show why in the fourth section, where their arguments will be dismantled.

Regarding the third point, it should be known, first, that death cannot be delayed in every possible way, nor can life be made perpetual. Second, the truth of the matter will be supported by its own pillars. 

Concerning the first, it should be known that <term>Ga.: Galen, the most influential physician of antiquity</term> wrote in his work *On Wasting* <note>original: "De Marasmo"</note> that a certain philosopher wrote a book showing how one could remain entirely "un-aging" <note>Incapable of growing old.</note>. He released this book while he was still in his forties. But eventually, when he reached eighty years of age, he became so thin that he took on the <term>Hippocratic Face: the hollow, sharp facial appearance characteristic of someone close to death</term>—a sharp nose, sunken eyes, and so on. In the end, he did not dare to teach others his method. Correcting himself, he said that not everyone can remain "un-aging," but only those who are excellently constructed from birth and who are carefully cared for from then on. To which **Galen** and others add a final note...

<meta>This page transitions from the astrological definitions of life—specifically the Hyleg (giver of life) and Alchocoden (giver of years)—to a physical and philosophical investigation into why living things must inevitably decay. The author reconciles Aristotelian physics with medical practices to argue that while death is certain, the speed of its arrival can be managed through the preservation of bodily moisture.</meta>

# ->Whether natural death can be delayed by some benefit, and life prolonged<-

It is considered a folly to think that anything which can be generated can escape being corrupted <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "generation" (coming into being) and "corruption" (passing away) are two sides of the same coin; what is born must die.</note>. This is confirmed by no few reasons drawn from the causes of animal constitution, both on the part of **prime matter** <note>original: "materie prime"</note> and its particular parts. For in any thing where a principle of corruption is found within itself, that thing must necessarily perish. Indeed, all mixed things <note>A "mixed" thing refers to a body composed of the four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> contain within themselves a principle of corruption, namely <term>Hyle: the fundamental, formless "matter" of the universe</term>, associated with the principle of **privation**, which constantly schemes for destruction and misfortune, as noted in the first book of the *Physics*. For when matter is under one form, it becomes weary of it and desires to be under another.

<margin>Aristotle</margin> Truly, the whole cannot satisfy the appetite of matter, just as in the heavens, the desire for form satisfies matter—if indeed it possesses it—or perhaps one exists and then another. By the reasoning of concrete matter, it is also shown that a mixture is composed of **contraries** <note>For example, the "hot and dry" of fire vs. the "cold and wet" of water.</note>; hence, the mixing itself happens almost by force, and the miscible elements remain in the mixture by a kind of violence, since each one naturally seeks its own place. Nature, however, by its own power, leads them to the mixture and holds them there for a time, with their contrariety being lulled to sleep, as it were. For a power is either drawn from within them or granted from without, which determines that they remain together for a time. For fire, through the rays of the stars and the sun, is drawn down into our generation, so that those things which are earthy might be surpassed. Yet, nothing violent—since it lacks the natural form implanted within it—is perpetual. 
<margin>manicule</margin>

This is also true on the part of the **form**, because the celestial influence acts like a form, and the giver of "being" <note>original: "esse"</note> terminates at the object, and the matter into which it is received is here. For an infinite power is never received into a finite matter, as stated in the eighth book of the *Physics*. And this is especially true when that form is intrinsic, as is the form of mixed bodies. 
<margin>10 p r b . 9 phys</margin> In the heavens, power and form are received as infinite in time, but not in vigor, lest movement should happen in no time at all. Yet even that is finite, according to the first book of *On the Heavens and the Earth* <note>original: "prio ce. & mu." referring to Aristotle's De Caelo et Mundo</note> and the Commentator <note>The "Commentator" refers to the Andalusian philosopher Averroes.</note> on the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*. But the power by which they move stands as something extrinsic, and not like a form inherent in the object. For the heaven moves through a separate principle, which is in it as the substance of the sphere. 

Furthermore, on the part of the **efficient cause**, which is the restoration of what has been lost, this is done by the natural heat of the body transforming food and converting it into nourishment by which it is repaired. Since this is a physical action, every physical agent is itself physically acted upon. 
<margin>3. p</margin> For nourishment is initially contrary to the body; because of this, the agent is weakened by the struggle with the contrary and must eventually fail. Just as wine mixed with much water eventually becomes entirely watery, as noted in the first book of *On Generation*. 
Furthermore, regarding the **final cause**: since inferior things are ordained toward generation so that they may endure, if corruption were to cease, generation would also cease. For as Aristotle says, the corruption of one thing is the generation of another, and vice versa. 
Moreover, speaking according to the laws, the number of the elements would never be complete, since the earth itself would not be able to nourish them all at once. 

<margin>3. p b t u</margin> These things are also apparent from the first book of the *Canon* <note>Referring to the Canon of Medicine by Avicenna (Ibn Sina).</note> and the *Problems*. For in the body of an animal, a manifold contrariety is found which is entirely causative of death: such as the primary qualities being adverse to one another, and the natural heat acting upon the moisture, which by accident eventually destroys itself in two ways—partly by consuming the natural moisture, and partly because an aqueous, undigested humor rises up as a result.

---

It suffocates the heat by its quantity and chills it by its poor quality. In this process, the constant resolution of bodies also plays a part, receiving the power of the stars into itself. Other "non-natural" things <note>The "six non-naturals" in medieval medicine were factors like diet, sleep, and exercise that humans could control.</note> also assist in this, being external to the bodies but constantly affecting them. Power also, as shown, is finite. Therefore, from these causes, it is necessary that life must eventually fail.

Regarding this, one should know that **death can be delayed by some aid**, or life prolonged by the same—not only accidental death, but even natural death.
<margin><insert>Death can be delayed, both accidental and natural, by some protection.</insert></margin> 
This is shown by the words of the physicians, if rightly understood. For while the art of medicine is the "preserver of health," it is not a faculty that makes us entirely safe from death, nor does it shield the body from all external harms, nor can it lead every body to the ultimate length of life which is possible for a human absolutely—say, 120 years, or 70 years, as touched upon in the ninth distinction. 

Indeed, medicine provides security in two things: by prohibiting putrefaction entirely, and by preventing the "resolution" (dissipation) of moisture so that it is not consumed too quickly. In its strength, it provides that the body remains until its "due time" according to its own individual complexion <note>The "complexion" is the specific balance of the four humors in a person.</note>. 

This happens in two ways, just as there are two causes of death. Regarding the first, an "anti-drying" regimen <note>original: "exsiccatiua"</note> acts by prohibiting the dominance of the causes of dryness from accelerating, meeting those causes of necessity; yet they cannot be prohibited forever, since it is proven that life cannot be perpetual. Against the second cause (putrefaction), a regimen is used that prohibits the generation of putrefaction by guarding the body from the power of external and internal heat. 

Thus, this discourse, if carefully explained, teaches that just as medicine prevents a violent death, it also delays a natural one. Otherwise, a body of the best construction would hardly need the curative art. Furthermore, Galen expressed no less on this in his work on "Wasting," saying it is impossible to finally prohibit the decay of old age, but it is possible to help extend life as much as possible. He adds that if it were possible to make the substance of the heart and liver more moist, life would be extended. But if there is no sufficient way to keep the liver and heart from becoming drier over time—and not just the viscera, but also the arteries and veins—then prohibiting old age seems impossible. 

He confirms this again by the words of Homer: through food, drink, baths, a soft bed, and sleep, the heart, liver, and indeed the whole body are refreshed. Since he teaches how to co-extend old age through such "moistening" (which is the opposite of natural death), and not merely through prohibiting the putrefaction of moisture, he indicates that natural death can indeed be delayed. 

<margin>manicule</margin> Furthermore, Haly <note>Haly Abbas (Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi), a famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note>, the physician and astrologer, making this truth plain, says it is possible that there are medicines which prohibit the speed of old age caused by the coldness and dryness of the limbs, and through them, a man's life is prolonged when his regimen is good; just as he says that men have lived for centuries.
<margin>Haly the physician and astrologer.</margin>
