<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether human life can be extended beyond its natural "programmed" duration. While the previous page established that all physical things must eventually decay, this page introduces the practical tools—medicine and astrology—that can be used to fight back against this corruption and delay the onset of death.</meta>

...years. And one of the things discovered in that context is the medicine known as **trifera** <term>Trifera: A complex medieval compound medicine, usually an electuary, believed to balance the humors and rejuvenate the body</term>. Indeed, it produces good digestion and a florid color. And it remarkably extends life, when combined with a good regimen, for a long time. So much so that perhaps those who have lived longer have already found medicines by which their lives were prolonged. For it is more possible to find an ultimate remedy in the production of life even beyond *trifera*. However, it is not possible to find a medicine that entirely prohibits death. 

Now, let the reasons for this be brought forward, lest anyone craftily wish to interpret the previously introduced discourses as if they only concerned violent death <note>The author wants to prove that "natural" death—not just accidental or "violent" death—can be delayed</note>. For anything whose constituent principles can be preserved more perfectly and vigorously by some benefit will be able to endure longer. Such are the principles constituting the human body, both material and formal, as previously stated. Materially, because the **radical moisture** <note>original: "humidum radicale"; the vital fluid or "lamp oil" of life that humans are born with and slowly consume</note> can be restored, as mentioned in the previous chapter. Heat can also be defended and tempered through medical art, lest by consuming the moisture, it brings dryness and coldness to the body, which are the qualities that cause death.

<margin>Trifera</margin>

Again, it was proved in Chapter 22 that a natural **complexion** <note>The specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) unique to an individual</note> can be changed. Let those of a "melancholic" type therefore change into a "sanguine" or temperate type, since the former has a shorter life and the latter a longer one, according to Chapter 21. Likewise, extrinsic heats that dry out the vital moisture can be tempered; by this means natural life will be prolonged, provided there is a due proportion of heat to moisture, and finally to the "third" principle, such as the heart, as cited in the previous chapter. Furthermore, the **formal principles** <note>The "form" or soul that gives the body its structure and life</note>, when perfected and invigorated, are preserved beyond their natural state if they are aided by the art of **astrology**. 

This happens in two ways: either by the physician predicting a future illness for someone once he has understood their **nativity** <note>The birth chart</note>. For by knowing the movement of the degree of the **Hyleg** <term>Hyleg: The "Giver of Life" in an astrological chart, used by medieval astrologers to calculate a person's lifespan</term> as it rises, and knowing that specific choleric influences moving toward the position of Mars will generate an illness from excess heat, the physician can cause the patient to be cooled and moistened, and the excess bile to be purged so that he does not fall ill, or is only slightly affected. 

<margin>Note</margin>
<margin>Centiloquium</margin>

Illnesses make death accelerate, even a natural one; hence in the **Centiloquium** <note>A famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note>: "The best astrologer will be able to avoid much evil that is to happen according to the stars, when he has foreknown its nature." Or, one can make the degree of the *Hyleg* and the Ascendant fortunate through **images** <note>original: "ymagines"; likely referring to astrological talismans or symbolic rituals used to harness planetary power</note> along with other indicators of life. For by adapting the image, and finally applying it to the person, the life-giving virtue of the stars is included through their rays, strengthening the birth-influence, as in Chapter 10. For just as the superior bodies [the planets] imprint common virtues through their motion and light, so also their more occult and specific virtues are fixed into this or that person, according to how fit the person was to receive them at birth. And this is what is said in the *Centiloquium*: "The wise soul assists the work of the stars," just as the sower assists natural strengths. Here it produces and extends the life of "vegetable" things <note>Meaning things that grow and consume nutrients</note>. 

Again: the end of anyone's life is not entirely prefixed, but rather contingent; it can not only be delayed but also accelerated, since it is natural for contraries to happen to the same thing. Such is the "period" of life. This is shown both by the superior formal principles [astrology] and even more by the reason of the inferior ones [matter]. 

First and foremost, according to the opinions of the astrologers: we see that the celestial bodies do not always pass through the same distances in the same amount of time; one moves faster and sometimes slower, though in the end the whole is perhaps rendered uniform. This is seen in the motion of the **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note>, which is now faster than it was in the time of **Abraham** <note>referring to Abraham Ibn Ezra</note> and **Ptolemy**, according to Chapter 9. Wherefore it is discovered, not only by art but by observation, that in these times years are elongated and nights are shorter during the winter and summer solstices because of the "precession of the pole" of the eighth sphere and the elevation of the zodiac, about which I have written a treatise. The Sun also, in traversing the space from the first minute of Aries to the first minute of Libra, spends seven more days than it does on the return trip, according to the third book of the **Almagest** <note>Ptolemy's foundational work on astronomy</note>. The Moon also, when swift in its course, travels 15 or more degrees of the zodiac in a day, but when slow, only 12. The average is about 13. There are many such diversities perceived in the heavens that cause these effects. 

That a precise "limit" of life cannot be set based on material principles is something **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay." = Aristoteles</note> testifies in *On Generation and Corruption*, book two. For after he had said that birth and decay happen in equal time, he adds: "But it happens many times that a thing is destroyed in a shorter time, because of mutual confusion." For since matter is unequal and not everywhere the same, it is necessary that life-cycles be unequal; some faster, some slower. This is also in the fourth book of *On the Generation of Animals*. Nature wills the truth of these things—that is, to count out births and deaths—but not with absolute certainty because of the "indeterminacy" of matter. 

Furthermore, since an action requires a matter that is ready for the agent, the more the matter is prepared, the easier the action will be. Thus even a weak agent can act upon it, since the material preparation is often the greater cause of the action, according to the first book of [Galen's] *On Fevers*. A physician is able, as shown, to prepare the matter, and the astrologer can render the result and the "form" more perfect. 

It is said that there are places where men live for a longer time, such as among the Indians, and places where they live shorter lives, such as among the "Blacks" <note>original: "nigrorū"; referring to people of sub-Saharan Africa</note>. For old age happens to them at 30 years. [32] Therefore, let one be moved from the land of the Blacks to India; his life will be rendered longer there, unless the specific virtue and influence impressed in the air should be contrary to him. As if an Indian were to take on the climate of a Slavic land, he would either die or fall ill, according to Aristotle. But that which is moved into a more life-sustaining climate becomes longer-lived. Since the particular life-path is distracted and disturbed, as **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Abraam Euenare"</note> says. For it happens that 40,000 men or more perish at once in war. One cannot say that all these died because of their individual astrological "birth-death," but rather because of a "superior nativity" [a bad omen for the whole group or city] drawing them into wars. Again, the same logic applies to the whole and the part. The life of the "universal" man is not fixed, for formerly it was longer and now it is shorter. Furthermore, if one of two contraries exists in nature, so must the other, according to *On the Heavens and the World*.

# Whether natural death can be delayed by any benefit and life prolonged

It is clear that life can be shortened. Likewise, contrary things are meant to happen concerning the same subject. Indeed, the brevity and length of life are contraries. It is accepted by everyone that life can be shortened. However, those with a perverted understanding attack this view with two arguments. They say, first, that the arguments about shortening life only conclude regarding accidental death, and not **natural death** <note>Natural death was seen as the body's internal clock running out, while accidental death was caused by external forces like injury.</note>.

This is manifestly false. Since the discourse of **Avicenna** <note>original: "Au." referring to the Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> is common even in cases that are not strictly true—as when he discusses introducing gold into fire and into water—it applies even more so to the natural life and its verification in death. Therefore, they offer no response that actually solves the problem. In the second argument, they add that death is fixed "unless something else is in its nature," assuming that nature is such that natural death cannot be delayed. The falsehood of this is shown by many examples that confirm the opposite. Likewise, the **soul** <note>the animating principle of a living being</note> is, in this case, the form most closely aligned with the body and more deeply impressed upon it than any external celestial influence. Yet often the movements impressed upon the body do not obey the soul. This is known from the study of the soul and the causes of animal motion, as seen in the heart and the appetites of the angry or the lustful, where the motion of the soul is perceived. Even natural processes are not entirely fixed, as the metrics of birds, the population of trees, and the generation of worms from rot indicate; for sometimes they occur earlier, and other times later, according to whether the sun is in Aries or Pisces, or whether Mars is joined with Saturn. Similarly, the **gestation periods** <note>the length of pregnancy</note> of mothers are not all equal. For some carry for seven months, others for nine, some for eight, some for ten, and so on.

Furthermore, the stages of life are not terminated by a single period, since one person is long-lived and another short-lived, as appeared in the case of the twenty-one-year-old mentioned earlier. Nor do the movement of the bones and the growth of the beard happen at the same time for everyone. Nor does the body remain the same itself, given the diversity of circumstances. Furthermore, we see dying people, even those already prepared for death, suddenly comforted and their death delayed through the administration of an **electuary** <note>a medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note> and aromatic wine. This is clearly seen in the effects of saffron, mace, and castoreum <term>Castoreum: A secretion from beaver sacs used in medieval medicine to treat hysteria and revive the senses</term> given with wine, such as Muscatel. So it is also said of the **apple** <note>original: "pomo"</note> in the book about Aristotle, who held it in his hands. He was refreshed by its scent, though he had supposedly been about to expire for a long time; had he not been sustained by the scent of that apple, his hands would have immediately begun to tremble, the apple would have fallen, and he would have died. This would not happen if the limit were absolutely fixed, like the arrival of light to an illuminated object. And this is especially true since the celestial bodies do not impose necessity upon us, but rather seek out disposed matter. And for those observing correctly, the rationality of the soul is more noble than the stars. **Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician</note> says in his fourth book on fevers: We see certain conjunctions that signify something great, preceding the actual effect by a long time, since they dispose the matter over time and finally bring about the form—just as the conjunction portending the Great Flood preceded it by 287 years, according to **Albumasar** <note>The famous Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar</note> in his first book on conjunctions. That which denoted the future of the **Mabari** <note>likely referring to a historical or legendary ethnic group or event described in astrological texts</note> preceded it by 52 years, according to **Alchabicius**.

<margin>Note</margin>
Thus, from all these points, it has been sufficiently shown to those with a clear intellect and a love of the science for whom this is written, that natural death can be delayed by the benefit of both medicine and astrology. But so that they may better understand...

...it must be known that death can be called "natural" in two ways. Either because it happens through the deprivation of the material and formal principles, and such is properly called natural; as when someone who had healthy material principles, was governed by a good regimen, and was aided by the benefit of an astrologer, finally passes away. The other is called natural in an improper sense, when it happens from the formal and internal powers alone, as they provide a certain quantity of life; whether it happens by swords or disease or rot, it can be called natural, since the formal principle of the power is taken away, and "nature" is spoken of regarding the form more than the matter.

But regarding the aforementioned things, a doubt arises: it was conceded that a certain "natural death" exists. This does not seem right, because old age and all defects and corruption are "according to nature" <note>Aristotle, *On the Heavens*, book 2</note>. Yet the contrary is also said: that growing old and corruption are "according to nature" <note>Aristotle, *Physics*, book 5</note>. It must be said that death is twofold. One is that which happens to the elements through the motion of the higher bodies; for the nature of the universe intends not only generation, but also corruption, since the corruption of one is the generation of another; and this death is called natural. There is another nature particular to each individual; and because everything always desires its own health and preservation, it avoids death and destruction. This kind of death is said to be "against nature," and especially against the **form** <note>the "blueprint" or soul of the creature</note>, which is divine and desirable; for this is not intended by the particular nature except perhaps by accident, as in those with a depraved appetite, or those wishing to be joined to a future divine life. And according to this intention, it is said in the *Generation of Animals* that a male is a "misbegotten" or struggling female. It can also be called natural if one considers that it proceeds from intrinsic principles, even if not intended. Some also say that natural death is such primarily because of the matter, on account of the deprivation and destruction joined to it, but not on the part of the form. To the first point, it must be said that **Job** <note>referring to the biblical Book of Job</note> does not speak implicitly but relatively, as concerning a common limit and not one narrowly precise. For a man's life is not extended to fifty years only, nor today to two hundred only; but between these broad limits, it is found to be terminated in different ways. Whence he says, "The days of man are short, you have appointed the number of his months, you have set his limits," and so on. Therefore, he is not speaking of a precise, particular limit.

To the second and third points, it must be said that **Avicenna** speaks of a common, indeterminate period, and not a precise particular one. Or he speaks of a period caused more uniformly by the motion of the higher bodies. Here, however, as will follow, it is added that because of the diversity of matter and inequality, it varies not a little. Thus, this understanding concludes the opposite of what was intended by the opponents. And it is a wonder that many great men were grounded in the idea that the period was so precise and its cause followed in an instant, like light follows illumination. To the other point, it must be said according to Avicenna and the Commentator, that God can do nothing...

Thus, the period <note>The fixed "period" or lifespan</note> induced into this lower matter by the celestial bodies cannot be unchangeable, for that would imply a certain filthiness, defect, and mutability in the First Cause <note>The "First Cause" refers to God, the origin of all things.</note>, as if he did not produce all things with supreme wisdom. For those things which are established by perfect reason cannot be changed, according to the **Timaeus** <note>original: "Thimeū," referring to Plato's dialogue on the creation of the world</note>. 

But because these thinkers spoke of the First Cause as if it were a certain agent of nature, it must therefore be said that since He is a **voluntary agent** acting through His own intellect, He disposes and changes all things as it pleases Him. This, however, has not been determined as truth, since these matters were investigated through natural and medicinal means, not through supernatural ones. 

Regarding the confirmation, it must be said that although God's knowledge is the cause of things, and things happen exactly as He foresaw from eternity, His foreknowledge or providence does not impose **necessity** upon things—as is argued in the **Consolation** <note>original: "de gſolone," referring to Boethius's "The Consolation of Philosophy," a foundational text on fate and free will</note>. For He produced and foresaw all things without motion and in an indivisible moment of time. We, however, perceive things through motion and time. Our minds cannot understand anything without continuous time and mental images; due to the weakness of our soul's intuition, we cannot reach those intimate things belonging to Him, just as the eye of a bat <note>original: "icorocis" likely "nycticoracis," the night-owl or bat</note> cannot look directly at the wheel of the sun. But since this discourse belongs to another and higher speculation, let it be suspended for the present. 

As for another point, it appears that just as a measure is broad and indeterminate, so is the thing measured once the measure is applied to it. To another point, it must be said that the first premise is true, but what is assumed under it is false. For it is clear that a **form** <note>the organizing principle or essence of a thing</note>, by the benefit of art, can remain in matter for a longer time. 

To another point, the answer is already clear: for the **life-giving power** is finite, but it is broad in its finitude, not narrow. To another point, it must similarly be said that the beginning of life and its "status" <note>the "prime" or peak of life</note> are not strictly determined. For some bodies begin earlier, others later, and they reach their peak in the same way, as is evident from the different times of gestation and the varying duration of youth. For some,

youth is placed at the **30th year**, while for others it is at the **35th**, according to the diversity of their **complexion** <note>original: "gplexiōis," the unique balance of "humors" or qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) in an individual</note> and such factors. To another point, it must be said that **astrology** is neither a lie nor useless. For just as an astrologer perceives the accidents emerging around a birth, so too does he perceive their remedies for the prolongation of life through the orderly application of art. Or, as it is said of many, their failure in correct prognosis is great, except in certain small details. Very few, however, use the aforementioned regimen for a productive life, since most live a **brutish life** <note>living by instinct rather than reason</note>, or are occupied with civil and domestic business. 

To another point, it must be said as shown: that life cannot be made perpetual <note>immortal</note>. What **Aristotle** <note>original: "Aʒ."</note> said is verified in "univocal causes" <note>causes that produce an effect like themselves</note> that are immediate in their effect. Such are not the superior celestial bodies in relation to these lower things; because these lower things are distant from them, they are rendered transformable and corruptible. Hence, in the book **On the Universe**:

<margin>God</margin>

**God**, according to the poet, resides in the highest power of the universe, and by His power, He primarily nourishes the body that is near Him, and then those that follow after it, down to our places near the earth. And those things seen upon the earth, being at a great distance from the divine benefit, are infirm and full of many movements. For an effect does not perfectly contain and represent the power of its cause; because of this, variety occurs little by little, as is seen in the whole order of the universe, descending from the first through the middle to the lowest. For the **First** remains simple, immobile, and entirely incorruptible. In the rest, however, there is composition, mobility, and corruption.

### CHAPTER 14.

**1. Wherein it is demonstrated that drink and food change us more than air does.** 

Because that which is simple does not change us further; but air, and even water, do not change us in an absolute sense. Whence the **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note> on the second book of **On the Soul**: "An animal whose nature is to be in water or in air does not produce any hot or cold quality in them." If, therefore, it does not feel the more perceptible and changing qualities, it will not feel the others. 

Furthermore, **Isaac** in his work **On Diets** <note>original: "yſaac i dietis," referring to the physician Isaac Israeli</note> says that simple things do not act upon composite things as composite things act upon composite ones. But food and drink are composite, whereas air is simple, according to the second book of **Physics** and the first book of **Primary things**. 

This is confirmed because there must be a likeness and proportion between agents and patients <note>the thing acting and the thing being acted upon</note>. Again, agents and patients share the same matter, according to the first book of **On Generation and Corruption**. These, however, do not share matter, since air is simple and food and drink are composite; their matters are opposite. 

Furthermore, **place** has a saving power, as in the fourth book of the **Physics**; for the nature of "place" is marvelous. But air is our "place." Therefore, it will save us unchanged. Again, that which has the least sensible differences and qualities changes us the least; air is of this sort. Whence in the first book of the **Physics**: "Air has no sensible differences." 

Also, that which remains longer is of a grosser mass; it is less yielding and changes us more. Such are food and drink especially, but not air, which is the subtlest of bodies after fire. Likewise, when the quality and the subject are weak, they change us the least. Just as very sensible things change us, the subject is receptive to many passions. The quality proper to air is **humidity**, as was shown in chapters 12 and 14; but this is the weakest of qualities and the least impressive. And thus, **dry illnesses** cannot be cured when they have become extreme, for they lack an equally powerful contrary. Therefore, air changes us less than food and drink.

<margin>Opposite</margin>

However, the entire crowd of doctors and philosophers holds the **contrary** view. Furthermore, that which possesses qualities in the highest degree, such as the elements, changes us more; for they are not measured by gradual measures. Again, that which changes others and is not changed itself, at least in its substance, is the air, since it is a simple body. Food and drink, however, are changed and finally rendered similar and uniform to the body. This is noted by the sign of **prisoners**: those suffering in bad air first seek good air, then, in their weakened state, they seek drink, and finally food. Similarly, certain animals in caves...

->### Whether Food and Drink or Rather the Air Changes Us More.<-

And you see birds leaving with their eggs or chicks, fleeing at the time of a plague <note>Plague or "pestilence" was historically attributed to "miasma"—poisonous or corrupted air.</note>, which occurs from the corruption of the air. <margin>Mortality</margin> This is found in the fourth book of the **Problems** <note>original: "qrto p’ia," referring to Aristotle's "Problemata," a work of encyclopedic questions.</note>. Therefore, the air changes us more than drinks and foods. Regarding the first point, it must be known that air is seen to be understood in three ways. First, as a **natural thing**, according to which it enters into the constitution of our bodies and others along with the other elements <note>The four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>; what this difference is was stated in section fourteen. It is also taken as one of the **six non-natural things** <note>In medieval medicine, the "six non-naturals" were external factors that affected health: air, food/drink, sleep/wakefulness, exercise/rest, evacuation/repletion, and emotions.</note>, according as it is a certain emanation reaching our spirits; which, by tempering and preserving them, exists as a cause of their improvement. Here, according to the fourth book of the **Theoretical Medicine** and **Johannitius** <note>original: "Iobãnitiũ," referring to Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a translator and physician whose "Isagoge" was a fundamental medical textbook.</note>, it varies in many ways. First, by the change of the rising and setting of the stars; by the force of the wind; by the situation of the land; and by vaporous qualities. And here the air still observes its natural changes. Third, air is taken as a thing made **outside of nature**, when its substance is changed into a rot that induces plague, or into a most evil quality. Regarding the second and even the third kind, a space of time is required for it to take effect.

What food and drink are is known to many scholars. In a broad sense, they can be called **natural things**, as when they are converted into the substance of the body—if they are not yet entirely transformative. Indeed, such things are truly called foods because they lack an excess of all qualities, such as bitterness, pungency, sharpness, and generally every superfluous quality. However, it is more customary to call them **non-natural things**, since it is necessary for them to be brought near to us (though not often) so that they may restore the substance of our body. Insofar as they themselves corrupt, they can be called things **contrary to nature**. For the same thing, according to its different application, can be a cause of health or its opposite. Hence in the art of medicine: "Each thing, if brought to a needy body in the proper quantity and quality, is healthful; but nothing offered to a body not in need, or not in the proper measure, establishes health." This change is an alteration from a pre-existing disposition. That which is changed the most is the **heart**; for even if it resists most strongly in itself, all motion proceeds from it and returns to it. It exists in the body just as the "first intelligence" exists in the celestial sphere.

Regarding the second point, it must be known that **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ay.," abbreviation for Aristoteles</note> in the first book of the **Problems** seems to feel that water, which is a true drink, changes us more than air and even more than food, since we consume more water in respect to food. For in food and in the lungs and in drink, there is very much. Whence he asks: <margin>In the Problems</margin> "Why do they say it is morbid to change waters, but not to change the air?" He, resolving this, assigns a triple cause. First, because water becomes nourishment—not that it nourishes in its actual state as an element, as said in the fourth book of the **Meteorology** and the first book of the **Problems**, but it aids in nourishing. For it mixes with the nutrients and, by its thinness, makes those which are hard in the stomach reach the narrow passages of the veins of the mesentery and the liver. It also moistens the parts and tempers excessive heat, and helps to expel what is superfluous through sweat; hence it follows. And those having foods and using them "descend"—that is, they make them descend and penetrate because of the water, but very little because of the air. That which is mixed with nourishment changes the body more, making it penetrate the narrow parts; this is the effect of water, not air. Second, that thing changes more which has more species and diversities within itself; this is true of water and not of air, for there are many species and differences of water, but not of air. Third, because that which arrives quickly and departs swiftly does not change the body as much as that which remains and stays. This describes air and not water. Whence he says: "This is also the reason why almost the same thing happens in the air as happens to those who are passing by," who can impress and change very little. Since this transformation is an alteration, it is perfected over time like other actions. In waters, it is different; for they remain longer, wherefore they can change the body more. For which reason he concludes that the change of water is rightly seen to be morbid <note>Likely referring to the danger of drinking "bad water" when traveling to new regions.</note>.

But because this discourse seems hostile to physicians who wish to claim that air changes us as much as drinks and food, and as it is said in the seventh book of the **History of Animals**, an infinite number of fish seem to fall into pestilence just as often happens in humans and in four-legged animals—namely horses, oxen, and other domestic and wild animals—this seems to happen more due to a more violent change of the air than of the water. Let us say, so that the <margin>Solution</margin> apparent contradiction may be put to rest, that air can be spoken of in two ways: either as it is changed from its being in substance or quality (such as the pestilential air mentioned), or as it preserves its own proper tenor. If the former, it must be said that this change of air changes us more than any water, since a more frequent and violent plague occurs from the corruption of air than of water. For sometimes it immediately strangles and extinguishes the heart when it enters, no less than a poison, as has been seen not a few times in the opening of caverns and wells.

But if the air preserves its own nature, it happens in two ways. Either the change of air is grand and distant, as from the first climate to the second, or suddenly in the seventh. Then it must similarly be said that the change of air perhaps hurts more than the variety of water, since "demons" <note>In this context, "demons" likely refers to "daemons" or spiritual forces/intelligences associated with specific locations or elements in Neoplatonic thought.</note> and specific virtues are infused in the air more than in the water, and they differ greatly in places; thus they are rendered disproportionate to individuals suddenly moved to a contrary climate. Whence in the first book of the **Problems**: "When the body of an Indian is made such as it is according to the complexion of a Slav, he will either fall ill or die." Or, the change of air is not violent and distant, but gradual and close, from the edge of one region to a neighboring one. And regarding this change, the discourse of **Aristotle** can be verified; for because of the simplicity of the air in such a small distance, it does not receive such great diversity as water does, since it does not undergo such ventilation. For water is of a more composite composition, both by its own nature and by the earth joined to it. <margin>From Picardy to Flanders</margin> This is indicated by what passes from **Picardy** into **Flanders** and many other places; for there the greatest diversity and malice of the water is perceived, not so much the air. Which the health and strength of those bodies indicates. Some have said that air changes the spirit more because of its proportional similarity <meta>to them</meta> to them; but water changes the humors <note>The four humors: blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm.</note> more.

<meta>This page continues a scholastic medical debate regarding environmental factors and human health. It builds on the previous page's discussion of the "six non-natural things," specifically comparing the transformative power of air versus the impact of food and drink on the human "spirits" and "humors."</meta>

This, however, might perhaps seem contrary to the mind of **Aristotle**, since he pronounces absolutely that water is more disease-causing than air. Furthermore, if air changes the **spirits** <note>In medieval medicine, "spirits" (spiritus) were subtle substances that carried life-force and sensory information through the body, distinct from the physical "humors" like blood or bile.</note> directly, then those things which are the immediate subjects of the **virtues** <note>The "virtues" or powers of the soul/body (natural, vital, and animal) which govern functions like digestion and heartbeat.</note> are changed; however, the humors are not such things, since by nature they are more remote from the spirits. For this reason, the following statement should be accepted: the truth seems to be that air changes the **vital** faculties more, while water changes the **natural** faculties more.

Regarding the third point, it must be known that air changes us more than drinks and foods specifically in relation to the **governing virtue** <note>The "virtue" that regulates the entire body's balance.</note> which is founded most essentially in the **heart**. For the heart is the first of all changeable things. Therefore, let the rule of proportion be faithfully observed: when the air is not natural, or exists in an unnatural state, it should be compared to drinks and foods in a proportional and not unequal way.

This is shown almost as much by authorities as by reasons. First, from the **Problems** <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Problemata*.</note>: bodies are similarly disposed to the seasons; the change of the air arises greatest and first from the seasons of the year. Again, in the **Regimen**: if the surrounding air is out of balance, it diminishes the tempering of all other "non-natural" things <note>The "six non-naturals" are external factors like diet, sleep, and air that determine health.</note> in proportion to how much the **eucrasia** <note>term: eucrasia; a healthy "good mixture" of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> of the surrounding air itself has been corrupted. 

<margin>~</margin> Therefore, he intends that when the air is changed in any of its qualities, the other non-natural causes must be led in the opposite direction proportionally. Thus, it is able to change us more than just food and drink, but more than all other things as well. Likewise, **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a 10th-century physician and philosopher.</note> in the fifth book of *On Fevers* says: Air is more harmful than food and drink because, when drawn in with the breath, it penetrates swiftly to the heart and lungs without any delay. Hence, in the ninth book of *On the Art of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio," referring to Galen's "De Methodo Medendi."</note>: the matter that surrounds us is impossible to flee, but it is necessary to use that which is present. And in the fourth book of the *Theory* and the first of the *Practice*: Air is one of the strongest causes of change because of the inevitable necessity for it. This is also suggested by common experience: a person's fatness begins to diminish immediately after a certain time because the surrounding air dries out the matter of his moisture.

¶ The reason why it changes us more is shown both on the part of the thing that changes, and on the part of the thing being changed, and the nature of the change itself. As for the "changer," such as the air: that which is most receptive to change also changes others the most, since a physical agent acts physically upon a physical subject. But air exists most powerfully in a state of change, whereas food and drink do not.

¶ This is shown in three ways: From the part of its substance, its quality, and its location. Regarding its **substance**: because it is of a subtle substance, and such a thing is easily changed. For a subtle substance receives an impression more than a thick one (as seen in the sixth book of *On Fevers*).

¶ Regarding its **location**: because it is mixed with the other elements more than the rest; just as it is joined immediately with water, and frequently reaches into the depths and heights of it. Regarding its **quality**: because the primary qualities of air are **moisture** (which is the most passive/receptive to others and the least impressive of itself) and, through association, **heat**, which by nature is suited for change and **putrefaction** <note>In this context, "putrefaction" refers to the breakdown or chemical change of substances through heat and moisture.</note>. Similarly, heat is presumptive of moisture. And therefore some have said that a hot and moist complexion will not last until the age of nineteen, since the "hot" acting upon the "moist" consumes it and induces dryness; hence we see those with hot and moist temperaments are subject to many passive changes. 

The aforementioned change is caused not only by what is in the air itself, but also by what is impressed upon it from above. For while other elements are acted upon by one planet, the air is acted upon by many. The **Sun**, with its sphere in which the source of heat and light is first found, is born to excite fire. The **Moon** acts upon water, which is why the sea flows and ebbs according to the Moon's ascent and descent above and below the middle of the sky, and according to its age (whether it is in conjunction or opposition). 

But **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, **Mars**, **Venus**, and **Mercury**, with their spheres, move the air in diverse ways; hence there exist different movements and various alterations, just as the motion of these planets is varied. For **coldness** is provided to the air by Saturn. **Burning heat** is from Mars. **Temperate heat** from Jupiter. **Temperate cold** also from Venus. But **mixability** and easy passivity come from Mercury, for it is indifferent to all things and changes easily. The **eighth sphere**, called the "starry" sphere, moves the earth, impressing various transformations upon it according to long periods of time. So much so that where there is now dry land, there was once sea, and vice versa, as stated in the *Meteorology* <note>original: "methauroꝝ," referring to Aristotle's "Meteorologica."</note>. For in that sphere there are forty-eight images <note>The 48 constellations of the Ptolemaic system.</note> which, through their movements, are generative of change and transformative of the earth.

<margin>333</margin> Because of this, various distinctions are found in it (differences 14, 16, and 9). Thus, since there are many things changing the air, its active and passive alteration will be greatest. 

Secondly, regarding the thing being changed: such as the **heart**. For passions begin from it and are directed toward it, as indicated by the pulse and the movement of breathing. 
<margin>~</margin> A change arising from any cause is very slight at first. For of all harms coming to the body, the first to encounter them is the heart, as if it were the **foundation of life**. **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (Mesue the Elder), a Persian Christian physician.</note> says in *On Simples*: its nature is the innermost and most powerful harmony. Such a thing is changed easily, as is clear in the eleventh book of the *Problems*.

Thirdly, regarding the change itself: it is shown in three ways—by reason of its **immediacy**, its **continuity/constancy**, and its **utility**. First, because air meets the heart almost immediately, changing it entirely according to its disposition. For that which changes something immediately changes it more strongly than that which changes through an intervening medium, since a medium hinders the impression.

But a doubt happens to arise here: 
<margin>Doubt?</margin> It does not seem that the air meets the heart immediately. For just as the stomach prepares and fits the food for the other members so that it does not reach them in a raw state, so the **uvula** and the **lungs** first change and alter the air so that it does not reach the heart without a medium. Furthermore, air is subtle, while food and drink are coarse. A subtle thing needs little change to make it familiar to the body, while a coarse thing needs much; therefore it seems air meets the heart through a medium just like food and drink. 

To which it must be said: first, that the lung induces only a slight alteration since it is a soft, loose member, easily affected, and especially since the air remains in it for only a short time. For as soon as it reaches the lung, it is swiftly transmitted to the heart to be associated with the **spirit**, as the heart requires the drawing out of smoky vapors lest it become inflamed.

<margin>returning to the heart</margin>

...the retained [matter] a destructive accident might occur. <margin>2nd part</margin> To the other point, it must be said that **air** is not altered more easily than food and drink, since in it there are many things requiring change. It also changes the most alterable member [the heart] above all. For something that is easily changed in respect to the stomach is not so easily changed in respect to the heart, since the heart itself would not endure any significant suffering. Third, concerning the parts of animals: even if I grant that air is more easily altered than food and drink by a single alteration, it nevertheless exists by reason of many factors. For air occurs to us almost continually, whereas food and drink occur at intervals. The reason for this continuity—or most frequent arrival—is that air, being inhaled and exhaled, meets the heart almost continuously, while food and drink do so with no small intervals. For if it arrives continuously as something altered, it changes the especially alterable member more than that which is transformed over time in members that are not as easily changed, such as the stomach. This [constant factor] is the air. But food and drink are not. Hence, in the ninth book of *On Generation* <note>Referring to Aristotle's "On Generation and Corruption."</note>, it is said: we can both choose and flee other materials, but it is impossible to avoid those which are constant; rather, it is necessary to use what is present. 

On the part of its utility, this is twofold: either because it arrives from everywhere—for it enters through the mouth and nostrils into the **respiratory organs** <term>original: "spiritualia" — the lungs and passages carrying the "vital spirit"</term> and immediately affects the whole body from the outside—which food and drink do not do in the same way; or because it is usually contained within drinks and foods. For all things are exposed to the air and are greatly affected by it. Hence, in the *Problems*, it says: **Mortality** <note>Used here to mean pestilence or epidemic disease.</note> corrupts trees and vegetation; wherefore those animals that eat them are corrupted. And therefore the men who feed upon them are corrupted. Mortality, or pestilence, arises from the corruption of the air. For it is itself a putrefaction that happens to the air, similar to the putrefaction of softened, foul-smelling water. Thus, air changes us more vehemently than drinks and foods, and then drink more than food.

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it must be said that even if pure elements change animals according to their exchange—since they lack changed qualities—they do so according to how they have been mixed with other bodies. Air is one of these elements. For the earth we tread upon, the water we drink, and the air we breathe are not simple elements. <note>Medieval science held that the "air" around us was a mixture, not the "pure" element of Air.</note> 

It is the sequence of the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the primary commentator on Aristotle.</note>: An animal that is naturalized to live in water or air does not feel any hot or cold quality if it is in the simplicity which it ought to have. Because that is its natural place, and the place is similar to the thing placed, as declared in the general discourses. It has been shown that the sensible object, before the act of perception, is a contrary. And since this is so, an animal does not feel heat or cold in air or water unless hot or cold bodies are mixed with them. He wishes, therefore, to say that simple elements do not change us, except insofar as they have been mixed with foreign bodies. Nor is "water" called such by the common people except because of the prevailing watery parts in it; just as **Anaxagoras** <note>Pre-Socratic philosopher who taught that "everything is in everything."</note> posited that a thing is named for what is predominant in it, such as "flesh" or something else. For the common people are accustomed to call it "water" as long as liquidity remains in it. 

To the other point, it must be said: simple things do in the composite what the composite things do in themselves, because according to **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a highly influential 10th-century physician and philosopher.</note>, they do not turn into the substance of the body with the others. Truly composite things, since they share in a more specific matter, do not operate like simple things in a composite. Yet the quantity of a simple thing can be added so continuously that it overcomes the action, since quantity is an assistant to action, specifically in simple drugs. Hence the **Commentator**: The powers of bodies follow their magnitudes. <margin>Commentator, Book 1, Chapter 2</margin>

To the other point, it must be said regarding the intemperate [state]: because simple and composite things share one matter, even if it is more specific to some and more remote to others. For all things that are generable and usually have a mutual transformation, there is one primary matter (from *On Generation and Corruption*). Or of all simple things through the contrariety of forms. 

To the other point, it must be said: air and water are the **place** of materially situated things. The form of this is the order and aspect toward the universe, which is always preservative, since it is something divine and desirable (from the *Physics*). Or water and air, insofar as there is in them a surface or boundary containing the body of the animal, have a preservative power. But in that foreign qualities are mixed with it, it has an accidental corruptive power. 

To the other point, it must be said: air has qualities that are minimally sensible in comparison to others, but through addition, it has qualities very sensible to our bodies. 

To the other point, it must be said: the opposite persuades more than the intended point; for because something remains longer, it transforms more, since it transforms that which is near to it. However, the transformer changes it less. Furthermore, food and drink are altered with difficulty in the [process] of alteration, but air is easy. And through this, the second part of that reasoning is clear. For there is no greater mass of drink and food by reason of the stomach than there is of air by reason of the heart; nor is it the stomach that is transformed longer, but rather the heart. 

To the other point, it must be said: although air, by reason of its substance or the quality of its moisture, is minimally impressive of change, yet because of the mixture of its substance with other foreign bodies, and the alteration made in its qualities by fumes from the earth and vapors from the water—as well as the ignitions and rays of the higher bodies mixing these lower things with themselves and altering them by motion and light—qualities both active and passive are most effectively imprinted upon it.

### DIFFERENTIA CXV.

-> It is shown whether life is shortened more in **Spring** than in the other seasons of the year. <-

Since in that time in which more diseases occur, life is shortened more—since disease is the most powerful cause of the shortening of life—and this is in the Spring according to **Hippocrates** and **Galen**, and even the **Aphorisms**. For in it, the diseases of all seasons coincide. It even produces, of itself, diseases of **repletion** <note>An excess of bodily fluids or humors.</note> and suffocating diseases. Hence the first problem: why are Spring and Autumn disease-bearing? 

Again: if that which meets its like incites it to fury, it is like fire upon fire. This is the case with Spring, since it pertains to heat and moisture. And human nature is hot and moist in the second degree, according to **Isaac** in his *Universal Diets*. For this reason, life will be further shortened in the Spring. 

The opposite of this is also shown: because Spring is most similar [to our nature] and least deadly, according to the *Aphorisms*. For health prolongs life.

<margin>First problem; see also: similarity and addition.</margin>

<margin>ISAAC.</margin>

<margin>3rd Aphorism.</margin>

Again, life consists of heat and moisture. Such a complexion is almost exactly what exists under the dominion of spring. Therefore, life is shortened the least in spring. However, it is shown that life happens to be shortened more in summer. Because that is the time when bodily strength is weaker, life is more likely to be shortened, since life is sustained by strength. This happens in summer, as they say and as the flow of humors shows, when heat exhales and moisture dissolves through the opening of the pores. Furthermore, life is prolonged by the perfection of natural virtues <note>In medieval science, "virtues" refers to the body’s innate functional powers, such as digestion or growth.</note> and especially by digestion. For through these, prepared material is supplied for nourishment. But this does not happen in summer; hence the first book of the *Aphorisms* <note>Referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates.</note> says: "In summer and autumn, they bear food most heavily."

Therefore, life will be shortened in summer. On the contrary, because in summer the humors ready to putrefy—which if retained in other seasons would cause rot—are expelled outward by the opening of the pores and the attraction of the surrounding heat. Whence it benefits <term>original: "pfert" — is advantageous for</term> phlegmatic people and the elderly, and strengthens their digestions. Again, in summer the sun approaches us or stays with us. Since the sun is the cause of generation, it is also the cause of life, since life is ordered toward it. Therefore, life is least shortened in summer. 

That it is shortened more in autumn is shown because autumn is cold and dry; and this is the way toward death. For it is proportioned to old age according to the theory of complexions.

<margin>1st Astronomical argument.</margin>
Similarly, the season which is contrary to the nature of life is what shortens it, since life is mostly taken away by such contrariety; such is autumn in the first instance. Therefore, it shortens life more.

<margin>2nd part, 2nd lesson, 1st chapter 6.</margin>
The opposite of this is shown because a temperate season does not shorten life but rather prolongs it. But the complexion of autumn is temperate in heat and cold, like spring. See the seventh book of the *Theorice* and Philaretus <note>Philaretus was a traditional medical authority often cited alongside Hippocrates.</note>. And this is confirmed because in autumn the sun is at the same distance and proportion to us as in spring. Since in both cases it is uniformly around the equator.

<margin>Albumasar</margin>

Whence Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> in the *Sadan* <note>The *Kitab al-Mudhakarat* or "Book of Conversations".</note>: "There is no life for the living, except through God, but through the sun and moon." But in spring, life is shortened the least. Again, life is shortened by an excess of qualities. Conversely, it is prolonged by their moderation. But in autumn, qualities are less excessive than in other seasons like summer and winter, since in autumn there is less heat than in summer and a more relaxed dryness. For the air is thinner in summer. In autumn, it already becomes moist, according to the first book of the *Meteorologica* <note>Aristotle's work on natural phenomena.</note> and the book on complexions. And the cold is more relaxed than that of winter. Furthermore, in autumn many people are seen to grow fat <term>original: "ancrastari" — to become fleshy or stout</term>; this, since it testifies to health and moisture, is advantageous for the prolongation of life. Furthermore, they write about the season and its constitution. But a cold and dry constitution, such as the northern one in autumn, renders bodies stronger, more mobile, and more perfect in other ways, according to the third book of *Aphorisms*. Therefore, the shortening of life is minimal in autumn. Thus, in autumn, life will be shortened only moderately. 

<margin>3rd Astronomical argument.</margin>
But that it is shortened more in winter is apparent, because in winter a destructive quality prevails, and cold is contrary to life, causing dissolution. Also, phlegmatic humor accumulates in it, which by the evil quality of cold, suffocates the body with its cold mass, and by its viscosity blocks the pores <term>original: "opilans" — obstructing or clogging</term> and narrows the passages, thus bringing on death. Furthermore, premature dissolution is a cause of the shortening of life; this occurs in winter according to Galen's <note>Galen of Pergamum, the most influential physician of antiquity.</note> commentary on the first book of *Aphorisms*. Therefore, life will be shortened most in winter. 

On the contrary, life stands by the support of the virtues. These are strengthened in winter, specifically those acting for life, as is evident from the first book of *Aphorisms*. Again, in winter there is a superabundance of heat and moisture because of good digestion and the invigorating of internal heat. Heat remains and dominates the moisture, strengthened by antiperistasis <term>original: "antiperistasis" — the process where a quality is strengthened by being surrounded by its opposite, such as internal heat being concentrated by external cold</term>. The cause of life is a proportionate abundance of heat and moisture, where the active qualities dominate the passive ones, according to Difference 12. Therefore, life is least shortened in winter.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that "time" is the number or measure of motion according to "before" and "after," from the fourth book of the *Physics*. For this motion of the first movable sphere is measured by the soul, under which the motion of the sun is also contained, as are other particular motions in which the sun traverses the zodiac; this is called a year. This is the space of time in which the sun, by its own motion, travels from west to east along its eccentric orbit placed directly under the ecliptic; it completes this in a space of 365 days and a quarter, minus a 161st part of one hour <note>This reflects medieval efforts to calculate the exact length of the tropical year.</note>. The year is divided into four parts called seasons: Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter. Of these seasons, a threefold distinction is found.

One is sensible and more medicinal, based on the effects found in them. This is because spring is the beginning of trees leafing out and when snow melts from the mountains; then we do not need many coverings because of the cold, nor few because of the heat. Autumn is the time of the changing of the color of leaves and the beginning of their falling. In it also, springs and water channels are diminished. The other two seasons are summer and winter. Of these, summer is very hot, in which leaves are rendered perfect, and at its end they begin to whiten and the early fruits wither. Nor do we need clothes for the cold, but rather the removal of them for the heat. Winter is very cold, the opposite of this. 

There is also another astronomical distinction of the seasons, which is also placed in the fifth book of the *Theorice* <note>Likely the *Theorica Planetarum*, a standard medieval astronomical textbook.</note>, which is considered according to the precise course of the sun in the zodiac. For by its passage through three signs of the zodiac—namely **Aries**, **Taurus**, and **Gemini**—which span the space of three solar months, it constitutes one season. And these spaces are truly equal. Spring now begins on the 13th day of March and ends on the 14th of June. Then the sun enters **Cancer**, and arriving at the end of **Virgo**, it constitutes another season as summer, which ends on the 16th of September; thus three solar months similarly arise. From there it enters **Libra**, and passing through **Scorpio** to the end of **Sagittarius**, which is the 14th of December, it completes another season as autumn, likewise having three months. And then, leaving **Capricorn**, passing through **Aquarius**, and arriving at the end of **Pisces** on the 13th day of March, it causes winter, consisting of three months. 

Thus, from every revolution of the sun in the "sign-bearer" <term>original: "fignifero" — the zodiac</term>, the year arises from four seasons and consists of twelve months. The third distinction is taken according to the rising and setting of certain stars, noted in Aristotle's book *On Air and Water* and expressed in the third book of *Aphorisms* and the fifth book of the *Theorice*. -> **Whether Life is shortened more in Spring than in other seasons of the year.** <-

Spring is said to begin when the Pleiades rise at the beginning of May; these are six stars gathered together with others in the heavens, now occupying the 19th degree of Taurus. 
<margin>Pleiades</margin> 
The middle of summer, however, occurs when the Great Dog star <note>Canis Maior, specifically the star Sirius.</note> emerges in the mouth of the "Little Dog" and rises before the morning sun; it is indeed larger and brighter than all other fixed stars. 
<margin>The Dog Star</margin> 
It currently rises on the 20th day of July, at the 5th degree of Cancer. Then the so-called "Canicular" <note>Often called the "Dog Days" of summer.</note> days begin, according to the fourth book of the *Aphorisms*: 
<margin>Canicular Days</margin> 
"Under the Dog Star and before the Dog Star, purges <note>Medical treatments intended to clear the humors, like bloodletting or laxatives.</note> are troublesome." Concerning this, Dionysius <note>Likely referring to a classical or medieval commentator.</note> says in his book: "The Dog star is a celestial constellation that glimmers morbidly at the foot of Orion." Autumn also begins when Arcturus rises before the sun at dawn, in the 15th degree of Libra. Every such rising is "heliacal" or solar. For there is a triple rising and setting: "Cosmical" (worldly), "Chronical" (temporal), and "Heliacal" (solar), as certain astronomical poets teach. 
The beginning of winter, however, is at the setting of the Pleiades, which is around the beginning of November; then follows the remaining time of spring after winter. 

And it should be known that the rising of the stars is not the total cause of the change of the air and seasons, but rather a sign. Indeed, the sun is like the whole cause; 
<margin>3rd book of *On Crises*</margin> 
whence it says in the third book of *On Crises* <note>A work by Galen regarding the turning points of diseases.</note>: "There is no cause for spring, summer, autumn, and winter except the sun itself." Ptolemy, in his *Introduction to the Art*, strove to confirm this. The stars also assist in this according to their conjunction with or separation from the sun. For when a star is joined to the sun, or the sun moves toward it, the change of the air toward heat is intensified. When, however, a separation occurs, it is lessened, according to theoretical measures. What "dual life" is, is noted elsewhere in sections 21 and 123. 
<margin>Dual life: 21 and 123</margin> 
It must also be assumed that of the parts of the seasons, the tempered one tempers the other; that is, because they correspond to each other. Thus they are such when, according to reason, the signs have been completed in the rising and setting of the stars. And if in autumn there were cold waters, and winter was moderate and at its end not very tranquil, nor over-abounding in freezing winds; and if in spring there were temperate waters as in summer; then it is fitting for the year to be very healthy regarding the air and water, as the first book of the *Aphorisms* states along with others. Similarly, the locations must be sufficiently tempered.

Regarding the same matter, it should be known that some have said life is shortened more in winter, while others say in summer, taking death to be twofold. One arises from the consumption of <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: "humidi radicalis" — the vital fluid believed by medieval doctors to be the "fuel" of life, which slowly burns away until death.</note>; the other from its putrefaction. The first of these, according to Avicenna, is natural and sweet, as it proceeds gradually from the beginning by the internal <term>natural heat</term> <note>original: "calore innato" — the innate warmth that drives biological functions.</note> acting upon the radical moisture. The second, however, is accidental, violent, and bitter, caused by decay. 

They say, therefore, that life is more shortened in winter—that is, when natural death is accelerated. Their reasoning is this: because at that time heat is more immersed and fixed in the radical moisture, it consumes it more extensively and consequently shortens life. This happens in winter, for the heat is driven inward into the moisture and strengthened by the surrounding cold, according to that old saying: "Stomachs in winter and spring are naturally warmest." 
When heat is thus concentrated, it consumes the moisture more greatly. And therefore, one can see more resolutions <note>The breaking down of substances in the body.</note> in it, as noted by Galen in the same place. By this sign they wish to show that 
<margin>Candle</margin> 
a candle burns faster in winter than in summer, unless the heat is dissolved otherwise by the summer air. They say this happens because in the density of the winter air, the flame is pushed more into the material of the candle, being unable to extend upward due to the resistance of the surrounding dense air. 

Conversely, they say the opposite happens in summer. Therefore, they conclude that life—as opposed to natural death—is shortened more in winter. In summer, however, because the natural heat is weakened by dissolution, the humors become unable to be governed. They say life—as opposed to violent death—is shortened more due to the putrefaction of the humors; for when the humors are not properly ruled by heat, they rot. For they do not putrefy unless they are destitute of nature's governance, as noted in *On the Differences of Fevers*. 

This position, however, as far as the first part is concerned, perhaps does not hold the truth—namely, that life is shortened more in winter as opposed to natural death. Rather, it is shortened more in summer and autumn, as will be declared in the third book of the *Opinions*. Nor is their reasoning entirely sufficient; for even granted that radical moisture is dissolved more in winter, this is compensated for by the "nutritable moisture" which is then generated more copiously. Those who posit this moisture say it restores the body and prevents such dissolution, as appears in chapter 12; although more is dissolved than in other times, more is also restored. And therefore, bodies seem more lively and stronger, as is evident to many. 

Nor does the sign they introduced <note>The candle analogy.</note> compel us, since there is no true similarity between an external flame and our internal heat, for the reasons already mentioned. For the greater consumption of a candle in winter is not compensated for by anything external coming in, whereas the radical moisture is said to be restored in winter by the inflowing nourishment. As for what they say about life being shortened more in summer by violent death, this can be understood as true. The Commentator <note>Referring to Averroes.</note>, in the fourth book of the *Meteorology*, says: "In winter, corruption is hastened, which occurs through freezing and desiccation, due to the victory of cold over that thing when natural heat is destroyed." This is because of external heat, and therefore winter illnesses are such. But in summer, putrefaction is greater than in winter, and this is because there is much external heat at that time due to the heat of the surrounding air. Whence the aforementioned corruption does not hasten then, but rather the corruption or putrefaction that occurs through dissolution and combustion is accelerated. For there is one putrefaction which is through external moisture and not through external dryness. 

And although this understanding may have truth, it does not distinguish the whole year into its necessary parts, perhaps only dividing the year into two. Regarding the third point, it should be known that if one wished to distinguish the whole year through everything, one would extend the argument further, since some natures and ages fare well or poorly in certain seasons—poorly indeed in summer, while phlegmatic people and women fare otherwise. 

However, as much as suffices for the present, it must be said simply that the time in which life is least shortened is spring. For in spring, moisture is sufficient and proportioned to the heat. Similarly, the heat is not entirely immersed in the radical moisture as in winter, nor is it dissolved and subject to putrefaction as in summer. Therefore, it is well said that spring is the healthiest season and the least lethal. 
<margin>Spring is the best time.</margin> 
And this is proved in the first book of the *Complexions*. It also shows that a tempered complexion lives longest. From then on, in winter, death is naturally accelerated, since in it there is more...

But against this, it seems to be what is said in the first of the *Problems*: <note>Referring to the *Problems* attributed to Aristotle, a collection of questions on natural phenomena.</note> why is it that people fall ill more in summer, but those who are ill die more in winter? Life will be shortened in summer. It must be said that in summer, as will be shown more clearly, this is true. And it must be solved according to Aristotle: he does not intend to say that more people simply happen to die in winter than in summer, but that more of the winter illnesses are fatal than the summer illnesses, because they arise from a more vehement cause. Whence he says that in winter, the beginning of the illness is a vehement thing; such a thing is consequently a source of corruption. For in diseases, those who are ill are in great danger. For if there are illnesses near each other, both those of winter and those of summer—say, thirty in summer and seven in winter—out of the thirty, it happens that more die because the total number of thirty exceeds seven. However, out of the seven in winter, more die proportionally—for example, three—than out of the thirty in summer, unless the illness was a pestilence affecting many at once. Therefore, life will be shortened more in summer and autumn.

Because of this, it must be known hereafter that life can be shortened in two ways: either by reason of the causes emerging from that time in its own property, or from things happening from other times. If in the first way, it is clear that summer shortens life more than the others; and secondarily, autumn. This is shown because when the qualities are most active, they produce more effective intensities and shorten life more, since life consists in a balance of temperaments. This happens in summer. For in it, heat thrives, which is the most effective of all primary qualities, as well as dryness among the passive qualities. It is, as it were, the file and sharpening of heat. Nor is there anything so hot that the heat of summer does not defend us from its resolution. Just as by chance we are defended and fortified by the cold of winter, because of which cold—even if it is naturally an enemy and a bringer of death—it is rendered accidentally a friend and a giver of life. But exceeding heat, in the manner mentioned, is rendered an enemy.

Furthermore, in summer, digestion is poorly celebrated <note>original: "prava celebratur digestio"; meaning digestion is performed poorly or becomes corrupted.</note>. According to that ancient proverb: "In summer and autumn, food is carried most heavily," and the naturally hateful humors, like burnt choler <note>term: <term>choler</term> (yellow bile), one of the four humors, associated with heat and dryness.</note>, and those prepared for a horrible putrefaction, are multiplied and open the pores. During this, the radical moisture <note>The "radical moisture" was believed by medieval doctors to be the finite fuel of life, like the oil in a lamp.</note> evaporates and the heat of nature dissolves. This is shown because the appetite is weakened, the body becomes thin, and illnesses emerge that are more troublesome due to the homogeneity of the time. This is also a sign: that in hot regions proportional to summer, life is seen to be shortened. For in the "land of the blacks," <note>A common medieval reference to sub-Saharan Africa or Ethiopia, used to illustrate climate theories.</note> old age arrives in thirty years. From which it is inferred that for itself, summer is the most shortening of life among the other seasons; but autumn is not so much for itself, but rather by reason of causes rising from other times, and it is the most shortening of both types of life, since it is not a little contrary to spring.

And therefore the first of the *Problems* states: autumn is more morbid <note>meaning: "more conducive to disease."</note> than spring. For a sick person is more affected when heat is turned to cold than vice versa; since cold is an enemy of nature, it finds the pores open through which it can seek the innermost parts of the body; for the pores begin to close in autumn, according to the first of the *Aphorisms*. <note>Referring to the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates, a foundational medical text.</note> Furthermore, its nature stands out as contrary to life. And again, nature does not tolerate sudden and manifold changes, since they dissolve its harmonic consonance. According to which, Damascenus <note>Likely referring to John of Damascus or a medical author known as "Johannes Damascenus."</note> says in the *Aphorisms* that a multitude of things are built up, but sudden changes intervene frequently in autumn toward cold, and then soon toward heat, because of the subtlety of the air acquired from summer (from the third of the *Aphorisms* and the second of the first). For the nights and mornings are cold, but the midday and even more the afternoon hours are hot, according to Aristotle.

Moreover, it receives materials "incinerated" by the summer and urges them on by its construction of the pores. For it is, according to Aristotle, the "relic of the leftovers" of summer illnesses. And its illnesses are for the most part very acute and very fatal, as per the third of the *Aphorisms*. Which, however, if they approach winter, the humor is softened and they are dissolved by the fortified heat. Such material is the cause of illnesses and brevity of life. Again, in the time when one walks under a very hot sun and in the night comes suddenly to cold. One also eats a multitude of fruits, which is a corruption of the humors. And in both cases, the body is weak, and life is shortened more by such things. This happens, as they say, in autumn. Because of which, it is more shortening of life than other times. And even if it brings forth little, it is for a few and for another reason. To sum up: spring shortens life the least; winter a little more; summer more for itself; but autumn the most of all for other reasons. Whence experience teaches us that more people die in autumn than in other seasons.

But concerning the aforesaid, it is doubted since "time" is a certain measure of motion numbered according to before and after <note>This is Aristotle's famous definition of time from his *Physics*.</note> according to its own nature in the genus of quantity, in which no alteration occurs, and similarly no mutation; since mathematics lacks sensible qualities, as appears in the third book of the *Metaphysics*. It must be said that "time" can be considered in two ways: either according to itself as touched upon, and thus in it and by it almost no mutation occurs in life; or by reason of a sensible quality joined to it, and thus a change occurs in it. For time is the cause of corruption for itself, according to the fourth book of the *Physics*. Whence the third of the *Aphorisms* says: "The names of the hours are not the causes of diseases, but the complexions." <note>term: <term>complexion</term> (the specific balance of the four humors in an individual).</note> Therefore, according to the first opinion: you should know that the effects of the mutations of the seasons are not because of the cause of "time," but because when the quality is changed, it has great efficacy in the operation of the changes of dispositions. Because of the fourth: to the first it must be said that although many illnesses happen in spring, yet not many of them are fatal as in autumn, since they are from the blood; also the virtue then becomes strong. Nor is that in itself true of spring, but rather through something else; because in it, with the strength being fortified and the pores beginning to open, nature—wishing to drive out materials—sometimes succumbs, just as when someone presumes more than they are able. To the other it must be said: although spring brings illnesses, yet they are fewer than in autumn, as Aristotle subjoins. And what it might be for the other, it has appeared.
