# Whether for a failing body preservation or conservation is due

The heat of human nature and its moisture, and the temperament of spring in its heat and moisture, are not mutually exacerbating and inciting to fury, since they are similar in species and nature, and thus preserve each other rather than being corruptive in kind. Regarding summer, it must be said that although in summer moist things tend to exhale and rot because of the thinness of the pores and the external attraction of the heat, the spirit that aids life—namely the blood, which is the support of life—exhales and dissolves. If the strength is so weakened that it cannot repel what is harmful, then while it may benefit some, it generally hinders the search for health. Regarding another point, it must be said that this approach and retreat is properly the cause of the generation and corruption of animals produced from putrefaction. In summer, the heat approaches and remains with us so much that its influence on the air becomes the cause of an excessive dissolution of strength. For a temperate life is preserved, not an excessive one; this only happens because foreign matter acts upon it, though the source of life exists of itself. Regarding autumn, it must be said that it is not a perfectly temperate season. For this, it should be known that something is temperate in two ways: either because within it, qualities are broken down and altered into a combined temperament for the constitution, and such is the temperament of spring, where all parts of the natural day correspond proportionally to it in qualities. The other way is when qualities are not broken down and mixed into one, but rather are placed near each other in a diminished state; such can be called the imperfect temperament of autumn in its heat and cold. This is indicated by the disposition of the day being the opposite of the former; hence, even if it is said to be somewhat temperate in its active qualities—because it is not as hot as summer nor as cold as winter—it is nevertheless very distempered in its passive qualities, as in its intense decline into dryness. For this reason, <term>Avicenna</term><note>The OCR "Aū." refers to Avicenna (Ibn Sina), the influential Persian physician and philosopher.</note> opposes those who think the <term>complexion</term><note>The balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, dry—within a person.</note> of autumn is like the temperance of spring just because it is the midpoint between summer and winter (see *Difference 66*). There, it will also be seen what should be said for confirmation. Regarding the other point, it must be said, as has already appeared, that as far as the excess of qualities is concerned, the shortening of life in autumn is not as great as in summer or winter. However, this is due to the sudden and frequent course of the qualities and because of other things inherent to it that are noted from other seasons, because of the suitability of its underlying substance for receiving them. Regarding the other point, it must be said that autumn helps some, such as those whose pores were thinned and dissolved by summer, since in autumn the pores begin to constrict; and those who do not have excessive moisture ready for corruption. Yet it profits few compared to those it harms. Regarding the other point, it must be said that such a constitution works by accident on the "falling" state, and the fortification of the internal composite of the body flourishes for a short time. For if what autumn does were to endure longer, it would work even more.

Regarding winter, it must be said that the quality is not inherent to it perpetually when it is restored temporally. Or, that this incidentally <note>original: "per accidens"</note> produces a strength of heat in many; but this is a winter-like thing. Regarding the other point, it also appeared: the reasons for the other part proceed in winter, and in other seasons, understood in their own way.

### DIFFERENCE CXVI.
<margin>1</margin>
**Whether** for a <term>failing body</term><note>original: "corpus lapsum," literally a "fallen body." In medieval medicine, this refers to a body that has deviated from perfect health but is not yet diseased.</note> preservation <note>original: "preservatio"</note> is due, and not conservation <note>original: "conservatio"</note> or a <term>regimen</term><note>A prescribed way of life, including diet and exercise, to maintain health.</note> through opposites and not likes. It seems that for a body in the best state of composition, everyone agrees on this. For if the body of a man is exactly in the middle of its complexion, it will be conserved by food that is in the middle of its complexion in its present state. But if it is somewhat hotter or colder or drier or moister, giving it foods and drinks of a middle complexion will do it harm; for it is necessary that each of these bodies be changed toward the opposite in as much as it stands apart from the exact middle of the complexion. For if the body departs from a well-complexioned and middle state toward cold by three degrees, and the same for moist and dry, it requires its own food. Furthermore, at the end of these three, things suitable for eating will preserve it without complaint, for whatever things are born in animals are similar to their own complexion. But for those who have a bad complexion from the start, or those acquiring one not yet at that state, the use of opposites is profitable. For those things which are naturally in a good state without complaint are preserved by similar things, but those which are poorly complexioned are led to a suitable state by opposites. This sounds the same as the eighth book of *On the Method of Healing* and the first of the *Aphorisms*. Furthermore, adding like to like makes it "rage" <note>original: "furere," meaning to intensify or increase uncontrollably.</note> in increase; it makes it more so by such additions (as in the third book of the *Topics*). Those things that act in this way make one fall further into decline. Again, the heart and the whole body are inspired and respired (see *Difference 71*), which is disproportionate to a failing body. The air that surrounds us is also very much a friend to the preparation of the innate spirit (according to the first book). At least in respect to air so changed, a regimen cannot be made through similar things.

Furthermore, in each of these, there is a predominant quality (*Difference 12*) which must be governed by opposites in the mixture so that it does not intensify, and thus the failing state would be made worse. Likewise, what is administered to a failing body will either be in a lesser excess of heat or cold, and thus it is not preserved in that same failing state unless it preponderates; or it will be in a greater excess and then it will increase the state; or in an equal excess, and thus no action or passion will occur, since it is similar. A thing does not suffer from its like (from the eighth book of *Problems*); and if it does not suffer, it does not act. For every physical agent thus suffers and acts. Because such a thing cannot conserve, since conservation is a certain action, it follows that conservation for a failing body will not be through similar things.

The opposite of this is in the *Regimen*: When one wishes to conserve the <term>crasis</term><note>The specific mixture of humors or qualities in an individual.</note> that the body has received, one should bring in things similar to it. For hotter bodies need hotter aids, colder need colder, moister need moister, drier need drier, and similarly in other cases in their own way.

Again, natural things, as was said, are preserved by similar things. But the failing body is natural, since it is placed within the "latitude of health" (that is, of the *Regimen*). Again, natural appetite is ordained toward the conservation of food. But here, in those things which are natural, it desires similar things. In non-natural things, however, it desires dissimilar things in the *Regimen*. Therefore, it is through likes that they are established. Furthermore, a sick body is not taught to be conserved by similar things (*Difference 174*). Much more so, then, a failing body. Therefore, conservation is due to the body and through likes. Furthermore, a thing does not suffer from that which is similar in species and nature (from the first book), since all passion is from an opposite; but a "fall" in the first degree, with heat in the same proper state, follows an equal stay...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how the four qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) affect the human body. It moves from the general theory of seasonal change to the specific medical philosophy of similarity: how like substances preserve the body and how "failing" health is categorized.</meta>

Something exists as **similar** in both species and nature. Because of this, it brings about neither a "passion" <note>In medieval philosophy, a 'passion' refers to being acted upon or undergoing a change caused by an external agent.</note> nor an "action." This is demonstrated when two bodies that are equally hot are applied to each other; for although the quantity of the individuals is equal, the quality remains stable within its degree. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known that the **lapsed body** <term>lapsed body: a body that has "fallen" away from perfect health but is not yet fully diseased</term> is threefold: namely, slightly, moderately, and greatly.
*   The **slight** is called a healthy-failing state.
*   The **great** is simply called "sick."
*   The **middle** is called "neutral."

Each of these categories has a wide "latitude" <note>The 'latitude' of health refers to the range or spectrum of physical states that fall under a single definition.</note>. Thus, in the *Tegni* <note>original: "tegni"; referring to Galen's *Ars Medica* (The Art of Medicine), a foundational textbook.</note>, the entire latitude of health is divided into three parts, which themselves have considerable breadth. Each of these three is further divided into a "more," a "less," and a "middle." These bodies are discerned between two extreme boundaries: 
1.  The best composition, simply and at this moment. 
2.  A composition that has just become diseased. 

These states are like middle grounds, and therefore their **regimen** <term>regimen: a prescribed way of life, including diet and exercise, to maintain health</term> must also be a middle ground. Thus, those closer to the best composition will participate more in its regimen, while the worst will deviate from it in every way. The middle state requires a moderate regimen. 

Furthermore, "preservation" is currently understood in two ways. In one way, it is **vital** <note>original: "spiritualit̄"; likely referring to the maintenance of the 'vital spirits' or pneuma within a healthy body.</note>, as it ought to be for a body that is perfectly healthy; in this case, all preservation exists through "likes" in every way. In a general sense, preservation is taken either to mean leading a body toward a better **temperament** <term>temperament: the specific balance of the four humors/qualities in an individual</term> or maintaining a state that already exists from the beginning. And so, under the heading of preservation, the "permutative" (changing) regimen is contained in the *Tegni*. There, **Haly** <note>Likely Haly Abbas or Haly Rodoan, famous medieval commentators on Galen.</note> names it a thing of its own kind; for this preservation seems to be the same as the **hygienic regimen** <note>original: "fastas regimētū"; likely a transcription error for "hygiasticum," the branch of medicine concerned with health maintenance.</note>, which is a category consisting of both the conservative and the permutative regimen.

<margin>**Similar**</margin>
<margin>Similarity. According to the second book of Boethius's *Topics*, in five modes.</margin>
<margin>The third book of the *Metaphysics*, the sixth book of the *Regimen*, the eighth book of *On the Preservation of Health*.</margin>

**Similarity** is understood in two ways. For one is called "truly similar," which is placed within a category; for its property is to be similar to itself. What is "dissimilar" is spoken of in terms of quantity (equal and unequal), but in terms of substance, it is "same" and "different." Hence Boethius, in the second book of his *Topics*, says: "Similarity in things is defined as the same quality." Fifthly, in the *Metaphysics*, two modes of similarity are touched upon. For those things are called "similar" which have been affected by the same thing, or many things affected by the same thing—as if many things were burned, or different things, such as if one person were beaten and another imprisoned. And those whose quality is one, like the whiteness and brilliance in snow and ice. There is also another mode where whatever happens to be altered by one of two contraries, that which has more of the proper quality is "similar" to it, as appears in the middle points between contraries toward the extremes. This is similarity in genus. 

Similarity is also used by Galen for **similarity in substance**. The knowledge of this is recognized by the "point" <note>Likely referring to the 'apex' or essential nature of the substance.</note> alone. By this similarity, flesh is said to be similar to lions. For horses, barley or oats are similar. For oxen, bitter vetch, and for pigs, acorns. For almost every species has its own food determined by its similarity in substance, which is dissimilar to others, as appears in the *Histories of Animals*. Man, however, is **polyphagous** <term>polyphagous: an organism that eats a wide variety of different foods; an omnivore</term>; though some foods are poisons to others—as henbane <note>original: "iusquiamus"</note> is eaten by thrushes and quails. This similarity is observed not only in species but also in individuals. For every figure and temperament of a man has a food that is convenient and similar to it. In food, there is a twofold similarity to the body: both in quality and in the substance of the temperaments.

***

However, this is not a "predicamental" substance separated from "accidents" <note>A reference to Aristotelian logic: a substance is what a thing is, while an accident is a property (like color) that can change.</note>, but rather a certain nature and property attributed to each animal species from a higher specific power, and even attributed to the individual. In this same specific way, it is written that a **medicine** <note>original: "pharmacū"</note> has the power to draw out the humor proper to itself, because of a similarity found in substance—that is, in its "form" or specific virtue. It should also be noted that all similarity mentioned here exists **potentially**, not actually <note>Meaning the food has the potential to become the body, but is not the body yet.</note>. For no food should be called "temperate" for a man except human flesh—or, more remotely, the flesh of hens. Since earthly science does not possess heat, they are not at all similar to the temperament of a man, which is hot. What a "generic difference" is, is shown in chapter 53.

Next, it should be known that Galen, in the fifth and sixth books of *On the Preservation of Health*, treating this discourse as it appears in the *Tegni*, says that some bodies have "lapsed" (failed) in their **temperament**, others in their **structure**, and some in their **common nature**. He attempts to write a regimen for all of them. Of those who have lapsed in temperament, some have lapsed "uniformly," where there is one proportional temperament throughout the whole. Others are "opposed," such as when the head inclines toward heat, the liver toward dryness, and the stomach toward excessive moisture, and so on. Such bodies do not preserve their connatural temperament, as they are further removed from health; they are also difficult to manage by regimen, since each part requires its own specific administration. Of those bodies that have lapsed uniformly in temperament, some have lapsed in their active qualities, others in their passive.

Furthermore, a twofold regimen is applied to bodies. One is **conservative**, through "likes," which is administered more safely for those performing "civil acts" <note>People with jobs, social duties, or public responsibilities.</note> and those hindered by many domestic occupations. There is another regimen, which is **permutative** (changing), leading the lapsed state back to something better through alteration. This is for bodies that are free, at leisure from civil acts, and minimally hindered by domestic affairs. Therefore, in the fifth book of the same work: "Whoever wishes to correct imbalances that are still within the latitude of health should do so with **contrary** diets." This is achieved for those who are not occupied; for those who are occupied, you should administer through **likes**, especially when they have become accustomed to them. But one of these happens more according to an "untaught nature," as we do not choose "likes" ourselves—for natural imbalances seek them out, as stated in the *Tegni*. 

Hence, in the first part of the third book: "Those at leisure can succeed in the desire to lead bad temperaments back to equality, for they can subdue their souls through long endurance, so that in time they return to equality in a coordinated way." To rule them without order would lead their bodies to sickness. They must be transferred to a better state gradually and with great care. 

For **sudden transformations** do not withstand nature. This regimen requires fuller diligence and more faithfulness than the previous one. Having admitted these things, it must be known that moist foods are proper to moist natures, and dry foods to dry natures. For **nutrition** is the perfect assimilation of that which nourishes to the body which is being nourished. Dry things are assimilated more quickly to dry things, and moist to moist.

<summary>This page discusses the medical theory of "similarity," explaining that health is maintained by consuming things similar to one's temperament, while illness is treated by contraries. It categorizes "failing" health into degrees and outlines two types of regimens: one for busy citizens and one for those with the leisure to undergo restorative changes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a technical medical debate from the previous folio regarding the "lapsed body"—a physical state that has fallen away from perfect health but has not yet descended into full clinical disease. # Whether a Preservative or Non-Preservative Regimen is Owed to the Lapsed Body

...mostly the **mixture** <term>crasis: the specific blending of the four qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—in an individual</term> uniformly throughout every lapse. For the more appropriate the nourishment is to the person, the more nutritiously it acts. This is because things that share a "symbol" <note>An Aristotelian term for a shared quality between two elements, which allows one to be more easily transformed into the other.</note> are more easily transformed. According to the first book of *On Generation and Corruption* and the first of the *Meteorologica*, transformation is easier among things within a proportional genus. Hence, from the second book of the *Aphorisms*: individual things are altered by those similar to their own mixture, because it is necessary that what is transformed be similar to that which transforms it, since very little distance is found between them.

If indeed you wish to change **dry or moist complexions** <term>complexion: the overall constitutional balance of an individual's qualities</term> by leading them toward a better state, then their contraries are suitable. But in a lapse toward heat or cold, the administration of contraries always occurs, because these are the most effective or "active" qualities. Therefore, they are more easily regulated by similar nourishments [when] they lead into a morbid disposition of bodies. Since dryness and moisture are weaker qualities, they are less active; they are indeed passive. This is taught by the stages of life, which remain affected for a long time. For from birth until youth, moisture endures. It is indeed almost superfluous, and the heat is nearly tempered. First, old age [comes] in the soul, and especially in seniority, which remains as dryness; since the complexion of the elderly is not moist—as some say—but those [saying so] are refuted.

It follows, therefore, that Galen’s opinion is directed toward one goal. For a lapsed body hindered by familiar occupations <note>The "familiar occupations" refer to the patient's daily work or social duties, which might prevent them from undergoing a rigorous or draining medical treatment.</note> and unable to use a transformative regimen <note>original: "regimen pmutatio"; a treatment designed to change the body's constitution back to health.</note> to return to a better state: it is expedient that it be ruled by a **preservative** one. This is also from the eighth book of the *Therapeutic Method* <note>original: "de ingenio"; referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi* or "The Method of Healing."</note>. For although it is simply more useful to transfer someone to a better state, it is not so when they are sick; since then it is expedient to preserve the pre-existing complexion. Just as when an enemy attacks, one should not neglect their defense to focus on preparing weapons they currently lack, but rather protect themselves with what is at hand, lest they succumb to the ambusher.

In bodies lapsed toward heat and cold, Galen also denies a preservative regimen as long as they are detained by their daily occupations. And briefly, all lapsed states [are treated thus] except for childhood alone. For a child is almost tempered, and therefore is governed by moisture. **Haly Abbas**, **Isaac**, and **Avicenna** <note>Major figures in the Islamic medical tradition whose works were foundational to European university medicine.</note> agree with Galen that for some, the regimen should be transformative and not preservative. And thus it appears that Galen would be consistent in governing even "passive" complexions by similar things, since he could not, without danger, use a transformative regimen for one who is occupied. Thus, they coincide theoretically: that whoever is in excess in passive qualities and occupied with civil acts must especially be ruled; but when opposites concur, they must be reduced by contraries.

---

Furthermore, since the body is subject to a **double transformation**: one indeed by the alteration of contrary qualities caused by things ingrained in them; the other by the "efflux" <note>The flowing out or depletion of bodily substances through heat.</note> induced by heat consuming the **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: the innate fluid believed to be the essential fuel of life and heat in the body</term>. It was necessary to resist the first by changing it through a contrary quality, but the second by replenishing what has been evacuated through something similar, which is achieved by nutrition. For to nourish is to restore to bodies what was previously lost from some similar substance. **Haly** [Abbas], raising this doubt, says that his speech in this art seems to contradict his speech in other books. For he wrote in the book *On the Preservation of Health* that hotter bodies need a regimen of cooling, and in others similarly...

---

...of complexions, and therefore he obscured his speech by not distinguishing between a preservative and a transformative regimen. And responding, he says: "I say that Galen did not forget his own speech, nor did he introduce a contradiction." For he did not mean by a preservative regimen here anything except that for a person having a hot complexion, foods should be offered which preserve their hot complexion, so that the regimen might be governed simply. This makes the hot complexion remain in him according to its own disposition, without addition or subtraction. If, however, he wished to change it toward an equal complexion, then he should add that by which it is ruled in cold, until the heat is diminished in them to the point that equality follows.

He provides an example of this matter, placing a certain body separated by **two degrees** <note>Medieval medicine measured the intensity of qualities in four degrees; a body "two degrees" from health was significantly unbalanced.</note> from equality and tending toward heat: it is preserved by a cooling regimen in the first degree, but transformed toward equality by an opposite regimen, such as a cooling regimen in the second degree. From which it appears that a preservative regimen (like cold in the first degree) is "hot" in relation to the cold in the second degree of the transformative regimen. For a cold thing is judged "hot" in relation to a greater cold; and thus the cold of the first degree will be reckoned similar to the hot of the second [degree], in comparison to the cold in the second.

To understand this place, he invites us, saying it would be difficult, and that those men are ignorant who, while following Galen, think they find a contradiction. His statement seems doubly detestable: First, because he does not correctly comment on the mind of Galen. For he is judged a perfect expositor who justly interprets the mind of the author, whether he speaks the truth or a falsehood. <margin>On the first book of the *Prognostics*</margin> Thus, his interpretation is held to be depraved since he does not explain Galen's mind. For Galen wants to compare the preservative regimen by similarity of the lapsed body to the regimen of a body of the best complexion. As appears when he says: "If, however, according to something from the best..." And finally he adds: "But those preserving its mixture [crasis] only change it from a well-tempered [eucrata] nature to the same degree as the mixture of the whole body is changed from that perfection." And he adds: "that a hotter and drier mixture is not made perfectly well-tempered by a hot and dry diet, but only by one as well-tempered as the mixture, and as much colder and moister as the nature is hotter and drier." For the preservative regimen does not intend to compare itself to the transformative regimen, as the **Commentary** <note>Likely referring to Averroes, known as "The Commentator," or a specific scholastic commentary on Galen.</note> falsely imposes upon him. It likewise falsifies when it breaks apart the preservative and transformative regimens and confuses them entirely. The falsehood of its intention is shown by the method of medicines.

---

For if the illness is of a more intense heat than the complexion of the medicine, the medicines of that kind preserve it and make it remain according to its disposition. And medicines that are hotter add to its heat. But medicines that are colder, or less hot, diminish the heat in them, though they do not heal it with a completed cure. So also it will be in **non-natural things** <note>The "six non-naturals" in medieval medicine: air, food/drink, sleep/waking, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and mental passions.</note>: that their administration in the first degree of cold will not preserve a "lapse" in the second degree of heat, but rather will diminish its heat, although it may not bring about equality entirely. Thus the interpretation is flawed; it neither explains the understanding of Galen, nor does it grasp the regimen well.

It harmonizes Galen's teachings with later authorities like Haly Abbas and Avicenna, emphasizing that treatment must account for a patient's daily responsibilities and the specific degree of their imbalance.</summary>

It specifically addresses the debate between using "similars" (like-with-like) versus "contraries" (opposites) to maintain the body, citing Averroes and Galen on how a body naturally drifts toward extremes and eventually decays through the consumption of its "radical moisture."</meta>

# On the Preservative and Transformative Regimen

Whether a preservative or transformative regimen can provide utility in practice. **Averroes** <note>original: "Au."; refers to the 12th-century Cordoban philosopher and physician Ibn Rushd</note> in the tenth book of his *Colliget* <note>The *Kulliyat*, Averroes' comprehensive medical encyclopedia</note> says: "I know there has been an inquiry regarding the contradictions of the authorities as to what should be added about these matters." I say that these **complexions** <term>complexion: the specific balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness in a person</term> depart from a balanced temperament toward an extreme, making them ready to fall into illnesses of the same nature as the complexion toward which they have slipped. This happens when some external cause comes upon them, finding a pre-existing aptitude in the body. And so I say that their regimen ought not to be carried out entirely by **similars** <note>The principle of "like treats like," used here in the context of maintaining a constitution rather than curing a disease</note> because their complexions do not remain the same. Rather, the body is mobile, moving toward a habitual complexion. For this reason, in the regimen of their foods, one must apply something contrary to their complexions so that the fear of external accidents is removed. From the perspective of the complexion alone, one would not need to fear using similars entirely; and this is the intention of those who hold this opinion, although they do not declare it fully. 

But who would say that such a regimen should be broken into one? Certain of our people have said that the "similar" is twofold: namely, in **potential** and in **act**. And the "contrary" is likewise: for one thing is hot and another is cold in potential and in act. From this, they say that bodies are preserved by things that are contraries in act, but similar in potential—such as treating warmer bodies with things that are warm in potential. Afterward, however, when they encounter the natural heat in the body, they become hot in act. Take, for example, **lettuce and purslane** <note>Both considered "cold" herbs in medieval dietetics</note> and the like, which are cold in the beginning and therefore alter the body, yet are also similar and thus preserve it. This specific opinion, however, opposes **Galen** and others who say such things occur by virtue of their essence and not by opposites. Furthermore, that is not a preservative regimen, but rather a transformative or curative one.

For this reason, it must be known that the animal body is subject to a threefold change and corruption. One arises from the **contrariety of qualities** acting and reacting upon each other. For in every mixture, one quality must dominate the others, as is said in the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "drā tactū. xyiii."; likely a reference to Aristotle's work on elements and qualities</note>. Otherwise, neither action nor passion would occur; because of this, a perfectly balanced complexion is denied to exist in practice. There is another subject arising from the action of **innate heat** upon the **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: the vital fluid a person is born with, which acts like oil in a lamp to sustain the fire of life</term>. From this action, as the moisture is consumed, the body is continually cooled and dried out from birth until death. From this also arise the various ages of life affected by different qualities, until finally it happens that the heat accidentally extinguishes and suffocates itself. 

There is also a third change arising from things that encounter the body: the **six necessary things** <note>The "non-naturals": air, food/drink, exercise, sleep, evacuation, and emotions</note> from outside and inside that alter it. Among these, the air and its surroundings are one of the principal causes, continually drying the body through **resolution** <note>The process of the body's substances being dispersed or evaporated</note>, no matter how much it is mixed with moisture. This is just like the nourishments occurring with other things; because they are opposite to the substance and quality of the body, even if they are transformed and acted upon by the body, they in turn cause the body to suffer from them. Eventually, the body is rendered impure and entirely watery, like wine so weakened by water that it can no longer effect a change. 

---

This is clear to any assembly of physicians who listen soundly. And therefore, in the *Regimen of Health*, it says the body has a threefold change. If the body were impassible and immutable, and the best complexion always remained, it would have no need of the art of preservation. But because it is changed, corrupted, and altered—not keeping the consistency it had from the beginning—it requires care. 

Therefore, the care for these three changes will be as follows:
1. For the first, it will always be by a **contrary**, so that excess may be restrained and the quality that is becoming dominant may be tempered. This is achieved by medicine or medicinal food, though the quality is more evident in the former.
2. For the second, provision should be made through **similars**—namely through food and drink—restoring what had been lost. And because that which was lost was hot and moist (which is clear because the body is said to be continually cooled and dried by the consumption of radical moisture), it shall be preserved by a similar heat and a balanced moisture. This must be done carefully, however, so that **putrefaction** <note>A common medieval medical fear where stagnant heat and moisture "rot," leading to fever</note> does not occur, which would induce fevers and other diseases of decay.

In this way, the body's change will also be managed for the most part through what it drinks, since the air—no matter how moist—continually dries and cools it. Nourishments act similarly with other things because of the contrariety they have with the body, at least in the beginning; for the nutrient in its totality is not transformed into the body as a perfect likeness. Rather, many **superfluities** <note>Waste products of digestion</note> (watery, serous, or smoky) are found in it. These are expelled from the body as much as nature is able. 

Therefore, although nature may be "untaught" <note>A common trope: Nature acts instinctively, while the Physician acts through reason</note>, she already chooses what is best. When there is a natural imbalance, a regimen that reduces the body back to a better state should be administered, which is more "preservative" through similars. This is supported by the fact that the quality or quantity in a body already predisposed [to illness] is on a downward slope toward an internal lapse. Furthermore, a physician cannot continually administer similars over a long period, since the exact extent of the **dyscrasia** <term>dyscrasia: an abnormal or "bad" mixture of the four humors</term> is not definitely known. Nor can the exact similar that ought to be applied be determined. In such applications, an error of excess could easily occur, leading to a significant lapse—especially since no body exists that is not sometimes subject to chance and unforeseen events. 

Therefore, it is commanded that a transformation toward things to which the body is not accustomed be done gradually, so that all things are eventually made customary. But on the contrary, many bodies are occupied in the pursuit of life, since human nature is a servant in many ways. It was said by **Galen** that such things are better preserved by similars. We must say that a good preservation ought to involve such a small alteration that it preserves the body from a lapse of a similar quality, and it should not be altered further unless it is being led back to the "best" state, as **Galen** intends. 

Regarding the fourth point, it should be known that although the paths of both sides have been introduced, for the sake of perfection and teaching, let them be spoken of briefly. To the first, it must be said according to the words of **Galen**: when they are accustomed to ruling a lapsed body by contraries, they touch upon a large or medium lapse, but not a small one. Or they are speaking of an idle body that is devoted entirely to its regimen...

It explains the three ways a body naturally decays: through internal elemental conflict, the consumption of radical moisture, and external environmental factors.</summary>

It references the seminal works of Galen, specifically his "Ars Medica" (Tegni) and "On the Preservation of Health," as well as the commentaries of Haly Abbas and Avicenna.</meta>

<page-num>74</page-num>

# Whether for a Lapsed Body there should be Preservation or Transformation

Concerning health alone, of which it was said it would be better to govern by **contraries**. Regarding another point, it must be said that this is true concerning "likes" in a general sense, such as when heat in the third or fourth degree is added to a body already in the first degree of heat. Under this broad similarity, there are underlying oppositions, and not small ones. However, this is not verified concerning that which is "like" in species and nature, such as cold or heat in its own proper dwelling <note>original: "mansione"; refers to the stable state or "degree" of a quality</note> compared with cold or heat in an unequal dwelling, as is gathered from the first book of *On the Preservation of Health* and the *Problems* <note>Likely referring to Aristotle’s "Problems" or Galen’s commentary on them</note>. 

Regarding another point, it must be said that although the surrounding elements are cold and might chill us, they nevertheless grow warm when they approach the body. The body’s own heat does not permit itself to be isolated by that external coldness; this is a clear and proven proportion. The temperament of the air also has an immense range, varying more or less, until one neither shivers from the cold nor sweats from the heat. Alternatively, the heat of the body can be changed by other **non-natural things** <term>non-naturals: the six external factors—air, food, sleep, exercise, etc.—that physicians used to manage health</term> toward a similar heat. 

For it must be understood thus when it is said that the body is governed by its like: that all the non-natural things are received and proportioned when they operate within the body at the time of the **third digestion** <term>third digestion: the process where nutrients are assimilated by the individual organs and limbs</term>. If the body has lapsed toward the heat of the first degree, they should induce only as much heat as is necessary to preserve what already exists; for that much was being lost through resolution. One should not, however, take each thing considered by itself in its own degree of heat, for in that way one would induce an immense excess of heat. One must also observe whether the transition of nourishment to the limbs is short or long, and its loss through the digestions, just as physicians attend to the loss of supplies in a kingdom during a journey.

Regarding another point, it was said that the body, on account of the similarity of its quality, should be governed by a transformative regimen of contraries. This is what the medical practitioners especially conclude, particularly those who say that **Galen** felt preservation is achieved through similars in regard to nutrition, but through contraries in regard to the other non-natural things. His discourse is nevertheless generally useful in all things, as **Haly Abbas** and **Avicenna**—his more faithful interpreters—bring him forward. 

Regarding another point, it should be understood that "similar preservatives" exist in an unequal degree; yet because of this, "action" and "passion" <note>In medieval science, "action" and "passion" refer to the way one quality acts upon another</note> are not removed. Even if similarity is introduced at the end, there was a contrariety at the start and along the way, at least in potential and act. Likewise, natural action and passion remain with any similarity of the agent to the patient found in animal bodies. In a body that is altogether tempered for justice <note>original: "iustitiam"; a perfectly balanced state</note>, the similarity of heat to the **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: the innate fluid that acts as the body's fuel; its exhaustion leads to old age and death</term> retains the contrariety of action and passion, yet not by casting anything out from the substance. 

Regarding another point, to be explained at length: concerning the first argument of the other part, it must be said that a diligent intellect, considering the discourses of Galen elsewhere—especially in the sixth book of *On the Preservation of Health*—and those which are collected succinctly in the form of chapters and conclusions in the *Tegni* <note>original: "tegnī"; Galen’s "Ars Medica," the standard textbook of the Middle Ages</note>, will be able to overturn the argument for contrariety. For when he wished to determine the causes applied to a lapsed body in the *Tegni*, he first spoke thus, explaining his intention: 

-> "If truly in some respect the body falls away from the best condition, yet not by much..." <-

Indeed, from this phrase "in some respect," a moderate "slip" is implied. For the term "lapse" denotes a certain diminution of that to which it is joined. This he explains clearly in what he adds: "not much," so that this body will be healthy as one approaching the very best condition, receding only a little toward the side of heat or cold, etc. Therefore, Galen, considering the body’s great affinity with the best condition, proposed that it be governed by things similar to it, such as heat or cold and the rest, just as with well-tempered <note>original: "eucrati"</note> bodies. And for this reason, he did not shudder in the *Tegni*, as he did in *On the Preservation of Health*, to lead the lapsed body even in its passive qualities through similars, especially referring his understanding to a body hindered by familiar business <note>i.e., the daily chores and duties of an active person</note>.

Those bodies that have a more vehement lapse are simply called "sick," just as the middle ones are called "neutral." These must be ruled by a transformative regimen rather than a preservative one—that is, by contraries. This is especially true in active qualities and in bodies that are idle or devoted to the study of preserving health. And therefore, immediately adding the transformative regimen for such people, he says: "But if he wishes to change it and transfer it to a better state," etc.

If anyone, being stubborn, wishes to claim that Galen’s discourse applies to all lapsed bodies, it must be said that he spoke this briefly as a summary of many things, which he explained more fully in the sixth book of *On the Preservation of Health*. This is apparent from the invitation with which he urges us in the *Tegni* toward that book. Or, he spoke this attending to the fact that few bodies are free, idle, and vacant for the sake of health; most are performing civil acts and services. As has been shown, these people cannot safely use a regimen of change based on excessive contrariety hidden under the guise of similarity, especially since we cannot arrive at what is certain in similarity, just as we cannot in the bodies of the sick. Therefore, Galen more safely advises the use of a conservative regimen for these bodies. 

Nevertheless, it should be known that when the hour permits, it is better to observe a transformative regimen. For it is proportioned in some way to a sickly disposition. For this reason, we see the **French** and others no less approving of a transformative regimen at last, provided the bodies are prepared as mentioned. Whence I say simply that the rule should be: **contraries for the contrary, and similars for the similar.** 

Regarding another point, it is true simply for a certain natural state, such as a tempered body, but where **dyscrasia** <term>dyscrasia: a bad mixture or imbalance of the four humors</term> is more mixed in, it must be governed by contraries rather than similars. And likewise for the other point, since it is not a simply natural appetite, but a middle state existing between two extremes. 

Regarding another point: that preservation is through "likes" in a certain respect and to a small degree, by reason of some natural state still existing, or through "contraries," as will be seen in chapter 74. Thus, in a transformative regimen, difficulty and fear arise on the part of the alteration of nature that soon occurs. In preservation, however, it occurs through the prayer <note>original: "oratione"; likely meaning a slow, systematic application or plea to nature</note> of a gradual and longer administration of similar things.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether a body in a state of "distemperament" (an imbalance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, dry) seeks out its like or its opposite. It expands on the definitions of "natural" and "appetite," drawing heavily from Aristotle’s natural philosophy and Galen’s medical theory.</meta>

...by the restoration of a failing quality and ignorance of direct application, it intends through itself the lapse, etc.

**Natural distemperaments** desire like things, and **disease-based** ones desire contraries. On the occasion of the present question and also a point of doubt, it is stirred up because it seems that a natural distemperament desires contraries. For in the *Problems*, section ten <note>Aristotle, *Problemata*, Book 10</note>: "Whatever animals are dry by nature desire moisture more, for these are in greater need; those that are moist desire the dry, for they are established in that need." Again, in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*</note>, the eyes are easily harmed by things similar to their own temperament and are helped by contraries used in moderation, which is a general rule in every recognition of the complexion <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four humors/qualities in a person</term> of every part. It must also be remembered that in the same work, a cold lung is perceptibly harmed by cold inhalation and is helped by heat as if by a friend; and a hot lung conversely. And yet these are natural distemperaments. Likewise, nothing natural desires its own corruption, but rather its preservation, since it desires to exist for a long time; but if it should desire its contrary, it would desire its own corruption, since it is said that "like is stirred up in form," just as fire is spurred by fire. Furthermore, that which desires does so as if for something perfect, since it is driven by need; but that which it desires is its own proper end which directs the appetite. Such things are often contraries. Therefore, a natural distemperament desires the contrary and not the like. 

However, it seems that an **unnatural** distemperament desires its like, as seen in the *Problems*, section twenty-seven. In those who are "out of their minds"—that is, the insane—and those who through pleurisy <note>original: "pypleumoia"</note> desire wine, which is hot by nature; and yet these are unnatural distemperaments, as will be seen. Also, nothing desires its own corruption as its primary aim; but that which desires a contrary desires that which leads to its destruction and corruption, as happens in an unequal distemperament. Furthermore, if a disease-based distemperament desired its contrary, then it would cure itself without any external medicine, which is certainly absurd. Conversely, one bitten by a rabid dog, after the dryness of the rabies has taken hold, abhors and trembles at water and generally all moisture. <margin>chapter 79</margin>

Also, one abounding in colder and more humid winds sometimes desires mud, chalk, or dry coals; <margin>section 13</margin> and again, one desires cold water when it already abounds in it, for this is the material cause of dropsy <note>original: "ydropisiz"; a buildup of fluid</note> where the matter is overflowing. <margin>chapter 4</margin>

Therefore, a natural distemperament will desire likes and not contraries. The opposite of these two views is written with others in the *Tegni*. Furthermore, every thing desires that by which it can be preserved and remain in being. Ноt that will be when a natural distemperament desires its like, and a disease-based one its opposite. For it is shown that preservation is achieved by the like, while reduction <note>returning to a balance</note> and cure are achieved, as will be shown, by the contrary. <margin>chapter 53</margin> Thus, a natural distemperament will desire what is like itself, and an unnatural one the contrary. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known that a certain distemperament is a "complexion" <note>temperament</note>, and this is threefold. One is simply "well-mixed" <note>original: "eucrata"; perfectly balanced</note>, such as that of a perfectly healthy body, or at least a living one. <margin>chapter 18</margin>

The second is simply infirm, more or less, such as a coldness of the body. The other is a middle state, and this is threefold: for some approach the first state, like a very healthy body or one slightly lapsed; the other two are like the infirm, such as a body that is implicitly sick. Some occupy the middle, which is like the body of a simply sick person, as seen previously from the *Tegni*. This first and middle state falls under the heading of "dryness," both more and less.

<margin>Natural</margin>
"Natural" is said in two ways in the present context. One is from nature generally understood: as that which is produced by some intrinsic principle in whatever order to the "difference of art," whose principle is from without. In this way, not only health is natural, but even sickness. Whence in the fifth book of the *Physics*: "Neither is generation according to nature, nor is corruption against nature." For growing old is according to nature. Nor is one generation to be seen as according to nature and another against nature. Otherwise, in a proper sense, that which follows a principle is simply for the perfection and preservation of the order of nature, or its opposite. Being is natural to the first, but unnatural or "beyond nature" to the second, such as death.

<margin>Appetite</margin>
**Appetite** is a certain inclination toward something else, and it is twofold. Either it happens with some apprehension or knowledge, or without it. But it is directed rightly by some director, like an arrow toward a target by an archer, as is said of the intellectual appetite. Whence it is indicated in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*: "the work of nature is the work of intelligence," and natural appetite is twofold, which is seen as nothing other than a certain inclination, and an inclination according to its own nature toward its end. In this way, "matter is said to desire form," in the first book of the *Physics*, "as the base desires the good and the female the male." This is seen to be natural toward which it is inclined and ordered into form, which is the end of matter, as is clear in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*. Just as potentiality is ordered toward act and the imperfect toward that which perfects it, since matter by its nature is in potentiality to form. 

This appetite exists in all inanimate beings, and even more so in animate ones, insofar as the soul participates in the vegetative or natural power, as in plants, and also in animals indifferently, according to which they are nourished and grow. For they communicate in these things from the beginning. This appetite in these things is the simple attraction of nourishment without the mind, just as a magnet attracts iron, as appears in the second book of the *Collections*, perfected by heat and dryness as its instruments.

<margin>Animal</margin>
The appetite which is with some knowledge is **animal**. This is twofold. One is common and involves movement; the other is more particular and can be without prior movement. The first is "appetitive" in seeking to acquire sensible things that perfect it; the other is intellectual, called the "practical intellect," in the third book of *On the Soul*. Whence in the *Problems*, section three: "Desire arises both from food and from the intellect." By these two desirable things, animals—both brute and rational—direct their movement toward their proper ends. The remaining one is the appetite of the stomach, being composed of the natural appetitive power and the animal instinctive power. For it feels.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of "appetite"—the biological or natural drive of an organ or organism—specifically focusing on whether an imbalanced body (a "distemperament") seeks out things that are similar to its state or things that are opposite to it.</meta>

-> ## Whether every distemperament desires its like, its contrary, or neither? <-

Iohannicius <note>The Latinized name of Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a 9th-century physician</note>, relying on coldness and dryness as instruments for his **emptiness**, and concerning those things which provide their own **appetite**, his discourse is verified; yet Haly <note>Haly Abbas, another major Persian physician</note> hesitates on these points in his *Accomplishments*. What we have said regarding the stomach, you should also understand to apply to the other limbs; their disposition is the same. Nevertheless, this is not merely for that reason, but because there is a **natural appetite** in them, and the appetite of the stomach is put forward from both a natural and a sensory power, and not a natural one alone. As for what was seen before—that which is called "contrary"—it will be seen in Chapter 13. Regarding the second point, it should be known that according to the saying of Empedocles, it follows that **natural distemperaments** <term>distemperament: an imbalance of the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry</term> would rather desire contraries, and unnatural ones would desire their likes no less. For instance, when he placed aquatic creatures in a cold and moist place, they would be those that are hot and dry. Indeed, they are preserved by fleeing the excess of greater heat. This is also found in the book *On Inspiration and Respiration* <note>original: "de inspiratione et respiratione," a work by Aristotle</note>. The sign of this deficiency, along with what is challenged there, will appear from what is to be said. Some also seek answers from what has been introduced, and especially the followers of Aristotle were perplexed by this question in no small measure, not knowing how to escape its difficulties; about these things, it will also appear generally.

Regarding the third point, it must first be known that **natural distemperaments** <note>imbalances that are part of a person's innate "normal" makeup</note> especially desire like things which are sustaining, while **sickly ones** <note>imbalances caused by disease</note> desire contraries. Then it must be seen what incites it, and whether either "temperate state" <term>temperantia: the ideal balance of qualities</term> desires the like or the unlike. Regarding the first, it should be known here that in the *Art of Medicine* <note>original: "in tegni," referring to Galen’s *Ars Medica*</note>, the truth is written thus: Sickly distemperaments of the stomach are distinguished from the natural ones by the fact that they crave **contraries** and not likes, just as natural ones crave their own **likes** and not contraries. Whence, in the first part of the *Theory*: Understand the difference between a naturally bad <gloss>imbalanced</gloss> complexion of the stomach and one that is bad outside of nature; for those who have a naturally bad complexion, the stomach seeks those things which are **similar** to it. But truly, for those who possess a complexion that is outside of nature <note>i.e., diseased</note>, the stomach desires things that are diverse and contrary. From this, it is gathered that a moist stomach desires moist things, just as a dry one desires dry things; and this occurs when the moisture or dryness is **according to nature**. But if this happens accidentally <note>through illness</note>, it occurs through the contrary, because one having a dry stomach then desires moist things, and a moist stomach desires dry things.

That this is so is persuaded by reason, since **all appetite is because of need**; for it belongs to one who does not have. But a natural distemperament needs the restoration of that which has been dissolved no less than before; and that, as has been seen, can be achieved through **like things**. An unnatural one, however, needs the casting out of its own excess, which is accomplished by the **contrary**, since one thing is the destructive excess of the other, and it must be led back into a certain measured state, as is clear in the *Art of Medicine*.

Furthermore, every appetite is ordered toward **permanence**, just as those things which exist before the end are in the same state; for all things desire this permanence, since all things, whatever they do, act according to nature so that they may always participate in the divine and immortal insofar as they are able, according to the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "secundo de anima," by Aristotle</note>. This, then, is the appetite of a natural distemperament, since it craves what is like itself, because through this it restores what has flowed away and been lost from the body, as with **nutrition, growth, and generation**, which are ordered in whatever way they may benefit the existence of like things. By contrast, the appetite of an **unnatural distemperament** is for contraries; for through that, it is desired that the pre-existing disposition in the body be destroyed, which is done by its contrary. Whence, regarding unequal distemperament: things are increased and nourished by their likes, but they are destroyed and corrupted by their contraries. Again, as it is in the whole, so it is in the part, since the power of both is the same, as in the first book of *On the Heavens and the World* <note>original: "prio de ce. et mu." i.e., De Caelo et Mundo</note>. For one is ordered into the other.

Secondly, according to the whole in a natural disposition, they desire **likes**, which their location declares; for nature is preserved in its proper places, especially according to Aristotle's *On Inspiration and Respiration*. For a "place" possesses a **preservative power**, according to the fourth book of the *Physics*; as land-dwellers are on the earth, swimmers are in the water, and winged creatures are in the air. For in these, they naturally flourish; but when they perceive an excess in their place, they flee it. Thus, land animals seek the air in a time of corruption, fleeing it; and aquatic animals at a colder hour stay near the shores. Wherefore in summer, fish flow forth into cold, rocky places, but in winter into warm, muddy ones. Winged creatures, when the atmosphere is imbalanced, change to the opposite, as in the eighth book of the *History of Animals* <note>original: "octauo hystoriarum az." i.e., Historia Animalium</note> and in *On Inspiration and Respiration*. Those which have an exceeding heat are saved when placed in a colder spot, and those with exceeding cold in a warmer spot. The location reduces the excess held to a measured state.

In the same way, it happens in the part: namely, that natural limbs—or those still existing under a natural state—will crave those things which are **like them** as if they were suitable, but those in an opposite state will crave the **contrary**. For their reasons stand as diverse: in a proper temperate state and a natural imbalance, it will desire likes; but in an unnatural one, the opposite, as the difference in Chapter 14 also indicates. Thus, natural distemperaments seek likes, and sickly ones seek contraries. Know, indeed, that a temperate state and also a natural distemperament principally desire something as **nourishment**, and generally as a quality, such as hot or cold. An unnatural one, however, is a state of need. Whence Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> in his *Problems*: "Why do those with fever thirst more, but do not hunger, while those recovering do the opposite?"

Regarding the second point, it should be known that what incites **good health** <term>eucratia: the perfect, healthy balance of humors</term> and also natural distemperament to collectively desire like things, stands in the stomach as a preceding and immediate perception; to which natural desire also moves with a "fear of a vacuum" <note>the physical principle that nature abhors a vacuum</note>. Then comes the drying out of the veins themselves from the belly and the stomach, and finally a natural desire for them, and at last a sensory one. For these are also appetitive movements, as is declared in the third book. But an **unnatural state** is not incited to crave contraries except by occasion; because as a distressing thing, it forces one to depart from the sick state toward a temperate one, so that having been incited, it moves toward seeking a certain beginning, or the divine mercy provides a restorative for it, which will be the contrary. This is in the same way that **matter**, existing in potentiality, is naturally inclined toward **form** as if by touch, since it is incited by privation <note>privation: the absence of a form that should be present</note>; when it is under one form, it desires to be under another. This very thing is often imagined toward a "bad thirst," as in the first book of the *Physics*. And because the heavens do not have matter, or at least matter joined to privation, they are not transformed to exist under another form; wherefore the heavens are **incorruptible and ungenerated**. Regarding the fourth point: to the first, it should be said that Aristotle speaks of a body involved in a sufficiently imbalanced sickness, which should rather be preserved by contraries...

Out of a certain irrational habit, some are so strong and persistent—and so prone to drinking—that in fevers they absolutely cannot abstain.

## DIFFERENTIA CXVII.

-> **Whether those of a hot and moist, tempered, or hot and dry complexion can more easily endure fasting?** <-

Because fasting is consumptive and weakening—for hunger dries out bodies, as is stated in the *Aphorisms*, book seven—the humors of the body are dissolved by it. Dissolution occurs when the "fumes" produced exit through the pores. But the three mentioned complexions resist consumption and weakness better, which is shown by their longevity in the 21st Differentia; the others are oppositely disposed toward life.

Furthermore, specifically regarding the **hot and moist**: since they sustain the act of coitus, which is both evacuating and drying, without significant harm (according to the *Tegni*, book one). Again, regarding the **temperate**: because this exists as the middle between all extremes. Such a person is most removed from harms; hence, regarding their proportionate composition, they are placed in the middle of all causes of sickness. Moreover, it measures all things for itself with moderation. Again, it seems the **hot and dry** endure it well because, both due to the dryness and the heat, their matter is thickened and made compact so that it cannot be easily dissolved by heat; hence, young men and old men endure fasting more easily than children for this reason. This is confirmed because the Armenians, Greeks, and Saracens, inhabiting hot regions, are especially practitioners of fasting.

That the **cold and dry** also endure it easily is shown because these qualities are most opposed to consumption (since consumption happens through heat and moisture). Fasting, however, chooses and consumes. Again, regarding the "extracted" complexion, since one is the effect of the other, the cause and effect are proportional. But the cold and dry age tolerates fasting better than others (as per the first book of *Aphorisms*). Therefore, it is difficult to change, just as old age is cooled in... which I have translated from Cassius the Physician, the Sophist. This is shown in those who are melancholic <term>melancholic: the cold and dry humor/personality type</term>, who fast the most and without harm. Regarding simple complexions, it should be argued from these halves. Thus, the different complexions can endure fasting differently and easily.

The opposite of all this seems to be written in the eighth book of *On Method*, where he suggests that a **cold and moist** complexion easily tolerates fasting because it is not harmed by it but rather helped. Hence, in the *Preservation of Health*, book two, it is written that those dominated by phlegm <term>phlegm: the cold and moist humor</term> incur less harm than others by skipping a meal. Likewise, their heat is modest and least consumptive, and their moisture resists the blunting heat. For when the agent is weak and the patient resists strongly, the battle can last a long time without injury. Therefore, complexions declining toward the side of coldness and moisture, whether simple or composite, will be able to carry fasting more easily than the others.

Fasting, according to the laws, is parsimony directed toward God. Simply speaking, however, it is the withdrawal of diet. This is considered in two ways: one by reason of quantity—for instance, if in the space of 24 hours one takes two pounds of nourishment...

## **Whether a constitution of heat and moisture easily bears fasting**

It was customary for someone to take [food], but now they take it only once. Or perhaps by reason of the service performed: the quantity is not diminished, so that if they were accustomed to eating twice or three times, they now eat only once. And this is how fasting is commonly understood, especially in **religious practice**; for thus, filling themselves once so that no empty space can be assigned within them. For this reason, the other method [of fasting] here more closely accords with the views of **physicians**. However, it is easy to tolerate fasting when one does not crave nourishment and abstinence does not harm them. Regarding this, Galen says that to "bear" it is to do so without injury. On the contrary, more will be heard in the verification of the question in the twenty-seventh distinction. And therefore, [the ability] depends on being of the same age; for **infants**, even if they are of a good and cold constitution, bear fasting with more difficulty than the elderly or hot and dry youths. Let there be a similarity of humors, members, virtues, sex, form, and custom. Let the diet also be similar, so that one does not always use thin liquids that evaporate quickly, while another uses the opposite. Let there also be an identity of region, the constitution of the time, and the north wind. For in hot [weather], fasting is borne with more difficulty; hence **Damascenus** <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century scholar</note> says: "Fasting in summer dries out bodies, but in the cold it is easier." And similarly in physical or mental exercise and other things, provided the body is not also evacuated due to some irregular fasting.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have said that a **hot and moist constitution** <note>the Sanguine temperament</note> bears the lack of food <term>incibationem</term> <gloss>the state of being without food</gloss> more easily than all others.
<margin>How</margin>
This seems to be supported by the science of constitutions in this way: Those who have wide veins and a multitude of blood are able to fast twice as much and without harm. Such indeed are the **sanguine** types. For they have large veins in the skin and much blood, since this is the proper nature of blood. Another argument is that this constitution possesses more than others the principles of life which oppose the "resolution" <note>the breaking down or wasting of the body</note> resulting from fasting. Hence, the human constitution which is placed as hotter and moister than others is judged to have a longer life, as proven in the causes of length and shortness of life.

Again, since this constitution has a proportion to **air** in its moisture by predominance, as shown in distinction fourteen, this heat will exceed by dulling itself and becoming viscous. Similarly, the appetite is perfected through the cold and dry, which the humor of **melancholy** <note>black bile</note> indicates when the desire is incited. Since, therefore, the constitution is hot and moist, the appetite will be perfected only after a long period of abstinence. Therefore, from these and similar points, they wish to show that the hot and moist constitution has a greater tolerance for being without food. To these things it must be said: although this constitution bears fasting more easily than many others, and especially more than the hot [and dry] ones, nevertheless the **cold and moist** and perhaps those that are only moist and cold tolerate it more easily in a certain way, as will be shown in the third point of the discussion.

Regarding the statement by Galen introduced by them, it should be said that he intends to compare the **sanguine** to the **melancholic** rather than to the **phlegmatic**. For it must be conceded that melancholics, by their nature, bear fasting more easily than the sanguine. For he said before: those who indeed have narrow veins are poor in blood and do not bear long fasts; these indeed would be the melancholic. For the **phlegmatic**, although they have slender veins in the skin, do not have them to the same degree as the melancholic, since in the latter two causes exist simultaneously: narrowness of the veins and coldness combined with dryness; whereas in the former [phlegmatics] there is only moisture. Similarly, they do not have so little blood. And melancholics also abound in phlegm, which is very close to blood, since it has little coldness in respect to the body and is born to be changed into blood through further "decoction" <note>the metaphorical 'cooking' or digestion of humors in the body</note>. Furthermore, even if the sanguine are perhaps little harmed by fasting and thus bear it more easily, they nevertheless do not feel it "lightly" because they do not [lack] appetite, since the heat in them is greater than the consumption in cold types. And let the motion of apprehension be vigorous and ordained in them.

To the other point, it should be said that although the sanguine may fast more easily than the phlegmatic by reason of the natural moistures of the members, nevertheless by reason of any "extraneous" moisture located in the vessels, the **phlegmatic** carry the lack of food more lightly than the others. To the other, it should be said that although the hot and moist constitution has more of the principles of life if it is duly ruled, nevertheless if it is led immoderately, it will participate more in the principles of death, since it is more "resolvable" <note>prone to breaking down</note> than others, especially when it is hot and moist with an airy moisture that is easily affected. Hence, in the ninth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." referring to Galen's De Ingenio Sanitatis</note>: bodies that are moist, hot, and thin evaporate most quickly, even if they have much moisture resisting consumption. It has, however, another consumption. And that moisture is also airy, thin, and liable to evaporation and consumption. Nor is it of longer life than the phlegmatic; that is the same constitution but for a different cause. For the **phlegmatic** die due to the extinction and suffocation of heat which occurs to them, since the cold watery humor increases because of the lack of heat, overwhelming the small heat with its bad cold quality and covering it with its quantity; hence a swift death follows. This differs in the **sanguine**, since the heat is not so overcome by the moisture as it is in the phlegmatic; for them, death happens more through the way of consumption of moisture caused gradually by heat. Since they have more moisture than others, they are judged by **Averroes** <note>original: "Af." referring to the philosopher Ibn Rushd</note> to be of longer life.

To the other, it should be said that although the sanguine constitution has a proportion to air and the phlegmatic to water—which resists consumption more—nevertheless its moisture does not simply always exceed the heat. But sometimes it does, as in childhood. In other ages, however, it exceeds, as in youth and old age. Thus, the constitution maintains a range. Nor does it easily allow the appetite to bear being without food, since it is not just about not being harmed, as happens in **bulimia** <note>here meaning a pathological or intense hunger</note>, in which there is little or no appetite despite a violent injury.
<margin>On account of <unclear>the third</unclear></margin>
On account of the third point, it should be known that the **cold and moist constitution** sustains the lack of food more easily than the others. This is shown by the testimony of the eighth book of *On the Method of Healing* and by many reasons and signs. For cold and moist and cold and dry constitutions are not easily occupied by fevers. Nor, if they are seized by some ephemeral fever and fast, do they cross over into those fevers that last many days. But for some of them, when a multitude of moistures happens to accumulate without corruption—for such things accumulate continuously—fasting is most beneficial to the cold and moist, especially the second [the cold and dry] after this.

<summary>This page analyzes how the four temperaments tolerate fasting, concluding that while sanguine types have the most "life force," phlegmatic types (cold and moist) bear the lack of food best due to their internal moisture reserves.</summary>
