The fourth is indeed that which is cold and dry. Thus, according to **Galen** <note>original: "secundum Ga." - refers to Galen of Pergamon, the foundational Roman-era physician</note>, a primarily cold **complexion** <term>complexio: the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a person's temperament</term> and humor is not only able to tolerate fasting more easily, but is actually helped by it. However, an uncertainty arises regarding this point, since it seems to be gathered 

<margin>Note here: that the melancholic complexion bears the deprivation of food <note>original: "icibationem" - literally "un-fooding" or fasting</note> more easily [than] the sanguine. The contrary of which is said according to the [standard] theory of complexions.</margin>

It must be said, however, that **Galen** here only compares against one another those complexions declining toward the side of coldness and moisture, whether simply or in combination, and not toward the side of heat. For in that case, he would have prioritized a hot complexion and humor [as being less able] to easily bear fasting than any of those four. Or, perhaps a hot complexion and humor naturally carries the deprivation of food more easily than the others, while certain other types do so only by accident. I say "naturally," because in a **sanguine** <term>sanguine: the temperament dominated by blood, characterized as hot and moist</term> body, there is more moisture to be immediately restored by eating than in any other body—especially when it has not been very passive—which is able to stand in place of that which is prohibited from entering the stomach. For this reason, we see sanguine people and athletes abounding in much blood who easily bear the deprivation of food after one day; hence, by natural intention, the animal does not feel hunger for a time due to the abundance of food-matter stored in the liver. I say "by accident," however, when there are raw **phlegmatic** <term>flegma: the humor associated with coldness and moisture; "phlegm"</term> humors in the vessels of a body which, when digested over a longer time, are converted into blood to nourish the body. This occurs in those who decline toward the side of coldness and moisture. This is what 

<margin>Galen meant when he said: "when it happens that a multitude of moistures has accumulated without corruption," etc.</margin>

Hence, in the first intention: Moist bodies possessing natural moisture are prone to rapid "resolution" <note>the dissipation or burning off of bodily fluids</note>; yet they do not tolerate hunger as well as dry bodies that have little moisture. This is also touched upon in the first [part] regarding the fourth [complexion]: There are certain people with an exuberance of flesh who, when food is cut off from them, become weak and incur wasting, wherefore they do not tolerate the deprivation of food. And it is added in the previous discourse: unless they were full of moistures other than those which are in the substance of the limbs when they are good, fitting, and receptive, so that nature may convert them into a fully realized nutriment. Hence, in the first book of the *Practice*: You should command him who has an excess of phlegm in his body to diminish his food and make it light; for this is sufficient by itself without the use of laxatives. For this lightens the humor and assists nature in altering it into good blood, since it is food that is already "half-cooked" <note>referring to the internal "cooking" or digestion of humors</note>. For if food is diminished and lightened while the natural heat is comforted, it is cooked thoroughly and becomes blood; however, this does not happen in the **melancholic** <term>melancolia: the cold and dry humor, often associated with "black bile"</term> or **choleric** <term>colera: the hot and dry humor, associated with "yellow bile"</term> humor because of their dryness. Thus, a complexion that is not only cold but [also] moist sustains fasting more easily than a hot and moist one. Indeed, even a cold and dry one [bears it] more easily when it has accumulated raw humors, though its primary nature is otherwise. Yet a pure melancholic, because the melancholy humor excites the appetite, will not easily be able to fast as such, although it often does not harm them. Therefore, one may accept this order of tolerance for the deprivation of food: that the cold and moist type fasts more easily than the others in any way, provided its moisture is not easily dissipated—which perhaps does not happen.

The ranking is as follows: first, those who are moist only; then the cold only; afterwards the hot and moist; then the cold and dry together; after that the temperate; then the hot only; and lastly the hot and dry. For this last type sustains the deprivation of food with the most difficulty of all and is most harmed by it, as is known from the books on therapeutics and according to the *Regimen of Acute Diseases* <note>original: "re. a." - referring to the Hippocratic/Galenic text *Regimen Acutorum*</note>. That the cold and moist type excels the others, and the order that follows, is shown from what was just touched upon: because that phlegmatic moisture is suited to be converted into blood, which is not the case in hot and dry types, except perhaps by accident from a very strengthening regimen. For one must imagine that a properly cold and moist complexion has food within itself which it eventually converts into blood and finally into nourishment. This does not exist in other natures, and especially not in the hot and dry.

But regarding this, a doubt arises: because in phlegmatic people, raw humor does not seem to aggregate in a way that, once cooked, it can be converted into nourishment. This is according to **Damascenus** <note>John of Damascus, 8th-century theologian and scholar</note> saying in his *Aphorisms*: bodies naturally cold and moist receive little in the stomach, and return even less—that is, they transmit less nourishment to the limbs. Their stomachs are the most easily harmed. If, therefore, they have so little [nutriment] that it was already exiting by a flux, they will not be able to tolerate the deprivation of food. It must be said that Damascenus is not speaking of bodies that are cold and moist naturally (that is, excessively). This is apparent when "long-lasting infirmity" is mentioned later. Hence it should be said that they receive little within themselves in relation to hot bodies. And even if their stomachs are "loose," they still receive enough to suffice for the restoration they need and for the tolerance of fasting. Also, the stomachs are narrowed because of the deprivation of food, while the humors, transformed through the blood, nourish them.

Furthermore, such a complexion resists [external] causes better than others, since the heat in them is weak and easily preserved, and the watery moisture checks the heat. And therefore, they are helped in these warming things: in exercises and in intercourse; so it is said in chapter 123. Again, since moisture abounds and is agitated by the heat during fasting, and the mouth of the stomach is softened thereby, they are rendered without appetite for a long time. Further, in the ninth book of the *Therapeutics*: thick, viscous, and cold bodies are difficult to evaporate, especially when the habit of the body is hard and dense, so that—to put it all together—it is rendered difficult to evaporate. Such is the nature of phlegmatic people above all in these three ways. Conversely, the reasoning for opposites is opposite: the choleric and phlegmatic complexions are opposites. The **choleric** type bears fasting with more difficulty than all others; hence, in the *Regimen of Acute Diseases*: the tolerance of fasting in one where phlegm is dominant is easier than the tolerance in one where choler is dominant. The other two humors, being intermediate between these, will behave moderately regarding the ease or difficulty of bearing fasting.

Furthermore, in the first [part] of the third [book]: it is beneficial for those who are parched and moistened to tolerate thirst and sleep with it; it is harmful to those having fevers from red choler. But to tolerate thirst is a kind of fasting. For it is, as has been said, a withdrawal of the way or the diet. And in the fourth [part] of the *Proper [Attributes]*: Everyone whose innate heat is very strong, as with the choleric, or very abundant, as with the sanguine and those with large livers, or whose innate heat...

# Whether one should first Drink or Eat
.vii. Angè

...is very weak. Just as the weak, dried-out nature of **melancholics** <term>melancholic: the temperament associated with black bile, characterized as cold and dry</term> cannot release its food. The **phlegmatic** <term>phlegmatic: the temperament associated with phlegm, characterized as cold and moist</term> appears to be the middle ground between these. For their heat is not very intense, nor very abundant or weak, but moderate; and therefore, they are able to release food through the opposite process. Again, observations confirm this. For we see animals that are cold and moist, such as bears, foxes, and other cave-dwelling creatures, remaining without any external nourishment. They do not waste away from this, but are rather restored; having gathered moisture during the raw summer time, it is converted into blood and nourishment. However, hot and dry creatures, like lions, horses, and sparrows, cannot live without eating even in the winter time. Indeed, heat invigorated by cold makes them more ravenous. We also observe that children, women, and especially phlegmatic women, endure fasting more easily than men, and specifically more than **choleric** <term>choleric: the temperament associated with yellow bile, characterized as hot and dry</term> men. This also happens in cold times and regions, and in similar natures; for they are helped by the cold penetrating to the interior, just as when thin bodies are bathed in cold water. And for this reason, it has been seen that women have sometimes remained without food for a long time, as related in *Differentia* 112. Therefore, those of a cold and moist complexion endure fasting more easily than the others, and then others in turn and in what manner.

Regarding the fourth point, <margin>A d</margin> first it must be said that although hot and moist (tempered) complexions, and hot and dry ones, are of longer life than the others, they do not, however, as has been shown, tolerate fasting more easily. This is because death does not arise solely from the consumption of moisture, but also from the extinction and suffocation of heat, as was touched upon before. Regarding the other point, it should be said that they do not fail, because a hot and moist complexion facilitates substance and evacuation, like a seed, because of the blood in which it abounds, which bloodletting <term>phlebotomy: the medical practice of drawing blood to balance the humors</term> removes, and which the phlegmatic lacks. A hot and moist complexion is of stronger power than a cold and moist one, and for this reason, even a small amount of sexual activity <note>original: "ueneris" - literally "of Venus," referring to sexual intercourse</note> harms others. The phlegmatic, as was touched upon, is even helped by coitus, because the natural phlegm, being converted toward corruption, is emitted. It is harmful, however, if they engage in it much, because of the loss of spirits, by which they become impoverished. It is not so with fasting; for they are not harmed by it but rather helped more because of the conversion of phlegm into nourishment, as has been shown.

Regarding the other point, it should be said that although a tempered state is harmed less by intensive injuries than other complexions, it is harmed most by extensive ones, since all extremes are in some way opposite to them. For a well-proportioned body is prepared to be quickly transformed in every way, because of the homogeneity of its parts (*Problemata*, section 5). And therefore, such a body bears fasting with more difficulty than the cold and moist, although for some it is easier. Regarding the other point, it should be said that they measure everything for themselves, not needing an external measure regarding the "six non-naturals" <term>sex necessariorum: the six factors essential for health, including food/drink, sleep, and exercise</term>. For they desire only as much as they can digest well, unless something hinders them, like overeating or other things. Indeed, when hindered, they are more distressed in a certain way than others because of their balanced state, just as in the human complexion compared to others.

Regarding the other point, it should be said that hot and dry complexions bear fasting with more difficulty than others, because of the multiplication of **choler** <term>cholera: yellow bile, the hot and dry humor</term> and its inflammation into a fever; and although the matter may be compact, the heat is nonetheless powerful, dissolving and inflaming the whole body. And so *Differentia* 134 will show that, above all others, they require a refined regimen. Indeed, even in the hour of fever, food must sometimes be given, as in the 10th book *On Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." - referring to Galen's Methodus Medendi</note>. Nor do men of many other religions endure fasts more easily than we do, except because either their moisture and bodies are more compact, while we lead a more delicate life, or we are less devout than they, being given over to luxury and gluttony. Regarding the other point, it should be said that cold and dry types support fasting with difficulty, unless raw moistures are present from indigestion, because of the weakness of their power and their resolution. And if by the compaction of moisture they can resist corruption, because it is nonetheless small, more is dissolved from a small amount than from a large amount in a hot and moist person; just as a poor man is harmed more by a small loss than a wealthy man by a large one. For this is the worst of the complexions (*On the Preservation of Health*, book 6), since it quickly kills with old age and death from the beginning.

Regarding the other point, it should be said that it is not the same concerning age and complexion. For likeness is by reason of quality, not substance; because every complexion can exist with any age and substance, but not vice versa. For a cold and dry complexion can exist with an infant's substance (which is more easily consumed), and with a dry earthly substance resisting consumption, and with a middle substance. But age is not so. As for those who fast for a long time and without harm, this happens either because of their specific idleness and a shadowed life, as often happens to those in prison and especially underground; for because of lack, more raw phlegmatic superfluities accumulate in them, since their complexion sometimes generates this with difficulty. Or because one power sometimes weakens the others. For the powers hinder each other (*On Natural Faculties*, book 6), because they act with a single instrument, namely the natural heat. Since they are continuously looking toward God with the animal power, the natural power is weakened, so that the harm from fasting does not seem to be perceived. And custom in these things, as in others, is no small matter. And through this, it appears what should be said to men of many other religions, etc.

For a thin substance is more receptive to being acted upon. This is confirmed by those released from prison, who first seek air, then drink, and finally food (*Differentia* 114). Furthermore, the rule of the middle is that the gross should precede the thin lest nature be trapped. Drink is thin, and food is grosser; therefore, it ought to precede it. # Whether one should first Drink or Eat
.vii. Angè <note>Probably an abbreviation for a specific chapter or author, likely "Angelus" or a similar scholastic reference.</note>

...behaving in this way very quickly. According to the fourth book of Rhazes' *Almansor*: 
Water must not be drunk at the table until after one has eaten and the upper parts of the belly have been eased. Again, in the first book of his *Practice*: When a man has had enough to eat and the food has settled in the stomach, let him drink as much cool, pleasant water as is necessary. Likewise in the third part of the first book: After eating, let him drink as mentioned above, and not at the hour of eating, any quantity that might be added to the food. This is supported by two main arguments: 

First, because when drink is taken with food, it surrounds the substance of the stomach and prevents it from "gripping" the food; thus, perfect digestion <term>digestion: in medieval medicine, this was viewed as a "cooking" process driven by the body's internal heat</term> cannot be completed, since the stomach must touch the food directly to act strongly upon it. This is shown by the appetite for food and its opposite. 

Second, because that which draws undigested food out of the stomach—such as the movement of drinking—should not be added yet. Such is the nature of drink, whether water or wine; hence in the first section: Wine after food is among the things that cause the most hindrance, because it digests quickly and penetrates, and it causes the undigested food to penetrate with it, leading to obstructions and putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the dangerous "rotting" of undigested food within the body, thought to cause disease</term>. This is even more the case when it is taken along with food without water. 

And for this reason, in the same place: A child must not be permitted to drink water on top of food as much as possible, lest the raw food penetrate before it is digested. Whence Avicenna wrote to Alexander: 
<margin>Avicenna to Alexander</margin>
Restrain your soul from drinking cold water on top of food until it becomes a habit for you, because it chills the stomach, extinguishes the fire <term>innate fire: the vital heat centered in the stomach that "cooks" food</term>, confuses the food, and creates an impediment if much is drunk. Again, drink is cold and moist, either in act or in potential. When there is thirst—which according to the Master of Aphorisims <note>original: "Aꝑ." likely referring to Hippocrates</note> is an appetite for cold and moisture—it follows that such a thing, according to Haly Abbas, hinders digestion when it is in full force. For it chills the stomach and what is contained within it, just as water suddenly coming into a boiling vessel. 

It is shown that drink should not be taken at the same time as food because it either induces fluctuations and gurgling that pour upward toward the head, or, by staying there, the digestive power of the stomach is weakened by the lubricating moisture, and the expulsive power is prematurely invigorated. From this, the corruption of digestion will occur. Therefore, one ought to put food before drink. 

However, as to the idea that one should drink and eat at once: this is the custom especially of the Greeks and the Latins. Again, in the fourth book on *Simple Medicines* and the sayings of the practitioners: 
<margin>The mouth tastes well, it nourishes well.</margin>
What tastes well, nourishes well, because a very sweet flavor is a path to nutrition. But it tastes well and is a delightful drink when taken together with food, unless one's habit has been changed to the contrary. So, eating and drinking should happen together. 

First, it must be known that "first" here implies an order of time and not of nature. Drink is also a "non-natural" thing <term>non-naturals: the six factors in medieval medicine (like diet, sleep, and exercise) that humans can control to maintain health</term>, being moist in act, serving to mix the foods in the belly and carry them to the various parts. Here, a threefold distinction is made: for some drink is purely drink, like water, whose office is to distribute nourishment through the parts. Some drink is given against an imbalance of humors <term>dyscrasia: an abnormal disproportion of the four bodily humors</term>, providing support with some substance, such as honey-water or julep <term>julep: a sweet medicinal syrup, often made with rosewater</term>. Other things are both food and drink, such as wine, beer, and cider; for these both nourish and distribute nourishment through the limbs. 

Drink is also divided because some is "mixing," such as that taken together with nourishment. 

---

Another is "conveying," such as that taken after digestion has occurred in the belly and is halfway through the liver. There is also "altering" drink, which is given for the sake of medicine. 

Secondly, it must be known that some have said drink should be taken with food for mixing, but the "conveying" drink should come later. Therefore, the Arabs are said to speak of "conveying" drink in agreement. Although this contains the truth, it does not fully express their mind, since the Arab authorities simply and without distinction deny that one should drink while taking food, nor should one drink immediately after, except perhaps for the sake of medicine. 

Indeed, some—and especially those who followed this—wanted all the food to be eaten first, and then, after it had settled at the bottom of the belly, to drink, as their words and actions show. From this, some have fallen into wicked diseases, although some try to pervert these sayings with interpretation. 

Others, however, such as the English <note>original: "āglici"</note>, take a drink after half the meal is consumed, and then begin to drink. Their error will be shown subsequently. 

Furthermore, it should first be known that no drink should be taken on an empty stomach, except for the sake of medicine. Second, that one should eat and drink at the same time. Regarding the first point, it must be known that simple water as a drink is not to be taken on an empty stomach, as the Greeks and Arabs testify. Indeed, it is numbered among poisons, and especially 
<margin>Water</margin>
after exercise, sexual intercourse, or a bath. Reason also concludes this: for drink is given either for the sake of mixing or for conveying nourishment to the parts. But neither of these should be taken before food, since it would have nothing to mix with, nor anything to carry to the limbs. 

Again, water—whether cold—is received into the body as it is by nature, and then by its extreme coldness, finding the belly (which is cold by nature) almost empty, it harms it vehemently. Since a general thing brings its proportional part to fury. Or, it has acquired an external quality, such as lukewarmness or heat, and thus it weakens the stomach by greatly relaxing it. For lukewarm water properly softens things, and its substance pours out <unclear>something</unclear> of digestion; for this reason, when it is necessary to induce vomiting, lukewarm water is given. And therefore it is commanded in the same place that heat, and not lukewarmness, should be applied even to the outside of the stomach. Hot water, however, weakens the stomach, as stated in the third part of the first book. 

Moreover, wine is no less accused than water when taken upon an empty stomach. This can be shown by the same reasoning as water. Since it performs neither the task of mixing nor conveying. Also, wine, by its heat and its subtle, sharp substance, penetrates the nervous substance of the stomach, dissolving it, especially when it is strong; whence the saying of Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus, a famous 10th-century physician</note>: Though the speech is detailed, if they drink wine before food is offered, they receive no good, but are greatly harmed, being quickly seized by spasms and "desipientia" <term>desipientia: a medical term for delirium or loss of reason</term>. 

For this reason, a servant of a grammarian, drinking old wine while staying awake, subsequently developed a fever and, being seized by delirium, died. Therefore: A wise man ought to beware lest he drink wine while fasting, or after exercise, and especially after intercourse, so that it is then numbered among the...

# Whether One Should Drink or Eat First

...intervening. And properly what is dense and sweet. Nor indeed does it help for the reason that food, being of a dense and earthy moisture, cannot perfectly restore what has been lost without a thicker nourishment. I have spoken "simply," because sometimes drink is taken before food, and after it, and during it; even those who hold the opposite view absolutely proceed with drink.

This can happen in two ways: either by custom, which is called a "second nature" (according to the 98th distinction). Hence, from the beginning, there are things that exist outside of reason. This is shown by the drunkards I have mentioned, who, by a depraved custom, demand to be in the taverns almost before the light of dawn. Or it is for the sake of medicine, as when there is coldness in the belly; then a drink such as wine in a small quantity—the best and aged, such as Doric wine—is required. This is also considered regarding water. Or it may be because of a burning of the stomach; whence Rhazes says in the fourth book of the *Almansor*: 
<margin>Digestion</margin>
"No one should drink water while fasting <note>original: "in ieiuno"</note> unless they have a great burning in the stomach." Or it may be by reason of hot weather, which dries out the moisture, creating a bad "hot complexion," or when choleric humors <term>choleric humors: in medieval medicine, "yellow bile," a hot and dry bodily fluid associated with heat and irritability</term> are accumulating in it. For this reason, Aristotle wrote to Alexander that he should sometimes take water in this way. 

Thus, let it appear that food should "simply" precede drink, and that drink is postponed relative to it. Regarding this, the following must be known: if one is to eat and drink, one should first eat, then drink a little, and finally eat. And so on in succession, so that a better mixture is made. One should not drink the whole amount in one, two, or three go's, as many Spaniards and English do <note>A common medieval stereotype regarding the heavy drinking habits of Northern and Western Europeans</note>. Many today observe the method mentioned above, as indicated in the 22nd section. For we do not only drink sometimes for the sake of what we eat, but also after food for the sake of pleasure or the like. Whence, in the first book on "Preserving Health": In many foods and at hot hours, when children come to cold water, I grant them its use. This is proven because things taken in are ordained for the restoration of what has been lost; however, what is lost is both a moist substance (which is restored by drink) and a dry one (which is restored by food), provided no other cause occurs to consume them. 

Again, one must satisfy a "right appetite," since it proceeds according to nature. But food is desired together with drink, especially when it is dry. Likewise, the mixing and uniting of the two is ordained for <term>digestion</term>, and this for nutrition, and finally for the preservation of health. Indeed, a more lasting mixture occurs when one eats and drinks together, because food is of a denser substance...

<margin>Digestion</margin>
...for a good mixture, it is necessary for a liquid to be mixed in, as the mixture of different existing natures indicates. And "digestion is the perfection achieved by one's own natural heat from the opposing qualities," according to the fourth book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "quarto methaurorum"; a reference to Aristotle's work on natural phenomena</note>. Therefore, where the logic of digestion is better preserved, a more perfect nutrition will follow. This occurs in the instantaneous mixing of food with drink. Furthermore, since opposing qualities arrive, they temper one another. And it is confirmed because everything that must be digested must become the substance of a "ptisan-like mass" <note>original: "masse ptisanarie"; referring to a consistency like barley water or gruel</note>. Whence, in the first [book of] *Principles*: "Nutriment, when it is digested, becomes its own essence in many animals with the help of what is mixed with it." Therefore, what is drunk is mostly <term>chyle</term> <note>chyle: the milky fluid drafted from food in the intestine during digestion</note>, and it exists in the liquid substance of a ptisan-like thickness. 

This happens through diligence when food and drink are taken together. Since food is usually dense in its penetration and slow, it is necessary to mix it with something that renders it liquid and allows it to penetrate; this thing is drink. Therefore, one should eat and drink at the same time. However, sometimes food is so liquid that it has the substance of a drink, with which it is not so necessary to drink. There are also some people with stomachs so moist and soft that they need little or no drink. Those who are loudly thirsty must drink in every way, not only with food, but before it and during it. Yet it is better for those with a "false nighttime thirst" <note>original: "fiti mendose nocturne"; likely referring to a thirst caused by bad humors rather than true dehydration</note> not to obey it, according to the seventh book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio"; likely Galen's *De Ingenio Sanitatis*</note>. 

<margin>M. Division / of Tudela (?) / for health.</margin>
If they are thirsty during dinner, they should abstain from drink entirely; it becomes sad and useless. Indeed, a little drink should be given to mitigate the anxiety and humble the thirst. Without a doubt, drink must be given to those who are excessively thirsty. Whence, in the first book of "Preserving Health": Children are not to be entirely prohibited from drinking cold water, but let them drink cold water often with food and in hot hours. Know also that food should be hot, or in summer lukewarm; drink, however, should be hot or lukewarm as mentioned. But in the colder winter, everything partakes in the coldness of that air, except for those things which are better in summer. Nor should one then drink water intensely cooled by ice or snow, especially when the recipient has cold viscera, is flatulent, or has weak nerves. And

especially those who drink much diluted wine. The Greeks, however, because of a certain misuse, continually drink hot things. In ancient times, they also thought it helped the sick, though perhaps in certain diseases, such as those of the chest, it may be expedient, especially in winter. 

Regarding the first part, it must be said that subtle, airy moisture is not consumed more quickly; for although it is more prepared for consumption than the dense kind, nature nevertheless applied a greater quantity to the limbs. For this reason, even if it is thin, it can resist consumption when combined with the dense. For a thing that is "enough" can resist better than a thing that is "little." Furthermore, moisture is found in foods, and this subtle moisture resists consumption. Nor does the confirmation cause distress, since this method is for healthy people living freely in the air. Or rather, this is sought more for the sake of medicine and correction than for anything facilitating nourishment. 

Regarding the other point, it must be said that thin food should precede dense food—preparing food for food—but not drink before food, as the logic seemed to suggest. Whence it needs thinner and more liquid food, such as broth, which is easily permeating and nourishing. Or perhaps it is to be interpreted this way: do not drink immediately after dinner before the food is digested, but rather drink...

It references the authority of Galen, Rufus of Ephesus, and Rhazes to determine whether movement should precede or follow a meal.</meta>

<margin>Galen, *On the Preservation of Health*, Book 6</margin>
...at the meal. However, some do not tolerate this for a long time. But against this is what Galen testifies in the sixth book of *On the Preservation of Health*: Galen himself, at the fourth hour of the day, would take simple bread and never drink with such food. Others, however, ate with this dates, acorns, or olives with honey or salt, and some of them drank. It must be said that Galen should not be heard on this now, because of a change in habit. Or perhaps moisture was overabundant in his stomach. Nevertheless, a <term>choleric: associated with yellow bile, which is hot and dry</term> matter may sometimes present itself in the upper stomach. Regarding the other point, it must be said through interpretation: when it more [closely] joins the substance of the stomach and is taken in larger amounts, it adheres better, provided that the drink is of sufficient quantity to be absorbed by the food. This occurs when the food is coarse and lasting—the kind eaten by healthy people—rather than the opposite, which is for the sick. Indeed, coarse and lasting food draws in and absorbs [liquid] just as a sponge absorbs water. Regarding the other point, it must be said by way of negation: rather, the food taken (as has already been shown) is held back when it has absorbed the drink, rather than sliding through the members, since a perfect mixing is achieved, unless the quantity of the drink is greater than the food can absorb. Avicenna also is heard when he explains this. Regarding another point, it must be said that although a drink may be cold, it is nevertheless stripped of that quality when it is mixed more diligently with food, both because of the heat of the stomach and the heat of the food itself. For the food is hot and dry in such a way that it indicates an appetite for it. Regarding the last point, it must be said (as has already appeared) that neither <term>didones: likely referring to ringing in the ears or head-related noises</term> nor rumblings nor vapors rising into the head occur, nor is the digestive purpose disturbed or hindered. Instead, everything is better gathered and retained in the stomach—and this is when the drink is proportional to the food through the intervening absorption of the drink. For if the drink is so great that it floats amidst the food and the walls of the stomach, it corrupts digestion.

Because it has been judged that, due to eating [immediately after] exercise, the nourishment slips from the stomach undigested, there is a doubt concerning the time of exercise. For it seems it should be done after eating, because of the meaning of the *Aphorisms*: <note>original: "Cibus semper exercitium preoccupet"</note> "Food should always precede exercise." Hence, in the first part of the *Tripartite*, Rufus says: "This walking pleases me specifically before lunch, because it prepares the goodness of the operation of the dinner." Also, in the 10th book of the *Theory*, the greatest utility of exercise is when a meal has preceded it. Therefore, since a comparison suggests a position, even if it does not precede, it will truly follow that there is utility. Such utility is to be acquired.

The same is true concerning the bath and exercise, since both draw heat outward from the inside. This is shown by the anxiety of the bath and exercise [mentioned by] Hali Abbas and Johannicius. But the bath is judged for children and those with many <term>dyscrasias: imbalances of the bodily humors</term>, since a temperate body is rarely found. Whence it says in the first book of *On the Preservation of Health*: In faulty dispositions of the body and [physical] constrictions, it is better to offer food before baths. For the same reason, one should also prescribe exercise. It is not the same for the healthy or those without fault. Likewise, digestion is the principal thing, since it is the end toward which the others preceding it are ordered. Digestion, however, occurs in rest. But exercise should be done before eating, for the sake of appetite; or afterward, once digestion is already completed. And where there is hunger, one ought not to work. But it is done before eating because one eats on account of it. To exercise is, in a way, to labor. 

Exercise, therefore, should only be after eating. On the contrary, physicians are before the <term>coitus: joining or meeting (here likely meaning the meal or a specific medical regimen)</term>; whence in the fourth section of the sixth book of the *Epidemics*: "Let labors predispose the food." Also, Galen, reciting the *Aphorisms* and *On the Preservation of Health*, says: "Labors should precede food." Whence in the fourth book of the *Almansor*: <note>original: "Sicut motus ante qmestionem fcus sanitatis e conservativus. Ita q post qmestionem egritudis inveit generativus."</note> "Just as movement made before eating is preservative of health, so that which is made after eating is found to be generative of illness." Again, exercise is done for the sake of expelling <term>superfluities: waste products or excess humors that the body needs to purge</term>; these are already sequestered before eating, and then it is necessary to expel them. Furthermore, exercise performed before eating kindles the heat of the body and the stomach, by which digestion is laudably perfected. Therefore, exercise alone is appropriate before eating. How it is neutrally appropriate is shown: because exercise is movement, as will be seen. This is made distinct by what is in the fourth book of the *Physics*. Indeed, such a corruptive thing goes out; for by being distant from its beginning, some corruption happens to it (according to Avicenna, *On the World*). Furthermore, since exercise is movement, and that is the act of a being in potentiality (according to the third book of the *Physics*), nothing conserving could be caused by it by nature. Therefore, exercise is appropriate neither before nor after food. 

Regarding the first point, it must first be known what exercise is. Finally, what rubbing is, since it predisposes and perfects it. Regarding the first, it must be known that "exercise" can be taken in two ways. Either in general, as for labor and also movement. Whence the meaning of the *Aphorisms*: "I do not understand labor to be only the more vehement thing we call exercise." And in the second book of *On the Preservation of Health*: "Labor, movement, and exercise are the same." Or it is taken in a special sense, as it is said against <unclear>buig</unclear>. For not every movement of nature is labor, since labor exists as a necessity or violence. Exercise, however, is that which is voluntary. Nor is every movement of a human [exercise], because it is not a small but a vehement thing; moreover, in the second book of *On the Preservation of Health*, movements that do not alter respiration are not yet called exercise. It is, however, that which alters respiration by its vehemence. Whence in the first part of the *Tripartite*: It is a voluntary movement because of which great and frequent panting is necessary. Exercise is divided just as movement is, essentially: for some is strong, some weak, and some intermediate. Also, some is fast, some slow, and some moderate. Additionally, some is long, some short, and some intermediate. From these differences, there are nine simple types of exercise. Others are composed of many species, which are hardly applicable to the perception of the senses. There arise, however, 19 types when two differences are joined: for instance, long and strong, long and fast, long and weak, long and slow, long and intermediate, long and moderate; strong and fast, strong and short, strong and slow, strong and mediocre or intermediate, strong and intermediate; fast and short, fast and weak, fast and mediocre, fast and intermediate; short and weak, short and slow, short and intermediate, short and mediocre. When, however, three are joined, 27 arise, just as there are differences in a great pulse; also the compound differences total 82: Long-strong-fast, long-strong-intermediate, long-strong-slow, long-fast-intermediate, long-intermediate-intermediate, long-slow-intermediate, long-weak-slow, long-weak-intermediate, long-weak-fast, short-strong-fast...

# Whether exercise should be done after eating, and so forth.

Short strong medium; short strong slow; short fast medium; short medium medium; short slow medium; short weak slow; short weak medium; short weak fast. **1v.** Of these, those carried out in action are very difficult. The remaining ones, which are more intense, might be handled by a colder constitution; the more relaxed ones by a warmer one. They are distinguished accidentally because exercises are infinite in terms of the materials in which they are performed, such as plowing, sewing, throwing a stone, etc.

Furthermore, some exercise is common to the whole body and moves it proportionally, such as running, digging, hoeing, reaping, and the like. Other exercise is specific, attributed to individual parts, such as writing with the hands, shouting for the chest, kicking with the feet themselves, weaving with the hands, and similar things. Again, some common exercise consists of movement that is only labor, such as building or digging. Other movement is only exercise, such as dancing and playing ball. Some, however, are both, such as plowing, rowing, and pruning.

The hour to begin exercise is after the <term>superfluities: waste products like urine and feces</term> of the first digestion have been expelled. This is when the nourishment first taken has been processed. For either the humors will be rendered undigested, or they will be transferred into the veins in a raw state. Indeed, urine discerns this time. For when the substance is medium, and the color is moderate and thin, one should exercise. When, however, the water is pale/whitish, it is not yet time; if it is fiery and <term>choleric: related to yellow bile, indicating excessive heat</term>, by no means, for the hour has already passed. For other bodies, this must be proportioned from a measured standard.

Exercise should be ceased when the breath begins to thicken, or rather when sweat begins to break out, redness appears, and the vessels swell significantly. For as long as the heat increases and provides strength, the movements are still light; and until the swelling of the parts becomes great, one must not desist from exercise. A temperate person should almost spontaneously stop exercising. A <term>flatulent: here meaning one prone to "wind" or gas in the limbs</term> person should be encouraged to exercise even when he wants to stop. But a choleric person should be restrained even while he still wishes to continue.

There are three benefits to exercise performed in this way. First, it imparts hardness to the organs as they are rubbed against each other, from which arises their durability and strength of action. Third, the movement of the <term>spirits: the vital forces believed to circulate through the body to enable life and movement</term> is more violent, by which vigor the pores are opened and superfluities are driven out, forced out through every path.

# Damascenus on the Aphorisms
<note>John Mesue the Elder, also known as Johannes Damascenus, was a 9th-century Syrian Christian physician whose medical "aphorisms" were widely studied in medieval universities.</note>

<margin>2. Book m. : [regarding] cooking</margin>
...existing. **Difference 29.** It is not appropriate to exercise after the consumption of food. We say this because digestion is perfected through rest, as previously mentioned. However, exercise after eating is ill-advised because, when the motion becomes violent, its agitation forces undigested food to descend into the intestines; this often causes a blockage <term>opilatio: a medieval medical term for a blockage or obstruction in the internal organs, especially the liver or veins</term> and distracts the natural heat. Consequently, it weakens and corrupts the digestion, which ought to be completed in a state of rest. Therefore, exercise is not suitable after nourishment, but rather before it; for then the internal heat is prepared to receive food, it expels superfluities <term>superfluities: excess waste products or "bad humors" the body needs to discard</term> to the exterior, and it strengthens the power of the whole body. This is true provided the person is not famished, for one should not labor when hungry, especially if the person is of a choleric <term>choleric: a personality or physical type dominated by yellow bile, characterized as hot and dry</term> temperament. 

However, in certain rare cases, movement is appropriate after eating. This might be because a person has taken more food than their digestion can master; therefore, to encourage it to move downward after consumption, they are agitated unless sleep provides a better remedy. This is because bodily movement causes a disturbance, as shown in the aphorism regarding sailing <note>original: "nauigatio afforismoz q̄rta . Vü ." refers to Hippocrates, Aphorisms 4.8, which discusses how the motion of sailing causes internal disturbance</note> by Hippocrates. After dinner or lunch, such people ought to sleep for the full duration of the night—that is, as long as the night lasts. The Commentator <note>This likely refers to Galen, the primary commentator on Hippocrates</note> notes that if they do not sleep, they will not be able to resist the discomfort unless they walk very slowly and gently. And this is the intention of Aristotle, as is clear from what precedes. For Hippocrates recites the aforementioned opinion when he says: "Rufus says <note>Rufus of Ephesus was a famous Greek physician whose works on dietetics were highly influential</note> that this walking pleases me," etc., as introduced before. 

It is also perhaps appropriate when we wish to stimulate the heat of a cold and dry body, and to send the dryness of the food into the deep parts of the body. In this way, some scholars have wished to explain the praise of physicians for those who are "leisurely," so that by such movement, the food might catch up with the exercise. But the falsity of this is soon apparent when he adds that this should be done for both the healthy and the sick. Hippocrates and Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon, the most influential physician of antiquity</note> testify to the contrary in the Greek texts. Nevertheless, it can be said in the same way that a bath is taken for the purpose of moistening after nourishment. The same is said in the third part. 

Furthermore, exercise or movement—more so if it is minor—is beneficial after food so that the food may descend downward from the stomach into the bottom of the belly, especially when the belly was windy and bloated before the meal. Hence, in the third part: a small movement after eating causes the food to rest in the stomach. For this reason, Aristotle in the *Problems* <note>original: "Ar. ꝑoliticoy" likely an error for *Problemata*, where Aristotle discusses health and walking</note> says: "To walk after dinner is healthy, lest the foods float around the mouth of the stomach." 

Certain accustomed laborers do not seem to be continually harmed after eating, although they may eventually come to grave illnesses. # Whether heavy foods should precede [lighter ones]

In this matter, a careful observer must be diligent so that they do not consume something light <note>original: "subtile"; refers to "thin" or "subtle" foods like broth or light fish</note> and easily digested after a heavy <note>original: "forte"; "strong" or "heavy" foods like beef or unleavened bread</note> and harder food. In all dietary books, the ancients agree that foods that descend quickly and easily penetrate the veins should be eaten before foods that are slow to do so.

<margin>On universal sayings.</margin>
Furthermore, one ought to eat first that which is quickly digestible and easily passes through the bowels. For if the quickly digested food is mixed with heavy, undigested food at the bottom of the stomach, and the heavy food does not allow it to pass, both will happen to be corrupted. Additionally, according to Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus, an influential 10th-century Jewish physician and philosopher whose works on diet and fevers were foundational in medieval medicine.</note>, the stomach is a receptacle for gases. It is also heavy, and thus seeks the bottom. It is naturally cold, moist, and viscous, which can impede digestion. Therefore, so that it may digest more easily, it requires light food to be presented first, as it is more obedient to digestion than heavy food. Furthermore, that which restores lost strength most quickly should be eaten first; this is light food, as it digests more swiftly and penetrates more deeply than heavy food. The opposite is shown in the first [book of] *Practice* <note>Likely referring to the *Practica* or practical section of a major medical compendium like the *Pantegni* or the *Canon* of Avicenna.</note>: "Heavy food, not quickly digestible, should precede quickly digestible food." Furthermore, in the third [book of] *Aphorisms*, it says one should not eat "praiseworthy" <note>referring to highly nutritious or "clean" foods</note> food first if heavy and hard food is to be taken afterward. Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon, the 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note>, in *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio"; refers to Galen’s *De methodo medendi*, often called the *Megatechne* in the Middle Ages.</note>, commands that heavier and more "earthy" foods, such as bread, be given at dinner first, and then more liquid and light foods, like a dish of rock-dwelling fish. Again, art imitates nature: nature places heavier and weightier things first, with their opposites following, just as one sees in the foundations of buildings. Therefore, it is appropriate for the heavy to precede the light.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that food has been defined in chapters 126 and 127. "Heavy" and "light" are two qualities that the physician, as a sensory craftsman, names after the substances they resemble, since these qualities appear to be joined to the primary substances here hidden. Heavy and thick is that whose substance is thickened by cold or heat, yielding with difficulty and penetrating through the parts slowly; light is the opposite.

<margin>Hard and liquid food.</margin>
Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have answered the question by distinguishing that food is twofold: hard (masticable) and liquid (non-masticable). They argue that if two foods are taken, one being masticable and the other not, the non-masticable should precede the masticable. This is moved by the idea that if the non-masticable is given afterward, being quickly digested but unable to pass through, it will corrupt itself and the preceding heavy, undigested food. However, if both foods are masticable, the heavy should precede the light. This position, however, is false regarding its first part and cannot stand, for the same reasons given previously regarding the difference between drink and food. Indeed, liquids are joined together in one space so that a more perfect mixture—and finally digestion and nutrition—may occur. For if a light, non-masticable food is placed first, it will pass through quickly and lead the other undigested food out of the stomach with it. Furthermore, the belly, being in its lower part a "fire" <note>a reference to the "innate heat" required for digestion</note> disproportionate to light food, would burn it with excessive quality, preparing it—

---

—for the generation of choler <term>choler: also known as yellow bile; one of the four humors, associated with heat and dryness</term> in the liver. Therefore, that position cannot stand regarding its first part. Regarding the third point, certain necessary truths should be set forth first. Regarding the first of these, it should be known that our bodies presently exist in two states. For there is a body that is simply healthy, whose actions proceed perfectly, having all members—and especially those of digestion—proportionate to each other and to the whole. There is also another body opposite to this, whose particular actions are deficient in some way, and especially those of digestion which are not proportionate to each other. These are either weak, allowing food to exit before perfect digestion (into the stool), or strong and "constipated," preventing even the digested superfluities from passing. Foods also fall into two categories. Some are true nourishments, like bread, meat, and wine, as praised in the third [book of] *Aphorisms*. Others are foreign to nutrition, being medicinal foods <note>original: "cibaria medicinalia"</note> like fruits and vegetables, some of which are styptic <term>styptic: substances that contract tissues or "bind" the bowels, often used to treat diarrhea</term> and others are softening <term>mollientia: substances that soften or loosen the bowels, acting as mild laxatives</term>. 

<margin>Foods are twofold: pure and nourishing, and impure foods.</margin>
Regarding the second point, it should be known that if the bodies have "fallen" bowels—such that the stool passes too quickly—then heavy and styptic things should precede light and softening things. This is so that the constipation may retain the light food for a time, so that one single digestion may be perfected. 

<margin>Towards digestion.</margin>
However, if the bowels are constipated, the light, liquid, and softening food should precede the heavy, earthy, and styptic food, so that the belly may be softened by it. 

<margin>Note.</margin>
As for other bodies, which are the primary subject of this discourse, they should be governed by this order of precedence and post-positioning of foods: If two or more foods are taken, one of which is medicinal, light, and softening, and the other is nutritious, then the light food, which descends easily, should be placed before the one that lingers longer. 

<margin>First Practice.</margin>
In the first [book of] *Practice*, it says a person should put foods that descend easily from the stomach before those that linger, so that they soften the belly; those that "bind" should come after, so that the food descending quickly prepares a path for the one that lingers. Examples include melons and peaches, which should be taken before bread or meat, so that by softening the belly they prepare a path for the "binding" food. Similarly, one should first take boiled vegetables prepared with brine and oil, rather than pears or quinces <note>original: "coctana"; a type of small Syrian plum or quince known for being astringent/binding</note>. The reason for this is that they are easily passed and have medicinal qualities. Therefore, so that they may be expelled from the belly as is expedient, and not corrupt the rest of the food if they were taken afterward, they must be placed first. It is in this sense that the third [book of] *Aphorisms* intends its command that light food be placed before heavy food. 

However, if the items taken are true nourishments, consumed solely for the sake of nutrition and not as medicine, then the heavy should precede the light. Hence, Haly Abbas <note>Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi, a famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note> in the aforementioned place says that heavy food, which is not quickly digestible, should precede quickly digestible and light food—such as placing mutton, poultry, or beef before sheep’s meat. This is also what [Aristotle] signifies in the place mentioned, saying that it is not appropriate to eat "praiseworthy" <note>light/nutritious</note> food first if a strong and hard food is to be taken after it. For every natural agent requires a certain time for its action. In a longer time, a stronger action is perfected, and heavy, strong food requires a stronger action [of digestion].

<summary>This page explores the medical debate over the order of food consumption, concluding that while medicinal or laxative foods (like fruit) should be eaten first to clear the bowels, heavy, nutritious foods (like meat) should generally be eaten before lighter ones to ensure proper digestion time.</summary>

They mix in digestion because the proportion of the foods (thin to heavy) matches the proportion of the lower stomach's digestion to the upper part, which is less digestive due to its nervous <note>sinewy or fibrous</note> nature. This discourse is more true for healthy bodies in which no humor—of which one must be cured—abounds in the stomach. In these, the medicinal food should be placed first, which is warming, digestive, and divisive, and then the phlegmatic matter contained therein should be led out by vomit or stool. 

As for the thin food being consumed faster than the heavy: this is true when they are of equal quantity. But when the thin is multiplied over the heavy, they are consumed equally.

### DIFFERENCE 120.

-> 1 <-

This section shows that one should eat only once in a natural day. Since that which is contrary to the body and harmful to it should be applied rarely, and food is of such a kind (according to [Aristotle's] *On Generation and Corruption*), it follows that it should be rare, which is once a day. Furthermore, an animal that performs noble acts should be less preoccupied with eating so that it may intend to do those things more fully (from the seventh [book] of Galen's *On the Usefulness of the Parts*). This is true of man. For this reason, he should eat rarely and little, such as only once a day. 

However, it seems that one should eat twice, according to Cornelius Celsus <note>A 1st-century Roman medical authority</note>, who advises taking food twice a day rather than once. 
<margin>
Cornelius Celsus
</margin>
For nourishment is ordained for the restoration of what is lost, and this loss seems twofold. One occurs at night, when the heat is gathered and strengthened, performing a more powerful—albeit hidden—work of restoration, as they say happens in winter. The other is the diurnal depletion <note>original: "resolutio"; the loss of humors and energy during the day</note> caused by the pores, the heat, and the light. Again, the appetite for eating is ordered; but appetite usually occurs twice a day, therefore one should eat twice. 

Furthermore, for someone with much heat, it is expedient to administer much and frequent nourishment (from the first [book] of *Aphorisms*). This is true of man, as he is the warmest of animals. Moreover, for one who has weak digestion and rapid depletion, one should provide small amounts frequently. Such is man, as he is devoted to many occupations that hinder digestion, and he is of a rarer and better habit of body. Again, in a natural day, there are four combinations of qualities of specific times, just as the moon causes no small alterations in us (Difference 178), which one must resist with food. Thus, one should eat four times. But also, because a living animal is continually being depleted—as natural heat always feeds on moisture—this is resisted by the administration of proportional nourishment. Furthermore, some small animals seem to eat continually; why then not the larger ones more so? Thus, it seems one should eat continually. 

The opposite of all these is held by the Arabs, who wish for there to be three meals in two days. This is seen because undigested food must be avoided; according to Avicenna, one should not take food while previous food remains undigested. This happens if one eats more than twice...

# Whether one should eat only once in a natural day.

...as will be declared, let him eat. For it is necessary to allow the body to feel hunger, which occurs if meals are administered in a number fewer than this. For this reason, in the space of two natural days <note>A "natural day" refers to a full 24-hour period (day and night), whereas an "artificial day" refers only to the hours of sunlight.</note>, they should eat three times. Regarding the first point, it should be known that eating is the reception of nourishment by the mouth. Some of this is solid and chewable, some is liquid and sippable, and sometimes it is liquid and drinkable, such as wine, which is both nourishment and drink. Also, "once," "twice," and "thrice" are adverbs denoting discrete quantities. What a natural day is and what an artificial day is has been seen in Difference 4. Regarding the second point, it should be known that Isaac <note>original: "Y."; referring to Isaac Israeli, a famous 10th-century physician</note> along with Galen <note>original: "Ga."</note> seems to suggest that eating should be once or twice a day. He implies this when he says: "For he who is accustomed to eating once or twice a day," and so on, regarding those for whom it is not a custom to lunch and yet they do so. And if someone 
<margin>On the Regime of Health, Book 6.</margin>
eats once a day against their habit, or twice, Galen says of himself that he eats twice a day. But in the seventh book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de īge."; referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note>, he prescribes three meals for those who are "dried out" or weaker. 
<margin>4th book of Almansor.</margin>
However, the inquired regime looks to the preservation of health. 
<margin>☞</margin>
The Arabs recommend—as touched upon by this one man—that one should eat three times over the course of two days. Whence in the fourth book of *Almansor* <note>A famous medical work by the Persian physician Rhazes</note>: "Let the healthy be refreshed three times during two days, as much as they can endure." Also in the first book of *Practice*: "It is appropriate that he eats twice on this day, and once on that day." The reason for this follows: so that his stomach may be lightened from the food of the day on which he took it twice, and may work on the remainder of the preceding food and digest the food with the appropriate subsequent cooking <note>original: "decoctīōne"; in medieval medicine, digestion was viewed as a "cooking" process driven by internal heat</note>. Also in the first book: "Of the frequencies of eating, it is better that a man eats once on one day and twice on the other, namely in the morning and evening." The motive for this could be the precept that nothing should be eaten unless the food has descended from the stomach. In an average constitution, food remains in the stomach from 22 to 26 hours. The average time is between 12 and 22, which is about 16 hours. Thrice 16 is 48 hours, which completes two natural days. He prescribes eating in the morning and evening on one of the days so that he does not eat in the middle of the night, for that is the time for deeper digestion and rest. This, however, varies among those in different latitudes due to the brevity or length of the days. What should be said about eating twice will be seen following this. 

Regarding the third point, it should be known that just as bodies differ in other ways regarding natural things, non-natural things, and things against nature, so it is with the frequency of eating. What these things are is well known from many sources; however, here a variation of natural and non-natural things is sought, since the discourse concerns healthy bodies. For some of these are hot and moist, thick, sufficiently dense, and compact, with commendable bellies and livers filled with decent blood, and not subject to external distractions. In temperate places and times and constitutions, and having a sufficient supply of the things necessary for life: for these, it suffices to eat once around midday in a natural day. This is what certain of our fat priests <note>A common medieval observation regarding the sedentary and well-fed lifestyle of some clergy</note> observe doing. Whence in the fourth book of *Almansor*: "Bodies that are thick and fat are harmed by being refreshed twice a day." 

For such people take in much nourishment. They also abound in raw humors that require digestion. And therefore, as they are strong in virtue and their bodies are not in need, they should be given food rarely and in large amounts. Those who are the opposite, with wide pores and thinner passages, perhaps need to eat more often. Wherefore in the fourth book of *Almansor*: "It harms bodies that are thin and dry to eat only once a day." Those in the middle of these should be refreshed three times in two days or twice every day. And the reason for this is taken from the opposite of the former. 

Age must also be especially observed along with other factors, as well as habit. For infants and children, and especially those who are more active, sometimes need to eat twice, three times, or even more. Since they are like a lamp ready to be extinguished, they require more frequent attention. Old men, however, should eat once, twice, or three times in two days. Adolescents along with youths should eat twice a day, according to whether they are more or less active. The reason for this is taken from their more intense or relaxed heat, with a substance that is harder or softer, and thus more or less apt for dissolution. Custom <note>original: "consuetudo"</note> must also be strongly observed in this. For some are accustomed to eating once a day, others twice, and some three times; if they change from their custom, and especially if they do so suddenly, they are harmed greatly, as declared in the second book of *On the Regime of Health*. And habit must be strongly observed in this, because it is said that habit becomes a certain "second nature" which one ought to govern like a daughter. For the diversity of habit causes not a few problems. For some eat once a day, others twice. And of these, some eat earlier, others toward evening. 

They should also be refreshed more often if they have sensitive stomachs where bile flows, requiring a little more substantial food. In hot regions, times, and constitutions, and for those using light or thin diets, it is necessary to increase the number of meals. In moderate cases, a moderate amount. In opposite cases, the reverse happens in every way. It is also necessary to add to the number of meals for those who work with their hands, because of the great dissolution <note>metabolic exhaustion or loss of substance</note> caused in them by sharp heat. 

Drink should also be taken at the time of eating, as declared in chapter 18. Drink is a "mixer." But "conveying" drink can also be taken outside of mealtime, for instance, when digestion is finished in the stomach and half-finished in the liver. From these brief points, one can see the truth of this question more fully. And note also that it stands from the nature of the thing itself. Thus, the naturalists feel that one should eat twice a day more often. Regarding the fourth point: to the first objection, it should be said that although nourishment may harm by its contrariety if applied twice or more, yet if this is done duly, a greater benefit follows the harm when necessity demands it. To the other, it should be said that although man is made for noble operations, it is not good for him to be continually engaged in them unless appropriate nourishment is supplied in the right way. For eating three or two times in two days, or more, is of great benefit.

# DIFFERENCE 121.

**Whether dinner should be larger than lunch.**

That dinner <term>cena<explanation>The evening meal, usually taken near sunset.</explanation></term> should be larger than lunch <term>prandium<explanation>The midday meal, typically taken around the fourth hour of the day (mid-morning/noon).</explanation></term> is shown thus: Because first, in his work *On the Diet of Acute Diseases*, Galen says juice should be given to the sick for lunch, but for dinner, change the juice for food. Indeed, food—such as unstrained barley-groats <note>original: "ptisana nō colata"</note>—is more nourishing than juice, such as strained groats. Also in the fourth book of the same work, he says to use a watery honey-drink in the morning, and a "sip" (namely the juice of barley-groats) toward the evening. Again, it is said in Difference 118 that Galen, on a day of thirteen equinoctial hours, used to take simple bread without drink around the fourth hour. But at dinner, he then took coarser meat with bread so that they might eat more substantially. Also in his *Practica*, Book 1: Dinner is more praiseworthy than lunch because everyone sleeps quietly after it. For the heat sinks into the depths of the stomach and the body and digests the food with a full and good digestion.

Likewise, as it is in other times, so it is proportionally in this particular time, since it receives its power from the other. But in [colder] times, such as winter, one digests better; therefore, in a particular time like the night, it is the same because it is proportionally similar in coldness. But when one digests more, more food is required. Again, digestion is achieved through sleep. For sleep makes all natural operations strong and provides a temperate rest with sufficient governance of heat; these things occur at night. Furthermore, at the time when digestion is most strengthened and distribution is greatest, more nourishment is required. This occurs at night because digestion is strengthened then, partly due to the gathering of heat as it draws itself inward away from outward actions (the animal virtues being at rest), and partly because of the darkness, from which the digestive heat and spirits flee, seeking the interior parts. On the other hand, more should be eaten at the time when the greatest consumption has preceded it, since food is ordained for the restoration of what was lost. This occurs during the day because of the containing heat and the necessary acts of life by which the body is thinned. Therefore, dinner should be made larger than lunch.

To the contrary: Because those who exercised in ancient times were content with eating meat alone in the morning and only bread at dinner, as seen in the first book of *On the Method of Healing*. But eating meat seems greater than eating bread, since it nourishes more. Furthermore, nourishment is given for the recovery of what was lost. But this loss will be greater during the day because of the quickened natural and solar heat and the actions by which the heat dissolves the body, leaving it un-restored due to the body's porosity.

Furthermore, if a greater consumption preceded during the night due to the internal union of heat, then a greater restoration would be required during the day, which is fulfilled by lunch. Therefore, lunch should be made larger than dinner. Regarding the first point, it should be known that lunch is commonly the reception of nourishment around the fourth hour of the day, while dinner is around the eleventh hour. Or, it is when eating occurs twice most especially. However, the time of lunch and especially of dinner varies according to the length and especially the shortness of the days. Regarding the second point, it should be known that in this matter, many ways of speaking are found. This happens because of the diversity of complexions <note>The balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, customs, dispositions of times, regions, and the like. For some simply preferred that dinner should be larger than lunch because of the strengthening of the digestive instrument at night. Others said that phlegmatic and cold people should lunch better than they dine, because their heat ought to be assisted by the heat of the day, which at night—being a soft flame—would be almost suffocated if a larger dinner were made. Choleric and "dried out" people, on the other hand, should do the opposite for the contrary reason. Some say that one should proceed according to custom, which does not require much debate. Still others testify that for the healthy, it is better to dine more, since heat is strengthened more at night. But for the sick, it is better to lunch more, unless the illness primarily occurs at night; for then dangers usually appear more often due to the absence of the sun, which gives life, as shown in Difference 3. Some also said that in hot weather and similar regions, lunch should be <margin>3 The French</margin> larger than dinner; but in cold weather, the opposite—which custom the French <note>original: "Galli"</note> observe. And perhaps they derived this from their stay in a hot region such as Syria; for there and in similar places, the heat of the night increases and disturbs digestion. Although all these opinions touch upon some truth, the defects of each will appear in what follows.
