# Should Dinner be larger than Lunch?

<margin>2170</margin>
...are more or less according to how they can be digested. For it is not from those things which are swallowed, but from those which are digested, that food is provided to the whole body, as stated in the eleventh book of <note>original: "terapētice"</note> <term>Therapeutics (Galen's Method of Medicine)</term>. Digestion, moreover, can be considered in four ways: either by reason of the frequency with which nourishment is applied to the body to be digested; or by the subject in whom the action is exercised; or by the reason of the disposition between the active and passive elements; or by the environment in which the digesting subject is held. If indeed by the first way: nourishment is provided either once a day, or three times in two days, or twice or three times in one day. Regarding the first: if it is once, then it must be said that it is better to be provided in the evening, provided the person does not have sensitive eyes or a sensitive brain.

<margin>Dinner harms the eyes and the brain.</margin>
For dinner harms the eyes and the brain of the sick in no small measure, as noted in the first book of medical practice. This is because <term>crude humors</term> <note>Unprocessed bodily fluids that have not yet been "cooked" by the body's heat.</note> and <term>superfluities</term> <note>original: "superfluitates"; waste products or excess fluids that the body must expel.</note> do not remain in the limbs themselves when there is sufficient time for exercise. If, however, dinner is taken when the subsequent time of night and the time of digestion arrive—which are long periods—all things are strengthened by digestion. However, this is not the focus of the question.

If, however, one eats twice, the midday meal should be larger because of the reasons just stated and those to be said. If one eats three times, it seems then that it is more preferable to have a better dinner because of the longer time for sleep and the coming rest. This too is not the primary question. If, however, the consideration refers to the subject, one must know that this person is either within the <term>latitude of health</term> <note>The medieval medical concept that health is not a single point but a range or "latitude" between perfect health and actual sickness.</note> or has already fallen into sickness. If they have fallen into sickness, it is either with a <term>vice of the humors</term> <note>A corruption or imbalance of the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> or without. If it is without, then more should be eaten at dinner, as in the seventh book on hygiene. In the evening, we consider that stronger food should be given, except to those few people who are suffering in the way described. This is also persuaded by reason: for those having any bad <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of qualities—hot, cold, moist, dry—unique to an individual.</note> without a vice of the humors, whether in the whole body or in part, are weak and have wasted bodies. Therefore, because of their weak virtue, they need little nourishment at one time; because of their consumption, they need it often. This should be done during the day; but in the evening, not so much, so that nature may rest at night and not fall into bad habits. And because a long time of sleep and rest intervenes, they need more nourishment at dinner. Furthermore, nature in such people is intent only on the digestion of food, not on the <term>maturation</term> <note>The process of "ripening" or preparing waste products for expulsion.</note> of superfluities, for they lack them. Again, since such people are dry and some of them are hot, they are helped by the contrary disposition of the night. Therefore, more nourishment shall be given to them at dinner.

But if they suffer with a vice of the humors, it must be said that it is more convenient to make the midday lunch larger, as in the first section of the third book on the cure of epidemics. He whose custom does not allow him to eat only once should divide his food, which is less than a full meal, into three parts: let him take two-thirds at lunch and the third part at dinner, after light exercise. This is also persuaded by reason: because at that time when nature is weak, it is helped in digestion by the life-giving <term>solar heat</term>, and more superfluities are resolved when food is to be taken; and this is during the day. For these people are like those who wash in the cold winter and are harmed by the cold because their bodies are thin and their heat is weak, but they are helped by the heat of summer, such as women and <term>phlegmatic</term> people, as mentioned in the third section. Furthermore, at that time, the resolution of superfluities is more active, 

---

and exercise is found in moderation. Likewise, the vital heat of the sun and light is present, and digestion occurs since it is the principle of life. For just as fruit is digested <note>In the sense of ripening or being processed by heat.</note> by a double heat—its own and the sun's.

<margin>Theophrastus, *On Plants*.</margin>
Theophrastus, in the fourth book of *On Plants and Medicines*, says similarly that in the digestion of animals, a double heat will operate. Finally, at night, such people must rest from taking much food, both because nature is strong and sufficient for digestion during sleep, and also because at night nature is more intent on the digestion of superfluities in such people and their expulsion. Furthermore, when superfluities are retained because respiration is hindered and they move outward, nature must not be impeded by the provision of much food. This happens at night, and in the time of old age. For although the heat in many is strengthened at night by its contraction and return to the center, it cannot in these people do two things at once: digest both nourishment and superfluities. Therefore, in these cases, it is more convenient to keep the meal small.

If, however, these bodies are within the "latitude of health," they are either sufficiently healthy, robust, and lacking in sensible superfluities because they expel all through their own channels—like <term>athletes</term>. For these, it is required to make the dinner larger, as in the seventh book of hygiene.

<margin>Aristotle, 7th book of hygiene.</margin>
Athletes have found it reasonable, not by reason alone but by long experience, to take whatever foods are stronger in the evening. This is shown firstly because their digestion at night is intent only on the digestion of food and not on the maturation of superfluities, since they almost lack them; and secondly because they intend only the strength of the body, which they acquire more at night, when a fuller <term>sanguification</term> <note>The process of turning digested food into blood.</note> and distribution occurs.

Again, those who are at leisure during the day, though they move with very vehement exercise, are praised for having a heavy dinner. But if the bodies are distant from that temperament and strength—as are most people who are now falling into sickness—one must see if they exercise with almost continuous and vehement exercise or not. If in the first way, like those who seek their living with their hands <note>Manual laborers.</note>, it is better for them to make lunch larger than dinner. Thus it was said that those who exercised in ancient times were content with the eating of meat alone in the morning and bread alone in the evening. This is confirmed because nourishment is required not only for the sake of nutrition, but also to moisten and "dew" the limbs so they do not become parched from strong movement, and so that they might resist the "resolution" <note>Here meaning the melting away or breaking down of the body's substance.</note> coming from the fire of the heat.

<margin>Nourishment, 2nd book of *On the Soul*.</margin>
Whence it appears in the second book of *On the Soul*: nourishment in the beginning is contrary to the body, but in the end, it becomes like it. Thus food has the power to temper the heat of our body and prevent its desiccation; for which reason one ought to provide more food at lunch. Nor does nature cease from the digestion of these things because of exercise, since they are so accustomed to it. For a thing is according to nature through habit. There is also a vehement heat because of exercise, which is able to overcome both labor and digestion. For this reason, we see them eat three times a day and digest with appetite.

Furthermore, concerning the health of many men of the city who are occupied with the goods of fortune and their own well-being: sometimes they are moved by strong and laborious exercise, such as those who spend a long time riding horses or traveling, or those doing something more strenuous than their accustomed exercise. For these, it is more useful to increase **dinner** more than lunch. However, <note>original: "Halyabas"</note> **Haly Abbas** <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note> instructs such people not to eat lunch at all, because the body ought to be exercised while it is "clean" <note>Empty or fasted.</note> in order to maintain health. Otherwise, one will incur a corruption of digestion and the diseases that result from it. This is persuasive because if they were to eat, and since they are not accustomed to such strong and laborious exercise as their predecessors, their digestion would be corrupted by the generation of <term>bad chymes</term> <note>Fluid produced by the stomach during digestion; "bad chymes" refers to poorly processed nutrients.</note>. Furthermore, because of excessive movement, their heat is weakened by being scattered. Indeed, the concentration of this heat is the most powerful cause of strength and digestion, which requires a stronger focus. This [unification of heat] happens at night. Furthermore, since they previously did not engage in laborious exercise, their bodies are so full of moisture that it can resist the dissolution and drying out that occurs through movement during the day, so that they may enjoy a small amount of food. Thus, it appears clear from the points mentioned above. 

When, however, they engage in their exercises and other occupations of life, it should be prescribed to them that it is better to eat a larger **lunch** than dinner. This is supported by 

<margin>Anthicus the physician. Telephus the grammarian.</margin> 

experience, and in the fifth book of the "Preservation of Health" by <note>original: "Anthico medico"</note> **Anthicus the physician** and **Telephus the grammarian**, who lived for very long times by making their lunches larger than their dinners. This is also evident from bodies that are not currently sick. For since such people have weak digestion, they are assisted by the sun's heat and light, which are very life-giving. These strengthen the <term>spirits</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids that carried life and sensation through the body.</note> because of their affinity; for light itself is either the spirit or has the likeness of light. They are also helped because <term>superfluities</term> <note>Waste products or excess fluids.</note> are then better expelled through the open pores during the day than at night. 

Furthermore, at night they ought not to be filled with much food, but only a little, since nature is then more intent on the digestion of **raw humors**, which sleep is especially meant to digest and reduce to a healthy state. For although the digestive power is fortified at night, it is not so fortified in these people that it can digest both food and superfluities at once. 

<margin>At night, the resolution of superfluities does not occur.</margin> 

Similarly, at night, superfluities are not resolved because the pores are closed, and because the movement into sleep and the night air oppose their evacuation. Likewise, the [digestive] power is strong at night—especially the natural digestive power—due to the retraction and unification of heat. However, a strong power does not seek food, especially when it is busy with the digestion of superfluities, working to reduce them to a healthy state or to expel them. 

On the other hand, those who eat a larger lunch can better engage in exercise, which is the most important thing for the preservation of health; for it invigorates the **innate heat** and makes all the powers strong by the expulsion of superfluities. This is shown by the fact that he who exercises must have the food already digested in the stomach, liver, and veins. This is gathered from the first and third parts of the sixth book <note>Likely referring to Galen's "De Sanitate Tuenda".</note>. It is necessary that all digestions be completed when exercise occurs. This happens when dinner is smaller than lunch, since food remains in the belly for more than twelve hours. In that case, in the morning, they will need to rise from sleep and move before the digestion of the liver is finished, which is helped by sleep and rest (just as the digestion of the stomach is helped by the movement of heat from the exterior to the interior). Thus, when morning comes, the digestion perfected by sleep will be disturbed when it is time for exercise. 

But when one eats a larger lunch, the digestive power will digest the offered nourishment during the day, so that the digestion of the belly is completed when night comes. And similarly, the digestion of the liver begins and ends by morning, so that when day arrives, there is a movement from the internal parts to the external ones. For the digestion of the limbs seems to imitate this movement outward. Thus, one will be able to exercise better before lunch, at the time when the **third digestion** <note>The final stage of nutrition where nutrients are assimilated into the tissues.</note> is completed, which could not happen if a larger meal had been taken at dinner, as the third digestion would not yet have been finished. Thus, the quantity of food to be given at lunch or dinner varies according to the condition of the subject in whom digestion takes place.

If, however, the present disposition of the active and passive [elements] is considered—which is a certain familiarity and habit born of our nature, according to **Hippocrates** and **Avicenna**—and since it is a matter of nature, it is expedient to provide more or less nourishment at lunch or dinner according to custom. For custom is the greatest thing in preserving health and curing illness. This is shown by the fact that a change in custom, especially a sudden one, is violently harmful. Whence <note>original: "Damascenus"</note> **John of Damascus** says: to change a custom is harmful and troublesome, especially for the elderly. And therefore, in the fourth book of "On Foods": **Bad habits should be abolished, but not all at once**, because nature does not sustain sudden changes in the regimen.

If indeed it must be observed by reason of the environment, it will be either temperate, hot, or cold; or mixed, or quickly changing. If it is temperate, one ought to follow what was said before: to make lunch larger than dinner for the reasons stated. If the environment is hot, because when night comes, the digestive power is not strong enough to digest both food and superfluities together, the **Egyptians** and **Syrians** inhabiting hot regions eat a larger lunch than dinner. 

If, however, it is cold: since in many people digestion is strengthened by daylight and superfluities (which abound in them) are resolved then, the nature of the body at night—intent on the surrounding cold—is busy digesting those superfluities. Whence it is not expedient to administer much nourishment at dinner. This is the rule observed by the <term>Ultramontanes</term> <note>People living "beyond the mountains" (the Alps), usually meaning the French or Germans.</note> inhabiting cold regions, and especially the **French**, who use reason more than others. 

Thus, the diversity of the quantity of nourishment taken appears from several considerations. And since most illnesses are material in nature, and since most bodies have declined [from perfect health], lunch should be made larger than dinner. 

Regarding the first objection, it must be said that **Hippocrates** was speaking about bodies that are currently sick; but this discourse is about the regimen of the healthy. Alternatively, the bodies he spoke of were already digested in the expurgation of matter. For it is conceded that for the sick who are not full of superfluities, it is better to eat dinner. Nor should it be added, as some say, that in the morning one should use a watery **honey-water** <note>original: "mellicrate"</note>; rather, one should listen to the reason for the honey-water.

### SECTION 122.

<margin>
Wine is a great remedy for melons.
</margin>
->**W**hether one should drink after fruit is shown.<-
In particular diets, peaches should be eaten on a fasting or empty stomach, and afterward old, fragrant wine should be drunk. For they are easily corruptible, which their smell denotes when they are cut with iron. Thirst indeed exists in these and others. Still, the rumor is not entirely lost by which many people speak, in the seventh book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics.</note>. For the celestial impulses follow them more. But it is a famous saying that some wine is potent and aromatic, and therefore good for melons <note>original: "peponibus"</note>. Again, that should be provided after fruit which corrects their "malice" <note>A medieval medical term for the harmful or indigestible properties of certain foods.</note> and drives away their harmful effects; since they are almost always of bad humor, filling the blood with wateriness. But wine, since it is hot, is a rectifier of putrefaction, moving all excretions (11th book of *On Hygiene* <note>Referring to Galen's work on the preservation of health.</note>). And it leads them outward because of the <term>cholera</term> <note>Bile, one of the four humors.</note> which it moves. And therefore it is given before the third hour to youths. And it is like a <term>great theriac</term> <note>A universal medicinal mixture used as an antidote or general cure-all.</note>, cooling hot bodies, heating cold ones, moistening dry ones, <margin>In particular diets.</margin> and drying moist ones in particular diets. Likewise, the fruits consumed are either hot or cold. If indeed they are cold, a drink like wine is suitable for them since it is hot, a corrective of their coldness by the opposite. If indeed they are hot, some of the cold drinks [are suitable], such as water; and similarly if they are dry or moist. Thus, after fruit and generally after food of bad humor, a drink is suitable, and especially wine. On the contrary, to drink wine after food of <term>bad chyme</term> <note>Poorly processed digestive fluids.</note> while eating, or before or after it is digested, is bad, because it makes the bad chyme penetrate into the extremities of the body. And he adds elsewhere also regarding fruit. According to the Arabs, one must not drink after food, and specifically wine, unless after the stomach has settled for a longer time (chapter 118), lest a distance be made between the intention and the foods so that it cannot touch them. Or else the undigested nourishment is carried into the parts. But fruits are some food after which one should drink even more, fearing their malice. And since they are more medicinal foods, nothing should be added to them that has the power of carrying or nourishing as much as possible. And therefore regarding nourishments, it teaches that it is allowed to be taken through time, but truly first before the simple assumption of food. Thus, after fruit, nothing is to be drunk. But for the first, it should be known: that fruits are the seeds of vegetables produced from their superfluities. These are diversified in many ways, separated by their quantity, discrete and continuous, and by the quality of the one consuming them, their substance, origin, effect, and time.

<margin>Distinction of Fruits</margin>
They differ in quality, namely in nature, taste, smell, and color. In nature, because some are hot and dry, others hot and moist, some cold and moist. Others are cold and dry, and some, as far as possible, are temperate. In taste, in every way, such as sweetness, bitterness, and the rest; and in smell similarly, in whatever way it is possible to denote. Likewise in color, which mostly pertains to greenness, which is more removed at the time of ripeness, and changes to whiteness or blackness. In substance, because some are soft and watery, others earthy and hard, some viscous, others brittle, some heavy and others light, and for whom. In origin, because some are of the vegetables, like those which participate in a greater wateriness of oil, but others in less of these. In effect, because some are portable for nourishment, like figs, grapes, and riper dates; others are far removed, especially like <term>cornels</term> <note>Small, tart red berries from the Cornelian cherry tree.</note> and medlars. Some are truly middling, like nuts, apples, and such. Some even loosen the belly and provoke urine, like plums, riper grapes, melons, and gourds. Others are constipating, like pears, sorb apples, medlars, and myrtles; some are truly middling. They are also diversified according to the seasons, because they ripen in almost all times, though mostly in summer and autumn. Truly, I hear wine is drunk after fruit while they are consumed, or immediately after they are eaten. What the drink should be was shown in chapter 118. Thirst <note>original: "Sitis"</note> <margin>Thirst is of two kinds.</margin> indeed happens for a double cause, according to the first book of *Medicines*: either from a lessening of moisture, as happens from the stomach and generally from the natural parts; or from a vehement dominance of heat, as from the spirits. Bodies consuming fruit also vary in their natures and in their disposition, just as the fruits are: some are hot, others cold, and so on. And some are <term>styptic</term> <note>Astringent; substances that contract body tissues.</note>, some laxative, and others middling, and diversified by many differences. Because of this, it must be known: that some simply asserted that one should in no way drink after fruit, nor generally after food, much less after fruit (as per the previously mentioned chapter). Others truly from subtle arguments...

# Concerning Fruit...

They have commanded that drinking should be done over them <note>The fruits mentioned previously.</note> as if the drink would correct their "malice" <note>In medieval medicine, "malice" refers to the harmful qualities or humors produced by certain foods.</note>. What should be thought of these matters will appear clearly from what is to be said. Regarding the third point, it must be known that thirst is either powerful, "crying out," and especially certain, or it is not so. If indeed it is the former, a drink should be offered before any meal; whence, in chapter 118, it is noted without a doubt that a drink should be shown to those who are excessively thirsty. Wherefore, in the seventh book on cures: "Who would not further endure thirst unless, as he said, choosing to die rather than live in sorrow?" And similarly concerning <term>marasmus</term> <note>A state of severe malnutrition and wasting, often associated here with extreme dehydration.</note>. Whence in the fourth book of Almansor <note>The *Liber Almansoris* by the Persian physician Rhazes.</note>, and in the first book of practice: if necessity urges, let him drink a little water over his food, but not for the sake of satisfying thirst to satiety.

<margin>Thirst</margin>
Because it supports this: that a living creature must be led away from vehement passion and anxiety. Such indeed is thirst, whether it happens from innate quality or from inflammation, since it dissolves the moisture of the natural heat's fuel and support. For if what is said regarding the thinner moisture or the thicker dregs... as it indicates at the end of the title: "May the gods give you bare hearths, a long old age, long winters, and perpetual thirst." <note>A quote from Ovid's *Ibis*, used here to illustrate the misery of thirst.</note> Even the poets have made riddles about such great things. And because of this, one should drink over fruit. If truly there is no such thirst, then it must be observed whether the drink is sought for the sake of medicine or for nourishment. If the first, one must consider whether the fruits taken are cold, easily corruptible, and similarly windy <note>Producing gas or "wind" in the stomach.</note>; for then an old, fragrant wine should be provided, which is hot and dry in degree. And this intention is held in the diets; hence in the third book and the first part: let them drink a little wine, not mixed with water, for one who has been accustomed to it. For such wine, taken in such measure, alters and digests the meal previously accepted without it being drawn into the veins beforehand. This is what wine does over fruit especially. But if the belly is especially hot, so that its heat might be remitted, a drink such as water should be offered, which should be in a small quantity and specifically when he is thirsty, fearing lest they be converted into <term>cholera</term> <note>Yellow bile, one of the four humors.</note> or putrefaction, to which two previously introduced things lend support.

But if the drink is intended for the sake of nourishment or transport, or with this, for nutrition—as other drinks, specifically wine with others, by its heat, subtlety, and wonderful nature, enters into the parts over food of bad <term>chyme</term> <note>The pulpy acidic fluid which passes from the stomach to the small intestine, consisting of gastric juices and partly digested food.</note>—and especially over fruits that are mixed and watery and quickly corruptible, a drink is not to be taken, especially when it is of a greater quantity. For it strives to penetrate the wicked moisture to the extremities of the body. As Avicenna <note>original: "A."</note> wished, with the things brought forward in this part at the beginning, the man commands that wine is not to be drunk after food, since it is among the things that impede more; for it digests too quickly as it passes through. From these things, an understanding person will be able to join together the diversities of fruits, bodies, and drinks in substance and quality and the aforementioned things. And in these, he may judge whether a drink over fruit is to be given, or not at all.

<margin>Water is not a healthy drink for fruit.</margin>
Know, however, that if it happens that one drinks over many fruits for the sake of nourishment, it is less blameworthy that he drinks water than wine, since they are softened by it more than by wine. And they are led to this because it is most friendly to nature and to those accustomed to wine. Wine, however, "saves" the fruits more and impels them to the innermost parts of the body. Whence experience teaches that it is less harmful to drink water over fruit and figs than to drink wine. This is shown by the external infusion of them in water and wine. For some have suffered more intense pains over fruit from the drinking of wine. Others have died from the same, drinking over figs; whence not only over these is drinking least commanded. Truly, it is useful over food since it is among the things that impede more; for it digests quickly and penetrates, forcing the food, still undigested, to pass through. Wherefore it creates opinions of inheritance, which of all sicknesses—especially chronic ones—are from putrefaction and finally cause fevers and <term>apostemes</term> <note>Internal swellings or abscesses.</note>. But concerning the aforesaid, there is doubt, because daily we see people drinking strong and much wine over watery fruits, and proverbially especially over melons.

<margin>Opinion</margin>
<margin>Doctrine</margin>
It must be said that they do not suffer here in the present from an altered vigor; they will be harmed finally in the future by the gradual aggregation of superfluities. Whence in the first book of *On Aliments*: it is not necessary to neglect making all things pure for the knowledge of eating. Recognizing that although the harm of them is not perceived through individual days because of their smallness, yet what is aggregated from them over time becomes manifest to others. Wherefore in the third book of the same: I counsel abstaining from all things regarding eaten foods, even if they are easily digestible for some. For a wicked <term>chyme</term> collected from these lies hidden in the veins for a long time, which on a slight occasion leads to putrefaction, producing a fever of an evil character. Or it must be said that usage is a thing outside of reason. Whence in the same place: although every drink is denied simply over food, he adds that to drink two or three "briela" <note>A specific small liquid measure.</note> over it does not harm him who is accustomed to it. For custom is a most powerful thing in the preservation of health. Because of which, regarding the first point, what should be said has now appeared.

<margin>Part of Almansor.</margin>
To the other point, it must be said: that the discourse commends those things in the way that it is verified as was seen, such as when it is drunk over fruit for the sake of medicine or vehement thirst. To the other point, it must be said with the induction of the same, that they take the drink with many concessions for the sake of correction and in small quantity, unless the wine is to be led to the external parts entirely for evacuating bile, so that it leads it out more through the urine than through the belly. For thus it ought to proceed into the veins and lead them to the internal parts; for bile is found in the stomach in very few cases. To the other point, it must also be said that they perform that drinking for the sake of medicine, not for the sake of nourishment, for which reasons one is reasonably granted and the other denied. To those things also which were said higher up, what should be said has appeared; for the first stands known by Avicenna, introduced when he denies drinking over fruit for the sake of nourishment. And so the rest proceed, especially according to the position of the Arabs.

# Whether it is Better to Sleep on the Right Side

Again, when one sleeps on the right side, the stomach—in which the things to be digested are contained—is placed over the warm and moist **liver** <note>original: "epati"</note>. In this way, digestion is like a **cauldron over a fire** <note>A common medieval analogy: the stomach acts as a pot and the liver provides the "heat" to "cook" or digest the food.</note>. When the digesting organ is placed beneath it, it cooks better that which is contained in the vessel above, since heat naturally seeks the upper parts continuously. Furthermore, it is better to sleep on that side from which the liver and the organs of nourishment can better and more appropriately attract the food and the **chyle** <term>chyle</term> <note>A milky fluid consisting of fat droplets and lymph, drained from the small intestine into the lymphatic system during digestion.</note>. This truly occurs when one sleeps on the right side, because of the proximity of the liver to the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: "mesaraycas"; these veins carry nutrients from the digestive tract to the liver.</note> and the other organs.

Furthermore, darkness contributes to better sleep because in the light, the spirits are moved to go outward due to the similarity they have to the light itself; whence light and the illumination of the eyes are set down as a cause of <unclear>fevers</unclear> <note>original: "fabare", likely a scribal error for "febrium" (fevers).</note> in the third book, first part. But since sleeping on the right side involves a turning toward the darkness, it completes the external rest. Conversely, there is a fatigue that arises from being propped up on the left side during wakefulness. Therefore, one should sleep on the right. 

On the contrary, in the thirteenth book, third chapter <note>Likely a reference to Galen's *On the Usefulness of the Parts* or a similar medical authority.</note>, it is said: Sleep on the left side is of the greatest help in strengthening digestion because of the way the liver **encompasses** the stomach. Furthermore, one should sleep in the most comfortable way, so that superfluities <note>Waste products or undigested matter.</note> may run down to the proper place, just as it is also commanded to sleep with the head elevated for this reason. Moreover, the "vile" side is the left side—see difference 47. Again, one should sleep on that side upon which we lie most delightfully; this is the left side—see Problem Six. For on that side, it is easier to be supported. It also resists cold in those who are full, and likewise resists **melancholy** <note>One of the four humors; here associated with coldness and heavy digestion.</note> when the warm side, like a blanket, is placed beneath it. For these reasons, it would be better to sleep on the left side.

When it is asked whether one should sleep on both sides, it seems to be drawn from the *Prognostics* <note>A work by Hippocrates.</note>, specifically from my translation thus: "It does not befit the physician to find the sick person lying on either the right or the left side." This indicates a state of ignorance or a lack of distinction. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known that the "side" here is defined as the surface of the body upon which a person leans when moving from an upright or sitting position, or the middle ground between them. There are four sides: right, left, front, and back. What the right and left are will be shown in difference 184. The front is that in which the senses are most present; the back is truly for motion. To lie on the front—that is, on the belly—is to be prostrate. To lie on the back is to be supine. What is imported by the act of sleeping is found in the chapter on vision, chapter 108. 

Regarding the second point, it must be known that some have praised sleeping on the right side more, and have taught that one should simply sleep that way. Others have favored the left, whose motives have been touched upon. But the deficiency of these views will appear subsequently; for it is not simply true to state this, but rather it requires a fuller determination.

<margin>Chapter 8</margin>
<margin>Alexander</margin>
<margin>Avicenna, Book 3, part 1</margin>

Regarding the third point, it must be known that for bodies that are sufficiently and blamelessly healthy, one must first begin sleeping on the **right side**. Then, one should sleep on the **left side** for a long time so that the digestion of the stomach may be perfected, and finally, one must return to the **right side** again. Whence **Avicenna** <note>original: "Ay."</note> says to **Alexander**: "Sleep first on your right side for one hour, then on your left, and there complete your sleep." This discourse is completed where it says: "O, that after eating, he should first sleep on his right side for a short time, then turn to the left, and afterwards turn himself back to the right." 

One must sleep on the right first so that the nourishment seeks the bottom of the stomach, in which—because of its fleshiness and proximity to the liver and the **omentum** <term>omentum</term> <note>original: "zirbū"; a fold of fatty tissue that hangs over the intestines, often called the "fatty apron."</note>—digestion is made more perfect. For when one lies on the right side, the bottom of the stomach of each person naturally inclines more toward the left and is situated downwards; then the liver acts as a **cushion** <note>original: "culcitra"</note> upon which the stomach spreads out. Thus the nourishment better seeks the lowest parts. And for this reason, I command those taking medicines to lie on the right, so that the vapors released from the medicines can better pass through the parts; afterwards, however, when they dissolve, they should turn to the left. 

When the food has descended (after a short time), then let him return to the left side, because the bottom of the stomach stretches laterally in a certain way toward the senses. It will also have the liver placed above it, warming it with its own heat... <unclear>continually</unclear>, with a certain compressive weight so that the food is fixed more vehemently therein. The liver also embraces and contains the stomach on every side, just as someone might take hold of something with their fingers spread wide and then slightly constricted over it. And therefore it was said in the thirteenth book, third chapter: Sleep on the left side is of the greatest help because of the liver's **embrace** of the stomach. From this application and union, the liver impels [the food] more toward the mesenteric veins and the intestines so that it can deliver the chyle from all of them through the shorter paths into the liver and attract it. 

After this, however, once digestion in the stomach is already perfected, let him return to the right side so that the bottom of the stomach, inclining to the right, may open as was said before, so that the superfluous weight of the stomach contained within it may descend. Whence in the thirteenth book, third chapter: "Sleep on the right side is the cause of the speed of the food's descent," because the preparation of the stomach and its equal positioning makes that necessary when the bottom directly seeks that which is downward. 

Some, however, have a habit of sleeping only on one side, either because of the depth of their sleep or the shortness of the night, being filled with vaporous foods, so that they are not roused nor move from that side before it is time for them to wake. These people should be led back gradually to what has been described. If, however, one does not turn in their sleep, it is better that after the food has descended to the bottom of the stomach—either by standing upright or by a modest walk—they lay themselves down on the left side. 

I spoke of "healthy people" with this distinction: because if anyone has a belly suffering from a **flux** <note>Diarrhea or excessive fluid discharge.</note>, it is appropriate for him to lie on the left because of the reasons touched upon. If, however, he is **constipated**, he should lie on the right for the opposite reason. Similarly, one who has a "hot liver" should take care not to sleep upon it. One who has a "cold stomach" should lie on the left side.

There are also two other mentioned ways of sleeping, such as on the **belly**, which indeed wonderfully strengthens digestion and prepares for the expulsion of superfluities through their proper paths; whence also in the first book: Lying on the belly brings great enough help in digesting, because it encompasses and retains the natural heat.

<margin>The effect of lying on the back is the worst and is most contrary to digestion.</margin>
Because [waste] increases. There is also a way of lying back, such as lying flat on the back <note>original: "supine"</note>, which is the worst of all, causing the parts of digestion to move apart and preventing superfluities <note>In medieval medicine, "superfluities" are waste products or metabolic byproducts that must be expelled to maintain health.</note> from being excreted, instead driving them into the brain, the spinal cord <note>original: "nucha"</note>, and the nerves. Indeed, the back has no place through which superfluities may be excreted, wherefore many diseases arise there; hence, lying on the back is bad, preparing the way for wicked ailments such as **apoplexy**, **phrenitis** <note>Inflammation of the brain or "brain fever."</note> (that is, lethargy), and **incubus** <note>original: "incubum"; refers here to sleep paralysis or the sensation of a weight on the chest, then attributed to rising vapors.</note>, because it causes superfluities to sink toward the back and be retained there. For they can find no path to the palate or the nostrils. It also aids good digestion to lie in a curled position rather than extended. For then the organs of digestion are brought closer together and the remaining space is left empty of winds <note>original: "ventositantibus"; intestinal gas or "vapors."</note> so that they may rest undisturbed (see *Problems*, section six). Furthermore, it is asked whether lying on the right or left side is for the sake of preserving health, as mentioned before, or sometimes for the sake of prognosis. For when someone lies on their back—unless it is out of habit or fatigue—it denotes that the animal virtue <note>The "animal virtue" or *virtus animalis* was the power of the soul centered in the brain, responsible for sensation and movement.</note> is so collapsed, along with its instruments, that it is unable to support itself upon the muscles of the sides; because of this, it falls back onto the spine like a corpse. The Commentator notes in the same place that this is a bad sign. Similarly, lying on the stomach out of habit is condemned. Whence in the first book of *Prognostics*: "To lie upon the stomach, for one to whom it is unaccustomed when healthy to sleep so, is bad, for it denotes frenzy <note>original: "desipientiam"</note>." Or it denotes those who have pain around the belly, such as those with **iliac** or **colic** pain. Thus, let the truth be touched upon with these brief supports. 

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it must be said that lying on the right side happens by chance during sleep, perhaps due to the laborious movement one had while awake, especially in those who work. Or it should be said that although sleep occurs more easily on that side, one should not sleep upon it [exclusively] since, as has been shown, digestion would not be celebrated and the excretion of superfluities would be hindered. To the other point, it must be said that when the **liver** <note>original: "epar"</note> is placed over the stomach, it heats it more than when it is placed beneath it, just as a piece of steel placed above a flame is damaged more than when placed beneath it. For it helps by the weight pressing down and by compression. Nor is it the same for simple heat in a subtle body which seeks the heights, as it is in a compact body where the compression of one body acts upon another. 

To the next, it must be said that the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: "mesarayce"; the veins that transport nutrients from the intestines to the liver.</note> are not closer to the liver when one lies upon it, since they are more dispersed when the liver is expanded. Even if they were, the mesenterics do not attract anything unless it is digested, and it is digested more laudably—as was declared—by lying on the left side. To the other, it must be said that the reason given by **Avicenna** <note>original: "Ay."</note> is probable and perhaps follows the opinion of others. For he speaks thus many times in that book. For he imagines the right eye sees more clearly. Therefore, when you lean on the right side, the right eye is hidden so that it does not see. But when on the left, the contrary happens. Or it must be said that this is true in a bright place. In a dark place, however, as one sleeps more, it does not seem to matter. To the other, it must be said that he concludes sleep happens on the right with delight for some, but it does not achieve more perfect digestion for most, nor the excretion of superfluities. As for the arguments of the other side...

---

...it has long since appeared. For we sleep more delectably on the left side, just as we lie down, unless preceding labor leads us to the contrary. To the last point, it has also appeared what should be said, since here we seek the benefit of the lying position and not its prognostic significance.

### CHAPTER 24

->That **coitus** is not suitable in a regimen of health is shown.<-

Since that which shortens life cools and dries the body and dissipates the natural heat—because no small part of it is led out of the body—it is not expedient in a regimen of health; such a thing is done by **coitus** <note>sexual intercourse</note>. For many things that do not mate are of longer life, like the mule compared to the donkey and horse from which it is born. And females live longer than males if they are prone to mating, which is why male sparrows are of shorter life than females, for reasons of longevity and brevity. The reduction of the body and the collapse of strength that occurs therefrom also denotes the dissolution of natural heat. Furthermore, whatever can evacuate superfluity without injury should be preferred over coitus, which is led out with harm. Such is exercise, especially with the small and large ball (as in the fourth book of the *Regimen of Health*). This is also clear from the benefits shown in the little book on *Exercise with the Small Ball*, which I translated into Latin. Whence **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "baly"; 10th-century Persian physician.</note> says: he who escapes the sickness of the constriction of sperm is he from whose body this superfluity is resolved either through exercise or another purgation. Again, this superfluity which coitus leads out could be consumed through abstinence without injury, since it is a perfect medicine according to **Galen** in the fourth book of the *Viaticum*. Furthermore, if coitus is not suitable for an adolescent, it would be suitable for no one according to the rules of logic, because labor, food, drink, and sleep are common to every age. But sexual matters belong to adolescents alone (from the *Regimen of Health*). Yet it is not suitable for these, since they are still in their "increase" <note>Growth phase.</note>, which would be greatly hindered. Again, that which is not born for everything ought not to be evacuated, since nature is nourished by it. Such is the **sperm** led out by coitus (from the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*). Therefore, coitus does not benefit a regimen of health.

On the opposite side are the physicians and the philosophers. Still, in a regimen of health, it is expedient that all members perform their own act. But coitus is the act of the reproductive organs. Furthermore, if coitus is suitable for <unclear>priests</unclear> <note>original: "afgrtecis", possibly a corruption of a term for those suffering from excess seed or a specific class.</note>, it will also be suitable for many others who are even better disposed to it. To them, indeed, it is beneficial; rather, it aids their passions (see *Problems*, one and four). Therefore, coitus is suitable in a regimen of health.

<margin>Coitus</margin> Regarding the first point, it must be known that coitus is the application of the male and female in the reproductive organs, by which superfluity is expelled for the end of the species or the ordained individual. For a twofold end of it exists: one is more principal, for the generation of the species. Whence in the fifth book of *Theories*: Nature established coitus in the animal for the sake of generating, so that the species of animals might remain. And therefore **Isaac Israeli** <note>original: "Ysaac"; 10th-century Jewish physician.</note> in the sixth book of the *Viaticum* says: God exhibited an admirable and inseparable delight in the coitus of animals, lest perhaps generation be destroyed by an abomination of coitus. For through the generative power which uses the sperm as an instrument, they participate as much as they can in the divine and immortal species (from the second book of *On the Soul* and *On the Generation of Animals*).

### Whether Sexual Intercourse is desirable in the Regimen of Health.

<margin>Note</margin>
Wherefore the Commentator <note>Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher widely cited in medieval universities.</note> says: Divine providence, since it could not make an individual animal remain forever, took pity on it by giving it a power by which it could remain through its species. One type [of appetite] is indeed healthy, which is twofold here: one as necessary and approved, ordained for the **regimen of health**, of which the present writing treats. The other is truly useless and rather illicit, as it is done for the sake of pleasure and wicked habit; many people place this end, which is foreign to the act itself, before other necessary ends. Whence in the fifth [book] of *Theory*: The majority of men, in desiring sexual intercourse, put the cause of pleasure first; truly, for a few, the end and purpose is the production of children. It is rightly said "the majority of part," because those practicing philosophy especially despise pleasure in their dignity, because [pleasures] are not among the necessary dispositions of being, let alone among its perfections, as the Commentator says in his *Accession to Physics*. Whence also in the fourth and sixth [books].
<margin>A foul thing, so it is said</margin>
Diogenes <note>Diogenes the Cynic, famous for his radical rejection of social norms.</note>, the most patient friend of all good men, being made for every work of continence, used to resort to manual relief in matters of Venus <note>sexual matters</note> when in need. Wherefore, wishing to lay aside the distress which he felt from the [build-up of] seed, and not for the sake of any good of pleasure—while his "female friend," as they say, was slow to come to him—he expressed his seed by hand, touching his private parts. When she finally arrived, he dismissed her, saying that he had anticipated the god of marriage <note>original: "ymeneū" (Hymen)</note> with his hand and had won the contest. Or, as some others do, they abstain for the sake of leaving behind an inheritance of a certain amount. However, for a healthy person, there is a due observance of the six <term>non-natural things</term> <note>The "six non-naturals" in medieval medicine were air, food/drink, sleep/waking, exercise/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the soul.</term> along with a certain discourse and sometimes the administration of a lighter use of medicines to the body.

Regarding this, it must be known that some, such as Epicurus, as introduced in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Ars Medica" or "Microtechne," a foundational medical textbook.</note>, denied that sexual intercourse was suitable in the regimen of health for a tempered body, saying that no use of Venus could be healthy. Whence in the sixth [book] of the *Colliget* <note>Averroes' medical encyclopedia.</note>: Many of the wise prohibit the use of coitus in the preservation of health.
<margin>Epicurus. 3rd of the *Tegni*: he is not called a physician.</margin>
Epicurus, however, was in my estimation the proper name of a physician who adhered to the opinion of Democritus and Leucippus, just as Asclepiades [followed] Empedocles. Whence in the first [book] on *Disease*: "The soul is not one thing and the body another," just like the Epicurean atoms. In the first book of the *Ethics*, in which the positions of such men are recited, some suppose that bodies are composed of indivisible units <note>original: "athomis"</note>, as did those around Epicurus. Who, however, being unmindful of this, said he was a great and famous man. To whom, indeed, the motive of Epicurus could be this: because since he supposed the body, according to himself, was made of atoms, he argued that [intercourse] was not suitable in the regimen of health because it draws atoms out of the body, and thus dissolves its composition. This is what coitus does. Because of this, he wished to conclude that none would be healthy.

This position Galen, as will appear, weakens. His motive is also taken from Avicenna <note>original: "Ay."</note> in several places and in the first of the *Ethics*. For the body is composed of elements in their quantitative nature—four in the first [place]. This he prohibited along with Democritus the physician and with their alterable qualities. This Asclepiades denied along with Empedocles. Furthermore, even if this is granted, you will find it stands nonetheless, since some atoms are necessary in the composition of the body, while others are for the sake of its being perfect. Not a few, however, are <term>superfluous</term> <note>waste or excess matter</note>, as also happens to those who posit that the body is composed in the other aforementioned way, although they

are in themselves impassible <note>incapable of suffering or changing</note>. Yet they suffer by reason of their composition (from the first [book] on *Disease*). And the defect of this [view] will appear more fully in the third [section] of our discussion. Some half-learned men <note>original: "sciolí"</note>, however, following the sect of Epicurus, wanted to be called Epicureans, so they say that according to that school, no use of coitus would be healthy but entirely for pleasure. For they wanted these philosophers to be called "Epicureans" only because they cared for the pleasures of the skin and the body. But far be it that such men ever were or should be called philosophers, since philosophy is the love of wisdom, abstinence, and the victory over concupiscence <note>The *Secret of Secrets* (Secretum Secretorum), a popular pseudo-Aristotelian text.</note>. While they were, as far as was possible for them, practicing philosophy correctly, having despised pleasures, as I have said. 

For the sake of which, it must be known that there were three **heresies** <note>In this context, "sects" or "schools of thought" rather than religious heresy.</note> of philosophers. The first was this one [the Epicureans]: which, not being able to reach the form and the end, nor to distinguish between the senses and the intellect, posited that the senses are from nature and did not posit anything unless it were bodies.
<margin>6th [book] of the *Metaphysics*</margin>
And therefore they established natural science as the first philosophy in the sixth of the *Metaphysics*. Because of this, they were deservedly called "Epicureans," as if "caring for what is above," because they only perceived what was superficial in a thing—as if in an equal body—such as only the accidents and sensible things. Whence they posited that there were no substantial forms (first [book] of the *Metaphysics*), for they were not able to reach the substance and the "marrow" of the thing. They were assimilated almost to the perceptions of brute animals. Wherefore Averroes says in *On the Sense and the Sensible*: Man comprehends the differences of things and their own intentions which are in the sensed thing, like the marrow from the fruit; brute animals, however, comprehend the extrinsics, like the rinds of fruits.

There was another sect, that of the **Stoics**, which discovered through study and meditation that there are substantial forms beyond bodies; their study began with the Pythagoreans and was finally consumed <note>reached its peak</note> in the Platonics. The third was that of the **Peripatetics**, which existed in a circuit through the schools; for they hurried about so that by disputation—which is the best instrument for inquiring after truth—they might arrive at the knowledge of hidden things. Their leader and prince was Aristotle the Stagirite.

For the sake of the beginning, it must first be known what the benefits and harms of coitus are. And finally, for what natures it is desirable and for what it is not. Then the truth of the question shall be opened. Regarding this, it must first be known that its benefit to the body and soul, if duly administered, is manifold. For it renders a man more cheerful, bolder, less prone to anger, less brooding, more ingenious, more grave in his habits, lighter in body, and sleeping better. It excites **natural heat** <note>The vital energy or "innate heat" that powers digestion and life.</note> and strengthens the virtues <note>In medieval medicine, "virtues" are the functional powers of the body, like the digestive or retentive virtue.</note>. It is also helpful for **melancholy**, pains of the kidneys, and flatulent illnesses, provided that the heat is sufficiently strong. It even preserves one from abscesses <note>original: "apātībus," likely *apostematibus*</note> of the groin and the genital parts, and recalls the "fumes" seeking the head <note>Vapors rising from the stomach to the brain, believed to cause headaches.</note>. It removes dimness of vision, dizziness, and heaviness of the head, and specifically when the seed has been constricted by the omission of intercourse.

There are also many harms of it, both to the soul and the body, when it is performed improperly. For it shortens life, causes old age to accelerate, and weakens the intellect, the senses, and all the powers of life, and it corrupts the heat and the spirit...

<meta>This page continues the medical discussion on sexual intercourse (coitus) from page 33. It focuses on the physical dangers of excess, the "indications" based on a person’s biological temperament (complexion), the appropriate age for such activity, and the seasonal and daily timing recommended for health according to authorities like Galen, Avicenna, and Rhazes.</meta>

<margin>folio 34.</margin>
[Excessive intercourse] weakens the very motors of the body, dissolving the nerves and the joints, especially the hips, and generally weakens the limbs used for walking, the spinal marrow <note>nucham: refers to the spinal cord or the marrow within the vertebrae, then believed to be connected to the brain and reproductive fluids</note>, and the belly. It acquires a wicked disposition for the entire body. At its peak, it dissipates the whole soul and corrupts the body. This is especially induced when one engages in it with great pleasure, since a greater quantity of heat and fluid is emitted from it. And therefore, in the twenty-third [chapter], it is noted that while intercourse with the immature <note>original: "Coitus infantilis." The text notes this practice was prohibited by law but preferred by "the multitude of nations," yet warns it is more physically exhausting than intercourse with women.</note> is prohibited by law among many peoples, it is sometimes preferred; nevertheless, it exhausts the body more through its impact than the other kind.

For this reason, one must know that if anyone wishes to order the use of intercourse rightly for the sake of health, they must take their indications from "natural things," from things "connected to nature," and from "things against nature" <note>This refers to the "Galenic" system of the six non-naturals: categories like diet, sleep, and exercise that affect health.</note>. From natural things, such as from the **complexion** <note>complexione: the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—in an individual.</note>: because hot and moist bodies are especially helped by proper intercourse and are least harmed by it. Next are the temperate; then the choleric; then the phlegmatic. Those of a melancholic nature <note>The melancholic temperament was considered cold and dry; since sex was thought to deplete heat and moisture, it was seen as dangerous for them.</note> are least relieved by it; indeed, it harms them much and often. And in these complexions, the same observation is found proportionately in simple temperaments where heat or moisture prevails. Whence, in the sixth book of *On Preserving Health* <note>original: "sexto re. sa." refers to Galen's *De Sanitate Tuenda*.</note>, it is said: Venereal acts are harmless only to those who are moist and hot, and to all those who naturally have much seed. Intercourse is most contrary to those with dry complexions. And it is even more so when dryness is mixed with coldness, and especially when it is accompanied by thinness of the testicles. For this complexion is a path toward death. 

Regarding the third type of complexions: for this reason, in the fourth book of *The Almansor* <note>The *Liber ad Almansorem* by the Persian physician Rhazes (al-Razi).</note>, it says that bodies having a dry nature ought to beware of intercourse as an enemy that weakens them. And because of this, it is clear for whom this intercourse is expedient and abundant, and for whom it is not. Similarly, in the limbs and in the power of the body: it is suitable for those who are robust; but for the weak it is least suitable, as they are greatly weakened by it.

# In the Ages of Life

Regarding ages, it especially suits the end of adolescence <note>The medieval "adolescence" often extended to age 30 or 35.</note> when the growth of the body begins to cease, and then in youth. In early adolescence, however, even a small excess is most harmful, since growth is still sufficiently intense, and the parts are still diminished and weak. Then, in old age it is less suitable, and in extreme old age <note>senio: refers to the final, frail stage of life.</note> least of all. Whence, in the third book of *On Preserving Health*, with the instruction for the administration of the "six things," it says: Begin with labors [exercise], then follow with food and drink, then sleep; afterward, venereal acts for those who ought to use them. For all other things are common to every age, but venereal acts are for the youthful alone, and only when the opportunity is right for them. For in the earlier and later ages, they either do not produce seed at all, or the seed is not generative or is of a poor quality. And hence it is that all the theoretical benefits of intercourse are ascribed to adolescence and youth. Older men should diminish their intercourse as much as they can; the very elderly should avoid it entirely.

It is also suitable for those of a fleshy habit, then for those of an equal habit, and afterward for those who are fat. Perhaps it is suitable for those with thinned matter, but least of all in cases of inequality or wasting <note>synthesis: likely referring to a state of bodily consumption or "syntexis."</note>. Also, it especially suits those with a red or yellow complexion <note>indicating a sanguine or choleric temperament</note>; but for the white or the black, it is not so suitable, as they have different proportions.

---

It also suits those accustomed to it more than those who are not. Nor should one suddenly cut off such a habit, for sometimes a kind of "poison" is generated in the body, inducing sudden death and many illnesses, and a wicked disposition is acquired for the body and its principal parts. This often happens to those who are religious or widowed who suddenly vow to abstain. This appears in the sixth book of *Internal Afflictions*. Indeed, its disordered use harms the male sex especially; it harms the female little, as she labors less in it.

The indication for it is also taken from "non-natural" things, and especially from the **time** [season], for which other things are suitable. This is twofold: either as one of the four parts of the year, and thus it is principally suitable in Spring, then in Winter, then in Summer (less so), and least of all in Autumn. Whence, in the first book of *Practice*: Let intercourse be diminished in Autumn and in times when grave and pestilential diseases loom. According to the saying: "If you wish to be safe in Autumn, beware the vulva" <note>original: "sang in autumno fore siuis perito cunno." A medical mnemonic warning that sex depletes the "blood" or vital spirit needed to survive the disease-prone autumn.</note>. And similarly, one should hear concerning other things ascribed to the air. Whence Democritus says: Intercourse is more certain in the times of Spring and Autumn. But Autumn is rendered suspect, though his colleague Oribasius says: "We, however, say that Autumn is a convenient time for exercising venery."

# Which is to be Detested

This is not a little to be detested, but perhaps it is a way to evacuate superfluous melancholy. Or, [time] is considered as the **hour**, or particularly how it happens to the body in relation to other things. This is also twofold: since it has been said that intercourse is ordained both for the species and for the preservation of the individual. If it is for the first [reproduction], then it should be done after the digestion of food in the stomach and its descent, and before sleep, so that after it is completed, one may sleep and rest. For this is the best time for conception, because after sleep the seed of the woman and the man is strengthened in the womb. Also, the generative spirit is vigorous at this hour with the matter of the seed. It should not be done during digestion when food is "crude" [undigested], nor upon a finished digestion when the body is empty.

And although the first book of *Practice* intends intercourse for both ends [reproduction and health], I listen most to that which is ordained for generation. And therefore Avicenna, in the twenty-third [chapter], speaking of intercourse especially as it is ordained for the health of the individual, says: Good intercourse is that which happens at an hour when the evacuation of superfluities follows it. This will be after a perfect digestion has been celebrated in the belly, and more than half-finished in the liver, so that it happens when the nourishment of the "third digestion" is already in expression <note>The medieval medical theory of "three digestions": 1. in the stomach, 2. in the liver, 3. in the tissues/members.</note>. Let the time also be when the body is, as much as possible, in a "middle" of all circumstances: neither too full nor too empty, neither too heated nor too cooled, neither too moistened nor too dried. And generally, a moderation of everything occurring to the body should be observed. 

As for the time divided by the number of days or weeks, it is not easily defined. However, some common limit can be adapted to the indications and inspected. Because one comes to the act of intercourse especially for the sake of pleasure, as was said, Galen often considers that when the bridle of sobriety is absorbed, one happens to sin, since the "concupiscible power" <note>concupiscibilis: the faculty of the soul responsible for desiring pleasures.</note> obeys reason the least. In the seventh book of the *Ethics*, he says: That if one sins in the use of intercourse, and the sin is small, it is deservedly so, because there is little [harm] in it.

# Whether Intercourse Should Occur Annually or at Other Times.

<margin>
Excessive intercourse
greatly and
most severely
weakens [the body]
as noted.
</margin>

...becomes a serious matter. For it evacuates the very **treasure of nature** when it is not performed properly. Indeed, when it exceeds measure, it is not just the quantity—like a flood of blood—that is evacuated, but rather a more violent dissolution of the vital power occurs. This is discussed in the fifth book of *The Theory of Animals* <note>original: "aialiū A." refers to Aristotle’s *De Generatione Animalium* (On the Generation of Animals)</note>. When a large amount of sperm leaves a man, it discolors and weakens his body more than if blood were to leave his body forty times over. This is because the substance is prepared <note>habilitata: refined or "ennobled" by the body's internal heat</note> to pass into the limbs. It is, in fact, the emission of pure and natural heat, as stated in the fifth book of *On the Generation of Animals*.

Furthermore, according to **Galen**, when this occurs as a matter of choice, it is most beneficial for one who is hot, moist, and full—the opposite of one who is lacking in these qualities. Therefore, regarding the dispositions related to heat and moisture, since semen is proportional to them, let the same be heard concerning the other "non-natural things" <note>The "six non-naturals" were the pillars of medieval health: air, food/drink, sleep, exercise, evacuation (including sex), and emotions.</note>. Nothing should be retained against nature when it reaches the body, for it prostrates the soul and the power of the body more than anything else. It is well-known that this provides relief for certain illnesses, especially those involving "tightness" <note>coartatōis: likely referring to a sense of constriction or pressure in the body or mind</note>, and specifically for those of a **phlegmatic** <note>term: flegticis (phlegmatic). One of the four temperaments, characterized by being cold and moist.</note> nature. Difference 186.

All these things together show that this practice is generally appropriate for those with hot and moist dispositions. In those who are cold and dry, it should be done least of all; in those of a medium temperament, it should be done moderately. Since intercourse evacuates heat and moisture from the body, those who have an abundance of these are helped by it. For others, it is the opposite, though it happens more or less depending on the person. Such are the dispositions shown before, which is why it is preferred for some and not at all for others. In others, it should be kept moderate.

Regarding the second point: intercourse is fitting as a part of the **Regimen of Health** <note>term: re. sa. (regimen sanitatis). A personalized plan of living to maintain health and prevent disease.</note> in the proper time, measure, and according to the declared dispositions. This is demonstrated because in the *Regimen of Health*, the administration of the six necessary things is profitable, as the body is necessarily changed by them. Indeed, intercourse is one of these, for according to **Haly Abbas** and **Johannitius**, it is contained under the category of "inanition and repletion" <note>Emptying and filling the body</note>. However, **Galen** and **Haly**, in the *Art of Medicine*, reduce it to the "accidents of the soul." For its primary act belongs to the soul, while the physical "filling" or "emptying" is an accidental result.

It also causes a great change in the soul by drawing heat from the interior to the exterior, which results in delight or something similar. Furthermore, in the *Regimen of Health*, there is a need to lead out **superfluities** <note>term: supfluitates. Waste products or "leftover" humors that the body did not use; if they remain, they were thought to rot and cause disease.</note>, since they have many ways to corrupt the body if retained. This is especially true of the sperm, which, because of its temperament and refined quality, corrupts very quickly so that a poisonous vapor is emitted from it. That which is emitted in intercourse is a superfluity. This is confirmed because it comes from all the members, and principally from the "principal members" <note>Heart, brain, and liver</note>. Again, because it provides the aforementioned benefits and removes many harms, it is profitable in the *Regimen of Health*. This is shown to be true when the act of intercourse is experienced; thus, intercourse is fitting for health.

Regarding the fourth point, and first: it must be said that intercourse induces the aforementioned symptoms when it is "superfluous" <note>excessive</note> and not performed at its proper time. However, when it is measured and performed as it ought to be, it induces the opposite. Or, though the act itself might seem to cause a loss of spirit, yet after it is done, those effects do not remain long and instead bring about the opposite results. This is what **Avicenna** suggests regarding stallions that engage in excessive intercourse.

At the same time, such an animal lives longer than another horse, provided it is not used for excessive intercourse, but used moderately. Furthermore, perhaps all abstinence is harmful to the horse and the donkey. In the mule, however, it is different because the material is dispersed throughout the entire body. In the former animals, the material for generation corrupts in the vessels unless it is led out.

If it is argued against this that natural heat is led out by intercourse—and that this heat, however strong it may be, does not diminish in power, but rather from it comes the strength of the spirit and "audacity" <note>boldness or courage</note> in the soul, as stated in the first book [of Aristotle]—it must be said that the fluid emitted is not purely natural to the individual, but exists for the sake of a future individual. Or, though it be natural and seems to harm the body in the present, it profits it much in the future. In this same way, spitting is said to be harmful because, according to Aristotle, **innate heat** <note>The "vital spark" or internal biological fire believed to sustain life</note> falls away in the saliva.

To the other point, it must be said that although exercise has the power to evacuate other superfluities or prepares them for evacuation, it does not do so for this one. This is not a simple superfluity; it is not defined by its quality but only by its quantity. And because it is ordained by nature to be sent to the testicles for the sake of generation, the body cannot quickly turn it away without injury. This is not the case with many other superfluities. Exercise evacuates superfluities by tending them toward the skin so they can be expelled, but it does not move the material of the sperm in that way. It is difficult to evacuate that material, just as material contained deep in the intestines is poorly led out by vomiting rather than by a bowel movement.

To the other point, it must be said that abstinence harms those predisposed to intercourse more, and it does not evacuate except by accident. Nor is it the kind of evacuation that is required. And though abstinence and exercise are excellent for the excretion of superfluities, they are not sufficient in all cases. Therefore, it was said at first that exercise brings many benefits when the rest of the regimen is appropriate and correct.

To the other point: intercourse is appropriate in **adolescence** <note>note: In the medieval life cycle, "adolescentia" lasted until age 30 or 35.</note> and specifically near the end of it, when bodies begin to stop growing. Thus, "youth" can also be understood by the term "adolescence." Or it should be said that in the Greek text it is written as *akmasontōn* <note>original: "akinaſontū" - a Latinization of the Greek word for those at their peak or in a state of stasis</note>, which properly means a "state of standing still." For *akmi* is interpreted as a "state." Hence, in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*</note>, where it speaks about the age of growth, the Arabic translation has "in the hour of the state of adolescence." Sometimes, however, it is translated as "adolescence" and sometimes as "youth."

To the other point: sperm is not naturally intended to remain in the body of the one who generates, but exists in respect to the one to be generated. For although sperm does not physically "fall away" from the entire body in reality, it nevertheless possesses the power of the whole. Difference 34.
