...disturb with diseases, either every single year, or perhaps once every two years. Certain people, however, fall ill twice within a single year. When someone falls ill in this manner, it is necessary to anticipate it with an **evacuation**, since such diseases are "material" in nature <note>A "material" disease was thought to be caused by an actual physical excess or corruption of the humors (fluids like blood or bile), rather than just a change in temperature.</note>.
Furthermore, when this pre-selection and corruption is present, it requires evacuation through **bloodletting** <term>phlebotomy: the surgical opening of a vein to release blood</term> and **purgative drugs**. But this should be done in the spring and autumn; for spring is associated with fullness <note>Spring was seen as the season of "blood," leading to an excess or "plethora."</note>, while autumn is prone to diseases of corruption.

Again, bodies are similarly disposed by the seasons. But since the time in the year varies in a fourfold way, it impresses at least a fourfold disposition upon bodies; from which the four **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> will increase or intensify, which then must be led out. Just as a particular cleansing relates to a particular time, so does a general use seem to relate to the time of use, since a harmony is seen in both. In a particular time, cleansing is granted more often, as in vomiting once or twice a month, as prescribed in the fourth book of **Al-Mansuri** <note>original: "Almaſoris" refers to the *Liber ad Almansorem* by the Persian physician Rhazes.</note> and the first part of the fourth book. Therefore, in the general time of use, one must evacuate at least once, so that it might even be done four times in a year. Because of this, one should evacuate every year.

<margin>
Opposite view.
</margin>
The opposite of this is written in the sixth book of the *Collectio*. For it says that evacuation should be done in "weeks of years" <note>This refers to a seven-year cycle, a concept common in medieval medicine and astrology.</note> and at their midpoints. Furthermore, the sixth [book] of the *Assumptions* does not say one must simply evacuate in the spring, but does so conditionally: that for whomever bloodletting or drugs are beneficial, it is truly appropriate to perform bloodletting or administer drugs for them in the spring. Furthermore, evacuation is done for **preservation**, so that one does not fall into a future illness, as appears in the sixth of the *Assumptions*. But many are not prepared to fall ill since they are sufficiently healthy. Otherwise, they would fall ill every year, which happens very little. Again, such an evacuation would happen in one of the four seasons of the year. But it will be suitable in none of them; for it is not truly necessary when there is no cause of evil. For a body may be most healthy and least prone to death. Nor should it be done in summer, because during and before the **Dog Days** <note>The "Dog Days" (mid-July to August) were considered dangerous for purging because the extreme heat was thought to weaken the body's internal forces.</note> purgations are troublesome; for in summer, because of the vehement heat which dissolves and works against the movement of the drug, purging is prohibited, as appears in the fourth of the *Assumptions*. So too in winter, because of the vehement cold, the humors settle in the center of the body and cling to the internal organs. Nor is it suitable in autumn, because the [vital] power is then weak. For autumn is contrary to human nature, according to the first book of the *Aphorisms*, since it is cold and dry; and because bodies are resolved <note>Weakened or "thinned out."</note> by the preceding summer, they suffer from a state of lack. Therefore, one should not evacuate every year.

<margin>
Augustine? on variation.
</margin>
Regarding the first point, however, it should be known that what is shown regarding the years is called a "difference" <note>original: "drā." abbreviation for *differentia*.</note>. Cleansing is twofold: **Universal** and **Particular**. Universal is that which is properly called bloodletting, and it is especially celebrated in the spring, for it evacuates all the humors. For it equally evacuates all the humors mixed in the veins, as noted in the books on drugs and the second of the *Assumptions*. Therefore, in the first part of the fourth book: Bloodletting is a general evacuation which evacuates a multitude [of humors]. It also draws from the whole body more than other evacuations. Spring, above all other seasons, indicates and tolerates a general evacuation, as the ancients testify. **Particular** evacuation, indeed, which is properly called **purging**, is the leading out of certain specific, distressing humors. This is called "particular" by reason of what it leads out—

---

for it does not lead out humors equally, but only one at a time, and by reason of the part [of the body], compared to bloodletting. However, it can be called "universal" if it is done at a universal time, like spring, in relation to others, as will appear in the "Greater Differences," sections 161 and 163. There is, moreover, a twofold hour for any evacuation: the **elected** <note>Chosen by a doctor or astrologer for the best results.</note> and the **necessary**. (Difference 163). One is done for the sake of preservation, like the one this argument concerns; the other for the sake of a cure, which in particular cases seeks the disease regardless of the time, unlike the former.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some want to be evacuated every year, not only by bloodletting but also by drugs. And they are moved to this by the disordered course and the "boiling" of the humors toward putrefaction in the summer. 

Others, however, despise this, caring only for what is urgent. Since the time in the year varies in a fourfold way, a fourfold [treatment] is necessary, which happens more in colder regions, just as the rest happens more in hot ones. Some, indeed, hold a middle path. Thus, it happens that physicians attend to their evacuations at a minimum; whence I recall that men were commonly purged around the **beginning of May**, though now they omit it. Some, however, like **Avicenna**, considering the "periods" <note>The cycles or critical days of a disease.</note> in which the movement of nature occurs, wanted to draw out [humors] every year, but more so during those periods. How much of error or truth this contains will appear in the third of the propositions.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that the truth of this inquiry refers either to the judgment of the **physician** or the **astrologer**. Since these two craftsmen especially have the duty to consult and provide for human nature. Wherefore it must first be seen in which of the seasons evacuation is most suitable and in which it is least. And finally, for whom it is expedient and for whom it is not. Regarding the first,

</margin>
it should be known that **spring**, as touched upon before, is the suitable time for evacuation for three reasons. First, because it touches the other seasons, and in such a time evacuation is sought, as was said. There is also in it a sort of strength because of the "temperate" quality which evacuation requires. Also, because of its order among the seasons; for winter preceded it, generating many humors, and those which are preserved from autumn follow it, as does the summer. Unless an evacuation precedes it, the humors will move toward regional and putrid diseases; consequently, it is expedient in autumn, because it resembles a disease of corruption. Corruption, however, needs to be cut away. And because it is a season that is somewhat temperate (Difference 66). Yet the [vital] power then is weak, and therefore one must evacuate cautiously, and specifically blood, since it is then very diminished; and finally, even less so in summer. If necessity compels it, let it be performed more with **lenient medicines** <note>Mild laxatives or "slippery" substances rather than harsh purges.</note> and lubricants. In **winter**, however, [evacuate] least of all, since the humors are at rest; and therefore they are not to be agitated, especially by drugs. In some seasons, drugs are granted more safely than bloodletting, such as in summer and autumn. In others, bloodletting is better, as in winter. In some, they are almost equal, such as in spring. Regarding the second, it should be known that some bodies are temperate and always healthy; some are now ill; others have "slipped" <note>Refers to *lapsus*, a state between health and sickness.</note>. Indeed, some of these people follow a proper **regimen** <term>regimen: a prescribed way of life, including diet and exercise, to maintain health</term>, even if only a few. Some follow a praiseworthy regimen tending toward lightness and refinement, while others do the opposite. <meta>This page continues the technical discussion regarding the administration of purgative medicines, specifically focusing on whether a patient should sleep after taking them, based on the astrological timing and the nature of the drug.</meta>

<margin>
Haly on the
*Centiloquium*
Commentary: the Moon
with Jupiter and
Venus.
Part 1.
<note>Haly refers to Ali ibn Ridwan, a medieval commentator on the *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy.</note>
</margin>

Furthermore, sleep should not be introduced after a medicine is taken, as it might disturb and corrupt the medicine’s action. This is because **sleep** causes a movement from the circumference <note>the outer parts of the body/limbs</note> toward the center, which is contrary to the movement of the medicine. Opposing movements counteract one another. Likewise, Haly says in the *Centiloquium*: The effect of a medicine is not natural to the body, but rather it draws out humors, overpowering the natural forces. And for this reason, it is forbidden to give medicine during a **conjunction of the Moon with Jupiter**, or as Ptolemy says in the same place, **with Venus**, because nature is then strengthened. Nature would then be able to overcome the many powers of the drug, since nature itself is fortified by sleep. For sleep makes all natural actions strong, because it settles the heat within. <note>Medieval physicians believed sleep concentrated "vital heat" in the stomach to aid digestion, which might cause the body to "digest" and neutralize a purgative drug instead of letting it work.</note> When this happens, the drug will not be able to loosen the bowels. It supports this because, when nature is invigorated, its power overcomes the weakness of the medicine.

Others say one should sleep after taking medicine, whether it is weak or strong. Not at first, however, because the power of the medicine would be weakened further, since weaker medicines are closer to food than others. Nor should one sleep after a strong medicine, because even if the drug's vigor is not fortified by sleep, nature might be able to bring the medicine's power into action. It would therefore be idle. Therefore, one should not sleep after taking medicine.

On the contrary, since medicines for intercourse <note>likely "coitus" here refers to the "coming together" or application of the drugs</note> are administered around the first quarter of the night, and it is our custom to sleep at night. This is a bad habit that should not be immediately cut off. Also, that which quickly brings the medicine from potentiality into action, fortifying it and restraining its "malice" <note>harmful side effects or violent intensity</note> and unbridled nature, should be introduced after taking it. **Sleep** is such a thing, as it is the instrument of nature’s heat. Furthermore, that by which the medicine (and specifically an "attractive" one) is resolved into vapors and fumes up to a determined point should be joined to it. This acts to "draw" in a certain way. Sleeping does this to the medicine because it strengthens the heat internally around the drug. When this heat is kindled, it is refracted from the center to the circumference; because of this, it tends toward the humors as was said before. Therefore, one should sleep after receiving the medicine.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that "medicine" <note>original: *farmacū*</note> is understood in three ways.

<margin>
"Medicine" is taken
for every remedy.
</margin>

Commonly, it denotes every **medicine** or title of Galen’s book *On Medicines*. Secondly, it refers to **laxative medicine**, as used here according to the ancient saying: "In medicines, if such things need to be purged." It is also taken from the Greek idiom for something "pernicious" <note>The Greek word *pharmakon* can mean both "cure" and "poison."</note>. Here, a double meaning is heard: that which is "evacuative" and that which causes "secession" <note>bowel movements</note> through the anus. Some of these are **violent**, opposing nature, such as **scammony** or **euphorbium** <term>euphorbium: a very harsh, caustic plant resin used as a drastic purgative</term>. Others are **weak**, such as **manna** <term>manna: a sweet herb used as a gentle laxative</term> and **cassia fistula**. Some are **moderate**, like **rhubarb** and **agaric** <term>agaric: a type of tree fungus used in medieval pharmacy</term>. Furthermore, any of these is described either by its substance, its power, or the quality it possesses, such as its proportion. For a violent medicine is constructed of a grosser and more compact substance, such as **troches** <note>medicinal lozenges</note> and **pills**. A weak one is liquid, like **decoctions** and **syrups**. A middle one is moderate, like **powders**. Their durability, or lack thereof, reveals this. The former last much longer, especially when prepared with **honey**, and even more so if they contain narcotics like **opium** and such.

---

The others last less time and are specifically prepared with **sugar**. For honey preserves more against corruption. Or they are categorized by the humor to be expelled—whether with difficulty or ease—such as **melancholy** <note>black bile</note>, **choler** <note>yellow bile</note>, or **phlegm**. Know also that mixed medicines given in a grosser and more compact substance, like **pills** and **electuaries**, must be prepared several days before they are taken, so that from the action and passion of the combined ingredients, a single intermediate nature results. Particles require a great deal of time to act and react upon one another in various ways. In **liquids**, however, and specifically those where **fire** has driven the mixing, this is not necessary, since the actual heat can quickly induce the same effect. The ways and means by which a medicine works are shown in Chapter 61. What "to sleep" or "sleep" means is seen in Chapter 108.

Sleeping after taking a medicine is understood in two ways: either immediately after it is received, or after it has begun to work. It is taken by someone with a robust, warm stomach and a healthy body, or one who is weak or average. Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have said one should not sleep after medicine because its power is dissolved. Others say the opposite, since it is invigorated by it. The defects of these views will be shown in the third and fourth points.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that if the medicine is an **emetic** <note>original: *uomitiuū*, meaning it induces vomiting</note>, one should not sleep at all. This is suggested by the fourth authority: when someone has drunk **hellebore** <term>hellebore: a powerful and toxic plant used to induce vomiting</term>, they should move the body more. For sleep and immobility hinder its movement. If the term is used simply, this is what is understood. Hippocrates says in the *Aphorisms*, Book 5: "Again, when nature is invigorated by sleep, a vomit-inducing medicine could become a purgative of the bowels," because that path is more natural and ready.

Furthermore, Hippocrates says: "Vomiting is prescribed at midday," because it is then nature’s habit to be very awake. Therefore, one should not sleep after an emetic medicine, unless one wishes to restrain its unbridled force, according to that Hippocratic rule: "When you want the hellebore to rest, produce sleep and do not move."

If, however, the medicine is for **purging the bowels** and is **strong** by reason of its power, or especially its composition, or if the patient is "viscous" <note>full of thick humors</note> and "gross," one should sleep not long after taking it. This applies regardless of the state of the stomach—whether strong, weak, or warm—for then nature will be sufficiently fortified, the power of the medicine will be perfectly brought into action, and its "malice" will be resisted.

If the medicine is **weak**, and the stomach is either strong or average with sufficient heat, then one should **not** sleep after taking it, for its power would be dissolved. It does not have any "malice" that needs correcting, and the heat is sufficient to bring it into action without any help. Whence the fourth authority says: "When someone has drunk a medicine that loosens the belly, it will be better for them, if it is a strong one, to sleep before it works, for it will work better. But if it is a weak one, it will be better not to sleep, for nature would digest the medicine." If, however, the medicine is weak and the stomach and the whole nature of the person is feeble...

It concludes that sleep helps the body handle strong purgatives but can cause the body to "digest" and neutralize weaker ones.</summary>

### Whether Theriac is beneficial after taking medicine.

<margin>Note</margin>
I do not recommend sleeping after a medicine has been taken so that nature may rest and the heat may strengthen the weak; rather, one must bring the medicine into action. For unless nature acts upon the drug, the drug will not act upon the body. <note>original: "id nō agēt in eam prīo q̄rta"</note> For everything that is led from potentiality into action must be led out by something already in action, according to Aristotle’s *On the Generation of Animals*, book 2. And as experience shows, I recommend that for a very weak medicine, a little sleep may be allowed so that the power of the medicine is not further weakened by wakefulness, but rather that nature is comforted. However, all this should be heard regarding the time *before* the medicine begins to work; afterward, one must not sleep as long as its action lasts, unless it becomes excessive. This is because the movement of sleep is contrary to the action of the medicine, and they impede each other when they occur at the same time.

<margin>Part 3, Chapter A, according to Avicenna</margin>
Hence, **Avicenna** <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was the most influential Persian physician of the Middle Ages.</note> says: When the medicine begins to work, it is better not to sleep on it in any way. And **Rhazes** in the fourth book of *Almansor* says: One must abstain from sleep entirely after the purging begins. This is also apparent from the *Aphorisms*, section four. But **Avicenna** seems to argue the opposite: that one should certainly sleep upon a weak medicine. For he writes in the first book of the third Fen: Easy solutions for purging the head are <term>aloetics</term> <note>medicines containing aloes, known for their bitter, laxative properties</note> from which a large pill is taken; it ought to perform its work sufficiently over time and not cause harm.

<margin>For piercing pain</margin>
Because of its small size, it may be repeated, and the patient may sleep upon it so that movement and wakefulness do not destroy its action. It must be said that there are two ways to empty the bowels with medicine. One is a total evacuation at a certain hour, and regarding this, the question stands. The other is a partial evacuation at an uncertain hour, as is often taken for constipation, so that the belly remains loose and the vapors seeking the head do not cause pain through the blockage.

<margin>Note what should be done regarding the aforementioned medicine.</margin>
And it is more praiseworthy to take this medicine in the evening than in the morning, because of the movements and labors that occur during the day. Its effect is not destroyed by frequent use, nor does it cause harm because of the goodness of the **aloe**. Indeed, it is less harmful than other medicines. And so it must be understood here.

<margin>Macer. Oribasius.</margin>
<margin>x/according to</margin>
Whence **Macer**, on the authority of **Oribasius**, <note>Oribasius was a 4th-century Greek medical compiler; Macer Floridus was the pseudonym for a medieval author of a famous herbal.</note> prescribes taking two or three pills formed with cabbage juice, the size of a bean or chickpea, often in the evening. He who is purged by these will scarcely ever be vexed by any pain of the head; and believe me, nothing is more healthy for the eyes than these. Regarding the first point, the answer appears: it is not the same for vomiting and bowel movements, since the latter is faster and stronger, irritating nature further. Regarding the other point, although at the beginning heat moves from the circumference to the center, in the process the opposite occurs because of the "refraction" <note>the counter-balancing effect</note>, and the movement becomes conformed to the medicine. For as soon as the medicine is received, it dissolves into vapors and affects the natural heat. To the other point, it must be said: a medicine should be assumed to be so strong and proportioned that it is invigorated by sleep rather than destroyed, once nature itself is invigorated. Nor is the power of the medicine weakened as long as nature is sufficient and powerful enough to use it for its own support, in the same way that

<margin>Question: Buenierius</margin>
it uses food in times of health, according to the seventh book of the *Breviary*. To the other point, regarding whether one should sleep on a weak drug, we have already seen the answer. The potential of a medicine cannot come into action unless nature is fortified; and sleep is resisted not only for a strong medicine as shown, but also to repress its malice and invigorate the heat so that it may more quickly attract and expel matter from the body. To the first point of the other part, it must be said: strong medicines are given at that hour; weak ones, however, are given more toward the fourth part of the night <note>the early hours of the morning</note>, so that sufficient sleep has already preceded. This is granted for a weak stomach or nature, or as a common practice. To the others, it must be said: they conclude correctly regarding stronger medicine, but not concerning the weaker sort.

### DIFFERENCE XXVII.

<margin>Bezoar.</margin>
<margin>V: Canon</margin>
<margin>1</margin>
That **Theriac** <note>Theriac was a famous ancient "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh.</note> is suitable after taking a medicine is shown in the first book, section four. Likewise, he who has a great flux of the belly <note>severe diarrhea</note> from a preceding medicine, or from drinking something poisonous, will be healed immediately if he drinks it, according to **Avenzoar**. <note>Avenzoar (Ibn Zuhr) was a famous 12th-century physician from Al-Andalus.</note> Furthermore, it retains nature, according to the first book of the *Summa* and the seventh book of **Serapion**. This is required especially when a purgative becomes unrestrained. Furthermore, medicine is of the nature of poison; but **Theriac** works against poisons so that in one respect it is better than <term>Mithridatum</term> <note>A complex herbal antidote similar to Theriac, named after King Mithridates VI.</note> and is the antidote for serpent venom. Additionally, because it removes the accidents arising from the medicine and improves the disposition of the body after medicine, it is helpful. Theriac is better because it removes the "tardum" <note>sluggishness</note>, the flux, and the windiness from which pain arises; it thins the viscera, cleansing them by propelling what is trapped toward the outside, and comforts the principal organs. Also, Theriac warms, whereas medicine cools by evacuating the body's heat or humors. Healing is achieved through contraries. Thus, it is clear that Theriac is appropriate after a medicine has been taken.

<margin>Opposing view</margin>
On the contrary, however, illustrious physicians seem not to exhibit it, and they are not to be dismissed as insufficient. Furthermore, Theriac is not suitable for weakness or dissolution, since according to **John of Damascus** <note>Likely referring to Mesue the Elder, often confused with John of Damascus in medical texts.</note> in his *Aphorisms*, it dissolves, cleanses, and disperses things that those who have been purged do not need, since the purgative has already done enough. Therefore, Theriac is not sought after a medicine. Regarding the first point, it must be known that there are two kinds of Theriac. One is the most "solemn" <note>grand or official</note> and effective of medicines, surpassing even Mithridatum, especially in expelling serpent venom. But in other matters, it is not less

<margin>Theriac: the mother of medicines.</margin>
than Mithridatum, about which we must be careful. Indeed, it is a greater added help in many things and of more certain utility according to **Avicenna**. And it is named from the *tyrus* serpent <note>The word "Theriac" comes from the Greek *therion* (wild beast/viper).</note>

<margin>Mithridatum is not less than Theriac.</margin>
because its flesh enters into it. These vipers are like the root and basis of this medicine, so much so that if they are removed, the medicine is destroyed. This is also observed in other solemn medicines,

<margin>Aloe is the base in Hiera.</margin>
such as **aloe** in <term>Hiera Picra</term> <note>A classic laxative powder; the name means "Holy Bitter."</note> and cassia or colocynth in the "Great Hieras." For the composers of medicine looked to the industry of nature, which places in each member a composite part and quality by which its actions are perfected. There are many preparations of Theriac. However, the most fundamental is that of **Andromachus**, <note>Andromachus was Nero's physician and the credited inventor of the refined theriac formula.</note> who constructed a singular remedy for every case; whence Avicenna says it is the most perfect of medicines...

<margin>Averroes, *Colliget*, Book 5</margin>
Just as Galen and others strove to add to the prescription of <term>Theriac</term> <note>Theriac was a famous ancient "universal antidote" made of dozens of ingredients, including opium and viper flesh.</note>, they did so not necessarily because of a compelling need for that specific ingredient, nor because of something else calling them to it, but because they sought to leave a trace of themselves in the recipe, just as a trace remained from **Andromachus** <note>Andromachus was Nero’s physician, credited with improving the formula for Theriac.</note>. And my advice indeed is that they should not remove any proven helpful ingredient they find. For perhaps that complexity with that specific weight is the sign of its found helpfulness; so much so that when it is removed from its proper weight, it no longer follows its specific property. Its approval is accepted from three sources according to Galen, Serapion, **Haly Abbas**, and Averroes.

<margin>
Tests of Theriac according to Galen, Serapion, Averroes, and Haly Abbas.

First, it is given to one who has taken a strong laxative or emetic medicine, such as <term>scammony</term> or <term>colocynth</term> <note>Scammony and colocynth (bitter apple) are extremely harsh purgatives that can be poisonous in high doses.</note>, in the quantity of a lupin bean. If it prevents the perceived purge, it stands as strong and perfect. If not, then it is less so. Second, according to Galen, a wild cock—which Averroes thinks is a male pheasant—should be bitten by some venomous animal. If it survives after the administration of the Theriac, it is effective; if not, by no means. Third, it is given to someone who has taken a medicine that kills by its coldness, such as **opium**, **mandrake**, or **henbane**; if it causes him to escape, it is youthful and perfect. If not, the opposite.

<margin>Ages of Theriac</margin>
It is also distinguished by its ages. For it has infancy, puberty, adolescence, old age, and death (or senility). After six months, it becomes an "infant," since before then it does not have a perfected being. Then it begins to reach "puberty" and increases until the time in which it stays stable, up to the 10th year in hot regions and the 20th in cold ones. Then it stays stable for 10 or 20 years. Then it declines after 20 or 40 years. Finally, it is stripped of its theriacal power after 30 or 60 years, and it becomes a composition declined from the grade of Theriac. Our wicked vendors, however, commonly give it after four months and consume it before two or so years, when it does not even ferment until after 10 or 20 years. <note>original: "drā.clxxviii"</note> The time of its ages in temperate places will be the middle between these extremes.

And it is necessary that for a bite, the medicine given in a drink should be that which is fresh and strong. For the other conditions for which it is administered, let another be given which is weaker. It is strong and fresh after five years (according to some) or 12, up to 30. And this medicine, like others, has its judgment from its simple components and from its "total form." From its simple parts, it works in a twofold way: first by cooling and numbing through its [opiate] power; then by heating and dissolving through the hot medicines eventually overcoming the coldness of the opium. But its "total form" works toward the expulsion of poisons through a specific form resulting from the simple ingredients.

As will be seen in section 178. The rest however is [discussed] according to Dan Ezra and in section 179. What the drug shows is shown in the premise. But perhaps that is not valid, as will appear in the third and fourth points. Thirdly, it should be known that a drug either purges sufficiently or excessively. If the first, then Theriac is in no way suitable, nor is this much suggested by any of the distinguished authors. This is confirmed by:

From this it appears, both from the rule cited and from the fact that he associates it with Philonium <note>An opiate-based electuary named after Philo of Tarsus.</note>, that he understands Theriac insofar as it stands as one of the opiates. Because of this, the discourse explains the fourth priority: when the solution of the belly is excessive in a drink, you will give Theriac or Philonium. For such things alter the bad hot complexion induced by the drug, cool the vapors, thicken the parts of the humors, and bind and press them together, rendering them almost insensible so that they are not moved into audacity and unbridledness, but their motion and agitation are quelled. For if young (fresh) Theriac were given then, they would be further weakened by its heat and movement, and by expanding them, it would induce a greater opening of the vessels and a stronger biting of the purgative.

->## Whether a bath is suitable after purgation.<-

<note>original: "An Balneuz opetat p[er] purgatio[nem]"</note>

...by the vapors of the medicine, and from that, pain is caused; whenever a violent fever comes upon them and a decline of superfluities <note>Superfluities are excess humors or waste products in the body that the medicine aims to remove.</note> is diverted, water is transmitted through the part. If, however, the discharge is excessive, they should not give a strong <term>Theriac</term> <note>A complex medicinal paste used as an antidote and general restorative.</note>, but another kind. From these things, therefore, it appears false what some have said: that on the same day as the <term>confection</term> <note>The mixing or preparation of the drug.</note> it is proper to administer a Theriac that still possesses the power of opium. But for phlegmatic or melancholic patients, it may be given more strongly. On the third day, however, in a phlegmatic person who was first filled with crude humors, a strong Theriac can be laudably administered to dry them out. 

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it must be said that through Theriac a youth is not helped—that is, rather, as has been explained, a fresh <term>opiated</term> medicine. And similarly, it must be said to **Zoroates** <note>Likely a reference to a specific medical authority or a misreading of a name like Rhazes or Hippocrates; in this context, it refers to an opposing medical opinion.</note> either that he considered here the correction of the poisonous nature of the medicine more than the unrestrained action of the discharge—which, once removed, is halted by itself—or that he was of an opinion for which I find no other supporters. To the other point, it must be said that although a Theriac may bind the belly and its application is of good quality, it nevertheless induces other harms to the person; hence it should not be administered when the flux can be restrained by other means, as **Mesue** and **Avicenna** teach. To the other point, it must be said that although drugs are without the danger of poison—specifically strong, "evulsive" <note>Drugs that forcibly pull or pluck out humors.</note> drugs—Theriac is not specially required, since the toxicity of those drugs can be expelled before they are taken. Just as when they act unrestrainedly, their lack of restraint can be removed through other means.

To the other point, it must be said that a drug rarely acts without restraint when the physician acts with caution, so that it is not necessary to administer Theriac after every flux for fear of that unrestrained action. Nor indeed is there anything that would improve the disposition of the body since the flux rarely exceeds what is necessary. It is also bad for superfluities to be removed at a great distance from the path of the intestines; nor do they strengthen the viscera unless they are no longer inflamed. To the other point, it must be said that a drug, by drawing out hot humors, does not chill the body, but rather protects it and strengthens nature by expelling what is distressing it; nor are the spirits so weakened and dissolved that they are not soon restored once the harmful matter is expelled. Hence they do not need Theriac, as they would be further dissolved in whatever temperament they were transmitted to. So much so that the body would be forced to move by two contrary motions.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.

<note>Large blank space for initial 'Q'</note> That a bath is not suitable after purgation is shown here. First, from the *Fourth Book of the Canon* <note>Referring to Avicenna’s Canon of Medicine.</note>: After medicine, no one should enter a bath, because it draws matter toward the exterior; and it is not good except for binding the belly. In this opinion **Mesue** agrees in the first book. Furthermore, traction <note>The pulling or drawing of humors.</note> should not be made in different directions. For one movement hinders the other and overturns nature; although a conflict of traction occurs here, for medicine draws from the circumference to the center, while a bath does the opposite. Even if the bath cannot draw matter with a stronger power than the drug, the body will be sufficiently purged, nor will the bath be able to accomplish that; according to the dialectic, it is weaker. Nor is it suitable during the act of purgation because, once the matter is irritated and agitated, it flows even more. Furthermore, the same authority teaches that the unrestrained action of a <term>cathartic</term> <note>A strong laxative.</note> is halted by sleep and rest. For when you wish to stop it, make the patient sleep and do not move them. But a bath is twice contrary to this, since according to **Johannitius** and **Haly Abbas**, it is reduced to the category of exercise and motion. The action of contraries produces contrary results. Those who have been recently purged remain, by the nature of the drug's action, inflamed, emptied, and dried out. But a bath, under the intent for which it is administered, increases such states. Also,

<margin>Opposing view</margin>
a bath does not help after cleansing. The opposite of this is written in the *Fourth Book*. Likewise, that which can draw out what the medicine could not—due to the distance—is suitable after the emptying. Such things are those located near the skin. This is the role of the bath, as it evacuates only what is near the skin; nevertheless, it is associated with the medicine. And because it removes the inflation and wasting of the limbs and takes away fatigue. According to **Almansor** <note>The title of the medical work by the Persian physician Rhazes.</note> in the fourth book, it is suitable after purgation since the body remains affected by these things. This bath, however, when properly measured, cools the limbs by tempering the humors and causes superfluities to breathe out. Furthermore, sometimes after a purgation has been undertaken, people are excessively emptied. But a bath binds the belly, according to **Almansor** in the fourth book; hence in the *Theory*, book five, it says: A bath cuts off the discharge of a laxative medicine. Therefore, a bath is highly beneficial after purgation. Regarding the first point, it should be known that a bath is a subtle or liquid body meeting the body circumferentially and changing it. 

The word "bath" <note>original: "balneum"</note> is derived from what is <note>original: "balaneyon"</note> in Greek, from *valo*, which means "I send in through a cutting." After removing the 'A' and the diphthong, and dropping the 'i', it is called *balneum*. The 'o' is also changed as in many words. It is, moreover, a manifold thing, as its definition suggests. For one kind is of the air, which is touched upon by the word "subtle," which is first called a bath. Another is aqueous, truly called a "sweet washing," which is suggested when "liquid" is mentioned. For sometimes we use only the wind or air as a bath, such as a <term>therma</term> <note>A hot dry bath or sauna.</note> or other "stuffa" <note>A steam room or stove-heated room.</note>; sometimes one uses fresh water by immersing the body in it or pouring it over oneself. And of these, one is hot and another cold, and sometimes we use both, as often happens in hot springs. Hence, in the tenth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio [sanitatis]" by Galen.</note>, he distinguishes four parts of the bath:

<margin>8th book of Almansor, 5th book of Theory. What a bath is and how it should be applied to the sick.</margin>
<margin>Galen, *On the Method of Healing*.</margin>
the first of which is the hot air with which the person entering first connects. The second is the entry into the tub. The third is the exit into the cold. And the fourth is the wiping away of sweat.

Furthermore, the bath is diversified: for one kind is simple, like the two mentioned above. The other is composite, which is also twofold. For one is naturally such, such as sulfurous, pitchy, or aluminous <note>Containing alum.</note>. The other is constructed by art; as when herbs, branches, and other hot or cold things are decocted in the water of the bath or strewn in the air, according to the utility intended by the physician. For a bath, according to the fifth book of the *Theory*, varies in three ways. First, because of the air, according as it may be hot, cold, or medium, inducing different effects in bodies. Or on the part of the water, as has been said. Or because of the quality of its use, since some of us use it with simple rubbing. Others with the rubbing of oils; some with the rubbing of grain flour and other things, according as it seems most expedient to fulfill their intentions.

First, however, the natural action of the bath is...

...to warm with its air and to moisten with its water. For the first room <note>original: "casa seu masio"</note> or chamber is cool and moist. The third, however, warms and dries. This is so that a sudden, harmful alteration of nature does not occur upon entering or exiting; it was necessary for the bath to be distinct with three chambers. Whence **Haly Abbas** <note>Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi (d. 994), a famous Persian physician.</note> says: there are three "airs" of the bath. The first is the air of the first room and it is tepid, bringing no heat into the body. The second is medium in heat, warming the body with some heat and dissolving [humors] with a certain dissolution. The third, however, is that which vehemently warms the bodies and dissolves many **superfluities** <term>superfluitates</term> <note>Excess waste products or humors that the body needs to expel to maintain health.</note> and evacuates them from the body. Nor is there a dissonance between **Haly Abbas** and **Avicenna** <note>Abbreviated as "A." in the text.</note>, because **Haly Abbas** touched only upon the air, while here [Avicenna] speaks of the mixture of air and water. It can also be that the space of the first [room] is made to match the exterior air. And it was placed around for the diversity of other things taken internally, or those which are applied externally, which do not just pass superficially through the bodies but either tend toward the center—as things sent inside—or are situated on the outer part. 

It was said, however, to act differently since among the things that act within us, some are such by **potency** <term>potentia</term> or by **virtue** <term>uirtute</term> <note>The inherent medicinal power or quality of a substance, such as "heat" in pepper even if the pepper is physically cold to the touch.</note>, such as chamomile and pepper. Others, however, act by **actuality** <note>Direct physical action, like hot water actually being hot.</note>, such as hot or cold water and the air of the bath; and everything hot warms, and everything cold cools. Another acts by **accident** <note>An "accidental" effect is a secondary or unintended consequence of a primary action.</note>, as a hot bath might cool in a twofold accidental way: either by opening the pores and resolving the hot **choler** <note>Yellow bile, one of the four humors, associated with heat and dryness.</note> outward, or by agitating the humors inside the body and dissolving them over sensitive members, which, being moved, act with more actual coldness. In this way, those who bathe while having undigested matter <note>original: "indigestis"</note> incur shivering and cold. 

Apart from this, he distinguishes a triple bath. Since a certain kind prepares for evacuation, according to practice: one wishing to take a laxative first needs to adapt the body so that it receives the medicine more effectively. For two or three days, take a bath of temperate heat and a gentle pouring of tepid water over the body. Wherefore in the first [part of the] fourth [book]: to enter a bath for several days before the belly is loosened is among those things that prepare well, unless something prohibits it. For this reason, those who are to be **bloodlet** <note>original: "flothomados"</note> or **cupped** <note>original: "uentososandos"</note> having thick blood should first be bathed. It is necessary, however, that a small amount of time intervene between the bath and the drinking of the medicine.

There is, however, another prohibited bath, such as that administered at the hour of the operation of a **cathartic** <note>A strong laxative.</note>; since its action is contrary to the action of the cathartic and distracts from it, unless the drug’s action is unrestrained. A certain [bath], however, is "perfecting," which is administered according to some when the action of the cathartic has ceased. For it resolves that which the medicine was unable to lead out.

<margin>A. 2 Mes.</margin>
<margin>4. p.</margin>

What the difference is regarding purgation is shown in [chapter] 125 with others. Regarding the second point, it should be known that the illustrious physicians **Avicenna** and **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (c. 777–857), known as Mesue the Elder.</note> seem to contradict each other in this, which is a fiction. For first [Avicenna] writes in the fourth [book]: He who drinks a loosening medicine should enter the bath on the second day; because if any of the humors remain, the bath itself will be able to cleanse them. And this is the common mode of practitioners: if the **virtue** <term>uirtus</term> <note>The patient's vital strength or "life force" required to withstand treatment.</note> is firm, the bath should be entered on the second day after purgation. **Mesue**, however, 

---

regarding drugs, wants no one to bathe after taking a drug unless the action of the medicine is unrestrained. Wherefore, in practice: if in someone the loosening [of the bowels] so exceeds measure that a failure of the **virtue** <note>vital strength</note> is feared, introduce him to a bath and pour hot water over him, especially on the feet and hands. And in this **Mesue** coincides, repelling those who prescribe such people to be bathed in cold and **styptic** <note>Substances that contract tissues and stop secretions.</note> waters. They are ignorant because these constrict the pores and turn the medicines and vapors back inside, whence the cause of the **flux** <note>An excessive discharge or diarrhea.</note> is increased. And therefore it is seen as no small mistake to place a cold, styptic **epithem** <note>A local application or poultice.</note> over the belly, as it increases the flux and even incites blood to flow, which it rarely benefits except in bodies already pure. 

On the contrary, the magnificent intention ought to be to dilate the pores and attract [matter] to the exterior; and properly when the bath is made of sweet waters in which pore-opening herbs are decocted, such as chamomile, wormwood, marjoram, citrus leaves, and such things. And in this, frictions and sweats provoked by ingenious means are of no small benefit. The common people, however, and those unskilled in the art, commonly bathe both those in whom the drug did not over-perform and those in whom it was unrestrained. 

Their error is shown first: because a bath pulls toward the exterior, whereas medicine pulls toward the interior. Because of this, [humors] that ought to be pulled to the interior by the medicine cannot be evacuated when the action of the bath is pulling in the contrary direction toward the exterior. Instead, remaining in the parts, moved but not led out, they harm them. It also fatigues the **virtue** <note>vital strength</note> and dissolves it because of the attraction made toward opposite parts, since in such motion a "cutting" <note>An internal conflict of forces.</note> must intervene. This is the apparent opinion of the physicians. Therefore, in the fourth of the Aphorisms, drugs are inhibited from being exhibited under the **Dog Star** <note>The "Dog Days" of summer, considered medically dangerous for strong treatments.</note> and before the Dog Star. Also, that evacuation is perverse which causes the passage of matter over the **noble members** <note>The vital organs, such as the heart, liver, and brain.</note>. <margin>ch. 187</margin> But through a bath, matter moved to the outside is transmitted from the ignoble parts through the noble parts to the ignoble—as from the belly to the surface of the skin through noble organs situated in the middle. Again, matter is better led out through the nearest ways and ducts, and especially the accustomed ones through which it is nature's habit to evacuate. Whence the first Aphorism says that one must act where nature most seeks to go, and lead from there through convenient places. 

Furthermore, because of such contrary action, the matter—robbed of its purpose—generates all sorts of things in the passages. Or, if led out into the skin, it causes defilements therein. Therefore, a bath after medicine is not appropriate except when the drug is unrestrained, for then it helps to constrict the belly. **Avicenna** concedes, however—though he seems slightly dissonant in this question—that immediately after taking medicine, it is not to be feared to enter the first room of the bath, and specifically in colder times, provided that the heat is in no way an impediment to attraction. Since intense cold harms the effect of the medicine. 

Regarding the third point, it should be known that the capacity for bathing is either strong, or it is a prostrated weakness. When the latter exists, one must cease from the bath entirely in any case. For since the **virtue** <note>strength</note> is dissolved, the spirits resolved, and the body consumed, and the bath increases these things, one must be spared lest the virtue be dissolved further. Whence, in **Marasmus** <note>A state of severe malnutrition and wasting.</note>, the taking of a bath is prohibited when the person is weak...

**uirtute** <note>catchword: strength/virtue</note>

<meta>This page continues the technical medical discussion regarding the timing of baths in relation to purgative treatments. The previous page detailed the physical structure of the bathhouse and its three chambers. This page moves into the clinical debate over whether a patient should bathe immediately after taking a laxative or wait until the "agitation" of the humors has ceased, citing authorities such as Galen, Avicenna, and Mesue.</meta>

<page-num>411</page-num>

### Whether the Bath is Recommended After Purgation

...safely; and if the condition demands it, lest death occur. This is what happened to the doctor who bathed the young boy, the first of the **Gnostics** <note>original: "gnosticorum"; likely referring to a specific sect of physicians mentioned in Galen’s commentaries.</note>. And to **Archigenes** and **Theagenes** <note>original: "Artalo Teagene"; likely a corruption of Archigenes, a prominent Greek physician from the 1st century AD.</note> in the thirteenth [book] on the **nature of the mind** <note>original: "de ingenio", referring to Galen's *De Ingenio Sanitatis* or *Methodus Medendi*.</note>. If, however, vigor remains constant, then either the medicine has ceased its action <note>original: "effrenitatus"; literally "unbridled," here meaning the active phase of the drug has ended.</note>, and thus it is universally agreed one should bathe—not indeed with cold styptics, but with those that are appropriately tempered and opening—or it has not ceased its action. And this occurs in two ways: either the motion and agitation of the medicine has stopped, or it hasn't. As for the first: if the patient is sufficiently purged with everything being beneficial, there is no need for him to be sent to the bath after purgation, since no benefit but rather harm would be received from it. Others, however, bathe these patients out of ambition, so that they may seem to be doing something more diligent, perhaps hoping to receive more [payment] therefrom (from the eleventh [book] on the **nature of the mind**).

This is noted in the first [part] of the fourth [book]. If a youth placed in a bath after medicine does not find delight in it but suffers a burning heat within, expel him. For the medicine did not find a need for **restoration** <term>resotio</term> <note>A term for restoring the body's moisture and strength after the harsh effects of a purgative.</note>; but under what pretext is the speech of **Mesue** verified? He holds especially that no one should bathe after taking a medicine unless it has ceased its action. 

If, however, the motion of the humors and the agitation of the **purgative** <term>kathartici</term> has ceased, and the patient has not been sufficiently purged, nor has every reasonable benefit and removal [of waste] followed, or if it was a matter of habit for him, he should be instructed to bathe on the third day after the medicine, and especially at its end, and perhaps on the third day so that all agitation may be quieted. And especially when one is being evacuated of matter that is difficult to move, either because the humors are thick and remote—such as those in the joints—or because they have been carried toward the external parts. This is particularly true when bodies are fat and compact. In these cases, the power of the medicine could not reach the outermost parts of the body at all. 

As **Avicenna** <note>Abbreviated as "A." throughout the text.</note> notes: if you see that the bath is pleasant to him and he delights in it, this will be a sign that the bath itself is cleansing what remains [of the waste]. Therefore, leave him in it. And this is supported because after a general purgation, when the body has not been purged in its entirety, a particular purgation ought to follow. This is achieved through a bath that evacuates the matter near the skin. Whence in the [book] on the **chest**, **Galen** says: The evacuation that occurs through exercise and the bath is of the subtle humors that reach the parts of the skin and are ready for exit. Furthermore, bodies are rendered dried out by medicine, and superfluities are especially moistened on the exterior, since many vapors during the action of the medicine tend from the center toward the circumference. 

But the bath has the power to move [humors], because it moistens what is dried and dries what is moistened, according to the dominant conditions, when it is administered properly. Whence from the **Table of Health** <note>original: "de tba. be."; likely referring to the *Tacuinum Sanitatis* (Tables of Health).</note>: This is a wonderful thing in hot baths, that they are beneficial to dryness, and cold baths [benefit] coldness. Just as it makes the thirsty not thirsty. In the thirsty, however, they remain thirsty. And it operates almost like wine, as is clear regarding it in the 30th **problem** and in the *Particular Diets*. Wherefore **Damascenus** <note>John of Damascus, an influential scholar whose medical aphorisms were widely studied.</note> says: Baths are not necessary for us solely for cooling the hot or heating the cold, but so that they may dissolve and cause sweating, dry, and moisten. He says also that the bath and a temperate drink help both the cause and the contrary of the cause. Therefore, a bath after purgation is appropriate in this case. And nothing in **Mesue** detracts from this premise, since the interior humors are purged and quiet, and are not moved to the skin from the lesser to the noble parts. Nor does it evacuate except where nature is found. Nor does it infect the skin, but rather purifies it, since the superfluities are led out from it. 

<margin>A Doubt</margin> Regarding the aforementioned, there is a doubt, because it seems one should bathe not only on the second day, but even on the same day. For in the second section of the **Introduction** <note>original: "Nazitiō"; likely referring to the *Isagoge* or an introduction to a medical text.</note>: It is expedient for one who intends to take <margin>22. 3. 1</margin> medicine to take it early in the morning and delay his food. Then after three hours, he should take twenty [parts] of bread with wine and a little water, and after six hours enter the bath and leave. 

It must be said that **Avicenna** is speaking here in the cure of joint pain with a medicine that is a mild laxative for the belly at the start, and not a strong purgative, so that mildness and softness may be acquired by nature; and especially when this is done with dry matter. He says also that he should enter the bath and leave immediately, so that the medicine is not agitated further. If, however, the medicine is in the act of purging and the matter is in **flux** <term>fluxus</term> <note>The active movement or discharge of humors caused by the medicine.</note>, and we do not fear it has ceased its action, one should not bathe at all. 

<margin>The Son of the King of Bohemia</margin> Just as a certain **Son of the King of Bohemia** <note>An anecdote likely referring to a contemporary or historical medical failure where a royal died or suffered from bathing too soon after a purgative.</note>, after a medicine was given to him, was found in a bath despite certain preceding warnings. And that is what **Avicenna** meant: that through a medicine taken a short time before, no one should enter the bath while the matter is being drawn to the exterior. And according to this understanding, especially of **Mesue**, the reasons proceed. Regarding the fourth point from **Avicenna**, what should be said has appeared from **Mesue**'s first point. 

To the other point it must be said: that traction should not be made in different directions while the medicine is still evacuating, unless, as was said, the action of the medicine is to be stopped. To the other point it must be said: it is true that medicine and the bath would lead out through the same path. But it has been shown that they act through different ones: for the bath touches the skin, but not the medicine; whence it can operate more through it. 

To the other point it must be said: it is not inappropriate for the same thing to be cured in the aforementioned ways though they are not taken for the same reason. For <margin>Sleep stops the flow of medicine</margin> **sleep** cures the flow of excessive medicine because it draws from the circumference to the center, which is the contrary of the cause of the flow's motion, and by strengthening the power, gathering the natural heat, and making it vigorous for the dissolution of the medicine's vapors. Still, if it happens that sleep occurs in the fact of it <note>original: "in facto esse"; i.e., in the state of being asleep</note>, yet while the heat is being moved inward, motion intervenes. Baths, however, stop the flow and the vapors of the medicine by drawing them to the opposite [the skin] and resolving them, since they lead them out by the opening of the pores; thus sleep and the bath draw the flow in opposite ways, though in different manners. 

To the other point it must be said: if those who have been medicated are weakened or dried out or vehemently emptied, they should not bathe as described except after their strength is resumed. If we wish to touch their bodily state to bring them back to a better condition as convalescents through moistening agents, [we note] that not all baths are **resolutive** <note>original: "resolutiva"; meaning they break down and disperse humors.</note>, but many are moistening. The arguments of the other side are also true, when understood in their proper context.

<summary>This page discusses the clinical timing of baths following purgative medicine, weighing the dangers of bathing while humors are still agitated against the benefits of using baths to cleanse remaining waste from the skin and joints. It harmonizes conflicting views from Avicenna, Galen, and Mesue, concluding that baths are therapeutic only after the medicine's primary action has ceased.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the specific practicalities of bathing after medicine to a broader theoretical debate: whether the administration of purgative drugs (pharmacy) is strictly part of "preventative medicine" (the regimen of health) or "curative medicine." The previous page discussed the immediate physical reactions to baths; this page looks at the classification of health states—healthy, neutral, and sick—to determine when drugs are appropriate.</meta>

->**Does pharmacy belong to the Regimen of Health?**<-

### DISTINCTION XXIX.

1. It is demonstrated that <term>pharmacy</term><note>In this context, "pharmacy" (farmacia) refers specifically to the administration of purgative or laxative drugs rather than the general preparation of medicines.</note> does not belong to the <term>regimen of health</term><note>A branch of medieval medicine focused on lifestyle, diet, and habits to maintain health and prevent disease.</note>. This is shown because **Galen** in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*, a foundational medical textbook.</note> and **Avicenna** in the third [chapter] of the first [book], where they discuss the preservation of health, do not teach how to administer drugs, but rather in the fourth book where they discuss the curative part of medicine. Furthermore, in the *Aphorisms* [of Hippocrates]: those who have healthy bodies are difficult to purge. And those with healthy bodies who are purged by drugs are quickly weakened; for they grow dark, are tormented, and waste away. However, bodies under a regimen of health are measured and healthy. For a regimen is either preservative or curative, since all such practice is one or the other. Moreover, medicine provides us security regarding two things: the total prohibition of putrefaction and the defense of moisture so that it does not quickly dissolve. Drugs, however, are sought for humors that are putrefying and corrupt. And the principles and natures of opposites are themselves opposite. Since the curative branch commands the use of drugs, the preservative branch must therefore forbid it. Again, if a body must be purged, it will be in relation to some other measured body; but a healthy body cannot be purged since drugs dissolve and melt it away, as has been stated. Therefore, drugs are not desired in a regimen of health.

On the contrary, in the sixth [book] on the regimen of health, they command that moist bodies prone to putrefaction be purged through **aloe** <note>A common bitter purgative derived from the aloe plant.</note>. Also, in the first [book] of the *Practice*, along with the third [book] of **Al-Mansur** <note>Referring to the *Liber ad Almansorem* by the Persian physician Rhazes.</note>, the method of purging and evacuating "sinning" humors <note>original: "peccātīū huōrū"; a medical term for humors that have become unbalanced or diseased.</note> is touched upon. Furthermore, the sixth [book] of the *Aphorisms* commands that a need for pharmacy or <unclear>surgery</unclear> should be addressed in the spring. Such people are considered "healthy" according to the commentator there. These are the ones to whom the regimen of health is applied. Also, people are called "healthy" in one sense as long as their actions are not sensibly <note>In the sense of "perceptibly" or "noticeably" to the senses.</note> hindered. For in the first [book] on disease, health is said to be the ability to exercise one’s actions without sensible hindrance. But some people with <term>cacochymia</term><note>An imbalance or "badness" of the humors.</note> or <term>plethora</term><note>An overabundance of blood or humors.</note> can exercise their sensible actions without harm. Those who are in such a state require the removal of humors. Again, if an optimally healthy body requires purging—which seems less likely—then other bodies require it even more, since they are more prone to slip and fail. This is necessary because in childhood and old age, no one stands in a "neutral" state; from infancy to youth, one exists in almost superfluous moisture and a kind of tempered heat. In old age and senility, one collects more superfluities that require removal. This is confirmed because a tempered body encounters more opposites by which it is harmed than a distempered one. And a tempered body—no less than others—can be affected by a pestilential constitution of the air or an unfortunate alignment of the stars, whereby the bodies collect many superfluities requiring removal. Therefore, pharmacy is appropriate in the regimen of health. Concerning the first point, one should know what has been seen regarding the nature of pharmacy in chapter 126.

<margin>Regimen of Health</margin>
The regimen of health is the measure of things occurring to the body, properly attributed to healthy bodies. When this concerns the bodies at hand, it must be heard diligently: it is necessary to look at the distinction of bodies. For some of these are healthy, and some are sick. Both of these are twofold. For some are such "temporarily," as in currently healthy or sick, in whom actions are either performed sensibly or similarly harmed. Others are such "simply" or by nature, as mentioned in distinction 125. These can also be understood in two ways: taking health narrowly, and thus only the body that is always or optimally healthy is contained under the regimen of health, since its care is sought for its own sake. Or, more commonly, according to what occurs in practice where one does not sensibly fail; and thus the body that has "slipped" a little, or the body that is very "neutral" or "simply" sick—whether equally or unequally—can be placed under the extension of health, according to what was cited from the first [book] on disease. Thus, in the *Art* <note>Referring to Galen's *Ars Medica*.</note>, the entire breadth of health is divided into three parts: those having a wide range, namely the healthy, the neutral, and the sick. These are established between two terms in the *Tegni*: between the simple best condition and that which is preserved "for now," and that which is a temporary or current sickness, as well as those being simply the healthiest or the sickest in whatever manner.

From these deductions, it should also be known that in the widest sense, "regimen" is taken commonly for any and all proper administration. And so, "regimen" is even called curative, according to the first [chapter] of the fourth [book]: "Regimen and nutrition are one." Properly, this refers to what is owed to a "slipped" body, not for the sake of preservation but referring to the whole genus; this is called the "properly preservative" or "pre-custodial" regimen. Most properly, however, it refers to what is owed to a body existing in the better of its forms. What health actually is was shown in chapter 82. Regarding this, it should be known that some have said pharmacy is not expedient in the regimen of health, because a body should be ruled by "like things," and drugs are not such, since most of them are highly contrary to nature.

But these people are deceived, hearing "healthy body" and taking it only as "optimal health" at a single point, whereas health is multifaceted and broad, as in distinction 18. Nor do they seem to perceive the infinite diversity of drugs.

Others have said, from the same root, that pharmacy is not sought in the regimen of health for the sake of the present, but rather because of future danger, wishing these healthy bodies to remain sufficient. But they err because, as appeared in distinction 116, just as a body that has slipped toward heat or cold is not only governed so that it does not fall into disease—which would be a small thing—but so that it may be reduced no less to a perfectly healthy body. For its actions, even if not sensibly harmed, can be affected by some *cacochymia* which a measured pharmacy purges. Regarding the third point, it should be known that pharmacy is expedient in the regimen of health, as touched upon, and it will be specified more as a "commensurate" pharmacy according to Galen, compared to the others, according to whether the body has slipped more or less. Thus, when a tempered body reaches further old age, according to the "neutrality" of senility, it may sometimes require lighter purges. And finally, for whom? The first point is confirmed by reason: since distempered bodies require alteration by their opposite, so too does pharmacy work in its own way when an excess of some humor follows their distemper. They require that drug. Furthermore, every "slip," when the time is right, must eventually be corrected, as appears in the sixth [book] on health. But a body placed under the regimen of health for the most part slips into excess, both in quantity and quality.

<summary>This page discusses the theoretical debate over whether purgative drugs belong in the "regimen of health," concluding that they are necessary when a body slips into a "neutral" or slightly unbalanced state. It provides a classification of health, ranging from the "optimally healthy" to the "simply sick," to justify the use of preventative pharmacy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into "pharmacy" (the use of purgative drugs). Having previously questioned if pharmacy belongs to the regimen of health, the author now lists specific mild and strong drugs and debates whether people recovering from illness—convalescents—should be purged.</meta>

->**Whether pharmacy is a task for convalescents.**<-

And therefore the art of medicine was established to aid the constitution and governance of the body. Furthermore, since many animal bodies are very prone to decline, not only in simple quality but also with a lack of humor, they eventually require evacuation. Hence, **Job** <note>Likely a reference to the Biblical Job, often cited in medieval medicine regarding the frailty of the human condition</note> says the healthy are "disposed to be sick." Therefore, in the regimen of health, <term>pharmacy</term><note>The use of laxatives or purgatives to clear the bowels and "humors."</note> is appropriate at times, and especially in the spring or even in autumn. **Distinction 130.** But against this, some say strong pharmacy should be administered to such people. It must be said that this is not primarily for the sake of a present lapse, but rather for a future one.

However, these two types of things that purge such bodies are of two kinds. For some are simple, or nearly so, such as: **Mallows**, **broth of half-cooked cabbage**, **mercurialis** <note>Dog’s mercury, a plant used as a laxative</note> which I find greatly restores the appetite and prevents stomach blockages; **bindweed** (from which **Antiochian scammony** <note>A harsh resinous purgative derived from *Convolvulus scammonia*</note> is made when they decoct it with fatter, tempered things, such as old cocks and hens); and likewise **dried prunes**, **cherries**, **mature grapes**; **sweet pomegranates**, **tamarinds**, **cassia fistula** <note>The "pudding-pipe tree," a mild laxative</note>, **manna**, **goat whey** <note>original: "sex caprinuz," likely *serum caprinum*</note>, **turpentine**, **epithymum** <note>Dodder of thyme, used to purge melancholy</note>, **senna**, **tartar**, **polypody** <note>A type of fern</note>, **safflower**, **larch fungus**, **aloes**, **turpeth**, and **myrobalans**. These are used according to the various movements of the humors and complexions, though it must be said some are milder than others, while some are harsh. Others, however, are compounds, like <term>Diapolicon</term><note>A famous digestive and laxative compound</note>, which is discussed in the fourth [book]

<margin>Diapolicon</margin>
of the regimen of health; it is made from nitre <note>saltpeter</note>, pepper, cumin, and seeds of water-rue. When one wishes to dissolve more, [the dose is increased], but when less, a medium portion is cast in, and that further incites the <term>phlegm</term><note>One of the four bodily humors, associated with cold and moisture</note>.

<margin>Hiera</margin>
There is also **Hiera** <note>original: "Yera," from *Hiera Picra* or "Holy Bitter," a traditional aloe-based purgative</note> made with aloes and seven other medicines; from the seventh [book] of the *Therapeutics* <note>Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note>, which moves the <term>choler</term><note>Yellow bile, the humor associated with heat and dryness</note> with windiness, and properly when larch fungus or turpeth is mixed with it.

<margin>Aloe Pills</margin>
There are **Pills** made of aloe and mastic. Another, which is especially useful for common folk: **Take 10 drachms of tamarinds** and dissolve them in warm water; [take] **one drachm of fresh rhubarb**, or two scruples. Let the mixture sit for a day and a half, then strain the whole; to this add one ounce of **citron peel syrup**. Another useful for commoners: **Take senna, polypody, epithymum, tartar, and cinnamon**, [and] **Arabian stoechas** <note>French lavender</note> in equal parts; let it be made with enough sugar or honey. Another common one: **Take one and a half ounces of cinnamon**; **tartar and senna pods**, six drachms each; **safflower**, two drachms; **nitre**, one drachm; **anise and ginger**, one and a half drachms each; **turpeth and Barbary rhubarb**, two scruples each. Let an **electuary** <note>A medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note> be made, or let it be taken in a powder before eating with broth.

<margin>V 3</margin>
Some use a certain **Diacatholicon** <note>A "universal" laxative meant to purge all four humors</note>, that is, they use it by choice; yet the continuous use of such things leads the body to a bad end, especially when they are more medicinal [than dietary]. Regarding the fourth point: even if such things appear to have been introduced, it must be said regarding the first point that although "pharmacy" is not explicitly named in the *Tegni*, it is understood by the brevity of the speech. For when it teaches how to govern healthy bodies in their composition, it also includes those things that pertain to <term>surgery</term><note>In the medieval sense, this could refer to any manual or invasive intervention, including strong purging</note>. Also, **Aristotle** touched upon light or moderate laxatives in the *Regimen of Health*, but the fourth, stronger ones certainly pertain to the curative part. To the other point, it should be said that the aforementioned bodies are perfectly healthy, which is not the case for everyone in the regimen of health. **Galen** <note>original: "Y." for *Ypocras* or *Galenus*</note> also understood by "to be purged" and "to be medicated" those things which work more strongly. To another, it should be said

that medicine prohibits putrefaction by applying pharmacy where it is appropriately beneficial. For although the humors of these bodies are not actually putrefied and corrupt, they are nevertheless in a certain disposition close to it. To another, it should be said that it is true that something might be in one of two opposites by its own nature, and not by the effect of a higher genus—just as whiteness and blackness are seen, not through themselves but through color. Thus, pharmacy is not curative through itself, but through the practice under which it is contained, such as the preservative [branch of medicine]. To another, it should be said that pharmacy is not spoken of in relation to the "best body" while it remains so, but when it becomes sick by some occasion, and properly when it neglects the observed regimen. For it is by no means appropriate when it is in its best disposition. To the first point of the other part, the answer has already appeared. To the other, it is similarly seen that it is granted that minor or medium pharmacy is appropriate for them. Or one is purged, especially more strongly, not by reason of the present disposition but the future. To the other, it has also appeared in its own way. To another, it must be said that although humidity may seem superfluous in the first age <note>youth</note> by reason of the temperate heat, it is not so in the other three ages. It is also granted sometimes to offer a light laxative to a temperate body that has become somewhat sluggish. And even if this meets with many objections, it is least harmful when the opposition is slight, like the middle compared to the extremes, relative to the distempered compositions which are extreme to extreme. Even if the parts suffer together, the injury of one part is lessened as it reaches all through the body. To another, it must be said that this is understood while the natural constitution of the time exists, as is supposed in the section on **Crises**, when signs of fever are placed. And similarly, it is said concerning an unfortunate constellation; for the physician does not have to consider this, but the astrologer. [See] the first section, and the fourth, first, and third *Fen*.

### DISTINCTION CXXX.

That it is a task to purge a **convalescent** <note>someone recovering from illness</note> is shown by the tenth [book] of the *Almansor* <note>Rhazes' *Liber ad Almansorem*, a major medical encyclopedia</note>, the first of the practice, and the fourth of the *Secta*. Furthermore, if something seems more present, it is not because something else is less. Moreover, it seems that nature in a time of health is better able to evacuate what is superfluous than in a time of sickness or a comparable disposition; but then it cannot. Hence, in the first section: evacuation alone is not complete; rather, without a doubt, a cleansing and impression remains from the superfluity of any digestion. Similarly, if nature in a time of health needs evacuation, since it is much stronger then, there will be much more need at the hour of convalescence; for it is still weakened by the sharpness of the disease. But it needs it in health, which is shown by the fact that evacuation is given to almost all bodies every year. **Distinction 130.** Also, in a convalescent, the blood is scanty according to the *Tegni*. But due to the scantiness of it, an increase of other humors follows. These require education/removal since they are foreign. Likewise, the whole body in a convalescent turns out colder. From this follows a bad digestion, since digestion is perfected by heat. By a bad digestion, superfluous humors are generated, which are hateful to nature and in need of removal. Therefore, a convalescent needs evacuation. To the contrary: in the fourth [book] of the *Secta*, a convalescent should be prohibited from evacuations, and properly from sexual intercourse.
