<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether people recovering from illness (convalescents) should be given purgative drugs or undergo bloodletting. It draws heavily on the authority of Isaac Judaeus, Almansor (Rhazes), and Haly Abbas, distinguishing between a "true" recovery and an incomplete one.</meta>

### On the Purgation of Convalescents

**Isaac Judaeus** still maintains in the fourth book of *On Fevers* that recovery cannot occur unless a good <term>crisis</term><note>A "crisis" in medieval medicine was the turning point of a disease, where the body's "nature" successfully expelled the "corrupt matter" causing the illness.</note> has preceded it. But a convalescent has already declined from the peak of the disease, since they are outside the initial period of sickness (as noted in Chapter 3a). Through a praiseworthy crisis, all superfluous matter is led out. Therefore, if a convalescent is evacuated—either of blood, which is not expedient since there is little good blood left in the body, or of other resisting humors—it is harmful. One should not use those humors as targets, since <term>medicine</term><note>The author refers specifically to "pharmacy" or purgative drugs here.</note> is of the nature of poison (Book 20, section a). This especially prostrates the body and the stomach, particularly because convalescents remain very weak.

Furthermore, a person is consumed by the sickness during convalescence. Hence, in the simple parts of the body, they are drier because their <term>virtues</term><note>The "virtues" were the innate biological powers—such as the "attractive," "retentive," and "expulsive" powers—that kept organs functioning.</note> are weaker. One who is in this state does not need evacuation, but rather "addition" (restoration). Therefore, a convalescent does not need to be purged.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that a convalescent is what is called a **"neutral body"** rising from illness. This status is fourfold, considered either by reason of age—and this is twofold: either the earlier stage, and thus a **child**, or the later stage, and then an **old man** or an **elder** (for a youth is in the middle of their strength)—or by reason of disposition. This also happens in two ways: either the future state, and thus one **falling ill**, or the past state, and then the **convalescent**. These individuals require at least two days of careful management by the regimen, as noted in Distinction 130, so that a sudden change does not overthrow their nature and force them back into the disease. Let their regimen be handled with all solicitude and caution, especially for those whose crisis was minimal or diminished. This applies both to the administration of the <term>six non-natural things</term><note>The "six non-naturals" were the factors of lifestyle that doctors controlled: air, food/drink, sleep/wakefulness, motion/rest, evacuation/repletion, and passions of the mind.</note> and the application of medicines if expedient, as taught in the tenth book of **Almansor’s** *Practice* (Books 1 and 4, Chapter 3a). What evacuation is, and how often it should be performed, is shown in Distinction 164, which here refers to the taking of blood and the drawing out of other humors.

<margin>Chapter 3, Distinction</margin>

Regarding the second point, it should be known that the common operations of practitioners often purge the convalescent, and especially the **unskilled**. This happens for two reasons: either because not only the physicians, but the sellers of medicines, wish to appear as if they are doing something to receive higher rewards—waiting to take more (as noted in Book 11 of *On Method*). Their defect will soon be apparent. They also err because they frequently purge after a crisis when they do not yet perfectly recognize that the person is a convalescent. Furthermore, the "nature" of the body, exhausted by the peak of the disease, is further prostrated. This is because there is nothing so powerful as a sudden evacuation that battles against nature. A drug also excites a laborious and "wicked disposition" in the person.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that first of all, one must distinguish between types of convalescents. From this, the truth will be shown. First, it should be known that some recover from an **immaterial** illness, and others from a **material** one <note>An "immaterial" illness was caused by a simple change in heat or cold (dyscrasia), while a "material" illness involved an actual excess of a humor like phlegm or bile.</note>. And either type can be twofold: there is the **certain** (or true) convalescent, and the **uncertain** (or untrue).

The **true** convalescent is the one whose crisis was praiseworthy in every way and whose recovery followed all the good conditions assigned in Distinction 103, or in whom almost no symptoms of the disease remain. The **untrue** is the opposite: one in whom signs remain or are diminished, such as thirst, dryness of the mouth, lack of appetite, and disgust (as found in the text of the *Epidemics* and the discourses on crises, Book 4, Chapter 3a). This distinction resolves the contradictions we encounter. For instance, in one regimen a bath is recommended, but in the tenth book of **Almansor** it is denied. This is because if the convalescent is "certain," they can bathe—especially if they are accustomed to it and their illness was one of "boiling" and "drying." But the "untrue" convalescent should not bathe at all.

Furthermore, it should be known (Chapter 30) that a "certain" convalescent does not need the evacuation of blood or any other humor, nor even an alteration of the body. This is confirmed because "those things which are judged and have been judged [by a crisis] should not be moved, nor should one make a new pharmacy or any other provocation" (Aphorisms, Book 1). A true convalescent has been "judged" by nature. Also, no one whose blood is good and scarce should be purged in any way, since the drawing of blood requires an abundance. Evacuation is a force that clears out a multitude; but a certain convalescent lacks this multitude because of the preceding illness and crisis. Their "animal and vital spirits" and their simple parts are drier, their virtues are weaker, and their whole body is colder.

Furthermore: **Whatever bodies are pure do not need evacuation.** Since "it is difficult to medicate bodies that are in good condition" (Galen), it is dangerous for them. In those with healthy flesh, it causes a **spasm**. This is because, according to **Galen**, when a medicine does not find its proper humor to attract (such as bile, phlegm, or melancholy), it seeks out the blood and melts the flesh to attract something from it. Therefore, if every convalescent were to be purged, then every crisis and every evacuation performed by nature would be imperfect. This would be a ridiculous thing to say, since nature always leads toward perfection unless hindered. Therefore, a certain convalescent does not need evacuation, nor any alteration, since no "dyscrasia" (imbalance) remains in them.

If, however, the convalescent is **"untrue,"** they do need evacuation, because they did not have a crisis or had an imperfect one. Rather, their illness only seemed to quiet down for one of these reasons:
1. The alignment or aspect of the **planets**.
2. The heterogeneity of the matter: such as when sharp and thin matter gathers first, and then thick and slow matter follows.
3. Because of **opiated** (numbing) matter that prevents putrefaction.
4. The matter falling into an "insensible" part of the body (as when nature carries it to the lungs).
5. Accidents of the soul that create "good hope," such as an **immense confidence in the physician** (Distinction 135).
6. The nature of the disease itself, such as "hepatic dysentery," which often seems to quiet down even without the fever ending, only to return again soon.

In such cases, perhaps the time is right. The illustrious authorities testify to this; hence **Almansor** says: "If anything remains of the bad accidents, let a vein be opened or diminished, or give things that extinguish it." **Haly Abbas** also observes: "If signs of blood are manifest in him, diminish and lead out the blood, for the work and strength require it; one rising from disease needs an increase of good blood." But if there are signs of bile or another humor, the body should be loosened with a subtle laxative, such as **cassia fistula**, **violets**, and similar light things. Hence: "Perhaps the malice of the blood will compel you to help the patient, because of what remained in him from the ashiness of bad humors." It is better that this be done gently and not suddenly, and especially...

->**Whether vomiting benefits the Eyes.**<-

When sweat increases, it is expedient to perform a small **bloodletting**<note>original: "minutio," the practice of opening a vein to restore the balance of humors.</note>. Perhaps one also requires evacuation, and a "subtle flux of the belly" <note>diarrhea</note> is more suitable. This is supported by the fact that matter left behind after a <term>crisis</term> returns on the sixth day, as noted in the *Epidemics* <note>Referring to the "Epidemics" of Hippocrates with Galen's commentary.</note>. For diseases that signify a lingering presence after the crisis are prone to relapse. As I translated from the Cretan authors at the beginning: it is not a small matter if material is saved after a crisis when that crisis was not "laudable" <note>A "laudable" crisis was a perfect turning point where the body successfully expelled all disease-causing matter.</note>, or if no evacuation preceded it, as many signs indicate. 

The disposition of the convalescing and the elderly is similar. But many elderly people require evacuation because "crude" <note>undigested or raw</note> superfluities collect within them. Likewise, one must evacuate bodies that are not pure; for according to the ancient saying: "The more you nourish impure bodies, the more you harm them." <margin>Plato</margin> This is like nourishing "impure souls"—the more you instruct them, the more you harm them, as **Plato** says in the *Politics* and **Galen** in the first book. However, some convalescents are "impure" and also require nourishment to restore the strength of their <term>virtues</term>. Therefore, it is expedient to evacuate a convalescent, specifically through <term>pharmacy</term> <note>purgative drugs</note> and the extraction of choleric humors. Yet, for a true convalescent, this is not always true. One must still alter the body after the illness or address the material remains. According to the rule: "Those having one common precept should first cut off each cause, and then come to the illness that resulted from that cause," such as a "bad complexions" <note>An imbalance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> left over from the previous sickness.

Regarding the first point, it appeared what should be said. Regarding the other, it must be said that evacuation is not part of the proper administration of the **six non-natural things** <note>The "six non-naturals" were the foundations of medieval health: air, food/drink, sleep/wake, motion/rest, evacuation/repletion, and passions of the mind.</note>, among which **exercise** is numbered. Exercise makes our internal heat "grow young" and forces superfluities to breathe out through the pores. This occurs by necessity. Therefore, an evacuation happens through "invisible pores" rather than through the manifest openings of nature or art. A true convalescent requires this kind of ordered evacuation. As it says in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Art of Medicine," a foundational textbook.</note>: "If they become much better for this, they may gradually reach their accustomed works." For Nature, though it lacks a mind or intellect, does not expel superfluity unless it perceives a harm to itself. Yet, there is a certain instinct and order in Nature, directed by "intelligences," by which it rightly reaches its ends. 

Regarding the other point: even if these bodies do not fail manifesty in their actions (so that they fall within the common range of health), they are still "neutral" <note>In Galenic medicine, the "neutral" state is a third condition between health and disease.</note>. Because they are full of superfluities, they require evacuation to avoid future danger. This does not apply to a "true" convalescent. 

Regarding the other point: **blood** is understood here as the "bloody mass" in which all humors exist proportionally, not as a single humor separated from the others. 

Regarding the other point: bad digestion does not happen because of this, provided that nourishment and other necessary things are administered correctly to the convalescent. If blood and spirits are few, they are invigorated, and the heat of true convalescents becomes continuous so that digestion is rendered more perfect over time. 

Regarding the first point of the other part: **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> speaks of a "certain" (true) convalescent. Or, he prohibits the convalescent from evacuations, and specifically from **sexual intercourse**. <margin>+ p^.</margin> Hence **Haly Abbas** <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note> says: "Intercourse should be greatly avoided, for it evacuates good matter from the body." Therefore, the virtue <note>bodily strength</note> is thinned and eventually dissolved entirely. 

Regarding the next point: **Isaac Judaeus** <note>A 10th-century Jewish physician and philosopher.</note> speaks of the aforementioned "decline" of the disease which a laudable crisis indicated, but not an incomplete one. 

Regarding the other: blood is good and scarce in a true convalescent, but not in the opposite case. For it is said by **Aristotle** that the "malice" <note>bad quality</note> of the blood sometimes forces you to perform **phlebotomy** <note>bloodletting</note>, even though phlebotomy should normally be done for a "multitude" <note>excess volume</note> of blood. Similarly, although many medicines are poisonous, not all are; some are "blessed." It was also said that the flux of the belly should be subtle. And because **vomiting** is the strongest of evacuations, I find it is least used when things are "expressed" <note>forced out</note>. Finally, that series of arguments applies to a true convalescent. A "non-true" convalescent—who is naturally drier in their simple parts—is nevertheless "moistened" by an accident of many superfluities that have been minimally or imperfectly evacuated.

### DIFFERENCE CXXXI.

->**Whether vomiting benefits the eyes.**<-

->It seems that vomiting benefits the eyes.<-
->Because whatever clarifies the sight helps the eyes.<-
This is because sight is their primary function. Again, whatever draws out harmful matter and fumes benefits the eyes. <margin>What vomiting is</margin> This is what vomiting does, as it is a strong evacuation, drawing from the lower parts and "eradicating" from the upper parts. Furthermore, whatever is done by the **natural virtue** <note>The body's innate biological power.</note> is beneficial, as it is one of the dispensations of the animal virtues. And this is vomiting, for it happens through natural virtue. 

Additionally, the eye is perfected by a **lucid and ethereal spirit** <note>Medieval optical theory suggested the eye functioned via a "visual spirit" made of light or fire.</note>. Therefore, **Plato** posits that the eye is of the nature of fire. But through vomiting, the superfluities that impede and disturb this "lucid spirit" are led out, especially since vomiting is the strongest of evacuations. Also, whatever benefits eye pains helps the eyes themselves. Purgative medicine does this, and it is also achieved through vomiting. Therefore, vomiting helps the eyes.

**The Opposite View:** <margin>Opposite</margin> On the contrary, it is shown that vomiting is harmful. Whatever leads matter through the "nobler parts" <note>such as the brain or lungs</note> toward a suffering part harms it. Vomiting does this, as it leads matter through the nobler respiratory parts toward the "animal parts" where the eye is located. Matter is also moved toward the eyes in every "heavy" state. The stomach is assigned to **attraction**, while the intestines are for **expulsion**, according to **Mesue** <note>A famous Christian physician in the Abbasid Caliphate.</note> on pharmacy. Also, that which requires the eyes to be protected during the act must be harmful to them. And this is vomiting; for in the fourth book of **Almansor** <note>The "Liber ad Almansorem" by the Persian physician Rhazes.</note>, it is commanded that during vomiting, the eyes should be bound with two pads or small cloths rolled into circles. Again, what harms the ears harms the eyes, since the sensory parts of the body are interconnected. But vomiting harms the ears (as it often causes deafness). Therefore, vomiting harms the eyes. To this, indeed, the "subversion of the soul" <note>This refers to nausea, which was often described as a psychological or spiritual distress alongside the physical urge to vomit.</note> and nausea are proportionate, though they are lesser in degree. For "subversion" is an expulsive movement that is not yet accompanied by the actual expulsion of matter, as occurs in vomiting. Second, the truth shall be shown so that the discordance introduced by the authors may finally be reconciled.

<margin>Things harmful to the eyes:</margin>
Regarding the first, it must be known that these things weaken and make the eyes grow old: Excessively harsh air, and especially in its qualities; wild winds, particularly when moving against the eyes; constant gazing at one thing, especially a small thing, such as the constant inspection of small letters or shapes; and bright white things, especially when they are in motion. Much sun is hot for the eyes; hence some have been nearly blinded by a long inspection of the sun while watching an eclipse. Dust, smoke, and excessive weeping; dry, sharp, and heavy foods; vapors from difficult digestion; and drinking too much followed by a long sleep; and drunkenness. Also foods such as: leeks, onions, cress, arugula, dill, *andachocba* <note>Likely a transliteration of an Arabic herb, possibly a type of endive or chicory.</note>, basil, and especially mustard, fenugreek, lentils, beans, and cabbage.

<margin>Chicken heads</margin>
**Avenzoar** <note>Ibn Zuhr, an influential Andalusian physician.</note> says that the heads of chickens have a property that causes blindness, specifically such that one cannot see after the setting of the sun; just as they said that the brains of chickens increase the intellect. Also salt, much dry or salted meat, gross or viscous fat (especially from pork), and excessive labor of both the body and the soul. Likewise, frequent sexual intercourse is a most harmful thing, especially upon a vaporous repletion <note>A full stomach</note> and particularly after dinner. However, the following preserve and strengthen the health of the eyes, being the opposites of those listed: especially eye-washes <note>original: "colliria"</note> prepared from tutty <term>thucia</term><note>Zinc oxide, used for centuries in eye salves.</note>, antimony, the juice of fennel, and pomegranate. Also from the gall of birds of prey, goats, and fish, especially if exposed to the heat for 50 days. Frequent foot-baths <note>original: "pediatio"</note> after digestion help, as they divert vapors from the eyes to the skin. Submerging the eyes in clear water, looking at green things and polished mirrors (though not in the sun's rays), and the practice of reading medium-sized letters strengthens the sight. Also anointing with the fat of a serpent and the eating of its flesh; yet this is to be feared <note>likely due to its potency or potential for poisoning if prepared incorrectly</note>.

<margin>Dove eggs. Turnips:</margin>
**Avenzoar** also commends the regular eating of dove eggs boiled with turnips, and young pigeons cooked in them, and similarly chickens cooked with them in the summer, without their heads and legs. Whence in the fifth book: Turnips have a wonderful property for illuminating the eyes. But perhaps, I say, they ought to harm them, especially when they hurt the stomach, because their vapor fills the head with wind and multiplies <term>rheum</term><note>Thin, watery discharge from the eyes or nose, believed to be a waste product of the brain.</note> in the eyes. Or perhaps you will say they creep downwards and provoke urine. Thus, the eye is harmed by many things and needs many helps, both because it is of a weak, watery reception, and because it is almost without skin and exposed to the elements, and most of all because it arises from the brain as if from the body's chimney.

Regarding this, it must be known beforehand whether, when vomiting is performed, there is already some lesion in the eyes or not. If there is, it will be either through "idiopathy" <note>A disease starting in the eyes themselves.</note> or from the brain, or through "sympathy" <note>A condition caused by another organ.</note> transmitted to them from the stomach via crude, undigested fumes and vapors. This often happens not only to the eyes but to the whole head from the interior. Furthermore, the vomiting may be a strong force instituted at the proper time of purging (such as the beginning of summer), drawing from the whole body by the effect of a strong medicine, or a particular evacuation for light cleansing, which is celebrated in the stomach once a month or at most twice, provided the precise time and number of days is observed, lest it become a bad and inevitable habit for nature. Let it also be after the fullness of food, especially when the vomiting is difficult; for to vomit without a full stomach is hard and cannot be done without great labor and effort. **Almansor** and the fourth book of **Macer** say: one should eat and drink various poorly-chewed, sweet, and greasy foods, and after an hour take a decoction of radish, orach, and bulbs, and then vomit.

One harm of vomiting occurs during the act itself, and another after it is done. These differ according to the "complexion" <note>The specific balance of humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) in an individual.</note>, form, or flexibility of the stomach's opening, and whether the habit is intense or relaxed, as well as the hour and the region. For he for whom vomiting is most beneficial is the choleric man, as noted in the fourth book. Or perhaps there is no lesion at all. Now, from these points, let the harm or benefit to the eyes from vomiting be shown. If no lesion exists in them, it must be said that vomiting harms them in every way, as it brings disturbing materials and vapors toward them, propelling them outward, just as when vomiting is performed for pains of the joints or kidneys while the eyes are healthy. But if a lesion has reached the eye from itself or from the brain, vomiting harms it even more, both during the act and after, as it raises the aforementioned parts toward them and affects the head. Therefore, it is forbidden in headaches, especially strong ones, when the pain is not caused by "sympathy" with the stomach. As it is in the first part of the third book: Vomiting is from...

It is also prescribed in the fifth book of the *Theory* that a patient suffering from melancholy caused by humor contained in the stomach should celebrate vomiting. The truth, therefore, is elicited from these: that vomiting harms any passions specifically belonging to the head. And this statement is verified in the first book of the *Practice* already cited: "But if damage happens to the eyes through a passion specifically of the stomach, then vomiting is the procedure," just as in other such passions transferred to the head. And this is indeed well-reasoned and apparent. Yet it must be noted that vomiting is harmful because it directs matter and vapors into the brain and eyes. And therefore, care must be taken so that little harm is caused by it; it should be a partial, weak, and infrequent vomiting, performed in one prepared for it. It is beneficial, however, after it has occurred, because it leads out the matter and consequently removes the "raw smoke" <note>Noxious vapors from undigested food.</note> that causes the injury to the eyes. For the cure is completed by removing the cause. And the statements of the authors cited are to be understood in this way. From which it is also clearly preferable to use vomiting, at least after it has occurred, when the matter is in the lower parts and especially in the part that contains it. And know that unless the humor existing in the stomach that harms the eyes is led out, they remain subject to it. Whence in the fourth book of the *Aphorisms*: for those having a "suffusion" <note>A cataract or clouding of the vision.</note> of the eyes from the stomach, **Galen** specifically offered "Hiera Picra" <note>A famous ancient purgative made of aloe and herbs; the name means "Holy Bitter."</note>. And for those suffering from lethargy, he commanded it in more distant parts. These, however, require the stomach to be purged downwards. Because of this, even if it now appears what should be said to the first point, to the other it is said: that if it leads out the harmful matter and smoke existing in the stomach, it helps—at least after the fact—but not for those things which the head or eyes would attempt to lead out through vomiting, since the harming agent would not be led out this way. For it is better for the matter to be drawn downwards. For the upper parts are more effectively emptied through the lower ones than vice versa. To the other point it must be said: that vomiting is not said there to be completed by the "natural virtue" <note>The body's innate biological power.</note> because its act would be entirely natural. But it is said in contrast to sneezing, which is done by the "animal" power, and coughing, which is done by the "vital" power. For vomiting is caused by a thing harming the stomach internally.

---

<margin>Whether in hotter and drier air it is beneficial to strew poplar.</margin>
By its nature, it strives to lead out the vomit. Since this occurs only in the outer tunic, it is a work of the "natural" powers, because in it there are wide, spread-out fibers <note>original: "villi"</note>. In the inner tunic, however, there are long, attractive fibers. In Distinction 46: It is very difficult in respect to bowel movements, because both tunics of the intestines are involved, with the fibers of both being wide. And therefore, a laxative medicine is more often returned as vomit than the other way around. In Distinction 141: To the other point, it appeared that it clears the "spirit" <note>The "pneuma" or subtle fluid thought to inhabit the nerves.</note> when the cause of the eye injury is a raw smoke sent into them from the stomach, and not when the matter is in the brain. For then, rather, the opposite occurs.
<margin>**Mesue**. Physiognomy.</margin>
To the other point it must be said that **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a Persian physician.</note> in his *Practice* explains that through "pharmacy" he means a flux of the belly; he says it benefits phlegmatic, choleric, and melancholic pains via the belly. And regarding those things which belong to the other part, it is clear that although these things happen and are bad in the act of vomiting, they are nevertheless beneficial in the becoming, when the matter is led out of the belly, and are tolerable enough compared to the injury already present in the eyes. Since, therefore, nothing helps without some harm, as per the eleventh book of *On Medical Issues*, it behooves the physician to be sharp, practiced, and diligent to discern between both, so that he may prefer the benefit over the harm.

## CHAPTER XXXII.

That poplar leaves should be strewn in hotter and drier surroundings is shown, because many of the Latin practitioners commonly command it in their work. Again, as the place is, so nature works. <margin>On Inspiration and Respiration</margin> Whence in *On Inspiration and Respiration*: The nature of matter is such as things are in it; for those in water are moist, those in earth are dry, and those in air are hot. But the poplar is found in moist and watery places, so that it does not germinate in hot or dry places. And it must be noted that it cools and moistens the air. Such indeed is the poplar. For it moistens moderately, according to **Dioscorides** <note>Ancient Greek physician and botanist.</note>. It also cools, which its resin <note>original: "karabre" (amber/resin)</note> shows to be cold. Whence in the second book of the *Practice*: "Karabre" <margin>Karabre or Kakabre</margin> is cold and dry. Another thing which is placed in cold medicines as a base is similar. Of this plant, certain extremities are called "poplar eyes" <note>The resinous buds of the poplar tree.</note>. For they are used in the "Populeon" ointment, noted by some as a principal ingredient which gives its name to the whole compound. It is cold, for it takes away heat and provides sleep according to **Nicolaus**. Therefore, poplar leaves are to be strewn in the air surrounding us. On the opposite side: <margin>Opposite</margin> Because this should not be applied to hotter and drier air, as it is not strong enough to specifically change it to coldness. Such is the poplar, since it is one of the things growing from the earth. For in them, actual heat is not found—according to the fifth book of the *Collections*—but only in animals. It will therefore be in "potentiality," and then it will not be able to cause a change in the air, since every action is completed by that which has "actuality," according to the ninth book of the *Metaphysics*. For it is not applied to bodies that have heat. Likewise, none of the distinguished physicians, whom it is not right to call insufficient, teach the strewing of these leaves in the air. Rather, they teach certain others that are cold and moist, such as vines, willows, myrtles, mastic trees, roses, violets, water-lilies, and especially when collected with the dew. Whence in the ninth book of *On Medical Issues*: Flowers and leaves...

<meta>This page continues the medical and dietary discourse from the previous page, shifting from the properties of amber and resins to the practical application of nutrition in the treatment of various diseases, specifically debating the timing of meals during acute and chronic illnesses based on the theories of Hippocrates and Galen.</meta>

<margin>
What hurts the healthy <gloss>sometimes</gloss> benefits the sick.
</margin>

...and before the "peak" <note>The *status* or climax of an illness.</note> of the disease, when the feverish heat and symptoms are intensifying. However, moist diets are beneficial for all those suffering from fevers. Conversely, what hurts the healthy also hurts the sick <gloss>namely, in reality</gloss>. But food hurts the healthy, therefore it also hurts the sick. Whatever hurts the sick requires a cutting off <note>Meaning a reduction or total abstinence from food.</note>. And thus, we must conclude that food must be given continuously in every disease. Regarding this, it must first be known that there are 72 different kinds of diseases. However, for our present purposes, disease exists in two forms:

<margin>
Twofold Disease:
1. Acute
2. Chronic
</margin>

**Acute** and **Chronic** <note>original: "cronicus"</note> or long-lasting. Indeed, an **acute disease** ends with great danger <note>original: "periculosus"</note> and quickly reaches its peak. This type also exists in two forms. One is called "simply acute," the limit of which is defined by **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Ypocrate"</note> as the fourteenth day. The other is "relatively acute," which is multifaceted. Either it slightly exceeds the 14th day—and then it is the type **Hippocrates** mentioned in the first book of the *Prognostics*, which he said terminates on the 40th day—or it is moderately acute, terminating on the 27th or 34th day. According to **Galen**, an acute disease is one that passes with a transition or change within 14 days; this is further diversified by its approach to the 14th day, such as those that reach a crisis <note>original: "creticat"; refers to the *crisis*, the turning point of a disease.</note> on the 12th or 9th day. Or, it may be judged by its approach to the beginning of the illness, such as those judged on the 3rd, 4th, or 5th day. These are called "very acute" or "highly acute." Thus, they terminate in the middle of these days, such as the 7th, which is called "very acute" or "peracute," and even the 4th.

<margin>
Oribasius does not explain the Lord <gloss>Hippocrates</gloss> correctly.
</margin>

For it should not be explained as **Oribasius** and certain others say, that an acute illness is terminated in 14 "critical days" <note>Days on which the disease's outcome is decided.</note> so that they might agree with the first statement of the first book: that in 40 days, 14 crises occur. These 40 critical days are: the 4th, 7th, 9th, 11th, 14th, 17th, 21st, 28th, 27th, 31st, 34th, 37th, and 40th. Furthermore, to bolster his error, **Oribasius** wrongly introduces the idea that **pleurisy** <note>An inflammation of the lungs' lining.</note> either terminates on the 14th day or becomes "empyemic" <note>original: "empica"; characterized by a collection of pus.</note> on the 40th day, or dissolves, or turns into **phthisis** <note>Tuberculosis or a wasting of the body.</note>. Therefore, a disease is not resolved by a distinction on the 14th day, but rather concludes or extends to the 40th. But one must say the opposite of this according to **Galen**. I shall set down the rule to teach: No acute illness passes the 14th day with equal intensity. If it is not severe in the first days and the second crisis, it is a chronic illness that is sometimes failing. Also, the aforementioned series of days is forced by those who use the term "day" equivocally. Again, if they take the true critical days, there would only be nine up to the 40th: namely the 7th, 9th, 11th, 14th, 17th, 20th, 27th, 34th, and 40th. If they add the 24th, 31st, and 37th, there would still only be twelve and not fourteen. But if you wish to collect all the days—both the true critical days and the intervening ones—then there would be many more than 14, according to **Oribasius**: namely, besides the 1st, the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th, 11th, 13th, 17th, 18th, 20th, 21st, 24th, 27th, 31st, 34th, 37th, and 40th. **Oribasius** also errs because he places the first day as a critical day, whereas the first period of time is on the 4th day according to **Hippocrates**, or on the 3rd by virtue of that same rule.

<margin>
Ephemeral fever does not have a crisis. Diocles opposed this.
</margin>

For **ephemeral fever** <note>A fever lasting only one day.</note>, even if it terminates on the first day, does not have a crisis, since a crisis only occurs in an acute and dangerous disease. **Diocles**, however, posited that it does have a crisis. Although unity is the potential of every number according to arithmetic, it does not suffice here where the act and the form are required. Perhaps, however, the first day very rarely has a crisis.

<margin>
Chronic
</margin>

Regarding the fourth [rule] of the first [book]: **Tertian fever** <note>A fever that recurs every other day.</note> is sometimes resolved in one paroxysm <note>A sudden attack or increase in symptoms.</note> because of the thinness of the matter, in which vomiting or a cleansing of the bowels occurs. A **chronic disease**, however, reaches its peak slowly, lacking great intensity, and extends beyond the 40th day—to 60, 80, or 120—and then runs through months and finally through years. These are governed better by the soul, or rather by the phases of the moon according to **Galen** and **Ptolemy**. What the food of the sick should be and how it is distinguished is written in what follows. Here, food is taken as a medicine. The "peak" <note>original: "status"</note> is one of the four periods of a healthy recovery from disease, as it is divided into the beginning, the increase, the peak, and the decline.

<margin>
Food. The 3rd stage: the peak.
</margin>

The peak is indeed the hour in which the disease remains in one disposition in all its parts. This, like the other three times, is distinguished in several ways. One is according to the struggle and fury of the symptoms; whence the first aphorism: the peak is nothing other than when the labors and symptoms are at their greatest. Or, it is the greatest point of the sickness, as in **synochal fevers** <note>Continuous non-intermittent fevers.</note>. Fourthly, the peak is the hour in which a vehement battle occurs between nature and the matter <note>The "matter" or "humors" causing the disease.</note>, and the victory of one of them over the other appears; it is the hour of the fight. Others also distinguish it based on whether the matter is digested or the opposite, as with the other periods of time. Thus: "there at the peak, the trace of digestion or its opposite is completed." In most diseases, the distinction of the periods of the disease coincides with the intensity or remission of the symptoms and the digestion of the matter. In some, however, the distinction of the digestion of the matter precedes the distinction based on the labors and symptoms, as in **pleurisy** and **peripneumonia** <note>Inflammation of the lungs.</note>, according to the first book *On Crises*. Regarding this, it should be known that some speeches of **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and others seem to suggest that in a very acute illness, no food should be given until the peak. Others, however, command the opposite: that food be given twice. Of these, some say food should be given continuously from the beginning until the peak, as will appear in the arguments. Others say food should not be given until the third day has passed, then feeding every other day, as seen in the *Tegni* by **Thessalus**.

<margin>
Cornelius Celsus.
</margin>

Whence **Cornelius Celsus** says: There are two kinds of abstinence. One where the patient receives nothing; the other where he receives what is necessary.

<margin>
Plato.
</margin>

In the *Viaticum*, **Galen** was asked what the perfect medicine would be; he replied: **abstinence**. **Plato** says there are two types of abstinence: total and partial. The first is not to eat unless the appetite is great and vehement. The second is to use specific things that oppose the dominant elements. **Cornelius Celsus** adds: Most of the ancients fed the sick late, often on the fifth or sixth day. And perhaps that was permitted in **Thrace** or **Egypt** by reason of the climate.

<margin>
Asclepiades.
</margin>

**Asclepiades**, when he had exhausted the patient with drink for three days, intended to give food on the fourth day. For food is also given to the sick in a combined way; they are fed on even days, for then the paroxysms seemed to happen less frequently—not when the fever began, but when it had ceased. In Africa, however, because the climate allows for better digestion, there is no such rule...

### Whether there are some diseases for which no food should be given:

<margin>Indications of the physician's skill.</margin>
...there is a rightful necessity of cutting off food. For what reason should other foods be given in Africa? <note>original: "Affrica"; likely referring to the works of Constantinus Africanus or the specific climatic medical conditions of North Africa.</note> The explanation of these things will become clear from what is to be said. It must also be known that it is the task of the physician to weigh contrary indications to determine whether food is expedient, or whether it should not be given before the **peak** <note>The *status*, or the highest point of intensity in a disease.</note>. From these things, the truth shall arise. First, it must be known that an "indication," or a showing of the method of cure—by which the application of medicinal things to nature is examined—is a single, most general category: the opposition to the disease which brings about healing. This can be divided into two parts: the present disposition, which is called **illness**, and the previously held health, which is called **according to nature**. These are further divided into three types of indications.

<margin>The visible archetype.</margin>
One of these is taken from **natural things**. The second from

<margin>Indications of Nature which produce others.</margin>
**non-natural things**. And the third from those which are **contrary to nature**. From the first, it is taken in two ways: from the natural things themselves and their "annexes." Among the natural things, it is taken principally from the **virtue** <note>The *virtus* or "vital power" of the patient’s body to heal itself.</note>. For the indication of the virtue itself eclipses and hides all other indications. Indeed, it founds the highest of all intentions, such as the disposition of the humors and the substance of the flesh and the "spermatic" <note>Referring to the fundamental, structural tissues of the body.</note> parts. From the "annexes," indications are taken from age, sex, the quality or form of the body, and habit. For the substance itself is placed among natural things. From all these, the method of providing the thing indicated is gathered. Attention is also paid to the **region** and the **time**, such as one of the four seasons of the year, or a particular day or hour, or the environment—such as the constitution of the air during the rising of the **Dog Star** <note>The "Canicula" or Sirius; historically associated with the "dog days" of summer and increased risk of fever.</note>. From these, the indication is usually received by applying the opposite. Regarding those things which are contrary to nature:

<margin>From here concerning the nature of philosophy.</margin>
These are threefold: the **cause**, the **disease**, and the **accident** <note>The "accidens" or symptoms resulting from the disease.</note>. From these, the method of the power of cure is taken by opposites. For this reason, it must be known that whoever wishes to apply this work must be practiced in all these things and prudent by nature, so that by subtly considering the power of each indication and comparing them to one another, he may gather a single primary summary of the indications for the laboring patient, as described in the **eighth book of the *Method of Healing***.

<margin>8th book of the *Method*.</margin>
But above all other indications, as has appeared, is the significance of the **virtue**. For according to **Hippocrates**, nature itself is the healer of diseases; this is found in the beginning [of the *Aphorisms*] and the eighth book of the *Practica*. For the virtue is like money to be spent; the physician is like a merchant, and the healing of the disease is the profit arising from the trade. Food is also proportioned to the "stipends" <note>Wages or provisions provided for a journey.</note> of a pilgrimage; the sick person is the pilgrim, and the peak of the disease is the end of the journey. Wherefore it is suggested that the physician must use the virtue in such a way that, while health is always strengthened and introduced, the sickness is destroyed. Thus, he should order food for the patient, either by subtracting or adding what is necessary so that the patient may reach the "peak." Furthermore, it must be known that if the virtue is robust and the body is qualified by the aforementioned dispositions—even in an acute illness—all food except thin broth

---

should be denied until the **seventh day**. But so that this may be understood, the series of instructions forbidding the opening of veins on the same day <note>A reference to the "Diatritarii," a school of ancient physicians who waited three days before starting treatment.</note> agrees with this. **Galen** supposes in the first book of the *Regimen in Acute Diseases* two patients with pleurisy. One has these conditions: a dry complexion, in the prime of age, of a thick bodily quality, with large veins and strong virtue, accustomed to eating much food, living in a cold and humid region, having previously had a delightful and quiet lifestyle with many nourishing foods, and a robust stomach. The disease of pleurisy happened to him in a very cold winter. Let the other be of a humid complexion, a child, of a sparse habit with tiny veins and weak virtue, accustomed to assuming a large quantity of food but weary from the heat of summer, eating few and unusual foods such as vegetables and such things providing little nourishment, with a naturally weak stomach; and let the disease fall upon him in the heat of summer. For the first of these sick men, according to the beginning of his illness until the peak, one should not permit continuous nourishment until the **seventh day**, according to the opinion of the **Diatritarii** <note>original: "dyatritarīoz"; a medical sect that believed in treating patients in three-day cycles.</note> who do not grant food nor open a vein until the third day has passed. For it is first expedient for him to be governed only by drinks until the peak on the seventh day. For it is hoped the illness will not extend beyond that.

<margin>Physician of the Ancients.</margin>
He also says that he had long experience that this regimen would be very helpful. If the contrary should happen—namely, that one who should abstain until the peak is fed, while the other is fed continuously from the beginning—

<margin>Proven by reason.</margin>
both will die before the fourth day: one indeed "suffocated" by the food, the other with their virtue "prostrated." This is what **Aristotle** signifies in his own works. Thus, it is clear from the speech of **Hippocrates** and **Galen** that in an acute illness, it is sometimes not expedient to offer food until after the peak, when the virtue is strong and the other qualities are vehement. It is also seen from the opinion of **Galen** in the first book [of *Acute Diseases*] that in an acute case with strong virtue, it is not expedient to be fed. He shows this by reason: for in that time in which nature is intent on the vehement **digestion** of the humors, it ought not to be hindered by the digestion of food or other things, since a distracted operation would be disturbed in every way. But in an acute illness, nature from the beginning until the peak is entirely intent on the digestion of the matter, so that it may expel it at the peak, trusting in its own strength.

<margin>Page 4.</margin>
Furthermore, food hinders nature and intensifies and increases the disease; when food is the cause of this, it should not be administered, since nature must always be kept unharmed. Food hinders nature when it is given in these illnesses with strong virtue; although it may be a "friend" in one respect <note>i.e., as nourishment.</note>, it is an "enemy" in another respect, since it is a friend to the enemy <note>i.e., the disease or the excess matter.</note>. Nature is then distracted, converting toward the undigested matter. At that time, severe "accidents" <note>Symptoms.</note> of the nature of the disease and inflammations often occur, which prohibit feeding. Therefore, in such illnesses, food should be given only after the peak. However, because today men are more **delicate** than usual, devoted to the throat and luxury, as seen in the sixth [book], they are also weakened by nature from the start by their parents, as shown in the ninth. And because according to the ancients, "the sick err in thin diets," which is why they are more harmed, in modern times the regimen should not be the same as it was in antiquity.

<margin>The delicate people of today.</margin>

...to refine the diet. Indeed, one must yield even further so that the <term>vital force</term> <note>original: "virtus"; in medieval medicine, this refers to the body's innate strength and ability to function and heal.</note> remains, as mentioned in the previous distinction. For once, certain medicines were used because they were considered useful, which are now entirely rejected because they are disproportionate to the underlying nature. For a weak body cannot endure cures carried out through feedings as an aid, nor can weak **stomachs** resist accidental disturbances. 

But so that what has been said may shine more clearly, let the aforementioned indications be adapted to the purpose. For the natural parts

<margin>Note.</margin>
<margin>2</margin>
are traversed in order. If the vital force is weak, it is expedient to feed the patient, disregarding all other indications. For an indication 

<margin>3</margin>
taken from the vital force directs and conceals all others. But if the vital force is strong, let it be governed rightly by "subtiliating" <note>Refining or thinning the diet, usually by using light liquids instead of solid food.</note>, such as with **honey-water** or a **barley water**, whether thin or thick or thicker, according to whether the illness is more or less acute. 

If, however, the <term>complexion</term> <note>The balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) in an individual.</note> is hot and quite moist, it dissolves either gradually or quickly, as shown in Distinction 117. If the composition of the body is porous, and the humors and spirits are subtle, then right from the beginning, a somewhat thicker food must be continued until the "status" <note>The peak or plateau of the disease's intensity.</note>. Yet there are some such patients to whom food must be given both at the peak and in the hour of the worst **paroxysm** <note>The period of greatest severity in a fever or fit.</note>, fearing a failure of the vital force in the restoration of the spirits. This is according to the tenth book of *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "decio de inge."; Galen’s *Methodus Medendi* or *De Ingenio Sanitatis*.</note>. 

But if the opposite of these conditions exists, it is expedient to thin the food as much as possible. In a middle disposition, one should diet with moderation. This same thing must be observed on the part of the "instruments" <note>The organs of the body.</note>. For if it is the age of childhood—since infants and children tolerate feedings poorly, but old men do so easily—and if the sex is male, and the quality of the body is soft and porous, and the habit of eating is frequent (since it is necessary to govern nature according to habit, and not to suddenly alter even a bad habit), then for these, the food must not be thinned. Nor should it be thinned much in very acute illnesses, especially since the nature of such people is consumed by itself; food must be provided so that the <term>vital force</term> can reach the peak of the illness, like a traveler reaching the end of his journey. In the contrary disposition, the food should be thinner. In a middle disposition, feeding should be moderate. 

By reason of non-natural things: in a hot region during the summer time, since summer is a time of dissipation, one lacks food by constitution and by the hour of the heat. It will be necessary to feed more abundantly because of the great "resolution" <note>The "melting" or loss of bodily fluids and spirits due to heat.</note>, yet in small amounts and often, because a defect of the <term>vital force</term> prevents the digestion of much nourishment at a single serving. This is seen in the "emptiness" of the bodies of those from Ethiopia, as mentioned in the *Aphorisms*. In a cooler region or season, by reason of the constitution, food should be given according to the middle or moderate disposition. 

As for things "beside nature," such as the disease and its cause, it is never expedient to give food when the cause and the disease are intensified by it. Whence, in the first book of *Acute Diseases*: through food itself, no help is given in the disposition of the illness. For we say that food is the friend of nature and the matter [of the disease]. Indeed, in an "immaterial" illness <note>A disease not caused by a physical mass of humors, but by a simple quality like heat or cold.</note>, it is appropriate that food acts not only as its matter but rather as a medicine acting by its quality, unless perhaps the illness itself is "consumptive." 

As for the "accidents" <note>The symptoms or secondary effects of a disease.</note>, it must be said that since they are threefold and diverse in many forms, they shall be ordered as declared in the fifth Distinction. Regarding the fourth point:

<margin>Ψ</margin>
As to the first, it has been seen what should be said. As to the other, it is said 

according to the commentator <note>Likely referring to Averroes or another major commentator on Galen.</note>, who calls these "spurious" and "wandering" fevers, and says that they do not have a peak. He did not want a precise amount of food to be administered in these unless the "error" <note>The irregular cycle of the fever.</note> ceases, choosing and observing the time to begin. And then these must be met competently, as has been said. 

As to other things brought in by **Galen**, it now appears what should be said, since he speaks of very acute illness when the vital force is strong and the conditions are proportional and corresponding to it. To the first of the contrary arguments, it must be said: **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Y." for Ypocras.</note> speaks more generally of simply acute illnesses, and not of the "very acute" or "specially acute" in which, as shown, food must be given continuously from the beginning until the peak, because the <term>vital force</term> is not strong enough to reach the peak without food for so long a time. In these, he warns (with the conditions added by **Galen**) lest the patient's path be left to the danger of death; thus, food should be given without the imposition of a fasting day. 

To the other, it must be said that this is verified in a natural complexion or in a habit that should not be changed, but not in a diseased disposition—especially when a change or "supposition" intervenes in this disposition, and not in nature or a habit made natural by long use. To the other, it must be said that moist diets, insofar as they are moist, always benefit a person with a fever, since a fever is a bad "dry" complexion needing moisture; but this is not always because of the material of the food or its softness, as shown before. For in food, one must attend not only to the quality but also to the substance and the quantity. To the other, it is said to be **true** regarding a change falling into nature where naturalness exists in both, but not regarding "unnaturalness," since the sick, because of the matter existing in them beside nature, can hunger and abstain with less harm than healthy people who lack such matter.

### DISTINCTION 134.

<margin>1</margin> **W**hich regimen in diet precedes by **thickening** and not by **thinning**; for example, that at the beginning of a disease a thin diet is provided, and thereafter it is thickened. This is shown by **Hippocrates** in the first book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*: when the sputum is of greater quantity than the residue, more [diet] should be applied until the peak. But then the illness is in its "increase" or at its "peak" when signs of digestion appear, which are shown at these times.

But wine is a "thick" diet compared to the drink which ought to be given to those with fever. Similarly, in the twelfth book of the same, once the matter is digested, "fleshy" foods are allowed, such as **rooster testicles**, **roasted pig brain**, and **egg yolks**, which are a thick diet. <meta>This page continues the discussion on dietary choices in medical treatment, specifically weighing the decision to provide a "subtle" (thin, liquid-based) diet versus a "gross" (thick, substantial) diet based on the progression of a fever and the patient’s vital strength. ->Whether a Dietary Regimen Should Proceed by Thickening.<-

# Whether a Dietary Regimen Should Proceed by Thickening.

In the fifth and fourth days of fever, it is right that the regimen should incline toward a certain **refining** <note>original: "subtiliatõez"; the process of making the diet lighter or more liquid to aid digestion during illness.</note> of the patient, especially in the early stages of quartan fevers. And this means they should abstain from meat; then the diet is ordered to be thickened. This same reasoning seems to apply to the cause of a six-day fever and similar illnesses. Likewise, in the cure of paralysis up to the fourteenth day. Furthermore, on the first, third, ninth, eleventh, and twenty-fourth days, abstinence from food and wine is ordered at the beginning, or at least a major reduction of them. Therefore, a refining of the diet proceeds either by reason of the <term>vital force</term> <note>The body's innate strength and ability to function.</note>, the disease, the cause, or the symptoms. But none of these seem to apply here: not by reason of the vital force, since it is strong at the beginning and does not need the support of food; yet at the peak of the illness, it is needed because the body emerges weak. Nor is it purely because of the disease, since the diet is formed not only for the subtraction of strength but rather for the opposition of the illness. For the diet of the sick must be qualified more by opposition. According to that ancient rule: for all those suffering from fevers, they prefer this diet...

<margin>~</margin>
But at the peak of the disease, when the sharpness of the illness rises most, a diet more opposed to it will be necessary; but this opposition cannot occur unless it is prescribed in a great quantity. For an agent does not operate unless it is associated with a large quantity. Therefore, it is for this reason, not the cause; for in the beginning, the cause is greater, especially in those who are to be saved. In the peak, however, it is less. If the diet is then too rich, it will nourish the impurity of the body. This is against the teaching of <term>Hippocrates</term>: "In bodies that are not pure, the more you nourish them, the more you harm them." Likewise, you will cause the matter to become raw by a multitude of food. In the peak, whatever happens follows; for the causes are not in the entry. Regarding symptoms that dissolve the vital force, <term>Galen</term> in the first book of the *Aphorisms* orders food to be given soon. But symptoms dissolve the strength; for the paroxysms are noted especially at the peak, since they are weaker at the beginning and stronger toward the peak. Again, as it is in the particular times of the disease, so it seems to be in its general stages, since in both cases there are four similar and proportional times. But it happens in the particular times that the hour of the worst feeding is the beginning; whence...

<margin>~ }</margin>
<term>Galen</term> says in his first book: "The worst of hours is the hour in which the limbs are found in the worst disposition, and it is manifest that this is the hour of the onset of the paroxysm." Yet at that time, food seems to be given in which nature is least occupied with the business of food; this is at the peak, when the natural unity is preserved, according to the second book of the *Aphorisms*. Furthermore, at the peak, one ought to increase the **natural heat**, so that the heat of the disease may be diminished and finally extinguished. For a larger flame placed near a smaller one extinguishes it, for reasons of the length and shortness of life. But natural heat is increased by food, as stated in the first book of the *Problems*.

<margin>~ }</margin>
In quartan fevers, one ought not to thin the patient, but to create fire in the bodies through food. For since much fire draws a little to itself, it is necessary to create much fire in the body so that the <term>fever</term> <note>original: "febris"; here referring specifically to the morbid heat of the illness.</note> may have only a little. For the heat induced by food aids digestion. Again, there is a fever of the blood that is "apuntic," that is, a declining diet as it continuously decreases until the peak; after its refining, it will be necessary to thicken the diet. Therefore, the diet proceeds by thickening and not by refining. The opposite of which Hippocrates seems to say when he says:

To those for whom the peak is continuous, one ought soon to refresh them thinly. And <term>Galen</term> says the same in the *Art of Medicine*. Yet nature does not sustain sudden changes. If one thins the diet much from the very beginning, a sudden change is introduced when previously a thicker diet was used. Therefore, the dieting should follow a process of thinning.

<margin>What was said above.</margin>
<margin>}</margin>
Regarding the first point, it must be known that "diet" can be understood in two ways: commonly and properly. First, taken commonly, it is a certain rule of living accommodated to the use and utility of the human body. Properly, however, it is called the perpetual exhibition of food and drink, measured in quantity, quality, time, labor, and order. The exposition of which extends to the parts, and finally shows how it should be administered to bodies.

<margin>Definition of proper diet.</margin>
<margin>}</margin>
Regarding the first, it should be known that diet is not called simply an exhibition of food, but one adds "perpetual" because the definition of diet includes not only the administration of food and drink, but even the subtraction of them. For that diet is elegantly ordered when it knows where and when it is expedient to be brief and to subtract. But the regimen of food is flexible, as gathered from Hippocrates and Galen. For to some, a diet must be given that is vehemently thin, such as the prohibition of all food or a small amount of <term>honey-water</term> <note>original: "mellicrati"; a mixture of honey and water, often used as a light nourishment.</note> or a <term>julep</term> <note>original: "iuleb"; a sweet medicinal drink.</note> according to Galen. Another kind is very thick, such as the food of healthy people; while another holds a middle ground.

<margin>}</margin>
And one of these inclines more toward the side of thinness, such as the juice of pottage, then a <term>julep</term>, then thin **barley water**; afterward thick, then vegetables, such as orach, spinach, and lettuce. Another tends toward the side of thickness, such as poultry and their extremities, then pheasants, partridges, and chickens; then small birds, and afterward soft-boiled eggs in small quantity. Above these is a thicker <term>barley water</term> <note>original: "ptisana"; a medicinal porridge or water made from crushed barley.</note> with its dregs, and bread similarly crumbled into water that has been washed many times. Even thinner food exists. The middle ground is "kises," that is, <term>barley water</term> with its dregs. Furthermore, the diet varies in its thinness and thickness by reason of quantity and time. In terms of quantity, a diet that is thick in itself can be called thin if it is given in a small quantity and rarely. And a thin diet given many times is rendered thick. Also, a diet is called thin by reason of quality when its nourishment is small even if the quantity is sufficient. A thick diet is the opposite if it is joined to a due quantity. Regarding time, a diet is called thin when it is exhibited rarely and at long intervals; thick is the opposite. Drink also is twofold: simple, such as water which is given raw in diseases, or boiled (the difference in their administration will be seen in chapter 171). Otherwise, it is compound, and here it is either wine (for it also contains the nature of food, the administration of which is indicated in chapter 172). Likewise, there is a diversity of drinks in chapter 118. And a drink is called a potion that turns the nature of the body toward it. And this is manifold, such as a simple <term>syrup</term> <note>original: "syrꝝ"</note>, a compound **oxymel** <note>original: "aceto sy"; a mixture of vinegar and honey or sugar, often with herbs.</note> with common roots and seeds, violet syrup, honey-water, or <term>honey-water</term> and <term>juleps</term>. Indeed, simple...

<margin>Oxymel.</margin>
**oxymel** is a useful drink for those suffering from fever. For it benefits those suffering from <term>burning fever</term> <note>original: "causõē"; a high, inflammatory fever.</note> and choleric fevers and all other fevers. For some, it is by reason of digestion; for others, it is by reason of alteration and digestion together.

It explains how different foods—from honey-water and barley to poultry and eggs—are classified by their "subtlety" or "thickness."</summary>

**It** cools, indeed, and extinguishes viscous <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance was thought to determine health.</note>; it cuts and thins thick ones, and opens obstructions so that it may lead out putrid matter. According to the third book of the *Practice*, and in the fourth part: **Vinegar syrup**, whenever it settles thirst, also cuts and dissolves [humors]. And **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (c. 777–857), a Persian or Assyrian physician influential in the medieval West.</note> in his *Antidotary* says: The virtue of vinegar syrup is magnified among the "verifiers" <note>original: "uerificatoris"; likely referring to authoritative physicians who test or prove medicines.</note> because of its excellence in common use—namely, that it can be used for hot, cold, thin, thick, viscous, or adhering matters. And its virtue, if any part of it remains inside, is quickly removed by its power of penetration without that power being lost. And this is what **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire (c. 129–216 AD).</note> testifies: that its power is common to all matters, so that it even acts upon <term>black bile</term> <note>The humor associated with melancholy and heaviness.</note> by dividing it and causing medicines to penetrate into it. (Part 2, Distinction 170). It is harmful, however, to a coughing chest and to the intestines where sharp humor tends to flow; just as is said of <term>oxymel</term> <note>A medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar.</note> which has a similar quality. From whatever source it is digested, the **Compound** [syrup] 
<margin>Cave</margin> 
<margin>(3.posit)</margin>
of vinegar also benefits those who are phlegmatic and melancholic; for it diffuses into wider matters, thinning them, provoking urine, and opening obstructions. **Violet syrup** 
<margin>julep</margin>
also softens matter, soothes the roughness of the chest and lungs, calms the sharpness of bile, and mitigates thirst; but it harms those who have a weak stomach and those with undigested matter in their viscera, because it can lead to illness. It does not benefit cold natures or matters, as it may cast down the appetite and induce a loathing for food. **Honey-water** also, and **honey-wine**, thins and cuts thick and viscous matters without much cooling; it procures the digestion of matters but nevertheless heats up hot natures, and therefore it harms those with burning fevers. The **Julep**, however, which is prepared from sugar and common water—to which a little rose water is sometimes added—mitigates thirst and procures the digestion of matters, and works a cleansing, though less so than honey-water.

**Indeed**, as has been touched upon, the regimen is diversified according to quantity: for some [foods/medicines] are many, some few, and some moderate. And according to quality: for some are hot, others cold, some moist, and some dry. Likewise, some are very nutritious, others moderately so, and some poorly so, as seen in the first section. According to this, the time varies, for in winter a hotter diet and a larger quantity are expected, while in summer the opposite is true. It should also be taken at a hotter hour in cold weather and a cooler hour in hot weather, unless habit especially dictates otherwise. And what is said of time should also be heard regarding habit and region. It is also diversified according to the craft [of preparation] in many ways: for some things are boiled, sometimes roasted or fried, or prepared otherwise according to the differences of the stomach and liver. As much as it pertains to order, the scheme of the diet is said to be twofold: either by reason of what comes before and after, or even by number. First, when someone uses several dishes, the thinner ones should be placed before the thicker ones. For nature is "imprisoned" when thick food is put before thin, unless there is a looseness of the bowels (Distinction 119). Regarding these things, one must know what is more fully heard: that one must attend to "natural things" and those annexed to them, the "non-natural things," and those "contrary to nature." For according to these, the entire regimen is ordered. These are: complexion, virtue (especially), age, form, law, and custom. And finally: the temperament, the constitution, the hour, the region, and whether something is repeated. And finally, the cause and symptoms of diseases. And according to the quantity of the body for which these dispositions exist. Also according to the **complexion** <note>The unique balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in an individual.</note>: because in a hot complexion, more food and more frequent meals are required, just as better digestion is needed. In a cold one, the opposite. It is also required similarly in a cold, hot, moist, or dry state. Natural temperance, however, should be observed continuously, especially in diseases where one must not alter the complexion through transformation. Regarding **virtue** [strength]: if it is strong, a small amount of food is sought, especially when the state of the illness is not far off. Sometimes, however, no food is given if the strength is greater and the state [of the illness] is continuous. If, however, it is weak and the distance to the state of the illness is far, the opposite. According to **age** it varies: for in the age of infancy, much food is sought, following that saying of the inventor of medicine [Hippocrates]: "Old men easily endure fasting," etc. In old age, however, little is needed. In the second stage of life, a moderate amount, administered many times. In the middle ages, it should be given moderately. And this is done for the sake of the humors, the members, and the spirit. According to the **quality of the body**: for those with "porous" bodies who are easily resolved by transpiration, food and drink should be given at the time of the illness's peak, according to the former authority. There are also certain bodies with soft flesh that are quickly resolved, which, even if they appear fat, cannot bear abstinence. For those opposite to these, a thin diet suffices for up to seven days, and food should be shown minimally. According to **sex**: a male nature requires more food than a female nature, since it is hotter, unless the weakness of his strength exhausts him, in which case food is ordered to be given at once. Also according to **custom**: for it is found to be safe at all times in the preservation of health. Therefore, custom becomes a second nature through habit. And so it should be followed; for when the hour of eating coincides with the peak of the illness, it is best that they try to eat. Regarding the **non-natural things** <note>A set of six environmental and lifestyle factors (air, food, sleep, etc.) that physicians believed were the primary causes of health or disease.</note> and first the time, the order of the diet varies: for in winter, hot food should be given, and once a day in bodies of a hot nature. In others, perhaps equal reason and hour apply, and in cold weather, it should be given more sparingly. In hot weather, the opposite. But in the middle [seasons], one should diet moderately. In the **constitution**, it is the same as in the time. In a cold **region**, more diet and hotter, "cutting" [thinning] foods are sought, given in fewer instances and in larger quantities. In a hot region, the opposite happens. Also according to the **quantity of the body**: whether large, small, or moderate; one must vary the diet accordingly. How the diet should be ordered regarding things "contrary to nature" will be made manifest later, about which we have also seen in the distinction. Regarding this, one should know that some of the ancients proceeded by "thickening" [the diet], showing nothing for up to three or four days; wherefore the ancients say: "I know physicians who, acting more quickly than is opportune, keep [the patient] from everything in the beginning for two or three days or more; afterwards, they permit them to take broth and drink." Their motive was that a change should be most contrary to a change. But the principal change for the sick is from that which they loathe; because of this, they change the diet from thick to very thin. Others, whom **Galen** in the *Part on Curing* calls the **Dyatritarios** <note>Followers of the "Methodic" school of medicine who waited for a three-day period (*diatritos*) before beginning treatment or feeding.</note>...
