# Whether the Dietary Regimen Should Proceed by Increasing in Substance

Those who call for abstaining from every diet until the third day has passed, ordering this in their general opinion, perhaps did so because they followed the persuasion of **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire (c. 129–216 AD).</note>, as can be gathered from his words. For he did not recognize the sickness at the beginning and therefore waited until the third day, including the start, so that the movement of the illness might be weighed; for every <term>humor</term> <note>Bodily fluids thought to control health: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> coming on the fourth day or later—unless it leads to a quintan or sextan fever, or those rarer ones emerging—Galen himself confesses in his first book *On Fevers* that he did not perceive them at first. 

But this cannot stand, as is said in the third book of the *Pantegni* <note>The "Universal Art," a medical encyclopedia by Haly Abbas.</note>. Hence, in the first book of the *Regimen*: **Take care that you do not allow the veins to be emptied for even a single day**, but do not cease to give food without the intervention of a day, unless perhaps it is necessary to use drinks or <term>clysters</term> <note>Enemas used to clear the bowels.</note>. And in the same work: where <term>ptisana</term> <note>original: "ptisane"; a medicinal porridge or water made from crushed barley.</note> is needed, begin giving it from the start of the disease. I confess it is better that the emptying of the veins should precede it; afterwards, however, on the third day of the disease, or the fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh, it ought to be given according to what is to come. Their motives are not valid, since a diet is a natural and customary administration not only for the healthy but especially for the sick. Anything that is not entirely found to be contrary should not be changed, according to that **Hippocratic** <note>Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BC), the "Father of Medicine."</note> maxim: *To heat or cool too much or too suddenly is dangerous.* Hence in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Art of Medicine."</note>: Nature does not sustain sudden changes. For the greatest change should not be made into the absolute opposite, but only as much as nature can sustain; for it must be provided for the sake of utility and harmony for safety. In the second book of the *Regimen*, it says: such a sudden change should be one that falls against the enemy [the disease] while remaining safe, not one that turns against nature itself. 

Those who give food or drink only after the third day often cause destruction, and in many specific ways. As is told in the tenth book of *On the Method of Healing*, a youth was not fed, and before he could be given a drink by **Galen**, he fell into <term>syncope</term> <note>Fainting or sudden loss of consciousness due to a drop in blood pressure.</note> in the presence of his relatives and the doctors of the **Diatritarii** <note>A medical sect that believed in fasting patients for three-day intervals (the "diatritos").</note>. They could not stop Galen when he secretly ordered the doors of the house to be closed and the keys removed [to feed the patient].

For this reason, the **Diatritarii** are to be blamed, since such a method of feeding occurs among them due to their ignorance in recognizing the sickness. Against whom the second book of *On Crises* thunders: "If you do not recognize a certain <term>tertian fever</term> <note>A fever that spikes every third day, typically malaria.</note> by the signs after it has occurred twice, but still wait, you are not a mocking Diatritarian like **Thessalus** <note>Thessalus of Tralles, a famous proponent of the Methodic school of medicine.</note>, but a <margin>3</margin> mere stone." And he who cannot distinguish a tertian from a <term>quartan fever</term> <note>A fever that spikes every fourth day.</note> immediately according to the first day is not a doctor. 

Finally, today almost all follow the sect of these men. At the beginning of the disease and thereafter, they thin the food exceedingly; then, seeing the strength of the patient fail toward the peak of the illness, they are forced by necessity to provide "gross" <note>Heavy or substantial nourishment.</note> restoration, even giving meat. They are deceived in this way, as was said, because they cannot recognize the stage of the sickness. Against these, **Hippocrates** and **Galen** frequently complain. In the second book of the *Regimen*, it is said: in these [doctors] the greatest error of the ancients is contained. They submit to these errors, and if complications occur, they are often filled from head to toe with "crude," undigested <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile; one of the four humors.</note>, from which insomnia and other symptoms happen. And therefore, in the fourth part: the doctor often errs in these sick people in another way than at the beginning of the disease; for he gives them food when the peak approaches and he knows their strength is failing, and he must feed them at that hour. Now he has erred doubly: for if he fed them at the beginning, it was an error, and there is ignorance beneath this error. In these sick people, bad complications occur, such as <term>catarrhs</term> <note>Excessive buildup of mucus.</note>, nausea, <term>colic</term> <note>Severe abdominal pain.</note>, and wakefulness because of the lack of digestion. Those suffering in their sides roll from side to side and become alienated; the matters constrict their strength, and vapors multiply within them. Wherefore they hear things not imagined, they tremble, and their lower lips twitch because of stomach pain, and their souls are saddened by the heaviness of the matter. 

Regarding the third point, it must be known: there is a certain sickness in which no food ought to be given from the beginning until the peak, as appeared in the previous distinction, which is not the subject of this discourse, since food should only be given after the peak. To this patient, the diet is finally ordered in a way contrary to the requirements of the sickness. For first, it is expedient to diet with the thinnest things, such as pomegranate juice, <term>julep</term> <note>original: "iuleb"; a sweet medicinal drink, often made with rose water.</note>, or <term>mellicratum</term> <note>A mixture of honey and water.</note>, then the water of ptisana, and finally barley <term>kyse</term> <note>A thick, strained cereal or cream.</note>. Hence the second book of the *Regimen*: He who administers ptisana mixed with dregs commits a harmful change. He also does harm who only provides juice or only gives drink, but their harm to those [patients] is not only because it introduces a sudden change. 

There is also another sickness in which food is required immediately from the beginning, nor should you allow the veins to be emptied for a single day. And this is likewise twofold. For one is cured by immaterial emptying, as in <term>hectic fevers</term> <note>original: "ethice"; a wasting fever associated with chronic illness like tuberculosis.</note>; these patients ought to be dieted uniformly according to the stages, or perhaps more in the progression than at the beginning, since the body is more thinned and the inflammation becomes more vehement—provided that the digestion can tolerate it. Hence in the fourth part: **When hectic fever occurs, increase the food quickly** and the pulse will become very strong and begin to enlarge. 
<margin>No</margin>
<margin>Take care</margin>
And because of this, it happens to foolish doctors that they prohibit food to them because of the occurring symptoms, and thus they destroy them; for the heat increases more in those who are unfed. 

There is another material sickness where the matter is either appearing in fact—as in a true <term>aposteme</term> <note>An internal swelling or abscess.</note>—or appearing similarly as in the labor of an abscess, or at least it possesses almost the whole body uniformly. Its diet should generally proceed by thinning, perhaps with the exception of <term>epimastic</term> <note>A type of recurring fever.</note> fevers; so that more is administered at the beginning, but in the progression it is continuously made thinner until it reaches the peak, at which point all diet must be entirely thinned. One must also consider the brevity of the peak or its length. First, however, this should be authorized and shown by reason. Then, that which must be dieted by relation to the cause, the disease, and the symptoms. Regarding the first, it should be known that the first book of the *Aphorisms* prescribes the order of dieting to be observed when it says: *To those for whom the peak is soon, diet most thinly; to those for whom it is later,* and so on. Hence in the third book of the *Practice*: "The regimen of diet according to the stages of the disease should be thus: **It is beneficial at the beginning of a disease for the food to lean toward thickness (substance)**, lest by chance a transition from thick to thin food at once harms him more, dissolves his strength, and weakens him."

...gradually and day by day until the disease reaches its <term>peak</term> <note>original: "statum"; the middle stage of a disease when symptoms are most intense.</note>.
In this diet, there is indeed much subtlety, such as the skipping of the midday meal and the beginning of a julep, honey water, and syrup of violets, lest by chance the <term>virtue</term> <note>The body's innate healing power or "vital force."</note> be occupied with the digestion of foods and turn all its focus away from resisting and expelling the disease. But when the disease begins to have its decline, the food should begin to be thickened, and the sick person should return to the regimen of those rising from infirmity. For this reason, and according to the first book of the *Aphorisms* <note>Referring to the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates, the foundational text of clinical medicine.</note>:
Indeed, it is necessary for you that the beginning of your regimen be thick, and at the last, reaching the peak, it should be thin, and you should proceed by degrees in that which is between them. Thus, as much as the illness is prolonged toward the peak, you should then focus upon the <term>matter</term> <note>The "materia peccans" or the harmful humors causing the illness.</note> so that you are not occupied with anything else. The aforesaid method of dieting is also confirmed by reason, as at the peak earlier. For at that time when Nature is more intent upon the digestion of the matter, and the fourth [day] of the onset of symptoms requires a more plentiful supply of food. In which, however, there is more or less; the first is at the beginning of the disease, the second truly at the peak.
Because at the beginning, Nature has not yet begun to act openly upon the matter, and therefore signs of digestion do not appear manifest in it. In these cases, however, they begin to be manifested at the end. Therefore, in the first book of the *Aphorisms*: "Signs of concoction <note>The "cooking" or processing of humors by the body's heat.</note> indicate the beginning," which occurs through the whole exit of the sickness. Likewise, the onset of symptoms is not yet so great, according to that old proverb:
"Regarding the beginnings and the ends, etc." But at the peak, the accidents <note>Symptoms or secondary complications of a disease.</note> are extreme. For in that stage, Nature is most intent upon the digestion and expulsion of the matter and can scarcely suffice for those things.
In the first book of the *Aphorisms*: "Then also vehement accidents arise," since immediately nothing else remains but the greatest part of the sickness, as in <term>symptoms</term> <note>original: "stitomatibus"; likely a corruption of "symptomatibus."</note> or when there are labors and their ultimate accidents in that same place. Furthermore, if because of the <term>fluxes</term> <note>Discharges, such as diarrhea or sweating.</note> and labors inseparable from acute sicknesses it is feared to give foods worthy of reason. In the peak stages, this is much more to be feared, when the aforesaid accidents arise more sharply; but one must wait in <term>peracute</term> <note>Extremely sharp or fast-progressing diseases.</note> cases. Therefore, in the peak stages, one must be more cautious.

Again, since a united power is more pleasing and innate than one which is multiplied; it is stronger in itself than when dispersed, for the reasons in the book with *Mesue* <note>Masawayh, or Pseudo-Mesue, a major source for medieval pharmacology.</note>.
But food given at the peak stage multiplies the virtue of Nature by dissipating its strength. For there would be a need for a surplus of similar nature for the regimen and the digestion of food; because of which, Nature either would not begin to be occupied with the digestion of food and would abandon the management of the matter, or the reverse. And so the food, remaining undigested, would further intensify the disease by multiplying its cause, or its own <term>dyscrasia</term> <note>An imbalance of the four humors.</note>. For it is not able to perfect both at once, since the <term>innate heat</term> <note>The fundamental biological heat believed to reside in the heart.</note> is not a sufficient instrument for this. For in the fourth book *On the Soul*, *Aristotle* says: "The powers hinder themselves when they all work with one instrument," such as innate heat. Therefore, the regimen of the diet ought to proceed by thinning and not by thickening.

I say this, however, because certain bodies cannot tolerate the aforementioned method of dieting, as was touched upon in the earlier sections. Because of these things, one must also know a second point: that the cause of disease is manifold, according to which the dietary regimen varies. For some are hot, some cold, etc. Furthermore, some are thin, others thick, some viscous, some much, others little, and some moderate. Therefore, if the cause be little and thin, it requires little time, so that the diet is similar to the sickness itself—

—having been handled quickly. In the opposite case, it is the reverse; and let it be with a good thinning and cutting [of the humors]. For everything must be referred back to the "virtue" or strength of the patient, for it is the person we feed and not the disease, according to the first book of the *Aphorisms*, unless perhaps the sickness was one of total consumption of the health, as touched upon before. The mode of diet according to the disease was stated earlier. For it must be considered that some diseases are acute, some chronic, and both are sub-distinguished as before.
Some, however, according to whether they are short or long or medium, must be dieted at the peak and at other times, having constant relation to the patient's strength. It must also be observed that of sicknesses, some are entirely at the peak, others in decline, some in the increase. Those which are <term>sanguine</term> <note>Caused by an excess of blood.</note> fevers always require a diminished regimen. Similarly, the peak of some sicknesses is short; of others, long; of these, however, it is moderate. According to all these diversities, one must diet in diverse ways.

The <term>accidents</term> <note>External symptoms or complications.</note> also vary the peak and the mode of diet, as touched upon. For some are from the essence of the sickness, others from the physician’s doing, such as excessive abstinence; some are those which prostrate the strength, either because they are harmful in themselves, like <term>syncope</term> <note>Fainting or sudden loss of consciousness.</note>, or because they evacuate something from the body like blood; as when there is an immoderate flux from the belly, or vomiting, or the rupture of an <term>aposteme</term> <note>An internal swelling or abscess.</note>. If any food should be given at first, it does not behoove one to withhold it, for if it were withheld, it would increase the same [weakness]. Hence, according to the King *Haly Abbas*:
"It has not been found by me that any physician can know the condition of the sick person as well as he ought, if he does not know whether they suffer a defect of the parts from an emptying of the veins, or from some other fury or labor afflicting the sick, or from some other natural accident." For it is a great evil when a patient is in pain and in the sharp stage of the disease, and [the physicians] permit them to take drink and broth or food on the day of the <term>crisis</term> <note>original: "divortii die"; the turning point of the disease.</note> because they estimate that very defect to be from emptiness. If, however, it was an accident perceived by the physician to be because of just abstinence, food is to be exhibited immediately. How great a gift this always is, you will see a plebeian physician, or one of the rustics or common people, in the departure of the dead, reviving the work of a previous great physician. If, however, the accident was one prostrating the strength, such as syncope, and especially when it occurs with an emptying of the consciousness, then food must be given quickly; see the twelfth book of the *Therapeutics* <note>Galen's *Methodus Medendi* (On the Therapeutic Method).</note>. But a doubt happens regarding this: since a certain syncope arrives from cold, viscous humors filling the passages, a diet is prohibited, since it does not need nourishment; since those who assist can turn this aforesaid fullness into nourishment. It must be said that since the curative intention turns upon two things especially—namely, the virtue and the disposition—as far as the reason of the latter is concerned, it does not require nourishment as touched upon, but rather abstinence and a thinning education, especially if it is through light friction at the beginning. # Whether the Regimen of Diet Should Lose its Thickness

->**Whether the Regimen of Diet Should Lose its Thickness.**<-

In this situation, we are compelled to give not only food but also some wine; we do this to immediately avert danger, not necessarily to cure the underlying condition. For the cure for such people is better achieved without adding more <note>original: "non adiecto"; referring to not adding more matter to the body during a crisis</note>. Indeed, when a patient suffers from <term>syncope</term> <note>fainting or a sudden loss of strength</note>, and specifically when there is no feverish "flow," bread should be given, though not much, soaked in wine; this brings about a rapid restoration of strength, according to Alexander in his *Problems*. It is also necessary to provide nourishment in small amounts, little by little, not a lot at once. For though it may be coarse and substantial, it should be of a warming and "thinning" nature. 

Therefore, let us consider what should be done. It may be argued more fully that if symptoms are present that cause the <term>virtue</term> <note>The body's innate vital force or healing power.</note> to fail due to a "flux" <note>an abnormal discharge or loss of fluids</note>, food must be provided, since food itself is ordered toward maintaining that strength; as seen in the *Aphorisms*. Sometimes, due to the weakness that follows an attack, we are forced to feed the patient. For the highest intention of all medical care is the intention derived from preserving the virtue. This is the primary concern, and the physician must be more worried about the virtue than the disease itself. 

Regarding the timing of meals, although diets vary according to the illness, nothing should be given during a <term>paroxysm</term> <note>original: "pocimum"; the period of highest fever or the "fit" of the disease.</note>; instead, what was added should be withdrawn unless the aforementioned cause (extreme weakness) occurs. Thus, in the *Aphorisms*: in paroxysms, one must subtract food, because adding it causes harm. In a paroxysm, food should not be given, but rather taken away, especially if it was wrongly provided before. This can be proven by the rule that food should not be consumed during the "peak" of the illness. But if there is no paroxysm, then food should be given at the usual and more quiet hour, at least by reason of maintaining the patient's strength. Next, one must ask how many hours before or after the departure of the paroxysm one should feed the patient. It must be said first that a greater span of time should be allowed for feeding before the paroxysm than after it, because before the attack, the "battle" <note>the physiological struggle against the disease</note> is approaching, and after it, the battle has already receded.

<margin>
Galen, Aphorisms.
4th book.
</margin>
<margin>
Not at the peak.
Preceding the attack.
Before or after.
</margin>

When the soles of the feet are cold, then all juice and any drink must be most strictly denied. But when the heat has already descended into the heel, food may be given, for now the decline of the paroxysm is imminent. Therefore, according to the third book: if the fever is immobile and varies little, the patient should be prohibited from food for six hours before the time of the onset, until the heat declines and the upper parts of the body are clear. He should not be refreshed while the heat is still in the upper parts or diffused through all the limbs. But when the burning heat has ceased in the chest and moves from the belly toward the extremities, he may be fed.

<margin>Galen, Aphorisms.</margin>

Galen also clearly states that from this point, one should specify the time of the beginning of the paroxysm and the end of the feeding in a single sequence. It should be noted that the timing for a pure <term>tertian fever</term> <note>A fever that returns every third day, typically associated with malaria.</note> is set differently by various authors.

<margin>Timing of the beginning</margin>
Serapio says in the sixth book of his *Breviarium* that the time before the "period" (which is the paroxysm) should be three or four hours, or after the fever has settled.

<margin>Serapio, XI.</margin>
<margin>Almansor, X.</margin>
Almansor, in his tenth book, says: Let there be a long span of time between the meal and the beginning of the invasion. Let the patient be nourished three or two hours before the onset, or after it has receded.

<margin>Haly Abbas</margin>
Haly Abbas also says that on the day of the fever's onset, barley water should be given as little as possible, and the meal should be deferred until the onset is entirely consumed or until the time of alleviation.

<margin>Isaac, On Fevers.</margin>
<margin>The Viaticum</margin>
Isaac, in his fifth book on fevers, warns that nothing should be given at the hour of the fever's onset. In the *Viaticum* <note>A famous medical traveler's handbook by Ibn al-Jazzar.</note>, it is said that food should not be given during the paroxysm nor in the three hours preceding it; instead, sustain the patient with syrup of violets or roses until after the fever's onset. Haly Abbas says of the tertian fever (not the pure kind): use food after the onset has been dismissed; the food should be light and refined after the "type" <note>the pattern of the fever</note> has been established, so that on the day the fever does not rise, the strength is preserved. But on the day of the onset, the body is occupied with the enemy disease, and the matter is being consumed.

Avicenna says: feeding every day or near the time of the feeding is among those things that harm them; rather, they should be fed one day and not the next. According to Serapio, the time for a <term>quotidian fever</term> <note>A fever that returns every day.</note> should be after the fever has quieted, or three or four hours before its "peak" <note>original: "statum"; the author explains this means before it becomes fixed and intense.</note>. I explain "peak" here as before it settles into its state of being, not as one of the formal stages of the disease, because then one would be feeding during the beginning or the "increase" stage. Almansor, remaining on the same point, says the hour of eating should be distanced as much as possible from the hour of the onset. Haly Abbas indeed says: Observe that you should give barley water no fewer than six or four hours before the onset.

<margin>In the Quotidian</margin>
Isaac says: We also say that a space of six hours should be made between the food and the onset. Indeed, the hour for food is after the time of the paroxysm and its "uprooting," and at least four hours before the next paroxysm.

<margin>In the Tertian</margin>
In a <term>quartan fever</term> <note>A fever that returns every fourth day.</note>, total abstinence is commanded on the day of the paroxysm. Whence Haly Abbas: You should prohibit foods on the day of the fever's onset, so that nature may be more occupied in resisting the disease. In the *Viaticum*: When twenty days have passed, one must abstain from food on every day of onset. In another place, it says on the tenth day one may eat a little. But Galen says: one must be prohibited from eating on the day of the paroxysm, and fasting is commanded; specifically, one should skip one meal that day, such as dinner or lunch. For if the fever is to invade after noon, lunch should be omitted. If at the beginning of the night, omit dinner. Yet, the patient should not be without food for the whole day, especially in their "natural" state, because since the affliction lasts twenty-four hours, and if the abstinence were certain for a thirty-six-hour span, the patient could fall into a <term>hectic fever</term> <note>A persistent, wasting fever often associated with consumption/tuberculosis.</note> or a collapse of strength.

Cornelius Celsus <note>A Roman medical encyclopedist.</note> also hesitates regarding the time of feeding. Since food must be given, there is no small debate. For some command it be given in the morning, because that is when the remission of the sick seems to be. But the response is that it should not be then, because the midday hour follows, at which time every sick person tends to get worse. And therefore others order it to be given in the evening. But this is not well, for at that time the sick are in a poor state. Therefore, it is feared that the movement of the fever might rise then. Because of this, he resorts to the middle of the night, the time of the paroxysm having finished and being at the longest possible distance from the next one. This follows a time in which the patient can sleep healthily, for almost everyone sleeps most then. This is true as long as the fevers are not erratic, or perhaps if there is a fixed contrary habit. In the eleventh book *On the Method of Healing*, it says the time of food in putrid fevers (which have only one paroxysm) is until the end, when good health and habit are the intentions; for then food should be given when they are most comfortable, and especially according to that time of day when they were accustomed to being fed before they were sick. Nothing is better according to Haly. These are the spans of time mentioned before.

The central debate is how to nourish the patient's "vital force" without fueling the "matter" of the disease during a feverish attack.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the timing of meals during illness, specifically focusing on the "paroxysm" (the peak of a fever) and how different medical authorities like Hippocrates and Avicenna reconcile their views based on geography and the specific type of fever.</meta>

<margin>Note</margin>
...the paroxysm <note>original: "pocismum"; referring to the period of the highest intensity or a "fit" of the disease</note> and afterward, the diet and hours are measured by physicians. Those who seem to differ from one another do not actually disagree at all if one observes that they wrote while looking at different regions and customs alongside others. And this is especially true regarding what must be measured and observed in any given matter. Whence it is said in Distinction 78: "Acute illnesses that occur in the lands of Hippocrates in the Southern parts end acutely." It should also be noted that in quartan and tertian fevers <note>Quartan fevers recur every four days; tertian every three. These were common ways to categorize malaria-like illnesses in the Middle Ages.</note> that are truly intermittent, as far as the reason of the paroxysm is concerned, we can keep food far away from the paroxysm, both before and after. For a true tertian fever has thirty-six hours of rest and twelve of labor <note>the "labor" refers to the period of active fever or suffering</note>. A quartan fever has forty hours of rest and twenty-four of affliction. In a true quotidian fever <note>a fever that recurs daily</note>, however, we are certainly burdened, since it has eighteen hours of labor and only six of rest. Within that rest, it subsides so little that it is almost never separated. Whence, for those who command that food be given six hours before the paroxysm, if it is a true quotidian fever, they would be feeding the patient while the previous paroxysm is still occurring. And for this reason, perhaps, the counsel of those who only set a space of four hours before the paroxysm is more acceptable, so that two hours or fewer remain after the paroxysm ends. For it is better, as will appear, to move away from the beginning of a paroxysm than from its end.

<margin>Answer</margin>
Regarding the aforementioned, a doubt arises because it was granted that food may be given in a paroxysm when necessity urges. But since the paroxysm itself, like the whole illness, contains four periods, in which period is the diet worse? It seems to be at the beginning. Because, in the first reason: when the coldness of the feet is at its height, which is at the start of the paroxysm, then especially broth and all other drink must be denied. Furthermore, Galen says in the same place: the hour in which the parts of the chest and belly are in their worst disposition is the hour of the onset of the paroxysm. Whence the first afflictions. In those things which are ordained for the paroxysm, their beginnings must be avoided; that is, so that we nourish them with things already prepared or about to be done. The opposite of this is written in the Fourth Fen, Book One <note>A reference to Avicenna's *Canon of Medicine*</note>: "Colic-prone bodies, and specifically those accustomed to eating much, when they are not fed—at least at the beginning of the fever, or rather in the hour which is worst in it, which is the peak—do not escape without being obstructed and dying if they were weak during the paroxysm." If, however, they remain strong, they incur exhaustion. To this, some respond by correcting the text through other findings, noting that sometimes "outer" <note>extrinsecus</note>, for example, a purer place, might be noted instead of "worse." Or it must be said that a more extensive and worse harm follows from the exhibition of food at the beginning of the paroxysm, since it lasts through all the following times; but not at the peak. However, in the peak itself, the harm stands out as more intense, since the symptoms are then more strained; for this is the "peak" as defined above. It remains now to follow the part of a certain distinction written above, which was whether the matter causing the illness was either truly apparent or collected internally. And certainly, if the disease happens from a manifest and powerful cause recently impressed—such as a dislocation or a fracture—then indeed one must diet thinly from the beginning; and then tend toward the peak, as the discourses in the sixth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio sanitatis"; Galen's *Therapeutike Methodos*</note> suggest. This is what Galen seems to think in the first book: for those beginning to feel dryness in the organs, when nothing flows from them in whatever viscera they may be, they should receive some moistening things before taking any gruel. Such things are <term>hydromel</term> <note>a mixture of honey and water</note> and wine, which are of greater moistening power. These, however, are thinner than gruel. From which it seems he feels that in these cases, the diet proceeds by thickening, as in the third book of the first part of *On the Cure of Exhaustion*. Regarding a certain apparent condition in the instructions on the cure of an appearing abscess of the liver: its cure begins and lasts up to a week. And let the patient be content with the food of barley water <note>original: "aqua ordei"</note>. When the fever is alleviated, let his foods be from herbs and verjuice <note>original: "agresta"; the tart juice of unripe grapes</note> with chicken. Therefore Alexander in his *Problems* asks: why did Hippocrates, fleeing from food in fevers, change his mind to granting it at the peak in pleurisy and pneumonia patients? This is what Avicenna explicitly called for in those locations: for in the Fourth Fen of the First Book, he says: "And when you know the virtue is strong, then perhaps the disposition makes it necessary that you be content with <term>julep</term> <note>a sweet medicinal drink</note> alone, even if it lasts no more than one week, and specifically in fevers from abscesses." And if you fear weakness, be content with barley water. Also in the Third Fen of the First Book regarding <term>karabito</term> <note>a medieval term for a heavy headache or lethargy, derived from Arabic</note>, first begin to nourish him with thin nourishment so that you are content with <term>oxymel</term> <note>a medicinal drink of honey and vinegar</note>. Then after this, for one or two days, change him to thin barley water with oxymel, and then to thick. 

Regarding the cure of <term>quinsy</term> <note>original: "squinantie"; an inflammation of the throat or tonsils</note>: they must be content in their foods until the third day with oxymel. Then a gradation should be made to barley water with certain delightful medicines, and then to egg yolk. Furthermore, regarding the cure of <term>pleurisy</term> <note>inflammation of the lung lining</note>: if it be great, be content with barley water until the condition is revealed to you, specifically according to the sputum; and if thinness of the regimen is retained, be content with barley water and syrups as much as you can. Retain this near the beginning. For then the matters are undigested. And therefore Aurelius commands those with pleurisy to abstain from food for three days. Also regarding the cure of a "beaten" liver: it is necessary that at the beginning a thinning of opening food be administered. And be content with barley <term>ptisan</term> <note>original: "kise"; likely a variant of 'ptisana', a medicinal porridge or decoction</note> and vinegar syrup. Then after that, let there be administered the opening foods which we mentioned, and sippable egg yolks and soothing gruels. And to the highest degree in the cure of all abscesses. This is also confirmed by reason because when you see the accidents of the illness are stronger at the beginning, one must start with a great thinning of food, unless a collapse of the "virtue" <note>vital strength</note> is feared. In the third book of the first part, it was also stated above that when violent symptoms are present, it is necessary to diminish food. But in abscesses, the cruel symptoms rise up more quickly near the beginning than in other diseases, since in them the state of the digestion of the matter differs from the state of the symptoms. Furthermore, when the matter is digested, the symptoms are quieted. And just as it is digested, so it needs to be led out, and especially since it is not expelled by one expulsion but by many little by little. Thus, by these series and reasons, it can be demonstrated in the solution of the unequal that a diet should proceed by thickening, since soon the symptoms in them become lighter. Because of this, one must thin the food at the beginning more than in the progress. So that this may be more fully declared and considered from the induction of these alone: the distinction of the "peak" <note>status</note> is stated as precious by the prior authority. Next, it should also be noted that dieting is twofold: one indeed used in the whole disease...

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the dietary management of fevers, reconciling the seemingly contradictory advice of ancient authorities. It concludes the discussion on the timing and quality of food before transitioning to a new "Difference" regarding the psychological impact of a patient's trust in their physician.</meta>

->**Whether the confidence of a sick person in their physician contributes to their health.**<-

from the beginning to the end. The other is particular, occurring at any particular time or during a paroxysm <note>original: "pocifmo"; the peak intensity of a disease</note>. It refers to the specific disposition of the patient. Indeed, the regulation of the diet is directed toward three things: primarily the strength of the patient, the stage of the disease, and the aforementioned symptoms. 

Regarding the first point, it must be said that Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> speaks of long-lasting fevers in which the matter <note>The "matter" refers to the excess or corrupted humors (like bile or phlegm) causing the illness.</note> is not expelled by a single expulsion. In these cases, it is necessary to thin the diet from the start. This is different from cases where everything is expelled in one go. Regarding the other point, it must be said that the reasoning of Hippocrates concerns those who have been without food from the beginning of the illness until the "status" <note>The "status" is the peak or plateau of the disease before it begins to decline.</note>. Regarding those who have been taking food continuously from the beginning, another approach is needed. 

Regarding another point, it must be said that Hippocrates speaks of those who were without food until the peak; in those cases, as shown, it is necessary to administer food by the contrary method. For in some of those who are fed right from the beginning, one must proceed by thinning the diet; in others, however, one must proceed by thickening it. Regarding the next point, he is speaking of short illnesses with strong bodily virtue <note>term: "virtue" (Latin: *virtus*); in medieval medicine, this refers to the body's natural power to heal itself and maintain life functions.</note>, where the disease is brief and they can reach the peak without food. 

Regarding another point, it must be said that Galen <note>A highly influential Roman-era physician and philosopher.</note> does not prescribe giving wine for the sake of thickening the diet, but for the sake of medicine; for wine, by its thinness and its ability to penetrate, draws out the matter. Indeed, it moves all excretions, and the symptoms are also somewhat calmed by it. Regarding the next point, the reasoning of Galen concerns fevers prone to fainting <note>original: "fricopolibus"; likely referring to syncopal fevers</note> caused by a lack of appetite, in which, because of the thinness of the humors and the opening of the pores, the body itself is weakened by dissolution. Therefore, one should administer substances that are moderately binding <note>term: "stiptic" (Latin: *stiptica*); substances that contract tissues or stop secretions.</note>. 

Regarding another point, it must be said that Haly Abbas <note>A famous Persian physician of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> understands the "middle" as the passing of the peak. For there is a single time of illness itself which does not pass through a middle, such as the beginning. Regarding the next point, that treatment by Isaac <note>Isaac Israeli, a prominent 10th-century physician and philosopher.</note> and Avicenna is tentative and not a true cure, like the administration of heating agents. But they wish to test right from the beginning if a sixth-day or fourth-day fever can be cured by thinning the diet for up to three weeks. If it is not, they immediately prescribe thickening the diet and providing meat and such things. And this is what is said regarding the cure for paralysis. 

The same must be said for other cases, such as fainting or syncope. Regarding the next point, Galen is strong and right that in the beginning we do not feed the patient for the sake of the present, but for the sake of the future; namely, so that strength remains for what follows. We want to strengthen the body during the time when nature is not hindered by the digestion of matter or by symptoms, so that at the time when it is doubly occupied, it may be able to resist them. Otherwise, we would necessarily feed them as shown in the same text. 

For at the peak, a diet must be provided because of the moisture, since although it might be beneficial because the moisture resists dryness, it might perhaps harm the substance and quantity by distracting the body's strength from the matter of the disease. Or, moist diets are not simply beneficial for those with fevers, but must be given with a determination of quantity, quality, and time. Nor should one stop feeding in the beginning even if the body is "unclean," because feeding is twofold: one for the sustenance of strength, and the other for the robustness and growth of the body. Hippocrates denies the latter, but not the former.

Furthermore, the matter filling the body in the beginning, since it is "raw" <note>term: "raw" (Latin: *cruda*); undigested or unprocessed humors that the body has not yet "cooked" or matured for expulsion.</note> and quiet, is not in a state to be corrupted as it is in the progression of the disease. Nor should the matter be made more raw, since the food should be only slightly prone to putrefaction and easily digestible. Nor do the blockages so dissolve the strength that food is necessary, but rather specific and determined things to which that name was perhaps given. For they denote a "cutting" <note>term: "concision" (Latin: *concisionem*); a surgical or medicinal cutting down of the humors.</note> as has been said. 

Regarding the next point, it must be said that the similarity is not total, but only in this: that just as every disease progresses through four known times, so a paroxysm progresses through four particular stages. But it fails in many other ways. For in the beginning of the disease, food is generally allowed. According to the ancient saying: *In the beginning of diseases, etc.*, but not in the beginning of a paroxysm. In the beginning of the disease, the matter is undigested, but not in the particular paroxysm of many illnesses. Thus, in the total beginning, the symptoms are more remitted, while in the particular paroxysm, they are not a little intense, and so on for others. 

Regarding the next point, although the "natural virtue" may be safe, the "animal virtue" <note>term: "animal virtue" (Latin: *virtus animalis*); the power of the soul/brain governing movement and sensation.</note>, being tired, turns all the natural heat (the instrument of nature) to itself, so that the natural virtue, impoverished of heat, would not be able to digest the food. Rather, the undigested food would turn into the matter of the disease. Or if it drew the heat to itself to digest, the "crises" <note>The critical point where the disease is decided.</note> and the management of the disease would be neglected. Or the natural virtue is still working on dividing the matter, even if not on "cooking" <note>term: "decoction" (Latin: *decoctio*); the metaphorical cooking or ripening of humors by bodily heat.</note> it. For digestion consists of decoction and distribution—that is, the separation from the walls of the members.

Regarding the next point, it must be said that this is true in cases where the heat is moderate, such as in quartan and daily fevers. Whence in these cases, warm electuaries are provided, such as theriaca or "diatriton piperon" <note>margin: Theriaca, Diatriton piperon</note> <note>Theriaca was a complex herbal paste used as a universal antidote; Diatriton piperon was a medicine made primarily of three types of pepper.</note>, especially when the matter has been digested. But in "inflated" fevers, these should not be given when both heats are intense, as we do not wish to increase the natural heat while the external heat is increasing. Indeed, it must often be introduced then because, although it helps the digestion in cold matter, in hot matter it harms by increasing the imbalance and extinguishing the innate heat. Nor is the heating of very hot matter "digestion," but rather a tempered cooling. 

Regarding the next point, because if a fever remains solely for expulsion, food should be thinned around the peak so that it does not occupy itself with the digestion of food, but only with the expulsion of the matter. Either this fever has a unique way of dieting compared to others. And let these arguments suffice for how much the arguments of the other side are convinced.

# DIFFERENCE CXXXV.

<margin>Theriaca, Diatriton piperon</margin>

That the confidence of the sick person in the physician does not contribute to their own health is shown by this: agents and patients must communicate in a common matter or genus, yet be distinct in their underlying location. But health and confidence do not agree in matter, since one is a bodily being and the other belongs to the soul and intention. They are both supported within the sick person. Furthermore, things that are beneficial resist by action, but health is achieved by motion. For it is proper for action to be in motion, according to Gilbert <note>Likely Gilbertus Anglicus, a famous English medical writer.</note>. Confidence, however, has very little motion in it, since it is a property of the soul, in which motion does not exist in itself.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the psychological dimensions of healing, specifically focusing on whether a patient's trust in their doctor (confidentia) has a physical effect on their recovery. The text uses Aristotelian natural philosophy and Galenic medical authority to bridge the gap between the mind and the body.</meta>

...nothing is moved unless it is a body, according to the sixth book of the *Physics* <note>Aristotle’s *Physics*, a foundational text for medieval science. The argument here is that if the mind is not a "body," it shouldn't be able to move or change the physical health of the body.</note>. Furthermore, health is a certain disposition caused by the proper tempering of the hot, the cold, the moist, and the dry, and by the equality of the substance in quantity, number, and position, according to the first book of the *Regimen of Health*. This health belongs most greatly to the natural faculty <term>natural faculty: the unconscious biological power responsible for nutrition and growth</term>, as is shown by its operations. Confidence, however, pertains to the animal faculty <term>animal faculty: the psychological power responsible for sensation, emotion, and thought</term>. For it inheres in opinion, according to the third book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle’s *De Anima*.</note>. And this is confirmed because when faculties impede one another—as in the fourth book of *On the Soul*—if the confidence of the animal faculty is strengthened, the natural faculty will be weakened, because the heat which is the instrument of nature (by which it performs all its actions) is drawn away from it. For all faculties are supported by their own proper instruments. Furthermore, nothing acts beyond its own species <note>original: "ultra suam speciem"; meaning a mental thing shouldn't produce a physical result</note>, since every action is ultimately from a specific form. Therefore, since confidence is of a different species and nature than health—for one, as has appeared, imitates the nature of the body, while the other is more of the soul—it follows that... etc.

<margin>hand</margin> In the first part of the fourth book <note>Likely referring to Avicenna’s *Canon of Medicine*.</note>, only three things are established by which medical treatment is completed: regimen (diet), medicine, and surgery. None of these is "confidence." Therefore, it is not sufficient to indicate there that confidence contributes greatly to the health of the sick. However, Galen in the first book of *Prognostics* and Aristotle in the fourth of *On the Soul* hold the contrary view. Furthermore, a mental image of something hot, whether painful or pleasant, is in some way the same as the thing itself, which is why it causes motion in living beings. But confidence is a certain hope of the soul existing in the animal faculty of greatest power. Therefore, confidence in health will be like health itself, and thus it contributes to it by being assimilated to it. 

Regarding the first point, it should be known that confidence is a strong intention impressed upon a hidden apprehension. What remains of the definitions appeared in the first and tenth distinctions. Regarding the second point, it should be known from the first book of *Physics* <note>original: "naturali primo"</note> that some authors, such as the Asclepiads <note>Followers of Asclepiades of Bithynia, who held a mechanistic view of the body and often denied the soul's influence.</note>, expressly announced that there is no power of the soul in us by which we think or understand. Rather, they regarded us as being driven like beasts by sensory passions, testifying that wisdom, sobriety, and continence are a "grand joke." They claimed that people do not love one another or their descendants, and have no care for such things. They furthermore despised dreams, divinations, counsels, and all astrology. Since, therefore, confidence exists (as will appear) in the power of the rational soul as its proper recipient, it will be regarded by these same people as no small joke that confidence could lead to health. Yet Aristotle "scented" them out in his works, noting that the body suffers due to the affections of the soul, such as the emotions and imaginations of the soul. This occurs, for example, in the case of someone who strongly imagines a fall while the seed is being received into the womb <note>A reference to the medieval belief that a mother's imagination could physically mark or affect a developing fetus.</note. These are things that men shrink from believing because they do not know the habits of difficult dispositions. But those who love wisdom do not deny them as things that cannot be. Those who baselessly disparage themselves, speaking vanities, should not be listened to; one should not dwell on their stupidity, but rather listen to those who provide reasons, as in the third book of the *Metaphysics*. For it is foolish to be troubled by the opinions of anyone offering contradictions, as the first book of the *Topics* says; and as the third book of *On the Parts [of Animals]* says, perhaps it is the mark of a fool

to search deeply into the speeches of fools, especially since their falsehood will appear clearly from what is to be said.

Regarding the third point, it must be shown first that confidence benefits the sick person. Secondly, the manner of this shall be declared. Regarding the first, it should be known that experience <note>original: "empeiria"</note>—the universal indicator—shows that confidence contributes no small amount to the health of the sick; authority testifies to it, and reason proves it. First, because we see not infrequently that the infirm are led into a great recovery because of their hope in a famous and long-desired physician, so much so that he often seems to work more than others. This happens even with the actual external operation of healing, as Galen testifies of himself sometimes: "I perceived through myself no small effect, even when I was sometimes doing nothing more than others." This is shown by proof in this way: when the human mind is certified that a certain thing (which otherwise has no natural help) is useful to it, that thing helps the body through the intention of the mind alone. Whence the beginning of the *Prognostics* says: "The physician who is well-persuaded [confident] heals more." And the Commentator says that the patient has faith that the doctor is able to know the nature of illnesses. Because of this trust, the sick speak of him and commit themselves to him vehemently. The doctor in whom the sick trust, and into whose hands they commit themselves, heals illnesses more fully. Aristotle, along with Al-Ghazali <note>Algazele; a Persian philosopher whose works on logic and soul were influential in the West.</note>, asserts this so strongly as to say that an action depending on confidence will be more effective than what the physician does with his instruments, means, or medicines. 

It must be noted, however, that this confidence benefits in different ways depending on the varying disposition of the body and age. For example, those with a soft, delicate body are more fit for receiving this effect, as are those of a youthful or needy age, and according to whether they are gifted in intellect or imagination or any internal sensory faculty. Confidence is received through the expectation of that which operates more actually on the outside, since the action happens here by a very direct reasoning. For confidence founded in the intellect benefits less in saving the patient than that situated in the imagination. And it is even much less effective in the imagination than in the external reality. For that which is most "impressed" is that which is apprehended as a particular thing. For this hope exists even in a certain confused way, then more absolutely in the common sense, then in the "cogitative" fantasy, and then in the estimation. It is least effective in the intellect.

# Whether Confidence itself acts as a medium toward health.

<margin>Second book of *On the Soul*: The intellect which was first in the senses. Second [book] of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*. The author is referencing the principle that all human knowledge begins with sensory experience.</note>.</margin> Since all teaching and learning arises from pre-existing knowledge—specifically sensory perception—and because confidence is of a small essence and distant from actual physical health, it nonetheless contributes, though not as much as "imagined confidence." In this way, confidence works more or less effectively depending on how strongly it focuses on the desired outcome. If the body is more or less receptive, like the sense of touch, it responds accordingly. Such confidence leaves a powerful impression on those with a strong imagination, such as melancholics <note>In the "four humors" theory, melancholics were thought to have a dry, cold temperament that made them prone to deep thought and vivid, sometimes obsessive, imagination.</note>, who are the opposite of the moist, phlegmatic types. For the actions of an agent are impressed upon a subject that is disposed to receive them. It should finally be noted that confidence sometimes moves the body by internalizing the effect—which is what we are speaking of now. At other times, some say it brings forth power from another source, through which health immediately arises. This is according to the Gospel of Matthew: **"Your faith has made you well."** <note>original: "Fides tua te saluam fecit" (Matthew 9:22). The author uses this biblical miracle as a case study for medical psychology.</note> This ultimately stands to reason. Because that which changes and alters the body according to heat, cold, and so on, is capable of inducing health. For health itself is a good disposition of the body, caused by a proper balance. Confidence performs this work. For confidence is a certain "species" <term>species: here meaning a mental image or representation</term> of the soul. A species moves the body according to the likeness of a thing existing outside of it. Hence, concerning the cause of motion in animals: fantasies, senses, and meditations alter the body. For the senses are immediate alterations, which is why it is said that confidence existing in the senses works more than that existing in the intellect. And it is added: Fantasy and understanding possess the power of real things. For in some way, the "species" of heat or cold, or of pleasure or sadness, exists in the intellect in the same way as the actual quality of the things themselves. And therefore, people tremble and feel fear simply by thinking of them. Furthermore, that which incites the "innate heat" <term>innate heat: the vital internal fire believed by ancient doctors to drive digestion and life</term> against a sickness contributes to health. For heat, as the instrument of nature, cures sickness. For either the sickness is cold, and the heat cures it through opposition; or it is hot, and the heat then moves the "spirit" <term>spirit: a subtle, vapor-like substance that carried life-force through the arteries</term> to destroy the sickness by making its matter evaporate and resolve. This is the primary and secondary way. Confidence acts in this manner, as will be shown. If it is said that confidence might incite the heat too much toward "fury" or "rage," especially in a hot sickness, it should be answered that the opposite happens. For the benefit gained by evaporating, resolving, and opening blockages <term>blockages: original "opilationem," referring to obstructions in the body's channels</term> is greater. Indeed, that which works in this way has more of a cooling effect than an increase in heat; there is almost no harm from the heat incited by confidence. This motion is light and gentle, not a sudden or violent alteration.

Furthermore, the body suffers along with the passions of the soul, as seen in the study of physiognomy <note>The ancient practice of judging a person's character or health from their physical features.</note>. This is apparent regarding love, fear, and sadness; and this is from the introduction to *On the Soul*. All passions of the soul seem to exist alongside the body. This includes mildness, fear, mercy, confidence, as well as joy, love, and hate. For the body suffers something simultaneously with these. This is apparent because even when no terrifying thing is present externally, we are sometimes moved to the passion of fear. But confidence, as has been said, is a passion of the soul; therefore, the body will suffer an effect from it. And because the subject suffers according to what is impressed upon it by the agent, anything that has a proportion or suitability to the outcome can produce it. Each thing is produced by something similar and suitable to itself. But the imagined and understood confidence of health is suitable to external health, as if depending on it. For it is drawn and led out from sensory things. For "health is made from health," according to the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*. Furthermore, that which changes the body with a less sudden alteration can contribute most to health, because nature does not endure sudden changes. Confidence in health works this way, as it induces alterations gently. It does not work as violently as many material medicines applied internally or externally. In those material medicines, sometimes no healing benefit is found, only injury. For they provoke nature with their foreign qualities, harsh substances, and excessive quantities. However, because a sickness is often so great that health must be introduced by force, and because the body is indisposed and the strength is weak, and because the confidence of health is only weakly impressed on the intellect or the senses, health cannot be induced without the application of a material thing. Indeed, the material medicine is often necessary for health to be introduced. Again, since confidence is a certain rational affection of the soul arising from an opinion of a desired, suitable thing, it contributes [to health], as gathered from Aristotle's *On the Soul*. For every opinion <margin>3rd book of *On the Soul* of Aristotle. Every opinion is followed by faith/conviction; but this does not exist in beasts.</margin> is followed by faith or conviction, but this does not belong to any of the beasts. But the confidence of health which a sick person receives from a doctor is a rational affection of the soul, which is why it would contribute to the health of the patient. Regarding this, one should secondly know that Aristotle's view partly agrees with Algazel <note>Algazel (Al-Ghazali, d. 1111) was a Persian philosopher whose works on logic and soul were widely read in Latin.</note> and partly disagrees with the Great Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note>. For he wrote in the fourth book on the soul that souls are of a double nature. For some are so exalted, noble, and capable of such great and miraculous works <margin>Avicenna, Algazel.</margin> that they do not only work in their own body through alterations and changes, but even in another person's body, and without any physical medium. An example is the work of the "fascinating eye" <note>The "evil eye." Medieval science often tried to explain the evil eye as a physical projection of the soul's power.</note> which works destruction. For example, it can cast a man into a pit or a camel into a cauldron <note>This is a famous scholastic example from Avicenna (Ibn Sina) illustrating "fascination" or the power of the mind to affect the physical world directly.</note>. For when the soul of someone is focused on the corruption of another whom they encounter, the other yields and obeys, being transformed and corrupted at the command of the first person's will. For it is felt that the "inferior nature" obeys the "superior" as if by a nod. Therefore, such a soul can heal the sick and...

<meta>This page continues a scholastic inquiry into the relationship between the mind (soul) and the body, specifically how mental states like "confidence" or "imagination" can manifest physical changes. It draws heavily on Avicenna’s theories regarding the soul's power to manipulate matter, while also contrasting these with the Aristotelian (Peripatetic) and Christian viewpoints.</meta>

...to weaken or corrupt <term>natures</term><note>In this context, "natures" refers to the inherent physical properties or dispositions of a living thing.</note> and to change them. This power is so great that it can make what is not fire behave as fire, and what is not earth behave as earth. And by the will of such a soul, rains, fertility, the swallowing of the earth, and mortality occur. This is because the matter of the soul is much more obedient [to the will] than one of the opposing physical elements is when it overcomes another. This is also one of the specific properties of **prophetic powers**.

What perhaps moved him <note>Likely referring to Avicenna.</note> to swim so superstitiously in the study of <term>physiognomy</term><note>The practice of judging a person's character or future from their physical appearance.</note> was the desire to assign a specific cause to all things. He accepted that incantations and <term>fascinations</term><note>The "evil eye" or the power of a gaze to cause physical harm or change.</note>—which are posited by their defenders to come from the aforementioned powers of the soul—are received from the celestial bodies, as the soul is made in the image of their motion and light. For a soul that possesses such power is able not only to move the body joined to it, but the entire world that lies beneath the <term>sphere</term><note>In medieval cosmology, the "spheres" were the concentric layers of the heavens moved by divine or celestial intelligences.</note> which its mover (of whom the soul is an image) controls. 

For the soul has two aspects: it is a soul, and it is an image of the movers of the spheres, such as **Saturn** or **Jupiter** or similar bodies. Thus, it follows the reflection and shadow of that power which moves the things subject to that sphere. When it moves by its own power, it can impede matter, or it is able to stop matter from its natural act and order. The Hebrews, writing on the deeds of the prophets, recorded such things. However, **Christians** <note>original: "Christicoli" — literally "Christ-worshippers."</note> do not attribute the primary cause of these things to any human soul. Rather, they attribute these wonders to **Divine Power** operating above nature through men called prophets, who act as instruments and hold a middle ground between us and God. This opinion, as will appear, has become ridiculous to the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The followers of Aristotle, known for their focus on natural, physical causes rather than supernatural ones.</note>.

<margin>Note</margin>
There is, however, another type of soul: one that is weak and infirm, unable to achieve its operations without physical instruments and means. This is apparent in a person performing a ritual <note>original: "scarificante" — likely a reference to one performing a sacrifice or ritual act.</note> who cannot introduce the form of the ritual into himself except through instruments and media, because of the weakness and idleness of his own soul. 

A similar situation occurs in the disposition of a sick person when they **believe they are recovering**, or a healthy person when they **believe they are falling ill**. It often happens that because the "form" of health or sickness is strengthened in the soul, actual health or sickness follows. This action is often more effective than what a doctor does with his instruments—as has been said—and his means, such as medicines. 

This is also why a person can walk across a beam laid flat on the ground, but cannot do so if it is raised high like a bridge over deep water. In the latter case, the "form" of falling is so vehemently impressed upon the soul that the physical nature obeys it <note>This is a classic medieval psychological example: fear of falling creates the physical reality of falling.</note>. Hence, regarding liquid motions: thought communicates with the body and "suffers" alongside it in its accidents. For perhaps a man sees a snake suddenly and turns pale. Or, walking upon the peak of a pinnacle or a high mountain, his feet tremble. Similarly, if he sees someone vomiting or urinating, he is provoked to do the same, as if the sight and understanding of it were occurring in his own limbs. On this, there are many examples in the *Seventh Book of Problems*. 

Therefore, this mode of thinking agrees more with the opinion of **Avicenna** and **the Commentator** <note>Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher who wrote famous commentaries on Aristotle.</note>, who posit that no operation occurs from any source without motion and change in these lower things. Indeed, every agent, the more distant it is from contact with the person being acted upon...

...requires more instruments and media so that it may be drawn out and articulated for its work. However, the truth of the Law <note>The religious or theological truth.</note> strives for the opposite, often positing that the **Creator** of all creatures produces them immediately without motion or change, and has the power to do so. On this, see distinction 64. 

According to this same mode, it must be posited that **confidence in health** is a path by which specific meditations on health are led back into the <term>fantastic virtues</term><note>The "virtus fantastica" or imagination—the faculty that creates and stores mental images.</note> or into the intellect. From there, it is brought forth to produce that very health. For when it is in the intellect, it is led to the fantastic powers, such as the estimative faculty, then to the cogitative and imaginative faculties. And then, having become like a "material" and specific thing, it is rendered to the instruments of nature, such as **heat**. It excites this heat and, especially as it moves everything subject to its sphere, it rouses the **vital spirit** to change, dissolve, and destroy the things that were causing the illness. Thus, the vital spirit, which was bound as if in a prison in the nobler part of the heart, is raised up into the principal parts and finally into the whole body. See distinction 72. This question is also touched upon in article 156.

Regarding the four objections: To the first, it should be said that agents and patients share the same physical matter. In such an action, every agent is prepared by the third book of the *Physics*. However, in an action that is in some way **supernatural**, this truth does not hold—such as the action of the higher celestial bodies upon these lower things. For they do not share the same matter, except perhaps through the mediation of "forms," as the Commentator says, or because such matter is proportioned to this specific soul through confidence.

<margin>13</margin> Although **real health** and **health moved by confidence** exist in the same subject, they are distinct in different partial subjects. One is rooted in the **heart**, while the other is in the **intellect** or the imaginative faculty. Thus, this mode is verified in the action as a proper conversion. 

To the next point, it should be said similarly that this is verified especially concerning the aforementioned conversion. For according to the wisdom of the Peripatetics, motion and action do not properly belong to the soul or its passions, but only to the body and its opposite. Nevertheless, we place action and motion in the powers of the soul and the intellect according to a certain "similitude." Indeed, a reflexive circle can arise in the same thing.

<margin>14</margin> To the next, it should be said that although health principally belongs to the "natural" virtue, it nonetheless belongs to the "vital" and "animal" virtues in those who possess them. Nor should it be said that the operation of the **animal virtue** (such as confidence) hinders the **natural virtue** which receives health. For as has been shown, its motion is very transformative and not at all hindering. Furthermore, the instrument—such as heat—which the animal virtue uses in its operation tends toward the same end as the heat which the natural virtue uses in its governance. When virtues are ordered toward a single end with their instruments, they do not hinder each other as was suggested, but rather strengthen each other more. 

To the last point, it should be said that although **healing confidence** and **real health** are different in their definitions, they do not differ so much that one cannot contribute to the existence and production of the other, as has been declared.

**T**hat medicine derives its species <note>In this context, "species" refers to the specific nature or essential quality of a substance.</note> and <term>constitution</term><note>Latin: *complexio*; the specific ratio of the four primary qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) that defines a person's health or a substance's effect.</note> from our **innate constitution**. Because, as stated in the first part: we do not say a thing is hotter or colder except in comparison to the impression of the **innate heat** which is within us. Likewise, constitution and heat are proportioned to each other just as a primary and secondary agent are, when one is ordered toward the other. But innate heat is that which brings the "potential" of a medicine into "act" <note>Drawing on Aristotelian logic: medicine has the potential to heat, but it only becomes "actually" hot when triggered by the body's natural warmth.</note>. Whence it is said in the second [book] of the first [part]: when the carrier of the medicine has been acted upon by the innate heat which is in us. Thus, it is also with the innate constitution. And so, a medicine will be "good" because of the relationship it has to the innate constitution, which is proportioned to such heat. Furthermore, medicine seems to derive its nature from that which provides the most certain test of its operation in our body. But this comes from the innate constitution and not the "influencing" <note>Latin: *influens*; the "influencing" or "acquired" constitution is the temporary state of the body, whereas the "innate" is the permanent natural balance.</note> one, since the truest experience of medicines occurs in a temperate body—as stated in the first [book] of *On Simples* <note>Referring to Galen’s *De Simplicium Medicamentorum Facultatibus* (On the Properties of Simple Medicines).</note>. But the innate constitution is temperate in relation to the person's current state; for that [acquired state] stands out as more elevated and more distempered.

Again, in common diets, the human constitution is temperately hot and moist in the second degree. For it either adds to the constitution by "weight" or by "justice" <note>Terms from medieval pharmacy: *complexio ad pondus* (balance by equal weight of elements) vs. *complexio ad iustitiam* (the balance appropriate or "just" for a specific species’ nature).</note>. Not by weight, because it was shown in Difference 18 that this is not found. It will therefore be by justice. But since this is twofold—influencing and innate—it will be necessary to verify the statement regarding one of them. Certainly not the influencing one, since it is separate from the innate cause. And because of each one and that which is more. Therefore, since there are no more constitutions to provide, the statement will be verified regarding the innate constitution alone. Because of this, medicine derives its own constitution from the innate, and not from the influencing.

> ¶ But that the opposite is true—that it is derived from the influencing—is shown thus: Everything derives its nature from that which it is in "act," and through which it has its being and is distinct from others. Act is that which separates and distinguishes. But the innate constitution is primary; for it primarily qualifies the moisture and parts, such as the touch, as stated in Difference 48. > ¶ Again, medicine derives its species and its name from that which directs it toward its proper "end" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "end" (*finis*) is the purpose for which a thing exists.</note>; for it is just that all things be named from their end—from the second [book] of *On the Soul*. But that it derives from neither is shown thus: one "act" is not constructed from several existing beings in act—Difference 16. But each of these is in act. This is known regarding the influencing one, and it also appears regarding the innate, since it qualifies the entity and disposes the "vital virtue" <note>Latin: *virtutem vitalem*; the life-force that governs pulse and breathing.</note> which follows it to receive the primary principle and the primary soul. Furthermore, a thing ought to derive its nature from those things out of which it is composed. But medicine, like any other thing here, is composed of the four elements. Therefore, medicine does not receive its constitution from the constitution of the body. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known what medicine is and how many ways it is spoken of; this was shown in the third Difference and will also be seen in the following. Truly, however, it should first be noted that medicine, as it is taken here, is a thing whose property is to **alter our natures**, just as food is a thing that increases our substance and adds to it.

Food is that which replaces the natural parts of the one fed, and this part is in the "species" of the dissolved part <note>Meaning food becomes the same kind of substance as the body part it replaces.</note>. Medicine, however, although it replaces the natural parts of the one fed, does not do so in the "species" of the dissolved part. Rather, it has within itself an active and "alterative" power. That which is digested by nature strengthens the bodies and is called nutriment. But there is a difference by reason of medicine and properly of "loosening" <note>Latin: *solutie*; referring to purgatives that "loosen" the bowels.</note>; as if there were in the digestible thing an excess of heat or cold that cannot be overcome by the heat of animals. That which overcomes and is easily "flowing" through the two vents—namely upward and downward—by reason of quality and quantity is called an "expurgation" there. 

Medicine thus accepted is twofold. One is **simple**, such as wormwood. The other is **compound**, such as **theriac** <note>Latin: *tyriaca*; a famous ancient and medieval poly-pharmaceutical compound used as an antidote and general cure.</note>. Likewise, the simple is twofold: for one is **alterative**, such as chamomile; the other is **loosening** [purgative], such as **scammony** <note>Latin: *scamonea*; a plant resin used as a potent laxative.</note>. And the compound is similarly twofold. One is for general use, attributed to no determined part, such as **Mithridatum** <note>A famous semi-mythical panacea or universal antidote.</note>, *scelithes*, and such. The other is **singular**, assigned to a specific part, such as a **collyrium** <note>Latin: *colerium*; an eye-salve or eye-wash.</note> of thucia [zinc oxide], an enema, and such things. And therefore the books of antidotes are separated into two parts. Know clearly that the constitution of any medicine heard of here is not according to how the whole is caused by the production of elements; since it is not ordered toward its own "end," but rather toward the **human body**—namely, according to what effect it produces in our body.
