...possibility and the diversity of matter so that we cannot collect them by signs. It was also said that **complexions** <note>In medieval medicine, a "complexion" is the specific balance of the four qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—within a body or substance.</note> would be infinite in the first theorem. Furthermore, **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a famous Andalusian philosopher who critiqued Al-Kindi's mathematical medicine.</note> refutes **Jacob** <note>Al-Kindi (c. 801–873), known in Latin as Jacobus, who proposed that the strength of a medicine increases geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8, 16) rather than arithmetically.</note> secondly because, even if he conceded what Jacob posits, then the latitude <note>The range or span of a specific degree of intensity.</note> of the third degree will not be proportional to the latitude of the second relative to the **temperament** <note>The "temperament" is the ideal point of health where all qualities are perfectly balanced.</note>, and similarly the second to the third. Since such latitudes ought to be located within a degree, and since there is no equality between these orders, there could be no greater error in this art than that. 

Furthermore, thirdly, he fights the same man with a discourse taken from the fifth book of **Medicines** <note>Likely referring to Galen's *On the Composition of Drugs*.</note>. This is because **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire, whose works formed the basis of medieval medicine.</note> understood that to be "hot in the first degree" which has an excess over the temperament in one part beyond it. And according to this, when a comparison of the "double" is placed in the excess of degrees, it will not be necessary that a medicine in the fourth degree is double over a medicine that is tempered sixteen times by doubling. This is what Galen sensed when he said: "And my intention in the first degree is that thing which is first manifested to the sense in the change of the body." If Galen’s intention were that the first degree was double the temperament, the change manifested by the medicine in the body would not be the *beginning* of the change; rather, if there were something before this, that would be the beginning of the changes. And this which is posited as the beginning would not be a beginning, but rather something already existing beyond the beginning. This is also what **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), author of the *Canon of Medicine*.</note> invites us to consider when he says: "The second degree is so that the operation becomes stronger than that [the first]."

Beyond this also, I can proceed against the counsel of Al-Kindi so that his erroneous position may be removed—a position previously loved by a few unrefined people on account of their wonder at it. For he first adopted a poor method of teaching. For natural things—among which is this distinction of the degrees of medicines—cannot be demonstrated from arithmetic and music, especially since this natural method is found to be quite sufficient. For "demonstrations from one genus to another genus do not fail" <note>A principle from Aristotle’s *Posterior Analytics* stating that you cannot use the rules of one science (like geometry) to prove things in another (like biology).</note>. Because of this, the school of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>, along with the third book of the *Critique*, detests **Pythagoras** and **Plato** in many places, because they wished to cause and demonstrate natural things through mathematics.

Furthermore, it remains insufficient because just as a double string or <term>diapason</term> <note>original: "dyapaſſon"; the Greek musical term for an octave, representing a 2:1 ratio.</note> [is in music], so Jacob errs in this part; and especially since that, as he shows, is possible and in some way harmonious with natural things. **Pliny** <note>original: "Palyn"; likely referring to Pliny the Elder.</note> in the third book of *Histories* and *On the World* says: "Nature does not commit a leap" <note>original: "Natura ſaltum non committit"; the principle that nature changes continuously rather than in sudden jumps.</note>, but passes from extreme to extreme gradually and step-by-step, so that by its continuity the boundary and the middle are hidden. But he who proceeds from the temperament to the double, and from there to the quadruple, and then to the octuple and sixteen-fold, certainly commits a sudden leap, not preserving an equal proportion.

Even as in the human complexion, even the natural one, there are infinite stages in "more and less," as touched upon by variety; much more so is this the case in sickness, since it is raised higher and recedes from the middle more than natural human complexions. Therefore, a sickness receding from the temperament will be according to 5 parts of heat, or 6, or 7, or 9, or 10, or 11, or 12, or 13, or 14, or 15, because the excess from the temperament is caused uniformly, since it is a movement, as said, from extreme to extreme through a middle. But the aforesaid distemperaments cannot be cured when, according to Jacob’s position, medicines are not found opposite to them as they are sought in the <term>Microtegni</term> <note>original: "microtegni"; the *Ars Medica* or "Small Art" of Galen, a foundational medical textbook.</note>. For according to him, one only finds opposition in the double, quadruple, octuple, and sixteen-fold ratios. 

Again, a medicine which is in the first degree of coldness will not be able to bring a medicine which is in the third degree [of heat] to the second degree, as everyone senses. Because in a hot medicine of the third degree, there are eight halves <note>original: "medietates"; units of quality used in these calculations.</note> of a part of coldness and one of heat, whereas the second degree has four of heat and four of coldness. Now, however, two halves of coldness of the first degree will remit eight halves of heat of the third degree, reducing it to 15 halves. And because in the first degree there was a half of coldness which was remitted from the eighth coldness of the third degree, the hot medicine in the third degree will be reduced by the cold medicine in the first to a sixth of heat and one half, with an eighth part of one half removed. If, however, it were led to the second degree, it would be necessary to repress it to four halves of heat. For this description is posited for the second degree. 

From these things, therefore, is raised up a wicked error that has long sprouted. Similarly, none of his motions are valid; for if the double proportion (or <term>diapason</term>) is more natural, sweeter, and more delightful than others, and the distinction of degrees is assigned according to it, then every numerical and harmonic proportion of sounds or voices would be made idly through it alone, for the others discovered would then be useless. For although it is as he reports—preferred among proportions in itself—it is not so in this matter. Just as although it is more noble to be in the air than in the water or earth (since air is more formal), it is not so for aquatic or earthly animals. Rather, such a process [as Jacob's] commits a deception relative to a certain thing and simply. 

Jacob himself also detests the distinction assigned second by a certain insufficient <term>algoristic</term> <note>original: "algoriſtica"; referring to the use of Arabic numerals and arithmetic processes.</note> reason, saying it would be false through the way of experiment and argument. For if a hot medicine in the fourth degree be mixed with a cold medicine in the same degree, and the medicine be equalized, there would be in it three parts hot and two cold; whereas previously in the posited position, five hot and three were added...

<meta>This page continues the technical rebuttal of Al-Kindi’s (referred to as "Jacob") mathematical system for determining medicinal potencies. ...cold in the same way in the second degree. According to this, therefore, there will be five parts hot and one part cold; but previously, six parts were placed as hot and two as cold. If, however, a third part is added, there will be six parts hot, so that the entire medicine will be hot, possessing no coldness. Previously, however, seven parts were hot in this degree and one was cold. Furthermore, I say that there will be no way in which it is possible to assign a fourth degree. 

Moreover, the very foundation of this position cannot stand, because a **temperament** <note>The "temperament" is the ideal point of health where the four qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—are perfectly balanced.</note> does not only result from hot and cold things in the fourth [degree], but even from degrees of opposing substances and temperaments—such as a third degree of heat with a third degree of cold, a second with a second, a first with a first, and a balanced state with a balanced state. 

Again, whatever would be hot in the fourth degree would, according to this, have no coldness at all—which is a ridiculous thing to say. For with that [heat], cold, dryness, and moisture exist not simply in these things, but I speak of them according to **dominance** <note>original: "a dominio." The theory that a substance is called "hot" because heat is the dominant quality, even if cold is still present.</note>. For in the beginning, heat, cold, dryness, and moisture were left as simple and absolute. 

Indeed, a sound mind does not grasp the distinction of **Constantine** <note>Constantine the African (c. 1020–1087), a physician who translated Arabic medical works into Latin.</note> when a degree is established (as it appeared according to Jacob) by the retreat from the temperament. Natural heat, however, as he imagines, is not perfectly tempered, but rather tends toward the second degree of heat. Furthermore, natural heat, tempered from the first form, is soothing and sweet; and if this and the human **complexion** <note>The specific physiological makeup or balance of an individual.</note> are placed in the second degree of heat by a relation of weight. Or perhaps he understands natural heat to be innate and not "running," or a third thing composed of these. Again, since according to the second collection and the first canon, natural heat is hot and moist, and exists as the form of the limbs, it will be in the second degree almost equal to the coldness of that degree, or to its dryness, since cold and dryness are graduated through it; for which reason, as in many other things, let it be omitted as ambiguous.

I also hear better of the fourfold division of degrees which he attributes to **Galen** <note>The primary authority in Roman and medieval medicine.</note> and **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), author of the "Canon of Medicine."</note>, although the **son of Al-Kindi** <note>original: "Alchindi filius." This may refer to a follower or a specific intellectual lineage of Al-Kindi.</note> says that Galen disapproved of it. Nevertheless, because he is rendered suspect here, I do not spurn this distinction of degrees, since it avoids the inconveniences that follow Jacob and others. 

Let the natural, gradual, and hidden process of nature be observed, continuously filling every distance in "more" and "less," distinct from the temperament all the way to the extremes of the four degrees, so that the end of one degree immediately touches the beginning of the next—just like the connection of the universe, such as the elements among themselves and to the celestial orbs, and those to one another. This appears in the fifth [book] of **Medicines** <note>original: "farmacorum." Likely Galen’s work on simple medicines.</note> and the first of the second. 

For a medicine is called hot, cold, dry, or moist—whether it is eaten, drunk, or applied—in the **first degree** when it warms the body with a warming that is not manifestly perceived; rather, it requires the demonstration of reasoning and logic, unless by accident, such as when it is repeated many times. 

That which consists in the **second degree** is such that it operates more strongly than the aforementioned. For its operation is manifest and understood, yet it does not change the course of nature nor its acts, unless by accident, such as if it occurs many times or remains for a long time. For something is placed in a degree in two ways: either directly by reason of quality, or laterally on the part of quantity, whether discrete or continuous. 

That which produces a strong action, yet not to the ultimate point so that an essentially harmful result arises, and which is manifest but does not deaden or corrupt, holds the **third degree**. 

But that which, by its operation, burns with heat or essentially **mortifies** <note>To "mortify" here means to kill or cause tissue death.</note> with cold—such as is the property of poisonous things—that is placed in the **fourth degree**. 

Since these degrees are referred to as indeterminate within the temperament, just as in a rule for directing inequality. It is that [temperament] itself when something meeting the body does not impress itself upon the senses, nor does it drive them away in any manner of flight. For that which it has is similar to itself, from which it does not happen to suffer. 

Galen also separated each single degree into three "mansions" <note>Stages or sub-divisions of intensity.</note> so that twelve result in total; whence in the *Segni* he names seven numbers and ten according to the excess from the temperament. This happens because a "degree" refers to an excess in "more" and "less," and where there is that and a middle, three things arise from it. In the smallest things, there is a middle. 

And if each of the degrees has "mansions" implanted in it (as was touched upon), it is nevertheless not possible for us to distinguish them. Galen proves the partition into the third degree because the drying of **mustard** <note>original: "sinapi."</note> is not like the drying of a **cautery** <note>A branding iron or caustic substance used to burn tissue.</note>, although both are such things in the fourth degree. Thus it appears from the discourses of these men and the sub-distinction into three parts for any degree, that the total distance of the boundaries is varied by gradual increase in "more" and "less," so that nothing falls into a vacuum, as followed erroneously from the position of Jacob. 

If, however, I should wish to curiously distinguish the degrees even better than Jacob according to numerical or **harmonic proportions** <note>The author is proposing a system where medical degrees correspond to musical intervals like the octave and fifth.</note>, so that a mathematical or harmonic distinction proportionally concurs with the natural one approved above, it shall be done by positing that:
*   The **fourth degree** stands to the first in a quadruple proportion, or a quadruple **octave** <note>original: "dyapason."</note>. And it is this which was granted: that the fourth quadruples the first.
*   The **third degree** triples the second [according to] a **fifth** <note>original: "dyapente."</note> and an octave.
*   The **second degree** doubles, or acts as an **octave**.
*   The **first degree** relates to the temperament, as far as its second "mansion," in a **sesquialteral** <note>A 3:2 ratio; original: "emiola."</note> proportion or a **fifth**; but as for the first [mansion], in a **sesquitertial** <note>A 4:3 ratio; original: "epitrica."</note> proportion.

It defines the degrees based on their observable effects on the human body, ranging from unnoticeable (1st) to lethal or caustic (4th).</summary>

In this way, therefore, the distinction of degrees more soundly and naturally serves arithmetic and musical proportions. Regarding the second point, it should be known—as will appear according to **Averroes** <note>original: "Aueŕ." Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a high-authority Andalusian philosopher and physician who often critiqued Galen.</note> in the 143rd distinction—that one necessary reason for joining one medicine with another is to strengthen or weaken the medicine's power. This can be done in two ways. One is that it is mixed with its opposite, as when we lack a medicine that is hot in the second degree, we mix a medicine that is hot in the third degree with a medicine that is cold in the first degree, and it is rendered into a medicine that is hot in the second degree.

The second way is when a strong medicine is joined with another that is not its opposite in quality and virtue, but is instead similar, or rather, one will be perceived by the other. For instance, when a medicine that is hot in the third degree is joined to a medicine that is hot in the first degree, it then brings it down to the second degree. **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of antiquity (c. 129–216 AD), whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> proves this through the mixing of lukewarm water with boiling water, which causes its heat to decline to a degree that might be called "the second." Galen therefore intends that a medicine that is hot in the first degree can reduce one in the third degree to the second. Tenthly, this is also confirmed in practice as follows: The composition of two medicines is sometimes necessary so that a **complexion** <note>The balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within the body or a substance.</note> opposite to an ill complexion is united. For example, to cure a disease, one might need a medication that is **heating** <note>original: "calefaciente."</note> in the second degree; if such a thing is not found, one may take something hot in the third degree and join it to what is hot in the first. From these will result a medium heating effect in the second degree. For that which is hot in the first degree diminishes the heat of the third and recalls it to the second, as was seen in the case of hot and lukewarm water.

However, Averroes subsequently opposes this, primarily through two arguments. One is because, he says, this would be a contradiction; for if we see a person suffering from a hot illness in the fourth or third degree and we give them a hot substance in the second degree, they will be greatly harmed by it. Yet, according to Galen’s words, the patient ought to be cooled. For example, if we were to give honey <note>Honey was traditionally classified as "hot."</note> in a drink to someone having a **burning fever** <note>original: "causonem." A high, acute fever often associated with bile.</note>, would they not be harmed immediately with great injury? And similarly, if someone had a very cold ailment in the head and was anointed with rose oil <note>Rose oil was classified as "cold."</note>, would it not do much harm? He adds that those who support Galen on this matter should be careful. The second argument is that it would follow that a hot medicine would diminish and repress a hotter one just as much as a cold medicine would. According to Galen, a first-degree hot medicine reduces a third-degree hot medicine to the second, but it is well enough established that a first-degree cold medicine also brings a third-degree hot medicine to the second degree. For the first degree [of cold], by its coldness, represses the third degree of heat and brings it to the second. What will be seen concerning this follows.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that, agreeing with Galen, I say his statement can be verified in three ways. Two of these are somewhat favorable to Averroes, such as the idea that a hot medicine in the first degree does not directly reduce a hot medicine in the third degree to the second degree of heat, but rather remits some of its heat. He says that if it is as Galen says, it happens in this way: the medicine we call "hotter" is that which has a greater proportion of heat to coldness than the "less hot" medicine. Therefore, there will be coldness in both, but in an opposite way—that is, in the hotter one there will be a smaller proportion of coldness, and in the less hot one, a greater proportion of coldness. For example, the proportion of heat to coldness in a **dram** <note>original: "drag." A unit of weight.</note> of pepper is greater than in a dram of **spikenard** <note>original: "spice." An aromatic herb used in ancient pharmacy.</note>. And if in one dram of pepper there are five parts of heat and one of coldness, when two drams are mixed together, the proportion of heat to coldness in this mixture will be smaller than it would be in the pepper alone. This is because along with the two parts of heat in the spikenard, there is much coldness, just as there was one part in the pepper with five parts of heat. Thus Galen explains that a reduction from the third to the second degree is not strictly achieved, but rather a certain weakening of the third degree while it still remains within its own range.

There is also another way of explaining this "by accident," as when it happens more by reason of an imbalanced quantity in which an immense quality is subsequently contained. Or if it has been repeated many times—just as one dram of pepper, if applied extensively or more often, heats more than it would later. However, this is not by reason of proportional, extensive qualities, such as when much lukewarm water is added to a little boiling water. Yet this way of speaking seems more foreign to the subject, since the proportion of principal qualities and virtues is what is required.

And because of this, according to Galen and others, a third way will be the most excellent, and is already manifest from what has been said: since each degree is divided into three **stages** <note>original: "mansiones." Literally "mansions" or "dwelling places," used to describe subdivisions of medicinal potency.</note>, the third stage of the second degree immediately touches the first stage of the third degree. For it is posited that all the stages, distinguished according to more and less, are contiguous to one another. This is what **Al-Kindi** <note>original: "Iacob Alkindi." An 8th-century Arab philosopher who attempted to use geometric progressions to calculate medicinal degrees.</note> was unable to preserve. Therefore, when something is weakened even a little from the first stage of the third degree—and especially when it was at its very beginning—it will be reduced to the extremity of the third stage of the second degree. If it is weakened further, it will cause that which is in the third degree to arrive even more into the second. But then it is doubted, because since there are three stages for each degree, Galen's word does not seem to be verified except for one. For that which is hot in the first degree will not reduce what is hot in the third degree toward the cold, and much less to the first stage of the second degree. It must be said that perhaps Galen’s word was more...

Regarding the fourth point: what should be said to the first part has already been shown. To the other part, it must be said that although the quantity—and consequently the quality—of the heat is multiplied, the quantity of the coldness is multiplied no less. Just as when many logs are added to a weak fire: they dull it and repress it. For an agent primarily requires a patient [a subject] disposed toward it, for from this comes the action; lacking this, it cannot operate, especially when that which is joined with a large quantity is weakly active. Moreover, that which, when added, makes something "more" of its kind must be similar in species and nature, not just in genus.

To the other point, it must be said that this holds true in contraries that are directly opposed and equally vigorous, resisting each other in a long struggle like strong men dueling one another for a long time. For when one then overcomes the other, he seems more severe over him than if he had overcome him quickly with little resistance. But heat in the first degree and heat in the third are not such contraries. To the other point, if I wish to agree with **Averroes**, I will say that heat in the first degree has a "sensible" [perceptible] heat, as the authority of physicians testifies. Alternatively, although the heat of the first degree may not be sensible in comparison to the heat of the second, it is nevertheless felt in comparison to a temperate state, and especially the final mansion of the first degree. Or it should also be said that although the operation of the first degree is not sensible in act, it is so in potential, such that when it is raised by being joined to a quality like the third degree, it is immediately felt. For it does not happen that there is no sensible mode in some way.

To the other point, it should be said that this does not prove the case, but rather denotes the curious laziness <note>original: "ignauia curiosa"</note> of **Jacob** <note>Refers to Ya'qub al-Kindi (Al-Kindi), an 8th-century philosopher whose mathematical theory of degrees was often criticized by later scholastics for being overly complex or "curious."</note>. > It is shown that there is no way by which a medicine can be led from potentiality into act, and especially a cold one. Because 

this will occur either on the part of the medicine brought into act, or on the part of the innate heat. Not indeed on the part of the medicine as medicine, since it is such in potential or virtue—as taught in the **Tegni** <note>Galen's "Ars Medica" (The Art of Medicine).</note> and the eleventh book of the <term>Therapeutics<note>Galen's "Methodus Medendi."</note></term>. For it is taught that a medicine should be chosen according to its virtue [power] and not according to its appearance or its present act; whence in the third book of the <term>Colliget<note>Averroes' medical encyclopedia, "Kitab al-Kullyat."</note></term>, earth-born things that are hot are also placed in potentiality as such. However, that which lacks act in every way cannot have a progression into act. Neither can it be on the part of the substance itself, especially in concrete accidents, since its operation comes from its matter; but that retains the nature of food and not of medicine. Neither is it on the part of the heat existing in the body, since heat does not have a way of cooling by leading a cold thing into act. For the leading into act must be done by something already existing in act.

Furthermore, if a cold medicine is led into act, either that which leads it will be hot in act or cold, since only such things are operative. It cannot be heat, because natural heat has no way of generating coldness (as noted in the fifth book of the **Colliget**). Nor can it be cold in act, since life and activity do not stand with it [the cold] except through heat, as they say. Furthermore, it will not be through division into the smallest parts <note>original: "minima"</note> as **Galen** thinks, because that which is the "minimum" does not act, because a natural form requires a due quantity in matter. For regarding poison and fire, they can be taken in such a small quantity that they will not be felt.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the "degrees" and "mansions" of medicinal qualities, specifically focusing on how a medicinal substance moves from a state of "potentiality" (having the capacity to act) to "actuality" (performing its cooling or heating function) upon the human body.</meta>

# Whether there is a mode by which **medicine** might be led from **potentiality** into **actuality** by the proportion of **cold**.

Not only that it harms the third books of *On Complexions* and *On Simple Medicines*. On account of which there is no mode to assign by which a medicine—and especially a cold one—can come into actuality. Yet our senses show us the contrary, since we see a substance that is cold in potentiality, when applied to the body, arrive at the actuality of coldness; and similarly for other qualities. And that which acts, having previously been non-acting, has been led from potentiality into actuality; such are all things that encounter the body.

<margin>medicine</margin>
Therefore, it is necessary to establish some mode by which this happens. Regarding the first point, it should be known what a medicine is and in how many ways its difference is described, as shown in the third book, chapters 136 and 137. A medicine is that thing which alters the body by its quality without the conversion of itself into the body <note>Unlike food, which is transformed into the body's own substance, medicine is supposed to change the body's state (its "quality") without becoming part of it.</note>. For it differs from food because food works through its matter and enters the body, preserving and increasing it through diversified nourishment. For food takes the place of what has been lost or adds more in many cases.

<margin>cold medicine</margin>
A medicine is also called "cold" if it possesses that quality in the highest degree or by predominance, such as water and air, or mixtures of cold things like **perfoliatum** <note>original: "perfolatrū," likely *Bupleurum perfoliatum*, an herb used for its cooling properties.</note> and **poppy**; for each body is such either simply and in the highest degree, or by a difference (chapter 16).

<margin>Potentiality</margin>
<term>Potentiality<note>A concept from Aristotelian philosophy: the capacity of a thing to become something else or to act in a certain way, even if it is not doing so right now.</note></term> is an imperfect thing born to receive a disposition with which it is born, such as a rational human when they are born, or a hunting dog.

<margin>Actuality</margin>
<term>Actuality<note>The state of being "at work" or fully realized; the opposite of potentiality.</note></term> conversely, will be a perfected thing already possessing the disposition with which it is born.

Potentiality is twofold: one is *per se* (natural), the other is *per accidens* (accidental), such as cold water curing the Theban from a "repletion" <note>The "Theban" refers to a famous patient mentioned in the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates; "repletion" is an overabundance of humors.</note> in the fifth book of the **Aphorisms**. The first type is also twofold: the most principal kind in which nature itself tends toward perfection with no external thing hindering it (which is seen as the first actuality or the second potentiality, being the "form"); the other remains with the matter so that something might come from it. This happens in many ways, according to whether it is "proximate" or "remote," such as when flesh is made from blood, or food is twice-cooked and entirely easy to mix like bread, or generally the elements of the complexions. Secondly, regarding *On the Soul*, potentiality is also twofold: one is first and remote, such as when something progresses from non-being to being (as the existence of minerals and plants is raised from the potentiality of the elements, and the potentiality of animals rises from their existence). The other potentiality or power is second, which is the "form" of the thing by which it has being and action. **Galen** calls this the "power" of a thing, its perfection, or its true existence (as in the 16th distinction on touch). This power is also threefold: one is "remote"—not the same as the "first potentiality" mentioned before—which is the power considered through the operation that our bodies perform upon its substance. When the carrier of that medicine suffers from our innate heat, then that which was in potentiality will arrive at actuality; such is the potentiality of medicines of the first and second degree especially. The "proximate" potentiality exists in the intensity of a habit, such as the power of **aconite** <note>original: "napelli," or Monkshood, a highly toxic plant.</note> and the venom of vipers to kill our bodies. There is also another between these. One part of this middle potentiality holds more to the "remote" kind, which exists with an aptitude for a good purpose, like sulfur or a medicine made from sulfate and moist "alpateo" <note>original: "alpateo," possibly a corrupt term for a mineral or botanical resin.</note>. The other is more akin to the "proximate" potentiality, having a greater aptitude for moving into actuality, as seen in the power of poisonous medicines like **opium** and **euphorbium**. All this "second potentiality" has an inclination toward actuality because it is very little distant from it—much less so than the "first potentiality" called "remote." For the remote kind, because of its great distance, is only led into actuality through intervening alterative transformations. The second potentiality is denoted in the second book of *On the Soul* as the first actuality, existing as the middle "form" from which the substance of the thing arises, from which—through middle qualities—the second actuality arises, which is called "operation."

<insert>3 2</insert>
Regarding the second point, it should be known that **Galen** posited in the books on *Complexions* and *Simple Medicines* that medicine is led into actuality—both hot and cold—by its division into the smallest parts. For they acquire motion from the outside, such as from the heat of our body.

<margin>Dry wood is more easily ignited.</margin>
He tries to show this by the fact that in divided and minute things, heat is first incorporated and dominates them more, as appears in small pieces of dry wood. In green wood, full of moisture and whole, heat (like fire) cannot prevail because it does not find open "paths and pores" <note>original: "vias & poros," referring to the internal channels through which heat was thought to travel.</note> for itself to enter. This position, although it seems to contain truth on the surface, does not simply explain the cause of the question, but rather states the cause or the occasion. Because if a cold medicine only cooled by being divided into its smallest parts, then when it had undergone that division, it would already be "actually" cold. This is not the case, since it appears that it is led from potentiality into actuality by this process. And therefore **Averroes** says: one cannot say that it is already actually cold simply by being divided into the smallest parts.

<margin>Mathematical things neither act nor suffer change.</margin>
<margin>3rd book of the Metaphysics, page 8 and 2nd commentary.</margin>
Furthermore, division regards "quantity"; for if quantity is removed, the substance remains indivisible (from the first book of the *Physics*). To quantity, however, neither "actuality" nor "passion" <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the capacity to be acted upon or changed by an external force.</note> is attributed. For mathematical things have neither motion nor place, nor are they measured by time, nor are the "end" and the "good" found in them—which are the principles of motion. They only have "being," and consequently they do not act or suffer change except perhaps metaphorically (from the third book of the *Metaphysics* and the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*).

<margin>In Aristotle, On the Soul, Book 2</margin>
On account of which, regarding the division concerning quantity, the leading forth from potentiality into actuality—since there is no [specific] quantity assigned to it—this mode of action cannot be assigned. For I have shown from the masters <note>likely referring to the established medical authorities or "lords" of the faculty</note> that every action is completed by qualities, since they then exist in a state of contrariety, which is proper to qualities. Furthermore, if [the body] were to lead medicine from potentiality into actuality, then those things which are the smallest <note>original: "minima," referring to the smallest particles of a substance that still retain its form</note> could not have an operation, since form requires a determined quantity and matter. For it is possible to assign the "smallest parts of flesh" according to Aristotle, as was introduced concerning poison and fire. Just as the body is lessened, so the power is diminished, the second from the first. On account of which it is concluded from the division of medicine into minute parts that its potentiality cannot rise into actuality. And therefore **Averroes** and **Galen** speak of it as something "fleeting." It should be noted, however, that although the division of medicine into smaller parts is not the *cause* of the arrival of potentiality into actuality, it is nonetheless a cause in a certain way—much like fire is to nutrition and food in the second book of *On the Soul*. For things that are convertible and able to be led from potentiality into actuality are more easily led into action when they are converted into small parts, as is testified by **Galen**; this also appears in wood that is dry and chopped small versus that which is moist, green, and whole. For as [the processes of] "gathering" and "scattering" are not themselves generation and corruption <note>Generation is the creation of a new substance; corruption is its destruction. Aristotle argued these were more than just the reshuffling of parts</note> as the ancients posited, they nevertheless contribute to generation and corruption. For things gathered and separated easily become corruptible, according to the first book of *On Generation*; so it is in the present proposal. But that—

<margin>Averroes, 5. Colliget</margin>
—the second "A" <note>likely shorthand for a specific proposition or author</note> seems to hold the manner of **Galen**, saying that a "subtle" medicine is one whose property is such that when it is acted upon by the natural power within us, it is divided in our bodies into its smallest parts. It must be said that "A" did not say this to provide a universal mode for leading the potentiality of medicine into actuality, but rather to describe a subtle medicine by that which was better known to him in relation to others that do not have [the same] substance. **Averroes**, however, in the fifth book of the *Colliget* <note>Averroes' major medical encyclopedia</note>, posits that a cold medicine is converted from potentiality into actuality through the heat existing within it; not that the innate heat [of the body]—which is similar in some way to that heat—stirs it from potentiality into actuality in the cooling of the **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid of digested food</term> and consequently the body. For he says that a cold medicine does not cool except because in the sites of digestion it is converted into a lesser heat than the heat of the body, so that the chyle generated from it is "diminished" by the body's heat. And therefore it is said that it truly cools—

<margin>Note</margin>
<margin>Commentary on the text, 2. On the Heavens and the World</margin>
—in the same way that he says in the second book of *On the Heavens and the World* that the stars do not produce coldness, but rather heats similar to each of the elements. He detests the one who posits that some things cool [directly], about which he inquired in Problem 25. He also tries to prove this by saying that natural heat has no way of generating coldness; on account of which it seemed to him that every—

---

### [Column 2]

—cold medicine reaches the actuality of coldness because of the proportioned heat existing within itself, which is somehow related to the heat of the body. This position, however, along with its reasoning, suffers no small degree of criticism. For in this way, his mode would apply only to medicine reaching the stomach, since it is there that chyle is generated, and not to medicine applied in any other way.

Furthermore, if the medicine were [simply] converted, it would not act by its quality but by its matter. And in such a case, we would never call anything truly "cold" except in relation to an animal body, even though, if that were removed, certain things would still be cold in themselves and in relation to the elements, according to their various operations. Further, if there is "the hot," there is also "the cold"; for if one of two contraries exists in nature, so does the other, according to *On the Heavens and the World*. But "the hot" is found truly as something that heats, therefore "the cold" must truly be something that cools. Again, since an operation makes the form known, that which sensibly harms or destroys operations by its coldness is truly cold. There are many such medicines; wherefore they shall be cold, since just as a thing is, so should it be conceived and signified. For "cold" is named from "to cool," just as "hot" is from "to heat." Likewise, if a cold medicine were discovered and led from potentiality into actuality because of heat, then a *less* cold medicine would reach the state of coldness *more quickly*, since it would have less contrariety to heat than a colder medicine. We see the opposite of this in **houseleek**, **stonecrop**, and **dog-grape** <note>original: "semperuiua uermiculari uua canis"</note> on one hand. On the other hand, in the deadly **nightshade**, **henbane**, **mandrake**, **Egyptian poppy**, and such things that have a more intense coldness, they nevertheless cool the action of the one suffering more swiftly.

Furthermore, if the heat of the body does not lead a cold medicine from potentiality into actuality except because of the heat found within it, then one must ask what "superior cold" within it leads it to actuality? Either there will be something that is not led into actuality because it lacks heat, or in an entirely cold medicine there is still heat present through which it reaches actuality—and thus it would not be cold, but rather hot. His induction is perhaps not valid. For heat is present in it "by accident" for the purpose of cooling, just as it is for cold water to heat by accident, and even to cure cold diseases, as in the "Theban" <note>likely a reference to a specific medical preparation or region</note> and such things in the third book of *On Complexions* and the fifth book of the *Aphorisms*. For it cools the heat either by consuming its proper matter or by opening the pores of the body, so that when opened, they exhale [the heat] outward. Certain others dream that heat leads cold medicine into actuality by removing a prohibition <note>i.e., removing an obstacle that prevented the cold from acting</note>. In that case, indeed, the cold medicine would be something other than the cold that constitutes it. # [Handwritten note at top]
->Whether there is a way by which medicines can be led [into action]... by the touch [of heat]...<- <note>The handwritten Latin is abbreviated and difficult to decipher, but it poses the central question of the chapter: the mechanism of medicinal activation.</note>

<margin>3rd mode</margin> It is necessary to recognize a certain mode by which a thing that is cold in "potentiality" <note>Potentiality refers to a latent power that is not yet active.</note> is more conveniently led into "actuality." <note>Actuality refers to the state where a power is actively functioning.</note> **That it is indeed** so led, the senses indicate along with reason, because every action is performed by a being already in a state of "act." It is apparent that certain things now possess an operation which they previously lacked; therefore, they have proceeded from potentiality into act. For in the same sequence, potentiality always precedes act (according to the third book of the *Metaphysics*). Now, the reason for leading a form from potentiality into act is identity and similarity in terms of origin or matter. However, it is a specific alterity and dissimilarity <note>original: "dissimilitudo specialis"</note> that allows for action; for the agent and the patient <note>The "agent" is the thing doing the action; the "patient" is the thing receiving it.</note> and all contraries are the same and similar in their "genus" <note>General category</note> but different and dissimilar in their "species." <note>Specific type</note> For active and passive things are contrary to one another and are "mediates" <note>middle-states</note> according to the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. For when the heat of the body acts upon a medicine that is cold in potentiality—because, as has been shown, its potentiality is not far distant from the act to which its form belongs—it is stirred up by its contrary and led into act. Indeed, when active and passive contraries are strong and disposed and applied to one another for a [sufficient] time, according to <term>Aristotle</term> and <term>Galen</term>, it is impossible for them not to act. **This mode** is indicated to us by what we see happen in other things, both those that are hot in potentiality being led into act by their contrary, and also those that are cold. For in slaked lime <note>original: "calce... extincta"</note> heat remains in "virtue" <note>power</note> after a long time, which, when its actual contrary (cold) arrives, reaches the act of heat. The heat of the lime is besieged and strengthened by the coldness of water, which chills it and closes its pores, because of which the heat, contracted into itself, is invigorated and excited, finally overcoming the actual coldness of the water. So also from the passage of cold water over sulfurous minerals, which have a potentiality near to being led into the act of heat <margin>$\dot{z}$</margin>, the heat in these minerals is excited by the water itself and it is made hot, according to the *Properties of the Elements*.

**In this same way**, a concoction of sulfur and asphalt which certain curious people build, when exposed to rain, is inflamed, by which someone could burn down an enemy's house. **Which also** the new food for the limbs indicates, occurring in the *Ethics* <note>Likely referring to Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics* or perhaps a biological work regarding how food is "conquered" by body heat.</note>. And vinegar also... Similarly, a cold potentiality comes into act from heat, as is also shown by marble exposed to the sun and wrapped in cloths. **Which also appears** in ice, hail, and "glassy phlegm" <note>A medical term for a specific type of cold, thick humor in the body.</note> when the heat is stirred by a clyster <note>An enema.</note>. In these things, not only does actual coldness exist, but also potential coldness. For when they melt, they cool more vehemently. Thus, in our body, a cold medicine will be led to the act of cooling by the stirring of the heat that is contrary to the cold. Thus, the colder things, since they oppose the body's heat more than the less cold things, by more quickly suppressing the heat and being moved by it, they come into the act of coldness; as the nature of a narcotic shown when administered with warm wine or with some small amount of heat, such as castoreum <note>A pungent substance secreted by beavers, used as a stimulant.</note>, added to it. For when these are stirred up and not restrained, they are led into the act of cooling 

more quickly and more strongly. For it cools even if it is administered quite hot. Whence, in the third book of *Complexions*: just as hot water thrown on a flame extinguishes it, so also opium cools and brings the danger of death even if you have heated it to the maximum. **It happens, however**, that one might doubt the aforesaid in two ways. <margin>$\dot{z}$</margin> First, because since hot medicine shares with the body's heat not only in genus or matter but even in species (if it can). For all things that appear are of an indistinguishable species (according to the fourth book of the *Topics*): thus, the rest are of the same quality. Therefore, it cannot be led into act. And this opposes the reason given, that contraries come into act, since there must then be both alterity and dissimilarity in species. Whence also, in the ninth book of the **Metaphysics** and *On the Generation of Animals*, it is said that an actual being always comes from a potential being by means of an actual being: as a man from a man, and a musician from a musician. And hence it is said that everything that is led from potentiality into act is led out by something that is such in act. Which is not found at all in the leading of medicine from potentiality into act, as was touched upon. <margin>$\dot{z}$</margin> **To the first** it must be said that the potential heat of a medicine and the heat of the body, although they seem to agree, they do not agree except remotely and in genus. In species and nature they differ greatly, just as there is heat of the first, second, third, and fourth degree. <margin>...</margin> For "intermediates" have a contrariety to the extremes, and not only the extremes to themselves (according to the first book of the *Physics*). Also, one heat is in potentiality while the other is in act, and one is a composite (like the heat of the elements and the body). And although all appear to be the same in that they are heat, they differ in their act. **To the other [doubt]** it must be said that for something to be led from potentiality into act is nothing other than for a certain "generation" to occur. For generation is the leading from non-being to being. In generation, a three-fold similarity is observed: <margin>$\dot{z}$</margin> first, the similarity of the form of the species, by which perfect things are generated, as a man generates a man and a horse a horse. And it is necessary for this generation to happen from a being in act that has a "univocal" <note>Of the same name and nature.</note> similarity with the thing generated; indeed, sometimes similarity is found in individuals, as in parents who pass on scars and marks (from the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*). And another is a "virtual" or "equivocal" similarity, by which the sun generates us, and also those things which are of plants and animals from putrefaction alone. Thus also wine generates drunkenness and motion generates heat by an "effective power" only, and not by form; for such things do not remain "informally." And in this [type of] generation, although an existence that is active on the outside is required, a formal identity is not required: a "virtual" identity alone is sufficient. **And there is a third** similarity between these two middle points, such as when two species of animals close in size and gestation time join together for the generation of a third [species]...

<summary>This page explains the scholastic concept of how a medicine's latent properties (potentiality) are triggered into action (actuality) by their opposites, such as a cold drug being activated by the body's heat. It uses analogies from chemistry (slaked lime, sulfur) and biology (generation, opium) to justify how heat can cause a cooling effect.</summary>

as in the case of the mule and the leopard in [Aristotle's] *On the Generation of Animals*.
In these cases, a formal similarity <note>Similarity in physical appearance or essential structure.</note> is not observed, but rather a virtual one, or both. Therefore, an agent, besides existing in "actuality," must also introduce a similarity derived from a "virtual" and "special" breaking down. Since the similarity of a medicine to the body is only virtual and not formal—for if it were formal, the medicine would be the very substance of our body, as argued in the first part—it is sufficient that it be an agent leading the body from potentiality into act, being itself in such a state of "act" with a certain virtual similarity, but not a formal one. We have already seen this in the first chapter. For this reason, it is clear in the fourth place what must be said regarding the arguments: the cause by which a cold medicine is led from potentiality into act is a "proximate potentiality" <note>A state where something is almost ready to change.</note> toward that act, since it is its form, and not a "remote potentiality" toward being; and the heat of the body exists in "actuality" by its power alone. It has also appeared in what manner the heat of the body has the power of cooling. Regarding the first point, however, it must be further said that a medicine is led from potentiality into act both on the part of the medicine, as a passive principle, and by the action of heat as an active principle, so that a hot medicine is directly led into act. A cold medicine, however, is led, as it were, "from the side" <note>Indirectly.</note> by way of a certain contrariety. For contraries are born to act and suffer upon one another. Regarding the other point, it has also appeared that heat has the power of cooling "by accident." <note>An "accidental" property is one that is not essential to the thing's nature, but happens due to circumstances.</note> What should be said to the other point has similarly been seen already.

### DIFFERENCE 141.

<margin>Damascenus, Aphorisms</margin>
Whether an attractive medicine <note>A medicine intended to draw humors (bodily fluids) toward a specific area for expulsion.</note> travels to the humor to be attracted and does not remain in the stomach is shown by Aristotle in the first book of *Problems*, problem 41, where he says: "When medicines enter the belly and are spread, they are carried through the same pores as nourishment is carried into the veins." Furthermore, Damascenus <note>John of Damascus, an influential theologian and writer on medicine.</note> says in his *Aphorisms*: "For the purpose of purging, medicine should be converted into the likeness of food by ingenuity, so that nature may receive it from its part and, having retained it, carry it back through the veins." Furthermore, 
<margin>Wisdom 7, Brief Summary</margin>
in the seventh [book] of the *Brief Summary*: "When the members remain in their natural disposition, they attract what is similar and proper to them, namely food. However, when a disposition departing from nature happens to them, they attract what is contrary to them because of a desire for rest from the injury." These are the attractive medicines, since they are of the genus of poisons according to the second book of [Galen's] *On Affected Parts*.
<margin>In the 2nd book of the Practice / 2nd book of the Canon / Agaric</margin>
Again, in the second books of the *Practice* and the *Canon* [of Avicenna]: "Agaric <note>original: "Agaricus"; a species of fungus (larch polypore) used as a laxative.</note> causes purgative medicines to reach the extremities of the body." They also say that hermodactyls, <note>original: "hermodactili"; likely *Colchicum*, a plant used since antiquity to treat joint pain and gout.</note> being of a proper dissolving nature, attract from a distance, such as from the joints, and leave an astringency <note>A drying or contracting quality.</note> in them, which is why they are very beneficial. They would not induce this astringency unless their substance reached the joints themselves. Furthermore, either the substance passes to the humor, or the virtue <note>The "virtue" (uirtus) is the medicinal power or essence of the drug, as opposed to its physical bulk.</note> alone, since one cannot assign more than these primary options. If it is the substance, then the medicine itself will go to the humor, and thus the proposition is proven. If it is the virtue alone without the substance, then an "accident" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" (like a color or a power) cannot exist without a "subject" (a physical thing) to hold it.</note> will exist without a subject, and a virtue will migrate from one subject to another. But virtue is an accident located in the category of quality, which is against the Physicists and the first books of *On Generation*, and even against divine intellect. Again, the administration of food or drink, such as very cold water, after a medicine makes it work, which does not seem possible otherwise than by the water pushing the medicine into the humors and the members.
<note>A drawing of a small hand pointing to the text appears in the left margin</note>
Again, every action is completed by contact, according to the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. All contact is placed there within the body. Therefore, the medicine with its substance will pass to the humor. The opposite of this is the opinion of excellent physicians such as John Serapion, Hali Abbas, Avicenna, and Mesue. For their discourses sound more as if the medicine remains in the belly when it attracts the humor. Furthermore, if the substance of the medicine proceeded to the humor, it would be weakened and dissolved on the way, so that the similarity it has for attracting the humor would be destroyed; for it is posited by Galen to attract. Therefore, it remains in the belly, with its virtue being sent out and preserved to attract the humor. For if, as some say, it were dissolved into vapors as it traveled, a new thing would be generated from there, the previous one having been corrupted—just as spirit is generated from thinned humors, being something different from them. Because of this, the virtue of the medicine alone tends toward the humors. Let the first question asked before be explained. And finally, let it be shown to which place the medicine attracts. For this, one must first know that an attractive medicine is an essential quality which, by a virtue implanted in it by its species, attracts from the humors what is proper to it to pull out. What attraction is, and how many times and how it occurs—whether by quality alone, as Avicenna with Averroes perhaps seems to feel; or through indivisible atoms, as Epicurus (introduced in the first book of *Natural Philosophy*) accepting the position of Democritus and Leucippus; or from the whole substance or species, or from the virtue following it—has been shown in Differences 51 and 60. It was said, however, to be an essential quality, as explained in Difference 71. It is added, "by a virtue implanted in its species." Since certain medicines dissolve by their whole species, which are called hot and dry attractive dissolvents. Others, however, dissolve by a quality, and these either by their weight, such as myrobalans <note>original: "mirabolani"; fruit used for purging.</note> and quinces <note>original: "cithonia".</note>; or by soothing, such as cassia fistula <note>The "golden shower" tree, used as a mild laxative.</note> and violets, among others; or by lubricating, such as the mucilage of psyllium <note>original: "psillii"; fleawort seeds.</note> and plums, as Avicenna and Mesue feel. According to the *Practice*, certain medicines are felt to dissolve by their sharpness, such as euphorbium, <note>A caustic plant resin.</note> which the aforementioned authors say dissolves by a hidden virtue. There is, however, a difference between an attractive medicine and the three or four types of purgatives, because the attractive one by itself draws to the belly or the intestines; then nature, having rendered them hateful, educes them through vomiting or stool.

It weighs the opinions of ancient authorities like Aristotle and Galen against medieval physicians like Avicenna and Mesue regarding the mechanism of "attractive" medicines.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the mechanics of medical attraction. Having previously discussed the "virtual similarity" required for a medicine to act on the body, the text now focuses on "attractive medicines"—those we might call laxatives or purgatives—and how they specifically target different bodily fluids (humors).</meta>

# Whether an attractive medicine moves to attract the humors. 2.

<margin>4th part</margin>
Regarding the first point of the fourth part: When a <term>humor</term> <note>One of the four vital bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> is to be attracted to the stomach or intestines, the nature of this humor is moved so that nature may expel it outward. Other medicines, and specifically the three previously mentioned, seem by themselves more likely to dissolve or descend by their own weight through compression. And if a certain <term>attractive power</term> <note>The specific quality of a substance that draws fluids toward it, similar to a magnet.</note> must be placed in <term>myrobalans</term> <note>A dried fruit used as a staple laxative in medieval medicine.</note>, it is because they evacuate <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile.</note> or <term>melancholy</note> <note>Black bile.</note>—sometimes from a distance—by either soothing nature (as in the case of the ducts of the limbs' expulsion) or by lubricating the matter and making it ready for flow; this distinction is noted in the <term>Third Canon</term> <note>Referring to the *Canon of Medicine* by the Persian physician Avicenna (Ibn Sina).</note> where he speaks of <term>lenitives</term> and lubricants, stating that choleric matter should be evaporated with that which soothes nature and lubricates the material.

<margin>1st part of the 3rd [book]</margin>
It was further added regarding the humors that certain medicines attract one specific humor by their own property, such as <term>scammony</term> <note>A resin from the root of *Convolvulus scammonia*, known as a drastic purgative.</note> attracting choler. Others, however, attract two, though one principally—as <term>aloes</term> <note>original: "aloes anthonomafice," likely meaning aloes par excellence.</note> attracts choler, but consequently phlegm; and <term>polypody</note> <note>A type of fern used as a purgative.</note> attracts melancholy and thick phlegm. Some medicines attract all humors except blood, because an attractive medicine for blood is not possessed today. For <term>Galen</term> <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire.</note> caused that knowledge to be suspended, the presiding judge deciding that he alone knew it (Chapter 44).

<margin>Note</margin>
Nevertheless, the blood is purified by them, as with <term>agaric</term> <note>A type of mushroom or fungus used in medicine.</note>, according to Galen; hence also <term>Mesue</term> <note>A name attributed to influential Arabic medical authors, often called the "Pharmacists' Educator."</note> and <term>Democritus</term> said it would be a "family medicine"—that is, common and familiar to the people. For by evacuating all matter and drawing it out from all the limbs, it provides no small help to each. Therefore, the cause of this duality or plurality of attraction can happen as much on the part of the medicine as on the part of the humors to be attracted. On the part of the medicines: because their heat is not "actual" in its own right—in the way a magnet attracts iron to itself by its own inherent power—but is acquired and brought into action (since it is only "potential") through the heat by which nature affects it. Otherwise, it would never operate in the first place, as is seen in the bodies of the dead. This heat must be determined and proportioned to the medicine in the proper quantity and quality. For if the quantity of the medicine is increased, it will also purge another humor; and similarly if the quality is strengthened by types of <term>elephangine</term> <note>A compound medicine, often pills made with aloes.</note>. Thus, attraction does not occur except by way of a certain proportion of "affinity." For in medicine, the power of attraction is, as it were, bound and in a state of potentiality, more than can be brought into action by the heat of the body in order to attract. However, the proportion of the magnet to the iron is not exactly like this. For the power of the magnet’s attraction is more powerful and free in attracting iron. On the part of the humors: it is not far-fetched that all humors have a proximity within one genus, since they are generated by almost the same specific power and the same common heat and organ. They are, however, not a little different by reason of the <term>medium</term> <note>The substance or environment through which they are created.</note> from which they are generated, about which the aforementioned doubts (29) arise. Therefore, since they are strongly related, if the quantity is increased along with the power of the medicine attributed to one specific humor, it will consequently draw out others, especially those that are "disposed," such as choler and its related humors. Therefore, a medicine attractive to choler attracts it first, then phlegm, then melancholy, and lastly blood—which nature, as the thing most dear to itself, preserves and hides away until the end. However, driven by the agitation of the medication and its vehement fervor, nature may yield some part of the blood so that the substance of the medicine may expel it from the body, just as an honest man leads a dishonest one away from himself, leaving behind what belongs to him. That medicine which specifically attracts phlegm will afterward attract choler, then melancholy, and blood last of all. But that which attracts melancholy finally attracts surplus choler, then phlegm, and finally blood (Difference 144).

<margin>The Belly</margin>
"The belly" is here taken for the stomach, as is commonly said among us; it is the hollow place in which food and drink are first placed to be digested. Galen, however, takes it to mean the esophagus or the "meri." What it is and how often it is mentioned has been sufficiently shown (Difference 54). Regarding the second point, it should be known that an attractive medicine either draws things out through vomiting (when nature is incited) or through the stool. If it acts through vomiting, while staying in the stomach it draws from the humors that which is its property to attract. When these humors reach the stomach and touch the medicine, the attraction ceases, since the attractor exits at the same time as the thing attracted. And then nature—irritated by the foulness of the humors and the sharpness of the medicine—rises up against these things that have become hateful to her, so that she may expel them through the act of vomiting. If, however, the medicine educes through the stool, remaining in the stomach and finally descending to the intestines, it attracts the humors to those intestines and not to the stomach. This happens "by accident," however, as in a disorder of the lower stomach or by its strength, or the weakness of the upper stomach, or by the dominion of some heavenly body—as when someone takes a purgative medicine while the Moon is in a "ruminating" <note>Signs like Aries, Taurus, or Capricorn, associated with chewing the cud.</note> sign, and with the lord of the ascendant being in the middle of the sky or joined to a planet there. In such a case, the medicine will evacuate through vomiting, as the doctors say in the <term>Centiloquium</term> <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms, traditionally attributed to Ptolemy.</note>.

<margin>Note</margin>
<margin>Astronomy</margin>
Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have wished that even a purgative medicine attracts humors to the stomach. <term>Serapio</term> <note>Yahya ibn Sarafyun, a 9th-century Syrian Christian physician.</note> refutes them in several places in the first book of his *Practice*. First, because if humors were attracted by a medicine to the stomach, both would remain in one place (the stomach), just as a magnet is not separated from the iron attracted to it and joined to it; and thus, neither a bowel movement nor vomiting would occur.

<margin>Opinion</margin>
<margin>Serapio argues against it and then [?]</margin>
Furthermore, nature always acts in the way that is better, faster, and easier. For we see her in all things...

It explores the hierarchy of these fluids, the role of bodily heat in activating medicine, and the influence of astrology on whether a drug causes vomiting or a bowel movement.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on how laxative medicines function within the body. While the previous page introduced the concept of "attractive power" using scammony as an example, this text now disputes the specific physical route the medicine takes, arguing that medicines do not physically travel to distant limbs to "fetch" humors, but rather act through complex Aristotelian principles of "agent" and "patient."</meta>

...doing the best possible for both youth and old age. This happens if the medicine remains in the intestines and does not go to the stomach, which is heavily damaged due to its <term>sensibility</term> <note>The stomach was considered a highly sensitive organ in medieval medicine, prone to "feeling" the harshness of drugs more than the intestines.</note>, especially when the humors are <term>choleric</term> <note>Related to yellow bile, associated with heat and bitterness.</note> and burnt. **Furthermore** <note>original: "Palyn" (Greek: again/furthermore)</note>, there is no necessity for humors drawn to the intestines to reach the stomach, since they can be expelled more briefly and safely downward through the bowels. Moreover, the stomach is designed for <term>attraction and digestion</term> <note>The scholastic view was that the stomach's primary job is to "attract" food and cook it (digestion), not to handle waste.</note>. It attracts using two forces, but it expels using only one, which is called the extrinsic force. The intestines, however, are ordered for expulsion and the reception of waste, which they propel using two <term>tunics</term> <note>Layers of tissue or muscle.</note>. 

Again, the intestines are accustomed to receiving sharp and constant wastes, for <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile.</note>, along with other wastes, similarly flows through them continuously. The stomach, however, is not at all accustomed to this, but is used to receiving foods and drinks that are delightful and proper to it. Also, <term>governing nature</term> <note>The innate intelligence of the body that manages health.</note> never leaves a near path to choose a remote and laborious one, since it is the work of intelligence to dispose all things in the best way (as seen in the **12th book of the Metaphysics** <note>A reference to Aristotle’s work on the prime mover and natural order.</note>). This would happen if the humors were brought back to the stomach. Not only does this rarely happen, but more importantly, a <term>vomitive medicine</term> is made <term>secessive</term> <note>A medicine that causes a bowel movement (laxative) rather than vomiting.</note> because of the downward inclination of the medicines, since they are heavy. For they are mixtures in which heavy elements predominate, allowing them to move further downward. Or, it is because the channels and ways through which the parts expel waste are more connected to the intestines than to the stomach.

**Furthermore** <note>original: "Palyn"</note>, nature chooses to transmit waste and harmful things from **noble parts** to **vile, ignoble parts**, and not the other way around. But the stomach, with its parts, is more noble than the intestines. Likewise, nature, working rightly, always leads via the nearest paths. That which it must expel, it sends out quickly. Again, the <term>stellar influence</term> <note>The belief that planetary positions and "breaths" from the stars affected the movement of fluids in the body.</note> mentioned by **Ptolemy** contributes to this. From these various arguments collected here into one, it is repeated that a laxative medicine, by itself, in no way leads humors to the stomach. 

Regarding the location where an attractive medicine remains, people have differed. For some have proposed (as in the **second book of the Practice** <note>Likely referring to Avicenna's Canon of Medicine.</note>) that the substance of the medicine physically reaches the humor to attract it. They said that when someone drinks a laxative medicine, upon reaching the stomach, it goes out lightly from there to the limbs where there is waste, tending toward it because of a "suitability" for it. But when it has attracted to itself what it must from the wastes, the limb is then moved to expel it because of the "discord" and contrariety it has toward it, and the injury felt from the sharpness of the humors and the medicine. Thus, the medicine returns with the attracted waste to the intestines, or likewise to the stomach, and so finally the purging is finished. 

This cannot stand, as will be shown. Some have proposed that the substance of the attractive medicine is dissolved into **fumes**, while a significant part of it remains in the stomach or intestines. These fumes reach the humors to be attracted through the same paths by which food is spread to the limbs. The vigor of the medicinal part remaining in the stomach, along with the expelling power of the limbs, then brings them back. Although this contains fewer impossibilities than the previous theory, it still opposes the truth significantly. For many further absurdities follow from this. 

First, the attraction of humors by a medicine is similar to the attraction of **iron by a magnet**, or **straw by amber**, or **nutriment by the limbs**. A magnet, amber, and the limbs never travel to the iron, the straw, or the food. The "attractor" does not move toward the "attracted"; rather, the attracted is carried toward the attractor, as **Haly Abbas** <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note> testifies. 

Furthermore, the **agent** <note>The thing doing the action.</note> is more excellent than the **patient** <note>The thing being acted upon.</note> (according to the **3rd book of On the Soul** <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*.</note>). But the medicine is the agent and the humor is the patient. If the medicine went to the humor, it would then be the patient and viler than the passive humor. 

**Furthermore** <note>original: "Palyn"</note>, when things find their place in matter, motion ceases (according to the **1st book of On Generation and Corruption**). Therefore, if the medicine reached the humor, since its form would then be joined with it, the motion of attraction would cease, just as attraction rests when iron is joined to a magnet. Therefore, those who claim the medicine travels entirely to the humor can in no way explain the attraction and leading out. 

Moreover, that which is perfect never moves <margin>§</margin> toward the imperfect, but rather the opposite. The medicine is **perfect**, while the humors to be attracted are **imperfect**, such as those that are corrupt or ready to be corrupted. Nor is it resolved into fumes in order to attract, because if it were entirely or mostly turned into fumes when it reached the humor, the attraction (and consequently the leading out) would cease as soon as it touched it. 

Again, since it is the nature of fumes to tend upward, the medicine would almost always lead things upward and result only in **vomiting**, the opposite of which is found to happen in experience. It might be said that these fumes are governed by nature and therefore spread to all parts of the body. But this is impossible, because then in the "loosening" caused by the medicine, there would be no resistance or victory of nature. The opposite of this is written in the **fourth [book]** and by **Haly in the Centiloquium** <note>A collection of astrological and medical aphorisms.</note>. 

Likewise, some medicines are hard, compact **minerals**, such as <term>lapis lazuli</term> and <term>Armenian stone</term> <note>Blue minerals used in crushed form as strong purgatives, specifically for "melancholy."</note>, from which almost no fume is raised, especially when they are given ground up. Therefore, at least in these cases, the "fume" method will not work. Additionally, a fume applied to the humors to be attracted, having overcome the part of the medicine remaining in the stomach or intestines, would not allow the humors to be brought back to them, since they would have already acquired their "perfection."

<summary>The author argues against the idea that laxative medicines physically travel to the limbs or turn into vapors to "fetch" humors, using Aristotelian logic and the metaphor of a magnet to show that the medicine remains in the gut and "draws" the fluids toward itself.</summary>
