<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on how medicines exert "attractive" power. Having previously discussed whether the stomach or intestines are better suited for the expulsion of humors, the text now addresses the mechanical path that these bodily fluids take when "drawn" by a drug. It uses Aristotelian physics—specifically the motion of projectiles and the properties of magnets—to explain how a medicine sitting in the gut can affect the far reaches of the body.</meta>

# Whether an attractive medicine is able to draw out humors.

<margin>Regarding the third question</margin>
**F**or this reason, the substance of an attractive medicine never approaches the humors it intends to draw out, neither in its own physical form nor by being dissolved into vapors. Regarding this third point, however, it must first be understood how the mode of attraction is demonstrated, so that the truth of the matter may finally be brought forward.
<margin>Regarding the first point</margin>
Regarding the first part of this, it should be known that a medicine often attracts humors from remote parts of the body. If these <term>humors</term> <note>The four vital fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile, whose balance determined health.</note> are located in the lower parts, such as the spongy tissues of the simple members, the heat and agitation [of the medicine] thin them down to such a degree that they are forced to enter the ends of the small veins. From there, they are drawn to the medium and large veins, and finally to the largest, until they reach the "hollow vein" <note>original: "vena concaua"; the Vena Cava.</note> called *kilim* <note>original: "kilim"; a Latinization of the Greek 'koile,' meaning hollow.</note> in Greek. From there, they pass through the liver to the <term>mesenteric veins</term> <note>Veins connecting the intestines to the liver.</note> and finally to the intestines. This occurs if the medicine is a <term>laxative</term> <note>original: "secessiua"; a medicine that moves the bowels.</note>. However, if it is an <term>emetic</term> <note>original: "uomitiua"; a medicine that induces vomiting.</note>, they are forced by the power of attraction to ascend toward the belly and the stomach. If the humors are located in the upper parts of the simple members, such as the head, they similarly enter the ends of the small veins and reach the large and then the largest veins, such as the <term>jugulars</term> <note>original: "originales siue iugulares".</note> if they are drawn from the head. From there, they go to the great vein located near the right auricle of the heart, and finally through the liver to the hollow vein as before, and ultimately through the mesenteric veins to the intestines; thus they are propelled through them if the medicine is a purgative. If it is an emetic, they reach the belly through those same paths and through the intestines, and then, as nature is irritated, they are led out by vomiting. However, humors residing under the brain and around the epiglottis, the esophagus, and the lung are sometimes attracted to the belly without entering the veins, as authorities testify. For when they have been thinned by the power of attraction—strengthened by the proximity of the locations—they exit the spaces where they are contained, penetrating the walls and <term>tunics</term> <note>Membranous layers of organs.</note>, and are transferred into the cavity of the belly.

These are finally propelled outward by vomiting or by stool, according to the nature of the medicine. For when they have been attracted to the intestines or the belly, the attraction of the medicine ceases, since the humors are now present with it. At that point, because of the weight and sharpness of the humors combined with the unpleasantness of the medicine, the belly and intestines are stirred up so that nature may expel them either by stool or by vomit. For this reason, it is wisely said that a <term>dissolutive</term> <note>A medicine that breaks down thick humors.</note> medicine is a purgative by accident.
<margin>3rd point</margin>
Regarding the second point, it should be known that the substance of the medicine, either in itself or resolved into vapors, does not reach the humors to be attracted. The speeches of illustrious and preeminent physicians demonstrate this. For the <term>Son of Serapion</term> <note>Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century Arabic medical author whose work was foundational in Western scholasticism.</note> in his seventh book, assigning the difference between an <term>altering</term> medicine and an <term>attractive</term> one, says that an altering medicine cannot act from a distance like a purgative can, because the purgative alone, when it is far away, can attract its own specific humor to itself. But when the humor is brought near and joined to it, the attraction is diminished.

For it attracts the harmful humor from a distance and places it into the pathways through which food penetrates, until the humor reaches the medicine itself. And he adds this, repeating: a purgative medicine does not attract unless it is at a distance from the humor. Therefore, when it approaches the humor and is joined with it, it rests from attraction. First, indeed, the fourth point:
<margin>4th point</margin>

> If a medicine had an attractive power that accompanied the humor, it would be more worthy of the nature of an <term>expulsive power</term> <note>The natural force that pushes waste out of the body.</note>, so that in a healthy and strong person it would prevail, even though the medicine only attracts toward designated paths. But the disposition of an emetic medicine is different from this, because when it is in the stomach, it remains there and attracts the humor from the intestines to itself, and by its own power it prevails over the natural power to make it stay.

<margin>Mesue</margin>
<term>Mesue</term> <note>Masawayh al-Mardini, or Pseudo-Mesue, an influential source for pharmacy and purgatives.</note> also says: a medicine reaching the stomach does not draw out the humor it must evacuate by penetrating toward it physically; rather, by the power of attraction sealed within it, it chooses and attracts from the humors that which is proper for it to attract. Some people try to demonstrate it in this way: the medicine, remaining in the belly or intestines, alters and transforms the medium placed near it and next to it, first imparting to that medium a power similar to its own. Then, this medium having been so affected, it transforms the next part in sequence, until finally it reaches the humor to be attracted, which is moved and drawn by the alteration of the affected medium. And finally, as it is said, it is driven out by the body's expulsive power.
<margin>3rd point</margin>
A similarity to this is seen in the <term>throwing of a stone</term>.
<margin>On the throw... of a stone</margin>
For the thrower first moves the particle of air near him, which moves another, and so on in sequence, as long as the power of the thrower—or the power of the pushing air and the air being pushed—remains. This is declared in the fourth and eighth books of the *Physics* <note>Aristotle’s *Physics*, the standard textbook for motion and causality.</note>; hence, only the "power" of the medicine is transmitted.
<margin>3rd point / 2nd point</margin>
Further declaring this position, some—wishing to remove the difficulties that arise—say that the medium does not change the power truly and "really," but rather "intentionally" and by way of likeness, just as the air and the pupil of the eye are changed by a color. They wish to say that the medicine, through its power and intention, multiplies the likeness of its own species through the disposed medium, and thus effects the attraction.
<margin>Not concerning the principal quality...</margin>
And such appears to be the action of a <term>magnet</term> upon iron. For nothing "real" is dissolved from the magnet, as <term>Epicurus</term> used to say.
<margin>Epicurus</margin>
And not departing much from this last position, I propose that a medicine attracting from remote parts is heated and altered by nature, and is dissolved into certain vapors to a degree, so that it can better multiply its "species" and likeness through the medium to attract more effectively. Thus <term>amber</term> <note>original: "karabe"; from the Persian/Arabic 'kahraba,' meaning 'straw-robber.' It refers to the electrostatic property of rubbed amber.</note> is seen to seize straws more strongly when heated by friction; then, as has been touched upon, it multiplies its power through the medium. Which motive of the position is sufficient...
<margin>3rd point</margin>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into how medicines "draw" or attract humors from distant parts of the body. The previous page established that while a medicine remains in the gut, it can influence the "hollow vein" (vena cava) and remote tissues. This section explores whether this influence is a physical movement of matter or a "virtual" transmission through the body’s medium.</meta>

<margin>Averroes.</margin> I am able to draw conclusions from the probable arguments of **Averroes** <note>original: "A." or "Aue."; Referring to the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd.</note> concerning the alteration of a medium by an odor. For he writes in the second book of *On the Soul* that an odor physically changes the medium, since it appears that fragrant things, such as an apple, decay, shrink, and are consumed. <margin>Commentator on Aristotle.</margin> The **Commentator** <note>Also Averroes, known in the Middle Ages as "The Commentator" for his works on Aristotle.</note> also perceives in the second book of *On the Soul* that the medium is altered only "intentionally" <note>An "intentional" change (immutatio intentionalis) is a medieval concept where a quality—like an image or a scent—travels through the air without the physical matter itself moving, much like how a mirror reflects an object without the object entering the glass.</note> because tigers and vultures, being five hundred leagues away, arrive at a carcass with no guide other than the scent. Otherwise, it would mean that the slaughtered bodies—having been resolved through evaporation and smoke into some part—truly and physically changed the medium all the way to that distant place. Therefore, the medium is altered over a vast space "virtually" and through "images." This can happen here because the sense of smell, which perceives such things, holds a middle ground between the "spiritual" senses, like sight and hearing, and the "material" senses, like touch and taste, as also appears in chapter 55. In the same way, a medicine, when it attracts from afar, will physically change the medium up to a certain point; however, this physical change does not occur in the humors themselves, for the inconveniences mentioned before would occur. Rather, across a longer distance, the change is "intentional" only.

Both of these occur in a seasoned manner. The first occurs through the carrier of the medicine, which must be acted upon by "innate heat" <note>The natural biological heat of the body believed to power digestion and vital functions.</note> as has been shown frequently, especially since the action of medicine is not as free and absolute as that of a magnet. For a magnet, according to a proper distance, can be carried into the act of attraction by its own power. The second point is also evident because the color **red**, when looked at intently, stirs the blood and induces its flow; therefore, a person whose nose is bleeding is forbidden from looking at it. Similarly, looking at the color **yellow** stirs the yellow bile. It is said that those suffering from **jaundice** <note>original: "ycterici"</note> are helped by contemplating yellow things. For that moves nature to expel all the yellow matter to the skin, which provides relief, as noted in chapter 35. These, however, are "intentional" alterations. <margin>Haly</margin> Furthermore, certain medicines held under the sole of the foot attract from the whole body, according to **Haly Abbas** <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note>. Similarly, certain aromatic balls are made from strongly attractive substances which, by scent alone, have the power to draw humors from the whole body. Sometimes, pills that are made too hard are excreted almost entirely whole. This happens more often when the "expulsive virtue" <note>The body's natural power to push out waste.</note> of the patient is strong and the humors are thin. Therefore, a medicine will cause a change physically up to a certain point, and thereafter "intentionally." But this seems to contradict the seventh book of [Aristotle's] *Physics*, which argues that the attractor and the attracted must not be separated, but must be together, with no medium falling between them. It must be said that this is true in "univocal" attraction, where physical contact occurs. The attraction of medicine, however, as appears from the book, is more "equivocal," where

---

virtual contact occurs. Regarding the fourth point: for the first part, it should be said that it is true according to "power" (virtue) and not "substance." However, because the writings of **Averroes**, if diligently inspected, seem to suggest a diffusion of the medicine according to its substance, it must be said that he held that opinion. For certain physicians of his time held that view, and in that passage, he assigns the causes of certain sayings by physicians such that he speaks in no small way according to the opinion of others. Furthermore, as shown in the 60th distinction, <margin>Aristotle</margin> **Aristotle** posited that every action is completed by a quality, and none by what is called "specific form." In the action of a quality, which is completed by alteration, the thing altering touches that which it alters, as appears in the seventh book of the *Physics*. To the other point, it should be said that he was then of that opinion; or better, because he is speaking of "food-like" medicine, as his speech indicates, and not of "dissolving" medicine as is sought here. For in the *Aphorisms* of **John of Damascus**, the medicine seems to have been **Cassia fistula** <note>A tropical tree whose pods were used as a mild laxative.</note>, which is blessed.

Regarding the next point, it should be said that he is then speaking of "altering" medicine, which is led to a limb by that limb's own attractive power, and finally about "dissolving" medicine, which (as has been argued) he did not want to reach the limb, but to attract while remaining in the belly or intestines. To the other point, it should be said that **Agaric** <note>A type of fungus used in ancient medicine as a purgative.</note>, **Hermodactyl** <note>Literally "Mercury's Finger," likely Colchicum, used for gout and joint pain.</note>, and such things do not only have an attractive power, but also an "incisive" <note>The power to cut through thick or sticky humors.</note>, "thinning," "styptic" <note>An agent that shrinks tissues or stops bleeding.</note>, and "strengthening" power, and such qualities by which the powers of dissolving agents reach the extremities of the body. For such things, when mixed with dissolving agents, help their powers more than they attract them. Averroes hints at this when he says they "sometimes help" and so on, but not "always" or "often." Or it should be said that although the "styptic" effect, as with Hermodactyls, occurs in parts not very far from the belly and intestines, it nevertheless strengthens the joints because it no longer permits the "rheum" <note>A discharge of watery fluid; in this context, the cause of swelling or gout.</note> to flow toward them. To the other point, it should be said that although the "power" alone is posited to reach the humor, it does not follow that the "accident" is separated from the subject and exists without it. This is because the power existing in the medicine alters the medium and transforms it, and that in turn transforms another until it reaches the humor, just as fire heats the air, and the air then heats other bodies. For the transformation does not jump from subject to subject, but is rather a new generation. Or it should be said that this "power" is not "real" and "true" but "intentional" and "likeness-based," which can be imprinted on another thing and exist without the subject in which it had been. For at one and the same time, two or more "species" or "intentions" can remain together in one thing according to the same part—such as the intentions of blackness, whiteness, and redness in the air, and similarly in the pupil of the eye. This does not happen in true, physical forms and powers. To the other point, it should be said that regarding the drink or food taken after the medicine...

->Whether an attractive medicine, if it does not purge, is changed into the humors it was intended to attract?<-

---

The purging is not strengthened by the medicine's physical substance being pushed toward the humor, but because the medicine's power multiplies its "image" and "intention" through the medium, and because the body's own stimulated expulsive power is incited. Regarding the other point, it should be said that contact is twofold: "real" contact, which belongs to physical bodies; and "virtual" contact <note>Virtual contact (contactus virtualis) refers to a force acting at a distance without physical touch, much like a magnet's influence.</note>, which can belong to other things. Because the power of the medicine penetrates while its physical substance does not, virtual contact is sufficient and appropriate.

### DISPUTATION 142.

<note>The initial letter Q is missing in the source, as it was intended for a rubricator to paint in later.</note>
[Q]uestion: Whether an attractive medicine, if it does not purge, is minimally converted into the humors it is meant to attract. It seems not. Since Aristotle <note>The text uses "A.", likely referring to Avicenna's Canon, Book 1, Part 4, or a commentary on Aristotle's physics.</note> in the first [book], fourth [part], when recounting the opinion of Galen on this matter, says these statements are not fitting. Furthermore, this conversion would occur either by reason of the medicine's substance or its natural acting power. Not by the first, because when something is converted into another—for instance, into a humor—it is necessary for its resolution to occur down to "prime matter," <note>Prime matter (materia prima) is the basic, formless "stuff" of the universe in Aristotelian philosophy that can take on any shape or nature.</note> as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> believe. For in this way, the "substantial form" of the medicine is destroyed, and consequently its accidental qualities. Since prime matter is indifferent toward all forms—as nothing is distinguished in it—it exists in potential to all humors indifferently, and not only to that specific one it was supposed to attract. Nor does it happen through the power of the natural body, since according to Aristotle, an attractive thing draws. A medicine, however, is meant to alter and transform. Those things that have opposite effects are themselves contrary; but food and medicine are opposites, as seen from their definitions in Disputations 136 and 137. Since food is meant to nourish and increase the body, while medicine is meant to alter and change it, one will not be transformed into the other. Again, the attraction of a humor by a medicine is similar to the attraction of iron by a magnet. But a magnet is never converted into the iron it attracts; therefore, neither is a medicine converted into a humor. Furthermore, in the first [book], second [part]: in that which is converted into blood, its original qualities remain—this is especially true when the nourishment was medicinal. This is seen in blood generated from lettuce, in which a lesser degree of coldness exists for a time than in the blood of the rest of the body. If blood generated from safflower (*carthamus*) <note>Carthamus tinctorius, used in medieval medicine as a purgative.</note> were converted into phlegm—since these things are hot and dry—heat and dryness would exist within the phlegm. This is false, since phlegm is cold and moist, and contraries cannot exist in the same thing at once. Moreover, it appears that a medicine for phlegm, at least an attractive one, is not converted into that which it attracts. This is not because of its "complexion" <note>Complexion (complexio) refers to the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within a substance.</note>, since turbith, nettle seed, safflower, and such things are hot and dry (the opposite of phlegm); nor is it because of the medicine itself, because a medicine acts through its quality, whereas true nourishment is suited to the body without such external qualities. Nor does it happen through a "hidden property," <note>A "hidden" or "occult" property is a power a substance has that cannot be explained by its heat or moisture alone, such as a magnet attracting iron.</note> because the logic of nutrition does not consist of that. Again, since a transformation into a humor begins with a similarity, and a medicine is hot and dry, it would only be transformed into bile <note>Choler or yellow bile, which is also hot and dry.</note>. Therefore, a medicine will not be converted into that which it is meant to attract, otherwise it would effectively become food.

<margin>
Material matter.
Opposition 4.
Proposition.
</margin>
<margin>1</margin>
The opposite view is held in the third book of *On Simple Medicines* and the first book, fourth part [of the *Canon*]. Whence Damascenus <note>Referring to the "Aphorisms" attributed to Johannes Damascenus.</note> says: "A medicine given, if it is overcome by nature, does not expel those humors we seek; it remains in the body, and having changed into their quality, it tends to generate diseases." Again, just as that which seems less likely to be present is present: it seems even less likely that a poison could be converted into humors and the body, yet it can be so converted, as will be shown.

<margin>2</margin>
Therefore, an attractive medicine that does not purge will be converted into the humor to be attracted. Regarding the first point, it should be known—for the sake of the medicine currently under discussion—that "medicine" is understood in two ways. One is materially, for the subject in which its essence is grounded, which is a mixture of the substances of the elements according to a resulting form. The other is formally, insofar as it is a medicine with a specific "complexion" and property arising from the mutual active and passive alteration of contrary qualities, as shown in Disputation 71. In this way, a medicine becomes "alterative" or "attractive" through its power.

<margin>3</margin>
Conversion is also a certain stripping away of the proper form and the introduction of another. Those things are said to be "converted" which, according to Aristotle, are acted upon by the matter receiving a form. This seems to be nothing other than nutrition. The essence of nutrition is the perfect assimilation of the thing nourishing into the proper quality and substance of that which is nourished (Disputation 30). Indeed, the logic of nutrition seems to arise from the mixing of elements, unless it is corrupted. For some mixtures are, in their ultimate state, suited for nourishing; these are things simply called "nourishment," such as wine, rooster testicles <note>Often prescribed in medieval medicine for vitality and reproductive health.</note>, soft-boiled eggs, and the like. Other things are so remote that no matter how much is consumed, they are never converted into true food, but always provide injury and corruption. These are, by their nature, contrary to human nature—as Galen says in the third book of *On Simple Medicines*—such as things that corrode and putrefy our body, especially "sublimated" minerals like burnt copper, verdigris, arsenic, or realgar <note>Realgar is arsenic disulfide, a toxic orange-red mineral.</note>.

It distinguishes between substances that can be assimilated as nutrition and toxic minerals like arsenic that always remain contrary to the human body.</summary>

This page continues the discussion on whether a medicine, if it fails to be expelled from the body, can be transformed into the humors it was intended to purge. The text moves from theoretical physics to specific examples of toxic and medicinal substances, referencing the famous "Poison Damsel" legend and the physiological theories of Galen and Asclepiades.

...and the rest, in which, because of their sharp fieriness and immense dryness, no capacity for nutrition remains, since all nourishment must partake in a temperate heat and moisture. And therefore, in certain sharp and bitter seas, no animal is generated or lives, as was touched upon in distinction 101. Some things, however, hold a middle ground between these extremes. Of these, some approach the side of the former group <note>referring to the nutritious side</note>, such as the "medicinal foods" mentioned before—for instance, dried grapes, dates, and similar things—as well as kinds of pot-herbs like turnips, cabbages, and so on.

Yet several others belong to the other extreme, such as those simply called <term>poisons</term> <note>original: "venena"</note>, like <term>snake venom</term> <note>original: "virus serpentum"</note> and <term>monkshood</term> <note>original: "napellus"; a highly toxic plant also known as wolfsbane</note>. For even if these are contrary to the whole species of human nature, they can still be taken in such a small quantity that the logic of nutritional mixture is preserved within them, rather than their specific poisonous power. This is because there is a "minimum amount of flesh" that can exist naturally, as found in the first book of the *Physics*. Indeed, poison and fire can be taken in such a small mass that they not only do no harm, but their effects will not even be felt, according to the third book of *On Complexions and Simple Medicines*. For a form and its operative property require a due or sufficient quantity of matter to act.

That snake venom and monkshood can provide nourishment is testified by the aforementioned wise men. For in the *Book of Secrets* attributed to Aristotle <note>The "Secretum Secretorum," a popular medieval pseudo-Aristotelian treatise on statecraft and health</note>, it is said that there was a certain girl nourished on snake venom. Likewise, in the fourth [book], sixth [part], it is recounted that Galen <note>A Greek physician whose work formed the basis of Western medicine for centuries</note> wrote of a certain old woman who, at the beginning, took a small amount of monkshood, and then did not cease using it until her nature was so accustomed to it that she could use it boldly without harm. It also seems that Rufus wrote

<margin>☜</margin> of a girl nourished on poison so that she might kill the kings who lay with her <note>This refers to the "Poison Damsel" myth, where a woman is raised on toxins until her very touch or breath is lethal to others</note>. Those things that exist in the middle of these categories possess the nature of a medicine more than that of a food or a poison. Of these, some participate less in the nature of medicine, such as "food-like medicines" like <term>purging cassia</term> <note>original: "cassiafistula"; a tropical pod used as a mild laxative</note>, tamarinds, mustard, and watercress. Others belong more to the nature of poison, such as those called poisonous medicines, like <term>euphorbia</term> <note>original: "euforbium"; a caustic plant resin</note>, <term>hellebore</term> <note>original: "elleborus"; a potent and toxic purgative</note>, and <term>scammony</term> <note>original: "scamonea"; a harsh resinous laxative</note>. Some are truly in the middle and are more accurately called medicines, such as <term>safflower</term> <note>original: "carthamus"</note>, nettle seed, agaric, iris, and the like. It should be noted that the humor into which a medicine is converted—if it is not expelled—is a "natural" humor. This is because in the appearance and form of a medicine, the natural humors are more considered than those that are against nature, since the causes of both are natural.

This is apparent because a medicine meant to draw out yellow bile, phlegm, or melancholy will evacuate them even if there is no "sin" <note>i.e., no pathological excess or imbalance</note> in them. This is indicated by medicine that evacuates blood. However, a medicine can also be transformed into an unnatural humor when it finds that humor more ready and abundant. Furthermore, natural and unnatural humors agree in that both are still called "humor"—for instance, phlegm, melancholy, or yellow bile. Indeed, not only do the natural and unnatural of the same species agree, but all humors communicate with one another

<margin>ᵟ</margin> with no small difference from the former. Regarding the second point, it should be known that <term>Asclepiades</term> <note>A Greek physician in Rome who disagreed with Galen's four-humor theory</note>—as attributed to him in the second book of *Elements* and the first of *Natural Things*, and as will be touched upon in distinction 144—wanted attractive medicine (whether poisonous or not), if it were not expelled, to be converted into the very thing it was supposed to evacuate. He posited that it does not evacuate any specific humor, but rather the thinnest ones first. Thus, those helped by medicine are not aided by the removal of a specific humor, but rather by the logic of general evacuation. This could have been his motivation for saying that even a poisonous medicine is converted into what it is meant to attract when it is not expelled. This is because conversion or nutrition (as mentioned) is perfected through "likeness," and an attractive medicine attracts through the likeness by which it is attracted, according to the third book of *Simple Medicines*.

Galen, however, weakened and denied this position. His reasoning is that a poisonous medicine—especially one taken in such a large quantity that it was expected to be expelled, but was not due to causes occurring in the body or the power of the stars—cannot be stripped of its poisonous nature so as to be converted into food. Rather, it leads the body to destruction. For although a small quantity of venom or poisonous medicine can be converted by the body, this is not possible when the amount is large, as the malice within it is invincible to the body. Nor is his <note>Asclepiades'</note> motive valid: for even if there is a similarity between the attractor and the attracted, there is nonetheless such a great contrariety between them by reason of the poisonous nature and the extreme quality (when taken in a large quantity) that it destroys the likeness and brings about its opposite, since it cannot be overcome by nature. Galen also, in the third book of *Simple Medicines* and Aristotle in the first [book], fourth [part], testify that...

It also debates the theory of Asclepiades, who argued that medicines turn into the humors they attract, a view Galen rejected on the grounds that large doses of poison remain inherently destructive.</summary>

# Whether an attractive medicine, if it does not purge, is turned into the humor it was meant to attract.

Medicine is simply converted into the humor it attracts, but with three conditions added: first, that it is not poisonous; second, that it does not purge but is digested; and third, that it is assimilated. For some medicines, even if they do not purge, they do not harm the body but act as food, because between every <term>purgative medicine</term> <note>A medicine designed to expel excess humors from the body.</note> and the <term>humor</term> <note>The four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that medieval doctors believed governed health.</note> it targets, there is an inherent similarity or "assimilation." However, some medicines are altered and converted into a state that corrupts and kills. The aforementioned conditions are explained as follows:

A medicine must not be poisonous if it is to be converted into the humor to be attracted. This is because it has been shown that when a poisonous substance is present in a large quantity in the body, it cannot be converted into nourishment, as the logic of nutrition—derived from the mixture of elements—is destroyed due to the medicine’s total opposition to the body's nature. For that which nourishes must ultimately be overcome and assimilated by the body.

Secondly, the medicine must not purge. For if it were to purge, it would not remain in the <term>digestive sites</term> <note>Medieval physicians believed digestion happened in stages: first in the stomach, then the liver, then the individual organs.</note> long enough to be digested. Instead, despite its opposition to the body’s resistance, it would be driven with the humors it attracted toward the belly or intestines and expelled upward by vomiting or downward by stool.

Thirdly, it is required that the medicine itself be digested. This is because every nourishing thing must pass through the three locations of digestion: the stomach, the liver, and the various members of the body. In **Difference 54**, it is noted that even the nourishment of the stomach lining from contact with food is not considered "simple nourishment" by doctors, but rather a kind of "qualitative refreshment," according to the <term>Colliget</term> <note>The *Kitab al-Kulliyat* (The Book of Generalities), a famous medical encyclopedia by the philosopher Averroes.</note>. But more was seen on this in the previously mentioned "Difference."

Regarding the third point, it should be known according to the aforementioned doctors that, once these three conditions are met, an "attractive medicine" is converted into the humor to be attracted. This refers to the medicine's "material" name—that is, the physical substance that carries the medicinal property. For "formally" speaking, as a medicine, it is never changed into a humor regardless of the conditions, since it would have to be digested and ordered toward nutrition—which is the nature of food, not medicine.

That medicine can be so converted is demonstrated thus: whatever things agree in genus but differ in species are transmuted into one another, as stated in the first book of *On Generation*. The substance upon which the medicine is based and the humor generated from it meet in a certain community of matter—at least <term>hyleal</term> <note>Related to "hyle," the Greek term for prime or fundamental matter.</note> matter. For there exists one single matter for all things that can be generated and corrupted. They also differ in "specific differences," as shown by their definitions. Furthermore, since it has been said that the logic of nutrition most effectively strips away the preceding oppositions through the mixing of elements, wherever this uncorrupted mixture of elements occurs, nutrition can be completed. This is found in medicine that is not poisonous, since the nature of the body is able to remove the oppositions that hinder nutrition.

Moreover, nutrition is achieved through similarity, since nutrition is a certain conversion of one thing into another. Things that are similar are more easily transmuted into each other. For those possessing a <term>symbol</term> <note>In Aristotelian physics, a "symbol" is a shared quality (like heat or moisture) that makes it easier for one element to turn into another.</note>, the transition into one another is easier (per the first book of *On Generation*), and conversion happens more easily within a proportional group than into something foreign. But according to **Galen**, medicine is similar to the humors it is meant to attract. And this is confirmed: if similarity is the cause of conversion into another, then where the similarity is more intense, the transmutation will be more powerful. This is the case between an attractive medicine and a humor. Indeed, according to Galen, there is a "similarity in substance." Therefore, since things similar in quality are converted into one another, much more so are those similar in substance, as they possess a more powerful similarity.

<margin>Note</margin>
This is also shown by the fact that we see "empirical" doctors helping a sick limb by administering a similar limb. For they say that the bones of a human skull help with diseases of the head and **epilepsy** <note>original: "epydimie"; a likely corruption of *epilensia*.</note>. They also say that the brain of chickens strengthens and increases the human brain. They testify that it restrains blood flowing from the nostrils, and that the lungs of a fox or a hedgehog help with ailments of the lungs. The inner lining of a chicken's stomach is said to greatly help a severely weak stomach. The entire belly of birds (especially the fleshy part) and the liver of a wolf are said, by their own specific properties, to suit the human liver. For ailments of the intestines, they write that intestines (especially when applied for colic) are effective. Similarly, kidney helps kidney (**book 3, chapters 18 and 22**). They even testify that some experts have believed—and there are those among the bold who have used them and were entirely healed of gout and joint pains—that burnt human bones should be given in a drink to those suffering from joint pains.

<margin>See the *Colliget*</margin>
Hence, in the fifth book of the **Colliget**, it is said that any accustomed limb strengthens the similar limb of the person eating it, as mentioned in the "Difference"...

It has also been seen in section 68. Therefore, it is proven that conversion and strengthening are caused primarily by a similarity that is mostly hidden from us. For human reason cannot reach it, not because of the thing's own obscurity, but because of a third factor appearing in its nature. Its knowledge is also hindered because it exists as infinite compared to infinite things. And therefore, it is gathered in section 6. Infinite preparations in <term>matter</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "matter" is the underlying "stuff" of the world, while "form" gives that stuff its specific identity.</note> will be unknown to us, since our intellect only extends to that which is finite.

### Regarding the fourth point

Regarding the first point, it must be said that A. <note>Likely referring to a commentator like Averroes or an "Author" like Aristotle.</note> did not intend to say that the words of **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of antiquity, whose theories dominated medieval medicine.</note> were "inconvenient"—that is, contrary to the truth—as some wrongly interpret, since he accepts his words in the third book of *On Medicines*. Rather, they are not "convenient"—meaning they are not similar, but dissonant—namely the sayings of **Asclepiades** <note>A Greek physician who often disagreed with Galen, favoring a theory based on atoms and pores.</note> and Galen.

For **Asclepiades** simply and indifferently claims that any medicine is "attractive" when it has not been evacuated into that which it has to attract and convert. Galen, however, as shown, applied three conditions. Now, the "simple" and the "conditioned" are opposites, let alone the same thing; for a greater assimilation exists, as also appeared by the logic of similarity in <term>substance</term> <note>The essential nature or "being" of a thing.</note> than in quality, since qualitative similarity is caused by the similarity of the substance. For matter with form is the cause of all <term>accidents</term> <note>Attributes that can change without changing the thing’s essence, like color or temperature.</note>, just like a mother. What kind of similarity there is in substance was shown in section 71.

<margin>?</margin> But if someone objects—since qualitative similarity, as established, is caused by similarity of substance—that **safflower** <note>original: "carthamus"</note> and **nettle seeds**, which are of a hot and dry <term>complexion</term> <note>The balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) in a body or substance.</note>, would never be something that converts into **phlegm** <note>A cold and wet humor; the objection is: why does a hot/dry plant turn into a cold/wet fluid?</note> through similarity of substance, but rather they should be cold and wet so that the effect matches its cause.

<margin>§</margin> To this it must be said: either because of some other preparation found in the matter of the substance (in which the aforementioned similarity is observed) such a diversity arises; or because similarity of substance is ordered toward the *act*. For **Form** is that which gives "being" and consequently "operation." But it cannot act except by having the appropriate **instruments**. Now, the instruments of action are the **qualities**. The most appropriate instruments for an "attractive" medicine are heat and dryness, since it is the nature of heat to attract and dryness to sustain its movement. They are also stronger than the other active and passive qualities. For this reason, since everything that exists is made to hold its own operation, it will also have its own "instruments" proceeding from its substance—even if they seem opposing to us at first glance. Just as we see the movement of an animal, which is performed by heat in the nerves, yet the heart and nerves themselves remain cold.

***

Regarding the other point, it must be said that according to the "gradual forms," the resolution of a composite thing does not happen all the way down to <term>prime matter</term> <note>The most basic, formless state of matter.</note>, but rather down to other forms always remaining in the matter. Because of these, some similarity remains in the thing that is destroyed or generated, due to the remains of such a form.

According to those who philosophize rightly about the truth of forms in all things—except perhaps in man, for some concede two forms in him—it must be said that although a resolution of the composite happens down to prime matter (so that all dispositions following the prior form are corrupted), when the matter receives another form, more perfect dispositions similar to the preceding ones are introduced. This is because a subsequent form always brings with it, as something more perfect, that which was in the first, according to the *Generation of Animals*.

Thus, by the power of the subsequent form that arrives having similarity with the prior, the dispositions left behind are not the *same*, but *similar*. This is also shown in the generation of fire from air; in which the "symbol" (the quality, number, and being) does not remain the same in the thing generated, but is the same in species or essence, as explained in the first book of *On Generation*. Hence, it implies a true **similarity** rather than "identity."

Nor does the natural attractive power always attract what is suitable and helpful; sometimes it is deceived, appearing to be drawn by sweetness or smell. Wherefore, it is commanded in the fourth and sixth [books] that one should not consume things of dominant flavors or odors if one fears poisoned drink or food. Nor is a medicine poisonous if it is converted, as has been shown.

<margin>§</margin> Regarding the other point, it must be said that the similarity of a **magnet** to iron and of an attractive medicine to a humor is quite broad and differs significantly by the aforementioned difference.

Regarding the other point, it must be said that when qualities in a generated thing seem to remain prior for a time, that thing is not yet perfectly transmuted and generated from the preceding corrupted thing. And for this reason, **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina, the Persian "Prince of Physicians."</note> indicates that it would not remain forever, but only for a time. Or it must be said, as already appeared, that those qualities are not the *same*, but remain *similar*.

Regarding the other point, it must be said that although medicine and food are formally opposed in as much as they are "medicine" and "food," nevertheless, as was said, the subject in which that medicine or food is grounded is not necessarily opposed.

Regarding the other point, it must be said—as appeared—that **turbith** <note>An herbal root used as a potent laxative to purge phlegm.</note> and similar things are converted into phlegm principally by reason of being a medicine. Nor is food called "without quality" unless it is "true nourishment" in the <term>third digestion</term> <note>The final stage of digestion where nutrients are assimilated into the tissues.</note>, which does not have qualities that are instrumentally opposed in complexion or property, and so on.

->Whether emollient and lubricating methods should be mixed with astringents. 7<-
i 5

### SECTION 143.

<margin>Mesue</margin>
<note original: "Mesue">Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, known as Mesue the Elder, was a Persian physician and educator in the early Islamic Golden Age whose works were foundational to medieval European pharmacy.</note>
That an emollient <note>original: "lenitiua"</note> and lubricating medicine should be mixed with an astringent <note>original: "compressiue"</note> is shown by **Mesue** in his works on simple medicines and his *Aggregator*. It is also shown in the first part of the fourth book [of the Canon] where he dissolves things using a decoction of <term>myrobalans</term> <note>Dried plum-like fruits used in medieval medicine as both laxatives and astringents depending on the variety.</note> with tamarinds, <term>turbith</term>, <term>cassia fistula</term>, and so on; among these, one is astringent and the other is emollient. Furthermore, those things should be mixed together where one corrects the other. For this is one of the primary reasons for mixing medicines, as will be shown in what follows. 

However, regarding an emollient or lubricating medicine—since the same judgment applies to both—there is a removal of foreign qualities from the medicine. For an emollient softens the matter and the parts of the organs, and it remolds and weakens them. A lubricating medicine, on the other hand, acts on the matter by making it slippery, and by a certain subtle softness, it urges the matter downwards. An astringent medicine, by contrast, strengthens and draws the viscera back together. Therefore, it will remove contraction and sticking through the emollient or lubricating medicine, so that the astringent medicine might correct the defects of the former. 

Again, emollients and astringents are joined with dissolving medicines because of their strong attractive properties, such as <term>cassia fistula</term> with rhubarb or <term>agaric</term>, and myrobalans with <term>scammony</term>, which dilate one another more than emollients and astringents do. Since a dissolving medicine has a much more powerful virtue than these, it also draws from distant parts, which the others could never do. 

Again, one method of medicinal composition is that it can benefit various different conditions at once. Suppose someone has a stomach and upper intestines that are robust and dense, but lower intestines that are weak and loose. In that case, the composition of an emollient with an astringent is useful, because the emollient acts first on the upper parts—to which an astringent, styptic, or contracting medicine would be harmful. But this [astringent] will finally act laudably against the lower parts of the intestines, and it calms the disturbance of the soul and nausea. Such a medicine, as they say, is an astringent medicine. Therefore, an emollient medicine should be associated with an astringent. 

The opposite of this view seems to be held in the first and fourth books, and in the fifth book of the *Colliget* <note>The "Colliget" or "Book of Generalities" was a major medical encyclopedia written by the philosopher-physician Averroes.</note>. Furthermore, those things whose operations joined together corrupt each other should not be mixed, just as one does not mix sweet things with strong vinegar. But an astringent medicine corrupts the action of an emollient since they are contraries: for one softens and smooths, while the other roughens and contracts. For contraries are mutually destructive. Also, things that have entirely different intentions should not be associated, since the intended quality is frustrated, and the action of such opposites is laborious and agitating. But astringents and emollients are of this kind, since an astringent is chosen to constrict the belly after it has been loosened; it is specifically praised for diarrhea and dysentery. An emollient, however, is meant to loosen the belly gently and to keep it open thereafter. Therefore, it is often given to those who are deprived of the benefit of a bowel movement. Thus, an astringent medicine should not be mixed with an emollient.

Regarding the first point, it must first be known what a composition entails; second, what forced physicians to compose medicines; and finally, which medicines so composed are made better and which are corrupted. The first point has already been shown in sections 137 and 141. 

<margin>Double mixture</margin>
Mixture, as seen in section 16, is twofold: there is one in which the mixed things are led into a certain common nature between alteration and corruption—this is the union of qualities, which is perceived by the intellect rather than the senses, such as the mixture of elements that constitutes living beings. There is another kind of mixture which is a gathering together of bodies, where their own forms remain unaltered, and this is perceived by the senses, such as the joining of beans together. There is also a mixture in which things are brought together over a long period, and some in a short time. Furthermore, one kind is made by fire, where one part penetrates another because of its sharpness and subtlety, such as in decoctions and syrups. Another kind is made by the application of bodies minutely blended together, such as pills or troches <note>A small medicated tablet or lozenge.</note>. For they are made and joined together in many ways, as in section 16. 

Regarding this, it must be known that whoever wishes to compose a medicine properly must first attend to the bodies which they must treat: their complexion <note>The "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) in an individual.</note>, age, strength, habits, constitution, and the rest. Similarly, they must consider the disposition of the air and the region, as well as the <term>non-naturals</term> <note>The "six non-naturals" were external factors like diet, sleep, and exercise that affected health but were not part of the body's nature.</note> and things against nature, such as the cause of the disease and its symptoms, so that they may compose the medicine skillfully and apply it proportionally to the natures of the bodies. 

I say "skillfully compose" because if a simple medicine could perform the whole task, a compound would not be chosen. But because it cannot, we do not find all the virtues we seek in one simple medicine; or perhaps we wish to increase or decrease the strength of a medicine because it contains virtues we do not need. We were therefore forced to compose medicines for these three reasons. Those who compose them distinguish them in two ways: first, according to the nature of the infirmity or disease and the weakened organs; second, according to the nature of the simple medicines. 

Regarding the nature of the patient: for example, if they have a firm belly but a hot liver, we mix a hot medicine with a cold one, such as wormwood and mastic with endive and barberry. Similarly, if the intestines are weak and prone to flatulence, but the stomach is strong and not prone to "rheum" <note>In this context, "rheum" refers to a flow of excess humors or catarrh.</note>, as in the case of a bilious passion or diarrhea, we might use radish or something similar. 

Regarding the nature of the disease, medicines are composed for several reasons: either because the disease is distinguished from its cause—as when a putrid fever arises from thick, cold humors. In this case, because of the hot and dry imbalance of the fever, we need a cold and moist medicine as its opposite; but because of the putrefaction from thick, cold humors, we need a hot and dry medicine which, by its heat and dryness, may digest the humor by thinning and dividing it. Or they are mixed because of the diversity between the disease and its symptoms, as occurs in a "syncopal" fever <note>A fever accompanied by fainting or a sudden loss of strength.</note>...

It explains that while contraries can cancel each other out, they are often combined to treat complex conditions where different organs (like the upper and lower digestive tracts) require different treatments simultaneously.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of pharmaceutical compounding, specifically detailing the diverse clinical and practical reasons why a physician should mix multiple ingredients rather than using a "simple" (single-ingredient) medicine. It builds on the previous section's debate regarding the mixing of opposites like emollients and astringents.</meta>

...[treating] **syncope** <note>Fainting or sudden loss of consciousness, often attributed to a failure of the "vital spirits."</note> with hot and dry remedies, such as aromatic, spirited wine, musk lozenges, and similar things. For this reason, **theriacs** <note>A famous ancient "polypharmacy" or "panacea" consisting of dozens of ingredients, originally used as an antidote to poison.</note> were developed to assist the body by resisting various harms and opposing poisons. 

Or, compounding is used because of the **diversity of illnesses**, as happens in a fever involving various types of matter and locations. An example is the **hemitritaeos** <note>A "semi-tertian" fever, considered complex because it combined the characteristics of a daily (phlegmatic) and a three-day (choleric) fever.</note> caused by a mixture of choler and phlegm, in which one matter is contained within the veins and the other outside of them. Regarding this, in the fourth book, **Galen** <note>original: "G." – The most influential Greek physician of antiquity.</note> and those before him cured the hemitritaeos with barley water in which the potency of pepper was present. In this way, he used one thing against each distinct nature. The learned mind is able to do this by obeying the Sublime and Glorious Creator. 

<margin>p. 4</margin>
Secondly, compounding is necessary due to a **diversity of conditions** collected in a single illness, such as a "bastard" tertian fever, which requires both cooling and heating agents due to the presence of both choler and phlegm.

<margin>p. z / xi. 3</margin>
Or, it is due to the **extreme malice of a disease**, which a single simple medicine cannot overcome through opposition. 

<margin>p. 5</margin>
Sometimes a medicine is needed that is heating to the fourth degree <note>Medieval medicine graded the "potency" of drugs from 1 to 4.</note>. Or, it is because of the **variety of the state** itself, which changes perceptibly—requiring cold at one moment and heat at another, or perhaps cold-repelling and heat-evaporating agents simultaneously, as happens in many illnesses according to the hours of the day or the status of the "flow" <note>Referring to the movement of humors or discharge from a wound/swelling.</note>. 

Or, it is because the disease is such that a **simple medicine cannot be found** that directly opposes it. For example, if a disease requires a medicine that is heating in the **second degree**, but none is available, one may compound it from a medicine that is heating in the third degree and one in the first degree; from these, a second-degree heating medicine will arise. This is discussed in the *Touch* <note>original: "tactu" - likely referring to a specific medical authority or text on the degrees of qualities.</note>, chapter 139.

The composition also varies according to the **weakness of the parts**, or because of their diversity and utility. For instance, when an <term>aposteme</term> <note>An internal swelling or abscess.</note> occurs near strong organs that are essential for the preservation of life, such as the heart and the liver. In these cases, one must use evaporating medicines, but in the state of the swelling, one must also use **styptics** <note>Astringents that contract tissues to stop bleeding or secretions.</note> and aromatic strengtheners so that their virtues are preserved; for these organs manage the nourishment for the whole body. This is found in the eleventh and thirteenth books of the *Art of Healing*.

Furthermore, it may be because of the **location of the organ**. One medicine is mixed with another to make it reach the intended location more quickly. For this reason, **saffron** is mixed with **camphor lozenges**, even though saffron itself might harm the heart's complexion in certain conditions. For this same purpose, some physicians added **celery** to medicines for epilepsy, and **cantharides** <note>"Spanish Fly," a beetle used in medicine, known for being extremely harsh and irritating.</note> to medicines for the bladder, or **vinegar** to a plaster for sciatica.

Or, it is because of the **connection or alliance of the organ**. For example, in a hot disease of the stomach, one does not need a very cold remedy because of the nerves sent to it from the brain; therefore, heating things are mixed with the cold medicine, since cold is the enemy of the nerves, according to the ancients. 

Or, because of the **great sensitivity of the part**, such as the mouth of the stomach and the eyes. These are the most sensitive parts of the body, as noted in the fourth book of *Accident and Disease*. Therefore, mild and painless medicines called <term>anodynes</term> <note>Pain-relievers.</note> should be mixed into their treatments. 

Sometimes it is because of the **diversity of the disease and the organ** together, because the organ affected is a "principal" one. For example, even if the organ is suffering from a "hot" disease, one must be careful not to cool it too much or too suddenly because of its noble nature and leadership over the body. Therefore, heating things must be mixed with the cooling ones. 

The composition of medicines is also determined by their **nature**, when a simple one does not suffice. Either to **increase the virtue** of a medicine (as when one hot or cold medicine is joined to another to strengthen it), or so that its virtue **endures for a longer time** without dissolving. This is why **iris root**, **acorus** <note>Sweet flag, a medicinal plant.</note>, and **agaric** <note>A type of medicinal mushroom/fungus used as a purgative.</note> are added to theriac. 

Or, it is to **lessen the strength** of a medicine. Since some medicines are hot and sharp, one must compound them with cold, slimy things to reduce their power and take away their sharpness. For example, **Arabic gum** or **fenugreek** is mixed into theriac, or gum is used in eye salves. 

Or, to **remove the harm** of the medicine itself. Just as **ginger** and **anise** are joined to **scammony** <note>A harsh purgative resin.</note>—which is harmful to the stomach and liver—and cooked in food, or **tragacanth** and **Arabic gum** are joined to **aloe**. 

Or, to **break its adversity**; for example, **castor** <note>Castoreum, a secretion from beavers used as a stimulant.</note> is joined to **opium** when there is a need to induce sleep <note>To prevent the opium from being too "stupefying" or dangerous.</note>. 

Or, because although a medicine might help in one way, it harms in another. A medicine to **remove the injury** is joined to it. For example, in breaking [kidney] stones, **cantharides** are used, but slimy, painless things like **milk** or fatty broth are added to them. 

Or, because a medicine has a "regard" for reaching two paths—namely, the veins and the urinary passages. Therefore, we add to it medicines that **draw it toward the urinary paths**, as we mix provocative agents with cantharides. 

Or, so the medicine remains **undispersed** in its place while completing its action. For instance, **wax** is associated with **balsam** so that it becomes slimy and does not disperse before it has finished its intended task. 

Or, so that the medicine **remains uncorrupted** for a longer time, as **honey** is mixed into confections. 

Or, to **remove loathsomeness and horror** [of taste or smell] so that it can be taken; once taken, it must remain in the stomach to complete its action. Therefore, **carrot**, **celery**, and **mountain parsley seeds** are associated with **hellebore**, and **anise** is joined to **scammony**. For this reason also, **sugar** and **honey** are added to many medicines. 

Or, so that the **goodness** of a medicine is acquired by a simple one, and its **malice and defect** are removed. For example, **yellow myrobalans** are joined to **scammony**. Indeed, they help its property in purging choler and they correct its excess. For since scammony inflames the stomach and weakens the heart, and dissolves and excoriates the parts, myrobalans remove all such things. Whence **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh.</note> says: "He operated best who mixed scammony with yellow myrobalans." 

In the same way, **ginger** invigorates and corrects **turbith** <note>A root used as a purgative.</note>. For when subtle phlegm occurs and is slow to be drawn out from the nearby parts, ginger mixed with it removes all these defects. Ginger does not allow the virtue of turbith to be "stupefied" <note>Rendered inactive or sluggish.</note>. 

To say it in a word, all types of **alaphangine** <note>original: "alephangie" - Aromatic bitter pills used for the stomach and head.</note> (that is, hot and aromatic ones) work this way when joined to weak and slow medicines. 

Thus, from these collected words from the sayings of the wise, the causes appear for why one simple medicine is joined with another or with others. Know that in the instructions for medicines, and especially the more solemn ones, one medicine is spread as a **basis** for the others compounded with it...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the compounding of medicines, specifically focusing on whether one should mix ingredients with opposing actions, such as "lubricating" (softening) and "expressive" (astringent/squeezing) substances. It draws heavily on the theories of Al-Kindi and Galen regarding the degrees of qualities in compound drugs.</meta>

## Whether lubricating and softening medicines should be mixed with expressive ones. -

<margin>It is not necessary</margin> ...according to the son of **Al-Kindi** <note>original: "filiū Alkindi" — Al-Kindi was a 9th-century Arab philosopher and "Physician of the Arabs" who developed a mathematical system for pharmaceutical dosages.</note>. Although there are almost infinite ways to arrange medicines, there are six primary types. This is because one either compounds a hot medicine with a hot one, a cold with a cold, a hot with a cold, a tempered with a tempered, a tempered with a hot, or a tempered with a cold. In the first three modes, a triple distinction exists: for one either joins equally hot with equally hot, or joins them with less or more heat. The same applies to cold with cold, and hot with cold. Whence we gather in the fifth book: The **simple medicines** <note>Single-ingredient drugs, the "building blocks" of pharmacy.</note> from which a **compound medicine** <note>A drug made of multiple ingredients.</note> results are either all of one kind, such as all hot or all cold, or of contrary kinds, where some are hot and others cold. Under both modes, he added that medicines will either be in the same degree of heat or cold—such as the second or third degree—or in different degrees, such as the first and third, or the second and fourth. Regarding this third point, it should be known that just as foods compounded in one way are rendered more vigorous and perfect, but in another way are made contrary, so it is with medicines. Whence the first *Problemata*: Certain nutrients by their nature corrupt one another in one way, but not in another. Those which are compounded in the second and first ways are disposed in three manners: they either invigorate their actions, destroy them, or rectify them by removing their "malice" <note>Harmful side effects or undesirable properties.</note>. They are invigorated, for example, when **panicum** <note>original: "panigiu" — a type of millet.</note> and millet are boiled with milk, or with pork fat or oil. For since these have little nourishment—indeed, they are more critical than other grains—they are rendered much more nourishing by these primary and particular diets. Whence **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."</note> in the third book of *On Foodstuffs*: It is clear that this <margin>Galen, 3. On Foodstuffs</margin> food is much better than if eaten alone, because the milk is led by the nature of those foods toward **good chyme** <note>original: "euchima" — healthy digestive fluid.</note> and other benefits. They also "corrupt" each other, such as sweet things mixed with sour things, because they do not "seal" <note>Harmful interaction where the qualities do not blend harmoniously.</note> together. Whence in the first and third sections: I have seen experimenters—and others have already said it—that milk must not be eaten with sour things, nor fish with milk, for from this come permanent illnesses, such as **leprosy**. Nor should one eat "sour milk" <note>original: "lac acetoſū" — likely yogurt or curdled milk.</note> with radishes; for although these are laudable enough in themselves, when they are mixed they corrupt, because they do not "seal" together. Similarly, the "perfection of heat" mentioned by **Gegyseb** <note>A medieval authority on dietetics, possibly a corruption of an Arabic name.</note>, the author on diets, is achieved by sufficiently compounding with praiseworthy things, such as pine nuts, almonds, sesame oil, and sugar. But when they are compounded in another way they corrupt each other, because an abominable blockage is made that passes slowly <margin>Gegyseb: Common dietaries of the East</margin> into the veins; yet it benefits those suffering from diseases of the chest and urinary tracts who need smoothing and soothing. They are **rectified**, however, when hot things are mixed with cold, and vice versa. Whence in the first and third sections: That which is cold, like cucumber and gourd, is tempered by that which is contrary, like garlic and leeks. If it be hot, it is tempered by that which is contrary, like cucumbers and **purslane**.

In the same way, the actions of medicines are invigorated, destroyed, or rendered better when they are joined.

An example of the first is the roasting of **turbith** <note>original: "turbith" — a root used as a purgative.</note> with ginger, as touched upon before, and **epithyme** <note>A parasitic plant, often dodder of thyme, used to purge "melancholy."</note> with pepper, or **rhubarb** with **bole armoniac** <note>original: "boloarmēo" — a medicinal red clay from Armenia used as an astringent.</note>. In rhubarb there is a strong power of contraction, but with this also an opening power which <margin>Aloe, Bdellium, Tragacanth, Myrobalans</margin> diminishes its astringent action; therefore, if it is mixed with bole armoniac or **acacia** <note>Used here for its tanning/astringent properties.</note>, it contracts vehemently. And for this purpose **saffron** is mixed with rose, camphor, and coral, so that it may cause them to reach the heart. For this reason also, radish seed is coupled with subtle and penetrating things so that it stays in the liver long enough to complete its actions. An explanation of the second <note>Medicines that destroy or weaken each other.</note> is **violet** mixed with **myrobalans** <note>original: "mirabolais" — astringent plum-like fruits used in tanning and medicine.</note>, and generally the joining of a softening thing with a "compressing" <note>astringent</note> thing, or barley water with **oxymel** <note>original: "ſyrupo acetoſo" — a syrup of vinegar and honey.</note>. Whence in the fourth and first sections: To aggregate oxymel and barley water together is unpraiseworthy, for it corrupts the barley water.

The third type <note>Rectifying or correcting "malice."</note> is shown by the mixture of **aloe** with **tragacanth** <note>original: "dragagāto"</note> or **bdellium** <note>A semi-transparent resin.</note>, and generally with anything that prevents sharp stripping of the gut, like the pulp of **colocynth** <note>A powerful and potentially toxic purgative.</note>. For aloe loosens and cleanses the intestines, but it strips them and opens the orifices of the veins; but by the mixture of the aforesaid things, this "malice" is removed. Such a society and coupling of medicines sometimes attends to the primary qualities so they may correct each other, or sometimes they are "corrupted" for the sake of an effect, just as myrobalans are said to emend the evil effects of **scammony** <note>A harsh resinous purgative.</note>. Sometimes it is for the emendation of bad properties, which it has by its own nature to correct, such as the poisonous nature and enmity of a thing, which is why **bezoar** <note>original: "bezabart" — a stone-like mass found in the stomachs of animals, believed to be a universal antidote.</note> is mixed with medicines. And if a mixture is to be sought from these, they should "seal" each other so that after they have been joined by action and passion and innate virtue, one single virtue rises from the whole. Such is the mixture of turbith with ginger, and radish with **hermodactyl** <note>A bulbous plant used for joint pain.</note>, but not radish with turbith, for they do not "seal" together. This is shown because it is the property of scammony to harm the heart. It also causes bile to become inflamed and leads to much dissolution of the limbs. **Amber** <margin>Amber, Crystal, Gallia</margin> <note>Likely ambergris or yellow amber.</note> strengthens the heart, and **crystal** extinguishes inflammation, and **gallia** <note>A medicinal paste or "musk-apple."</note> strengthens the dissolution of the limbs; yet a mixture of these with scammony is not suitable. For they do not "seal" into one thing. Therefore, their mixture is not useful. In the first book of *Simples*, Galen says: "I placed **wolf's liver** <margin>Wolf's liver</margin> <note>original: "epar adib" — 'adib' is the Arabic word for wolf.</note> in a medicine of **eupatory**, and I did not find it to increase the benefit beyond what usually came from it." Some things corrupt each other by their properties, such as strings made from the intestines of sheep and wolves placed together, or the feathers of a dove with those of a hawk. Regarding the second mode, it is written in the first and fourth sections: That which causes "slipping" <note>A laxative effect.</note> should not be joined to that which aids by "compressing" <note>An astringent effect</note> in such a way that their powers are equal. Rather, it is better in such cases that one be delayed after the other, so there is one path for the two medicines: the one that softens performs its work first, and then the "expressive" one arrives and expels what was softened.

Also in the second and first sections: Those things which destroy through mixing are like two medicines performing one action but with two contrary powers. When they are aggregated, if it happens that one of them precedes the other in its action, it will complete its work; but if it does not precede, one will prohibit the other, like violet and myrobalans. For violet loosens by softening, and myrobalans loosen [by another means].
