It references the works of Mesue, Serapion (the Aggregator), and Avicenna.</meta>

...by expressing and thickening. When, therefore, they come upon the matter, both of their operations destroy themselves. And if **myrobalans** <note>Astringent plum-like fruits used in medieval medicine as a purge that also "strengthened" the organs.</note> come first, and then **violet** follows and softens; or if the myrobalans follow after and "express" <note>Squeeze or constrict</note>, the operation is stronger. This is also gathered from the fifth book. Physicians mix 

<margin>3</margin> myrobalans with **cassia fistula** <note>The "purging cassia," a mild, sweet laxative.</note> and **turbith** <note>A powerful root used to purge phlegm.</note>, but they do not know the proper method of healing. This is contrary to their nature, but in practice it is done thus: Some drink simple myrobalans with sugar and **manna** <note>A sweet plant exudate used as a gentle softener.</note>; and in this way, some prefer them crushed with double the amount of sugar. Manna is indeed a "lenitive" <note>A medicine that softens or eases the bowels.</note>. Furthermore, this seems sufficient for the simple medicines. 

<margin>3</margin> However, some have said that the mixing of myrobalans with "labificative" <note>Slippery or lubricating.</note> and lenitive medicines is not good, because their operations in the same body push against each other. But I do not see it that way; rather, the "stickiness" <note>original: "adherentia"</note> and "wrinkling" <note>original: "corrugatio" — referring to the way astringents can shrink tissues</note> are removed from them by these [lenitives], and an easy passage is acquired. 

Further, the **Aggregator** <note>Serapion the Elder, a 9th-century Syrian Christian physician whose medical compendium was widely used.</note> says: when we wish to prepare myrobalans to be given in a drink, they should be crushed and infused in hot water, then strained, and sugar should be added to the strained liquid; we will then grind them to press out their "stypticity" <note>The quality of being astringent or mouth-drying.</note>. And those who wish to increase the goodness of their preparation should cook them with **prunes**, **sebesten**, and **jujubes** <note>Fruits known for their mucilaginous, soothing properties.</note>, and administer it. For in these medicines there is a viscosity that tempers the stypticity of the myrobalans. And these three species of myrobalans are mixed with **tamarinds**. 

Therefore, according to these authors, a lenitive medicine is to be mixed with a "compressive" <note>Astringent/binding</note> one. But the truth of this will soon appear. Regarding the third point, it must be known from what has been said that the truth becomes clear: the mixing of one medicine with another is either "true" or "nearly true," and enough time has passed over it so that one single **complexion** <note>The overall balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) resulting from a mixture.</note> and form results from all the mixable parts. For the particles of the mixed bodies—the primary elements—require time to act and be acted upon by each other in a necessary way. In this way, a lenitive medicine can be joined with a compressive one, since the contrarieties they held are then "put to sleep" <note>original: "sopite" — neutralized or dormant</note> and reduced into one shared nature. For thus we see through time one perfect thing being constituted and rising up from contraries. 

Otherwise, the mixture was merely "sensible" <note>Apparent to the senses but not chemically unified.</note> and by "juxtaposition," made in a short time. In such a case, the mixing of a lenitive medicine with a compressive one is not useful, especially if the compression preceded the lenitive, as happens when they are mixed in equal parts. This is noted by the clever arguments introduced in this part. It can also be said more sweetly and otherwise, gathered from the aforementioned speeches of the physicians: either the ingredients in the mixture are equal in power, or unequal. If they are equal—as when we wish to help the "solution" <note>The loosening or purging of humors.</note> of one medicine with the solution of another, such as **agaric** <note>A medicinal fungus used as a purge.</note> with turbith—then a lenitive medicine should not be joined to a compressive one. This is because their adverse actions would destroy each other, as **Avicenna** <note>A — refers to the famous Persian polymath Ibn Sina.</note> and **Averroes** <note>Ax/An — refers to the Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd.</note> believe when they say their powers are equal. The reasons of this part deduce this clearly. 

But if they are not equal in power—if one greatly surpasses the other—this happens when a medicine is joined to another not for the sake of an equal "solution," but rather to remove the "malice" <note>Harmful side effects or harshness.</note> and defects from that medicine. For example, **yellow myrobalans** are added to **scammony** <note>A very harsh, resinous purgative.</note>, or **ginger** to turbith, or **roses** to scammony, and **bdellium** <note>A semi-transparent resin.</note> to **aloe**. In these cases, the mixing of a lenitive medicine with a compressive one is useful as a way of "correction" and "amendment" of the harm. And this is what **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a royal physician in Baghdad.</note> meant when he said that in myrobalans—which are a compressive medicine—the stickiness and wrinkling are removed by the addition of a lenitive medicine, and thus a solution <note>A bowel movement</note> is easily granted. 

It also appeared clearly from the **Aggregator Serapion** that he speaks of a preparatory mixing for the sake of providing "goodness" and removing "malice." Similarly, the virtue of myrobalans removes the "superfluous lubrication" from cassia fistula, which weakens the stomach and intestines so much that it passes through the weak and "slippery" <note>Those prone to diarrhea.</note>, especially in winter. The clever arguments of this part show this first. 

Regarding the fourth and final point, it appears from the reasons of both sides what should be said, though it is a question of greater teaching. To the first, it seems we should say that the authorities of **Haly Abbas** <note>Halyabatis — a 10th-century Persian physician.</note>, Mesue, and the Aggregator deduce this. To the other, it should be said that a mixture of unequal power is useful for the sake of "correction," but not for the sake of performing a "solution" equally. And thus, what Avicenna introduces should be heard. To the next, it should be said that a "dissolving" <note>Strongly purging</note> medicine is joined to others for the reason of correction, not for the sake of the solution itself since it is already strong; in this way, the joining of a lenitive and compressive medicine is granted. Or it should be said that there is not such a great opposition of a dissolving medicine to others as there is of a lenitive to a compressive; for although it is of stronger virtue than the others, a contrariety and impediment to the solution does not arise from it. To the next, it should be said that here one can be helped by the mixing of lenitive and compressive, not of equal but of unequal power. Or even a mixture equal in power and "true," which has been constructed over a long time. And through this, to the next: because a "styptic" <note>Astringent</note> thing can help another medicine if the compressive mixture is granted. Similarly, the opposite appears from the speeches of Avicenna and Averroes. To the next, it should be said that the operations of lenitives and compressives do not corrupt each other; rather, they improve and amend each other if they are mixed in the predicted way. To the next, it should be said that he argues about "true" mixture, which arises from a long time into a certain "medium" <note>A third, balanced state.</note> from all the extreme parts.

### ->Whether Phlegm is drawn out by the "unbridling" of a medicine after the evacuation of Melancholy<-

A laxative draws by similarity: so that eventually nature is stimulated to an attractive force. But **melancholy** <note>original: "mīia" (melancholia); the "black bile" associated with cold and dry temperaments.</note> and **phlegm** <note>original: "flā" (phlegma)</note> agree with each other because both are cold and moist. Whence it is gathered in the 5th book: Medicines that draw out melancholy also draw out phlegmatic humors, because they agree in one of their qualities. Therefore, after the leading out of melancholy, phlegm will be evacuated. On the contrary, Galen says in the

<margin>3</margin> third book of *On Elements*, and the third of *On Medicines*. Serapion in the *Antidotary*. And Isaac in his first book of *Diets*. That humor ought to be evacuated after melancholy (and generally after the appropriate one) which is less proper and familiar to nature. Such a humor is indeed **yellow bile** <note>original: "colera"; the "choleric" humor associated with heat and dryness.</note> and not phlegm, since phlegm is born to nourish the body by being converted into blood, which yellow bile is not. Section 30. Palyn. <note>likely a reference to a specific commentary or author</note> says that what is hotter is more easily led out, because heat is well-suited for movement. According to the book *On the Generation of Animals*, this describes yellow bile, not phlegm. Therefore, after the leading out of melancholy, a medicine will draw out yellow bile and not phlegm. Regarding the first point, it must be known that

<margin>3</margin> what is evacuated will be shown in section 173: This specific evacuation is properly called a "purging," because once the other humors are led out, the blood remains purified. Whence Galen says in *On Medicines*: For this reason they are named "purgatives" by everyone, because they leave the blood pure of other superfluities. What a medicine is has also been seen in section 127. That which is called **unbridledness** <note>original: "effrenitās"; a term for when a medicine acts with excessive, uncontrolled violence.</note> occurs when it leads out humors not by the law of medicine, but by the violence of its degenerating nature. For it falls upon a humor foreign to it like a man falling into a rage. For a humor is evacuated in two ways. Either by pure property, when a determined medicine draws determined humors—for a certain medicine evacuates one humor, such as **scammony** <note>A harsh resinous juice used as a strong purgative.</note> for yellow bile, **lapis lazuli** for melancholy, and **turbith** <note>The root of *Operculina turpethum*, used to purge phlegm.</note> for phlegm—or certain medicines draw several, such as **aloes** and **rhubarb** for yellow bile and phlegm. **Agaric** <note>A wood-growing fungus used as a universal purge.</note> perhaps draws all three. Another way is through "unbridled" qualities, as seen in section 141. What melancholy and phlegm are has been seen in their proper sections.

<margin>Others say through the science of Empedocles. Opinion.</margin> Regarding the second point, it must be known, as also seen in section 141, that the ancients were divided concerning these qualities. For **Asclepiades**, acting as a defender of the opinion of **Empedocles**, held that the qualities of the elements are unalterable and untransmutable from age to age; thus denying that Nature acts with providence and a kind of art. He said that no humor is drawn out by any determined medicine; rather, the medicine transmutes, converts, and alters, corrupting whatever is poured out into its own nature. Furthermore, he held that the utility followed in purgings does not come from the purging of a specific humor, but by the common reason of evacuation: because, indeed, it evacuated in general, and not because it moved this humor or that one. The annulment of this position is written in the second book of *The Aphorisms*, the first book of *Physics*, and the third book of *On Simple Medicines* and *On Melancholy*; for if he were right, bloodletting and medicines for this or that humor would help indifferently. This leads to a manifest absurdity, since these things help in one case but clearly do harm in another. For bloodletting does not benefit those who are dry and thin, nor do medicines benefit their opposites. Again, experience teaches that a medicine evacuates this humor and not that one, and that this person is helped and not that one. Why a medicine is not simply dissolved and converted into the humor it is supposed to draw was shown in section 142. 

**Erasistratus** is also mistaken, thinking—after the true things said by Asclepiades were denied—that all types of what is evacuated are saved. He was refuted in the first and second books of *Physics* and in *On Medicines*. He wanted it to be that, just as in bloodletting there is an equal evacuation of all humors, it is similar in purgings. In that case, every medicine, since it is subtle, would lead out everything. For that which draws by the nature of a vacuum draws the thinnest thing first, and then the rest in order. Section 51.

<margin>Erasistratus: what they evacuate first</margin> Others, however, said almost the opposite: that a medicine 

<margin>3</margin> tears away that which is increased among the humors. But this is not valid, because then a medicine would not lead out by choosing what is proper to it, and thus it would not determinately evacuate all phlegm.

<margin>3</margin> since the number of medicines for the humors is now greater. However, some practitioners of the "familiar art" have said that a medicine, having been drawn in, first tears away yellow bile; then, if it becomes "unbridled," phlegm; then melancholy; and finally blood, since it is familiar to nature and loved like a son. But if after that it degenerates, it draws yellow bile, and from there melancholy, and finally blood. And in these points all are at rest. But if it has the property to draw melancholy according to Galen (attributing this to Hippocrates), Serapion, and Isaac, as previously introduced, that is torn away first; then yellow bile; then phlegm; and blood last. **Ali Abbas** <note>Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician.</note> along with **Haly**, as introduced, want phlegm to be evacuated after melancholy. **Avicenna** <note>indicated by "A."</note> seems to agree with them. Indeed, for this or another ordering of the humors being led out one after another, I find four modes of causes established. For **Mesue**, in *On Medicines*, touches on the cause of utility and the insufficient fitness of the humors. Galen, however,

<margin>Ali Abbas, Haly, Avicenna</margin> in the third book of *On Medicines*, assigns the cause of this to the subtlety and thickness of the humors, and their property, or their rest within the body, and the opposite of this. Serapion also and Isaac coincide with Galen on the first point, but not on the second; they place the cause of this in the lightness and gravity of the humor, or its speed and slowness of motion. Avicenna, however, agreeing with the others on the first cause, says the second cause is the multitude or scarcity of the humors. What should be seen regarding this generally: Concerning the third point, certain necessary things should be set forth first so the truth may be joined. And thirdly, the practitioners most seen in the art are brought in to reconcile the disagreement. Concerning the first of these, it must be known that a medicine, as assumed, sometimes becomes unbridled. This happens in three ways: by the weakness of the vessels; or by the openness of their pores; or by the biting sharpness of the medicine. Section 127. Furthermore, according to Serapion, the inquiry is verified by three added conditions: that the power of the medicine does not fail in the succession of humors until the leading out of the blood; and that the medicine has the property to tear away only one humor. For a certain medicine, as said, moves multiple humors. And that the humor to be led out exists in a place suited for the medicine's extraction. For if a medicine attractive to melancholy finds yellow bile in a place suited for tearing away, like the belly, but finds the melancholy placed in narrow passages; now the yellow bile is led out first by the paths of the accidents. Because the stomach is shaken by the medicine, and the sharpness and gravity of the humors, its power will be excited to expel the yellow bile before the melancholy. Whether or not every bitter thing is hot is shown here.
Because of the books *On the Soul* and *On Sense and the Sensible* <note>Works by Aristotle.</note>.
What color expresses more fully. The species of tastes are like the species of colors, and equal to them. But any color, such as white and black, with others that are their extremes, are caused by heat and cold. Therefore, the **bitter taste** <note>original: "sapor amarus"</note> and the sweet are, according to **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ar."</note>, from the extremes from which the intermediate ones arise. Also, in the fourth book of *On Simples* <note>likely Galen's *De simplicium medicamentorum temperamentis*.</note>:
Certain fruits turn from bitterness to sweetness, such as many citrons and melons. This is attributed to cold and moisture. Furthermore, if "sweet" is commonly said to be hot, then its opposite, "bitter," will be cold. For contrary effects argue for contrary causes. Heat and cold, with other qualities, are the causes of all things, according to the fourth book of *Metaphysics*.
Again: That whose carrying substance is cold, is itself cold. But the carrying substance of a bitter taste is something cold, because it is thick. Thickness seems to be caused by cold, by aggregating and contracting. Conversely, it is preserved from rot, because rot is caused by heat. But bitter preserves from rot (according to the first book of *On Simples*).
Likewise: all bitter things are simultaneously indigestible (according to the *Problems* <note>A work attributed to Aristotle.</note>). But everything indigestible is cold, since the digestive force is hot and cannot cause it; therefore, not every bitter thing is hot, but some are cold and others hot. The opposite of this is what most doctors and physicists believe. This is also shown because the difference of quantity from sweet through a further quality becomes salty and nitrous, and then bitter. This is noted in the boiling of honey and sugar, although honey is the sweetest of all things. Third, in food. And **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a Greek commentator on Aristotle.</note> in his *Problems*. Conversely, in *On Sense and the Sensible*, taste is attributed to quality and humidity. Bitterness is also a taste. But this reasoning destroys the flavor between cold and dry especially. And they themselves will say so.

<margin>opposite</margin>
Therefore, every bitter thing will be hot. Regarding the first point, it must be known that for one wishing to know what "bitter" is, it is necessary first to show what "taste" is and what its distinction is, since it is a species of it. According to Aristotle, **taste** <note>original: "sapor"</note> is an experience of the sense of taste from terrestrial dryness and moisture, brought from potentiality into actuality by an altering power. He says "terrestrial dry" to distinguish it from a substantial evaporation, which is the cause of smell. The altering power brought into act is heat, which from mixing with other qualities, brings the taste from potential into act. I say "act" which is a form and not an action; for such arises when what is tasted is in effect. For there is a double taste: in potential and in act. As in salt: when it is tasted in effect, its taste is then perceived, which was previously in potential. **Avicenna** also agrees: Taste is caused by the mixing of a dry part with a moist part, which has been digested by some heat of digestion.

<margin>TASTE</margin>
**Isaac**, if he identifies taste sufficiently in general foods, wishes it to be nothing else than a certain sensible quality of the sense of taste, which is either abhorred or delighted in.

<margin>The distinction of taste</margin>
For taste can be distinguished in three ways: either by the reason of its primary qualities, or the substance carrying them; or by whether it is delightful, or abhorred, or neither.
According to the first distinction, some tastes are hot, some cold, and others intermediate. The hot ones are **salty**, **bitter**, and **sharp**. The cold ones are **sour**, **astringent**, and **harsh** <note>original: "acerotus" (acetosus), "stipticus", "ponticus". These terms describe degrees of acidity and dryness in classical medicine.</note>. The intermediate ones are **oily** and **sweet**, and according to some, **insipid** <note>tasteless</note>.

<margin>ISAAC</margin>
Furthermore, Isaac places them in determined grades of primary qualities: for he posits that **salty** is hot and dry in the second degree; **bitter** in the third; but **sharp** in the fourth. Whence we have from Isaac: the salty taste is hot in the second degree, and bitter in the third. Truly, its heat is less than the heat of the sharp. And in the genus of cold: Isaac says **vinegary** is cold and dry in the second degree. Which, however, is not entirely soundly said, since the nature of vinegar is rather cold in the first and dry in the first. **Astringent** is in the beginning of the third; **harsh** is in the end of the same or the beginning of the fourth. **Oily** and **sweet** are especially placed by the experts as being between the third and fourth of the simples. For a sweet thing is agreeable to the nature of our body specifically, and the human body is hot and moist with equality. And Isaac also wishes to bring **insipid** to this nature.

<margin>First Distinction: regarding substance</margin>
This, however, is for him the balance of justice <note>original: "iusticie tēpamtū"; referring to the ideal physiological balance or "temperament."</note>, which is nonetheless hot and moist. In the book *On the Sense and the Sensed* <note>original: "i szo" (De Sensu et Sensato by Aristotle).</note>, the human **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body or substance.</term> is said to be balanced in heat and moisture. The same book also distinguishes the aforementioned qualities according to their substance. This occurs implicitly, because some substances are <insert>subtle</insert>, others are medium, and some are truly gross <note>In medieval science, "gross" refers to thick, heavy, or coarse matter.</note>. Gross substance carries the **pontic** <term>pontic: a harsh, tart, or astringent taste, like that of an unripe fruit.</term> and the bitter. Subtle substance carries the sharp and the sour. The medium substance includes all others, though they are more or less diversified. For the unctuous <note>original: "unūuosa"; oily or fatty.</note> is more moderate; then follows the sweet, then the salty, and finally the **styptic** <term>styptic: a highly astringent taste that "contracts" the tissues of the mouth.</term>; after these, the insipid holds a middle place between these distances. And this distinction can be joined with the previous one, such that a gross substance is bitter and hot in the third degree.

<margin>Second Distinction: regarding taste</margin>
It is distinguished in a third way, because according to **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a foundational authority on the science of "fever" and dietetics.</note>, a certain taste is not suited to the sense of taste, such as that which is called **insipid** <note>original: "īsipid9" (tasteless).</note>. This exists in two ways: either because it is truly insipid, such as the taste of simple water and other elements. For these lack taste, since taste arises from the mixing of elements. There is another kind of insipidness, not because it lacks the "form" of a taste—for it already possesses the primary form of a taste—but because it cannot perform its work. This is because nothing is dissolved from it into tiny parts that can be fixed into the pores of the tongue, through which, when mixed with moisture, the perception of flavors is created, as appears in the book *On the Soul*.

<margin>That is, it tastes like iron or stone</margin>
And so we call **iron**, by its hardness, or **adamant** <note>original: "adamantū"; historically referring to diamond or an unbreakable hard stone.</note> almost indissoluble and insipid. Even if something were dissolved from it and mixed with the tongue, it is not said that a definite taste is perceived. Perhaps this is not properly called "insipid," just as **phlegm** and **gourd** <note>original: "cucurbita"; often used as a medical example of a cooling, bland substance.</note> are so called. There is another taste suited and adapted to the sense of taste, which also exists in three types. For it is either abominable and repugnant to the sense, separating the junctions of the tongue (proportioned more or less to boiling water), such as the salty, the bitter, the sharp, and the sour, arising from a subtle substance. Or it is horrific and harmful to the sense because it excessively constricts and binds, assimilated to cold water; such are the **pontic** and especially the **styptic**. By reason of its quality, it may also be sour. Or it is pleasant and well-tempered, holding the middle between both extremes, such as the unctuous and the sweet. Each taste also receives many degrees and stays, being more or less diversified; hence one taste is rendered not unlike another. And therefore, according to **Avicenna**, the sweet and the unctuous are placed as almost the same, as are the salty and the bitter. This diversity arises in sweetness, for a fourfold distinction is found by Isaac. For one is pure and middle among all qualities; another pertains to thickness and viscosity; another is joined to insipidity; and some are mixed with sharpness. That which is pure is proportioned to the balanced nature of humans. As has now appeared, there are eight tastes. And one which is deprived of taste is called insipid. Some have placed only eight, as **Galen** in the first book of *Simple Medicines*, and Avicenna comprehends them in this number, just as with colors, although he explains the same by counting eight. Some also omit the "pontic," such as **Almansor** <note>Rhazes (al-Razi), in his book *Liber ad Almansorem*.</note> and **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a Persian Christian physician.</note>, reducing it to the "styptic." Others do the same for the other, which happens because these two tastes differ very little. And among these, according to

Galen, in *On Aliments*, seems to reduce it to the styptic and the pontic even more. And perhaps the translators induced this diversity. This poor science, once hidden, lacked both things and words.

For each taste is attended to according to certain proportional numbers, mixtures, and motions—or indeterminate and disproportionate ones. For those which induce delight are those which consist of proportional numbers alone. The opposites hold themselves otherwise. Hence, know also from *On the Sense and the Sensed* and the second book of *On the Soul* that tastes are caused by the hot, cold, moist, and dry; and those are contrary which are most distant from each other, yet the contrariety in the species of tastes is not attended to according to the maximum distance of hot, cold, moist, and dry, but according to their order to the sense of taste, insofar as it is born to be changed by a taste with horror or with pleasure. Hence, it is not necessary that the sweet and the bitter be the maximum hot, cold, dry, or moist, but that they behave most differently in this or that change of the sense of taste. From these things, therefore, it can appear what "bitter" is.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the elemental nature of tastes, specifically investigating whether the quality of bitterness is always a result of "heat" or if it can coexist with "cold," using substances like opium and roses as case studies.</meta>

->## Whether everything bitter is hot? ##<-

It is found in conjunction with coldness, as is demonstrated in fruits in their first growth, which shows a cold nature <note>original: "calm̃"; likely "caliditatem" or "colorem," but here referring to the initial state of growth.</note>. And thus it is not impossible that some sweetness might be cold. It appears, indeed, that plants of a bitter taste were sweet or insipid at the beginning near their completion. A sign showing that tastes behave this way is that plants possessing a specific taste do not transition from bitterness to sweetness—in those that are meant to become sweet—except by the mediation of some of those other tastes. In the fourth [book] it is also gathered: regarding the nature of the bitter, it is said that the **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body.</term> is thus earthy. This can be born from both the hot and the cold. And the sign separating one from the other is in the indication that comes from cold: namely, that it becomes sweet after it has been bitter, such as occurs with woody acorns and some types of gourds.

Furthermore, opium is at the limit of bitterness, yet it induces sleep by its coldness. This finally removes the argument of the cavillers, for you cannot say that bitterness does not proceed from the cold part but only from the hot. For bitterness is a "differing" <note>original: "d̃ians"; likely "distinguens" or "differens."</note> in its taste, and taste is a means for judging the nature of a thing; whence it ought to be judged according to this that it is more hot than cold. And regarding what we have said about the bitter, the physicians who preceded us did not perceive it; even Galen <note>original: "Ga."</note> attributed it to heat alone. The position of those who speak of a reasonable annulment will be shown in the third [book] of the sayings. Here, however, let it only be shown that the arguments introduced do not remain quiet.

<margin>Avicenna and Averroes</margin>
Nevertheless, it must first be known that there is nothing among those things having tastes that possesses a truly "pure" taste, according to the fourth [book] of *On Simples*. For there is no taste to which other tastes are not mixed; since the humors <note>original: "bu."; likely "humoribus."</note> from which they are caused are also not pure. For all things are composed of the four elements, making in each thing a different representation, such as mixtures or complexions. For there is a double commingition or complexion. The first is according to the physical and in the natural and fiery things, as the "milkiness" signifies, and the composition of the **tyriac** <term>tyriac (theriac): a famous ancient medical concoction used as an antitoxin, often containing dozens of ingredients.</term>. The first is indeed made; the first of these is that which results from the primary complexion in the induction of the elements, which the sense of touch follows most closely, since it is a certain material and factual presence, very close to the primary natures. The sense of taste, which is a kind of touch, also follows this closely. There is a second [complexion] resulting after that primary one from the action and passion of the contrary qualities of the elements. This happens because one quality eventually gains strength over the others, as happens in many things that are sharpened by the process of time. This happens either because of the surrounding air, or because of some celestial virtue, or perhaps an immense imagination in the things possessing it. This is followed slightly by color, then odor, and lastly taste, appearing in the 37th [chapter] of the *Mime. dia.* <note>Reference unclear; possibly a specific medical or philosophical commentary.</note> For color is something almost spiritual and immaterial; for it changes easily from any light thing, since it is like an **epiphany** <term>epiphany: used here in the Aristotelian or Pythagorean sense (epiphaneia) to mean the "surface" or "outward appearance" of a body.</term> according to some followers of Pythagoras. In taste, however, there is no necessary "suffocation" of the sense <note>original: "suffocatõ pe ity"; likely referring to the direct impact on the palate.</note>, such that a specific taste argues for such a complexion entirely or for a substance for the most part. And after tastes, it is in odors. For it is in them as if without confidence, according to the fourth [book] of *Simples*.

<margin>Epiphany</margin>
Colors do not give an ordered knowledge by which an expansion or expression occurs, such as from the universal into the particulars; rather, they signify indifferently regarding the goodness or malice of certain medicines. The cause of this stands out: because odors and colors impress themselves without the obstruction of their bodies, but it is not so in tastes. And therefore something can be resolved from a thing according to the secondary complexion and not the primary, from which second [complexion] color and especially odor follow more, testifying nothing regarding the primitive complexion or mixture. This can indeed happen reasonably when in one of these mixtures there is something thick and gross, while in the other there is something subtle, superficial, and smoky. In taste, however, these two natures imitate each other more, either according to the second or the primary complexion. The fallacy of color is shown by the generation of "milk" from two golden pieces of **euphorbia** <term>euphorbia: a genus of plants (spurge) known for their caustic, milky sap.</term>. For the sight will judge this to be milk <note>i.e., cold/soothing</note>, although it is hot, as the taste suggests. And therefore here in practice: in testing medicines in human bodies, there are dangers to the souls.

<margin>Euphorbia with milk</margin>
It must also be known that taste, as a sign denoting the quality in a thing, is found indicating coldness in its cause: because heat is the most efficacious quality, adapting and assimilating all things to itself. And by this way a cause can be assigned as to why opium, in its bitterness, abounds with coldness. Avicenna <note>original: "Auicẽ."</note> suggests: or perhaps it acquires bitterness from a certain combustion, because it is roasted upon a fiery iron plate and becomes red.

<margin>Avicenna and Averroes</margin>
<margin>How in opium bitterness stands with coldness</margin>
However, that such a nature is found in mixtures is tasted more or less by Galen in many places, and especially in his books on pharmacy. This is shown especially by milk, cabbage-stalks, and lentils. But it is not so in chamomile, in which **stypticity** and "unbinding" <note>original: "ifolutõ"; likely "insolutio" or "dissolutio."</note> are tasted; even less is it shown in tempered food. This diverse composition is testified by [the Book of] Medicines in many [chapters] on simples. For it says the rose is mixed from parts even of excellent differences, such as from cold and watery parts providing its stypticity, and from airy parts giving it sweetness and aromaticity, and from fiery parts providing it with bitterness. This is also said to happen in the simple **agaric** <term>agaric: a type of mushroom used in medieval medicine as a purgative.</term>; for it has sweetness with stypticity and bitterness. And therefore Hermes says: see regarding the centaury...

<margin>Hermes to Averroes</margin>
These things having been premised, it must be said to Avicenna first: that the bitter taste is not caused by the cold; rather, it is only from the hot, as will be shown. Nor is it of the species of tastes in the same way as is universal of the species of colors, because tastes like bitter and sweet are not opposites according to Avicenna, as it appeared, because they are caused immediately from coldness and heat just like colors. But because they are caused by a numerical proportion and a commixtion, say, either delightful or horrid, by which tastes are finally caused in a moderate middle. To the other [point], it must be said: it is not true that fruits change from bitterness into sweetness. Rather, the sweet always precedes the bitter. For in woody-cleansed acorns and certain gourds there is not a bitter taste and **austerity** <term>austerity: a harsh, dry, and astringent taste.</term>; rather, it is more **pontic** <term>pontic: a sour, tart taste.</term>, according to the fourth [book] of *Simples*. Or it is "austere" from the styptic, which is mixed with the pontic. Whence, it is proved: styptic acorns are placed, and again, bitter, styptic, and pontic gallnuts are judged. Or if there is a bitter taste there, it exists from the heat of some subtle part. To the other point regarding opium: what was said has already appeared, since opium is twofold, as in the beginning...

...otherwise, they would be of a different nature. Or it must be said that opium is not actually at the extreme of bitterness, as is testified, but rather possesses a taste composed of a certain bitterness and an urgent, horrible quality. Nor is the argument valid that opium would then be hot; for though it may be hot by reason of its taste and a certain bitterness, its other [cold] parts overcome the heat. Indeed, a small amount of substance can change the taste and smell, and especially the heat, since these are material qualities and not the primary nature of the thing. Galen finally wishes to support this when he said: "And if we were to say that everything sweet is hot, and everything bitter is hot, we must say that this is only in respect to the human body, not the inherent nature of the thing." For although experience in the human body testifies to this, the nature of these tastes demonstrates it otherwise. For the word of Galen is not true regarding the complexions <term>complexion: the specific mixture of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a substance's nature.</term> of tastes according to their own natures. Whence he says this concerning the "flowing" <note>likely referring to the *Meteorologica* or a treatise on fluids</note> and the "fixed": sweetness is attributed to heat and moisture, but bitterness to heat and dryness, or to coldness and dryness in respect to the moisture of sweetness. Thus, since Galen's word is relative—as is the case with any craftsman speaking of comparable matter—his argument does not constrain us; rather, it shows him speaking as one not learned in medicine. Furthermore, what nature judges the tastes of a thing? None but the sense of taste. Regarding the third point, it must be known that every bitter thing is hot, as all physicians know. Whence in the fourth [book] of *Simple Medicines*: "A bitter thing is beyond doubt hot, though according to more or less, insofar as it recedes more or less from sweetness." Therefore, according to practical science, the bitter is fiery and earthy. And in the first [book] of *Physics*: the "sharp" <note>original: "acutū"; often referring to acidic or pungent tastes</note> can be called the hottest, then the bitter, then the salty. This also seems to have been the opinion of Aristotle. For he says regarding the "flowing" and "fixed": bitter and salty are almost the same thing. Whence in the 23rd *Problem*...

Furthermore, in what was previously introduced concerning the generation of the sea, he speaks of it as the most bitter of all tastes, for the drinkable part has been exhaled from it. And in the 24th *Problem*: the ash of all burnt things is bitter, but moisture is hot. Further, whatever is burnt is hot, but the bitter is something burnt (23rd *Problem*). Palyn <note>likely a commentator on Aristotle</note> in the *Meteorology* (130), placing saltiness as caused by heat creating an evaporation in a subtle, airy moisture, perceives that when the evaporating heat is greater, not only is saltiness generated, but even bitterness, as he mentions regarding the lake of Palestine and cider <note>original: "cidra"; likely a reference to the bitter fruits of Sodom or a specific fermented drink</note>. ...chickpeas <note>original: "cicri"</note> are so bitter that in them no animal is born nor lives. Furthermore, the bitter is that which scrapes and roughens the tongue, though without actual burning, as was said. But that which is such is hot. Palyn...

...for he whose actions are hot is himself hot, since an action leads to the knowledge of the form. But the actions of the bitter testify to heat. For it heats, dries, and induces thirst; it opens the orifices of the veins; it attracts, cleanses, dissolves, purges, excoriates, causes the flow of blood, and expels wind <term>carminative: a substance that relieves gas and flatulence.</term>, as they say of it. Again, a sweet thing in time becomes bitter, then sharp, as is shown by wine, sugars, and honey; this, however, seems to happen only by heat and not by cold, for it would never become sharp [by cold]. Likewise, nothing oily or sweet has been seen to become bitter by cooling; rather, it becomes rancid. Therefore, every bitter thing, insofar as it is bitter, is exceedingly hot, occurring in the third degree according to Isaac <note>likely Isaac Israeli, the 10th-century physician</note>. But as to that which is in the fifth [book] of *Simples*, Aristotle says: the bitter opens, cleanses the passages, wipes away, thins, and cuts through thick humors, besides its manifest heat. It must be said that this was said in comparison to the "sharp" <note>acutū</note>, which performs these tasks more effectively, but not in comparison to the salty, and much less the sweet. Regarding the fourth...

But regarding the first, as it appeared, Aristotle did not wish there to be such a strict division <note>original: "febre"; likely "serie" or "distinctione"</note> in the species of tastes as there is in colors. It is not as if tastes are immediately caused by hot and cold in the same way colors are. But just as white and black are opposites and from them intermediate colors are caused, so sweetness and bitterness are opposites and produce intermediate tastes. Then, by another reasoning, taste and color arise, as has been declared. To the other [point], it must be said either that the bitter is hot insofar as it is moist, or that the term is properly used for the "austere" <note>harsh or astringent</note>. Perhaps also the word was corrupted by a faulty Arabic translation. To the other, it must be said to be true if tastes are caused immediately in some way by their causes, just as colors are. For the cause is twofold: the remote, which is less distinct and leads to the effect, and the proximate, which is more so. To the other, it must be said that the substance carrying bitterness, although it may be "coarse" in the category of substances carrying hot tastes, is actually a subtle earthiness. It is not cold, because a coarse substance is not only caused by cold, but indeed also by heat. For if moderate heat acts upon something by digesting it, it aggregates like parts and expels unlike parts, rendering the substance moderate, such as sweetness or oiliness. But if the heat is intended more strongly, causing the subtle moisture to expire, it makes the substance coarser, such as that which carries saltiness. If it is intended even further, it forces all moisture to expire, whence the substance remains pressed and thickened, like those things from the sea. If the heat prevails even more than this, it liquefies the remaining moisture in the heated thing, whence it becomes necessary to bring out the pores and the subtlety of the substance; and this is the substance that carries the "sharp" taste. This can be seen in wood when it turns into glowing coal and then into ash. To the other, it must be said that it is not true that only the cold is preservative against putrefaction. Indeed, heat is as well; nor does every heat cause putrefaction, but rather a weak heat overwhelmed and aided by moisture. For a powerful heat, by heating and causing the moisture prone to rotting to expire, preserves from putrefaction. For Aloes and Myrrh, and everything salty and bitter, by their subtle quality, resolve and glue together moisture; but their earthy substance [fills] the pores...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the qualities of tastes, specifically investigating whether bitterness is inherently linked to heat and how the process of "cooking" or "decoction" alters the fundamental nature and taste of substances.</meta>

It constricts and obstructs, not permitting the natural heat and moisture to exhale, nor allowing external influences to enter; for in this way, putrefaction is generated. To the other point, it must be said that something is rendered indigestible not only by reason of coldness, but indeed also by reason of heat. For heat can exist within a thick and hard substance, as has been seen, and such a compact thing is rendered indigestible. As is said in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's "De Anima"</note>: the radish digests and does not digest. Or concerning bitterness: just as I wrote in the exposition on Avicenna, one should not only understand the specific flavor of bitterness, but indeed every "horrible" or repellant taste. This is what is meant by the saying that "all medicines are bitter," even though some are truly bitter while others are affected by different tastes.

But concerning a certain argument brought forward by the opposing parties, it became known that one must doubt the Lord Avicenna's claim that taste is attributed to heat and moisture. This does not seem to be the case, since certain tastes are cold. Furthermore, the same is found in *On the Soul*: Taste seems to follow moisture and dryness more than it follows heat and coldness.

It must be said that taste is caused by a certain "digestion" <note>In this context, "digestion" refers to the internal "cooking" or processing of a substance by heat.</note>. However, all digestion is fundamentally perfected by heat and generated in moisture. Therefore, it is granted that taste is an "affection" <note>A quality or state produced in a substance.</note> celebrated by heat acting within a terrestrial dryness. Thus, although this process is "hot" with respect to the taste produced, it can nevertheless be "cold" in relation to the human body to which it is applied. To the other point, it must be said: Avicenna and others say that taste follows moisture and dryness more than heat because the *internal* cause of taste seems to be the dry and the moist, while the *external* cause is heat. For the heat that performs the "digestion" often remains outside, such as the heat of the sun which contains it. Thus it must be said that "little heat" is sometimes dominant in a taste, as in cold tastes; however, heat is never entirely absent, since all taste is perfected by heat. And therefore, taste follows dryness and moisture more closely, which gives the diverse qualities, as is stated in the *Book of Urines*, chapter 85. What compels us to doubt here is that active qualities—especially heat—operate most fully, since heat is the most effective of qualities, just as moisture is the most passive, followed by cold and dry.

# DIFFERENCE 146

->Whether further boiling makes a substance more bitter.<-

> It is shown that further boiling <term>decoctio: the process of boiling down a substance in a liquid to extract its medicinal or nutritional essence.</term> renders a thing more bitter. For it is written in the second book of *Natural Things* as follows:

Who does not know that each of those things which are boiled further becomes first salty, and afterwards truly bitter? And in the *Problems* attributed to Aristotle, which I have translated: "Every sweet thing, when heated, first becomes sharp; finally, when overheated, it is made exceedingly bitter." Furthermore, through further boiling, that which is watery and airy exhales, while that which remains is the thick, burnt, earthy part. In such a base, a bitter taste is found, just as in the former state it was oily or sweet. This is apparent in the fourth book on medicines. Furthermore, just as it is in natural "digestions" that happen within, so it is in artificial ones performed outside, since art is the image of nature. But in those, further boiling makes the substance bitter and sharp; for example, "insipid" chyle <note>The milky fluid produced during digestion.</note>, which by further boiling and digestion is sweetened and converted into blood, and finally by further boiling is turned into bitter, sharp, and highly burnt yellow bile <note>original: "colera"; one of the four humors, associated with bitterness and heat.</note>. This is proven in the eleventh book.

<margin>Garlic. Leeks.</margin>
Boiled garlic is mild; leeks have a viscosity. And honey testifies to this, being sweeter than all things; yet as said before, by further boiling it is made bitter and thereafter sharp. Milk also, when outside the veins, possesses an insipidity; but when it is boiled further, it becomes sweet. Whence in the fourth book on medicines: "If milk digested in the stomach and veins could be tasted, I estimate it would be sweeter than the taste of honey." And the same is true of sugar and other juices. Thus, some things are rendered more bitter and sharp by boiling. On the opposite side: according to the *Aphorisms*, preparation should "remove the more biting tastes," just as in cabbage and legumes, which removal is done by transferring them during boiling from one water into another. And in the third book of *On Aliments*, it is written: "A solid substance that is boiled is not made bitter, but rather is sweetened more." Furthermore, whatever is expressed from a thing by boiling that is nitrous, ferrous, or sharp, that thing is made sweet and oily. But boiling does this, as radishes and lupines <note>A type of bitter legume.</note> show when they are soaked and boiled; as do coldness, sharpness, and garlic with the rest. Also, whatever is "digested" is sweetened, since all digested things are rendered sweet. But boiling operates this way on wild acorns, sorb apples, and the like. Therefore, further boiling renders a thing sweeter or more oily.

<margin>
Honey after further boiling is made bitter.
Milk [in the] 4th [book of] Medicines.
</margin>
<margin>The opposite changes in the 4th.</margin>

For the first point, it must be known that boiling is a certain softening caused by heat. This results in two types: one is natural, and this is twofold. Either it is "perfective," which is properly called digestion or *pepansis* <note>Greek: ripening or cooking of humors.</note>, such as that of fruits. Or it is "harmful," such as the maturation of corrupt humors, which is more truly called a ripening through which they are prepared for expulsion. The other type is artificial, and this is either by boiling <note>original: "elixando"; also called "epselis".</note> or by roasting <note>original: "assando"; also called "optesis".</note>.

<margin>
• pepansis. Digestion is twofold.
epselis. optesis.
</margin>
<margin>
Indigestion is threefold.
Omothesis.
Molinsis.
[See] the 4th [book of] Metaphysics.
</margin>

There are three types of indigestion <note>original: "indigōnēs"</note>, which are the opposites [of the above]: namely *omothesis* <term>omothesis: rawness or lack of "cooking" in the humors.</term>, *molinsis* <term>molinsis: "leadenness" or incomplete boiling.</term>, and *statelis*. Know also that a thing is boiled for many reasons: so that it may be rendered more digestible, such as solid food; or so that it may penetrate more easily, like water; or so that its "malice" or sharpness may be diminished, such as an attractive medicine; or so that it may be preserved from putrefaction, as with glass and many juices. Or so that a better mixture may be made among them, as in the construction of medicines; or so that it may become more "soluble" <note>likely meaning laxative or easy to break down</note>, like a roasted squill <note>a sea onion used as a medicinal plant</note>; or so that it may lose its [laxative] power and acquire "contraction" <note>astringency</note>, like roasted myrobalan and rhubarb; or so that they may be made poisonous, like sublimated mercury and arsenic. What makes a thing bitter, sweet, or of other tastes was seen in the previous section.

<margin>Galen, On Aliments, chapter 29... directed to Brachas.</margin>
<margin>Paraxagoras. Philotimus.</margin>

Regarding the second point, it must be known that some, such as Paraxagoras and Philotimus, estimated that whatever hard things were "salted" or "nitrous" became bitter when boiled at the beginning of their preparation as food. Galen, however, speaking against them, says: "A solid or hard body boiled in water loses the qualities existing in it from the beginning, so that in the succeeding time it is rendered without quality and watery, not retaining its saltiness, bitterness, pungency, or stypticity <note>astringency/biting quality</note>." This is shown most clearly when the water is changed from one to another; for thus you will find that the boiled thing casts off its own quality and takes on the quality of that in which it is boiled, both because of this and because it often "digests" what was raw within itself.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on how the process of "cooking" or "decoction" changes the qualities and tastes of substances, moving from the definition of taste to specific examples of plants and minerals.</meta>

remained. Just as bitter lupins <note>original: "lupi amari", a type of legume known for its bitter taste unless soaked</note>, when they are boiled or infused in water, make that water bitter; the same occurs with wormwood <note>original: "abrotanum", a bitter herb used medicinally</note>, antimony, and similar things. The solid bodies of such things, once boiled, remain less bitter. Indeed, if you change the water and boil them a second time or more, they lose their bitterness entirely.

The same occurs with pungent things, such as garlic, onions, and leeks; and with fruits like medlars, pears, and unripe rowan berries. All things of this kind, when cooked in water, leave behind their original quality <note>They transfer their flavor to the water</note>. In themselves, they are rendered either sweeter or more oily. But if you boil the juices alone without their solid substances, they first become tasteless, then sweet; then, with further boiling, salty; and finally bitter and sharp, as was shown with honey and sugar.

In this way, solid things become sweeter when boiled in multiple changes of water, but liquid juices are made bitter. Similarly, harsh or "biting" wines become sweet of their own accord over a long period of internal <term>digestion</term> <note>In medieval science, "digestion" referred to any refinement or ripening process driven by heat</note>. This happens more quickly when they are transported to Asia and exposed to the sun in jars on the rooftops, or when they are smoked with a great fire from below. However, weak wines are ruined by this and become acidic, as stated in the fourth book of *On Medicines*.

From this, it appears that the views of Paraxagoras and Philotimus <note>Two ancient Greek physicians often cited in scholastic texts</note> are true in these specific cases, though not in the earlier ones. For the truth of this matter is perceived through a distinction and not as an absolute rule.

Regarding the third point, it must be known that things which are boiled are either <term>homogeneous</term> <note>uniform in substance</note> and simple, or <term>heterogeneous</term> <note>composed of different parts</note> and mixed. 

If they are simple, they either have the flavors of "cold" things, "middle" things, or "hot" things. If they are cold, like tasteless endives or similar plants, it must be said that sufficient boiling makes them sweet and oily. But when such things are already prepared and then boiled further, they are made salty, bitter, or sharp, depending on whether the boiling is moderate or extensive. 

This is demonstrated thus: Boiling causes maturation by removing raw, undigested qualities and introducing their opposite; it makes moisture penetrate the soft parts of the boiled item. However, when it is boiled further, the "subtle" moisture—composed of air and water—begins to evaporate, so that the substance is rendered salty. When it is boiled even more, and more moisture evaporates, what is left behind is the "coarse" terrestrial matter and heat, which we know brings a bitter taste. When the substance is reduced to a purely intense heat, it not only forces the moisture to transpire, but indeed burns it away.

<margin>Pumice stones from Mount Vulcan <note>Likely referring to Mount Etna or volcanic regions in general</note>.</margin>

This is like the pumice stones seen in the sea, thrown from a volcano, which are made subtle, light, and hot. It is known that such a substance possesses a sharp taste. Thus, a simple, homogeneous substance can pass through all flavors by means of boiling.

If, however, the thing to be boiled is a mixed, heterogeneous substance, then it is either roasted by fire or boiled in water. If it is roasted, I say it can acquire all the tastes mentioned before. The juicy part, excited by heat and mixed with dry terrestrial matter, changes its nature. This is shown to us in fleshy fruits, beans, and rowan berries; or in wild fruits when they are roasted, they become pungent or sharp. The reason for this has already been made clear.

But if it is boiled in water, then the water in which it is boiled takes on the quality of whatever was boilable. The substance itself, having left behind its original nature, is sweetened for human use. For only the sweet taste is pleasant and agreeable to humans. Therefore, the more it is infused and the water changed with sufficient boiling, the more savory it becomes. 

Know also that water is rendered salty or bitter by the boiling or infusion of such things. It can eventually take on any flavor of the original simple substance. But let it be said for now that the water becomes quite different from the substance infused or boiled in it. It is also the case that whatever is boiled in any way will eventually be rendered extremely sharp and poisonous; for fire, turning everything toward itself, corrupts things to such an extent that they no longer have the power of nourishment, but become treacherous poisons, which can in no way be converted into the nature of the body. Indeed, they corrode and corrupt the body so that they are more destructive than monkshood <note>original: "napello", the poisonous plant Aconite</note> or snake venom—even though we hear of a girl and an old woman who were nourished on such things <note>A reference to legends of people who built immunity to poison by gradual consumption</note>. Thus, from these points, let the truth of this whole inquiry be summarized briefly.

Regarding the fourth point: It was seen before what should be said, for it speaks of simple homogeneous things, such as certain purified juices. Regarding the other point, it also appeared that when such a thing is boiled extensively, it passes through all tastes. This does not happen when it is a mixed, heterogeneous substance. 

To the next point, it must be said that the reasoning proceeds similarly for simple homogeneous things, where it was shown how extensive boiling makes things bitter and sharp; for humors are like certain juices. 

And regarding what should be said to the other view: how some things lose their "biting" quality or are made sharper by boiling. This perhaps happens when they are boiled for a very long time and violently, so that while the original moisture was vigorous, a certain "stickiness" does not rage as much. Similarly, an onion possesses sufficient moisture. But when the boiling of garlic is not as violent, the "biting" or sharpness is consumed by the evaporation and the duration of boiling, and they are turned into a sweet, digested state. 

This is also a work of solar heat, especially at the time of the full moon, appearing in the fruits of the Cretans <note>Theophrastus frequently used Cretan plants as examples of high-quality ripening</note>, by digesting their moisture and their harshness, with which their own heat is associated. For they digest by a twofold heat: the solar heat and their own internal heat, as noted by Theophrastus in the fourth book of *On Plants* and *On Simple Medicines*. 

Similarly, regarding those things which appeared in the other part: they proceed from mixed heterogeneous things, from which through boiling or infusion the water is given the foreign quality of the boiled item, while the remainder is left sweetened. This was the opinion of Galen, along with Paraxagoras and Philotimus, in the third book of *On Foods*. 

To the other point, it must be said that all things, insofar as they are digested, are made sweet. They can, however, be bitter or the like because of a quality impressed upon moisture that is not yet sufficiently digested. Eventually, as touched upon, these also change their tastes through boiling.

## Whether a Little Pepper Provokes Urine and Much Loosens the Belly, and for Scammony the Reverse

A little [pepper] provokes urine, and much of it loosens the belly. But the opposite is true for scammony <note>Scammony is a resin from the root of *Convolvulus scammonia*, used as a powerful purgative</note>. Again, a small amount of pepper is a weak laxative. Since moderate laxatives [work differently], when a quality is weak, it provokes [urine], because that is easier than loosening the bowels. If, however, the quality in these things is strong, it will loosen the belly, since the action of the strong is greater.

First, pepper is used in a small quantity, but second in a large one. A small quantity of scammony, however, loosens the belly because its nature allows it to be regulated and sustained as it is distributed through the members. But a large amount [of scammony] is resisted; it is quickly driven out through the wider urinary paths. 

Furthermore, a little pepper does not "bite" the belly and intestines with its sharpness, even though it is considered hot and dry in the fourth degree <note>In medieval "humoral" medicine, drugs were ranked from 1 to 4 in intensity of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness</note>. Since every effect requires a certain magnitude to act, and a small amount lacks this, it allows itself to be carried through the veins to the liver and the urinary paths. On the contrary, a large amount [of pepper] bites and stimulates these same areas, forcing them to cause expulsion and a bowel movement. 

Conversely, a small quantity of scammony is tolerated by the belly and intestines, and it loosens the belly by attraction. But a large amount, being intolerable, is propelled outward through the urinary ways as if it were "unconquerable" <note>original: *invincibilis*</note>; for the belly and intestines will not tolerate it because of its "wildness" <note>original: *effreitate*, referring to the harsh, unbridled nature of the resin</note>. 

Therefore, a smaller quantity of pepper provokes [urine] and a larger quantity loosens [the belly]. For scammony, a little loosens and much provokes [urine]. This is the opposition: that much pepper taken provokes urine, but a little loosens the belly; for scammony, it is the other way around. 

Because of this, according to the properties <note>original: *propria*</note>, a large amount of pepper loosens the bladder <note>The transcription *venticam* is likely a clerical error for *vesicam*, bladder</note>, but a little loosens the belly. Scammony in a large amount loosens the belly, but a little and aged amount loosens the bladder. 

Hence, Serapio <note>A 9th-century Christian physician from Damascus, famous for his medical compendium</note>, the aggregator of the *Book of Questions*, says: "If someone uses much pepper, it provokes urine, and if he uses a little, it causes the belly to give well; but scammony is the opposite in this." Furthermore, scammony, when it is not too old, does not provoke urine but relaxes the belly. When old, it provokes urine and does not relax. Hence, some have said in the second *Canon* <note>Referring to Avicenna’s *Canon of Medicine*</note> that when there is a small quantity of old scammony, it provokes urine and does not loosen the belly.

Additionally, much pepper, with its added heat, passes through the mesenteric veins into the liver; there, melting the moisture, it seeks the urinary paths, as it is hot and subtle. A little pepper, lacking this power, remains in the intestines, stimulating them to a bowel movement by its sharpness. Scammony, however, first "bites" the intestines and, irritating them, expels itself in a bowel movement. A little scammony, being weaker, is tolerated—especially if it is older—so that it penetrates the veins to reach the liver and finally the urinary passages. 

Furthermore, for any agent to produce its proper action, it must be of sufficient quantity; otherwise, it would have no power over the object. But the proper action of pepper is to provoke [urine], and of scammony to loosen [the belly]. Hence, Avicenna <note>transcribed as *Ay.*</note> asks which of the two is more mobile. Pepper is called a <term>diuretic</term> <note>a substance that promotes the production of urine</note>, while scammony is "downward-bearing" <note>a laxative</note>. The improper action of pepper is to loosen, and of scammony to provoke urine. In these, the effects can be altered by their quantities. Thus, much pepper provokes, but a little loosens. It happens differently with scammony.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that pepper is an aromatic species, hot and dry, sharp, and a powerful corrector of cold and moist complexions. It is three-fold. For there is one that is immature and has an oblong shape, which for that reason is called

<margin>Long pepper</margin>
**Macropiper**. It is hot in the third degree and dry in the second. There is 

<margin>White pepper</margin>
also a round white one called **Leucopiper**, which is heating and drying and especially strengthens the belly. According to the sixth book of *On Simple Medicines*, it is better than the black variety. Hence, in the fifth *Canon*, it is said to comfort the stomach more than other spices and peppers. It is neither small nor shriveled, and its skin is not thick, yet it is heavy in weight. There is also found a third, called simply pepper, or black pepper

<margin>Black pepper</margin>
(**Melanopiper**), which is hot and dry in the fourth degree. Some believe these three differ only in time and quantity. For it is said that "long pepper" is the fruit when it is moist and raw. When it matures, it shrivels and separates and becomes white pepper. When this happens even more, it turns black and is called black pepper. Hence, in the second *Canon*, Galen says that when the fruit of the pepper first rises, it is long pepper; then it separates into grains. Because of this, long pepper is moister than [black] pepper. In this, Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> also agrees in his work on simples, as does the "Prince of Pharmacists," Galen, in his sixth book.

Scammony is the juice of a certain climbing plant. According to Mesue <note>A Persian physician, likely Mesue the Younger, whose work on purgatives was standard in the Middle Ages</note>, four types are found. One is called "tree-rope," "hops," or *humulus* because it involves itself around them. Its flower is white, shaped like a long bell, and contains milk; this is the large climbing plant. Another has branches that creep over the ground and herbs; its flower is small, like an expanded little bell, whitish-yellow in color, and also contains milk; children delight in eating it.

There is another with rough leaves, like those of a citron, with flowers like attached flasks; it is called "poor man's hops." There is a fourth, and its root is like that of a bryony <note>transcribed as *tanni*, likely *taminia* or *bryonia*</note> but larger, having small, narrow leaves like winged arrows, which fall off easily; it has milk which is called *lacticiin ioy*, from which scammony is made. Its complexion is hot in the third degree and dry. The *Aggregator* <note>Serapio</note>, however, following Galen, presents it as hotter than pepper, although others declare it to be of the aforementioned complexion. Scammony draws out <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile, one of the four humors</note> with great force. Indeed, its action is "furious," and therefore it is only used [cautiously]. It requires many "correctors" because it offends the primary parts of the body. Its dose is from 5 to 12 grains according to Mesue. According to Avicenna, it is one *danich*—which is the sixth part of a drachm. According to Serapio, from one *kirat* up to one drachm. 

<margin>Dose of Scammony</margin>

<margin>Diagridium</margin>
It is cooked inside a paste-wrapped quince under the ashes so that its "malice" <note>its harsh, toxic side effects</note> is lessened, and then it is called **Diagridium**. It is also corrected significantly by mixing it with myrobalans <note>A plum-like fruit used in medicine to balance purgatives</note>. The climbing plant itself from which it is derived loosens the belly gently, so that it may be administered to children and to those in the regimen of health. What it is to the belly, urine, loosening, and provoking is noted in its properties. At present, these things should be known: that the action differs according to the agent, the patient <note>the person receiving the medicine</note>, and the mode of action. For a strong agent works differently than a moderate or weak one, just as scammony is compared to pepper, since it is more unbridled and more inimical to human nature. As for the patient, one belly or part of the body is more sensitive and passive than another...

...is moderate. Truly, the modes [of action], as touched upon before, regarding **pepper**, principally have the power to provoke [urine] and to loosen [the bowels]. Regarding **scammony**, however, they cause excretion. Concerning the second point, it must be known that this has already appeared from the arguments. Furthermore, in the third place, he will manifest this by saying: regarding the third point, it must be known that the first discourse is considered truer and is the declaration of **Aristotle**; and thereafter let him attend to whether there is any flavor of truth in what **Avicenna** says. 

Regarding the first of these, it must be known that a larger quantity of pepper, by its heat and <term>acuity</term><note>Sharpness or stinging quality</note>, "bites" the belly and the intestines, and especially attacks the more sensitive parts; from here, passing through the **mesenteric veins** into the paths of the liver, it dissolves and balances the subtler humors. And because the heat of [pepper] itself is weaker than that of scammony, and less [hostile] to human nature, it cannot lead the aforementioned humors back through the mesenteric veins to the belly and intestines. This is especially true since its substance does not remain in the belly or intestines, as happens with "attractive" medicines <note>Medicines that draw humors toward them</note>. By its vigor, the attraction to the aforementioned places is achieved. It leads them out through the urinary passages, which are wider and more ready for it, since its function here is also to evacuate. 

If, however, a small amount is present, the internal parts—being less delayed—will not expel it into the veins. And especially since they are more sensitive, and the remission of the substance is not capable of its own proper act, it remains there for a longer delay due to its qualities and quantity. It liquefies some humors and veils them. It will lead them out with the dung through a meeting [in the bowels], just as other bean-like or sharp things do, as is manifest in the **Alexandrian** diet. 

In the case of **scammony**, the opposite occurs. For first, its power in its proper act remains in the belly and intestines as a purgative; and passing through the pores through which nourishment is carried into the veins, it is first dissolved into fumes over some space of time. Finally, it intentionally changes the aforementioned differences. These fumes, finally carried to the humors, agitate, liquefy, and dissolve them. Because it is very thick and earthy, by the vigor of the attraction of the substance remaining in the belly or intestines, it recurs through the mesenteric veins in this manner. Nature, struggling against this hateful thing, repels it from itself, so that it is entirely excreted by the belly. 

Whence **Avicenna** says: scammony, in a large dose because of its strength, remaining for a long time, brings about much purgation and earthy [excretion] from above. A small dose, however, and especially old scammony—being almost totally dissolved into fumes—reaches the humors in the way previously described but is not effective, because it would require much and thick substance to excite them. Rather, it is small and subtle. And because of this, it cannot lead them to the belly and intestines, since nothing of it remains in them. And therefore, it turns itself to a more proper and lighter act, which is to provoke [urine]. Thus the aforementioned discourse of **Avicenna** is verified. 

Regarding the second point, it should be known that:
<margin>¶</margin> either the discourse of **Aristotle** has been poorly or falsely explained, or that he heard "much" and "little" differently than **Avicenna**, diversifying the quantity according to "moderate" and "maximum." 

Or it must be said that pepper loosens the bowels in one way, by liquefying humors with its sharpness like <term>euphorbium</term><note>A very caustic plant resin used in medicine</note> and other things that are vehemently hot. And scammony [acts] in another way, namely by dissolving and attracting. Therefore, when there is a large quantity of pepper, stinging the belly and intestines with its sharpness—especially if they are sensitive—they do not tolerate it for long enough for it to reach the urinary passages; rather, they propel it outward, and thus it moves the belly. And perhaps that quantity is the "maximum." But when its quantity is smaller, being tolerated by the aforementioned parts, it can reach the passages and provoke urine. And perhaps this smaller quantity is the "moderate" one. 

Scammony, in a large dose, loosens the urine, perhaps because nature does not sustain it for long enough to lead the attracted superfluities back to the belly and intestines; instead, it immediately propels them into the paths more ready for it: the urine. A small dose is tolerated by the same, so that it leads them to the places mentioned before. Thus the discourse of **Aristotle** is shielded, and I have written similarly about this, which is sufficient in the explanation of **Abubacer** <note>Original: "Ay." Likely referring to Ibn Tufayl/Abubacer or a similar commentator</note>. 

Regarding the fourth point, it must be known that things induced proceed by their own paths. Whence what should be said has already appeared in the first point. To the other, it must be said that smaller and weaker medicines tend to provoke [urine], but large and stronger ones loosen the belly if they are of that nature—but not if they are for the urine, like pepper. Regarding the other part of this reasoning in scammony, what should be said has already appeared. 

To the other, it has also been seen what should be said: namely, that a little pepper remaining for a long time in the intestines, by its certain sharpness, liquefies and dissolves something. Whence it accelerates the stool. But a little cannot reach the urinary paths, since scammony is penetrative and weak. 

To the remaining part of this reasoning about scammony, it is seen similarly. To the other, it also appeared that scammony could be of such a quantity that it is heard [felt] everywhere; which, as soon as it is taken, nature—terrified by it—would propel it outward by a certain meeting with the dreg-like humors, as discussed in the tract 91.

### DIFFERENCE 148.

<margin>1</margin> **That the water of milk, or whey, is hot.**
In the discussions, the water of milk [whey] is indeed hot. 
<margin>2</margin> Secondly, in the third book: "The wateriness of milk is hot." 
Also in the same place: "In the water of cheese [whey] because there is in it a <term>nitrosity</term><note>A salty, alkaline, or cleansing mineral quality</note> acquired in the blood; and it is clear that there is a certain heat." 
In the *On Diets*: "One of the three substances of milk, the subtle and clear part, has a certain sharpness." 
The subtle and clear part of milk has a certain sharpness, therefore because of the sharpness, it has subtlety and heat, etc. 
**Mesue** also: "The water of milk is of a hot and dry complexion in the first degree, even up to the second." 
Furthermore, in the third book of the *Aphorisms*: "Milk has no small amount of serum [whey] in itself. This is purgative by nature, and therefore it recently induces mouth sores <note>Original: "alcula," likely aphthae</note> in the newborn." 
Whence in the first [book of] the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Art of Medicine"</note>: "The scraping of the wateriness of milk is very harmful to an infant, leading them to mouth sores." 
**Dioscorides**, however: "Whey has a purgative power, leading out the humors of the belly." 
That this is hot [is shown because] purgation is performed by heat alone. Whence these things are declared hot and dry by **Galen**. 
Again, that which opens blockages of the viscera and cleanses and subtilizes humors is hot. Such is the water of milk. Whence **Mesue**: "It is washing and cleansing because of its nitrosity and is laxative by the biting of the stomach." 
Furthermore, that which quickly turns into fumes and fire is hot...

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on the purgative effects of pepper and scammony to a new inquiry regarding the medicinal properties of milk and its components, specifically whey (serum).
