## Whether whey is hot.

---

...the passage of food is made easier. The byproduct of this is the water of milk <note>Whey</note>. 
Regarding this, it is said that for all those suffering from head pain and for those with fevers, they draw out the whey from the milk just as the wateriness of urine comes from the humors. But urine takes on heat. Therefore, the water of milk is hot. 

<margin>☛</margin> In contrast, it is written in the fourth book of *Simple Medicines* and the seventh book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>Two major works by the Greek physician Galen</note> that in the cure of a "hot" <term>mal-complexion</term><note>An imbalance of the four bodily qualities; here, an excess of heat</note> of the belly, the froth of the milk is administered. And in the third book, chapter eighteen, it is said that in a certain "water of cheese" <note>Whey</note>, one is cooled. Furthermore, that which is watery and freezes with cold is whey. Whence in the fourth book of the *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle’s work on natural phenomena</note>: "Certain wines, vinegar, lye, whey, and watery <term>ichor</term><note>A thin, watery discharge or fluid</note>; all these are coagulated by cold." Furthermore, the same logic applies to the whole as to its parts, according to the principle of histories. Such is the nature of milk. Whence it is concluded that if substances have been thickened so that heat previously caused no coagulation, it must be said that they are cold and moist, just as milk is coagulated by intense cold. Therefore, the water of milk is cold.

Regarding the first point, however, it should be known that milk is an animal's white surplus, generated in the breasts by a double <term>decoction</term><note>A biological "cooking" or refining process where the body transforms one substance into another</note>. 
<margin>☛</margin> For it is blood twice cooked, as **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a Persian Christian physician</note> says in his *Practice*, and it is changed into whiteness. And if this second decoction does not instill heat but rather cold, it is because of the mammary flesh, which is glandular, cold, and moist. For just as the animal spirit is twice cooked—namely in the heart and the brain—so too is milk in the liver or heart and then the breasts. And milk is a medium between <term>phlegm</term><note>The cold, moist humor</note> and blood, yet declining more toward the nature of blood, according to the second book of the *Practice*.

Milk is also diversified by its own nature and by external factors, such as timing. By nature, because its complexion is twofold: one part rising from its components, such as the balance of the water of milk, the butter, and the cheese within the milk. The other is the finished product, resulting from those three prior parts, just as the complexion of **theriac** <note>A famous ancient herbal "cure-all" compound</note> acquires its qualities from its simple ingredients. And by its nature, milk is cold and moist in a temperate way. Whence **Almansor** <note>Referring to the medical text by the Persian physician Al-Razi</note> in his third book says: Freshly milked milk comes out near to a temperate state, although it pertains slightly to coldness and moisture. 

Generally, however, milk is cold and moist. Wherefore, in the second place, it should be known that because milk declines toward cold, it harms those who are "windy" <note>Prone to gas or flatulence</note>. It is also diversified by time. Whence in the *Common Diets* it is said that "milk" is spoken of generally or implicitly: for it is either sweet, flowing recently from the breasts, or sour, having been kept for a long time, or something in the middle. Sweet milk is moderately warm, being in the middle of the first degree <note>Medieval medicine graded qualities from 1 to 4</note>, which its flavor demonstrates; whence in the fourth book of *Medicines*: "The taste is sweet and pleasant." It therefore possesses a temperate quality. Sour milk, however, is considered whey-like and dry, for the pre-existing heat and moisture in it have evaporated. And know that the nature of milk varies according to the species of animals, their natures, their ages, the regions, the pastures, and such things.

<margin>3. On Foods</margin> Regarding whey, it should be known that **Galen** appears to contradict himself in this distinction. For he says in the third book of *On Foods*: "These things happen to milk not only because it has a whey-like nature in itself." And he adds: "Neither in a <term>choleric</term><note>Hot and dry</note> and very hot belly does sour milk yet possess a hot and stinging quality and power, because milk participates in heat through the whey." This occurs without the influence of any rennet or other hotter mixture. 

But in the fourth book of *Medicines* he writes thus: milk is composed of three substances differing in quality. One is the thick substance from which cheese is made; the second is the fatty, buttery part; the third is the watery part called the water of cheese. And each of these substances has its own complexion. For the fatty, buttery part is of greater equality <note>balanced</note>; the cheesy part is below that in the equality of its complexion. But the watery part is cold and moist, whence the heat of the whole milk is rendered below the quality of the whole body's temperate heat. And therefore, of itself, it does not change into bitterness, but into sourness. The definition of this "discord" of properties will appear in the third book. Wherefore some have said that the water of milk is of a twofold substance: one is watery and tasteless, and this is cold and moist. The other is <term>choleric</term>, nitrous, and sharp, by which it opens, wipes away, and purges; and that part is hot and dry. This is what **Avicenna** seems to suggest in the premises. 

But it must be said that if this nature of heat and sharpness belonged to it by its dominant nature, it would not be, as **Galen** testifies, cold and moist. What more may be shown of this will be clear from what is to be said. Regarding the third point, it should be known, as **Galen** says in *On Medicines*, that the water of milk—provided it is considered by itself in whatever way—is cold and moist. 

<margin>☛ 3. Water of milk is divided in three ways</margin> And finally, regarding what he says to himself in *On Foods*, I say "by itself," since the nature of the "water of cheese" can be changed into a hot nature through the artifice of extraction. For it is often drawn out from milk after being separated from the other two substances by the power of a hot and dry <term>coagulant</term><note>Rennet or a similar agent used to curdle milk</note>, which alters and changes this water. It is then called whey, just as semen acts upon menstrual blood. 

But others will object: for by the same reasoning, it ought to change the fatty and cheesy substance of the milk. Furthermore, the quantity of this coagulant is very small compared to the milk. It also enters the cheese not by its mass, but rather by its power and vapor, like semen in an embryo. It must be said that because the wateriness of milk is of a subtler substance, it is the first to receive the "impression" <note>the effect</note> of the heat. The other two substances are thick and more compact; they do not receive such a great change from the coagulant, since the action of agents is strongest on material that is disposed to receive it. To the other point, it must be said that although the coagulant put into the milk is small in quantity, it is nevertheless powerful by the nature of its principle. For it acts in the milk like semen in menstrual blood. For it induces a certain boiling, almost by way of putrefaction. Whence even the various types of cheese are altered in flavor thereby. 

However, this wateriness can be derived from milk through something cold, like the juice of sour grapes, and then it remains cold and moist. For milk is coagulated by many substances put into it, such as the flower of the mullein, boxwood, rennet, dried milk, safflower, and the like. Whence **Avicenna** says: "The dried milk of animals coagulates milk." There is also an artifice for separating the wateriness from the milk: one should have a round vessel, like a large <term>cucurbit</term><note>A gourd-shaped chemical vessel</note>, and the milk is put into it with hot round stones and shaken for a long time. Then the fatty substance which floats on top is drawn out by hand, and thereafter it is shaken strongly in the same way.

...until it is all thrown off, and finally through strong straining, this water is separated from the remaining cheesy substance. Whence in the fourth book <note>referring to Galen’s *On the Capacities of Simple Medicines*</note>: "Cheese water obtained from the vessel <note>original: *dogo*</note> after vigorous straining, which is properly called the water of milk <note>Whey</note>."

<margin>☞ Manicule pointing to following paragraph</margin>
That this wateriness, extracted in itself and by art, is **cold** and **moist**, is seen. For all milk, as has been said, is cold and moist, such that the fatty substance <note>The butter</note> is more balanced, and the cheesy substance is within this same equality of <term>complexion</term> <note>The balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>. But if the whey were hot, then since the buttery substance is temperately hot, the milk would be hot because of its two parts, even though the cheesy substance is of a moderate coldness. To this, Avicenna <note>abbreviated as A.</note> might respond: for he posits that fresh cheese is cold and moist in the third degree; he claims the other two substances change it so much that the milk is rendered cold. Furthermore, since the effect leads to knowledge of the nature, that which mitigates the thirst of those with acute fevers and cools the <term>hectic</term> <note>Those suffering from wasting fevers or consumption; original: *ethicos*</note> is cold. Such is the nature of whey. Whence in the fourth book: "it is effective for settling the thirst of those with acute fevers; it is a remedy made from bread together with the cheese water obtained from the vessel after vigorous straining." And in the same place: "The whey of cow's milk from which the butter has been extracted cools those with hectic fevers."

Someone might perhaps object that although it mitigates thirst and cools those who are vehemently inflamed, it does not do so for others. To which it must be said that this argument is not valid; rather the opposite is true, since a semi-hot thing would heat a hot person more than someone who is colder. Therefore, the water of milk <note>whey</note> is cold and moist. To that which was brought up regarding foods, it must be said again that there, the moist water is compared to acidic whey, and not to the body of a temperate complexion; and then it is certainly hot. And even if it were cold, it would be so by the measure of its equality, according to the fourth book of *Medicines*. And I certainly am not ignorant of the fact that other physicians, even along with Galen in his book *On Foods*, seem to feel that cheese water is more hot and dry. Let it be decreed now, however, with the fourth book of *Medicines*, that it is cold and moist. Regarding that fourth book, it must be said to the first group that they were of that opinion because they understood "whey" to be that derived from milk after curdling <note>original: *pro coagulum*</note>, or because they saw some "choleric" <note>pertaining to yellow bile</note> part existing within it. To the other point, it must be said that although a woman’s milk has a significant amount of purgative <term>serosity</term> <note>the watery part of the fluid</note>, nature intended this for the newborn; thus it causes ulcers of the gums, yet not in relation to a balanced body, to which the fourth book of *Medicines* is compared. For the subtle wateriness of the milk penetrates into their very tender lips, and boiling there, it induces ulceration—especially when the nurse's milk is hotter than other milk. And such milk is hot and moist in act, and not only in potential, as is the reason here. Nor is every purgative, aperient, or thinning substance—or that which relaxes the belly—hot by dominance; this is shown by barley water. It can also work by its thinness, as vinegar denotes. Certain things also loosen by softening or lubricating, or by pressing down with weight, or by liquefying or dissolving. <note>See Differentia 141</note>. And these last two cases alone are hot and dry. To the other point, it was shown to be apparent. To the other point, it must be said:

that the easy conversion to heat <note>literally "to fire"</note> comes not only from the part of heat, but also in no small part from the thinness of the substance, which is easily affected. To the other point, it must be said that the serum extracted from milk after curdling, which some call "milk water," is altered toward heat and dryness. Or it must be said that just as urine is not hot in respect to blood or bile, so whey is only hot in relation to butter, but not to cheese. Therefore, let it be accepted as probably passed down in this way.

## DIFFERENTIA. 161.

<margin>☞ Manicule pointing to following paragraph</margin>
That **Mint** is cold is shown as follows. For that is cold which cools. Indeed, it cools. Whence, in *Problems* 20 <note>A work attributed to Aristotle</note>, it is said that "one should neither eat nor plant mint in time of war." Solving this, it says: "either because it cools," which is declared by the corruption of the sperm, which is the genus <note>source</note> of strength and boldness. And further, in Mint there is a power to corrupt the blood. Furthermore, mint has a **styptic** <note>astringent</note> flavor; and this is cold according to Differentia 145. Since from the flavor, a sufficient knowledge of the thing is obtained.

On the other hand, in it there is a superfluous crude moisture according to Aristotle and Galen. That such a substance, which dulls, associates coldness with itself is likely. Also, that it excites the appetite is similar. Because it is acidic and seen to be styptic, it flourishes in coldness and dryness. Mint, as they pass down, strengthens the appetite. Likewise, they say it helps with the spitting of blood when taken with vinegar. That it should be so effective for the cold, when it causes hot blood to flow out, according to the fifth book of *Aphorisms*.

Furthermore, if it were hot, it would be of one nature, since it is the nature of heat to make each thing uniform. But it is pronounced to have diverse flavors. For some posit it is styptic; others bitter with stypticity. Some say it should be said to have sweetness with bitterness; others a certain pungency with sharpness. Therefore, mint is cold.

<margin>☞ Manicule</margin>
On the opposite side, however, is the view of Avicenna <note>original: *Ay.*</note>, whom I have seen positing that it is sufficiently **hot**. Again, that which bites the tongue with a swift sharpness is hot. Mint is of this kind, especially its leaves. For they participate in no small amount of heat. And it is supported because, according to Galen and Avicenna, it is of a thinner substance than other herbs. Therefore, mint is hot. Regarding the first point, it should be known that mint, called <gloss>dyofmon</gloss> in Greek <note>original: *dyofmon*, from *diōsmos* meaning "sweet-smelling"</note>, is a commonly known herb. It is of two types: one is domestic, which is itself twofold; one has broad and sharp leaves, being hotter and called **Roman mint** or **Saracen mint**. The other is smaller in its leaves, whose stem is square and about a cubit in height, almost like a border. It is commonly placed as **hot** and **dry** in the second degree. Some have extended it into the third degree, considering the festive biting and sharpness that exists in its leaves and top, although the stalk itself participates more in stypticity. And so, the accounts found regarding its flavor are various; whence for strengthening the stomach and for its stypticity, its leaves are to be chosen in no small measure, as is found in wormwood according to Avicenna. And it indeed excites sexual intercourse; for it is hot and dry with a certain superfluous moisture. Such things are windy and provocative of Venus <note>arousing sexual desire</note>.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that **Avicenna**, as it appeared, wrote that mint, unlike other things, cools the body. Which is shown because that thing is hot which heats its own parts and dries up the surrounding moistures; it procures digestion and excites intercourse in cold natures. For it is <term>flatulent</term> <note>original: *iflatia*; causing wind</note>; it kills worms; it resolves swellings. Such is mint, as certain experience testifies along with the writings about it. This is shown by the sharpness and the stinging of its juice, and especially of its top. Therefore, in short, all science holds mint to be hot and dry. It is such in the second degree, since its action does not reach the point of hindering the operations of the body, unless by accident; as when there is too much of it, or if it is repeated. Or the cold parts help even with heat and dryness; and in those where such humors abound. The appetite also flourishes by tempered coldness and dryness, since extreme <term>dyscrasia</term> <note>An imbalance of the humors</note> properly dissolves actions and virtues. *Aphorisms*, book 2. To the other point it must be said similarly: that mint benefits the spitting of blood by its dryness and astringency, its heat being moderated by the admixture of vinegar; and this in those who are not naturally hotter. It can also help sometimes by inciting and causing the sick person to expectorate. To the other point it must be said: that this is true, unless there were a heterogeneity of matter. Which arises from the diverse flavor of the root, the stalk, and the leaf, and its superfluous moisture. Or this is so when the heat is more powerful.

### CHAPTER 160.

> That **hemlock** is cold is shown by **Democritus**, who associates it with cold things thus: Apply to the kidneys the juice of nightshade and purslane and henbane or hemlock. <meta>This page continues the discussion of medicinal herbs, transitioning from Mint to a detailed investigation into the properties and classification of Hemlock (Cicuta). The text focuses on a scholastic debate: whether the plant is fundamentally cold (as the Greeks and Macer claim) or hot (as some Arabic authorities and Constantine suggest).</meta>

<margin>
MACER'S
verses.
</margin>
**Macer**, speaking above all else regarding hemlock <note>original: *conio*; from the Greek *kōneion*</note>, says: "The nature of hemlock is of a nearly deadly power of cold." Whence it kills those who drink it after the manner of a chilled poison. In the *Synonyms* <note>A common medieval reference work for plant names</note>, and also according to **Stephanus**, *conion* is explained as hemlock. And in sum, it is that which by its own action induces coldness. Such indeed is *conion* or hemlock. For they write that it freezes or numbs; it restrains the flow of blood and <term>sperm</term> <note>original: *spmatis*</note>. It prevents the growth of hair and forbids the enlargement of the testicles and breasts. It settles <term>erysipelas</term> <note>A skin infection, often called St. Anthony's Fire</note> and <term>formica</term> <note>literally "ant"; likely referring to a crawling skin ulcer or shingles</note>. It is also a deadly poison. Every drop of it is pure poison, along with the other accidents that are asserted to come from immense coldness. This is supported by the fact that it numbs living creatures and prostrates them into immobility. In this state of numbness, birds can be caught by hand using a preparation made from its juice, wine dregs, and flour—this material being particularly suited for them to consume. Therefore, among other things, it is concluded that *conion*, hemlock, or *succaram* <note>A term sometimes used for a toxic draught or a specific preparation of hemlock</note> is cold.

<margin>
Constantine.
Averroes.
Circa instans.
Opposite
opinions.
</margin>
On the other hand, **Constantine** <note>Constantine the African</note> testifies concerning certain types that it is hot and dry in the third degree. Similarly, **Averroes** <note>abbreviated as Ax.</note> in the fifth book of his *Colliget*, and also the author of *Circa instans* <note>Mattheus Platearius</note>, agree. In no way do they disagree in its <term>complexion</term> <note>The constitutional balance of heat/cold/moisture/dryness</note> or its degree. Furthermore, any plant is hot which is not aquatic and remains green in winter. This is said to distinguish it from things like <term>water lilies</term> <note>original: *nenuphar*</note> and the like. However, hemlock is not of that sort, as it remains green at all times, especially the smaller terrestrial kind.

<margin>
Hemlock is
of two kinds.
</margin>
Therefore, hemlock is hot. Regarding the first point, it should be known that hemlock is twofold: one is terrestrial, the other is aquatic. The terrestrial kind is also twofold: one is indeed smaller and branched, remaining green at almost every hour, though changing with new flowers and resembling **parsley**. The other is large, rising to the height of a man, with a hollow stem inside like a reed or a <term>ferula</term> <note>Giant Fennel</note>, marked by certain nodes. In its leaves, it resembles the former kind, and upon it grow whitish flowers. The seed is like that of **anise**. The aquatic kind, however, has a shorter, thicker, and more immediate stalk, with a heavier and more pungent odor. Whenever "cold" and "hot" are mentioned, and how they should be understood here, one should consult the fifteenth <term>differentia</term> <note>chapter/division</note>.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that the authors have disagreed most strongly on this question, as is seen. There were perhaps two causes for this. One is that few of the earlier authors heard *conion* called hemlock. The **Arabs**, however, mostly think it is <term>henbane</term> <note>original: *iusquamus*</note>. Whence, in the first and third books on medicines, where the Greek has *conion*, the Arabic translator rendered it as *iusquamus*. And where **Galen** has *iusquamus* according to the Arabic in the aforementioned degrees, he says it is food for birds and poison for humans. **Avicenna**, in his second book, wrote it down as <term>napellus</term> <note>Monkshood or Aconite</note>, and in the fourth and sixth, being more hesitant, he says Galen calls it that. In the third book of *Simple Medicines*, he identifies it as *Alfarfa* and thinks it is *napellus* or a killing poison. For it kills men but not <term>thrushes</term> <note>original: *turdos*</note>, because due to the narrowness of their veins, it does not reach their hearts unless vehemently altered. In man, however, it is otherwise, the true cause of which is noted in the third book on *Complexions*, based on the proportion of the agents and patients acting upon one another. And so Avicenna, receiving this cause from him, attributed it to himself as if by theft...

---

...remaining silent about the primary great cause. And I say this method is a certain way of finding Galen's defect. **Haly Abbas**, inquiring into this matter in his *Practice*, says it does not harm; for where the Greek writes *conion*, it chills humans so much that it chills them unto death. For it is food to those birds, just as it is not expedient for **hellebore** to be food for humans, even though it is food for thrushes. Where the **Monk** <note>likely referring to Constantine the African</note> translated it as henbane, it does not kill sparrows; rather, it nourishes them. It is not necessary for humans to be nourished by it just as <term>quails</term> <note>original: *coturnices*</note> are. Whence in the third book of *Complexions*, they strive to interpret Galen's series: *conion* is food for the thrush but a drug for man, and hellebore is food for the bird but a drug for man. Galen interprets this dissonant series similarly. Avicenna, having recited many opposing opinions about *succaram* that exist, finally agrees with **Dioscorides** in the discussions of *conion*, reciting his words. Regarding which he says in his *Practice*: *Succaram* is a deadly sleep-inducer due to its coldness; if anyone takes a little of it in wine, he falls asleep. Some also say that *succaram* is a species of henbane, just as was said of *conion*. Whatever it may be, it seems cold and poisonous, as the initial effects prove; because of which people die from an immoderate amount if they drink much of it while already weakened. Or just as heat is gradually extinguished by *conion* in its own way, but in another way, this which congeals by cold is cold and moist. Wine, however, by its own heat, extinguishes natural heat.

There could be another cause, which is written in the *Synonyms*: *Harmel* <note>Syrian Rue; *Peganum harmala*</note> is a herb found in Toledo and is similar to hemlock. In that place, **Constantine** put hemlock and erred, as some say. For the Arabs want *harmel* to be a type of **rue**. Whence Dioscorides, at the end of his discussion on rue, says: "There is another kind of rue which the citizens of Macedonia, Galatia, and Asia call *molim*, and which many also call *harmela*." Therefore, **Almansor**, **Avicenna**, and **Serapio** discuss *harmel*. In the fourth and seventh books, they say wild rue is not *harmel* according to what some have estimated; rather, it is a species of rue itself, and they coincide with Dioscorides' *osiaría* <note>possibly a corruption of *rutam montanam* or a specific Greek term</note>, although he ascribes more to it. But whatever it may be, *harmel* seems to share many attributes with hemlock, so much so that it is estimated to be the same herb. For it is written of *harmel* that it purges winds and viscous humors and provokes menstruation; similarly, it intoxicates like wine and brings on sleep. Likewise, they say hemlock purges phlegm and that which is thick and viscous. They write that both *harmel* and hemlock cause vomiting. But I have learned that by eating its root, it induces drunkenness and sleep. Indeed, its parts are considered deadly and poisonous due to the numbness they cause. Others say it causes a dissolution of the spirits; whence the author of *Circa instans* says Hemlock has the power of dissolving and consuming. Therefore, we do not use it internally, because it is poisonous in its substance and quality; for it dissolves so much that the spirit is weakened, from which the spirit and the limbs are mortified.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that, as is said for the present, hemlock is twofold: terrestrial and aquatic. The terrestrial is hot and dry. What then is its effect? That heat of itself is also that which cuts through viscous and thick humors, thinning them and leading them out. It provokes urine and menstruation, and cures colic and windiness.

<meta>This page concludes the investigation into hemlock (cicuta) and begins a new section on the properties of quicksilver (mercury). # Whether Quicksilver is hot and dry.

...it cures the <term>dissolution of the intestines</term> <note>likely referring to chronic diarrhea or dysentery</note>. It assists those with epilepsy when cooked with wine. It promotes conception. If any woman who has been purified <note>referring to the end of menstruation</note> on any tenth day takes its root for several days until conception; I was told of a certain wise woman who, after she had not conceived for seven years, used some of the roots of the <term>lesser hemlock</term> <note>original: *cicute elixate minoris*</note> and conceived a male child. Such are the determinations regarding hemlock made by **Constantine**, **Axi**, and the author of *Circa Instans*.

<margin>vi. rã i. c. ix.</margin>
And it is supported by the fact that when it is tasted, it strikes the tongue with a certain biting and sharpness, just like <term>pellitory</term> <note>original: *piretrũ*; a root known for its pungent, heat-inducing sensation</note>. Furthermore, that which is rare, light, and quickly turns into fire is of a hot complexion. Such is the nature of both types of hemlock, especially when dried. Also, its odor—or rather its stench—is great and truly horrible, striking the organ of smell, which denotes a great heat and shows its wicked and highly <term>heterogeneous</term> <note>composed of diverse or conflicting elements</note> composition. This is also indicated by its foul-smelling remains. Therefore, unless a better opinion occurs to me, it is my judgment that terrestrial hemlock is hot and dry. However, aquatic hemlock is undoubtedly poisonous and pestilential, as proved by experience. I believe it kills more by its coldness than by its heat, because the place where it grows is not a little colder. It kills very swiftly, which heat does not do; rather, heat works more slowly unless an occult power is joined to it, as in <term>monkshood</term> <note>original: *napello*</note> and the venom of serpents. For according to **Avempace** <note>original: *Auẽperras*; a 12th-century Andalusian philosopher</note>, such things move in a circular fashion very quickly. The determination of heat is also found in the fourth and fifth sections of the *Aphorisms*. Regarding the questions asked: to the first, it must be said that **Democritus** estimated hemlock to be a kind of <term>henbane</term> <note>original: *iusquami*</note>, as interpreted by some. To **Dioscorides**, it must also be said that perhaps *conion* <note>the Greek name for hemlock</note> is not hemlock as some explain it, though they testify it to be a species of henbane. Or perhaps it is something else of this sort. Or, it may be granted that *conion* is the poisonous aquatic hemlock. Regarding the other point, for confirmation: it must be said that if a substance seems to induce stupor and immobility, it is not therefore necessary to conclude it is cold. For <term>wild rue</term> <note>original: *barmel*; likely *Peganum harmala*</note> is hot and dry in the third degree according to the experts, yet it is seen to cause sleep, for it induces immobility and drunkenness. Similarly, <term>darnel</term> <note>original: *loliũ*</note>, hemp seed, <term>amomum</term>, Indian aloes, and very strong wine taken in excess cause the aforementioned effects because by their heat and <term>effumation</term> <note>the giving off of vapors</note> they send vapors into the brain. By these vapors, the spirits are disturbed, whereby the reason is first dulled, and finally sleep and immobility are caused. In this way, the aforementioned hemlock is also thought to induce such states.

### DIFFERENCE CLI.

<margin>Dioscorides. The Aggregator.</margin>
1 **T**hat quicksilver <note>original: *argentuʒ uiuũ*</note> is of a hot and dry complexion is shown because that which bites and corrodes parts is hot and dry. Corrosive things are placed among those that are vehemently hot and dry. Such indeed is quicksilver; whence **Dioscorides** says: the power of quicksilver is homicidal, eating through the intestines by its own weight. Wherefore the **Aggregator** says: it corrodes everything it meets among the internal members. It is also shown to be of a hot and moist nature because that which is quickly turned toward something else seems to possess its nature. For such things are "symbols" that easily transmute into one another. But quicksilver is very swiftly turned into air by means of smoke. And generally, its motion testifies to its heat. For everything that is perfected finally reaches heat through itself. On the other hand, it seems to be cold and moist because it causes cold and moist diseases, such as <term>paralysis</term> <note>original: *paliſim*</note>, <term>apoplexy</term>, and the like. Even its name in Greek, according to **Dioscorides**, shows this. For it is called *hydrargyros* <note>original: *urdias. ſurpecydrar. gyros*—the scribe's garbled Greek</note> from *hydor* which is "water," and *argyros* which is "silver," as if it were "water of silver." And water is cold and moist. That it is also cold and dry is shown by the injury it inflicts on the nerves and all cold and dry members, and the mortification and general denunciation of life it brings. Furthermore, it is attributed to **Mercury**, which although it is indifferent, nevertheless pertains more to coldness and dryness according to the astrologers. And generally, the cold injuries occurring from it denote coldness. Therefore, quicksilver is of a diverse nature. From these points, the opposite of each can be gathered.

<margin>O: cold through moisture. O: cold through dryness.</margin>
**R**egarding the first point, it must be known that quicksilver is a metal in continuous motion, defined by an external boundary, and infused with a shining white color. Because it does not adhere to the touch, and because of its "earthiness" and "wateriness" and the roundness of its figure, it moves continuously. For according to **Avempace**, water moves in a circular fashion, as indicated by its ebb and flow. The principles of metals are also set down differently by different people. For some of the <term>alchemists</term> <note>original: *alchimiſtaꝝ*; here meaning those who work with humors or liquids</note> said they are fashioned from "fetid spirits" and "living water," which can be called "dry water." Others placed the principle of metals not in quicksilver and sulfur in their own nature, but in an altered and transformed state. Some said metals are fashioned from water flowing through the passages of the earth, finding a dissolvable substance in its bowels, which when joined with the water becomes one body. Some of the more skilled simply testify that the principles of metals are quicksilver, acting as the mother and matter, and sulfur, acting as the father and the agent. There are, moreover, seven metals, following the number of the planets. The alchemists, wishing to hide their esteemed science, speak in metaphors after the manner of the Platonists. Wherefore they called quicksilver "Mercury" and the "fleeing servant," because just as Mercury is vehemently mobile and turns easily toward all planets since it is indifferent, so also is quicksilver unstable, like a servant. Thus also this metal, of which **Aristotle** says in the fourth book of *Meteorology*: Quicksilver is like water mixed with earth by a very subtle and strong sulfurous mixture until it does not rest on a flat surface; and this is from the great dryness that is in it, and therefore it does not stick to the touch. And its whiteness comes from the clarity of the water and the whiteness of the subtle earth that is in it, and also from the mixing of air with it. Silver is compared to the Moon because it is proportioned to it in substance and color and...

**GEBER** in his *Alchemy*
</margin>

...is established. These indeed belong to Venus because of their color and their internal complexity. To the Sun, they give gold because of the preciousness of both. To Mars, indeed, iron. To Jupiter, however, tin, both because of the nature of their mutability and their color. To Saturn also lead, because of the substance and weight of both being similar. Which things, even when transferred, he makes use of. But if anyone should object that **Geber**, in his *Alchemy*, only posits six metals—for he does not enumerate <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; literally "living silver," known to us as mercury</note>—it is because it does not seem to be a singular metal, since it is the very matter from which they are made. It must be said that it is not a simple metal, but rather it is so by a certain assimilation and reduction; thus simple things are reduced into compounds situated in a direct line. Because, however, it is not purely simple like the nature of prime matter, but participates in a <term>complexion</term> <note>the balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> as will be shown, it can therefore be numbered among the metals in some way.

Concerning the second point, it should be known that diverse opinions are found regarding this quality. For it seems that its nature cannot be perceived, just like that of the planet Mercury, because of its instability, appearance, and ostentation. For some have pronounced it to be cold and moist, as **Aristotle** does in 
<margin>
Diverse opinions on its classification
</margin>
the second book [of *On Generation and Corruption*]; others in the fourth. Others say it is hot and moist in the fourth degree, as with **Constantine** in the *Circa Instans* regarding <term>bulbs</term> <note>likely referring to medicinal plant roots</note> and in his *Practice*, book two. **Haly Abbas**, however, says in the same place that it is sharp and burning. **Al-Mansur** also says in his third book that that which extinguishes burning things is itself burning. **Geber**, however, seems to pronounce it to be a viscous water united by a temperate heat. Therefore, the diversity of this quality is apparent. What also introduces difficulty here is that few authors express its complexion clearly. But concerning this, it shall be shown briefly.

Concerning the third point, it should be known that **Geber** posited it to exist as such, as was said immediately above. In which it is finally manifest that the quicksilver which is called "Mercury" by the use of the ancients is a viscous water in the bowels of the earth, composed of a subtle white earth united by a most temperate heat in a most minute union, until the moist is tempered by the dry, and the dry equally by the moist. Therefore, it flees a flat surface easily because of the moisture of its water. This perhaps cannot stand according to **Avicenna**, since it is said in the fourth book of the *Meteors* that the water of liquids is least thickened by itself alone, unless coldness turns it into earth. For it is in no way "cookable" by heat. Furthermore, it happens that it does not stick to the touch because of the subtle earthy part which is in it, as previously introduced by **Aristotle**. Quicksilver is, as it were, the material substance of the metals and like a <term>menstruum</term> <note>a solvent or base liquid used in alchemy to dissolve or "digest" substances</note> for mixtures. From this, by the power of sulfur digesting and "burning" it, this metal is generated. When, however, it begins to be converted, it is first reduced into a "glandulous" form of moisture; thereafter, little by little, it begins to stand and be converted. In this substance, according to the wise, two dominating substances are found. One is indeed aqueous; the remaining is earthy, and this possesses something of sulfur. Thus, quicksilver can be considered in two ways: either in regard to the sulfurous earthy part—and thus it participates in heat and dryness, which is manifested by its "extinction" and its power of <term>sublimation</term> <note>the process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again, used here to show mercury's "hidden" heat</note> once the aqueous moisture has evaporated. And regarding this, it was said by **Al-Mansur** 
<margin>
Al-Mansur
Haly Abbas
</margin>
that it is "extinguished burning" and "combustive." And **Haly Abbas** says it is sharp, that is, when sublimated it is burning. Whence **Aristotle** says: "Sublimated [mercury] is a killer because of its vehement incision." For according to the *Aggregator*, fire burns it so. Or, it can be considered in regard to its aqueous substance, which exists as its matter. This immediately evaporates into fumes when heat is applied because of its imperfect mixture with the earthy sulfur. And this induces diseases and other harms of coldness. Whence **Aristotle** says: its vapor causes palsy and tremors to happen. And according to **Abugerig** <note>likely a corruption of an Arabic name, possibly referring to a medical authority</note>, the smoke is very harmful, for by its constant use it destroys the nerves and induces palsy and takes away sense and motion. It destroys sight and hearing, and even according to **Aristotle**, it induces a stench of the mouth with the rotting of the teeth, as women who use <term>makeup</term> <note>original: *fucantes*; mercury was famously used in "ceruse" or white face paint, leading to systemic poisoning and tooth loss</note> demonstrate. And looking toward this part of its nature, he pronounced it cold and moist in the second degree.

It is therefore apparent to anyone paying attention what ought to be said. The **Monk** <note>referring to Constantine the African</note> seems to exceed in this as in many things, when he claims it is hot perhaps in the fourth degree; for it does not allow moisture to remain with it in an equal state, at least in relation to its temperament, as discussed in chapter 138. Which the rest of the matter also declares. For we see mixed parts constructed from different substances; according to one substance—as with hot and dry <term>nitre</term> <note>saltpeter or a similar alkaline salt</note>—it may loosen the belly, but according to another earthy and <term>styptic</term> <note>astringent or contracting</note> substance, it may constrict it, as is shown in <term>chickpeas</term> and lentils, the first of foods.

The truth of its quality appears not a little when considering the manner in which quicksilver is constructed. For **Dioscorides** writes that a certain kind is prepared from <term>minium</term> and <term>cinnabar</term> <note>red ores of mercury</note>, otherwise called *canuaria*. For it is placed in an earthen pot and secured with an iron lid sitting over it; it is placed in the hearth, and after two hours it is opened. And that which has adhered to the lid, collect it, for this is quicksilver. This, however, the *Aggregator* does not recite. There is indeed another quicksilver according to **Aristotle** which is purged or extracted from its own mine and found "living" (liquid); whence **Dioscorides** says: "It is also found in metals when silver is collected," and I myself have heard many times of this water running from mountains. There is also a third type which is extracted from the mountains and stones of its own mine, in which it is generated through "combustion" with fire, just as gold and silver are torn from stone. And this, because of its sharpness, is said to be of the genus of poisons. But then someone will say that gold and silver thus extracted would also be sharp and pernicious—especially gold—when nevertheless it is more temperate. It must be said that this matter is disposed differently than that which is treated by fire; for it suffers differently, as sweat and venom show, and humors, and the juice of <term>monkshood</term> <note>original: *napelli*; a highly toxic plant</note> itself. Thus, that which is constructed by the artifice of fire will be more hot and dry. But that which nature produces will participate more in coldness and moisture. From which things the diligent intellect will be able to terminate the inquiry. Yet in a more elegant way than before. Nor is it valid to judge as the author of *Circa Instans* indicates, who said some authors placed it as cold in the fourth degree because it is very cold to the touch; for physicians do not consider such things in bodies based on their actual appearance, but according to their power and presence...

# Whether Colocynth should be ground much?

...to understand. Regarding the fourth point, it now appears what should be said to the first: that according to its earthy, sulfurous part, it is hot and dry. Or it must be said that it corrodes whatever it encounters by its weight. However, according to **Aristotle**, this word is not understood in that way. To the next point, it must be said that it does not follow that it is hot and moist because of this, for that which evaporates into smoke is not necessarily hot—at least not of its own nature—but rather is a watery substance moved by heat, just as the vapor of water is drawn upward when heated by the rays of the heavenly bodies. 

To the next point, it must be said that this motion does not belong to it immediately from its fall, since other things are not moved continuously just because they are fallen, but rather because of the subtle earthy part mixed within it with the watery part, which is limited in a certain way; therefore, it looks down upon a flat surface and flees easily. To another point, it should be said that by sight, because of its cold wateriness mixed with moisture in the smoke, it causes the aforementioned accidents. From this, its name was imposed upon it, because this [wateriness] is more manifest than its earthiness. 

To the next point, it must be said that it does not harm the nerves and other dry things by reason of moisture, but rather by reason of coldness, just as moisture harms through its wetness. To the final point, it must be said that it is ascribed to **Mercury** for the reason stated first, and not because of its <term>complexion</term> <note>The balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>. For gold is temperate; the Sun is hot and dry; Saturn is cold and dry; lead is cold and moist; Mars is also hot and dry; and iron is cold and dry. Their complexion in active properties is not found to be sufficiently expressed by the more expert authorities.

### DIFFERENCE CLII.

<margin>Democritus. Mesue.</margin>
<margin>The Aggregator</margin>
->**Whether colocynth should be ground much?**<-

That **colocynth** <note>original: *coloquintida*; the Bitter Apple, a powerful and toxic laxative used in the Middle Ages.</note> should not be ground much is shown by **Serapion** in his *Book of Simples*. Again, in the third book, he says: "Take of colocynth, surely not crushed." Also, in the tenth book of his *Practice*, **Galen** commands that those medicines of the antidotes which are soluble should be ground moderately; for if they are ground diligently, they work less effectively. This is also apparent in the fourth book regarding roses. 

Colocynth is of this kind, since it cannot be taken in decoctions, syrups, or powders due to its bitterness, but rather in pills. Furthermore, according to the first book, in all medicines where excessive labor is spent on their <term>trituration</term> <note>The process of grinding or crushing a substance into a fine powder.</note>, their operations are destroyed. However, the grinding of this substance produces extreme results. Again, that which is ground to the extreme cannot be washed away or wiped off because of its penetration into the <term>villi</term> <note>original: *villi veneris*; likely a corruption of *villi ventris*, referring to the shaggy, velvet-like lining of the stomach and intestines.</note> and the intestines. Because it is of such a nature, it will cause excoriation <note>skin-stripping or internal scraping</note> and inflammation. This is confirmed because that which is ground much, by its subtlety, adheres and becomes stuck to the villi of the belly and intestines. Because it is moist—and especially when it is bitter—it strips the lining and causes ulcers more than other things. Such is colocynth when it is vehemently ground. 

Furthermore, **scammony** is the greatest of laxatives, so much so that according to **Democritus**, it is the "laxative" by excellence. And so, according to **Mesue**, it is supported by him because **Mezereon** <note>A toxic shrub (Daphne mezereum) used as a violent purgative.</note> is a violent laxative; it is commanded not to be ground much. Whence in the tenth book of the *Practice* and the *Aggregator*: "Grind the mezereon not too finely, lest by chance it harms by adhering to the villi of the stomach and intestines." Likewise, **Mesue** says: "Every trituration, of whatever kind it may be, ought to be done with ease and measured against the substances being ground." For laborious grinding dissolves the virtue [medicinal power]. This happens when grinding to the extreme.

<margin>Opposition.</margin>
Therefore, colocynth should not be ground much. 
However, **Serapion** in the seventh book of his *Breviary* tastes that it should be ground not a little, but to the extreme. And perhaps because a powerful laxative can cause injury, it is commanded to be "comforted"? But it is perfected by great trituration. For by this, the "malice" [harshness] of the laxative is settled. For it is not the case that whenever the body of the substance is diminished, its virtue is preserved in proportion to the diminution; rather, it is impossible for the diminution of the body to reach a point where it no longer induces its proper action, since "minimal matter" is found in the first book of the *Physics*. For a natural form requires a due and precise quantity in matter in order to act. 
<margin>Aristotle's *Physics* Book 8</margin>
Hence, it is not necessary that if a certain strength—say, ten men—can carry a weight a certain distance in a day, that half of them (five men) can carry it half the distance; rather, they might not be able to move it at all. This appears in the first and seventh books of the *Physics*. 
<margin>*Physics* Book 8</margin>
For united virtue is stronger than divided virtue. 

Again, art assists nature. It is in the nature of colocynth to reach remote parts, such as drawing [humors] out from the joints of the extremities. That which is ground to the extreme is more able to reach the extremities. For this reason, it is expedient for colocynth to be ground to the extreme. 

Regarding the first point, it should be known that colocynth, according to **Dioscorides**, is a plant emitting branches and leaves spread upon the earth, similar to those of the domestic gourd, white and hairy, burning to the touch, and having incisions. **Mesue** and the Persians call it the "Gourd of the Desert," which is also called "Gall of the Earth," because in its entire circumference it kills the herbs around it, being as a poison to them. And therefore the Arabs call it the "Death of Plants." It produces a round fruit similar to a ball. It is vehemently bitter, composed of many burnt fiery and earthy parts. And it is of two kinds: male and female. The male is hairy, woolly, heavy, tending toward roughness and blackness. The female, however, is praised and is collected in autumn, specifically when it has lost its skin and acquired a lemon-yellow color. When the plant is in a stony place, or the fruit is on the plant, it is pernicious. For all the "malice" and violence is collected within it. For it is a rule that among praiseworthy and "blessed" medicines, however much of them there may be in a place, their goodness is diminished by being sequestered into many parts; in this case, however, the opposite is true. We use the pulp or the "fat" of it, by which viscous fluid is attracted from more remote places like the joints. 

Trituration is the sequestering of the body into many parts. These are diversified in quantity and number according to whether one labors more or less in the grinding. And this is threefold, according to the variety of the substance being ground. For a coarse substance must be ground the most; a subtle one the least; and a moderate one in the middle. Trituration is also seen for a fourfold reason...

<margin>Galen's advice on moistening and moderation</margin>

<summary>This page discusses the preparation of Colocynth, debating whether it should be finely ground. While some argue fine grinding causes the drug to stick to the intestines and cause ulcers, others claim it is necessary to help the medicine reach the joints to treat ailments like gout.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on medical preparation, specifically transitioning from the physical properties of substances to the technical processes of grinding (trituration) and its effects on the potency and safety of drugs like colocynth.</meta>

...to be done. One reason is that a better mixture may be made and the signs of the medicines may assist each other, just as is useful in <term>thariac</term> <note>Also known as Theriac, a famous ancient "universal antidote" made of dozens of ingredients.</note> and in other common compositions, so that nature may purge the rest from them. Some, however, are ground so that a speed of penetration for the medicine is acquired, which is necessary when it must reach distant parts of the body; for this reason, <term>hematite</term> <note>original: "lapidem ematitem," a reddish iron ore used to stop bleeding.</note> and coral must be ground most vehemently when they are mixed with medical powders. Another reason is so that a certain property of the medicine may be obtained, where by its action a different manner of effect is induced, as seen in the fourth book of *On the Preservation of Health* <note>Referring to Galen's "De Sanitate Tuenda."</note> regarding cumin. For when it is ground only slightly, it leads to a bowel movement. However, when it is ground most thoroughly, because it is weakened, nature evacuates it through the urinary passages; since the medicine becomes weak and unable to draw out the feces, being refined, it turns itself toward the urine. Hence, **Avicenna** and **Mesue**, following **Galen**, agree that in the final pulverization of cumin, when it is dissolved, it becomes a provocative of urine. 

A fourth reason is so that the "malice" <note>In this context, "malice" refers to the harsh or toxic side effects of a potent drug.</note> may be removed from the medicine, and this is on account of itself, because it may be violent and an enemy to nature. For this cause, **colocynth** <note>Also known as Bitter Apple, a powerful and potentially toxic purgative.</note> must be ground extremely. Or, it is on account of the noble and most sensitive part of the body which it encounters, such as the eye in practice. For the eye is the most sensitive particle of the body (from the 13th book of *On the Method of Healing*); therefore, it is necessary to grind powders or <term>alcohol</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "alcohol" referred to any fine, impalpable powder, particularly those used for the eyes, rather than a liquid.</note> which are administered to the eyes to the ultimate degree. 

Regarding the second point, it should be known that the great authorities are divided on this distinction. Some, such as **Ibn al-Jazzar** <note>original: "filius Gezar"</note> and the author of the *Aggregator* with the *Servitor* concerning the preparation of drugs, argue that colocynth should not be ground finely, lest by adhering to the villi of the stomach and intestines, it causes ulcers. For they imagine that by its fineness, it might penetrate so deeply into the parts through which it passes that it could not be washed away or wiped off from them. Others, however, totally oppose this, such as **Serapion the Younger**, **Avicenna**, and **Mesue**. For these testify as one that colocynth must be ground to the ultimate degree. Hence **Avicenna** says: "It is necessary that its grinding reaches the ultimate, and one should not be content that it is already very well ground." **Mesue** also expresses this opinion, though some ascribe it to **Serapion**. What the truth is regarding this will be seen generally.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that grinding is threefold. For some is coarse, some is most refined, and some is medium. This is what **Avicenna** suggests from the premises. I say here, therefore, that medium grinding is to be detested entirely, because in it, sensible parts remain that adhere to the villi of the organs, so that they are separated with difficulty. 

<margin>bracket in margin</margin>

Nor are they reduced to such smallness by grinding that the malice of the colocynth is sufficiently repressed. This is what he meant here by saying one should not be content that it is "very well ground." Yet both extremes of grinding can contain the truth. For those who say it should not be ground much look at its lesser adhesion to the internal parts and its easier removal from the same, being supported by other subtle arguments. The others, however, seek the acquisition of safety through ultimate grinding and the rejection of harm. 

Indeed, I support and defend these latter ones more in the present case, wishing with them that colocynth be ground to the ultimate degree, so that no part of it is manifest to the senses; rather, that it reaches a mixture where the intellect perceives it as if almost the minimum of one part touches the minimum of the other, as much as is possible. But that is only achieved by the ultimate grinding. Hence **Mesue** says: "It seems to me that in the ultimate grinding, its power is broken by the mixing of its joined parts, and it passes through the locations of the viscera without the impression of injury in them." Furthermore, that which adheres to the villi of the stomach and the folds of the intestines—which causes inflammation, ulceration, and pain—must be prohibited. Colocynth acts in this way when it is not ground to the extreme, but as they say, ground moderately or only a little. Also, a drug works according to its vapors dissolved within it. But this is more aptly achieved when it is ground to the extreme. For it has been said that ultimate grinding helps medicines to penetrate into parts which they could not reach before; and colocynth is such a substance. And this is confirmed because, as was premised, it is most bitter and of a coarse substance. Such a thing is said to sustain a most vehement nature without its own destruction. Therefore, colocynth is to be ground to the ultimate. 

Regarding the fourth point, what should be said to **Serapion** concerning simples has appeared. To the other point, what **Avicenna** said also seems to apply. Either he speaks of colocynth which is administered by <term>clyster</term> <note>An enema.</note> for colic, and not by mouth as below. Or there are other books that lack the negative particle. To another point, it must be said that this is true, and therefore colocynth is to be ground to the ultimate, so that its violence and laborious attraction may be blunted; yet its power is not entirely taken away by the grinding, since it is a violent and coarse substance. Or that speech is verified in many cases, whereas few medicines are of such a coarse substance and so violent. To the other point, it should likewise be said that they are destroyed either entirely or in part, and are diminished from that which they were. To another point regarding the "washing away," it must be said: it can indeed be washed and wiped away, and therefore the aforementioned harm is not induced. Hence **Avicenna**, teaching that colocynth should be ground to the ultimate, commanded that it first be infused in <term>hydromel</term> <note>A mixture of honey and water.</note>, then ground once dried. Furthermore, even if it could not be washed and wiped away like that which is not much ground, yet the grinding (as touched upon) having weakened it, it could inflict no injury or only a slight one. And especially because it is taught to be mixed with certain styptic and viscous things, such as <term>bdellium</term>, <term>tragacanth</term>, and <term>mastic</term>, and the like. 

Regarding the confirmation, it appears what should be said: that the power is released by the grinding so that it cannot harm. To the other, it must be said: the case of <term>scammony</term> <note>Another potent purgative resin.</note> is not the same as the "fat" or pulp of colocynth, since scammony is of an acute and subtle substance. Its force is destroyed by laborious grinding, but this coarse substance sustains extreme grinding. To the confirmation, it must likewise be said: perhaps there was an opinion among them regarding <term>mezereon</term> <note>A toxic shrub (Daphne mezereum) used in medicine.</note> just as in colocynth. To another, it must be said: that the substance of the fat or pulp of colocynth, because it is a coarse substance, can undergo the most refined grinding. It is also granted that the vigor of colocynth is in some way dissolved by grinding. Those things which proceed from the other side follow in a similar manner.

<meta>This page transitions from the practical preparation of drugs (the previous page discussed grinding cumin and colocynth) to a high-level theoretical debate: the fundamental medical principle of "Contraries." The author examines whether every disease must be cured by its opposite—such as cooling a fever—or if "Like" can sometimes cure "Like."</meta>

# Whether Every Cure is Accomplished by the Contrary

The rule meets a false objection here. Furthermore, in the same place: water is cold and moist, and yet it is said to cure regional <term>tetanus</term> <note>A condition of muscle stiffness; the author is puzzled why water (cold/moist) would cure a condition caused by phlegm, which is also considered cold and moist.</note> arising from the structure of phlegmatic humors. Also, in the sixth book of *On Epidemics*: "Pain dissolves pain," which is why two pains occurring at the same time [cancel each other out]. In the fourth book of the *Topics* <note>Aristotle’s treatise on logical argumentation.</note>: "Nothing is contrary to fever and <term>ophthalmia</term> <note>A general term for severe eye inflammation.</note>," and yet cases of them are cured. From the third book of *On the Preservation of Health*: "It is necessary to resolve labor with labor." And at the beginning of the *Megategni* <note>Referring to Galen's "Ars Medica" or "The Great Art," a foundational medical textbook.</note>: "One must cure moist bodies with moist things, and dry with dry." And also at the start: "Labor is cured by labor." Again, in the fourth book of the same: "Not every response, nor every 'malice' of a <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of humors (hot, cold, moist, dry) that makes up an individual’s constitution.</note>, is medicated by its contrary <margin>vol. 3</margin> through evacuation and opposition." 

Furthermore, in the third book of the same: "A refining regimen is harmful to one who has a foul cause from coarse food on account of <term>cholera</term> <note>In this context, "cholera" refers to "Yellow Bile," one of the four humors.</note>." And in the same book, chapter 16, according to **Hippocrates**: "Vomiting is sometimes stopped by vomiting, and a flux by a flux." Again: natural heat is hot, yet it cures diseases that appear hot, as stated in the first book of the *Physics*. Many things are also cured by their <term>Specific Form</term> <note>The "Specific Form" is an internal, essential property of a substance that gives it power (like a magnet attracting iron) beyond just its heat or moisture.</note>, to which nothing seems to be contrary. Again: <term>scammony</term> <note>A harsh herbal laxative derived from a Mediterranean vine.</note> is hot and dry, yet it cures a choleric fever <note>Which is also hot and dry.</note> both by reason of the fever and the matter. 

Furthermore: if every cure is accomplished by a contrary, then a disease of number or quantity could not be cured. This is because in the "Categories of Quantity" <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Categories*; logic dictated that things like "size" or "number" have no opposites, unlike "hot" and "cold."</note>, <margin>Injury</margin> nothing is placed as a contrary. Furthermore, if the cure is perfected by contraries, they would be opposites in degree and manifestation, according to the *Tegni* <note>The "Art of Medicine" by Galen.</note>. But things that exist in such a way either will not act upon one another if there is total equality, or they will provoke further fury. Thus, the reasoning stands that not every cure is completed by a contrary. 

The opposite of this view is written in *On Human Nature* and in the *Aphorisms*: "Diseases are not caused by fullness of every kind," etc. Hence, in the second book of the *Ethics*: "Medicines are naturally made to act by the contrary." Also, every action is from a contrary, as stated in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. But a cure is a certain kind of action. Therefore, a cure of a sickness is by the contrary. 

First, it must be known that a "cure" is the providence or care of something so that it may remain, while that which is harmful is driven away. This exists in two ways. One is "vile" or common, such as taking care of someone in any manner; according to the saying: "Cure him," that is, "provide for him." There is another "particular" cure, such as that perfected by opposition. For it cares for the subject—namely the body—so that it may remain in its being by cutting off the disease, just as moral care does for the soul. A "contrary," however, is a distance within the same genus. Regarding this, four things must be seen: first, how "contrary" is taken in multiple ways according to **Avicenna**; second, how it is understood by **Galen**; and finally, what is added concerning the modes of the contrary taken from the discussions of physicians.

<margin>Contraries.</margin> Regarding the first point, it should be known that according to **Avicenna**, "contrary" is found to be used in multiple ways. One is the proper sense, as it is found in qualities. In these, contrariety is most truly found according to "place," such as the center to the circumference. See the Commentator <note>Referring to **Averroes**, the famous 12th-century philosopher who wrote standard commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in the 8th and 10th books of the *Metaphysics*. Since in qualities the "maximum distance" is preserved—for of true contraries, one is the maximum and perfect thing, having no excess in that genus, while the other is distant from it through all things— <margin>2nd book of the Metaphysics?</margin> therefore, in the 10th book of the *Metaphysics*: "Contrariety is a difference...

---

...that is, a perfect distance." For as the Poet says, under the same genus, contraries are those things which are most distant from each other. They occur in the same recipient, and according to the same respect they cannot exist at once in the Categories. Hence, in the 11th book of *On the First Philosophy* <note>Often referring to Aristotle's Metaphysics.</note>: "Contraries are those things which are most distant from one another according to some one genus." Thus, the nature of true contraries is that they are most distant from each other, are in the same genus, and have the same recipient although they differ. And therefore, in such contraries, it does not happen that one thing has many contraries, as noted in the 10th book of the *Metaphysics*. For only one thing is the opposite of one thing. 

There are also other interpretations of contraries in the 5th book of the *Metaphysics*. For things are said to be "contraries" which cannot exist in the same being if they differ according to genus—for example, music and whiteness. Also, things that differ "first," because they exist in the same recipient, such as white and black. And also those things which are most distant among those that are in the same genus, such as a man and a donkey. And those things which differ the most among those that are under the same power. These last two modes of the four seem to properly carry the name of "contrariety." 

According to these four modes, contraries are also said to be joined. Some have them in such a way, others in the receiving. The rest is in active or passive things, or being agents or patients, such as rejections or acceptances, or habits or privations. In these, contrariety seems to be drawn from qualities. They are also called "contraries" commonly whenever they are diverse according to one category; for in the same way that "being" and "one" are spoken of in many ways, so are other things that follow from them. In this way, all things that are divided equally in any manner are called contraries. In this sense, even the "Categories" <note>Aristotle's basic classifications of all things that exist.</note> are called opposites. 

It is also said that it is not only extremes that are contrary to extremes, as shown in the 10th book of the *Metaphysics*. Rather, even the "middle" is contrary to them. For example, a middle voice is contrary to the furthest voice, just as a high pitch is to a low one. A high pitch is contrary to a deep one, and "dim" is related to white just as black is, and white appears [contrary] to black in the 5th book of the *Physics*. 

Regarding this, second, it must be known that **Galen**, considering the multiplicity of "contrary," says in the 11th book of *On the First Philosophy*: "If you do not wish to say that the cures of contraries are contraries, you may say that the cures of opposites are opposites." As **Hippocrates** felt along with **Plato**. <margin>Divine Plato</margin> Indeed, he says that **Plato** is "divine" and must always be followed; it is necessary to disregard the names of things, but not the teaching of the facts, since it contributes much to health, and the failure of such things ends in ruin. And whether we use names properly or improperly, the laboring patient is not affected more or less by this. For it is not only in qualities, but also in quantities that this kind of contrariety is found, which the **Aristotelians** call "opposition." 

For they do not say that "large" is the contrary of "small," but rather its relative opposite; nor likewise "much" to "few." And in the same way, neither "dense" to "rare," nor "relaxed" to "intense" in the Categories. All such things, however, are named as contraries according to **Hippocrates** and **Plato**, who make generation come from contraries. **Avicenna** also says that he does not observe the strict rules of language in names when he places the principles of Physics—namely matter and form with privation—as "contraries," which yet are not qualities but substances.

<summary>This page explores the scholastic debate over the principle of "contraries" in medicine, questioning whether diseases are always cured by opposites or if "like cures like" in certain cases. It reconciles medical practice with Aristotelian logic and Platonic philosophy, defining what constitutes a "contrary" in a medical context.</summary>
