<meta>This page continues the theoretical discussion on the principle of "Contraries" in medicine. It moves from specific objections to a systematic explanation of how nature and the physician use opposing forces to restore health, citing Aristotle's physics and Galen's medical theory.</meta>

<margin>Aristotle, *On Generation and Corruption*, Book 2</margin>

Furthermore, Aristotle wrote in *On Generation and Corruption* <note>original: "de generatione & cor."</note> that water is contrary to fire, and earth to air. And if they are under substances, they are indeed constituted from contrary passive qualities. Whence Galen also says that healing primarily and for its own sake <note>original: "per se"</note> must be directed toward the disposition or the disease, but only secondarily and by accident to the symptoms <note>original: "accidentia"</note>. This is because a symptom follows a disease like a shadow follows a body, as stated in the beginning of *Accidents* and the eleventh book of *On the Local Affections* <note>original: "de ingenio," referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note>. Therefore, when the disease is destroyed, the symptom is also destroyed. It can therefore be understood from this that a "contrary" is two-fold: one is an immediate contrary which opposes the disposition itself; the other is a mediate contrary which acts for the sake of another thing. One is for its own sake, the other is by accident. One is specific, the other is general. Even among symptoms, a certain contrariety can be granted: for example, a "flowiness" caused by the opening of the pores is the contrary of a "retention" caused by their narrowing.

<margin>2nd part: colcodea</margin>

$\P$ Regarding the third point, it must be known that in the specific practice of medicine, the "intention" of a contrary toward a disposition is found to be three-fold. For one is **intrinsic**, another is **extrinsic**, and yet another is a **mixture** of both.

$\P$ The **intrinsic** is differentiated in three ways. First, by reason of the governor—that is, the power of nature which rules the body—concerning which it is said in the *Tegni* <note>Galen’s *Ars Medica*, a standard medieval textbook.</note>: "The nature of all things is the worker, and the physician is the servant." Whence it is said in the *Metaphysics* concerning drugs, and in the eighth book of *Practice*: "It is the role of Nature to cure, not the physician." To Nature, as the more worthy power, belongs the work of offering something to the body. On the part of that which supports, this is the nature of the body called the <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> and the composition, and the common nature of both. The vigor of the complexion is the primary factor, since it is the more powerful cause of the composition and the common nature. Complexion is the principle of action because of the qualities from which it arises, since every action is eventually completed through a quality. 

Second, it is differentiated by reason of the instrument, namely the **innate heat** and the **spirit** <note>In medieval medicine, "spirit" (*spiritus*) was a subtle gas that carried life-force through the body.</note>. For the spirit is the instrument of nature by which it acts. It is the nature of this heat not only to attack and destroy coldness (its contrary quality), but also to oppose "foreign" heat in a certain way. For the spirit itself moves to expel the harm of external heat by removing the vapor and dissolving it, or by burning up the matter. **Coldness** does not have this nature. It does not attack and destroy anything except the heat that comes against it; it does not attack coldness at all. For this reason, heat is called "innate," but coldness is not. And therefore, life is not attributed to the coldness of the <term>colcodea</term> <note>A term likely referring to the vital or formative principle of the body.</note> of the body (that is, the giver of life), which is what we seek in heat.

**Extrinsic** contraries vary in three ways: either by the influence of the heavens, for sometimes such a superior influence occurs that it removes or lessens a sickness through one of the aforementioned modes of contrariety—for example, when the Moon is joined to a strong star, or is applied to a place where the stars were fortunate at the patient's birth, as has been often touched upon. Or by reason of service, and thus the physician acts as a contrary to the disposition. For he is the servant of nature, although acting through another medium as nature works. For fortune (which is a benevolent influence) and the craftsman work through intermediate materials; but Nature herself works through herself, completed by three parts: namely, the substance of the spirit, the spermatic members, and 

---

the formal substance of the flesh (eleventh book of *On the Local Affections*). Or, the contrary is differentiated by the instrument through which the sicknesses of the sick are met: the suitability of the assistants and the prompt adaptation of external things which are set against the disease to destroy it, as the first *Aphorism* instructs.

$\P$ A **mixed contrary** is when one disease is set against another disease for the sake of a cure, occurring either by nature or by art. For example, a fever supervening upon a spasm, or a quartan fever <note>A form of malaria characterized by paroxysms every fourth day.</note> curing epilepsy.

Regarding the second main point, it must be known that everyone has finally agreed that a cure is perfected by the contrary, as it is the very **principle of the art**. This should be as well-known as the "door in a house" which no one is ignorant of (as the Commentator <note>Averroes, the famous commentator on Aristotle.</note> says in the *Metaphysics*). For no one denies a first principle unless through ignorance. However, different thinkers have posited the "contrary" differently because they believed bodies were constructed in different ways. Some said they were composed of the four alterable and passive elements (like Hippocrates and Aristotle); or of opposites like Empedocles and Asclepiades; or of atoms and "unconnected bodies" <note>original: "corporibus anarmis"</note> as Democritus and Epicurus claimed. These latter thinkers place diseases and their specific contrariety only in the "position" of things—such as the narrowing or widening of the pores—rather than in the <term>complexion</term> itself.

Regarding the third point, it must be known that the universal rule remains that a cure is by the contrary, as derived from the ancients and Aristotle. Whence in the *Tegni*: "Healing has one mode, and its most general intention is to resolve the condition by its contrary." This is what Galen was seen to establish by induction: that cold is the contrary for a hot disposition, and heat for a cold one, and similarly for other simple and composite conditions. He also confirms this in the eleventh book of *On the Local Affections* and in the *Aphorisms*, saying that **Empiricism** <note>Knowledge based on observation and experience rather than just theory.</note> makes this so manifest that it requires very little reasoning. Indeed, it is the greatest and first principle of the healing art. There is no "reason" behind first principles; they are the end-point for all things that follow. 

Nevertheless, reason sometimes tries to confirm it: when two contraries of roughly equal power are applied to one another, a "middle point" composed of both must necessarily arise from their action and passion. This is apparent in the joining of snow or ice with fire, or with water that is not quite boiling. For since an immoderate condition (the disease) is a certain contrary "beyond nature," and a moderate condition is "according to nature" (health), it is necessary that this immoderate thing be brought back to a moderate state by the administration of another immoderate contrary—that is, calling health back by opposites. And in *On Unequal Distemper*: "All things are ended and corrupted by their contraries." Since therefore health is the destruction of the diseased disposition, it must necessarily be accomplished by the contrary. 

If anyone should snap at Galen <note>original: "mordeat Galenum"</note> that this great principle of healing ought not to be "proven" (since it is self-evident to those who possess the art), the answer is: No universal or particular science proves its own subject, as stated in the first book of the *Metaphysics* and by the Commentator in the second book of the *Physics*. For all reasoning proceeds from things that are better known.

> No science proves that its own subject exists. (Aristotle, *Metaphysics* Book 1, and Commentator, *Physics* Book 2).

<summary>This page establishes "Cure by Contraries" as the fundamental principle of medicine, explaining how nature (intrinsic), physicians (extrinsic), and even other diseases (mixed) act as opposing forces to restore the body's balance.</summary>

<header>Whether every cure is effected by its contrary. 7</header>

# Whether every cure is effected by its contrary. 7

<margin>Book 3 of the *Physics*</margin>
It must be said that Galen reinforced this principle, not so much as a physician, but rather as a natural scientist <note>original: "naturalista"</note>. It was through this same method that he introduced demonstrations in confirmation of the support of nature, and the number of elements in those books <margin>Book 1 of the *Physics*</margin> concerning them. Just as Aristotle disputes in the first book of the *Physics* against Parmenides and Melissus—who testified that all things are one and immobile—it leads to what is attested in the *Metaphysics*. Or rather, a science does not go about declaring its own subject except through certain later effects and signs to declare its own text <note>original: "verbum"</note> in whatever way, and especially the causes of the thing itself.

<margin>The Commentator on the *Physics*</margin>
Whence the Commentator <note>Averroes, the influential 12th-century philosopher</note> says on the text of the *Physics*: it is impossible for any universal or particular science to declare that its own subject exists, whether through a sign or through demonstration. This is not the case regarding the causes of the subject, since the scientist declares them through signs and not through simple demonstration. Or perhaps it was better for Galen to remain silent about demonstration in such a brief art, just as he did in the *Aphorisms*. Know also that a certain cure is not perfected by just any contrary, but by a contrary through an opposite that is equal in degree. This is fourfold, each of which is divided into three mutations <note>stages of change</note>, according to doctrine 139. And whatever work is done, it happens by joining and extending a duality to the medicine, so that something is lost in the transition, as when a suffering part lies in the depths, according to that passage in the *Art* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica* or *Tegni*</note>: if it happens that the number according to the text is exceeded by heat, and so forth.

This is also verified when a sufficiently robust power <note>original: "virtute," referring to the body's vital force</note> is assumed, so that it can tolerate a contrary correctly disposed as the opposite to the condition. For many times we do not evacuate the entire repletion through the opposite, nor do we attempt to destroy the condition through a contrary alteration, because the vigor of nature does not suffer the cure of the diseases by something opposed to itself. Whence in the first book of the text: when a great departure <margin>Book 2 of the *Physics*</margin> from equality <note>the healthy balance of the humors</note> occurs, the proportional and the non-proportional are diversified by it, because the power of the body is weakened. And therefore, this kind of treatment is omitted in the eleventh book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio," referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note>, lest the benefit of health be disparaged by unskilled people <note>original: "idiotis"</note>. However, the equality of such a cure by contrariety and duality is confirmed by reason. Since, as has been shown, if a cure is by a contrary—and if simply to the implicit, then more to the more, and most to the most, according to the text of the *Topics*—then the cure will be perfected most by the truest and greatest contrary. This, however, is according to an equal excess of degree. Furthermore, in doctrine 116, "similar" is twofold: <margin>The similar is discussed in Book 4, Article 1, and Book 5, Part...</margin> one indeed in genus, the other in species and nature, in which the definition of similarity is truly preserved. Because of this, it was shown in that same place that preservation happens most through similarity. For like is not acted upon by like, according to the eighth book of the text; thus, by reason of contrariety, a contrary will be assigned in two ways: one namely in genus, the other in species and nature, through which the cure and the destruction of the sickness will most effectively happen, since the principle of contrariety is most powerfully observed in it. This contrary, according to the text, is in an equal excess of degree to the excess of the contrary degree. Just as the dry is similar if it is productive with its own like, being at the same point in the same degree. Thus, the cure is perfected by the contrary located in an equal excess of degree. However, we cannot reach this certain degree of excess in contrariety. If we could, then our science would be like that which was attributed to Asclepius or Aesculapius <note>the Greek god of medicine</note>.

<margin>Book 3 of *On the Method of Healing*</margin>
Whence in the third book of *On the Method of Healing*: "I indeed, if I could know the nature of each individual, would be of the same science as that of Asclepius. But since this is impossible, I have studied to omit nothing of those things which human nature can comprehend in any way." For in every nature there is a certain proper moisture which can in no way be explained by the tongue. And because we cannot reach that which is certain, we administer to the "artificial nature" <note>the medical art</note> in a cure that is not by an exact equal, but by as much as we can through a contrary, trusting in its sagacious and diligent work; so that what has been added superfluously beyond the equal excess of contrariety, nature itself may cut away, and what is lacking, it may supply and increase. Regarding the fourth point: it must be said that as far as true immediate cure is concerned, as shown, it is perfected by contrariety, such that in cold cases it is necessary to re-warm. Nevertheless, because of the fear of a side effect <note>original: "accidentis"</note>, such as a future flow of blood resulting from the thinning heat in the pores and the blood being drawn outward, the warming of the coldness is prohibited from being extended immediately. Commonly, however, the flow can be warmed once it has been quieted. For although the cure should principally be directed at the dispositions <note>the underlying causes</note> and not the symptoms, as it appeared, sometimes the treatment of the symptoms themselves diverts and destroys the cure of the dispositions. Just as is shown in colic caused by "glassy phlegm" <note>a very cold, thick, and transparent humor</note> which is extremely cold; in this case, because of the intensity of the symptom (the pain), we are forced to administer a numbing <note>original: "stupefactive"</note> medicine, such as Philonium <note>a famous ancient opiate electuary</note>, opium, and the like (doctrine 24), so that sensation is removed from the limb. This is not because they remove the cause of the condition; on the contrary, such things increase and extend it further. To the other point it must be said <margin><insert>Commentator on the *Physics*</insert></margin> that nothing is contrary to those things named by the same name, such as justice to justice. For according to the Commentator on the fifth book of the *Physics*, the species of health are contrary to the species of sickness, and so forth (doctrine 65). To the other point, it must be said that he is speaking of the cure of the "dissolution of continuity" <note>a wound or break</note>, the cure of which is union through the opposite. Through the "similar," however, it is reduced back into that which had been according to nature, and then the flesh will be cured by moist things and the nerves by dry things (doctrine 107). Or there is an intrinsic general contrary to them, such as health in general, even if not singular. For health is a most specific species, as touched upon before, according to the extrinsic particular, such as the due six non-natural things <note>environmental factors like air, diet, sleep, etc.</note> and the exhibition of medicines. To the other point, it must be said that the contrary was mediated and remote. Or that nature rules with its own instruments, such as the complexion and the innate heat, and performs the cure in this way, which is set to oppose the conditions. To the other point, it must be said that this is true when their regimen is too subtle, and for that reason it causes harm in another way. For too much smallness of a mixture in a foul state brings harm; just as a substance of the world generates "cholera" <note>yellow bile</note> and exhales a bran-like vapor, which causes no less pain than heavy, pressed food, as it induces more or less of the same differences in the *Art*. Whence, when they have not attained the correct contrarieties, a cure does not follow, but rather a *synocha* <note>a type of continuous fever; OCR: "finothoa"</note> intervenes. To the other point, it must be said similarly, except only... To the other point, it must be said...

It also discusses the practical dilemma of treating painful symptoms (like colic) with medicines that might technically worsen the underlying cold disposition.</summary>

For cold water, by gathering natural heat together again and creating *antiperistasis* <note>A physical phenomenon where a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as internal heat being concentrated by external cold.</note>, heats by strengthening that very heat. This ultimately, by way of contrariety and as an instrument, heats and dissolves cold and moist humors. This is a visible proof. This is because it stirs nature, along with the spirits and humors, to pass from one part to another, so that the matter is removed from the painful place and the pain subsides. For it evacuates the bile that is the cause. Furthermore, in such an action, the previously mentioned "contrariety of position" is preserved, because the scammony occupies one place and the matter to be drawn out occupies another. This is shown by the attraction of the bile. For when the action of the scammony reaches it, it acts like a magnet applied to iron. And perhaps there is a

He suggests that through a moistening diet, scammony <note>original: "dygridiū," dacrydium, the thickened juice of scammony</note> gains strength. Thus, that which is hot and dry (and therefore contrary to a "choleric" or bilious quality) is invited by the diet to deposit the humor. Therefore, we offer cold and moist foods, such as lettuce and soft-boiled eggs. By the contrary, the flame is heated and put down. The matter is heated and moistened, and thus the humors are deposited. But then I would say the attraction occurs not through an "occult virtue" <note>A hidden or inexplicable power</note> but rather through their manifest quality. Many find this explanation burdensome. Furthermore, they would never draw anything out unless predisposed by foods. This is not strictly necessary, though it completes the process more suitably. Regarding another point, it must be said that "contrary" is taken commonly for any opposition or diversity that can be found in quantity. Or better, because disease is not simply a matter of quantity, but of quality, since it is a quality or disposition that naturally harms action. It is founded, however, sometimes in continuous or discrete quantity, as when there is too much humor. To another point: perfectly equal things are not found. Or if they are, one overcomes the other through frequent repetition, as a medicine overcomes a disease. Furthermore, nature here governs the auxiliary medicines, but it would be stirred to fury if the medicine remained for too long, immediately passing into that which it dominates.

## SECTION 154

**T**hat the cure of a disease should be initiated with a strong medicine is shown by the second book of Aphorisms. Following the principle of those illnesses from which the patient hopes to be saved, one must attempt to offer greater aids. This is also supported by Galen in the fourth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio [sanitatis]"</note>, where he detests Erasistratus <note>An ancient Greek anatomist who often disagreed with the Galenic/Hippocratic tradition</note> for beginning even in a strong illness with a weaker medicine. Also, in the fourth part of the fourth book: when ulcers are being cured, they need a "bite" <note>a sharp or stinging sensation</note> at first, and then gradually one should arrive at a milder treatment. Furthermore, when the matter is plentiful and clinging to the parts, it needs a very powerful medicine. For a strong medicine is truly needed when the illness is "firmly established" according to the fourth book of *Aphorisms*. This happens at the beginning of a disease when the matter has not yet been changed in any way. Again, as in the previous section: a cure is perfected by a contrary of equal power in a gradual disease, but at the start of a disease, the medicine exceeds it in quantity and quality, since no evacuation or alteration has yet been undertaken by nature. Again, everything harmful should be expelled from the body quickly and forcefully since it is corrupt. Such is a disease even at its beginning, since by its nature it essentially harms the body's operations. Also, when nature is strong, it requires a strong medicine; and nature is strong at the onset of a disease, as it has not yet been exhausted by the illness. The symptoms indicate this. For around the beginnings and the ends, all symptoms are weaker according to the ancients; but around the "status" <note>The peak or height of the disease</note>, they are stronger. Therefore, in the beginning of a disease,
<margin>3</margin>
the treatment should start with a strong medicine. The opposite of this is also written: that the cure should begin with a weak medicine. For it is written in the first part of the third book that we should start with a weaker medicine and proceed gradually until we know from the disposition of the disease that it has been cut off. Whence Mesue <note>A famous Persian or Arab physician, likely Masawayh</note> says in his *Practica*: Let us begin with the lighter things, just as those who precede us moved to greater things. Likewise, in the fourth book, he teaches to cure acute illnesses and "phlegmonous" <note>Inflamed or swollen</note> areas of the upper abdomen at the beginning with bloodletting, while detesting the use of drugs <note>original: "farmacie"</note>, since they draw nothing from the inflamed parts nor remit the passion, but rather the resistance to the disease and the healthy parts are gathered. But bloodletting is a lighter treatment than drugs. Again, art is the image and follower of nature. Nature itself always begins from weak things and proceeds to stronger ones. Whence it is proved: nature at the end achieves its goal quickly, but not at the beginning. Therefore, 
<margin>4</margin>
the cure should be started with a weaker medicine. Regarding the first point, it must be known how a cure is performed, as noted in the previous section. For it is the removal of a disease through its opposite, as it was said that it is always perfected by a contrary. What a disease is, and what a medicine is, has been shown. Medicine itself is an aid that expels disease by alteration or evacuation. It is
<margin>5</margin>
therefore twofold: One is "altering," acting through quality without entering the substance of the body, by heating, cooling, drying, or moistening. The other is "evacuating" in the ways previously touched upon.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the methodology of treatment. Having previously discussed the principle of contraries, the text now enters a debate on the "Differentia" or specific question of whether a physician should initiate treatment with powerful, aggressive remedies or gentler, weaker ones, citing the historical disagreements between Galen and Erasistratus.</meta>

->## Whether the Treatment of a Disease Should Begin with Strong Medicine<-

Indeed, **Erasistratus** <note>Erasistratus of Ceos (c. 304–250 BCE), a Greek physician known for his anatomical studies but often criticized by Galen for his conservative treatment methods.</note> used to begin the treatment of severe and dangerous illnesses with weak medicine, such as the avoidance of bloodletting. **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 CE), the most influential physician of antiquity whose works formed the basis of medieval medicine.</note> attacks him in *The Method of Medicine* <note>original: "de ingenio," referring to Galen's *De methodo medendi* (On the Therapeutic Method).</note>, comparing him to a sailor who neglects his ship while it is still seaworthy until it is broken apart, and then hands each person a plank, telling them to escape if they can. Some, however, began with weak medicine out of fear that a strong medicine might cause a sudden, harmful change in the patient's nature. Their error is revealed in the third and fourth points to be discussed. Regarding the third point, it must be known that disease is of two types. One is dangerous and "crafty," <note>original: "uersuta," meaning a disease that is complex, deceptive, or rapidly changing.</note> whether the danger is imminent or delayed. The other is the opposite. The first type must be treated with strong medicine immediately from the beginning, unless the strong medicine is contraindicated; for example, an acute enema <term>clyster: an intestinal wash or enema</term> should not be used first in cases of fecal colic <note>Colic caused by an obstruction of stool.</note>. In such a case, the priority is first to soften the blockage and then proceed with the rest. For other diseases, weak medicine should be used. Hence, against Erasistratus, Galen says: we ought not to act like small and weak doctors who claim that the beginning of a cure must always be made with small and minute medicines, and only if those do not prevail, should great and strong ones be used. While that may be a safer path in minor ailments, in those diseases from which a patient may die—such as if **consumption** <note>original: "ptisim" (phthisis), a wasting disease, usually pulmonary tuberculosis.</note> has set in—the beginning must not be made with small medicines, but with strong and frequent ones. <margin>3<br/>4^o</margin> Therefore, as stated in the first and fourth parts: in illnesses where there is fear, and safety is not guaranteed due to a lack of strength, if we delay what we ought to do, or if we alleviate the treatment too much, we must begin with strong medicine first. However, in those where no such fear exists, the treatment should proceed in order toward the stronger, if the weak medicine does not suffice. <margin>Alexander</margin> For this reason, **Alexander** <note>Likely Alexander of Tralles (6th c. CE), a Byzantine physician.</note> relates that in a case of **quinsy** <term>synanche: a severe sore throat or peritonsillar abscess that could lead to suffocation</term> he knew that the veins under the tongue were incised in the morning and evening, and a dose of **barley water** with **diagridium** <note>A preparation of scammony juice, a potent purgative.</note> was given in the evening. Each part of this distinction is proven by authority. For according to **Hippocrates**: <margin>Hippocrates</margin> For extreme diseases, extreme treatments are most effective in their certainty. A "dangerous disease" is categorized among these extreme cases. Furthermore, one should administer drugs in very acute cases if it is desired on the same day, because in such cases, delay is an evil. <margin>Aphorisms</margin> This is from the fourth of the *Aphorisms*. <margin>3<br/>4^o</margin> But on the same day the disease begins, it is "in the beginning," and **pharmacy** <note>In this context, "farmacia" refers to the administration of strong purgative drugs.</note> is called a strong medicine. Also, for extreme fullness, an extreme evacuation is required, according to the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*, often called *Tegni* in the Middle Ages.</note>. And similarly, for every disease, the ultimate remedy is required through its opposite and direct contrary. But this applies to the "craftier" or more complex disease; therefore, at the onset of such a disease, strong medicine must be used. But on the contrary, **apoplexy** <note>A sudden loss of consciousness or paralysis, similar to a stroke.</note> is the most dangerous and crafty of diseases. Yet in the third part of the first book, it is written that you should begin with the weakest of ointments if the patient can bear it, and if not, change to that which is stronger. It must be said that in the aforementioned disease, one should begin with a strong medicine that is inherently strong in its ability to evacuate, especially in preparing and altering the humors. Such an ointment is not of that kind. It speaks also of "testing" the patient: when he says "if he can bear it," just as Hippocrates says the cure for **pleurisy** is with heating agents (as in the 30th rule of *On Acute Diseases*). Or he says this because evacuation must be preceded by preparation. The other side of the aforementioned distinction is also demonstrated: because when the matter is undigested, resting, and nearly immobile, it does not need a stronger "altering" or "uprooting" agent. Such is the state in the beginning. Again: Nature does not endure sudden changes, since everything sudden is an enemy to nature (according to the second book of *Aphorisms*). But if one begins with a strong medicine at the start of a disease when nature is weak and fearful, a sudden change is introduced; because nature is weak, it cannot hold up under it. Nature still possesses its natural character, which one ought to alter gradually and through similar things rather than violent ones. Therefore, here one must begin with weak medicine. The first part of the opposing argument is also shown by recorded experience, and consequently, it is a known fact. Indeed, those cures ought to be applied to the disease and its symptoms by altering and evacuating. Regarding the reason for **alteration**: if a **burning fever** <term>causonic: a high, inflammatory fever</term> should be so burning and scorching that an inflammation of the brain and stomach, and finally a spasm, is feared, it is commanded that it be extinguished violently and immediately with a cooling substance. <margin>Ethics<br/>in the Method</margin> Even in a desperate case of **hectic fever** <note>original: "Ethica," referring to a slow, wasting fever associated with consumption.</note>, it is commanded to cast the patient immediately into cold water, so that he might pass into the "hectic of old age," in which he can live longer than in the former states (from *The Method of Medicine*). In a **spasm**, however, we are taught to assist with warm applications. Regarding **evacuation**: blood should be drawn even unto **fainting** <term>lipothymia: a clinical swoon or fainting fit, often induced by physicians to stop a hemorrhage or reset the system</term> in fevers caused by it, and further in other diseases like **apoplexy** and **quinsy**, provided other factors allow. And similarly, in cases of intense pain and the most burning fevers, the drug is ordered to be given on the first or second day even unto fainting and exhaustion. The symptom itself demands this, as seen in the most violent **colic**, in which for fear of a swift death, a **narcotic** is administered, or **wine** in a case of **syncope** <note>Fainting or loss of consciousness due to a drop in blood pressure.</note> arising from a similar cause. Therefore, in a minor disease, a light medicine should be used first; in the other, a stronger one. But on the contrary, **Avicenna** <note>original: "A.," referring to the Persian physician Ibn Sina (980–1037 CE).</note> concerning the cure for **paralysis**: <margin>A. 2. 3.</margin> Do not rush into the use of strong medicines at the beginning of the matter; rather, wait until the fourth or seventh day. What if the disease is strong even until the seventeenth day? They say, therefore, to treat with strong medicines when the disease is strong. It must be said that although paralysis is "strong" by reason of the matter having become viscous <note>Sticky or thick humors, such as phlegm, which were thought to cause nerve blockages.</note>, it requires much digestive preparation with altering agents before a strong evacuation; however, it is not "strong" by reason of the acute effect of the disease or its symptoms, which is the primary subject of this discussion. Regarding the fourth point, although it may appear from what has been said, it must still be stated. What then is used for the first? To the other point, it must be said that the condition in a **pruritic** <note>Itchy or stinging.</note> ulcer is not the same at the beginning and later; since at first it is more discharging and less sensible. Hence, Avicenna says: Sensation does not feel it at first. For it requires cleansing with something that can achieve this without pain. To the other point, it must be said that although the matter is...

# DIFFERENTIA 155

<margin>1</margin>
Whether odor cures only by altering and not by nourishing: it is asked whether it nourishes itself. For according to *On the Sense and the Sensible* <note>Aristotle’s *De sensu et sensato*</note>, that which is smellable does not contribute to nourishment, but clearly to health. For just as flavor is to nourishment, so is the smellable to health. This is proven in a twofold way against the **Pythagoreans**, who proposed that certain animals are nourished by odors. Perhaps they believed this because of the air, because they found the internal organs of these animals empty upon dissection, as it was said. Since just as the things nourished are composed of matter, so must the food be, for no simple, incorporeal thing nourishes. But an odor of this kind, since it is a certain spiritual and intentional quality <note>In medieval philosophy, an "intentional" quality is one that exists in the senses or the mind as a representation, rather than as a heavy physical substance.</note>, as will be seen. This is supported by the fact that simple, pure water, which seems more likely to nourish, does not do so, even though it appears more substantial and corporeal than air, in which the aforementioned quality is placed. It would similarly be necessary for a surplus of it to be produced internally as in animals, or externally as in plants. Furthermore, that which nourishes has need of a place for its own digestion, such as the entrails. But the "flow" of odor is in the head. Moreover, the objects of the senses are unmixed, as are the senses themselves, since they are distinguished by opposites. But the objects of touch nourish the animal and precede the sense of smell. <margin>4th [book of] Boethius's *Topics*</margin> For one opposite species does not help another to exist, according to the fourth book of **Boethius's** *Topics*. Also, the matter from which one is nourished is the same as that from which one is first constituted, according to the *Generation of Animals*, book 13. For all things are nourished by the same things from which they are made, from the *Generation and Corruption*. But we are not made of odors, but rather from spermatic humors. Furthermore <note>original: "Palyn," Greek for "again" or "furthermore"</note>, nothing nourishes unless it first passes through the threefold place of digestion, according to the third book of *Complexions*. But odor, though it reaches the nostrils, does not pass through this place, since it seeks the brain through the nostrils. Also, everything that nourishes must be transformed into a mass of "parts" <note>original: "p̄tistana riaz," likely a corruption of "prostitanariaz" or similar scholastic terminology for processed matter</note> and finally be converted into a humor, since it is almost alone in being said to nourish. Therefore, odor does not cure by nourishing, but rather by strengthening through alteration.

On the contrary is **Galen**, with the majority of physicians, following the opinion of the *Aphorisms*. Whatever things require the swiftest addition of moisture are best for the restoration of strength. Where indeed is there a swifter path than through smelling? Also, that which delights, refills and completes, nourishes, since it pertains to the reason of that which is nutritional. Such indeed is odor. Whence, in the sixth book of *Epidemics* <note>Hippocrates' *Epidemics*</note>: odors are "lighteners," that is, resolved into a vaporous emanation, delightful, refilling, and completing. Furthermore, in the eleventh book of *On the Generation [of Animals]*: the substance of the "virtue" <note>original: "uirtutis," meaning the vital power or spirit of the body</note> is filled by a carniform <note>flesh-like</note> substance, both by the spirit and by the solid. For from the likenesses of each, it is necessary for the spirit to operate its virtue. For the spirit, it is generated through respiration, transpiration, and the evaporation of the blood; for the solids, through solid food. Thus is generated the carniform species through the nature of the "black" <note>original: "melā," likely referring to black bile or a dark humor</note> of moist and solid bodies. But the prior mode of nutrition is of the spirit, at least through the introduction of the vapor of a smellable air. Therefore, odor also has the power to cure by nourishing, and not only by altering. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known that odor is the nature or form of a dry *euchimus* <term>euchimus: a Greek-derived term meaning "good humor" or "healthy juice"</term> <margin>Odor</margin>—that is, something humor-like—in a moist medium, namely one that is washable and cleansable; for by such a moisture it is born to be washed and cleansed. For the smellable is not an affection of the air and water insofar as they are transparent (which is common to them), but rather by reason of a certain washing and cleansing of the dry *euchimus*. Note that the ancients commonly said that odor is a smoky evaporation. Which is surprising, because up to now **Aristotle** attributes this to the moderns, though he himself attacks it, saying it occurs for animals in water, such as fish, and in air, such as others. But a smoky evaporation is an affection of the earth and air, and not of water. Therefore, according to this, aquatic animals would not smell, since such a smoky evaporation cannot exist in water, whose affection is vapor. Neither can it be said that odor is a certain "outflowing," because then it would not remain in the air, but in water alone. But I say that if something common to water and air is found, then according to this attack of Aristotle, it will be a suitable description of odor. Let it be said that odor is a vaporous diffusion or emanation. For one of these seems to belong to water, and the other to air. Nevertheless, it is placed in the fourth [book of the *Meteorology*?] and is quite improperly called vaporous, since that is a common affection of all four elements. For he intends that the vapor of the earth, through a correspondence in one of the qualities, is received by the water; and by the water, for a similar reason, by the air. And so, that which is from the air is from the fire. And thus, being dissolved, it reaches our sense. The followers of Aristotle, however, attack the aforementioned description of odor differently, saying that odor is not a smoky evaporation or a vaporous diffusion, because odor sometimes reaches—as happens with the incense of the Greeks—for five hundred leagues, and even a thousand, following the diameter in the opposite direction...

<margin>Note that the odor of corpses in battle reaches five hundred leagues.</margin>

-> **Whether Odor cures by altering or by nourishing.** <-

# Does an odor cure by altering and not by nourishing?

<margin>In primary cases / through the nasal passage / in the nostrils / with almost alone... / nourishment. B cures / thus it is found / in the fici <note>possibly referring to "ficus" or growths</note> / truly more quickly / it refills before the end.</margin>

As stated directly. However, it is absurd to think that the aforementioned evaporation happens in such a way. And perhaps someone besides them will say: that they place odor as a real thing in the medium <note>In medieval philosophy, the "medium" is the substance, like air or water, through which a sense travels.</note>. If this evaporation were "intentional," the description would be corrected and saved. However, this vaporous diffusion is called the cause of the odor rather than the odor itself. Whence, **Aristotle** <note>original: "A.", standard abbreviation for Aristotle</note> says in the first book of *On Sense and the Sensible*, the primary cause in proximity to the power of smelling is a subtle, vaporous **substance**. And this speech is indeed more exquisite in the exposition of the *Problems*, part twelve. 

Truly, there are two types of odors. One which is called "per se" <note>essential or in itself</note>, such as a sweet or foul odor—pleasant or horrible—like that of flowers or corpses. The other is "per accidens" <note>accidental or by association</note>, and by its similarity to flavors; thus it is called delightful or distressing, depending on how one is affected by **nourishment**. It is also called sweet, bitter, and so on. For we have a poor sense of the types of odor, since we have this sense much more weakly than other animals (as noted in book 45). It should also be noted, according to the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the "Great Commentator" on Aristotle</note> on the second book of *On the Soul*, that just as color has a twofold existence—one in the defined or colored body, which is its natural existence, and another in the medium or transparent substance, which is external to it—so too does odor. <margin>Truly another</margin> For one existence is in the separable moisture or the odorous body, which is its physical and natural existence. The other is in the medium, which is spiritual and external. I add also that in the medium it also has a twofold existence. One is real or natural, when the medium is not very far away and there is an odorous vaporous emanation of no small size, such as a very subtle airy evaporation over burning coals, provided its body is nearby. But when the medium is very wide, or the odorous thing is not such as to alter the extreme, it reaches toward the organ "intentionally" or "spiritually" <note>In this context, "intentional" means the smell travels as an image or "species" without the physical vapor particles reaching the nose.</note> alone, as shown by the sense of touch. 

I assert also that in whatever way the odor reaches the organ—whether the odorous thing is present or not—it arrives "intentionally" alone, since the sense is a receiver of forms without matter (from the second book of *On the Soul*). Whence Aristotle says in the same place: To sense is to receive the form of the thing stripped of its matter, and to be informed by it. This "intentionality" is almost material and as if bodily compared to the spirituality of color, and especially in the medium and in sound, approaching the nature of touch and taste. This is shown by the fact that many contrary "intentions" of sight can be perceived in the same medium, and to some extent sound, but odors cannot. Know then that although the intentional odor may change the organ more, it can exist in the medium both "really" and "intentionally," depending on whether the distance is small or great. This is shown by the fact that an object of touch, such as heat and cold, can exist "really" in the medium and change the object "intentionally" as a species of heat and cold. 

What nutrition is was shown in distinction 30. To nourish is also twofold: one is proper, such as **nourishment** acting on its own matter; the other is metaphorical, as an agent altering and strengthening by its own quality, which true nutrition eventually follows. That thing needs nutrition which <margin>1</margin> is dissolved and lost. Our substance is threefold: **spirit**, flesh-like substance, and solid **spermatic** <note>In medieval medicine, "spermatic" tissues were the solid parts like bone and nerve, thought to be formed from the original reproductive "seed."</note> substance, as said before. 

What it means to "cure" and "alter" is known from its own inquiries. Regarding the second point, it should be known that there is a disagreement in this question, as appeared from the arguments. Some have even said that nourishment occurs through touch alone via moisture. But regarding these, it will appear in the third part of the propositions, and more in the fourth. 

Regarding the third point, it should be known that odor nourishes with true nutrition, specifically the **spirits**, and properly the "animal spirits" <note>The "animal spirit" (from *anima*, soul) was a refined fluid in the brain responsible for sensation and movement.</note>. This happens in the medium first through vaporous emanation, then passing through the windpipe into the lungs and heart, and finally through the youthful arteries into the **wonderful net** <note>The "rete mirabile," a network of vessels at the base of the brain where spirits were thought to be refined.</note>, where it is digested significantly; and reaching further into the brain and being more fully digested, the **spirit** nourishes and repairs those that are dissolved. It does not, however, truly nourish when it meets the organ of smell, for then it is a certain simple quality and almost more "intentional." But before that, as it exists in the medium, it participates in "bodiliness." Therefore, odor and heat can be understood in two ways: for the odorous body itself and for the odoriferous quality. It nourishes the grosser parts, like the flesh-like and solid parts, more by strengthening them with that quality than by substance. 

Whence, in *On the Utility of the Parts*, it was said in the discourse on breath according to the opinion of **Hippocrates**, that it has a twofold utility: one and the chief is the preservation of innate heat; the other is the soothing nutrition of the animal spirit. And in the seventh book of *On the Benefits*, the third utility of breath is to feed the animal spirit. And in the ninth book of *On the Generation of the Spirit*, the spirit is irrigated and nourished through inspiration and the presentation of what is folded back from the net-like structure. Furthermore, in the eleventh book, in many cases of syncope <note>fainting or loss of consciousness</note>, one must begin and work with that which nourishes the **spirit** from good odors, unless the syncope is caused by a "suffocation of the womb." Whence, in *Medicines for the Heart*: of two medicines equal in power, the sweeter and more aromatic one is of more effective help; and therefore the attractive power of the mind receives it more strongly, and the spirit is nourished more quickly from it, if it has the power of nourishing. And it is more quickly affected by it insofar as <margin>3</margin> it is a medicine. 

Even **John of Alexandria**, commenting on the passage "Lifting Odors": some report a miracle about **Democritus**, that when he wished to depart this life, mocking it, a solemn festival was to be celebrated in the city of Abdera where he was. And the Abderites <margin>4</margin> asked him not to die, lest the city be in mourning during the festival. Democritus responded to them: "For how many days do you want me to wait?" They said, "For three or four days, which are the days of the feast." And he then ordered a vessel of honey to be brought to him, and he remained there for four days smelling it <margin>John of Alexandria / Democritus / in life</margin>. Others, however, said that he ordered an oven to be opened and bread to be baked in it, and thus he survived on the odor of the bread. And this is perhaps what **Oribasius** recites in his *Aphorisms*. A certain philosopher reports that he lived for forty days on the odor of honey. But I think the text is corrupt.

It can happen that one reaches the other when the acting and receiving parts are joined by contact. Moreover, a liquid is less [airy], and that which has gone further. And there, a light, pure **animal spirit** is made.

Theorica, book 3.
</margin>

Thirdly, according to theory: Air was necessary for **concoction** <note>original: "coctio"; the physiological process of "cooking" or digesting food and humors using natural heat</note>. For external air also nourishes and increases the vital spirit. And because the vital spirit is the matter of the animal [spirit], it nourishes this generally.

<margin>
Alexander.
</margin>

Whence **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle</note> in the *Problems* says: Air entering through inspiration is refined in the heart and, ascending through the arteries to the brain, is constituted as the food of the brain and the animal spirit. If it exists as a body, it is shaped to the body. If, however, it is a most pure and splendid subtle smoke, it is directed by the rational soul.

<margin>
Nicolaus the Peripatetic.
</margin>

**Nicolaus the Peripatetic**, however, in his *Problems*, says: It is necessary to know that the preservation of heat happens through air, not (as some think) for its cooling, but rather for its nourishment. For in small animals, the heat is small. Therefore, sufficient air can enter through the pores of the body for its nourishment. Thus, odor not only cures by altering, but even by nourishing, and it especially nourishes the spirit by a true nutrition, as prefigured.

<margin>
Odor contributes to nutrition.
</margin>

Odor also, insofar as it carries an "intentional" quality, contributes—though not properly and only indirectly—to the spirits. Truly, it nourishes with the soul and comforts the parts. Once this is done, they truly nourish, just like the "accidents" of the soul, bringing joy and delight. Also, a most sweet odor is the food of the soul (Aristotle, *On the Secrets*). And **Damascene** <note>John of Damascus</note> in his *Aphorisms*: Smell—and especially if the smoke reaches the head—assists the brain more quickly than what one drinks. But there is a doubt concerning the aforementioned...

---

...since it was proposed that air nourishes. The opposite of this is written in *On Sense and the Sensible* thus: Neither does water tend to nourish by itself without being mixed. And this is much more reasonable regarding air. Furthermore, no "simple" <note>a pure element like air, water, fire, or earth</note> nourishes, since it is necessary to restore the same kind of thing that was lost. From the first book of *Elements*: Those things which are composed of several parts are preserved entirely by such things as those which compose them. But that which is lost is a composite mixture. And therefore, in book 10: It is not as some think, that air alone is converted so as to become spirit, just as water alone does not nourish; rather, each thing is joined, or is a part of the nourishment, or causes it to penetrate by its lubricity. But water is for the nourishment of the body, and air for the nourishment of the spirit. And each of the two—namely, the nourishment of the body and of the spirit—is a composite body, not a simple one. And therefore, in *The Collectio* <note>possibly the *Collectio Salernitana* or a similar medical compendium</note>, book 3: It is impossible for a composite to be nourished by a simple element; for then the animal would be simple, made from one single element, contrary to **Hippocrates** in *On Human Nature*. Therefore, air does not nourish anything.

It must be said that "air," and indeed "all things," can be understood in two ways. Either as it is a pure, simple, and singular element—and in this way, as argued, it does not sufficiently nourish—or as it exists mixed with others in its sphere, as happens most especially in this discussion (book 32). For those things, such as earth and vapors, are mixed as they ascend, and fire flows down through the solar rays, and from the refraction of those rays reaching the earth and water, the same is stirred up. Whence, from the first book of *Elements*: It is not necessary to seek pure, unmixed earth in animal bodies, because you cannot point to such a thing even in the world. For no matter how small a part you take, it soon participates in heat, humidity, and air. And it is the same in others. Wherefore, in the first book of *Medicines*: None of the four elements we use is pure; there is no element that is not mixed with another in our speech and use. Water, however, is far from this; it is pure and clean. But that which is so mixed can even truly and properly nourish, because it requires little nutrition—as is shown especially by the spirit, and specifically the animal spirit. For in the most subtle and clear water, **basil** <note>original: "ozimum" (Ocimum basilicum)</note> lives and is nourished; it continually grows and flourishes, not even losing its scent. And in the same way, I observe fish in clear, subtle spring water, uniquely pressed against the stones—especially **trout**, **crayfish** <note>original: "cancralia"</note>, and the like—living and being nourished for a very long time; even worms in wells of limpid and clear water likewise. And the little lizard called the **Salamander**. And from this, it appears what must be said regarding the previous points, when the element is concluded to be simple and pure. Regarding the fourth point: For the first, it appeared that one must say that when Aristotle takes odor as a simple "odorous quality" and not as a vaporous diffusion. For it has been shown that an element can nourish when it is impure <note>i.e., mixed</note>, nor does odor nourishing in this way have a sensible excess as if it were received in a physical place; for it breathes through without being sensed. Regarding the other point, it must be said that there are...

It must be said that an odor of this kind is truly nourishing to the **sensible body** <note>the physical body capable of sensation</note>, being a certain vaporous diffusion affected by the primary and secondary qualities of touch, but not the tertiary ones. For then it brings about a simple sensory emptiness.

Regarding the other point, it should be said that we are composed of odors; for the principles of our generation were watery and airy matter, emanating more vaporous things from the beginning. To the next point, the answer is already apparent.

Regarding another point, it must be said that we should hear this concerning nutrition in its sustaining parts, specifically those of the coarser parts. The **subtle spirit** <note>original: "spiritus subtilis"; the refined "vapor" believed to circulate in the nerves and arteries to facilitate life</note>, however, is nourished by subtle parts. That which is properly nourished is innate and implanted within the principles of our construction. For that which is flowing or "running" is generated daily from food through the motion of the heart and the digestion of the arteries; it is refined and turned into the aforementioned spirit, as discussed in the fifth book of *Simple Medicines* <note>original: "simpliciū quinto"; referring to Galen's work on simple drugs</note>. This "running" spirit, however, does not truly nourish, since it becomes smaller or larger with almost every intake, as noted in the eleventh book of *On the Art of Healing* <note>original: "xi. de inge."; likely Galen’s *Methodus Medendi*</note>. That which truly nourishes must remain.

Regarding the points made about other parts, the answer is now clear. For it is concluded that odor nourishes insofar as it is a body dissolved from an odorous object and taken inward; but certainly not insofar as it exists as a simple, intentional quality.

## DIFFERENCE 156

->**Whether prayer contributes to a cure.**<-

That incantation <note>original: "precantatio" and "incantatio" are used interchangeably here to mean rhythmic prayer, chanting, or spells</note> does not contribute to a cure is shown as follows. Regarding the cure for love: "No thing will set aside the cares born in the heart." Galen, in the sixth book of *Individual Simples*, is said to speak against certain doctors who use incantations and "sworn herbs."

Furthermore, in the first book of *On Interpretation* <note>original: "pyermenias"; from the Greek "Peri Hermeneias" by Aristotle</note>, because of affirming or denying, a speech will not be true or false <note>in the sense of having physical power over reality</note>. An incantation is a certain affirmative or negative speech. Just as a thing relates to truth and falsehood, so it relates to action, according to the tenth book of the *Metaphysics*. Therefore, because of an affirmation or negation, it will do nothing to our bodies. Also, nothing acts beyond its own species. But an incantation, since it is a speech, belongs to the category of **Quantity** <note>original: "quantitatis"; in Aristotelian logic, speech is a "discrete quantity" because it is measured by syllables</note> in the *Predicaments*. Health, however, is in the category of **Quality**, or perhaps **Relation**. These differ not only in species but even in genus. Also, an incantation moves something only intentionally <note>mentally or symbolically</note>, while health is something real. Furthermore, in the first part of the fourth book: the work of healing is perfected by three things—namely, nourishing things like drinks or medicine, and manual operation <note>surgery</note>. Whence, in Galen's *To Paternianus*: the medicine of the whole body is reduced to these three: drugs, iron, and fire. But an incantation is none of these, as is shown by an examination of them. Again, that which heals must be able to "alter" the body, since health is introduced into it. But an incantation does not alter matter; for things of this kind must share in matter, which is not present in an incantation, as was touched upon before.

Therefore, incantation does not contribute to healing.

<margin>
Homer
</margin>

**On the contrary:** Because **Homer** <note>the Greek epic poet</note> relates in the first rhapsody <note>Book 1 of the Iliad</note> how the priest **Chryses** <note>original: "beris"; likely a scribal error for Chryses</note>, on account of his daughter **Chryseis** <note>original: "Briseydaz", though the priest's daughter was Chryseis; Briseis was the woman taken from Achilles</note> being snatched by Agamemnon, returning along the shore of the whispering sea, having not obtained her, prayed with an incantation to the Sun <note>Apollo</note>, saying how he had sacrificed to him and would sacrifice again if he would take vengeance on the Greeks. Thus the Sun, being summoned, sent arrows or rays from his bow and caused a plague, first in the mules and white dogs, and finally in the men, so that Agamemnon was forced to return the girl to the priest. Calchas the son of Thestor assigned the cause of the plague to this. Also, in the third book, first part, *On Love*: words contribute to this chapter. Furthermore, in *On the Cause of the Motion of Animals*: in a certain way, a perceived form is the cause of heat or cold, or of delight or stability, just as each thing exists; because of this, those who understand tremble and fear, even when things are not present but only through the power of **imagination** <note>original: "ymaginatō"; the author suggests that if the mind can cause physical chills or heat through thought, words can too</note>. This, as will appear, is what an incantation is. Furthermore, that which generates confidence in health in a sick person helps in the cure. Such is the incantation, as reason will judge. Therefore, it contributes to the cure.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that **Socrates** <note>the Greek philosopher</note> is written to have said that incantations are "words deceiving human souls." But to speak on the present matter: an
<margin>
Socrates
</margin>
<margin>
Incantation
</margin>
incantation is an admirable speech explained with a helping affection for the one being incanted, especially for one who is confident. It is called a "speech" to distinguish it from meaningless terms; when it concerns wondrous and occult things, the one being incanted will value it more, and it will benefit them more. And therefore, one should use secrecy as much as possible. For he diminishes the **Deity** <note>the divine power or sacredness of the rite</note> who broadcasts mystical secrets. The **Notory Art** <term>Ars Notoria</term> <note>a medieval system of "angelic magic" intended to gain knowledge through prayers and figures</note> also teaches that the practitioner must utter the incantations with even greater diligence, so that they are regarded as more worthy by both the practitioner and the patient, thus providing more benefit. For when the patient is more confident in it, it will help him the most, according to that saying: "He heals more illnesses in whom more people have confidence."

It is also proven to be beneficial by its explanation. Since speech is threefold, according to **Boethius** in his commentary on *On Interpretation*: one kind is formed in the mind as a concept; another in pronunciation, according to the *Categories* (I call this speech as a spoken voice); and the third in writing, such as that which is expressed in letters and characters and finally tied to the neck or elsewhere <note>as an amulet</note>. Furthermore, the incantator must be shrewd, believing, affectionate, and of a strong, impressive soul. And rightly so; for since an incantation is something intentional, it does not act effectively unless the aforementioned conditions are found, since the "action of agents is in the patient" and the recipient must be predisposed. Therefore, the practitioner changes and alters that which is most changeable—namely, the animal powers, and especially in dreams, when other bodily motions cease. For these are especially powerful in opposing things: first the vital power, and finally the natural power, as it is more material than the others. For example, **estimation** <note>the internal sense that judges intentions, like a lamb fearing a wolf</note> changes a human more than a brute animal. For one is moved more by a giant than by any other... <note>The final sentence fragment discusses the psychological and physiological reactions of humans compared to animals.</note>

Either because they were crude unbelievers, not thinking that any actions could occur unless by a material and coarser means, through certain immediate primary qualities <note>the basic qualities of hot, cold, wet, and dry</note> of the more sensible powers. For they cast spells on medicines, sprinkled them, and fumigated them divinely when they pulled them from the ground, so that they might hang them around the neck or elsewhere for the sake of help in the manner of **phylacteries** <term>phylacteries (filateriarum): protective amulets or charms, often containing written texts, worn on the body</term>. All of which is false and foolish, and a detestation of the medical art. For those who cling to such things have abandoned the proper methods of the art. Others, however, standing outside this opinion, and fearing to contradict incantations, proceeded through both of the aforementioned paths. Therefore, it must first be known: that an incantation does not benefit in a cure insofar as it is itself [the spoken words]. But finally, insofar as it is such—namely, as it is received from the one delivering or swearing it, or from the one instituting or causing it. Therefore, first it must be known <margin>4</margin> that if an incantation benefited insofar as it is a simple prayer, then all would. The falsity of which is obvious. And also, such a chant consists in a certain sonorous explanation. Because such a thing does not by itself alter the body toward health, since it induces an alteration that does not change it; hence the second and third books of *On the Soul*. It is manifest that neither light nor darkness, nor sound nor odor, produces any effect in bodies, namely, except by accident; for instance, if by a sound being driven out a blow occurs, as in thunder splitting wood. And similarly from things seen and smelled, a motion is made...

...accidentally by motion. For we are affected by primary qualities, but not by tertiary ones. Therefore, in chanting, the cure is not completed as such. Therefore, second, it must be known: that experience can demonstrate, and finally reason can persuade, that incantation confers benefit. Regarding this, in both physics and purpose, there are many empirical examples. For instance, that greatest sacrament, along with many others, shows the power of the Eucharist. Divine names also confirm this in the notorious art <note>the *Ars Notoria*, a medieval grimoire</note> and the art of prayer. Also, with magical words spoken into the ear of a bull, when the enchanter persisted in the face of death in the presence of a Silurus <note>possibly a reference to a type of fish or a river deity</note>: he caused it to come back to life again. This is also confirmed by the movement of bread to find a theft, or of a psalter or a sieve <note>divination techniques where objects move to identify a culprit</term>. Also, certain words spoken in the ear of any man make him eager to grant you whatever you have asked. Similarly, an incantation spoken or written so that those being tortured never reveal secrets. They also walk upon a very sharp sword and live coals. And by applying one of their fingers to each other, they lift a very heavy man or weight on high. They also stupify snakes so they do not bite. They calm raging horses with a song, while rendering others immobile. In this way, also, those who are slaughtered escape danger. First, they please the stars of astronomy with prayer, and they are carried for our aid, as the epilogue of their prayers clearly suggests; whence Albumasar <note>an influential Persian astrologer</note> in *Sadan*: The kings of the Greeks, when they wished to beseech God for some business, placed the **Head of the Dragon** <term>Head of the Dragon: the North Node of the moon, considered highly auspicious in medieval astrology</term> in the middle of the sky with Jupiter, or a favorable aspect from it, and the Moon joined to Jupiter, or receding from it, and seeking a conjunction from the Lord of the Ascendant. Furthermore, when the Head was in a friendly figure, then it was said their petitions were heard; whence Almansor in the *Aphorisms*: If anyone shall ask anything from God with the Head being in the middle of the sky, etc., he shall not pass by without briefly obtaining whatever he seeks. And I indeed, in five configurations of this world <margin>3</margin>, seeking knowledge from the First <note>the First Mover or God</note> <margin>4</margin>, have seen myself profit further in that. Also, with an incantation for those who cannot sleep, by the representation of the one constantly enchanting in the imagination. It even induces pollution <note>nocturnal emissions</note> in dreams. What shall be in the future is thus clearly revealed about something. Also, an arrow fixed in a bone so firmly that by no other skill or fingers, but by two fingers applied laterally, it is easily and without pain drawn out. Cancer also is killed. Worms are killed. Blood flowing from anywhere is stopped by this and a **character** <term>character (karactere): a magical symbol or sigil believed to hold power</term>. A paroxysm of **epilepsy** <term>epilepsy (epylēfia): often called the "falling sickness" in this period, sometimes attributed to demonic or planetary influence</term> is carried away by the names of the Magi. Or carrying the names upon oneself forces all things to cease. The epileptic is healed, and the lunatic is stabilized by these with others. When the father or mother, during the four seasons on Wednesday, leads him to the church, and on Friday, and then on Saturday, it is chanted over him, and that Gospel of the Lord is suspended from his neck: "this kind of demon is not cast out except by prayers and fasting." Similarly, by a character and a song, a kidney ailment is cured. The future is known beforehand. And that which is absent is found, as **geomancy** <term>geomancy: a method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand</term> teaches, and many such things.

# Whether prayer or incantation benefits treatment

This, however, is certainly persuaded by reason, and they reduce the effects to their respective causes. For this happens either from an immediate internal cause, or a lower or exterior one. If it is the first [internal], it occurs in two ways. Either on the part of the one chanting <note>original: "cantantis"; referring to the practitioner of the incantation</note> with great affection, when his soul is so elevated that it can dominate this worldly matter; and [the things] themselves, having received the vigor of intelligence, allow themselves to be transformed. Or, it occurs on the part of the one being incanted upon, such as through the vigor of their own "estimation" <note>the faculty of "estimatio" in medieval psychology, which perceives non-sensory intentions like fear or hope</note>, which aids significantly. And this indeed is the mode that the Peripatetic <note>a follower of Aristotle’s school of philosophy</note> concedes in Difference 135. Either of these is sufficient, for this latter one [the patient's belief] especially supports the former [the healer's power].

But if it is from an exterior cause, it is likewise twofold: either that substance is more universal, or more particular. The universal one is like the presence of the causes, by whose virtue the prayer or incantation receives its effect, since it [the First Cause] has, in a certain way, a concern for us, as shown in Difference 101. For the First [God] can, by his own sheer kindness—since he is a supernatural agent acting through will without motion or change—operate in these lower things. Whatever the Peripatetic says in his submissive discourse, since He is the highest good, it is within His nature to be diffusive and communicative of Himself. Otherwise, He would not be the highest good at all. Nor because of this—since He is what is most divine and most honored, according to the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*—does He change into something needy by understanding [lower] essences. For He does not understand things actually outside of Himself; rather, by understanding Himself, He understands all things, since they shine back in Him as in their cause. For He does not contemplate them as they are material and base, but in a more noble and higher way, by which He understands Himself to be the cause of such things. In this way, even the knowledge of the basest and most abominable animals is rendered noble and decorous to Himself. Whence, in the first book of *On the Parts [of Animals]*: "In things not pleasing to the sense, the theory is similar." For it provides wonderful delights to those able to know the causes. And therefore Mesue <note>Yahya ibn Masawayh, a famous Persian Christian physician</note> says: "God alone heals diseases."

If, however, the substance is more particular, it is either absolute or joined to a mobile body. If it is the first, it is either benign, like an angel—who is placed as our administrator by divine decree and as a messenger carrying prayers before the First—just as Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note> felt in the tenth book of his *Metaphysics*, of which the testaments are not a little full. If, however, it is depraved, then it is a demon or spirit, whose efficacy is very great, since there is no power on earth that can be compared to it. This [spirit] indeed obeys incantations and sacrifices greatly, so that it may deceive those it has incited, or appear to be performing many things, and it is especially obedient to simpler "little women" <note>original: "mulierculis"; a common medieval term for unlearned or superstitious women</note>. For it is able to deceive them more quickly than the wise. Wherefore I see these [women] pursue movement and effect from their incantation or conjuration very well. This does not happen to the wiser person, no matter how much he works with them. 

There is also, as if experienced, a vigor of either prior [influence] or familiarity in places where divine worship is celebrated. Peripatetic philosophy might not express this, for its way was not like that of Plato—since it [the Peripatetic way] arrives at the "movers" from sensible and mobile things, as appears in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*. Nevertheless, Ptolemy asserts it in the fourth book of the *Quadripartitum* <note>Ptolemy’s famous work on astrology</note>. If indeed the Moon is the lady of the "mastery" <note>an astrological term for the planet ruling one's profession or actions</note> being in Sagittarius or Pisces, one will divine by the dead and will compel malignant spirits to move even from place to place. Whence the commentator says there: "The spirits who are called devils will be moved," or other spirits because of which one will divine. 

If, however, it [the cause] is joined to such a mobile substance, it is either incorruptible—like the intelligence and soul of the heaven, or the latter only according to Alexander and Themisteus <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias and Themistius, famous commentators on Aristotle</note>—and this in two ways. Either the one performing the incantation is moved by the one above, since they are ordained toward our concern in a way previously touched upon; and let it be such that he understands [the heaven] so that he utters it [the incantation] by its orb and star, or performs the office according to how it was differently incanted. Not a few of the Magi observe this, invoking Jupiter, Saturn, or another by the name of the Intelligence leading the same, in Difference 9, when they are fortunately or otherwise disposed. This is even what the priest Brysis <note>possibly Chryses from the Iliad, or a similar legendary figure</note> felt. And as I have experienced, they [the practitioners] bring about no small continuous attraction in matters of love or hate through song. 

Or, the incantation seems to help not because it contributes [directly], but because the "direction" <note>an astrological calculation of a planet's movement over time</note> of the "significator" <note>the planet representing a person in a chart</note> of some person happens to reach our [position], so that he ought to obtain the love of such a person, or something similar. In this case, the incantation or that which is done contributes nothing except by chance. According to that [phrase] in the first book of the *Posterior [Analytics]*: "It lightened while you were walking" <note>a classic example of a coincidental correlation</note>. And thus all such people dismiss these prayers and things of that sort. But that is not so: for it is not likely that what they say could happen only once in a while, and not always or for the most part. Since the "direction" of a significator to a place rarely happens for such a singer, in Difference 63, since we see that then, very often, the one acting through incantation or another means achieves the intended effect.

If, however, it adheres to a corruptible mobile substance—like the aforementioned agent intelligence from Aristotle—what should be thought about this and the present topic is explained in Difference 1 and 135. Or it may even be because in the movement itself, the incantation of "expelled nature" <note>meaning a physical reaction triggered by a psychological state</note> occurs. As happened when a certain nobleman taught a poor little old woman to pray [over a patient], saying: "Two and three make five, and three are six and two" <note>a nonsense rhyming charm based on simple addition</note>, while a fishbone was fixed in her throat and torturing her. She was finally called and, arriving at him, said she knew no other medicine except that which she had learned from him. He, however, was moved to a most vehement laughter, and he sent the bone out along with some blood. 

Regarding the fourth point: what should be said to the first [argument] has appeared. For Ovid held such precepts so as to deny the touch <note>meaning he denied the physical reality of the effect</note>, since they stood against his intention there. Also, many things are heard "according to the proverb of the poets," in the *Metaphysics* of the philosopher [Aristotle]. Similarly Galen, the most clear of physicians, did not have the touch of such things mixed with his [work].
