# What a dream is. 3

<margin>On sleep and waking</margin>

An incantation does not alter or transform anything by itself. Therefore, it does not heal, since it only indicates a command of the mind. Regarding those things that appear on the opposing side: they proceed in their own way. Since incantations act through some cause, what they do is led through a path where their effectiveness can be preserved. For words bring forth love most effectively for rational beings. Indeed, they excite their reason so that, having conceived a love for it, they might turn away from something as if it were shameful. Let this suffice as a topical discussion on this question.

### DIFFERENCE 157.

It is shown that a dream does not contribute to a cure because that which is indifferent in itself does not contribute to healing, since healing is determined by the science of medicine—at least as other parts contain truth while this contains lies. A dream is of this nature; hence in the third book of *On Sleep and Waking* <note>Aristotle’s "De somno et vigilia"</note>, regarding the divination that happens in dreams, it says that what occurs from dreams is neither worthy of contempt nor of belief. Furthermore, that which deceives is not suitable for treatment, since treatment is perfected by certainty. Such a thing is the dream, according to that ethical proverb: "Do not heed dreams: for dreams deceive the common people." <note>original: "Somnia ne cures: nam fallunt somnia plebes." A common medieval hexameter often attributed to Cato.</note> Again, if it did contribute to a cure, it would be by way of some motion, since healing is a kind of doing, which is said to be perfected by motion. But in a dream, motion is not found, since it is a certain property and "passion" <note>an experience or state of being acted upon</note> of sleep. Moreover, every property is at rest, while motion proceeds from animal power. Sleep is the rest of the animal powers with the intensification of the natural ones, and the "binding and immobility of the primary sense." <note>A classic Aristotelian definition of sleep.</note> Difference 104. Also, the matter of medication is perfected by three things: diet, potion, and manual action <note>surgery</note>; and a fourth, prayer. A dream is none of these. For it is not contained under diet, since diet is the proper administration of "non-natural" things <note>The "Six Non-Naturals" in medieval medicine: air, food/drink, sleep/wake, motion/rest, evacuation/repletion, and passions of the mind.</note>, of which the dream itself is none, as one goes through them individually. That it is not a potion or surgery is evident. Therefore, with the others set aside in Difference 135, a dream does not contribute to health.

On the contrary, in the third book of *On Sleep and Waking*, the most gracious of physicians say one must pay close attention to dreams. This is only because they ultimately contribute to the cure, as will appear. Whence, in the same book: a certain "splenetic" <note>someone suffering from a disease of the spleen</note> dreamed that he was commanded in his sleep to drink his own urine three times every day, and he would be healed; having tried it, he found it marvelous. Also in the fourth book, third section: some, by obeying a dream vision, were cured of leprosy. Hence in the 13th book of *Therapeutics*, Galen <note>written as "G."</note> praised his son <note>or "the son of G." likely referring to a case study</note> who was [cured] by a dream. Likewise, that which proceeds from Him who heals all ailments contributes to the cure. Such is the dream. Wherefore: "Dreams are from God, the blessed and sublime, and God alone heals ailments." <note>A quote often attributed to Galen or Rhazes regarding the divine origin of true dreams.</note>

Furthermore: that which signifies the dominance of a humor before it affects the body, and signifies a future evacuation, aids the treatment; since every signification is ordered toward it. Such is the dream, for each of the humors causes a dream when it is dominant, so that the physician is directed to its removal. Whence in the fourth book: many times a sick person sees the kind of thing that will be his "crisis." <note><term>Crisis</term>: the turning point of a disease where the patient either recovers or declines.</note> Thus, one who is about to have a crisis through sweat sees himself entering a bath and preparing himself. Therefore, the dream is useful in the cure.

First, it must be known that a dream is a "phantasm" <note>an internal mental image</note> created by the movement of "idols" <note>original: "filacroꝝ" for "simulacrorum," the sensory images that persist in the mind</note> in a person who is sleeping. Regarding this, Aristotle <note>Ax.</note> and Avicenna <note>Ay.</note> speak in this treatise. For there are three such types of apprehensions: namely, dreams which are said to be from angels; divinations from demons; and prophecies which are from God and without an intermediary. A dream is divided in many ways: for one is true, another false. Furthermore, one is based on repletion <note>fullness/excess</note>, another on inanition <note>emptiness/lack</note>, and some on a medicinal indisposition. Likewise, one is natural, another "animal" <note>pertaining to the "anima" or soul's activities</note>, and sometimes celestial or divine. I call that "natural" which happens from the dominance of the complexion and the humors. Whence, from the fourth book *On the Soul*: natural dreams are those that come from the temperament of the powers of the humors, since they carry the formal and imaginative power. For when the nature of **blood** dominates in someone, he will see red and delightful things in his dream, or he will seem to swim in blood, or see roses and lilies. When **choler** <note>yellow bile</note> dominates, he sees fiery things, yellow things, flights, quarrels, rages, and such things. If the nature of **phlegm** dominates, he will dream of waters, snow, cold, stupors, and the like. If **melancholy** <note>black bile</note> dominates, he dreams of great passing things, mournings, falls, places of the dead, and the like, which either remain liquid for a long time or slip away, according to whether the body's nature participates in dryness or moisture. I call an "animal" dream that which is caused by the great worry of the soul about something while awake. For when the greater motion—the exterior one—is quieted because of the withdrawal of the spirits, the smaller interior motion is perceived. For the greater motion, according to Avicenna, disturbs and drives out the smaller. And indeed, such a

<margin>concerning himself</margin>

dream troubled me many times for over two years, caused by a vehement impression from my journey to the University of Paris to study. I hear that a "divine" or "celestial" dream is that which is caused by the souls of the heavens, which are also called the movers of the spheres; these, according to Aristotle, sometimes work a form in the imagination according to their own disposition and the disposition and aptitude of our souls. For our souls have a greater kinship with separate substances than with sensible bodies. According to this, that saying of Galen is perhaps verified: "Dreams are sent by God, the blessed and sublime."

Secondly, it must be known that some have denied dreams, not only regarding their usefulness in cures, but even simply all things that belong to order and nature. Whence in the first book of *Natural Philosophy*: some expressly declared that the soul has no power by which we think, despising dreams, divinations, counselors, and all astrology. See also Difference 135. Advice against their error is found there. Others directly denied dreams. Wherefore Aristotle says: certain men deny dreams and say they happen by chance. I say this perhaps happens because they have seen the closest ones to be false, not knowing how to distinguish between them. Or perhaps they immediately reduced all things to the First Cause (Difference 101), whose defect appeared there. Concerning...

Regarding the first point, it must be known that a dream assists in healing, both by way of cause (when it heals immediately) and by way of sign. Not immediately [after birth], but truly after four or five years. Some people have even never seen a dream.

One who is of a moist complexion receives them quickly but loses them swiftly, nor does he remember the dream for long. One who is of a hot complexion will be agile in their movements but unstable, having changing dreams. One who is cold is slow, lazy, and forgetful. ### DIFFERENCE 158.

Whether it can be shown that unnatural heat digests.
Because it is proven: a specific command is given for it to be increased in quartan fevers. Such a command does not seem to be made except for the digestion of the matter <note>the "materia" or diseased humor causing the fever</note>. For whatever is exhibited in material fevers and is properly medicinal is for this end: that the matter may be digested and rendered obedient to nature. But fire or fiery heat is unnatural. Furthermore, that which can do the greater can also do the lesser. But even unnatural heat can do more, since it can produce an animal from putrefaction; whence in the fourth book of the *Meteorology*: "Animals are produced in those things which putrefy." This is a greater thing than simply disposing matter for nature, since it rouses a soul from the potentiality of matter. Also, that which causes the illness to end in health causes digestion, since digestion is nothing more than nature dominating and overcoming a wicked humor, whatever it may be, according to Haly <note>Haly Abbas or Haly Rodoan</note>. But unnatural heat terminates the illness; whence in the fourth book of the *Aphorisms* <note>of Hippocrates</note>: "When a fever supervenes upon a person having a spasm or tetanus, it dissolves the illness." Fever also cures epilepsy, especially a long-lasting quartan fever, according to the third and first books. And Mesue in his *Practica*. But fever is unnatural heat. Again, since some effect is produced by two causes, it is true to say that both operate toward it. But the "cooking" <note>fauces</note> around which digestion is observed is caused by both natural and accidental heat, as will appear in the present Difference. Often, wishing to digest matter, we induce external heat into the body, since digestion is perfected most of all by heat, such as electuaries, syrups, and the like. Therefore, unnatural heat performs digestion. On the contrary, because digestion is a completion by one's own natural heat, according to the fourth book of the *Meteorology*. But unnatural heat is not natural, nor is it one's own, but external. <meta>This page transitions from the psychological and prophetic aspects of dreams discussed on the previous page to a technical medical debate regarding the role of heat in the human body. Specifically, it addresses whether unnatural heat—such as that found in fevers—can perform the function of digestion, a topic central to medieval physiology and the works of Galen and Averroes.</meta>

# Whether Unnatural Heat Performs Digestion

The heat which is natural is that which exists in the bodies of animals. Such heat is not <term>unnatural heat</term><note>In medieval medicine, "natural heat" is the vital force that sustains life and processes food, while "unnatural heat" (like a fever) is seen as a foreign or destructive force.</note> as is clearly expressed here. It is said that unnatural heat putrefies, mortifies, and corrupts; it does not digest. Natural heat vivifies and builds. This is the operation of natural heat, while the other is unnatural, as others testify. Furthermore, the reasons for contraries are themselves contrary: but natural heat has the function of digesting; therefore, unnatural heat will perform the opposite, such as putrefying. Again, the most excellent of physicians <note>referring to Galen and his followers</note>, whom it is not right to consider insufficient, have written this very thing. Therefore, unnatural heat does not digest.

Regarding the first point, one must know what heat is, and what is "natural." In how many ways it is spoken of and its differences have been shown in books 10 and 11 <note>likely referring to Aristotle’s *Physics* or a similar commentary</note>, through the opposite of which unnatural heat will be known; for he who defines a thing well also signifies its contrary, according to the sixth book of the *Topics*. Therefore, unnatural heat will be the <term>instrument of disease</term> by which nature is corrupted. This heat is either entirely unnatural, such as that of <term>atrophy</term><note>original: "marcoris," a wasting away or decay of the body's moisture</note>, or it is unnatural in a certain respect—that is, a middle ground between the natural and the entirely unnatural, such as the heat of <term>pus</term><note>original: "saniei," the discharge from a wound or ulcer</note>. For this heat is a mixture of the natural and the putrefiable, where the natural is ultimately winning. It has been shown in books 10 and 62 that there are different types of digestion.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have said unnatural heat does not digest. Because digestion is a work of the <term>natural digestive virtue</term><note>The innate power of the body to process nourishment</note>, just as that virtue is natural, so it is necessary for its heat to be natural, so that there is a proportion of the principal agent to the instrumental and secondary agent. They also say that if unnatural heat should cure anything, such as the touch of a sickness, it would be <term>by accident</term><note>Meaning it is a side effect, not the primary intended function</note>. Nor does it do this by way of digestion, but rather by reason of corruption, resolution, or breathing out. This indeed appears to be the case from what has been said. For digestion is nothing other than nature dominating and overcoming a "vile humor" in whatever way—even by unnatural heat. What truth there may be in this, since its motion contains a certain state, the third point will show.

There were also some who simply maintained the opposite: namely, that unnatural heat digests not only in harmful states but even in helpful states of disease. Therefore, that which prepares for the <term>nutritive virtue</term> and the <term>expulsive virtue</term> is said to digest. In a helpful state, it proportions the nourishment for the virtue of nutrition. In a harmful state, it prepares the matter for expulsion by the digestion of the matter. Unnatural heat does these things: it prepares for nutrition by changing and altering the food. It also aids the expulsive virtue by "incinerating" <note>drying out or burning up excess humors</note> the matter and refining it into vapors and smokes to be expelled. Because of this, they conclude that unnatural heat performs the work of digestion.

That this latter position is more absurd than the first is shown by the third point. The reasoning is also minorly absurd. For if unnatural heat digested, then those suffering from fever would digest better than healthy people, which is against <note>the teachings of</note> Galen and the sense of the *Aphorisms* <note>Hippocrates' *Aphorisms*</note>. Nor is that which is "incinerated" actually digested, since it is rendered more obedient to the expulsive power and the victory of nature. And therefore we see "incinerated" matter being cast out in sicknesses. Nor does that which is refined into smoke obey nature in every way and properly, especially when the matter was plentiful and gross. Or perhaps they hear of unnatural heat coming from non-natural things, and especially from the air, when it shortens diseases.

Regarding the third point, it should be known: whether the heat is entirely against nature or not, but rather mixed in some way with natural heat, it has no way of performing "helpful" digestion as such. Because the end goal determines the nature of the things ordered toward that end, since the end necessitates the things preceding it. But the end of digestion in a helpful state is the preservation of the natural; and if it is sometimes helped by heat acquired from motion or from foods or medicines, nevertheless all this is ordered toward the natural heat. Furthermore, that whose virtue and form are natural uses media by which nature operates, since the effect is proportional to the cause. But the virtue and form of digestion is entirely natural, as the effect indicates. Likewise, nothing acts beyond its own species. Therefore, since natural and unnatural heat are different species, their actions will also be different. And so if the natural digests and perfects, the unnatural putrefies and destroys.

If, however, digestion should exist in a "harmful" state, it must be said that in it, unnatural heat—that is, heat that is in every way against nature—does not digest in any way, but continuously putrefies and corrupts, since it overcomes the natural heat by putrefying its matter. Such is the heat producing atrophy or <term>virulence</term> or putrefaction, the natural heat having finally been overcome and having entirely departed from its equilibrium, as in pernicious ulcers and in mortified bodies. Just as natural heat, when it is strong, can administer to the humors through nature, by way of ripening and digesting and guarding them, and preventing them from being moved by an external heat so they do not putrefy; so, when external heat finds humors not governed by the administration of natural heat, it seizes them and makes them obedient to itself, moving them with a foreign motion. Whence putrefaction occurs, according to the first <term>Aphorism</term><note>referring to Hippocrates</note>. This shows that what is simply against nature will never induce a natural work, since it is a cause entirely disproportionate to the effect. But this heat, being contrary to nature, is such a thing. For it does not have the power to digest of itself (as natural heat does), nor by accident, since it is a corrupted power. It is deprived of the work of digestion entirely.

But if this unnatural heat is not entirely <margin>Question 3, *Colliget* <note>referring to the *Colliget*, a medical encyclopedia by Averroes</note></margin> against nature, but rather a mixture of natural and accidental heat, such as <term>feverish heat</term>, and especially when it has not yet come to suppress nature, it performs digestion after a fashion; whence it is gathered in the third <note>book of the *Colliget*</note>.

For the heat of a fever and the heat of pus is "extrinsic" <note>foreign/external</note> because it harms the actions and passions of the limbs. And it appears from the part where it is manifested in the very operation of the heat, by digesting humors internally and receiving healing. And this is not like the extrinsic heat found in the bodies of the dead. And from this it is also natural. And it is the truth, because it is a "putrescibilis" heat <note>heat capable of causing putrefaction</note>. ...of natural heat. Still remaining, there occurs a disposition of the blood composed of both an unnatural disposition and a natural disposition. Therefore, a part of it putrefies into an unnatural state because of the disposition. Whichever of these heats prevails, its signs will then appear more dominant in the substance, odor, and heat of the <term>pus</term><note>original: "saniei," referring to the discharge from a wound or infected humor</note>. Hence, in the third book of the *Aphorisms*, a threefold transformation of the blood is distinguished: One is simply benign, whose conversion into parts becomes the animal's own substance. Another is absolutely wicked, such as that by which putrefaction becomes fully purulent. 87. This is also demonstrated by reason and by example. Since that which produces an effect "by accident" works in a certain way toward that same effect, and the aforementioned unnatural heat contributes to digestion "by accident"—insofar as it heats the material, dissolves it, and opens the pores—its action is accepted by the natural heat which regulates it, assuming the natural heat is the stronger of the two. Because of this, unnatural heat contributes to digestion in some way, as is seen in the cure of <term>tetanus</term><note>original: "spasmi s. tbetani"</note> and other fixed illnesses brought on by fever. We see these illnesses terminate more quickly and for the better when the accidental heat is sharpened during the third stage of a <term>crisis</term><note>A turning point in a disease</note>. For here, the heat agitates the matter, opening the pores and exciting the innate heat. Further, it is shown that the <term>external cause</term><note>original: "fxtas" (extrinsicas)</note> making a difference in digestion is more averse to nature than the extraneous heat itself. They illustrate this by comparing it to the works of nature in human affairs. For just as the captors of cities place the conquered in front of their own troops so they might seize the remaining cities—
<margin>Attila the Picard: the subverter of Italy</margin>
—as they say Attila the Picard observed during the conquest of the Italians. For these subjugated people, who are placed in front in the war with their captors behind them, fight only because they are forced by the fear of those rising up behind them. This is apparent because if those forcing them were to stop attacking the rebels, the subjugated would most bitterly turn and attack them instead. Thus natural heat acts with unnatural heat; for with the unnatural heat regulated and restrained, it acts as a secondary instrument to achieve the digestion of the material, even though the unnatural heat by itself plots mischief and destruction. It works "by accident" more effectively when it pre-exists, as the species could not be preserved in the prior individual state. And so, among the principles, it is treated as a third cause, even if it is proven only by accident. This is shown because if the natural heat were weakened, it would immediately induce a work of putrefaction and corruption, with the unnatural heat acting simply and unmixed.

Regarding the fourth point, it must be said to Avicenna <note>original: "Au."</note> that by "fire" he did not mean natural heat, but rather a medium that nonetheless pertains more to natural heat. This is apparent because he added "through foods." For it is not necessary in similar material things—such as <term>phlegmatic</term> and especially <term>quartan</term><note>A fever that recurs every four days</note> conditions—to thin the foods, but rather they are exhibited in a thickened and abundant state so that as the heat is increased, a little of the feverish heat is destroyed. For a great heat draws a small one to itself, and a larger flame extinguishes a smaller one. 

Regarding the other point: it is not unnatural heat that generates animals from putrefaction <note>referring to the theory of spontaneous generation of insects/worms from rot</note>, but rather celestial heat, as in Difference 48 and 100. But this is said to be of minimal value, for if one says unnatural heat digests by virtue of the celestial. In putrefying things, at least some general proportion of heat remains in the moisture, through which the generation of "imperfect" animals can occur, even if the specific previous form is corrupted. For the generation of imperfect animals does not require as great a proportion as is required for "complete" animals (Difference 35). Moreover, this natural heat is not preserved in heat that is simply unnatural; or if it is preserved and contributes to the digestion of harmful things, it happens "by accident." Or perhaps in the production of animals, the power of the <term>constellations</term><note>Astrological influence on biology</note> works more than digestion does; thus it is a lesser thing to produce an animal than to perform digestion, as happens from other causes in Difference 100.

Regarding the other point: unnatural heat digests material distinctly and causes it to exhale "by accident" insofar as it is the instrument of natural heat. Similarly, regarding the other: although pus is initially created by unnatural heat, it is perfected by the natural heat prevailing, especially when it is "laudable" and well-digested; this is much more true for a fever or any other material illness that is similar to pus. 

Regarding the other point: the heat acquired from foods and medicines is more natural than unnatural, since it is ordered toward the body as a digestive instrument. To those things in the other part, the answer is similar. For Avicenna and Galen <note>original: "Ga."</note> speak of digestion in a simple state, which is said to be perfected by natural heat absolutely. Regarding the other: this is true of heat that is entirely inanimate, but not of the other. Regarding the other: this must be understood as being essentially and per se in contraries, but not in those things which occur by accident, such as natural and extraneous digestion. For nothing prohibits that which someone does "by accident" from being done by another "per se" in its own way. For cold and heat both chill and warm (it is said), one doing so "per se" and the other "by accident," as is often felt. Regarding the other: the authors mostly enumerated the essential causes completing digestion, since they are more effective than accidental ones. Or they touched upon them as was said. <meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the timing and nature of digestion in relation to disease, specifically whether digestion must occur before a "conjoined cause" or if it belongs to the "antecedent cause." # Whether digestion ought to occur before the conjoined cause, as an antecedent. 1

The substance of putrefaction remains even while it is present. For <term>digestion</term><note>original: "digō" (digestio). In this context, it refers to the "ripening" or "cooking" of humors by the body's internal heat to make them easier to expel.</note> is an alteration that causes putrefaction to cease while the substance remains, as noted in the *Ars Medica* <note>original: "in tegni," referring to Galen's *Ars Medica*, also known as the *Microtegni*.</note>. Likewise, putrid vapor does not require digestion, since it evaporates and dissolves by itself. It does not have qualities that are disobedient to expulsion; rather, as will be shown, it is the <term>conjoined cause</term><note>The immediate, active cause of a disease that is present as long as the disease lasts.</note>. However, respiration and putrefaction are <term>antecedent causes</term><note>A pre-existing condition, like an imbalance of humors, that leads to a disease but is not the disease itself.</note>. Furthermore, foresight belongs only to the antecedent cause; indeed, the very name "pre-vision" denotes this. But through digestion, a certain foresight is obtained. For it is reduced to a benign antecedent cause, or it is prepared for expulsion so that it does not cause further harm.

Likewise, in a putrid fever, when an illness occurs, one part is considered already happened, and another part is "about to happen." If that which has already occurred requires only a cure and the application of contraries, this is seen to be caused by the conjoined cause. However, that which is "about to happen" is due to the antecedent cause which is placed below it. It is also said that one must first "digest" the matter and then evacuate it. For this reason, <term>Mesue</term><note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (c. 777–857), a Persian or Assyrian Christian physician.</note> 
<margin>Mesue</margin> 
in his *Antidotary* says that Galen testifies to the power of **Oxymel** <note>original: "syrupi Acetosi," a medicinal syrup of vinegar and honey.</note> for all common matters. But the antecedent cause is the matter itself, not the conjoined cause, since it is the "efficient" part according to the *Ars Medica*. One must first cut off every efficient cause, and then come to the illness that was made by it. However, the efficient cause and the material cause do not coincide in nature, since one holds the role of "action" and the other "potential." Digestion, therefore, belongs to the antecedent cause and not the conjoined cause.

On the contrary: Putrefaction is commonly considered the conjoined cause of fever. But digestion is owed to it, since it is an alteration—as was said—an action making putrefaction cease while the substance remains, which certain causes happen to do. Furthermore, art and the physician imitate nature. But nature digests the conjoined cause when it dominates and overcomes it. Whence <term>Haly</term><note>Haly Abbas (930–994), a famous Persian physician.</note> 
<margin>Haly.</margin> 
says: Digestion is nothing more than nature dominating and overcoming a bad humor, whatever it may be. Moreover, digestion is a certain curative cause in the *Ars Medica*; this truly belongs to the conjoined cause. For preservation is more necessary beforehand, as in the eleventh book of *On the Method of Healing*. Elsewhere, evacuation and digestion are appropriate where they are seen to be ordered toward emptying the body. According to the words of <term>Hippocrates</term>: 
<margin>Hippocrates</margin> 
"Medicate things that are digested [ripe]." But putrefaction, which is considered the conjoined cause, requires evacuation, according to that rule: Evacuation is the drawing out of the whole substance from the body. Also, digestion is the preparation of the substance of the matter so that it may be ordered for easy expulsion. But putrefaction resists expulsion because of "indigestion" (lack of ripening), because it is too thick or too thin or otherwise disposed. Therefore, digestion ought to belong to the conjoined cause.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that a "cause" in general is that upon which something else follows according to nature, or a disposition through which it has the state of being a cause; it is the first principle of a thing having its being through another. To a physician, a cause is that which is prior, and from which some disposition in the human body proceeds, or its prior secondary fixation. Some causes are healthy, others are sickly, and some are neutral, as in the *Ars Medica*. These exist in two ways: either they are such from birth (and thus some are healthy, sickly, or neutral, just as the body is threefold), or they come after birth or over time.

Strictly speaking, all causes are "healthy," as it is said in the *Ars Medica*: "We shall henceforth run through the healthy causes for those who are clearly sick." For every cause is either preservative of health or effective of health; the latter is posterior in nature but prior in time. For a cause applied to a sick body is properly called "healthy" when it is ordered toward health as its end. Movement receives its name and species from the end toward which it naturally tends (as in the *Physics*, book 5). 
<margin>Physics book 2.</margin> 
And it is right for everything to be named 
<margin>On the Soul</margin> 
after its end (from *On the Soul*). Improperly, however, a cause can be called "sickly" by reason of the subject it is applied to (the sick person) or because of its administration, which will appear as bad. 

There are also certain **necessary causes** without which it is impossible for our body not to be affected, such as:
1. Air
2. Motion and rest
3. Sleep and waking
4. Food and drink
5. Emptiness and fullness
6. Passions of the soul

Certain other causes are not necessary but are their opposites—rather, they are casual or accidental. For dealing with swords or wild beasts is not necessary. And therefore, the art of medicine does not concern itself with these in the human body. However, another art, such as **astrology**, can exist regarding these. For although they are not [scientifically] existent as casual things, they are rather necessary [in a cosmic sense]. And indeed, all these are causes of health and sickness as their "matter"; but they rise into "forms" when they are applied to the body in the proper (or opposite) quantity, quality, time, manner of use, and order (from *On the Preservation of Health*, book 1). 
<margin>On the Preservation of Health.</margin> 
Or also from Johannitius, chapter 19. Of these, the principal things are quantity and quality. What is meant by digestion has been shown in the first part.

But the particular causes of health and sickness are three: **Primitive** (or manifest), **Antecedent**, and **Conjoined**, which relate to the disposition of the <term>complexion</term><note>The balance of the four humors/qualities.</note>, the composition, and the common state. **Primitive causes** 
<margin>Primitive Causes</margin> 
are things that are not bodily—that is, they do not exist from the substance of the body—although some of them may be bodies in themselves, such as food and drink, from which sickness happens mediated or unmediated. For sometimes the heat of the sun immediately induces a one-day fever; but sometimes, by means of the "boiling" it induces in the humors, it causes a putrid fever.

**Antecedent causes** are bodily causes, such as the humors 
<margin>Antecedent</margin> 
or the complexions or compositions, from which sickness does not happen immediately, but by means of something else: namely, the conjoined cause—for example, through fullness or emptiness.

**Conjoined causes** are also bodily causes, from which 
<margin>Conjoined</margin> 
sickness rises immediately as a "prior secondary" state; when these are present, the infirmity is present, and when they are absent, it ceases. At times they harm the function of another part by means of a disease (from the *Theorica*, book 6). But on the contrary, the *Ars Medica* says that a function is principally harmed by a conjoined cause, which is seen to happen immediately. To explain this further: illness is twofold. One is simple and single, such as a hectic or one-day fever, in which no underlying cause is making it. For everything has passed; nothing remains in the body to generate it (from *On Unequal Distemper*). There is another kind where the conjoined cause alone makes the disease, not receiving anything further from an antecedent cause...

...regarding the state, no less. And such an illness is that which is cured by a "resolved disposition"—that is, by the <term>conjoined cause</term><note>original: "cā giuncta." In medieval medicine, this is the immediate cause of the disease symptoms, present as long as the disease is present.</note> and not the primary one, since it lacks it. From this conjoined cause, the function is harmed principally—that is, by itself and immediately—with respect to the <term>antecedent cause</term><note>original: "cā añcedētē." A pre-existing condition, such as an excess of a certain humor, that disposes the body toward a disease.</note>, by which it is harmed secondarily and very mediately. Indeed, we say that this conjoined cause is the cause of the illness. For it is the principal cause, since the illness turns with it. Or, in which illness it is harmed principally—that is, simply and immediately—and not only by relation to the antecedent cause, as before, and the rest as mentioned earlier.

Yet, to the subtle observer, it should be known that some causes are only antecedent, such as a repletion of humors before it reaches the "mine" <note>original: "minera," referring to the specific site or source where the humors begin to decay.</note> of putrefaction. Some are only conjoined, such as the putrid <term>soot</term><note>original: "fuligo." This refers to the smoky or sooty vapors believed to be produced by decaying humors.</note> or smoke of this kind which, resulting from the "mine" of putrefaction, reaches the ventricles of the heart, [acting as] the primary cause of fevers. 

Hence, in the fourth book [of the *Ars Medica*], the primary humor receiving putrefaction is of such a sort that a vapor exits from it, which is a very subtle smoke. If it is blood, that which evaporates is a subtle vapor. If it is <term>phlegm</term><note>original: "flā" (flegma).</note>, a thick vapor evaporates from it. If it is <term>melancholy</term><note>original: "melācolia."</note>, a thick, dusty, smoky vapor rises from it. However, it is shown here that this horrible smoke or putrid soot is the conjoined cause that correlates with the fever, and not the putrefaction itself. Since it is sometimes possible to find putrefaction in abscesses or in the veins, but not a fever, because the putrid soot has not yet reached the heart. Nor could a thicker putrefaction tend toward the heart in that way; or if it did arrive, it would induce worse things and the symptoms of death. 

But if someone should insist and say that putrefaction is commonly defined as the conjoined cause of fever, it must be said that by this "putridity" they partly mean the putrid smoke, which truly is the conjoined cause, and partly they trace it back to the antecedent cause. Hence, in the eleventh book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "xi. de īge" (De Ingenio Sanitatis).</note>, an obstruction is a symptom caused by the detention of perspiration, in which again the putrefaction of humors is the antecedent cause of fever. Here, however, because of the need for careful teaching, it was necessary to explain Galen and Avicenna. 

This can rightly be done, for putrefaction is a certain corruption in each thing of this kind, occurring properly and according to the nature of heat [being corrupted] by a foreign quality, as stated in the fourth book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "metbauroꝝ qrto."</note>, from wherever it arises. Whether it is a transformation of the whole substance of the body putrefying into corruption by external heat, as in the eleventh book of *On the Method of Healing*. Hence, in the fifth book of *On Fevers*, putrefaction is the corruption of a humor and occurring in liquid bodies on account of the "boiling" and turbulence of foreign heat. 

But as to what is said—either because it moves and flows—the opposite is written in the twenty-second book of the *Problems* <note>original: "p̄bf.xxii" (Aristotle's *Problemata*).</note>: "certain things are all moved [to] putrefy." It must be said that movement is twofold: namely, "local" (moving from place to place by itself) and "alteration" (impressed by another). Indeed, things moved in the first way, when they are aired out and expel superfluities, are preserved from putrefaction, as seen in animals, air, and water. But those things that are moved [only] as bodies resting in the air putrefy. For the foreign heat of the surrounding environment, entering into them, corrupts their own heat, causing boiling and alteration in their humors. And thus wine turns sour in a vessel when it is not full, and specifically when nothing is drawn out of it. For the air moves and agitates it more when it is half-full than when it is full.

Regarding this, in the fourth book of the *Meteorology* and the third book of the *Colliget* <note>original: "collz tertio," the medical compendium by Averroes.</note>, a twofold cause exists. One is "by itself"—namely, foreign heat, which forces the natural heat to exhale, especially when it is joined with a violent quality. The other is "by accident," such as coldness. For when coldness dominates the internal heat, it extinguishes it, and then from the matter, another "foreign" heat is generated. 

There is, however, a five-fold cause why some things putrefy more or less. [1] Either because of the surrounding environment; hence in winter things putrefy less, because in the air and water there is little heat, and similarly in the bodies of animals; and therefore they get sick less then. However, if they happen to get sick, they perish more quickly, according to the first book of the *Problems*. [2] Or because it is congealed, and especially by iron or metal, or fat. [3] Or because it is burning, like fire and spirit. [4] Or because it moves and flows, like water and spirit or arterial blood. [5] Or because it is of a larger mass. For in a large mass, the proper heat is better [preserved]; and therefore water that is divided putrefies faster, but when joined together it putrefies least, as appeared... and in the first book of *On Fevers*. 

It is threefold according to whether it participates more, less, or moderately in the foreign heat. The first is caused either because the digestive power is entirely weak, so that it can transform nothing into a benign state from the putrefying superfluity. Even when the bad humor itself is measured, or when the power is not entirely weak, the putrescible moisture remains larger. And such putrefaction has neither a determined color nor odor, but according to its substance, that which putrefies is always altered and varied; it participates in some putrid color, white and foul-smelling, being very thin and equal throughout, as in the first book of the *Prognostics*. These [substances] which settle like "wool" <note>original: "laniei," likely referring to the fleecy sediment in urine called 'laniculi'.</note> denote the digestion of the putrefaction, as appears in material fevers. But that which exists in the middle is judged as moderate. 

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have said digestion belongs to the conjoined and antecedent cause. Those who finally contradicted themselves proposed it only for the antecedent cause. I think these men, by their own speeches, have a sound understanding, since they wish the antecedent cause to sometimes be twofold, and similarly the conjoined cause. In this, however, they seem to feel that the putrid smoke reaching the heart does not receive digestion; perhaps, as will appear, this does not contain the truth. 

What should be seen regarding this third point? Regarding the third, it should be known that <term>digestion</term> principally belongs to the "middle cause" between the truly conjoined and the antecedent cause—namely, the "mine" of the putrefaction. Secondarily, it belongs to the antecedent cause noted before, and finally, very minimally to the conjoined cause properly so called. This is shown because digestion especially belongs to that which it always and by itself concerns; such is putrefaction. For digestion causes the putrefaction itself to cease while the substance remains. But the antecedent cause is not of this kind; for blood sinning in quantity alone does not properly owe [anything to] digestion, as Avicenna and Galen feel, soon caring for the soul...

# Whether a Humor is the Efficient Cause of Fever as its Matter.

...falling short. Nor indeed is <term>digestion</term><note>In medieval medicine, "digestion" refers to "coction" or maturation—the process by which the body's natural heat acts upon humors to make them healthy or ready for expulsion.</note> owed to "furious" matter, unless perhaps someone says it ought not to be digested by accident. This is because nature, in its own time, does not tolerate such unrestrained force without greater danger, as Galen notes in many places. Or rather, it should be said that these matters are proportioned once digested. This is seen from their own agitable and furious motion. Wherefore, in the first book of *On Crises*: in matters that are merely raging, one would reasonably use medication according to the principles, having cooperation toward the ease of attracting the motion of overabundant humors. Similarly, moderate matter existing many times in the stomach or head can be evacuated without digestion, especially when it is "floating" <note>This likely refers to humors that are loose or not yet fixed in the tissues.</note>. However, because the primary aspect of the <term>antecedent cause</term><note>A pre-existing condition, such as an excess of humors, that disposes the body toward a disease.</note> is viscous, thick, thin, or otherwise disobedient to the urge of expulsion, digestion is therefore owed to it. This is discussed concerning "pre-preserved" causes in the *Regimen* <note>original: "regni." Likely referring to Galen's *Ars Medica* or "Tegni," a foundational medical textbook.</note>. Indeed, certain causes of <term>synochal fever</term><note>original: "fynoche." A type of continuous, non-intermittent fever caused by the fermentation of blood.</note> are appropriate when they do not have the aforementioned disobedient qualities for evacuation. Since it is then hotter or drier, or more biting or sharp, or more poisonous than is expedient, it requires digestion. And for that reason, in the state of a more vehement burning, syrups and other administrations of coldness are made, which mitigate the parts and strengthen those that are dissolved, specifically the heart. They also repel [the heat] from the heart by strengthening <term>epithems</term><note>Topical applications or poultices, often applied to the chest or stomach.</note> placed over it. And for this intention, in efficient fevers, we administer cold drinks and medicines.

Furthermore, in Book 11 of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." referring to Galen's *De Ingenio Sanitatis*.</note>, Galen seems to say: Because putrefaction occurs in a living body, it can be altered and digested and reduced to a benign state; whatever of the putrefied things are minimally putrid and <unclear>seeded</unclear> <note>original: "senimata." Possibly "seminata" (seeded/elemental) or a transcription error for "sanata" (healed).</note>, he raises their power toward healing. And in those who are being restored to health from fever, it is necessary to make the putrefaction cease so that two intentions are carried out: one from the fever, the other from the putrefaction. Thus, that which was produced by the putrefaction itself may be cured, which is achieved by those [medicines] that open [the pores]. And what is prohibited or achieved is the inhibition of obstructing humors. Of these, I say one regards the putrefaction—the intermediate cause—and the other the antecedent. Finally, he adds that the [remedy] for the putrefaction of humors is exercise and cooling, and for things already putrid, it is digestion. Yet that which has more "disobedience" toward evacuation, a greater contrariety to nature, and remains longer, principally requires digestion, which compels such things to cease. This is putrefaction, since every kind of indigestion is found more thoroughly in it than in the antecedent or truly <term>conjoined cause</term><note>The immediate, active cause of the symptoms.</note>. Thus, digestion primarily belongs to the "mine" <note>original: "minera." The localized site of the diseased humor.</note> of putrefaction, then to the antecedent cause, and finally to the conjoined causes, such as <term>soot</term><note>original: "fuligi." The smoky vapors produced by decay.</note> and its putridity. 

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it must be said, with the previous exposition, how digestion or alteration makes the putrefaction cease while the substance remains. This is seen to be interpreted in two ways: one according to the Arabic translation, which has: "it is necessary that you make an alteration, that is, to cause the putrefaction to rest, and the substance which existed before the putrefaction remains in the bodily substance which was the humor." Thus, according to this, "while the substance remains" refers to the substance of the humors, since it no longer

passes from the antecedent cause into the conjoined cause, as another translation seems to sound, about which the speech was made when it said: "For they say, if it happens thus in putrefying humors, a fever is kindled." In another, more pleasant way: that the alteration makes the putrefaction cease, not indeed according to its form entirely (for then it would no longer be the state of the fever, since it would cease from putrefaction, even if it remained in a state beyond nature). But rather that it removes the substances and actual qualities existing in it that prevent it from being expelled, while the substance remains internally, not yet evacuated, which is finally led out through evacuation, as is added shortly after: evacuation is that which leads the whole substance out of the body. Just as digestion specifically applies to the disposition of the substance that prevents its leading out. And by this, what must be said appears: that although the matter is digested, the substance of the humor or putrefaction remains, since digestion itself removes more of the [difficulty of] evacuation. Some indeed say the "substance of putrefaction"—which is the matter—remains, but not the "form," since it has already been removed by digestion. This does not contain the truth in every respect, since no small amount of horribleness and opposition is still found in it toward the <unclear>nature</unclear> <note>original: "vulturam." Context suggests "vultum" (aspect) or "naturam" (nature).</note>, such that not only the matter is shown therein, but also the form. 

To the other point, it must be said that although putrid smoke/fume does not require digestion on account of its substance, it requires it nonetheless on account of its contrary and specific qualities, as has been shown to be extraneous. Nor is it entirely resolved in this way when it finds the [vessel] walls thick and resistant. And therefore, as will be shown in [chapter] 162, it is beneficial for frictions and ointments to happen to the body. To another, it must be said that it was granted before. Also, that provision is not simple but composed of the aforementioned "pre-cautionary" and "curative" cause, from the second [book] of *Aphorisms* and the 11th of *On the Method of Healing*. To another, it must be said that although a cure is appropriate for truly conjoined causes, some mode of digestion is also fitting, as has been shown. To the other, it must be said that the antecedent and intermediate cause (like putrefaction) have the nature of "matter," to which digestion is properly owed.

<margin>
Putrid fume is the efficient cause.
</margin>

However, putrid fume is the <term>efficient cause</term><note>The agent or force that brings about a change or effect; in this case, the trigger that "ignites" the fever.</note>, and is something different from the two aforementioned things. Just as the vapor that comes from the thinness of humors is different from the humors themselves, so also putrid fume is different from the "mine" of putrefaction, and even more so from the preceding cause. Or, it cuts away the efficient cause—that is, the cause making it to be. And thus also the matter, and universally every cause, can be called "efficient" since it produces the effect. This is something that some, being unable to understand, often pervert in their exposition of the healthy understandings of the great masters. Which, on the other hand, appears to be an acute point.

The cause of this lighter inquiry debates whether a humor is the efficient or material cause of fever. For it seems that it is the efficient cause, according to that one common precept: "to cut away each of these causes first, etc." And the discourse exists in the treatment of synochal fever. And it is supported as touched upon: For if a humor, in addition to being the efficient cause of fever, were also the material cause, then the matter would coincide with the agent in one thing, which is denied in Philosophy [Aristotle], specifically in the second book of the *Physics*. For then, potentiality and act (which are greatly opposite, according to the Commentator [Averroes] in the prologue to *On the Soul*) would stand as one. Indeed, three causes many times come together in one in number, such as form and end. Or in species, as the agent with the aforementioned: for man generates man.

It concludes that while humors are the material cause requiring digestion/maturation, the "putrid fumes" they produce act as the efficient cause that kindles the fever.</summary>

It focuses on the Aristotelian distinction between "material cause" (the substance a thing is made of) and "efficient cause" (the agent that triggers the change). The text references key authorities including Aristotle's Physics and Metaphysics, and Galen's Ars Medica (referred to here as the "Tegni" or "Principles").</meta>

# Whether a Humor is the Efficient Cause of Fever as its Matter

Still regarding the work *On the Sense and the Sensible* <note>original: "de sensu & sensato"; a treatise by Aristotle.</note>. Neither health nor infirmity is possible for those lacking life. But a **humor** lacks life, since it is a consistency formed through nourishment. Such a thing does not nourish [of itself], but provides nourishment; for this reason, a humor will not be the **material** of fever but its **agent** <note>In Aristotelian logic, the "agent" or "efficient cause" is the active force that produces an effect, whereas the "material cause" is the physical substance involved.</note>. And he confirms this in the first book of the *Principles* <note>original: "p[ri]o p[ri]n"; referring to the *Ars Medica* of Galen, the foundational textbook of medieval medicine.</note>. It is established as the proximate **subject** <note>The underlying substance or physical location where a quality like health or disease resides.</note> of health and sickness.

Also, the agent is the first principle of change, while the "end" is the principle of rest. Such is the humor, because of the depraved dispositions implanted within it. Matter is that "from which something is made," provided it remains within the thing, according to the second book of *Physics* and the fifth of *Metaphysics*. But a humor is not the humor "toward" the fever, since fever is an **accident** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change (like being hot or sick) without changing the essential nature of the substance (the human being).</note>, and it does not have matter *from which* it is made, but rather matter *in which* it exists. Therefore, a humor is not the material cause of fever.

On the contrary, in the first book of the *Principles*: for the material causes in which health and sickness are measured are the "remote subject," namely the humors; he does not express them there among the effective causes. And in the same way, the **antecedent causes** are the bodily causes—whether humoral, complexional, or compositional. He also writes concerning fevers in the fourth book of the *Principles* that there are three types of fevers, distinguished according to a triple subject: for **ephemeral** fever is founded in the **spirits** <note>Fine, vaporous substances believed to circulate through the heart and brain to sustain life.</note>; **humoral** (or more accurately, putrid) fever is in the humor; and **hectic** <note>original: "ethica"; a chronic fever that has "dried out" the solid tissues or limbs.</note> fever is in the **limbs**. Again, matter is that "from which" [something is made]. But humor stands in such a relationship to fever. For it is a certain excess of heat and moisture, according to the first book of the *Physics*. The word "from" implies a material cause.

<margin>¶</margin>
Therefore, humor is the material cause of fever, and not the efficient cause. Regarding the first point, it should be known that the difference of humor was shown in chapter twenty-nine. Regarding the second, it should be known that some have said humor was twofold: one kind is in the limbs—for it is imbibed and mixed with them—and such is the matter of health and sickness. The other is in the cavities of the veins, and this stands as the efficient cause of health and sickness. But this [distinction] is not valid, because in the first case, the humor does not remain but has passed into the limb. Nor is it the efficient cause as they propose, but rather the material cause, as will be seen in general. And so, some explain "humors" as **spirits**, because they are closely related to the spirits and limbs. Others, moved by prejudice, have simply asserted that humor would be the efficient cause and not the material one. Yet others, explaining the "material" as the "efficient," say that the material cause is also the "maker" <note>original: "faciens"</note>, since it is one of the four causes, according to what is added at the end. It is manifest that it is among the "making" causes. This will also appear from what is to be said.

Regarding the third point, it should be known (as they have argued not poorly) that humor relates to fever or sickness in the role of both material and efficient cause, as collected in the third book. The occasions of material sicknesses are when the four humors depart from their temperament in quantity or quality. And this happens either on the part of the matter or on the part of the agent. He adds also that humors depart from nature in two ways: from the material part and the efficient part simultaneously. This is confirmed because just as a good humor exists for health, so a depraved one exists for sickness. For the effects and causes of contraries are likewise contrary.

But a humor remaining under the grace of nature stands as the material cause of health. For from it arises the temperament of the parts; whence in the seventh book of the *Physics*: health is a certain commensuration of heats and colds, or of those things within—that is, the humors from which the body is composed, as they explain. Similarly, a humor by its tempered nature preserves or produces health. So it also happens in sickness, that a humor can have the role of both material and efficient cause. Furthermore, everything that is made is made "from something" (as a principle) or "in something" (from an agent). Since any generation or making proceeds from potentiality into act through some being already in act, according to the ninth book of *Metaphysics*. But fever is made; for an effect [is made] "from something" or "from something and into something." That which is properly generated is "from something and into something," because a **substance** is more properly generated from something (namely, from matter), whereas an **accident** <note>Such as a disease or a quality.</note> more properly occurs "in something" as its subject. And it is confirmed that two things are found in a humor: the matter (or the subject itself) and the quality. Therefore, a humor can have the role of both material and efficient cause toward fever. And similarly in other material diseases.

However, someone might appear to say that a humor is the material cause of fever and not the efficient cause, because that which causes humoral fever (such as a putrid one) is the **vapor** or putrid **soot** <note>original: "fumus seu fuligo"; medieval medicine taught that putrefying humors released smoky, toxic vapors that traveled to the heart to cause fever.</note> as mentioned. This, however, is not the humor, just as the spirit is not the blood; indeed, it is generally called something else by physicians, even though it is constituted from it [the humor], according to differences 48 and 59. Nor does the humor itself perfectly produce the fever as matter, since it must eventually reach the heart through the aforementioned soot. Regarding the fourth point:

To the first, it should be said: either that the same thing is not both material and efficient cause, since humor (as seen) is generally distinguished from putrid soot and from the "mine" of putrefaction likewise. Or it should be said that in generation and coming-to-be, it will be as a certain substance. This is verified especially since agents and patients in it ought properly to be distinct in subject and location. But in generation regarding an accident (such as health and sickness), this is not necessary, as is shown in the matter of vapor, which has heat implanted within it, and the hidden form raised in **theriac** <note>original: "tyriaca"; a famous polypharmaceutical compound used as a "universal" antidote.</note> by which poison is repelled, according to distinction 178. For the subjects of the simple [elements] are their matter, and their qualities are the agent. Hence, in the *Principles* <note>original: "regni," i.e., the *Tegni*.</note>, the **six non-naturals** <note>The six external factors that govern health: air, food/drink, sleep/waking, motion/rest, evacuation/repletion, and passions of the soul.</note> are placed as the matter of health and sickness. But according to whether they are administered to the body in appropriate use, they become preservers and providers of health. So also, those "sinning" against temperament are the causes of sickness. It suffices, therefore, in this kind of distinction of reason for there to be a real identity of the subject. Or, although matter and agent do not coincide as one in number or species, they can nevertheless concur in that which is the same in subject. This denotes the matter and the quality in a mixture. In which the substance of the elements are the matter and their qualities are the agent; similarly in the present case. Someone could also explain "efficient" as "maker"; for every cause "makes" something in some way. On this, Haly [Abbas] says that this would not properly be the case except in sicknesses that are only at their first beginning. To the other, it should be said that health...

And he referred disease to the whole, as in the animal in common, and not to any parts whatsoever. This is because he finally adds: It is necessary for an animal, insofar as it is an animal, for each [part] to have life, and yet according to the parts themselves there is no sense <note>original: "insus" for "sensus"; meaning the parts only "sense" as part of the whole living being.</note>. Just as he shows that the natural philosopher must determine the principles of health and disease, which are passions of life, since he must deal with life. Or it should be said that **spirits** and **humors** can be said to live, for they are ordered toward life from proximity. And what is lacking to a small degree seems to the intellect as if it has nothing at all, according to Aristotle in the *Physics* <note>original: "phīs ī .sio."; likely referring to the principle that small differences are often ignored in general definitions.</note>. Or that health and disease, and the state of the member, are finally caused from other prior things. For from praiseworthy humors and spirits, the tempered composition of the whole originates. Then follow the composition and the common nature. From these, health is in the part; likewise, disease, induced from these corrupted things, finally settles in the member. This is because the injury to the whole follows the injury of the part.

It is supported indeed that "subject" <note>term: subject <gloss>the underlying physical substance or location where a disease resides</gloss></note> is used in two ways. Either properly, as that in which a disposition is grounded—and thus the humor is the subject of putrefaction, the spirit of effervescence, and the member of hectic fever <note>original: "rbice" / "ethica"; a fever that has settled into the solid parts of the body, often associated with consumption.</note>. Or as that in which the physical operations or corruptions are manifested. And one should know that the member is the primary subject of health and disease. For the dispositions of this are first—that is, immediately—in the member, though they occur in the spirits and humors; but first—that is, before anything else—in the humors and spirits. As to the other part, it appears that the humor is well granted the role of mediated efficient cause, and also of material cause. Since the effect always immediately corresponds to its cause, as fever does to the **purulent soot** <note>original: "fuligini purulēte"; medieval doctors believed putrefying humors released a "sooty" vapor that traveled to the heart to cause fever.</note>, which is joined to them by its own transformative power; for it proceeds from it without a medium. But in the material cause, such as **repletion** <note>term: repletion <gloss>an excess of humors, often from overeating, considered a primary cause of disease</gloss></note>, the cause is mediated.

**W**hence he shows that digested matter cannot cause fever or disease. Because the alteration that takes place causes putrefaction to cease, while the substance remains, as in the prior difference. But digestion is a brief alteration. For alteration is owed to the matter, just as there are differences of health. Furthermore, if the cause is removed, the effect is removed, since it followed it. But putrefaction follows fever after the **joined cause** <note>original: "causam conjunctam"; a cause that exists simultaneously with its effect.</note> convertibly. While the cause exists, the disease exists. When it recedes, according to Johannitius <note>original: "lobāīciū"; Johannitius (Hunayn ibn Ishaq) was a foundational translator and medical authority.</note>, health follows. When we prohibit putrefaction, fever will not be generated from it. But "digestives" remove this—such as food, drink, exercise, and medicine. Furthermore, when the **boiling** <note>term: ebullitio <gloss>a "boiling" or fermentation of humors during the process of putrefaction</gloss></note> in the putrefaction ceases, the fever ceases, since the putrid smoke does not seek the heart. But in digested matter, the boiling ceases; otherwise, it would not be digested. Also, that which is moved by nature in an equal and well-ordered way does not cause fever. Since fever is caused by the "victory" and inequality it obtains over nature; but the digested matter is that which stands apart from this. Again, digestion is a completion by one's own natural heat from the passive qualities—Difference 50. How then, since it is subdued by nature, can it cause fever at all? Galen <note>original: "Palyn"; likely a corruption of Galenus.</note> in the fourth book of *Symptoms and Accidents* suggests this. But digested matter removes its subject—namely, the humor in which it was grounded—as seen in the prior difference by Haly Abbas <note>original: "abice"; likely Al-Abbas, the author of the *Liber Regalis*.</note>. Indeed, by an alteration such that you make that same putrefaction and substance which was before putrefaction remain in the body. Wherefore Haly says: "One of the intentions of cure is the mutation of the humor until the putrefaction rests." Therefore, digested matter does not generate fever in any way.

Some argue the opposite from the first book of Avicenna's *On Fevers*. While the digestive virtue still remains, the humor that putrefies within reaches such an alteration. From the book *On Crises* they also offer a sequence, and ask whether something is "laudable" <note>original: "laudabile"; in medicine, this meant "healthy" or "properly formed," as in "laudable pus."</note> except for the humor causing the sickness which is already digested. From these and others, they argue that fever can occur even when the matter is undergoing digestion. Likewise, since an effect does not remain once the cause is removed, if putrefaction inducing fever were to cease through digestion, the fever itself would rest when the matter was digested. But in the **state** <note>term: status <gloss>the "acme" or highest point of intensity in a disease's progress</gloss></note>, the matter is fully digested—first book *On Crises*. Therefore the fever should cease. But we experience the opposite, since at that time the symptoms [accidents] are most intense. For concerning the state of a disease, it was pronounced by Hippocrates that all symptoms are then more severe. Furthermore, the matter which is assumed to be digested is putrid; but a humor is normally according to nature and disobedient to corruption. Which of these can sustain a fever? Therefore, digested matter **can** cause fever.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that the matter of putrid fever is complex. One indeed is remote, such as a humor or repletion. Another is nearer, such as the material of putrefaction. The third indeed is the joined cause by reason of the efficient humor, such as the soot or putrid smoke seeking the heart immediately—as in the preceding difference. What digestion is, Difference 50 showed. What fever is, Difference 87. Regarding the second, it must be known that some have doubted both sides of this question, leaving it in a treatise with great hesitation, either because its explanation seemed difficult or lengthy. Whence others have well suggested that perfectly digested matter does not cause fever, because it is immediately joined to the expulsion of the disease. This then exists only by accident, as will appear. Some others have stated more clearly that digestion makes the putrefaction causing the fever cease; thus, once the matter is immediately digested, it will not perfectly induce fever. However, they say a certain quality impressed upon the members makes an extrinsic fever. Which perhaps is not valid, neither as to the first... nor as to the second, because thus it would already be putrid in all with hectic fever, since putrid fever resides in the humor, but hectic fever in the member.

**A**gain, a certain brief passion makes no impression on the part, for which after its departure there is need of care for what remains. Regarding the third, it must be known that digested matter—such as putrefaction, for which it was said that before digestion it causes fever—can still foster it. This is indicated in the fourth book of *Symptoms*: that there may be a rising of the fever with the appearance of digestion, just as there is no intense pain with the appearance of digestion. Furthermore, because until the curative intentions are fulfilled, the fever-removing actions will remain, and it cannot be made to cease by other means; but in digested matter, all curative intentions are not yet complete.
