<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the nature of fever and whether humors that have undergone "digestion" (the body's natural process of ripening or breaking down harmful substances) can still cause or sustain a disease. The author cites Galen, Avicenna, and Haly Abbas to distinguish between the process of putrefaction and its end products.</meta>

...are completed. For there are three types mentioned in the 11th book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." – *De Ingenio Sanitatis*, Galen's work on the therapeutic method.</note>: the putrefaction of good humors that are excreted and cooled, and the semi-putrefaction of those that are digested. Therefore, in the third book of *Practice*, it is said that one must use three means in the healing of fevers arising from putrefaction: First is the extinguishing of the heat of the fever and its countering. Second is the evacuation of the putrid humor. Third is the regimen of food and the choice of drink. This benefits by using digestive foods and drinks and medicines, as he explains in general. However, only two methods are touched upon in the *Royal Book* <note>The *Liber Regalis* or *Kitab al-Maliki* by Haly Abbas.</note>: alteration and evacuation. Regarding this, Haly Abbas <note>original: "baly"</note> says that Galen was silent about the cure for fever with <unclear>stris</unclear> and humors because of its obviousness. And since his discourse was on the preservation of health. 

->Berthold the German<-

Berthold the German, however, says that Haly Abbas was an "unrelenting stimulus." I say that Galen was not silent, but he follows up at the end of the chapter where he says: "Then one should come to that which has been made into a disease by that [cause]." Which a certain group of people <note>original: "gentis"</note> attacks in many ways, even if he [Galen] has been unclear in several places. For a disease is not truly "made" from a disease unless it remains after the fever has been cut off. When the fever has ceased through the cessation of its cause, since it depended on it, a certain other "distraction" remains in the members, which is not yet so far progressed that it is habitually ingrained. 

->The Analogy of the Fire<-

It is just as when, after the removal of a massive and long-lasting fire, heat remains for some time in the walls even though the fire is gone.

This is certainly held by what he says: "Whosoever [comes] as if to that which is still in the process of becoming." And through this, it is finally manifest that the healing of these imbalances <note>original: "discrasia."</note> is a restoration. Also, in the fourth book of the *Aphorisms*, it appears that in the healing of material disease, three things must happen: namely **digestion**, followed by **separation**—that is, distinction—and thereafter **evacuation**. But in digestion, only one thing occurs; for in it, there is neither evacuation nor the separation that is ordered toward evacuation.

There is, however, a certain separation which is the parting of the humor from the parts to which it was adhering. Thus, the separation regarding the matter to be led out is twofold. Or perhaps threefold, if the "cutting" of viscous matter <note>term: <term>incisio</term> — a medical process of breaking down thick, sticky humors using specific medicines or heat.</term> is called separation. For the principal goal of digestion is to make the matter uniform through its separation, so that it suffers no obstacle in its expulsion through the open passages <note>original: "meatibus."</note>. Whence after digestion, the final expulsion must follow. Therefore, digestion alone is not sufficient. 

Wherefore in the *Prognostics* [it is said]: "Oftentimes the disease is already digested, but there is no procession of phlegm <note>original: "sputi."</note> as there ought to be." This happens because of the weakness of the virtue <note>term: <term>virtus</term> — the body’s innate biological power or "nature" that drives functions like healing and movement.</term> that moves the matter. Whence in the fourth book of *Internal [Diseases]* according to Hippocrates: "Certain paraplegics, having expelled the digested matter, lived but a short time." One cannot say that this happened by accident. For if the matter had acquired all the "goodness" of digestion, it would not devise any craftiness <note>note: "craftiness" here refers to the disease's ability to persist or cause harm.</note> even if the virtue were weak. Likewise, sanies <note>term: <term>sanies</term> — a thin, greenish or blood-stained discharge from a wound or sore; considered "digested" because it has been processed by the body's heat.</term> is digested matter, as appears in the *Prognostics*. For sanies is made when natural heat finally triumphs, distinguished by its proper characteristics, so that it is already digested by the natural heat prevailing in it. But being so disposed, it is less easily led out; whence in the *Aphorisms*: "Concerning the generation of sanies," etc.

Furthermore, it is confirmed because the putrefaction of humors which is in the vessels is similar to that which occurs in inflammations, apostemes <note>term: <term>apostemata</term> — abscesses or swellings filled with purulent matter.</note>, and other pustules. But in those appearing as sanies made through digestion, the fever still remains; indeed, in some, the eruption increases. *Prognostics*: "Again, in which a not small part is contained against nature, it is able to nourish the begun fever," and especially when the members are already disposed to receive it. Such is sanies, however much it is conquered by nature. For even in it, things against nature still persist that are not small. *Prognostics*: "Appearing in the first [stages] of fevers," and in the fifth book of *On Drugs*. Still, that which remains in it is hostile to nature: horribleness, inflammation, and "seriousness" <note>original: "seriositas."</note>, which can produce an aptitude for fever. These things are found by those diligently observing sanies or matter, no matter how much it is digested. For through alteration, nothing more is removed from the matter except its "disobedience" to expulsion, since this digestion is nothing else [than preparation].

From these things, it is proven that putrefaction—not only while it is happening but also when digestion is complete—can nourish a powerful fever, as will appear in the resolution of the arguments. But regarding the aforesaid, it is doubted: for from these things at least it is held that when matter is digested, the fever and its accidents <note>term: <term>accidentia</term> — the secondary symptoms or clinical signs accompanying a disease.</term> ought to be mitigated, since it has been mastered by nature. Yet we experience the opposite. 

It must be said that these things should be mitigated because of the matter's digestion, as argued. But that they [the symptoms] increase happens either because of the body's weakness, or more so because of the "impetus of nature" toward the excretion of the matter. Whence in the fifth book on the accidents of a burning fever <note>original: "febris causoica."</note>, when a rigor happens: because the matter of this fever, being red bile, while it is moved strongly, it is increased and ignited more, and in no way recedes unless a "voiding" <note>original: "egestio."</note> follows or a great sweat happens. And the second *Aphorism*: "To whomsoever a crisis occurs, to them the night before the paroxysm <note>term: <term>paroxysmus</term> — the point of greatest intensity in a fever or disease cycle.</term> will be difficult and unbearable." The Commentator says: This happens while nature is discerning the harmful from the helpful and preparing for excretion. For the animal virtue is greatly fatigued according to its state, even if the vital [virtue] remains strong and 

<margin>natural</margin> 

Therefore, regarding the fourth point, it must be said: To the first, that through digestion the "essence" <note>original: "esse."</note> of putrefaction is not removed. For as long as it exists as putrid, it can never be as if it were natural. But digestion removes from the putrefaction the excessive qualities that are actually rebellious to the expulsive virtue. If the cause was cold, it is warmed; if moist, it is dried, and so on. If it is thin, it is thickened, and vice versa. Also, viscous matter is "cut" [broken down] as in the *Royal Book*. For it cannot repel the habit from itself even when it is currently susceptible, especially when there is a disposition to fever. 

Or it should be said that putrefaction is twofold: one indeed "in the making" <note>original: "fiens."</note>, the other "completed" <note>original: "facta."</note>. 11th book of *Method of Healing*. Alteration indeed makes the "in the making" putrefaction cease, but not the "completed." For it corrects and terminates the antecedent cause, lest it be produced under the joined cause. Know, however, that "putrefaction" is properly said of that which is "in the making," and not that which is in the "completed" state. Since according to Avicenna <note>original: "Ay."</note> it is a corruption, and according to Galen <note>original: "Ga."</note> a transformation; they pronounce it to be a thing "in the making" and not in a "completed" state. But "completed" putrefaction—and even more so "in the making"—is of a nature to cause a fever that has been started. To the other, it must be said: that the "mine" <note>original: "minera" — the source or site of production.</note> of putrefaction is not a truly joined cause of fever, but rather the putrid soot <note>original: "fuligo."</note> reaching the heart immediately... Whence those saying that putrefaction is a cause united and convertible with fever...

<summary>This page discusses the medical theory of "digestion" (pepsis) in fevers, arguing that even after the body has processed harmful humors into "sanies" (pus), a fever can persist or even intensify during the crisis phase as nature struggles to expel the matter. It distinguishes between putrefaction currently occurring and putrefaction that has already been completed, using the analogy of residual heat in a wall after a fire.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the causes of fever, specifically focusing on the distinction between the "material" cause (the humors themselves) and the "efficient" cause (the process of putrefaction or the resulting vapors). It transitions into a new "Differentia" (scholastic inquiry) regarding the timing of medical intervention, specifically whether a patient should be purged or bled at the very onset of an illness.</meta>

# Whether evacuation is appropriate at the beginning of a disease.

...they set down the causes. Although there are expressly three, two are more material, as if prior, and one is efficient, like a foul smoke <note>original: "fumus putidus"</note> arising from a real mineral-like rot, just as the spirit <note>In medieval medicine, "spirit" refers to a subtle vapor that carries life force through the blood.</note> is generated from the blood. And here, many modern physicians have stood obsessed, strongly asserting the same thing against Avicenna <note>original: "Au." - Referring to the Persian physician Ibn Sina.</note>, positing both a material and an efficient principle. This is because in the *Techne* <note>original: "tegn̄" - Galen's *Ars Medica* or *Techne*.</note> they think the humor is called the efficient cause of fever. Which it is not; rather, it is the soot <note>original: "fuligo" - metabolic waste products or vapors.</note> called by the same name already produced by another, as seen in Difference 87 and earlier. It has long been apparent how much food, medicine, and other things can provide from the benignity of what is putrid. Regarding the other point, it must be said that the boiling <note>original: "ebulitō" - the metaphorical boiling of humors during fever.</note> does not cease until it reaches its end, and the opposition that putrefaction has toward nature, as touched upon, is especially true when putrefaction is in the process of becoming. To the other point, that which was said through the first appeared: it extends from the same root. To the other point, it must be said that the discourse on the root of digestion concerns youth; here, however, the reasoning concerns the harm itself. To the other point, it must be said that putrefaction can be understood in two ways: more by quality and by the body; and putrefaction which is not an accident but a substance acting in no other subject. The authorities introduced for the other part also claim that putrefaction is more "in the making" than "already made," of which there is no doubt it causes fever. Therefore, it has appeared why a fever is also caused in the state of completed putrefaction and which of its aspects are intensified.

# DIFFERENCE 161.

-> Whether evacuation is appropriate at the beginning of a disease. <-

Because Hippocrates says: "In the beginning of diseases, if anything seems moved, move it." <note>A famous medical aphorism suggesting early intervention.</note> Whence the Commentator <note>Usually Galen, commenting on Hippocrates.</note> says: It is better to evacuate in the beginnings, so that the material, having been made smaller, can be more easily digested by nature. Likewise, in the 8th and 13th books of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." - *De Ingenio Sanitatis*.</note>, he orders evacuation at the beginning. Furthermore, all medical practitioners hold this principle: in fevers of the blood, one should evacuate even until fainting <note>original: "lippotomiā" - *leippothymia*, a controlled faint during bloodletting to shock the system.</note>. They also order immediate and diverse evacuation in cases of apoplexy <note>stroke</note>, quinsy <note>original: "sqnantia" - *synanche*, a severe throat infection</note>, and such things. Also, one should evacuate at that time when the strength <note>original: "uirtus" - the patient's vital force</note> is stronger, since it is disturbed by the evacuation itself. Thus, the primary indication for evacuating is taken from the strength, according to the first book of the *Aphorisms*. That, however, is at the beginning, when the nature has not yet been weakened by the struggle with the disease. Also, because evacuation is forbidden at the beginning, this happens because of the rawness <note>original: "indigōne" - lack of "digestion" or ripening</note> of the matter; for which reason, Hippocrates ordered to medicate things that are digested and to let nature evacuate. But some matters are already digested even at the beginning, such as many blood-related humors floating in the stomach. And perhaps furious choleric humors, since they have nothing preventing them from being moved, as will be shown in what follows. Therefore, one must evacuate at the beginning.

On the other hand: Because Hippocrates orders us to treat with drugs things that are ripe <note>original: "pepana"</note> and to move things that are not crude; but in the beginnings, they are crude. Also, because they evacuate the matter of undigested things, and especially when it has been collected at a specific part, they evacuate nothing of the [harmful] matter, but instead destroy the healthy parts resisting the sickness—according to the fourth book of the *Aphorisms* and the first of *On Crises*. Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century medical writer.</note> says: In pleurisy, which often comes from blood in the side, he orders the vein to be cut when the pain ascends to the shoulders; but then the passion already appears to be in its increase. Again, in the ninth book of *On the Method of Healing*, he ordered a young athlete suffering from a putrid continuous fever <note>original: "synocha putrida"</note> to be bled at the eighth hour of the third night. But the fever seems to have already passed its beginning, since the first stage is terminated in the fourth—according to the third book of *On Crises* and the first. Furthermore, digestion is the making-ready <note>original: "babilitatō" - *habilitatio*</note> of the humor so that it may be easily expelled by nature, as was shown in Difference 50. But at the beginning, such readiness cannot yet exist due to the shortness of time. For in order for a praiseworthy judgment <note>original: "iudiciū" - a "crisis" or turning point in the disease.</note> to occur, digestion and "cooking" <note>original: "excoctiō" - the process of humors being refined by body heat.</note> must have preceded—fourth book of *Aphorisms*. Likewise, in the first book, chapter four, listing many diseases, he says: You ought to know that while these people fear illnesses and have not yet fallen into them, bloodletting is granted to them more safely; but when they have fallen into them, in their beginnings, bloodletting should be omitted, because it thins the humors and makes them flow through the body, and mixes them with the healthy blood. And it is also the case that nothing of what is necessary is evacuated. Furthermore, the Medical Art imitates nature. But nature does not evacuate in the beginning because the matter is unrefined. Therefore, one should not evacuate at the beginning, but perhaps more in the "state" <note>original: "statu" - the peak or plateau of a disease.</note> when the matter has been digested.

Regarding the first point, one must know what evacuation is and in how many ways it is spoken of; this <margin>Evacuation generally</margin> will be shown in Difference 164. Indeed, evacuation is commonly understood as any drawing out, whether it be an abundance of blood with other humors or one specifically. It is also known what the "beginning" is and in how many ways it is taken—Difference 106 and 112. Because as it is one of the periods of a disease, it is taken in the fifth sense. Regarding the second point, it must be known that it is written in seven ways that expulsion is appropriate once digestion has occurred. But when digestion does not appear, then a disagreement is found among physicians. For Galen and the greater part of physicians say we should by no means purge while the matter is undigested, unless the sickness <margin>Rhazes</margin> is at the ultimate peak of its sharpness. And he adds afterwards that in phrenetic and melancholic fevers, Rhazes purges at their beginning. And that was entirely his opinion. <margin>Galen</margin> Galen, however, says the opposite clearly: that we should by no means purge at the beginning of melancholic fevers. And he writes this very thing in the *Letter to Glaucon*, Book 2, because the end of these sicknesses is safe and does not wait for bad digestion. However, there is a series [of instructions] in the book to Glaucon, saying: do not give any medicine rashly at the very start, nor perform purging or withdrawal of semen or blood unless you perhaps see an excessive abundance of blood. Then bleed from the left arm. But when you clearly see the signs of the cause's digestion, you will then give a melancholic purgative, drawing it out not just once, but as often as you think required. After these things, we persuade you to take theriac <note>A famous ancient "all-cure" or antitoxin.</note> or *diacythibe* <note>A specific medicinal preparation, likely containing germander.</note> within a few intervening days, and other such things. From which it is proven to us that all hold the same opinion as Hippocrates. But if you give such a thing twice right at the beginning, it is greatly objected to. <margin>10. From one quartan fever there were two; from two there were three; thus everything comes from an imagination of Averroes which I seek.</margin> For out of one quartan fever <note>A fever recurring every four days.</note> you will make two, and out of two you will make three, or from a light one a stronger one, and you will lead the person into danger, making it so he does not live. Finally, the discourse is continued by Averroes: but a phlegmatic condition is of bad determination, and because of this, it is necessary that the sick person be evacuated before perfect digestion is expected. And therefore the physician first...

It emphasizes that while early intervention can be vital in acute cases, improper purging can worsen fevers, potentially turning a single quartan fever into multiple recurring ones.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic discussion on medical treatment, moving from the theoretical causes of fever to the practical application of purging and bloodletting (evacuation) at the start of a disease. <margin>+ Since evacuation is twofold: eradicative and minorative</margin>
...to begin with thinning and cutting medicines for one week <note>original: "ebdomodā unam"</note>. In what manner should one begin to administer pharmaceuticals? What should be felt regarding this will be shown in the third point of our discussion. Regarding the third point, let the truth first be opened concerning its quality, and thereafter the order of its grace: whether it should be done in certain hours, or whether one should be entirely silent. Regarding the first, it must be known that evacuation is of two kinds: one is **eradicative** and perfect, by which the sinful material <note>original: "peccas materia" — corrupt humors that cause disease.</note> is totally removed from the body. The other is **minorative** and imperfect, through which some of the material is evacuated so that nature, made more powerful, may eventually prevail over the residue. Hence, in the eleventh book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "xi. de ige." — Galen's De Ingenio Sanitatis.</note>: for by a lightened evacuation, nature manages the body and lays down what was weighing it down, just as a load will be easily managed by the remainder; and it will digest what can be digested and excrete it. This also appears in the first part of book four and book fourteen, and the third book.

Next, it must be said regarding the four conditions, that for a sickness to which evacuation is owed, either it should be evacuated, or there is hope for health, or not at all. Indeed, if signs of future death are already appearing <margin>}</margin>, in such a case—according to book eleven of <margin>2</margin> *On the Method of Healing* and the first and second *Aphorisms*—one ought not to evacuate nor, as it were, apply medicine. One should not strive in cases where life is lost <margin>}</margin>, but rather predict the future and thus withdraw from them, since in such cases it is vain to be disparaged by <margin>4</margin> unlearned people <note>original: "ydiotis" — laypeople or those without formal medical training.</note> on account of those aids which heal many others. Nevertheless, physicians sometimes—lest a defect appear in the art or the artist—strive to practice upon such patients, as even with the **apoplectic**, those **spasming** from emptiness, those with **irrecoverable fainting**, and those in the final stages of **consumption** <note>original: "ptificos pfcōs" — advanced phthisis or tuberculosis.</note>; though the signs mentioned above appear in *On the Method of Healing* and the *Prognostics*. Hence Mesue <note>A 9th-century Persian Christian physician.</note> says of apoplexy: "Lest a defect appear on the part of the practitioner, you shall strive from the beginning to subtract material insofar as it is possible."

But if a disease exists in which there is hope for health, the material is either gathered in one place or dispersed through all or several parts of the body. The first is twofold: because this material is either entirely in a "flux" <note>A flowing motion of humors toward an organ.</note> so that it may aggregate in a place, or it has already become massed together in great quantity in that part, as when an **aposteme** <note>A swelling or abscess.</note> occurs, which is a disease of the parts already formed, and in part future (from book thirteen of *On the Method of Healing*). But if it is in the process of becoming, and specifically when the material is **sanguine** <note>Pertaining to blood.</note> and has flowed through the veins, an evacuation—even an eradicative one—is owed to it at the beginning, provided the strength and other factors are proportionate (from the first of the *Aphorisms*). For when the material blood flows into a place to collect into an inflammation, once it is evacuated, the future swelling will either be entirely quieted or only a small amount will remain. This can also happen with **choleric** <note>Pertaining to yellow bile.</note> material, since a swelling can happen because of it.

But if the material has been massed together for the most part in a place, and the disease is partially formed, then the same **minorative** evacuation is owed (according to book thirteen of *On the Method of Healing* and the *Techne*). For I evacuate the whole not only in a **plethoric** <note>An excess of blood or humors.</note> disposition, but also on account of the magnitude of the suffering, even when the humors are in moderation in the whole body. For the pain and heat of an **inflaming** part become the cause of a "rheum" <note>A flow of humors.</note>, even if it exists without an overall superfluity in the body. By this evacuation, nature is lightened over the residue. Thus the fear of a rupture is avoided, even if it is through maturation. Hence in the first part of book four: he who has a small swelling <note>original: "apā" - apostema.</note> is better off when it is feared it might open before it matures, even if he did not require it and there was no great quantity.

An eradicative evacuation is not owed to such a person; hence, as touched upon in book four: those who, with an inflammation at the beginning of diseases, immediately strive to dissolve it with strong pharmacy, take away nothing of the inflammation. For the raw suffering is not remitted, but the resistance to the disease and the healthy humors are liquefied. Wherefore, in the first part of book four: when a humor is trapped in one member, let it be moved in no way until it matures and has a tempered essence. For if you do otherwise, it will be as if one tried to pull up a tree from the earth by pulling it sideways without separating it; it would be necessary either to break the tree or not pull it up at all, except with a great tearing of the earth. And thus one should not evacuate at the beginning, but in the "state" <note>The peak or plateau phase of a disease.</note> of the illness, as long as nature does not come to the rescue.

If, however, the material is dispersed through many or all parts of the body, then it constitutes either a long-lasting <note>original: "eroicam" — likely a scribal error for "chronicam" (chronic).</note> or an **acute** disease. If indeed it is long-lasting, such as that arising from **phlegm** and the like, or if the body is "full" either from an injury or fear, then one must not evacuate in that manner, which Galen perhaps suggests in his work *To Glaucon*, unless perhaps a swelling were feared from a fall or a blow. But if it is moderately full, it needs a minorative evacuation at the beginning so that nature may be strengthened over the residue, both through bloodletting, as appeared in books eleven and thirteen of *On the Method of Healing*, and also through pharmaceuticals in its own way. For Al-Mansur <note>Referring to the Book of Almansor by Rhazes.</note> in book ten teaches to evacuate cold humors minoratively in their beginning; hence in the first part regarding **phlegmatic fever**: "I do not like the waiting for digestion and softening in those things we spoke of first; rather it is necessary that something be evacuated, and one should wait for the rest until it digests." They also exhibit a medicine made of **turbith** <note>A purgative root.</note> constructed from ginger <note>original: "zinzib."</note> and sugar, powdered. In the cure of **quartan fever** <note>A fever that returns every fourth day, associated with black bile.</note> in the same place, there are signs of hope in which they agree. For all reduce at the beginning. It is also added after a bit: if it is necessary to evacuate something at the beginning of a fever-causing humor to lighten and cleanse it, this evacuation should be small, and done by evacuating lightly with a weak medicine, not with a strong eradicative one, so that the thin part is evacuated and the thick remains fixed and undigested. For in that way, nothing of the material is evacuated, but rather the healthy parts resisting the disease are weakened, especially when the material is thick and compacted.

But if the material is not chronic, then it will be either of great sharpness, because it is "furious," or otherwise. If the former, it will be either **choleric** or **sanguine**. For these materials sometimes turn furious, either by reason of quality (like choler) or quantity (as when blood is entirely exuberant). Sometimes a disease is also called **furious** by reason of its location, when whatever material is collected in a place where it hinders noble actions <note>The functions of vital organs like the heart or brain.</note>. Thus a disease can be called furious in three ways: **properly**, <margin>}</margin> like the choleric type—for that, according to Galen, is the one which moves suddenly like animals driven to mate, unbridled in its thinness and heat; **commonly**, <margin>3</margin> where blood is called the "furious" material; and **improperly**... <margin>}</margin> <margin>4</margin> <margin>}</margin> <margin>2</margin>

-> Properly -- From Choler. <-
-> Commonly -- From Blood. <-
-> Improperly -- From its Location. <-

<meta>This page continues the scholastic discussion on medical treatment, moving from the theoretical causes of fever to the practical application of purging and bloodletting (evacuation) at the start of a disease. It addresses the debate between aggressive treatment and waiting for the "digestion" of humors.</meta>

-># Whether evacuation is appropriate at the beginning of a disease...<-

And it can be said by way of similarity by reason of the place within us, or where the matter is contained: such as the matter causing **apoplexy** <note>original: "appopliaz"</note> in the brain, or in the throat <note>likely referring to quinsy or inflammation</note>, or in the intestines causing **iliac** or **colic** pain with the greatest vehemence. This "furious" matter should properly be evacuated at the very beginning according to Hippocrates <note>original: ".y." — Ypocras</note> and others, even by <term>eradicative purging</term> <note>total removal of the corrupt humor</note>; this is out of fear of its mobility and "fury," lest it be transferred to the heart and kill the patient instantly, or collect in another principal organ and induce an <term>aposteme</term> <note>an inflammatory swelling or abscess</note>. Furthermore, such matter is subtle, mobile, and already "digested" <note>original: "digesta" — in medieval medicine, this means the humors have reached a state where they are ready to be expelled</note> and prepared for extraction; for it shares little in the conditions that would prohibit its expulsion due to the indigestive state of the humor.
<margin>Regarding the crisis.</margin>
Hence, regarding the **crisis** <note>the turning point of a disease</note> at the start: in these cases alone is it reasonable to use pharmacy at the beginning, as it aids in the ease of attracting the overabundant humors. And it follows that where the humors are most acute, they are subtle, because there is no thickness nor viscosity to prevent the action of the laxative medicine. But since laxative medicines are by nature warm and dry, which might further incite such matter to "fury," it must be said that they only cause harm if they exceed in their qualities, incite fever, and stir up the disease in its progress. However, this can be avoided by mixing them with cold and moist things, such as mixing **scammony** with **yellow myrobalans**, pomegranate juice, syrup of costus, syrup of rob <note>a thickened fruit juice</note>, and such things. These confer no small benefit in such a state, or they alleviate the symptoms by being given in small quantities, or by being drawn out with "blessed" medicines <note>gentle, well-regarded remedies</note> that are moist and lubricating. If the matter is **sanguine** <note>bloody</note>, dissolving by its own superfluous quantity, it is immediately necessary to evacuate it from the beginning, such that many physicians agree it should be led out even unto fainting <note>original: "licopī" — likely a corruption of lypothymia</note>. And this is rightly so, 
<margin>Avicenna</margin>
<margin>to be read when it is in the third [stage]</margin>
because in the case of blood, one does not wait for "digestion" as in other humors. When the intention is to remove blood, it is not of the kind where digestion is expected—an expectation used for other humors—but rather it is feared lest it run into the principal organs, extinguishing the innate heat by suffocation, or lest the vessels burst. This is according to the first book of the *Aphorisms* regarding "good habit" <note>a state of physical fitness</note>. Yet note that this evacuation at the beginning is for "eradicating" the cause, not merely treating the symptoms, so long as the strength of nature persists. For it is similar to feeding a patient at the wrong hour—for instance, during the peaks of a fever <note>original: "paroxismis"</note>—when one must preserve the strength. In both cases, the goal is to ensure that the patient's strength does not succumb to the labor of the coming struggle.

If, however, the matter is not of such vehement acuteness—such as those that terminate within the first, fourth, or seventh day—but is simply "acute" and not "furious," resting and giving nature space for digestion so that the strength may endure until the hour of maturity, then a <term>minorative evacuation</term> <note>a partial reduction of the humors</note> at the start is sufficient, provided the body is not already empty. Thus nature, being unburdened, may act upon the residue; one should not use eradicative purging when the matter is not yet digested, nor subtle, nor mobile, nor overly sanguine. This appears from the words previously cited from *On the Method of Healing* and the *Tegni* <note>Galen's Ars Medica</note>. In a sanguine fever, it is necessary that evacuation be done by "diminution" <note>bloodletting</note> if it is superfluous at the beginning—that is, 

minorative—and if the superfluity remains until maturity, which is often removed at the hour of phlebotomy. If the matter is of a colic nature, just as blood must be evacuated (as seen in the tenth book of Almansor <note>Rhazes' medical compendium</note>), so in **tertian** <note>a fever recurring every three days</note> and **burning fevers** <note>original: "causone"</note>, he teaches to evacuate lightly at the beginning. Haly Abbas <note>an 11th-century Persian physician</note> agrees with this. Why? Because you must hurry at first and soothe with a certain gentleness. And regarding "bastard" tertian fever <note>original: "notba"</note>: concerning purging at the start, let those things be used which are closer to equality. Hence, those sicknesses which are not extremely acute and arise from subtle humors—such as true tertian fever which does not pass beyond the seventh paroxysm—Avicenna says we ought to wait for digestion, because the digestion of a subtle humor involves its thickening. Therefore, it appears that at the beginning, a minorative evacuation is appropriate if the matter is not extremely acute; if it is, then use eradicative purging. Regarding this, it should be known
<margin>Note</margin>
that during the "increase" of the disease <note>original: "iaugmēto"</note>, eradicative evacuation is not appropriate, for by then the "furious" matter would have already brought about destruction. At that time, the matter is already partly settled in the organs and the strength is under attack. Minorative purging, however, can be appropriate, especially in long illnesses where one must digest and evacuate by parts almost all the time, so that nature does not remain overwhelmed. In the "status" <note>the peak of the disease</note>, one must observe: if the matter is digested and nature is winning, then the physician should do nothing by art, but commit everything to nature. As the first book of the *Aphorisms* says: "Things that are being judged or have been judged... [leave them be]." It is better to remain silent during the peak if nature is prevailing.
<margin>Avicenna, Aphorisms 4, part 3</margin>
For nature is such that it saves more than die, unless it be a pestilential constitution. If, however, nature is powerless to expel the digested matter at the peak, then the physician must supply nature's defect and evacuate it. As is added: "Those things which must be moved, move them where nature tends." And in the fourth book: "If the humor is not digested, 
<margin>Aphorism 4</margin>
do not move it except at the beginning." At the peak, do not move anything until nature prevails and digests. And if nature does not move it, you move it at the hour of its motion. And if nature is moving or has moved it, then leave it and its operation alone. In the "decline" or similar stage, when the crisis has perfectly succeeded at the peak, one should not evacuate by art, since nature has evacuated sufficiently. This is a common error among practitioners who want to evacuate everyone who is recovering, hoping to gain more [money or credit], thereby making the act and the crisis of nature incomplete. For those truly recovering do not need evacuation, as they have little and good blood. 
<margin>Not the spirit</margin>
But for those not truly recovering, it is the opposite. If something remains, it must be completed by the physician's help. Know that just as evacuation is appropriate at the beginning of the disease and sometimes at the peak, so it is in the seasons of Spring and Autumn. Thus it is said that those who seek the benefit of purging should choose Spring and Autumn. Regarding the fourth point: a minorative evacuation is granted at the start, which is what Hippocrates meant, but not an eradicative one, unless the matter...

# Whether evacuation acts only on the resting cause

If the humor were of great acuity, which according to Hippocrates <note>original: "ypocrate"</note> rarely happens. To the other point, it should be said that Galen <note>original: "Gā."</note> hears of "minorating" evacuation <note>a partial removal of humors to relieve pressure</note>, but it is not "eradicative" <note>a complete removal of the cause</note>. To another point, it appears similarly: because such matter is called "furious" in a similar way. And similarly, the term "furious" being extended to another point, these diseases can indeed be called "furious." To another point, it should be said that although the strength may be strong at the beginning, it does not yet exist <note>as a stable state</note>. To another point, similarly to what has already been seen. The parts of the other side are introduced similarly through their own paths. To the first and second of these, it must be said that once evacuation is perfected, the matter already **digested** <note>matured or processed by the body’s heat</note> must be evacuated, and not before, since nature is not yet evacuating it. To another point, it should be said that Hippocrates first treated **pleurisy** <note>original: "pleurefiz"</note> with a trial cure rather than starting with heaters. Or, because the disease is still at the beginning, when the pain ascends into the ribs and specifically when it is of a longer duration, those treating it now evacuate at the very beginning, before it might be better weighed. To another point, it should be said that Galen would have performed a **phlebotomy** <note>bloodletting</note> on the youth immediately from the start, had there not been other physicians who ordered it to be done. To the other point, it appears similarly through the aforementioned. To another point, the distinction appears in **Chapter 164**.

<margin>To this argument, see Book 9, Chapter 8 of *De Ingenio*.</margin>
<margin>Phlebotomy, when postponed at the beginning of a disease, is harmful.</margin>

Or it must be said that Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note> does not simply deny that phlebotomy should be performed. But rather that it is not as safe when someone has fallen into a disease as it was before, and he feels this on the fourth day. For when phlebotomy is postponed at the beginning of a disease, it is not his intention, and perhaps the patient is killed by the arrival of the weakness of strength. And therefore he advised that phlebotomy should be suspended as far as is possible, either because in the aforementioned diseases the blood is subtle, thin, and good, and the bad humors are boiling over due to the disease, or they are raw and violent. Raw humors coming out before they begin to generate diseases must be evacuated with caution. But once they are already feverish, in no way; for now it is to be feared lest phlebotomy snatch away the good blood and leave the bad. Or, he denies eradicative evacuation then, but not minorating. To the other point, it must be said that eradicative evacuation is not expected unless the matter is digested; provided that it is at least "furious." To the other point, the difference is noted in **Chapter 146**.

### DISTINCTION 162.

It is shown that evacuation is expected only for the **joined cause** <note>original: "giuncte" — the immediate cause of the symptoms</note>. Because it is owed to that which causes the disease: for evacuation is administered because of the causative agent of the disease, and this cause exists as "joined." Again, in the *Tegni* <note>original: "regni" — Galen's *Ars Medica*</note>: It is necessary to cut away each of the efficient causes. A cause of this kind is "joined," for it causes the disease by itself. And the disease does not cease except by the immediate cutting away of that cause, which is the "joined" cause, as the cure of **enrasis** <note>likely a corruption of *emphasis* or a specific Greek-derived clinical term for an obstruction</note> signifies in the *Tegni*. Therefore, evacuation is appropriate only for the joined cause. 

On the opposite side, it is shown only for the **antecedent** <note>original: "anti" — the prior buildup of humors</note> cause. Since when a joined cause is in a state of use or can be moved, evacuation would then be more appropriate for it, the falsity of which will appear in the present distinction. Furthermore, evacuation is done for preservation, but such should be for the antecedent cause. This is shown from the *Tegni* regarding the pre-guarding against disease. Thus, evacuation ought to be for the antecedent, and not the joined cause. Regarding the first point, it should be known what evacuation is, what purging is, and how they are named, and how they agree; the difference will be seen in **Chapter 164**.

Here, evacuation is also commonly understood as any drawing out of a humor, whether the humor is "sinful" <note>peccant/unhealthy</note> in quantity or quality. Regarding the second point, it should be known that some of the sharpest thinkers have said that evacuation belongs only to the antecedent cause and not the joined; their error will be shown from what has been said. Regarding the third point, it must be said that evacuation is primarily owed to the antecedent cause, and secondarily to the joined cause, whether it be a mineral of putrefaction <note>the source of rot</note> or the "true joined" tension, or the smoky vapor or its putridity. This is shown because evacuation is suited primarily and by itself to the preceding cause, not even waiting for digestion; but the mineral of putrefaction is not evacuated except after digestion, since digestion causes it to cease, as in **Chapter 160**. 

And digested things ought to be medicated. For that <note>the raw humor</note> resists extraction the most, but not so much the repletion <note>overabundance</note>. Furthermore, evacuation ought to happen before the humor is prepared to be corrupted; for corruption is the first thing to be guarded against. But the antecedent cause is like the humor which is apt to be corrupted, while the putrefying humor is already corrupted. Furthermore, the antecedent cause is owed evacuation through phlebotomy, **scarification** <note>making small surface cuts in the skin</note>, or purging. Putridity, however, is very rarely owed evacuation through this, since it has withdrawn from those things to be evacuated, not by nature’s power; for it does not fill the vessels in the same way.

That this is so is manifest from this: In exercises to the smoke with other mites. Whence in Book 8 of *De Ingenio*, those are better evacuated who previously went from **cacochymia** <note>original: "chacbochimie" — bad humors</note> of the purgings to obstructions. Therefore, it is appropriate for the prior antecedent cause. That which is written in the *Tegni* regarding the drawing out of putridity: "When any humor contrary to nature is contained in a limb." The cure is by imperfect evacuation, just as in putrid fevers. In Book 11 of *De Ingenio*: "It is necessary to purge the putrefied parts of those bodies laboring from putridity through urine, the belly, sweat, and vomit." 

I say also that for the joined cause, such as putrid smoke or soot, a certain evacuation is appropriate, such as through respirations according to the skin. For such a thing is found in Chapter 13 of the *Tegni* and Book 10 of *De Ingenio*: the cure is to effect the exclusion of the hot vapor. And in those suffering from **syncopal** <note>fainting-related</note> humors of the humors, there is no better cure than **friction** <note>massage</note>, and finally anointing. In Book 12 of *De Ingenio*, I find no other evacuation in them except that which is through friction. Therefore, what the monk does besides friction, I do not know. For the pores are opened thereby, and this corrupted smoke breathes through. Thus, from these points, it is concluded that evacuation is suitable for the three mentioned causes, but more principally it is owed to the antecedent, secondarily to the mineral of putrefaction, and generally to the putrid soot or smoke. What remains concerning the quality of the humor is shown in the prior and following distinction. Regarding the fourth point, it should be known that from the aforesaid it became known what objects were given to each part. Since it must be granted that even a certain joined cause of smoke requires evacuation. And similarly in a state where nature cannot complete the evacuation it wishes. For then it is the physician's command to lead it out from wherever it is found, especially through the quiet places.

But if putrefaction is called a simply joined cause, evacuation is nonetheless less suited to it, since once it is expelled, the putrid smoke ceases. Similarly, it must be granted that evacuation is suited to the antecedent cause, and principally to those who are filled by it; for repletion by itself...

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding medical interventions—specifically purging and bloodletting—and whether they should be performed during the active phases or "movements" of a disease. It follows a discussion on how the physician must balance the need to remove harmful matter with the risk of disrupting the body's natural healing process.</meta>

# Whether action should be taken during the movements of a sickness.

Evacuation is necessary: though by accident it is often not performed when dispositions occur that prohibit the drawing out of the matter. And for that reason, in the general practice of the physician, **digestion** <term>digestion: the process by which the body's heat "ripens" or matures harmful humors so they can be expelled</term> should come first, however much is to be evacuated. They caution, however, not to promote digestion in those who are overly "full" <note>plethoric, or having an excess of blood</note> unless some evacuation has preceded it. <margin>This is a small point.</margin> This is for fear that from the heat of the digesting agents, the expanded matter might induce a more violent obstruction, and consequently putrefaction and fever, or drive the sick person to suffocation. <margin>Galen, *On the Method of Healing*, Book 7.</margin> There is danger when we take away an obstruction: before we evacuate, the obstructions may become more deeply wedged in.

### DIFFERENCE 163.

**It** is shown that action should be taken on the day of the disease's movement. Because in the eleventh book of *On the Method of Healing*, in the cure of putrid **synochas** <term>synocha: a type of continuous, high fever</term>, Galen commands evacuation through vomiting, stool, and urine. These fevers are always generated in **paroxysms** <term>paroxysm: a sudden attack or increase in symptoms</term>, since their nature remains the same from the beginning to the end, according to the ninth book of the same work. And yet he commands evacuation there until **lipothymia** <term>lipothymia: fainting or swooning due to loss of blood or strength</term> occurs in them, as if the cure according to Galen were then perfected. And this is supported by the fact that he himself performed a **phlebotomy** <term>phlebotomy: bloodletting for medical treatment</term> on a certain person with a putrid synocha at the eighth hour of the night, at the very onset of the paroxysm. For the fever was from putrefied blood, the "subtle" [thin] part of which turns into **choler** <term>choler: yellow bile, thought to be hot and dry</term>, and the thicker part into the matter following the fevers and **crises** <term>crisis: the turning point of a disease, often involving a sudden change</term>. Choler is moved from the beginning into the "third" stage. Also, a "furious" disease breaks out in a paroxysm and most violent movement; and then it is commanded to evacuate immediately by any means. Galen, in the fourth book of the *First Principles*, commands movement to be made before the paroxysm, and yet there is then some movement of the disease.

**Again**, in the same place, the physician is the helper of nature and not its hinderer. But on the day of the disease's movement, the vital faculty labors to expel what causes distress. Therefore, when aid is required, nature should be helped by the physician's assistance; for it is not right to hinder it. Further, in the first book of the *Aphorisms*: Wherever nature tends, it should be led through the appropriate places. And similarly: Whenever Hippocrates <note>original: ".y." for Ypocrate</note> was brief, many things are understood in a single word, as Galen often testifies of him. Likewise, matter that is in motion is expelled more fully and quickly than that which is at rest; and on the day of the disease's movement, this motion occurs.

Furthermore, the physician imitates nature, according to the first and fourth books of the *Aphorisms*. But nature evacuates on the day of the disease's movement, and even commendably so; therefore, one should evacuate on the day of the disease's movement.

On the contrary: Neither phlebotomy nor evacuation should be performed on the day of that movement. Because it is a day for resting and seeking sleep, and the day of the **ebullition** <note>a "boiling up" or surge</note> of the sickness. And afterward some add that in all acute fevers, from their beginning and on the **periodical day** <term>periodical: the day a recurring fever is expected to return</term>, one must beware of **diminution** <note>a technical term for bloodletting</note>, according to the first and fourth books. <margin>4th book of *On the Method of Healing*.</margin> Also in the fourth book of the *First Principles*: Do not evacuate a flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note> on a periodical day, nor perform a phlebotomy. Also in the chapter on the cure of a pure **tertian fever** <term>tertian fever: a fever that spikes every third day, typically associated with malaria</term>: You must not move anything on the day of the paroxysm, except by necessity. Likewise, nature is not to be hindered, especially when it operates correctly. But he who moves [acts] on the day of the disease's movement hinders nature, since he distracts its operation on what it is focused. Especially since nature works secretly in the six principles; thus it is the artifice and work of those things which are most excellent in the art. The physician will be able to imitate its acts. Furthermore, the movement of art [medical intervention] fatigues nature.

---

For nothing reaches the body, however suitable it may be, without changing nature in some way from it, since the genus itself exists before it. So that when a moderate departure from equality happens to someone, and the balance is cut away from them, it is contrary. But the movement induced on the day when it attempts to move is of this kind. Also, nature is laboring by itself after digestion and distribution. Therefore, to act then is to join affliction upon affliction. Therefore, one should not act on the day when the disease moves.

Concerning the first point, it must be known that "to move" is to evacuate or to lead out. Evacuation is manifold, Difference 166: for some is of blood, and others of other humors. It also happens through many paths. There is both a violent, vehement kind, and some that are weak.

It is also shown there that evacuations are multiple; they are differentiated in greater or lesser degree by the movement exercised. Now, the "day of the disease's movement" is either the day of paroxysms, or the **indicative day** <note>a day when signs appear predicting a crisis</note>, or the **critical day** <term>critical day: a day when the disease is expected to reach a turning point, such as the 7th or 14th day of illness</term>. And this is twofold: one is the movement it receives from another, or from other superior causes, Difference 104; and another which it receives strongly from the nature of the humor. For some movements are continuous, while others are **interpolated** <term>interpolated: occurring at intervals, such as an intermittent fever</term>. This interpolated kind is threefold, or even more, Difference 169 and 59. This movement is finally reduced to the former. The movement is also differentiated not a little based on the location of the matter, according to whether it exists inside or outside the veins, and by reason of its quantity and quality. For larger and hotter matter moves more quickly and strongly than its opposite; so that choler [yellow bile] is sometimes moved on the fourth day, and **phlegm** <note>original: "sla" for phlegma</note> on the third, and otherwise; and matter is moved on the fifth, sixth, and ninth, as in the aforementioned Difference. The former is indeed twofold: namely, the **indicative movement** <margin>Indicative.</margin>, in which it is shown how nature will operate upon the sickness; and thereafter the indicative or **critical movement**, by which nature itself clearly rises against the sickness, aided by the conjunction or aspect of the celestial bodies, so that it might expel it. By the term "day," one must understand the natural day, containing both day and night, bounded by a span of twenty-four hours.

Concerning the second point, it must be known that some of the **Salernitans** <note>physicians of the School of Salerno, the most famous medieval medical center</note> wished that action should simply be taken on the day of the disease's movement, led by certain superficial appearances. <margin>Led by the Salernitans.</margin> For they observed diseases cured by nature on this day, whom the physician is commanded to imitate. For then heat acts upon the matter, so that it appears ready for digestion and expulsion. They showed this from empirical cases where healing occurred on the day of the paroxysm, sometimes in fevers. But how much this position is repugnant to the truth and the opinion of the wise is manifest from what has been said. Those of **Montpellier** <note>original: "mōtis peſulaī", a rival medical school in France</note> fell into a nearly burgeoning and strange error, opening a vein two days before a crisis, drawing out a quantity of two ounces of blood. <margin>The practice of Montpellier.</margin> For they say that by this, nature is rendered more powerful over the remaining matter. But as will appear, this error is obvious and contrary to the teaching of the ancients; since the disease is then at its "state" <note>the peak or height of the illness</note> or near it, a time when it is commanded to remain still. Those who distract the movement of nature perturb it, and clearly incite the matter into a "fury."

Concerning the third point, it must be known first of all when one should cease from action and when one should act on the day of the disease's movement, and thereafter how one should act in particular. Regarding the first, it must be known that nature moves toward a crisis, sometimes perfectly, and sometimes in a diminished way, just as in its other works.

It contrasts the views of the schools of Salerno and Montpellier with the traditional teachings of Galen and Hippocrates, ultimately warning that improper timing can disrupt the body's natural healing crisis.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a technical scholastic debate on medical timing, specifically whether a physician should intervene during a "crisis" or the "paroxysm" (peak) of a disease. It draws heavily on the Aphorisms of Hippocrates and the commentaries of Galen and Rhazes.</meta>

## Column 1

...it happens in these actions. If indeed the first concern is that there should be the **six conditions of a good crisis** <term>crisis: the "turning point" of a disease where nature either overcomes the illness or succumbs</term>, as noted in Difference 171. Then, certainly, one must not intervene on the day of the movement of the sickness; whence the ancient saying: <note>This refers to a famous Hippocratic aphorism (I.20).</note> *Those things which are in the process of being judged or have been judged should not be disturbed.* Therefore, fourthly, in the first part: if nature is moving or has moved, then leave it alone and trust its operation. For the physician’s help would be in vain since nature is sufficient by itself to bring about the crisis; indeed, the physician might disturb it further, as he cannot entirely measure the place of evacuation, the timing, the quantity, or the quality. Furthermore, since nature should not be agitated by food on the day of the sickness's movement, it is commanded that in every disease involving physical matter, while the strength of the body is suffering, nourishment should be withdrawn.

Much more, then, will medication not be necessary, as it would alter the matter even further. In such a case, the acting physician is like a friend who brings help to someone who does not need to be sent away. If, however, nature should move to diminish the crisis—as when the aforementioned conditions of a good crisis are lacking, either all of them or the most important ones—then it is necessary for the physician to help nature and fight alongside it so that the crisis may be completed. For the physician is the **helper of nature** and its minister. Whence Hippocrates says: *Those things which must be done, wherever nature leads, there one must follow.* For example, if nature is attempting to evacuate a humor but is too weak to do so, the physician should evacuate it through the same part of the body, even with such a great mass. Even if nature moves improperly, it is necessary to govern it and lead the matter to convenient places. Because of this, fourthly, it is said: *If nature does not move, you must move it at the hour of its movement,* during which hour it is useful to hear all the aforementioned things, according to what was said by Hippocrates regarding "convenient regions" <note>This refers to the "paths" of evacuation, like sweat, urine, or stool.</note>. This is supported by the fact that just as sometimes on the day of the sickness's movement one must strengthen nature with food (as when the body is weak and the symptoms are overwhelming, as noted in Differences 173 and 134), so too must one sometimes help with medication. Although the body labors during the action of the medicine, that which is drawn out of the matter makes nature more powerful over what remains. Nevertheless, these helps should be light, for patients live more tolerably with **diaphoretics** <term>diaphoretics: medicines that promote sweating</term> which promote sweat and urination, rather than with those that draw out blood or cause vomiting, which have their own order among themselves (Difference 166). Regarding the second point of this kind, it should be known that if by "the day of the movement of the sickness" one understands the "indicative day," then it seems no movement should be made, both because the matter is not yet **digested** <term>digested: in medieval medicine, this means "ripened" or ready for expulsion</term> and because nature, through a failed indication, would be thrown into confusion. Whence, regarding the time of the crisis and its manner, one cannot be certain thereafter. If, however, one hears "the day of movement" as the day of the **paroxysm** <term>paroxysm: the peak of a fever fit or the most intense moment of a disease's cycle</term>, then one must consider whether the sickness is severe and acute or the opposite. If it is the former, one must not intervene because of the matter, especially at the hour of the paroxysm or on the day itself, whether the fever is continuous or intermittent; for such matter is easily moved and would further stimulate nature if stirred by medicine. If, however, the disease is chronic, coming from raw matter that moves slowly, then one should intervene with light evacuations on the day of the paroxysm, but not at the hour of the paroxysm itself, so that nature is not fatigued or disturbed in its act. This movement should not be done from anywhere or by any means, but rather through a light vomiting or sometimes a **clyster** <term>clyster: an enema</term>...

---

## Column 2

...whence in the third book of the *Practice* concerning **quartan fever** <term>quartan fever: a malarial-type fever that returns every fourth day</term>: *On the day of the accession, vomiting should be provoked,* for the humor is in a tumult on the day of accession and the febrile heat liquefies it. Therefore, regarding the same point, Avicenna says: *Vomiting is especially appropriate before a meal, but after is also convenient, and specifically on the day of the paroxysm before the peak.* And Al-Mansur <note>This refers to the medical text by Rhazes.</note>, in book ten: *Vomiting should be given on the day of accession.* Also in the daily fever, Avicenna says: *After the seventh day, he also provokes vomiting after the peak of the paroxysm,* as if for an hour it is useful to administer some light provocative and cleansing agents, so that the remains of the matter moved in the paroxysm may be expelled. Because of this, syrups prepared with vinegar or **oxymel** <term>oxymel: a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</term> are preferred in such conditions in their proportional ways. Nor should this vomiting be prohibited since it is light and empties the stomach; to make it easier, it should be done after a meal, because vomiting on an empty stomach is difficult. According to Al-Mansur in book four: *A strong or universal vomiting that empties the whole body, and strong medicine on the day of the disease's movement, must be avoided,* as it is even more violent than a purge (Difference 166). Nevertheless, there is a time when the matter is stubborn and disobedient to being drawn out because of its coldness and thickness; in such a case, it is a sign of greater worth, or if the sickness has preceded for a long time and the strength of the patient is strong with a robust belly, medicine may be given at the state of the paroxysm when the heat and other symptoms are most intense. And below: *In fevers, and especially quartans,* empirics <note>Healers who rely on experience rather than theory.</note> sometimes give medicines with a praiseworthy effect, such as those that give **asarum** <note>original: "asseri", likely wild ginger</note> or **dwarf elder** <note>original: "ebuli"</note> or myrrh and frankincense, or many things of this kind; however, they give such things without distinction, and therefore they not infrequently torment the sick. Concerning the day of the movement of the sickness (that is, the day of the crisis), it is said that "crisis" (Difference 153) is understood in two ways: first, as a commotion (that is, before the evacuation), as when the symptoms of the crisis intensify. On such a day, one must not intervene, since nature—and especially the distributive and expulsive virtues—is laboring greatly. Moreover, the physician cannot know for certain whence or how nature intends to move. Therefore, one should not move then, neither with any kind of medicine nor even with food, since then the symptoms are from the fury of the sickness, not from something the physician can understand as coming from evacuation or abstinence. <margin>☞ See Column 5v.</margin> There is also a crisis by sudden alteration which is followed by evacuation, which is the aforementioned kind of crisis. And on such a day of movement—that is, after the alteration—it is necessary to intervene not a little, when the symptoms have been mitigated and nature attempts to evacuate through one of the regions, though in a diminished way as explained above. Know also what is written in the fifteenth book of Galen: <margin>q L 40</margin> *In the majority of cases in fevers, bloodletting should occur on the day of rest, but in other diseases like **ophthalmia** <term>ophthalmia: severe inflammation of the eye</term> and abscesses, it is done more at the time of the greatest pain* and its vehement assault. And I say this because the nature of the sickness takes on a furious quality. Regarding the fourth point: to the arguments of both sides, even if they appear however they may, one must say: First, in an acute sickness which is entirely in its paroxysm and continuous struggle, one must evacuate at the more convenient hour, and in the beginning when the symptoms are not yet intense and crushing the strength of the patient; for "concerning the beginnings and the ends," as in the Aphorisms. Whence, since Galen commands evacuation once the sickness is mitigated...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the timing and limits of medical intervention, specifically focusing on when "evacuation"—the removal of excess humors, usually through bloodletting—becomes dangerous. It transitions from a general discussion of "furious" fevers to the specific risks of "syncope" or fainting during treatment.</meta>

# Whether one should evacuate even until fainting.

The matter is already primarily digested. Regarding the confirmation of what must be said, it has already appeared from the previous discussion. Whence it must be said that **synocha** <term>synocha: a type of continuous, high fever traditionally attributed to an excess of blood</term> is a "furious" sickness more by reason of its quantity than from an over-inflammation of the blood. That which is from putrefaction [of humors] is on account of quality; but if it is otherwise, it is from quantity. 

When the matter is "furious," it is immediately necessary to evacuate; in this hour, it is a matter of necessity, not choice. <margin>☞</margin> A clear distinction appeared for the patient: for instance, a certain sick man, unable to suffer the fury of the sickness any longer at the **eighth hour of the night** <note>In the Roman and medieval system, the "eighth hour of the night" would be roughly 2:00 AM.</note>, sent for Galen. Moreover, the sickness was not far from its beginning; similarly, in a stagnating sickness, it is safer to evacuate at any hour, since the vital strength lasts longer than in other sicknesses. This is the distinction for the patient in Difference 168.

To another point, it must be said that a "furious" sickness is privileged above others regarding evacuation, both at the beginning and when the disease is being uprooted; this is because its mobility suggests that "digestion" <note>In medieval medicine, "digestion" refers to the process where the body prepares harmful humors to be expelled.</note> is occurring, as it is a precursor to expulsion. Regarding the other point, what was needed has appeared. Regarding another, it is said that if nature is strong, it is not necessary to help it, both because the physician cannot entirely measure nature’s own movement, and because the things with which he would help it might incite nature toward something worse and weaken it.

To another point, it must be said that it has already appeared when one ought to help nature and when not. To another, it is said that it would be true and praiseworthy unless the medical treatment fatigued nature while using that help. For when nature is already incited by the disease, if it were moved again by medicines while already agitated, affliction would be joined to affliction. Regarding another point, it has also appeared: for the physician imitates nature when it is weak in such a way that he provides what nature lacks, which is not the case here. Regarding those points, it also appears as said elsewhere. For the discourses of **Aristotle** <note>original: "A."</note> have already been explained; having heard from the discourse of the patient, I now enter into this voluntarily.

Regarding the other, it also appears: for nature is not to be helped unless the movement that precedes it proceeds weakly. However, the physician must imagine from where and when he wishes to move those humors. It is also said that nature is said to operate "secretly" because no one, no matter how perceptive, can immediately weigh its action; rather, he perceives it through the distance of time, just as the **growth of plants** shows itself over time. Whence, although the physician may not be able to perceive the perfection of its action in the moment, he will weigh it little by little over time. Regarding the other, it is said that although the movement of the medical art fatigues nature, it does so more or less depending on the case. And therefore the physician must be provident, so that he moves nature in such a way that it is helped more than it is harmed, since it is very difficult to find a remedy that is perfectly beneficial without being in some way harmful.

## DIFFERENCE 164.

That evacuation should not be performed until **fainting** <term>lyppotomia: from the Greek leipothymia, meaning a sudden loss of consciousness or fainting</term> is shown from the collections of the seventh book of **Galen**, who says much about this biting issue. Furthermore, the physician ought not to bring about that which vital strength must resist; but this thing is **syncope** <term>sincopis: syncope or fainting, often viewed as a temporary "death" of the vital powers</term>. Whence, in the twelfth book *On Method*, it is said: *In every disposition, syncope must be resisted.* Again, one must guard the strength of the presiding power, since that is the guardian of life (ninth book *On Method*). That which must be most cared for is the vital strength. And therefore, the indication taken from strength itself overshadows all other indications. In the ninth book *On Method*, it is said: **fainting** prostrates the strength above all other conditions, since it is a fall and a **half-death** <note>original: "mors dimidiata"</note>. 

It is also commanded in the first book of the *Aphorisms* that excessive evacuations should be avoided; but evacuation until syncope is excessive. For nothing is more immense than that. This is confirmed because there, among athletes as well as others, they are ordered to be avoided. Likewise, since the physician must measure the strength in every way (first book of the *Aphorisms*), one must fear lest, through excessive evacuation, the strength succumb so that it cannot be raised from its fall. Therefore, it is advised in the first and fourth books that it is better to stop short than to evacuate too exquisitely. Therefore, one should not evacuate until fainting. This contrary view is felt in the first and fourth books of the *Aphorisms*. In the *Letter to Glaucon*, however, he commands phlebotomy <term>fleubotomari: to perform bloodletting</term> without commemorating fainting; whence, on account of many things which they thought, he did not yet construct a more sparing rule. And especially because he authorizes it from his other works; for I find it introduced only in the book *On Crises*, which other physicians also perform even until fainting. To the ultimate "repletion" <note>Repletion is an excess of humors.</note>, the ultimate evacuation is owed. Some are indeed sometimes "ultimately replete"; evacuation until syncope is the ultimate evacuation. Again, of two evils, the lesser must be chosen as expedient (*Topics*, Book 3). It is a lesser evil to lead someone to fainting—from which, when it has been induced as it ought, he can rise again—than to leave him to succumb by chance to the perils of death. 

<margin>Fainting</margin>
Therefore, one might be led to fainting. Regarding the first thing to be known: "evacuation" is understood in two ways. In one way, commonly, for the drawing out of any humor; as by bloodletting or any other mode, whether by pharmacy or phlebotomy. As it is hinted: if one who is sick takes food and vomits, it signifies that he needs evacuation. In another way, it is used properly for the drawing out of blood mixed with other humors through **phlebotomy** <term>fleubotomia: the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood</term>. For evacuation is owed to humors that sin in quantity, as phlebotomy primarily is. **Scarification** <term>scarificatio: making small incisions in the skin to draw blood</term> is another form. Whence in the *Aphorisms*: *Evacuation is the equalizing of all humors.* This is certainly done most surely through phlebotomy, and properly through scarification of the knees. In the fourth book: Phlebotomy is a universal evacuation that evacuates the multitude of humors. The drawing out of humors that are faulty in quality (other than blood) is properly called **purgation** or **cleansing**, through medicines.

<margin>And Greek Syncope</margin>
**Lyppotomia** is a Greek compound name from *lyppi*, which is "defect," and *thimos*, "soul" or "fury"; that is, a defect of the soul’s vitality. In the ninth book *On Method*, it is called a "defect of the spirit." It is also named **syncope**, or *leipopsychia*, or "malefaction," or "dissolution": a half-death and an anguish. There is, however, in syncope, an acute cutting of the strength, or a sudden fall of the strength (twelfth book *On Method*). In the fourth book of *On Fevers*, it is described as a defect of the heart, a gathering of the whole strength into itself, and a removal of the spirit's outward flow. In the third book, **Syncope** is the destruction of the greater part of the primary motive and sensitive strength, on account of the weakness of the heart, and the aggregation of the whole spirit to it. 

<margin>Cause of Syncope: double/triple</margin>
This happens either because of a cause moving it to the interior, or because of a cause suffocating it within so that it finds no breathing space, or because of its own smallness and thinness. Therefore, it does not overflow beyond that which is found in the "mine" <note>Likely referring to the "source" or "vessels" of the blood/spirit.</note>. This event is known to happen from a double cause: either from a sudden translation of spirits into the heart, suffocating it, or from a sudden dissolution of the same.
