<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding "evacuation"—specifically the practice of phlebotomy (bloodletting)—to the extreme point of "lipothymia" or fainting. The author is weighing the risks of such a drastic procedure against the opinions of authorities like Averroes and Galen.</meta>

<margin>
Averroes, *Colliget*, Book 7.
</margin>
Dissolution, for it is twofold: one indeed comes from exhaustion <note>Original: *repletione*, likely meaning a "filling up" or congestion</note>, the other truly from emptiness. In the 12th book of *The Method of Healing* <note>Original: *De ingenio*, referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note>. For the sake of the third point, it should be known that Averroes, in establishing his first principles for healers, declared that one should only use evacuation until fainting <term>lipothymia: a medical term for a sudden loss of strength or fainting</term>. In Book 7 of the *Colliget*, he strives to destroy the notion that the quantity of blood removed during fainting is unscientific and erroneous. He argues that art imitates nature, but nature never healthily reaches a "crisis" <note>In medieval medicine, the "crisis" is the turning point of a disease</note> by drawing out blood to the point of syncope <term>syncope: a temporary loss of consciousness caused by a fall in blood pressure</term>; rather, that happens only in cases of bad crises. And the intention of evacuation, regarding the blood, is only to remove what is superfluous while preserving the natural quantity of the body. This is impossible to achieve in an evacuation to the point of fainting, since that which is natural is especially drawn out. Furthermore, once the evacuation is done and the vital power is utterly prostrated, a state and readiness for putrefaction can be left in the body, whereby, with the fever still sustained, nature would be led to its destruction.

<margin>
Averroes on [Aristotle's] *Physics*, Book 2, Text 1.
</margin>
Regarding this, although the speech of Averroes might trouble a physician with fear, nevertheless, what he asserts should not be held as an absolute rule in its own form. The image of his argument is refuted thus: a movement from "never" to "not able" is not valid. For although art is the follower of nature, many things are done through art that are completed by nature, and vice versa. As the Commentator <note>Referring to Averroes himself</note> says, following Alexander [of Aphrodisias] on the *Physics*, folio 30: For certain things are initiated by art and perfected by the same, such as houses and statues. Some truly are entirely from nature, such as absolute health or the growth of a plant. Others truly are mixed: they begin from nature and are perfected by art, like the health introduced into matter, or the cultivation of a wild plant. Some are the opposite, like the sowing of seeds. For art begins by scattering them in the earth, and nature completes the work. In some cases, art can do more than nature: for art is able to remove a finger, but nature is not. Similarly, nature can do things that art cannot, such as the production of humans or flesh. Whence art can kindly evacuate to the point of fainting, but nature cannot. This is demonstrated because evacuation to the point of fainting is not appropriate except when the vital strength is standing firm; specifically, at the beginning [of the illness], but not in its full "state" <note>The peak or *fastigium* of the disease</note> when it is fatigued by sickness. Nature never evacuates kindly at the beginning, since it is nature's way to evacuate digested matter, which can least happen at the beginning, but rather in the state of the disease (Difference 163). Art, however, is truly able to evacuate everything; thus art can preserve the patient while evacuating to the point of fainting, whereas nature cannot. To the other point, it must be said that although a great quantity of natural blood and heat is drawn out in this evacuation, there remains just enough to suffice for the existence of life, provided it is managed under the given conditions, so that danger is avoided, the cause of the disease expelled, and nature afterward strengthened so it can return to its own functions.

<margin>
Scholars. Regarding "until." Double meaning according to some.
</margin>
Regarding the other point, as will appear, in a continuous fever <term>synocha: a continuous, high fever</term> resulting from putrefaction, it is more to be feared to lead the patient into fainting if there is fear that the fever will not be entirely extinguished, but rather persist near it; in that case, one should not arrive at fainting. Certain scholars <note>Original: *scioli*, often used to mean those with a smattering of knowledge or "know-it-alls"</note> have touched upon the writings of Hippocrates and the commentaries of Galen, saying that this word "until" <note>Original: *usque*</note> can be held in a twofold way. Either **exclusively**, as in "until fainting," meaning that one approaches it but does not actually fall into it; or **inclusively**, that is, so that fainting actually occurs. They say that Galen intended the first meaning—the exclusive one—and not the second. Their discourse openly contradicts other physicians who describe this evacuation; whence in Book 9 of *The Method of Healing*, [Galen says]: "I took away blood by design so that a failure of the spirit, that is lipothymia, might occur." Wherefore, in the fourth book of *On the Crisis of Fevers*, he recites that when the friends of a blood-filled man saw him led into fainting by Galen, they began to murmur against him, saying, "Alas, alas, you have killed our dearest friend!" Wherefore Serapion says: "If the vital strength helps, evacuate the sick man until syncope comes upon him." Haly Abbas also says: "Draw out a very large quantity of blood so that even a falling away occurs." And in the fourth book of the *Pantegni*: "Do not cease phlebotomizing until the patient approaches fainting, or falls into fainting." Thus it appears from their speeches that the adverb "until" does not imply exclusion, but rather inclusion. There were also others distinguishing between "reparable" fainting, from which the patient escapes, and "irreparable" fainting, in which it happens that he perishes. They wish, therefore, for the evacuation to be performed until "reparable" fainting, but not "irreparable." They say this because in fainting, a failure of the vital spirit <note>Original: *animositatis*</note> is noted, intending that one should not reach the state itself but only its approach. Whence, in the 12th book of *The Method of Healing*: "Raw humors sometimes do not cause fainting, but what are called failures of the spirit, namely when they do not obstruct or weigh down." Yet from the diversity of translators, it clearly appears that the sequence describes lipothymia, or the failure of the spirit, or syncope, as all meaning the same thing, so that the names seem to be synonyms. Galen also called them "failures of the spirit," but did not explain them in an absolute sense. Again, this distinction of theirs, which they want to attribute to Galen and Averroes to support their view, is unscientific; it creates discord and in no way reconciles the differing opinions. For everyone, whether they deny evacuation to the point of fainting or applaud it, always refers to "reparable" fainting, since the physician is the helper of nature, not its destroyer.

Even if this distinction were removed, it still happens that the question is solved, since that is the correct solution; if the opposite were granted, the problem could not be solved (from the *Sophistical Refutations*). It is therefore unscientific and crude, though it seems entirely gilded <note>i.e., it looks good on the surface but is hollow</note>.

Regarding the first, it should be known that it is primarily appropriate in "synocha" <note>fever from excess blood</note> and in "synocha" arising from putrefaction, and in the most vehement pains. <meta>This page continues the technical discussion on whether medical evacuation—specifically bloodletting—should be performed until the patient faints. ### Whether evacuation should be performed to the point of fainting ---

<margin>From age 12 or 14 they are strong.</margin>
Regarding this method, it should be known that the indications for all [treatments] in this third part of the book are frequently taken from three sources: from things natural, things non-natural, and things contrary to nature.
Regarding **natural things**, indications are taken especially from the **vital power** <term>vital power: the "virtus" or innate strength of the patient to survive treatment and disease</term>. For this must be guarded above all things so that it remains true to itself. Hence, those who do not respect this power have suffered not a little; for it is said in the ninth book of *The Method of Healing* <note>Original: *De ingenio*, referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note> that two men, in the hands of certain doctors, underwent bloodletting to the point of fainting and have not yet been restored to health. The vital power must, therefore, be very strong. From the **complexion** <gloss>truly</gloss>, for if the complexion has been previously examined, the diseases are more easily met, and the vital power becomes more robust. But in a very cold or very hot complexion, such evacuation is prohibited, because of the cooling of phlegmatic persons and the "boiling" of choleric persons. Regarding **age**, it is established that for those under 12 years old, bloodletting—or even up to 14 or 16—is prohibited; according to the precept in *To Glaucon*, one should not only avoid bleeding them to the point of fainting but should cease the drawing of blood entirely. This is because the spirits and good fluids in this age are quickly dissolved, as this age is hot and moist and easily dissolved. In the ninth book of *The Method of Healing*, it says that in old age, one must also cease evacuation, and rightly so, because the fullness of humors ceases along with the vital power. From **sex, form, and color**, the physician likewise takes his indications. If according to **habit**, it is as if from a natural disposition; for habits themselves stand out like a second nature. Thus, for those accustomed to being evacuated, when it is necessary, one may even dare to lead them to the point of fainting.

Indications are also taken from **non-natural things** <note>In medieval medicine, "non-naturals" were six external factors affecting health: air, food/drink, sleep/wakefulness, motion/rest, evacuation/repletion, and passions of the mind</note>, which are predicted in two ways: namely from the time, the constitution [of the air], the hour, the region, and the art. Regarding **time**, it is twofold: either it is one of the four seasons of the year—for in a season of intense cold, like winter, it denies evacuation; and in the opposite season, like summer (as in the first part of the fourth book), and especially in autumn, because it is a time when the fluids are susceptible to corruption. And therefore, it is beneficial to perform evacuation properly in the spring, as is advised in the same work. And the **constitution, hour, and region** must be observed proportionally with the **art**, as is often declared. Or, the "time" is one of the four stages of the disease, and then such evacuation is appropriate at the beginning, but not at other times when the vital power is already fatigued. Hence, in the first book of the *Aphorisms*: In acute illnesses, use evacuations at the very beginning, either on the first day or shortly thereafter, while the strength is still intact. This is also ordered in the sixth book of the *Breviary* under the title of "practice." Therefore, Isaac [Israeli] says in the fourth book of *Fevers* that after the beginning, the vital power lies prostrate under the sharpness of the disease; and if the region is unknown, the doctor perhaps already attempted to perform future evacuations. To these indications are also added four things which I have taken from a Greek commentary, which prohibit us from evacuation: namely, a stomach that is easily affected, fearful disposition, a tendency for humors to flow toward the stomach in those with colic (with excessive flux), and the rawness <note>Original: *cruditas*, meaning undigested or "unripe" humors</note> of the humors. These are also touched upon in the ninth book of *Therapeutics*. Whence Galen, in the fourth book of *The Regimen of Acute Diseases*, says: dare to lead them even to fainting if the vital power is strong, the patient is a laboring youth of a sanguine temperament, and the habit is dense, hard, and not easily dissipated, and if the hour of the year and the region are well-balanced <term>eucrate: a state of healthy, balanced temperament or climate</term>. To which things ten factors demonstrate the correctness of the evacuation. First, four are to be brought forward: the composition [of the body], the vital power, the proportional symptoms, and the figure. Then: age, time, air, region, habit, and art. Afterward, the urinal must be inspected: if the urine is red and thick. Regarding the things "beyond nature" <note>The disease itself and its symptoms</note>, it appeared that evacuation is beneficial in the aforementioned diseases whose cause was a moist and hot humor, or also hot and dry, with acute symptoms. These follow the natural dispositions. But if the humors are very undigested and viscous, or the midriff is tense, inflated, and excessively burning, or the viscera are inflamed—such bodies must be "prepared" before purging, according to that old saying: "Where bodies are to be purged, they must be made fluid."

Regarding the third point, it should be known with Hippocrates and Galen: perhaps one may dare to include evacuation to the point of fainting, and not rarely, especially in "inflammatory synocha" <term>synocha: a continuous, non-remitting fever</term>. Whence in the ninth book of *The Method of Healing*, he says: I take so much blood from the vein that fainting—that is, a failure of the spirit—occurs.

<margin>9th book of *The Method of Healing*.</margin>
<margin>Democritus / Oribasius / to Eustachius</margin>
And Democritus with Oribasius, in the work to Eustachius, say that a sick man must be evacuated until he faints, because from this "narrowness" <note>Referring to the physical crisis of fainting</note> comes great help; for sweats follow, and fevers are extinguished.

This is shown both from the side of the cure—where you look for the remedy alone—and from the side of the vital power. From the **cure**: because for the ultimate diseases, the ultimate cures are best. And for the ultimate symptoms, the ultimate evacuation is prescribed (in the *Tegni*). Now, the disease for which such a cure is required is an ultimate one, and fainting-evacuation is likewise extreme. By **reason of the vital power**: since it is strong, this outcome is sought. For this disease, such as a 

<margin>Sanguine fever does not occur except in a robust heart and fleshy [body].</margin>
sanguine fever, does not happen except in a fleshy body with robust vital power. For it does not like to occur in any other, as per the ninth book of *The Method of Healing*. Furthermore, that evacuation should be performed by which the body is soon cooled, or by which vomiting or sweat is excreted, and which the laboring patient can sustain more delightfully and gently. Such, according to Galen, is the fainting-evacuation, which experience confirms, as in the first book of the *Aphorisms*.

Fainting-evacuation, therefore, is to be celebrated in this illness when the indications are present. Whence in the first [book], fourth [part]: if the body is strong, do not cease to evacuate until the patient falls into syncope. For syncope weakens a strong temperament. But because the demonstrations for such evacuation are many, but the actual occasions are very rare—or because many requirements must concur upon this one thing—one should not frequently prescribe such an evacuation to be done. For this reason, **modern doctors**, being fearful and knowing that bodies now are no longer as strong as they used to be (according to the ninth book), and fearing they might incur the charge of accidental homicide and indignation, choose instead to stop somewhere in the middle rather than evacuate to the extreme. They take the counsel of the first [book], fourth [part]: in a doubtful case, do the least harm. Also in the seventh book of the *Colliget*: in a synocha fever, if it is from putrefaction and the patient is not sweating, it is done with [the bloodletting] we spoke of. One should therefore cut the vein immediately, evacuating until fainting, where he had said above "until lipothymia," that is, until there is a failure of the soul. But finally, he adds that this applies to synocha fevers, which exist in a state of strong constriction; in these, evacuation is often without danger to the vital power. But in other illnesses, the extreme is dangerous because of the corruption of the humors. It is safer, therefore, to explain here that up to—

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding bloodletting (phlebotomy) and whether it is safe to bleed a patient until they faint (syncope). It transitions from the dangers of excessive evacuation to discussing "symptomatic" evacuation—evacuation caused by the disease's own symptoms rather than the physician's intervention.</meta>

# CLXV

->Whether symptomatic evacuation is beneficial<-

## DIFFERENTIA CLXV.

...should be held as excluded, as <term>Alexander</term> <note>original: "A.", referring to the 6th-century physician Alexander of Trallianus</note> invites you to say, until it approaches fainting. Hence, regarding the treatment of <term>phrenitis</term> <note>An acute inflammation of the brain or its membranes, often involving delirium</note>, the first requirement is that bloodletting be performed with caution, recognizing the patient's disposition toward fainting—whether they have fallen into it or are close to it—and the blood should be retained when fainting is imminent. This is also supported because, as one reasoning by <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: "Ax."</note> brought forward, and Galen suggests in the ninth book of *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "nono post euōne," referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note>, that for fainting in a <term>putrid synochal fever</term> <note>A continuous, high fever believed to be caused by putrefaction of the blood</note>, one should not act with total security as long as some movement of pulsation remains. This is sufficient because <term>Rhazes</term> <note>original: "az.", the Persian physician al-Razi</note>, in the ninth book of the *Liber Almansoris*, recounts that bloodletting did not cure a synochal fever. And in the previously mentioned cases, if two people are not yet relieved from fainting, some may fall into a long illness because they have acquired a broken <term>complexion</term> <note>The physical and mental constitution of a person, determined by the balance of their four humors</note>, so that they remain for their whole life unable to revoke the harm caused by that immoderate evacuation.

Others have remained discolored and in a bad state for all time. Not a few have been seized by dropsy, difficulty of breath, and weakness of the stomach and liver. Some indeed have incurred <term>apostemes</term> <note>deep-seated abscesses or swellings</note> and paralysis. Thus, one must proceed modestly here, fearing beforehand that they might fall into fainting, which the pulse can teach you. For when it tremors, drops, and becomes disorganized—so that you find one pulsation large and another small—it signifies the approach of fainting. Although we follow the teachings of Master Galen, the priority should not only be for fainting through the drawing of blood but also through <term>pharmacy</term> <note>The administration of purgative drugs</note>. In that case, however, one should not presume as much as in bloodletting, since drugs themselves are of a more intense danger <note>original: "pictī. dīa. clxvi.", likely referring to a later distinction on the dangers of drugs</note>, which authors show by opposing the injuries caused by pharmacy even more. Likewise, other humors require preparation before being expelled, whereas blood requires little or none. And truly, if possible, fainting should be avoided in every evacuation. Hence, the *Regimen of Health* <note>original: "re. fa.", likely the *Regimen Sanitatis*</note> says in the fourth book: it is better to allow the removal of blood twice in one day than to lead the patient to a loss of consciousness once. Because of this:

<margin>☛</margin>To the first point, as has appeared; to the other, it must be said that Galen speaks there of a "syncopal fever" in which the vital power is weak, and therefore evacuation is to be avoided entirely. To the other, it must be said that although it prostrates the vital power during fainting in the present, it nonetheless helps in the future; nor does it cast it down so much that, provided the previously mentioned conditions are observed, the patient cannot recover and escape the danger of death, rather than being led to a loss of consciousness. To the other, it must be said that such outcomes are ultimately to be avoided if they can be escaped by the <term>palatines</term> <note>likely referring to "palatines" as those in the physician's immediate care or high-status patients</note>, which is not the case with the previously mentioned ailments where evacuation is appropriate; when fainting is handled with less intensity, they are moved more fully, and precious help follows. In athletes, however, since there is no prior illness, evacuation can be done gradually or precisely. To the other, it must be said that although a physician cannot measure the vital power perfectly in every way, he can nonetheless do so through a certain "artificial conjecture" close to the truth, based on the *Aphorisms* and the teaching of <term>crises</term> <note>The turning point of a disease</note>. To those points from the other side, as has appeared: in every kind of reception, if the vital power can tolerate it, evacuation should be performed. For it does not stand on its own property alone, but more so for the sake of the vital power, as is often taught. To the other, it should similarly be granted, since all signs persuade and demonstrate it.

### DIFFERENTIA. CLXV.

<margin>Symptomatic</margin>
Whence he shows whether **symptomatic evacuation** is beneficial.
Since that which is evacuated from the beginning of a disease is drawn out symptomatically, it nonetheless helps; hence the tenth reason.
Diarrhea or a flux of the belly in the beginning of <term>pleurisy</term> <note>Inflammation of the chest lining</note> is a good sign; indeed, it is a helpful thing. This is confirmed by common vomiting, or that of <term>eruginous</term> <note>Vomit that is greenish, like copper rust, usually indicating bitter bile</note> matter, and the swift nature of taking poison. Also, evacuation in fainting—since it is an acute "cutting" of the vital power—is symptomatic, as was said in the previous distinction. Again, that which draws out matter which, by its quantity or quality, could produce death, is seen to be beneficial. This can happen through symptomatic evacuation, since by the removal of the matter, nature is relieved, so that it is seen that some are healed little by little. Furthermore, it is said that a physician often imitates nature by supplying its defect, such as by evacuating "furious" <note>violent or untamed</note> undigested matter in the beginning, which nature would benefit from if it could evacuate it by itself. Therefore, since art and nature help each other, and the effect is proportioned to them, it follows that evacuation helps even when it is symptomatic. On the opposite side, nothing is brought forth kindly if its evacuation is not ruled by nature, but symptomatic evacuation is erratic, as its very name indicates. There are reasons to the contrary, but natural and symptomatic evacuation are of the same kind, and since one helps, the other will harm; therefore, symptomatic evacuation does not help.

<margin>Why for the symptom</margin>
Regarding the first point, it should be known what evacuation is, as seen in the previous distinction. A **symptom** is a "cutting" or an accidental evil stimulated by whatever nature is leading. Symptomatic evacuation happens by reason of the **quantity** of the humor, or its **quality** (such as its sharpness), or both; or from the malice of the <term>region</term> <note>The local part of the body affected</note>, or from some celestial application, or burning, or a malignant aspect [of the planets] such as **Saturn** or **Mars**, as is proven in the *Aphorisms*. For just as a weak porter is stimulated by a heavier weight and drops it before the destination, so too does nature rule; because it is not able to sustain the humors and digest them in time, it is stimulated and compelled to expel them before the appointed hour, as seen in the third book of *Crises*. To be beneficial, however, is to provide some benefit to nature. Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have said that symptomatic evacuation can be beneficial "by way of cause," because the wicked matter which would have caused no small harm has been led out of the body. But it always harms "by way of sign," denoting a wicked disposition of the body. But this cannot stand: although something can be good or bad by way of cause and sign, it cannot be good by way of cause and bad by way of sign at the same time. For a thing's relationship to being is the same as its relationship to being understood and signified, as is taught in the *Metaphysics*. For one is ordered to the other by way of cause or effect. Therefore, when something is "kindly" (beneficial) by way of cause in its being and causing, it will also be so by way of sign in making itself known, and vice versa. Again, the cause and effect are proportional; but the disease and the sign are proportional, for both come from a cause, except that the disease is caused immediately by the cause, while the sign or accident occurs as the disease falls upon the patient.

...it imitates it like a shadow <note>original: "ūbra," referring to the relationship between a sign and its cause</note> as in Differentiation 73; and thus it is led by the cause, since whatever comes from the cause is also the cause of the thing caused. Therefore, something is not praiseworthy if it arises by way of the cause, but is evil if it occurs by way of a sign of the disease. Some, however, respond by saying the sign should be referred to the <term>virtue</term> <note>The vital power or strength of the body's natural systems</note> and not to the cause or the disease. But this is not valid, because then it would no longer be a sign, since it would not refer to its essential meaning, namely the cause or the disease.

<margin>$\P$</margin> Indeed, significations must always be joined to the things they signify (Aphorisms, Book VI). For the signs of virtue are not sought from a triple origin <note>original: "triplici sūpta nata," likely referring to the three types of spirits or powers in Galenic medicine: natural, vital, and animal</note> but rather from the matter itself. Nor does the motion of the primary causes prevail here; for if an evacuation is to be praiseworthy and free of <term>symptoms</term> <note>original: "syntbomate," meaning distressing side effects of the illness</note>, it is not enough that the patient merely escapes the disease, but the manner in which the matter is drawn out must be inspected—whether it was prepared by nature or otherwise. This does not happen in a symptomatic evacuation, as is shown when it is mixed with symptoms. Some have also said that a symptomatic evacuation is perpetually harmful in itself, though it may help by accident; the defect of this view will be shown in what follows, since everything that helps by accident must first be led back to something that helps by itself.

<margin>$\P$</margin> Regarding the third point, it should be known that a symptomatic evacuation, as such, always tends to inflict injury and never brings help. This is confirmed because that which precedes the work of nature causes harm; so it is always induced. A symptomatic evacuation causes this, as the name itself indicates and the nature of the thing shows, when something is drawn out from the body while the natural virtue is stimulated by injury. Furthermore, that is a symptomatic evacuation which draws out matter before <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "dignōē" for "digestionem," the process where the body "cooks" or matures diseased humors so they can be expelled</note> or through inappropriate parts of the body. All such things are considered evil. For nothing is benignly evacuated by nature unless it has been pre-digested, which cannot happen at the beginning of a disease. Hence, the fourth book of Aphorisms says: "At the beginning of a disease, if there are signs of lack of digestion, the evacuations are bad signs." Such an evacuation of humors will always be bad because it comes before the <term>critical signs</term> <note>Signs indicating a "crisis" or turning point in the illness</note> of digestion. Similarly, whatever is drawn out through inappropriate places must be restrained and directed toward the proper channels (Aphorisms, Book I). Likewise, an evacuation that induces death or a long illness according to the weakness or vigor of the virtue signifies a bad sickness. Experience certifies that a symptomatic evacuation is such a thing. For it would be praiseworthy to retain the matter and finally evacuate it naturally. Even an evacuation that is prompted by art <note>The physician's skill</note> is not helpful if it should be assisting nature, but instead exists as a symptomatic one. Hence, the first book of Aphorisms: "Every physician must attend to the work of nature." In one part, he must serve and cooperate with what is happening. But if something happens that is contrary and harmful, he must prohibit, transfer, or <term>revulse</term> <note>Drawing humors away from one part of the body to another</note> it (Aphorisms, Book I). Thus, symptomatic evacuation does not help in itself or directly. Regarding the fourth point:

To the first, it is said in Differentiation 192: This is not a symptomatic evacuation when the matter has been pre-disposed beforehand and nature then wishes to expel it; or it is praised in relation to the evacuation performed, as in <term>pleurisy</term> <note>Inflammation of the lungs/chest</note> where the liver is already denoted as weakened. To the second point, it is said that because bile is so depraved and poisonous, the materials do not need a delay inside to be "ripened" because of the conflict they have with nature. For they can never be reduced to a benign state or suited for a praiseworthy expulsion, since they do not receive the specific <term>natural heat</term> for digestion, but rather corrupt the form like a poison (Collection, Book III). To the other point, it is said that such a <term>syncope</term> <note>Fainting</note> or symptomatic extraction is done in part to avoid the danger of a great crisis, of which we are not speaking here. For a good <term>crisis</term> <note>original: "crisis bona"</note> through evacuation does not usually go as far as fainting (Collection, Book VII). To the other, it is said by way of interception, and properly so if the matter to be drawn out required preparation. For if it were retained and then evacuated spontaneously, it would be most praiseworthy. To the other, it must be said as appeared in the previously cited Differentiation: although art imitates nature in some things, it does not in all, since art can do things nature cannot—such as removing a sixth finger, or benignly evacuating at the beginning of an illness. Also, the matter may be "furious" <note>Uncontrollable or acute</note> and almost digested by its own mobility and subtlety, as touched upon before.

## DIFFERENTIA CLXVI.

<margin>$\P$</margin> **Whether Pharmacy in a pregnant woman is more dangerous** <gloss>than</gloss> **evacuation by phlebotomy.** <note>original: "Vod farmacia inpregnāte ſit piculoſior eūo fleubōtoīa." "Pharmacy" here refers to the administration of strong purgative drugs; "phlebotomy" is bloodletting.</note> This is argued by <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: "Aũ."</note>, in Book VII of the *Colliget*, who believes so. Indeed, pharmacy is a matter of great fear and danger, while phlebotomy is least so. Furthermore, pharmacy here is a dissolver of matter; but such a thing is of the nature of poison, and every poison is destructive, especially when the matter is obedient and easily acted upon, as it is in an <term>embryo</term>. Again, pharmacy induces a vehement agitation in a pregnant woman, since the operation of medicine is not natural to the body, but violent. The *Commentator on the Centiloquium* <note>Likely referring to a commentary on Ptolemy</note> says these agitations loosen the <term>matrix</term> <note>The uterus</note>, from which an <term>abortion</term> <note>miscarriage</note> follows, which happens least of all in phlebotomy. Furthermore, pharmacy is either violent—and then it causes the aforementioned harm—or it is weak, and thus it might move the humors but not evacuate them, inducing bad symptoms. It would also be necessary to take a large dose of them, which is laborious for nature (Book I, Part 3). If medicines were not poisonous, it would not be so laborious for nature to drink them. Therefore, in a pregnant woman, pharmacy is more dangerous than phlebotomy.

On the contrary, the fifth book of Aphorisms allows pharmacy and detests phlebotomy. This is confirmed: because in a weak virtue, phlebotomy does not hold to purging even moderately. Likewise, phlebotomy immediately evacuates blood, which is the nourishment of the pregnant woman and the generator, nourisher, and augmenter of the embryo. Other humors do not do this (Differentiation 30), and pharmacy draws those out. We do not know a medicine that draws out blood by dissolving it (Differentiation 194). Therefore, phlebotomy is more dangerous

<meta>This page continues the scholastic medical discussion on bodily evacuations. While the previous page focused on whether disease-driven evacuations are beneficial signs of the body's strength, this page categorizes the different types of evacuations—natural versus artificial—and enters a specific debate regarding the safety of bloodletting and medicinal purging during pregnancy.</meta>

Every evacuation is a leading away of something from the body. Beyond what was previously said, it occurs in two ways: one is natural, which nature alone performs <note>The author distinguishes between "Nature" as the body’s internal healing force and the "Art" of the physician.</note>, and which should not be interfered with unless it is so excessive that it overthrows the body's <term>virtue</term> <note>The vital power or strength of the patient.</note>. The other is artificial, which is accomplished with the help of a physician, who almost always imitates nature.

Each of these is further divided into universal and particular. A universal evacuation is one where all the humors <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> are evacuated proportionally, such as a spontaneous flow of blood or <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>Bloodletting, the surgical opening of a vein.</note>. Or, it is universal because it affects the whole body, such as a spontaneous flux of the bowels or a strong <term>pharmacy</term> <note>In this context, "pharmacy" refers to the administration of a purgative drug or laxative.</note>. Finally, a particular evacuation is one that draws out matter from a specific place, such as purging the chest through spit, or the ventricles of the brain through the filters of the nostrils and the palate. Or, it is particular because it evacuates a specific material held somewhere, such as in a <term>decoction</term> <note>original: "apatū" likely referring to an apozema, a medicinal syrup.</note>.

Furthermore, in some evacuations, the whole body is evacuated immediately, such as the stronger types like a flux of the bowels, or through the stomach, urine, or sweat. Others are mediated, such as by friction or baths and the like. For through these, nothing is evacuated except what remains under the skin, and not what is dispersed in the depths (according to the third book of Aphorisms). Accidental evacuation always occurs through abstinence or hunger, because it removes that which induces repletion <note>An "overfilling" of the body's vessels with humors.</note>. For one thing's presence deprives the other of its place. Some of these evacuations are also done by "permutation," as in a decoction; others by a drawing out to the surface. There are also parts through which some evacuations occur more "occultly" <note>Hidden or invisible to the naked eye.</note>, such as through sweat and even more so through deep sleep.

Of the remaining types, some are more manifest. A woman is said to be "pregnant" when, the seed being retained, an embryo is formed. Regarding this, it should be known that <term>Galen</term> <note>original: "Col l. vii. Ax." likely referring to Galen's Commentaries.</note> strives to show that the use of drugs is more dangerous in a pregnant woman than bloodletting, which seems to contradict <term>Hippocrates</term>. Having recited this, I say that bloodletting is not bad when repletion is present, which the embryo does not need. But I do not believe a drug reaches a good end; rather, it harms the embryo because it contains a poisonous substance in its essence. Furthermore, it perhaps causes bad humors to flow toward the embryo so that they harm it. Also, purging medicines are provocatives of urine; and that which provokes urine is of the same genus as that which provokes the menses <note>The monthly period.</note>. Such a thing induces an abortion. For these three reasons, he concedes that bloodletting is less difficult.

But as will appear, if one listens at length, that position cannot stand; indeed, the opposite is more true. Nor do his arguments convince: for just as bloodletting in a pregnant woman is not to be condemned in a time of repletion, so much more should it be said of a drug when there is a need for it. There are, however, certain "blessed" drugs lacking in poisonous qualities, about which one may presume (as they write) they are safe for pregnant women and children—such as <term>cassia fistula</term> and <term>manna</term> <note>Cassia and Manna were considered "gentle" laxatives, unlike "drastic" purges like hellebore.</note> and the like. These, being sufficiently friendly to nature, do not force humors to flow in a way that harms the embryo. Being of such a kind, they provoke neither urine nor menses.

<margin>1</margin> It is, however, necessary
<margin>2</margin> to provoke the menses sometimes by placing a
<margin>3</margin> suppository in the neck of the 
<margin><term>manicula</term> <note>A "little hand" or pointing finger drawn in the margin to highlight this instruction about the womb.</note></margin>
womb gradually, and cleansing it many times. This is especially true when an impurity has been created in the womb of a pregnant woman. This is also sufficiently heard in the 21st book of Galen, so as to deny bloodletting entirely

---

and drugs conditionally, depending on the necessity and the time. Hence the fifth book of Aphorisms says: *A pregnant woman, if bled, aborts*, and especially if the fetus is larger. Yet the fourth book of the same work commands pregnant women to be purged from the fourth month inclusive up to the seventh month inclusive. From these points, it is gathered that a pregnant woman should be given drugs, but not bled. The "Brutal Saxons," however, commonly perform bloodletting on pregnant women.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that vomiting is more dangerous than stool, and other evacuations, all other things being equal (as is known from the Aphorisms). And after that, bloodletting in a pregnant woman is safer than drugs. Regarding the first, it should be known that an evacuation is more difficult and dangerous the more it exists contrary to the inclination of nature. Such is vomiting, since the stomach is assigned by nature for attraction, and the intestines for expulsion (according to the third book of *On Natural Faculties*). Vomiting is performed by the stomach; the stool by the pylorus of the belly and the intestines. The stomach is also very sensitive and the path is shorter. But the power of nature is broader and more prone downward than upward. Also, the act by which it is performed is more laborious and dangerous because of the parts involved; for in vomiting, only the outer tunic <note>A layer of tissue.</note> performs the work, whereas stool involves two layers of the intestines. 

Furthermore, vomiting induces worse accidents than stool—namely, suffocation or the rupture of a vessel in the chest or lung. Because of these dangers, vomiting is more difficult and dangerous than stool, and generally more so than other evacuations. That stool and similarly vomiting are more sharp/dangerous than bloodletting is shown by the "acute fevers." Because in bloodletting, nothing of a more [dangerous] nature falls; but in the loosening [by drugs], many times a "terror" occurs, especially when you are not a knower of the patient's nature. For there are those who are loosened with difficulty by medicines, others easily, and some moderately. Because of this, one must fear to give drugs, especially to those unknown and inexperienced. For a drug unduly administered either loosens too much, or moves the humors but does not draw them out, causing many twistings, anxieties, and pains. 

The drug itself is also categorized as being of the genus of dissolving poisons. For the nature of loosening medicines is contrary to the nature of the bodies to be loosened, and generally they are destructive and killing. They especially harm the heart and destroy its strength; for of all the harms coming to the body, the first rush is toward the heart as if to the base of life, and the stomach as if to the receptor of troubles (according to <term>Mesue</term> <note>Masawayh, or Mesue the Elder, a famous Persian Christian physician.</note> *On Drugs*). However, this is not because the principal parts are the most difficult to affect by a drug; for the hair and nails, which are the least principal, are more difficult to affect. But medicines are harmful to the belly and especially to its opening, since it is of the highest sensitivity. Because the nerves are weakened in it, the motion cannot be perfected, just as a shot arrow cannot be called back. But bloodletting can be compelled and moderated, unless perhaps it occurs from the larger arteries. Therefore, stool and vomiting are much more bitter and dangerous than bloodletting, and vomiting most of all.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into medical evacuations. Having previously defined natural and artificial evacuations, the author now turns to a specific debate: whether phlebotomy (bloodletting) or pharmacy (the use of purgative drugs) is more dangerous or effective, with a particular focus on the risks these treatments pose during the different stages of pregnancy.</meta>

# Whether Pharmacy is More Dangerous than Phlebotomy

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
This is still proven by the method of withdrawal. But regarding the things mentioned above, a doubt arises: specifically, concerning the matter of the fact. For in those with weak <term>virtue</term> <note>The vital power or strength of the patient's body</note>, the humor should never be diminished; however, it should be moderately purged. According to Haly <note>Haly Abbas, a famous 10th-century Persian physician</note>, it is more suitable and requires greater caution for those of an equal age, just as blood is drawn out. Furthermore, more noble things are evacuated through <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>The surgical opening of a vein to draw blood</note> than through pharmacy, such as blood and the <term>spirits</term> <note>In medieval medicine, these were subtle substances in the blood that carried life and sensation</note>. Therefore, phlebotomy is more dangerous and troublesome than pharmacy. It must be said, however, that pharmacy is more dangerous, because it cannot be perfected according to the physician’s wish as precisely as phlebotomy can; pharmacy also induces greater labor in the sick person than phlebotomy, specifically through vomiting. But in terms of what is actually led out of the body, phlebotomy is more dangerous than pharmacy, unless the drug itself draws out and evacuates the blood forcefully, or if the "pharmacy" is itself a drawing out of blood. Furthermore, according to the mind of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon, the primary authority on medicine in the Middle Ages</note>, regarding a person with pleurisy accompanied by fever and other acute symptoms, one must fear the quality and movement of the drug in the lower parts, and therefore one should turn more to phlebotomy.

<margin>Note.</margin>
<margin>1</margin>
To the first point: just as one must not perform phlebotomy when the patient’s virtue is weak, neither should one purge with a dissolving pharmacy. However, some light or lubricating treatments can be used. There is a greater range of options in pharmacy than in phlebotomy; wherefore, if it is performed within a proper timeframe, pharmacy is no less to be feared than phlebotomy.

<margin>2</margin>
To the second point: Haly compares phlebotomy to the swelling of the belly and the reduction of food and drink, but not to the taking of pharmacy.

<margin>3</margin>
To the third point: it has appeared that for the sake of the matter, it should be well known that some drugs are strong, dangerous, and abound in much poisonousness, such as the "dissolving" ones like scammony, mezereon, and euphorbium <note>These are all powerful herbal purgatives that can be toxic in high doses</note>. Others are weak and safe, such as those that "express" humors, and even more so those that are light and lubricating, such as <term>myrobalans</term> <note>A fruit used as a mild laxative</note>, manna, tamarind, <term>cassia fistula</term> <note>The pods of the "golden shower tree," used as a gentle laxative</note>, and psyllium mucilage.

<margin>Cassia is a suspect laxative; a gloss.</margin>
<margin>4</margin>
Cassia fistula dissolves without harm and without a biting sensation, so much so that it is suitable for pregnant women and relieves them. However, for those having weak intestines or suffering from <term>lientery</term> <note>A type of diarrhea where food passes through the body undigested</note>, it is viewed with suspicion.

<margin>Myrobalans</margin>
<margin>5</margin>
As for myrobalans, they can lead out humors primarily. For I am forced to admit that some power of primary attraction exists in them, just as we see that the black ones lead out <term>melancholy</term> <note>Black bile</note> from the whole body, the yellow ones lead out <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile</note>, and the others phlegm. This would not be the case if they only "expressed" humors like quinces or pears; rather, they first draw the humors into a designated place, and then finally, by aiding nature, they dissolve and release them by the pressure of their own weight. Medication does not only work through dissolution; it draws humors to the designated pathways, and afterward, nature—sensing the sharpness and the humor—strives to expel it.

<margin>Aloe, Agaric, Rhubarb</margin>
A third type of drug is found as a good middle ground, even if it is dissolving, such as aloes, agaric, and rhubarb; these can be suitable here and are especially comforting. Next, know that the time of pregnancy is divided into three periods; in a natural birth of nine months, each period contains three months. In other cases, it may have fewer or more, such as when one is born in the seventh month or on the tenth day of the forty-ninth... in which months

->The time of pregnancy is divided into three periods.<-

---

the fetus is disposed in different ways within the womb. For in 

<margin>In the first months</margin>
<margin>1</margin>
the first three, the fetus is small and weak, content with little nourishment. It is weakened daily by the things it is bound to, like a newly produced sprout.

<margin>2</margin>
In the next three—the fourth, fifth, and sixth—it is larger and stronger, requiring more nourishment, blood, and growth. Then it is strongly attached to the womb, just as fruit in the middle of the season adheres more vehemently to the trees. For now the juicy moisture that binds it is soft and fluid as it was in the beginning, nor yet softened by maturation and weighed down by the weight of the fetus, which happens to them when the term is completed.

<margin>3</margin>
In the remaining last three months, the fetus is strong and large, and draws much blood for its nourishment and growth. Then the ligaments begin to weaken, partly because of the weight being heavier than usual, and also because of nature's purpose. For they proceed toward weakness so that the birth may be easily released, and like mature fruit, the fetus is disposed to fall. This happens similarly in the other time periods.

<margin>Causes of abortion.</margin>
Note also that although there are many causes of abortion, two are the principal ones: first, the subtraction of nourishment from the embryo, because blood is removed by phlebotomy or other means. For the embryo is nourished from the purer part of the menstrual blood. The second is agitation and violent motion, by which the ligaments of the fetus are dissolved, as <term>tenesmus</term> <note>A distressing urge to evacuate the bowels</note> shows, which a stronger pharmacy induces.

<margin>4</margin>
These things being briefly touched upon, it must be said that while both phlebotomy and pharmacy are dangerous, pharmacy stands out as more dangerous, as the ancient authorities also believed. Reason proves this: because phlebotomy does not seem suitable except in the first three months and especially in the middle of them, since then the embryo is small and weak and does not demand much nourishment. If bloodletting is done, let it be done gradually and in small quantities at intervals. Phlebotomy measured in this way does not induce such agitation that the fetus's ligaments are dissolved (since that is more the effect of pharmacy), nor does it lead away so much blood that it greatly hurts the fetus, since the embryo is content with minor nourishment. This does not apply to pharmacy, especially the strong dissolving kind. These were better known to Hippocrates; for perhaps at that time these "blessed" familiar medicines <note>A common medieval term for effective, well-known drugs</note> had not yet been discovered, nor were they so needed then as they are now, when bodies were more robust.

<margin>5</margin>
In the second period—the three following months—it is certain that phlebotomy is more dangerous than pharmacy. The embryo, being larger and stronger, seeks much blood for its nutrition and growth. If this is subtracted, abortion happens quickly. However, the body tolerates pharmacy then, since it does not subtract the blood (the fetus's food) but rather the other humors. The fetus is also strong and firm enough that its ligaments can tolerate the agitation and motion of pharmacy unharmed, especially when the drugs are from the "blessed" category. In the last three months, although the body bears both pharmacy and phlebotomy with more difficulty, phlebotomy is slightly less burdensome...

<meta>This page continues a scholastic medical debate regarding the timing and safety of evacuations—specifically bloodletting (phlebotomy) and purgatives (pharmacy)—during pregnancy and acute illness. It contrasts the opinions of major authorities like Galen, Hippocrates, and Haly Abbas.</meta>

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
<margin>Haly Abbas, 10th book of the Theoretical part.</margin>

...it requires nourishment and the growth of blood, for the reason that the fetus increases continually. But if necessity drives one toward <term>pharmacy</term> <note>purgative drugs</note>, let it be mild, as it appears most appropriate in the third month. If Hippocrates <note>original: ".y."</note> abhors the use of pharmacy, it is because stronger drugs were known in his time, as is found in the <term>Aphorisms</term> <note>A famous collection of medical principles by Hippocrates</note>, where by "to medicate" or "to purge," Hippocrates understands a medicine that dissolves the body. Therefore, more than in others, pharmacy is to be granted in a pregnant woman rather than <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>bloodletting</note>. Against the aforementioned things, a doubt arises: because the time of pregnancy is divided into three parts—the fourth month is joined to the middle time, and the seventh to the last—whereas phlebotomy might still be granted more cautiously in the first months than in the second. But in the third [book], chapter 21, it is said: one must beware before the fourth month and after the seventh, and in that period which is between them. Here, Galen first alludes to the reasoning of <margin>He attacks Haly Abbas.</margin> Haly Abbas. On the contrary, in the first part of his *Practice* <note>The *Liber Regalis* was divided into "Theory" and "Practice"</note>, and somewhat in his *Theory*, he is emphatic. Similarly, a pregnant woman at some time needs her blood to be diminished or to be purged by a <term>cathartic</term> <note>a strong laxative or purgative</note>. Because of certain <term>passions</term> <note>suffering or diseases</note>, one should not rush this in the early stages, until the pregnancy has reached four months; indeed, one should do this in the fifth, sixth, or seventh month. You shall beware of this same thing in the eighth or ninth month. For in those months the fetus is weak and has need of food. But indeed, the <term>inanition</term> <note>emptying of the body</note> diminishes the food, whence the fetus dies. Also, in the eighth and ninth month, the fetus has grown and needs more abundant food; in these months, if bloodletting occurs, it diminishes the food of the fetus, nor does it remain alive. Finally, the advisor adds: if necessity drives one to inanition in these times, and they fear for the death of the woman if it is delayed, do not care for the fetus; let the mother be dearer to you than it. It must be said that the speech of Haly Abbas is perhaps not entirely sound. First, when he places the fourth month with the three prior ones, he contradicts Hippocrates and Galen, who say: "Pregnant women should be purged if there is a need after the fourth month." Also, the seventh month ought not to be joined with the fifth and sixth, but rather with the eighth and ninth, as was said. For according to Galen, one must purge after the fourth month and up to the seventh month—that is, by excluding the seventh. This appears from that which is added: namely, "that which is in the middle of conception," since it is held most certainly in the <term>physics</term> <note>natural science/philosophy</note> of those who conceive. If, however, the seventh is composed with the fifth and sixth, then it will not be in the middle of conception except perhaps by a very loose geometric measure. Likewise, some are born in the seventh month; many also do not complete the ninth, but take only a portion of the time for themselves. For this reason, it seems more reasonable to couple the seventh month with the third period [the end] and not with the second, as is commonly said by many. That he seems to grant phlebotomy in the fifth, sixth, and seventh, and deny it in the first four months, I do not much accept; since it is declared reasonably by those things said before, it shows directly the opposite regarding phlebotomy. For it is <margin>A certain pregnant woman who menstruates has a healthy fetus.</margin> seen that some women at the beginning of pregnancy menstruate healthily for one or two periods. And perhaps Haly Abbas feared the motion of phlebotomy more than the loss of blood it would induce. Know also that sometimes phlebotomy is expedient even when signs of <term>fullness</term> <note>plethora, or an excess of blood</note> do not exist—for instance, when the disease is severe and the patient's strength is robust, or even in fear of an <term>aposteme</term> <note>an internal swelling or abscess</note>, as in a blow or a fall. Sometimes, however, necessity removes the abstinence from phlebotomy, or softens the belly through pharmacy, baths, exercise, rubbing, and other things in pregnancy; just as in the fourth [book] of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." - *De Ingenio Sanitatis*, Galen's work</note>. Regarding the fourth point, it appears as Avicenna said. Regarding the other thing Galen saw, and another point that pharmacy is a vehemently dissolving thing and of the nature of poison—not so the others mentioned, by which a purging can be performed kindly. Or, if it were necessary to administer it in a case where the time is critical. Regarding the other point, it must be said that a pre-selected pharmacy is not harmful. If such is administered, it is necessary to do it at the time when the fetus is more firmly joined, as in the fourth, fifth, and sixth months. Perhaps also the medicine is not very violent; and if the <term>humors</term> <note>bodily fluids like blood, phlegm, and bile</note> are agitated, it is by its nature mobile and disposed toward exit, as if they were digested things; and therefore they can be evacuated in the beginning. Otherwise, they remain to the great prejudice of nature if unevacuated. Regarding the other point, it must be said that a weak and not a strong pharmacy is to be given, as seen; nor will it move much in evacuating since it has no attraction, but rather a meeting of substances. If it does not evacuate, it will not harm sensibly, since it is even apt to be converted into food. But if the nature of the patient is fastidious, let a drug of lesser loathing be chosen, or prepared with sweet or acidic things. Or, as Aristotle says, let them use it with whatever they are accustomed to at the time.

### DIFFERENTIATION 167.

That in an acute illness one should not perform phlebotomy after the fourth day is shown because physicians commonly command phlebotomy at the beginning, which is before the fourth day—namely the first, second, and third days—as Hippocrates feels. Rhazes <note>9th-century Persian physician</note>, above all Isaac [Israeli] in *On Fevers* in the fifth book, and Haly Abbas in the third book of *Practice*. And in the fourth [chapter], first [part]. Since phlebotomy is placed at the beginning of the illness, it is no longer intended afterward. And perhaps it would kill the patient due to the arrival of the weakness of their strength <note>virtue</note>. The "beginning" in these illnesses terminates before the fourth day, nor does it seem right to evacuate on the fourth day, since in such an illness that is the time of the movement of nature or the <term>critical</term> <note>creticus</note> day. Differentiation 173. <meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the timing of medical interventions, shifting from the treatment of pregnant women to the specific question of whether bloodletting is permissible after the fourth day of an acute illness. It compares the stricter "days-based" rules of some traditions with the "strength-based" approach of Galen and later Arabic physicians.</meta>

# -> Whether in an acute illness one should perform phlebotomy after the fourth day. . 7 <-

Nature begins to prepare itself toward the expulsion of the disease. Since a physician cannot sufficiently weigh the specific action and mode of evacuation <note>The process by which the body naturally rids itself of "corrupt" humors during a crisis</note>, it is not necessary to provoke it with an evacuation when this happens. Furthermore, <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>bloodletting</note> is required when there is a "sin" <note>an imbalance or excess</note> of blood in itself. Such sanguine fevers mostly terminate in the fourth crisis of the third [book] and the fourth of the first. Therefore, one should not perform phlebotomy after the fourth day in an acute illness.

However, the opposite is also felt in the ninth [book] of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio"</note> and the first [book], fourth [part of Avicenna's Canon]. Whence Democritus says: "When such fullness <note>an excess of humors</note> exists, or an illness appears where phlebotomy is necessary, you shall wait for neither nature nor the hour, but you shall immediately decide upon phlebotomy." Likewise, in the third book of *On the Regimen of Acute Diseases* <note>original: "re. a."</note>, it is ordered that in <term>pleurisy</term> a vein be cut when the pain ascends to the shoulder blades, even if this occurs long after the fourth day.
<margin>2. On the Regimen of Acute Diseases.</margin>
Whence the first of the *Aphorisms* states: "On the eighth day the elbow vein was cut." Haly Abbas <note>original: "Aux. ioti."</note> says: "When there is an abundance of blood and the strength is tolerant, phlebotomy is appropriate; this indeed can happen after four days when the blood abounds in a strong nature." For this reason, sanguine fever is only loved <note>tends to occur</note> in such people. Distinction 173. Furthermore, <term>pharmacy</term> <note>the use of purgative drugs</note> is granted after the fourth day in the fourth book of *On the Regimen of Acute Diseases*. Therefore, much more so is phlebotomy granted, since it is said in Distinction 71 that pharmacy is more difficult <note>harsher on the body</note> than phlebotomy. 

Therefore, phlebotomy should be performed in an acute illness after the fourth day. For this reason, it should be known that phlebotomy is a "distinction" introduced by common sense, and it is no small thing that phlebotomy primarily ought to address the quantity of the "sinning" humor, and secondly its quality. Regarding what an illness is, and what "acute" means, and how they are distinguished, see Distinctions 72 and
<margin>Question. Definition. Acute.</margin>
133. Now, a certain illness is "acute" by reason of its matter, either according to quantity—such as <term>synocha</term> <note>a continuous, non-intermitting fever</note>—or quality, such as <term>tertian</term> <note>a fever that peaks every third day, like malaria</note>. Some are acute by reason of their location, such as <term>quinsy</term> <note>original: "sqnatiā" - a severe inflammation of the throat</note>; others by reason of the "accident" of pain, such as <term>colic</term>. In some cases, all the aforementioned are contained, as in <term>syris</term> <note>likely a reference to a specific burning fever</note> arising from colic blood. In that case, the blood "sins," and its sharpness and its quantity are the cause. It is also in the brain, which is the most noble member after the heart (7th book of *On the Method of Healing*); the worst accidents also happen in it, such as <term>phrensy</term> <note>brain fever/delirium</note> or <term>karabitus</term> <note>a medieval term for a lethargic or heavy-headed condition</note>, involving alienation or a mixing of the senses.

Know also that the fourth day was proposed more than others because it is the day when acute illnesses most often reach a conclusion <note>original: "conterminat"</note> in the beginning. On that day, nature also moves, as it is one of the days of "indication" or "crisis." 

Regarding the second point, it should be known that Galen and the Greeks generally seem to grant phlebotomy more freely than the Arabs. For in the eighth book of *On the Method of Healing*, he grants that phlebotomy be performed in <term>plethora</term> <note>an excess of bodily fluids</note> even when no disposition toward disease is present, but rather a middle state between health and sickness, with the humors being similarly thick and viscous. For this reason (11th book on Illnesses), it is said: "The best thing is to cut a vein, not only in continuous fevers, but in all others that involve the putrefaction of humors." This is done provided that age or strength do not forbid it; for once the nature is alleviated, the body is managed and set down, and that which weighed upon it like a burden will be easily ruled by the remainder. Indeed, in other indeterminate cases, Galen ordered phlebotomy to be performed even until <term>lipothymia</term> <note>fainting</note>. In the same 11th book, as if correcting his own speech, he says: "Because it is not possible to cure opinions and putrefaction through phlebotomy alone when they require other aids." 

One must set down the blood during the time of cure, lest we be forced to feed the patient intemperately; for as much as the body is evacuated, it needs food. Thus, it would then be necessary either to increase the fever by nourishment or to dissolve the patient's strength by lack of nourishment. Therefore, it is better that the blood—the animal's own food—should melt into the particles. In the same 11th book, however, modifying his view, he says: "One must set down the blood during the time of cure so that necessity never takes us to feed the patient intemperately."

The Arabs, on the other hand, seem to suspend phlebotomy more. Whence in the first [book], fourth [part], 
<margin>2. t. p. <note>likely referring to a specific book/tractate</note></margin>
it is said that the turns of phlebotomy should be many.
<margin>3. p. q. <note>likely referring to "prima quarta"</note></margin>
Where it is not possible [to do it all at once], a multiplication of the number [of sessions] is better than a multiplication of the quantity [taken at once]. Avicenna <note>original: "m. a." - Master Avicenna</note> also grants leading the patient to fainting, but with greater fear and distinction, which Haly Abbas <note>original: "Ax."</note> rejects in Distinction 173. This happens perhaps because although Galen handed down the canons of cure for the whole world—and not just for Italy (5th book of *On the Method of Healing*)—they are nonetheless more directly adapted to temperate climates, such as the regions of the Greeks, from which he originated (Pergamum). In those regions, bodies are stronger and blood is more abundant, since blood is a more temperate and multifaceted humor. For everything is generated by something similar to itself and remains at rest. From such people, the indication for phlebotomy was greatest. 

The Arabs, however, inhabit "distempered" and hotter regions. Therefore, illnesses in those regions become more "choleric" <note>bilious/hot</note>. For this reason, the 7th book of the *Collection* <note>original: "collx."</note> says: "Illnesses which are simply acute in the lands of Hippocrates are 'peracute' [extremely acute] in ours." In these regions, due to dispositions opposite to those in temperate regions, they require phlebotomy less. For temperate blood requires evacuation, but <term>cholera</term> <note>yellow bile</note> requires purgation.

Entering more into the particulars, it is said in the 9th book of *On the Method of Healing* that phlebotomy is granted even after the fourth day. Indeed, the best time, as you have seen, is when we act not only on the sixth or seventh days, but according to the needs of those whom you will bleed thereafter.
<margin>3. ix. d' īge.</margin>
Finally, phlebotomy may be done at any time, provided the strength of the patient can bear it. 
<margin>3. xv. cōnneris. <note>Refers to the 'Continens' of Rhazes</note></margin>
Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis"</note> in the 15th book of the *Continens* said: "Therefore, do not look at the days, but perform the bloodletting until the [fever] recedes." Whence 
<margin>f. vi. Breuiaī. <note>Refers to the 'Breviarium' of Serapion</note></margin>
in the 6th book of the *Breviary*: "One should not consider the number of days, for when strength remains, be content to perform phlebotomy on the sixth and seventh, and even on the remaining days." 
<margin>4o</margin>
Wherefore in the first [book], fourth [part]: "When you must perform phlebotomy in fevers, do not heed what some say—namely, that it is not good to perform phlebotomy after the fourth day—for it is good even after forty days." And this is according to the opinion of Galen, although it is better to do it before the fourth day and prepare by later digesting [the humors] when the signs are certain. Wherefore the 7th book of the *Collection* says: "The time for performing phlebotomy follows the strength of the person, because strength is at its greatest in the beginnings of illnesses; for this reason, some ordered phlebotomy to be performed in the beginnings." There are many sick people who endure phlebotomy even until the seventh day. And to remove the opinion of those others, Galen says that the weakness or strength of the person [is the true guide].

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the timing of phlebotomy (bloodletting) in acute illnesses. It specifically addresses the "fourth-day rule" and provides counter-arguments and refinements based on the patient's vital strength, the type of illness (such as smallpox), and astrological influences like the lunar cycle.</meta>

...the number of days does not strictly follow. For those who say that one should not perform <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>bloodletting</note> after the fourth day, as was already touched upon in the general [discussion], and particularly in the fifth [book] on the practice of <term>phrenitis</term> <note>original: "frenefi"; an acute fever with delirium</note>: you should use the lancet on the first, or the second and third day, if the vital strength is sufficient. On the fourth day, however, you should touch none of these. But what should be said concerning these things will soon appear.

<margin>3/4</margin>Regarding the third point, however, the indications showing the evacuation of blood before the fourth day or even after it should first be seen. And thereafter, they should be applied to the act. Regarding the first of these,

<margin>1/2</margin>it must be known what such indications are. And the authorities on these matters were touched upon in <note>original: "dis. clxiiii & clii"</note> distinctions 164 and 152. Regarding the second of these,

<margin>1/2</margin>it must be known that if all the signs—or several of the more significant ones—testify to phlebotomy, such as the vital strength and disposition of the organs along with their principal functions, and with this, the urine is thick, dense, and tending toward red; and provided there is no nausea, nor indigestion of the stomach, nor its weakness, nor an excess of susceptibility [to pain]; and if the principal organs are still somewhat strong with their adjacent and subservient parts, but the <term>matter</term> <note>the diseased humors</note> is not yet so "digested" <note>the process where humors are ripened by the body's heat for expulsion</note> that nature can expel it without the help of art; and if there is a filling of the veins or putrefaction with a certain quality of the blood—if, also, the illness is expected to last beyond the seventh day—then it is better to perform phlebotomy before the fourth day while the vital strength is strong. For it is rare in the first or second day for the vital strength to be feeble, unless it happens due to the bad habits of the patient or old age. It can also be performed beyond the fourth, fifth, or subsequent days if it was previously omitted due to nausea, discord [of symptoms], ignorance, and similar reasons. This is the opinion of Galen and those who follow him. If, however, all or most intentions disagree—especially the most principal ones, such as the vital strength being weak—and the urine is the opposite of what was described; and if nausea is present and the principal organs with their administrators are weak, and the matter tends toward digestion of its own accord, and there is blood outside the vessels; then phlebotomy must be suspended, not only after the fourth day, but even quite a while before it. This is perhaps what Avicenna <note>original: "A."</note> meant when he said: "My counsel in phlebotomy is that it should be avoided as much as possible." 

If, however, the known signs and other general conditions are in a middle state, phlebotomy should not be performed in an absolute way as in the first case, nor should one entirely desist as in the second, but one should maintain a middle course, so that phlebotomy will be performed moderately around two [days]. From these points, therefore, because these things have been more fully ordered elsewhere, a serious mind will be able to artificially conjecture the truth among these contradictions. 

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it is said that he <note>Avicenna</note> orders phlebotomy at the beginning of the illness because it results more laudably, provided there is no impediment as mentioned before. Nevertheless, if it was omitted, it can still be done after the fourth day, as was declared. To the other, it is said that Avicenna speaks in a general way, not in a specific one, when the blood specifically requires evacuation. The method of the Arabs and the Greeks in performing phlebotomy also appeared to differ. To the other, it must be said that in a <term>tertian fever</term> <note>a fever that recurs every third day, traditionally associated with yellow bile</note> choler dominates and will quickly reach a <term>crisis</term> <note>the turning point of a disease</note>; therefore phlebotomy is not owed to it, or if it is, it should be in the first days. To the other, it is said that it is different 

in smallpox <note>original: "uariolis"</note> than in other illnesses arising from blood or its heat. For the matter of smallpox and measles <note>original: "morbilloꝝ"</note> must clearly tend toward the exterior surface if the termination is to be praiseworthy. Phlebotomy, however, after two or three days, diverts it and draws it back toward the inside on the fourth day. This does not happen in other blood-related illnesses, as they do not terminate in this manner. To the other, it must be said that Hippocrates <note>original: "y."</note> suggests, as it appeared, that it is better to evacuate at the beginning; but nevertheless, he does not deny that phlebotomy can be performed after the fourth day. And Galen says the same. To the other, it is said that nature is not always prostrate after the fourth day. If it were, phlebotomy would have to be suspended as said, since the principal inclination is taken from it. To the other, it is said as a concession: since the movement of nature is already tending toward a crisis of its own accord, phlebotomy should not be performed, as the physician's energy should be conformed to nature. Nor can one measure perfectly its subtle action. For nature perhaps attempts its goal through one path, and you might take a different one while wishing to be its imitator. To the other, it must be said that although <term>synoche</term> <note>a continuous, non-intermitting fever</note> fevers mostly terminate on the fourth day, there are other illnesses with an abundance of blood which are judged beyond the fourth and seventh days, where phlebotomy is required due to the fault of other humors in the veins.

Regarding the first point of the other part, it must be said that Galen, Avicenna, and Democritus speak of illnesses in which the blood "sins" by purging and the vital strength is strong. This is found in the ninth [book], where he treats the cure of <term>synoche</term> fevers and fistulas. Avicenna, in the first [book] on phlebotomy, ordains it for the evacuation of blood. To the other, it must be said that perhaps Hippocrates delayed phlebotomy from the beginning because he considered that he could heal the illness already attempted; for through the various warming applications he applied, more signs then appeared for phlebotomy.

To the other, it is said that the pleurisy of Anxion was not "simply acute," even though pleurisy usually is, but was a "tropical" <note>perhaps meaning localized or of a specific type</note> kind since it terminated on the 34th day. This discourse here is about the "simply acute." Let the other reading be conceded as a healthy understanding. To the other, it is said that medication is conceded and phlebotomy is more denied after the fourth day, not because phlebotomy is a stronger evacuation, but because after the fourth day it happens more often that matter is found needing education by medicine rather than by phlebotomy. For blood in illnesses should mostly be regarded and guarded as a treasure; it is also converted into bile and other things. How phlebotomy and medicine become safer, and how they do not differ in power, is seen in Distinction 166.

### DIFFERENTIA. 168.

> That phlebotomy is more looked for in the first quarter of a lunation
> than in the others is shown.
> For there are four general times of the year
> proportioned to their natures. Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Albūasar"; a famous Persian astrologer</note> in his fourth *Introduction*: Because the first quarter is like Spring, it is placed
> as hot and moist. The spring of infancy is proportioned to blood.
> The second quarter is hot and dry, like summer and youth, attributed to choler.
> The third is cold and dry, like autumn and old age, added to melancholy.
> The fourth is cold and moist, like winter and senility, proportioned
> and attributed to phlegm. In that quarter, therefore, in which blood
> and nature given to it dominates, phlebotomy is expedient.
