<meta>This page continues the scholastic examination of phlebotomy, shifting from the timing based on the progression of a disease to the timing based on the phases of the moon and astrological influences. It reflects the medieval medical belief that the moon governs the "moistures" (humors) of the body just as it governs the tides.</meta>

# Whether Phlebotomy is More Effective in the First Quarter of the Moon than in Others

This is shown as follows. Phlebotomy <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>the practice of opening a vein to let blood out</note> ought to be performed when the power of the spirit, or the heat and the <term>humors</term> <note>the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, are increasing, since it leads out a multitude of these humors. But this occurs in the first quarter, when the humors and spirits are increased and intensified by the governing power. For the moon, in its first phase, possesses the strength to generate internal heat and a multitude of fluids. Also, phlebotomy must be qualified according to the quantity and the type of medicine used. For heat and moisture, which are associated with the blood, abound in the first quarter; in the second, heat and dryness; in the third, cold and dryness; and in the fourth, moisture and cold. These qualities are attributed to the quarters, and the medicine <note>here meaning the bloodletting treatment</note> must correspond to them. For it is required when the qualities of the humors are failing. Likewise, according to the *Centiloquium* <note>a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note>, the moisture of bodies increases in the first quarter and recedes in the second; it will follow this proportion in the other two quarters, for in the third it arrives and in the fourth it recedes. When they increase, <term>diminution</term> <note>bloodletting</note> is required; for then they are augmented, whereas when they recede, the opposite is true. Therefore, phlebotomy is suitable in the first quarter, but not as much in the others. On the contrary, in the first quarter, the humors are not yet fully increased, nor have they "boiled" <note>reached a state of peak activity or agitation</note> at the beginning of the month; therefore phlebotomy is not suitable then, nor is <term>cupping</term> <note>the use of heated cups to create suction on the skin</note>. Therefore, one should not perform phlebotomy.

It is shown that it is not suitable in the second quarter because, as touched upon, it corresponds to <term>choler</term> <note>yellow bile</note>, for which phlebotomy is not sought, but rather for blood. Furthermore, one fears that as the humors boil over, phlebotomy might move them toward a state of pulsation. For it is commanded at the time of the movement of illnesses to desist from evacuation as much as possible. Moreover, the aspect of opposition <note>an astrological term where the moon is 180 degrees from the sun</note> falls within it, which is judged to be a position of enmity in terms of its breadth. In this state, the astrologer commands one to rest from evacuation and natural movement, since it possesses a contrariety of nature. Therefore, one should not perform phlebotomy in the second quarter. On the contrary, because the vital strength is then strong and the humors seek the exterior parts, phlebotomy is suitable for these. Additionally, a <term>trine aspect</term> <note>an auspicious astrological angle of 120 degrees</note> is found in it; then it is most suitable, as this is an aspect of friendship and the light is already abundant. Therefore, phlebotomy is very appropriate. However, that it is suitable in the third quarter is taught especially to Alexander in the *Secret of Secrets* <note>original: "secreta edocēt Ay." referring to the pseudo-Aristotelian "Secretum Secretorum"</note>.
<margin>Haly Abbas</margin>
Likewise, Haly Abbas <note>an influential 10th-century Persian physician</note>, in the book *On Elections* <note>astrological choices</note>, says that when phlebotomy is performed, the moon should be in the waning of its light; this happens most in the third quarter. And in that phase, the moistures arrive. Even then, the humors are increased and the vital strength is strong, which are conditions that command phlebotomy. Therefore, one should evacuate then. The opposite of this is written by Haly Abenragel <note>an 11th-century Arab astrologer</note>, who wishes phlebotomy to be done in the first half of the month. Furthermore, because of what was mentioned regarding the aspect of opposition, phlebotomy is prohibited. Moreover, when the humors seek the interior parts while diminishing themselves, there is no place for phlebotomy; but that occurs during the decrease of the moon. Therefore, it is not expedient. That it is suitable in the fourth quarter is argued because when moistures abound and are diffused, phlebotomy is appropriate; but this is during the failure of the moon’s light, as it is in the air, for then the worst vapors are raised and rains become more frequent. Again, it imitates the nature of menstruation, which indeed occurs in the fourth quarter and at the end of the month. Wherefore

in the *Posterior Analytics* <note>a work by Aristotle</note>: At the end of the month, the Nile flows more, because the end of the month is more "spring-like" due to the moon's light failing.
<margin>Aristotle, Posterior Analytics</margin>
<margin>From the Histories: many physicians have many good things</margin>
Furthermore, in the ninth book of the *History of Animals*, it is explained thus: The movement of the menses in women occurs around the waning moons. Whence in the fourth book of *On the Generation of Animals*: Menstruation occurs naturally more as the months fail <note>at the end of the lunar cycle</note>. Therefore, one should perform phlebotomy in the fourth part of the lunation. Others, however, think the opposite. And <term>phlegm</term> then abounds, for which evacuation is not owed, but rather a true purging. Additionally, a <term>square aspect</term> <note>a 90-degree angle, often considered tense or difficult</note> is found, which is at least a position of contrariety; the moon also seeks the solar rays. Therefore, one should not evacuate in it. Regarding the first point, however, it must be known which quarter of the lunation is denoted by the lunar month. But the "month" is multifaceted, as shown in
<margin>Quarter of the month of conjunction</margin>
distinction 164. But here we mean the "month of conjunction" <note>the synodic month</note>, constructed from the "month of pilgrimage" of the moon through its whole orbit, which is completed in a space of 27 days and almost 8 hours, and from two days and four hours besides, the number of which rises to 29 and a half days. For the moon, receding from the sun with its swifter motion, does not return to the sun in the place where it was first joined, but advances almost through a [zodiac] sign; and it is to this that the moon, after a time of two days and four hours, joins itself again. When, therefore, this month is divided into four parts, four quarters will also arise, each of which will contain 7 days and 9 hours, in which the light of the moon varies by division. In the first quarter, it will be half-full, or <term>dichotomous</term> <note>original: "dyacorona"; the moon when half its disk is illuminated</note>. In the boundary of the second, it is completely full, or <term>Bederen</term> <note>from the Arabic "Badr," meaning full moon</note>. At the end of the third, it is rendered half-full again. In the fourth and last, it is burned by the sun <note>the new moon phase</note>, joined to it, lacking light and vigor. It also receives other particular configurations according to the third book of *On Critical Days* and Messahallah's <note>an 8th-century Jewish-Arab astrologer</note> *On the Rotating Sphere*. It can also be said that the quarter of the lunation is according to how the moon moves by the lead of the
<margin>3. Critical Days</margin>
"First Mover" <note>the outermost celestial sphere</note> in a natural day, from the east to the middle of the sky, and from there to the west, then to the middle of the earth, and finally back to the east. According to that aphorism of the *Centiloquium*: moistures increase in the first quarter. It must also be observed that in phlebotomy, and indeed in every evacuation, there is a double hour: the "elected" hour, which is the most suitable, in which all conditions or the more worthy ones are observed in the best way—such as in the clearer light of day, with superfluities evacuated, and following the expert's judgment. And there is the "necessary" hour, when it must be done regardless, so that almost nothing intervenes to prohibit it—as happens rarely, such as in a "bloody apoplexy" <note>a stroke</note>. In the first quarter, the third book of the *Aphorisms* <note>by Hippocrates</note> commands that in acute diseases, one should medicate on the same day. Indeed, the day has a great latitude so that the orbit and the planets can be configured differently at different times. Because of this, there is no disagreement between physicians and astrologers, but rather they are in the highest accord of understanding. This is sought even if it involves both types of hours, though it is verified more in the "elected" hour. What phlebotomy is has been made known in distinction 163. Regarding the second point, it must be known that certain physicians have said phlebotomy should be performed more in the first quarter. Since, as touched upon, it corresponds to the blood in sharp matters, being hot and moist.

# The Determination of the Proper Time for Phlebotomy

However, this argument does not hold at first glance. It is because astrologers recommend that phlebotomy should be performed first in the second quarter before the opposition <note>original: "oppositio"—the full moon, when the moon is opposite the sun</note>, and in the third quarter after it. Likewise, in the first phase, the humors <term>humors</term> <note>the bodily fluids that were believed to dictate health and temperament</note> are not yet fully moved toward the exterior of the body. Indeed, even if their movement were sufficient, although the moon varies in nature according to its quarters relative to the light it receives—being called cold and moist at one time, and cold and dry at another—yet when compared to Jupiter, which is proportioned to human nature, the moon as a whole remains cold and moist. Thus, it is more appropriately proportioned to the blood, which is hot and moist, as it approaches the hot and moist nature of humanity.

There were others who recommended phlebotomy at the time of opposition <note>the full moon</note>, because the "winds" do not apply at the beginning of the month <note>original: "mensis"—the lunar month</note> as some have reported, or because the humors have not yet been moved or "boiled up" <note>original: "ebullierunt"—referring to the medieval medical theory of humors heating and expanding like boiling water</note>. Nor should it be done at the end of the month, because they are then diminished; but rather in the middle of the month, when the humors are boiling and follow the increase of the moon's light. They argue that in the first quarter, the moistures increase most significantly, as the moon becomes, so to speak, a "lesser sun." In the middle of the month, the moon exists in its proper prevention <note>original: "preventione"—a technical term for the phase leading to the full moon</note>, standing directly opposite the sun.

<margin>Decision</margin>

<margin>{</margin>
Even then, there is an increase of moistures and a flow. However, as shall be declared, this position cannot stand, since that aspect of opposition <note>the moment of the full moon</note> is an hour of nature that is forbidden by all astrologers. Nor should their reasoning be accepted, either because the author <note>likely referring to a specific source like "A."</note> does not speak from his own knowledge but from others, or because he intends the middle of the latitude's degree and not an arithmetic point, so that the "middle" is said to be when the aspect of opposition is separated, which covers a space of twenty-four degrees. Furthermore, because the humors are then moved by an excessive "boiling" and are fluctuating too much, they should not be disturbed.

Regarding the third point, it must first be known which quarter of the moon is suitable for phlebotomy, and subsequently which is for scarification <note>a method of bloodletting by making small shallow cuts in the skin</note> and the use of leeches. Regarding the first, one must know that the moon can be considered in two ways: either by the changes it undergoes according to its quarters, or by the reception of its light. If the first is considered, the governing power of the body <note>the "virtus regitiva"</note> varies according to the increase and movement of the humors. When the moon moves from conjunction <note>original: "complexio"—here meaning the new moon</note> toward opposition <note>the full moon</note>, this power is strengthened. For the humors and the spirit <term>spirit</term> <note>the "pneuma" or vital force that carries heat and life through the body</note> assume an increase, and their movement tends toward the exterior. From the opposition of the moon <note>symbolized here by the sign of Leo ♌</note> back toward conjunction, a weakening occurs. 

Therefore, Albertus <note>referring to the scholar Albertus Magnus</note> introduces in his third book: those who fall ill at the beginning of the month will have bodies stronger for repelling infirmities. At the end of the lunar month, the opposite occurs. This is confirmed by the "critical movement" <note>the "crisis" in a disease</note>, which is a kind of expulsion from the interior parts to the exterior; the moon has this same movement from conjunction to opposition. An illness is nothing less than a state of emptiness, since it requires an increase of moisture and the vigor of power. From the opposition toward the conjunction, the opposite happens to both.

I say, therefore, that phlebotomy is more appropriate in the **second quarter**, excluding the specific hours of the opposition aspect; generally in the third; more so in the first; and least of all in the fourth. This is also shown from what was said before: because whenever the vital power is strong, the indication for evacuation and the increase of humors is principally made. When the humors are abundant, phlebotomy should not be performed sparingly, and their movement seeks the exterior. Phlebotomy should follow the movement of the fluids. This occurs principally in the second quarter of the month. For the power is then strong due to the greater reception of the moon’s light, from which the humors are also increased and seek the outer parts because of the heat moving from the center to the circumference. For the moon, when magnified with light, creates impressions of heat. Thus, in the fourth part <note>of the *Metaphysics* or a similar Aristotelian work</note>: the nights of the full moon are hotter because of the light of the moon, which occurs in the second quarter and especially near its end. 

After that, in the third quarter, even if moisture is still sufficient and the power is strong, they nonetheless seek the interior parts more. However, phlebotomy is more permissible there than in the first quarter. Whence Haly Abenragel <note>original: "balybamec"—a corruption of the name of the famous Arab astrologer</note> says: after the full moon, bloodletting is better than at the very beginning of the light; however, in other places, the "airy signs" are found to be better after the full moon. For bloodletting at the very beginning of the month is praised more only in comparison to the end of the month. In the first phase, the power is not yet strong, nor are the humors fully increased, even though their movement begins to tend toward the exterior. In the fourth quarter, none of these conditions are found, especially beyond its midpoint. 

Thus, phlebotomy is most suitable in the **second quarter**, then in the third, less in the first, and least in the fourth. Know also that the quarters differ according to whether they are before or after the opposition. For it is less suitable at the very beginning of a phase than at the end (excluding the degrees of opposition); but after the opposition, it is more suitable in the beginning of the phase than at the end. 

If the moon is considered on the part of its position, this can happen in three ways: by reason of the sign <note>Zodiac sign</note>, the house, or its conjunction with other planets or fixed stars, or by its aspect. Regarding the first, astrologers say that in phlebotomy one must especially observe the **airy**, **fiery**, and **mobile** signs. **Fixed** signs <note>symbolized by Leo ♌</note> and common signs are generally to be avoided. But not all airy signs are to be chosen; for although Gemini and Libra are airy, phlebotomy is not granted in them for two reasons. One specific reason is that Gemini signifies the large hands <note>or lower arms</note> where phlebotomy is principally performed. For they say that phlebotomy is not suitable in the arms while the moon is in Gemini, just as scarification is not suitable while it holds Cancer in the shoulder blades. In these parts, injuries often occur. Whence it is said in the *Centiloquium*: "To touch a limb with iron while the moon is in the sign of that limb is a terrible thing." 

The signs govern the body as follows:
*   **Aries** signifies the head.
*   **Taurus** signifies the neck.
*   **Gemini** signifies the shoulders and large hands.
*   **Cancer** signifies the shoulder blades.
*   **Leo** signifies the heart and stomach and what is there.
*   **Virgo** signifies the belly and its surroundings.
*   **Libra** signifies the lower parts of the belly, such as the loins.
*   **Scorpio** signifies the private parts, bladder, and anus.
*   **Capricorn** signifies the knees.
*   **Aquarius** possesses the shins down to the lower parts.
*   **Pisces** <note>symbolized by ♌</note> denotes the feet.

And all this refers to the "essential" significance; for "accidentally" it can happen that Pisces denotes the head and Aries the neck, as when someone's birth coincides with Pisces ascending <note>the rising sign</note>, or as others say. However, this notation does not...

# In the fourth quarter of the moon, phlebotomy should be performed more than in the others.

Knowledge precedes and arises from a natural, well-ordered understanding. This work requires judging rightly, wishing to attend to both the denoted and the observed. However, another factor is universal: because Gemini is a **common** sign <term>common sign</term> <note>also known as mutable signs (Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces), which represent transition</note>, when the moon is held in it, the day is not suitable for phlebotomy. They signify that the bloodletter <note>original: "minutorem"</note> might strike more than one blow, so that the necessity of the bloodletting is interrupted by a moderate delay for the other person.

There are, however, **fixed** signs <term>fixed signs</term> <note>Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius; these were thought to be stable but resistant to change</note> to be avoided when we wish to change something, just as they are to be chosen when a matter is to be made firm. Some, <margin>these quarters are excellent</margin> however, do not approve of Scorpio. There are also **mobile** signs <term>mobile signs</term> <note>also known as cardinal signs (Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn), which initiate change</note>: Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn. The fixed are Taurus, Leo, and Scorpio, and Aquarius; the rest truly are common.

One should especially choose for the moon to be in Aries or Libra, and for Venus or Jupiter to be joined to either. For this denotes that everything will be good for the person undergoing phlebotomy. As much as it pertains to the **house** where the moon is located, the first, second, and third—which is the house of its joy—or the seventh or fifth are good, but not in the **ascendant** <note>the sign rising on the eastern horizon</note>. For the moon's grace is diminished in its own heat and dryness. Neither should it be in the **fourth house**, for that is the house of the pit <note>original: "fovee" - referring to the *Imum Coeli*, often associated with the grave or hidden things</note>, nor in the **sixth**, which is the house of infirmity, nor in the **eighth**, which is death, nor the **ninth**, because it is opposite its joy. Nor the **twelfth**, which is the house of enemies, sadness, and prison, and of every evil thing; nor with the lords of these houses, nor if the lord of the ascendant is in these places; but rather in the **tenth house**.

If, however, the conjunction of the moon is observed, let it be joined to Venus or Jupiter, or both. Let it not be joined to the Sun unless it is a **union** <note>original: "unitio"—likely referring to the state of *cazimi*, being in the heart of the sun</note> where the limit is within sixteen minutes before or after. For all planets are said to be strengthened in union with the Sun. This, however, is brief and almost like a point, and thus does not greatly suit medicine. Or let it be under its rays for fifteen or twelve degrees before or after. Or in conjunction with Saturn—specifically when the moon is diminished in light—or with Mercury.

Regarding Mars, however, because it denotes curative and especially material medicine, astrologers disagree. For **Baly Bamec** <note>likely Albohali, an 8th-century Arab astrologer</note> says that phlebotomy should be performed when the moon is in a masculine sign joined to Mars; they should not fear him unless he is ascending in latitude and in the circle of the moon's apogee <note>original: "lune augis circlo"</note>, and if the lord of the moon's house regards him with a favorable aspect. Hence, contrary to what was said before, Mars is a fortune <note>a lucky planet</note> in every work involving the opening of the veins of the blood, and the diminishing of the blood through cupping <note>original: "ventosas"</note>, or in medicating the sick.

Many, however, detest the conjunction and even the aspect of Mars as being primarily evil. Whence **Baly Babe Ragel** <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century astrologer</note> says: "It is not a good bloodletting when the moon is going toward Mars." And **John of Seville** <note>a famous 12th-century translator of Arabic scientific texts</note> says: "Let the moon not be joined to Mars." For it signifies a movement of choler <note>the yellow bile humor associated with anger and heat</note> after the bloodletting, just as a connection to Saturn signifies melancholy. I agree with these more, fearing the deceits of Mars. For in fortune they are greedy and unfaithful; for when they have provided something good, they regretfully try to take it away. **Almansor** <note>the physician Rhazes</note> says this in his aphorisms.

Thirdly, one must consider the reason of the **aspect** <term>aspect</term> <note>the geometric angle between planets</note>. Since it is fourfold—namely sextile, quartile, trine, and opposition—a bloodletting should be performed when the moon is in a **trine aspect** with Jupiter or Venus, or secondly when in **sextile**. The **quartile aspect** of these does not harm, nor does the **opposition**, though it does not help. But the aspect of opposition should be avoided specifically, and finally—

---

<margin>Sextile Aspect ✶</margin>
—the quartile aspect to Saturn and Mercury, and especially the deceptive one to Mars. The **trine aspect** and likewise the **sextile** of Mars perhaps help, because this is the artifice of Mars, which is not in Saturn and Mercury.

The **sextile aspect** <note>60 degrees</note> is that containing a sixth part of the heaven—for example, two signs—and it is divided in two, just as others provide the opposite. For it regards a planet existing in the third sign before it and after it; for example, one who starts at the beginning of Aries regards one who is at the start of Gemini and Aquarius. This is called the aspect of friendship.

<margin>Quartile □</margin>
The **quartile** <note>90 degrees</note> is that containing a fourth part of the heaven, such as three signs. It is twofold like the first; for example, when one looks at what is before it in Cancer, and after it in Capricorn. This is called the aspect of "half-enmity."

<margin>Trine △</margin>
The **trine aspect** <note>120 degrees</note> is that containing a third part of the heaven, such as four signs. For example, when from Aries one sees that which is in Leo and Sagittarius. This is called the "perfection of love."

<margin>Opposition ☍</margin>
The aspect of **opposition** <note>180 degrees</note> is simple, as from any given sign into the seventh; it will be the perfection of contrariety and enmity. And what was said regarding a planet starting in Aries and others, so it happens by a similar distance in the rest of the signs.

This vision in the moon lasts according to the quantity of its light, just as in the others, which is twelve degrees preceding and following it. Whence, since the aspects of opposition and also quartile are evil, phlebotomy must be suspended for the predicted twelve degrees before and after. And because trine and sextile <margin>Trine and Sextile are Praiseworthy and Good.</margin> are praiseworthy, phlebotomy should be performed during these visions, observing the predicted quantity of degrees.

Whence, in the first trine aspect, when the moon has already obtained two parts of three of its light, and is a benevolent planet sufficiently distant from the fourth house, in no case is phlebotomy more recommended than in that trine aspect. But when the moon has receded from opposition, having sufficient light, I praise the first aspect more, since it proceeds with increasing light, while the latter proceeds with decreasing light.

The **sextile aspect**, although it is moderately benevolent, because the moon possesses little light, should not be valued except slightly; the first is stronger, as with the trine. As for the **fourth vision** <note>the quartile</note>, it is disliked, for it is of moderate contrariety. However, because the moon receives more light in it than in the sextile aspect, phlebotomy is granted more safely than in the former. The vision of **opposition**, because it is of total contrariety, must be avoided entirely. For its malice forces the bloodletter to err, or causes the one being bled or the attendants to sin, and external things to be administered inconveniently. Because of this, before its limit of twelve degrees, one must primarily take heed, and generally for twelve degrees afterward.

If it is said that in the predicted cases nature does not go out in the sextile or trine vision, but rather strengthens itself and prepares the matter—but in the sixth [aspect] as on the seventh and twenty-second day, and in opposition as on the fourteenth—thus the physician is a follower of nature, whose opposition is confirmed. It must be noted from many differences, especially from rule 155, when and how the physician imitates nature. According to this, it should be known that at the same time and manner, blood is to be evacuated by cupping and also by leeches just as by phlebotomy; the predicted declarations can be similarly adapted, and they do not differ except in degree.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on phlebotomy from the previous page, focusing on the distinction between bloodletting and cupping, and how the timing of these procedures is governed by the lunar cycle, the "boiling" of humors, and the tides.</meta>

For the blood is thinner when it is drawn through **cupping glasses** <term>cupping glasses</term> <note>original: "ventosas"; glass vessels used to create suction on the skin to draw out "corrupt" blood</note> than that which is drawn through **phlebotomy** <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>the traditional practice of opening a vein to balance the humors</note>. Regarding this, Haly Abenragel <note>An 11th-century Arab astrologer whose "Book of the Skilled in the Judgments of the Stars" was a standard medieval text</note> sufficiently indicates that there is a difference between phlebotomy and cupping. He notes that when you wish to extract blood through cupping, it is good for this to occur after the **opposition** <term>opposition</term> <note>The Full Moon, when the Moon is opposite the Sun</note> in the latter half of the month. But if you extract it from a vein, it is better that it be done in the first half of the month, provided other previously noted celestial configurations have been inspected. 

Here, however, a very difficult point is raised: that the humors escape differently through phlebotomy than through cupping. For in phlebotomy, the humor is expelled, whereas in cupping <note>original: "sycia"; a term for cupping</note>, it is drawn out. Because the **humors** <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health</note> are "boiling up" <note>original: "ebulientes"</note> before the opposition and increasing afterward, there is a fear that too much suction from cupping might lead to a harmful deduction of the humors, and consequently an outpouring of them. This does not happen after the opposition, when the humors have already begun to quiet and decrease. But this risk does not occur in phlebotomy, if it is done properly at any time, since in that act there is an expulsion rather than a suction.

<margin>The hour of phlebotomy</margin>
It should be noted that the best time for phlebotomizing is from the morning until the **third hour** <note>Approximately 9:00 AM in the medieval system of unequal hours</note>. This is particularly true when one phlebotomizes because of an excess of blood, as those physicians who practice astrology teach. They divide the day into four parts of six hours each. From three hours before dawn until the third hour of the day, **blood** dominates. From then until the ninth hour of the day <note>approx. 3:00 PM</note>, **yellow bile** <note>original: "colera"</note> dominates. Phlegm <note>original: "fla"</note> rules for six hours of the night. And because each of the humors is best evacuated when it is in motion and undergoes an "evaporation," the blood is best evacuated in the aforementioned six hours, and especially in the three hours of the morning. For in those hours, the body is better prepared for the choice of phlebotomy, as the worthy elements are celebrated and the superfluous ones expelled. At that time, phlebotomy and cupping are to be performed, just as vomiting is to be encouraged at midday.

<margin>I say that it is advised (?)</margin>
The hour for vomiting <note>inducing emesis to clear the stomach of bile</note> is better in summer and at midday. For at that time, the yellow bile is rising, which is led out by vomiting; the Sun indeed rises upward and lightens it. Just as at midnight, phlegm is most easily led out.

<margin>Toward the opposition</margin>
Because of the opposition of the humors, astrologers also place the "Lord of the Ascendant" in the mid-heaven and join the Moon to it in some way when they wish to provoke vomiting. But when they wish to encourage a movement of the bowels, they place the Moon in the "angle of the earth" <note>the 4th astrological house, associated with the bottom of the sky</note> and join it with some conjunction or aspect, as appears in the **Centiloquium** <term>Centiloquium</term> <note>The "Hundred Sayings," a famous collection of astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note>. 

Regarding the first point, it has already been shown that the first **quarter** <term>quarter</term> <note>the phases of the moon</note> is entirely moist. Regarding the second, although phlebotomy is appropriate in its own way in the first quarter, it is not as much so as in the second or third. This is because things are not yet fully established in the first quarter. 

Regarding the other point, one must say almost the same as the first: that the humors "offend" <note>cause illness</note> more in the second quarter than in the first, in relation to human nature. Regarding the claim that humors move according to the quarters, I do not mean the quarters in which the Moon passes through its eccentric orbit (even though the commentator on Haly perhaps explains it perversely that way), but rather I mean the quarters of the **natural day**. One of these is from the horizon to the mid-heaven. Therefore, when the Moon has crossed from the horizon to the mid-heaven, the moisture in bodies increases, just as the tides of the ocean increase. But from the mid-heaven, when it tends toward the setting, the humors decrease, seeking the hidden inner parts. This happens in the third quarter as it did in the first, and in the fourth as in the second. By this increase of moisture, the life force is so strengthened that almost no one dies unless by violence or extreme sickness—except perhaps when the Moon occupies the 12th house. In the other two quarters, the vital powers are fortified.

For it often happens that someone seems to be dying when the Moon moves from the mid-earth to the hemisphere, or from the mid-heaven to the west; and then afterward they are so invigorated that hope of health is seen by those standing by. But when the Moon is finally snatched from the mid-heaven toward the west, or from the angle of the earth toward the east, death arrives swiftly. This is even known by the "idiots" <note>unlearned or common people</note> who inhabit the shores of the ocean, in which the flux and reflux is more manifest. For seeing someone brought to the extreme, they pronounce that the person will die when the ebbing of the sea occurs. I clearly perceived this in those whose "Hyleg" <term>Hyleg</term> <note>The "Giver of Life," a specific planet or point in a birth chart used to determine longevity</note> was the Moon; this was seen significantly in the death of **Azzo, Marquis of Este** <note>Likely Azzo VIII d'Este, a powerful nobleman of Ferrara who died in 1308</note>, so much so that for two days those standing by wondered greatly.

Regarding the other point, one must say that such a great agitation does not occur that the moist humors are moved to putrefaction. Specifically, the sight of the opposition must be avoided, and one should perform phlebotomy when no such aspect is near. Regarding Haly's writings on the third quarter, one must say that was his opinion. Or perhaps he wished phlebotomy to occur after the opposition because the humors do not "boil" then as they do in the second quarter, fearing their overflow. Or he imagined that in the third quarter, the "praiseworthy" <note>healthy</note> blood already begins to seek the inner parts. Because the life force is stronger in the approach to the Full Moon than in its waning, and the humors are more inclined to be led out, I have preferred the second quarter over the third.

...or its power. Firstly, because since the Moon possesses a humid power in its movement, when it is vigorous (as at the Full Moon), it is certainly able to move and disperse those increased humors; just as a powerful leader of an army <note>original: "dux exercitus"</note> is capable of ordering and restraining his subordinates by his own motion. Secondly, when the Moon begins to be "under the rays" <note>A term for the New Moon, when it is so close to the Sun it is invisible</note>, it is deprived of light—for it has none except from the Sun, like the other celestial bodies. The Sun’s heat and dryness also dry up its natural moisture. Therefore, being so weakened, it cannot rule the moisture; rather, the fluids run about of their own accord through the places where they were situated. In the first case, when the Moon rules the moisture with orderly motion by dominating it, and is rendered strong in all things, **phlebotomy** <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>bloodletting</note> is expedient; but in the second case, it is not, as the Moon is rendered weak.

Regarding another point, it should be said that the movement that causes menstruation <note>original: "motus menstruorum"</note> at the end of the lunar month is not due to the vigor of nature, but rather because the body is rendered powerless in its weakness, and the moisture (having been rendered thin by certain opposites) slips out of its own accord. Therefore, since this does not happen because nature is strong or specifically intending it, menstruation does not have to "imitate" the Moon—or if it does imitate it in the provocation of blood, it is not so much in drawing it out through other incisions <note>i.e., surgical bloodletting</note>. Also, menstruation does not only flow at the end of the month, but also in its middle, as is indicated in the fourth book of *On Generation* <note>Likely referring to Aristotle’s "On the Generation of Animals"</note>. For when the Moon changes specifically in its light, the humors in animals are changed. But concerning the 
<margin>3 Du 4</margin>
aforementioned, one might doubt whether the flow of menses is unnatural at the end of the month, since it was said in the sixth book of *On Accidents* that every flow of blood is unnatural except for that of the menses. It must be said that the flow at the end of the month is not "unnatural" in terms of the blood itself being expelled as a superfluity, but rather because it happens when the vigor of nature is lesser than at the full moon; in that sense, it can be called "unnatural" in a certain way. The distinction between the natural and unnatural flow of blood was shown in chapter 187.

# DIFFERENTIA CLXIX.

<margin>4</margin>
¶ Whether **barley ptisan** <term>ptisan</term> <note>A medicinal porridge or water made from boiled barley, the standard "sick food" of the Middle Ages</note> is beneficial in fever is shown. This benefit would either be on the part of the "agent" and the "patient," or the fever itself. Not the first, because the agent and patient must communicate in their matter if one is to impress upon the other by altering it and bringing it toward itself. But ptisan is a substance, and fever is an "accident" <note>In medieval philosophy, an "accident" is a property (like heat) rather than the thing itself</note>. For fever is a corrupt **complexion** <term>complexion</term> <note>The balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> of heat and dryness; they do not coincide in matter. Nor is it the second, because since there are three types of fevers—**ephemeral**, **putrid**, and **hectic** <term>hectic</term> <note>"Ethica"; a deep-seated fever affecting the solid tissues of the body</note>—it does not benefit ephemeral fevers because they are in the "spirit" <note>The vital breath</note>, for the heart is hotter than any other part of the body. It would only increase the inflation. Nor does it benefit hectic fever, since its heat is more immense than the heat of the ptisan. Nor even putrid fevers, such as **tertians** <term>tertian fever</term> <note>A fever that spikes every third day, associated with yellow bile</note>, because the **cholera** <term>cholera</term> <note>Yellow bile</note> that is its matter is hotter than the rest of the body, being an unequal distemper. Blood, the matter of **synochus** <term>synochus</term> <note>A continuous, non-intermittent fever</note>, is the next hottest after bile. Those which are putrid or phlegmatic are rendered hotter as they reach the third or fourth day. 

Ptisan, however, is characterized by coldness and moisture, located near the beginning of the second degree. Because such a thing does not reach the 
opposite of equal duality, as taught in the *Tegni* <note>The "Technê" or "Art of Medicine" by Galen, a fundamental textbook</note>. For just as the final response ought to be communal, so too should other bodies be altered by their opposite. Nor does it benefit fevers whose matter is a substance, since by moistening it, it would rather increase it. This is supported by the fact that cold and moisture prohibit digestion except in "concocted" matters, according to Haly. And ptisan is a food above every other grain-based meal, as noted in the first book of *On Regimen in Acute Diseases* <margin>Hippocrates, On Regimen in Acute Diseases</margin>. It is given either for the sake of the fever or for the sake of strength. Not the first, because a disease in its vigor perhaps does not require food (from book 11 of *On Ingenuity*); nor for strength, since strength is often strong enough not to require food. This is confirmed because food is an enemy to both, and the "foster-mother" of the disease (from the first part of book 4). Furthermore, barley is cold and dry and "windy" (gassy), as taught in the second book of the *Canon* <margin>2. Canon</margin> <note>The "Canon of Medicine" by the Persian physician Avicenna</note>. All barley water is inflating; but such a thing does not benefit fevers, since it would increase the distension of the vessels. Furthermore, if it were beneficial to fevers, it would be administered to all and at all times; but in very acute cases, it is prohibited (chapter 133). During **paroxysms** <term>paroxysms</term> <note>The periods when a fever is at its highest intensity</note>, the old precept of silence was held. Likewise, that which is viscous does not benefit material fevers, and ptisan is viscous, as Hippocrates says <margin>Hippocrates, On Regimen in Acute Diseases</margin>. Therefore, it does not benefit fevers.

On the opposite side is the consensus of all physicians and philosophers. Above all grain-based foods, it is held as the most excellent for acute passions. It possesses all the goodness and utility for the sick and benefits those with fevers; among the ancients, ptisan is the first of nourishments <margin>Among nourishments, ptisan is first</margin>. Thus, ptisan helps in fevers. 

Regarding the first point, it should be known that ptisan is a medicinal food or a food-like medicine made from barley and water, cooked to perfection. For its use, especially when strained, belongs more to the work of medicines than foods (from book 5). It is usually made from water and barley, though sometimes almond milk is added, and finally sugar is added to the unstrained version. Similarly, in the strained version, vinegar and white poppy seed are mixed in, for the sake of cooling hotter natures or perhaps inducing sleep. Secondly, according to **Galen** <note>The 2nd-century Greek physician whose work dominated medieval medicine</note>, the power of pepper and often fennel and celery root is added. The strained version requires more cooking than the thick/dreggy version. It is constructed in multiple ways from the barley; often through carefully prepared flour and water. Secondly, barley water is composed from barley in many ways. The first of these is from **Almansor** <note>Rhazes (al-Razi), a 9th/10th-century Persian physician; his "Liber ad Almansorem" was a standard text</note> in his first book: when they grind the raw barley in a mortar and do not dissolve it, cooking it over a fire and adding starch so that it seems sufficiently succulent through the decoction. This version is very inflating and most difficult to digest. It is even worse when sweet wine is put into it, or prepared water, then ground in a mortar and rubbed with the hands through a rough linen cloth. The end of the grinding should be when the husk <note>original: "cortex"</note> is cast off. For when the barley is pounded, the thin surrounding tunic is not cast off, and therefore it is soaked and ground in a mortar, then sufficiently...

Let it be boiled. Some indeed boil the barley first in water, then roast it, and then make a flour from it which is finished with sugar. Once it has inflated greatly, let it be carefully and moderately husked. One measure of this should be taken and placed in a tin-plated vessel or a cauldron, over which fifteen measures of water are poured. Let it boil over a temperate fire until only two measures of water remain—I speak of the liquid only—in which decoction there should be diligent stirring and beating with a large spoon until it is perfectly mixed and strained.

According to Isaac, the barley should be crushed so the husk can be removed. Take one measure of barley and ten of water; then let it be strained and given as a drink, which is useful for the preservation of health and the hydration of the body. In the fourth specific method, it is said that "water of barley" is better than "barley water": take twenty measures of water and one of barley—approximately 37 and 1/3 ounces—and let it be reduced by boiling to a specific quantity. From this, a subtle red liquid is obtained, which provides less nutrition but greater hydration.

In the fifth collection, it says: Barley water should be made in this way—whole grains of barley, not crushed, should be soaked in water. For one part of barley, twenty parts of water should be added. Let them sit for four hours, then boil them in that same water until they acquire a redness like that of wine. In the tenth book of *On Aliments*, the broth is constructed in these ways: **Barley water** <term>ptisana</term> <note>a medicinal drink made from pearl barley</note> hydrates when it has been prepared as it should be, which is when it has boiled at length during the decoction. Afterward, let the juice be made over a gentle fire. It should be mixed according to the time it takes to boil perfectly. When it has been boiled, one should diligently add fine salt shortly before eating. This method of construction is perhaps healthier than the others.

This is used later by boiling it, or by drinking it infused in water to quench thirst. Note that regarding the preparation of barley water—and especially the strained version—the Parisians err in two ways: first, because they commonly prepare it from **oats** <note>original: "auena"</note>, which, according to the book *On Aliments*, is food for beasts of burden <note>original: "subiugalium"</note> and not for good men, except perhaps in times of extreme famine when it provides sufficient warmth. This is shown by grains that do not grow when cut or broken. They do not sprout when deprived of that attractive power. # Whether Barley Water is preferred for fever. 2

<margin>Galen, Book 3, On the Method of Healing, regarding fevers...</margin>
...more a medicine than a food. Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, Roman author of Natural History</note> notes that it possesses a cleansing and scouring quality and causes less windiness <note>internal gas or flatulence</note>. Others, however, seek to have it provide nourishment or to create a more pleasing preparation of crushed barley. Thirdly, there is a similar doubt because barley is established as being cold and dry. For this reason, Haly <note>likely Haly Abbas, a Persian physician</note> says: The primary power of barley is cooling and drying in the first degree <note>The Galenic system ranked the intensity of a substance's qualities—heat, cold, moisture, dryness—from the first to fourth degree</note>. Therefore, Almanzor <note>Refers to the medical work *Liber ad Almansorem* by the Persian physician Rhazes</note> in his third book says it generates blood close to black bile <note>original: "cole nigre"; one of the four humors, associated with coldness and dryness</note>. On the other hand, in the first book of *On the Properties of Foodstuffs*, it seems to be perceived as moist when its essence is extracted; not only is barley cold and moist, but it is also cooling. Wheat, however, is warm in the first degree, and is considered temperate in moisture and dryness by Galen and others. Since that which is temperate in moisture is considered moist, barley must therefore be moist. It should be said that barley is naturally dry, which is demonstrated by its low nutritional value, but it possesses a certain extraneous, undigested, and windy moisture which is removed by sufficient boiling. It is moist and windy, which causes it to be digested weakly by the heat it encounters. From beans, however, windiness cannot be removed, since it is inserted into them, as it were, in a subtle way; so much so that if those who cook them were to boil them for three days and nights, stirring them on the tables, they still could not exclude the gas. This is discussed in the books on acute diseases and the primary elements of foods. Regarding the second point, it should be said that some have said
<margin>fevers...</margin>
that barley water is not at all preferred for some fevers, because it might hinder digestion in some patients due to its coldness. It also induces certain symptoms <note>original: "accidentia"</note>. But what should be said regarding this third and fourth point will appear in the following discussion. Regarding the third point, it should be known that barley water is generally preferred for fevers, as is declared in the first book of *On the Method of Healing*, especially for acute fevers, and particularly when it is strained. This is demonstrated because its administration is indicated in cases where other things—whether they are "natural" or "non-natural" things—are not. <note>The "six non-naturals" in medieval medicine were external factors affecting health, such as air, food/drink, sleep, exercise, etc.</note> From the first perspective, the cause is threefold, since the cause of fever is threefold, as are its symptoms. On the part of the disease itself—the fever—barley water is always sought by reason of the alteration it induces, and more specifically when it is finely strained. This is confirmed because every cure is achieved through its opposite; barley water is the opposite of fever, since they declare it to be cold and moist, not just in the first degree of its essence, which is apparent to anyone who diligently considers the nature of barley and water and the craft of preparing them. However, its temperament <note>term: complexio (the balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, dry—in a person or substance)</note> can be made more difficult by adding certain things to it. Fever, however, stands as a "bad temperament," being hot and dry. Therefore, things that are cold and moist are opposed to a hot and dry fever; for it is the nature of fire that an imbalance should be reduced to a temperate state by its opposite. But boiled barley is the first among nourishing foods; this is barley water, as appeared from its construction, which is why it is beneficial for fever. It also assists by reason of the symptoms, for it mitigates thirst, the roughness of the mouth, and generally clears the respiratory passages. It makes breathing easier and pushes down the vapors that cause headaches, leading to urination and sweat. By performing such actions, it treats the symptoms of fevers. Since barley water is described as having such properties, it is therefore beneficial. On the part of the cause: either it is hot by essence, such as in fevers of the bile and blood, and then it is clear that it is beneficial by intervening with a contrary alteration, a division of the matter, and a scouring wash. Or it is hot by accident, for instance by putrefaction; and in such a case, perhaps a simple alteration does not confer a notable benefit unless the cause is an antecedent one, where the putrefaction has not yet become inflamed. Nevertheless, it is useful by reason of the contrariety of the joined cause, when it has reached a state of heat, and because it washes and scours just as perhaps it did before. On the part of the "non-naturals," such as the time of year or the region: it should be said that it is beneficial in hot conditions, but not in the same way in cold ones, since a change in time always indicates that an imbalance should be corrected by its opposite. By reason of "natural things" like the patient’s strength and other annexed factors, it should be said that barley water—and especially the thicker kind—is always beneficial, specifically when the strength is weak. For when the strength is robust, it requires no nourishment, because it might bring harm along with its help by diverting nature away from the management of the diseases. And therefore, in the peak and the most critical stages of acute diseases, it is ordered to be withheld, as it might be converted into the "matter" of the disease. Thus it is shown how barley water assists in fevers. Regarding the fourth point, to the first argument it should be said that barley water is beneficial for fevers by reason of the fever itself, and because barley water shares the same "matter" with them. For all things that can be generated and corrupted, whatever they may be, meet in a common matter, just as even some celestial bodies do, positing one matter for all under various forms. Barley water does not act merely through its substance, but through the qualities and symptoms existing within it, such as coldness. It also benefits by reason of the quality of the fever; for although a fever may be hotter and drier, barley water can be administered in great quantity and frequently, so that the
<margin>Rhazes, on the opposite</margin>
quality of the fever is gradually opposed. For that which is in the first degree, if applied much and often, will slide into the second degree. Even colder things, as mentioned, can be immersed in the barley water. Other cold things are also present with which it acts as a medicine against the fever; nor does the body always require food to be administered by opposites, but sometimes more by things that are similar. To the rest of this argument, what has been said already appears: that in the case of a cold fever, it does not harmonize by reason of alteration. To the other point, it should be said that it does not help the fever in the way that food does, but rather in that it possesses the power of a medicine that alters the body. Similarly, it is granted that when the strength is robust, there is no need to provide it for the sake of nourishment specifically; nor is it necessary, if it does a little harm, to turn away from it entirely when it is needed, considering its help is greater than the injury. For it is difficult to find any
<margin>refer to Book 1, On Accidents</margin>

To the other point, it should be said that dryness is removed from the barley through the mixing in of water, and windiness through sufficient boiling, as has been shown. And if barley water is at all "inflating" (that is, causing gas), it is either because it is not sufficiently boiled, or when it does not suit a predisposed body; in such a case, it should not be administered to a dry belly, as per the first book. To the other point, it is said that barley water, insofar as it relates to the fever by alteration, is always appropriate, as shown; but in terms of certain symptoms...

It is not administered, as it is sometimes seen that its power distracts from its action regarding the treatment of the disease. Or, something more subtle is exhibited in its place. To the other point, it must be said that viscosity <note>stickiness or thickness of bodily fluids</note> is twofold. One kind is an adhering obstruction, which is not beneficial when it has been sufficiently built up and becomes dreg-like. The other is a continuity of parts joined together, by which windiness <note>internal gas or flatulence</note> is judged to exist within it, such that the distant parts are not easily separated; and this is the viscosity that is beneficial.

### CHAPTER 170.

**T**hat vinegar syrup or that which is like it, such as **oxymel** <note>a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</note>, does not seem to be beneficial in every type of matter <note>the "matter" of a disease refers to the specific humors—blood, phlegm, choler, or melancholy—involved</note>. This is because it either benefits by reason of its quality or its substance; for example, by "cutting" <term>incisio: the medical process of breaking down thick or viscous humors</term> or by penetration. It is not beneficial by quality, because the dryness of the vinegar harms choler <note>yellow bile</note>. Both [vinegar and honey] harm those suffering from windiness or those who are melancholy. Nor is it beneficial for "cutting," since cutting matter is hot and dry, and would agitate the humors and further incite them by making them more viscous... especially when it is quite acidic. Nor is it beneficial for the blood, since digestion should not be expected in those cases.

Even if it were beneficial in the first or second degree <note>The Galenic system ranked the intensity of a substance's qualities—heat, cold, moisture, dryness—from the first to fourth degree</note>, or because of its active quality, it is not so here; for it cools, thickens, and coarsens some matters more than others by its cold quality. Nor is it beneficial as a food. Nor even in a third way, by reason of its specific property, since it arises more from nature. Chapter 179. Again, it is not beneficial for choler, because subtle <note>thin or refined</note> matter needs to be digested by thickening. Hence, in the first book on *Medicines*: "That which is subtle and of extreme thinness escapes from the vinegar," and it is not able to constrain or restrain it, as is the case with the humor of choler. This syrup, however, is held to provide thinness. Nor is it for phlegm or melancholy, because by "cutting" and agitating them, it will become a greater cause of obstruction. Furthermore, such a thing is harmful to everything. Moreover, treatments are the opposites of the things they treat, since medicines are naturally made to act through the contrary. But the aforementioned matters are contrary, as their qualities and substances show. Therefore, vinegar syrup will not be suitable for every matter. On the opposing side, **Mesue** <note>likely Mesue the Younger, an influential 11th-century Arabic medical authority</note> 
<margin>Opposition.</margin>
regarding compound medicines: the power of vinegar syrup is greatly praised among those who verify its excellence, namely in its common ability to act upon matters whether they be hot or cold, thin or thick and viscous, or adhering. 
<margin>Against.</margin>
Hence, **Galen** <note>the most famous Roman physician, whose theories dominated medicine for centuries</note> says its power is common to all matters. And in *The Collectanea*, book 7: [Vinegar] and barley water are praised in the cure of fevers. This appears in the fourth part of the first book, in which he commands vinegar syrup to be administered in almost every fever. Because it quickly quenches thirst, "cuts," and dissolves abscesses while doing the least harm, it is beneficial in every matter.

Likewise, because it seeks out the paths and channels of the body, aiding in the expulsion of humors and leading other medicines to them, it is suitable for the same. Such a syrup is indeed vinegar-based, through its "cutting" and its universal, subtle penetration. For all matter requires some of these benefits. Therefore, vinegar syrup is beneficial to all matter.

<margin>Syrup.</margin>
First, it should be known that "syrup" is derived from **rob** <note>original: "rob"; a term of Arabic origin for a thickened fruit juice</note>, which is a thickened juice. Hence, in the fourth part of the first book: the difference between syrups and *robub* <note>the plural of rob</note> is that *robub* are juices thickened by themselves, while syrups are decoctions <note>liquids prepared by boiling</note> and juices thickened with sweetness. For sometimes they are made with honey, but most often with sugar. **Rob**, however, 
<margin>Rob. Sapa.</margin>
was commonly used for the "must" <note>freshly pressed grape juice</note> of small sweet grapes, which is thickened by boiling. Therefore, it is called a "thickened decoction," because the boiling reduces it by a third; **carenus** is sweet, and **faramphena syreon** according to Galen. There are two types of vinegar syrup: namely, "simple," which is heard when "vinegar syrup" is 
<margin>Simple.</margin>
pronounced on its own; and "compound." The first is made from vinegar, water, and sugar, brought to a thickness by boiling. Galen, in the 4th book of his work *To Glaucon*, constructs it from white vinegar, skimmed honey, and **robana**. There is also a compound vinegar syrup made with hot medicines, and sometimes with cold ones, as necessity urges. Similarly, **oxymel** (or *fecaniabin*) is twofold: simple and compound. 
<margin>Vinegar syrup 1st, 2nd, 3rd [degrees].</margin>
Vinegar itself, which is naturally cold in the first degree and dry in the third, is the base of this, just as viper’s flesh is in **Theriac** <note>a famous ancient "universal" antidote</note>, and aloes are in *Hiera Picra* <note>a bitter purgative medicine</note>, and hellebore is in the great *hieras*, or colocynth, in the way that similar parts are the base and vigor of the entire compound organ. Chapter 143. Here, vinegar is used properly. However, its nature can be adjusted with fresher and whiter sugar and reach the second degree of coldness, considering the natures of the components. It varies, however, according to whether it is more or less acidic. For when its sourness is intense, the vinegar moves away from heat. The matters of the fourth kind are the simple, known ones: blood, phlegm, choler, and melancholy. It ought to be administered in large or small amounts according to the size or smallness of the cause, the condition, and the illness or its 
<margin>Of Vinegar.</margin>
symptoms. Know also from the first book of *Medicines* that physicians have differed regarding the "complexion" <note>the balance of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) in a substance</note> of vinegar. For some have placed it as hot, because it sharpens, stings, corrodes, irritates, and thins—traits associated with heat. Others, however, have declared it cold, because it naturally liquefies and resolves the stickiness occurring in the blood, since by its coldness it aggregates and squeezes out in every way, as if something were being compressed by the fingers. Both sides have exceeded the truth, as the aforementioned complexion shows. But it is doubted again: if vinegar is placed as cold by nature, how is it that a weak heat is then perceived from it? Galen responds that this happens either because it is perhaps composed of contrary powers, like milk, or perhaps because it traps heat and aggregates it, and invigorates it so that by its penetration, sharpness, and stinging, pain is caused, by which hot matter is drawn to that place. Also in *On Fevers*, book 2: I say, therefore, that vinegar, aided by its thinness of substance, brings a dormant heat (resulting from putrefaction) into a certain state of active heat when mixed with the fluids of the body, as was declared at the end of Chapter 140. Of which this is a sign...

# Whether Vinegar Syrup is appropriate in fevers and acute diseases

<margin>Galen, *Prognostics*, Book 3</margin>
First, according to Galen, it cools at first, but after some hours it warms. This is because it firms the earth <note>referring to the solid parts of the body or the "earthy" humor, black bile</note> while the air entering within is forced to exit, since multiple bodies cannot occupy the same place. Galen admits he was at one point ignorant of the cause of this. Secondly, it should be known that some have said vinegar syrup is not beneficial for every type of matter <note>the "matter" refers to the specific humor—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, or black bile—causing the illness</note>, because vinegar harms the melancholic <note>those with an excess of black bile</note> while it benefits the choleric <note>those with an excess of yellow bile</note>. Hence, in the third book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*: the acidity of vinegar helps those who have "bitter choler" <note>yellow bile</note>, but not those who have "black choler." For yellow bile, by vanishing, is transformed into the nature of wind <note>internal gas</note> when it is agitated by vinegar. But black bile boils and increases by multiplying, because vinegar helps black bile to be created. Therefore, it harms women more than men because of the womb, a member that is melancholic by nature and akin to the nature of vinegar. Furthermore, it seemed to some that certain syrups were more appropriate and suited to individual matters, such as simple or compound **oxymel** <note>a mixture of honey and vinegar</note> for cold matters. It must be said that vinegar syrup is suitable, as will be shown hereafter, for all matter. Nor is the argument they bring forward valid; for vinegar is not administered plainly, but "broken down" <note>tempered or diluted</note> and reduced into one substance from three, though the power of the vinegar remains dominant. Even though it may cause harm by reason of its melancholic quality, it nonetheless benefits by the subtlety of its substance. Nor should it be said that it does not benefit in every matter, even if some syrups are found to be more specifically appropriate for certain matters. For in this syrup, a greater "commonality" is found over all matter than in the rest of those other

<margin>Mesue, Book 2</margin>
matters. This is achieved chiefly because of the vinegar. Whence, in the first and third parts [of his work], he says: vinegar is common to all matters. For its cooling is such that it can be easily broken by a light cause. Furthermore, its ability to penetrate deeply remains along with the medicines and its power of <term>incision</term> <note>original: *incisio*; the medical process of thinning or breaking up thick, viscous humors</note>, and it performs this when administered in cold matters. In the maturation of hot matters, however, nothing is chosen above it. Thus, vinegar syrup helps all matter. Regarding the fourth point: first, it must be said that it has been seen how it benefits by the quality of the vinegar and by reason of "cutting" <note>thinning the humors</note>. Nor is vinegar's "cutting" ability due only to its quality; rather, its substance works no small amount toward that end. Even if it is "cutting" and thus might seem hot, it can nevertheless be cold for another reason, just as opium, despite its coldness, is bitter.

<margin>Opinion</margin>
Similarly, it should be said that although blood does not require as much <term>digestion</term> <note>the process of "cooking" or preparing a humor for expulsion</note> as some of the other humors, this syrup nevertheless provides no small benefit when the blood is not in its natural state. Hence, in the first and fourth parts: **phlebotomy** <note>bloodletting</note>, when the intention is to draw blood, is not of the kind in which "digestion" is expected—specifically the kind of digestion required for laxative medicines. To the other point, it must be said that vinegar syrup can act upon the matter like a **julep** <note>a sweet medicinal drink</note> or **mellis-cratum** <note>honey-water</note>, and more so by its quality, as has been shown. To the other point, it must be said that Galen's discourse was concerning vinegar itself, and not the syrup. To the other point, it must be said that the claim is verified in essential groups and by itself, but not in opposites. (158). For vinegar syrup benefits choler and blood, but it also benefits other matters.

<margin>Prognostics, Book 2</margin>
That cold water is not appropriate in fevers and especially in acute cases is shown chiefly because it must have some action within the body of the feverish person; otherwise, it would not be suitable. But it is shown that it can have no such action in the body. For according to **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a famous 10th-century physician</note> in his *Elements and Universal Foods*: a "simple" thing does not act upon the intended subject in the way a "composite" thing acts upon a composite. Now, water is a simple body, but the human body is composite. Hence, **Abenguefith** <note>original: *beben gueſen*; an 11th-century Arab physician</note> says: a simple thing does not produce the operation of a composite thing upon a composite thing. For nothing acts except upon that which is similar to it in potential; and the "agents" and "patients" <note>the things acting and the things being acted upon</note> must share a common matter. Water and [human] bodies do not coincide in one matter, but it is spoken of as a simple thing and a mixture. Furthermore, a cure is perfected by applying a contrary in the same degree and directly opposite, as in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*</note>. But a fever has a "degree" <note>a measurable intensity on the scale of hot/cold/moist/dry</note> since it is a sickness, although some pseudo-scholars have said the opposite, raving that in the first book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases* it is pronounced that the substance of fire exists in a "degree" while the other elements are placed at the minimum, since its nature is simple and in the "highest" state. But water is not in a "degree" since its coldness is considered an extreme difference. (13). For a "degree" implies respect and comparison. (139). Also, that which harms the healthy harms the sick. (See Book 3 of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*). But water harms the healthy because it is cold, at the very least. For coldness is added to coldness. It also harms those who are hot <note>feverish</note> because of its quick penetration when their pores are open. It harms those who are "temperate" <note>of balanced humors</note> because they require a regimen of similar things, which water is not, since it is cold in the highest degree and...

...[baida] <note>This appears to be a fragment of a name or term from the previous page, possibly referring to a specific author or preparation.</note> Or such a thing is not appropriate. On the other hand, it is generally seen that water does not benefit an **ephemeral fever** <note>a "one-day" fever believed to affect the "spirits" or vital breath rather than the humors or solid parts of the body</note>. For it is not the case that it suits it, since its subject is the *spiritus* <note>the "spirit" or vital breath</note>, which is greatly harmed by cold. *Difference 116*. For there is a subtle "fire-like" quality that is more easily resolved than anything else due to an unequal distance.

And this is confirmed because the heat of an ephemeral fever is almost soothing and pleasant, like that of one who has been bathed. Such a person does not need a remedy as strong as one who requires [intense] cooling.

Nor is it appropriate for a **hectic fever** <note>original: "ethice"; a long-term wasting fever affecting the solid parts of the body</note>, since it renders the body cold and bloodless. For the body is impoverished of its own heat. To such a person, water does no small amount of harm. *On the Method of Healing, Book 9*. And it is supported by the fact that hectic fevers flare up after meals, however weak the patients may be. This happens because of the moisture dispersed over the inflamed members, just as when water is poured over lime, it causes a struggle as the parts dissolve. *Galen*.

Therefore, there will be much more of a struggle from the contact with water, as a more intense battle will arise between opposites throughout the parts. *Difference 140*. Nor is it suitable for a **putrid fever**, because it induces **obstructions** <note>original: "opilatōnē"; blockages in the vessels or pores</note> by its coldness. For the matter is delayed in passing through. *Book 4*. From this, transpiration is prohibited, and thus the putrefaction and the fever increase.

Furthermore, cold and moisture—the qualities of water—greatly prohibit the "digestion" <note>the process of the body processing and ripening the diseased humors</note> of the matter. **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a Persian physician</note> says that digestion is essentially perfected by heat and moisture. *62*. It likewise increases the "accidents" <note>symptoms</note> such as inflammation or burning and thirst, because in **choleric** patients <note>those with an excess of yellow bile</note>, in whom choler dominates under the diaphragm, water is transformed into the nature of choler. *Regimen in Acute Diseases, Book 3*. Whence the *Practica* says: If it happens that choler dominates in the stomach, water corrupts it and converts it into choler.

<margin>2</margin>
That cold water is not appropriate in fevers, either universally or particularly. On the contrary, in the fourth [section], the **Commentator** <note>Averroes</note> says: No one has died to whom I gave cold water at the appropriate time, unless they were in a dangerous and incurable state. For he himself, along with others, shows that water is to be administered cold, as will be seen. On the other hand, **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli the Elder</note> in his third book says: I have found no use for water except that it is drunk in acute diseases. And many fevers are acute. Indeed, it is the most troublesome of diseases. *On the Method of Healing, Book 8, Appendix*. Again, it is the property of every medicine to be contrary to the disease; but water is contrary to every fever, being cold and moist, while fever is hot and dry. Likewise, the accidents of fever, such as thirst, burning, and headaches caused by hot vapors rising to the head—as well as the distress that follows almost all fevers inseparably—are settled and removed by a drink of cold water. Therefore, cold water is appropriate in fevers.

Regarding the first point, one must know what water is and how it is distinguished. *Difference 13*. Let it be said here, beyond those things determined in the book on simple medicines and other places, that we are now considering potable water imagined as "sweet," such as rainwater, spring water, river water, or well water. For those that have foreign qualities mixed in and flavors are certainly not [simply] cold and moist, like potable water, which is sought not for the sake of thirst or carrying nourishment, but rather as a medicine.

Regarding the second point, one should know that some have shrunk from the idea of giving cold water in fevers,

---

either because it was sometimes administered unskillfully and a [bad] outcome followed. *On the Method of Healing, Book 9*. Note also that **Averroes** in the *Colliget*, Book 7, does not prefer simple water here, saying it seems to him that **watermelon water** <note>original: "aqua angurie"</note> is far better than water cooled in snow in such cases, as in a **burning fever** <note>original: "causone"</note>. This is because simple water, although it is at the ultimate degree of coldness, quickly receives heat; furthermore, since water is a simple substance, it hardly restores the body and provides nothing but a cold quality. But watermelon water restores the body and adds to the making of blood according to its quality. What then is desired regarding this third point from the premises?

Regarding the third point, it should be known that since fever is a genus of "complex" diseases, the genus to which water is compared should first be considered. One should look at the evidence showing whether it should be administered entirely, denied, or given in a middle way. Next, it must be shown where it is necessary to give it and when, as well as the opposite.

<margin>3</margin>
Regarding the first point, one should know that some indications always precede the use of cold, such as those taken from the disposition or the fever itself. For since it is a "bad complexion" <note>an imbalance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, dry</note> that is hot and dry, its proper remedy is cooling and moistening. *Difference following*. Therefore, for the species of fever, cold water is appropriate. However, there are some indications that prohibit it entirely, such as those taken from the **virtue** <note>the "virtus" or vital strength of the patient</note> and mostly from the spirit, for the strengthening of virtue is more immediately perfected by food and especially by wine. *Difference 75*. Water does not directly strengthen virtue; rather, of itself, it weakens and prostrates it, though it may help by accident. For it corrects the complexion which supports virtue like an instrument. So also it weakens the spirit—the carrier of virtue—more by itself, as its quality blunts the tempered state. For the spirit is a tempered vapor of the blood. *On the Use of the Parts, Book 6*. And its substance may render it dark and immobile. Nevertheless, by accident, it can be beneficial, as touched upon regarding virtue.

If one also refers to the complexion of the feverish person, it should be known that it is either hot or cold. If it is hot, for the sake of the cure, a cold drink is owed to him. If it is cold, on the other hand, for the sake of the cure, a hot drink is owed. However, for the sake of preservation, a hot person should have hot, and a cold person cold. Here, however, the opposite is more sought after, in which the cure consists, rather than the similarity in which preservation is founded. If anyone looks to the humor, then if the humor is hot—sanguine or choleric—he needs a cold drink, even if the matter is undigested, and especially the choleric person. Whence the *Aphorisms, Book 4*: The digestion of the choleric humor is such that it is turned from its thinness and made thick. Cold water does exactly that. But if the humor is cold and raw, even after digestion, a cold drink is not appropriate for him. *Practica, Book 3*.

<margin>4</margin>
As much as must be considered regarding the members: if a member is weak, obstructed, or has an **abscess** <note>original: "apostematū"</note>, cold is not appropriate for it. This is especially true when the liver and the stomach with its parts first perceive the harm of the water. *On the Method of Healing, Book 7, Appendix*. In the opposite disposition, it is otherwise. Regarding the "annexed" things, such as age, it should be said that since youth is a hot age, it allows it. But a cold age, like old age, prohibits it. Similarly it is in sex, color, and...
