# Whether Cold Water is Effective in Fevers and Especially Acute Ones

...appearance, since those who show themselves to be of a hot [constitution] seek it, while those of a cold [constitution] reject it. This is also seen in a fleshy habit <note>the physical build or "constitution" of the body</note> and a vivid color. It is also necessary to observe custom <note>habitual behavior</note> not a little, as one is accustomed to it, and so on; but this is desired. For nature is a kind of second habit. If, however, one considers non-natural things in general, we should say that insofar as they incline toward heat, temperate things allow for cold ones; but insofar as they incline toward cold, they are forbidden. For those coming from a hotter region are harmed by [cold] water because of its quick penetration into the pores of those who are opened by the heat. If, however, one looks at the nature of the cause of the fever, then they allow it in part, such as when the matter is hot; but they also forbid it in part, as when it is cold and undigested.

Similarly, the accidents <note>symptoms or secondary occurrences</note> of inflammation, burning heat, and thirst demand it. Other things, however, deny it, such as rigors <note>shivering fits or chills</note>, acid belching, nausea, coldness of the feet, and the like. Regarding these, you have also seen why they forbid a drink of cold virtue: <margin>Galen, Book 3</margin> weakness of power <note>original: "uirtutis"; the body's internal strength or vital force</note>, a lack of innate heat, cold and raw blood, indigestion of the humors, weakness of a part such as those of the belly, the intestines along with the viscera, the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: "dyaflamate"; the muscular partition between the chest and abdomen</note>, and the bladder; thinness, being unaccustomed to the drink, obstruction of the internal viscera, pain, and the appearance [of a swelling]. It is prepared with warm and cold water with a temperature of nine, ten, and the first of the fourth. Regarding this, it should be known specifically that in <term>ephemeral fevers</term> <note>one-day fevers</note>, a cold drink is prescribed, especially in those where the inflammation is more intense while the strength remains, with other things added, and properly in the beginnings. Whence in the first of the fourth [it says]: It is necessary that cold water not be forbidden in the beginning of the matter, <margin>Galen, Book 3</margin> <margin>Galen, Book 4</margin> because the strength is strong, concerning which there is no fear. Therefore they do not fear its weakness, and cooling is better. This is known from the *Method of Healing* <note>original: "de igenio", referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note>, where in a fierce fever, and properly from anger, burning heat, and the <term>canicular heat</term> <note>the "dog days" of summer</note>, and especially when fearing a fall into a <term>hectic fever</term> <note>original: "ethicā"; a wasting fever of the solid parts</note>, he orders cold things to be drunk, and rightly so. For then the inflammation is so great that the spirit <note>original: "spiritus"</note> would be removed along with other things; [cold water] removes the fear of falling into a hectic state, so that insofar as it is by reason of an ephemeral fever, the water should not be very cold, but by reason of the inflamed parts or the fear of falling into other fevers. In a hectic fever, however, since its heat is more intense than a temperate one, according to A. <note>likely referring to Avicenna or Aristotle</note>, cold [water] should be exhibited for the sake of the fever. Whence from the tenth [book] of the *Method of Healing*: It is necessary that as quickly as possible, both through the juice of <term>ptisan</term> <note>barley water</note> and through soups that are fed through <unclear>pdrū</unclear> and bread that is added; then care for the laboring patient with a drink of cold water. For it extinguishes it immediately and the <unclear>fialz</unclear> of the fever rests, provided that, as was said, neither <term>phlegmon</term> <note>an inflammatory mass or abscess</note> grows from it, nor the putrefaction of the humors. For the drinking of cold water is most useful in <term>colliquative fevers</term> <note>fevers characterized by the "melting" or wasting of body tissues</note>. It is most contrary to <term>phlegmon</term>, and so on, in the fourth. Sometimes, even when a phlegmon exists, water must be chosen to be given; whence under <margin>Galen, Book 8, Method of Healing</margin> the aforementioned part being touched: I have given it to many such people, thinking it better because soon the phlegmons increase with heat than to sustain a person falling into a hectic fever; indeed, he prescribes cold water to be thrown in so that the fever does not convert into a hectic state of old age, choosing rather that he should die more quickly of <term>marasmus</term> <note>severe malnutrition and wasting</note>, though with reason. For those who have little blood and have thin flesh, the drink of cold [water] is quickly deceptive; it passes through to the solid particles of the animal and finds nothing by which it may be broken. Therefore, for hectic fevers, neither

pure water is appropriate, nor do they similarly require much cold, because of their thin bodies and little blood. Wherefore in the first of the fourth: Cold water that is not of a violent coldness is not a bad thing if given to hectic patients as a drink, if there is no <term>aposteme</term> <note>original: "apā"; a swelling or abscess</note> or anything else prohibiting it, such as a swelling under the <term>hypochondria</term> <note>the upper abdomen below the ribs</note>, or putrefied or raw <term>chymes</term> <note>the partially digested humors</note> undigested in the whole body. For although these things prohibit it, if you fear the malice of the heat and thirst, and you estimate that it leads through it to dryness, do not forbid cold water. For the addition of a swelling and rawness is better than the wasting [of the body]. One must fear, however, in a swelling of the lung and the diaphragm because of <term>spasm</term> and faster suffocation. Thus, therefore, it appears that in hectic fevers, even if there are many prohibiting factors, having considered the greater benefit over the harm, it is necessary to exhibit cold things to them moderately and with caution. If, however, the question refers to <term>humoral fevers</term> <note>fevers caused by an imbalance of the four humors</note>, it should be said that sometimes a cold drink is suitable, and sometimes not, according to the indications allowing or prohibiting it. For in this, it must be properly observed. Those things which allow it are a <term>choleric humor</term> and blood, also health and strength of the members and the innate spirits with a powerful principal heat, fleshiness, a hot age <note>youth</note>, habit, and a temperately cold region. The absence of a swelling in the viscera [allows it], unless it be pure <term>erysipelas</term> <note>original: "erisipila"; a bacterial skin infection, here used to mean a specific type of hot inflammation</note>. <margin>Note this in the drinking of cold [water]</margin> Whence in the ninth of the *Method of Healing*: Erysipelas is most certainly never cured by anything with cold. Therefore, concerning marasmus: If the disposition is erysipelatous, it is necessary to abstain from almost everything. Cold water, however, according to the state of the disease, should be used "agonistically" <note>original: "agonistice"; meaning a bold or aggressive therapeutic intervention</note>; for I have been accustomed to name it so when I give it suddenly and very cold. In the beginning, however, it should not be used unless forced by the laboring patient and it being a habit for him, and when he cannot bear the thirst. In the first of the fourth: in fevers of swellings, the drink of cold water is not granted, nor is the entering of a bath. He means that in a swelling of erysipelas, cold things are applied externally, such as lettuce, purslane, and <term>houseleek</term> <note>original: "sempuia"; likely *sempervivum*</note>; however, water is not offered internally. Whence on wasting: It is necessary to place cooling things on the outside, expressing those things aforesaid. But if nothing profited, force it to flow inside the body. The opposites to these are those which prohibit it, which are many. For of humoral fevers, there is one with a swelling, concerning which it has already appeared appropriate to give [water]. Another is without it; some are called <term>synochal</term> <note>original: "fynoca"; a continuous fever</note> from the inflammation of the blood alone; others indeed with putrefaction, in which cold [water] is sought in its own time, the harm and benefit having been weighed... arising in the ninth of the *Method of Healing*, unless a stronger prohibition occurs. And perhaps in the drink of thirst until it makes one tremble, and it will. For perhaps it heals in [a certain] way. Therefore to Glaucon: Spring water is to be chosen in a synochal fever because it is lighter, and it should be exhibited on the <term>critical day</term> <note>the day a disease was expected to change for better or worse</note>. If, however, the fever is from cholera, or from an intermittent or continuous <term>tertian fever</term>, or <term>causus</term> <note>original: "causon"; a burning remittent fever</note> when the fault is by reason of the <term>dyscrasia</term> <note>an imbalance of humors</note> especially, a drink of cold water is properly owed. <margin>Galen, F.</margin> <margin>Haly Abbas</margin> Whence to Glaucon: Causus is most certainly extinguished if one drinks much and very cold water. Haly Abbas, however: While the consistency of the fever holds its period, for the patient...

Cold water ought to be administered at the time of the onset of the medicine <note>likely referring to the peak of the fever's paroxysm or the time a specific remedy is given</note>. But in the beginning, the intake of cold water should in no way be permitted. Concerning the **burning fever** <term>causon</term> and the continuous **tertian fever**, do not listen to or pay attention to what is said by foolish physicians—namely, that a large amount of "extinguishing" <note>the process of cooling or quenching the febrile heat</note> delays the **crisis** <note>the turning point of a disease</note>. For I have already experienced both ways and found this one [using cold water] to be safer, more favorable, and less fearful. And those who died of this fever under this regimen are much fewer than those who died under the first regimen.

For to abandon the extinguishing and the refinement of the regimen as the crisis approaches is to abandon the sick man to death, without a doubt, unless a surplus of moisture is expected in the whole body, or he disobeys the physician and drinks very cold water or eats the food he most desires. If that happens, it affects the brain and their stomach so that they suffer spasms; wherefore the eyes and jaws are loosened, and a distortion occurs from the affliction of the stomach and brain, and a spasm in the nerves. And it is not forbidden in this fever for the sick person to take cold water when he wishes, and whatever he desires from cold and moist foods. Whence, in the fourth book [of his authority], he says: "The drink of cold water with which we have often cured burning fevers, with no one dying to whom I gave cold water as mentioned." If, however, the fever is less acute and the **humor** is raw <note>undigested or not yet matured for expulsion</note>, a drink of cold water must be forbidden.

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, that water acts upon the body of the feverish person since the action is accomplished by quality; and it exists in water just as in other elements in the highest degree. Nor did <term>Isaac</term> <note>likely Isaac Israeli</note> intend to say that a **simple** [element] does not act upon a **compound** in any way, but that a simple does not act as strongly upon a compound as a compound acts upon a compound, or a simple upon a simple. Because the most powerful action arises from agreement combined with some contrariety. For agents must agree in genus but be opposed in species <note>differentia xvi</note>. And although a simple does not act on a compound in the same way a compound does, the quantity of the simple will multiply the effect.

For thus it will work more strongly, since when the quantity is increased, the quality is also intensified. It should also be said that water and fever share in matter. For she is the first giver, namely the **matter** <note>original: "yle", from the Greek hyle</note> of all things generable and corruptible. To another point: healing is well accomplished by a contrary in the same degree, or at least in vigor. For although water is not in the extreme degree of humidity and cold, nevertheless, as it appeared, because a simple does not act on a compound as a compound does on a compound, it can also be taken from water in which the quantity and cold are tempered such that they reduce the degree of the fever. -> **Whether wine is suitable in fevers and in acute diseases.** <-

...because cold and humid things hinder digestion unless the material is choleric <note>referring to yellow bile, which is hot and dry</note>. Or because when water is given, for the most part, the material is already digested. Regarding the final part of this [argument], it must be said that cold things, as has appeared, soothe the "accidents" <term>accidētia</term> <note>in medieval medicine, 'accidents' are the symptoms or secondary effects of a disease</note> which are caused by heat. Nor is it converted into bile <note>original: "colera"</note> except when it is of a small quantity, such that it is not overcome by the fervor of the fever. For then the febrile heat covers it, just like a small amount of water thrown upon the fire in a furnace, as those who invigorate a blacksmith's fire do. However, when it is given in a large quantity, it extinguishes the febrile heat just like a fire. And therefore, they prescribe that it must be given in a large quantity until the face shivers, having been cooled. One should not listen to the common talk that water is converted into bile since it is a simple substance without other qualities; but this is an effect of the heat covering it, which strengthens the heat so much that it inflames the material so that it turns into bile. For from it, as if from bile, a smoke then rises.

# SECTION CLXXII.

<margin>1</margin>
**That wine is not suitable in fevers and especially in acute ones** is seen from the fourth book of *On the Preservation of Health* <note>Galen's "De sanitate tuenda"</note> and the eighth book of *On the Power of Foods* <note>Galen's "De alimentorum facultatibus"</note>, **following the Hippocratic voice.** Again, if wine is suitable in fever, it will be either by reason of the thing itself, or the cause, or the disease (such as the fever or its accidents), or nature (that is, the "virtue" or strength of the patient). It is certainly not the first, since fevers are made of things having no cause, such as hectic <term>ethice</term> <note>a fever associated with wasting diseases like tuberculosis</note> and many ephemeral ones. Nor even in those having causes, namely putrid ones, since wine agitates them, mixing the malignant with the benign and making them run together into one. There are also certain hot causes for which wine will be harmful by similarity. For it acts like fire upon fire, as in the case of choleric, bloody, and burnt materials; and as long as the material cause of the fever exists as putrefaction affected by excess heat and dryness. Nor is it suitable by reason of the fever itself, since that is a "bad complexion" <note>an imbalance of the four bodily humors</note> of heat and dryness, and wine is similarly hot and dry in specific diets. At the very least, it harms because it is hot and humid. <margin>Difference 70</margin> For every fever is naturally healed by cooling and moistening. <margin>Book 9, *On the Method of Healing*</margin> Whence, in the 11th book, "a cold drink is always the healing of a fever." Similarly, it is not conferred by reason of the accidents, because the inseparable accidents that always occur and are not separated from them are headache, thirst, and distress of the spirit. And in the second book on fevers, all these are intensified by the oily heat and vaporous subtlety of wine. Nor is it suitable on the part of the "virtue" <term>uirtutis</term> <note>the patient's vital power or strength</note>, because contraries are [not] assisted. The strength of the sick is not to be increased but, as it is found, to be guarded; nor should the body be further nourished. For the more you nourish impure bodies, the more you harm them. But according to Isaac <note>likely Isaac Judaeus, a famous 10th-century physician</note>, wine is more than other things an augmentative and nutritive of the spirit and the body. And it is entirely proportional to the instrument of nature, namely the spirit. <margin>Difference 70</margin> Furthermore, wine is flammable, as they teach, like oil poured into a lamp. That wine is such is shown from the inflammation of "water of life" <note>distilled spirits or alcohol</note> and from a vial full of boiling wine.

<margin>Note well.</margin>
On the opposite side, in the third book of *On the Preservation of Health*, it is conceded that wine may be used even in acute cases, and Galen likewise in no few than eleven places in *On the Method of Healing*. Again, wine evacuates the cause of the fever. For it moves all excretions in the previously cited 11th book. It also moistens and cools in particular diets. It also soothes accidents such as thirst, and relieves "syncope" <term>sicopi</term> <note>fainting or sudden loss of strength</note> above all other things, corroborating the virtue <margin>Book 12, *On Method of Healing* & Difference 70</margin>. Again, wine is humid. <margin>Difference 70</margin> But humid diets are beneficial to all those suffering from fever. A great fire snatches a small one to itself, for a larger flame extinguishes a smaller one. <margin>*On the Cause of Long and Short Life*</margin> And therefore the fire in the sun is dissolved and more quickly extinguished. Since wine is hot, it should be given so that it increases the innate heat, by which increase the attracted febrile heat may be dissolved. Therefore, wine is to be exhibited in fevers. Regarding the first point, one must know what wine is and what fever is, as noted in Differences 70 and 87.

<margin>Galen 15. Thin, watery wine</margin>
Regarding the second point, one should know that Galen, in the 9th book of *On the Method of Healing*, delivers such a speech: "Know that I give wine to all these people, which is watery in appearance and in power; for this wine is better than water, aiding digestion above all, and promoting urine and sweat." It is manifest, moreover, that Hippocrates gave wine not only in ephemeral fevers but also in acute ones. This is seen from the books he wrote on the diet in acute diseases. But according to Galen's *Commentary*, just as Hippocrates (or his son Thessalus) forbids wine not only to those in fevers who are of hot complexions, but even in a time of health. For he advises a hot nature to be cooled, and to drink water, and to rest; unless perhaps one uses more water than wine according to such natures, as it pleases some, and I have said it should be removed by him. And because that seems difficult and long-lasting to endure, he adds that this very thing should be sought in itself. He supports this by the fact that we see some to whom we give wine, while for others we prohibit it entirely. Just as some allow meat to those in fever, but others deny it altogether—as the Gauls <note>the French</note> concede less wine than the Italians.

<margin>On the part of the wine.</margin>
What should be seen about this will appear from what is to be said. Regarding the third point, it should be known that one wishing to diligently administer wine in fevers must attend to the "indications" <term>indicatiōib9</term> taken from things natural, non-natural, and against nature <note>the 'six non-naturals' in Galenism were factors like diet, sleep, and exercise that affected health</note>. According to these, it must then be given or denied. And the parts are taken from the side of the wine, then from the side of the suffering <note>the disease</note>, and from the subject <note>the patient</note>. Regarding the first of these, it should be known that when wine is administered in large amounts, it must be watery in appearance and power. Whence, in the third book of *On the Preservation of Health*: "Wine will be suitable for one having an acute sickness if it is watery, its color is white, its substance is thin, and in which none of the [strong] qualities stand out, such as stipticity <note>astringency</note>, bitterness, harshness, sweetness, or gassiness." For that alone is deprived of the harm of water and of those things that other wines cause. This is given more as a medicine for altering, dividing, and purging, and rather for making the water penetrate. For wine makes water penetrate like a medicine <margin>Book 1</margin> rather than as a nutrient. For wine is among the "nutriments" <term>alimētoy</term> and not just a drink, contrary to what some say.

<margin>3. Nutriments.</margin>
<margin>X. Al-Mansur.</margin>
Sometimes, however, an old, potent wine is required, so that it may alter the material and break it down, as in a long-lasting quartan fever <note>a fever that recurs every fourth day, often associated with malaria</note>. Whence Al-Mansur in the 10th book: "Let old and pure wine also be drunk." Regarding the second point, it should be known, as was said before, that wine—especially if thin—is absolutely for those who are hot...

<meta>This page continues the medical debate regarding the use of wine in patients suffering from fevers, building on the previous discussion of cold water treatments. It focuses on the specific conditions—physical, environmental, and symptomatic—under which wine might be permitted or strictly forbidden.</meta>

<margin>Wine is prohibited in fevers.</margin>
...for those who are naturally vigorous, youthful, fleshy men. It is also forbidden for those who are sufficiently lean and high-colored, and those accustomed to hot and dry conditions, or living in hot and dry air. The same applies to those on a strict diet <note>literally "diet of the son," likely referring to a meager or restricted regimen</note>, or those subjected to strenuous movements, wakefulness, anger, and fury, or when the cause of the illness is hot. In these cases, with similar symptoms, wine should not be given at all unless a major crisis occurs, such as <term>lipothymia</term> <note>fainting or sudden loss of strength</note>. However, for those with the opposite conditions, it may be granted more freely. For those in the middle, it should be administered with moderation, as nature indicates the sufficiency of the matter. Furthermore, it should be stated that for the most part, wine is suitable for <term>ephemeral fevers</term> <note>fevers lasting only one day</note>, as is clear from the discourse of Galen, especially when the fever is declining. Hence Galen says in his work *To Glaucon*: those who have a light fever and are not at all plethoric <note>having an excess of blood or bodily fluids</note> should not be entirely prohibited from wine, but for those of the opposite condition, it should be entirely forbidden. White and thin wine should be given to those who cannot sleep, provided they do not suffer from a headache, or at least not a pain in the temples. This rule must be observed. Likewise, those who are boiling with anger, anxiety, or excessive thought should abstain from it.

<margin>pp</margin>

$\P$ Fourthly, on the contrary: Wine of many mixtures is a good medicine for an ephemeral fever caused by distress. For since this is a specific passion of the heart, according to **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli, a prominent 10th-century physician</note> in the *Book of Fevers*, wine has the power to comfort the heart and the spirit above all else. Similarly, it benefits fevers arising from sadness, worry, and fear. In fevers caused by wakefulness, wine is placed among the most beneficial things. By raising vapors to the head, it causes sleep through the good digestion that follows. It similarly benefits ephemeral fevers of the <unclear>inflammatory</unclear> <note>original: "scōpoli," likely referring to synochus or continuous inflammatory fever</note> type and those arising from exhaustion, since it excites the spirit and increases moisture. However, it harms those with fevers arising from nauseating satiety and <term>obstruction</term> <note>original: "opilatione," referring to a blockage in the vessels or organs</note>, perhaps especially as they are declining. For it is to be feared that by its smoke and disturbance, it might induce <term>putrefaction</term> <note>the breakdown of humors that turns a simple fever into a dangerous one</note> or generate a prior inflammation, two things one must always watch for in fevers of the spirits. Perhaps, however, by reason of the subject in whom the fever is not rooted—such as the spirit—no harm comes from the wine, but rather a benefit is acquired, unless it was caused by anger or fury and the like. For the spirit is greatly comforted by wine. However, as for why it is not suitable in a <term>hectic fever</term> <note>original: "ethica," a fever involving the consumption of the body's solid tissues</note>, although it is not explicitly stated in the tenth book of *On the Method of Healing*, Galen writes concerning <term>consumption</term> <note>original: "thabe," referring to wasting diseases like tuberculosis</note> as follows: Wine is extremely useful in the final stages of a cold consumption. But in that which comes from "roasting" <note>fevers that "dry out" the body</note>, it must be avoided. Others, however, more determinately say it should be given if many conditions are added: both on the part of the patient—that they are not of a hot nature along with other similar factors, and the fever is not intense—and on the part of the wine, that it be weak and mixed with much water. For such a mixture cools and moistens, since the water makes it penetrate quickly. Whence **Almansor** <note>Al-Mansur, referring to the Persian physician Rhazes</note> says in his tenth book: If neither the heat nor the sharpness is strong, let a white and subtle wine be drunk, which has so much cold water mixed in that the taste of the wine is hidden. Therefore, it is appropriate. Perhaps it is necessary sometimes to give the patient a drink of a little subtle wine mixed with much water. If, however, we refer to <term>putrid fevers</term> <note>fevers where the humors are literally decaying</note>, it is given with caution as before; wine is least suitable for a hot nature. In contrary cases,

<margin>In tertian fever</margin>

<margin>Part 4, perhaps in quartan fever.</margin>

it is not as it will appear; in some it should be prohibited, in others exhibited in moderation or prohibited. Furthermore, some fevers are deadly, in which neither signs of digestion appear nor are the strengths of the body vigorous. It is impossible for these to be healed, and such patients should not be bathed, nor anointed with things that open the pores, nor should wine or water be given. For in the eleventh book, chapter nine of the *Therapeutics*, it is said that where hope is lost, it is a vain thing to be criticized by the unlearned for using those aids that heal many, as is said in the *Aphorisms*.

$\P$ There are others, however, for whom there is hope of health. Some of these arise from an <term>aposteme</term> <note>an internal swelling or abscess</note> in which wine must be prohibited. For it stirs up the material by its heat and subtle penetration and leads it to the site of the putrefaction, unless perhaps the material is very cold and crude and the illness is in decline. Others are without an aposteme. These either decline while the material is digested, or they do not. In the first case, wine is granted in the eleventh book of *On the Method of Healing*, as touched upon before, especially because the strength is weak. For at this time, watery wine being drunk moves all the excrements. Following this, after the fever has become moderate and the strengths are not strong, if there are signs of digestion, baths and the drinking of wine benefit such people. But if the fever is strong and the material undigested, and especially if the strength is robust, wine must not be given. Whence in the same place: If at any time the magnitude of the fever flares up, as in <term>synochus</term> <note>a continuous, non-putrid fever</note>, neither wine nor baths nor anointing with pore-opening things should be used; yet wine is to be avoided even more when the material is intensely choleric and inflamed, perhaps even if it is digested. And therefore, in the seventh book of the *Collectio*: In fevers that are not acute, we can provide aromatic and light wines that can sustain a little water, specifically for <term>phlegmatic</term> and <term>melancholic</term> fevers. But in burning fevers, they must be distanced from wine entirely. Since the materials of acute fevers are hot both essentially and by accident by reason of putrefaction. Chronic fevers, however, are cold in themselves, although by reason of putrefaction they are rendered hot in some way, so much so that in a <term>quartan fever</term> <note>a fever recurring every four days, associated with "black bile" or melancholy</note>, perhaps a preparation of wine is required. Whence *To Glaucon*: One should use thin, white, and moderate wine for those with a hot natural vigor. **Almansor** also, before the fortieth day of the illness, prescribes drinking a subtle and very tempered wine. But against this, it is argued: In the beginning of the *Practice*, it is said it is expedient for the master of this fever to be given wine after the maturation of the humors, and let the wine be not old but of a new nature and mixed with water. It must be said that before the fortieth day, the material of a quartan fever can be digested in some way. Or for those for whom the wine is weak, watery, and given after a longer fast. In a <term>tertian fever</term> <note>a fever recurring every three days, associated with "yellow bile"</note>, however, after digestion, **A.** <note>likely Avicenna or Aristotle, but context suggests a medical authority</note> grants a bath and subtle white wine mixed with much water. For it causes them to sweat when they are covered in their beds. Whence *To Glaucon*: In a tertian fever, abstain entirely from wine as long as you see it being done for the sake of digestion and coming toward health; let it be white, thin, and watery.

$\P$ In a <term>phlegmatic fever</term>, he says *To Glaucon*: You shall give to drink, before the paroxysm, a wine that is subtle and white in color and moderately tempered and warm. **A.** however: When you see that digestion is desired and especially when the material is very cold, it is not bad to use a little pepper and a little wine.

# Whether Bathing is Suitable in Fevers

<margin>
40
On the six [principles of] health <note>The "six non-natural things" essential for health: air, food/drink, sleep/wake, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions.</note>
</margin>
...thin [wine]. For thin wine <note>original: *vinum subtile*</note> benefits through its thinning action because it strengthens innate heat, provokes [the humors], and causes one to sweat. Hence, in the third book on the *Preservation of Health*: Wine, above all else, digests crude humors, and provokes sweats and urine, which is why it is beneficial. It appears, therefore, for what reason wine is allowed or forbidden, and also what kind of wine it should be and how much. Regarding the fever itself, it must now be known that wine is never suitable when that illness exists as a hot and dry <term>complexion</term> <note>the balance of the four bodily humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, as was said. Indeed, wine is balanced against this in every way, judging by its hot and dry nature, and according to those who attest that it is hot and moist when it consists of sweet, oily matter like bile. This is especially true when they find a great deal of heat in the body. Also, when a cold drink is made for those cured of fever, as touched upon before, wine is generally judged to be hot. Therefore, wine should not be given to someone currently suffering from fever. /

<margin>
Viri. Cotta <note>Possibly a reference to a specific medical commentator or a shorthand for a source.</note>
</margin>
But if it is administered, it is either by reason of the cause [of the illness] or due to the weakness of the patient's strength <note>original: *virtutis*</note> caused by the "accidents" <note>symptoms or secondary complications</note> that occur, as will be seen later. I said "as itself," because by "accident," wine extinguishes fever; a more intense heat draws a weaker one to itself and consumes it. For this reason, in the first book of the *Problems*, it is commanded that the heat of nature in a <term>quartan fever</term> <note>a fever that recurs every four days, often associated with malaria</note> be increased by hot things, so that once the heat is increased, the fever has no heat of its own, as everything concurs with the heat of nature. Therefore, it appears that at the time of a greater inflammation, hot things taken internally extinguish this fever. (Differentia 163). If, however, it is asked in the accidents of the disease whether wine is suitable in fever: because some accidents cast down the strength by evacuating something from the body, for which a restorative is soon needed. Wine, indeed, is the best [restorative] since it is both food and drink, especially with bread. Alexander [of Tralles] in the first book, 7th aphorism, says: For dissolutions and cuttings-off of strength, feeding is most beneficial. There are also accidents that cast down strength because the heart suffers, especially with <term>lipothymia</term> <note>fainting or sudden loss of consciousness</note>, for which wine is most desired because it strengthens and repairs the <term>spirits</term> <note>the vital forces believed to circulate in the blood and nerves</note>, being very proportional to them. (Galen, 12th book of *The Method of Healing* and 4th book of the *Problems*). Hence, in the 7th book, it is gathered: In this case, nothing better is found than wine, so that it is even permitted for Saracens <note>Muslims</note>, who do not drink it by the command of their law, to drink it then. Just as it is permitted to eat the meat of animals that died naturally for those in necessity. But a doubt arises concerning this, as it was said now and in Differentia 70.

<margin>
Is?
Differentia on wine. 2nd book of the *Metaphysics*?
</margin>
Differentia [states] that wine strengthens the virtue <note>bodily power</note> above all else. To which the opposite is written in the third book: There is a difference between the power of wine and honey when given pure and unmixed. For he who drinks a double portion of pure wine strengthens the power more than the same amount of honey, provided it softens the belly. It should be said that pure, strong wine, given only once or twice, strengthens the power more than the same amount of honey alone. But when given in larger amounts, even a half-portion of honey compared to wine has more power to strengthen, because it inflames the spirits less and dries the innate moisture less, so that perhaps even with water it might extend life. Hence Galen says: since honey does not soften nature by its own property, it is possible to use it for many days. Regarding the fourth point: Firstly, it should be said that there is a fermentation <note>or "boiling"</note> in the matter of the fever that remains undigested, as with strong wine. Or in hotter matters and natures in which wine must be avoided. Hence, in the 5th book on the *Preservation of Health*: Hippocrates said this to me so absolutely, but concerning a nature that is extremely hot according to a distemper. To the other [point], it should be said that it is now known how wine is suitable by reason of the cause, and how it is not similarly suitable for the fevers and the symptoms.

As for what Isaac says—that in an inseparable fever there are difficulties in breathing, thirst, and headache—this is verified in burning and acute fevers. For such symptoms follow inseparably from the vehement heat and dryness of the fevers. Or, it is said that thin, watery wine given here would not induce the opposite, but rather, by making the water penetrate, would cool and moisten more. To the other point, it should be said that when the strength is strong, wine should not be given because it causes weakness of that strength. In the infirm, there is no need to increase strength when it appears strong. Hence, the true translation of the determination contains this: it is so rare that while we hasten to work with a stronger power than that which we have taken up, we do not nourish it so that it leads to the robustness of the body, but only to the sustenance of the living being.

To the other point, it should be said that the wine administered is very weak and watery, so that the inflammation and oiliness are lulled or removed entirely. To those things also mentioned by the other side, it can be clear that Hippocrates, with Galen, does not concede simple wine in fevers, and especially acute ones, but only after much consideration, as Hippocrates himself professes. What those considerations are has now been shown. To the other point, it should be said that wine performs the aforesaid works when the fever is already declining and the matter is matured. Wine also previously granted as a medicine has the power to cool and moisten.

To the other point, it is said that although wine benefits by reason of its humidity, it does not do so by reason of its heat. Or, its humidity is oily and inflammatory, unless the wine has been pre-prepared by reason of itself and the reception of similar things. To the other point, what should be said has already appeared. For Avicenna speaks of quartan fever, in which wine and hot water are more suitable than in other fevers, both because of the coldness and thickness of the matter, and because by "accident," a larger flame extinguishes a smaller one. And if it is said that many of the aforesaid solutions do not apply to the proposed "quality," that white, thin, watery wine is not truly wine in appearance or power. Since everything mentioned simply should be understood in its best state. (3rd book of *The Method of Healing*).

It should also be said that although wine in its best state is denied for almost every fever, this [prohibition] applies not only to the name of wine itself, but also to everything else that participates in its nature. Therefore, so that one may be saved from the reproach of the complexions, it is necessary to touch upon wine in every sense of it. (1st and 3rd books of *The Method of Healing* with the *Regimen of Health* and the 12th book on cures previously mentioned).

<meta>This page continues the medical discussion on treatments for fever, moving from the use of wine to the controversial use of baths. The text cites classical authorities like Galen and a physician named Philip, weighing the benefits and risks of bathing for different types of febrile patients.</meta>

<margin>
Philip [in] *Method of Healing* <note>original: *Physhop' mēd'*, likely referring to the physician Philip as cited by Galen in *Methodus Medendi*</note>
Book 10, Chapter 8 of *Method [of Healing]*
</margin>
...that it is not suitable because it increases the febrile <term>dyscrasia</term> <note>an abnormal imbalance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>. Neither should a cold bath strike the limbs with its coldness, as it causes obstruction by inducing rot (putrefaction), nor is a lukewarm one suitable, since it is softening and possesses a nature midway between hot and cold extremes. Furthermore, a bath is sought either for the sake of moistening or for the sake of evaporation or <term>resolution</term> <note>the process of dispersing or "melting" harmful humors so they can leave the body</note>. Not for the first reason, because water, whether drunk or applied externally, is not naturally suited to moisten the solid parts of an animal, as stated in the fourth [book of] the *Aphorisms*. Nor does it evaporate or resolve; rather, it attracts humors to the exterior and then obstructs and clogs [the pores]. Furthermore, in books 9 and 10 of the *Method of Healing* <note>original: *De Ingenio Sanitatis*, a common title for Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note>, a bath is said to be most harmful to those who have a "repletion" <note>an excess of bodily fluids</note> either in practice or in potential strength. But it seems all feverish patients have one of these—specifically in potential—since their strength is weakened by the fever. Also, in the *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, it is said that "windy" humors are not resolved by a bath since they are thick and viscous, and consequently, melancholic humors even less so. Choleric humors, however, are further inflamed by it. For according to Galen, they "boil" in the body because of the bath. Therefore, it is not suitable for such people.

Again, because it moves quiet humors and prepares them for putrefaction, making them fall upon weak limbs, a bath is thus not suitable in fevers, as seen in the first [book of] *On the Regimen in Acute Diseases*. Therefore, a bath is not suitable in fevers. On the contrary, physicians commonly prescribe bathing even in acute fevers; and in the *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, it is said that bathing is more helpful in <term>peripneumonia</term> <note>inflammation of the lungs or pneumonia</note> than in acute fevers. Since, therefore, it leaves a positive benefit in the former, it will similarly be helpful in the latter. Furthermore, that which opens the pores of the body and resists a bad <term>complexion</term> <note>the specific internal balance of hot/cold and moist/dry</note> is beneficial in fevers; and such is a well-tempered water bath. Therefore, a bath is helpful in fevers. Regarding the first point, one must know what a bath is and its various types (see section 118), and similarly what a fever is and its remains (see section 87). Regarding the second point, it should be known that certain physicians, like Philip (mentioned in books 9 and 10 of the *Method of Healing* and *On Wasting*), prohibit baths even in <term>hectic fevers</term> <note>chronic, wasting fevers often associated with consumption</note>. He was perhaps moved by some bad effect he encountered when a bath was administered improperly, or driven by the reasoning that heat increases febrile dyscrasia, while cold weakens and kills the parts of the body. Or perhaps because he bathed people incautiously—for instance, when rot or an <term>aposteme</term> <note>an internal swelling or abscess</note> was present—or he wanted to bathe them as if they were healthy, not observing the method handed down in the 10th book of the *Therapeutics*. These arguments do not hold up, since it has been found many times by illustrious physicians that a bath, when properly administered, confers no small benefit in fevers. Universal reasoning does not arise from a single, accidental experience unless the attribute belongs to the subject by its very nature, as appears in the third [book of] *Aphorisms*. Perhaps Philip encountered a deceptive experience because the attendants and other necessary things were not properly arranged (see *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, book 3). Furthermore, a bath is not only hot or cold, but a medium between them: namely, lukewarm. This opposes the bad febrile complexion by cooling the limbs and moistening them, thus preventing the consumption of the "radical moisture" <note>the vital fluid believed to sustain life and heat in the body</note>. Nor does the cold [part of the bath] hurt when the heat has preceded it, as will be shown from the sayings of Galen. 

Galen, however, in his book *To Glaucon*, proceeds somewhat indistinctly regarding the bath. For although that book is his, I rarely find him citing his own words from it in other places, except for the section on crises. Those things determined in that book do not seem to be of the same nature or method as his other exquisite works. Regarding the third point, it must be known that since there are three types of fever, bathing is generally praised in **ephemeral fevers** <note>short-lived fevers lasting about a day</note>, and especially in those which arise from manifest causes, and specifically when they have begun to decline. Hence, in the eighth [book] of *Method of Healing*: One ought to lead everyone to the baths during the decline after the <term>paroxysm</term> <note>the peak or "fit" of the fever</note>. Those, however, who have a fever from fury, sadness, lack of sleep, or anxiety do not need baths or many rubbings. Therefore, in the fourth [book of] the *First [Principles]*, a bath is conceded in ephemeral fevers when their paroxysm is consumed, for the sake of the "accidents" <note>symptoms</note>, among which are the need for moistening, soothing, and the opening of the pores. From these comes a cooling in the ingrained condition; but it is prohibited where a risk of rot is feared. One should not avoid the bath unless the person has an ephemeral fever from an "oppilation" <note>a blockage or obstruction of the internal passages</note>, because bathing then generates a putrid sickness; similarly for one who suffers from a nauseating fullness. Hence, in the eighth [book] of *Method of Healing*: Allow bathing if it is most certain that the fever is [only] ephemeral. Also for one who suffers an ephemeral fever from a <term>bubo</term> <note>a swollen lymph node</note>: in these cases, it is feared that the humors, stirred up by the bath, may fall into putrefaction. A sign that they should not bathe is the arrival of a rigor [shivering] caused by the bath itself. That a bath is suitable in ephemerals is clear: it opens the skin, thins the spirits, and strengthens them, making them fit to expel "sooty vapors" <note>waste products of the body's internal heat</note>; it also thickens the humoral matter when it is not yet ready to rot. In these cases, one should not fear that the water clogs the pores; rather, it opens them, both because of the heat (which opens) and because of the spirit that enters the pores and makes a way, pushing the extrinsic spirit outward. And it is better for all these patients to stay in the water of the bath rather than in the air of the bathhouse, unless the fever was caused by a hardness and thickness of the skin. For these people, it is suitable to stay longer in the air of the bath until they sweat, so that the pores may be opened. Those suffering from **hectic fever** and the "hectic of old age" should be bathed more freely, as almost everyone except Philip testifies. The method of bathing these is sufficiently noted in the 10th [book] of *Method of Healing* and *On Marasmus* [Wasting]. They ought to stay in the air of the bath in a similar way to those with ephemeral fevers. First, they should bathe in well-tempered [lukewarm] water, and finally in cold water, so that the pores are tightened and the moisture of the water remains contained within them. It is also sometimes expedient to splash cold water on them, especially when they are already wasted and incurable. In this way, they are led back from a hectic state to [the natural dryness of] old age, and life is granted to those who were otherwise about to die quickly. A bath certainly suits those with hectic fevers more than others, as it tempers their febrile heat and moistens them, especially preparing food to be distributed through the body...

<summary>This page discusses the medical debate over using baths to treat fevers, distinguishing between ephemeral, hectic, and putrid fevers. It concludes that while bathing can be dangerous if humors are "full" or "blocked," it is highly beneficial for moistening the body in hectic fevers and aiding recovery in ephemeral cases.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the medical debate regarding the use of baths in fever treatments. While the previous page touched upon the potential for baths to worsen a patient's condition by stirring up humors, this page focuses on the specific conditions, timing, and types of baths—moistening versus purging—that a physician must consider, citing authorities like Avicenna, Galen, and Averroes.</meta>

# Is the Bath Suitable in Fevers?

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
One should not fear the flow of matter here as in other places; universally, every cure is achieved through **contrariety**. Indeed, water—through its opposition—assists in this fever along with other aids; it is of no small benefit not only to the feverish but to all those suffering from wasting, as is apparent in [Galen’s] *The Method of Healing*, Book 7. Therefore, the ancients were not a little concerned with the regimen of the bath. If, however, it is said that the bath does not help here because it is among those things that "evacuate" <note>original: *evacuantibus*, meaning to drain or purge the body of fluids</note> and "resolve," <note>original: *resolventibus*, the process of thinning and dispersing harmful humors</note> one must respond that the bath is of multiple types. For here, a purging or dissolving bath is not sought, but rather one that is more **moistening and replenishing**, such as one of fresh water with a well-balanced and measured degree of heat and cold.

In those suffering from a putrid fever, if it occurs with an **abscess** <note>original: *apostemate*, a localized collection of infected fluid or swelling</note>, bathing is to be greatly feared in almost any manner. For the bath excites the matter and leads it toward a weakened area. This eventually becomes the cause of a greater fever and danger. Whence Avicenna says: In these cases, the drinking of cold water is not permitted, nor is the entering of a bath. If by chance it is suitable, it will be extraneous and very much "by accident," such as for the mitigation of pain; however, this should not be attempted unless the matter has been **digested** <note>original: *digesta*, meaning the illness has reached a stage where the body has processed or "cooked" the harmful humors for expulsion</note>. I also know [this from] Rhazes and Averroes; even then, it does not seem to benefit by this intention when the pain is already subsiding. For during the generation of pus, pains and fevers are greater than after the pus has formed.

Whence [Galen], in Book 10 of *The Method of Healing*, says: Inflammations increase because of the bath. For they pour out humors from the heat; the vessels of the membranes are stretched by the power [of the heat], and the faculty of the body suffers badly. And in the third [book] of *Acute Diseases*, he posits that the bath is beneficial in "burning" fevers where no hot abscess exists, nor any abscess made solely of yellow bile. For these boil within the body.

If, however, the putrid fever is simple, then it will either be in its **decline** <note>original: *declinatio*, the stage where the disease begins to fade</note> with the matter already digested, and thus it is commonly prescribed to bath with the intention of opening the narrowness of the pores and evacuating the matter through them. For the whole body evacuates through the skin. Likewise, the water moistens and tempers the body. In this stage, Galen in Book 11 [of the *Method of Healing*] curatively permits the feverish to be bathed and to use thinning <term>fomentations</term> <note>warm, medicinal applications to the body</note>, or to drink cold water or wine when you see the signs of those things which are digested. Finally, he adds: When the body has breathed out moderately, the bath produces universal utility, evacuating from it all "smoky" superfluities—provided the internal organs are not of a weak nature prone to shivering from the bath itself.

<margin>Three things to be observed in the bath for the feverish.</margin>
For one must have three intentions in all fevers regarding the bath. One is that it occurs **without shivering**; for shivering generates and increases fever. Second, that none of the principal parts remain weak; for the humors poured out by the bath are received by those weak parts. Third, that there is not a multitude of **crude humors** <note>unprocessed or "un-cooked" fluids that the body has not yet prepared for expulsion</note> within the veins. For the whole body is restored by it.

Also, in the first [part] of the fourth [book of the *Canon*], it is written that it is not bad to administer the bath and the drinking of subtle, mixed wine, and anointing with soothing oils. He says it is "perhaps not bad" because one must consider the custom of the bathers and their love for it. For bathing does not harm those who love it, even if you prescribe it twice a day. I know [this from] Rhazes and Averroes. Whence Avicenna, regarding the cure of **tertian fever** <note>a fever that spikes every third day, historically associated with yellow bile</note>: It is necessary that baths are not approached except after digestion and at the decline [of the fever]; it is then the best cure for them, and properly for those accustomed to it. From there, regarding the cure of a "windy" fever: when the sickness declines, entering a bath before food is then not bad.

<margin>Colliget, book 7, on the decline.</margin>
In the seventh [book of the] *Colliget*, know that he praises the bath during the decline of the fever. Because it evacuates superfluities. At the beginning, however, he praises it least, because it has the power to provoke rigors, dissolves humors, multiplies obstructions, and disperses superfluities throughout the whole body; it is not safe lest an abscess arises in some principal organ. For although the bath evacuates the heat of the fever, it multiplies the dryness. If, however, the matter is undigested, then the bath is sought either for the sake of moistening or for the sake of evaporating and dissolving. Regarding the latter, it already appears that the bath should not be done. For it brings many inconveniences.

<margin>The Breviary, book 6.</margin>
Whence in Book 6 of the *Breviary*: Let them beware lest they bathe before digestion. Since when we do so, we attract three bad things: Because the matter is poured out, which generates obstruction and rot; and because matter that is retained and putrefied in one limb is poured out when heated and mixes with other, non-putrefied moisture. Thus, a mixture of the benign with the malignant occurs, and consequently, a greater corruption and fever is returned. And because the bath resolves what is subtle, the thick matter remains stuck.

<margin>Part 4.</margin>
Whence in the first [part] of the fourth [book]: The bath makes undigested humor descend; therefore, it pours it into the place of putrefaction and mixes the bad humor with the rot, and it resolves the subtle [parts] and makes the thick [parts] remain. And these things happen more at the beginning of a disease.

<margin>Oribasius</margin>
Oribasius says: It is not good to be washed in baths from the beginning, but only when signs of digestion already appear. If, however, the intention of the bath is moistening and moderate heating, then sometimes it is seen [as acceptable]. In the first [part] of the fourth [book], even before the digestion of the matter, he permits the bath for the cure of **quartan fever** <note>a fever that spikes every four days, associated with "black bile"</note>. For among those things that provide help is sitting in warm, fresh water before every meal and bathing that moistens and does not cause sweating nor excite heat. But this seems to be opposed by the *Practica* regarding the cure of melancholy, thus: One must not use this bath in fevers at all, unless its peak has passed and its decline has begun. For the nature of the bath is to evacuate subtle humors. It must be said that the bath, as recently shown, is of two kinds. For one is **moistening and temperately heating**; such a bath is suitable even for undigested matter in a quartan fever, since the humor is cold, dry, and not ready to be stirred up and poured out by the bath many times. There is also the **exciting bath** which evacuates and resolves humors, which Haly Abbas wished to be unsuitable there. It should be noted that the bath must be avoided especially in **syncopal humorosa fever** <note>a fever accompanied by fainting spells, thought to be caused by an excess of humors</note>. In Book 12 of the *Method of Healing*, baths are most contrary to it; therefore, it is not fitting to bathe when there is weakness of strength, which prohibits the bath. Whence in Book 3 of *Acute Diseases*: the bath is not suitable for the exhausted. One should also know that the operation of the bath, as seen, is diversified by reason of habit and the climate of the air.

<margin>Greeks and Arabs.</margin>
For the Greeks and Arabs even unto this day seem to [value it] more...

<summary>This page analyzes the medicinal use of baths in treating fevers, distinguishing between moistening baths and purging baths. It warns that while baths can help during the recovery phase (decline), they are dangerous at the start of an illness or when the body contains "crude" humors that have not yet been "digested."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the medical debate regarding the use of baths in fever treatments, specifically addressing the physiological risks for "modern" patients and the varying requirements for different temperaments as established by Galen and Hippocrates.</meta>

...the Latins <note>original: *latinis*; referring here to Western Europeans</note> delight in these things and have made them a habit; because they enjoy them more, they are less harmful when they occur appropriately, but more harmful when they occur at the wrong time. This is also evident for a fourth reason. There is also another factor: the Latins, because they are exceedingly devoted to gluttony and luxury, prepare various delightful foods, which stirs up the **humors** <note>the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to control health</note> more toward flux and putrefaction.

For universally, human nature has now been rendered much more delicate; in ancient times, people were content with acorns <note>original: *glans*; likely a reference to the "Golden Age" where people lived simply</note> and eating chestnuts for their nourishment. As noted above in **Boethius's *The Consolation of Philosophy***, humors that are further stirred up by a bath turn into **abscesses** <note>original: *apostemata*; internal or external swellings filled with corrupt matter</note> and putrefactions. Therefore, I hesitate to use baths not only during the decline of a fever but even after they have ceased, given the state of bodies today. I have rarely found a praiseworthy result from bathing in those suffering from putrid conditions.

<margin>Warning</margin>
Regarding the fourth point: concerning the authority of Philip, it should be said that his intention was not to accuse the practice, but rather to show how authoritative it might be rendered. To the other point, it should be said that a bath is not only "hot" or "cold," but can also be "medium" and "temperate." To this end, even a hot bath is beneficial, as shown in its proper time, by opening the **pores** and evacuating the matter. Likewise, a cold bath is suitable at its own hour and disposition. Whence **Galen** says in the 11th book of *Therapeutics*: "If there is a young man, strong and fleshy, of a hot and dry constitution, and you plunge him into a cold swimming pool, he soon sweats, and in some of them, the belly erupts with bile." Thus, in this scheme, the cold does not strike or mortify the limbs, but rather gathers and strengthens them; the "medium" bath, though it tastes of the nature of the extremes, does not have their full operation since it participates in them only partially. 

To the other point, it should be said that a bath has the power to **moisten**, as does water universally when applied externally and internally; hence what was said above. One should not heed the words of those who say that water does not moisten the internal parts when it is drunk or when it meets the limbs. But because it seems that Galen apparently contradicts this in the *Aphorisms*, section four, it should be known for the sake of truth that "moistening" is twofold: one is "true moistening," which is...

<margin>Double moistening</margin>
...the conversion of something into its proper form within the nature of the body; in this way, things are properly said to "moisten" which are more truly **nutrients**, as Galen asserts. Since this type of moistening is like nourishing, simple water will not moisten in that way, for no simple substance provides nourishment. There is another kind of moistening, which is a certain "sprinkling" or "bedewing," and in this sense, simple water and every liquid are said to moisten. Similarly, the "resolution" <note>the thinning and dispersal of fluids</note> caused by a bath does not result in the drawing in or blocking of matter when the body has already been made porous and the matter has been **digested** <note>original: *digesta*; meaning the "cooking" or ripening of humors so they can be expelled</note>.

To the other point, it should be said that those having a "repletion" <note>an excess of fluids or blood</note> in their vessels should not be bathed unless that excess is first drawn out; otherwise, a danger of suffocation is imminent. Nor should those who are weak in virtue be bathed, even if the matter is already digested and the body thinned, because a certain effect of the "virtual repletion" remains. While the cause of the illness remains, one must not bathe; however, once the cause is expelled, or in the process of being expelled, one may bathe. 

To the other point, it should be said that a flatulent or **melancholic** humor is not resolved by a bath in the early stages of illness, but rather in the decline, when the humor has been "subtilized" <note>refined or thinned</note>. At that time, the bile is not inflamed, but rather, once digested, it is restrained from its sharpness by the soothing and well-temperate warmth of the water, and is led out through the manifest and open pores. To the other point, it should be said that the bath performs the aforementioned actions *before* the digestion of the matter, but not *after* it. Therefore, it should be prohibited then, but not now, as the opposing arguments show.

However, because **Hippocrates** simply prefers bathing in cases of **peripneumonia** <note>inflammation of the lungs</note> and pleurisy to mitigate pain, it should be known that this is not to be done absolutely, but only after the digestion and deduction of the matter. Whence the commentator says on that passage: Hippocrates says that bathing settles pain and ripens the matter that must be excreted through the sputum; yet it is clear that you must use the bath after the evacuation of the body. Know also that if a bath is administered to the body universally *before* evacuation, it draws the matter to the areas under the **hypochondria** <note>the upper abdomen, under the ribs</note>. If it is used *after*, it aids in ripening. For with hot baths, there is no safety regarding the flow of humors to the lungs, heart, and brain. Cold baths, however, prohibit the flow but increase the blockage.

### DISTINCTION 173.

<margin>1</margin>
That a young man or a **choleric** <note>someone with a hot and dry temperament</note> person suffering from a **burning fever** <note>original: *causon*; a high, acute fever</note> requires more extensive cooling than a child or a flatulent person is shown in the 7th book of the *Collectanea*: I say that it is clearly apparent that those who say the opposite are not speaking the truth. For they claim that an old man or a flatulent person in a cold time, region, and diet needs more vehement cooling than a young, choleric person. This is proven by reason: for he who requires cooling for more reasons needs more cooling than one who does not require it for as many. But a young, choleric man with a burning fever is such a person. He needs it both for the reduction of his natural complexion <note>the specific balance of humors in an individual</note> and his age, since a hot and dry complexion requires cold and moisture to temper its excess (as in Distinction 116). He also needs it because of the feverish imbalance. An old or flatulent person, however, needs it only for the feverish imbalance, and not for the preservation of their nature—especially the flatulent person who actually needs heat and dryness. The old man does not need cold for his preservation, even if he needs moisture. Therefore, the choleric person with a burning fever needs more cooling than the flatulent person. And if a burning fever happens to the elderly or the flatulent—though it is of a double nature according to the 4th book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, namely from bile and from "false" wind—the flatulent person will have a smaller "flame" than the choleric, being more proportional to their nature. But the choleric fever, because it is proportional to the choleric and the young, will come upon them more fiercely. Therefore, since the curative cause must be proportional to the illness, the "flatulent" burning fever has a lesser flame and requires a milder extinction. Furthermore, cold water is administered to a young man with a burning fever, but not to an old man (Distinction 171). For the nature of the old is to have little blood and weak innate heat, which are cold conditions that prohibit the drinking of cold things. Therefore, for the young man with a burning fever, a more abundant...

<meta>This page continues a scholastic medical debate, transitioning from the general use of baths to a specific case study: whether a young, "choleric" man suffering from "causon" (a burning, ardent fever) requires more intensive cooling than an elderly or "windy" (flatic) person. It pits the classical authority of Galen against the medieval Arabic philosopher Averroes.</meta>

## Whether a Young Man, as a Choleric suffering from Ardent Fever, requires [more cooling] than a Child or a Phlegmatic person

---

Cooling is appropriate for the elderly. On the opposite side, doctors are in agreement. This is ultimately attested in the seventh [book] of the *Therapeutics* <note>original: *tadē* or *tegni*; likely referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note> and is proven by reason. A similar thing is seen regarding this and regarding a bad **humoral temperament** <note>original: *complexio buōrali*; the balance of the four humors in the body</note> in the flesh, caused by a natural rupture of continuity, which requires a more powerful desiccation <note>drying out</note> than in the flesh, because it stands further from its natural temperament when it suffers from this bad temperament than the [healthy] flesh does. But a nerve requires greater drying than flesh.

Again, regarding the first part of the reasoning, that which requires more intensive extinction of the causes is that which is its opposite. Here, however, is the **phlegmatic** <note>original: *flaticus*; referring here to a "windy" or cold/moist temperament</note> or elderly person, at least in part. Because the natural temperament is preserved by things that are cold and moist. For hotter things require hotter remedies, and colder things require colder ones, as in the *Art of Medicine* <note>original: *tegni*; refers to Galen's *Ars Medica*</note>. One also requires [remedies] because of a febrile **dyscrasia** <note>an imbalance of humors, specifically in a fever</note>. A young man, however, only requires them because of this imbalance; he does not require them for natural preservation—rather, he requires the opposite, such as hot and dry things, as is shown by the previously mentioned discourse. Likewise, a disease produced by a more powerful cause requires a more powerful removal; such is the case when it occurs with a disproportion of the particular [humors].

This is found in the first [book] of the *Aphorisms* and the *Physics*. **Ardent fever** <note>original: *causon*; a high, "burning" fever often associated with yellow bile</note> occurring in the elderly is, as is known, with a disproportion of these [humors]. But when it happens to a young man, it is with a certain harmony of them. Therefore, an elderly person suffering from ardent fever requires more powerful cooling than a young man.

<margin>Regarding the third part of the first [section], it should be known what constitutes a "choleric" and a "phlegmatic."</margin>
The difference was noted in [chapter] 21; regarding the elderly and the young, in [chapter] 26; and regarding the one suffering from ardent fever in the following.

<margin>Regarding the third and fourth [points].</margin>
Furthermore, it should be known that **Galen**, along with many others, feels that an elderly person suffering from ardent fever requires significantly more cooling than a young person. Whence in the eighth [book] of *On the Method of Healing*: a part with a hotter nature is sick with a hot disease; it needs a small and brief cooling; a colder part, however, needs a colder [remedy], and similarly for moist and dry things. Since therefore the elderly and the phlegmatic are cold and yet suffer from a hot sickness like ardent fever, they will require a more powerful cooling than a young man and a choleric who are [already] hot and dry and suffering from this sickness.

They also show this by reason. For nature intends to return every temperament to that which is according to nature, insofar as it was overturned toward that which is against nature. For when an elderly or phlegmatic person is sick with a hot disease, a great overturning from that which is according to nature has occurred. Therefore, they are in greater danger. In the young and the choleric, however, the opposite happens, and therefore they are not in such danger. Those who claim to be more faithful interpreters of Galen bring forward the aforementioned reasons in their arguments, though it appears they explain him more with ingenuity than with truth.

**Averroes**, however, feels the contrary. He strives to show this against Galen with not a few reasons. For, as he says, there is a sensible argument: because a young man suffering from ardent fever cannot be cured except with things that are intensely cooling, such as **cucumber water** and **camphor**. If these were given to an elderly person with ardent fever, they would extinguish his **natural heat** and he would die.

Even if a choleric young man of a hot temperament in the first degree <note>the scholastic system of "degrees" measured the intensity of a quality from 1 to 4</note> should be found to have a fever that transfers him to the third degree of heat, he would now be distant from his own temperament by one degree. Though he cannot be cured with things cold in the second degree, this happens because of the strong transformation that medicines undergo in the body of a young man toward an **igneous substance** <note>a fire-like quality</note>.

But if a sickness should overcome a phlegmatic elderly person who is cold in the first degree, leading him to the second degree, he will now be more distant from his natural temperament than the young man was, removed by one degree. Indeed, his removal from his natural temperament is by two or more degrees; yet even if this is so, we cannot administer cold things to the elderly person through the opposite in an equal degree of opposition, because such things would be cold in the third degree, which would destroy him because of his **radical coldness** <note>the fundamental cold nature of old age</note> and consequent weakness. For these things would remove him so far from his balance that they would be the cause of death or a severe illness.

Likewise, the opposite follows for those who hold that the medicines of the elderly and the young should be in an equal degree of coldness; because if a hot body is heated up to the second degree, and a cold one similarly up to the second, one body will not be hotter than the other. His discourse stands on this: that although the elderly person is colder than the young person, enough heat is added to him so that he equals the heat of the young person. Furthermore, it should be known that if hot medicines were given to a young man beyond his natural temperament, they would not harm him but rather help him, since a strong power exists in their transformation. Therefore, they do not reach the degree where nature is destroyed. But rather, they lead it back to a balance, which does not happen for the elderly because of the coldness of their **radical members** <note>the primary organs like the heart and liver</note>, and therefore a medicine cold in the second degree suffices for him, even if he has a very hot fever, for the reasons mentioned above. Furthermore, the body of an elderly person does not have the power to convert medicines into an igneous substance like the body of a young man.

And these things have already been touched upon. This also touches upon a great "trap for doctors" <note>original: *medicorū decipulā*</note>. What led doctors into this error is a general rule which they posed without a prior distinction regarding the degree of distance of the elderly person from his natural heat to an extraneous heat, especially when they said the distance is greater. For this is impossible; for you know that extraneous heat is rarefied from the natural heat... since the elderly person has little natural heat, little extraneous heat is intensified in him. And he adds: if it were possible for the distance to be equal, then truly, according to the path of cure by opposites, the cooling agents for the elderly would necessarily have to be much stronger, even to the third degree. But this is not the truth in this case, regarding how much the extraneous heat of the elderly is raised. Therefore, he does not require such great cooling. Averroes holds these things in his "reproof of doctors." However, many would attack his views from the opposite side. For in the first induction, it will perhaps be said that the heat of the young man is ready to be extinguished by the coldness of medicines, since his body is more porous and thus quickly affected, and especially since it is said that hot things are easier to receive coldness than cold things are to receive heat. Regarding the other point, it should be said that perhaps his first [premise] is not...
