<meta>This page continues a scholastic medical debate regarding whether a young man or an elderly man requires more intensive cooling treatments when suffering from "causon" (a burning, ardent fever). It explores the tension between the patient's "disposition" (their natural state) and their "vital strength" (their ability to withstand treatment).</meta>

...the rest, at least by reason of the body’s disposition, contains the truth. Regarding the other point, it should be replied that in cooling the elderly, the opposition should not be made by comparison to an absolute equality of justice <note>In a medical context, "justice" refers to a perfect balance or "neutral" state of the humors</note>, but rather to their own natural balance; in that case, there will not be an equal degree of cooling for both, but rather the elderly person requires more as they have exceeded their balance further. The other point introduced coincides significantly with the first. And so these things are apparent. Regarding the other matter, it must be said that although doctors do not explicitly state the distinction between a "greater" and "lesser" **ardent fever** <term>causon: a severe, acute fever characterized by intense thirst and heat</term>, they nevertheless imply it. For an old man falls into ardent fever in no small part due to the disproportion of his natural heat, which happens to him through poor lifestyle management. However, this discourse of **Avicenna** <note>original: *Auē.*</note> encourages us to investigate the middle ground of truth. Regarding the third thing to be known, the rule of comparison is based on the difference [found in] book 27. Here it is necessary to use **indications** <term>indicatio: a symptom or circumstance that points to a specific remedy</term> taken from things natural, things non-natural, and things contrary to nature, as declared in section 133 and also 171, with the two following.

Furthermore, since the quality of the subject is almost twofold, we must first see whether the elderly man requires more cooling than the young man, and finally whether he requires it with the speed of a **choleric** <note>original: *coleritate*; referring to the yellow bile humor associated with heat and speed</note>.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that by reason of the underlying disposition of the similar parts and their surroundings, an old man with ardent fever requires more intensive cooling than a young man. This is the understanding that the apparent discourses of **Galen** <note>original: *Ga.*</note> imply. However, by reason of his **vital strength** <term>virtus: the innate power or energy of the body to function and heal</term>, he cannot tolerate this "extinction" <note>the total quenching of the feverish heat</note>. For his strength is weak and his nature is cold; he cannot endure it. Therefore, more intensely cold remedies should not be applied. For it is said that the indication taken from the patient's strength outweighs all other indications. This is what the superficial discourses of **Averroes** <note>original: *Auerroy*</note> signify, and the reasons shown here and there suggest that each side is true in part. Indications very often oppose one another, yet one must pay great attention to the vital strength, as happens in this proposal, sometimes even neglecting the disposition. At other times, one looks to the disposition while the strength remains sufficient, such as when one might tolerate **evacuation** <note>bloodletting or purging</note> at the start of a disease, but the disposition does not allow it because the cause of the illness is **undigested** <term>indigesta: humors that have not yet been "cooked" or processed by the body's heat for expulsion</term>. For in the beginnings of diseases, unless the matter is "furious" <note>violently active</note>, one must not evacuate. If it is drawn out, it is not for eradication, but rather for minor relief. Galen seems to have felt this in the seventh [book of] *Therapeutics*, stating: Whichever parts are naturally hotter suffer more from coldness, and they will need to be warmed for a longer time; in cold parts, however, it is the opposite. For it is necessary to return each of the **dyscrasias** <term>dyscrasia: an imbalance of the four humors</term> to that state which is according to nature. Conversely, for a part naturally hotter, the rest is as prescribed. Wherefore in the eighth [book]: If any suffer from fever, the common indication is for cooling and moistening. But what of the rest? Namely, the **temperament** <note>original: *complexio*</note>, the habit, the hour, and the constitution? He who has an indication for cooling and moistening must be cooled and moistened not just slightly, as it happens, but very strongly and greatly. 

But for one whose indication from all other factors is not for moistening and cooling, but rather their opposites—heat and dryness—the alteration is made in cooling by comparison. Whence in the third [book] of the *Practica*: It is necessary for the cure to be made according to the natural temperament of the body; thus, if the natural temperament of the body is cold, we need things in fevers that cool powerfully, because this body has been removed very far from its natural cold temperament. But if the temperament of the body is hot, it is necessary to use fewer moistening and cooling medicines. For the body has not been removed very far from its natural temperament. This also occurs in the cure of all diseases that happen poorly due to diversities of temperament. First, if the healthy temperament was cold and the diseased temperament is hot, then there is already a great distance from the [natural] temperament, and thus it requires much cooling. But if both were hot, a little cooling will suffice. That <margin>Averroes</margin> **Averroes** <note>original: *Auē.* or *Auer.*</note> agrees with these things is shown in what follows; for he says: If a cold disease comes upon a cold member, for instance the brain, it is a sign that it is a slight distance from its natural temperament, whence it will be cured by medicines having weak heat. But when a hot bad temperament comes upon it, then it is moved far from its natural temperament. Wherefore the doctor must treat it with much coldness, if other members are to be cooled and not the brain itself; and the same is said regarding the young and the old. Whence one must fear cooling the brain, both because it is naturally cold and because it is the principal organ performing noble operations with help. And one must not only fear cooling a cold member, but even a hot one having the aforementioned signs. And therefore he says that one must fear cooling in the end the **liver** <note>original: *epar*</note>, although it may be overheated; and since the same judgment applies to the part and the whole, it will be fearsome to cool the whole body of an old man, which is weak and cold, especially one advanced in years. Wherefore it is concluded that an old man suffering from ardent fever requires less cooling than a young man. But if someone, wishing to see this truth, should say that the old man simply requires more "extinction" because his body is cold and his pores are condensed so that cold cannot induce injury in him, it must be said that the harm an old man incurs is greater because of his weakness and his own coldness, which is quickly increased by its like. According to **Diocles** <note>original: *Dyodis*</note> and **Aristotle** <note>original: *Ay.*</note>, like increases like, and it stirs into a fury, just as fire in fire. On the other hand, in the disposition of the matter previously shown, the pores are still opened and the elderly body is disposed to the reception of heat on account of fevers. And therefore some, acting as mediators and wishing to avoid many inconveniences, said (not incorrectly) that an old man suffering from ardent fever throughout the whole time of the cure requires more intensive cooling than a young man, but in particular applications the opposite happens, since a weak agent can do the same over a longer time as a strong agent does in a shorter time. [As in] the fourth [book] of *Medicines*. For it is necessary to cool the old man...

# Whether a Disproportionate or Dissimilar Disease is More Restricted than a Proportional and Similar One.

...even when the **vital strength** <term>uirtus: the body's natural power to maintain health and resist disease</term> is weak and naturally cold, and often **because of** the heat of the **ardent fever** <term>causon: a high, burning fever often associated with bile</term> according to that dietary rule. And for those to whom it once occurred, he strives here by a similar reasoning to preserve every intention according to the parts to be suppressed, so that the **indication** <term>indicatio: a symptom or sign that points toward a specific medical treatment</term> taken at the same time might guard the strength and the disposition. **Because of** this, it must be known that a phlegmatic <note>original: *flāticus*</note> suffering from ardent fever, other things being equal, is more severely affected than a choleric, because not rarely is the phlegmatic's vital strength less and his pores denser. For they do not open themselves as they do in a choleric, as is evident; and by reason of his birth temperament, even if he has dilated pores, the physical composition follows the temperament, as it almost always happens that the body of a phlegmatic is held in that proportion from then on. Truly, the young person is affected by summer according to that saying, "the bellies in winter," etc. And therefore it is proven that the more violent attacks occur in winter and autumn than in summer and spring. For bodies then are compact and do not breathe through the skin. A choleric, indeed, has a heat that is subtle and easily dissolved, and pores so suited [to this] that **because of** the intensity of this suitability, he is rendered more violently susceptible to being affected by the cold.

<margin>Book 3, Chapter 7, Commentary 1</margin>
According to that [text], chapter 7: Know that dryness is more difficult to moisten than moisture is to dry, just as cold things are naturally more difficult to receive heat than hot things are to receive coldness.

<margin>Book 7, Chapter 8, On the Method of Healing</margin>
Which is perhaps hinted at regarding the "Method of Healing," where it says: These indeed are certain ends of time for both heat and cold. It is said, however, in what way and perhaps why cold operates more intensely upon the hot than vice versa: because the hot is more disposed to receive the operation of the cold than the reverse; for the actions of agents are in the disposed patient. Or someone might say that **Galen** <note>original: *Gal.*</note> looked more at the similarity and homogeneity of the incoming heat to the pre-existing natural heat, yet the first reason is to be considered more likely. The discourse of **Avicenna** <note>original: *Aueī.*</note>, however, as is his custom, differs from **Aristotle** <note>original: *A.*</note> in the first, fourth, and third [books], chapter 13, stating that the time for cooling and heating is the same, and the interval for heating the cold is the same as for cooling the hot. Nevertheless, after the aforesaid things, he adds how this diversity can be resolved. For he says that to heat a cold temperament is difficult when it is already fully infused, but very easy in the beginning. And finally, to heat the cold at the beginning of the matter is easier than to cool the hot at the beginning. But to cool the hot at the end, although it is difficult, is nevertheless easier than to heat the cold at the end, since excessive coldness is itself the death of the innate heat, or very close to it.

The phlegmatic, indeed, according to Galen, even in moist conditions, needs [cooling] both **because of** the preservation of his natural temperament through similar things, and also **because of** the **dyscrasia** <term>discrasia: an imbalance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile)</term>, and specifically because the fever is more intense when a discoherence of the parts occurs.

Therefore, a phlegmatic suffering from ardent fever requires more cooling than a choleric. But perhaps someone will speak against Galen: that the phlegmatic, **because of** his temperament, does not need cold and moist things, but rather hot and dry ones, since a fallen body, especially in its active states, needs a reduction through opposites and not preservation through likes (Difference 116); similarly, the choleric's natural temperament will need to be cooled and moistened.

It must be said that this is true of a "fallen" natural temperament, but not of an "illness-induced" temperament, since the task is to preserve the latter in whatever state it exists, as seen more widely, since such is the nature of the matter now under discussion. **Regarding** the fourth point, or to the first, something has been seen.

<margin>To the Arguments</margin>
To the other point, it must be said that this reasoning is conceded in the case of the old and the young, but in the case of the choleric and the phlegmatic, according to Galen, it is conceded by giving a more opposite reason than if it were concluded simply; for a hot and dry body in ardent fever requires [what is] dry so that its natural temperament, according to Galen, may be preserved. Or it must be said that one should not simply look at the multitude of causes, but at their vigor; just as with prognostic signs, one good sign overcomes many bad ones, and vice versa (Aphorisms II); so it is in causes. For those which reach the form and the end are more powerful than those which reach the nature and the agent. <margin>~</margin>

<margin>Cause folio 145, 2 Final</margin>
To the other point, what should be said appeared in the rule of comparison. To the remaining point, it is said that this reasoning has already been conceded in the old and the young, or a method of gradual administration was given by some. But as to the rest of the question, I say first that, just as was shown, I will not deny giving cold water to the phlegmatic when the heat is intense and is the cause itself, and when the accidental heat of nature sharpens the [innate] heat and acts upon the cold by heating it. He also has heat defended by the covers of denser pores than the choleric, nor is his blood meager, although he is called phlegmatic; indeed, perhaps he participates more in the choleric nature since phlegm is close to blood and bile, and here he is more moist than hot. For he is a "son of the air," nor is he weak as was said; the old man is equal [in this], and especially so. To the points introduced for the other side, and first to those of Galen and others, what should be said has now appeared. To the other point, it must be conceded in part, as in the phlegmatic and choleric; but in part denied, as in the old and the young. For there is no similarity, as has been shown. Since the dry and the moist are not troublesome to nature and strength because of their lack of actuality, as heat and cold are because of their opposition to nature (Difference 116), and especially the cold, which provokes the native heat. To the other point, it appears from its opposite comparison; for it is now known that it concludes in part according to one thing in the touched quality, but according to the other, not at all.

<margin>Indication from the strength, above.</margin>
The last point I concede in the case of the choleric and phlegmatic, but not the old and the young; for although the indication taken from the part of the disposition and other factors requires this, nevertheless a more venerable indication taken from the vital strength forbids it. What if it is said that the ardent fever of an old man will be phlegmatic, and that of a young man choleric? It must be answered in two ways: either **because of** the causes of a greater "sin" <note>In medieval medicine, a "sin" or *peccatum* refers to a harmful error in the "six non-natural things" like diet or sleep</note> in the lifestyle management of the old man, as touched upon; not only can a phlegmatic ardent fever happen to him, but even a choleric one, which is a worse accident, even though he is more disposed to the phlegmatic than the choleric. Or because it is necessary for each to suffer ardent fever—the phlegmatic or the choleric—so that the rule of comparison remains unharmed.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding medical prognosis, specifically whether a disease that aligns with a patient's temperament (proportional) is more dangerous than one that opposes it (disproportional). It builds on the previous discussion of "causon" (ardent fever) and the vital strength of phlegmatic versus choleric individuals.</meta>

...dissimilar; a disease is more dangerous when its opposite is seen. First, according to the *Prognostics* <note>original: "pronoſtic." — referring to Hippocrates' work on predicting the outcome of illnesses</note>. For example, suppose the cause of an infirmity is labor, fasting, or distress in the heat of summer and hot air; and the patient is a choleric youth with a vehement, bilious fever, whose pulse shows a failure of **vital strength** <term>uirtus: the body's natural power to maintain life and resist disease</term>. My assessment of the sickness would then be that his face denotes a swift death unless he is first nourished as he ought to be. Now, let us suppose another patient in whom none of these reported signs are found, neither on the first day nor the third, and his face looks as Hippocrates <note>original: "Y." — a common medieval abbreviation for Ypocras (Hippocrates)</note> described. If such a state arises from wakefulness or a flux <note>a "flux" usually refers to an abnormal discharge of fluids, like diarrhea</note> or a lack of food, he would be estimated to be less cunningly afflicted. Of these, the former seems to suffer with a particular proportionality <note>meaning the disease "matches" his natural hot/dry temperament</note>, while the latter is the opposite.

Also, the further one is removed from one's natural state, the more dangerous the sickness, since life consists of that balance as well as health. Suppose there are two people, both hot and dry, or the same person at a different time. Let the first suffer from a most intense **ardent fever** <term>causon: a high, burning fever often associated with yellow bile</term>, and the other from paralysis. Indeed, the ardent fever is more dangerous than paralysis because it is three degrees and two stages removed from the natural state, whereas paralysis appears to depart by only two degrees and a single stage. <note>Medieval medicine categorized temperaments and diseases by four degrees of intensity.</note> The middle ground holds the logic of the indivisible, as also appeared previously; however, the ardent fever remains similar to this sickness, while paralysis is dissimilar to it, or dissimilar to the same person at a different time.

<margin>Pleurisy of the side similarly / & Gout is worse.</margin>
Furthermore, according to the *Diaries* <note>original: "dia." — likely referring to Galen's De crisibus or similar diagnostic texts</note>, pleurisy of the left side and gout are worse and more dangerous than those on the right. But pleurisy of the left side is proportional to the patient when it arises more from bile, and because of the sharper heat of the heart on the left side; when it approaches a choleric person, it renders them worse. **Gout** <term>podagra: a painful form of arthritis, traditionally associated with the feet</term>, however, occurs because of the coldness of the feet being distant from the fountain of heat <note>the heart</note>, and is therefore more stable when it arises from a cold breath, which is more common on the left. Furthermore, in the fifth book of *Practice*, **spasms** <term>spaſmi: involuntary muscular contractions or convulsions</term> resulting from "evacuation" <note>bloodletting or purging</note> in a child around seven years of age are perhaps easily cured; yet infants are freed from a "dry spasm" quickly, even though it is not proportional to them. Additionally, fasting in a choleric person, to whom it is proportional, dries them out and thins them, and thus is more dangerous than in a phlegmatic person, to whom it appears disproportional. According to the eighth and tenth books of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." — Galen's *De Methodo Medendi*</note>, a disease is less dangerous when it resists its own cause and tends toward its own destruction; its opposite, however, is unlike the others and appears contrary.

Again, the danger of a disease is perceived either by the vital strength or the method of cure. But in a proportional disease, the curing strength is weakened because of the joining of "like with like"—much like fire in fire, it is incited into fury and destruction. In a dissimilar disease, the opposite happens. The mode of cure will be similarly hindered because of the direct lack of opposition <note>the medical theory of "contraries cure," where hot diseases need cold remedies</note>. Many partial examples regarding infants could be brought forward against individual sections of the Aphorisms; however, for the sake of brevity and because of the present consideration, I know many of them will seem repetitive if spoken, so let them be passed over for now.

<margin>Aphorism.</margin>
The opposite is written in the *Aphorisms*, Book One: "In diseases, the sick are less endangered when the disease is <margin>Properly</margin> **proper** to their nature, age, and the rest." Likewise, it is asked why more people die in winter according to the aforementioned Aphorism. This is because in winter it is necessary for the beginning of a disease to be vehement, as the heat is strengthened internally. When such a thing happens to be corruptive, it is different in summer. Hence, in the fourteenth section: "Why are ardent fevers greater in cold regions and seasons?" Again, a diverse "bad complexion" <note>an imbalance of the four bodily humors: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile</note> always causes worse harm than a similar and equal one, even if it is bad. First, however, it was said that in a proportional case, it is similar or equal. Therefore, a proportional disease is more dangerous than its opposite.

Regarding the first point, one must know what a disease is. According to the seventy-second vision, what is proportional, similar, dangerous, or opposite will soon appear from these propositions. Regarding the second point, it must be known that sometimes a disease is called proportional as being much less dangerous, while an imbalanced one is sometimes worse than the other. This is suggested by the instances added to the contrary and many others, so that the understanding of Hippocrates may be grasped: this happens "more or less," meaning it is very rare for the sick to be endangered in diseases that are proper to their nature. But because Galen seems to make this Aphorism more universal, and there is a visible rejection of these instances, one must speak more fully to the man and to the reason.

Regarding the third point, one must know—supposing the rule of compassion—where proportion and disproportion in a disease are caused. Next, the danger and its opposite. And third, in which diseases the question is verified. Regarding the first of these, one must know that disease is essentially an impediment to our "energies" <note>active bodily functions</note>. For it is a disposition of the body contrary to nature that primarily harms its action. It implies a dependency regarding operations, which have a relationship to **vital strength**. For strength is the beginning of operation, and no operation proceeds except from strength. Strength and disease exist locally, at least by reason of the subject. That which relocates and preserves us is the "container" <note>the physical body or the spirit that holds the life force</note>. For without it, it is impossible to either end a disease or have health. According to the ninth book of *On the Method of Healing*, it is in the "container" that the healthy and the sick state must necessarily remain. One must attend not only to these three things but also to those reduced to them. For the strength of the things constituting the body is more principal, because through it, life is made and established. In the ninth book of *On the Method of Healing*, it is compared in two ways: to those things immediate to it, or to those through a medium. The first is threefold: either as the subject in which it is founded—which is also twofold, either near, like a limb and spirit, or a medium, like a humor, or more remote, like an element...

# Whether a disproportional or dissimilar sickness is more dangerous than one that is proportional and similar.

...or as if toward an efficient cause, as when the **complexion** <term>complexio: the unique balance of the four humors in an individual</term> or the bodily state, such as the spirits, is of equal quality; for these lead the **vital strength** <term>uirtus: the body's innate power to maintain life</term> into action and also preserve it; or toward a final cause, such as an emotion or suffering. For the end of vital strength is that by which everything is ordered into action as if by its own gift. If indeed the vital strength is considered in relation to those things which are called "annexed" to it, which are placed alongside natural things by means of the complexion, they are existing in three ways: either they are closer, such as sex and age, or more remote, such as custom <note>meaning the patient's personal habits or lifestyle</note>, concerning which a joining or middle ground is seen, such as form and color. Next, since a sickness is a certain middle point between two circumstances, it will have a relationship to that through which it receives its being—namely, the cause—and to that which follows from it, such as an accident, or the body itself, or a sign. 

The environment surrounding us is considered in two ways: either in the arrangement of things comparable to it, understood as the five other **non-natural things** <note>The "Six Non-Naturals" were environmental factors medieval doctors believed governed health: air, food/drink, motion/rest, sleep/wake, evacuation/repletion, and emotions.</note>, namely motion and rest, food and drink, evacuation and repletion, sleep and wakefulness, and the passions of the soul; or considered more broadly in itself, which happens to the mind in various ways: either by reason of the season—and that of the four universal ones, such as spring, summer, autumn, and winter—or of the "constitution," such as the **Dog Days** <note>original: "canicula" — the hottest time of summer</note> or its opposite, or a partial hour like the day, or a part such as one of the twenty-four equinoctial hours, or on the part of the rising and setting, the conjunction and separation of the stars from one another, or the winds, or the disposition and site of lands. All these things are somehow disposed by the first four natures <note>the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>.

If, therefore, all things concur with one another according to heat and dryness, or in whatever other way, it is called "proportional" or "comparable" to the sickness. If, however, they are entirely opposite, they are judged as more or less proportional. This can be explained individually, but for the sake of brevity, let us pass over it. Because of this, it is to be known that

If it is robust, it dispenses all things for the best; if it is entirely weak, then for the worst. In that case, a similar or proportional sickness stands out as dangerous, since whatever similarity or diversity exists may harm it. First, it cannot endure the application of contraries to the body. If it is middling, it must be judged by itself. In the same way, by reason of the disease—either because of its species, such as

Indeed, some signs are so severe that one is not permitted to use a regimen for the disease or the cause, as noted in book twelve of *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "xii. de igẽi." — referring to Galen's *De Ingenio Sanitatis*</note>.

Often, however, the cure of a disease is carried out more mildly; for the disease is removed like a shadow from the body, for so it follows it. The cure is also diversified

either by reason of the materials or the aids, such as the six non-natural things with whatever medicines; or on the part of the method. For those things in which cold flourishes induce a worse harm; not so those where heat is present. Similarly regarding the dry and the moist; whatever they report, either on account of a more intense or remiss action. For heat and dryness imprint themselves more powerfully, while cold and moisture are least suffered, since they are more active and resistant to suffering. Therefore, the less simple the moisture is, the more it is elevated. 

The method of administration is observed in quantity, quality, and manner of use, as in the book *To Glaucon* <note>original: "ad glauconẽ" — Galen's *Ad Glauconem de Methodo Medendi*</note>, which are forms of regimen. From these things, it clearly appears that a sickness is rendered dangerous by the feebleness of the vital strength, whether it be dissimilar or disproportional. According to the **Commentator** <note>original: "Cõmẽtatoris" — likely Averroes, the "Great Commentator" on Aristotle and Galen</note>: it is not simply said that in the elderly, **hoarseness** <term>brancos</term> and **catarrh** <term>corifas: a cold or "running of the head"</term> do not mature, but they do so with great difficulty. For in the elderly, all things are dangerous because of the weakness of their vital strength. In the same way, **pneumonia** <term>piplemonia: an inflammation of the lungs</term> is common in the elderly; since it arises from cold humors, they die from it more than the young, whom the disease resembles <note>meaning the cold/moist nature of the disease matches the naturally "cooling" temperament of old age</note>. Hence, in the second book of the *Prognostics*, it says that among the elderly who suffer from pneumonia, more die; but in other types of suffering, the young perish more often.

In the case of an opposite vital strength, it happens differently, and when it is middling, the danger is middling. If, however, the sickness is viewed by reason of the preceding causes, then that one is always more dangerous whose causes are disproportional and opposite to it, since it happens from an internal and more abundant cause.

<margin>Note</margin>
For indeed, because a disproportionality of many causes—which are opposed to a sickness—cannot prevent that sickness from occurring, it is judged to be more cunning. For an immense fire burning in water, according to what I have read, is related to the infinite sin of Lucifer <note>The author uses the fall of Lucifer as a metaphorical illustration of an overwhelming force (fire) acting against its contrary (water/grace) without a mediating influence</note>: lacking an impeller, but not having an Adam. In a similar way, it happens conversely when many things concur in the generation of a sickness that are fitting in **virtue** <term>uirtus: the body's innate vital power</term> and also in the body's own suitability for them. If, however, with all this, the sickness tends toward a subject into which it has entered, then although it may not originally be more dangerous, it is rendered fully perilous; thus, a partial **empyema** <term>empyema: a collection of pus in the cavity between the lung and the membrane surrounding it</term> and things in disposed subjects exist as less dangerous than in those that are opposed, since the same cause remains in both. But that it is more dangerous in those "prepared" happens because of the narrowness and weakness of the chest, which is unable to purge the **digested matter** <note>In medieval medicine, "digestion" or "coction" referred to the process of a humor ripening or being prepared for expulsion from the body</note> as the teachings state.

Similarly, this happens in a **solution of continuity** <term>solutio continuitatis: a medical term for a wound, fracture, or any break in the body’s physical integrity</term> in a softened body, or a cancer drifting into a leprous state. For they are rendered dangerous by reason of the subjects upon which they come, and not because of an affinity of causes. For if they came upon their opposites, they would exist more safely. In the same way, a sickness arises full of danger because of the depraved character of the **accidents** <term>accidents: the symptoms or secondary effects of a disease</term> that supervene, and especially because of a report of pain not existing in relation to the cause of such a thing. Whence *Prognostics* IV [says]: younger men and those with golden skin <note>likely referring to a jaundiced or bilious appearance</note> suffering pain with an acute fever perish within one week, and older men even more quickly than this disease, though they are usually slower. So indeed, **pleurisy** <term>pleuresis: inflammation of the membranes surrounding the lungs</term> of the left side and in a young person is worse than the opposite. But if the friendship and contrariety of remedies are considered, then that which is cured by cold things will be more dangerous than that cured by hot things, since they are enemies to nature and more vastly different, like an immense burning fire compared to something cold and moist. As far as the vigor of the matter and its opposite are concerned, the sickness is more dangerous which is made from a more effective quality, such as hot and dry, or cold and moist contraries, like a **spasm** <term>spasmus: a convulsion or involuntary contraction of the muscles</term> from repletion. But that which comes from **inanition** <term>inanition: exhaustion or emptying, often due to lack of nourishment or loss of fluids</term> is worse, since its opposite (moisture) is ineffective for the cure. Nevertheless, if a spasm should happen from so great a cause, the dry one would be worse, mortifying the limb in every way. And if a sickness requires the form of remedies through diligent prayer <note>meaning extreme care or careful consideration</note>, whether a greater quantity or a more intense quality or other noted things, the 133rd **difference** <note>a reference to a specific section or "differentia" in a medical textbook, likely by Galen or Avicenna</note> says the opposite is more dangerous, especially when the indications occur to themselves as seen in books VIII and IX of *On the Method of Healing*.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
Regarding the aforesaid things, it happens to be doubted: whether the stated **aphorism** <term>assorismũ: a concise medical principle, specifically referring here to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates</term> is verified universally, so that it also applies in **species** or in **composition** <term>conpositio: the physical structure or arrangement of the body parts, as opposed to the complexion/humors</term>. The **Commentator** <note>The Commentator is the standard title for Averroes, the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician</note> feels the opposite, narrowing it to the **crisis** <term>crisis: the turning point of a disease</term> of the body. It must be said that he did not mean it is not verified at all in species, but so that he might awaken the mind of the reader, indicating that a sickness would not be dangerous solely by reason of antecedent causes, but by those things which follow the subject inseparably or separably, such as incisions, since even the composition follows the **complexion** which is discussed in the 63rd difference. Regarding the third point of this, it is known that the question is verified in a **complexional disease** <note>a disease caused by an imbalance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile)</note> in whatever way, as seen since proportionality and dissimilarity appear chiefly in it, and universally in every disease, such as a **compositional** one, just as touch is dependent on the composite. For the form or composition depends on the complexion, and finally, unity depends on those same common things (63rd difference), all of which are joined in an **aposteme** <term>apostēate: a swelling or abscess</term> (95th difference), and in the cause and its accident in its own way. Therefore, the aphoristic canon admits no exception, safely as now explained. Since **Hippocrates** (Y.) in this, along with **Avicenna** (Ay.), transferred themselves to the preceding causes so that a demonstration might be formed from them: that disease is more dangerous because it arises from a more vehement cause, since it derives its whole being from it; but this, as declared, stands as a disproportional and not a similar suffering. On the other hand, a disease is more severe when it could not be resisted even by causes opposite to its generation, compared to one which the causes contested; but such a thing is disproportional and not, as appeared, opposite. And so, a similar disease is said to be more dangerous and proportional. These things could be declared further by descending into them one by one, but for the sake of brevity and because this is written for those who understand, they are omitted.

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it must be said that the proportional does not compare to the dissimilar as some have thought; nor to the similar only, but it can happen from a hidden internal cause and a manifest external one; for always, as it were, the former is more terrifying. To the other, it must be said that not all things are equal, as experience shows. For from a more vehement and more active cause, this **burning fever** <term>causon: a Greek medical term for a highly acute, inflammatory fever</term> happens rather than a paralysis, since the quality is raised further toward the extreme and works more vehemently (as shown in the 138th difference). For if both departed equally from the natural state, it would be equal, and the qualities of the disease would be similar in action with the quantities. For this disease is worse than that by its very species. Whence **John Damascene** <note>Johannes Damascenus, an 8th-century theologian and physician often cited in medieval Latin medicine</note> says in his *Aphorisms*: "Hot diseases are more deadly than cold ones because of the speed of the fiery motion."
<margin>Distinction</margin>
To the other, it must be said that it does not happen because of the proportionality of the preceding causes, but because of the more severe accidents, as in left-sided pleurisy, or a weaker virtue, as in **gout** <term>podagra: specifically gout of the foot</term>, even on the left side with great narrowness of motion. To the other, it must be said that a spasm exists as an **official disease** <term>official disease: a disease of the "offices" or organs/limbs themselves, rather than just the humors</term>. I know that this is verified in the complexion, but not in the composition; it is also said in the fifth book of the *Practica*. **Avicenna** adds similarly: [It happens] immediately because of the moisture of their complexions and the moisture of their food.

Someone also explained that infants are freed from a spasm quickly because they incur it very little. To the other point, it also appears that if natural consumption happens in both places, more will be consumed of that which is **phlegmatic** than **choleric**, since it is greater and smaller because of the contraction of what is capable of drying out, and a relation should not be made of watery moisture as if it were phlegm.

-> # Whether Phlebotomy Should Be Repeated in Burning Fever <-

Regarding the moisture of the **choler-type** <term>colerici: relating to yellow bile, one of the four bodily humors, associated with heat and dryness</term> which was previously stated as an opposite, once the established rule has been presupposed, it is found to be compatible. To the other point, it must be said that the opposite rather concludes the matter when it is justly deduced, as has been shown. For if the aforementioned resistance were to prevent the coming sickness, then it would be beneficial. However, a small cause is judged to be weak, while the remaining hidden or more vehement cause is judged such that it generally teaches the contrary along with the disease; this disproportion always renders the disease more dangerous. When it supervenes, it makes a simple case more harmful, as it is directed toward the cure as if it were a similar incident, making it more perilous than the prior or subsequent stages of the illness, increasing both the duration of the treatment and the danger. This environment shows where the great Commentator <note>Typically referring to Averroes, the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician</note> bit into **Diomedes** <note>likely referring to a medical authority whose views were being challenged</note>. To the other point, it must be said that it is more allowed through interception. For although "like is joined to like," it does not incite fury because of the vehement ability of the subject and the minor causes by which the disease can happen. For such a thing is disposed as a measured body, as is found in the **Fifth Book of Problems, Problem 3** <note>A reference to the pseudo-Aristotelian "Problems," a collection of questions on various scientific and medical topics</note>. To the other part of the induction, it is seen what was said.

### DIFFERENCE 175

It is demonstrated that **phlebotomy** <term>phlebotomia: the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood, a standard treatment in medieval medicine</term> is appropriate in **burning fever** <term>causone: (from Greek *kausos*) an acute, inflammatory fever often associated with yellow bile</term>. **Cassius Felix** <note>A 5th-century Latin medical writer</note> says: "In the beginning of burning fevers, if the strength of the sick person permits, perform bloodletting in the arm, especially if the patient is a young person." In the eleventh book of **On the Method of Healing** <note>original: "de ing." for *De Ingenio Sanitatis*, a work by Galen</note>, it is said: "It is best to cut a vein not only in **synochous fevers** <term>synochis: a continuous, non-intermitting fever</term> but also in others that involve the putrefaction of humors, provided that age or strength do not prohibit it." And **Oribasius** <note>A 4th-century Greek medical compiler</note> says: "Those who suffer from fever due to the putrefaction of humors should soon be bled if their vital force is strong." But burning fever is a fever of this kind.

Furthermore, in the **Fourth Book of First Principles** <note>likely referring to Avicenna's *Canon* or a similar compendium</note>: "The cure for burning fever is the same as the cure for pure **tertian fever** <term>tercian: a fever that spikes every third day, traditionally attributed to yellow bile</term>, both when they require evacuation and otherwise; but evacuation ought to be performed when the offending humors are excessive in quantity." This is done through phlebotomy. For phlebotomy is a universal evacuation that draws out a multitude of humors. Again, art is the imitator and follower of nature; but nature terminates a burning fever through a flow of blood from the nostrils. Whence **Hippocrates** <note>noted as "Y." for *Ypocras*</note> in the fourth book says: "If blood flows from the nostrils, the passion is resolved." Finally, for such a burning fever, it is not resolved unless blood flows from the nose. Wherefore in the Fourth Book of First Principles: "It is mostly consumed by vomiting, or by loosening of the belly, or by sweat, or by a flow of blood from the nostrils." **Palin Assor** <note>likely a reference to Rhazes or another Arabic authority</note> in the first book says: "In the strongest of fevers, phlebotomy is commanded; such indeed is the burning fever, for as its name says, it is the most intense fever." For it is named from "heat" (*caumate*), and in it, the nature of the fever is seen to be preserved to the maximum degree.

<margin>Firstly</margin>
And since burning fever implies a fire, the cure requires cooling. For a cure is perfected by its contrary; however, phlebotomy does not induce this. In the ninth book of the **Therapeutics** <note>Galen’s *Methodus Medendi*</note>, it is confirmed that only through phlebotomy is not only the quantity of the blood addressed when it is at fault, but also its quality. Therefore, phlebotomy is appropriate in burning fever. **To the contrary:** because common doctors do not prescribe bloodletting in burning fevers. Likewise, for distressing humors, **purgation** <term>purgatio: specifically clearing the bowels or using emetics</term> is owed, not evacuation; however, this fever is caused by choler and "false phlegm," from which this suffering is said to arise. For a strong disease, a strong medicine should be used according to Galen, so that a direct contrariety may occur; but phlebotomy is not a strong medicine (Difference 166), since in it, nothing more intense is intended than vomiting or loosening. Therefore, phlebotomy is not appropriate in burning fever.

Regarding the first point, however, it must be known that burning fever is an incendiary fever caused by choler or false phlegm, the material of which is located in the veins near the heart. That it is incendiary or "burning," the name itself indicates. It also afflicts the patient continuously without any sensible intermission of its tenor until the **crisis** <term>crisim: the turning point of a disease, after which the patient either recovers or dies</term>, so that in it, neither addition nor diminution is found. But if **Almansor** <note>Rhazes, author of the *Liber ad Almansorem*</note> writes that the burning fever becomes stronger on one day and less strong on another, it must be said that he is referring to a tertian fever preceding the burning fever, or a continuous fever, because of which this happens. That it arises from choler or false phlegm, Hippocrates asserts in the fourth book. Know also that the discourse of **Averroes** <note>noted as *Auer.*</note> is quite spread out on this matter.

<margin>In Burning Fever</margin>
<margin>3rd of the Colliget</margin>
Thirdly, in the third book of the **Colliget** <note>Averroes' major medical work, the *Kitab al-Kullyat*</note>, he says that illnesses coming from **eruginous choler** <term>eruginosa: "rusty" or "verdigris" colored bile, considered highly toxic</term> and **prassine choler** <term>prassīā: "leek-green" bile</term> are incurable since they do not undergo **digestion** <note>original: *digestio*; in medieval medicine, this is "coction," the process where the body's heat ripens a humor for expulsion</note>, nor are they changed by natural heat; instead, they corrupt the specific form of the heat like a poison. Fourthly, he says the worst species of burning fever is that which comes from "vitelline" (egg-yolk like) or prassine choler, and the most proximate cause of that is long-lasting, because then he says burning fever lacks a **paroxysm** <term>paroxismo: the periodic return or intensification of symptoms</term>. And he adds: "Because of the disobedience of that humor to receiving digestion." He also says in the second book that it is not possible for choler to undergo any digestion because it is not possible for a thing that has passed the limit of "cooking" (*decoctionis*) to return to it. Just as it is not possible for a roast to return to being boiled, because what is already cooked cannot be made raw again.

<margin>4th of the Colliget</margin>
And this discourse, as it appears, is also brought forth by **Haly Abbas** <note>A 10th-century Persian physician</note> in the chapter on humors; it is verified concerning natural choler. In the fourth book of the *Colliget*, he says: "A fever cannot occur in the body from choler alone, because such a fever is necessarily deadly, since choler is not fit to receive any digestion." And from this, it seems that it cannot receive digestion even by the probability of the material's expulsion by the vital power. In the third book, however, he says: "As if it had become a contrary." There are fevers that are appropriately assigned to pure choler and others to impure choler. Also, in the seventh book, it is found that a fever rarely arises from pure choler. Know indeed that although he speaks this way, it will be stated indistinctly in Difference 30: that "pure" is said in two ways. Either because it has no mixture of another, like a wine that is pure in every way; or that which has a little, or that which has a bit of water mixed in. In the first way, according to Hippocrates, no humor is found to be pure (Prognostics II). For when choler is pure, it signifies the victory of vehement heat, and pure phlegm signifies coldness. For both of these humors, when they are...

<margin>}</margin>
Even in the <note>original: "collz.iiii." referring to the fourth book of the *Colliget*, a medical encyclopedia by Averroes</note> **Averroes** argues that a **burning fever** <term>causon: a severe, acute fever characterized by intense heat and thirst</term> is caused by non-putrescible matter, and not only in the digestive regions but also in the third stage of digestion, which is quite discordant with the views of others. Or perhaps he understands it, I know not how, through a mixture of putrid matter with <term>hectic fever: a persistent fever often associated with wasting diseases like tuberculosis</term>. <margin>}</margin> Furthermore, the matter of **burning fever** is contained in the veins of the mouth of the stomach, or specifically in parts of the liver, and at its peak in the noble organs near the heart, as stated in the fourth [book]. On this point, **Hippocrates** and **Galen** seem to disagree in the sixth [book of the *Aphorisms*]. For **Hippocrates** says: *In whomsoever tremors occur in a burning fever, the delirium is released.* <note>original: "Quibuſcūqz in cauſone tremores fiunt alienatio ſoluit"</note> However, **Galen** does not think this aphorism is truly his [Hippocrates'], because even if the matter of the burning fever shifts from the veins and arteries into the nerves and the fever is released, it is not the habit of **Hippocrates** to say a disease is "solved" when a more vehement one takes its place. For when the **burning fever** is resolved, a **mental confusion** <term>mentis pmixtio: delirium or cognitive impairment</term> supervenes which is no less dangerous, since it leads to <term>phrenitis: an acute inflammation of the brain or its membranes, often called "frenzy"</term>. However, **Hippocrates** is agreed with elsewhere, in the third [book], where he says that if a tremor occurs in a **burning fever**, then the mental confusion resolves the fever from the patient. **Galen** does not concede this aphorism is true, yet it is not among those things that lack reason. In the fourth [book], he explains it with approval thus: It is likely that since the brain is greatly heated and the nerves are heated, and it is a **burning fever** with mental confusion, it is resolved through tremor because of the expulsion of matter toward the nerves. From these words, the truth—as **Avicenna** suggests—can be investigated. For mental confusion can arise from **phrenitis**, as **Galen** wants, and thus the aphorism is proven false. Or it arises from fumes and horrid vapors carried into the brain by the movement of matter seeking higher parts, as happens when a <term>crisis: a turning point in a disease</term> is achieved by vomiting or a nosebleed, and thus the aphorism can be verified. Regarding what **phlebotomy** <term>phlebotomy: the practice of opening a vein to let blood</term> is and how it is applicable, see distinction 114. Regarding the second point, it should be known that there remains an ambiguity in the words of the physicians concerning this question. For many simply prescribe purging the bowels, sweating, and vomiting. Among them, **Democritus** and **Oribasius** say: *Do not bleed them; for perhaps it will inflame them, though perhaps it will help them if there is turbidity and redness,* <note>original: "Non fleubotomet fortaſſis nāqz inflamabit eos..."</note> that is, urine that is thick in substance and red in color, or if the face and body appear so. Whence the **Averroes** concludes in the seventh [book]: In this fever, purging with attractive medicine is appropriate at its beginning, as is reducing the blood if its signs are apparent. But some have said that **phlebotomy** is not appropriate in itself, but is suitable *per accidens* <note>by accident; due to specific circumstances rather than the nature of the disease</note> when the matter is "furious" [raging]. It is clear that this is not a healthy evacuation, because since a **burning fever** arises from choleric matter, it must be led out by medicine <note>purgatives</note>, not **phlebotomy**. 

Regarding the third point, it should be known that regularly and most frequently in any **burning fever**, **phlebotomy** is not appropriate. Yet it is occasionally suitable *per accidens*, as when the matter is raging and mixed with the blood. Almost all authors have remained silent on this, which shows that **phlebotomy** is an evacuation that removes a <term>plethora: an excess of blood or total bodily humors</term>, which does not exist in **burning fever** since one humor prevails in it, such as choler or "salted" phlegm, rather than all humors together. In this case, there is no plethora of humors, but rather a <term>cacochymia: a bad quality or "corruption" of the humors</term> of quality, which requires pharmacy [purging], just as plethora requires **phlebotomy**. Again, it is not appropriate in **burning fever** because it incites the fever further into a fury; for blood is the obstacle and the "rein" of choler, and removing it would be the opposite of what is needed. For "boiling" choler, rendered raging and moved to a nobler place, either causes an <term>aposteme: an abscess or swelling</term> or extinguishes the <term>innate heat: the vital heat believed to be centered in the heart and necessary for life</term>, just as a larger flame destroys a smaller one. Whence some have already been lost to sudden death. And therefore, in the fourth [book], take the greatest care lest you lead to one of these two things: the boiling of the choleric humors or the <margin>☌</margin> chilling of crude matter. Thus, regularly, **phlebotomy** is not suitable in **burning fever**. Perhaps, however, it is very rarely suitable when the **burning fever** has been made with an abundance of blood, or perhaps when its origin was from the corruption of blood. For when blood is corrupted, according to **Galen** in distinction 89, its subtle part is converted into choler and its thicker part into melancholy. In this transition, at the beginning when the blood is not yet fully transformed, **phlebotomy** can be appropriate, even though it is subsequently owed to humors that are faulty in quality. <margin>}</margin> Therefore, **phlebotomy** is sometimes suitable in **burning fever**. This is suggested by **Averroes**. Regarding the fourth point, it must be said that it is true assuming some abundance of blood. This is confirmed because in putrefaction, and not just of humors, **Galen** says with **Oribasius** that the blood itself is also at fault. Or it must be said that here the Greek [physician] was bolder in "inflaming" and more universal than the Arab, as in distinction 167. To the other point, it must be said that "evacuation" is understood not only for quantity but also for quality, as in distinction 163. To the other point, it must be said that it is rarer for **burning fever** to remain in the state of a nosebleed. Therefore, by **Avicenna**, this is placed as a final judgment. Or it must be said that although nature at the end leads out through a nosebleed because the blood is in a state filled with choleric humors—due to their movement to the upper parts—it is not so in the beginning. Whence **Galen** says: *In acute fevers, boiling blood is carried to the head.* Therefore, when nature pours this out while it resides in the veins, a part of it—along with gathered vapors—dominates the rest. To the other point...

It highlights a historical tension between Greek and Arabic medical authorities regarding whether these fevers are caused by an excess of humor (quantity) or a corruption of humor (quality).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic discussion on medical treatments, shifting from the specific case of burning fever to the general application of bloodletting and "repercussion" (driving back humors) in cases of inflammatory swellings.</meta>

-> **Whether repercussion is appropriate for an aposteme.** <-

It should be said that these <term>phlegmons: inflammatory swellings caused by an excess of blood</term> are very strong as they are from the blood. For "strongest," even if it first denotes quality, can also denote quantity according to the <term>Aphorisms: a famous collection of medical principles by Hippocrates</term>; strictly speaking, a phlegmon is said to be large or small, though it could also be called intense or mild. Regarding the other point, it should be said that **bloodletting** cools the body when the "sinning" blood is evacuated. However, when <term>choler: yellow bile, one of the four humors</term> is at fault and is evacuated, it tends to inflame rather than cool, as it has been shown that its "bridle" is removed. Regarding the "constriction," it should be said that it is used improperly, or that it is suitable when all humors are putrefying. Furthermore, for the opposite part, it appears with its own most certain and regular causes, where a <term>cholagogue: a medicine that promotes the discharge of bile</term> or <term>phlegmagogue: a medicine that promotes the discharge of phlegm</term> is appropriate, depending on whether the patient is choleric or phlegmatic. In certain cases, it is sought because of the corruption of the humors and inflammation. 

Hence **Democritus** and **Oribasius** <note>Oribasius (c. 320–400 AD) was a Greek medical writer and personal physician to Emperor Julian</note> state that not only those full of blood require bloodletting, but also those in whom <term>rheumatic: related to the flow of humors</term> passions and certain inflammations arise in the body without full plethory, whether by a blow, or by wind, or if the blood is constricted either externally or internally by a choleric cause or if the pain is quite vehement. For anyone is bled either because of the multitude of blood, or its bad quality, or both, as noted in the first of the *Fourth [Books]*. Regarding the other point, that it can be hindered because bloodletting is not a "strong" medicine by reason of the danger emerging in the act itself (as a drug treatment might be, since that power can be resisted), it is nevertheless "strong" and even "stronger" by reason of what is drawn out by it—namely blood, which is proper to our nature and familiar, unlike the other humors. 

## DIFFERENCE 176

It is shown that **repercussion** <term>repercussion: the medical practice of using cooling or astringent topical agents to drive a swelling back into the body</term> is not appropriate for an **aposteme** <term>aposteme: an inflammatory swelling or abscess</term>. Since an aposteme is formed either by way of congestion from the residue of surplus nourishment in a part, or by way of rheum where one strong member expels its superfluity <margin> d. 95 </margin> to a weaker one. <gloss> } </gloss> But to neither of these is repercussion suitable: not to the first, since it is the expulsion of a part's superfluity which nature itself cannot expel, and it ought rather to be drawn outward than repelled inward by an <term>apocrustic: a repellent medicine</term> agent. Nor is it suitable in the second case, since that is the expulsion from principal members to other parts—and internal parts are more noble and principal than external ones, just as superiors in a government are to inferiors. 

Furthermore, the forms of fevers and apostemes are similar. In fevers, repercussion is not used, but rather evaporation and drawing the matter to the exterior. Moreover, whatever narrows the pores of a limb and condenses the matter by entangling and thickening it is not appropriate in apostemes; such is the act of repercussion, since it proceeds from cold and dry astringents. Again, in the sixth [book] of the *Aphorisms*: *It is not good for an <term>erysipelas: a bacterial skin infection, here used generally for red inflammation</term> formed on the outside to be turned inward; but from the inside to the outside is good.* <note>original: "Eriŝipilam extrinŝecus factam intus conuerti non bonum. Intrinŝecus Xo extra bonum."</note> The commentator applies this universally to any aposteme. Repercussive medicines turn an erysipelas or aposteme from the exterior to the interior. 

Furthermore, whatever violates the action of nature is not appropriate, since it is a medical precept to imitate nature. Yet repercussion does exactly that, as its very definition denotes. Therefore, repercussion is not appropriate for an aposteme when administered at its beginning. 

On the contrary, the opposite is felt by almost everyone, who command that at the beginning, simple <margin> Apocrustics </margin> <gloss> } </gloss> **apocrustics** <note>repellents</note> are to be applied. Whence, in the thirteenth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "xiii. de īge." referring to Galen's *De Ingenio Sanitatis* or *Methodus Medendi*</note>: it is common to all phlegmons that if one uses only repercussive aids at the very beginning, he will not sin. In the *increase* of the swelling, however, **resolutives** <note>medicines that dissolve or disperse the matter</note> must be mixed with the repercussives. Then, in the *state* (peak), both should be equaled. In the *declination* (fading), one should use only softening repercussives. This is proven because that which prevents the enlargement of the aposteme and prevents its malice from spreading into the part is what belongs to its cure. Repercussion does this. For this reason, apostemes are to be repelled at the start. 

Regarding the first point, one must know what an aposteme is, its causes, and the mode of its generation, as shown <margin> d. 95. <br/> Aposteme - <br/> Repulsion. </margin> in Difference 95. <gloss> } </gloss> **Repercussion** is the act of a medicine whose property, on account of its coldness, is to cause cold to reach into the limb, so that it is thickened, its pores are constricted, its attractive heat is broken, and that which runs to it is congealed and thickened so it does not flow into the limb—which prevents the limb from receiving it. 

To the last point: repercussion is to drive back matter by coldness and astringency from the surface of the place <gloss> a </gloss> from which it recedes. One must also know that some have felt that repercussion is owed to hot apostemes but not to cold ones, imagining that hot matter can be repelled and cold induced, but not cold matter since it is "dull." The error of this will appear in the third part of what is to be said; for even cold apostemes, such as windy ones, require repercussion, though not as much or with the same agents as hot ones. In the thirteenth [book] of *Method of Healing*, Galen commands that a new sponge soaked in water and a little vinegar be applied, along with medicines made of "memite" <note>likely *mimycite* or a mineral astringent</note>, which are cold repellents. And in the second [book] *To Glaucon*: *Immediately you shall place a new <margin> repelled. </margin> <gloss> } </gloss> <gloss> } </gloss> soaked sponge upon it and you will heal it with <term>oxycrate: a mixture of water and vinegar</term>.* Or according to some, a wash of grape-dregs called *marellum*. And if the person suffering has a strong body or flesh and hard skin, the application ought to be sharper. Whence in the first of the *Fourth [Books]*: It is necessary that cold, astringent, constricting, and repercussive medicines be of a pure cold complexion if the apostemes are acute. If they are cold, they must be mixed with something that has a warm power, like <term>squinanthum: camel grass or lemongrass used medicinally</term> or *blatta byzantia* <note>an operculum of a shell used in ancient pharmacy</note>. And finally, in the fourth of the *Third [Books]*, Galen adds cleansers. Regarding the third point, certain things must first be set forth from which the truth may be hunted, and finally the truth concluded. First, know that some apostemes are from a primitive cause, like a fall or a blow, while others are from an antecedent cause, like...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic medical debate regarding the treatment of "apostemes" (inflammatory swellings or abscesses). It focuses on the classification of these swellings by their cause—whether from the four humors, "windiness," or "wateriness"—and discusses the contraindications for "repercussion" (driving the humors back into the body).</meta>

**Fullness** <note>original: "repletio"</note> results from the four humors, along with an excess of water and windiness, which eventually develops into a <term>conjoined cause: the immediate physiological cause of a disease</term>.

### Classification of Swellings
At the beginning, there are sometimes five types named for their duration, while others are named for their internal location, such as **frenzy** <note>inflammation of the brain</note>, **pleurisy**, or an **abscess of the liver, kidneys**, and similar organs; others are external. Some are inherently "hot" by their nature, such as those made of **sanguine** <note>blood-based</note> and **choleric** <note>yellow bile-based</note> matter. Others are hot only by "accident"—specifically through **putrefaction**—such as those composed of **phlegm** and **melancholy** <note>black bile</note>. For although the material of these latter types is inherently cold, they become hot when they decay. These ailments are discussed in the first and third books of the *Canon* <note>referring to Avicenna’s Canon of Medicine</note>. Certain other swellings are hot both due to their material and due to inflammation or putrefaction, such as **buboes** and those arising from putrefying blood or bile. 

Sometimes the material is also suitable for internal movement. There are also certain swellings resulting from severe or corrupt wounds. Furthermore, some are **universal**, affecting almost the entire body, such as **smallpox**, **measles**, and other types of **pustules** <note>original: "bothorum"</note>, as well as **dropsy** <note>edema or swelling caused by fluid</note>; others are restricted to a specific part. Some occur in soft members, such as the **brain**, others in hard parts, such as **bones and teeth**, and some in the "middle" parts, such as **muscles** and the like. There are also those found in locations designated for receiving the waste matter of the principal organs, such as those that occur in the **throat, the armpits, and the groin**. Some are **critical** <note>occurring during the "crisis" or turning point of a disease</note>, which most often happen in the aforementioned places and in the joints. Others arise from "venomous" matter, such as types of **anthrax** and pustules, which are discussed in the "Hidden Things" of Hippocrates. With these, the body is either <term>plethoric: overfull of blood</term> or <term>cacochymic: full of corrupt humors</term>, or it is not.
<margin>}</margin>

### The Use of Repercussion
Because of this, I will next discuss what appears to be the case. For that which happens first is not simply predicted by **repercussion** <note>the medical practice of applying cold/astringent topicals to drive fluids away from a swelling</term>. That they do not require it is more often an accidental occurrence; hence the first and fourth points: For swellings of the <term>emunctories: organs or areas like the armpits and groin that "drain" the body’s waste</term>, nothing should be applied that restrains <note>original: "infrenet"</note> them. This is not because it would not serve as a medicine for the swelling itself, but because we do not wish to treat the swellings of the emunctories themselves; rather, our effort is to increase them and draw the matter toward them, not caring if the "malice" <note>the severity of the infection</note> is increased in those spots, so long as the principal organs are kept safe by this expulsion. This follows the teaching of **Galen**, though understood in the opposite sense; he likewise shows that if the body is plethoric or cacochymic, **evacuation or purging** must precede the use of medicines. 

In the thirteenth book of *On the Method of Healing*, it is noted that what prevents the formation of a swelling strengthens the limb, alters the corrupt complexion, and removes the "sinning" composition; it prevents the loss of continuity from spreading and greatly mitigates the pain of the abscess. This <term>repercussive</term> method works by its quality and substance. Just as for those wishing to treat particular cases of cold matter that has become hot by "accident" through putrefaction—such as phlegmatic or melancholic swellings—they require repercussion, but not as much as those that are inherently hot. Indeed, something hot should be mixed with the treatment, as has been said. Therefore, at the proper time, repercussion stands as the preferred treatment.

However, that which occurs almost by accident is because either the cause is a **primitive swelling** <note>caused by an external factor like a blow</note>, in which case little or no repercussion is suitable—especially if the body is not plethoric—but rather medicines that cause "flux" <note>movement of fluids</note> should be used at the start. Hence **Avicenna** says: those things which happen due to primitive causes where there is no repletion of humors should be treated at the beginning with things that cause flux and dissolve. 

---

Or, if it is generated by way of **congestion** <note>a natural gathering of fluids by the body</note>, then repercussion is not expedient unless one fears a flow of other materials to the site of pain. In other cases, or if they are internal, no or very little repercussion is appropriate, just as in those which are external and especially those near the heart—such as a swelling of the side <note>pleurisy</note>—lest the matter be repelled back toward a principal organ. 

Hence **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (c. 777–857), a Persian or Assyrian Christian physician</note> states: the first task in curing **pleurisy** is the administration of medicines that strengthen the organ itself so that it is safely unified, and that the organ does not begin to fail as the matter flows down toward it. For this, plasters are made from hulled lentils with vinegar, or from bean flour with vinegar, or from bitter vetch with vinegar, etc. 

But this is suspicious unless done with great caution, or at the very beginning when the matter has not yet "crept" into the place. Or if the swelling is from cold matter that does not become hot by accident or putrefaction—such as **nodes, scrofula** <note>swollen lymph nodes in the neck, often tubercular</note>, and the like. In these cases, softening and dissolving agents are needed, not **apocrustics** <note>repelling or cooling medicines</note>, for fear of causing a spasm, mania, or "crudity" <note>undigested or raw humors</note> of the stomach. 

Or, as it says in the thirteenth book of *On the Method of Healing*: treat everything that occurs in a "phlegmatic" part that cannot yet be treated with repercussion, for it is time to move toward evaporation. Or because it is a universal condition, such as **measles, smallpox, leprosy, and dropsy**; for there is no "safe" place to which such a vast amount of matter can be expelled. With fear of such quantity, repercussion is avoided, as is the case in **scabies**. Furthermore, those in the bones, since they are hard, do not allow for recession. Neither should repercussion be used for those things which happen during the expulsion of matter from principal organs, especially in the three designated locations <note>the emunctories</note>, nor for those that are critical or venomous, lest the work of nature be disturbed and deadly matter be repelled at the beginning—especially when the expulsion is moving toward the emunctories and the joints. 

Therefore, a reasoning of the first principles can be formed: that which hinders the motion of nature, or drives a non-obedient matter toward a place that cannot receive it, is not suitable for a swelling. Such is the case for these exceptions to repercussion. Therefore, in these instances, it is not appropriate.
<margin>} 45</margin>

Regarding the fourth point, which relates to the first: as shown, repercussion is not suitable in itself when a swelling is formed by way of congestion. However, when it is formed by way of **rheum** <note>a flow of humors</note>, which happens more frequently, it is more suitable, provided that the principal organs are not harmed, because the matter is taken up in the intermediate empty spaces—especially when the body is not plethoric or has already been evacuated. For the site remains a defenseless recipient. And it is much more expedient that the internal parts suffer only a very small amount than that a great injury occurs in the exterior parts, especially in the skin, which would restore the "spermatic" sense <note>the vital or formative power</note> and beauty. 

To the other point, it should be said that the forms of fevers and swellings are similar in some ways. For just as they putrefy from the four humors, and some are simple while others are composite, so too are swellings; and just as those require maturation and drawing out in general, so do these. Yet, in specific details, they differ: because abscesses occupy a particular place, they can receive repercussion, but fevers cannot, since they involve the whole body and there is no place to which the matter can be repelled.

To the other point, it should be said that the matter, before the pores are constricted...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the treatment of "apostemes" (inflammatory swellings), specifically debating the risks of "repercussion"—the practice of driving diseased humors back into the body using cooling agents. It then transitions into two specific inquiries: the physical removal of "formica" (a type of wart or pustule) and the treatment of leprosy through evacuation.</meta>

Or the cooled matter itself will be propelled inward. For although the pores may be narrowed on the outside, they are not yet narrowed on the inside while the liquid matter, still remaining, flows inward; and this is especially true since a "vacuum" <note>the medieval belief that nature abhors a vacuum</note> cannot occur. To the other point, it should be said that **Hippocrates** <note>abbreviated as "Y." for Ypocras</note> speaks of matter that is expelled by way of a **crisis** <note>term: "creticum" - a turning point in a disease where the body attempts to expel the cause</note>. Or, the repulsion is not so great that it prevents the matter from being expelled; rather, it comforts the limb and provides it with a kind of **digestion** <note>the process of "ripening" or breaking down morbid humors</note>. To the other point, it must be said that the physician ought to imitate nature when it is operating correctly—not when it operates incorrectly by expelling matter into a vital part, except in those cases which are exceptions. Alternatively, although the physician may seem at first to hinder nature, he subsequently assists it and strengthens it by the power of the body part and the heat of digestion being strengthened in that place.

->Regarding the occasion of the previous inquiry,<-
the question arises whether the cure for **Formica** <note>literally "ant"; a term used for both a type of stinging pustule and a specific kind of wart</note> is achieved by the hardness of the hollow of a quill or something proportional to it. And it seems that it is. For in the fourth book of his science, **Galen** said it is appropriate that there be something like a **plunger** <gloss>original: "embula," a surgical instrument or piston</gloss>, such as a pipe made from the end of a quill or another object with a sharp end that can "swallow" the **formica**, etc. This is the series of Galen's thoughts, as translated from *On the Method of Healing*, book 14: he similarly treats a wart by placing a reed around its circumference. It must have a capacity proportional to the thickness of the wart, and it should tightly grip it on all sides and then be driven downward as quickly as possible; for in this way, the wart is removed along with its very root. And that which removes the disease completes the cure. According to book 11 of *On the Method of Healing*, such a reed should be used so that it immediately extirpates the harmful growth upon contact. On the contrary, because the **formica** is of a hot and painful nature, the act of treating it might draw more matter to the location, filling the space. For a **formica** is a pustule or pustules that break out and cause a stinging abscess, and they "walk" <note>spread across the skin</note> and perhaps ulcerate, and perhaps resolve. Briefly, it should be said that for the pre-defined cure of **formica**, a reed is not appropriate, as that is for a wart or rather an **acrochordon** <note>a hanging wart or skin tag</note>.

<margin>Note</margin>
**Avicenna** responds that [the questioner] seems to be deceived, or he falls into a fallacy of **equivocation** <note>using one word to mean two different things</note>. For "formica" denotes two things. According to **Albucasis**, it refers to a wart or **acrochordon**. According to **Hali Abbas** and **Dioscorides** and the ancients, it is called **mirmicia** <gloss>formicalis, or "ant-like" pustule</gloss>, from *mirmix*, meaning "ant." Therefore, according to the second canon on vines, its "tears" <note>sap</note> are effective against ant-like warts. Thus, the "ant" is a warty pustule named because its bite feels like an ant's.
<margin>Note</margin>
According to **Avicenna**, as mentioned before, it signifies a hot, burning, and spreading pustule like an ant, and thus the reed treatment is not appropriate for it, but rather for the former type (the wart).
