### DIFFERENCE 177.

Regarding whether evacuation <note>purging or bloodletting</note> should be repeated in **leprosy**. Because in a major, more fatal **apoplexy**, and even in **mania**, evacuation is commanded. Much more so, therefore, in this disease, since the one suffering from it remains alive. Furthermore, according to the first and fourth *Aphorisms*, the physician ought to imitate nature; nature expels corrupt humors outward, as shown by the pustules and scales dispersed on the skin. Furthermore, in book 18 of *On the Method of Healing*, regarding **cancer**, which is of the same matter as leprosy and in which the matter is very thick, evacuation is commanded with iron <note>surgery</note> and **epithems** <note>topical applications</note>.

Likewise, for the ultimate sicknesses, the ultimate cures are the most certain. Such is evacuation, since it assists nature in no small way. Leprosy is the worst of illnesses. A leper lives for a long time. It must be treated like other material diseases: first by evacuating what is corrupt, and then by altering the **dyscrasia** <note>imbalance of humors</note> for the better. Therefore, evacuation is appropriate in leprosy. On the contrary, evacuation is the removal of the bad from the body while the good is retained; for thus nature acts in expulsion. In leprosy, however, everything is corrupt. For it is like a cancer common to the whole body. Furthermore, in a disease whose matter does not undergo digestion, it should not be evacuated, as one should medicate and move soft things, not "raw" <note>undigested</note> things. But such is leprosy, since the humors in it are so diversely corrupt that they cannot be brought to a healthy state nor undergo digestion to prepare for expulsion. For nature lacks support, and every movement must be regulated by art, and a strong art at that.

<margin>Leprosy, first part of the *Theorica*</margin>
<margin>*Viaticum* books 3 and 4</margin>
Regarding the first part, it must first be known what leprosy is; second, its types; and finally, how it progresses. Regarding the first, it must be known that leprosy, or **elephantiasis** (according to book 8 of the *Theorica*), is a disease that dries out the limbs of the body and corrupts them with dryness, acting like a cancer that affects the whole body. In the *Viaticum*, leprosy is a passion arising from **black bile** <note>original: "colera nigra"</note> that has been "burnt" and putrefied, appearing on the surface of the body. Third, leprosy is an evil infirmity resulting from the infusion of black bile into the whole body, whereby the complexion and shape of the limbs are corrupted. Thus, in the end, their continuity is lost to such an extent that they are corroded and sometimes fall off. It is then like an abscess of the whole body generated from [corrupt] matter, although some classify it as a defilement of the skin. As for what evacuation or general emptying seeks, it is twofold: either a large or intense exit, or a small and proper one.

Regarding the second part, it should be known that leprosy is either **congenital** <note>from birth</note> and inherited from parents—for it is a disease that is inherited in the seed—or because the conception occurred before the menstrual blood was purified, or it occurs from the air being corrupted by **pestilence**. For [the air] is an ancient and general cause. Or it comes from other parts of the body, or from bad foods and melancholic drinks, and thus from a bad diet. Whence the Indian experimenters and others said that milk should not be eaten with vinegared things, nor fish with milk, because from this comes...

...permanent illnesses such as leprosy, which can occur due to staying among lepers. For they posit that this illness is contagious. It may also occur through intercourse with a leprous woman, or especially with a woman with whom a leper has recently had intercourse. For, due to the heat of the man and the openness of the pores of the male member, vapors rising from the corrupt womb <note>original: "matrice corrupti"; the medieval belief that the uterus could harbor corrupting "vapors"</note> quickly corrupt him. Thus, one must beware of coupling with a menstruating woman. A woman, however, is not infected in this way except perhaps by frequent intercourse with lepers, since her womb is cold, dry, and dense, and thus less receptive to injury. Furthermore, the seed of a leper received by her is quickly cast out, or if it remains inside, it is extinguished.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that **Serapion** <note>Yahya ibn Sarafyun, a 9th-century Syrian Christian physician</note> says in his fifth book that leprosy is caused by excesses of black bile. This arises in two ways: one arising from the combustion of yellow bile, the other from that which is naturally melancholic. According to theory, there are two species of "elephantia" <note>term: "elephancie" - often used interchangeably with leprosy in this period</note>: one which comes from black bile (which we have said is the dregs and purgation of the blood) and which does not cause the falling off of limbs and is sometimes cured; the other comes from the black humor generated by the combustion of red bile. In this type, there is a "devouring" of the limbs and they fall away, from which no remedy can bring recovery.

<margin>
<note>A pointing hand (manicule) indicates the start of this section on the types of leprosy.</note>
</margin>
According to **Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century philosopher and physician</note> in the *Viaticum*, the four types of leprosy are distinguished by names arising from the four humors. The first is caused by burnt blood, which is called **alopecia** or "fox-like" disease, in which the skin is excoriated as a fox is in its behavior; this name is specifically applied to this passion of the scalp. Another type, from corrupt phlegm, is called **tyria**, named for the likeness of that serpent's [the *tyrus*] shedding of skin, and is also attributed to the peeling of the scalp. A third comes from burnt yellow bile, called **leonia** [lion-like] because it is hotter and more severe, producing a terrifying face like a lion, or because it happens to lions. The remaining type, from the combustion of black bile, is named **elephantia**, because just as the elephant is varied with spots, so is the skin of those suffering from this; or because just as the elephant is the largest and strongest of animals, so is this form of leprosy called the "greatness of skin" <note>original: "magnitudo... crutis"</note> and the strongest type. These explanations by **Avicenna** and **Isaac** have been expanded upon by all the Latin authors. **Avicenna** posits that it arises from burnt bile as in the "leonia" type, and from burnt humors as in the first type, and from the dregs of the blood, which he considers the worst, generating the first and third types.

Regarding the fourth point, it should be known whether this humor putrefies or not. If it does, it is either within the veins, causing a continuous quartan fever, or outside them, causing an interpolated quartan fever. If it does not putrefy, the species is either expelled to one part or to the whole body. If it is retained deep within the limbs, or if it is propelled to the surface: if the former, the matter is thick and generates hardness or "sepbiros" <note>term: "sepbiros" - a medieval term for a hard, scirrhous tumor</note>; or it is thin and corrosive, generating "herpes esthiomenos" <note>term: "herpetẽ beltionomenū" - a "devouring" or "eating" skin ulcer</note>; or it is mid-range, causing cancer. If it moves to the surface, it causes **morphea** <note>a skin condition causing discolored patches</note>, **serpigo** <note>a "creeping" skin disease like ringworm</note>, and **scabies**. There are indeed 180 differences of leprosy and similar conditions. If, however, it is propelled into the whole body so that leprosy is fully formed, then according to **Serapion** and **Avicenna**, one must consider whether evacuation of the humors is permitted. Sometimes it is granted, sometimes not at all; what is desired regarding this will be said with the fourth point. Concerning the third part, it should be known that in leprosy, evacuation is sometimes appropriate and sometimes not at all.

---

And thereafter it must be considered whether the evacuation should be sudden and immediate, or little by little. Regarding the first, it should be known whether the leprosy is "on the way" to becoming confirmed, or is already established and confirmed. If it is the first, it must be evacuated by a sudden or strong evacuation, whether it be blood or whichever other humor is at fault. Whence **Serapion** says: "The intention in the cure of leprosy is to evacuate the humor, and this is at its beginning before it hardens and passes into a stony hardness." For it then obeys the medicines that evacuate and draw it out. Consonant with this, **Avicenna** says: "One must begin the cure of leprosy with evacuations and cleansing before the illness thickens." **Haly Abbas** and **Rhazes** <note>two influential Persian physicians</note> also agree on this. For in the beginning, it is sometimes cured, as stated in the fourth book of the *Practice*. It is cured by removing the cause, as with other material illnesses; this is removed by evacuation.

Evacuation should therefore be performed then, as argued by many authorities. But if the disease is already established, one should not evacuate suddenly or violently, but little by little. Whence **Serapion**: "When the matter has reached a thick state, it does not resolve entirely." This is because the bad humors use the nutrition within themselves, and if they are purged, the patients are quickly weakened due to the abundance of bad humors. Furthermore, anything that agitates the matter and rouses it to a "fury," mixing the more malignant with the benign, is not appropriate in such leprosy. Thus, a strong or sudden evacuation is not suitable when the matter is found to be already indisposed. The complexion is also corrupted... cleansing the humors of a leper is like someone wishing to purify a well of corrupt water by throwing a flask into it; it purifies nothing, as the passing water becomes dominated by the corruption already present. In such a state of leprosy, evacuation is not suitable.

**Avicenna** grants a small and gradual evacuation. In confirmed cases of leprosy, one should not be occupied with strong medicine for the bowels, because the superfluities move but do not separate; rather, relief is found by inclining the matter toward the intestines and administering external things that soothe and resolve. For since such cases cannot be cured—which is proven especially when their blood is placed in a vessel and after being strained <note>original: "ĩ śaccello" - in a small bag or cloth</note> one sees sandy, black, burnt pieces of flesh, and not whitish ones—then they must be soothed and palliated as much as possible. This is done by supporting their internal organs with troches of capers <note>medicinal lozenges</note> and opening the intestines and urinary passages with gentle movers and moisturizers.

One may also palliate the surface of the face, specifically with metal filings, or with turtle blood and oil of bitter almonds. Others use **theriac** <note>a famous poly-pharmaceutical "universal" ointment or medicine</note> mixed with opiates, and some use a dark ointment with turpentine. The blood of young children <note>original: "śanguīe pueroz̃ recētī"</note> is also praised, and "areoticon" <note>perhaps a specific medicinal mixture</note> with ivory filings.

# Whether Theriac Expels Poison Through Its Alterative Power or Its Specific Property

<margin>Sixth Doubt</margin>
...not in others. The truth regarding this is briefly indicated by **Rhazes** <note>Al-Razi, a 10th-century Persian physician</note>: this disease is either beginning, or it has evacuated something from the body, or it has already reached its ultimate peak. I have indeed doubted what is prescribed in the *Viaticum* <note>A standard medical manual, likely by Ibn al-Jazzar</note> regarding leprosy concerning crow’s blood <note>original: "sanguine corue"; possibly a specific symbolic or literal ingredient</note>. It should not be taken from the median vein when the matter is between the vessels. If it is outside the veins, one must be careful as it may cause much harm. For corrupt matter is drawn into the veins and must then be led out by pharmacy. To which the opposite seems to be felt by others, since they place leprosy as being diffused through the whole body like a creeping cancer. It should be said that the words of the *Viaticum*, **Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician</note>, and others are perhaps not heard in the same way. I understand, however, that he is introducing a distinction in leprosy based on whether it resulted from corrupt blood or from another humor.

Regarding this word, it should be known that **Rhazes** prescribes that the evacuation be done small and gradually, in several sessions and hours—that is, when the disease is beginning. It is necessary that it be evacuated with bloodletting in every month, and that a "loosening" <note>purging of the bowels</note> occur in the extraction of blood and the loosening of the belly in every week with those things which lead out <term>black bile</term> <note>Melancholy; the humor associated with earth, coldness, and dryness</note>, and let this be done strongly. Whence in the fifth book, it is recounted that a certain leprous youth, in the space of five months and a few days, loosened his belly more than forty times. But this could not happen if much were led out all at once. And it is confirmed by what was shown in chapter 154: that in a disease that is not violently dangerous, giving time, the beginning should be made from lighter medications, since nature cannot sustain sudden changes.

**On the contrary:** **Serapion** says that in the beginning of this disease, an evacuation must be made with the extraction of much blood in the beginning, if the strength and age of the patient allow it. In the fourth book of *Practica*: when <term>elephantiasis</term> <note>A term for advanced leprosy characterized by thickened, "elephant-like" skin</note> is in the beginning, before the face begins to fail and become deformed and the limbs to ulcerate, diminish the blood from the two organic veins <note>likely the jugulars</note> and the two veins that are behind the ears and those of the forehead, and sometimes from the median vein, until a deficiency appears. Whence it is said by **Aristotle**: "It will be necessary that you begin with the ultimate bloodlettings." That is, to lead out much and quickly. And it is confirmed by that which is said: "For the ultimate diseases, ultimate powerful cures." And for the ultimate fullness, an ultimate evacuation is owed, and by many extractions. It should be said that "much and quickly" can be said in two ways: either by reason of the infection and the malice of the matter, which cannot be cured in one or three turns but requires many extractions. For the strength of the patient would not suffer it. And therefore it is better to remain below the limit than to evacuate to the point of exhaustion. And thus the first authorities are to be heard. Or, it is on the part of the mass of matter filling the body, which soon transforms itself into a greater <term>cacochymy</term> <note>A general state of bad humors or "bad juice" in the body</note>; and thus the second view is understood. The first authorities, therefore, took their indication from the patient's strength; the second, however, from the multitude of the bad humors.

<margin>Note</margin>
And know that milk is very little suited to this suffering, and especially when it is from matter that is not so burning and in a colder region. By accident, however, it sometimes helps for the sake of secondary symptoms, such as difficulty of breathing and its constriction, or irritation and hoarseness of the voice, especially when the body has already been evacuated. And specifically when it is warm and fresh, like sheep’s milk according to **Aristotle**, specifically when exhibited according to his rule. Leprosy is incurred when someone uses it too often and immoderately, and especially when it has little watery part, and in colder, less breathable places, and from salted sea fish, old salted meats, and specifically from buffalo and beef. And therefore in **Saxony** and above the **Flemish sea** and in **Carmonia**, it is common to find lepers, just as in **Alexandria**, from the mixing with others. Regarding the fourth point, however, it should be known that although it appears so, it should be seen in chapter 185. For the same things do not occur when the matter of the two is different. Regarding the other point, it is stated in chapters 18 and 165. For that which flows to the external parts and causes scars and defenses of these causes is not by way of the evacuation of matter eradicated from the internal parts, in which the malice of the disease comes out more to the surface, harming everything. To the other point, it should be said that the evacuation made in cancer with <term>whey and epithymum</term> <note>Epithymum is "dodder of thyme," a parasitic plant used as a purgative for melancholy</note> when it is confirmed is not much or violent, but rather a little and owed by way of a certain preservation or palliation. Know, however, that a confirmed cancer is of a worse cure than leprosy, because its malice is fixed in one place, whereas in leprosy it is diffused and thus rendered more "virtuous" <note>powerful or active</note>. Likewise, by administering cures, leprosy is sustained and does not act upon the simple limbs; but in cancer, it is not so.

To the other point, it should be said that this is true if the strength would tolerate it and the corrupt matter were expelled; but it is not true that this should be cut short; rather, this would be to "wake a sleeping wolf" <note>original: "lupum suscitare sopitum"; a proverb meaning to make a bad situation worse</note>. To the other point, it also appears what should be said: because a leper who is not yet "confirmed" <note>fully symptomatic or advanced</note> is to be cured even with a larger evacuation, but not so afterward. For this disease differs from others in its corruption. Those things which are brought in from the other part proceed in their own way.

### DIFFERENCE 178.

<margin>Question</margin>
Whether **Theriac** <note>A famous ancient medical concoction of dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh, used as a universal antidote</note> expels poison by its quality and not by its specific property is shown in the seventh book of the *Breviary*: that Theriac performs its operations through the common complexion resulting from the other simple ingredients composing it. Furthermore, a "property" arises in something when the whole species or substance, when the simples have been mixed and digested, reaches the vigor of a preceding, perfect, and specific complexion. But the things mixed in Theriac are not simples, but rather composed of the four elements. For no element by itself enters its constitution. Furthermore, if a property results in something when it follows the "substantial form" <note>The essential nature of a thing in Aristotelian philosophy</note> (chapter 71), it would have to be introduced through a generation that happens in the first preceding thing by resolving the matter. But that is done by nature and not by art, since nature is an intrinsic principle transforming the whole into the whole, while art is extrinsic. Generation also proceeds when the subject is nature in potentiality, whereas art is in act; since art is only a transforming alterative, and Theriac is made by art and not by nature. Again, nothing acts beyond its own species; this would happen if the art of making Theriac had a specific property, since that belongs to nature and not to art. For it follows the substantial form, as was said; for art is weaker than nature...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into Theriac, moving from the general introduction of the "Sixth Doubt" into a detailed scholastic debate regarding whether this "universal antidote" works through its physical qualities (like heat) or its "specific property" (a hidden, essential power). ...even though he labors much on this in the fourth book of the *Meteorics* <note>Aristotle’s treatise on natural science; book 4 was often attributed to Avicenna in the Middle Ages</note>. **Avicenna** states again: if a "property" could be introduced by art, it would bring with it the [essential] form which it follows substantially; and thus gold could be constructed through alchemy <note>original: "palchimia"</note>, which **Avicenna** denies in that same place.

**Theriac**, therefore, repels poison by its quality and not by its property. However, other physicians think the opposite, as will appear later. Furthermore, **Damascenus** <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian and scholar often cited in medical texts</note> says in his *Aphorisms*: Theriac is most necessary so that it may dissolve, dissipate, and change [the poison]. These actions are performed by its constitution <note>term: <term>complexio</term> (complexion/constitution); the specific balance of the four humors—hot, cold, moist, and dry—in a substance</note>. By the power of this preparation, another work will be more inherent to it: namely, to expel poisons, which is perfected by its "property." Again, that which is universally opposed to poisons acts by its property, since an action involving quantity or constitution is limited. Such is the nature of theriac. For it expels poison whether it is hot or cold. Therefore, theriac does this by its property and not merely by its [elemental] nature.

Regarding the first point, it should be known what theriac is and what the other terms related to it mean. <margin>Difference 127</margin> Poison is properly defined as something destructive to the substance of the human body, and it is two-fold. One type is destructive to the moisture of the human being, which happens from the corruption of the internal matter. Whence **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician</note> says: Poison is an aqueous, subtle, horrible humidity of a quality or of animals of this kind; it is subtle, sharp, and destructive of human nature, especially such as that of a serpent or a scorpion. The other type of poison comes from minerals or vegetables, such as arsenic, or sublimated lead, monkshood <note>original: "nappelli"</note>, or poppy.

There is also a type that kills by its property or its "specific form" <note>the hidden essence of a thing that gives it unique powers beyond its heat or moisture</note> or substance, as monkshood does most powerfully. Or it kills by its quality, and that in a fixed way, like opium and henbane; or in a sharp way, like spurge <note>original: "euforbium"</note> and cashew nut <note>original: "anacardus"</note>, though these are more dangerous because of their coldness. There are also those that poison the whole body, like almost all those mentioned above. Some, however, poison only a part, such as quicksilver <note>mercury</note> when introduced into the brain through the ears, or the sea-hare <note>a marine mollusk historically believed to be toxic</note> by ulcerating the lungs, and cantharides <note>the "Spanish fly" beetle</note> by affecting the bladder.

Furthermore, "quality" (by which things are called "qualified" in the *Categories* <note>Aristotle’s work on logic and classification</note>) is twofold: one belongs to a simple thing, and the other to that which is composed of it. Also, according to **Galen**, qualities are threefold. First: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. Second: hardness, softness, roughness, and density, heaviness, and lightness, and those that follow these. Third: odor, taste, and color. Here, we are hearing about quality in the fixed and primary sense.

What a "property" is has become known in Book 1, Difference 60. For it follows the substantial form of inherence in such a way that the action is sometimes attributed to the whole substance. For when simple ingredients are mixed by the vigor of a more perfect constitution in which heat dominates, and they have been perfectly digested and purified from the stain and filth of their previous property, the old form is corrupted and another is introduced. Its power or powers inhere according to an alignment with a determined heavenly sphere, which is most occult and wonderful, raised up from the potentiality of the matter, like the human soul. These are also followed by a constitution, once the previous one is corrupted and the next remains. And if all things were to exist at the same time, the substantial form naturally precedes, then the properties follow, and finally, the constitution follows. 

Regarding the second point,

---

it should be known that some have said that **theriac, mithridatum** <note>a complex semi-mythical herbal remedy similar to theriac</note> and things of this kind—such as a bitter or sweet confection of musk—benefit against poisons only by quality and not by property, moved by the aforementioned arguments. Those who say this are moved by the fact that from the mixable elements of such confections, measured in their due proportion, a constitution results that is so agreeable to human nature. It is so wonderful that it invigorates the spirits and the principal parts, and thus all the malice of hot or cold poison is removed. This is supported by the second book of the *On the Elements* <note>likely referring to a work by Galen or Isaac Israeli</note>: When an external heat wishes to destroy equality, the innate heat exists within in resistance to foreign things, so that it even refrains hot poisons. It does not expel nor corrupt their substance unless the innate heat itself—which exists as the instrument of nature—expels the harm of the arriving heat. Therefore, it moves the spirit to expel it, to remove its vapor, to resolve it, and to burn up its matter. 

According to the first point, it also expels harm when it occurs. For coldness does not have this property; it does not fight or act unless against an arriving heat by its own primary quality, but not against an occurring coldness. This is the opinion of **Avicenna**, the cunning of one who wishes every action to be performed by quality in whatever elementary way. **Alexander** <note>likely Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> is so reliant on this that he even wrongly feels the human soul arises from the power of the elements (Difference 71). But perhaps this is not valid, because then theriac would greatly strengthen its power by the addition of stones <note>bezoars or gems used in medicine</note>, which happens very little.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that after these views, a more familiar way of speaking is added, which follows what is said in the first book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics</note>: how theriac and things like it expel poison. It would be foolish, according to **Cicero**, to depart from things correctly discovered by the ancients. According to his own words: "Everything I have said well stands out." Theriac and such things do not only work by their constitutional quality, but also by the property of an occult quality. In this way, it expels fixed-quality poisons like opium and similar things, and by its property it expels hot ones like those of the serpent and its kind. In a certain way, it works by both, as with those which, through coldness, have a property destructive to the heat of life, such as the poison of a scorpion. 

That theriac and its like expel poisons by property is supported by the authorities. Whence **Serapion** <note>a 9th-century Syrian physician</note> says in book 7: There are certain operations which theriac does not do by its property—namely, operations that follow the primary qualities, like expelling worms. In the tenth book of the *Practice*, it says: Theriac, by its own property, benefits the bites of reptiles and not by its [elemental] qualities. In the fifth book of the *On Simple Medicines*, it says: Theriac does not perform these operations except specifically because of the property of that form following the composition of its simples. Whence the *Colliget* <note>a medical work by Averroes</note> says: It is not far-fetched to find properties in medicines whose composition was made over a long time, because the constitution is more confirmed in them. However, a property begins more in a natural mixture than in an artificial one, and only wisdom comprehends its property. Thus **Avicenna** declares this property in his *On Cardiac Medicines*.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on whether Theriac works through its elemental "complexion" (heat, cold, etc.) or a "specific property" (a hidden, essential power). He says that in <term>theriac</term> <note>a famous ancient "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh</note> and **Mithridatum** <note>a precursor to theriac, named after King Mithridates VI of Pontus</note> something is "known"—namely, what arises from the <term>simples</term> <note>individual, unmixed medicinal ingredients</note>, or as it is said, that theriac overcomes venomous things because those very things enter into the medicine and are directed against them. 

Another part, however, is "unknown," such as that which comes from them after they are mixed together by a nature that is highly suitable to human nature, just as the <term>complexion</term> <note>the specific balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> prepares for the receiving of the soul. The origin of this property is drawn from an external source. Furthermore, the quantity of the proportions of the medicines found within it is unknown, so that such a "property" may be introduced, just as we are ignorant of the composition of other natural things—as also appears in the third book of the *Therapeutics* <note>original: "terapentice"; referring to Galen's *Method of Medicine*</note>. 

And therefore, the wiser ones say precisely that the direction for the composition of theriac and such things comes from divine inspiration and providence, or from an art inspired by the same. For human reason cannot reach the secret of their composition; their mixing is almost like the work of God, which exists entirely in the first complexion of nature. Therefore, the mixing of such things is not grasped by reason, but rather by **experience**. 

Indeed, the "property" of theriac does not emerge except after an intense mixing of its ingredients. The ancients even feared that the mixing of the simples entering into the theriac would destroy their individual properties. But revelation and divine providence lead us to understand that they are not corrupted, as experience also shows. 

And so it is said in **Difference 126**: "My advice is that nothing should be removed from theriac which **Andromachus** <note>physician to Emperor Nero and the credited inventor of the refined theriac formula</note> found to be helpful by experiment." **Galen** even exerted himself to ensure this formula was ascribed to him. For perhaps that specific complexion, with that exact weight of ingredients, signifies the one whose benefit was found by experience—so much so that when it is moved from its proper weight, it no longer possesses that specific property. 

And know from the tenth book of the *Practice of Heart Medicines* <note>likely referring to a work by Avicenna or a similar authority</note> that the benefit which comes from them is found to be sufficiently grasped only in **fermented** theriac. According to the moderns, this fermentation is completed in ten years, but according to **Galen**, it takes twenty years, depending on the distance of the region in terms of heat and friction <note>the local climate affects how fast the medicine "matures"</note>. Yet among some moderns, its benefit is hoped for after only six months, which **Galen** does not allow. And if it is said that it becomes healthy after six months in **Difference 127**, the experts nevertheless feel it is not inconsistent that through the working and interaction of the simples joined into one, after a long time, the "property" arises and ferments in the theriac. By this property, it may expel venomous spirits and strengthen the innate heat. Therefore, they are specifically helped by those things that act against the contrary qualities and overcome their powers.

And so it should be known that "property" can be understood in two ways:
1. **Properly**, according to how it is truly found in things produced by nature (as explained in **Difference 21**).
2. **Improperly**, according to a certain similarity, such as from the application of things entering theriac made by art. 

In this artistic composition, perhaps the "aspect of the stars" is not strictly observed, unless one considers the existence of the "luminaries" <note>the Sun and Moon</note> in determined locations at a suitable time, as shown in **Difference 125**. When theriac is made, some property eventually arises in it and its parts. This is shown by the fact that if the operation of theriac happened only because of the complexion of the simples and not because of the composition from which the property is raised after a long time, then **fresh** theriac would be more effective and useful. However, the opposite is seen in **fermented** theriac; for when it is fresh, it provides little benefit. 

Furthermore, if theriac repelled poisons by quality or complexion alone, then it would act by contrariety so that the heat would not be corrupted by those poisons. But the opposite is seen: it helps magnificently against "hot" poisons, like those of the serpent and its like, and "cold" ones, like those of the scorpion. 

Again, consider the color and odor constructed by art, and also of theriac. These too have properties:
*   **Red** color moves the blood outward and induces flow; therefore, it is forbidden for a person to look at red things when blood is flowing from their nose.
*   **Citrine** <note>yellow</note> is preferred in cases of jaundice; hence in **Book 15, Chapter 3**, it says that those suffering from jaundice are helped by looking at yellow things. For that color moves nature to expel all the yellow matter to the skin. 
*   Similarly, **odor** seems to incite the hidden power into motion. 

Thus, in theriac and similar things, the property arises after no small space of time. This is also marked by other joined arts, such as with scorpions, bees, and the like. 

You should also know that some things resist poisons by their **complexion**—just as hot bodies resist cold ones, like <term>castoreum</term> <note>a secretion from beavers</note>, white <term>dynacardinon</term>, and others. Or they resist by **property**, such as the "napellus mouse" <note>a legendary creature said to live on the poisonous monkshood plant, acting as an antidote</note>, a little worm born in its root; and as they say, theriac or things that comfort the heart, such as hyacinth, gold, and <term>dyamuscus</term> <note>a musk-based cordial</note>. 

Other things work by narrowing the paths and passages so the poison cannot proceed into the body, such as <term>terra sigillata</term> <note>medicinal "sealed earth" or clay</note>; or things that help by making the paths to the heart slippery and oily so the poison is prevented from reaching it—which is what much butter, oil, walnuts, hazelnuts, and others do. Or they work by inciting the heat itself so that it moves against the poison and dissolves it, as do all hot, dry, subtle, aromatic things, and those that especially comfort the heart. 

Know, moreover, that theriac does not only work to drive out poisons because of the property arising from the simples, but also through its complexional operations, which are helped and perfected by that property. Hence, concerning heart medicines: some physicians attack theriac, thinking that the heat of theriac and Mithridatum is perhaps stronger than that of *dia triton pipereon* <note>a pepper-based digestive</note> or *diacimini* <note>a cumin-based medicine</note>, and therefore they should give a "golden mean" quantity. But this is false. 

For in those things concerning heart medicines, **Avicenna** says he found the heat of theriac to be at the end of the second degree, and Mithridatum a little below it. However, estimation suggests that the complexion acquires heat from the outside through fermentation, which cannot be grasped so easily, but only through artificial and experimental estimation. This is shown by the great change it causes when taken into the body. 

Regarding the fourth point: something appeared to the first, since **Serapio** <note>an influential 9th-century Arabic Christian physician</note> stated that the actions of theriac come through...

...resulting from the combination of simple medicines, some of which do not act by their own specific property <note>In medieval medicine, a "specific property" is a hidden, total power of a substance that goes beyond its basic qualities of heat or moisture</note>, since he already said that theriac does not perform certain actions by its own property. But he says this, rejecting the idea that theriac works only through the simple complexion of the things mixed in it. Or, he was of the opinion that the property was something beyond the complexions, as seen in Difference 71.

Regarding the other point, it appeared that something else must be said: because that property is more truly verified in a "property of nature," which results entirely through nature without the help of art. However, that property which rises up initially from art exists as a "property of imitation," not a "certain" or fixed one, which imitates the prior natural property, just as art follows nature. For it results, as has been declared, in a certain way from the simple medicines composing the theriac, just as its property results from the simple elements in relation to a certain position in the world.

Regarding the next point, it must be said that although a property is primarily and perfectly introduced by nature, it can be raised up initially and consequently by the power of art, by imitating nature. And just as by this imitation art does not achieve the same result as a natural mixture, so the generated property that rises from such things is not "certain" but exists more as a likeness. Regarding the other point, adding to what was said before: nothing acts beyond its own species in its own power, yet it acts by the power of another, just as heat, by the power of fire, generates fire from air and water.

Regarding the next point, it must be said that it is conceded by some that **alchemy** <note>The medieval precursor to chemistry, focused on the transmutation of matter</note> is a true science, and that **gold** and **silver** can be constructed by art. This is because they posit that all metals share one close nature and do not differ except in being more or less pure. They are like sick bodies whose health and perfection are acquired by art, just as in the bodies of the healthy. Hence, the Commentator <note>Averroes, the 12th-century philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> says in the third book of *On the Soul* that we are masters of those artificial skills which seem possible but are only unknown by chance—for example, the art of alchemy. This is shown by the double mode of generation of certain things through both nature and art, such as scorpions and bees. Thus, Aristotle says in the 15th book of *On Animals*: "I have already seen a man who made scorpions, which afterwards generated others." And two faithful men have testified to me that they made silver by the art of decoction <note>The process of boiling or heating substances to extract their essence</note>—truly by every test—yet they did not make a profit from it.

# DIFFERENCE CLXXXIX.

Whether **Theriac Diatesseron** <note>original: "tyriaca dyatefferon"; a simpler version of theriac made of only four ingredients: Gentian, Aristolochia, Myrrh, and Frankincense</note> is beneficial for the bite of a rabid dog is shown here. For it is written in the fourth book, section six: "It is said that Theriac Diatesseron is vehemently beneficial for those bitten by a rabid dog." Furthermore: what is in the parts is also in the whole, since the whole is nothing other than a gathering of parts, as the Commentator says in the first book of the *Physics*. But in the parts from which this medicine is composed, there exists the power to drive away poisons and to be beneficial for the bites of dogs, as they say. Again: that which comforts the heat or the spirit, provokes urine, and dries out poison should be beneficial for the bite of a rabid dog. Such is this theriac, since it is constructed from various hot, dry, and <term>diaphoretic</term> <note>medicines that induce sweating</note> substances. Furthermore, that which is sharp and ulcerative, and which draws poison toward the outside, is especially beneficial; and this medicine is such a thing. Therefore, Theriac

Diatesseron is beneficial for the bites of a rabid dog. On the opposite side: neither Serapion, Rhazes, Haly Abbas, Avicenna, nor Mesue <note>These are the primary authorities of medieval Islamic and Greco-Roman medicine</note>—among whom there is no lack of knowledge in their proper subject—wrote that this theriac provides help in the bites of a rabid dog. Furthermore, it would either help by its complexion or its property. Not by its complexion, since the theriac is hot and dry, and the venom of this dog is also hot and dry. But every cure is achieved by the opposite; moreover, they are dried out and inflamed by such a poisonous bite. Nor does it help by property, since such properties are found in the <term>simples</term>, but not in composites, except perhaps in "solemn" medicines, such as the **Great Theriac**, **Mithridatum**, and the "Perfections of Musk" mentioned before. For that property is introduced by the generation of the mixture, which is an effect of nature and not of art. Therefore, Theriac Diatesseron does not benefit the bite of a rabid dog.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that theriac is manifold according to the diversity of its components, as seen in Difference 127. However, the one for which that name is most properly sought is the **Great Theriac** of Andromachus or Galen, in which the flesh of the <term>tyri</term> serpent <note>The Tyrus or viper; its flesh was the signature ingredient of the most potent theriacs</note> is included; from which it takes its name. But that which does not contain this is called "theriac" metaphorically, such as the Diatesseron, because it drives away the harm of poisons in likeness to the great one. It is called so from *dia*, which is interpreted as "of" or "from," and *tessera*, meaning "four," hence **Diatesseron**: "of four." For besides the cooked honey, it is constructed from four medicines in equal parts: **gentian**, **long birthwort** <note>original: "aristologia longa"</note>, **myrrh**, and **frankincense** <note>original: "thure"</note>, of which the dose is one *aureus*. 

Indeed, some have put **costus** <note>an aromatic root</note> in place of myrrh. Others added costus. Nicomachus also reports that some added to the previous ingredients: fenugreek, nigella, zedoary, diptany, and even in other places ivy and <term>calcanthum</term> <note>a type of vitriol or copper sulfate</note>. These the earlier Greeks and Arabs reasonably omitted, saying that the composition itself is wonderfully beneficial for windiness, the corrosion of the belly and intestines, and for the liver and spleen. Also for pains of the liver and the chest, tremors, and the stings of crawling things like scorpions and spiders. And for poisonous drinks, especially cold ones. 

The bite of a dog, however, is a grasping with the teeth themselves, by which a solution of continuity <note>a physical wound or break in the skin</note> is induced, which becomes worse. Sometimes, however, it kills the person in a very short time. A **rabid dog** is an animal that has turned completely treacherous toward all, whereas before it was a familiar domestic pet, a guardian of strangers, or devoted to hunting. They go rabid either from corrupt food and drink, or from carcasses and putrid waters, so that their humors are turned into a great burnt state, or from the air. This happens most often in autumn and spring, according to Aristotle and the *Viaticum* <note>A famous medical traveler's handbook by Ibn al-Jazzar</note>. For the heat of summer burns the humors, but the vehement cold of winter makes them turn toward blackness. Others, however, write that this happens most in the "dog days" <note>the hottest days of summer</note>, but very rarely in winter. For the end of one season is the beginning of another, according to the *Aphorisms*. Moreover, not only dogs become rabid, but also wolves, foxes, monkeys, weasels, and sometimes mules. ...of discretion or the opposite. Authors note many things concerning the bite. For when the time of the bite proceeds, terrible and wonderful signs appear, such as the **fear of water** <note>original: "pauor aque"; this refers to hydrophobia, a classic symptom of rabies</note>, even though they desire it vehemently and look for liquid; they see shapes as if presented in a mirror and meanwhile bark like dogs. They also sometimes urinate a fatty substance in which wonderful things can be seen, as if they were animals, and they appear like puppies. Other such cunning things happen, namely hallucinations; scarcely anyone ever escapes once the fear of water has arrived. For now the malice has entered the heart, according to that line from **Ovid’s** *Metamorphoses*: *Nor does he help with the trembling waters.* <note>original: "Nec trepidantis auxiliatur aquis"; Ovid, Metamorphoses IV.551, describing the madness of Ino and Athamas</note>. However, **Avicenna** <note>referred to as "A." in the text</note> records two men who escaped this condition, though they were not bitten by a rabid dog directly, but by a man who had been bitten.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that it is commonly estimated that the **Theriac of the Four** <term>Diatesseron: a medical mixture composed of four main ingredients: gentian, laurel berries, birthwort, and myrrh</term> is beneficial for this disease. This is why **Nicolaus** <note>Nicolaus Praepositus, author of a famous medieval medical text, the Antidotarium</note> expressed it in his antidote, perhaps because it happened that way or because he saw that **gentian** conferred magnificent benefit. Or perhaps he was focused on the addition of medicines which more illustrious physicians put into this perfection; however, what should be felt about this will appear more clearly later. Some, however, have asserted that this theriac benefits the bite through its "specific property," but it is vain to say this. For then one would have to assign a specific property to any medicine whatever, the falsehood of which can appear from the previous distinction and later from the teachings.

Therefore, for the sake of the third point, let the truth of the first be opened. Next, for this reason, I will add whether a solution is appropriate at the beginning of this, and finally, let the cause of certain accidents of the bite be assigned with probability to those things that occur. Therefore, regarding this first point, it should be known that this **Theriac of the Four** does not benefit by helping the bite—which is what must be cured—especially when it is taken internally. In fact, it might even do more harm because it is vehemently hot and dry. And so, as it appeared to the more illustrious physicians, they did not profess this virtue for it, but rather for many other medicines and for the **Great Theriac**. 

If it does benefit, it is either for tender and fat children by heating and drying out this venom, and by strengthening the body through the property of the **gentian**, since the gentian is not totally corrupted in this medicine. Nor is it lasting enough, since it is so vehemently hot and dry, that its property rises up through maturation and fermentation like that of the **Great Theriac** <note>The "Great Theriac" or Theriac of Andromachus contained dozens of ingredients, including viper's flesh, and required long fermentation</note>, as per the aforementioned distinction. Or it works by the provocation of urine and the drawing out of the poison from the internal parts to the outside. Hence, **cantharides** <note>Spanish fly beetles, used as a potent diuretic and blistering agent</note> are especially praised for the provocation of urine and the drawing out of blood, even with the excoriation <note>skinning or irritation</note> of the bladder.

It is more beneficial, however, when it is applied as a plaster over the site, because it is quite hot, dry, inflammatory, ulcerating, and attractive <note>meaning "drawing" or "pulling" the toxins out</note>. For ulceration and attraction soon pull toward the exterior, just as **cupping glasses** should be applied to the bitten place, and then sharp, ulcerating things such as **garlic, onion, mustard, and rocket** <note>arugula</note>. For this reason, **Nicolaus**, in his *Greater Antidote*, especially for bites, prescribes that the **Theriac of the Four** be applied as a plaster. 

The medicine praised by everyone here above all others is the one which **Galen** wrote to **Monteus**, and which **Ascimus the Elder** proposed; he used to disparage all medicines except this one, saying that no one would die who used it for 40 days. Its composition is as follows: 

->**Recipe:** Ash of burnt river crabs <note>burnt in a vessel of red copper</note>, 10 parts; gentian, 5 parts; frankincense, 1 part.<-

The dose of this is one large spoonful powdered over water, and one should drink no less than three drams of it. According to **Avicenna**, it should be taken in the morning on an empty stomach, and in the evening. Some, however, provide two drams, and some only one, as long as the fear of water has not yet appeared. 

**Astadion the Experimenter**, according to the *Aggregator*, commanded that this medicine be prepared when the **Sun is in Leo** and the **Moon is 18 days old**; after the preparation, it should be taken for many nights, though they differ among the experts in number and weight. Over the site, **Galen** used to firm up this plaster: 

->**Recipe:** One *kist* <note>a Greek measure of volume</note> of vinegar, three ounces of opoponax <note>a medicinal gum resin</note>, and one pound of pitch; let them be combined and applied as a plaster to the bitten place.<-

Regarding the second point, it should be known that **Almansor** <note>The Persian physician Rhazes (al-Razi), author of the Book for Al-Mansur</note> in the seventh book commands that at the beginning of such a treatment, one should begin to loosen the belly with pills and the medicines named in the chapter on theriac. The contrary of this seems to be written in the fourth and sixth books; or, it is not necessary in the first days to hurry toward evacuation, but rather to be occupied in drawing the poison to the exterior. For sometimes evacuation helps the venom to penetrate to the depths, prohibiting the attraction to the outside. For that which pulls humors to the interior also drags the poison along with them. Some say that in the very beginning, evacuation according to **Avicenna** should not be done, fearing the attraction of the venom further inward. 

For the "beginning" has a certain breadth: one part of it belongs more to the certain start, another to its end, and some to the middle. And rightly so, since before the wicked symptoms come upon the patient, a little time passes—sometimes seven days, sometimes forty. Sometimes six months, and sometimes, according to others, a year. And some have said—though it is not believed—that such things appear after seven years. **Almansor**, therefore, took the middle part of the beginning as the start, whereas **Avicenna** excluded the first part as the initiating beginning; hence he adds, "after the attraction from the site." When you have drawn out what is possible for you after two or three days, then occupy yourself in evacuating that which has perhaps already penetrated.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that some have said the bitten person is terrified of water because their complexion has become badly equalized, so that they flee grace and desire thirst. For natural imbalances seek similar things, while sickly ones seek grace <note>In this context, the text debates whether the body's altered state "prefers" the dryness of the disease or is repelled by the "goodness" of water</note>. Hence, in the fourth and sixth books, **Rufus** says they are not terrified by water and love to roll in the earth, except because their complexions have already loved dryness, which is why they abhor the grace of the complexion and love what is convenient. On the contrary, **Avicenna** says he detests it immensely. To this discourse there is no turning away. For a turning away toward that which is convenient to the complexion is near to those things to which it does not run; an equal complexion does not introduce...

Even in mirrors and polished glass reflecting images, fear is struck into them. Conversely, those with wasting <term>marasmus: a state of severe malnutrition and energy deficiency</term> and a disordered "complexion" <note>the balance of the four humors</note> that is equally hot and dry still vehemently desire water.

->**On the Corruption of Imagination**<-

Therefore, it is said that this happens more from a **corrupted imagination**. For they "fantasize" <note>original: "fantasiantur"</note> dogs in liquids and polished surfaces, and even within their own internal organs. **Almansur** and **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "balyabbas"</note> and **John** agree: they dread water and abhor it even though they suffer from that great thirst. This reveals that the damage is fixed in the **principal members** <note>the brain, heart, or liver</note> and especially in the brain, according to the eighth book of *Theory*. For the **animal spirit** <term>spiritus animalis: a subtle substance thought to transmit sensation and motion through the nerves</term>, along with the other spirits, is turned toward a "melancholic" nature, from which fear naturally arises. When this happens by accident, it is no wonder if they suffer sadness, fear, and a suspicion of death, with **melancholy** serving as the foundation for the mistress of the rational soul. For nothing occurring from the outside seems to bring as much fear as darkness does.

Indeed, **Rufus** <note>Rufus of Ephesus, a Greek physician</note> says in the eighth book of *Theory* that this passion is a certain species of melancholy. Here, the spirit is so corrupted that it forces one to imagine things that do not exist, and eventually these are perceived by sight, hearing, or the other senses. Thus, in the third book of the *Colliget* <note>the medical encyclopedia of Averroes</note>: because of some fixed sickness, fear or sadness arises, and a vapor that dissolves the brain ascends, into which a thought-form is impressed. By the assent of this form, the animal spirit is generated in such a way that it reaches the **imaginative juncture**, through which the **common sense** <term>common sense: the faculty that integrates the five senses</term> is moved. This then stirs a particular motion so that it is perceived externally.

However, some believe that this fear is sent by **angels or demons**. For when the spirit of sight is burdened by this corruption and encounters liquids or polished surfaces representing an image, it acts by the power of the "dog-likeness" and causes it to be seen. And because the patient has this dread, it strikes a vehement fear. For this reason, physicians command that the liquid they take for their trembling be hidden by a "camel" <note>likely a reference to a specific type of curved straw or hidden vessel</note> which the patient avoids.

I recall, indeed, when I was disturbed by a certain madness during a recovery, it happened to me through a corruption of my imagination that every sight seemed to be my recently deceased grandmother. Likewise, when I had stared into a fire for a long time with eyes wide, there appeared a high, darkish smoke which vanished through a circular motion; this proportional phenomenon is touched upon in the third book of the *Meteorology*. According to **Alexander**, something similar happened to **Antipheron** <note>a classic case cited by Aristotle of a man who saw his own reflection in the air due to weak sight</note> because he saw weakly and not sharply; it was as if he were always looking at his own idol <note>image</note> appearing from the opposite direction. Truly, forms are represented in the "fats" separated in the urine, because every effect is drawn out by the strength of the agent and the aptitude of the matter; this happens here because that poison is vehemently hot, dry, and sharp.

---

Every thing that is derived from another retains a mark of that from which it is produced. For things begun from principles excel in their completion. Also, the matter in which the effect is represented is subtle and easily affected, according to **Galen**. Therefore, the effect of the "forms of dogs" can be generated in the urinal, which, if shaken, causes a dissolution so that nothing appears to remain. This is further argued by the light formative power and the disposition of the urine in the flask, as the heavier parts denote more at the top of the urine, and the lower parts in the middle of the vessel are struck by the dominating parts. Likewise, the "circle of the sediment" <note>original: "ypostasis circulus"</note> acts with the other contents.

Regarding the fourth point, to the first it must be said: **Avicenna** speaks according to their opinion. For his method is often not to affirm something, but to write what the assembly of physicians indicates, besides the prognostics of **Hippocrates** attributed to the prognostics. To the other point regarding the "Diatesseron" <note>the Theriac of Four</note>: it is only seen to be beneficial because of the **gentian**, which treats diseases; if it works otherwise, it is not from the other components, but from this one alone. To the other point: in some cases these things provide help, in others perhaps very little. These were given more as a method by the philosophers than arising from other medicines. Therefore, such things should not be heavily credited to this. To the other point: it appeared that the external application of **theriac** is granted to be beneficial for bites.

### DIFFERENCE 180.

> That in **scabies** <note>an itchy skin disease</note> bloodletting is not to be looked for in all cases. **Avicenna** <note>A.</note> commands it very little in the fourth and seventh books, where he says it is insufficient to apply it when

others have stood out more particularly. Furthermore, **phlebotomy** <term>phlebotomy: the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood</term> is for those whose humors are equally abundant, since it is an evacuation that leads out a multitude of humors, according to the first and fourth books. But in scabies, the humors do not abound equally; rather, it is a "burnt" humor or "false phlegm" that predominates.

Again, wherever **Nature** is found to act, she does so through the most appropriate places; since the physician is an imitator of Nature, and Nature is found to lead things to the skin (as shown by sweat in those undergoing a healthy crisis), the physician should follow. Furthermore, when the blood is good but the humors are few and mildly bad, phlebotomy will snatch away the good and leave the bad behind, according to the first and fourth books. For the same reason, **intercourse** <note>original: "coitus"</note> is prohibited here, because it moves material toward the exterior and excites a hot vapor that reaches the surface of the skin where it putrefies, according to the eighth book of the fourth volume. So too with phlebotomy, because it causes motion in the humors by elevating vapors and fumes from them. Therefore, according to the first and fourth books: "Bloodletting is a disturbance until it clots," and thus sleep follows phlebotomy. Therefore, in scabies, phlebotomy is not always appropriate. <meta>This page continues a scholastic medical debate regarding the treatment of skin conditions, specifically whether bloodletting (phlebotomy) is appropriate for scabies. It moves from the specific case of hydrophobia (rabies) on the previous page to the broader category of "superficial foulness" of the skin.</meta>

The opposite is found in the sixth book of the *Breviary* <note>A common title for medieval medical compendiums, possibly that of Rhazes or Serapion</note>. The occurrence of scabies arises from thick blood that putrefies. For this reason, its treatment begins with **phlebotomy** <term>phlebotomy: the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood, a primary treatment in medieval medicine to balance the humors</term>. Yet **Theodorus Priscianus** <note>A 5th-century Roman physician</note> says that one must first provide aid by a "double extraction" <note>likely referring to bleeding from two sites</note> and frequent purging of the belly. 

Again, bloodletting is commonly prescribed in cases of leprosy. **177.** It is said, moreover, that scabies is a species of leprosy. Furthermore, in the eleventh book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." referring to Galen's "De Ingenio Sanitatis"</note>, the opposite is stated: that opening a vein is only for humors in "synochal" <note>continuous</note> fevers; but it is also used in all other conditions involving the putrefaction of humors. In these cases, a physician can more safely approach the cure. My advice regarding bloodletting is that it should be delayed as much as possible. But in scabies, as is admitted, there is no suspicion of bringing about danger. 

Therefore, bloodletting is beneficial in scabies. First, however, it must be known that **scabies** is a defilement of the body or its surface accompanied by an itchy stinging and moderate ulceration. For this reason, it is numbered among the "common" diseases, as it occupies almost the entire surface of the body, which is how it differs mostly from conditions located under the skin. It does not ulcerate deeply, but with a certain acrimony and stinging due to the "nitrous" or **borax-like** quality <note>original: "bauracitatem," referring to salt-like or caustic properties of the humors</note> acquired by the humor. 

It is called a "superficial foulness of the skin" because it is not commonly treated under the category of "sickness," but rather among those things which are discussed as matters of **decoration** <note>medieval "decoratio" covered what we now call dermatology and cosmetics</note>. For this reason, know that scabies can be regarded in two ways: either it essentially hinders the actions of the whole body—and in that case, it takes on the nature of a sickness, since that is the definition of a disease—or it does not harm all operations but only one, namely that of the skin. From this latter case, a total injury to the body does not arise. And so, it is called a matter of "decoration" insofar as the rest of the body is concerned, though it remains a "disease" in regard to the skin. This is like a small injury to a finger: even if it does not hinder the action of the whole person, it is still a disease of the part in which it occurs, so that the virtues <note>natural powers</note> of that part are hindered in their proper actions; it is a disease not of the finger, but only of the part it falls upon. But because scabies rarely hinders the whole body, it is placed under "disfigurement" rather than "sickness."

The cause of scabies, like many other complex sicknesses, arises from several factors. The **primary causes** are things like salty, sharp, and bitter foods and drinks; a lack of bathing; not changing clothes; and a lack of exercise and rubbing. The **antecedent causes** are humors "sinning" <note>being out of balance</note> mostly in the blood. The **conjoined causes** occur when a corrupt humor is driven toward the skin.

Regarding this, it must be known that the matter driven toward the skin is either uncorrupted and natural, or it is corrupt and putrefying. If it is the former, it is either "serous" <note>watery</note> or earthy—though more or less thick—from which hair and nails are generated. Or it is moist and vapory, which happens in three ways: 
1. It is subtle, and thus is sent out insensibly as vapors through a not-so-hidden transpiration. Whence the authorities say: "Our body always emits a certain warm vapor from itself, warming the nearby air." 
2. It is thick, remaining under the skin and, being affected by the heat of the body and an external power, it turns into **lice** <note>medieval science believed lice were spontaneously generated from corrupt vapors trapped under the skin</note>. 
3. It is of a middle consistency, which is sent out as sweat. 

If, however, the matter is corrupt and virulent: it is either subtle, and from it come **dandruff** <note>original: "furfures"</note> and itching, though to a greater or lesser degree. Or it is thick, and thus it is **scabies**. Or it is even thicker, and thus it causes **alopecia** <note>hair loss</note> and **impetigo** <note>skin infections</note>. 

And note that scabies sometimes stands as a "crisis" <note>the turning point of a disease</note> for certain illnesses, especially chronic ones. And it is a **contagious disease**. What bloodletting is was shown in section 164, along with other details. 

Concerning this, it should be known that some have omitted bloodletting in scabies, following the view of **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."</note>. For phlebotomy, while useful for evacuating humors, should be used for humors that "sin" in quantity, but not for those that are "persistent," which are the kind that generate scabies. And because the matter of scabies seems to exist outside the veins, as is shown in the third and fourth propositions. 

Nevertheless, it must be known that bloodletting is appropriate in scabies, as almost everyone states or allows, provided that other indicators do not stand in the way—those taken from the "virtue" <note>the patient's strength</note> and its consequences, and from the "non-natural things" <note>the six environmental factors of health: air, food/drink, sleep, etc.</note> that intermediate between strength and disposition. 

This is demonstrated as follows: because its matter exists **inside the veins**, not outside. Indeed, first, since blood dominates here, phlebotomy is beneficial. For that is the proper evacuation for blood. This is confirmed because, in the fourth and seventh books, it is said that the matter from which scabies is generated is either **sanguineous matter** <note>blood-based</note> mixed with **choler** <note>yellow bile</note> which has perhaps turned into "malice" <note>toxicity</note>; or a part of it has turned into malice as matter mixed with "salt phlegm" or borax-like salt. Whence the fourth book of *Practice* says: Scabies arises from salt phlegm mixed with melancholic blood. When blood "sins" alone, or even when mixed with other humors, bloodletting is appropriate. It appears in book eight of *On the Method of Healing* that one is not always bled primarily for a multitude of blood, but also because of its "malice" (bad quality), or both. 

Again, it is necessary to cut off each of the efficient causes of a sickness; such blood can be an antecedent cause or an immediate cause, like those which are conjoined. For this is a cause that is entirely antecedent. Furthermore, a more common treatment should be applied to a common ailment, so that each thing is proportionally matched. Bloodletting and scabies, as introduced, are such things. Therefore, bloodletting is suitable in scabies. 

If, however, the humors causing it were **not** in the veins, but had already been driven to the skin—being very much alienated from the blood—then, conversely, bloodletting would not be appropriate. In that case, one would fear that the corrupt matter would be drawn back **inside the veins**, where it could putrefy further and cause a fever. This must be avoided above all else, since that would be a sign of some greater sickness; rather, the matter should be drawn toward the skin as much as possible, as is commanded to be done during the "crises" of abscesses. 

Therefore, in such a case, one must bloodlet for a single purpose: in scabies and itching, **pharmacy** <note>medication/topical treatments</note> is more necessary than bloodletting, since the humors from which they are caused are far removed from the blood—such as that which is the "cleansing of the blood," purifying it from the infections of other superfluities. 

Regarding the first point, it must be said that **Avicenna** does not deny bloodletting; rather, he makes it even more recommended when he says: "The first and best cure of scabies is evacuation," along with that which brings the humors to a state of being burned away.

### DIFFERENCE 181.

¶ **Whether a breach of continuity** <term>breach of continuity: "solutio continui," a medical term for a wound where the natural connection of tissues is broken</term> **penetrating to the interior of the skull can be treated without the lifting of the bone**, according to nearly every authority of all writers and practitioners. **Galen** indeed says so in the first part of the sixth book of *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "terapeutice"</note>; **Albucasis** <note>An influential medieval Andalusian surgeon</note> in the 13th part of his manual operations; **Haly Abbas** <note>A 10th-century Persian physician</note> in the ninth [book] of the *Practice*, parts four and five; and the *Colliget* <note>The medical compendium by Averroes</note> in book seven. These authors, and others as if with one voice, require that the bone be removed from its surroundings. Still, the reason is threatening. If that which seems less likely to occur is present, then also that which is more likely. It seems less likely when a bone of other parts besides the skull is improperly restored and bound, where the fracture penetrates to the marrow, that one must repeat the restoration and binding lest the **sanies** <term>sanies: a thin, greenish, or bloody discharge from a wound or ulcer</term> corrupt the marrow along with the bone. But this must be done because of the accident that follows. Since, therefore, the aforementioned happens in any other bones, how much more so in the bone of the head, since it cannot be bound and restored like the bones of other parts? Therefore, much more so here. Again, if the fracture is a small "capillary" one, because of the thickness of the surrounding parts, the power of the medicine will not be able to reach into the depths, according to the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Art of Medicine"</note> and the seventh book of *On the Method of Healing*. Nor can the matter that has fallen through and become clotted <note>original: "scrossata," likely meaning curdled or thickened</note> in the interior be drawn out through a small fissure. Furthermore, if you say that the treatment of the breach of continuity is done by medicines such as a plaster or ointment without the removal of the bone, it will be necessary that this medicine extract the generated sanies from the inside to the outside. This can only happen in two or three ways. For all attraction in the nature of things happens either by a quality of power—as the **magnet** <note>original: "magnes"</note> draws iron to itself—or by the intention of that which is evacuated. Not indeed before this, because a specific power is a certain natural potential governing the introduction of form into matter according to some aspect of the sphere. But this introduced form, through which such an operation follows, exists by art, and is thus accidental. For all accidental forms are "accidents," which is why this cannot happen by a specific power. Nor by a vacuum, because for the general evacuation to occur, the things attracted must be more subtle than the containing vessel, and not dispersed; these conditions are not found in a plaster or ointment applied externally. For the attraction can be saved by a gap <note>original: "casm", likely 'chasm' or 'cavern'</note> because this is the primary attraction to fill a vacuum. Thus, there is no way to preserve the attraction. Likewise, in a fracture of the bone, a bad "complexion" <term>complexion: the specific balance of humors in a part of the body</term> is introduced not only externally but also internally, which cannot be healed unless the same is removed. Therefore, the medicine must reach the internal place. But the motion of the attractive medicine moves away from that. Again, all wounds except those that are bruised ought to be dried. But drying holds itself with the end, because greater dryness than is proper renders the body colder than it ought to be. This will further block the opening of the wound and trap the sanies inside. Therefore, it is necessary to lift the bone.

The opposite view has also been held, though no one worthy of trust has yet confirmed it by authority. Nevertheless, it can be approached by reason and experiment. By **Experience** <note>original: "Emperia"</note>: Since it is the task of anyone to add what is missing, and especially for a physician. Certain people operating in such a way today cure the primary wounds more laudably and without greater slicing. Also by **Reason**: Because that which brings more severe accidents to the sick person ought not to be admitted, and such is the lifting of the skull bone. For there follows no small pain of the brain, confusion, spasm, and sudden death, as the aforementioned wise men testify. Furthermore, in a strike to the skull, the fracture occurs first, and afterward follows the bad complexion. This bad complexion, as they say, must be removed first in every cure. This is achieved by the applied medicine and not by the lifting of the bone; indeed, the lifting induces a worse complexion. Therefore, one should persist with plasters or ointments without lifting the bone. Regarding the first, it should be known that a breach of continuity or an unequal [wound] happens to all members and is healable, except for the **heart**. For that does not tolerate a breach of continuity. Or unless it reaches the innermost part of the internal side, such as the ventricles of the brain or the depths of the liver, according to the sixth book of *Aphorisms*. For to this, an immoderate exit of blood follows. **Galen** indeed says in the same place: "I have often seen a cutting of the brain be healed." For once in **Nubia, a city of Samaria** <note>This geographical reference is likely a scribal error or a specific medieval tradition; Samaria is in the Levant, while Nubia is in Africa. Galen practiced in Rome and Pergamum</note>, I saw someone have a brain cut very large and deep, and yet they escaped death, which happens very rarely. This breach of continuity receives different names according to the different members it affects; for if it happens to the skin, it is called an **excoriation** or **scarification**; if to the flesh, it is a **plaga** <note>strike/wound</note> or **vulnus** <note>wound</note>.
