<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on skin diseases (scabies) to a detailed surgical classification of wounds and fractures, particularly those of the skull. It references the surgical methods of the "ancients" like Galen and medieval Islamic authorities such as Albucasis and Haly Abbas.</meta>

If an ulcer occurs in a bone or cartilage across its width, it is called an **incision**; if it is along the length and of small size, it is called a **fissure**; if it is large, it is a **perforation**. When it happens to the muscles <note>original: "lacertis"</note> across the width, it is called a **separation**. If it occurs at the extremity—that is, in a tendon <note>original: "corda"</note> or nerve—along the length, it is called a **liquefaction** or **dissolution**. When it occurs at the very end of these, as in a tendon or nerve, it is called a **bruise**. If it occurs in the arteries or veins, it is called an **opening** <note>original: "apto," likely referring to *apertio*</note>; if width-wise, an **incision** or **separation**; if lengthwise, it is named a **fissure**. If it occurs in a membrane <note>original: "panicuľ," referring to the *panniculus* or thin tissue layers</note>, it is called a **rupture**. If in the joints, it is called a **separation** or **dislocation**.

### Differences in Diagnosis
What the skull <term>craneum: the bony structure of the head</term> is and its composition is discussed in section 39. Next, it must be known that the modes and shapes of the **solution of continuity** <term>solution of continuity: a medical term for a break in the natural connection of parts, such as a fracture or wound</term> of the head, along with their names and causes, are multiple. Some are simple, and others are compound. The simple type is also manifold: one is in the skin only; another is in the skull, which is properly called a **fracture**. Furthermore, some fractures reach halfway through the skull. The skull is composed of two layers <note>original: "ptibus," parts</note> with many small cracks and windings between them, which are called **tables** <term>tables: the inner and outer layers of the flat bones of the skull</term>. Some of these fractures penetrate entirely to the interior. There is another type that breaks the **dura mater** <term>dura mater: the tough outermost membrane enveloping the brain</term> and the **pia mater** <term>pia mater: the delicate innermost membrane enveloping the brain</term>; another reaches the marrow of the brain, and some reach the ventricles, which is judged to be **mortal**. 

There is also a type of **contusion** where the outer skin does not appear injured, yet the bone inside is fractured—or even if not fractured, there is a rupture of continuity and a bruise inside. Another type is broad, where the bone is broken into many pieces. In another type, the broken bones are pushed inward. Some are extremely fine and do not appear except by using a "closure" <note>likely an ink-test</note> or by applying a colored liquid which sinks into it; this is called a **capillary** or hairline fracture. It also happens sometimes that the skin or bone is not broken, but it is dented inward like a metal vessel when it is struck hard; this occurs in the soft heads of children.

Fractures are also distinguished by the objects that cause them. One is caused by the strike of a sword which removes the whole bone until it penetrates the membrane; this is called an **axial fracture**, for it is similar to an incision made in a piece of wood. Or, the sword cuts only the upper part of the bone without full penetration, which they simply call a fracture. That which is caused by a stone or other blunt object is called an **attrition** <note>a crushing injury</note>. A **perforation** also occurs in the skull, caused by sharp-pointed tools. These may occur at the top, front, back, right, or left side, and each can be either penetrating or non-penetrating. A **compound fracture** is when the break or rupture of continuity is accompanied by the loss of flesh and ulcers. 

Because of this, it must be known that these various separations of continuity are healed in different ways according to the indications they present. Regarding all such fractures, omitting the method of treatment for the moment, the **capillary fracture** is taken as the primary example, as it serves as a pattern for the others.

<margin>A.</margin> All those writing up to now have treated this type of rupture by the **scraping** or removal of the skull bone, 

---

devising this through the invention of many suitable instruments. One of these is a narrow and thin-edged, very sharp instrument; after this, they command a wider one to be used, and even wider still if necessary. There is also another instrument, a **fine saw** skillfully made, with which the bone is lightly sawn. Another is called a **borer** or **trepan** <term>trepan: a surgical drill used to remove a circular piece of bone from the skull</term>, which has a sharp point proportioned to the thickness of the skull. So that it does not penetrate too far, a rounded "guard" is left on top to prevent it from reaching the interior. With this instrument, the bone is perforated with frequent holes, and then the spaces between them are cut with a sharp divider, just as one bores through walls with a small drill. However, they use this instrument on stronger people and thicker skulls.

There is also another instrument called the **lenticular** <note>original: "lenticlare"</note>, so named because its protruding tip is shaped like a lentil <note>original: "lens"</note>, which is struck with a mallet. This is perhaps the instrument praised for this purpose which **Galen** calls the *colophisos*. Before using these, if the skull is not already open, they command that a **crucial incision** <note>a cross-shaped cut</note> be made over the site. If blood flows out, they order the spot to be stayed with a **rosate cloth** <term>rosate cloth: a linen cloth soaked in rose oil or water</term> and wine until the swelling subsides.

They command that this elevation of the skull be delayed longer unless it has reached the dura mater. However, they distinguish between **summer** and **winter**, for it is done sooner in the former and later in the latter. Whence **Albucasis** <note>A famous 10th-century Andalusian surgeon</note> says: *In the days of winter, you must strive to remove the bone before the 14th day, according to the condition. But if it is in the days of summer, you should hasten to remove the bone before the 7th day, before the membrane under the bone becomes corrupted.* If this corruption happens, severe symptoms occur, denoting a "loss of majesty" <note>likely a loss of vital function or consciousness</note>, such as a flare-up of bile, loss of intellect, loss of voice, fainting, acute fever, and bulging or reddening of the eyes. Patients are rarely cured when these conditions are present.

**Haly Abbas** <note>A 10th-century Persian physician</note> determined the time for bone removal thus: *If it is winter, it is necessary to take out the piece of bone before the 14th day. If it is summer, before the 7th day, before the aforementioned symptoms are suffered.* For if they are suffered, you should apply no cure, as death is imminent. Lest pus be poured into the interior, the bone must be extracted if the head wound is "complete"—that is, if it does not require the removal of the bone <note>meaning the wound is already open enough</note>. Otherwise, it should be cut as previously described if it is not "complete," so that there is no delay in its restoration. It must not be delayed beyond 7 days in summer or 10 to 14 in winter. The faster it is done, the better, and the further one is from great harm. 

But if the rupture of continuity reaches only the dura mater, they command it be treated on the first or second day in the manner described. In these fractures, they also take care that the perforation they make is not in a place where a nerve might run or where a membrane exits the brain. Similarly, they bore into the thinner part and place of the skull from which the **sanies** <term>sanies: a thin, greenish-yellow discharge from a wound, often mixed with blood</term> can be more freely purged. Whence **Galen** says: *For I know that we saw a certain man's head where the skull was fractured and the bone which they call the **temporal** <note>original: "tympore"</note> suffered...*

...because there was an incision in the skull <term>craneo: the bony part of the head</term> and the sick man was restored to health. And he lives still. For if I had neglected the skull, the membranes <note>original: "pellicłe," referring to the meninges</note> that were beneath it would certainly have rotted before the bone could solidify, because unless I knew that the pus <term>sanies: an infected discharge of blood and thin pus</term> would always descend from the upper to the lower parts, the incision of the bone would not have been useful.

### Differences in Bone Healing
The bones of the head also differ from other bones. For when they are broken, nature does not restore over them a "callus" <term>porum/ros bo͠m: a hard, bony substance that forms around a healing fracture</term>, just as it brings and causes to grow over other bones; rather, it remains a weak thing. This also appeared in the clever arguments from the discourse of Galen <note>original: "Ga.," the famous 2nd-century Greek physician</note>. However, that which moved them to the incision or perforation of the bone and its elevation was the purging of the pus and its retention, which is done lest the brain be corrupted. Whence, in the seventh book of the *Collections*: "If the fracture is in the skull bone such that it penetrates all the way to the membrane, then it is necessary that the bone be removed around the cut so that the membrane can be cleansed of pus, lest it be corrupted; and if it were not done so, it could not be healed." 

But in this place of ours, those who know how to do this are not found. Regarding the third point, it should be known that there is a need to teach another empirical method <term>empiricū: based on observation and experience rather than just theory</term> for curing the aforementioned solutions of continuity without the elevation of the bone. And this indeed is accomplished with the application of plasters <term>empsoʒ/emplastrum: a medicated paste spread on cloth</term> or ointments alone, without any elevation of the bone. 

### Guidelines for Treatment
One must observe, however, that these should not be applied in cases where the severe symptoms mentioned before already appear, as the foolish and "Methodic" <note>A medical sect that followed rigid formulas regardless of the individual case</note> practitioners do, using these medications without any indication except from the disease, and still smelling foully <note>possibly referring to the improper preparation of medicines</note>. Nor should they be applied in places where, because of a contusion of the skull, humors have gathered internally upon the **dura mater** <term>dura mater: the tough outermost membrane enveloping the brain</term>, or when the fracture does not penetrate and the aforementioned course has occurred. This can be understood through the fearful symptoms noted.

Therefore, these two conditions having been first established, let this empirical mode of cure be recounted, which is twofold. Some, after the flow of blood has ceased in whatever way after the second, third, or fourth day, apply this plaster: 

#### An Empirical Recipe
They take **Doric** or **Malvasia wine** and soak **tow** <note>original: "stuppas," coarse flax or hemp fibers used for dressings</note> in it. Then they wring it out and finally have powders of **plantain** and **fern**, not too violently crushed. First, they sprinkle the powder of plantain over a small cushion of tow and put it on in a larger quantity; then they add the fern in a smaller quantity. Some also add a portion of **black beans**, toasted and crushed in the same way. Over this cushion, they place many other things soaked in the aforementioned wine and wrung out, applying them diligently. They leave it for three or four days, especially in winter. Finally, to draw out the matter further, they use a **leaven plaster** externally. For its nature is to pull matters out from the depths of the body. Afterward, they use some consolidating agent. 

I have seen this method to be useful and have tested it sometimes, though they do not apply it to other members besides the head. For just as I have seen idiots elsewhere applying prepared things that did not fail to pull toward the part, there is a more artificial, useful, and common method now made effectively, such that after the hemorrhaging of blood, such an ointment is applied over it:

...it measures by quality and a certain astringency <term>stipticitatem: a binding or contracting quality used to stop bleeding or dry out wounds</term>, also strengthening the injured parts. From these qualities, something balanced arises that is contrary to every injury. Haly <note>referring to the Persian physician Haly Abbas</note> shows that it is possible to draw out the aforementioned matter to the exterior. Indeed, he prepares for us medicines to be placed under the navel to attract humors <term>humores: the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that governed health</term> from the body; he suggests holding medicine in the hand to attract humors, or placing it under the foot to draw them from the head.

Therefore, a plaster or ointment applied to the area will be better able to attract humors, since its path is through the small pores <note>original: "rimulas," literally "little cracks"</note>. Likewise, pain arises for two reasons: a bad "complexion" <term>complexionem: the specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in an organ</term>—caused by a sudden alteration—and the continuous dissolving of the parts. These causes often lead to worse symptoms, such as the brain being affected by the elevation of the bone, leading to its protrusion, fever, spasms, fainting <term>lincopim: a medieval Latinization of "syncope"</term>, and not infrequently, death. One should not choose a treatment that does not work; the elevation of the skull causes these dangers, as the same authority testifies. For the skull is the shield and defense of the brain.

Similarly, in the sixth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." referring to Galen's *De Ingenio Sanitatis*</note>, a preparation called *Colofisos*—which is highly praised by him and others—is said to be less troublesome to the brain than others. Yet it is not entirely free from suspicion, since the skull of the head is moved by it, at which time the head must necessarily be kept still. Thus, treatment with plasters or ointments is more praiseworthy than that induced by the elevation of the bone. But the reason all do not agree on this mode of cure is that they are ignorant of the medicine, or because they are truly afraid to depart from their accustomed school of thought, wishing to keep their reputation unharmed and lofty. For vain ideas surrounding various "heresies" <note>here meaning "schools of thought"</note> are like a difficult itch; it is indeed curable by a natural principle, yet they fear to imitate this new and unaccustomed method. 

For as Galen says, doctors commonly used a medicine to mitigate the pain of the head after the elevation of the skull bone. However, a certain senior doctor in our city used to work upon the membranes <note>the meninges covering the brain</note> which are under the skull; as soon as he stripped them from the bone, he placed a preparation called an *epithema* <note>original: "effisios," a topical poultice</note> and over the ointment he placed a mixture of honey and vinegar. He was very studious in this medicine; I have not seen it done by anyone in Rome, nor did I have the audacity to perform it myself. Regarding this, however, I will be a witness before God: if you wish, many were cured by him with this medicine in Asia <note>likely referring to the Levant or Byzantine territories</note> than by those who applied pain-mitigating medicine. Therefore, I want to prove this myself when I am in Asia. Because I am in Rome now, I have postponed it because I have followed the Roman surgeons. Wherefore Avicenna <note>original: "A."</note> in the third book, while citing these two methods of treating a skull fracture, says: "A greater safety comes through the latter method than through the former," and this is not surprising since the complexion of the bone and the membrane is dry, according to Galen. Thus it appears that Galen doubted the power of the medication, lest the local virtue be frustrated. So even now, many rightly doubt—perhaps lest the effect appear as praiseworthy as it does in Arabic regions, where this method of healing originated. This doubt is unnecessary, since experience of it has been verified in those regions; and perhaps in temperate regions its effect is even more praiseworthy, as it can most effectively prevent the "wine-like" <note>possibly referring to the color or consistency of the discharge</note> state, although it does less harm than other things. 

Let this method of treatment, therefore, be brought into use more securely from now on. Regarding the fourth point—concerning the authority of the writers—it has already appeared what should be said. Regarding the other point, it must be said that the applied medicine does not allow the poured-out matter to rot; for it draws it out first. Or if it begins to rot, it does not become so foul, nor does it stay so long that it harms the things of the brain. In the counter-argument, however, it was assumed that the pus was already causing harm.

To the other point, it must be said that it can indeed penetrate by the power of nature, aided by the medicine. For nature, in a time of sickness, draws the medicine to itself, just as it draws food in a time of health—as stated in the seventh book of the *Breviary* <note>a medical compendium</note>. This is both because the ointment, through its own thin and subtle moisture, "breathes" through the parts of the bone and opens the surrounding areas, and because the substance of the medicine, resolved into a subtle vapor, can penetrate through the narrowest crack. Matter can also be drawn out through even a hair-thin crack. For if it penetrated from the outside to the inside, it can also be led back out, because of nature expelling it and the medicine thinning and attracting it. If, however, it did not enter that way, the crack will still be treated in that manner. If the matter has truly gathered inside, which is known by its signs, then it is necessary—as has been said—to procure the elevation of the bone as the ancients taught. 

To the other point, it must be said that attraction occurs by its own power in the case of a restorative medicine. If it is said that a "specific virtue" is not found in artificial things, it must be answered as in the 178th *Differentia*. To the other point, it must be said that wise nature first draws the vapor of the medicine to itself, which resists the bad complexion; then, nature expelling and the applied medicine attracting from the outside, it expels the dissolved matter. And thus, by removing the cause of the bad complexion, it removes the complexion itself. Finally, it is true that wounds must be dried when we wish to consolidate <note>to close and heal the wound</note>; but by this medicine we do not intend to consolidate yet, but rather to open and purge the rotten matter. When the purging has been completed, then one proceeds to the cure with dry astringents, especially since "consolidation" means the coupling of previously distant parts, which is achieved by temperate heat and more so by dryness. And the untrained practitioner <term>idiota: a person lacking formal medical education</term>—the detractor of medicines—not knowing how to change the medicine after the purification of the settled matter, errs by thinking the aforementioned medicine should be for consolidation. Similarly, he erred because he wanted to cure every sickness with this, even though it is specific to the head. However, I hear from experts that it is also used in chest wounds to evacuate fluid from the breast. One must be careful, though, when and for whom it is applied, and with what "bridle" it is restrained, lest it induce a greater action than is expedient.

### DIFFERENCE 82.

> That in apoplexy <term>apoplexia: a sudden loss of consciousness or paralysis, similar to a stroke</term> nothing should be operated upon within 72 hours, as the fifth book of *Practica* testifies.

Furthermore, in a fatal illness, one should not operate but only use prognosis <term>pregnosticia: the art of predicting the course and outcome of a disease</term>. Wherefore the first of the *Aphorisms* <note>referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates</note> says: "In those states where death follows, we use only the prognostic part of the art, foretelling what will happen."

<meta>This page continues the medical discussion from the previous section, transitioning from the surgical treatment of skull fractures to the diagnosis and prognosis of apoplexy (stroke). ...which will happen as we know in the account of those things that occur. And in Section 3 of the same: **One should not strive in the case of the conquered.** <note>This refers to a common medical maxim suggesting that physicians should not attempt heroic interventions when a patient is clearly beyond saving, to avoid bringing medicine into disrepute.</note> Also in Section 11 regarding the eye: In cases where health is despaired of, it is vain for the ignorant to disparage those treatments that have healed many aids. 

But **apoplexy**, and especially the "greater" kind, is mortal. According to that ancient saying: *To resolve a strong apoplexy is impossible.* Furthermore, in a crisis <term>crisis: a turning point in a disease where the patient either begins to recover or declines toward death</term>, nothing is to be done, according to the first book of the *Aphorisms*. <note>A reference to Hippocrates' Aphorisms, the standard medical textbook of the era.</note> Since some apoplexy occurs during a crisis—as stated in the third part of the first book—when an apoplectic patient has a fever, wait on their condition until the outcome is revealed. Perhaps it is a crisis; let there be a delay of up to **72 hours**, for such a time the ancients command burial to be deferred. <note>Medieval physicians often warned against premature burial for stroke victims, as they might appear dead but eventually "awaken" if the crisis passed.</note> 

Again, in the fourth book of the *Aphorisms* and the first book on *Crises*: whoever attempts to resolve phlegmatic humors <term>phlegmatia: an excess of phlegm, one of the four bodily humors, thought to be cold and moist</term> with medicine at the very start of illnesses gains nothing, because the raw passion <note>original: "cruda... passio," meaning a disease caused by "undigested" or "unripened" humors</note> is not diminished; instead, the medicine liquefies the healthy parts and the resistance to the illness. 

The reason for this is that the matter of apoplexy is sometimes appearing and deeply "wedged." This is supported by the third book: know that appearances and **palsy** <term>palisis: paralysis or loss of motor function</term> constrict the passages of the brain, because there are no medicines that cause a proper evacuation of the specific matter causing them. **Hippocrates** <note>original: "ypocras"</note> commands one to rest in that state, but apoplexy, like other very acute illnesses, is immediately in a state of crisis according to the first book of the *Aphorisms*. 

And the physician operates with three instruments: **diet, potion, or surgery.** These are the three tools through which he assists the necessities of nature. Not indeed with diet, since according to the maxim: *For extreme diseases, extreme cures*—meaning to give nothing—are best for certainty. This is the case with apoplexy. Nor should one use a potion, because it either alters the undigested matter, or (if it is hot and dry) it liquefies and dissolves it, which actually increases the matter and wedges it further. Hence, in the eighth book of *Therapeutics*: "It is better to leave the foul humors <term>cacchomicam: from the Greek 'kakochymia,' meaning bad or corrupted humors</term> to be purged later." Nor should evacuative medicines be used, since one should medicate and move matter that is "digested," not "raw," which is the state of apoplectic matter. Nor is manual operation <note>surgery</note> used, as it presupposes the aforementioned tools. 

Therefore, in apoplexy, **nothing should be done before 72 hours** or three days, so that some action of nature may first appear. **Mesue** <note>a famous Persian Christian physician</note> thinks the opposite in his practice. Again, in the fourth book of the *Aphorisms*: to medicate in very acute cases if the patient faints on the same day it is delayed is a bad sign. This is especially true in apoplexy, for it is very acute and rational. 

Since the physician is the diligent minister and helper of nature, he must govern it more in the most dangerous cases. Such is the case of those with apoplexy, since in them, all governing power is immediately taken away. Therefore, one must operate quickly within 72 hours.

## On the Causes and Modes of Apoplexy

First, one must know what apoplexy is; second, its many causes and modes; and third, how it comes about and differs from certain other conditions. 

Regarding the first: know that **apoplexy is a "softness" of the whole body** with the removal of the governing power, as stated in the third book on accidents. Hence, in the third book of the *Aphorisms*: *It is the sudden insensibility and immobility of the whole body.* **Cassius Felix** <note>a 5th-century Latin medical writer</note> says this disease is so named because the patients collapse from a "deadly blow" to both body and soul. Hence **Theodorus** says: They are called apoplectics because they are struck as if by a sudden blow. 

Furthermore, in the third part of the first book: It is the idleness of the limbs from sense and motion due to an obstruction occurring in the **ventricles of the brain** and in the passages of the **sensible and motor spirit** <term>spiritus: a subtle substance believed to carry sensation and motion through the nerves</term>. It is an "accident" <note>a symptom or secondary condition</note> just as epilepsy is, because of the wicked convulsive motion in it. Indeed, the action of the body is damaged. It is an acute passion accompanied by spasm, and a disease insofar as it damages the very shape and fills and obstructs the receptacles.

Regarding the second point, know that apoplexy is sometimes caused by an **external cause**, such as:
*   **Extremely cold air**, as sometimes happens to travelers in a time of great frost; the cold constricts and narrows the internal moisture and spirits so they cannot pass through the parts. 
*   **A blow or a fall**, which immediately deprives one of motion.
*   **Drunkenness**, as the fifth book of the *Aphorisms* states: *If someone who is drunk suddenly becomes speechless and develops a spasm, he dies unless a fever takes him,* or unless he speaks within the hour that the "hangover" <note>original: "crapule"</note> is resolved. 
*   **Constriction of the neck**: One can constrict the arteries and the **jugular veins** and nerves under the chin so vehemently that he falls into apoplexy. When the arteries and veins are obstructed from the vehemence of fullness, it results in the same thing that happens when the two "apoplectic veins" <note>the carotid arteries</note> are constricted.

Or it arises from an **internal cause**. This is mostly generated by blood, and least by other humors. These obstruct by their sheer multitude, either appearing suddenly (which induces a more pernicious apoplexy) or occurring gradually in the brain itself or in the passages of the spirit. This happens when blood or excessive phlegm is poured into the ventricles of the brain, or in the passages of the spirit to the brain when the arteries and veins are obstructed by extreme fullness. Thus, the spirits have no passage. 

Apoplexy is also commonly considered a disease of the brain by physicians. However, according to **Aristotle** <note>original: "Ap̄," likely referring to the Philosopher</note>, it is a disease of the **heart**. He says that in the elderly, when a coagulated or dissolved liquid falls into the heart, it causes a collapse due to the weakness of the innate heat. And rightly so, because apoplexy happens to those of a certain age. **Avicenna** <note>original: "Ay."</note> wishes to say that when moisture moves toward the "apoplectic" veins of the heart, it suffocates them immediately. This follows the common ancient series: *To the elderly, catarrhs <term>catarrhi: a downward flow of humors from the head</term> cause rapid death.*

According to **Hippocrates**, there are two types of apoplexy: **strong and weak** (or major and minor). While it is impossible to resolve the strong, the minor is not easy. According to **Avicenna** and **Avenzoar** <note>original: "3oar," a famous Andalusian physician</note>, there is one type worse than all others, in which neither breathing <note>original: "hannelitus"</note> appears, nor foam, nor the voice of a strangled person; it is so severe that it is not far from death.

...dead. And there is another [form] in which motion and **breathing** vanish, or the spirits are so weakened that breathing becomes difficult; indeed, in that state, there is a foaming, and the person’s voice is like that of someone being strangled. This description is common to the first and third types, for **Aristotle** <note>original: "A." refers here to Aristotle, though in other contexts it may signify Avicenna.</note> writes of the former, and thus there will be only two types. 

There is also a third type in which the damage does not greatly affect the breathing, and what is put into the throat penetrates [is swallowed by] the patient, who does not faint from the severity, although one may have confidence in their recovery. Regarding the **Aphorisms**, however, four or five types are identified according to **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note>: 

1. One in which **insensibility** is suddenly rendered in the whole body, except for respiration alone; if this breathing is eventually blocked, it will be the greatest and most acute apoplexy.
2. Another in which the patient breathes, but with a violent and extreme vehemence; this is a strong apoplexy. 
3. Another which is strong but less so than the previous, where the patient has an unequal, disordered, and difficult respiration, yet without such tension and violence.
4. And the remaining type in which some order is preserved, though it is weak; this type may perhaps be healed if all appropriate measures are taken.

Regarding the aforementioned, one may hesitate because so many different species of apoplexy are enumerated. It must be said that the condition is distinguished either by its end—which leads to death or to life—just as the description of any illness is marked by its **crisis** <term>crisis: a turning point in a disease where the patient either begins to recover or declines toward death</term>. Thus, there are two modes. Or it is distinguished by the symptoms, such as the state of the breath and the spirits; in that case, three, four, or five categories can exist depending on how they are considered. 

Furthermore, a doubt is raised because it was said previously that in the stronger apoplexy, sense and motion are taken away from the whole body, except for breathing. Note, however, that in some cases breathing does not appear, yet their **pulse** does not entirely fail. It must be said that Galen touches upon a certain apoplexy in which the motion of every part fails, such as that which is greatest and most acute. Or perhaps he is speaking of the loss of motion caused by the **animal virtue** <term>animal virtue: the power centered in the brain responsible for sensation and voluntary movement</term>, but not the **vital virtue** <term>vital virtue: the power centered in the heart responsible for life-sustaining functions like the pulse</term>. For Aristotle <note>original: "A."</note> does not simply deny that any motion remains, but rather the motion of the animal virtue; the motion of the vital virtue, such as the pulse, can still be present. Respiration fails because it is an act of the animal virtue, the defect of which signifies apoplexy. When the brain is obstructed in apoplexy, the **animal spirit** <term>animal spirit: a subtle substance thought to travel through nerves to cause movement and sensation</term> is unable to proceed from the brain into the nerves and muscles; the movement of the chest ceases, and the living being is suffocated.

It should be known that apoplexy shares characteristics with several similar diseases, either in the affected organ or the symptoms. However, it differs in not a few ways from **epilepsy**, *subeth* <term>subeth: an Arabic-derived medical term for a state of deep, morbid sleep or coma</term>, stupor, "congelation" (catatonia), syncope, and **suffocation of the womb** <term>suffocation of the womb: a historical diagnosis where the uterus was believed to migrate and cause respiratory distress</term>. 

*   Apoplexy and **epilepsy** agree in their subject (the brain) and their cause (mostly obstruction by vapors), and in the symptom of labored breathing. 
*   They differ in degree, for apoplexy is more severe; it either kills quickly or turns into **paralysis**. 
*   Apoplexy differs from *subeth* because the apoplectic patient makes a sound with labored breathing and a total loss of sense and motion, whereas the *subethic* patient can be understood and even roused. 
*   It also differs from "congelation" and stupor; those with stupor keep their eyes closed, while those with **catalepsy** keep them open. 
*   *Subeth* differs from **syncope** (fainting) because the pulse in *subeth* is stronger and similar to a healthy pulse, whereas in syncope it is weaker and harder. In syncope, the skin turns yellow or deathly pale and the extremities grow cold, which does not happen in *subeth*. 
*   Similarly, *subeth* differs from "suffocation of the womb," for in the latter the patient understands and speaks, while the *subethic* patient understands with difficulty and is entirely mute. 

Regarding the treatment of the apoplectic patient—whether by diet, medicine, or other means—less weight should be given to diet and more to medicine. Some authors teach that in apoplexy, nothing should be done without a prior warning [of the danger of death], such as **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli (c. 832–932), a highly regarded Jewish physician and philosopher.</note> and **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."</note>. Others, like **Mesue** <note>Mesue the Younger, a name associated with influential 11th-century pharmaceutical texts.</note>, argue that one must act immediately so that the physician's failure does not appear to be the cause of death. Delay leads to a swift death. Even if the disease itself is rarely cured, as Isaac testifies, you should attempt from the beginning to withdraw the matter—whether it be **sanguine** (blood-based) or **phlegmatic** (phlegm-based)—as much as possibility allows. 

Others practice out of honor and to provide comfort to the soul. As **Theodorus Priscianus** <note>A 4th-century Roman physician.</note> says: *We visit patients placed under the full weight of despair, not so much for medicine as for the consolation of their minds.* Still others are moved by piety; for if we leave them in this state, death will occur according to everyone’s expectation.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on the treatment of apoplexy (stroke). If the patient's face is red, livid, or green and full of humors, you should use a lancet on the **cephalic vein** <note>The vein in the arm traditionally bled for head-related ailments.</note> or the **saphenous vein** <note>A vein in the leg.</note> so that the material may be drawn from distant locations. Blood should be drawn according to what the situation allows and the quantity of the fullness.

But if you do not see these signs, do not move the patient, nor provide any food or medicines until 72 hours have passed. **Almansor** <note>Referring to the *Liber ad Almansorem* by the Persian physician Rhazes (865–925 AD).</note> in the ninth book says: "If foam comes out from the mouth, the apoplectic patient is not to be treated." Hence it is sometimes said that the action which must be taken in a "true" apoplexy <note>A genuine, severe stroke as opposed to a minor one.</note> results in the patient's health, yet even then, one should not always treat, but only when there is hope of a cure. 

Sometimes, however, a "cloaked" <note>original: "palliata"</note> treatment is performed so that the failure of the art or the physician might not be seen; thus they judge that something should always be done. But what pertains to these matters will be shown in the third and fourth books of the doctors.

Regarding the third point, let the truth be submitted first; then let it be seen why **Balyabas** <note>Likely a Latinized name for an Arabic authority, possibly Yahya ibn Sarafyun (Serapion the Elder).</note> commands a delay of action in apoplexy for 72 hours. I say, therefore, first that one must act immediately from the beginning, and specifically with evacuations in apoplexy, nor should any time be waited for. This is partly so that a failure in the operation—such as appearing to lack mercy or causing the sadness of friends—does not occur as previously mentioned, but rather the opposite, since in acute diseases, prognostications of health or death are not always certain. This indeed is the most acute of diseases. 

For every individual, from their material construction, cause, and humors, and from the celestial bodies, has hidden virtues and properties to which the human intellect cannot reach. <margin>Difference 115</margin> For we cannot reach certainty in the knowledge of such things, since sometimes strangeness—that is, "monstrosities" <note>original: "monstruositates," meaning medical anomalies or outliers.</note>—occurs in diseases, just as in natural things like ulceration of the lungs. 

This is further confirmed by **Aristotle** <note>original: "p. A." likely refers to Aristotle here or perhaps Avicenna.</note> saying: "It happens that a man falls into apoplexy and there is no difference between him and a dead man, nor does any breath appear, yet afterward he revives and is healed." And we have seen many such people. Furthermore, the matter of apoplexy brings a certain "fury" <note>original: "furiositatem," referring to the rapid and violent onset of the disease's matter.</note>. In these cases, it is commanded to act quickly. Again, prescribed documents for such an operation are not found in every season. Therefore, one must operate immediately in apoplexy, though with a disclaimer of the outcome.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that **Balyabas** wanted a delay of action for 72 hours—though some books erroneously, and even contrary to **Rhazes** and **Aristotle**, say 70. For 72 hours constitute three full days, in which it is declared that every humor is vented. <margin>Difference 89</margin> Even a minor illness completes its period in four days. And for this reason, **John** in the ninth chapter <note>A reference to the Gospel of John, chapter 11, regarding the death of Lazarus.</note> says that when **Lazarus** had been dead for four days and was even smelling, which cannot be found in an apoplectic patient, it was ascribed more to a miracle than to nature. Here also the number three is preferred by the philosophers, so much so that it is instituted in sanctifications. 

**Balyabas**, fearing to disturb the hidden action of nature, perhaps also assigned a cause based on the movement of the moon through the zodiac circle according to its quarters and halves. For in the space of three days, the moon reaches the middle of a quadrant. But this can be challenged. For the moon does not reach the middle of a quadrant unless its course is accelerated; for then, as is clear, it moves 15 degrees in a natural day. Three times 15 makes 45 degrees, which is the middle of a quadrant since the whole contains 90 degrees. But if its motion is slowed, it moves only 12 degrees, so that in three days it travels only 36 parts, and thus falls short of the middle of the quadrant. When it is between these two states, it walks through the middle degrees of the zodiac.

But there is doubt regarding the aforesaid, because, as cited, **Almansor** denies treatment when foam appears. But this occurs in the third type of apoplexy according to **Aristotle**; therefore one should not operate when foam is present, and much less in the first type. It must be said that **Almansor** should be listened to in the very act of foaming, because then the patient is being strangled. Regarding those being suffocated or dissolved but not yet dead, they do not report whatever foam is around the mouth. But when foam does not yet appear, there is a space of time to operate, as contained in the writings of **Balyabas**; this opinion coincides here. For many see that cures are more suited to "minor" apoplexy.

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it must be said that **Balyabas** was of that opinion which is not approved at present. To the next, it must be said that in a mortal illness, when one is certain of a very swift death, nothing should be done—which does not always happen here—or nothing should be done without a disclaimer. Ethical physicians undertake the care of the dying without promising health to parents and friends, but only a prolongation of life for days, months, or years; or they act so that the failure of the procedure is not imputed to the physician's ignorance by others. 

To the next, it must be said that nothing should be done during a **crisis** <note>The turning point of a disease.</note> when it happens equally; for then nature must not be disturbed with medicines, according to that **Hippocratic** saying: "one must act especially when nature's drive is greatest." To the next, it must be said that apoplexy does not always arise from what is apparent, which is very bad. Whence **Aristotle** says: "After the speech, I am encouraged." But if it is not so, but there is decay and putrefaction, then it is fatal. It was also said that the matter of apoplexy has the image of "fury," compelling evacuation immediately at the beginning. 

To the next, it should be said that apoplexy, like other illnesses, has a beginning, even if it is brief. One must rest in that state if nature operates sufficiently. If, however, it is not moved, then that is the hour of its motion. To the last, it is said that one should not operate much with diet as long as the apoplexy happens from an internal cause, except after 72 or more hours, and specifically when a minor apoplexy ends in paralysis. But one must negotiate more with evacuation; for although the matter is raw, it has a "furious" habit, requiring evacuation immediately at the start. Which parts and how much they are changed has been shown previously.

Concerning the aforementioned things, a doubt arises because we say that **fever** happens to coincide with **apoplexy**. This does not seem to be the case. Because the **Aphorisms** <note>The *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates, the foundational text for medical students.</note>, in sections five and six, state: "Acute illnesses are rare which are without fever," yet such is the nature of apoplexy. Also, **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina (c. 625–690 AD), a Byzantine Greek physician.</note> says: "Apoplectic patients lie without fever." If a practitioner searches through the practical manuals, he will very rarely find fever associated with apoplexy. Likewise, apoplexy happens suddenly, as if by a touch; hence it is also called "the stroke." Apoplexy, because of its sudden generation, indicates a cold humor, either thick or viscous, suddenly filling the principal ventricles of the **brain** <note>The ventricles were thought to be the seat of the "animal spirits" that controlled movement and sensation.</note> and not according to a **dyscrasia** <note term="dyscrasia">An imbalance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that causes disease.</note> of the whole substance itself. 

But a fever does not happen suddenly. For it is necessary that putrefaction be produced by its preceding causes, then that it be resolved, and then that the putrid vapor seek the **heart**; finally, from the heart, it is spread through the whole body (Difference 88). Fever is also a dyscrasia. It truly comes on gradually. Furthermore, as was said, in a fever it is necessary that the putrid soot seek the heart. However, this cannot happen in apoplexy because, as is seen, a total obstruction intervenes—which does not happen in epilepsy. And it is established that even the most subtle animal spirit cannot be diffused into the more subtle parts (Aphorisms, section 2). Again, because of apoplexy, a very great necessity for ventilation <note>Breathing or the cooling of the innate heat.</note> is induced, so that suffocation alone intervenes (Aphorisms, section 6). 

If, therefore, a fever should supervene, it will be multiplied so much further that life cannot remain; for fever increases the necessity of extinction in no small way (Aphorisms, book 4), since it is a passion of the heart diffused through everything. Therefore, fever cannot coincide with apoplexy. On the contrary, as is seen in **Almansor** <note>Rhazes' *Liber ad Almansorem*.</note> and the gloss on the ninth book: "Apoplexy sometimes happens in the ventricles of the brain from **wind** <note>Refers to gaseous humors or "pneuma," not just digestive gas.</note>, sometimes from superfluous blood, and sometimes from an **aposteme** <note term="aposteme">A swelling, inflammation, or abscess within the body.</note> of the brain." An aposteme of such a noble member will induce a fever (Difference 95). 

**Aphorisms**, book 6: "To whomever pains suddenly occur in the head and they immediately become voiceless and snore, they perish in seven days unless a fever takes hold." But according to the commentaries, this is apoplexy. Therefore, fever falls together with apoplexy. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known what apoplexy is and what its causes and modes are, as was seen before, and what a fever is (87). Regarding the second, it must be known that it appears from the sharpest signs. Regarding the third, it must be known that fever can sometimes coincide with apoplexy. For that which is caused by a "plurian" matter <note>Likely referring to a complex or overflowing humors.</note> soon suffocates by obstruction, just as a fire is corrupted by a covering; and with this brevity of delay, as was proven, it is not able to coincide. Since this most great matter happens to be windy, fever is opposed to it in substance and quality. 

Another type happens from a smaller matter, so that when the brain is invigorated, it is expelled to the side, more often the right side (Difference 183), causing **paralysis**. And with such a movement and agitation of nature, and not because of an aposteme, a fever can be associated, and laudably so, as **Hippocrates** judges; for according to the Commentaries, it heats and dissolves the thick and inflated windiness or the windy matter where it happens. Wherefore, Almansor says: "When an apoplectic patient has a fever, make a delay in that thing <note>Wait before acting.</note> until he is uncovered; for perhaps it is a **crisis** <note>The turning point of a disease where the patient either recovers or dies.</note>." The delay lasts up to 72 hours, as was seen. If these two matters...

---

...should be of a medium quantity, properly speaking, blood that is not immediately suffocating but is sufficiently entering can cause an aposteme. And because such a thing occurs more rarely, it happens less often, as Almansor indicates. This is proved because fever coincides with an aposteme of this noble internal part, as seen in Difference 95; but the brain can suffer an aposteme, as shown in 96. And even with an aposteme, they still suffer apoplexy, especially from blood. Whence also **Aphorisms**, book 2: "All apoplexy happens when the animal virtue cannot flow through into the lower parts of the head, either because of some **phlegmatic** <note>Related to the humor phlegm, associated with cold and moisture.</note> disposition existing in the brain itself or its ventricles being filled with windy moisture." 

And where it is possible to find a joined cause of fever, it will be found in that same inseparable fellowship. But in apoplexy, it is possible that this "soot" seeking the heart is found internally because of the "corruption" <note>original: "sanie"</note> of the apostemes. For it gives a time of three or four days sometimes, in which the joined cause can be sufficiently produced. Furthermore, since the **arteries** are parts of the heart and are ordained for its service, if an extraneous, harmful heat seeks them, it will soon lead back to a suffering of the heart. But this happens to them from an aposteme. 

It is confirmed that when these accidents occur, the first recourse is to the heart as the "base of life." **Mesue** <note>Masawayh (777–857 AD), a famous Persian Christian physician.</note>, *Particularities*, book 2: "Fever can again sometimes coincide with apoplexy, especially a phlegmatic one, though more often without it." Whence Almansor: "When there is fever with apoplexy, then there is an aposteme according to most." 

But a doubt occurs regarding this. Because he says that apoplexy resulting from an aposteme follows a prior apoplexy. Therefore, it does not give time for the production of fever. It must be said that apoplexy exists in three ways, as was touched upon. One is the "pre-eminent" <note>The most severe or sudden form.</note> type and is immediately suffocating. Some are "phlegmatic," and the third is less severe, like those which cause a person to fall into paralysis. From this third type, escape is not rare when one acts against it quickly. From the first, death happens suddenly. But from the middle type, it is deferred for a time, as was seen; yet the last is more severe. Whence Almansor: "If the fever is because of an aposteme and putrefaction, then it is deadly." Thus, according to the physicians, it is more often pre-eminent/deadly. 

Yet there is hesitation because in the *History [of Animals]* book 4, it says that in the brain there is no moderate or large vein or artery; for it has no blood in it and is very dry. Thus, an aposteme cannot be made of blood. It must be said that although an artery or vein is not in the *substance* of the brain, it is nevertheless in the **pia [mater]** <note>The delicate innermost membrane surrounding the brain.</note> enveloping it immediately, and in the **rete [mirabile]** <note term="rete mirabile">A complex of arteries and veins at the base of the brain, once thought to be where "vital spirit" was turned into "animal spirit."</note>, and in the **dura [mater]** <note>The tough outermost membrane surrounding the brain.</note>, so that from there a continuation with the heart is made. By reason of this fellowship of the arteries, the suffering of the brain enters. 

Regarding the fourth point, they have transferred themselves to those things which happen most often, such as the first of the three types of apoplexy. Thus many, as is seen, claim it happens simply from wind. To another, it must be said that it is signified to the mind that apoplexy also happens according to an immediate dyscrasia, since there is no disease without a "complexional" suffering. To which, however, as was shown, a febrile dyscrasia sometimes supervenes. To the other, it must be said that although there is an obstruction of the **nerves** in apoplexy, through which the animal spirits for sense and motion are carried, it is not so with the arteries; thus the putrid soot of the disease is able to seek the heart, especially as was said...

It uses this coexistence as a prognostic sign, noting that a fever can sometimes help "melt" the cold humors causing the blockage.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the medical discourse on apoplexy (stroke) and its related conditions, specifically transitioning into a detailed comparison of paralysis (palsy) affecting the right versus the left side of the body. It relies on the authority of Paul of Aegina and Serapion the Elder to debate which side is more difficult to cure and why.</meta>

In cases of phlegmatic apoplexy, the sudden suffocation of the patient is not found to be caused by an excessive quantity of matter. From this, another point becomes clear: because there is a smaller amount of matter, the necessity for total extinction of life is not so great, allowing life to remain for several days. Perhaps some of the matter even dissolves. Therefore, the necessity of death will no longer be so pressing. This is clearly seen in cases of spasm caused by repletion <note>A "spasm of repletion" was believed to be caused by an overabundance of humors stretching the nerves, as opposed to a "spasm of inanition" caused by dryness.</note>, as the truth of the Aphorisms teaches us.

### DIFFERENCE 183.

<margin>1</margin>
**Whether** palsy of the left side is more difficult to cure than that of the right is a matter of debate, with **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century medical authority.</note> stating it is so. There is a reason why the cure is greater in the latter case: since healing is achieved by its contrary, it is completed more effectively that way. Right-sided palsy occurs because that side is naturally hot and dry, which stands in opposition to the cold and moist matter that causes this passion <note>In medieval medicine, a "passion" (passio) refers to a suffering or a pathological condition of the body.</note>; it is not so in its contrary, the left side. Furthermore, where the vital spirit rules, nature is stronger. Since, according to **Hippocrates**, healers act as the assistants of nature, the illness is easier to cure when the matter can be evacuated and the sickness expelled. This occurs in the right side because that side is more noble and expansive. However, the illness is rendered more difficult to cure when its cause is greater. But more cold matter collects in the left side because it is weaker, and from this, the illness arises most frequently.

Likewise, defects and faults occur in the "ignoble" <note>In this context, "ignoble" refers to parts of the body considered less central to the life force or less anatomically dominant.</note> parts more than in their opposites. According to the third book on the parts of animals, the right side is nobler than the left, just as the back is to the front and the top is to the bottom. Let us consider the same regarding palsy and **pleurisy** <note term="pleurisy">Inflammation of the chest cavity; in medieval medicine, it was often categorized by which side of the ribs it affected.</note>, and even more regarding tremor and **sciatica** <note term="sciatica">Pain resulting from the "sciatic" nerve, often attributed to cold humors settled in the hip joint.</note>. But pleurisy of the left side is worse than that of the right. Tremor and sciatica follow the same rule. In the *Viaticum* <note>The "Viaticum" was a standard medical handbook for travelers and students, originally by Ibn al-Jazzar.</note>, it says: "In the left part it is difficult." Therefore, left-sided palsy will be worse to cure. On the contrary, an illness is harder to cure when it occurs in a nobler part. Thus, illnesses of the **heart** are perilous. So too is palsy of the right side, since it is nobler than the left. Again, an illness is more difficult to cure if it does not tolerate strong medicines, especially when the illness requires strong remedies. But this is the case for right-sided palsy, as it must be cured with hot things. The right is hotter and more vulnerable than the left. Therefore, right-sided palsy is harder to cure than the left.

To understand this, it must first be known that "palsy" is understood in two ways: commonly and properly. In the common sense, it signifies the weakening of any part of the body. Properly, however, it is the loss of sensation and motion in half of the whole body. Otherwise, palsy is called the loss of sensation and motion throughout the whole body, which is the same as **apoplexy** <note term="apoplexy">A stroke; derived from the Greek word for "to strike down."</note>, a name which signifies a "dissolution." Palsy differs from numbness and tremor; in palsy, sensation and motion are entirely absent, but in numbness there is only a weakness of sensation, and in tremor, a weakness of motion. For these two conditions are precursors to palsy. Know also that a greater remedy is required in this than in **tetanus** <note term="tetanus">Used here to describe rigid muscle contractions.</note>, and subsequently in spasm, and finally in tremor, numbness, and leaping. In those, sensation and motion are not entirely lost.

Palsy sometimes occurs on its own, but not infrequently results from another condition, such as choleric apoplexy, acute fever, and similar things. It is also often caused by a vice of the humors, specifically cold humors, but sometimes from a simple quality. According to authorities, it happens from apoplexy, from a crisis of colic and acute illness, dislocation of the vertebrae, cold, a fall, a blow, tight binding, poison, and so on. The right side of an animal is the nobler of the two parts because it is the side that moves, while the left is the baser part that supports. For movement is in the right, while support is in the left.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that Paul and others, following the reasons introduced above, claimed that left-sided palsy is more difficult to cure than right-sided. This is perhaps proven by the weakness of the location itself, since the right side is easier to cure, not considering what happens by accident. First, it should be known that palsy occurs more often in the right side than the left, and finally, that the right side's palsy is worse.

<margin>22</margin>
Regarding the first point, it should be known that experience shows the right side is paralyzed much more frequently than the left. This is especially true when it occurs from a minor apoplexy. Hence, the Aphorisms state that in those who are quite elderly, **catarrhs** <note term="catarrh">A buildup of phlegm; here specifically phlegm descending from the brain.</note> occur because of the rarity and thinning of the passages, so that they perish suddenly; or they become apoplectic or paralytic on the right side. Thus, by a swift transition, they either die or suffer palsy on the right side. But concerning air and water, in others, the sides are dried out. This is because palsy mostly happens from a minor apoplexy due to matter that, when it flows, fills the ventricles of the brain less than in a major one. This flow is naturally expelled to the right side, both because the greater part of this matter collects in the left side (since it is weaker than the right), and because nature always expels superfluity to the weaker part. But once the left is filled, expulsion cannot occur there, as a full part does not receive, only an empty one. Therefore, it is expelled to the less-filled right side. Also, support is in the left, while movement and expulsion are in the right; further, the paths and passages are wider in the right than the left because of heat, and because heat is particularly attractive.

Therefore, it occurs more frequently on the right side. But the opposite seems true: it seems to happen more in the left than the right. As **Serapion** <note>Serapion the Elder, a 9th-century Syriac physician.</note> says: if viscous humor abounds in the two anterior ventricles of the brain, it causes apoplexy. If it is in the posterior, it induces palsy. If it is moved to the weaker side, which is the left, it is evident. Thus it happens more in the left.

It must be said that the "weaker side" in this labor of apoplexy is that which nature, having been stimulated, renders more fit to receive the matter propelled from the brain into the side. Hence, according to Serapion, nature does not delay in preserving one of the two sides by purging, so that it expels the matter to the side that is weaker and more susceptible to receiving the matter first. That side is the right, as has been shown. Regarding the second point, it should be known that right-sided palsy is harder to cure than left-sided. For according to the ancients, it is worse.

...disease which happens with a lack of harmony and disproportion of the particular parts. But such is the case with palsy of the **right side**, as it is more contrary to the body’s nature than that of the left, which is demonstrated by the heat of motion and strength, along with other factors. Nor should we insist on that reasoning used by the moderns <note>The "moderns" likely refers to contemporary 13th or 14th-century scholastic physicians who interpreted Galen and Hippocrates.</note> in their discourse on **Avicenna** regarding acute diseases, where he writes in the first and second sections that epilepsy does not occur in those inhabiting northern regions because they are healthy internally and their innate heat is moderate; but if it should occur, it will be severe, because it only happens due to a powerful cause. And in the same way, in the third part, section 14, he says that a man who suffers from a very severe thirst when dropsy <note>Term: <term>dropsy</term> (Latin: *ydropisis*); an old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid, often linked to liver or heart failure.</note> comes upon him is one whose natural complexion is hot and dry. Note: a person does not fall ill by the contrary of their cause except by some great circumstance. **Epilepsy** and **dropsy** are chronic illnesses, except when epilepsy involves spasms. Furthermore, that illness is more difficult to cure which more severely damages the "fountain" and the matter of life and nutrition, and thus the foundation of the cure. Such is the case with palsy of the right side more than the left, since the heart, by its power, has more regard for the right. 

### Difference 47.

The liver <note>Latin: *Epar*.</note> also, if it is considered in the same light, and any disease that collects a broader matter that is disseminated and inserted throughout, is rendered worse for healing. But this is the nature of right-sided palsy, as has been shown. Nor can we support the basis of the cure in this case, since the noble parts are injured. Therefore, right-sided palsy—especially that which follows a major apoplexy—is worse to cure than that of the left. Perhaps, however, if there were some particular palsy or softening of the parts accompanied by a lesion of the brain and the "nut" <note>Note: "nux" or nut often referred to the medulla oblongata or a specific part of the brain stem in medieval anatomy.</note> and other principal organs, it might be that the left side is more affected than the right, as occurs in gout <note>Latin: *podagra*.</note> affecting the left or right; in such primary passions, the curative principles are better preserved. And thus one should listen to **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina.</note> when he says that palsy of the right side is easier to cure than the left. 

Regarding the first point: to the first argument, let it be said as follows. To the other, let it be said by way of interruption here: even if the right side is hotter and drier than the left, once it is strongly weakened, broken down, and moistened, it does not remain in a state where the "spouse" <note>Note: likely a metaphorical term for the restorative power of nature.</note> of the cure can be easily had, just as if it were in the left side by way of "rheum" <note>Term: <term>rheum</term>; a discharge or flow of humors thought to cause various illnesses.</note>, which takes up more matter in the left. To the other similar point, the truth appeared: it is not because the right side remains in its natural disposition that this happens. To the next, it must be said that although through a mode of congestion or aggregation of matter, an excess of nourishment comes more to the left part than the right by way of rheum, as seen, it falls more heavily upon the right. To the other, it should be said that this mode is verified in the relation of the parts remaining to the heart; however, if injury happens to it from some stronger cause, it is more difficult to remove since no help comes to it from elsewhere, as shown in the lesion of the heart. To the last, it should be said that it is not similar, since these diseases do not damage the parts where they occur as much as palsy resulting from apoplexy. For the principles are more naturally damaged in some way, whereas in a particular palsy of touch, it can happen differently.

### .DIFFERENCE. 184.

->**Whether in facial distortion a local remedy should be placed upon the side that appears healthy.**<-

It is shown by **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a Greek commentator often cited in medical texts.</note> in his *Problems* why, in palsy of the jaw, aids are not applied to the jaw itself but to the other side. Furthermore, a local remedy ought to be applied to the side that falsely appears infirm, since the physician is a practitioner of sensibility and evidence. But that side is the one which *seems* healthy, as Alexander says in the same place. They see the muscle which is on one or the other side of the jaw as the weakest, and the weakest appears as if it were healthy. Also, a local aid should be placed on the "flowing" side <note>The relaxed or paralyzed side.</note>, since in that part the composition is corrupted; but that side, as they say, is the one which *looks* healthy. Conversely, the remedy should be applied to the softened or resolved part so that it may dry out the humidities soaking into it; but this part appears healthy because it does not pull back toward its origin, but rather the other part seems to be pushing it. Therefore, the local aid should be situated on the side that appears healthy. 

To the contrary, in the third part of the second book of **Avicenna**, some have said that the side which is ill in a facial twist <note>Latin: *tortura*; a twisting or distortion of the face.</note> is the one that *appears* healthy, even though the cause is within it, and the healthy side acts by its own power. But this is not entirely true. For **anatomy** <note>Latin: *anothomia*.</note> and what is known about the disposition of the facial muscles <note>Latin: *lacertoz*; literally "lizards," the medieval term for muscles based on their shape.</note> make you understand this corruption. Likewise, the remedy must be applied over the place where the disease is, even if it does not appear to be the unhealthy side, since the sickness exists in the proportion of the parts. Hence, in the fourth book of the *Internal Affections*, it is said: "The healthy side, as you know, is pulled toward the softened side." 

Again, those whose origins are different require different remedies. In this case, one or the other side is twisted. Therefore, the local remedy must be fixed upon the side that is infirm and does *not* look healthy. Regarding the first point, one must know that a "twist" is an official <note>Term: <term>official disease</term>; a disease of an "official" or "instrumental" organ (like a hand or face) rather than a "similar" part (like bone or flesh).</note> disease in the face in which one part is drawn toward its natural side, and the natural form is changed, so that the proper meeting of both lips and both eyelids is removed. The cause of this is seen to be a softening or palsy or dissolution of the "string" <note>Term: <term>corde</term>; can mean a nerve, tendon, or ligament.</note>, namely of the muscles of the face and eyelids. Concerning the second cause: **Serapion** <note>Serapion the Elder, a 9th-century physician.</note> says that nature is sometimes corrupted as in elephantiasis <note>A form of leprosy or severe skin disease.</note> and similar things. Sometimes, however, it is by accident, as in those who are dissolved or paralyzed or spasmed, or those with phlegmon <note>An inflammatory mass.</note> or hardening, or where a nerve is cut, or where the "string" is tied by hard scars. In all these cases, a creeping occurs in one part because of another. For this twist happens through a lesion made in the nerves coming from the **third conjugation** of brain nerves and the **fifth** buried and hidden under the bones of both pairs, and from the nerves coming from the nearby vertebrae of the neck, from which—along with ligaments and flesh—the muscle of the film of the neck is constructed. From which certain passion, even if the two "broad-angled" muscles known by this name in **Avicenna** (which are like cushions according to **Galen**) are affected, nothing less is suffered by the four muscles of the lips and the two of the nose, in which passion the muscles of the eyes and eyelids are also twisted, especially in the area of the distortion. If therefore the location is common, just as when an injury is recognized in the finger from a prior cause, it is because of the injury that happens in the sixth pair of the nerves of the neck. It appears, therefore, from these series that according to the fifth and sixth vertebrae, and finally less so according to the seventh, and least of all according to the eighth, the nerves are carried into the hands. 

To the contrary, in the first book of the *Interiors* <note>Galen's *De locis affectis* (On the Affected Parts).</note>, a certain man falling from a vehicle while he was going to Rome was struck in the top of the shoulder blade <term>spatula: the scapula</term>; sensation had already failed in three fingers of his hand for thirty days, while motion remained unhindered. Regarding this, Galen presumed that in the first cutting of the nerve which is after the seventh vertebra, the blow caused a certain phlegmatic, hard disposition. But the nerve which is after the seventh vertebra and before the eighth comes out from the eighth pair of nerves. Whence, in the fifth book of the *Practice*, where he relates this case, he concludes thus: this disadvantage happens to the nerves which carry sensation to the ring finger and the middle finger, whose origin is from the seventh vertebra of the neck. Wherefore, in the second and first books of the *Theory*, the author expresses this more clearly: the fullness of the seventh pair of nerves of the neck reaches the upper arm. Yet certain branches go to the neck, head, back, and diaphragm <note>original: *dyaflama*</note> associated with the branches of the fifth. But all those of the eighth, after mixing and association, reach the arm and the ulnae <note>the bones of the forearm</note>; nor do any of them reach the diaphragm. However, the branch which is from the fifth pair, having been cut, did not pass through the direct part of the hand and shoulder blade, nor did the one from the seventh reach the upper arm; but that which comes from the shoulder blade into the arm is from the eighth, mixed with the first branch that is born from the vertebrae of the back and tends toward the back. 

This second discourse is truer and more detailed. But he who heard about the "accidents" generally across the hand heard of their supreme beginnings, such as the shoulder blades with their joints, to which the branches of the fifth and sixth pair of nerves are said to reach; or the lesion made in the implantation of the nerves around the fifth vertebra was not of it alone, but communicating with those below. 

That which was acceptable before, he shows to be worthy by what I saw regarding a certain youth falling from the stairs onto his neck, where he incurred a blow around the seventh vertebra, in which motion was diminished and prohibited throughout the hands. But when I was helping him, he began to have better

motion in the right hand, reassuming it from the forearm bones <term>focilia: the radius and ulna</term> forward. But he could not move the end of the upper arm with the forearm bones; in the left, however, it was more so. This happened according to the injury or health of the nerves originating from the seventh and eighth vertebrae. Finally, he was healed perfectly by the dissolving of the swelling through medicine. Let it be said for the present, however, only concerning the variety of this authority. For perhaps a fuller discourse of his will occur hereafter. 

The face is the part which is under the cranium in the front, written of properly in man alone in the first book of the *Histories*. Local aid is what is needed after general evacuation or purging, which is administered first, since in few or none of such people does this sickness happen without a fullness of the body or a bad habit of the humors <note>original: *cacbocimia* (cachexia/cacochymia)</note> which first require evacuation or purging. 

The thing indeed seems to be one thing and is that itself, such as gold or a man. Sometimes, however, it is not seen and does not exist, like a "man-donkey" <note>A reference to a chimera or a logical impossibility</note>. Sometimes also it is seen and is not, as fixed distant stars appear not to twinkle, yet they do twinkle. Sometimes it is and is not seen, as by the placement of different colors, a surface that is flat appears concave from a distance. 

Regarding the certainty of these things, there are two extremes: one which is the exit of sight, but which often deceives faith. For the second part, it must be known that some, paralyzed by the ambiguities and series of different authors, have said the healthy side seen was the sick one. To others, the contrary. And therefore, according to this, the local remedy must be applied in different ways. What, however, should be seen of this will soon be clear from what has been said. 

For the third part, it must be known that enervation or a "twist" <note>Refers to facial distortion/Bell's Palsy.</note> is made by "softness" or by the dissolution of a cord or a visible cutting, which is then placed on the healthy side seen, which is the remedy since it is sick in such a way. And therefore, the flowing [humor] draws from the healthy side, acting directly. For it appears superficially in a distortion that the side which is drawn back is the healthy one. For the side contracting and receding from its due position is sick, like two ends of a rope pulling in different directions fixed to a wheel. For the one that pulls more seems to be repressed and the other raised. 

If, however, the distortion happens from a spasm—either moistening or drying—or from a manifest hardness of a scar, according to Galen, the local aid must be placed upon the part appearing sick and truly being so, such as when hardness or a knotty thing is in the other side to be suspended. This is hinted at in the preceding series. It is also supported by a shorter means, since whatever local remedy is to be applied, even if the appearance is sometimes fantastic <note>i.e., deceptive to the eye</note>, it must be applied over the truly sick part. In a distortion caused by "softness" or something proportional to it, the "healthy-looking" side is actually the sick one, because it has lost its tension and allows the other side to pull it. Therefore, in this case, the local remedy is placed on the side that appears healthy, since it is actually the diseased one. In other distortions, it is placed on the side that is both sick and appears so. This is discerned by certain signs: for when the enervation happens from "dissolution," sensation and motion are dull and slow in it, there is a smoothness in the skin, and the muscles are without extension, and the lower eyelid and other parts droop.
