<margin>Distinction 70</margin>
Regarding the membranes of the palate, the following distortion is softened, moist, and lax; and because it looks toward the lower parts, it appears to be the suffering side. One must consider this: the signs of a dry or moist spasm <note>Latin: *spasmus*; a contraction or convulsion of the muscles.</note> are noted in the spasming part as a contraction with resistance, not as a tightening due to dryness. This causes the skin of the forehead to wrinkle on that side and to be stretched smooth on the other side. There is also a lack of saliva and phlegm, along with an impairment of the senses. The signs of an abscess <note>Latin: *apostema*; a localized swelling or collection of pus.</note> are truly noted in its own part. 

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it must be said that **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Trallians, a 6th-century Byzantine physician.</note> speaks of distortion caused by "softening" <note>Flaccid paralysis or loss of muscle tone.</note> in which he grants that the remedy must be placed upon the side that appears healthy <note>In facial palsy, the healthy side often pulls the mouth toward it, making the healthy side look "distorted" and the paralyzed side look "normal" to an untrained eye.</note>. To the other point, it must be said that although a physician is a craftsman of the sensible and the evident, his perception and manifestation must be true and not "sophistic" <note>Misleading or appearing one way while being another.</note>, such as those distortions that appear due to "dissolution" <note>A loss of structural integrity or nerve power.</note>. For it has been said that some things appear to be but are not; therefore, a local remedy should not be applied to them. 

Similarly, one must proceed when the injury is on the side that appears healthy. 
<margin>Nature</margin>
For although on the weak side the disposition appears corrupted, it is not properly so, but occurs through the "binding" <note>The physical connection and balance between opposing muscles.</note> that the muscles of one side have with those of the other. For when those on the other side are softened, those exercising their action on the opposite side are contracted because they have nothing of equal power to pull against. To the other point, it must be said that this distortion happens from palsy or dissolution; therefore, the remedy must be placed where the disease originated. Regarding those things that appear on the other side, it must be said that in this discourse the distortion is caused by a spasm or an abscess. And because it happens very often that those things said of softening are suitable, Alexander says this is not always true for the common people. To the other point, it must be said that there is no "disease of composition" in the healthy place, even though the distortion from softening happens there in appearance but not in truth. For when a muscle on both sides has its action to perform, if those on one side fail, those on the other side—not being restrained or pulled back—contract into themselves and look infirm, though they are actually performing their action. In a distortion from a spasm, however, the opposite occurs.

## DISTINCTION 185.

<margin>Whether wine...</margin>
**W**hether wine is suitable in diseases of the nerves is shown because, in the second section, old wine in small amounts is very beneficial for all diseases of the nerves. This is confirmed because, in the fifth book of *Practice* <note>Likely referring to the *Almansor* by Rhazes.</note>, it says: "Offer old wine in a moderate quantity as the belly allows." And **Celsus** <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a Roman medical encyclopedist.</note> says the same. Since these diseases are of the nerves, it is even more true that wine which is moving away from its youth <note>Medium-aged wine.</note>, when compared with old wine, is largely suitable to nature, for the difference varies by time. 

<margin>Distinction 70</margin>
Furthermore, this disease will either be from "inanition" <note>A state of depletion or emptiness of the body's vital fluids.</note>, and thus wine is highly preferred because it is treated by moistening; for wine moistens in both act and potential, since among other things it enters the parts quickly and extensively. For it quickly refills bodies subject to depletion, according to the second section. The logic of nutrition is especially preserved in it, since it is warm and moist. 

<margin>Distinction 70</margin>
Or the disease will be from a repletion of humor <note>An excess of bodily fluids.</note>, such as windiness, choler, or similar things, or blood. For these, it is uniquely beneficial; for it digests, cuts through, and resolves. It draws red choler into the urine and makes black choler pass out quickly because it forces it out by the logic of contraries. In the first section, it also clarifies the blood, deriving its dregs to the parts that evacuate them. Furthermore, because it alleviates the animal virtues <note>The "virtutes animales" were the powers of the brain, including sensation and motion.</note> and makes them flourish, it is beneficial to the nerves, since it serves the brain, which is the foundation of the nerves; this is also true of intoxicating wine. 

In the fourth book of *Almansor* and the third book of the *First* <note>Likely referring to Avicenna's *Canon of Medicine*.</note>, it is said that healing and restoration are achieved by the contrary; nerves are cold and dry, while wine (as said) is warm and moist. Thus, the reasoning for contraries is found in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption*. 

But wine causes "repletion-based" diseases of the nerves, such as palsies, spasms, and general paralysis. It will therefore cure those that come from depletion. Therefore, wine is beneficial for passions of the nerves. 

On the opposite side, in the fifth book of *Theory*, the specific nature of wine is to harm the brain and the nerves, for it causes "matters" <note>The harmful humors causing disease.</note> to penetrate them, according to the second section. Hence, **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a Persian physician.</note> says in his *Practice*: "One must avoid wine." For it causes matters to penetrate into the nerves which perhaps would not have penetrated otherwise. And know that wine is an enemy to the eyes and the nerves. Furthermore, everything is changed and corrupted by its contraries in a state of unequal distemper. Wine is contrary to the nerves since it is warm and moist. The nerves themselves are cold and dry, not departing much from an acute temperament. Therefore, wine is not suitable for diseases of the nerves.

Regarding the first point, one must know what wine is (given its variety) and what the distinction of nerves and diseases shows in chapters 70, 41, and 42. Know also that wine is taken either for the sake of nutrition—as it carries itself as food into the parts and is converted into them—or for the sake of medication, namely so that it may alter and comfort. 

Regarding the second point, it must be known that some have said wine is suitable for passions of the nerves both because its heat remits their coldness and because it cooks and digests their superfluities. But these arguments are not valid when those more zealous for the truth contradict them. For although it may heat and moisten the nerves, the nature of the nerves is so refined that contraries in excess harm them. By its very "subtlety" <note>Thinness or ability to penetrate.</note>, it harms by carrying superfluities into them; nor does it help their materials in any way except when they have been digested, at which point it rouses nature to expel them. Others have said it is beneficial because it comforts the virtue and procures digestion, especially when the humors are raw; hence, in the fourth book of *On Preserving Health*, it says wine digests semi-raw humors better than anything else. But this likewise does not hold, because this happens to them in a different way than it appears here. 

Regarding the third point, it must be known that wine simply and by itself harms the nerves, especially when given for the sake of nourishment, as more illustrious authors commonly explain; specifically thin, sharp, yellow wine when it is old is most opposed to them. This is confirmed because that which relaxes the nerves and dissolves matters by leading them into the nerves does not help them, but rather hurts them greatly; and such is wine itself, for its exit is through thin penetration. In the nerves also...

# CLXXXVI

With weak digestion, [wine] is turned into indigestible matter. As has been affirmed, nothing is more harmful to the nerves than vinegar, to such an extent that it has been said by **Rhazes** <note>original: "re.a." (Ratio/Rasis); likely referring to the Persian physician Rhazes.</note> that it is more harmful to women than to men because of the damage it does to the womb, which is of a nervous nature. And already, according to the foremost teachings, wine should be avoided by those suspected of having nerve ailments, as it induces and harms the nerves themselves. But wine is of such a nature as described in the second [book] of *Complexions* <note>A reference to Galen’s *On Temperaments* (De complexionibus).</note>. This is supported by evidence. For we see that men who do not drink wine, whether because of their law—such as the **Hagarenes** <note>A historical term for Muslims, referring to their religious prohibition of alcohol.</note>—or because of a lack of it in places where it is not produced, or out of a fatal loathing or religious zeal, suffer very little from nerve afflictions. 

Thus, wine is simply harmful to the nerves and does not help them; the same applies to cider and especially apple-wines. However, **incidentally** <term>per accidens (incidentally): a secondary effect not arising from the thing's primary nature.</term> and for the sake of medication, it can sometimes benefit them because it moistens them when they have become dried out, especially when mixed with a great deal of water, as in the case of a <term>spasm from inanition</term> <note>A convulsion caused by depletion or extreme dryness of the body's fluids.</note>. In such cases, wine mixed with water should be given as a drink. If wine is mixed with the water one drinks, it is not far from a restorative effect. Indeed, in the first book of the *Breviarium* <note>Likely the medical compendium of Serapion the Younger.</note>, it says one should take a subtle wine of swift penetration, which I judge does not differ much from a strong wine that has been mixed with much water. This is confirmed because water and wine together appear to pass through more firmly than they stay. Wine mixed with water acquires a subtleness and power of penetration, so that reaching the nerves without harm, it moistens them in a twofold way: substantially because of the wine softened by water—so that it moistens them without dryness—and it "kindles" <note>Refers to stimulating the innate heat.</note> because of the water, which is like a dew from the outside. 

It also confers another benefit incidentally because it stimulates digested matter toward expulsion by supporting the natural heat of the organs. Yet, at the same time, it can make matters worse and cause no small harm, which the eleven symptoms of fever indicate; but curatively, it profits because it strengthens and confirms the **virtue** <term>virtus (virtue/power): the body's innate ability to function and heal.</term>. This is shown in its use for **syncope** <note>Fainting or sudden loss of consciousness.</note>, where it is given without distinction. For it comforts the spirit and the heart universally; it gladdens the soul and causes it to rejoice, so much so that nothing is found to take its place. 

According to **Almasor** <note>The *Liber ad Almansorem* by Rhazes.</note> in the fourth book, it helps only in specific cases and incidentally. Know also that wine generally harms when given for nutrition. However, for the sake of medicine, it sometimes profits. Or if by chance it harms the nerves simply, it may still benefit them through the appetite, which is diversified according to whether it is taken in lesser or greater amounts, inducing different effects. Whence **Dioscorides** says: "Old wine, if drunk in excess because of its great strength, is contrary to the nerves and the senses; but for the sake of its pleasantness, if drunk in moderation, it is good." 

Regarding the second point touched upon: a little old wine helps almost all ailments of the nerves; however, a large amount of it is a more harmful thing, so that what is said of the **squill** <note>A medicinal sea onion (Urginea maritima), used as a diuretic or stimulant.</note> is also said of it: it harms healthy nerves while helping a little with pains of the nerves and joints, paralysis, and especially sciatica. Just as wine must be prohibited in nerve passions, so also in those of the arteries. For it harms the nervous and fragile parts...

Nor is the substance of the eye certainly born to be dominated by the nervous, but rather by the watery, according to the 64th distinction. 

Even if wine—according to the fourth book of Almasor—absolutely harms the eyes, it helps them incidentally by aiding their matter or spirit, as the sixth aphorism of **Hippocrates** <note>Abbreviated as "moy" or "afforis".</note> indicates. A small quantity is also permitted. To the other point, it must be said that wine does not help a spasm from inanition simply, but truly when mixed with water as touched upon before, or otherwise; for wine benefits the nerves by reason of medicine, but harms them as we have seen by bringing raw matters into them when it dissolves their subtleness. Similarly, it is seen how wine confers benefit and when, for the sake of the matters contained in them. 

To the other point, it must be said that even if wine simply harms the foundation of the nerves and their power, yet it alleviates them and causes them to rest by means of the instrument, namely the **animal spirit** <term>spiritum animalem (animal spirit): in medieval medicine, the subtle vapor that carries sensation and motion through the nerves.</term>; it also provokes urine and sweat, leaving behind the superfluities. And therefore **drunkenness**, as they say, must not be constant. One must be careful, especially for one whose brain is weak. For the greatest of the harms of wine is in the brain. Truly, the passion of the nerves occurs in those who have a preparedly weak brain. 

To the other point, it must be said that although wine is opposed to the nerves in complexion <note>Wine is hot/moist; nerves are cold/dry.</note>, such that it might reduce them or cure their passions, other more harmful things mentioned before are present in it. Wine is more hot and moist than the nerves, which are cold and dry, since the sense of touch is immediately and properly tempered like the skin, so that [wine] neither reduces them nor directly opposes them. To the other point, it must be said that it is true in itself, but not in those things that happen incidentally, as it has been seen that wine provides help or harm to the nerves incidentally. For it harms **paralysis**, especially when taken in great quantity by multiplying the matter and fixing it more deeply in the nerves; but when taken in small amounts, it has already been said to confer benefit.

<meta>This page continues the medical discourse on whether certain activities or substances are beneficial or harmful to specific bodily conditions. The previous page discussed the effects of wine on the nerves; this page transitions into a detailed scholastic debate on the medicinal utility of sexual intercourse—referred to here as "coitus"—specifically regarding "windy" or flatulent diseases.</meta>

...the superfluity of the final nourishment, which is blood. This is proven as follows:
37. It is consistent with windy <term>flatulent: relating to "wind" or vapors (flatus) produced by the body's humors during digestion</term> suffering itself, because it is the material that brings them forth. And this is supported by the fact that it is impossible for food to be converted into <term>chyle: the milky fluid produced in the small intestine during digestion</term> unless windy superfluities are generated from it, since <term>phlegm: one of the four bodily humors, associated with cold and moisture</term> is the first stage of indigested food. This is found in Difference 34. However, that which is such is as far removed from sperm as can be. Furthermore, because it dries out the body and diminishes the natural virtue, it is not beneficial for a cold illness—since the illness itself is cold—nor does it help the "windy" condition, not in itself, but according to its nature. Intercourse is the subject here. Again, that which most harms the part of the body that causes and receives wind during the cure of an illness generated from it does not help. Indeed, the part that receives it sustains a much greater harm than any benefit. This part is the stomach. Whence we know from [Difference] 14: the phlegm found in the stomach is either generated in it or comes from the food. Therefore, **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Y." (Ypocras)</note> posits it as the receptacle for phlegm; but here it is especially weakened, as if by a miracle, by intercourse. Furthermore, it either helps by its own nature or by accident. Certainly not by its primary nature, because that would require a mediating cause. Such things are to be chosen for their own sake according to their virtue, and not according to accident or appearance.

Furthermore, if sexual desire helped windy diseases, it would be prescribed by physicians for them; yet it is not among the practices of doctors to prescribe it, just as they do not prescribe **theriac** <note>original: "tyriā"; a traditional herbal "universal" medicine</note> or similar things for acute fevers, which would not help the "wind" but rather the opposite. Therefore, intercourse does not benefit windy sufferings.

->**On the Contrary**<-

**Hippocrates**, in the *Epidemics*, Book 5, along with other philosophers, says: That which makes the soul cheerful and lightens the body benefits those suffering from phlegmatic and melancholic illnesses especially; and this is intercourse. **Almansor**, in Book 4 and in the *Royal Book*, appears to say this. Also, that which warms and dries benefits windy diseases, since they are cold and moist. But such is the nature of intercourse; for from much exertion the body warms and dries. Therefore, intercourse benefits windy disease.

Regarding the first point, one must know what intercourse is in its multiplicity, as seen in Difference 123. What is illness? (72). A windy illness, like other complexional <note>relating to the balance of the four humors</note> illnesses, is of two kinds: one is without the vice of humor, and the other is with it (74). And it is either diffused through almost every part, as in fever, leprosy, scabies, "hyposarca" <note>a type of dropsy or swelling under the flesh</note>, cachexia, and such; or it is consolidated in a specific part, such as in the intestines, colic, and so on. Regarding the second point, it should be known that some, and especially **Epicurus**, denied that intercourse helps anyone here (Difference 133). Some philosophers, noting the losses in intercourse, hesitate to call it beneficial at all. But what more appears regarding this will be shown.

Regarding the third point, it must be known that intercourse benefits windy diseases when it is modified [moderated], as will be shown. Whence **Hippocrates** says: Sexual desire is beneficial for windy diseases. **Democritus** also says: The use of Venus [sexual activity] is a great aid for diseases that arise from wind. Wherefore **Oribasius** <note>A 4th-century Greek medical writer</note> says to Eustochium: Venus is suitable for those suffering from wind.

And in the *Problems*, Books 1 and 4, it is asked why intercourse benefits diseases that come from wind. And according to the theologian [?]: It helps the smallest suffering. It also benefits windy diseases. Third, [Difference] 25: Intercourse benefits windy diseases. However, so that these things may be verified, one must first rely on certain indications, as I have shown and as is proven by **Avicenna's** <note>original: "Ay."</note> exposition. And finally, the same is to be confirmed.

Regarding this first point, it must be known that a strong innate heat is required for intercourse, which the exit of sperm does not destroy, which is indicated by a desire for food. But how, one might ask, can there be a strong innate heat in a windy disease?

It should be said: not simply, but in some way. For a windy disease can be in some of the parts, especially the belly and the heart, while the other principal parts remain sufficiently strong in heat. Let the disease also be with a vice of the humors. For those who are "full," intercourse is sought. Let it not be present in a weak or prostrate stomach, and especially a melancholic one. For intercourse harms that most of all. In the *Canon* [of Avicenna], Book 3, Fen 13: Intercourse is among the things most harmful to the stomach, and abstaining from it is among the things most beneficial. Whence in [Fen] 20: The reduction of intercourse is a very convenient thing for him who has a weak stomach. Nor should his nerves, along with the brain, eyes, and heart, be weak. For intercourse primarily harms the nerves. Although it might benefit on account of the material that is drawn out, the harm perhaps arises more on account of the nerves. This is shown by those suffering from lesions of the joints. It also does not allow anything ready to be corrupted to remain in the body, as in windy **scabies** <note>A skin disease</note>. Whence in [Book 4, Fen 5]: Those with scabies should avoid intercourse entirely. For it moves materials to the exterior and excites a putrid, hot vapor coming to the surface of the skin. Therefore, it becomes putrid there. And similarly in **leprosy** <note>original: "lepra"</note>, when it is caused by wind and theriac-like <note>original: "tyria"; referring to a specific type of leprosy characterized by serpent-like skin shedding</note> humors (175), in which the preparation is not rarely brought into action. Whence in [Book 4, Fen 3]: It is necessary that the leper be alienated from intercourse entirely, lest the whole body be putrefied as in fevers, or in part, as in a specific infection. For by intercourse, the body would be inflamed and dissolved. Furthermore, it would mix the malignant with the benign through motion and agitation. Therefore, in these cases, intercourse is not prescribed, but rather quietly prohibited.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that intercourse, when applied in a measured way as shown (124), benefits windy diseases. Because that which draws out windy material excites the dormant natural heat and warms and dries the body, it helps windy diseases; such indeed is intercourse. For it draws out a non-small part of the wind, since in such cases there is especially a certain superfluity blown into the sperm. Whence **Avicenna**: Intercourse benefits windy diseases because the superfluity of wind is purged by it, and it acts upon the wind. Insofar as intercourse takes away much wind, it helps. And therefore I see that those with windy conditions have frequent and many emissions, especially when windiness assists the erection. And this similarity occurs because the rest of it, with its origin, is windy. The first material of the sperm descends from the brain (Difference 34). Whence in *On Airs, Waters, and Places*: For those in whom the veins behind the ears are cut, they are first deprived of generation. And therefore, those things that harm the brain by intercourse are very many. It also excites the natural heat by motion and extraction. From these two things, warming and drying follow. Again, it is noted by a sign that one can see pure "windy" people suffer much from windy diseases and remain smaller and duller. But when they begin to have intercourse, they are rendered healthy; they grow in stature and speed greatly. Therefore, intercourse helps diseases...

To the other point that was said: that this is true when the intercourse has been exceedingly superfluous for the body, and in whatever quality; this is not the place for that discussion. To the other point seen: since a great injury to some principal part or virtue might arise through intercourse due to the dissolution of the exhaled spirits. To the other point: that intercourse by itself <note>original: "per se"</note> is beneficial because it profits not by accident or chance, even though it may occur through some mediating factor, such as movement or evacuation. To the other point: it has appeared that in the aforementioned illnesses, intercourse is prohibited. Or it is silently understood as harmful. ## DIFFERENCE 187.

¶ **Whether blood flowing from the upper parts should be restrained.**

It is our opinion: Because that which is against nature <note>original: "praeter naturam"</note> is to be restrained since it hinders and prostrates the body. Such is the flux of blood occurring from above. For every flow of blood, except for the menstrual flow, comes forth against nature. From *The Accidents*, book 5: such a thing does not come from external causes. Likewise, every evil is to be restrained since it is an injury to nature. Such is this flux here. Indeed, the fourth **Aphorism** says: Blood flowing from above, of whatever kind it may be, is bad; but flowing downward it is good, if it be black. 

Again, that which leads out the "son and treasure of nature" <note>A poetic medieval term for blood, the most vital humor</note> from the body—and specifically through the upper part, which is assigned to attraction, as the lower is to expulsion (as in Difference 166)—must be restrained. And such a flux of blood from above acts specifically against that which is most intimate and familiar to nature. Second: the deviation and passage of matter toward the principal organs must be prohibited. But here, a flux of blood happens when the brain is overwhelmed from above. Therefore, blood flowing from above is to be restrained.

**On the contrary:** In the *Almansor*, book 9 <note>The 'Liber ad Almansorem' by the physician Rhazes</note>: For those to whom an exit of blood from the mouth happens with intervals, from which they feel no harm, no remedy is to be applied. Again: that which is healthy or salubrious, providing tranquility and help, is not to be restrained. Such is this blood flowing from above. Whence **Aphorisms**, book 7: "Whoever vomits blood, if they do so without a fever, it is healthy." And according to the *Commentary* on book 13: "Many times in a vomit of two pounds of blood, for example, there is tranquility and help." Furthermore, the movement of nature is not to be restrained, especially when it has been sufficiently regulated. And it has been found that blood flowing from above is no small thing, since a <term>rheum: a watery discharge or flow</term> of blood from the nostrils shows itself to be helpful. Therefore, the flux of blood from above is not to be constrained.

Regarding the first, it should be known what blood is and how many times it is mentioned, as shown in Difference 30. "From above" refers to that which is above the diaphragm <note>original: "dyaslate," likely a corruption of "diaphragma"</note>. "From below" refers to the rest. From which parts blood flows from above will be seen in Difference 190.

Regarding the second, it should be known that some followers of **Erasistratus** <note>An ancient Greek anatomist who often disagreed with bloodletting</note> said that the flow of blood must be restrained, avoiding even spontaneous flows. Others, agreeing with **Galen** <note>The most authoritative ancient Greek physician</note> who denoted every flux as against nature except for menstruation, claimed that the flow from above, specifically from the nose, must be restrained. Some, however, assert this of all flows. But what I know of these propositions will be shown.

Regarding the third, it should be known, as was recently made clear, that a flux of blood occurring from above is either from the nostrils or from the mouth. First: it is either <term>symptomatic: a secondary sign of another underlying disease</term>, such as from another bad complexion of the containing parts, or from the sharpness and biting nature of the blood, or its quantity stimulates nature to excrete the blood; and thus the blood is to be restrained by removing its cause, since being made by a symptom, it is against nature. 

However, if it is a <term>critical: relating to a "crisis," a turning point in a disease where nature attempts to expel the illness</term> flow, with preceding signs of "digestion" <note>In medieval medicine, this meant the humors were "ripe" for expulsion</note> or otherwise periodic, one must consider whether it is sufficiently expelling that which is superfluous. If help follows from its exit, then since it is a movement of nature operating naturally, it is not to be restricted—unless it becomes excessive, whereby the humors are exhausted and the spirits are dissolved, so that the strength finally fails; then, as they feel it, it must be restrained. 

If indeed it is from the mouth, it either exited its proper place or is contained within it. If it has exited, it must be led out in whatever way nature incites to that medication. Because blood poured out against nature into a "belly" (that is, a cavity) must necessarily putrefy. From **Aphorisms**, book 6: "That which putrefies causes fever," and whatever follows. But if it is contained within its own place, then it either comes from the upper parts like the mouth, or from the middle parts. And thus it is to be restrained and led to the lower parts, since the evacuation demands opposition of both the place and the specific area where it is intended to be diverted. If, however, it glides from the parts internal to the mouth...

...it is brought out either by a cough or by vomiting. Indeed, if it comes by a cough, then it exits from the respiratory organs <note>Latin: *spiritualibus*, referring to the organs of breathing or the "vital spirits" housed in the chest.</note>. Whence the **Aphorisms**, book 7 [states]: *Blood exiting from the lungs with sputum is not healthy* <note>original: "Sanguis a pulmone cū fputo exiens nō ē salubris"</note>, especially for those lacking a fever. For if this suffering is prolonged, it is necessarily followed by a wasting disease. According to that same book 7: *In the spitting of blood, consumption and the loss of hair follow* <note>original: "In sanguinis fputo ptifis & fluxus capilloz"</note>; but where the saliva is retained, the person dies. 

If also the blood has exited its primary location, such as falling into the cavity of the chest, it must be drawn out lest it corrupt everything else by putrefaction. For this reason, drawing liquids <note>Medicines intended to "draw out" or evacuate fluids.</note> should be mixed with a vinegar that is not too sharp, so that by its cutting action and by a certain provocation of coughing—once the active flow has ceased—it may lead the residue of the blood out of the chest. 

However, in between these cases, it often happens in the mediating locations, such as in an abscess of blood. And then, unless it is at the very beginning, it must be led out entirely by soothing and "maturing" medicines for the chest <note>Medicines intended to bring an abscess to a "head" or maturity so it can drain.</note>, so that its cure may be perfected through digestion and evacuation. 

If, however, the blood is brought out by vomiting, like that which is contained in the belly, then it has been poured into it. This will be either because of a **leech** <term>sanguisuga: a common medieval medical concern was accidentally swallowing a leech in drinking water, which would then attach to the stomach lining</term> fixed in the stomach, or some other cause; and thus, as it appears, it must be emptied out so that it does not rot there. If the same blood settles in the stomach from other places, one must consider from where it is periodically driven out by the vigor of nature, perhaps because of some abandoned "consumptions" <note>This likely refers to the cessation of habitual evacuations.</note> or the prohibition of accustomed emptyings. This is seen in those who have been mutilated, or in the cessation of **menstruation** and **hemorrhoids**, or when accustomed exercises have been abandoned, as is shown elsewhere. 

And this series of facts is verified by **Al-Mansur** <note>The *Liber ad Almansorem* by the Persian physician Rhazes.</note> along with the 7th book of the **Aphorisms**. And truly, the evacuation is more symptomatic due to the cause of a simple provocation, or it matures, or it is due to a provocation of the spirit. And thus, as if it were according to nature, a flow should be decreased, just as I have seen it to be harmful in women who were still menstruating. And concerning these things, it appears in the fourth book of the **Critic** <note>Likely a reference to a specific medical commentary or a section of Galen's works.</note>. 

Know indeed that "good" or "bad" is understood in two ways: either simply, as when we say a gift is found and we honor the givers, or it has its opposite—that is, "good" in a relative sense—just as pleasure or throwing cargo into the sea during a storm is a "good" choice to avoid being overwhelmed, or as the cutting off of a finger is "good" for the sake of the whole body, or the contrary of the same. 

Or it is that which is simply "good" here, such as the flow of **menstrual blood**, but only insofar as it is appropriate for a woman and tempered in her kind; but it is not "good" in a tempered man. This flow is "natural" because it cleanses and orders the woman for offspring; for then she is more likely to conceive. Whence in the 20th and 21st [chapters]: *By the custom of menstruation, this blood having fallen to the womb at the time of pregnancy is retained, the womb being closed, so that the embryo may be fashioned, nourished, and cherished by it.* Therefore, this natural flow is ordained for the individual and even more for the species, as is seen because many sterile women menstruate the least. 

Others, truly, though these flows are simply "bad," are nevertheless commendable in some respect, such as through vomiting; a periodic and helpful flow, though bad in itself, stands in relation to the menstrual flow, or a flow of blood from the nose, or through **hemorrhoids**, or similarly in the intestines. For it contains a degree within the breadth of health. Whence **Aphorisms** 6.4: *Downward, truly, it is good,* etc. It is fitting to understand "good" not in its proper sense, but as "better"; as if it were said: it is better that black fluids exit downwards. For truly, who would not choose for blood to be carried back downwards rather than exiting through the mouth in any way? 

It appears, therefore, from these things, that the truth is of no small importance. Let there be, then, a flow of blood which is entirely "unnatural" <note>Latin: *innaturalis*.</note>, such as that of a perfectly healthy body. Another is simply "unnatural" in a relative sense, but for the sake of help it can be called "natural" because it arises from within, such as that from the nose and hemorrhoids. Another truly is a "good middle," such as that which occurs in some kind, like the menstrual flow, which a woman even when tempered needs to have. 

Regarding the first point—that what is natural is taken very strictly—it consists in the equality of all natural states when it is said that "every flow of blood happens outside of nature" <note>A standard Galenic/scholastic medical axiom: in a perfect state of health, no blood is lost.</note>. According to what **Diocles** said: *Sweats are outside of nature.* And similarly **sediment in the urine** <note>Latin: *ypostafis* (hypostasis).</note>; thus anything will be "unnatural" in a tempered body, for certainly no sensible superfluity ought to be emitted through manifest paths. Rather, everything is excreted insensibly. And thus, superfluity of sweat or sediment will not be present in such a body. For which reason it was said by some that every flow of blood is entirely unnatural. 

Broadly speaking, however, taking "nature" to include many flows of blood—besides the menstrual—they are natural in providing help, such as those of the nose and hemorrhoids, which occur in many bodies that are healthy and within the "latitude" <note>The "latitude of health" was a medieval concept that health is not a single point but a range of acceptable balances.</note> of health, even if they are healthier than others. 

As for the other point, it should now be clear. For every flow of blood made from above—besides that which comes from the nose—as the **Commentator** <note>Usually referring to Averroes, the great commentator on Aristotle and medical texts.</note> explains, is not simply bad, but bad in respect to the flow which goes downward, like hemorrhoids. When he says, *Downward, truly, black is good,* it contains a degree of goodness, as has been declared. Just as when blood has been vomited periodically from its proper places from the rest of the body, it would be more commendable, lovable, and decent for the same to be dismissed through the intestines. 

To the other point, it should be said that although blood is the "child and treasure of nature" <note>original: "sanguis sit filius & thesaurus nature"</note>, and not a little beloved by her, yet when it sins in quality or quantity, according to **Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus, an influential 10th-century physician.</note>, it then becomes an opponent. For just as a father is angry with a delinquent son (all the more when he ought to have been subject to him), so nature expels the blood from itself as if it were beaten. It also happens that it is kindly expelled through the stomach, and especially when nature finds a way there. 

To the other point, it should be said that the flow of blood from above, even if directed by a principal organ like the brain, is not therefore commendable simply, but only in a relative sense. 

Similarly, it appears from the other part that a flow of blood made periodically through vomiting is "good" in some respect and provides a remedy, and is not to be restrained. 

To the other point, it should be said that the vomiting of blood is not simply commendable. But that which is without fever is commendable in relation to that which is with fever, since the latter is pernicious. Whence **Avicenna** [says]: *All vomiting of blood with fever is bad.* But when there is no fever there, sometimes it is not bad. That it is "wicked," however, is shown by **Hippocrates**. And one should resist it with styptics and cooling agents, and through this, its tranquility and the nature of its help become apparent. 

To the other point, it appeared when it was granted that some flow of blood from above exists as something commendable.

Furthermore. Albucasis, *Surgery*, book 3. In those suffering from **quinsy** <note>Latin: *squinantia*, a severe inflammation of the throat or peritonsillar abscess that threatens breathing.</note>, one must avoid the cutting of the epiglottis <note>Here used generally for the larynx/airway area.</note> since no benefit is achieved by it. Indeed, it would cut the muscles ordained for dilating in the attraction of air. Whether it exists in the epiglottis itself, it is the worst of the quinsies. Furthermore, through the hole of the **tracheotomy** <note>Latin: *subscanatio*, an incision into the "scanum" or throat; a precursor term for tracheotomy.</note>, blood may run down into the lung causing suffocation, and the air, soon being unaltered and changing into a bad disposition, [would corrupt] it. And therefore, for this double reason, the cutting of the uvula <note>Latin: *uuee* (uvae).</note> is rendered suspect. *Prognostics*, book 3: from this, no small fear can loom. Again, for those whose health is beyond hope, the physician must predict death so that he may withdraw from them, lest he be blamed for their death. Distinction 182.

Where truly it is a quinsy: for a tracheotomy is a primary resort when other things do not help and the matter is placed in desperation. And it is confirmed because if it is held by a fever... it is mortal. *Aphorisms*, book 3. Likewise, if a cut in the neck of the bladder or the intestine is mortal, since that part is not so noble as the "pipe" <note>Latin: *canna*, referring to the trachea or windpipe.</note>, then a cut to it is also mortal. But that [the bladder] is mortal is according to *Aphorisms*, book 6: *The bladder being cut, or the brain... is mortal.* Furthermore, if the pipe is cut, it cannot be consolidated <note>Healed or closed back together.</note> according to the following aphorism: *When a bone or cartilage or nerve or thin jaw or the foreskin has been cut, they do not grow back nor glue together.* By the nature of some of these things is the "pipe," since it is nervous and cartilaginous. The fear, therefore, toward the inability to consolidate is as mentioned. Therefore, in quinsy, tracheotomy is not appropriate. The opposite of which is written in the ninth book of the *Practice* by Rhazes and Avenzoar <note>Latin: *Zoar*.</note>.

Furthermore, incisions no less than these are dangerous, such as those of the chest, liver, navel, bladder, and groin, and ruptures, which nevertheless are permitted to be done. Again, for the ultimate illnesses, the ultimate cures are powerful for perfection. Quinsy is truly an ultimate and most pernicious illness appearing in the *Prognostics*. Manual operation is the ultimate cure since it is the extreme instrument of medicine. Therefore, in quinsy, it is appropriate to perform a tracheotomy. 

Regarding the first point, it must be known that quinsy is a suffocation around the throat arising from an abscess. Indeed, this suffocation, as a genus, can happen from many causes: either an external cause like a noose, or from poisonous things taken in such as henbane <note>Latin: *iusquiamo*.</note> and fungi, and specifically *andochoca* <note>Likely a reference to a poisonous plant or mandrake variety.</note>; or from a bolus that is vehemently styptic and viscous, or a thorn fixed in the throat. Or from an internal cause like intense dryness, or from weakness of the muscles moving the parts that attract air. Or from material blocking the breathing passages, or from material fallen into the lung, or as superior catarrhs dissolving quickly. Or because of a quinsy-causing abscess or a dislocation of the vertebrae of the neck caused in whatever way. For quinsy is caused much by an abscess. Sometimes truly from a dislocation [according to] the *Aphorisms* and the fourth book of *Internal [Diseases]*. Which also for the most part happens from the contraction of an abscess in its dislocation. Sometimes truly by chance or by a blow. 

Rhazes in the *Divisions*: Know also that quinsy is distinguished in two ways: sometimes indeed by reason of the material, such as blood, choler, phlegm, and melancholy, [as in] book 3, [chapter] 9. For it is added in that book, besides the others, that it happens from melancholy. Rarely, however, of which the *Viaticus* <note>A medical manual by Constantine the African.</note> feels the contrary below: *This abscess never happens from melancholy, because this disease prevails quickly since it is most acute, but melancholy operates over a long time.* Wherefore it would be impossible for it to be generated from melancholy. 

Whence, Avicenna <note>Latin: *A.*</note>: Some say that it does not happen at all from melancholy, since the effusion of melancholy is lessened from one member to other members suddenly. Finally, joining these, he determines the truth in such a way: truly it is not far-fetched, despite its rarity, that it might happen suddenly or gradually and then suffocate; nor is it necessary, as the *Viaticus* reports, that melancholy always leaves its impression over a long time. For although this is inherent to it by reason of its quality, it can nevertheless, on the part of its mass and thickness, quickly obstruct any passage whatever with its heaviness. 

Further, according to Avicenna, the suffocation is sometimes prolonged for 40 days. Sometimes truly quinsy is distinguished by reason of location alone, as in four or five modes only [according to] the fourth book of *Internal [Diseases]*. For the following words of Hippocrates <note>Latin: *Y.* (for Ypocras).</note> expand on this not a little, when he submits only three known modes of it in the third book of the *Prognostics*. For sometimes it is in the external muscles declining from the epiglottis toward the anterior and inferior parts, in which redness appears in the anterior part of the neck and chest. Or in the muscles toward the back of the neck with the commonality sometimes of the vertebrae and the "nut" <note>Latin: *nuce*, likely the nucha or nape of the neck.</note>, and then redness and heat are perceived in the mouth. Or it is in the internal muscles of the esophagus <note>Latin: *meri*.</note> and those which follow it, constricting the breath, appearing least to the senses because of its proximity. Or in the internal muscles of the epiglottis and in the membrane covering it, which is worse than the others and not manifest to the senses at all. And sometimes from these abscesses, two or more can be gathered together. And know that some call the first species of this passion by a "q," *squinantia*; the second by an "s," *sinancia*; the third truly by an "s" and a "q," *squinantia*, and by a "c," *chinantia*, or by *achinantia*. This is from the *Aphorisms* and the fourth book of *Internal [Diseases]*; it does not help to neglect the study of the names of things. 

This, however, is **tracheotomy**: the solution of the continuity of the trachea, subtly perforating it. Regarding the second point, it must be known that physicians commonly do not perform this sectioning. Whence Albucasis: *I have not seen anyone in our land who has done this, because they are inexperienced, fearful, and afraid of the danger and infamy which they might incur.* And specifically...

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding "subscanatio" (tracheotomy) as a treatment for "squinantia" (quinsy). The previous page established the risks of the procedure, particularly the fear of blood entering the lungs; this page provides arguments in favor of the surgery, citing clinical observations and historical anecdotes from authorities like Platearius, Albucasis, and Avenzoar.</meta>

...I say [these are] less reputable and work unskillfully. For the common people do not grasp those things which are greater. But what should be held regarding this will appear subsequently from what is to be said. Regarding the third point, it should be known that **tracheotomy** <note>Latin: *subscanatio*. While literally "cutting under the structure," in this context it refers to the surgical opening of the windpipe.</note> is not infrequently appropriate here. And the method for it will be shown following this. 

Regarding the first part of this, it should be known that some suffocations <note>Latin: *prefocatio*, referring to the internal obstruction of the airway.</note> are so savage that other medical remedies do not help them, so that one might almost despair of them entirely. Some, however, are opposed to these [remedies]. In the first place, when there is a constancy of courage, a tracheotomy—which is understood and proposed everywhere—will be appropriate, as the illustrious prefaces of physicians testify. And in a case where someone would by no means wish to receive any medical help except this incision, as will be conceded below in **Avenzoar** <note>Original: *bezel* (Abumeron Avenzoar), *dria. cxcix* (Distinction 199).</note>, it may be done; provided, however, that a prediction is made so that if anything should happen, the physician is not defamed. 

An exception is made if the abscess <note>Latin: *apostema*.</note> is inclined toward the outside; it can be cured with medications and incisions made under the jaw if it is expedient. Or if it is appearing internally when the mouth is open. Whence **Platearius** <note>Matthaeus Platearius, a 12th-century physician from the school of Salerno.</note> advises—although he never did it himself—that in imminent danger of suffocation, a polished wood should be placed in the open mouth so that the film of the abscess may be ruptured, though this must be done with the greatest caution. 

For my father said that while he was playing at dice with a certain man of **Salerno**, the man was suddenly seized by quinsy <note>Latin: *squinantia*, an acute, life-threatening inflammation of the throat.</note> so that he could not speak; and when he already began to suffocate, he began to point to the painful place with his finger. My father, as if perceiving the cause, placed a wedge in his teeth, pushed a key inside, and the film of the abscess was ruptured; and thus, with blood flowing in great quantity, he recovered. I say, however, that one must fear to do it in such a way when the abscess is hidden internally, as no small danger could be imminent. Indeed, I have seen some suffocate more quickly from the greater downflow of humors. 

Furthermore, a tracheotomy is performed for the sake of drawing in air to cool the heart, but not for the sake of leading out the matter of the abscess or for nourishment; for if there were an abscess in the [internal] middle, one should not reach it by incision so that nourishment might be taken once the matter is led out, since death could quickly occur from that.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; That a **tracheotomy** <note>Latin: *subscanatio*.</note> ought to be performed is proven. Since in the seventh book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>Latin: *de ingenio*, referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*.</note> and the first [book], fourth [chapter]: "You ought to have greater concern for the thing which incurs the greater fear," while still managing that which is beneath it. But a greater fear is incurred from the sudden suffocation caused by quinsy than from an incision in the part of the artery <note>In medieval anatomy, the "rough artery" (arteria aspera) referred to the trachea.</note>, as will be shown. Moreover, just as we see in other perforations of the "pipe" <note>Latin: *canna*, the windpipe.</note> made by accident, so it is in those which are made by art; but the former often happen without danger, as I have seen and heard. Whence **Albucasis** <note>The great Andalusian surgeon Al-Zahrawi (936–1013).</note> says: A maidservant took a knife and plunged it into her throat so that she cut the lung-pipe <note>Latin: *canalem pulmonis*, the trachea.</note>; called to her cure, I found her lowing like a dead person. Uncovering the wound, I found only a little blood coming out. I was confident, therefore, that she had not cut the [jugular] vein nor the [carotid] artery. And nothing happened to the maid except a hoarseness, which after [some] days returned to the better state of her disposition.

---

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Furthermore, just as it happens in other animals—and especially the more perfect ones that resemble man—so it is in the internal apparatus of man. But in these [animals] I have often seen that when they are hung and their "pipe" is perforated indifferently and without art, they live.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Again, that which prepares air for the heart for its cooling not only helps, but rather is of great necessity. Such is the **tracheotomy** when air is drawn from there into the lung.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Also, we see that in perforations and even more dangerous ones reaching into the cavity of the chest, life is not then entirely corrupted. Therefore, neither in that of the "pipe." Thus, tracheotomy is beneficial for quinsy; indeed, it is to be performed as a necessity in determined cases. Regarding the second part of this, it should be known that the patient ought to sit in the sight of the operator upon a seat raised at the back so that his back is supported and his head is lifted. The skin should be stripped back <note>Excised or pulled away.</note> with the small membrane that lies beneath it, and it should be pulled in different directions with hooks. Then, between three or four or more of the semicircular rings of the **epiglottis** <note>Here used to refer to the larynx/trachea structure.</note>, between one cartilage and another in the membranes, let three or four round fissures be made, so that two are toward the right and the other two toward the left; or perhaps two lateral ones are sufficient. Let them be left open until the danger has receded. After the external parts occurring laterally have been treated as is expedient, let the "incarnation" <note>The healing and knitting of the flesh.</note> be consolidated with medicine. Whence **Avenzoar** <note>Latin: *Zoar*.</note>, after much investigation regarding this, says: "I once cut the lung-pipe after the incision of the skin and the membrane; I cut from the substance of the pipe itself an incision less in quantity than a **lupin** <note>A small bean, used as a standard for measurement.</note>; then I washed the wound with water and honey until I consolidated it."

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Regarding the fourth point: To the first, I say that you do not argue through these [reasons], but rather you accuse those who are so fearful and inexperienced in the works of the art. For tracheotomy is to be done as in the case pre-figured, since according to **Albucasis**, they are thereby saved from death.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; To the other, I say that Albucasis did not simply deny it, but rather commanded that a tracheotomy of the epiglottis be made beneath almost three or four of its rings. He denied it, however, in the [body of the] epiglottis itself. Because of this, according to him, all the veins and the lung are weakened. For the muscles of the epiglottis, which dilate and constrict it for the attraction and emission of air, are injured, as was touched upon. To the other, I say that blood will not run to the lung, but all [will flow] externally, since the pipe is not cut except by a small incision and in a membranous place lacking blood. Nor is it...

...similarly to what is introduced concerning the **uvula** <note>The fleshy hang-down at the back of the throat.</note>. Neither does the air cause harm, since it can be changed into the tempered **complexion** <note>The specific balance of qualities—hot, cold, moist, or dry—of an organ.</note> of the lung. Nor will that [incision] remain for a longer time, just as in the cutting of the uvula. To the other point, it is said that **Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician whose works dominated medieval medicine.</note> speaks of those in whom the strength is completely prostrated and weak, such as those who are not assumed to be in the state where an intervention for suffocation is introduced. Or rather, Galen's speech is not absolute, but rather appears as a warning regarding the operation in cases of thickening [of humors], in the fifth book of his *Method of Healing*, so that **Mesuë** <note>An influential Persian or Arab physician often cited in medieval Latin texts.</note> commands one to operate even in a major **apoplexy** <note>A sudden loss of consciousness, similar to a stroke.</note> lest a defect appear in the art or the artisan.

For confirmation, it is said that before that sudden suffocation, a life-saving intervention could precede. To the other point, it is said that an incision of the bladder is mortal when a large part of it is cut, which does not happen here. According to the **Commentator** <note>Usually referring to Averroes, the 12th-century philosopher and physician.</note>, this mortality is inherent to the bladder because it is thin and without blood, but the **trachea artery** <note>The historical term for the windpipe, then thought to be a type of artery that carried air.</note> is not entirely like that.

To the other point, it is said that this [harm] is perceived when it has been cut—that is, when a large part of it has been lost—which does not happen here; or it does not knit together by the "first and true knitting" or consolidation according to the **first intention** <note>The surgical ideal where a wound heals by direct union of the edges without scarring or infection.</note>, but according to the second intention of the art. Furthermore, even if the parts of the trachea artery were not to knit together in any way, the overlying parts would nevertheless be consolidated and united, and the openings of the "reed" [the windpipe] would be closed.

# DISTINCTION 189.

That gargles are beneficial in ailments of the chest is shown. Because in **asthma** and constriction of breath, which is made easy because of **catarrh** <note>Excessive mucus draining from the head into the throat or lungs.</note>, it is necessary to work with care to prohibit the catarrh and to cause the spitting out of what has gathered, as mentioned in the thirteenth book of this work or regarding diseases of the chest; but the gargle performs the aforesaid actions since it stops the catarrh by thickening it and by **constricting** <note>Original: *stipticādo*. Using astringent medications to shrink tissues and reduce fluid flow.</note> and strengthening the parts. It divides and thins the matter when it has been viscous and thick, and it soothes the roughness, propelling it into sputum.

<margin>1</margin>
Furthermore, that which strengthens the brain and checks catarrh and turns it away from the parts of the chest is beneficial in ailments of the chest. Of this kind is the gargle, composed of things helping the brain, and of constricting and strengthening things of the expulsive parts. Again, for the same reason that head-purgatives are suitable, the gargle also seems to be beneficial, since in both cases catarrhal matter is prohibited from entering the parts of the lung. Head-purgatives are suitable as will be more fully declared. Moreover, that which is beneficial in ailments is that through whose motion and agitation the [vital] power is brought to the site. Such is the gargle. For because of its shaking and agitation, vigor is propelled inward. **Again** <note>Original: *Palyn* (Greek: *palin*), meaning "on the other hand" or "again."</note>, by reason of the continuity of the parts, it extinguishes the inflammation existing in the chest, or remits the heat, or removes another evil disposition. For such a thing provides help to the same.

Therefore, gargles are beneficial for diseases of the chest. On the contrary, no author is found—and they are not insufficient—who expresses that gargles are beneficial in ailments of the chest; rather they are for the head and neck. Furthermore, for those things whose parts and ailments are different, the remedies will also be different, since the judgment of the cure is taken from these; but the parts of the head, neck, and chest are different. But for the former, as will be shown, a gargle is suitable. Therefore, they are not beneficial in diseases of the chest. Regarding the first point, it should be known that "gargles" is an artificial name taken from the similarity of this sound. Or from ***gargareon*** in Greek, which is the uvula. For in ailments of the uvula and the parts surrounding it, gargles are used. A gargle is a local moist medicine helpful in ailments of the head and neck, from the agitation of which a certain sound is perceived in the throat. It is called a local liquid medicine or remedy because it is applied specifically to a place, unlike something that affects the whole body. It exists as a liquid to moisten, smooth, cleanse, and wipe away; its liquid is water or another liquor in which the necessary medications are boiled. Authors also use it for ailments of the head and neck because it meets those parts more immediately as their appropriate locations, and its use is not small in ailments of the neck. Which, being different, is administered according to the expected benefits. For one is [for checking] some simple or compound imbalance; another is for thickening flowing sharp matter; another is **opening**; another is **soothing** for roughness; another is **dissolving**. The rest is for **cleansing** and **purifying** something contained in the aforesaid parts, such as dust or something else, and even for the expulsion of a **leech** <note>Original: *sanguisuge*. Leeches were sometimes accidentally swallowed or lodged in the throat.</note>, which is often administered hot and sometimes cold, according to how it is differently required to alter and change the condition. The chest, however, is the protection of the heart and other organs of life, organized for its ventilation, constructed from 12 **vertebrae** <note>Original: *spōdilibus*.</note> and 24 ribs and the thoracic bone. For the **thorax** or thoracic bone is a sevenfold part of its front, with which 14 ribs are connected (Distinction 192). What an ailment or disease is was shown in Distinction 72. Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have simply stated that a gargle is beneficial in diseases of the chest because it incurs a "fall" or other things which a gargle assists, which it induces in all its long-term ailments. But that this is not effective will be shown in the third point of the discussion. For even if they bring some help, the harm...

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding treatments for respiratory issues, specifically moving from the risks of tracheotomy to the utility of gargles (gargarismata) and other remedies for chest ailments and catarrh.</meta>

...as will be shown, it is greater than that. And therefore, they have sometimes said with a **distinction** <note>A formal logical or medical classification used to clarify a point.</note> that an ailment of the **chest** <note>Latin: *pectus*.</note> is either already occurring—and thus, as will appear, a **gargle** <note>Latin: *gargarisma*.</note> is not suitable—or it is about to occur soon, for instance from a **catarrh** <note>A discharge of mucus or "downflow" from the head to the respiratory tract.</note> that is innate or viscous, descending to the chest. And then it is beneficial when it has thickened the matter or divided it with a suitable alteration. For according to **Mesuë** <note>An influential Persian or Arab physician often cited in medieval Latin texts.</note>, a gargle is sometimes chosen when he fears lest the **matter** <note>The physical substance (like phlegm or bile) causing the disease.</note> flow to the **noble parts** <note>The vital organs, such as the heart, lungs, or brain.</note> and when the catarrh is **choleric** <note>Caused by yellow bile, usually characterized as hot and sharp.</note>, acute, or of great viscosity and thickness. 

But as will be made manifest in the third of the proposed points, that does not hold value; while this discourse is more frequently denied in catarrh, it is especially denied in ailments of the chest, in which even if a gargle might confer some benefit, it nevertheless causes harm, as will be shown, by reason of the motion and agitation of the **cough** <note>Latin: *tussis*.</note> it induces. Regarding the third point, it should be known that a gargle is not appropriate in ailments of the chest or the **lung** <note>Latin: *pulmo*.</note> because the matter is agitated by its own motion into the chest—as if expressed by nothing more excellent—and because it does not assist its downfall in these ailments, especially when it results from catarrh. What demonstrates this is that a gargle performs its action with motion and agitation; here, however, it drives the matter into a weak place naturally disposed to receive it. 

Furthermore, it may incidentally cause a cough; this harms most chest ailments since it leads more matter to the location and causes a **break in continuity** <note>Latin: *solutionem continuitatis*; a medical term for a wound, lesion, or tear in the tissue.</note> and induces a widening of the same. Again, consider either the "body" of the gargle or its "virtue" <note>Its medicinal essence or power.</note>. Certainly not the body, because if it accidentally falls upon the **epiglottis** <note>Latin: *cimbalaris*; literally 'the cymbal-like part,' a common medieval term for the flap covering the windpipe.</note>, it induces agitation and a cough, which are often harmful to chest ailments. Nor does its "virtue" or any subtle passing vapor seem to confer benefit, because due to its weakness, it cannot oppose the **dyscrasia** <note>An imbalance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile).</note> that is prevalent in the chest; rather, being overcome, it increases it—just as the sprinkling of water upon a fire often invigorates the heat. 

Even if a gargle is mostly prohibited in catarrh, it must especially be avoided in illnesses of the chest, since it is said to be a medicament for the head and neck, but is not a small prohibition in this case. Whence Mesuë says: In four cases, it is suspect to administer a gargle in catarrh. First: the fear and suspicion of it being accustomed to flow to the chest and lung. Second: if the matter is of the kind that is acute, thin, and **biting** <note>Latin: *mordicantium*; stinging or corrosive humors.</note>. Third: in suffocations that happen suddenly. Fourth: if the matter is vehemently abundant. In these cases, indeed, gargles agitate the matter and turn it toward the passages of the chest, lung, and throat, multiplying them. 

Therefore, a gargle is not suitable in chest ailments. However, a **mouthwash** <note>Latin: *collutio oris*.</note> and the retention in the mouth of some moist medicine beneficial to chest ailments—from which no motion or agitation arises—is not prohibited, or rather is more greatly prescribed, such as the placement of a **looch** <note>Latin: *loch*; a thick, syrupy medicine intended to be licked or dissolved slowly in the mouth.</note> and things of this sort. 

Know also that **strangury** <note>Latin: *stranguria*. Note: In this context, the author likely means "sneezing agents" (*sternutatoria*), as the description of "great agitating motion" fits sneezing better than the urinary condition of strangury. This may be a transcription or scribal error.</note> confers no benefit here in any way, since because of their great agitating motion, they drive the matter into the chest; indeed, they are suspect in catarrhs because the matter remains while not yet being **digested** <note>In medieval medicine, "digestion" or "concoction" refers to the process of humors being ripened or prepared by the body's heat for expulsion.</note>, especially if the chest is weak and receptive. From this remedy, I have seen certain catarrhs lapse into **empyema** <note>A collection of pus in the space between the lung and the chest wall.</note> and **phthisis** <note>Latin: *ptisim*; a wasting disease of the lungs, typically tuberculosis.</note>. 

**Head-purges** <note>Latin: *caputpurgia*; medicines designed to draw humors out of the head via the nose or mouth.</note>, however, help vehemently, just as the aforementioned things harm, since they divert the matter descending into the chest toward the opposite side without injury. This is confirmed because those having phthisis and those sufficiently prepared for it cast nothing out of the nostrils, but everything is led into the mouth through the **strainer** <note>Latin: *colatorium*; referring to the ethmoid bone or the nasal passages thought to act as a filter for the brain.</note> so that from there—and especially during sleep—it may fall into the lung or the stomach, causing phthisis or diarrhea. Therefore, how good it is to divert it to the opposite side. 

Regarding the fourth point: To the first argument, it appeared that a gargle can confer benefit by somewhat altering and changing the catarrh as introduced. Nevertheless, it harms by reason of the cough and the superfluous agitation it induces. To the other argument, it appeared that there is a greater harm than benefit. The brain can also be comforted by other things and the catarrh calmed, as introduced, such as by the retention of something in the mouth or between the teeth, or by a mouthwash. To the other, it is said that it is not similar, as was shown, because a gargle is by no means suitable. A head-purge, however, is beneficial in every way, and specifically when the head is not entirely **plethoric** <note>Latin: *plectoricum*; an overabundance of humors.</note>. To the other, it is said that it would be true if that medicinal "virtue" could meet the chest ailments without injury, which is not the case, as seen before. Also, the virtue of a gargle often does not confer benefit unless it meets the disease by **opposition** <note>The principle of *contraria contrariis curantur* (opposites are cured by opposites).</note>. To the other, it must be said that it has been seen that if a gargle could perform its cause without injury, it would certainly benefit; but as shown, it does not avail.

### DISTINCTION 190.

->That **centaury** <note>A bitter herb (*Centaurium erythraea*) used in traditional medicine.</note> does not benefit the **spitting of blood**.<-

It is shown that what **excoriates** <note>To strip or scrape the skin or internal lining.</note> and induces the flow of blood does not benefit the spitting of blood, but rather incites it. Of such a nature is centaury, for it is extremely bitter; and that which is bitter, above all else, tends to excoriate since it is hot and "gross" in its parts, so much so that it exceeds that which is sharp in this regard; and they testify that it draws out a "solution" of blood. Furthermore, that which is hot harms the spitting of blood, since it induces its flow, according to the fifth book of the **Aphorisms** <note>Referring to the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates.</note>; and therefore in that same place, there is a need to warm whatever things have been cooled, except for those in whom blood is about to flow. But centaury is hot and dry in the second degree, or at the beginning of the third. Furthermore, because it opens **obstructions** <note>Latin: *opilationes*.</note>, dissolves **abscesses** <note>Latin: *apostemata*.</note>, and ripens and provokes the **menses** <note>Latin: *mētrua*; menstrual flow.</note>, and because such things proceed from heat, it does not help one spitting blood, but rather...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on respiratory treatments, specifically evaluating the use of the herb centaury for patients coughing up blood, and providing an anatomical guide to the various origins of bloody phlegm.</meta>

...it falls to its outflow that they write of **centaury** <note>A bitter medicinal herb, likely *Centaurium erythraea* or *Centaurea centaurium*, highly valued in medieval pharmacy.</note> in such a way. Again, because it causes agitation and movement in the **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to govern health.</note>, even remaining in the stomach, it does not assist the sputum. Indeed, centaury exists for this purpose since either kind <note>The Greater or Lesser centaury.</note> is a purgative for both primary **phlegm** and **black bile**, and the Greater centaury is specifically for these. The Lesser, however, acts with the former on **red bile**. The aforementioned difference of it remaining in the stomach produces the purgative effect.

### 141. 

On the other hand, that which is opposed to benefiting bloody sputum harms it most. This is centaury, as it is hot and dry in approximately the **third degree** <note>Medieval physicians graded the intensity of a drug's qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—on a scale of one to four.</note>, in which **purslane** <note>A succulent herb (*Portulaca oleracea*) known for its cooling properties.</note>—its direct opposite—is most usefully placed. Therefore, centaury does not benefit the spitting of blood. 

In opposition to this is **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*.</note> along with **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire.</note> and others, saying it is a singular protection for **asthmatics** and those with **hemoptysis** <note>Original: *emothoicis* (from Greek *haimoptysis*), those who spit or cough up blood.</note>. Furthermore, because it mitigates a cough, it benefits bloody sputum, even though by its movement it may sharpen the flow; this is how centaury stands. Whence Galen, in his writing to **Paternianus**, says it benefits those who are coughing and gasping for breath. Again, that which consolidates a rupture of a part helps in bloody sputum; such is the nature of centaury since it is hot and dry. For indeed, dryness consolidates wounds. "If they are not perfectly dried, they are not healed," according to the sixth book of the **Aphorisms** <note>Referring to the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates.</note>. But because it is hot, it resists the superfluous cold moisture of the lung. Thus, centaury is beneficial in bloody sputum. 

Regarding the first point, it should be known that centaury is of two types: **Greater** and **Lesser**. The Greater, according to Dioscorides, is abundant in Lycia and Arcadia. It has certain leaves like the **royal walnut** <note>The common walnut (*Juglans regia*).</note>—that is, the common family—long and green like small stalks, round and notched on the outside like three fingers. It has a stalk similar to **sharp dock** <note>Latin: *lappacio acuto*, likely *Rumex acutus*.</note>, two or three cubits long <note>Approximately 3 to 4.5 feet.</note>, having many branches emerging from a single root, upon which are small heads similar to those of the poppy, round and tending toward length. Its seed is similar to **cardamom**, and the flower is like wool. Its root is thick, as much as two cubits, with a sharp taste, a little **astringency** <note>A puckering or mouth-shrinking quality.</note>, and sweetness; its color is red, the color of blood-dye, growing in rich places exposed to the sun and in shady mountains. And what is administered from it is the root, the flavor of which, according to Galen, is composed of diverse qualities. For in it there is sharpness, a stinging sensation, and astringency with a little sweetness. And this is twofold according to **A.** <note>Possibly Avicenna (Ibn Sina).</note>: namely, white and yellow. And this centaury is unknown among us, but we use a certain other kind not much different from the Lesser, having leaves with a stalk that are larger and longer. 

There is another type according to Dioscorides called the **Lesser**, known to some as **amaratum** or **fever-fleeer** <note>Latin: *febrifuga*, a plant that "shaking off" or chases away fevers.</note>, growing in watery places, similar to **hypericum** <note>St. John's Wort.</note> or **oregano**, having a long, jointed or square stalk with a red flower turning toward purple. Its leaves are tiny and oblong like those of **rue**, and the seed is like

---

wheat. Its root is bitter and is of no help. And it is this one which is universally and commonly called the "Greater" here <note>The author notes a local confusion in plant identification.</note>. However, the one called the "Lesser" among us is more universally known. 

Centaury also, according to **Mesuë** <note>A famous Persian or Arab physician (Yuhanna ibn Masawayh), a standard authority in medieval pharmacy.</note>, is composed of earthy parts that have been "burnt," which in part give it its bitterness, and parts not burnt mixed with wateriness. For this reason, it is rendered astringent. There is also a sweetness in it from airy parts and a sharpness from fiery parts, whence the bitterness in it is more immense than the astringency or its sweetness, and its sharpness is mild without stinging. Nor is this inconsistent, since even in the human body there are clearly different complexions of the parts, finally reduced into one more universal whole—first things first—since every single thing is composed of the **four elements** <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>. And indeed, the Lesser is better in every way according to Mesuë. Some, however, praise the Greater.

The **spitting of blood** is caused either from the upper parts—and thus either from the "strainer" of the nose or from the **meninges** <note>Original: *miringis*, the membranes covering the brain.</note> of the brain, which they draw out with a certain attraction—or it is excreted. Sometimes, however, it comes from the middle parts, such as the lips, gums, or tongue, and it is thin, small in quantity, mixed with saliva, and brought out with a certain rinsing. Or it comes from the lower parts, such as the throat or the **windpipe** <note>Latin: *canna*, the trachea.</note>, depending on whether it comes out with a smaller or larger "scraping" <note>A clearing of the throat.</note>, or according to whether it is much or little; for the blood from the windpipe is less than that from the throat. 

Sometimes it is even emitted without a cough through vomiting, and it comes from the stomach, the belly, or the liver by a mutilation of the part; and universally it can happen from the whole body, which is discerned by color and pain. 

Sometimes it is brought out with a cough, thus proceeding from the **spiritual organs** <note>The organs of breathing: the lungs and chest.</note>. And this is either from the chest—and it is thicker, more clumped, and darker, with some pain and less fear of duration, and with a faster return to health—or it is from the lung. If it is from its substance, it is then yellow, thin, very frothy, and also painful. Or it is from a vein, that is, the **venous artery** <note>Latin: *artaria uenalis*. In the Galenic system, this refers to the pulmonary vein, which was thought to carry "pneuma" and blood.</note>. For I do not hear that the **arterial vein** <note>The pulmonary artery.</note> of the lung, which has two tunics <note>Layers of the vessel wall.</note> like an artery and is as if immovable since it is disseminated in the lung toward the back (where it remains almost quiet), is able to be ruptured. Rather, it is the venous artery, having only one tunic and disseminated toward the interior part of the lung where vehement motion exists. And thus much hot blood is brought out, halfway in consistency between that which comes from the chest and that from the substance of the lung; this indeed seeks the three-fold blood currently under inquiry. 

And know that this flow is either by way of **sweating** <note>Exudation or "oozing" through the vessel walls without a total break.</note> from the ends of the veins or arteries, or from a bloody abscess, or by sweating as if from the retention of the menses or hemorrhoids, or by universal **plethora** <note>An overabundance of blood in the system.</note>, or by way of a rupture.
