<meta>This page continues the investigation into the medicinal properties of centaury, specifically addressing the apparent contradiction in its ability to both open vessels (causing bleeding) and seal wounds (stopping bleeding). It cites a range of classical and Arabic authorities to explain how the same herb can have opposing effects depending on its preparation and application.</meta>

...and the opening of a vessel or an ulcer, and the corrosion that occurs within it, and sometimes from a leech. Regarding the second point, it should be known that **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and medicine.</note> doubted, and had reason to doubt, because it was said that **centaury** <term>centauream</term> <note>A bitter herb, likely *Centaurium erythraea* or *Centaurea centaurium*, used since antiquity for various ailments.</note> would open the veins and cause blood <term>sanguis</term> to flow, even though it is conversely a medicine for flesh-forming <term>incarnatiua</term> and sealing <term>sigillatiua</term> of ulcers. This doubt is justified because it was stated by **Dioscorides** <term>Dya.</term> that it provides a singular protection for those coughing up blood <term>emotboicis</term> <note>Original: *emotboicis*, a corruption of the Greek *haimoptoikos*, referring to hemoptysis or spitting blood.</note>. For this reason, **Al-Kindi** <note>A 9th-century Arab philosopher and physician known for his work on the dosages of medicines.</note> uses it for the spitting of blood <term>sputo san.</term>, bringing parts together for its retention and the sealing of the site of the discharge. 

**Mesue** <term>Me.</term> <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a prominent Persian-Christian physician and translator.</note>, resolving this ambiguity, says that a close investigation satisfies the inquiry. Since it is said to be composed of different parts in which **bitterness** and **astringency** <term>stipticitate</term> <note>The quality that causes tissues to contract and "dry up," often used to stop bleeding.</note> dominate, the first action to occur from these is aggregation and sealing <term>sigillationis</term>. Indeed, the action follows from the dominant quality. However, when after a long period of action its **heat** <term>caliditas</term> and **sharpness** <term>acrimonia</term> are stirred up, an action arises from a newly sharpened stinging <term>mordicativa</term> power, due to the heat more strongly "cooking" and examining everything in its innermost part. Thus, by cooking the blood, it draws it out of the vessels and opens them—which does not always happen, but specifically when its purging is unbridled <term>effreni</term>. 

Furthermore, the difference in how it is applied externally works in no small way toward this. For when it is hot and finds the body's action to be weak, it induces flesh-forming <term>incarnationis</term> and sealing; but if taken internally, and it finds the vessels to be sharp, it causes the stripping of the vessels <term>excoriationem</term> and induces the flow of blood <term>san.</term>. For four reasons, a thing works differently when applied externally than when taken internally, and vice versa. First, because of the temperaments, as seen with **onions** <term>cepe.</term>, **garlic** <term>allea.</term>, salted **fish** <term>pisces</term>, **white lead** <term>cerusa</term>, and the like. Second, because when taken internally, the retentive power soon holds it and breaks it down, and the digestive power—altering and changing it with immense heat—weakens its vigor. Or because the natural power converts what is superfluous and benign into blood. Or because it is eaten in large amounts when mixed with other things, even though according to **Galen** <term>Gal.</term> it should be taken in a small quantity. Or because it is mixed with the remaining humors of the belly which submerge it. For a region is never found empty, neither in the womb, nor the belly, nor either of the bladders. Or because, when taken internally, it moves continuously by the motion of alteration or even transport; whereas according to **Avicenna** <term>A.</term>, it is mostly bound and held tightly on the outside. Thus, since **white lead** <term>cerusa</term> is of a thick substance, when it is applied from the outside where the heat is not so vigorous, it does not penetrate and reach the spirits or the principal organs; but when it is received within, the opposite happens, as has been shown to occur with centaury. This is rightly so, because the agent is diversified according to the nature of its own vigor and that of the patient, and the actions of the agent and patient coincide in the disposition of the patient, as stated in the second book of *On the Soul*.

Regarding the third point, it must first be known that **centaury** is beneficial for the spitting of blood <term>sputo san.</term>, and thereafter the more common simple and compound medicines for this should be touched upon for the sake of truth. Regarding the first of these, it should be known that besides what has been cited from the discourse on simple medicines, it is shown in other actions that centaury is beneficial for spitting blood; thus, centaury brings parts together for the retention of bloody spit and for cleansing. For this reason, those with fevers drink it with water, and others with wine. And the **Slavic people** <term>sclaui</term> indeed cure people with a decoction of the roots of **Greater Centaury** <term>centauree ma.</term>. For I say that this centaury is the one praised by **Dioscorides** and **Galen** in this chapter. This is confirmed because that which forms flesh, consolidates <term>consolidat</term>, and seals <term>sigillat</term>—which are the most difficult of such actions—also cleanses, restrains the movement of blood, and settles the symptoms associated with spitting blood; it is of great benefit. Such a thing is centaury. Indeed, it is so powerful in the former actions that it is even said to consolidate different meats when they are put into a pot. It also cleanses, being a medicine that draws out **phlegm**, **yellow bile**, and **black bile** as mentioned; also, with its **cold astringency** <term>stipticitate frigida</term>, and especially when its substance is weakened upon reaching the lung, it restrains the agitation of the blood. It even mitigates symptoms like a **cough** <term>tuffim</term> by its certain sweetness, especially when it has been prepared, because of which it is found to be of no small benefit for the spit. 

But regarding the aforesaid, one might hesitate because it was said that when taken internally—which is the case here—its **sharpness** <term>acuitas</term> and **pungency** <term>acrimonia</term> are specifically stirred up so that it can cause a flow of blood, especially as it tends toward the lung which it greatly overheats, being altered over a long time so that its sharpness and unbridled nature are further elevated. It must be said that this is due to its different administration: when it is sought for purging, it is taken in a larger quantity; but when strained for the spit <term>sputo colatam</term>, it induces different impressions in the body. For when given for the sake of purging, it is taken in a larger quantity, such as from a third of an **ounce** of the substance itself according to **Mesue**, up to an ounce and a half. In a decoction, however, from one ounce up to three. But when it is given for spitting blood <term>sputo san.</term> to those with fever, with water and not with wine according to **Dioscorides**, two **drachms** <term>drg</term> are offered. According to **Galen**, two **aurei** <term>aurei</term> <note>A unit of weight roughly equal to a drachm, named after the gold coin.</note> are similarly mixed with other things that can remove its pungency and comfort the sealing astringency with sweetness, such as **rose sugar** <term>rosatum zuccarum</term>. Such things must also be ground so they can penetrate more swiftly, as noted by **Dioscorides**; thus it is weakened in the process so that a smaller quantity <term>qtitas</term> of it...

To the lung, through longer paths and narrow passages, the medicine arrives; its "sharp" alteration is so weakened by heat that its piercing power and sharpness are diminished. <meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the treatment of respiratory ailments, shifting specifically to pleurisy (inflammation of the chest lining). It follows the previous discussion on hemoptysis, moving from internal medicines to the controversial use of "repelling" or "repercussive" topical treatments and bloodletting.</meta>

...turning itself toward less noble parts. Again, **repulsion** <term>repercussio</term> <note>a treatment intended to drive "bad humors" away from an inflamed site</note> is not appropriate, especially when the body is **plethoric** <note>overfull of blood or humors</note>, unless **bloodletting** <term>fleubotomia</term> is performed first. This, however, cannot be done when there is a drawing and a demand upon the heart, specifically when the bloodletting is done on the side opposite to where the **pleurisy** <term>pleuresis</term> is located.

Furthermore, that which is contrary to the cure of pleurisy should not be introduced; this refers to the administration of **repellents** <note>medicines that drive humors back</note> since they are cold and dry. These hinder the "digestion" or ripening of the pleurisy, as that process is achieved through heat and moisture, as is its resolution. For an inflammation is resolved in two ways, like all other **abscesses** <term>apostematum</term>. Very rarely does it turn into a hard tumor. Therefore, in pleurisy, repulsion is not appropriate, even at the beginning.

**On the contrary:** Since repulsion is appropriate for abscesses, especially hot ones—as noted in distinction 176—and pleurisy is an abscess, it does not seem that it should be excluded from this rule. Furthermore, cold repulsion is appropriate for **erysipelas** <term>erisipille</term> <note>a skin infection, here used as an analogy for choleric inflammation</note>; hence in the ninth book of *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio"</note>: "You shall not heal erysipelas, which is most certain, in any other way than with cold water." Erysipelas is a choleric abscess, and pleurisy is most often caused by **yellow bile** <term>colera</term>, as noted in distinction 89. Again, **astringents** <term>stiptica</term> repel because they thicken the parts by compressing them, so that what is contained is forced to be propelled in the opposite direction. 

However, this should be practiced with moderation in the chest. For there are some parts that entirely require astringents, such as the stomach and the liver. Others, however, not at all, such as the intestines, the **peritoneum** <term>sipbac</term>, the muscles of the midriff, the bladder, and the womb. Some are in the middle of these, such as the kidneys and the chest (from book 11 of *The Method of Healing*). 

Therefore, in pleurisy, repulsion is appropriate. 

Regarding the first point, one must know what pleurisy is and everything shown in its distinction (89). What repulsion is can be found in distinction 176. Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have said—and it has become almost common practice—that repellents are not suitable for pleurisy, supporting this with the words of **Hippocrates** <term>Ypoci.</term> and the aforementioned reasons. But that this should not be asserted simply, nor put into practice without distinction, will appear from what follows.

Regarding the third point, it must first be known that for some types of pleurisy, repulsion is appropriate. And finally, because one of the arguments touches on bloodletting, let its rule be added here. Regarding the first of these, it should be known that whether the pleurisy is "true" or "spurious," repulsion is appropriate under these conditions: **Bloodletting** must be performed first if the body was plethoric or moderately full, provided it was not exposed to "emptiness" <note>extreme weakness or lack of humors</note>, in which case pleurisy perhaps never occurs unless from a hidden cause. But if it occurs from an open cause, such as a fall or a blow, one must bleed. Similarly, it is done because of the flow of humors. For when the body is 

---

plethoric, or even in a state of moderate fullness, it does not respond at all to repellents. The work also requires the matter to be hot and specifically **choleric** <note>related to yellow bile</note>, and not cold, **phlegmatic**, or **melancholic**—from which pleurisy is very rarely generated. This is because hot matter requires cooling, which is acquired through repulsion, and it is mobile and changeable from place to place, a quality that cold matter possesses very little. 

It is also necessary for the matter to be in a state of "flow" and not already gathered in one part. Hence, in book 11 of *The Method of Healing*, it is impossible for an inflammation to be helped by astringents when nothing more is flowing into it, and once it is fixed, it is difficult to dissolve because the humors have become thick in the affected part. And for this reason, **Mesue** <term>Me.</term> <note>a 9th-century physician</note> says: "A medicine that aids by gathering and strengthening is suspect unless used with great caution, or at the very beginning when the matter has not yet filled the area." For when it has already been collected and wedged in, it does not obey transmission but, through astringency, it becomes crusted and hardened. 

Let the matter also be little, not much. Hence, in the thirteenth book: "If the matter is much, then cold plasters and applications are harmful; if it is little, they do no harm." For it is to be feared that when this matter, finding no place and being increased, might be transferred to a more principal part.

Furthermore, an indication taken from the part itself suggests that repulsion is useful only in small amounts, or not at all. Hence, book 11 of *The Method of Healing*: "Astringents should be used less in the chest." For they sometimes expel the humors toward the **lungs** <term>pulmonem</term> and the heart. I say "not at all" when it is first necessary to purge what is contained in the chest and lungs. And it is confirmed that whatever repels matter back to the place from which it was sent, and cools it, and invigorates and comforts the limb, that is what should be done. Such indeed is repulsion, as appears in the *Art of Medicine* <note>original: "tegni"</note> and *The Method of Healing*, provided the aforementioned conditions are added. 

Therefore, one should repel immediately. But because these conditions rarely concur at once, physicians almost always begin by applying **relaxing** <term>calastica</term> and **pain-relieving** <term>anodina</term> remedies to the chest. For they are rarely called at the very onset when repulsion is said to be appropriate. To the sides of the patient, one should apply things such as a **wax-salve** <term>cerotum</term> made of violet oil, strained wax, and crushed **tragacanth** <note>a natural gum</note> (according to **Serapion**). 

In the *Viaticum* <note>a famous medical manual</note> also, let the place be anointed with violet or rose oil, white wax, and tragacanth. Similarly, **poultices** <term>cathaplasmata</term> should be made of **psyllium**, **purslane**, and violet oil, if the matter is very sharp and choleric. Hence **Mesue** says: "First, medicines that comfort the limbs and gather their strength should be administered, so that the limb does not receive nor is overcome by the matter flowing to it." Such is a plaster made of **peeled lentils** cooked with vinegar, or bean flour cooked with vinegar, or **sumac** <note>original: "fauich", likely a corruption of sumac or similar astringent</note> with vinegar. ...the intent is **evaporation** <note>a treatment using medicinal vapors</note> performed with a sponge soaked in a decoction of vinegar, roses, or **pomegranate flowers** <note>original: "balaustiarum"</note>, or similar things. Regarding the second point of this science, it must be known that **bloodletting** <term>fleubotomia</term> is almost always to be performed first, provided that the patient's strength and age allow it, though more or less according to what the indications show. Indeed, it should be done on the side opposite the **abscess** <term>apostematis</term> <note>an internal inflammation or swelling</note> if the body is **plethoric** <note>overfull of blood/humors</note> and the matter is in **flux** <note>actively moving or spreading</note>. If, however, the matter is not in flux, some assert it should be done on the same side. But if the matter is in the membrane of the chest, one must distinguish whether to bleed on either side indifferently or more on the right. Yet because physicians mostly call the collected matter a "not small amount," they evacuate from that same side. For when matter flows, it must be evacuated from the opposite side, especially when you wish to **derive** <note>to draw humors away from an organ</note> it: for this purpose, a more distant diversion is expedient. However, when the matter is "fixed" <note>settled into the tissue</note>, bloodletting performed on the opposite side is powerless to evacuate anything from the matter of the abscess; instead, it weakens nature and prohibits **digestion** <note>the ripening or breaking down of the "bad" humor</note>. The same is to be understood in cases of **pneumonia** <term>perypleumonia</term>. It must also be considered that if the **pleurisy** <term>pleuresis</term> is in the upper part of the chest, the **median vein** <note>original: "mediana"</note> is to be bled more; if it is in the lower part, the **basilic vein** <note>original: "basilica"</note> should be used, as the former evacuates what is higher and the latter what is lower. Nor does a "draw" occur upon the principal organ when bloodletting is performed on the side opposite the pleurisy, because the veins that go to the muscles of the chest branch out from the **great vein** <note>likely the vena cava</note> ascending from the heart near the collarbone. And even if it passed through the heart, since such matter is not yet corrupt, there would not be such great harm as there is benefit following from it.

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it must be said that as is commonly stated, the cure taught by **Hippocrates** <term>Yp.</term> <note>original: "Yp." for Ypocras</note> in that place is not "true" <note>definitive</note>, but rather **tentative** <note>experimental/exploratory</note>, such as in the case of a quartan fever where a three-week fast is prescribed. This is apparent because, seeing that the patient is not helped by a heating treatment, he immediately orders bloodletting and pharmacy. Or it should be said that **Hippocrates** <term>Y.</term> intended to apply heating treatments more to the **accident** <note>the symptom, in this case, pain</note> than to the underlying sickness, as taught in *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio"</note>. Whence he says: "First, indeed, the application of a heating agent for the purpose of dissolving pain is not useless." Similarly, **cupping glasses** <note>original: "ventose"</note> are not to be administered at the beginning when the matter is present. Nor should they be used in hot matter, but more in cold, and in "false" pleurisy rather than true pleurisy. To the other point, it must be said that he does not repel the matter into a more principal organ once the appropriate conditions are met, but rather, after bloodletting is performed, the matter is sent back to the parts from which it was transmitted by strengthening the limb with **styptics** <note>contracting/astringent medicines</note>. To the confirmation, it must be said that repellents in the previously assigned case eventually drive the matter outward rather than inward. Or it should be said that it is good for every internal abscess to be moved to the outside according to nature, yet not always according to the medical art, nor at all times. Or it is good thus; however, sometimes the matter gathered within is broken back by a strengthened unity, bringing destruction, as is shown in **anthrax** <note>original: "antraces"; refers here to a carbuncle or severe localized infection</note> and such things. What should be said to the other point has already appeared. To the other, it must be said that when **repercussion** <note>driving matter back</note> occurs at the very beginning, the digestion of the matter is not prohibited, nor is its resolution, but rather the matter is lessened and prepared for digestion. Also, regarding the induction of the other part: pleurisy does not arise universally from pure **choler** <note>yellow bile</note>, so much so that cold water is not applied externally in **erysipelas** <note>original: "erisi pila"</note> but is rather taken internally, for it has the power to extinguish and resolve purely choleric matter, just as **nightshade** <note>original: "psolattū," likely Solatrum</note> has the property of resolving hot abscesses that are hidden.

## DIFFERENCE 192

> <gloss>q</gloss> Whether a flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note> cures an abscess of the chest or pleurisy.

It is shown that it does. Because the same matter that heals the pain of the side heals the first and second. This is the **flux of the belly** <note>diarrhea</note>, and the "side" is this portion of the chest. And it is confirmed because **diarrhea** <term>dyaria</term> and **dysentery** <term>diffinteria</term> heal diseases of the eyes and the spleen, according to the sixth book of *Aphorisms*. These are also fluxes of the belly. Furthermore, that which cures material illnesses most universally will cure abscesses of the chest. This is the flux of the belly, since it is the most preferred evacuation and the one most accustomed to nature; through it, superfluities are more freely led out, so much so that it even cures diseases of the head. Furthermore, a "regional" sickness is cured by evacuation, since every cure is perfected by its **contrary** <note>referring to the principle of "contraries cure contraries"</note>, according to distinction 153. But an abscess of the chest is a disease consisting of **repletion** <note>fullness/excess</note>. A flux of the belly, however, is a disease of **inanition** <note>emptiness/evacuation</note>. Again, that which preserves one from a future illness can cure that illness after it has happened by evacuating the matter causing the sickness. But a flux of the belly preserves one from a future material sickness; hence, in humid air and water, those with naturally "moist bellies" do not fall into pleurisy or other cold-induced illnesses. Therefore, a flux of the belly will cure an abscess of the chest.

**On the contrary:** According to the sixth book of *Aphorisms* and **Avicenna** <term>Auicen̄.</term>: "In one who has pleurisy or **pneumonia** <term>perypleumonia</term>, a supervening **diarrhea** <term>dyaria</term> is a bad sign." These [pleurisy and pneumonia] are abscesses of the chest. That [diarrhea], however, is a flux of the belly. Great "softness of nature" <note>loose stools</note> is to be avoided in this disease unless it is vehemently necessary. In an **abscess** <term>apostemate</term> <note>a localized collection of pus or a swelling</note> of the chest, the pain is indeed inseparable and located above the **diaphragm** <term>dyaslama</term> <note>original: "dyaslama," referring to the midriff or dividing membrane</note>, and this is especially true in **pleurisy** <term>pleuresi</term>. Furthermore, that treatment is effective which evacuates the matter causing the sickness through its own appropriate and convenient region. In the case of a chest abscess, this is the upper part, which is evacuated via sputum through the **tracheal artery** <note>the windpipe</note>, just as the region of the hollow of the liver is evacuated through the stool, and the convex part of the liver through the urine. Regarding the first point, it should be known that the difference between the flux, the belly, and the abscess is shown in chapters 254 and 95. The chest is the **furnace of the breath** <note>an evocative metaphor for the respiratory system</note> and the instrument of breathing, constructed from 12 **vertebrae** <term>spondilibus</term>, 24 ribs, and the seven-fold bone called the **thoracic bone** <note>the sternum, which medieval anatomists often described as being made of seven segments</note>; it is also composed of seven muscles, which Galen (along with Haly Abbas in chapter 22) places between the ribs for both dilating and constricting. However, Avicenna and Al-Mansur in chapter 88 divide each of these 22 into four parts. For between the 12 lines, 11 distances <note>intercostal spaces</note> fall, but there are 19 on the outside, remaining more according to the upper and lower parts. Of these, the 11 upper ones are for dilating and the 9 lower ones for constricting (Difference 99). And know that the **diaphragm** <term>dyasla</term> is the most principal of the muscles, for from its very beginning proceeds the movement of the lung according to Galen—and indeed of the whole chest—which by its motion is numbered among the muscles of dilation, but by its rest is placed among those that restrain it. There is also the **perforated vertebra** <note>the spinal canal</note> through which the **spinal cord** <term>nuca</term> <note>from the Arabic 'nukha'</note> travels. Of the 24 ribs which rest upon the 12 vertebrae, 14 are "true," surrounding the chest on all sides and firmly connected at the front to the cartilaginous thoracic bone. Ten, however, are called "false" ribs. These are not joined to one another but remain detached to allow for the swelling of food [in the stomach] and the carrying of offspring <note>pregnancy</note> (from the second part). Because their extremity is near the belly, it remains cartilaginous so that the belly is not harmed. It is also known that an abscess of the chest is **pleurisy** and is treated by **bloodletting** <term>phlebotomiam</term>. For the heart never, or very rarely, sustains an abscess, since death would occur first (Chapter 91). Regarding the second point, it should be known that as appeared from the sharp arguments, a contradiction is gathered among the authors, the explanation of which will be shown from what has been said. Although this contains truth, a sounder understanding is needed of what it seeks to reveal. Regarding the third point, it must be known that an abscess of the chest, and especially pleurisy, is either in the beginning

It is supported because it signifies that nature is powerful in evacuating and it draws out the offending matter; such a flux at the beginning of such a suffering indicates the power of the expulsive virtue. But against this, it is argued that no evacuation at the beginning of a disease is praiseworthy, as they write, since every symptom must be treated and moved when **digested** <note>ripened or processed by the body's heat</note> according to the ancient [authorities], and not when **crude** <note>raw or unprocessed</note>, as the matter is in the beginning. The Commentator says this suffering is still beginning and not yet confirmed, and if three days pass, they escape; yet when this suffering is intense in a noble member, no one escapes once it is confirmed. Or it is said that the flowing matter of this [abscess] is somehow digested. For nature was moving toward a spontaneous flux after a certain neutrality, so that being unable to expel the matter, a small part of it was collected into an abscess, while the rest ran to the belly; having slipped away from there, it first makes the abscess smaller, and finally the matter that was contained in the abscess is removed by the flux—which I have seen by experience. But if the abscess is [fixed] and there is a flux of the belly, it will either be because the matter of the abscess is evacuated from there, or because of the weakness of the liver, with the belly suffering along with the "spiritual members" <note>the heart and lungs</note> in which the abscess is located. For they have a connection to one another that is not small, both real and through the vessels: for the whole is continuous with the whole, and it flows and breathes together by a natural connection. And if it is the former, then either the matter of the abscess is much and not perfectly mastered by nature, and thus the flux is bad since the matter passes through or around the heart, and travels over noble parts, omitting its proper place of expulsion (such as occurs through the tracheal artery), whence bad symptoms follow threatening death; or it was [matter] which was mastered by nature by the power of its quantity, and thus the flux of the belly can terminate in good with a strong nature...

<meta>This page continues the medical analysis of chest diseases. It specifically examines the prognostic value of diarrhea (flux of the belly) in patients with pleurisy and pneumonia, and initiates a new "Difference" (Chapter) on the curability of phthisis (tuberculosis/consumption). ...nothing repugnant exists. But if the **flux** <note>diarrhea</note> occurred because of the shared suffering of the liver and the belly, then it does not cure the **abscess** <term>apostemate</term> <note>a localized collection of pus or a swelling</note> of the chest, but rather stimulates nature [to more distress]; whence it is said that diarrhea supervening upon someone who has **pleurisy** or **pneumonia** <term>pypleumonia</term> <note>peripneumonia, an inflammation of the lungs</note> is an evil sign. According to the **Commentator** <note>Averroes, the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on medical texts were standard in European universities</note>, diarrhea occurring as an additional symptom will be a bad sign because the liver itself, as is required, is not able to draw in and transform the nutrients.

This also happens sometimes because of the belly corrupting the food within itself. Therefore, in the thirteenth [section]: When a **flux of the belly** <note>diarrhea</note> comes to a patient with pleurisy at the end, it signifies that his liver is already very weakened; for as it was noted in the touch of the sign, it marks such a great debility of the spiritual organs that the natural organs also suffer with them. Nevertheless, nothing of the matter of the abscess is evacuated thereby, and it acts in the manner of a **fistula** <note>an abnormal passage in the body</note>. For this more intense flux is induced when nature is weakened and the body is deprived of nourishment, which is certainly very bad—just as when a long-lasting **dysentery** <term>dissinteria</term> comes upon those with **spleen disease** <term>spleneticis</term>. Because it prostrates the strength and evacuates nothing of the [chest] matter, it does not cure the chest abscess. Such is the nature of this flux. Therefore, it does not cure him. This flux can also intervene either by the belly's own malice, whence the **Commentator** says: sometimes it happens from the corruption of the stomach's food, which is corrupted within itself; although this is bad, it is not as bad as the first case.

The Commentator, however, seems to distinguish between a large abscess and a small one; for if the pleurisy or pneumonia are small, they can be resolved when diarrhea supervenes, especially if the current cause of the diarrhea is such that it evacuates that same matter. But it is not resolved by a flux occurring due to food or drink. Because a large chest abscess—acting as a malignant burden—is not healed by the same flux of the belly, but rather its malice extends further. 

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it appeared to be conceded. For it is possible for **lientery** <note>a form of diarrhea where food passes through undigested</note> or a flux of the belly at the beginning—or when the matter is small and dominated by nature—to lead the chest abscess toward health. Nor is it entirely the same here as in the cure of eye and spleen ailments through diarrhea and dysentery, since those do not happen from a suffering of the spiritual parts, but rather from the vigor of nature, which expels the matter prepared by nature from those places. I say "prepared" because a longer dysentery in those with spleen disease induces **dropsy** <term>ydropisim</term> <note>edema or swelling caused by fluid</note> or lientery, according to the sixth [section] of the *Aphorisms*.

To the other point: a flux of the belly cures sicknesses when it occurs by the vigor of nature, expelling digested material, and not as a secondary symptom or from the suffering of the more noble organs. To the other point: respiration is not cured by just any kind of evacuation, but it requires the proper region. For the chest purges through the **tracheal artery** <note>the windpipe</note>, the stomach through vomiting, and the intestines and the mass of the liver through the stool. It also requires a time in which the acting force works so much upon the matter that it exposes it for evacuation worthily, which the flux of the belly does not do. Although it is mentioned in chest abscesses, it is nevertheless a more universal path for other evacuations. To the other point: perhaps it is not true, since it leads out matter differently when it is wandering and not yet confirmed in a part, and differently when it is collected in it. For when it wanders, it can be evacuated more freely through many parts; but when it is confirmed, it stands determined and defined, requiring a specific evacuation. 

How much one part can overcome the other will also appear. Because even if a chest tumor is sometimes cured by a flux of the belly, it is healed more fully and perfectly by the drawing out of the matter through sputum; even if it is found elsewhere, unless it is more vehemently impeded, it must always be drawn out.

## .DIFFERENCE. .CXCIII.

**Whether phthisis can be cured.** It is shown that it can, because in the twenty-eighth [section] it is proved: Dionysius of Tyre, during a siege or blockade, according to Nicholas the Peripatetic, ceased drinking until he suffered from **phthisis** <term>ptifis</term> <note>consumption or tuberculosis</note>, until he again changed himself back to his former habit of overindulgence. 

Furthermore, **Medicine** <note>likely referring to a specific medical authority or text</note> says that the number of those who have been healed by the use of **sugar of roses** <term>zuccari ro.</term> <note>original: "zuccari rosati," a common medicinal syrup or conserve made from sugar and rose petals</note> is beyond counting, which also contributes to healing. **Galen** in the fifth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "De Ingenio Sanitatas"</note>, reciting two cured cases where they were spitting out the thin skin of the inner lung passages. **Avenzoar** <note>Ibn Zuhr, a famous 12th-century Andalusian physician</note> cites two cases, and in the thirteenth [section]: one woman was healed and fattened up who had reached such a point that everything necessary for death was already prepared. Wherefore his brother cured her with sugar of roses and eating bread. 

Also, the creation of **pus** <term>sanies</term> <note>a discharge of pus and serum from a wound</note> in ulcers is a great certainty of safety for health; for it is impossible for it to be troublesome or dangerous when pus is formed in ulcers, according to the fifth [section] of the *Aphorisms*. But in phthisis, pus is generated, and often even of a "laudable" kind. Again, if it were not healed, it would either be on the part of the organ, which is not the case because then no ulcer [of the lung] would heal; or by reason of the motion, which also is not seen since it prohibits putrefaction and consolidates the artery—even the breaking and separating of moving parts. Or it would be on the part of the method of applying medicines. But this also does not happen, since it can be applied to the body both internally and externally. Again, a flux of blood from the lung is cured, according to the fifth book of *On the Method of Healing*; here it is already shown to be putrefied, since if natural blood is poured into the belly, it must necessarily be converted into pus, according to the sixth [section] of the *Aphorisms*. Therefore, phthisis can be healed.

On the opposite side: in the fourth book of the *Interior Parts*, several are recited of whom none eventually escaped. And **Serapion** <note>an influential 9th-century Syrian Christian physician</note>, having given the signs of phthisis, says: phthisis that exists according to this disposition has no cure. **Avenzoar** indeed says that this sickness, even in which the sputum appears white, is not healed according to the judgment of physicians, but falls into the sickness called phthisis, from which he posits that death arrives. Likewise in the *Viaticum*: if it is neglected for so long that the lung gathers wounds into pus, the wounds are incurable. In phthisis, the wound exists in the lung. Furthermore, from phthisis, because of the copious putrid vapor that is retained by the motion of the lung, in dulling and exhausting, it passes into wasting and consumption, gradually dominating, from which it happens that no one escapes. Therefore, phthisis cannot be cured. Regarding the first point, it should be known, as was touched upon in [chapter] 93, that "phthisis" or "corruption" is found to be understood in various ways. Commonly, indeed, it is taken for any natural or accidental consumption indifferently; and thus it is more universal, since every **hectic fever** <term>ethic9</term> <note>a fever associated with wasting diseases like TB</note> is phthisical, but not the other way around. For it can happen that nature, from a total corruption of the **radical moisture** <note>the vital fluid thought to sustain life and heat in medieval medicine</note>...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on respiratory diseases, moving from the complications of pleurisy and pneumonia to a detailed examination of phthisis (consumption). It focuses on the physical characteristics of susceptible patients and the anatomical and pathological reasons why the disease is so difficult to cure.</meta>

...from a hot humor, phthisis <term>ptisiz</term> <note>also known as consumption or pulmonary tuberculosis</note> ultimately arrives at this point, as appears in some degree. And properly speaking, it takes hold of those who are "prepared" for it, such as those having a weak brain, a long and slender neck, a prominent epiglottis <note>the flap of cartilage at the root of the tongue</note>, shoulder blades elevated like wings, and a narrow chest, bare of flesh and full of windiness in the lungs; such people are frequently invaded by a slight cough, even without cause, along with a stabbing pain in the shoulder blades or breasts, especially if they are of a choleric temperament and easily angered. 

It is also defined most specifically as a consumption of the whole body with ulceration of the lung. Whence **Cassius Felix** <note>A 5th-century North African medical writer whose work "De Medicina" was a primary source for medieval physicians</note> says: **Phthisis** is an ulceration of the lung and thorax with a wasting away of the body. Wherefore, it is a wasting of the constitution falling upon the body from the heat of hectic fevers or from an ulcer of the lungs; and in this way, every phthisical person is hectic, but not vice versa. These latter two types of phthisis touch upon the essence of the matter. Concerning both, it is pronounced a grave evil, especially in spring; whence the sixth book of the **Epidemics** <note>a work by Hippocrates</note> says: "Phthisis in autumn is bad; it is also bad in spring when the leaves of the fig tree are equal to the feet of a crow." 

Regarding the final stage, there is a discourse here that it is caused by an acute **catarrh** <note>a descent of fluid or mucus</note> falling into the lung, perforating it with ulceration, just as water hollows out a stone by frequent dripping; or it occurs because of the spitting of blood, according to that **Aphorism** in the seventh section: "From spitting of blood comes the spitting of pus; from the spitting of pus comes phthisis." Or it follows a preceding pneumonia <term>pypleumonia</term> or pleurisy which turns into an **empyema** <term>empima</term> <note>a collection of pus in the space between the lung and the chest wall</note>, according to the Aphorism in the fifth section: "If those who become empyemic from pleurisy are not purged within forty days of the rupture, they pass into phthisis." For the remaining pus becomes acrid and corrodes the lung. It also happens sometimes from corrupt matter remaining a long time in the lung, followed by putrefaction and ulceration. This passion, according to the ancients, mostly occurs from age 18 to 35. Whence **Cassius Felix** says: "It is a symptom that creates itself more in young men than in the old, and is more troublesome, arriving more often in men than women, and in adolescents and youths more than children and the elderly." For children are more easily susceptible to cures than others. It is also among those diseases that are inherited through the seed, and it is worse when it appears to originate in the lung rather than in the chest initially. 

The lung is a rare and soft member, ordained for the fanning <note>cooling</note> of the heart; it joins above with the **rough artery** <term>aspa artaria</term> <note>the trachea</note>, and into it is dispersed that which is hard and composed of almost cartilaginous rings and the membranes investing it. Laterally, however, the **arterial vein** <note>the pulmonary artery</note> and the **venous artery** <note>the pulmonary vein</note> meet it from the heart, from which it is nourished, sustained, and moved; and that part which is laterally around the heart is shaped so that it may contain and embrace it, especially at the time of its dilation. Of this lung, there are five **lobes** <term>pennulae</term> <note>literally "little wings"</note> or appendages, the larger of which lies toward the back and is less moved, acting like a supporting cushion for the major vein; the other four are lighter and more mobile, blowing through the heart during its dilation and constriction, embracing it in the front. 

But the cure is administered through the application of opposites to the body to introduce health, which is twofold: one is the **true cure**, by which the disease or its cause is totally removed. Some cures, however, are **apparent or palliated**, such as when remedies are used so that the disease does not extend further, which serves for incurable diseases. 

<margin>
Note this **Cassius Felix**, of whom several fragments are referred to in this "Difference" <note>chapter</note>. Concerning him, see **Clericus** in the *History of Medicine*, Part II, Book 3, Chapter 2. The works of the aforesaid Cassius were still in existence during the time of **Pietro d'Abano** <term>Petri Aponensis</term>, that is, around the year 1300 and beyond. Today, namely in the year 1771 in which I write these things, they have long since perished or lie hidden.

**Ludovico Castellini** <note>Likely the owner or a commentator of the manuscript</note>
</margin>

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have said phthisical patients can hardly be cured because they are ulcerated in the lung. For they admit that an ulcer of the lung is not only difficult to cure but is even incurable. This is affirmed by reason and by experiment in the fifth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>Galen's "De Ingenio Sanitatis"</note>; whence at the beginning of the tenth book: They say that ulcers of the lung do not heal at all because consolidation <note>healing/closing of the wound</note> requires rest, and there is no rest there. But **Galen** differs from them; for he thought that motion alone does not prevent consolidation unless the rest of the phthisis is joined to it. The significance of this is that the lung is always moving, and yet sometimes its ulcers are healed. This diversity of opinion has already appeared among the learned. 

But what is to be felt about this will be seen later. Regarding the third point, it should be known that the phthisis intended here is for the most part not cured, especially that which has already become chronic and has impressed the "signs of terror," having been caused in the lung by an acute, corrosive catarrh descending into it, most especially into the more mobile lobes mentioned before. Whence **Cassius Felix** says: "The ancients say those are worse and incurable which are of the lung; such a cure is impossible, as the empyema indicates." For from that sight, we see that few or none escape it. Reasoning also confirms this. Since if phthisis is to be cured while there is an ulceration of the lung, that ulcer must be cured. But this is an impossible cure since there are many impediments: such as the softness and tenderness of the lung, the heat, thinness, and sharpness of the blood, and the constant motion. For that which must be consolidated requires rest. Furthermore, the pain excites and stimulates the rheum <note>discharge</note>, along with the magnitude, width, and hardness of the lung's vessels. The lung also receives catarrhs ascending and descending, which hinder consolidation by softening the tissue. It is also necessary that the pus be cleared out by coughing, but the coughing itself dilates the ulcer. 

A bad **complexion** <note>humoral imbalance</note> is also introduced there, which hinders consolidation, leading to a hectic fever. Because the damaged lung is unable to freely vent the heart, the smoky, putrid, and carbonaceous vapors are retained, inflaming the heart and then the whole body, leading into hectic fever. Similarly, medicines taken internally cannot reach the lung unless they are much altered and weakened in their transit by the heat of many body members and the distance. Moreover, it is necessary that they be very subtle in substance, by nature and by art, so that they may pass through. Wherefore it is commanded in the **Tegni** <note>Galen’s *Ars Medica*</note> that their strength must be increased externally; for example, if there is a **dyscrasia** <term>diferafia</term> <note>an imbalance of humors</note> of the lung of the 11th degree, a medicine of the opposite quality of the 10th degree of heat should be chosen. For three degrees are estimated to be lost on the way. Perhaps such an elevation of the medicine's strength would harm the lung and surrounding parts. And therefore, physicians have been ingenious...

<meta>This page continues the clinical discussion of phthisis (consumption), focusing on the pharmacological delivery of medicines via "lochs" (syrups) and the anatomical reasons why lung ulcers are notoriously difficult to heal compared to wounds in the chest wall. It cites major authorities like Avicenna, Galen, and Avenzoar to weigh the possibility of a cure.</meta>

One should construct moist, sippable <term>electuaries</term> <note>medicinal pastes usually mixed with honey or syrup</note> called **lochs** <note>original: "locath"; a linctus or licking-medicine designed to dissolve slowly</note> so that, when held in the mouth while the patient lies on their back, they may gradually dissolve into vapors. These vapors descend somewhat toward the lung, passing smoothly through the esophagus, and alter the substance of the airway and the lung. In the same way, medicines applied externally reach the lung with great difficulty because of the thickness of the chest walls. Furthermore, medications often hinder each other because this condition requires opposing treatments. For the purging of **discharge** <note>original: "sanies"; the thin, foul-smelling pus from an ulcer</note>, hot and dry medicines are needed; but for the **hectic fever** <note>the wasting fever associated with consumption</note>, cold and moist ones are required. Whence **Avicenna** and **Mesue** say that the drying treatments required for the closing of the ulcer prevent the bringing up of phlegm, thereby worsening the fever. Cleansing agents, meanwhile, soften the ulcer and perhaps make it more malignant. 

Therefore, a case of phthisis that demands such a cure is either impossible to treat or perhaps "monstrous" <note>in the sense of a rare medical anomaly</note>, for even in diseases, a "monstrosity" occasionally occurs. Whence the **Seventh Collection** says: some escape from illnesses by chance. Just as in natural things, "strangenesses" sometimes occur, though they are among the rare events—such as the ulceration of the lung and similar things—so too death in consumptive patients is often delayed for a long time, so much so that **Avicenna** saw one live for about twenty-three years or a little more with phthisis.

It is rare then, and for the reasons touched upon, that phthisis can be cured, especially when it has not become chronic or when no terrifying symptoms have appeared. A cure may also happen when there is a simple break in tissue or an ulcer that is not discharging pus, located higher up near the windpipe of the lung, or perhaps in the "greater addition" of the so-called "greater vein" <note>likely referring to the pulmonary vessels or major bronchi</note>, or those wounds that are not in the lung itself but in the chest. For a break in the continuity of the chest is healed with less difficulty than one in the lung for many reasons. 

One reason is the fewness of the "instruments" <note>anatomical structures like vessels and nerves</note> in the chest compared to the multitude in the lungs. Another is because the vessels of the chest are smaller and narrower than those of the lungs. A third is that the discharge of a chest ulcer flows into its own cavity, whereas the lung's discharge does not, as it is trapped in narrow channels. A fourth is that the chest is fleshier than the lung and contains thick blood, while the lung has many divisions of channels whose substance is not fleshy but rather "nervous" <note>fibrous or membrane-like</note>, containing thin, choleric blood. This can be seen in the sixth book of *The Benefits [of the Parts]*. That which is fleshy consolidates better, as the fleshy part of the **diaphragm** <note>original: "dyasantis"</note> shows when it is wounded. The fifth reason is that the motion of the lung is more continuous and stronger than that of the chest. Add to this a sixth: the immense weakness of the materials by the time they reach the lung.

Phthisis occurring from a break in continuity around the **trachea** <note>original: "tracea artaria"</note> toward the lung is not so difficult or impossible to cure as that which occurs in the pure substance of the lung. Since these channels are solid, they are more receptive to closing up, as **Galen** notes. Wounds that are in the internal channels of the lung—namely the membrane, and especially that which is near the throat—can possibly be cured. Indeed, he [Galen] had many patients...

---

...who received treatment and were restored to health. ♣ 

That phthisis can be cured—provided the physician is not negligent—is proclaimed by experience, as noted before. I myself have healed some and have seen others cured, especially children and women. Reason also confirms this; for when the injury is small and the remedial causes are great, it can certainly be cured. This happens in phthisis when the air is altered in a way that is highly beneficial; thus, even in a time of pestilence, one can find air that dries and purges the discharge of the lung or chest, as **Stabrius** <note>possibly a corruption of a name like Strabo or a specific medieval author</note> says in his 207th chapter. Nor are the obstacles to healing previously mentioned always so immense as to prevent it entirely. Thus, rarely and by chance, some cases of phthisis can be cured. 

And know that there is perhaps a medicine, though hidden from us, capable of curing almost every phthisis. According to **Hermes**, "There are wonderful virtues in minerals and vegetables which, if men knew them, they could perform whatever is achieved by the magic art." Such things, however, are better known to the brute animals than to us. Whence **Avenzoar** <note>The 12th-century Andalusian physician Ibn Zuhr</note> says: "There are medicines for the ulceration of the lung and its infirmities existing in the world, yet unknown to us." For it happens that ulcers occur in the lungs of sheep; they wander and go about seeking something to find. And shepherds told us that those sheep eat certain herbs, and having eaten them, they soon revive and are perfectly healed of their ulcers. And I, he says, have seen the lungs of sheep in which a trace of a former break in continuity had begun to form, and it was visible in one part. In another part, the work of healing was manifest in the closing of the lung's flesh. But now there is no one who knows that herb, nor do I believe there was anyone before us who knew it.

Regarding the fourth point, even if it appears difficult, it is like the first point: **Avicenna** understood phthisis as a consumption of the body in general, but specifically as a condition similar to phthisis.

<margin>A</margin> To the second point: **Mesue** speaks of phthisis in the second way mentioned, which is cured only rarely and by chance, although many cases may occur that are cured over a long period of time. For he himself previously asserted that the healing of phthisis was impossible.

<margin>B</margin> To the other point: **Galen**, as it seems, speaks of those in whom there was an ulceration higher up around the channels of the windpipe membranes, and who were spitting [blood/matter]. He says these were healed by the dryness of pestilential air. Similarly, I will say that **Avenzoar** and **Avicenna** saw cases cured, provided the discharge was "laudable" <note>a medical term for pus that indicates a healthy healing process</note>; the cure is not prevented by the discharge itself, but by the secondary symptoms that follow when such matter lies in that part.

<margin>C</margin> To the final point: this happens because the motion of such a member [the lung] hinders consolidation. For although motion prevents putrefaction by causing "transpiration" <note>the movement of air/vapors</note>, it nonetheless happens to increase the matter by bringing pain and the ulcer to that location.

It also includes a fascinating account from Avenzoar regarding sheep instinctively finding medicinal herbs to cure their own lung ulcers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the pathology of phthisis (consumption), transitioning from the mechanical difficulties of healing lung ulcers to a debate on whether environmental dryness causes the disease, and finally beginning a new section on the suitability of milk in the patient's diet.</meta>

...to be solidified. And though some say that the arteries or the diaphragm, when moved, do not heal, this is not true of all, but specifically of those in children; nor is it the case everywhere, but only in the fleshy parts rather than the nervous ones. Similarly, it is seen how physicians and their methods of application hinder the cure of **phthisis** <term>phthisis: a progressive wasting disease, usually pulmonary tuberculosis</term> when it has become deep-seated. Regarding another point: it is said that blood poured out against nature into the belly or a cavity becomes putrid if it remains there. However, if it is drawn out very quickly, it does not putrefy. Regarding the first point of the other side: **Galen**, **Serapio**, and **Avenzoar** <note>original: "Zoar"</note> speak of the "worse" phthisis, which is defined as being impossible to cure. And regarding the rest, they speak similarly.

<margin>o</margin>
On the occasion of what has been touched upon regarding the causes of phthisis, it is doubted whether phthisis can be caused by **dryness**. And it indeed seems so according to the **Aphorisms** <note>original: "affoy."; referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates</note>. In dry spells, phthises and eye inflammations occur. Furthermore, phthisis arises from moisture, as appears in the commentary there, which **catarrh** <term>catarrh: a buildup of mucus in the nose or throat, believed in medieval medicine to flow down into the lungs</term> also demonstrates. Again, every constitutional disease of the lung happens just as it does to the other organs, one of which is dryness. And this is confirmed because by drying out, the continuity of the tissue is dissolved; thus, he denotes a "cracked" dryness, and therefore in the first and second [books] he writes that pain occurs by accident, as the dissolution of continuity causes it. That which is a great and evil contrary also causes phthisis; such a thing is dryness, as shown by **Autumn**, which is bad for the phthisical, revealing what was hidden, according to the Aphorisms and the first and second [books]. Since a dry autumn causes great harm, therefore dryness causes phthisis. To the contrary, **Galen** on the Aphorisms says otherwise, as will be seen. Furthermore, when the causes of phthisis are sufficiently enumerated, dryness was not included; and he confirms that dryness stops catarrh by drying and consuming it, and universally hardens and strengthens a part so that blood does not slip from it—and these are the causes of phthisis. Therefore, it is not caused by dryness.

Regarding the first point, one must know what phthisis is seen to be and how it is distinguished. Dryness is also noted as the third difference. Regarding the second, it must be known that **Galen** detests this saying of **Hippocrates**, stating that phthisis is caused by extreme cold in the respiratory organs—especially when a strong movement follows—and by heat combined with moisture. But when dryness is tempered with heat and cold, it leads more to other ailments than to phthisis. Or perhaps "phthises," as some have explained, is not to be taken properly on its own, but in conjunction with eye diseases, so that one might speak of "phthises of the eyes," meaning a **consumption** <note>original: "consumptōeʐ"</note> of the eyes during ophthalmia. Regarding the third point, it should be known that phthisis in the "third mode" mentioned previously does not happen because of dryness; rather, dryness helps once it has begun, as it dries out the **discharge** <note>original: "saniem"; inflammatory pus</note> and consumes the causes of it. Nor can such great dryness perhaps occur in the lung that its continuity is dissolved by it, both because cold can act as a passive quality (especially following a vehement movement, as touched upon) since it is active, and also because the lung receives moisture...

...from the air drawn in. For it is the receptacle of the spirit, and also because of catarrhs ascending and descending. Truly, dryness can cause the first two modes—and especially the second—when a similar thirst is joined to it, stirred to a fury so that it consumes like fire upon fire. Or we say that dryness causes phthisis not primarily, but as a consequence. For the cough itself is the mechanism, since every bad constitution causes it. But the cough induces phthisis by dividing or dissolving the continuity of the respiratory organs and inducing an influx of blood, or by stirring up catarrh in the lung, which, by its constant falling or its sharpness, ulcerates the lung, especially when the body is full and the constitution of the air is preceded by **cholera** <note>here referring to the "yellow bile" humor, associated with heat and dryness</note>. Regarding the fourth point: even if it now appears what should be said to the first view, to the second it must be said that moisture of itself does not cause phthisis unless it is joined with a moist catarrh, as with heat or cold. But dryness of substance alone is at least not mixed with such **rheum** <note>original: "reumati"; watery discharge from the mucous membranes</note>. To the other point, it also appears that dryness is prevented from intensifying to the point of a tear because of the moisture in the lung. To the other, it must be said that Autumn does not harm the phthisical only by reason of dryness; indeed, it helps the "third" type more in terms of drying the flesh and the discharge, as much as it harms because of its inequality. Let us now approach those things which belong to the other side.

### DIFFERENCE 194.

<margin>q</margin>
#### It is shown that milk is not suitable for the phthisical.
> According to the ancients, milk is bad for the **hypochondria** <note>the upper abdomen; here referring to internal inflammation or "heat"</note>. But the phthisical are like this: they thirst on account of febrile inflammation and the "whey-like" nature of the discharge, which suspends the passages. They omit lunch on the second day, and so on twice, because of the wasting. Likewise, in the second [book], he says milk harms those with **weak heads**. The phthisical are such, whence **Mesue** says those exposed to falling into phthisis are those having a weak brain. Again, since there are three substances in milk, as shown in Difference 148—namely the watery, the buttery, and the cheesy—it is suitable by reason of none of these. Not the watery part, whether it be given hot (as some feel), because then the febrile **dyscrasia** <term>dyscrasia: an imbalance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile)</term> will be increased; nor cold, because then it will not be cleansing or abstergent, but rather, by its coldness, it will cause blockages. Nor for the sake of the buttery part, since it is hot, oily, and easily flammable. For an oily substance in a fever is like oil poured into a lamp. Nor even on the part of the cheesy substance, since it is cold and thick, thus increasing the imbalance and causing blockage with difficult digestion.

Furthermore, milk is one of the most changeable things (as in the seventh [book] of *On the Method of Healing*); for it is corrupted soon after leaving the vessels. It is not suitable for phthisis, which in Greek...

Furthermore, in the same place, the reasoning is that if milk could be tasted after it has been digested in the stomach and the veins, it would be sweeter than the flavor of **honey**. But honey is considered hot and dry in the second degree <note>Medieval medicine categorized substances by "degrees" of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness; the second degree indicates a significant effect</note>, and therefore it tends to be converted into bile, appearing especially in the "ignited" states in the second [book] of *Natural [Faculties]* regarding diets and uses. Therefore, milk is not suitable in phthisis.

On the opposite side, in the fifth of the **Aphorisms**: Milk is suitable for consumptives and specifically for those with fever, provided it is not severe.

Also, milk is prescribed in **hectic fever** <note>original: "ethica"; refers to *febris hectica*, a slow, persistent fever common in tuberculosis</note> about which less will be seen later; indeed, it acts as an eradicator, and specifically **ass’s milk** in the first part of the fourth [book]. But every distinction for the consumptive follows from the former. Therefore, milk is beneficial to the consumptive. Regarding the first point, however, it should be known what milk is and how it is distinguished, and similarly the different ways phthisis is affected. (148)

Know, however, that different types of milk are useful here according to different intentions. When the primary goal is the **cleansing** <term>abstersio: the process of cleaning out an ulcer or wound</term> and spitting out of the ulcer's matter, **camel's milk** is suitable, followed by **goat's milk**, and then **ass’s milk**. This is because, due to its thinness, it is suitable for easy penetration. If, however, a **sealing** <note>referring to the closing or healing of the lung ulcers</note> is sought, along with more nourishment and firmness of the belly, **cow’s milk** will be useful. But if balance and a temperate quality [are sought], **goat’s milk** is best. If a specific property is desired alongside these, **human milk** is most familiar to the body, especially when it is sucked by mouth directly from the breasts, according to **Prodicus** and **Euriphon** in the seventh [book] of *On Disease and Wasting*.

It is also necessary that the animal [providing the milk] be fed on certain things when the goal is the cleansing of the ulcer's pus—namely with **hyssop**, **wormwood**, **field cypress**, **fennel**, and **southernwood**—and then the milk is more suitable in the spring than at other times. When the goal is consolidation and the scarring of the ulcer, [the animal should be fed] with **bramble**, **tannin-sumac**, **willow**, **thorns**, **myrtle**, **oak**, **shepherd's staff**, and similar plants; then the milk will be more praiseworthy after the middle of summer. Let the milk also be taken from a young animal that is neither close to giving birth nor too far from it. It should be taken on an empty stomach, and nothing else should be eaten until it has been digested; other such precepts should be observed here.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have hesitated to give milk to consumptives, fearing their **feverish imbalance** <term>distrasiam: dyscrasia, an imbalance of the four humors</term> and the increase of **catarrh** that sometimes follows when they have administered it. For instance, that there is no active flow of **catarrh**, but that it has already settled; for it often happens that catarrh dripping into the lung causes ulceration over a long period, eventually producing pus. Sometimes it also occurs from a rupture of an artery or a vein in the chest, or the substance of the lung itself, caused by a fall, a blow, a heavy weight, or other causes like the **sea-hare** <note>original: "lepore mario"; the Aplysia, an aquatic mollusk believed in antiquity to be a deadly pulmonary poison</note> which acts as a poison to the lung, corroding it, and sometimes from an **empyema** <term>empyema: a collection of pus in the cavity between the lung and the chest wall</term> as seen before. For the ancients chose it because it is of a nature similar to human nature. That which is preferred, however, is especially that of the camp in **Campania** near Rome by the sea; if you fear its curdling in the stomach, you shall mix a little **honey** with it, especially if you seek a more vehement cleansing. For this reason, **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (c. 777–857), a Persian physician</note> says that milk fulfills three intentions: for it is a nutritive substance and very well-liked, and is among those things that are swiftly converted into blood. For it is a "costus" <note>likely meaning a restorative or aromatic agent here</note> of the blood. It also stands as a medicament that cleanses the ulcer by the power of its wateriness <note>original: "serositatis," referring to the whey-like part</note> and glues the thing itself together by the power of its cheesiness.
Indeed, at the most, eight things are found in milk that are beneficial to the **consumptive** <term>phthisicus: a person suffering from phthisis or pulmonary tuberculosis</term>. For it is easy to digest, good to consume, well-digested, penetrates quickly, and specifically—in the case of camel, horse, and donkey milk—provides excellent nutrition. Whence **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), author of 'De Materia Medica'</note> says: It nourishes the humors well. Also, according to **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), author of 'The Canon of Medicine'</note>, it is soothing, moisturizing, consolidating, and sufficiently washing and cleansing.

### Milk is therefore quite suitable for consumptives.
But regarding this, a doubt arises: because it was said that the wateriness of milk cleanses and scours, which is an action of a "hot" medicine according to the fifth [book] of *Simple [Medicines]*, yet in the 148th distinction, it is stated to be **cold**.
It must be said that although the wateriness is cold, it nevertheless acquires a certain cleansing serosity and sharpness through being warmed during the long journey it takes to reach the lung, since it is of a subtle substance and easily susceptible to any impression. For a subtle substance is very quickly changed; or perhaps, along with its watery coldness, it possesses a certain sharpness in its particular parts.
Regarding the fourth point: To the first it must be said that consumptives who do not have a strong fever do not thirst much. Thirst also happens more because of **inflammation** produced in the humors, specifically the bilious ones in the organs. This is shown by the fact that those with fistulas are not very thirsty, nor is the watery discharge of the pus so great that it makes them thirsty. It also passes quickly through the parts where thirst originates.
Furthermore, "suspended" <note>original: "suspensus"</note> in a consumptive is said in two ways. Either because he is hanging downward on account of a heavy swelling and a blockage—and in such a case milk is not suitable, as it would "suspend" and block him further. Or because it [the milk] clings vehemently to that which it is joined—and in this second sense, milk is not denied but rather granted, so that he may be built up by fattening where the previous conditions do not interfere.
To the other point, it must be said that if the consumption is **catarrhal** <term>catarrhalis: caused by an excess of mucus or "catarrh" flowing from the head</term>, caused by a weakness of the head, milk should not be granted until the brain is strengthened and the catarrh quieted, as was touched upon before.
To the other point, it must be said that milk is suitable because of all its parts, as has been declared. For the watery substance is not hot, but rather cold according to distinction 148. It is also shown to be very useful for those with fevers. Similarly, although it may be slightly cold, it becomes warm on the way to the lung so that it is able to cleanse. The **buttery** part is also allowed, since it is slightly warm, as long as the fever is not vehement. It is also balanced by the cheesiness, nor does it 

---

participate in so much coldness and dryness that it causes harm when measured against other substances; nor are consumptives [always] exposed to blockage.
To the other point, it must be said that although milk changes easily when administered, when it is mixed with **rectifiers** <note>medicines intended to "correct" or balance the qualities of another substance</note>, as shown before, its alteration is slowed down. Nor is there a corruption of the humors or the whole body in phthisis. Nor is it given when the stomach and other parts of nutrition are excessively out of balance.
To the other point, it must be said that although milk in the veins becomes sweeter, acquiring a sweet flavor in them like that of honey, it does not entirely take on its temperament <note>complexionem</note>, especially since the cheesy substance resists it. Whence this is true of the buttery part; the sweet flavor itself is not hot and dry in the second degree except in respect to the weight of its composition, but is rather tempered in relation to a balanced state.
And these previous points proceed when the fever is intense. Therefore, it is denied then; but it is granted when the fever has been remitted, as much as possible through foods and medicines, so that the consumptive is disposed to the consumption of milk. As for the other points brought up regarding consumption, it has been sufficiently shown how much they weigh.

<margin>p</margin>
### On this occasion, it is also asked and hesitated upon whether **rose sugar** <term>zucarum rosaceum: a medicinal preparation of sugar and roses</term> is suitable for consumptives.
For it stands as highly praised, just as milk was mentioned before. And it seems that it is not, because consumptives need the cleansing of pus and its expulsion. But that material is strongly expelled by medicine when it is contained in the chest and lung; whence, as far as medical skill is concerned, physicians wanting to cleanse the chest and lung of pus give a very strong **incisive** <term>incisiuam: a medicine that "cuts" through or thins thick humors like phlegm</term> medicine. Rose sugar, however, is not of this kind, but rather the opposite.
Furthermore, it is either administered "new" or "old." Not new, because it loosens the belly—which is feared here—and it is so cleansing that a flux of blood might be feared. Nor is the old suitable, since it dries out and narrows the paths through which the matter is expelled, and it thickens the pus.
Again, since it is dry, it will increase the febrile heat through a bad dry **dyscrasia** <term>discrasia: an imbalance of the four bodily humors</term>. **Isaac Judaeus** <note>Isaac Israeli ben Solomon (c. 832–932), a significant Jewish physician and philosopher</note> teaches to resist this in all those with fever by administering moist things. Likewise, it is cold, and cold things are enemies to the chest.
Additionally, if the simple components do not suit, neither do the compounds. For they receive their being and vigor from the simples; but the simples, such as sugar and roses, do not suit, since one [sugar] heats, dries, and cleanses excessively. The other [roses] dries, acts as an astringent, and consumes and squeezes out moisture. Therefore, rose sugar is not suitable in phthisis.
However, many [authorities] think the opposite, as will appear. Furthermore, that which is suitable for consumptives is that which serves them as both medicine and food; such a thing is rose sugar, since it is a cold alterative for a bad habitual dyscrasia on account of the dominance of the roses and...

...it is highly nutritive, especially because of the sugar. It also purifies and scours because of the sugar, which is said to be necessary for the **consumptive** <term>phthisicus: a patient suffering from pulmonary tuberculosis or wasting disease</term>. Therefore, rose sugar is suitable in cases of phthisis.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that there are two types of sugar. One is from a reed; the other is called *alusar* <note>original: "alusar," likely referring to a type of manna or sugary exudate from a plant</note> from the letter A, and it is a manna falling upon the *alusar*, which is a light, thick, straight, and beautiful wood. To this, the legs and arms of ladies are compared. 

However, the sugar from the reed is taken from the marrow of a certain cane whose nodes are close together, similar to a golden cane, which is placed in a vessel. Because it then distills from it, the liquor is subtler and very sweet, which is called "cane honey," in the same way that moisture flows from grapes that have not been trodden. Then a boiling of the canes is done, and what is first gathered from it after cooling is the whitest, purest sugar called **tabarzeb** <term>tabarzeb: a Persian term for highly refined, hard white sugar</term> or *cassiebi*. Then it is boiled a second time and pressed, and it becomes a "loaf," which is called sugar-loaf. Finally, from a third boiling, a yellow powder arises, as the sugar increases in color through the boiling process.

### On Roses
**Rose sugar** <note>original: "rosaceum"</note> is so named from roses, of which some are domestic and others are wild; and of these, some are white while others are red. The white ones are indeed colder than the red ones, less dry, and more "soluble" <note>meaning they have a laxative effect</note>, whereas the red ones are more strengthening. When they are fresh, they loosen the bowels, but when they are aged, they constipate. Violets, however, act in the opposite way.

### The Construction of the Remedy
Its preparation is as follows: Take white or red roses and spread them upon a table in the shade until their excess moisture is resolved, and they are of a more suitable medium dryness. Then they should be brought into a stone vessel. Next, let there be thrown over them **tabarzeb** sugar, triple their weight, and let them be placed in a glass vessel. Let its mouth be stopped with parchment and exposed to the sun for three continuous months, stirring it frequently; then let it be removed from the sun and stored. 

Indeed, some make it with immature roses, which is found to be more **astringent** <term>stipticum: a substance that shrinks tissues and stops bleeding</term>. There are also some who do not grind them but cut them with scissors and rub them with their hands with a deep rubbing; then, as before, they expose them to the sun. 

### The Properties of the Remedy
There is a "new" version of this remedy, which has the power to cool and moisten, and especially when taken cold, to scour and consolidate. There is another "old" version, whose property is to dry, bind, and consolidate. There is also a "medium" version, which works moderately.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have said that rose sugar does not benefit the consumptive. They were moved to this view because many authors do not testify to it, and for the reasons touched upon earlier. But why this view is invalid will be shown in the third and fourth points. For if someone has not touched upon it, it happened either because he preferred brevity (though its presentation demands a longer explanation), or perhaps because they did not perceive its experience, as empirical medicines are discovered daily.

### Evidence of Success
Regarding the third point, I will first show that rose sugar benefits the consumptive, and finally, the time and manner of administration shall be touched upon. Concerning the first, it should be known that one of the things most beneficial to consumptives...
