...is rose sugar. Whence in the thirteenth book <note>likely referring to a specific medical authority or book number</note>: Among those things which have been tested for a long time in various bodies and various regions is that one should use bread with fresh rose sugar of its own year, every day, as much as one can. And if one's breath smells because of the dryness of the roses, let him take in his drink a syrup of hyssop or of poppy according to the quantity of necessity. And if a fever is inflamed, let **troches of camphor** <term>trocisci: medicinal lozenges or tablets</term> be given in his drink, and let this care not be interrupted, for it heals. 

And therefore, if I did not fear being called a liar, I would narrate wonders regarding this intention and report the case of a certain consumptive woman. For the matter reached a point where the sickness was so prolonged that she reached the brink of death, such that the things necessary for death <note>likely funeral rites or a shroud</note> were prepared. And then a certain brother of hers rose up and treated her with this cure for a long time, and she revived and was healed. And almost the same happened to me in the case of a certain youth.

**Avenzoar** <note>Ibn Zuhr (1094–1162), a famous Arab physician</note> also says: Food will be rectified by the refinement and improvement of all foods, which is rose sugar with bread made wisely. Whence **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh</note> says: Among things of wonderful help for the consolidation and healing of ulcers of the lung is fresh rose sugar, specifically that which has not passed its first year. For there is gathered in it the power of scouring from the juice of the roses and the power of consolidation from the part of their substance. 

And **Galen** commanded that rose sugar be given every day in partial quantities, even with medicinal things, foods, and drinks, and according to every mode of its administration, so that it is even used with bread. They used it especially after meals, and the number of those who were healed by its use is incomprehensible.

### The Logic of the Cure
This is confirmed because that which lightly purifies, scours, consolidates, seals, nourishes, and comforts, succeeds excellently in phthisis. Such is rose sugar. By reason of the sugar, it especially purifies and scours, as do the roses (especially when fresh). For in them, above anything else, there is a power of washing. On the part of the roses, it more so consolidates and seals, especially when it is old or medium. It also nourishes by reason of the sugar and somewhat because of the roses, by whose aromatic quality it comforts. Therefore, rose sugar—especially the new or medium kind, and the old in its own way—benefits the consumptive.

Regarding this, it should be known that doctors often err concerning the cure of phthisis because, wishing to purify the **pus** <note>original: "saniem," referring to the discharge from an ulcer</note>, they only use scouring agents to purge it, so that bloody sputum is induced anew. They also err on the other side because they administer astringent-purgatives like rose sugar (especially the medium or old kind) and particularly with Armenian bole <note>a medicinal clay</note> and other things, when the purification of the pus is not yet complete; these materials then further <margin>clog the lungs. Whence Mesue says that rose sugar must be administered</margin> with preceding purifiers. For those who use it from the beginning, when purification has not preceded, are deceived. It is necessary, therefore, first to sufficiently scour the pus and afterwards to consolidate and seal. Of these, rose sugar is often not able to perform the first, especially the medium and old kinds. Regarding the fourth...

### 1
**That** cupping glasses in the retention of menses should be applied under the breasts with **scarification** <term>scarificatio: the act of making small incisions in the skin before applying a cup to draw out blood</term> is shown by what Hippocrates indicated. For in this condition, as in many others, he prescribes **phlebotomy** <term>fleubotomia: bloodletting</term>, and after its use, a particular and local cupping follows; this evacuation is perfected by scarification. Furthermore, this diverts and evacuates the matter to the opposite location in the case of menstrual retention, just as is prescribed in other flows. Now, scarified cups perform this, which simple cups do not do since they do not draw out blood. Again, they are placed with scarification, and then they either achieve the intent or they do not; by drawing to a weak, receptive part, they might induce a flow of matter in that part. According to the fifth book of the Aphorisms: "In women whose blood turns toward the breasts, it signifies mania." <note>original: "Mulieribꝝ qbꝝ ad mamillas san. uertit ur maniaʒ significat"</note> Nor will they draw if they lack penetration through an obstacle. And this is because, assuming the blood turns toward the breasts, it will return again by its own weight when the cup is removed. Again, the attraction of cups is achieved by a vacuum, according to Galen, which evacuates; but when they are placed with scarification, a greater vacuum occurs because of the "solution of continuity" <note>an old medical term for a break in the skin or tissue</note>, or because that which is evacuated follows the rest of the blood by attraction. Therefore, these should be placed with scarification under the breasts in the retention of menses. On the opposite side are Viaticus and A. <note>likely Avicenna</note> with the common practitioners. In these cases of retention, the intention is not just the evacuation of blood—lest she be further weakened by a superfluous flow—but rather **derivation** <term>derivatio: the medical practice of drawing humors away from an affected part to a nearby area</term>, as is prescribed when there is a scarcity of blood along with a weakness of vigor; this occurs when cups are used without scarification. Also, whatever retains the menses is better treated with the least injury. This is seen when the cup is applied without scarification, for in that case, no pain occurs. Therefore, cups should be placed under the breasts without scarification. 

First, it should be known that cupping glasses are an instrument for attracting something from the body by the power of a vacuum, and they can be constructed from various materials. Most commonly they are made from their own rounded gourds <term>cucurbitis: literally "gourds," the traditional shape and name for cupping vessels</term>. Sometimes they are made of glass, which perhaps draws more strongly because it is more solid and more applicable. Sometimes horns perform a similar function; as in the 14th book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio," referring to Galen's 'De Methodo Medendi'</note>, where they are applied by the breath of the mouth and draw less than those applied by themselves. According to Cornelius Celsus, they are applied with fire, where something combustible is applied to their orifices. Elsewhere, for lack of other things, drinking cups are applied. Cups applied with fire are more powerful at pulling things out. And note that sometimes cups draw the flesh to themselves so strongly that they cannot be separated without breaking the flesh; therefore, those made of gourds are then more commendable, for they can be perforated and the hole can then be plugged. 

Some cups are applied with scarification, which cleanses the parts of the skin more than phlebotomy, and they draw out thin blood more than thick. To whom they should be preferred and in what places they should be applied is taught further. Others are fixed without scarification, which is done for many reasons: either so that an excessive menstrual flow may be restrained (when placed on the breasts); or so that a deep **abscess** <term>apostema: a localized collection of pus or a swelling</term> may be drawn to the exterior so that medicine can better reach it; or so that the matter of a swelling may be drawn from a noble organ to a closer, less noble one. Or so that a passage may remain open, as they are applied to the neck in **quinsy** <term>squinantia: a severe throat infection or peritonsillar abscess</term>. Or so that a limb deprived of heat may be warmed by the attraction of blood and spirits, and coldness and **flatulence** <term>uentositates: literally "windiness" or gas trapped in the body</term> contained there may be resolved. Or so that a part may be reduced to its original place from which it was separated, as in an inguinal rupture [hernia]. Or so that an obstruction or stone may be removed when they are placed over the kidneys according to Albucasis. Or indeed, so that pain may be settled, as in colic where a cup is more necessary, and generally in all pains and especially windy ones. Or lest a limb be moved from its place, as in the hip joint. Or so that a windy and cold swelling may be medicated. Or so that it may suck out poison and draw it to the exterior part when it has been inflicted, which is why it is applied after the use of leeches in the 12th, 13th, and 14th books of *On the Method of Healing*. 

The **menses** <term>menstruum: the monthly discharge of blood from the uterus</term> is superfluous blood which is naturally emitted by a woman at a determined time. For every non-natural flow of blood—except for the menses—is described in the sixth book of *On Accidents*; it usually runs from about the 14th year until the 45th, according to different temperaments, more or less; since in material things there is no fixed limit to be found, as appears in the first book of *On the Days of Crises*, it is useful to note the range of health. When this flow is more natural, it happens more at the end of the lunar month. For "menses" is derived from "month." When, however, it becomes non-natural, it returns sooner...

<meta>This page continues a discussion on female physiology and the regulation of menstrual cycles, specifically focusing on the anatomical connection between the breasts and the womb. ...it was, however, slower. Hence the law: "A woman who is purged twice in a month is not healthy." <note>original: "Mulier que bis purgatur in mense sana non extat." A common medical aphorism suggesting that excessive menstruation is a sign of illness.</note> For some women who are more hardworking and of a "virago" constitution <note>referring to women with a more masculine or robust physical nature</note> living in cold places, it happens later, so much so that they may lack them entirely. The [menstrual] flow usually lasts for five days, more or less, for quite a few.

The breast is the instrument for the production of milk, which is composed of arteries, veins, nerves, and white, sensitive flesh. For just as the liver is made purple so that blood might be generated—as discussed in the fourth book of theoretical benefits—so also the flesh of the breasts is white so that the blood within it might be further "cooked" <note>the medieval concept of 'coction' or 'digestion' of fluids into other forms</note> and turned white into milk. To the breasts come arteries and veins branched from the womb, originating from the vessels lying opposite the thigh. For they return again to the breasts just as the veins and arteries, divided from the vessels ascending above the **collarbone** <term>furcula: literally "little fork," the medieval term for the collarbone or the notch at the top of the breastbone</term>, join with the aforementioned ones by descending in branches.

**Scarification** <term>scarificatio: the medical practice of making many small, shallow cuts in the skin to draw out blood or "humors"</term>, or *carassatio*, is a frequent, superficial incision of the skin, whereas a phlebotomy <term>phlebotomy: a single, deep incision into a vein to draw a larger amount of blood</term> is a single deep one. Know, according to Democritus and Oribasius <note>Oribasius was a 4th-century Greek physician and biographer of Galen</note> his colleague, that **cupping glasses** <term>ventosa: a suction cup used to draw blood to the surface; "ventosa" means "windy" or "full of air"</term> are not appropriate at the beginning of an illness, nor while a **plethora** <term>plethora: an unhealthy physical state caused by an excess of blood or bodily fluids</term> remains, but rather after the fullness has been evacuated. This is also found in the thirteenth book of *On the Method of Healing*. <note>original: "de ingenio," referring to Galen's *De Ingenio Sanitatis*</note> Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have wanted to apply cups with scarification, claiming they evacuate the fullness. But this is not effective, since it would be better while the fullness remains to allow it to pass through the womb so that it is released. Or, if it must be evacuated, it is more convenient to draw it out through phlebotomy, since that properly evacuates fullness, which scarification does not. And therefore others have said that cupping glasses are effective through **derivation** <term>derivation: the medical strategy of drawing "bad blood" or "vapors" away from a diseased organ to a healthy part of the body nearby</term>...

Regarding the third point, it should be known that cupping glasses ought to be placed absolutely without scarification <note>this is "dry cupping," using suction without cutting the skin</note>. Hence the *Viaticum* <note>a famous medical handbook for travelers, likely that of Ibn al-Jazzar</note> says: "We should apply cupping glasses to the breasts and suck without scarification." They are sometimes placed so that, by the nature of their suction, the blood is pulled away, such as when they are applied to the breasts to stop the course of menstrual blood. Reason confirms this. Since menstrual blood is thick and earthy, that which is drawn out through scarification is instead thin and watery. Furthermore, the blood drawn by scarification is superficial, since it is contained in the smallest veins near the skin. But the blood that exists in the veins which branch from the womb to the breasts is deep, and the attraction of cupping glasses [with cuts] cannot reach it as effectively. Again, if they are applied with scarification, the necessity of the vacuum ceases more quickly because the skin is broken; once this happens, the "pull" or attraction is destroyed. But when the blood is not evacuated—which happens in cupping without scarification—the "necessity of the vacuum" remains vigorous and pulls the blood more strongly, retaining it in the place where the attraction reached. Therefore, cupping without scarification should be applied here.

Regarding the fourth point... a diligent craftsman will cease the attraction to a place when he sees that a "stasis" <note>a standing still or blockage of fluids</note> might be born, so that the blood attracted to the breasts is not retained there to rot and cause a tumor. Rather, it is drawn to itself when there is no excess flow. There is such an obstacle of flesh that the power of the cupping glass cannot reach the arteries and veins to pull from them. For this reason, the following support appears: the attracted blood does not run backward, but is distributed into the rest of the body that needs it. To the other point, it is said that through a vacuum, the benefit to that which is evacuated is greater, especially since when the attracted blood flows, the softness of that which fills the cupping glass is immediately removed.

### .DIFFERENCE. .CXCVI. <note>Difference 196</note>

That hot things are suitable in the cure of a **hot disease of the heart** <note>likely referring to a fever or inflammation of the heart</note> is shown in the third book, chapter eleven. Furthermore, in the *Megatechni* <note>the "Great Art," a title for Galen's work on therapeutics</note> book three: "It is necessary to cure dry bodies with dry things and moist with moist things." Therefore, one should treat hot causes with hot things, and cold with cold. Now, the disease here is assumed to be hot. Likewise, a physician should treat according to the ancient and Christian [tradition]... For the heart itself is supported by the instrument of internal heat. This heat remains through hot things and is destroyed by cold things, especially. Again, the **spirit** <term>spiritus: in medieval medicine, a subtle substance (not a soul) that flows through the arteries to give life and movement</term> is strengthened by fragrant things because it is nourished by them; hence in the twelfth book [it is said]: "In a fainting fit, one should work with that which nourishes the spirit from good odors," for the restoration of the **virtue** <term>virtus: the innate biological power or "faculty" of an organ to perform its function</term> to its proper form is swifter through fragrance. This is because aromatic things are hot, and the odor is caused by the evaporation of fumes. The spirit is the "root" of the heart, as will be seen.

Moreover, the heart must be preserved and defended above all other members, since it is the primary root of all the parts, demanding virtue from them by means of the arteries. Also, in all accidents occurring to the body, there is first a recourse to the heart as if to the "base of life." In *On Simples*, it is said that preservation and defense should be through "likes" and not through "contraries," since contraries are rather destructive. Heat was also a "daughter" to the heart, for the formal complexion <note>the specific balance of hot/cold/moist/dry qualities</note> of the heart is hot and dry. Therefore, in the cure of a hot sickness of the heart, the administration of hot things is appropriate.

On the opposite side is the common use of physicians, who apply cold things to "hot distempers" of the heart. Furthermore: "All cure is through the contrary," as stated in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's *Ars Medica*</note>. But the disease designated here is hot. Again, in the eleventh book: "In a visible hot condition of the heart, a cooling of the chest with snow and camphor is prescribed." ...like fire in fire. For this reason, in the case of a healing passion <note>original: "passiois"; here meaning a medical condition or suffering</note> of the heart, hot things are not beneficial, but cold things.

<margin><unclear>da</unclear></margin> **Regarding the first point, it must be known** that what constitutes a cure, what a disease is, what heat is, and also what the heart is, has already been shown in the preceding sections.

<margin><unclear>ad</unclear></margin> **Regarding the second point, however, it must be known** that from many sources it is sufficient, as the speeches of the physicians are heard, that for hot diseases of the heart—as with the other parts—cold things are sought and moved from the aforementioned principles, and especially according to Galen <note>original: "cañ." likely referring to the Canon of Avicenna or a Galenic principle</note>, where a cure is achieved through contraries. And since hot diseases are more deadly than cold ones on account of the speed of their fiery motion—as Damascenus <note>John of Damascus, or the medical author known as Mesue the Elder</note> says in his aphorisms—the most dangerous are those of the hot heart, for which some reasoning and investigation will be seen in what must be said. 

But concerning the aforesaid, a doubt arises because the reasoning is gathered: Fevers that come from wind <note>original: "a flante"; referring to "flatic" or windy humors</note> are more dangerous than choleric fevers. A "windy" fever, however, is a disease of cold, while a choleric one is of heat. Furthermore, a disease involving a disproportion of particular circumstances—according to the ancients—is more dangerous than a proportionate one; but such a disease is cold and not hot, since the healthy human nature is hot and moist. 

Moreover, a disease that causes great detriment to nature is more mortal than the rest. A disease of this kind is one that comes from cold, since coldness is mortifying and produces paralysis, while heat is called the friend of nature. In [Proposition] 62, Palladius <note>original: "Palyn"; likely Palladius or a similar commentator</note> says that a cold disease stands in relation to a hot one as a cold season stands to a hot one; but in a cold season, disease is more mortal than in a hot one because of the disproportion of the particularities. Therefore, cold sicknesses are more pestilential and cause more falls. 

To the contrary, in the *Prognostics* [of Hippocrates], book 30: bloody and windy matters are of lesser malice than matters which are of the genus of yellow or black bile; but "wind" is hot according to the choleric [classification]. And if it is joined to a fever, it incites one to fury; it is, indeed, like fire in fire. This happens in a hot disease when the matter is hotter than nature. Therefore, a hot disease is more mortal than a cold one. 

It must be said briefly that a disease is either simple (that is, without matter) or conjoined to it. If it is the former, a hot disease is more dangerous than a cold one because of the efficacy of its active quality. A cold disease is not [as dangerous], although it is more contrary to nature—as indicated by hectic fever <term>febris ethica: a wasting fever often associated with consumption or tuberculosis</term> and those diseases of old age, as in the [tenth book] of *On the Method of Healing*. Explain how he teaches that one with a hectic fever should be placed in cold water, so that one in old age might be led to live longer. 

If it is the latter, a disease is more mortal in two ways: either by reason of a soft matter covering the innate heat and extinguishing it (and thus a cold disease is particularly dangerous, and sometimes a bloody hot disease is more mortal than a choleric hot one), wherefore thirdly it is added that windy fevers are more dangerous than choleric ones because of the thickness of the wind and the blockages <term>opilatione: the medieval term for an obstruction or blockage in the vessels or pores</term> caused by it. Or by reason of not allowing the physician to err or the sick man to sin <note>referring to the difficulty of management</note>. 

And thus a hot disease is more mortal than a cold one, either because its essence is opposed to the primary principle of life (and then the cold is more mortal than the hot), and finally, hot diseases are more deadly than cold ones because the hot ones are disproportionately present, destroying by their sharpness, whereas if they were equal in number, the cold ones would be more mortal because of their contrariety. 

To the first point, therefore, it is replied that a windy fever is more dangerous by reason of the quantity of the matter or the injury it causes in the stomach; as they say, it kills more. To the other, it is said that human nature is not [purely] hot but tempered in relation to the temperament of justice <note>original: "ad iusticiā"; likely referring to the 'balance' of the humors</note>, not of weight, as sought in [Proposition] 341. To the other, it has already appeared as such. To the other, it is said that this is true, but more diseases happen in summer than in winter, and thus more die, though not observed by a just comparison. To those things of the other part, it is now clear from the first and second points through the solution of the fourth earlier.

**Regarding the third point, it must be known** that although in cold diseases of the heart hot things are absolutely sought, in hot ones they are not always beneficial, but rather the reduction of those [qualities]—on account of which this is first shown from [Book] 3, Chapter 11. Secondly, let it be supported by reason, and finally, let it be told what things are sought for this medicine. 

**Regarding the first of these, it must be known** that when we wish to change a hot disposition, we are bold in doing so with physicians mixing hot things with cordials <note>medicines intended to stimulate the heart</note>. But when we wish to change a cold disposition, we are not content with cooling things, because the substance for which the heart was created—and the spirit <term>spiritus: the vital breath or pneuma believed to carry life through the arteries</term> poured out and existing within it—is a hot substance by innate heat, not by a heat harmful to the body. Wherefore, when something happens to it that might extinguish it because it is not mixed with hot medicines (whose property it is to strengthen the innate heat, which is not entirely done by their heat but also with an absolute property associated with their heat), it is possible that it might harm the root (that is, the spirit), even if it benefits the branch (which is the body of the heart). 

And therefore we do not find that the wise men among the ancients treated the malice of a hot complexion in the heart (and that which happens in fever) without a mixture of cold medicines with hot cordials; they sat [to consider] whether nature were strong enough to discern between cooling and heating, so that it might bring cooling to the heart and radical heat <term>calorem radicale: 'radical moisture/heat' was the essential life-fuel in medieval medicine</term> to the spirit. Therefore, those who removed saffron <note>original: "crocum"</note> from the camphor troches <note>original: "trociſcis camphore"; medicinal lozenges</note> and blasphemed the previous camphor troches, gave little help. And if it is fever, for the same reason Galen <note>original: "Gal."</note> orders that in the cure of a hemitritaeus fever <term>emitritei: a semi-tertian fever, often associated with malaria</term>, the power of pepper be mixed into the barley water, which is the proper reasoning.

**Regarding this second point, it must be known** that indications for the principal parts ought to be aimed at: one taken from the virtue <note>original: "virtute"; the vital power of the patient</note>, another from the disposition, and a third from the part itself. The contrary of these indications obscures and blackens the others, as in *On the Method of Healing*, Book 9, especially in a dangerous passion that is very difficult to judge; for when that [virtue] fails, all things are in vain. Since that which is natural ought to govern it like a daughter and fight for it in every way. The showing of the disposition, taken from its own spirit, indicates its intention through the contrary. Regarding the heart, however, I hear that the heart and its innate spirit are the greatest and flow out like the aforementioned root. 

Let it be said, therefore, that in the cure, attention is paid either to the virtue (and thus as it remains hot, it should be strengthened, and similar things would be harmful), or in the passion of those [parts] where, however much the case requires hot things, a mixture of broken fevers <note>meaning mitigated or tempered fevers</note> is beneficial, especially in the heart since life proceeds from it. For there is in it a continuous motion from the heart...

<meta>This page continues the technical medical debate regarding whether "hot" or "cold" remedies are appropriate for the heart. In limbs that have weakened, this [treatment] benefits from heat and is harmed by cold, because the spirit, which is the bearer of its virtues, is similarly affected by heat and cold. Therefore, let it be done as you have sung. If, however, the disposition is considered, since it must be cured by its contrary—because every cure happens through this, or by a similar grace, or by elevation so that it is not lost by injury. And for the most extreme illnesses, the most extreme cures are powerful enough to proceed; and for the final findings, let the final evacuation be expedient. Thus, a condition of the heart is never [properly] described as a "falling sickness" <note>likely referring to syncope or fainting</note> except perhaps by accident, when the heat intensifies into a greater imbalance.

If, however, the heart itself is considered by reason of cure—since its composition is "sung" <note>original: "cantata"; possibly meaning "determined" or "composed"</note> as such—it formally, naturally, and even in its sickly state, requires only cold. From the perspective of preserving its natural complexion, it requires hot things, since its preservation is achieved through its like. If the other part is considered—the composition of the spirit, which is like the root—then in a "hot" suffering of the heart, it requires temperate heat, not excessive; for by excessive heat the spirits are quickly dissolved. 

Indeed, the spirit is most changeable because it is the most subtle [substance] resulting from imbalance. Because of its subtle substance, it readily receives the suffering of a feverish heat; and for this same reason, extreme cold must not be administered, especially since it is contrary to the spirit and its actions. This disposition suffers most quickly from rarity <note>meaning thinness or porosity of the substance</note>. Furthermore, hot qualities make a medicine reach the heart better, as is shown by saffron <note>original: "crocus"</note>. Thus, whether by reason of virtue or on the part of the spirit and the preservation of the natural complexion, the heart requires hot things, though with its feverish heat suppressed, especially in heart disease. Yet, it requires cold things for its absolute disposition and for the restoration of the heart.

Thirdly, it must be known that of the things administered here, some are **simples** and some are **compounds**.

**Simples** act in various ways:
*   **From matter:** such as egg yolks, meat broth, and wine.
*   **From complexion:** such as zedoary <note>a root similar to ginger</note> and stoechas <note>French lavender</note>.
*   **By property:** some of these do not purge, while others do, such as lapis lazuli and Armenian stone <note>a blue mineral used to treat melancholy</note>. Those that do not purge include hyacinth <note>likely a gemstone preparation</note>.
*   **By both complexion and property:** such as lemon balm <note>original: "melissa"</note> and bugloss, which have a marvelous virtue in every suffering of the heart according to the manner of its administration, especially the unwashed bark of the root.

**Minerals** help by carrying the virtue of the medicines to the heart, just as saffron and musk do; and with this, they have other natures. Some parts of the heart and spirits are brought together by **astringency** so they do not dissolve, such as myrobalans and lily. There are some things that **strengthen** the heart so it does not easily suffer from poisons, such as musk and doronicum <note>leopard's bane</note>. Indeed, every fragrant thing, whether hot or cold, is beneficial since it is proportional to the spirit and the soul.

There are also **compounds**, and these are the most perfect, such as theriac, mithridatum, and diamuscum <note>a musk-based confection</note>, and various confections in which, among other things, certain metals like **gold** and **silver** are included, as well as precious minerals. Such are the confections called "of the stones," among which the most noble, effective, and temperate—so that it can be administered in every suffering of the heart, whether hot or cold—is that which I have constructed. Its efficacy is attested by what follows. Sometimes it is administered as it is; sometimes with an choice wine like muscatel, or another when there is a need to quickly strengthen the virtue.

But regarding the aforesaid, a doubt arises: it was said the heart is the "branch" and the spirit the "root," yet it seems that the spirit is generated in the heart by its motion and the friction of the arteries. ## .DIFFERENTIA. .CXCVII. <note>Difference 197</note>

<margin>q</margin> It is shown that in an inflammation <note>original: "apante," referring to an aposteme or abscess</note> of the liver, and especially in a sanguineous one, phlebotomy <note>term: <term>phlebotomy</term>The surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood, a standard treatment for balancing "humors."</note> is performed on the foot and not the hand. For matter ought, according to the ancients, to be evacuated through the parts in which it is found. Those things which are heavy seek the lower parts, just as light things seek the upper, since this is their proper place. But the superior blood is thin and light, while the inferior is thicker... First, the thinnest which is the purest blood is in the head. The liver, however, since it is situated under the diaphragm <note>original: "dyaflante"</note>... and the feet are below, while the hands are indeed above.

And it is supported by the fact that those who suffer pains above the diaphragm signify they require medicine from above. Whosoever, however, suffers below, the flow is downward. Again, first: take care that the passage [of blood] does not happen over a principal organ. This happens over the heart, which is the most principal of all, when one performs phlebotomy in the hand for a liver inflammation. For the blood to be led out is drawn through the vein from the convex part of the liver through the diaphragm into the heart... and finally to the hands and to the rest of the branches above, which does not happen in phlebotomy of the feet. Again in the same place: it is not necessary that you make it in two diameters across the length, but in only one which is the longer diameter. When phlebotomy is done in the hand, it happens across two diameters, because from the liver to the hand a diagonality occurs, since it is constructed from length and breadth. In phlebotomy of the foot, however, only one distance occurs, namely length and breadth, and because the diameter to the foot is longer than that to the hand. Furthermore, it is commanded in the *Tegni* <note>term: <term>Tegni</term>Galen's "Ars Medica," a foundational medical textbook in the Middle Ages.</note> that matter existing in the convex part of the liver should be led to the urinary paths... not to the hand or foot. Moreover, phlebotomy is owed to matter existing within the veins when blood is led out through it, which is contained only in the veins and heart. Matter of an abscess, however, has already crossed the veins and fallen into the spongy parts...

Therefore, not the hand but the foot should be bled, or neither should be bled at all. The opposite, however, is held by almost all physicians, who in an inflammation of the liver command bleeding the hand and not the foot. Whence, in the 13th book of *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingenio san." referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*</note>, it is commanded to cut the inner vein of the right elbow, that is, the basilic vein <note>term: <term>basilic vein</term>A prominent vein in the arm, historically favored for treating diseases of the liver or upper body.</note>, because it follows a straight and wide path to the vena cava; if it does not appear, the median vein should be cut, and if that does not appear, the third should be cut. And finally, when the liver begins to inflame, the veins in the right hand should be cut, but for the spleen, the left. Furthermore, the vein that corresponds to the part to be bled should be bled; such is the basilic vein which is of the hand, whence the 4th book says: the basilic vein evacuates that which is from the upper parts to the lower; here the liver is situated. Therefore, in an abscess of the liver, the hand should be bled and not the foot.

Regarding the first, it must be known what an abscess is, what the liver is, and what phlebotomy is, as shown in Differences 95, 48, and 173. Now, the "hand" is twofold: the "great hand" including the arm and the "small hand" which is the remainder; and similarly, the "foot" exists twofold. The "great hand" and "great foot" are more often intended here. Regarding the second, it must be known that some specific doctors said a vein should be bled here which is after the joint of the ham <note>the back of the knee</note>, such as the saphenous vein. And they established this should be done when matter seeks the upper parts, like the head. And in the 13th book of *The Method of Healing* on the cure of liver abscesses: cut either the inner or median or humeral vein, or that which is by the knee or leg. Which perhaps cannot stand, since an inflamed liver draws blood to itself like a suction... and especially since it rules over the blood, those paths being wider and more direct, so that on account of the length and the narrowness of the paths, phlebotomy of the foot could not effectively lead blood out from the liver. Furthermore, downward evacuation is a kind of derivation <note>term: <term>derivation</term>A medical theory of drawing "bad" humors away from a diseased organ to a nearby site.</note>; this ought to be done for an abscess... Regarding the other point, there is no talk then of phlebotomy for a liver abscess since it was touched upon sufficiently above. But whether evacuation happens through such a vein or another is determined by consideration... either it is a "revulsion" <note>term: <term>revulsion</term>Drawing humors to a distant part of the body to relieve an organ.</note> or a certain partial derivation. Therefore, the foot is not to be bled here. Regarding the third, it must first be shown that the hand is more to be bled here, and the foot also at times; then whether on the same side or the other, such as the right or left. And finally, which vein should be bled. Regarding the first of this, know that I find all simply agree on this: that the vein of the hand should be bled. For in the *Aphorisms*, book 6: in diseases of the upper parts above the liver, bleed from the hands; in inferior parts, cut the veins from the inner knees or above the heel. Hippocrates <note>original: "Ydre"</note> was accustomed, provided the indications allow for phlebotomy and pharmacy, as declared many times in this edition. Because if all agree, or the principal ones, and especially if the vigor of the strength is present, then extract what is necessary of the blood at one time. If not, divide the phlebotomy into several times... And it is supported because evacuation must be made across a moderate distance, so that it is neither entirely close nor entirely remote, and looking toward a wide and direct path; therefore the hand should be bled as anatomy indicates and not [the foot].

Regarding the second point, it should be known that everyone commands phlebotomy to be performed on the same side and not on the opposite side. The opposite is criticized. For the left basilica vein is so far from the liver that the evacuation would occur across two great diameters. Also, the liver is "phlebotomizing" <note>acting like a blood-letter</note>, drawing blood to itself like a dry-nurse <note>original: "sica," likely "sicca" or a suction device</note>, according to the seventh book of *On the Method of Healing*. Therefore, one must evacuate by a path that draws out vehemently, and this is the **right basilica**. This is true even in pleurisy where, if the body is plethoric, the matter is ordered to be bled from the opposite side when a shorter distance is found; however, for an inflammation of the liver, the attraction of blood is so great [that the same side is required]. Regarding this, thirdly, it should be known that commonly the basilica is ordered to be bled because it evacuates more quickly the parts neighboring the liver. The **cephalica**, however, concerns the neck and upper parts. The **median** is common. The **black vein** <note>original: "nigra," often referring to the median cubital or a branch of the basilic</note>, the **purple**, the **matrix**, and the **vein of the heart** <note>various medieval names for veins of the arm</note> follow. These parts are below the middle, according to the fourth book of the first section. If anything prevents using the basilica, then use the median, and after that the cephalica. If these also "rebel" against you or do not appear (as said before), or if you fear the danger that sometimes follows bleeding the basilica because of the artery, or the median because of the nerve, then according to Avicenna <note>original: ".A."</note> in book 14: perform phlebotomy if possible from the basilica. If not, from the "black" vein, and if not that, from the cephalica. And thus it appears here why in the divisions it is commanded to bleed the cephalica more than the basilica or median; this would not be understood unless the cephalica were explained, for no one would think there was any utility in it, just as in the fourth book of *On Accidents* <note>original: "Asso."</note> a red cloud appearing in the fourth crisis is denoted... Although this is demonstrated more fully according to Galen's appearances. For he did not simply say that phlebotomy of the cephalica should be done, but added "up to the week," saying that in the beginning phlebotomy should be from the basilica, but in the process of time, if necessary, from the cephalica. Regarding the fourth point: To the first objection, it is granted that although blood naturally seeks to go downward when left to its nature (since in every mixture earth and water predominate, tending downward), nevertheless, because of the heat and the nature of the spirits joined to it, it often seeks the higher parts. Even though the blood in the lower parts is thicker than that in the upper, it is not so thick that it cannot seek the higher parts in no small measure. For when a vein is opened anywhere, the blood runs there due to the pain, along with the spirits and humors and the impulse of the flow, by which even thicker blood is drawn to the upper parts or the exterior. Also, the liver

---

holds the middle of the whole body. To the affirmation, it is granted that Hippocrates <gloss>Ypocr.</gloss> pays more attention to the inclination of the matter than to the deduction of other humors from the blood. To the other point, it is granted that although the passage occurs over the heart, nevertheless more help than harm follows. Since the blood is not yet corrupt when phlebotomy must be performed, nor is it distended in its substance, but rather runs laterally through the vein upward to the part where it receives its bifurcation and finally inclines to the arm. For it has sometimes been seen that the "sanies" <note>infected discharge or pus</note> of the liver is derived through the heart into the lungs and exits, allowing for health. Generally, however, it is better if it can be done so that the passage of matter—especially pernicious matter—never occurs over a principal organ, as stated in chapter 192. But if it cannot be done otherwise, the physician should choose the path that is less terrifying, without neglecting the rest. Hence, from the seventh book of *On the Method of Healing*, part three: One must apply greater care to the thing that causes greater terror, also ruling over that which is beneath it. And if in phlebotomy of the foot the passage does not fall over the heart, nevertheless it does not provide as much help as that which is more direct. To the other point, it is granted that the transition does not occur across two diameters but across one, which is distant from the lower and upper, as the arm denotes a direct upward elevation. For a diameter must pass through the whole body from top to bottom, from left to right, and front to back, which does not happen here. Also, the diameter extending to the feet is longer... especially since the feet... otherwise it would not meet all the conditions required for an elegant evacuation by diameter. Or it must be longer, not simply, but in the disposition of the two parts of the head, namely the right and left. To the other point, it is granted that the matter which is led from the liver to the belly or the bladder is different from the blood which remains under its natural equality. To the other point, it is granted that in a forming inflammation, when phlebotomy is first sought, the matter is not yet totally outside the veins... Or, once the body is evacuated, the matter that was causing the heaviness re-enters the vessels, especially when it is driven by styptic <term>apocrustic</term> <note>Medicines that repel humors from a site of inflammation.</note> drugs.

### DIFFERENTIA. CXCVIII. <note>Difference 198</note>

> <insert>T</insert>hat the liver should always be poulticed <note>original: "epitimandum," from epithem</note> with **white lead** <note>original: "cerusa"</note> is shown by Pseudo-Dioscorides <note>original: "PDyafco"</note>, who says: Endive leaves mixed with vinegar and white lead help all hot things <note>i.e., hot inflammations</note>. Hence, according to the rule: endive water with white lead and vinegar is a wonderful poultice in cooling that which seeks refrigeration; here, however, it is sought for the liver... Furthermore, the cure is perfected because white lead is cold and dry in the second degree. Again, since the liver is located deep within, it needs something to conduct the coldness to it; this is found in white lead, as it is of a subtle nature. For it is composed of lead and vinegar, which are subtle in their parts... White lead is of vehement subtlety and penetrates deeply, especially that which is prepared with vinegar. Furthermore, if lead is applied over the loins to the kidneys for cooling, it prevents the seminal vessels from causing involuntary emissions <note>original: "pollutonem," nocturnal emissions</note> according to Avicenna <note>original: "Ax"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of topical treatments for liver ailments, specifically debating the use of ceruse (white lead). The previous page concluded with a discussion on phlebotomy (bloodletting) for liver and spleen inflammation. Here, the author shifts to pharmacology, citing classical authorities to warn against the improper use of cooling agents like lead on deep-seated organs.</meta>

...much more strongly **ceruse** <note>original: "cerusa," also known as white lead, a pigment and medicinal substance made by exposing lead to vinegar</note>. Since it is said that it is equal to **lead** in its nature and its powerful thinning effect, it is more potent than lead when it exudes, but lead is more precipitating. In Book 6 of *On the Preservation of Health* <note>original: "vi. de re. sa. a Ga.," referring to Galen's "De Sanitate Tuenda"</note>, **Galen** notes that it is applied to the loins based on the experience of the trainers of athletes. Furthermore <note>original: "Palyn," from the Greek "palin" meaning "again" or "furthermore"</note>, when **ceruse** has been dissolved and applied as a dressing, it remains unresolved for a long time, working upon the site by its own binding nature. Even when mixed, it remains effective for a long time when applied. 

Thus, should **ceruse** be applied to the **liver** <term>epar</term><note>The Greek-derived term for the liver, commonly used in medieval medical Latin.</note> if it is overheated? On the contrary, all authorities agree: nowhere is it found among the simple or composite remedies for the liver that it should be prescribed by itself, but rather it is more often applied with other cooling agents. For I have heard no compatible opinion among the physicians I have consulted, except for one who was long ago moved to uproot this worst of errors. 

Furthermore, because **ceruse** is a **styptic** <note>A substance that contracts tissues and stops secretions.</note> made of coarse parts, it is unable to reach the liver; instead, because it covers the surface, it blocks the heat inside and covers it up, and will further overheat it. In Book 8, it is noted that **lead** is colder than wool <note>A common paradox in Galen's physics: lead feels cold but because it is dense, it can trap body heat like a thick garment.</note>. For it first warms that which it covers. This is especially true because the liver is situated deep within. Moreover, it will prohibit the transpiration of the vapors. Therefore, the liver should not be treated with an **epithem** <term>epithima</term><note>A liquid or semi-liquid topical application, such as a compress or poultice.</note> of ceruse if it is inflamed.

Regarding the first thing to be known—what the liver is—this has already been made known in chapter 47. The liver is said to be overheated when its heat increases beyond its natural state, whether without the fault of the humors or with them. 

**Ceruse**, however, is a medicine made from **lead** and **vinegar**. It is poisonous when administered internally, but soothing <note>original: "lenitivum"</note> when applied externally. I say "commonly," for in the second section it is written that it is sometimes made from salts, and sometimes from vinegar. Regarding the use of lead and vinegar, it is taught that white grapes should be added; although different methods of preparation are taught by various people, they all coincide in the same outcome. 

### Preparation of Ceruse

Let a glass or glazed vessel be taken, wider at the bottom than at the top, and let the strongest vinegar be poured into it along with its dregs <note>original: "fece," the lees or sediment of the vinegar/wine</note>. Some add white grapes. Then, let plates of lead be suspended four fingers above the vinegar by pieces of wood or a stiffer cloth. Next, seal the vessel very well and bury it—most especially in **pig manure** <note>The fermentation of the manure provided a steady, low heat to speed the chemical reaction between the vinegar fumes and the lead.</note>—up to two-thirds of the vessel. It should be in a covered place, not windy at all, and left thus for ten days. 

Some, however, prescribe four months. Then, let the diligent operator open the vessel wisely, lest they be harmed by the pestiferous and paralyzing fumes <note>A remarkably early recognition of the dangers of lead vapor (lead poisoning).</note>. Then, scrape off the **ceruse mucilage** blossoming upon the plates. This should be taken and kneaded by hand, then washed in a basin with water in the sun, and allowed to settle until it sinks. This should be done repeatedly until it becomes entirely white; for that which is snowy is best. In the summer, according to **Dioscorides**, it is prepared thus. And because it is somewhat stinking, certain women wash it and prepare it with **rose water**. This is the common method of its preparation. Sometimes all ceruse is made with vinegar, sometimes with salts, and sometimes by the methods mentioned in the second section.

An **epithem** is a local medicine applied to external parts. According to the fourth rule, epithems are made of good medicines that reach the illness itself. These are similar to plasters, but they are called epithems because plasters are hard, while epithems are runny and soft. Whence **Serapio** says in Book 7: A "tyle" <note>likely referring to a specific form of medicinal paste</note> is an epithem made of aggregated parts and is spread under the fingers. 

Know also that of such applications, some are entirely coarse in substance, like plasters and dry heating agents, which are sometimes bound on and sometimes placed in small bags. Some are entirely soft and liquid, like **embrocations** <note>original: "ebroce," liquid liniments poured over a body part.</note>, which are appropriate medicines for that which must be resolved from the head and other members. Their operation must be changed according to the fourth rule. These are constructed from medicines sufficiently boiled in water, and then poured over the part from above so that their power may penetrate more deeply. Others are intermediate, such as **ointments** <note>original: "ungenta"</note> or **maran** <note>possibly a corruption of "myron" or a specific fat-based preparation</note>, which receive fats or oils. Some lean toward one extreme, such as **cerates** <note>original: "cerotum," a wax-based ointment</note> or **epim** which are constructed from medicines receiving a unifying agent like wax, ladanum, pitch, and oil, so that they can be spread. Then there is the **fomentation**, which is made from decocted things or other warm items and applied. Others reach toward the other extreme, like the **sinapism** <term>linapisma</term><note>A mustard plaster used to irritate the skin and draw out "bad humors."</note>, which is better when a powder is thrown over a part moistened with a viscous liquor. After this is the **epibima** <note>a variation of epithem</note>, as when powder is thrown into fragrant waters and applied to the heart or liver.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that certain "wild" <note>original: "silvestrium," perhaps meaning unlearned or non-traditional</note> physicians attempt to treat the liver with an epithem of ceruse, but they are deceived by the arguments they bring forward. This must be refuted. 

First, it must be known that **ceruse** should never be applied as an epithem over an inflamed liver, neither alone nor mixed. This is a new and erroneous doctrine, unheard of before. This is shown because if it were to be beneficial, its power would have to reach the liver; but it cannot, since it is **styptic**, according to **Dioscorides** and **Galen**, and consists of coarse parts. Because it is applied from the outside, it does not penetrate the pores; or if it does penetrate, it does not reach the vital spirits nor the principal members. The liver is such a member. Nor can it penetrate even when mixed with another liquid, for it will remain in the outer pores because it lacks the nature to sink deep. Furthermore, even if it did penetrate, it would bring harm to the liver’s composition, its spirits, and its power, since it is poisonous when internal—as all attest—even if it is soothing when applied externally. Thus, it poisons if it is absorbed. Secondly, anything applied over the principal members, and especially the liver, ought to be **aromatic**, according to Book 11 of *On the Method of Healing*. 

Thus, let it be briefly inserted as something doubted by no intelligent person: the liver, if it is overheated, must not be treated with an epithem of any kind of ceruse. 

Regarding the fourth point: the intention of **Dioscorides** was not that the prescribed epithem should be applied over the liver for its own sake, but he speaks of it in a general sense within the field of operations and properties...

...protection of the limbs, because that famous and common explanation must be applied when we wish to cool those parts which are on the outside and not those which are on the inside, such as the **liver** <term>epar</term><note>The Greek-derived term for the liver.</note>. For then, **ceruse** <note>white lead</note> is effective not only by standing on its own, but when gathered for a long time because of the equal viscosity arising from it, it manages to dominate the area. It should also be noted that although **A.** <note>Likely Avicenna or Albucasis</note> says the aforementioned remedy is wonderful in cooling with an **epithima** <note>original: "epithima," a medicinal compress or poultice applied over an internal organ</note>, such that nothing is more wonderful than it, he also notes that **camphor** or others may be received into the composition in the third or fourth degree of potency.

Regarding another point: it should be stated that according to what appears in the entire therapeutic section, one should take the indication for cure not only from the disposition of the diseased part, but no less from its **virtue** <note>the innate functional power or "spirit" of an organ</note> and its location. It has been said that **ceruse** harms both the virtue and the instrument of an organ like the liver. It also benefits from the addition of aromatics, of which ceruse has very little. Regarding another point: it is said that **ceruse** is composed with **vinegar**, which acquires a stickiness, thickening, and a stupifying quality because of the "lead-ness" of the lead; and by this artifice, it acquires dryness. For while lead may be humid in effect, vinegar is dry in the beginning. Thus, through the artifice of constructing the ceruse, the humidity is removed from the lead so that it becomes dry to the touch; thus, drying is achieved. Note that **A.** says it possesses a report of powerful subtlety, as that which is made from vinegar compared to that which is constructed from salts. 

Regarding another point: it is said that lead and ceruse are not the same, as they differ greatly in their innate properties and species. Note also concerning the liver—being a principal limb—and the kidneys, which are receivers of the waste of the principal organs: note that a **lead plate** <note>original: "plumbea lamia"</note> is to be applied over the loins, unless it has been perforated with many small holes, for fear that it might induce a greater heat in the flesh itself <note>by trapping the body's natural heat against the skin</note>. It is also necessary that beneath the plate, an application of juices be made for the purpose of cooling, such as **houseleek** <note>original: "sempervive"</note>, **psyllium**, or juices applied to the navel of the belly, such as **plantain**, **purslane**, **sorrel**, with **rose oil** and similar things, as mentioned in Book 6 of *On the Preservation of Health*. It is also expedient that there be two plates with a distance of two fingers between them, so that the **nucha** <note>The spinal cord or the back of the neck; here referring to the spinal column in the lower back</note> is not harmed. Let them be joined together with leather or something else, and with this, one must take care not to let them overheat; they should be removed and a new application of the aforementioned moistures should be placed under the plates. Indeed, this is applied more because of the quality of the "enveloping vessels" in which it is said (in *Diax 25*) that sperm is generated, which is warmed by thin heat, and the place is also warmed by no small amount of motion and friction there, and thus horsemen and those who rub the area are stimulated to intercourse.

Regarding another point: it is argued that **ceruse** should be excluded from cooling the internal parts, which is granted regarding the interior, since it has been shown that it cannot penetrate; hence the earlier practical advice. If they apply a **cataplasm** <note>a soft, moist mass of material, typically of bran or herbs, applied to the body</note> over acute inflammations, it settles them; and therefore it is put into ointments for burns from fire or boiling water, and in **cancerous ulcers**.

### .DIFFERENCE. .CXCVIX. <note>199</note>

->That **bezel** <term>bezeɫ</term><note>From the Arabic "fasil" or "basil," referring to an incision or the act of tapping/puncturing to drain fluid.</note> or incision above the navel is suitable in **dropsy** <term>ydropisi</term><note>An old term for edema or the swelling of soft tissues due to the accumulation of excess water.</note> is shown. As in *Aphorisms*, Book 6: "Those who burn or cut for dropsy..." whereupon the Commentator says: Physicians are accustomed to **cut** dropsical patients more than to **burn** <note>cauterize</note> them. Indeed, in *Epidemics*, Book 6: "Quickly cut those with water..." <margin>draining the fluid</margin>... Furthermore, the cure is perfected by the removal of the conjoined cause, since it turns into a disease with it. Indeed, the conjoined cause is seen to be in the dropsical patients that which is led out by incision.

---

Also, **cauterization** <note>burning the skin with a hot iron to create a permanent opening or "fount"</note> is suitable according to **Albucasis** <note>The great medieval surgeon of Islamic Spain</note>, as he declares it to be manifold, which seems more difficult than incision, since incision is done only once. And in Book 13 of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de inge." referring to Galen's "De Ingenio Sanitatis"</note>: Surgery in dropsical patients is done by a nearby incision. Furthermore, it leads out by incision that which is "drops" and preternatural. All such evacuation is considered laudable. Again, if it seems right for dropsy, since there are certain swellings to burn and others to cut, but the others often require sectioning. Therefore, and further, whence in Book 14: When the corruption from the rupture of the <unclear>membrane</unclear> or exit breaks into the cavity, it is received under the **peritoneum** <term>syphac</term><note>From the Arabic "sifaq," the lining of the abdominal cavity.</note>; it is cured by being cut at the two groins until the peritoneum is opened, such that a **cannula** <note>a small tube for draining fluid</note> is introduced to let it run outward. 

Likewise, art imitates nature, since art is the rule and image of nature. But nature evacuates the dropsical patient not a little through the **navel** <term>umbilicum</term>, and takes the path by which in the womb it returned urinary waters to the navel. For then it does not urinate from the bladder, but by that way. And also by a rupture near the beginning of the hips... it is a thing to be feared. Furthermore, the precept in Difference 197 is that evacuation should not happen by passing over a principal organ; but that happens especially when the water of the dropsy is led out by diuretics. Also, purgative medicines, since they are of a poisonous nature (as mentioned by **A.** in the *Canon*), harm the stomach and weaken the liver, which an incision does not do. Therefore, the **bezel** <note>incision</note> is suitable for the dropsical. In the opposite view, in Book 7 of the *Practice*, and also **Galen**. Furthermore, the cure of a disease is its removal and not the bringing on of another; but in an incision, there is a "solution of continuity" <note>a surgical wound</note>. 

And according to **Erasistratus** <note>original: "Archistratem," a famous Greek anatomist and royal physician</note>, the liver is rendered heavy either by an abscess or by the soaking up of water. Or the spleen contracts the diaphragm and the rest of the spiritual organs downward, whereby the **vital virtue** <note>the life-force seated in the heart</note> is violently struck. For this reason, incision is not suitable for a dropsical patient. 

Regarding the first point, however, it should be known what dropsy is, and what and how many its species are, and the difference of their causes. What an incision shows is shown in Differences 181 and 208. Below the navel is a part of the belly; for the whole is divided into three: the **hypochondrium** <note>the upper abdomen</note>, the area around the **navel**, and the **pecten** <note>the pubic region</note> (*Aphorisms*, second section). Regarding the second point, it should be known that some have simply allowed the incision to be made. For physicians were accustomed to cut dropsical patients (*Aphorisms*, Book 6). This is shown because the pain is a more intense cause when administered by the multitude of cauteries. But that is not valid because in the "bursting," there is a great danger (*Practice*, Book 7). Also, the incision penetrates to the interior parts, evacuating the water from the belly almost suddenly, which is followed by the **resolution of the spirits** <note>fainting or death due to the sudden loss of vital energy</note> and the commotion of the humors; whence fever often arises. But according to **Albucasis**, the "cooked" <note>the cautery</note> does not lead it out so suddenly, nor does it stir the humors, but leads it out little by little since it does not pass through the skin [all at once], whereby a greater defect will appear in the beginning. 

Regarding the third point, however, the discourses of the authors are first brought forward and confirmed by reasons thereafter. Afterwards, the site of the muscles of the belly in which the incision falls should be explained, and finally, the manner of incision and cauterization should be joined similarly. Regarding the first, this sequence should be known...

<meta>This page transitions from a discussion on external medicinal applications (like ceruse) to the surgical interventions for dropsy, specifically paracentesis—the draining of fluid—and the anatomical structure of the abdominal wall.</meta>

Regarding this point of **Serapion** <note>Yuhanna ibn Sarapion, a 9th-century Syriac Christian physician</note>, we have perhaps already seen many who underwent the **tapping** <term>bezel</term> <note>original: "bezel," a medieval term for paracentesis or surgical tapping to drain fluid from a body cavity</note> and only a few of them escaped death. Those who did survive were those who, after the **tapping**, made use of movement and exercise; their **virtues** <note>the body's innate vital powers or strength</note> were still intact, and their bodies were not overly thinned. For these reasons, I believe they survived. Therefore, one ought not to administer the **tapping** except in bodies whose **virtue** is stable and whose health is sufficient according to the level of necessity, and who have not descended into extreme wasting and thinness. It is also necessary, when one administers this **tapping**, to do so with extreme caution. We must treat them and make the severity of the **tapping** known, as well as the fear of death involved, so that we are not later blamed for their death.

In the seventh and also the ninth [books] of practice, it is noted that there is great danger in **rupturing** <note>original: "crepando," referring to the surgical piercing of the abdominal wall</note>, and it should not be applied except in one whose **virtue** is powerful. For there are few who are liberated by **rupturing**. Indeed, I have not seen it applied to anyone except one, and even he was not perfectly cured. **Galen** reports that he saw no one to whom **rupturing** was applied who was liberated, except for one man whose **virtue** was powerful and whose body was robust.

In the thirteenth [chapter] of the third [book] concerning the **incision of the abdominal wall** <term>mirach</term> <note>original: "mirach," an Arabic-derived term used in medieval medicine to denote the abdominal wall, including the skin, fat, and muscles</note>. Know that it profits few except in a very strong body, since the person must be able to tolerate moderate thirst and a reduction of food in this manner. Hence, one should not dare to perform it while any other cure is possible. **Albucasis** <note>Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi, the famous Andalusian surgeon</note> also says: "If your treatment with medicines does not help, then consider: if weakness has already followed the infirmity, or if there is some other illness along with the **dropsy** <term>ydropisim</term> <note>the accumulation of excess fluid in the body tissues or cavities; modern ascites</note>, such as a loosening of the bowels or colic, then beware of treating him with the iron <note>the surgical knife</note>, for there is fear of death." But if you see a patient of exuberant **virtue**, and there is no illness except the **dropsy** alone, and he is neither a child nor an old man, then the major procedures may be performed well. 

Regarding this, one must first know that the indication for this incision must be taken from the nature of the subject being treated and the condition of the subject. Simply put, the **virtue** must be strong, the body fleshy and youthful, not prostrated by any other illness, and—after despairing of health through other medicines—powerful enough to tolerate abstinence and exercise. Regarding the nature of the condition: in **dropsy**, it is appropriate for **ascites** <note>fluid in the abdomen</note>, but not for **anasarca** <note>general swelling of the whole body</note> or **tympanites** <note>swelling due to gas</note>. **Haly Abbas** <note>Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi, a Persian physician</note> and **Albucasis** agree that there should not be so much wateriness contained within him that the attendants, by compressing his sides, cannot force it downward. 

Know also that some illness is "curable"—that is, not having anything that prohibits medicine—while others are not. If the illness is truly and simply curable, then the **tapping** or rupture is in no way appropriate. This is shown from the previously mentioned indications, whether the patient is strong or weak. If he is strong, he is to be cured with medicines such as purgatives and diaphoretics <note>medicines that induce sweating</note>, in which the cure is completed without danger. If he is weak, the incision is already forbidden. Furthermore, from the indication of the cause and disposition, the cure is the removal of the cause; a rupture is not performed when **dropsy** arises from a bad condition or an obstruction or an abscess in the **liver** or other organs. In such cases, the heart eventually suffers; otherwise, it is almost never the primary cause. But in surgery, the disease often meets more disease with the dissolution of **virtue** due to the drawing out of the **spirits** <note>the vital breaths or subtle fluids thought to sustain life</note>. Again, organs that are abscessed or rendered heavy by the soaking up of water tend to move downward after the evacuation by incision, dragging the diaphragm and other spiritual organs with them, from which pain and difficulty follow according to this text.

**F.** also says, according to the authorities, that in **dropsy** one receives a poor prognosis because of which surgery is not suitable for curable **dropsy**. But if it is "incurable" <note>meaning resistant to standard drugs</note> or there is a defect in the art of medicine, a rupture may be performed, provided the aforementioned indications are observed—for instance, when someone chooses it because they abhor all medicines. Thus **Serapion** says: "In patients who did not tolerate the administration of laxatives and diuretics and things that diminish the water of **dropsy**, they instead chose a single surgical medicinal drink." So **Galen** relates of a certain patient who preferred to suffer anything rather than be **pitched** <note>referring to a surgical procedure involving cautery or sharp intervention</note>. Or some avoid medicines through which the cure is seen to proceed slowly, thinking that it will be completed more quickly by evacuation, trusting in their own strength; or perhaps because they are poor and cannot afford moderate living, or for some other such reason. If such a person survives by the strength of their **virtue** and the fleshiness of their body, the cure could have been praise-worthily completed by the help of physicians.

For the beginning of this, it must be known that the muscles situated in the lower belly are eight in number. Two of these, located under the skin, cover the whole belly, beginning from the lower part of the chest around the **sword-like extremity** <note>the xiphoid process of the sternum</note> and extending along the groin as long muscles. There are also two others whose fibers proceed across the width with the posterior ones, forming right angles, located under the two near the lower chest. Others run according to the fibers diagonally to each other in the manner of a **cross** <note>the Greek letter Chi, χ</note>. In this positioning of the eight, the first two are the most prominent, under which the longitudinal or "round" ones provide support. As I have read in the Greek book, he expressed this with his own words, as did **Al-Mansur** <note>Rhazes</note> and **Averroes**. The theoretical reason places the diagonal or oblique muscles immediately under the straight ones. Considering again the anatomical vision, one perceives the order of the muscles by touch. For some appear so deep that they cannot be discerned, and therefore their position is described in different ways. The parts of the belly encountered preceding the **tapping** itself are first the skin, then the fatty tissue, then the **small cloth** <note>original: "panniculus," a membrane or layer of tissue</note> or membrane extended under it, and then the muscle.
