<meta>This page continues the surgical discussion of dropsy (edema), moving from the general risks of "tapping" to the specific anatomical layers of the abdomen and the precise techniques for incision and cautery as practiced by medieval authorities.</meta>

The **abdominal wall** <term>mirach</term> <note>original: "mirach," an Arabic-derived term for the external layers of the abdomen, including skin, fat, and muscle</note> is described first, then the **peritoneum** <term>siphac</term> <note>original: "siphac," the inner lining of the abdominal cavity</note>, which is the thin, firm membrane of the belly muscles, and finally the inner lining. It is a truth always held that the *siphac* is a surrounding or extended membrane under which the **omentum** <term>zirbus</term> <note>original: "zirbus," the fatty tissue covering the intestines</note> and the intestines are contained. There is a three-fold benefit to these muscles and the parts with them: first, that by their compression, they force the intestines, bladder, and womb to expel what they contain at the proper time; second, that they support and strengthen the **diaphragm** <note>original: "dyafla"</note> when it is strained during the exhalation of breath and assist in the protection of the voice; and third, that they increase the heat of the belly for the digestion of food. Furthermore, they provide a constant utility by lifting the weight of food from the organs and increasing the thickness so that no rupture occurs when the belly happens to be distended by bloating.

Regarding the fourth point, it should be known that the evacuation of water in this "sickness" <note>original: "sanie"</note> must be done gradually by **cautery** <note>the use of a hot iron to create an opening</note>, according as the patient's strength can tolerate it. For according to the ancients, some **empirics** <note>physicians who rely on experience rather than theory</note> or those suffering from **dropsy** <note>original: "ydropici," fluid retention</note> are burned or cut, and while the fluid or water flows out in great quantity and suddenly, they perish entirely, since every sudden change is an enemy to nature—as stated in the **Aphorisms** <note>referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates</note>.

The method of incision for **ascites** <note>original: "ascliticus," fluid in the abdominal cavity</note> is to stand the patient upright or in an elevated seat so the abdominal area is stretched; then the assistants press the sides of the belly downward. One must consider whether the dropsy arises from the intestines, the kidneys, the liver, or the spleen. If it is from the intestines, the incision should be made directly three fingers' breadth below the navel. If it is from the liver, let it be done on the left side. But if from the spleen, let it be done on the right, so that the drainage happens through the **opposite side** <note>a common medieval medical theory that draining from the opposite side of the affected organ balanced the body's humors</note>. Then the skin should be lifted upward so that the incision pierces the *mirach* and the *siphac* in different spots; this is so that when the skin is let down, it covers the opening, just as happens at the entrance of the ureters into the bladder, from which the urine does not flow backward.

<margin>
Regarding another point: although it is regularly commanded to avoid passing through a **principal organ** <note>such as the liver or heart</note> as much as possible, it is sometimes permitted when the matter is not corrupt, is small in quantity, and passes through quickly. From this, a greater benefit follows than harm, such as when water is drawn out by **diuretics**. For some of these pass through the liver and the rest, perhaps thinned out, descend through the veins to the kidneys, according to that **Aphorism** [Book VII]: "In those whom the kidneys and belly..." etc. If, however, anything should ascend to the liver through the lower parts, it is rendered dissolved into vapors so that it does not cause harm. Similarly, although medicines may not be poisonous or inherently violent, the milder ones should be chosen, and their "malice" <note>harmful side effects</note> is corrected with things that strengthen the liver, such as **spikenard**, **hemp-agrimony**, **endive**, and fat for the liver.
</margin>

**Asclepiades** <note>an ancient Greek physician</note> wished for the urine to be collected by "sweating" through the same natural passages. Once a rupture is made, a metal **cannula** <term>tube</term>—either silver or a thin one—is inserted, and as much water is evacuated as the strength of the patient's **virtue** <note>innate vital energy</note> allows, which the pulse will indicate. There are also some who use their ingenuity to make the water flow to the surface, and they cut gradually; others make an incision near the bone. Others prick the area with many needles so that the water has a way to "sweat out" through the punctures. In the seventh book of Practice, this rupture is considered dangerous.

According to **Albucasis** <note>original: "Albuca," the great 11th-century Andalusian surgeon Al-Zahrawi</note>, the method is this: four **cauteries** <note>surgical burns</note> are made around the navel: one toward the stomach, another over the liver, one in line with the chest, and the last in line with the [lower] stomach. The depth of the cautery should be equal to the thickness of the skin. Then it is left open for a long time so the water can flow through gradually. This should be managed according to their specific condition; if the patient is weak or if they prefer it, fewer cauteries should be made and done in stages so that strength is preserved as much as possible. Because the pain of the burning afflicts them, many flee from it and choose the incision instead.

Regarding the first point: **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Y." for Ypocras</note> does not simply command that an incision be made, but advises that if it is done, the water should be drawn out gradually, lest by a sudden evacuation **fainting** <note>original: "sincopis"</note> and death should follow. Or he speaks of the previously noted case where the dropsy is a non-curable sickness. 

It appears what should be said regarding the point brought up by the **Commentator** <note>likely Averroes or Galen</note>. It is also clear what should be said to the other point. By this, **ascites** is compared to **hyposarca** <note>original: "yposarticos," a general swelling of the flesh or systemic edema</note>. Whence it is added: a physician does not happen to cut a patient with *hyposarca*. 

Regarding another point: although a three-fold cautery may be expedient, it can be done successively and not all at once; although this may trouble the patient more, it is not as much as an incision. This is similar to what is said about **actual and potential cautery** <note>actual cautery used hot iron; potential used corrosive chemicals</note>. 

To another point: perhaps the "joined cause" <note>the immediate cause of the disease</note> is not only the water, but a bad disposition in the liver or a condition where water is the joined cause; and though the dropsy is removed, the cause remaining in the liver generates water again. Just as when smoke is removed, it was the joined cause of the soot, but the fire does not cease on account of this. It is possible for the preceding cause to remain. 

To another point: it is not enough for a cure that the thing causing the distress or the unnatural thing be evacuated, but according to the ancients, one must "bear it well and not just bring it together," as appears in the incision of the head of one of the two, which happens in this proposal. 

To another point: it is not the same because the water of **abscesses** <note>original: "apostematu"</note> and other things, when evacuated, do not leave behind such a depraved disposition in the part that it rises up again, as is left in the liver, as seen before. The manner of a dropsical swelling is different and induced differently. 

To another point: sometimes art does not imitate nature. Since sometimes nature is more powerful. Nor are the evacuations of water made through the navel or through a rupture near the groin and anus properly made by a "victorious nature," but rather they are caused by the weight of the matter being stimulated, which is shown by their bad outcome.

Fen 3, Section 11 <note>This refers to the third "Fen" (a division of a book) of Avicenna's *Canon of Medicine*.</note>

# ## DIFFERENCE 100 <note>original: "C.C." represents the Roman numeral 100, likely a chapter or distinction number.</note>

That the **flux of the belly** <term>fluxus ventris</term> <note>a general term for diarrhea or any loose discharge from the bowels</note> occurring at the beginning of a disease should be stopped is shown by the fact that such a flux should be restrained because it evacuates nothing in a healthy or natural way, but rather **symptomatically** <term>sinthomatice</term> <note>meaning the discharge is a harmful symptom of the disease itself rather than a "natural" healing crisis</note>. Indeed, a flux at the beginning of an illness is simply an evacuation of every kind [of humor]. Hence the specific **Aphorism** <note>Referring to the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates</note>: "Of those things that are excreted, those that are evacuated according to the reason of nature are beneficial, but those that are entirely symptomatic of conditions are contrary to nature." For at the time when nature is being produced by sickly causes and there is an **indigestion of the humors** <note>the body's inability to "cook" or process the bodily fluids properly</note>, it is impossible for anything to be evacuated in a benign manner.

Furthermore, that which corrupts the order of nature must be stopped, since goodness in things exists through proper order (as stated in the 12th book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note>). But such a flux does exactly that. For first, it evacuates when digestion ought to precede it, followed by discretion <note>the separation of good and bad humors</note>, and only then evacuation, according to Galen in the same place. Here, the opposite is committed. Likewise, that which is evil by way of cause and wood <note>original: "lignum," likely a metaphor for the "material" or root cause</note> must be cut away; and such is the aforementioned flux. For it is a **critical sign** <term>signum creticum</term> <note>a sign of a "crisis" or turning point in a disease</note> and a cause preceding the signs of digestion; since it never appears at the beginning, these are not good signs when they appear quickly in the belly. Indeed, those critical signs that precede digestion denote death or a long-lasting sickness, such as a relapse of a previous crisis (according to the Aphorisms).

Also, that which cannot do the lesser cannot do the greater; much more so nature, which cannot induce the motion of **alteration** <note>the process of changing the quality of humors</note> at the beginning of a disease—which is easier to cause than the motion of **expulsion**—cannot properly move things locally. For in local motion, a thing changes its place entirely, whereas in the motion of alteration, it changes according to its parts (as in the first book of *On Generation* <note>Aristotle's *On Generation and Corruption*</note>). Therefore, that which nature cannot handle must be restrained, as it is a burden to her. Again, if a cause must be prohibited, so must its effect, especially when it leaves a greater impression. But the cause [the disease] must be prohibited, therefore also the flux, which is its effect. For these are accidents caused by diseases, which is why a flux occurring at the beginning must be stopped.

**To the contrary:** In the seventh book of the *Practice*, it is commanded that when disturbance, anxiety, or a **choleric passion** <note>an illness related to yellow bile, often involving vomiting and diarrhea</note> occurs, one should not occupy themselves with stopping it as long as the patient's strength remains firm and the evacuation does not exceed its limits. Rather, it should be assisted with **rose water** <note>original: "aqua rosa"</note> and **sweet almond oil** <note>original: "oleo dulciū amigdalay"</note> so that the stomach may be purged of superfluities. This should similarly be observed in a flux of the belly, as it is associated with the same condition.

Furthermore, that which is a good sign and a helpful thing should not be restrained. Such is the flux occurring at the beginning of a disease, as stated in the tenth [text]. When a person with **pleurisy** <note>inflammation of the lung lining</note> experiences a difficulty at the end, otherwise a flux of the belly signifies that his **liver** <note>original: "epar"</note> has already been weakened, which is very bad; yet at the beginning, it is a good sign—indeed, it is a helpful thing. Also, according to Hippocrates <note>original: "Y." for Ypocras/Hippocrates</note>, if **sputum** <note>phlegm</note> appears immediately, it shortens the onset of the disease; similarly, a flux occurring at the beginning will shorten the disease, since in both cases the matter of the disease is led out. Often it excuses the physician from his work, so it should not be cut off; such is a flux occurring naturally at the beginning, since a physician should not rarely evacuate at the beginning.

---

Again, that which leads out humors that are suffocating by their quantity or extinguishing by their quality (or both) should not be restrained. This flux seems to accomplish this. Therefore, it is not expedient to constrict a flux of the belly at the beginning of a disease.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that a flux is a passage of humors through the body made from the center toward the circumferences, which is either an evacuation of the belly through the path of the intestines. This happens either from an external cause, such as air, water, or the environment; or from food or drink and simply from the improper administration of the six non-natural things <note>A medical concept: air, food/drink, sleep/wake, motion/rest, evacuation/repletion, and passions</note>; or from an internal cause and even a "solution of continuity" <note>a physical break or injury in the tissue</note>. This arises from one of the four humors, especially **choler** <note>yellow bile</note>, or from an organ like the brain, stomach, intestines, **mesenteric veins** <term>mesarayca</term> <note>the veins connecting the intestines to the liver</note>, liver, or spleen; or simply from the whole body or some food-based cause from indigestion. This happens due to a "bad complexion" <note>an imbalance of the primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, or dry</note> of the stomach and intestines, whether simple or mixed, as when the mesenteric veins and liver are unable to attract [nutrients].

Another type is **humoral**, and that is manifold according to the diversity of the humors themselves, especially when the humors are in opposition to the organs. Furthermore, a flux is sometimes a disease and other times an accident <note>a secondary symptom</note>; likewise, one occurs with the strength of the patient's power, and another with weakness. Finally, one is **critical** <note>natural/healing</note> and another is **symptomatic** <note>harmful</note>. What the "belly" is, the 54th distinction shows. The "beginning" is taken here as one of the four stages of a disease.

Regarding the second point, some have said simply that this flux should be stopped since it evacuates nothing naturally or benignly, but rather symptomatically as nature is further stimulated. Others say it should not be constricted since it leads out the matter of the disease. The defects of these positions and their motions will appear.

Regarding the third point, it should be known whether this flux is a disease or an accident. If it is the former, it should not be stopped unless it precedes things so much that it prostrates the patient's strength, just as even critical fluxes are restrained. Hence Damascenus <note>referring to Mesue the Elder</note> in the Aphorisms says: if for a long time they have had neither vomiting nor a loosening [of the bowels] and it suddenly happens, see that you do not hasten to constrict it, because here the body is purged of wicked humors. For this reason, blood that is not exercised often carries out strength and **pus** <note>original: "sanie"</note>, and this purging and evacuation is praiseworthy. From this, the looseness that happened due to the omission of exercise is removed. If, however, it is an accident, it either arises from food due to indigestion or it is humoral. If it is the former, it should be stopped lightly with things that procure digestion in the belly and intestines, whether taken internally or applied externally, such as **wormwood** <note>original: "abstinthiū"</note>, **mastic** <note>a resin</note>, **spikenard** <note>original: "spica"</note>, **quince** <note>original: "cithonia"</note>, and similar things. If it is from the mesenteric veins, liver, or brain, it should be cured by strengthening those organs.

<margin>No</margin>
<margin>Great bedside determination</margin>
Whether it arises from a fault of the **constitution** <term>complexion</term> <note>the balance of the four "humors" or qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within the body</note> or otherwise, or in specific active locations, the following are clearly effective: spikenard, Arabian lavender <note>original: sticados arabicum</note>, and agarwood <note>original: xiloaloes</note>. For it is necessary to check this flow when the **vital power** <term>virtus</term> <note>the body’s natural ability to heal and sustain life</note> is flattened and nothing of the diseased matter is being expelled. However, if the flow is humoral, it is either due to an excessive quantity of humors or an intense quality. In either case, one should not stop the flow violently, but rather by soothing it, so that the diseased matter does not retreat to any of the principal organs and cause death or an **aposteme** <note>an internal swelling or abscess</note>. You should manage this so that some of the matter is evacuated, especially when it is excessive and sharp, because it may not wait for proper digestion. Nature sometimes acts like a warrior who, feeling strong and perceiving harm, moves indiscreetly because he is too confident in himself. If, however, the vital power is weak, the flow must be stopped cautiously and gradually, partly to preserve the power and partly by soothing the flow. It is not only necessary to bind a beginning flow, but even a critical one when the body's strength cannot tolerate it. For the indication taken from the vital power itself blunts all other indicators, as the therapeutic discourse says. That which must be most carefully looked after is the vital power. For it is the healer, not the medicine. When the flow is checked, the **spirit** <note>the "vital breath" or energy believed to circulate through the arteries</note> is preserved. Because any critical or further flow, when it is excessive, dissolves the vital power, it must be restrained. I have constructed an effective **electuary** <term>electuarium</term> <note>a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</note> for this restriction.

> **Recipe**
> Take seeds of wild grapes, fruits of the red dog-rose, cypress nuts, the dung of a donkey, goat, and hare, plantain seeds, the ash of a sponge, and cloister-ink, 4 drachms of each; mastic, fine frankincense, gum arabic, tragacanth, myrrh, acacia, myrtle, sumac, and *ramech* <note>a compound astringent medicine</note>; seeds of water-lily, barberries, cumin and bishop's weed toasted and infused in vinegar; oak galls, pomegranate peels, pomegranate flowers, red coral, dragon’s blood, Armenian bole, sealed earth, "star-clay," and mummia <note>original: mumie; a resinous substance used in medieval medicine</note>, 3 drachms of each; half a measure of spodium <note>ash of ivory or metals</note>, seeds of white and black poppy, seeds of white henbane, purslane seeds, endive seeds, lettuce seeds, and toasted rhubarb, 2 drachms of each; mouse-ear hawkweed, horsetail, knotgrass, hypocistis, barberry, spikenard, fennel, celery seed, caraway seed, lovage, and anise, 2 drachms of each; quince pulp, 5 drachms; medlars, service-berries, wild pears or pomegranate seeds, and cornelian cherries, 7 scruples of each; all types of sweetened and charred myrobalans, 5 scruples of each; amber, sandarac, and red rose petals, 4 scruples of each; opium, saffron, castor, cassia wood, and camphor, 2 drachms of each. Let a sugar electuary be made once the ingredients are sufficiently crushed.

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it is said that something can be evacuated by the vigor of nature and benignly in two ways. Either simply—and thus no such flow occurring at the beginning is beneficial—or in a certain respect, as if expelling an evil in a time of necessity. Thus, a flow made by the power of nature can be said to evacuate something benignly. It is not an evil thing to restrain the matter, especially when it is abundant and sharp, for fear that it might decline toward one of the principal organs if repelled, particularly when it is not being evacuated elsewhere and the vital power is still standing firm. To the other point, it is said that the order of nature is not absolutely corrupted, but follows what is most permitted; though a thing may be completed poorly, if necessity compels it, it can be finished however possible. To the other, it is said in the same way that it is better to choose a relapse or a long illness than the rushing of the matter to a principal organ. To the other, it is said that nature sometimes seems able to do less because it is not using its full strength. However, when it uses its gathered strength, it can do more, as appears in the **ant-like pulse** <term>pulsu formice</term> <note>a very weak, small, and frequent pulse that feels like an ant crawling under the skin</note>, or the very thick and **worm-like pulse** <term>uermiculante</term> <note>a pulse that feels like a creeping worm, signaling extreme weakness</note> made near death when the power is defeated. A **large pulse** <term>pulsum magnum</term> always requires three conditions: the strength of the vital power, the obedience of the "instruments" (the arteries), and necessity. If the pulse becomes disobedient, it becomes fast. If, with this, a weakness of power occurs, it will be "thick" (frequent). If the thickness increases more, it becomes **worm-like**. If it increases further and the power is worn down, it becomes **ant-like**. Finally, when the power is prostrate, it ceases to move due to weakness, and the pulse again appears worm-like, signifying a greater weakness than before. Finally, when the power is completely exhausted and collapses into itself, the pulse becomes slow, and then the "fire" of the vital power is extinguished and death is near. Some beats become sluggish because the soul is exhaling. From this, the true harmony of conflicting ideas appears. For it is written that the **ant-like** pulse shows a greater weakness of power than the **worm-like** pulse.

Regarding the other point, it is said that the effect should not be prohibited entirely if it leads to the destruction of the cause, just as a flow in some way removes the cause and the disease. To those things which were touched on elsewhere, it appears as follows: first, that a flow of the belly should not be prohibited, especially when some bad matter is being evacuated while the vital power remains firm. To the other, it is said that there, "A" <note>likely a reference to an author like Aristotle or Avicenna</note> understands the "beginning" to mean a space of three days, and not one of the four stages of a disease.

# DISTINCTION 201.

<margin>1</margin>
He shows that dysentery caused by **blood** <term>sanguis</term> is more difficult to cure than others. Since that suffering is the hardest to treat in which a humor is evacuated that is more "familiar" and closer to the body’s nature; here, according to them, it is blood. Furthermore, a disproportionate disease is worse than a proportionate one, according to the rule in "On Diseases" and the remainder of Distinction 179. But blood is disproportionately related to causing dysentery, since dysentery is a **tearing of the intestines** <gloss>original: scissura intestinorum</gloss> which is caused by some sharp humor; blood is not such a thing, as it is hot, moist, sweet, and mild. Therefore, dysentery caused by blood is worse to treat. 

However, it is written in the *Aphorisms* <note>Referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates</note> that dysentery from **salt phlegm** <term>flegma salsum</term> is worse. Again, an illness caused by a humor that resists being drawn out is harder to cure than its opposite; and this is the case with phlegm, since it is cold and viscous. Therefore, it is worse to treat. 

On the contrary, some say that **sanguine** <gloss>bloody</gloss> and **phlegmatic** <gloss>phlegm-based</gloss> dysentery are easier to cure because, according to the second book of *Prognostics*, sanguine and phlegmatic matters are of less "malice" <note>harmful intensity</note> than **yellow bile** <term>colera citrina</term> and **black bile** <term>colera nigra</term>, and those things which induce such diseases are easier to cure. 

He demonstrates that dysentery caused by **yellow bile** <term>cholera</term> is of a worse cure because dysentery is an **excoriation** <term>excoriatio</term> <note>a scraping or stripping away of the internal lining of the gut</note>. This is caused by a bitter, sharp quality, which is the specific property of yellow bile. Furthermore, it is hot, thin, and penetrating, which makes it the greatest inducer of such excoriation. Therefore, dysentery is more incurable when it comes from yellow bile. 

In contrast, some argue it is easier to cure because a thin humor is quickly expelled, and the dysentery that follows is more curable. 

Regarding **black bile** <term>melancholia</term>, it seems to be the most difficult cure because a disease caused by a humor further from the nature of the body is harder to treat; such is black bile, as it is cold and dry by nature, whereas human nature is hot and moist. Likewise, a disease caused by a humor that is difficult to expel from the body is harder to cure; such is black bile, since it is earthy, thick, and moves with difficulty. Therefore, this cure is worse than the others. 

On the contrary, according to the sixth book of *Aphorisms*, dysentery occurring in those with **splenic disorders** <note>diseases of the spleen, often associated with excess black bile</note> is good. Again, by its coldness, dryness, and **astringency** <gloss>original: ponticitate</gloss>, it has the power to pull parts together and comfort them, which is the opposite of dysentery. Likewise, black bile is naturally proportionate to the intestines; therefore, if dysentery happens to be caused by black bile, it is most easily cured.

Regarding the first point, one must know what dysentery is, and which is true, and which is metaphorical, and how many types there are. Indeed, **intestinal dysentery** <term>dissinteria intestinalis</term> is caused by an external cause, such as a poison or an unrestrained poisonous drug, and sometimes from sharp and salty feces. It also arises from an internal cause, such as black bile, and specifically "burnt" <note>adusta; humors that have become overheated and toxic</note> bile, or from a cancerous discharge in the intestines which is distinguished by the breaking down of the tissue, or the discharge of blood from yellow bile, or from salt phlegm due to the intensity of its viscosity—for when it is rooted out, it wounds—or from the rupture of an **aposteme** <note>an internal abscess or swelling</note>. Sometimes it happens from the tearing of veins when the blood in them becomes too much; for they are thinned and burst by the abundance of blood. 

There are also others who say it happens from **leek-green** <gloss>prassina</gloss> and **verdigris-colored** <gloss>eruginosa</gloss> bile <note>These colors indicated highly toxic, "burnt" states of yellow bile</note>. Regarding the second point, some say that dysentery arising from **choleric black bile** <term>melancholia colerica</term> is the worst to cure because of its violent onset and its deadly, poisonous quality. But this argument is not valid, as he includes all unnatural modes of black bile under the term "colic" for the sake of brevity. He expresses this one specifically as it is the most famous and most frequent, since yellow bile is more prone to "burning" because of its heat, dryness, and thinness of substance. Yet, as will be shown, **medical black bile** <term>melancholia medicinalis</term> exits with more violence and lack of restraint. 

Some also said that the hardest cure is the dysentery caused by leek-green or verdigris bile, as the illnesses caused by these are incurable, destroying the specific "form" of natural heat like a poison. To these it is replied that if dysentery were caused by these, it would indeed be impossible to cure, but I find no authentic author writing that dysentery is caused by these; for Hippocrates denies in the fifth book of *Epidemics* that diseases are generated by them, as they are either immediately expelled or they destroy the body, as shown in Distinction 91.

Regarding the third point, it must be known that the dysentery worst to cure is that which is said to come from **melancholy** <gloss>black bile</gloss>, as stated in the fourth book of *Aphorisms*: "Dysentery, if it begins from black bile, is fatal." This is confirmed by reason because that cure is worse which involves qualities that are more unrestrained and contrary to human nature, and likewise more acute. Such is the case with black bile; for it boils and ferments the earth, inducing bubbles like boiling lye or vinegar, from which flies flee and which animals will not taste. This is found in the third book of *On the Use of Parts* and the fourth book of *Aphorisms*. First, this occurs in two ways: either from the "burning" of thick natural black bile or thin black bile. That which comes from the thicker sort is harder to resolve from the limb. Where it is more sharp, it is worse; and this is generated from the burning of the thinner black bile. But if help is present at the very beginning, it will receive medication more quickly. That which boils upon the ground, however, is slower to overcome...

It concludes that dysentery caused by "burnt" black bile is the most lethal, often fatal, due to its corrosive and "fermenting" nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of dysentery, specifically categorizing its severity and curability based on which of the four humors is responsible for the intestinal ulceration. It references the Aphorisms of Hippocrates and the works of Galen, Haly Abbas, and Avicenna.</meta>

...to be refreshed and narrowed, and to receive medication. It is more unrestrained, as seen in Distinction 33. Moreover, that **dysentery** <term>dysenteria</term> is worse to heal which is in no way different from an **ulcerated cancer** <note>original: "cancro ulcerato"; a reference to the incurable, corrosive nature of malignant growths applied here to the intensity of the intestinal sores</note>, since here it becomes a corrosive, incurable thing even in an external site upon which remedies can reach by touching and remaining. Such indeed is the dysentery caused by **black bile** <term>fel nigrum</term>, according to the *Aphorisms*, Book 4. 

This is followed in severity by that which is said to happen from the emission of **gangrene** <term>cancrena</term> in the intestines arising from **blood** <term>sanguis</term> mixed with this humor, as mentioned in Book 9 of the *Theory*. These two types are the worst and are deadly, especially if that humor is accompanied by a stench. For the humor is so savage and pernicious that it is only generated due to a cause that stretches nature to its absolute limit; such a cause opposes nature especially when the effect is proportionate to the cause. Therefore, the dysentery arising from such humors is worse to cure than others.

After this, the next worse is that which happens from the **burning** <note>original: "adustio"; the Galenic concept of humors becoming "burnt" or scorched by excessive heat, making them toxic and sharp</note> of **red bile** into **melancholy**; for this is second in severity and of faster corruption than phlegmatic and sanguine melancholy, even though **phlegm** <term>flegma</term> has a stronger power of sticking <note>viscosity</note>, while the burning of the bile is already diminished. Those are of slower severity and hindrance; however, melancholy is susceptible to cure, as noted in the *First of the First*.

This is shown by the fact that the lesser of these melancholies has a sequence of severity within itself, as it is generated from a humor that is less savage. For a thing generated retains some nature of its generator—either a more subtle nature which can be more quickly drawn out, such as that from bile, or a more difficult nature, such as that made from **salty phlegm** <note>original: "falsedine"; a humor thought to be irritating because of its salt content</note>. 

Whence the *Aphorisms* pronounce that dysentery most difficult because the **choleric humor** <note>bile</note>, through its thinness, makes its exit. Phlegmatic humor, however, remains because of its viscosity and adherence; when saltiness is added to it, it causes more ulceration. Thus, there is more harm from the viscosity of the phlegm than from its opposite quality, as phlegmatic quality is less biting and sharp. 

So, after this comes the choleric; after these, in order, another is generated from a humor that is corrupted in whatever way, such as the melancholic, as hinted in these Aphorisms in Book 6: *Whoever among those with spleen disorders are seized by dysentery...* and so on. In those with spleen disorders, the onset of dysentery is good when it is of brief duration and moderate. Whence it is known in Book 16: *When melancholy does not bubble up and does not have a vinegar-like smell, then it is a surplus of melancholy which nature expels, and health is hoped for.*

Next is that which is created from the intensity of the fixing of some extremely phlegmatic viscosity, which is less sharply biting in the intestines, such as **glassy phlegm** <note>original: "flegmatis vitrei"; a thick, transparent mucus described in the "Viaticum," a medieval medical manual</note>. For the separation of this leads to a great ulceration, as the **lining of the intestine** <gloss>original: pellicula intestini</gloss> is stripped away and causes pain. Therefore, they bite into it as the surpluses run together and pass through there. 

Finally, that which is generated from blood is more difficult to cure, though I think this is rare; nor is it born from blood remaining in its proper state, because that would perhaps generate a **hepatic dysentery** <term>dysenteria epatica</term> <note>liver-related flux</note> or something similar. For when a vein is torn, the intestine becomes malignant, just as a **virulent wound** <gloss>original: virulentia</gloss> happens in an external loss of continuity, which causes a mode of ulceration.

That which is caused by the rupture of an **abscess** <term>apostema</term> will be harder or easier to cure according to the quantity and severity of the matter itself, and similarly those generated from poisonous and sharp, watery dregs.

Thus it appears that the worst dysentery is that which happens from **melancholic melancholy**, then that from choleric, phlegmatic, and sanguine melancholies, and afterwards that from salty phlegm. After these, that from bile; then that from melancholy and that from the adherence of intense viscosity; and finally the sanguine from unburnt blood, and that from the rupture of abscesses and others according to their greater or lesser cause.

But the opposite seems to be what is said about **black bile** <term>colera nigra</term> by **Haly Abbas** and **Avicenna**, who posit that melancholy generated from the burning of bitter bile is worse than black bile. On the contrary, because it is said that an intestine ulcerated by black bile—as if in a remedy—is more difficult to help than one by yellow bile; for the latter is less deterring than the former.

It must be said that by reason of rapid impact, the worse harm comes from choleric melancholy; consequently, from melancholy that is less thick, then from that made from thicker melancholy, and finally from the sanguine and phlegmatic, with a difference. However, regarding the difficulty of rooting it out, it is worse as indicated in the *First of the First*. Or, as Galen says, burnt matter is not compared to choleric matter, but rather that to unburnt bitter bile. 

Yet one may doubt. For it happens that dysentery is simply fatal if it begins from black bile. In the *Distinctions*, it is written that dysentery caused by melancholy is a bad, chronic evil, from whose evacuation the **earth bubbles** <note>referring to a chemical reaction or fermentation of the stool upon hitting the ground</note> and a smell of vinegar is perceived; if this stripping of the lining is old, it is not healed. He hints, therefore, that in the beginning, if help is present quickly, it might be cured.

It must be said that if dysentery begins from black bile and has already proceeded so far as to ulcerate the intestine, then according to the *Commentator*, it is a **cancerous ulcer** and it is not possible for it to be healed. Or, dysentery is caused by greater or lesser quantity and similar severity. 

Regarding the fourth point: To the first, it must be said that in sanguine dysentery made by excoriation <note>scraping of the lining</note>, although blood comes out, its quantity is small. If it were much, as happens in hepatic dysentery sometimes, then this would be of worse cure. To the other, it must be said that those Aphorisms, according to the *Commentator*, have a place in complexional illness, or it stands true when the blood coming out is very great. 

Another point, as it appeared, must be conceded. To the other, it must be said that although it is true that when it ulcerates, the illnesses of blood and phlegm are safer by reason of their quality than the choleric and melancholic ones, they are nonetheless worse by reason of quantity, inducing **suffocation** <note>blockage or overwhelming of the vital forces</note> more quickly when they abound too much in the body. To the other, it must be said that although these traits are in the bile, it does not induce dysentery in most humors...

# DIFFERENCE 202.

<margin>1</margin>
->**That styptics are appropriate in hepatic dysentery**<-
->**is shown by the *Viaticum* and the seventh book**<-
->**of the *Practice*, which prescribes that in this condition**<-
**styptics** <term>stiptica</term> <note>Medicines that contract tissues to stop bleeding; astringents</note> should be administered in no small measure, such as **amber lozenges** <note>original: "trociscos de karabe"; amber was used in medieval medicine to stop hemorrhaging</note> with syrup of pomegranates, or **purslane** and **barberry water**, and those things which are also beneficial for the spitting of blood. Furthermore, this dysentery is a kind of "flux" or flow; since styptics condense and block, they restrain this flow and are highly effective for healing. Likewise, in other diseases of the liver in which they do not seem so appropriate, styptics are nonetheless ordered to be administered. It appears from medical skill that they should be mixed with medicines that resolve or mature the humor. Whence, in the first part of the fourth book: "When it is time to resolve the obstructions of the liver and stomach, you must not fail to mix in styptic medicines that have a good scent." This is supported by the "minor" premise. It holds because those things are appropriate which thicken and restrain the thin blood flowing from the liver—blood which resembles the **water used to wash meat** <note>original: "aque loture carnis"; a classic diagnostic description for hepatic discharge</note>. Whence, in the fifth book of *Internal Diseases*: "When you see bowel movements like the washings of newly slaughtered meat, let the knowledge of a liver affliction be certain." Styptics achieve the cure for this. Furthermore, when an evacuation is harmful to someone, retention is beneficial due to the principle of "cure by opposites." But what is led out here is harmful, since blood and spirit are evacuated, which are the cause of life. Therefore, their retention will be beneficial. Thus, in hepatic dysentery, styptics are appropriate.

The opposite view is found in the sixteenth section of the third book. It is argued that whatever cools the liver and removes it further from its nature, and which packs and condenses the matter within it, preventing its "breathing out," does not benefit this sickness. Such are styptics, since they are very cold. This is confirmed because the passages of the liver are extremely narrow, like **capillary hairs** <note>original: "capillares entes uilli"</note>. Furthermore, since the liver is like "congealed blood," whatever freezes it further causes injury to it. Styptics are pronounced to be quite cold. Therefore, in such a disease, styptics are not appropriate, but rather **aperitives** <term>aperitiua</term> <note>Medicines that open the "pores" or passages of the organs</note>.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that, as the name designates, **dysentery** <term>dissinteria</term> is a flow with an "erosion of the internals." For the name denotes an intestinal issue: *interon* means "intestine," and thus *enteria* means "intestinal." This exists in three forms. One is when the fat existing upon the intestines is excreted. Another is when the superficial internal membrane is led out. The third is when the actual substance of the intestine is scraped away. This last one is properly called dysentery according to the logic of the word.

Hepatic dysentery is called "dysentery" by a **metaphor** <note>original: "metbaphora"</note>, since an actual excoriation or scraping of the gut rarely occurs in it. Thus, in the fifth book of *Internal Diseases*: "Many physicians are deceived and judge this hepatic condition to be dysentery." It is, in fact, an emission of pure blood not mixed with stool. According to some, it is a bloody flux of the belly without the scraping of the intestines. But because pure blood is not always emitted in every hepatic dysentery—indeed, it is sometimes **rusty** <note>original: "eruginosus"</note>—and sometimes occurs with a following or preceding scraping, one might say that hepatic dysentery is a flow of humors through the intestines caused by a bad disposition of the liver. The humor emitted in this case is either a liquid like the washings of newly slaughtered meat, or like the **dregs of blood** <note>original: "fanguis fex"</note>. In the beginning, bloody liquids are excreted; as time proceeds, they become thick and very bloody; at the end, they are certainly **black bile** <term>nigra colera</term>.

**Galen** and **Haly Abbas** in the sixth book of *Accidents* list four types of bloody bowel movements, three of which pertain to this liver disease. One happens from the cutting off of some great color or the stopping of exercise; another happens from bright melancholic blood; the fourth is blood flowing little by little from the intestines. Many authorities list various types of humors exiting the liver, differing in their substance and their cause. For the substance which is expelled is sometimes **chyme-like** <term>chimośa</term>, sometimes watery (a washing), sometimes bile-like, sometimes virulent, sometimes black (like dregs), or melancholic black; some are foul-smelling and some lack stench; or it is pure blood which is otherwise expelled by vomiting; and some is a thick black substance that comes near death, which is the very flesh of the liver. The cause of their expulsion is sometimes a ruptured **abscess** <term>apostēa</term>, an opened obstruction, a tear, an ulcer, or a failure of the digestive power; sometimes the cause is total fullness, or the cessation of exercise, or an excess of food and drink.

From these points, one must further descend to the causes assigned to particular bowel movements according to the doctrine of **Avicenna**. There is a difference between hepatic and intestinal dysentery: because what comes from the intestinal type is gradual, involves **scaly scrapings** <note>original: "rasura squamośa"</note>, and is painful and stinging; but what is in the hepatic type is without pain, is plentiful, and is not continuous but occurs with breaks. Furthermore, in the intestinal type, there is a mixing of dung with what is excreted, which is not the case here...

In the stomach-related flux, however, this is not the case at all. Know that **hepatic dysentery** is understood in two ways. One is general, for any flux of moisture passing through the liver <note>original: "epar"</note> toward the lower parts, distinguished from the stomach-related flux. Inexperienced doctors greatly disregard this, so that it sometimes seems to them that the patient is laboring without any fever. If they do have a fever, the doctors think it happens because of fasting for the sake of appetite, and therefore when they see them sometimes even exercising or bathing, they allow them to neglect their diet. What a **styptic** <term>styptic</term> <note>An astringent substance that shrinks tissues and stops bleeding</note> is, is shown in chapter 145, which differentiates the more and the less, like other comparable things.

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some practitioners, using **styptics** vehemently and without distinction, fail to discern in this suffering. They are moved by the fact that they think they can cure this flux simply with constricting agents, such as styptics. Furthermore, they believe that in all sufferings, the liver is especially strengthened by styptics. These things, however, are not absolutely effective, as will be seen in the third book, and rightly so, for many are deceived in the cure of this suffering. This is partly because it is difficult in itself; hence the *Practice*, book seven, says: **The remedy and cure for hepatic dysentery is extremely difficult, and few are freed from it.** This is also due to the ignorance of doctors. Wherefore it adds: **For many recognize little of the liver's weakness and its cause.** Indeed, **Galen** <note>original: "Ga."; the influential 2nd-century Greek physician</note> said he had known certain people who had hepatic dysentery caused by the weakness of the liver, and they perished from a lack of knowledge regarding its cure. For sometimes this suffering happens from an acute humor flowing out to the intestines and ulcerating them, which they treat with the intestinal cure for dysentery, whereas it requires the wisdom of the liver; therefore, the patient perishes. The same is found in the third book of the *Breviary*, which I see happening even more today. And indeed, I have observed this cruel suffering to be especially prevalent in the regions of **Gaul** <note>France</note> and neighboring areas. At other times, hepatic dysentery follows from the intestinal kind when it extends itself because the **mesaraic veins** <term>mesaraic</term> <note>The mesenteric veins that carry nutrients from the intestines to the liver</note> suffer along with the intestines. This suffering is sometimes caused by the mesaraic veins, and the liver eventually suffers as well, which the unskilled neglect, believing it to be simply intestinal. Regarding the third point, it should be known that if hepatic dysentery happens from a repletion of blood throughout the whole body, then its cure is the removal of blood through another region and the avoidance of everything that produces blood, while adhering to their opposites. In this case, one only needs a moderate amount of styptics so that the matter, having been diverted and removed, does not receive more and the liver is strengthened. For one must not use styptics excessively during the time of the flux, lest the overabundant matter be suppressed inside; and here the 

---

cure is not difficult, though it is improperly called dysentery. But if it happens from a fault of the liver, it will either be because it is so weakened it cannot attract the **chyle** <term>chyle</term> <note>The liquid resulting from the stomach's digestion</note> to itself, so that the belly remains liquid and the body becomes emaciated with a weakness of appetite. In the cure of this, hot things with a certain stypticity are appropriate so that the vigor of the liver may be strengthened. Hot things indeed help attraction when the liver, being weak, cannot attract the chyle, or when within its substance an equivalent mass accumulates from a dominance of heat or cold. If it is cold, thick, and causing an **obstruction** <term>opilatio</term> <note>A blockage in the vessels or "pores" of an organ</note> in the liver, then by reason of the suffering, styptics are in no way appropriate. 

Wherefore **Avicenna** <note>original: "A."; the 11th-century Persian physician</note> in book three, section 16, detesting those who administer styptics, says: **The error that occurs in this chapter is that constipating medicines are given to those who have an obstructive hepatic flux, adding to the obstruction and reinforcing it to 'bind nature,' and this leads to the greatest error.** And many times the foolish person rubs the liver with things that thicken the blood with their coldness, in which there is death and the beginning of putrefaction. Rather, when the cause of this suffering is an obstruction in the mesaraic veins and the liver, one must intend to open the obstruction. And they have already praised **fat raisins** <note>original: "passu las pingues"</note> in this chapter, so much so that some estimated they could heal the difficult "washing flux." This was not experienced by those who took a long view. Wherefore book three, section 14, says: **Raisins benefit the weakness of the liver so that they drink a solution similar to meat-water.** It was seen in the previous demonstration that such matter obstructs and thickens in the liver, and because of this, it prepares for putrefaction when coldness is added, destroying its strength; it does not benefit hepatic dysentery, for such styptics are like adding fury to a similar fury.

Therefore, stypticity is not suitable for this suffering, except for the sake of the part that requires styptics. For the liver and the stomach, so that their strength may be preserved, always need to be invigorated by styptics above all other laboring parts, as very clever teachings show. If indeed a subtle hot matter dominates in the liver due to the dominance of heat, like subtle blood similar to the washings of meat which eventually turns into a **rusty discharge** <note>original: "eruginosā"; likely bile-colored or greenish</note>, then it is necessary to use cold things to temper the bad hot complexion of the liver while restraining it with moderate styptics so that the liver is invigorated and the subtle blood is thickened. Yet they should not be so styptic as to prevent what has already slipped down from descending; for if retained, it would cause excoriation and putrefaction. Therefore, these styptics are more appropriate than others both by reason of the part and the suffering, as the writings of the **Practice** <note>A medical textbook</note> confirm. When the liver doctor recognizes the suffering, he must cure it with strengthening agents and those things that turn away its bad complexion, and thereafter begin to use those things that will heal the blood so that the inconveniences of this suffering are cut off. Such things include **sealed lettuce** <note>original: "lactuca trasigillata"; likely lettuce used with Terra Sigillata</note> and **cypress** <note>original: "ciprina"</note> among others. Once these things are known, you will be able to cure the other hepatic discharges previously mentioned. And for the highest cure of this sickness...

### DIFFERENCE 204.

That **ileus** <term>ileus</term> <note>A painful and life-threatening blockage of the intestines</note> arising from **strangury** <term>strangury</term> <note>A condition where urine is passed painfully and drop by drop</note> is not cured by a supervening fever is shown by the Commentary, loathing the aphorism of the sixth section through the whole Hippocratic profession. The series of which is: **To whomsoever ileus is born from strangury, they perish in seven days, unless, a fever supervening, much urine flows.** Again, that which weakens the principal members, corrupts digestion, and inflames the spirits does not heal ileus. This is the fever, since it is a disease more hostile than others; as in the eighth [book] of *On Design*. For it is an abundance of foreign heat diffused through the whole animal body. Again, whenever a harm is joined to a harm, it does not result in a benefit, but rather incites a "frenzy." For when like is joined to like, it is like fire added to fire; for like meeting like intensifies the frenzy. This happens when fever, a more severe disease, is coupled with another disease. Even if fever were to cure ileus, it would be that arising from cold, viscous humors; for that made from hot humors would be further inflamed and harmed, as in an **aposteme** <term>aposteme</term> <note>An internal swelling or abscess</note>. But when ileus is caused by cold, viscous material, there is no fever. Whence in the *Viaticum*: "Ileus from cold humors has neither tumor nor extension nor fever," unlike that which happens from a hot aposteme. Therefore, ileus caused by strangury is not healed by a supervening fever. On the opposite side is the previously introduced aphorism. Whence in the sixteenth [section] Hippocrates says: "When ileus happens from a distillation of urine, that person dies on the seventh day unless a fever happens to him and much sweat runs with it." And in the nineteenth: "He who has difficulty of urine, and there comes upon him after it a **tenesmus** <term>tenesmus</term> <note>A distressing and continual urge to evacuate the bowels</note>, dies on the seventh day unless a fever happens and makes a great provocation [of fluids]." Behold how he waveringly discusses what the aphorism introduces, as he is accustomed to always lead in the extorted speeches of others. Or he alludes finally to Galen <note>original: "G."</note> wanting the bladder to compress the **longaon** <note>The rectum</note> and not the iliac intestines. Furthermore, just as a fever supervening upon a spasm or **tetanus** <term>tetanus</term> <note>A condition of muscle contraction or rigidity</note> which occurs from cold, viscous humors destroys them, so it cures ileus from the same. Whence the fourth aphorism: "A supervening fever dissolves the sickness of a spasm or tetanus." And know that **epilepsy** is often dissolved by fevers which the sufferer tolerates, especially those that are long-lasting. Therefore, ileus made on account of strangury is removed by a supervening fever. Regarding the first, it should be known that **strangury** is a small and very frequent mixture [of urine], according to the sixth aphorism. A. <note>Avicenna</note> says it is when urine is passed drop by drop and exits quickly, which happens from sharpness or burning, or a defect in the bladder's capacity. A defect also comes from an aposteme, a wound, an intemperate complexion, or from thick windiness. **Dysuria** <term>dysuria</term> <note>Painful or difficult urination</note>, however, is when the bladder completes its action with hardness and narrowing, and not without great pain. What a fever is, the 87th [section] showed. **Ileus** is a pain of the intestines preventing the stool from exiting from the upper part, sometimes forcing it to be vomited; whence the *Commentary* on the sixth aphorism says: "In ileus, nothing exits from below, and even if a sharp **clyster** <term>clyster</term> <note>An enema</note> is applied, the patient is not helped." Paulus <note>Paul of Aegina</note> says it is a most acute suffering, full of pain, by which they perish a miserable death, rejecting stool through the mouth. In the ninth [book] of *Theory*, it is called the suffering *yleos* and is interpreted as "vexation," a heavy pain in the intestines. In the idioms, its explanation is **"Lord have mercy"** <note>original: "miserere mei"; ileus was historically called 'miserere' because the pain was so great the patient could only cry for mercy</note>, especially when it happens from a hot aposteme. For it descends from *eleos* <note>The text mistakenly links the Greek 'ileos' (intestinal) with 'eleos' (pity/mercy)</note> which in Greek means "mercy," from which comes *yleos*. Whence I know Hippocrates says: "When there occurs in a colic—from which may God protect us—vomiting and hiccups and mixing..."

...and spasm, then the whole of it is a bad sign.

There are, however, three ailments that are generally similar; for they often arise from a similar material and in the same general location with nearly similar pain, not differing in particular except by degree. These are **strophus** <note>original: "strophus" — a twisting or tortion of the bowels</note> (torsion), **colic**, and **ileus** <term>ileus</term> <note>A painful obstruction of the ileum or other part of the intestine</note>. For when the material is brief, it induces a twisting, according to that passage in the *Tegni* <note>Galen's "Art of Medicine," a foundational textbook</note>: "Twisting in the belly is a precursor to colic." This indeed, according to the truth, occurs in the large intestines—such as the **colon**, from which the name is derived—and those parts following it, and it is much more difficult to treat than a simple twisting. **Ileus**, however, is properly generated in the slender <note>small</note> intestines; nevertheless, in certain places, ileus is considered a type of colic because it is very similar to it. 

In section sixteen, Garipontus <note>An 11th-century medical writer</note> says it is an acute ailment that acts within a short time. Whence it says in the *Viaticum* <note>A traveler’s medical manual by Constantine the African</note>: "Generally, this disease is pestilential and mortal, sometimes killing on the second day, sometimes on the third, and it is rarely cured." Avicenna notes, however, that ileus most often occurs in autumn, appearing as an epidemic and contagious disease; thus he says it passes from some people to others through a change in the pestilential air and then to the earth by the shift of coming sicknesses. 

It occurs for many reasons. For it is caused either by a hot **inflammation** <term>aposteme</term> <note>An internal swelling, abscess, or inflammation</note> in the thin intestines, or from a thick, viscous, phlegmatic humor, or from an obstruction caused by **dung** or dry feces by which the intestine is twisted, or from a rupture of the **siphac** <term>siphac</term> <note>The medieval term for the peritoneum, the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> when the displaced intestine falls into the bone <note>likely referring to an inguinal hernia</note>, or from a lack of food, or the administration of a deadly medicine. According to the ninth book of the *Theorica*, it also happens according to Avicenna due to drinking cold water unnecessarily, along with all the causes that produce colic. 

Regarding this, it should be known that the *Commentary* <note>Galen's commentary on Hippocrates</note> simply rejects the previous aphorism, both because ileus cannot arise from **strangury** <term>strangury</term> <note>Painful, frequent, and drop-by-drop urination</note>, and also because a supervening fever does not cure it but rather intensifies it further. First, he [Galen] says he has seen many in his time reach death from strangury, whose bladders appeared full, distended, and painful, yet none of them suffered from ileus. Furthermore, it seems it should rather happen from an inflammation of the **uterus** <note>original: "matrice"</note>, since the uterus ascends all the way to the **diaphragm** <note>original: "dyaflagma"</note>, where it ought to compress the intestines more, yet ileus does not occur from that. 

Again, if the bladder were inflamed, it would only compress the **rectum** and not the slender intestine in which ileus is said to occur. He concludes, therefore, that ileus is very rarely caused by strangury; perhaps someone might hear "colic" instead of "ileus" as mentioned. As to the second point—that ileus cannot be helped by a fever—he tries to show this because it is caused by an inflammation of the bladder. A supervening fever does not cure it, but rather increases its malice. Moreover, a fever only cures a disease if it arises from coldness, whether alone or with phlegmatic humors or thick and inflating windiness, of which ileus does not consist; rather, it consists of inflammation. Therefore, a supervening fever does not cure it.

---

Avicenna, however, defending the aphorism of Hippocrates <note>original: "Yp."</note>, says that Galen did not know the cause, because "phlegmatic and windy" ileus is indeed helped by a fever. If someone perhaps opposes Galen, he will take away his arguments, saying they have little validity. To the first point, it should be said that even if Galen did not see ileus caused by strangury in his time and region, it was nevertheless seen by others, from which the observation arose. Indeed, something experienced in many regions can be heard of; as he says in the first book on fevers: "I have not yet clearly seen a **quintan fever** <note>A fever recurring every fifth day</note> nor any other beyond a **quartan** <note>every fourth day</note>." Regarding this, Avicenna in the fourth book of the *Canon*, essentially attacking Galen, says that Hippocrates confirmed the account of finding **septan** <note>seventh-day</note> and **nonan** <note>ninth-day</note> fevers. And a certain faithful person has already reported to me that he saw a nonan fever. As for the quintan, we have seen it many times. For diseases ought not to be denied just because they do not happen in a certain time and region, or because one's kind has not encountered them due to their rarity. 

Similarly, in the sixth book, it is said that in a certain place in Arabia, things called **traguntia** <note>The Guinea worm (Dracunculus medinensis), a parasite that looks like a nerve or vein</note> occur; they are nervous, similar to worms in color and thickness. I have heard many people say they have seen this. Although I myself have no certain knowledge of their generation or substance, this ailment in the seventh book of the *Almansor* <note>The medical handbook of Rhazes</note> is called the "civil vein," and in the fourth book of the third part, the "**Medina vein**," because it abounds in 그 city. Wherefore it is added: Galen said that nothing manifest was understood of its nature upon which one could rely, because he never saw it at all. The writer himself <note>The author of this manuscript</note> once observed it in a nun. I also do not find **goiter** <note>original: "bocium"</note> commonly mentioned by the Arabs, although it is very common among the Italians.

To the other point, it should be said that ileus does not arise from an inflammation of the uterus in the same way as from the strangury of the bladder, because the bladder (especially in men) has a much stronger connection and tighter binding with the intestines than the uterus does. For the uterus is bound weakly and loosely, as shown by its descent and ascent and its turning around the vertebrae. And therefore, the **regulative power** <note>The body's natural self-governing force</note> pushes it toward the muscular parts of the belly when it ascends to the diaphragm, so that it does not cause an ailment in the intestines by compressing them. To the other point: although the bladder compresses the rectum more immediately, it is nevertheless able to compress the rest by a certain "community." For the "society" or community through which one ailment suffers with another is manifold: either because they are continuous in nature, between which some instrument provides continuity (such as the brain and the stomach through the continuity of the nerves between them, and the uterus and the breasts through the continuity of the veins); or because one is the path for the other (like the groin for an inflamed leg); or because they are neighbors in location (like the brain and the lung); or because one is the root and principle of the action of the other (like the diaphragm for the lung in the drawing of air); or because one serves the other (as the nerves serve the brain); or because they are associated in another way (like the brain with the kidneys because each is associated with the liver and the stomach). In this way, the bladder is associated with the **iliac regions** <note>the area of the small intestines</note> indirectly.

straight to the intestines. Or it must be said that through this association of suffering, there will be an abundance of material caused by the bladder, which, reaching the small intestines, induces **ileus** <term>ileus</term> <note>a painful intestinal obstruction</note>. This is according to that seventh Aphorism: "In those whose **omentum** <term>omentum</term> <note>the fatty tissue covering the abdominal organs</note> is filled with water, the belly is filled with water and they die." Furthermore, the orifice of the bladder is narrower than that of the **uterus** <note>original: "matricis"</note>. Regarding the argument that a fever coming upon ileus does not help but hinders, the opponent would say that Galen was perhaps dreaming when he thought ileus arose from a hot **inflammation** <term>aposteme</term> <note>original: "apāte," short for apostemate; a localized swelling or abscess</note>. When he says, "I say a hot inflammation," or while he believes it does this, I do not believe this constipation is made from thick, viscous humors, even though all his followers affirm that the **iliac passion** <note>another term for ileus</note> happens because of them. However, what most excited Galen to put forward such things was that he did not perceive the experience of the aphorisms as true.

Regarding the aforementioned matters, a doubt arises because it was said by Galen that the uterus ascends as far as the **diaphragm** <note>original: "dyaflagma"</note>. The opposite of this is seen in the sixth book of the *Introduction*: the uterus will reach neither the diaphragm nor any other place. For it does not appear to be pulled back as far as the belly. It must be said that the uterus does not reach those parts by its own capture like a self-moving animal, but rather by a certain instinct or divine clemency. For in the aforementioned sixth book, Plato and others are rebuked for thinking the uterus is an **animal** <note>Plato famously described the womb as a "wandering animal" that causes distress when it cannot conceive</note> desiring the procreation of children. Or it must be said that Galen does not intend for the uterus to physically and absolutely reach all the way to the diaphragm, but rather mediately or by its power; as if he says it ascends a great deal when its ligaments are loosened or dissolved, compared to the bladder which remains almost immobile. Or, in the manner of a litigious person, Galen, wishing to obtain all things in this way, includes whatever he can, just as many other things were brought in there as a false accusation, as they are able to suffer no small sight. Regarding the third point, two things must be known which Galen seems to deny: first, that ileus can arise from **strangury** <term>strangury</term> <note>original: "strāguiria"; painful, drop-by-drop urination</note>. Either from an abundance of material, as touched upon by the deduction from the bladder into the small intestines for the sake of commonality and the impulse of nature from a nobler and more sensible member to one that is not so. This is shown by a **torsion** <note>original: "strophus"</note> or twisting of the intestines when someone is forced to retain urine out of respect or another reason, as in the sixth book of *Accidents*. The slender <note>small</note> intestines do not primarily receive this material, since they are more sensible, more prone to suffering, and less protected by defenses than the thick ones; as is shown by the extremity of the penis, which soon becomes more painful when a suffering of the bladder occurs, both because it is closer to the first sensation and because it is less covered by viscosity and fat.

Or one might say this happens because when the bladder is full of urine, nature turns it away from the bladder as much as it can, directing it toward the intestines. It fears that if it reaches the rectum, it might make the bladder even more painful by compression. Therefore, nature forces it to remain in the slender intestines. In this way, it is said that the difference follows: **colic** <note>inflammation of the large intestine</note> is generated from ulcers and pustules; thus ileus can be caused by strangury.

Second, that since every cure is perfected by its contrary, and fever is a bad, hot, and dry **complexion** <term>complexion</term> <note>the balance of the four bodily humors</note>, whereas ileus is established to occur from cold, phlegmatic, and windy moisture. Whence the sixth Aphorism: "Constipation or windy and inflating thickness, or a cold intemperance of complexion, is cured by fever." For it liquefies and dissolves the material that generates the constipation and the bad windiness, bringing it toward a balanced complexion.

Again, in the same place, it would be good to say that thick, crude, viscous, and cold humors create this disease, and it is cured with fever and the purging of urine. But this disease, according to others, is ileus; who would not perceive Galen's view? And therefore Avicenna <note>original: "A."</note> said he was ignorant of its cause in this matter. Therefore, some ileus can be cured when a fever comes upon it, especially when it was caused by strangury, and particularly when a multitude of urine or sweat has flowed. Regarding the fourth point, to the first it must be said that it has already appeared; for Galen was not conceded as far as he went. To the other, it must be said that the benefit someone follows from the dissolution of the matter of ileus through fever is greater than the harm from it; just as fever coming upon a spasm or **tetanus** from repletion is curative, according to his own words. To the other point, what must be said is well known: although fever through itself generally causes harm, by accident, however, insofar as it heats and dissolves cold and windy material, it confers much more benefit. For when a disease occurring upon another is founded on its material, adapting it and leading it toward the better, it does not work an injury but a benefit; but when the opposite occurs, it is necessary that it be most dangerous, as happens in **dropsy** <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "ydropisi"; swelling from fluid retention</note> with fever, and in **hemoptysis** <note>original: "emothoica"; coughing up blood</note> with pleurisy. To the other, it is said that fever soon assists a certain disease, such as ileus caused by an inflammation. To another, however, finally as to that which is caused from crude humors, just as it occurs to a spasm from repletion. From this, however, fever comes upon it, either by a certain prompting of nature, or by ingenuity or art, so that the harmful thing may be expelled. Nor should it ever be understood that fever is not present in ileus from a cold cause, but it is very little in relation to that which is made from a hot inflammation. Of these, however, Galen seems to have felt the first, thinking fever is only associated with a hot inflammation of the bladder, or that it is not a fever nor with such cruel symptoms as that which would have been made from a hot inflammation.

## DIFFERENCE CCIIII.

> That narcotics are not suitable in colic
> is shown. Since a cure is through the
> contrary, the cutting off of the disease or its cause; however,
these numbing agents do not cut it off but rather increase it, since they induce a wicked quality with their coldness, which things by their substance simultaneously thicken and make the matter of the colic more fatty and block the intestines further. Moreover, so that there may be reasoning in a universal way, every sickness requires a cure. Colic is indeed a sickness; it also is cured either by altering the complexion toward the better or by evacuation. From these, the ingenuity of a cure must simply be taken. None of these do narcotics provide.
