...they act. But rather the opposite is true. For they lay low the **virtue** <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "virtutem"; the body's natural vital force or innate strength</note> since it remains with the heat, as is shown by its action: a movement triggered and unfolded by heat as if continually. Because of this, a limb is also rendered unfit by **mortification** <note>the death of tissue</note> from receiving these substances, through which the limb has its being and its function. It appeared that they ruin any **complexion** <term>complexion</term> <note>the specific balance of humors in an individual</note> either by altering it wickedly or by preventing evacuation.

Again, it is argued that what induces pain is not sought in **colic** <note>severe abdominal pain</note>. But these substances cause pain, for the sedation of which someone might say they were administered. Since they immediately alter the complexion toward coldness and cause a "solution of continuity" <note>a medical term for a break in healthy tissue or a disruption of natural flow</note> when they push and aggregate matter into a part, dissolving it. These things, secondly, are the causes of pain. Also, an **accident** <note>a symptom or secondary effect of a disease</note> follows a disease as a shadow follows a body. Therefore, the accident cannot be removed except by the removal of the body itself. Thus, an accidental pain cannot be sedated by **stupefacients** <term>stupefacients</term> <note>medicines that dull the senses or cause stupor; narcotics</note> if its subject—the disease—is not removed by its own cause, if it has one.

Furthermore, if narcotics are beneficial in colic, why are they not administered at the beginning when the virtue is robust? In acute passions, one should medicate on the same day and at the second hour. Otherwise, we shall incur the same detestation as the sailors of **Erasistratus** <note>a Greek anatomist and royal physician</note>, who used remedies at the beginning for both strong and weak illnesses. Therefore, in colic, stupefacients are not appropriate. 

The opposite, however, is what the community of physicians professes. Furthermore, that which causes the virtue to rest and sedates the "accidents" is appropriate in colic, since such things vehemently attack nature. These things, as will be declared, are **narcotics**. And that which alters a bad complexion and thickens the substance of the matter is beneficial—especially when the matter is hot and thin, as is the case in colic which sometimes arises from hot humors. Again, since this arises from **windiness** <note>gas or flatulence</note> which is caused by suppressed heat, it will be destroyed by a strong cold, just as winter indicates. For windiness is generated in temperate times, not in those that are very hot or very cold, as appears in the second book of the *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle's work on natural phenomena</note>. These things, however, are narcotics. 

Because of this, narcotics are beneficial in the cure of colic. First, it should be known that a **narcotic** is a medicine that sedates pain, the nature of which is vehemently cold along with dryness. They are elevated to the end of the third degree and even to the fourth <note>referring to the four degrees of intensity in medieval pharmacology</note>. Some are "simples" <note>single-ingredient drugs</note>, such as **opium**, which is stupefying above all others. Also the juice of the Egyptian **poppy** <note>original: "papaueris egyptiaci"</note>. And universally both poppies, though more so the black; also **henbane** <note>original: "iusquiamus"</note>, **mandrake**, the greater **nightshade** <note>original: "psolatrum"</note>, and the so-called "inverted bean" <note>likely a species of hellebore or similar toxic plant</note>. 

The rest are "compounds" <note>multi-ingredient formulas</note>, such as **Philonium** <note>a famous sedative electuary named after Philon of Tarsus</note> (that is, the "friend"), **Dyaspermaton**, **Trigona**, or the **Troches** <note>lozenges</note> which they name "the triads." Also the **New Theriac** <term>theriac</term> <note>a complex "universal" antidote and medicine</note> (aged up to six months), the **Greek Apolonia**, and the **Babylonian**, **Golden**, and **Alexandrian** formulas, the **Requies**, the **Red Troches**, and many others. A good version of these is constructed from **saffron**, **cassia wood**, and **opium** in equal parts. The best electuary is that which is written.

Know also that those which are simples are worse than the compounds. Therefore, they are compounded with others so that their "malice" <note>harmful toxicity</note> and audacity may be restrained. For many harms are feared from them, since they are all contrary to life—congealing and mortifying—especially when used "naked" <note>pure/unmixed</note>. For this reason, it is necessary to correct them by the art of medical mixing to remove the harm. This is done for three reasons:
1. To remove their mortifying congelation; this is what **castoreum** <note>a secretion from beavers</note>, **pepper**, and **saffron** do. These are the "theriac" of narcotics. Castoreum and pepper are **carminative** <note>gas-relieving</note> and resolving; saffron sedates and ripens, while also strengthening the virtue of the heart.
2. So that the virtue of the limbs is comforted and the spirit is restored; this is the work of "cordials" and "stomachics" such as saffron, **spikenard**, **basil**, **zedoary**, and the like.
3. So that **stipticity** <note>astringency/constriction</note> and constriction are induced in "rheumatic" cases. For pain sharpens the "rheum" <note>flowing humors</note> and the fever. Things that do this are **myrrh**, **mastic**, **olibanum** <note>frankincense</note>, and **sandarac**.

Furthermore, older medicines are to be chosen because they become weaker with time; the coldness is put to sleep by the heat of the things mixed with it, though it becomes less active. 

Moreover, since these are so contrary to the nature of life, they should not be administered if they can be avoided. But if not, it must be done with fear and caution. Hence, it is better that they be administered in scents, ointments, or plasters than taken internally—unless perhaps for the eyes, because of their sensitivity and the transparency they require. They are most harmed by these, whereas some parts, like the teeth, are least harmed by these opposites. Also, they do less harm when administered via **clisters** <term>clister</term> <note>an enema</note> or suppositories than when swallowed. 

It is also necessary that they be given, if possible, in the evening before sleep, because by inducing sleep, they sedate the pain. One should also begin with weak doses, proceeding gradually to stronger ones, keeping in mind the rules from the fourth book of the *Canon* <note>likely referring to Avicenna's Canon of Medicine</note>. If it is necessary to induce stupor, do not transcend something like the poppy, which, along with its stupor, is "domestic" <note>safe/familiar</note>. Caution must be taken not to give it after food, nor when the body is full, but only after food is digested and evacuated. Nor should their exhibition be continuous, but rather highly intermittent, as it leads to a bad end—specifically to blindness and deafness in those parts, and finally to stupor and death. They should be given with warm wine, for they are more quickly brought into action.

But a doubt occurs regarding the aforesaid: for it was said that opium is so vehemently stupefying that a dose the size of a large lentil is a poison that kills by congealing and extinguishing the **innate heat**. However, in parts of **Egypt**, they use it in any manner and quantity, even making oil from it for seasonings. Therefore, it does not seem to stupefy to such an extent. It must be said that perhaps the mode of the poppy is different here and there. Or, more certainly according to **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> in his *Problems*, it must be resolved that just as Egyptian wine is cold even though the region is hot... <note>text cuts off</note>

Rarifying the pores of the earth, it exhales the heat placed within the bowels of the earth, which then associates with the external heat. Appearing first, it is such that vines are nourished by the cold. In **Scotland** <note>original: "Scotia"</note> however, the pores of the earth remain obstructed by cold so that its heat cannot exhale; for this reason, vines nourished by heat produce a wine that is warm and strong, because it is difficult to find a **Thorysius** <note>possibly referring to a specific volcanic or stony region known for its soil heat</note> where the stony, temperate earth is warmer than others and more fertile, digesting what it bears better. For small stones prevent the heat and moisture of the earth from exhaling. Plants also change greatly according to the diversity of the earth, as **Galen** <note>original: "boleum", likely a transcription error for Galenum</note> shows in his twenty-second book on differences; wine and cabbage are particularly noted in cases of **paralysis** <note>loss of muscle function</note>. So it seems it must be said of the **poppy** <note>original: "papauere"</note> in Egypt and in places similar to it, as well as in those around the poles. Nor is **opium** <term>opium</term> <note>the dried latex of the poppy</note> made from the seed of the poppy as it is eaten, but from the milk that is gathered from the green poppy heads. For after the sun has dried the dew, subtle incisions are made in the head of the poppy with a knife, not deep enough to go through the cortex but only superficially, and the juice or milk that comes out without compression is scraped off. It is gathered a second and third time until no more comes out.

Again, let it be known that compound narcotic medicines are more harmful, especially if they are prepared such that **theriac** <term>theriac</term> <note>a famous ancient "universal" medicine containing dozens of ingredients</note>, because of the opium it receives, induces a certain stupor and checks the spitting of blood. Hence, in the fifth book of the **Method of Medicine** <note>original: "de inge." referring to Galen's *De Ingenio Sanitatis*</note>: at the hour of sleep, theriac of four months' age was given for three days; because it was near its freshness, it had the power of opium, and therefore it induces sleep, dries up flows, and thickens nourishment. Because of this, it neither expels poison nor does other things that require heat. This seems unlikely since heat is a stronger quality than coldness. Similarly, it receives many more hot ingredients than cold ones. The heat of the body should also lead heat into action better than cold, since it has a proportion with it. To which it must be said that opium, because it overcomes many things at first, induces its own action because it is of a more vehement coldness than any hot thing, since the levels of degrees are almost infinite. **Galen** <note>original: "cxxxix. & xxii." probably citing specific book/chapter references</note> discusses this, and a great quantity follows, especially in the original description of **Andromachus** <note>physician to Nero and creator of Theriac</note>. It is also a substance of **pancbimeres** <note>a term likely referring to a substance composed of similar or all-encompassing parts</note> and of a unifying virtue, so that it more strongly unites its own power with other things that do not resemble it in degree—that coldness which is vehemently announced as an enemy to all nature. The hot parts of the body open the pores, preparing it to suffer more. They also oppose the coldness of the opium so that it is more fiercely excited into action; eventually, however, the heat wins since the hot elements thereafter concur into one nature. These things having been deduced, the inquirer can rest with some hesitation as to why...

***

**Colic** <term>colic</term> <note>severe, fluctuating pain in the abdomen caused by intestinal gas or obstruction</note> is a very painful sickness of the **colon** intestine, in which its natural exit is prohibited by an obstruction. Now, the intestines are members longer than the others of the body, composed of a double tunic, serving to help and contain the surplus received. They are six in number:

*   First, the **duodenum** <note>original: "duodenū"</note>, so called for being twelve fingers long.
*   The **jejunum** <note>original: "ieiunū"</note>, so named because it is found empty in the dead of animals.
*   The **subtle** or **ileum** <note>original: "ylion"</note>, in which three the more useful nourishment is contained.
*   The **one-eyed** <note>original: "monoculū"</note>, the **cecum** <note>original: "cecū"</note>, or the "blind" gut, which contains purely dreg-like matter.
*   Then the **colon**.
*   And finally the **hastale** <note>the rectum</note>, also called the "long" gut, the end of which is called the **sphincter** <note>original: "sicteris"</note>. In these three, simpler fecal matter is contained.

That the pain in colic is immense, **Galen** testified from his own experience of it. Feeling himself internally as if he were being pierced by a **drill** <note>original: "terebro"</note>, he nevertheless thought he was suffering from a stone. The aforementioned obstruction arises from many causes, as appears in book 203. Causes arise from warm matter, but most especially from cold humor such as **phlegm** <term>phlegm</term> <note>one of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture</note>. But according to **Anaxagoras** <note>pre-Socratic philosopher</note>, it is called "vitreous," which often happens either from a sharp hot humor, or from windiness, or from a descent of the intestines into the bone <note>a hernia</note> in whatever manner, or from an excoriation which naturally abhors emitting what is contained through the intestines, or from worms, or from hard dung that has adhered to the intestine, which happens in many ways according to **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a Persian physician</note> and in the sixteenth book of the **Techné** <note>Galen's "Art of Medicine"</note>. From these things, it appears that the natural exit is hindered.

Regarding this, it should be known that some, fearing the danger of inducing it, avoided **narcotics**. This is supported by **Serapion** and **Rhazes** <note>influential Islamic physicians</note>; in their discussions with **Avenzoar** <note>original: "zoar"</note> they do not seem to touch them. But what follows from this will appear, since the aforementioned authors do not avoid them entirely, but rather, out of brevity of speech, they remain silent, leaving them to be supplied in the antidotes by those who come after.

Furthermore, it should be known that at present, the indication for cure is taken from things natural, non-natural, and against nature, as has often been touched upon. From the first, namely from the **virtue** <note>vital force</note> with its attachments, which will be strong, weak, or medium. From the third, namely from the cause with its effect and **accident** <note>secondary symptom</note>. For the cause is sometimes cold and other times hot, and the accident is sometimes pernicious, casting down the virtue in every way, such as pain, and sometimes it is minimal, where a middle ground is found. From the non-natural things, because the middle of these must be judged moderately.

If indeed the virtue is strong and the matter fixed and the pain small enough to be endured, one should not presume to use narcotics, since the cure can be achieved otherwise through alteratives, **anodynes** <note>pain-relievers</note>, and evacuants. For there are three types of things that sedate pain: 
1. Those that evacuate the matter which is the cause of it. 
2. Those that alter the bad complexion, such as those that are moderately hot in the first degree, like the complexion of the body, according to **Behen** <note>a medicinal root</note>, which lead the spirits and are almost intoxicating, such as **chamomile**, **dill**, **linseed**, and **wild celery** <note>original: "zcy." likely for 'apii'</note>. 
3. Or those that remove sensation from the limb, such as the narcotics treated here. 

If the virtue is weak, the cause hot, and the pain strong, then it is finally expedient to presume to use narcotics. In middle cases, one must act moderately. For that is what the physician should be most concerned about.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the administration of narcotics (stupefacients) for pain management, specifically addressing the risks and benefits based on the patient's humors and the severity of the condition. It transitions into a new chapter (Differentia CCV) concerning why diuretics should not be used in certain urinary tract diseases.</meta>

One must preserve the **vital strength** <term>virtus</term> <note>The innate power of the body to heal and maintain life</note>, especially if it has become weak. According to the fourth book <note>likely referring to Galen's commentary on Hippocrates' *Prognostics*</note>: if the humors are sharp and thin, then **narcotics** <term>narcotica</term> <note>substances that induce stupor or dull the senses, like opium</note> are used, because they dull the flow, cool intense heat, and thicken the substance of the humors. In such cases, they provide much benefit and do very little harm; therefore, one may use them with confidence. 

However, when the humors are **cold and thick**, or consist of **glassy phlegm** <note>original: "flegma uitreū"; a very thick, clear, and cold humor considered difficult to digest</note>, or crude windiness, a great danger is incurred. In these instances, the relief felt is only an appearance or a fantasy. Afterward, a more intense pain will arise because the underlying cause of the pain increased while the senses were dulled. Therefore, in these cases, narcotics must be used only with the greatest caution and out of absolute necessity. 

Even if they cause some harm, it is perhaps possible to correct that harm later. As it says in the twelfth book of *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingen. xii.", referring to Galen’s *De Ingenio Sanitatis*</note>: to save a person, one must choose the immediate relief over the harm that might follow later. For it is better to harm one part of the body than to allow the patient to perish. Although a cure is generally achieved by cutting away the cause, one must nevertheless focus on whatever is currently distressing the patient's nature the most. For the medical art first rises up against the cause that is most urgent. 

Hence the rule: 
-> **If the symptom <note>original: "accidens"</note> overpowers the disease, then we provide care for the symptom and ignore the disease.** <-

For example, in **colic** <term>colica</term> <note>severe abdominal pain often caused by obstruction</note> we give stupefacients so that the intensity of the pain may be removed, even though these drugs may actually be harmful to the underlying cause of the colic. On the second or third day, the pain may return more troublesome, especially when the matter is cold; nevertheless, cold matter is not as immediately painful as hot matter, though cold is more "mortifying" <note>likely meaning it leads to tissue death or lethargy</note>. 

In that hour, the pain is calmed; in the next, evacuate the bowels, lest by the frequent use of narcotics you lead the patient to death. This is an "apparent" or palliative treatment, similar to those used for confirmed leprosy, which certain **deceivers traveling the world** <note>original: "deceptores orbē percurrentes"; refers to itinerant quacks or unlicensed healers</note> dare to use. These are the same people who claim to cure arthritic pains by the application of a **living stork** <note>original: "ciconie... uiuētis"</note> along with some white lead and vinegar.

That it is sometimes necessary to use narcotics according to the aforementioned rules is shown by the principle: **Of two evils, the lesser must always be chosen.** As it says in the third book of the *Topics* <note>Aristotle’s *Topics*</note>: just as merchandise is thrown overboard for the sake of a person's safety during a storm. 

To use stupefacients is sometimes a fearful thing, yet neglecting them can lead to death. In the time between doses, the vital strength rests and is comforted, and the cause of the pain can perhaps be digested and evacuated. This drug is suitable because it removes that which prostrates the strength; for pain, more than anything else, casts down the vital power. Furthermore, as Galen swore <note>original: "ceu sacramētatus Gal."; suggesting Galen spoke with great authority or as if under oath</note>, it is good to resist things that consume the body, especially those that suddenly and vehemently cast down the strength, of which pain is a primary example. 

Narcotics work by destroying the sensation in which the pain is rooted. Therefore, narcotics are sought after in certain cases and times, provided they are used with moderation so that the benefit outweighs the harm, which is the intention of every healer. It is very difficult to find any remedy that offers a great benefit without doing some harm (see book 11 of *The Method of Healing*). What has been said regarding **colic** and **iliac passion** <term>yliaca</term> <note>a severe and often fatal intestinal obstruction</note> should be understood as applying to similar conditions.

### ON THE ADMINISTRATION OF STUPEFACIENTS
Regarding the pain that occurs from windiness, it is harsh and longer-lasting because of its constant generation. In this case, narcotics are to be feared greatly, because they thicken the spirit and condense the limbs so that the windiness cannot be resolved (dispersed).

In response to the first point: it must be said that a true cure is achieved by cutting off the cause, not by a false or deceptive palliative that only appears to work. To the second point: narcotics, when administered correctly, do not destroy the vital strength, but rather save it so that it may rise again later, even if they weaken it in the moment. It is also chosen so that one part may be "sacrificed" for the safety of the whole. A hot humor is not harmed by them but rather helped; however, a cold humor is harmed, though the patient supports this harm for the sake of the relief gained.

To the next point: stupefacients would only cause pain if the subject's senses remained intact. But the sensation is removed, and thus the pain is calmed regardless of its cause. Similarly, a symptom follows not only the disease but also the nature of the person. It is not possible for health or disease to exist in things lacking life, sensation, and the sense-object. A symptom is said to "imitate" the disease because it seems to be caused by it immediately. Finally, in the beginning, the body is full and the strength is strong, and one hopes for a cessation of pain. In such circumstances, it is not appropriate to induce a stupor.

## DIFFERENTIA. CCV.

<margin>1</margin>
**That diuretics are not suitable for diseases of the urinary pathways is shown here.** 

Because **diuretics** <term>diuretica</term> <note>substances that increase the production of urine</note> draw matters toward the pathways where they are already fixed; however, one should not draw matter toward a damaged part, but rather toward the opposite side. Hence the rule: when the member from which matter is expelled is the same member through which the evacuation must be made, but there is an old or recent disease in it, there is fear that the humors will flow into it. They must therefore be transposed to another part. 

Wherefore, in book 13 of *The Method of Healing*: you should not move the bowels when there is an inflammation of the anus or nearby parts. In the same way, you should not command a patient to swallow diuretic drugs if there is an issue with the bladder, the private parts, or the kidneys. Nor should you provoke the menses in a woman if the disease is in the womb or the private parts; rather, you should always perform a **revulsion** <note>original: "euulsione"; a medical technique of drawing blood or humors to a distant, opposite part of the body</note> to the furthest possible place. 

Furthermore, since a cure is achieved by contraries, a suffering in the lower part of the body should be treated by those things which draw toward the upper parts, such as vomiting. Hence the saying: **Vomiting is the best way to cure ulcers of the kidneys**, because it cleanses and evacuates by drawing the humors to the opposite side of the kidneys. 

Again, because the matter drawn to the suffering place increases the blockage, and by that very process the substance is hardened and turned to stone <note>referring to the formation of kidney or bladder stones</note>, while simultaneously causing pain through the stimulation of the **rheum** <note>a flow of humors</note>, diuretics are not beneficial in these diseases.

It also begins a new section on why diuretics are contraindicated in urinary tract diseases, suggesting that humors should be drawn away from infected organs rather than toward them.</summary>

# On the Urinary Passages

Regarding the **urinary passages** <term>viae urinae</term>, some argue that **diuretics** <term>uritica</term> <note>Medicines that promote the production and flow of urine</note> are of no use in such conditions, because they are vehemently hot, dry, and sharp, as stated in the fifth book of *Simple Medicines* and the third book of *Practices*. 

It is asked whether they provide benefit through **similarity** or **contrariety**. Certainly not through similarity, for then they would not act at all, since every action is perfected through contrariety. Furthermore, such things do not profit when they are deprived of their proper end. Nor do they profit through contrariety, because when contraries are joined together, they are destructive; hence, concerning unequal **distemperance** <term>distemperantia</term> <note>An imbalance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, all things are destroyed and corrupted by their contraries. Therefore, in diseases of the urinary passages, diuretics do not confer benefit.

On the opposing side are the authorities who not infrequently command that these substances be swallowed in these illnesses. Again, in the first book of the *Aphorisms* <note>Referring to Hippocrates</note>, it is said that one ought to act from wherever nature most strongly repairs itself. Therefore, the fourth precept states that those who are slender and easily vomit should be purged from above. Conversely, in these passions, nature repairs itself through the inferior part, since evacuation occurs through the closer passages.

And in the same precept regarding the **diaphragm** <note>original: "dyaslagma," a corruption of "diaphragma"</note>, it is noted that pains above the diaphragm indicate a need for medicine for the upper parts. However, for those below, the provocation is downward. The provocation of urine is similar to the purging of the belly, but these pains and passions are below the diaphragm. Furthermore, whatever draws out matter from the urinary passages cleanses them and benefits them; and these are the diuretics. Therefore, they do benefit the passions of the urinary passages.

Regarding the first point, it must be known that a **diuretic** or **uritic**—that is, a urinary medicine—is a medicine that is hot, dry, and sharp, which thins the blood, separating the thin from the thick, and evacuating the thin part into the urinary passages. Examples include the seeds of **parsley** <term>apii</term>, **fennel** <term>feniculi</term>, **sweet flag** <term>acorus</term>, and similar herbs. 

For some medicines are moderately heating and not drying, such as those that generate milk. There are two types of milk-generating substances: those that are hot and moist, producing much matter for the blood itself; and those that are hot and dry, cutting into the blood and thinning it so that the matter of the seed is converted into milk by being reduced. Others, however, heat and dry more moderately, such as those used for the provocation of **menstruation**. Those that heat and dry even more than these, with a strong cutting power, are **stone-breaking** <note>original: "lapidis frangitiue"; lithontriptic medicines used to break up kidney or bladder stones</note> medicines. If they participate even more in heat and dryness, they are provocative of urine. For those that break stones are not as hot and dry as these diuretics, because if they were, they would aggregate, thicken, and harden the stone. This is from the fifth book on **pharmaceuticals** <term>farmacorum</term>; and therefore, in the gloss, the opinion of **Al-Mansur** <note>original: "Almansoris"; referring to the Persian physician Rhazes and his work *Liber ad Almansorem*</note> is not rejected by this discourse of **Galen**. For it is necessary that diuretics be hot and dry so that they may open the passages, thin the humors, and heat the kidneys so that they may attract them with vigor. 

But a doubt arises concerning the aforementioned definition, for a diuretic medicine is stated to be hot, dry, and sharp, yet some include certain cold and moist things among the diuretics, such as the four or five "cold seeds" <note>A standard medieval medical formula usually consisting of cucumber, gourd, melon, and watermelon seeds</note>. To this, it must be said in two ways: either a diuretic is properly hot and dry—as **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Halyab"; the Latinized name of the physician Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi</note> says: medicines truly provoking urine must be both hot and sharp. Likewise, **Mesue** <note>original: "Heben Guesfo"; likely a corruption of "Ibn Masawayh" or "Yuhanna ibn Masawayh"</note> says: all things that heat and dry are urine-provokers, of which the sharpest are the best. 

And so, a medicine is called a diuretic either commonly—and then some of these cold things are called "uritic" because they have a certain subtle moisture and an **opening quality** <term>apperitīaz</term> <note>The ability to open blockages in the vessels or organs</note>, and can thus be named diuretics. Just as properly a laxative medicine is only attractive, but in a certain way three other types are more so. Or it must be said that diuretics, as such, are hot and dry, but they may also contain another quality or complexion. Just as everything bitter is hot, such as **opium**, even if it is judged to be cold. And because in the husks of these seeds there is less coldness and moisture than in the marrow, they are made more opening. These diuretics also differ in being more or less hot or cold.

At present, there is a triple benefit to them: 
1. By reason of **alteration**, in that they alter the body by their own qualities. 
2. By reason of **eduction**, because they evacuate matter from the urinary passages. 
3. By reason of **deduction**, because they carry medicines to the site of the disease, just as **saffron** <term>crocus</term> carries medicine to a suffering heart; thus it is administered even in hot diseases. 
4. Or perhaps even by reason of **ablation** <note>The removal or taking away of a substance</note> of a certain kind. 

What a disease is has already been seen. It is twofold: simple, such as a bad complexion without matter; or with matter, a bad composition divided into four natures. It can be a **breach of continuity** <term>solutio cōtinuitatis</term> <note>A physical injury like a cut or fracture where the body's natural connection is broken</note> occurring in many parts according to different names and times, or a composite one like an **aposteme** <term>apā</term> <note>An internal swelling or abscess</note>.

The **urinary passages** are the parts serving its eduction, such as the **emulgent veins and arteries** <note>The renal veins and arteries</note>, the kidneys, the **ureters** <term>port urinales</term> <note>Literally "urinary gates," the tubes carrying urine from kidneys to bladder</note>, the bladder, its muscle, and the penis in men. For these parts are ordered by nature so that the superfluity of urine may be led out of the body, with the muscles of the belly assisting in this work. What urine is has been seen previously. 

Know also that the urinary passages are either vehemently weakened or only slightly so. Regarding the second point, it should be known that according to **Thessalus** <note>Thessalus of Tralles, a famous physician of the Methodist school</note>, they indiscriminately command the administration of diuretics in diseases of the urinary passages, since the indication for him depends only on the use taken from the disposition, and not on the particular member or other factors. For this reason, he claimed that the science of medicine could be learned in six months—indeed, even less than six months—which is ridiculed by many. For he was a **Methodist**, or rather one of those "un-Methodical" ones who, considering only the general "path," treated nothing of the particulars in which experience exists and where the limit of medicine is reached. Others, working more commonly, indiscriminately command that diuretics be swallowed because it seems to them that matter abounds in the urinary passages, and thus they act as if on a specific part. The defect of their reasoning will be seen in what follows.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that if the disease is here without a vice of the humors, diuretics benefit it by reason of **alteration** and **deduction**. First, because the method of cure is founded upon contrariety, and especially since it is conceded that diuretics vary the different complexions—even if the diuretic itself is hot and dry. On the part of deduction, it is because it carries the prepared medicines to the site, though not by eduction since that lacks the presupposed...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the use of diuretics, specifically addressing when they are beneficial or harmful based on the state of the body’s humors and the specific nature of the urinary ailment.</meta>

...the matter of the disease <note>original: "passio materia"</note>, and let these passages not be entirely loosened. 
<margin>·</margin> If, however, there is a faulty **complexion** <term>complexio</term> <note>The specific balance of the four humors in an individual</note> due to a vice of the humors, or if the body is **plethoric** <note>Overfull of blood or humors</note> or **cacochymic** <note>Full of "bad juices" or corrupted humors</note>, then that which must be evacuated or purged must first be dealt with by a universal cleansing before a particular drawing out of fluids is attempted. 

And from there, if the location allows, **diuretics** should sometimes be used. If neither of the aforementioned conditions exists, and if the nature of the body allows for diuresis once the universal evacuation has been performed, it is helpful to draw out the "lye" <note>The waste products or sharp fluids</note> through the affected part so it may be more perfectly expelled. Therefore, in that case, diuretics can be beneficial in the three ways touched upon previously: by the alteration of the complexion, by the transportation of medicines to the site, and by the evacuation of matter. 

If, however, there is a faulty composition, specifically a blockage <term>opilatio</term> in the receiving vessels—whether caused by humors, a **stone** <term>lapis</term>, or fleshy growth—then diuresis should be encouraged to lead out the offending humor, provided the limb can tolerate it. However, this must be done temperately, lest more matter flow into the part and increase the obstruction. 

When there is excessive heat in the **kidneys** <term>renibus</term> combined with a certain viscosity, it is converted into a stone; for this reason, vehemently heating substances are forbidden when trying to break a stone. Through continuous use, diuretics also diminish fleshy excrescences; they moisten and soften, especially those that are cold and humid, which thin the dryness of the limbs from which the blockage arises. 

If the disease is on the surface, such as a type of **scabies** <note>A term used historically for various itchy skin eruptions</note>, diuretics can assist the body's predisposition, at least for the sake of "washing" the system, so that eventually **astringents** <term>stiptica</term> and healing agents may follow. 

Indeed, a disease involving these quantities—whether of few numbers or improper position—can rarely be cured by diuretics. If there should be a **break in continuity** <term>solutio continuitatis</term> <note>A medical term for a wound, fracture, or ulcer where the body's tissues are physically separated</note>, it will either be a fresh wound through which blood is continually drawn (as in a rupture of the **emulgent veins** <note>The renal veins</note>), and in that case, diuretics should by no means be administered. As stated, they thin the blood and force it to flow even more—unless perhaps the blood is trapped, as happens in **clots** <term>trumbis</term>. This is diagnosed by a feeling of heaviness and the retention of urine. Even then, for such an unequal break, one should use milder diuretics combined with astringents, as the stronger ones are to be feared. 

<margin>·</margin> If, however, it is an old break in continuity, such as an **ulcer**, and the body is predisposed to evacuation toward the opposite side, then if the condition is mild, one should work with milder diuretics like **alkekengi seed** <note>Winter cherry, used to clear the bladder</note>, **marshmallow** <term>altea</term>, and similar substances that cleanse and wipe away impurities. Afterward, use binding agents for healing, where diuretics are not helpful unless perhaps for the sake of leading matter away. But if the ulcer is malignant, it requires stronger agents to wipe away the thick and viscous matter within it, such as **maidenhair fern** <term>capilloueneris</term>, **orris** <term>yreos</term>, and **bitter vetch flour** <term>fata orobi</term>; finally, use "incarnative" <note>Medicines that help regrow flesh</note> and solidifying agents. 

According to **Serapion** and **Avicenna**: If the proposed sickness is like an **abscess** <term>apā</term> <note>original: "apostema"</note> in the body, first the offending matter must be evacuated. Then, while the matter is still undigested, it must be ripened <note>brought to a "head"</note>; but diuretics should not be used until it is ripened, so that the diuretics may break the abscess and lead the **pus** <note>original: "faies," likely "saniem"</note> outward. Care must be taken that these diuretics are not too strong, lest they provoke the premature movement of the matter into the passages, which generates constipation, or lest they thicken the pus, causing it to harden and "petrify" <note>Turn to stone</note>. 

<margin>·</margin> Because of this, the best medicine in such cases is **Cassia fistula** <note>A tropical pod used as a mild laxative and cleanser</note>, always assuming there is some remaining strength in the urinary passages. 

And know that it is best to administer diuretics far from the consumption of food. For if they are taken with or shortly after food, they draw undigested material into the passages along with the urine, thus becoming a cause of greater harm. Therefore, common practitioners err when they mix diuretics into feasts. It is necessary to take them hours before, just like laxatives for the belly. Hence, in the second book of **Almansor** <note>A work by the Persian physician Rhazes</note>: for purging the belly, it is beneficial to take prunes, then drink sweet wine, and allow some time to pass, and not to dine immediately after. This should be kept in common memory for all things that loosen the belly. Therefore, one must wait much longer with diuretics, since they seek the urinary paths more quickly than belly-softeners do. 

But on the contrary, in the fourteenth book of *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "de ingeio," referring to Galen's "De Ingenio Sanitatis" or "Methodus Medendi"</note>: when there is a stony constitution in the kidneys, give **capers** with **oxymel** <note>A mixture of honey and vinegar</note> at the beginning of the meal until the heaviness passes. To this it must be said that this diuretic should not be in such a quantity or for such a purpose that it draws out undigested food; it is not so. When it is said to "give capers," etc., it means they are taken on an empty stomach before everything else, but not so that food follows immediately. 

One must also avoid diuretics, especially when there is an intense **burning of urine**. By drawing heat to the infirm place, they force more "migration" of humors and thus induce greater pain. 

<margin>·</margin> Thus has this more universal question been briefly treated. Regarding the fourth point: to the first, it must be said (as it appeared) that when parts are vehemently injured, evacuation should not be performed through them. Hence, **Avicenna** says that one either speaks under this pretext, or when the matter is largely undigested, it must first be diminished and digested. And similarly, it is clear what should be said to **Galen**, since his speech also exists regarding an abscess that is not yet ripened. 

<margin>·</margin> To the other point: when the matter "sins" <note>Is excessive or corrupt</note>, it should be led to the opposite side; but when it has been diminished, it can be evacuated through the same part, unless it has been entirely weakened. Nor does Avicenna entirely deny diuretics in the cure of kidney ulcers, even if he praises vomiting more. To the other point, what should be said has appeared: because when an abscess happens with this, diuretics are not appropriate. For thus the body is prepared and such diuretics are administered so that the aforementioned accidents do not occur. To the other point: diuretics can be beneficial, for they are not entirely similar nor entirely contrary, but "middle" things, as they communicate with the urinary passages in matter but differ in their specific forms. For such things are active and passive. To those things which belong to the other part, it has also been seen what should be said; for it has been declared which diuretics, and when, and how they are conceded to the learned. To the final point: from wherever nature repairs itself, there one must lead, if the region is suitable; which is often not the case. Therefore, according to Galen in the same place, one must "revulse" <note>Draw away humors to a distant part of the body</note> and transform them toward their contraries.

### DIFFERENCE 206.

¶ It is demonstrated that in **gout** <term>podagra</term> <note>Gout specifically affecting the foot</note> caused by blood in the right foot, **phlebotomy** <term>fleubothomia</term> <note>The surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood</note> should be performed from the left hand, and in the left foot, from the right hand. This is because **Rhazes** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian physician</note> in the *Divisions* says: If the gout is in the right foot, bleed from the left hand; if in the left, from the right. Whence, concerning the joints, the same is said: If the pain is in the left foot, we ought to diminish blood from the right hand, and vice versa, from the **basilic vein** <note>A major vein in the arm, then thought to be connected to the lower body</note> or from certain branches of it, and you should not go to any other vein. Wherefore **Avenzoar** <note>Ibn Zuhr (1094–1162), an Arab physician</note> unworthily orders the **cephalic vein** <note>A vein in the arm usually associated with the head and neck</note> to be cut. And he confirms this because Rhazes in the *Almanzor* and the *Divisions*, in cases of **elephantiasis** <note>A term then used for severe skin diseases or leprosy</note>, commands the basilic vein of the opposite side to be bled. Furthermore, **Garinpontus** <note>An 11th-century Salernitan physician</note>, constructing his *Passionarius* from the series of **Galen’s** *Letter to Glaucon*, **Alexander**, **Paul**, **Theodore**, and **Priscian**, says: If the gout is "hot" and the pain of one foot is great with swelling and redness—provided the strength and age of the patient allow it—let him be bled from the arm of the healthy side. The healthy side is that which is positioned in contradiction to the infirm one, such as the right foot to the left hand, and the left foot to the right hand. Again, **Serapio** <note>Yahya ibn Sarafyun, a 9th-century Syrian physician</note> says that in the sickness of gout, we bleed from the joint opposite the sick foot; this, however, is not the other foot but the hand, and he commands it be done quickly, or not at all, lest it "attract" more matter than it "evacuates." True "opposition" is reserved for things that are contradictory, since everything is ultimately reduced to that principle. As it is said in the *Regiment of Acute Diseases*, the right foot to the left [hand] and vice versa is an opposition of contradiction. Furthermore, a cure is performed through its simple contrary. Therefore, it is better and most effective, because if the simple leads to the simple, the "more" leads to the "more," and the "most" leads to the "most," according to the second book of *Dialectics*. Whence, in the twenty-second section: If the gout is caused by blood, or with a dominance of blood, it is necessary that you administer phlebotomy from the contrary side. A greater contrariety exists when it is both "upper and right" compared to "lower and left" simultaneously, rather than just "upper and lower." This occurs when, with gout in the right foot, one bleeds from the left hand, and in the left foot, from the right hand. It is *not* so if one bleeds from the right for the right, or left for left. Again, if the body is **plethoric** <note>Overfull of blood</note>, not only is evacuation or attraction required, but also **derivation** <note>Drawing fluid from a nearby site</note> or a closer extraction. But when gout is in the right foot and one bleeds from the right [side], or left from left, it will not be able to cut off the flow, because bleeding from the same side in cases of **sciatica** <note>Pain along the sciatic nerve</note> or the **saphenous vein** <note>A large vein in the leg</note> would agitate the matter further. Therefore, for a right foot suffering gout, bleeding from the left hand is appropriate, and for the left foot, the right hand.

->In opposition to the *Almanzor*, Book Nine<-

If the patient hurts in the right foot, he should be bled in the right hand; and if in the left, the left. Furthermore, in the thirteenth book of *On Method*, [Galen says] if a hand is in bad condition, we shall cut or scarify the legs; if one leg is suffering, we treat the other. Whence in the first part of the *Fourth*: you should not make the extension across two diagonals, but only in one that is the furthest diagonal. Whence, if the matter is in the upper part of the right side, it is not to be drawn to the lower part of the left, but rather to the lower part of the same right side. This is more necessary because the opposite is found when one bleeds from the right hand for a gouty left foot, or from the left for a right foot, as a double diagonal intervenes—namely, that of upper to lower, and right to left. Wherefore, in the *Almanzor*: If an **aposteme** <note>An internal swelling or abscess</note> is in the right hand, blood should be drawn to the left hand, and vice-versa; and if it is in the right foot, draw blood lower down from the side that is directly in line with it. Again, art imitates nature: a spontaneous flow from the right nostril is praised in cases of an aposteme of the **liver** <note>Located on the right side</note>. In a case of the **spleen** <note>Located on the left side</note>, the left nostril. The opposite is criticized in Difference 197. Again, it is expedient for evacuation to happen through the most suitable part; this is the right through the right and left through the left, as the "community" or agreement is more intense between right and right than otherwise. Therefore, one should bleed from the right hand for a gouty right foot, and from the left for a left foot.

To understand this, first know that according to the *Viaticum*, **podagra** is pain of the heel and sole of the foot with tension of the nerve and pulsing, arising from "evil humors" descending to the heel. This suffering takes its name from the foot, just as **chiragra** <note>Gout of the hand</note> denotes the hand <note>original gloss: "a cir. i. manus"</note>, and **pleurisy** <note>Inflammation of the chest lining</note> comes from *pleura*, the rib. Sicknesses claim names for themselves in Difference 99. In this suffering, as with general joint pain, one must consider the producing, the suffering, and the instrumental cause. The "acting" cause is twofold: universal/preceding (such as a bad regimen in the **six non-natural things** <note>Historical health factors: air, food/drink, sleep/waking, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions</note>, especially strong or subtle wine that inebriates, sexual intercourse, the retention of accustomed evacuations, and the treatment of **catarrh** <note>Excessive mucus</note> and **colic**), and the particular/present cause. This latter is twofold: **complexion** <note>The balance of humors</note> or matter. The matter may be blood alone, or blood mixed with wind, or **choler** <note>Yellow bile</note>, or **melancholy** <note>Black bile</note>, or **phlegm** alone, or a multitude of raw humors. This suffering often comes from phlegm mixed with choler; for choler, with its biting sharpness, incites the nature and the spirits to run and prepares a path. Then, the phlegm, by its weight and slipperiness, descends into the path prepared by the choler—followed by the raw humor, then blood, and then choler again.

...and from melancholy, rarely [according to] **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rasis"</note> in the *Scientia*, book 22. Regarding the cause in the suffering patient, I mean the limb receiving the humor, it occurs because of weakness or a bad **complexion** <term>complexionem</term> <note>The balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within a person or a specific limb</note> impressed upon it, especially a cold one, or because of a poor structure from birth or acquired over time.

Indeed, the instrumental cause [relates to] the opening of the passages, whether by nature or by accident, toward which there is a superfluous movement of humors, especially after eating. Emptiness, looseness of tissue, bathing, tight footwear, and similar accidents work not a little [to cause this]. Those more prone to the passion of the joints are those entangled in chronic diseases and those recovering, especially those whose cure was mild and whose symptoms were calmed [prematurely], rather than being fully cleared and evacuated.

The more fitting times for the generation [of these pains] are [spring and autumn] because of the movement of humors and the malice of their qualities caused by indigestion. For **gout** <term>podagrica</term> and mania are moved in the spring and autumn, as is commonly noted.

<margin>vi.</margin>
Pain also multiplies in the joints because they perform more labor than other parts of the body. Hence, when they are heated, they attract humors, since by their natural structure they demand moisture for the sake of stability. They are also empty and receive [fluids] easily because their **complexion** is weak and they are further from the source of life <note>The heart, seen as the source of vital heat</note>. Also, this passion is inherited in the seed. And know that there are six differences of location by which bloodletting is regulated: above and below, before and behind, right and left. Sometimes these occur simply, and sometimes in combination, such as when two or three [locations] are involved. One should observe the flow; for example, if the right foot is suffering, you should bleed from the left hand, and vice versa. Three [locations] perhaps do not divide this way. Regarding this, it must be known that some have preferred a simple [rule]: for gout in the right foot, one must bleed from the left hand; for the left, from the right. Others say the opposite: for the right foot, one must bleed from the hand on the same side, and for the left, from the left. Both of these views were supported by earlier authorities. But the defect of their simple views will be shown generally by the teachings. In truth, it must be known that this truth appears not a little from the reasoned arguments in Difference 197: for the body is either **plethoric** <term>plectoricum</term> <note>Overfull of humors, specifically blood</note> or of strong constitution. If the illness is at its very beginning, bloodletting should be done from the contradictory <note>The opposite side and opposite limb, i.e., diagonally</note> location, and not just the contrary one. For a plethoric state requires the drawing away [of matter] to a distant place; it weakens the strength more to draw it from a distance, which is why bleeding the foot is more effective than the hand for certain weaknesses. And when matter flows too much, one must lead it to more distant parts, which happens at the start of the passion.

There are similar cases. In the *Divisions* and the *Almansor*, for **sciatica** <term>sciatica</term>, it is commanded to bleed the **basilic vein** <note>A large vein in the arm</note> on that side, and in swelling of the testicle, to bleed the basilic on the side of the swelling. Furthermore, the matter not only requires extraction but also attraction [away from the site], which is achieved by the diversity of distance. In this, one does not only wait for the first bloodletting, but also the second, which is performed from the basilic vein of the infirm side after a minor bleeding has been done on the healthy side.

If, however, the body is not plethoric, nor the strength great, nor the disease licensed [spreading], then one should bleed not contradictorily but contrarily <note>On the same side or in a simpler opposition</note>; for instance, for gout on the right, the left should be diminished, and vice versa. But because healthy blood is abundant in this passion, and it might otherwise lead to apoplexy or a rupture of a vein or most grave suffocation, the contradictory bloodletting remains [the standard], even if this passion, according to the masters, arises from indigestion of the blood, as earlier authorities noted in the opposite manner. Regarding the fourth point, even if it appears so: to the first, it is said that according to **Rhazes**, either he is [to be followed], for in parts of his books it is found that if it is in the right foot, they should bleed from the right hand; if in the left, from the left. The *Almansor* agrees with this. There are, however, some books not containing the truth, saying if the passion is in the right foot, one should bleed in the left hand, and if in the left foot, from the right hand. 

To that which is brought up regarding the joints, it is said that they contain [humors] deeply, and you will say the opposite: for example, if the pain is in the left foot, we must diminish [blood] from the left hand. This consideration is not similar to **elephantiasis** <term>elephantia</term>, which happens from a greater fullness than the passion of the joints. To another point, it is said that to **Gariopontus** <note>An 11th-century Salernitan physician</note> it appeared from the arguments in the *Scientia*... which can nevertheless contain the truth. To another, it is said this is verified in the *Canon* <note>Avicenna’s Canon of Medicine</note>, that bloodletting is perfected by contradiction...

Furthermore, the cure is not always perfected by the contrary immediately, but also by other similar means, as in Difference 154. A cure is perfected not only by contrariety but more by the constancy of the strength. To another point, it appeared that the second [bleeding] should be performed from the **cephalic vein** <note>A vein in the arm</note> or from the basilic on the side separate from the first, or from one of its branches. To those things which touch on the present, it must be said that according to that author, it is verified when the body is not entirely plethoric. With the maturation of the evacuation, the eradication of the matter from its place to another place occurs either by attraction to a distant part or to a near one, when there is no fullness of any passion in the body. But what is referred to... for the sake of evacuation... contradictory bleeding should be done most gravely when this replenishment is minimal or rarely said to happen. To another, it is said that although art follows nature, it is not always as shown in Difference 163. To another, it is said that it is not always necessary for right to right or left to left to be bled, because the contrariety or suitability is more intense... whence it is sought through the passages, especially when there is a counter-flow and a "breathing together" <note>original: "conspiratio"</note> through the same [parts], a natural ejection of the whole from the whole.

### DIFFERENCE 207.

<margin>1</margin>
¶ That not every **ulcer** <term>ulcus</term> requires drying is shown. Whence **Rhazes** in the *Continens*, book 15: Every ulcer ought to be dried except that which occurs from bruising and stretching in the flesh, which ought to be moistened and heated so that the matter in it may become pus more quickly. Whence, in the fourth [book]: All ulcers need drying, except those made from the bruising of the muscles and the crushing of the same. For these need, in the first place, to be softened and moistened.

<meta>This page continues the medical distinctions regarding the treatment of bodily ailments, specifically moving from the causes of joint pain to the nature and treatment of ulcers and wounds.</meta>

Furthermore, in the fourth book of **The Art of Healing** <note>original: "de inge." referring to Galen's *Methodus Medendi*, often titled *De Ingenio Sanitatis* in the Middle Ages</note>, according to **Hippocrates** <note>original: "y."</note>: Not every wound should be moistened; therefore, some ulcers should be moistened. But an ulcer is truly something other than a wound; indeed, nothing is added to it except something more, such as **putrefaction** <term>putrefactione</term> <note>The decay or rotting of tissue within a wound</note>. In Greek also it is written, as will appear, as *helkos* <note>original: "eleos"</note>.

Likewise, because an ulcer greatly needs **incarnation** <term>incarnatione</term> <note>The growth of new flesh to fill a void</note>, consolidation, and scarring; however, these are perfected through "gluing" <note>original: "inviscationem," a process where tissues adhere to one another</note>. This gluing is caused by moisture, as appears in the third book of *On Generation and Corruption* and the fourth book of *Meteorology*. Furthermore, in an ulcer, there is no small loss of flesh which must be regenerated, since the cure leads the part back to that state in which it previously existed; but flesh is generated primarily from blood through its kinship and moisture, according to the third book of *On Generation*. Therefore, it is appropriate and according to the art that it be nourished by blood, since it is a follower of it. Even if ulcers occur in a dry body or a dry part, since every cure is perfected through moisture, it needs it in no small measure.

And it is probable: for when one suffers from **chilblains** <note>original: "punices"</note> or cracks in the heel called **fissures** <note>original: "mugas"</note> from a bad cold and dry **complexion** <term>complexione</term>, as happens in frost, there is a need for warming and much moistening, but not for drying. Therefore, any ulcer requires minimal consolidation.

On the contrary, in the fifth book of *The Art of Healing*: Experience testifies and reason confirms. One of the intentions in treating ulcers is that they be dried; hence, in the first [part] of the fourth [book], the intention in healing ulcers is drying. Furthermore, in an ulcer, there is a loss of the part's natural heat due to the flow of spirits and humors, which not rarely induce pain. All these things, when they attract moisture to the place, cause a soft, moist substance, as seen in the third book on fevers. Therefore, every ulcer requires drying.

Regarding the first point, however, note that "ulcer" is often used for "wound" and vice versa. Nor do I think they differ in essence, but rather by accident. For a wound is declared to be a recent blow in a fleshy body. An ulcer, however, is a wound or blow that has putrefied. At the same time, putrefaction follows in a wound, which above all appears as **pus** <note>original: "saniem seu pus"</note>, which is a change of the putrefying humors toward whiteness and lightness, in which the natural heat is finally overcome, as noted in the third book of *Aphorisms* and the first book of *Prognostics*. And this is said because that which is putrefying is either watery in substance with a strong heat, requiring maximum drying—which is a subtle and horrible quality—or it is thick and earthy, such as filth or **decay** <note>original: "macor"</note>, requiring drying and cleansing especially.

The cause of such putrefaction is twofold: internal or external. The primary internal cause is the weakness of the limb. Then, the other parts of the same nature assist with the flow of moisture and heat, accompanied by pain. The external cause is a medicine that is too hot and moist applied to the part, along with other external factors already mentioned.

The distinction of wounds, beyond what was touched upon before in the first and third books of *The Art of Healing* and the fourth [book] of the *Practica*, is twofold: for one is **simple** <term>simplex</term>, which is associated with nothing against nature except for the break in continuity, so that in it there is only a minimal change, not requiring correction and having a small amount of praised pus. The other is **compound** <term>compositum</term>, either by reason of the cause, the disease, or the accident, such as wicked superfluities flowing into it, or an added **eschar** <term>eschara</term> <note>A piece of dead tissue that is cast off from the surface of the skin</note>, or excessive flesh, or a cavity, or blood poured out into it. What is "dry," and how many ways it is spoken of, is explained in the fifteenth [Difference].

---

Regarding the first point, it should be known that in this case, as it appears, the indication for treatment is chiefly taken from the part itself. Therefore, the **Thebalites** <note>Followers of a specific medical school or author, possibly Thabit ibn Qurra</note>, accepting no indication from the part in the first book of *The Art of Healing*, but only from the contraries, would say that not every ulcer should be dried, but some should be moistened and others dried by their opposites, as argued from the previous points. But their defect in this doctrine will be wonderfully clear.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that every ulcer and even a wound joined with filth—that is, those that are dirty and impure—require drying as the nature of the matter dictates. For they require unity, which cannot occur without the thickening of the blood, which is perfected by dryness; hence in the third book of *The Art of Healing*: Wounds or ulcers, and specifically ulcers, are to be dried. And therefore wine, in which there is a certain power, is a supreme medicine for all.

But it is said "in ulcers" because if it were due to an effusion, it is ordered to be moistened, as introduced before from the fourth book of *The Art of Healing*. However, so that this may be clear, it should be known that one cure is **immediate**, when the medicine falls directly upon the thing to be removed, such as water for a fever; and another is **mediated**, when it acts through something else, as when cold water cures a spasm of repletion or scammony cures a fever.

Therefore, dryness is suitable for an ulcer and a wound in itself; moisture is suitable only by accident. Cold water, for instance, is not hidden from this, for it is "biting" to ulcers according to the fifth book of *Aphorisms*. For corrosive ulcers where there is no putrefaction, a wash <note>original: "embrocatio"</note> with cold water and much pure water is beneficial if there is heat. It must be said that for these ulcers, cold is appropriate, just as for pure **erysipelas** <note>a skin infection</note> and burning fevers.

From this, you also know the distinction that a "contrary" is taken for everything that expels a disease in whatever way. Therefore, whether the disease of the ulcer and the break in continuity happens in any way, the goal is "union" [healing]. Let them say, therefore, that if an ulcer is simple, drying is immediately required, unless something else is observed that diverts the cure. This is confirmed because the pure separation of the joint requires union. All this, as the substance of the matter denotes, calls for union to bring it back to its prior state. This is achieved by drying the blood and gathering it together. Furthermore, the wound requires drying and cleansing, which also strengthens the parts and closes the pores so that it does not receive more superfluities to be poured out.

If, however, the ulcer or wound is compound, although by reason of what is joined to it a moistening treatment might be appropriate immediately, nevertheless, the ulcer itself fundamentally requires drying as shown before. Sometimes, both the associated condition and the ulcer require drying.

For example: an ulcer might be dry and **escharous** <note>covered in a hard crust</note> and hard due to its complexion, so that the parts cannot be joined. Since this is achieved by something moist, then a moistening and softening work is necessary. Hence, in the fourth book of *The Art of Healing*: If there is a corrupted complexion in the flesh, one must investigate whether it is hard and dry; if it is so, foment it with warm water until it swells and becomes red. Once the bad dry complexion is removed and the eschar-like flesh is calmed by gentle moistening, then you lead it to drying, just as the nature of the part requires.

### FROM BOOK III OF THE ART OF HEALING

In which three **complexions** <term>complexiones</term> <note>The balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determines a person's physical and mental state</note> are to be considered. For if the complexion of the body is dry and the members are drier, such as the bones, ligaments, and the heart, it is necessary to make the substance of the medicines themselves drier. But if the complexion of the whole body along with its members is moister, a medicine that is less drying is helpful, although it is necessary to act and observe according to similar principles. If, however, a middle state occurs, a moderate medicine is needed.

Likewise, if an **ulcer** <term>ulcus</term> <note>A persistent open sore that fails to heal naturally</note> is accompanied by bruising or contusion, it must first be moistened and warmed so that **pus** <term>sanies</term> <note>original: "sanies"; a discharge of pus and fluid from a wound, often seen by medieval doctors as a sign the body was expelling harmful matter</note> is generated, which expels the harmful matter; afterward, one should return to drying it. Unless the contusion or bruising ceases, the ulcer cannot be healed. If, however, there is a cavity associated with the ulcer, or excess flesh, or a severed vessel, the ulcer or wound will require a drying medicine so that the lost flesh may be regenerated; it then requires consolidating and scarring treatments.

However, in destroying excess flesh, it is necessary to join heat with dryness. In checking the flow of blood, coldness is used, unless it becomes necessary to check it with **cauteries** <note>Tools or substances used to burn tissue to stop bleeding or remove growth</note> once scarred.

The model for this is the **aposteme** <note>A swelling or abscess</note>. In the beginning, it needs drying help to repel what flows to the ulcer and to block the pores and strengthen the part. In its increase and peak, it needs moistening and **maturation** <note>The process of a swelling "ripening" into pus</note>. In its decline, it needs drying mixed with heat, and finally, a unifying drying treatment. For the cure of an ulcer is supported by drying agents, as was previously said.

Intermediary cures appear clearly from the nature of things. For everything that hinders union is an intermediary that must be removed by its opposite. This is either moist or dry; therefore, one must sometimes dry and sometimes moisten in the middle. From this, it also appears that an ulcer of a "difficult cure" requires many different healing intentions, especially when it is in a more noble part of the body, or is of great quantity or malignancy.

Know also that a simple ulcer only needs consolidation when there is no loss of substance in it. A compound ulcer, specifically one with a great loss of flesh, requires more drying agents. Every ulcer, therefore, needs drying agents at some point, though they differ in degree.

An exception is granted for contused and bruised ulcers, which are moistened so that the flow to the part is matured. For ulcers cannot be healed unless matured pus appears; as it is said in the **Aphorisms** <note>Referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, Book 5</note>: "In an ulcer, the cure of pus is a great certainty of safety." It is impossible for an ulcer to be dangerous or troublesome while pus is being formed.

Regarding another point: that series was corrupted by a monk and cannot be verified except externally. From the Greek, I have translated it thus: "Ulcers are universal and should not be extended without wine." This is clear from what is added, teaching the cause: **"For the dry is near to the healthy; the moist is not healthy."** <note>original: "Siccum enim vicinum est salubri, humidum vero non salubri"</note> Because wine, despite its moisture—and especially old, dry wine—is effective in its power, it softens and extends the part, which does not happen with water or other liquors; therefore, it is the best medicine for wounds or ulcers.

Regarding another point: flesh is generated from heat and moisture. Regarding the generation of bone, it is said to be generated from heat like a tile in a furnace. Regarding fat, it is generated from cold and moisture. Regarding the cure: although the material of a cure may be moist, its formal effect arises from its drying. For while blood is moist when flowing, it helps by adhering through dryness.

It is necessary to restore what was lost. The substance of blood is dried; therefore, the operation will be drying, more or less, depending on the member and its complexion. As it says in the third book of *The Art of Healing*: If there are two ulcers or wounds with moisture, one in a moist body and the other in a dry one, the one in the dry body needs drier help, while the one in the moist body needs more drying agents. This must be done according to the diversity of dryness and moisture. For flesh in ulcers must be created to replace what was lost. Therefore, if the part is dry, it is helpful to dry the ulcer or wound further. If it is moist, the medication must be even more drying.

## DIFFERENCE CCVIII.

**Whether a potential cautery is more praiseworthy than an actual one.**

The best of physicians is he who can cure bad, fraudulent, and corroding ulcers with medicines that do what an incision with iron or a **cautery** <term>cauterium</term> <note>A tool for burning the skin</note> with fire does. In this, the operation of the prudent man over the imprudent is shown. **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a famous 10th-century Persian physician</note> says: A potential cautery is made from medicines; in an actual one, fire is mixed with some metal. Furthermore, **Damascenus** <note>Johannes Damascenus, often identified with the medical writer Mesue the Elder</note> says in his aphorisms: "He who can cure with diet without medicines will find prosperity." Haly says: "A cure made with food is better than a cure made with medicine." But as diet is to medicine or a potion, so a potion is to surgery. Therefore, if one prospers by curing with diet without medicine, one also prospers by healing with a potion without surgery. Again, that cautery is worse which causes a more sudden change. For nature does not withstand sudden alterations. But an actual cautery causes a more sudden change because of the fire.
