...actuality. It is not, however, potentiality, since it is necessary for that which is in potentiality to be introduced into **actuality** <term>actualitas</term> <note>In medieval science, "actuality" refers to an immediate effect (like fire), while "potentiality" refers to something that has the power to act once applied (like a chemical that burns the skin over time)</note> little by little through the influence of the carrier itself upon the body. Again, the physician who proposes a medicine that is less harmful is more to be chosen, which is the cautious **potential cautery** <term>cauterium potentiale</term> <note>A chemical "burning" agent, such as a strong acid or caustic herb, that works more slowly than a hot iron</note>, since it makes a greater impression on a soft body; however, it does not do so on a hard, dry body such as those that are sinewy and bony. But the **actual cautery** <term>cauterium actuale</term> <note>A metal tool, usually made of iron or gold, heated in a fire and applied directly to the flesh</note> is able to press its power into all parts for this reason.

Furthermore, Galen in many places teaches us to choose such things according to their virtue or power, such as through their form or essence. One should reject things according to their "act" or accidental properties, such as through the senses or appearance. But the cautious potential cautery is placed in the first rank, and the actual in the second. And for that reason, the cautious one makes for a better operation because it is more proportional to the human body, since contraries without heat are mutually corruptive; therefore, the cautious one is naturally placed there since it is graduated, not acting as an immediate heat like the fiery quality in smoke. Therefore, potential cautery is preferred over actual.

On the contrary, **Albucasis** <note>Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (936–1013 AD), a famous Andalusian surgeon whose work "Al-Tasrif" was a standard medical textbook in Europe</note> at the beginning of his *Surgery*, extols actual cautery as more wonderful than potential. Furthermore, that cautery is more to be chosen in which the utility of the whole purpose of cauterization is more perfect, which is the actual. Whence in the ninth book of the *Practica*: in the care of cooking <note>original: "coquendi"; here referring to the "digestion" or maturation of humors in a wound</note>, a delicate treatment is necessary, such as with pepper and **euphorbia** <note>A genus of plants with a caustic, milky sap</note>, and burning, such as with lime and **flower of brass** <note>original: "floris eris"; likely verdigris or copper oxide</note>. But when both assist in the completion without burning by fire, it is actual cautery; otherwise, it is potential.

And if actual cautery is to be chosen over potential, first it must be known what is potential cautery and what is actual cautery, and the differences between them, and next which conditions they suit and which they do not, and finally at what time it is most expedient to cauterize. 

According to the first section of the fourth book, **cautery** <term>cauterium</term> <note>The practice of burning a part of the body to close a wound, stop bleeding, or remove diseased tissue</note> is a very noble medicine helping to prohibit the spread of corruption, to strengthen a member whose proportions we wish to rectify, to resolve corrupt matters retained in a member, and to restrain a **flux** <term>fluxus</term> <note>An abnormal or excessive discharge of bodily fluids, such as blood or diarrhea</note>. And these four benefits, with the kind of treatment given, especially suit actual cautery, which is evident because actual cautery by iron or gold acts immediately, while no potential cautery acts simply by touch. 

Potential cautery is that which is made from burned or caustic medicines, hot and dry in the fourth degree. For these, when applied to the body and influenced by natural heat, perform their action. Cautery is diversified by reason of its substance, quality, and quantity. In substance: one is a hard, dry substance, such as **sublimated arsenic** <note>A highly toxic chemical compound often used in medieval medicine to "eat away" diseased flesh</note>, lime, verdigris, and similar things. Another is in liquid substance, such as the water of nitre, arsenic, and prepared sulfur. There is also another in a middle substance, constructed from these extremes, such as with soap, crushed herbs like **flammula** <note>Spearwort, a plant known to cause skin blistering</note>, **thapsia** <note>The "deadly carrot," used as a skin irritant</note>, wild rue gum, **water-crowfoot** <note>original: "apio ranio"</note>, and similar things. 

Actual cautery is that in which the quality of fire impresses an act, the material of which is metal, such as gold or iron, and some moderns have tried silver and brass. Regarding the suitability of cautery in conditions, Albucasis testifies that it prefers every natural **complexion** <term>complexio</term> <note>The patient's elemental balance (hot, cold, wet, dry)</note> when it is with matter and without matter. In a hot and dry condition without matter, it is least suitable, and especially potential cautery, so that principally cautery suits a cold and moist condition, both with and without viscous matter, since it is said to animate the proportion of the member and resolve the matters retained in it. For alteration in a passive state is located only in quality, and every addition is perfected by its contrary. For the virtue of cautery is to heat and dry; therefore it is suitable for a simple cold and moist condition, then for hot and moist, and especially for material conditions, and then for cold and dry. 

Regarding hot and dry, and also cold and dry, there seems to be no small doubt, since it was said that cautery animates the proportion of the member, which it does by its contrary; for this reason, some have held that cautery does not suit a hot and dry condition, since this is the nature of fire. But others have maintained that it does suit it, because although a person's condition may be somewhat hot and dry, it is nevertheless cold and moist in preparation for cautery, especially actual cautery. So that perhaps the reasoning is not exquisite to the intent, since it is necessary for the cure to occur through the opposite in the same degree; however, Albucasis feels here that cautery is beneficial, as experience has testified to him in no small measure. 

It is necessary, however, for the one performing this to be upright and practiced in the act of cautery. It is also necessary to know the diversity of the proportions of men, the dispositions of illnesses, causes, accidents, and the spans of time of the illnesses themselves, so that he makes the cautery fall upon the matter needing resolution and not upon the constitution and nature in such a way as to cause harm. For cautery performs the aforementioned benefits, though not all at once, but sometimes many, and other times only one. 

All these things are more clearly seen in actual cautery than in the first [potential]. For potential cautery is not properly suitable except in a cold and moist condition, and especially with matter, because of the harms that frequently occur with actual cautery. 

The time for cautery is twofold: one which relates to the time of the season, the other to the configuration of the body being healed. Regarding the first, surgeons are of different hearts. For some say that cautery is only suitable in the **Spring** <note>Spring was considered the balanced season, ideal for many medical procedures like bloodletting or purging</note>, since then the complexions are altered and the humors are moved. Others, however, among whose number is Albucasis, say that cautery is suitable at any time, because the harm occurring due to the time is removed by the benefit of the cautery, especially if the cautery is required because of a sudden pain prostrating the strength entirely, or a flux of blood, especially from an artery. 

This ambiguity can be clearly decided from the fourth book [of Galen]. For as in phlebotomy you distinguish two hours, the "elected" and the "necessary," so in purging and cautery and generally in every work of medicine, a twofold time must then be observed. Thus, the elected time is Spring and specifically other times, yet in such a way that Spring follows or joins in goodness, then Winter, and afterwards Summer. 

The time related to the body is that cautery must be done after sufficient general and particular purging of the body, lest by its pain the agitated humors should run to the place. For it must be done after the first medicines do not help, so that cautery is called by some the "last resort of medicine." 

Therefore, it should be known that some have absolutely chosen potential cautery over actual, moved by the sudden pain it induces, and likewise because some abhor it more than potential. But this position cannot stand, as is shown in the second proposition; nor does it argue for the motion generally but particularly, since in some cases actual cautery must yield to potential. There are also others erring about cautery, such as the common and dull-witted surgeons who think that illness...

This, however, is not the case, since a recurrence can happen by occasion of **natural things** <term>res naturales</term>, **non-natural things** <term>res non naturales</term> <note>In medieval medicine, these are external factors affecting health, such as air, food, sleep, and exercise.</note>, or things existing beyond nature. Similarly, it is argued that the cautery is the final refuge of medicine, yet the healthy can also be under medical care. For we use it when we see that other remedies do not help. First, the body must be guided by diet and drink; finally, however, one turns to **surgery** <term>cyrurgia</term>, under which the cautery is placed. If, however, one wishes to refer to this such that after it no other medicine confers help, it has already been said that this is false, since there may be another medicine necessary according to the disposition of the parts already mentioned.

Regarding the third point, it should be known that the **actual cautery** <term>cauterium actuale</term> <note>A metal tool heated by fire.</note> is always to be preferred to the potential one, because, as has been shown, the actual is suitable for almost every complexion, whereas the potential is not, but rather is more for those that are cold and humid, and specifically when the matter is in a stronger body and at an appropriate time. Furthermore, the benefits for which the cautery is described are more diligently adapted to actual cautery than potential. **Paulus** <note>Paulus Aegineta</note> says the potential cautery, by penetrating, harms the principal members more than the actual, especially when it is near them. Furthermore, the potential cautery—and especially the liquid kind—once it has been impressed, does not remain within our power to stop, unlike the actual cautery which leaves as soon as it is removed. Thus, there is a seen difference between potential and actual cautery, just as there is between **alchemy** <term>falacia</term> <note>Here used to imply a deceptive or artificial process.</note> and **philosophy** <term>floia</term>. For in philosophy nothing is lost or falls away; in alchemy, however, a great difference is found. Also, that cautery which is used not only reaches the place to be cauterized but also heals and collects; yet it hurts the members and provides a longer-lasting pain, perhaps causing an inflammation in members that are difficult to heal and perhaps even causing death, whereas the other does not transcend the place or harm the underlying natural members. The first, as they say, is the potential cautery; the second is the actual. For the potential, being brought little by little from potentiality into act, induces a boiling in the spirits and humors, making the pain run to that place no less than if the members were dried out, causing them to shrink toward the heart itself, inflaming them, and causing them to fall into fever; and rightly so, because it acts by **putrefying** <term>putrefaciendo</term> <note>Chemical caustics work by "rotting" or breaking down the tissue chemically, which is slower and more prone to infection than a heat-sear.</note>. Hence, in the third book of the *Farabi* concerning vehement medicines, it is attested that the potential cautery induces a more intense and longer pain, and for this, the length of time of its operation is not small. The actual cautery, however, does not induce this, since it is "simple" according to **Albucasis** <note>The famous 10th-century surgeon from Islamic Spain.</note>, and its pain is most quickly quieted by its own subtlety and goodness, unless it is used excessively and in the wrong place. The weak cannot tolerate the violence of the cautery when it is brought toward the internal members, which is very dangerous, especially when it is near the nobler organs. Therefore, the actual cautery is to be preferred over the potential. Sometimes some are **faint-hearted** <term>pusillaimes</term>, abhorring and greatly fearing the actual cautery, as said in the distinction 199, choosing for this reason the potential over the actual. To them, it seems that the actual induces more vehement pain, which is not the case except perhaps in its intensity. Hence, if a **splenetic** <note>Someone suffering from a diseased spleen.</note> person does not tolerate fire, let medicines be used as cauteries, according to the fourth book on *Ingenio*. Some, being of tender flesh and unwilling, wish to be cured over a long time; the pain of the actual passes quickly, but the potential induces a greater pain extensively, since its action is measured over a longer time while it performs its work by putrefying. Others, however,

are fleshy places, or have a **fistula** <term>fistola</term> with a narrow and deep opening, which the actual cautery could not reach without great injury to the surrounding parts. Sometimes potential cautery is also administered when we fear injury to the nerves or veins; for the potential, if duly applied, harms these less. Regarding the fourth point, it must be said to the first that those medicines are not cauterizing but rather cleansing, abstergent, and lightly drying, along with a proper diet and the ordering of evacuations. And if they are said to do that which incision and cautery with fire do, this is through a middle way of compression. For every fullness and every malice of the spirit is medicated by its own reason, and if these are cauterizing, they ought not to be placed under the second type of medicine. Since the duty of surgery is to cut, to sew, and to cook <note>In this context, "to cook" refers to the application of heat to transform or "ripen" tissue.</note>. To the other point, it is similar: caustics should not be placed under "drink" but under manual operation. To the other, it is said that what is repetitive changes into its own disposition and does not harm its cause; however, that which harms the nature of the limb, and especially destroys its congenital habit, is harmful. Actual cautery falls into the category of things "beside nature" if it is administered properly and not "against nature," which is shown by its quick effect. To the other, it is granted that in other cases, the cautery is potential. To the other, it is said that **Galen** does not define all things simply but through the act, since with their actual presence they can induce an effect like an actual cautery. But because at the beginning they were deceptive, the action does not remain, just as appears in hot water: although it begins to warm, it cools afterward and freezes more vehemently than before. To the other, it is said that potential cautery seems to be more proportioned to the spirit of the body than the actual, because of its long stay in the part; but because of all the accidents it induces, it causes more harm than the actual. The actual does not harm the surrounding parts like the potential does. For opium, although it is more proportioned to the human spirit than water (since it is gradual in its nature, while water is in the highest degree of coldness), nevertheless it harms and chills it more. So says **Hippocrates** <term>Y.</term> <note>Abbreviated as Y for Ypocras/Hippocrates.</note> regarding spirits. Its action is simple. Or also, although the actual cautery changes things more quickly, it does not do so afterward like the potential one does.

->**For the reason that follows, it is asked whether actual cauteries are more laudably made with iron**<-
than with gold. Because in a cautery, and specifically an actual one, what is sought (as has appeared) is drying and burning. But this is found more in **iron** <term>ferrum</term> than in **gold** <term>aurum</term>, since iron is drier in itself and is a more active subject in which the impression of fire, once received, can work more strongly than in gold. Furthermore, of the metals, only iron is ignited <note>Meaning it can reach a glowing, incandescent state without melting immediately.</note>. Every cautery must be ignited.

->**Also, a cautery is more laudable if made of that material in which we can better measure the heat of the fire, which is the reason for**<-
iron. Since gold, being of a reddish-fiery color, does not show when it is sufficiently hot as iron does, which shows a color participating almost in white <note>Incandescence or "white heat."</note>. Moreover, gold is a body less dense and more porous than iron, so that when heated it dissolves and yields into thin leaves. For which reason the craftsman falls into difficulty. If it is only slightly heated, its action cools before the cauterization is complete, whereby danger can follow...

It also makes a technical case for iron as the ideal material for cauteries due to its ability to hold heat and visibly indicate its temperature.</summary>

...the physician, so that the pain and scarring which happen with iron do not occur. On the other hand, according to the **astrologers** <term>astrologos</term> <note>Medieval medicine closely linked the planets to parts of the body and surgical tools; Mars was traditionally associated with iron and cutting.</note>, they attribute medicine, and especially surgery, to **Mars** <term>Martis</term>. Iron is clearly of his nature. Therefore, the application of a gold cautery is preferred over iron. 

In opposition to the first point, which was the fourth: **Gold** <term>aurum</term> is a better material for a cauterizing tool. For a cautery made of gold is better and more quickly healable. This is also attested by **Dioscorides** <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> along with the first reasoning: that when one cauterizes with a gold tool, it does not produce **blisters** <term>vesicas</term> <note>original: "uesicas"</note> from the cauterization itself, and leads to a better cure. 

Furthermore, a cautery is elegantly made from that which is more closely related to the human constitution, as it inflicts less harm and heals more quickly. Such is the gold cautery, but not the iron one. This is fixed because gold is tempered and proportional to the human constitution. Iron, however, is sufficiently hot and perhaps dry. It is expressed well enough in these acts which qualities are innate to them. Therefore, when cauterizing with gold, blisters and **pustules** <term>pustule</term> do not follow as they do with iron, nor does **discharge** <term>sanies</term> <note>original: "saies"; likely meaning inflammatory fluid or pus</note> remain in the cauterized limb. It also allows for faster consolidation and a more perfect scarring because of the tempering and quality of the operation itself. It is also shown that a mark made on the flesh is made more easily than with iron; for incision and cauterization are proportional. Gold, both in its substance and its color, is more closely related to the human body than iron. Furthermore, a cautery made of a more noble material, and one more proportional to life, is itself more noble. This is gold and not iron, since gold is a companion to life and declared to be its origin; iron, however, belongs to Mars and is an origin of corruption. Therefore, the gold cautery is to be preferred to the iron one.

Regarding the first point, it should be known what iron is and what gold is, along with the difference in their use. They say cauteries are of various shapes according to the diversity of the places that must be cauterized; for some must be round, some curved, others thin and long, some thick, some with one head, and others with many. **Albucasis** <note>Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi, a hugely influential medieval surgeon.</note> indicates this sufficiently along with others. But one can also burn with juices and inclusions, or with metallic **cannulas** <term>canulis</term> <note>Small tubes used to protect surrounding tissue during internal cautery.</note>, especially when it is necessary to cauterize internal parts like the inner ears, the anus, or the mouth.

Regarding the second point, we should know that authors here seem to contradict themselves. For the predecessors, as **Albucasis** likewise attests, chose the gold cautery over the iron one. Yet, in practice, the iron cautery is preferred over the gold. His motivations were mentioned above regarding the color and substance of gold. Other medicinal parts were also touched upon earlier. What should be seen regarding this is as follows:

Regarding the third point, it should be known that the **actual cautery** <term>cauterium actuale</term> <note>A tool that uses physical heat, rather than chemicals, to burn tissue.</note> can be considered in two ways: in itself, and in relation to those operating it. For there are two types of practitioners: those educated by long experience (who are rarely skilled) and those who are unskilled and inexperienced, among whom there is almost no knowledge. According to **Al-Mansur** <note>likely referring to the *Liber Almansoris* by the Persian physician Rhazes</note> in the seventh book: most of those who exercise this art are **idiots** <term>idiote</term> <note>In this context, meaning unlearned laypeople rather than a slur.</note>, rustics, fools, and especially bone-setters. If gold is considered in itself, it is a nobler metal and more prepared and proportional for the human body, causing less injury and easier healing; there is no doubt it is the more elegant choice for cauterization. Thus, in the 22nd canon: "Let the **sciatica** <term>sciaticę</term> be cauterized with red gold." This is also indicated when it is ordered that **smallpox** <term>uariolas</term> <note>original: "uariolas"</note> pustules be broken with a golden needle. 

But because someone could be deceived by the color or substance, it is necessary to be forewarned. The choice lies more in the practitioner than the tool. Thus the arguments of Albucasis are shown on the contrary side. 

---

And therefore, the skilled and experienced say to use gold and not iron, especially when noble and visible parts are to be cauterized, such as the face—for instance, the lips, the nose, or the eyelids. For the face is nobler than the rest of the body, as it is uncovered. 

If, however, the iron cautery is considered in itself, it is less noble than gold. Yet it is to be chosen by the unskilled and inexperienced who do not know how to measure the heat of fire in gold. One must choose what does the least harm when a person can hardly step away from their ignorance. For a flame in thick materials causes more obvious errors, while those who are ignorant might rush headlong into thin materials, even though the latter provide more help when administered properly. This is why the food of those who experiment with sacrifices is praised. 

Similarly, **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire.</note> says that inexperience falls into error when reason is omitted, since it is quite difficult. Thus, in general, gold does not excel iron in terms of preventing harm, so iron might be chosen simply because people lack gold through poverty or greed. A gold cautery is better the purer it is, the more compact it is, and the slower it is to melt. Iron, however, is better when it is purer, drier, rougher, and more compact. Cauteries made of silver or **brass** <term>auricalci</term> are not approved because of their instability, even though some modern practitioners have tried them.

Regarding the fourth point: a cautery does not require total drying or burning, but a sufficient tempering. As shown, gold induces this better than iron. To the other point: it is said that gold does not "ignite" <note>original: "igniri"</note>—not because it does not receive the impression of fire, but because it is not diminished by the fire and remains pure, unlike other metals. To the next point: an experienced person knows how to measure the heat of a gold cautery and should therefore prefer it over all others. To the other: perhaps it is not true that gold cools faster; it remains sufficiently hot when it is of the proper thickness. It can be heated so that it will not cool before the cauterization is finished. To the other: the argument is irrelevant because it argues from logic rather than from the specific nature of the thing. Or, one could say that while iron is not preferred over gold in the act of cauterization itself, it is preferred by the nature of **Mars** <term>Martis</term> <note>The planet/god associated with iron.</note> regarding the separation of parts, as shown previously. The earlier arguments of the other side, however, proceed in their own way.

### DIFFERENCE CCIX.

<margin>1</margin>
Whether the composition of other medicines can perform the action of **laxative medicines** <term>mēiciay ſolutiay</term>. 

Because **Dioscorides** <note>original: "Diaſ"</note> says that those vexed by pain in the feet or the root of **arthritis** <term>arthietice</term> should be given **wild cucumber** <note>original: "oxi elle"</note> to eat, and in this way you will purge the **sciatica** <term>sciatico</term> so well that one could hardly believe such power exists. Yet none of these ingredients is a laxative in itself, and thus he mentioned it with admiration. 

Also, a worthy **antidote** <term>ātidoto</term> of pills to be taken before food and during it: they gradually cause the ejection of food, destroy nausea and over-fullness, loosen the belly, and resolve **colic** <term>colicā</term>. 
Take: **Ginger** <term>ȝiȝi.</term> <note>original: "ziziberis"</note>, **Black Pepper** <term>pip. ni.</term>, **Long Pepper** <term>pip. lō.</term>, **Gallic Musk** <term>gallie. nerēſch.</term> <note>original: "gallie muschate"</note>, and **Peony seed** <term>ſe. peoie.</term>. Take 10 drams of each. Add **Tabasheer** <term>tabarȝe</term> <note>A silica secretion from bamboo used in medieval medicine.</note> and sugar. Make into pills. These cause one to go to the stool from two to five times, according to the quality of one's nature and strength. Yet none of the ingredients entering this composition is a laxative on its own.

Still regarding the coverage. The body is evacuated by heat when it is sufficiently made. In the **Commentary on Medicine** <note>likely referring to a commentary on Galen or Avicenna</note>, it states that a medicine acts through a similarity of its heat upon the humors. It is also said that a **purgative** <term>pharmacaria</term> <note>original: "fafacū" / "pharmacaria"</note> denotes that which loosens, but one is distinguished from others and it is more effective to compare them by heat. Therefore, they are loosened more strongly if they are applied like-to-like. Again, in the second point on loosening, heat is seen to be required. In the **Aphorisms** <note>referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates</note>, it is said that all purgative medicines are hot, as is seen in their use. For by heat, almost everything is aided; however, every specific action is indicated by its essence. For a **laxative** <term>solutivum</term> operates not by a similarity of quality, but by its substantial power. However, these emerge from simple **alteratives** <term>alterativis</term> <note>Medicines meant to change the body's condition (e.g., making it warmer) without necessarily purging it.</note> according to their kind. This is shown by the specific internal power which is implanted in things. And this is supported by the similarity of how a metal is constructed by nature and—according to **Alchemy**—by the skill of the art.

Similarly, the nature of a **scorpion** <term>scorpio</term> is produced both by nature and by art, which also generates others. One produces another. Hence **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and botanist</note> recounts that if a stone protects the "of basils" <note>original: "basilicorum"; likely referring to the herb basil</note>, scorpions are born. Furthermore, in the book *On Food*, it is said that if a pot is placed empty, they are generated very quickly in a few days; they say this of scorpions, and especially on a day when the pot has been heated in the sun. However, **Serapion** <note>An influential Arabic medical writer</note> adds that this is only so if it is empty. Also, the **Cow of Plato** <note>A reference to the "Bugonia," the ancient belief that bees could be spontaneously generated from the carcasses of oxen.</note> teaches how to construct bees from the flesh of a bull.

And **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher</note> says in Difference 60: **White Hellebore** <term>eleborus albus</term> <note>A plant used in antiquity as a violent purgative and emetic.</note> is light and purges upwards by causing vomiting; **Scammony** <term>scammonea</term> is heavy and affects the back. **Elaterium** <note>A potent purgative derived from the juice of the squirting cucumber.</note> and **Raphanus** <term>raphanus</term> <note>radish</note> act in both ways. But one can be added to others in all these cases, whether of light or heavy or moderate transformative power. If nature can construct a purgative from simple elements, art will be all the more able to do this when joined to it. But that happens when simple things are altered, even if not by the hand of art, they are combined in the required weight. 

Thus, from alteratives, a purgative can always arise. On the contrary, **Theriac** <term>tiriaca</term> <note>A famous ancient "universal" antidote and medicine made of dozens of ingredients.</note>, **Anacardium** <note>marking nut</note>, and **Pistacia** <note>original: "fistiaca"</note> are commended because they are properly composed, and especially theriac would not be purgative if constructed in a certain way. Likewise, that which is separated from its opposite does not coincide with the other, since one species does not help the other to exist. But "alterative" and "purgative" will be distinguished as opposites, as will be seen. Furthermore, nothing can act beyond its own species. For the power of an **alterative** is to alter; that of a **purgative** is to draw [humors] to itself. Therefore, a purgative cannot be produced from alteratives. 

Regarding the first point, it should be known that medicines are called purgatives in Difference 136 and 141. Indeed, I hear here of a purgative or laxative medicine of sufficient heat, though its power arises from the species which looks toward the celestial sphere <note>Medieval medicine believed a drug's "specific form" or ultimate power was granted by the influence of the heavens.</note>. This is properly called "pharmacaria" according to **Isaac** <note>likely Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician</note>, but they are "alteratives" by their own quality, either in the elementary action that moves the belly or naturally softens it, as in the softening of the limbs, such as **cassia**, **violets**, and the like; or by making the passages slippery, such as the mucilage of **psyllium** <note>original: "psilii"</note>; or by their subtle quality penetrating the pores and thinning the moisture, which causes a flow. For every medicine by its thinning nature relieves nature, even if there is no purgative power in it initially, as in those with sharpness like **Euphorbium** <note>A caustic resin from a succulent plant.</note>, although others say this dissolves more. For that which a medicine loosens is by its weight, like **myrobalans** <note>A fruit used as a mild laxative.</note>; others by loosening, like salt and sharp things or Euphorbium; others by viscosity, like honey; and some by the power of attracting humors, like **Scammony**, which specifically draws out bile. And of this **Martha** <note>Unclear reference, possibly a misreading of a source name</note> noted in Difference 161. 

Regarding the second point, it should be known that some, moved by examples...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the nature of medicines, moving from the mechanical action of laxatives to the philosophical and practical limits of alchemy and the shelf-life (durability) of medicinal compounds versus simple ingredients. It references Aristotle’s "De Anima" and "Meteorology," as well as "Metaphysics."</meta>

This purgation is through a **laxative** <term>solutivum</term> <note>original: "solutū"</note> in a slow manner, which is shown by **oxymel** <note>original: "oxiel"; a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</note> because it irritates the bowels with its sharpness and stimulates them, which aids the evacuation that follows. 

Regarding the other point, that the medicine—though it consists of sharp, biting species—encounters flatulent, viscous, or colicky humors and by its sharpness agitates, liquefies, and dissolves them. But there it is found that it expels any bite <note>original: "morsã"; referring to stinging or sharp pains</note> because it occurred before and not through those things which flow together from another laxative, as indicated in that passage. Furthermore, it is evacuated by sufficient pharmacological means. It is also found that watery medicine induces or constricts a flux, but that which was beginning is disposed toward it. Hence, in the third book of the **Basilicum** <note>likely referring to a "Royal" medical compendium or the "Canon" of Avicenna</note>, it is noted that it constricts, but if it finds it already prepared, it loosens. But it is a wonder how such a small dose can operate in such a way. Hence, a corruption fell into the written text, and the numbers were multiplied.

To the other point, that when pharmacological means are not sufficient for a **laxative** <term>solutivum</term>, but rather for an **alterative** <term>alterativam</term> <note>a medicine that changes the body's condition rather than purging it</note> according to the **Commentary**, they draw the heat of the humor to the skin, dissolving it into a vapor which at last is resolved into the air, specifically when it has been made subtle. This is seen from those things which are submitted to purgations through which a laxative is sent, and in clysters, sweats, and vomits. For a fivefold method of evacuation was touched upon. Nor was the pharmacology here for a laxative method, but rather for one that acts through alteration. To the other point, that while an alteration is present through heat, the power of loosening cannot be absent, as was shown. For it co-aids with the principal attraction by itself, or it does not stand as sufficient. For this is approved by the fact that in water, the power of congealing is not given, but rather it pertains to water as something similar. Chapter 178: it is not the same thing, because an alterative differs greatly from a laxative; for the simple constructive things differ from the power which exists in them, especially since both of its natures are more of an alterative kind. Furthermore, this power of a **Theriac** <term>theriaca</term> <note>original: "tiāca"; a famous ancient polypharmaceutical compound used as an antidote</note> endures for 10 or 20 years. Chapter 178: An alterative medicine, however, cannot last for such a time, as is seen in troches or pills, unless opium or other things are preserved within it. These would, however, impede the power of loosening. 

Regarding the confirmation, it is said that **metal** <note>original: "metallū"</note> cannot be made by art from another, but only transmuted, since art only effects a permutation in **accidents** <term>accidentibus</term> <note>surface qualities like color or hardness</note> and not in **substance** <term>substantia</term>; hence perhaps that possibility is unknown. Hence, the third book of **On the Soul** <note>Aristotle's "De Anima"</note> says of the artifacts of metals that they are possible to be, but they were causes of unknown things, such as in **Alchemy**. And even if it were perhaps established, this would be more by accident and divine inspiration than by the wisdom of art, as was said of the property of Theriac in Chapter 121. For art cannot arrive at a point where the agent knows how to proportion the matter with time so that a new metal is established. If it should appear to be so, it will be because art is a deceiver and cannot by any ingenuity detect nature. Hence, I do not think gold or silver constructed by art is the same as that produced by nature from the depths; but one cannot show its deception to the art. Faithful men have experienced that agents can be made through art by decoction, but they do not truly appear to profit all men who use the experiment. 

It is also not similar because one of the metals agrees more with another, since they have a greater possibility of alteration in the matter which is native to that medicine. For there exists a more formal way in which it undergoes passion, and therefore one is more distinct from another. Finally, the **Alchemists** say that all metals can meet in one liquid matter, in which each is compared to the other, just as through that which they lead by purification into a more noble metal, and from those bodies through regimen and medicine, health is attained. 

Regarding the generation of **scorpions** or **bees**: the first of these is not similar, since it is necessary that the matter from which they are generated must putrefy and extend to its own proper matter, which does not happen here. This could happen if the sharp heat of the alteratives caused putrefaction toward the essence and proper matter. To the other point: see chapter 60. To the other point, that it cannot generate a laxative from simples, since that is the proper matter of generation in which a more celestial cause of generation exists, and not from simples compounded by art, since there is no matter from which nature could work with them while the actual power remains.

## THE DISTINCTION <note>original: "DIFFERENTIA"</note>

¶ That compounds last longer than simples is shown here. For **Theriac** <term>theriaca</term> is a medicine of a more compound nature than others, even lasting thirty years for the rejuvenation of youth, according to the diversity of regions, as touched upon in Chapter 178. However, none of the simples is found to last beyond these years. Furthermore, since a thing needs to be as it is. For nature is similar in the disposition of the entity in act and in power, as seen in **Metaphysics** II; it acts more strongly than simples, as seen in Chapter 143, which is more strongly for well-being. Again, since art intends to follow nature, as it happens in the natural and in art. But in those things which are not durable, they were compounds, such as those things generated through seed or sperm from which they are produced. Also, things are more united and powerful and persistent through a genus than through diverse multiplied things. Therefore, compounds are more durable than simples. 

On the contrary, because in the second book of **Causes** <note>likely "Liber de Causis"</note>, every power lasts up to three years; two years for others, and they do not remain for a longer time, and therefore herbs are excluded, which ought to last two or three years; whereas minerals and stones remain for a long duration. No compound, either by itself or through itself, remains for such a long time as will be declared. Likewise, if simples are placed before compounds, they are constructed from them, but those which are compounded from them also persist for a longer period, since they are greater than them; and their time follows their magnitude. **Commentary** on **Generation and Corruption**: Simples therefore persist longer than compounds. 

Regarding the first point, it should be known that duration in time consists of the constancy of vigor. For thus vegetables are said to endure and live when they are strong in act. Here, a simple medicine is one produced by nature alone. A compound, however, is one constructed from simples by art, which mixes many into a nature, applying them to one another. Hence, simple is twofold: one which is simple according to nature, like an element; the other according to art, like a single medicine. Similarly, by opposition, a compound is twofold. Know that simples and compounds endure for a longer or shorter time for multiple reasons. For those things which are cold and dry, being simpler, are less exposed to putrefaction and resolution, and they persist for a longer time without life, as touched on in Chapter 21. Those which are hot and moist are more exposed to putrefaction; and those which are hot and dry, to resolution. Cold and moist things, as seen in Chapter 138, are more dull and fail more quickly. Those which have hard, compact substances, with bitter, stiptic, and harsh tastes, are more durable than their opposites, as minerals and juices show. For soft, watery things do not persist for long, such as fuchsias <note>likely "fucosities" or surface dyes/washes</note>, unless constructed by art and decoction; likewise leaves, roots, and stalks, unless they are very moist. Those soft things, however, are drier and harder, and consist in others in their own way. Similarly, those things which are of a larger quantity putrefy less, as is seen in the opposite. Hence, in the fourth book of **Meteorology** <note>Aristotle</note>: much putrefies less than a little. For in a larger thing, there is more heat. Furthermore, those things exposed to the air and to agitation are more subject to continuous alteration and resolution, and specifically soft things are preserved from corruption. <meta>This page concludes the "Conciliator," continuing the discussion on the shelf-life and "vigor" of various pharmaceutical preparations. It specifically addresses the shelf-life of theriac, syrups, and ointments, comparing the practices of "modern" apothecaries to ancient authorities like Serapion and Haly Abbas. The text concludes with a formal colophon detailing the printing information for the 1472 Mantua edition.</meta>

...frequent and lacking, although they are also made incorruptible by certain powers when they are prepared on the Sabbath, and likewise those which have their own seasonal properties. This is because the way is moved and putrefies, which are otherwise full and immobile. However, this contradicts what is said in the fourth book of the **Meteorology** <note>Aristotle’s treatise on the elements and physical change</note>, concerning which many things were touched upon in the twenty-second [section]. And when some simple or **compound** <term>composita</term> <note>medicines made of multiple ingredients</note> ingredients are mixed, it is sufficient to use honey, either added directly or cooked for a long time. For this reason, those wishing to make **compounds** <term>composita</term> more durable construct them with honey and not sugar, because all things prepared with honey are more lasting. Even those things which are kept in the sun for a long time endure with more vigor than those kept in other places, which indicates a difference in their age. Also, those things collected in the summer and in dry times, in the north wind and under a dry moon, endure longer than their opposites because they possess less moisture.

Likewise, those whose substance or matter is fatty, homogeneous, and uniform endure longer than others. Regarding the second point: according to the author, simple and compound medicines endure for many years, perhaps up to four. For the continuity of their permanence cannot be assigned a literal hour because of the aforementioned reasons. Furthermore, Serapion and Haly Abbas <note>Haly Abbas (930–994 AD) was a famous Persian physician</note> treat the durability of **compounds** <term>composita</term> more specifically and carefully with great authority. For it is said that the vigorous permanence of many compounds, such as **theriac** <term>tyriaca</term> <note>original: "triaca"; a famous universal antidote and panacea containing dozens of ingredients</note>, lasts up to thirty years and even longer if it is constructed with honey; and especially if opium is present, it endures for a longer time—say five or seven years—if it is mixed with sugar and without sun. But properly prepared medicines that are cooked do not last seven years when they are sold in the shops under various conditions.

Moreover, those things of large quantity that are compressed and less exposed to the air endure longer, provided that the mouths of the liquid vessels are filled with honey or oil so that the movement of the air and the entrance of corruption cannot occur. Those that are of smaller movement endure for a short time, such as **troches** <term>trocisci</term> <note>medicinal lozenges or disks</note> and **pills** <term>pilulae</term>, lasting perhaps three or five months, in which they differ from what Serapion and Haly Abbas say. And therefore it is better, as is customary, for the mass of these things to be stored in their entirety. Those which are prepared for the sake of the beginning <note>perhaps referring to initial fermentation or mixing</note> endure for a shorter time, such as for two months or thereabouts. For as long as the body is lessened, the vigor is also consolidated (Canon, Book II, Fen III). They endure until they begin to grow rancid and lose their odor.

But only **balsam** <note>original: "balsamũ"</note>, **opobalsam** <note>the resin of the balsam tree</note>, and **camphor** water: the older they are, the more excellent they become. **Plasters** <term>emplastra</term>, **ointments** <term>unguenta</term>, and similar things endure for years. Syrups, however, it is said can last two or five years, and up to four years because they are excellently constructed and thickened by cooking. Among our **modern apothecaries** <term>apotecarios</term>, they hardly last one or two years. Whence it is said: the medicine of the ancients was a science that either had great strength or was made fortuitously; yet in those years it possessed no change in quality of taste, smell, or color. And this is what Haly Abbas says: it was durable until the power failed. 

Note that those things which are compounded with one another—and specifically those with honey—do not work immediately upon being constructed, but require a "delay" <note>original: "mora"; a period of maturation</note> in the interval, during which action and passion concur so that they may fall into a single nature. Whence it is said that they need a delay before use so that they may act and react upon one another in various ways, and thus the whole becomes perfected within itself. Therefore, we use **compounds** <term>composita</term> when they have aged, and they begin to be effective at least six months after they are made, so that they are unified into one and the narcotic malice is put to sleep. Some take one or two months to be attributed to this process. Thus, syrups and similar things are perfected after their preparation, so that from the day of their construction they need two [months].

And consequently, all letters, ointments, and others endure. Pills and troches, however, last at least four to seven years if kept in an appropriate place. Thus, the time of permanence for compounds briefly appears. But regarding the aforementioned, a doubt arises because Dioscorides says that both white and black [hellebore] can last only one year. To which the opposite is said by the aforementioned authorities: that it lasts not only two or three years, but even longer. This is because their substance is subtle and they dissolve easily, yet they are more violent in modern bodies and are harmful, as was touched upon; therefore, from one year onwards they weaken until the end of their activity in us, even though they might endure for a long time as a substance, as was said concerning the thirty-year duration.

It should be known that all things prepared with many **simples** <term>simplicia</term> <note>single-ingredient drugs</note> are more durable than compounds. This is shown by the discourse of experience and reason alike. For permanence is through the essence; for it is that which gives being and duration. That which is more perfect can better receive duration. But this is the nature of **simples**, whereas **compounds** are artificial. Nature is more perfect than art because its principle is intrinsic, while the other is extrinsic. Again, it is said that whatever diminishes the body diminishes its vigor; compounds are diminished more laboriously and through necessity than simples. And thus the cause of corruption and the lack of permanence is heterogeneity; for no simple is corrupted in its permanence except by accident. Therefore, artificial things constructed from many parts are more exposed to the opposite of nature than simples, which are homogeneous, while compounds are heterogeneous.

Furthermore, those things endure less in which the active and corruptive properties are balanced; but this is the case in compounds, whereas in a simple, there is a single nature. Therefore, simples endure for a better and longer time than compounds. To the first point, it is said that theriac and honey endure longer, not because of the uniformity of the compounds, but because of one maximum simple ingredient, such as opium, and thus the intent of the compound is achieved or verified. To the other, it is said that it is not necessary for something to be more durable just because it is stronger or more vigorous; for agents like fire or spiritual things are stronger in their essence but have less life or permanence, as is seen in many cases.

To the final point, it is said that although simples and components are more durable than compounds, such as theriac, the vigor in compounds is compacted together, though not because of the unity of their joining, but rather because it is hidden as in a simple. For the many parts of a compound are not joined by nature but by art. For it is the action of the elements that approaches nature, and it cannot reach a natural and true mixing through art. Of which clearly we may be able to enjoy the benefit hereafter.

<margin>👉</margin> **TO THE MOST REVEREND** Father in Christ and Lord, Lord N. <note>historically identified as Pope Nicholas IV, though Peter served several popes</note>, by divine providence Supreme Pontiff. Peter of Abano, the least of physicians, with devotion intends to fulfill both your request and my duty to provide, according to my ability, a useful and brief treatise on poisons to your Holiness, both for the benefit of the body and for the advancement of knowledge. First, I shall make a division of poisons; for whatever parts divide a whole are better known to us. Second, I will resolve each member of the division down to individual terms; for the knowledge of any thing is completed by descending from the most general to the most specific. Third, I will describe the way in which poison kills and causes harm to the human body. For from this, the knowledge of the cure is hunted out in the art of medicine. Fourth, I will speak on the safeguard and caution so that poisons are not administered, or if administered, do not harm. Safeguard...

<meta>This page continues the introductory goals of the treatise and begins the first chapter, which categorizes poisons by their origin (mineral, vegetable, animal) and their mode of action (physical qualities vs. occult properties).</meta>

...for the art is indeed curative and protective. Fifth, I shall set forth the signs and cures for whatever poison has been consumed and for the harms introduced by it. Sixth and finally, I shall describe the <term>bezoartic</term> <note>original: "bezoarticas"; referring to substances that act as universal antidotes</note> virtues—that is, those that liberate from death—which act through an occult and divine power rather than through their <term>complexion</term> <note>the specific balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> or nature, according to each poison. And with this, I shall resolve two very difficult questions: the first will be concerning the "Great Theriac," <note>a famous ancient poly-pharmaceutical antidote</note> whether it acts as a bezoar or a medicine for any specific poison. And the second will be whether any poison can be drunk that is timed to kill at a certain future point, so that the person dies at that time and not before.

# CHAPTER 1.

->On the division of poisons.<-

¶ Because poison is the opposite of the food of our body, just as food itself is made into a part of our body and assimilates itself entirely to our nature—taking the place of the parts that have dissolved—so too does poison draw and convert our body (or the part to which it is applied) toward its own poisonous nature, and finally assimilates the body to itself. Just as animals and things growing from the earth (whose nature converts food into the species of the nourished) are converted into our nourishment and species when eaten by us, so too whatever bodies are joined with poison, if they are eaten by us, they transform our bodies into poison. For every active agent is more powerful than the thing it acts upon; thus our substance, as the "passive" element, passes into the presence of the poison, which acts as the "active" element, just as straw subjected to fire turns into fire. For fire is entirely active toward the straw. Therefore, the wise among physicians have said that poison belongs to the class of things that infect and destroy the **complexion** and **composition**, and sometimes induce a "solution of continuity" <note>a physical rupture or wound in the tissues</note>, so that the illnesses which happen because of poisons are of general types rather than specific ones.

Poison is divided in three ways. In the first way, the division of the genus into species is considered. According to this, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian physician</note> and Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd</note> said that one type of poison is **mineral**, another is **vegetable**, and another is **animal**. 

From the **minerals**, there are those generated under the earth that have a ruinous nature, such as quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, gypsum, copper, and certain stones like the magnet and unwashed Armenian stone, burnt lead, arsenic, realgar <note>arsenic sulfide</note>, white lead <term>ceruse</term>, and many others of which we shall speak specifically below. 

From the **vegetables**, there are those plants whose natures are most contrary to food, such that they are not suited to be converted into nourishment for the species, but are instead ready to convert the body, such as hellebore, black turbith, <term>napellus</term> <note>monkshood or aconite</note> and the gum of monkshood, certain fungi and truffles, "widow-maker," mezereon, oleander, "laughter-parsley" <note>original: "apiū risus"; likely the Sardinian water dropwort which causes a sardonic grin</note> and many others of which we shall speak specifically. 

From the **animals**, poisonous things are all those whose nature is furthest removed from the human complexion, or is opposed and hostile to the species. These include serpents, dragons, venomous beasts, vipers, the sea-hare, and meats that are roasted and then immediately suffocated <note>likely referring to spoiled or improperly prepared meat</note>, cold fish, the flesh of animals that died naturally, putrid meat, those struck and killed by lightning, and whatever animals are suffering from rabies, and many others which will be mentioned specifically below.

In the **second way**, poison is considered in relation to us. According to this, they say one poison is **taken inside the body**, and another is **outside**. That which is taken inside is of the nature of ruinous potions given under the appearance of food, drink, or medicine; and this is what happens most often, against which kings, prelates, and those with enemies must be on guard. That which is outside is said to be from the bites of reptiles, or through sight, hearing, taste, touch, or smell. 

By **sight**, just as the basilisk poisons. By **hearing**, as a certain serpent in Nubia poisons, which is as thick as two palms, having a sharp head and being green in color, which is called the *regulus* <note>the "little king"</note>; for by its hissing, it kills the birds and animals that hear it. By **taste** as well, such as the "deaf asp" which kills those it touches with its spit, or the *tirus* and the viper which kill those they bite. By **touch**, like the serpent which a soldier (of whom Avicenna speaks) killed with a lance; from the contact of the lance, the soldier's hand and his whole body were killed. It is also like the fish called the "numbing-fish" <note>the Torpedo or electric ray</note>, of which Galen says that while it enters the fisherman's net, the hands and arms become so numbed that they are rendered insensible. By **smell**, as certain ruinous mushrooms of which Rhasis <note>the Persian physician Al-Razi</note> says that when they are pulled from the earth and smelled, they kill the one smelling them.

In the **third way**, poison is considered according to its **specific difference**, which distinguishes one species from another. According to this, all physicians and natural philosophers have said that one poison is that which performs its work by its **quality** (that is, its complexion), and another is that which does the same by a **virtue** flowing from its **entire species**, which physicians call the **specific form**. This is nothing other than the merit which each thing composed of the four elements (according to the greater or lesser proportion of those elements in the compound) receives strongly or weakly from the influence of the fixed stars, which look upon the species of inferior compounds according to how the matter of those things was prepared. According to this, the virtues of the stars come down to the lower world by means of pyramidal and straight lines which are formed in the light of those stars; this light, brought from the stars through diverse lines, carries the **specific virtues** which it leaves in the compounds according to what the components deserved. 

And this is what Avicenna rightly said in his *Canon*: that such a "specific form" comes to things *after* the primary complexion of the elements in the compound. And because we are ignorant—and shall be ignorant forever—of the exact quantities and weights of the elements in these compounds, it is necessary to be ignorant of such incoming specific forms. We cannot know more about them than what human **experience** provides. Therefore, in such matters, experienced physicians contribute more than those who rely only on reason, as Aristotle well says in the beginning of the *Metaphysics*. 

Poison, therefore, which performs its work by **quality alone**, varies according to the diversity of the qualities: for one is hot, another cold, another dry, and another moist. The **hot** poison kills in two ways: either by heating until it corrodes the interior when taken in, all the way to the heart and beyond...

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on how poisons act by transforming the body into their own nature. It completes the classification of poisons by their primary qualities (hot, cold, dry, moist) and then begins Chapter II, which examines specific mineral poisons in detail.</meta>

applied even to the marrow of the bone, and thus it kills by dissolving the continuity of the tissues, such as the <term>sea hare</term> <note>original: "lepus marinus"; a marine mollusk (Aplysia) believed in antiquity to be a deadly poison if touched or eaten</note>; or by heating, it causes inflammation both inside and out, reaching all the way to the heart, and thus it kills the <unclear>life</unclear> of the heart by suspending it through inflammation—and this is like <term>euphorbia</term> <note>a caustic plant resin</note> and <term>hellebore</term>. A cold poison likewise kills in two ways: either by stupefying [the body] because of its extreme coldness until the heart is rendered immobile—and this is such as <term>opium</term>—or by obstructing the pathways of breath and closing them so that they almost cannot breathe, and the breath is taken away from the heart—and this is such as <term>burnt lead</term>. A dry poison, however, kills in two ways: either by consuming the moisture of the blood of the heart and turning it into a crust—and this is such as <term>unslaked lime</term> and <term>colcothar</term> <note>original: "colcotar"; iron oxide, often a byproduct of making sulfuric acid</note>—or by separating part from part until all members down to the heart are dissolved into the smallest pieces (not liquified, but broken apart)—and this is done by something like <term>realgar</term> <note>arsenic sulfide</note>. As for a "moist poison," it is said that such a thing is not found, because moisture does not reach the fourth degree <note>in medieval medicine, qualities like hot or cold were ranked 1 to 4; the fourth degree was considered potentially fatal</note>, and the fourth degree renders a quality poisonous because it is corruptive and mortal. But <term>Galen</term> <note>original: "G."; the famous 2nd-century Greek physician</note> tells of a certain man whom a serpent bit while he was asleep; when he woke up, unable to rise, he was pulled by the hand and his flesh remained behind, corrupted and putrefied upon the earth, and his bones appeared stripped bare. From this hidden putrefaction and easy dissolution of the flesh, Galen proves that a poison can be "moist." According to some, <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum" (living silver)</note> seems to be of this kind of poison, which he admits is moist only in the third degree. But poison that kills by its "total species"—dissolving the power of the soul or by its whole substance or specific form—kills not because it is hot, nor cold, nor dry, nor moist, but because it is "such a thing"—that is, because it possesses a power opposite to human life and health. And this poison, in whatever small quantity it is taken (even so that it escapes the internal senses), kills by multiplying itself; for whatever moisture of our body it finds, it immediately converts into poison, and this by the power of its species. Such a thing is <term>aconite</term> <note>original: "napellus"; also known as monkshood or wolfsbane</note>.

# CHAPTER II.
## On each poison in particular.

We shall speak only of the known and famous poisons of minerals, plants, and animals, lest by describing hidden things we might "add venom to the snakes." <note>a classical idiom meaning to make a bad situation worse</note> These things are written for this reason alone: so that harms, being foreseen, may hurt less or never hurt at all; they are not written so that we may teach how to harm others. Therefore, some mineral poisons are from nature, and some are procured by art. Those from nature are those generated in the belly of the earth. One of these is **mercury**, which if taken internally sometimes kills by its moisture, causing the natural moisture of the heart to putrefy; sometimes, however, it kills by its actual coldness, congealing the heart. <margin>//</margin> A sign of this is a certain apothecary who, when he was thirsty during a night in a time of great heat, found a flask full of mercury while searching [for water]; he drank it, and in the morning he was found dead. When they found the mercury exiting his anus, he was anatomized <note>dissected</note>, and the blood around the heart was found clotted and the heart itself was cracked. They found almost one pound of mercury in his stomach. Another kind is the **mercury**

which is made by art, <term>sublimated</term> with egg white in an <term>aludel</term> <note>original: "alutel"; a pear-shaped ceramic pot used in alchemical sublimation</note>, which is a vessel of the alchemists; and this is worse and more pernicious than the natural kind. For the mineral kind often passes through the belly or is removed by a clyster <note>an enema</note>, but the sublimated kind, when taken internally, corrodes the intestines, causes the heart to swell, retains the urine so its exit is prohibited, and the person dies. Mercury is also "extinguished" by a strong mixture of human saliva until it disappears; if you throw boiling water upon it and it returns to its first state, it was not extinguished. This is even worse than pure mercury and less evil than the sublimated kind. The **second poison** which is from the nature of the mine is **gypsum**; when taken internally, it congeals the blood with its coldness, thickens the spirits, and induces difficulty in breathing, after which the person dies. This happens when it is given raw and ground up in a drink; when cooked, however, it is not a poison but a very <term>styptic</term> <note>astringent/blood-clotting</note> medicine. It is born in the veins of mountainous earth. The **third** is **copper**, which has a metallic nature composed of mercury and burning sulfur brought to a red form; when it is struck and hammered by smiths, the scales that fall off, if given in a drink, are poisonous and cause the belly to purge strongly—and doctors call this **copper dross** <note>original: "tubel eris"</note>. From this also, if wine is stored in a vessel of brass, copper, or <term>electrum</term> <note>an alloy of gold and silver</note> and then drunk, it causes vomiting. The **third** <note>the author repeats "third"</note> is the **dross of rusty iron** and the rust itself, which if taken internally dries out the moisture and the body by adhering to the intestines; they induce old age and a certain sickness which doctors call **marasmus** <note>a wasting away of the body</note>. Doctors, however, use consolidated iron dross in the cure of many illnesses. The **fourth** is the **magnet stone** <note>lodestone</note>, which if taken internally makes the recipient melancholic, lunatic, and "bewitched" <note>original: "pistrigiatum"; likely meaning suffering from hallucinations or delusions</note>. Doctors, however, use it consolidated with other medicines in the treatment of melancholy. This stone is of two species. One is that which draws iron, turning it toward the North pole, where the mine of the magnet is said to be. The other is that which draws human flesh, turning the draw toward the South pole, where its mine is said to be. This stone, ground and given in a drink, contracts the viscera and turns them into a ball. The **fifth** is the **Armenian stone** <note>azurite</note>, which is red; if taken internally without being washed according to the teaching of doctors, it is a poisonous emetic that subverts the entire body. When prepared, however, doctors use it in the cure of the melancholic passion. The **fifth** <note>repeated numbering</note> is the **starry stone** which doctors call **lapis lazuli**; if it has not been washed and is given in a drink, it subverts the stomach and causes pain in the intestines; doctors use it against quartan fever. The **sixth** is **arsenic** or **orpiment**, which is a species of gypsum as **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, the famous 13th-century polymath</note> says; because of its heat, dryness, and pernicious nature, it is a most evil poison, causing putrefaction and being highly mortifying. But if it is sublimated according to alchemy in an "abathel" vessel <note>another term for a sublimation vessel</note>, it is the most evil of all.

poison taken internally; and if it is frequently **sublimated** <note>Sublimation is a chemical process where a solid turns into gas and back to solid, used here to purify or concentrate a substance.</note>, it becomes very white and an even more potent poison. There are also poisons made by human art, such as **litharge** <note>Lead oxide</note>, which is made from lead melted in a pot with crushed oyster shells; if taken internally, it causes such great constipation of the intestines that one can almost never evacuate, and things that are usually expelled through the bowels are instead cast out through vomiting. There is also **ceruse** <note>White lead, often used as a pigment</note>, which is collected from lead plates placed over vinegar; due to its coldness and dryness, if taken internally, it causes paralysis and contractions. There is also **chalcanthum** <note>original: "calcecumenon"; likely a form of copper sulfate or verdigris</note>, which is green copper made from copper plates exposed to vinegar; it is a corrosive and deadly poison. There is also **burnt lead**, made from sulfur and **orpiment** <note>original: "auripigmento"; arsenic trisulfide</note>, which is a poison that obstructs the breath and kills by suffocation. There is also **Water** made from **lapis lazuli**, which is a drying poison. There is also **realgar** <note>Arsenic sulfide</note>, which is made from sulfur and lead, existing as a corrosive poison when taken internally.

Among **vegetable poisons**, some are the juices of herbs, some the fruits of trees, and some their seeds. Of the juices, there are: **hemlock**; the juice of **spurges**; the juice of **squirting cucumber**; the juice of **usnea** <note>a type of lichen</note>; the juice of *bothormarien* <note>likely an Arabic-derived name for a toxic plant, possibly a variety of chamomile or daisy used in excess</note>; the juice of **coriander**; the juice of **mandrake**; and the juice of the **black poppy**, from which **opium** is made. There is also the juice of the **milky bindweed**, from which **scammony** <note>a harsh purgative resin</note> is made; the juice of the **sardonic herb** <note>original: "apii risus"; literally "laughter parsley," a plant said to cause fatal muscle contractions resembling a grin</note>; the juice of **chervil**; the juice of **sunflower** <note>original: "giraffolis"</note>; the juice of **monkshood** <note>original: "napelli"</note>; the juice of **oleander**; the juice of **mezereon** <note>Paradise plant</note>; and the juice of **black hellebore**. There is also the juice of **white vine** <note>original: "asseffite"</note> and the juice of **bryony** (that is, the **wild gourd**). Of the fruits, there are: **oleander pods**; the pods of the **bedeguar** <note>rose gall</note>; **cashew nuts** <note>original: "anacardi"</note>; **rancid hazelnuts**; **nux vomica** <note>the source of strychnine</note>; **colocynth** <note>bitter apple</note> that grows solitary on its vine; **Pharaoh’s figs**; and **mandrake apples**. Of the seeds, there are: **henbane**; **spurge laurel**; **rancid laurel berries**; **caper spurge**; **nettle seed**; **black poppy seed**; **hellebore seed**; **hemlock seed**; **moist coriander seed**; and the seed of **snakeweed**. All of these, if eaten or drunk, either kill in the ways described above or weaken and alter the body.

Among **animal poisons**, some come from their brains, some from their tails, some from their blood, some from their saliva and spit, some from their gallbladders, and some from their whole bodies. In the **brain of a cat**, there is a pernicious poison that makes a man lose his mind; the same is true of the **bat’s brain**. In the **tail of a deer**, there is a most wretched poison, which is why hunters cut off the tip of the deer's tail when they wish to eat it. Similarly, poison is found in the **tail of the scorpion**, the **spider** <note>original: "rutele"</note>, the **wasp**, the **bee**, and among **hoofed animals** and certain **serpents**. In the **blood**, it is found in the blood of an **old ox**, the blood of a **toad** (and its spit), the blood of a **furious red ox** in a state of rage, in **menstrual blood**, and in the blood of a **leper**. Regarding **spit** or **saliva**, that of a **fasting man** is poisonous, 

not to humans, but to the scorpion and the serpent. It is also found in the **spit of a toad**, and the **saliva of a viper**—which, when it wishes to mate with a fish, deposits its poison on a certain stone on the shore, then returns to collect its poison again. It is also in the **saliva and foam of a rabid dog**, and the **saliva of a cat, monkey, and mouse**, and the **saliva of a fasting man** when they bite. Of the **gallbladders**, such is the **gall of a leopard**, which is a poison that kills immediately by its specific form. Of the **whole body**, such are **cantharides** <note>Spanish fly</note> and the **salamander**. Regarding all of these, the sum of the matter is that the poison kills either by its quality or its species.

### CHAPTER III.

->Regarding the knowledge of the manner in<-
->which poison kills or harms.<-

**E**very poison, insofar as it is a poison, has a quality opposite to our body. This opposition creates a great doubt: how and by what path does the poison pass to the human heart? For either the poison is drawn to the heart like iron to a magnet, or it travels to the heart by itself, or it happens in both ways (that is, the heart attracting and the poison running toward it). If it is none of these ways, it would have to be asserted that the poison cannot reach the heart at all, and thus the opposition of the poison to the heart would cease. In that case, we would say that poison is not destructive to the heart—the opposite of which we see to be true. For when a deadly poison like **monkshood** <note>original: "napellus"</note> is taken, **syncope** <note>fainting</note> appears immediately, which is a suffering of the heart, along with **tremors of the heart**, failure of the pulse, and all the accidents of **cardiac distress**. Therefore, it must be understood that while the heart is healthy, like the other members, it attracts nothing except blood similar to itself and **spirit** <note>In medieval medicine, "spirit" (spiritus) was a subtle substance that carried life and sensation through the body.</note>, one of which it stores in the right ventricle and the other in the left. But when it is sick, it draws to itself a contrary quality to its own harm—just as something that is overheated attracts cold air and cold blood to itself. This it does through the **natural power** of attracting its like while it is within the power of nature, and through the **sensitive animal appetite** by which every injured limb seeks delight and to feel what is suitable, yet [accidentally] draws in the contrary which harms it. Thus, since poison shares nothing with the complexion of the heart, the heart does not attract it while it is healthy; rather, it flees from it as an opposite enemy. But when the heart is weakened, it would seek and draw in the opposite of its suffering through the sensitive appetite. It is in this way that **poison is cured by poison**. For when someone has taken a poison—say, **opium**, which kills by cooling the body all the way to the heart and then coagulating the heart's blood—before the heart is deprived of sensation, feeling the harm from the coldness of the opium, it desires a hot medicine. If **castoreum** <note>A pungent substance secreted by beavers, considered a "hot" medicine.</note> is given, which is itself in the category of poisons, the heart will attract that castoreum by means of its sensitive appetite—not as a poison opposite to the heart's substance, but as an opposite to the [cold] quality...

<summary>This page catalogs various mineral, vegetable, and animal poisons before explaining the physiological theory of how toxins reach the heart, notably suggesting that a "sick" heart may accidentally attract poison while trying to heal itself.</summary>
