<meta>This page continues the discussion of how poisons affect the body, moving from a list of specific substances to a theoretical debate on whether the heart "attracts" poison or if poison spreads through a process of transformation and multiplication. It also explores environmental toxins and individual susceptibility based on temperament.</meta>

...wrongly introduced through opium. This reasoning, however, shows no more than that the heart attracts poison to itself unless every diseased limb draws to itself an opposing quality. Furthermore, granted that when the heart feels the harm of a "cold" poison, it might, by the power of its sensitive appetite, desire a "warm" medicine and draw it to itself; the question still remains how that first poison given passes to the heart. Therefore, it seems it should be said that in no way does the heart ever draw poison to itself. This is because poison is neither like the heart (having no similarity to it), nor is it drawn as an opposite (since the heart was never of such a disposition as poison is). 

You cannot infer from this that there is no opposition between the heart and poison. For although the heart does not "draw" the poison, and although the poison does not "run" to it, there is another way in which direct opposition and manifest destruction appear. For poison—being active because of its ruinous form and destructive to the heart—converts whatever it touches in the human body into its own poisonous species. It multiplies itself by infecting the fluids of our body into a poisonous nature; once multiplied, the power of the poison increases. For it is said in geometry that a doubled quantity increases the power; thus, from a small amount of poison consumed, by converting what it touches into something like itself, its power is increased and multiplied. 

In this way, as if through a continuous body where the ends touch, a small quantity of poison reaches the heart itself. When it touches the heart, it converts it also into poison. From this, the **vital spirit** <note>The "vital spirit" was believed to be a refined substance produced in the heart that carried life and heat through the arteries.</note>, no longer having a proper organ in which to reside, yields to the form of the poison. Departing from the heart, it leaves the heart and the body without motion—and this is death. The sign of this is that if the resulting corpse is eaten, it acts as a poison to the eater.

It must still be known, however, that the arteries and the ventricles of the heart, by their motion of <term>diastole</term> <note>original: "dyastoles"; the expansion of the heart and arteries</note> and <term>systole</term> <note>original: "systoles"; the contraction of the heart and arteries</note>—that is, by the natural motion of attracting and expelling which they perform continually as long as the animal lives—draw in the surrounding spirit <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to the air or vital breath</note>. Thus, even the arteries that terminate at the skin draw the external air surrounding us through their pores all the way to the heart; and through these same paths, the heart expels heat and fumes by breathing out. 

If the air surrounding us is poisonous and pestilential, it is drawn in by the motion of expansion through these arteries and infects the heart, from which pestilential illnesses arise. This is not because the artery or the heart draws poison by its own nature, but because a poisonous vapor enters under the guise of air and attracted spirit. According to this, the wise men have said that it is poison to sleep or stay under a **walnut tree** <note>original: "arbore nucum"; medieval folklore often claimed the shade of the walnut tree was toxic</note>, or in cabbage gardens, or under the shade of an oleander, or to bathe in waters where oleander and poisonous trees grow along the banks. 

For **Galen** <note>original: "G."; a prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> tells of a certain man who bathed in a bath heated with wood cut from the dens of serpents; he died from the vapor of the wood, which was infected with the poison of the serpents. And **Avicenna** <note>A 11th-century Persian physician and philosopher</note> says in his book *On the Properties of the Elements and Planets* that in the time of King Philip, all merchants passing along a certain road leading to a city would immediately die when they reached a part of the road between two mountains. Then **Socrates** <note>The text here attributes a legendary story to the philosopher Socrates, often involving his use of a mirror or glass to defeat a basilisk or serpent</note> had a glass cage prepared; entering it, he ordered himself to be carried there. He looked out and saw two serpents—one on one mountain and another on the other—which were infecting the air of that place, causing those passing by to die. 

**Rufus** <note>Likely Rufus of Ephesus, a Greek physician</note> also says that ancient kings had a girl nourished on <term>aconite</term> <note>original: "napello"; also known as monkshood or wolfsbane</note> so that those copulating with her or receiving her breath and embrace would die. Similarly, people are poisoned in the bilges of ships, in deep caverns, in uninhabited places, and in foul-smelling places because of the air they breathe. 

Indeed, Avicenna says in the first chapter that nothing is more an enemy to the innate heat and the heart than a great stench, from which the vital spirit suddenly retreats from the heart. The warmer and more porous a person’s heart and arteries are, the more quickly poison—whether drunk or breathed—destroys and kills them. This is because a warm heart attracts more breath than a cold one, and the pathways in the arteries of a warm heart are wider. 

Thus, **henbane** <note>original: "iusquiamus"</note> does not kill sparrows because of the narrowness of the passages to their hearts. In humans, however, it does, because they have wider paths through which the passage of poisoned spirit is easier. Furthermore, the warmer a poison is in its own temperament, the worse its effect when given to a warmer man, because the heat of both aids in a single effect. But when given to a colder nature, the poison's effect is delayed. 

Nevertheless, natural heat could be so great that it might overcome and repel even a warm poison, preventing harm or death. This is why, among many people poisoned by the same food and in the same quantity at the same dinner, one person dies, another escapes, and another loses his skin or falls ill. For example, I once saw at a certain dinner four people who had been poisoned, each eating from a poisoned dish. One died immediately; another escaped entirely; the remaining two were sick unto death. The one who escaped was courageous and had a "warm" heart. The one who died was of a less warm temperament. Those who were sick were naturally warmer than the one who passed away, but less so than the one who escaped. 

This can only be because the innate heat, which moves toward the form of life, resists accidental heat—whether from fever, warm poison, pestilential air, or the heat of the **dog days** <note>original: "diey canicularium"; the hottest days of summer, associated with the star Sirius</note>—all of which move toward the alteration and dissolution of the body's composition. Hence, Avicenna said in the first chapter that nothing exists that resists evil...

It highlights how environmental factors, such as foul air or toxic shade, and individual physical temperaments determine a person's vulnerability to various poisons.</summary>

...to the qualities and febrile heat more than the innate heat <note>original: "calor inatus"; refers to the vital heat believed to sustain life</note> does, to such an extent that it even resists "hot" poisons—not just through a balance of qualities, but through its very essence. This is because the innate heat is shaped and generated by our soul, which moves toward life using this innate heat as its instrument. Therefore, it is said that every work of nature is a work of the intelligence that rules it. This is why nature is specifically associated with "heat" by both philosophers and physicians when they speak of "innate heat" and not "innate coldness." This heat is proportioned—as the astrologer Dorachius <note>likely Dorotheus of Sidon</note> says—to the *giver of life* <note>original: "alcotodeum"; the Alcocoden, or the planet that determines the length of life in a horoscope</note>, that is, to the constellation and place in the heavens which is called the giver of life. Conversely, a "cold" poison given to a person with a cold temperament <note>original: "compositione"; refers to the balance of humors</note> kills much faster due to the coldness of both, compared to when it is given to someone with a warmer temperament. However, if the poison is one of those that kills by its entire species <note>meaning it is inherently lethal regardless of temperature</note>, such as monkshood <note>original: "napellus"; aconite</note>, toxic gum, leopard’s gall <note>a substance historically believed to be highly poisonous</note>, or viper venom <note>original: "tyrus"</note>, then the temperament of the person possessing the poison neither hinders nor helps, except insofar as the pathways in a "warm" person are wider for the poison to pass through, while in a "cold" person they are narrower.

->CHAPTER IV.<-
->On precaution and care, so that either poisons are not<-
->administered, or if administered, they do not cause harm.<-

**I**t is necessary for anyone who suspects or fears a poisonous drink or food to use a two-fold regimen. The first is defense through caution; the second is the destruction of the consumed poison through its medicinal power. Defense with caution involves ensuring that before eating at the table, there are things present among the dishes and drinks that can discern and signal if poison is present. One of these is "serpents' horns" <note>likely fossilized shark teeth or narwhal tusks, often called "tongue stones," believed to sweat in the presence of poison</note> which "sweat" upon the arrival of poisons, specifically monkshood, viper venom, and leopard's gall, though not with other poisons. Another is a certain stone called *Prase* <note>original: "prassius"; a leek-green quartz</note>, which is the "mother" or "palace" of the emerald because it is found with it. It is green, having a thick greenness like a leek, and is sometimes found with red spots and sometimes with white. It has been proven that this stone protects kings from poisons. For if that stone is on the table where poison is placed, it immediately loses its luster in the presence of the poison, and when the poison is removed, the luster returns. Regarding this stone, it is said in the letter of the philosopher Aesculapius to Octavian that poisons and battles fear it. Hence, Alexander of Macedon often had it with him in battles. When he was returning from India and was washing himself in the Euphrates, he laid aside his belt in which the stone was hanging; a certain serpent bit it off and vomited it into the Euphrates. This story is mentioned by writers in the book on the nature of serpents. 

There is also another thing written in the *Book of Persian Kings*: that if you have a kneeling figure carved into a hematite stone, girded by a serpent whose head he holds in his right hand and tail in his left, and you place this stone in a golden ring with crushed serpentaria <note>snakeroot</note> root underneath the stone, wearing this ring protects against all poison. I myself once had this prepared and kept for the aforementioned use. Let everyone also beware that the vessels in which their wine is carried or kept do not stand uncovered in wine cellars, nor should wine be left uncovered, because every poisonous animal naturally licks wine and wine vessels, and sometimes they are found drowned in them. 

Also, beware of dishes, drinks, and confections that have very sweet or very clashing, pervasive, and diverse flavors, because people are accustomed to hiding poison in these. The emerald <note>original: "smaragdus"</note> is also excellent; it has been proven that if a toad <note>original: "buso"</note> looks at one, its eyes will burst in its presence. If held on the table, it weakens poisons, and if held in the mouth, it takes away the poison's power to infect. If it is given crushed in a drink after poison has been taken, it frees one from death most effectively. The dosage should be two scruples <note>a small unit of weight</note>, which I have occasionally tested, and Avenzoar <note>an 11th-century Andalusian physician</note> discovered this, as is written in the book translated for Pope Boniface. 

One should also frequently eat, before any food: chestnuts with dried figs; or rue with hazelnuts; or green walnuts with rue; or dry walnuts with dried figs; or fresh or dried calamint in fried cakes; or crushed dittany <note>original: "diptami"</note> root drunk with wine. As a precaution against all poison, one should also drink on an empty stomach a cup of excellent pure wine in which two live serpents were suffocated during the time of the new wine harvest <note>original: "tempore musti"</note>. 

Another proven preventative to be taken every morning is two drams <note>original: "ʒ . ii ."</note> of the theriac <note>a universal antidote</note> called "Sealed Earth" <note>original: "terra sigillata"; a medicinal clay from Lemnos stamped with a seal</note>. It is made as follows: Take 4 drams of laurel berries and 1 dram of Sealed Earth. Let them be ground and mixed with one pound of clarified honey. Let it be stored in a glass vessel and taken in doses of two drams.

The destruction of consumed poison is done as follows: if the type of poison is known, then let it be destroyed by the medicine specific to that poison which is called a *bezoar* <note>a stone-like mass found in the stomachs of animals, highly prized as an antidote</note>. I shall provide a unique chapter on this below for identifying each poison by its own signs and there the bezoar-like powers will be discussed. If, however, the poison is unknown or a doctor is absent, and there is doubt about the poison's type, then immediately let the person drink butter and warm water mixed together, and force them to vomit. After vomiting, let them be forced to vomit again with butter and honey-water. Once the stomach is cleansed, let the "Great Theriac" <note>a complex poly-pharmaceutical antidote</note> be administered immediately with a decoction of wine in which dittany roots have been boiled. Let the dose be 2 drams of theriac and 2 ounces of wine. The person should not eat for seven hours. Then, let them be nourished with "windy" foods <note>foods thought to move "pneuma" or vapors</note> such as figs, raisins, and hazelnuts, and the broth of a very fat hen, or a year-old lamb or kid. 

If burning or pain is felt in the intestines, an enema should be injected, made with honey-water dissolved with duck or hen fat. After that enema is expelled, let another be given with warm sheep's milk; after that is expelled, let the person be fed with the broth mentioned above. If a biting sensation or pain still remains in the stomach or intestines, then give a small amount of balsam dissolved in one cup of warm milk as a drink. This frees the poisoned if the things mentioned are applied quickly. If, however, there is a bite or a poisoned blade wound, a live hen—disemboweled—should be placed immediately over the bite. This should be repeated with another live one. Or, let the place be sucked by the mouth of some lad or servant, and let the servant's mouth be washed often with wine in which dittany has been boiled. Then, let the Great Theriac be applied to the spot, and when the theriac has dried, let another fresh application be put on.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of theriac's application to wounds and shifts into a list of specific botanical antidotes. It then moves into Chapter VI and Chapter VIII, focusing on the clinical signs and treatments for poisoning by mercury (quicksilver) and gypsum.</meta>

...until the area no longer dries out the theriac <note>original: "tyriacam"; a famous ancient poly-pharmaceutical used as a universal antidote</note>. If, however, the site of the bite or the poisoned wound is dry, then theriac should not be applied. Instead of theriac, **wild lettuce** <note>original: "lactucella"</note> should be bound over the wound and renewed repeatedly until the site is moistened; only then will health be restored. Just as theriac dries, wild lettuce moistens even more.

Your Reverence should understand that there are seven herbs whose universal nature has instilled in each plant a singular and specific essence. They are endowed with this power not through their elementary "complexion" <note>the balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>—that is, not simply because they are hot or cold, dry or wet—but because of their specific nature, granted by the stars. This power frees the body from poisonous foods and drinks, as well as from lethal venom from a wound or bite.

The first of these is **Hypericum**, which is also called "perforated herb" <note>St. John’s Wort, known for the tiny oil glands in its leaves that look like holes</note>; Pliny <note>the Roman naturalist</note> says that Achilles discovered it in the Trojan army through an oracle of Apollo. The second is **Vincetoxicum** <note>literally "poison-conqueror"</note>. The third is **Elecampane** <note>original: "enula"</note>. The fourth is **Radish**. The fifth is **Dittany**. The sixth is **Birthwort** <note>original: "aristologia"</note>, both the long and round varieties. The seventh is **Wild Lettuce**, which is said to drive out theriac from poisoned wounds just as it does other substances.

When any of these aforementioned herbs is given in a drink, it purges and heals wounds infected with poison; this was the method the ancients used to cure such wounds before they had knowledge of theriac. For the bite of a poisonous animal, any of the aforementioned herbs, mixed with theriac and placed upon the bitten site, effects a cure. For swallowed poisons, a "holy powder" <note>original: "puluis scūs"</note> made from any of these herbs and given in a drink of wine or honey-water is effective.

Note also: water in which a rooster has been boiled, drunk with water, immediately draws out all poison through vomiting. Furthermore, **donkey’s milk**, whether eaten or drunk during a lunch or dinner, ensures that no poison—except for **monkshood** <note>original: "napellū"; aconite, considered the most lethal poison</note>—can do harm.

Theriac, however, is the proportional and specific opponent to every poison, and is directly opposed to monkshood. It works "according to its entire species"—that is, through the perfect blending of the many medicines that enter into the artificial making of theriac. From this mixture results something almost divine and a formal power that destroys all poison, as will be discussed specifically below. One should take two or three drachms <note>original: "ʒ. ii. ul. iii."</note> of it for three continuous days, because it breaks down the toxin and liberates the patient by inducing sweat.

**Sealed Earth** <note>original: "Terra sigillata"; a medicinal clay, usually from Lemnos, pressed into tablets and stamped with a seal to guarantee its purity</note>, whether eaten or drunk after a meal, has this property: if it finds poison in the stomach, it expels it through vomiting. If, however, the poison is administered after the earth has been taken, it never allows the poison to travel through the body; thus it defends the heart and guards its chambers. Kings and princes of the Eastern and Southern regions—where the wicked and most nefarious practice of clandestine poisoning began and grows daily—eat sealed earth at their dinners and lunches. For this reason, such earth was stamped with the seal of kings, and so it was called "sealed earth." Nowadays, trust in these seals has perished, although that which is brought to us is still legally and elegantly "sealed." It is well known that **Rhazes** <note>original: "Ralsis"; a famous 10th-century Persian physician</note> and experience itself testify to this.

Rhazes said in his *Book of Divisions* that for the poison of monkshood, theriac seems to be of little or no use. For this reason, one must flee to another remedy entirely. Because of the very short span of time in which monkshood acts, the power of medicine in the form of theriac cannot prevent the poison from reaching the heart. This is because if it is not blocked very quickly, a person will die within one or three days. But this will be discussed below, where I shall introduce specific medicines for specific poisons.

### CHAPTER VI.
### On the signs and cures for each individual poison administered.

He who has taken **quicksilver** <note>original: "argētū uiuū"; mercury</note> will suffer pain in the intestines and sides, or a sense of heaviness, which ultimately leads to epilepsy or apoplexy <note>a sudden loss of consciousness, often a stroke</note>, at which point he falls and becomes still. If the mercury was "sublimated" <note>original: "sublimatū"; corrosive sublimate or mercuric chloride, which is highly toxic</note>, it causes corrosion and a "gnawing" of the intestines; a coating forms on the tongue and stomach, the heart becomes inflamed <note>original: "apostemat cor"</note>, and the person dies. The cure for this is an **enema** <note>original: "clistere"</note> made with duck fat or butter, followed by one of honey-water. If it is believed that the poison was the sublimated form, vomiting should be induced immediately before it descends to the intestines; otherwise, it will flay the intestines, causing blood to pass and inducing **tenesmus** <note>a distressing and constant urge to evacuate the bowels</note>. In that case, one must focus solely on enemas. Once the mercury has been cleared out, one must attend to the three lingering symptoms: first, a bad "complexion" in the intestines that is too cold and moist; second, weakness of the heart and trembling of the limbs; and third, wounds in the stomach or intestines.

First, we counteract the cold with strengthening, "styptic" <note>contracting or binding</note>, hot, and drying substances. We should give **myrrh** <note>original: "mitrā"</note> and **castoreum** <note>a secretion from beavers used in medicine</note> boiled in wine, along with sage and crushed rue, offered as a drink with water in which cypress nuts have been boiled. Second, we counteract the weakness with doses of **diamargariton** <note>a medicine made from pearls</note> and **diamuscus amari** <note>a musk-based tonic</note>. Third, we counter the wounds with "sealing" medicines; these are taken by enema if the wounds are in the intestines, or as a drink if they are in the stomach. The best of these is **Trissera Minor** <note>an electuary used for flux and wounds</note> or red wine in which **myrobalans** <note>astringent plum-like fruits</note> have been cooked. If the urine is retained because of the mercury, we should place the patient in a warm water bath and afterward apply a sponge to the bladder that has been soaked in a decoction of juniper and celery seed several times. We shall give him the best pure wine to drink, in which **cyperus root** has been boiled, and we shall anoint the groin and testicles with oil of rue and oil of juniper. Also, **bezoar** <note>a stone-like mass found in the stomachs of animals, prized as an antidote</note> is effective, as is **costus** <note>an aromatic root</note>, etc.

### CHAPTER VIII.
### On Gypsum.

He to whom **gypsum** <note>plaster of Paris or mineral sulfate</note> has been given in a drink will suffer from difficulty in breathing, coldness in the stomach, a binding of the belly <note>constipation</note>, and lips that appear white or deadened. His cure shall be to drink warm water with butter and then vomit; afterward, he should drink warm water with honey and vomit again. Then, give him two drachms of **Mithridatum** <note>a famous semi-mythical panacea and antidote</note> with excellent wine. If the bowels remain bound, he should be given an enema with fat.

<meta>This page continues the toxicological manual, providing specific treatments for mineral and metallic poisonings. It maintains the two-column layout of the previous folio, detailing symptoms, topical treatments, and specific antidotes known as "bezoars."</meta>

...of a duck and with oil, and they should anoint the belly with oil of **kerva** <note>original: "kerva"; castor oil, derived from the Ricinus communis plant</note>; and its **bezoar** <note>in this context, a "bezoar" refers to a specific or sovereign antidote for a particular poison</note> is mouse dung, ground and drunk, and let it be given with one ounce of wine.

### CHAPTER IX. On copper dross.

The one to whom **copper dross** <note>original: "scoria eris"; the waste product of smelting copper</note> has been given in a drink will have frequent bowel movements or vomiting, accompanied by pain and a stinging sensation in the intestines and stomach. The cure shall be a bath in which the heads of goats or snails have been boiled. Give him mint juice to drink, and anoint the stomach and belly with warm rose oil. Its bezoar is the juice of **sweet flag** <note>original: "accori"; Acorus calamus, a medicinal root</note>; let two ounces be drunk with wine.

### CHAPTER X. On iron dross.

The one to whom **iron dross** <note>original: "scoria ferri"</note> or copper rust has been given will dry out daily; the belly will "stick to the ribs," and he will suffer from **wasting** <note>original: "marasmu[m]"; a state of severe malnutrition and physical decay</note>. The cure is to moisten the entire body with baths in which tortoises have been boiled. Administer an enema to the belly with a decoction of the feet of kids <note>young goats</note> or with marshmallow water. The patient should eat fresh butter and fatty broths. The bezoar is **magnet stone** <note>lodestone</note>, ground and given in pills with an equal amount of the juice of **mercury-herb** <note>original: "mercurialis"; Mercurialis annua</note> and **blite** <note>a spinach-like plant</note> formed into pills. The dose of the magnet should be one ounce.

### CHAPTER XI. On magnet stone.

The one to whom **magnet stone** has been given <note>perhaps referring to unrefined or unwashed stone</note> will be made lunatic and melancholic or suffer from **heroic malady** <note>original: "heroicū"; likely referring to "amor heros," a severe form of melancholy or mania associated with obsession</note>. The cure is to give a drink of gold leaf and fragments of fine emeralds with wine. Let an enema be given with sheep's milk and sweet almond oil. Its bezoar is ground emerald, given in a drink three times over the course of nine days.

### CHAPTER XII. On lapis lazuli.

The one to whom unwashed **lapis lazuli** has been given in a drink will suffer a "turning" of the stomach, sadness, and a desire for solitude. The cure is to drink much fresh cow’s or ass’s milk every morning for eight days, and to eat small birds roasted on a spit. Its bezoar is two **scruples** <note>a small unit of weight</note> of ground **amber** <note>original: "carabe"</note> given in a drink with wine.

### CHAPTER XIII. On sublimated arsenic.

The one to whom **sublimated arsenic** has been given will suffer excoriation <note>scraping or tearing</note> of the intestines and stomach, along with burning, biting pains, and thirst. His tongue will be dried out so that he cannot spit, and finally, he will suffer from **fainting** <note>original: "lico pīz," likely a corruption of "leipopsychia" or syncope</note>. The cure is for him to drink butter with warm water in which turnips have been boiled, then let him vomit and be given an enema. Afterward, give him sweet almond oil twice every day and feed him the broth of a very fat hen. Its bezoar is **crystal** finely ground and given in a one-ounce dose in a drink with sweet almond oil. If the arsenic was not "sublimated" <note>purified through heating into a vapor</note>, the symptoms will be milder, but the cure remains the same.

### CHAPTER XIV. On litharge.

The one to whom **litharge** <note>original: "litargiro"; lead monoxide, often used in glazing and medicine</note> has been given in a drink will be unable to defecate and will vomit everything up, including what should have passed through the bowels. The cure is the same as for **colic**: an enema made from honey-water and the fat of a hen or duck. Give him sweet almond oil to drink, and have him eat dried figs before meals. Anoint the stomach with celery juice and the belly with butter. Its bezoar is two ounces of ground **kerva seed** <note>castor seed</note> given in a drink.

### CHAPTER XV. On white lead.

The one to whom **white lead** <note>original: "cerusa"; a lead pigment</note> has been given in a drink will suffer from white vomit (the color of the lead), have black teeth, and experience pain in the belly and throat. He will pass blood and suffer from **tenesmus** <note>the constant, painful urge to evacuate the bowels</note>. The cure shall be induced vomiting with water in which turnips and dill have been boiled. Afterward, provide an enema for the belly with boiled cabbage broth and saltless oil. Give him **mithridate** <note>a famous complex semi-liquid antidote</note> or theriac with excellent wine to drink. Its bezoar is a drink of the clearest, purest white wine, taken almost to the point of drunkenness.

### CHAPTER XVI. On verdigris.

The one to whom **verdigris** <note>original: "uiride eris"; the green pigment that forms on copper</note> has been given in a drink will suffer obstruction and suffocation of the lungs. He will have difficulty breathing and suffer internal "solutions of continuity" <note>a medical term for open wounds or ulcers</note>, as well as ulcers in the intestines and corrosive stinging. The cure must be immediate: induce vomiting with butter and warm water, repeating this often. Then, administer an enema made with ass’s milk and sweet almond oil. Afterward, give him one ounce of **tragillata** <note>a type of medicinal paste or electuary</note> in white wine. If this does not help, prepare a bath in a tub of olive oil deep enough to reach his stomach. Its bezoar is two ounces of ground red coral given in a drink with wine.

### CHAPTER XVII. On burnt lead.

The one to whom **burnt lead** <note>lead that has been oxidized by fire</note> has been given cannot speak and dies suffocated. His voice cannot be heard except as a heavy, "leaden" sound, and his lips and tongue become the color of lead. The cure is to give two ounces of **Great Theriac** every day for five days with honey-water. Clothe him in new fox or sheep skins and place him inside the warm belly of a recently slaughtered mule or ass, repeating this entry often. Its bezoar is two ounces of cleaned, ground **citron seeds** given in a drink of sweet, boiled-down wine.

### CHAPTER XVIII. On azurite, minium, or cinnabar.

The one to whom **azurite** <note>blue pigment</note>, **minium** <note>red lead</note>, or **cinnabar** <note>mercury sulfide</note> has been given will suffer vomiting and constipation; the vomit will be the color of whichever pigment was taken. The cure for all of these is the same: give butter with warm water in which turnips have been boiled, and let him vomit. After the initial spontaneous vomiting, give an enema of honey-water and oil. Its bezoar is two ounces of **spodium** <note>ash produced from burning animal matter, here specifically ivory</note> made from burnt ivory, given in a drink with wine.

### CHAPTER XIX. On realgar.

The one to whom **realgar** <note>original: "realgar"; arsenic sulfide, a bright red-orange mineral</note> has been given in a drink will suffer from thirst, extreme heat, drying out, and the consumption of his bodily fluids. Unless he is helped, he will die or remain paralyzed and physically contracted.

<meta>This page continues a practical manual on toxicology, moving from mineral poisons to plant-based toxins. It details the physiological effects of various poisonous herbs and provides specific antidotes (bezoars) and regimens for recovery.</meta>

I saw and cured a youth to whom was given ground **realgar** <note>original: "realgar"; arsenic disulfide, a highly toxic mineral</note> with roasted pig's liver. I saved his life, but he remained nearly immobile in all his joints due to excessive dryness. His cure is vomiting with butter and warm water often repeated, and enemas with donkey milk repeated, and giving in the morning a drink every day of five ounces of donkey milk, and feeding him fatty soups, and anointing the whole body with oil of sweet almonds, and soothing his thirst with **julep** <note>original: "iuleb"; a sweet medicinal syrup</note>. His **bezoar** <note>in this text, a "bezoar" refers to a specific or sovereign antidote for a particular poison</note> is oil of pine nuts given in a drink immediately, or on the first day, in a dose of three ounces.

## CHAPTER XIX.
->On Hemlock.<-

He to whom the juice of **hemlock** <note>original: "cicuta"</note> has been given in a drink will lose his stupor and sensation; it was by this that **Socrates** was put to death by the Athenians. Its cure is to take in a drink two **drachms** <note>original: "ʒ.ii."; a drachm is a medicinal unit of weight, roughly 3.5 grams</note> of **theriac** <note>original: "tyriacā"; a famous "universal" antidote composed of dozens of ingredients</note> diluted with a decoction of **dittany** <note>original: "diptami"; an aromatic herb believed to draw out poisons</note>. Its bezoar is ground **gentian** <note>original: "gēciana"</note> given in a drink of two drachms with wine.

## CHAPTER XX.
->On Spurge Juice.<-

He to whom the juice of **spurge** <note>original: "titimalloꝙ"; plants of the Euphorbia genus, known for their milky, irritating sap</note> has been given will suffer a flux of the belly and vomiting and the symptoms of a **choleric passion** <note>original: "colerice passiōis"; a state of severe digestive upset associated with yellow bile</note>. Its cure will be the great theriac with wine in which dittany has been boiled. Its bezoar is ground **mumia** <note>original: "muia"; a medicinal substance made from mineral bitumen or powdered mummified remains</note> drunk with wine, in a dose of one drachm.

## CHAPTER XXI.
->On Squirting Cucumber Juice.<-

He to whom the juice of **squirting cucumber** <note>original: "cucumeris asinini"; Ecballium elaterium, a potent purgative</note> has been given in a drink will suffer from excoriation <note>raw, scraped skin</note> in the throat, a loosening of the belly, and pain in the intestines. Its cure is the great theriac with a decoction of **laurel berries** and two drachms of honey. Its bezoar is one ounce of **mint juice** <note>original: "fucus mente"</note>.

## CHAPTER XXII.
->On Wolfsbane Juice.<-

He to whom the juice of **wolfsbane** <note>original: "usnee"; though usnea usually refers to moss, the text identifies this as "strangulator lupi," a common name for Aconite or Wolfsbane</note> has been given will suffer a discharge of superfluous humors to the mouth and throat, so that he appears to be strangled; for this reason, this herb is called **wolf-strangler**, as it strangles wolves that eat it. Its cure is to take immediately in a drink two drachms of **sealed earth** <note>original: "trā sigillata"; a medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos</note> with warm water and to vomit; after that, take two drachms of theriac with a wine decoction of gentian. Its bezoar is **long birthwort** <note>original: "aristologia lōga"</note>.

## CHAPTER XXIII.
->On the Cyclamen Root.<-

He to whom the juice or root of **cyclamen** <note>original: "bothor marien"; an Arabic-derived name for Cyclamen europaeum</note> has been given in a drink will suffer strangulation and a kind of suffocation, because of which it is called **sowbread** <note>original: "panis porcoꝙ"</note>. Its cure is two drachms of ground laurel berries given in a drink. Its bezoar is two drachms of ground white pepper.

## CHAPTER XXIIII.
->On Coriander Juice.<-

He to whom the juice of **coriander** has been given will suf-

---

fer a kind of destruction of the intellect and will appear as if drunk, and at last dies in a stupor. Its cure is two drachms of the great theriac with the best wine. Its bezoar is the herb called **swallow-wort** <note>original: "uicetoxi"; Vincetoxicum</note> given in a drink of two drachms.

## CHAPTER XXV.
->On Mandrake Juice.<-

He to whom the juice of **mandrake** <note>original: "mādragore"</note> or its fruit or its root has been given in a drink will suffer redness in the face and eyes, a stupor in the mind, alienation of the mind, madness, and a deep sleep. Its cure will be to take immediately in a drink the great theriac diluted with the best wine, and to delay eating for one day, and to drink the best pure wine, and to smell strong vinegar. Its bezoar is **radish root** eaten every day for up to three days with bread and salt.

## CHAPTER XXVI.
->On Black Poppy Juice.<-

He to whom the juice of the **poppy** has been given will suffer a stupor of the mind, sleepiness, and **foolishness** <note>original: "bebeciā"</note> like those who eat too much oil. Their cure is to drink the great theriac and **dyacastoreum** <note>a medicine made from castor</note> or **opopira** <note>a compound medicine</note> or a confection of **marking nuts** <note>original: "anacar dis"; the fruit of the Anacardium tree</note>, two drachms with wine. Its bezoar is raw garlic, eaten.

## CHAPTER XXVII.
->On Opium.<-

He to whom **opium** has been given in a drink, if he is forced to vomit, the smell of opium will appear in the vomit, and he will be dull, sluggish, and drowsy without sensation, neither understanding nor feeling anything; and if he is not helped, he will die. His cure is to drink the strongest wine, and to rub the extremities with **niter** <note>saltpeter or natron</note> and soap, and to provoke sneezing with pepper introduced into the nostrils. His bezoar is ground **castoreum** <note>a secretion from the beaver used in medicine</note> given in a drink with wine, in a dose of two drachms.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.
->On Scammony Juice.<-

He to whom the juice of **scammony** <note>original: "scamonee"; a harsh purgative resin</note> has been given in a drink will suffer a failure of the heart, fainting, thirst, overheating, dysentery, and fever. His cure is to drink barley water often and enter a bath of lukewarm water, then after that drink syrup of roses and **bugloss** all day, and to provoke sleep, and to smell water lilies, roses, and myrtle, and to be fed with food made with **sumac** or **barberries**, and to plaster the belly and stomach with the pulp of **quinces** <note>original: "citonioꝙ"</note>. Its bezoar is the herb called **currant** <note>original: "ribes"</note> and its juice.

## CHAPTER XXIX.
->On Sardonian Smallage.<-

He to whom **sardonian smallage** <note>original: "apiū risus"; literally "parsley of laughter," likely Ranunculus sceleratus, which causes a facial spasm resembling a grin</note> has been given in a drink, it makes the man out of his mind and he laughs continually; because of this, it is called the "parsley of laughter." His cure is to provoke sleep with a drink of good wine...

### CHAPTER XXX.
### On the juice of **cherue**.

<margin>1</margin> He to whom the juice of **cherue** <note>original: "cherue"; likely the Castor Oil plant (*Ricinus communis*), derived from the Arabic *al-khurwa*</note> has been given in a drink will suffer continuous vomiting and pain in the belly. His cure will be the **great theriac** <note>a complex, "universal" medieval antidote</note> given in a drink of two **drachms** <note>roughly 7 grams</note> with excellent warm wine. Its bezoar is **St. John’s Wort** <note>original: "ypericon"</note>.

### CHAPTER XXXI.
### On the juice of **monkshood**.

<margin>1</margin> He to whom the poison of **monkshood** <note>original: "napelli"; Aconite, one of the most lethal plants known to medieval toxicology</note>—whether its fruit or its substance—has been given will die within the space of one to three days. Before this, he will suffer **syncope** <note>fainting or loss of consciousness</note>, heart failure, and a gradual blackening and darkening of all his limbs; then the whole body swells, his eyes bulge out, and he cannot keep his tongue in his mouth. He must be helped instantly by giving **sealed earth** <note>original: "terrā sigillatā"; a medicinal clay used to absorb toxins</note> dissolved with butter and water to make him vomit. Immediately after, let there be administered two drachms of the finest ground **emerald** <note>original: "smaragdus"; precious stones were often ground into "cordial" medicines for the wealthy</note> with wine, and place upon his heart **raw silk** <note>original: "siricū elidū"</note> soaked in the juice of **bugloss** <note>an herb thought to hearten the spirit</note> and rose water, and let this be repeated. He will be a dead man unless he receives the emerald. Its bezoar is the **mouse** that is born in the root of the monkshood, dried and given in a drink of two drachms <note>A legendary medieval antidote based on the idea that a creature living off a poison must contain the cure for it</note>.

### CHAPTER XXXII.
### On the juice of **oleander**.

<margin>1</margin> He to whom the juice of **oleander** or its "horns" <note>likely referring to the seed pods</note> or its bark has been given in a drink will suffer syncope, distress of the heart, and anxiety. His cure is to take **diacastoreum** <note>a medicine made from castoreum, a secretion from beavers</note> given in a drink of two drachms. Its bezoar is ground **juniper berry** in a quantity of two drachms with wine.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.
### On the juice of **mezereon**.

<margin>1</margin> He to whom the juice of **mezereon** <note>original: "mezerion"; *Daphne mezereum*, a highly toxic shrub</note> has been given in a drink will suffer a flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>, thirst, anxiety, and the stripping away of the lining of the intestines. His cure shall be **syrup of roses** with barley water and the smelling of cold, fragrant fruits. Its bezoar is **oregano**, roasted and drunk.

### CHAPTER XXXIIII.
### On the juice of **hellebore**.

<margin>1</margin> He to whom the juice of **hellebore** or its root has been given will suffer a strangling of the throat and choking; perhaps he will be suffocated suddenly, and for this reason it is called "dog-strangler." His cure is to take honey-water in a drink immediately and to rest in a quiet place. Then let his bezoar be given, which is the flower of the **water lily** <note>original: "nenu faris"; from the Arabic *nilufar*</note>, dried and ground, in a dose of two drachms.

### CHAPTER XXXV.
### On **alfesira**.

<margin>1</margin> He to whom **alfesira** <note>original: "alfesira"; likely White Bryony, from the Arabic *al-fashira*</note> has been given will suffer a stripping of the belly and vomiting. His cure will be to give honey-water in a drink, then to provide roasted **quince**. Its bezoar is **pimpernel** <note>original: "anagallus"</note>.

### On the juice of **bryony**.

<margin>1</margin> He to whom the juice of **bryony** <note>original: "brionie"</note> has been given will suffer **scotoma** <note>dizziness or dark spots in the vision</note>, stupor, and shortness of breath. His cure will be two drachms of theriac with a wine decoction of **elecampane** <note>original: "enule"</note>. Its bezoar is **pepper**.

### On the "horns" of **lavender**.

<margin>1</margin> He to whom the "horns" <note>spikes or flower heads</note> of **lavender** <note>original: "spice"</note> have been given will suffer twisting of the belly and nausea. His cure is two drachms of theriac with a decoction of wine in which **dittany** has been boiled.

### CHAPTER XL.
### On the "horns" of **oleander**.

<margin>1</margin> He to whom the "horns" of **oleander** have been given, or he who eats meat roasted on a spit cut from oleander wood, or he who sleeps under the shade of an oleander, or he who drinks the water of a river beneath whose banks oleander grows—which is found in abundance on the island of **Sardinia**; and I have experienced this and seen it—he will suffer over-heating, madness, and a rumbling of the belly. And if a bath has been heated with oleander wood, he who bathes there will suffer syncope in the bath. His cure and bezoar are what we stated above in the chapter on oleander juice.

### CHAPTER XLI.
### On the "horns" of **bedeguar**.

<margin>1</margin> He to whom the "horns" of **bedeguar** <note>original: "bedeguar"; a gall caused by a wasp on rose bushes, from the Persian *bād-āwar*</note> have been given in a drink will suffer difficulty in swallowing. His cure is to take oil of sweet almonds. Their bezoar is **mulberries** <note>original: "mora celsi"</note>.

### CHAPTER XLII.
### On **cashew nuts**.

<margin>1</margin> He who takes **cashew nuts** <note>original: "anacardis"; specifically the Marking Nut, which contains caustic fluids</note> will suffer a powerful burning in the throat and instability of the senses; it will cause an acute sickness and alienation of the mind. Its cure is with oily things, such as almond oil, sesame oil, butter, milk, and chicken broths. If he has pain in the intestines, then a bath is appropriate. If they induce an acute fever, then it is appropriate to use a thinning, cold, and moist diet. If there is alienation of the mind, sleep should be provoked with lettuce seed and white poppy. Its bezoar is **pine nuts**, roasted and eaten.

### CHAPTER XLIII.
### On **walnuts** and **hazelnuts**.

<margin>1</margin> He who eats rancid **walnuts** or **hazelnuts** will suffer bad accidents, namely nausea, loss of appetite, vomiting, and a weakening of the animal virtues <note>the vital powers of the mind and senses</note>. His cure will be a **rob** <note>a thickened fruit syrup</note> of quinces or apples. If he experiences a burp having the odor of rotten flax, then he could die. His cure will be **diacyminum** <note>a cumin-based digestive</note> or **diapepion**, and let pure wine be given to him in a drink, and let the stomach be warmed with oil of **spikenard** <note>original: "nardino"</note>.

### CHAPTER XLIV.
#### On bad castoreum.
He to whom bad **castoreum** <note>original: "castoreo"; a yellowish secretion from beaver scent glands used in medieval medicine, which could be toxic if spoiled or adulterated</note> has been given in a drink will suffer from shouting, quarreling, and pain; he will have his tongue protruding from his mouth and will suffer a fever. His cure shall be to induce vomiting with butter and honey water until the vomit no longer has the odor of castoreum; then let him be given a syrup of blackberries or lemons. Its **bezoar** <note>a specific or sovereign antidote</note> consists of two **drachms** <note>original: ".3.ii"; approximately 7-8 grams</note> of roasted and ground coriander seeds.

### CHAPTER XLV.
#### On bad mushrooms.
He who eats bad mushrooms—especially those that grow upon iron, or upon **spurge** <note>original: "anabulla"</note>, or in bad soil, or in the locations of hot springs—will suffer choking and pain in the pubic region; his urine will be suppressed and he will have pains in his belly. If he should even smell a bad mushroom or bad tubers, he will suffer from epilepsy and perhaps die. Before that happens, he should be given excellent wine in which black pepper has been boiled, and then he should be given an enema with honey water and salt, and his thighs should be rubbed with **nard oil** <note>an aromatic essential oil derived from the spikenard plant</note>. Their bezoar, when mushrooms are being cooked or eaten, is pears cut into pieces and cooked with them; the bezoar after they have been eaten is raw garlic.

### CHAPTER XLVI.
#### On nux vomica.
He who drinks or eats **nux vomica** <note>the seeds of the Strychnine tree, containing highly toxic strychnine</note> will suffer terrible vomiting and a dissolution of his mind. His cure is syrup of quince and myrtle, and a drink of garlic wine. Its bezoar is the rind of a **citron** <note>original: "cortex citri"</note>.

#### On colocynth.
He who eats a **colocynth** <note>original: "coloquintida"; the "bitter apple," a powerful and potentially lethal purgative</note> that has grown solitary on its vine has consumed a lethal poison. Unless he is helped quickly, he will die on the third day. Its cure and bezoar, administered together at once, is two drachms of the finest ground **emerald** given in a drink.

### CHAPTER XLVII.
#### On the Pharaoh’s fig.
He who eats **Pharaoh’s figs** <note>original: "ficus pharaonis"; likely the Sycamore Fig (*Ficus sycomorus*)</note> will immediately suffer a fever and a crushing sensation throughout the whole body, and he will appear to be **dropsical** <note>swollen with fluid/edema</note>. I myself saw this in <term>Sardinia</term> in the <term>Judicate of Gallura</term> <note>original: "iudicatu galurie"; one of the four districts of medieval Sardinia</note> where there is an abundance of these figs. He who ate one suffered one fever; he who ate two suffered two; and he who ate three suffered a triple fever; for the most part, these were **tertian fevers** <note>a fever that returns every third day, common in malaria</note>. The cure for this is prepared barley water or goat whey. Its bezoar is two drachms of the cleaned and ground seeds of a cucumber, given in a drink.

### CHAPTER XLVIII.
#### On the seed of henbane.
He to whom the seeds of **henbane** <note>original: "iusquiami"</note> have been given in a drink will suffer drunkenness, alienation of the mind, stupor, and the immobility of all his limbs. His cure is two drachms of ground long pepper given in a drink. Its bezoar is **pistachio nuts** <note>original: "grana sistucorum"</note>, either eaten or drunk.

### CHAPTER XLIX.
#### On the seeds of mezereon.
He to whom the seeds of **mezereon** <note>original: "cocognidii"; seeds of the Spurge Flax, a violent purgative</note> have been given in a drink will suffer vomiting, a flux of the belly, and distress in the stomach. His cure is two drachms of **great theriac** <note>a complex "universal" medieval antidote</note> with wine. Its bezoar is bitter almonds.

### CHAPTER L.
#### On rancid laurel berries.
He who eats rancid **laurel berries** <note>original: "bacbalauras"</note> will suffer the same symptoms as one who eats rancid nuts. His cure and bezoar shall be the same as those.

### CHAPTER LI.
<margin>cherue</margin>
#### On spurge.
He who eats **spurge** <note>original: "cataputias"; likely the Castor Bean or Caper Spurge</note> will suffer the same symptoms as one who drinks the "sun-turner" which was called **ehenia** above; the cure and bezoar are the same.

### CHAPTER LII.
#### On the seed of nettle.
He who eats the seed of **nettle** <note>original: "urtice"</note> will suffer a scouring and burning of the throat, mouth, and tongue, and a burning during urination. His cure shall be to drink sweet almond oil. Its bezoar is ground quince seeds drunk with hot water.

### CHAPTER LIII.
#### On the seed of black poppy.
He who drinks or eats the seeds of **black poppy** will suffer the same symptoms as one who has taken opium, though they will be milder; the cure and bezoar are the same.

### CHAPTER LIIII.
#### On the seed of hellebore.
He who drinks or eats the seed of **hellebore** will suffer the same symptoms as one who drinks the juice or root of hellebore; the cure and bezoar are one and the same.

### CHAPTER LV.
#### On the seed of hemlock.
He who drinks the seed of **hemlock** <note>original: "cicute"</note> will suffer the symptoms of one who has drunk its juice, though they are more mild; the cure and bezoar are the same.

### CHAPTER LVI.
#### On the seed of fresh coriander.
He who drinks or eats the seeds of **fresh coriander** <note>original: "humidi coriandri"</note> will suffer symptoms similar to one who drinks its juice; the cure and bezoar are the same.

#### On the seed of snakeweed.
He who eats the seed of **snakeweed** <note>original: "serpentarie"</note>...

### CHAPTER LVIII.
### On bites or punctures from 
### any venomous animals.

If indeed there should be a bite or a puncture from some venomous animal and it is unknown which animal's puncture it is, then let the place of the puncture be bound tight, and let **cupping** <note>original: "uentofe"; the application of heated glass or ceramic cups to create a vacuum on the skin</note> be applied over it with **scarification** <note>the making of small incisions in the skin to draw out blood or venom</note>. Let the place be sucked by a warm mouth, and then let crushed crabs be placed over the site. If the site begins to reach a state of corruption, let the limb be cut off, if the site is suitable or the limb is appropriate for amputation. If not, let it be **cauterized** <note>burned with a hot iron to seal the wound and stop the spread of poison</note>. For when a place begins to blacken or putrefy, it will be a sign that the puncture was from a pernicious animal. However, as long as it has not begun to tend toward putrefaction and corruption, even if there is vehement pain, as long as there is not yet a swift traveling [of the poison] through the body, it is not an evil sign unless the puncture was near the heart or near a great artery.

<margin>m</margin>
### CHAPTER LIX.
### On the bite of a viper.

For him whom a viper has bitten, the highest medicine and **bezoar** is the **Great Theriac** <note>original: "tyriaca magna"; a famous and complex multi-ingredient ointment and internal medicine used since antiquity as a universal antitoxin</note>. And perhaps **mithridate** <note>another complex ancient antidote</note> and a medicine of **asafoetida** <note>a pungent resin used in medicine</note> and old butter and a medicine of **barberry** <note>original: "berbo"; likely barberry or a similar astringent herb</note> may be beneficial, as well as the eating of garlic and the drinking of pure wine.

<margin>m</margin>
### CHAPTER LX.
### On the bite of a scorpion.

For the stinging of scorpions, the vapor of oil and garlic is beneficial, as is the **theriac of four ingredients** <note>original: "tyriaca dyatefferō"; a simpler version of Theriac made of four components: aristolochia, bay berries, germander, and myrrh</note> and the rubbing on of old oil. And its **bezoar** is the body of the scorpion itself, crushed and placed upon the site.

<margin>m</margin>
### CHAPTER LXI.
### On the bite of spiders.

For the biting of spiders, the juice of apples or pears is beneficial, or the repeated application of cold iron. And its **bezoar** is **endive** <note>a bitter salad herb</note>.

<margin>m</margin>
### CHAPTER LXII.
### On the bite of the *rutela*.

For the biting of the **rutela** <note>original: "rutele"; likely referring to a species of venomous spider or tarantula</note>, a very hot bath is beneficial, as is being buried in sand or hot ash and drinking the powder of **black cumin** <note>original: "nigella"</note>.

<margin>m</margin>
### CHAPTER LXIII.
### On the bite of bees.

For the biting and puncturing of bees, a poultice with **Armenian bole** <note>a medicinal red clay</note>, vinegar, and camphor is beneficial. And he who washes his hands and face with the juice of **mallow** <note>a flowering plant known for its soothing mucilage</note> will not be stung by bees.

<margin>h</margin>
### CHAPTER LXIIII.
### On the biting of animals.

If, however, biting animals leave their stingers or teeth in the bitten places, then it is useful for the place to be rubbed gently with oil and ash; then let a plaster be made over the site from **leaven** <note>original: "fermēto"; sourdough or yeast starter</note> with oil, and thus the venomous stingers or teeth will be drawn out.

<margin>h</margin>
### CHAPTER LXV.
### On the bite of a dog.

If anyone has been bitten by a dog and doubts whether it was rabid or not, let a morsel of bread be rubbed under the site of the bite and then let it be offered to other dogs; if they refuse it, the dog was rabid. If they eat it, not at all. The signs that it is rabid besides this are: that the dog thrusts its tongue out, and tucks its tail between its thighs, and has a hoarse voice, and shrinks away from healthy dogs and men, and bites the masters of its own house and all who encounter it, and other dogs flee from it. And he who is bitten, unless he takes precautions and is cured within 40 **dog days** <note>original: "caniculares dies"; the hottest days of summer, traditionally associated with the star Sirius and the madness of dogs</note>, will become **hydrophobic**—that is, fearing water. This is because, on account of the rabies, he becomes **congested** <note>original: "fisticulosus"; possibly referring to a sensation of a "pipe" or blockage in the throat</note> and craves water, but when he sees it, he will imagine that dogs are in the water; and dying of thirst, out of fear of those immense dogs, he will flee the water. And then there is no hope of safety. As the sickness proceeds, he himself becomes rabid and emits semen in his involuntary emissions in the manner of puppies, and sometimes he brings up phlegm in the manner of puppies; this is because the continuous imagination which he has regarding the dog imprints the form of dogs into his bodily fluids. And know that horses, mules, donkeys, monkeys, and oxen also suffer from rabies around the time of maximum cold or maximum heat. And its cure is that cupping with scarification be placed over the site of the bite, and crushed garlic or onion mixed with cow's butter be placed on top. Let him take a drink of an **electuary of river crabs** <note>a medicinal paste made from crabs</note> and enter a bath every day, and let him work on the cure for **ethibos** <note>original: "ethiboy"; possibly a corruption of a term for hectic fever or a specific wasting disease</note> and melancholics. Let him bathe in seawater before 40 days have passed. And its **bezoar** is river crabs, burnt and powdered; let 4 **drachms** <note>original: ".3.iiii"; about 15 grams</note> of these be given in a drink every three days.

<margin>h</margin>
### CHAPTER LXVI.
### On Spanish flies.

If someone drinks **Spanish flies** <note>original: "cantarides"; toxic beetles used in small doses as an aphrodisiac or diuretic, but highly poisonous</note>, he will suffer the passing of blood [in the urine] and overheating and pernicious accidents. Its cure is that he take a drink of sheep's milk with almond oil, and then let the ulcers of the bladder be treated. And its **bezoar** shall be 10 grains of **winter cherry** <note>original: "alkekēgi"; Physalis alkekengi, used for bladder and kidney issues</note>.

<margin>h</margin>
### CHAPTER LXVII.
### On milk.

If someone drinks milk and it becomes curdled in the stomach, he will suffer a softening of the stomach and nausea, and he will sweat a cold sweat. Its cure will be to drink very strong vinegar; afterwards, let him take one **drachm** of asafoetida or one ounce of **oxymel** <note>original: "firupo acetoso"; a syrup of honey and vinegar</note>, dose after dose.

<margin>h</margin>
### CHAPTER LXVIII.
### On smothered roast meat.

If someone eats "smothered" roast meat, which is wrapped in bread when it is pulled from the oven, he will suffer a vertigo similar to epilepsy. And its...

...the care is that he should vomit and be purged; let him take in a drink the juice of **styptic** <note>original: "stipticoy"; referring to substances that contract tissues to stop secretions or bleeding</note> fruits and rose juices with **wood-aloes** <note>original: "xiloaloes"; a fragrant, medicinal wood</note> and **mastic** <note>a resin from the mastic tree used in medicine</note>, and let him seek sleep and enter a bath.

# CHAPTER 69.
## On cold fish.

If anyone should eat "cold" fish <note>in the medieval humoral system, fish were considered "cold and moist"</note> that has been caught for one or two days, or if anyone eats meat killed the day before yesterday, or before the third or fourth day, or carrion, or animals killed by lightning and storms, or those destroyed by a pestilential disease; the same effects happen as from the eating of bad mushrooms. Their cure is that he should vomit and take in a drink pure wine with pepper, and let him be treated with the cure for mushrooms, except that he should not eat pears.

# CHAPTER 70.
## On the brain of a cat.

He to whom the brain of a cat has been given in a drink will suffer from **stolidity** <note>a state of dullness or lack of mental agility</note> and will appear **hallucinatory** <note>original: "instigiosus"; likely referring to being haunted or having visions</note>. His cure is **sealed earth** <note>original: "terra sigillata"; a medicinal clay from Lemnos used as a universal antidote</note> and vomiting with it twice every month; and let him take the confection **dyamuscus** <note>a restorative medieval medicine based on musk</note> every day at the crack of dawn. Its **bezoar** <note>here meaning its specific antidote</note> is a half-scruple of ground **musk** <note>a strong-smelling substance secreted by deer</note> given in a drink with white wine.

# CHAPTER 71.
## On the tip of a deer's tail.

He to whom the tip of a deer’s tail has been given will suffer the symptoms of **monkshood** <note>original: "napelli"; a highly toxic plant, also called aconite</note>. Its cure is a potion of a half-scruple of ground **emerald** given in a drink with wine, and then a rubbing of the whole body with oil made from **citron seeds**. Its bezoar is **great theriac** <note>original: "tyriaca magna"; a famous poly-pharmaceutical antidote containing dozens of ingredients</note>, two drams.

# CHAPTER 72.
## On bovine blood.

He to whom old bull’s blood has been given in a drink will suffer **mortification** <note>numbness or the "death" of sensation in the limbs</note> and will vomit up clotted vomit. His cure is very sharp hot vinegar, then vomiting, then theriac, and finally a bath of warm water.

# CHAPTER 73.
## On the blood of a toad.

He to whom toad's blood has been given in a drink will suffer difficulty of breath and heart palpitations. If anyone should consume its spit, he will be near death, just like one who has drunk monkshood. Its cure is a potion of one scruple of emerald, then entering the body <note>the patient would be placed inside the eviscerated carcass of a large animal to draw out toxins</note> of a large four-legged animal, such as an ox, donkey, mule, or horse; this should be repeated, and then drink two drams of theriac. Its bezoar is the stone found in the head of a toad which among lapidaries is commonly called **borras** or **trepanide** <note>the "toadstone," a mythical gem thought to be found in a toad's skull, used as an antidote to poison</note>.

# CHAPTER 74.
## On the blood of a red-haired, choleric man.

He to whom the blood of a red-haired, **choleric** <note>possessing a "hot and dry" temperament, associated with anger</note> man has been given in a drink—extracted at the time of his strife or fury—will suffer furies of the mind, confusion of the intellect, and shamelessness, and then he will gradually be dried up. His cure is to drink the water of Palestinian cucumber and to chew its seeds and swallow the juice, and to drink **water-lily syrup** <note>original: "sirupū nenufarinū"</note>. Its bezoar is one ounce of the **troche of Tyre** <note>original: "trociscus unz de tira"; likely a medicinal lozenge from Tyre used against venom</note>.

# CHAPTER 75.
## On menstrual or leper's blood.

He who drinks menstrual blood or the blood of a **leper** will appear to be bewitched, moon-struck, cursed, and forgetful. His cure is to drink one dram of ground pearls with honey-water, to bathe in lukewarm water, and to have sexual intercourse with a girl according to the law, and to socialize and embrace girls and youths. Its bezoar is to eat snakes from which the tails and heads have been cut off by a palm’s length.

# CHAPTER 76.
## On the bite of a fasting man.

He who has been bitten by a man who is fasting should place chicken dung over the bite; otherwise, he will suffer a venomous ulcer that is difficult to heal.

# CHAPTER 77.
## On the bite of any snake.

He who has been bitten by any snake should immediately bind the place with deer hide, and then apply theriac and drink from it. Let him place emerald, coral, and pearls near the heart, and let him make the site of the bite "flee" from a deer <note>likely a reference to using deer products or the presence of deer as a counter-agent</note>.

# CHAPTER 78.
## On the gall of a leopard.

He to whom leopard gall has been given in a drink will suffer the symptoms of monkshood and the viper. Its cure and its bezoar are the same [as those].

# CHAPTER 79.
## On the salamander.

He who drinks [the essence of] a salamander will suffer the symptoms of **Spanish fly** <note>original: "cantariday"; a toxic beetle used as a medicine and aphrodisiac</note>. Its cure and its bezoar are one and the same.

# CHAPTER 80.
## On the sea-hare or sea-frog.

He to whom a sea-hare or a sea-frog has been given in a drink will have oily vomiting, and his whole body will become swollen and inflated like **yposarca** <note>a type of dropsy or edema where fluid accumulates under the skin</note>, and his breath will stink. Its cure is swift vomiting with butter and honey-water, and then to take theriac **diatessaron** <note>a simpler theriac made of four ingredients</note> for three days, and to be fed with the meat of sparrows and to drink good wine. Its bezoar is roasted and eaten fox meat.

# CHAPTER 81.
## On the bite of a mouse, monkey, and cat.

For a man bitten by a mouse, monkey, or cat, let him place chicken dung over the bite and treat it as was said regarding the bite of a fasting man.

# CHAPTER 6.
## On the description of the universal bezoar...

**Bezoar** is said **antonomastically** <note>i.e., by its most famous name</note> to come from a certain...

--- Page 728 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of sovereign remedies against toxins, transitioning from specific biological cures to a deep exploration of the "bezoar"—both as a physical stone and as a theoretical medical category—and concluding with a scholastic debate on the nature of Theriac, the most famous universal antidote of the Middle Ages.</meta>

...by the stone which is so called <note>the Bezoar stone, a mass trapped in the gastrointestinal system of animals, believed in the Middle Ages to be a universal antidote</note>. Its proper and specific virtue against lethal poison is such that it delivers one from death suddenly, without any need for a physician's skill. And therefore, any medicine that can deliver a person from death, whether from some sickness or a poison, can be called the **bezoar** of that disease—whether that medicine be a stone, a grain, a dye, or some compound medicine. 

Whoever possesses this stone is safe from all mortal poison. It is also ground up and given in a drink, in the amount of one drachm <note>original: "ʒ. i."; a unit of apothecary weight</note>. It is said that by this very stone the Lord King of England, **Edward**, was delivered in the city of Acre when he was wounded by the poisoned sword of the Sultan's assassin <note>refers to the attempted assassination of Edward I during the Ninth Crusade in 1272</note>. This stone was given to him by the Grand Preceptor of the Temple <note>the leader of the Knights Templar</note>. 

I myself have seen one like it. It is red, powdery, light like a sponge, and as brittle as gypsum. Every poison—whether mineral, vegetable, or animal—has its own proper opposing medicine, by which opposition and specific virtue a person is delivered from death. Therefore, a **bezoar** is that medicine for any given poison which cures such a poison without relying on elemental virtues <note>meaning it works through "occult" or "specific" powers rather than just being "hot" or "cold"</note>. I have already set forth a treatise on every kind of bezoar above, in the treatment of each poison at the end of its description, so that it is no longer necessary to repeat that discussion.

### On the question of whether Theriac, etc.

The question arises whether **Theriac** <note>original: "tyriaca"; the most famous and complex poly-pharmaceutical antidote of antiquity and the Middle Ages, often containing dozens of ingredients including viper flesh</note> is a "bezoar"—that is, whether it delivers one from poison by its **specific form**, or whether it works by its **elemental matter**, delivering one through its humoral temperament <note>original: "complexione"</note> and not by its form. 

Some have wished to say that it was entirely a bezoar, basing themselves on the reasoning of **Galen**. When he looked back at the philosopher **Andromachus** <note>the physician to Nero who refined the recipe for theriac</note>, who first discovered Theriac, Andromachus had proved that it was only useful in "cold" diseases because of the opposition of many "hot" ingredients, and in "hot" diseases because of the opposition of many "cold" medicines within it. Galen said that the Theriac of Andromachus was balanced in its temperament; but by adding the flesh of vipers and **sealed earth** <note>original: "terra sigillata"; a medicinal clay used as an antidote</note>, Galen made it effective **formally** <note>by its "specific form" or essential nature</note> against poison, though more so for some and less for others, sometimes given alone and sometimes with additives.

Others, however, said it acted through its elemental temperament, as does anything that operates in the human body. They based this on the weakness of its operation or its utter vanity when given against **monkshood** <note>original: "napellū"</note>, or against a viper, or against the gall of a leopard; in short, against any lethal poison that acts according to a "specific form," against which Theriac seems to offer little or nothing, as **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rasis"; the influential Persian physician Al-Razi</note> said.

The solution to this doubt is that the cure for any poison happens in four ways: 
1. The sharpness of the poison is broken.
2. Its substance is dissolved.
3. It is expelled.
4. It is corrupted through specific opposition and its virtue is entirely taken away.

An example of the first is **opium**, which breaks the power of **euphorbium**, and **castoreum**, which breaks opium. An example of the second is **sealed earth** and **garlic**, which resolve the substance of the poison either through vomiting or through sweat. An example of the third is the **emerald**, which puts the poison to flight and draws it out to the very tips of the limbs. An example of the fourth is the **specific form** opposed to the poison, which is found in natural things like the bezoar stone, and in artificial things like the divine and noble composition of Theriac, resulting from the mixture of all its medicinal components fashioned together. 

And because Theriac contains the power of the temperament of many medicines that break poison through the opposition of qualities, and medicines that resolve and expel it, it is well said that Theriac is a **temperamental medicine** against poisons. Yet, because from such a composition results a "divine thing" which comes from without rather than from within—namely, an artificial form that is opposed to all poison—it is also well said that it is a **bezoar** for all poisons, albeit more for some and less for others. And though some things are more "bezoar-like" toward certain poisons than Theriac is, Theriac is effective against all. For this reason, it has been called the **Mother of all Medicines** by physicians.

# The Manuscript Binding

->**Exterior Front Cover**<-

This page presents the physical exterior of the manuscript. The book is bound in dark, aged leather, decorated with a technique known as <term>blind-tooling</term>. <note>Blind-tooling is a decorative method where heated metal tools or stamps are pressed into dampened leather to create permanent, recessed designs without the use of gold leaf or ink.</note>

The cover features a central rectangular panel filled with a repeating pattern of circular <term>rosettes</term>. <note>A rosette is a stylized floral ornament, a very common motif in late medieval and early modern European bookbinding.</note> This central design is framed by a border of straight, impressed lines. 

At the corners of this frame are four prominent, star-shaped decorative <term>stamps</term>. <note>Individual stamps like these often help scholars identify the specific workshop or region where a book was bound.</note>

On the left edge of the cover, a metal plate remains where a <term>clasp</term> was once attached. <note>Before the age of modern climate control, books—especially those with parchment pages—were fitted with metal clasps to keep them tightly closed. This prevented the pages from warping or "springing" due to changes in humidity.</note>

<summary>This page shows the manuscript's historical leather binding, decorated with blind-tooled rosettes and star-shaped stamps. It serves as an example of the craftsmanship and functional hardware used in early book production.</summary>
